## Front Matter of the Volume

## Title Page of the Series

The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, complete, uniform, convenient, economical Library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition during the first twelve centuries of the Church, prepared with the utmost care according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margins of the individual pages and indicating their subject matter; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on the texts of the individual books of Scripture, and in which places in their works they did so.

The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others, if the following features are taken into account: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, and the modest price; and especially this collection, a single, systematic, and chronological gathering—here for the first time in our library—of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, assembled from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

## First Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great.

Under the direction of J.-P. Migne. The Patrology of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning, was issued in two printed editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin.—The purely Latin edition is sold for 1,200 French francs for 200 volumes; the Greek-Latin edition for 1,300 francs for 800 volumes.—The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are given in it only in Latin translation.

# In the Year of Our Lord 538–555. Pope Vigilius

[Note: We have transcribed the notes placed opposite the text in Mansi’s edition, whether inserted within the text in brackets or placed below the columns with superior reference numbers. Editor.]

[Column 0009]

## Notice from the *Pontifical Book*

[Column 0009A] Vigilius.

[Note: When Vigilius, introduced into the apostolic see through the favor of the empress Theodora after the death of Silverius, had craftily resigned the pontificate, perhaps hoping that he might be lawfully elected through the influence of Belisarius, fear seized the clergy of the Roman Church as they were about to elect a new pontiff: if they elected Vigilius, notoriously stained by many crimes, they would violate the sacred canons; but if they passed him over, they would provide an opportunity for schism and the most dangerous heresy. After a long consultation, Vigilius was elected—by divine inspiration, perhaps with everyone’s consent—to avert the danger of schism and heresy. He was indeed Catholic, [Column 0009B] but through ambition had been defiled by association with heretics.

After he had issued a confession of faith and condemned every heresy, he was raised to the pontifical throne on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, in the year of Christ 540, which was the fourteenth year of Justinian. The outcome proved that all these things had happened by God’s will. For it occurred, in an astonishing example, that the man who had previously been induced to curse God’s people was converted to bless them; and the man whom the empress Theodora had elevated in order to restore Anthimus to the pontifical see, after his lawful election confirmed again the anathema pronounced against that same man and his fellow heretics.

When the emperor Justinian was informed of Vigilius’s lawful election, following the custom of his ancestors he made a confession of faith to him through an envoy and a letter, as is clear from Vigilius’s reply, in which, contrary to the expectation of the empress Theodora, he pronounced an anathema against Anthimus and his fellow heretics.

In Italy, without any valor on the part of the generals, the city of Ravenna was surrendered, and Vitiges, king of the Goths, [Column 0009C] was defeated by Belisarius in the year of Christ 540. Because of this Belisarius suffered the envy of his rivals and was brought under suspicion of aspiring to tyranny, and was recalled to Constantinople. When he arrived, bringing the defeated enemies with him, he was not permitted to celebrate a triumph, perhaps because, by obeying the impious empress too readily, he had attempted something impious and sacrilegious against the pontiff.

The Gothic king Theobald restored the scattered forces. After his death, Totila, Theobald’s nephew—the scourge of the Greeks who ruled in the West—was raised to the kingship. After winning several victories against the Romans, he took possession of Campania, where what Saint Gregory reports in Book III, chapter 18, of the *Dialogues* concerning Saint Benedict, the monk of Cassino, happened to him. When Riggo came to investigate the Lord’s prophecy, Benedict said to him: “Put down, my son, put down what you are carrying; it is not yours.” To Totila himself, when he came to him, he foretold, saying: “You do many evil things; you have done many evil things. Cease at last from iniquity. Indeed, you are going to enter Rome and cross the sea; you will reign for nine years and will die in the tenth.”

When Totila had taken possession of Rome after almost all Italy had been subdued, we shall speak of it below. During his time, four or more invasions of the Romans by the Persians took place under Chosroes, king of the Persians; Procopius describes them in *The Persian War*.

In the seventh year of Vigilius’s pontificate, which was the year of Christ 546, Peter, bishop of Jerusalem, died. [Column 0010A] Macarius II succeeded him, and by an erroneous judgment incurred suspicion of heresy.

The empress Theodora, a Severian heretic intent solely upon the overthrow of the orthodox faith, ruled for twenty-one years, according to Procopius. In the twenty-third year of Justinian’s reign, she was struck by Vigilius with the dreadful dart of anathema and, plainly by divine vengeance, miserably perished.

With what credibility, then, Anastasius says that Vigilius was removed from the church of Saint Euphemia at Chalcedon by order of the empress, we shall explain below. If Belisarius had not been excessively obedient to the rule of this impious woman and had not withdrawn his violent hands from Silverius, he would have been the most fortunate of military commanders. But because he placed God below a woman, he was miserably cast down from the highest glory to the lowest fortune. For when he was accused, and perhaps also convicted, of plots prepared against the emperor Justinian, he was stripped of all his possessions and honors, blinded, and reduced to such poverty that he was forced to beg alms.

Zonaras, Cedrenus, Volaterranus, and others; Baronius, under the year 561.

What was said, written, or done during Vigilius’s time concerning the Three Chapters—the writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia and Theodoret, and the letter of Ibas—will be made clear below through letters, councils, and edicts.

The metropolitan see of Justiniana was first adorned with dignity, prerogative, and authority by Vigilius. *Novella* 131, chapter 3.

He adorned the basilica he had built with sacred paintings of images, as Pope Hadrian says in his letter to Charlemagne. He endowed with privileges and immunities the monastery founded by Childebert, king of the Franks, as Saint Gregory writes in Book VII, Letter 115.

Vigilius also condemned, by his own decree, the bishop Origen, who had previously been condemned several times. Cassiodorus, *Institutions of Divine Readings*, Book I, chapter 5.

From the acts of this pontiff, everyone may recognize the singular providence of God toward the Roman Church and the admirable authority of the apostolic see. Although the empress and others may have hoped that the little ship of Peter would be steered wherever their desire moved Vigilius, who had been violently and sacrilegiously introduced into the apostolic see through their efforts and favor, nevertheless Christ, seated within it, turned the whole ship hither and thither according to his will. Though contrary waves pressed upon it, and winds blowing against it sometimes drove it in the opposite direction, that little ship never, throughout the whole period of Vigilius’s legitimate pontificate, struck the rocks or ran aground on shoals; nor, broken apart by the more frequent blows of the waves, did it founder. Rather, it remained unharmed and, having received all the water that entered through its wide openings, repeatedly expelled it entirely until it was completely dry.

Let the heretics who are introducing innovations therefore see how prematurely they triumph over the shipwreck of this little ship when Vigilius was at its helm. If he is the author of that letter and confession of faith which they produce from Liberatus’s *Breviary*, they have conquered nothing except that, at that time, while he was still a false pope during Silverius’s lifetime, Vigilius wrote the letter by professing heresy in an external declaration, in favor of the empress and in hope of obtaining or retaining the pontificate. Even if they could prove that Vigilius had erred, or had been a heretic and a simoniac, they would cast no stain upon the orthodox Church or its doctrines.

But the fact that, after Silverius’s death, when through the love or approval of the Roman clergy he began to be the legitimate pope, he said, wrote, or did none of these things will be shown by the sentences of anathema that, according to Gregory, he pronounced against Anthimus—previously condemned by his predecessors—and against the empress Theodora.

What should be thought of that letter, taken from Liberatus under the name of Vigilius, we shall state below in the notes to his letters.

Severinus Binius.]

A Roman by birth, son of the consul John, he occupied the see for seventeen years, [Note: Baronius writes that Vigilius held the apostolic see for sixteen years, under the year 555. Severinus Binius.] five months, [Note: The Lucian manuscript has “seven.”] and twenty-six days.

At the same time, the patrician Belisarius waged war [Note: Procopius writes that Vitiges, without any battle being fought or any valor on the part of the generals, was surrendered together with the city of Ravenna to Belisarius in the fifth year of the Gothic War, which was the year of Christ 540. Severinus Binius.] against Vitiges, king of the Goths. John, master of the soldiers, surnamed “the Bloodthirsty,” pursued him as he fled by night, seized him, and brought him to Belisarius and Vigilius at Rome.

Then they gave him pledges in the basilica of Julius [Note: The same manuscript has “Julia.”] that they would bring him safely [Column 0011A] to the emperor Justinian. When they had brought him to Constantinople, the emperor rejoiced, made him a patrician and a count, and sent him near the Persian frontier; there he ended his life.

The emperor asked Belisarius how he had conducted himself with the Romans, or how he had installed Vigilius in place of Silverius. Then the emperor and the empress gave him thanks [Note: The letter of Justinian to Menna, printed above under Silverius, indicates that Justinian was not aware of the plan to restore Anthimus to his see, but rather that all these matters had been arranged through the secret plotting of the empress Theodora with Vigilius. At the end of that letter, among the other heretics who were to be condemned, he lists Anthimus, bishop of Trebizond. Hence it is clear that the emperor himself did not thank Belisarius for this reason, unless perhaps he had been persuaded that Silverius had been condemned by a just sentence and that Vigilius had lawfully succeeded him. The same author.] and, having conferred rank upon him, sent him again to Africa. [Note: These events seem to have occurred during the pontificate of John II, in the year of Christ 533. The same author.]

When Belisarius reached the borders of Africa, he treacherously killed Gontharis [Note: The same manuscript reads “Widtharim.”], king of the Vandals, under the pretext of peace, and Africa was brought under imperial rule.

Then the patrician Belisarius came to Rome and, from the spoils of the Vandals, offered to the blessed apostle Peter through the hands of Pope Vigilius a golden cross adorned with jewels, weighing one hundred pounds, on which he had inscribed his victories; two large gilded silver *cerostata* [Note: In the same manuscript, “silver” is absent.], which still stand today before the body of the blessed apostle Peter. [Note: This offering, also mentioned by the author of the *Historia Miscella*, was perhaps made under the pontificate of Silverius, in 537, when Belisarius had subdued Rome after defeating the Goths. If, however, any gift was made to Vigilius, it must have been offered by Belisarius’s agents during his absence; for Procopius shows that Belisarius himself did not enter Rome in the fourth year of the Persian War. The same author.]

He also gave many other gifts and alms to the poor. The patrician Belisarius likewise founded a hospice on the Via Lata and, on the Flaminian Way near the city of Ostia [the manuscript has “Ortas”], the monastery of Saint Juvenal, to which he donated many estates and gifts.

At the same time, the empress Theodora wrote to Pope Vigilius:

“Come; fulfill for us what, of your own willing inclination, you promised concerning our father Anthimus, and restore him to his office.”

Vigilius replied:

“Far be this from me, empress. Previously I spoke wickedly and foolishly; now I will in no way consent to your restoring a heretical and anathematized man. Although unworthy, I am the vicar of the blessed apostle Peter, just as my most holy predecessors Agapetus and [Column 0011C] Silverius were, and they condemned him.””

Then the Romans made their accusations [Note: Baronius, under the year 546, number 54, proves that the history which follows, up to the words “When he entered Sicily,” is of suspect credibility. He bases this on the fact that Vigilius was summoned only because of the Three Chapters, whereas Menna of Constantinople and the leading bishops of the East were unwilling to subscribe until the Roman pontiff had consented. Justinian thought that the pontiff should be won over by whatever flatteries might be employed and invited only honorably, lest, if he opposed, every effort concerning the promulgated edict be frustrated; all the bishops of the East depended on him. The same author.] against Vigilius, because blessed Pope Silverius had been deposed with his counsel.

“We bring this to your piety’s attention,” they said, “because he behaves wickedly toward your Roman servants and toward his own people, and because we accuse him of murder.”

He became so enraged that he struck his notary on the face; the man immediately fell at his feet and died. Vigilius also gave his nephew, the son of a widow, to the consul Asterius. As a consequence, he had him seized at night and beaten until he died.

When the empress heard this, she sent the *scribo* Anthimus to Rome with her order and with a large force, saying:

“If you find him in the basilica of Saint Peter, spare him. But if you find Vigilius in the Lateran, in the palace, or in any church whatsoever, immediately put him on a ship and bring him to us. For if you do not, by Him who lives forever, I will have you flayed.”

Anthimus the *scribo* came to Rome and found him in the church of Saint Cecilia on the tenth day before the Kalends of December—for it was her feast day—distributing gifts to the people. They seized him, took him down to the Tiber, and put him on a ship.

The common people followed him, crying out that they might receive a prayer from him. When he had given the prayer, all the people answered, “Amen,” and the ship began to move.

When the Romans saw that the ship on which Vigilius was sitting had begun to move, the people began to throw stones, sticks [with kicks, and] pots after him, saying:

“Your hunger go with you! Your plague go with you! You have done evil to the Romans; may you meet evil where you are going!”

Some of his supporters followed him from the church.

When he entered Sicily [Note: Procopius reports that the pontiff remained longer in Sicily and from there sent grain intercepted from the Goths to the city suffering from famine. The same author.] and reached the city of Catania, he was permitted to perform ordinations during the month of December: priests and deacons. Among them, he sent back to Rome Ampliatus, the priest and his deputy, and Valentinus, bishop, to Saints Rufina and Secunda, to guard the Lateran and govern the clergy.

After taking leave of everyone, he entered Constantinople [Note: Vigilius, setting out for the imperial court contrary to the example of Saint Leo and his other predecessors, exposed the little ship of Peter to great danger; he would have held its helm more safely by remaining seated at Rome, as will be shown below in the notes to his letters and councils. Severinus Binius.] on the eve of the Nativity [Column 0013A] of Our Lord Jesus Christ. [Note: Procopius, in *The Gothic War*, chapter 3, writes that after the winter had passed and a suitable season for sailing had returned, Vigilius departed from Sicily and reached Constantinople. This agrees better with the foregoing words of Anastasius. For if he held ordinations in December shortly before Christmas, as he says, how could he have reached Constantinople on the eve of that same Christmas? Baronius, under the year 547, number 36. The same author.]

Then the emperor came to meet him. They kissed one another and began to weep, while the people sang before him all the way to the church of Hagia Sophia, saying:

“Behold, the Lord, the ruler, has arrived,” and so forth.

For two years, however, there were disputes [Note: The same manuscript has “intentions.”] concerning Anthimus the patriarch: they showed how Vigilius had promised to restore and return him to his office, and they produced the written guarantee of his own hand, showing that he had promised to restore him to his rank.

But Vigilius absolutely refused to consent to them. Strengthened by such power, he preferred to die rather than live.

Then Pope Vigilius said:

“As I see it, the most pious princes Justinian and Theodora did not have me brought to them; today I know that I have found Diocletian and Eleutheria. Do as you wish; for I receive what my deeds deserve.”

[Note: What follows occurred after Theodora’s death, in 551, when persecution was again stirred up against him through Theodore, bishop of Caesarea, and he had to flee to Chalcedon, to the basilica of Saint Euphemia, as is clear from Vigilius’s letter written to the whole Church. Therefore the reader should restore to their proper places the several matters Anastasius henceforth recounts, mingled and confusedly, about the empress Theodora, who had already been dead for three years. The same author.]

Then someone struck him in the face, saying:

“Murderer, do you not know to whom you are speaking? Do you not know that you killed Pope Silverius and killed the widow’s son with blows of heels and sticks?”

Then, fleeing to the basilica of Saint Euphemia, he grasped the altar column. He was dragged away from it and thrown outside the church.

The empress Theodora ordered a rope to be put around his neck and had him dragged through the entire city until evening. Then he was sent into custody and given only a small amount of bread and water.

The Roman clergy who had been sent with him were exiled to various places to cut metal in the mines.

Then the Goths made Badiulla their king [Note: The same source has “Badua.”], who was called Totila. He came down and besieged Rome. [Note: The siege began in the year of Christ 546. In the following year the Isaurian soldiers betrayed the city to Totila, while the Romans, oppressed by dreadful famine, lacked even the most filthy necessities and many collapsed dead. After occupying the city, Totila had already begun to demolish it and reduce it to pasture for sheep, but after repeatedly reading Belisarius’s letters wisely dissuading him from this, he abandoned the plan.

Belisarius recovered the city after defeating Totila again in a pitched battle in the same year, 547. How, in the year 550, the same city was once more betrayed to Totila by the Isaurians and was embellished by him with new buildings, and how Narses, commander of the Roman army, relying on God’s help and the intercession of the blessed Virgin Mary, freed it from barbarian rule after killing the king and the Gothic army, we shall explain below. The same author.]

A famine arose in the Roman city so severe that the people even wished to eat their own children.

One day he entered Rome through the gate of Saint Paul, in the thirteenth indiction [the fourteenth]. All night he had the trumpet sounded until the whole population had fled or hidden themselves in the churches, lest the Romans’ lives be ended by the sword.

The king lived among the Romans like a father among his children.

Then certain senators who were fleeing—Citheus [Techeus], Albinus, and Basilius, the patrician and consul [Note: The same source has “patricians and consuls.”—]—entered Constantinople and were presented before the emperor, afflicted and desolate.

The emperor then consoled and enriched them, as they deserved, as though they were Roman consuls. [Note: The same source lacks “as though.”]

At the same time, the emperor Justinian sent Narses, his eunuch [Note: In the year when, at the insistence of Pope Vigilius, the emperor revoked the edict concerning the Three Chapters and presented himself as obedient to the Roman pontiff, Narses, commander of the Roman army, relying on God’s help through the intercession of the blessed Virgin Mary, defeated and killed Totila together with his entire army in the tenth year of Totila’s reign, as the monk Saint Benedict had foretold to him. He recovered the city itself for the second time after Totila had occupied it for the second time, namely in the year of Christ 553. According to Procopius, Narses sent the keys of the city gates to the emperor Justinian at Constantinople. Thus the emperor gained possession of the city’s keys when he acknowledged the keys of Peter in Vigilius. The same author.] and chamberlain, to Italy. When he engaged the Goths in battle, God granted him victory; the king was killed, and a multitude of Goths were slain.

Then the assembled clergy asked Narses [Note: There is no doubt that Vigilius was freed from exile at Narses’s request and confirmed the Fifth Synod, held for the condemnation of the Three Chapters, especially since the emperor was pressing this most vehemently and could not otherwise be reconciled with him in friendship and peace. See Baronius, under the year 554, numbers 3–6. The same author.] to join their petition in asking the emperor that, if Pope Vigilius were still alive, or if the priests, deacons, or clergy who had been deported into exile with Vigilius were alive, they might return.

When the emperor received Narses’s report, or that of the whole Roman clergy, he became joyful, as did all his nobles, because God had granted rest to the Romans.

Immediately he sent his orders to the various places where they had been deported into exile, to Gissa [Note: The same manuscript has “Gypso.”] and Proconnesus, and the emperor brought them before him, saying:

“Do you wish to receive Vigilius, as he was your pope? I give thanks. Is that not enough? Here you have your archdeacon Pelagius, and my hand will be with you.”

They all replied:

“May God govern your piety. Restore Vigilius to us now, and when God wishes him to depart from this world, then, by your command, let our archdeacon Pelagius be given to us.”

Then he released them all together with Vigilius.

They came into Sicily, to the city of Syracuse, where Vigilius, afflicted and suffering from the pain of a stone, died. [Note: The deacon Pelagius incurred suspicion of having killed Vigilius; but he cleared himself of the accusation brought against him, as is evident below in the Life of Pelagius. Severinus Binius.]

His body was brought to Rome and buried at Saint Marcellus on the Salarian Way.

He performed two ordinations during the month of December: forty-six priests, sixteen deacons, and eighty-one bishops in various places.

The episcopal see was vacant for three months and five days.

# Letters and Decrees of Pope Vigilius

(C, S)

## Letter, Formerly II, of Vigilius, Still a False Pope, to Eutherius

[Note: In Mansi’s edition the first is entitled “A letter written in the name of Pope Vigilius by a certain Eutychianus”; it may be seen transcribed, with accompanying notes, in Liberatus’s *Breviary*. Editor.]

He responds to Eutherius’s questions.

[Column 0015B]

[Note: This letter was hitherto addressed to Eutherius or Eleutherius, as we formerly noted in the annotations to *Gratiarum*. It is certain, however, that it ought to be addressed to Profuturus, who was bishop of Braga. This is proved not only by the authority of the most ancient codex of the Church of Lyons, but also by two excellent and very old Colbertine codices, numbered 408 and 3970, in which various chapters of this letter are reproduced from a letter of Pope Vigilius to Profuturus, bishop.

Moreover, the letter survives complete with this same inscription in another excellent and ancient codex, number 449, of the same Colbertine library; in that manuscript, however, the chapter on the primacy of the Roman Church is absent. Indeed, although the other chapters are reproduced in full in Colbertine codex 408 and in the Lyon manuscript, those same manuscripts do not contain what is added concerning the primacy of the Roman Church in the collection bearing the name of Isidore.

Furthermore, the letter to Profuturus is explicitly mentioned in the acts of the First Council of Braga, where it is said to have been written in response to his questions and, because of its length, not to have been inserted into the acts.

As for the day and year in which it was delivered, I consider it pointless to debate the matter, since the Colbertine codex establishes that it was written in the year in which John was consul after Belisarius, that is, in the year 538. Baluzius, *New Collection of Councils*.

Yet much greater confidence ought to be placed in all the remaining codices, both the very ancient manuscripts of Spain examined and collated by the most illustrious Loaisa and the printed copies in which the chapter on the primacy of the Roman Church is found, than in a single Colbertine manuscript. There may be a considerable suspicion that the latter was written in Gaul during the period when the cases of bishops appealing to the apostolic see were being disputed, especially toward the end of the ninth century, under Pope Nicholas I, and later in the case of Gerbert of Rheims, near the end of the tenth.

For it could easily have happened that those who, against the bishops Hincmar of Laon and Rothad of Soissons as they appealed to the apostolic see, were attempting to wrest from that see judgments concerning bishops, mutilated Vigilius’s letter by cutting away the chapter by which they themselves were condemned.

Car. de Aguirre, *Councils of Spain*, vol. II, p. 278.

Leaving these matters aside, Baluzius transcribed this letter from the Colbertine codex; from it we have selected the following variant readings.]

To his most beloved brother [Note: Colbertine codex: “To beloved brother Profuturus, bishop: Vigilius.”] Eutherius [Eutherus] [Note: Vatican Palatine codex: “Profuturus.”], Vigilius.

We gratefully received the letters of your charity addressed to us, full of the anxious concern of Catholic inquiry [and of inquiry and concern], blessing the clemency of our God because, in the most distant regions of the world, he has deigned to provide such shepherds for his sheep, through whom they may abound in wholesome pastures and be preserved from the rapacity of the ancient enemy [wicked wolf], so that they may not fall into the snares of his deception. [Note: Colbertine codex: “and, preserved from wicked rapacity, may not fall into snares,” and so forth.]

It is therefore certain that the grace of the promised blessedness will follow you, since the perfection of heavenly teachings is sought from you through such desirable questioning.

For it is written: “Blessed are those who search out his testimonies; with their whole heart they seek him” (Psalm 118).

Therefore, dearest brother, as we consider with our whole mind the purpose of your inquiry, we affirm [are confident] that this too proceeds from you: you strive to hold the rule of the Catholic faith in the very footsteps in which you recognize it to have been founded upon apostolic faith [Note: The same codex has “the apostolic see.”]

And although the sound of those teachings has gone forth through the whole world, and their words have been extended to the ends of the earth, proving the heart of your charity faithful to Christ, nevertheless, if anything among those matters has not yet shone forth in full clarity in the Church entrusted by God’s help to your governance, you return to the same fountain from which that life-giving stream flowed. [Note: The same codex has “to the place to which.”]

We have embraced this with the charity that was owed, because you wished our answer confidently to confirm those matters concerning which, as you said, observance among them was uncertain.

Therefore, greeting your charity in the Lord, we believe that you should be instructed concerning each point: what the authority of the apostolic see holds according to Catholic discipline, with certain chapters of the sacred canonical rules added below.

### I.

First, concerning those whom you have indicated to be defiled by the vices of the Priscillianist heresy, you judge [the same manuscript reads *judices*] that they must be censured with the holy detestation befitting the Catholic religion: they appear, under the pretext of simulated abstinence, to withdraw from eating meat, and are shown to do this from a spirit of execration rather than devotion. Since in this matter they are proved to be like the most impious Manichaeans, they have rightly been forbidden by the decrees of the venerable Fathers to persist in this superstition, under threat of anathema, when [the Colbertine manuscript reads *ne quando . . . crederent*, “lest at any time . . . they should believe”] they believe that some food is polluted by contact with meat [or: that something is polluted by contact with carnal foods]. For of all that God’s mercy has provided [or: bestowed] for human nourishment, nothing is judged unclean by Catholics.

Thus the Apostle Paul, teacher of the nations, admonishes Titus, saying: “All things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean; rather, their mind and conscience are defiled. They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him; they are detestable and unbelieving, and rejected for every good work” (Titus 1).

Likewise, in another passage, he preached to Timothy about avoiding errors of this kind, saying: “In the last times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy and having their conscience seared, forbidding marriage and abstaining from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have come to know the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected when it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Timothy 4).

Accordingly, the following decrees of the venerable Fathers specifically judged that those must be condemned who, while abstaining from meat, also believed that whatever seemed to have been mixed with meat was to be avoided. For our Lord Jesus Christ himself gave this warning, saying: “It is not what enters into the mouth that defiles a person, but what proceeds from the mouth—this is what defiles a person” (Matthew 15).

Therefore, we neither reject abstinence that is pleasing to God, nor do we admit into our fellowship those who execrate the Lord’s creation.

**Note:** The Colbertine manuscript reads *exsequentia* (“the following,” rather than *sequentia*).

### II. Concerning baptism

Concerning baptism also, which is solemnly to be administered by three immersions [the Colbertine manuscript reads: “Concerning baptism, likewise, of those being reborn, solemnly by three immersions, etc.”; the Vatican Palatine manuscript reads: “Concerning baptism also, of those being reborn, solemnly by three immersions”], your Charity will clearly recognize below what the apostolic authority has either decreed or observes.

We judge it to be an error of recent origin that, although all Catholics customarily say at the end of the psalms, “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit,” some, as you indicate, removing one connective syllable, attempt to diminish the complete word *Trinity*, saying: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, to the Holy Spirit” [the Colbertine manuscript reads: “Glory to the Father, Son, Holy Spirit”; the Vatican Palatine manuscript: “Glory to the Father, Son, Holy Spirit”].

Although reason itself clearly teaches us that, when one syllable is removed, they thereby designate the person of the Son and of the Holy Spirit as somehow one [the Colbertine manuscript reads: “the person of the Father and of the Son, etc.”], nevertheless, to refute the error of such people it is enough that the Lord Jesus Christ, indicating that baptism must be celebrated in the invocation of the Trinity, said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew, last chapter).

Since he did not say, “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, of the Holy Spirit” [the Colbertine manuscript reads: “of the Father, of the Son, etc.”], but commanded that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit be named with equal distinctions, it is evident that those entirely depart from the Lord’s teaching who wish to detract anything from this confession [the Colbertine manuscript reads: “subtract”; it then adds: “Therefore let your Charity strive by every means to recall them to the path of right confession. But if, God forbid, they should persist in error, etc.” The Vatican manuscript reads: “subtract,” etc., as Baluzius notes].

If they persist in error, they cannot be our associates.

### III.

Concerning those who, after receiving the saving grace of baptism, were baptized a second time among the Arians and have been plunged into the death of a deep abyss, we have disclosed [or: brought forth] and sent below from our archives the chapters in which the decrees of our predecessors have judged what should be done for each rank and age; these decrees are arranged in a variety of ways.

Nevertheless, in these matters it is also appropriate to observe this with particular charity: since that iniquity arose among the nations because of many sins, the matter should be left to the judgment of your Fraternity and of the other bishops in their dioceses, so that, if the character and devotion of the penitent are approved, he may also be near to the remedy of indulgence.

Their reconciliation, however, is not effected by that laying on of hands which takes place through the invocation of the Holy Spirit, but by that through which the fruit of repentance is acquired and restoration to holy communion is accomplished [the Vatican manuscript reads: “by the restoration of holy communion”].

### IV.

Concerning the restoration of any church, if it has been destroyed, and whether the solemnity of consecration ought to be repeated in a place where no sacred vessels [or: sanctuaries] remain, we judge that it causes no difficulty [the Colbertine manuscript reads: “causes no effect”] if blessed water [or: exorcized water] is not sprinkled through it at all. For we know that the consecration of any church in which no altar of the Holy Spirit is placed [the Colbertine manuscript reads: “in which no sacred vessels are placed”; the Vatican manuscript: “in which no holy altar is placed”] consists only in the celebration of Masses.

Therefore, if a basilica of the saints has even been renewed from its foundations, without any doubt, once the solemnity of Masses has been celebrated in it, the sanctification of the entire consecration will be completed. But if the sacred vessels which it had have been removed, it will again receive the reverence of sanctification through their replacement [or: arrangement] and the solemnity of Masses.

### V.

Know that, if God wills, we shall celebrate the coming Easter on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May [the Colbertine manuscript reads: “the eighth day before the Kalends”; the Vatican manuscript: “the eighth day before the Kalends”].

We also declare that at no time and on no feast do we have a divided order of prayers in the celebration of Masses [the Vatican manuscript reads: “a different order”], but always consecrate the offerings made to God according to the same form.

Whenever the feast of Easter, the Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, the Epiphany, or one of God’s saints is to be celebrated, we add the individual sections appropriate to those days, by which we make commemoration either of the holy solemnity or of those whose festivals we celebrate; the rest we continue in the customary order.

Therefore we have also sent below the text of the canonical prayer, which, by God’s favor, we have received from apostolic tradition. And so that your Charity may know at which points you should attach material appropriate to the various feasts, we have likewise [or: together] added the prayers for Easter day.

Having answered your Fraternity’s inquiries in these matters, we earnestly beseech our God, insofar as we are able, that he may multiply the gifts of his grace among all the churches of the Catholic religion and concerning all whom he makes faithful to himself, and that he may deign to keep all his peoples free from every ambush of the spiritual and carnal enemy.

We also indicate [or: We have indicated] that we have sent you relics of the blessed apostles and martyrs, as we hope [the Colbertine manuscript reads: “as you hope”], trusting that henceforth your faith will be more fully aided by their merits [the Colbertine manuscript ends the letter here, with the following words: “May God keep you safe, dearest brother. Given at Rome, on the third day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Flavius John, most illustrious man.”].

### VI.

If any bishop or presbyter, in accordance with the Lord’s command, does not baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, but in one person of the Trinity, or in two, or in three fathers, or in three sons, or in three paracletes, let him be expelled from the Church of God [here the Vatican manuscript ends].

### VII.

No one who has even a slight understanding, nor anyone fully wise, is in doubt that the Roman Church is the foundation and form of the churches; no right-thinking believer is unaware that all churches took their beginning from it.

For although the election of all the apostles was equal, it was nevertheless granted to blessed Peter that he should surpass the others. Hence he is also called Cephas, because he is the head and beginning of all the apostles; and what went before in the head must necessarily be followed in the members.

Therefore the holy Roman Church, consecrated by the Lord’s voice on account of his merit and strengthened by the authority of the holy Fathers, holds primacy over all the churches. To it the most important affairs, judgments, and complaints of bishops, as well as the greater questions of the churches, must always be referred as to their head.

For one who knows that he has been placed over others should not be displeased that someone has been placed over him. That Church which is first has entrusted its functions to the other churches in such a way that they have been called to share in its concern, not in the fullness of its power.

Hence it is clear that the judgments of all bishops who appeal to the apostolic see, and all the business of major cases, have been reserved to that same holy see, especially since its counsel must always be awaited in all such matters. If any priest should attempt to oppose its course, let him know that he will have to render an account of his cases before that same holy see, not without danger to his honor.

Given on the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Volusianus [or: Vuilisiarius, incorrectly] and John, most illustrious men (A.D. 538).

## From a letter of Pope Vigilius to Profuturus of Braga

(From the Supplement to Mansi, vol. 1, p. 417.)

He must be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit—not in the name of the Father, Son, Holy Spirit. If the altar is moved, the church must be consecrated anew. If the wall is renewed and the altar has not been moved, it must be exorcized [perhaps: blessed] with salt alone. There must be a threefold immersion in baptism.

## Note

From the authority of this excerpt we learn that the best title of this letter is the one indicated to Baluzius by several manuscript codices. For it was addressed not to Eutherius, as in the printed editions, but to Profuturus; and we firmly establish from this excerpt that he was the same man as the bishop of Braga who flourished at that time.

As for the matters concerning the baptismal formula and the consecration of churches contained in this epitome, comparison of the two texts proves that they were plainly taken from sections 2 and 4 of the same letter, which in the printed editions is read as addressed to Eutherius. Nevertheless, the author of the excerpt may have obtained a more corrected and complete copy of Vigilius’s letters and therefore expressed those decrees somewhat differently from the form found in the commonly printed letter to Eutherius.

The decree that follows in the epitome concerning threefold immersion in baptism is not mentioned even by a single word in the letter; conversely, the letter contains several matters of which there is not even a trace in the excerpt. Hence it is easy to conjecture that the letter reached us not as a whole, but pieced together from fragments of several letters.

The learned Baluzius suspected this before me. Having found in the Colbertine manuscript a much shorter text ending with section 5, he judged that everything which subsequently follows in the commonly printed versions of the same letter—especially what is stated there concerning the primacy of the Roman Church and appeals from the whole world being brought before it—was added later and ought to be entirely removed.

Yet Baluzius’s manuscript is not more complete, since it neither represents the material found in our excerpt nor is it considered free from anachronisms. For that Baluzian text is dated to the third day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of John, most illustrious man, which indicates the year 538. In the letter itself, however, the coming Easter is assigned to the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, something that never occurred under Vigilius.

Perhaps, therefore, only the earlier paragraphs, through the fifth, are presented in the printed editions as the letter to Profuturus. The remainder has been sewn together from other letters, whether of Vigilius or of others.

Finally, I think it should be added here that the Fathers of the Council of Braga, assembled in the year 563, ordered this letter of Vigilius to Profuturus to be read to them in the full synod. For thus it is read in the acts of that council in Labbe, volume 6, column 520, Venetian edition:

“The authority of the apostolic see addressed to a certain bishop Profuturus was reread; because of its length it has not been inserted in these acts.”

The Fathers of that same council indicate in canons 4 and 5 that this letter contained regulations for administering baptism and the rite of celebrating Mass; and these are indeed the two matters found in Vigilius’s letter.

# Testimonies of ancient canons concerning threefold immersion (S)

## From the Council of the Apostles, title 49

(From Baluzius’s new collection.)

### That baptism ought to be administered in the name of the Trinity

If any bishop or presbyter, in accordance with the Lord’s command, does not baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, but in three principles without beginning, or in three sons, or in three paracletes, let him be cast out.

## From the same, title 50

### That there ought not to be one immersion in baptism, as though it represented the Lord’s death

If any bishop or presbyter does not celebrate the threefold immersion of the one mystery, but immerses once in baptism, which is understood to be given in the Lord’s death, let him be deposed.

For the Lord did not say, “Baptize in my death,” but, “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” Amen.

# Letter (formerly III) of Vigilius, still a pseudo-pope, to Caesarius of Arles

He responds to Caesarius, who had consulted him concerning the imposition of penance on King Theudebert for an incestuous marriage.

### Vigilius to his dearest brother Caesarius

If, for the observance of heavenly commandments, it is fitting for priests to instruct the sons of the Catholic Church, whether opportunely or importunately, how much more necessary is it to respond in an appropriate order to those who, with praiseworthy devotion, come for counsel concerning matters about which they are uncertain?

For this reason we have decided to receive the inquiry of our glorious son, King Theudebert, who believed that we should be consulted through his envoy, Modericus, an illustrious man. In it he desires to be instructed as to what sort of penance might cleanse the offense of one who rashly presumed to enter into an unlawful marriage with his brother’s wife.

We have accordingly taken care to communicate this to him in a letter, the text of which your Fraternity will find below: such an offense can be expiated only through no small affliction of heart. But since—as we trust your Charity well knows—the measure of penance is entrusted rather to the scrutiny of the priests of the present time, so that the remedy of pardon may also be granted according to the merit of contrition, we believe that this matter should rather be left to your judgment.

Therefore, having examined the entire character of the affair and the contrition of the penitent himself, let your Charity not fail to instruct our aforementioned glorious son, the king, concerning the proper observance of time, and earnestly require that no such thing be presumed again.

The greatest care must be taken that he who is known to have committed this offense does not return to the same vomit, but that, although they continue to dwell in the same place, their residences should nevertheless be separated, so that they may be rendered free from every suspicion of the crime committed.

May the Lord keep you safe, dearest brother.

Given on the day before the Nones of March, in the consulship of John, most illustrious man.

# Letter (formerly IV) of Pope Vigilius to Justinian

When the emperor Justinian had professed the faith before Vigilius, who had been lawfully elected, he was changed from an enemy into a defender, from a persecutor into a preacher, and from a blasphemer into a confessor; and he pronounced a sentence of anathema against Anthimus and his associates, who were heretics.

### Vigilius, bishop, to the most glorious and most merciful son, Justinian Augustus

Having received, with our accustomed veneration, the letters of Your Clemency brought by our glorious son Dominicus, an ex-consul and patrician, we have perceived that the universal Church ought to rejoice with manifold joy because you permit the Christian faith, by which the divine Trinity is honored and worshiped, to be in no respect different and in no respect discordant; and because, through your most merciful rule, you increase by tireless works the grace of God, whom you serve by reigning and whom you serve by your reign.

Thus it is rightly and suitably recognized that the preaching of the Apostle is fulfilled in the things which the Lord, in his singular mercy, has granted you for the integrity and devotion of your faith: “The saints through faith conquered kingdoms” (Hebrews 11).

What kingdoms you have conquered more by the weapons of faith than by bodily strength is shown by the multitude of nations subject to you. The greater their number becomes, the more it is overcome by the perfected working of the one mystical miracle.

Therefore it is altogether fitting that we should glory in the Lord, because he has deigned in his mercy to grant you not only an imperial but also a priestly spirit. What all bishops request when offering sacrifices of the ancient tradition—namely, that the Lord may unite, govern, and preserve the Catholic faith throughout the whole world—you have accomplished with the greatest strength.

For throughout every region of your kingdom and to the ends of the earth, you command that the faith which is known to have been irreproachably established by the venerable synods of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus I, and Chalcedon, which must always be embraced according to the judgment of the Christian confession, be preserved in unshaken peace. Nor do you allow anyone to be called Christian who separates himself from the unity of the aforementioned synods; and anyone who does not defend their faith with every strength and effort, you judge not merely to be subject to judgment, but already judged [the words enclosed in parentheses, omitted in Labbe, have been restored from the Roman edition].

What priestly exultation and infinite joy, then, would this not bring about: that, by the grace of our God, the light of evangelical truth inserted into your heart, after the night of pernicious and heretical doctrines has been dispelled, shines throughout the universal Church?

Therefore let it be far from us that what we profess generates joy for all our brother bishops should not be mingled with our own joy along with all the rest, or—what is more worthy—that it should not rise above them all.

For this reason, venerable emperor, we receive with devoted reverential thanksgiving the fact that, inflamed by the ardor of faith and stirred by a gracious indignation, you have also sent us pious words in which, with praiseworthy affection, you recall Coelestine and Leo of blessed memory, pontiffs of the apostolic see. In accordance with the divine dispensation entrusted to them, they condemned the individual heresies with synodal assembly and established by an enduring law what all Christians ought generally to follow.

Our predecessors of holy memory, Hormisdas and the elder John, as well as Agapetus, preserving their praiseworthy decrees in every respect, struck down with the sword of a just sentence all the followers of the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies.

Let Your Clemency recognize without doubt that we follow this with all our strength and defend it with every effort. We also entirely embrace and defend with the charity that is required the letters of blessed Leo addressed to Flavian, then bishop of the city of Constantinople, and to Leo, emperor of most clement memory. In them, with a reasonable argument and by God’s inspiration, he confounded the impiety of the heretics, namely Nestorius and Eutyches.

Although, with God’s protection, the sincerity of our mind and faith permits us in no way to oppose these things, your admirable prudence ought nevertheless to consider that those bishops are not judged worthy who have not inviolably preserved the established decrees of the aforementioned pontiffs of the apostolic see.

Therefore, following in every respect the matters concerning the faith that were reverently defined by the Fathers of the four holy synods, by the letters of Pope Leo of blessed memory, and by the decrees of our aforementioned predecessors, and condemning with the commendable authority of the apostolic see those who oppose their teaching, we anathematize whoever attempts either perversely to dispute or unbelievingly to doubt the exposition or correctness of this faith.

We separate from the unity of the Catholic faith those who think contrary to the matters concerning the faith contained in the holy synods of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus I, and Chalcedon, as well as in the letters of our predecessor Leo of blessed memory, which we have mentioned, or in everything sanctioned by his authority. We embrace and approve in every respect the statement of your faith which, in the pious service of our office, Your Orthodox Clemency once delivered to our predecessor Agapetus of pious memory.

In it you also made clear, by the testimony of Scripture, the convictions which you hold in your mind for the instruction of future generations. We preserve nothing that deviates from the faith of our often-mentioned predecessors under any pretext—unless, after the darkness in which they wallow has been cut away, they should wish to follow the truth concerning the faith stated above through suitable correction by repentance; and unless, having condemned everything that certain people have said with the most wicked impiety against the matters we have mentioned, they should be converted by canonical discipline, rejecting all the errors of the heretics in their own subscriptions and with their own voices.

Then they may deserve the mystery of sacred communion, when they have fulfilled everything we have mentioned according to canonical and apostolic discipline, since it is not fitting for us to deprive anyone who corrects himself of the opportunity for repentance.

As for the matters in which Your Clemency ordered that our brother and fellow bishop Menna, mindful of his own statement which he had presented to our predecessor Agapetus of blessed memory at the time of his ordination, with the consent of Your Clemency, should follow the discipline of the apostolic see and pronounce anathema against the heretics listed below—namely, Severus the Eutychian, Peter of Apamea, Anthimus, who had also invaded the Church of Constantinople through wicked ambition, Xeneas, Theodosius of Alexandria, Constantine of Laodicea, and Antonius of Versentum, of the Eutychian heresy, as well as Dioscorus, who is read to have been condemned among others at the Council of Chalcedon, together with their defenders and followers—such condemnation pronounced against heretics by our aforementioned brother or by anyone else is in no way displeasing to us.

We gladly embrace it and confirm it by the authority of the apostolic see, striking the associates of the condemned with a similar punishment of anathema. This is to be done on the understanding that, as we mentioned above, in accordance with the decrees of the pontiffs of the apostolic see, we shall open the way to repentance and communion for those who have come to their senses and have accepted the decrees of the preceding synods or of the aforementioned pontiffs of the apostolic see.

But since we know that those who destroy heretical unbelief benefit themselves more by avoiding association with the erring than by adding any firmness to the sentence of the aforementioned Fathers, already established in many ways and known to stand securely by God’s authority, we have therefore hitherto judged that a condemnation not newly issued requires no new response.

For those who are found to be followers either of the heresies mentioned above or of all the others condemned by apostolic definition and decree have been struck down not merely by a new law but by the condemnation of their authors, which was issued long ago.

And although a malicious interpreter might wish to suspect or understand Your Clemency’s attitude otherwise because of our silence, nevertheless, since the Apostle Peter (1 Peter 3) established us by pious tradition as people who must give an account to everyone who asks, we have willingly recognized that we ought to satisfy Your Christianity.

We humbly hope [or: request] that, in your most Christian times, you permit none of the privileges of the see of blessed Peter the apostle to be diminished in any respect through the ambushes of anyone who might insinuate himself. If these privileges should be disturbed—which we do not believe—or diminished in any respect, let them be recognized as signs [or: offenses] of violated faith.

For Your singularly wise piety knows that it will in every respect merit that recompense from the authority of blessed Peter the apostle which you will have preserved either in his privileges or in our humble person, with God assisting you.

Nevertheless, so that all matters may instruct Your Clemency and nothing further remain ambiguous through the cunning of a crafty plotter, we have added the decrees of our predecessor Pope Leo of blessed memory that were sent to the East at different times, insofar as we have judged many of them necessary at present.

Through him, whose cause you hasten and desire to pursue completely with Christian affection, we ask that Your Piety deign to read everything, so that nothing at all may remain unread.

For I know that, just as God has given you the will to obey the law, so, in handling all matters, you arrange them by the wisdom singularly granted you by God, so that none of the faithful priests may be harassed in any respect either concerning religion or concerning any prejudice.

Let it suffice, then, that we have given an account of these matters insofar as we were able, as the merit of Your Christianity required. Although no one, however clever and subtle, will be able to find that we have committed or attempted anything against the synodal decrees or the decrees of our predecessors, the pontiffs of the apostolic see.

I do not fail to suggest those matters which are beneficial to the Catholic faith and to our soul—for, as Your Piety knows, both on account of the priestly office and because of the many favors granted by Your Clemency, I have more reason than others to consider this matter.

First, we earnestly implore and, through the intercession of blessed Peter the apostle himself, whom you love, request that you always deign to send to this apostolic see, for the administration of the interests of your state, persons who are orthodox, pleasing to God, and without wrinkle or blemish in the faith. Through them, the matters appropriate to your public administration may be salutarily ordered, and the integrity of Catholic discipline may in no way be disturbed for the sake of your soul’s reward.

Thus all may truly recognize that Your Piety already possesses—as we also believe—the gift of heavenly grace which Solomon was still requesting from the Lord when he said: “You shall give your servant an understanding heart, to judge your people in justice and to discern between evil and good” (1 Kings 3).

And because we have instructed our son Dominicus, the bearer of this letter, to communicate certain matters orally, we hope that, with the Lord assisting you, you will deign to hear them willingly and, above all, arrange in your customary Christian spirit and prudence those matters which will benefit ecclesiastical peace and, thereafter, the tranquility of the whole community.

# Letter (formerly V) of Pope Vigilius to Menna

He congratulates him for condemning the heretics and embracing the four holy universal synods; those who recover from heresy ought to be received.

### Vigilius, bishop, to his dearest brother Menna, bishop

Although, insofar as by God’s help we were able and believed it expedient, we have communicated everything concerning ecclesiastical matters to our lord son, the most serene and most Christian emperor, through the words of our representation, we nevertheless judged it necessary also to send writings to Your Charity through the person of our most Christian son, the patrician Dominicus.

Know that we received them with great exultation and joy, because you affirm that you inviolably preserve the holy synods of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon, in which the foundations of the orthodox and apostolic faith are displayed, just as the reading of the promise given by you at that time to our predecessor Agapetus of holy memory testifies. Above all, you affirm that you follow in every respect the decrees of our predecessor, blessed Leo.

What honor more worthy of Your Charity could there be than not to depart from the teaching of the Roman pontiffs? Or what could be more joyful or pleasing to us than to embrace in the love of Christ our Lord and Savior those who preserve the deeds of our elders and predecessors?

Therefore, greeting you spiritually, we exhort you and address you unceasingly with the affection appropriate to us: follow in every respect the norm of that man, his admonition, and his decrees, just as you have promised and indicated.

For the archives of your Fraternity are full of the writings of our predecessor Leo, of holy and venerable memory, which that pontiff is read to have sent to your predecessors; and in the same place are reread the promises which your predecessors made to ours.

But let this suffice to have said. For the Apostle’s saying is before our eyes: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Corinthians 1).

Concerning the fact that, mindful of the statement which you had delivered to our aforementioned predecessor and following the decrees of apostolic teaching, you pronounced anathema against the heretics listed below—namely Severus of Antioch, Peter of Apamea, Anthimus, the invader of the Church of Constantinople, Theodosius of Alexandria, Constantine, Antonius of Versentum of the Eutychian heresy, and Dioscorus, who is read to have been condemned among others at the Council of Chalcedon, together with their defenders and followers—we have learned that you added nothing new to the sentence once decreed by the Fathers.

Nor did such a sentence, given by the vicars of blessed Peter against the authors of those heresies, in fact need such bishops, since one recognized as a follower of a condemned heresy has been struck down not merely by a new law but by the condemnation of its author, already issued long ago.

We gladly and willingly embrace this, and confirm it by the intervention of the authority of the apostolic see over which God has willed us to preside. All their associates, and all heretics, will likewise be subject to the same sentence of condemnation.

We reserve only this matter in every respect, as is appropriate to apostolic moderation: if any one of them, or any of the erring, should wish to return as though having recognized the truth of the Catholic faith and doing penance, and, rejecting the error in which he wallows, should condemn in a written profession the whole depravity of his errors and of his associates, and, following the decrees of apostolic teaching, should pronounce anathema against anyone who either does not follow the four aforementioned synods in the matter of faith or does not confess in every respect the venerable decrees of our predecessor Leo of blessed memory, and does not follow them with every strength and with complete purity of mind—then, under the apostolic and canonical satisfaction mentioned above, he will in every respect be admitted to our communion, which it is not fitting for us to deny to any penitent.

For our Redeemer did not come to destroy anyone, but in his mercy to save everyone.

And in the hand of the lord pope:

“By God’s help, through his grace, I, Vigilius, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, have examined and subscribed these sheets of the letters written above, which I dictated with God’s help and, with his assistance, have acknowledged.”

And in another hand, the subscription of Flavius Dominicus:

“I, Flavius Dominicus, most illustrious man, count of the household troops, ex-consul and patrician, having reread, compared, and approved these sheets concerning the faith, composed by the most blessed and apostolic Pope Vigilius for our lord Justinian, most pious and most Christian emperor, and also for Menna, most blessed archbishop of the city of Constantinople, have subscribed, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Justinus, most illustrious man” (A.D. 540).

# Letter (formerly VI) of Pope Vigilius to Auxanius of Arles

He postpones granting the use of the pallium, which Auxanius had requested, until he can inform the emperor more fully.

### Vigilius to his dearest brother Auxanius
The documents concerning the ordination of Your Fraternity, brought by our son, the presbyter John, and also by the deacon Teredius, we received with spiritual rejoicing of heart, giving thanks to the Lord because in the Church of Arles [Col. 0027A] something was done that accords both with the canons and with the regulations of our predecessors: namely, that Your Fraternity should be advanced from the succeeding order of the priesthood to the summit of pontifical dignity, and that the judgment of divine election concerning you should be fulfilled, as it is written: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow caused by turning” (James 1). And again the Apostle Paul, teacher of the nations, says: “No one takes the honor for himself, but only he who is called by God, as Aaron was” (Hebrews 5).

It remains that God, who in his goodness mercifully grants us, though unworthy, to possess pontifical honor through his ineffable mercy, may also grant the reward, so that what the words of Christ our God and Savior attest may be fulfilled in us, when he says: [Col. 0027B] “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord” (Matthew 25); and again: “Who, then, is the faithful and wise servant whom the lord has appointed over his household, to give them their measure of grain at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom, when his lord comes, he finds doing so” (Matthew 24).

There are also examples which, by God’s grace, urge Your Fraternity to perform good works. For if you wish to imitate those deeds of your predecessor by which he equaled in action what he had received as good teaching from the apostolic See, founded upon the rock of the Lord’s teaching, and if you deviate in nothing from the ordinances of the apostolic See, then, as it is written, “You will without doubt receive the crown which God has given to those who love him.”

As for the matters which Your Charity requested should be granted to you by us, both concerning the use of the pallium and concerning other matters, we could willingly have done this at once [Col. 0027C] in the present circumstances, had we not wished, with God as our guide, to make the matter known to our most Christian lord, our son the emperor, as reason requires. Thus the cause of what has been granted may become more agreeable to you, when what you requested is reported with the consent of the most Christian prince, and we may be judged to have preserved the honor due to his faith with appropriate reverence.

May God keep you safe, dearest brother. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, the second time after the consulship of Basil, the illustrious man (A.D. 513).

## LETTER (formerly VII) OF POPE VIGILIUS TO THE SAME

He delegates his functions to him in Gaul and grants him the use of the pallium, admonishing him to pray to God for the emperor and to strive to preserve peace between him and King Childebert.

[Col. 0027D]

To his dearest brother Auxanius, Vigilius.

Just as, out of affection for Your Charity and in response to the Christian devotion expressed in the instructions of our most glorious son, King Childebert, we have entrusted our functions to you with the greatest willingness, so it is fitting that Your Fraternity should, through conduct worthy of the authority of so great a See, use and administer the authority entrusted to you in works pleasing to God, so that, becoming known through good deeds, you may show the sound judgment of our affection toward you.

For it is fitting that we recall the instructions of the Teacher of the Nations, by which he exhorts his disciple Timothy with holy admonitions, saying: “Be an example to the faithful in speech, in conduct, in charity, in faith, and in purity” (1 Timothy 4). And likewise the first of the apostles, giving salutary instruction, says: “Feed the flock of God that is among you”; and then adds in exhortation: “Becoming examples to the flock from the heart; and when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory” (1 Peter 5).

Therefore, if any disagreements should arise among our brothers and fellow bishops in the places presently entrusted to Your Charity’s authority—should that ancient iniquity’s author sow his accustomed weeds—then, after summoning with you a suitable number of priests, examine the cases with canonical and apostolic equity, and bring them all to an end by a judgment that can in every respect accord with the God-pleasing regulations of our predecessors.

But if any disputes should arise, God forbid, concerning the religion of the faith, or concerning any matter which, because of its importance, cannot be settled there, then, after carefully examining the whole truth with diligent judgment, send us a written account and reserve the matter for settlement by the apostolic See. Thus, when everything has been properly arranged by Your Fraternity, the peace which, according to the Savior’s word, has been bestowed upon the Church of God—which is one and spread throughout the whole world—may be preserved with steadfast firmness, and may not be disturbed by the accusations of the ancient enemy, but may persist in the stable foundation established upon that rock, Christ our God, Lord, and Savior.

So that Your Fraternity may better fulfill all these duties by God’s grace, the sequence of our authority has been communicated to all the bishops over whom we have wished you to preside. Therefore none of the bishops entrusted to your administration through these functions, as our instruction given to them likewise declares, may dare to travel to any distant places unless, according to solemn custom—as they had been accustomed to do when our predecessor made a similar grant to your predecessor—he has received a canonical letter (*formata*) from Your Charity.

It is therefore fitting that Your Fraternity pour out prayers to our God in unceasing supplication, asking him always to protect our lords and sons, the most merciful rulers Justinian and Theodora. They have graciously assented to these matters being entrusted to Your Charity, at the urging of our most glorious and excellent son, the patrician Belisarius, for whom likewise it is fitting that you pray.

We also exhort you, in the exercise of your priestly office, by fatherly encouragement to preserve the tokens of the favor established between the glorious King Childebert and the aforesaid most merciful prince. For we rightly keep before our eyes the commands of our Lord and Savior which we proclaim to the peoples, in which he says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5).

And because we consider it fitting that the one performing our functions should not lack the adornment of the pallium, we grant you, by the holy authority of blessed Peter, its use, just as our predecessor, Saint Symmachus of blessed memory, is recorded to have granted it to your predecessor.

As for the matters which we have marked by a written command concerning this present appointment, we wish them to reach all the bishops through Your Charity.

May God keep you safe, dearest brother. Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, the fourth time after the consulship of Basil, the illustrious man (A.D. 545).

## LETTER (formerly VIII) OF POPE VIGILIUS TO AUXANIUS OF ARLES

Concerning the investigation of the case of Bishop Praetextatus.

[Col. 0029A]

To his dearest brother Auxanius, Vigilius.

Although, by virtue of the functions of the apostolic See assigned to Your Fraternity, which we have entrusted to you by direct authority, you generally have permission to examine cases as they arise, nevertheless, because a petition has been presented concerning the misconduct of Praetextatus by our sons, the presbyter John and the deacon Teredius, whom Your Charity sent to us, we have considered it very necessary to instruct you by our present authority to investigate this particular matter.

Therefore, returning the fraternal greetings of visitation appropriate to the charity by which we are joined in Christ, we exhort Your Charity, after summoning with you a suitable number of our brothers and fellow bishops, to arrange the matter, once it has been examined according to canonical truth, with wise judgment and in accordance with the statutes of our predecessors. Take care especially that no priest may easily admit anyone from the laity into the sacred orders by a precipitous leap.

May God keep you safe, dearest brother. Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, the fourth year after the consulship of Basil, the illustrious man.

## LETTER (formerly IX) OF POPE VIGILIUS TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL

He announces that Auxanius has been appointed vicar of the apostolic See, explains the duties of this office, and orders everyone to obey him.

[Col. 0029C]

To our dearest brothers, all the bishops of every province throughout Gaul who are established under the kingdom or authority of our most glorious son Childebert, king of the Franks, and also to those who, according to ancient custom, have been or are consecrated by the bishops of Arles, Vigilius.

To the extent that divine power has established us as holders of the See of the first of the apostles—not on account of our merits, but through the ineffable goodness of its mercy—to that extent it is fitting that we should care for the ordering, peace, and condition of all the Churches, since the Apostle says concerning the nations: “My daily burden is the care of all the Churches” (2 Corinthians 11).

How, then, can holy and God-pleasing concord remain among the Lord’s priests unless, when the enemy of the human race wishes through his ancient wickedness to sow his customary weeds, the one who represents our absence through the spiritual grace of exercising the functions of the apostolic See removes the conflict that has arisen?

Therefore, let Your Charity know that we have entrusted our functions to our brother and fellow bishop Auxanius, bishop of the city of Arles, so that, if any dispute should arise—God forbid—he may assemble there our brothers and fellow bishops and, examining the cases by canonical and apostolic authority, settle them with equity pleasing to God.

But if any disputes arise concerning the matter of the faith—may the Lord remove them—or if some matter should arise which, because of its importance, ought rather to be settled by the judgment of the apostolic See, let him, after examining the truth, bring the matter to our attention without delay.

And because, with God’s favor, it is necessary that the bishop of Arles exercise our functions at appropriate times, whenever he judges that bishops ought to assemble for the sake of providing common consolation, let no one be disobedient to his commands. If anyone is, let him be suspended from the assembly, unless bodily illness or a just excuse prevents him from coming. Even then, if he can reasonably defend himself against failing to appear, let him send to the synod, in his own place, a representative from among his presbyters or deacons, so that whatever decision has been determined and settled by our vicar with the assembled brothers may be communicated through his representatives to the one who was absent and preserved with sincere and inviolable stability.

For whenever the servants of the Lord gather in the Lord’s name to deliberate on matters pleasing to him, the presence of the Holy Spirit must not be absent. Thus the commands of Christ our God, Lord, and Savior instruct us, when he says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew 18). What, then, does he think he will undergo who, through pride hateful to God, refuses to attend that assembly in which our Lord declares by a gracious promise that he will be present?

With equal authority we command that no bishop dare travel to more distant places without a canonical letter from the aforesaid brother and our bishop. For the holy commands of our predecessors likewise define this concerning his predecessors, to whom they most willingly entrusted their functions: namely, that when obedience pleasing to God has been preserved in all these matters, the peace which Christ our God, Lord, and Savior left in the Church of God to the apostles as an inheritance by name may be preserved with firm stability; for that Church is one and spread throughout the whole world.

May God keep you safe, dearest brothers. Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, the fourth year after the consulship of Basil, the illustrious man (A.D. 545).

## DECREE OF THE EMPEROR JUSTINIAN (S)

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, God.

The Emperor Caesar Flavius Justinian, Alamannic [Note: Read *Alamanicus*.], Gothic, Frankish, Germanic, Antic, Alan, Vandal, African, Pious, Fortunate, Illustrious, Victorious, and Triumphant, ever Augustus, to the most blessed bishops and patriarchs: Eutychius of Constantinople, Apollinarius of Alexandria, Domninus of Theopolis, and Stephen, George, and Damian, most religious bishops acting in place of Eustochius, the most blessed archbishop and patriarch of Jerusalem, and to the other most religious bishops residing in this royal city from various provinces.

It has always been the concern of our orthodox and pious imperial fathers to cut away the heresies that arose from time to time through the assembly of the most religious bishops, and, after sincerely proclaiming the right faith, to preserve the holy Church of God in peace.

Therefore Constantine, of pious memory, when Arius was blaspheming [Note: The older books read *Arrio*.
