This is approximately how the Latin manuscripts generally have it.] and saying that the Son was not consubstantial with God the Father but a creature, made from things that did not exist, assembled at Nicaea three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers from different dioceses [Note: The same books read *diocesibus*. This too is approximately how the Latin manuscripts generally have it]. Since he himself was also present at the council and supported [Note: The same books read *adjuvasset*, “had supported.”] those who confessed the Son to be consubstantial with the Father, he condemned the Arian impiety and took care to preserve the right faith.

After the holy creed, or statement of faith, had been set forth, the holy Fathers thereby confessed that the Son is consubstantial with God the Father, something that until then had been doubted by many.

Likewise, when Macedonius denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit, and Apollinarius, or Magnus his disciple, blasphemed concerning the dispensation of the incarnate Word of God, saying that God the Word had not assumed a human mind, but had been united to flesh possessing an irrational soul [Note: Read *recepisse Deum Verbum*, “that God the Word had assumed [a human mind].” This is a typographical error in the Labbe edition, corrected here], Theodosius the Elder, of pious memory, assembled one hundred and fifty holy Fathers in the royal city. Since he too had taken part in the council, he condemned the aforesaid heretics together with their impious doctrines and caused the right faith to be proclaimed.

For these same holy Fathers, following the right faith set forth by the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers, explained the divinity of the Holy Spirit and taught perfectly concerning the dispensation of the incarnate [Note: Read *incarnati*. Here too the Labbe edition suffers from a typographical error, reading *incarnata*.] Word of God.

Again, when the impious Nestorius asserted that there was one God the Word and another Christ [Note: Paris: “and the Son, another Christ”], introducing the one as by nature the Son of God the Father and the other as a son by grace [Note: The Paris codex lacks the word *Filium*, “Son,” here], and denying that the holy glorious Ever-Virgin was the Mother of God, and when that same Nestorius had filled nearly all the eastern regions with his impiety, Theodosius the Younger, of pious memory, assembled the first holy synod at Ephesus. The holy Fathers Celestine and Cyril presided over it. He sent judges who were to attend the council and compelled Nestorius himself to come there, so that judgment might proceed on his account [Note: The same codex reads *propter eum contra eum procedero* (“on his account / against him, [uncertain *procedero*]”).].

After this examination had been conducted, the same holy Fathers, following in every respect what had been defined concerning the faith [Note: The words “concerning the faith” are absent from the same Paris manuscript] by the earlier holy Fathers, condemned Nestorius together with his impiety.

After these events [Note: The same codex reads, “And after these events”], when the followers of the impious Nestorius rose up against Cyril, they hastened, as far as they could, to refute the condemnation made against Nestorius. But the aforesaid Theodosius, of pious memory, defending what had rightly been judged against Nestorius and his impiety, caused the condemnation made against him to remain firmly in force [Note: The same codex reads *fuerunt*, “were,” for *fuerant*, “had been”].

After this, when the madman Eutyches again arose, denying that the Lord’s flesh was consubstantial with ours, and while many disturbances were being stirred up both at Constantinople and at Ephesus, such a great conspiracy of heretics was made on his behalf that Flavian, the bishop of the royal city, of religious memory, was even expelled because of him.

Marcian, of pious memory, assembled the holy Fathers at Chalcedon. Although great contention arose among the bishops, he came to the council not only through his judges but also in person [Note: The older books read, “he came to the council.”], and brought everyone to agreement.

Those holy Fathers, following in every respect what had been defined concerning the faith by the aforesaid three holy councils, and what had been judged concerning the condemnation of the heretics and their impiety, condemned and anathematized the madman Eutyches and his impious doctrines, as well as Nestorius with his impious doctrines, since at that time certain people had hastened to defend Nestorius and his impious doctrines [Note: The same books read, “since even then certain people had hastened…”].

Moreover, those same holy Fathers at Chalcedon anathematized those who had handed down or were handing down another creed besides the one set forth by the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers and explained by the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers.

After all these things had occurred at different times, our aforesaid fathers, of pious memory, strengthened and confirmed by their laws what had been judged at each council, and expelled the heretics who tried to resist the definitions of the aforesaid four holy councils and to disturb the Churches.

After Marcian, of divine memory [Note: Paris manuscript: “of divine memory.”], had died, when there was controversy in various places concerning the holy Council of Chalcedon, Leo, of pious memory, wrote to all priests everywhere, asking each of them to make known his own judgment concerning that holy council. Without one bishop waiting for another, they replied to what they had been asked.

After a short time had passed, the followers of Nestorius and Eutyches rose up again and caused such disturbances in the holy Churches of God that divisions and schisms arose among them, and the Churches had no communion with one another. No one dared to come from one city to another and communicate, nor could a cleric come from one city to another and enter the church [Note: The older books read, “from one city to another”; and: “enter the Church.”].

When the Lord God, according to his mercy, entrusted us with the government of the state, we made the joining together of the divided priests of the holy Churches of God, from East to West [Note: Paris manuscript: “as far as the West.”], the beginning and foundation of our rule. Cutting away all the controversy that was being stirred up against the holy Council of Chalcedon by the followers of the impious Eutyches and Nestorius [Note: From “by Eutyches” through “holy synod” the scribe of the Paris exemplar omitted the text], we caused that same holy synod to be proclaimed in the Churches of God together with the aforesaid three other holy councils [Note: Paris manuscript: “with the other holy councils”], knowing with certainty that what it set forth concerning the faith agrees in every respect with the other three holy councils [Note: The Bellovacensis manuscript reads, “and composed”; and shortly afterward, “agree.”].

We satisfied many who opposed that same holy synod; but those who persisted in opposing the holy council we expelled from the holy Churches of God and venerable monasteries in such a way [Note: The older books do not recognize the word *sic*, “thus,” nor do the older editions] [Note: Read “in the holy Churches of God.” This is a typographical error in the Labbe edition, corrected here] that, while concord and peace among the holy Churches and their priests were firmly preserved, the one and same faith confessed by the four holy synods might be proclaimed in the holy Churches of God.

After all these measures had been taken and established by us, with God’s favor, for the stability of the four holy synods, the followers of Nestorius, wishing to attach their own impiety to the holy Church of God and not admitting that they were doing this through Nestorius, hastened to introduce it through Theodore of Mopsuestia, the teacher of Nestorius, who blasphemed many things worse than Nestorius. In addition to his countless other blasphemies against Christ our God, he said that there was one God the Word and another Christ [Note: The older books read, “and another Christ”], and likewise through the impious writings of Theodoret, which he set forth against the right faith, against the first holy Synod of Ephesus, and against Cyril of holy memory and his Twelve Chapters, and furthermore through the criminal letter [Note: Bellovacensis: “and furthermore through the criminal letter”] which Ibas is said to have written to Maris the Persian. That letter is full of all the impiety of Theodore and Nestorius.

By means of this impious letter they hastened to free from condemnation not only the impiety but also the very persons of Theodore and Nestorius, whom it especially praises [the Joly text reads *vindicat*, “defends”] and approves [Note: The older books read *vindicat*, “defends”]. They likewise hastened to free this same impious letter from condemnation [Note: Bellovacensis reads *condemnatione*; Paris, “to free them from condemnation”], claiming that it had been accepted by the holy Council of Chalcedon.

They say this not in defense of the holy synod, but in its name, as they think, hastening to confirm their own impiety. It is certain, however, that the intention of those who defend these matters is impious: namely, that if they succeed, God the Word will not be proclaimed to be a holy man, nor will the holy glorious Ever-Virgin Mary be proclaimed Mother of God [Note: Read “the glorious Ever-Virgin”; these words were omitted in the Labbe edition]. Theodore and Nestorius impiously set these things forth in their writings, and the one who wrote the letter blasphemes in it [Note: The Paris manuscript reads “blasphemed.”].

Therefore, following the holy Fathers and wishing the right faith to be proclaimed in the Churches of God without any stain [*quadam*, “some”; perhaps *aliqua*, “any”; Note: the older books read *praedicare*, “to proclaim”] and wishing to cut off the attempt of the impious, we first questioned you, while you were residing in your Churches, about the aforesaid Three Chapters. You made your will clear to us, and for this we approved you [Note: The Paris manuscript reads “we questioned, and about the aforesaid…”], because you confessed the right faith without hesitation and with complete eagerness, and condemned the impious doctrine.

But since, after the condemnation you had made, certain persons nevertheless remain in those same views, defending the same impious Three Chapters, we summoned you to the royal city and jointly urged you, when you had assembled, once again to make known your will concerning these matters.

When Vigilius, the most religious pope of elder Rome, had arrived at this royal city [Note: The conjunction is absent in the same Paris manuscript. Paris reads: “the pope of elder Rome, when he had arrived at the royal city, after everything concerning the aforesaid three impious Chapters had been carefully set forth, we also asked him what he thought concerning this case; and he anathematized the impious Three Chapters not once or twice, but repeatedly in writing and without writing”], we explained everything carefully concerning the Three Chapters and asked him what his view was concerning this matter [*hac causa*, “this case”]. He anathematized the impious Three Chapters not once or twice, but repeatedly, both in writing [Note: Bellovacensis and the edition read, “in writing and without writing,” that is, in written and oral statements].

He also made clear by many other means that he had always held the same view concerning the condemnation of the Three Chapters, including the condemnation of Rusticus and Sebastian, at one time deacons of elder Rome, whose written statements are also preserved among us.

[Note: In Migne, the sections of text “Romae, cujus etiam . . . vos volumus, etc.” and “Romae: qui cum . . . illos patres et sacerdotes” are printed in parallel.]

[Col. 0034B] [Note: From the Paris manuscript of Claudius Joly, canon and cantor of the Church of Paris.]

At Rome, whose written statements are also preserved among us. After this he issued what is called the *Judicatum*. It was made known to all the priests as having been issued by him, and in it he likewise anathematized the aforesaid impious chapters [Note: Perhaps *praedicta*, “aforesaid,” rather than *praedicata*, “proclaimed”] in these words:

“And since, in the words written and presented to us concerning Theodore of Mopsuestia, many statements contrary to the right faith are read, therefore, following the admonition of the Apostle Paul, who teaches, ‘Test everything; hold fast what is good,’ we anathematize Theodore, who was bishop of Mopsuestia, together with all his impious writings, and those who defend him.

“We also anathematize the impious letter said to have been written by Ibas to Maris the Persian, as contrary to the right faith of Christians, and all who defend it or say that it is orthodox.

“We also anathematize the writings of Theodoret which were written against the right faith and against the Twelve Chapters of Saint Cyril.”

These statements were inserted in what is called the *Judicatum*.

We think that Your Religiousness was not unaware that he deposed Rusticus and Sebastian, his deacons, and other clerics who at first accepted what he had done in the *Judicatum*—in which, as has been said, he anathematized the same impious chapters—but afterward defended and vindicated those same impious chapters.

Not only this: in writing to Valentinian, bishop of Scythia, and to Aurelian, bishop of Arles, which is the first of the Churches of Gaul, he made the condemnation of those same chapters known and ordered them to accept nothing written by those who had been condemned against the aforesaid *Judicatum*. And, to put it briefly, he always remained steadfast in the same position.

We have ordered all these matters to be communicated to you.

Afterward, when you came to the royal city, written exchanges took place between Your Holiness and Vigilius, the most religious pope of elder Rome, so that all of you might assemble together and, because of those who defended the impiety of the Chapters either through ignorance or knowingly, pronounce a judgment corresponding to what had been defined by the four holy councils.

Now the same most religious Vigilius has acted contrary to his own position, unwilling to assemble together with everyone in accordance with what had been agreed. Instead, he wished to meet with only three patriarchs and one other bishop, [Note: Perhaps *ut per*, “so that through”] so that the case might be provoked through opposition, saying that he had only three bishops [Note: Perhaps, “that he himself had only three bishops”], although many bishops from the West are with him.

When we heard this, we repeatedly instructed him, both through our judges and through several of you, to assemble with everyone and [Note: Perhaps *ut*, “so that”] pronounce a judgment consistent with the right faith; alternatively, that each patriarch should meet with him and his bishops together with five or three bishops; or, if he did not choose this but wished the matter to be conducted through opposition, that judges should be appointed according to synodal custom and as our predecessors had done. They would have to debate what was raised by each side, since the same persons cannot both oppose and judge.

When he was unwilling to meet any proposal, we informed him that we had also questioned Your Holiness and the other patriarchs in writing concerning this matter: namely, that these impious Chapters should be condemned by everyone, or, if anyone thought them orthodox, that he should clearly make his position known.

For it is alien to Christians, while accepting the right faith, to accept impiety and fail to distinguish what is right from what is evil.

We wish you to know, and so forth.

[Col. 0034B]

Of elder Rome: those who had initially accepted the *Judicatum* made by him, in which he anathematized the same impious chapters, afterward also accepted and defended their impiety.

Moreover, he wrote to Valentinian, bishop of Scythia, and to Aurelian of Arles, which is the first among the most holy Churches of Gaul, and made known the condemnation of these Chapters. He ordered them to accept nothing contrary to the aforesaid *Judicatum* that was written by the condemned deacons. And, to put it briefly, he always remained steadfast in the same position.

In due time we shall make all these matters known to you.

Afterward, when you had arrived, as has been said, at this royal city [Note: The older books read, “when you had truly arrived”], letters were exchanged between Your Holiness and Vigilius, the most religious pope of elder Rome, so that all of you might meet together and, concerning those who defended the impiety of the Chapters either through ignorance or knowingly, pronounce an appropriate judgment corresponding to what the four holy synods had defined concerning the faith.

We also instructed him through our judges and through some of you to assemble with everyone and deliberate together concerning the aforesaid Chapters, so that a form consistent with the right faith might be established. We questioned both him and Your Holiness in writing concerning this matter, so that either the Chapters might be condemned by everyone as impious, or, if he thought them orthodox, he might openly make his position known.

For it is alien to Christians, while accepting the right faith, to accept impiety and not distinguish what is right from what is evil.

He, however, informed us that he would prepare and present to us his own statement concerning the aforesaid Three Chapters. Therefore we also exhort you to deliberate on these matters.

For we wish you to know that we preserve, defend, and follow what was set forth and defined concerning one and the same faith by the four holy councils—the Nicene, Constantinopolitan, first Ephesian [Note: The word “first” is absent from the Paris manuscript], and Chalcedonian—and what was regularly arranged concerning ecclesiastical order. We accept and embrace everything that agrees with these.

Whatever does not agree with them, or whatever is found written by any person against what the four holy councils or one of them defined concerning one and the same faith, we utterly abominate as alien to piety.

In everything, however, we follow the holy Fathers and teachers of the holy Church of God: Athanasius, Hilary, Basil, Gregory the Theologian, Gregory of Nyssa [Note: The Paris manuscript corruptly reads *Numusemum*], Ambrose, Theophilus, John of Constantinople, [Col. 0035D] Cyril, Augustine, Proclus, and Leo. We accept everything written and expounded by them concerning the right faith and the condemnation of heretics.

Remaining, therefore, in all the foregoing matters, those Fathers and priests …

We receive those who preserve and proclaim in the holy Church of God what has been set forth concerning the faith by the four holy councils and preached by the aforementioned holy Fathers. But when heretics, wishing in every way to defend Theodore and Nestorius and their impiety, as has been said, also claim that the impious letter said to have been written by Ibas to Maris the Persian was accepted by the holy Council of Chalcedon, we exhort you to consider what Theodore impiously wrote both elsewhere and in the Jewish creed [Note: That is, Theodore’s creed], which, having been produced at Ephesus and Chalcedon, was anathematized by both synods, together with those who have held or hold such opinions. Consider also what the holy Fathers wrote about him and his blasphemies, what our predecessors promulgated, and what the writers of ecclesiastical histories have related about him.

From all these things you will learn that from that time both he himself and his blasphemies were condemned by the holy Fathers, and that on account of them his name was formerly erased from the sacred diptychs of the Church of which he had been bishop. We also exhort you to examine that vain claim advanced by those who say that heretics ought not to be anathematized after death [Note: Older books: “to anathematize after death”], and to follow in this the teaching of the holy Fathers [Note: The same books: “and to follow also in this teaching”], who not only condemned heretics while they were alive but also anathematized them after death, since they had died in their impiety; just as they restored after death those who had been unjustly condemned and inscribed them in the sacred diptychs. This was done also in the case of John and Flavian, bishops of Constantinople, of religious memory.

For your Reverence knows what is stated by the Lord in the Gospel concerning him: “Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God” (John 3). It is clear that this was said not only of the living but also of those who died in their impiety.

Furthermore, we exhort you to examine what Theodoret impiously wrote against the orthodox faith, against the first holy Synod of Ephesus, against Cyril of holy memory, and against his twelve chapters, as well as what that same Theodoret impiously composed in defense of Theodore and Nestorius and their blasphemies against Cyril of holy memory. Examine also the impious letter said to have been written by Ibas to Maris the Persian. In it, its author denies that God the Word became man [Col. 0036D] and denies that the holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mary is the Mother of God. That same impious letter condemns the first holy Synod of Ephesus, as though Nestorius had been condemned without judgment or investigation; it calls Cyril of holy memory, the teacher of the Church, a heretic and calls his twelve chapters impious; while it defends and praises Theodore, Nestorius, and their impiety.

And since, as has been said, some presume to say that the letter containing the aforesaid impiety was accepted by the holy Council of Chalcedon [Note: Older books: “by the holy Chalcedonian Council”], we exhort you to compare what was said by that holy council in its definition setting forth the faith with what is contained in the impious letter [Note: Paris alone: “with the contents of the impious letter”], so that the orthodox may be confirmed in every respect and the impious condemned.

Therefore, examining all the matters mentioned above with the utmost care, as is fitting for priests, keeping in mind the fear of God and the coming judgment, and preferring nothing to piety, orthodox faith, truth, the glory of God, and his honor, also bearing in mind the apostolic pronouncement uttered against those who teach things contrary to the orthodox faith, which plainly says: “Even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached to you [Note: Bellovacensis, here and shortly afterward: “to you”], let him be accursed” [Col. 0037B]. As we have said before, so now I say again: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1).

Knowing also the command of the apostle Peter, who says: “Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the hope that is in you” (1 Peter 3), make your will known promptly concerning the matters about which we have questioned you. For when one who is questioned about the orthodox faith delays for a long time, it is nothing other than a denial of the orthodox confession. In questions and answers concerning the faith, there is no first or second place; rather, whoever is found more ready in the orthodox confession is acceptable to God.

May the Divinity preserve you for many years, holy and most religious fathers.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of May, at Constantinople, in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of our lord Justinian, the perpetual Augustus, and in the twelfth year after the consulship of Basil, the most illustrious man [Col. 0037C].

Stephen, George, and Damian, most religious bishops, acting on behalf of Eustochius, the most holy patriarch of Jerusalem, through one of their number, Stephen, the most religious bishop of Raphia, said:

“Let Theodore, the illustrious man, depart, once he has satisfied the command of the most pious emperor.” And when the distinguished *silentiarius* had gone out, the holy synod said:

“Since certain documents have been established whose contents are included in the imperial document that has been read, and since certain writings concerning the present case have been exchanged between us and Vigilius, the most holy pope of Old Rome [Note: Read: “since writings concerning the present case have been exchanged.” This is a typographical error in Labbe’s edition, corrected here], we think it necessary that these be made known by reading before anything else.”

And when Stephen, the notary and recorder, had received them, he read them aloud.

## Letter (formerly X) of Pope Vigilius to Aurelian of Arles

After Auxanius’s death, Vigilius delegates his authority in Gaul to Bishop Aurelian.

[Col. 0037D]

Vigilius to his most beloved brother Aurelian.

We gladly entrust the administration of our vicariate to your Fraternity, and we trust that through the service of your charity all things will be diligently accomplished in works pleasing to God, since divine grace has judged you worthy to share in the highest priesthood, and since the Christian and God-pleasing goodwill of the most glorious Childebert, king of the Franks, has added its testimony on your behalf.

Therefore, by this authority we entrust our vicariate to your charity, so that by doing and observing all that the statutes of our predecessors or the canons have decreed in accordance with God, you may demonstrate that both our judgment and that of the aforesaid glorious king concerning your charity were right. For the authority of the holy Scriptures teaches us that Christ our God, Lord, and Savior first wished to do all that is good before teaching it. For it is written: “The first account I composed, O Theophilus, concerning all that Jesus began to do and teach until the day when, after giving instructions through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up” (Acts 1).

Likewise, we confidently believe that your Fraternity always keeps before its eyes what the Apostle, the teacher of the nations, says when admonishing Timothy: “Be strengthened by the grace that is in Christ Jesus; and what you have heard from me through many witnesses, entrust to faithful men who will be capable of teaching others also” (2 Timothy 2). And again he himself says: “Take diligent care to present yourself approved to God, an unashamed workman rightly handling the word of truth” (ibid.). And again: “Work as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. Understand what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding in all things” (ibid.).

If, therefore, the devil, the ancient enemy of the human race, should by his customary wicked craft sow any tares among the brethren, or if a complaint concerning any priest should be brought before your Fraternity, while all the provisions of the Fathers are observed in every respect, then, having associated with yourself brothers and fellow bishops in a number appropriate to the nature of the case, you shall examine the matter according to canonical and apostolic ordinance and settle it by a judgment that accords with the statutes of our predecessors and is pleasing to God, who is attentive to equity in all things.

But if, God forbid, any dispute concerning the religion of the faith should arise, or some such matter should emerge that, on account of its magnitude, could not be settled there, we exhort you, after examining the truth and setting out the sequence of the report distinctly, rather to refer it for the consideration of our See. For the record of our archives testifies that your predecessors, who are shown to have acted as vicars of our predecessors, did so. Thus, by preserving this arrangement, the unity of the Church may continue with firm stability and enjoy in every respect the blessing of peace—peace which Christ our God, Lord, and Savior, is read to have left to his disciples as an hereditary gift, when he said: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 13).

And so that your entire Fraternity may be able to fulfill all these matters with diligent judgment, we signify that we have sent instructions to the bishops over whom we have wished you to preside in our place, so that they may render you the obedience that is due, while your Fraternity, embracing them in the charity of Christ, may continually invite them by examples of good works to do what is pleasing to God.

By the same authority we have also decreed that no one may dare to depart for distant places without a *formata* issued by your Fraternity; rather, he must observe the custom that the vicary of our See is known always to have possessed, and, if they intend to undertake longer journeys because compelled by the needs of their cases, they must request a *formata* from you.

But lest the vicary of our See should appear in any respect inferior to his predecessors, we have thought it necessary to grant you by the present authority the use of the pallium, just as we have hitherto given it to your predecessor, so that, with the blessed Apostle Peter assisting you, you may not lack adornment of character and of every good quality.

It is therefore fitting that your charity should always, with priestly zeal, preserve the bonds of unimpaired grace among our most clement lord sons and princes, and especially with the most glorious man, that is, our son King Childebert. For you know—and it is not fitting that you should be ignorant—that you necessarily proclaim what Scripture declares, saying: “Blessed are the feet of those who evangelize peace, who evangelize good things” (Romans 10).

We also desire this expression of your affection: that you send written thanks to the glorious man, our son the patrician Belisarius, who spared your man the labor of traveling to the most clement prince; as soon as he had received a reply, he informed us of it by his letter.

May God keep you safe, dearest brother.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, in the fifth year after the consulship of Basil, the most illustrious man (A.D. 546).

## Letter (formerly XI) of Pope Vigilius to the Bishops of Gaul

He announces that he has delegated his authority in Gaul to Aurelian and orders them to obey him.

[Col. 0039C]

Vigilius to his most beloved brothers, all the bishops established throughout Gaul under the rule of our most glorious son, King Childebert.

The ministry of our office, conferred by the gift of divine mercy, reminds us that, under the protection of the Lord’s grace, we should avoid the danger of a negligent watchman and instead strive and deserve to receive the palm of the promised reward through good works. Therefore, to the extent that Christ our God, Lord, and Savior has granted us, by the ineffable generosity of his goodness, to occupy the place of the first of the apostles, to that extent it is fitting that we should be unceasingly concerned for the peace of all the Churches—which, although many in number, are nevertheless one, spread throughout the whole world.

For the words of the holy Scriptures diligently instruct us that, when Moses, the servant of God, wished to ascend the mountain in obedience to the divine commands, he is read to have left Aaron and Hur in his place, saying: “Wait here until we return to you. You have Aaron and Hur with you; if any question arises, refer it to them” (Exodus 24).

Thus peace among the priests of the Lord, pleasing to God above all things, can be preserved if there is one who, supported by the authority of our vicariate and representing our person in the regions of Gaul, according to the custom assigned by our predecessors, diligently guards wisdom; and if the ancient enemy of the human race should attempt to sow his customary tares among the servants of God, removes the scandals that have arisen by a wise moderation, associating with himself our brothers and fellow bishops.

Therefore, since long ago we had entrusted the concern for our vicariate to Auxanius, formerly bishop of the city of Arles, but he departed this life after completing the course of his present existence, and our brother Aurelian is known to have succeeded him, we have considered it absolutely necessary that this responsibility should be entrusted by us to the aforesaid man. We are confident that, in accordance with the dignity of his office, he can accomplish everything that is pleasing to God through good works, especially since our glorious son King Childebert has offered testimony to his good conscience through his Christian devotion.

It is therefore fitting that your charity should render him due obedience in all matters that, while preserving the canons throughout, he determines by our authority according to the salutary decisions of our forefathers. And since it is altogether necessary that, with God’s help, he should convene a synod of bishops at appointed and suitable times to deliberate with the brethren on various matters, we decree by the present authority that no one may dare to excuse himself from attending at the place or time he has appointed, except on account of illness, which human frailty cannot avoid, or when a valid reason for excusal prevents someone from coming.

Let everyone nevertheless know that Christ our Lord and Savior declares in his gracious instruction: “If two of you agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18). How, then, can anyone believe that what he asks may be granted to him if he thinks he may avoid the gathering of the holy assembly, where the Lord has promised in every way that his presence will be present?

But, as we have said, if a just cause prevents him from coming to the synod, let him not delay to send in his place either a priest or a deacon, so that through them he may learn what has been decreed and fulfill what has been determined.

By the same authority we order that no one may dare to depart for distant places without the aforesaid *formata*, especially since the statutes of our predecessors’ predecessors, to whom they are read to have entrusted their vicariate in former times, likewise decree this. If all these provisions are observed with obedience pleasing to God, the peace of the Churches will continue with firm stability, and, as the Apostle, the teacher of the nations, says (Ephesians 5), the Church of God may remain without wrinkle or blemish.

May God keep you safe, dearest brothers.

[Note: Since the schismatics had everywhere spread by written letters that Pope Vigilius was attacking the Council of Chalcedon by condemning the Three Chapters, and since many had withdrawn from his communion, Valentinian of Scythia, Aurelian, bishop of Arles, and several other more prudent men wrote to him asking whether what was being spread was true. On this occasion he replied that, adhering to the footsteps of his predecessors, he approved and venerated the four holy councils. He added what is contained in the arguments of each of them. SEV. BINIUS.—Concerning this letter of Vigilius and Anastasius, who is mentioned in it, see what is related in another letter addressed to the Frankish legates, which will be placed below in its proper location, in the year of Christ 552, the forty-first year of King Childebert. JAC. SIRMONDUS.]

## Letter (formerly XIII) of Pope Vigilius to Aurelian of Arles

Written at Constantinople. He affirms that he has done nothing against the general councils or the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, and exhorts Aurelian to urge King Childebert to write to the king of the Goths, that he may not allow anything in the Roman Church to be disturbed.

[Col. 0041A]

Vigilius to his most beloved brother Aurelian, bishop.

We received the letter of your Fraternity on the day before the Ides of July [Note: Older books: “on the day of the Ides of June”], delivered by Anastasius, and we give thanks to the divine clemency, because we read that your concern in the matter of the faith and concerning our personal reputation accords with the sacred commands, so that the words of God may fittingly and appropriately be applied to your charity, in which he says: “I have chosen you as a priest from among all, ascending to my altar, and you shall bear before me [perhaps: “in my presence”] a great name throughout all the days of your life” (1 Kings 2). [Note: Older books: “that you may ascend.”]

It is therefore necessary for us, in the meantime, to relieve your Fraternity’s concern briefly, as far as we can given the circumstances of time, by conversation, so that you may be completely confident that we have done absolutely nothing that might be found—God forbid—to be contrary to the statutes of our predecessors, to the four synods of the holy faith, which is one and the same faith, namely, those of Nicaea, Constantinople, the first of Ephesus, and Chalcedon, or to anything injurious to the persons who subscribed to the definition of that same holy faith, or contrary to the determinations of our holy predecessors Celestine, Xystus, Leo, and the other pontiffs who preceded and followed them.

Rather, we unquestionably show toward all the aforesaid synods one veneration and one belief in the faith. We reject those who do not follow all the aforementioned four synods in the rectitude of the faith, who corrupt one or all of them in matters of faith, or who attempt to corrupt [variant: *reprobare*, “reject”], injure, or repudiate them. We have judged—and have established that they are to be judged—that those things which are spoken or found written to the injury of that same holy faith must be anathematized and execrated.

We also impose a similar punishment upon those who have called impious the faith of the blessed Cyril, which our predecessor Leo of holy memory is read to have approved and praised in letters sent to your predecessors and to others, and which the venerable holy Council of Chalcedon is read to have set forth, as well as the faith of the other Fathers whom the bishops of the apostolic See received and followed.

Therefore, let your Fraternity, who is known to be the vicar of the apostolic See through us, make this known to all the bishops, so that they may not be disturbed by false writings, lying words, or messengers of any kind, but rather follow, as is fitting, the words of the first of the apostles, who says: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour; resist him, strong in the faith” (1 Peter 5). Let them also follow what the Apostle, the teacher of the nations, says [Note: Older books: “the same teacher”]: “I urge you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause dissensions and scandals contrary to the doctrine that you have learned, and avoid them” (Romans 16).

Trusting in the Lord, because, as we have said above, we have held, hold, venerated, venerate, and defend with sincere devotion the faith handed down by the apostles, declared by the aforesaid four holy councils, preached by our predecessors and by the aforementioned Fathers, and preserved inviolate, we condemn by apostolic authority those who act against it.

But it is necessary for us, through our son Anastasius, to make known to you briefly as much as we can about what has taken place; and when our most clement lord son the emperor, as he promised, orders us to return, with God’s help—who holds his heart—we shall send you, God willing, a man who will inform you carefully about each matter.

We have not yet done this because both the severity of winter and the necessity of Italy, which is not unknown to you, have hindered us, until the most serene prince, as he desires, may receive the Lord’s help [Note: All the older books: “until the most serene prince, with the Lord assisting him, may receive help.” The same is found in Sirmond’s edition].

We also believe that we should hope for this, because it is written: “A brother helping a brother will be exalted” (Proverbs 18); and because the Scripture of the Acts of the Apostles testifies concerning those who believed in the Lord: “The believers were of one heart and soul” (Acts 4). Therefore, let your Fraternity be concerned also in this matter, and do not cease to beseech our glorious son King Childebert—whom we know to display, through his zeal for Christianity, complete veneration toward the apostolic See over which God has willed us to preside—that, in such a great crisis, he may show Christian devotion and concern for the Church of God, as we trust he will.

Since the Goths are reported to have entered the Roman city with their king, may he deign to write to them so that they do not interfere in prejudice to our Church, as though it were subject to an alien law, nor do anything, nor permit anything to be done by any means, whereby the Catholic Church could be disturbed [Note: Paris: “by any means”].

For it is fitting, and appropriate to a Catholic king such as he is, that he should defend with every strength the faith and the Church in which God willed him to be baptized. For it is written: “I live, says the Lord: those who glorify me, I will glorify” (1 Kings 2).

Hasten, therefore, dearest brother, so that, persevering in the sincerity of the holy faith, you may, with God’s favor, guard with due concern the peace of the Churches entrusted to you either by God through the merit of the priesthood [Note: Older books: “through the merit of the priesthood entrusted to you”] or by us through apostolic authority and vicarious power; and show by works pleasing to God that you are a worthy vicar of our See.

May God preserve you [Note: Regius and Colbertine manuscripts: “May God keep you safe and sound”], dearest brother.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of May, in the twenty-fourth year of the reign of our lord Justinian, the perpetual Augustus [Note: Regius and Colbertine manuscripts: “while our lord Justinian, the perpetual Augustus, was reigning, in year twenty-four”], and in the eighth year after the consulship of Basil, the most illustrious man [Note: Parisian, Regius, and Colbertine manuscripts: “in the ninth year”], by the man whom Anastasius sent.

[Note: Vigilius, harassed by several of his own clerics who were schismatics, assembled the bishops of Italy who were in Constantinople and issued a sentence of excommunication and deposition from every rank and order against them, especially against the deacons Rusticus and Sebastianus. Yet the schism was not thereby brought to an end; rather, it was intensified, as the defenders of the Chapters joined together with their opponents against Vigilius. Baron., year 550. SEV. BINIUS.]

## Letter (formerly XIV) of Pope Vigilius to Rusticus and Sebastianus

He excommunicates Rusticus and Sebastianus.

Vigilius, bishop, to Rusticus and Sebastianus.

For a long time, Rusticus and Sebastianus, we delayed, in accordance with apostolic moderation, imposing upon you the punishment appropriate to the canons and to the provisions of our predecessors. But because we see fulfilled in the hardness of your hearts—which we mention with profound sorrow—the words of the teacher of the nations: “Do you not know that God’s patience is leading you to repentance? But by your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath” (Romans 2), we shall meanwhile identify, insofar as we can, a few of your many offenses.

When we came here to the imperial city, you, Rusticus, while reading certain things unknown to us—things that a man of your position ought not at all to have read—and while you were said to have committed many other acts that could also have harmed our reputation and soul, had we not prevented you, God forbid [Note: Older books: “could have harmed”], we repeatedly and secretly admonished you with fatherly affection. This was done both because Paul the deacon had told us certain things about you in your presence, as was proper, and because of the family connection by which you were joined to us through a brother whom we loved, and because we had promoted you to the Levitical office.

We warned you to refrain from such things if you recognized any part of what was being said about you, lest, since we would not permit the cause of God to be abandoned without investigation by any means, canonical judgment should proceed against you.

But you not only refused, with a malevolent spirit, to heed our admonition, as it is written, “Reprove a wise man, and he will love you; reprove a fool, and he will hate you” (Proverbs 9), and again, “He refused to understand how to act well; he meditated iniquity on his bed” (Psalm 35); your wickedness was carried to the point that, having despised our admonition, you instead broke out into hatred and sought an opportunity whereby, under the pretext of the matter of the Chapters—that is, concerning the sayings and person of Theodore of Mopsuestia, as well as the letter said to have been written by Ibas to Maris the Persian, and also the writings of Theodoret [Note: The same books: “of Theodore”] that were directed against the orthodox faith and against the synodical letter of Cyril of blessed memory to Nestorius, together with the twelve chapters—which the first holy Synod of Ephesus accepted, and which the blessed Council of Chalcedon is read to have included in its definition of the faith in order to refute the madness of Nestorius—you might demand that these matters be condemned.

It is certain that you did so insist, even proclaiming to our sons, the deacons Sapatus and Paulus, and to Surgentius, first of the notaries, not only that the name and writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia ought to be condemned by us, but also the territory itself [Note: The word “itself” is absent from the Parisian manuscript] where he lies; and that, if anyone should tear his bones from the grave, cast them out of the burial place, and burn them together with that territory, you would gladly approve it.

And when it was necessary that the case brought before our tribunal should be concluded by a sentence, with you yourself, above all the others of both the sacred and the subordinate order, consenting, this was done. No one is unaware what you did with that judgment, or how urgently you acted in the palace so that it might quickly be delivered to our brother Menna [Note: Older books and editions: “Mena”], to whom we had written.

Thus, when our son Surgentius, first of the notaries, asked for a copy of our judgment so that he might keep it with him in the proper place according to custom, you absolutely refused to give it to him for many days. Instead, you sent copies through numerous priests and laymen, and through the glorious man Tyrannus, master of the soldiers [Note: Bellovacensis: “Tyrannius”; Paris: “Turranius”], and other laymen, to the province of Africa—something that has never been done in our Church by a deacon—and you sent copies of it even though we did not know.

For on Holy Saturday, when we issued that judgment with you, as we have said, pressing the matter, you are known to have gone into the church, sat down [Note: Older books: “sat in the church with us”], communicated, and fulfilled your office. And on that same day, when returning from the church, you told our fellow bishop Julianus, as he reports, that nothing could have been done better than what had been done in the judgment, and you urged him to pray to God that what had been done should not be removed [perhaps: “lest what had been done should be removed”; Note: Paris: “lest what had been done be removed.” This confirms the conjecture added in the margin of the Roman edition].

You acted similarly on the following Sunday, Easter Day, and, persisting for a long time in the same opinion, you nevertheless urged others to follow our judgment willingly.

When we delayed giving copies of that judgment to the representatives of the Church of Antioch, who were asking us for them, and instead told those representatives that it would be more just for them to request copies from our brother Menna, to whom it appeared to have been issued by us, you publicly demanded them, saying that Lord Leo had sent copies of his letter in various directions and asserting that we ought to do the same. You said this because you feared that, unless everyone possessed copies of our judgment issued from our archives, it might later somehow be concealed [Note: Bellovacensis: *editaon teneret*; Paris: *edita non teneret*].

Then, when you had found an opportunity to travel to Sicily, you wished to send to our sons Pelagius the deacon and others, as a precaution, our judgment and the commendations of it—on which it is clear that our son the first of the deacons and the first of the notaries had also subscribed with you—so that it might perhaps not be found by anyone. Without our knowledge, you sent it written on parchment [Note: Older books: *membrano*, “on parchment”; the same reading occurs shortly afterward], folded four times into a small compass and written in extremely minute letters.

[Additional textual apparatus: At “But when,” older books read “Since indeed.” At “formerly erased,” older books read *a super. temp.* At “We also exhort you,” the Paris manuscript reads “But we also exhort you.” At “For your Reverence knows,” read “For your Reverence knows”; the printed Labbe edition has a typographical error, corrected here. At “It is clear,” read “that this was said not only”; this too corrects a typographical error in Labbe. For the date of the first letter, Bellovacensis and the older editions read “Given,” while older books read “the third day before the Nones” rather than “the fourth day before the Nones.”

At the synodal proceedings, older books read “most reverend” for “most religious” bishop Stephen; Paris reads “who, when he had satisfied” for “once he has satisfied”; and the corrected text is “since certain writings concerning the present case have been exchanged between us and Vigilius,” with *concerning the present case* added to repair Labbe’s typographical error.

In Letter XIII, Paris and Regius read *legimus* (“we read”) at “we read that your concern”; older books read “that you may ascend” in the biblical quotation; Paris reads *indubitanter* (“unquestionably”); Regius, Paris, and Colbertine manuscripts read *reprobant* (“reject”) for *repravant* (“corrupt”); Paris reads *cuius* (“whose”) for *quem* (“which”) concerning Cyril’s faith; Bellovacensis reads *cui* (“to whom”); older books read *praecessores* (“predecessors”) for *praedecessores*; and *sancta* (“holy”) after “venerable Council of Chalcedon” is absent from all ancient manuscripts. Paris reads “his heart” for “the emperor’s heart.” At “by any means,” Paris reads *aliqua*. 

In Letter XIV, Paris reads *commodica* for “profound” sorrow; older books read “and that we may identify your offenses” for “we shall identify”; Paris reads *adstante* (“standing by”) for *instante* (“insisting”); the same manuscript reads “deacons,” while Bellovacensis reads “deacon,” for the reference to Sapatus and Paul; older books read *consentientibus* (“with [them] consenting”) for *consentiente* (“with you consenting”); and Paris reads “and this the more” for “but this the more.” The note “the same books: *Theodoreti*” merely repeats the printed form and supplies no distinct English reading.]

For you also wrote in like manner to our son Pelagius the deacon through Vincent, subdeacon of the second region, whom we later sent again to Sicily. But because the aforesaid subdeacon sailed so successfully that he could have preceded the man who was carrying what had been written on parchment, Pelagius the deacon, as he reported to us, received in that man’s presence what you had written on the parchment [Note: Paris reads “written” (scriptum).]. [Col. 0045B]

Therefore, when the judgment brought forward—while you above all were pressing for it—had been issued, and when you had written for a long time with such ardor in its praise, and had acted so that we never believed you could depart from this rectitude, we learned through public report that afterward you had suddenly been changed by a certain levity of mind and had begun secretly to confer with the adversaries of the Church—those who were striving against the tenor of our judgment [Note: Bellovac reads “because [they were] against” (quia contra)] and had been suspended by us from communion under the terms of that judgment. And when our son Paul the deacon [Note: Older books and editions read “the deacon Paul.”] wished to depart for Italy [Note: Paris reads “from Italy.”], after the report had also reached him that, while still remaining in our communion, you were secretly attempting here and in the African province [Note: Older books read “the African province,”] to cause the scandal of the Church—where previously you had sent copies of our judgment in its defense and praise—he then began to confront you and say that, if it were true, you ought to produce it [Note: Paris reads “reveal it.”]. When convicted, you could by no means conceal it.

Then the aforesaid deacon began to press us, saying that you ought either to promise in the presence of our clergy to correct the things you were illicitly doing there, or else that we ought to accept from him the petition against you, and the account of your inconsistency and deceit, which he also held in his hands. You were brought by your own will to the point of touching the Gospels and giving an oath, so that your words, written down by the notary [Note: The same codex reads “notaries.”], might be kept in our archives; among other things, you are recorded as having promised that you would never wholly withdraw from our service.

But after Sebastian, worse than you, was known to have arrived—coming solely to create scandal, as both the beginning of his arrival in Constantinople showed and its worse outcome made clear—you, immediately forgetful of your oath, formed a conspiracy with one another against the canonical statutes, without our knowledge, and both burst into open scandal.

But so that everyone may know your evil deeds, Sebastian—not insofar as they are, but insofar as we can report them—and may recognize that you have justly, though rather late, undergone canonical judgment, let us turn to the beginnings of your ordination.

When our sons the deacons Anatolius and Stephen were absent [Note: Older books read “the deacons Pelagius, Anatolius, and Stephen.”], you asked us to make you a deacon temporarily in place of the absent men, for the fulfillment of the office during that period. We granted this for the time being to your expectation because, before your ordination, you had voluntarily read to us a written undertaking, which you also confirmed by witnesses and sealed with a bodily oath upon the Gospels: that whatever we might enjoin upon you for the benefit of the Church, you would faithfully and without any fraud fulfill; and that you would discharge the office and place of deacon [Note: Paris reads “the place of the diaconate.”] without any fault, without any pride, and without any neglect, until the aforesaid deacons returned, or for however long we might wish you to serve in the order of the Levites [Note: The manuscripts omit te, “you”; Bellovac reads ordinationem (“ordination”); Paris, ordinem (“order”)] [Col. 0046B] with all humility and diligence, without neglect, in every way.

In the same undertaking you added that, if you failed to fulfill anything of all that you had promised under oath, with your bodily hand touching the Gospels, then you would be suspended from holy communion; and that, if from the day of your offense you were unwilling within a year to bow your neck in penance, you had said, writing it with your own hand, that you would be anathema to yourself. Thus, for the time being, you became a deacon under the condition that you had hoped for and promised.

Afterward you repeatedly begged with the greatest urgency to be sent by us to the patrimony in Dalmatia. Since we were confident because you had made such an undertaking, we granted this willingly. But when you had arrived in the city of Salona [Note: Older books read “in the city of Salona”] for the administration of the patrimony, we later learned from the reports of many that you had involved yourself in ordinations which were illicit and prohibited by the Apostolic See. Those whom Honorius, then bishop of the aforesaid city, had admitted to sacred orders contrary to the custom of the Roman Church and of his own Church, and contrary to the constitutions of the Apostolic See [Note: The same books read “had admitted”], you not only refused entirely to prohibit, but did not even wish to report the matter to us in writing, or to tell us how it had occurred [Note: The same books read “or how” (vel quomodo)]; nor, when you had encountered us at Thessalonica, did you wish, mindful of your conscience, to mention it to us even in a word. Rather, you consented, in the spirit of greed, to proceed with them as though they had been ordained in a legitimate and reasonable order, and you were found to be their associate through the sale of communion.

Again you were sent from Thessalonica to Dalmatia to administer the patrimony [Note: The same books read “Again, from Thessalonica”]. From that province we frequently admonished you not to depart before you had collected, according to your promise, all the revenues both of the Dalmatian patrimony and of the Praevalitan patrimony.

But you disregarded everything and hurried to Constantinople solely to create scandal, as the subsequent outcome also made clear.

Nevertheless, rereading the text of our decree—which we have read that we delivered concerning the aforesaid chapters to Menna, bishop of this city—you praised it aloud in the presence of the deacons, subdeacons, and all the clergy [Note: Paris reads “you proclaimed”], so that you might declare publicly to all the clergy, as we have said, that our judgment had been ordained and issued from heaven. You asserted that you had found in the city of Rome, among certain books, statements of Theodore of Mopsuestia, which you affirmed were filled with every execration and blasphemy. While saying these things, you publicly fulfilled the office of the diaconate in our service, in the church, and in the Placidian building.

The day of the Nativity of Christ God, our Lord and Savior according to the flesh, arrived in the past year. We summoned you because the report of what we have mentioned above that you had done in Dalmatia had recently reached us. As was fitting, we said to you [Col. 0047B]: If you proceeded with those who had been admitted to sacred orders contrary to the constitutions of the Apostolic See, or if, as is said, you joined yourself to their communion, it is necessary for us—if God deigns to recall us to our Church—to investigate these matters [Note: Paris reads “to investigate whether these matters”] and, after learning the truth more clearly, to punish them according to the canons.

But you, terrified by the guilt of your conscience because you had acted against the apostolic constitutions, concealed your purpose and sought an excuse for leaving. For when we had sent you on an assigned mission [Note: Older books read mandato, “on a mission”] with John the bishop, Surgentius the primicerius, and Saturninus, our consul, to Menna, our brother and bishop of this city, you returned to the Placidian building. With many present, you and Rusticus fulfilled the deacon’s office in the customary manner [Note: Paris reads “the office of the diaconate”]. And when the most clement emperor, our lord and son [Col. 0047C], sent a referendary so that we might promise him that we would proceed to the church on another day, you and Rusticus urged us, together with the other deacons [Note: Older books read diaconibus rather than diaconis, both “deacons”] and clergy [Note: The same books read fuissetis, “you had been”]. You will likewise be shown to have both been present at the meal at our table.

But just as Judas, after receiving the morsel, thought about the Lord’s betrayal, so you also departed during the night [Note: Paris reads “during the night hours”] to stir up scandal in the Church. On the following day we sent you word that you should either proceed and fulfill the place of deacon in the customary manner, or recognize that you had been suspended from communion.

But you, Sebastian, said this to our brothers John and Julian, bishops [Note: The printed Labbe edition mistakenly has episcopos; read episcopis, “bishops”], whom we had sent among others, as they reported: “I follow the judgment issued by the pope, provided that he punishes those who act against the judgment.” You likewise said to them, as they testify [Note: Bellovac reads in illis; Paris, in illius], to such an extent that you declared that Lampridius [Note: Older books and editions read “Lampredius”] and Felix, monks who had refused to accept our judgment, had come there [Note: Older books read venisse ibi] and that you had told them: “We cannot see you, because you have one cause and we have another.”

Afterward your wickedness proceeded to the point that, with an arrogant spirit, you dared to communicate contrary to the canons with persons who had been excommunicated—that is, with the aforesaid men or others whom the text of the same judgment showed to have already been suspended by us from communion because they had written against our judgment. The Catholic Church has demonstrated that you accepted, consented to, and communicated in accordance with that judgment, as we have mentioned above. It is therefore clear that you have been justly condemned according to the rules of the canons.

For the canons define:

“If anyone who has been excommunicated presumes to communicate before a hearing, he has pronounced condemnation upon himself.” [Note: See Additamenta to the Fourth Book of the Capitularies, chapter 54.]

Again, the whole council decreed: “If anyone has been excommunicated for his negligence, whether a bishop or any cleric, and during the time of his excommunication presumes to communicate before a hearing, he shall be judged to have pronounced the sentence of condemnation upon himself.” [Note: See Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 30, and Book VIII, chapter 26.]

You also added, with execrable pride, that which neither is read nor has anyone of your order ever presumed to do without the command of his own bishop: you claimed for yourselves the authority to preach contrary to every custom and canon. You attacked and reproached the First Synod of Ephesus and blessed Cyril [Note: Read “the blessed Cyril”; this typographical error has been corrected], and with similar madness defended blasphemies spoken against Jesus our Lord [Note: Older books read “against Christ”]. You wrote deceitfully throughout all the provinces that you had committed nothing which could be found contrary to the definition of the holy Council of Chalcedon, which agrees in faith with the three preceding councils: Nicaea, Constantinople, and the First Council of Ephesus.

Thus your deceitful activity reached such a degree of wickedness that you turned the minds of all who did not know your malice—those who, receiving your writings as writings from Roman deacons [Note: The same books read “from deacons”], believed them simply—to such a great crime that human blood was shed in certain places within the church, which is unspeakable. You wished in an arrogant spirit to trample upon every ecclesiastical law, and you insulted the continuity of the holy canons by deceitfully proclaiming throughout all the provinces against us things that were impious and unlawful.

Recently, adding worse things to your earlier evils, you dared to assert in a written statement addressed to the most Christian emperor, our lord and son [Col. 0048D], that our predecessor, Lord Leo, had given his agreement to and confirmed writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia which are read to be contrary to the true faith. Let no Christian believe that the holiness of so great a bishop could have accepted anything of this kind—anything found written by anyone against the true faith [Note: The word quod (“that/which”) is absent from the ancient codices]—for he is read in all his letters to have condemned Nestorius, Eutyches, and those who held similar views with an equal sentence [Note: Older books read suscepisse (“to have accepted”) rather than suscepisset (“could have accepted”)].

In that same writing you also attempted to inflict sacrilegious insults, contrary to the divine Scriptures, not only upon many bishops but also—what is unspeakable—upon the emperor himself, so that you might deceive the Christian people, whom you regarded as ignorant, still further by diabolical cunning [Note: Paris reads “as though”].

Although we endured these things [Note: Bellovac reads Haec enim ergo, “For these things therefore”] for long periods of time [Note: Paris reads “for a long time and through many periods”; Bellovac reads “for long periods of times,” apparently formed from “for a long time” and “through long periods”], we delayed cutting them off with priestly patience, believing that perhaps you would recover your senses and refrain from unlawful acts. But because, after being admonished once and again by our brother bishops John of Marsica and Julian of Cingoli, by our son and deacon Sapatus [Note: Paris reads “deacon”], and also by the glorious patrician Cethegus, the religious man and likewise our son Senator, and our other sons, you refused to listen and refused to return either to the Church or to us, and, as in everything, you chose detestable pride [Note: Older books read “contentiousness”], it is necessary for us to punish you canonically, lest we appear to be subject to the interpretations of the divine Scriptures.

For it is written: “You saw a thief, and you ran with him [Note: Paris reads “you ran together with him”]; and you placed your portion with adulterers” (Psalm 49). And our Lord and Savior himself says: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it from you. For it is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body be thrown into Gehenna” [Note: Older books read “into gehenna”] (Matthew 5).

And since this meaning ought properly to be applied, with sound judgment, to ecclesiastical offices or to neighbors who act wrongly and bring scandals into the churches, as he also warns us elsewhere, saying: “It is necessary that scandals come, but woe to the one through whom they come” (Matthew 18); and the blessed Apostle proclaims in like manner: “Would that those who unsettle you would cut themselves off” (Galatians 5); and again holy Scripture admonishes us, saying: “Cast out the pestilent man from the assembly, and strife will go out with him” (Proverbs 22).

Therefore, after so many admonitions, it is now necessary for us [Note: The same books read “it is now necessary for us in you”], Rusticus and Sebastian, by the authority of blessed Peter—whose place the Lord has wished us to serve—to punish you canonically, lest, if we delay any longer, the whole ecclesiastical order be dissolved.

Accordingly, what must be said by us with grief but with the authority of blessed Peter, we decree: because of the offenses written above, you are alienated from the honor of the diaconate [Note: The same books read “from the honor of the diaconate”], and we wholly remove from you the aforesaid honor and every ministry of the Levitical office. You have no further permission to presume to do anything under the Levitical name or rank, or to trouble the Church of God again by writing under the name of deacons. For, by apostolic authority and the rules of the Fathers—against which you have acted in many ways with an arrogant and irreligious spirit—we depose you by our present authoritative sentence, since you have long been worthy of condemnation.

And so that everyone may know that we have acted rightly in this matter, in the place where God has willed us to be and by the authority of the blessed Apostle Peter, we have set forth the canonical decrees which the holy Council of Chalcedon read aloud in its assembly and approved.

The archdeacon Aetius reread:

“If any presbyter or deacon, despising his bishop, separates himself from the communion of the Church, secretly holds an assembly, and establishes an altar, and refuses to respond to the bishop when summoned, and refuses to obey him when summoned a first and a second time, let him be condemned absolutely; let him never obtain healing, and let him not be able to recover his honor. But if he persists in making disturbances and seditions in the Church, he must be restrained as a seditious person by external authority.”

(All the most reverend bishops cried out: “This is a just rule; this is the rule of the Fathers.”)

We likewise decree that, if while we are alive—as we hope—you recognize in humility and meekness, through canonical penance, the Church as your mother, pardon shall appropriately be granted by us [Note: Bellovac reads competens; Paris, compatens, for competenter, “appropriately”]. But if—which we do not desire—you delay returning to the mother Church under regular penance, through your customary pride, the censure of the councils whose rules we have set forth shall remain in force against you. Thus no one, after our passing, shall dare, contrary to the decree which we issue by the authority of blessed Peter, whose place we hold though unworthy, while carrying out the rules of the canons, to restore you, or John, Gerontius, Severinus, Importunus, John, and Deusdedit to an ecclesiastical rank [Note: The text should read “after our passing, [to restore] you contrary to our decree”; Labbe’s edition has a typographical omission, and vos (“you”) is supplied from ancient copies]. They are known to be participants in your conspiracy and confederacy. We had made them, as powerful and good men, serve the Church over which, by God’s authority, we preside.

Nevertheless, so that they themselves and others may know, they should recognize that by this present sentence they have been deposed from the office of subdeacons, notaries, or defenders, and that they retain no rank whatever in our Church thereafter—unless, as we have said, while we and they still live in this world, they also submit their necks to canonical penance.

We likewise establish a regular sentence against Felix, the African monk who is said to have presided over the monastery at Gillitanum, and who is known, through his levity and inconsistency, to have scattered the congregation of that monastery through various places, and to have been the instigator of your depravity; and against all who, whether clerics or monks or laymen, after the present prohibitions, pollute themselves by any association with him or with you, or offer consent and counsel. In these matters, as is likewise read above, we establish a sentence of warning, so that, with canonical order observed in these remedies, no one may presume thereafter to disturb the peace which the Lord loves in the Church.

We are known to have transmitted this present sentence to you through our brothers and fellow bishops John of Marsica, Zacchaeus of Squillace [Note: Bellovac reads “Scillacenus”; Paris, “Squillacenus”], and Julian of Cingoli; through our sons and deacons Sapatus and Peter; through our son Surgentius, primicerius of the notaries; through Servus Dei, subdeacon of the first region; and through Vincent, subdeacon of the second region, of our Church over which, by God’s authority, we preside [Note: Paris reads “of our Church over which, by God’s authority, we preside.”] [Col. 0051A].

## Letter (formerly XII) of Pope Vigilius to Valentinian, Bishop of Tomi

What was done at Constantinople concerning the Three Chapters.

Vigilius to his most beloved brother Valentinian, bishop of Tomi in the province of Scythia.

As we reread the writings of your Fraternity, we gladly recognized that you possess episcopal concern; for the prophetic words can appropriately be applied to you: “I will save my flock, and I will raise up over it a shepherd who will feed it, my servant” (Ezekiel 34).

Your Charity ought therefore also to follow those words of our Lord by which he said: “I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel; you shall hear a word from my mouth, and you shall announce it to them from me” (Ezekiel 3). You should continually exhort those whom you reported to have been scandalized by various rumors, lest they perhaps be led astray by those who, under a Catholic pretext and with a most wicked spirit, attempt by their deceit to ensnare the hearts of simple Christians. Following the practice of their father, the devil, with a malignant spirit, they desire to disturb the Church entrusted to you with various lying writings. To them the apostolic reading appropriately applies, saying: “I urge you, brothers, to watch out for those who create dissensions and offenses contrary to the teaching that you have learned, and avoid them” (Romans 16). And below: “By pleasing words and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent” (ibid.).

Your obedience, however, has been proclaimed everywhere, so that, frequently admonished by your Fraternity’s exhortation, no evil announcement may move the minds of the faithful from the straight path, which is Christ, who says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14). But if, as ought not to happen, they have been disturbed by the adversaries and perhaps fear that something has been done against the faith—which God avert—let them follow with the gentleness fitting for Christians the prophetic words that say: “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will say to you” (Deuteronomy 32); and the other prophet: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth” (Malachi 2).

And because Basinianus [Note: Paris reads “Basilianus,”] an illustrious and magnificent man, our son, is known to have said, together with those who are watching over the affairs of your Fraternity’s Church in Constantinople [Note: Older books read “to Constantinople”], that the enemies of God also falsely claimed that the persons of the bishops Ibas and Theodoret had been condemned in our judgment—which God forbid—let them read what we find that we defined when writing to our brother Menna, bishop of the city of Constantinople, concerning the matter that was raised here. Then they will recognize [Note: The same books read cognoscunt, “they recognize”] that, with God guarding us, we committed or decreed nothing that can be found contrary to the faith and preaching of the four venerable councils, which defined one and the same faith: Nicaea, Constantinople, the First Council of Ephesus, and Chalcedon. Nor should they insult any one of those who subscribed to the definition of the aforesaid faith of Chalcedon, or anything that may be found—God forbid—contrary to the constitutions of our predecessors and antecedents [Note: Older books and editions read “predecessors”; Labbe altered the text]. Rather, in all things we have resisted the adversaries of the bishops of the Apostolic See, of Pope Leo of blessed memory, and of the aforesaid councils [Note: The same books read “we have restored.”].

We believe that your Fraternity is not unaware that the enemies of the Christian faith have always contrived, with worldly and reprehensible cunning, to show that the four evangelists had spoken things contrary to one another—which God forbid. The holy Fathers opposed them with heavenly wisdom through books demonstrating the harmony of the Gospels.

The adversaries of the holy Council of Chalcedon are now doing the same. Among them we have discovered Rusticus and Sebastian to be the authors of this scandal; because of their deserts we formerly suspended them from sacred communion, and your Fraternity should know that, unless they quickly recover their senses, we shall pronounce canonical judgment upon them. They are striving, under the pretext of a false defense, to show that the same council spoke against the aforesaid three councils—which God forbid.

To those who attempt such things the words of the prophet appropriately apply: “Truly, the lying pen of the scribes has worked falsehood. They have rejected the word of our Lord, and there is no wisdom in them. They have taught their tongue to speak lies; they labored to act wickedly” (Jeremiah 8–9). If they do not repent, the sentence invoked by the Psalmist will come upon them: “That you may destroy the enemy and the defender.”

We believe that what we then wrote to our brother and fellow bishop Menna—the things concerning the blasphemies of Theodore of Mopsuestia and his person, concerning the letter said to have been written by Ibas to Maris the Persian, and concerning the writings of Theodoret [Note: The same books read scripta Theodoriti rather than scriptis Theodoriti: “the writings of Theodoret”], which were composed against the true faith and the Twelve Chapters of the holy Cyril—can abundantly suffice for the Catholic sons of the Church.

For it can be carefully recognized in our decree, designated above, that in the very definition of faith which the bishops of the holy Council of Chalcedon issued according to the three other holy councils preceding it [Note: Paris reads alios sanctos, literally “the other holy [men/saints]”], they changed nothing; rather, praising everything enacted by the earlier councils, they confirmed and established it forever by their holy definition [Note: Bellovac reads “by its strength”; Paris, “by honor and strength”].

Nevertheless, if after this anyone should wish to doubt—which we do not believe—we urge him to hasten to come to us with the arrangement of your Fraternity [Note: Paris reads “let them hasten”; and below, “let them recognize”], so that by clear instruction he may recognize that everything enacted and written in the times of our predecessors and of the aforesaid four councils concerning the one and the same faith has been inviolably preserved by us. Once this has been understood, and the scandal removed from Christian minds as is fitting, may peace pleasing to God remain undefiled in his Church.

We also believe that your Fraternity should be admonished not to receive any further writings from the aforesaid Rusticus and Sebastian, or from those who are proved to share in their depraved presumption. You should also warn all who belong to your jurisdiction not to read anything sent by those men, nor to give their minds any further credence to their falsehood.

May God preserve you safe, most beloved brother.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the twenty-third year of the reign of our lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus, and the ninth year after the consulship of Basil, a man of illustrious rank, through John the presbyter and apocrisiarius; and he himself sent it through Maxentius, his own man. [Col. 0053B]

[Note: Sirmond published it after the appendix to the Theodosian Code. It is in a very ancient manuscript collection in the library of the Paris College of the Society of Jesus. Hardouin.]

## Encyclical Letter (formerly XV) of Pope Vigilius to the Whole Church
