He explains the reasons for his withdrawal to Saint Euphemia, what he did there with Justinian’s legates, and inserts a confession of his faith.

Vigilius, bishop of the Catholic Church, to the entire people of God.

While we were being detained in the basilica of Saint Euphemia, suffering from a serious illness, the most pious and clement emperor, on Sunday [Note: The Lucca codex reads “on the Sunday,” that is, the fifth day before the Kalends of February], the Kalends of February [Note: Hardouin reads “the fifth day before the Kalends of February,” that is, 28 January 552], deigned to send his glorious judges to us: Belisarius and Cethegus, former consuls and patricians; Peter, former consul, patrician, and master; and Justin, former consul and master of the imperial household [Note: The same codex reads “count of the excubitors”], together with Marcellinus the quaestor [Note: The same codex reads “the religious man Constantine the quaestor,” and so forth]. They were to tell us that we ought to receive an oath and return from the church of Saint Euphemia to the royal city.

With God’s help we gave them this reply:

“We did not flee to this basilica for any financial or private reason, but solely because of the scandal of the Church, which has now become known throughout the whole world because of sins. Therefore, if the cause of the Church is put in order, so that its peace—which the most pious emperor established in the time of his uncle—may now also be restored by him, I have no need of oaths, but shall depart immediately. If, however, the cause of the Church has not been settled, I likewise have no need of oaths, because I have no intention of leaving the basilica of Saint Euphemia unless the scandal has been removed from the Church of God.”

For after the most pious emperor ordered his edicts to be posted for all the bishops of the various regions, and also for the priests, deacons, and clergy of the Church of Constantinople who came to us, in the Placidian residence [Note: “Palatine residence” in the same manuscript; in the year 551, in the month of August], before we took refuge in the basilica of Saint Peter [Note: “Called the Hormisdas,” Hardouin], we spoke face to face as follows:

“Ask the most pious emperor to deign to remove the edicts which he ordered to be posted, and to await the common decree; that is, let the bishops of the Latin tongue who have been scandalized either come to the synod, or, with all violence removed, declare their judgments in writing. But if he should refuse to hear your requests, do not give your assent to anything that tends toward the division of the Church, and do not act against the decree under any threat. For if, which we do not believe, you should do this, know that from this day you are suspended from communion by the seat of the blessed Apostle Peter, through the ministry of my voice, as transgressors [Note: The word “communion” is absent from the Lucca codex].”

And since by these actions not only were the things that had been committed in no way corrected, but even worse things were attempted on that very day, for other reasons, to the prejudice of ecclesiastical rules and the injury of the Apostolic See, we no longer allowed them to share in our communion, nor did our eyes receive their presence after so many transgressions.

For what we had publicly declared by word concerning the aforesaid excommunication to all the bishops, priests, deacons, and other clergy of the Church of Constantinople, we later also confirmed in writing on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September recently past [Note: 14 August 551, Hardouin], in the basilica of blessed Peter at the Hormisdas [Note: The Lucca codex reads “the ninth day before the Kalends”; it is absent from the Hormisdas manuscript]. In that document we also deposed and condemned from the episcopal order the man who, under episcopal clothing, like a ravenous wolf, continually lies in wait for the Lord’s flock and, assuming leadership of the entire scandal, has disturbed and continues to disturb the universal Church of God. We suspended the others mentioned above from communion.

But until now we have been unwilling to publish the page of that condemnation because we trust that, by considering the divine judgment, the most clement emperor may recall what has been done in connection with so great and serious a scandal, and because it was fitting for us to reserve a period of repentance for all those aforesaid, imitating blessed Peter, whose seat we hold, though unworthy.

We handed the document of excommunication and condemnation itself to a certain Christian person for safekeeping, so that, if perhaps those who had transgressed should in no way wish to correct themselves, or if any force should be inflicted upon us, or any disturbance should occur, or indeed if, by the lot common to humanity, our passage from this light should take place, he might immediately display it in the most prominent places, so that its contents, made known to all Christians, might be preserved for the future.

While we were saying these things to the aforesaid judges, we asked and solemnly adjured them, invoking the judgment of almighty God, to communicate this also from our name to the most clement emperor: namely, that he ought not to communicate with those whom we have excommunicated, among whom is also the man we mentioned, lest—God forbid—he incur a grave sin.

While matters stood thus, on the day before the Kalends of February, through the magnificent man Peter the referendary, a certain document was brought to us. We did not in any way believe that it had been sent by the most clement prince, since it had not been subscribed by his pious hand. When we told the aforementioned referendary to subscribe it and likewise to indicate the day on which it had been brought by him, he altogether refused to do so. This plainly confirmed our suspicion that the document itself was unknown to the most pious prince.

For it is shown to be so full of matters removed from the truth and of insults that no one could believe that the gentleness of an imperial mouth had dictated it, especially against the vicar of the first of the apostles, whose former reverence he has frequently professed in his letters to be his obligation.

Although the aforementioned document possesses no force in itself, nevertheless, with God’s help, a truthful and straightforward answer is given to each of its points, so that its falsity—always hateful to wise men—may be more fully excluded from everyone’s mind.

Now we have also taken care to make this known to all people: we departed for the basilica of Saint Euphemia in great fear and anxiety. For when, in the previous month of August, we had fled to the basilica of blessed Peter founded at Hormisdas, no one, we trust, is unaware that, when a company from the praetor came into that same church with a multitude of armed soldiers, drawn up as though for battle, we were seized and dragged by the feet from the holy altar; and the altar table itself would have fallen upon us had it not been supported by the hands of our clergy.

Afterward, when we were told that from there we would be dragged away with every kind of violence unless we were willing to receive the sacramental oath, the aforementioned judges, sent by the most pious emperor, wished to administer the oath to us. We gave them a written memorandum by which we requested that an oath be administered in writing to our person. The most clement prince did not grant that it be administered in the form we desired; instead, he directed through his judges that it be given in the form he himself preferred.

When the aforementioned judges had placed the memorandum upon the altar, upon the lattice of blessed Peter the apostle, upon the cross which contains enclosed within it a piece of the wood of the Lord’s Passion, and also upon the keys of blessed Peter the apostle, and had sworn the bodily oath, we returned to Placidia, as though we would suffer nothing harmful thereafter, in accordance with the will of the most pious prince.

While there we repeatedly suffered many intolerable evils, which, we trust, are now known to everyone, we believed that we ought to summon the aforementioned judges to witness our case: verbally, when they had often been sent to us by the most clement prince, and also once, twice, and three times in writing, so that they might keep the oaths they had given and report to the most pious emperor that we should suffer no disturbances or hardships, just as had been sworn to us.

Since our repeated protest, whether verbal or written, achieved nothing, and we suffered worse things day by day, two days before the Nativity of the Lord we learned for ourselves and heard with our own ears that guards were stationed at every entrance of the aforementioned house, so that those who were laying ambushes for us were seen by many of our people, and on the night when we departed we heard their shouting in the bedroom where we were staying.

When this had happened, and during the night hours we were held under profound desperation and the affliction of great fear, we fled, as that place itself will be able to show to all people. For if one considers why and to what extent, under the pressure of fear, we looked upon the danger with despair, and how, after being forced to pass through a small wall built by workmen, we were compelled to proceed in the darkness of night amid the greatest pain, then it can clearly be recognized how great our necessity was at that time for the sake of the Church alone, and how great the guard was which compelled us to depart under such danger.

But lest anyone, in accordance with the wickedness of perverse men, should perhaps fabricate something about our preaching to religious and God-fearing minds, we have thought it right to append to this brief account of the evils we endured a declaration of our faith.

Let all therefore know that we preach, hold, and defend that faith which, handed down by the apostles and inviolably guarded by their successors, the venerable Council of Nicaea, of 318 Fathers, received through the revelation of the Holy Spirit and reduced to a creed. Then three other holy synods—namely, the Council of Constantinople, of 150 Fathers, held under the pious-emperor Theodosius the Elder; the First Council of Ephesus, presided over by our predecessor, Pope Celestine of blessed memory, and by Cyril, bishop of Alexandria; and the Council of Chalcedon, of 630 Fathers, which assembled under the pious-emperor Marcian and which our predecessor, Pope Leo of holy memory, presided over through his legates and representatives—published that same faith at great length, declaring it with one and the same understanding and spirit, as the condemnable opposition of various heresies required.

For this reason our God armed the pastoral office from heaven against the savagery of such errors, commending it to the blessed apostle Peter with a threefold injunction when he said: “Feed my sheep” (John 21). And rightly was the care of feeding them entrusted to him whose splendid confession of faith was praised by the mouth of God.

To him who made the saving confession and said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16), everlasting blessedness is repaid; he is called the son of the dove, and he receives the keys of the heavenly kingdom.

When the Lord asked whom they said the Son of Man was, he confessed, in the wondrous brevity of the question and answer, that this same one was both the Son of Man and the Son of God: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

Thus he disclosed the mystery of his most sacred incarnation: while the distinct properties of both natures were preserved in the unity of the person, the same one remained both human and God—both what he received in time from his ever-virgin mother and what, born from the Father, he was before the ages.

God the Word, our Emmanuel, united to himself flesh without confusion, without division, without alteration, and in personal union, came as the one whom the Law and the prophets had announced and awaited. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1): wholly in what was his and wholly in what was ours, taking from the womb flesh together with a rational and intellectual soul. As it is written, “building himself a house,” and “coming forth like a bridegroom from his chamber” (Psalm 18), through an ineffable and saving mystery, he who in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word, became incarnate.

God the Son, from God and through the Holy Spirit, took the beginning of his humanity from blessed Mary, ever-virgin, so that he might make us coheirs of his eternity. He deigned to become a sharer in our nature so that he might make us participants in his immortality. “Though he was rich, he became poor, so that by his poverty we might be enriched” (2 Corinthians 8). He forgave all that is ours, cancelling the bond recording our offenses, as the Chosen Vessel taught:

“Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2).

He accomplished this through the hidden depth of so inscrutable a mystery and dispensation that Christ Jesus, the man who is the mediator between God and human beings, might free the first earthly man, who was held fast by the curse in the bonds of death, through the second, heavenly man, by trampling death through death (1 Corinthians 15).

The Son of God suffered in the flesh for us; he was crucified in the flesh; he died in the flesh; and on the third day he rose again. Thus, while his divine nature remained impassible and the reality of our flesh was preserved, we confess both the sufferings and the miracles of one and the same Lord, our God Jesus Christ.

So that the whole body of the Church, beholding the glorification of its head, may await at the coming of future glory in those who are his members the same kind of firstfruits from the dead as it sees in our head, Christ God and Lord.

Our Redeemer therefore sits at the right hand of the Father, one and the same, without confusion of either nature and without division of the person, believed to remain from and in two natures. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.

The Father, with the same only-begotten Son and the Holy Spirit, is one in divinity, equal and of an undivided nature.

After his resurrection our Lord entrusted the fullness of this faith to the apostles, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 18). He said “in the name,” not “in the names,” so that where there is one power, one authority, one divinity, one eternity, one glory, one omnipotence, one blessedness, one operation, and one nature, there might also be the integrity of one name.

For nothing is divided in the Godhead, although the distinct property of the persons is marked by a clear distinction. Therefore, all that the Trinity is remains consubstantial and undivided divinity.

This faith, which I have briefly set forth and which accords with prophetic and apostolic teaching, was explained at greater length by the assertion of the Fathers mentioned above, when either the opposition of the attacking heretics was refuted or the authority of sound doctrines was effectively declared.

The praiseworthy confession written by the four aforementioned synods, and by the letters of our blessed predecessors composed concerning the integrity of the faith, also contains this faith. It is shown to be wholly like the teaching of the see of the first of the apostles and discordant with it in no respect.

Therefore, we condemn as heretics all who contradict this faith or anything that was defined by our holy Fathers in the four councils mentioned above: namely, Arius, Macedonius, Eunomius, together with their doctrines, and all who have agreed or agree with their error.

We also anathematize Paul of Samosata, Photinus, Bonosus, and Nestorius, together with their impious teachings, and all who have at any time given or give assent to their blasphemies.

Likewise, we anathematize Valentinus, Manichaeus, Apollinaris, and Eutyches, together with Dioscorus, their defender, and with their execrable opinions and preachings; and all who remained entangled in their errors until the day of their death.

But if we have omitted any heretics by name, we condemn, reject, and repudiate, together with their own errors, all who have been polluted by any error and have remained in it until their end.

We preserve, through the operation of the Lord’s grace, only the Catholic faith which the apostles handed down, which the four holy councils mentioned above received, and which their successors, through their expositions, have transmitted inviolate down to our own times.

And since no Christian ought to remain uncertain about knowledge of events that have taken place up to the present day, we also recount in a similar manner what happened after the addition of so extensive an account.

Yesterday—that is, on the Sunday which fell on the day before the Nones of February [Note: 5 February 552]—the magnificent man Peter the referendary returned to us with instructions from the most clement prince. He said: “When do you wish the judges to come and administer oaths to you, so that you may leave this church in which you are residing and return safely to the imperial city?”

We answered him publicly as follows: “Through the illustrious judges of the palace, as we said above, when your Magnificence came with them to Saint Euphemia, we gave the instructions stated earlier; and now through you we again say that these matters should be communicated to the most clement prince.

“We departed from our city seven years ago [Note: 22 November 549] in order to hasten to your piety without any private business. Now also we suggest and ask, for the sake of the peace which God formerly granted to the Church through your piety, that you not allow it to be disturbed further by anyone’s insinuations, nor permit Theodore, the author of the entire scandal, to harass the Catholic faith any longer.

“For six months ago he was deprived by us, together with others, of sacred communion and was deposed from the episcopate because of his depravity—by the document which, out of regard for your gentleness and in the hope of his conversion, we have, as stated, delayed publicly producing.

“We also make this known to his ears through your Magnificence: concerning the Church’s case, we cannot give any answer through you, because you profess that you cannot communicate to his clemency certain things that we tell you to report.

“Therefore, if he deigns to send two judges, whose names we have just disclosed to you, and to administer oaths, so that thereafter, without fear of danger, he may receive in our place our brother Dacius, bishop of the Church of Milan, or others whom we send with him, we are prepared to dispatch them, so that through them all that we have commanded concerning the Church’s case may be truthfully made known.

“We do not demand that any oaths be given to us on account of the Church’s case. Rather, we immediately hasten to give thanks to his piety, since, with God’s help, nothing except the scandal frightens us from continuing to remain in the basilica of Saint Euphemia.

“For we beseech our God and desire with unwearied prayers that, through him, the peace which he himself brought to the Church in the days of his uncle of pious memory may be restored after the dissension has been removed [Note: Under the emperor Justin, in the year 519].

“For if any further delay occurs, we must settle the matter by every means. We place neither our relatives, nor other family members, nor any property whatsoever above the judgment of our soul or that of the most pious prince.”

Given on the Nones of February, while our lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus, was reigning, in the twenty-fifth year, in the year after the consulship of Basil, the most illustrious man, year 10 [Note: “Year 11” should be read in place of “year 10”; the fact that Justinian’s twenty-fifth year coincides with the month of February makes this clear. Accordingly, this encyclical was issued in the year of Christ 552.] (A.D. 551).

[Note.]

Theodore, bishop of Caesarea, with intolerable audacity and impudence, relying on the emperor’s favor and power, deposed Zoilus, bishop of Alexandria, because he refused to condemn the Three Chapters, and substituted Apollinaris in his place, as Liberatus records in chapter 23 of his *Breviary*. He despised Vigilius, the Roman pontiff, who opposed him so that he would not consent to the emperor’s edict; and, although Vigilius forbade him, he dared to celebrate Mass and commit many other intolerable acts.

For these crimes Vigilius, with unbroken strength of mind and truly apostolic spirit, although he was in foreign territory, summoned whatever Latin bishops he could and pronounced against Theodore this most severe sentence of excommunication and deposition at Constantinople, in the church of Saint Peter, to which he had fled in fear of the violence of the emperor’s officials, as is clear from the encyclical letter written to the universal Church.

After this had happened, someone struck him in the face at Constantinople, as Anastasius relates in the *Life of Vigilius*, saying: “Murderer, do you not know what you are saying?” and so forth.

Wishing to be safe from the violence of the sacrilegious emperor, he fled across to Chalcedon and decided to live there with his followers in the church of Saint Euphemia.

From that place he wrote the following circular letter to the universal Church, from which the events that followed are known with certainty. See how great was the power and force of the chair of Peter. Justinian, compelled by the authority of Pope Vigilius, ordered the edicts concerning the Three Chapters that had been promulgated and posted to be removed, and ordered that nothing concerning them be disputed before a general synod.

Theodore, the author of all the evils, repentant and humble, presented a supplicatory petition to the pontiff, in which he professed the right faith, approved the four holy ecumenical councils, postponed the controversy about the Three Chapters—which he himself had provoked—to the decision of the council, and asked pardon for the injuries and insults directed against the innocent pontiff.

Mennas, bishop of Constantinople, did the same. When Vigilius had received both of them into repentance and into the communion of the Church, peace was restored to the Church.

These matters are taken from the decree of Pope Vigilius, which we append here.

Baronius, years 551 and 552. Severus Binius.

## Fragment of the condemnation of Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, issued by blessed Pope Vigilius

Theodore, bishop, is deprived of the priesthood and communion. The bishop of Constantinople and the other bishops conscious of that crime are excommunicated.

[Col. 0059C]

Vigilius, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, said:

It is indeed in accordance with the divine command to show patience toward sinners, but patience ought not to be extended so far that, through the hope of continuous impunity, sin is committed continually without correction. [Cod. Luc.: *ad hucusque* for *adusque*.]

Therefore, Theodore, bishop of the city of Caesarea in Cappadocia, since from the time of your ordination you have not endured remaining for even a year in the Church whose helm you had undertaken, but, abusing the authority of your episcopal name, have not ceased generating scandals throughout the universal Church [Cod. Luc.: *universali* for *universalis*]; and since, now admonished by us familiarly, now entreated by prayers, sometimes corrected by fraternal reproof, and often warned by the authority of the divine Scriptures or convicted by examples of ecclesiastical custom, you have always promised improvement in words but rejected it in your most wicked deeds, you have never ceased from your perverse intention.

We, however, have shown our long-suffering, granted by divine generosity, both toward you and toward those whom you led astray, during nearly five years now elapsed.

First, we showed it in this: in order to restrain the scandal, we accommodated ourselves to the minds of certain people whom we believed should be moderated by some measure of dispensation [or: “dissipation”; the reading is uncertain], because you, as an extremely restless agitator, had inflamed them for several years. For the time being we judged that certain things should be arranged medicinally, on the condition that, once every disturbance had been put to rest thereafter, no one should presume to do anything further in that matter, either in word or in writing.

But you, driven by the audacity of your perverse habit, did not then wish to cease composing or preaching novelties. Thus, after the bishops’ petitions had often been delivered, and after condemning your agreement with them by your own confession, you had repeatedly asked us to grant pardon for their excesses or for your own.

After this, when neither shame from human modesty, nor the burden of the priesthood, nor fear of divine judgment restrained you from your accustomed presumption, and when we extended patience to your crimes beyond what was just, the matter was brought to the point that, with everything that had been arranged by anyone in word or writing concerning the Three Chapters set aside [Cod. Luc.: “concerning the questions of the Three Chapters, how by …,” etc.], we might discuss in an assembled synod of the African, Illyrian [Cod. Luc.: *Iliarum*], or other regions [reading uncertain: “Gallican regions”] what ought to be done about the matter itself, requiring above all the presence of those whose fraternity had been scandalized.

We also agreed at length with the most clement prince, in the presence of Mennas, bishop of the city of Constantinople, Dacius, bishop of the city of Milan, and other Greek and Latin bishops—with all of whom you too, Father Theodore, were present—as well as in the presence of the judges, officials, and the entire senate, that no one should attempt [Cod. Luc.: “should try”] to do anything concerning the aforementioned Three Chapters until the stated decision of the council.

Then, in accordance with your custom and at your instigation, a document containing the condemnation of those Chapters was freely read in the palace, while you were present and instructing the proceedings, before certain Greek bishops, from whom you demanded the favor of their support through your words.

As a result, both you and the bishops who agreed with you, although rebuked by us more mildly than was fitting, hastened to obtain pardon through a pretended satisfaction.

Who could sufficiently recount the evils committed at your instigation and under your direction? To mention only a few of your great excesses: you were the instigator and source of the entire scandal and sedition. Sitting at home, hiring copyists at a high price, you wrote down the things which you had repeatedly confirmed under oath that you would not do before the appointed time; and under the pretext of religion you perpetrated things that divided the Church of God, as is also recognized from the events themselves.

You brought the mind of the most Christian prince to such a point through false suggestions that his clemency—which had always appeared merciful even toward his enemies—was gravely stirred against us.

But your restless mind so scattered all our good desires, which unquestionably labored for the peace of the Church, that matters which ought to have been reserved for fraternal discussion and the peaceful judgment of bishops were suddenly condemned according to your decision, contrary to ecclesiastical custom, contrary to the traditions of the Fathers, and contrary to all the authority of evangelical and apostolic teaching, through the posting of edicts.

No believer is unaware through whom our Lord and God commanded his people to be instructed in heavenly doctrines, or to whom he gave on earth the power of binding and loosing.

Then, in the house of Pacidiana, you met with the bishops of the Greek or Latin regions [variant: “other regions”] who were present in the imperial city, and with the priests and deacons of the Church of Constantinople. There, amid loud protest, both we and our brother, the bishop of Milan, forbade all of you to give assent to the violation of the common decree, despising fraternity.

But you disregarded, through us, the authority of the apostolic see that was forbidding you. You dragged the others with you to the church in which those edicts were hanging, went there, and, adding other violations, celebrated the solemn rites of the Mass [reading in one manuscript: “you celebrated”].

And as though it were not enough for you to have despised the bishop of the first see while he was present and objecting, you also removed from the diptychs our brother Zoilus, priest of the Church of Alexandria, whose name had been included in your commemoration until that very day, and joined to yourselves a certain Apollinaris, a perverse man and adulterer of that very Church. Thus your wickedness was made evident not only in removing the most innocent priest but also in receiving the perverse man.

For the moment we pass over other acts which you are shown to have committed on that same day to the injury of the apostolic see and of the canons, lest, detained by the enumeration of the offenses whose inventor [variant: “author and instigator”] you are shown to have been, we postpone for too long what properly concerns you.

Although thirty days earlier we had removed you from participation in the communion of the apostolic see because of your aforementioned excesses, believing that, in keeping with your priestly purpose, you would more readily correct what had been done wrongly through suitable satisfaction, nevertheless, in the name and by the authority of blessed Peter the apostle, whose place we occupy, although unworthy, together with Dacius of Milan, John of Marsica, Zacchaeus of Scyllacium, Valentinus of Silva Candida, Florentius of Matelica, Julian of Signia [Cod. Luc.: *Cinglano*; perhaps *Cingulano*], Romulus of Numana, Dominicus of Calliopolis, Primasius of Hadrumetum, Verecundus of Luna [variant: “of Junca”], Stephen of Rimini, Paschasius of Aletrium, and Jordan of Croton, our brothers and fellow bishops, we decree by the promulgation of this sentence that Theodore, formerly bishop of the city of Caesarea in Cappadocia, is deprived alike of priestly honor and Catholic communion and of every episcopal office and authority.

We judge that you are to be occupied henceforth with nothing except tears of repentance, by which, once remission of your offenses has been obtained, you may receive your place and communion, either from me or, after my death, from my successor—if you should deserve it—as an act of indulgence.

And you, Mennas, bishop of the city of Constantinople, who are bound by no dissimilar guilt, together with all the metropolitan and suffragan bishops belonging to your diocese, and also your Eastern bishops [Cod. Luc.: “you”] and the bishops of the major and minor cities of the various provinces who gave assent to these excesses for which we condemned Theodore, formerly bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, we suspend from sacred communion by a more merciful sentence, out of regard for God, until each of you, recognizing the error of your violation, has cleansed your own guilt before us through suitable satisfaction.

This is the subscription of the holy pope:

With God’s help and by his grace, I, Vigilius, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, have subscribed this condemnation and excommunication of Theodore, formerly bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, and of Mennas, bishop of the city of Constantinople, and of the others who communicated with him [variant: “this excommunication”].

Given on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September, while our lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus, was reigning, in the twenty-fifth year, in the eleventh year after the consulship of Basil, the most illustrious man [10] (A.D. 551).

# Letter of Eutychius to Vigilius

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0063]

To the most holy and most blessed lord, brother and fellow-minister Vigilius: Eutychius.

Having seen how many blessings the peace of God brings about—guarding the hearts and thoughts of the faithful, gathering them so that they may think one and the same thing in the confession of the right faith and in the fulfillment of the divine commandments, and making God favorable to those who agree in what is right—for this reason, eager to preserve unity, we make it clear to the apostolic see of your blessedness that we have always guarded, and do guard, the faith originally handed down by the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ to the holy apostles, proclaimed by them throughout the whole world, clarified by the holy Fathers, and especially by those who assembled in the four holy councils. We follow and receive them always and in all things: namely, the 318 holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea, set forth the holy creed, or lesson of faith, and anathematized the madness of Arius and those who have thought or think as he did.

We also receive the 100 holy Fathers who assembled at Constantinople. They clarified the same holy lesson, made clear the matters concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit, and condemned the heresy of Macedonius, the fighter against the Spirit, and the impious Apollinaris, together with those who have thought or think as they did.

We also receive the 200 holy Fathers assembled at the First Council of Ephesus. They followed in every respect the same holy creed, or lesson, and condemned the impious Nestorius and his filthy doctrines, together with those who at any time have thought or think similarly to him.

In addition, we receive the 630 holy Fathers assembled at Chalcedon. They too agreed in every respect with the three councils mentioned above and followed the aforementioned creed, or lesson, set forth by the holy Fathers and clarified by the 150 holy Fathers.

They anathematized those who dare to teach, set forth, or hand over to the holy churches of God anything other than the creed that has been stated. They also condemned and anathematized Eutyches and Nestorius, their impious doctrines, and those who have thought or think similarly to them.

Since these things stand thus, we make it clear that we have guarded and do guard everything judged and defined by the four holy councils mentioned above. For although the four holy councils took place at different times, they nevertheless guarded and proclaimed one and the same confession of faith.

We also receive and embrace the letters of the presidents of the apostolic see at Rome, both those of the others and those of Leo of holy memory, written concerning the right faith, concerning the four holy councils or one of them.

Since, then, we have guarded and do guard all the things mentioned above, and since in these matters we agree with one another, it is necessary to discuss the Three Chapters, concerning which a dispute has arisen for some people.

Therefore we ask that, with your blessedness presiding over us, calmly and with priestly gentleness, with the holy Gospels placed before us, those same Chapters be brought forward in a common discussion, investigated and compared, and that a conclusion pleasing to God and consistent with what was defined by the four holy councils be placed upon the inquiry.

For this contributes to the increase of peace and to the concord of the Churches: when all dissension has been removed, the definitions of the four holy councils may be preserved unshaken, while reverence for the holy councils is maintained in every respect.

To these matters we have also subscribed.

And the subscription:

Be strong in the Lord, most holy and most blessed brother, and pray earnestly for us.

I, Eutychius, by the mercy of God bishop of Constantinople, New Rome, have subscribed to all the foregoing.

[Note.]

The same petition was also written by Apollinaris, the most holy archbishop of the great city of Alexandria, and by Domninus, the most holy archbishop of Theopolis, and by the most God-loving bishops under them, who were also present in this imperial city, to the same most holy Vigilius.

[Col. 0064A] He professes the Catholic faith and agrees that the question of the Three Chapters should be settled in a council.

To the most holy and most blessed lord and fellow priest Vigilius: Eutychius.

Knowing how many blessings the peace of God brings about, guarding the hearts and thoughts of the faithful, gathering them so that they may think one and the same thing in the confession of the right faith and in fulfilling the divine commandments, and making God propitious to those who agree in what is right, we therefore hasten to preserve unity.

To the apostolic see of your blessedness we make it clear that we have always guarded and do guard the faith handed down from the beginning by the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ to the holy apostles, proclaimed by them throughout the whole world, explained by the holy Fathers, and especially by those who assembled in the four holy synods. We embrace and receive them in every respect and in all things.

That is, we receive the 318 holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea, set forth the holy creed, or lesson of faith, anathematized the impiety of Arius, and anathematized those who have thought or think similarly to him [Note: Bellovacensis: “who have thought or think differently from him.”]

We also receive the 150 holy Fathers assembled at Constantinople, who explained the same holy lesson, clarified the divinity of the Holy Spirit, and condemned the Macedonian heresy, which attacks the Holy Spirit, and the impious Apollinaris, together with those who have thought or think similarly to them.

We also receive the 200 holy Fathers assembled at the First Council of Ephesus, who followed in every respect the same holy creed, or lesson, and condemned the impious Nestorius, his impious doctrines, and those who at any time have thought or think similarly to him.

In addition, we receive the 630 holy Fathers assembled at Chalcedon, who likewise agreed in every respect with the three synods mentioned above [Paris: “the aforementioned three synods”] and followed the aforementioned creed, or lesson, set forth by the 318 holy Fathers and explained by the 150 holy Fathers.

They anathematized those who presume to teach, set forth, or hand over to the holy churches of God anything other than the aforementioned creed [Note: Older books: “to the churches of God”]. They also condemned and anathematized Eutyches and Nestorius, their impious doctrines, and those who have thought or think similarly to them.

Since these things stand thus, we make it certain that we have guarded and do guard all that was judged and defined by the four holy synods mentioned above [Note: The word “four” is absent from the Bellovacensis manuscript]. For although the aforementioned four holy synods were held at different times, they nevertheless guarded and proclaimed one and the same confession of faith.

We also receive and embrace the letters of the bishops of the apostolic see of Rome [Paris: “of the see and apostolic”], both those of the others and those of Leo of holy memory, written concerning the right faith and concerning the four holy councils or one of them.

Since, then, we have guarded and do guard all the foregoing, and since in these matters we agree with one another [Bellovacensis: “and if in these very things we agree among ourselves”], it is necessary to discuss the Three Chapters, concerning which a dispute has arisen for certain people.

Therefore we ask that, with your blessedness presiding over us, calmly and with priestly gentleness, with the holy Gospels placed before us, those same Chapters be brought forward in a common discussion, investigated and preserved [Paris: “confessed”; Bellovacensis and all editions before Labbe: “compared”], and that a conclusion pleasing to God and consistent with what was defined by the four holy councils be placed upon the inquiry [Paris: “a conclusion pleasing,” feminine].

For this contributes to the increase of peace and to the concord of the Churches: when all dissension has been removed, the definitions of the four holy councils may be preserved unshaken, while reverence for the holy synods is maintained in every respect.

To these matters I have also subscribed, in soundness in the Lord. Pray for us, most holy and most blessed brother.

I, Eutychius, by the mercy of God bishop of Constantinople, New Rome, have subscribed to all the foregoing.

[Note.]

The same petition was written by Apollinaris, the most holy archbishop of the great city of Alexandria, and by Domninus, the most holy archbishop of Theopolis, and by the most God-loving bishops under them, who were also present in this imperial city, to the same most holy Vigilius.

# Letter, formerly XVI, of Pope Vigilius to Eutychius

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0065]

To the beloved brother Eutychius and to the bishops under your authority: Vigilius.

“Our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation” (Psalm 125), because, once the confusion of dissension had been removed, God restored peace to his Church, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one” (Psalm 132).

For it is very fitting that we exult in the Lord, because a written declaration of your love has been presented to us [Greek correction: *hēmin*, “to us,” for *hēmōn*], whose substance is as follows.

[Here the preceding letter of Eutychius is inserted; the subscription here is fuller by several words, as in the Latin edition.]

To these matters we have also subscribed. Having gladly embraced the brightness of this orthodox confession, accepting the same things in every respect and in all things, we profess, with our God going before us, that we will guard and preserve them blamelessly and inviolably.

Since, therefore, everything contained in your confession remains permanently in its proper force, your fraternity requested that, with us presiding, the Three Chapters, concerning which a dispute has arisen, be compared calmly and with priestly gentleness, with the holy Gospels placed before us, and that a conclusion pleasing to God and consistent with what was defined by the four holy councils be placed upon the inquiry.

Thus, when every dissension has been removed, the definitions of the four holy councils may be preserved unshaken, while reverence for those councils is maintained in every respect.

We judge this confession, which recalls the traditions of the Fathers and follows them, to be filled with every praise—both in your fraternity and in all who have confessed and do confess the same things—and by the matter itself we truly recognize them as our brothers.

Therefore we beseech the loving-kindness of God that all of us, remaining steadfast in this confession and in the traditions of the Fathers, may be found worthy of our profession and may not be found liable, on the day of divine judgment, for any violation of the regulations of the Fathers.

Since these matters have been said, and recognizing the longing expressed in your request, we have assented: that, concerning the Three Chapters over which a dispute has arisen, a canonical council should be held, and, with justice preserved in the matter and the holy Gospels placed before us, we should conduct a comparison together with the brothers united with us, and that a conclusion pleasing to God and consistent with what was defined by the four holy councils should be given.

For we know—as the testimony of the common confession also shows—that reverence for the four councils mentioned is preserved in every respect.

Subscription:

May God preserve you in health, most honorable brother.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of January, in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of our lord Justinian, eternal Augustus, and in the twelfth year after the consulship of Basil, the most illustrious man.

[Note.]

In the same form he also wrote to Apollinaris, the most holy archbishop of the great city of Alexandria, and to Domninus, the most holy archbishop of Theopolis, and to their synod.

[Col. 0066B] He commends his faith and agrees that the matter of the Three Chapters should be treated in a council.

To the most beloved brother Eutychius and to the bishops established under you: Vigilius.

Our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation [Note: Bellovacensis: “our tongues”] (Psalm 125), because, every source of discord having been removed, God has restored peace to his Church, so that what was said might be fulfilled [Note: Older books: “written”]: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity” (Psalm 132). For it is altogether fitting that we rejoice in the Lord, since a written profession from your Charity has been presented to us, whose wording is as follows [Note: Paris: “is thus”]: “Knowing how many blessings are caused by the peace of God, which guards the hearts and thoughts of the faithful and gathers them together so that they may hold one and the same understanding in the right confession of faith,” and so forth.

To this we too subscribed, gladly embracing the clarity of this orthodox profession, and, approving it in every respect and in all its particulars, we profess [Note: Read: “we profess.” This is a typographical error in the edition of Labbe, corrected here.] that, with God as our author, we will guard and inviolably preserve it [we profess]. Since, therefore, everything contained in your profession was to remain permanently firm, your Fraternity requested that, while we presided, the matter of the Three Chapters, from which the controversy had arisen, should be discussed with priestly tranquility and gentleness, with the holy Gospels set before us [Col. 0066D] [Note: Bellovacensis: “placed before us”], and that an end pleasing to God and consistent with what had been defined by the aforesaid four holy councils should be imposed upon the controversy itself; so that, all dissension being removed, [Col. 0068A] what had been defined by those same four holy synods might be preserved unshaken, with reverence for those synods maintained in every respect.

We judged this profession, mindful of and faithful to the traditions of the Fathers, both in your Fraternity and in all who have confessed and confess similarly, to be altogether worthy of praise [Note: Older books: “we judge”], and we recognize them on this account as our true brothers [Note: The same books: “true,” not “truly”]. Therefore we beseech the divine mercy that, as we all remain in this confession and in the traditions of the Fathers [Note: The same books: “and in the traditions of the Fathers”], we may be found worthy of our office, and that on the day of divine judgment we may be found liable to no violation of the constitutions of the Fathers.

When we had learned of your desire through the requests stated above [your request], we gave our assent: namely, that, when a regular assembly had been convened concerning the Three Chapters from which the controversy had arisen, equity being preserved, we should hold a conference with the united brothers in the presence of the holy Gospels, and that an end pleasing to God and consistent with what had been defined by the four holy councils should be granted [perhaps: “that you should hold a conference”]; for we know, as the testimony of our common profession also makes clear, that reverence for the aforesaid synods is maintained in every respect.

May God preserve you in safety, dearest brother. Given on the eighth [seventh] day before the Ides of January, in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of our lord Justinian, the perpetual Augustus, and in the twelfth year after the consulship of Basil, the most illustrious man.

[NOTE.]

In the same form he also wrote to Apollinarius, the most holy archbishop of the great city of Alexandria, and to Domninus, the most holy archbishop of Theoupolis, and to the synod subject to them.

## Vigilius the Pope’s Constitutum concerning the Three Chapters (C)

[Col. 0067C]

To the most glorious and merciful son, Justinian Augustus, Vigilius, bishop.

Amid the countless anxieties by which the imperial dignity is burdened, we have recognized as praiseworthy the purpose of Your Clemency: namely, that, after removing all the seeds of discord which the enemy of the human race had scattered in the field of the Lord, you hastened to restore all the Lord’s priests to unity and concord, after first requiring them to submit professions as testimony to their consciences—professions by which they would be shown to adhere to the definitions and judgments of the holy Fathers, of the venerable four synods, and of the bishops of the Apostolic See. We set forth here, inserted in the present page just as it stands, the form of those professions, so that it may be handed down to posterity as an example to be embraced for ecclesiastical peace. [Col. 0067D]

### Copy of the first profession which they made at the church of Saint Euphemia

All the faithful, and especially the priests of God, ought to pursue peace and sanctification with everyone, without which, according to the Apostle (1 Thessalonians 4), no one will see the Lord. Therefore, following the apostolic teaching and hastening to preserve ecclesiastical concord, we present this document.

First, we accept the four holy synods: the Nicene synod of 318 Fathers; the Constantinopolitan synod of 150; the First Ephesian synod of 200, at which, through his legates and representatives—that is, the most blessed Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria, the bishops Arcadius and Projectus, and the presbyter Philip—the most blessed Pope Celestine of elder Rome is known to have presided; and the Chalcedonian synod of 630 holy Fathers.

In every respect and in all their particulars, whatever was defined, judged, established, or arranged by common agreement with the legates and representatives of the Apostolic See in all the acts of the Council of Chalcedon and of the other aforesaid synods, as it is found written in those same four synods—at which, according to their respective times, the predecessors of Your Holiness, the most blessed popes of elder Rome, presided together with the synods’ legates and representatives—whether concerning the faith or concerning all other matters, judgments, constitutions, or arrangements, we promise to follow without wavering, inviolably, irreproachably, and irrevocably, without any addition or diminution. We will admit nothing contrary to them that might, under any pretext or innovation, pertain to their censure, retraction, alteration, or injury; nor will we consent to anyone presuming to do such a thing. [Col. 0069A] Rather, whatever was said there by common agreement with the orthodox legates and representatives of the Apostolic See, that we venerate and accept as orthodox.

Whatever they anathematized or condemned, we too anathematize and condemn. Everything found to have been judged, defined, established, or arranged by those same synods in common agreement with the representatives of the Apostolic See, we preserve irrevocably and unalterably.

We also promise to follow and preserve in every respect the letters of Pope Leo of blessed memory and the constitutions of the Apostolic See which have proceeded both concerning the faith and concerning the firmness of the aforesaid four synods.

We anathematize every person belonging to the orders and dignities of the Church who attempts, under any pretext or dispute, to act against what we have promised above. As for the document concerning the Three Chapters, over which the controversy has arisen, contrary to the constitutum of the most pious prince and of Your Holiness, I myself have composed none; but I wish and consent that all the documents which have been composed in this form be returned to Your Holiness.

As for whatever injuries have been inflicted upon Your Holiness or your See, I did not inflict them; but because one must hasten by every means toward the peace of the Church, I ask pardon for them as though I had inflicted them. Furthermore, because during the time of discord I received into communion persons who had been excommunicated or not received by Your Holiness, I likewise ask pardon.

In this form made their professions Mennas, bishop of Constantinople; Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia; Andreas, bishop of Ephesus; Theodore, bishop of Antioch in Pisidia; and Peter, bishop of Tarsus. Many other bishops did the same.

### Copy of the profession which the remaining bishops made to us on the day of the Epiphany

Knowing how many blessings are caused by the peace of God, which guards the hearts and thoughts of the faithful, gathers them together so that they may hold one and the same understanding in the right confession of faith, leads them to fulfill the divine commandments, and renders God propitious toward those who agree in what is right, we therefore hasten to preserve unity and make known to the Apostolic See of Your Holiness that we have always preserved, and continue to preserve, the faith handed down from the beginning by the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ to the holy apostles, preached by them throughout the whole world [Col. 0069D], and expounded by the holy Fathers—especially by those who assembled in the four holy synods. In every respect and in all their particulars we follow and accept them: namely, the 318 holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea, expounded the holy creed or statement of faith, anathematized the impiety of Arius, and those who have held or hold the same views.

We also accept the 150 holy Fathers who assembled at Constantinople, who further explained the same holy statement of faith, clarified the deity of the Holy Spirit, and condemned the Macedonian heresy that opposed the Holy Spirit, as well as the impious Apollinarius, together with those who held or hold the same views as they did. [Col. 0070A]

We also accept the 200 holy Fathers assembled at the First Synod of Ephesus, who followed in every respect the same holy creed or statement of faith, and condemned the impious Nestorius, his wicked doctrines, and those who at any time held or hold views similar to his.

In addition, we accept the 630 holy Fathers assembled at Chalcedon. They too agreed in every respect with the three aforesaid holy synods and followed the aforesaid creed or statement of faith expounded by the 318 holy Fathers and explained by the 150 holy Fathers. They anathematized those who presume to teach, expound, or hand on to the holy churches of God anything other than the aforesaid creed. They also condemned and anathematized Eutyches and Nestorius, their impious doctrines, and those who held or hold views similar to theirs. [Col. 0070B]

Since these things stand thus, we make it certain that we preserve everything judged and defined by the aforesaid four holy synods; for although the aforesaid four holy synods were held at different times, nevertheless they preserved and preached one and the same confession of faith.

We also accept and embrace the letters of the bishops of the Apostolic See of Rome, both those of other bishops and those of Leo of holy memory, written concerning the right faith, and concerning the four holy councils or any one of them.

Since, therefore, we have both preserved and continue to preserve all the aforesaid matters, and agree with one another concerning them, it is necessary to confer [confess] concerning the Three Chapters, over which a controversy has arisen for certain persons. Therefore we ask that, with Your Holiness presiding over us, in tranquility and priestly gentleness, with the holy Gospels set before us, the same chapters be brought forward for common discussion, examined, and considered, and that an end be imposed upon the controversy—an end pleasing to God and consistent with what was defined by the four holy councils. For it pertains to the increase of peace and the concord of the Churches that, all dissension being removed, what was defined by the aforesaid four holy councils should be preserved unshaken, with reverence for the holy synods maintained in every respect.

To this we, your brothers and fellow bishops, also subscribed in the following manner.

Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople; Apollinarius, bishop of Alexandria; Domninus [Domnus] [Col. 0070D], bishop of Antioch in Syria; Elias, bishop of Thessalonica; and the other bishops who had not made the first profession but either subscribed to this second profession or made the same profession separately.

When these arrangements had been made, we indeed desired, venerable Emperor—as we very frequently requested in humble prayer—to go to some place in Italy, or at least to Sicily, and, after summoning to us the priests of the African provinces and of the other Latin-speaking provinces, or the ordained clergy of our own Church, to deliberate according to custom and return to Your Piety a fully considered answer concerning the controversies over the Three Chapters.

Since Your Serenity did not consent that this be done, it was then established that, after we had submitted to Your Gentleness the names of bishops from the aforesaid provinces who were to be brought in with us for deliberation, Your Clemency should cause them to come. To this arrangement also we gave our assent, out of love for ecclesiastical peace.

Afterward, very recently, before the holy day of Easter, Your Piety determined—again with the agreement of our brothers, the bishops of our regions—that, with the number of those bishops made equal to that of the bishops presently in the city of Constantinople, we should begin a discussion concerning the Three Chapters over which the controversy turns, according to the profession of our brother bishops set out above.

But while we were hastening to fulfill what, by Your arrangement, had been agreed upon with our brothers concerning what was to be done for the preservation of the peace of the Churches [Col. 0071B], so that, after a sound deliberation had been held jointly and all the proceedings between us had been committed to writing and set forth, our judgment concerning the Three Chapters brought into question might emerge from these materials, Your Piety immediately, after that volume which you had sent us many days before Easter through the magnificent Theodore, a decurion of the palace—in which you explained what you meanwhile thought concerning the Three Chapters—requested that we give an answer on the same matter. [Note: Perhaps: “Your Piety produced that document.” Hardouin.]

Therefore, since our brothers would neither sit with us in equal numbers nor permit what we were doing or discussing to be committed to writing, as though—God forbid—we were speaking things inconsistent with rectitude and were afraid to write them [Col. 0071C]; and since, in addition, Your Clemency persisted, after sending the most glorious nobles to us, that we ought to produce our answer concerning the affair of the Three Chapters as quickly as possible, we nevertheless did not cease desiring to obey Your Clemency.

We asked only that, in view of the weakness of our body, which is unknown to no one, you grant us a postponement of twenty days, so that, after discussion had been held with us, with God’s help, we might pronounce our judgment on the appointed day, once our definition had been written.

We sent our son, the deacon Pelagius, to our brothers and fellow bishops, from whom, as you said, you likewise demanded an answer on the same matter, with the following instruction: Since the established procedure for holding a conference had been set aside, they ought at least to await for twenty days, on account of the aforementioned weakness of our body, which they knew, our definitive answer concerning the Three Chapters. They were to preserve the ancient and regular order, so that before the promulgation of the judgment of our See—that is, of the Apostolic See over which, by God’s grace, we preside—they would not attempt to issue anything from which an occasion for renewed scandal might arise, though that scandal had been put to rest.

Accordingly, after the matters had been placed before us and carefully examined insofar as the nature of each chapter brought into question required, and after the synodal books and acts had been produced—documents which some of those same Fathers are shown to have answered in writing [variant: “sat”] either in the four holy synods or in one of them—and after the synodal letters had been examined, we nevertheless also considered the constitutions of our predecessors, the bishops of the Apostolic See, and the other necessary instructions of approved Fathers.

If any of the matters brought into question had been examined, concluded, and settled by our Fathers, we took care to investigate them, mindful of the professions specified above. Examining certain doctrines lying in the first part of a parchment volume sent from Your side through our brother Benignus, bishop of Heraclea in Paphlagonia, we found that their wording, according to the interpretation set out below, had to be inserted into the present definition in order to exclude every error of ambiguity. We perceived them to be filled with utterly detestable blasphemies and exceedingly hostile to the orthodox faith—which, according to the evangelical and apostolic teaching, is read as having been defined credibly and irreproachably by the four holy synods, Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon, with the cooperating presence of the Holy Spirit—and to be rejected far from Christian understanding. Therefore, as detestable doctrines, and as doctrines long ago condemned without hesitation by the holy Fathers, we too, by our judgment, anathematize and condemn them. The first chapter is as follows:

## Chapter I of Theodore

[Note: As in the Fifth Council, Session 4.]

How then do you say that the very one who was born from a virgin is God and is to be considered consubstantial with the Father, you whom, above all, it most befits to govern souls—unless, perhaps, you do not wish his creation to be attributed to the Holy Spirit?

But who is God from God and consubstantial with the Father? The same one who was born from a virgin—O astonishing claim!—and who, according to the divine Scriptures, was fashioned through the Holy Spirit and received his formation in a woman’s womb?

Perhaps he was present in him as soon as he had been fashioned, and he received him as a temple of God. Yet we must not consider God to have been born from a virgin, unless perhaps we must likewise consider that what was born, what is the temple in the one born, and God the Word who is in the temple are all the same. Nevertheless, not even according to your statement should it be proclaimed at all that God was born from a virgin and is consubstantial with the Father from God.

For if the one born from the virgin is not a man who was assumed—as you say—but God incarnate, how can the one who was born be called God from God and consubstantial with the Father, when flesh cannot receive this designation?

For it is indeed madness to say that God was born from a virgin. This means nothing other than saying that he was generated from David’s seed, from the substance of the virgin, and fashioned in her; for what is from David’s seed and from the substance of the virgin exists in the mother’s womb, and we say that, fashioned by the power of the Holy Spirit, it was born from the virgin.

Suppose, however, that someone grants them the right to say that God from God and consubstantial with the Father was born from the virgin because of the one born who is in the temple—but that God the Word himself was not born, only incarnate, as this wise man says.

If, then, they say that he was born together with the flesh, and that what was born is God from God and consubstantial with the Father, it is necessary also to call the flesh this. But if it is not flesh for this reason—because it is neither God from God nor consubstantial with the Father, but from the seed of David and consubstantial with the one whose seed it is—then it is not the case that what was born from the virgin is God, from God, and consubstantial with the Father.

Unless perhaps he means a part of the one born, just as below he calls the deity a part of Christ. But the divine nature was not born from the virgin. The one born from the virgin is constituted from the substance of the virgin; God the Word was not born from Mary. The one born from Mary is from David’s seed; God the Word was not born from a woman. Rather, the one fashioned in her by the power of the Holy Spirit was born from a woman.

He was not born from his mother consubstantial with the Father—for, according to the statement of the blessed Paul, he is without a mother—but the one who in later times was fashioned in the mother’s womb by the power of the Holy Spirit, and who for this reason is said to be without a father.

### Vigilius’ response

In the first chapter quoted above, it appears to be argued at length that a mere human being was born from the holy virgin Mary. The statement is made: “If we confess that God the Word, who is consubstantial with the Father, was born in the flesh from the same virgin, we must consequently say that the flesh too is consubstantial with the Father.”

Therefore, whoever holds, teaches, believes, or preaches such an understanding, and does not believe that the same Word and Son of God was incarnate and born through a second birth from holy Mary, let him be anathema.

## Chapter II of Theodore

[Col. 0073C] [Note: In the Fifth Council, Session 4, read the same excerpts from Theodore that appear here through Chapter XIII.]

Immediately, in the one who had been fashioned, God the Word became present. For he was present not only in the one ascending into heaven, but also in the one rising from the dead, since he also raised him according to his promise. Nor was he present only in the one rising, but also in the one who was crucified and baptized, who carried out the evangelical manner of life after baptism, who fulfilled the legal ordinance after baptism, who was presented according to the Law, circumcised, and wrapped in swaddling clothes.

Perhaps he was also in the one who was being born, and in the one who was in the womb from the very first fashioning. For he imposed order upon the dispensation concerning him, gradually bringing him to perfection.

## Chapter III of Theodore

Leading him in due course to baptism, afterward to death, then raising him according to his own declaration, leading him into heaven, and seating him at the right hand of God through his union with him—through which he both sits and is worshiped by all and will judge all—God the Word held the completion of all these things within himself while he was in him, and completed everything in due order.

He judged that this order was good through the determination and will which he had previously established concerning the things that were to occur; and, through the good will which he likewise had toward him from the beginning, he was present in him, while by an ordered purpose he led him toward perfection.

### Vigilius’ response

In the second and third chapters quoted above, it appears to be argued that God the Word was present in a fashioned man as one person in another. For the text says that he seemed gradually to impose order upon the dispensation concerning him and, because of the good will which he had toward him, to prepare and bring the one who had been assumed to an advance toward perfection.

By such expressions a duality of persons in the one Lord and our God Jesus Christ appears to be introduced in an utterly detestable manner, as though any human being had progressed through stages of time by the grace of God the Word.

Therefore, whoever holds, teaches, believes, or preaches this understanding, let him be anathema.

## Chapter IV of Theodore

He supplied his cooperation for the works proposed to the one who had been assumed. When he does this, it means that the faculty of perception was separate from the one who had been assumed; for he did not grant cooperation to just anyone, but the faculty of perception occupied his place.

And if even now he granted a particular kind of cooperation to the one who had been assumed, he did not do this by causing the faculty of perception to possess the place of the deity. But if the deity served as the faculty of perception for the one who had been assumed, according to your words, how did he receive fear during the Passion?

Why did he need more fervent prayers in the face of the impending necessity, prayers which, according to the blessed Paul (Hebrews 5), he offered to God with a great and loud voice and with many tears, while the Evangelist clearly says (Luke 22) that his sweat fell like clots resembling blood?

Why did he need the coming and visitation of an angel who restored his soul in the experience of evils, strengthened his eagerness, trained him for the impending necessity of the Passion, urged him to endure evils courageously, pressed him toward patience and endurance of suffering, and showed him the fruit of the present evils arising from the Passion and the change into future glory that would come to him after the Passion?

For the angel who strengthened him, as the Evangelist says (in the same passage), made him strong by these words, urged him to become superior to the weakness of nature, and, by strengthening his thoughts, made him strong.

### Vigilius’ response

In the fourth chapter quoted above, the meaning appears to be that, just as God granted his cooperation to other human beings, so it is said to have been granted to the one who had been assumed—although in a particular way, nevertheless in the same manner as to other human beings. Thus a mere and weak human being is said, in connection with the Passion, to have needed the protection of an angel, so that future glory might be promised to him for strengthening his thoughts through endurance of the Passion.

If anyone holds, teaches, believes, or preaches this, let him be anathema.

## Chapter V of Theodore

“Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me, because you do not think the things of God but the things of men” (Matthew 16; Mark 8). Death is not a disgrace to me; I do not flee from it as something unbecoming, looking toward human glory. I will endure the experience of death with a better spirit, for the sake of the many future blessings in which I too shall share, and for the sake of all, lest you injure or disturb my courage by urging me to flee from the experience of death as though it were something deserving disgrace.

### Vigilius’ response

In the fifth chapter quoted above it is said that Jesus Christ rejected the words of the apostle Peter when he said to him, “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me, because you do not think the things of God” (Matthew 16; Mark 8), so that Peter’s dissuasion would not disturb his mind and cause him to shrink from the Passion, and because through his Passion he would advance toward, and thereby obtain, many blessings.

Therefore, whoever holds, teaches, believes, or preaches this, and does not rather believe that by his own flesh he accepted death for us and bestowed the rewards of eternal life, let him be anathema.

## Chapter VI of Theodore

For what is said—“He was led by the Spirit” (Matthew 4)—clearly means that he was governed by the Spirit, strengthened by it for the virtues proposed, led by it toward the things that were necessary, taught by it what was fitting, and strengthened by it in his thoughts, so that he might be sufficient for the contest. As the blessed Paul says: “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Romans 8).

By saying that those are led by the Spirit who are governed by it, taught by it, established by it for what is better, and receive from it instruction suitable to them, the Evangelist, after saying that he returned from the Jordan full of the Holy Spirit, clearly demonstrated that for this reason he received the indwelling of the Holy Spirit at baptism: so that from it he might obtain the virtue he had set before him. Hence, for that contest which he was to undertake against the devil on our behalf, he was led by the Spirit.

### Vigilius’ response

In the sixth chapter quoted above, he is again presented as a mere human being, led in everything by the Spirit—whose presence he is said to have received after baptism—strengthened and taught just like other human beings, concerning whom, as the passage appears to say, the Apostle declares: “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Romans 8).

If anyone holds, teaches, believes, or preaches this, and does not believe, confess, and preach that Christ is one, God the Word incarnate, let him be anathema.

## Chapter VII of Theodore

Let the wisest of all tell us: if the deity had become, as they say, a substitute for the faculty of perception in the Lord Christ according to the flesh, why did Christ need the operation of the Holy Spirit for these things?

For the deity of the Only-Begotten did not need the Spirit for justification; it did not need the Spirit to conquer the devil; it did not need the Spirit to perform miracles; it did not need the Spirit in order to be taught what it was fitting to do; it did not need the Spirit in order to appear immaculate.

For if the deity was sufficient as a substitute for the faculty of perception, and its power was sufficient for all things, everything ought necessarily to have been accomplished through it, so that the indwelling of the Holy Spirit would have been superfluous.

But now he says that Christ was anointed with the Spirit, that the Spirit dwelt in him, that it aided him in all the tasks proposed, that from it he received teaching and power, that from it he obtained justification, and that from it he was made immaculate.

### Vigilius’ response

In the seventh chapter quoted above, the meaning is understood to be that, like other human beings, Christ needed the indwelling of the Holy Spirit for his justification, for conquering the devil, for performing miracles, for being taught what it was fitting for him to do, and for appearing immaculate; and that he was aided by that Spirit in all the tasks mentioned.

Whoever holds, teaches, believes, or preaches this, and does not believe that Christ, as true God, performed through his own deity everything he wished and will wish to perform, but says that, as a mere human being, he needed the assistance of the Holy Spirit, let him be anathema.

## Chapter VIII of Theodore

He says that what existed before the ages was made in the final times, as certain people confess this. Yet no one who cares for piety tolerates in him such a disease of madness as to say that the one who exists before the ages was made in the final times.

From this he infers that what exists in the final times must also exist before the ages, and he accuses those who do not say everything in the same way with reversal, as though those who confess one Son were obliged to say everything with reversal.

And who would not call your madness blessed? Who would not wish such teachers to be obtained—men who introduce such confusion into the reasoning of piety that they say that what exists before the ages was made in the final times, alienate this from its own nature, and bring it down to something inferior; and then reverse the statement, saying that what exists in the final times also exists before the ages?

Perhaps it would have been necessary to say that the one who existed before the ages assumed the one who existed in the final times, according to the statement of the blessed Paul (1 Timothy 4).

Following your laws, therefore, and accepting the reversal established by your wisdom—or rather, the subversion—let us confuse everything together at once. Let there now be no distinction between the form of God and the form of a servant; between the temple that was assumed and the one who dwelt in the temple; between the one who was released and the one who raised him; between the one who was perfected through sufferings and the one who perfected him; between the one who deserved remembrance and the one who was remembered; between the one who was visited and the one who visited; between the one who was made a little lower than the angels and the one who made him lower; between the one crowned with glory and honor and the one who crowned him; between the one appointed over the works of God’s hands and the one who appointed him; between the one who received these things for exaltation and the one who granted the exaltation.

### Vigilius’ response

In the eighth chapter quoted above, a duality of persons appears to be introduced in various ways by the statement: “It is not the same one who existed before the ages who should be said to have come in the final times,” as though the person who assumed humanity were one and the person assumed were another.

Therefore, if anyone holds, teaches, believes, or preaches this, and does not confess that the same God the Word, who was born from the Father before the ages, was incarnate and born in the final times from the blessed Virgin Mary, so that one and the same Christ exists in both natures, let him be anathema.

## Chapter IX of Theodore

When he had raised this man from the dead and shown him to be the judge of all for the faith of those to come, according to the statement of the blessed Paul (Acts 17), he deemed this man worthy of himself by a unity of merit [Note: In Session 4, “meritoriously.” Hardouin.]. Through the union made with him, he made him a participant in such things that he also shared in adoration: while all rendered to the divine nature the adoration due to it, they also comprehended in their adoration the one whom they know to be inseparably united with it.

From this it is clear that he brought him to greater things.

### Vigilius’ response

In the ninth chapter quoted above, by the use of the terms “union” and “participation,” as though a union of God with the human Christ had taken place, Christ is asserted to be adorned with divine works. Through this, once again, a duality of persons is introduced.

Therefore, if anyone holds, teaches, believes, or preaches this, and does not recognize and believe one and the same Christ, our God and Lord, while the distinct properties and differences of the natures remain in their proper integrity, let him be anathema.

## Chapter X of Theodore

“I, whom you see, can do nothing according to my nature, since I am a man; but I act because the Father, who remains in me, does everything.
