For I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14). God the Word, the Only-Begotten, is in me; it is certain that the Father also remains in me together with him and performs the works.

It is not surprising to hold these things concerning Christ, since he himself clearly says concerning other human beings: “Whoever loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (the same passage).

If both the Father and the Son make their dwelling with each one of such human beings, what should we think? Should both be regarded as dwelling together in the Lord according to the flesh of Christ, perhaps receiving their communion according to substance and also a communion of dwelling?

### Vigilius’ response

In the tenth chapter quoted above, God the Word is said to be present in the man Christ in the same way as the Father, so that either the Father too appears to have become incarnate, just as the Son did; or the Son too is not incarnate, just as the Father is not; or, rather, both dwell in the third person, the man.

Therefore, whoever holds, teaches, believes, or preaches this, let him be anathema.

## Chapter XI of Theodore
Thus also, having first accepted the soul as human and immortal and constituted as a participant in sensation, and having established it through the resurrection in incorruptibility, he likewise granted us, through the resurrection, participation in these same things. Before the resurrection from the dead, therefore, he rebukes Peter, as scandalizing his fellow disciples by his words [Col. 0078A]; and, placed in great fear during the time of the Passion, he requires the appearance of an angel to strengthen him for the endurance and tolerance of the evils impending. But after the resurrection from the dead and the ascent into heaven, having become impassible and wholly immutable, and sitting at the right hand of God, he is judge of the entire world, since it is the divine nature in him that exercises judgment.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the eleventh chapter quoted above, the same points seem to be repeated that were already stated earlier in the fourth: namely, that before the Passion Christ was so weak that, placed in great fear at the time of the Passion, he appeared to have needed the comfort of an angel. Since this seems to signify a mere human being who would require such assistance, whoever thinks, teaches, believes, or proclaims this way, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XII

Thus here also you teach us to understand Christ’s mind as possessing the greatest wisdom of all: he had the Holy Spirit, and the one who possessed Christ’s mind [or: “those having the mind of Christ”] fulfilled a certain power, supplying him with prudence for everything that had to be done. As we demonstrated in the preceding passages, he was led by that power into the wilderness for the contests against the devil; but from it he received his anointing, knowledge, and power for the things that had to be done. Having become a participant in it, he not only performed miracles but also knew precisely how miracles ought to be used, [Col. 0078C] so that he might make piety known to the nations, suffer the weaknesses of those who labored, and thus bring his will to fulfillment; and by this he was justified and shown to be undefiled, whether through the restoration of those in worse condition, the preservation of those in better condition, or even through gradual progress toward better things.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the twelfth chapter quoted above, the same things seem to be expounded as in the seventh chapter: it is asserted that our Lord Jesus Christ was instructed in everything through the indwelling of the Holy Spirit and reached, over time, the perfection of his anointing with the Spirit’s assistance. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or proclaims that he was not perfect through his own deity but was assisted as a mere human being in need of the anointing of the Holy Spirit, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XIII

How, then, does it follow from the fact that God became human that one should say that a human being is God the Word? For if a human being is God the Word, as you say, we shall apply to the human being in every respect what the Evangelist says about God the Word. What does he say? “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God; he was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made” (John I). Therefore, if a human being is God the Word, we shall say of him: “In the beginning was the human being, and the human being was with God, and God was the human being; the human being was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, [Col. 0079A] and without him nothing was made that was made.” For if a human being is God the Word, as you say, everything that the Evangelist says about God the Word will appropriately apply to him.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the thirteenth chapter quoted above, God the Word is apparently denied to have become human, and conversely the human being is denied to be God the Word, so that, as stated earlier, a duality of persons may be introduced. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or proclaims this way, and does not instead believe that, while the distinction of natures remains unchangeably and indivisibly in our Lord Jesus Christ, he is one person—or subsistence—in such a way that God the Word is human without any change in his divine nature, and that the assumed humanity is unchangeably God on account of the singularity of the person, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XIV

[Note: The same excerpts from Theodore, through chapter 60 inclusive, may also be read in the fourth session of the Council of Constantinople, under the same chapter. HARDUIN.]

What, then, is this: “To my Father and your Father, and my God and your God” (John XX)? No one is so insane as to say that this applies to anyone else except the human being who, having been assumed as the temple of God the Word for our salvation, died, rose again, and was about to ascend into heaven; who ascribes God as Father to himself together with his disciples; and who, having obtained adoption by grace, calls him his God because he received being in the same manner as the other human beings. Therefore, on account of the commonality of nature, he says, “my Father and your Father, and my God and your God.” But he again distinguished his person from theirs, signifying the beginning of grace, by which, through union with God the Word, he is honored by all human beings in the place of the true Son.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the fourteenth chapter quoted above, the Gospel’s words, “I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John XX), are understood to mean that Jesus Christ, our Lord and God, received adoption by grace, like the other human beings, so that he might be called the Son of God and, as though through union with God the Word, might be worshiped by all in the place of the true Son. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or proclaims this way, and does not rather understand and believe that the one Jesus Christ, the Son of God and our Lord, exists in two unmixed and inseparable natures, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XV

He says “Receive,” instead of “You will receive.” For if, when he breathed upon them, he had given the Spirit to the disciples—as they very foolishly supposed—then it would have been superfluous afterward to tell them, especially at the time of his ascent into heaven, not to depart from Jerusalem but to await the promise of the Spirit; and later: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you” (Acts I). Luke says that the coming of the Holy Spirit itself upon the disciples took place on the fiftieth day after the resurrection, following the ascension. It must nevertheless be observed that, if they had received the Spirit from the breathing, he would not have said, “Receive,” but “Since you have received.” For the word “Receive” is appropriate to those who have not yet received.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the fifteenth chapter quoted above, it is said that our Lord Jesus Christ, breathing upon the faces of his disciples after his resurrection, did not give them the Holy Spirit but indicated that he would give it, so that thereby either the truth itself—which God forbid—might be thought to have lied, or he might be regarded as a mere human being who did not possess anything to give by that breath, or who was entirely unable to give it. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, or proclaims these things in this way, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XVI

He says to Thomas: “Put your finger here and see my hands; and extend your hand and put it into my side, and do not be unbelieving but faithful” (John XXVIII). Since, he says, you do not believe, and think that touch alone is sufficient for you to believe—for in saying this you have not escaped my notice—touch with your hand, make trial, and learn to believe rather than doubt. When Thomas had believed in this way, he said, “My Lord and my God.” He did not mean that he was the Lord and God himself. For the knowledge of the resurrection did not teach him that the one who had risen was also God; rather, as though for a miracle that had occurred, he praised God.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the sixteenth chapter quoted above, concerning the Gospel passage in which the apostle Thomas, touching the marks [Note: In the Vulgate edition, *fixuras*, and in Baronius. HARDUIN.] of the nails, said, “My Lord and my God” (same passage), it is asserted that the apostle Thomas did not confess Jesus Christ himself as Lord and God, and that the knowledge of the resurrection did not teach him that the one who had risen was God; rather, the apostle Thomas praised God because of the miracle that had occurred. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or proclaims this way, and does not instead believe that Thomas’s confession declared both that Jesus Christ is true God and that he rose in true flesh, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XVII

He said that they ought to repent for the offense of the cross, acknowledge Jesus Christ the Savior and author of all good things, and, since he had attained these things and been assumed from the divine nature, place their faith in him and become his disciples—above all, approaching baptism, which he himself handed down to us. It had a foreshadowing of future things, but it was to be celebrated in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. For the statement, “Let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ” (Acts II), does not mean that, abandoning the invocation made in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, they should invoke Jesus Christ in baptism. Rather, this is like the statement that they were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea: they were separated from the Egyptians beneath the cloud and the sea and delivered from their slavery, so that they might heed the laws of Moses. In the same way, when they had approached him as Savior, author of all good things, and teacher of the truth, they were to be called by him, as author of good things and teacher of the truth, just as it is customary for all people who follow a sect to be called by the inventor of its doctrine—Platonists, Epicureans, Manichaeans, Marcionites, and others of this kind. In the same way, the apostles judged that we too should be called Christians, as thereby establishing that his teaching must be followed. Thus they were also to receive the baptism given by him: instituted first in him, who was himself first baptized, and then handed down by him to the others, so that it might be celebrated according to the foreshadowing of future things.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the seventeenth chapter cited above, from the words of blessed Peter, who says in the Acts of the Apostles, “Let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ,” it is asserted that Christ is not included in the invocation made in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and that the apostle Peter said they ought to be baptized in Christ’s name, so that, according to this interpretation, a quaternity appears to have been introduced. It is also added in the same chapter that we are called Christians by Christ in the same way that the followers of various sects and errors receive their names from their inventors and teachers: from Plato, Platonists; from Marcion, Marcionites; [Col. 0081C] and from Mani [Manes], Manichaeans. Whoever thinks, teaches, believes, or proclaims these things in this way, let him be anathema. For we are called Christians and are Christians because, receiving our Lord Jesus Christ in baptism, we put him on; with him as our head, we all become one body in him.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XVIII

He occupies the place of an image for two reasons. Those who love certain people often erect images of them after their death and consider this sufficient consolation for their death; looking at the one who is not seen and is not present as though in an image, they think they see him, thereby soothing the flame of longing and the intensity of their desire. Likewise, those who have images of emperors throughout the cities appear to honor, through the worship and veneration of the images, those who are not present as though they were present and watching.

Both of these things are fulfilled through him. All who are with him, follow virtue, and are ready to repay what they owe God love and greatly honor him. Although the divine nature is not seen, they fulfill their love for it in the one who is seen by all, so that everyone thinks that, through him, they see the divine nature itself and are always present to it; and they attribute every honor to him as to an imperial image, since the divine nature is, as it were, itself in him and is contemplated in him. For if the Son is also said to indwell him, the Father too is with him, and every creature believes that he is altogether inseparably with the Son. The Spirit too is not absent, since he was also made present to him in the place of anointing, and is always with the one who was assumed. Nor is this surprising, since he is also said to be with any human beings who follow virtue, together with the Son and the Father: “For we will come, I and the Father, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John XIV). It is certain to everyone that the Spirit likewise is inseparable from such human beings.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the eighteenth chapter quoted above, Christ is asserted to be the invisible image of God in such a way that images of absent rulers are worshiped for their honors. Whoever thinks, teaches, believes, or proclaims this way, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XIX

The statement, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Luke III), demonstrates adoption in the baptism, but not by comparison [or: “according to the comparison”] with Jewish adoption. For it had also been said to them: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High,” and, “I have begotten and exalted sons” (Psalm LXXXI). It reveals the distinctive character of this adoption by saying, “Beloved,” and, “In him I am well pleased” (Isaiah II). For this reason the Father’s voice also occurred, confirming the adoption; and by naming him “Son,” it demonstrated through adoption by grace the one who is truly Son. His union with the one who is truly Son established him in true and firm adoption. The Holy Spirit also descended in the form of a dove and remained upon him, so that, in union with the one who is truly Son, he might remain devoted to his cooperation, possessing the firm dignity of adoption. In every respect, the baptism in which adoption was first enacted—I mean the baptism of the Lord Christ from the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—was thereby completed.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the nineteenth chapter quoted above, where the Gospel according to Luke appears to be expounded concerning Christ’s baptism, there are two accusations: first, that a duality of sons is introduced, since Christ appears to be called the Son of God through adoption; second, that he too is asserted to have been baptized in the name of the Trinity, by which a quaternity is unmistakably displayed. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or proclaims these things in this way, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XX

Therefore the psalm shows us only the distinction between God the Word and the human being who was received. These things are divided in the New Testament: the Lord himself takes up the opening words of the psalm, in which he is said to be the maker of creation, to possess majesty exalted above the heavens, and to be wondrous throughout all the earth. The Apostle, however, applies the words cited above to the human being who deserved so many benefits. How could it not be evident that divine Scripture teaches us clearly that the one is God the Word and the other a human being, and shows us their great difference? For the one remembers, while the other deserves to be remembered; the one visits, while the other, when he deserves visitation, is called blessed; the one, by granting a benefit, makes the other a little lower than the angels, while the other received a benefit through such a lowering; the one crowns with glory and honor, while the other is crowned and is called blessed for these things; and the one appointed him over all the works of his hands and subjected all things beneath his feet, while the other deserved to rule over things over which previously he had no power.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the twentieth chapter quoted above, where the eighth psalm appears to be expounded, Christ is asserted to be a naked human being—as has already been said elsewhere—and is shown to be divided from the Word; thus a duality of persons is introduced. Whoever thinks, teaches, believes, or proclaims this way, and does not understand that in Christ the Lord the two natures are invisibly and without confusion united, so that, while the distinction of those natures remains, he himself, one and the same, is truly the Son of God and truly the son of a human being, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XXI

But because they do not wish to consider these things, they attempt to draw all the words toward the Lord Christ, so that they might understand in the same way the things done to the people and provoke laughter among the Jews, when the sequence of the writings shows that the words have no bearing on the Lord Christ.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XXII

The same applies to the statement, “His soul was not abandoned in Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption” (Psalm XV). The prophet places his providence concerning the people above measure, wishing to say that he preserved them from all evils while they were exposed to trials. But since this received a true fulfillment in the Lord Christ through the events themselves, blessed Peter, speaking of him very frequently, uses the words, showing that what had been said above measure about the people by the prophet’s use of a certain expression received its true fulfillment in the Lord Christ through the events themselves.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the twenty-first and twenty-second chapters quoted above, it appears to be said that the prophecy spoken in the person of Christ—“You will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will you allow your Holy One to see corruption” (Psalm XV)—was not foretold of Christ himself but of the people of the Israelite race; and that the blessed apostle Peter wished to apply this prophecy to Christ by its fulfillment (Acts II). Therefore whoever thinks, teaches, believes, or proclaims these things in this way, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XXIII

The same interpretation applies to the statement, “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast a lot” (Psalm XXI). It is certain that the psalm in no way applies to the Lord. For it was not appropriate for the Lord Christ, who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found (1 Peter II), to say: “Far from my salvation are the words of my offenses” (Psalm XXI). But the Lord himself, when he was oppressed in the Passion according to the common law of human beings, uttered, “My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?” (Matthew XXVII); and the apostles clearly applied to him the words: “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast a lot” (Psalm XXI). For what David had previously said beyond measure on account of the evils inflicted upon him occurred in the Lord Christ through the events themselves: his garments were divided, and his tunic was subjected to the casting of lots.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the twenty-third chapter quoted above, while expounding certain words of Psalm XXI—“They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast a lot”—it is denied that they apply to the Lord Jesus Christ. Instead, it is said that David spoke of himself because of certain evils he had suffered, and that the Evangelist applied the words to Christ on the basis of their fulfillment. It is added that the Lord Jesus, who committed no sin, could not say, “Far from my salvation are the words of my offenses” (same passage). Therefore whoever thinks, teaches, believes, or proclaims these things, and does not understand that the passages in which offenses are mentioned pertain to his body, which is the Church and cannot be without sin in this world, while the passages concerning the division of the garments were not specifically foretold of the head himself—that is, our Lord God Jesus Christ—but were believed to have been fulfilled in him, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XXIV

[Note: [Col. 0083D] This is also the reading in the fourth session. HARDUINUS.]

“They pierced my hands and feet” (Psalm XXI), and they examined everything—the things I was doing and the things I was attempting. For “they pierced,” he says by a figurative rendering, refers to those who try, by piercing, to investigate what lies in the depths. “They counted all my bones” (same passage): they became masters of all my strength and all my substance, so that they even subjected my possessions to counting. He said this according to the custom of enemies, who, whenever they have gained possession, count and make a precise inventory of what they have found [the passage is corrupt]. Therefore, immediately afterward, when he says, “They themselves looked and saw me,” he adds: “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast a lot.” Looking at me, he says, and seeing that everything they desired had happened to me—for “to see” is used here as among us, meaning “he saw in him what he wished to inflict upon him”—they now, as enemies, after laying waste to and capturing me, divided my possessions and made their division by lot, as though I had been wholly handed over to evils. The Evangelist, taking the words from what occurred in the Lord, used them, as we have said in other passages. For we have clearly shown above that the psalm does not pertain to the Lord. But blessed David said these things to an even greater degree concerning what was done by Absalom: when David had departed, Absalom entered the capital by right of war and took possession of all the royal property, nor did he shrink from defiling his father’s bed.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the twenty-fourth chapter quoted above, concerning the words of the same Psalm XXI—“They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones; but they themselves looked and gazed upon me”—it is asserted that these were not foretold of Christ. Rather, David said this about himself because of the tyranny of Absalom, who had seized the royal city and the substance of his father and had counted everything on the ground; but the Evangelist applied these words to Christ’s person on the basis of their fulfillment. Whoever therefore believes, thinks, teaches, or proclaims these things in this way, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XXV

[Note: Alternatively, “How.” HARDUINUS.]

Since foods and drinks become pleasant in a time of joy but unpleasant and bitter in sorrow, such, he says, were the things done by them: because of sorrow and anger, food became for me as gall, and drink was no different from vinegar. This occurs especially in anger accompanied by tribulation, such as they were likely to suffer at the hands of their own people. The Evangelist used this testimony concerning the Lord, and the Lord himself likewise said of himself, “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (John II). Blessed Paul, speaking about the Jews, says, “Let their table become …” (Romans XV), and blessed Peter concerning Judas, “Let his dwelling become desolate” (Acts I). And certainly, although the circumstances were different, this was not said once in the psalm about one matter, then again about him, and again about another; rather, because many things were said about the Jews who separated themselves from God and the Law, convicting their devotion, it was necessary to use testimonies drawn together from the events, such as: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm LXVIII).

### Vigilius’s Response

In the twenty-fifth chapter quoted above, concerning the passage of the psalm that says, “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink,” it is expounded contrary to the evident truth of the Gospel: it is said that the Lord was not actually given vinegar to drink, but that the drink was offered in place of vinegar and the food in place of gall because of the sorrow and anger of those offering them; and that the passage was not foretold of him, but that the Evangelist used this testimony in the Lord on the basis of its fulfillment. Therefore whoever thinks, teaches, believes, or proclaims these things in this way, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XXVI

Just as Nathanael is shown by such a confession not to possess knowledge of the deity—for Jews and Samaritans, who hoped for such things very greatly, were far removed from knowledge of the Word of God—so Martha too is proved, by that confession, not at that time to have possessed knowledge of the deity. Clearly, neither did blessed Peter. For at that time it was still sufficient for them, as they received that revelation, to gain from him something exceptional beyond the opinion held concerning the other human beings. After the resurrection, however, when they had been led by the Spirit to knowledge, they then also received perfect knowledge of the revelation, so that they might know that what was exceptional in him beyond the other human beings did not come from God through some merely pure honor, as in the case of other human beings, but through unity with God the Word, through which, after his ascent into heaven, he shares in every honor.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the twenty-sixth chapter quoted above, it is denied that Peter possessed recognition of Christ’s deity before his resurrection; instead, he is said to have received only an imaginative understanding, superior to that of the other human beings. A duality of sons is again introduced when the human being is said to have become a participant in the Word after ascending into heaven. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or proclaims this way, and does not understand that Christ our Lord is one and the same Son of God and of a human being, while the distinction of the natures united in him remains, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XXVII

After the temptations, the Evangelist Matthew says, “Angels came and ministered to him” (Matthew IV), that is, they stood with him and cooperated, ministering to God in everything concerning him; for through the contests against the devil he had already been shown to be more glorious. We also learn from the Gospels that angels were present with him when he was about to suffer. When he rose, they were seen at the tomb (Matthew XXVIII; Luke [Col. 0086B] XXII). In all these things Christ’s dignity is displayed: angels were inseparably present with him and ministered to him in everything concerning him. For just as they separate themselves from sinners, so they assist those honored on account of merit. Therefore the Lord rightly says: “You will see greater things, and heaven will be opened to all through me, and all the angels will always be with me, now ascending and now descending, as to the friend and intimate of God” (John I).

### Vigilius’s Response

In the twenty-seventh chapter quoted above, where the Evangelist Matthew is expounded as saying that, after the temptations had been completed, angels came to minister to Christ, it is said that angels assisted Christ, who had been honored on account of merit, as they assist others; and that angels ascended and descended to Christ in heaven as to the friend and intimate of God. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or proclaims these things, and does not believe that, as the true God and Son of the true God, one and the same with the perfect humanity assumed from the Virgin’s womb, Christ was and is served by angels as their Creator and Lord, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XXVIII

The Lord was more troubled and engaged in a greater struggle with the passions of the soul than with those of the body, and by a better disposition he conquered the desires, with his deity assisting him toward perfection. Hence the Lord also appears to have undertaken his struggle chiefly for this purpose. Not deceived by the desire for money and not overcome by the longing for glory, he gave nothing to the flesh—for it was not his nature to be conquered by such things. But if he had not received a soul, and it was the deity that conquered these passions, then none of what occurred would profit us. For what similarity is there, for the perfection of conduct, between deity and a human soul? The Lord’s struggles also appear not to profit us but to have occurred for the sake of some display. If it is impossible to say this—for it is certain that those things happened for our sake, and that he undertook a greater struggle with the passions of the soul and a lesser one with those of the flesh—then how much more and more greatly must he have been troubled, and how much more were those things in need of medicine, since, assuming both flesh and soul, he struggled for both: in the flesh he put sin to death and subdued its desires, making them easily subject to the better reasoning of the soul; while he instructed the soul and trained it both to conquer its own passions and to restrain the desires of the flesh. The deity indwelling him accomplished these things; indwelling him, it healed both of them.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the twenty-eighth chapter quoted above, Christ is again introduced as a mere human being: by means of the soul, he is said to have subdued the desires of the body, instructed the soul, and trained it to conquer its own passions and restrain the desires within the flesh. Yet it says that both of these were accomplished by the soul with the deity assisting. Thus, according to this, we no longer have the one and same Jesus Christ, mediator between God and human beings, but the deity appears to have been mediator for the flesh and the soul. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or proclaims these things in this way, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XXIX

But if it was flesh, he says, that was crucified, how did the sun turn away its rays, darkness seize the whole earth, earthquakes occur, rocks split apart, and the dead rise? What, then, will they say about the darkness that occurred in Egypt in the time of Moses—not for three hours but for three days? And what will they say about the other miracles performed through Moses, and those performed through Joshua, who made the sun stand still? The sun also moved backward, contrary to nature, in the time of King Hezekiah. And what of the remains of Elisha, which raised a dead man? If the things that occurred on the cross demonstrate that the Word of God suffered, and they do not allow them to have occurred on account of the human being; and if the things in the time of Moses did not occur on account of the race of Abraham, nor those in the time of Joshua, nor those in the time of King Hezekiah, then—if those things were wondrously done for the Jewish people—how could the things that occurred on the cross not have occurred for the temple of God the Word all the more?

### Vigilius’s Response

In the twenty-ninth chapter quoted above, while apparently opposing Apollinaris, who involved the divine nature in sufferings, the argument departs from the straight path and exceeds the proper measure of assertion, so that a mere human being is thought to have hung upon the cross. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or proclaims this way, and does not believe Christ to be true God while confessing that, with his deity remaining impassible, he himself suffered in his own flesh, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XXX

It is evident that unity is appropriate: through it the united natures formed one person according to unity. For just as it is said of a man and a woman that they are no longer two but one flesh (Matthew XIX), so let us also say rationally, according to the principle of unity, that there are not two persons but one, namely, with the natures distinguished. For just as in that case the fact that two are called one flesh does not harm the number two—for it is certain that they are called one according to a particular respect—so here too the unity of the person does not harm the difference of the natures. When we distinguish the natures, we say that the nature of God the Word is perfect and that his person is perfect; for it is impossible to speak of a perfect subsistence without a person. Likewise, the nature and person of the human being are perfect. But when we look to the union, we then say that there is one person.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the thirtieth chapter quoted above, a very bad example is used in an attempt to show how one person in Christ can be understood: just as it is written of a man and a woman coming together, so in Christ, with the natures distinguished, there is said to be, as it were, one person. It then follows that the nature of God the Word and his person are perfect, and likewise that the nature and person of the human being are perfect. Thus it appears that both from the example of the man and woman, where there are two persons, and from what follows—although the number is not stated—a duality is introduced in the one person of Christ. Whoever thinks, teaches, believes, or proclaims this way, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XXXI

He designates Christ according to the flesh and the assumed form of a servant, and the one who assumed it as God above all; yet he states this according to the union, so that by the signification of the names he may make the division of the natures plain. Therefore let no one call the one who is from the Jews according to the flesh God, nor again call God, who is above all, one who is from the Jews according to the flesh.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the thirty-first chapter quoted above, in the exposition that appears to have been made of the creed of the 318 Fathers, not only is a division of the natures asserted, but, by saying absolutely that neither the one who is from the Jews according to the flesh—a mere human being without deity—nor God, who is pure and without flesh, is to be called God, it declares that there are two persons, as though separate and distinct. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or proclaims these things in this way, and does not confess unity in the one Christ in such a manner that the singularity of the person or subsistence is acknowledged, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XXXII

For he says that Jesus was from Nazareth, “whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts X). But whoever is anointed with the Spirit of God undoubtedly receives something from it. What madman would say that the divine nature received something from the Spirit? And yet he also speaks of participation: for he calls those who themselves are anointed participants in it. Those who are anointed, and who have rightly become participants in it through this, are said to share in the anointings only in relation to the one who was assumed. This very thing demonstrates that he received a just reward: “For this reason,” he says, “because you loved righteousness and hated iniquity, you deserved the preeminent anointing.”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the thirty-second chapter quoted above, in the commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews, Peter’s statement is introduced in which he says, “Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power.” It is then inferred: “Whoever is anointed with the Spirit of God undoubtedly received something from it.” It is added: “What madman would say that the divine nature received something from the Spirit?” Through these words Christ is introduced as a mere human being who became a participant in the divine nature through the anointing of the Holy Spirit, just like the others; and, under the name of a just reward, because he loved righteousness and hated iniquity, he is said to have deserved the preeminent anointing. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or proclaims this way, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XXXIII
Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the king of Israel: that is, you are the one who was proclaimed beforehand from afar, Christ. For this is evidently what he hoped concerning Christ, just as one made familiar to God above all.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XXXIV

He himself was indeed certain that he was the Son of God—not speaking according to the birth of deity, but according to the fact that he was familiar to God; for by this means human beings who had been constituted familiar to God through virtue were meanwhile called sons of God.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid thirty-third and thirty-fourth chapters, in the interpretation of the Gospel according to John, Nathanael’s words to the Lord are introduced: “You are the Son of God; you are the king of Israel.” It is then stated that he spoke of Christ as one familiar to God, so that Christ himself is not God, but is more familiar to God than other human beings. It is said that, just as other holy men are called sons of God, so Christ too was named God by Nathanael because of the familiarity he possessed with God. Whoever thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches in this way, and does not confess that this same Christ is true God and true man, perfect in both natures and one in both, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XXXV

For when he says, “Concerning his Son, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh,” it is certain that here he does not call the one who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh God the Word, but the assumed form of a servant. For God was not made according to the flesh, nor was God made from the seed of David; rather, it was a man assumed for our sake whom the blessed Apostle plainly calls “Son.”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid thirty-fifth chapter, when the Apostle’s passage from the Epistle to the Romans is expounded—“Concerning his Son, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh”—only the form of a servant is brought forward. It is said that here he does not call the one who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh God the Word, but a man assumed for our sake, whom the blessed Apostle plainly calls “Son.” These words show that, as has been said, a mere man is being proclaimed. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches in this way, and does not believe that the one who was born from the seed of David according to the flesh, in accordance with the testimony of David and the Apostle Paul, is himself also God over all, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XXXVI

One who was reborn became another in place of another: no longer a part of mutable Adam, enveloped in sins, but of Christ, who through the resurrection was made altogether blameless.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid thirty-sixth chapter, where it is said to the baptized person, “Because, having been reborn, he became another from another, no longer a part of mutable Adam, enveloped in sins, but of Christ, who was made altogether blameless through the resurrection,” these words seek—God forbid—to make Christ appear to have been culpable before the resurrection. Whoever thinks, teaches, or preaches this, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XXXVII

So that he might indeed show great diligence toward him, but make all things belonging to him his own and endure them, through all the passions by which he perfected him according to his virtue; and, not departing from the dead according to the law of his nature, but freeing him by his presence, operation, and grace from death and the evils arising from it, while raising him from the dead and leading him to a better end.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid thirty-seventh chapter it is said that, in Christ’s passions and death, God the Word was present with him by presence, operation, and grace. If this is so, it will appear that one was present to the other and bestowed grace and operation upon the other. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches in this way, and does not say that God the Word himself, while the impassibility of his divinity remained intact, voluntarily endured in the flesh—animated by a rational and intellectual soul, which he united to himself from the very conception from the Virgin—all that is written concerning his passion, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XXXVIII

Then, showing for what reason he suffered, he introduces a diminution: “So that, apart from God [or: without God], he might taste death for all” (Hebrews 2). Because the divine nature so willed, having been separated, he himself tasted death for himself [or: through himself], for the benefit of all. And, showing that the deity was indeed separated from the one who suffered according to the experience of death—for it was not possible for it to undergo the experience of death—he nevertheless says that it was not absent from the one who suffered with respect to its care.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid thirty-eighth chapter we recognize that the Apostle’s testimony has been falsified. For where it reads, “So that by the grace of God he might taste death for all,” it is found here as, “So that without God he might taste death for all.” This is asserted as though to prove that, once the divine nature had been separated, he himself—or a mere man—tasted death for the benefit of all. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches in this way, and does not confess that God the Word never abandoned the flesh which he united substantially to himself from the very conception, neither in the passions nor in death, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XXXIX

“Jesus of Nazareth,” he says, “whom God anointed with the Spirit and with power” (Acts 10), whose anointing he merited, and through which he was made immaculate in all respects and merited union with the divine nature. For he would not have received that union unless he had first been made immaculate, so that he might thus befit its unity.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid thirty-ninth chapter, again expounding what the blessed Peter said—“Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Spirit and with power”—he says that through the anointing of the Spirit, which he merited, Christ was made immaculate in all respects and merited union with the divine nature. These words plainly designate Christ as a mere man. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches this, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XL

“For this statement also—‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’ (Matthew 3)—it is manifest madness to think that he says it concerning God the Word. For he who said, ‘This is my beloved Son,’ and added, ‘in whom I am well pleased,’ clearly indicated that he said this by comparison with the other sons, who neither became beloved nor were able to please him greatly.”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid fortieth chapter, in the interpretation of the Gospel according to Matthew, where it says, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,” it is added and stated: “It is manifest madness to say that he is God.” For he who said, “This is my beloved Son,” and added, “in whom I am well pleased,” indicated that he plainly said this in comparison with the sons who neither became beloved by him nor were able to please him greatly. These words once again clearly show Jesus Christ to be a mere man and an adoptive son. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches this, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XLI

“Remaining until, according to his creaturely condition and virtue, he released the pains of death and freed him from its ineffable bonds; and, raising him from the dead, he transferred him to immortal life. Making him incorruptible, immortal, and immutable, he led him into heaven.”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid forty-first chapter it is said that, by releasing the pains of death, he freed Christ from those ineffable bonds; that, raising him from death, he transferred him to immortal life; and that, making him incorruptible, immortal, and immutable, he led him into heaven. Through all these words it is declared that Jesus Christ is a mere man. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches this, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XLII

He caused Christ, justified and made immaculate through the virtue of the Holy Spirit—as the blessed Apostle says at one point, “He was justified in the Spirit” (2 Timothy 3), and at another, “Through the eternal Spirit he offered himself immaculate to God” (Hebrews 9)—to die according to the law of human beings. But, having made him sinless through the virtue of the Holy Spirit, he raised him from the dead and established him in a better life, making his soul immutable in its thoughts and his flesh incorruptible and indissoluble.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid forty-second chapter it is said that Christ was justified and made immaculate by the virtue of the Holy Spirit. It adds: “He caused him to die according to the law of human beings; but, having made him sinless through the virtue of the Holy Spirit, he raised him from the dead.” By these words a man is so presented as separated from the Word of God that he is asserted to have been made immaculate and sinless by the virtue of the Holy Spirit, as though he were some righteous man. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches this, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XLIII

“But thanks be to God, who gave us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15). He says that God was the cause of these things for us, giving us victory over every adversary—whether death, sin, or any evil arising from them. Taking our Lord Jesus Christ as a man for our sake, he transferred him himself through the resurrection from the dead to a better end, made him sit at his right hand, and granted us communion with him.

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid forty-third chapter, while expounding the Apostle Paul’s words, “But thanks be to God, who gave us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ,” and after several further statements, it is added: “Our Lord Jesus Christ, taking a man for our sake, transferred him through the resurrection from the dead to a better end.” By these words he is presented as though he had existed as a man and had been assumed by God the Word, so that they appear to have been two, with one bestowing something upon the other. Whoever thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches this, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XLIV

“When they ask, then, whether Mary is to be called the mother of a man or the mother of God, let us say: both—the one according to nature, the other according to relationship. For she is the mother of a man according to nature, because he was a man and was in Mary’s womb, and he came forth from it; but she is the mother of God because God was in the man who was born—not circumscribed in him according to nature, but present in him by an inclination of will.”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid forty-fourth chapter it is said: “When they ask, then, whether Mary is called the mother of a man or the mother of God,” as though speaking in the person of the respondent, it says that she is to be called both. It adds: “The one according to the nature of the matter, the other according to relationship”; and further: “For she is the mother of a man according to nature, because he was a man and was in Mary’s womb, and he came forth from it; but she is the mother of God because God was in the man who was born.” It then adds: “He was not circumscribed in him according to nature, but was present in him by an inclination of will.” These words likewise demonstrate both one human being, Christ, and two sons of blessed Mary. Whoever thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches this, and does not recognize and believe that God the Word, ineffably born from the Father before all ages, was the same one incarnate and born from the holy Virgin Mary through a second birth—as we said in the first chapter—one in both natures, without confusion and without separation, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XLV

[Note: As in the Fifth Council, sessions 4 and 5.]

“By grace he is the son who is a man from Mary, but by nature he is God the Word. What is according to grace is not according to nature, and what is according to nature is not according to grace: there are not two sons. Let what is according to grace—sonship, glory, and immortality—be sufficient for the body that is from us. Since it has been made the temple of God the Word, let it not be elevated above nature, and let God the Word not be insulted by the thanksgiving owed by us. What insult is it to unite him with the body and to think that he needed the body for perfect sonship! God the Word himself does not wish to be David’s son, but Lord; yet he did not merely begrudge this body’s being called David’s son, but was present for this very reason.”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid forty-fifth chapter it is said that the one born from Mary as a man is a son by grace, whereas God the Word is so by nature. It reasons as follows: “What is according to grace is not according to nature, and what is according to nature is not according to grace.” It adds: “It is sufficient for the body that is from us to have sonship according to grace; it must not be elevated above nature, and God the Word must not be insulted by the thanksgiving owed by us.” These words signify a mere man from the Virgin Mary, who is called the Son of God by grace. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches this, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XLVI

[Note: As in the Fifth Council, session 5.]

“When there is a question concerning births according to nature, so that the Word of God may not be thought to be the son of Mary: for mortals beget mortals according to nature, and a body like themselves. God the Word did not undergo two births—one before the ages, and the other in later times.”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid forty-sixth chapter it is said that God the Word must not be thought to be the son of Mary, with the addition: “Because a mortal begets a mortal according to nature, and a body like himself.” These words signify both a mere man from the holy Virgin Mary and the introduction of two sons. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches this, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XLVII

“Therefore let them now cease from their shameless struggle and desist from their vain contention, ashamed of the obviousness of what has been said; for they introduce many sons, bringing them into glory. Behold, then, the Apostle appears in the matter of sonship (1 Timothy 3), counting the assumed man among the others—not because he is a participant in that sonship, but because he likewise assumed sonship by grace, while deity alone possesses natural sonship.”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid forty-seventh chapter, expounding what the Apostle says—“He brought many sons to glory” (Hebrews 2:10)—it is stated that the holy Apostle counts the assumed man among the others because he likewise received the grace of sonship, while deity alone possesses natural sonship. These words, as was said above, introduce two sons: one by grace and the other by nature. Whoever thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches this, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XLVIII

“But to this they say that the name Jesus signifies ‘savior.’ If he is called Savior, how can he be called that man? They have forgotten that Jesus was also called the son of Nun; and what is remarkable is that he was not called this accidentally at his birth, but was renamed by Moses. It is certain that he would not have permitted this name to be imposed upon a man if it signified the divine nature in every respect.”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid forty-eighth chapter, by an argument concerning the name Jesus, which signifies “savior,” the claim is denied, and it is said: “If ‘savior’ signified the divine nature, such a name would never have been imposed upon a man.” By these words Christ is absolutely shown to be a mere man, and two persons are understood. Whoever thinks, believes, or preaches this, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER XLIX

“Therefore he not only calls him ‘Son,’ separating him from God the Word, but he is also shown to share, according to the account of sonship, with the other participants in sonship. For he too was a participant in sonship by grace, not born naturally from the Father, though he possessed superiority over the others, since by union with him he possesses sonship, which grants him a firmer participation in the reality itself.”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid forty-ninth chapter it is said that Christ was a participant in sonship by grace, while possessing superiority over the others because he was granted a firmer participation in the reality itself. Whoever thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches this, and does not rather understand and believe that God the Word, together with the assumed flesh, is one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, true Son of God and that same true Son of man, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER L

“Jesus the man was like all human beings, differing in nothing from human beings of the same nature except that he gave him grace. But grace bestowed does not change nature; after the destruction of death, God gave him the name above every name.”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid fiftieth chapter it is said that Jesus the man differs in nothing from all human beings of the same nature except that God gave him grace. These words make our Lord Jesus Christ appear to be one of the righteous human beings, understood not to be exalted by his own deity but to have obtained something greater than other human beings through grace. Whoever thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches this, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER LI

“But my brothers, who are sons of the same mother as I, say to me: ‘Do not separate the man and God, but call him one and the same man, saying: “I call him of the same nature as myself; I call him God.”’ If I say, ‘of the same nature as God,’ I ask: ‘How are man and God one? Is there one nature of man and God, of master and servant, of maker and creature? Man is consubstantial with man, and God is consubstantial with God. How, then, can man and God be one through unity—the one who is saved and the one who saves, the one who existed before the ages and the one who appeared from Mary?’”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid fifty-first chapter it is denied that God and man can be called one and the same, with the question: “How can man and God be one through unity—the one who saves and the one who is saved, the one who exists before the ages and the one who appeared from Mary?” These words introduce two persons in Christ. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches this, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER LII

“He spoke well when he added: ‘For I too am a man’ (Matthew 8), meaning: ‘There is nothing remarkable in your being able to do this, since you are a man receiving it from God; for since I too am such a one, I receive those who obey, having once received the power to command through the indulgence of the giver.’”

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER LIII

“Therefore it is neither incongruous for you, having received this power from God, to drive away diseases by a mere word, nor did the centurion approach you as the Son of God, who existed before the whole creation and was its creator.”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid fifty-second and fifty-third chapters it is said that the centurion told Christ that there was nothing remarkable in his being able to do this, since he was a man receiving it from God: “For since I too am such a one, I receive those who obey, having once received the power to command through the indulgence of the giver.” Although, from what follows—namely, that the centurion did not approach him as the Son of God who created the whole creation—he may seem indeed to confess him to be the Son of God and maker of the whole creation, nevertheless Theodore did not form a sound judgment even concerning the centurion’s understanding. For the Lord would not have praised his faith by saying, “I have not found such faith in Israel” (ibid.), unless he knew that the centurion understood him to be God. From these chapters, the preceding chapters, and other statements, Christ is now said to be the Son of God not by unity of subsistence but by grace; and Christ appears to be introduced as a mere man who, on account of his merit, received power through the indulgence of the giver. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches this, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER LIV

“And the Apostle also says consistently: ‘And manifestly great is the mystery of piety, which was manifested in the flesh, was justified in the Spirit’ (1 Timothy 3), saying that he himself was justified in the Spirit—either because before baptism he observed the law with appropriate exactness, or because even after it he completed a life of grace through the cooperation of the Spirit with great exactness.”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid fifty-fourth chapter, Christ is asserted to have been justified in the Apostle’s statement, “What was manifested in the flesh was justified in the Spirit,” either because before baptism he observed the law with suitable exactness, or because after baptism he completed a life of grace through the cooperation of the Spirit with great exactness. Since these words likewise show that Christ, as a mere man, needed justification, whoever thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches this, and does not rather believe that he himself, as true God consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit, justifies the ungodly through faith, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER LV

“We say this justly also concerning the Lord: God the Word, knowing his virtue and according to his foreknowledge, graciously willed immediately at the beginning of his formation to dwell with him; and, uniting him to himself by an inclination of will, he bestowed upon him a greater grace, namely, the grace that was in him and was to be distributed among all human beings. Hence he also preserved his will intact with respect to good things. For we shall not say that this man had no will, but that he indeed willed the good, while there was voluntarily present in him to a very great degree both desire for the good and hatred of the contrary. His will, however, was preserved intact by divine grace from the beginning, God knowing with subtle precision what he would be like; and, in order to strengthen him, he provided him with great cooperation through his indwelling, for the salvation of us all. Therefore let no one say that it was unjust that something extraordinary was given, beyond all others, to that man who was assumed by the Lord.”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid fifty-fifth chapter it is said that God the Word, knowing through foreknowledge the virtue of the man Christ, graciously willed to dwell in him immediately at the beginning of his formation, and, uniting him to himself by an inclination of will, bestowed upon him a greater grace. From these words and from what follows, two persons are plainly introduced, and the Son of God appears to dwell in the son of man through inclination, grace, and relationship. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches this, and does not recognize and believe one and the same Christ in two perfect, undivided, and unconfused natures, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER LVI

“For discrimination between good and evil is indeed proper to a rational being; but since they are not opposites, it was not possible for him at first to discern anything. Therefore, in the things that were created, he first made a great opposition.”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid fifty-sixth chapter it is said that discrimination between good and evil is proper to a rational being. Shortly afterward it follows: “Therefore, in the things that were created, he first made a great opposition.” If these words are spoken with the intention of introducing evil’s nature in the same way as the nature of good, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER LVII

“But because Adam did not obey, he was afterward subjected to death. This happened on account of disobedience, although even apart from disobedience it was done by the Creator for our benefit. We have all been instructed in sin.”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid fifty-seventh chapter it is said that, even if Adam had not been disobedient, this would nevertheless have been done by the Creator for the benefit of human beings, and that we were instructed in sin. May it be far from the Catholic faith to believe that God could have instructed us in sin so that we might become sinners. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, or preaches this, and does not rather confess that sin was introduced through the fault of the first man, despite God’s prohibition, and that by God’s just judgment he and his offspring underwent the punishment of death on account of their disobedience, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER LVIII

“Nor, therefore, did he impose death upon human beings unwillingly and contrary to his own judgment, nor did he give sin access for no benefit. For this could not happen against his will. Rather, because he knew it to be beneficial for us—and especially for all rational beings—that access should first be given to evils and worse things, and that these should afterward be destroyed while better things were introduced, God therefore divided creation into two states: the present and the future. In the latter he will bring everything to immortality and immutability; in the present, however, he temporarily leaves creation in death and mutability.

“For if he had made us immortal and immutable immediately from the beginning, we would have had no distinction from irrational beings, since we would not know our own good. For, not knowing mutability, we would not know the good of immutability; not knowing death, we would not know the gain of immortality; not knowing corruption, we would not praise incorruption; not knowing the burden of sufferings, we would not marvel at impassibility—to put it briefly, so as not to prolong the discourse; not knowing the experience of evils, we could not acquire knowledge of those goods.”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid fifty-eighth chapter it is said that God gave sin access because he knew this to be beneficial for us, and especially for all rational beings, so that access might first be given to evils and worse things and, after these had been destroyed, better things might be introduced. It is added: “For if he had made us immortal and immutable immediately from the beginning, we would have had no distinction from irrational beings, since we would not know our own good.”

By these words, first, God is asserted—contrary to the rule of faith—to have introduced sin as something beneficial for us. Second, since the statement embraces all rational beings, it is made to apply also to the angels and the entire heavenly host, which is endowed with reason. Third, the claim that the devil persuaded the first human beings that, if they ate from the forbidden tree, they would be like gods, knowing good and evil, is presented as having benefited them in the manner of a gift. [Note: Perhaps: “they would be like gods.” Harduinus.]

Whoever thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches this, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER LIX

[Col. 0098B] “It is necessary that all rational beings together—I mean the invisible beings and ourselves, whose body is mortal but whose soul is in every respect of the same kind as the invisible and rational substances [perhaps: “immortal, with those same invisible and rational substances”]—should here undergo present mutability, so that we may be instructed in the best teaching of religion and established in benevolence.”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid fifty-ninth chapter it is said: “It is necessary that all rational and invisible beings together, and ourselves, whose body is mortal but whose soul is in every respect of the same kind as the invisible and rational substances, should here undergo present change, so that we may be instructed in the best teaching of religion and established in benevolence.”

If by these words the angels of light and all the heavenly and invisible powers are asserted to be subject to mutability to the same extent as human souls, let him be anathema.

## THEODORE’S CHAPTER LX

“For he knew that they would certainly sin, but he permitted this to happen because he knew that it was expedient for them. For it was impossible that the one who had brought into existence beings that did not previously exist, had shown himself their lord, and had set before them such great goods for their enjoyment should not also prevent access to sin if he knew that this was expedient for them.

“But it was not otherwise possible for us to learn sin, the troubles of sufferings, the worse things, and our weakness as demonstrated in these, so as to display the greatness of the immutability that he would afterward give us, unless these things had been arranged by God from the beginning in such a way that, through comparison with and experience of innumerable evils, we might know the greatness of good things. For this reason, since he allowed sin to enter as something that would benefit us, man found great assistance in the battle against that sin.”

### Vigilius’s Response

In the aforesaid sixtieth chapter it is said that God, knowing that man would sin, permitted him to sin because he knew that this would be expedient for him. For this reason he did not prevent access to sin, since God had arranged things from the beginning so that, through comparison with and experience of innumerable evils, we might know the greatness of good things; and for this purpose, since he allowed sin to enter as something that would benefit us, man found great assistance in the battle against that sin.

These words are alien to the sense of divine Scripture, since they assert that sin was introduced by God for our benefit. Whoever thinks, teaches, believes, or preaches this, let him be anathema.

For the holy Catholic Church holds and believes this with certainty: God both prohibited the first man from sin and punished sin through disobedience with a just penalty. Yet, making good use even of our evils, he freed us by a singular remedy from the bonds of all sins through the incarnation, passion, death, and resurrection of his only-begotten Son, that is, our Lord Jesus Christ.

Having therefore duly condemned these matters by the authority of the apostolic judgment and in accordance with the rectitude of the orthodox faith, we decree that, from all those things which we have condemned by apostolic authority while adhering to the statutes and traditions of the Fathers, no opportunity be provided for insulting the preceding Fathers or teachers of the Church—an act which undoubtedly provokes scandals against the most holy Church. We anathematize every person belonging to the ecclesiastical orders who wishes in any way to attribute or inflict an insult upon the Fathers and teachers of the Church on account of the impieties set out above.

And since the aforementioned doctrines, which according to the interpretation given of them we have subjected to anathema and condemnation, are said to have been marked with the name of Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, in the volume recently sent to us by your Piety through our brother Bishop Benignus, we consequently directed the attention of our concern to this matter: if anything had been investigated by the Fathers concerning the person or name of the aforementioned Theodore, or if any canonical decisions or arrangements had been made by them concerning his name, we should seek this out with the greatest diligence.

While investigating these matters, we observed that Cyril, of blessed memory, bishop of the city of Alexandria, in replying to John, bishop of the city of Antioch, of reverend memory, or to the Eastern synod, concerning the deceased Bishop Theodore, stated among other things as follows:

“The definition brought forward in the holy Synod of Ephesus as having been composed by Theodore, as those who presented it said, contained nothing sound. The holy synod therefore nullified it as full of perverse interpretations, condemning also those who think in this way. But, as a matter of administrative prudence, it made no mention of the man, nor did it subject him by name to anathema, nor did it do so with respect to others.”

Carefully reviewing the First Synod of Ephesus itself, we found that it makes no reference to the person of Theodore of Mopsuestia. Rather, it concerns the creed which the presbyter Charisius presented there, especially because it had been sent to the churches of Philadelphia by Antony and James—who possessed only the names of presbyters—from Athanasius and Photius, who at that time adhered to the heretic Nestorius.

From this it is clear that the blessed Cyril, as he professes in his letter, understood that the name of the deceased Bishop Theodore had been brought forward by the presenters of the creed. In his prudence, preserving ecclesiastical moderation with priestly wisdom concerning the dead man, he did not wish his name to be included even in the synodal records, on account of the rule that must be observed concerning those who have died in the priesthood.

The blessed Cyril also added below in the same letter how what he had said was to be understood as having been done administratively, so that he had not wished the man’s name to be subjected to anathema, extending the matter to the ecclesiastical rule. He said:

“But those who provide such causes will hear justly, even if they do not wish to. You forget yourselves when you stretch your bows against ashes; for the one who was inscribed among them is no longer present. Let no one accuse me for having advanced to these words; rather, let them yield entirely, namely, to my predecessor.”

For it is a grave matter to insult the dead, even if they were laymen, and all the more those who ended this life in the episcopate. To prudent men it appears most just to yield to the one who foreknows—the God, of course, who knows the will of each person and knows what each one will become.

It is likewise established that the blessed Proclus, bishop of this imperial city, responded in a similar manner by letter to the aforementioned John, bishop of Antioch, saying among other things:

“When, in writing to Your Holiness, did I say that Theodore or certain others who died long ago ought to be subjected to anathema? Or when did I mention anyone by name?”

And shortly afterward:

“I rejected those chapters that were appended, since they lacked precision in matters of piety. I wrote neither about Theodore nor about anyone else who has already died, most beloved of God, either that he should be anathematized or that he should be rejected. Nor did the most beloved deacon Theodotus, who was sent by us, receive such instructions.”

The blessed Proclus himself also says the following in a letter to the deacon Maximus, after other matters:

“How, then, have I now learned by letter that the names of Theodore of Mopsuestia and certain others have been placed at the head of chapters for anathematization, when they have already departed to God? It is superfluous to insult after death those who have already left this life, whom we never blamed while they were alive.”

And shortly afterward:

“After the signing of the tome and the rejection of the chapters—whose authors we do not know—immediately prepare for the deacon Theodore to come to the imperial city.”

Therefore let the singular wisdom of your Piety consider [Col. 0100D] that Proclus, the most learned of priests, who lived not long after the lifetime of Theodore of Mopsuestia, then openly declared that he did not know whose the evils were which he had willingly condemned. Nor do we find that anything contrary was decreed or said in the holy and venerable Council of Chalcedon concerning the name of the often-mentioned Theodore of Mopsuestia, bishop. For in the report which that same venerable synod sent to the emperor Marcian of pious memory, and which you too have commendably adduced in your own constitutions as testimony—when you affirm that, in an orthodox confession, Christ our God and Lord is one of the Holy Trinity—the letters of John of Antioch, sent together with the Eastern synod to Theodosius, then the most pious ruler, are reverently recalled. [Col. 0101A] In those letters the person of Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, is defended, so that he should not be condemned after death.

After this, we examined with still greater care whether our predecessors, themselves of holy memory, had decreed anything concerning those who had already died and who had not been found guilty while alive. Having inspected their decisions, we recognized that the venerable constitutions of the bishops of our predecessors in the Apostolic See had handed down to us most clearly the form of this caution and prudence. For the most blessed Pope Leo says the following, among other things, in his letter to Theodore, bishop of Forum Julii:

“We do not need to review the merits and deeds of those who died in such a condition, since our Lord God, whose judgments cannot be comprehended, reserved to his own justice the matter of one who was unable to fulfill the priestly mystery.”

Likewise, the blessed Pope Gelasius, in the letter which he wrote to the bishops of Dardania concerning the case of Acacius, says the following, among other things:

“After he had once again entered the fellowship of wickedness, he rightly deserved to be excluded from apostolic communion; but since he died while persisting in that condemnation, he cannot now, after death, obtain the absolution which, while alive, he neither sought at all nor deserved. For it was entrusted to the apostles themselves by Christ’s word: ‘Whatever you bind on earth, and whatever you loose on earth’ (Matthew 18). But concerning one who has been placed in the divine judgment, it is not lawful for us to decree anything else except that in which his final day found him.”

[Note: [Col. 0101D] See also Facundus, *Book Against Mocianus*.]

Likewise, the aforementioned Pope Gelasius, of blessed memory, clearly taught this in the synodal proceedings composed concerning the absolution of Misenus, bishop of Cumae:

[Note: [Col. 0102D] From the Roman Council under Gelasius, in the year 495. HARD.]

“Let us leave to divine judgment everything that exceeds the measure of our authority. They cannot charge us with wrongdoing for remitting to the living the offense of transgression, something which, by God’s gift, is possible for the Church; nor should they ask us to grant pardon to the dead, something which plainly is not possible for us. For since it has been said, ‘Whatever you bind and loose on earth,’ God has reserved those whom it is now clear are no longer on earth, not to human but to his own judgment. Nor does the Church dare to claim for itself what it sees was not granted even to the apostles, because the case of the living is one thing and that of the dead another.”

This rule is also known to have been observed in the cases of the saints John, bishop of Constantinople, whom they call Chrysostom, and Flavian, bishop of that same city, both of venerable memory. Although they were violently excluded, they were nevertheless not treated as condemned, because the Roman pontiffs always preserved their communion inviolate. They neither could nor can be said to have been cut off from the Church, since apostolic authority judged them to be inseparably united to itself.

Moreover, in the seventh book of the *Ecclesiastical History* of Eusebius, also called Pamphilus, we read that Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, concerning a certain Egyptian bishop named Nepos, who had lived long before, acted as follows. Nepos, the bishop, is said to have written about the thousand years during which, according to what the blessed Apostle John says in the Apocalypse, the saints would reign with Christ after the first resurrection; and he is said to have understood them in a Jewish sense. After his death, when what Nepos had left in writing reached Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, and all Egypt thought that those books were in possession of some great and hidden mystery, Dionysius proceeded to the place where the question had arisen—for he reports that it had been raised in the Arsinoite district—and, writing against them, destroyed and overturned those same books. But he inflicted no injury upon Nepos, who had written them, chiefly because Nepos was already dead. Whoever wishes to learn these matters more fully will find them in the aforementioned seventh book of Eusebius’s history.

Having carefully examined all these matters, we find that although our Fathers discussed them in different words, they followed one and the same understanding: they preserved unharmed, within ecclesiastical peace, the persons of priests who had died; and the constitutions of the Apostolic See mentioned above likewise define the matter as a rule:

No one is permitted to judge anew the persons of the dead. Rather, each person is to remain in the condition in which his final day found him. And specifically concerning the name of Theodore of Mopsuestia, what our holy Fathers decided has been clearly expressed above. We do not dare to condemn him by our own sentence, nor do we permit him to be condemned by anyone else.
