Nevertheless, far be it from us to tolerate, even by hearing, the aforementioned chapters of doctrine—which, according to the meanings set out below, are known to have been condemned by us—or any statements written without a name, if they are incompatible and inconsistent, not merely in meaning but even in sound, with the evangelical and apostolic teaching, with the teaching of the four synods—Nicaea, Constantinople, the First Council of Ephesus, and Chalcedon—and with that of the Apostolic See.

Concerning the writings circulated under the name of the venerable Theodore, formerly bishop, we are first astonished that anyone should find it necessary, in the name of that priest, to drag anything whatsoever into reproach through another’s zeal. More than a hundred years ago he stood before the judgment of the holy and venerable Council of Chalcedon, subscribed without hesitation, and gave willing assent to the letters of the most blessed Pope Leo.

Furthermore, although Dioscorus and the Egyptian bishops were then present and claimed that he had anathematized Saint Cyril and that Theodore himself was also a heretic, our holy Fathers, after hearing these accusations and thereafter examining Theodore most carefully—questioning Theodore himself in the presence of those assembled—are known to have demanded nothing else from him except that he immediately anathematize and condemn Nestorius and his impious doctrines. They judged this alone sufficient, because Theodore did so before the entire council and, in a clear voice, condemned Nestorius together with his doctrines, while all the Fathers listened.

From this it plainly appears that whatever has been or is produced under anyone’s name and seems to agree with the doctrines of the impious Nestorius was then undoubtedly condemned by the venerable Theodore at that holy council. It is therefore profoundly contrary and undeniably hostile to the judgment of the Council of Chalcedon to condemn now, under the name of that priest, certain Nestorian doctrines—when he, together with the holy Fathers, then openly anathematized the same impious Nestorius and his detestable doctrines, as we have said.

For what else is it than to display the Fathers seated in the holy Council of Chalcedon as liars or pretenders to a profession of right faith, if one says that some of them thought like Nestorius, by whose judgment Nestorius and his doctrines are seen to have been condemned?

Nor should it be supposed that our blessed Fathers in the holy Council of Chalcedon disregarded the insults supposedly directed by the venerable Theodore against Cyril of holy memory through his criticism of Cyril’s twelve chapters. Rather, either—because they had all the recent events before their eyes—they judged that Theodore had done nothing of the kind, or they considered the example of Cyril himself, of holy memory, worthy of imitation. After many serious written proceedings had been carried out against him by the Eastern bishops at Ephesus, when he was later reconciled with them, Cyril left those matters in silence, as though they had never occurred, out of love for peace, so that he might fulfill the apostolic saying which he writes to the Corinthians:

“Whomsoever you have forgiven anything, I also forgive” (2 Corinthians 2).

The holy Council of Chalcedon must also be believed to have intended this: when the aforementioned bishop Theodore received the teaching of Saint Cyril with such devoted conviction from the letters of Cyril that had been read and accepted in that same council, and even used testimonies from Cyril’s teaching in praising the letter of the most blessed Pope Leo, he appeared to have made complete satisfaction—even if it were established that he had formerly insulted Cyril—by reverently embracing the faith of the man whose error he had falsely suspected.

Therefore it is not fitting for us now to seek out or reopen anything supposedly omitted by our Fathers; and by every means we reject those who now approve of Cyril’s criticism or think that our holy Fathers approved of it.

Having therefore weighed the truth of these matters, we establish and decree that no one may do or publish anything under the charge of the name of Theodore, bishop of Cyrus, that would insult or disparage that most highly approved man of the Council of Chalcedon. But, while preserving in all things reverence for his person, we anathematize and condemn any writings or doctrines published under his name or under that of any other person [Note: Perhaps: “under his name, or that of any other person.” Hardouin] that are shown to agree with the errors of the wicked Nestorius and Eutyches.

For it is enough, and ought to be more than sufficient, that when we condemn and anathematize Nestorius together with Paul of Samosata and Bonosus, and Eutyches together with Valentinus and Apollinaris, as well as their errors and all other heretics with their doctrines, we likewise condemn those who, entangled in their errors and remaining incorrigible, have departed from the life of the present age. Thus we leave no perverse doctrine which is not found to have been excluded from the holy Church by the sentence pronounced by us with apostolic authority.

**I.** Again, however, we state this specifically: if anyone, while preserving the immutability of the divine nature, does not confess that the Word became flesh and that, from his conception in the Virgin’s womb, he united to himself the principles of human nature according to subsistence, but says that God the Word was present as though in an already existing man, so that the holy Virgin is not believed truly to be the Mother of God but is called so merely in words, let him be anathema.

**II.** If anyone denies that the union of the natures in Christ was made according to subsistence, but says that God the Word dwelt in a man existing separately, as in one of the righteous, and does not thus confess the union of the natures according to subsistence, so that God the Word remained and remains one subsistence or person with the flesh assumed, let him be anathema.

**III.** If anyone divides the evangelical and apostolic expressions concerning the one Christ in such a way that he also introduces a division of the natures united in him, let him be anathema.

**IV.** If anyone says that the one Jesus Christ, the true Son of God and that same true Son of man, possessed ignorance of future things or of the day of the last judgment, and that he could know as much as his divinity, dwelling in him as in another person, revealed to him, let him be anathema.

**V.** If anyone interprets the Apostle’s statement in the Letter to the Hebrews—that he learned obedience through experience and offered prayers and supplications to God with a loud cry and tears, to him who could save him from death—as referring to Christ stripped of divinity, who was perfected through the labors of virtue, so that this appears to introduce two Christs or two sons, and does not believe that one and the same Christ, the Son of God and man, is to be confessed and worshiped as existing from two natures and in two inseparable and undivided natures, let him be anathema.

Having thus rejected and condemned all these and similar blasphemies, by the provision of this present constitution we take the greatest care that, as we said above, nothing should be taken away from persons who rested in the peace and communion of the universal Church on the pretext of the perverse doctrine condemned by us. Rather, now that the detestable doctrines of the heresiarchs Nestorius and Eutyches and all their followers have been condemned, no insult should arise against those priests who died in the Catholic peace of the Church, as has been said—lest an occasion for injury arise from the very place where the reverence due to the holy Fathers ought instead to be preserved.

Concerning the letter of the venerable Ibas, formerly bishop of the city of Edessa, about which you likewise inquired, we nevertheless investigated with careful examination whether anything had been raised, debated, sought, or decided concerning it in former times by our Fathers. Since we are ignorant of the Greek language—as is known to everyone, and especially to your Piety—we searched most diligently through the records of the holy and venerable Council of Chalcedon in the synodal books, with the aid of our people who appear to possess knowledge of that language. We found clearly and openly that the case of the aforementioned venerable Ibas had been examined in two sessions of that council. From the proceedings held before Photius, bishop of Tyre, and Eustathius, bishop of Berytus, it appears that, among other matters, the letter in question was produced against him by his accusers.

When the discussion of his case had been concluded and the venerable Fathers were asked what seemed appropriate to be established concerning Ibas’s case, the following judgments consequently proceeded.

Paschasinus and Lucentius, most reverend bishops, and Boniface the presbyter, holding the place of the Apostolic See—for apostolic envoys have always been accustomed to speak and give confirmation first in synods—said through Paschasinus:

“Having reread the documents, we recognize from the judgment of the most reverend bishops that Ibas, the most reverend bishop, has been approved as innocent; for, having reread his letter, we recognize him as orthodox. Therefore we decree that the honor of the episcopate be restored to him and that the Church from which he was unjustly expelled while absent be restored to him. As for the most holy bishop Nonnus, who was appointed in his place shortly before, it will belong to the venerable bishop of the Church of Antioch to determine what ought to be decided or confirmed concerning him.”

Anatolius, most reverend archbishop of Constantinople, New Rome, said:

“The faith of the God-loving bishops and judges, together with the reading of all that followed, demonstrates that the most reverend Ibas is innocent of the accusations brought against him. Therefore I now remove every suspicion, since he agrees with and subscribes to the judgment concerning the faith which has now been issued by the holy council, and to the letters of the most holy archbishop of Rome, Leo. I judge him worthy of the episcopate and of having charge of the Church in which he formerly served.”

Maximus, most reverend bishop of Antioch, said:

“From what has just been reread, it is evident that the most reverend Ibas has been found innocent of all the charges brought against him. From the rereading of the letter, which was approved by the man who is his opponent, it has been shown that his written statement is orthodox.”

Since these matters thus stand in the judgment and decision of the holy Council of Chalcedon, and since they were declared in the interventions of the venerable bishops who held the place of the Apostolic See and in the statements of the other Fathers, we clearly understand that those known to have held the place of our most blessed predecessor Pope Leo in that holy council said:

“Having reread his letter, we recognize him as Catholic”;

and that Anatolius of Constantinople said:

“The reading of all that followed demonstrates that the most reverend Ibas is innocent of the charges which his accusers brought against him”;

while Maximus of Antioch said:

“From the reread text of the letter, which was brought forward by his adversary, his written statement has been shown to be Catholic.”

The other bishops are known not merely to have offered no opposition to these interventions but also to have given them the clearest assent.

Because of the proclamation of the faith through which Cyril, bishop of Alexandria and of venerable memory, John, the most reverend bishop of Antioch, and all the Eastern bishops returned to concord through Paul, bishop of the city of Emesa—and because Ibas, praising that proclamation in the same letter, willingly embraces it—the writing of Ibas the bishop was pronounced orthodox by the Fathers.

But the statements in Ibas’s own priestly letter which, through an error of understanding, were made as insults against Cyril of blessed memory were not accepted by the Fathers when they pronounced the letter orthodox at the holy Council of Chalcedon. Indeed, the venerable bishop himself, after receiving a better understanding of Cyril’s chapters, rejected those statements by changing his position, as is shown most clearly by the intervention of Eunomius, bishop of Nicomedia, who was present at that same holy Council of Chalcedon. It reads as follows:

Eunomius, bishop of Nicomedia, said:

“From what has now been reread, the blessed Ibas has already been approved as innocent. In those writings he also appears, by what he said, to have wrongly blamed the most blessed Cyril; but at the end he rightly confessed and rejected what he had blamed. Therefore I too decree that he is worthy of the episcopate, since he anathematizes Nestorius and Eutyches and their impious doctrines, agrees with what was written by the most holy archbishop Leo, and concurs with this universal council.”

The intervention of Juvenal, of venerable memory, signifies the same thing: Ibas the bishop, having previously detracted from Saint Cyril because he understood Cyril’s chapters otherwise, later professed that, after Cyril had explained them and Ibas had understood them, he had devotedly entered into communion with him and had changed his mind concerning what he had formerly understood otherwise. For this reason Juvenal decreed that Ibas should be restored to the episcopate, since he was orthodox with regard to his profession of faith. Juvenal said:

“Holy Scripture commands that those who turn back are to be received; therefore we also receive those returning from heretics. Accordingly, I foresee that the most reverend Ibas deserves mercy, because he is also an old man and, being orthodox, should retain the rank of the episcopate.”

From these words it is understood that if we receive those who come back from heretics, how could we fail to receive Ibas, who is orthodox and who, after hesitating in his understanding of the chapters of blessed Cyril and appearing to oppose him, has now turned away from the understanding in which he was mistaken, when it is certain that he is orthodox?

For Bishop Juvenal would not have said that Ibas was orthodox unless he had judged, from the words of his letter, that his profession of faith was orthodox. And that the intervention of Juvenal agrees with the intervention of Eunomius is shown by the very words of Eunomius’s intervention, which include the following:

“For in those writings he appeared, by what he said, to have wrongly blamed the most blessed Cyril; but at the end he rightly confessed and rejected what he had blamed.”

These words clearly show that nothing was reproved in Ibas’s confession of faith, which is known to have been praised; rather, Ibas rejected the wrong opinion he had held about blessed Cyril through a misleading understanding.

The same venerable bishop Ibas is also clearly said, from the preceding proceedings themselves, as the judgment of Photius and Eustathius contains, to have accepted and received everything done at the First Council of Ephesus, to have judged equally valid what had been established at Nicaea, and to have considered there to be no difference between that council and the others. He declared that he had praised Cyril’s holiness exceedingly and that Ibas had rightly known that care should be taken concerning those who, whether through suspicion or in some other way, might injure Cyril’s reputation for doctrine.

After the twelve chapters of blessed Cyril had been explained, and after the understanding which Saint Cyril had intended in those chapters had been made clear to him, Ibas also professed that he had regarded Cyril as orthodox together with all the Eastern bishops and had remained in communion with him until the end of his life.

From this it appears that Ibas first rejected the twelve chapters of blessed Cyril with an orthodox understanding, before he understood them, when he suspected that they proclaimed one nature in Christ; but that after their explanation he reverently received, with an orthodox understanding, what he recognized to have been rightly said.

It is also indubitably clear to the minds of all the faithful that Dioscorus, together with Eutyches, more gravely insulted blessed Cyril and the First Council of Ephesus at the Second Council of Ephesus through a heretical interpretation. They believed that Saint Cyril, in his twelve chapters, had proclaimed one nature in our Lord God Jesus Christ.

For this reason Dioscorus condemned certain Eastern bishops who refused to accept the proclamation of one nature. Among them he condemned Bishop Ibas as a heretic, specifically because of his profession of faith, in which he most openly confessed two natures, one power, and one person—that is, one Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. He recalled Eutyches as a Catholic because of his proclamation of one nature, while also condemning the person of Flavian, of holy memory, because he had spoken of two natures.

Dioscorus himself was therefore found more intent on destroying the First Council of Ephesus, which he defended under the guise of a detestable interpretation. Dioscorus and Eutyches, by praising Cyril, maligned him more gravely than Ibas did by criticizing him through the error of a false understanding.

For since praise and blame were directed toward one and the same interpretation, Dioscorus and Eutyches, who offered praise, were found to have praised with a heretical spirit and were therefore condemned by the holy Council of Chalcedon. Bishop Ibas, however, who initially criticized the chapters because, through error, he thought that they proclaimed one nature, later declared, after their intended meaning had been explained to him, that he was in communion with blessed Cyril together with all the Eastern bishops; and he was judged by that same Council of Chalcedon to have remained steadfast in the Catholic faith.

Therefore that council, seeing that Dioscorus and Eutyches—who attempted falsely to conceal themselves beneath the veil of blessed Cyril—were rather shown by Cyril’s own proclamations to be opposed to him, because they proclaimed with a blasphemous spirit one nature after the union, condemned Dioscorus together with Eutyches by the same and identical sentence. It destroyed the Second Council of Ephesus and confirmed the First.

Since the words of the prophet Ezekiel are brought against us—those which he spoke in the person of the Lord against the priests of Jerusalem who failed to distinguish evil from good:

“Her priests have despised my law and polluted my holy things; they did not distinguish between the holy and the profane, and they did not discern between what was clean and what was unclean” (Ezekiel 22),

your Piety, together with us and with the hearts of all the faithful, ought to understand from these words why we dare not reopen the judgment of the Council of Chalcedon. Otherwise the priests who sat there would, God forbid, be branded with the stain of heretical plots: they might be accused of having been unable to distinguish between the holy and the profane, and between what was clean and what was unclean, if they saw us now retracting, on any pretext, the cases of that holy council, which were concluded by its judgment with the assent of the Apostolic See.

Therefore, preserving in all things the discipline and judgment of the holy Fathers, and making every arrangement according to the account which we have given and which was declared by the judgment of the Council of Chalcedon—and since the truth shines with sufficient clarity from the words of the letter of the venerable Ibas rightly and piously understood, from the proceedings held before Photius and Eustathius, and from the examination of the intention of Bishop Ibas himself in the presence of those who were present—we establish and decree by the authority of our present judgment that our Fathers sitting at Chalcedon most justly pronounced the faith of that venerable man, Bishop Ibas, orthodox, and that they recognized the criticism of blessed Cyril, which had arisen humanly through an error of understanding, as cleansed by an appropriate satisfaction.

Accordingly, in all matters, and also in the often-mentioned letter of the venerable Ibas, we decree that the judgment of the Fathers sitting at Chalcedon remains unimpaired.

Nor do we permit anyone belonging to ecclesiastical orders or dignities ever to presume, concerning the case of that letter or concerning other matters judged, ordered, defined, and arranged at the Council of Chalcedon with the agreement of the vicars of the Apostolic See, to introduce any rash novelty—as though those matters were incomplete or blameworthy—whether by addition, subtraction, alteration, or in any other manner.

By the same reasoning we decree that no one may suppose that anything should be taken away from the letter of blessed Cyril to which the twelve chapters are appended, or from the chapters themselves promulgated against the perfidy of Nestorius. For it is established that Ibas, after the meaning of those chapters had been explained to him, remained throughout his life in communion with blessed Cyril among all the Eastern bishops, rejecting and refusing to accept those interpretations which would imply, whether from the aforementioned letter of Ibas the bishop or from everything judged, ordered, defined, and arranged at the holy Council of Chalcedon, that anything had been adapted either to assert Nestorius’s perverse doctrine by the authority of that council or to excuse Nestorius himself.

And lest anyone perhaps consider it uncertain that the blessed Pope Leo had instructed the aforementioned legates and vicars of the Apostolic See only concerning the faith, and not also concerning the restoration of bishops who had been improperly deposed—and lest anyone think that the case of Ibas, bishop of the city of Edessa, had been discussed before the holy Fathers as though unnecessarily—let him know that the most blessed Pope Leo wrote the following, among other things, to the holy Council of Chalcedon:

“Since we are not unaware that the condition of many Churches has been disturbed by evil rivalries, and that many bishops who refused to accept heresy were driven from their sees and carried into exile, while others were substituted in the places of those who were still alive, the medicine of justice must first be applied to these wounds, so that no one may be deprived of what is his own or make use of what belongs to another.”

And lest anyone doubt whether the proceedings concerning the restoration of bishops at the Council of Chalcedon were brought to the knowledge of the most blessed Leo and confirmed by him, let him rather take care to read the report of the council sent to our most blessed predecessor Leo. At its end, among other things, it says:

“We have taken care to inform you of the whole force of the proceedings, both for the stability of our position and for the confirmation and arrangement of what has been done by us.”

After receiving this report, the same most blessed Pope Leo wrote to the Augusta Pulcheria, of pious memory, giving thanks for the restored bishops:

“Let your Clemency therefore know that the entire Roman Church greatly rejoices over all the works of your faith, both because you have assisted our legation with pious affection in every respect and because you have brought back the Catholic priests who had been unjustly expelled from their Churches.”

Thus, since all the proceedings were sent to the most blessed Pope Leo, knowledge of the matters carried out was brought to him; and in the action of returning thanks, confirmation of those proceedings is made clear.

We do not doubt, therefore, that it has been made evident to the understanding of all the faithful what form of administering affairs was entrusted by the blessed Pope Leo to his vicars, who were present at the council in his place; what actions they received from him for overcoming the opposition; and what was established by that general council while the bishop of the Apostolic See presided and consented through his vicars. These decisions may neither be diminished, increased, violated, nor lawfully reopened by anyone.

That the statutes of the venerable Council of Chalcedon may not be overturned or reopened under any pretext or title is taught by a few of the many constitutions of our predecessors, especially by the letters of that blessed predecessor of ours, Leo, under whose supreme authority the holy Council of Chalcedon flourished through his vicars.

For in a letter to the Augusta Leo, of pious memory, he says:

“These gifts of God are bestowed upon us by divine generosity only if we are not found ungrateful for what has been granted and do not, as though we had received nothing, instead await contrary things. For to seek what has been revealed, to reopen what has been completed, and to overturn what has been defined—what else is this than to fail to give thanks for what has been received and to reach out, through the wicked desires of deadly cupidity, for the fruit of the forbidden tree?”

And a little later:

“Let your Piety therefore know, venerable emperor, that those whom I promise will be sent from the Apostolic See are not coming to fight against the enemies of the faith or to contend with them, because we dare not enter into any debate concerning matters defined at Nicaea and Chalcedon according to God’s will, as though they were doubtful or unstable—matters which such authority, through the Holy Spirit, has brought to completion.”

Likewise, the same blessed predecessor of ours, Pope Leo, wrote in another letter to the aforementioned venerable Augustus:

“Do not permit struggles already extinguished to rise again through renewed disturbances against the triumphs of the right hand of the Almighty, especially since it is wholly impermissible to revive the assaults of heretics long ago condemned [perhaps: “these”], and since this fruit is owed to pious labors: that the fullness of the Church may remain secure in the solidity of its unity, and that nothing whatsoever may be reopened of what has been rightly established. For to wish to contend after legitimate and divinely inspired constitutions is not the attitude of a peaceful spirit but of a rebellious one, as the Apostle says: ‘Contending over words is useful for nothing except the subversion of those who hear’ (2 Timothy 2). For if it were always permissible to dispute by human persuasion, there could never be a lack of those who would dare to resist the truth and rely upon the verbosity of worldly wisdom.”

Likewise, a little later:

“We must piously and steadfastly take care lest, while such disputation is admitted, authority be diminished in matters that have been divinely defined.”

Likewise, in a letter of Pope Leo to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople:

“Let your diligence see to it that this exhortation may come to the knowledge of all the brethren, because—as must often be said—the entire Christian religion is disturbed if anything whatsoever is torn away from what was established at Chalcedon, or if you permit anything composed by divine disposition to be violated by any novelty.”

The most blessed predecessor of ours, Pope Simplicius, likewise says the following to the Augustus Zeno, among other things:

“Let no one who is uncertain in reason and fearful in mind expect that anything new will be reopened after the Council of Chalcedon against its definitions, because throughout the world what has been established by the universal body of priests is maintained with unbreakable observance.”

Likewise, the aforementioned Pope Simplicius to the Augustus Zeno:

“Let no access be opened to the ears of your Piety for minds bent on destruction; let no confidence be granted for reopening matters of the greatest antiquity. Thus, when the machinations of all heresies have been struck down by ecclesiastical decrees, they are never permitted to restore, through renewed assaults, the conflicts that have been crushed.”

Likewise, the aforementioned Pope Simplicius to the aforesaid Augustus Zeno:

“Command that the constitutions of the Council of Chalcedon, and what my predecessor Leo of blessed memory taught fully according to apostolic tradition, remain unimpaired, because what has been put to rest by their definition cannot in any way be reopened.”

[Col. 0111A] It is therefore clear from the testimonies cited above of the Fathers what caution we must maintain for the rectitude of the Apostolic See and for the welfare of the universal Church. Mindful of this caution ourselves, we now annul, insofar as it concerns the case of the Three Chapters, the letter which we had formerly sent to Mennas, bishop of Constantinople. That letter had been received when Mennas, bishop of holy memory, presented it to your Clemency in the presence of several priests and the glorious senate, and when your Piety, with his agreement, returned it to us.

Yet we have in no way ceased to exercise the vigilance appropriate to our position and purpose. We have taken care to show everyone the proper reverence owed to the Council of Chalcedon, as the text of that same letter bears witness. To demonstrate our caution, we have appended a very small portion from among many passages. When these are carefully examined, it is clearly shown how the holy Council of Chalcedon has remained and continues to remain inviolate among us.

For in that same letter of ours we are certain to have written the following concerning the council, among other things:

“Since it is plainly clear to us by manifest reason that anyone who attempts to do anything as an insult to the aforementioned council will harm himself rather than it.”

Likewise, after other matters:

If it had been clearly demonstrated to us that these matters were contained rather in the official records themselves, no author of such presumption would dare to judge as doubtful anything that had been brought before that most holy judgment. For it must be believed that those who were then present, having a more immediate memory of the events, could have sought out more carefully than the written record some things, or defined more certainly what, after so long a time, appears to us obscure and ambiguous, although this too is owed to the reverence due to synods: even in matters less understood, their authority must be accepted. Further on:

“While everything defined in the venerable councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus I, and Chalcedon, and confirmed by the authority of our predecessors, remains intact and in its perpetual validity; while all those condemned in the aforesaid holy councils are without doubt condemned, and those whom the same synods decreed to be absolved are likewise absolved.”

Further on:

“We subject also to the sentence of anathema anyone who accepts as possessing any validity whatever is found to have been done or written, either at present or at any time in this matter, whether by us or by anyone else, against the aforesaid Council of Chalcedon. And let the holy Council of Chalcedon, whose validity is great and unshakable, retain its perpetual and venerable authority, just as the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, and Ephesus I possess theirs.” Further on:

“We anathematize also anyone who does not faithfully follow and equally venerate the most holy Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus I, and Chalcedon, consonant with the apostles in one and undefiled faith and strengthened by the bishops of the Apostolic See; and anyone who wishes to correct as wrongly stated, or to supplement as incomplete, what was done in those councils that we have named.”

Behold, venerable emperor, it is demonstrated more clearly than daylight that we have always held this intention regarding the reverence due to the four holy synods: that whatever was defined, established, or judged by the holy Fathers assembled in them should remain inviolate. Since, therefore, everything contained concerning the person of Ibas and his letter in the interventions of the holy Fathers and the vicars of the Apostolic See remains in force, let this suffice for all of us and for all Catholics, with equal resolve—namely, what the holy synod itself there loudly declared sufficient for it, saying: “Let him now anathematize Nestorius and his doctrines.” By this anathema, repeatedly pronounced by Bishop Ibas against the most wicked Nestorius and Eutyches, the will of the entire synod was fully satisfied.

Having therefore arranged these matters with every precaution and diligence on every side, in order to preserve the inviolable reverence due to the aforesaid synods and to their venerable decrees, and remembering that it is written (Proverbs 22) that we must not overstep the boundaries of our fathers, we establish and decree that no one belonging to ecclesiastical orders or dignities may write, publish, compose, or teach anything contrary to what we have asserted or established by this present decree concerning the often-mentioned Three Chapters, nor raise any further question after the present definition. If anything concerning those same Three Chapters has been or shall be done, said, or written contrary to what we have asserted or established here, in the name of anyone belonging to ecclesiastical orders or dignities, and if it is found anywhere by anyone, we reject it in every way by the authority of the Apostolic See, which by the grace of God we preside over.

## SUBSCRIPTION

With God’s help and by his grace, I, Vigilius, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, have subscribed to this decree of ours.

Given on the day before the Ides of May, during the reign of our lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus, in the twenty-seventh year, and in the twelfth year after the consulship of Basil, a man of most distinguished rank, in the city of Constantinople (A.D. 553).

# LETTER DIRECTED BY THE CLERICS OF ITALY TO THE FRANKISH LEGATES WHO WERE SETTING OUT FOR CONSTANTINOPLE

In this letter they urge the legates to endeavor to provide support and assistance to Pope Vigilius and to Dacius, bishop of Milan, who were being harassed in that same city by the emperor Justinian on account of the controversy over the Three Chapters. (C)

[Col. 0113]

## JACQUES SIRMOND’S NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LETTER

[Col. 0113B]

We were persuaded to place the following letter here not merely because it mentions the letter of Pope Vigilius to Aurelian of Arles, which we presented shortly before, and because, since it was written to the Frankish legates, it seems in no way foreign to our purpose; but chiefly because it contains much material for illuminating the history of Vigilius that is scarcely found elsewhere. As for the events it mentions as having been carried out by force against him in the Basilica of Saint Peter in the Hormisda district, these are confirmed by Vigilius’s own Letter 15. Since that letter is mutilated in the commonly circulated copies, it survives complete in a manuscript of Saint Mary of Reims, from which we also drew this letter of ours.

[Note: [Col. 0113C] Although the letter bears no subscription, the letter itself reveals the year in which it was written: it counts the sixth year from Pope Vigilius’s entry into the city of Constantinople, and the second from the time when Anastasius had been sent from Aurelian by the bishop to Vigilius. For Vigilius’s Letter 7 shows that Anastasius reached Vigilius on the day before the Ides of July in A.D. 550. Marcellinus, in his Chronicle, states that Vigilius entered Constantinople at the beginning of A.D. 547. We therefore assigned the letter to the year 552. JAC. SIRMONDUS.

—Sirmond published this little work after Baronius’s death and believed it to have been written in the year 552, as did Cointius in his notice for the year 552. Cardinal Norisius, however, demonstrates in his dissertation on the Fifth Synod that it was written in 551, on the ground that it makes no mention of Vigilius’s flight to the nearby city of Chalcedon. Secondly, the work says that a certain Anastasius, whom the holy bishop Aurelian of the city of Arles had sent to the most blessed pope two years earlier, was lying about something there in Gaul, because he too, in order to be allowed to leave Constantinople, promised that he would incline the minds of all the Gallican bishops to condemn the Chapters on account of which these scandals had arisen. They gave him many rewards and compelled him there to swear solemnly that he would fulfill this promise; nor did they allow the most blessed pope, through this same Anastasius, to write to his brother bishops in Gaul about what was being done in the matter, and so forth. But Anastasius delivered the letter of the bishop of Arles to Vigilius on the day before the Ides of July in the year 549, as is stated at the end of that letter. Therefore, since he came to Vigilius two years earlier, this little work was written in 551.

Furthermore, it says in the work: “For the most blessed Pope Vigilius came there six years ago—or rather, to speak more truthfully, was brought there almost by force.” And in his encyclical, dated 5 February 552, Vigilius testifies that he had left Rome seven years earlier. Thus, if the year 552 is the seventh year from Vigilius’s departure from the city of Rome, the year 551 is the sixth from that departure—not from his arrival in Constantinople, which the clerics of Italy do not have in view.

Nor should anyone say, with Sirmond, that the letter counts the sixth year from Vigilius’s entry into Constantinople and the second from the time Anastasius was sent by the bishop of Arles to Vigilius, and that Anastasius reached Vigilius on the day before the Ides of July in A.D. 550, while Vigilius entered Constantinople at the beginning of 547. For Anastasius reached Constantinople not in the preceding year but in 549, as Vigilius himself testifies in the letter cited immediately above and quoted by Baronius in its proper place. That letter was written on the third day before the Kalends of May in the year 550, and Vigilius states that he received it from Anastasius on the day before the Ides of July; hence the date was the day before the Ides of July in the year 549.

Finally, that little work cannot have been written in 552, since, as its title states, it was delivered to the Frankish legates who were setting out for Constantinople. They were sent to Constantinople by Theudebald, king of the Franks, in 551, the seventeenth year of the Gothic War, which continued until the spring of the following year. It should not be supposed that the legates set out during the winter of that year. For Procopius, in Book IV of the Gothic War, chapter 24, speaking of events in the seventeenth year of the Gothic War, says that when the Franks and Goths had agreed not to attack one another with arms in Italy, Justinian Augustus sent Leontius the senator as an envoy to Theudebald, king of the Franks, asking him to join him in taking up arms against the Goths and to surrender the places that Theudebert had occupied in Italy contrary to the terms of the treaty. But Theudebald replied to Leontius that he could not come to join the war against the Goths and, as for those places, that his father Theudebert had not taken them from the Romans. “But concerning these matters,” said Theudebald, “we shall shortly send envoys to Byzantium.” Having said this, he dismissed Leontius and sent Leudard, a Frank by birth, to Justinian Augustus together with three others. When they reached Byzantium, says Procopius, they accomplished satisfactorily the business for which they had come. If, therefore, that embassy took place in 551, this little work was written and delivered to the legates in that year. ANT. PAGI.]

# LETTER TO THE LEGATES

[Col. 0114C]

The Christian faith spreads among all peoples through the operation of divine grace, so that, however much anyone may prosper in this world, through that faith and love he desires all the more to obtain the things that are eternal, knowing that in this life no one can exist forever, whereas in the next he will be either in rest or in everlasting punishments.

Therefore, having heard that Your Glory had been sent on an embassy to the royal city, and having also learned from certain persons who claimed to know you of your reputation and wisdom, we have sent you, to instruct you on whatever occasion may arise, a brief account of the many things that have taken place. Through it you may learn of the persecutions and acts of violence suffered there by Catholic priests and by all who wish to observe the ecclesiastical rules.

For when the most blessed Pope Vigilius came there six years ago [A.D. 547, in January]—or rather, to speak more truthfully, was brought there almost by force—they began to await his making a condemnation of certain Chapters by which the holy Council of Chalcedon, which under the leadership of the most blessed Pope Leo had then defended the Catholic faith against various heresies, would in every way be undermined.

But when Pope Vigilius refused to give his consent in this matter, such violence was already being used that he publicly cried out in an assembly: “I call you to witness that, although you hold me captive, you cannot make the blessed Apostle Peter captive.”

Nevertheless, after discussions had been held, the aforesaid holy Pope Vigilius arranged the matter under a certain dispensation, carefully warning that the aforesaid synod should suffer no injury under any pretext. Although the African and Dalmatian priests did not agree to accept even what the pope had done, the often-mentioned most blessed Pope Vigilius was again compelled to condemn the Chapters outright, without any mention of the Council of Chalcedon.

But the pope refused to do this, and seeing that he was being pressed too severely, he then said to the most serene emperor: “Let five or six of our brothers, bishops from every province, come here, and whatever, after discussion and in tranquillity, appears right to all, we shall settle peacefully. For without the consent of all I will in no way agree to do this alone—something that both causes the Council of Chalcedon to be called into question and creates scandal for my brothers.”

The most merciful emperor therefore sent envoys to Africa and Illyricum, so that the bishops might come. But no one from Illyricum was willing to come. When it was being reported that some men from Africa were already approaching the royal city, Pope Vigilius told the emperor that, if what he had previously decreed was not sufficient for him, he should restore it and have the matter discussed anew with those whose arrival had been announced.

God therefore granted that, by this means, the holy Pope Vigilius publicly withdrew the decree he had made in this matter, declaring that if any Greek bishop, until the matter had been considered by a universal council, did anything concerning these Chapters or consented to those who did so, he would be separated from communion with the Apostolic See. For the Greek bishops themselves had frequently condemned the Chapters at the emperor’s desire—the very action from which the controversy arose—but the most blessed pope had received their signatures back from the most serene emperor.

The Greek bishops possess rich and wealthy churches, and they cannot endure being suspended for two months from control of ecclesiastical property. For this reason, according to the time and the wishes of the emperors, they agree without dispute to whatever is demanded of them.

When the African bishops, so often mentioned, had arrived in the royal city, they began to extort their consent to the condemnation of the Chapters, now by blandishments and now by threats. But when they could not extort it from them by any means, a case was fabricated against the holy Reparatus, bishop of Carthage, on the pretext that he had caused Areobindus, master of the soldiers, to be killed by Guntarith, the tyrant in Africa; and under this pretext he was deported into exile.

Seeing this, two others, distinguished among them both for the holiness of their lives and for their knowledge of the divine Scriptures, fled to holy Euphemia in Chalcedon. To this day they remain there in such distress that, although suffering from bodily illness and not even deemed worthy of finding a physician, they endure immense dangers.

The prefect of Africa, whenever he found in Africa bishops who either had personal cases, or were simple and ignorant, or were venal and ready for a reward, gathered them together and sent each one away from there. One of these, however, had been expelled from the royal city in disgrace seven years earlier on account of his adulteries, placed on a ship, and sent to Africa.

And behold, through what sort of men dissensions and scandals are generated in the holy Church throughout the various provinces. They also sent to Carthage and had another bishop ordained in the place of the bishop Saint Reparatus, contrary to every rule and every decree of the Fathers. They are said to have done this with an enormous shedding of blood and the slaughter of many innocent people.

At Constantinople they again began to compel the most blessed Pope Vigilius to condemn the same Chapters with the Greek bishops if the African, Illyrian, and Dalmatian bishops were unwilling to do so. But when the most blessed Pope Vigilius absolutely refused, they caused edicts issued in the emperor’s name to be posted both in the Constantinopolitan Church and in various places, ordering that the same Chapters be condemned.

After this had been done, the most blessed pope warned all the bishops, saying: “Whoever wishes to give his consent to these edicts should know that he is suspended from communion with the Apostolic See.”

Saint Dacius, bishop of Milan, also submitted a protest on behalf of all, with a loud outcry, saying: “Behold, I, together with that part of all the priests among whom my Church is established—that is, those of Gaul, Burgundy, Spain, Liguria, Emilia, and Venetia—call you to witness that whoever consents to these edicts will not be able to have the bishops of the aforesaid provinces as his communicants, because it is clear to me that these edicts disturb the holy Council of Chalcedon and the Catholic faith.”

Because of this, the imperial anger was kindled against the most blessed pope and against Bishop Dacius. They began to act against them with such severity that, unless they had taken refuge in the basilicas of the saints, they would have been put to death.

Yet the most blessed Pope Vigilius did not even deserve to have a safe seat in the Basilica of Blessed Peter. Indeed, a praetor—the official to whom only thieves and murderers are normally assigned—was sent there. He entered the aforesaid basilica with a multitude of soldiers carrying drawn swords and bent bows.

When the holy pope saw this, he embraced the altar columns. But the praetor, aroused by ferocity and anger, first dragged his deacons and clerics from the altar by their hair. Then some seized the holy pope by the feet, others by the hair and beard, and cruelly dragged him away.

But when he would not release the altar columns, the altar collapsed, and some of the columns were broken; and, as far as they were concerned, he would have been thrown there among the pieces upon the altar. But God, who deigns always to be present in such distress, moved the hearts both of some of the soldiers and of the people who had come in response to the tumult to pity. They began to utter shouts and cries, and so it happened that the aforesaid praetor, that unjust judge, terrified, fled with the agents of his cruelty.

Afterward, however, the most blessed pope, Saint Bishop Dacius, and all who had taken refuge with them in the holy places received assurances under oath that no one would use violence against them thereafter or extort anything from them against their will concerning the ecclesiastical case; and thus for the time being they came out.

Even today they generate various disturbances and annoyances both against them and against the different persons in their service, sending clerics and servants against them with bribes so that they may stand in their presence and publicly insult them, and eject some of those placed in their service from their lodgings.

But those men endure everything patiently with God’s help, provided that they do not appear to give assent to any prejudice against the holy Church or to any innovation.

Some men were also sent to the provinces of Italy, so that, if possible, by lying about their names—that is, about the most blessed pope and the holy Bishop Dacius—they might stir up hatred against them in those regions and persuade people to ordain other bishops in their place who would consent to innovations.

They even secretly solicited one notary descended from the servants of the most blessed pope. He is said to imitate the hand of the holy pope, and, as we have learned, they had certain documents falsely written in his name. They sent a certain Stephanus, one of those whom they had solicited, to Italy with envoys of the Goths, so that through falsehoods and deceit they might appear to stir up the minds of some people in those regions against the most blessed pope—something God forbid should happen.

Therefore we beseech and adjure Your Glory, by the future judgment of our God, which every human condition fears, to report all these things quickly to your provinces, lest either these men who have been sent deceive them, or a certain Anastasius, whom the holy bishop Aurelian of the city of Arles had sent to the most blessed pope two years earlier, lie about something there in Gaul.

For when he himself was unable to leave Constantinople, he adopted the plan of promising that he would incline the minds of all the Gallican bishops to condemn the Chapters on account of which these scandals had arisen. They gave him many rewards and compelled him there to swear solemnly that he would fulfill this promise. Nor did they allow the most blessed pope, through this same Anastasius, to write to his brother bishops in Gaul about what was being done in this matter, except only about other matters and about the fact that he guarded and preserved the Catholic faith and the reverence due to the four synods according to the tradition of the Fathers.

Therefore may your prudence, so that it may receive from Almighty God both great recompense in this world and eternal life in the next, deign to write about all this to the province with every precaution and haste. Warn them that the bishops of those regions should send letters to the most blessed pope and to holy Bishop Dacius, steadfastly refusing to allow any innovations, and that they should strengthen their hearts by fraternal consolation.

But also hasten, with God’s help, to assist the holy Bishop Dacius in the royal city as much as you can in this matter. Ask that he be permitted to return to his Church after fifteen or sixteen years. For, as you know well, since almost all the bishops whom he ordinarily ordains have died, an immense multitude of the people is dying without baptism.

Ask also that you be allowed to see that same holy Dacius and to inquire from him what the reason is that he has not returned to his Church for so long a time.

Nevertheless, be careful: those who wish the Chapters to be condemned pretend that they are defending the Catholic faith and venerating the Council of Chalcedon together with all of us, so that those who do not know their intention may think that they are seeking something unjust.

You, Christian and noble men, be vigilant, so that you may appear to have provided some remedy or consolation to the priests of the Christian people, who, under the weight of persecution, utter groans from the deepest parts of their being. Thus may God, on the day of recompense, grant a great reward and splendid gifts in return for this service.

For certain utterly trustworthy persons who came from Constantinople have truthfully confirmed that all these things took place in this way. They have also reported that many cruel acts were committed, or are being committed, against various African deacons and clerics who refuse to consent to them, and that all Romans have been forbidden to approach the most blessed pope.

We have hastened, in our anxiety, to inform Your Glory briefly of all these matters, so that, for the remedy of your souls, you may make it your concern above all your actions to consider this matter, which belongs especially to God. Thus, on the day of judgment, as it has been said, you may find not offense on account of negligence but reward for a good deed.

# COPY OF THE SACRED LETTER OF JUSTINIAN WRITTEN TO THE MOST BLESSED JOHN, METROPOLITAN BISHOP

We inform Your Holiness that you are to gather all the most religious bishops who belong to your synod, proceed to the city of Mopsuestia, and conduct a careful inquiry among all the elderly men assembled there, whether clerics or laymen. You are to learn from them whether they know the time when the name of Theodore was removed from the sacred diptychs.

[Note: [Col. 0119D] Older books read: “Theodore from the sacred…”]

[Col. 0119B] But if they do not remember when this took place,

[Note: [Col. 0119D] The same books read: “But if.” A little later they read “but the other,” and “but you.”]

let them confess precisely this: that they do not know the name of Theodore to have been inserted or proclaimed in the holy diptychs. Let the diptychs themselves also be brought before you, so that you may learn whose name was inserted in his place. Having received such confessions into the official records and joined them to your reports, let Your Holiness and the other most religious bishops subscribe to them. Then send one copy to us and another to the most holy pope.

Let this also be made clear: let each of those who confess state and make known how many years ago this occurred. You, for your part, must indicate in your own confessions the aforesaid Chapter and whom you found inserted in Theodore’s place.

We have also written to the magnificent Marthanius concerning this, so that these matters may be carried out without any delay and sent to us.

I have read it.

Given at Constantinople on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, in the twenty-fourth year of the reign of our lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus, and the ninth year after the consulship of Basil, a man of most distinguished rank (A.D. 550).

[Note: [Col. 0119D] Read “perpetual,” that is, *perpetui*. The same applies in the following letter.]

# ANOTHER LETTER OF JUSTINIAN TO COSMAS, MOST HOLY BISHOP OF MOPSUESTIA

We inform Your Holiness that we ordered John, the most blessed metropolitan of the city of Anazarbus [Justinianopolis], to gather all the bishops of the province, proceed to your city, and conduct a careful inquiry among all the elderly men assembled among you, whether clerics or laymen. They are to learn from them whether they know when the name of Theodore was removed from the holy diptychs.

[Col. 0119D] But if they do not remember the time when this occurred,

[Note: [Col. 0119D] Older books read: “But if.” Later they read “but the other.” Immediately afterward: “And let this also…”]

let them also confess this very thing: that they do not know the name of Theodore to have been inserted or proclaimed in the holy diptychs in the church itself.

The sacred diptychs themselves must therefore be brought forth, so that all the most religious bishops may learn in what order the names of the bishops are recited in the diptychs. You must make this known through your report. Having received the confessions into the official records and joined them to your reports, let all the bishops assembled subscribe, and then send one copy to us and another to the most holy pope.

Let this also be made clear in their confessions: each one must state and make known how many years ago this occurred.

I have read it.

Given at Constantinople on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the twenty-fourth year of the reign of our lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus, and the ninth year after the consulship of Basil, a man of most distinguished rank.

# REPORT OF THE SECOND ECUMENICAL COUNCIL OF CONSTANTINOPLE TO VIGILIUS (C)

[Col. 0120B]

It was truly fitting that, since you have attained the first dignity among priests,

[Note: [Col. 0119D] Parisian manuscript: “first.” Perhaps: “among the priesthood.”]

[Note: [Col. 0119D] Older books: “of the priesthood.”]

most holy one,

[Note: [Col. 0119D] Parisian manuscript: “most holy.”]

the matters concerning the condition of the holy Churches should be made known to Your divinely honored Blessedness.

Our most Christian emperor, considering this carefully,

[Note: [Col. 0120D] The same codex reads: “considering this most earnestly.”]

ordered that certain matters raised concerning Theodore, formerly bishop of the Church of Mopsuestia, be reported to your knowledge.

For in a pious letter addressed to us,

[Note: [Col. 0120D] The same codex reads: “in a letter sent to us.”]

he urged us to assemble in the city of Mopsuestia, which is one of the cities of Second Cilicia, and to investigate carefully when Theodore, formerly bishop of that city, was removed from the sacred diptychs, and to make the matter clear both to his tranquillity and to Your divinely honored Blessedness.

Therefore, immediately approaching Mopsuestia,

[Col. 0120C] we gathered the most religious clergy and the faithful people of the city, choosing those who were older and who might perhaps retain in memory the details of what was being investigated.

[Note: [Col. 0120D] Bellovacensis manuscript: “might have been able to retain.”]

Presenting them with the divine and revered Gospels, so that they might cleanse their testimony of suspicion, we invited them to say whether they knew at what time the name of the ancient Theodore had been removed from the sacred diptychs.

But they swore that it was many years ago, beyond the reach of their memory, since no commemoration of that same Theodore had been entered in the sacred diptychs. They asserted that Cyril, of revered memory, bishop of the city of Alexandria, had been inscribed in his place,

[Note: [Col. 0120D] The same books read: “had been inscribed.”]

and that they had heard this from their fathers.

[Note: [Col. 0120D] Parisian manuscript: “they assert that they had heard this.”]

Investigating the details of what they said, we also examined the sacred diptychs themselves and were considering the enumeration of the deceased bishops.

[Note: [Col. 0120D] The same codex reads: “we considered.”]

We found no mention of Theodore in the earlier periods. But at the very end of the sacred diptychs Theodore was written, and everyone said that he had recently died and that he came from the province of Galatia.

[Col. 0121A] We all know that he, having become a member of our council, died three years ago.

[Note: [Col. 0121B] Older books read: “your council.”]

[Note: [Col. 0121B] Parisian manuscript: “we learned.”]

Let the official records themselves make these matters known to you, most holy ones. We have attached them to our humble report and sent them for your information.

But we ask you, divinely inspired and most religious men, who are pleasing to God,

[Note: [Col. 0122B] Older books read: “who appease God.”]

not to disdain supporting us by your prayers.

# OATH OF POPE VIGILIUS

The most blessed Pope Vigilius swore to the most pious emperor, in our presence—that is, in the presence of me, Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, and of me, the patrician Cethegus—by the power of the holy nails with which our Lord God Jesus Christ was crucified, and by the holy four Gospels, and likewise by the power of this holy bridle and by these holy four Gospels:

that he would be of one mind and one will with Your Piety in wishing and striving for this, and would act, insofar as he was able, so that these Three Chapters—that is, Theodore of Mopsuestia together with his writings, the letter called the letter of Ibas, and the writings of Theodoret against the orthodox faith and against the Twelve Chapters pronounced by Saint Cyril—should be condemned and anathematized;

and that neither he nor anyone whom he could trust, whether from the clerical order or among the laity, would act, speak, or secretly give counsel concerning these Chapters against the will of Your Piety.

If anyone said anything contrary to him, whether concerning these Chapters, the faith, or against the commonwealth, he would reveal that person and what he had said to Your Piety without fear of death. on condition that, because of his position, Your Piety would not betray his person.

And while he observed these obligations toward Your Piety, you promised to preserve his honor in every respect, as well as to safeguard and, with God’s help, defend his person and reputation, and to preserve the privileges of his Church.

You also promised that these documents would be shown to no one.

[Perhaps: “that these documents be shown to no one.”]

Furthermore, I promise that, in this matter of the Three Chapters, whatever ought to be done, we shall discuss jointly,

[Col. 0122B] [Perhaps: “let us discuss jointly”;]

and whatever seems useful to us, we shall do with God’s help.

This oath was given on the fifteenth day of August, in the thirteenth indiction, in the twenty-third year of the reign of our lord Justinian, nine times after the consulship of Basil, a man of most distinguished rank.

I, Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia by the mercy of God, have subscribed as witness to this oath-document.

I, Flavius Cethegus, patrician, have subscribed as witness to this oath-document.

[Note: [Col. 0121] The Reverend Father John Garnerius proves this to be a spurious letter in his notes on Liberatus’s *Breviarium*. HARDUIN.]

# DECRETAL LETTER OF POPE VIGILIUS IN CONFIRMATION OF THE FIFTH ECUMENICAL SYNOD

(From a manuscript in the Royal Library.)

[Note: [Col. 0121] The Greek and Latin versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0121]

[Col. 0121C] To the beloved brother Eutychius: Vigilius.

## To the beloved brother Eutychius, Vigilius

No one is unaware of the scandals which the enemy of the human race has stirred up throughout the whole world. He has driven each person, intent on fulfilling his own evil purpose by whatever means toward the overthrow of the Church of God established throughout the entire inhabited world, to fabricate various things—not only in his own name but also in ours and in that of others—by speaking or writing. He has brought matters to such a point that, while we were living in the imperial city with our brothers and fellow bishops, defending the four councils with equal reverence and continuing blamelessly in the one same faith of those four councils, he attempted by the sophistries of such wicked cunning to divide us, so that we, who have become and remain united in one faith, might disregard brotherly love and be led into discord. [Col. 0121D]

But since Christ our God, who is the true light, which darkness does not overcome, has recalled the inhabited world to peace, after removing every confusion from our minds, and has restored the Church, so that what ought to be defined by us might be salutarily accomplished through the Lord’s revelation and the discovery of truth, therefore let your entire brotherhood know that we, together with these same brothers of ours, accept in every respect and with devout mind venerate, and unanimously preserve, the four councils: namely, that at Nicaea, that at Constantinople, the First at Ephesus, and that at Chalcedon. And we judge those who do not follow these holy councils in everything defined by them concerning the holy faith to be aliens from the assembly of the holy and catholic Church.

Therefore, wishing your brotherhood to know what has been done by us, we make it manifest to you in this letter. Since no one doubts how many and how serious matters have been stirred up concerning the Three Chapters—that is, concerning Theodore, formerly bishop of Mopsuestia, and his writings, as well as the writings of Theodoret, and the letter said to have been written by Ibas to Maris the Persian—and since various things have been said and written concerning those three chapters, then, if in every matter reason requires that what is being investigated be reconsidered, and if it ought not to be a matter of shame that what was omitted at the beginning but later discovered through zeal for truth should be made public, how much more fitting is it that the same practice be observed in ecclesiastical controversies?

This is especially so since it is clear that our Fathers, and above all the most blessed Augustine, who shone in the divine Scriptures and was a teacher of Roman eloquence, reconsidered his own writings, corrected what he had said, and added what he had omitted but later discovered. We too, encouraged by such examples, never ceased investigating, in the matter of the Three Chapters mentioned above, what more truly might be found concerning those three chapters in the writings of our Fathers. Hence it became clear, through manifest truth, that the writings of the aforesaid Theodore of Mopsuestia, everywhere denounced, contained many things contrary to the orthodox faith and to the teachings of the holy Fathers. Accordingly, the holy Fathers, writing against him, left their own treatises for the instruction of the holy Church.

For among his other blasphemies we plainly find that he said that the Word of God was one and Christ another, harassed by the passions of the soul and the desires of the flesh, and that, gradually withdrawing from lesser things toward better ones, he attained this through progress in his works and became blameless in his conduct. He also said that a mere man had been baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, that through baptism he had received the grace of the Holy Spirit and been deemed worthy of adoption, and that Christ was worshiped in the person of the Word of God, after the likeness of an imperial image. He said also that after the resurrection he became immutable in his thoughts and completely sinless.

Moreover, he said that the union of the Word of God with Christ was of the same kind as that which the Apostle described between man and woman: “The two shall become one flesh” (1 Cor. 6). And he said that after the resurrection, when the Lord had breathed upon the disciples and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” he did not give them the Holy Spirit.

He likewise dared to say that the confession which Thomas made after touching the Lord’s hands and side after the resurrection, saying, “My Lord and my God,” was not spoken by Thomas concerning Christ (the text apparently should read τῷ Θωμᾷ, “to Thomas.” —Editor)—for Theodore does not say that Christ is God—but that Thomas, astonished at the miracles of the resurrection, glorified God and uttered those words.

What is worse, in the commentary which the same Theodore supposedly wrote on the Acts of the Apostles, he made Christ comparable to Plato, Manichaeus, Epicurus, and Marcion. He said that, just as each of them called his own disciples Platonists, Manichaeans, Epicureans, and Marcionites from the doctrine which each had discovered, so Christ, having discovered a doctrine, called his followers Christians from it.

Therefore let the whole catholic Church know that we have proceeded justly and without reproach to the matters contained in this our decree. Accordingly, together with all the other heretics condemned and anathematized—as is manifest—by the aforesaid four holy councils and by the catholic Church, we condemn and anathematize Theodore, formerly bishop of Mopsuestia, and his impious writings; likewise the writings composed by Theodoret against the orthodox faith, against the Twelve Chapters of the holy Cyril, and against the First Council of Ephesus, as well as those writings which he composed in defense of Theodore and Nestorius.

Moreover, we anathematize and condemn the letter to Maris the Persian heretic, said to have been written by Ibas. It denies that Christ the Word, incarnate from the holy God-bearer and ever-virgin Mary, became man; rather, it says that a mere man was born from her, whom it calls a temple, so that from this it is understood that the Word of God is one and Christ another. It slanders the holy Cyril, teacher and herald of the orthodox faith, as a heretic and as one who wrote things resembling those of Apollinarius. It censures the First Council of Ephesus as though it had condemned Nestorius without judgment or investigation. The same letter calls the Twelve Chapters of Saint Cyril impious and contrary to the orthodox faith; but it defends Theodore and Nestorius and their impious doctrines and writings.

Accordingly, we anathematize and condemn the aforesaid three impious chapters: namely, the impious Theodore of Mopsuestia together with his impious writings; whatever Theodoret impiously wrote; and the letter said to have been written by Ibas, in which the profane blasphemies mentioned above are contained. We also subject to the same anathema anyone who at any time believes that the aforesaid chapters ought to be accepted or defended, or who attempts to overturn this present condemnation.

But those who, preserving the orthodox faith proclaimed by the aforesaid councils, have condemned or do condemn the three chapters mentioned, we define to be brothers and fellow priests. Whatever has been done, whether by me or by others, in defense of the aforesaid three chapters, we annul by the decree of this present writing of ours.

Far be it from the catholic Church that anyone should say that any of the blasphemies set forth above was accepted by the aforesaid four councils, or by one of them, or that they accepted those who think and follow similarly. For it is entirely clear that none of those concerning whom suspicion had arisen was admitted by the holy Fathers mentioned above, and especially by the holy Council of Chalcedon, unless he rejected the blasphemies contained above, or things similar to them, or the heresy of which he was suspected, or denied and condemned the blasphemies regarding which he had fallen under suspicion.

## Subscription

May God preserve you safe and sound, most honored brother. Given before the sixth day before the Ides of December, in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of our lord Justinian, the eternal Augustus, after the consulship of Basil, the most illustrious man, in the twelfth year [of the indiction; A.D. 553].

(End of the book, or of the holy council assembled at Constantinople. Christ God, glory to you. Amen.)

## Dissertation of Peter de Marca on Vigilius’s decretal letter for the confirmation of the Fifth Synod

### I

It recently happened, fortunately, that, at the time when the acts of the Fifth Ecumenical Synod were being printed at the royal press, an old collection of *chrēseis*—extracts drawn from the ancient Fathers and councils—came to my attention. It had once been compiled by an ancient theologian against the heretics known as the Acephali and Monothelites.

That Greek manuscript volume is preserved in the Royal Library. It was accurately copied by Leo Cinnamus and deposited by him at Constantinople in the imperial library in the time of Michael Palaeologus, in the year of the world 6784, or A.D. 1276. The copyist testifies that he transcribed it from an autograph preserved in the ancient library of the Roman Church, written by hand in the year of the world 6267, or A.D. 753. I have noted this so that there might be no room for doubt concerning the antiquity and reliability of the manuscript.

Among the many excellent passages from which that collection was assembled, I happened opportunely upon several extracts from the ancient acts of the Fifth Synod: namely, Eutychius’s letter to Vigilius, part of which was produced in Greek at the Council of Florence; Vigilius’s reply to Eutychius, which survives only in Latin in the first session of that synod; and the fourteen anathemas issued by the same synod, which are preserved only in Latin in the eighth session.

I therefore thought it useful for students of ecclesiastical antiquity that, since the injury of the times had deprived us of a copy of the Greek acts, they should at least not be without these Greek fragments. This is especially so because, by comparing the anathemas with the Latin edition, they may obtain substantial assistance in discovering the true judgment of the synod, against the evasions of the Nestorians and Eutychians.

Moreover, reader, we present to you Vigilius’s letter, which has not yet appeared in print and which ought to be valued above gold. By it the acts of the Fifth Synod are confirmed by the authority of the Apostolic See. Only those who understand how greatly many people detract from the dignity of the papacy on the ground that this Fifth Synod obtained ecumenical force and weight although it had encountered Vigilius’s resistance—since he preferred to suffer exile rather than approve its definition by his vote—will know the worth of this letter.

The distinguished author of the annals indeed argues from Evagrius and other writers that the synod was confirmed by Vigilius, but he postpones that approval to the time when Vigilius was released from exile, at the request of the general Narses, after Italy had been liberated from the Goths. Yet he requires a fair-minded reader willing to let himself be led by conjectures in a matter of such importance. For, by contrast, not only innovators but also many of the most learned men have usually maintained that the Greek writers who speak of Vigilius’s agreement were mistaken, since Anastasius states that Justinian drove him into exile with several bishops because he opposed the synod. According to the same Anastasius, Vigilius was recalled through the prayers of the Romans and of the general Narses; yet Anastasius makes no mention at all of that confirmation.

I am not unaware that learned men attribute ecumenical authority to this Fifth Synod because it was listed under the name of the Fifth Synod by Pelagius I, Gregory the Great, and other popes after the other four. Others, however, explain this in such a way that those popes should rather be said to have yielded to the authority of so great a synod than to have added authority to it.

### II

I have said these things in order to commend Vigilius’s letter, found in the Royal Library, which overcomes all those difficulties and is expressed in terms appropriate to a pontiff of the Apostolic See.

The Greeks themselves considered it so important for establishing the authority of the Fifth Synod that they inserted it into the acts of that synod and appended it to the synodal definition, as will be shown below. Hence it is clear that Evagrius wrote with complete accuracy that Vigilius agreed with the synod “in writing” (*engraphōs*), for he had read that letter among the acts of the synod.

These are Evagrius’s words (Book IV, chapter 34):

> Βιγίλιος μὲν οὖν ἐγγράφως συνθέμενος, συνεδρεύειν οὐκ εἵλετο  
> “Vigilius agreed with the council by letter, but did not choose to attend.”

Photius, Zonaras, Cedrenus, Euthymius, and Nicephorus undoubtedly drew from the same acts what they transmit concerning Vigilius’s agreement.

The Sixth Synod also recalls that agreement in its address to the emperor Constantine Pogonatus. After reporting that the condemnation of Eutyches had been decreed by Leo I and accepted by the emperor Marcian together with the Council of Chalcedon, it adds these words:

> Οὕτω νῦν μετὰ ταῦτα Βιγίλιος Ἰουστινιανῷ τῷ πανευσεβεῖ συμπεφώνηκε, καὶ τὸ τῆς πέμπτης συνέδριον, τὰ φωραθέντα καὶ λαθόντα τινῶν ἀναθεματίζων συντάγματα βδελυρίας πληρέστατα.

An old translator renders this as follows:

> “Likewise Vigilius afterward agreed with Justinian, the most devout emperor, and the Fifth Council was constituted to anathematize the writings of certain persons, discovered either openly or secretly, and full of abomination.”

These words can be explained in two ways. They may mean that Vigilius agreed with Justinian that a council should be summoned for the condemnation of the Three Chapters, although the pope persisted in the contrary opinion. Or they may mean that he agreed with Justinian altogether, both concerning the convocation of the council and concerning the condemnation of the Three Chapters.

The latter explanation is necessary; otherwise, if we adhere to the first, the Fathers would appear to have introduced an example foreign to their intention and entirely unlike what they had proposed in the preceding words concerning the agreement of Leo and Marcian and of the entire synod.

### III

To this may be added the remarkable testimony of Pelagius II in his letter to the bishops of Istria (chapter 7). Its wording is so explicit that one must wonder how men otherwise exceptionally perceptive could have overlooked so clear a judgment concerning Vigilius.

For there it is stated at length that the Apostolic See, through Vigilius, at first approved the Three Chapters and labored for a long time in their defense, contending for them over an extended period even to the point of suffering injuries—a statement that can refer only to Vigilius—and that afterward he yielded when the truth had revealed itself.

Those words refer to Vigilius’s letter, in which he writes that, after the matter had been examined more carefully, the truth had shone upon him and that he had condemned the Three Chapters, as will shortly be explained more fully.

### IV

For a clearer understanding of the judgment expressed in this letter, and at the same time in order to safeguard Vigilius’s reputation and dignity, it will not be irrelevant to say a few things about his policy in the controversy over the Three Chapters.

Those three chapters were these:

1. The letter of Ibas, bishop of Edessa, to Maris the Persian;
2. The person of Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, and his writings;
3. The disputations of Theodoret against the Twelve Chapters of Cyril of Alexandria.

From these three chapters the Acephali, a branch of the Eutychians, seized an opportunity to reject the Council of Chalcedon, as though it in some way favored Nestorius. They inferred this from the fact that the synod had approved the letter of Ibas, which nevertheless criticized Cyril, praised Theodore of Mopsuestia as the author of the Nestorian heresy, and used Nestorius’s blasphemous expressions; it also claimed that Nestorius had been condemned at the Council of Ephesus without the proper judicial procedure.

They inferred it also from the fact that, although Theodoret had been received into communion, the Council of Chalcedon had not condemned his writings against Cyril’s Twelve Chapters, by which the Nestorian heresy had been proscribed. The Nestorians likewise attempted to revive their heresy from those same chapters, producing testimonies from Theodore of Mopsuestia and dissertations by Theodoret against Cyril.
