Since Justinian was intent above all on attacking the Acephali, who were causing serious disturbances in Egypt and the East, Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a supporter of the Acephali and a follower of Origen, who had been condemned only a few years earlier, stirred up the controversy concerning the Three Chapters. He did so both to avenge the measures taken against Origen and to avert the danger threatening the Acephali, thereby disturbing the peace of the Church.

Relying on the favor he enjoyed with the emperor, who was otherwise zealous for ecclesiastical peace, he undertook the matter by covert means. He led Justinian to hope that an agreement with the Acephali could be reached if, besides Theodoret’s writings against Cyril, the letter of Ibas of Edessa, read at the Council of Chalcedon, were rejected as impious, and if Theodore, who was praised in that letter, were condemned as the parent of Nestorius. The bishop of Caesarea was hostile to Theodore also because Theodore had once refuted the ravings of Origen.

### V

Justinian, moved—as he thought—by considerations of the public good, condemned those three chapters in a fairly extensive document and arranged for them to be condemned by the bishops of the East.

Since the matter of the Three Chapters had not been prejudged by any synodal judgment, and indeed seemed in some way to violate the dignity of the Council of Chalcedon, the patriarchs of the East who had subscribed Justinian’s decree declared to Stephen, the representative of the Roman See, that they had been compelled by force. Menas, bishop of Constantinople, added the condition that, if these measures were not approved by the Roman bishop, his own signed document should be returned to him—a promise made to him under oath.

Thus Justinian, perceiving that nothing in this affair affecting the condition of the Churches could usefully be attempted without the judgment of the Roman pontiff, summoned Vigilius from Rome. As Vigilius was leaving Rome, the Roman Church, and also the provinces of Africa, Sardinia, Greece, and Illyricum, appealed to him, as Facundus testifies, not to yield in any way to this innovation.

Before explaining what he did in this matter, it must be observed, with Pelagius and Blessed Gregory, that the controversy was not about the faith but about persons. Pelagius I testifies to this in his letter to Childebert, king of the Franks, in which he writes that certain matters had then been debated in the East outside the faith.

Blessed Gregory likewise warns the bishops of Ireland that the synod had dealt only with certain persons; or, to use the words of Pelagius II, that nothing else had been at issue but persons. Vigilius too, in the letter which we publish, expressly noted that the controversy was not about the faith but about persons.

It follows that there was freedom to form different judgments in this matter without injury to the Christian religion. Consequently, Vigilius, who changed his opinion several times, should not be exposed merely to suspicion of fickleness or fear. Indeed, he ought to be so far removed from such suspicion that he appears rather capable of gaining praise for exceptional prudence from what he did in this affair.

### VI

Those experienced in ecclesiastical affairs know that the supreme pontiffs formerly used to proceed in two ways in questions submitted to them which concerned discipline: either with the strictest application of the law or with relaxation.

There was a place for this moderation and relaxation of the canons when, for the good of unity and for restoring peace to the Church, it seemed necessary to employ such clemency. The Greeks call this clemency *oikonomia*; the Latins, following their example, call it *dispensatio*, or dispensation, as I have shown elsewhere [Book III of *On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*, chapter 13], adducing testimonies from the ancient Fathers and councils.

Vigilius used both methods in this controversy, now the force of law and the canons, now their relaxation, showing himself wholly devoted to the faith and peace of the Church. Learned men have indeed observed that the apparent inconsistency of Vigilius ought to be attributed to prudence and mature deliberation; but they have not shown that his manner of acting depended upon canonical discipline.

### VII

At first, immediately after his departure from Rome, nothing else should have been expected from him than that, by favoring the wishes of the Westerners, he would present himself as a defender of antiquity. Accordingly, in a letter sent from the journey to Menas, he criticized the condemnation of the Three Chapters and asked, through legates sent to Justinian, that he permit its rescission.

He then entered Constantinople on the eighth day before the Kalends of February in the year 547. He suspended Menas and the other condemners of the chapters, as well as those who communicated with the condemners, from communion. Yet five months later, at the request of the empress Theodora, he restored communion to them.

His principal reason for opposing the condemnation of the Three Chapters was that he believed that nothing done at the Council of Chalcedon could be reconsidered, since the authority of general councils is such that matters once ordered and settled by their judgment ought not to be debated again. This is what jurists mean by *retractatio*, which the Greeks call *anapsēlaphēsis* or *palindikia*. Thus he resisted the desire for innovation by invoking the exception of a matter already adjudicated.

He also appealed to the authority of Pope Leo, who, by expressly confirming the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, had forbidden that matters defined at the synod should be reconsidered under any pretext. Moreover, whereas under imperial laws reconsideration of the decisions of the prefects of the praetorium had to be undertaken within two years, this reconsideration of the Three Chapters against a universal council confirmed by the agreement of the whole world was being pressed after a hundred years, as Facundus of Hermiane complains.

It remained only to show that the council of Chalcedon had already dealt judicially with these chapters. Vigilius explains this clearly in his *Constitutum*, and Facundus does so more fully in his books addressed to Justinian. Yet it did not follow from this that the synod had admitted anything contrary to the faith.

### VIII

Although Vigilius could not be compelled by force to subscribe, he finally agreed, in the year 548, that the matter should be discussed at a gathering of seventy bishops in Constantinople. After the individual votes had been submitted to him in writing, he issued his *Judicatum* to Menas, in which he condemned the Three Chapters.

He did this *kat’ oikonomian*, that is, by canonical relaxation and dispensation, in order to preserve peace with the Easterners at that time. If anyone thinks that I have invented this, let him hear Vigilius himself, who speaks on his own behalf in his encyclical against Theodore of Caesarea:

> “First, because we yielded in order to restrain the scandal, accommodating ourselves to the minds of certain persons whom we believed could be moderated by some dispensation—since you, as a most persistent agitator, had inflamed them for several years—we judged that certain things should be arranged for the time being, on this condition: that, once every future disturbance had been silenced, no one should presume to do anything further in this matter, either by word or by writing.”

The Roman clergy likewise appealed to the same ground of dispensation in their letter to the Gallican legates:

> “Afterward, however, following a discussion, the aforesaid holy pope Vigilius, under a certain dispensation, settled the matter itself, carefully warning that the aforesaid synod should suffer no injury through any pretext.”

But Vigilius could not obtain from the African, Illyrian, and Dalmatian bishops that they yield to his judgment; rather, they suspended themselves from his communion. Facundus pursues the causes of their withdrawal in harsher language in his pamphlet against Mocianus the scholastic and in his *Letter on the Catholic Faith*, where Vigilius is therefore called a prevaricator.

He therefore acted with the emperor, in the presence of Menas the patriarch, many bishops, and the senate, so that, after rescinding what had been done on both sides in this affair, a synod might be summoned at which the bishops of the African and Illyrian provinces would be present. Their brotherhood, as he himself put it, had been scandalized, and matters approved by the votes of all would thereby obtain a place in the peace of the Church.

### IX

When the emperor summoned bishops from Africa and Illyricum, and they obeyed only with difficulty, if indeed they obeyed at all, an arrangement was made with Vigilius in the year 551 that, if the Western bishops were unwilling, he alone should condemn the Three Chapters together with the Greeks.

When the pontiff refused, Justinian’s edict condemning the Three Chapters was publicly presented at the instigation of Theodore of Caesarea. Vigilius threatened the Greek bishops with suspension from his communion if they supported the edict; Dacius, bishop of Milan, made the same declaration.

Accordingly, Justinian became so enraged that Vigilius took refuge in the basilica of Saint Peter at Hormisdas. The praetor attempted to drag him away by force, but was driven back by the uprising of the people.

At last, after receiving an oath from the emperor’s legates, Vigilius returned to the Placidian house. But after suffering many further injuries and being subjected to plots, he once again departed by night, on Christmas Eve, for Chalcedon, to the church of Saint Euphemia. Senators sent by Justinian, and separately Peter the *referendarius*, once and again attempted to summon him, but could not do so.

Rather, he wrote an encyclical concerning his sufferings, issued a sentence of deposition against Theodore of Caesarea, and suspended Menas, patriarch of Constantinople, from communion in the year 552.

This firmness of Vigilius was followed by the result that, after the edicts had been withdrawn, the emperor agreed to leave the complete discussion of the Three Chapters to a future synod. Menas, Theodore, and other bishops then asked Vigilius’s pardon for the injuries done to his Beatitude or to the Apostolic See, as their petitions inserted in Vigilius’s *Constitutum* testify.

After Menas’s death, Eutychius succeeded him. In January of the year 553 he immediately presented Vigilius with a profession of faith and asked that the controversy which had arisen be settled by common discussion.

Vigilius replied that he was pleased that the discord should be quieted:

> γινομένης κανονικῆς συνόδου  
> “provided that a canonical synod be held,”

at which discussion and debate might take place:

> ἅμα τοῖς ἐνωθεῖσιν ἡμῖν ἀδελφοῖς σύγκρισιν ποιησόμεθα  
> “and together with the brothers united to us we shall undertake the examination.”

Vigilius wished the synod to be held in Italy. But when the emperor opposed him concerning the place, they finally agreed that, before Easter, the matter of the Three Chapters should be discussed after the number of bishops of the Latin language had been made equal to that of the Greek bishops then present at Constantinople, as Vigilius testifies in his *Constitutum*.

The emperor, however, impatient of delay, summoned the synod contrary to the agreements. In letters addressed to the patriarchs of Constantinople, Alexandria, and Antioch, to the representatives of the patriarch of Jerusalem, and to the other Eastern bishops who were in the city, he urged them to undertake the controversy concerning the Three Chapters.

In those letters he mentioned the *Judicatum* previously issued by Vigilius, so that there might appear to be no room for doubt concerning the pontiff’s judgment; yet he concealed the rescission of that *Judicatum* and the other conditions agreed upon with Vigilius.

### X

The synod therefore convened on the fourth day before the Nones of May. An illustrious delegation consisting of Eutychius of Constantinople, the other patriarchs, and sixteen metropolitans approached Vigilius and asked him whether he wished to debate the case of the Three Chapters with the other bishops, as he had promised Eutychius in his letter.

Vigilius pleaded illness and postponed his answer until the following day, promising then to make known what he thought of such a gathering. His words do not mean what learned men have supposed—namely, that he intended to satisfy the synod by a written statement—but rather indicate that he did not regard that gathering as a canonical synod and that he would address the matter two days later.

This passage is of great importance for forming a definite judgment about Vigilius’s policy. He had especially desired the convocation of a synod in order to heal the feelings of the Western bishops, who had been offended by the dispensation he had used to reconcile the Easterners. Justinian had approved that condition; therefore, in Vigilius’s view, a gathering of Easterners alone could not be considered a legitimate and universal council.

When the synod’s legates approached him a second time, he replied bluntly that he could not meet with them at that time, as is clear from the report which the legates presented to the synod. Their words are these:

> “He replied that he could not meet with us, because there are many Eastern bishops here but few with him. He would, however, give his judgment in writing by himself and present it to the most devout emperor.”

The legates, on the other hand, argued that the gathering should not be postponed because of the absence of the Western bishops, especially since at the other ecumenical synods scarcely two or three Western bishops had been present, whereas Vigilius himself was now present, together with several priests from Italy, Illyricum, and Africa.

They further insisted that his reply remained in force, by which he had promised Eutychius that he would discuss the matter with the brothers united to him and that he himself would be joined with Eutychius in communion.

Vigilius’s reply is not inserted in the acts, but it can be gathered from the sequence of events which we noted above. The legates were concealing the words of his reply, in which he had promised to deal with the matter in a canonical synod. But a synod could not be canonical if, according to the practice observed at the other ecumenical synods, it did not consist of representatives of all the ecclesiastical provinces.

Nor could they object that few Western bishops had attended the other councils, since the synodal acts show that those bishops had represented the Roman pontiff and the whole council of the Western dioceses. This practice ought to have been observed with still greater care in the present case, because the matter concerned the scandal inflicted upon the Westerners. It was also the custom of the Roman Church, when those whose interests were involved had been summoned, to remove offenses, as the letters of Leo I to the legates sent to the East make clear.

In this matter too Vigilius had often made his position known in the words contained in the letter of the Roman clergy:

> “Without the consent of all,” Vigilius said, “I will in no way agree to do alone what both causes the Council of Chalcedon to be called into doubt and generates scandal for my brothers.”

When the patricians whom the emperor had delegated, and the bishops in the name of the synod, appealed to him again, he promised that within a few days he would send the emperor in writing what he thought about the controversy.

There is therefore no reason for learned men to allege Vigilius’s absence on the ground that supreme pontiffs were not accustomed to attend general councils. The true reason must be sought in his refusal to make an incomplete gathering ecumenical by his presence, to the offense of the Westerners.

The synod nevertheless undertook its examination of the Three Chapters and eventually condemned them in its definition.

### XI

Meanwhile, within the twenty-day postponement which he had requested on account of illness, Vigilius delivered to Justinian his *Constitutum*, in which he set forth at length his judgment concerning the Three Chapters. He condemned Theodore’s blasphemies, but spared his name, following the example of the Council of Ephesus. He declared it superfluous, and tending toward Theodore’s reproach, to condemn his writings against Cyril, since Cyril himself and the Council of Chalcedon had required nothing else of him than that he anathematize Nestorius. As for Ibas’s letter, he held that nothing needed to be retracted after the Council of Chalcedon. He then prohibited anyone of ecclesiastical rank or order from teaching concerning the Three Chapters otherwise than he had expressed in his *Constitutum*.

Nevertheless, I observe that he did not add an anathema against those who maintained the contrary opinion. He did this with the greatest prudence, to show that the matter was of such a kind that it could incline in either direction, if ecclesiastical peace might thereby be served. He could not have answered otherwise when Justinian asked for Vigilius’s judgment: the emperor was asking for Vigilius’s opinion, not treating of a dispensation intended to restore harmony between the Westerners and Easterners, which could not otherwise be achieved than by an agreement reached without insulting the Westerners.

### XII

Here I cannot conceal that I am far removed from the opinion of the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius (*Ecclesiastical Annals*, under the year 553), who thinks that Vigilius’s *Constitutum* was sent by Justinian to the synod. He infers this from the fact that the arguments advanced in the *Constitutum* in favor of Ibas’s letter are discussed and refuted in the sixth collation.

I am led to think otherwise more by love of truth than by the insolence of innovators, who believe that from this narrative a substantial argument can be drawn against pontifical authority. They infer that the pope’s writings were not only discussed but refuted in the synod, and that a definition contrary to them was issued, together with an anathema, in the promulgated decrees.

Indeed, if the *Constitutum* had been reread in the synod, its recitation would have been recorded in the acts, into which even readings of lesser importance were inserted. The arguments in favor of Ibas’s letter that are discussed in the sixth collation were well known and commonplace, since for six or seven years they had been vigorously deployed by the opponents, even in extensive books, as happened in the case of Facundus of Hermiane. There is therefore no need to have recourse to Vigilius’s *Constitutum*, as though those arguments necessarily had to be excerpted from it.

Moreover, publication of the *Constitutum* would have been contrary to the emperor’s purpose and prudence. Since he was wholly intent upon condemning the Three Chapters, he ought not to have obstructed his own wishes by producing Vigilius’s authority, which disapproved that desire. Rather, so that he might more easily attain the result he had proposed, and so that no one might wait to hear what Vigilius would answer the emperor—as Vigilius had promised he would do—Justinian, through Constantine, quaestor of the sacred palace, suggested to the synod that Vigilius’s mind had been sufficiently expressed by what he had repeatedly taught on this matter, both in writing and orally.

To encourage the sacred assembly to condemn the Three Chapters, the same quaestor also arranged for letters written by Vigilius on this subject to Aurelian of Arles and to Valentinian, bishop of Scythia, together with the judgment issued by that same pontiff against his deacons Rusticus and Sebastian, supporters of the Three Chapters, to be presented for reading after being translated from Latin into Greek.

These are Constantine’s words:

> “When he was invited to attend in common—that is, Vigilius—and to do this together with your holy synod, he promised that he himself would do so and present it to the most pious lord. Therefore, so that, hearing also what he himself has often done for the condemnation of the Three Chapters, you may become more eager to issue a form concerning these matters quickly, he has sent through me to your Holiness the condemnation pronounced by the most religious Vigilius himself, and so forth, with everything translated into the Greek language for the easier understanding of your Holiness.”

He who thought that the Fathers would be made more eager to condemn the chapters after Vigilius’s prior judgment had been read was not so obtuse as to impede their momentum by presenting a contrary definition of that same pontiff.

Furthermore, this was precisely the place to speak of the *Constitutum*, when the quaestor was recounting Vigilius’s promise to the emperor. Yet he not only failed to mention it; he deliberately concealed it altogether and substituted other documents in its place.

The most illustrious scholar says that by producing these documents Justinian attempted to accuse Vigilius of prevarication, since Vigilius had decided otherwise in the *Constitutum* than he had earlier. But the emperor’s intention cannot be discovered more clearly elsewhere than in the speech of the quaestor, who invoked Vigilius’s written authority against the chapters in order to arouse and encourage the Fathers, not to insult the pontiff.

Certainly, if anyone examines more carefully the order maintained in ecumenical councils, he will depart as far as possible from the opinion that violates the dignity of the apostolic see, and will easily agree with me that Vigilius’s name was employed to construct a step toward the synod’s definition against the chapters.

For the judgment of the Roman pontiff was always first in ecumenical synods, and it was not customary to decree anything before awaiting it. The practice was analogous to senatorial decrees issued in response to the emperors’ speeches, as I shall explain in Volume II of *On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*.

For the present I shall rely only upon Vigilius’s testimony, by which he claimed that right for himself in this matter. For after promising the emperor that within the twenty-day postponement he would issue his definition concerning this affair, he sent the deacon Pelagius to the bishops to warn them not to decide anything on the matter before his judgment was promulgated:

> “Preserving the ancient and regular order,” he said, “so that before the promulgation of the judgment of our see—that is, of the apostolic see over which, by God’s grace, we preside—they would not attempt to issue anything from which an occasion for scandal, once quieted, might arise again.”

Thus Justinian, so that Vigilius’s authority might not appear to have been disregarded in this matter, suppressed the *Constitutum*, but presented to the synod other earlier judgments of Vigilius, which he had issued in preceding years *oikonomically*—that is, as an accommodation—so that everything in the acts might appear to have been done properly and solemnly.

Accordingly, the synod itself also placed great weight upon the fact that Vigilius had condemned the Three Chapters repeatedly, both in writing and orally. It did complain that, although invited by an illustrious embassy, he had refused to attend the assembly and had preferred to promise that he would send his own judgment to the emperor.

The synod, however, remained entirely silent as to whether the pontiff had kept his promise. It considered that it had fulfilled its duty if it relied upon judgments issued by Vigilius and produced in court by the emperor’s command, especially since there was no solemn and procedurally regular evidence of the pontiff’s contrary opinion.

### XIII

What greatly distressed Vigilius was that he saw the restoration of peace among the Westerners—which he desired above all else—being undermined by Justinian’s devices. Not only had the number of Western bishops not been made equal in the synod according to the agreements previously discussed; Vigilius’s decree had also been withheld by the emperor and had not been promulgated in the synod. Vigilius had expressly stated in his *Constitutum* that this would lead to an occasion for even greater scandal if it occurred.

Therefore, amid the general confusion of affairs, he refused to give his consent to the bishops’ definition. For this reason the emperor drove him into exile, together with several bishops and clerics who opposed the synod, as Anastasius testifies.

There is complete silence concerning that insult in Evagrius and the other Greek writers. Unless, perhaps, one wishes to suspect that some knowledge of this disagreement reached Michael Cerularius, patriarch of Constantinople, and provided him with an occasion for a certain egregious blunder.

Around the year 1051, in order to remove from himself the disgrace of having rejected Roman communion with the utmost wickedness, Michael wrote in a letter to Peter, bishop of Antioch, that the pope’s name had already been erased from the ecclesiastical diptychs from the time of Vigilius himself.

A custom had become established among the principal sees: the pope’s name was inscribed first, followed by the names of the other patriarchs, in the ecclesiastical tablets called diptychs, and the names were recited in the order of the liturgy as a testimony to the communion of the universal Church. If any one of them fell out of that communion, his name was erased from the diptychs. This is shown, among other things, by the fierce controversies over restoring the name of John Chrysostom and erasing that of Acacius.

Peter immediately corrected Michael’s error. He was distressed that communion with the Roman Church was being dissolved. He tried to preserve it by letters concerning his ordination and by testimonies of faith addressed to Leo IX, and he achieved his desire, as is clear from Leo’s reply.

I shall quote Peter’s own words from his letter to Michael, which is preserved in a manuscript codex of the Royal Library, since they show not only what Peter thought about Vigilius’s affair but also the time at which the Greek patriarchs erased the Roman pontiff’s name from the diptychs. In their later efforts to restore it—of which they spoke as the “recitation of that name” (*hou onomatos anaphoran*)—they labored so greatly to restore the unity of the Church, as Georgius Pachymeres and Nicephorus Gregoras testify. I shall discuss this elsewhere.

> [Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following paragraph are printed in parallel in Migne.]
>
> “Your sacred letters report that a rumor has reached your ears: that I recite the pope in the sacred diptychs, and that the other patriarchs do the same; and that I ought not to have been ignorant of so great an error—especially I, before the others—since I know that from the holy Sixth Ecumenical Council down to the present the pope’s name was cut out of the recitation in the sacred diptychs because at that time Vigilius did not attend the synod, nor anathematize what Theodoret had written against the orthodox faith and the Twelve Chapters of Saint Cyril; and from then until now the pope has been cut off from our most holy church.
>
> “As for the matter concerning Vigilius, how much heedlessness does it not additionally testify against your pious chartophylax? For although the man is, as we hear, a sophist learned in rhetorical studies, he is still young and has not yet acquired sufficient experience in ecclesiastical matters. Vigilius belonged to the time of the Fifth Council, not the Sixth. The interval between the two councils is 129 years.
>
> “It happened that his name was omitted from the recitation for a short time because he had quarreled with the most holy patriarch Menas and subjected him to deposition, until the chief bishops made peace with one another and were reconciled.
>
> “At the time of the Sixth Holy Council the sacred pope was Agatho, an honorable man and wise in divine matters. Read what concerns the Sixth Council, which used to be read on Sunday after the Exaltation of the Precious Cross. You will find the aforesaid Agatho gloriously proclaimed by that holy council.
>
> “In addition to these things, I am an unimpeachable witness, as are many other distinguished men of the Church with me, that under the most blessed patriarch of Antioch, lord John, the pope of Rome, also named John, was recited in the sacred diptychs.
>
> “When I came to Constantinople forty-five years ago, under the most blessed patriarch, lord Sergius, I found that the aforesaid pope was recited in the divine mysteries together with the other patriarchs.
>
> “How his recitation was later cut off, and for what reason, I do not know.”

> [Latin version, Col. 0136A–C:]
>
> “Your Holiness’s sacred letters contain the report that it has come to your ears that I have restored the pope to the sacred diptychs, and that the other patriarchs have done the same. This fault ought to have been absent from me above all others, since I knew that from the time of the Sixth Synod down to this age the pope’s name had been cut out of the diptychs, because Vigilius refused to attend the synod and to condemn what Theodoret had written against the right faith and Cyril’s Twelve Chapters. And from that time until the present the pope has been cut off from your [our, in the Greek] most holy Church.
>
> “The matters concerning Vigilius display what great heedlessness on the part of your religious chartophylax! For although, as they say, he is highly accomplished in rhetoric, in his youth he has not yet sufficiently mastered ecclesiastical matters. Vigilius belongs to the Fifth, not the Sixth, Synod. The interval between the two synods is one hundred and twenty-nine years. It happened that he was omitted from the recitation for a very short time because of his disagreement with the most holy Patriarch Menas, whom he had subjected to suspension, until the bishops returned to peace with one another. At the time of the Sixth Synod the pope was Agatho, a most distinguished man, skilled in divine matters. Read what concerns the Sixth Synod, which is customarily reread on the Sunday after the feast of the Exaltation of the venerable Cross. You will find that the aforesaid Agatho is extolled with the highest praises by that holy synod. Moreover, I am a witness beyond all exception, as are very many distinguished men of the Church with me, that under the most blessed lord John, patriarch of Antioch, John, the Roman pope of the same name, was recited in the sacred diptychs. Indeed, forty-five years ago, when I came to Constantinople under the most blessed lord Sergius, patriarch, I found the aforesaid pope recited with the other patriarchs during the divine mysteries. How his recitation was thereafter cut off, and for what reason, I know absolutely nothing.”

From this it is clear that the patriarch Sergius, who held the see of Constantinople from 997 to 1017, was in communion with John XIX—or, rather, John XVII—who sat from 1003 to 1009 (Baronius, *Annals*, under the year 1009), as the illustrious author of the *Annals* also observed from Peter’s letter.

But after several years had passed, the Greeks again departed from the unity which John’s diligence had restored. Peter of Antioch professes that he does not know the cause of this final disagreement—that is, he does not regard it as justified.

Otherwise, it would not have been difficult to identify it, if one considered the rejection suffered by the legates sent by Eustathius of Constantinople to John XVIII in 1026, in order to obtain the pontiff’s consent, through lavish gifts, to the granting of the title “universal patriarch” to the bishop of Constantinople. This would have allowed the Church of Constantinople to be called and regarded as universal in its own sphere, just as Rome was universal throughout the world, as Rudolph Glaber puts it (*Book IV*, chapter 1).

### XIV

Returning to the affairs of Vigilius, it should be observed that the definition of the Fifth Council was issued in the year 553, on the fourth day before the Nones of June, in the twenty-seventh year of Justinian’s reign and after the twelfth consulship of Basil, as is clear from the eighth collation.

Before the sixth day before the Ides of December of that same year—that is, six months after the dissolution of the synod—Vigilius issued a decretal letter to Eutychius, because he condemned the Three Chapters. From this it can be seen that his stay in exile was brief.

It is worthwhile to examine what words he used in so complicated a matter by which he could defend his dignity against the Constantinopolitan synod without offending either the emperor or the bishops.

If we love truth, we must frankly acknowledge that the traditional opinion concerning the supreme authority of the apostolic see had by then struck deep roots in people’s minds. The supreme pontiffs were accustomed to speak of the other ecumenical synods with such reverence—and Vigilius himself did so in this decree—that they professed to accept, embrace, and venerate them with devoted minds, since they had been confirmed by the support of the apostolic see and the consent of the universal Church.

Vigilius does not even honor this Fifth Council with the name “synod.” He was moved to do so because he had not consented to its celebration under the conditions in which it took place, as we noted in section X. Moreover, even if he had subsequently concealed its defect, the promulgation of his *Constitutum* had been discontinued, as I have explained.

As for the substance of the matter, by his own authority and decree he condemns the Three Chapters. All those who had already condemned them—by these words he means the Constantinopolitan synod—he declares to be brothers and fellow priests, embracing the faith preached by the four councils. That is, he admits them to his communion and grants their judgment that authority which they ought to derive from agreement with his own decree.

He had expressed the same judgment earlier in the letter in these words:

> “The things which, with the Lord revealing and the truth investigated, ought to be defined by us have been salutarily completed.”

It was as though he were saying that this question, although discussed by the bishops in synod and decided by their votes, had to be definitively settled by a decree of the apostolic see. For this reason he calls his decree a *diatyposis*, following the example of imperial decrees.

### XV

Accordingly, so that there might be no future doubt concerning the authority of the Fifth Council, the Greeks inserted this decree of Vigilius into the acts immediately after the council’s definition. This may be inferred from the fact that the ancient copyist of the exemplar we are presenting testifies that this letter was placed at the end of the council’s acts.

The solemn word used by ancient scribes to mark the end of a work was *telos*, or *explicit*, a word sometimes used by Jerome. Our copyist faithfully transcribed it from the acts into his excerpt:

> “The end of the eighth book of the synod assembled at Constantinople.”

Moreover, the heading or title of this letter sufficiently shows that the acts of the synod were written before it in the same codex:

> “The letter of Vigilius to Eutychius and to the entire holy synod mentioned above.”

For this reason Photinus, patriarch of Constantinople, although an extremely hostile enemy of the Roman Church, could not refrain from words that signify Vigilius’s authority in confirming this synod and sufficiently show that the pontiff’s decree followed the holding of the synod.

These are his words:

> “He was present in the city, but he was not present at the synod. Although he did not willingly join the gathering of the sacred assembly, nevertheless he confirmed the common faith of the Fathers by a written petition.”

The same view is reported in a very ancient Arabic manuscript containing a collection of canons for the use of the Church of Alexandria. The distinguished Gilbert Gaulmin, master of requests and highly skilled in Arabic and the other Eastern languages, possesses it.

These are the words of the collection:

> “The synod excommunicated even the dead, something not previously done except against those alone. This was done with the knowledge of the Roman patriarch, who also confirmed it and professed his faith in a written statement given to the emperor.”

We also owe to the diligence of the same man the following testimony: he excerpted and translated from an Arabic manuscript the ecclesiastical history of Ibn Patric. In the passage above it says:

> “The Roman patriarch was present but neither attended the synod nor sent a legate; he gave his consent, however, and accepted what the Fathers had said.”

This author, Patric, is often praised by Georgius Elmacin, the writer of the history of the Saracens, published in earlier years by Erpenius.

### XVI

By this decree of Vigilius the Fifth Council was admitted as universal, not only in the East but also in the West.

Thus Pelagius I claims for it the title of universal council in a letter to Narses, patrician and duke of Italy, when speaking of the bishops of Liguria, Venetia, and Istria who had withdrawn from communion with the apostolic see because of that synod:

> “If anything perhaps moved them concerning the judgment of the universal council recently held at Constantinople during the first indiction just past, they ought, as has always been done, to have sent some of their own to the apostolic see who could give and receive an account.”

Pelagius II and Gregory the Great also accepted that synod. Gregory declares in a letter to John of Constantinople that he venerates it under the name of the Fifth Council together with the other four, to say nothing of the other supreme pontiffs and of the Fathers of the Sixth Council, who received that synod with equal worship and reverence.

Nor should anyone persuade himself that it was hated by the learned men of that age because Cassiodorus made no mention of it in his *Divine Institutions*. We shall shortly investigate another reason for that silence, one that has been partly indicated by others.

### XVII

Indeed, lest anyone think this decree of Vigilius ambitious, he himself assigns the reasons that moved him to this judgment. The offenses and scandals which the enemy of the human race had brought about through the dispute concerning the Three Chapters had already been quieted; peace had been restored to the Church after their condemnation; and truth had shone forth in these ambiguous controversies.

From this it may be inferred that the bishops of the Illyrian and African provinces repented of their earlier judgment and, having consulted with Vigilius, embraced communion with the Easterners. For this reason they are not afterward counted among the schismatics.

In the rest of the West, the Franks and Spaniards retained communion with the apostolic see. So too did the bishops of Italy, after the Tuscans, warned by Pelagius I, immediately returned to their duty.

Only the bishops of Istria, Venetia, and Liguria, who lived under Lombard rule, stubbornly maintained the schism until the time of Gregory the Great, who cured that disease even among the Irish.

The mention of peace and of scandals being quieted opens the way for the accommodation which Vigilius renews in this final decree. I cannot refrain from attributing this final definition of Vigilius also to an accommodation, since I see that Leontius the Scholastic, who flourished in this period, supports the decree of the Fifth Council on that sole ground: that it was issued *kat’ oikonomian*, “by way of accommodation,” as he says. Justinian believed that, once these chapters had been condemned, the Acephali, or Hesitants, would embrace the unity of the Church and the Council of Chalcedon.

Leontius’s words are these, in Action 6, concerning the sects:

> “Justinian did this by a certain accommodation. For when he saw the Hesitants rejecting the synod on this account, he thought that, if he anathematized them, he would cause the synod to be accepted. He therefore decided to anathematize two men, although they ought not to have been anathematized, so that he might bring everyone into unity; and for this reason he anathematized them. Yet even in this way the Hesitants did not accept the synod.”

The Latin translator renders this badly as “according to a certain council.” The meaning is:

> “For when he saw the Hesitants rejecting the [Council of Chalcedon] because of this, he thought that if he anathematized them—that is, Theodore and Ibas—the synod would be received. Therefore he decided that the two should be anathematized, although they by no means ought to have been anathematized, so that he might bring everyone into unity. For this reason he subjected them to anathema. Yet even so the Hesitants did not receive the synod.”

### XVIII

Vigilius assigns another reason for this final decree: recognition of the truth, which at last had shone upon him after he had anxiously and carefully searched the writings of the ancient Fathers.

He says that it belongs to an upright and prudent man to depart from an earlier judgment after the equity of the matter under discussion has been discovered. He teaches that this applies especially to ecclesiastical controversies, and he proves it by the distinguished example of blessed Augustine, who, after reviewing his own works, added some things and corrected others.

Pelagius II follows the same path in defending Vigilius’s decree, in the lengthy letter addressed to the bishops of Istria. Gregory the Great wrote it while he was engaged in ecclesiastical records under Pelagius, as Paul the Deacon testifies (*History of the Lombards*, Book III, chapter 20; Pelagius II, letter to the bishops of Istria, chapter 7).

The Istrian bishops alleged, in excuse for their schism, that at the beginning of the controversy the apostolic see, through Pope Vigilius, had resisted the condemnation of the Three Chapters.

Pelagius replies that the Latins, ignorant of Greek, had recognized their error only slowly. He adds:

> “The sooner they ought to have been believed, the more their steadfastness deserves credit: until they recognized the truth, they did not cease from the struggle. Your Fraternity would surely despise their agreement if they had consented with rash audacity before recognizing the truth. But after they had labored over it for a long time and fought for an extended period, even to the point of suffering insults, let your Fraternity consider that they would not suddenly abandon such labors unless they had recognized what is true.”

He proves by two examples that it belongs to the order of divine providence that the work of those who have long struggled against the truth should often commend it.

God made Paul, who had been obstinate against the Gospel, a preacher of the faith, so that he might show to all those to whom he was going to preach through him how truly divine the Gospel is, since it was preached by one whose great hardness had been overcome.

He adds the example of Peter, who, after being rebuked by Paul for urging Gentiles newly converted to the faith toward the ceremonies of Judaism, changed his judgment.

He concludes:

> “If, then, in the affair of the Three Chapters one thing was said while the truth was being sought and another after the truth had been found, why is a change of judgment charged as a crime against this see, which the whole Church venerates in its founder? It is not a change of judgment but steadfastness of understanding that is blameworthy. Therefore, when an unchanging intention remains directed toward the recognition of what is right, what objection is there if someone abandons his ignorance and changes his words?”

### XIX

It remains to ask what truth Vigilius attained that had previously been hidden from him.

This can be inferred by comparing that letter of Pelagius II with the words of Vigilius’s *Constitutum*. The first rule established in the *Constitutum* is this: nothing that had been arranged in any way at the Council of Chalcedon could be brought into question or retracted. Vigilius sought proof of this rule in the letters of Pope Leo to the emperor Leo and in the letters of Simplicius to Zeno.

Pelagius, by contrast, teaches that only the matter of faith defined at the Council of Chalcedon is irretractable; all the other matters discussed in that synod concerned private affairs. He interprets Leo’s testimonies and proves from them that permission is granted to retract whatever was done there concerning persons outside the matters of faith.

Accordingly, he rightly concludes that Ibas’s letter could be debated again, even if it had been approved at the Council of Chalcedon.

The second rule according to the *Constitutum* is that those who died in the communion and peace of the Church cannot be subjected to anathema after death. Vigilius confirms this rule by citing the testimonies of Leo and Gelasius. It followed that Theodore could not be condemned after death.

Pelagius, however, teaches from Augustine that those who professed heresy may rightly be condemned after death, since guilt committed in matters of faith is not released by death. He compares this to the case of traitors, whose memory is condemned after death and whose goods are confiscated, although all crimes are extinguished by mortality, as Papinian says.

As for Theodore’s doctrines, they are condemned in the *Constitutum* as impious and blasphemous, although the text indicates that it was not entirely clear whether Theodore had actually written them.

In his final decree, however, Vigilius teaches that it had at last become completely clear to him, “by transparent truth,” that Theodore had polluted his books with very numerous blasphemies.

### XX

From the letters of Vigilius and Pelagius one may gather two rules of great usefulness and wide application in all ecclesiastical disputes.

The first is that the canon of faith cannot be changed and that questions of doctrine once settled by the judgment of a universal synod ought not to be revived.

> “The rule of faith,” says Tertullian (*On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 1), “is entirely one, alone immovable and unreformable.”

The second is that in other matters outside the faith—that is, in disciplinary questions, which concern not only what was done but also what ought to be done—the truth may at one time be hidden and at another revealed. Once it has disclosed itself, earlier constitutions must be changed, whether they originated with general councils or with supreme pontiffs.

Vigilius professes this not only in our letter but also Pelagius II (*Letter to the Bishops of Istria*, chapter 19):

> “The special concern of synodal councils is faith. Whatever, therefore, is done apart from faith, Leo teaches that nothing prevents its being recalled for judgment.”

Tertullian likewise says:

> “While this law of faith remains, the remaining matters of discipline and conduct admit the novelty of correction, as the grace of God works and advances until the end.”

Lest anyone object that Tertullian wrote these words out of hatred for the “Psychics,” as he calls them, in order to assert the new discipline of his Paraclete, the rule we have proposed must be confirmed by the clear testimony of blessed Augustine:

> “The very plenary councils are often corrected by later councils, when, through experience of events, what had been closed is opened and what had been hidden is recognized—without any swagger of sacrilegious pride, without any inflated arrogance, without any contention born of spiteful envy, but with holy humility, Catholic peace, and Christian charity” (Augustine, *On Baptism*, Book III, chapter 3).

There can be no doubt that judgments issued by the apostolic see in private matters may be retracted and, if necessary, corrected by that same see in a council, whether general or particular, as I have shown at length elsewhere.

### XXI

It may appropriately be asked here why this letter is absent from the Latin acts.

I think the reason is that the Greek acts were translated into Latin immediately after the chapters had been condemned and were delivered to Vigilius, so that he could deliberate about approving or rejecting them. No one afterward took care to add Vigilius’s letter to the Latin acts, since it seemed sufficient that, following the example of the other pontifical letters, it was contained in Vigilius’s register. Since, however, those registers have been lost, this letter too necessarily disappeared.

There should be no doubt that someone skilled in both languages immediately undertook the Latin translation for the use of Vigilius and the Western Church. The ancient translations of the anathemas of the Council of Ephesus, of the complete acts of Chalcedon, and of the Sixth Council show that such a practice was customary.

In this case the Latin translation had to be prepared with particular speed, so that the acts could be presented to Vigilius, who would then deliberate, as I have said, concerning the condemnation of the Three Chapters.

Therefore, immediately after the eighth collation had ended, where the condemnation of the Three Chapters is contained, the acts of the synod were undoubtedly translated into Latin and delivered to Vigilius.

We learn that the Latin translation is ancient not only from the acts of the Sixth Council, where it is reported that a Latin exemplar of the Fifth Council was preserved in the patriarchal archives of Constantinople, but also from Gregory the Great, who sent Latin copies of this synod to Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards.

### XXII

Since we infer that the Latin acts now extant are ancient, we must also regard them as genuine and remove from them every suspicion of forgery and mutilation, although learned men have introduced such suspicions with some plausibility.

They think that the letter to John of Antioch, produced under Theodoret’s name in the sixth collation, has the appearance of a forgery. They suppose that some Eutychian scoundrel inserted it into the acts in order to assail Cyril with insults.

They say that it is contrary to Theodoret’s modesty for him to present himself as hostile to Cyril after Cyril’s death, since, while Cyril was alive, Theodoret had embraced his concord and communion together with John of Antioch.

They add, from the chronicle of Patriarch Nicephorus, that John of Antioch died before Cyril, so that Theodoret could not have congratulated John on Cyril’s death.

On this basis one may plausibly say that an error entered the heading of the letter and that, instead of “John,” “Domnus, John’s successor” should be restored. This is especially likely because immediately after the letter a fragment of an address is recited which Theodoret delivered at Antioch in the presence of Domnus. In it, exulting over Cyril’s death, he declares that envy had died, contention had been buried, and the East and Egypt had been placed under one yoke.

Theodoret had always shown himself particularly harsh toward the memory of Cyril, even after Cyril’s death. This can be learned from his letter to Domnus of Antioch, numbered 112 among the published letters, where he says that the bishops of the other dioceses do not know the poison implanted in Cyril’s Twelve Chapters.

Yet it may also be said that the letter to John of Antioch should not be understood as referring to Cyril. The person who excerpted the passages from Theodoret that were recited in the sixth collation at the command of the Fifth Council must have made an error.

Rather, Theodoret seems to be speaking of some bishop subject to the see of Antioch, since he attributes to John of Antioch the right and authority to make a decision concerning that bishop’s tomb.

> “It must be arranged,” he says, “and your Holiness must hasten to undertake this and order the corporation of those who carry away the dead—that is, the grave-diggers or corpse-bearers—to place some very large and extremely heavy stone upon the tomb, lest he should ever come here again.”

## XXIII

The learned prove that the Latin acts are truncated and mutilated from the fact that no investigation into the case of Origen is undertaken in them, although it is established that such an investigation was conducted at the Fifth Synod. From the antiquity of the Latin translation, however, one must infer why that condemnation has been omitted from our acts, although it was decreed in the following order.

Meanwhile, while Vigilius was deliberating whether he preferred to yield or to contend on account of the Three Chapters, Justinian addressed an edict to the synod, urging it to strike down the followers of Origen with an anathema. The emperor had been approached by a petition presented to him by the monks Eulogius, Conon, Cyriacus, and Pancratius, who complained that there were certain monks in Jerusalem professing the impious errors of Origen. He appended a copy of that petition to his letter sent to the synod, together with his own edict, by which he had formerly refuted those trifles and had obtained from Vigilius an anathema against Origen and against the blasphemous chapters excerpted from his works. He therefore asked the synod not only to condemn those chapters again by its own authority, but also those who either then or thereafter should hold the same opinions.

After the condemnation of Origen and of his followers Didymus and Evagrius had been carried out, a report, or *anaphora* (ἀναφορά), of the matter was sent to the emperor, from which Evagrius excerpted several words. It is clear from the testimony of that same Evagrius that the proceedings concerning Origen and his supporters took place in this order; for he expressly noted that, after the condemnation of the Three Chapters, the case of the Origenists was examined.

His translator, however, must be corrected in passing. Departing from the author’s meaning, he writes that the petition was presented to the council by the monks, whereas Justinian transmitted to the synod a copy of the petition—namely, the petition presented to him—in accordance with the procedure observed in a similar case by Marcian at the Council of Chalcedon and by Justinian himself at the synod under Menna.

Moreover, the very sequence of the acts of the Fifth Synod clearly shows that the investigation of Origen followed the investigation of the Three Chapters. The synod was convened on account of the affair of the Three Chapters; its examination was immediately begun and completed in eight sessions, in a single continuous process, with no other matter inserted, so that no interval can even be found into which an investigation of Origen could be fitted.

Nevertheless, the most illustrious author of the *Annals* judged that the case of Origen had been discussed before the Three Chapters, because Cedrenus, in his narrative, followed that order, recording the condemnation of Origen first. To support this conjecture one might also add the distinguished testimony of Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem, who flourished before the Sixth Synod. In his synodal letter to Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople, cited at the Sixth Synod, session 11, he declares that, together with the other four synods, he embraces the Fifth Ecumenical Synod, which confirms the Council of Chalcedon and

> “removes and utterly casts out, to destruction, in the first place, Origen the madman”  
> (ἀναιρεῖ καὶ ἐκρίπτει πρὸς ὄλεθρον πρωτοτύπως Ὡριγένην τὸν ἄφρονα),

and also his ravings, as well as the impious doctrines of Didymus and Evagrius; and

> “after them it casts out Theodore of Mopsuestia”  
> (μεθ’ οὓς Μοψουεστίας ἐκτίλλει Θεόδωρον).

But it must necessarily be said that Sophronius placed the condemnation of Origen first, not because this was the order of the synod’s investigation—as has been demonstrated—but because this article seemed to him more serious and more important than the other three that were discussed at the synod.

For the same reason, the emperor Constantine Pogonatus, in the edict issued for the confirmation of the synod; Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, in his manuscript excerpt concerning the six synods; Cedrenus; and the other Greek writers all record in the same order the condemnation of Origen and of his followers Didymus and Evagrius, whom Sophronius calls “Origenist hierophants” (Ὁριγένους μυστηριάρχας). For the same reason also, the Seventh Synod, omitting the Three Chapters, mentions Origen, Didymus, and Evagrius as condemned by the Fifth Synod.

## XXIV

Indeed, although in the Latin acts of the Fifth Synod an anathema is incidentally pronounced against Origen in the eleventh chapter of the anathematisms, the full investigation instituted concerning that matter is not recorded. Justinian’s letter to the synod, together with the monks’ petition, is absent, as is the same emperor’s edict to Vigilius for the condemnation of Origen and his followers. The synod’s discussion of the matter and the report sent to the emperor are absent as well.

The most illustrious historian of the *Annals* believes that the Greek acts were first corrupted and mutilated by the heretical Origenists, and that the Latin translation later emerged infected with that defect. But those acts are so far from being corrupted that Greek writers, from reading them, drew what the Latins learned only from those Greek writers concerning the condemnation of Origen, Didymus, and Evagrius.

For the Latin acts that were initially brought to the West contained nothing at all except the condemnation of the Three Chapters. Pelagius I and Pelagius II, as well as Gregory the Great, speak only of those chapters when they report the decrees of the Fifth Synod. Otherwise, they would not have been silent about Origen and his ravings, since the Fifth Synod—so vehemently rejected by the schismatics—could have been strongly commended on that account.

Indeed, when blessed Gregory, in his letter to John of Constantinople, professes that he embraces the faith of the five synods, he lists the heresies condemned by the first four and the Three Chapters rejected by the Fifth Synod. He would not have omitted the condemnation of Origen if the Latin acts had made that matter known to him. For this reason Vigilius also pronounced his decree only concerning the Three Chapters, which were the subject of controversy.

From this ignorance of Origen’s condemnation at the Fifth Council it resulted that not only Cassiodorus but also the Second Council of Braga, held in the year 572, omitted the Fifth Synod when listing the first four Ecumenical Councils. Since those authorities knew only that the Three Chapters had been rejected by that synod—and those chapters concerned private affairs and certain persons who had died, not the Catholic faith—there was no reason for them to attach the Fifth Synod to the other four, which they cited for the overthrow of the heresies condemned in them, rather than, in the manner of historians, undertaking a catalogue of the councils held in the Church.

Hence it also happened that Gregory the Great, otherwise a most vigorous defender of the Fifth Synod, professed that he venerated the four synods with equal reverence to the Gospels, namely because of the truth of the doctrines that they had asserted against heresies. That aspect of dignity was lacking in the Fifth Synod, at least in the Latin acts, because the condemnation of Origen had been omitted.

For the same reason, Gregory himself, as well as the other supreme pontiffs and councils, omits the Council of Sardica, because it struck down no new heresy but chiefly involved itself in judgments concerning persons.

## XXV

Now it is worthwhile to investigate the reason that moved Vigilius to restrict his decree to the Three Chapters. Although the acts delivered to him did not contain the investigation conducted concerning Origen, nevertheless, by the time of our present reply addressed to Eutychius, which was issued six months after the council, he knew that judgment concerning Origen had been carried out at the synod. It therefore appears that it belonged to his office not to omit confirmation of that judgment.

Nevertheless, so that this omission may not be charged as a fault, it should be observed that sixteen years earlier—that is, in the year 538—Justinian, at the urging of Pelagius, deacon and *apocrisiarius* of the Roman Church, had condemned Origen and his blasphemous trifles by his own pronouncement. These had long before been proscribed by Anastasius, bishop of Rome, and by Theophilus of Alexandria. Justinian had also urged Menna, patriarch of Constantinople, to subject them to anathema together with the bishops residing in the imperial city.

By sending his own edict, he sought and obtained the same judgment from Pope Vigilius and the other patriarchs. Liberatus bears witness to this in the following words (*Breviarium*, chapter 23):

> “At his command”—that is, Justinian’s, although he speaks more mildly; for he does not use the word “command,” but rather “we exhort” (προτρέπομεν)—“a condemnation by anathema was pronounced against Origen and those chapters, which, together with Menna the archbishop, they found and subscribed at Constantinople. Then it was sent to Vigilius, bishop of Rome, to Zoilus of Alexandria, to Ephrem of Antioch, and to Peter of Jerusalem. When these received it and subscribed it, Origen was condemned, dead though he was, having formerly been condemned while alive.”

Liberatus alone does not prove that Vigilius’s authority had intervened in Origen’s condemnation at that time. Cassiodorus does so as well (*Institutions of Divine and Secular Learning*, book I, chapter 1):

> “Although the authority of so many Fathers opposes this man”—Origen—“it is nevertheless established that in the present time he has again been condemned by the most blessed Pope Vigilius.”

Vigilius had decreed the condemnation by subscribing his annotation to the emperor’s edict, as Liberatus observed. Hence Evagrius makes an elegant observation (*Book IV, chapter 37*): Justinian, in the letter that he sent to the Fifth Synod for the condemnation of Origen, appended what had been sent to Vigilius on that matter—that is, the edict that the emperor had sent to Vigilius in the year 538 and to which, as we have said, Vigilius had already subscribed an anathema against Origen.

Evagrius’s words are:

> συζεῦξαι καὶ πρὸς Βιγίλιον περὶ τούτου ἀπεσταλμένα

In interpreting these words, the Latin translator went astray, understanding them as referring to letters written by Vigilius. Although Justinian’s edict had in fact been sealed with Vigilius’s subscription, Evagrius’s words nevertheless mean nothing [lacuna] except an edict sent to Vigilius.

Justinian also understands this edict when he asks the Fifth Synod to condemn by anathema the blasphemies described “in the exposition set forth below” (ἐν ὑποτεταγμένῃ ἐκθέσει). Nor was this without good reason. Since the emperor had in his archives the subscriptions of Menna of Constantinople and of his synod, as well as those of the other patriarchs, placed on an equal number of copies of his edict, he selected that copy of the edict which had been sent to Vigilius and subscribed by him.

For he knew well that the first definition of matters to be enacted in synods, or their subsequent approval, and *the authority* (τὸ κῦρος), ought to be awaited from the Roman pontiff. Thus, with Vigilius as its authority, although he was absent, the Fifth Synod dealt with Origen’s errors.

Accordingly, that supreme pontiff did not include Origen in his final decree, which he necessarily had to issue concerning the Three Chapters, because he had formerly fulfilled his role in condemning Origen and because, under his auspices, the Fifth Synod had issued its decree concerning Origen. There was therefore no reason for him to contribute his efforts anew to a matter on which it was unnecessary for him to pronounce, just as he himself indicates that it had been necessary for him to settle the controversy concerning the Three Chapters by his own authority, although it had already been resolved by the votes of the bishops residing at Constantinople.

[Col. 0143]

# THE CONSTITUTUM OF POPE VIGILIUS FOR THE CONDEMNATION OF THE THREE CHAPTERS, ISSUED IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 554. THE DEFINITION OF THE FAITH OF THE HOLY COUNCIL OF CHALCEDON. (S)

[Col. 0143C] Aetius, archdeacon of Constantinople, New Rome, said:

The holy, great, and universal synod which, by the grace of God and by the decree of our most pious and most Christian emperors, the Augusti Valentinian and Marcian, was assembled at Chalcedon, the metropolis of the province of Bithynia, in the martyrium of the holy and venerable martyr Euphemia, defined the following.

Our Lord and Savior Christ, confirming the knowledge of the faith to his disciples, said: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you,” so that no one should disagree with his neighbor in the doctrine of piety, but that each should equally display the proclamation of the truth.

But because the most wicked one does not cease to rise up and sow his tares among the plantings of piety, always devising something new against the truth, for this reason our Lord, in his customary care for the human race, raised up this pious and most faithful emperor to zeal for the faith and summoned to himself the leaders of the priesthood from every quarter, so that, through the grace of the Lord of us all and through Christ’s working, he might remove every plague of falsehood from Christ’s sheep and make them fertile with the shoots of truth.

This indeed we have done: by common decree we have driven away the doctrines of error, renewed intact the faith of the Fathers, proclaimed in every respect the creed of the three hundred and eighteen, and enrolled as members of our household those Fathers who accepted this composition of piety—namely, the one hundred and fifty who later assembled at great Constantinople and who themselves also subscribed the same faith.

Therefore, preserving the order and every form of the faith, we define that the holy synod formerly held at Ephesus, whose presidents were Celestine, of holy memory, bishop of the city of Rome, and Cyril, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, should retain its authority; that the exposition of the correct and undefiled faith of the three hundred and eighteen holy and most blessed Fathers assembled at Nicaea under the pious emperor Constantine should shine forth; and that what was defined by the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers at Constantinople should also prevail—at that time for the destruction of the heresies that had arisen, but for the confirmation of this same Catholic faith of ours.

## The Creed of the Three Hundred and Eighteen at Nicaea

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things were made; who for us human beings and for our salvation came down, and was incarnate and became human, and suffered, and rose again on the third day, and ascended into heaven, and will come to judge the living and the dead; and in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was once when he was not,” and “Before he was begotten he was not,” and that he was made from things that did not exist, or from another subsistence or substance, and who say that the Son of God is either capable of conversion or changeable, the Catholic and Apostolic Church anathematizes.

[Col. 0145A] Likewise, the creed of the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers who assembled at Constantinople.

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things were made; who for us human beings and for our salvation came down, and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary and became human; and was crucified for us under Pontius Pilate, and was buried, and rose again on the third day, and ascended into heaven, and sat at the right hand of the Father; and will come again with glory to judge the living and the dead, whose kingdom will have no end.

And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father, worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son, who spoke through the holy prophets; and in one Catholic and Apostolic Church. We confess one baptism and the forgiveness of sins. We await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

This wise and salutary symbol of divine grace would indeed suffice for a full knowledge and confirmation of piety. For it teaches perfection concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and faithfully presents the Lord’s incarnation to those who accept it.

But because those who attempt to reject the proclamation of the truth have generated new expressions through their own heresies—some presuming to corrupt the mystery of the Lord’s dispensation that exists for our sake, and refusing to call the Virgin Mary “God-bearer”; others introducing confusion and mixture, foolishly fabricating one nature of flesh and divinity, and monstrously asserting by their confusion that the divine nature of the Only-Begotten is passible—for this reason the present holy, great, and universal synod, wishing to close every contrivance of theirs against the faith, teaching this proclamation as unshaken from the beginning, has defined above all that the faith of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers must remain inviolable.

And on account of those who fight against the Holy Spirit, it confirms the doctrine concerning the substance of the Spirit handed down by the Fathers who later assembled at Constantinople, one hundred and fifty in number. They made that doctrine known to all, not by implying that anything was lacking in the earlier statements, but by declaring through testimonies of Scripture their understanding concerning the Holy Spirit against those who attempted to reject his lordship.

But on account of those who strive to corrupt the mystery of the dispensation, shamelessly raving that the one born from the holy Virgin Mary was a mere human being, it accepted the synodical letters of blessed Cyril, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, to Nestorius and to the others throughout the East, since they were appropriate for refuting the madness of Nestorius. It also joined to them, for the interpretation of those who desire to know the salutary creed with pious zeal, the great letter of the most blessed and holy archbishop of the elder city, Leo, written to Flavian, archbishop of holy memory, to destroy the wicked understanding of Eutyches. That letter was consistent with the confession of that great Peter and served as a kind of common pillar for us against perverse doctrines, fittingly confirming correct teachings.

For it opposes those who strive to divide the mystery of the divine dispensation into two sons, and expels from the sacred assembly those who have dared to call the divinity of the Only-Begotten passible. It resists those who seek a mixture or confusion in Christ’s two natures. It drives away as deranged those who say that the form of a servant which he assumed from us is heavenly or of some other substance. It condemns those who invent two natures of the Lord before the union but fabricate one after the union.

Accordingly, following the holy Fathers, we all unanimously teach that the same one is confessed as Son and our Lord Jesus Christ: the same one perfect in divinity and the same one perfect in humanity; truly God and truly human; the same one consisting of a rational soul and a body; consubstantial with the Father according to divinity and the same one consubstantial with us according to humanity; like us in every respect except sin; begotten from the Father before the ages according to divinity; and in the last days, for us and for our salvation, the same one born from the Virgin Mary, the God-bearer, according to humanity.

We teach that the one and the same Christ, Son, Lord, Only-Begotten, is to be acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation; with the distinction of the natures nowhere removed because of the union, but rather with the property of each nature preserved and coming together into one person and one subsistence, not divided or separated into two persons, but one and the same Only-Begotten Son, God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ, just as the prophets formerly taught concerning him, as Jesus Christ himself taught us, and as the creed of the Fathers delivered to us.

Having therefore set forth all these matters among ourselves with complete precision and diligence, the holy and universal synod defined that no one may produce, write, compose, think, or teach another faith. Those who have dared to compose, produce, teach, or transmit another creed, whether wishing to convert Gentiles to the knowledge of the truth, or Jews, or converts from any heresy—if they are bishops or clerics, they are to be deprived of their episcopate and clerics of their clergy; but if they are monks or laypeople, they are to be anathematized.

## To Flavian, his most beloved brother, Leo

[Col. 0146D] Having read the letters of Your Affection, which we are surprised were so long delayed, and having reviewed the sequence of the episcopal proceedings, we finally learned what scandal had arisen among you against the integrity of the faith. Matters that had previously seemed concealed were now laid open to us. From these it became clear that Eutyches, who appeared worthy of the honorable title of presbyter, was very imprudent and exceedingly ignorant, so that what the prophet said of him could now be applied: “He was unwilling to understand so as to do good; he meditated iniquity in his bed.”

What is more unjust than to hold impious opinions and refuse to yield to wiser men and teachers? Yet those who, when some obscurity obstructs them in their effort to know the truth, turn not to the prophetic utterances, not to the apostolic writings, and not to the authority of the Gospels, but to themselves, fall into this folly. Therefore they become teachers of error, because they were not disciples of the truth.

And the rest of the contents of the same letter, through its conclusion.

Given on the Ides of June, in the consulship of Asterius and Protogenes.

## I

After we have set forth the exposition of the blessed Council of Chalcedon, or the letter of blessed Leo concerning the holy and orthodox faith—which is one and the same faith of the three preceding synods, namely, those of Nicaea, Constantinople, and the First Council of Ephesus—and after Your Fraternity and the universal Church have recognized that, with God’s help, we persist in it with all the devotion of a sincere mind, we believe it very necessary, in order to preserve its reverence in every respect, that we carefully examine all the questions concerning the aforementioned Three Chapters and define them by a cautious promulgation of judgment.

We therefore consider it appropriate first, as we proposed, to make entirely clear what is to be said concerning the letter said to have been written by Ibas to Maris the Persian.

When Bishop Ibas had been wickedly attacked by Samuel, Mara, and his other clerics, and when, as though charged with the grave crime of having attacked the holy faith, the letter to Maris the Persian had been brought against him by those same accusers, and when he had been acquitted by the bishops Photius and Eustathius, to whom the pious emperor Theodosius of blessed memory had then delegated the investigation; and when afterward, for the very crimes from which he had been cleared, he had been condemned through the wicked proceedings of the Second Council of Ephesus, in his absence and on the testimony of false witnesses who insisted above all that the same letter to Maris was his—when he came to the holy Synod of Chalcedon, he is read to have alleged the following in his own defense.

From the Council of Chalcedon, in the session concerning Bishop Ibas, after other matters, as follows (*Act 9*):

The most reverend Ibas, bishop of the city of Edessa, entered and said:

> Having suffered injustice from Eutyches and false fabrications, I have come here after being absent from forty stations and condemned, to obtain mercy. I have approached the sacred and immortal summit, and Your Magnificence has ordered, together with this holy and universal synod, that the proceedings against me be investigated. I therefore beseech you to recognize that I endured a false accusation and calumny from certain clerics. Order the judgments rendered by the most reverend bishops Photius and Eustathius to be reread.
>
> For Bishop Uranius of the Hemeritae, acting entirely out of favor toward Eutyches, prepared certain clerics to accuse me and arranged for judgment to be transmitted to himself and to those previously mentioned. I was found innocent of the blasphemies brought against me, and the judgment was issued by the aforementioned most reverend bishops, demonstrating that the accusations against me had been brought through calumny and testifying that I am Catholic.
>
> Order everything done in my absence at Ephesus to be annulled and justice to be preserved for me, since I am guilty of nothing, and let both my episcopate and my Church be restored to me. All the Edessene clerics, through whom they wrote to the aforementioned bishops, also testify that I am Catholic, and I am alien to the wicked blasphemies brought against me; and so forth.

Likewise, from the eleventh session of the same synod:

The aforementioned most reverend man Ibas entered and said:

> I beseech Your Magnificence and this holy universal synod. Eutyches fabricated certain false charges against me concerning the faith and did not permit me to enter the holy synod.

And after other matters:

> For this reason, as I have already explained, I approached the sacred and immortal summit, and Your Magnificence and the holy synod ordered that the proceedings against me be heard. And you recognized from the decree that I was found guilty of nothing.

## II

It is therefore clear that, from the very beginning when Ibas, bishop of the city of Edessa, is shown to have entered the holy Synod of Chalcedon, he denied that the letter alleged to have been composed [perhaps, *confingitur*, “fabricated”] by him for Maris the Persian was his own. He admits this most plainly when he declares that, in the wicked proceedings of that Second Council of Ephesus, he suffered injustice from Eutyches and false fabrications.

It is established, moreover, that in that same Second Ephesian hearing, held against the aforementioned bishop in his absence, the accusers especially demanded that, through the testimony of witnesses produced earlier, they might demonstrate that Bishop Ibas had confessed the letter written to Maris the Persian to be his own. From this it appears that he had been condemned, as he himself complains, by an unjust judgment.
