Since Bishop Ibas asserts that, through false fabrications, a false accusation, and calumny, this had been spoken against him in the wicked judgment of the Second Council of Ephesus, it is most clearly demonstrated by the aforementioned Bishop Ibas that he had denied the letter written to Maris the Persian to be his own.

To this may be added the fact that, in the wicked proceedings of that council, the very submission [the text has *praelatio*; perhaps *prolatio*, “production”] of the witnesses’ testimony by the adversaries of Bishop Ibas, through which they endeavored falsely to demonstrate that the letter was his, indicates nothing other than that this could not be proved to be the letter of Bishop Ibas in the judgment of Photius and Eustathius.

For if it had been proved there, the accusers at the Second Council of Ephesus would have relied on the proceedings held before Photius and Eustathius rather than on witnesses. The necessity of producing witnesses arises not concerning manifest matters but concerning uncertain ones.

Therefore Bishop Ibas acted most justly before the holy Council of Chalcedon when, refuting those same witnesses as false, he complained that, in his absence at the Second Council of Ephesus, he had suffered accusation through fabrication rather than through truth. He knew that in the judgment of the aforementioned bishops Photius and Eustathius he had not been convicted by any allegation from those same accusers. On the contrary, in order to demonstrate his innocence more fully, he requested that the judgment of the bishops Photius and Eustathius be reread.

In their judgment, when a petition had previously been presented by the accusers, it read as follows (*Act 10*):

> We indeed wished to live out the whole time of our lives without litigation. But because the things boldly done against our Church and against the most holy faith of our Fathers by our venerable bishop Ibas, being close to injustice, compelled us to descend to this accusation; and the rest.

When those same investigators had decreed by an interlocutory decision that, abandoning a general accusation, the accusers should individually designate in writing the chapters of their charges against Bishop Ibas, the written accusation is known to have contained nothing else, so far as matters of faith are concerned—that is, nothing that seemed to attack the faith of the Fathers—except this: that he called blessed Cyril a heretic and was therefore shown to be a Nestorian.

Thus it says:

> Because he is a Nestorian and calls blessed Cyril the bishop a heretic.

It is certain that the letter read to have been written to Maris the Persian contains this accusation in particular.

The judges immediately testified in their interlocutory decision that they had accepted this statement as involving the grave weight of heresy, saying as follows (*Act 10*):

> When an accusation follows a chapter involving danger to the soul, we judge it superfluous to conduct an investigation of the others. Choose first those matters that have plainly been condemned by the canons and the laws and that are openly hateful to those who fear God, and persist in them. It seems to us that, first of all, the man who exercises the priesthood must be of correct faith and must likewise be free from every form of immorality; and so forth.

## III

Who, then, could doubt that the judges said the chapter concerned the danger of the soul, and that from it a priest who called blessed Cyril a heretic was to be judged not to possess the correct faith, since before that interlocutory decision nothing else had been stated in the accusation concerning matters of faith except that he was a Nestorian and had called blessed Cyril a heretic?

It is therefore sufficiently clear that the letter written to Maris the Persian, which called blessed Cyril a heretic by declaring that Cyril’s doctrines—through dissent from which Nestorius is known to have been condemned—were contrary to the right faith, was in no way proved by the adversaries of Bishop Ibas to have been the letter of Ibas himself, nor had Ibas himself confessed it to be his.

For if it could have been demonstrated before the aforementioned judges that the letter had been written by Ibas, Ibas would never have deserved acquittal by their judgment. With the great weight of their interlocutory decision, they first wished the matter of the faith to be examined thoroughly, before they judged the case to be especially grave because of blessed Cyril, whom Ibas was said to have called a heretic.

The text of the subsequent decree also clearly demonstrates, in the passages set forth below in their proper places, that it agrees with what has been said.

For, at the request of Ibas, after the sequence of the judgment had been reread in the aforementioned holy Council of Chalcedon by the bishops Photius and Eustathius, the following is clearly stated in the judgment of those judges, after certain other matters, when they were discussing the order of the accusation instituted against Bishop Ibas (*Act 9*):

> When they had therefore presented certain chapters and requested that these be carefully investigated, we applied ourselves to the chapters and found in them a certain fabrication against the most reverend Bishop Ibas, as though he did not think correctly but taught something other than the doctrine of piety. We were therefore necessarily compelled first to conduct a careful investigation of this matter.
>
> For we ordered the accusers to state what, as they themselves claimed, Bishop Ibas was saying that was alien to the doctrine of piety. They stated certain things of their own. And when many matters had been raised, which have been inserted into the acts—

And shortly afterward the same judges said:

> Putting piety everywhere before our counsels and inquiries, we prepared the most reverend Bishop Ibas—who himself also understood that he should give satisfaction concerning what had been lightly said [perhaps, “concerning the faith”]—to provide in writing what he believed or understood concerning our pious faith; and he did so.
>
> Moreover, in addition, the aforementioned most reverend man promised that, both in the church of his own city and publicly, he would anathematize Nestorius, the originator of wicked impiety, and those who think as he does, as well as those who use his books or codices.
>
> He confessed that he believed as the letters contain that had passed between the most reverend and holy Bishop John of the great city of Antioch and Cyril, bishop of the greatest city of Alexandria, and which had been delivered by Paul, bishop of the city of Emesa; from these a universal agreement is produced.
>
> He also confessed that he agreed in every respect with what had recently been done by the holy synod assembled in the imperial and Christian city of Constantinople, and that he accepted everything approved at the metropolitan Council of Ephesus, which was moved by the Holy Spirit; that he judged what had been established at Nicaea to be equal to these and regarded no difference between that council and the others.
>
> And we praised his holiness exceedingly because he had wisely taken care to protect those whose doctrinal reputation might be harmed by suspicion or by any other means; and so forth.

## IV

Having carefully considered the tenor of the decree issued by the venerable men Photios and Eustathios, in which it is said that, when the accusers presented their articles—which, as is read above, could not in fact have been presented except in writing—the judges found that an accusation had been fabricated against Bishop Ibas, alleging that he did or taught something beyond the pious doctrine, it is clear that they pronounced nothing else [Col. 0150C], once the matter had been thoroughly investigated, as they themselves record, than that the accusation against Bishop Ibas had been maliciously brought forward through fabricated imputations, not out of a zeal for truth.

And what else had the accusers brought in writing against Bishop Ibas concerning the matter of faith, except that he was a Nestorian, since he called the blessed Cyril a heretic and affirmed that Cyril had fallen into the heresy of Apollinaris and had composed a heretical letter, said to have been written to Maris the Persian? Hence it is clear that this letter had not been Bishop Ibas’s, since the judges attest that, through the falsity of the fabricated imputation, he had been charged with what that same letter contained. The place in the above-mentioned decree plainly corresponds to the question put to Bishop Ibas, by which he complains that, at the holy and venerable Council of Chalcedon [Col. 0150D], Bishop Uranius, acting on behalf of Eutyches, had prepared certain clerics to persist in their accusation against him.

From this it sufficiently appears that Photios and Eustathios, by their own judgment, denounced the fabrication, silently omitting the name of the person who had introduced it, whereas Bishop Ibas openly identified it in the holy Council of Chalcedon by expressly calling it a contrivance. It is therefore not doubtful that what was brought forward against the blessed Cyril as a charge, and against Ibas as heresy and schism, and which is shown to have been contained in the letter, was fabricated by the accusers’ cunning device and exposed as such by the accused man’s denial and by the judges’ decision.

## V

The same page of the decree further states that, in satisfaction for what the accusers had said lightly [possibly: “concerning the faith”], Bishop Ibas wisely undertook in writing to state what he believed or understood concerning the pious faith. Hence it consequently appears that the accusers of Bishop Ibas are marked throughout by falsehood. They had slipped, through the unconsidered heat of hostility, into accusing Bishop Ibas lightly rather than truthfully. Thus, although the tenor of the letter written to Maris the Persian asserted, in disparagement of the blessed Cyril and his Twelve Chapters, what they had alleged—and although Ibas could not be convicted of having said the same things, despite the accusers’ equal levity and falsehood—Bishop Ibas nevertheless showed in writing what he believed concerning the pious faith, as though he did not consider it sufficient for his own vindication that he could not be convicted of having said anything against the true faith, unless he also publicly declared, by his own statement, how he had always held that faith in his mind [Col. 0151B].

This would have been wholly unnecessary either for the judges or for Bishop Ibas himself if it could have been shown that the aforementioned letter was both his own and composed in an orthodox sense. Therefore, careful attention must be given to the statement that, in satisfaction for what had been said lightly, Bishop Ibas wisely undertook in writing to show what he believed concerning the pious faith.

For it is plainly evident that the text of the letter to Maris is so contrary to pious doctrine that, although it was charged against Bishop Ibas through the accusers’ levity rather than through the truth of the matter, nevertheless, lest even what had falsely been attributed to him should detract from his Catholic faith, he wisely undertook to show, against that impiety, what he believed concerning the pious faith. Nor would it have been necessary for him to set down in writing what he believed concerning the sincerity of the orthodox faith [Col. 0151C], unless it had been evident in that letter, which had been charged against him, that there was the stain of unbelief which he avoided.

It is therefore established both that the letter, which is asserted on the basis of the accusers’ levity to have been charged against him, was not his, and that it was opposed to the true faith; and that, in response to its accusation, the true faith was set forth in writing.

Again, and still more clearly for the acquittal of Bishop Ibas, the same judgment states that Bishop Ibas, “out of an abundance of caution,” had promised openly to anathematize Nestorius, the leader of malicious impiety, together with those who held opinions like his and those who used his books or codices; and that he accepted everything approved at the Council of Ephesus, which was moved by the Holy Spirit, and regarded it as no different from what had been established at Nicaea [possibly: “as not differing from the Council of Nicaea”].

Moreover, the letter read as having been written to Maris the Persian is shown not only [Col. 0151D] not to contain what was done at the First Council of Ephesus, but also to have rejected and condemned it with grave execration. For it records that Nestorius was condemned without judgment or investigation; it defines, with obstinate and sacrilegious error [possibly: “with obstinate and sacrilegious”], that the blessed Cyril had fallen into the heresy of Apollinaris and had written similar things; and it had called the Twelve Chapters of the blessed Cyril full of every impiety and contrary to the true faith.

From this it is most clearly declared that, on the basis of Bishop Ibas’s profession—which, as the judges testify, declares that he accepted and preserved everything done at the First Council of Ephesus—the letter was denied to have been his. For if it had been established that the letter was his, the letter in which, as has been said, the First Council of Ephesus was attacked, the judges would not have said that Bishop Ibas had “out of an abundance of caution,” among other things, promised to accept everything approved at the First Council of Ephesus. Rather, they would have said that, for the sake of demonstrating his correction, the aforesaid bishop had been necessarily compelled to accept what he himself had rejected in the letter [Col. 0152A].

For Bishop Ibas would not be said to have made his profession “out of an abundance of caution” if, compelled by the necessity of the facts themselves, he confessed these things in order to appear orthodox. The words of the same judgment that follow contribute to this clear reasoning. They say (Act. 10): “For thus we praised his holiness, because he had wisely undertaken to care for those who, whether through suspicion or in any other way, might injure his reputation for doctrine,” and so forth.

From these words it is completely clear that Bishop Ibas also made this profession “out of an abundance of caution,” by which not only the truth—which had not been proved against him—but even suspicion, if it could have arisen, would be removed [Col. 0152B]. Since the letter written to Maris the Persian is read to contain not merely matters capable of creating some suspicion, but open and manifest accusations against the First Council of Ephesus and the Twelve Chapters of the blessed Cyril, no one can doubt that the letter had not been approved as belonging to Bishop Ibas, who was shown to be free even from suspicion through his abundant precaution.

And how could a man be accused of the truth of a reprehensible act who wished to be shown free even from suspicion?

## VI

Since these matters stand thus, consistently and with the same justice urging it, there follows the statement of the legates of the Apostolic See. On the basis of the decree itself of the venerable bishops Photios and Eustathios, it declares Bishop Ibas to be innocent and free from every accusation, both with respect to what the accusers had presented in writing [Col. 0152C] and with respect to what they had said during the proceedings. It asks only that Photios and Eustathios, the venerable men, should acknowledge their own judgment and confirm it by their signatures.

The record reads as follows (Act. 9):

“Paschasinus and the other bishops said through the presbyter of the Apostolic See: ‘If the most holy bishops who, by their own decree, declared the most reverend Ibas innocent and free from every accusation recognize their own judgment, let them state so.’

“Photios, the most reverend bishop of Tyre, said: ‘It is also our decree.’

“Eustathios, the most reverend bishop of Berytus, said: ‘The subscription is mine’;” and so forth.

Since in this inquiry the judges had merely reminded them to acknowledge their judgment, expressing no doubt about the character of the judgment, and indeed approving that Bishop Ibas had thereby been found free from every accusation, it is clearly and openly shown that the decree of the venerable bishops Photios and Eustathios also received the unquestionable agreement of the legates of the Apostolic See, because, as has been said, Bishop Ibas had been found free from every accusation.

After the judgment of the bishops Photios and Eustathios, which Bishop Ibas had produced on his own behalf, had been reread, and after the same judges had acknowledged it by repeating their profession, as stated above, the examination of the person of Bishop Ibas was carried over to the following day. Again Bishop Ibas entered, and is read to have complained as follows (Act. 10):

“I appeal to your magnificence and to this universal holy synod. Eutyches fabricated certain false charges against me concerning the faith, and did not permit me to enter the holy synod. He sent me through forty stations, in different ranks one after another; I changed twenty or more prisons, as though there were no prison in Antioch, while the members of the comitiva said to me, ‘You have been condemned.’ If it seems good, therefore, to your magnificence and to your holy synod to annul what was done against me in my absence without judgment, it will be in your power. For this reason, as I have already explained, I approached the sacred and immortal summit, and he ordered your magnificence and your holy synod to hear what had been done against me; and from the decree you learned that I was found guilty of nothing.”

## VII

When these complaints had thus been brought forward, it is clear that Bishop Ibas, in his most explicit lamentations, asserted (printed *alligare*, “to bind”; perhaps *allegare*, “to allege”) that what had been done against him concerning the faith in the criminal proceedings of that wicked Second Council of Ephesus had been contrived [possibly: “fabricated”] by Eutyches. As has already been stated above, there they had attempted, by introducing the responses of witnesses against an absent man, especially by means of the letter to Maris the Persian, to prove that the letter was his.

In this passage it is plainly apparent that Bishop Ibas denied the letter in two ways, as was also asserted above. First, it is demonstrated that the production of witnesses by his accusers would have been necessary only against a man who denied the charge. For no one needs the responses of witnesses against a man whom he sees confessing what he is accused of having done. Bishop Ibas made this denial still clearer by showing it through the accuser’s fear, saying: “Nor did he permit me to enter the synod” (ibid.). For by this he testifies that the other had prepared false witnesses against him: while complaining that his absence had been brought about by the adversary’s deliberate effort, he confirms that he could not have been convicted had he been present.

Second, when Bishop Ibas was present at the holy and venerable Council of Chalcedon and complained that what had been done against him at the Second Council of Ephesus by the testimony of witnesses [possibly: “through witnesses”] and in other ways had been fabricated [possibly: “fabricated”], he undoubtedly professed that he rejected as alien to himself the letter which, according to the responses of the witnesses there, had falsely been declared to be his.

Consequently, it appropriately follows that the judges residing there at Chalcedon, on the basis of the decree of Photios and Eustathios [Col. 0153D], recognized him as guilty of nothing, openly professing that what the accusers had said against him concerning the faith—both in the petition presented to Bishops Photios and Eustathios, in which they said that he uttered many things against the faith of the Fathers, and in the articles given in writing, in which they said (ibid.), “He is a Nestorian and calls the blessed Cyril a heretic”—as well as what they said he had publicly declared, “I do not envy Christ, made God; for insofar as he was made, I too,” had been falsely reported against him by the accusers.

Thus the judgment of the venerable bishops Photios and Eustathios established that these statements had been made lightly and falsely, to such an extent that, on the basis of the same decree, he was declared free from every accusation and found guilty of nothing [Col. 0154A].

Since this is so, it is clearly demonstrated that the letter written to Maris the Persian—which says that the Twelve Chapters of the blessed Cyril are full of every impiety and contrary to the true faith, and that Nestorius was condemned without judgment or investigation—was in no way approved as belonging to Bishop Ibas. For he himself openly declares concerning himself that what the accusers had said against him concerning the faith had been falsely said. If he had either acknowledged the letter as his own or had been convicted by some proof brought by the accusers, he certainly would not have been judged completely innocent by Bishops Photios and Eustathios, before whom these matters had been dealt with (printed *flagitate*; perhaps *agitata*, “discussed”).

Bishop Ibas had therefore been attacked by his accusers lightly, falsely, and through some fabricated imputation; under compulsion he anathematized Nestorius and voluntarily testified that he accepted everything approved at the First Council of Ephesus, just as he accepted what had been done at Nicaea. These things are plainly shown to have been rejected on behalf of Nestorius by the letter said to have been written to Maris the Persian.

For this reason no one can doubt that, with respect to what we assert was falsely said against us, we categorically deny that it was said or done by us; and that what we assert was received “out of an abundance of caution,” we affirm had been held previously as well.

## VIII

As further and indubitable evidence of this denial, the sequence of the following proceedings is appropriately connected. When certain persons in the holy Council of Chalcedon had attempted to raise an objection to the acquittal of Bishop Ibas, and the judges had ordered his accusers to enter, the deacon Theophilus entered with others. When asked whether he had come to accuse Bishop Ibas, he replied as follows (Act. 10):

“The accusers are manifest, and they are not here. I am a deacon, and I know the violence of the city. And if I accuse, the witnesses are not present, and he denies.”

This response of the accuser shows that Bishop Ibas had denied what was charged against him before Bishops Photios and Eustathios in such a way that, at the Council of Chalcedon, when he knew that the same charges were being brought against him, the accuser confirmed that Bishop Ibas would deny them.

Hence the contention of certain people is extremely astonishing. They falsely claim that Bishop Ibas confessed that the letter written to Maris the Persian—which had been brought forward by the accusers as a serious crime and which, on the basis of the proceedings held before Bishops Photios and Eustathios, was again produced at the Council of Chalcedon to convict Bishop Ibas, as they supposed—was his own. Yet, as has been stated above, his accusers, having already experienced his denials and knowing that he would certainly deny what they intended to bring against him from the aforementioned proceedings, testify that he would deny it.

Indeed, they knew Bishop Ibas to be so bound (*subnexum*; perhaps *subnixum*, “supported”) by the strength of his conscience in the judgment of Bishops Photios and Eustathios, and knew that he had denied what had been brought forward by the accusers, that at the holy Council of Chalcedon, even in the presence of Photios and Eustathios themselves, before whom the matter had earlier been examined, they again confirmed that he would deny it [Col. 0155A]. For an accuser would never say that Bishop Ibas would deny something while the same men were again sitting in judgment if he knew that Ibas had already confessed it in the earlier judgment before them.

Afterward, when the judges residing at Chalcedon asked the accusers of Bishop Ibas whether they could provide written proofs of anything concerning the matter, the deacon Theophilus said: “I have records concerning these proceedings, both those held at Berytus and those held at Ephesus,” and so forth.

## IX

It must therefore be observed that the adversaries of Bishop Ibas said that they had nothing else to bring against him at the Council of Chalcedon except the records concerning him that had been produced before Bishops Photios and Eustathios and later at the Second Council of Ephesus.

From this it appears that they did not think it sufficient for them—or rather, they thought it would work against them—if only what had been done against Bishop Ibas before the aforementioned Bishops Photios and Eustathios were read. In those proceedings he was shown to have been convicted neither by witnesses nor by his own confession. They therefore demanded that the things wickedly done at the Second Council of Ephesus also be produced, in which they could employ the falsehoods of those who deceitfully claimed that Bishop Ibas had confessed the letter written to Maris the Persian to be his own.

It is therefore certain that the adversaries had no document which they thought constituted proof against Bishop Ibas except this one thing: what, in that council—which ought not to be called a council—Bishop Ibas asserts was fabricated against him in his absence. The judges residing at the holy Council of Chalcedon, moved by the truth of the matter, removed this by a just interlocutory decision [Col. 0155B]. They asked Bishops Thalassius and Eusebius, who had been present at the Second Council of Ephesus with the others, whether Ibas had been present at their hearing. They replied (Act. 10): “He was not present.”

When this response had been heard, the Eastern and Pontic bishops cried out at the Council of Chalcedon: “No one condemns an absent man.”

Their interlocution, thus pronounced, plainly nullifies what had been done against Bishop Ibas at the Second Council of Ephesus, referring the entire matter back to the proceedings of those men—namely, Photios and Eustathios—by whose judgment they already knew Bishop Ibas to have been acquitted.

This is marked in what follows by an even clearer judicial interlocution: they forbade the wicked proceedings of the Second Council of Ephesus against Bishop Ibas to be reread as matters held for execration and falsehood [Col. 0155D].

But in order that it might be made more clearly understood that Bishop Ibas had unquestionably denied everything which his adversaries had charged against him in the judgment of Bishops Photios and Eustathios, and which they were now going to charge against him at the holy Council of Chalcedon from the proceedings produced by Theophilus, the questioning of the judges residing at Chalcedon, or the response of Bishop Photios, disclosed this without any obstacle of ambiguity. It reads as follows (ibid.):

“The most magnificent and glorious judges said: ‘Was the most reverend Bishop Ibas therefore convicted by his accusers?’

“Photios, the most reverend bishop, said: ‘No,’” and so forth.

What could be said more clearly or more conclusively than this proof—that the bishop confirmed that Bishop Ibas would deny what the accuser was about to bring forward? Did not Photios himself, the judge before whom the matter had earlier been examined, confess that Bishop Ibas had not been convicted, and thus plainly testify that Ibas had denied what had been charged against him?

The sequence of the following proceedings makes clear that this denial especially concerned the letter read as having been written to Maris the Persian. For, when they had produced as documentary evidence what they had earlier submitted in writing in the judgment of Photios and Eustathios—namely, that Ibas was a Nestorian and had called the blessed Cyril a heretic—and had brought forward those blasphemies which they thought they would prove by witnesses, namely, “I do not envy Christ made God” (Act. 10), but had been unable to establish any of these matters once the witnesses were rejected, they returned to what they had previously submitted in writing. They charged him with what the letter written to Maris the Persian contained [Col. 0156B]: namely, that he had called the blessed Cyril and his Twelve Chapters heretical.

The judges Photios and Eustathios, therefore, as they themselves professed above, applied themselves more carefully to the matter. At one moment they questioned Bishop Ibas himself; at another they demanded proofs from the accusers, asking most earnestly and shrewdly whether anything had been said against the blessed Cyril by the aforementioned Bishop Ibas after the unity of the Churches had been established.

In response to these charges, Bishop Ibas, through all his defenses, opposed the letter read as having been written to Maris the Persian, asserting that after unity and peace had been established between the blessed Cyril and the Easterners, he had in no way disparaged the blessed Cyril.

## X

Moreover, the aforementioned letter written to Maris the Persian, after unity and peace had been restored to the Churches, confirms that the blessed Cyril had fallen into the heresy of Apollinaris and had written similar things; it asserts that his Twelve Chapters were contrary to the true faith; and it states that Nestorius had been condemned without judgment (the printed text has *judicium*; perhaps *sine judicio*) or investigation.

The writer of the letter does not say that the error arose through his own understanding or that of anyone else, so that the blessed Cyril might be thought to have composed heretical doctrines. Rather, the same fabricator of the letter persists in that depravity and so presents the orthodox doctrines of the blessed Cyril as heretical that he even asserts that the blessed Cyril withdrew from them as though he were rejecting what he had wickedly written.

Anyone who reads these things with a pious and upright heart understands that they are contrary to Bishop Ibas’s profession, as the adversaries’ charge presents it. For if the judges, while investigating Bishop Ibas to determine whether he had said anything after the unity that might lightly disparage Cyril, had established that the blasphemous letter so plainly belonged to him, they would not have permitted the matter to pass without punishment, nor would they have said that he was not convicted.

What greater injury could be sought or inflicted against the blessed Cyril than to define as heretical the doctrines he set forth at the First Council of Ephesus—through whose orthodox proclamation he remains venerable and revered by all, living and dead? Since the letter written to Maris the Persian, after the blessed Cyril and John, bishop of Antioch, had been united, plainly attacks these doctrines with wholly profane language, how could anyone of sound mind suppose that Ibas, while denying that he had said anything against the blessed Cyril after the unity, had not denied the letter which, after that union, defines Cyril’s doctrines to be heretical?

Unless, perhaps, someone should depart so far from human reason as to believe that Ibas said nothing contrary to the blessed Cyril if he testified that Cyril had written heretical things, and should suppose that Ibas preserved reverence toward Cyril’s person while accusing the holy teaching by which Cyril is revered by all.

Therefore, if condemning the doctrine of the blessed Cyril is a singular injury against him, and if openly derogating from Catholic teaching appears to be a profession of heresy, then, if the letter were proved to be Ibas’s—the letter in which both are manifestly contained—Ibas could never have earned acquittal by denying both charges.

Furthermore, it is demonstrated more clearly than daylight that no time can be found—neither before nor after the union of the blessed Cyril with the Easterners—at which the same letter could be shown to have been written by Bishop Ibas. For the tenor of the letter plainly shows that it was composed after unity and peace had been restored to the Churches, in disparagement of the blessed Cyril and his doctrines. Yet Ibas testifies that after the union of the blessed Cyril with the Easterners he said no such thing.

It is therefore established that the letter in question was not written by Ibas: not before the union, because this is not read in the tenor of the letter; and not after the union, because Ibas denies it by his own profession.

## XI

And so that it may be entirely beyond doubt that Bishop Ibas persisted in the same denial with which he had begun, that the judges understood this from the words of Ibas himself, and that the accusers treated him as one who denied it but could not prove their case, we must weigh the words of the judges’ interlocution and the accusers’ argument, which are read in the holy Council of Chalcedon from the proceedings of Photios and Eustathios. They read as follows (Act. 10):

“The most reverend bishops, namely Photios and Eustathios, said: ‘If, after the death of the blessed Cyril, the most reverend Bishop Ibas appears to have called him a heretic and to have regarded him as a heretic, show it.’

“Maras said: ‘We prove it.’”

The judges would certainly not still have sought proof of this, nor would the accusers have promised to prove it, if Bishop Ibas had not denied it.

Although what has already become abundantly clear from the proceedings held before Photios and Eustathios and from their judgment—namely, the denial of Bishop Ibas, demonstrated in many ways by the interlocutions of the judges, the arguments of the accusers, and Ibas’s own defenses—would have been sufficient, nevertheless, even if something less explicit had been read in the judgment of Bishops Photios and Eustathios, the single profession of Bishop Ibas denying the letter at the Council of Chalcedon would have sufficed.

For when the letter written to Maris the Persian had been read from the proceedings held before Photios and Eustathios, Ibas immediately responded with the voice of one who denied it, saying:

“Let your clemency order the letters of the clerics of Edessa to be reread, so that you may know that I am alien even to the things brought against me and that I have suffered violence.”

Here one must first carefully observe that, after the text of the letter written to Maris the Persian had been read, the judges residing at Chalcedon are shown to have passed over that same letter in silence. They knew that it had already been refuted so many times by the denials of the accused.

For if they had seen in it anything that could assist the acquittal of Bishop Ibas, they would immediately, moved by its reading, have decided that the accusers were bringing forward in vain from the proceedings of Bishops Photios and Eustathios, as a charge of heresy, something by which Bishop Ibas was instead shown to be orthodox. Finally, they would not have ordered the letter of the Edessene clerics to be reviewed in their interlocutions—the letter which Bishop Ibas requested to be reread on his behalf against the one said to have been written to Maris the Persian—if the letter produced by the accuser had shown the accused man’s merit to be praiseworthy rather than blameworthy [Col. 0158B].

Moreover, when the same letter to Maris the Persian had been reread, Bishop Ibas himself did not undertake to defend its character, nor did he demonstrate the rectitude of his faith from the profession contained in that letter. Immediately, if it had been his own or had contained doctrines that were orthodox [Note: Cotelerius correctly advised reading: “or if he had known that it contained orthodox doctrines”], he would have risen against his accusers and said:

“With blind hearts they attack me, so that they may charge me with heresy on the basis of things by which I can be proved orthodox. Rather, they have shown themselves to be heretics, since they accuse as heretical a letter whose composition asserts the Catholic faith.”

But Bishop Ibas knew both that the letter was not his and that it was wholly opposed to pious doctrines. Therefore, he opposed it with the letter of the Edessene clerics, which testified that he had never said anything against the Catholic faith [Col. 0158C]. He followed what he had alleged earlier, upon entering the holy Council of Chalcedon, saying:

“For all the Edessene clerics, through whom they wrote to the aforementioned bishops, testify that I am Catholic” (Act. 9).

Thus, already at the judgment of Photios and Eustathios, and afterward at the holy Council of Chalcedon, while denying that the letter to Maris the Persian charged against him was his own, he knew that it was contrary to the orthodox faith, to such an extent that he sought proof of his own faith not from the text of that letter but from the testimony of the Edessene clerics.

## XII

If, therefore, the judges, not only judging that Bishop Ibas’s case was not helped by that letter but actually seeing it as wholly contrary to him, ordered by their interlocutions another letter, which the accused had sought for his vindication, to be reread; and if the accused Bishop Ibas himself, instead of defending the letter to Maris the Persian, requested that the letter of the Edessene clerics be reread precisely in order to refute it, then it is established by the judges’ interlocution and by Bishop Ibas’s profession that the letter written to Maris the Persian was denied to have been his and was shown to contain criminal doctrines.

Therefore Bishop Ibas, moved by the fervor of an innocent mind and hastening to add at the Council of Chalcedon an even clearer proof of his denial, requested that the letters of the Edessene clerics be reread from the proceedings held before Photios and Eustathios—proceedings which his adversary had produced. As the following demonstrates, the accuser had deliberately omitted that part of the proceedings by which he knew that Ibas would be more clearly assisted [Col. 0159A].

Next, we must observe what Ibas’s own words plainly assert. He continues, as we recalled above, as follows (Act. 10):

“Let your clemency order the letters of the Edessene clerics to be reread, so that you may know that I am alien both to the things brought against me and that I have suffered violence.”

These words make it perfectly clear that, because Bishop Ibas immediately after the reading of the letter to Maris the Persian asserts that he is alien to the things brought against him and that he has suffered violence, and because of this requests that the letters of the Edessene clerics be reread, he spoke as though he were pointing with his own hand to the letter to Maris the Persian, from the charge of which he was hastening to clear himself.

When he said, “I am alien to the things brought against me,” he showed that he was entirely alien both to the other matters previously brought against him and to the letter written to Maris the Persian, which had just been reread.

Here too we must consider what was read above: when Bishop Ibas entered the holy Council of Chalcedon, he complained most seriously that he had been attacked by false accusations at the Second Council of Ephesus, that he had not been permitted to enter the council, and that he had changed more than twenty prisons. After the reading of the letter, he did not omit to add this again, so that it might appear that what he had alleged upon entering the holy Council of Chalcedon—namely, the injustice inflicted upon him at the Second Council of Ephesus—belonged to the cause of this letter.

After its reading, he asserted that he was alien to the things brought against him and added the violence which he had suffered from Eutyches.

The letter of the Edessene clerics was therefore read, as Ibas had requested, from the proceedings of the judges Photios and Eustathios, to whom that letter had in fact been addressed, and who had requested it so that Photios and Eustathios might insert it into the proceedings. Those proceedings were produced by the adversaries of Bishop Ibas at the Council of Chalcedon.

The reason why the reading of that letter had been desired is recognized from its own words, which read as follows (Act. 10):

“From many and various people coming to us from Phoenicia, we learned what had been done by those who rose up against our most holy and most reverend bishop, Ibas. We were terrified by what was reported to us: words which surpass even those of the godless, unbelievers, heretics, Jews, and pagans. It was said that the same most reverend bishop had spoken these words in our presence:

‘I do not envy Christ who was made God, because I too, if I wish, can become like him.’

“We all, whom they say heard the things they report, make it manifest before your reverence and in the presence of the clemency of God that we have never heard such a statement from him or from anyone else, nor has anything of the kind ever entered our ears. We anathematize ourselves and make ourselves liable to the terrible Gehenna if we know that any such statement was made by him, or anything else contrary to the Catholic faith.

“For if we had suffered ourselves to communicate with one who had spoken any such words, or to celebrate the Mass with him, we would have been liable to the ultimate punishment, as men communicating in such an error [Cotelerius reads: ‘horror’],” and so forth.

### XIII

Under these circumstances it is clearly shown that, according to the testimony of the Edessene clergy, all the things which the accusers alleged that Bishop Ibas had said—both in the written petitions submitted [Col. 0160A] and subsequently in their spoken statements recorded in the proceedings—were not said by Bishop Ibas. For when they say that they do not know that he ever made either such a statement, namely, “I do not envy Christ, who has been made God,” or anything similar—that is, anything which might appear in any respect to agree with Nestorius’s doctrines—or anything else contrary to the true faith, it is perfectly clear that, by their testimony, they also cleared Bishop Ibas of the contents of the letter written to Maris the Persian.

For since the aforesaid letter, by saying that blessed Cyril had fallen into the heresy of Apollinaris and had written things similar to him, and that his Twelve Chapters were full of every impiety and contrary to the true faith, and that Nestorius had been condemned without judgment or investigation [Col. 0160B], appears not merely to say something against the true faith but, by attacking it, even to reject that true faith itself, whereas the Edessene clergy testify that Bishop Ibas said nothing contrary to the true faith, it is evident from their testimony that the letter read as having been written to Maris the Persian was refuted.

What Theophilus the accuser then proceeded to do must be examined more carefully. He did not think that this letter of the Edessenes should be omitted as superfluous or as something which, in his judgment, could contribute nothing to overturning the letter written to Maris the Persian. Rather, he made every effort, with the full concentration of his mind, to assert that this letter of the Edessene clergy had been falsified. He was especially moved to do so because they had testified that Ibas had said nothing contrary to the catholic faith. Seeing, therefore, that by this statement the letter written to Maris the Persian [Col. 0160C], which speaks most openly against the true faith, had been refuted, he wished to accuse this Edessene letter of forgery, since he saw that by it all his objections had been defeated.

The subsequent order of the proceedings helps establish this. For when Theophilus, Ibas’s adversary, as above, so here too, demanded that the proceedings held at the Second Council of Ephesus—by which he sought to establish his case—be sought from all the bishops then sitting at Chalcedon, the acts held at the Second Council of Ephesus were forbidden to be reviewed. From this prohibition it is evident that the assertion of Bishop Ibas was confirmed: he had declared that he was being attacked by Eutyches through slander and false fabrications. It is clear that, when lying witnesses were produced, it was fabricated that Ibas [the bishop] had said that the letter written to Maris the Persian [Col. 0160D] was his own.

Among the statements of the Fathers concerning the annulment of the Second Council of Ephesus, nothing other than the deposition of Domnus and the ordination of Maximus is certainly shown to have been confirmed. It is clear that Domnus was condemned for no other crime than that he had forbidden the preaching of blessed Cyril’s Twelve Chapters. Thus, by manifest reasoning [*manifesta ratione*], it is evident that if the holy Fathers sitting at Chalcedon had found that the letter to Maris the Persian—which declares blessed Cyril’s Twelve Chapters heretical and says that blessed Cyril wrote things similar to Apollinaris—was in some way [the text appears to lack a word indicating its relation to] Bishop Ibas, they would certainly have decided that he could not be acquitted of the more serious charge in the same case [Col. 0161A]. They did not permit the condemnation of Domnus, bishop of Antioch, to be overturned when it had been imposed solely because he had forbidden the preaching of those same Twelve Chapters, and they confirmed the ordination of Maximus.

For how could those same judges, in one and the same case, decide by their statement that Ibas—condemned by the Second Council of Ephesus—should be acquitted, while allowing Domnus to remain condemned, unless they had approved that the man whom they decided to acquit was not involved in the same crime? Since at the holy Council of Chalcedon such execrable abuse of blessed Cyril and his Twelve Chapters prevailed that, because of them, they allowed Domnus—condemned at the discredited Second Council of Ephesus—to remain condemned, how great must have been the innocence of Bishop Ibas demonstrated at that holy Council of Chalcedon, when it determined that he should be acquitted even though he had been condemned for the same crime in the wicked proceedings of the Second Council of Ephesus! In this case he could never have appeared innocent if that criminal letter to Maris the Persian could have been shown to be by the same Bishop Ibas.

### XIV

After everything has therefore been examined and clearly argued—by which it became evident, both from the proceedings held before Bishops Photius and Eustathius and from their judgment, as well as in many other ways, that Bishop Ibas entirely denied that the letter written to Maris the Persian was his and could never be convicted on the basis of its accusation—it remains for us, with similar truth, to show how the aforesaid letter written to Maris the Persian appears to be alien to the understanding, definition, or professions of the venerable Fathers sitting at Chalcedon, and to conflict with their judgments.

To make this clear to everyone, we must first examine what our Fathers sitting at the Council of Chalcedon professed in proclaiming and receiving the letter of blessed memory of our predecessor, Pope Leo, and in explaining the holy faith, and what pious doctrine they handed down as something to be held. Once these matters have been considered, it will be demonstrated from them how much the letter written to Maris the Persian differs from and contradicts their definition and tradition; and thus it will become apparent that it was in no way approved by the judgments of our Fathers.

In the fourth session of the Council of Chalcedon, after the letter of blessed memory, Pope Leo, had been read, when our Fathers were speaking about confirming that letter, they said as follows (Act 4):

Anatolius, the most reverend bishop of imperial Constantinople, said:

“The letter of the most holy and apostolic archbishop Leo agrees with the creed of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers who gathered at Nicaea and with that of the one hundred and fifty who afterward assembled at Constantinople, who confirmed the same faith; and it also agrees with the things enacted at Ephesus under blessed and most holy Cyril by the universal and holy council, when it condemned the accursed Nestorius. Therefore I have agreed and gladly subscribed to the same letter.”

Paschasinus and Lucentius, most reverend bishops, and Boniface the presbyter, representatives of the Apostolic See, spoke through Paschasinus:

“It is manifest, and it cannot be doubted, that the one faith of the most blessed pope, the ruler of the Apostolic See [Col. 0162A], agrees with and is preserved by the three hundred and eighteen Fathers at Nicaea, and also by the one hundred and fifty priests assembled at Constantinople who confirmed the same faith, and also by the decrees of Cyril, the man of holy memory, at Ephesus, when Nestorius was condemned for his error, without differing from them in any respect. Therefore the letter of the most blessed pope, which is recognized to have expounded that faith because of the error of Eutyches, appears to be joined to that faith in one meaning and one spirit.”

Maximus, the most reverend bishop of Antioch in Syria, said:

“The letter of the most holy archbishop Leo of imperial Rome agrees with the expositions of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers at Nicaea, with those of the one hundred and fifty at Constantinople, the New Rome, and with the exposition of the faith set forth at Ephesus by the most holy Bishop Cyril; and I have subscribed.”

After the other bishops had made similar statements, thirty-two Illyrian bishops dictated from a written document, through Sozomen, bishop of Philippi, as follows (Act 4):

“We both preserve the faith of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers, which is our salvation, and pray to complete our life in it. The one hundred and fifty agree with the aforesaid faith [perhaps, ‘with the aforesaid faith’], and we preserve and diligently follow it; and we acknowledge and follow all that was done and decreed at the First Council of Ephesus, whose presidents were the most blessed Coelestine, head of the Apostolic See, and the most blessed Cyril of the great city of Alexandria; and we have recognized our holy Father Archbishop Leo to be orthodox [perhaps, ‘the orthodox’].”

The remaining bishops likewise made similar professions.

### XV

Since these matters stand thus, no one can doubt [Col. 0162C] that our Fathers reverently believed that the letter of blessed Leo should be received by them because they asserted that it agreed both with the doctrines expounded at the Councils of Nicaea and Constantinople and with those of blessed Cyril at the First Council of Ephesus.

And if the letter of so great a pontiff, shining with such great light of the orthodox faith, must be approved by these comparisons, how can the letter to Maris the Persian—which expressly rejects the First Council of Ephesus and declares the dogmas expounded by blessed Cyril to be heretical—be believed to have been called orthodox by those same Fathers, since it condemns the very things by comparison with which, as stated, the teaching of so great a pontiff deserved praise?

Moreover, the acclamation of the universal Council of Chalcedon most clearly proved that the faith and teaching of both—namely, blessed Leo and blessed Cyril—were one, saying as follows (Act 2):

“Leo taught piously and truly. Cyril taught thus. Eternal memory to Cyril. Leo and Cyril taught alike. Anathema to anyone who does not believe thus.”

Thus the letter to Maris the Persian is shown not merely not to have been received, but even to have been anathematized, since it calls the doctrines expounded by Cyril at the First Council of Ephesus heretical; and whoever does not follow them is condemned, by the judgment of the holy Council of Chalcedon, to the punishment of anathema.

To this is added the judgment expressed in the profession of faith of that venerable Council of Chalcedon, which reads as follows (Act 5):

“Therefore, preserving the order and all the forms of the faith, and also what was done at the holy Council of Ephesus—whose presidents were Coelestine, bishop of the city of Rome, of holy memory, and Cyril of the Church of Alexandria—we define that the exposition of the true and undefiled faith of the three hundred and eighteen holy and most blessed Fathers gathered at Nicaea under Constantine, the prince of pious memory, shines forth; and that the definitions of the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers at Constantinople also remain in force, for the overthrow of the heresies that had arisen and for the confirmation of this same catholic faith of ours.

“The Creed of the three hundred and eighteen at Nicaea.”

And later (Act 5):

“Because of those who attempt to corrupt the mystery of the dispensation, shamelessly raving that the one born from the holy Virgin Mary was a mere man, it receives the synodical letters of blessed Cyril, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, to Nestorius and to others throughout the East, as appropriate for refuting the madness of Nestorius”; and so forth.

### XVI

Behold, it is evident to the understanding of all the faithful that our holy Fathers sitting at Chalcedon, when they expressed their judgment concerning the explanation of the catholic faith, professed that they preserved the order and all the forms of the faith established at the First Council of Ephesus, presided over by Coelestine of blessed memory and blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, just as they professed that they preserved the common care of the Nicene and Constantinopolitan [perhaps, “council”] councils. They undoubtedly testified that the definitions of those councils were their own faith.

From this it appears that whatever differs from the order or forms established at the First Council of Ephesus, and is shown to be contrary to them, is likewise assailed by the judgments of the blessed Fathers of Chalcedon [the text has *impugnare*, perhaps for *impugnari*, “to be assailed”].

Furthermore, the letter written to Maris the Persian, by saying that blessed Cyril was a heretic, that his Twelve Chapters were impious and contrary to the true faith, and that Nestorius was condemned without judgment or investigation, is shown to be contrary to the entire order and all the forms established at the First Council of Ephesus.

It follows that it is exceedingly absurd to suppose that, by their decrees, the Fathers received a letter which most openly attacks their judgment concerning the faith, so that by this they would appear not only to destroy the earlier Fathers but also themselves by some contradiction—which it is impious even to say.

For it is seen, with the clearest light of truth, from what follows that all such things as were said or were to be said in derogation of the First Council of Ephesus were also condemned in this exposition of the faith issued by the holy Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon. It reads as follows (ibid.):

“Having therefore arranged these matters with every care and diligence on every side, the holy and universal council defines that no one may bring forward, write, compose, hold, or teach another faith in any way. But those who dare to compose another faith, or to bring forward, teach, or hand down another creed to those wishing to turn to the knowledge of the truth either from paganism, or from Judaism, or from any heresy whatever—if they are bishops or clerics, they shall be alienated from the episcopate and the clergy; but if they are laymen or monks, they shall be anathematized.”

Since, therefore, our Fathers said that they preserved the order and all the forms of the faith of the First Council of Ephesus, and that no one was permitted to bring forward, write, hold, hand down, or teach another faith, and since they condemned all who presumed to do such things, we must certainly affirm that the letter written to Maris the Persian, which in every respect attacks the doctrine expounded by blessed Cyril at the First Council of Ephesus, did not merely teach differently but even taught in opposition to it. It is therefore clear that it was included under the sentence of the same condemnation by synodical judgment. Consequently, since the letter to Maris the Persian is read as having been expressly condemned by those whose statements are cited, it is even clearer that it was not received by them.

### XVII

Nor should any of the faithful be disturbed by the fact that some, by stealth, attempt to maintain that certain things were said in this letter to Maris which can be shown to agree with the things it says correctly. For it is the custom of heretics to conceal their poisons beneath embellished speech, to utter first words which seem to harmonize with orthodox professions, and to reserve [Note: [Col. 0163D] This appears to be a corrupt manuscript. HARD.] for their malignity hidden entrances through which the pestilence of their error may be introduced, just as the prophet testifies concerning them: “They have softened their words more than oil, but they are darts” (Ps. 54:22); and again: “For they were many against me” (Ps. 54:19). Concerning them the Apostle, teacher of the nations, also says: “Having the appearance of piety, but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3:5).

For it does not benefit Nestorius to confess two natures and one Son, although this profession is also common to the orthodox, since Nestorius himself, refusing to say “one subsistence” of the two natures—which is proper to the orthodox—plainly reveals that he fraudulently said “two natures and one Son.”

Therefore, because the aforesaid letter to Maris the Persian made such a manifestly wicked assertion about blessed Cyril and the Fathers who first assembled at Ephesus, there can be no doubt what its author thought while defending Nestorius or accepting his perverse doctrine. For he wrote such impious and abominable things about the condemners of Nestorius and their holy doctrines. It is therefore established by open truth that the same letter to Maris the Persian was written through the fraud and perversity of a Nestorian mind.

And although this alone might seem more than sufficient to preserve reverence for the holy Council of Chalcedon and to exclude the snares of heretics who falsely claim that the letter to Maris the Persian was approved by our Fathers, the many arguments set out above also testify that our Fathers could in no way have judged it worthy of reception. From the very beginning, when Bishop Ibas appears to have entered the holy Council of Chalcedon, the proceedings of Photius and Eustathius and their judgment made clear that he complained of having suffered violence and false accusations at the Second Council of Ephesus, and that the letter was not his.

This is shown most clearly after the text of the same letter had been read from the proceedings of Photius and Eustathius at the Council of Chalcedon: Ibas’s profession denied it as well, in order to exclude that other letter to Maris, and requested that the Edessene letter be read on his behalf [Col. 0165A].

The support of Theophilus, Ibas’s enemy, abandoned by the support of truth, nevertheless demonstrates the matter with evident reasoning. He did not dare to assert the letter to Maris the Persian which he had brought against Ibas; rather, he attempted to accuse as false the letter which Bishop Ibas had requested to be read on his behalf.

The sentence of our own Fathers sitting at Chalcedon likewise made this unmistakable: in the same case, they allowed [perhaps, “of those allowing”] Domnus, who had been accused, to remain condemned, while deciding that Ibas should be acquitted. The text says “saying” [perhaps, “of those saying”] that their faith was the faith attacked by the letter to Maris, and thus [perhaps, “and through this”] showed that the letter had been condemned by the judgment of those whose statement is falsely alleged to have received it.

### XVIII

Although it appears indubitably from the foregoing light of truth that we are under no necessity to inquire from the text of which letter certain Fathers sitting at Chalcedon declared in their statements that Bishop Ibas had appeared catholic—for it is quite sufficient for us to have demonstrated most clearly that they could not have rendered any such judgment concerning the letter written to Maris the Persian—this sufficiently supports us against the devices of heretics. They wish that this letter to Maris the Persian should appear to have been received by the holy Council of Chalcedon; but we have shown not only that it was not received, but that it was altogether rejected by our Fathers, who by a judgment plainly pronounced condemned it among the enemies of their true faith.

Therefore, since, as we have said, the question against the adversaries of the holy Council of Chalcedon seemed to be whether it can truly be shown to have been received or not received, and since, while they needlessly suppose it received, we have shown from the very words of the Fathers that it was rejected, we need not be compelled to say concerning which letter our Fathers thought in those statements. It is enough that they did not think concerning this letter [perhaps, “although this is the letter”] about which the controversy turns. Nevertheless, if the individual statements of the Fathers are examined and fitted to the consistency explained above, those who pursue a devout understanding will also be able easily to see concerning which letter they spoke.

### XIX

First of all, we must carefully and shrewdly observe that the concordant judgments of our Fathers, delivered with one sense and one mind concerning the acquittal of Bishop Ibas, declared that the same Bishop Ibas had been proved innocent [the text reads *obnoxius*, apparently for *innoxius*] of all the charges brought against him by his accusers. For the statement of the legates of the Apostolic See begins thus:

“Having reread the documents, we have learned that, by the judgment of the most reverend bishops, the most reverend Ibas has been proved innocent.”

This is plainly followed by the statement delivered by Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, expressing that he had been found innocent of the charges brought against him by his accusers. For he says (Act 10):

“The faith and reading of the most reverend bishops and judges, and of all that followed, show that the most reverend Ibas is innocent of the charges which his accusers brought against him.”

The judgment of Maximus of Antioch, further establishing the sense of the foregoing, is accordingly added:

“From what has now been reread it is manifest that the most reverend Ibas has been found innocent of all the charges brought against him.”

We must therefore consider how the judgment of these three judges, who hold the first place, agrees with the judgment rejecting [the text has *adiciendam*, perhaps for *abiciendam*, “to be rejected”] and refuting the letter to Maris the Persian; though uttered by different mouths, it was dictated by one Spirit.

For what does it mean that Ibas is pronounced innocent of all the charges brought against him by his accusers, according to the decision of Photius and Eustathius and from the documents reread, except that the letter which, in disparagement of the teaching of blessed Cyril and in defence of Nestorius, endeavours, so to speak, to overthrow the foundations of the orthodox faith, was brought by his adversaries, as it truly is, against Bishop Ibas as a great crime, and was found foreign to him and most plainly rejected by the decrees of the aforesaid three Fathers?

For he would not appear justly pronounced innocent of all the charges brought against him if the letter to Maris the Persian, which is the chief part of the accusations—indeed, in which all the crimes alleged against him are contained—were not proved excluded by these statements. And therefore, since it is certain that, if it were taught that this was his letter, he could not be pronounced innocent, it follows that, since he was pronounced innocent, it was not his letter.

Since it has thus been made perfectly clear that these statements were delivered, with a sense and purpose most fitting for the acquittal of Bishop Ibas, chiefly to exclude and refute the letter to Maris the Persian, it follows that we must examine with equal truth the determinations of the other Fathers who thought the same, passing over for a little while the statements of the most reverend bishops Juvenal and Eunomius; although we have shown elsewhere that, from another aspect, they agree with the same meaning.

Thus Thalassius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, says (Act 10):

“Since the most reverend bishops Photius and Eustathius established Ibas’s case and did not condemn him, persuaded by their judgment I too wish him to remain in the priesthood, as it also seemed good to the most holy bishops, because he especially accepted the proceedings by anathematizing what his accusers had laid against him in writing.”

To what lover of the faithful and evident truth is it not clear that all the reasoning which we have given above concerning the letter to Maris the Persian as denied or refuted, and shown to agree with the statements of the preceding Fathers, is fully and briefly set forth also in this judgment delivered by the most reverend Thalassius?

For when he says that he follows the judgment of Photius and Eustathius, who established Ibas’s case and did not condemn him, and then adds that Bishop Ibas, to complete the proof of his innocence, condemned the things brought against him in writing by his accusers, he shows beyond doubt that both in the examination of the Council of Chalcedon and in the judgment of Photius and Eustathius Ibas’s authorship and conscience had been found free from the charge of the letter to Maris the Persian: there all things were rejected, not merely because the adversaries did not prove them or Bishop Ibas denied them, but because he himself condemned them.

It follows that the letter to Maris the Persian, which contained the charges brought by the accusers, was condemned not only by the judgment of the Fathers sitting at Chalcedon but also by Ibas’s own judgment, as the Fathers in question, instructed by the decision of Photius and Eustathius, affirm.

The judgments of Eusebius of Ancyra, Stephen of Ephesus, Diogenes of Cyzicus, and Romanus of Myra in Lycia, though delivered in different places, likewise confirm the decrees of the preceding judges with one meaning. For some recall the judgment of Photius and Eustathius, while others establish the innocence of Bishop Ibas from his condemnation of Nestorius and his heresy; they testify that the letter to Maris the Persian, which excuses Nestorius and calls blessed Cyril a heretic, not only did not belong to Bishop Ibas but was condemned by him.

John, bishop of Sebaste, Seleucus, bishop of Amasia, Constantine, bishop of Melitene, Patricius, bishop of Tyana, Peter, bishop of Gangra, and Artanius, bishop of Trapezus, agreed in the same way, saying (Act 10):

“The decision of the most reverend bishops Photius and Eustathius shows that the most reverend Ibas is innocent. Likewise, his denial makes us more inclined to believe what he received.”

From this statement of the aforementioned bishops it is clear that Bishop Ibas was found innocent of the matters on which he was accused for these two reasons: the decision of Bishops Photius and Eustathius and his own denial.

Now the decision of Photius and Eustathius declares that, although he had been falsely attacked by his accusers, he nevertheless thought it right, to answer even the false accusations, to profess in writing what he believed concerning the true faith; and, beyond this, he anathematized Nestorius and said that he held all that had been approved at the First Council of Ephesus.

Moreover, his denial also made the minds of the judges more inclined: after the reading at the Council of Chalcedon of the letter to Maris the Persian—which is wholly contrary to Bishop Ibas’s open and pious confession—he declared himself to be free of the charges brought against him. Thus, rejecting and refuting what he denied, they might believe that he had held before as well only what he professed that he had held and received.

Once this has been shown, it is clear that the letter to Maris the Persian, being contrary to everything which Ibas said that he received and defending instead the things which Bishop Ibas anathematized, was in no way composed by Bishop Ibas.

### XX

For, in order to make it manifest to all that by denying the matters brought against him Ibas rendered more certain the matters which he confessed concerning the pious faith, the statement says:

“And his denial made us more inclined to believe what he received.”

This is as though it said: We receive more credibly what he professed concerning the pious faith because he denied the matters brought against him; thus he would not seem to show what he thought concerning the pious faith as one convicted by the truth of the accusations and correcting himself from necessity, but, being cleared rather by his denial of the accusations, would be believed to have thought before as he professed that he thought.

For just as the confession of a deed could make a man guilty even regarding the past, so an unrefuted denial made him innocent even regarding past matters.

The statements of Bishops Eunomius and Juvenal fit suitably with this denial, through which Bishop Ibas is shown to have refuted the letter to Maris the Persian. We must first show, with God’s help, that these statements agree, and then show how they confirm that the letter was denied by Ibas. They read thus (Act 10):

Juvenal, the most reverend bishop of Jerusalem, said:

“Those who are converted, the divine Scriptures command us to receive. Accordingly, we also receive those returning from heretics. Therefore I consider that the most reverend Ibas deserves clemency, because he is an old man and is catholic, so that he may retain the rank of bishop.”

Eunomius, bishop of Nicomedia, said:

“Indeed, from what has been reread the venerable Ibas has been proved innocent. In those matters in which, by speaking ill, he seemed to blame the most blessed Cyril, he afterwards confessed rightly and refuted the things which he had blamed. Therefore I decide that he is worthy of the episcopate, since he anathematizes Nestorius and Eutyches and their impious doctrines, and agrees with what has been written by the most holy Archbishop Leo and by this universal council.”

We must first examine Eunomius’s statement, which more clearly sets out Bishop Ibas’s meaning and explains what Bishop Juvenal also thought on this matter. For, in saying that Ibas was proved innocent from the documents reread, he approves without ambiguity, like the preceding Fathers, the judgment of Photius and Eustathius; and by these words he appears also to include Ibas’s denial and the testimony on Ibas’s behalf of the letter of the Edessene clergy.

Accordingly, attending properly to the order of the proceedings held before Photius and Eustathius, lest any scruple should remain in anyone’s mind against Bishop Ibas because before the union he had once, through a different understanding, spoken against the teaching of blessed Cyril, he necessarily clears him by showing that Ibas, having corrected his understanding, received blessed Cyril’s orthodox doctrines, confessed them to be right, and refuted the error of the understanding which he had held before the union of the Churches. Thus he shows most plainly that Bishop Ibas denied that the letter read as addressed to Maris was his.

For, since Eunomius approves Ibas as having departed from what he had said concerning blessed Cyril before the union of the Churches and as having confessed after the union that those things were right, while the letter to Maris the Persian, written after the union, falsely alleges that Cyril’s sayings are heretical and invents that he had fallen into the heresy of Apollinaris, it is certain that Ibas denied this letter also, according to the testimony of the present statement.

The judgment of Bishop Juvenal agrees with this meaning without ambiguity: since it maintains that Ibas was orthodox, it shows that he denied the letter written to Maris the Persian, as hostile to sound doctrines, and approves the judgment of Photius, Eustathius, and the others as agreeing with it.

When Juvenal says that a convert ought to be received, he agrees with Eunomius: concerning the dogmas of blessed Cyril, of which he had thought differently before the union, he approves Ibas, now after it thinking rightly as he ought, as converted to a fitting understanding. From this, as has already been shown repeatedly, it follows that the letter which speaks contrarily after the union was not Bishop Ibas’s.

### XXI

Although, therefore, it has already been sufficiently and undeniably demonstrated from all the assertions set out above and from the statements of the Fathers sitting at Chalcedon—statements which agree completely concerning the acquittal of Bishop Ibas—that the letter to Maris the Persian, hostile to the true doctrines and contrary to Ibas’s own profession, was denied by him, rejected in many ways by the judgment of the Fathers, and therefore could not have been received by any of them, nevertheless it is useful, for completeness, to understand which letter the representatives of the Apostolic See or Maximus of Antioch seem to have had in mind in their statements, and to demonstrate that nothing contrary to this can be found in the decrees of the Fathers, as ought to remain fixed in the minds of the faithful.

It is most clearly believed that our Fathers referred in their statements to the letter of the Edessene clergy, which Bishop Ibas requested to be read on his behalf. He hastened to have this Edessene letter read from that portion of the proceedings held before Photius and Eustathius which his adversary had cunningly and deceitfully omitted. He did so in order to refute the letter to Maris which had been read against him from those same proceedings. Through that letter the adversaries attempted to show that Ibas had attacked the true faith and had said that the doctrines of blessed Cyril handed down at the First Council of Ephesus were full of impiety and contrary to the true faith.

It was therefore necessary that Ibas should ask that the letter previously delivered by the Edessene clergy to Bishops Photius and Eustathius, reviewed in their judgment and inserted into the proceedings themselves, be read at the Council of Chalcedon as well, for his own defense. Among other things, it says as follows (Act 10):

“We anathematize ourselves and make ourselves liable to the dread Gehenna, if we know that he ever said anything of this kind or anything else contrary to the catholic faith. For if we had knowingly communicated with the man who said anything of this kind, or celebrated the liturgy with him, we would be liable to the ultimate punishment, as having shared in such an error,” and so forth.

By this the Edessene clergy asserted that he had said nothing of this kind, nor anything else contrary to the orthodox faith. Thus they would exclude [perhaps, “excluded”] everything contrary to the true faith contained in the letter to Maris the Persian, which the adversaries falsely claimed had been said by him in order to attack Bishop Ibas [Col. 0169D]. At the same time, Bishop Ibas most clearly confirmed his own denial, when shortly before he had said: “I am also alien to the things brought against me.”

## XXII

Therefore, with this letter of the Edessene clergy’s representatives before their eyes, the apostolic see’s legates, after first declaring from the reading of the documents and from the judgment of the bishops Photius and Eustathius that Ibas had been proved innocent, went on to say (Act 10): “For, having reread his letter, we recognized that he was Catholic.” Thus, first, from the very sequence of the proceedings conducted before Photius and Eustathius, they are believed to have judged concerning that letter—the Edessene letter—which is shown to have been reread last before them, in their own interlocutions.

But since, by designating it as his—that is, Bishop Ibas’s—letter, they seem to indicate the letter which he requested to be reread on his behalf, they show that it was rather the letter to Maris the Persian, which had been brought forward against him, that was not his, by the manner of speaking which all people undoubtedly use concerning both others and themselves, so that documents, papers, and letters are called those of the persons who use them on their own behalf and whose interests they are shown to serve.

For which letter would those most holy examiners more reasonably judge to belong to Ibas, whom they were absolving: the letter to Maris the Persian, which his opponents had produced against Ibas in order to attack him on account of the grave crimes contained in it, or the Edessene letter, which cleared him of all the charges brought against him? The letter to Maris, which Ibas himself, when it was brought against him, denied—as has been shown in many ways—or the Edessene letter, which he demanded should be reread in order to refute that letter to Maris and to establish his orthodox faith? The letter to Maris the Persian, which asserted that he had attacked the true faith, if it were proved to be his, or the Edessene letter, which testified that he had said nothing contrary to the Catholic faith? The letter to Maris the Persian, after whose reading Bishop Ibas immediately stated that he was alien even to those things that had been charged against him, or the Edessene letter, through which Theophilus, his opponent, recognizing that he had been convicted, sought to undermine him by accusing him of falsehood?

Therefore, that letter to Maris the Persian was most justly judged, or ought to be judged, by all to belong rather to the accuser who produced it but did not prove it than to Ibas, who denied it.

Now we must examine more attentively by which letter Bishop Ibas was chiefly judged orthodox by the representatives of the apostolic see: by the letter to Maris the Persian, which most openly contradicts the First Council of Ephesus and the faith set forth there by blessed Cyril, which the Council of Chalcedon confirms and follows, and which therefore reveals its author as a heretic; or by this Edessene letter, which, confirming under the imposition of a terrifying oath and anathema that Ibas had never said anything contrary to the Catholic faith, caused him to be declared orthodox after he had been cleared of his opponents’ accusations?

Was it by the letter to Maris the Persian, which the holy Council of Chalcedon struck with the penalty of anathema among those who do not believe as Cyril expounded at the First Council of Ephesus, or by the Edessene letter, which, agreeing with the judgment of those same Fathers, imposes anathema upon those who communicate with persons who say anything against the Catholic faith?
