All these points are also seen to accord with the interlocution of Maximus, bishop of Antioch, by the same truth that has been set forth. For, when he names the “reply of the letter,” he is shown to have meant not the letter to Maris the Persian but the letter of the Edessene clergy.

For how could Maximus be thought to have called the letter to Maris the Persian orthodox, when it is certain that this letter attacked the doctrine of the First Council of Ephesus and of blessed Cyril proclaimed there? As we have already fully stated above, when he was giving judgment concerning the reception of the letter of blessed memory, Pope Leo, he declared that it ought to be received because it agreed with the faith expounded by blessed Cyril at Ephesus, saying as follows (Act 4): “The letter of the most holy archbishop of royal Rome, Leo, agrees with the expositions of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers at Nicaea, of the one hundred and fifty at Constantinople, the New Rome, and with the faith expounded at Ephesus by the most holy bishop Cyril; and I have subscribed.”

Who, then, could be found so removed from all human reason as to believe that this priest, in the matter or definition of the faith, was so self-contradictory that, although he judged the letter of so distinguished a pontiff and teacher—blessed Leo—to be orthodox by comparing its plainly pious doctrines with the teaching of blessed Cyril expounded at Ephesus, he would conversely call orthodox the writing of that other letter which, in a heretical voice, endeavored to overturn the very doctrines of blessed Cyril?

Since it is impossible that one and the same judge, in defining the faith, should either reject what he approved or approve as pleasing to himself the very thing he rejected, it must be clear to everyone that he judged not the letter to Maris the Persian but rather this Edessene letter, which was read later, to contain an orthodox composition.

## XXIII

Nor should anyone be disturbed by the fact that, in the same interlocution, a “reply of the letter” is mentioned, brought forward by the man who was his opponent, so that, from these words—as the enemies of the orthodox faith wish to maintain in order to attack the First Council of Ephesus—it might seem that Maximus, bishop of Antioch, judged concerning the letter read as having been sent to Maris the Persian, which Ibas’s opponents had produced against him in the judgment of Photius and Eustathius.

We have already proved above, by suitable and manifold reasoning, that this was far removed from the meaning of Maximus himself. For there is no doubt that the wording produced by his opponent refers to this letter of the Edessene clergy. Since Theophilus, Ibas’s opponent, had brought forward against him at the Council of Chalcedon nothing except the proceedings conducted before Photius and Eustathius, and, as is clearly evident, had maliciously suppressed that section of the proceedings in which the letter of the Edessene clergy was contained, causing only the part by which he thought Bishop Ibas could be burdened to be read, Bishop Ibas then requested that the part fraudulently omitted by him be reread, so that it might become more evident—[something is missing]—from the very documents produced by that same opponent, by which the letter read against him was proved to have been excluded, and so that he might more effectively demonstrate that his opponent Theophilus himself was convicted by what he had produced.

Accordingly Bishop Maximus, expressing the force of an adequate proof, declared, after the Edessene clergy’s letter had been reread from the documents produced by the opponent, that Ibas was orthodox (Act 10).

But, so that the contentious minds of the heretics may be overcome more fully, it is shown in various ways that this Edessene letter was not produced by Ibas at the Council of Chalcedon as something new, but had long before been handed over to the bishops Photius and Eustathius and inserted into their proceedings.

First, because it is read as having been given to them at the time of the judgment, there can be no doubt that it was delivered to those to whom it was addressed, especially since in their judgment Ibas needed its assistance for his clearance from the charges that had been brought against him.

Next, in the same letter the Edessene clergy are repeatedly read as having earnestly requested the aforesaid Photius and Eustathius to arrange for it to be inserted into their official proceedings; and the order of the judgment itself likewise demanded that this be done.

The truth of the present argument demonstrates that these things were recorded in this manner; so too does Ibas’s own testimony, extracted above both at the Council of Chalcedon and in the examination before Photius and Eustathius.

For when Bishop Ibas entered the holy Council of Chalcedon, asserting that he had been acquitted by the decision of Photius and Eustathius, he said as follows (Act 9): “For all the Edessene clergy, through whom they wrote to the aforesaid bishops, testify that I am Catholic.” He plainly showed that the writing had been addressed to them and that, already in their judgment, he had been cleared of all the charges and declared Catholic by the reply of the Edessene clergy.

Again, in that section of the proceedings conducted before Photius and Eustathius which, as stated, Ibas’s opponents requested to be reread against him, when the aforesaid bishop rejected the three witnesses whom his opponents had tried to produce against him in the judgment of Photius and Eustathius, he said as follows (Act 10):

“Our clergy are very numerous—about two hundred names, more or less; for I do not retain the number. All the clergy testified, whether I am orthodox or a heretic, through written confessions which were both sent to the most holy bishop Domnus and written to Your Reverence. If the testimony of so many clergy agrees with the three witnesses, as he himself says, who came with them to accuse me at Constantinople and are now with them, it is for you to judge.”

From this it is plainly evident that, in the very judgment of Photius and Eustathius, in refuting the witnesses brought forward by his opponent, Ibas made mention of the letter of the Edessene clergy in such a way as both to show that it had already been delivered to the judges and to demand, on the basis of the reply of the entire Edessene clergy known to those same judges, that the testimony of a few clergy ought not to be admitted.

Therefore, there is no doubt that the opponents deliberately omitted that section of the proceedings in which the letter of the Edessene clergy on behalf of Ibas had been inserted, and that Ibas necessarily requested that this very Edessene letter be reread from the section that had been suppressed. For this reason Bishop Maximus declared, from the reply reread from the proceedings produced by the opponent, that the composition of the reply of the letter—that is, of the Edessene letter—had been declared orthodox.

That the section of the proceedings omitted by the opponents, by which Bishop Ibas was more clearly cleared of the charges, was also suppressed is shown in other ways. For in the same sentence of Photius and Eustathius, in which they report everything that had been done by Bishop Ibas in their judgment, it is stated that Bishop Ibas had shown by a written document what he thought concerning the pious faith, and that, in addition, he had anathematized Nestorius, and had promised to express these things in the church of his own city, along with other matters made evident by the tenor of their judgment.

That entire material is absent from the section of the proceedings reread at the Council of Chalcedon in accordance with the wishes of Ibas’s opponents. Nevertheless, their sentence declares that these things had been recorded in the judgment of Photius and Eustathius. Thus it is established beyond doubt that the opponents maliciously suppressed those sections which, they write, would have benefited Bishop Ibas still further.

And that these matters were inserted into the official proceedings before the bishops Photius and Eustathius is made entirely unambiguous by the judgment of Thalassius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, who was residing at Chalcedon. After other matters, it says as follows: “Because, above all, the proceedings accepted that he should anathematize in writing those things which his accusers had deposed against him.”

Since this is not read in that section of the proceedings which was recited at the request of Ibas’s opponents, it is clear that the aforesaid Bishop Thalassius knew, from the report of the proceedings conducted by Photius and Eustathius in their judgment, what had been inserted into the official record.

Therefore, by the full light of truth it has been proved that the section of the proceedings containing the Edessene clergy’s letter was suppressed by the opponents in the same way as this other section was omitted so that it might not be reread. It is not from the section which the opponents wished to be reread but from the sentence of the bishops Photius and Eustathius concerning what had been done before them that this is established.

## XXIV

Therefore it plainly appears, beyond doubt, from those proceedings which the opponents did produce but deliberately suppressed in part, that Ibas the bishop requested that the Edessene letter be reread on his behalf, and that Bishop Maximus of Antioch, in his interlocution, spoke of the reply of that letter which had been produced by the opponent.

Which letter could have been declared to have an orthodox composition has been amply established above; and it will become still clearer from this that, in his preceding argument, Ibas asserted that he had been proved orthodox by the reply of the Edessene clergy.

Accordingly, the composition of that same Edessene letter was called orthodox, through which Ibas himself requested to be judged orthodox by the judges and by whose sentence he was declared orthodox.

Let the shamelessness, therefore, of the perverse—both followers of the Eutychian and of the Nestorian heresy—give way. By heretical fraud they strive to persuade people that anyone sitting at the Council of Chalcedon could have said or thought anything orthodox concerning that letter to Maris the Persian, which was full of every kind of impiety.

For when Bishop Ibas entered at the beginning to be examined by the holy Council of Chalcedon, he proceeded by saying that, through the testimony of the Edessene clergy, he had been judged, or ought to be judged, Catholic. He likewise maintained before the bishops Photius and Eustathius, for his own clearance, that it ought to be sufficient that the Edessene clergy had testified through their confessions, which they had written to those same bishops, that he was Catholic.

Again, remaining in that same defense after the reading of the letter to Maris the Persian, he requested that the letter of the Edessene clergy on his behalf—which he had often mentioned—be reread. What opponent of such evident truth could there be who would not recognize from the text of this Edessene letter, through which Ibas, having been accused, requested to be judged [perhaps: requested that he be judged] orthodox, that the Fathers considered its composition orthodox and pronounced Ibas himself Catholic, but would instead think that the composition of the letter to Maris the Persian had been judged orthodox—a letter which was brought against him as a crime of heresy and by which, if it had been proved to be his, he could have been judged a heretic?

## XXV

Accordingly, we anathematize and condemn the aforesaid letter which Ibas is falsely alleged to have written to Maris the Persian the heretic. It denies that God was incarnate and became man from holy Mary, the Mother of God and ever-virgin, but says that a mere man was born from her, whom it calls a temple, so that from this one God the Word and another Christ may be understood. It accuses holy Cyril, who was a teacher and preacher of the true faith, as a heretic and as writing things like Apollinaris; it censures the First Council of Ephesus as though it had condemned Nestorius without examination or investigation; and the same letter calls the twelve chapters of holy Cyril impious and contrary to the true faith, while defending Theodore and Nestorius and their impious doctrines and writings.

Therefore, we anathematize and condemn the aforesaid letter to Maris the Persian, in which the abominations of the blasphemies designated above are contained. Whoever at any time believes that it should be accepted or defended, or attempts at any time to dissolve this present condemnation, we condemn with the same anathema.

But those who contend that the aforementioned letter to Maris the Persian, containing the blasphemies designated above, was accepted from the present time by the holy Council of Chalcedon, as is made known to them by the text of our present decree, or who strive to assert that it was pronounced orthodox by any of those Fathers residing at Chalcedon, we strike with the same penalty of anathema. For they strive not only to inflict an injury upon the holy and venerable Council of Chalcedon, but also declare themselves instigators and renewers of a suppressed scandal, through which the universal Church could again be shaken; so that they may rightly seem to be struck by the sentence of the Apostle to the Gentiles, who says: “Would that those who trouble you would even cut themselves off!” (Galatians 5:12).

## XXVI

Having completed what had to be discussed or defined concerning the quelling of the question of the first chapter—that is, concerning the letter to Maris the Persian—it is necessary for us to explain what the order of ecclesiastical unity and the safeguard of the faith handed down by the holy Fathers require to be done concerning Theodore of Mopsuestia and his writings.

We have considered that the beginning of this question too flowed from the muddy source of the heretics. For when, many years ago, the Nestorians were unable to insert the impious doctrines of Nestorius under the name of Nestorius himself, who had been condemned, into the minds of certain people whom they wished to deceive, they found, through carefully contrived frauds, an opportunity to bring forward their error. From the books of Theodore of Mopsuestia, whom they boast to have died in the peace of the Church, they strove to introduce anew the impious doctrines of Nestorius, now renewed with still more monstrous blasphemies.

Their poisons, secretly creeping along for long periods and now flowing forth in open profession, have stirred the minds of ourselves, of the most Christian emperor, and of all the orthodox, who observe that remedies must no longer be postponed where, through patience nourished by dissimulation, the destruction of so great an evil appears to have grown.

For no one can doubt that these Nestorians publicly and continually assert the following: “We venerate as our father not so much Nestorius as Theodore of Mopsuestia, and we embrace his books with the full devotion of our minds. Nor will anyone be able to resist us, since our doctrine is everywhere affirmed by the widely circulated books of the ancient teacher Theodore.”

A considerable number of the uneducated populace is daily deceived by the perverse seduction of the Nestorians’ words. Since it is clear that, through the name and writings of the deceased Theodore, the error of the Nestorian heresy is being introduced among the people more extensively than Nestorius, while alive, could have introduced it, we believed that we would incur not merely the danger of negligence but also the guilt of connivance [perhaps: the crime of connivance], if we allowed the remedies required by necessary correction—which the administration of the endangered Church demands—to be postponed any longer.

Nor, as some groundlessly spread abroad, can it benefit the defense of Theodore and his writings that the name of Theodore or his writings appear to be praised at length in the letter to Maris the Persian. For in the preceding assertion it was demonstrated in many ways that the same letter was justly condemned both by us and by the holy Fathers residing at Chalcedon. Rather, this is fully sufficient to demonstrate Theodore’s evils: his name and writings were praised there where blessed Cyril and the First Council of Ephesus are attacked.

Nevertheless, since these things are so, we did not cease to scrutinize Theodore’s writings through more reliable interpreters, although they had previously been published for us in some form. From this it has now become entirely clear, with the brightest truth, that the aforesaid book of Theodore of Mopsuestia contains things contrary to the true faith and to the teaching of the holy Fathers.

Accordingly, the holy Fathers who wrote against him left their books for the instruction of the holy Church. For among other blasphemies we have clearly found that he said that God the Word is one and Christ another; that Christ suffered the troubles of the soul and the desires of the flesh, gradually withdrew from worse things, reached better things by progress in his works, became immaculate in his manner of life, and was baptized as a mere man in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; that through baptism he received the grace of the Holy Spirit and earned adoption; that Christ was worshiped in the likeness of the imperial image, in the person of God the Word; and that after the resurrection he became unchangeable in his thoughts and altogether without sin.

He also said that the union of God the Word with Christ was of the sort of which the Apostle spoke concerning man and woman: “The two shall be one flesh”; and that after the resurrection, when the Lord had breathed upon the disciples and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” he did not give them the Holy Spirit.

He also dared to say that Thomas’s confession, made when he touched the Lord’s hands and side after the resurrection—“My Lord and my God”—was not said by Thomas of Christ (for Theodore does not say that Christ is God), but that Thomas, astonished at the miracle of the resurrection, glorified God and said these things.

And in the interpretation which the same Theodore wrote on the Acts of the Apostles, he made Christ similar to Plato, Manichaeus, Epicurus, and Marcion. He said that, just as each of those men caused his disciples to be called Platonists, Manichaeans, Epicureans, and Marcionists from the doctrine he had discovered, so also, when Christ had discovered a doctrine, Christians were called from it.

The depravity of Theodore of Mopsuestia’s books has exposed these blasphemies, and it is plainly evident how falsely certain people who foster Theodore’s statements think that Theodore was not condemned during his lifetime. For, when we examined the synodal decrees of our predecessor, blessed Damasus, issued long before Theodore of Mopsuestia assumed the episcopal office—decrees issued after the Council of Nicaea by the Catholic bishops who had gathered in Rome to discuss the Holy Spirit, together with blessed Ambrose, bishop of the city of Milan—we found it most fully defined that those who affirm two Sons, one before the ages and another after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin, as Theodore was shown above to have asserted, had been struck by the penalty of anathema.

There not only those who were followers of his heresy at that time, but also those who in succeeding times would follow the same error, are found bound by the same bonds of anathema.

Theodore of Mopsuestia must necessarily have been subject to this condemnation, since he became a follower and preacher of a heresy already condemned. For we do not otherwise regard those whom we now find entangled in the Arian or any other heresy as already condemned by the penalty of anathema, except because they themselves are found condemned in the errors already condemned which they follow.

Nor should we omit the fact that those who in their books and disputations teach belief in two Sons nevertheless deny that they profess two Sons. This denial in empty words does them no good, since through their doctrines and books they are also convicted of deceitfully asserting it.

Thus Nestorius, as we have already said above, while pretending to confess two natures and one Son, and persisting with every fraudulent intention in persuading people that one is born from God the Father and another proceeds from the Virgin Mother, was unable to escape the penalty of the deserved condemnation. Nor could that deceitful confession of one Son free him, since his doctrine was proved to contain something else.

For followers of this perversity are punished by their own authors: they do not cease to teach what they are ashamed to profess, and they do not write for reading what they deny should be said.

[Note: Cotelerius correctly emends the reading to *conscribunt* (“they write down”).]

## XXVII

For all these reasons, therefore, let the universal Church recognize for whose benefit our concern is laboring: so that the people of Christ our God may no longer be led astray.

We have already stated that this benefit is harmed through Theodore’s name and writings, and that we have therefore proceeded justly and without any reproach to the measures which we establish by the present authority.

Therefore, just as all the other heretics whom the holy four councils and the Catholic Church are known to have condemned and anathematized, we likewise condemn and anathematize Theodore, who was once bishop of Mopsuestia, together with his impious writings, and also the writings composed by Theodoret against the true faith, against the twelve chapters of holy Cyril, and against the First Council of Ephesus, as well as those which he wrote in defense of Theodore and Nestorius.

For, for the sake of ecclesiastical benefit [Note: *pro* may perhaps be deleted. HARD.], he also requested that the aforementioned writings of Theodoret be condemned, because the Nestorians repeatedly appear to use these writings, under the name of that bishop who is read to have been accepted by Pope Leo of blessed memory and by the holy Council of Chalcedon, as support for asserting their own error. They fail to consider that not only did the holy Fathers gathered at Chalcedon condemn Nestorius together with his doctrines and also condemn these writings, but Bishop Theodoret himself, in the holy Council of Chalcedon, openly rejected all the statements that appeared contrary to the doctrines set forth by blessed Cyril at the First Council of Ephesus, and accepted the definition of the holy Council of Chalcedon, in which it is clear that the doctrine expounded by blessed Cyril at the First Council of Ephesus is proclaimed.

And thus, just as the entire council of the holy Council of Chalcedon expressed in its interlocution, it is established that he was accepted by that same council.

Therefore it is clear that by this condemnation we establish nothing new, but anathematize those things which the holy Council of Chalcedon also rejected and which Bishop Theodoret himself likewise condemned there by his profession.

## XXVIII

Therefore, we anathematize and condemn the three aforesaid impious chapters: namely, the letter said to be Ibas’s letter to Maris the Persian, in which the abominable blasphemies designated above are contained; the impious Theodore of Mopsuestia, together with his abominable writings; and the writings which Theodoret composed impiously.

Whoever at any time believes that these things should be accepted or revered, or attempts at any time to dissolve this present condemnation, we condemn with the same anathema.

But those who, preserving the true faith proclaimed by the aforesaid four councils, have condemned or do condemn the three aforementioned chapters, we regard as brothers and fellow priests.

Whatever has been brought forward in my name or in the name of anyone else in defense of the three aforementioned chapters, or has been found anywhere, we invalidate by the authority of this present full decree.

Far be it from the universal Church that anyone should assert that the aforesaid four councils, or any one of them, accepted any of the blasphemies designated above, or accepted those who thought or followed such things. For it is clear from the holy Fathers mentioned above, and especially from the holy Council of Chalcedon, that no one concerning whom suspicion existed was accepted except one who rejected the blasphemies designated above, or similar things, or the heresy of which he was suspected, or denied and condemned the blasphemies concerning which there had been doubt about him.

Therefore, those who wish to assert that the aforementioned letter to Maris the Persian, containing the blasphemies designated above, was accepted from the present time by the holy Council of Chalcedon, as is made known to them by the text of this decree, or who strive to assert that it was pronounced orthodox by any of those Fathers residing at Chalcedon, we strike with the same penalty of anathema. For they strive not only to inflict an injury upon the holy and venerable Council of Chalcedon, but also declare themselves instigators and renewers of a suppressed scandal, through which the universal Church could again be shaken; so that they may rightly seem to be struck by the sentence of the Apostle, who says: “Would that those who trouble you would even cut themselves off!”

[Note: Read, as above, “the Apostle to the Gentiles.” HARD.]

And after the subscriptions.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of March, in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of our lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus, and in the thirteenth year after the consulship of Basil, illustrious man, at Constantinople.

[Col. 0177]

# THE BOOK OF THE EMPEROR JUSTINIAN AGAINST ORIGEN

[Note: Liberatus mentions this letter in chapter 23—this is what Justinian himself calls it at the end—and says that it was composed at the urging of Pelagius, deacon and *apocrisiarius* of the Roman Church, and was later approved by Pope Vigilius.]

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

(C)

## [AGAINST ORIGEN.]

A discourse of our most pious emperor Justinian, sent to Menas, the most holy and most blessed archbishop of the prosperous city and patriarch, against the impious Origen and his profane doctrines.

[Col. 0177D]

It has always been, and still is, our concern to preserve in every way the upright and undefiled faith of Christians, and the untroubled condition of the most holy Catholic and apostolic Church of God; and we place this care before all others.

Through it, we have believed that the kingship in the present world has been entrusted to us by God and is preserved, and that the enemies of our government are subjected; through it, we hope also to find mercy before His goodness in the age to come.

For although the enemy of the human race devises various pretexts by which he strives to plot against human souls, nevertheless God’s loving-kindness, abolishing his wickedness and exposing his opponents, does not permit His own flock to be harmed or scattered.

We have said these things because it has come to us that some people, who do not keep the fear of God in mind and do not know how to distinguish correct doctrines, have abandoned the divine Scriptures and the holy Fathers, whom the Catholic Church of God holds as teachers and through whom every heresy everywhere has been driven away and the orthodox faith has been clarified.

[Note: This passage is transcribed, though with many omissions from time to time, in Royal manuscript codex 2935, under this prefixed heading: “The holy and ecumenical Fifth Synod took place under the emperor Justin [for Justinian], which anathematized Origen and his impious writings, and the strange doctrines of Evagrius and of Didymus, who held Origenist views. From the book of the Acts of the holy Fifth Synod, from the discourse of our most pious emperor Justinian to Menas, the most blessed archbishop of the prosperous city. He also speaks of Origen and of his Greek and Manichaean doctrines,” etc. The manuscript is no more than 160 years old. HARD.]

They lay claim to Origen and to his Greek, Arian, and Manichaean doctrines, through which he fell into the pit.

How can such people be counted among Christians when they claim to deliver the doctrines of Greeks, Manichaeans, Arians, and the other heretics, having labored to do so? Origen, above all, blasphemed against the holy and consubstantial Trinity, daring to say that the Father is greater than the Son, the Son greater than the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit greater than the other spirits.

He added [read: προστέθεικε, “he added”] this to his impiety, saying that the Son was unable to see the Father, nor the Holy Spirit the Son; that the Son and the Holy Spirit are creatures; and that what we are in relation to the Son, the Son is in relation to the Father.

He also added the following to his blasphemies in the first book of his *On First Principles*, saying in the very words:

“God must be said, at the conceived beginning, to have brought into existence by his will such a number of intellectual substances as he was able to sustain; for God’s power too must be said to be limited, and its limitation must not be removed under the pretext of euphemism. For if divine power is infinite, it is necessary that it should not even understand itself; for by nature the infinite is incomprehensible. Therefore he made as many things as he was able to encompass, hold in his hands, and sustain under his providence, just as he also prepared as much matter as he was able to adorn.”

What greater blasphemy against God could Origen have uttered than this—he who even devised grades within the holy Trinity, wishing thereby to introduce polytheism, and who absurdly claimed that God’s own power is bounded?

And there is also that tale of his, full of every kind of impiety: his claim that all genera and species are coeternal with God; and that rational beings who sinned and therefore fell from the condition in which they had existed were cast into bodies for punishment according to the proportion of their sins; and that, after being purified, they would again ascend to the condition in which they had formerly been, entirely laying aside their wickedness and their bodies; and that again, a second time, a third time, and repeatedly, they would be cast into different bodies for punishment.

He also supposes that different worlds both have existed and continue to exist—some in the past, others in the future. Who is so foolish that, hearing such things, would not shudder in mind at the excess of impiety? Who would not abhor the madman Origen, who fashioned and committed to writing such blasphemies against God?

Since these things are forbidden to all Christians and plainly bear the proof of impiety, we have considered it superfluous to deem them worthy of refutation.

If, then, all heretics have been expelled from the most holy Church for deviating in one doctrine, or perhaps two, and have been subjected to anathema together with their particular doctrines, what Christian could endure Origen and claim his wicked writings—the man who uttered so many blasphemies, provided almost all heretics with such abundant material for destruction and blasphemy, and who was therefore long ago made subject to anathema by the holy Fathers together with his foul doctrines?

For even if someone were to grant that Origen, the God-fighter, as is also found among other heretics, mixed something from correct doctrines into his wicked writings [read perhaps ἐναμῆξαι, “to mix in,” or ἀναμίξαι, “to mix”], these things do not belong to him but to the holy Church of God.

And he himself contrived this deceitfully, to mislead the simple. For, brought up on the myths of the Greeks and wishing to extend them, he pretended to interpret the divine Scriptures, so that by mixing his foul doctrines with the commentaries on the divine Scriptures, he might wickedly introduce his Greek and Manichaean error and his Arian madness, and might ensnare those who had not accurately understood the divine Scripture.

For what else did Origen set forth beyond what Plato had said, the Plato who expanded Greek madness? Or from whom else did Arius take the material from which he wrote down his own disease, when, to the destruction of his own soul, he devised grades within the holy and consubstantial Trinity? In what respect does this man fall short of Manichaeus, when he says that human souls were cast into bodies for punishment on account of sins—souls that were first minds and holy powers, then became satiated with the contemplation of divine things, turned toward what was worse, and for that reason grew cold toward the love of God, and from that point were called souls and cast into bodies for punishment?

This alone would have been sufficient for his complete condemnation, since it belongs to Greek impiety.

For when God said, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness,” according to that man’s empty arguments it turns out that only the body, without a soul, was made according to God’s image and likeness—if indeed a soul existed beforehand and, after the body had been made, was cast into it or attached to it.

It is altogether necessary, then, to say that God himself, the creator of man, is also a body, since he made the body according to his own image and likeness.

But how can a body be an image of the incorporeal? Therefore, far be it from Christians to agree with such people.

And if, according to Origen’s blasphemy, souls existed beforehand and were sent down into bodies for punishment because they had sinned, so that after being disciplined they might become sober, they ought no longer to sin. For if the body was given to the soul as punishment on account of sin, so that, suffering pain, it might be disciplined to honor God, how does the body cooperate and struggle with it in order to sin—something which does not happen to those being punished [read οὐ γίνεται, “does not happen”]?

Chains, prisons, fetters, and, in short, such things are given to those being punished to restrain them from wrongdoing and sin. A chain is not given to one who has sinned as an accomplice in further sin, so that he may sin more, but so that, being tormented by the chains, he may cease from sinning.

It is therefore evident that, according to their nonsense, souls were not cast into bodies for correction of sins committed earlier, but that God created both body and soul at the same time—that is, he created the complete human being.

Thus we await recompense for the things we have done through the body, whether good or evil. For the divine Apostle Paul also hands this teaching down to us, saying: “We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive the things done through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or bad.”

We must therefore attend to the Apostle’s words, because he did not say that the one being judged must receive according to what he did before the body.

If a human being is punished by the judge of the earth, or deemed worthy of the honor he deserves, solely for things done through the body, and no memory is made of earlier sins, it is clear that souls do not exist before bodies. For if they existed beforehand, the Apostle would have said: just as for the things done through the body, so also for those done before the body.

That human souls are intellectual and rational is among the acknowledged truths; nor do we think that those who claim Origen’s views would deny this.

Let those who hold Origen’s views, then, say this: if their souls, as they assert, existed before bodies, before they entered bodies, in what condition did they exist, and what did they do? They ought to know where they were, if they existed beforehand, and how they came here.

If it is impossible for them to say this, because it is not true, it is evident that their doctrines are myths.

Perhaps they will say that, after souls entered bodies, they are then able to distinguish and know the things they themselves do. But if they say this, according to their own empty arguments the body is found to be more honorable than the soul, since it grants the soul the capacity to become intellectual and rational. To say this, however, is full of every kind of folly and absurdity.

Why, indeed, if the soul existed beforehand, as they say, does it need some learning or instruction after it comes to be in the body, being gradually introduced and progressing toward greater and more perfect things?

For if it existed beforehand, it would know what was beneficial without needing any instruction, and, possessing knowledge, it would be corrected by attentiveness. If it knew the error, it would not be taught, since it already knew it in advance. But if it is taught because it is ignorant, it did not know beforehand. And if it did not know beforehand, it did not exist beforehand; rather, it is clear that it did not exist beforehand.

For God alone is the cause of our coming-to-be. Just as he made us when we did not exist, so, once we have come to be, he saves us by his own hand [perhaps: by his grace], if we prove worthy and suitable.

For when God said, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness,” he created both at once: that is, he fashioned the body and created an intellectual and rational soul.

At the same time God fashioned the body and created the soul, completing the perfect human being. For neither is a body without a soul a human being, nor is a soul without a body a human being.

But if the soul existed beforehand, as Origen babbles, why did the most holy prophet Zechariah say, “Forming the spirit of man within him”? For if it existed beforehand, he ought rather to have said, “Attaching” or “sending down the spirit of man within him.”

But now, by saying “forming,” the prophet shows that, just as the body, so also the soul—although it did not exist beforehand—was made by God through his own power and goodness.

As has been said, the fact that man was made according to God’s image and likeness and deemed worthy of the divine inbreathing shows that the soul was created not only intellectual and rational but also immortal, so that it might rule all the things made upon the earth.

This is also what the theologian Gregory says concerning the soul: that it participates in what is from God, is divine, and belongs to the nobility from above.

The soul is not, as some imagine and say, a part of the divine essence, but came into being through God’s inbreathing and received from him the gift of being intellectual, rational, and immortal, and of not dying together with the body like irrational animals, but of participating by grace in the nobility from above—that is, immortality.

The holy John, patriarch of Constantinople, also bears witness to these things in his eleventh discourse on creation. For he says:

“And he breathed,” he says, “into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul.

“Here some thoughtless people, moved by their own reasoning and conceiving nothing worthy of God, without considering the condescension of the words, attempt to say that the soul is from God’s essence. Oh the madness! Oh the derangement!”

Thus far the Father concerning the matters before us.

Consider also that, concerning all the other things made upon the earth, God said, “Let it come to be,” and “Let the earth bring forth,” and it came to be. But concerning man he says, “Let us make man”—and not merely “Let us make,” but “according to our image and likeness.” Taking dust from the earth with his own hands, he fashioned man and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul.

From this, therefore, one may see how God made man more honorable than all the other creatures upon the earth.

All the other things he spoke into being, and they came to be; but man, as has been said, he himself created with his own hands, according to the divine Scripture. And all the things made by him upon the earth he subjected to man, who was made on the sixth day, so that he might rule all the creatures of the earth that had already come into existence and been prepared for him, while he himself was ruled by the Creator.

The holy theologian Gregory also teaches this in his discourse for the New Sunday, saying:

“Thus one thing is first numbered in days, and a second, and a third, and so forth, up to the seventh day, the day of rest from the works. By these days the things that come to be are divided, appointed by ineffable words, and not all brought forth at once by the all-powerful [for *παντοδυνάμῳ*, ‘almighty’] Word. For merely to conceive and say it is an accomplished work.

“And if man was manifested last, honored by the hand and image of God, this is nothing surprising. For just as a palace must exist beforehand for a king, so the king is brought in, already escorted by all.”

If, then, according to the teaching of the theologian Gregory, man was manifested last, honored by the hand of God and by the image, and everything was prepared for him by God, and, as for a king, the palace existed beforehand, so that he was brought in by God as a king already escorted by all, how do those who rave according to Origen say that souls existed beforehand and were sent into bodies on account of sins, being required to suffer punishment for sins previously committed?

On the contrary, the holy Gregory says that man was made last of all, honored by God, and made ruler of everything on earth.

This is not an indication of punishment but, on the contrary, of the greatest providence and beneficence of God.

In agreement with the words of the theologian Gregory, the holy John, patriarch of Constantinople, also teaches us in his eleventh discourse on creation, saying:

“But perhaps someone might say: ‘And why, if the soul is more honorable than the body, is the lesser created first and then the greater and superior?’

“Do you not see, beloved, that the same thing happened in creation? For just as heaven, earth, the sun, the moon, and everything else were created, and after all these things man was created, who was about to be entrusted with authority over them all, so likewise, in the very fashioning of man, the body is formed first and then the soul, which is more honorable.

“Just as the irrational creatures that were to be useful for service were created before man, so that the one who was to enjoy their use might have their service ready, so the body is created before the soul, so that, when the soul is brought forth according to his ineffable wisdom, it may have its proper activities to display through the movement of the body.”

These things have been said to show the hearers that we speak in agreement with the holy Fathers, who everywhere abolish the pre-existence of souls.

Again, holy Scripture says concerning Adam and Eve: “God blessed them and said, ‘Increase and multiply, fill the earth, and rule over it.’”

How, then, if souls existed before bodies, would those things that already existed, according to their myths, be about to increase in accordance with the divine command? And how could God bless souls that had already fallen into sin, so that they might increase and multiply? For, having sinned, the souls would have been worthy of curses rather than blessings.

And if souls existed beforehand in another condition, according to the myths of the Origenists, why did God create only Adam? Was Adam’s soul alone the one that had sinned at that time, and for this reason did God create one body? For if other souls had existed before this, other bodies too ought to have been fashioned at the same time to receive the souls.

And how was the soul that, according to their arguments, had sinned and been cast into a body for punishment placed by the Lord in the paradise of delight? For if it had been cast into a body for punishment, it would have been placed not in a paradise of delight but in a place of punishment.

But God loved man so greatly—man whom he fashioned after all the other creatures—that [F. reads ὥστε, “so that”] even after he violated the command given to him by God and was therefore expelled from paradise, while the human race increased and sin multiplied because human thought was diligently directed toward worse things, God, being good, did not disregard his own creature. Instead, he admonished him in various ways, as is shown by holy Scripture.

But when, because of the increasing severity of the diseases, we needed a greater remedy and healing, the only-begotten Word of God, the One—namely, the one Person of the holy Trinity—through his loving-kindness became man while remaining God. He neither changed his divine essence into the human nor transformed his human essence into the divine.

He is one and the same, known in both natures without confusion and without division. Remaining what he was, he became what he was not.

Taking in his own flesh the death owed by us because of the condemnation resulting from transgression, he freed us from eternal death. He became the beginning of those who had fallen asleep, and, rising as the firstborn from the dead, he raised us with himself and seated us with him in the heavenly places, as the apostolic tradition teaches us.

For although at the beginning human nature was deprived of paradise through disobedience, nevertheless, as has been said, the only-begotten Son of God, because of the great love with which he loved us, united our nature to himself inseparably according to hypostasis in the womb of the holy, glorious, God-bearing and ever-virgin Mary, and deemed us worthy of greater grace, granting us the kingdom in heaven.

The holy John, patriarch of Constantinople, also bears witness to these things in his discourse on the Ascension, saying:

“We who were shown to be unworthy of the earth have today been taken up into heaven. We who were not worthy even of rule below have ascended to the kingdom above; we have passed beyond the heavens and taken hold of the royal throne. And the nature for which the Cherubim guarded paradise itself sits today above the Cherubim.”

It has therefore been demonstrated that, contrary to Origen’s babbling, souls did not first exist in heaven, then sin, and afterward come down into bodies for punishment.

Rather, the whole of human nature—body and soul—was created on earth and, through God’s surpassing goodness, was deemed worthy of the kingdom in heaven.

Thus human beings who keep and fulfill God’s command are deemed worthy to share the company of the angels in heaven; and while on earth we have been commanded to imitate them through our confession toward God.

For God, wishing through his ineffable loving-kindness to be glorified on earth by human beings just as he is glorified in heaven by the holy powers, created man as a second angel on earth, so that everything might be filled with the glory of God.

Therefore the Lord, handing down how we ought to pray, says:

“Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come; thy will be done, as in heaven so also on earth.”

In agreement with what we have said, the holy theologian Gregory also teaches in his discourse on holy Easter, saying:

“Desiring to display this, the artisan Word creates man as one living being from both—the visible and the invisible nature. From matter, already existing, he takes the body; from himself he places life in it, which the Word knows as an intellectual soul and an image of God. He establishes him as another world, great in a small compass, upon the earth; another angel, a worshiper, a mixed being, an observer of visible creation, an initiate of the intelligible, a king of the things upon earth, ruled from above.”

Pay attention, therefore, that when the Father says that God made man from both, he adds that he took the body from matter already existing. But he does not say that the soul existed beforehand, nor that it came from some pre-existing substance. Rather, he says that God placed life in it from himself, which the Word knows as an intellectual soul and an image of God.

The Father’s statement that God made man a king on earth, ruled from above, also abolishes the claim that souls were cast into bodies for punishment. For to rule on earth and to be ruled by God alone is not punishment but a great gift of God.

Moreover, we consider it necessary to say this to those who assert the pre-existence of souls: if it were true that souls existed before bodies, they would know and remember what they did before entering bodies, just as after death they know and remember the things done by them in bodies.

We shall demonstrate from the very words of the Gospel that the soul knows, after its departure from this life, what it has done. For our Lord and Savior Christ says in the Gospel according to Luke, in the passage concerning Lazarus and the rich man:

“There was a certain rich man, and he clothed himself in purple and fine linen, rejoicing splendidly every day. But there was a certain poor man named Lazarus, who had been cast at his gate, covered with sores, and desiring to be filled from the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table. Even the dogs came and licked his sores.

“Now it happened that the poor man died and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried. And in Hades, lifting up his eyes while in torments, he saw Abraham from afar, and Lazarus in his bosom. And he himself cried out and said:

“‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am suffering in this flame.’

“But Abraham said:

“‘Remember, child, that you received your good things during your life, and Lazarus likewise his bad things; but now he is being comforted, while you are suffering. And besides all these things, a great chasm has been established between us and you, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can those from there cross over to us.’

“And he said:

“‘Then I ask you, father, to send him to my father’s house—for I have five brothers—so that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torment.’”

Let those who claim Origen, then, be ashamed even by the words of the holy Gospel.

For if souls existed before bodies, they would know also what had been done to them before the body, just as after death they remember what was done to them through the body.

This is what we have learned from the sayings of the holy Gospel.

That the holy Fathers, following the divinely inspired Scriptures, condemned such doctrines, together with Origen, who invented these myths, we have already demonstrated clearly from the words spoken by the holy Fathers themselves. Nevertheless, we shall demonstrate it no less through the testimonies of the holy Fathers that follow. First we shall cite Saint Peter, who became bishop of Alexandria and a martyr, bearing witness to our statements in the following words.

## From the First Discourse of Saint Peter, Bishop and Martyr of the Great City of Alexandria, concerning the proposition that the soul neither pre-existed nor sinned and was therefore cast into a body

“We consider it appropriate to set forth what concerns the first man, the earthly one fashioned from the ground, in order to show that the inner and outer man, even if at some points each is separately named, came into being one and the same at the same time. For although, according to the saving Word, the one who made the inner man also made the outer, nevertheless he made them once and at one time—that is, on the same day—when God said, ‘Let us make man according to our image and likeness.’

“From this it is perfectly clear that man was not generated from a conjunction, as though one entity had previously existed and another had come together from another place. For if there had been a conjunction, why was the thing made also recorded?”

And a little later:

“Thus it is impossible for souls to sin in heaven before bodies (F: ‘to sin’), or for them to subsist at all before bodies. For this teaching belongs to Greek philosophy, which is foreign and alien to those who wish to live piously in Christ.”

## From the same saint Peter’s Mystagogical Instruction to the Church, delivered when he was about to receive the crown of martyrdom

“For this reason I exhort you: keep watch, for you are again about to enter into tribulation. You know how many dangers my father and bishop, Theonas, who brought me up, endured at the hands of madmen devoted to idols; I succeeded him in his see—would that I had also succeeded him in his manner of life! Likewise, consider how the great Dionysius was driven from place to place in concealment, and in addition suffered under Sabellius.

“What shall I say of Heraclas and Demetrius, the blessed bishops, and the trials they endured from the deranged Origen, who himself introduced schisms into the Church—schisms that have stirred up disturbances in her down to the present day?”

How, then, can anyone of sound judgment oppose what the holy martyr and bishop of Alexandria, Peter, said concerning Origen? Having undertaken the noble contest on behalf of Christ, he not only repudiated Origen and his detestable doctrines, but also testifies that the holy fathers before him endured many trials because of Origen’s insanity.

## Testimony of Saint Athanasius, formerly bishop of Alexandria

In his discourse on the life of the blessed Antony, he says:

“How, then, do you dare to mock us when we say that Christ was manifested as man, while you, defining the soul, assert that it was once a mind, wandered astray, and fell from the vault of heaven into a body?”

Those who hear this must observe that Saint Athanasius clearly opposes those who say that the mind pre-existed, and that from it the soul came into being after sinning and falling from the vault of heaven into a body.

## From the second discourse of Saint Athanasius Against the Arians

“All visible creation came into being in six days. On the first day, the light, which he called day; on the second, the firmament; on the third, having gathered the waters, he displayed the dry land and brought forth upon it various plants; on the fourth, he made the sun and the moon and the entire host of stars; on the fifth, he created the generation of the creatures in the sea and of the birds in the air; on the sixth, he made the quadrupeds upon the earth, and finally man, consisting of a rational soul and a body.

“‘His invisible attributes are clearly perceived from the creation of the world through the things that have been made.’ Neither is the light like the night, nor the sun like the moon, nor irrational creatures like rational man, nor angels like thrones, nor thrones like authorities. All are creatures, but each of the things that came into being exists and remains according to its kind and its own nature, as it came to be.”

Behold, Saint Athanasius also teaches that after all the creatures God made man, consisting of body and intellectual, rational soul. He did not say that the body came into being after everything else so that a pre-existing soul might enter it; rather, he said that man, consisting of rational soul and body, came into being after all the creatures. He thus shows that God created both together—that is, both body and soul.

Since this doctrine is also stated among Origen’s other blasphemies—that the Lord’s soul pre-existed and that the Word of God was united to it before his incarnation from the Virgin—Saint Athanasius himself, refuting this foolish claim in his Letter to Epictetus, says:

“Rightly will all those condemn themselves who suppose that the flesh derived from Mary existed before Mary, and that the Word of God possessed a human soul before that flesh, and that he had always existed in it before his coming.”

If, then, according to what Saint Athanasius has said, the soul of our Lord Jesus Christ—who became like us in every respect except sin—did not pre-exist his coming in the flesh, what madness would it be to say that the other human souls pre-existed their bodies?

## From Saint Basil, in his discourse on “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God”

“Take care lest the similarity of the expression deceive you. For how could the human word have been in the beginning, when man received the beginning of his generation only later? Before man there were beasts, livestock, reptiles—those of the land and those of the water—birds of heaven, stars, sun, moon, vegetation, earth, sea, and heaven.”

Behold, the Father expressly warns us not to be carried away by Origen’s fables concerning the pre-existence of souls. He does not teach that the human word—that is, the soul—was in the beginning; rather, he plainly proclaims that man’s generation occurred after all God’s creatures.

If, then, all the creatures existed before man, how could souls have pre-existed? The Father did not say that everything came into being before the body, but before man, who is soul and body; and from this it is shown that both were created together.

## Saint Gregory of Nyssa, in his treatise On the Making of Man

“Perhaps it is not outside the scope of our present inquiry to examine the disputed question among the churches concerning soul and body. Some of our predecessors, among whom was the author of the treatise On First Principles, appear to say that souls pre-existed, like a kind of populace in a peculiar city. There, they say, examples of vice and virtue were set before them; and if the soul remained in the good, it remained untested until its union with the body. But if it flowed away from participation in the good, it slipped down into this life and thus came to be in a body.

“Others, attending to the order of man’s creation according to Moses, say that the soul is second to the body in time. For God first took dust from the earth and fashioned man, and then animated him through his breath.”

And a little later:

“Those who follow the former account and dogmatically assert that the souls’ manner of life existed before life in the flesh do not seem to me to be free from the Greek tales about transmigration. For if one examines their argument carefully, one will necessarily find that it is dragged toward this conclusion.

“They say that one of the wise men among them declared that he had been a man, had put on a woman’s body, had flown with the birds, had frequented the bushes, and had obtained an aquatic life. In my judgment, the man who said this about himself was not far from the truth. Such doctrines are worthy, in fact, of the chatter of frogs, the cawing of jackdaws, the irrationality of fish, or the insensibility of oak trees: to say that one soul passes through so many forms.

“The cause of such absurdity is the belief that souls pre-exist. For once the beginning of such a doctrine has been made, the argument proceeds by consequence toward what follows and lies adjacent to it, continuing in its wonder-working until it reaches this point.

“If the soul, separated by some vice from the higher mode of life, becomes a human being, and if life in the flesh is admittedly more subject to passions than the life of the eternal and incorporeal beings, then the soul’s life in such a condition—where there are more opportunities for sin—must necessarily involve greater vice and greater subjection to passion.

“Now the passion of a human soul is likeness to the irrational. Once it has become attached to this, it flows into an animal nature. And once it has begun to travel through vice, even when it has entered an irrational creature it will never cease its progress toward evil.

“For the cessation of evil is the beginning of the impulse toward virtue, but virtue does not exist in irrational creatures. Therefore it will necessarily always be changed for the worse, advancing continually toward what is worse and more dishonorable, and always discovering something worse than the nature in which it presently exists. As the sensible is lower than the rational, so from the sensible there is a further descent into the insensible.

“Thus far their argument proceeds, and it is already carried outside the truth; yet by a certain sequence it takes one absurdity from another. From this point onward, through its incoherences, it turns the doctrine into a fable.

“The sequence indicates the complete destruction of the soul. For once it has slipped from the higher mode of life, it will not be able to stop at any measure of vice. Through its relation to the passions it will pass from the rational to the irrational; from there it will be transferred to the insensibility of plants; and after the insensible comes the lifeless, and after the lifeless comes the nonexistent. Thus, by this sequence, the soul will finally pass altogether into nonbeing.

“Therefore its return again to what is better will be impossible. Yet they bring the soul back from a bush to a human being. Thus they prove by their own argument that life in a bush is preferable to incorporeal existence. For it has been shown that, as the soul’s progress is toward what is worse, it will reasonably descend toward what is lower. The lifeless is lower than the insensible nature, and to this the beginning of their doctrine leads the soul by consequence.

“But since they do not wish this conclusion, they either imprison the soul in the insensible, or, if they bring it back from there to human life, they will, as has been said, prove the wooden life more honorable than its original condition—if the descent into vice occurred from that condition, while the return to virtue occurs from this one.

“Such an argument is therefore shown to be headless and incomplete: it makes souls live independently before life in the flesh and claims that they were bound to bodies because of vice.”

Since the Father’s teaching is clear and rejects the claim that souls pre-exist bodies, let us hear also Saint Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, from the discourse written to certain monks who held Origen’s opinions:

“Therefore, as we anathematize Origen and the other heretics, so do I and Anastasius, bishop of the holy Church of Rome—a glorious commander, appointed from earlier contests over a distinguished people, and followed by the entire council of blessed bishops in the West, who accept the condemnation pronounced by the Church of Alexandria against the impious.”

## From the same Theophilus’s Letter to the Holy Ones in Scetis

This letter was written against those who objected to Origen’s condemnation:

“Some have dared to say that Origen is a teacher of the Church. Is it fitting to tolerate such people? If Origen is a teacher of the Church, then Arians, Eunomians, and Greeks may boast: the first blaspheming against the Son and the Spirit, the others, in addition to sharing their impiety, mocking the resurrection of the dead.

“It has therefore become clear from what has been said that anyone who follows the holy fathers has no doubt that those who hold Origen’s views follow Greek error and Arian madness.”

## Saint Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria, in his Letter to the Monks at Phoua

Against those who said that there is no resurrection of bodies, he says:

“They say that some among you deny the resurrection of human bodies, which is part of our confession when we approach saving baptism. For when we confess the faith, we add that we believe also in the resurrection of the flesh.

“If we abolish this and do not believe that Christ has risen from the dead in order to raise us together with himself, our faith is lame, and abandoning the royal road we walk along the crooked one.

“Such false doctrine belongs to Origen’s madness. Our fathers repudiated and anathematized him as one who distorted the truth. He did not think as a Christian, but, following the babblings of the Greeks, went astray.

“The beginning of his disease came from this. For he says that souls pre-exist bodies, that they were diverted from holiness into evil desires, and that they departed from God; and that for this reason God condemned them and embodied them, so that they are as though in a prison in the flesh.”

## From the same Letter to the Monks at Phoua

“The Church, following the divinely inspired Scriptures, does not know a soul existing before bodies, nor one that sinned before them. For how could what did not subsist have been capable of sinning? We say that the Creator of all fashioned the body from earth and animated it with an intellectual soul. This is the constitution of man.”

And a little later:

“That the human soul was not condemned because of earlier sins and sent into this world will be confirmed by the all-wise Paul, who writes: ‘For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what was done through the body, according to what he did, whether good or evil.’

“Why does he say that only what was done through the body will be brought to light, and not also what occurred before the body, if he knew that the soul pre-existed and had sinned beforehand? If we are judged only for what was done through the body, then evidently we have no earlier sin committed before the body.

“For the human soul did not subsist at all before the human being; and the force of the Law also confirms this. If, as the misguided Origen says, the soul received the body as punishment or chastisement for earlier sins, why did he threaten death to those who sin? It would rather have been necessary for the righteous to die, so that they might be freed from their bonds and punishment, while the wicked should live, so that they might be punished without being released from their bonds.”

## From the Synodal Letter issued by the bishops in Egypt and Alexandria against Origen’s doctrines

“This Origen, then, who has been brought forward, has appeared in the midst of the true Church like the abomination of desolation. Although he was ordained presbyter by the canonical and true hand, he possessed the dignity of presbyter merely and only in name, just as the thief and betrayer Judas possessed the apostleship.

“When he began to deliver blasphemous discourses, the then-blessed Heraclas, the bishop, being a truthful ploughman and cultivator of the Church’s field, plucked him from the midst of the good wheat as one who truly was a noxious weed.”

And a little later:

“Having fallen to the earth from heaven like lightning, like his father the devil, breathing great and fierce anger against the truth, he sailed to the region called Palestine. Settling in the metropolitan city of Caesarea, he there completely unveiled his mask, vomiting out the dark and black poison of his life—like the cuttlefish, which some call the squid, that emits darkness according to its nature—and stamped it there in writing. Like a Jewish merchant, he mixed bitter with sweet under the appearance of good.

“For what does this evil contriver and madman say? ‘The soul existed in heaven before the body,’ he says, ‘and after sinning there God imprisoned it—that is, sent it down into the body—for purification and correction of the sins it had committed in heaven.’ From the outset the most impious man invents myths and wishes to fight against the truth.”

And a little later:

“If the soul existed in heaven and sinned there, as the mad and God-fighting Origen said, the most holy prophet ought not to have said, ‘forming the spirit of man within him,’ but rather ‘bringing the spirit of man near him,’ or perhaps ‘sending it down.’

“But by not saying this and instead saying ‘forming it within him,’ he shows that this man is a most savage wolf, with the fleece worn outwardly for the deception and destruction of others. For, as though he had clearly come from heaven and knew the things formed there, the notorious man says that the soul not only pre-existed but had also sinned beforehand.”

It has therefore been demonstrated through both divine Scripture and the holy fathers that the heretics’ fantasies concerning the pre-existence of souls agree neither with the true faith of Christians nor with right reason.

Among Origen’s other follies is this: his claim that heaven, the sun, the moon, the stars, and the waters above the heavens are living and rational powers. Saint Basil clearly forbids this as well, in the third discourse of his Commentary on the Hexaemeron, speaking against Origen’s doctrines as follows:

“We also have an argument against those from the Church who discuss the separated waters. Under the pretext of higher interpretation and supposedly more exalted meanings, they have taken refuge in allegory, saying that spiritual and incorporeal powers are symbolically signified by the waters: the better powers remaining above upon the firmament, while the evil ones are confined below, in earthly and material places.

“For this reason they say that the waters above the heavens praise the Lord—that is, that the good powers, worthy because of the purity of their ruling faculty, render fitting praise to the Creator. The waters beneath the heavens, they say, are spiritual powers of wickedness, having fallen from their natural height into the depth of evil. Because they are turbulent and rebellious, tossed about by the disturbances of the passions, they are called seas on account of the changeability and instability of voluntary movements.

“Having dismissed such arguments as the confusions of dreams and old-wives’ tales, let us understand water as water, and let us accept the separation made by the firmament according to the explanation that has been given. Even if the waters above the heavens are sometimes taken in praise of the common Lord of all, we do not on that account assign to them a rational nature.

“For the heavens are not living beings because they declare the glory of God, nor is the firmament a sensible animal because it announces the works of his hands.”

The listeners must observe that when the Father says, “We have an argument against those from the Church,” he is speaking about Origen, who had been expelled from God’s grace and from God’s holy Church, together with those who shared his views. He did not say, “against those in the Church,” but, “against those from the Church”; by saying “we,” he indicated the members of the Church, and by saying “those from the Church,” he signified those who had fallen away from it.

The impious Origen had only one aim: to strengthen Greek error and sow weeds in the souls of the weaker. Therefore we have considered it appropriate to add the following statement of his, which is laughable but nevertheless was made by him, concerning the resurrection of human beings from the dead.

He says that at the resurrection human bodies rise spherical.

O the folly and ignorance of this deranged man, this interpreter of Greek doctrines! Blinded in mind and eager to mix fables into the Christian faith, he strove to insult the very hope and salvation of Christians—that is, the resurrection promised to us—not even respecting the Lord’s resurrection.

For when the Lord rose from the dead and became the firstfruits of those who had fallen asleep, he appeared to the disciples and showed them the wounds in his hands and feet and the wound in his side. After the resurrection he ate—not because he needed food, but in order by this means to establish the nature of the risen body.

Indeed, when the Lord was being taken up, the angel said to the disciples: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.”

If, then, as Origen madly claims, the Lord’s body was spherical, how could he have shown the wounds in his hands and feet or the wound in his side? How could he have eaten, or been recognized at all by the disciples? And how could the bodies of the saints, raised after the Lord’s resurrection and seen in the holy city, have been recognized by the others if they had another form than the one they had possessed in life?

The impious Origen, not at all founded upon the rock of faith, put forward these and much worse blasphemies. Accordingly, at the time of his martyrdom he denied Christ and worshiped the Greek polytheism introduced by him.

This too occurred by God’s providence, so that he would not be received into the Church as a martyr and thereby cause harm to Christ’s flock. For if there are even now some who acknowledge his fall while claiming his doctrines, would they not have defended his teachings as those of a martyr and father, if he had died without worshiping idols?

No one who holds fast to the truth falls away from God or is abandoned by him, according to what is said in divine Scripture: “Look upon the ancient generations and see: who believed in the Lord and was forsaken? Or who hoped in him and was disregarded?”

The impious Origen did not confine his blasphemies to himself, but through his writings transmitted his own error to many others. Thus the saying of the holy apostle Paul is entirely appropriate to him: “The sins of some are manifest, going before them to judgment, while for others they follow after.”

For the succession of his error, creeping through the souls of the weaker, causes the sins committed by him from the beginning to follow after him.

As though those who glorify Origen did not have enough of the impiety concerning the pre-existence of souls, his other empty talk, and his blasphemies concerning the holy Trinity, they add this to their own error, guided by his distorted arguments: that the punishment of all impious human beings and even of demons has an end, and that the impious and demons will be restored to their former rank.

By saying this they make people careless about fulfilling God’s commandments, turning them away from the narrow and afflicted road and leading them astray toward the broad and spacious one. They also utterly oppose what was said by our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.

For he teaches in the holy Gospel that the impious will go away into eternal punishment, while the righteous will go into eternal life. Again, he says to those on his right: “Come, blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world”; but to those on his left: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.”

Since the Lord plainly promises through the holy Gospel that both punishment and the kingdom are without end, those who prefer Origen’s fables to the Lord’s declarations stand manifestly convicted. Their folly is exposed even by the consequence of their own argument. For if someone supposes, according to Origen’s nonsense, that punishment has an end, he must also assign an end to the eternal life promised to the righteous. The word “eternal” is applied equally to both. If punishment and enjoyment have an end, why did our Lord Jesus Christ become incarnate? Why the crucifixion, death, burial, and resurrection of the Lord? What benefit would there be for those who fought the good fight and bore witness for Christ, if demons and impious people were to receive through restoration the same rank as the saints?

May these things fall upon the heads of those who tell such fables. The words of Christ remain unshaken in the souls of believers and in the very truth of realities.

Those who defend Origen’s false doctrine, fleeing the irrefutable refutations concerning these matters and wishing to conceal their error, twist certain sayings of the holy fathers and distort them according to their own meaning, adapting them to their own disease. They do the same with the divine Scriptures. We shall demonstrate from the holy fathers themselves that such arguments of theirs are futile.

Saint Gregory the Theologian says in his Apologetic Discourse:

“For us, whose concern is the salvation of the blessed and immortal soul—which will be punished or praised immortally because of vice or virtue—how great must we consider the contest to be, and how much knowledge is required?”

And a little later:

“What false defense is there? What skillful plausibility? What invention can deceive the tribunal against the truth and steal the just judgment that places everything in the balance—deed, word, and thought—and weighs the better against the worse, so that what inclines may prevail and the verdict may go with the greater weight? After that there is no desire, no higher judge, no defense through subsequent deeds, no oil from the wise virgins, nor from those who sell it when the lamps are failing; no repentance of the rich man melting in flame and seeking correction for his own; no period granted for amendment.

“The tribunal is enduring, fearful, and final, and more just than it is terrifying—or rather, therefore more terrifying, because it is just. Thrones are set, the Ancient of Days takes his seat, books are opened, and a river of fire is drawn forth; light is set before them and darkness prepared.

“Those who have done good go to the resurrection of life, which is now hidden with Christ and later to be revealed together with him. Those who have done evil go to the resurrection of judgment, by which those who do not believe have already been condemned by the Word who judged them.

“The ineffable light receives the former, and the grace of the holy and royal Trinity shines forth more clearly and purely, with the whole mind mingling with the whole. This alone I call the kingdom of heaven. For the others there is punishment, and before all else the fact of being cast away from God, together with the shame in conscience that has no end.”

## Basil, Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, from his Canonical Book

**Question:** When one passage says, “He will be beaten with many blows,” and another says, “with few,” how do some say that punishment has no end for those who are punished?

**Answer:** What is ambiguous and appears to have been spoken obscurely in certain passages of divinely inspired Scripture is clarified by what is stated plainly elsewhere.

Since the Lord has declared that “these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life,” and elsewhere sends us into “the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels,” and elsewhere calls it “the Gehenna of fire,” adding, “where their worm does not end and the fire is not quenched”; and since long ago through the prophet he said of certain persons, “their worm will not end and their fire will not be quenched”—since such and so many things are repeatedly stated in divinely inspired Scripture, it is one of the devil’s devices that many people, as though they had forgotten these and so many declarations of the Lord, dare to prescribe for themselves an end to the punishments of sin in the age to come.

For if eternal punishment will ever have an end, eternal life must also have an end. But if we do not accept this meaning of the text in the case of life, what reason is there for assigning an end to eternal punishment? The addition “eternal” stands equally with respect to both: “These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”

### From the same author’s Exhortation to Baptism

“Because of a momentary pleasure of sin I am punished immortally; because of the pleasure of the flesh I am handed over to eternal fire.”

### Saint John, Bishop of Constantinople, from his First Letter to the Monk Theodore
