“Consider these things continually, and the river of fire: ‘For a river of fire flowed before him.’ Once delivered to that fire, one should not expect an end to punishment.

“The senseless pleasures of life differ in nothing from shadows and dreams. Before the deeds of sin are completed, the pleasures are extinguished; but the punishments for them have no end.”

### From the same author’s Commentary on the First Letter to the Corinthians

“Our present question is not a small one, but concerns matters of the greatest necessity. Everyone asks whether the fire of Gehenna has an end. That it does not, Christ declared when he said: ‘Their fire will not be quenched, and their worm will not end.’ Paul also shows that it is immortal when he says: ‘Those who sin will suffer an eternal destructive penalty.’”

Since divine Scripture and the holy fathers plainly teach that the punishment of the impious and of the demons served by them has no end, what restoration do those who hold Origen’s opinions imagine, when punishments have no end? The holy Church of Christ proclaims eternal life without end for the righteous and likewise hands down unending punishment for the impious.

These matters may suffice here. We have decided to bring forward a few things from the many statements of divine Scripture and the holy fathers in order to refute the impiety of the Origenists.

## Letter against Origen

Wishing to remove every stumbling block from the most holy Church, so that no stain might remain in her, and following the divine Scriptures and the holy fathers—who expelled Origen and his detestable and impious doctrines and justly subjected them to anathema—we address this present letter to Your Blessedness.

Through it we urge you to assemble all the most reverend bishops residing in this imperial city, together with the most God-loving superiors of the pious monasteries here, and to arrange for all of them in writing to anathematize the impious and God-fighting Origen, also called Adamantius, formerly a presbyter of the most holy Church of Alexandria, together with his detestable and impious doctrines and all the chapters set out below.

You should also send copies of what is being done by Your Blessedness for this purpose to all the other most holy bishops and superiors of the pious monasteries, so that they too may, by their own signatures, anathematize Origen and his detestable doctrines, together with all the heretics who will be named.

Henceforth no one is to be ordained bishop or appointed superior of a monastery unless, together with all the other heretics customarily anathematized in the documents that have been issued—namely Sabellius, Arius, Apollinarius, Nestorius, Eutyches, Dioscorus, Timothy the Cat, Peter Mongus, Anthimus of Trebizond, Theodosius of Alexandria, Peter formerly of Antioch, Peter of Apamea, Severus formerly of Antioch, and the aforesaid Origen, who was afflicted with Greek and Arian madness—they anathematize Origen and his detestable and impious doctrines.

For it must be proclaimed to everyone that no one may at all claim such a heretic or his writings, but that everyone must hate, reject, and anathematize them with all his soul and mind, since they are alien to Christian tradition and cause great damage to the souls of the simple.

We have written these things not only to Your Holiness, but also to the most holy and most blessed pope of elder Rome and patriarch, Vigilius, and to all the other most holy bishops and patriarchs—namely, those of Alexandria, Theoupolis, and Jerusalem—so that they too may take responsibility for the matter and bring it to completion.

Wishing all Christians to know that the writings of Origen are wholly alien to the true faith of Christians, we have decided to cite a few of his many and immeasurable blasphemies in his very words. They are as follows.

## Extracts from Origen’s writings

### That the Son is inferior to the Father, and the Spirit to the Son

From the first discourse of the book On First Principles:

“God the Father, holding all things together, reaches each of the beings, imparting to each from himself its being. The text here is corrupt (‘ᾯ γὰρ ἐστιν ἔλαττον’); an alternative reading gives: ‘The Son, being less than the Father, reaches only rational beings, for he is second to the Father’; and the Holy Spirit, being still less, reaches only the saints. Thus the power of the Father is greater than that of the Son and the Holy Spirit; the power of the Son is greater than that of the Holy Spirit; and the power of the Holy Spirit is in turn greater than that of the other holy beings.”

### That the power of God the Father is limited

From the second discourse of the same book:

“One must say that the power of God is limited and must not, under the pretext of praise or laudatory language, remove its boundary.”

And a little later:

“He therefore made as many things as he was able to grasp, hold in his hand, and keep under his providence; just as he prepared as much matter as he was able to order.”

### From the fourth discourse of the same book

“Let no one take offense at the argument if we impose limits even upon the power of God. For it is naturally impossible to comprehend infinite things. Since the things that God himself grasps are once and for all finite, there must necessarily be a limit corresponding to the number of finite things for which his power endures.”

### That the Son is a creature and generated

From the same discourse:

“This Son, begotten by the Father’s will, ‘who is the image of the invisible God, the radiance of his glory and the exact impress of his substance, the firstborn of all creation,’ is a creature and wisdom. For Wisdom herself says: ‘God created me as the beginning of his ways, for his works.’”

### That the Father contains the Son with the other creatures

From the fourth discourse of the same book:

“That the Son is also contained by the Father together with the other creatures, and that in every respect the Father is greater than the Son and is invisible to him.”

From the same book On First Principles:

“If the Father contains all things, and the Son is one of all things, it is clear that he contains the Son also. Someone else may ask whether it is true that God is known by himself in the same way as he is known by the Only-begotten; and he will conclude that the statement, ‘The Father who sent me is greater than I,’ is true in every respect. Thus even in understanding, the Father is understood by himself more greatly, clearly, and perfectly than by the Son.”

### From the first discourse of the same book

“Since we were made according to the image, we possess the Son as the archetype, in truth, of the beautiful forms within us. The Son himself is, in relation to the Father, who is truth, what we are in relation to him.”

### From the same discourse

“Thus, I think, it may properly be said of the Savior also that he is the image of God’s goodness, but not goodness itself. Perhaps he is also a good Son, but not good in the absolute sense.

“And just as he is the image of the invisible God and is therefore God, but not the one of whom Christ himself says, ‘That they may know you, the only true God,’ so he is an image of goodness, but not good without distinction as the Father is.”

### That the Holy Spirit too is a creature

“Having called the Holy Spirit a creature along with the Son, he counted it among the other creatures; therefore he calls them ministering living beings.”

From the book On First Principles.

**[Note: [Col. 0215D] Read αὐτούς, that is, “the Father and the Son,” which agrees with the Latin ipsos. EDIT.]**

From the same book:

“That everything generated apart from the Father and God of all things follows from the same argument.”

And after some material:

“The Hebrew said that the two six-winged seraphim in Isaiah, crying out to one another and saying, ‘Holy, holy, holy is the Lord Sabaoth,’ are the Only-begotten of God and the Holy Spirit. We think also that in the song of Habakkuk, ‘In the midst of two living beings you will be known,’ the reference is to Christ and the Holy Spirit.”

### From the second discourse of the book On First Principles: that the Lord is merely a man

“For this reason Christ also became man, receiving this status because of his virtue, as the prophet testifies when he says: ‘You loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.’ It was fitting that the one who had never been separated from the Only-begotten should be called by the same title as the Only-begotten and be glorified together with him.”

### That creatures are co-eternal with God

From the first discourse of the book On First Principles:

“How could it not be absurd for God, who did not possess something proper to him, to come into possession of it? Since there was never a time when he was not almighty, these things must always exist through which he is almighty. They were always being ruled by him and serving him as their ruler.”

### From the same discourse

“All genera and species have always existed.” [Another reading: “But someone else will say that each individual also exists eternally.”] In either case it is shown that God did not begin to create after having previously been inactive.

### Concerning the pre-existence of souls

From the first discourse of the book On First Principles:

“Because of their own cause, those who do not attend vigilantly to themselves undergo changes (variant: ‘falls’) sooner or later, falling either more or less, according to divine judgment proportioned to each one’s better or worse movements and to what is deserved.

“One will possess in the coming arrangement an angelic rank, or a ruling power, or authority over certain beings, or a throne over subjects, or dominion over servants. Those who have not fallen very far will possess administration and assistance in the matters just mentioned. Thus, for the most part, the human race will be constituted from those under the principalities, authorities, thrones, and dominions; perhaps at times it will even be constituted in their place, in each individual world.”

### From the same discourse: if demons change for the better, they will eventually complete humanity

“I think that those subject to the inferior principalities, authorities, and world-rulers in each world—or, in some worlds, perhaps certain minds (alternative reading: ‘minds of what world?’)—may, if some are benefited more quickly and wish to change, eventually complete humanity.”

### Concerning the descent of those above into a body

“Since the world is of such extraordinary variety and contains so many different rational beings, what other cause should we say produced its existence than the varied falling-away of those who flowed away from the Monad in different ways? And at times the soul chooses an aquatic life.”

### From the second discourse of the book On First Principles

“The soul, flowing away from the beautiful, inclining toward evil, and remaining in it for a longer time, is turned into an animal by folly and made bestial by wickedness.”

And a little later:

“It chooses to become irrational and to live, so to speak, an aquatic life; and perhaps, in proportion to the extent of its deeper fall (variant: ‘falling’) into evil, it puts on a body (variant: ‘bodies’) of such an irrational animal, not dry but watery [read: ‘watery’].”

### From the same discourse: that bodies will eventually be completely put off

“If the things subjected to Christ will at the end also be subjected to God, all will put off their bodies. I think that then there will be dissolution into nonbeing, when the nature of bodies comes to subsist a second time, should rational beings descend once more.”

### From the third discourse of the same book, on the same subject

“When God is said to become all things in all, just as we cannot leave evil behind—otherwise God would become all things even in evil—nor irrational animals, lest God become all things in irrational animals, so neither can we retain lifeless things, lest God become all things even in them; likewise, neither can we retain bodies, which by their own nature are lifeless.”

### From the second discourse of the book On First Principles

“Through the fall and the cooling that resulted from ceasing to live by the spirit, the soul that now exists came into being. It is also capable of returning to what it was at the beginning, which, I think, is what the prophet means when he says, ‘Return, my soul, to your rest.’ Thus the whole of this was mind [possibly, ‘was a mind’]. How, then, did it become soul, and how does the soul, when perfected, become mind?”

### From the same discourse, on the same subject

“As the Savior came to save what was lost, yet when what was lost is saved it is no longer lost, so the soul whom he came to save, as he came to save what was lost, is no longer a soul when the saved soul is saved; nor is what was lost still lost.

“Let the matter be examined further. If what was lost existed when it was not lost and will one day exist when it is no longer lost, then likewise the soul existed when it was not a soul and will be when it is no longer a soul.”

### From the fourth discourse

“The nature of bodies must not exist previously, but must come into being intermittently because of certain conditions arising among rational beings who need bodies. When the restoration is fully accomplished, bodies must again be dissolved into nonbeing, so that this may always occur.”

### From the first discourse of the same book: that the sun, moon, and stars are living beings

“That the soul of the sun is older than its attachment to the body, after reasoning from comparison with man, and from this I think it can be demonstrated from the Scriptures.”

### From the same discourse

“It is better to depart and be with Christ, for that is much better. I think the sun might say: ‘It is better to depart and be with Christ, for that is much better.’ Paul says, ‘But to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake’; the sun says, ‘To remain in this heavenly body is more necessary because of the revelation of the children of God.’ The same should be said concerning the moon and the remaining stars.”

### From the fourth discourse of the same book: that Christ must be crucified for demons also, repeatedly, in the ages to come

“Even if someone examines the matter only as far as the Passion, he will seem bold if he searches for the heavenly place itself. But if there are spiritual powers of wickedness in the heavenly places, then, just as here we are not ashamed to confess that he was crucified for the destruction of those whom he destroyed by suffering, so there also, granting that something similar occurs, and continuing likewise until the consummation of the entire age, we shall not be afraid.”

**[Note: [Col. 0221D] Some wish to read ‘until the consummation’; but nothing should be changed. Hardouin.]**

### From the same discourse

“Who possessing understanding would define a first, second, and third day, evening and morning, as having occurred without the sun, moon, or stars?”

Since these matters stand thus, and all the blasphemies spoken by Origen have become evident to everyone, his anathema ought to be pronounced as follows.

### Anathemas

If anyone says or holds that human souls pre-exist, having formerly been minds and holy powers, but, having become satiated with divine contemplation, turned toward what is worse and therefore cooled from the love of God, and were consequently called souls and sent into bodies for punishment: let him be anathema.

If anyone says or holds that the soul of the Lord pre-existed and became united to the Word of God before his incarnation and birth from the Virgin: let him be anathema.

If anyone says or holds that the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was first formed in the womb of the holy Virgin, and that afterward the Word of God was united to it, together with the soul as having pre-existed: let him be anathema.

If anyone says or holds that the Word of God became like all the heavenly orders, becoming a Cherub to the Cherubim, a Seraph to the Seraphim, and in general becoming like all the powers above: let him be anathema.

If anyone says or holds that at the resurrection human bodies rise in spherical form, and does not confess that we rise upright: let him be anathema.

If anyone says that heaven, the sun, the moon, the stars, and the waters above the heavens are living and material powers [Paganinus Gaudentius correctly observes the alternative reading ‘rational powers’]: let him be anathema.

If anyone says or holds that the Lord Christ will be crucified in the coming age on behalf of demons, just as on behalf of human beings: let him be anathema.

If anyone says or holds that the power of God is limited, or [read: “that”] he created only as many things as he was able to grasp: let him be anathema.

If anyone says or holds that the punishment of demons and impious human beings is temporary and will have an end after a certain period, or that demons or impious human beings will be restored: let him be anathema.

Anathema also to Origen, called Adamantinus, who set forth these doctrines, together with his detestable and accursed impious teachings, and to every person who holds or defends these doctrines, or at any time dares in any way to claim them.

# Letter of the Emperor Justinian to the Holy Synod concerning Origen and his adherents

We have always been—and still are—concerned to preserve undisturbed the holy and apostolic Church of God, and to condemn everything that in any way rises up against the orthodox faith.

Since we have learned that certain monks in Jerusalem follow Pythagoras, Plato, and Origen called Adamantius, together with their impiety and error, and teach these doctrines, we have thought it necessary to undertake care and investigation concerning them, lest through their Greek and Manichaean deception they utterly destroy many.

Among the many things they say, let us mention a few: that there were minds without any number or name; that all rational beings were one in their identity of essence and activity and in their union and knowledge directed toward the Word of God; and that, when they became satiated with divine love and contemplation in differing degrees, each clothed itself in bodies more subtle or denser according to its individual turn toward what is worse, and received names. From this arose the heavenly and ministering powers.

They also say that the sun, moon, and stars themselves belonged to that same unity of rational beings, and that they became what they are through their turning toward what is worse. Those rational beings that had cooled more extensively from divine love were called souls and were cast into denser bodies like ours. Those that had advanced to the extreme of evil were bound in cold and gloomy bodies and became demons.

They say also that from an angelic condition there arises a psychic condition, and from the psychic condition a demonic and human one.

Only one mind, they say, remained steadfast and unmoved in the divine love and contemplation throughout the entire unity of rational beings; this mind became Christ, King, God, and man.

They say that there is a complete abolition of bodies, with the Lord himself first laying aside his own body and all the others following. All are then brought back into the same unity and become minds, just as they were in their former pre-existence. The devil himself and the other demons are likewise restored to the same unity, as are impious and atheistic human beings together with the divine and God-bearing men and the heavenly powers. All possess the same union with God as Christ possesses, just as they did before; so that Christ differs in no respect from the other rational beings—not in essence, knowledge, power, or activity.

Pythagoras said that the Monad is the origin of all things. Again, Pythagoras and Plato, speaking of a kind of multitude of incorporeal souls, say that souls who fell into some sin are sent into bodies for punishment. Hence Plato called the body “enclosure” and “tomb,” as though the soul were bound and buried in it.

Then, concerning the future judgment and recompense of souls, he says:

“The soul of one who has practiced pederasty and lived badly, though with philosophy, is allowed to be punished on the third circuit of a thousand years; and thus, having grown wings, it is cast out and departs in the three-thousandth year. When the others complete this life, some go to places of judgment beneath the earth and pay both penalty and account, while others, lifted by judgment to some heavenly place, spend their time there according to their deserts, as they lived.”

It is easy to understand the absurdity of this argument. Who taught him the cycles and millennia of the years? Who taught him that, once a thousand years had passed, each soul then departs to its proper place? The intervening matters were unfit to be mentioned even by the most wanton men, let alone by such a philosopher. For he yoked those who had achieved a pure manner of life with the unchaste and pederasts, and said that both would enjoy the same things.

Pythagoras, Plato, Plotinus, and those of their faction, having agreed that souls are immortal, said that they pre-exist bodies, that they are a multitude of souls, and that those who fail fall into bodies, as I have said. They say that the bitter become wicked beings [possibly “sluggish beings” or “donkeys”], predators become wolves, deceitful persons become foxes, and effeminate persons become horses.

But the Church, following the divine teachings, says that the soul was created together with the body, not that one came first and the other later, according to Origen’s madness.

For these wicked and destructive doctrines—or rather, absurdities—we urge Your Most Reverend Beatitudes, gathered together in one place, carefully to read the statement set out below, and to condemn and anathematize each of its chapters, together with the impious Origen and all who hold or will hold such opinions to the end.

# Treatise of the Most Pious Emperor Justinian, sent to Mennas, the Most Holy and Most Blessed Archbishop of the Fortunate City and Patriarch, against the impious Origen and his wicked doctrines

## [Col. 0178D]

It has always been our concern, and remains so now, that the right and irreproachable faith of Christians and the state of the most holy catholic and apostolic Church of God be preserved everywhere free from disturbance. This is our first and most ancient care. Through it we believe that the empire entrusted to us by God in the present age is both preserved and maintained, that the enemies of our commonwealth are subdued, and that in the age to come we shall obtain mercy in the presence of his goodness.

For although the enemy of the human race devises various opportunities by which he strives to injure human souls, God’s humanity nevertheless breaks and nullifies his wickedness and malice, rebukes his adversaries, and does not permit his flock to suffer harm or be scattered.

We have said this because it has been reported to us that certain persons do not possess the fear of God in their hearts and do not discern the distinction of right doctrine, by which everyone who knows the truth is saved. Abandoning the divine Scriptures and the holy fathers, whom the catholic Church of God recognizes as teachers—through whom every heresy has everywhere been expelled and the orthodox faith declared—they affirm that Origen and his doctrines are related to the errors of pagans, Arians, and Manichaeans, through which he fell into the pit.

How can such people be numbered among Christians, when they defend a man who tried to transmit the doctrines held by pagans, Manichaeans, Arians, and other heretics? Above all, he dared to utter blasphemies against the holy and consubstantial Trinity: that the Father is greater than the Son, the Son than the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit than the other spirits.

Moreover, he added this to his impiety: that the Son cannot see the Father, nor the Holy Spirit the Son; that the Son and the Holy Spirit are creatures; and that the relation between us and the Son is the same as that between the Son and the Father.

To his blasphemies he added the following in the first discourse of On First Principles, saying:

“In that beginning apprehended by the mind, God established, by his intelligible will, as many rational substances as he judged sufficient. For one must say that the power of God is finite; nor, under the pretext of praise and laudatory language, should its limitation be removed. For if divine power is infinite, it must be unable even to understand itself, since nature cannot comprehend what is infinite.

“Thus he made as many things as he was able to grasp and keep under his providence, just as he prepared as much matter as he was able to govern, distinguish, and adorn.”

Could Origen have uttered any greater blasphemy against God? By devising ranks within the holy Trinity, he seeks to introduce a multitude of gods and monstrously asserts that God’s power is bounded.

It is also full of impiety to say, according to his fable, that all genera and species are co-eternal with God; that rational beings who sinned and therefore fell from their condition were, in proportion to their sins, cast into bodies as punishment and, after being purified, were again raised to their former condition, having laid aside both wickedness and bodies; and that they were again, a second, third, and many times, cast into different bodies as punishment.

He further posits that different worlds existed and exist—past worlds as well as future ones.

Who is so foolish that, hearing these things, does not shudder at their extreme impiety? Who would not execrate the mad Origen, who invented and committed such blasphemies against God to writing? Since they are forbidden to all Christians and plainly bear the marks of impiety, we have thought it unnecessary to honor them with a refutation.

If all heretics have been expelled from the most holy Church and subjected, together with their doctrines, to anathema because of the perversity of perhaps one or two doctrines, what Christian could possibly tolerate defending Origen and his wicked writings? He uttered so many blasphemies and provided nearly every heretic with such abundant material for destruction and blasphemy; therefore he was long ago subjected by the holy fathers to anathema together with his criminal doctrines.

Even if someone grants that Origen, who opposed God, expressed something of right doctrine in his wicked writings—as is found among other heretics—that is not his own; it belongs to the holy Church of God. He maliciously attempted this very thing to deceive the simple. For, having been nourished on pagan writings and intending to propagate them, he pretended to interpret the divine Scriptures, so that by maliciously mixing his wicked doctrine into the monuments of sacred letters he might introduce his pagan and Manichaean error and Arian madness, and ensnare those who had not accurately grasped the sacred Scripture.

What else did Origen expound than the doctrine of Plato, who spread the madness of the pagans? And from whom else did Arius borrow when he fashioned his own poisons? Origen devised ranks within the holy and consubstantial Trinity to the destruction of his own soul.

Is he not also close to Manichaeus, who says that human souls are sent into bodies for punishment because of sins? He asserts that they were first minds and holy powers, then became satiated with divine contemplation, turned toward what is worse, and therefore cooled from the love of God; hence they were called by the Greek name ψυχαί, “souls,” and were placed in bodies for punishment. This alone would have been sufficient for his complete condemnation, since it arose from pagan impiety.

When God said, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1), his empty statements imply that only the body, without the soul, was made according to the image and likeness of God, if the soul pre-existed and was cast into the body after it had been made, as into a vessel. It would then be necessary to say that God, the maker of man, is himself a body, since he made the body according to his own image and likeness. But how could a body be the image of the incorporeal? Therefore, let Christians not assent to these things.

If, according to Origen’s blasphemy, souls pre-existed and were sent into bodies as punishment for their sins so that they might be corrected and repent, they ought not to sin any further. For if the body was given to the soul as punishment for its sins, so that through suffering it might be corrected and honor God, how does the body help and strengthen it to sin? This does not happen to those who are punished. Bonds, prisons, fetters, and, in short, all such things restrain the injustices and sins of those who are already undergoing punishment.

Bonds are not added to someone who has sinned in order to help him sin further, but so that through the torment of the bonds he may cease sinning. It is therefore clear that souls were not placed in bodies, as those men babble, to punish earlier sins. Rather, God created both body and soul together, that is, the complete human being.

Accordingly, we await recompense for what we have done through the body, whether good or evil. The divine apostle Paul also teaches this when he says: “For we must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done through the body, whether good or evil” (1 Corinthians 5).

The apostle’s words must therefore be heeded. He did not say that the one being judged would receive according to what he had done before the body. If a human being is punished or rewarded by the judge of the earth solely for what he has done through the body, and no mention is made of sins committed before it, it is clear that souls do not exist before bodies. For if they pre-existed, the apostle would have said that each receives according to what was done both through the body and before the body.

It is acknowledged that human souls possess understanding and reason; even those who defend Origen, we suppose, cannot deny this. Let those who share Origen’s views say, then: if their souls existed before bodies, as they assert, in what condition were they before entering them, and what were they doing? If they existed beforehand, they ought to know where they were and how they came here. If they cannot say this in any rational manner—and indeed it is not true—it is obvious that they are telling fables.

Perhaps they will say that once souls entered bodies, they were then able to discern and know what they themselves were doing. If they say this, their empty argument will result in the body having greater value and honor than the soul, since the body would provide the soul with understanding and reason as a benefit. But to assert this is full of madness and absurdity.

Why, if the soul existed before the body, does it require instruction after entering the body and gradually develop toward what is better and more perfect? If it pre-existed, it would certainly know useful things and would need no instruction; and if it possessed knowledge, it would not require care and diligence to be educated. If it knew what offense was, it would not be taught what it already knew. But if it is taught, then, being in ignorance, it did not know before; and if it did not know before, it did not exist before.

It is therefore evident that it did not exist beforehand. God alone is the cause of our origin. Just as he made us when we did not exist, so, once we were born, he preserves and saves us by his grace and his own hand, if we are judged worthy and fit.

For when God said, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1), he made both together: he formed the body and created the intellectual and rational soul. Together he fashioned the body and created the soul, presenting the complete human being. For man is neither body without soul nor soul without body.

If the soul pre-existed, as Origen raves, why did the most holy prophet Zechariah say, “Forming the spirit of man within him” (Zechariah 12)? If it existed beforehand, it would have been more appropriate to say, “Pouring the spirit of man into him as into a vessel,” or “sending it down into him.” But when the prophet says “forming,” he shows that God made the soul, as he made the body, by his own power and goodness, not that it pre-existed.

That man was made, as has been said, according to the image and likeness of God, and was deemed worthy of divine inspiration, makes it clear that not only was the intellectual and rational soul created, but it was also created immortal, so that it might rule over all things made upon the earth.

This is what Gregory the Theologian says concerning the soul: that it is from God, divine, and participant in heavenly nobility—not, as some suppose and say, that the soul is of the divine substance, but that it was made by God’s inspiration and received from him the grace to be understanding, rational, and immortal, and not to die together with the body like irrational animals, but by grace to share in heavenly nobility, that is, immortality.

Saint John, patriarch of Constantinople, bears witness to this in his eleventh discourse on creation. He says as follows (Homily 13 on Genesis 2):

“‘And he breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul.’ Here some uneducated men, moved by their own thoughts and having nothing worthy of God in mind, without considering the condescension of the words, dare to say that the soul is of God’s substance. O madness! O insanity!”

The Father says that, concerning all the other things made upon the earth, God said, “Let it be,” and, “Let the earth bring forth,” and it came to be. But concerning man he says, “Let us make man”—not merely “Let us make,” but “according to our image and likeness.” Taking dust from the earth, he fashioned man with his own hands and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul.

From this it may be perceived that God made man more honorable and precious than all the other creatures upon the earth. He made all the others by a word: he spoke, and they came to be. But man, as has been said, he himself made with his own hands according to divine Scripture. And all that he made upon the earth he subjected to man, who was made on the sixth day, so that, with all the earthly creatures already made and prepared for him, he might rule over them, himself obeying the command of his maker.

The holy theologian Gregory also teaches this in his Oration on the New Sunday (Oration 43):

“Thus one day is counted first, another second, another third, and so on up to the seventh day, on which there was rest from the works. By these days the things that came into being are distributed, arranged by an ineffable order and not produced all at once by the Word who is powerful over all things, for whom to think a thing and to say it is to accomplish it. If man was designated last, and that by the hand of God, and honored with his image, there is nothing strange in this. For, since he was to be king, it was fitting that the royal palace should first exist and then the king, as judge, surrounded and protected by all his attendants.”

If, therefore, according to Gregory the Theologian, man was designated last, made by the hand of God, honored with his image, and everything was prepared for him, with the palaces first subject to him as king, and he was introduced by God surrounded by all the service of creation, how can those who are mad after Origen say that pre-existing souls were sent into bodies to pay the penalty for sins previously committed?

On the contrary, Saint Gregory says both that man was made last of all and that he was honored by God and made ruler over all earthly things. This is not a sign of punishment, but of singular providence and beneficence.

The teaching of Saint John, patriarch of Constantinople, in his eleventh discourse on creation agrees with Gregory the Theologian. He says (Homily 13 on Genesis):

“Perhaps someone may say: Why, if the soul is more precious than the body, is what is inferior made first and what is greater and nobler afterward? Do you not see, beloved, that the same thing occurred in creation itself? Just as heaven, earth, sun, moon, and all the rest were fashioned, and man came last, to whom dominion over all was to be entrusted, so in the fashioning of man the body is formed first and then the soul, which is more honorable.

“For just as the irrational creatures, which were prepared for utility and service, existed before man, so that the one who was to enjoy their benefits might have prepared servants, so the body was fashioned before the soul, so that when the soul was introduced according to God’s hidden wisdom it might carry out its proper functions through the movement of the body.”

These testimonies suffice to show the hearers that everywhere we hold and teach the same things as the fathers who abolish the pre-existence of souls.

Furthermore, since holy Scripture says concerning Adam and Eve, “God blessed them and said, ‘Increase and multiply, fill the earth, and rule it’” (Genesis 1), how, if souls were older than bodies, could those souls—which, according to their fables, already existed—be destined to increase and multiply according to the divine command? How could God bless souls that had already fallen into sins so that they might increase and multiply? Souls polluted by sins deserved a curse rather than a blessing.

And if souls pre-existed and, according to Origen’s fables, existed in another order, why did God fashion only Adam? Had Adam alone sinned in his soul, and was one body therefore fashioned by God? If other souls had existed previously, other bodies ought also to have been fashioned to receive them.

And how could a sinful soul, which according to their reasoning was cast into a body as punishment, have been placed by God in a paradise of delights? If it had been sent into a body to pay a penalty, it should have been placed not in paradise but in a place of punishment.

God loved man so greatly—man whom he had fashioned after all the other creatures—that when he transgressed the command given to him and was therefore expelled from paradise, and when the human race increased and sin grew because human thought inclined with wicked zeal toward worse things, God, being good, did not neglect his creation. Instead, as holy Scripture indicates, he rebuked and chastised it in many ways.

When we needed a greater remedy because of more serious diseases, the only-begotten Word of God, one—that is, one person—of the holy Trinity, became man because of his goodness, remaining God. Neither was his divine substance changed into human substance, nor the human into the divine. He is one and the same in both natures, known in them without confusion and without division.

Remaining what he was, he became what he was not. Taking in his own flesh the death owed to us because of the condemnation of transgression, he freed us from eternal death. He became the firstfruits of those who sleep and the firstborn from the dead, raising us with himself and seating us together in the heavenly places (1 Corinthians 15; Colossians 1; Ephesians 2), as apostolic tradition teaches us.

Although human nature was deprived of paradise from the beginning because of disobedience, nevertheless, as has been said, the Only-begotten Son of God, because of the great love with which he loved us (Ephesians 2), united our nature to himself indivisibly according to his hypostasis in the womb of the holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mary, the Mother of God, and deemed us worthy of even greater grace, granting us the kingdom of heaven.

Saint John, patriarch of Constantinople, bears witness to this in his discourse on the Ascension (volume 3 of his works), saying:

“Today we, who had been unworthy of the earth, have been raised into heaven. We, who were not worthy even of the lower dominion, have ascended to the kingdom above. We have passed beyond the heavens and attained the royal throne. The very nature for which the cherubim guarded paradise (Genesis 3) today sits above the cherubim.”

It has therefore been demonstrated that souls did not, as Origen babbles, first exist in heaven and then get sent into bodies to pay the penalty for sins committed. Rather, the whole of human nature—body and soul—was fashioned on earth and, through divine goodness and condescension, attained heaven. Thus those human beings who guard and fulfill God’s command may be deemed worthy of the angels’ heavenly way of life, whom we have been commanded to imitate on earth through confession of God.

For when God wished, because of his ineffable humanity, to be glorified on earth by human beings just as he is glorified in heaven by the holy powers, he fashioned man as another angel on earth, so that God’s glory might fill all things.

Therefore, when the Lord teaches how one ought to pray, he says:

“Our Father, who are in the heavens, hallowed be your name; your kingdom come; your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.”

The things we have said agree with what the holy Theologian Gregory teaches in his sermon [Col. 0192A] on Holy Pascha (Oration 42, which is the second on Pascha). For he says:

“Since the Word, the Craftsman, wished to demonstrate this matter, he fashioned one creature from both kinds of nature, namely, the visible and the invisible: man. Taking a body from matter that already existed, and giving it life from himself—for reason knows this to be an intelligent soul and the image of God—he established upon the earth, as it were, another world, a great thing in miniature: another angel, a mixed worshiper, a contemplator of visible nature, and an industrious student of that which is grasped by the mind alone; an emperor of earthly things, subject to heavenly rule.”

Therefore it must be noted that, when this Father said that God made man from both, he added that the body was taken from matter previously existing; [Col. 0192B] but he did not say that the soul had previously existed, nor that it was born from some substance that existed beforehand. Rather, he said that God himself gave it life, which reason knows to be an intelligent soul and the image of God.

When the Father says that God made man an emperor on earth, bound by heavenly rule, he overturns the assertion of those who say that souls were sent into bodies for punishment [Col. 0191B]. For reigning on earth and being held under the rule of God must not be regarded as a place of punishment, but as a great benefit and gift of God.

[Col. 0192B] We also consider it necessary to say the following against those who assert pre-existence: if it were true that souls existed before bodies, they would know and remember what they had done before they came into bodies, just as after death they know and remember what they did while in bodies.

We shall demonstrate from the very words of the Gospel that the soul knows after departing from life what it has done. For our Lord and Savior Christ says in the Gospel according to Luke, in the passage concerning Lazarus and the rich man (Luke XIX):

“There was a certain rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen, and feasted splendidly every day. And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, who lay at his gate, full of sores, desiring to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table; moreover, the dogs came and licked his sores. Now it happened that the beggar died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried. And in Hades, lifting up his eyes while he was in torments, he saw Abraham from afar and Lazarus in his bosom. And he himself cried out and said: ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame.’ And Abraham said to him: ‘Son, remember that you received your good things during your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, while you are tormented. And besides all this, a great gulf has been fixed between us and you, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can they cross from there to us.’ And he said: ‘Then I ask you, father, to send him to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come to this place of torment.’”

Therefore let those who defend Origen be ashamed, even in light of the words of the holy Gospel. For if souls existed before bodies, they would know what they had done before the body, just as after their departure from life they remember what they did in the body [Col. 0194A]. This is what we have learned from the words of the holy Gospel.

That the holy Fathers too, following the divinely inspired Scriptures, condemned such teaching together with Origen, who invented it, we have already shown clearly from what they said. Nevertheless, we shall demonstrate it no less from the testimonies of the Fathers that follow. First we shall present the holy Peter, bishop and martyr of Alexandria, who bears witness to these arguments of ours.

### From the first sermon of Saint Peter, bishop and martyr of Alexandria: that the soul neither pre-existed nor, having sinned, was for that reason sent into the body

“We have set forth certain things concerning the first earthly man formed from the earth, so that it may be demonstrated that one and the same man was made at one and the same time, although he is sometimes described in particular as the inner and outer man. For although, according to the saving teaching, he who made the inner things also made the outer things, nevertheless God made them once and at the same time, that is, on the same day, when he said: ‘Let us make man according to our image and likeness.’ From this it is clear that he was not made through a conjunction, as though something else had preceded and had come together from another place. For if there had been such a conjunction, why was what had already been made described?

“And later:

“Therefore it is not to be accepted that souls sinned in heaven before bodies existed, since they did not exist even before bodies. This doctrine comes from pagan philosophy, which is foreign and alien to those who wish to live piously in Christ.”

### From the same saint’s mystagogical address to the Church, delivered when he was about to receive the crown of martyrdom

“Therefore I beseech you: be vigilant. For you are about to enter affliction again. You know the dangers endured by my father and bishop, Theonas, who raised me, at the hands of those who raged against the idols; I succeeded to his seat—would that I had succeeded also to his character! You know how great Dionysius conducted himself, hiding from place to place while Sabellius was additionally persecuting him. What more shall I say of the blessed bishops Heraclas and Demetrius? What temptations they endured from the madman Origen, when he was sowing divisions in the Church—divisions that continue to stir up trouble for him to this very day!”

Can anyone of sound judgment, then, oppose what the holy martyr and bishop of Alexandria, Peter, said against Origen? In undertaking his noble contest for Christ, he not only rejected Origen and his wicked teaching, but also testifies that the holy Fathers who preceded him endured many trials because of that man’s madness.

The holy Athanasius, who likewise was bishop of Alexandria, also said in his sermon on the life of the blessed Antony:

“How dare you mock us, who say that Christ was manifested as a man, when you, defining the soul to be mind, also say that it went astray and fell from the vault of heaven into a body?”

Let those who hear this observe that Saint Athanasius openly opposes those [Col. 0196A] who say that mind pre-existed and that the soul arose from it, having defiled itself through sin and fallen from the vault of heaven into a body.

### From the second sermon of Saint Athanasius against the Arians

“Every visible creature was made in six days. On the first day, light, which he called day; on the second, the firmament; on the third, having gathered the waters, he displayed the dry land and produced upon it various fruits; on the fourth, he made the sun and moon and the entire host of stars; on the fifth, he established the generation of the creatures that swim in the sea and of those that fly through the air; on the sixth, he made the four-footed creatures upon the earth, and finally man, who consists of a rational soul and a body.

“And his invisible things are perceived and seen from the creation of the world through the things that have been made (Romans I). Light is not the same as night, nor the sun as the moon, nor angels as thrones, nor the latter as powers. All are creatures, but each of the things that have come into being persists and remains according to its kind in its own substance, as it was made.”

Behold, Saint Athanasius too teaches that, after all the other creatures, God made man from body and an intelligent, rational soul. He did not say that the body was made after everything else, so that a pre-existing soul might enter it. Rather, he said that after all the creatures man was made, consisting of a rational soul and a body, showing that God fashioned both together, namely, the body and the soul.

Since Origen added this to his other blasphemies [Col. 0196C]—that the Lord’s soul had existed beforehand, and that God the Word had been united to it before he was incarnate from the Virgin—the holy Athanasius himself overturns this delirium in his letter to Epictetus, saying:

“Rightly will all condemn themselves who suppose that the flesh which came from Mary existed before Mary; and that God the Word possessed a human soul before that flesh, and was always in it before his coming.”

Therefore, if, according to what Saint Athanasius said, the soul of our Lord Jesus Christ, who became like us in all things except sin, did not exist before his coming in the flesh, what madness is it to say that the other human souls existed before their bodies?

Let us also hear Saint Basil in his sermon on the words, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (Homily XVI). He says:

“Take care lest the ambiguity of the expression ever deceive you. For how could human reason have been in the beginning, when man received the beginning of his generation last? Before man there were beasts; before man, domestic animals; reptiles, both terrestrial and aquatic; the birds of heaven, the stars, the sun, and the moon; plants, earth, sea, and heaven.”

Behold, the Father openly warns us not to be led astray by Origen’s fables concerning the pre-existence of souls. He teaches that human reason, that is, the soul, existed in the beginning; but he plainly declares that the origin of all God’s creatures preceded that of human beings. If all creatures therefore existed before man, how could souls have existed earlier? The Father says that everything existed not before the body, but before man, who is soul and body [Col. 0198A]. From this it is shown that both were fashioned together.

Saint Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, also says in his *Dispute concerning Man* (Chapter 28):

“It may perhaps not be foreign to the purpose of our discussion to examine what is disputed in the Churches concerning the soul and the body. For some who lived before us and composed treatises on first principles have held that souls existed beforehand, like a certain people in their own city; and that examples both of virtue and of wickedness had been set before them there. They say that the soul which remained in virtue and goodness did not undergo the encounter and conflict with the body at all; but that if it departed from participation in the good, it descended into this life and thus came to be in a body.

“Others, attending to the order of the making of man as transmitted by Moses, say that the soul is later than the body in time, since God first took dust from the earth and fashioned man, and afterward gave him life by inspiration.

“And a little later:

“Those who defend the first account and assert that souls, like an older city, existed before bodily life do not seem to me to be free from the pagan fables that arose concerning the migration of souls from one body into another. For if anyone examines the matter carefully, he will find that their reasoning necessarily comes to this. They say that one of the wise men of their sect declared that he had been a man, had put on a woman’s body, had flown with the birds, had been a little tree, and had obtained an aquatic life. In my judgment, one who asserts such things about himself is not far from the truth. For a discipline that says one soul passes through so many things is truly worthy either of the croaking chatter of frogs and jackdaws, or of the irrationality of fish, or of the insensibility of trees.

“The cause of these absurdities is that they believed souls to pre-exist. For once such a doctrine has been established as its starting point, it proceeds by consequence toward related and accompanying claims, extending its fictions to this point. For if, through vices, the mind is drawn away from a higher life and becomes human, and if it is admitted that bodily life is more subject to passions than eternal and incorporeal life, then the soul dwelling in this life, in which it has greater opportunities for sinning, must be involved in more vices and be more affected by passions.

“The passion of the human soul is likeness to irrational creatures. Therefore the soul bound to this life descends into the nature of animals; and once it has entered into vices and become involved in irrationality, it will have no limit to its progress in wickedness. For where wickedness comes to a halt, the impulse toward virtue follows; but there is no virtue in irrational creatures. It will therefore necessarily change for the worse, continually progressing toward what is worse and more shameful, always devising worse things in accordance with the nature in which it exists.

“Just as the sensible is subordinate to the rational, so from the sensible there is a fall to the insensible. Thus, when their reasoning reaches this point, it departs from the truth and, by a kind of consequence, proceeds from absurdities to absurdities. From that point their doctrine advances like a fable through things that do not cohere with one another. The consequence itself reveals the soul’s complete destruction.

“For once the soul has fallen from the higher life, it sets no limit to its wickedness; through the habit and practice of the passions it will pass from the rational to the irrational, and from there be changed into the insensibility of plants. What is lifeless follows upon the insensible, and what does not subsist follows upon the lifeless. Thus, by this chain of reasoning, the soul will finally pass altogether into non-being. It will then have no capacity to return to better things.

“Yet they bring the soul back from a shrub to man; thus they show that life in a shrub is superior to incorporeal life. It has already been shown that the soul’s progress toward worse things is therefore a progress toward lower things. But the lifeless is subordinate to insensible nature; and by consequence their doctrine’s beginning brings the soul to this point. Since, however, they do not want this, they either confine the soul within the insensible, or, if they bring it back from there to human life, they show, as has been said, that the life lived in a plant is superior to the soul’s first condition: for from the former there was a fall into wickedness, while from the latter there is a return to virtue.

“Therefore that account is shown to be without beginning and without end which asserts that souls lived separately before bodily life and were bound to bodies because of their crimes.”

Thus far Gregory of Nyssa.

Since this Father’s teaching is clear and condemns those who say that souls existed before bodies, let us also hear the holy Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, from a sermon written to certain monks who supported Origen. He says:

“Therefore, following our example and that of Anastasius [Col. 0200C], bishop of the holy Roman Church, who, distinguished by ancient struggles, was appointed leader of that most noble people, and whom the entire synod of the blessed bishops of the West follows—a synod that received and approved the judgment pronounced by the Church of Alexandria against the impious man—we beseech you to anathematize Origen and the other heretics.”

### From the same Father’s letter to the holy men who were in Scetis, concerning those who complained about the condemnation of Origen’s teaching

“Some have dared to say that Origen is a teacher of the Church. I ask you, are such men to be endured? If Origen is a teacher of the Church, the Arians and the Eunomians and the pagans have great confidence in themselves: the former blaspheming against the Son and the Spirit, and the latter being impious in the same way as they, and also mocking the resurrection of the dead.”

From these words it is clear that one who follows the holy Fathers does not doubt that those who agree with Origen follow the error of the pagans and the madness of the Arians.

Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, also says this in his letter to the monks in Phua, against those who assert that there is no resurrection of bodies:

“They say, then, that there are among you some who deny the resurrection of human bodies. This is part of our confession, which we made when we approached saving baptism. For when we profess the faith, we add that we believe also in the resurrection of the flesh. If we remove this, we do not believe that Christ rose from the dead in order to raise us together with himself; our faith is lame, and, turning aside from the royal road, we follow a crooked path.

“Such a wicked opinion comes from the madness of Origen, whom our fathers rejected and anathematized as a corrupter of the truth. For he did not think as a Christian, but, following the absurdities and trifles of the pagans, fell into error. From this came the beginning of his disease. He asserts that souls existed before bodies, and that, having been drawn away from holiness into desires and wickedness, they defected from God; for this reason they were condemned by him, bound to a body, and placed in the flesh as in a prison.”

### From the same Father’s letter written to the monks who were in Phua

“But the Church, obeying the divinely inspired Scriptures, knows neither that the soul existed before bodies nor that it sinned before them. For how could that which did not subsist have sinned? We affirm instead that the Maker of the universe fashioned the body from the earth and gave it life through an intelligent soul; and this is the constitution of man.”

And later:

“That the human soul was not condemned because of alleged former crimes and wicked deeds, nor sent down into this world, the most wise Paul makes clear when he writes: ‘For we must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil’ (1 Corinthians XV). Why, then, does he say that we must appear for the things done through the body alone, and not rather also for the things done before the body, if he knew that the soul had existed before and had sinned beforehand? But if we are brought to judgment for the things we have done in the body alone, then we have not sinned before the body; for the human soul simply did not exist before it [Col. 0202C].

“The force of the Law’s text also makes this plain. If, as the wandering Origen says, the soul received a body as a place of punishment and penalty for former deeds, why did the Law threaten death to the wicked and criminals? It would rather have been necessary for good and righteous men to meet death, so that they might be freed from their bonds and punishment, while the wicked and depraved should live, in order to be punished, with no release from their bonds.”

### From the synodical letter of the bishops of Egypt and Alexandria against Origen’s teaching

“This Origen, then, who is under discussion, stood in the midst of the true Church like the abomination of desolation. Ordained presbyter by a canonical, single, true hand, he possessed only the bare and solitary dignity of the presbyterate, just as the thief and betrayer Judas possessed the honor of apostleship. When he began to deliver blasphemous homilies, Heraclas, of blessed memory, then bishop, as a lover of truth and a cultivator and vintner of the ecclesiastical field, tore him out from the midst of the beautiful and flourishing crop, since he truly was a noxious weed.”

[Note: [Col. 0201D] The successor of Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria.]

And a little later:

“Therefore, falling from heaven to earth like a thunderbolt, just as his father the devil did, breathing great and savage anger against the truth, he sailed to the region of Palestine. Having stayed in the metropolitan city of Caesarea, once he had removed the character he had assumed and revealed himself, like a fish called by some the cuttlefish—signifying what was pleasing to him—and having vomited forth the dark and black poison of his life, he expressed it there in writing. Like a Jewish innkeeper, by the appearance and pretense of goodness he mixed the bitter with the sweet.

“For what does this man, devising evil and raging, say? ‘The soul existed before the body and pre-existed in heaven. When it sinned there, God cast it into custody, that is, sent it down into a body, for the purification and correction,’ he says, ‘of the crimes committed in heaven.’ Thus the most impious man immediately begins to fabricate and to strive against the truth.”

And a little later:

“If the soul existed previously in heaven and first sinned there, as the deranged and God-opposing Origen said, the most holy prophet ought not to have said: ‘And forming the spirit of man within him’ (Zechariah XII), but rather: ‘Plunging the spirit of man into him as into a wineskin,’ or perhaps, ‘Sending it down.’

“Since he does not say this, but says ‘forming it within him,’ he shows this most grievous wolf to be clothed externally in sheep’s clothing for the deception and destruction of others. For, as though he had come from heaven and openly knew what had been established there, the senseless man says not only that the soul pre-existed, but also that it sinned beforehand.”

Therefore it has been demonstrated both from divine Scripture and from the holy Fathers that the heretics’ imaginings concerning the pre-existence of souls agree neither with the true faith of Christians nor with sound reason.

Moreover, Origen’s madness is also shown by his assertion that heaven, the sun, the moon, the stars, and the waters above the heavens are living beings, and that some of them are rational powers. Saint Basil clearly refutes this in the third sermon of his commentaries on the *Hexaemeron*, arguing against Origen’s teaching as follows (near the end):

“We must speak to those who have separated themselves from the Church concerning the separated waters—those who, under the pretext of an anagogical sense, that is, of more elevated meanings, have resorted to allegory and assert that certain spiritual and incorporeal powers are figuratively signified by the waters. They say that the better powers remained above in the firmament, while the worse persisted below in earthly and wooded places. For this reason, they say, the waters above the heavens praise the Lord—that is, the good powers, which, because of the purity of their superior portion, are worthy to render fitting praise to the Creator. But the waters beneath the heavens are spiritual forces of wickedness, which have fallen from their natural height into the depth of evil; and they wish these to be called seas because, being turbulent and seditious and tossed by the tumult of passions, they undergo easy change and instability in their voluntary movements.

“But let us reject such arguments as confused dreams and old wives’ tales. Let us understand that the substance is water [Note: [Col. 0203D] The Greek would more coherently read, ‘let us understand water to be water.’ EDITOR.] and accept the separation made from the firmament according to the account that has been given. And whenever the waters above the heavens are summoned to glorify the common Lord of all (Psalm CXLVIII), let us not therefore suppose that they are a rational nature. For the heavens are not animated merely because they declare the glory of God (Psalm XVIII), nor is the firmament a living creature endowed with sensation because it announces the works of his hands.”

Thus far Basil.

The hearers should also note that, by using the expression, “We have a certain discourse for those who are outside the Church,” the Father speaks of Origen as expelled from the grace of God and from the holy Church of God, together with his followers. For he did not say, “We have a discourse for those who are in the Church,” but, “We have a certain discourse for those who are outside the Church.” By the word “we,” he signified the people of the Church; by “those who are outside the Church,” he designated those cast out from it.

Origen’s one and only concern was to confirm the error of the pagans and to plant weeds in the minds of the weaker. Therefore we have decided to add, as something truly laughable, this further statement of his concerning the resurrection of human beings from the dead. He asserted that, at the resurrection, human bodies would be raised in a rounded form.

O the madness and ignorance of this deranged man, this interpreter of pagan teaching! Blinded in mind and striving to mix fables into the Christian faith, he attempted to violate through insult the very hope and salvation of Christians, namely, the resurrection promised to us, showing no reverence even for the Lord’s resurrection.

For when the Lord rose from the dead and became the firstfruits of those who sleep (John XX), he appeared to the disciples and showed them the holes in his hands and feet and the wound in his side. After the resurrection he also ate, not because he needed food, but in order by this means to confirm the nature of the resurrected body.

And when the Lord ascended, the angel said to the disciples: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I).

But if, as Origen raves, the Lord’s body was rounded, how could he have displayed the holes in his hands and feet or the wound in his side [Col. 0206C]? How could he have eaten, or been recognized at all by the disciples?

And since [Note: [Col. 0205D] “In what manner” must certainly be read, so that the sense may be complete. EDITOR.] the bodies of the saints who rose after the Lord’s resurrection and appeared in the holy city (Matthew XXVII) could have been recognized by others, if they had a different form from that which they had possessed in life, is also inexplicable.

Since the impious Origen was in no way established upon the rock of faith, but had uttered such blasphemies and others far more atrocious than these, it is not surprising that, at the very moment of martyrdom, he denied Christ and worshiped the multitude of gods cultivated by the pagans, which he himself introduces.

This happened by the providence of God, so that he would not be accepted in the Church as a martyr and thereby cause harm to Christ’s flock. For if even now there are people who confess his downfall but defend his teaching, would they not have defended it as the teaching of a martyr and a Father if he had been brought to his end without offering worship to idols?

No one who holds fast to the truth falls away from God or is abandoned by him, according to what divine Scripture says: “Look, children, at the nations of human beings, and you will know that no one hoped in the Lord and was put to shame. Who has remained in his commandments and been abandoned? Or who has called upon him and he has despised him?” (Ecclesiasticus II).

But the impious Origen did not confine his blasphemies to himself. Through his own writings he transmitted his error to many others, so that the saying of the holy apostle Paul applies to him very appropriately: “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment; but some also follow afterward” (1 Timothy V). For the succession of his error, creeping into the souls of the weaker, causes the sins he himself committed at the beginning to follow him [Col. 0208A].

As though it were not enough for those who follow Origen’s opinions to embrace the impiety of the pre-existence of souls, together with his other empty talk and blasphemies concerning the holy Trinity, they add this to their distinctive error. Taking his perverse teaching as their guide and author, they say that the punishment of all impious human beings, and also of the demons, will come to an end, and that both impious human beings and demons will be restored to their former order.

When they say this, they make human beings negligent in carrying out God’s commandments. They turn them away from the narrow and constricted way and lead them into the error of the broad and spacious way [Col. 0208B].

But they plainly contradict the words of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ. For in the holy Gospel he teaches that the impious will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life (Matthew XXV). Again he says to those on the right: “Come, blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world”; but to those on the left: “Go away from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid.).

Since the Lord plainly and continually proclaims both punishment and the kingdom in the holy Gospel, it is clear that these people prefer Origen’s deliriums to the Lord’s judgments.

Their madness is also refuted by the following. If anyone, according to his foolish notions, supposes that punishment will cease, he must necessarily also establish an end to the eternal life promised to the righteous; for the word “eternal” is applied equally to both. But if both punishment and the enjoyment of glory have an end, why did our Lord Jesus Christ become incarnate? Why his crucifixion, death, burial, and resurrection? What advantage is there for those who have fought the good fight and suffered martyrdom for Christ, if demons and impious human beings are to have, through restoration, the same order as the saints?

But let this return upon the heads of those who invent such things. The words of Christ remain unshaken in the minds of the faithful and in the very reality of things.

[Col. 0208C] Those who defend Origen’s wicked opinion flee from these firm arguments. Trying to conceal their error, they seize upon certain sayings of the holy Fathers and, receiving them badly and interpreting them perversely according to their own view, adapt them to their disease. They do the same with the divine Scriptures.

We shall show from the holy Fathers themselves that their arguments are empty and futile. Saint Gregory the Theologian writes the following in his apologetic oration:

“For us, whose blessed and immortal soul is at stake, and which is destined to enter either everlasting punishment or everlasting praise because of wickedness or virtue, how important is this contest, and how much knowledge is required!”

And a little later:

“By what false defense, by what artful persuasion, by what contrivance opposing the truth, will the right be circumvented and the just judgment deceived—a judgment that places all things in the balance, all deeds, words, and thoughts, and sets wicked acts against better deeds, so that what weighs more may prevail, and the sentence may be pronounced according to the greater number, from which there is no appeal: neither a higher judge, nor a defense based on other deeds, nor oil taken either by the prudent virgins (Matthew XXV) or by those who sell it when their lamps are failing, nor the repentance of the rich man who is tormented by the flame (Luke XVI) and seeks correction for his relatives, nor a day appointed for change.

“Rather, the judgment is certain and stable, fearful and final, more equitable and just than the terror it inspires—indeed, terrifying because of its justice—when thrones are set in place, the Ancient of Days sits, the books are opened, a river of fire is drawn forth, light is before him, and darkness is prepared; when those who have done good go into the resurrection of life (John III), which is now hidden in Christ but will afterward appear with him, while those who have done evil go into the resurrection of judgment. Those who do not believe this have already been judged and condemned by the Word that judged them.

“Some are received by ineffable light and by the grace of the holy and reigning Trinity, shining more openly and purely and inserting itself wholly into the whole mind. This alone, in my judgment, is the kingdom of heaven. Others, together with other evils, are cast away from God—indeed, this comes before all else—and experience the shame and disgrace of conscience, which has no end.”

[Col. 0210B] From the book of Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, *The Rules*.

**Question:** If Scripture says, “He will be beaten with many blows, and then with few” (Luke XII), how can some people say that the punishment of those who are punished will have no end?

**Answer:** What is ambiguous and seems to have been expressed obscurely in some passages of the divinely inspired Scriptures is explained elsewhere by other statements that are acknowledged and clear. Since, then, the Lord declared, “These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew XXV); and in one place he sends us into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels; and elsewhere he names the fire of Gehenna and adds, “where their worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished” (Mark IX); and again, through the prophet, he foretold concerning certain people, “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished” (Isaiah LXVI)—since these and similar statements are repeatedly set forth by the divinely inspired Scripture, it is also one of the devil’s arts and stratagems that many people, as though they had forgotten such great and numerous sayings of the Lord, dare to imagine for themselves that the punishments of sin will eventually end.

“For if eternal punishment will one day have an end, eternal life will certainly also have an end. If in the case of life we do not understand the Gospel saying in this way, what reason is there to assign an end to eternal punishment? For the word ‘eternal’ is applied equally to both. ‘These will go away,’ he says, ‘into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life’” (Matthew XXV).

### From the same Father’s exhortatory sermon on holy baptism

“Because of the brief and temporary pleasure of sin, I am tortured by everlasting punishment; because of the pleasure of the flesh, I am consigned to eternal fire.”

### From the first letter of Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, to the monk Theodore

“Keep these things continually in your mind, as well as the river of fire: ‘For a fiery and rapid river proceeded from before him’ (Daniel XVII). No one devoted to that fire should expect an end to punishment. The wicked pleasures of this age differ in no way from shadows and dreams; before sin reaches its end, pleasure is extinguished, but the punishments endured for wicked deeds have no end.”

### From the same Father’s commentaries on the First Epistle to the Corinthians

“A serious question is set before us here, concerning matters of the greatest necessity. Everyone asks whether the fire of Gehenna will have an end. The Lord declared that it would not, when he said: ‘Their fire will not be extinguished, and their worm will not die’ (Mark IX). Paul, showing that it is everlasting, says: ‘Sinners will suffer eternal destruction’ (2 Thessalonians I).”

Therefore, since divine Scripture and the holy Fathers teach us that there is no end to the punishment of the impious and of the demons whom they worship, what restoration do those who agree with Origen imagine, when punishment has no exit?

The holy Church of Christ, just as it proclaims unending eternal life for the righteous, likewise teaches that perpetual punishments remain for the impious [Note: [Col. 0211D] The syntax and the Greek text require that *perpetua* be read. EDITOR.].

These matters, then, are sufficient here. We have judged that only a few of the many authorities from divine Scripture and the holy Fathers should be brought forward for the refutation of the impiety of the Origenists.

When, moreover, we wish to remove every scandal from the most holy Church, so that no stain may remain in it, obeying the divine Scriptures and the holy Fathers who overthrew Origen himself and his criminal and impious teaching of this kind, and rightly subjected him to anathema, we have sent this letter to Your Beatitude [Col. 0212C]. In it we urge you to convene an assembly of all the most holy bishops now residing in this imperial city and of the God-beloved superiors of the holy monasteries here, and to arrange that all of them, in writing, anathematize in every way the aforementioned impious and God-opposing Origen—also called Adamantius, who was a presbyter of the most holy Church of Alexandria—as well as his wicked and impious doctrines and all the chapters set out below. You should send copies of whatever has been done for this reason by Your Beatitude to all the other most holy bishops and superiors of the venerable monasteries, so that they too may, by their own signatures, anathematize Origen and his criminal doctrines, together with all who are identified as heretics.

[Col. 0212D] In future, however, let no bishops or superiors of monasteries be appointed unless, together with all the other heretics who are customarily anathematized in published documents—namely, Sabellius, Arius, Apollinarius, Nestorius, Eutyches, Dioscorus, Timothy the Cat, Peter Mongus, Anthimus of Trebizond, Theodosius of Alexandria, Peter who was bishop of Antioch, Peter who was bishop of Apamea, and Severus formerly of Antioch—they also anathematize the aforementioned Origen, who was afflicted with the madness of the pagans and Arians, together with his execrable and impious doctrines.

Everyone must be warned that absolutely no one should dare to defend such a heretic or his interpretations; rather, each person must hate and reject them with his whole soul and all his mind, and anathematize them as alien to Christian tradition and as bringing grievous disease and pestilence upon the souls of the simple.

We have written these same things not only to Your Holiness, but also to the most holy and most blessed pope of senior Rome and patriarch Vigilius, and to all the other most holy bishops and patriarchs—that is, of Alexandria, Theopolis, and Jerusalem—in order that they too may provide for this matter and bring it to completion.
