Since we desire all Christians to know that Origen’s writings are wholly alien to the true [Col. 0214B] faith of Christians, we have judged that a few of his many and immense blasphemies should be set down verbatim. They are as follows.

### That the Son is less than the Father, and the Spirit less than the Son

From the first book of *Periarchon*.

That God the Father, who contains all things, reaches every individual being, imparting existence to each from his own; for existence is lesser; but the true Father reaches the Son only among rational beings, for he is second after the Father. The Holy Spirit is still lesser, reaching only the saints. Thus the Father’s power is greater than that of the Son and the Holy Spirit; the Son’s is greater than that of the Holy Spirit; and, again, the power of the Holy Spirit is superior to that of the other holy beings.

[Note: [Col. 0213D] It should read, “all things,” from Book I of *Periarchon*, chapter 3. The remaining passages quoted here from Origen should likewise be corrected in the Greek, which was translated from the Latin. Hardouin. The passage is obscure and corrupt also in the Greek; perhaps it should be restored as follows: “For he himself is the one who is; but the Son, being less than the Father, reaches only rational beings.”]

### That the power of God and the Father is finite

From the second book of the same work.

For one must say that the power of God too is finite; nor should its limitation be removed under the pretext of praise. A little later:

For he made as much as he was able to grasp and possess under his hand and to contain within his providence, just as he also constructed as much matter as he was able to administer and adorn.

### From the fourth book of the same work

Let no one be offended if we assign a limit even to God’s power. For by nature it is impossible to encompass infinite things; since, once the things comprehended by God himself are finite, there must necessarily be a limit extending as far as he himself is sufficient for finite things.

### That the creature and the Son are created

From the same book.

This Son, generated by the will of the Father, who is the image of the invisible God, the radiance of his glory, and the form of his substance, the firstborn of every creature, is a creature and wisdom (Colossians I; Hebrews I; 1 Corinthians V). For Wisdom herself says: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, for his works” (Proverbs IX).

[Col. 0216A] ### That the Son is contained by the Father together with the other creatures, and that the Father is greater than the Son in all things, and is also invisible to him

From the fourth book of *Periarchon*.

If the Father contains all things, and the Son is among all things, it is clear that he too is contained. Let someone else inquire whether it is true that God knows himself equally as he is known by the Only-begotten; and he will assert that the saying, “The Father who sent me is greater than I” (John X and XIV), is true in all respects. Therefore the Father, when understanding himself, understands himself more fully, clearly, and perfectly than he is understood by the Son.

### From the first book of the same work

Thus we, having been made in the image, possess the Son, since he is the truth, the model of the beautiful formations within us [Col. 0216B]. But what we are in relation to the Son himself, he is in relation to the Father, who is the truth.

### From the same book

Thus I think that it can suitably be said even of the Savior that he is the image of God’s goodness, but not goodness itself; perhaps also that the Son is good, but not simply good. And just as he is the image of the invisible God, and therefore God, yet is not the one of whom Christ himself says, “that they may know you, the only true God” (John XVII), so he is the image of goodness, yet not so immutably as the Father.

### That, by calling the Son and the Holy Spirit creatures, he numbered them among the other creatures, and therefore called them ministering animals

From the fourth book of *Periarchon*.

[Col. 0216C] Since, then, everything whatsoever apart from the Father and God of all is created, we are led to the same conclusion. A little later:

The Hebrew said that those two seraphim in Isaiah, having six wings, crying one to another and saying, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isaiah VI), are the Only-begotten of God and the Holy Spirit. We, however, think that the statement also found in Habakkuk’s song, “You will be known in the midst of the two animals” (Habakkuk III), should be referred to Christ and the Holy Spirit.

### From the second book of *Periarchon*: that he calls the Lord a mere man

For this reason Christ also became man, attaining this by his own merit, as the prophet testifies, saying: “You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm XLIV). For it was fitting that the one who was never separated from the Only-begotten should coexist with the Only-begotten and be glorified together with him.

### That creatures are coeternal with God

From the first book of *Periarchon*.

Who would think it absurd that God should become possessed of something appropriate to him when previously he did not possess it? Since, therefore, he was never not omnipotent, these things, on account of which he is omnipotent, ought to be eternal. They were therefore always subject to his dominion, using him as their ruler.

[Col. 0218A] From the same book.

All genera and species always existed; no one would say the same about individual things differing numerically. Nevertheless, in both respects it is shown that God did not begin to create at some point, as though he had once been idle.

[Note: [Col. 0217D] As though he had once been idle. See Paganus, *Gaudentius*, chapter 25.]

### On the pre-existence of souls

From the first book of *Periarchon*.

Through their own fault, those who do not vigilantly attend to themselves undergo falls, sooner or later, either for longer or shorter periods; and the daytime judgment, for this reason, measures out a fitting recompense for the movements of each person, whether good or evil. In the future arrangement of the world, one will have an angelic rank, or the virtue of a principality, or authority over some beings, or a throne over subjects of a kingdom, or dominion over servants. Those who have not fallen very far will have the administration and assistance that we mentioned. Thus, for the most part, from among those who are under principalities, powers, thrones, and dominions, perhaps even at some time the human race will be appointed in their place in one of the worlds.

[Col. 0218B] From the same book: that if demons change for the better, they will eventually complete the human race.

I think that from among those who are subject to the worse principalities and powers and rulers of the world in the several worlds, or from among the minds of some world, those who receive benefit more quickly and wish thereafter to be changed by them may eventually complete the human race.

### On the one who, having been made from above, fell into a body

Since the world consists of the greatest variety and contains such a vast difference among rational beings, what other cause should be said to account for its existence than the various modes of falling of those who do not fall in the same way from unity? And sometimes a soul chooses an aquatic life.

From the second book of *Periarchon*.

A soul falling away from the good and inclining toward wickedness, and embracing it for a longer time, unless it draws itself back from folly, passes into animals and, because of its depravity, becomes fierce. A little later:

It chooses even a life in which it becomes brutish—an aquatic life, so to speak. And perhaps, in proportion to the greater merit of its fall into vice, it assumes aquatic bodies of such a brutish animal.

### From the same book: that there will be a complete abandonment of bodies

If at last those subject things are subjected to Christ and to God, bodies will be laid aside by all (1 Corinthians XV); and I think that there will then be a dissolution into non-being. The nature of bodies will begin again if rational beings descend once more.

### From the third book of the same treatise, on the same subject

Since God is said to become all things in all things (ibid.), just as we cannot abandon wickedness, so neither does God become all things in all things; nor does he become what the brute animals are, lest, when God becomes all things, he should also become what wickedness and brute animals are. Nor does he become what inanimate things are, lest, when God becomes all things, he should become what they themselves are. Likewise, he does not become what bodies are, since by their own nature bodies are inanimate.

### From the second book of *Periarchon*

Because it fell away and grew cold—he calls the falling away from spiritual life *psyxis* in Greek—the thing that is now called a soul, *psyche* in Greek, came to be; and it admits a return to what it was at the beginning. I think this is signified by the prophet when he says, “Return, my soul, to your rest” (Psalm CXIX), so that the whole of this may be mind. Mind, therefore, became soul, while soul, restored through right actions, becomes mind.

### From the same book, on the same subject

Just as the Savior came to save what had perished (Luke XIX), and what had perished, once it is saved, is no longer said to have perished, so the soul that he came to save, in order to save what had perished, is no longer a soul once saved, nor can what previously could be said to have perished be said to have perished. This still requires consideration. If, just as what perished was once a thing that had not perished and will someday be a time when the thing that perished will no longer exist, so too the soul did not once exist as a soul and will someday be a time when it will no longer be a soul.

[Col. 0220C] ### From the fourth book

It is necessary that the nature of bodies not pre-exist, but subsist intermittently on account of certain falls of the surrounding rational beings who need bodies; and, once perfect correction has been achieved, that these bodies again be dissolved into nothingness, so that this may always occur.

### From the first book of the same work: that the sun, moon, and stars are animate

That the soul of the sun is older than its attachment to the body has already been established by comparison with man; but I think this can also be demonstrated from the Scriptures.

### From the same book

“It is better to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians I), for this is much better. The sun too, I think, would say this very thing: “It is better to depart and be with Christ, for this is much better.” Paul, however, says, “But to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake” (ibid.); the sun would say, “But to remain in this heavenly body is more necessary for the revelation of the children of God.” The same things must be said concerning the moon and the other stars.

### From the fourth book of the same work: that Christ must also be crucified for demons, and this repeatedly throughout the ages to come

If someone should raise a question even about the Passion itself, he will certainly seem bold to inquire about it in connection with the heavenly regions. But if spiritual wickedness exists in the heavens, just as here we are not ashamed to confess that he was crucified in order to destroy what he destroyed by suffering, so there too, granting that something similar takes place, we shall fear nothing in what follows until the consummation of the whole age.

[Col. 0222A] From the same book.

Who in his right mind would suppose that the first, second, and third days, and evening and morning, existed without the sun, moon, and stars?

Since these things therefore stand thus, and all Origen’s blasphemies have been made manifest, it is fitting that the anathema against him be pronounced as follows.

### I

If anyone says or thinks that human souls pre-existed, being previously minds and holy powers, and that they became satiated with divine contemplation, turned toward what is worse, and therefore grew cold toward the love of God, and that from this they are now called *psychai* in Greek—that is, souls—and were sent down into bodies as a punishment: let him be anathema.

### II

If anyone says or thinks that the Lord’s soul existed previously and was united to God the Word before the incarnation and birth from the Virgin: let him be anathema.

### III

If anyone says or thinks that the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was first formed in the womb of the blessed Virgin and that afterward God the Word and the soul were united to it, since the soul had existed previously: let him be anathema.

### IV

If anyone says or thinks that God the Word was made similar to all the heavenly orders, and became a cherub among the cherubim and a seraph among the seraphim, and was made plainly similar to all the heavenly powers: let him be anathema.

### V

If anyone says or thinks that, at the resurrection, human bodies will be raised round, and does not confess that we shall be raised upright: let him be anathema.

### VI

If anyone says that heaven, the sun, the moon, the stars, and the waters above the heavens are certain animate and material powers [endowed with reason]: let him be anathema.

### VII

If anyone says or thinks that the Lord Christ will be crucified in the age to come for demons, just as for human beings: let him be anathema.

### VIII

If anyone says or thinks either that God’s power is finite or that he made as much as he was able to comprehend: let him be anathema.

### IX

If anyone says or thinks that the punishment of demons and impious human beings is temporary and will someday have an end, or that there will be a restoration and renewal of demons or impious human beings: let him be anathema.

Anathema also to Origen, also called Adamantus, who expounded these things, together with his wicked, execrable, and criminal teaching; and to anyone who thinks or defends them, or at any time presumes in any way whatsoever to uphold them.

[Note: [Col. 0222D] These letters belong to the synod held by Menas around A.D. 543.]

## Letter of the Emperor Justinian to the holy synod at Constantinople concerning Origen and his followers

It has been and remains our purpose to safeguard the holy and apostolic Church of God from disturbances, as is proper, and to condemn whatever in any way arises against the orthodox faith.

Since we have learned that there are certain monks in Jerusalem who follow and teach the impious errors of Pythagoras, Plato, and Origen Adamantius, we judged that care and investigation should be applied to them, lest they ultimately destroy many people through their pagan and Manichaean deceptions. For they say—to mention only a few of their many claims—that minds existed wholly without number or name; that all rational beings are one in identity of substance and activity and in power before God the Word through union and knowledge. When these minds have received, according to each one’s capacity, satiety of divine love and contemplation, they put on, through their change for the worse, either denser or subtler bodies and receive names; and from them the heavenly and ministering powers came into existence. Indeed, the sun, moon, and stars too, since they likewise belong to the unity of rational beings, began through a change for the worse to be what they are.

Those rational beings in whom the love of God grew colder are called *psychai*, that is, souls, and are placed in denser bodies such as ours. Those who reached the extreme of perversity are inserted into cold and dark bodies, and become and are called demons. Thus from the angelic state one becomes animal, and from the animal state demonic and human.

They say that only one mind among the entire unity of rational beings remained undisturbed and unmoved from divine love and contemplation, and that this was Christ, king, God and man. They further assert that bodies will wholly perish: first the Lord’s body, and then all the others will cast off their bodies; and that afterward, when all return to the truth itself, they become minds according to the being they previously possessed. Thus even the devil is to be restored, and the other demons, into that unity, together with impious and wicked human beings, with holy and God-filled men, and with the heavenly powers. In the same manner as Christ, they are to be united with God, just as they had previously been united; and Christ differs in no respect from the other rational beings, neither in substance, knowledge, power, nor activity.

For Pythagoras said that the beginning of all things is unity. Pythagoras and Plato, again, while saying that there is a multitude of incorporeal souls, also say that, if they fall into some sin, they are sent down into bodies as punishment. For this reason Plato called the body *desmos* (that is, “bond”) and *sema* (that is, “tomb”), because the soul is bound and buried in the body. Then, speaking again of the future judgment and recompense of souls, he says:

“The soul of the man who, together with the pursuit of wisdom, polluted himself with love of boys and a shameful life will pay the penalty through three thousand circuits; and thus, when he has recovered his wings after a thousand years” [Note: [Col. 0223D] Plato, in the *Phaedrus*: “after three thousand years”] “he is brought out and departs. But the others, when they depart from this life, are brought by judgment—some beneath the earth to a place of judgment, where they will undergo punishment and give an account; others are brought by judgment to a certain heavenly place and will enjoy happiness according to the merits of their life.”

[Col. 0226A] It is easy to perceive the absurdity of this opinion. Who taught him these thousand-year revolutions, and that after the passage of a thousand years each soul reaches its proper place? The things he inserts here would scarcely be appropriate even if spoken by the shameless, however licentious, much less by such a great philosopher: for he joined those who lived a life full of purity to the intemperate and lovers of boys, and said that both groups would enjoy the same blessings.

Pythagoras, Plato, Plotinus, and the other followers of these men, who unanimously confess that souls are immortal, assert that they precede bodies and that there is a multitude of souls. Those that sin are sent down into bodies, as I have said: the souls of the sluggish go into asses, those of the predatory into wolves, those of the deceitful into foxes, and those of men who enjoy the love of women into horses.

But the Church, agreeing with the divine Scriptures, affirms that the soul was created together with the body, neither preceding nor following it, contrary to what foolish Origen thought. Therefore, on account of these wicked and destructive opinions—or rather, these absurdities—we exhort you, most holy Fathers, [Col. 0225B] gathered together, to read carefully the exposition set out below, condemn each of its chapters, and, together with Origen, anathematize all who think or will think the same to the end.

[Note: [Col. 0225D] In the Bohier manuscript: “Edict of the most pious emperor Justinian containing a confession of the right faith and a refutation of the heresies opposed to the Catholic Church of God.” But on page 794 of the *Alexandrian Chronicle*, as it is called, edited by our Raderus: “A proclamation, or rather a teaching and exact exposition, concerning our Christians’ blameless and orthodox faith,” where there is also another version distinct from the following.]

# CONFESSION OF THE RIGHT FAITH OF THE EMPEROR JUSTINIAN AGAINST THE THREE CHAPTERS

[Note: [Col. 0225] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0225]

In the name of God and the Father, and of his Only-begotten Son Jesus Christ our Lord, and of the Holy Spirit.

The Emperor Caesar, Christ-loving Justinian, Alamannic, Gothic, Frankish, Germanic, Antic, Alanic, Vandalic, African, pious, fortunate, glorious, victorious, triumphant, ever-revered, Augustus, to the entire body of the catholic and apostolic Church.

[Col. 0225C]

Knowing that nothing so heals the benevolent God as for all Christians to hold one and the same belief concerning the right and undefiled faith, and that there be no schisms in the holy Church of God, we have considered it necessary, removing every pretext for those who are scandalized by or scandalize the confession of the right faith proclaimed in the holy Church of God, to make that faith manifest through the present edict. Our purpose is both that those who confess the right faith may preserve it securely and that those who contend against it, upon learning the truth, may hasten to be united with the holy Church of God.

[Col. 0225D] We therefore confess that we believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: a consubstantial Trinity, one Godhead—that is, one nature, substance, power, and authority—in three hypostases, or persons, whom we glorify, into whom we have been baptized, in whom we have believed, and to whom we have been committed. We distinguish their individual properties, but unite the Godhead.

For we worship a unity in Trinity and a Trinity in unity, possessing a paradoxical division and union: unity in respect of the account of substance, that is, of the Godhead; Trinity in respect of the properties, that is, the hypostases or persons. It is divided indivisibly, so to speak, and joined while remaining distinct: for the Godhead is one in three, and the three are one, in whom the Godhead exists—or, to speak more precisely, each of those who is the Godhead is God, whenever the mind alone considers the inseparable separately.

The three, understood together, are God by the sameness of their activity and nature [perhaps: “power”]. Since one must both confess one God and proclaim three hypostases—that is, three persons—each together with its property, we neither make the union a confusion [perhaps: “confessing”], as Sabellius did when he said that the Trinity is one three-named person, the same Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, nor, by dividing the properties, estrange the Son and the Holy Spirit from the substance of God the Father, as in the madness of Arius, cutting the Godhead into three different substances.

Therefore there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things; one Only-begotten Son, through whom are all things; and one Holy Spirit, in whom are all things.

[Col. 0227C] We confess also that the Only-begotten Son of God, God the Word, was begotten timelessly and before the ages from the Father, not made; that in the last days he descended from the heavens for us and for our salvation; that he was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and from the holy, glorious, God-bearing and ever-virgin Mary; and that he was born from her. He is the one Lord Jesus Christ, one of the Holy Trinity, consubstantial with God the Father according to his Godhead, and the same consubstantial with us according to his humanity—passible in the flesh, but impassible in the Godhead.

For it is not someone other than God the Word who accepted suffering and death; rather, the same impassible and eternal Word of God, accepting the birth of human flesh, fulfilled all things. Therefore we do not know one God the Word who performed miracles and another Christ who suffered, but we confess one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, the Word of God incarnate and made man, whose miracles and sufferings were voluntarily endured by him in the flesh.

No human being gave himself for us; rather, God the Word himself gave his own body for us, so that our faith and hope might not be in a human being, but that we might place our faith in God the Word himself.

In confessing him as God, therefore, we do not deny that he is also man; and in calling him man, we do not deny that he is also God. For if he were God alone, how did he suffer? How was he crucified and die? These things are alien to God. But if he were man alone, how did he conquer through suffering? How did he save? How did he give life? These things are beyond man. Now, however, the same one suffers, saves, and conquers through suffering: the same one is God and the same one is man, the whole of both [Col. 0229A], each one being one in such a way as to be alone.

Therefore, when we say that one composite Christ was formed from each nature—that is, from divinity and humanity—we do not introduce confusion into the union. And while recognizing in each nature, that is, in divinity and humanity, the one Lord Jesus Christ, the Word of God incarnate and made man, we do not impose on his one hypostasis any division or separation into parts [variant: “in accordance with the parts”]. Rather, we indicate the difference between the natures from which he was composed, a difference not abolished by the union, since each nature exists in him.

For when composition is acknowledged, the parts exist in the whole, and the whole is known in the parts. The divine nature was not changed into the human, nor was the human nature transformed into the divine. Rather, since each is understood and exists within the boundary and definition of its own nature, we say that the union was accomplished according to hypostasis.

The union according to hypostasis signifies that God the Word—that is, the one hypostasis among the three hypostases of the Godhead—was not united to a pre-existing man. Rather, in the womb of the holy Virgin, he fashioned for himself from her, within his own hypostasis, flesh endowed with a rational and intellectual soul, which is human nature.

The divine apostle also teaches us this union according to hypostasis of God the Word with the flesh when he says: “Who, existing in the form of God, did not regard being equal with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.”

By saying, “who, existing in the form of God,” he showed that the hypostasis of the Word existed in the substance of God. By saying, “he took the form of a servant,” he signified that God the Word was united with the substance of man, not with a hypostasis or person. For he did not say, “He took the one existing in the form of a servant,” lest he show that the Word was united to a pre-existing man, as Theodore and Nestorius impiously blasphemed when they called the union relational.

Following the divine Scripture and the holy Fathers, we confess that God the Word became flesh, which means that he united human nature to himself according to hypostasis. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ is one, possessing in himself the perfection of the divine nature and the perfection of human nature. He is Only-begotten and Word, as begotten from God the Father, and the same one is firstborn among many brethren when he became man; for the Son of God became the Son of man.

Remaining what he was, he did not change what he became. Therefore we confess two births of the same Only-begotten Word of God: one before the ages, bodiless, from the Father; the other in the last days, when the same one was incarnate and became man from the holy, glorious, God-bearing and ever-virgin Mary.

For he who shone forth from the Father beyond conception rose from his mother beyond explanation. Being true God, he truly became man. Therefore we confess that holy, glorious, and ever-virgin Mary is properly and truly God-bearer—not because the Word of God received his beginning from her, but because, in the last days, the Only-begotten Word of God, who existed before the ages, became incarnate from her without change and became man. Invisible among his own things, he became visible among the things that are ours; and although he was God impassible, the immortal did not disdain to become passible as man and to submit to the laws of death.

The holy apostles proclaimed that this one, born at Bethlehem from the seed of David according to the flesh, made like human beings, and crucified for us human beings under Pontius Pilate, is himself God, himself man, himself Son of man, himself from heaven, himself from earth, himself impassible, himself passible.

For the Word who was ineffably, indescribably, incomprehensibly, and eternally begotten from the Father above is himself born in time below from the Virgin Mary, so that those previously born below might be born a second time above—that is, from God. Thus he alone has a mother on earth, while we have only a Father in heaven.

For, taking Adam, the mortal father of human beings, he gave human beings his own immortal Father, according to the saying: “He gave them authority to become children of God.” Therefore the Son of God tastes death in the flesh because of his fleshly father, so that the sons of man might share in his life because of their Father according to the Spirit, God.

He, then, is Son of God by nature, whereas we are so by grace. Again, he became son of Adam according to the economy and for our sake, while we are sons of Adam by nature. God is his Father by nature, while ours is so by grace. God became his God according to the economy, because he is man; but by nature he is our master and God.

For this reason the Word, who is the Son of God the Father, united with flesh became flesh, so that human beings, united with the Spirit, might become one spirit. Thus the true Son of God bears us all, so that we all might bear one God.

Even after the incarnation, the Only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, remains one of the Holy Trinity, composite from both natures.

We confess Christ as composite, following the teaching of the holy Fathers. In the mystery concerning Christ, union by composition excludes confusion and division; it preserves the property of each nature, while showing one hypostasis—that is, the person of God the Word—together with the flesh. The same one is perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity, not as two hypostases or persons, but recognized in the divine and human nature, so that he is one in both respects: perfect God and perfect man, the same our Lord Jesus Christ, one of the Holy Trinity, glorified together with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

For the Holy Trinity did not admit the addition of a fourth person when one of the Holy Trinity, God the Word, became incarnate.

We preserve this good deposit that we received from the holy Fathers, in which we live and conduct ourselves, and which we hope to take with us when we depart: the confession of the Father, Christ the Son of the living God, and the Holy Spirit.

While confessing these things, together with the other teachings of the holy Cyril concerning the right faith, and accepting his statement, “one incarnate nature of God the Word,” we confess that one Christ was constituted from the divine and human nature, and not one nature, as some wrongly attempt to understand the expression.

Indeed, the Father himself, whenever he said “one incarnate nature of the Word,” used the word “nature” in place of “hypostasis.” In the passages where he used this expression, he generally added immediately afterward either “Son,” “Word,” or “Only-begotten”—terms that signify not a nature but a hypostasis, that is, a person.

The hypostasis of the Word, having become incarnate, constituted not one nature but one composite Christ, the same God and man. Yet, while confessing Christ as God and man, it is impious to speak of one nature or substance in him. For it is impossible for our Lord Jesus Christ, according to one and the same nature or substance, both to exist before the ages and to exist in time, or both to be impassible and passible. These things we rightly confess of his one hypostasis or person.

From the very statements of the same holy Cyril we shall demonstrate his clearest teaching concerning this expression. In his first letter to Succensus, after saying “one incarnate nature of the Word,” he immediately added:

“Accordingly, insofar as concerns conception—indeed, merely seeing with the eyes of the soul how the Only-begotten became man—we say that there are two natures which have been united, but one Son and Christ and Lord, the Word of God the Father, who became man and was made flesh.”

By these words the Father, wishing to set forth the manner of the incarnation and preserving what is indivisible and without confusion, showed the number of the natures that came together and proclaimed one Christ—not one nature of divinity and flesh.

In his second letter to the same Succensus, teaching similar things, he writes:

“For if, having said one nature of the Word, we had remained silent and had not added ‘incarnate,’ but had as it were placed the economy outside it, their question might perhaps have appeared plausible when they pretended to ask: Where is the perfection in humanity? Or how has our substance subsisted? But since the perfection in humanity and the manifestation of our substance have been introduced by saying ‘incarnate,’ let them cease, having set up a reed-staff for themselves.”

For it was appropriate to reproach the person who excluded the economy and denied the incarnation for depriving the Son of perfect humanity. But if, as I said, by saying that he became incarnate there is a clear and unambiguous confession that he became man, nothing further prevents us from understanding that Christ, being one and the only Son, is the same God and man, perfect in divinity and likewise perfect in humanity. Your Perfection has set forth the discourse concerning the saving Passion most correctly and wisely, without asserting that the Only-begotten Son of God himself, insofar as he is conceived and exists as God, suffered in his own nature the things of the body, but rather that he suffered in his earthly nature.

For both things must necessarily be preserved in the one and truly existing Son: that he does not suffer divinely, and that he is said to suffer humanly. His own flesh suffered.”

In the thirteenth chapter of the *Scholia*, the same holy Cyril, likewise rejecting both those who introduce two sons and those who say that there is one nature of the divinity and flesh of Christ, writes:

“We must not, therefore, divide the one Lord Jesus Christ into a man separately and a God separately, but we say that Jesus Christ is one and the same Lord, recognizing the difference of the natures and preserving them without confusion toward one another.”

If, then, as the holy Cyril teaches, our Lord Jesus Christ is one, perfect in divinity and the same one perfect in humanity, and he did not suffer in the divine nature but in the earthly nature; and if he recognizes the difference of the natures and preserves them without confusion toward one another in one hypostasis, it is clear that the Father says that the same one is recognized in the divine and human nature, and that each nature exists in him, from which he was composed.

No one could be so insane as rightly to think that those who say there is one nature or substance of the flesh and divinity of Christ are correct, making the same nature both divine and earthly, both passible and impassible.

Since some also attempt from another direction to establish that there is one nature of the divinity and humanity of Christ, presenting the example of man and saying that, just as man, composed of soul and body of different kinds, is called one nature, so we too ought to say that Christ, composed of two natures—divinity and humanity—has one nature, we shall answer them as follows.

Although man is composed of different things, namely soul and body, he is called one nature because this is predicated generally of all hypostases or persons belonging to the same species. Although each hypostasis or person—for example, Peter and Paul—is separated from the other by its individual characteristics, they are nevertheless not divided in nature; both are human beings.

Again, neither soul without body nor body without soul is a human being or humanity; rather, humanity was created from non-being into being from soul and body. Every creature, although composed of different things, is nevertheless said to possess one nature, according to which it was created by God.

Christ, however, is not so. He does not signify one nature or substance predicated generally of many hypostases or persons, as “man” does. For if that were the case, many Christs would be found, of whom the common nature would be predicated; and this is impious even to say.

Nor was Christ created from the beginning out of divinity and humanity, as man is from soul and body, so that this might be the nature of Christ. Rather, the Word, being God before the ages, of the same nature or substance as the Father, and Creator of all, united human nature to himself according to hypostasis in the last days and became man without ceasing to be God.

Christ, therefore, is one hypostasis or person, and he possesses in himself the perfection both of the divine and uncreated nature and of the human and created nature.

How, then, when two natures—uncreated and created—are recognized in him, can one nature or substance be spoken of in his case? Although Christ is one hypostasis or person, the same one is consubstantial with God the Father and consubstantial with us, but not according to one and the same nature or substance.

If Christ had been one nature or substance, then either, being without flesh, he would be consubstantial only with God the Father [Latin: “Father,” thus read in the Alexandrian Chronicle] and the Spirit, since the Godhead has one substance or nature; or, being a mere man, he would be consubstantial only with us, since humanity has one nature; or the two natures, being changed, would have produced something of another kind.

According to their view, Christ would have been constituted contrary to the things that came together: he would have remained neither God nor become man, and therefore would be consubstantial neither with the Father nor with us. Such a view is filled with every kind of impiety.

We say these things without being unaware that some of the holy Fathers also used the example of man in the mystery concerning Christ. They did so to show that, just as one man is constituted from soul and body and not two men, so Christ, composed of divinity and humanity, is one and is not divided into two Christs or two sons.

These people, however, use the example of man in order to introduce one nature or substance of the divinity and humanity of Christ, which we have shown to be alien to piety.

When they are refuted on this point, because they fashion within themselves one nature or substance of divinity and flesh contrary to the orthodox teaching of the Fathers, they turn to other arguments, saying that one ought not to speak of a number of natures in Christ, since number introduces division.

Let them know, then, that when number is predicated of different persons or hypostases, it indicates a division of the things themselves into parts, as with two or more human beings. But when it is predicated of united things, it possesses division only in word and thought, not in the things themselves, as in the case of one human hypostasis composed of soul and body.

Here too two natures are contemplated: one belonging to the soul and another to the body. Yet the human being is not thereby divided into two human beings; we know one human being and one hypostasis.

Thus, in the mystery of Christ, once the union has taken place, although the united things are contemplated as different, the things from which our Lord Jesus Christ was composed are not actually and separately divided from one another. Nevertheless, because we understand the difference and wish to signify it, we employ number and say that there are two natures in Christ. The one Christ is not thereby divided into two Christs or two sons.

The holy Gregory the Theologian bears witness to what we have said in his first discourse to Cledonius, writing:

“If anyone introduces two sons, one from God the Father and a second from the mother, but not one and the same, let him fall from the sonship promised to those who rightly believe. For the natures are two, God and man, since soul and body are also two; but the sons are not two, nor are the gods two. Nor are there two human beings here either, although Paul called the inner and outer parts of man by these names. And, to speak briefly, the things from which the Savior consists are one thing and another, if the invisible is not the same as the visible and the timeless is not the same as what is subject to time; but he is not one person and another—God forbid.”

[Col. 0239A] Through these words the holy Gregory clearly teaches that, in the mystery concerning Christ, the person who speaks of number with reference to persons is condemned as impious; but the person who applies number to the natures from which the one Christ was composed confesses correctly. In this way he signifies the difference of the natures that came together, without in any way making a division into separate parts.

Just as the nature of the soul is different from that of the body, yet one man is constituted by composition and not two, so in Christ, although two natures are contemplated—one of divinity and the other of humanity—two Christs or two sons are not thereby introduced.

Therefore, those who refuse to speak of the number of the natures in Christ in the manner described plainly deny their difference and introduce confusion into the economy. If they confess the difference, they must necessarily also speak of the number of the natures that came together without confusion into one hypostasis. For wherever difference is preserved, number necessarily follows it.

To confirm what we have said by the testimony of the holy Fathers, we shall show that they say that, in the mystery concerning Christ, expressions are distinguished according to the difference of the natures—divinity and humanity—from which he was composed, and that number is used in this connection, but that they do not actually divide the natures separately into two hypostases or two persons.

The holy Cyril says in his interpretation of Leviticus:

“Consider again clearly in these things the mystery of our Savior and the purification through holy baptism. For he commands two living and clean birds to be taken, so that through the birds you may understand the heavenly man and God together, divided into two natures insofar as concerns the proper account of each, for the Word who shone forth from God the Father in flesh from a woman was there—yet not divided; for Christ is one from both.”

Again, the same holy Cyril writes in his second letter to Succensus:

“But they failed to understand that the things which are accustomed to be divided only in contemplation do not necessarily depart from one another altogether and individually into a separate identity.”

The holy Basil, in the fourth discourse against Eunomius, explaining “The Lord created me” and “He begets me before all the hills,” writes:

“We must therefore understand ‘he begot’ of the Son of God, and ‘he created’ of the one who took the form of a servant. In all these things we do not speak of two—God separately and man separately—for he was one; rather, we consider each nature according to conception.”

The holy Gregory the Theologian, in his second discourse on the Son, teaching how we must distinguish the natures in our Lord Jesus Christ according to conception, writes:

“When the natures are separated in conception, the names are separated with them. Hear Paul saying: ‘The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory’—God of Christ, but Father of glory. For although the whole is one, it is not so by nature, but by their coming together.”

The holy Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, in the fourth discourse against Eunomius, teaching us the same things, writes:

“And lest anyone should attribute the suffering on the cross to the incorruptible nature, he corrects such an error more clearly through other expressions, calling him mediator of God and human beings, God and man himself, so that, when two things are said concerning one, what is appropriate to each may be understood: impassibility concerning the divine, and the economy of suffering concerning the human.

When conception divides what has been united through philanthropy but is distinguished in speech, whenever it proclaims what is exalted and surpasses every understanding, it uses the higher names, calling him in all things God, great God, the power of God, wisdom, and the like. But whenever it describes in speech the experience of sufferings necessarily assumed for the sake of our weakness, it names the whole from our side, calling him man—not making the one signified common with the remaining nature by the expression, but preserving piety concerning each.”

Since these things have been demonstrated through the teaching of the Fathers, let those who make the number of the natures in Christ a pretext for their own error, and who attempt by denying the difference through this means to introduce confusion, cease.

For how could number not be necessary, when the Fathers used it to signify the difference of the natures united into one hypostasis, and not to indicate their division into separate parts?

Since it has been demonstrated from every side that it is impious to say that there is one nature or substance of the divinity and flesh of Christ, we shall also say this: just because we call the divinity and humanity of Christ one hypostasis, it is not thereby possible to call Christ one nature, since nature and hypostasis are not the same.

All the holy Fathers unanimously teach us that nature, substance, and form are one thing, and hypostasis or person another; nature, substance, and form signify what is common, while hypostasis or person signifies what is particular.

If some say that, just as Christ is called one composite hypostasis, so one ought also to say one composite nature, we shall demonstrate that this too is alien to piety.

When we speak of one nature or substance of the Godhead, we glorify three hypostases in it, recognizing the same nature or substance in each hypostasis. In accordance with piety, we say that from the three hypostases one hypostasis—the hypostasis of the Word—has been composed together with the flesh.

No one has ever dared to say in the catholic Church that, just as there are three hypostases, so there are three natures of the Holy Trinity, so that one could say that one nature was composed from the three natures together with flesh. Arius alone dared to say, as a blasphemer, that there are three natures in the Holy Trinity, and he was condemned.

Therefore, according to right reasoning, we speak of the union of two natures and one hypostasis. The Son of God, being other than the Father according to hypostasis but of the same nature as the Father, fashioned flesh for himself in his own hypostasis, endowed with a rational and intellectual soul. This signifies that the Word of God was united to human nature, and not to the hypostasis or person of some particular man.

The Word of God, therefore, even when incarnate, is one hypostasis recognized in each nature: in the divine nature, in which he existed according to the words, “who existed in the form of God,” and in the human nature, according to the words, “having become in the likeness of human beings.”

For this reason one may piously speak of one composite hypostasis of God the Word rather than of one composite nature. When nature is spoken of simply in itself, without the addition of some particular person, it signifies something indefinite and without hypostasis; but what is indefinite cannot be composed with anything.

If anyone, even after these arguments, should look only toward contentiousness and attempt to oppose them, saying that, according to the definition given of nature, Christ’s human nature must have its own hypostasis or proper person, it is obvious that such a person says that the Word was united to a pre-existing man and that the union was relational.

For it is impossible for a union according to hypostasis to take place between two hypostases or persons. Thus the person who says these things, striving to empty the power of God through words of human wisdom, does not understand the great mystery of piety, which is believed in the heart for righteousness and confessed with the mouth for salvation.

The human nature of Christ is never spoken of simply, nor did it ever possess its own hypostasis or person; rather, it received the beginning of its existence in the hypostasis of the Word.

Therefore we confess that God the Word himself became man without change, and that he did not come into some man. Since the same God the Word became incarnate, the birth from the Virgin belongs to him; and for this reason the holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mary is God-bearer.

For this reason, both before and after the incarnation of God the Word, we speak of three hypostases—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—and the Holy Trinity did not receive the addition of a fourth hypostasis or person.

All these things refute those who say that there were two natures before the union, since they say that a man pre-existed and was thus united to God the Word, according to the madness of Theodore and Nestorius, the impious. Those who say that after the union one ought not to speak of two natures in Christ, but of one nature, introduce confusion and phantasy [“they introduce”], according to Apollinarius and Eutyches, the impious.

But enough of them.

[Col. 0243D] The holy Fathers, contemplating after the incarnation of the Word the things from which Christ consists, and recognizing that the natures remained without confusion, have rightly said that there are two natures in Christ, the divine and the human. For there were not two natures of the Lord before the incarnation, nor did the two become one after the incarnation, even though they are recognized in one hypostasis.

[Col. 0243D] Having been taught these things both from the divine Scriptures and from the teaching of the Fathers, we have rightly written them for the overthrow of those who confuse and divide the mystery of the divine economy. By making clear the things from which Christ exists and in which he is recognized, we do not introduce confusion or division into the divine economy.

Indeed, while presenting praise and the account of the union, we confess and worship together with the Father and the Holy Spirit one Christ, Son and Lord, the Word of God incarnate and made man.

Since these things are confessed by the catholic Church of God, we wish all Christians to know that, just as we have one God and Lord, so also we have one faith. For there is one rule of faith: to confess and rightly glorify the Father, Christ the Son of God, and the Holy Spirit.

We preserve this confession, into which we too were baptized. It was given by the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ to his holy disciples and apostles, and was proclaimed by them throughout the whole world.

The three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea against Arius, condemning him together with his impiety, handed down this same confession—or creed and [Latin: “holy”] lesson of faith—to the holy Church of God. After them, the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers assembled at Constantinople against Macedonius the fighter against the Spirit and Magnus the Apollinarian, condemning them together with their impiety, and following in all things the same holy creed handed down by the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers, clarified the doctrines concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit.

Furthermore, the holy Fathers previously assembled at Ephesus against the impious Nestorius, and the holy Fathers assembled at Chalcedon against the impious Eutyches, following in all things the holy creed, or lesson of faith, condemned the aforementioned heretics together with their impiety, as well as those who thought or think like them.

In addition, they anathematized those who hand down another rule of faith, creed, or lesson to those approaching holy baptism or returning from any heresy, contrary to that handed down, as has been said, by the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers and clarified by the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers.

Since these things stand thus, we have judged it appropriate to append chapters containing both a brief confession of the right faith and the condemnation of the heretics.

If anyone does not confess the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, a consubstantial Trinity, one Godhead—that is, one nature and substance—and one power and authority worshiped in three hypostases or persons, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not confess that God the Word, begotten before the ages and timelessly from the Father, descended from the heavens in the last days [and—Latin addition—became incarnate] from the holy [glorious—Latin addition] God-bearing and ever-virgin Mary, and became man, being born from her, and therefore that the same God the Word has two births—one bodiless before the ages and the other according to the flesh in the last days—let him be anathema.

If anyone says that the God Word who performed miracles is one and Christ who suffered another; or says that God the Word was with Christ, who was born from a woman, or was in him as one person in another, but does not confess one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, the Word of God incarnate and made man, whose miracles and sufferings were voluntarily endured by him in the flesh, let him be anathema.

If anyone says that the union of God the Word with man took place by grace, activity, merit, equality of honor, authority, reference, relation, or power; or according to homonymy, by which the Nestorians, calling both God the Word “Christ” and the separate man “Christ,” say that there is one Christ merely in name; or if anyone says that the union took place according to good pleasure, as the heretic Theodore says in these very words—that God the Word was pleased with the man because it seemed good and beautiful to him concerning him—but does not confess that the union of God the Word with flesh endowed with a rational and intellectual soul took place according to hypostasis, and therefore that his hypostasis is one and composite, let him be anathema.

If anyone calls the holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mary God-bearer only by reference or improperly, or calls her man-bearer or Christ-bearer, as though Christ were not God, and does not confess that she is properly and truly God-bearer because God the Word, begotten before the ages from the Father, became incarnate and was born from her in the last days, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not confess that our Lord Jesus Christ, crucified in the flesh, is true God, Lord of glory, and one of the Holy Trinity, let him be anathema.

If anyone, while speaking of two natures, does not confess the one Lord Jesus Christ, the Word of God incarnate, as existing in divinity and humanity, and does not use the expression to signify the difference of the natures from which he was composed, but uses it to introduce a separate division in the mystery concerning Christ, as though the natures were separate and possessed their own hypostases, as Theodore and Nestorius blaspheme, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0247D] If anyone, while confessing the number of the natures in the one Lord Jesus Christ—that is, the incarnate Word of God—does not understand their difference, from which he was composed, in contemplation, as this difference was not abolished by the union, but uses number to indicate a separate division, let him be anathema.

If anyone, saying “one incarnate nature of God the Word,” does not understand it in the sense that one Christ was constituted from the divine and human nature, consubstantial with the Father according to divinity and the same one consubstantial with us according to humanity, but understands it to mean that one nature or substance of the divinity and flesh of Christ was constituted, according to the false belief of Apollinarius and Eutyches, let him be anathema.

For the catholic Church equally rejects and anathematizes those who divide or cut apart, and those who confuse, the mystery of Christ’s divine economy.

If anyone does not anathematize Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Apollinarius, Nestorius, Eutyches, and those who think or thought things similar to theirs, let him be anathema.

If anyone supports Theodore of Mopsuestia, who said that the God Word is one and Christ another, the latter troubled by the passions of the soul and the desires of the flesh, improved through progress in works, baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, receiving through baptism the grace of the Holy Spirit and being deemed worthy of adoption, worshiped as the image of the king in equal honor in the person of God the Word, and becoming unchangeable in his thoughts and entirely sinless after the resurrection; and who further said that the union of God the Word with Christ took place in the manner in which the Apostle spoke of a man and woman: “The two shall become one flesh”; and who, in addition to his countless other blasphemies, dared to say that, after the resurrection, when the Lord breathed on the disciples and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” he did not give them the Holy Spirit but merely breathed symbolically; and who said that Thomas’s confession, made after touching the Lord’s hands and side following the resurrection—“My Lord and my God”—was not spoken by Thomas concerning Christ, since he says that the Lord is not God, but that Thomas, astonished at the wonder of the resurrection, praised the God who raised Christ; and, worse still, who in his alleged interpretation of the Acts of the Apostles compared Christ with Plato, Mani, Epicurus, and Marcion, saying that just as each of them, having discovered his own doctrine, caused those who became his disciples to be called Platonists, Manichaeans, Epicureans, and Marcionites, so likewise, when Christ discovered his doctrine, Christians were called from him—if anyone therefore supports Theodore, who blasphemed in these ways, but does not anathematize him, his writings, and those who think or thought like him, let him be anathema.

If anyone supports the writings of Theodoret that he published on behalf of the heretic Nestorius and against the right faith, the First Holy Council at Ephesus, the holy Cyril, and his twelve chapters, writings in which he impiously calls the union of God the Word with some man relational; and in which, blaspheming concerning him, he says that Thomas touched the one who had risen and worshiped the one who raised him; and for this reason calls the teachers of the Church impious, those who confess the union of God the Word with the flesh according to hypostasis; and, in addition, denies that the holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mary is God-bearer—if anyone therefore praises the aforementioned writings of Theodoret but does not anathematize them, let him be anathema. For these blasphemies he was expelled from the episcopate, and afterward, at the holy Council of Chalcedon, he was compelled to do the opposite of everything contained in those writings and to confess the right faith.

If anyone supports the impious letter said to have been written by Ibas to Maris the Persian heretic, a letter that denies that God the Word became man and says that it was not God the Word, incarnate and born from the Virgin, who was born from her, but a mere man born from her, whom it calls a temple, as though God the Word were one and the man another; and which moreover insults the First Council at Ephesus, saying that it condemned Nestorius without investigation or judgment, calls the holy Cyril a heretic and his twelve chapters impious, and praises and defends Nestorius and Theodore together with their impious writings—if anyone therefore defends that impious letter or says that it, or any part of it, is orthodox, but does not anathematize it, let him be anathema.

Since that letter was rightly anathematized on account of the blasphemies contained in it, those who impiously think like Nestorius or Theodore attempt to say that it was accepted by the holy Council of Chalcedon. In saying this they slander the holy council, while under its pretext striving to free Theodore, Nestorius, and the impious letter from the condemnation they deserve—the letter concerning which Ibas, although frequently accused, did not dare to claim it as his own because of the blasphemies it contained.

We shall demonstrate these things from the various proceedings held concerning the matter. In the proceedings conducted at Tyre by Photius and Eustathius, the aforementioned Ibas, being accused concerning his insults against the holy Cyril, openly declared that after the union of the Easterners with the holy Cyril he had said nothing insulting concerning him. But the letter filled with the blasphemies mentioned, for which Ibas was accused, contains many insults against the holy Cyril and thereby shows that it was composed after the union with the Easterners; from this it is clear that Ibas repudiated it.

Therefore the aforementioned Photius and Eustathius formally set down, on the basis of the accusers’ report, that Ibas had done everything contrary to the letter, as the judgment issued by them concerning the matter demonstrates. Since Ibas did not fulfill what they had judged, he was expelled from the episcopate because of the blasphemies of the aforementioned letter, and Nonnus was ordained in his place; Nonnus also took his seat at the holy Council of Chalcedon.

When the aforementioned Ibas was accused at Chalcedon of the same things, after the impious letter had been read he did not dare to claim it as his own, but immediately added in its very words: “I am alien to the things brought against me.”

Therefore the holy council, not being satisfied with Ibas’s denial concerning the impious letter, compelled him to do the opposite of what it contained: namely, to confess the right faith that it rejected, to accept the First Holy Council at Ephesus, to acknowledge the holy Cyril as father and teacher, and to anathematize Nestorius and his impious doctrine. The impious letter praises and defends these very things.

If Ibas himself, although accused in various ways concerning the impious letter, did not dare to claim it as his own, and if the holy Council of Chalcedon compelled him to do everything contrary to it, how could that same holy council have accepted the letter and fallen under the judgment of the impiety contained in it, from which it strove to free Ibas?

Since the heretics, surpassing all the blasphemies contained in the letter, bring forward only this one statement from it to deceive the simple—namely, “two natures, one power, one person”—we shall show that even in this the author mixed his own impiety into the statement.

For what person would speak of two natures and one person if he denied that God the Word became incarnate and was born from the holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mary? It is clear that he assigns a separate person to each nature, as Theodore and Nestorius set forth in their own blasphemous writings, which the author of the letter also defends together with their impiety.

They plainly speak of two persons, one of God the Word and the other of Christ, whom they call a mere man. They say that, through a relational conjunction and the same rank and honor, one person appears.

Moreover, by saying that there is one power or dominion of the two natures, the author of the letter clearly follows the aforementioned heretics here also: Theodore, in the various impious discourses he published concerning the incarnation, and Nestorius in many writings, especially in the letter written to Alexander, the heretic bishop of Hierapolis, in which he says that of the two natures there is one authority, one power or dominion, and one person according to one rank and the same honor.

From these things it is demonstrated that the author of the letter, in accordance with their false doctrine, used the designation of natures in place of persons. For “one authority,” “one power” or “dominion,” “one rank,” and “the same honor” are not predicated of different natures but of different persons of the same substance, as we confess concerning the Holy Trinity.

Therefore the holy Fathers anathematized those who say that God the Word was united to Christ—a mere man, as the followers of Theodore and Nestorius call him—by authority, power or dominion, rank, or equality, but do not confess that the union of the Word with flesh endowed with a rational and intellectual soul took place according to hypostasis.

These things would be sufficient to refute the impiety of those who defend that foul letter. Nevertheless, near the end of the same letter its author also reveals his own false doctrine by saying that one must believe in the temple and in the one dwelling in the temple, thereby plainly introducing two persons.

The author of the letter learned this impiety from Theodore and Nestorius. The catholic Church, however, condemning such false doctrine, hands down that one must confess and believe not in the temple and in the one dwelling in the temple, but in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Word of God incarnate and made man.

Nor is it surprising that the author of that impious letter used the terminology of the natures. It is customary for heretics, to deceive the simple, to employ expressions used piously by the orthodox and to transfer their pious meaning and interpretation to their own impiety. The same expressions, when rightly interpreted and understood, belong to piety; but when wrongly interpreted and uttered by heretics, they contain impiety.

Thus, although Nestorius said “two natures and one person,” because he did not confess their union according to hypostasis, the First Holy Council at Ephesus, presided over by the holy Celestine and Cyril, did not accept him but condemned him.

Following the teaching of the holy Fathers in all things, we have demonstrated above with greater clarity both the union of the two natures from which our one Lord Jesus Christ, one of the Holy Trinity, God the Word incarnate, was composed, and the fact that their difference was not abolished by the union.

What we have said would be enough to convince those who do not wish to be contentious. But since, having once turned toward impiety, they attempt further arguments, we must also show that their pretexts are futile.

They say that the impious letter ought not to be blamed because it is found in certain books. But if anyone accepts this according to their folly, he must also accept Eutyches and Nestorius, since many things concerning them appear in the records of the council. No sensible person will pay attention to what they say.

For statements concerning heretics brought forward in councils and becoming part of the records are not received in order to free them, but for their refutation and for their greater condemnation, as well as that of those who think like them.

Although, as has been said, records from the impious letter have been inserted in certain books, they are nowhere found in the authoritative records signed by the most reverend bishops. Those who investigate the truth must also attend to this: in councils, certain things are often said by individuals present, whether out of partiality, opposition, or ignorance. No one pays attention to what individuals say separately, but only to what is defined by all through common agreement.

For if someone wished, as they do, to attend to such contradictory statements, every council would be found overthrowing itself.

For these reasons, if they truly accepted the holy council, they ought not to attach such accusations to it, but should follow the teachers of the catholic Church, especially the holy Athanasius, formerly bishop of the Church of Alexandria, who undertook many great struggles for the right faith of Christians against every heresy, and especially against the most impious Arians.

When those same Arians, to deceive the peoples, tried to draw Dionysius into their party—Dionysius, who had been bishop of Alexandria many years before the holy Athanasius—and said that Dionysius too had held opinions like theirs, Athanasius the Great, teacher of the Church, demonstrated by many written arguments that Dionysius had proclaimed the right faith from the beginning and had in no way shared the impiety of the Arians.

These people, however, holding the opinions of the heretics, strive to attach their own impiety to him.

The divine Scripture also teaches us what condemnation and what curse awaits those who sin against fathers. When Ham, the son of Noah, saw his own father naked and did not cover his father’s bodily nakedness, but went out and reported it to his brothers, while they covered it with a garment, Ham himself and those born from him came under a curse, whereas those who covered him were deemed worthy of a great blessing.

How much more deserving of a greater and still heavier condemnation are those who strive, through the impiety of the letter and of Theodore, to attach to the council a dishonor that was in no way present in it.

But neither will the impious letter nor those who defend it thereby escape condemnation for their impiety. Nor will Theodore, who surpassed Greeks, Jews, and all heretics in impiety, escape it.

For, in addition to his other blasphemies, he was not content merely to misinterpret the creed of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers for his own error, but, scorning it, he produced another creed filled with every kind of impiety. In it he dared to anathematize those who thought or taught otherwise, so that, according to their madness, all the holy apostles and Fathers would be condemned.

This impious creed of Theodore was brought forward at the First Council of Ephesus and read at Chalcedon; both councils condemned it, together with its author and those who accepted it.

Since some, making a case for Theodore, pretend—when his impious writings are brought forward because of the blasphemy contained in them—to say that the writings are impious but refuse to anathematize the person who vomited forth such impiety, we marvel at their folly. They plainly dare to oppose the divine Scripture, which says: “The impious person and his impiety are equally hateful to God.”

For the deed will be punished together with the person who committed it. If both the impious person and his impiety are equally hateful to God, it is clear that such a person is separated from God and is rightly subjected to anathema.

For anathema signifies nothing other than separation from God, as the judgment concerning anathema in the Old and New Testaments makes clear.

The Lord also says in the Gospel according to John, speaking to the Jews, that those who are not in the word of his truth are separated from the Church:

“Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. The slave does not remain in the house forever, but the son remains forever.”

That the house named by the Lord is called by divine Scripture the Church of the living God, the Apostle testifies in the First Letter to Timothy.

If some say that Theodore should not be anathematized after death, let those who defend such a heretic know that every heretic who persists in his own error to the end is more justly subjected to perpetual anathema even after death.

This has happened to many heretics, both ancient and more recent: Valentinus, Basilides, Marcion, Cerinthus, Mani, Eunomius, and Bonosus. The same happened to Theodore, who was accused during his life and anathematized after death by the holy Fathers.

If his defenders, as heretics, do not wish to obey these authorities, let them at least believe the impious letter that they defend. Although it strongly defends Theodore, it plainly says that he was anathematized in the churches by the holy Fathers, and that afterward there was much investigation concerning his writings, since they were evidently filled with impiety.

At that time the members of the catholic Church did this so that the simple, when reading his impious writings, would not be led astray from the right faith.

That the impious, even if they do not receive anathema personally during life, are nevertheless anathematized after death by the catholic Church is demonstrated by the holy councils. The council at Nicaea anathematized anonymously those who upheld the impious opinion of Arius. The council at Constantinople likewise anathematized the most impious heresy of Macedonius. Yet the holy Church of God anathematizes Arius and Macedonius by name even after death.

Refuted by many proofs and shown to be defending Theodore and his impiety in vain, they flee to another empty pretext, saying that he should not be anathematized because he died in communion with the churches.

They ought to know that those die in communion with the churches who preserve to the end the common doctrine of piety proclaimed in the catholic Church.

Theodore, however, having died in his own impiety, was expelled from every church. Indeed, the entire body of the Church at Mopsuestia, in which he is said to have been bishop, because of his blasphemies—on account of which he was numbered by the holy Fathers with Greeks, Jews, and Sodomites—afterward erased his name from the sacred diptychs of the Church, as the records composed concerning him at the council of the province in that same city demonstrate.

We therefore marvel at those who defend Theodore and claim both him and his impiety as their own, when the church in which he had been bishop rejected him as a heretic long ago.

That Theodore’s defenders put forward this pretext to their own condemnation can also be learned from the dreadful judgment concerning Judas.

Judas thought that he could escape the notice of the one who knows the hidden things of human beings. He shared the mysteries with the apostles, but even communion under hypocrisy did him no good. Nor does the fact that, after his death, the disciples continued to be called twelve, as the evangelist John says—“Thomas, who is called Didymus, one of the twelve, was not with them when Jesus came”—either remove Judas from condemnation or cause him to be counted among the apostles.

Indeed, after the Lord’s ascension, the apostles, by their own vote, condemned that same Judas even after death and appointed another in his place.

That their claim that dying heretics should not be anathematized is an empty pretext can also be demonstrated from the Lord’s own words. He calls the impious, even while they are alive, dead, saying: “Let the dead bury their own dead.” In the same way he calls the righteous who have died living. For concerning Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob he says that God is not God of the dead but of the living.

If, then, according to their arguments, dying heretics ought not to be anathematized, neither should living heretics be anathematized, whom the Lord calls dead because they are separated from him, since he says: “I am the life.” According to them, therefore, neither living nor dead heretics would be anathematized; and in vain the apostolic teaching handed down that those who preach contrary to what we received should be anathematized; in vain the holy councils condemned heretics; and in vain the other holy Fathers and teachers of the Church anathematized them.

They would also have to blame the prophet Jeremiah, who says: “Cursed is the one who does the works of the Lord negligently”; and the prophet David, who says: “Cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments”; and, to speak briefly, all divine Scripture, which in many places imposes such condemnations upon the impious.

If those who negligently perform the Lord’s works and sin against his commandments are subjected to such condemnations, how much more justly is Theodore the impious condemned and anathematized, since he blasphemed in such ways against the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ himself?

These things, together with the proofs set out above and in other works of ours, would be sufficient to demonstrate that heretics must be condemned even after death, to put Theodore’s defenders to shame, and to make them cease from such impiety.

But because they obstinately persist in the same arguments, we shall say more. Some of those assembled at the holy Council of Nicaea, who had signed the rule or creed of faith issued by that council, afterward appeared to hold contrary opinions. Some while still alive and others after death were anathematized by Damasus, pope of senior Rome of holy memory, and by the Council of Sardica, as the holy Athanasius also testifies.

Furthermore, the holy Council of Chalcedon condemned Domnus, formerly bishop of Antioch, after his death, because he had merely dared to write that the twelve chapters of the holy Cyril ought to be passed over in silence.

Source/review notes: The draft contained a few substantive shifts: the preserved names were restricted to places; Theodosius’s ‘pious end’ was generalized to ‘pious memory’; Gregory’s promised adoption was rendered as hope; and Cyril’s statement made the Word, rather than the flesh, originate from a woman.

Because the Theodore-party heretics, having fallen away from every proposition and undertaking, have attempted to say, for the deception of the ignorant, that Cyril, of holy memory, praised Theodore in a certain passage of a letter, it is demonstrated by many proofs that their undertaking does not accord with what the holy Cyril said in various writings against the impious Theodore. In these writings, having shown him to be more impious than all the other heretics, and unable to endure the number and magnitude of his blasphemies uttered against the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, he declared as follows:

> “At this the heaven was astonished, and was exceedingly horrified, says the Lord. Woe to the unspeakable wickedness! Woe to the tongue that speaks injustice against God and lifts up its horn!”

And again:

> “Put a door and a bar upon your tongue, O man. Cease lifting up your horn on high and speaking injustice against God. How long will you leap against Christ, who endures patiently? Bear in mind what was written by the divinely inspired Paul:
>
> ‘Thus, when you sin against the brothers and wound their weak conscience, you sin against Christ.’
>
> And, to utter something from the prophetic books:
>
> ‘Sodom was justified by you.’
>
> You have overcome the reckless speech of the Greeks, which they directed against Christ, considering the cross folly. You have shown the accusations of Jewish madness to be nothing.”

Since these things were therefore said by the holy Cyril for the condemnation of the impious Theodore, even if someone were to grant, according to their arguments, that the holy Cyril said something in Theodore’s defense, not even this exempts him from condemnation. For we find that many of the holy Fathers accepted certain heretics, as did the holy Damasus, Athanasius, and Basil in the case of Apollinarius, and Leo, of holy memory, in the case of Eutyches. Yet, when the impiety of these men became manifest, the heretics did not escape, on account of that acceptance, the condemnation and anathema subsequently pronounced against them personally and against their impiety.
