So great, however, is the madness of Theodore’s defenders that they dare to slander even Gregory the Theologian and John of Constantinople, claiming that they sent Theodore letters filled with praise. This is wholly false. For when Gregory, after contending for the truth in Constantinople and turning the peoples from the error of the Arians to the orthodox faith, returned to his native country, he did not write the letters maliciously cited by the heretics to Theodore of Mopsuestia, but to Theodore, bishop of Tyana, which is the metropolis of the Second Cappadocia. Nazianzus also belongs to that same region, of which the same holy Gregory became bishop, as does the village of Arianzus, from which he came.

The letters themselves clearly show this: they mention peoples, synods, and the village of Arianzus itself, as well as other villages of the same province; months named in the local dialect of the Cappadocians; the bishop Bosporius, subject to him in the city of Colonia; and other bishops, rural bishops, and monasteries subject to the same Theodore. The names of these persons, places, and institutions are preserved even to the present day. What connection, however, did the Cappadocians have, then or now, with those of Second Cilicia, since the administration of those provinces was separate? Or what bishops could the bishop of Mopsuestia have under himself, when he himself was subject to the metropolitan of that same Second Cilicia?

John of Constantinople did write a letter to Theodore of Mopsuestia, but it was not filled with praise; rather, it was full of reproaches and admonitions, since Theodore had fallen away from piety. For, having practiced the solitary life together with him in one and the same monastery, John reminds him of their companionship there. So testify Sozomen, Hesychius, Socrates, and Theodoret, who extended many speeches and praises in Theodore’s defense.

But if they produce testimonies from John of Antioch and the Eastern synod under him, offered in defense of Theodore and his impiety, they must necessarily also accept those actions which John and his associates dared to undertake, insofar as they contributed to the condemnation of the holy Cyril and the rejection of the orthodox faith—and the writings in which they defended Nestorius and his evil doctrine for a very long time. This is shown by various speeches and letters of theirs written to Theodosius, of pious end, and to various others.

[Col. 0265A]

These matters having been set forth, and so that we might omit nothing pertaining to precision, we have thought it necessary to mention also what was written by Augustine, bishop in Africa, of holy memory. When, after his death, an inquiry arose concerning Caecilianus, on the charge that he had departed from ecclesiastical tradition, and when certain people on this account separated themselves from the catholic Church, the same Augustine of holy memory writes to Boniface that no one ought for this reason to separate himself from the catholic Church.

For if the charges brought against Caecilianus had been true, and he had been shown to have held opinions contrary to the catholic order, they would have subjected him to anathema even after his death. Moreover, a canon of the holy synod in Africa decrees that bishops who, by testament or intestate succession, hand over their property to a heretic must also be anathematized after death.

In addition to all this, who is unaware of what happened in our own times in the Church of elder Rome concerning Dioscorus? Though he had committed no offense against the faith, he was anathematized after death by that most holy Roman Church itself, solely on account of an ecclesiastical matter.

If, then, bishops who had committed no offense against the faith are subjected to anathema, even after death, on account of an ecclesiastical matter and a financial cause, how much more Theodore, who was impious toward God himself?

As for the folly of those who say that people who die in their own impiety must not be anathematized after death, then, by their reasoning, neither ought Fathers who were unjustly condemned to be restored after death. Yet this is precisely what happened in the case of John, bishop of Constantinople, of holy memory, who was restored after death by the catholic Church; and in the case of Flavian, also of holy memory and bishop of Constantinople, who was unjustly condemned while alive but was justly restored after death by Pope Leo, of holy memory, and by the holy synod at Chalcedon.

According to their arguments, therefore, it follows that heretics are to be counted among the holy Fathers, as though they were released from the condemnation owed to them, while the holy Fathers who were unjustly condemned are to be joined to the heretics, as though the unjust condemnation imposed upon them were not annulled.

But the most credible teacher of all is the Lord and our God Jesus Christ, who speaks concerning himself:

> “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him. Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.”

And the Holy Spirit says through the prophet David that the impious will not rise in judgment.

Since, then, such a judgment has been pronounced by the Lord against every impious person, and makes no distinction between living and dead heretics, how do they dare oppose this judgment and say that those who have once been impious, and for that reason have already been condemned by the Lord, must not be condemned after death?

The divine Apostle, moreover, having Christ speaking through him, pronounced such a judgment not only against human beings but also against angels, saying in the Epistle to the Galatians:

> “But even if we ourselves, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be anathema. As we have said before, so now I say again: if anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be anathema.”

And who is so impious as to dare say that the impious writings of Theodore, or even a part of them, were ever handed down to the holy Church of God, rather than that the person who dared to utter anything of the kind was immediately subjected to anathema by the holy Fathers?

[Col. 0267B]

If, then, after this correct confession and condemnation of the heretics, while preserving the pious understanding, someone wrangles over names, syllables, or expressions and separates himself from the holy Church of God, as though piety consisted for us only in names and expressions and not in realities, such a person, rejoicing in schisms, will give an account before the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ on the day of judgment, both for himself and for those deceived—or destined to be deceived—by him.

Amen.

## Formulary of the Emperor Justinian addressed to the holy synod concerning Theodore of Mopsuestia and the others

It has always been the concern of the orthodox and of our pious predecessors who have ruled as emperors to cut off, through the most holy synods of priests, the heresies that arise from time to time, and, while the orthodox faith is clearly proclaimed, to preserve the holy Church of God in peace. Therefore Constantine the Great, when Arius was blaspheming and saying that the Son was not consubstantial with God the Father but a creature brought into being from nothing, gathered the three hundred and eighteen Fathers at Nicaea, and himself attended there. After Arius had been condemned and anathematized, Constantine took care to strengthen the orthodox faith.

By that confession the divine Fathers declared that the Son is consubstantial with God the Father, and not a creature brought into being from nothing; and this confession is sung even to the present day [probably: “they sing”].

The elder Theodosius likewise, when Macedonius denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit, and Apollinarius, his disciple, blasphemed concerning the dispensation of God the Word, asserting that the Word of God had not assumed a human mind but had been united to flesh possessing an irrational soul, gathered the 150 Fathers at Constantinople, took part himself in the synod, and, after the heretics just mentioned had been deposed and anathematized together with their impious doctrines and like-minded associates, arranged that the orthodox faith should be proclaimed.

The younger Theodosius, likewise, when the impious Nestorius asserted that God the Word was one and Christ another, introducing the impious doctrine that the former was by nature the Son of God and the Father, while the latter was a son by grace, and denying that holy Mary was Theotokos, gathered at Ephesus the first synod of the two hundred holy Fathers. He sent officials who were required to attend the synod, ordered Nestorius also to appear, and commanded that judgment be rendered against him.

[Col. 0269A]

After a careful examination had taken place, they condemned Nestorius, anathematizing him together with those who shared his opinions. When these events had unfolded, the adherents of the accursed Nestorius rose up against Cyril, the most holy, and did their utmost to overturn the judgment that had been rendered against Nestorius.

Nevertheless, the Emperor Theodosius, supporting those who had truly been judged rightly against Nestorius and his wicked doctrines, arranged that the judgment rendered against him should be firmly maintained [the Latin translator reads: “thus”].

Moreover, when certain people had poured out other foolish accusations against the divine Cyril, Cyril wrote to the Emperor as follows:

> “Since I have learned, most pious Emperor, that certain people accustomed to literary disputation buzz like savage wasps and belch forth wicked words against me, saying—as though it had been brought down from heaven and not taken from the holy Virgin—that Christ’s divine body came from elsewhere, and that we confess, according to Nestorius, two sons, I thought that I ought to say a few words to them on this subject, as follows:
>
> “O foolish men, who know only how to slander, how have you been led to such an opinion, and how have you fallen into such madness? You ought clearly to have understood that almost the whole of our struggle for the faith consisted in affirming that holy Mary is Theotokos.
>
> “But since, as they say, we declare that Christ’s divine body came from heaven and not from her, how could she be understood as Theotokos? What, indeed, did she bear at all, unless it is true that she bore Emmanuel according to the flesh?
>
> “Let those who have uttered such things and similar nonsense against me be laughed to scorn. For blessed Isaiah does not lie when he says:
>
> “‘Behold, the virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which means “God with us.”’
>
> “The archangel Gabriel also certainly speaks the truth when he says to the Virgin:
>
> “‘Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God; and behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he will save his people from their sins.’
>
> “When we say that our Lord Jesus Christ came from above, from heaven, we do not mean that his holy flesh was brought down from heaven from above. Rather, we speak in accordance with the holy Paul, who says:
>
> “‘The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man, the Lord, was from heaven.’
>
> “We also remember the Lord himself saying:
>
> “‘No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man.’
>
> “Although he was born according to the flesh, as has been said, from the holy Virgin, nevertheless, since God the Word who descended from above, from heaven, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and was called the Son of Man while remaining what he was—that is, God—for by nature he is unchangeable and immutable, he is understood as one together with his own flesh and is therefore said to have come down from heaven. He is also called a man from heaven, being perfect in divinity and the same person perfect in humanity, understood as one person.
>
> “For there is one Lord Jesus Christ, even though the difference of the natures from which we say that his ineffable union was accomplished is not ignored.
>
> “Therefore we confess the only-begotten Son, the Word of God, perfect God and perfect man, consisting of a rational soul and a body: begotten before the ages from the Father according to his divinity, and in the last days the same person born from Mary the Virgin, for us and for our salvation, according to his humanity; the same person consubstantial with the Father according to his divinity and consubstantial with us according to his humanity.
>
> “For there has been a union of two natures; hence we confess one Christ, one Son, one Lord.
>
> “We also truly confess the holy Virgin to be Theotokos, because God the Word became flesh and became man, and from the very moment of conception united to himself the temple taken from her.
>
> “If you will, let us take as an example the composition that exists in us, by which we are human beings. We are composed of soul and body, and we observe two natures, one belonging to the body and another to the soul. Yet one human being results from both by union; the fact that he is composed of two natures does not make the one person two human beings.
>
> “Rather, by composition there is one human being, as I said, the one composed of soul and body.
>
> “For if we remove the assertion that the one and only Christ is from two different natures and remains undivided after the union, our opponents will say:
>
> “‘If the whole is one nature, how did he become man, or what flesh did he make his own?’
>
> “But as for those who say that a mixture, confusion, or fusion occurred between God the Word and the flesh, may your piety deem it worthy plainly to silence them.”

After these events, when Cyril had died, a certain monk and archimandrite named Eutyches arose and drew after him a considerable portion of the people, endorsing the opinions of Nestorius and his evil doctrine, and asserting that the flesh of the Lord was not consubstantial with us.

Soon afterward, when a devilish hand had grown strong, another synod took place at Ephesus—a robber synod, not a holy one. Flavian of Constantinople was brought there, while Dioscorus of Alexandria possessed the entire authority. The divine Flavian was killed while defending the orthodox faith, and the first synod at Ephesus was overturned, when certain bishops signed under murderous compulsion; among them was Basil of Seleucia.

From that point, when the wicked doctrines of Nestorius, Dioscorus, and Eutyches were being published and great disturbance arose, especially in the East, Proterius, the great priest, and many others were killed.

While matters stood thus, King Marcian arose by divine providence. He gathered at Chalcedon the synod of the 630 Fathers; Dioscorus and Eutyches were present, and Marcian himself also attended. Dioscorus and Eutyches were condemned, and Nestorius was again anathematized. But they accepted Theodoret, Ibas, and Basil of Seleucia after they had subscribed, and, once the robber synod had been overturned and anathematized, the divine Fathers brought everyone into one agreement.

After these four synods had thus taken place, been confirmed, and prevailed in the Church of God, those who held Nestorius’s opinions attempted once more to strengthen their heresy through Theodore of Mopsuestia, who blasphemed much more grievously than his disciple Nestorius.

Therefore we too, following our Fathers and desiring that the orthodox faith be preserved unharmed, urge you, after examining the blasphemies of this man, to pronounce judgment against him and those who share his opinions.

In addition to his countless other slanders against Christ our God, he said that God the Word was one and Christ another; that Christ was troubled by the passions of the soul and desires of the flesh; that he gradually departed from worse things toward better things through progress in his works; and that he became blameless through the excellence of his way of life.

He also said that Christ, as a mere man, was baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; that through baptism he received the grace of the Holy Spirit and was deemed worthy of adoption; that Christ was worshiped as the likeness of a royal image, in the person of God the Word; and that after the resurrection he became immutable in his thoughts and sinless.

Furthermore, he said that the union of God the Word with Christ was of the same kind as that which the Apostle described concerning man and woman:

> “The two shall become one flesh.”

I also urge you to examine what Theodoret and Ibas wrongly wrote against the first holy synod at Ephesus, and likewise to pronounce judgment against them.

The divine Fathers, having investigated these matters with equal care, replied as follows. The divine synod at Chalcedon, after loudly denouncing Theodoret and Ibas, did not receive them unless they first anathematized their own wicked writings, as well as Theodore and Nestorius.

We, for our part, condemn and anathematize, together with all the other heretics condemned and anathematized by the four holy synods just mentioned, Theodore, who became bishop of Mopsuestia, and his impious writings.

We also condemn the writings wrongly composed by Theodoret against the orthodox faith, against the Twelve Chapters of the holy Cyril, and against the first holy synod at Ephesus, as well as everything he wrote in defense of Theodore and Nestorius.

In addition, we anathematize the impious letter said to have been written by Ibas to Maris the Persian. It denies that God the Word, having become incarnate from the holy Virgin Mary the Theotokos, became man; it slanders the divine Cyril as a heretic; it reproaches the first holy synod at Ephesus as having deposed Nestorius without judgment or investigation; it rejects the Twelve Chapters of blessed Cyril; and it defends Theodore and Nestorius, together with their God-hated writings and doctrines.

[Col. 0273D]

Therefore, concerning the reckless tongues of these heretics and of all others, their most impious writings, and the heretics themselves who remained to the end in their own evil doctrine and wickedness, we shall rightly say, counting them with the father of lies, the devil:

> “Walk by the light of your fire and by the flame that you have kindled.”

[Note: [Col. 0226D] This is the version of the older translator, which the illustrious Ducange published in a more accurate form from a Colbertine manuscript. Leuclavius first published the Greek from the Alexandrian Chronicle, which had not yet been published. Hardouin.]

In the name of God the Father, and of his only-begotten Son Jesus Christ our Lord, and of the Holy Spirit. The Emperor Caesar Justinian, lover of Christ, Alamannic, Gothic, Frankish, Germanic, Antic, Alanic, Vandalic, African, pious, fortunate, illustrious, victorious, triumphant, ever venerable, Augustus, to the entire assembly of the catholic and apostolic Church.

[Col. 0226C]

Knowing that nothing else can so please the merciful God as for all Christians to hold one and the same opinion in the true and undefiled faith, and for there to be no dissensions in the holy Church of God, we have judged it necessary, removing every occasion for those who are scandalized or who cause scandal, to make clear by the present edict the confession of the true faith proclaimed in the holy Church of God. Thus those who confess the true faith may guard it firmly, while those who contend against it, learning the truth, may hasten to unite themselves to the holy Church of God.

We therefore confess that we believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: the consubstantial Trinity, one divinity, or nature and substance, power and authority, worshiped in three subsistences or persons. In these we were baptized, in these we believe, and in these we have made our confession, distinguishing the properties but uniting the divinity.

For we worship unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity, possessing a marvelous division and union: unity according to the account of substance or divinity, and Trinity according to the properties, subsistences, or persons.

It is divided without division, so to speak, and joined while divided. For the divinity in the three is one, and the three are one, in whom the divinity exists. Or, to speak more precisely, the three themselves are the divinity: God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit, when each person is understood individually, the mind distinguishing things inseparable; and the three are one God when they are understood together, because they possess the same power and the same nature.

For we must confess one God and proclaim three subsistences, or three persons, each with its own property.

In confessing unity, we do not introduce confusion according to Sabellius, who said that the Trinity was one person with three names, the same Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Nor, by dividing the properties, do we separate the Son and the Holy Spirit from the substance of God the Father, falling, according to the madness of Arius, into three different natures within the divinity.

Therefore there is one God the Father, from whom are all things; one only-begotten Son, through whom are all things; and one Holy Spirit, in whom are all things.

[Col. 0228C]

We confess that the only-begotten Son of God, God the Word, begotten from the Father before the ages and without time, not made, descended from heaven in the last days for us and for our salvation, became incarnate from the Holy Spirit and from holy, glorious Mary, the Mother of God and ever-virgin, and was born from her. He is the Lord Jesus Christ, one of the Holy Trinity, consubstantial with God the Father according to his divinity and the same person consubstantial with us according to his humanity; passible in the flesh, but the same person impassible in divinity.

For it was not someone other than God the Word who received passion and death; rather, the impassible and eternal God the Word himself deigned to undergo human birth and fulfilled all things.

Therefore we do not acknowledge one God the Word who worked miracles and another Christ who suffered, but one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, God the Word incarnate and made man. We confess that his miracles and sufferings are those of the same person, which he voluntarily endured in the flesh.

For no mere human being gave himself for us; rather, God the Word himself gave his body for us, so that our faith and hope would not be in a man, but that we might place our faith in God the Word himself.

Thus, while confessing that he is God, we do not deny that he is also man; and while calling him man, we do not deny that he is God. For if he were God only, how could he suffer? How could he be crucified and die? These things are foreign to God. But if he were man only, how did he conquer through suffering? How did he save? How did he give life? These things were above human nature.

Now the same person suffers, saves, and conquers through suffering: the same person is God and man, both as one, and each as complete in itself.

[Col. 0230A]

Therefore, saying that from both natures—that is, divinity and humanity—one composite Christ has been formed, we do not introduce confusion into the union.

In both natures, moreover—that is, in divinity and humanity—we recognize one Lord Jesus Christ, God the Word incarnate and made man. We do not introduce into his one subsistence a division into parts or a cutting apart; rather, we signify the difference of the natures from which he is composed, a difference not abolished by the union, since both natures are in him.

When we speak of composition, we must necessarily confess both that the parts are in the whole and that the whole is recognized in the parts. For the divine nature was not changed into the human nature, nor was the human nature transformed into the divine nature.

Rather, while each remained in the property and character of its own nature, a union was made according to subsistence.

Union according to subsistence signifies that God the Word—that is, one subsistence from the three subsistences of the divinity—was not united to a man formed previously. Instead, in the womb of the holy Virgin, he created for himself, within his own subsistence, flesh taken from her and animated by a rational and intellectual soul, which is human nature.

Teaching us this union according to subsistence of God the Word with the flesh, the divine Apostle says:

> “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2).

By saying, “Although he was in the form of God,” he showed that the subsistence of the Word is in the nature of God. By saying, “He took the form of a servant,” he signified that God the Word was united to the nature of man, not to a subsistence or person.

For he did not say that he took the one who was already in the form of a servant, lest he show that God the Word had been united to a previously formed man, as the impious Theodore and Nestorius blasphemed when they asserted a merely affective union.

Following the divine Scriptures and the holy Fathers, we confess that God the Word became flesh. This means that he united human nature to himself according to subsistence.

Therefore our one Lord Jesus Christ possesses in himself the perfection of the divine nature and the perfection of human nature. He is the only-begotten Word, being born from God the Father, and also the firstborn among many brothers: the same person when he became man—for the Son of God became the Son of Man—and, while remaining what he was, did not change what he became.

Therefore we confess two births of the same only-begotten God the Word: before the ages, born incorporeally from the Father; and in the last days, the same person incarnate and born [Greek: made man] from holy, glorious Mary, the Mother of God and ever-virgin.

He who shone forth from the Father beyond understanding was born from his mother beyond explanation [variant: “beyond speech”]. Although he was true God, he truly became man.

Therefore we properly and truly confess holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mary to be the Mother of God—not because God the Word received his beginning from her, but because, in the last days, the only-begotten God the Word, who existed before the ages, became incarnate from her and immutably became man.

Though invisible in what was his own, he became visible in what was ours; though God was impassible, he did not disdain to become passible as man; and though immortal, he submitted to the laws of death.

The one who was born at Bethlehem from David’s seed according to the flesh, became like human beings, and was crucified for human beings under Pontius Pilate, the holy Apostles proclaimed to be God himself and man himself; the Son of God himself and the son of man himself; himself from heaven and himself from earth; himself impassible and himself passible.

For God the Word, who was born above from the Father ineffably, indescribably, incomprehensibly, and eternally, was himself born below in time from the Virgin Mary, so that those who had first been born below might be born a second time above—that is, from God.

He therefore has only a mother on earth, while we have only a Father in heaven. For when he received Adam, the mortal father of human beings, he gave human beings his immortal Father, according to what is said:

> “He gave them authority to become children of God” (John 1).

Therefore the Son of God tastes death according to the flesh because of his fleshly father, so that the sons of men might become participants in his life because of their Father according to the spirit, God.

He is therefore Son of God by nature, while we are sons by grace; and again, according to the dispensation and for our sake, he was a son of Adam, while we are by nature sons of Adam.

God is his Father by nature, while ours is by grace. God was his God according to the dispensation, because he became man; but by nature the Lord and God is ours.

Therefore God the Word, who is the Son of God the Father, became one with the flesh and became flesh, so that human beings, united to the Spirit, might become one spirit.

The true Son of God therefore clothed himself with all of us, so that we might all put on the one God.

Even after the incarnation he is one of the Holy Trinity, the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, composed of both natures.

We confess Christ to be composite, following the teaching of the holy Fathers.

[Col. 0232D]

For in the mystery of Christ, unity according to composition rejects confusion and division, preserves the property of each nature, displays one subsistence or person of God the Word together with the flesh, and shows the same person to be perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity—not as existing in two subsistences or persons, but as recognized in the divine and human natures: one in both, perfect God and perfect man; the same Lord Jesus Christ, one of the Holy Trinity, to be glorified together with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

Nor did the Holy Trinity receive the addition of a fourth person when one of the Trinity, God the Word, became incarnate.

We therefore preserve this good tradition, which we received from the holy Fathers, in which we live and conduct ourselves, and which, as we depart from this life, we pray to have with us: the confession that is directed toward the Father, Christ the Son of the living God, and the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0232D]

While confessing these things, in addition to the other teachings of the holy Cyril concerning the true faith, and accepting what he said—“one incarnate nature of God the Word”—we confess that one Christ has been made from the divine and human nature, and not “in one nature,” as certain people, misunderstanding the expression, attempt to say.

Accordingly, whenever the Father said “one incarnate nature of the Word,” he used the term “nature” in place of “subsistence.” In the books in which he used this expression, he frequently explained it in what followed [Note: sometimes “Son,” sometimes “Word”; sometimes “Son,” sometimes “Word”]: whether he said “Son,” “Word,” or “Only-begotten,” these terms signify not nature but subsistence or person.

The incarnate subsistence of the Word therefore produced not one nature but one composite Christ, the same person God and man.

It is impious to say that those who confess Christ as God and man should call him one nature or substance.

[Col. 0234B]

For it is impossible for our Lord Jesus Christ, according to one and the same nature or substance, both to exist before the ages and to exist in time, or to be both impassible and passible. This is what we rightly confess in his one subsistence or person.

From the words of the same holy Cyril we shall demonstrate his clear teaching concerning the expression just mentioned. In his First Letter to Succensus, after saying “one incarnate nature of God the Word,” he immediately added:

> “According to the meaning of the term, and merely by looking with the eyes of the soul, we say that the Only-begotten, having become incarnate, consists of two united natures, but is one Son, one Christ, one Lord, the Word of God the Father incarnate and made man.”

By these words the Father, wishing to make clear the manner of the incarnation, preserving the union undivided and unconfused, demonstrated the number of the natures that came together, and proclaimed one Christ, not one nature of divinity and flesh.

In his Second Letter to the same Succensus, teaching similar things, he writes:

> “For if, when saying ‘one nature of the Word,’ we had remained silent and had not added ‘incarnate,’ but had set the dispensation aside as something external, they might perhaps have had a plausible reason for asking, ‘Where is perfection in humanity, or how does our human substance subsist?’ But since perfection in humanity and the demonstration of our substance have been introduced by saying ‘incarnate,’ let those who prop up a reed as their support cease. For one who removes the dispensation and denies the incarnation ought rightly to be accused of taking away from the Son perfect humanity.
>
> “But if, as I said, by saying that he himself became incarnate, the confession is clear and indisputable that he became man, nothing prevents us from understanding that, since Christ the Son is one and alone, the same person is God and man, perfect in divinity and likewise perfect in humanity.
>
> “Your Perfection most correctly and prudently explains the meaning of the saving Passion, not asserting that the only-begotten Son of God, insofar as he is understood and is God, suffered in his nature the things of the body, but rather that the earthly nature suffered. For it is necessary that both things be preserved for the one true Son: that he not suffer according to divinity, yet that the same person be said to have suffered according to humanity. His flesh suffered.”

In the thirteenth chapter of his Scholia, the same holy Cyril likewise rejects those who introduce two sons and those who say that Christ’s divinity and flesh are one nature. He writes:

> “One must not divide the one Lord Jesus Christ into a man separately and a God separately. Rather, we say that there is one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, recognizing the difference of the natures and preserving them mutually unconfused.”

If, then, as the holy Cyril teaches us, our one Lord Jesus Christ is perfect in divinity and the same person perfect in humanity; if the divine nature did not suffer but the earthly nature did; and if he recognizes the difference of the natures and that they are preserved mutually unconfused in one subsistence, it is certain that the Father says that the same person is recognized in the divine and human nature, and that both natures are in him, from which he is composed.

No one should therefore be so mad as to suppose that those who say that the flesh and divinity of Christ are one nature or substance—both divine and earthly, passible and impassible—are thinking rightly.

[Col. 0236B]

Since certain people also attempt in another way to demonstrate that the divinity and humanity of Christ are one nature, putting forward the example of a human being and saying that, just as a human being consists of different natures, soul and body, and is called one nature, so too, since Christ consists of two natures, divinity and humanity, we ought to call his nature one, we shall say to them this:

Although a human being consists of different elements, namely soul and body, he is called one nature because this is predicated commonly of all subsistences or persons that belong to the same species.

Although each subsistence or person, such as Peter and Paul, is distinguished from the other by individual properties, they are not divided according to nature; both are human beings.

Again, neither soul without body nor body without soul is a human being. Rather, from what he was not, he was created as what he is, from soul and body.

Although every creature consists of different elements, it is said to possess that one nature according to which it was created by God.

Christ, however, is not like this. For “one nature” or “substance” does not signify something predicated commonly of many subsistences or persons, as “human being” does.

If this were so, many Christs would be found in whom the commonality of one nature could be predicated—and to say this is impious.

Nor was Christ created at the beginning from divinity and humanity as a human being is from soul and body, so that this would constitute Christ’s nature. Rather, although God the Word existed before the ages and was of the same nature or substance as the Father and the Creator of all things, in the last days he united to himself human nature according to subsistence and became man while remaining God.

Christ is therefore one subsistence or person, and possesses in himself the perfection of the divine and uncreated nature and the perfection of the human and created nature.

How, then, can one nature or substance be said to exist in him in whom two natures are recognized, the uncreated and the created?

Although Christ is one subsistence or person, and the same person is consubstantial with God the Father and consubstantial with us, this is not according to one and the same nature or substance.

If Christ were one nature or substance, then either he would be without flesh and consubstantial only with God the Father [and the Spirit, Greek], because there is one substance or nature of divinity; or, existing as a mere man, he would be consubstantial only with us, because there is one nature of humanity; or, with the two natures changed, one would have become another nature beyond those that came together.

According to that view, Christ would have remained neither God nor become man, and therefore would be consubstantial neither with the Father nor with us. To think in this way is wholly impious.

We say these things without being unaware that certain holy Fathers also used the example of a human being in the mystery of Christ [Note: Saint Athanasius, in the creed bearing his name]. But they used it to show that, just as a human being is made one from soul and body and is not two human beings, so Christ, composed of divinity and humanity, is one and is not to be divided into two Christs or two sons.

These people, however, use the example of a human being to introduce one nature or substance of Christ’s divinity and humanity. We have shown that this is foreign to piety.

When they are refuted by these arguments, because they have fabricated one nature or substance of divinity and flesh contrary to the correct teaching of the Fathers, they turn to other arguments, saying that one ought not to speak of the number of the natures in Christ, since number introduces division.

[Col. 0238C]

Let them understand, then, that when number is spoken of with respect to different persons or subsistences, it involves division of the things themselves into parts, as with two or more human beings.

But when it is spoken of things that are united, it involves division only in speech [variant: “only in reason”] and in thought, not in the things themselves, as in the one subsistence of a human being constituted from soul and body.

Here too two natures are understood, one of the soul and another of the body. Yet the person is not thereby divided into two human beings; we know that there is one human being and one subsistence.

Thus, in the mystery of Christ, after the union has taken place, although the things united are understood as different, the elements from which our Lord Jesus Christ is composed are not separated from one another in reality or into parts.

Nevertheless, because we consider the difference and wish to signify it, we use number and say that there are two natures in Christ. Nor is the one Christ thereby divided into two Christs or two sons.

The holy Gregory the Theologian bears witness to what we have said. In his First Letter to Cledonius he writes:

> “If anyone introduces two sons, one from God and the Father, and the other from the mother, and not one and the same son, let him fall from the adoption promised to right-believing persons. For there are two natures, God and man, as soul and body; but not two sons, nor two gods.
>
> “Nor are these two human beings, although Paul called them so (1 Corinthians 4), referring to what is within a human being and what is external. To state the matter briefly: the things from which the Savior is composed are one thing and another, since the invisible is not the same as the visible, nor the timeless the same as what is under time; yet they are not one person and another. Far from it.”

[Col. 0240A]

By these words the holy Gregory clearly teaches that the person who speaks of number in the case of persons is condemned as impious, whereas the person who applies number to the natures from which one Christ is composed rightly confesses the faith, signifying by it the difference of the natures that came together, without in any way producing division by parts.

For just as the nature of the soul is one and the nature of the body another, yet one human being is produced by composition and not two human beings, so in Christ, although two natures are understood—one of divinity and the other of humanity—two Christs or two sons are not thereby introduced.

Therefore those who refuse to speak of the number of the natures in Christ according to the manner stated above clearly deny the difference of the natures and introduce confusion into the dispensation.

If they confess the difference, it is absolutely necessary, in order to signify it, also to speak of the number of the natures that came together without confusion in one subsistence. Wherever difference is preserved, number necessarily follows in every respect.

To confirm what we have said, using the testimony of the holy Fathers, we shall show that they teach that in the one Lord Jesus Christ the concepts are distinguished according to the difference of the divine and human natures from which he is composed, and that they employ number for this purpose, while not dividing the natures themselves in reality or into parts into two subsistences or persons.

[Col. 0240C]

The holy Cyril says in his Interpretation of Leviticus (Leviticus 14):

> “Consider again clearly in these things the whole mystery of our Savior and the purification that takes place through holy baptism. For he commands that two living and clean little birds be taken, so that through the flying creatures you may understand the heavenly man, at once man and God, to be divided into two natures, insofar as this pertains to the account proper to each. God the Word, who is from God the Father, shone forth in flesh which is from a woman; nevertheless, he is not to be divided, for one Christ comes from both.”

Again, the same holy Cyril says in his Second Letter to Succensus:

> “But they did not understand that things customarily divided by thought alone are not therefore necessarily and in every respect separated from one another into an otherness that exists by parts.”

The holy Basil, in the fourth book Against Eunomius, interpreting the words, “The Lord created me” and “Before all the hills he begot me” (Proverbs 9), writes:

> “We must understand the word ‘created’ as referring to him who took the form of a servant. In all these matters we do not speak of two, God separately and man separately, for he was one; rather, we understand the nature of each by thought.”

The holy Gregory the Theologian, in the second book On the Son, teaching us how we ought to distinguish by thought the natures that are in our Lord Jesus Christ, writes:

> “When the natures differ in thought, the names too are divided together. Hear Paul saying: ‘So that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory’ (Ephesians 1): God of Christ, but Father of glory. For although both are one, they are so not by nature but by conjunction.”

The holy Gregory of Nyssa, in the fourth book Against Eunomius, teaching us the same things, writes:

> “And lest anyone apply the passion of the cross to the incorruptible nature, he corrects such an error more clearly elsewhere, calling the mediator himself of God and human beings (1 Timothy 2) both man and God himself. Thus, when two things are said of one person, what is appropriate to each is understood: impassibility with respect to divinity, and the dispensation of suffering with respect to humanity.
>
> “When thought divides what is united in compassion but distinguished in reason, and when it proclaims the one who is exalted and surpasses every sense, it uses higher names—God over all, the great God, the power of God, and the wisdom of God (Romans 10; Titus 2; 1 Corinthians 1), and similar names.
>
> “But when it signifies in words the experience of sufferings necessarily assumed for the sake of our weakness, it names both from our own condition and calls him man, without assigning by that expression the one signified to the other nature, but preserving piety with respect to both.”

Having demonstrated these points from the teaching of the holy Fathers, let those who make the number of natures existing in Christ an occasion of their error cease trying to introduce confusion by denying the difference of those natures [Greek: denying the difference on account of the denial of the number]. For how could the number not be necessary, when the Fathers used it to signify the difference of the natures united in one subsistence, and not their division into parts? It is therefore demonstrated in every way that it is impious to say that the deity and flesh of Christ are one nature or substance. We say this also because, just as we say that the deity and humanity of Christ are one subsistence, so it is not possible to say that Christ is one nature, since nature and subsistence are not the same.

All the holy Fathers unanimously teach us that nature or substance and form are one thing, and subsistence or person another. Nature, substance, and form signify what is common [Col. 0242D], whereas subsistence or person signifies what is particular. But if some should say that, just as Christ is called one composite subsistence, so one ought also to say that he is one composite nature, we shall show that this too is foreign to piety. In saying that the deity is one nature or substance, we confess [Greek: glorify] three subsistences, recognizing the same nature or substance in each subsistence. And rightly, out of the three subsistences, we call the one subsistence of the Word composite with respect to the flesh.

For no one in the catholic Church has ever dared to say that, just as there are three subsistences, so there are three natures of the holy Trinity, so that it might be possible to say that one nature was composed from three natures and united to the flesh. Arius alone dared to say that there were three natures in the holy Trinity, and he was condemned as a blasphemer. Therefore, in accordance with right reasoning, we speak of the union of two natures and of one subsistence. For the Son of God, while being another according to subsistence than the Father, yet possessing the same nature as the Father, fashioned for himself in his own subsistence flesh animated by a rational and intellectual soul. This signifies that God the Word was united to human nature, and not to some subsistence or person.

God the Word, therefore, incarnate, is to be recognized as one subsistence in both natures: in the divine nature, in which he existed, as it is said, “Who, although he was in the form of God” (Phil. II); and in the human nature, according to the fact that he “was made in the likeness of human beings” (ibid.). Therefore someone may more correctly say that the subsistence of God the Word is one composite subsistence than that it is one composite nature. For when nature is spoken of absolutely and by itself, without the addition of the particular person to whom it belongs, it signifies something infinite and non-subsisting; but the infinite cannot be composed with anything.

If, however, someone, even after these arguments, looking only toward contention, attempts to object that, according to the definition of nature just given, Christ’s human nature must also have its own subsistence or proper person, it is evident that such a person is saying that God the Word was united to a man who already subsisted, and that the union was merely one of will or affection. For two subsistences or persons cannot be united according to subsistence.

Whoever says this, hastening to empty God’s power by human words of wisdom, does not understand the great mystery of piety, which is believed in the heart for justification and confessed with the mouth for salvation. For Christ’s human nature is never spoken of absolutely and by itself; nor did it possess its own subsistence or person. Rather, human nature received the beginning [Greek: received the beginning of its existence] of its being in the subsistence of God the Word. Hence we confess that God the Word himself immutably became human, and did not come into a certain human being. We confess also that the birth from the Virgin belonged to this same God the Word incarnate, and for this reason that holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mary is the Mother of God.

Therefore, both before the incarnation of God the Word and after his incarnation, we say that there are three subsistences: of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For the holy Trinity did not receive the addition of a fourth subsistence or person.

By all these points, then, those are refuted who say that there were two natures before the union, since they say that a man had already been fashioned [or: subsisted] and that he was then united to God the Word, in accordance with the madness of the impious Theodore and Nestorius. Those, on the other hand, who say that after the union one ought not to speak of two natures in Christ but of one, introduce confusion and fantasy, in accordance with the impious Apollinarius and Eutyches.

But enough concerning them. The holy Fathers, considering after the incarnation of God the Word the things from which Christ consists [Col. 0243D], and recognizing that the natures remained unconfused, most rightly said that there are two natures in Christ, divine and human. For there were not two natures of the Lord before the incarnation, nor did two natures become one after the incarnation, although they are recognized in one subsistence.

[Col. 0244D] Taught these things by the divine Scriptures and by the teaching of the Fathers, we have rightly written them to refute those who confuse and divide the mystery of the divine dispensation. We do not, by declaring the things from which Christ consists and in which he is recognized, make confusion or division in the divine dispensation. Accordingly, proclaiming the glory and the account of the union, we confess and adore, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one Christ and Son and Lord, the Word of God incarnate and made human.

While confessing these things with the universal Church of God [Note: [Col. 0245D] “Let the universal Church of God confess.” Greek. The Bohierian manuscript likewise has this reading], we wish all Christians to know that, just as we have one God and Lord, so also we have one faith. For the one definition of faith is to confess and rightly glorify the Father, Christ the Son of God, and the Holy Spirit.

We preserve this confession, in which we were also baptized: a confession given by our great God and Savior Jesus Christ to his holy disciples and apostles, and preached by them throughout the whole world. The three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea against Arius, after condemning him together with his impiety, handed down to the holy Church of God this same confession, namely, the holy definition and creed of the faith.

After them, the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers assembled at Constantinople against Macedonius, who opposed the Holy Spirit, and against the great Apollinarian, condemned them together with their perfidy and, following in every respect the same holy creed handed down by the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers, explained the matters concerning the deity of the Holy Spirit (Acts 5).

Furthermore, the holy Fathers who first assembled at Ephesus against the impious Nestorius, and the holy Fathers who met at Chalcedon against the impious Eutyches, following in every respect the aforesaid holy creed or definition of the faith, condemned the aforesaid heretics together with their impiety, as well as those who held or hold opinions like theirs.

In addition, they anathematized those who hand down another definition of the faith, whether creed or definition, to those approaching holy baptism or converted from any heresy, other than the one handed down, as has been said, by the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers and explained by the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers.

Since matters stand thus, we have judged it appropriate to append chapters containing both a concise confession of the true faith and the condemnation of the heretics.

### I

If anyone does not confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and the consubstantial Trinity, one deity—or nature and substance—and one power and authority to be worshiped in three subsistences or persons, let him be anathema.

### II

If anyone does not confess that he who was begotten from the Father before the ages and beyond time, God the Word, descended from heaven in the last days, became incarnate from the holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mother of God, Mary, and became human, being born from her—and that for this reason the same God the Word has two births [supplement: namely, the eternal one and] the one in the last days according to the flesh—let him be anathema.

### III

If anyone says that the God the Word who performed the miracles is one person and that the Christ who suffered is another; or says that God the Word was with Christ as he was being born from a woman, or was in him as one person in another, but does not confess one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, God the Word incarnate and made human, and does not confess that his miracles and sufferings are those of this same person—sufferings which he willingly endured in the flesh—let him be anathema.

### IV

If anyone says that the union of God the Word with a human being was made according to grace, operation, dignity, equality of honor, authority, relation, affection, or power; or according to homonymy, by which the Nestorians call both God the Word “Christ” and the human being “Christ” separately, while saying that there is one Christ only in name; or if anyone says that the union was made by good will, as the heretic Theodore says in these very words, as though the human being pleased God the Word because he was well-pleasing to him, but does not confess that the union was made according to the subsistence of God the Word with flesh animated by a rational and intellectual soul, and therefore does not confess that his subsistence is one and composite—let him be anathema.

### V

If anyone says by relation or abusively that the holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mary is the Mother of God, or the mother of a human being, or Christotokos, as though Christ were not God, but does not properly and truly confess her to be the Mother of God, because he who was begotten from the Father before the ages, God the Word, became incarnate and was born from her in the last days—let him be anathema.

### VI

If anyone does not confess that our Lord Jesus Christ, who was crucified in the flesh, is true God, Lord of glory, and one of the holy Trinity—let him be anathema.

### VII

If anyone, while speaking of two natures, does not confess our one Lord Jesus Christ, God the Word incarnate, as one in deity and humanity, and does not use the number to signify the difference of the natures from which he is composed, but takes the expression as division into parts, as though each nature separately had its own subsistence, as Theodore and Nestorius blasphemed—let him be anathema.

[Col. 0248D]

### VIII

If anyone, while confessing the number of the natures in the one Lord Jesus Christ, that is, God the Word incarnate, does not understand this as the difference of the natures from which he is composed, a difference not abolished because of the union, but uses the number for division into parts—let him be anathema.

### IX

If anyone, saying “one incarnate nature of God the Word,” does not understand this to mean that one Christ was produced from the divine nature and the human nature, consubstantial with the Father according to deity and the very same person consubstantial with us according to humanity, but instead says that one nature or substance of the deity and flesh of Christ was produced, in accordance with the perfidy of Apollinarius and Eutyches—let him be anathema.

[Col. 0250A]

### X

For the universal Church of God equally rejects and condemns both those who fall into division or divide the mystery of Christ’s divine dispensation and those who confuse it.

If anyone does not anathematize Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Apollinarius, Nestorius, Eutyches, and those who held or hold opinions like theirs—let him be anathema.

### XI

If anyone defends Theodore of Mopsuestia, who said that God the Word is one person and Christ another—Christ suffering the troubles caused by the passions of the soul and the desires of the flesh, being improved through the progress of his works, being baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, receiving through baptism the grace of the Holy Spirit, and earning adoption; and who said that Christ was to be worshiped in the person of God the Word [variant: worshiped] in the likeness of an imperial image; and that after the resurrection he became immutable in his thoughts and altogether incapable of sin;

—and who further said that the union of God the Word with Christ was of the same kind as the union of man and woman described by the Apostle: “The two shall be one flesh” (Eph. V);

—and who, in addition to his other innumerable blasphemies, dared to say that after the resurrection, when the Lord breathed upon his disciples and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX), he did not give them the Holy Spirit, but merely breathed symbolically;

—and who also [Here also Greek] said that the confession made by Thomas when, after the resurrection, he touched the Lord’s hands and side, saying, “My Lord and my God” (ibid.), was not spoken by Thomas about Christ—for Theodore did not say that Christ was God—but that Thomas, astonished at the miracle of the resurrection, glorified the God who raised Christ;

—and, what is worse, in his commentary on the Acts of the Apostles Theodore made Christ similar to Plato, Mani, Epicurus, and Marcion, saying that just as each of them, from the doctrine he had discovered, caused his disciples to be called Platonists, Manichaeans, Epicureans, and Marcionists, so also, when Christ had discovered a doctrine, Christians were called from it;

—if anyone, then, defends this same Theodore, who blasphemed in such ways, and does not anathematize him, his writings, and those who held or hold opinions like his—let him be anathema.

[Col. 0250D]

### XII

If anyone defends the writings of Theodoret which he composed on behalf of the heretic Nestorius against the true faith, the First Holy Synod of Ephesus, Saint Cyril, and his twelve chapters—writings in which the same Theodoret calls the union of God the Word with a certain human being a union of affection, and, blaspheming, said that Thomas touched the one who rose and worshiped the one who raised him; and for this reason calls impious those teachers of the Church who confess the union of God the Word with flesh according to subsistence; and in addition denies that the holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mary is the Mother of God—if anyone, then, defends these aforementioned writings of Theodoret and does not anathematize them—let him be anathema.

Because of such blasphemies he was deposed from the episcopate [Col. 0252A], and afterward at the holy Council of Chalcedon he was compelled to do everything contrary to those writings of his and to confess the true faith.

### XIII

If anyone defends the impious letter said to have been written by Ibas to Maris the Persian heretic—a letter which denies that God the Word became human and says that not God the Word was incarnate and born from the Virgin, but that a mere human being was born from her, whom it calls a temple, so that God the Word is one person and the human being another; and which further insults the First Synod of Ephesus, as though it had condemned Nestorius without inquiry or examination, calls Saint Cyril a heretic, declares his twelve chapters impious, and praises and defends Nestorius and Theodore together with their impious writings—if anyone, then, as has been said, vindicates this same letter, or says that it is correct, or that any part of it is correct, but does not anathematize it—let him be anathema.

Since this impious letter was rightly anathematized because of the blasphemies inserted in it, the followers of the impious Theodore and Nestorius try to say that it was accepted by the holy Council of Chalcedon. They say this while slandering the holy Council of Chalcedon and hastening, under its name, to free Theodore, Nestorius, and the impious letter from the condemnation they deserve. Ibas, who was repeatedly accused because of that letter, did not dare to call it his own because of the blasphemies inserted in it.

We shall demonstrate this from the various proceedings that took place concerning the matter. In the proceedings held at Tyre before Photius and Eustathius [variant: by Photius and Eustathius], when the aforesaid Ibas was accused of insults against Saint Cyril, he plainly confessed that, after the union which had been effected between the Easterners and Cyril of holy memory, he had said nothing insulting about him.

The letter, however, which is full of the aforesaid blasphemies for which Ibas was accused and contains many insults against Saint Cyril, is shown to have been produced after the union with the Easterners. This demonstrates that Ibas denied it. Therefore the aforesaid Photius and Eustathius, satisfying the accusers, declared in writing that the aforesaid Ibas was doing everything contrary to the letter, as the judgment which they issued concerning the matter shows.

But when Ibas did not fulfill what they had judged, he was deposed from the episcopate because of the blasphemies of the aforesaid letter, and Nonnus was ordained in his place; Nonnus also took his seat at the holy Council of Chalcedon.

When the same Ibas was accused at Chalcedon, after the impious letter had been read he did not dare to confess that it was his own. Instead, in the very words that followed, he declared himself a stranger to the charges brought against him. Therefore, since Ibas’s denial concerning the impious letter was not sufficient for the holy synod, it compelled him to do the opposite of what the letter contained: that is, to confess the true faith which it rejected, to accept the First Holy Synod of Ephesus, to acknowledge Saint Cyril, whom the same impious letter insults, as Father and teacher, and to anathematize the impious Nestorius and his impious doctrine, whom the impious letter defended and praised.

If Ibas himself, repeatedly accused because of the impious letter, did not dare to call it his own, and if the holy Council of Chalcedon compelled him to do everything contrary to it, how could that same holy synod have accepted the letter and subjected itself to the condemnation of the impiety contained in it, from which it hastened to free Ibas?

Since the heretics omit all the blasphemies of the letter and produce from it only the statement which its author made to deceive the simple—namely, “two natures, one power, one person”—we shall demonstrate that in this very statement he mixed in his own impiety.

For whose two natures and one person could he mean, when he denies that God the Word became incarnate from the holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mother of God, Mary, and was born from her? It is certain that he assigned its own person to each nature, just as Theodore and Nestorius, blaspheming in their books, set forth; the author of the letter defends them together with their impiety.

They plainly say that there are two persons, God the Word and Christ, whom they call a mere human being, but that through a union of affection, and through the same dignity and honor, they appear to be one person. The author of the letter, likewise saying that there is one power or authority of two natures, clearly follows the aforesaid heretics in this also: Theodore, in his various impious expositions concerning the incarnation, and Nestorius in many writings, especially in the letter written to Alexander of Hierapolis the heretic, say that of two natures there is one authority and one power, or force, and one person [according to one], through dignity and the same honor.

From this it is shown that the author of the letter used the term “natures” in accordance with their perfidy, intending persons. For “one authority,” “one power or force,” “one dignity,” and “the same honor” are spoken not of different natures but of different persons of the same substance, as we confess concerning the holy Trinity.

Therefore the holy Fathers anathematized those who say that God the Word was united to Christ—whom the followers of Theodore and Nestorius call a mere human being—by authority, power or force, dignity, or equality of honor, but do not confess that the union was made according to the subsistence of God the Word with flesh animated by a rational and intellectual soul [Col. 0253C].

[Col. 0254C]

These points would have been sufficient to convict the impiety of those who vindicate the criminal letter. Nevertheless, at the end of that same letter its author also reveals his perfidy, saying that one must believe in the temple and in the one who dwells in the temple. By this he plainly introduces two persons.

The author of the letter learned this impiety from Theodore and Nestorius. But the Catholic Church, condemning such perfidy, hands down the teaching that one must confess and believe not in a temple and in the one who dwells in the temple, but in our one Lord Jesus Christ, God the Word incarnate and made human.

There is nothing surprising if the author of that impious letter used the term “natures.” Heretics often use expressions which are rightly spoken by the orthodox in order to deceive the simple, but transfer their correct meaning and interpretation to their own impiety. The same expressions, when properly explained and understood, are sometimes compatible with piety; but when wrongly understood and uttered by heretics, they contain impiety.

Accordingly, the First Synod of Ephesus, whose leaders were Coelestine and Cyril of holy memory, did not accept Nestorius, who spoke of two natures and one person but did not confess their union according to subsistence; rather, it condemned him.

Following in every respect the teaching of the holy Fathers, we have demonstrated more clearly above both the union of the two natures from which our Lord Jesus Christ—one of the holy Trinity, God the Word incarnate—is composed, and the fact that their difference was not abolished because of the union.

The points we have already stated would indeed be sufficient to satisfy those who do not wish to contend. But since those who have once turned toward impiety attempt to raise other objections, we must also show the emptiness of such pretexts.

They say that the impious letter ought not to be condemned because it is found in some copies. But if anyone should accept this as sufficient according to their madness [variant: receive it], then one ought also to accept Nestorius and Eutyches, since many statements concerning them are contained in the records of the proceedings held before the synod.

No sensible person will pay attention to their arguments. Statements made in synods concerning heretics and incorporated into the acts are not inserted for their release, but for their greater condemnation [Col. 0256C], and for the condemnation of those who hold opinions like theirs.

[Note: [Col. 0255D] These words are absent from the Bohierian manuscript and from Leunclavius.]

Although copies of the impious letter which circulate have, as has been said, been inserted in some manuscripts, they are not found at all in the authentic copies on which the most holy bishops subscribed.

Those who investigate the truth must also attend to this: perhaps in councils certain things are said by particular people assembled there, whether through favoritism, opposition, or ignorance. No one pays attention to things said individually by some persons, but only to those defined by all in common agreement. For if anyone wished, following their method, to attend to such contradictions, every synod would be found destroying itself.

For these reasons, if they rightly accepted the holy council, they ought not to attach such blasphemies to it, but should follow the teachers of the Catholic Church, especially Saint Athanasius, who was bishop of Alexandria and undertook many great labors for the true faith of Christians against every heresy, and especially against the most impious Arians.

When the Arians, in order to deceive the peoples, tried to join Dionysius to their error—Dionysius having been bishop of Alexandria many years before Athanasius—and said that Dionysius too held opinions like theirs, Athanasius, the great teacher of the Church, demonstrated in his writings in many ways that Dionysius had preached the true faith from the beginning and had in no way shared the Arian impiety.

But these people, holding heretical opinions, hasten to attach their own impiety to that synod.

Divine Scripture also teaches us what condemnation and what curse await those who sin against the Fathers. When Ham, the son of Noah (Gen. IX), saw his father naked, he did not cover his father’s bodily nakedness but went out and reported it to his brothers, who covered it with a garment. Ham himself, and those born from him, were placed under a curse; those who covered him, however, earned a great blessing.

How much more deserving of a greater and more extensive condemnation are those who, through the impiety of the letter, hasten to attach to that holy synod a disgrace which has nothing to do with it, together with Theodore!

But for this reason neither the impious letter nor those who defend it will escape condemnation for their impiety; nor will Theodore, who surpasses pagans, Jews, and all heretics in impiety.

For the impious Theodore was not satisfied, in addition to his other blasphemies, with falsely interpreting for his own error the creed of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers. Even after disregarding it, he composed another creed full of every impiety, in which he dared to anathematize those who held or transmitted different opinions, so that, insofar as his madness was concerned, all the holy apostles and Fathers would have been condemned.

This impious creed of Theodore was both produced at the First Synod of Ephesus and read at Chalcedon. Both synods condemned it, together with its author and those who accepted it.

Since certain people, speaking on behalf of Theodore, when his impious writings are produced, pretend, because of the blasphemy inserted in them, to say that the writings are impious but refuse to anathematize the person who spewed forth such impiety, we marvel at their madness. They act contrary to divine Scripture, which plainly says that before God the impious person and his impiety are equally abominable (Wisdom XIV).

The deed will be punished together with its author [variant: actor]. If the person who acts impiously is as abominable to God as the impiety itself, then such a person is certainly separated from God and is justly subjected to anathema.

For anathema signifies nothing other than separation from God, as the judgment concerning anathema signifies in both the Old and the New Testament.

The Lord also says that those who do not remain in the word of his truth are separated from the Church. Addressing the Jews in the Gospel according to John, he says:

“Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. A slave does not remain in the house forever; but the son remains forever” (John VIII).

The Apostle testifies in the First Letter to Timothy (chapter III) that the house which the Lord names is called by divine Scripture the Church of the living God.

If some say that Theodore ought not to be anathematized after death, those who defend such a heretic should know that every heretic who remains in his error until the end of his life is justly subjected to perpetual anathema even after death. This has happened with many heretics, both earlier and more recent: Valentinus, Basilides, Marcion, Cerinthus, Mani, Eunomius, and Bonosus.

The same thing happened with Theodore: he was accused during his life and anathematized after his death by the holy Fathers. If his heretical defenders do not wish to believe the Fathers, let them at least believe the impious letter which they themselves defend. Although that letter praises Theodore, it plainly says that he was anathematized in the Church by the holy Fathers, and that a great investigation was made concerning his writings because they were full of impiety.

The teachers of the Catholic Church did this at that time so that the simple, when reading his impious writings, would not turn away from the true faith.

The holy synods demonstrate that the impious, even if they did not receive anathema against their own persons during life, are nevertheless anathematized after death by the Catholic Church. The Council of Nicaea anathematized without naming them those who embraced the impious sect of Arius [variant: the impious sect]. The council assembled at Constantinople likewise condemned the impious heresy of Macedonius. Nevertheless, the holy Church of God anathematizes Arius and Macedonius by name even after their deaths.

Since they are refuted by many proofs and shown to act vainly and impiously in defending Theodore and his impiety, they flee to another empty pretext, saying that he ought not to be anathematized because he died in communion with the Churches.

They ought to know that those die in communion with the Churches who preserve to the end the common doctrine of piety preached in the universal Church. But Theodore, remaining in his impiety until death, was expelled from every Church.

Indeed, the entire body of the Church of Mopsuestia, in which he is said to have been bishop [supplement: because of the blasphemies on account of which he was numbered with pagans], when it discovered that the holy Fathers had counted him among pagans, Jews, and Sodomites, erased his name from the sacred diptychs of the Church, as the records prepared concerning this matter in that same city before the council of the bishops of the province demonstrate.

We therefore marvel at the followers of Theodore, who defend him and his impiety as though they were their own, although the Church in which he had been bishop expelled him as a heretic long ago.

That the defenders of Theodore propose such a pretext to their own condemnation may also be learned from the fearful judgment enacted against Judas. He thought that the one who knows the secrets of human beings did not know him, and he shared in the sacraments with the apostles; yet it profited him nothing that he shared in them deceitfully.

Although after his death twelve disciples are named, as the evangelist John says, “Thomas, who was called Didymus, one of the twelve, was not with them when Jesus came” (John XX), this does not free Judas from condemnation or cause him to be counted among the apostles. Therefore, after the Lord’s ascension, the apostles themselves condemned that same Judas by their judgment even after his death and introduced another in his place (Acts I).

That they offer a vain pretext when they say that dead heretics ought not to be anathematized, we shall also show from the Lord’s own words. He calls the impious, even while they are still alive, dead, saying: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. VIII), just as he calls the righteous, though already deceased, living. For he says of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob that “God is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matt. XXII).

If, then, according to their words, dead heretics ought not to be anathematized, neither will those heretical men be anathematized whom the Lord calls dead because they are separated from him who said, “I am life” (John XI and XIV). According to their view, therefore, neither living nor dead heretics will be anathematized.

Then the apostolic teaching would hand down without cause that those who preach anything other than what we received are to be anathematized (Gal. I); the holy synods would have condemned heretics without cause; and the other holy Fathers and teachers of the Church would have anathematized heretics without cause.

Let them also accuse the prophet Jeremiah, who says, “Cursed is the one who does the work of the Lord negligently” (Jer. XLVIII); and the prophet David, who says, “Cursed are those who turn away from your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII); and, to speak briefly, let them accuse all divine Scripture, which in various places imposes such condemnations upon the impious.

But if those who do the works of God negligently and sin against his commandments are subjected to such condemnations, how much more was the impious Theodore, who blasphemed in such ways against the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, justly condemned and anathematized?

These things would indeed have been sufficient, together with the proofs mentioned above and inserted in our other books, which we have produced to show that heretics ought to be condemned even after death, to confound those who defend Theodore and restrain them from such impiety.

But since they obstinately persist in the same position, we add something further. Certain men among those who assembled at the holy Synod of Nicaea and subscribed to the definition or creed of the faith set forth by it later proved to hold contrary opinions. Some of them were anathematized while still alive, and others after death, by Damasus, pope of elder Rome of holy memory, and by the universal Synod of Sardica, as Saint Athanasius testifies.

The holy Council of Chalcedon also condemned Domnus, who had been made bishop of Antioch, after his death, for the sole act of daring to write that the twelve chapters of Saint Cyril ought to be silenced.

The heretical defenders of Theodore, having failed in every argument and attempt, presume to say, in order to deceive the ignorant, that Cyril of holy memory praised him in some part of a letter. From many sources it is shown that their effort does not agree with what St. Cyril said against the impious Theodore in various writings. There he showed him to be more impious than all other heretics and, unable to endure the many and great blasphemies he uttered against the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, cried out:

> “The heaven was astonished at this, and shuddered exceedingly,” says the Lord. “O intolerable wickedness! O tongue speaking iniquity against God and raising up its horn on high!”

And again:

> “Put a door and a bolt upon your tongue, O man. Cease raising your horn on high and speaking iniquity against God. How long will you insult the suffering Christ? Bear in mind what was written by the divine Paul: ‘In this way, by sinning against the brothers and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ’ (1 Cor. 8). And, to say something also from the prophetic books: ‘Sodom was justified in comparison with you’ (Ezek. 16).
