You surpassed the verbosity of the pagans who spoke against Christ, considering the cross folly (1 Cor. 1); you showed that the crimes of Jewish arrogance were nothing.”

Such, then, are the words spoken by St. Cyril for Theodore’s condemnation. Even if someone should concede, according to their claim, that St. Cyril said something in Theodore’s favor, this does not free him from condemnation. For we find that many of the holy Fathers praised certain heretics: Sts. Damasus, Athanasius, and Basil praised Apollinarius, and St. Leo of holy memory praised Eutyches. Yet, once their impiety became known, they did not thereby escape the condemnation and anathema that were later pronounced against them and their impiety.

So great, however, is the fury of Theodore’s defenders that they presume to lie even against Gregory the Theologian and John of Constantinople, saying that they sent letters full of praise to this same Theodore. That is false. When Gregory was laboring for the truth in Constantinople, and, after he had turned the peoples from Arian madness to the catholic faith, had returned to his own country, he did not write the letters which the heretics deceitfully produce to Theodore of Mopsuestia, but to Theodore, bishop of Tyana, which is the metropolis of Second Cappadocia.

Nazianzus, the city of which the same Gregory of holy memory had been bishop, and Arianzus, the estate from which he had come, also belonged to that province. The letters themselves clearly indicate this: they mention local customs and collections, the estate of Arianzus and other estates in the same province, the month called by the Cappadocians by its native name, and Bosphorius—or Bosporus—the bishop placed under that same Theodore, who at that time was bishop of the city of Colonia in the same province, as well as other bishops, country bishops, and monasteries subject to Theodore’s jurisdiction, whose names are still preserved to this day.

What communion could there have been between the Cappadocians and Second Cilicia, whether then or now, when the administration of those provinces was divided? And what bishops could the bishop of Mopsuestia have had under him, when he himself was subject to the metropolitan of Second Cilicia?

John of Constantinople did indeed write a letter to Theodore of Mopsuestia, but it was not full of praise; it was full of complaints and rebukes, since Theodore had fallen away from good conduct [variant: “piety”]. Because John had practiced monastic life with him in one and the same monastery, he reminded him of the conduct they had shared there. So testify Sozomen, Hesychius, Socrates, and Theodoret, who uttered many speeches and praises on Theodore’s behalf.

But if they produce as evidence the acts performed for Theodore by John of Antioch and the Eastern council under him, they must also accept those things which John and his associates wrote—so far as their position is concerned—for the condemnation of St. Cyril and the rejection of the true faith, as well as what they wrote in prolonged defense of Nestorius and his treachery. This is shown by their various writings and letters, which they addressed to Theodosius of pious memory and to many others.

[Col. 0266A] Such, then, is the situation. But, in order to omit nothing subtle or relevant, we have thought it necessary to mention also what was written by Augustine of holy memory, bishop of Africa. When a question arose after Caecilian’s death concerning him, because he was said to have departed from ecclesiastical tradition, and because of this certain people had separated from the catholic Church, the same holy Augustine wrote to Boniface that it was not right for anyone to separate himself from the catholic Church for that reason.

For, he said, if the charges brought against Caecilian had been true, and if he had been shown to have held anything contrary to the ecclesiastical order, I would subject him to anathema even after death.

Moreover, the rule of the holy African synod decrees that bishops who leave their possessions by testament, or intestate, to a heretic must also be anathematized after death.

Beyond all this, who does not know what has happened in our own times in the Church of Old Rome concerning Dioscorus? Although he had committed no offense against the faith, nevertheless, solely because of ecclesiastical order, he was anathematized after death by that same holy Roman Church.

If, then, bishops who have committed no offense against the faith are subjected to anathema, even after death, solely because of ecclesiastical order and a pecuniary matter, how much more Theodore, who sinned against God himself?

As for the folly of those who say that people who died in their impiety ought not to be anathematized after death: then those Fathers who were unjustly condemned ought not to have been recalled after death either. Such was the case with John, bishop of Constantinople, of holy memory, who was recalled by the universal Church after death; and with Flavian, also bishop of Constantinople and of holy memory, who was unjustly condemned during life but justly recalled after death, both by Pope Leo of holy memory and by the holy Council of Chalcedon.

According to their argument, therefore, heretics would be numbered among the holy Fathers, as having been released from the condemnation due to them, while the holy Fathers who were unjustly condemned would be joined to the heretics, as though the unjust condemnation pronounced against them had not been annulled.

But more than all others we must believe the Teacher, our Lord and God Jesus Christ, who says of himself:

> “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him. Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God” (John 3).

The Holy Spirit also says through the prophet David that the impious will not rise for judgment (Ps. 1).

Since, then, such a sentence of the Lord has been pronounced against every impious person, without distinguishing between living and dead heretics, how dare they resist such a sentence and say that those who once acted impiously, and for that reason have already been condemned by the Lord, ought not to be condemned after death?

The divine Apostle too, who has Christ speaking in him, pronounced such a sentence not only against human beings but also against angels, saying in the Epistle to the Galatians:

> “But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be anathema. As we have said before, so now I say again: if anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1).

Who, then, is so impious as to presume to say that Theodore’s impious writings, or any part of them, were ever handed down to the holy Church of God, and that the person who dared to say such a thing was not immediately subjected to anathema by the holy Fathers?

If, after such a right confession and condemnation of the heretics, while preserving the pious understanding, anyone disputes about names, syllables, or expressions, and separates himself from the holy Church of God as though our piety consisted not in realities but merely in names and expressions, such a person, delighting in dissensions, will render an account for himself and for those whom he has deceived and continues to deceive, to the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ on the day of judgment. Amen.

## Letter of the Emperor Justinian to the holy synod concerning Theodosius of Mopsuestia and the others

It was always the concern of our orthodox and pious imperial fathers to cut off the heresies that arose from time to time through the assembly of the most religious priests, and, with the true faith sincerely proclaimed, to preserve the holy Church of God in peace.

Therefore Constantine the Great, when Arius blasphemed and said that the Son was not consubstantial with God the Father but a creature, made from things that did not exist, assembled the three hundred and eighteen Fathers at Nicaea. Being himself present at the council, he sought to confirm the true faith after Arius had been condemned and anathematized. By that faith those divine Fathers confess that the Son is consubstantial with God the Father, not a creature and not made from things that did not exist; and this confession is sung to this day.

The elder Theodosius, when Macedonius denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit and his disciple Apollinarius blasphemed concerning the incarnation of the Word of God, saying that the Word of God had not assumed a human mind but had been united to flesh possessing a rational soul, assembled the one hundred and fifty Fathers in the city of Constantinople. He himself took part in the council and took care that the true faith be proclaimed after those heretics, together with their impious doctrines and followers, had been condemned and struck with anathema.

The younger Theodosius, when the impious Nestorius introduced the blasphemy that the Word of God was one and Christ another, that the Word was by nature the Son of God and the Father, but Christ was a son only by grace, and when he denied that holy Mary was the Mother of God, assembled the First Council of Ephesus of two hundred holy Fathers. He sent officials who were to attend the council and ordered Nestorius himself to be present and judged.

After careful examination, they condemned and anathematized Nestorius together with his followers.

When these events had taken place, the impious followers of Nestorius rose against the most holy Cyril and attempted, as far as they could, to annul the judgment pronounced against Nestorius. But the Emperor Theodosius defended the decisions rightly made against Nestorius and his impious doctrines and took care that the sentence of condemnation against him remain valid.

Moreover, when they frivolously brought other accusations against the divine Cyril before the emperor, Cyril wrote to the emperor as follows:

> “After I was informed, most pious emperor, that certain chatterers, like wild wasps, were buzzing in your ears with their whisperings and spewing curses against me, foolishly asserting that I say the divine body of Christ came down from heaven rather than being assumed from the holy Virgin, and likewise that I confess two sons according to the opinion of Nestorius, I thought that I ought to say a few things against them on this subject.
>
> “O fools, skilled in nothing except slander, how have you arrived at this opinion and conceived such madness? You ought to have clearly understood that almost our entire discussion of the faith arose from our insistence that holy Mary is the Mother of God. If, as they say, we claim that the divine body of Christ came from heaven and was not born from her, how can she be called Mother of God? Whom did she bear, if it is not true that according to the flesh she bore Emmanuel?
>
> “Let those, then, who babble such things about me be laughed at. Holy Isaiah does not lie when he prophesies:

> “‘Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,’ which means ‘God with us’ (Isa. 7).

> “And certainly the archangel Gabriel spoke truth when he addressed Mary:

> “‘Do not fear, Mary, for you have found favor with God. Behold, you will conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus; for he will save his people from their sins’ (Luke 1; Matt. 1).

> “When we say that our Lord Jesus Christ came from above, from heaven, we do not mean that we think he carried his holy flesh down from heaven. We follow the holy Paul, who says:

> “‘The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second is the Lord from heaven’ (1 Cor. 15).

> “We also imitate the Lord himself, who says:

> “‘No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man’ (John 3).

> “As for the flesh, he was born, as we have said, from the blessed Virgin. But because the Word of God, descending from heaven, emptied himself by assuming the form of a servant and became the Son of Man, while remaining the same as he had previously been—namely, God—for he is immutable and his nature is subject to no alteration, and because he is now understood to be one with his own flesh, he is said to have come from heaven.

> “He is also called a man from heaven, since he is perfect in divinity and likewise perfect in humanity; and he is understood to be one person. For there is one Lord Jesus Christ, although the distinction of the natures from which we say that ineffable union was made is not ignored.

> “We therefore confess the Word, the only-begotten Son of God, to be perfect God and perfect man, consisting of body and an intellectual soul. As regards his divinity, he was born from the Father before the ages; in the last times, for us and for our salvation, he was born from the Virgin Mary according to his humanity. He is consubstantial with the Father according to divinity and consubstantial with us according to humanity.

> “For a union of two natures has taken place. Hence we confess one Christ, one Son, one Lord, and also that the holy Virgin truly was Mother of God, because the Word of God put on flesh and became man and, at the very conception, united to himself the temple that he assumed from her.

> “If it pleases you, let us take our own composition as an example, insofar as we are human beings. We plainly consist of soul and body. We see two natures, one of the body and another of the soul, but the human being resulting from their union is one. The composition of two natures does not make us think of two human beings instead of one; we understand one human being composed of soul and body.

> “If we remove this—that one undivided Christ exists from the union of two different natures—the opponents will say: ‘If the nature of the whole Christ is one, how could he assume human nature, or take flesh as his own?’

> “May your piety deign to stop the mouths of those who say that a commingling, confusion, or mixture of the natures of the Word of God with the flesh took place.”

After these events, when Cyril had died, a certain monk and archimandrite named Eutyches arose. He gathered a considerable part of the people to himself, approving the sect of Nestorius and his impious doctrine and saying that the Lord’s flesh was not consubstantial with us.

Then, shortly afterward, when the devil’s hand prevailed, another council at Ephesus was compelled to meet—a council of robbers, by no means holy. Flavian of Constantinople was sent to it as well, while Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, held supreme authority there. The divine Flavian, defending the orthodox faith, was killed. The authority of the First Council of Ephesus was abolished, with certain bishops subscribing under deadly compulsion, among them Basil, bishop of Seleucia.

Since the destructive doctrines of Nestorius, Dioscorus, and Eutyches were then being taught publicly, and great disturbances arose especially in the East, Proterius the high priest and many others were killed.

In this state of affairs Marcian was divinely appointed emperor. He assembled at Chalcedon a council of six hundred and thirty Fathers, and, with Dioscorus and Eutyches present, took part in it together with them. There Dioscorus and Eutyches were condemned, and Nestorius was again anathematized. Theodoret, Ibas, and Basil, bishop of Seleucia, were received, although they had previously subscribed to the earlier [read: “prior,” as below] council.

Thus, after the acts of the predatory synod had been abolished and condemned, harmony was established among all by the holy Fathers.

After these four councils had been held, confirmed, and granted authority in the Church of God, the followers of Nestorius again confirmed their heresy through the works of Theodore of Mopsuestia, who blasphemed far worse than his disciple Nestorius.

We therefore follow our holy Fathers and desire to preserve the true faith without blemish. We urge you to examine this man’s blasphemies as well and to pronounce judgment upon him and his followers.

For, besides the countless other curses which he impiously spewed against Christ our God, he also asserted that God the Word was one and Christ another; that Christ, troubled by disturbances of mind and desires of the flesh, gradually abandoned worse things and became better through progress in his actions, living an irreproachable and excellent life.

He said that Christ, as a mere man, was baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, received the grace of the Holy Spirit through baptism, and was deemed worthy of adoption; that, in the likeness of a royal image, Christ was worshiped in the person of the Word of God; and that after the resurrection he was of steadfast mind and free from sins.

He further declared that the union of the Word with Christ was the union spoken of by the Apostle concerning a man and a woman: “And the two shall be one flesh” (1 Cor. 6).

I urge you also to examine what Theodoret and Ibas wrote wrongly against the holy First Council of Ephesus, and to pronounce the same judgment against them.

[Col. 0274B] The Fathers, having again carefully considered these matters, replied:

> “The sacred Council of Chalcedon, having severely reproached Theodoret and Ibas in words, received them back into favor on no other condition than that they first condemn their evil writings and Theodore and Nestorius.
>
> “We, therefore, in addition to all the other heretics condemned by the four holy councils and excluded from the Church, also condemn and proscribe Theodore, who was bishop of Mopsuestia, and his impious books; likewise the things wrongly written by Theodoret against the true faith, against the Twelve Chapters of St. Cyril, against the holy First Council of Ephesus, and in defense of Theodore and Nestorius.
>
> “Furthermore, we condemn the letter which Ibas is said to have written to Maris the Persian. It denies that the Word of God was incarnate and became man from the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, and portrays the divine Cyril as a heretic. It reproaches the holy First Council of Ephesus, as though it had condemned Nestorius without investigation; it spits upon the Twelve Chapters of St. Cyril; and it supports Nestorius and Theodore together with their impious writings and opinions.
>
> “Therefore, concerning the unbridled tongues of these heretics, their most impious writings, and finally the men themselves, who persist in their false opinions and wickedness, counting them with complete justice among the father of lies, the devil, we shall say: ‘Go into the light of your fire and the flame which you have kindled’ (Isa. 50).”

## Letter of the Emperor Justinian against certain persons who defend in writing the impious Theodore, his wicked doctrines, the so-called Letter of Ibas, and Theodore’s books against the catholic faith (C)

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### Copy of a letter sent by the most pious and most Christian Emperor Justinian to certain persons who wrote in defense of the impious Theodore, his wicked doctrines, the so-called Letter of Ibas, and the writings of Theodoret composed against the orthodox faith

[Col. 0275A]

We received your writings. After reading them, we were astonished that you had not understood the Lord’s teaching when he says, “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart,” but had been lifted to such a degree of arrogance that you despised all the priests of the Church of God and alone justified yourselves above everyone else, like that Pharisee who was justified without condemning even the tax collector.

While we had hoped that you would think like the other priests, contrary to our expectation we found you defending those things that oppose both God and the orthodox faith. Yet, while defending such impiety, you supposed yourselves equal to the apostles, saying that no one ought to reproach you as rustic men, since God also commanded rustic men to preach the gospel.

Even if we called you rustic, as the expression goes, this was why: because, being ignorant of ecclesiastical order and tradition and of the orthodox faith, you defend such impiety [variant: “you are defending”]. But the apostles, whom you call rustic [variant: “you call”], God chose for himself, filled them with his own Spirit, grace, and wisdom, and sent them to guide the nations that did not know God into the way of truth.

Therefore he said to the apostles alone: “You are the light of the world.” You have plainly shown yourselves to be what the Apostle said: “not understanding either what you say or concerning what you make assertions,” since you dared to equate yourselves with the apostles and insult the patriarchs and all the priests.

You have guarded ecclesiastical order so little that [variant: “so that”] you dared to do what had never been done by Christians at any time. Although all the most blessed patriarchs possessed unity with one another, none separated himself from the catholic Church unless he was openly possessed by heretical madness. This is what you have now undertaken to do.

Yet, even though this has happened on your part, we do not cease doing and writing everything that may bring about your correction.

Since you wrote that we had taken pains to condemn these three matters—namely, Theodore together with his writings, the so-called Letter of Ibas, and the writings of Theodoret—in order to fulfill the will of those who have separated themselves from the catholic Church, know that we did not do this on their account.

We did it first because of the impiety of the matters mentioned, and second because certain persons, pretending to keep silent about the name of Nestorius, attempted through those same writings to introduce Nestorius himself and his false doctrine, attaching the impiety of those matters to the catholic Church.

[Col. 0277A] Therefore, although the impiety of those matters was evident, we nevertheless asked the priests of the Church of God what they thought concerning them. They, wishing to show that the catholic Church never possessed and does not now possess such impiety, themselves condemned that wickedness, which had from the beginning been condemned by the holy Fathers.

For even those who have separated themselves from the catholic Church make no argument concerning these matters, knowing that no one bearing the name of Christian can defend them. They contradict the decree of the holy Council of Chalcedon concerning the faith, which was issued for the condemnation of Nestorius and Eutyches and of their unbelief.

Those who oppose the Church’s orthodox doctrines desire rather to defend the impious matters just mentioned against the holy Church of God, so that by this pretext they may deceive the simpler people and separate the Christian people from the Church.

Since you wrote about two supposed reasons why that impious letter should perhaps be accepted [variant: “should be accepted” or “ought to be accepted”]: first, that it rightly fought against Apollinarius; and second, that although the writer of the letter seemed to disparage Cyril of holy memory, he overturned this stain of insult at the end of the letter, and therefore, it is said, the same impious letter ought to be judged orthodox—you have shown that you understood neither the style nor the force of that impious letter.

It contains nothing against Apollinarius. Rather, it calls Cyril of holy memory an Apollinarian. Nor did the same impious letter overturn at the end what it had said against Cyril; rather, in its final statements it said worse things against him.

As we proceed, however, we shall demonstrate both the complete impiety of the so-called Letter of Ibas and the emptiness of the matters you sent.

After everything written by you had been read, we were deeply grieved that you had fallen into such an error, although you are people from that region in which the orthodox faith had always been preserved undefiled before your time.

Therefore we thought it necessary to answer the matters you set forth and to advise you to abandon this impiety and your impious teacher, who composed the matters mentioned above.

For, wishing to deceive you, he produced certain expressions from the divine Scriptures. Having misunderstood some of them, he attempted to attach them to certain expressions in the aforementioned impious letter. All heretics do this: they misinterpret certain expressions of the divine Scriptures and transfer them to their own perverted meaning.

It seems to us that your impious teacher either had not read that anonymous letter or had read it maliciously and brought forward certain expressions from it while concealing the greater and worse part.

For, when that same letter speaks of the blessed Cyril and the impious Nestorius, it says that each wrote harmful words against the other; that Nestorius said that blessed Mary was not the Mother of God, so that many thought him to belong to the heresy of Paul of Samosata; and that Cyril, wishing to overthrow Nestorius’s arguments, slipped and fell into the doctrine of Apollinarius.

It is evident that the writer of the letter was possessed by the madness of Nestorius. He says that Nestorius, who denied that the holy Virgin Mary was the Mother of God, had gone no further than the suspicion of certain people and had not thereby appeared to be a heretic. But he insists that Cyril of holy memory, the teacher of the Church, slipped and fell into the doctrine of Apollinarius.

He says this because Cyril declared that God the Word himself became incarnate and became man. Your teacher, knowing that anyone who says that Cyril of holy memory slipped and fell, and who calls his words heretical, condemns the whole Church, which rightly has Cyril as its father and teacher, omitted these expressions, as we have said.

How was he not terrified when he said that Cyril of holy memory was a heretic because he said that God the Word himself became man, and that by speaking in this way he did not acknowledge a distinction between the temple and the one dwelling in it?

By these words he censures not only Cyril of holy memory but also the Evangelist who says, “The Word became flesh,” and all the prophets who proclaimed the bodily coming of God the Word, especially Jeremiah, who says:

> “This is our God; no other shall be accounted beside him. Afterward he appeared upon the earth and lived among human beings.”

And again Isaiah, who says:

> “The child is the mighty God” (Isa. 9:6).

Before these, the Apostle Paul says in the Epistle to the Ephesians:

> “He who descended is the one who also ascended above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things.”

For, as your teacher says in his madness, the prophets, the Evangelists, and the Apostles deserve blame for saying that God the Word himself became man, as though by these expressions they taught that a transformation of divinity into humanity had taken place.

Those who do not confess that God the Word himself became man plainly show that they say Christ is a mere man and is called Son of God by grace, as the false doctrine of Nestorius and his teacher Theodore says.

The divine Scriptures, and the holy Fathers who followed them, say that God the Word himself—the invisible, incorporeal one, light from light, the one begotten timelessly from the Father before the ages—came down, became flesh, and became man.

St. Gregory says in his Oration on the Theophany:

> “God’s own Word, pre-eternal, invisible, incomprehensible, incorporeal, the beginning from the beginning, light from light, the source of life and the impress of the archetype of immortality, the unmoving seal, the unaltered image, the definition and Word of the Father, proceeds toward his own image and assumes flesh for the sake of flesh; and a rational soul is mingled for the sake of my soul, cleansing like with like. He becomes everything except sin, a human being, conceived from the Virgin, whose soul and flesh had been purified beforehand by the Spirit. For both birth had to be honored and virginity preferred.”

St. Athanasius says similarly in his discourse on the Holy Spirit against the Arians:

> “He who was ineffably, incomprehensibly, inconceivably, eternally begotten from the Father above is himself born below in time from the Virgin Mary.”

Again St. Basil, writing to Amphilochius in the eighth chapter, says:

> “For heaven, earth, the vastness of the seas, the creatures that live in the waters, land animals, plants, stars, air, seasons, and the varied adornment of the universe do not demonstrate such superiority of power as does the fact that God, whom nothing can contain, could without suffering be joined through flesh to death, so that by his own suffering he might grant us freedom from suffering.”

St. Augustine, bishop from the land of Africa, says in his Exposition of the Creed:

> “And you too, prophet Habakkuk, speak a testimony concerning Christ.”

[Editorial note, Col. 0281D: If agreement between the Greek and Latin texts is desired, read: “Say also to you, Habakkuk the prophet.”]

> “Lord,” he says, “I have heard your report, and I was afraid; I considered your works, O God, and I was astonished.”
>
> “What works of God did he marvel at and become astonished by? Was it perhaps the creation of the world? Far from it. Listen instead to what astonished him:
>
> “‘In the midst of two living creatures your works will be known,’ because you, God the Word, became flesh; in the midst of two living creatures you will be known.
>
> “‘Who are you, and how far have you descended? You have made me astonished because the Word through whom all things came to be was born in a manger.’”

St. Leo, Pope of Rome, says similarly in his letter to Flavian, archbishop of Constantinople: ‘Lord,’ he says, ‘I have heard your report, and I was afraid; I considered your works, O God, and I was astonished.’
>
> “What works of God did he marvel at and become astonished by? Was it perhaps the creation of the world? Far from it. Listen instead to what astonished him:
>
> “‘In the midst of two living creatures your works will be known,’ because you, God the Word, became flesh; in the midst of two living creatures you will be known.
>
> “‘Who are you, and how far have you descended? You have made me astonished because the Word through whom all things came to be was born in a manger.’”

St. Leo, Pope of Rome, says similarly in his letter to Flavian, archbishop of Constantinople:

> “The impassible God did not refuse to become a passible man, nor did the immortal refuse to be subject to the laws of death.”

These things have been said by the divine Scriptures and the holy Fathers. Yet, according to your accusations, they deserve blame for introducing a confusion of flesh and divinity because they said that God the Word himself became man. You have also said that Cyril of holy memory, by saying that God the Word himself became man, introduced confusion through these expressions.

But we shall show from the writings addressed by Theodore himself against the impious Apollinarius that the writer of the letter, possessed by Theodore’s madness, denied that God the Word became man.

In the fourth book he writes as follows:

> “You say that certain people among us gave you things that no one devoted to defending the ecclesiastical teaching would ever have given. We asked whether, when someone confessed that God the Word had become man, you then admitted it. And who with any understanding would say that God the Word became man in the sense that you affirm, unless he had previously fallen into the same madness as you?”

“For we most certainly say that God the Word took a man; but that he became a man according to your meaning, we could never endure saying.”

Since it has therefore been shown by what has been said that the impiety of the letter agrees with Theodore’s heretical madness, how could anyone who places his hope in God the Word who became incarnate and man not justly condemn both Theodore and that impious letter?

Since you praise the impious letter because it says that whoever declares that God the Word became incarnate and man removes the distinction between the temple and the one dwelling in the temple, know that the holy Church of God rightly proclaims a distinction between the natures from which the one Christ, our Lord and God, was composed.

But none of the holy Fathers taught a distinction between the temple and the one dwelling in it. Only the impious Nestorius and Theodore said this, wishing thereby to introduce two persons.

Although the divine Scriptures and the holy Fathers use the word “temple,” they mean by it the body of the only-begotten Son of God, as the Evangelist said:

> “But he was speaking about the temple of his body.”

No one says that there is a distinction of the one person of Christ in relation to itself, as though one were in another. They speak only of the distinction of the natures from which the one Christ was constituted without confusion and without division.

You, therefore, by defending the impiety of the letter, which denies that God the Word himself became man, plainly introduce two persons and understand Christ as a mere man.

The Apostle said to believers:

> “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you.”

According to your error, there would be no difference between us human beings and Christ, just as the heretic Theodore, the teacher of the writer of the letter, says in his third book against Apollinarius, speaking madly as though in Christ’s person:

> “I, whom you see, can do nothing according to my own nature, since I am a man. But I work because the Father, remaining in me, does everything.
>
> “‘Since I,’ he says, ‘am in the Father and the Father in me, and the Word of God, the only-begotten Son of God, is in me, it is clear that the Father also, together with him, remains in me and performs the works.
>
> “‘There is nothing astonishing in thinking this about Christ, since he himself plainly says concerning other human beings: “Whoever loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.”
>
> “‘If, then, the Father and the Son make their dwelling with each such person, what is astonishing if both are thought to remain simultaneously in Christ the Lord according to the flesh, since communion in essence naturally admits also communion of dwelling?’”

Since the impious Theodore said these things, it is not surprising that one who has fallen away from God should possess folly joined to his impiety, as the prophet Isaiah says concerning the impious:

> “The fool will speak foolishness, and his heart will understand vain things.”

For how can the one who maintains that the Father and the Son remain in Christ in the same way as in other human beings, and who does not confess that Christ is God the Word become incarnate and man, call him “Christ according to the flesh”?

The holy Fathers, confessing Christ to be God the Word become incarnate and man, rightly add “according to the flesh” whenever they say something lowly concerning him.

Even if it were appropriate for those who defend Theodore to avoid his impiety on account of this exceedingly great blasphemy, nevertheless, because of their shamelessness we shall bring forward other blasphemies of his by which he introduces two persons.

Reproaching those who say that God the Word, who existed before the ages, became man in the last times, he says in the fourth book against Apollinarius:

> “‘The one who existed before the ages became in the last times.’ Again, as though some had given this expression, and as though anyone devoted to piety could choose to suffer from such madness as to say that the one who existed before the ages became in the last times.”

[Editorial note, Col. 0285: Perhaps read: “The one who existed before the ages became in the last times again, as though certain people taught and said this; no one …”]

And elsewhere:

> “Following your laws, then, and accepting the reversal—or rather the overthrow—legislated by your cleverness, let us confuse everything into one, and let there henceforth be no distinction: not between the form of God and the form of a servant; not between the temple that was assumed and the one dwelling in the temple; not between the one who was loosed and the one who raised him; not between the one perfected through sufferings and the one who perfected; not between the one remembered and the one who remembered; not between the one visited and the one who visited; not between the one made lower than the angels for a little while and the one who made him lower; not between the one crowned with glory and honor and the one who crowned; not between the one set over the works of God’s hands and the one who set him over them; not between the one who received them in subjection and the one who gave the subjection.”

In view of these impious words of Theodore and his manifest blasphemy, those who claim to defend him and the impious letter should blush.

For repeatedly and shamelessly to say that God the Word is one and Christ another, one the benefactor and the other the one benefited, one the savior and the other the one saved, plainly denies the salvation that has come to us through the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ.

How can one who has received a benefit from another, or has been saved, save others? Those who defend the man who blasphemed these things—whose body and blood do they think they receive, that of the one benefited or of the one who bestowed the benefit?

If they say it is the body and blood of God the Word who bestowed the benefit, how can they say this while refusing to confess that he became incarnate and man? But if it is that of the one who was benefited, their hope is vain, since they advocate the worship of a man and have impiously worshiped the creature rather than the Creator.

We, all who belong to the catholic Church, confessing God the Word become incarnate and man, one of the holy Trinity, receive his body and blood for the forgiveness of sins and eternal life, as the Lord himself says:

> “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him on the last day. For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him. As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will also live because of me.”

This is what we believe and confess.

How much falsehood is contained in the passage concerning the Twelve Chapters of Cyril of holy memory in the impious letter mentioned above! It slanders him as saying in these chapters that there is one nature of Christ’s divinity and humanity, and therefore says that the chapters are filled with every kind of impiety.

Your teacher cunningly interpreted this [variant: “having interpreted, says”] by saying that the letter did not say that the chapters were filled with every kind of impiety because of the Twelve Chapters, but because it had said that there was one nature of divinity and humanity. This is an obvious falsehood.

Cyril of holy memory neither in his other writings, nor in the letter to which the Twelve Chapters are appended, nor in the Chapters themselves, is shown to have said that there is one nature of Christ’s divinity and humanity. Rather, he teaches that there is one hypostasis, or person, of Christ’s divinity and humanity.

This is what the holy Church of God proclaims and what all the Fathers taught, anathematizing those who say that there is one nature of Christ’s divinity and humanity.

Nature is one thing, and hypostasis, or person, another. Nature signifies what is predicated commonly and generally of all persons; hypostasis, or person, indicates what is particular. A person is not contemplated in another person.

That the foul letter says concerning Cyril’s Twelve Chapters that they are filled with every kind of impiety can be found from what follows in that same impious letter, where it plainly says that those Twelve Chapters are contrary to the orthodox faith.

Since the same impious letter called the Letter of Ibas also censures Cyril of holy memory for denying a distinction of expressions, know that both the writer of the impious letter and your teacher lie in this respect as well.

In all his own writings, when Cyril teaches concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, he says that there is a distinction of expressions: the lofty expressions refer to Christ’s divinity, the lowly expressions to his humanity. Yet he teaches that all of them are spoken from and concerning one and the same God the Word become incarnate. The same Cyril forbids these expressions to be distributed among different persons.

But because you wish to distribute the expressions among two persons, you say that Cyril denied a distinction of expressions.

Since your teacher, wishing to deceive you in this matter also, said that the so-called Letter of Ibas records the impiety of Apollinarius and therefore ought to be considered orthodox, you must know that he lied in this matter too.

As we said above, the letter was not written against Apollinarius. Yet even if, according to your view, this were true, the letter would not thereby be freed from condemnation. Even if a heretic speaks against a heretic, he is not thereby shown to be orthodox.

Arius spoke against Sabellius, Apollinarius against Arius, and Eutyches against Nestorius. Although all these men were held by different errors, none is judged orthodox on account of such opposition; all are likewise condemned by the catholic Church.

From this also it is clear that the writer of the impious letter mentioned above introduces two persons, for he said:

> “How can the Word who was in the beginning be taken as referring to the temple born from Mary?”

By these words he plainly shows that he does not say that God the Word became incarnate and was born from the holy Virgin Mary, but that Christ is a mere man whom he calls a temple.

That the writer of that foul letter also received this impiety from Theodore’s teaching is clear from what the same impious Theodore wrote in his third book against the heretic Apollinarius:

> “But God, from God and consubstantial with the Father, was in the one born from the Virgin, O admirable man, fashioned by the power of the Holy Spirit according to the divine Scriptures and receiving its constitution in the woman’s womb. Naturally he was present, since, as soon as the one was formed, he had also received the status of being God’s temple.
>
> “We must not, however, think that God was born from the Virgin, unless we are to regard as the same both the one born and the temple in the one born and God the Word in the temple.
>
> “Nor should we declare, according to your expression, that the one born from the Virgin is wholly God, consubstantial with God the Father. For if, as you say, the one born from the Virgin is not a man who was assumed but God made flesh, how could the one born be called God from God and consubstantial with the Father, when flesh cannot receive this expression?
>
> “It is indeed senseless to say that God was born from the Virgin. For this is nothing other than saying that he was formed from David’s seed, cut from the substance of the Virgin and fashioned in her. We say that what came from David’s seed and was constituted in the Virgin’s substance in the womb, fashioned by the power of the Holy Spirit, was born from the Virgin.”

Thus Theodore blasphemes and repeatedly asserts that it is impossible for God, who is from God and consubstantial with the Father, to become incarnate and be born from the Virgin, since the flesh is not consubstantial with the Father. Why, then, do those who defend such a heretic not blush?

He set forth things disgustingly contrary both to the divine Scriptures and to the holy Fathers, although it is clear to all that from the beginning, from the time God founded the Church in the orthodox confession, all God’s priests proclaimed that God the Word, who is from God, became incarnate from the holy and glorious Virgin Mary in flesh animated by a rational and intellectual soul, became man, and was born from her.

In teaching this they introduced neither a transformation of divinity into flesh nor a denial that, because of the flesh, he is consubstantial with the Father, as Theodore babbles. Rather, they taught that the one and same Lord and God Jesus Christ is consubstantial with the Father according to divinity and, according to humanity, the same one is consubstantial with us.

Again, in the work mentioned above, the impious Theodore blasphemously says:

> “The divine nature was not born from a virgin; what was born from the virgin was the one constituted from the substance of the virgin. God the Word was not born from Mary; what was born from Mary was the one from David’s seed.
>
> “God the Word was not born from a woman; what was born from a woman was the one fashioned in her by the power of the Holy Spirit.
>
> “The one consubstantial with the Father was not born from a womb—for he is without mother, according to the word of blessed Paul. Rather, what was fashioned in later times in the mother’s womb by the power of the Holy Spirit was born, and for this reason is also called fatherless.”

The impious Theodore thus reasons falsely concerning the Apostle’s teaching, who says in the Epistle to the Hebrews concerning the Lord:

> “First, by interpretation, king of righteousness, and then also king of Salem, which is king of peace; without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life.”

Although the Apostle speaks of one and the same person as without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, the impious Theodore says that one is fatherless and another motherless.

We shall expose the impiety of those who think this way from the teaching of the holy Fathers.

St. Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus, says in his discourse on the Theophany:

> “Who does not worship the one from the beginning? Who does not glorify the one at the end? Again darkness is dissolved; again light is established. Again Egypt is punished with darkness; again Israel is illumined by a pillar.
>
> “Let the people sitting in the darkness of ignorance see the great light of knowledge. The old things have passed away, and all things have become new; the letter withdraws, the Spirit speaks boldly; the shadows flee, and truth enters; Melchizedek is gathered up.
>
> “The one without mother becomes without father: without mother first, without father second. The laws of nature are dissolved; the world above must be fulfilled. Christ commands that we not resist.”

St. Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, says in his discourse on the Mother of God:

> “He who by nature is impassible became, through compassion, subject to many sufferings. Christ did not become God by progress—far from it—but God became man through compassion, and this is what we believe. We do not proclaim a man who was deified; we confess God become incarnate.
>
> “He who is without mother according to essence and without father according to the dispensation claimed his own handmaid as mother. For how, according to Paul, can the same person be without mother and without father? If he were a mere man, he would not be without mother, for he has a mother. But now the same one is without mother as Creator and without father as creature.”

St. Augustine says in his discourse on the exposition of the Creed:

> “We believe in his Son Jesus Christ, born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.
>
> “Why are you astonished at this birth, O unbeliever? Do not believe if the one born were only a man. But if he were God and man, he was born from whatever source he wished [variant: “from whom he wished”], since he was born as he wished.
>
> “Marvel rather that the Word took flesh and was not changed into flesh; that, remaining God, he became man.
>
> “Why are you astonished that the woman who gave birth gave birth to her own Creator, that the creature gave birth to the Creator? The Most High willed to be born humble, so that in this very humility he might display his greatness.”

These are the words of the holy Fathers.

That the divine Scriptures also, which the holy Fathers followed, teach that God the Word himself became incarnate, was born from the holy Virgin Mary, and became man is clear.

First the prophet Isaiah says:

> “Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,”

which means by interpretation “God with us.”

Then the prophet David says in Psalm 106:

> “He sent his word and healed them, and delivered them from their destructions.”

The holy Apostle Paul also says:

> “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, so that he might redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption.”

Since these things are so, who is so mad as to dare say that a man was in heaven and that he was sent so that he might be born of a woman and under the law?

Human beings were under the law before the incarnation of the Word. But God the Word himself, the only-begotten Son of God, who was not under the law but himself gave the law, was sent by the Father. Becoming from a woman, he came to be under the law so that he might redeem us who were under the law and so that we might receive adoption.

If, then, as the writer of that impious letter and the heretic Theodore madly claim, the one born of a woman was not truly and properly the Son of God, how could he grant us adoption?

The same impious letter further says that the words “You made him a little lower than the angels” cannot be spoken of the divinity of the only-begotten Son. You also put this forward as correctly said, claiming that the words can be spoken of the man but not of God the Word who became incarnate.

We shall show that the writer of the letter learned this impiety from the heretic Theodore, for Theodore says the same things in his fourth book against Apollinarius:

> “The man concerning whom the prophet says these things is clearly shown by blessed Paul to be the man assumed by the only-begotten. For, after saying, ‘Someone testified somewhere, saying: What is man, that you remember him, or the son of man, that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor; you set him over the works of your hands; you subjected all things beneath his feet,’ he adds:
>
> “‘We see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death’—
>
> “clearly showing that Jesus is a man concerning whom blessed David, astonished, says that the divine nature made remembrance of him at that time and deemed him worthy of its own visitation: ‘You made him a little lower than the angels in order that he might taste death, and you crowned him with glory and honor for all, so that through his union with himself he might also make him lord of all.’”

Again, in his interpretation of the eighth Psalm, concerning the same passage, the impious Theodore says:

> “Therefore the Psalm shows us the distinction between God the Word and the man who was assumed. These things are found expressed in the New Testament: the Lord applies to himself the first part of the Psalm, in which he is said to be the Creator of creation, to possess majesty exalted above the heavens, and to be praised throughout the whole earth; but the Apostle applies the latter part, concerning the man who was deemed worthy of such beneficence, to Jesus.
>
> “How is it not obvious that divine Scripture clearly teaches us that God the Word is one and the man another, and shows us that there is a great distinction between them?
>
> “One remembers, while the other is deemed worthy of remembrance; one visits, while the other is blessed as having been deemed worthy of visitation; one, as benefactor, makes him a little lower than the angels, while the other receives the benefit and is benefited by such lowering; one crowns with glory and honor, while the other is crowned and blessed for this; one sets him over all the works of his hands and subjects all things beneath his feet, while the other is deemed worthy to rule them, although previously he did not possess the authority.”

These are the manifest blasphemies of the impious Theodore and of that foul letter: they say that God the Word is one and Christ another. You, following them, have written that “You made him a little lower than the angels” was spoken concerning a man and not concerning God the Word become incarnate.

You ought to have understood that every human being is lower than the angels, but that this was said concerning the only-begotten Son of God. For, although he was God, he deemed it worthy to become man, accommodating himself to our weakness.

The Apostle teaches us this when he says:

> “But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death.”

If, then, as you say, the Jesus who was made a little lower than the angels is one person and God the Word who was not made lower is another, Christ is plainly a mere man who endured suffering. Thus, according to you, even the Apostle is lying when he says:

> “For if they had understood, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.”

Who is the Lord of glory except God the Word become incarnate, whom the Jews, not knowing that he was God, said:

> “Why, since you are a man, do you make yourself God?”

By this wicked interpretation your teacher followed the Jews more than the truth and spoke against our God.

For confirmation of your arguments you also added to your chapters the Apostle’s statement, “Although he existed in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” claiming that it agrees with your interpretation and was spoken not concerning God the Word become incarnate but only concerning a man.

Even if, following the error of the heretics in this matter also, you insist that the Apostle spoke of a man when he said that he emptied himself, it is clear to all orthodox Christians that the Apostle says that God the Word himself emptied himself, because, existing in the form of God—that is, in the divine nature—he deemed it worthy to take the form of a servant.

The form of a servant signifies human nature, which God the Word united to his own hypostasis in the Virgin’s womb and from her.

He was not united to a man formed beforehand, as the impiety of Nestorius and Theodore handed down to their followers. Nestorius says that God the Word was with the man born from Mary. Theodore says that he was present, as was fitting, in the one who was born.

That “You made him a little lower than the angels” and “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” were spoken concerning God the Word become incarnate is also taught by other words of the Apostle:

> “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, although he was rich, for your sake he became poor, so that you might become rich through his poverty.”

Who would dare say that a rich man became poor so that he might make us rich?

Since you say that if anyone speaks of God the Word, the only-begotten Son of God, become incarnate, that he was made lower or emptied himself, he introduces a transformation of the divine nature according to the impiety of Apollinarius or makes the divinity passible according to the madness of Arius, it is appropriate to say to you the Gospel saying:

> “You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God.”

What, then, will you say concerning the Lord’s statement:

> “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven”?

Does this mean that a man descended from heaven? It is clear that God the Word himself emptied himself by descending from heaven, becoming incarnate from the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, becoming man, and being born from her. The one who descended is himself the one who ascended. His lowering and emptying are spoken of because of his descent.

Since the Lord also said elsewhere in the Gospels, “My Father is greater than I,” do you perhaps think that these words were spoken concerning some man and not concerning God the Word who became man?

But it is clear that the one who said, “My Father is greater than I,” also said, “I and the Father are one.”

By saying, “I and the Father are one,” he indicates the equality which he possesses with the Father according to the divine nature. By saying, “My Father is greater than I,” the same one indicates the lowering that took place for our sake according to the dispensation.

Both—equality and lowering—are said concerning one and the same Lord and God Jesus Christ, that is, God the Word become incarnate.

The Arians, with wicked intent, deny from the lowly expressions that the Son is consubstantial with the Father and therefore assert that he is lesser. You, refusing to accept the lowly expressions concerning God the Word become incarnate, introduce another person into the Trinity according to the impiety of Theodore and Nestorius.

But we, speaking both the lofty and the lowly things concerning one and the same God the Word become incarnate, our Lord Jesus Christ, introduce neither confusion nor division of the natures from which we confess the one composite hypostasis of our Lord and God Jesus Christ. Nor do we introduce a fourth person into the holy Trinity.

That “You made him a little lower than the angels” was written concerning the only-begotten God the Word become incarnate, as stated above, was taught to us by the holy Fathers and teachers of the Church who interpreted the holy Scriptures.

Cyril of holy memory says in his letter to the Empress:

> “How, then, was he who is worshiped by the angels made lower than the angels? The reason is clear. He was brought down [variant: “was held”] within the measures of humanity. Taking a body naturally subject to death and making it his own, he willingly suffered in it and, because of the suffering, was crowned with the highest glories, since through it he abolished death and rendered corruption powerless, being himself immortality and life.
>
> “Whenever, therefore, he is called Jesus and is said to have been made lower than the angels, we do not understand a man separately and individually; rather, we understand the only-begotten himself, who, according to the dispensation, yields superiority to the holy angels, because he truly became man and was made lower than their superiority.
>
> “The holy angels possess superiority because they are outside flesh and are superior to death; the Son entered into these conditions through his voluntary emptying.
>
> “Yet he who was made a little lower than the angels according to the measure of humanity is worshiped by them in the superiority of divinity and is enthroned upon the seats around which they stand, continually glorifying him and calling him Lord of the powers.”

That the emptying also belongs to God the Word become incarnate is stated by the same Cyril in the writings against the objections of Theodoret, which Theodoret composed against Cyril’s fourth chapter:

> “I would hesitate to say without qualification that all human things are small in comparison with the Word who was born from God. But I ask: whose emptying could be understood to have taken place, and who suffered this voluntarily?
>
> “If, as they themselves say, the form of a servant—that is, what came from David’s seed—was assumed by God, how and in what manner was it emptied?
>
> “But if the Word himself, existing in the form and equality of God the Father, is said to have emptied himself, how and in what manner was he emptied, if he should refuse the emptying?
>
> “The emptying of God the Word, who knows no change, is the performance and utterance of human things because of the economy of his union with flesh.”

Again the same Cyril says in the same book against the Nestorians:

> “Has the divine Paul, speaking most clearly concerning the only-begotten to those sanctified through faith, perhaps deceived them when he said that, although he was rich, he became poor for our sake? Far from it; the herald of truth speaks truth in every respect.
>
> “But who is the rich one, and in what manner did he become poor? Let the word examine this for us.
>
> “If, as they boldly think and say, a man was assumed by God, how did the one assumed become poor, having been glorified and shining with honors beyond nature? For he has been glorified—or, if this is not true, their assumption has been slandered as bringing the measure of humanity down to what is lesser and more dishonorable.
>
> “But such an opinion is discordant. Therefore the one assumed did not become poor. It remains to say that the rich one, as God, entered into poverty according to us.”

Likewise St. Gregory the Theologian says in his discourse on the Theophany:

> “God came forth with the assumption, one from two opposites, flesh and spirit, of which the one deified and the other was deified.
>
> “O new mixture! O paradoxical blending! The one who is becomes; the uncreated is created; the uncontainable is contained through an intellectual soul mediating between divinity and the density of flesh; and the one who enriches becomes poor.
>
> “He becomes poor for my purification, so that I may share in his divinity; and the one who is full is emptied. He is emptied for a little while of his glory, so that I may share in his fullness.”

St. Athanasius, interpreting the Apostle’s words, “Although he existed in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” says:

> “What could be clearer or more demonstrative than this? He did not become better from something lesser; rather, although he was God, he took the form of a servant, and in taking it he was not improved but humbled himself.”

A little later:

> “What else is this than that the one who exists in the form of God, the Son of a noble Father, humbled himself and became a servant for us and on our behalf?”

And a little later:

> “The Word became flesh, and such a man is said to be from heaven and heavenly because the Word descended from heaven.”

St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, says in the third book against Eunomius:

> “We have believed these things concerning the one crucified. Therefore, exalting him according to the measure of our power, we do not cease, because the one whom nothing can contain, on account of his ineffable and inaccessible majesty, except himself, the Father, and the Holy Spirit, was able also to descend into communion with our weakness.
>
> “But those who make the Lord’s manifestation in flesh and on the cross proof that the Son is alien to the Father by nature say that the Father’s nature remained wholly in impassibility and could in no way receive communion with suffering, while the Son, because his nature had been altered toward what is lower, was able to undergo the experience of flesh and death.”

And later:

> “For this reason the cross is called the cross of the Lord of glory, and every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
>
> “If we must distinguish the remaining matters in the same way, let us consider what dies, what destroys death, what is renewed, and what is emptied. The divinity is emptied so that it may become accessible to human nature; the human is renewed through its blending with the divine and becomes divine.”

We have set forth these things from the teaching of the holy Fathers so that, understanding them, you may recognize that the things you have set forth are spoken impiously by Arians and Nestorians against our Lord and God Jesus Christ.

The Arians, striving to prove that the Son is a creature and alien to the Father’s substance, attribute the passion and the other lowly things to his divinity alone. The Nestorians, wishing to introduce two sons, speak separately of God the Word and separately of Christ as a mere man, assigning the lowly things to the man alone.

But the holy Fathers do not teach in this way. They do not speak of a transformation of the Son’s divinity because of the lowly things, nor do they divide humanity from divinity because of the lofty things. Rather, they teach that both the lofty and the lowly things belong to one and the same only-begotten God the Word become incarnate and man.

Since you also inserted into your chapters from the same letter the claim that it rightly spoke of two natures, one authority, and one person, let us expose the wickedness of the writer of the letter in this matter.

For the one who does not confess that God the Word himself became incarnate from the Virgin and became man—of what does he say that there are two natures? It is clear that he takes two natures in place of persons, according to Nestorius and Theodore, whom the impious letter praises.

Even if the letter seems to speak of one person and one son, Theodore and Nestorius say this too, claiming that Christ is merely a man who bears the person of God the Word, possesses the dignity and honor of God the Word, and the grace of adoption, and is worshiped in his place.

For this reason they pretend to speak of one son and one person of the Word and Christ, although the man shares sonship only in name. This is shown plainly by the letter’s statement that the two natures have one authority, as you also wrote.

“One authority” is not said of different natures but of different persons, as we confess concerning the holy Trinity.

Therefore the holy Fathers anathematized those who say that the man was united to the Word in power, dignity, authority, relation, or honor, and who do not confess that the union of the two natures took place according to hypostasis.

How those who hold the doctrines of Nestorius, whose leader in unbelief is Theodore, impiously interpret what the holy Fathers correctly said concerning the distinction of the two natures—speaking of natures in place of persons and advocating a relational union of persons while pretending to speak of one person—is shown by the impious Theodore himself in the fourth book against the heretic Apollinarius:

> “By these words he sufficiently indicates to us the difference of the natures: one is astonished that, because of extraordinary love for humanity, he chose to remember and visit what was so insignificant; the other is considered blessed as having been deemed worthy of such things.
>
> “Thus Scripture indicates both the division of the natures and the difference between the nature of the one who assumed and that of the one who was assumed. Yet, wishing also to indicate the union, or what came to the one who was assumed, it often says, according to the union, that each of the natures individually possesses the properties of the other, so that it might make clear to us the union of the one assumed with the one who assumed and whatever resulted for the one from his association with the other.”

Having shown that the impious Theodore speaks of natures in place of persons, let us bring forward an even greater blasphemy exposing him. What kind of union does he assert, to the condemnation of those who defend him?

In the eighth book on the incarnation he says:

> “It is clear that the matter of the union is appropriate. For through it the natures, brought together, constituted one person according to the union. Thus, just as the Lord says concerning man and woman, ‘They are no longer two but one flesh,’ so we too may appropriately say, according to the account of the union, that they are no longer two persons but one, while the natures remain distinct.
>
> “For just as there the number of the pair is not harmed by the flesh being called one—for it is clear in what sense it is called one—so here too the union does not destroy the distinction of the natures of the person.
>
> “Whenever we distinguish the natures, we say that the nature of God the Word is perfect and the person perfect; for it is impossible to speak of a hypostasis without a person. We likewise say that the nature of the man and the person are perfect.
>
> “But whenever we look to the conjunction, we then say that there is one person.”

Although it is dreadful to say such things to Christians, we have been compelled to set them forth because of the madness of those who defend Theodore and that impious letter. We pray that God may be merciful to us. By all these things it has been proved that that accursed letter is full of all Theodore’s impiety.

[Col. 0305C] We have answered all these matters contained in your compilation, by which you sought to defend that impious letter and, through it, renew the false doctrine of Theodore and Nestorius, whose impiety the same letter praises.

Since you omitted many passages from the aforementioned letter written to Maris the heretic, and did not dare to insert them into your chapters lest the Christian people among you learn from them the impiety which you defend, we considered it necessary to reveal these passages briefly.

Among the words of the impious letter omitted by you are these:

> “Cyril held captive the ears of all the bishops who assembled at the Council of Ephesus with the potion that blinds the eyes of the wise. He found an opportunity in his hatred of Nestorius, and the Council of Ephesus deposed Nestorius from the episcopate without any judgment or investigation.”

Again, the same letter says:

> “The Twelve Chapters written by Cyril, although contrary to the orthodox faith, were brought forward by the bishops assembled at Ephesus, confirmed, and approved by them as agreeing with the orthodox faith. Nestorius, because he was hated in his own city and by its leading men, could not return there.”

Throughout, the writer of the same impious letter not only defends and praises heretics but also denounces the orthodox.

Concerning the blessed Rabbula, bishop of Edessa, a distinguished man among bishops, whose tomb performs miracles to this day, he says in the same impious letter:

> “The tyrant of our city, whom you yourself do not fail to know, under pretext of the faith persecutes not only those living with him but also those who departed long ago to the Lord. One of these is the blessed Theodore, herald of the truth and teacher of the Church, who not only during his life chastised the heretics through his own faith but, after death, left spiritual weapons in his own books to the children of the Church, as your reverence knows from having spoken with him and having believed his writings. This man the one who dares everything dared publicly to anathematize in the churches.”

Again, the same impious letter contains, as an insult to Cyril of holy memory:

> “The Egyptian’s heart was softened, and without plunder he agreed with the orthodox faith. They rushed disorderly against the living and the dead, and are now disgraced as they defend their own offenses, teaching things contrary to their earlier doctrine, and saying that one must confess the temple and the one dwelling in the temple.”

We have taken care to make these things contained in the letter mentioned above clear to you, so that perhaps, even at this late hour, you may choose what is right and depart from this false doctrine.

So great is the impiety of the foul letter that even you did not dare insert into the chapters you sent everything contained in it, although you attempted to interpret some passages from it with a distorted meaning.

For who can be numbered among Christians without calling the letter impious, when it contains such and so many blasphemies?

Whoever defends the letter that calls the holy Cyril a heretic and casts out the First Council of Ephesus plainly accepts Nestorius and his impiety. The same letter says that he was condemned without judgment or investigation, not because of his doctrines but because of the hatred of his fellow citizens, and that he could not return to the Church.

The one who defends the impious letter not only errs in this but also condemns Pope Celestine, who said concerning Cyril, “Cyril’s faith is our faith.”

And the one who says that the Twelve Chapters of Cyril of holy memory are contrary to the orthodox faith condemns not only Cyril himself, Celestine of blessed memory, and the First Council of Ephesus, but also condemns the Council of Chalcedon, which inscribed Cyril as its own father and teacher.

He likewise condemns Leo, Pope of Rome and of holy memory, who, writing to the Council of Chalcedon, said concerning the Twelve Chapters of Cyril of holy memory:

> “The decrees issued by Cyril of holy memory against Nestorius must remain firmly established.”

Although filled with every kind of impiety, the foul letter was unable to conceal one truth: Theodore was anathematized by orthodox and holy men, expelled from the Church, and anathematized even after death.

The same impious letter calls the impious Theodore a teacher of the Church and a herald of the truth, although he blasphemed more than all the heretics.

We have already revealed to you, in another letter, a very small part of his blasphemies, using his own words, and have shown what the holy Fathers Cyril, Proclus, and Rabbula wrote against Theodore and his impious words, condemning him together with his impiety.

These are Theodore’s blasphemies, and they are so grave [variant: “so that”] that even you did not dare defend them, although you defend the one who set them forth. It is evident that no one who condemns evil defends the person who set it forth, unless that person has repented, abandoned his own error, and condemned those things.

To the other insults spoken in the same letter against Cyril of holy memory is added the claim that Cyril himself was shameless and that, after repenting, he set forth things contrary to his earlier teaching.

From this the writer of that letter is shown to be full of every kind of folly. Where did Cyril of holy memory set forth anything contrary to his earlier teaching, or repent? And how would the holy Council of Chalcedon have inscribed him as its father if he had repented, as the letter claims?

The person who repents is not numbered among teachers; he is received as one who has returned from error.

Finally, the writer of the letter concluded with this statement:

> “One must confess the temple and the one dwelling in the temple.”

From these words, insofar as they concern the impiety of the letter and those who defend it, the whole orthodox faith is overthrown.

For the catholic Church confesses one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God; it does not teach belief or confession in a temple and in the one dwelling in the temple.

Therefore those who seek holy baptism are instructed to confess and believe in one Father almighty, in one Lord Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, and in the Holy Spirit—not in two sons or two Christs.

This is what the letter to Maris the Persian indicates when it says that one must confess the temple and the one dwelling in the temple, thereby introducing a fourth person into the holy Trinity.

From all these considerations, then, it has been demonstrated that whoever praises or defends the aforementioned impious letter is alien to the orthodox faith.

But since you say that the holy Cyril was received by the Easterners for this reason—that he interpreted his own Chapters—we do not wonder at you, since you were likewise deceived by the Chapters sent by you, although you have failed to understand what was written in the First Council at Ephesus itself. For the holy Celestine, the First Council at Ephesus, the holy Leo, and the holy Council at Chalcedon accepted and confirmed the Chapters of the holy Cyril as they stood, and sought no interpretation of them. The interpretation was not made for the orthodox, but for the heretics who defended Nestorius and opposed the Chapters just mentioned. For, according to what you say, neither the holy Gospels, nor the Apostle, nor the other divine Scriptures are acceptable unless the holy Fathers have interpreted them.

You ought to blush when you say that the Easterners, who defended Nestorius, accepted the holy Cyril while he was interpreting his own Chapters. On the contrary, the Apostolic See of Rome and the holy Cyril accepted into communion the Eastern bishops who had condemned Nestorius and his impiety. Thus also the holy Xystus, pope of Rome, wrote with his own synod to the holy Cyril, praising his labors on behalf of unity, and among other things said:

> “The brothers have returned to us—I say, to us—those whom, after driving away the disease with united zeal, we took care to heal in soul.”

And again:

> “Rejoice, beloved brother, and exult as a victor when the brothers have been gathered to us. The Church was seeking those whom she has recovered. For if we do not wish any of the little ones to perish, how much more ought we to rejoice at the health of those who are leaders? We have read [read: ἀνέγνωμεν] how much joy one sheep brought back afforded, and we ought to reflect how much praise is due for gathering together so many shepherds. In each case flocks are contemplated; whenever action is taken concerning the health of the many, the matter is not sought for one alone.”

And again:

> “Let us rejoice that the priest of the Church of the Antiochenes is now being called by Your Holiness—a most reverent man and a lord. He is rightly called ‘lord,’ since he has recognized the common Lord, who confesses with us, in orthodox speech, the mystery of his incarnation.”

And again:

> “Afflictions are always desirable for the one who proclaims the faith. For a rich reward has been prepared in heaven, together with blessedness, for those who are commanded to endure insults, persecutions, and every evil for righteousness’ sake. You endured falsehood in order to make truth victorious. Therefore, now you must rise up against falsehood, since no one has been destroyed by truth.”

And again:

> “The holy brotherhood with me has written these things in reply to Your Reverence, accepting all that is yours and affirming your labors—labors which have not been burdensome or bitter, since they were undertaken for the sake of him whose burden is light and whose yoke is gracious.”

These things, then, the holy Xystus wrote to the holy Cyril concerning the Easterners.

But since you have also said this foolishly—that the condemnation of the impious letter to Maris damages the reputation of the holy Council at Chalcedon—we ask you: for what reason did you dare to write this? Do you perhaps think that the Definition of the holy Council at Chalcedon contains something resembling the impious letter? May no Christian ever say such a thing! For understand that everything contained in that impious letter and in Theodore’s writings is contrary to the Definition concerning the faith issued by the Council of Chalcedon.

Theodore and the letter say that the Word of God is one person and Christ another. But the holy Council at Chalcedon says that our one Lord Jesus Christ is the Word of God made flesh and unchangeably become man.
