The letter and Theodore do not confess that the Word of God was made flesh from the holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mary, the Mother of God, and was born from her; for this reason they deny that the holy Virgin Mary is the Mother of God. But the holy Fathers who assembled synodically at Chalcedon confessed that the holy Virgin Mary is the Mother of God.

The impious Theodore and the anonymous letter speak of two persons and fabricate one person by a relative union. But the Council, speaking of the union of the two natures according to hypostasis, proclaims one person—that is, one hypostasis—of Christ, the only-begotten Word of God.

Again, that impious letter condemns the First Council at Ephesus and the holy Cyril, and calls his Chapters impious. It defends and praises Nestorius and Theodore. But the Council at Chalcedon follows in every respect that First Council at Ephesus; it designates Cyril as father and teacher; it confirms his synodical letter, in which the Twelve Chapters are appended; it condemns the impious Nestorius; and, in addition, it condemns the Jewish creed fabricated by Theodore—condemned also at the First Council at Ephesus—which was later produced at the Council at Chalcedon, together with its author, and condemned in like manner.

The holy Council at Chalcedon set these things forth in its definitions, introducing nothing new concerning the orthodox faith, but following throughout the confession of faith which the Lord gave through the holy Apostles, which the holy Apostles preached, which the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers handed down to the Church of God, and which the one hundred and fifty Fathers confirmed by clarifying the divinity of the Holy Spirit. The holy Fathers who had previously assembled at Ephesus followed this same confession. The holy Council at Chalcedon also anathematized those who handed down another creed or exposition of faith besides that transmitted by the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers.

Since the truth stands thus, consider at last who rightly defends the holy Council at Chalcedon. Is it the person who demonstrates that, having followed the holy Fathers mentioned above, it set forth everything correctly? Or the person who strives to attribute to it the impious words of the heretics?

It is impossible to accept with a clear conscience and right intention the First Council at Ephesus, the holy Fathers Celestine, Cyril, and Leo, and the Definition of the Council at Chalcedon, while also accepting the foul letter to Maris, which contradicts all these. For who can accept together the teachers of the Church and those who teach contrary things; the orthodox and the heretics; those who condemned and those who were condemned?

So that you may understand more fully what was set in motion concerning Ibas and Theodoret, we have deemed it necessary to make these matters clear to you as well.

Know, then, that at different times, because of the impiety of Theodore and Nestorius contained in that same letter, and because of the insults spoken against the holy Cyril and his Chapters, Ibas was accused before Emperor Theodosius of pious memory [Note: [Col. 0313D] λήξεως, “end”; alternatively λέξεως, “wording.” Proclus, Archbishop of Constantinople.], before Proclus, the holy archbishop of Constantinople, before various archbishops of Antioch, and finally before the same emperor and Flavian, who had become archbishop of Constantinople after Proclus. The case brought against Ibas was assigned to Photius, bishop of Tyre, and Eustathius, bishop of Berytus. Before them Ibas was accused both concerning the faith and concerning insults committed against the holy Cyril.

In his defense he replied that after the union which had taken place between the Easterners and the holy Cyril, he had neither said nor written anything insulting against him. But this foul letter, produced by his accusers, shows that it was written after the union.

Ibas is therefore shown, by his own deposition, to have denied the letter in question. Accordingly, the bishops mentioned above, seeing the impiety of the letter, although Ibas did not acknowledge it as his own, nevertheless issued a decision entirely opposed to the impiety contained in that letter. For they decreed that Ibas should anathematize Nestorius, his impious doctrines, and those who defended him—precisely the persons whom the impious letter defended—and should likewise accept the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers and the First Council at Ephesus as having been assembled by the Holy Spirit, in the same manner as the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers. That Council at Ephesus, together with the holy Cyril himself and his Twelve Chapters, the same impious letter insults.

Ibas did not fulfill what had been decided by the judges; therefore he was deposed from the episcopate. After this, the holy Council at Chalcedon assembled. Ibas was neither summoned nor present as a bishop, since Nonnus had already been ordained in his place and was also summoned to the holy Council at Chalcedon.

But after the Definition concerning the faith had been issued, the aforementioned Ibas entered and requested that his case be examined—the case on account of which he had been deposed—and he produced the decision of Photius and Eustathius. When it had been read, his accusers also entered and produced the acts at Tyre, in which the same impious letter was contained. When it had been read, Ibas, knowing that if he acknowledged it as his own he would be condemned because of its impiety, interrupted the reading of the proceedings and said:

> “Order the letters of the clergy of Edessa to be read, so that from them you may learn that I am unrelated to the charges brought against me.”

When these letters had been read, the bishops, having understood the decision of Photius and Eustathius and the accusation brought against Ibas, required him to fulfill what had been decided by Photius and Eustathius, to accept the Definition pronounced by that holy Council, and to subscribe it. By doing so he also accepted the First Council at Ephesus, the holy Cyril, and his teaching. All these things, as we have said, that foul letter insults. From this it is demonstrated that the holy Council at Chalcedon arranged all these matters in order to condemn and overthrow that impious letter of Ibas.

We therefore marvel at you, because you defend that foul letter, which Ibas himself did not dare to call his own or defend, either at Tyre or afterward at the holy Council at Chalcedon. Rather, he used the letters of the clergy of Edessa and the decision of Photius and Eustathius to escape the accusation brought against him concerning the impious letter.

In addition to all the other matters which you have badly interpreted, you also turn the discourse of Eunomius concerning Ibas toward a false meaning, asserting that Eunomius’s discourse was made in defense of the impious letter. For that discourse is said to contain the following: after insulting the holy Cyril in the earlier part of the letter, Ibas corrected himself at the end. It is therefore clear that Eunomius’s discourse was not spoken concerning that impious letter, but concerning the deposition of Ibas made at Tyre by Photius and Eustathius.

For in the proceedings conducted before them Ibas clearly confessed, as we have said above, that before this, when there was dissension between them, he had insulted the holy Cyril together with the other Eastern bishops; but that after the union which took place between them, he had said nothing insulting against the holy Cyril. From this confession Eunomius found that Ibas had first insulted the holy Cyril, then defended himself and said that after the union he had said nothing insulting against the holy Cyril; and on this basis he composed the discourse in question.

That the aforementioned impious letter, called “the letter of Ibas,” is filled from beginning to end with every kind of impiety and with insults against Cyril is beyond dispute. But there is also no reason to believe that Eunomius first denounced the earlier parts of the letter as evil, and then praised the final parts, which were worse. No sane person accepts someone praising and blaming the same person at the same time concerning one and the same matter.

If, then, anyone dares to say that Eunomius’s discourse does not correspond to the deposition of Ibas made at Tyre, but agrees with the style of the aforementioned impious letter, he does not preserve the sequence of truth; rather, like a heretic, he strives to heap insult upon the Fathers.

[Col. 0317D] We also marveled at this: that you dared to write that the Chapters of the holy Cyril are obscure, while praising the impious letter as having been accepted with the Holy Spirit presiding. It is evident that you have advanced these words not from the Holy Spirit but from the activity of the evil spirit: you called the Fathers and teachers of the Church obscure, while praising the letter’s evil doctrine with blasphemy.

Therefore the saying of the holy Apostle Peter concerning those who misunderstand the letters of the holy Paul applies well both to you and to the others who think like you about the holy Fathers:

> “The ignorant and unstable twist these things—as they do the other Scriptures—to their own destruction.”

Thus, to you also, who misunderstand, the things set forth by the teachers of the Church and in the divine Scriptures appear obscure. These, then, are the matters concerning Ibas and that impious letter, as they are found arranged in certain books.

You ought to know that the proceedings in which that impious letter is contained are not appended to the authentic documents signed by the bishops. Copies of these authentic documents were also deposited in the most holy Church of Rome, in Constantinople, and in our imperial palace.

Since, then, that same impious letter is shown on every side to be filled with all impiety and to be contrary to the definitions of the holy Council at Chalcedon, those who say that it was accepted by the holy Council at Chalcedon are striving not only to defend their own evil doctrine, but also to heap insult upon that holy Council. For what was accepted and confirmed by that holy Council is contained by name in the Definition concerning the faith issued by it.

We wish you to know also that, because Theodoret wrote against the Twelve Chapters of the holy Cyril while defending Nestorius and his evil doctrine, he too was brought forward after the Definition of the holy Council at Chalcedon and was first required to anathematize Nestorius and his impiety, and to confess that the holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mary is the Mother of God; only then was he accepted.

Therefore both Ibas and Theodoret were accepted not as teachers and fathers, but as men who had repented, anathematized the evil doctrine for which they had been accused, accepted the Definition of the Council at Chalcedon, and subscribed to it. For it is customary in the catholic Church to receive into communion all heretics who depart from their own error and return to the orthodox faith, but not to number them among the Fathers as teachers.

Accordingly, the apostolic throne of Rome, the holy Cyril, and therefore also the holy Church of God, accepted the other Eastern bishops who, while defending Nestorius, had opposed the First Council at Ephesus and the holy Cyril, because afterward they anathematized Nestorius and his evil doctrine.

We also wish you to know that not only Ibas and Theodoret were expelled from the episcopate because they opposed the Twelve Chapters of the holy Cyril, but Domnus, archbishop of Antioch, was also condemned for writing that those same Twelve Chapters ought merely to be silenced. The condemnation pronounced against Domnus was accepted and confirmed even after his death by the Council at Chalcedon.

That this is true is testified by Theodoret himself in a letter to John, bishop of Germanicia, where he writes as follows:

> “Why do they also lie openly and say that no innovation concerning doctrine has taken place? For what murders and sorceries was I expelled? What adultery did this one dare to commit? What tombs did that one break open? It is clear even to barbarians. I ask [sic]: they expelled me and the others because of doctrines. For they also deposed Lord Domnus because he had not accepted the Chapters, calling them most praiseworthy and confessing that he would remain committed to them. I read their depositions, and they excommunicated me as the leader of the heresy.”

From this, then, it is demonstrated that Domnus, Theodoret himself, Ibas, and certain others were expelled because of the Chapters of the holy Cyril proposed against Nestorius. The holy Council at Chalcedon accepted Theodoret and Ibas after they had repented, accepted the Chapters mentioned above, and accepted the other matters on account of which they had been expelled. The others, however, who did not repent, were not accepted; and the condemnation of Domnus was confirmed even after his death.

[Col. 0321B] Since you have written that you anathematize the blasphemies of Theodore which were sent to you by us—“if they belong to anyone”—but have hesitated to anathematize Theodore himself because, as is said, he had already died in communion with the churches, know [F. supplies ὅτι, “that”] that those who say that Theodore may not be anathematized, but must be numbered among the bishops because he died in communion with the Church, as you have said, ought also to number Judas among the Apostles—Judas who thought he had secretly escaped the notice of the God who knows the hidden things of human beings, and who had received communion from him together with the other disciples.

For, so far as those who say these things are concerned, even the Apostles would deserve blame: after Judas’s death they brought forward a decision against him, condemned him, and introduced another in his place.

Again, since his name is read among the other Apostles in the holy Gospels, should he therefore be accepted as an Apostle, or should he have been exempted from the condemnation of anathema?

Understand, then, that the person who dies in communion with the churches is the one who preserves the orthodox faith to the very end of his life.

For even if a Manichaean, an Arian, a Nestorian, an Eutychian, or any other heretic, or someone dominated by pagan madness, secretly communicates with the Church and dies in that state, and afterward is shown to have been a heretic either from his writings or in some other way, nevertheless the orthodox faith is not harmed by this, nor is he released from condemnation because he is said to have died in [the manuscript reads ἣ, “which,” for ἐν, “in”] the peace of the churches. In general, death frees no heretic from condemnation for his evil doctrine; rather, it condemns him all the more for having failed to repent while alive.

That heretics who did not repent during their lives were condemned even after death is demonstrated by many examples. Eunomius, Apollinaris, Bonosus, and, in earlier times, Valentinus, Basilides, Marcion, Cerinthus, and many others, though not anathematized during their own lives, were condemned after death and anathematized by the catholic Church, because they died in their own error.

Likewise, those who were unjustly condemned during their own lives were recalled after death by the catholic Church—namely, John and Flavian, the holy archbishops of Constantinople. According to your understanding, then, heretics who died in their own error ought to be freed, while orthodox persons who were unjustly condemned ought not to be recalled after death. This is filled with every kind of impiety.

That it is an ecclesiastical tradition to condemn and anathematize heretics even after death we have demonstrated from these examples. Nevertheless, it is also shown by the ordinances of the holy Apostles. For when they say that almsgiving ought to be offered for the repose of the departed, they add:

> “We say these things concerning the godly. But concerning the impious: even if he gives the possessions of the world to the poor, it will benefit him nothing; for if, while he lived, the divine power was against him, it is clear that it is also against him after his departure.”

Since, then, the Apostles laid down this rule concerning the godly, who could say that heretics after death—or Theodore in particular—ought to be freed from the condemnation of anathema? The holy Fathers counted Theodore among those who were worse than Jews, Greeks, Sodomites, and all heretics because of his blasphemies, and condemned him together with his impiety.

That heretics must be anathematized even after death, as we said earlier, is also stated by the holy Augustine, bishop of an African city, in his letter to Boniface:

> “Even if what they brought forward against Caecilian and against you could be shown to be true, and even if he were dead, we would anathematize him. Nevertheless, we ought not to abandon the Church of Christ on account of any human being—the Church which is not changed by quarrelsome opinions but is confirmed by divine testimonies.”

These, then, are the words of the holy Augustine.

The holy Fathers do not anathematize after death only those who have erred concerning the faith, but also bishops who in their final wishes, or while dying intestate, leave their property to heretical relatives or to outsiders. For the eighty-first canon of the Council in Africa says:

> “Again it has been decreed: if any bishop prefers outsiders who are not of his family, or heretics—even if they are his relatives—or pagans, to the Church, let him also be anathematized after death; let his name not be read among the priests of God; and let him not be exempt from condemnation even if he dies intestate. For, having become a bishop, he ought in no way to have postponed the administration of his own property in a manner appropriate to his calling.”

If, then, according to the ecclesiastical canon, bishops are anathematized even after death for improperly administering their own possessions, how much more ought those who sin against God himself to be anathematized, since Holy Scripture says:

> “If a person sins against another person, they will pray for him; but if anyone sins against God, who will pray for him?” [The source breaks off here.]

Having demonstrated that in former times the holy Fathers decreed that those who had sinned either against the faith or against the canons ought to be anathematized even after death, we considered it necessary to make clear to everyone what has occurred in our own times, in order to remove every pretext from those who defend manifest heretics and their impiety.

Laurentius and Dioscorus, who at different times usurped the priesthood of the Apostolic See, were condemned and anathematized after death by the Apostolic See. Although they did not err concerning the faith, they nevertheless strove improperly to seize the episcopate.

[Col. 0325B] Since you have also added this to your writings: that if anyone anathematizes the leader of a heresy and says, in condemning him, “and those who hold the same opinions as he,” he thereby includes everyone who ever held those opinions; and therefore, since you anathematize Paul of Samosata, Photinus, Bonosus, and Nestorius, you ought not also to anathematize by name Theodore, who held opinions like theirs—know that, first, those who followed the leaders of the heresies in error are anathematized without being named individually, but not those who deceived others.

For the Church of God anathematizes the originators of the heresies by name. Theodore, however, was not only a teacher of Nestorius’s impiety; through his impious writings he also deceived many.

Just as the orthodox teachers of the Church are known and praised through their own expositions, so, conversely, all the leaders of evil doctrine are exposed and anathematized through their own impious writings.

Since Theodore therefore became a leader of heresy and spewed out innumerable blasphemies in his own books, you have no legitimate pretext for refusing to anathematize him.

Concerning the exposition of the faith which you inserted into your writings: although we had many criticisms to make, we nevertheless thought that, because of your ignorance and simplicity, it should for the present be passed over. In some places you have written carelessly. In certain places you have inserted words unknown either to the divine Scriptures or to the holy Fathers; in others, you have condemned the teachers of the Church insofar as this concerns you. In addition, you have omitted certain matters that contribute to the orthodox faith.

Therefore, according to the exhortation of the holy Fathers, you must either speak with knowledge, or remain silent in ignorance, and learn from those who possess understanding.

Since you have written to us asking how we ought to answer the Egyptians, we marvel at you: while defending that impious letter, Theodore, Nestorius, and their evil doctrine, you attempt to advise us about what answer we ought to give to those opposed to the Church.

For if anyone, agreeing with what you have written, advises the Egyptians to do nothing other than accept the heretics Theodore and Nestorius, condemn all the holy Fathers who condemned them and their unbelief, and thereby fall from one error into another, then—when you wrote to us that we should answer those opposed to the Church—you were calling that foul letter beautiful and orthodox.

Strive, then, first to correct yourselves, and only afterward to teach others.

For if anyone defends either Theodore, or the so-called letter of Ibas, or the writings of Theodoret composed against the orthodox faith, he numbers himself among the heretics and makes himself alien to the catholic Church, whose head is the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord and God Jesus Christ. By defending the impious letter and Theodore, you separate yourselves from him.

Therefore you ought to abstain from the impiety of the letter and from defending Theodore, who is so manifestly a heretic.

For if the holy Apostle Paul forbids anyone to be called by his own name in one instance and by the names of the other Apostles in another, and rebukes those who say, “I belong to Paul …”

Not a few things are missing.

## Copy of the letter written by the most pious and most Christian Emperor Justinian against certain persons who defend in writing the impious Theodore and his wicked doctrines, the letter called that of Ibas, and likewise the books of Theodoret against the catholic faith

[Note: [Col. 0275D] This letter, which had until now remained entirely unknown and which contributes greatly to advancing ecclesiastical affairs, is now brought to light with a Latin translation, elegantly prepared by the most distinguished monk of the Dominican family, Jo. Dominicus Stratico [Col. 0276D], from the recension of the most distinguished Angelus Maria Bandini, Doctor of Both Laws and prefect of the Caesarean Medicean library.]

[Col. 0276A]

We have received your letters. As we read them, we were greatly astonished that, paying no attention to that command of the Lord in which it was said, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29), you have been raised to such a height that you judge all the bishops of the Church of God worthless, while imagining that you alone, above all others, have attained justice—thereby resembling the Pharisee who was not justified because he condemned the publican as unrighteous (Luke 18:14).

Although we had hoped that you would think wisely, without differing from the other priests, we unexpectedly found that you uphold doctrines which conflict with God and with the right faith, and that, while defending such impiety with every effort, you take as your defense the claim that you are equal to the Apostles. You assert that no one may criticize you for ignorance and lack of education, since God himself entrusted the preaching of his Gospel even to uneducated and rustic men.

When we called you rustic, we used that manner of speaking because, neglecting the ecclesiastical rules and traditions and being ignorant of the orthodox faith itself, you were defending that impiety. God chose the Apostles whom you have taken pleasure in calling rustic, and filled them with his Spirit and wisdom; thus prepared, he sent them to be guides for the nations who do not know God, leading them onto the path of truth.

Therefore it was said uniquely to the Apostles: “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14). Be luminous, then, just as the Lord again said to them: “Do not consider what you will say, or what you will speak, or concerning what matter you will bear witness” (Matthew 10:29).

You have dared to compare yourselves with the Apostles and have not feared to assail all priests with insult. Indeed, you have so neglected the ecclesiastical sanctions that you have begun, with the utmost audacity, to attempt what no one in any age of the Christian religion has ever attempted.

While the most blessed patriarchs have always mutually preserved inviolate the tradition handed down among them, no one ever divided the Church by schism unless he had been openly seized by heretical madness. You have now arranged for this to happen. We burn with a vehement desire to heal the evil which you have undertaken to perpetrate, striving by both action and writing for this one purpose: that you may come to your senses.

Now, since you have written that we carefully arranged for these three Chapters—theodore, namely, together with his writings; the letter called that of Ibas; and likewise the writings of Theodoret—to be condemned, with the intention of satisfying our own will, because we were inflamed by an extraordinary desire that they should be separated from the catholic Church, understand that we did not do this on their account. We acted first because we had been gravely disturbed by the impiety of those Chapters, and afterward because there were people who, suppressing the name of Nestorius while favoring Nestorius’s party, attempted to introduce his erroneous faith and did not hesitate to attribute the impiety of those Chapters to the Church.

[Col. 0278A] Although the wickedness of the Chapters was manifest, we nevertheless asked the bishops of the Church of God, gathered together as one, what they thought should be decreed concerning them. When they wished to demonstrate by clear testimony that errors of this kind were neither approved by the Church nor had ever at any time been approved, they all, by their vote, proscribed that impiety, which had initially been condemned by the holy Fathers.

Those who have been separated from the Church because of their defense of the Three Chapters are completely silent. They plainly understand that such things cannot possibly be defended by anyone who is called a Christian. Instead, they openly oppose the holy Council of Chalcedon, which defined the doctrine of the faith in the condemnation of the errors of Nestorius, Eutyches, and those introduced by them.

Those who oppose the right doctrines of the Church, however, strive with all their strength to make it appear that the aforementioned three wicked Chapters were accepted by the Church of God and ought therefore to be upheld, so that in this way they may deceive the simpler and divide the Christian people by schism.

Thus, since you have written two principal things—if everything contained in those impious letters is compressed into a few words—you have said, first, that the letter rightly argues against Apollinaris; and second, that although its author appears at the beginning to insult Saint Cyril unjustly, he removed the stain of the insult at the end, and that consequently it is worthwhile to judge that impious letter catholic.

First of all, take this as certain: you have understood neither the sequence of words nor the force of the arguments in that impious letter. It does not conclude against Apollinaris; rather, it counts Saint Cyril himself among the followers of Apollinaris. So far is it from correcting at the end anything that was said against Saint Cyril that, toward the conclusion, its author appears to rage against Cyril even more viciously.

Therefore, beginning with this point, and also with the whole impiety of the letter called that of Ibas and the madness of the Chapters which you sent to us, we shall demonstrate the matter by arguments.

When we had read everything that you wrote, we were afflicted with the deepest grief that you, citizens of that city in which the right faith had always been preserved uniquely until the present time, had fallen into such great error. We therefore considered it necessary to write to you against the aforementioned Chapters and to warn you yourselves about their impiety, so that you might withdraw from your wicked teacher, who committed them to written record.

For since he had resolved to lead you into deception, he drew certain statements from the divine Scriptures and, twisting them into an evil meaning, undertook to confirm some opinions of that impious letter—just as it has always been customary for heretics to pervert certain testimonies of the divine Scriptures and distort them toward the opposite understanding.

We therefore think either that your teacher did not read through that anonymous letter at all, or that he read some passages in very bad faith while passing over in silence the rest, which were far worse.

[Col. 0280A] For since that letter relates that blessed Cyril and impious Nestorius assailed one another with insults, and that Nestorius affirmed that the blessed Virgin was not the Mother of God, as many followers of the heresy of Paul of Samosata preferred her to be called; and since it says that Cyril, who attempted to refute Nestorius’s error, had likewise fallen and descended into the doctrines of Apollinaris, it is clearer than daylight that the author of the letter is shown to have been seized beforehand by Nestorian madness.

He claims that Nestorius, who refused to confess holy Mary the Virgin as Mother of God, merely gave some people grounds for suspicion against himself, but was not thereby demonstrated to be a heretic. Cyril, however, the holy teacher of the Church, he explicitly says fell into the heresy of Apollinaris, because Cyril said that God the Word had become incarnate and had assumed humanity.

Your teacher passed over these words, although, as we noted above, he clearly understood that anyone who says that Cyril fell into heresy and maintains that Cyril defended heretical opinions pronounces a sentence of condemnation against the whole Church, since the whole Church honors Cyril as father and teacher.

How could he fail to shudder at calling Cyril a heretic because he taught that God the Word had become man, and then adding that, because Cyril taught these things, no distinction between the temple and the one dwelling in it is admitted?

By this manner of speaking he accuses not holy Cyril, but the Evangelist, who plainly declares that the Word became flesh (John 1:14); all the prophets, who foretold the coming of the Word in the flesh, especially Jeremiah, who says, “This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3); and Isaiah, who likewise says, “A child, the mighty God” (Isaiah 9:6).

He accuses above all the Apostle Paul, whose statement in his Epistle to the Ephesians is this: “He who descended is himself also the one who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things” (Ephesians 4:9).

If we wished to agree with your foolish teacher, we would accuse the prophets, evangelists, and Apostles of heresy because they said that the Word of God became man, as though by these forms of speech they had admitted a conversion of divinity into humanity.

But those who do not confess that God the Word became man plainly make Christ a mere human being, adorned with the name of Son of God only by grace, according to the erroneous opinion established by Nestorius and his teacher Theodore.

For the divine Scriptures, and the holy Fathers of the Church who adhere to them, most explicitly confess that God the Word himself—the invisible one, without a body, light from light, begotten from the Father before the ages and times—came, was incarnate, and became man.

For Saint Gregory, in his sermon on the Theophanies, or on the Nativity of Christ, says:

> “The invisible Word of God himself, he who is older than the ages, he who is incomprehensible, he who is incorporeal, that light from light, beginning from beginning, the fountain of life and immortality, the archetypal expression, the unmoved seal, the image wholly like the original, the limit and reason of the Father—he, I say, comes to his own image, bears flesh for the sake of flesh, and is joined to an intellectual soul for the sake of my soul, so that he may cleanse like with like. He assumes all that is human except sin, conceived from the Virgin, whose mind and body had been purified beforehand by the Spirit; for it was necessary both to honor the Nativity and to prefer virginity.”

Athanasius explains the matter in exactly the same way in the discourse against the Arians, concerning the Holy Spirit:

> “He who had been ineffably, inexplicably, immutably, and eternally begotten above in heaven from the Father was himself begotten below on earth in time from the Virgin Mary.”

Basil likewise writes in the eighth chapter of his book to Amphilochius:

> “Neither heaven and earth, nor the boundless seas, nor living creatures dwelling in water or on land, nor plants, nor stars, nor air, nor the hours, nor the manifold adornment of the universe commend the excellence of his power to us as much as this: that the incomprehensible God was so subjected to conflict in the flesh that the divinity itself suffered nothing, while through his death he bestowed immortality upon us.”

Saint Augustine, bishop of an African city, also explains the Creed in this manner:

> “The prophet Habakkuk brought you [Greek: profer et tu, ‘bring forward also’] a testimony concerning Christ: ‘Lord,’ he says, ‘I heard your report, and I was afraid; I understood your works, O God, and I was terrified.’ What works of God did he admire and fear here? The creation of the world? Certainly not. But hear why he was terrified. ‘In the midst of two living creatures your works shall be known, O God,’ he says, because you, God the Word made flesh, will be made known in the midst of two living creatures. What were you, and how far did you descend? You have astonished me, because you, the Word through whom all things were made, were born in a manger.”

Saint Leo, the Roman pontiff, says similar things in his letter to Flavian, archbishop of Constantinople:

> “The impassible God did not disdain to be a passible human being, and the immortal did not refuse to be subject to the laws of death.”

[Col. 0282C] Thus the divine Scriptures and the holy Fathers speak in this sense. Yet according to your judgment they must be corrected, as though they introduced a confusion of flesh and divinity, although they too explicitly declare that God the Word became man—precisely the same way in which you attacked Cyril for saying that God the Word became man, as though that manner of speaking introduced confusion.

We have clearly concluded from what the author of that letter wrote to the heretic Theodore against the impious Apollinaris that he was seized by Theodore’s delirious teachings and denied that God the Word became man.

For in his fourth sermon he writes:

> “You said that some of our people hold certain opinions which have never been approved by those who strive to adhere to ecclesiastical doctrines. When we asked them whether they confessed that God the Word became man, they produced an affirmative answer. But who [F. reads mentis, ‘mind,’ for meriti] in his right mind would say that God the Word became man in the manner you customarily propose, unless he were first afflicted with the disease of your madness? We, for our part, steadfastly confess that God assumed a human being; but we absolutely do not tolerate saying that he became man, as you are accustomed to express it.”

Since, then, by what he writes to Theodore he shows that the impiety of the letter agrees remarkably with Theodore’s delirious teachings, how could any just person, whose hope is placed in the incarnate and human-made Word of God, fail to condemn Theodore and, together with him, the impious letter?

Since you strongly approve what is taught in that execrable letter—namely, that the doctrine which calls the Word God incarnate and made man abolishes the distinction between the temple and the one dwelling in the temple—understand that the distinction of the natures from which Christ our one God and Savior is constituted is rightly proclaimed by the holy Church of God.

But no holy Father ever proposed this distinction of the temple and the one dwelling in it. It was invented only by the impious Theodore and Nestorius, because they had decided thereby to introduce two persons.

Whenever the divine Scriptures and the holy Fathers of the Church have used the figurative designation “temple,” they did so merely to signify the body of the only-begotten Son of God, exactly as the Evangelist says of him: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:21).

They did not introduce these distinctions into the one person of Christ, as though one thing were in another. They admitted only a distinction of natures, from which one Christ is perfected, without mixture or division.

You, therefore, by defending the impiety of that letter, in which it is denied that God the Word became man, are plainly convicted of admitting two persons in Christ. In this way, by teaching delirious things about Christ as though he were a mere human being, you speak about him in the same manner in which the Apostle said concerning believers: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (1 Corinthians 3:16).

Thus, if your error is taken into account, no distinction remains between us human beings and Christ, in accordance with what Theodore the heretic, the teacher of the author of that letter, foolishly devised in his third sermon against Apollinaris. Introducing Christ as speaking about himself, he writes:

> “I, whom you see, can do nothing according to my nature, since I am a human being. But I act because the Father, remaining in me, accomplishes all things. Indeed, he says, I am in the Father and the Father is in me. God the Word, the only-begotten, is in me. It is certain that the Father also remains with him in me and performs the works. Nor is it surprising that these things should be believed concerning Christ, since he himself plainly says concerning other human beings: ‘Whoever loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him’ (John 14:23). If both the Father and the Son make their dwelling with each such human being, what is surprising if, in the Lord Christ according to the flesh, both were likewise thought to remain together, their communion according to substance perhaps also receiving the communion of dwelling?”

Since the impious Theodore proposed these things in this way, it should not be surprising that, having fallen away from God, he joined folly to impiety, as the prophetic saying of Isaiah declares concerning the impious: “The foolish man will speak foolish things, and his heart will think senseless things” (Isaiah 32:6).

For whoever asserts that the Father and the Son remain in Christ in the same way as in other human beings, and does not confess that God the Word is Christ incarnate and made man, how can he call Christ himself “according to the flesh”?

The holy Fathers, confessing that Christ is God the Word incarnate and made man, rightly add “according to the flesh” whenever they say anything humble about him. It would therefore have been reasonable for the defenders of Theodore to be moved by this surpassing blasphemy and to withdraw from his impiety.

Nevertheless, to refute their shamelessness, we shall also bring forward his remaining blasphemies, by which he introduces two persons in Christ.

Thus, accusing those who confess that God the Word, begotten before the ages, became man in the last days, he writes in his fourth book against Apollinaris:

> “‘This one’ [Greek: ‘he who’] who existed before the ages, he says, became in the last times—as some confess this—although no one among those who care for piety would allow himself to suffer from such a disease of madness as to say that he who existed before the ages became in the last days.”

And shortly afterward he adds:

> “Following your laws, then, and accepting the reversal—or rather the subversion—established by your wisdom, let us confuse everything together, so that there may no longer be any distinction: neither between the form of God and the form of a servant; nor between the temple assumed and the one who dwelt in the temple; nor between the one who was released and the one who raised him; nor between the one perfected in sufferings and the one who perfected; nor between the one who merited remembrance and the one who was remembered; nor between the one who was visited and the one who visited; nor between the one made a little lower than the angels and the one who made him lower; nor between the one crowned with glory and honor and the one who crowned; nor between the one appointed over the works of God’s hands and the one who appointed; nor between the one who received these things for exaltation and the one who granted exaltation.”

Through these impious words of Theodore and this profane kind of blasphemy, all who opposed him and that impious letter were put to shame. For, repeatedly and shamelessly saying that the Word of God is one and Christ another; one the recipient of a benefit and another the giver; one the savior and another the one saved, he openly denies the salvation obtained for us through our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.

How can the one who, like the rest, received the benefit of salvation and was himself saved, save others? Whose body and blood, then, do those who defend this blasphemy think they receive? The body and blood of the one who granted the benefit, or of the one who received it?

If they answer that they receive the sacraments of the Word of God who grants the benefit, how can they say this when they do not confess that he became incarnate and made man? But if they say that they receive the body and blood of the one to whom the benefit was granted, their hope is foolish, since they venerate a human being and have worshiped a creature rather than the Creator (Wisdom 15:5).

[Col. 0286D] But all of us who belong to the catholic Church, confessing that the Word of God is incarnate and made man, one of the persons of the Holy Trinity, receive his body and blood for the remission of sins and for eternal life, just as the Lord himself taught us:

> “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day. For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him. Just as the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will live because of me” (John 6:54).

These things we believe and confess.

How full of falsehood, too, is what the impious letter mentioned above contains concerning the Twelve Chapters of the holy Cyril! For it slanders Cyril himself, claiming that in those Chapters he admitted one nature of divinity and humanity in Christ, and consequently concludes that the Chapters are full of every kind of wickedness. Your teacher craftily explained this by saying that they were not called full of every kind of impiety as an insult to Cyril, but because they teach that there is one nature of divinity and humanity.

This is a foul and obvious falsehood. Nowhere is Cyril shown to have said that there is one nature of divinity and humanity—not in the letter containing the Twelve Chapters, nor in any of the Chapters, nor in any other of his books. On the contrary, he explicitly teaches that there is one hypostasis, or person, of divinity and humanity in Christ. This is what the holy Church of God confesses, and what all the Fathers have perpetually taught, pronouncing anathema against those who say that there is one nature of divinity and humanity in Christ.

For nature is one thing, and hypostasis or person another. Nature is predicated commonly and generically of any person, whereas person, or hypostasis, expresses a particular property. Therefore one person is not considered in another.

Since the wicked letter says concerning the Twelve Chapters of the holy Cyril that they are full of wickedness, how false this is may be investigated from the sequence of the letter itself, by examining the points in which it asserts that those Twelve Chapters conflict with the right faith.

Since the impious letter called that of Ibas accuses the holy Cyril of abolishing distinctions among designations, know that in this matter too not only the author of the letter but also your teacher has lied.

For whenever the holy Cyril speaks in any discourse about Jesus Christ our Lord, he teaches this distinction of designations or names: exalted expressions belong to him according to divinity, while humble and lowly expressions belong to him according to humanity; nevertheless, all are predicated from and of one incarnate God the Word.

Cyril forbids such designations to be attributed separately to one person and another. You, however, plainly wishing to attribute such designations separately to two persons, slander Cyril by saying that he abolished distinctions among designations.

Since your teacher had resolved to lead you into error in this matter also, and had therefore invented the claim that the letter called that of Ibas was written against the impiety of Apollinaris and should consequently be judged orthodox, you should recognize that he lied there as well. For, as we indicated above, it was not written against Apollinaris.

Even if, as you wish, this were granted as true, the letter would not thereby be exempt from condemnation. A heretic does not become orthodox merely because he has argued against another heretic. Arius argued against Sabellius; Apollinaris against Arius; Eutyches against Nestorius. Although all adhered chiefly to different errors, none became orthodox because of such mutual disputes; all are condemned by the Church in exactly the same way.

It is therefore clear that the author of the letter introduces two persons when he says:

> “How can it be that the Word received from the beginning from the temple what was born from Mary?”

By these words he plainly shows that he does not confess that the Word, God, became incarnate and was born from the holy Virgin, but that Christ is a mere human being, whom he designates by the term “temple.”

It will likewise become clear that the author of the wicked letter drew this impiety from Theodore’s teaching if it is compared with what Theodore himself writes in the third book against the heretic Apollinaris:

> “But God, and from God, consubstantial with the Father, and that same one [Greek: ‘that one’] who was born from the Virgin—O wondrous one!—and who was fashioned through the Holy Spirit according to the divine Scriptures and received formation in a woman’s womb, was perhaps present because, as soon as he was fashioned and so that he might be the temple of God, he received him. Yet we must not suppose that God was born from the Virgin, unless perhaps we must also suppose that what was born, what is in the temple that was born, and God the Word who is in the temple are the same. Nevertheless, not even according to your expression should we say at all that God was born from the Virgin and that he is from God, consubstantial with the Father. For if the one born from the Virgin is not a human being, as you say, but God incarnate, how can the one who was born be called God from God and consubstantial with the Father, when flesh cannot receive this expression? For it is madness to say that God was born from the Virgin. This is nothing other than saying that he was from the seed of David and begotten from the substance of the Virgin and fashioned in her, because we say that what is from the seed of David and from the substance of the Virgin was formed in the maternal womb, fashioned by the power of the Holy Spirit, and was born from the Virgin.”

Thus, when Theodore blasphemes and repeatedly argues that it is impossible for God from God, consubstantial with the Father, to become incarnate and be born from the Virgin, because flesh cannot be consubstantial with the Father, how can the defenders of that heretic fail to be covered with the greatest shame? He introduced this teaching contrary to the sacred Scriptures and opposed to the tradition of the holy Fathers, among whom it is certain that God established his Church from the beginning in the right confession.

For all the priests of God proclaimed that God the Word—God from God—was born and became incarnate from the holy and glorious Virgin Mary, and assumed flesh vivified by a rational and intellectual soul, becoming man and being born from that Virgin. In teaching this they introduced neither a conversion of divinity into humanity nor the absurdity that he is consubstantial with the Father according to the flesh, as Theodore foolishly maintains. Rather, they taught that our one and the same Lord and God Jesus Christ is consubstantial with the Father according to divinity and consubstantial with us according to humanity.

[Col. 0292A] But again the impious Theodore blasphemes as follows in the aforementioned sermon:

> “It was not the divine nature that was born from the Virgin, but he was born from the Virgin who consists of the Virgin’s substance. God the Word was not born from Mary; rather, he was born from Mary who is from the seed of David. God the Word was not born from a woman; rather, he was born from a woman who was fashioned in her by the power of the Holy Spirit. He who was born from his mother is not consubstantial with the Father—for, according to the blessed Paul’s statement, he is without a mother—but he who in later times was fashioned in the maternal womb by the power of the Holy Spirit is called ‘without a father’ for that reason.”

Thus the impious Theodore distorts the Apostle’s teaching in the Epistle to the Hebrews concerning Christ the Lord, where he says:

> “First, indeed, he is interpreted as ‘King of righteousness’; then also ‘King of Salem,’ which is ‘King of peace,’ without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life” (Hebr. 7:3).

Although the Apostle speaks of one and the same person as “without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life,” the impious Theodore himself distinguishes “without father” from “without mother,” as though they referred to different persons.

Moreover, the impiety of such madmen is demonstrated also by the teaching of the holy Fathers. For Saint Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus, in the sermon entitled *On the Holy Theophanies*, or *On the Nativity of Christ*, says:

> “Who will not worship him who is from the beginning? Who will not praise and celebrate him who is at the end? Darkness is dissolved again; light is created once more. Egypt is again troubled by darkness; Israel is again illumined by the pillar. Let the people sitting in darkness behold the great light of knowledge. The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new. The letter yields; the spirit prevails. The shadows pass away; the truth enters. Melchizedek is gathered up: he who was without a mother becomes without a father—first without a mother, afterward without a father. The laws of nature are overturned; the upper world must be filled. Christ commands that we not resist.”

Saint Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, says similar things in his sermon on the holy Mother of God:

> “He who by nature is impassible,” he says, “was made subject to many sufferings through calamities [Greek: ‘through mercy’]. He was not made God by advancement in order that he might become Christ; rather, through mercy God was made man, in whom we believe. We do not proclaim a man deified, but we confess God incarnate. He who by nature is without a mother chose his own handmaid as his mother, and in the dispensation is without a father. For how, according to Paul’s statement, is he himself without father and without mother? If he is merely man, he is not without a mother, for he has a mother; but if he is naked divinity, he is not without a father, for he has the Father. Therefore he himself is without mother as Creator, but without father as creature.”

Saint Augustine likewise says in his sermon on the exposition of the Creed:

> “We believe in his Son Jesus Christ, born of the Holy Spirit and from the Virgin Mary. Why, unbeliever, do you disturb this birth? Do not believe either that he who was born was merely a man, or that, if he was God-man, he afterward wished to be born; for he was born as he himself willed. Rather, marvel that the Word became flesh and was not changed into flesh, and that, while remaining God, he became man. But why marvel that she who gave birth gave birth to her own Creator, and that a creature brought forth her own Creator? The Most High willed to be born in humility in such a way that he might display his magnificence in that very humility.”

These things, then, are discussed by the holy Fathers. Yet it is no less evident that the divine Scriptures, which the holy Fathers of the Church followed, teach the same thing: namely, that God the Word became incarnate, was born from the holy Virgin Mary, and became man.

First, the prophet Isaiah says:

> “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us.”

Again, the prophet David sings in the one hundred and sixth Psalm:

> “He sent his Word and healed them, and delivered them from their destructions.”

The Apostle Paul likewise says:

> “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law, so that he might redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive the adoption of sons.”

Since these things are so, who could be so foolish as to dare say that some man had been in heaven and that he himself had been sent to be born from a woman and under the law? Human beings, indeed, were under the law before the Incarnation; but God the Word himself, the only-begotten Son of God, who was not subject to the law but was himself the Lawgiver, was sent by the Father, made from a woman, and made under the law, so that he might redeem us who were under the law and so that we might receive the adoption of sons.

If, therefore, he who was born from a woman were not truly and preeminently the Son of God, as the heretical author of that impious letter and Theodore foolishly maintain, how could he have bestowed upon us the adoption of sons?

Moreover, that detestable letter contains the statement from the Psalm, “You made him a little lower than the angels.” It denies that this can be said of the divinity of the Only-Begotten—a proposition which you likewise presented as catholic, saying that it could be attributed to a man but not to the incarnate Word.

It will become clear to us that the author of the letter, having been similarly taught this impiety by the heretic Theodore, uttered such blasphemy from what Theodore himself discusses in the fourth book *Against Apollinarius*:

> “The blessed Paul clearly indicates that the man of whom the prophet speaks is the one who was assumed by the Only-Begotten, saying” [Greek: “when he had said”] “that testimony concerning him was brought by the one who said” (Ps. 8:6 ff.; Hebr. 2:9):
>
> “What is man that you are mindful of him, or the son of man that you regard him? You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor, and appointed him over the works of your hands; you subjected all things beneath his feet.”
>
> He continues in this way: “But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honor”—clearly declaring Jesus to be the man of whom the holy David speaks, amazed that mention had there been made of the divine nature which he possessed, and that he had deemed him worthy of his own visitation. He was made a little lower than the angels because he was about to taste death; he was surrounded with glory and honor so that the Lord might also be appointed over all things, on account of his union with him.

Again, in his exposition of the eighth Psalm, the same impious Theodore says:

> “Therefore this Psalm shows us such a difference between God the Word and the man received by him. These things are divided in the New Testament: the Lord receives the beginning of the Psalm, in which it says that he is the Creator of creation, that he possesses magnificence exalted above the heavens, and that he is wondrous in all the earth; while the Apostle receives the remaining statements concerning the man who merited the benefit, applying them to Jesus. How could it not be clear that divine Scripture teaches one to be God the Word and the other to be man, and shows us that there is a great difference between them? For the one remembers, while the other is remembered; the one visits, while the other receives that visitation and is called blessed. The one, by granting the benefit, makes him a little lower than the angels, while the other receives the benefit through such abasement. The one crowns him with glory and honor, while the other is crowned and is therefore called blessed. The one appoints him over all the works of his hands and subjects all things beneath his feet, while the other merits dominion over those things over which he previously had no authority.”

Thus far the impious Theodore, blaspheming openly in the same way as the detestable letter: one, he says, is God the Word, and another is Christ. Following him, you likewise wrote that the passage “You made him a little lower than the angels” was spoken of man and not at all of God the Word incarnate.

You ought to have understood that every human being is lower than the angels, but that this was said of the only-begotten God the Word, who, although God, deigned to become man and joined our weakness to himself. The Apostle himself teaches this when he says:

> “We see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels through the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honor.”

If, then, as your opinion holds, one is Jesus who was made lower than the angels, while another is God the Word, who was not made lower, then without doubt it is merely a man who endured suffering whom you call Christ. Consequently the Apostle becomes a liar when he says:

> “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

For who is the Lord of glory except God the Word incarnate? The Jews, denying that he was God, rebuked him by saying:

> “Because you are a man, you make yourself God” (John 10:33).

Your teacher, following the Jews in that impious interpretation, devised the same claim.

To confirm the opinions mentioned above, you placed before us in your chapters the Apostle’s statement:

> “Who, being in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:7),

asserting that it agreed splendidly with your interpretation and that the passage spoke not of the Word God incarnate, but only of a mere man.

Although here too you follow the error of the heretics and maintain that the Apostle spoke of a man when he said that he “emptied himself,” nevertheless it is clear to all Catholics that the Apostle teaches the self-emptying of God the Word himself. For, although he was in the form of God—that is, in the divine nature—he deigned to take the form of a servant. The form of a servant signifies human nature, which God the Word fashioned for himself from the Virgin’s womb and from his own subsistence; he did not add it externally to a man who had first been fashioned, as the impious doctrine of Nestorius and Theodore has transmitted.

Nestorius says that God the Word exists together with the man who was born from Mary. Theodore, however, declared that what was present in the man born from Mary was “similar.”

[Col. 0298B]

That the statement “You made him a little lower than the angels,” and also “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” were spoken of God the Word incarnate, we learn from another passage of the Apostle, where he says of him:

> “Know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: although he was rich, for our sake he became poor, so that by his poverty we might become rich” (2 Cor. 8:9).

Who would dare say that a man had been rich and had become poor in order to enrich us?

And since you again say that whoever declares the incarnate God the Word and only-begotten Son of God to have been made lower and emptied himself thereby introduces a change in the divine nature, according to the impiety of Apollinarius, or makes the divinity passible, according to the error of Arius, the Gospel statement applies excellently against you:

> “You are mistaken, knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God” (Matt. 22:29).

What, then, will remain for you to say about the Lord’s statement:

> “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13)?

He does not say that a man descended from heaven; rather, he most clearly asserts that God the Word is the one who emptied himself, who descended from heaven, became incarnate from the holy Mother of God, the ever-virgin Mary, became man, and was born from her. The one who descended is the same one who ascended; to him, on account of his descent, are attributed self-emptying and abasement.

[Col. 0298D]

When the Lord also says elsewhere in the Gospels, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), do not imagine that some man, rather than God made man, spoke of himself in this way. For it is most evident that the same one who said, “The Father is greater than I,” also said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

When he says, “I and the Father are one,” he indicates the equality of the divine nature which he has with the Father. When he says, “The Father is greater than I,” he shows his abasement, accomplished for our sake through his dispensation. Both the equality and the abasement were spoken of one and the same Lord Jesus Christ—that is, of God the Word incarnate.

The Arians, indeed, on the basis of such lowered modes of speech and through an erroneous opinion, deny that the Son is consubstantial with the Father and say that he is therefore inferior to the Father. But you, refusing to admit that these humble statements are to be understood of God the Word incarnate, introduce a new person into the Trinity, approving the impiety of Theodore and Nestorius.

We, however, explaining the humble statements no less than the exalted statements of one and the same God the Word incarnate and our Lord Jesus Christ, avoid alike the confusion and the division of the natures. We confess that from these natures there is constituted one subsistence of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and we do not introduce a fourth person into the holy Trinity.

The holy Fathers and teachers of the Church likewise, in expounding the sacred Scriptures, taught that the passage “You made him a little lower than the angels” was spoken of God the Word incarnate, the Only-Begotten, in accordance with what was argued above.

Saint Cyril says in his letter to Basilides:

> “How, then, was he made lower than the angels, when he is worshiped by them? The reason is evident. He sits in the condition of humanity and in the mortal body which he assumed and made his own. In it he willingly suffered, and because of his suffering he is crowned with supreme glory, since through it he destroyed death and removed corruption, while he himself exists as life and incorruption.
>
> “Therefore, when he names Jesus and says that he was made lower than the angels, we do not understand him to mean a man taken separately and individually, but the only-begotten Son of God, according to the dispensation, yielding in dignity to the holy angels because he truly became man and was made lower than their eminence.
>
> “The sublimity of the holy angels consists in being outside the flesh and not being subject to death, which he himself undertook through voluntary self-emptying. He who is made a little lower than the angels because of the condition of humanity, while existing in the sublimity of divinity, is worshiped by them and sits upon the thrones around which the angels stand, always glorifying him and continually proclaiming him Lord of hosts.”

That the same self-emptying pertains to God the Word incarnate is also established by Cyril in the book *Against the Refutations of Theodoret*, which Theodoret composed against his fourth chapter:

> “I will say without hesitation that all human things are small in comparison with the Word born from God. But let us ask whose self-emptying this is thought to be, and who voluntarily endured it.
>
> “Therefore, if, as others say, the form of a servant is that which is from the seed of David, how—or, [supply: ‘in what manner’]—I ask, was it emptied, if it was assumed by God? But if the Word himself, who exists in the form and equality of God the Father, is said to have emptied himself, how, or in what manner, was he emptied, if he rejected self-emptying?
>
> “I do not know how one can make self-emptying a change undergone by God the Word and call something human on account of the dispensational union with the flesh.”

Again, Saint Cyril says in the same book *Against the Nestorians*:

> “Did the divine Paul, then, deceive those sanctified by faith when he clearly spoke of the Only-Begotten, saying, ‘Although he was rich, he became poor for our sake’? Far from it. The herald of the Truth speaks entirely truly.
>
> “Who is rich, and how did he become poor? If, as certain people have dared to think and say, a man was assumed by God, how did he become poor? The one who was assumed would thereby be deprived” [Note: “*Derogabitur* should be expunged,” they insist; the Greek text and the syntax require it. EDIT.] “of the dignities that shine forth above nature, for he was glorified. Or, if this is not true, the text reads *ab eis assumptioni quod* [perhaps read: ‘they disparaged the assumption as though’]; it is absurd to suppose that the assumption had led him down to a lower and inferior measure of humanity. Therefore the one who was assumed did not become poor. It remains, then, for us to say that he who was rich as God became poor in our poverty.”

Similarly Saint Gregory the Theologian says in his sermon on the Nativity of Christ:

> “God came forth with humanity, one thing from two opposed to one another—namely flesh and spirit—of which one deified, while the other was deified. O new mingling! O wondrous combination!
>
> “He who is becomes what he was not; he who was not created is created; he who can be contained in no place is contained, through the intervention of a spiritual soul, between divinity and the density of flesh.
>
> “He who enriches others becomes subject to poverty; for he takes on the poverty of my flesh so that I may obtain the riches of his divinity. He who is full is emptied; for a brief time he is emptied of his own glory, so that I may become a participant in his fullness.”

Saint Athanasius likewise, expounding the Apostle’s words, “Who, being in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” writes:

> “What could be clearer or more certain than this? He was not made better from something worse; rather, although he was God, he assumed the appearance of a servant. Nor was he improved by assuming it; he humbled himself.”

And shortly afterward:

> “What else is this than that he who was in the form of God and was the noble Son of the Father humbled himself and became a servant for our sake?”

Again, shortly afterward:

> “The Word became flesh; and for this reason this man is called heavenly, from heaven, because the Word himself descended from heaven.”

Saint Gregory of Nyssa likewise argues in the third book *Against Eunomius* as follows:

> “We have believed these things concerning the Crucified One. Therefore, according to the measure of his own power, we do not cease to exalt him: namely, that on account of his ineffable and inaccessible magnificence, while remaining undivided from the Father and from the Holy Spirit, he was able to come into communion with our weakness.
>
> “They, however, establish this as proof that the Son is alien in nature from the Father, saying that the Lord appeared through flesh and the cross, so that, while the paternal nature remained impassible and was in no way able to share in suffering, the Son, transformed into a lower nature, came through flesh and death, having become fully capable of suffering.”

And afterward he adds:

> “For this reason the cross is also called the glory of the Lord, and every tongue confesses that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.
>
> “For if it is necessary to divide the other matters in the same way, we shall see who it was that died and who it was that destroyed death; what was renewed and what was emptied.
>
> “Divinity is emptied so that it may become capable of assuming humanity; humanity, however, through the mingling with divinity, is made divine and renewed.”

We have set forth these things from the teaching of the holy Fathers so that, understanding them, you may recognize that the positions established by you are precisely those which the Arians and Nestorians impiously maintain against our Lord Jesus Christ.

The Arians, attempting to demonstrate that the Son is a creature and alien to the Father’s substance, attribute suffering and the other humble things to divinity alone. The Nestorians, on the other hand, who strive to introduce two sons, confessing God the Word separately and a mere man separately, decree that whatever pertains to the humility of suffering must be assigned to the man alone.

But this is not what we learn from the holy Fathers. They do not admit a change in the divinity of the Son on the basis of the humble statements, nor do they divide divinity from humanity on the basis of the exalted statements. Rather, they handed down that both the exalted and the humble statements were spoken of one and the same God the Word, incarnate and made man.

Since in those same chapters you also added—drawing from the same letter—that it is correct to speak of two natures but one person and one power, it will likewise be worthwhile to expose the impiety of that letter’s author.

For if he does not confess that God the Word became incarnate from the Virgin Mary and became man, of whom does he say that there are two natures? It is clear that he admits two natures in place of a person, in the sense of Nestorius and Theodore, whom that detestable letter praises to the highest degree.

If the letter appears to indicate one person and one Son, Nestorius and Theodore also used this manner of speaking. They said that Christ was a mere man who possessed the person of God the Word, and that he possessed the honor and dignity of God the Word, as well as the grace of adoption, and that he was worshiped in his place. For this reason they pretend to speak of one Son and one person of Christ, agreeing only in the name of sonship. This is clearly gathered from the form of the arguments used in the letter, which says that there is one power of a twofold nature, just as you yourselves also wrote.

“One power” is not said of different natures but of different persons; we likewise recognize and confess this in the holy Trinity. For this reason the holy Fathers anathematized those who affirmed that the man was united to God the Word according to power, force, habit, or dignity, and who would not confess that the union had taken place in one subsistence of a twofold nature.

Thus, what was correctly said by the holy Fathers concerning the distinction of the two natures, the followers of Nestorius, with Theodore as their guide in unbelief, appropriate for themselves, naming natures in place of persons and venerating a union based on habit, so that they may pretend to speak of one person.

The impious Theodore himself demonstrates this. In the fourth sermon *Against Apollinarius the Heretic* he writes:

> “The distinction of the natures is sufficiently demonstrated to us by what has been set forth, since it is concluded that, as a result of an excess of benevolence, the memory and visitation of the man who was taken up were established in this way, and that he is considered most blessed as the cause of such condescensions [sic].
>
> “This also shows the distinction of the natures: divine Scripture itself shows us the distinction between the nature of the one who assumes and that of the one assumed. Wishing to indicate the union which pertains to the thing assumed, it brings out through unity or union that both natures have made themselves one another’s own, so that it shows us alike the unity of the one who existed and assumed, and of the one who was assumed—a unity which proceeded from the conjunction made with him.”

Since it has been clearly demonstrated that the impious Theodore used the word “nature” in place of “person,” we shall bring forward an even worse blasphemy of his, by which he teaches what he understands by the word “union,” so that his defenders may be condemned more fully.

In the eighth sermon *On the Incarnation* he writes:

> “It is clear what is implied by union. Through it, the natures, coalescing, are perfected into one person by union, just as the Lord says concerning a male and a female that they are no longer two but one flesh.
>
> “Similarly, the terms of the union are no longer two but one person, while the distinction of the natures always remains. Just as the doubleness of number is not removed when they are called one flesh—for it is clear in what sense they are called one—so likewise the distinction of the natures is not removed by the unity of the person [read *aufert*, not *aufertur*].
>
> “When we distinguish the natures, we confess the perfect nature of God the Word and also the perfect person—for hypostasis cannot be spoken of without person—and likewise the perfect human nature and its person. But when we direct our attention to the joining or conjunction of these, we then proclaim that there is one person.”

Although these statements are horrifying for Christians to hear, we have been compelled to bring them forward because of the madness of Theodore and of the defenders of that impious letter. We ask God to be favorable to us. Nevertheless, it has been demonstrated that the detestable letter is filled throughout with the whole of Theodore’s impiety.

[Col. 0306C]

We have answered all these matters concerning what was contained in your book of chapters, by which you attempted to defend the aforementioned impious letter and thereby to revive the perverse opinions of Theodore and Nestorius, whose impiety the letter commends.

Since, however, you omitted many things contained in the aforementioned impious letter written to the heretic Maris, and did not dare to insert them into your chapters—lest perhaps the Christian people should understand from them how great an impiety you were defending—we judged it necessary to point out these matters briefly as well.

For in that part of the letter which you omitted, it says [Note: This passage appears in the acts of the Second Council of Constantinople, Collection 5, in Labbé]:

> “Cyril, blinding the ears of all the bishops who had gathered at Ephesus with poison, gained control over the eyes of all the wise. He found a means, out of a preconceived hatred of Nestorius, to have Nestorius expelled from his see by that same Council of Ephesus without any investigation or judgment.”

Likewise, the same letter says:

> “Those twelve chapters written by Cyril, although they conflicted with the true faith, were presented and confirmed by the bishops of the Council of Ephesus; they agreed with them as though they were consonant with the true faith. Nestorius, however, because he was hated by his own city and its leading citizens, was unable to return there.”

In this way the wicked author of that letter not only protects and praises heretics, but does not hesitate to call them Catholics.

Concerning the blessed Rabula, bishop of Edessa, an eminent prelate of exceptional piety, at whose tomb miracles are performed even to the present day, he writes in that impious letter:

> “The tyrant of our city, whom you yourself also do not fail to recognize, uses the pretext of faith to persecute not only those who are living with him but also those who long ago departed to the Lord. One of them is the blessed Theodore, preacher of truth and teacher of the Church, who not only struck heretics through his own faith while alive, but also, after his death, left spiritual weapons for the children of the Church in his books, just as your Reverence learned when you spoke with him and placed faith in what he had written.
>
> “This man the one who dares everything dared to anathematize from the Church.”

Again, for the insult of Saint Cyril, the same detestable letter contains these words:

> “The heart of Egypt has been softened, and without disturbance it has assented to the true faith. Those who rush disorderly against the living and the dead are in confusion, making satisfaction for their offenses and teaching things contrary to their former doctrine, and that one ought to confess the temple and the one dwelling in it.”

We have attempted to place these scattered and entangled statements from the aforementioned letter clearly before your eyes, so that, even if late, you may at last think rightly and withdraw from those perverse opinions and errors.

[Col. 0308C]

The impiety of that criminal letter is so great that you yourselves did not dare, as the saying goes, to set forth in the chapters you sent everything that it contains, although you attempted to interpret some passages through a perverse explanation.

Who could be counted among Christians who would not call that letter impious, since it contains so many and such great blasphemies?

Whoever undertakes the defense of that letter, in which Saint Cyril is called a heretic and the First Council of Ephesus is rejected, plainly stands with the party of Nestorius and adheres to his impiety. The letter itself admits that Nestorius was twice condemned by investigation and judgment, but says that he did not return to the Church not because of his doctrines, but because of the hatred of his fellow citizens [Note: The phrase is entirely defective. If the Greek text and the preceding context are taken into account, it should be corrected as follows: “... whom the letter itself says was condemned without investigation or judgment, and not because of his doctrines, but ...” EDIT.].

Whoever defends the position of that letter is guilty not merely of sin for this reason, but also because he condemns Pope Celestine, who said of Cyril, “Cyril’s faith is our faith.”
