Likewise, whoever maintains that those twelve chapters of Saint Cyril conflicted with the true faith condemns not only Saint Cyril, blessed Celestine of holy memory, and the First Council of Ephesus, but also pronounces judgment against the holy Council of Chalcedon, which declared in writing that Cyril was its father and teacher. Moreover, he stands against Saint Leo, Roman pontiff, who, writing to the Council of Chalcedon concerning the twelve chapters of Saint Cyril, says:

> “The definitions proposed against Nestorius by Cyril of holy memory have remained secure” [Greek: “may they remain secure”].

Although that detestable letter is altogether full of iniquity, it nevertheless could not conceal one truth: namely, that after his death Theodore was anathematized even by pious and orthodox men and rejected by the Church. Yet that impious letter calls Theodore, a blasphemer among all the heretics who have ever existed, a teacher of the Church and preacher of truth.

In another letter we have already laid before you a small portion of his blasphemies. In the words of Saints Cyril, Proclus, and Rabula, we showed what they themselves wrote against Theodore and how they condemned him, his impious teaching, and his iniquity.

The blasphemies of Theodore are of such a kind that even you, who defend Theodore while he advances them, have not dared to defend them. Yet it is evident that no one who has condemned impiety by his own judgment can defend the patron of that same impiety unless he has first departed from error, come to his senses, and condemned the things he once taught impiously.

To the other insults hurled against Saint Cyril in that letter is added the charge that Cyril acted disgracefully, to such an extent that, repenting of what he had formerly taught, he put forward a doctrine opposed to it.

From this the author of the letter is shown to be utterly insane. For where did Cyril establish a doctrine contrary to his earlier teaching? When did he repent? Or how could he have been counted among the holy Fathers by the holy Council of Chalcedon if, as the letter claims, he had repented of his earlier doctrine?

A person who returns from error to soundness is not enrolled among teachers, but is regarded as one who has turned away from error.

Finally, the author of the letter concludes in this way:

> “It is necessary to confess and believe in the temple and in the one who dwells in the temple.”

From this statement, insofar as it concerns the impiety of the letter and its defenders, the entire true faith is overturned.

For the Catholic Church confesses one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God. It nowhere teaches that one must believe in a temple and its inhabitant, or that one ought to confess these things, as it instructs those admitted to the grace of holy baptism to confess and believe in one God, the Father almighty; in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God; and in the Holy Spirit—not in two sons or in two Christs, as the letter to Maris the Persian explicitly establishes should be believed, by proposing faith in the temple and in the one who dwells in it. The result is that a fourth person is constituted in the holy Trinity.

It has therefore been demonstrated by all these considerations that the patrons and admirers of the aforementioned abominable epistle have been judged wholly alien to the orthodox faith. Moreover, [Col. 0310D] since you say that Cyril was accepted by the Easterners for the reason that he interpreted those chapters of his, we are not at all surprised that you likewise have been deceived in the chapters you sent to us, since you plainly seem to be ignorant also of the acts of the earlier Council of Ephesus. For Saint Celestine, the first Council of Ephesus, Saint Leo, and even the holy Council of Chalcedon itself accepted those chapters of Saint Cyril and confirmed them by their own authority; they never sought any exposition of them. The explanation was supplied not for the sake of Catholics, but because of the heretics who, devoted to Nestorius’s party, were attacking the chapters in question. For, as you yourselves admit, neither the holy Gospels, nor the Apostle, nor the rest of the divine writings would be sufficiently understood unless they had been interpreted by the holy Fathers.

Moreover, you heap arguments of confusion upon yourselves, saying that Cyril was then accepted by the defenders of Nestorius in the East when he had expounded his chapters. On the contrary, the apostolic Roman See and Cyril admitted into their communion bishops who had pronounced judgment against Nestorius and condemned his impiety. Thus the holy Roman pontiff Xystus himself, writing with his council to Saint Cyril and praising the labors he had undertaken for the unity of the Church, says among other things:

> “The brothers have returned to us—to us, I say—we who, pursuing the disease with united zeal, have cared for the health of souls.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Rejoice, dearest brother, and rejoice victoriously with the brothers gathered again to us. The Church was seeking those whom she has received. For if we wish none of the little ones to perish, how much more ought we to rejoice in the recovery of the leaders? We read how much joy the return of a single sheep brought, and therefore it must be understood how much praise belongs to having recalled so many shepherds. Flocks are seen in each individual case; here the concern is not for one alone whenever the health of many is at issue.”

And again:

> “I rejoice,” he says, “that the priest of the Church of Antioch is now called by your holiness a venerable man and *dominus* [lord]. And rightly is he called *dominus* who has acknowledged the common Lord, who confesses with us, in catholic speech, the mystery of the incarnation.”

And again:

> “The troubles of those who preach the faith are always welcome; for abundant reward is prepared in heaven for those who, on account of righteousness, are commanded to endure curses, persecutions, and every evil. You suffered falsehood in order to make truth victorious, and therefore falsehood must now be mocked, since no one could perish for truth.”

And finally:

> “This brotherhood,” he says, “writes these things with me to your veneration, approving your actions in every respect and confirming your labors. Yet they could not have been burdensome or bitter, because they were expended for him whose burden we carry as light and whose yoke is gentle.”

These are Saint Xystus’s words to Saint Cyril concerning the Easterners. But since you have most foolishly asserted at the same time that the definition of the holy Council of Chalcedon is damaged by the condemnation of the epistle entitled *To Maris the Persian*, we ask by what reasoning you could have been moved to dare write this. Do not, therefore, suppose that the doctrine of the holy Council of Chalcedon embraces anything resembling what is contained in that impious epistle; to say so is not Christian. Rather, know that everything contained in that same epistle and in the books of Theodore is wholly opposed to the definition of the holy faith handed down by the Council of Chalcedon.

The epistle and Theodore assert that the Word of God is one, and Christ another; but the holy Council of Chalcedon acknowledges one Lord of ours, Jesus Christ, the incarnate Word of God, who became man without alteration of himself. The epistle and Theodore do not confess that the Word of God assumed flesh from the holy and glorious God-bearing and ever-virgin Mary, nor that he was born from her; consequently, they also deny that the most holy Virgin Mary is God-bearer. But the holy Fathers assembled at the Council of Chalcedon confessed the most holy Mary to be God-bearer.

The impious Theodore and the anonymous epistle, while admitting two persons, pretend at the same time to profess one person through a habitual union. The synod, however, affirming a hypostatic union of the two natures, proclaims one person—or rather, one subsistence—of Christ, the only-begotten Son of God.

Again, that epistle condemns the earlier Council of Ephesus and Saint Cyril, whose chapters it also calls impious; it defends and praises Nestorius and Theodore. But the Council of Chalcedon follows the earlier Council of Ephesus in all things, honors Cyril with the titles of Father and teacher, confirms his synodical epistle to which those twelve chapters are appended, and condemns Nestorius. Moreover, it likewise curses the Jewish creed cobbled together by Theodore, which had formerly also been condemned at the first Council of Ephesus and which, after the matters we have reviewed above, had been brought forward at that same holy Council of Chalcedon; together with its author, it anathematizes it.

These matters, then, were established by the definitions of the holy Council of Chalcedon. The synod spoke nothing obscure concerning the faith; rather, everywhere and in all things it followed the confession of faith graciously granted by the Lord through his apostles. That confession the holy apostles themselves proclaimed; the holy three hundred and eighteen Fathers delivered it to the Church of God; and the one hundred and fifty Fathers likewise confirmed it when they declared the doctrines concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit. The holy Fathers who first assembled at Ephesus followed it; [Col. 0314C] the holy Council of Chalcedon embraced it, and struck with anathema anyone who should offer any other creed or exposition of the faith than that handed down by the holy three hundred and eighteen Fathers.

Since these things are so, recognize at last which of the two more rightly defends the holy Council of Chalcedon: the one who maintains that it faithfully followed the aforementioned holy Fathers and rightly defined everything, or the one who tries to attribute to it the impious modes of speech of heretics. It is utterly impossible that those who accept the pure decrees and catholic expressions of the first Council of Ephesus, and who receive Saints Celestine, Cyril, and Leo together with the definition of the Council of Chalcedon, should also accept the wicked epistle to Maris, which is wholly opposed to them and to the matters we have reviewed. Who could embrace teachers of the Church who teach contrary things—orthodox and heretics alike—or the condemned together with those who condemned them? Moreover, so that you may understand more fully the matters confused by Theodoret and Ibas, we have thought it worthwhile to set these other points before you as well.

Know, then, that when Ibas was accused at different times before the most pious emperor Theodosius on account of the Nestorian and Theodorian impiety contained in that epistle of his, and because of the insults uttered against Saint Cyril and his chapters, and also before Saint Proclus, archbishop of Constantinople, and several archbishops of Antioch, finally, by the same emperor and by Flavian—who had succeeded Proclus in the see of Constantinople—Photius of Tyre and Eustathius, bishops of Berytus, were chosen to render judgment against Ibas. When Ibas was reproved by them concerning his faith and the insults he had hurled against Saint Cyril, and was given an opportunity for his defense, he denied that he had said or written anything insulting against Saint Cyril after the reconciliation established between the Easterners and Saint Cyril himself. But it was openly demonstrated at length by the accusers, who produced the incriminating epistle, that it had been written after the reconciliation.

Ibas, therefore, is known from that same deposition of his to have utterly repudiated the epistle in question. Consequently, the aforementioned bishops, considering the impiety of the epistle—even though Ibas did not at all admit that it had been published by him—issued a judgment entirely against the impiety contained in it. They decided that Ibas ought to anathematize Nestorius together with his impious doctrines, which had been collected in the wicked epistle; that the faith of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers ought to be accepted; and that the earlier Council of Ephesus, as having been assembled in the Holy Spirit, ought to be accepted in the same manner as the council constituted by those same three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers. That was the Council of Ephesus which, together with Saint Cyril and his twelve chapters, the impious epistle attacked with insults.

[Col. 0316C] Since Ibas did not carry out what had been decreed by the judges, he himself was deposed from the episcopate. Meanwhile, the holy Council of Chalcedon was convened. Ibas was neither summoned to it nor present as a bishop, since Nonus had already been substituted in his place by the laying on of hands; Nonus too had been summoned to that same holy Council of Chalcedon. After the matters concerning the faith had been settled, Ibas arrived and requested that the case concerning the substitution made in his place—the case by which he had been deposed from the episcopate—be heard. He produced the judgment of Photius and Eustathius. When it was being read, his accusers likewise arrived and produced the acts of Tyre, in which that impious epistle was also contained.

When the epistle likewise began to be read, Ibas realized that he would certainly be condemned on account of its impiety if he acknowledged it as his own. Interrupting the reading of the proceedings, he said:

> “Order the letter of the clerics of Edessa to be read, so that you may recognize how separate I am from those things of which I am accused.”

When these too had been read, the bishops considered the judgment of Photius and Eustathius and the accusation brought against Ibas. They again decreed that Ibas himself ought to fulfill what Photius and Eustathius had judged, and ought to accept the definition proclaimed by the holy synod itself and subscribe to it. That definition embraced both the first Council of Ephesus and Saint Cyril, as well as his doctrine—all of which, as we have observed, were scorned with mockery in that wicked epistle.

By these facts we are plainly taught that the holy Council of Chalcedon itself arranged for Ibas to do all these things in order to overthrow and condemn the frequently mentioned impious epistle. We therefore wonder that you still patronize that wicked epistle, which Ibas himself dared not call his own either at Tyre or afterward at the holy Council of Chalcedon, nor did he undertake its defense. On the contrary, he used the letter of the Edessene clergy and the judgments of Photius and Eustathius to evade the accusation brought against him on account of that impious epistle.

To all the other matters you have badly explained, you have also added this: that you would distort, by a false interpretation, the proclamation made by Eunomius concerning Ibas, asserting that Eunomius’s proclamation concerned that impious epistle. For it is reported that the following is contained in it: although Ibas had assailed Saint Cyril with insults in the first part of the epistle, nevertheless toward its end he corrected and amended himself. Yet it is manifest that Eunomius’s declamation has nothing at all to do with that impious epistle, but that he was speaking about the substitution made for Ibas at Tyre by Photius and Eustathius.

For in the proceedings before them Ibas plainly admitted—as we also indicated above—that previously, together with the other bishops of the East, he had insulted Saint Cyril, when their judgment and his differed. But afterward, once the union between them had been completed, he said that he had uttered nothing insulting against Saint Cyril. From this confession of Ibas, Eunomius, finding that Ibas had first heaped insults upon Saint Cyril but afterward repented and said that he had uttered nothing at all against Saint Cyril after the union had been established, composed the declamation in question.

No one can doubt that the impious epistle attributed to Ibas, from beginning to end, teems with every form of iniquity and with insults against Saint Cyril. There is no reason to believe that Eunomius wished to condemn the earlier portions of the epistle as wicked while praising the remaining portions, which are worse. No sensible person approves someone who is simultaneously the praiser and the censurer of one and the same similar thing. Whoever, therefore, dares say that Eunomius’s declamation refers not to the substitution made for Ibas at Tyre but to the [lacuna] of the aforementioned impious epistle—whoever, I say, dares assert this does not serve the truth; rather, like a heretic, he attempts to wrong the Fathers.

[Col. 0318D] We were also astonished that you were not at all afraid to write this: that Saint Cyril’s chapters were obscure, while you praised that impious epistle as though it had been made clear through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. It is manifest, therefore, that these words were uttered by you not through the power of the Holy Spirit but through the impulse of an evil spirit, since you reproached the Fathers and teachers of the Church for obscurity, while extolling the malice and blasphemies of that epistle with praise. Accordingly, what the Apostle Peter said about those who perversely understood the Epistles of Saint Paul rightly applies to you and to all others who think similarly about the holy Fathers of the Church:

> “The ignorant and unstable distort these things, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction” (2 Peter 3:16).

Thus, because you too perversely understand what has been handed down by the teachers of the Church, the things drawn from the divine writings seem obscure to you. These matters concerning Ibas and that impious epistle are found after investigation in certain books.

For it is worthwhile for you to know that the proceedings in which that impious epistle is contained are not included in those authentic records to which the bishops subscribed, whose authentic copies have been preserved in the most holy Roman Church, in Constantinople, and also in our sacred palace. Since, therefore, it is manifest on every side that that impious epistle is filled with every kind of iniquity and opposed to the holy definitions of the Council of Chalcedon, it remains that those who say that it is contained in the holy Council of Chalcedon must be judged not only to strive with every effort to defend their own malice, but also to inflict a grave injury upon the holy council. For everything approved and confirmed by the aforementioned holy synod is expressly contained in the definition of the faith handed down by it.

We also wish you to understand that after Theodoret had directed his pen against the twelve chapters of Saint Cyril while defending Nestorius and his depravity, after the definition of the holy synod he was commanded first to anathematize Nestorius and to confess the holy and glorious ever-virgin Mary as God-bearer—and he carried this out. Therefore, both Ibas and Theodoret were received not as teachers or Fathers, but as penitents who detested the pernicious opinions of which they had been accused, and who had embraced and subscribed to the definition of the Council of Chalcedon. In the Catholic Church it is customary for heretics who condemn their own error and return to the orthodox faith to be received into communion, but not to be counted among the Fathers as teachers.

Thus other Eastern bishops also—some of whom had supported Nestorius’s party and contradicted the earlier Council of Ephesus and Saint Cyril—were later received into communion by the apostolic Roman See and by Saint Cyril after they had pronounced anathema against Nestorius and his perverse opinion. For that reason they are understood to have been received by the holy Church of God.

We also wish you to observe that not only Ibas and Theodoret were deposed from the episcopate for attacking those twelve chapters of Saint Cyril; Domnus too, archbishop of Antioch, underwent the judgment of condemnation because he had written that it would be expedient for those twelve chapters to be suppressed in silence. The Council of Chalcedon approved and confirmed the judgment instituted against Domnus even after he had died.

That these matters are entirely true and happened just as we have explained them is testified by Theodoret himself in his letter to John, bishop of Germanicia, where he writes:

> “For what do the profane falsely claim and say—that no new division was made concerning the doctrines? Why, then, was I expelled—because of what murders or sorceries? What adulteries did anyone commit? Who violated any tomb? But it is known and clear even to the barbarians themselves that I and the others were deposed because of doctrines. Indeed, they also expelled Lord Domnus, as though he did not accept the chapters, calling those chapters entirely worthy of praise, and professing that they would remain in them. But me, who read their decrees, they proclaimed to be the leader of heresy.”

From these words it is clearly inferred that Domnus, Theodoret himself, Ibas, and several others were driven from their sees because of the chapters of Saint Cyril proposed against Nestorius. Theodoret and Ibas, however, having repented, approved the aforementioned chapters and all the other matters on account of which they had been expelled from their sees, and were received by the holy Council of Chalcedon. Those who did not repent were not received. The condemnation of Domnus, moreover, was confirmed even after his death.

[Col. 0322B] Since you have likewise written that you curse the blasphemies of Theodore which we ourselves sent to you, whoever he may be, but hesitate to pronounce anathema against Theodore because, as you have claimed, he had already died in the communion of the Churches, know that anyone who says that Theodore may not be anathematized but must be counted among the bishops, on the ground that he died in communion with the Church, can equally admit Judas into the number of the apostles. Judas was admitted by Christ into communion with the other disciples, although he remained hidden and was known only to God, who searches human secrets. For according to what those who speak thus seem to think, the apostles too deserve blame because, after Judas’s death, they passed judgment against him and substituted another in his place. Moreover, although his name is read among the other apostles in the holy Gospels, he is not for that reason received as an apostle, nor could he thereby be freed from the judgment of anathema.

Understand, then, that a person dies in the communion of the Churches if he has preserved the Catholic faith undefiled unto death.

Indeed, if some Manichaean, or Arian, or Nestorian, or Eutychian, or any other kind of heretic, or someone seized by the madness of the Greeks, lived in communion with the Church and died in that state, but after death was discovered to have been a heretic, whether from his writings or by any other means, the Catholic faith nevertheless suffers no damage, nor is he thereby freed from condemnation because he is said to have died in the peace of the Churches. In truth, death by no means frees heretics from the judgment of condemnation deserved by their perverse belief; rather, they are condemned all the more justly because, while alive, they did not repent.

This can be confirmed by many examples: heretics who did not return to soundness while alive were condemned after death. Eunomius, Apollinarius, Bonosus, and in earlier times Valentinus, Basilides, Marcion, Cerinthus, and many others who had not been subjected to anathemas while alive were condemned after death and are anathematized by the Catholic Church, because they died in their errors. Conversely, those who had unjustly suffered the judgment of condemnation—namely Flavian and John, holy archbishops of Constantinople—were restored by the Catholic Church itself after death.

According to your judgment, heretics who die clinging to their own errors must be freed from condemnation, while Catholics who have been unjustly judged must not after death be recalled to the peace of the Church. It is scarcely possible to say how full of iniquity this is.

By these examples we have plainly shown that the tradition of the Church has established that heretics can be judged even after death and condemned by anathemas. Moreover, the same point is demonstrated still more forcefully from the Constitutions of the holy apostles. At the place where they establish that offerings of alms are useful for the repose of the dead, they continue as follows:

> “We say this concerning pious persons. For concerning the impious: even if the entire substance of the world were distributed to the poor on their behalf, it would profit them nothing. For if divine things opposed someone while he was alive, it is certain that they will not profit him after he has been removed.”

Since the apostles thus defined the matter concerning pious people who have died, who would dare declare that heretics after death—and especially Theodore himself—ought to be free from condemnation? The holy Fathers ranked him with the Jews, Greeks, and Sodomites as one who blasphemed more grievously than they did, and condemned him together with his impiety.

Moreover, that heretics must also be condemned after death, as we established above, Saint Augustine, bishop of an African city, expressly teaches in his letter to Boniface:

> “Even if what they charged against Caecilian and us were true and could at some time be demonstrated to us, we would nevertheless anathematize him, although already dead. Yet we must not abandon the Church of Christ, which is not fabricated by contentious opinions but confirmed by divine testimonies, on account of any one person.”

Thus far Augustine.

Similarly, the Church and the holy Fathers anathematized after death not only very many people who had erred against the faith, but also bishops who had left their property either in their final wishes or by intestate succession to heretical relatives, or even to outsiders. The eighty-first canon of the African Council states:

> “It is likewise decreed that if any bishop should prefer heirs unrelated to him by blood, or even heretical relatives, or pagans, to the Church, then even after his death anathema shall be pronounced against him, and his name shall not be counted among the priests of God. Nor shall he have the excuse that he died intestate, since, having been made a bishop, he ought certainly not to have postponed the proper disposition of his property, consistent with his profession, to another time.”

If, therefore, as that ecclesiastical canon has decreed, bishops are struck with anathema even after death because their wealth was not properly distributed, how much more justly must those be subjected to excommunication who have sinned against God himself, as Scripture says:

> “If a man sins against another man, there will be someone who can pray for him; but if he sins against God, who will pray for him?”

[Col. 0326A] Since we have shown that in earlier times it was established by law among the holy Fathers of the Church that even after death those who had erred either against the faith or against the canons of the Church ought to be anathematized, we likewise see that it is necessary to make known to everyone what has occurred in our own age, so that every contradiction that might be raised by profane heretics and by the patrons of their impiety may be removed. For Laurence and Dioscorus, who at different times had usurped the sanctity of the apostolic throne, although they had committed no fault concerning the faith, were nevertheless judged and condemned by the apostolic See after their death, for the very reason that they had attempted to assume the episcopate by devious means.

[Col. 0326B] But since you have also added in your letters that if someone anathematizes a heretic and, passing judgment against him, includes all who share his opinion, that person thereby includes everyone who in any way has approved the very thing being condemned; and therefore, since you have condemned Paul of Samosata, Photius, Nestorius, and Bonosus, it is unnecessary to condemn Theodore by name as sharing their opinion—know first that those who have followed the authors of heresies in error, without themselves deceiving others, are anathematized without their names being mentioned; but the leaders and teachers of heresies are anathematized by name.

Theodore was not only the teacher of Nestorius, but also led very many people into error through his impious writings. For just as the orthodox teachers of the Church are recognized from their own doctrines and commended because of them, so, conversely, the authors of perverse opinions are exposed and anathematized from their own writings. Since, then, Theodore was a heresiarch and uttered nearly countless blasphemies in his books, you have no remaining reason for refusing to pronounce anathema against him.

Concerning the exposition of the faith that you inserted in your letters, although there are many points about which we would have grounds for complaint against you, nevertheless we thought that the whole matter ought to be excused as the result of ignorance and simplicity. In some places you wrote with affected cleverness; in others you used words that have never been employed either in the sacred writings or by the holy Fathers of the Church; elsewhere you condemned the teachers of the Church according to your own judgment; and you also passed over in silence someone who unquestionably belongs to the orthodox faith. Therefore, in accordance with the admonition of the holy Fathers, you must either speak knowingly or, if you are ignorant, remain silent and be instructed by the learned and those who possess knowledge.

Since you have now written how we ought to answer the Egyptians, we are astonished that you—who have defended that impious epistle, Theodore, Nestorius, and their perverse opinions—have undertaken to instruct us about what we should answer other enemies of the Church. For if anyone considers what you have written, nothing will encourage the Egyptians except that they should receive Nestorius and Theodore as heretics and reject all the holy Fathers who condemned them and their unbelief; thus they would fall from one error into another. Yet, when writing to us that we should answer the enemies of the Church, you have not hesitated to call that abominable epistle orthodox.

You should therefore first strive to correct yourselves, and afterward to teach others. For if anyone defends either Theodore, or the epistle of Ibas in question, or the writings of Theodoret composed against the right faith, that person is counted among the heretics and becomes alien to the Catholic Church. Its head is the only-begotten Son of God, our God and Lord Jesus Christ; and that impious epistle, together with the patrons of Theodore, is separated from his Church.

It is therefore expedient for you to cease defending that impious epistle and Theodore. For if the Apostle Paul forbids anything to be called by his own name or by the name of the other apostles, and rebukes those who said, “I belong to Paul, but I to Cephas, and so forth,”

A few things are missing.

**In the year of the Lord 556. Gildas the Wise.**

[Col. 0327]

## Notice (from Gallandius)

[Col. 0327C] **I.** Gildas, surnamed the Wise, is said to have been born in the year of Christ 493. For the author himself reveals that he was brought into the light in that year, in these words [Note: [Col. 0327D] Gildas, part I, *History*, chapter 26, below, col. 000.]:

> “From that time … up to the year of the siege of Mount Badon … and the forty-fourth year, as I know, is arising [or beginning], the first month already having elapsed, which is also the year of my birth.”

From this passage Vossius argues [Note: [Col. 0327D] Vossius, *On Latin History*, book II, chapter 21, p. 243.] that Gildas was born in the very year we have just indicated. For, he says, the Saxons came to Britain in the year 449, according to Bede [Note: [Col. 0327D] Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chapter 15.], and the Britons crushed them at Mount Badon. Thus the forty-fourth year from the first arrival of the Saxons rises to the year 493, which was Gildas’s year of birth, as he himself asserts.

John Smith, however, offers an interpretation of Gildas’s words different from that of Vossius in his notes to his excellent edition of Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History* [Note: [Col. 0327D] Smith, notes on Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chapter 16, p. 53, Cambridge edition, 1722.]. For the learned man thinks that the number of years given by Gildas refers rather to the time when he was writing than to the arrival of the Saxons: namely, that Gildas wrote in the forty-fourth year after the battle of Badon, a year especially notable to him because it was also his birth-year.

Mabillon had previously anticipated Smith’s opinion in these words [Note: [Col. 0328D] Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, first century, volume I, p. 130.]:

> “The forty-four years that Gildas mentions did not intervene between the arrival of the Saxons and the siege of Badon … [Col. 0328C] but between the siege and the writing of his little work. For he speaks of years whose last year was still in progress while he was writing: ‘the forty-fourth year,’ he says, ‘is beginning, one month having already elapsed.’”

So says this most learned man. In my judgment, however, this interpretation seems alien to Gildas’s own meaning, chiefly because the author was also called Badonicus, after the battle fought by the Britons against the Saxons at Mount Badon. He acquired this surname, evidently, because he was brought into the world in the very year of the siege of Badon.

**II.** Concerning the deeds of Gildas, the anonymous monk of Rhuys transmitted many details in a literary work, his *Life of Gildas*. John a Bosco first published it at Lyon in 1605 [Note: [Col. 0328D] Bosco, *Library of Fleury*, p. 426.], then Bollandus [Note: [Col. 0328D] Bollandus, *Acts of the Saints*, January, volume II, p. 958.], and finally Mabillon published a more complete version [Note: [Col. 0328D] Mabillon, cited work.].

From it we learn that our author was British by nation and a disciple of Hildutus. Under him he was first trained both in the liberal arts and in the study of the divine Scriptures; afterward, having been initiated into sacred orders, he embraced the monastic life and became famous for many distinguished virtues in the noble monastery of Banchor. He flourished at the time when five British kings ruled over different territories: namely Constantine, Aurelius Conanus, Vortiporius, Cuneglassus, and Maglocunus. Since he was safely established in Britain across the sea, he bitterly attacks all of them for their crimes and their bad administration of the state [Note: [Col. 0329C] Gildas, part II, *Epistle*.].

“Moreover,” says Gale [Note: [Col. 0329C] Gale, preface to the fifteenth historians of Britain, p. 9.], “our author is known to have recalled one of them to a sound mind. For in a certain Welsh chronicle I read the following about Constantine, whom Gildas rebuked: ‘The conversion of Constantine to the Lord.’”

### III

A man outstanding in faith and holiness, and likewise of the highest learning, when religious brothers who had come to him from Britain asked him, wrote a little epistolary work ten years after he had departed from there. These are the words of the monk of Rhuys who composed Gildas’s *Life* [Note: Anonymous, *Life of Gildas*, no. 19]. The work is entitled as follows: *A Lamenting Book on the Ruin of Britain*, divided into three parts: I. History; II. Letter; III. Rebuke of the Clergy. In the *History* he compresses much into little. Thereafter he proceeds at greater length, rebuking both the kings and the priests of his time.

It may be inferred that Gildas wrote this little work after the year 543 from his account of Constantine, the tyrant of Damnonia [Note: Gildas, Part II, *Letter*, § 2], who tore open with sword and spear, as though they were teeth, the sides of two royal boys and an equal number of their attendants between the sacred altars. Matthew of Westminster likewise reports that this occurred in the year 543. If, however, one follows Ussher [Note: Ussher, *Ancient Ecclesiastical History of Britain*, p. 532, second London edition, 1687], Gildas published his work in 564 and died in 570. Mabillon, however, takes a different view: he believes that Gildas died in 565, already an octogenarian [Note: Mabillon, cited work, p. 138, note a]. The authors of the *Gallic Literary History* follow Mabillon [Note: *Gallic Literary History*, vol. III, p. 280].

Moreover, among others, Bede [Note: Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chapter 22] and Alcuin remember Gildas and his little work; Alcuin calls Gildas “the wisest of the Britons” [Note: Alcuin, letter 28, *Works*, p. 1535]. Yet, as Smith observes [Note: Smith on Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chapter 22], “Gildas’s book *On the Ruin of Britain* is sufficiently well known today. Its author, Gildas, is almost entirely unknown, evidently because of excessive distinction. Hence so many surnames: Albanius, the Wise, the Badonic, the Historian; whereas in truth there is one and the same Gildas”; from whom, it is said, three were fabricated. On this subject Bollandus [Note: Bollandus, cited work, pp. 953 ff.], Mabillon [Note: Mabillon, cited work, pp. 129 ff.] and Fabricius [Note: Fabricius, *Medieval Latin Library*, vol. III, pp. 174 ff.] have written at greater length, to say nothing of Cave [Note: Cave, *Literary History*, vol. I, p. 539] and others.

### IV

Gildas’s little book first appeared in London in 1525, edited by Polydore Vergil. Yet, says Leland [Note: Leland, *Assertion of Arthur*, p. 32], his copy is defective, disordered, and mutilated—so much so that, even if it were restored to life, its parent would scarcely recognize the offspring. John Josselin appended a severe criticism of this Vergilian edition to his own edition of Gildas, likewise published in London in 1568.

The earlier edition of Polydore is reproduced by both Basel *Orthodoxographia* editions and by the Paris, Cologne, and Lyon *Libraries of the Fathers*. Commelin followed Josselin’s later edition in his *Collection of British Writers*.

“Yet these two editions,” says Gale [Col. 0330B] [Note: Gale, preface to the *Fifteen Historians of Britain*, p. 4], “whether that of Polydore Vergil or that of John Josselin, differed from one another so greatly that they deprived their author of all credibility, and one might still search for Gildas in Gildas. I therefore thought it most advisable to print him again, using a written manuscript which neither of the earlier editors had examined and which was free from the shameful and absurd interpolation that had disgraced the other copies. Nor did I rely upon a single book in purifying Gildas: I summoned assistance for this undertaking from elsewhere as well.”

Thus he edited Part I of Gildas’s work, namely the *History*, from an ancient manuscript in Cambridge; but the remaining two parts—the *Letter* and the *Rebuke of the Clergy*—from a Cotton manuscript. Accordingly, we have presented this edition—unknown to the just-mentioned authors of the *Gallic Literary History* [Note: *Gallic Literary History*, cited work, p. 283], certainly the best and most accurate of all, and published at Oxford in 1691 through the efforts of Thomas Gale—at the beginning of the work entitled *Fifteen Writers of British, Saxon, and Anglo-Danish History, Published from Ancient Manuscript Codices*. We have increased it with a few observations here and there, separately interwoven with the distinguished editor’s notes, and leave them to the judgment of scholars.

[Col. 0329]

## Gildas the Wise’s Lamenting Book on the Ruin of Britain (C)*

### Author’s Preface

[Col. 0329D] In this book [Note: The printed editions read “in this letter”], whatever I shall have pursued rather by lamenting than by declaiming—even in a humble style, though with benevolent intent—let no one suppose that I am setting myself against all men in contempt, or above them all, since I lament in tearful complaints the common loss of good things and the accumulation of evils. Rather, let him understand that I am grieving with my country over its misfortunes and wretchedness, and rejoicing with it in its remedies.

But since it has been appointed for me not so much to proclaim the dangers of savage war to the bravest soldiers as to the slothful, I remained silent—I confess—with immense anguish of mind [Note: The edition reads “with anguish of heart.” The remainder is wanting until “so that I might.”] [Note: The printed edition lacks *viro*, and rightly so, it seems; perhaps *vere*, “truly,” should be read.] and contrition of spirit, with a broken heart, repeatedly turning all these matters over in my mind in astonishment [Note: A finite verb seems to be missing, such as “I was accustomed,” or something similar], and—as the Lord is the searcher of my inmost parts—for the space of ten years, or even longer, as time passed.

Ignorance, as now also, together with my dearest friends’ injunctions, restrained me from writing any sort of admonition [Note: The edition reads: “together with my unworthy merits restraining me from writing any sort of admonition.” The printed editions continue as follows]:

> “Nevertheless I read of the astonishing lawgiver who, because of doubt about a single word, did not enter the desirable land; of the sons of the priest who, by bringing strange fire to the altar, perished by a swift death; of the people who transgressed God’s words—six hundred thousand, excepting two faithful men—and who, though especially dear to God (for their path had been made most level by the gravel of the Red Sea’s depths, their heavenly food was bread, their drink a new thing from the rock for the traveler, and their undefeated battle-line depended only upon the extended raising of their hands), fell scattered among the beasts, by the sword and by fire throughout the deserts of Arabia; of the unknown city’s gates and the opposing walls of the city, as though those of the Jordan, destroyed after the entrance at God’s command by the sound of trumpets alone; of the little cloak and the small amount of gold taken from what had been devoted to destruction, which brought many down; of the broken covenant with the Gibeonites, though extracted by cunning, which brought death upon some; of the sins of men, and the plaintive voices of the holy prophets, especially Jeremiah, lamenting the ruin of his city with an alphabet of fourfold form.

> “I also saw in our own time, as that man had lamented, a city sitting solitary and widowed which had formerly been full of peoples, mistress of nations, chief of provinces, and made tributary [that is, the Church] (Lamentations 1:1); gold darkened and the finest color changed (Lamentations 4:1) [that is, the splendor of God’s word]; the sons of Zion (that is, of the holy mother Church), renowned and clothed with the finest gold, embracing dung (ibid., 2). And what had grown intolerably for him, since he was a person of distinction, also increased, in whatever way, the burden of sorrow for me, though I am worthless, when he had described those same people flourishing in prosperity:

> “‘Her Nazarites were whiter than snow, more ruddy than ancient ivory, more beautiful than sapphires’ (ibid., 7).

> “As I gazed upon these and many other things in the ancient Scriptures as in a kind of mirror of our life, I also turned to the New Scriptures, and there I read more clearly what had perhaps previously been obscure to me, when the shadow had ceased and the truth shone more firmly. I read, I say, that the Lord had said:

> “‘I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel’ (Matthew 15:24);

> “and, conversely:

> “‘But the children of the kingdom will be cast into outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth’ (Matthew 8:12);

> “and again:

> “‘It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs’ (Matthew 15:26);

> “likewise:

> “‘Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites!’ (Matthew 23:13 and following).

> “I heard:

> “‘Many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven’ (Matthew 8:11);

> “and, in contrast:

> “‘Then I will say to them: Depart from me, workers of iniquity’ (Matthew 7:23).

> “I read:

> “‘Blessed are the barren, and the breasts that never nursed’ (Luke 23:29);

> “and, conversely:

> “‘Those who were ready entered with him into the wedding feast. Later the other virgins came, saying: Lord, Lord, open to us’ (Matthew 25:10–12).

> “They received the answer: ‘I do not know you.’

> “I certainly heard:

> “‘Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned’ (Mark 16:16).

> “I read in the Apostle’s words (Romans 11:17) that a branch of the wild olive had been grafted into the good olive tree, but that it would be cut off from the fellowship of its root and richness if it did not fear but became proud.

> “I knew the Lord’s mercy, and I feared his judgment. I praised grace, but I was afraid of the repayment to each according to his works. Seeing dissimilar sheep of one flock, I rightly called Peter most blessed because of his complete confession of Christ, but Judas most wretched because of his love of greed; Stephen glorious because of the palm of martyrdom, but Nicolaus wretched because of the mark of filthy heresy.

> “I certainly read:

> “‘Everything was held in common among them’ (Acts 4:32);

> “but also what was said:

> “‘Why have you agreed together to tempt the Spirit of God?’ (Acts 5:3).

> “I saw, by contrast, how much security had grown among the people of our own time, as though there were nothing to fear.

> “Turning these and many more matters over repeatedly in an astonished mind, which for the sake of brevity we have decided to omit, I said: If the Lord did not spare a people chosen from all nations, a royal seed and holy nation [to which he had said, ‘Israel is my firstborn’ (Exodus 4:32)], nor its priests, prophets, and kings through so many ages, nor the Apostle as minister, nor the members of that primitive Church, when they deviated from the straight path, what will he do with the black ink of such an age as this? Besides those unspeakable and monstrous sins which it shares with all the world’s criminals, it has also acquired a certain apparently innate and indelible weight of folly, and an unavoidable light-mindedness.

> “What shall I say to myself? Is such a task entrusted to you, wretched man, as though you were a conspicuous and eminent teacher, that you might withstand the blows of so violent a torrent and preserve the deposit entrusted to you against this chain of long-established crimes, stretched out intermittently and widely over so many years?

> “And: Be silent. Otherwise it is as though one said to the foot, ‘Watch,’ and to the hand, ‘Speak.’ Britain has rulers; it has watchmen. What are you planning to mutter in your trifling? It has rulers, I say—it has them, if not more, at least in due number. But because they are weighed down beneath so great a burden, they have no room to breathe.

> “My thoughts, as though fellow debtors, therefore anticipated and opposed one another with such objections, or ones much sharper than these. As I said, they struggled for no short time [since I had read that there is a time for keeping silence and a time for speaking (Ecclesiastes 3:7)] in a kind of narrow passageway of fear.

> “At last the creditor prevailed and conquered:

> “‘If you lack the boldness not to fear being branded with the fitting mark of golden freedom among the truthful rational creatures, creatures of a second derivation from the messengers, at least do not reject the impulse of the intelligent, though hitherto speechless, she-ass, inspired by God’s Spirit. Unwilling to be the conveyance of the turbaned magician bent on cursing God’s people, she crushed his unshod foot in the narrow space of the vineyard wall. Though for this she suffered hostile blows, she showed him the heavenly angel standing against him with a sword drawn from its sheath—whom he, blinded by brutish stupidity, had not seen—indicating him, as it were, to one ungrateful and furious and unlawfully striking her innocent sides.’

> “‘Therefore, in zeal…’”]

Consequently, in zeal for the house of the Lord, by the reasoning of the sacred law and of my thoughts, or compelled by the religious prayers of my brothers, I now discharge the debt exacted long ago: humble indeed in style [Note: This word is absent from the edition], but, as I think, faithful and friendly to all excellent Christians; burdensome and intolerable, however, to foolish apostates.

The former, if I am not mistaken, will receive it perhaps with tears flowing from the love of God; the others with sorrow—but sorrow wrung from indignation and the faint-heartedness of a conscience caught in the act.

Therefore [Note: The edition reads “But before the promise”], God willing, I shall undertake to speak briefly:

1. Of the situation;
2. Of obstinacy;
3. Of subjection;
4. Of rebellion;
5. Of the second subjection and harsh servitude [Note: The edition reads “also of subjection and cruel servitude”];
6. Of religion;
7. Of persecution;
8. Of the holy martyrs;
9. Of the various heresies;
10. Of the tyrants;
11. Of the two victorious nations [Note: The edition reads “devastating nations”], and of the first devastation [Note: These words are absent from the edition];
12. Of defense;
13. Of the second devastation [Note: The edition reads “also of devastation”];
14. Of the second vengeance;
15. Of the third devastation;
16. Of famine;
17. Of letters [Note: The edition reads “letters to Aetius.” Yet in the Paris *Library of the Fathers*, 1644, vol. V, p. 361, the words “to Aetius” are omitted, as they appear in the Cambridge manuscript];
18. Of victory;
19. Of crimes;
20. Of enemies suddenly announced;
21. Of the famous plague;
22. Of counsel;
23. Of the much more savage enemy than the first;
24. Of the destruction of cities;
25. Of the survivors;
26. Of the final peace [Note: Another reads “of the fatherland, of victory, which…”; the Paris *Library of the Fathers* has “of the peace which…”],

which final victory has been granted in our own times by the will of God [Note: The edition reads “we shall attempt”].

## First Part: History [Note: The edition reads “Letter.” The Paris *Library of the Fathers*, cited work, gives this heading: “Gildas the Wise, *On the Ruin and Conquest of Britain*, or a Sharp Rebuke against the Whole Order and People of the British Nobility.”]

### Of Gildas

[Col. 0333]

## Chapter I. Of the Situation of Britain

Britain is an island situated almost at the extreme limit of the world, toward the north-west wind [Note: Thus the Oxford edition from the Cambridge manuscript, as I believe. Another reading is *circum*, “around.” Unless one suspects an error either in the manuscript or in the printed English edition, the reading *circium* should be judged sound. For *circius*, as the lexicographers teach us, is a very violent wind blowing between the summer west and the north; it is so called from *circus* because of its whirlwind and gyration, by which it disturbs and overturns everything. Afterward I noticed that the manuscript reading *Circium* is sound and should be retained. For below, in chapter 11, the author mentions the Scots as coming from the *Circius*, and the Picts from the north. I am surprised that the Oxford editor passed over this passage], and toward the west, balanced, as they say, by the divine scales that weigh the whole earth. It stretches more toward the axis from the south-west to the north, and occupies a length of eight hundred miles and a breadth of two hundred, except for the longer reaches of its various promontories, which are surrounded by the curving bays of the Ocean.

By its extent and, so to speak, by an impassable circle enclosing it on every side, except for the strait on the southern side by which one sails to Belgic Gaul, it is strengthened by the mouths of two famous rivers, the Thames and the Severn, like arms through which overseas luxuries were once conveyed to it by ships, and by the influx of other smaller rivers.

It is adorned with twenty-eight cities [Note: The Fragment preserved by John a Bosco reads *Quaternis fulget*, literally “it shines with fours/fourfold things”; the fragmentary wording does not itself state “twenty-eight.”], and with several fortresses [Note: “It is adorned with fortresses.” Thus the aforementioned Fragment], walls [Note: “Walls also, and towers, serrated gates.” Thus the aforementioned Fragment. The Paris *Library of the Fathers* omits “serrated”], towers, serrated gates, and buildings whose roofs [Note: Josselin omits *-que*, “and”; the Fragment has “also buildings”] were raised to threatening heights [Note: Thus Josselin and the Fragment. In the Cambridge manuscript it is corruptly read *proteleritate*] and joined together in strong, elevated construction by works not unreasonably well fortified [Note: The Fragment has “are seen”; Josselin has “by fortifications.” The whole passage is read in the Fragment, not implausibly, as follows: “adorned with well-arranged fortifications”].

It has broad plains [Note: “It also shines with broad plains,” in the Fragment], hills beautifully situated and highly suitable for cultivation, and mountains [Note: Josselin omits *-que*, “and”; the Fragment has “mountains also”] well suited to alternating pastures for animals [Note: “Especially,” in the Fragment; the Paris *Library of the Fathers* also has “especially”]. Flowers of different colors, trodden by human feet [Note: Josselin has “whose various flowers”; enclosed in parentheses, the Fragment reads: “which are made pleasing to human eyes by flowers of various colors”], once impressed upon them a not unbecoming image or painting [Note: The edition lacks *quondam*, “once.” The Paris *Library of the Fathers* reads “they impressed upon them a not unbecoming image, as though a painting.” Correctly].

Like a chosen bride adorned with various jewels, it is watered by bright springs, whose frequent waters drive along, as it were, snow-white pebbles; by very clear streams creeping with a gentle murmur and offering, to those resting on their banks, a sweet pledge of refreshment; and by lakes pouring forth the cold torrent of living water [Note: The edition reads *ipsorumque*, “and of those same [streams],” rather than *quorumque*, “of whose [banks].” The Paris *Library of the Fathers* has *suavis soporibus*, “sweet for sleep”; perhaps *soporis*, “of sleep,” should be read, as in the Fragment above.].


### Restored textual apparatus for Chapter I

- At “by its extent,” the manuscript has *diffusione* (“by [its] breadth/extent”); the printed edition reads *diffusiore* (“more expansive”).
- At “the mouths of two famous rivers,” the manuscript has *duum* and the printed edition *duorum*, inflectional forms both meaning “of two.”
- For the buildings, the text has *quorum* (“whose”); the printed edition reads *quarum*, the feminine form “whose.”
- The text reads *in edito* (“on/in the height”); the Fragment has *in editum* (“to a height”). Where the text has *pangebantur* (“were fixed/joined”), the Fragment reads *cernuntur* (“are seen”). Where it has *molitionibus* (“structures/works”), Josselin reads *munitionibus* (“fortifications”). The Fragment gives the whole phrase as *non improbabiliter est adornata instructis munitionibus*, “it is adorned, not implausibly, with well-arranged fortifications.”
- For the landscape, Josselin reads *quorum diversorum* (“whose various [flowers]”). The Fragment’s parenthesis reads: “which are made pleasing to human sight by flowers of various colors.” From there through the end of the chapter the Fragment reads: “Like a chosen bride adorned with various jewels, it rejoices in bright and frequent springs; from them streams creeping with a gentle murmur offer weary travelers a sweet pledge of sleep. It is also improved by the mouths, like arms, of two famous rivers, namely the Thames and the Severn, by which overseas luxuries were once carried on boats to Britain; and it is watered by the influx of other smaller rivers.”
- The main text has plural *imprimebant* (“they impressed”); another reading has singular *imprimebat* (“it impressed”).

## Chapter II. Of Obstinacy

This island, standing with head and mind held high, has risen, from the time it was inhabited, now against God, sometimes against its citizens, occasionally even against overseas kings, and sometimes against its subjects [Note: The edition lacks the word *interdum*, “sometimes”].

For what business can be more deformed or more unjust in human undertakings, or be introduced into them, than to deny God the fear due to him, good citizens the affection due to them, and those established in higher dignity the honor owed to them without injury to faith; to break faith with the divine and human order; and, after casting aside fear of heaven and earth, to rule someone according to one’s own inventions and desires?

Therefore, omitting the ancient errors common to all nations, by which the whole human race was bound and shackled before Christ’s coming in the flesh [Note: The printed editions read *Igitur non omittens*, “therefore not omitting”; from the context the negative particle should be deleted, whether in the manuscript or in the editions. The following clauses are “nor enumerating,” “nor specifically denouncing,” and “remaining silent,” followed by “I shall nevertheless try to bring forward.”]; and not enumerating the very monstrous, almost numberless diabolical prodigies of the country, some of which we still behold with distorted features, standing in their customary fashion within or outside deserted walls; nor specifically denouncing the mountains, hills, or rivers once deadly but now useful to human beings, to which a blind people then heaped divine honor; and remaining silent about the ancient years of monstrous tyrants made famous in other distant regions—for Porphyry, that rabid eastern dog against the Church [Note: The edition reads “that rabid eastern dog against the Church,” with the order altered], in the style of his madness and vanity, even appended this statement: “Britain is a fertile province of tyrants,” he said [Note: The printed editions omit *est*, “is”]—I shall nevertheless try to bring forward those calamities which Britain both suffered in the times of the Roman emperors and inflicted upon other citizens living far away [Note: The edition reads “and upon distant citizens”].

As far as I can, I shall rely not so much on the writings of the country or on the records of its authors—for if any such writings existed, they have either been burned by the fires of the enemy or carried farther away in the fleet of citizens driven into exile [Note: The edition reads “of exiles,” which is more agreeable] and are therefore unavailable—as on overseas reports, which, interrupted by frequent gaps, do not make the matter sufficiently clear.


### Restored textual apparatus for Chapter II

- At “those established in higher dignity,” the manuscript has *compositis* (“ordered/established”); the printed edition reads *positis* (“placed”).
- After “by their own inventions,” the printed edition has the abbreviated reading *et lib.* (“and desires,” apparently). The editor considers that printed reading perhaps preferable to the other manuscript, but also argues that the negative in *Igitur non omittens* (“therefore not omitting”) must be deleted because the following coordinated clauses are “nor enumerating,” “nor denouncing by name,” and “remaining silent,” followed by “I shall nevertheless try to bring forward.” The resulting sense is therefore “Therefore, omitting.”
- The manuscript’s order is *numero vincentia Aegyptiaca*, “Egyptian [prodigies] surpassing in number”; the printed edition has *Aegyptiaca vincentia*, the same words in reversed order.

## Chapter III. Of Subjection

For when the Roman kings had obtained dominion over the world, and, after subjugating every neighboring region or island toward the East as far as the first peace with the Parthians and the frontier of the Indians—for after that peace wars ceased almost everywhere—had strengthened their power through periods of greater renown, the battle-line of flame, as it were, of unyielding force [Translation note: The governing source phrase is *non acies flammae quodammodo rigidi tenoris … cohiberi potuit vel exstingui*, “the battle-line of flame, as it were, of unyielding force … could neither be checked nor extinguished”; the Paris *Library of the Fathers*, cited work, p. 363, adds *terroris*, “of terror,” in the margin, yielding an alternative phrase “of unyielding terror.”] could neither be checked nor extinguished by the blue torrent of the Ocean toward the West.

Rather, crossing the sea, it brought the laws of obedience to the island without opposition. It subdued an unwarlike but faithless people—not so much by sword and fire [Note: The edition lacks the conjunction *et*, “and,” immediately introducing “engines”] and siege engines, as other nations, but by threats alone or by the shocks of judgments. The people displayed obedience to its commands only on the surface of their faces, while suppressing deep within their hearts the pain of doing so.


### Restored textual apparatus for Chapter III

- The main text reads *reges Romani* (“Roman kings”); the printed edition reads *reges Romanorum* (“kings of the Romans”).
- The main text has *vel cohiberi potuit, vel exstingui*, “could either be checked or extinguished,” within the governing negative; the printed edition transposes the first *vel*: *cohiberi vel potuit*. The source-bound rendering above expresses the resulting negative pair as “could neither be checked nor extinguished.”

## Chapter IV. Of Rebellion

When they soon afterward returned to Rome, as they say, because of a shortage of turf [Note: Josselin reads “as they were doing,” incorrectly. The Paris *Library of the Fathers* has “as they said”], and suspected nothing of rebellion, the treacherous lioness slaughtered the governors left behind to proclaim more fully or confirm the designs of Roman rule.

When these events had occurred [Note: Here chapter 4 begins in the Cambridge manuscript], and news of such things was brought to the senate, and an army hastened to take vengeance upon the crafty little foxes—as he represented them [Note: Another reading has “the crafty little foxes.” The Paris *Library of the Fathers* reads “with a successful army, to avenge the crafty little foxes,” omitting “as he represented them.” Nevertheless the manuscript reading *propero*, “hastening,” is preferable]:

there was no military fleet prepared to fight bravely for the fatherland upon the sea, nor a square battle-line, nor a right wing or any other apparatus of war drawn up on the shore [Note: The edition reads “nor a right wing or any other [forces] are drawn up.” The Paris *Library of the Fathers* has “are seen,” but wrongly omits *nec* or *neque*, “nor”];

instead, backs were offered to the pursuers as shields [Note: The edition reads “backs are offered as a shield.” Shortly afterward it has *efferetur*, “will be spread,” instead of *efferatur*, “is spread.” The Paris *Library of the Fathers* has *effertur*, “is spread,” and earlier *ita*, “thus,” rather than *ita ut*, “so that.” The editors’ reading *dantur*, “are offered,” is probably better than the manuscript’s *dabantur*, “were offered,” as suggested by the following verb *protenduntur*, “are stretched out”];

and necks were stretched out womanishly to swords, and hands to be bound, with a cold shudder running through the bones. Thus, as a proverb and derision, the saying was spread far and wide: “The Britons are not brave in war, nor faithful in peace” [Note: The Paris *Library of the Fathers* has simply “The Britons are not”; perhaps this is more correct].

## Chapter V. Of the Second Subjection and Harsh Servitude

Accordingly, after many of the treacherous had been killed by the Romans, and some had been reserved for servitude as slaves, lest the land be reduced entirely to a wilderness, the Romans departed for Italy, leaving behind certain of their own officials [Note: The edition reads “the Romans, after many…” and shortly afterward “leaving behind their officials.”]

They intended to make the native people’s backs bear whips, their necks bear a yoke, and the name of Roman servitude cling to the soil, and to wear down the crafty nation not so much with military force as with scourges [Note: The edition reads “with lashes.” The Paris *Library of the Fathers* has earlier “to impose the honor of Roman servitude upon the soil by name alone.” It then reads “to purchase the crafty nation…” and continues disastrously].

If circumstances required it, they would, as the saying goes, fit a sword drawn from its sheath to the side of that people [Note: The edition omits the word *populi*, “of the people”], so that the island would be considered not British but Roman [Note: The edition reads “Romania”], and whatever bronze, silver, or gold it could possess would be stamped with the image of Caesar [F: “of Caesar”].


### Restored textual apparatus for Chapter V

- At Britain, “lacking wine and oil,” the text reads *experte* (“lacking”); the printed edition has *experte relicta* (“left lacking”). The text then says *suorumque quosdam praepositos relinquentes*, “leaving behind certain officials of their own”; the printed edition has *suorum … relinquentes praepositos*, the same elements with “officials” displaced after “leaving.”
- The Paris *Library of the Fathers* reads earlier: “to make the honor of Roman servitude adhere to the soil in name alone.” It then has “to purchase the crafty nation … so that it would be reckoned not Britain but Roman,” readings the editor condemns as thoroughly corrupt. These are distinct from the text’s “wear down the crafty nation” and “be reckoned not Britain but a Roman island.”

## Chapter VI. Of Religion [Note: This chapter begins as chapter V in the manuscript codex]

Meanwhile, for the island stiffened by icy cold and, as though separated by a greater expanse of land, not near the visible sun, that true Sun—Christ—showed his radiant light to the whole world, not from the temporal firmament alone [Note: The edition omits *sol*, “sun,” and has “from the temporal firmament alone”], but also from the highest summit of heaven, which surpasses all times.

In the time of Tiberius Caesar, as we know, toward the end of his reign, when his religion was propagated without any impediment, while the prince threatened informers of his followers with death despite the senate’s opposition [Note: The Paris *Library of the Fathers* reads: “Christ, showing the radiant light of himself to the world, grants his rays, that is, his commandments, at the time, as we know, of Tiberius Caesar, toward the end of whose reign his religion was propagated without any impediment, with the prince threatening the informers of his soldiers with death against the will of the senate.” Everything is reversed], Christ first granted his rays—that is, his commandments.

## Chapter VII. Of Persecution

Although these things were received lukewarmly by the inhabitants, they were received completely by some and less completely by others, until the nine-year persecution of the tyrant Diocletian. During it, churches throughout the world were overthrown, and all the sacred Scriptures that could be found were burned in the streets, while chosen priests of the Lord’s flock were slaughtered together with innocent sheep.

Thus, if it had been possible, not even a trace of the Christian religion would have appeared in certain provinces [Note: The edition reads “in places of the province”]. There then occurred how many flights, how many slaughterings, how many punishments by various deaths, how many downfalls of apostates from the religion [Note: The printed edition omits *religionis*, “of the religion,” and shortly afterward reads *gloriosorum*, “of glorious [martyrs].” The Paris *Library of the Fathers* instead has *gloriosae*, “of glorious [religion],” associating “glorious” with religion.], how many crowns of the most glorious martyrs, how many frenzied rages of persecutors, and, in contrast, how much endurance of the saints there was, ecclesiastical history relates.

Thus, in a dense column, vying with one another, the whole Church hurried toward the pleasant kingdom of heaven, as toward its native home, leaving behind the darkness of the world.


### Additional textual apparatus for Chapter VII

- The word *permansere*, “there remained/continued,” is absent from Polydore Vergil and from the Paris *Library of the Fathers*. The editor observes that it may be omitted without loss because *fuere*, “there were,” occurs a few clauses later.

## Chapter VIII. Of the Holy Martyrs

God therefore magnified his mercy toward us [Note: The edition reads “God with us”—that is, Emmanuel, which is interpreted “God with us” (Matthew 1:23)], wishing all people to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4), and calling sinners no less than those who think themselves righteous [Note: The edition reads “those who think themselves righteous”] (Matthew 9:13; Mark 2:17; Luke 5:32).

By that aforementioned free gift, as we understand [Note: The edition reads “as we conjecture”], during the time of persecution, lest Britain be completely obscured by the dense darkness of black night [Note: The edition reads “lest Britain be wholly obscured”], he kindled for us the brightest lamps of the holy martyrs. Their burial places and the sites of their sufferings, if the grievous separation caused by barbarians had not taken very many of them away from their fellow citizens because of our sins [Note: The edition reads *divortio*, “separation,” rather than *divortione*, “by separation”], would kindle no small ardor of divine love in the minds of those who contemplated them.

I speak of the holy Alban of Verulamium, and Aaron and Julius, citizens of the city of the Legions, and of the others of both sexes who stood with the greatest courage in Christ’s battle-line in various places.

The first of these, after concealing in his house another confessor whom the persecutors were pursuing and who was already on the point of being captured [imitating Christ in this also, who laid down his life for the sheep (John 10:15)], first in his own home and then, after they had exchanged clothes with one another, willingly offered himself to be pursued in the garments of the brother mentioned above.

Thus, pleasing God [Note: The edition omits *placens*, “pleasing”; it is nevertheless found in the Paris *Library of the Fathers*], amid sacred confession and bloodshed before the impious, who bore the Roman brands together with a horrible phantom [Note: The edition reads “phantasy”], he was wondrously adorned by miracles of signs [Note: The edition reads “pleasing by miracles of signs,” except for the Paris *Library of the Fathers*, which correctly places *placens* above in its proper position].

Through fervent prayer he opened an unknown path, like that of the Israelites through the dry and less-traveled way—when the ark stood for a long time near the gravel of the covenant in the middle channel of the Jordan—crossing with a thousand men on dry feet beyond the bed of the noble river [Note: The edition reads “beyond the Thames”], while the torrents of the river, like precipitous mountains, hung on either side.

He made the former executioner, who witnessed such great wonders, change from a wolf into a lamb, and caused him both to desire more ardently to raise with him the triumphant palm of martyrdom and to receive it more resolutely [Note: The edition reads *sitire*, “to thirst,” rather than *sistere*, “to raise.” The latter is preferable].

The others, however, were tortured with various torments and mangled by unheard-of dismemberment of their limbs [Note: The edition omits *sunt*, “were”], so that without hesitation they fixed the glorious trophies of their martyrdom at the magnificent gates, as it were, of Jerusalem.

Those who survived concealed themselves in forests, deserts, and hidden caves, awaiting from God, the just ruler of all, severe judgments one day for the executioners, and protection for their own souls.

[Note: Here chapter VII begins in the Cambridge manuscript.]

Before the fifteen-year period of the aforementioned storm had yet been completely fulfilled, while the wicked edicts of its authors were withering through the death of those who had issued them [Note: The edition reads “while the decrees were being completed”], all Christ’s soldiers, with joyful eyes, like people receiving the mild and serene light of heavenly air after a long winter night, renew the churches destroyed to their foundations; they lay the foundations of basilicas for the holy martyrs, build and complete them; display them like victorious standards; celebrate feast days; perform the sacraments [Note: The edition reads “sacred rites”] with pure heart and mouth; and all the children rejoice, warmed, as it were, in the bosom of their mother, the Church.


### Restored textual apparatus for Chapter VIII

- The text has *et caeteros*, “and the others”; the printed edition reads *caeterosque*, likewise “and the others,” with the conjunction attached as a suffix.
- At the confessor sheltered by Alban, the printed edition omits *alium*, “another.”
- The text’s difficult order is *et discrimini se fratris in supradicti vestimentis … dedit*, “and he gave himself to the danger, in the aforesaid brother’s clothing.” The printed edition reads more plainly *et se discrimini in fratris supradicti [vestimentis dedit]*, “and he gave himself to danger in the aforesaid brother’s [clothing].”

## Chapter IX. Of the Various Heresies

This pleasing concord of the written head and members [Note: The edition lacks *-que*, “and.” The compact phrase *scripti capitis membrorumque consonantia* literally gives a concord “of the written head and members”; whether *caput* means the work’s heading, chief part, or another “head” is uncertain in the printed source.] remained until the Arian perfidy, fierce as a serpent—or rather, as it seems to me, like a serpent [Note: I would indeed prefer *ceu*, “as”]—vomiting overseas poisons upon us, caused brothers dwelling together to be disastrously separated [Note: The edition reads “to be separated disastrously.”]

Thus, as though a road had been opened across the Ocean, all the wild beasts, brandishing in their savage mouths the deadly poison of every kind of heresy, inflicted the lethal wounds of their teeth upon their homeland, which was always eager to hear something new and possessed nothing with certainty.

### Additional textual apparatus for Chapter IX

- Where the text has *edictis*, “edicts,” the printed edition reads *decretis*, “decrees.”

## CHAPTER X. On the Tyrants

And then at last, as the shoots of tyrants grew and were already bursting forth into an immense forest, the island sent to Gaul a sprout of its most bitter planting, retaining the Roman name, but not its customs and law—indeed, casting these aside—with a great accompanying crowd of attendants, and moreover with the insignia of an emperor, which he neither wore anywhere becomingly nor lawfully, but rather in tyrannical fashion, after being inaugurated by a mutinous soldiery: Maximus.

[Col. 0339B] By cunning art at first rather than by courage, he attached to his criminal kingdom, through the snares of his perjury and deceit, every neighboring district or province that he could, against the Roman order; extending one wing to Spain and the other to Italy, and establishing the throne of his unjust empire at Trier. He raged against his rulers with such madness that he drove out two legitimate emperors, one from Rome and the other from a life of most religious devotion. Nor was there delay: surrounded by such fertile acts of audacity, he was beheaded at the city of Aquileia—that man who had, so to speak, cast down from their royal necks the crowned heads of the whole world.

[Note: [Col. 0339C] The manuscript has VIII.]

[Note: [Col. 0339D] The editor reads *morem*, “custom,” instead of *mores*, “customs.”]

[Note: [Col. 0339D] The editor reads *imperatoriis*, “imperial,” instead of *imperatoris*, “of an emperor.”]

[Note: [Col. 0339D] The edition reads *non legitime*, “not lawfully,” in place of *nec legitime*, “nor lawfully.”]

[Note: [Col. 0339D] The edition omits *per*, “through/for”: “through” before the snares in chapter X, and “for” before the years in chapter XI.]

[Note: [Col. 0339D] The editor reads *feralibus*, “savage,” instead of *fertilibus*, “fertile.”]

[Note: [Col. 0339D] The editor omits *cervicibus*, “from the necks.” The edition also has *regno*, “from the kingdom,” for *regni*, “of the kingdom.”]

## CHAPTER XI. On the Two Victorious Peoples and the First Devastation

Thereafter Britain was left without all its armed soldiery and military resources, under savage rulers, stripped of its immense young manhood—which, having accompanied the footsteps of [Col. 0339C] the aforesaid tyrant, never returned home thereafter—and utterly ignorant of every use of war. For many years it endured and lamented being trampled down, first by two peoples from overseas, fiercely savage: the Scots from the northwest, and the Picts from the north.

[Note: [Col. 0339D] The editor omits *-que*, “and.”]

[Note: [Col. 0339D] The editor reads *licet*, “although,” instead of *linquitur*, “is left.”]

[Note: [Col. 0339D] The editor reads *usu penitus ignara*, “utterly ignorant of [war’s] practice,” instead of *omnis belli usus ignara penitus*, “utterly ignorant of every use of war.”]

[Note: [Col. 0339D] The edition omits *per*, “through/for”: “through” before the snares in chapter X, and “for” before the years in chapter XI.]

## CHAPTER XII. On the Defense

[Note: [Col. 0339D] The following is absent from the edition up to *ferens*, “bearing.” In the manuscript, however, this is chapter IX.]

The people of the Britons, therefore, unable to endure the Scots and Picts—on account of whose invasion and most grievous oppression [the editor reads *quarum*, “of whom,” instead of *quorum*, “of whom,” referring evidently to the preceding feminine noun *gentibus*, “peoples”; the preposition *a*, “by/from,” is absent both in the Cambridge manuscript and in the Oxford edition, where the context perhaps requires *ob eorum*, “on account of them”]—sent envoys to Rome with letters, begging in tearful appeals for an armed force to avenge them, and vowing with all the strength of their hearts that they would remain continually subject to Roman rule, if only the enemy were driven farther away.

[Col. 0340A] A legion, unmindful of the earlier disaster and sufficiently equipped with weapons, was promptly sent to them. Transported across the Ocean to their homeland in ships, it engaged the fierce enemies at close quarters, laid a great multitude of them low, drove them all from the borders, and freed the subjected citizens from the imminent captivity that was tearing them apart so cruelly.
