The legion ordered them to build a wall across the island between the two seas, so that, furnished with a body of men to repel the enemy, it might serve as a terror and as protection for the citizens. But because it was constructed by the common people without a ruler, not so much with stones as with sods, it was of no benefit.

[Note: [Col. 0339D] The editor reads *a turba*, “by the multitude,” instead of *turba*, “a body of men” (ablative in the supplied construction).]

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Second Devastation

When that legion was returning home with great triumph and joy [the edition reads *Illa domum cum triumpho magno et gaudio repedante*, “As it went back home with great triumph and joy,” omitting “legion” and changing *repetente*, “returning,” to *repedante*, “going back”; the Paris edition reads *Legione autem domum … repetente*, “But as the legion returned home …”], those former enemies—like ravenous wolves wasted by deep hunger—leapt over into the sheepfold with dry throats, [Col. 0340B] when the shepherd did not appear. Carried by the wings of oars and rowers’ arms, and by sails billowed by the wind [the editor reads *juvatis*, “assisted”; the Paris edition of the Fathers reads *velis ventorum plenis*, “by sails full of winds”], they broke through the boundaries, slaughtered everything, and reaped, trampled, and crossed over everything as though it were a ripe field of grain.

[Note: [Col. 0340C] The editor reads *ac si*, “as if,” instead of *ac quasi*, “as though.” Immediately afterward, the preposition *in* is omitted before *ovile*, “the sheepfold.” The Paris edition of the Fathers reads *ovile circumsilientes*, “leaping around the sheepfold.”]

## CHAPTER XIV. Again on the Same Devastation

[Note: [Col. 0340D] The manuscript has X. At the beginning of this chapter, the Paris edition of the Fathers reads *iterumque*, “and again,” instead of *itemque*, “and likewise,” which is preferable. In that edition *sabulone*, “sand,” is also written, more correctly than *sablone* in the Oxford edition.]

And so again complaining envoys are sent, with their garments torn, as the saying goes, and their heads covered with sand, imploring aid from the Romans. Like timid chicks crouching beneath the most faithful wings of their fathers [the editor reads *fidissimis*, “most faithful,” instead of *fidelissimis*, “most trustworthy”; the Paris edition of the Fathers reads *matrum*, “of mothers,” instead of *patrum*, “of fathers,” which may perhaps be preferable], they begged that their wretched homeland should not be utterly destroyed, and that the Roman name [the edition reads *Romanorum*, “of the Romans,” for *Romanum*, “Roman”]—which merely echoed in their ears through words—should not become worthless, having been gnawed away by the reproach of foreign peoples.

But the Romans, moved as far as human nature allows by the account of so great a tragedy, hastened the eagle-like flight of their cavalry on land and their sailors at sea. They drove the claws of their swords into the enemies’ necks, at first unexpectedly and then terribly [the edition transposes the words to *cervicibus infingunt mucronum ungues*, “they drive the claws of their swords into their necks”]. [Col. 0340C] They carried out this slaughter, likening it to the fall of leaves at their appointed season [the supplied *ad simulandam istam*, “to liken this [slaughter],” contrasts with the edition’s *assimulandam iisdem*, “to be likened to those same [falls]”]. It happens as if a mountain torrent, swollen by the frequent streams of storms, overflowing its channels with a roaring course, with furrowed back and sharp front, its waves rising, as they say, to the clouds—

[The supplied parenthesis is corrupt: *luminum quibus pupilli persaepe licet palpebrarum convolutibus innovati, adjunctis sibi minutissimarum rotarum tautonibus veluti fuscantur*. Its recoverable wording concerns “pupils of the eyes,” “often,” “although renewed by folds of the eyelids,” and their being “as if darkened,” with *tautonibus* of “very tiny wheels” joined to them; *tautonibus* and the precise construction are uncertain. The edition reads *convolatibus*, “flights/turnings,” for *convolutibus*, “foldings,” and *adjunctissimarum rotarum rivulis fuscantur*, “they are darkened by little streams of wheels set very close together.” The Paris Library of the Fathers omits everything after *alveos exundans*, “overflowing its channels,” up to *uno objectas*, the phrase beginning “with one [surge], the obstacles …”.]

—foaming wondrously, yet overcomes the masses set against it with a single surge: so those excellent rescuers quickly drove the enemy bands, if any had managed to escape, across the seas. For, [Col. 0341A] with no one resisting them, the enemies had greedily been carrying off their annual plunder across the seas. [The edition reads *ac si*, “as if,” for *ac fit, si*, “and it happens, if”; except for the Paris edition, it has *auxiliares*, “auxiliaries,” for *auxiliatores*, “rescuers,” and then *praepropere*, “very hastily,” for *propere*, “hastily.”]

The Romans, therefore, returned to their homeland, declaring that they could not be harassed so frequently by such laborious expeditions, and that so great and powerful an army should not be wearied on land and sea on account of unwarlike, wandering brigands, a disgrace to Rome. Rather, they advised, the island itself should, by becoming accustomed to arms and fighting manfully, defend its land, its little property, its wives, its children, and—what is greater than these—its freedom and life with all its strength; and it should not stretch out its hands as unarmed people to be bound in chains by peoples no stronger than itself, unless it had been dissolved by sluggishness and torpor [the editor reads *dissolveretur*, “were dissolved,” instead of *dissolverentur*, “they were dissolved,” and omits the following particle *ut*, “so that”], but should extend them armed with shields, swords, and spears, and ready for slaughter.

They advised this because they thought it would bring some advantage to the people they were leaving. They also built a wall, unlike the other one, [Col. 0341B] at public and private expense, with the wretched natives joining them, in the usual manner of construction, along a straight route from sea to sea between the cities that had by chance been established there out of fear of the enemy [the Paris edition of the Fathers reads *directo aedificant*, “they build in a straight line”]. They gave the fearful people strong admonitions; they left behind models for the preparation of weapons; and on the shore of the Ocean, toward the southern region where their ships were stationed [the edition reads *quo*, “where/to which,” for *qua*, “where/by which”], and from which the savage beasts of the barbarians were feared [the edition has *quia et inde barbaricae*, “because from there also barbarian [beasts …],” instead of *et inde barbariae*, “and from there [the beasts] of barbarism …”], they placed towers at intervals to overlook the sea. They said farewell, as though they would not return thereafter [the editor reads “and they said farewell”; the conjunction *et*, “and,” is also absent in the Paris edition of the Fathers].

[Note: [Col. 0341C] Here chapter XI begins in the Cambridge manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0341D] The editor omits *insula*, “the island.” The Paris edition of the Fathers reads *sed ut potius sola*, “but rather that it alone.” Earlier, it reads *Romana signa*, “Roman standards,” instead of *Romana stigmata*, “Roman marks of disgrace,” perhaps more correctly.]

[Note: [Col. 0341D] The editor reads *dissolveretur*, “were dissolved,” instead of *dissolverentur*, “they were dissolved,” and omits the following particle *ut*, “so that.”]

## CHAPTER XV. On the Third Devastation

[Note: [Col. 0341D] The manuscript has XII.]

And so, when those men had returned to their own country, [Col. 0341C] the foul bands of Scots and Picts emerged competitively from the small boats in which they had been carried beyond the Tithican valley [the editor reads *Styticam*, an uncertain place-name, instead of *Tithicam*; the Paris edition of the Fathers reads *Scyticam*, “Scythian.” Both also read *evecti*, “carried out/over,” for *vecti*, “carried”]. They were like dark masses of little worms emerging from the deepest small cavities of holes when the sun stands high and the heat grows hot [the supplied *cenci* is uncertain; the edition reads *cunei*, “wedges/masses,” and *caverniculis*, “little caverns,” for *cavernulis*, “little cavities”]. Their customs differed in part, but they were united by one and the same eagerness to shed blood. They covered their gallows-worthy faces with hair more than they covered the shameful parts of their bodies and the areas adjoining those parts with clothing.

When they learned of the return of their fellow-debtors and of the denial of their return, they took possession, with greater confidence than usual [the edition reads *confidentiores*, “more confident” (adjective), for *confidentius*, “more confidently” (adverb)], of the whole northernmost and farthest part of the land up to the wall, in place of the natives. Against them, a line of defenders was stationed on high ground for battle, incapable of flight and useless with their hearts trembling; day and night it languished on its senseless seat. Meanwhile, the [Col. 0342A] hooked weapons of the knots [the editor reads *nudorum*, “of naked men,” instead of *nodorum*, “of knots”] did not cease, by which the wretched citizens were dragged from the walls and dashed to the ground. This, evidently, was the punishment of premature death for those who were carried away in such a death; while by a swift end they escaped the pitiable, impending punishments of their brothers and children [the supplied *fratrum quo pignorum suorum* has an uncertain conjunction; the edition reads *quo fratrum pignorumque*, joining “brothers and children.” *Pignora*, literally “pledges,” here denotes loved ones or children].

What more should I say? [The editor omits *loquar*, “should I say.”] The cities and lofty wall were abandoned; again, there was flight for those to whom flight was possible [the editor reads *illis*, “for those,” instead of *quibus*, “for whom”]; again, dispersals more desperate than usual. Again, persecution by the enemy; again, massacres were hastened, more cruel; and just as lambs are torn apart by butchers, so the lamentable citizens were torn apart by their enemies, so that the comparison called to mind wild beasts.

[Note: [Col. 0341D] The editor reads *curucis*, “boats,” instead of *curicis*, “small boats.” The Paris edition of the Fathers reads *carruchis*, “wagons.”]

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Famine

For they tear one another apart, and in their brigandage they did not refrain from taking even the small provision of food that briefly sustained the wretched citizens [the edition reads *Nam et ipsos mutuo nec perexigui victus brevi sustentaculo miserrimorum civium latrocinando temperabant*, approximately “For they did not spare one another or the brief sustenance of the wretched citizens’ very scanty food in their plundering.” The supplied base sentence lacks a clear verb governing *nec*; the translation follows its recoverable sense]. Foreign disasters were also increased by domestic disturbances, by which [Col. 0342B] the whole region was emptied of every support of food through such frequent plunder [the editor reads *externae*, “external,” instead of *extraneae*, “foreign”; and *quod hujusmodi*, “because of this kind of thing,” instead of *quo et hujusmodi*, “by which also this kind of thing”], except for the relief provided by hunting.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Letters

Therefore the wretched survivors again sent letters to Aetius, a man of Roman authority [the Cambridge manuscript corruptly has *Agitio*, “Agitius”; this name is nowhere found among the consular fasti, so it must be corrected to *Aetio*, “Aetius.” He was Aetius III, or thrice consul, as Gildas says; in the year 446 he held the consulship with Quintus Aurelius Symmachus. See Baronius under the year 446, section 2, where he quotes this passage of Gildas], saying in this manner: “To Aetius, consul for the third time, the groans of the Britons” [the editor omits *inquiunt*, “they say”].

And after a little further speech [the editor reads *querentes*, “complaining,” instead of *loquentes*, “speaking”]: “The barbarians drive us to the sea; the sea drives us back to the barbarians. Between them arise [the editor omits *oriuntur*, “arise”] two kinds of death: either we are slaughtered or we are drowned.” They had no assistance of any kind on their behalf [the editor omits *nos*, “us,” in both instances].

Meanwhile, a dreadful and notorious famine clung to the wandering and wavering people. It compelled many of them to surrender without delay to bloody robbers, so that they might obtain a little food to revive their lives; others, however, surrendered nowhere [the editor reads *nunquam*, “never,” instead of *nusquam*, “nowhere”], but continued to rebel from the mountains themselves, the caves, and [Col. 0342C] the thickets thick with brambles.

[Additional readings, chapter XVII: the edition transposes *mittentes epistolas reliquiae*, “the survivors sending letters”; Paris reads *Igitur rursum miserae mittentes epistolas reliquiae ad Aetium Rom[anae potestatis virum]*, “Therefore the wretched survivors again sending letters to Aetius, a man of Roman authority.” The edition has *compulit*, “compelled,” for *compellit*, “compels.”]

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Victory

Then for the first time they inflicted slaughter on enemies who had been active in the land for many years [the edition inserts *praedas*, “plunder,” before *in*, giving “carrying on plundering in the land”]—not trusting in man, but in God, according to that saying of Philo: “The divine must be present when human assistance ceases” [the editor omits *exemplum*, “example”]. The boldness of the enemies subsided for a while, but not the wickedness of our people. The enemies withdrew from the citizens, but the citizens did not withdraw from their crimes.

[Note: [Col. 0342D] The editor reads *fidentes*, “trusting,” instead of *confidentes*, “trusting.”]

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Crimes

It was indeed the people’s continual custom—as it is even now—to be weak in blunting the weapons of the enemy, but strong and unconquered in [Col. 0343A] civil wars and in sustaining the burdens of sins. It is weak, I say, in carrying out the insignia of peace and truth, but strong in crimes and lies.

[Note: [Col. 0342D] The editor reads *fortis esset*, “it was strong,” omitting the rest.]

[Note: [Col. 0343D] The editor reads “bearing the burdens of sins” instead of “sustaining the burdens of sins.”]

[Note: [Col. 0343D] The editors omit “it is weak.”]

[Note: [Col. 0343D] Here chapter XIV begins in the Cambridge manuscript.]

Therefore the shameless raiders return to their winter homes, intending to return again after not much time [Josselin and Bede I.14 read *Hyberni domum*, “the Irish [return] home,” and subsequently *non longum*, “not a long [time]”]. The Picts then rested in the farthest part of the island, and thereafter as well, though they occasionally carried out raids and devastation.

During such intervals, therefore, a cruel scar was laid over the desolated people, while another, more poisonous wound began to sprout [the supplied *tactus* is grammatically uncertain; the edition reads *obducitur famis … tacite …*, “a scar of famine forms … silently …,” which the editor considers perhaps more correct]. When the devastation had ceased [the editor reads *vastitate*, “desolation,” instead of *vastatione*, “devastation”], the island overflowed with such abundance of riches that no earlier age was remembered to have possessed anything comparable; and along with them luxury grew in every form.

For it grew with exceedingly vigorous increase, so that at the same time it was said: “There is altogether such fornication as is not even heard of among the nations” (1 Corinthians 5:1).

[Col. 0343B] Nor was this the only vice; there were all the things that ordinarily arise in human nature [the editor reads *accidere*, “happen,” instead of *accedere*, “arise”], and especially—what even now overturns the whole condition of goodness in that land—hatred of the truth together with its defenders; love of falsehood together with its fabricators; acceptance of evil in place of good; reverence for wickedness in place of kindness; desire for darkness in place of the sun; acceptance of Satan in place of the angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14).

Kings were anointed, and not by God [the editor omits *et*, “and”], but those who proved more cruel than the rest; and shortly afterward they were slaughtered by their anointers, not after examination of the truth, with others chosen who were still more savage.

But if any one of them seemed gentler and somewhat nearer to the truth, against him, as though he were a destroyer of Britain [the edition transposes *Britanniae quasi* to *quasi Britanniae*, both meaning “as though [a destroyer] of Britain”], the hatred and weapons of everyone were hurled without restraint [the editor reads *contorquebantur*, “were hurled,” instead of *torquebantur*, “were hurled”]. Everything that had displeased God and everything that had pleased him [the edition reads *displicuerint, Deoque placuerint*, “may have displeased, and may have pleased God,” changing the verbal forms and placing “God” with the second verb] was [Col. 0343C] weighed in an equal balance, if not with greater favor shown to what displeased God.

Thus that prophetic example [the editor omits *exemplum*, “example”] announced to the homeland could rightly be applied—the example proclaimed to that ancient people [the editor reads *veteri*, “ancient,” instead of *veterano*, “veteran”]:

> “Children, without law you have abandoned the Lord, and you have provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger. Why do you still inquire, adding iniquity? Every head is sick, and every heart is sorrowful; from the sole of the foot to the crown, there is no soundness in it” [the editor reads *percutiemini*, “will you be struck,” for *percunctemini*, “do you inquire”] (Isaiah 1:4–6).

And so everything contrary to salvation was carried out, as though the true physician of all things bestowed no medicine upon the world [the editor reverses the order: “as though no medicine were bestowed upon the world by the true physician of all”].

And not only the secular men, but even the Lord’s flock and its shepherds—[Col. 0344A] who ought to have been an example to the entire people—were for the most part torpid and relaxed, as though soaked with wine, in drunkenness. They were consumed by swelling arrogance, contentious quarrels, the grasping claws of envy [perhaps “rapacious claws”], and undiscerning judgment between good and evil.

Thus it was plainly seen—as it is even now—that contempt was poured out upon rulers, and that they were led astray by their vain things and error [the editors omit “and that they were led astray by their vain things and error”; the Paris edition of the Fathers reads: “upon rulers, who made them err in a trackless place and not on the way”], “in a trackless place and not on the way” (Psalm 106:40).

[Note: [Col. 0343D] The editors omit *fuit* and *suis*, “was” and “with its.” Immediately afterward they have *amorque*, “and love.”]

[Note: [Col. 0343D] The editor reads *displicuerint*, “may have displeased,” and *Deoque placuerint*, “and may have pleased God,” instead of *displicuerant Deo*, “had displeased God,” and *placuerantque*, “and had pleased.”]

[Note: [Col. 0344D] The editor reads *mundo medicina … largiretur*, “medicine were bestowed upon the world,” instead of *mundo … medicinae … largiretur*, “bestowed medicine upon the world.”]

[Note: [Col. 0344D] The editor reads *haec*, “these things,” instead of *hac*, “by this.”]

[Note: [Col. 0343D] After the statement that the nation is weak in pursuing peace and truth, the edition reads *et fortis*, “and strong,” for *fortis*, “strong.”]

[Note: [Col. 0344D] The editors omit “and to be led astray by their vain things and error.”]

[Note: [Col. 0344D] The editor reads *vastitate*, “desolation,” instead of *vastatione*, “devastation.”]

[Additional readings, chapter XIX: *peccatorum onera sustinenda*, “the burdens of sins to be sustained,” for *onera peccatorum sustentanda*, the same sense with different word order and verb; *habere*, “to have,” for *haberi*, “to be had”; *et fuerunt*, “and there were,” for *fuerunt*, “there were”; *Deum … iracundiam*, “God … anger,” for *Dominum … iram*, “the Lord … anger”; *agebant*, “they did,” for *agebantur*, “were done.” The conjecture *rapacibus*, “rapacious,” is offered for *capacibus*, “capacious/grasping,” modifying envy’s claws.]

## CHAPTER XX. On the Enemies Suddenly Announced

[Note: [Col. 0344D] Here chapter XV begins in the Cambridge manuscript.]

Meanwhile, since God wished to cleanse his household and correct it, infected as it was by so great a stain of evils, by the mere report of tribulation, a winged flight of no unfamiliar rumour, as it were, penetrated the attentive ears of all: the ancient enemies were already approaching, intending utterly to destroy the whole region and inhabit it in their customary manner, [Col. 0344B] from end to end [the editor omits *totam*, “whole”].

Yet this did not profit them at all. Rather, like senseless beasts, fastening the bridle of reason firmly between their clenched teeth, they were running along the broad road of various vices, leading downward toward death [the editor reads “toward death,” instead of “and leading toward death”], abandoning the saving, though narrow, path.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Notorious Plague

Therefore, as Solomon says, “A stubborn servant is not corrected by words; though the fool is scourged, he does not feel it” (Proverbs 29:19), a deadly plague settled savagely upon the foolish people [the editor reads *incumbit*, “settles,” instead of *incubuit*, “settled”]. In a short time it struck down, without the sword’s being drawn, so great a multitude of them that the living could not bury them [the editor omits *tempore*, “time”].

Yet even by this they were not corrected [the editor reads *emendatur*, “is corrected,” instead of *emendantur*, “are corrected”], so that in that people too was fulfilled what the prophet Isaiah says:

> “And God called the people to mourning, [Col. 0344C] to baldness, and to the wearing of sackcloth. But behold, they began to kill calves and slaughter rams; behold, to eat and drink and say: ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die’” (Isaiah 22:12–13).

For the time was approaching when their iniquities would be completed, as those of the Amorites.

[Note: [Col. 0344D] The editor omits *tempore*, “time.”]

[Note: [Col. 0344D] The editor omits *populo*, “people.”]

[Note: [Col. 0344D] The editor omits *populum*, “the people.”]

[Note: [Col. 0344D] The editor omits *coeperunt*, “they began.”]

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Deliberation

A council was therefore convened: it had to decide, rather, what course would be best and most salutary for repelling the repeated and exceedingly savage incursions and plunderings of the peoples mentioned above [the editor reads “for resisting the savage and repeated incursions,” reversing the order and replacing *repellendas* with *refellendas*].

[Note: [Col. 0344D] The editor omits *potius*, “rather.”]

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Enemy Much More Savage than the First

Then all the counselors, together with the proud tyrant Vortigern, [Col. 0345A] leader of the Britons [the words “Vortigern, leader of the Britons” are absent from the edition], are blinded. They devised such a defense—or rather, such a destruction—for their homeland: that the fiercest Saxons, men of a detestable name and hated by God and human beings, should be admitted into the island, like wolves into sheepfolds, to drive back the northern peoples [the editor reads *retundendas*, “to blunt,” instead of *retrudendas*, “to drive back”].

Nothing more ruinous, nothing more bitter, was ever done to it. O deepest darkness of understanding! O desperate and savage dullness of mind! Those whom, while absent, they feared more than death, they voluntarily invited—as I may put it—beneath the roof of a single dwelling. “The princes of Thafnei are fools” [the edition reads *Taneos*, “of Taneis,” instead of the manuscript’s *Thafneos*], “giving the counsel of Pharaoh to one who is foolish” [the edition reads *insipiens*, “foolish,” instead of *insipienti*, “to one who is foolish”] (Isaiah 19:11).

Then a brood of whelps burst from the lair of the barbarian lioness in three *Cyulis*—as it is expressed in their language—“long ships” in ours, with favorable sails, [Col. 0345B] under a favorable omen and auspices [the editor omits *lingua*, “language,” and *secundo*, “favorable”]. Through these, a fixed prophecy had foretold to him that the land toward which he had directed their prows would be occupied for three hundred years; but for one hundred and fifty years—that is, half that time—it would also be repeatedly devastated [the edition reads *patriam*, “homeland,” instead of *terram*, “land”; the editor reads *librabat*, “he directed,” instead of *librarat*, “he had directed”; the editor omits *quoque*, “also”].

Having first landed in the eastern part of the island, at the tyrant’s command, he drove in his terrifying claws, as though he were going to fight for the homeland, but in fact intending to attack it more certainly. When the mother of the aforesaid band learned that its first contingent had prospered [the editor reads “having first learned that the contingent had prospered”], she sent another, longer array of attendants and dogs [the Paris edition of the Fathers reads *catervam*, “troop,” instead of *catastam*, “array”], which, carried over in ships, joined itself to the bastard companies.

From there, the shoot of iniquity, the root of bitterness, the poisonous planting suited to our merits, sprouted on our soil in savage branches and leaves [the editor reads *pullulat*, “sprouts,” instead of *pullulabat*, “was sprouting”].

The barbarians, therefore, admitted into the island, obtained provisions for themselves, as though they were soldiers and guests about to undergo [Col. 0345C] great dangers for their hosts’ benefit—as they falsely claimed. These provisions, supplied for a long time, closed, as the saying goes, the hunger of the dogs.

Again, they complained that their monthly allowances were not being distributed to them abundantly [the edition, except the Paris edition of the Fathers, reads *quaeruntur*, “are sought,” instead of *queruntur*, “they complained”], deliberately coloring their complaints with excuses; and unless a more lavish generosity were heaped upon them [the editor reads *ni*, “unless,” instead of *nisi*, “unless”], they declared that they would ravage the whole island once the treaty was broken. Nor was there delay: they followed their threats with deeds.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Overthrow of the Cities

For the eastern fire of just vengeance for the preceding crimes, fanned from sea to sea by sacrilegious hands, ravaged [Col. 0346A] every neighboring city and field [the editor omits *qui*, “which”], and did not cease burning until, consuming almost the entire surface of the island, with its red and savage tongue it licked the western Ocean.

In this Assyrian assault, to be compared with that once made upon Judea [the edition has *Judam*, “Judah,” for *Judaeam*, “Judea”; the Paris Library of the Fathers substitutes *facto*, “made,” for *comparando*, “to be compared”], the following was also fulfilled in us in its historical sense, as it is said [the edition reads *quod propheta deplorans ait*, “what the prophet says in lament”]: “They set fire to your sanctuary; they profaned the dwelling-place of your name upon the earth” (Psalm 73:7). And again he says [the editor omits *dicit*, “he says”]: “O God, the nations have entered your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple” (Psalm 78:1), and so forth.

Thus all the columns were laid low together by repeated battering rams, and all the settlers with the leaders of the churches, the priests, and the people, amid swords flashing everywhere and flames crackling [the editor reads *coloniae*, “settlements,” instead of *columnae*, “columns”]. A pitiful sight: in the middle of the streets, together lay [Col. 0346B] stones from towers torn from their lofty supports and from high walls, sacred altars, and fragments of corpses, covered with congealing crusts of purple blood, all seemingly mingled as in some dreadful winepress. [The construction *una turrium edito cardine evulsarum … saxa* is difficult: *una* can mean “together,” and *turrium … evulsarum* is plural, “of towers torn away”; *edito cardine* literally means “from a lofty hinge/pivot/support.” The edition reads *aedito … avulsarum*, with spelling and verb-prefix differences, “lofty … torn away”; Paris reads *una turrium cardine avulso*, an alternative construction with *avulso*, “torn away” (ablative singular), rather than *evulsarum* (genitive plural). The edition substitutes *sigillantibus*, “sealing,” for *gelantibus*, “congealing”; Paris has *crustis purp[urei cruoris]*, “with crusts of purple blood,” omitting the intervening wording.]

There was absolutely nothing except the terrible ruins of houses [the editor omits *horribiles*, “terrible”], with the bellies of beasts and birds serving as a burial-place in their midst—apart from the reverence due to the holy souls, if indeed many were found who during that period were carried by holy angels to the heights of heaven [the editors omit *per*, “during,” before “that time”; shortly earlier, Paris reads *quae ad ardua coeli*, “who [were carried] to the heights of heaven,” which is clearer]. For that once-good vineyard had degenerated into bitterness [the editor omits *versa*, “having been turned”], so that, according to the prophet, a cluster, or even [an uncertain final *ipsa*, “itself”] was rarely seen after the grape-gatherers or reapers had passed by (Micah 7:1).

[Note: [Col. 0345D] The editor reads *orientali*, “eastern” (dative/ablative), instead of *orientalis*, “eastern” (nominative with “fire”); the inflection changes the grammatical attachment.]

[Note: [Col. 0346C] The editor reads *coloniae*, “settlements,” instead of *columnae*, “columns.”]

[Note: [Col. 0346C] For the actual competing forms *edito/aedito*, *evulsarum/avulsarum*, and the Paris construction *una turrium cardine avulso*, see the textual note at the tower-and-carnage sentence above.]

[Note: [Col. 0346D] The editor omits *horribiles*, “terrible.”]

[Note: [Col. 0346D] The editors omit *per*, “during,” before “that time.” Earlier Paris reads *quae ad ardua coeli*, “who [were carried] to the heights of heaven,” which is clearer.]

[Note: [Col. 0346D] The editor reads *veherentur*, “were being carried,” instead of *vehebantur*, “were carried.”]

[Note: [Col. 0346D] The editor omits *versa*, “having been turned.”]

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Survivors

And so some of the wretched survivors, discovered in the mountains, were slaughtered in heaps; others, exhausted by hunger, approached and [Col. 0346C] surrendered themselves to the enemy to serve forever [the editor, except the Paris edition of the Fathers, reads *servaturi*, “to preserve,” instead of *servituri*, “to serve”]—if indeed they were not immediately slaughtered, which stood in place of the highest grace [the editor omits the preposition *in*, “in”].

Others sought regions overseas with great wailing, or as though in place of a rowing-song [the text should be corrected to *ceu celeusmatis*, “as though it were a rowing-song,” following the Paris edition of the Fathers], singing in this way beneath the folds of their sails: “You have given us like sheep for food, and among the nations you have scattered us, O God” (Psalm 44:12) [the editor omits *Deus*, “O God”].

Others, surrounded by mountain ridges, threatening precipices, dense thickets, and sea-cliffs [the editors omit the preposition *a*, “from,” and then read *vallatis*, “surrounded” (dative/ablative plural), for *vallati*, “surrounded” (nominative plural), changing its grammatical attachment], with ever-anxious minds regarding their lives as uncertain, remained in their homeland, though fearful.

[Note: [Col. 0346D] Here chapter XVIII begins in the Cambridge manuscript.]

After some time had passed, when the most savage plunderers had withdrawn home for a while, the survivors—strengthened by the Lord [the editor reads “by God,” instead of “by the Lord”]—gathered strength. [Col. 0347A] Wretched citizens flocked to these survivors from every direction and from different places, as eagerly as bees to a hive when a storm is imminent [the editor reads “from different places,” instead of “in different places”]. Together they implored him with all their hearts and, as the saying goes, burdened the heavens with countless prayers, asking that they should not be destroyed everywhere and all the way to extermination [the editor reads “to extermination,” omitting *ita usquequaque*, “everywhere and all the way”].

Under the leadership of Ambrosius Aurelianus, a modest man—who alone, perhaps, was a faithful, brave, and truthful companion of the Roman race [the words “was a faithful, brave, and truthful companion” are absent from the edition], and who had survived the collision of so great a storm, although his parents, clothed in the purple, had been killed in that same disaster [the Paris edition of the Fathers reads *indutus*, “clothed,” which may be preferable; the manuscript form is *indutis*], and whose descendants in our own time have greatly declined from their ancestral goodness—they challenged the victors to battle. By God’s assent [the edition reads “by the Lord’s assent”], victory, in accordance with their prayer, fell to them.

[Note: [Col. 0347C] The editor omits *qui*, “who.”]

[Note: [Col. 0347C] The editor reads *Domino annuente*, “by the Lord’s assent,” instead of *Deo annuente*, “by God’s assent.”]

[Note: [Col. 0347C] The editor reads *De diversis locis*, “from different places,” instead of *diversis in locis*, “in different places.”]

[Note: [Col. 0347C] The editor reads *internecionem usque*, “all the way to extermination,” instead of *ad internecionem ita usquequaque*, “everywhere and all the way to extermination.”]

[Note: [Col. 0347C] The editor reads *a Deo*, “by God,” instead of *a Domino*, “by the Lord.”]

[Note: [Col. 0347C] The words “was a faithful, brave, and truthful companion” are absent from the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0347C] The Paris edition of the Fathers reads *indutus*, “clothed,” which is more suitable.]

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Final Peace, That Final Victory Granted in Our Time by God’s Will

[Col. 0347B] From that time onward, now the citizens and now the enemies prevailed, so that in this people the Lord might test, according to his customary manner, the present Israel, whether the Lord loved him or not [the editor omits the second *Dominus*, “the Lord,” and rightly so. For why should the Lord test whether he himself loved Israel? Rather, the Lord was testing whether Israel loved HIM, namely, the Lord]. This continued until the year of the siege of Badon Hill, which is near the mouth of the Severn [the edition omits the clause “which is near the mouth of the Severn”], and almost the last, and by no means small, slaughter of the gallows-worthy men. That year, as I know, is the forty-fourth, which is now beginning [the editor reads *orditur*, “begins,” instead of *oritur*, “is beginning”], with the first month already completed [the edition reads *uno*, “one,” instead of *primo*, “first”], and which is also now the year of my birth [the editor omits *jam*, “now”].

Yet even now, as before, the cities are not inhabited [the edition reads “the cities of the homeland are not inhabited,” instead of simply “the cities are not inhabited”], but remain deserted and ruined to this day, although foreign wars have ceased, though not civil ones [the editor omits *tamen*, “however”].

For the memory of so desperate a ruin of the island and of unexpected assistance has remained fixed in the minds of those who were witnesses of both miracles. On account of this, [Col. 0348A] kings, public and private [the editor reads *privati*, “private,” instead of *privatique*, “and private”], and ecclesiastical priests maintained their own order [the editor reads “each maintained his own order”].

But when they had passed away, and an age succeeded that knew nothing of that storm and had experienced only the calm of the present, all the restraints of truth and justice were so shaken and overturned that among the aforementioned orders there appears, I will not say a trace, but scarcely even a memory of them [the editor reads *earum*, “of them,” instead of *eorum*, “of them,” correctly referring to truth and justice], except among a few, and very few indeed, who, because of the loss of so great a multitude that was daily inclined toward hell [the editor reads *ruit*, “rushes,” instead of *prona fuit*, “was inclined/headlong”], are regarded as being of so small a number [the editor, except the Paris edition of the Fathers, reads *numerus*, “the number,” instead of *tam brevis numeri*, “of so small a number”] that the venerable mother Church, as though they were reclining in her bosom, does not in some way see them, though she has them alone as true [ones] [the editor omits *ut*, “as though,” and reads *veros filios*, “true sons,” instead of *veros*, “true”].

Lest anyone think that I am attacking their excellent life, admirable to human beings and beloved by God—for our weakness is supported by their sacred prayers, as though by salutary columns and buttresses, [Col. 0348B] so that it may not collapse completely—I have said [the editor omits *dixi*, “I have said”] that if I have spoken somewhat freely about them, indeed mournfully, compelled by the accumulation of evils, I have not so much argued as lamented those who serve not only their belly, but the devil rather than Christ, who is blessed above all, forever God (Romans 9:5) [the edition reads “God forever” instead of “forever God”].

For what will the citizens conceal that the surrounding nations not only know [the editor, except the Paris edition of the Fathers, reads *nostrorum*, “of our people,” instead of *norunt*, “they know”], but also reproach them with?

[Note: [Col. 0347C] The editor omits the second *Dominus*, “the Lord.” The omission is indeed correct: the Lord was testing whether Israel loved HIM, namely, the Lord.]

## PART TWO. THE LETTER OF GILDAS

[Col. 0347]

### CHAPTER ONE. Rebuke of Constantine

[Col. 0347D] 1. Britain has kings [the *Fragment* reads: “Indeed, Britain has kings”], but they are tyrants; it has judges, but they are impious—often plundering and terrorizing the innocent; avenging and defending, but the guilty and robbers; having very many wives, but engaging in prostitution and adultery [Josselin reads *scorta*, “prostitutes”; the Fragment has *scorta et adulteras*, “prostitutes and adulteresses,” instead of the participles *scortantes et adulterantes*, “engaging in prostitution and committing adultery”]; frequently swearing, but committing perjury; [Col. 0348D] making vows, and almost continually lying; waging war, but conducting civil and unjust wars; throughout the country [another reading: “throughout the region”] zealously pursuing thieves, yet loving and even rewarding the robbers who sit at table with them [the Fragment reads *Eos autem qui ad mensam sedent latrones*, “But those robbers who sit at table”; Josselin, and likewise Paris, omit *latrones*, “robbers”; the Fragment also has *etiam munerantes*, “rewarding as well,” for *et munerantes*, “and rewarding”]; giving alms generously, but on the other hand piling up an immense [Col. 0349A] mountain of crimes; sitting in the seat of judgment [the *Fragment* reads *arbitrum*, “of judges” (contracted genitive plural), for *arbitraturi*, “about to judge”], but rarely seeking the rule of a right judgment; despising the innocent and humble; raising to the stars, as far as they can, bloodthirsty, proud, parricidal men, fellow-soldiers [the *Fragment* omits “fellow-soldiers” and the following *et*, “and”], adulterers, and enemies of God, if chance—as the saying goes—should bring them forward, although their destruction, name and all, ought to have been pursued with competing zeal [the *Fragment* reads “those whom …” and omits *certatim*, “in rivalry/with competing zeal”]; keeping many prisoners bound in jails, whom they oppress by their own deceit rather than on account of their deserts [the Fragment reads *Dolose potius quam merito poterunt*, “deceitfully rather than deservedly they will be able [to …],” with *poterunt* perhaps standing for *proterunt*, “they crush/oppress”]; lingering among altars by swearing oaths [the Fragment reads *intrando*, “by entering,” for *jurando*, “by swearing”; *inter altaria*, “among the altars,” is retained], and shortly afterward despising these same altars as though they were filthy stones [the Fragment transposes *paulo post saxa* to *saxa paulo post*, “stones shortly afterward,” with the same sense].

The tyrannical whelp of the unclean lioness of Damnonia [the Paris edition of the Fathers reads *Dannoniae*, “of Dannonia”], Constantine, is not unaware of such a foul sacrilege.

[Note: [Col. 0347D] The *Fragment* reads: “Indeed, Britain has kings.”]

[Note: [Col. 0347D] Josselin reads *scorta*, “prostitutes”; the Fragment has *scorta et adulteras*, “prostitutes and adulteresses,” instead of *scortantes et adulterantes*, “engaging in prostitution and committing adultery.”]

[Note: [Col. 0347D] The Fragment reads *Eos autem qui ad mensam sedent latrones*, “But those robbers who sit at table”; Josselin and likewise Paris omit *latrones*, “robbers.”]

[Note: [Col. 0348D] The *Fragment* reads “and rewarding as well.”]

[Note: [Col. 0349D] The *Fragment* reads *arbitrum*, “of judges” (contracted genitive plural), for *arbitraturi*, “about to judge.”]

[Note: [Col. 0349D] The *Fragment* omits “fellow-soldiers” and *et*, “and.”]

[Note: [Col. 0349D] The *Fragment* reads “those whom” and omits *certatim*, “in rivalry/with competing zeal.”]

[Note: [Col. 0349D] The Fragment reads *Dolose potius quam merito poterunt*, “deceitfully rather than deservedly they will be able [to …],” perhaps *proterunt*, “they crush/oppress,” for *poterunt*, “they will be able.”]

[Note: [Col. 0350D] The Fragment reads *intrando*, “by entering,” for *jurando*, “by swearing”; the phrase “among the altars” is unchanged.]

[Note: [Col. 0350D] The Fragment transposes *paulo post saxa* to *saxa paulo post*, “stones shortly afterward,” with the same sense.]

2. In this year, after the horrifying oath by which he bound himself never to deceive his fellow citizens—swearing first by God, and then by the choirs of the saints, with his mother accompanying and supporting him—he cruelly tore, between those very sacred altars, with a wicked sword and spear in place of teeth, the tender sides of royal boys, or the hearts of two men and of an equal number of their fosterlings, in the revered laps of two mothers, the Church and the flesh, beneath the mantle of the holy abbot. Their arms had been stretched out not toward weapons—which scarcely any human being handled more bravely than they did at that time—but toward God and the altar; on the day of judgment, at the gates of your city, Christ, they will hang forth the revered banners of their patience and faith. He tore them so that the purple coverings of the heavenly sacrifice, as though made of congealed blood, were touched by them. Nor did he do this after commendable merits had been achieved. For many years before, overcome by repeated and successive adulteries, he had rejected his lawful wife contrary to the prohibition of Christ and the Teacher of the nations, who said: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:6; Mark 10:9), and: “Husbands, love your wives” (Col. 3:19). For he had planted in the barren soil of his heart, hostile to good seed, a bitter shoot from the vine of Sodom: a sprout of unbelief and folly. Watered by the poisonous rains, as it were, of public and domestic impieties, and raising itself more eagerly toward offense against God, it produced in the open the crime of sacrilegious parricide. Yet he was not even then freed from the nets of his earlier evils; he adds recent crimes to his old ones.

3. Come now: I accuse you as though you were present, although I know that you still survive. Why are you astonished, executioner of your own soul? Why do you voluntarily kindle for yourself the flames of hell, which will never fail? Why, in place of enemies, do you willingly stab yourself with your own swords and spears? Have those poisonous crimes, as though they were cups, perhaps been able to sate your breast? Look back, I beg you, and come to Christ, if indeed you labor and are bent beneath an immense burden; and he himself, as he said, will give you rest (Matt. 11:28). Come to him who does not wish the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live (Ezek. 33:11). “Loosen,” according to the prophet, “the bonds of your neck, son of Zion” (Isa. 52:2). Return, I beg you, even from the distant retreats of sins, to the most loving father, who, when his son despised the filthy food of pigs, feared the death of terrible hunger, and returned to him, was accustomed in his joy to kill the fattened calf for his son and bring forth the first robe and the royal ring for the wanderer (Luke 15:13). Then, as though tasting in advance the flavor of heavenly hope, you will perceive how sweet the Lord is (Ps. 33:9). For if you despise these things, know that you are already at this moment being whirled about and burned in the inextricable, dark torrents of fire.

## Chapter II. Rebuke of Aurelius

4. What are you doing also, Aurelius Conan, “lion’s whelp,” as the prophet says (Ps. 16:12)—[Note: The edition, except the Paris Bibliotheca Patrum, reads *Canine*]? Are you not being savagely devoured by the same—or, if possible, more destructive—waves of the mire of parricides, fornications, and adulteries as the man mentioned above? Do you not, hating the peace of your fatherland like a deadly serpent, thirsting for civil wars and frequent unjust plunder, shut against your soul the heavenly gate of peace and refreshment? Left now alone, I beg you, like a tree withering in the middle of a field, remember the phantoms of your fathers and brothers, their youthful and untimely deaths. Will you, because of your religious merits, be preserved for a hundred years, or as Methuselah’s contemporary, with almost all your offspring? By no means. But unless you turn more quickly to the Lord, as the Psalmist says (Ps. 7:13), that King will soon brandish his sword against you, the one who says through the prophet: “I kill, and I make alive; I strike, and I heal; and there is no one who can rescue from my hand” (Deut. 32:39). Therefore shake yourself free from your filthy dust (Isa. 52:2), and turn with your whole heart to him who created you, so that, when his anger soon blazes forth, you may be blessed by hoping in him (Ps. 2:12). Otherwise, eternal punishments will remain for you: you will be crushed continually by the savage throat of Tartarus and yet never consumed.

## Chapter III. Rebuke of Vortipor

What are you doing also, Vortipor, like a leopard in character and variegated in wickedness, already gray-haired, stiffening stupidly on a throne full of deceit, your body from the soles of your feet to the crown of your head defiled by diverse parricides and adulteries? You are the wicked son of a good king, like Manasseh of Hezekiah; you are a tyrant of the Demetians. Why do the torrents of sins so violent—torrents that you swallow like the finest wine, or rather by which you are swallowed—not satisfy you as the boundary of life gradually approaches? Why, as though adultery were the summit of all evils, having put away your own wife, do you load your wretched soul with an inescapable burden through a shameless union with her daughter? Do not, I beg you, consume what remains of your days in offense against God, for now “is the acceptable time and the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2), shining upon the faces of the penitent, in which you can do good, lest your flight be in winter or on the Sabbath (Matt. 24:20).

Turn away, according to the Psalmist, from evil and do good; seek peace, and pursue it (Ps. 33:15–18), because the eyes of the Lord will be upon you as you do good, and his ears will be attentive to your prayers; he will not erase your memory from the land of the living. You will cry out, and he will hear you; and he will rescue you from all your tribulations. For Christ nowhere despises a heart that is contrite and humbled by his fear (Ps. 50:19). Otherwise, “the worm of your torment will not die, and the fire of your burning will not be extinguished” (Isa. 66:24; Mark 9:44).

## Chapter VI. Rebuke of Cuneglas

Why are you rolling about in the ancient dregs of your wickedness, Cuneglas, and why, from the years of your youth, have you been a bear, rider and driver of the chariot of the bear’s lair, a despiser of God and an oppressor of his strong one, a tawny butcher in the Roman tongue? Why do you wage such great war against human beings and against God—against human beings, that is, your fellow citizens, with deadly weapons [Note: The edition reads *specialibus*, “special,” rather than *exitialibus*, “deadly”]? against God, with endless crimes?

Why, besides innumerable disasters, after driving away your own wife, do you take her gallows-worthy sister, who promises God perpetual widowly chastity (as the poet says), as though she were the supreme delight of the nymphs of heaven—with all the reverence, or rather obtuseness, of your soul—contrary to the Apostle’s prohibition that adulterers cannot be citizens of the heavenly kingdom (Gal. 5:21)? Why do you provoke with repeated injuries the groans and sighs of the saints, who bodily mourn because of you and will one day shatter your bones in place of a savage lioness’s teeth [Note: The edition, except the Paris Bibliotheca Patrum, reads “who turn about”]?

Cease, I beg you, as the prophet says, from anger, and abandon the deadly fury that will torment yourself—the fury that you breathe out against heaven and earth, that is, against God and his flock (Ps. 36:6). Rather make them pray for you after your character has been changed; they possess the power, above the world, to bind those whom they have bound in the world and to release those whom they have released as penitents.

Do not, as the Apostle says, be arrogantly wise, or hope in uncertain riches, but in God, who supplies you abundantly with all things (1 Tim. 6:17), so that by reforming your character you may lay up for yourself a good foundation for the future and possess true life—everlasting indeed, not transient. Otherwise you will know, and will also see, how evil and bitter it is that you have abandoned the Lord your God and that his fear is not before you (Jer. 2:19). In the future you will be burned in the gloomy mass of eternal fires, yet you will not in any way die. For the souls of the wicked are immortal in perpetual fire, just as the joys of the saints are everlasting.

## Chapter VII. Rebuke of Maglocun

### 1.

What are you doing also, you insular dragon, Maglocun, suppressor of many tyrants both in kingdom and in life, latest in the writing of those mentioned above [Note: The preposition *in* is absent in the edition], first in wickedness, greater than many in power and likewise in malice, more generous in giving, more extravagant in sin, strong in arms but stronger in the destruction of souls? Why do you stupidly roll about, drenched, as it were, in such ancient blackness of crimes, like wine pressed from the vine of Sodom (Jer. 23:9)?

Why do you voluntarily bind around your royal neck such enormous, inescapable masses of sins, as though they were lofty mountains? Why do you not present yourself to the King of all kings—who made you higher than almost all the leaders of Britain both in kingdom and in the lineament of your exalted position—as better than the others in character, but, on the contrary, as worse? Listen calmly for a little to the unmistakable agreement of their reproaches, leaving aside the domestic and lesser matters—if indeed any are lesser—which public report, spreading far and wide through the air, bears witness to.

Did you not, in the first years of your youth, crush with sword, spear, and fire your royal uncle, together with almost the bravest soldiers, whose faces seemed scarcely different in battle from those of lion cubs? You gave little thought to the prophetic saying: “Men of blood and deceit will not halve their days” (Ps. 54:24).

What reward for this single act could you hope for from the just Judge, even if the things that followed had not followed, since the prophet likewise says: “Woe to you who plunder: will you not yourself be plundered? And you who kill: will you not yourself be killed? And when you have ceased plundering, then you will fall” (Isa. 33:1)?

Did you not, after the desire for a violent kingdom had yielded to you according to your wish, return, enticed by ambition, to the right path? At that time, by day and night, perhaps with your conscience gnawing at you because of your sins, you first pondered many things inwardly concerning divine fear and the decrees of monks; then, after learning the opinion of the people, you brought it forth [Note: The Paris Bibliotheca Patrum reads *cognitioni*, “to the knowledge”; the next words are “with the nets broken, as it was thought”]. You vowed to become a monk, without any regard for unfaithfulness, as you said, before almighty God, in the presence of angelic and human faces. You had broken the most capacious nets in which your fat bullocks are customarily entangled headlong: the tensions of the entire kingdom, of gold and silver, and—what is greater—of your own will.

You snatched a dove from a raven and carried it safely to the trustworthy caves and refreshment of the saints, as though it were avoiding, by winding turns, the shrill rush of dogs powerfully cutting the air and the savage talons of a swift hawk. What great joy you would have brought to Mother Church—if the enemy of all mortals had not mournfully dragged you, so to speak, from her bosom! What abundant kindling of heavenly hope would have blazed in the hearts of the despairing, had you remained in goodness! What great and glorious rewards of Christ’s kingdom would have awaited your soul on the day of judgment, had that crafty wolf not snatched you, a lamb made from a wolf, from the Lord’s sheepfold—not very unwilling—and intended to make a wolf like himself out of a lamb!

What great exultation would your salvation, if it had been preserved, have brought to God, the pious Father of all the saints, had not the unlucky father of all the lost, like a demon with great wings and claws, carried you, against divine and human law, away to the unhappy troop of his sons!

In short, your conversion to good fruit once brought as much joy and sweetness to heaven and earth as your wicked return, like a sick Molossian mastiff to its vomit (Prov. 26:11; 2 Pet. 2:25), has now brought sorrow and mourning. Once this had been done, your limbs were presented as weapons of iniquity to sin (Rom. 6:13) and to the devil, though with sound understanding they ought eagerly to have been presented to God as weapons of righteousness.

### 2.

With ears held alert, people listen—not to the praises of God sweetly modulated by the melodious voice of Christ’s recruits, nor to the breath of ecclesiastical harmony, but to your own menials, who are nothing, their speech stuffed with lies and at the same time foaming with phlegm, their heralds’ mouths clanging in the manner of bacchants, ready to destroy every neighbor with savage speech. Thus the vessel once prepared for God’s ministry is turned into the organ of the Devil, and what was thought worthy of heavenly honor is deservedly rejected into the abyss of Tartarus.

Yet your mind, dulled by such great stumbling-blocks of evil and by the mass of your folly, is not delayed as though by some obstacle. Rather, feverish, like a colt thinking every pleasant thing unexplored, it is carried with irrevocable fury across the extended fields of crimes, adding new offenses to the old.

For the first presumptuous marriage to your own wife, though unlawful, is despised after the monk’s vow has been made void; another wife is loved, belonging to a living man—not a stranger, but your brother’s son. Because of this, that hard neck, already burdened with many bundles of sins, is bent from the depths to lower depths by a twofold parricidal undertaking: the killing of the man mentioned above and of your wife, who had lived with you for some time. This was, as it were, the highest summit of your sacrilege.

Thereafter you took that woman, through whose collusion and prompting such great sudden masses of sins arose, into a public and—as the deceitful tongues of your parasites loudly proclaim, though only with their lips and not from the depths of the heart—lawful marriage, since she was a widow. But in truth, you took her into a most criminal union [Note: The words “but in truth” are absent from the editions].

What holy man, with his entrails stirred by such a story, would not immediately burst into weeping and sobs? What priest whose heart is open and upright before God, hearing these things, would not immediately say with great wailing the prophetic words: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep day and night for the slain of my people?” (Jer. 9).

Alas! You have paid too little attention to the prophetic rebuke that says: “Woe to you, impious men: you have abandoned the law of the Most High God; and if you are born, your portion will be in the curse. All things that are from the earth will return to the earth; so the impious pass from curse to curse” (Sir. 41:11–13)—that is, they will pass, if they do not return to the Lord [Note: The Paris Bibliotheca Patrum has *ibunt*, “they will go”; the Oxford edition lacks it]—if at least you do not return after hearing this admonition: “Son, you have sinned; do not add to it again, but pray concerning your former sins” (Sir. 21:1). And again: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, nor put it off from day to day” (Sir. 5:8–9). For his anger comes suddenly, because, as Scripture says, “When a king hears a wicked word, all who are under him are wicked” (Prov. 29:12). Indeed, as the prophet says, a just king raises up the land (ibid., 4). Certainly you are not lacking admonitions, since you have had an elegant teacher of almost all Britain’s precepts.

### 3.

Beware, therefore, lest what Solomon records happen to you: “Like one who awakens a sleeper from deep sleep, so is one who recounts wisdom to a fool.” At the end of the account he will say: “What did you say first?” (Sir. 22:8–9).

“Wash your heart from wickedness,” as it is said, Jerusalem, “so that you may be saved” (Jer. 4:14). Do not, I beg you, despise the ineffable mercy of God, who in this manner calls the impious away from sins through the prophet: “Suddenly I will speak to a nation and to a kingdom, to uproot, scatter, destroy, and overthrow” (Jer. 18:7). This greatly urges the sinner toward repentance: “And if that nation repents of its sin, I too will repent of the evil that I have spoken of doing to it” (ibid., 8).

And again: “Who will give them such a heart that they may hear me and keep my commandments, and that it may be well with them all the days of their life?” (Deut. 5:29). Likewise, in the song of Deuteronomy: “A people without counsel and understanding. Would that they were wise and understood, and considered their final destiny. How could one pursue a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight?” (Deut. 32:28, 30).

And again, in the Gospel, the Lord says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart; and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:28–29).

If you hear these things with deaf ears, despise the prophets, scorn Christ, and regard us—even though we are of the lowest standing—as entirely insignificant, although we preserve that prophetic saying with sincere devotion of mind—“provided only that I am filled with strength in the spirit and power of the Lord, to declare to the house of Jacob and to the house of Israel their crimes” (Isa. 58:1)—then we would be mute dogs unable to bark (Isa. 56:10).

And there is Solomon’s saying: “Whoever says that the impious person is just will be cursed by peoples and hated by nations; but those who rebuke will hope for better things” (Prov. 24:24–25). And again: “Do not be ashamed of the people in their downfall, nor withhold a word at a time of salvation” (Sir. 4:27). Likewise: “Rescue those who are being led to death, and do not spare those who are being dragged to slaughter” (Prov. 24:11), because, as the same prophet says, “riches will not profit on the day of wrath; righteousness delivers from death” (Prov. 11:4).

“If the righteous person is scarcely saved, where will the impious and sinner appear?” (1 Pet. 4:18; Prov. 11:31). That dark torrent of Tartarus will certainly enfold you in its savage whirling and waves, as though in the sharpest waters, always to torment you and never to consume you. Then you will have a late and useless, yet clear-sighted, awareness of punishment and repentance for evil—the conversion that is postponed from this present acceptable time and day of salvation to the right path of life (2 Cor. 6:2).

### 4.

This mournful and lamentable history of the evils of this age should surely have been concluded here, or even earlier, so that our mouth might no longer speak of the works of human beings. But lest they think us fearful or weary, as though we did not indefatigably guard against the Isaianic warning—“Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness, bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter” (Isa. 5:20)—and against those who, though seeing, do not see, and though hearing, do not hear (Matt. 13:13), whose heart is covered by a certain thick cloud of vices, I wish briefly to declare how many and how great the prophetic oracles of threats thunder against these revelers [the following parenthetical passage is omitted in the Paris Bibliotheca Patrum: “the satellites of Pharaoh, whose army, doomed to perish in the Red Sea, is vigorously challenged by five horses, and their like”], so that the structure of our little work may be most faithfully covered by them as by a beautiful covering, and may not remain penetrable to the rains of the envious rushing upon it all together.

Let the holy prophets therefore answer on our behalf, now as before—the prophets who have existed, in a certain sense, as the mouth and organ of God, forbidding mortals to do evil and favoring the good—so that the stubborn and proud rulers of this age may not say that we, by our own invention and merely loquacious boldness, are inflicting such threats and such terrors upon them.

For no wise person doubts how much more serious the sins of this age are than those of the first, since the Apostle says: “Anyone who transgresses the law dies on the evidence of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will the one deserve who has trampled underfoot the Son of God?” (Heb. 10:28).

### 5.

First Samuel meets us: the establisher of the legitimate kingdom at God’s command, dedicated to God before he was born, a truthful prophet known throughout the whole people of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, by unquestionably marvelous signs. From his mouth the Holy Spirit thundered against all the powers of the world.

First he denounced Saul, the first king of the Hebrews, because he had not fulfilled certain commands of the Lord, saying: “You have acted foolishly, and you have not kept the commandment of the Lord your God, which he commanded you. If you had not done this, the Lord would even now have prepared your kingdom over Israel. But your kingdom will by no means rise any further” (1 Sam. 13:13–14).

What crime comparable to the evils of this age did he commit—adultery or parricide? Not at all. He merely altered part of a command, because, as one of our people rightly says: “The issue is not the quality of the sin but the transgression of the command.”

Likewise, when Saul thought he had cleansed himself of the charge and skillfully appended defenses, as is customary for the human race, saying, “I did hear the voice of the Lord, and I walked in the way by which he sent me” (1 Sam. 15:20), Samuel punished him with this judgment: “Does the Lord desire holocausts and sacrifices, and not rather that his voice be obeyed? For obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen better than to offer the fat of rams. For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusing to comply is like the crime of idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, he has rejected you, so that you shall not be king” (ibid., 22–23).

And shortly afterward: “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today, and has given it to your neighbor, who is better than you. Moreover, the Triumphator in Israel will not spare, and will not be moved by repentance; for he is not a human being, that he should repent” (ibid., 28–29)—that is, over the hardened hearts of the wicked.

It must therefore be noted that he said it was the crime of idolatry to refuse to comply with God. Let these criminals, then, not applaud themselves because they do not visibly sacrifice to the gods of the nations. For by trampling, like pigs, upon Christ’s most precious pearls, they are idolaters. Yet although this one example, as an invincible witness, would be sufficient to correct the wicked, let us nevertheless pass on to the remaining examples, so that every evil of Britain may be established by the testimony of many witnesses.

### 6.

What happened to David when he numbered the people, when Gad the prophet said to him: “Thus says the Lord: Three options are given to you. Choose one of them as you wish, so that I may do it to you. Either seven years of famine will come upon you; or for three months you will flee your enemies, and they will pursue you; or certainly there will be pestilence in your land for three days” (2 Sam. 24:12–13).

Constrained by this condition, and wishing rather to fall into the hands of a merciful God than into those of human beings, he was humbled by the slaughter of seventy thousand of his people. Had he not, through apostolic charity toward his fellow tribesmen, wished to die so that the plague might not touch them, saying, “I am the one who sinned; I, the shepherd, have acted wickedly. These, who are sheep, what have they done? Let your hand, I beg you, be turned against me” (ibid., 17), he would have atoned for the thoughtless exaltation of his heart by his own death.

What does Scripture next relate about his son? “Solomon did what was displeasing before the Lord, and he did not fulfill what was required to follow the Lord as his father had. The Lord said to him: Because you have kept this within yourself and have not guarded my covenant and my commandments that I gave you, I will tear the kingdom away from you and give it to your servant” (1 Kings 11:6, 11).

Hear what happened also to the two sacrilegious kings of Israel, Jeroboam and Baasha, equally like these men. The Lord’s sentence was directed against them through the prophet, who said: “Because I exalted you as ruler over Israel, yet they provoked me by their vanities” (1 Kings 14:7). “Behold, I will raise up after Baasha and after his house, and I will make his house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat. Whoever of his people dies in the city, the dogs will eat; and whoever dies in the field, the birds of the air will eat” (1 Kings 16:3–4).

What did the holy and fiery mouth of Elijah, instructed by the Lord’s speech, threaten that other wicked king of Israel, a companion of these men, through whose collusion and the deceit of his wife the innocent Naboth was crushed because of his ancestral vineyard? He said: “You have killed, and moreover you have taken possession.” And afterward he added: “Thus says the Lord: In the place where the dogs licked Naboth’s blood, they will also lick your blood” (1 Kings 21:19). That this happened is established with complete certainty.

But lest, following the example of Ahab, the lying spirit speaking falsehood through the mouths of your prophets seduce you, so that you do not listen to the words of the prophet Micaiah—“Behold, God has permitted a lying spirit in the mouth of all your prophets who are here, and the Lord has spoken evil against you” (1 Kings 22:22–23)—know that even now there are certain teachers filled with a contrary spirit, asserting wicked pleasure rather than truth. Their words are softer than oil, yet they are themselves arrows (Ps. 54:22). They say, “Peace, peace,” though there will be no peace for those who persist in sins (Jer. 6:14; 8:11), as the prophet says elsewhere: “There is no rejoicing for the impious, says the Lord” (Isa. 48:22; 57:21).

### 7.

Azariah son of Obed also spoke to Asa when he returned from the slaughter of the Ethiopian army of a million men, saying: “The Lord is with you while you are with him; and if you seek him, he will be found by you; but if you abandon him, he will abandon you” (2 Chron. 15:2).

If Jehoshaphat, who brought aid to a wicked king, was rebuked by the prophet Jehu son of Hanani in these words: “Do you help a sinner, or do you love one whom the Lord hates? Therefore the wrath of the Lord is upon you” (2 Chron. 19:2), what will happen to those who are shackled by the very locks of hair of their crimes? If we wish to fight in the Lord’s battle, we must hate their sins, not their souls, as the Psalmist says: “You who love the Lord, hate evil” (Ps. 96:10).

What did the prophet Elijah, the chariot and charioteer of Israel, say to Jehoram, the parricide son of the aforementioned Jehoshaphat, who slaughtered his excellent brothers so that he might reign in their place? “Thus says the Lord God of your father David: Because you have not walked in the way of Jehoshaphat your father and in the ways of Asa king of Judah, but have walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, and in the shameful manner in which the house of Ahab acted, and have killed your brothers, the sons of Jehoshaphat, who were better than you, behold, the Lord will strike you and your sons with a great plague” (2 Chron. 21:12, 14).

And shortly afterward: “You will suffer a great illness, with an affliction of your intestines, until your intestines come out with the illness, day after day” (ibid., 15).

And concerning Joash, king of Israel, who abandoned the Lord like you, pay attention to what Zachariah son of Jehoiada the prophet threatened. Rising before the people, he said: “Thus says the Lord: Why do you transgress the commandments of the Lord and fail to prosper? Because you have abandoned the Lord, he will abandon you” (2 Chron. 24:20).

What shall I say about Isaiah, the author of the prophets, who began the preface, or vision, of his prophecy in this way? “Hear, O heavens, and listen, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: I have nourished and exalted sons, but they have despised me. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger; but Israel has not known me, and my people have not understood” (Isa. 1:2–4).

And shortly afterward, fitting deserved threats to such great folly, he says: “The daughter of Zion will be left like a shelter in a vineyard, and like a hut in a cucumber field, like a city that is laid waste” (ibid., 8). Addressing the rulers in particular, he says: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; perceive the law of our God, people of Gomorrah” (ibid., 10).

### 8.

It must certainly be noted that wicked kings are called “rulers of Sodom.” For while the Lord forbids sacrifices and gifts to be offered to him by such people—and we, greedily desiring them, accept what is not pleasing to God from every nation, while to our own destruction we do not allow the same things to be distributed to the needy and to those who possess almost nothing—he says to those who are burdened with extensive riches and intent upon the filth of sins: “Do not offer sacrifice in vain any longer; incense is an abomination to me” (ibid., 13).

He also declares: “When you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply your prayer, I will not hear” (ibid., 15). He shows why he does this: “Your hands are full of blood.”

At the same time, showing how he might be appeased, he says: “Wash yourselves; be clean; remove the evil of your thoughts from my eyes; cease to act perversely. Learn to do good; seek judgment; assist the oppressed; judge for the orphan” (ibid., 16–17).

Adding, as it were, a reciprocal exchange for appeasement, he says: “If your sins are like scarlet, they will be made white as snow; and if they are red like crimson, they will become like white wool. If you are willing and listen to me, you will eat the good things of the land. But if you are unwilling and provoke me to anger, the sword will devour you” (ibid., 18, 20).

Receive as a truthful and public witness, one who repays your good and evil without any veneer of flattery—not like the mouths of your parasites, whose beloved poisonous words hiss into your ears—testifying: “Your rulers are faithless, companions of thieves; all love gifts and pursue rewards. They do not judge for the orphan, and the widow’s case does not come before them.

“Therefore says the Lord of hosts, the Strong One of Israel: Alas! I will be comforted over my enemies, and I will avenge myself upon my foes. And the wicked and sinners will be crushed together, and all who have abandoned the Lord will be consumed” (ibid., 23–24, 28).

And below: “The haughty eyes of human beings will be humbled, and the loftiness of men will be brought low” (Isa. 2:11).

And again: “Woe to the impious, for evil will come to him; the recompense of his hands will be done to him” (Isa. 3:11).

And shortly afterward: “Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness and continue drinking until evening, so that they become heated with wine. Harp, lyre, tambourine, pipe, and wine are in your feasts; but you do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the works of his hands.

“Therefore my people have been led away captive, because they had no understanding; their nobles have perished from hunger, and their multitude has dried up with thirst. Therefore hell has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without limit; and its strong men, its people, and its lofty and glorious ones will descend to it” (Isa. 5:11, 14).

And below: “Woe to you who are powerful for drinking wine and strong men for mixing drunkenness, who justify the impious for gifts and take away the righteousness of the just from him. Therefore, just as a tongue of fire devours straw and the heat of flame burns it, so their root will be like ashes, and their shoot will rise like dust. For they have rejected the law of the Lord of hosts and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel. In all these things the anger of the Lord has not turned away, but his hand is still extended” (ibid., 22–25).

9. And after discussing at some length the day of judgment and the ineffable terror of sinners, he says:

“Wail, for the day of the Lord is near” (if it was near then, what should it now be thought to be?), “because devastation will come from God. Therefore all hands will be slackened, and every human heart will melt and be crushed; torments and pains will seize them; like a woman in labor, they will suffer. Each person will be astounded at his neighbor; their faces will be faces of flame. Behold, the day of the Lord will come, cruel, full of indignation, wrath, and fury, to make the earth a desolation and to destroy its sinners from it. For the stars of heaven and their brightness will not display their light; the sun will be darkened at its rising, and the moon will not shine in its season. And I will visit the evils of the world upon it, and their iniquity upon the ungodly; I will bring to rest the pride of the faithless, and humble the arrogance of the strong” (Isa. 13:6, 11). [Col. 0359A]

And again:

“Behold, the Lord will lay waste the earth, strip it bare, afflict its surface, and scatter its inhabitants. And it shall be: as the people, so the priest; as the servant, so his master; as the maidservant, so her mistress; as the buyer, so the seller; as the lender, so the borrower; as the one who demands repayment, so the debtor. The earth shall be utterly laid waste, and it shall be utterly plundered; for the Lord has spoken this word. The earth mourned and languished; the world languished; it grew weak because of its inhabitants, for they transgressed the laws, changed the right order, and dissolved the everlasting covenant. Therefore a curse shall devour the earth” (Isa. 24:1, 6). [Col. 0359B]

And below:

“All who rejoice in their hearts shall groan; the joy of tambourines shall cease, the sound of those who rejoice shall be quieted, and the sweetness of the lyre shall fall silent. They shall not drink wine with song; the drink shall be bitter to those who drink it. The city of vanity is broken down; every house is shut, with no one entering. There shall be a cry over wine in the streets; all joy is deserted, the gladness of the earth has been removed, solitude remains in the city, and calamity shall oppress the gates; for these things shall be in the midst of the earth and among the peoples” (ibid., 7, 13).

And shortly afterward:

“They have transgressed by transgressing, and by the transgression of transgressors they have transgressed. Terror, pit, and snare are upon you, inhabitant of the earth. And it shall be: the one who flees from the sound of terror shall fall into the pit, and the one who escapes from the pit shall be caught in the snare; for the floodgates from on high shall be opened, and the foundations of the earth shall be shaken. The earth shall be utterly shattered, the earth shall be utterly convulsed, the earth shall be utterly shaken; it shall be moved like a drunkard, and it shall be carried away like a one-night tent. Its iniquity shall weigh it down; it shall fall and shall not rise again. And it shall be: on that day the Lord will visit the host of heaven on high, and the kings of the earth who are upon the earth. They shall be gathered into one gathering, like a bundle, into the pit; they shall be shut up there in prison, and after many days they shall be visited. The moon shall blush and the sun shall be confounded, when the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and is glorified in the sight of his elders” (ibid., 16, 23). [Col. 0359C]

And after some further discussion, giving the reason why he threatened such things, he says:

“Behold, the hand of the Lord is not shortened, so that he cannot save; nor is his ear burdened, so that he cannot hear.
