But your iniquities have made a division between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you, so that he would not hear. For your hands are defiled with blood, and your fingers with iniquity; your lips have spoken falsehood, and your tongue utters iniquity. There is no one who calls for justice, nor anyone who judges truly; but they trust in nothing, speak vanities, conceive pain, and give birth to iniquity” (Isa. 59:1, 4). [Col. 0359D]

And below:

“Their works are useless, and the work of iniquity is in their hands. Their feet run toward evil, and they hasten to shed innocent blood. Their thoughts are useless thoughts; devastation and destruction are in their ways. They have not known the way of peace, and there is no judgment in their paths. Their paths have been bent for them; everyone who treads upon them does not know peace. Therefore judgment has been removed far from you, and justice will not overtake you” (ibid., 6, 9). [Col. 0360A]

And shortly afterward:

“Judgment has turned backward, and justice has stood far away, because truth has fallen in the street and equity could not enter. Truth has become forgotten, and whoever withdrew from evil was exposed to plunder. The Lord saw it, and it was displeasing in his eyes, because there was no judgment” (ibid., 14, 15).

Let it suffice thus far to have cited a few passages from the many utterances of the prophet Isaiah.

10. Now listen for a little while to what Jeremiah—who was foreknown before he was formed in the womb, sanctified before he came forth from the womb, and appointed as a prophet among all nations—pronounced concerning an unwise people and rigid kings, beginning his words gently in this manner: [Col. 0360B]

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Go and cry in the ears of Jerusalem, and say: Hear the word of the Lord, house of Jacob, and all the families of the house of Israel. Thus says the Lord: What did your fathers find in me as an injustice, that they went far from me, walked after vanity, and became vain? And they did not say: Where is he who brought us up from the land of Egypt?” (Jer. 2:1, 2, 4–6).

And shortly afterward:

“From of old you broke my yoke, tore my bonds, and said: I will not serve. I planted you as a chosen vine, wholly true seed; how then have you been changed into a perverse, foreign vine? Though you wash yourself with nitre and multiply for yourself the herb called *borith*, you are stained by your iniquity before me, says the Lord” (ibid., 20–22). [Col. 0360C]

And below:

“What do you wish to contend with me in judgment? You have all abandoned me, says the Lord. In vain I struck your children; they did not accept discipline. Hear the word of the Lord: Have I become a wilderness to Israel, or a late-growing land? Will a virgin forget her ornament, or a bride her breast-band? Yet my people have forgotten me for innumerable days” (ibid., 29–33).

“For my people are foolish; they have not known me. They are foolish and senseless children; they are wise in doing evil, but they have not known how to do good” (Jer. 4:22).

Then the prophet speaks in his own person, saying:

“Lord, your eyes look upon faithfulness. You struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to accept discipline” (Jer. 5:3).

And likewise the Lord:

“Announce this to the house of Jacob and proclaim it in Judah, saying: Hear this, foolish people, who have no heart; you have eyes, but you do not see; you have ears, but you do not hear. Will you not fear me, says the Lord, and tremble before my face? I who placed sand as a boundary for the sea, an everlasting ordinance that it cannot pass; its waves are shaken, but they cannot prevail; its waves surge, but they cannot pass over it. But this people has an unbelieving and rebellious heart; they have turned aside and gone away, and they have not said in their heart: Let us fear the Lord our God” (ibid., 20–24). [Col. 0360D]

And again:

“For wicked men have been found among my people, lying in wait like bird-catchers, setting traps and snares to catch human beings. As a cage is full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit; therefore they have become great and rich. They have grown fat and sleek, and they have passed beyond my words most wickedly. They have not directed the cause of the orphan, nor judged the judgment of the poor. Shall I not visit these things, says the Lord? Or shall my soul not take vengeance on such a nation?” (Jer. 5:26–29). [Col. 0361A]

11. But may what follows never happen to you:

“Speak to them all these words, and they will not hear you; you will call them, and they will not answer you. And you shall say to them: This is the nation that has not listened to the voice of the Lord its God and has not accepted discipline; faith has perished and has been removed from their mouth” (Jer. 8:27, 28).

And after some further passage:

“Will the one who falls not rise, and will the one who has turned away not return? Why then has this people in Jerusalem turned away with a contentious turning? They have grasped falsehood and have not been willing to return. I paid attention and listened: no one speaks what is good. There is no one who repents of his sin, saying: What have I done? All have turned to their own course, like a horse rushing impetuously into battle. The hawk in the sky knows its season; the turtledove, swallow, and stork observe the time of their coming; but my people have not known the judgment of God” (Jer. 8:4–7). [Col. 0361B]

The prophet, terrified by such vehement blindness in sacrilege and ineffable drunkenness, and mourning those who did not mourn themselves—as even the wretched tyrants now do—wishes that an increase of tears might be granted him by the Lord, saying:

“I have been crushed over the crushing of the daughter of my people; astonishment has seized me. Is there no resin in Gilead, or is there no physician there? Why then has the wound of the daughter of my people not been bandaged?” (ibid., 21, 22). [Col. 0361C]

“Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, so that I may weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people? Who will give me a lodging for travelers in the wilderness, so that I may leave my people and withdraw from them? For they are all adulterers, an assembly of transgressors. They have stretched out their tongue like a bow of falsehood and not of truth; they have grown strong in the land, for they have gone from evil to evil, and they have not known me, says the Lord” (Jer. 9:1–3).

And again:

“And the Lord said: Because they abandoned my law, which I gave them, and did not listen to my voice, and did not walk in it, but went after the perversity of their heart, therefore thus says the Lord God of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will feed this people with wormwood and give them water of gall to drink” (Jer. 9:13–15).

And shortly afterward—something the prophet also added repeatedly in his writing, speaking in the person of God:

“Therefore do not pray for this people, and do not take up praise or prayer for them; for I will not hear them at the time of their cry to me and their affliction” (Jer. 11:14). [Col. 0361D]

12. What, then, will the unfortunate leaders now do? Those few who find the narrow way, having rejected the broad one, are forbidden by God to pour out prayers for you who persist in evil and incite others so greatly; yet they could not bring vengeance upon those who, by contrast, return to God from the heart, since God does not wish a human soul to perish, but holds back lest the one who has been cast away perish completely. For Jonah could not do so either, even though that prophet had greatly desired vengeance upon the Ninevites.

But setting aside our own concerns for the moment, let us rather hear what the prophetic trumpet loudly proclaims:

“And if you say in your heart: Why have these evils come upon us? Because of the multitude of your iniquity. If an Ethiopian can change his skin, or a leopard his spots, then you too will be able to do good, once you have learned evil” (Jer. 13:22, 23)—that is understood to mean: because you do not wish to.

And below:

“Thus says the Lord to this people, who loved to move their feet and did not rest, and whom the Lord did not please: Now he will remember their iniquities and visit their sins. And the Lord said to me: Do not pray for this people for their good. When they fast, I will not hear their prayers; and if they offer burnt offerings and sacrifices, I will not accept them” (Jer. 14:10–12).

And again:

“And the Lord said to me: Even if Moses and Samuel stood before me, my soul would not be toward this people. Drive them from my presence, and let them depart” (Jer. 15:1).

And shortly afterward:

“Who will pity you, Jerusalem? Or who will grieve for you? Or who will go to plead for your peace? You have abandoned me, says the Lord, and gone backward; therefore I will stretch out my hand over you and destroy you” (ibid., 5, 6). [Col. 0362B]

And after some further passage:

“Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am devising a plan against you. Let each person turn back from his evil way, and straighten your ways and your practices. But they said: We despair; we shall follow our thoughts, and each of us shall do the perversity of his evil heart. Therefore thus says the Lord: Ask the nations: Who has heard of such dreadful things as the virgin Israel has done beyond measure? Does the snow of Lebanon ever fail from the rock of the field? Or can the cold waters that gush forth be torn away and cease to flow? For my people have forgotten me” (Jer. 18:11–15).

And shortly afterward, setting an alternative before them, he says:

“Thus says the Lord: Execute judgment and righteousness, and rescue the oppressed from the hand of the slanderer; do not grieve or oppress unjustly the stranger, the orphan, or the widow; and do not shed innocent blood. For if you truly do this word, kings sitting on the throne of David and descended from him will enter through the gates of this house. But if you do not hear these words, I have sworn by myself, says the Lord, that this house shall become a desolation” (Jer. 22:3–5). [Col. 0362C]

And again—for he was speaking about a wicked king:

“As I live, says the Lord: If Jeconiah were a signet ring on my right hand, I would tear him away from there and give him into the hand of those who seek his life” (ibid., 24, 25).

13. Holy Habakkuk also cries out, saying:

“Woe to him who builds a city with blood and prepares a city in iniquities, saying: Are these not from the almighty Lord? And many peoples have labored in fire, and many nations have been diminished” (Hab. 2:12, 13). [Col. 0362D]

And he begins his prophecy sorrowfully in this way:

“How long shall I cry out, and you will not hear? Shall I cry aloud to you? Why have you given me labors and pains to see—misery and impiety before me? Judgment has been made, and the judge has taken it. Therefore the law has been dispersed, and judgment is not brought to completion” (Hab. 1:2–4).

But blessed Hosea the prophet also—listen to what he says about rulers:

“Because they transgressed my covenant and rebelled against my law, they cried out: We have known you, because you are against Israel. They pursued what was good as though it were wicked. They reigned for themselves and not through me; they established rulers, but did not acknowledge me” (Hos. 8:1–4). [Col. 0363A]

But also hear holy Amos the prophet threatening in this manner:

“For three transgressions of the sons of Judah, and for four, I will not turn them away, because they rejected the law of the Lord and did not keep his commandments; their vanities led them astray. And I will send fire upon Judah, and it shall devour the foundations of Jerusalem. Thus says the Lord: For three transgressions of Israel, and for four, I will not turn them away, because they sold the righteous for money and the poor for sandals that tread upon the dust of the earth; they struck the heads of the poor with blows and turned aside from the way of the humble” (Amos 2:4–7).

And shortly afterward:

“Seek the Lord, and you shall live, lest he shine forth like fire upon the house of Joseph and devour it, with no one to extinguish it” (Amos 5:6). [Col. 0363B]

When Amos was forbidden to prophesy in Israel, he replied without flattering anyone:

“I was not a prophet, nor was I a prophet’s son; I was a shepherd and one who tended sycamores. And the Lord took me from the sheep, and the Lord said to me: Go and prophesy to my people Israel. And now hear the word of the Lord”—for he was addressing the king—“You say: Do not prophesy in Israel, and do not gather crowds in the house of Jacob. Therefore thus says the Lord: Your wife shall practice prostitution in the city, your sons and daughters shall fall by the sword, your land shall be measured by a measuring line, and you shall die in an unclean land; but Israel shall be led captive from its land” (Amos 7:14–17).

And below:

“Hear this, you who crush the poor utterly and exercise dominion over the needy of the land, who say: When will the month pass, so that we may acquire, and the sabbath, so that we may open our treasuries?” (Amos 8:4, 5). [Col. 0363C]

And shortly afterward:

“The Lord swears against the pride of Jacob: Surely he will not forget your works with contempt. Shall not the earth be shaken because of these things, and shall not everyone who dwells in it mourn? Shall not its destruction rise like a river? And I will turn your festivals into mourning, put sackcloth upon every loins and baldness upon every head; I will make it like the mourning for a beloved one, and those with him like a day of grief” (ibid., 7, 8, 10).

And again:

“All the sinners of my people who say, ‘Evil shall not draw near or come upon us,’ shall die by the sword” (Amos 9:10).

14. But holy Micah the seer also—listen to what he has uttered:

“Hear, tribes. And what will adorn the city? Is it perhaps fire? And the house of the wicked, storing up wicked treasures and injustice with violence. Will the wicked person be justified by an unjust balance and deceitful weights, by which they have filled themselves with riches in impiety?” (Mic. 6:10–12). [Col. 0363D]

But also hear the illustrious prophet Zephaniah and the threats he heaps up:

“The great day of the Lord is near; it is near and very swift. The voice of the day of the Lord has been made bitter and mighty; that day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of cloud and darkness, a day of trumpet and blast, a day of misery and destruction, a day of darkness and gloom over fortified cities and lofty corners. I will afflict human beings, and they shall walk like the blind, because they have sinned against the Lord. I will pour out their blood like dust and their flesh like the dung of oxen. Their silver and gold will not be able to rescue them on the day of the Lord’s wrath. In the fire of his jealousy the whole earth shall be consumed, when the Lord brings consummation and desolation upon all who dwell in the land” (Zeph. 1:14–18). [Col. 0364A]

“Gather together and join yourselves, undisciplined nation, before you become like a passing flower, before the wrath of the Lord comes upon you” (Zeph. 2:1, 2).

And consider also what holy Haggai the prophet says:

“Thus says the Lord: Once again I will shake heaven and earth, the sea and the dry land; I will overturn the kingdom, destroy the strength of the kingdoms of the nations, and overturn chariots and riders” (Hag. 2:22, 23).

Now consider also what Zechariah son of Addo, the chosen prophet, said, beginning his prophecy in this way:

“Return to me, and I will return to you, says the Lord; and do not be like your fathers, against whom the earlier prophets protested, saying: Thus says the almighty Lord” (Zech. 1:3, 4). [Col. 0364B]

And below:

“And the angel said to me: What do you see? And I said: I see a flying sickle, twenty cubits long—a curse that proceeds over the face of the whole earth, for every thief among them shall be punished unto death. And I will cast him out, says the almighty Lord; and he shall enter the house of fury and the house of the oath, where falsehood is sworn in my name” (Zech. 5:2–4).

Holy Malachi the prophet also says:

“Behold, the day of the Lord will come, burning like a furnace; and all the proud and all who commit iniquity shall be like straw. The coming day shall set them ablaze, says the Lord of hosts, and shall leave them neither root nor branch” (Mal. 4:1). [Col. 0364C]

15. Consider also holy Job, and what he discussed concerning the beginning and end of the wicked, saying:

“Why do the wicked live and grow old dishonorably? Their offspring are according to their desire, and their children are before their eyes. Their houses are fruitful, and there is neither fear nor the scourge of the Lord upon them. Their cow does not miscarry; their pregnant animal bears its offspring and does not go astray, but remains like everlasting sheep. Their children rejoice, and, taking up the psaltery and lyre, they end their life in good things; they sleep in the rest of the underworld” (Job 21:7–13).

Does God not see the deeds of the wicked? Certainly not; rather, the lamp of the wicked will be extinguished, and destruction will come upon them; pains like those of women in labor will seize them because of wrath. They will be like straw before the wind and like dust carried away by a whirlwind. May his children’s goods fail; may his eyes see his own slaughter, and may he not be released by the Lord” (ibid., 17, 18, 20). [Col. 0364D]

And after some further passage concerning the same people:

“They seized the flock along with the shepherd, carried away the orphan’s beast, pledged the widow’s ox, and turned the powerless aside from the way of necessity. Before the proper time they reaped a field that was not theirs. The poor worked the vineyards of the powerful without pay and without food. They caused many naked people to sleep without clothing; they took away the covering of their bodies” (Job 24:2–4, 6, 7).

And shortly afterward:

“When, therefore, he knew their works, he handed them over to darkness. Let his portion be cursed by the earth; let his plantations produce dry growth. Let him be repaid according to what he did; let every wicked person be crushed like wood without health. For when he rises in anger, he overturns the powerless. Therefore he will not trust in his life; when he begins to grow weak, he will not hope for health, but will fall into illness. For his pride has harmed many, and he has become rotten like mallow in the heat, or like an ear of grain when it falls from its stalk” (Job 24:18, 20, 22, 24). [Col. 0365A]

And below:

“If his children are many, they shall be for slaughter. If he gathers silver like dust and prepares gold like clay, all these things the righteous shall obtain” (Job 27:14–17).

Consider also what blessed Ezra, that prophet who was the library of the law, threatened, discussing matters in this fashion:

“Thus says the Lord God: My right hand will not spare sinners, nor will the sword cease against the one who pours out innocent blood upon the earth. Fire shall go forth from my wrath and devour the foundations of the earth, and sinners shall be like burning straw. Woe to those who sin and do not observe my commandments, says the Lord; I will not spare them. Depart, apostate children, and do not defile my holiness. God knows those who sin against him; therefore he will hand them over to death and slaughter. For many evils have already come upon the inhabited world” (4 Esd. 15:21–27). [Col. 0365B]

“A sword has been sent forth like fire; and who is there who will drive it back? Can anyone drive back a hungry lion in the forest? Or can anyone extinguish fire once the straw has been burned? The Lord God will send evils; and who is there who will drive them back? Fire will go forth from his anger; and who will extinguish it? He will flash like lightning; and who will not fear? He will thunder; and who will not shudder? God will threaten all things; and who will not be terrified? At his presence the earth will tremble, and the foundations of the deep will be shaken” (4 Esd. 16:3–12). [Col. 0365C]

16. Consider also what the outstanding prophet Ezekiel, that wondrous observer of the four Gospel creatures, declared concerning criminals. When he was first lamenting the wound of Israel, the Lord said to him:

“The iniquity of the house of Israel and Judah has become exceedingly great, because the land has been filled with iniquity and uncleanness” (Ezek. 9:9). “Behold, I am here: my eye will not spare, nor will I have pity” (Ezek. 5:8, 11).

And below:

“Because the land is full of peoples and the city is full of iniquity, I will turn aside the force of their strength, and their holy things shall be polluted. Entreaty will come, and they will seek peace, but there will be none” (Ezek. 7:23–25).

And after some further passage:

“The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, if a land sins against me by committing a transgression, I will stretch out my hand against it, break its support of bread, send famine into it, and remove human beings and animals from it. And if these three men—Noah, Daniel, and Job—were in its midst, they would not deliver it; but they themselves would be saved by their righteousness, says the Lord. Even if I brought evil beasts upon the land and punished it, and it became desolate, so that no one could pass through because of the beasts, and these three men were in its midst—as I live, says the Lord—if they could save their sons and daughters, they alone would be saved, but the land would become a ruin” (Ezek. 14:12–16). [Col. 0365D]

And again:

“The son shall not bear the injustice of the father, nor the father bear the injustice of the son. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him. And if the wicked person turns away from all the iniquities he has committed, keeps all my commandments, and practices justice and great mercy, he shall surely live and shall not die. None of all the offenses he has committed shall be remembered against him; in the righteousness he has practiced he shall live. Do I desire the death of the wicked, says the Lord, rather than that he should turn from his evil way and live? But when the righteous person turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity according to all the iniquities committed by the wicked, none of all the righteousness he has practiced shall be remembered. In the offense by which he fell away and in the sins by which he sinned, he shall die” (Ezek. 18:20–24). [Col. 0366A]

And after some further passage:

“All the nations shall know that the house of Israel was led captive because of its sins, because they abandoned me. I will turn my face away from them, and I will hand them over into the hands of their enemies; and all of them shall fall by the sword. According to their uncleannesses and according to their iniquities I dealt with them, and I turned my face away from them” (Ezek. 39:23, 24).

[Col. 0366B]

17. It is enough to have said this about the threats of the holy prophets. I considered it necessary to insert into this little work a few passages from the Wisdom of Solomon expressing exhortation or warning to kings no less than threats, lest they say that I wish to place heavy and unbearable burdens of words upon people’s shoulders but am unwilling to move them with my finger—that is, with a consoling address (Matt. 23:4).

Let us therefore hear what the prophet said:

“Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wis. 1:1).

This one testimony, if it were kept with the whole heart, would be more than sufficient to correct the rulers of the fatherland. For if they had loved justice, they would certainly love, in a sense, the fountain and origin of all justice: God.

“Serve the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart” (ibid.). [Col. 0366C]

Alas! Who will live to see these things accomplished by citizens, as someone before us said, if indeed they can ever be accomplished? “For he is found by those who do not tempt him, and he appears to those who have faith in him” (ibid., 2).

For these men tempt God without restraint. They contemptuously and stubbornly despise his commandments, and they do not preserve faith toward him whose gentle or somewhat severe oracles they turn their backs upon rather than their faces. “For perverse thoughts separate from God” (ibid., 3). This is clearly detected in the tyrants of our own time.

But why should our mediocrity intrude upon so evident a meaning? Let the one who alone is truthful speak for us, as we have said—the Holy Spirit, of whom it is now said:

“But the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (ibid., 5).

And again:

“For the Spirit of God has filled the inhabited world” (ibid., 7). [Col. 0366D]

And below, setting forth the end of the wicked and the good with discerning judgment, he says:

“How the hope of the ungodly is like down carried away by the wind, like smoke scattered by the wind, like thin foam dispersed by a storm, and like the memory of a passing guest who stays for one day. But the righteous shall live forever, and their reward is with God, and their thought is with the Most High. Therefore they shall receive a kingdom of splendor and a crown of beauty from the hand of the Lord. For with his right hand he will protect them, and with his holy arm he will defend them” (Wis. 5:15, 17).

For the righteous and the wicked differ greatly in character—just as the Lord said:

“Those who honor me I will honor; but those who despise me shall be held of no account” (1 Sam. 2:30).

But let us pass on to the rest.

“Hear, O kings, and understand; learn, judges of the ends of the earth. Give ear, you who govern the multitude and take pride in crowds of nations. For power has been given to you by God, and authority by the Most High, who will examine your works and scrutinize your thoughts. For although you were ministers of his kingdom, you did not judge rightly, nor keep the law of justice, nor walk according to his will. He will appear to you terribly and swiftly, because a very strict judgment will be made against those who rule. For the lowly may be pardoned out of mercy, but the powerful will suffer powerful torments. He who is Lord of all will not exempt persons from judgment, nor will he reverence anyone’s greatness, because he himself made the small and the great, and he cares equally for all. But a stronger torture awaits the stronger. Therefore, O kings, these are my words, so that you may learn wisdom and not fall. For those who keep what is just will be justified, and those who learn holy things will be sanctified” (Wis. 6:2–11). [Col. 0367B]

18. Thus far we have argued with the kings of the fatherland no less through the oracles of the prophets than through our own words, wishing them to know what the prophet said:

“Flee sins as from the face of a serpent. If you approach them, their teeth will seize you—their teeth that kill human souls” (Sir. 21:2, 3).

And again:

“How great is the mercy of the Lord, and his forgiveness toward those who turn back to him!” (Sir. 17:28). [Col. 0368A]

And although we do not possess within us that apostolic sentiment so as to say, “For I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers” (Rom. 9:3), still may we be able to say with our whole heart that prophetic word:

“Alas! The soul is perishing.”

And again:

“Let us examine our ways, seek, and return to the Lord” (Lam. 3:40, 41).

And also that saying of the Apostle:

“We desire each one of you to be in the depths of Christ” (Phil. 1:8).

For since I would willingly have rested here, as though tossed by the waves of the sea and carried by oars into the desired harbor—if I had not seen mountains of the wickedness of bishops, and of other priests or clerics even within our own order, raised against God—mountains that I must, according to the law, first shatter with harsh songs of words as witnesses, and then shatter the people, if indeed they cling to the ordinances, not so that they may be killed bodily, but so that, dead to their vices, they may live to God, lest I be accused of respect of persons—I would have been silent out of modesty. [Col. 0368B]

But I ask that, as I have already said above, pardon be granted me by those whose life I not only praise but even prefer to all the riches of the world, and of whose life I desire and thirst, if it could be, to become a participant before my death. Our sides are now fortified by the two invincible shields of the saints; the walls of adversity stand behind us; our head is firmly established and, as a helmet, most faithfully covered by the Lord’s help; and the cliffs of reproaches are repeatedly assailed by the flight of truthful birds.

## PART THREE. GILDA’S REBUKE OF THE CLERGY

[Col. 0367]

### CHAPTER ONE. Rebuke of the Clergy

Britain has priests, but they are foolish; very many ministers, but imprudent; clerics, but deceitful plunderers; shepherds, as they are called, but wolves prepared for the slaughter of souls. For they do not provide what is useful for the people, but seek the fullness of their own bellies. They have church buildings as their homes, but enter them for the sake of disgraceful profit. They teach the peoples, but by offering the worst examples, vices, and evil customs.

They rarely sacrifice, and never stand at the altars with a pure heart. They do not rebuke the people for their sins, clearly because they commit the same sins. They despise Christ’s commandments and strive by every means to fulfill their own desires. They usurp the seat of the apostle Peter with unclean feet, but, deservedly because of their greed, they fall into the pestilential chair of Judas the betrayer. [Col. 0367C]

[Col. 0367D] They hate the truth as an enemy and favor lies as though they were their dearest brothers. They regard righteous poor men, savage as serpents, with grim faces, while they venerate wicked rich men without the slightest sense of shame as though they were heavenly angels. With the highest part of their lips they proclaim that alms should be given to the needy, but they themselves give not even a coin. They remain silent about the unspeakable crimes of the people, but magnify their own injuries as though they had been inflicted upon Christ.

They perhaps drive a religious mother or sisters from their house, while indecently exalting foreign women as though for a more secret service—or rather, to speak the truth, though such conduct is foolish not so much to me as to those who do it, humiliating them. [Col. 0368C]

After this they pursue ecclesiastical offices more eagerly than the kingdoms of heaven, defend those whom they have accepted in tyrannical fashion, yet do not adorn them with legitimate conduct. When they occasionally hear the precepts of the saints—which they ought to hear from them very frequently—they are drowsy and stupid; but for entertainments and foolish tales of secular men, as though for a road journey that opens onto death, they are energetic and attentive.

For the sake of their fatness they are hoarse like bulls, and unhappily eager for illicit things. They hold their faces arrogantly high, while their minds, gnawed by conscience, are plunged into the depths or even into Tartarus. They are sorrowful over one lost coin and joyful over one coin sought and found. In the apostolic ordinances, through ignorance or the weight of their sins—and even stopping the mouths of those who know—they are dull and mute; but in the twists and turns of worldly affairs they are most skilled in lies. [Col. 0368D]

Many of them, because of their wicked way of life, rush into the priesthood, even purchasing it with nearly all their money. After obtaining the episcopal or presbyteral priestly seat—which they have nowhere rightly occupied—they roll about like pigs in the same old, accursed, intolerable mire of sacrilegious acts, having snatched only the priestly name, without having received its order or apostolic dignity. [Col. 0369A]

But those who are not yet fit for complete faith or for repentance from their evils—how can they properly approach and obtain any ecclesiastical rank, not to mention the highest rank, which only the holy and perfect, imitators of the apostles, and—as I may speak in the words of the teacher of the nations—men who are blameless, lawfully and without great sacrilege, undertake?

## CHAPTER II. On the same subject

For what is so impious and wicked as, in imitation of Simon Magus (Acts 8:18), even though other assorted crimes do not meanwhile intervene, for someone to wish to purchase the office of bishop or presbyterate at an earthly price—a dignity more properly acquired through holiness and upright conduct? Yet these men err more deliberately, or more desperately, because they buy their priesthoods not from the apostles or the successors of the apostles, but from tyrants and from their father, the devil—counterfeit priesthoods that will never profit them. Rather, as though placing a roof and summit over all their wickedness, under which their former or recent offenses, and the cravings of greed and gluttony, might not easily be reproached by anyone, they build this criminal structure of life above them, so that, as superiors over many, they may plunder more freely.

For if such a condition of purchase had been proposed by these shameless men not, I say, to the apostle Peter but to any holy priest or pious king, they would have received the same answer that their author, Simon Magus, received from the apostle, when Peter said: “May your money perish with you” (ibid., 20). But perhaps—alas!—those who ordain these ambitious men, or rather abase them and curse them instead of blessing them, while they make them not repentant sinners, as would have been more fitting, but sacrilegious and despairing men, have themselves been raised to the priesthood in the same way. Therefore they do not greatly detest in their sons—indeed, they venerate in them—that which, as is certain, came upon them in the same manner as upon their fathers.

Indeed, if they cannot find such a pearl in their own parish because the treasurers resist them and refuse them so valuable a profit, they are not so much reluctant as eager to cross the seas and traverse spacious lands, after first sending careful messengers, so that this singular kind and incomparable beauty—or, more truly, this diabolical illusion—may be obtained even at the price of selling all their possessions.

Then, returning to their homeland with great display and great fantasy—or rather, insanity—they portray themselves as walking more erect than before. Whereas they once looked upon the mountain peaks, they now direct their half-sleeping eyes straight toward heaven, or toward the highest fleece of the clouds; and they thrust themselves upon their homeland as new creations—or rather, as diabolical instruments—like that black pig Novatian, once the executioner of the Lord’s precious pearl at Rome. With violence they will extend their hands not so much toward venerable altars as toward the avenging flames of hell, hands worthy of being placed in such a posture [Note: [Col. 0369D] Perhaps *schemate*; “posture” or “form”].

## CHAPTER III. On the same subject: examples are proposed from Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Melchizedek, Moses, Phinehas, and Jesus son of Nun

What, then, unhappy people, do you expect from such men, whom the Apostle called “beasts of the belly” (Titus 1:12)? Are you corrected by those who not only do not stir themselves toward good deeds, but, according to the prophet’s reproach, “labor to act wickedly” (Jer. 9:5)? Are your eyes enlightened by such men, who eagerly observe only those things that readily lead to vices—that is, to the gates of hell? Or surely, according to the Savior’s saying (Matt. 15:14), if you do not flee from these most rapacious men, like wolves of Arabia, as Lot fled to the mountain from the fiery rain of Sodom, you will fall, blind led by the blind, into the pit of hell.

But perhaps someone will say that not all bishops or presbyters are evil in the manner described above, because they are not stained by the disgrace of schism, pride, or impurity. We do not strongly deny this either. Yet although we know that they are chaste and good, we shall answer briefly: What did it profit the priest Eli (1 Sam. 2:11–12; 3:12) that he alone did not violate the Lord’s commands by seizing meat from the pots with forks before the fat was offered to the Lord, when he was punished by the same wrath of death as his sons (1 Sam. 4:11)?

Who among them, out of envy of a better sacrifice carried up to heaven by heavenly fire, was killed like Abel (Gen. 4:8)—men who even disdain the reproach of an ordinary word? Who hated the counsel of the wicked and did not sit with the ungodly (Ps. 25:5), so that it could truthfully be said of him, as of Enoch: “Enoch walked with God, and he was not found” (Gen. 5:22)—that is, at a time when everyone, abandoning God, was beginning to limp after idols amid the vanity of the world?

Who among them, like Noah in the time of the Flood (Gen. 7:7), admitted into the saving ark—that is, now the Church—no one opposed to God, so that it might plainly be shown that only the innocent or the repentant ought to be in the Lord’s house?

Who, like Melchizedek, offered sacrifice and blessed those who belonged only to the victors and to the righteous man rescued among the three hundred— that is, through the mystery of the Trinity—after they had defeated the savage armies of five kings and victorious bands, and had desired nothing belonging to another (Gen. 14:18)?

Who, like Abraham, at God’s command willingly offered his own son to be beheaded upon the altar (Gen. 22:1), thereby fulfilling something analogous to Christ’s command that the right eye causing scandal must be torn out (Matt. 5:29), and taking heed of the prophet’s warning that the sword which holds back from bloodshed is accursed (Jer. 48:10)?

Who tore the memory of wrongdoing from his heart by the roots, like Joseph (Gen. 50:15)? Who spoke with the Lord on the mountain and was not thereafter terrified by the resounding trumpets (Exod. 19:16), but, like Moses, brought down the two tablets and the horned face—figuratively understood, unfit and dreadful for unbelieving eyes—(Exod. 34:29)?

Who, praying for the sins of the people, cried out from the depths of his heart, as Moses did: “Lord, this people has sinned a great sin; but if you forgive it, forgive it; otherwise erase me from your book” (Exod. 32:31–32)?

Who, inflamed with zeal for God, rose up energetically, like the priest Phinehas (Num. 25:7; Ps. 105:31), to avenge fornication without delay, healing the wound of sexual sin with the medicine of repentance, lest wrath blaze against the people, so that righteousness might thereby be reckoned to him forever?

Who among them has imitated Jesus son of Nun, whether in the moral sense by eradicating the seven nations from the Promised Land even to their destruction, or in establishing spiritual Israel for them (Josh. 24:11)?

## CHAPTER IV. Jesus and Phinehas—or rather Eleazar—Jephthah, Gideon, Samson, and Samuel are proposed as examples

Who among them showed how the final boundaries beyond the Jordan ought to be wisely divided among the people of God, so that it might be known what should be allotted to each, as Phinehas—[Note: [Col. 0371D] The author has suffered a lapse of memory. Read “Eleazar.”]—and Jesus did (Josh. 19:51)?

Who, in order to overthrow thousands of the nations hostile to the people of God while leaving that people unharmed, sacrificed his only daughter—understood as his own pleasure—when she came out to meet the victorious men with tambourines and dances (Judg. 11:31), that is, with carnal desires, imitating in this also the Apostle, who says: “Not seeking what is useful for me, but what is useful for many, so that they may be saved” (1 Cor. 10:33), and thus acted like Jephthah in offering a sacrifice of vowed appeasement?

Who among them, to disturb, put to flight, and overthrow the camps of proud nations through the mysteries of the Trinity, proceeded like Gideon, as we said above, with men holding jars (Judg. 7:6, 16) and excellent, sounding trumpets in their hands—that is, prophetic and apostolic understandings, as the Lord said to the prophet: “Raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58:1), and the Psalmist said of the apostles: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. 18:5)—and with jars flashing at night in the brightest light of fire, understood as the bodies of the saints, joined to good works and burning with the fire of the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7), after the cutting down of the grove of idolatry (morally interpreted as the dense and dark forest of greed) (Judg. 6:25), and after experiencing the evident signs of the fleece of the Jews in the heavenly rain (ibid., 37), and of the Gentiles moistened with the dew of the Holy Spirit, advancing with unwavering faith (Judg. 7:1)?

Who among them, desiring to die to the world and to live for Christ (Phil. 1:23), overthrew, like Samson, the innumerable luxurious banqueters of the nations who praised their gods (Judg. 16:23–25)—that is, thoughts exalting riches, as the Apostle says: “Greed, which is the worship of idols” (Col. 3:5)—by shaking the two columns with the strength of his arms (understood as the evil pleasures of soul and flesh, by which every human house of wickedness is in some fashion built and supported) (Judg. 16:29–30)?

Who, like Samuel, driving away fear by prayer and the sacrifice of a suckling lamb (1 Sam. 7:9), stirring up unexpected thunder and rains from the clouds (1 Sam. 12:17), appointing a king without flattery (1 Sam. 10:1, 24), and rejecting the same king when he no longer pleased God, anointing a better man in his place for the kingdom (1 Sam. 13:14; 15:28; 16:13), stood ready to take leave of the people and spoke in this manner: “Behold, I am here; speak before the Lord and his anointed, whether I have taken anyone’s ox or donkey; whether I have falsely accused anyone; whether I have oppressed anyone; whether I have taken a gift from anyone’s hand” (1 Sam. 12:2–3).

The people answered him, saying: “You have not falsely accused us, nor oppressed us, nor taken anything from anyone’s hand” (ibid., 4).

## CHAPTER V. Examples of Elijah, Elisha, and Isaiah are reviewed

Who among them, like Elijah the outstanding prophet, burned one hundred proud men with heavenly fire while preserving fifty humble men (2 Kings 1:10, 11, 15), and, without the disguise of flattery, announced the approaching death of the wicked king who consulted not God through the prophets but the idol of Ekron (ibid., 16), and struck down all the prophets of the image of Baal with a flashing sword—that is, with the word of God—(1 Kings 18:40), who, moved by zeal for God, deprived the wicked of the heavenly rains of the earth and shut them up, as though with the strongest lock of famine, for three years and six months (1 Kings 17:1), and, dying of hunger and thirst in the desert, complained: “Lord,” he said, “they have killed your prophets and destroyed your altars; and I alone have been left, and they seek my life” (1 Kings 19:10)?

Who among them, like Elisha, punished his most beloved disciple, burdened with earthly goods beyond his accustomed measure (2 Kings 5:23), with expulsion, if not with perpetual leprosy, because he accepted what he had previously despised, although he had been earnestly asked by him to take it (ibid., 16, 27)?

And who among them, like Elisha, revealed to a boy despairing of life and trembling at the unexpected military forces of enemies besieging the city in which they were, the vision of the soul through fervent prayer to God, so that he could behold the mountain full of the heavenly army of armed men, chariots, or horsemen, shining with fiery faces (ibid., 15–17), and believe that the power to save was greater than the enemies’ power to fight?

And who among them, by bodily contact (2 Kings 4:34), benefited another lying dead—dead, clearly, to God but alive to vices—as the one described above, dead to the world but living to God, so that he immediately sprang up and gave thanks to Christ for a restoration of health that almost all mortal tongues had deemed impossible?

Whose lips, like Isaiah’s, were cleansed by a burning coal brought from the altar with the tongs of a cherub, so that his sins might be wiped away through humble confession (Isa. 6:6–7), and whose army of one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians, aided by the effective prayer of the devout king Hezekiah (2 Kings 19:1, 14; Isa. 37:1, 15), was overthrown by the hand of an angel without any visible trace of wounds (2 Kings 19:35; Isa. 27:36)?

Who among them, like blessed Jeremiah, endured prisons with their filth and stench (Jer. 20:2; 32:2; 37:15; 38:6) and sudden deaths (Jer. 26:8, 14), because of God’s commands and threats given from heaven (Jer. 1:17), and because he proclaimed the truth even to those unwilling to hear it?

And, to say no more, who among them, as the Teacher of the Nations said (Heb. 11:37–38), endured wandering in the mountains, in caves and caverns, being stoned, sawn in two, and exposed to every kind of death for the Lord’s name, as did the holy prophets?

## [Col. 0373A] CHAPTER VI. Next, from the New Testament: James first, Peter, and Paul

But why linger over examples from the old covenant, as though there were none in the new? Let those who think they can enter the narrow path of the Christian religion without any labor, merely under the pretext of the priestly name, listen to us—those who pluck only a few flowers, as though they were the highest, from the broad and pleasant meadow of the saints who were beginners in the New Testament.

Which of you, who are sluggish rather than legitimately seated in the priestly chair, after being expelled from the council of the ungodly and enduring various blows from rods (Acts 16:23), gave thanks with all your heart to the Trinity because you were considered worthy to suffer disgrace for Christ the true God, as the holy apostles did (Acts 5:41)?

Which of you, struck repeatedly with a fuller’s club for bearing witness to the true God, died bodily like James, the first bishop in the New Testament alone?

Which of you was beheaded by the sword at the hands of an unjust ruler, like James the brother of John (Acts 12:2)?

Which of you, like the first minister and martyr of the Gospel, was stoned by impious hands for the sole crime of having seen God, whom the faithless could not see (Acts 7:57)?

Which of you, crucified with his feet turned upward out of reverence for Christ’s gibbet, breathed his final breath like that worthy keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom?

Which of you, after chains, prisons, shipwrecks, and bitter scourging with rods; after continual dangers from rivers, robbers, nations, Jews, and false apostles; after the labors of hunger, fasting, and vigils; after constant anxiety for all the churches; after anguish on behalf of those causing scandal; after weakness on behalf of the weak; after an astonishing circuit of almost the entire world in preaching the Gospel of Christ, was beheaded by the stroke of the sword for confessing Christ, like the chosen Vessel and Teacher of the Nations?

## CHAPTER VII. The example of Saint Ignatius the martyr

Which of you, like the holy martyr Ignatius, bishop of the city of Antioch, after his wondrous deeds in Christ, was torn apart at Rome by the mass of lions for bearing witness to Christ? When you hear his words as he was led to his passion—if your faces have ever been covered with the blush of shame—you will not merely think yourselves unworthy to be priests in comparison with him, but not even ordinary Christians.

For in the letter that he sent to the Church of Rome he says:

> “From Syria to Rome I fight with beasts by land and sea, day and night, bound and chained to ten leopards—that is, soldiers assigned to guard me—who become fiercer because of the benefits we have shown them. But I am instructed still more by their wickedness, though I have not thereby been justified. O blessed beasts prepared for me, when will they come? When will they be released? When will they be permitted to enjoy my flesh? I pray that they may be prepared to be more savage, and I shall invite them to devour me, and I shall beg them not to fear touching my body, as they have feared in the case of some. Indeed, even if they hesitate, I myself will use force; I myself will thrust myself upon them. Grant me pardon, I beg you: I know what is profitable for me. Now I am beginning to be Christ’s disciple. Let envy, human affection, and spiritual wickedness depart, so that I may be worthy to attain Jesus Christ—fires, crosses, beasts, scattering of bones, tearing apart of limbs, punishments of the whole body, and every torment devised by the devil’s craft may all be completed in me, provided only that I may be worthy to attain Jesus Christ.”

What do you see in these words with the eyes of your souls half asleep? What do you hear of such things with ears deaf to understanding? Shake off, I beg you, the dark and black gloom of your hearts, so that you may be able to see the radiant light of truth and humility.

The Christian who is not ordinary but perfect, the priest who is not base but supreme, the martyr who is not sluggish but outstanding, says: “Now I am beginning to be Christ’s disciple.”

But you, as though you were that Lucifer cast down from heaven (Isa. 14:12), raise yourselves by words though not by power, and in a manner chew over and display in your gestures what your author previously depicted:

> “I will ascend into heaven, and I will be like the Most High” (ibid., 13).

And again:

> “I dug wells and drank water, and I dried up with the sole of my feet all the streams of the embankments” (Isa. 37:25).

It would have been far more fitting for you to imitate and listen to the one who is truly the unconquered model of all goodness and humility, who says through the prophet:

> “But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Ps. 21:7).

O marvelous statement, that he called himself the reproach of men, when he had erased all the reproaches of the world! And again, in the Gospel:

> “I can do nothing of myself” (John 5:30),

although he, coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit, of the same essence, made heaven and earth with all their immeasurable adornment—not by another’s power but by his own.

And you arrogantly exalt your words, while the prophet says:

> “Why does earth and ashes grow proud?” (Sir. 10:9).

## CHAPTER VIII. The example of Saint Polycarp, with passages of Holy Scripture also brought forward

But let me return to the subject. Which of you, I ask, like Polycarp, the outstanding shepherd of the Church of Smyrna and witness of Christ, kindly set a table for the guests who were eagerly dragging him to the fire, and, exposed to the flames for the love of Christ, said:

> “The one who has given me the fire to endure punishment will grant that I may endure the flames steadfastly without being fastened with nails.”

I shall still add one example, besides the great forest of the saints whose words fly about everywhere: Basil, namely, the bishop of Caesarea. When threats of this kind were made against him by an unjust ruler—that unless he were stained by the Arian filth like the others by the following day, he would certainly die—he is said to have replied:

> “I shall indeed be tomorrow what I am today; would that you might not change!”

And again:

> “Would that I had some worthy gift to bring to the man who would release Basil sooner from the knot of this purse!”

Who among you firmly preserves, amid the assaults of tyrants, the rule of apostolic speech that has always been observed by all holy priests existing in every age, when they reject human counsel rushing headlong toward wickedness, saying:

> “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 3:29).

Therefore, as usual, let us flee to the mercy of the Lord and to the voices of his holy prophets, so that they may hurl at imperfect pastors the arrows of their oracles—as formerly at tyrants—by which they may be pierced and healed. Let us see what the Lord speaks through the prophets in threats against idle and dishonorable priests who do not teach the people well either by their examples or by their words.

That priest Eli in Shiloh was condemned to such punishment because he had not avenged his sons, who despised God, with the severe zeal worthy of God, but had admonished them mildly and indulgently, as a father moved by paternal affection. The prophet said to him:

> “I plainly revealed myself to the house of your father when they were serving Pharaoh in Egypt; and I chose the house of your father from all the tribes of Israel for my priesthood” (1 Sam. 2:27–28).

And shortly afterward:

> “Why did you look upon my incense and my sacrifice with an evil eye? And why did you honor your sons more than me, so that you blessed them from the beginning in all the sacrifices before me? And now this is what the Lord says: Those who honor me, I will honor; and those who treat me as nothing will be reduced to nothing. And let this be a sign for you: what will come upon your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas; in one day both will die by the sword of men” (ibid., 29, 31, 34).

If, then, such things happen to those who correct their subjects only with words and do not amend them through a punishment proportionate to their deeds, what will happen to those who exhort others to evil by sinning and drag them along?

What also happened to that true prophet is clear. After he had fulfilled the sign foretold by him, restored the withered hand of the impious king, been sent from Judah to prophesy at Bethel, and been forbidden to taste any food there, he was deceived by another prophet, as it was said, into taking a little bread and water. His host then said to him:

> “Thus says the Lord God: Because you disobeyed the mouth of the Lord and did not keep the command that the Lord your God gave you, but returned and ate bread and drank water in this place, although he had commanded you not to eat bread or drink water here, your body will not be placed in the tomb of your fathers.”

And it happened, he says, that after he had eaten bread and drunk water, he saddled his donkey and departed; and a lion found him on the road and killed him (1 Kings 13:21–24).

## CHAPTER IX. From Isaiah

Hear also the holy prophet Isaiah speaking in this manner about priests:

> “Woe to the wicked for evil; the reward of his hands will be given to him. My people have been plundered by their exactors, and women have ruled over them. My people, those who call you blessed are themselves deceiving you, and they destroy the way of your paths. The Lord stands to judge, and stands to judge the peoples. The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people and its rulers. You have devoured my vineyard; the spoil of the poor is in your house. Why do you crush my people and grind the faces of the poor? says the Lord of hosts” (Isa. 3:11–15).

And again:

> “Woe to those who make unjust laws and, by writing, write injustice, so that they may oppress the poor in judgment and do violence to the cause of the humble among my people, so that widows may become their prey and they may plunder orphans. What will you do on the day of visitation and calamity coming from afar?” (Isa. 10:1–3).

And further:

> “But these too have not known because of wine; they have gone astray because of drunkenness. The priests have not known because of drunkenness; they have been swallowed up by wine; they have gone astray in drunkenness; they have not known the seer; they have been ignorant of judgment. For all the tables are filled with vomit and filth, so that no place remains. Therefore hear the word of the Lord, you mocking men who rule over my people who are in Jerusalem. For you have said: ‘We have made a covenant with death, and with hell we have made an agreement. When the overflowing scourge passes through, it will not come upon us, because we have made falsehood our hope, and we are protected by falsehood’” (Isa. 28:7–8, 14–15).

And after a little:

> “The hail will overturn the hope of falsehood, and the waters will inundate the protection. Your covenant with death will be abolished, and your agreement with hell will not stand. When the overflowing scourge passes through, you will become its trampling ground; whenever it passes through, it will carry you away” (ibid., 17–19).

And again:

> “The Lord said: Because this people approaches me with its mouth and glorifies me with its lips, while its heart is far from me, behold, I will continue to astonish this people with a great and wondrous miracle. The wisdom of its wise men will perish, and the understanding of its prudent men will be hidden. Woe to those who are deep in heart, hiding their counsel from the Lord, whose deeds are in darkness, and who say: ‘Who sees us?’ and ‘Who knows us?’ This is your perverse thought” (Isa. 29:13–16).

And after a little:

> “Thus says the Lord: Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet. What is this house that you will build for me? And what is the place of my rest? My hand made all these things, and all these things came to be, says the Lord. But upon whom will I look, except upon the poor man, contrite in spirit, and trembling at my words? The one who sacrifices an ox is like one who kills a man; the one who slaughters a sheep is like one who brains a dog; the one who offers an offering is like one who offers swine’s blood; the one who remembers incense is like one who blesses an idol. They have chosen all these things in their own ways, and their soul has delighted in their abominations” (Isa. 66:1–3).

## CHAPTER X. From Jeremiah

Pay attention also to what Jeremiah, a virgin and prophet, says to foolish shepherds:

> “Thus says the Lord: What injustice did your fathers find in me, that they went far from me and walked after vanity and became vain?” (Jer. 2:5).

And shortly afterward:

> “You entered and defiled my land, and you made my inheritance an abomination. The priests did not say: ‘Where is the Lord?’ Those who held the law did not know me, and the shepherds transgressed against me. Therefore I will still contend with you in judgment, says the Lord, and I will dispute with your children” (ibid., 7, 9).

Again, after a little:

> “Astonishment and wonders have occurred in the land. The prophets prophesied falsehood, and the priests applauded with their hands, and my people loved such things. What, then, will happen at its end?” (Jer. 5:30, 3).

> “To whom shall I speak and testify, that he may hear? Behold, their ears are uncircumcised, and they cannot hear. Behold, the word of the Lord has become a reproach to them, and they do not receive it” (Jer. 6:10).

> “For I will stretch out my hand over the inhabitants of the land, says the Lord. From the least to the greatest, all are intent on greed; from prophet to priest, all practice deceit. And they healed the brokenness of the daughter of my people with disgrace, saying: ‘Peace, peace,’ when there was no peace. They were ashamed because they committed abomination; indeed, they were not ashamed of their shame, and they did not know how to blush. Therefore they will fall among those who fall; at the time of their visitation they will collapse, says the Lord” (Jer. 6:12–15).

And again:

> “All these rulers of those who turn aside, walking deceitfully, are bronze and iron; all are corrupt. The bellows have failed in the fire; the refiner has refined in vain; their wickednesses have not been consumed. Call them rejected silver, because the Lord has cast them away” (ibid., 28–30).

And shortly afterward:

> “I am he, I am he; I have seen it, says the Lord. Go to my place in Shiloh, where my name dwelt from the beginning, and see what I did to it because of the wickedness of my people Israel. And now, because you have done all these works, says the Lord, and I spoke to you, rising early and speaking, but you did not hear, and I called you, but you did not answer, I will do to this house in which my name has been invoked, and in which you trust, and to this place which I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh; and I will cast you away from my face” (Jer. 7:11–15).

And again:

> “My children have gone out from me, and they do not remain; there is no one who will extend my tent farther and raise my curtains. For the shepherds have acted foolishly and have not sought the Lord; therefore they have not understood, and their flock has been scattered” (Jer. 10:20–21).

And after a little:

> “What has my beloved done in my house? She has committed many crimes. Will holy flesh take away your wickednesses, in which you have gloried? The Lord called your name ‘a luxuriant, beautiful, fruitful, splendid olive tree’; at the sound of its words, a great fire blazed against it, and its branches were burned” (Jer. 11:15–16).

And again:

> “Come, gather together, all you beasts of the earth; hurry to devour. Many shepherds have destroyed my vineyard; they have made my desirable portion a desert of solitude” (Jer. 12:9–10).

He also says:

> “Thus says the Lord to this people, who loved to move their feet and did not rest, and did not please the Lord: Now he will remember their iniquities and visit their sins” (Jer. 14:10).

The prophets say to them:

> “You shall not see the sword, and there will be no famine among you; rather, the Lord will give you true peace in this place.”

And the Lord said to me:

> “The prophets prophesy falsely in my name. I did not send them, and I did not command them. They prophesy to you a lying vision, divination, fraud, and the deceit of their heart. Therefore thus says the Lord: Those prophets will be consumed by sword and famine. And the peoples to whom they prophesied will be cast out upon the streets of Jerusalem because of famine and sword, and there will be no one to bury them” (ibid., 13–16).

And again:

> “Woe to the shepherds who destroy and tear apart the flock of my pasture, says the Lord. Therefore thus says the Lord God of Israel to the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock and driven them away, and you have not visited them. Behold, I will visit upon you the wickedness of your practices, says the Lord” (Jer. 23:1–2).

> “For both prophet and priest have been polluted, and in my house I have found their wickedness, says the Lord. Therefore their way will be like a slippery path in darkness; they will be driven forward and fall upon it. For I will bring evil upon them, the year of their visitation, says the Lord. And among the prophets of Samaria I saw folly: they prophesied by Baal and deceived my people Israel. And among the prophets of Jerusalem I saw the likeness of adulterers and the way of falsehood; they strengthened the hands of the worst men, so that no one would turn from his wickedness. They have all become for me like Sodom, and its inhabitants like Gomorrah.

> “Therefore thus says the Lord to the prophets: Behold, I will feed them wormwood and give them gall to drink, for pollution has gone out from the prophets of Jerusalem over the whole land.

> “Thus says the Lord of hosts: Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you and deceive you; they speak the vision of their heart, not from the mouth of the Lord. For they say to those who blaspheme me: ‘The Lord has spoken: You shall have peace.’ And to everyone who walks in the perversity of his heart they say: ‘No evil shall come upon you.’ For who has stood in the council of the Lord, seen and heard his word? Who has considered his word and heard it? Behold, the whirlwind of the Lord’s indignation goes forth, and a storm breaking forth will come upon the head of the wicked. The Lord’s anger will not turn back until he acts and fulfills the thought of his heart. In the last days you will understand his counsel” (ibid., 11–20).

## CHAPTER XI. From Joel, Hosea, and Amos

For you think or do little concerning the fact that the holy Joel, admonishing inactive priests and lamenting the people’s loss because of their iniquities, also declared:

> “Awake, you who are drunk from your wine, and weep and lament, all you who drink wine to drunkenness, because gladness and joy have been taken away from your mouth” (Joel 1:5).

> “Mourn, priests who serve at the altar, because the fields have become miserable. Let the earth mourn, because the grain has become miserable, the wine has dried up, the oil has diminished, and the farmers have languished. Mourn, fields, over the wheat and barley, because the harvest has perished from the field; the vine has dried up; the fig tree has diminished; the pomegranate, palm, apple tree, and all the trees of the field have dried up, because they have confounded the joy of the children of men” (ibid., 9, 12).

All these things must be understood spiritually by you, lest your souls dry up through such a pestilential famine of the word of God.

And again:

> “Weep, priests who serve the Lord, saying: ‘Spare, O Lord, your people, and do not give your inheritance to reproach, and do not let the nations rule over them, lest the nations say: Where is their God?’” (Joel 2:17).

But you do not listen to these things at all; rather, you commit everything by which the indignation of divine fury may blaze more fiercely against you.

Consider carefully also what the holy prophet Hosea said to priests of your sort:

> “Hear this, priests, and let the house of Israel and the house of the king attend; give ear, for judgment is against you, because you have become a snare to the watchtower and like a net spread over Tabor, which hunters have fixed” (Hos. 5:1).

The Lord also intends this kind of alienation from you through the prophet Amos, who says:

> “I have hated and rejected your feast days, and I will not accept the fragrance of your solemn assemblies. For even if you offer me burnt offerings and sacrifices, I will not accept them; I will not look upon the saving declaration of your offerings. Take away from me the sound of your songs, and I will not hear the psalmody of your instruments” (Amos 5:21–23).

For the famine of evangelical food rages among you, consuming the very entrails of your souls, just as the same prophet foretold:

> “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will send a famine upon the land—not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God. They will move from sea to sea and run from north to east, seeking the word of the Lord, but they will not find it” (Amos 8:11–12).

## CHAPTER XII. From Micah

Also attend with your ears to the holy Micah, as though he were sounding more sharply like a kind of heavenly trumpet against the deceitful rulers of the people:

> “Hear now this, leaders of the house of Jacob. Is it not for you to know judgment, you who hate good and seek evil, who tear their skin from them and their flesh from their bones? Just as [Col. 0379B] they have eaten the flesh of my people, stripped their skin from them, broken their bones, and torn them apart as though for meat in a pot. They will cry out to God, but he will not hear them, and at that time he will turn his face away from them, because they acted wickedly in their schemes against them. Thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who lead my people astray, who bite with their teeth and proclaim peace to them, but when nothing is given into their mouths: ‘I have stirred up war against him.’ Therefore night shall be yours instead of vision, and darkness shall be yours instead of divination; the sun shall set upon the prophets, and the day shall grow dark over them. The seers shall be confounded, and the diviners ridiculed; they themselves shall rail against everyone, because there will be no one who answers them. But if I do not fill [myself] with strength [Col. 0379C] in the Spirit of the Lord, with judgment and power, to declare to the house of Jacob its impieties and to Israel its sins.

> “Hear this, then, leaders of the house of Jacob and remnant of the house of Israel, who abhor judgment and pervert everything that is right, who build Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquities. Its leaders judged for gifts, its priests answered for payment, and its prophets divined for money; yet they relied upon the Lord, saying, ‘Is not the Lord among us? Evil will not come upon us.’ Therefore, because of you, Zion shall be plowed like a field, Jerusalem shall become like a watchtower in an orchard, and the mountain of the house like a wooded height.” (Micah 3:1–12)

And a little later:

> “Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers straw at harvest and like a cluster of grapes at the vintage, when there is no bunch of first-ripe fruit to eat. Woe to me, my soul, because [Col. 0379D] [the Latin is corrupt or uncertain: ‘reverence always rises, reverent, from the earth’], and there is no one to set things right among human beings. They all strive for blood in judgment, and each one afflicts his neighbor with tribulation; they prepare their hands for evil.” (Micah 7:1–3)

## CHAPTER XIII. From Zephaniah, Zechariah, and Malachi

Attend also to what the outstanding prophet Zephaniah once argued concerning your predecessors—for he was speaking about Jerusalem, which spiritually is understood as the Church or the soul:

> “O city that was splendid and delivered, the faithful dove, she did not obey the voice or accept correction; she did not trust in the Lord and did not draw near to her God.” (Zephaniah 3:1–2)

And he shows why:

> “[Col. 0380A] Her leaders were like roaring lions; her judges were like wolves of Arabia, leaving nothing until morning. Her prophets were men bearing the spirit, contemptuous; her priests profaned holy things and acted wickedly against the law. But the Lord is righteous in her midst, and he will not do injustice; morning by morning he will bring forth his justice.” (Zephaniah 3:5)

But hear also blessed Zechariah admonishing you in the word of God:

> “Thus says the Lord Almighty: Judge with righteous judgment, and show mercy and compassion, each one toward his brother. Do not harm the widow, the orphan, the stranger, or the poor by force; and let no one of you remember his brother’s evil in his heart. But they were rebellious and refused to pay attention; they turned their backs in folly and made their ears heavy so that they would not hear. They made their heart unpersuadable, so that they would not hear my law and the words that the Lord Almighty sent by his Spirit [Col. 0380B] through the earlier prophets. Therefore great wrath came from the Lord Almighty.” (Zechariah 7:5–12)

And again:

> “Because those who spoke uttered troubles, and the diviners spoke false visions and false dreams, and offered empty consolation, therefore they became dry like sheep and were afflicted because there was no healing. My anger was kindled against the shepherds, and I will visit the lambs.” (Zechariah 10:2–3)

And shortly afterward:

> “The sound of the shepherds lamenting, because their greatness has been made wretched. The sound of the lions roaring, because the course of the Jordan has been made wretched. Thus says the Lord Almighty: Those who possessed them killed them and did not repent; and those who sold them said, ‘Blessed be the Lord, for we have grown rich’; and their shepherds suffered nothing on their account. Therefore [Col. 0380C] I will no longer spare the inhabitants of the land, says the Lord.” (Zechariah 11:5–6)

Hear also what the holy prophet Malachi announced to you:

> “You, priests who despise my name, have said, ‘How have we despised your name?’ By offering polluted bread upon my altar; and you have said, ‘How have we polluted it?’ In that you have said, ‘The table of the Lord is of no account.’ And you have despised what is placed upon it. For if you bring a blind animal for sacrifice, is that not evil? If you bring a lame or sick one, is that not evil? Offer it, then, to your governor: will he accept it, or receive your person? says the Lord Almighty. And now entreat the face of your God and beseech him. These things have been done by your hands; will I accept your persons? says the Lord Almighty.” (Malachi 1:6–9)

And again:

> “[Col. 0380D] You brought what was taken by violence—the lame and the sick—and you brought an offering. Shall I accept it from your hand? says the Lord. Cursed is the deceitful one who has a male in his flock, yet, when making a vow, sacrifices the weak to the Lord; for I am a great King, says the Lord of hosts, and my name is fearful among the nations.” (Malachi 1:13–14)

And now this command is addressed to you, priests:

> “If you will not hear and will not set it upon your heart, to give glory to my name, says the Lord of hosts, I will send poverty upon you and curse your blessings, because you have not set it upon your heart. Behold, I will cast the shoulder away from you and scatter dung upon your faces—the dung of your solemnities.” (Malachi 2:1–3)

[Col. 0381A] ## CHAPTER XIV. Again from Malachi

But in the meantime, so that you may more eagerly prepare the instruments of wickedness for good purposes, listen—if even the slightest degree of inward hearing remains in you—to what he says concerning the holy priest:

> “My covenant with him was one of life and peace”—

for historically he was speaking of Levi or Moses—

> “and I gave him fear, and he feared me; he was afraid before my name. The law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found upon his lips. He walked with me in peace and righteousness, and turned many away from iniquity. For the lips of a priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.” (Malachi 2:5–7)

Now he changes his subject and does not cease reproving the wicked:

> “But you have departed from the way and caused many to stumble in the law; you have invalidated [Col. 0381B] the covenant with Levi, says the Lord of hosts. Therefore I have made you contemptible and low among all the peoples, just as you have not kept my ways and have shown partiality in the law. Is there not one Father of us all? Has not one God created us? Why, then, does each one despise his brother?” (Malachi 2:8–10)

And again:

> “Behold, the Lord of hosts will come; and who will be able to contemplate the day of his coming? Who will stand when he appears? For he will go forth like a burning fire and like the soap of those who wash clothes. He will sit refining and purifying silver; he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver.” (Malachi 3:1–3)

And shortly afterward:

> “Your words have prevailed against me, says the Lord; and you have said, ‘It is useless to serve God. What profit is there in keeping his commandments and walking mournfully before the Lord [Col. 0381C] of hosts?’ Therefore now we shall call the arrogant blessed: indeed, those who commit iniquity have been built up; they have tested God and have been saved.” (Malachi 3:13–16)

## CHAPTER XV. From Ezekiel

Attend also to what the prophet Ezekiel said:

> “Woe upon woe shall come, and messenger upon messenger; vision shall be sought from the prophet, the law shall perish from the priest, and counsel from the elders.” (Ezekiel 7:26)

And again:

> “Thus says the Lord: Because your words are false and your divinations empty, therefore, behold, I am against you, says the Lord. I will stretch out my hand against the prophets who see falsehoods and those who speak empty things. They shall not be in the instruction of my people; they shall not be written in the writing of the house of Israel, and they shall not enter the land of Israel. And you shall know that I am the Lord. Because they have led my people [Col. 0381D] astray, saying, ‘The peace of the Lord,’ when there is no peace of the Lord. One builds a wall, and they plaster it, and it will fall.” (Ezekiel 13:8–10)

And a little later:

> “Woe to those who sew pillows beneath every elbow of the hand and make coverings over every head of people of every age, to overthrow souls. The souls of my people have been overthrown; they possessed souls and defiled me before my people for a handful of barley and a piece of bread, killing souls that ought not to die and preserving souls that ought not to live, while you speak empty words to the people who listen.” (Ezekiel 13:18–19)

And further on:

> “Son of man, say: You are a land that is not cleansed, upon which no rain has fallen in the day of wrath; in [Col. 0382A] it its leaders are like roaring lions, seizing plunder, devouring souls by their power, and accepting payments. Your widows have multiplied in your midst, and its priests have despised my law and profaned my holy things. They did not distinguish between the holy and the polluted, nor did they separate between the unclean and the clean; they turned their eyes away from my Sabbaths, and I was profaned in their midst.” (Ezekiel 22:24–26)

And again:

> “I sought among them a man who would walk uprightly and stand before my face at the time of wrath, so that I would not destroy her in the end, but I found none. I poured out my indignation upon her in the fire of my wrath, to consume them; I returned their ways upon their own heads, says the Lord.” (Ezekiel 22:30–31)

And a little later:

> “The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, speak [Col. 0382B] to the children of my people, and say to them: A land upon which I bring the sword—if the people of the land take one man from among themselves and appoint him as their watchman, and if he sees the sword coming upon the land, blows the trumpet, and warns the people; then, if one who hears hears the sound of the trumpet but does not take heed, and the sword comes and seizes him, his blood shall be upon his own head. Because he heard the sound of the trumpet and did not take heed, his blood shall be upon him; but because he took heed, he has saved his life.

> “If, however, the watchman sees the sword coming and does not blow the trumpet, and the people do not take heed, and the sword comes and takes a life from among them, that person has been seized because of his iniquity; but I will require his blood from the watchman’s hand. And you, son of man, I have appointed you watchman for the house of Israel. You shall hear the word from my mouth when I say to the sinner, ‘You shall surely [Col. 0382C] die,’ and you do not speak to turn the wicked from his way: that wicked person shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand. But if you warn the wicked of his way, so that he turns from it, and he does not turn from his way, he shall die in his iniquity, but you will have saved your life.” (Ezekiel 33:2–9)

## CHAPTER XVI. From the Gospel of Matthew

But let these few passages from the many testimonies of the prophets suffice—testimonies by which the pride or sloth of rebellious priests is beaten back—so that they may not suppose that we denounce such things against them by our own invention rather than on the authority of the holy law.

Let us therefore see what the evangelical trumpet, sounding throughout the world, says to disordered priests.
