For, as we have already said, our subject is not those who legitimately occupy the apostolic seat and know well how to distribute spiritual [Col. 0382D] food to their fellow servants at the proper time—if indeed there are many such at present—but ignorant shepherds who abandon the sheep and feed them with empty things, possessing none of the words of a knowledgeable shepherd.

It is therefore clear evidence that he is not a legitimate shepherd but merely an ordinary Christian if he rejects or denies these things—not so much our own words, for we are very insignificant, as the decrees of the Old and New Testaments. As one of our own people rightly said:

> “We earnestly desire that the enemies of the Church should also be our enemies, enemies without any treaty; and that our friends and defenders should be regarded not merely as allies, but even as fathers and lords.”

Let each person therefore bring his conscience before a true examination, and in this way they will discover whether they are seated [Col. 0383A] upon a priestly throne according to right reason.

Let us see, I say, what the Savior and Maker of the world says:

> “You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its savor, with what shall it be salted? It is good for nothing thereafter except to be thrown outside and trampled under people’s feet.” (Matthew 5:13)

This one testimony alone could sufficiently refute all the shameless. But so that it may be demonstrated even more clearly, by further confirmations from Christ’s words, under how many intolerable bundles of crimes these false priests crush themselves, something more must be added.

For it follows:

> “You are the light of the world. A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden. Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house.” (Matthew 5:14)

Which priest of the present age, then, is so possessed by the blindness of ignorance [Col. 0383B] that he shines like the light of a brilliant lamp in some house, illuminating all who remain there at night with the lamp of knowledge and good works? Who is held to be such a secure, public, and conspicuous refuge for all the children of the Church that he resembles a firmly established city on the summit of a lofty mountain?

But also, concerning what follows—

> “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16)—

who among them can fulfill this even for a single day? Rather, such a dense fog and black night of sins hangs over the whole island that it almost turns everyone away from the straight path and makes them wander along the trackless and obstructed paths of crimes. Through their works the heavenly Father is not merely left unpraised; he is even blasphemed intolerably. [Col. 0383C]

I would indeed like to interpret all these testimonies of Holy Scripture, whether inserted or to be inserted in this letter, in a historical or moral sense, as far as my mediocrity could manage. But lest this little work be prolonged to an immeasurable length for those who despise, disdain, and turn away not so much from our words as from God’s, the passages have been or must be gathered simply and without any circumlocution.

And a little later:

> “Whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven.” (Matthew 5:19)

And again:

> “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged; for with whatever judgment you judge, you will be judged.” (Matthew 7:1–2)

Which of you, I ask, will consider what follows?

> “Why do you see the splinter in your brother’s eye but do not consider the beam in [Col. 0383D] your own eye? Or how do you say to your brother, ‘Let me remove the splinter from your eye,’ while, behold, there is a beam in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3–4)

Or what follows:

> “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine, lest perhaps they trample them with their feet and, turning, tear you apart.” (Matthew 7:6)

This happens to you very frequently.

And warning the people not to be led astray by deceitful teachers such as you, he said:

> “Beware of false prophets who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will know them by their fruits. Do they gather grapes from thorns or figs from thistles? Thus every good tree bears good fruits, and a bad tree bears bad fruits.” (Matthew 7:15–17)

And further on:

> “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ [Col. 0384A] will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven.” (Matthew 7:21)

## CHAPTER XVII. Again from the Gospel of Matthew

What, indeed, will happen to you who, as the prophet said, believe in God only with your lips and not with your heart? (Isaiah 19:13)

How, moreover, do you fulfill what follows?

> “Behold, I am sending you like sheep in the midst of wolves.” (Matthew 10:16)

You who, reversing the order, go forth like wolves into the flock of sheep? Or how do you fulfill what he said:

> “Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.” (Matthew 10:16)

You are indeed wise enough to bite someone with your destructive mouth, but not wise enough to defend your head, which is Christ, by placing your body, as it were, before him—though you trample him by every effort of your evil works.

Nor do you possess the innocence of doves. [Col. 0384B] Rather, resembling the blackness of ravens and once flying out of the ark—that is, the Church—you have found the stench of carnal pleasures and have never flown back to it with a pure heart.

But let us examine the rest:

> “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.” (Matthew 10:18)

Consider which of these things you have done.

Which one of you, moreover, would not be wounded in the deepest secret place of his heart by the following testimony, in which the Savior speaks concerning wicked bishops to the apostles?

> “Leave them; they are blind guides of the blind. And if the blind guides the blind, both will fall into a pit.” (Matthew 15:14)

The peoples over whom you preside—or rather, whom you have deceived—certainly need to hear this. Attend to the words of the Lord speaking to the apostles and to the crowds, words that, as [Col. 0384C] I hear, you are not ashamed frequently to bring forward publicly:

> “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon the chair of Moses. Therefore, whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not do according to their works, for they say and do not do.” (Matthew 23:2–3)

It is certainly a dangerous and useless doctrine for priests when it is obscured by wicked deeds.

> “Woe to you, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven before people: you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow those entering to enter.” (Matthew 23:13)

For not only will you be punished in the future for the many crimes of evil that you commit, but you will also be punished with penal punishment for those who perish daily through your example. Their blood will be required from your hands on the day of judgment.

But consider the evil that the parable of the servant presents, when he says in his heart:

> “My master is delaying [Col. 0384D] his coming.”

For this reason, perhaps, he had begun to beat his fellow servants, eating and drinking with drunkards.

> “Therefore the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and he will cut him in two”—

that is, away from the holy priests—

> “and assign him his portion with the hypocrites”—

certainly with those who, under the covering of the priesthood, cast a great shadow over their wickedness—

> “where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” (Matthew 24:48–51)

Such things do not happen to them often in this life because of the daily ruin of the children of Mother Church or their longing for the kingdom of heaven.

## CHAPTER XVIII. From Paul’s Epistle to the Romans

But let us see what Christ’s true disciple, the teacher of the nations, Paul—whom every ecclesiastical teacher ought to imitate, as I also imitate Christ [Col. 0385A] (1 Corinthians 11:1)—declares in such a matter in the First Epistle:

> “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools.” (Romans 1:21–22)

Although this may seem to have been said about the nations, consider nevertheless how appropriately it can be applied to the priests and peoples of this age.

And a little later:

> “They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Therefore God handed them over to dishonorable passions.” (Romans 1:25–26)

And again:

> “Just as they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a depraved mind, to do what is improper, filled with every iniquity, [Col. 0385B] wickedness, impurity, fornication, greed, and malice; full of envy, murder”—

that is, of the souls of the people—

> “strife, deceit, and malignity; whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, insolent, proud, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, senseless, disorderly, without mercy, without affection. Although they knew God’s justice, they did not understand that those who do such things deserve death.” (Romans 1:28–32)

Which of those mentioned above truly lacked all these things? If there were such a one, he might perhaps be caught by the following clause, in which Paul says:

> “Not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them.” (Romans 1:32)

That is, none of them is free from this evil.

And further:

> “According to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous [Col. 0385C] judgment, who will repay each one according to his works.” (Romans 2:5–6)

And again:

> “There is no partiality with God. For whoever has sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and whoever has sinned under the law will be judged by the law. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified.” (Romans 2:11–13)

What severity, then, is coming upon those who not only fail to do what must be fulfilled and do not avoid what is forbidden, but even recoil like a most savage serpent from the very reading of God’s words, however lightly it may have been brought to their ears?

## CHAPTER XIX. Also from the Same Epistle and from the Two Epistles to the Corinthians

But let us pass to what follows:

> “What shall we say, then? Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound? Certainly not. For if we have died to sin, [Col. 0385D] how shall we live in it again?” (Romans 6:1–2)

And a little later:

> “Who,” he says, “will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” (Romans 8:35)

Which of you, I ask, will be inwardly possessed by such an attitude, when you not only do not labor for piety but also endure many things in order to act wickedly and offend Christ?

Or consider what follows:

> “The night has passed, and the day has drawn near. Therefore let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Let us walk honorably as in the day, not in banquets and drunkenness, not in bedrooms and indecencies, not in strife and rivalry; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and do not make provision for the flesh in its desires.” [Col. 0386A] (Romans 13:12–14)

And again, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians:

> “As a wise architect I laid the foundation, and another builds upon it. But let each one see how he builds upon it. For no one can lay another foundation besides that which is Jesus Christ. Now if anyone builds upon this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw, the work of each will become manifest. The day of the Lord will declare it, because it will be revealed in fire; and the fire will test what sort of work each one’s is. If anyone’s work remains, all things will be judged through fire; the one who has built upon it will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss.” (1 Corinthians 3:10–13)

> “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him.” (1 Corinthians 3:16–17)

And again:

> “If anyone [Col. 0386B] among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become a fool so that he may be wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God.” (1 Corinthians 3:18–19)

And shortly afterward:

> “Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole mass? Therefore purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump.” (1 Corinthians 5:6–7)

How will the old leaven—that is, sin—be purged, when it is accumulated day after day by every effort?

And again:

> “I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with fornicators—not at all meaning the fornicators of this world, or the greedy, or the rapacious, or those who serve idols; otherwise you would have had to leave this world. But now I wrote to you not to associate with anyone who is named a brother and is a fornicator, or greedy, or serves idols, or is a slanderer, or drunkard, or rapacious; with such a person [Col. 0386C] you must not even eat.” (1 Corinthians 5:9–11)

A thief, however, certainly does not condemn another thief for theft or robbery; rather, he wishes for him, protects him, and loves him as a partner in his own crime.

Likewise, in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians:

> “Therefore, since we have this ministry, just as we have received mercy, we do not fail; but we reject the hidden things of shame, not walking in cunning or falsifying the word of God.” (2 Corinthians 4:1–2)

In what follows he speaks in this way about wicked teachers:

> “For such people are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light. It is therefore no great thing if his ministers also disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness; their end will be according to their works.” (2 Corinthians 11:13–15)

[Col. 0386D] ## CHAPTER XX. From the Epistles to the Ephesians, First to the Thessalonians, and to the Colossians

Attend also to what he says to the Ephesians. Do you not know that you are in some respect held guilty for this?

> “I say and testify this in the Lord: you must no longer walk as the nations walk in the futility of their mind, with their understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, on account of the blindness of their heart. Having lost all hope, they handed themselves over to indecency, for the practice of every impurity and greed.” (Ephesians 4:17–19)

And which of you has willingly fulfilled what follows?

> “Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the will of God is. And do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit.” (Ephesians 5:17–18)

But also consider what he says to the Thessalonians:

> “[Col. 0387A] For we were never among you with flattering speech, as you know, nor with a pretext for greed, nor seeking glory from people, whether from you or from others, although we could have been honored as Christ’s other apostles. But we became gentle in your midst, like little children, or like a nurse cherishing her own children. In this way, longing for you, we were eager to share with you not only the Gospel of God but also our own souls.” (1 Thessalonians 2:5–8)

If you retain this apostolic affection in all things, you may know that you legitimately occupy his chair.

Or consider what follows:

> “You know what instructions I gave you. For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication; that each one of you know how to possess [Col. 0387B] his own vessel in honor and sanctification, not in the passion of desire, like the nations that do not know God; and that no one overreach or defraud his brother in business, because the Lord is the avenger of all these things. For God did not call us to impurity but to sanctification. Therefore whoever despises these things does not despise a human being but God.” (1 Thessalonians 4:2–8)

Which of you has also carefully and watchfully kept what follows?

> “Therefore put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, lust, and evil desire, on account of which the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience.” (Colossians 3:5–6)

You see, then, on account of which sins the wrath of God chiefly rises up.

## CHAPTER XXI. From the Epistles to Timothy and Titus

Hear, then, what that same holy apostle foretold about you and those like you by the prophetic Spirit, [Col. 0387C] writing openly to Timothy:

> “Know this: in the last days difficult times will come. For people will be lovers of themselves, greedy, boastful, proud, blasphemous, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, incontinent, harsh, without kindness, treacherous, reckless, conceited, lovers of pleasures rather than lovers of God, having an appearance of piety but denying its power. Avoid such people.” (2 Timothy 3:1–5)

As the prophet also says:

> “I have hated the assembly of the wicked, and I will not sit with the ungodly.” (Psalm 25:5)

And a little later—something we see flourishing in our own time—he says:

> “Always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth. Just as Joannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these people also resist the truth, men corrupted [Col. 0387D] in mind and rejected with regard to the faith. But they will not progress further, for their folly will be manifest to all, as theirs also was.” (2 Timothy 3:7–9)

He also clearly shows how priests ought to conduct themselves in their office, writing to Titus:

> “Show yourself as an example of good works: in teaching, integrity, seriousness, and sound, irreproachable speech, so that the one who is opposed may be ashamed, having nothing evil to say about us.” (Titus 2:7–8)

And again to Timothy:

> “Work as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself. And the one who competes in the contest will not [Col. 0388A] be crowned unless he has competed lawfully.” (2 Timothy 2:3–5)

This is an exhortation to the good. But what follows is also a denunciation of wicked people—as you plainly appear to everyone who understands:

> “If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the teaching that accords with piety, he is proud and knows nothing, but is sick with regard to questions and disputes about words. From these arise envy, strife, blasphemies, evil suspicions, and conflicts among people corrupted in mind and deprived of the truth, who suppose that piety is a means of gain.” (1 Timothy 6:3–5)

But why should we continue to rock in the little boat of our meager talent, using testimonies scattered here and there and waves of various meanings? At last we have judged it necessary to return to those readings—which were excerpted from almost the entire text of the sacred writings not only so that they might be recited, but also [Col. 0388B] so that they might support the blessing with which the hands of priests or ministers are initiated, and continually teach them not to depart from the commandments faithfully contained in them by degenerating from priestly dignity—so that it may be clearer to all that eternal punishments await those who have not fulfilled, according to their ability, the teachings and commandments contained in them through their works, and that those who have not done so are not priests or ministers of God.

## CHAPTER XXII. From the First Epistle of Peter

Let us therefore hear what blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, has marked out concerning such a matter:

> “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has regenerated us for the hope of eternal life through the resurrection from the dead [Col. 0388C] of our Lord Jesus Christ, into an incorruptible, undefiled, unfading inheritance, kept in heaven for you, who are guarded by the power of God.” (1 Peter 1:3–5)

Why, then, do you foolishly violate such an inheritance, which is not like earthly things, subject to falling, but is unfading and eternal?

And a little later:

> “Therefore gird up the loins of your mind, be sober, and hope perfectly in the grace that is offered to you in the revelation of Jesus Christ.” (1 Peter 1:13)

Search the depths of your hearts, then, to see whether you are sober and preserve perfectly the priestly grace that must be examined at the Lord’s revelation.

And again he says:

> “As children of blessing, do not conform yourselves to those former desires of your ignorance; but according to the one who called you, the Holy One, be holy in all your conduct. For it is written: ‘Be holy, because I am holy.’” (1 Peter 1:14–16)

**Note [Col. 0387; 0388D]:** The Vulgate has *sanctum* (“holy,” masculine singular) where the text here reads *sanctos* (“holy,” masculine plural). A little earlier it has *filii obedientiae* (“children of obedience”). The Greek likewise has the corresponding reading.

Which of you, I ask, has pursued holiness with such ardor of soul that he hastened to fulfill this, insofar as it lay within him?

But let us see what is contained in the second reading from the same Epistle:

> “Beloved, purify your souls for obedience to the faith through the Spirit, in love and brotherhood, loving one another sincerely and steadfastly, as those reborn not from corruptible seed but from incorruptible seed, through the living and abiding word of God.” (1 Peter 1:22–23)

These commandments were indeed given by the Apostle and read on the day of your ordination [Col. 0389A], so that you might keep them without violation; but they have not been fulfilled by you in the judgment, nor have they even been much considered or understood.

And further:

> “Therefore, laying aside all malice, all deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander, like newborn infants, desire the rational and guileless milk, so that by it you may grow toward salvation, because the Lord is sweet.” (1 Peter 2:1–3)

Consider whether these things too, though you have heard them repeatedly with deaf ears, are trampled underfoot by you.

And again:

> “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for adoption, so that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you from darkness into his wondrous light.” (1 Peter 2:9)

Not only are God’s virtues not proclaimed or made greater through you; by your most wicked examples they are even despised among unbelievers.

[Col. 0389B] **CHAPTER XXIII. From the Acts of the Apostles and again from the First Epistle to Timothy.**—You perhaps heard on that same day, when the reading from the Acts of the Apostles was read, Peter rising in the midst of the disciples and saying: “Men and brethren, the Scripture had to be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David concerning Judas” (Acts 1:15–16). And shortly afterward: “This man, therefore, acquired a field from the reward of iniquity” (ibid., 18). You heard this with an unconcerned—or rather, dull—heart, as though it had not been read concerning you. Who among you, I ask, does not seek a field from the reward of iniquity? Judas was plundering the money-box; you lay waste the offerings of the Church and the souls of its children. He went to the Jews in order to sell God; you go to tyrants and to your father the devil, so that you may despise Christ. He held the Savior of all for sale for thirty pieces of silver; you do so for even a single penny. What more? The example of Matthias is set before you for your confusion: he was chosen by the lot, through the election of the holy apostles or by Christ’s judgment, not by his own will. Yet, made blind to this, you do not see how far you stand from his merits, since of your own accord you have fallen into the love and practice of Judas the betrayer. Therefore it is evident that the man who knowingly calls you priests from his heart is not a true Christian.

Let me state plainly what I think. The rebuke could indeed be made gentler; but what benefit is there in merely stroking with the hand, or anointing with ointment, a wound which, already abhorrent to itself through swelling or stench, requires the cautery and the public remedy of fire—if it can in any way be healed—when the sick man seeks no treatment at all and withdraws farther from this physician? O enemies of God, and not priests; veterans of evil, and not bishops; betrayers, and not successors of the holy apostles; not ministers of Christ. You certainly heard the sound of the words of the Apostle Paul in the second reading—yet in no way preserved his admonitions and virtue, and, like idols that neither see nor hear, stood before the altar on that same day—words that then, and every day, thundered at you: “Brothers,” he says, “this is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptance” (1 Tim. 3:1). He called it faithful and worthy; you rejected it as unfaithful and unworthy.

“If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work” (ibid.). You desire the episcopate with the greatest eagerness for the sake of avarice, not for the purpose of spiritual advancement, and you do not possess the good work worthy of it. “Therefore such a person must be blameless” [Col. 0390A] (ibid., 2). In this saying, tears are needed more than words—as though the Apostle had said that he must be more blameless than all. “The husband of one wife” (ibid.). Why is this so despised even among us, as though it had not been heard—or as though it said the same thing as “the husband of wives”? “Sober, prudent” (ibid.). Who among you has ever even desired that these qualities be found in him? “Hospitable” (ibid.). If this should happen by chance, it is done for popular applause rather than because of the commandment, and it is of no benefit, since the Lord the Savior says: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6:2). “Well ordered, not given to wine, not violent, but moderate, not quarrelsome, not greedy” (1 Tim. 3:2–3). O deadly transformation! O dreadful trampling underfoot of the heavenly commandments! Do you not tirelessly seize the weapons of your deeds and words to overthrow—or rather, bury—these requirements, for the preservation and strengthening of which, if necessary, punishment ought to be willingly endured and life itself laid down?

But let us examine what follows: “One who rules his own household well,” he says, “having his children submissive with all chastity” (1 Tim. 3:4). The chastity of fathers is therefore imperfect if the chastity of their children is not added to it. But what will happen when neither father nor son, corrupted by the example of an evil parent, is seen to be chaste? “If anyone does not know how to preside over his own household, how will he take care of the Church of God?” (ibid., 5). These are words that are confirmed by unmistakable results.

“Deacons likewise must be chaste, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not pursuing shameful gain, holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience.” [Col. 0390C] “But let them first be tested, and then let them serve, having no crime” (ibid., 8, 10). Shuddering at these words, I have lingered over them for a long time. I can say one thing truthfully: all these qualities are changed into their opposites, so that clerics—something I confess not without pain of heart—being immodest, double-tongued, drunk, desirous of shameful gain, holding faith and, to speak more accurately, unbelief in an impure conscience, untested in good but known beforehand for evil works, are admitted to sacred ministry while bearing innumerable crimes.

**CHAPTER XXIV. Again from the Gospel of Matthew.**—You also heard on that day—when it would have been far more worthy and far more proper to drag you to prison or to the punitive scaffold (*catasta*) than to the priesthood—that, when the Lord asked whom the disciples thought him to be, Peter answered: [Col. 0390D] “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16); and that the Lord said to him for this confession: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (ibid., 17). Peter, therefore, taught by God the Father, rightly confesses Christ; but you, instructed by your father the devil, deny the Savior through evil deeds.

To the true priest it is said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (ibid., 18). You, however, resemble the foolish man who built his house upon sand (Matt. 7:26). It should be noted that, when foolish people build a house upon the shifting instability of sand, the Lord does not cooperate with them, according to the saying: “They made kings for themselves, but not through me” (Hos. 8:4). Likewise, what follows has the same meaning when it says: [Col. 0391A] “And the gates of hell shall not prevail” (Matt. 16:18): their sins are understood by this.

What is pronounced concerning your ruinous structure? “The rivers came, and the winds blew, and struck that house, and it fell; and great was its ruin” (Matt. 7:27). To Peter and his successors the Lord says: “And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16:19). To you, however: “I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Matt. 7:23; Luke 13:27), so that, separated on the left with the goats, you may go into eternal fire.

Likewise, to every holy priest it is promised: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19). But how will you loose anything so that it may be loosed in heaven, deprived of heaven because of your crimes and fettered by the cords of monstrous sins, as Solomon also says: “Each person is bound by the cords of his sins” (Prov. 5:22)? By what reasoning will you bind anything on earth so that it may also be bound above the world because of yourselves, who are so bound by iniquities and held in this world that you will by no means ascend into heaven, but, without turning to the Lord in this life, will fall into the wretched prisons of Tartarus?

[Note: So it rightly appears, according to the Paris *Bibliotheca Patrum*. For I do not approve the reading of the Oxford edition: “so that it may be bound even beyond measure, apart from yourselves.”]

Nor should any priest flatter himself merely on account of the consciousness of bodily purity, since, if any of those over whom he presides perish because of his ignorance, negligence, or flattery, their souls will be required on the day of judgment from his hands, as from those of a murderer. For the death inflicted by a good man is no sweeter than that inflicted by an evil one. Otherwise the Apostle would not have said, as though leaving a paternal inheritance to his successors: “I am clean from the blood of all. For I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts 20:26–27). [Col. 0392A]

[Note: Here again we follow the Paris *Bibliotheca Patrum*, rejecting the Oxford reading: “And indeed by much practice.”]

Having been drunk with the long habit and continual practice of sins, and battered as though by waves through the accumulating crimes that continually rush upon you, seek with all the effort of your soul one plank of repentance, as it were after a shipwreck, by which you may escape to the land of the living, so that the wrath of the Lord may be turned away from you—the Lord who mercifully says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. 33:11). May the almighty God of all consolation and mercy (2 Cor. 1:3) preserve the very few good shepherds from every evil, and, after the common enemy has been subdued, make them citizens of the city of heavenly Jerusalem, that is, of the congregation of all the saints—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

**A.D. 555–560. POPE PELAGIUS I.**

[Col. 0391]

**NOTICE (from the *Liber Pontificalis*).**

[Col. 0391C] Pelagius [Note: In the year of Christ the Redeemer 555, which was the twenty-ninth year of Justinian’s reign, the archdeacon Pelagius was appointed in place of Vigilius through the promotion of the same emperor Justinian. To avoid the impending injury to the Catholic faith, or the disgrace of the Council of Chalcedon, he approved the Fifth Synod. Therefore, when the Western bishops were divided by a greater schism, he arranged through Narses that they should be compelled, though repeatedly and unsuccessfully warned by letters from him. In his time the Franks, after devastating many regions of Italy, are said to have been defeated by Justinian and brought under the Roman Empire [Col. 0391D] [This is completely false.], according to Agathias. Pope Hadrian, in his letter to Charlemagne concerning images, writes the following about Pelagius: “Much more, however, his most holy successors, Lord Pelagius and Lord John, built from the foundations the church of the Apostles, of marvelous size, painting various histories both in mosaic and in diverse colors with sacred images, and even to this day they are venerated by us. Pelagius began this church, but John, his successor, completed it and consecrated it under the title of Saints Philip and James,” in accordance with the verse which, according to Baronius, the ancient monuments of the Vatican basilica, collected by Manlius, contain:

“Pelagius began it; Pope John completed it.”

Severinus Binius.]

A Roman by nation, born of John Vicarianus, he sat for eleven years, [Note: Others assign him ten years, ten months, and eighteen days; still others only six years.] ten months, and eighteen days [Note: The commentary of Anastasius, which, according to Baronius, is preserved in the Vatican library, says that Pelagius sat for four years, ten months, and eighteen days. Thus Baronius, year 559, no. 1. Severinus Binius.]. And since there were no bishops to ordain him, two bishops were found—John of Perugia and Bonus of Ferentino—and Andrew, a priest of Ostia; and they ordained him pontiff. For at that time there were none in the clergy who could promote him [Note: The Lucanian manuscript reads: “who could be promoted.” Monasteries and a multitude of religious persons.]. [Col. 0392C]

And a multitude of religious men, learned and noble, had withdrawn from communion with him, saying that he had involved himself in the death of Pope Vigilius, so that he might be afflicted with such punishments. At that same time Narses and Pope Pelagius, having taken counsel, set out with a litany from Saint Pancratius [Note: The same manuscript reads: “to Saint Pancratius.”], with hymns and spiritual songs, and came to Saint Peter the Apostle. Pelagius, holding the Gospels and the cross of the Lord above his head, ascended the ambo. And thus he satisfied the entire people and populace [Note: “And populace” is absent in the same manuscript.], because he had done no evil against Vigilius.

Pope Pelagius then added and said: “I ask you to confirm my petition, so that, if there is anyone who is to be promoted in the holy Church, from doorkeeper up to the rank of bishop, he may advance neither through gold nor through any promises—for you all know that this is simony—but, if there is anyone learned in the work of God and possessing a good life, we command [Col. 0394A] him [Note: “We command him” is absent in the same manuscript.] to advance to the first rank, not through payment but through good conduct.”

At the same time he appointed over the Church’s possessions [Note: “The Church’s possessions” is absent in the same manuscript.] his notary Valentinus, who feared God [Note: The same manuscript reads “appointed.”], and caused all the gold and silver vessels and vestments to be restored throughout all the churches.

At that same time the basilica of the Apostles Philip and James was begun. While it was being begun and constructed, he died [Note: From the ancient monuments of the Vatican basilica collected by Manlius, the following epitaph inscribed for Pope Pelagius is reported:

“Let these tombs perhaps enclose the earthly body,

which will detract nothing from the merits of the holy man.

He lives, blessed in the citadel of heaven’s light,

and here too he lives for all through pious deeds.

Certain to rise at the judgment, while an angelic hand

snatches him away to the right-hand side.

Let the Church of God number the titles of his virtues,

which future ages may be able to bear.

As ruler of the apostolic faith, he reverently unfolded

the doctrines which the Fathers clearly established.

Caring through his speech for those fallen into error’s schism,

so that their tranquil hearts might hold the true faith.

He consecrated many ministers under the divine law,

his unstained hand doing nothing for a price.

Redeeming captives, ready to aid the wretched poor,

he never denied them what he had acquired for himself.

Sharing in the sorrows of others, a generous governor of joy,

he believed another’s lament to be his own.”

The following is added in the same place: “Here rests Pope Pelagius, who sat for four years, ten months, and eighteen days. He was buried on the fourth day before the Nones of March.” These things are from Baronius, year 559.], and was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle on the sixth day before the Nones of March [Note: “On the sixth day before the Nones of March” is absent in the same manuscript.]. He held two ordinations during the month of December: twenty-six priests, nine deacons, and forty-nine bishops in various places. The episcopate then remained vacant for three months [Note: The same manuscript reads “two months.”] and twenty-five days.

[Col. 0393]

**LETTERS OF POPE PELAGIUS I. (C, G, S)\***

**LETTER I (formerly II). TO NARSES** [Note: Two different declensions of this name are used, as will easily be apparent to the reader. Editor.]. He urges him to provide assistance to the legates for correcting bishops who disturb the Church.

[Col. 0393C]

Pelagius to Narses, patrician and commander in Italy [Note: Anselm, book XII, chapter 46; Polycarp, same place.].

We believe that not only you, but many and almost all others, know with what judgment we rejoice over the zeal of your Excellency; and therefore, concerning what we are astonished to see being done there in your presence, we have now decided to complain confidently to your Excellency. Thracius and Maximilian, possessing only the names of bishops, are said both to disturb the ecclesiastical unity there and to appropriate all the Church’s possessions for their own uses—so much so that, against one of them, namely Maximilian, certain men, compelled by necessity to come to us over so long a journey, presented petitions without tiring.

For this reason we have decided to send to those regions Peter, a priest of our see, and Projectus, a notary, so that whatever they discover the aforementioned false bishops to have committed against the canonical statutes, they may either restrain there with fitting punishment or bring the men themselves all the way to us. And so, greeting your Excellency with paternal affection, we ask that you provide every assistance to those whom our see has sent; and do not suppose that it is a sin if such men are restrained. For both divine and human [alternative: worldly] laws have established that those who have been separated from the unity of the Church and most wickedly disturb its peace should also be restrained by secular authorities. Nor is there anything greater by which you can offer sacrifice to God than arranging that those who rage to their own destruction and that of others should be restrained with appropriate force.

**LETTER II (formerly III). TO THE SAME.** He warns him to restrain the schismatics.

[Col. 0394D] Let not the empty talk of men delay you—those who say that the Church commits persecution when it either represses crimes that are being committed or seeks the salvation of souls [Note: Polycarp, book VII, title 5; Anselm, book XII, chapter 45; Ivo, part X, chapter 95.]. The fabricators of such rumors are mistaken. No one persecutes except the one who compels someone to evil. But whoever punishes an evil already committed or prevents it from being committed does not persecute; he loves. For if, as they think, no one is to be restrained from evil or drawn away from evil toward good, then human and divine laws must necessarily be emptied of force—laws which, with justice as their guide, establish punishments for the wicked and rewards for the good.

That schism is evil, and that such men ought to be crushed even through external authorities, both the authority of canonical Scripture and the truth of the rules of the Fathers teach us [Note: 11, question 9, “If any priest”; Act 4 in the letter of the archimandrites to the same council at Antioch, canon 5.]. Whoever, therefore, is separated from the apostolic sees is unquestionably in schism and attempts to raise an altar against the universal Church. But let your Excellency consider what canon the Council of Chalcedon inserted concerning such men, where, among other things, it says: “He who suspends himself from communion, and holds an assembly and establishes an altar, and refuses to obey the bishop who calls him, and refuses to yield or obey him when called a first and a second time, is to be condemned absolutely, and is never to be thought worthy even of prayer, nor is he to receive honor. If he persists in making disturbances and seditions in the Church, he is to be restrained by external authority as a seditious person.”

And blessed Augustine says of such men (*Enchiridion*, chapter 72): “Many things must also be done with those who are unwilling, by a certain kindly severity, and their welfare should be considered more than their will. For in correcting a son, however harshly, paternal love is never lost; yet what he would not wish is done, so that he who appears to be unwilling may be healed through pain.”

Behold, you see how, according to the testimony of so great a Father, the Church does not persecute by restraining such men, but always loves by correcting them. Do you, therefore, also do what we frequently urge, knowing your Christian intention; and take care that such things may no longer be permitted to occur. Moreover—and I do not doubt that this is very easy for you—let those who have presumed to do such things be sent under suitable guard [Col. 0395C] to the most merciful emperor.

Your Highness ought to recall what God did through you at the time when Totila the tyrant possessed Istria and Venetia and the Franks were laying waste to everything: you did not permit a bishop of Milan to be made until you had referred the matter to the most merciful emperor; and you learned again from his letters what ought to have been done. Amid enemies raging everywhere, both the man who was being ordained and the man who was to ordain him were nevertheless brought to Ravenna through the foresight of your Highness.

What shall I say about the bishops of Liguria, Venetia, and Istria? Your Excellency is able by both reason and authority to restrain them, yet you allow them, in contempt of the apostolic sees, to boast of their rusticity. If anything concerning the judgment of the universal synod—which was recently held at Constantinople during the first indiction now past—troubled them, they ought to have sent a delegation to the apostolic see, as has always been done, choosing some of their own who could give and receive an account, rather than, with closed eyes, tear apart the body of Christ our God, that is, the holy Church.

Do not hesitate, therefore, to restrain such men by imperial or judicial authority, because the rules of the Fathers specifically established that if any person belonging to the ecclesiastical order resists the one to whom he is subject, or gathers separately, or raises another altar, or creates a schism, he is to be excommunicated and condemned. But if he should also despise this and persist in creating divisions and schism, he is to be crushed by public authorities.

Behold, my lord, what your mind perhaps fears, lest you appear to persecute: on the authority of the Fathers your mind has taken care briefly to have these instructions sent to you [L: I have taken care], although there are a thousand other examples and constitutions by which it is clearly recognized that those who create divisions in the holy Church ought to be restrained by public authorities not only through exile, but also through confiscation of property and harsh imprisonment.

**LETTER III (formerly IV). TO NARSES THE PATRICIAN.** That he should restrain the schismatics by whom he had been unjustly barred from communion.

[Col. 0396B] Pelagius to Narses the patrician [Note: Anselm, book XII, chapter 47; Polycarp, same place.]

On rereading your Excellency’s letter, we were deeply grieved by the injury inflicted upon you through the presumption of wicked men. But because we know that, by God’s hidden judgment, your soul has been kept from the contamination of schism—even through the iniquity and pride of others—we have given thanks to almighty God, who is accustomed to bring good even out of the evil deeds of men. For it must not be thought that it happened without his providence that senseless and perverse men went so far as to believe their division to be Catholic and to keep you from their own contamination.

Thus, through God’s mercy, this happened without their knowing it, so that, rescued from the faction of the schismatics, you might be preserved for the Catholic Church, which you love. Although, therefore, your advantage has resulted from their crime, do not permit the unpunished presumption of wicked men to rage unchecked. If what they presumed against your dignity is not suppressed by punishment, there can no longer be any doubt that they cannot be punished in lesser matters.

Exercise, therefore, the authority owed in such cases, and let them be restrained by your punishments, lest their spirit grow bolder to commit such things again. Indeed, by God’s will they presumed such things even against you so that, while correcting others, you might, with God’s favor, be able to protect others from the same crime.

The crimes of Eufrasius—which God no longer wished to remain hidden—clearly show what sort of men those are who flee the Church. In murder he considered neither the relationship of the victim, nor brotherly affection, nor the reverence due to the priesthood. By an incestuous adultery he even removed the possibility of punishment itself: for if you punish the adultery, nothing remains in which the incest can be punished; and if you impose punishment for the incest, the crime of adultery remains unavenged.

Behold the company from which those men come who, so far as their pride was concerned, attempted to inflict injury upon you, but who, so far as God’s providence was concerned, preserved you unpolluted for the Church. Remove such men from this province; make use of the opportunity God has offered you to crush the faithless. This can be done more fully if the authors of the crimes are sent [Col. 0397A] to the most merciful emperor, and especially the invader of the Church of Aquileia, who is both [perhaps [Col. 0398A] “is”] in schism and accursed in it, and will be able to retain neither the honor of a bishop nor his standing.

**CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON LETTERS II AND III (formerly III and IV) OF PELAGIUS I TO NARSES.**

[Col. 0397]

[Col. 0397A] Just as the distinguished Antonius Pagi, in his *Criticism of Baronius*, observed that Letter 10 of Pelagius I to Childebert had been assembled from two fragments of two entirely different letters, so I have no doubt that precisely the same thing happened with other letters of this same Pelagius. The two letters to Narses—the one printed as no. 5 and the other as no. 3 in Labbe—present one and the same continuous letter in the fragment published by Holstenius, which is read in volume VI of the Venetian-Labbean Collection and is addressed to the patrician Valerian. This fragment certainly gives first the whole of Letter 5 to Narses, followed in a single continuous sequence by Letter 3. Nor do those two letters have different subjects, and neither could conveniently be separated from the other.

**LETTER IV (formerly V). TO NARSES THE PATRICIAN.** He advises him to send the bishops of Aquileia and Milan under guard to the emperor.

[Col. 0397B]

Pelagius to Narses the patrician [Note: Anselm, book XII, chapter 4; Polycarp, book I, title 15.]

This is what we asked of you, and now ask again: that you send Paulinus, the false bishop of Aquileia, and that bishop of Milan to the most merciful emperor under suitable guard, so that the former—who in no way can be a bishop, because he was made contrary to every canonical custom—may no longer destroy others, and the latter—who presumed to ordain him contrary to ancient custom—may suffer the punishment of the canons.

Nor was it ever permitted to anyone, nor will it ever be permitted, to convene a particular synod. But whenever doubt arises for some people concerning anything from a universal synod, then, in order to receive an explanation of what they do not understand, either those who desire the salvation of their souls should voluntarily come to the apostolic see to receive an explanation, or, if they should perhaps—as it is written concerning such men, “When the wicked comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18)—be so obstinate and stubborn that they do not wish to be taught, it is necessary either that those same apostolic sees draw them by some means toward salvation or, lest they become the destruction of others, to restrain them according to the canons through secular authorities.

**LETTER V (formerly VI). TO THE BISHOPS OF TUSCIA.** He rebukes them for schism.

To the most beloved brothers Gaudentius, Maximilian, Gerontius, Justus, Terentius, Vitalis, and Laurentius throughout Annonarian Tuscia, Pelagius.

Having received the report sent by you and delivered by Jordan, the defender of our Church, we were sufficiently astonished that you should have forgotten apostolic authority to such an extent that you wished your division from the universal Church to be confirmed even by my consent—God forbid—and that those who ought to restrain popular ignorance through priestly teaching should wish to follow the judgment of the populace, to the insult of the apostolic see.

In saying this we do not mean that we grieve over an injury to ourselves, since, by the Lord’s gift, we have resolved, while patiently bearing all things, to preserve everything through the bond of fraternal peace; but, as we have said, I am profoundly astonished at your division from the universal Church, which I shall not be able to tolerate.

Since blessed Augustine, mindful of the Lord’s judgment by which he placed the foundation of the Church in the apostolic sees, says that whoever separates himself from the authority or communion of the bishops of those sees is in schism, and shows that there is no other Church except that which is firmly rooted in the bishops of the apostolic sees, how can you fail to believe that you have been separated from the communion of the whole world if, during the sacred mysteries, you keep silent about the customary remembrance of my name—in whom, although unworthy, you see the stability of the apostolic see existing at the present time through the succession of the episcopate?

But lest any suspicion concerning our faith perhaps remain among you or among the flocks entrusted to you, I desire your Love to know with complete certainty that, by the Lord’s gift, I preserve the faith established by the sacred teaching of the apostles, confirmed by the authority of the Council of Nicaea, and explained by the judgments of the holy councils of Constantinople, the First Council of Ephesus, and Chalcedon. I have neither diminished nor increased anything from the definitions of those councils, nor changed anything in them in any respect; rather, with God’s favor, I preserve inviolably everything they wrote concerning the purity of the faith.

Moreover, I subject to the judgment of anathema anyone who should at any time consent either in any way to weaken or—God forbid—to call into doubt any part of the faith of the four councils named above, or of the *Tome* of the most blessed Leo, bishop of the apostolic see, which was confirmed at the Council of Chalcedon.

Strengthened, therefore, by this profession of our faith, let your Love hasten—as befits priests—to instruct the ignorance of men in a spirit of gentleness, and by every means to recall them from their wrongful intention and restore them to the unity of the Church. If anyone should still believe that some scruple remains for him even after this, let him cease from his insane tumult and hasten rather to come to us, so that, having received a reasonable explanation of what he doubts, he may, with God’s favor, rejoice in the truth he has learned and be restored to the universal Church.

For, in accordance with the apostolic statement, we are ready to give an answer to everyone who asks us for a reason concerning the faith that is in us (1 Pet. 3), because, with divine grace protecting us, we know that we have deviated in nothing from the holy Fathers. May the Lord keep you safe, most beloved brothers. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the fifteenth year after the consulship of Basil, a man of most illustrious rank.

**LETTER VI (formerly VII). TO THE WHOLE PEOPLE OF GOD.** Concerning the Catholic faith.

Pelagius, bishop, to the entire people of God.

The blessed Apostle Paul, the vessel of election, speaking about the Jews who did not yet believe in Christ, declared that they possessed zeal for God; but, so that they should not be thought guiltless on this account, he appropriately added: “But not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10). Thus he showed that they necessarily needed correction through the teaching entrusted to him by God.

Your Love does not doubt that this testimony also applies to our own time. For although we find that some possess zeal for God, they are nevertheless plainly without knowledge in this respect: they have shaken themselves and continue to shake themselves through certain suspicions without knowledge of the truth, and with wicked animosity tear themselves away from the bosom of the one mother, the Church.

We could indeed, with the divine mercy cooperating with us, confidently explain the reasoning of the entire matter in order to quiet the rumors of men, and demonstrate through the clearest proofs that nothing at all is to be attempted (*tentandum*; variant: “has been attempted,” *tentatum*) against the faith of the Fathers or against the stability of the four councils; rather, that the purpose was to ensure that the stability of those councils should stand immovable and solid against all enemies.

But because we have not judged it necessary to present this to those who must be nourished with milk rather than solid food (1 Cor. 6)—so that, as the aforementioned Teacher of the Gentiles says, wisdom may be spoken among the perfect—we have perceived that what is sufficient in abundance even for little ones should meanwhile be brought to the knowledge of all.

This is the matter: that I should define my faith in the profession appended below, in which, by God’s favor, it will clearly appear that I adhere to the teaching of the apostles and to the footsteps of the Fathers, so that through you, who possess zeal for God together with knowledge, it may become known to the others, whom, through the working of the grace of our Lord, we trust will be liberated—not without your reward—from the irrational evil of their division.

Concerning the four holy councils—that is, the Council of Nicaea of 318 bishops, the Council of Constantinople of 150, the First Council of Ephesus of 200, and the Council of Chalcedon of 630—I profess with all my heart and strength that, with divine mercy protecting me, I have held and shall continue to hold until the end of my life the following conviction: I shall preserve them with complete devotion in the defense of the holy faith and in the condemnations of heresies and heretics, since they have been confirmed by the Holy Spirit.

Because their stability is the stability of the universal Church, I profess that I shall protect and defend them just as my predecessors unquestionably defended them. Among those predecessors, I especially desire to follow and imitate Leo, whom we know to have been the author of the Council of Chalcedon. In agreement with his name, he clearly showed himself to be a member of him who arose as the lion from the tribe of Judah, through the most vigorous vigilance of faith.

I therefore trust that I shall always show the councils named above a similar reverence, and I shall regard as orthodox all those who have been absolved by those same four councils. Never in my life, with God protecting us in all things, shall I diminish anything from the authority of their holy and true proclamation.

I also follow and venerate the canons received by the apostolic see, and, with God’s help, defend them; nor do I promise ever to conceal or depart from this profession. I also profess that, with the help of Christ our Lord, I shall preserve inviolably the letters sent at various times, for the defense of the Catholic faith and for the stability of the four councils named above and against heretics, both to emperors and to bishops or any others throughout the East, Illyricum, Dardania, and the other provinces, by the blessed popes of revered memory Celestine, Sixtus, and above all the blessed Leo, as well as by their successors Hilary, Simplicius, Felix, Gelasius, Anastasius, Symmachus, Hormisdas, John, another Felix, Boniface, another John, and Agapetus.

I profess that I regard as condemned all whom they condemned, and that I venerate among the orthodox those whom they received, especially the venerable bishops Theodoret and Ibas.

This, then, is my faith and my hope, which by God’s merciful gift exists in me. For this faith, blessed Peter says that we ought above all to be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks us for a reason (1 Pet. 3). With this profession I desire to live; with it I desire to stand before the tribunal of Christ. Through it I believe that I shall be absolved from my sins [Col. 0400D] and, by divine mercy, carried to the right hand of glory.

But whoever thinks, believes, or proclaims anything else, the holy and universal Church of God anathematizes him. May God keep you safe, most beloved children. Amen.

# JACQUES SIRMOND, S.J.: INTRODUCTORY NOTICE ON THE ORDER OF THE FOLLOWING LETTERS

[Col. 0399]

[Col. 0399D] The order in which we have arranged them is the very order presented by the ancient manuscripts—the Pithoean, the Lirinensis, and especially the Arlesian manuscript from which they were first copied and sent to Cardinal Baronius and brought to light. But what led that eminent man to alter the order was the corrupted subscription of the letter in the exemplar he had received: where “in the fifteenth year” had been written instead of “in the sixteenth year of Basil.” We have removed this error with the help of those same ancient books.

## LETTER VII (formerly VIII). TO SAPAUDUS, BISHOP OF ARLES

A greeting sent before receiving a letter from Sapaudus.

[Col. 0401A]

To his dearest brother Sapaudus, Pelagius.

We believe that what the grace of almighty God has accomplished among us has been conveyed to your Charity. For this reason it had been agreed that you should be sent to us, so that by a common visitation we might enjoy great joy in one another. Nevertheless, mindful of brotherly charity and finding an opportunity through the bearers of this letter, we offer the service of a fraternal greeting, desiring that, while living together in mutual charity in the fear of the Lord, we may frequently refresh one another through reciprocal conversation.

May God keep you safe, dearest brother. Given on the fourth day before the Nones of July, in the fifteenth year after the consulship of Basil, the illustrious man (A.D. 556).

## LETTER VIII (formerly IX). TO THE SAME

He modestly rejects the praises with which Sapaudus had adorned him in his letter.

[Col. 0401B]

To his dearest brother Sapaudus, Pelagius.

We received with gratitude the agreeable conversation of your Fraternity, delivered by Felix, an honorable man. After reading it, we gave inadequate thanks to our common Lord and God, because through its testimony we learned of the well-being of your affection, which is desirable to us. But although what your eloquence said in our praise plainly shows that you did what was fitting for you, we, recognizing nothing of our own in all that was said, are instead overcome with embarrassment, calling to mind the saying of a most learned man [Col. 0401C]: “As true praise adorns, so false praise chastises.” For the words of your charity greatly exceed the measure of our life and conduct.

Nevertheless, we desire that through the prayers of all the saints and your own prayers God may make us become such as, in your good will, you have portrayed us to be. And therefore, greeting you with the affection owed by charity, we inform you that, when recently an opportunity arose through certain people from your province who were coming to Rome, we were so inflamed with love for you that we could not bear to let such an occasion pass in silence.

Accordingly, we wrote to our most glorious common son, King Childebert, and also sent your Charity a letter, dictated as briefly as the shortness of time allowed. Moreover, as you wrote, the bearer briefly conveyed to us certain matters from your own mouth through your letter—matters that moved us considerably. We were astonished, of course, at how so unprecedented a thing had been undertaken, and we must take care that, if anyone comes, it may not appear that something has been slipped past us as though we were ignorant.

Your Fraternity will do better, however, if, after learning that those whom you suspect are coming to us, you also send a thoroughly instructed representative who can oppose them. For since your letter contains nothing concerning the matter, if the man who has now, at your request, privately reported it to us cannot then be found here, we will appear to have taken upon ourselves the office of accuser.

But if your Charity sends a representative, it will be our responsibility—both because of the affection we bear you and because of the novelty of what has occurred—to provide, while preserving equity, suitable support to the person whom your affection sends. May God keep you safe, dearest brother. Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the fifteenth year after the consulship of Basil, the illustrious man.

## LETTER IX (formerly X). TO CHILDEBERT, KING

He pronounces an anathema against those who hold a different opinion concerning the faith from that contained in the letters of Leo and in the Council of Chalcedon. He sends relics of the saints through Hominembonus the subdeacon.

To his lord son, the most glorious and pre-eminent King Childebert, Pelagius, bishop.

Rufinus, a magnificent man and envoy of Your Excellence, told us that certain people in the provinces of Gaul have also sown seeds of scandal, saying that something contrary to the Catholic faith had been admitted—may the Lord prevent it. And although, since the death of the divine empress Theodora, the Church of God in the eastern regions, by God’s mercy, has feared no questions concerning the faith, certain articles have nevertheless been debated outside the faith, concerning which it would take too long to give an account in an epistolary discussion.

Accordingly, following the admonition of the aforesaid magnificent Rufinus, we have judged that this brief statement should be made to heal the mind of Your Excellence, or of all our brothers and fellow bishops residing in the regions of Gaul: We declare that we anathematize and judge excluded from the rewards of eternal life anyone who has ever erred or departed, or shall ever err or depart, in a single syllable, a single word, or a single idea, from that faith which Pope Leo of blessed memory proclaimed in his letters and which the Council of Chalcedon, following that same bishop, accepted in its published definition.

Since matters stand thus, let neither Your Highness nor our brother bishops pay attention to the tales of those people who delight in scandals. For these things happened in this way: when your most merciful father, the emperor, overthrew all the heresies that, until the time of his reign, had their own bishops and churches in Constantinople, with great revenues and a variety of vessels, he transferred their basilicas, revenues, and all their other possessions to the Catholics.

Those, therefore, who remained in those errors gathered themselves into one body and are working vigorously to divide and disturb the Catholic Church. Indeed, while we were in Constantinople, they sent letters even here to Italy in our name, saying that we had declared the Catholic faith to have been corrupted. Now they even bring letters against us, with the names suppressed, so that it may not be known who sent them.

This is how the Christians in Constantinople act, although it is clear that they are not Christians. Above all, however, the adherents of the Nestorian heresy, because Nestorius asserted that the two natures in Christ were separated and divided, deceitfully attempt to say that their teaching is not far from the understanding of the Council of Chalcedon and Pope Leo. Yet Nestorius was condemned by the very doctrine of blessed Pope Leo because he asserted that the two natures were divided.

We have taken care to make this briefly known to Your Excellence, so that the ardor of your faith and your love of unity may not permit the tales or useless letters of any perverse person to receive attention. For here too they have troubled certain simple bishops who do not know even the first elements of the faith, so that they neither understand the matter itself nor discern how great a good it is not to depart from the Catholic faith, but only to refute whatever other charges the holy Church suffers from heretics.

Who could tolerate the belief that the blasphemies of Nestorius or his followers agree with the Catholic faith, since he asserted that the two natures in Christ were separated—that is, divided?

The circumstance briefly mentioned above caused us to suffer such long tribulations in Constantinople: while the empress was alive, we regarded as suspect whatever was stirred up in ecclesiastical affairs. For your most merciful father, the emperor, never in any way permits either the doctrine of blessed Pope Leo or the faith of the Council of Chalcedon to be violated.

As for the relics of the blessed apostles and of the holy martyrs, we have already sent some through the servants of God from the monastery of Lérins. We now also acknowledge that we have sent those which your envoys requested, assigning Hominembonus, a subdeacon from the clergy of our Church, to convey them, with the Lord’s command, as far as our brother and fellow bishop Sapaudus.

Given on the third day before the Ides of December, in the fifteenth year after the consulship of Basil, the illustrious man, through Rufinus the envoy (A.D. 556).

### Subscription

[Col. 0403C] Pelagius, by the mercy of God bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, have subscribed the copy of our letter.

## OBSERVATION OF P. ANTONIO PAGI ON THE YEAR OF CHRIST 556, NOS. 7–8

The letter of Pelagius to King Childebert, written on the third day before the Ides of December in the year 556, was pieced together from two other letters, one of which had been given by Vigilius to Childebert and the other to Justinian. This joining of the two letters—one to Childebert and the other to Justinian—which has hitherto been noticed by no one, nevertheless does not seem open to doubt.

For the conclusion and beginning of the letter said to have been written to King Childebert concern Gaul and the Frankish king, who, as is clear from another letter of Pelagius, had sent Rufinus to Rome to Pope Pelagius. Rufinus asked that the pontiff either inform Childebert that he agreed in every respect with the writings of blessed Leo, or send him a confession of his faith in his own words.

This is established by another letter of Pelagius to King Childebert, in which the pontiff says: “Rufinus, a magnificent man, envoy of Your Excellence, confidently and as was fitting, asked us either to inform you that we preserve in every respect the Tome of Pope Leo of blessed memory, or to send you a confession of our faith in our own words.”

The reason for this request was that certain people were sowing seeds of scandal in the provinces of Gaul, as though something contrary to the Catholic faith had been done in the Fifth General Council.

Therefore, in the letter sent to Childebert on the third day before the Ides of December of that year, Pelagius fulfilled the request and pronounced an anathema against those who held a different opinion concerning the faith from that contained in the letters of Saint Leo and in the Council of Chalcedon.

The compiler of the letter under discussion assigns its first part to the letter to Childebert, from the beginning up to the words: “For these things happened in this way,” [Col. 0404A] and likewise assigns the latter part from the words: “As for the relics of the blessed apostles and of the holy martyrs, we have already sent some through the servants of God from the monastery of Lérins,” and so forth to the end.

Everything else contained in the letter to Childebert the compiler took from certain letters given by Pope Vigilius to the Emperor Justinian. For, by way of example, these words could have been written only to the emperor of Constantinople: “For these things happened in this way: when your most merciful father, the emperor, overthrew all the heresies that, until the time of his reign, had their own bishops and churches in Constantinople, with great revenues and a variety of vessels, and, after removing their basilicas and revenues and all their other possessions, transferred them to the Catholics.”

It is certain that Justin the Elder transferred the basilicas of the heretics to the orthodox, and that Justinian was his adopted son. By contrast, Childebert’s father, Clovis the Great, was never called emperor, especially by the Roman pontiffs, nor could any Frankish king have overthrown the churches of heretics in Constantinople.

Moreover, the author of that letter shows below that the emperor whom he addresses can be no one other than Justinian: “The circumstance briefly mentioned above caused us to suffer long tribulations in Constantinople: while the empress—namely Theodora, whom he had already named in the same letter—was alive, we regarded as suspect whatever was stirred up in ecclesiastical affairs. For your most merciful father, the emperor, never in any way permits either the doctrine of blessed Pope Leo or the faith of the Council of Chalcedon to be violated.”

Where the text reads *patitur* (“permits”), one should read *passus est* (“suffered” or “allowed”).

I omit the other matters mentioned in that letter which could have been spoken by no Roman pontiff other than Vigilius after his return from Constantinople to Sicily. Finally, there is no connection among the three sections into which that letter is divided, as is evident to the reader.

## LETTER X (formerly XI). TO SAPAUDUS, BISHOP OF ARLES

He recommends to him the return of Hominembonus the subdeacon and asks him to suggest to his father Placidius that garments be purchased and sent to Rome for distribution among the poor.

[Col. 0404C]

To his dearest brother Sapaudus, Pelagius.

Because the envoys of our son, the most glorious King Childebert, requested relics of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of other holy martyrs, we found it necessary to send Hominembonus, a subdeacon from our clergy, to convey them reverently as far as your Fraternity.

And therefore, greeting you, we urge you, when an opportunity has been found, whether by ship or overland, to send him back to us, with the Lord’s help, by means of persons concerning whom there can be no suspicion of danger.

As for the things which the aforesaid envoys are known to have requested from us in honor of your charity, we are prepared, with God’s help, to grant them. But unless we receive your letter through you yourself, just as our predecessors granted the requests of your predecessors, we have judged it superfluous to send anything of our own accord.

As soon as, with the Lord’s help, you send one of your clergy to us with a letter, we promise, if the Lord wills and if we live, to do what is required.

Furthermore, we urge you to tell your most magnificent son, the patrician Placidius, your father, to send us what has been collected from the rents of the possessions of our Church, either through his own agent or through the bearer of this letter. For the estates of Italy have been so devastated that no one is capable of restoring them.

And, if possible, have him use those same solidi to purchase padded woolen cloaks for distribution to the poor, as well as white tunics, hoods, or sleeved garments, or any other kinds of clothing that are made in the province and, as we have said, ought to be distributed among the poor. Send them to us when an opportunity for a ship is found, so that we may give the greatest thanks to your Fraternity, since the solicitude of your charity will thereby have relieved our own concern in some measure.

We also urge you to arrange for Anastasius, the brother of Paul, the Church’s defender, to come to us.

May God keep you safe, dearest brother. Given on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the fifteenth year after the consulship of Basil, the illustrious man.

## LETTER XI (formerly XII). TO SAPAUDUS OF ARLES

He delegates his authority to him in Gaul and grants him the use of the pallium.

[Col. 0405B]

To his dearest brother Sapaudus, Pelagius.

Desiring, by the working of God’s mercy, to cling to the footsteps of our predecessors and, with divine assistance, to imitate their deeds in every respect, we entrust to your Charity authority throughout all Gaul on behalf of the holy apostolic see over which, by God’s grace, we preside.

For this is taught by the memory of antiquity; the Roman archives also testify that this was granted by the holy Fathers and our predecessors to your predecessors: that the eternal solidity of that immovable rock upon which our Lord and Savior founded his own Church from sunrise to sunset should, through the authority of its successors, firmly retain the summit of its primacy, both directly and through its vicars.

We, however, as the blessed Apostle says, do not boast beyond measure, but according to the measure of the rule which God has measured out to us, extending as far as you. For we do not overreach ourselves as though we had not reached you.

Thus, with shared responsibility, our predecessors governed the holy universal Church of God by God’s grace. Hence we too entrust such responsibilities to your Fraternity, so that, appointed vicar of our see, you may hold in the regions of Gaul, in our likeness, the place of the chief priest. Whatever must be undertaken for the government or administration of ecclesiastical affairs, you are to dispense with consideration of divine judgment, observing the rules of the Fathers and the decrees of the apostolic see.

Show yourself in the holy conduct with which you guard the canons to be the sort of vicar worthy of so great a position, mindful of the statement of blessed Paul the Apostle, by which the teacher carefully instructs his disciple Timothy, saying: “I testify before God and Christ Jesus and his chosen angels, that you observe these things without prejudice, doing nothing by turning aside to either side” (I Tim. 5:21).

Know, dearest brother, that by us the authority of a pontiff and the gentleness of a shepherd have been granted to you, through the generosity of grace, in the place of vicar, just as to your predecessors. For although with God there is no partiality, it is nevertheless clear that your Charity is distinguished even by bodily descent.

Therefore, the more the Lord has bestowed manifold blessings upon you, the more conspicuous should be the integrity of your conduct in priestly actions. For it is written: “From the one to whom they have entrusted much, they will demand more” (Luke 12:48).

We also gladly and affectionately grant you the use of the pallium, sending the pallium as well, so that, established at the summit of so great a position, you may also be adorned with a distinguished garment. Let all men of ecclesiastical rank know that no one has permission, without a formal authorization from your Charity, to seek more distant regions from any part of Gaul, lest those who presume to do what is forbidden appear to deprive themselves of their own office.

We have therefore taken care that these matters be written through Flavianus the deacon and Nestorius the subdeacon of your Church, through whom we received your letters. In their conduct also we recognized the praiseworthy discipline of your Charity.

May God keep you safe, dearest brother. Given on the third day before the Nones of February, in the sixteenth year after the consulship of Basil, the illustrious man.

## LETTER XII (formerly XIII). TO CHILDEBERT, KING

He announces that he has granted Sapaudus his authority and the use of the pallium, and commends him to the king.

To his lord son, deservedly the most glorious and pre-eminent King Childebert, Pelagius.

We reverently received Your Excellence’s letters, sent after those which your envoys had delivered, also through the men whom our brother and fellow bishop Sapaudus sent to us. Learning from them signs of your well-being, which we always desire, we gave thanks to the divine mercy, beseeching it to preserve you safe by its abundant compassion.

We have sent our letter to the aforesaid fellow priest of ours, Sapaudus, in accordance with your request, granting him the use of the pallium as well. For in the ecclesiastical archive we have found examples showing that these privileges were bestowed upon the bishops of Arles by our predecessors of holy memory.
