Therefore, greeting you with the respect owed to royal insignia, we ask that Your Excellence protect and support him and his Church with such favor that the man whom, through our authority, you have asked God’s mercy to exalt may not be held in contempt in any respect by any Gallican priest or by any person of ecclesiastical rank—which would be improper—and that the authority of the holy apostolic see and your own character, by which you come forward as his supporter, may not in any way be diminished.

May our God preserve Your Excellence completely safe, lord son, most glorious and pre-eminent.

## LETTER XIII (formerly XIV). TO CHILDEBERT, KING

Concerning Sapaudus of Arles, who had been ordered to submit to the judgment of another bishop contrary to the privilege of his see.

To his lord son, the most glorious and pre-eminent King Childebert, Pelagius.

Although divine mercy has bestowed many gifts upon Your Highness, the sincere love which you show toward his Church has nevertheless made you more illustrious than many rulers (Nicolas II, Letter 8, to Michael, emperor of the Greeks). For it is certain that, among the other concerns of your kingdom, you show particular solicitude for the tranquility of the holy Church.

Since this is so, we are astonished that, as the report of the present bearers has disclosed to us, you allowed yourselves to be deceived concerning our brother and fellow bishop Sapaudus, bishop of the city of Arles—whose Church is honored in the Gallican regions by the privilege of primacy and by the authority of the apostolic see—and, at the petition of a bishop ordained by him, ordered him to appear for judgment before the bishop of a neighboring city, something permitted by no ecclesiastical law or principle.

When he complains of the prejudice done to his position, the man who usurped this authority must necessarily be condemned for his unlawful presumption (Hincmarus, Letter 6, ch. 15).

Therefore, relying confidently upon your Christianity, we ask with paternal concern that, if anything of this kind has occurred, it be quickly ended by a suitable satisfaction, and that you not allow any precedent of this sort to remain for the disturbance of the Churches entrusted to you by God.

In the future also, it is fitting that you exercise careful vigilance in such matters, lest you grant anything contrary to ecclesiastical rules to those who make requests. For—something well known to your religious mind—our royal devotion can serve our God rightly in no other way than by preserving the integrity of the ecclesiastical orders through his providence.

May our God preserve Your Excellence safe, lord son, most glorious and pre-eminent.

## LETTER XIV (formerly XV). TO SAPAUDUS OF ARLES

Concerning the letter he had previously written to the king about the Catholic faith. He commends Romans who had taken refuge there out of fear of the enemy, and again asks that clothing be sent to the city.

[Col. 0407C]

To his dearest brother Sapaudus, Pelagius.

Our affection for your Fraternity is so great that we do not allow any opportunity to pass in silence. Accordingly, when Peter, a merchant of the city, was coming there, we made sure to send written communication to your Fraternity, desiring that through mutually provided opportunities we might also learn of one another’s well-being.

Therefore, greeting you with fraternal charity, we inform you that, by the Lord’s favor, everything here is proceeding successfully. We urge you, if the letter which we sent through the deacon and subdeacon of your Fraternity to our most excellent son, King Childebert— in which, concerning the institutions of our most blessed Fathers, we set forth in our own words the Catholic faith by God’s grace—has pleased that most glorious king, your Charity, and our other brother bishops, to let us learn more quickly through a reply from your Charity.

Furthermore, we especially commend to your affection the Romans who have taken refuge there out of fear of enemy attack, so that they may find the consolation of your Fraternity and the restraint which their exile requires. We also wish them to be commended on our behalf to our son, the most magnificent patrician Placidius, your father, so that in their proper conduct they may recognize how much our recommendation to your Charity has benefited them.

We also bring this to the remembrance of your Fraternity: as we wrote some time ago, arrange for garments to be purchased from what our lord son Placidius was going to send us from the rents of the ecclesiastical estates—namely, hoods, tunics, and cloaks—to be distributed among the poor, and send them, with God’s favor, to the Roman port, so that you may relieve our anxiety in some measure.

For such poverty and nakedness prevail in this city that, without grief and anguish of heart, we cannot look upon people whom we knew to have been born in an honorable station and to be capable.

May God keep you safe, dearest brother. Given on the Ides of April, in the sixteenth year after the consulship of Basil, the illustrious man.

## LETTER XV (formerly XVI). TO CHILDEBERT, KING

He sends his confession of faith and warns him not to allow divisions to be stirred up in Gaul by heretics.

To his lord son, the most glorious and pre-eminent King Childebert, Pelagius, bishop.

The Savior and Lord of the human race, teaching his disciples, says: “It is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that even one of these little ones should perish” (Matthew 18:14). He also declares that no one should be scandalized because of them without incurring a punishment of great magnitude.

Since, then, this form of command applies even to the little ones, with what zeal and effort must we strive to offer kings the service of our confession, in order to remove the scandal of suspicion, when holy Scripture also commands us to be subject to them?

For Rufinus, a magnificent man and envoy of Your Excellence, came and confidently, as was fitting, asked us either to inform you that we preserve in every respect the Tome of Pope Leo of blessed memory, or to send you a confession of our faith in our own words.

We immediately fulfilled the first part of his request, since it was easier, and, with God’s favor, we sealed with our own hand our profession to you that we preserve in every respect the Tome of the aforesaid bishop, written for the defense of the Catholic faith.

But, so that no occasion for suspicion might remain thereafter—God forbid—we also resolved to undertake the other part mentioned by the illustrious Rufinus, setting forth in our own words the confession of the faith which we hold.

I have also judged it necessary to make known in this present communication to Your Excellence that, with God’s help, we hold and defend the definitions concerning the same Catholic faith established in the four holy councils, as well as those of the aforesaid pontiff, which the universal Church has always held and continues to hold.

## THE FAITH OF POPE PELAGIUS

[Col. 0407D] I therefore believe in one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: namely, the almighty, [Col. 0408D] eternal, unbegotten Father; and the Son, begotten from the substance or nature of that same Father before absolutely any beginning, whether of time or of anything else, almighty from the Almighty, equal, co-eternal, and consubstantial with his begetter.

I also believe in the Holy Spirit, almighty, equal to both—the Father and the Son—co-eternal and consubstantial with them. Proceeding timelessly from the Father, he is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son.

These are three persons, or three subsistences, of one essence or nature, one power, one operation, one blessedness, and one authority: so that there is a threefold unity and a single Trinity, in accordance with the truth of the Lord’s words: “Go; teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

He says “in the name,” not “in the names,” thereby showing both one God through the undivided name of the divine essence and the distinction of the persons through the properties proper to them. For since the one name of divinity belongs to three, the equality of the persons is shown; and again, the equality of the persons permits us to understand nothing foreign and nothing added in them.

Thus each of them is truly and perfectly God: from the fullness of divinity, nothing less is understood in each individual and nothing more in the three.

From this holy, blessed, and consubstantial Trinity I believe and confess that one person—that is, the Son of God—descended from heaven in the last times for the salvation of the human race, without abandoning either his native dwelling or the governance of the world.

When the Holy Spirit came upon the blessed Virgin Mary and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, the same Word and Son of God mercifully entered the womb of that holy Virgin Mary and united to himself flesh from her, animated by a rational and intellectual soul.

The flesh was not created first and the Son of God came afterward. Rather, as it is written, “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Proverbs 9:1): at once flesh existed in the Virgin’s womb, at once it became the flesh of the Word of God. From then onward, without any change or transformation of the nature of the Word and the flesh, the Word and Son of God became one man in both natures, divine and human: Jesus Christ, true God and the same true man.

He came forth—that is, was born—while the integrity of his mother’s virginity remained intact, for she gave birth while remaining a virgin just as she conceived while a virgin.

For this reason we most truly confess that the same blessed virgin Mary is the Mother of God: she gave birth to the incarnate Word of God.

There is therefore one and the same Jesus Christ, the true Son of God and the same true son of man, perfect in divinity and the same perfect in humanity: wholly in what is his own and the same wholly in what is ours.

By his second birth he took from his human mother what he was not, without ceasing to be what he was by his first birth, through which he was born from the Father.

For this reason we believe him to exist from two natures and in two natures, which remain undivided and unconfused.

Undivided, because even after assuming our nature the one Christ, the Son of God, remained and remains one. Unconfused, because we believe that the natures were united into one person and one subsistence in such a way that, while the property of each was preserved, neither was changed into the other.

And therefore, as we have often said, we confess that the one and same Christ is the true Son of God and the same true son of man: consubstantial with the Father according to his divinity, and the same consubstantial with us according to his humanity, like us in every respect except sin; passible in the flesh and the same impassible in his divinity.

We confess that under Pontius Pilate he suffered voluntarily for our salvation in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh, died in the flesh, rose on the third day in the same glorified and incorruptible flesh, and after the resurrection lived with his disciples, clearly demonstrating to them in many ways the reality of his body.

On the fortieth day, while those same disciples watched, he ascended into heaven and also sits at the right hand of the Father.

I believe and confess that, according to the testimony of the angels, just as he ascended into heaven, so he will come to judge the living and the dead.

I confess that all human beings born and dead from Adam to the completion of the age, together with Adam himself and his wife—who were not born from other parents, but one was created from the earth and the other from the man’s rib—will then rise and stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive the things proper to the body according to what he has done, whether good or evil.

The just, through the most abundant grace of God, as vessels of mercy prepared for glory, he will grant the rewards of eternal life; they will live forever in the company of the angels, without any further fear of falling.

But the wicked, by the choice of their own will vessels of wrath fit for destruction, who either did not acknowledge the way of the Lord or, having acknowledged it, abandoned it after being captured by various transgressions, he will, by the most just judgment, consign to the punishments of eternal and unquenchable fire, so that they may burn without end.

This, therefore, is my faith and my hope, which exists in me as a gift of God’s mercy. The blessed Apostle Peter commands us to be especially prepared on its account to give an answer to everyone who asks us for a reason (II Peter 3).

It is now fitting that Your Excellence, because of the fervor of that same faith which we rejoice that you hold in your heart, exercise particular care throughout all the regions of your Gaul, so that those who sow scandals there, as they were attempting to do in these regions, may not run about driven on by the insolence of their shamelessness and stir other brothers and fellow bishops, or the peoples entrusted to them, into dissension.

For although they do not hold the right faith, they pretend, under the pressure of the pain of their oppression, to defend the right faith, so that they may make themselves agreeable to Catholics in nourishing scandals—especially among those who do not know their frauds and deceits.

But God, who in his mercy has prepared your glory at this time against the enemies of ecclesiastical peace, grants that you may be so vigilant and circumspect that they cannot sow the evil seeds of their weeds among the crops of the holy Church in those regions.

May our God preserve Your Excellence safe, lord son, most glorious and pre-eminent.

## LETTERS OF THE SAME POPE PELAGIUS I, OR RATHER FRAGMENTS FIRST RECOVERED FROM OBSCURITY THROUGH THE LABORS OF LUCA HOLSTENIUS

[Col. 0411]

Pelagius to John, the patrician and *caburtarius*, among other matters.

[Col. 0411A]

A shameful robbery, so to speak, is involved here: the bishop is not consecrated but desecrated. For if we examine the very name “consecration” with rational and vigorous understanding, he who refuses to be consecrated together with the universal Church can in no way be called or be consecrated. For to consecrate means to make sacred together. But one divided from the Church’s innermost members and separated from the apostolic sees rather desecrates and does not consecrate. Rightly, therefore, he may be called only desecrated, not consecrated, whom the Church does not recognize as being made sacred together with its united members.

Let us nevertheless see whether they have preserved even the custom of those regions in their ordination. Certainly, the ancient practice was that, because the distance or difficulty of the journey made it burdensome for them to be ordained by the apostolic see, the bishops of Milan and Aquileia were themselves to ordain one another—but in such a way that, in the city where the bishop was to be ordained, the bishop of the other city had to be present. Thus the choice of the person to be ordained could more properly and easily be recognized by the ordaining bishop who was present, with the consent of the universal Church over which he was to be placed; and the man who was to be advanced to the episcopate, though he was not to be subject to his own ordaining bishop, would be ordained in his own Church.

Do not continually pollute a Catholic mind with any association with schismatics. It is established that there is one body of Christ and one Church. An altar divided from unity cannot gather the truth into Christ’s body. Even those faults sometimes found in members placed within the body must be tolerated when, out of regard for unity, we cannot at times cut them away.

For our Savior taught that the evangelical farmer can cleanse a branch bearing little fruit, provided it remains in the vine (John 15:2); but we have learned from the truth of the same heavenly teacher that a branch cut off from the vine is fit for nothing except to be burned in the fire (ibid.). Therefore, do not consent to those who are fit for the fire—not to consecration but to desecration. Nor should you think that they can either be or be called the Church.

For since, as we have said, the Church is one, and in the Song of Songs it is said to it, “My dove is one” (Song 6), it is clear that there is no other Church except that founded upon the apostolic root; and there can be no doubt that from this root the faith has been propagated throughout the whole world.

Although this should be entirely well known to you, let us nevertheless confirm it by the testimony of blessed Augustine. Hear what that most illustrious teacher says about the Church in one of his works. He says:

“But if it cannot in any way rightly be called a Church in which there is schism, it remains that, since there cannot be no Church at all, the Church is that which has been established in the apostolic see through the succession and lineage of bishops. No human malice—even if it cannot be excluded when exposed—can in any way extinguish it; rather, according to the circumstances of the time, it is judged necessary to tolerate it.”

The same Pelagius to the illustrious Viator and Pancratius, among other matters.

[Column 0412A]

You must abstain from the sacrifices—or rather, the sacrileges—of schismatics. For “schism,” which is a Greek word, means a tearing apart. But there can be no tearing apart within unity. Therefore those who associate with schismatics do not share in unity. They have made divisions for themselves and, separating themselves from what is one—to use the words of the apostle Jude—they “do not have the Spirit” (Jude 9).

From all this it follows that, because they are not one within unity, because they have wished to be on the side of division, and because they do not possess the Spirit of Christ’s body, they cannot possess the sacrifice. Our question now is not whether the wicked should be tolerated, but whether we ought to associate with schismatics.

If they themselves, although confident in their own understanding, had sought the truth while remaining within their mother’s womb, they would not have been driven away by us until the truth of the matter had become clear to them under the guidance of reason. But because they have divided themselves from the universal Church, as blessed Augustine says, every Catholic safely detests that party which he knows does not share communion with the universal Church strengthened by the apostolic sees.

Their crime is not lessened—indeed, it is increased—by your statement that they long resisted admitting into their communion those who shared communion with the apostolic sees. For in this matter, although those who wished to communicate with such people are also blameworthy, much more deserving of condemnation are those who rejected communion with the apostolic sees not only in the case of priests but even in the case of laypeople.

Nor does it benefit them that, as you report in the same letter, they suspended themselves from communion with us either through ignorance of reason or through the simplicity of their understanding. That is precisely why they are schismatics: they were divided not by a considered judgment arising from differing opinions, but by a thoroughly evil opinion. They feared certain matters brought before them which nevertheless remained unknown to them, and they rashly believed against the apostolic see.

Blessed Augustine expressly declares that this is schism when he says of such people:

“He who rashly believes against the authority of those Churches which have deserved to receive the apostolic sees and letters will not be able to drive away from himself the monstrous crime of schism.”

In short, either you believe that they are the Church, and, since there cannot be two Churches, you will—God forbid—judge us to be schismatics; or, if it is established that the true Church is in the apostolic sees, recognize that they are divided from unity and that the question of communion has been settled, since true communion cannot exist except in unity.

Therefore, do not act as though there were no difference between schismatics and the Church, wishing indiscriminately to associate with the sacrifices of both. What a schismatic performs is not Christ’s body, if we are guided by the truth. No one can fabricate the claim that Christ is divided without rejecting the Apostle’s teaching.

As has often been said, it is established that there is one Church, which is Christ’s body, and it cannot be divided into two or more parts (1 Cor. 1:13). For as soon as anyone withdraws from it, he ceases to be the Church. There is one temple in Jerusalem; whoever divides himself must necessarily sacrifice to idols.

The same Pelagius to the patrician Valerian, among other matters.

This is what we requested of you and now request again: send Paulinus, the pseudo-bishop of Aquileia, and that bishop of Milan to the most merciful emperor under suitable custody. The former, who absolutely cannot be a bishop because he was made one contrary to every canonical custom, must not continue to destroy others; and the latter, who presumed to ordain him contrary to ancient custom, must suffer the punishment prescribed by the canons.

Nor was it ever lawful, nor will it ever be lawful, for a particular synod to be convened to judge a general synod. But (Ivo, part 4, chapter 239), whenever doubt arises for some people concerning a universal synod, either those who desire the salvation of their souls should willingly come to the apostolic sees to receive an explanation of what they do not understand, or, if they should perhaps be so obstinate and stubborn that they do not wish to be taught—as it is said concerning such people, “When the wicked comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3)—then it is necessary either that they be brought by whatever means to those same apostolic sees for their salvation, or, lest they be able to destroy others, that they be suppressed by secular authorities according to the canons.

Nor should the empty talk of men delay you in this matter, when they say that the Church is persecuting, while it either restrains offenses that are committed or seeks the salvation of souls. Those who spread such rumors are mistaken (Ivo, part 10, chapter 95). No one persecutes except the person who compels another to do evil. But whoever either punishes evil already committed or prevents it from being committed does not persecute; rather, he loves.

For if, as they think, no one is to be restrained from evil and led toward good, both human and divine laws must necessarily be abolished. These laws, with justice as their guide, establish punishments for the wicked and rewards for the good.

Both the authority of canonical Scripture and the truth of the rules handed down by the Fathers teach us that schism is evil and that people of this kind ought to be suppressed even through foreign powers. Whoever, therefore, is divided from the apostolic sees is undoubtedly in schism and attempts to erect an altar against the universal Church.

But let your excellence consider what canon the Council of Chalcedon inserted concerning such people (Act 4, ancient canon 5), where, after other matters, it says:

“He who suspends himself from communion, holds an assembly, establishes an altar, refuses to consent to the bishop who summons him, and refuses to yield or obey when summoned for the first and second time, is to be utterly condemned; he must never be considered worthy of prayer, nor may he receive honor. If he persists in causing disturbances and seditions in the Church, he is to be suppressed by foreign power as a seditious person.”

And blessed Augustine says of such people:

“Many things must also be done with a certain kind severity for the benefit of those who resist; their advantage should be considered rather than their will. For in correcting a son, however harshly, paternal love is never lost. Yet something is done against his will so that he may grieve—he who, even unwillingly, appears to be healed through grief.”

You see, then, from the testimony of so great a Father, how the Church does not persecute by restraining such actions but always loves by correcting such people.

Therefore do what we frequently urge you to do, knowing the purpose of your Christian devotion, and see to it that such things may no longer be done. Moreover—and I do not doubt that this will be far from easy for you—send those who have presumed to do such things to the most pious emperor under suitable custody.

Your Highness should remember what God accomplished through you at the time when Totila the tyrant possessed Istria and Venetia and the Franks were laying waste to everything. Even then you did not allow a bishop of Milan to be made until you had reported the matter to the most merciful emperor, had learned again from his letters what ought to be done, and, although enemies were raging everywhere, had brought to Ravenna both the man who was being ordained and the man who was to ordain him, through the foresight of your dignity.

Pelagius to the patrician Cethegus.

We have acknowledged your wish that the bishop of the Church of Catania should be appointed after a salutary process of election. Accordingly, on the following day we examined him according to custom and, on the third day after he came, arranged for him to be consecrated bishop.

In a similar way, at the very beginning of your distinguished career, we had wished to comply with your desire concerning the bishop of the city of Syracuse, had not several considerations compelled us to defer his priestly ordination for quite some time. His personal qualifications, or—as you know better than we do—a surviving wife or children, through whom ecclesiastical property is often endangered, caused our minds to remain suspended for a longer period regarding his ordination.

As far as human prudence permitted, we postponed it for almost a year, thinking that the choice of the Syracusans might yield a better result. But because they remained irrevocably fixed in their purpose, and no other person was found in that same Church, unless the matter were deferred for still longer periods of time—and because, as we learned from the testimony of our son, the magnificent praetor, they might otherwise become still more deranged—in the midst of these uncertainties we judged it more prudent to do the following: with appropriate foresight, and without prejudice to the council’s arrangement, we would safeguard the reason why the principal constitution forbids men with children and wives to be advanced to the episcopal order.

For this reason, before he could be ordained by us, we required him with the greatest care to provide a guarantee of the following kind. He was to acknowledge how small his present property was, according to the description of his possessions then made; he was never to seize anything belonging to the Church, whether through himself, through his children, through his wife, or through any relative, household member, or outsider; and he was to join to the ownership of the Church everything acquired during the period of his episcopate, leaving nothing beyond what had then been described to his children or heirs.

Pelagius to Bishop Eleutherius (Deusdedit, book 3, chapter 10).

Maximus, a deacon of your beloved Church, has informed us that, on an estate called Pancellus, he founded an oratory out of devotion and desires to consecrate it in honor of blessed Cantiana the martyr.

Therefore, dearest brother, if the building mentioned is lawfully situated in your diocese and it is established that no body has been buried there, after first receiving a lawful donation of the specified possession, yielding so many solidi free from fiscal assessments, and after the municipal records have been produced, you shall solemnly consecrate the said oratory without public Masses.

This is subject to the condition that neither now nor in the future shall a baptistery be built in that place, nor shall you appoint a cardinal presbyter (*presbyter cardinalis*). Rather, whenever he should wish Masses to be celebrated there, he must know that he is to request a presbyter from your Belovedness, so that no other priest may presume to do anything of this kind.

Pelagius to Bishop Asterius (ibid., chapter 10).

Vindimius the abbot informed us by a written petition that, as stated below, he founded an oratory out of devotion within his monastery, near the walls of the city of Salerno, and desires that it be consecrated in honor of the blessed martyrs Chrysanthus and Daria.

Therefore, if it is established that no body has been buried there, you shall consecrate the said monastery without Masses. This is subject to the condition that, if the founder mentioned should wish Masses to be celebrated there, he must know that he is to request a presbyter from your Belovedness.

Pelagius to the bishops Viventianus of Naples, Geminus of Puteoli, and Constantius of Misenum, after other matters (ibid., chapter 112).

Therefore, by the tenor of this present decree, we command your Charity that, with Constantine, the defender of our see, carrying out the matter, you cause the clergy or citizens of the Church of Paris and, conversely, those of the Church of Volturnum or of Vicus Feniculensis to come before your tribunal, and that you deliver a written judgment in the presence of the parties. The aforementioned defender of our see must in every way ensure that whatever has been established is put into effect.

Pelagius to the defender Benegestus, after a few preliminary matters (ibid., chapter 113).

For this reason, by the authority of this present letter, we command your Experience that, in cases where any person belonging to an ecclesiastical office appears as plaintiff and is bringing an action against a layman, he must not cease to present his claims before the provincial judge.

But in those proceedings in which a person belonging to an ecclesiastical office is sued, with every obstacle of the lawsuit removed, let him come without discrimination before the examination of the bishop or bishops appointed in the place where the dispute is being heard, not evading the pleading of the case through any delaying devices. Thus the entire substance of the matter, argued solely on the basis of its truth and solely according to the laws, may be brought to an end by the judgment arising from the clergy.

You must also endeavor to ensure that whatever happens to be decreed is put into effect. Henceforth no complaint concerning the contumacy of any ecclesiastical person who has been sued is to return to us, through which not only his disobedient excesses but also your negligence may be punished.

Pelagius to John, count of the patrimony, after other matters (ibid., chapter 114).

[Column 0416A]

Therefore, in accordance with your customary goodness, let your Glory provide our son, the presbyter Luminosus, with assistance on the journey mentioned, so that he may safely reach his appointed destination. Kindly also commend him there to your own men, so that, supported there by your assistance as well, he may more easily bring the business entrusted to him to its conclusion.

Pelagius to Count Anilanus, after a few preliminary matters (ibid., chapter 115).

We have decided to send our son Peter, a presbyter of the apostolic see, to correct the matters now under investigation. We judged that the outcome of all the cases would be easier if he were publicly sent from the apostolic see, since both the merits of the matter and the bond of charity would secure for him the assistance of the public authority.

For the statutes of both the canons and the laws admonish us that the humble are to be instructed and the spirit of the proud restrained. For sometimes, in minds that have despaired, teaching without power is despised, while power that lacks the reason of teaching is believed to possess authority.

We have therefore thought it necessary to attach to him Projectus, a notary of our see, so that, after taking counsel together, they may not delay in carrying out what is reasonable, with the Lord’s help, more easily fulfilling what has been ordered.

We therefore greet you in the language of paternal charity and ask you to provide assistance in every matter mentioned that concerns either ecclesiastical unity or the correction of offenses.

Pelagius to Elpidius, bishop of Catania, among other matters.

(Ibid., chapter 116.)

[Column 0416C]

Just as you will have seen to it that each of your clergy faithfully obeys your Belovedness in matters of ecclesiastical utility or administration, proceeding for the sake of that Church as far as justice and the laws permit, so also, through the effective exercise of your Belovedness, continue to pursue the merits of each person according to his faithfulness and diligence.

Pelagius to Laurentius, bishop of Centumcellae.

The report of the most devoted soldiers who are stationed there in the city of Centumcellae, sent directly to us, informs us that they have obtained from the most merciful emperor a sacred decree ordering that a presbyter, a deacon, and a subdeacon should be appointed for them.

Therefore we urge your Belovedness to examine the men themselves carefully and investigate whether they have committed anything contrary to the canons. If you find them blameless and observe an admirable testimony to their lives, then, when the middle week of Easter arrives, if the Lord wills and we remain alive, do not delay promoting each of them through the offices we have mentioned.

Let that presbyter take care never to celebrate the sacred mysteries without the recitation of both our name and yours—

# Fragments of the Letters of Pelagius I

*(From the Collection of Deusdedit.)*

[Column 0417]

Pelagius to the subdeacon Melleus, among other matters.

[Note: The Ballerini assert this in the preliminary dissertation to volume 3 of the works of Saint Leo the Great, page 306.]

[Column 0417A]

We have learned from the report of the notaries of our see that, from the time when the patrimony of the Church was first entrusted to you until now, the accounts of no indiction have been settled. They must therefore necessarily be examined and balanced, so that we may be able, by inspecting the records, to determine what is owed to ecclesiastical uses and what has been appropriated by anyone; and so that you, or your heirs in the future, may be fully protected by security and be able to suffer no disturbances.

Pelagius to Maurus, bishop of Praeneste, among other matters.

We have learned that, from the patrimony of Hilviade, you collected and paid what was owed for the first, second, and third indictions, while Ampliatus, formerly a presbyter, and Stephen, a deacon acting as the pope’s representatives in the city of Rome, were in office.

For the fourth indiction, according to the order of our son Narses, a religious man and son of the sacred palace, you delivered to our sons Dulcitius, Felix, and Spannes, presbyters, what had been collected. After we arrived and, by God’s grace, were ordained, you delivered from the same property what was owed for the fourth indiction. And so forth.

Therefore, at the request of your Belovedness, we have thought that your Fraternity should be protected by this security concerning all the aforesaid past six indictions, so that no one may in the future bring any accusation against your Charity.

Pelagius to the patrician Narses Anagnosticon, among other matters.

Let your Excellence know well that we in no way presume to give the goods of the poor to persons who have means, or to relatives who are under no necessity; for we know that this does not please you, nor do we judge that it is appropriate to our office.

Pelagius to Boethius, prefect of the praetorium of Africa, among other matters.

The Roman Church, over which by God’s authority we preside, after the continuous devastation of war that has afflicted the regions of Italy for twenty-five years and more, and which has scarcely yet withdrawn, obtains from nowhere else except foreign islands or places a stipend—though insufficient, at least a small one—for its clergy and poor.

Pelagius to Julianus, bishop of Cingulum.

It is established that your Belovedness has entered into the accounts of the Church, from the rents of estates or farms located beyond eleven [units] in Picenum, which were entrusted to the care of our son Anastasius, a banker and treasurer of our Church, five hundred solidi of gold from the seventh indiction.

I recorded this on the third day before the Kalends of August, after the consulship of Basil, a man of illustrious rank.

Pelagius to the defender Dulcitius, after certain matters.

Moreover, you sent us certain accounts, disguised in the Greek manner, concerning the payments of the sixth indiction, claiming that you had collected houses for fifty solidi from the deacon Varinus and for another sixty from some other person whom I do not know.

Although estates increase for you daily from here and there, you create difficulties for us concerning payments. Is it not enough that we could scarcely free you from the notaries and various other offices [lacuna], etc.?

Pelagius to the defender Vitus, among other matters.

Therefore, by this present command, we instruct you not to neglect the administration of the patrimony itself. Know that from you we shall now demand both the remaining sixth indiction and the payments of every individual indiction from the seventh onward, according to custom; and that you are to issue a written guarantee in the archive and be able to receive an inventory of that patrimony.

Pelagius to the subdeacon Melleus (Ivo, part 8, chapter 55).

Dulcitia, a servant of our Church residing on the Tarpeian estate, brought the following complaint to our attention. She stated that, after she had become widowed through the death of her husband, a certain Celerinus, reportedly born of a female slave of the Church, had sought through various flatteries and persuasions to incline the mind of the woman mentioned toward his companionship, and had fathered a son by her.

Now, after a considerable period of their union—indeed, after the son had already been born and raised—although, as is reported, there were no reasonable causes for doing so, he abandoned the same woman and proceeded to such insolence that, in order to evade the servitude he owed, he dared to assume the status of a curial.

It is also reported that he had as his first wife a woman born on Church property from the colonists of the Church, and that from her property he is said to retain to this day a certain small estate. He is also said to have possessed no small amount of other property of his own.

Therefore, once you have received the force of this present command, your Experience must carefully ascertain the entire truth of the case through the same “desento” Clarentius [sic], and must carry out whatever the ecclesiastical interest requires concerning the person and property of the man mentioned.

If you find that he was born of a Church slavewoman, or that in any other legitimate manner he is subject to the lawful rights of the Church, hasten to restore him, together with all his property, to the Church estate. You must also restore to union with him the woman mentioned, whom he himself took as his companion, and he must henceforth have no license whatsoever to abandon her.

# Appendix to the Letters of Pope Pelagius I

## Letter 16 (formerly 1)

[Note: Many things expose the audacity of the impostor.]

**He proves that the Father and the Son are one God.**

[Column 0419A]

Pelagius, bishop, sends greetings to Vigilius, bishop.

I rejoice in the devotion of your faith, because you graciously devote yourself to religious study and divine service (Saint Leo, letter 35), and especially because, while seeking the examples of the apostolic see, you strive against the enemies of the faith.

I have learned both from the bearer of your letter and from your letter itself that there are certain people among you who chatter, asking how the Father and the Son can be one God (Ithacius, *Against Varimadus*, chapter 2), since there is no God besides the Father who is said to be unbegotten and invisible.

If these people knew the gift of God and understood the rules of the true faith, they would certainly not mutter such things. But because they do not possess a pure heart with which they are able to see God’s secrets and understand divine mysteries, their hearts must first be cleansed through repentance, so that afterward they may be able to understand and receive the light of truth.

Nevertheless, for their illumination and that of many others, the error of such people must be corrected, and they must be answered with apostolic authority as follows:

How can you refuse to confess the Father and the Son as one? We show from the prophets and the apostles that they were preached as one and true God. We also believe that the Holy Spirit is not separated from them, since the prophet Isaiah says:

“I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Isa. 43).

And:

“By myself I swear: truth has gone forth from my mouth, and my word shall not turn back [shall return], because every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall swear by the Lord, saying: ‘Justice and glory shall come to him.’”

And so that you may recognize that this testimony concerns the Father and the Son together, hear Paul saying:

“So that at the name of Jesus,” he says, “every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth; and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father for all” (Phil. 2).

But if this Son is inferior to his Father, then the Father’s glory has been diminished in the Son. And where is the statement spoken by Scripture in Solomon?

“As you have been magnified among them,” it says, “so you shall be magnified among us, that they may know you as we also have known you, because there is no God besides you, Lord” (Sirach 36).

Pay careful attention and recognize that he is the Son who will be magnified in judgment when he comes to judge the living and the dead.

Also Isaiah: “Listen, house of Jacob and remnant of the house of Israel, you who have come forth from my womb and have been instructed from childhood even to old age. From the beginning I am, and until you grow old, I am. I made you, and I sustain you. I shall forgive, and I shall receive,” says the Lord (Isa. XLVI). And again: “I am the Lord God, and besides me there is no other God, declaring the last things before they happen, and immediately they were accomplished” (ibid.). Elsewhere: “Hear me, Jacob and Israel, whom I made. I am the Lord your God, and there is no other besides me.” Elsewhere: “I am the Lord your God, the first, and I am the last; and in the things that are to come at the end, I am” (Isa. XLIV). Elsewhere: “I am God, who created you, who helped you, and strengthened you with my right hand” (Ps. XLI).

And indicating the unity of the Father and the Son, he says: “You are my witnesses,” says the Lord God, “and my servant, whom I have chosen, so that you may know and believe that I am. Before me there was no other God, and after me there shall not be” (Isa. XLIII).

Choose one of two alternatives, heretic: either confess the Father and the Son to be one God, or, if you insist that the Father alone is God, then the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, will not be God for you, because it is written: “Before me there was no other God, and after me there shall not be” (Isa. XXXIV). If this is so according to you, why does the Apostle proclaim such things and indicate that the same Son is “God blessed above all”? “Theirs,” he says, “are the fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is above all, God blessed forever” (Rom. IX).

Isaiah likewise says: “The Lord God of Israel, who delivered him from Egypt. I am the first, and I am hereafter, and besides me there is no God, as I am, who stood and called and prepared for me, from the time when I made man in the world” (Isa. XLIII).

Elsewhere: “In you is God, and we did not know it; God, and there is no other God besides you. For you are God, and we did not know it, God of Israel, Savior” (Isa. XLV).

Are the Father and the Son not one God? Who is this God in whom God is said to be, besides whom the prophet repeatedly and expressly declares that there is no other God?

And Jeremiah says: “This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him, who discovered the whole way of knowledge and gave it to his servant Jacob and to his beloved Israel. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch III).

And in Solomon (Eccli. XXXVI): “Have mercy on us, God of all, and show us the light of your mercy, and send your fear upon the nations that have not sought you, so that they may know that there is no other God except you” (Deut. IV).

And there: “Lord God of Israel, there is none like you in heaven above or on earth below” (III Kings VIII).

And Psalm XVII: “For who is God besides the Lord, or who is God besides our God?”

And in Genesis: “The Lord rained fire and brimstone from the Lord upon Sodom and Gomorrah, and he overthrew those cities” (Gen. XIX). If the Father alone is God, answer me, I ask: who rained fire and brimstone from the Lord in order to overthrow the cities mentioned above?

And in Deuteronomy: “The Lord alone led them, and there was no foreign god with them” (Deut. II).

And the Apostle Paul: “The true God, who justifies circumcision by faith and uncircumcision through faith” (Rom. III).

And to the Corinthians: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.” And again: “There is no God except one” (I Cor. V).

And to the Galatians: “There is no mediator of one; but God is one” (Gal. III).

And showing the unity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, he confirms it by writing to the Ephesians: “Bearing with one another in charity, anxious to preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace. One body and one spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling. One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God” (Eph. IV).

For if the aforementioned heretics should wish to receive the unity of faith with a simple heart, from this testimony alone they can learn together the unity of the Father and the Son in one Spirit.

Therefore, as they themselves claim to have discovered in the divine writings, they can neither read nor prove at all that the Father is properly called “begotten.” But because Christian faith itself demands this, he is believed without any doubt to be unbegotten; nevertheless, according to the sequence of Scripture, he is shown to have appeared in the Son begotten by him.

But the Apostle Paul, foreseeing from far off the sending of the Son of God in the Holy Spirit (the same Ithacius, ch. 3), testified as follows when writing to the Roman Church: “For what was impossible for the law, in which it was weakened through the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and on account of sin condemned sin in the flesh, so that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled” (Rom. VIII).

Do you see that the Son was not sent by the Father according to his divinity, but according to the flesh, which in his mercy and piety he did not disdain to assume for us?

For that the Son himself sent himself, having emptied himself of the power of his majesty, the Apostle testifies, saying: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil. II).

And Isaiah: “It was not an ambassador or an angel, but the Lord himself who will come and save them” (Isa. XXXIII).

And there: “He appeared openly to those who were not seeking me” (Isa. LXV).

And in Jeremiah: “I abandoned my house, I left my inheritance, and I came and became for them an object of disgrace” (Jer. XII).

And in Micah: “Behold, the Lord will come, and the mountains will be shaken beneath him” (Mic. I).

And in Zechariah: “Rejoice and exult, daughter of Zion, for behold, I am coming, and I shall dwell in your midst,” says the Lord (Zech. II).

And the Apostle to Timothy: “The saying is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance: Jesus Christ came into this world to save sinners” (I Tim. I).

And Malachi: “Behold, suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire” (Mal. III).

And in the Gospel: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matt. IX; Mark II).

Again: “What have we to do with you, and what have you to do with us, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come before the time to destroy us?” (Mark I).

The same passage continues: “The Son of Man came to seek and save what had perished” (Luke XIX).

And there also: “I came so that they may have life, and have it more abundantly” (John X).

Again there: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven” (John III).

Is it not manifest in so many and such great testimonies, in which the Son of God declares that he came from himself, that he who mercifully assumed our flesh came voluntarily and was not sent by another? [Perhaps read *non* (“not”) in place of *dum* (“while”): Col. 0421B.] For since he remains in the Father and is present everywhere by his power, there was no place where he could be sent by the Father. We know that no part of heaven or earth is excluded from the Father’s presence, to which, according to them, the Son would have been sent by the Father.

Meanwhile, let your affection take care, as far as possible (St. Leo, Ep. 32), that it become known to all the sons of the Church what we preach against impious opinion—namely, the evangelical and apostolic teaching. For although we have written out in full what has always been and remains the position of Catholics, nevertheless we now add no small exhortation to strengthen the minds of all.

I remember that I preside over the Church bearing the name of the one whose confession was glorified by the Lord Jesus Christ (Matt. XVI), and whose faith destroys all heresies, but above all attacks the impiety of the present error. I understand that I may do nothing else than devote all my efforts to the cause in which the salvation of the universal Church is under attack.

And lest our writings have been unable to reach you through some occasion of negligence, we now believe that copies of them should be sent, so that the proclamation of the faith we defend may in no way be withheld from your knowledge and teaching.

Given on the fifth day before the Nones of May, under the most illustrious consuls John and Narses.

[Note: [Col. 0421B] Note. [Col. 0422B: Binius could have borrowed more from Baronius, but he feared falling into the impostures of his own Mercator.] The consular notation added at the end renders this letter suspect as to authenticity. Since all ancient monuments are found everywhere marked with dates after Basil’s consulship, repeatedly recorded, it is plainly indicated that no other consul was appointed in the meantime. In Cassiodorus, Basil’s consulship is found repeated twenty times. If the consulship of Narses or of others had been inserted in the fasti after Basil’s consulship, surely all those years would not have been inscribed after Basil’s final consulship, but after the consulship of Narses and John. — Sev. Binius.]

[Note: A false consular notation.]

## In the Year of Our Lord 560. Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator, Abbot of Vivarium

[Col. 0421]

## Dedication

### To the Most Illustrious Man, Michel Le Tellier, Chancellor of France

Since, by common custom, all books being published are referred to you, most illustrious man, as the arbiter of their destiny, Cassiodorus Senator alone, secure as though by a kind of right of his own and without a preface seeking permission, flies into your bosom—he who long ago entered wholly into your mind, slipped into it, and was poured into it.

For the successive stages of his honors, his blameless character, his manner of life, and the favor of the prince and the devotion of the populace have made him so like you that whoever praises Cassiodorus seems to praise Le Tellier.

First, under King Odoacer, Cassiodorus obtained the office of count of the private largesses and the sacred largesses; then, under Theodoric, various provincial offices; afterward he became prefect of the praetorium, and secretary of his letters, private affairs, and instructions; finally he earned the honors of patriciate and consulship.

What of all these things did Le Tellier fail to accomplish under Louis the Just, or fail to surpass under Louis the Great? Neither of them, moreover, rose through some fragile prosperity or flew to the summit of the fasces by the sudden turns of fortune’s game; rather, as virtues customarily grow, he ascended to the height of renown through the steps of dignities (Var. Book I, Letter 4).

In Cassiodorus, incorruptible faith, a mind most steadfast in what is right, and singular prudence flourished; in Le Tellier, all these qualities are found in the highest degree. In both, virtue grew more honorable with each day, and their reputation was not sought by artifice or subject to variation, but always and everywhere remained constant to itself.

Indeed, Cassiodorus administered the offices entrusted to him with such fairness that no one knew how to whisper anything contrary about him, and his integrity of conduct overcame those who wished to detract from him (Var. Book IX, Letter 24). Consider the same to have been said of Le Tellier, against whom even the most ill-tempered envy has never dared to set its teeth.

Through the labor of Cassiodorus, as Athalaric testifies, the empire was spared labor; and when the novelty of the kingdom required many matters to be organized, he alone was sufficient for diverse tasks, so that the public dictation, the king’s counsels, and the king himself required his services (ibid., Letter 25). This would be an appropriate place for speaking of Le Tellier, if it were now permissible to recall those most disastrous times of Gaul, when through his prudence and counsels he vigorously removed the ruin threatening the kingdom.

Finally, if Cassiodorus was praised by the mouth of Theodoric as “the highest glory of the age” (ibid., Letter 24), Le Tellier received from the most Christian king praises all the nobler because Louis the Great surpasses Theodoric by as much.

We enter upon a brief account of your praises, most outstanding man, not so that you may become more illustrious by comparison with Cassiodorus, but so that he may become more distinguished through you. Another might say that you are more just, more prudent, wiser, and more excellent than Cassiodorus; for me it will be enough to call you the Cassiodorus of our age—that is, of Louis the Great. Your modesty requires this measure, if indeed it is a measure to have pleased the greatest king to such an extent.

In this one virtue, lest he be thought inferior to Cassiodorus, you yourself would willingly contend with him. Indeed, this is the chief adornment of your virtues, most upright man: what in others was human, moral, and political is in you, to put it in a word, thoroughly Christian.

Permit the court, the people, and your own household to think and proclaim this about you. First, you undertook to restrain your household within the bounds of modesty—a task Tacitus says is scarcely less difficult for most men than governing a province. Then you yourself learned to shun in public pomp, ostentation, and applause, than which nothing is more effective for earning and increasing reputation.

Moreover, as a minister, you learned to refer your distinguished deeds to their author and leader, far from rivalry with your colleagues and far from contention with others. From this proceeds that courtesy toward everyone, that humanity which is dignified without arrogance and venerable without pride, so that Le Tellier’s mind, no less than his house, seems open to all.

Thus it has happened that the highest dignity, which ordinarily arouses rivals in others, has instead turned the minds, devotion, and applause of all toward you in greater measure. And certainly, where everything is devoted to modesty and beneficence, what place is there for envy? Rather, “he made greater things be wished for himself who confined great achievements within the bounds of modesty” (Var. Book I, Letter 4).

The king’s wise choice of you was quickly followed by the acclamation of every order. You alone seemed to force yourself into obedience to the prince, when the highest office of chancellor was conferred upon you even though you were almost refusing it.

“This,” you said, “will be the final title of honor placed upon me by the best of princes, since I shall soon die.” On the contrary, this will be the most abundant harvest of your merits, which will employ your vigorous old age for the benefit of public law and increase not your own dignity but that of the highest office through you.

For that honor adds nothing to Le Tellier—if one may speak so—except a new vote of Louis the Great, except the supreme crown of modesty. Certainly, like Cassiodorus, you have always been moderate in prosperity (Book IX, Letter 25), so that no favorable course of affairs, however successfully it proceeded, and no breath of popular favor ever lifted the equanimity and steadfastness of your great soul.

You recognize, I think, most illustrious man, your own image in Cassiodorus; indeed, even though you conceal it, everyone recognizes it. Yet, to pass over other matters, there is one respect in which you have surpassed Cassiodorus.

His family, as Theodoric testifies, was illustrious in both worlds; suitably fitted to the twin senate, it shone with pure brilliance, as though endowed with two eyes for two lights (Var. Book I, Letter 4). But Cassiodorus himself lacked the glory of offspring, who might transmit his father’s prudence and other virtues, together with his blood, to posterity.

You, however, most distinguished man, furnish the twin senate with twin offspring in both worlds: one devoted to sacred affairs, the other to political affairs. These are the twin eyes, one of which contemplates divine things and governs sacred matters, while the other surveys and directs human affairs. These are the heirs upon whom the glory of your virtues awaits—not late, but anticipated—not taken away from their father, but enlarged—

Yet, in turn, there is one respect in which, owing to your piety, you consider Cassiodorus happier and superior to yourself, most outstanding man: he ultimately obtained in his Vivarium retirement from public cares, the retirement you yourself sought at your estate in Couvilles. But when God calls you elsewhere, simply follow him, and live for the kingdom, live for your own people, live for everyone.

Until now, like him, you have adorned the palaces with the integrity of your conscience (Var. Book III, Letter 28); now illuminate and purify the tribunals of justice with the light of your equity. For the rest, continue, as you are accustomed and as we have so often proved, to love and support our order—that is, our congregation.

That same Cassiodorus, who is your author and example in this matter, restored through me to his full dignity under your patronage, most illustrious man, will be an everlasting monument of our grateful feeling toward you. Thus, in my name and in the name of us all, I make this vow.

[Col. 0425]

Your most devoted and obedient servant,

Fr. Jean Garet,

monk of the Congregation of Saint Maur.

Rouen, from the monastery of Saint-Ouen, on the Kalends of January, 1679.

[Col. 0425]

## Preface to a New Edition of Cassiodorus’s Works

[Col. 0425A]

Here, benevolent reader, you have a new edition of all the works of Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator. Since we are undertaking it, we must briefly explain why it is called new.

First, no one before us had gathered into one body all the separate writings of this most celebrated author that could until now be found. We collected them by searching manuscript codices with the greatest diligence and by opening the repositories of learned men.

Second, we restored from older manuscripts of proven reliability many things that were missing from the printed works. At times we supplied entire pages and filled gaps; throughout the works we corrected passages that had been shamefully corrupted either through the ignorance of copyists or through the fault of the press, so that sometimes, entirely disregarding the printed context, we were compelled to adhere solely to our manuscripts.

Nevertheless, throughout the work we burdened the margins with various readings which, although doubtful, might be considered sound by an impartial reader. [Note: [Col. 0425] Benevolent reader, you will find in our edition those variant readings appended to the text itself and distinguished by brackets. — Editor.]

Finally, this edition is called new because we have newly added certain works that had never been published.

As for the series of books or treatises that you see here, reader, we have arranged the whole work in two volumes. The first contains everything that our Senator wrote as a politician and historian; the second contains what the author published on Sacred Scripture, his books on the Institutions of Divine and Human Letters, and finally the book he entitled *On the Soul*.

But lest the matters that we now wish to make your concern escape you, we shall say a little about each.

We begin with the notable work of the *Variarum*, which is completed in twelve books. It is a collection of letters of various kinds that Cassiodorus frequently wrote under the Gothic kings Theodoric, Athalaric, Theodahad, and Witigis, and in their names; he also addressed letters in his own name while serving under those kings as prefect of the praetorium.

It also contains various formulas for dignities to be conferred under that Gothic monarchy. Through this style of writing our Aurelius won renown among all people, although some complain that its barbarous style does not attain the dignity of its subject matter or the majesty of the royal name.

Others protest, while not denying Cassiodorus his own stylistic graces; even the strictest Aristarchus would not deny that nowhere else is there to be found such acuteness of intellect, such weight of reasoning, such gravity of thought, such abundant variety of learning, or such a well-stocked treasury of both kinds of wisdom as in our illustrious Senator.

For although he does not display the beauty and elegance of style that flourished together with the majesty of the Roman empire under Augustus, he nevertheless possesses, in a rude age and under barbarian kings, a quality that you may rightly admire and to which writers of better rank properly bear witness.

We examined every edition of these books that we were able to obtain, and collated all of them with several manuscripts of different ages, correcting them from those manuscripts.

Our principal assistance came from the manuscript codex of Saint-Ouen, although books V, VI, and VII are missing from it, and from the ancient parchment manuscript of Saint-Remi at Rheims, in which, however, everything after the first four books is absent.

We also possessed from our library an edition of these books published by Mariangelo Accursio in 1533, which the highly distinguished and learned Claude Grulart, formerly president of the supreme senate of Normandy, had collated with the copy of the celebrated Cujas at Bourges.

But we cannot determine what sort of copy Cujas’s manuscript was, since on the front of our book we found only these words, written in Grulart’s hand: “I collated it at Bourges, on the Nones of November 1575, with the copy of the illustrious man Monsieur Cujas.”

Whatever that copy of Cujas may ultimately have been, Grulart’s book certainly supplied us with very many excellent corrections and observations. Anyone who reads them will easily see for himself how greatly they have illuminated the text and notes of our edition.

Since it has not yet been clear to us whether those observations should be attributed chiefly to Cujas’s copy or to Grulart’s own genius and labor, we have decided to append each of them in its proper place under the names of both men.

Finally, the most learned Francis Juret was of particular assistance to us. The very distinguished Monsieur Bouhier, president and mitred head of the supreme senate of Burgundy, and heir to Juret’s writings, most courteously transmitted to us Juret’s annotations and variant readings for the books of the *Variarum*, written in Juret’s own hand and based on the testimony of several manuscript codices.

We have now appended at the end of each letter all the observations on these books that we received from learned men, so that the learned reader may survey everything, as it were, at a single glance.

There he will again see what Fornerius and Brossaeus had already made public, but not without some correction. For we have added to their work Juret’s notes, remarkable for their varied learning. These not only illuminate our Senator’s words and thoughts but also correct Fornerius’s own observations, and either correct or restore several authorities which Fornerius had cited incorrectly, whether from jurists or from other authors.

Some men with too much leisure prefixed summaries or synopses to the individual letters of Cassiodorus, but with such dull judgment and perfunctory effort that many think they either did not read the letters or failed to grasp their meaning.

We took greater care to miss the target by less, publishing other summaries, which we willingly submit to the judgment of our readers.

To ensure that nothing should be lacking from this edition of the *Variarum*, we took care to explain whatever we thought difficult, obscure, or not readily accessible to anyone. We also provide information about dignities, places, rivers, and many other matters of the same sort that can be found in that work and that are especially worthy of notice.

But lest the bulk of this volume become excessive, this small work of ours will be issued separately after we have put the finishing hand to this edition.

[Note: We have found this *Notice* nowhere. — Editor.]

The books of the *Variarum* are followed immediately by the *History*, which is called *Tripartite* because Cassiodorus had collected it in twelve books from three Greek authors—namely, Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret—into a single body.

“Our Senator,” he says, “having clothed their works in Latin eloquence through Epiphanius Scholasticus, judged it necessary, with the Lord’s help, to bring their selected statements into the continuous course of a single style and to make one discourse out of the three authors” (*On Divine Literature*, ch. 17, in the preface to the *Tripartite History*).

And lest an undifferentiated work confuse anyone, he says that he placed headings throughout the entire text. He testifies that he had no other aim in this work than to ensure that this history, wonderfully written by those authors, as he says (*On Divine Literature*, ch. 17), would not be lacking to his monks at Vivarium: “Lest eloquent Greece,” he says, “boast that it possesses something which it judges has been withheld from you.”

We know that Beatus Rhenanus attacked Epiphanius’s translation bitterly and abusively (in the letter prefixed to the works of Eusebius), charging him with ignorance of both Greek and Latin. Wearied by its sluggishness and by typographical errors, Rhenanus, not without arrogance, announces that he corrected, deleted, and supplied many passages.

But everyone who compares this edition of ours, sincerely restored according to the manuscripts, with Rhenanus’s additions will admit how little justice there is in his abuse of the translator.

Perhaps he will be surprised that Rhenanus corrected almost nothing except certain words which, judging them to be barbarisms and solecisms, had aroused his bile and stomach in a remarkable way through an excessively delicate fastidiousness.

We do not deny that Epiphanius’s translation contains little pure Latinity and much Gothic barbarism. But it did not err so shamefully that the whole appearance of the work should perish because of barbarous trivialities and uncultivated language—just as no one could rightly say that the other Gothic writers should be eliminated for the same reason.

Therefore, we thought that all educated readers, who have always preferred the reading of authors to that of interpolators, would be grateful if we restored the entire work of Cassiodorus Senator and Epiphanius, as it is, to its original integrity—especially since it differs in meaning from the translation of the most learned Valesius in very few places, and since we see that Valesius himself not infrequently made successful use of our translator in his observations.

An ancient codex of the monastery of Blessed Mary at Lyra, written in an excellent hand about four hundred years ago, therefore came to the aid of our revised edition. No less useful was another manuscript from Saint-Thierry near Rheims, whose script is approximately six hundred years old.

We cannot conceal that these manuscripts contain the figures of speech which Rhenanus called barbarisms and solecisms. But they should be forgiven more generously in a Latin translator living among Goths and writing for Goths, who perhaps thought that, in order to render the Greek phrase more accurately, he ought to express it word for word.

[Col. 0427D]

Rhenanus’s work would certainly have been most useful if he had corrected the faults of the copyists as he corrected Epiphanius’s Latinity. For it is clear that many errors have crept into these books, errors that mislead readers and cause no small difficulties.

We have attempted to correct many of them with the help of the manuscripts. Yet we must admit that we lingered long and greatly over two principal passages, and it is worthwhile explaining them once and for all to the reader.

The first is the passage of the *Tripartite History*, Book IX, chapter 38, made famous by the disputes of so many learned men, where we read: “For the Romans fast continuously for three weeks before Easter, apart from Saturday and Sunday.”

But the manuscript codex of Lyra and an old edition derived from other manuscript codices have not three but six weeks.

Until now we hesitated whether that reading should be admitted, since men of the highest learning do not identify an error there in the *Tripartite History*, but many suspect that the fault lies either in Socrates’ error or in the negligence of the historian who wrote that account.

After considering the matter seriously and at length, however, we inserted the reading of our manuscript and of the old edition into our text. We were led to do this not merely by the authority of both witnesses but by more weighty arguments.

First, several very learned men have demonstrated admirably that a six-week fast before Easter was observed at Rome in the time of Socrates.

Second, our Cassiodorus clearly teaches that the Romans fasted for the same number of weeks in his explanation of the title of Psalm XL, where he says: “For forty days Saint Moses abstained from bodily foods . . . In the same way Elijah . . . The Lord himself also fasted for the same number of days and nights, so that he might show us the pattern of blessed purification. We are likewise taught by his example concerning Lent itself. A period of abstinence is set before us so that, our sins’ filth having been washed away, we may approach the Lord’s Resurrection with pure minds.”

Cassiodorus would certainly not speak in this way about a forty-day fast if, in the time of Socrates, the Romans had fasted for only three weeks, excluding Saturday and Sunday—that is, if they had fasted for only fifteen days before Easter. For he had lived with many men who had flourished at Rome in the age of Socrates, and from them he would have learned with certainty what the observance of the Lenten fast was then among the Romans.

Third, it is absolutely certain that some error of the author must be acknowledged in this chapter of the *Tripartite History*, a fact that even the heterodox do not deny. For immediately after the words quoted above—“The Romans fast continuously for three weeks before Easter, apart from Saturday and Sunday”—we read: “At Rome they fast on every Saturday, and all the more during Lent.”

Who, then, can know whether Cassiodorus originally wrote six rather than three weeks there, and whether the reading was later changed either deliberately or through the carelessness of copyists?

We know that the most learned Quenellius solved this exceedingly difficult problem (*Dissertation on the Saturday Fast*) by attributing the entire error to Socrates, a Greek living far from the city of Rome and deceived by false rumors. He says that Cassiodorus copied the error not through malicious intent but in fulfillment of the translator’s office, since, acting there as interpreter, he ought faithfully to render all of Socrates’ words.

We would gladly have accepted this most excellent observation, by which our Senator is cleansed from every fault, if a very small scruple did not still hold us back.

For Cassiodorus assumes not only the office of interpreter but, as he himself says, that of a selector—that is, he writes a continuous history by taking some material from one author and some from another, either accepting or rejecting it.

This is plainly signified by the words that we quoted above from him, and even more clearly by the same preface to the *Tripartite History*: “But after rereading their works and examining each of them with careful judgment, we recognized that they had not all explained every matter with equal clarity and precision; rather, now one, now another had handled a particular part better. And therefore we judged that we should collect selected passages from each speaker.”

If, therefore, he collected only what he considered better, he must not be said to have written anything that he thought false.

[Col. 0428D]

I readily admit that Socrates contains many things worthy of knowledge which Cassiodorus wished to teach his monks. But he could have done this without sacrificing the truth—for example, by passing over Socrates, as he often does elsewhere, and borrowing from Sozomen, who discusses the same matters but does not speak about the Romans; or, at least, if he wished to use Socrates’ words, he could have omitted the few words concerning the Roman fast.

That he did this elsewhere will be clear from the single passage of Sozomen that we shall shortly cite.

Since this is so, someone might perhaps not rashly subscribe to the opinion of those who suspect that the passage of the *Tripartite History* has been corrupted. We nevertheless most willingly leave our conjectures to the judgment of the learned reader. We have therefore relegated to the margin the reading that has “three weeks,” not so that anyone should reject it, but so that whoever judges it more truthful may embrace it of his own accord.

[Col. 0429A]

We make the same declaration concerning another passage of the *Tripartite History*, namely in chapter 39 of the same book, where the following is taken from Sozomen: “In that Church—that is, the Roman Church—neither the bishop nor anyone else teaches before the people.”

Most very learned men contend that this is false, and certainly we do not see how it could be true. But how could it have happened that the Senator passed over what precedes and follows and copied only what he knew with absolute certainty to be false?

For Sozomen continues immediately after the words of Cassiodorus just cited: “But among the Alexandrians only the bishop of the city of Alexandria preaches. They report that this custom, which had not existed previously, was introduced from the time when the presbyter Arius, discoursing on the doctrine of faith, brought in new doctrines.”

Cassiodorus omits all of this, and nothing more. Who, then, would think it probable that an Italian writing to Italians, an abbot writing to his monks, would report from a Greek author what they falsely believed to be done at Rome, while deliberately keeping silent about what was taking place at Alexandria, although it was true and most worthy of notice?

[Col. 0429B]

Perhaps the person will have guessed more successfully who supposes that some copyist’s error slipped into the *Tripartite History* through carelessness.

Indeed, the codex of Saint-Thierry reads *dicit* (“says”) instead of *docet* (“teaches”); and this reading produces an entirely different and entirely truthful meaning.

Cassiodorus is speaking there about the chanting of the Alleluia in this manner: “Among the Romans, in each year, they sing the Alleluia once, on the first day of Easter, so that the Romans regard it as an oath that they may deserve to hear this hymn.”

Valesius’s translation has: “so that it may happen to them to hear and sing this hymn.”

The *Tripartite History* immediately adds: “In that Church neither the bishop nor anyone else before the people says it”—with “it” understood as the first Easter Alleluia.

That this was Cassiodorus’s meaning, and no other, will be proved by the fact that, if he had been speaking about Roman sermons or catechetical instruction, he would never have fraudulently passed over in silence what Sozomen said there about the Alexandrians.

Nor would I deny that Sozomen’s Greek history reads διδάσκει (*didaskei*, “teaches”). But who would dare assert that the text of the Greek author was not corrupted?

Everyone knows how easily unskilled copyists err in transcribing Greek. Perhaps lovers of truth and antiquity will one day discover the correct reading if they come upon Greek manuscripts of better quality; or at least they will correct it from the various manuscript codices of the *Tripartite History*, which we were unable to obtain from the other libraries where they lie concealed.

Cassiodorus, when compiling his *Tripartite History*, nowhere disclosed, apart from the names of the authors, either the book or the passage from which he borrowed his words. Therefore, I think our work will be neither unwelcome nor useless to the reader: in the margins we have indicated, for each writer, the book, chapter, and page according to the editions of Christophorson and Valesius, wherever the material found in our *Tripartite History* appears there. Whenever the chapters are the same in both editions, after citing them we have indicated only the page of the Valesian edition and the letter identifying the passage.

For the rest, we have used both editions in such a way that, in the more difficult passages and in those corrupted either by the punctuation of scribes or by the ignorance of orthographers, they have contributed no little assistance to our emendation of the *Tripartite History*. Finally, wherever they differed especially from our manuscript and printed codices, we have occasionally noted this in the margins of our text. We have also frequently added the years of the Christian era corresponding to the consuls recorded in the *Tripartite History*.
