An impartial reader will observe that we calculated these, perhaps not by uncertain reckoning, always ascending from the year of Christ 514, in which it is established that Senator was made consul.

[Note: What Garetius here says he would note in the margins, we have restored within parentheses in the text, except for the indication of authors, which we have transcribed at the end of the passages cited, in the manner of a siglum. — Editor.]

We gave the third place in this volume to the *Chronicle* of our Senator, which he composed at the command of King Theodoric. Onuphrius Panuinus attacked this work of Cassiodorus with utterly incredible anger and rancor; Joseph Scaliger did nothing to restrain his anger, and he too assailed the *Chronicle* of Senator with no less arrogance. They chiefly criticize the points to which the author adhered in recording the consular fasti from Tiberius Caesar to Diocletian. But the same charge of excessively severe criticism ought to be stamped upon Prosper, so great a man, and upon Victorius, to whom perhaps, as Bucherius says (*Commentary on the Canon of Victorius*, chapter 13), the enormous medley of suffect consuls in that period produced this confusion.

Scaliger himself gives another explanation (in his notes on Eusebius, pages 96 and 425) of why the author deviated slightly from the true epochs: namely, that, following Eusebius as his guide, he placed the consulship of Junius Brutus one complete Olympiad earlier. But even if this error were certain and genuine, it ought to have been forgiven without haughtiness in a man who had rendered the greatest service to letters, who was burdened with greater concerns, who was the Atlas of the entire Gothic kingdom, and who cited a most weighty witness for his opinion. This is especially true since others, less distracted by affairs, commit graver errors without damage to their reputation and without anyone reproaching them.

Moreover, these excessively fastidious faultfinders, Onuphrius and Scaliger, cannot deny that Senator’s *Chronicle* satisfied the wishes of many who committed ecclesiastical and Roman imperial affairs to writing. Indeed, we see often enough that both of them themselves used it in their works, neither unwillingly nor unsuccessfully. What is more, Onuphrius himself, its accuser, admits, even against his will, that Cassiodorus served as a guiding light to him in many matters. Finally, Scaliger himself, although he shared Panuinus’s rancor, repeatedly acknowledges (in his notes on Eusebius, pages 9 and following) that our Senator followed Eusebius and Jerome so closely that he appears not to have differed from them even in wording.

Yet he did not have only these guides, excellent though they were. He also followed Livy, Aufidius Bassus, and Paschal—that is, as Bucherius says (*Commentary on the Canon of Victorius*, chapter 13), the Paschal Canon of Victorius—and, without disregarding them or the others who at that time stood out above all in the ordering of chronology, he did not wish to regard anything as fixed.

I therefore more readily agree with Baronius, Bucherius, and Juretus, who, after more mature consideration of the matter, judge that the anachronisms should be attributed not to the author but to the ignorance of the copyists. Nor will learned men hesitate to subscribe to their view, for they cannot doubt how easily these chronological errors—often arising in the transcription of consular names—creep in through the fault either of printers or of copyists.

Accordingly, so far as we were able, we have corrected these errors by preparing a new edition of our Cassiodorus’s *Chronicle*, modeled with the greatest exactness on all the ancient witnesses. Above all, however, we followed Onuphrius and Cuspinianus, who testify that they had seen manuscript codices. Whenever their readings differed, we have all noted them in our margins, so that a learned reader will be unable to miss anything found in any other edition. We have also added to this *Chronicle* a Paschal Computation, about which we shall say a few things toward the end of the life of Cassiodorus Senator.

Cassiodorus had published a history of the Goths divided into twelve books, as will be clear from what is said in his life; but no one can say by what fate it perished, and everyone has mourned its loss. Only the sort of synopsis and abbreviated rendering of this history that Bishop Jordanes—or Jornandes—of Ravenna collected from it and left to posterity can in some measure lessen the universal grief.

Therefore, so that none of Cassiodorus’s works might escape our diligence, this volume will close with that brief and carefully wrought collection of Senator’s history, inscribed to Castalius, concerning the origin and deeds of the Getae, or Goths. In order to make our edition of this *Chronicle* sound and as free from blemish as possible, we used the edition printed in the Netherlands by Bonaventura Vulcanius, in which the entire work is clearly divided into chapters and the most accurate chapter summaries are supplied. After comparing it with other editions, we added various readings and observations of Juretus, as well as the notes of Bonaventura Vulcanius himself, so that the erudition of these men might make the obscure diction of Jordanes clearer.

The second volume contains works relating to Holy Scripture or to its sacred study. It is rightly and properly headed by the illustrious *Commentary on the Psalms*, or *Exposition of the Psalter*. We know of no edition of this outstanding work of Cassiodorus Senator except the first, published at Basel, and then the Paris edition, printed in Gothic characters and with a more frequent use of abbreviations. Since these forms were less suited to the needs of people in our own time, and the work could scarcely, if at all, be found in the larger libraries, it left among scholars a profound desire for it.

Therefore, so that learned and devout men would not be deprived of this luminous exposition of the Psalms, composed by Cassiodorus with such great care, I undertook the difficult task of issuing it again publicly. This later gave our labor its first occasion for publishing all the author’s works. Since our copyists could not use the previously printed books because of their Gothic characters, faulty punctuation, frequent abbreviations, and countless other errors, I transcribed the less corrupt Basel exemplar in full with my own hand, and compared and corrected it against four manuscripts of better quality.

The first three of these contain the entire *Commentary*; the fourth, mutilated in one portion, does not extend beyond the first hundred psalms. The first was supplied from the library of Saint-Germain at Paris by the Reverend Father Dom Lucas Dacherius. No one will deny that this codex was written approximately nine hundred years ago. The second, which may be judged to have been written five hundred years ago, we owe to the monastery of the Most Holy Trinity at Fécamp. The third, of approximately the same age, was lent by the monastery of Blessed Mary of Lyre; our royal abbey of Saint-Ouen at Rouen preserves it, having received it freely. The fourth is likewise of great antiquity and belongs to the monastery of Bec. After carefully consulting all of these, we diligently corrected more than six hundred passages that were teeming with serious errors.

[Note: Nevertheless, we corrected the edition of Garetius in more than two hundred passages. — Editor.]

We also indicated the scriptural texts and passages that are either cited incorrectly or absent from the two preceding editions. This was not accomplished without labor and frustration, because of the lack of concordances for the version of the Seventy Interpreters, which Cassiodorus used as familiar to him and almost exclusively. I wished to reduce his citations to the form of the Vulgate edition.

It was also necessary to expose and eliminate an error in the manuscript codices, in which, usually through the carelessness of copyists, one prophet is cited in place of another—Jeremiah in place of Isaiah or Daniel. Those who worked on the Basel and Paris editions had thought it preferable to omit such citations altogether. As for the version of the Psalms followed by our Cassiodorus Senator in his *Commentaries*, it is clear that he adhered to the more ancient Roman version. Yet, as Faber Stapulensis testifies, he had compared it with the original purity of the Hebrew text and with the earlier editions then in circulation, as may be gathered from chapter 16 of his preface and from his commentary on Psalms 13:6 and 54:3, among other passages. Hence the division of the verses of the Psalter is not always the same in Cassiodorus as that found in the Vulgate edition.

We also identified other texts of the holy Fathers whom Senator cited without naming their books or indicating their chapters, both in the manuscript codices and in the printed editions. Consequently, more than once we had to reread entire treatises and books of the Fathers so that, once the source had been discovered, the passage of even a single authority cited by Cassiodorus could be identified.

Some recent writers think that these *Commentaries* of Cassiodorus are merely an epitome of Augustine’s works, which that celebrated doctor composed in a more expansive style. But this is entirely gratuitous. First, the version of the Psalms followed by Cassiodorus differs greatly from the one to which Augustine consistently adhered, as Faber Stapulensis noted before us: “Augustine followed the old Psalter, which is less corrected than the others; Cassiodorus followed the Roman psalmody.”

Second, Cassiodorus spared neither expense nor effort to bring this *Commentary* into the public sphere as a work completed in every respect. For this reason, as he himself indicates (in the preface to the Psalms, chapter 16), he summoned experts in the Hebrew language from everywhere and compared everything that he himself was writing on the Psalms with their volume. A mere abbreviator of Augustine could easily have dispensed with all this.

Third, Senator himself makes the matter still clearer in his own words, when he says (in the *Preface to the Psalms*, near the beginning): “To steal something from his understanding”—that is, Augustine’s—“would be like taking Hercules’ club from his hand.” And shortly afterward: “Yet, after so wonderful a master, I have added certain things newly discovered, relying only upon the Lord’s permission, who gives confidence to the little ones, sight to the blind, and so forth.”

Fourth and finally, it is most evident that the learned abbot did not devote himself to Augustine alone in these *Commentaries*, but gathered abundantly the opinions of other holy Fathers as well: Cyprian, Origen, Athanasius, Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, Leo, Chrysostom, Cyril, Didymus, Facundus, Primasius, Sedulius, and others. He used the works and authority of all these no less than those of Augustine. Our venerable Bede also acknowledges this: “In the *Exposition of the Psalms*, which he composed with great distinction, Cassiodorus carefully considered what Ambrose, Hilary, Augustine, Cyril, John, and the other Fathers had said.”

Nor will we deny that Augustine’s teaching was familiar to our Senator, and that he often pursued it in his other works. But he did so by selecting what pleased him most, not by choosing one authority to whom he would adhere with greater zeal and exclusively. He himself freely and gratefully acknowledges this concerning his *Commentary on the Psalms*, which is now under discussion, when he says (*On Divine Literature*, chapter 4): “Borrowing, as is customary, light from light, I wrote certain things about it”—that is, about the Psalter—“by the Lord’s gift.”

He certainly followed Augustine’s footsteps so diligently for no other reason than that he knew with complete confidence that Augustine had always opened the safest path. As he himself observes (in the *Preface to the Commentary on the Psalms*), Augustine is found to be “entirely orthodox, entirely catholic.”

There are, however, some who have on their side the most eminent Cardinal Baronius and who think that Cassiodorus undertook his *Exposition of the Psalms* not of his own initiative but at the command of the supreme pontiff. They summon Baronius himself as a witness, since he speaks as follows (in the *Preface to the Psalms*): “Therefore, apostolic Father, you who have restored heavenly letters to holy conduct, by God’s favor, summoned by your invitation, I shall enter the divine abysses—you who mercifully correct errors and do not harshly impute what you amend.”

The conjecture will seem weightier if someone observes with us what, so far as we know, no one previously has noted: throughout all his works Cassiodorus addresses no one with the title “apostolic Father” except Saint Leo. This indicates that he directed his speech to one of the supreme pontiffs.

It may nevertheless be answered that this address was directed to Saint Jerome, who had been mentioned shortly before. This is supported by the fact that the printed editions, and Baronius himself, read “provoked by imitation of you,” not “provoked by your invitation.” By these words Cassiodorus would merely have suggested that he undertook his *Exposition of the Psalms* following Jerome’s example.

In truth, however, Senator clearly indicates that he applied his hand to this work not under another’s impulse but of his own accord, when he says at the very beginning of the prologue: “When I had tasted the honey of the heavenly Psalter…” By this he shows that he was gently drawn by its sweetness to reveal to his monks the richer delights of the hidden Spirit beneath the veil of the letter—delights of which he had already happily tasted.

Who could believe that a man of such refined humanity, who had continually lived amid the splendor of the court, would have addressed abruptly, as the saying goes, a supreme pontiff whom he had never previously greeted, of whom he says not the slightest word either before or afterward? Yet they wish this pope to have been Agapetus. But how could Senator have addressed him so ineptly when Agapetus had already been dead for many years by the time he began his commentary on the Psalms? We do not, however, wish to remove anything here from the judgment of readers, so that each person may retain his own opinion.

Immediately after this genuine offspring of Cassiodorus, his *Commentary on the Psalms*, we placed another on the *Song of Songs*. We read it under his name in our manuscript codices and in the German edition; everyone who has transmitted a catalogue of Cassiodorus’s books followed that attribution, with the sole exception of the Reverend Father Philippe Labbe, S.J. Perhaps they were deceived by these concluding words of the *Commentary on the Psalms*: “Now let us consider Solomon’s sayings, which are known to have their own interpreters.”

Cardinal Baronius, however, understood these words differently and reached a different conclusion: namely, that our abbot of Vivarium had written on Solomon’s Proverbs, but expressed this opinion in so singular a statement that no one except him appears to have guessed it.

Many things demonstrate that this *Commentary* is a spurious product falsely attributed to Cassiodorus.

1. In this little work on the *Song of Songs*, Gregory the Great is cited, especially his work on the Gospels. Gregory did not undertake that work until he had already been called to the pontifical office, which occurred in the year of Christ 592. By then at least seventeen years had elapsed since Cassiodorus’s death, and the common opinion of authors is that he did not survive the year 575.

2. This commentary on the sacred nuptial song differs greatly from Cassiodorus’s style and manner of writing.

3. Our Senator nowhere mentions having composed this treatise, and he maintains complete silence about it in the preface to his book *On Orthography*, where he lists all the books he had published as a monk. Finally, it is characteristic of our Cassiodorus to present scriptural texts according to the version of the Seventy, whereas this fictitious work does otherwise.

Why, then, is it being issued publicly despite lacking so illustrious a parent? The only reasons were the benefit to readers and the dignity of the book, which is so great that it has a place among the works of Isidore of Seville. Yet Isidore’s version is so compressed and condensed that it appears to be merely an epitome of the work we publish here in full.

It was also necessary to preserve this *Commentary*, lest it perish when the German edition disappeared; that edition is rare and unique. The same edition, along with many other works from his immense private collection of books, was most generously lent to us by the distinguished Emeric Bigot, sufficiently celebrated among learned men for his erudition and wholly devoted to the advancement of letters.

In third place we have placed the books *On Divine and Human Literature*, or *Readings*, with which the abbot of Vivarium instructed his monks in the study of Holy Scripture as necessary preliminary exercises and prolegomena. Some think that Cassiodorus originally divided the book *On Divine Literature* into two books, because in all the printed editions, after chapter 23, the following words are added: “The first book ends. The second book begins.”

But all the manuscript codices dispel this error: none contains such a division. Nor should anyone be surprised that these words were not yet removed in the latest editions. Although these books have been printed so many times, they have nevertheless not lost their blemishes and great lacunae, as could be observed in chapters 12, 15, and 28.

To correct and repair them, we used ancient parchment manuscripts at least five hundred years old, supplied both by our library of Saint-Ouen and by the monastery of Noa on the border of the dioceses of Évreux and Coutances. We also obtained, with equal success, many corrections that the learned Juretus had transcribed from other manuscript codices, and we added several observations that he had made on this book of Cassiodorus.

The book *On Human Literature* is completed, though quite concisely, in seven treatises: on grammar, rhetoric, dialectic, arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy. It was published together with the book *On Divine Literature*, but was so corrupted, mutilated, and full of gaps through the ignorance of copyists that you would scarcely recognize it if you compared it with the text we now give you, reader.

The codex of Saint-Germain-des-Prés was of assistance; its age is assigned to the time of Hincmar of Reims. No less help was supplied by the Reverend Father Dom Simon Bougis, secretary to the Very Reverend Father Dom Vincent Marsolle, superior general of our congregation. He compared the printed edition with the most ancient manuscript of the Thuana Library and sent us its various readings.

The most obliging Pierre Pelhester, librarian of the metropolitan church of Rouen, supplied us with other variant texts from a manuscript of the Royal Library. Its script indicates that it is at least eight hundred years old; nevertheless, it ends at the conclusion of the book *On Arithmetic* and is marked with the number 1467.

We restored the preface to this book. It is found among the works of Alcuin after the treatise *On Virtues and Vices*, and we establish that it is genuinely Cassiodorus’s preliminary work as follows.

1. The preface begins: “The preceding book, completed by the Lord’s favor, contains the *Institution of Divine Readings*. It is known to comprise thirty-three titles.” But no one except Cassiodorus published a book *On Divine Literature*, or *Readings*, arranged in thirty-three titles. Therefore it is called the preceding book because it must be referred to the later book that he composed on human literature.

2. The author of this preface promises to discuss the seven arts that he lists there. Alcuin, however, discussed only three and proceeded no further. Only our Senator reached and completed the full number seven.

3. The words “We must speak about the art of grammar,” which occur in this preface, through the words “which are inscribed under this title,” followed by chapter 2, “On the Art of Rhetoric,” are found both in the printed editions and in the manuscripts bearing Cassiodorus’s name. Our parchments do contain that second chapter on rhetoric, but in a somewhat reversed order.

It is certain that the book *On Grammar* is incomplete. None of our codices could supply its deficiency, not even the Thuana manuscript, which extends farther. The *Commentary on Donatus*, of which we shall speak shortly, will nevertheless abundantly fill the gap.

Those who first published these seven treatises warn the reader at the beginning of the book *On Rhetoric*: “We have restored what follows concerning rhetoric, aided by this abridgment carefully collected by a certain student of the arts.”

As far as we can understand, these words suggest either that they lacked manuscripts of Cassiodorus’s work or that they had obtained only mutilated copies. Because of this scarcity, they resorted to the meager abridgment or synopsis of some compiler, so that the book *On Rhetoric* might at least appear not wholly unlike Cassiodorus’s original work.

Fortune smiled more favorably upon us, reader. We discovered the manuscripts mentioned above, which preserve Cassiodorus’s genuine and complete work, and we give it to you. We rejected the earlier editions, which, as their editors admit, resemble the commentary of some diligent student more than the author’s text.

Anyone who consults the printed editions of the book *On Dialectic* will encounter no small number of passages reversed in remarkable confusion, especially where definitions and interpretation are discussed. We restored everything to its proper place according to the authority of the manuscript codices, to which alone we adhered.

Concerning the book *On Arithmetic*, it is enough to note that at the beginning of the third division the printed editions contain this warning: “This third division has been added; it was lacking in the manuscript.” But they say nothing at all about where or how it was taken, and we cannot guess. We know only that the material printed there differs entirely from what is found in our manuscripts.

Therefore, wishing to safeguard the truth, we rejected all that material and followed only our parchments, word for word and letter for letter. In this codex of Saint-Germain another little book on arithmetic follows, entitled *A Brief Compendium of Arithmetic*. Since it is a synopsis, or brief collection, of certain chapters from the first book of Severinus Boethius’s *Arithmetic*, we thought it better to pass it over, since it can easily be found among Boethius’s works.

A great deal relating to the elements of geometry had been absent from the books of our Cassiodorus published up to that time, although he sometimes cites it in his *Commentaries on the Psalms* or refers the reader to it. Thus, in his exposition of Psalm 96, speaking of the point, line, circle, triangle, quadrilateral, and so forth, he says: “Diligent reader, you will find fuller knowledge of these matters in the books of the discipline of geometry.”

Yet no such material is found in the printed editions; it is contained only in the manuscript of Saint-Germain. Therefore, although it appears to have been excerpted from Euclid’s *Elements*, we have included it here, since it is absolutely certain that Cassiodorus wrote on these matters and since the material appears under his name in so ancient a codex.

Our Aurelius, when listing the books he had already published as a monk, states that two commentaries on Donatus had appeared from his pen. At the beginning of the book *On Grammar* he refers to them as follows: “We have left behind two commentaries on him,” namely, Donatus. Until now, we did not know whether these works had been published.

We give one *Commentary on Donatus* by Cassiodorus, supplied by a very ancient manuscript of the library of Saint Michael on the Mount, or at Peril of the Sea. From its title, almost destroyed by excessive age, we were able to recover only the following.

On the first line: “Here begins the Commentary of S . . . . .”

On the second line: “CII. On the Sentence and on the eight . . . . .”

And on the third line: “. . . parts of the Sentence.”

If one permits a conjecture, these fragments yield the following complete heading: “Here begins the Commentary of Senator, a name also proper to Cassiodorus, the illustrious man, on the Sentence and on the eight parts of the Sentence.”

Nor are we perhaps far from the truth, both because we know with certainty that Cassiodorus wrote books on Donatus and because the material found here and that found in the book *On Grammar* consistently correspond. Thus what is lacking at the end of this work can be abundantly supplied from the other.

We carefully compared all the editions of Cassiodorus Senator’s book *On Orthography*, especially the one published at Antwerp by Ludovicus Carion, with the Montane codex mentioned above, the only manuscript we possessed on this subject.

Cassiodorus mentions (*Preface to the Orthography*) that, by the Lord’s favor, he had compiled another book by Sacerdos on figures of speech, and he says that this compilation contains ninety-eight tropes, excerpted from the book of a certain author named Sacerdos.

Two printed books circulate under Cassiodorus’s name *On Figures and Tropes*, and the same books are attributed to the venerable Bede in volume 1 of these works. From this source an error entered all editions of Cassiodorus, except the Nivellian edition, so that the books appeared under both names with this title: “A Collection of the Great Aurelius Cassiodorus on Figures and Tropes, excerpted from Sacerdos—that is, from the priest Bede.”

Even the inexperienced can recognize the enormous chronological error in this attribution, since it is certain that Bede lived approximately two hundred years after Cassiodorus. The safer conjecture would be that Cassiodorus preceded Bede, as he also preceded Isidore of Seville, among whose works the same book *On Figures* is listed. The difference is that Isidore borrows his tropes or figures from secular writers, whereas Bede borrows his from Holy Scripture and the holy Fathers.

The ancient parchments of the monastery of Fleury contain the same treatise that we read in Bede, and they attribute it to Cassiodorus under this title: “Here begins Cassiodorus’s book *On Figures or Modes of Expression*, which the Greeks call *schemata* or *tropes*, sent to Galertus the deacon.”

This, however, does not establish that it is genuinely the work of Cassiodorus Senator.

1. It is certain that he directed this book to his monks at Vivarium, not to another person named and addressed individually.

2. Gregory the Great is cited in it twice, although he wrote after the time of our Cassiodorus.

3. Senator himself contradicts it, for he states that he had collected ninety-eight *schemata* or tropes, whereas the Fleury codex, stitched together from Bede’s writings, barely reaches half that number.

We therefore left this book among Bede’s works. It seemed better to us, and more suited to the intention of our Senator, to gather these same figures—which are encountered throughout his *Commentary on the Psalms*—into a single body arranged alphabetically, adding one or more examples to each figure. For the reader’s benefit, we extended the collection not merely to ninety-eight tropes but to 120 and more, adding certain rhetorical passages that were found scattered throughout the same *Commentary*.

Although Cassiodorus wrote the book *On the Soul* before embracing the monastic life, we nevertheless thought it appropriate to place it immediately after the treatises he published in old age. If one considers the customary order of philosophical works, no position suits it better, since a treatise on the soul fits reasonably well with the others we have listed.

We removed its blemishes with the aid of manuscript codices—our own of Saint-Ouen at Rouen and that of the abbey of Noa. Above all, Juretus assisted us through his observations and marginal notes on Cassiodorus’s works.

Cassiodorus wrote many more things, but they have escaped our diligence and the wishes of everyone. If that immense store of books which he had gathered for the benefit of his monks’ studies at his monastery of Vivarium still existed, there is no doubt that this collection would be larger and more numerous.

Perhaps we might see a book *On Divisions*; another *On Titles*, which is elsewhere called *Memorial of Sacred Scripture*; brief commentaries on the Epistles of the Apostles, their Acts, and the Apocalypse of John; a treatise *On Etymologies*; and certain others about which we shall say a little in his life.

One author came to our attention: Hincmar of Reims, who testifies that he had read Cassiodorus’s scholia on the Epistle to the Romans (*On Predestination*, chapter 25). We know of no others to whom these works on sacred literature were known.

You may perhaps encounter more than once other books upon which the celebrated name of Cassiodorus has been imposed through the empty fraud of falsehood, such as these two volumes preserved at Cambridge in the library of Corpus Christi: the first *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, the second entitled *Sentences of Cassiodorus from Saint Cyprian*.

In the Oxford Library and in the possession of a certain private Englishman, two copies are seen bearing Cassiodorus’s name: *The Sparkler of the Scriptures*. And Peter of Natalibus, when listing Cassiodorus’s works, counts a book *On the Trinity* among his genuine offspring.

But all contemporary and near-contemporary writers maintain profound silence about these works. Nor is their attribution supported by Cassiodorus Senator, who nowhere mentions any of them, not even when he composed a catalogue of his own works.

No less mistaken are those who think that the lives of Saints Paphnutius, Spyridon, and the others, which Lipomanus gathered into the first part of his *Legendary*, were first written by Cassiodorus. They rightly belong to the earliest writers of the *Tripartite History*.

The opinion of Gesner in his *Bibliotheca* appears still less plausible. There he attributes to our Cassiodorus sixteen books *On Rural Matters*, which he vaguely suggests are found in the library of the monastery of Saint Michael on the Mount. They should rather be attributed to Columella, who wrote sixteen books on that subject, as Cassiodorus Senator himself testifies (*On Divine Literature*, chapter 28).

In codices 114 and 1469 of the Vatican Library another book is found bearing this title: “Cassiodorus’s *Etymologies of the Books of Divine Scripture*.” But the text contradicts that heading, for it is entirely concerned with *Divine Literature*.

[Col. 0436D] A greater controversy may arise concerning the book *On Friendship*, which is attributed to our Cassiodorus in some printed copies and in no small number of manuscripts. But the style of the entire book does not support this attribution; rather, it points conspicuously to Bernard or Peter of Blois.

Furthermore, this book *On Friendship* uses the text of the common edition of Holy Scripture, whereas Cassiodorus never used it. Our Senator nowhere mentions this book among his works. The latest edition of Peter of Blois’s works, recently reissued, sufficiently vindicated the book’s true parentage.

Each of the two volumes of Cassiodorus’s works closes with its own very full index. Before them I have placed the life of our Senator, a man certainly outstanding but not yet sufficiently known, together with a dissertation on his monastic life. In composing these I was assisted by the work of our Nicolas Nourrit, who shared my studies and participated in the labor.

[Col. 0437]

# THE LIFE OF THE GREAT AURELIUS CASSIODORUS SENATOR

## PART ONE

[Col. 0437A] **PREFACE.**—Such are the achievements of the great Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator, and such are the praises with which writers everywhere adorn him, that they would easily have led anyone to undertake committing the history of so great a man to writing, had the difficulty of carrying out such a task not deterred most people from that undertaking.

Indeed, only a few exercised their style in writing the life of this highly distinguished Senator. The eminent Cardinal Baronius, Antonius Yepezius, and Cuspinianus are known to have written more extensively about him than the others; yet, in a condensed—or, so to speak, abbreviated—course, they appear to have traversed so immense and difficult a road.

But I, who am undertaking a new edition in which all the works of our Cassiodorus are to be committed to the press, have thought it worthwhile to investigate somewhat more carefully the events of his life and place them at the beginning of this book. Therefore, if I seem to have entrusted myself too boldly to this labor, the reader’s kindness will grant me pardon. I profess that I have brought into this account of his life nothing that I did not draw from the books of our most celebrated writer or that is not confirmed by his authority.

[Col. 0437B] ## § I. On Cassiodorus’s Names

Although the name Cassiodorus belonged to several people, it is nevertheless plainly evident that it was proper to the family whose history we are here bringing to light, as is clear from King Theodoric: “Although this name,” he says, “may seem to occur among others, it is nevertheless established as the particular name of the family” (*Variorum*, book 1, letter 4).

Whether, however, the outstanding man was called by the surname Senator as his proper name is so uncertain that some have thought it was added to him by *antonomasia*—that is, by a title used in place of a personal name. Others, and more reasonably, have judged that it was bestowed upon him to distinguish him from the others whom we read were called Cassiodorus.

When serving as praetorian prefect, he was accustomed to sign the letters he wrote with the single name Senator. Indeed, he wished his consulship to be designated by this name alone. Jurists also use the distinguished title of this name when, in their writings or judgments, they invoke the authority of this most illustrious man.

There is scarcely an author or manuscript codex that does not designate Cassiodorus with the praenomen **Magnus**. I do not deny, however, that Gesner, in his *Bibliotheca*, and certain more recent writers call our Senator not Magnus but Marcus, although they give no reason at all for this new designation.

Perhaps they thought that Cassiodorus should be given the praenomen Marcus, just as Cicero is, because the letter *M* was placed before both their names. Whatever the case may be, I would confidently declare that almost innumerable writers of better quality have honored Cassiodorus with the distinguished title Magnus, so that the greatness of his name might correspond to his great resources, his great lineage, his great dignities, his piety, and his learning.

## § II. Cassiodorus’s Family

[Col. 0438A] There is no doubt that the family of Cassiodorus was adorned with those distinctions by which the nobility of a most illustrious lineage is commended. This is clearly established by the finest titles of glory that King Theodoric bestowed upon it. For whether one considers its antiquity—“an ancient offspring,” he says (*Var.*, book I, letter 4); or the fame and reputation of its name—“a praised ancestry”; or the lofty honors to which it rose—“distinguished among the wearers of the toga”; or the strength of spirit and virtue—“outstanding among brave men”; or, finally, its exceptional physical endowments—for “they flourished both in bodily health and in stature.”

Add to this that this highly distinguished family carried the splendor of its name into both halves of the world: “A lineage,” says the same Theodoric (ibid.), “renowned in both worlds.” And those whom ancient and new Rome admitted from this family into the senate for their own adornment bound both communities to themselves by every kind of service: “This lineage,” Theodoric says again (ibid.), “[Col. 0438B] fittingly suited to the twin senate, shone with the purest brilliance, as though endowed with two eyes.” Finally, no family attained as much glory in East and West alike as this most noble house: “For what nobility ever extended itself farther than this, which deserved to be renowned in both worlds?” (ibid.). To these distinctions were added the most ample resources, sufficient not only to advance its own dignity but also to muster and maintain armies.

## § III. Cassiodorus’s Grandfather and Father

To come closer to Cassiodorus’s immediate parents, it is appropriate to turn to Theodoric (*Var.*, book I, letter 4), from whom we shall take the whole account. First, his grandfather was surrounded by the distinction of office. He freed Sicily and the Bruttii from the invasion of the Vandals by defending them with arms. The Republic owed it to his virtues that Genseric—whom Rome later endured as a savage enemy—did not invade those neighboring provinces. [Col. 0438C] Therefore, as a reward for his outstanding courage, it granted him the right to hold the foremost position in those provinces that he had defended from so savage and sudden an enemy.

Cassiodorus’s father likewise earned no lesser praise through his distinguished achievements under the Emperor Valentinian. Thus Theodoric writes (ibid.):

> The father of the candidate—that is, of Cassiodorus—served under the Emperor Valentinian in the office of tribune and notary, a dignity then bestowed upon outstanding men.

A close relationship united him with Aetius, such as ordinarily joins those whom both an exceptional love of country and virtue rising above ordinary souls elevate:

> As those equal in spirit always choose one another, he was joined to the patrician Aetius by great affection for the sake of assisting the Republic.

Such was his courage in both civil and military affairs, and such his prudence, that the emperor, because of his wisdom and his glorious labors for the Republic, followed him in every matter of counsel. [Col. 0439A] Indeed, he enjoyed such a reputation for virtue and wisdom with Valentinian that the emperor selected him as the chief member of the embassy sent from Rome to Attila, who was threatening the city.

But what was the outcome of an embassy undertaken in such dangerous circumstances, amid affairs so afflicted and almost ruined, to the most ferocious of conquerors? Hear it from Theodoric himself (ibid.):

> He was appointed, not without purpose, to the duty of an embassy to Attila, mighty in arms. Fearlessly he looked upon the imperial power that he feared; relying upon truth, he scorned those terrifying and threatening faces; nor did he hesitate to confront the arguments of one who, seized by I know not what madness, seemed to seek dominion over the world. He found the king arrogant but left him pacified; and he so demolished his false accusations by the force of truth that the king would have wished to seek the favor of one with whom it was in his interest not to have peace, despite his richest kingdom. By his steadfastness he raised the spirits of the fearful, and those who appeared to be armed with such ambassadors were not thought unwarlike. He brought back a peace that had been despaired of. The success of his embassy may be understood from the fact that it was received with as much gratitude as it had evidently been desired.

[Col. 0439B] Nor should it be concealed how restrained Cassiodorus’s father was in his own praises, since in his *Chronicle* he testifies that peace was obtained from Attila through the efforts of Pope Leo:

> With him, Pope Leo, sent by the Emperor Valentinian, made peace.

Nevertheless, Theodoric’s words sufficiently show that Cassiodorus’s father exerted himself greatly in carrying out this embassy. I should judge him worthy of no less praise because, in place of a reward, he asked the emperor to permit him to withdraw from the court to the Bruttii, from burdensome labor to honorable leisure, and from noise to silence.

This unexpected request caused Valentinian extraordinary grief; yet he could not refuse the prayers of a man who had served both himself and the Republic so admirably. But he—these are Theodoric’s words—was “enriched by an exceedingly great native moderation.” Accepting an honorary retirement, he sought as the place of his reward “the delightful region of the Bruttii.” The emperor could not deny the desired repose to the man who had made him secure from a savage enemy; “sadly he left his service, though he knew that the man had been indispensable to him” (ibid.).

[Col. 0439C]

## § IV. Proba, Galla, and Symmachus, Cassiodorus’s Relations; and Heliodorus, His Kinsman

Cassiodorus boasts that the most noble virgin Proba, once an ornament of Rome, was related to him by blood. For in his book *On Divine Letters* (chapter 23), he calls Proba his relative. She was the sister of Galla and therefore the daughter of Symmachus. From this it is easy to understand that Cassiodorus was related by marriage to that most illustrious Patrician.

It would be lengthy to enumerate the entire family. It will therefore be sufficient to add Heliodorus to Proba. Just as not a few of her relations distinguished the senate of ancient Rome by their virtues, so Heliodorus adorned the government of new Rome through the merits of his upright conduct.

To use Theodoric’s words (*Var.*, book I, letter 4), Heliodorus,

> who, in that Republic—that is, in the East—held the prefecture with distinction for eighteen years in our presence,

is shown to have belonged to their kin. [Col. 0439D] This eminent man, second to none in the distinction of his lineage, after successfully performing the Republic’s highest offices, spent the remainder of his life as a private citizen. Yet in his altered condition he turned everyone’s affection and love toward himself alike. In the province he lived both with the honor of a judge and with the security of a private citizen; superior to all in nobility, he attracted everyone’s affection, so that those who could not be subjected by the right of liberty seemed rather to be gently bound by his continual benefactions (ibid.).

But so that nothing might be lacking from the happiness of this outstanding man, he was heaped with the richest resources. He used them for generosity, not for oppressive domination:

> He also took pride in such abundance of patrimony that, among his other possessions, he surpassed princes in his herds of horses, and by giving so often he avoided incurring envy for his name (ibid.).

## § V. Scyllacium, Cassiodorus’s Homeland

From these most illustrious parents Cassiodorus was born at Scyllacium, which was then the principal city of the Bruttii. A writer of no little reputation takes the opposite view, however, failing to consider sufficiently that the Romans made different divisions of the provinces of Italy at different times.

[Col. 0440A]

Perhaps he had not weighed Cassiodorus’s own words, in which he paints the exceptionally pleasant situation of his homeland with such an elegant pen that I trust it will be most agreeable to the reader if I set his words down here (*Letters*, book XII, letter 15):

> Scyllacium, the first of the cities of the Bruttii, is shown to touch us with patriotic affection. The city, situated above the Adriatic Gulf, hangs upon the hills in the form of Botrys—not rising through a difficult ascent, but so as to look out with delight upon the green fields and the blue back of the sea. From its very cradle it beholds the rising sun, where the coming day does not send the dawn ahead; rather, as soon as it begins to rise, the splendor, shaking its lamp, reveals it. It looks upon Phoebus in joy and shines there with the brightness of its own light, so that it might itself be thought more truly the homeland of the sun, surpassing the reputation of Rhodes. It enjoys a clear light; blessed also with a temperate climate, it experiences sunny winters and cool summers. And life passes there without any sorrow, where threatening seasons are not feared, etc.

[Col. 0440B]

## § VI. Ravenna Was Not Cassiodorus’s Homeland

Nothing further would need to be added to such exquisite words, with which he so beautifully commends the advantageous situation and other benefits of Scyllacium, were it not that several writers, held by an erroneous opinion, call Cassiodorus Ravennate, as though he had been born at Ravenna.

They can easily be disabused of this view if they observe that elsewhere, more than once, in his writings Cassiodorus celebrated the Bruttii and Lucania as his native land and homeland (*Var.*, book I, letters 3; book XII, letters 5 and 12).

## § VII. Whether Cassiodorus Was Born in the Year 479 or 480

It would certainly have been desirable if Cassiodorus had used the same care in specifying the time of his birth as he did in describing his city. The difficulties that entangle nearly all the writers who have transmitted his memory would undoubtedly be resolved. Some of them, such as Augustine of Florence and the Reverend Father Angelo della Noce in his *Cassinese Chronicle*, assign his birth to the year 480 of Christ:

> He died, they say, in the year 575, at the age of ninety-five.

Bucelinus likewise writes:

> [Col. 0440C] He rested in a holy end around the year of Christ 575, at the age of ninety-five.

Others, such as Sixtus of Siena in the *Bibliotheca*—where his birth is inferred from the time of his death—prefer the year 479:

> He died, he says, at the age of ninety-seven, in the year of Christ 576.

Barius, or Cardinal Sirleto, writes in the *History of the Bruttii*:

> He died at the age of ninety-six, in the year 575 from the birth of Christ.

Although these are the opinions of learned men, I cannot agree with them, since I find them inconsistent with Cassiodorus’s letters.

There Theodoric praises him for having been devoted to him at the very beginning of his reign—that is, in the year 493—and for having compelled the restive Sicilians, who at that time could not endure peace and settled rule, to pass over to his side through the victorious persuasion of Cassiodorus:

> At the very beginning of our reign, when the hearts of the provinces were still wavering amid unstable circumstances, and novelty itself allowed the new lord to be neglected, you turned the suspicious minds of the Sicilians away from reckless obstinacy: removing guilt from them and the necessity of vengeance from us. Beneficial persuasion accomplished what forceful severity could scarcely [Col. 0440D] have corrected. You turned to profit the losses of a province which, in its loyalty, deserved to know nothing of such losses. There, under military discipline, while preserving civil laws, you judged public and private interests as an incorruptible arbiter; and, disregarding your own wealth, you brought back the riches of character without incurring the envy of gain. You excluded either a hearing for complaints or an opportunity for slander; and from the place where patience usually returns only silence, voices of praise served you.

Who could believe that a youth of thirteen or fourteen years could demonstrate his virtue through so many outstanding achievements? Yet this praise would have to be attributed to Cassiodorus if the opinions just cited were correct.

Moreover, in that same year, 493, he was Theodoric’s secretary. In Theodoric’s name, as Baronius notes (*for the year 493*), he wrote to the Emperor Anastasius requesting peace (*Var.*, book I, letter 1). Shall we therefore suppose that Cassiodorus had scarcely entered the first years of adolescence when Theodoric advanced him to this office?

[Col. 0441A] Finally, from book I, letter 4 of the *Variae*, we understand that under Odoacer, Theodoric’s predecessor—that is, before the year 493—Cassiodorus had already acquired considerable glory. It is established that at that time he held the offices of *comes privatarum* and *comes sacrarum largitionum*. No one will deny that a thirteen-year-old youth was unequal to such responsibilities. That, however, would have been Cassiodorus’s age if we agree with the authors mentioned above.

What is more, for the year 493 of Christ, Baronius counts him among those senators whose counsel and assistance Theodoric used in governing political affairs at the beginning of his reign. We must therefore acknowledge that Cassiodorus had then passed beyond the years of adolescence.

## § VIII. The Year of Cassiodorus’s Birth

As for the year in which he was born, the remaining authors who wrote about him established nothing certain. Trithemius indeed says:

> He flourished for more than ninety-five years, in the year of the Lord 575.

But what consistent or stable conclusion can be drawn from the phrase “more than”?

[Col. 0441B] Baronius and several others passed over the matter in silence because they judged that nothing could be determined about it. The arguments so far brought against the first opinion, together with what will be said in the course of this history, seem to show that Cassiodorus had reached approximately his twenty-third or twenty-fourth year at the beginning of Theodoric’s reign, namely in 493.

This is especially so since it is established that he performed great deeds in the first flower of his life under Odoacer, and since Theodoric testifies that, still a young man, he entered his court immediately after Odoacer’s death and administered the burdens of office with distinction. It is therefore permissible to infer that Cassiodorus was born at Scyllacium in the year of the Lord 469 or 470.

## § IX. Cassiodorus’s Education and the Offices He First Held under Odoacer

During his manageable childhood, every care appropriate to young men of distinguished nobility was provided for his education. To the military discipline by which his more mature age was properly formed were added the adornments of learning. Although these studies may have retained the scent of the uncultivated barbarism of that extremely troubled age and of foreign domination, he nevertheless made such progress in them that he surpassed every expectation.

[Col. 0441C] Not long afterward he gave such outstanding evidence of talent and learning that Odoacer, king of the Heruli and ruler of all Italy, seeing a noble youth who had attained so much ability and prudence within the years of his youth, honored him with the offices then considered foremost in the government.

First, he adorned him with the dignity of *comes privatarum* (*Var.*, book I, letter 4). This office involved custody, as it were, on behalf of the public and the legitimate magistrate: ensuring that no one polluted himself by mixing with the nearest of kin, that no one violated the rights of tombs, and that perishable goods and deposited funds were assigned to the royal treasuries (*Book VI, formula 8*).

A considerable burden was certainly imposed upon Cassiodorus when he had scarcely emerged from boyhood. Yet Odoacer was not to be blamed for imprudence in appointing as judge of matters of the greatest importance one whom his age seemed to exclude from handling such affairs. There was no reason to fear that a youthful governor would err in issuing judgments through fickleness of spirit, since senile maturity had already outweighed his youthful years.

[Col. 0441D] In fact, Theodoric says that Cassiodorus discharged so great an office so properly that Odoacer’s discerning prudence was approved by everyone: Odoacer had judged him equal to bearing the burden, and although placed at a rank where the vices of youth might have caused him to fall, he not only did not collapse in a precipitous fall but also shone with the splendor of virtues that could have provoked even the envy of old men.

> For the first entrance, as you know (*Theodoric, book I, letter 4*), into public administration was established through the weighty office of *comes privatarum*. There, he did not stumble from the weakness of inexperience, nor innocently err through the fault of novelty; rather, with the foundation of self-restraint firmly established, he lived as an example for imitation.

Why should we now weary the reader’s mind with new arguments to make clear how exceptionally the virtues of Cassiodorus’s youth ennobled him? The testimony already cited of a most trustworthy prince will serve as the equivalent of every proof. Through it, it is clearer than noonday that neither the splendor of his lineage, nor the turbulent spirit of a luxuriant age, nor the corruption of ancestral morals, nor the disorder of circumstances dragged him toward the easy road of vice.

[Col. 0442A] The wise administration of his first dignity made a step toward greater honors for our young man. Accordingly, Odoacer appointed him *comes sacrarum largitionum* (*Var.*, book I, letter 4). In this office he was placed in charge of distributing royal gifts, striking coinage, advancing all commercial dealings, confirming offices and dignities, and so forth (*Book VI, formula 7*).

Senator rose as much through the splendor and merit of his virtues as through his offices. In carrying out this duty, his fairness of spirit and moderation were such that Theodoric himself became the herald of his praise. His distinguished words are these (ibid.):

> Soon afterward, having undertaken the office of *comes sacrarum largitionum*, he grew as much in the praise of his conduct as he had advanced in dignity. Why should we recount the discipline restored to the provinces? Why the measures of justice infused into different classes of men? He lived with such self-restraint that he both established equity by his admonitions and taught it by his example.

[Col. 0442B]

## § X. What Cassiodorus Did after Theodoric Overcame Odoacer

Nor did the praiseworthy virtue of his youth, already consecrated to public service, stop there. Toward the end of Odoacer’s reign, he achieved such a reputation for prudence in the conduct of affairs that it would provide political thinkers with an entirely sufficient reason for admiring and proclaiming his wisdom forever.

In the year of the Lord 490, Theodoric entered Italy and moved against Odoacer with such success that he forced the defeated and routed king to withdraw for refuge into the city of Ravenna. After establishing his camp near the city, after the third year of the siege he accepted the suppliant king under agreed conditions—and inflicted upon him the death that Odoacer suspected was being prepared for Theodoric.

What counsel do you think Cassiodorus adopted amid the radically changed fortunes of the two rulers? When, I say, he saw Theodoric gaining the power from which he had stripped Odoacer, to which side would uncertain Cassiodorus turn amid this fluctuating state of affairs? At last he withdrew to the region of the Bruttii.

[Col. 0442C] When he understood that it had happened by divine providence that the rule of Italy should fall to Theodoric, he set private advantage aside, restrained the rebellious spirit of the Sicilians, and compelled them to obey the new king through the power both of eloquence and of arms. Thus he gained entrance to the king’s court, offering a province that came under the ruler’s authority without the disadvantages of war or any expense.

> At the very beginning of our reign, when the hearts of the provinces were still wavering amid unstable circumstances, and novelty itself prevented them from neglecting their new lord, you turned the suspicious minds of the Sicilians away from reckless obstinacy, etc. (*Theodoric, Var., book I, letter 3*).

[Col. 0442D]

## § XI. Cassiodorus Becomes Theodoric’s Secretary

After honorably completing the duties entrusted to him by King Odoacer, and after proving himself equally capable before Theodoric, Cassiodorus passed by his own willing service from the favor of the former to the friendship of the latter, and from the former’s palace to the latter’s court.

Thus Theodoric continues (*Book I, letter 4*):

> Having been trained in these exercises under the preceding king, he came to our palaces with honors well earned.

The king received him with the honor owed to the splendor of his lineage and his rare virtue. Admiring in the young man the many virtues joined to his gifts of intellect, he wished him to serve as his secretary.

Cassiodorus laid the first foundations of this office in the elegant letters that the king sent to the Emperor Anastasius, seeking more easily to obtain the peace he requested from him. The emperor’s friendship was then judged most useful for stabilizing Theodoric’s kingdom.

## § XII. The Favor of Arian Princes Did Not Weaken Cassiodorus’s Religion

The fact that Cassiodorus earned the favor and affection of Arian princes should not cause anyone to suspect his faith or religion. His solid piety testifies that he was free from every taint of error; his distinguished services to the Church demonstrate his devotion; and his most submissive obedience toward the supreme pontiffs and bishops continually commends him. [Col. 0443A] Finally, all his writings firmly establish this, since in them he utterly refutes the Arians and every other kind of heretic.

It is also recorded concerning Odoacer (Baronius, for the year 476):

> He interfered with no ecclesiastical business, although he was an Arian.

The deacon Ennodius likewise records that this same prince granted many requests made by orthodox bishops.

Some also report (Baronius, for the year 493) that Theodoric respected the authority of the Roman Church, and that he did not prevent any bishop of that see from exercising with full authority everything belonging to the rights of the Apostolic See.

Moreover, at the beginning of his reign he not only did not stain it by persecuting the orthodox, but also pursued them with every kind of service. He went so far that anyone who, in pursuit of royal favor, crossed over to the Arian side found him angered. We have a most vivid example of this, as reported by Zonaras and Cedrenus.

[Col. 0443B] A certain courtier, extremely dear to Theodoric, had defected from the true faith to the Arian sect in order to insinuate himself more deeply into the king’s favor. When Theodoric learned of this, he ordered the man to be beheaded, adding these distinguished words:

> If you have not preserved sincere faith toward God, how will you provide a sound conscience to me, who am only a man?

No one, therefore, should regard it as a fault that Cassiodorus was highly esteemed by kings, and indeed by Arian kings, since he used the authority and favor he possessed with them no less religiously than prudently to promote the good of the Church.

## § XIII. Cassiodorus Is Appointed over the Bruttii and Lucania

Theodoric, whether mindful of the great service Cassiodorus had energetically rendered to the royal majesty when Sicily was added to the empire of the Goths, or wishing to bind the wavering minds of the Bruttii and Lucanians more closely to himself, allowed himself for a time to be deprived of the comfort and presence of so necessary a man in order to entrust those provinces to his administration.

Theodoric clearly explains this himself when discussing Cassiodorus (*Var.*, book I, letter 3):

> But not content with that limit of praise, we gave you the customs of the Bruttii and Lucania to govern, so that the fortune of your native land might not remain unaware of the good that a foreign province had earned.

[Col. 0443C] During his year-long prefecture, Cassiodorus excavated the fishponds and stagnant lakes of Scyllacium by laboriously cutting into the heart of the mountain. He presents this outstanding work as though it were placed before the eyes in the letter that, after being established in the praetorian seat, he wrote to Maximus, chancellor of Lucania and the Bruttii:

> We constructed the barriers of Neptune. For at the foot of Mount Moscius, after excavating the heart of the rocks, we fittingly admitted the streams of Nereus’s deep waters. There a school of fish, playing in free captivity, refreshes the spirit with delight and charms the eyes with wonder (*Letter 15, book XII*).

He already seemed to be dedicating that place to the construction of a monastery, as though he were then meditating on a retreat for contemplating heavenly things, even while the broadest path to the highest honors lay open before him.

[Col. 0443D] How much good his authority and presence brought to those regions, he himself testifies—not with boastful arrogance but in the straightforward movement of his words (*Book II, letter 39*):

> They experienced me as their judge, and those whom I had benefited as a private citizen through my ancestors and forefathers, I strove more vigorously to assist through my official authority.

These achievements will seem few and insignificant if compared with the greater works that he undertook prudently and completed energetically in the prefecture for the defense of justice.

What more? Neither ambition nor love nor hatred ever turned him away from equity when he delivered judgment. In truth, neither affection for his homeland, nor the claims of kinship, nor any other persuasion of human reason violated the integrity of his spirit.

Finally, he proved himself such an upright judge that he received these exceptional praises from Theodoric:

> By displaying your accustomed devotion, you bound us to yourself through a service by which we think we have repaid you everything—thereby increasing our debt precisely where it might have been thought discharged. Throughout all your actions you conducted yourself as a judge wholly free from error, neither depressing anyone through envy nor raising anyone through flattering favor. Although this is difficult everywhere, it becomes glorious in one’s homeland, [Col. 0444A] where either kinship must provoke favor or long disputes must intensify hatred (*Book I, letter 3*).

## § XIV. What Cassiodorus Did after Being Recalled to Theodoric

After completing his year-long magistracy, Theodoric recalled Cassiodorus to himself so that he might employ his services, counsel, and eloquence whenever letters had to be written to kings and princes or to the kingdom’s chief administrators; whenever kings or queens came into the senate to approach the prince and had to be received with a panegyric speech; and, finally, in any especially serious affairs. He could also occasionally mingle conversation with his friends through discussions that were no less useful than agreeable.

Commending this intimacy with the king, Athalaric says:

> You acted as the Lord of affairs’ familiar judge and his intimate nobleman (*Book IX, letter 24*).

Who would believe that Theodoric, more renowned for the glory of arms than for devotion to letters, and occupied with organizing the affairs of a kingdom recently acquired, was so wonderfully affected by Cassiodorus’s learned eloquence that, whenever he could snatch a little leisure from public cares, he devoted it entirely to seeking from him the opinions of wise men and statesmen? [Col. 0444B] He loved to ask him about the hidden wonders of nature, the secrets of philosophy, the courses of the stars, the abysses of the sea, and the channels and courses of springs.

If anyone thinks that I should not be believed, let him hear the most authoritative witness, Athalaric, speaking in these words (*Book IX, letter 24*):

> When Theodoric had been relieved of public concerns, he drew the opinions of the wise from your conversations—that is, from those of Cassiodorus—so that he might match ancient men in his own deeds. As a most penetrating investigator, he inquired into the courses of the stars, the bays of the sea, and the marvels of springs, so that, after examining more carefully the natures of things, a man clothed in purple might seem to be a philosopher.

Perhaps these words of Athalaric led some writers, including Cuspinianus, to assert that Theodoric studied literature under Cassiodorus as his teacher. Yet they offered no proof for the assertion.

[Col. 0444C] The prudent reader should therefore consider whether King Theodoric, having spent nearly his whole life in military affairs and having neglected the study of the sciences, listened as Cassiodorus’s pupil. I can scarcely believe that anyone could easily persuade himself of this.

## § XV. The Order in Which Cassiodorus Held His Offices

Although Cassiodorus brought to great affairs a spirit so immense and serious that he seemed incapable of attending to still greater things, he had so often demonstrated the excellence of his exceptionally capable mind to the most discerning king that Theodoric, as a fair judge, thought him able to undertake still higher responsibilities.

Therefore, when Cassiodorus returned from the prefecture of the Bruttii and Lucania, Theodoric gradually promoted him to the highest honors. Nevertheless, it is scarcely possible to explain either the chronology and sequence of the years in which he held the offices or even the order of the honors themselves.

If anything certain can nevertheless be discovered, we shall derive the whole account from his writings.

[Col. 0444D]

## § XVI. Cassiodorus Becomes Quaestor

After the prefecture of Lucania and the Bruttii, Cassiodorus became quaestor. This is why Athalaric praises him for assuming that dignity (*Var.*, book IX, letter 24):

> Finally, through you we can demonstrate the prince’s exceptional policy: when he received you, still in the first flower of youth, into the office of quaestor, he soon discovered you endowed with integrity of conscience and mature in knowledge of the laws.

And shortly afterward:

> How often did he reckon you among gray-haired nobles, when they were not equal to your beginnings—men whom such great length of life had instructed?

Cassiodorus himself, in the first preface to the *Variae*, lists the office of quaestor among the principal offices he held before the mastership and the prefecture of the praetorian seat. Its chief function was to serve as “the voice of the royal language” (*Book VI, formula 5*).

No one was advanced to this honor who was not commended by his learning and by a mind capable of handling affairs, as Theodoric rightly teaches (*Book V, letter 4*):

> We judge all whom we raise to the summit of the quaestorship to be most learned, such as interpreters of the laws and participants in our counsels ought to be. This is a dignity found neither in wealth nor in mere birth; only learning, joined with prudence, can obtain it, etc.

[Col. 0445A] Cassiodorus, fully equipped with these gifts of mind and adornments of virtue, was appointed to this office. When he bore its burden in a manner worthy of his dignity, everyone praised the king’s exceptional judgment in bestowing honors.

The closer Senator approached the royal majesty as the rank of his office raised him, the more the prince’s singular affection for him increased. His freedom from vice made him especially dear to the king. Hence Athalaric writes (*Var.*, book IX, letter 24):

> You seemed to be joined to the most equitable prince by glorious affection because you were separated from vices by a commendable withdrawal.

Thus the king admired in his quaestor an integrity of mind empty of every form of greed, and eagerly received the delightful wit of his conversation. Athalaric continues:

> He found you pleasing in dictation, stern in the cause of justice, and free from desires.

The king entrusted the actions and complaints of litigants to Cassiodorus’s judgment for resolution:

> The wisest of arbiters burdened you with the weight of those who appealed to you. He had such confidence in the deliberation known to exist in your mind that, as a benefit, he offered your judgment without [Col. 0445B] hesitation to those who were in distress (*ibid.*).

Senator hated the sordid profit of a venal spirit and never attempted the unjust means of acquiring wealth through assessments imposed by office. He placed the honorable wealth of virtue far above goods destined to perish:

> You did not sell his benefits—that is, those of Theodoric—through any detestable assessment, so that your honor might advance toward the riches of reputation while remaining entirely beyond a price. It was plainly an exceptional quality in you that your spirit was open to earning benefits but closed against the vices of greed (*ibid.*).

Anyone who weighs these words with an impartial mind will undoubtedly attribute to Cassiodorus the commendation of praise that he earned in carrying out the office of quaestor before the king and his subjects.

[Col. 0445C]

## § XVII. Cassiodorus Holds the Office of Master

This is relevant because, as a testimony of grateful affection, Theodoric honored the quaestor, whose integrity was universally known, with the office of master. Athalaric bears witness to this (*Book IX, letter 24*):

> Let us come to the dignity of master, which you obtained not through the generosity of money but through the support of your character.

To the man who held this office belonged the discipline of the palace, the weight of lawsuits, the judgments of others, the care of the messengers, and so forth. Through him senators were presented to the king and the arrival of ambassadors announced. Finally, among the praetorian cohorts and the soldiers of the urban prefecture, he held the highest rank.

Since Cassiodorus had been raised to this summit solely by the steps of virtue, he then flourished with that integrity of justice which befits an upright and prudent man. He defended the rights of the prince and the interests of his subjects in such a way that everyone who had dealings with him became his friend.

This great office, full of demanding business and scarcely equal to a man of the most capable mind, did not overwhelm Senator’s outstanding intellect. Indeed, although Cassiodorus had been appointed to the office of master, Theodoric wished him also to remain available for the chief duties of the quaestorship.

Athalaric writes:

> Once you had been placed in the office of master, you were always present for the quaestors. And whenever the gravity and importance of affairs demanded no ordinary eloquence, the matter was entrusted to your intellect (*ibid.*).

[Col. 0445D] Can you call a man fortunate whose counsel and industry the king judged so necessary that he was compelled to demand from him what he knew he had not entrusted to anyone else (*ibid.*)?

Can you regard it as a singular favor that, while others were left idle, he alone touched the summit of affairs?

> By a certain prejudicial favor, he allowed the others to remain without work so that he might crown you with the abundant praise of his judgment (*ibid.*).

But consider what disastrous circumstances and what hostile weapons of envy would have followed this happiness and this favor of the prince, had not the exceptionally skilled political intelligence of this wisest man taken precautions.

Through his prudence and equity he achieved this: he was not harmed even by the slightest bite of his detractors; indeed, his opponents were compelled, against their will, to praise his integrity.

> No one knew how to mutter anything adverse against you, although you endured envy because of the prince’s favor. Your integrity of action overcame those who wished to disparage you; your adversaries often spoke under compulsion what their hearts did not contain (*Book IX, letter 24*).

[Col. 0446A] Moreover, no one will wonder that in the greatest affairs he always possessed the greater spirit and always earned the greater merit of virtue, if he considers these words of Athalaric (ibid.):

> No dignity under you kept within its proper limits, since it is established that your conscience was entrusted with what many nobles would have had to carry out with complete sincerity.

## § XVIII. Cassiodorus Is Made Praetorian Prefect

From that point he was raised to the praetorian prefecture, the highest summit of honor. Yet, once established in that office, he was not inflated by the breath of vanity, which commonly brushes even nobler minds:

> For he did not, as is customary with many, exalted by Fortune’s favor, raise himself on the buskin of great power; rather, he caused greater things to be desired for him by restraining great authority within the bounds of modesty (Book I, Letter 4).

This evenness and moderation—by which he considered himself unworthy of such great offices—did not diminish his devotion of mind to the prince’s glory or to securing the welfare of his subjects. Through his benevolent inclination he gently won the hearts of the provincials, while making himself an object of respect to the soldiers:

> Thus, as you know, he was respected by the soldiers and gentle toward the provincials (Book I, Letter 4).

He was so steadfast in justice [Col. 0446B] that, whenever someone was engaged in litigation, he would choose Cassiodorus as arbiter of the case. Although he administered the unpopular task of imposing taxes upon the peoples, he distributed them to each with such equity that no one complained of being burdened by the assessment, and no one refused to pay. Theodoric praises this equity magnificently (Variae, Book II, Letter 3):

> By arranging everything through prudent governance, you showed how light it is to pay assessments under an upright judge; for no one offered grudgingly what he paid under equity.

What sort of ability, I ask, do you think belonged to a man who knew how to reconcile the prince’s assessments and rights with the devoted obedience of the peoples, so that he incurred the hatred neither of the prince nor of the people? Indeed, his subjects gladly did what they knew was justly demanded by the prince. Theodoric’s words are these (Book I, Letter 4):

> He has joined our advantages with the joy of everyone: generous to the treasury, and gracious to those who pay justly.

Cassiodorus was so beneficent toward everyone that, far more eager to give than to receive, he condemned the avarice of judges who stain their dignity by accepting gifts from their clients:

> Eager to give, disdainful of receiving.

Never did this great man, when his mind had remained unstained by the contagion of crimes, fail to turn it toward love of virtue:

> A hater of crime, a lover of equity.

Who, then, will wonder that the memory of his right actions in the exercise of the prefecture wonderfully delighted the prince’s mind? “It delights us,” says the king (Book I, Letter 3), “to recall the acts of your prefecture.” And indeed, how pleasing it was for Theodoric to call to mind the distinguished modesty, justice, and fidelity of his subject! Having governed everything with equity, he did not render our favor toward him fruitless.

It was especially pleasing for him to be able to proclaim, with complete truth, this concerning the praetorian prefect whom he himself had appointed: that the state had then experienced in him, from that Romulean assembly, a man of innocence; and that, although he had made himself glorious by self-restraint, he had nevertheless contributed something greater by leaving an example of good conduct for those who followed (Book I, Letter 4).

## § XIX. What He Did When Theodoric Went to Rome

I would never finish if I wished to report individually how diligently, as governor, he cared for the provinces and cities, both in defending the rights of citizens and in settling disputes among common people. Yet one feature of the provident prefect’s painstaking diligence cannot be passed over: he arranged for the City to be adorned and prepared for Theodoric’s royal entry.

The king had established the seat of his empire at Ravenna. From there it became necessary for him to proceed to Rome, which he had made tributary to himself, in order to suppress the seditions and disturbances that had been stirred up by the antipope Laurentius against the legitimate pope Symmachus, dividing the clergy and senate into factions and tearing the City apart.

Although royal authority had likewise supported Symmachus’s canonical election, it had not restrained the authors of revolutionary upheaval. Therefore, when the king yielded to the wishes of the orthodox Romans, he planned to come to Rome, so that by his presence he might calm the storm that had arisen and restore the desired tranquillity of the Christian commonwealth.

As soon as the praetorian prefect Cassiodorus learned that the king intended to travel to Rome, he immediately sent letters to Constantinianus, whom he calls a man of exceptional experience, and to his deputy Maximianus in the City. In them he ordered that they take care that nothing be lacking for the splendor of the king’s solemn entry: that they arrange for the public roads to be repaired if necessary, the bridges restored, and tables furnished with food worthy of a king.

> For this purpose, he writes to Maximianus, know that we have sent a soldier of our household, who must supervise you and your office, so that he may report to us that everything is ready; for what is known to be entrusted to our responsibility cannot be left to chance (Variae, Book XII, Letters 18–19).

I do not deny, however, that it is uncertain whether this letter was written during the reign of Theodoric or under his successors, who likewise went to Rome with Cassiodorus as praetorian prefect. Nevertheless, we have recalled here that splendid deed of Senator because Maximianus is mentioned nowhere except in letters sent in Theodoric’s name. From these letters it can certainly be understood what standing Cassiodorus had with the king and with the Roman people, and what he was capable of undertaking.

Even if anyone should still consider this date doubtful, he must at least admit that nothing more diligently—much less more ingeniously—could be found or devised by our Cassiodorus concerning the entry into the City of whichever prince it may have been.

The king therefore proceeded from Ravenna to Rome with his nobles, among whom Cassiodorus stood foremost. He was received with immense joy and applause by the citizens and settled the divided minds of the Romans, cutting away the deadly plague of schism that had afflicted the clergy and senate.

Let each person now consider for himself how justly Cassiodorus, whose influence over the king’s mind was so great, ought to share in the praise that Theodoric attained when, by his authority, he suppressed the worst infection of schism and restored the property of the orthodox according to the canons of the Roman council. For in this affair Cassiodorus was the prince’s chief helper and partner in counsel and action.

## § XX. He Is Raised to the Dignity of Patrician

Scarcely had he completed his tenure of the prefecture when Theodoric raised him to the dignity of patrician. His rare merits, both toward the king and toward the state, demanded this advancement by a kind of legitimate right.

“Moved by so many and such outstanding praises,” says Theodoric (Book I, Letter 3), “we confer upon you the summit of the patriciate as a just recompense, so that what is a prize for others may be, for you, a repayment of merits.”

He then asked the senate to confirm by common consent the patrician whom the royal decision had selected:
