> You remember—and the memory of recent events still supplies the evidence—with what moderation he occupied the height of the praetorian office (Book I, Letter 4).

We know from Formulary 2 of Book VI how lofty this honor was, since kings considered it honorable to receive a dignity known to stand below only the summit of the consulship.

> He precedes the prefects and men of the other dignities, yielding only to that one splendor which, as we know, is sometimes assumed even by us (Theodoric, Book VI, Formulary 2).

This dignity did not surround the patrician with the brief duration of a yearly honor, but with perpetual splendor:

> An inseparable ornament, a faithful belt, which does not know how to depart before human beings depart from the world (ibid.).

When Theodoric indicated that Cassiodorus’s distinguished deeds had prompted him to burst forth into these exceptional praises, he exhorted him also to display in the patriciate the equity and virtue that he had shown so remarkably in the offices previously conferred upon him.

Cassiodorus’s mind, however, did not need to be stirred by such admonitions toward the glory of virtue. He had cultivated virtue so greatly in the courts of princes that he had always shown himself an outstanding example of integrity to nobles and to men distinguished by the purity of their character. Theodoric recalls such a man when he commends the patrician’s unblemished fidelity (Book I, Letter 26):

> The pure faith and integrity of the magnificent man Cassiodorus, Patrician, have been proved to us, and so forth.

We shall present so many still-existing and most certain proofs of this in the course of this life that no one will be able to doubt the praised integrity of this most excellent man.

## § XXI. In What Year Cassiodorus Became Consul

Writers do not agree about the year in which he held the consulship. Some assign it to the year 513, as does Cuspinianus in his Commentary on the Chronicle of Cassiodorus. I do not wish to take account here of the error that slipped into an edition which places his consulship in the year 512; for the year 451 is found counted twice.

Other chronicles, however, place it more plausibly in the year 514, including those of Marcellinus, Onuphrius, and Bucherius; Cardinal Baronius agrees with them. This diversity of opinion was caused by the carelessness of scribes, who, while copying Cassiodorus’s Chronicle, omitted the consulship of Dexecratus and Volusianus, which occurred in the year 503.

That Cassiodorus’s consulship should be assigned to the year 514 can also be proved by an observation I have made, which does not occur in the authors cited above: namely, that according to Cassiodorus (Variae, Book II, Letter 2), Felix received the consulship from Theodoric in the fourth indiction, which fell in the year 511; and that in his own Chronicle he lists two consulships between the consulship of Felix and his own. From this reckoning it follows that his consulship must be assigned to the year 514.

## § XXII. During Cassiodorus’s Consulship the Schism of the Antipope Laurentius Is Extinguished

What need is there now to recount how splendid were the adornments and how lofty the responsibilities of this most exalted honor? Anyone who wishes to know them should learn them from Formulary 1 of Book VI of the Variae.

It will be enough to note that Cassiodorus saw, with immense joy of heart, the flames of the renewed schism extinguished during his consulship. We have already stated on what occasion Theodoric formerly came to Rome: namely, to suppress the dissensions that had arisen from the schism.

After the king’s departure, the faction of Laurentius stirred up a new storm, like some terrifying north wind, and the tranquillity of the Church was miserably disturbed until the death of Symmachus, which occurred in this year.

When Symmachus had been taken from the living, the agreement and diligence of upright men finally brought the opposing parties together and caused the election of Pope Hormisdas to be confirmed by common consent. For this reason the remnants of the schism were entirely dissolved, as Cassiodorus himself testifies in his Chronicle in the most restrained terms:

> While I too was consul, to the praise of your times—namely, Theodoric’s—with the clergy and the Roman people united, the desired concord returned to the Church.

Would that the other writers had explained this more fully! It would certainly become clearer how much effort the magnanimous consul expended, in keeping with his dignity and with his most devoted piety toward Mother Church, to recall divided minds to peace and to ensure that the supreme pontiff was elected according to the canons and decrees of the Church.

Nevertheless, our consul’s inclination toward the welfare of the Church and the salvation of the state, together with his diligent concern, does not permit this to be doubted.

## § XXIII. How Impatiently Theodoric Endured Cassiodorus’s Absence

While Senator was holding the consulship—or at approximately that time, when he was going to Rome or traveling elsewhere—an unquestionably very serious matter demanded his attention. Consequently, he had to be absent for some time from the royal palace.

But Theodoric could not long endure his absence. The chief affairs of the kingdom depended upon Cassiodorus’s counsel, and Theodoric considered it most beneficial to nourish his mind with Cassiodorus’s learned conversation. He therefore sent a letter earnestly asking him to return to the court as quickly as possible.

From this you may infer how highly Cassiodorus valued this royal exchange of letters: among the letters that he wrote in the king’s name to various persons, he preserved this one (Variae, Book III, Letter 28). It is very brief, but in condensed language it contains all the praises with which a subject can be honored by a prince.

Theodoric says that he rightly required the presence of a man to whom he confessed himself greatly indebted for the increase of his dignity and glory:

> It is fitting that you too should be sought, since you have caused our times to be proclaimed with distinction.

He confidently affirms that his palaces were adorned by Cassiodorus’s splendid character:

> You have adorned the palaces with the integrity of your conscience.

He acknowledges that the peoples owed to Cassiodorus the welcome leisure of peace:

> You have given the peoples profound tranquillity.

He declares that Cassiodorus was full of faith and so devoted to equity in issuing judgments that those over whom he pronounced judgment suffered no loss:

> When presented before the tribunals, they saw you as judge without any fear of loss.

He approves the fact that Cassiodorus was commended so earnestly to everyone because, setting aside his own interests, he made himself readily available to each person:

> You became more precious to everyone because you were not for sale at any price.

He gratefully recalls that Cassiodorus undertook no labor or service for the prince’s sake unwillingly, and that he had therefore repaid him with public praises and testimonies of gratitude:

> With the palace as witness, we have praised your greatness, proved by glorious service to us.

He exhorts him to hasten to the court, where everyone’s highest prayers awaited him:

> Turn your steps this way; hasten your arrival.

What, I ask you, could be added to this heap of praises? It would exceed the merits of anyone else. Yet it scarcely equals the virtues of the great Cassiodorus, whose outstanding greatness, already known from his previous deeds, supplies abundant material for praise without any fear of injuring the truth.

## § XXIV. He Writes Letters, Panegyrics, and a Chronicle

Cassiodorus, therefore, while distinguishing himself in the king’s court from the rest of the nobles by his virtues, wrote letters in the king’s name and delivered panegyrical speeches to kings and queens:

> You frequently pronounced praises to queens and kings in commendation of the whole community (First Preface to the Variae).

At the king’s command he also composed a Chronicle, carried from the beginning of humankind in a concise style down to his own times—that is, to the consulship of the emperor Justin and of Eutaricus Cillica, which was reckoned as the year 519 of the Christian era.

We have no room here to discuss this Chronicle at greater length. We have explained in detail in our preface how differently the authors judge it.

## § XXV. He Composes a History of the Goths

Under the same king, Cassiodorus published a History of the Goths divided into twelve books, as he himself states in the earlier preface to the Variae. King Athalaric, writing to the senate, gives a general outline of this history when he says (Book IX, Letter 25):

> He brought forth from the hiding place of antiquity the kings of the Goths, long concealed by oblivion; he restored the Amals together with the glory of their lineage, clearly showing that we possess a royal stock extending through the seventeenth generation. He made the Gothic origin into Roman history, gathering, as though into a single crown, the flowering shoot that had been scattered here and there across the fields of books.

The loss of this work arouses an ardent longing that must be deeply lamented by lovers of history, since from it splendid monuments of antiquity could surely have been unearthed.

Nevertheless, Jornandes—or Jordan, bishop of Ravenna—places some limit upon our longing, since he entrusted to posterity an epitome of the entire history. He introduces it to Castellius in these words:

> You urge me to compress, in my own words, the twelve volumes of Senator concerning the origin and deeds of the Getae, descending through generations from ancient times to the present, into this one small book—a sufficiently difficult command, and so forth.

If these final words of Jordanes are understood by those who know how laborious it is to write history, they should show how much labor Cassiodorus devoted to arranging his history. Certainly everyone will continue to marvel that a man occupied with the public affairs of the kingdom not only undertook so arduous a work but completed it through vigorous labor.

## § XXVI. Cassiodorus Again Assumes the Office of Master

In the year of Our Lord 526, the last year of Theodoric’s reign and life, Cassiodorus was again summoned to the office of master. Thus Athalaric says:

> We found him indeed as master (Book IX, Letter 25).

It might undoubtedly seem surprising that, after so many and such extensive offices had been commendably administered for the king’s benefit and glory, Theodoric should, contrary to ordinary practice, invite Cassiodorus once more to undertake the duties of the mastership—duties he had already fulfilled with distinction and which, in view of his merits, he might have looked down upon without compromising his modesty.

But Senator possessed too lofty a spirit to judge the king unfairly or to place private advantages before the king’s commands. We shall see that he offered the clearest evidence of this under Theodoric’s successors.

Since Cassiodorus knew that it would be of the greatest benefit to the king for him to undertake the office of master, he accepted it with no less evident joy than the higher dignities, and always discharged it with equal equity and prudence.

The fortunate outcome of events showed that he had been appointed to this office more by heavenly providence than by Theodoric’s command. For it is impossible to express how greatly he assisted the youthful Athalaric by his counsel and service at the beginning of his reign, when untimely disturbances could have been stirred up by seditious men because of the king’s tender age.

## § XXVII. How He Assisted Athalaric at the Beginning of His Reign

Theodoric had died without leaving any male offspring except the eight-year-old Athalaric, whom his daughter Amalasuntha had borne by Eutaricus Cillica, who had died before his father-in-law.

Amalasuntha assumed the government of the kingdom on behalf of her son. She would certainly have been unequal to administering it unless Magnus Cassiodorus had, so to speak, placed his hand and his Herculean shoulders beneath so great a burden.

In this new situation he never deviated from faith and duty. Indeed, he assisted the beginning of the kingdom with his resources, writings, and arms (Variae, Book IX, Letter 25), as Athalaric himself gratefully boasts.

Nor was the outstanding Senator content merely to restrain a single province, as formerly he had restrained Sicily. He achieved something greater when he subjected the entire Gothic nation to Athalaric. Thus it came about that the desired happiness of public peace followed upon his labor and prudence. To speak with Athalaric:

> It was achieved through his labor that the empire might not have to labor (ibid.).

Athalaric was truly fortunate to have obtained, at the very beginning of his reign, an administrator upon whom his tender age and the novelty of the kingdom could safely rely; a man capable both of asserting royal dignity and of bearing the weight of affairs.

Since the novelty of the kingdom required many things to be ordered, Cassiodorus alone was sufficient for everything. Thus, whenever public matters had to be discussed, no one was more prepared or better equipped with eloquence.

If counsel was needed in pressing affairs, a new sun poured light upon obscure matters through the splendor of his genius. A new Oedipus easily explained doubtful and ambiguous questions. There was nowhere any need to despair of the outcome of a matter that someone had entrusted to his judgment.

> Public dictation demanded him; our counsels demanded him (Athalaric, ibid.).

The beginnings of the kingdom, burdened with the most serious affairs of Amalasuntha and Athalaric, found in him a man adorned with exceptional wisdom for governing political affairs and deeply knowledgeable in military matters for conducting wars.

> While concern for the coasts occupied royal thoughts, he was suddenly drawn forth from the inner chambers of letters and, undaunted, supplied a command equal to that of his ancestors (ibid.).

Who, then, will not admire Cassiodorus, a man made wondrous by so many and varied praises of virtue? I venture to say that under Athalaric he was the greatest ornament of the Gothic kingdom—he who under Theodoric had unquestionably been the chief glory of the age (Book IX, Letter 24).

## § XXVIII. He Becomes Quaestor Again

He had scarcely completed a year’s service in the office of master when he was compelled to undertake the quaestorship again. He had previously held that office through Theodoric’s favor, with the faithfulness and integrity that both the king and his subjects had openly exalted with deserved praises.

The beginning of Athalaric’s reign gave him a broad opportunity to administer this dignity once more in an even more outstanding manner:

> He fulfilled for us the office of quaestor, and, dispensing rewards with the most just prudence, which he had learned from our founder, he willingly devoted it to the interests of the heir (the king himself—or rather Amalasuntha—Book IX, Letter 25).

The quaestor’s devotion to the king and the state did not stop there:

> Adding something greater to these achievements, he arms the armies of the Goths after the manner and example of his forebears, and, improved by good instruction, preserves through inherited generosity the sound practice he received from his forebears (Book I, Letter 4).

At his own expense he maintained Gothic forces assigned to forestall disturbances, which frequently arose at the beginning of the unstable kingdom under a child king. He fed the Goths assigned to this duty from his private resources, so that he would neither alarm the provincials nor burden our treasury with the expenses (Book IX, Letter 25).

Such was the nobility of his mind and his willingness to benefit each person that he was not merely beneficent toward citizens but even toward the king. He was so attentive to the welfare of others that his arms caused no harm to property owners.

How justly, then, is he praised before the senate by Athalaric when he calls him the guardian of the provinces! He was truly the most faithful guardian of the provinces.

Who, indeed, was ever a more conscientious and courageous defender of royal majesty, more lavish of his goods and his life? Neither the beginnings of a wavering kingdom under a child king, nor the uncertain state of affairs, nor unstable fortune could ever deter him from his purpose.

He was the most faithful conservator of the royal treasury, but a provident—indeed, almost no—guardian of his own resources. Possessed of a generous spirit, he set aside these and other considerations by which he might have been led to care for his private affairs and raised himself to higher things. Since his fidelity was bound by no limits, he spared nothing for the service of the king.

## § XXIX. What He Did in the Quaestorship after the Soldiers Were Dismissed

When he had withdrawn from military affairs, he devoted all his care and genius to assigning each person his rights according to equity. Athalaric testifies to this as follows (Variae, Book IX, Letter 25):

> When the care of war had been set aside, he exercised his genius rather as a guide of the laws.

With the confusion of war dissolved, he found almost everything corrupted, the laws dispersed, and even the judgments of judges—whom avarice had invaded—put up for sale.

What did he do? He devoted himself to repairing these injuries and eliminating this plague, with such praise of prudence and justice that the crowds of litigants could desire nothing more equitable than his judgment:

> By signing, without harm to the litigants, what had previously been known to have been torn apart without payment (ibid.).

If you wish to know whom Cassiodorus followed in this, listen to Athalaric himself (ibid.):

> We read that such was the leadership of Metellus in Asia and of Cato in Spain; they were praised more for their discipline than for their weapons.

He did not merely attain their stature by imitating them; he surpassed them by far. Athalaric gave such distinguished testimony to his exceptional virtue that he did not hesitate to affirm that Cassiodorus,

> while he did not know how to seek what belonged to others, knew only how to offer generously what was his own (ibid.).

Hence, he says,

> he was so benevolent toward everyone that he seemed not the master of his possessions but their outstanding distributor.

Yet even when affairs proceeded successfully, and even when he was buoyed by popular favor, his moderation of mind was never elated. Firmly grounded upon the solid foundations of Christian humility, he was always restrained in prosperity.

But from what teacher had he learned these laws of good conduct, which worldly prudence usually rejects? Certainly from no one except Christ the Lord, whom he had heard teaching in the sacred books. Divine reading therefore strengthened these habits (Book IX, Letter 25).

From these springs he drew the virtues that he transmitted as an eternal example for all political officials. Under this heavenly Teacher he learned to conform his character, through the humility of Christ, to the greatest honors with the most modest conduct.

Here the clear knowledge of all virtues is acquired; here wisdom is seasoned with the savor of truth. Thus the man whom heavenly teaching has instructed is made humble in all things (ibid.).

While Cassiodorus was exercising his mind in these virtues of Christian piety, he was compelled to undertake the duties of another office. As recently under Theodoric, so under Athalaric he wrote, by Athalaric’s command and in his name, many letters to the supreme pontiff, to bishops, to the clergy, senate, and Roman people, to the emperor, to the king of the Vandals, and to many others—letters remarkable for singular piety and refined expression. They may be seen in Books VIII and IX of the Variae.

## § XXX. Cassiodorus Is Amalasuntha’s Only Hope as She Mourns Athalaric’s Removal from His Studies

Athalaric was eight years old, as we have seen, when he assumed the government of the Gothic empire. His mother Amalasuntha had entrusted him to be instructed in all the disciplines and arts that befit a Christian and great king.

But the Goths, a fierce people, arrogantly refused to obey a king devoted to learning. They thought that the glory of arms could not coexist with the study of letters, which, they believed, softened and weakened the vigor of the mind [Col. 0452A].

They resisted the queen’s will and salutary counsel with such obstinacy and ferocity that she was finally compelled to yield to their fury. Consequently, Athalaric’s soft and unstable youth, deprived of the seeds of virtue and the best arts, easily turned toward vice; and the wretched corruption of nearly all his subjects quickly followed the worst example of the king.

Amalasuntha, a pious queen above all, could not see the universal degradation without tears or without the bitterest anguish of heart. The miserable condition both of the royal household and of the kingdom inflicted immeasurable grief upon her and upon all good people.

Nevertheless, her supreme sorrow was lessened by the one hope she placed in Cassiodorus’s integrity. She knew how greatly he had supported the king’s youth by his counsel and service, by his care and resources; how many unjust laws he had rescinded when he became quaestor; how many that had been most wickedly overturned he had justly restored.

She therefore trusted that all vicious and corrupt customs would soon be corrected by the man whom she then considered a gift from God, destined to restore the state’s former splendor [Col. 0452B].

## § XXXI. He Is Made Praetorian Prefect Again

For this reason, all who cherished the glory of their homeland ardently desired that the praetorian prefecture should be administered by the unimpeachable Senator. They had repeatedly requested this of Athalaric.

Yielding to their prayers, the king made him praetorian prefect in the twelfth indiction, that is, in the year of Our Lord 534. Athalaric indicates this with no small commendation of Cassiodorus when he says (Variae, Book IX, Letter 24):

> By delaying you for so long, we wearied everyone’s wishes, in order to test the general affection toward you, and so that you might arrive all the more desired by everyone.

The king praises his subject equally when he informs the senate of the reason why he had made him praetorian prefect: namely, so that, desired by the wishes of all, he might more easily correct every corruption and evil practice.

> We have entrusted to him the dignity of governing this praetorian prefecture, so that, with God’s help, he may settle through his integrity all complaints gathered through the unfaithful practice of trading favors, and may make himself so greatly desired that he can be beneficial to everyone (Book IX, Letter 25).

The king further explains that he appointed him prefect so that he might relieve the provinces oppressed by unjust judges:

> So that the provinces, which we know have hitherto been wearied by the conduct of wicked men, may receive a proven judge without fear (Book IX, Letter 24).

And because Cassiodorus had always abstained from sordid profit, he was to repair the damage caused by avarice:

> You have indeed been accustomed not to sell justice; but now you must come more earnestly to the aid of those injured by injustice (ibid.).

What more? The king says that he who had previously provided admirable examples of restraint while holding office should now, by the incorruptible integrity of his character, eradicate and utterly remove every abuse and fraudulent practice:

> Let your incorruptible judgment keep watch against hands accustomed to wrongdoing (ibid.), and so forth.

For this reason he declares that he had placed Cassiodorus in the praetorian seat as though on a watchtower, so that no evil might escape his vigilant prudence which he could not punish or correct:

> We have brought you as a light into hidden affairs, since no one will be able either to deceive your prudence or to test your fidelity with any offering (Book IX, Letter 24).

Yet he declares that Cassiodorus should not need to be induced by any example to undertake great actions. Why do you think this was? Listen to Athalaric; he gives a remarkable explanation of this unusual matter:

> We set before you no examples of others: you have fulfilled the ancient examples through your character and the wishes of everyone (ibid.).

No one could encompass the most complete praise of a great man more briefly or more effectively than in these few but brilliant words:

> You have fulfilled the ancient examples through your character and the wishes of everyone.

## § XXXII. What, Why, and How He Wrote to Pope John II

It is remarkable how constant Christian humility always remained amid Cassiodorus’s highest praises. For as soon as he had been made praetorian prefect, he immediately wrote a supplicatory letter to Pope John II. In it he begged, as a son, that the pope pray earnestly to God on his behalf, so that he might be capable of carrying out with dignity the province and responsibilities of the state entrusted to him.

> I ask, he says (Variae, Book XI, Letter 2), that you pray more fervently, so that my mind may shun whatever is foreign to what is right; so that my intellect, illumined by heavenly light, may never depart from the truth; and finally, so that I may show myself such a judge as the Catholic Church requires.

These words could not be better set down than in his own language, engraved in lasting bronze (ibid.):

> May he open to me, your son, the sense of understanding, so that I may follow what is truly useful and avoid what must be shunned. May that rational vigor of the soul provide us with counsel; may the face of truth grow bright. Let bodily darkness not cloud our mind. Let us follow what is within, lest we be outside ourselves. May that which savors of true wisdom instruct us; may that which shines with heavenly brightness illuminate us. Finally, may public action receive such a judge as the Catholic Church sends forth as a son.

And because he professes himself not only the son but also the disciple of the supreme pontiff, he asks, in that capacity, that if he should err in carrying out his office, his teacher admonish him, so that he might correct himself more quickly.

He says that he is certain he cannot depart from what is right if he has the pope as the monitor of all his actions:

> Instruct me in what must be done; even when corrected, I desire to act well, because the sheep that longs to hear the shepherd’s voice is less likely to go astray, and the person whom a constant admonisher attends does not easily become vicious. I am indeed a judge of the palace, but I shall never cease to be your disciple.

He adds:

> We conduct these matters rightly if we depart in no way from your rules (ibid.).

Finally, with words threatening in form but most gracious in substance, he presses the pope to assist him with prayers and counsel. If he should find these lacking, whatever he did contrary to what was right in the prefecture would be chargeable to the pope:

> Since I desire from you both to be admonished by counsel and assisted by prayers, you must now be held responsible if anything in me should be found otherwise than was desired (ibid.).

He asserts that the supreme pontiff owes these things to him because he sits in the chair of Peter. Admiring its splendor and authority, he indicates how highly he regards it in these words (ibid.):

> May that seat, wondrous throughout the whole world, shelter its own devoted servants with affection. Although it has been granted to the world as a universal seat, it is known also to have been assigned locally to you.

From this he says that the pope presides over the Christian world (ibid.) by the right and authority of the pontificate:

> For you preside as watchmen over the Christian people; in the name of the Father you love all things. The security of the common people therefore looks to your reputation, since divine providence has entrusted their guardianship to you.

He closes this most Christian letter with the following words (ibid.), in which he eternally testifies to his supreme reverence for the apostles, always wishing them to be his patrons:

> We hold something belonging to the holy apostles . . . . . Therefore we fear nothing with such patrons, provided that the bishop’s prayer is not lacking.

Let whoever reads these words consider, I beg, whether the slightest suspicion of violated faith or religion could fall upon this most wise administrator of civil affairs, since we see in him such an extraordinary union of Christian piety with the office of judge.

## § XXXIII. How He Wrote an Encyclical Letter to the Bishops

In precisely the same spirit he sent an encyclical letter to the bishops, whom he calls spiritual fathers (Variae, Book XI, Letter 3). In it he asks them to beseech the most holy Trinity that, in administering his prefecture, he might always be an incorruptible and unimpeachable judge.

> You, spiritual parents, who behold the Author of all things with an illumined mind, earnestly supplicate the Holy Trinity on my behalf. May he who has deigned to confer tribunals grant integrity of conscience; may he make me an unoffending judge, lest I condemn one who has gone astray. May they obtain for me that, in my judgments, I may always behold, love, and follow God who judges. May he be most favorably present to us, so that unfortunate vices may be kept away; may he grant his love, so that, in his mercy, he may exclude the opportunity for sinning (ibid.).

He then adds a very full petition of piety, which most clearly demonstrates how great was the hope and confidence he placed in the fasts prescribed by the Church and in other exercises of stricter penitence:

> Therefore, true parents of my soul, I implore you with an affectionate petition to supplicate the Lord through the appointed fast, that he may prolong the life of our princes under a flourishing kingdom, that, as defender of the state, he may diminish its enemies, grant peaceful times, and abundant occasions for the praise of his name (ibid.).

The entire letter would have to be transcribed if I wished to disclose the innermost sentiments of piety and holiness with which Cassiodorus’s mind was moved. But since anyone may read it in full in its proper place, I think I should add only this: he urges the bishops, when praying, to love the people with the affection of paternal charity, yet without departing from the laws of the kingdom or allowing excessive indulgence to give others an opportunity to go astray. Thus, in Cassiodorus’s own words (Var. XI.3):

> Do not, through excessive piety, take away the place of the laws while you seek to aid the unfortunate. For if something has perhaps offended the strictness of the law, give such admonitions to all that you may be able to render judgments in a spirit of repose.

No one, therefore, I think, will be so captious a critic as to suppose that Cassiodorus’s dutiful loyalty in serving a corrupt and Arian ruler deserves condemnation, since he is nowhere found to have violated the integrity of religion or conscience so long as he remained faithfully attached to him.

[Col. 0454B] § XXXIV. How the Supreme Pontiff Replied to Senator. It is not recorded what letters either the Supreme Pontiff or the bishops sent in reply to Cassiodorus. If there are any, they doubtless extend at considerable length in his praise. Yet he again directed a letter to John II, in order to induce him to explain all the mysteries of the Catholic religion. This may be inferred from the letter of Pope John to Cassiodorus, preserved by Baronius (Annals, A.D. 534), written at the request and urging of several senators, in which he expounds at greater length the orthodox faith concerning the most holy Trinity.

§ XXXV. Cassiodorus’s Letter to the Senate and His Edicts to the Other Magistrates. Before writing to Pope John and the bishops, M. Senator sent a letter to the Senate filled with expressions of grateful feeling, because he had been requested by the Fathers to assume the praetorian prefecture; and he showed himself especially mindful of the benefits received from those who had deserved well of him. But he also proved himself an ardent lover of justice in letters separately addressed (Var. II.1) to the magistrates and judges of the provinces, and in an edict promulgated throughout the provinces he earnestly admonished them to regulate their conduct carefully according to the straight rule of virtue:

> All of you, devote yourselves to good actions; always conduct yourselves innocently (XI.8).

He adds that they must not, driven by greed for money, seek unjust profits through unjust causes:

> Why do you confuse honorable dealings with lawsuits? If you seek profits, avoid rather ruinous litigation (ibid.).

In the same letter he declares that he will conduct everything according to the laws of equity:

> Promise all men justice, all moderation; for no disgraceful trafficking will be known to me: my words are not hung up for sale like garments.

He promises that no one will suffer injury or loss at the hands of the praetorian officials, since he has taken precautions lest they unjustly demand money under the false pretext of official duty or expenses:

> No soldier shall extort anything from you at his own pleasure; no collector shall burden you with additional inconveniences. We have kept safe not only our own hands, but also those of our office, from wrongdoing.

He then explains why he has confirmed these principles not merely by words but above all by his own example:

> With God’s help, we have displayed self-restraint, so that we may command it without shame.

He further promises that the advancement so long desired by him will increase the public welfare, not diminish private fortunes, and that each person will be free to plead his own cause without payment, without purchasing another’s patronage, and without purchased eloquence:

> Our administration will look solely to the public advantage, not to private thefts … the originator of a cause, without having redeemed it, will use his own tongue. No one will return from us less wealthy than when he came.

Finally, he implores them to approach right counsel and the purpose of preserving justice with united minds, so that he may show himself a father rather than a judge:

> Devote yourselves to all your duties, so that you may make me the father of the provinces rather than their judge.

He issued another edict to the provincial judges, so splendidly illuminated with maxims and so filled with pious instruction that one might suppose it had been dictated by a bishop of the Church rather than by a prefect of the palace. It would take too long to reproduce every part here; nevertheless, we cannot omit the passage in which he addresses the judges placed under his authority (XI.9):

> Know that judgment is so called as if it were “jurisdiction.” It is not fitting for a governor to do what another person accuses him of doing. What should a defendant fear when he sees the crime established in the symbols of office?

§ XXXVI. What Senator Wrote to John and Ambrose. In writing to each magistrate, Senator exhorted them to observe equity with such force of language and such vigor of mind that no one can sufficiently wonder at his ardent devotion to justice—justice alone seemed to animate him, and to it alone he appeared to have devoted himself entirely from childhood. Indeed, no one demanded from those whom he had appointed as his chancellors a readier willingness in carrying out instructions or more incorruptible fidelity in reporting the petitions of supplicants; no one more strictly forbade them to stain their hands with money or gifts; no one more earnestly commanded them to discharge the office entrusted to them in such a way that the outstanding equity both of the chancellors and of the praetorian prefect might be approved by all.

This is clearly evident in his letter to John (Var. XI.6):

> Through you, let the desire of the suppliant become known to our ears; carry out our commands without any spirit of venality. Conduct everything in such a way that you may commend our justice, and so forth.

He specifically identifies what John must perform in office and commands him carefully to consider how attentive he ought to be to these instructions, lest he displease anyone or be criticized for having been advanced by him to this rank of public honor. In almost the same terms he writes (XI.5) to Ambrose, who was acting as his representative at Rome, urging him not to spare himself in securing the peace of the peoples. He adds that Ambrose must not be unaware how greatly the negligence of judges harms the laws of justice, and commands him to ensure that justice be restored to its proper splendor:

> May your labor secure peace for all. You know what disgrace neglect has brought about: the place where another stumbled must be avoided (ibid.).

§ XXXVII. Senator’s Edicts and His Concern That Taxes Should Not Burden the Peoples. Taxes seemed to give collectors an opportunity to violate the laws of equity with impunity. This matter deeply disturbed the prefect and moved him to drive such license far away. Accordingly, in written letters he admonished the provincial judges to act more severely against those who transgressed in this matter, and commanded that a landholder pay nothing except what was publicly owed.

He very carefully prescribed the times at which each tax was to be paid, lest fraudulent and commercially motivated delay should impose the burden of an abominable bargain rather than relieve such obligations:

> Let detestable and avoidable cunning be far from our times. Just as we do not wish fiscal burdens to be increased on any pretext, so, at the appointed times, we command that the prescribed payments be completed, with God’s help (XI.7).

He condemns these impious profits in the clearest terms (ibid.):

> Profit is made through equity rather than rapacity. For what, indeed—an aureate saying—is thought to be gained where a good conscience is lost? Or in what respect can a person prosper if he is proved to have lost his innocence? Do not suppose that what seems to belong to a good conscience will go without reward.

And, in order to encourage the judges whom he so sharply admonished to be faithful observers of justice, he promises that he will reward generously anyone whom he discovers to have been especially steadfast in justice while fulfilling his office:

> I promise to be a rewarder of the man whom I discover to have treated some matter with integrity (ibid.).

§ XXXVIII. Cassiodorus’s Same Concern in Matters of Lesser Importance. Let us now consider how upright Senator’s mind was in its love of justice, since he went so far as to promote the public welfare even in matters of lesser importance. For this reason he ordered, in two edicts (Var. XI.11), that a moderate price limit be imposed upon grain, fearing that the poorer classes might be oppressed by the monstrous greed of the buyers.

In the first edict he provided that goods should be sold at a just price. And, lest the words of the edict be twisted to some alien meaning, he removed every ambiguity by requiring each individual kind of merchandise to conform to an equal standard of weight; he also enacted, in language immediately clear to everyone, under threat of the gravest punishment, that no one should dare anywhere to lower or raise the price he had established.

In the second edict he took precautions that innkeepers should not exceed the fair public price in receiving guests:

> Let a guest be received at the stipulated prices; let one invited as a favor not suffer greedy unfairness.

He subjected violators of this decree to the same penalties that he prescribed for preserving the first edict. And, so that no one would be left with any ground for complaint, he assigned a praetorian soldier to public eating-houses and inns, so that, together with the leading citizens and bishops, he might establish the price of grain. Thus he writes:

> Our soldier, assigned to this task, shall determine the prices after taking counsel with the citizens and the bishops of the places concerned.

Nor should we omit the reason he adds:

> Honest profits from citizens ought to suffice for everyone, lest the roads seem rather to be beset by robbers.

We must therefore acknowledge that he was most devoted to justice, as is demonstrated by the laws, edicts, and decrees he enacted to have justice administered and preserved in every individual matter. And although he was wholly disposed toward humanity, when zeal for equity moved him, he sometimes inclined his mind toward severity. Yet, in his ardor for justice, this prudent man joined such even-tempered moderation to paternal love for his subjects that he would personally examine matters involving some difficulty, or refer them only to the bishops, who are spiritual Fathers.

§ XXXIX. Cassiodorus Comes to the Aid of Rome Suffering from Famine. He gave especially admirable evidence of his love for his fellow citizens when Rome was suffering from an extreme shortage of grain. As soon as he learned of it, he devoted all his attention to relieving the city’s distress, undertaking every possible effort to remedy the public calamity as quickly as possible, even by embarking upon a long and arduous journey. He testifies to this himself in writing to Ambrose, who was acting as his representative in the City (Var. XI.5):

> We entered upon the hardships of travel and so many anxious thoughts for this reason: so that that people, accustomed in the most blessed times of former rulers to ancient pleasures, might enjoy relief from its necessities.

The reason he gives makes it perfectly clear with what paternal affection he cherished the inhabitants of Rome, mistress of the world, exhausted by hunger. He says (ibid.):

> Far be it from us that we should be satisfied while any of that city is hungry; their need, God forbid, is our want.

What more is there to say? He continues:

> We cannot be happy unless we hear that they too are rejoicing with us.

Who has ever expressed in more ardent words the astonishing love felt by those whose affection for the commonwealth earned them the most glorious name of “Father of the People”?

And, so that he might meet the extreme poverty of all the citizens as fully as he desired, the provident prefect arranged for such a quantity of grain to be transported into the City that its happy abundance might enrich the poverty of the unfortunate. Accordingly, he instructed Ambrose (ibid.) to gather grain of such unimpaired freshness that bread baked from it might seem intended not for disgust but for enjoyment.

Since he foresaw that soldiers and transporters might fraudulently obtain some profit from the grain exported, beyond the established price, and that the people might thereby suffer some loss, he ordered Ambrose, acting in the City in the prefect’s place, to prevent this harm as carefully as his authority allowed:

> Whatever is wrongly undertaken there makes an assault upon the injury of my own mind (ibid.).

He adds, as an expression of his supreme goodwill toward the Roman people:

> We more readily allow ourselves to exceed the proper measure than tolerate any diminution of the Romans’ interests.

He nevertheless denies that he is caring for Roman affairs in order to win popular favor, but rather so that he may demonstrate, through a dutiful expression of love, his inclination and desire toward those entrusted to him:

> Not for favor, or popular applause, but so that, with God’s help, I may fulfill my chosen affection for them (ibid.).

The following words sufficiently indicate how far he was from the pursuit of human approval. He says that it was accomplished not by his own foresight but by the prayers and tears of good men, so that Rome might no longer be oppressed by the harsh sufferings of hunger. Thus he writes to Pope John II (XI.2):

> Hunger among the people has been driven away by ecclesiastical fasts; ugly sadness has departed through tears of reverence; and through holy men it has been hastened that what was burdensome should not be prolonged.

§ XL. In What Year Athalaric Died, How Theodahad Succeeded Him, and How Great Cassiodorus’s Constancy Then Was. While Cassiodorus was administering the prefecture so admirably, Athalaric’s death caused him immense grief. The youthful king died unexpectedly in the very flower of his age, when he was entering his sixteenth year and the eighth year of his reign. The harsh condition of premature death spared neither the flourishing age of the prince nor the dignity of royalty. Cassiodorus then saw the face of the kingdom overturned for the third time; nevertheless, no change of circumstances weakened the steadfast constancy—or even the fortune—of that great soul.

Theodahad, Amalasuntha’s cousin, was substituted for Athalaric in the kingdom by Amalasuntha around the middle or end of the year 534. This is easily established from Cassiodorus’s letters (Var. X.6–7). Theodahad appointed Patricius quaestor in the thirteenth indiction, which fell in the year 535; but in the preceding year, that is, 534, Athalaric had appointed Cassiodorus praetorian prefect in the twelfth indiction, in which Athalaric himself consequently died.

§ XLI. What Cassiodorus Did at the Beginning of Theodahad’s Reign. The new prince, aware of how greatly Senator had aided his predecessors by his work and counsel, resolved to employ that outstanding man in directing affairs, believing that he would not withdraw from the obedience and services by which he had served Theodoric and Athalaric. Accordingly, as soon as he assumed the administration of the kingdom, in addition to the dignities he had already obtained and continued to hold, he wished to have him serve as an assistant in letters sent to the emperor Justinian, to the Senate, and to various others.

In this capacity Cassiodorus wrote in the name of Queen Amalasuntha to the same emperor and to the senators, asking them to honor the election of King Theodahad made by her with their support and authority. He also lent his hand at various times to letters written by Gudelina, Theodahad’s wife, to Justinian and the Empress Theodora, letters intended to reconcile the emperor and Theodahad after their broken alliance.

Theodahad had rightly fallen under suspicion because of the murder inflicted upon Amalasuntha, through whose favor he held the government of the kingdom. For this reason he seriously offended the emperor Justinian, who had always honored the queen with exceptional distinction and knew her to be adorned with extraordinary gifts surpassing those usually associated with her sex.

What moved Theodahad to commit such a crime is not readily apparent. Perhaps he could not endure a partner in the kingdom, or perhaps, remembering the injury Amalasuntha had inflicted upon him shortly before she raised him to royal power, he did not fear to stain his impious hands with royal blood. Whatever the case, Cassiodorus had repeatedly experienced that queen’s very great devotion toward himself, and there is no doubt that he was struck by incredible grief at her extinction in so pitiable a manner. Nevertheless, he was eventually compelled to place a limit upon grief for which he knew no remedy now remained.

§ XLII. Cassiodorus’s Third Administration as Praetorian Prefect and His Moderation in Collecting Taxes. Theodahad, now master of affairs, therefore appointed Senator praetorian prefect for the third time. It is not sufficiently clear, however, whether he held this dignity under that king for one year or for several. The matter is obscured by the differing opinions of authors, who do not agree about the time of Pope Agapitus’s pontificate or of his embassy to Justinian. Nevertheless, if we follow our customary method and settle the whole matter from Cassiodorus’s writings, Letter 35 of Book II and Letter 2 of Book XII, dated in the thirteenth indiction, clearly indicate that he was praetorian prefect in the year 535.

The death of Queen Amalasuntha provoked the Goths to seditious disturbances and the emperor to seek revenge for so great a crime by war. Theodahad, unused to arms and terrified by the impending burden of battles, had sought peace from Justinian by every possible means, but in vain. Thus, in that year, Mundus invaded Dalmatia and Belisarius Sicily. To resist them, the king first ordered his subjects to pay taxes for the expenses of war, and he entrusted to Senator the extremely difficult task of collecting money from barbarous peoples hostile to their own ruler.

That command seemed harsh to a man so devoted to the peoples and so respectful of Theodahad. Nevertheless, he bore the burden with such skill that he aroused the greatest admiration in everyone and offended no one; indeed, his success was such that he gave God the greatest thanks he could for an outcome beyond hope. He begins the second letter of Book XII in these words:

> I give thanks to the Divinity, because the provincials did what I advised and I fulfilled everything I promised.

He then commends his own integrity and that of his associates in collecting the taxes, saying that the peoples found their judges kindly disposed; that he compelled no one to give what he was not bound to offer; that he caused the terrors of former times to be forgotten; and that no one had been afflicted by him, either publicly or privately.

He adds that no excuse can be accepted from a judge who withdraws from his duty; that nothing base or covetous becomes a judge; that a judge mounts the tribunal so that he may be raised by the steps of moral character; and that a judge’s blemishes become conspicuous if he himself, upon whom many look, is stained by any fault.

Afterward he addresses those from whom the taxes had been demanded—not with harsh, threatening, or insulting words, but with gentle and dutiful language announcing the equity that must be preserved toward all:

> Let the landholder willingly offer me the public monies; I will pay him his taxes in the assembly of justice.

§ XLIII. He Attempts to Establish Sacred Schools at Rome. We have just seen with what concern Cassiodorus served the interests of the ruler and his subjects. But just as he acknowledged the Creator himself to be far greater than the things created, so he always judged the interests of the Church of God to be preferred to all other business.

We possess the richest testimony to this. Senator feared that the many vicissitudes of the Gothic kingdom and the wars in Italy would eventually drive divine and ecclesiastical learning out of Rome, replacing it with the barbarism of peoples who themselves recoiled from the very names of peace and literature. Therefore he left no stone unturned, together with Pope Agapitus, to establish schools for the exposition of the sacred Scriptures.

Yet he experienced especially at that time how much more difficult it generally is to accomplish plans in proportion to the benefit they promise. The disturbances in Italy prevented this project, as he himself states in the preface to his book *On Divine Letters*:

> I attempted, together with the most blessed Agapitus, bishop of the city of Rome, to arrange that, just as it is reported that such an institution existed for a long time at Alexandria, and as the Hebrews are diligently said even now to expound the Scriptures in the city of Nisibis among the Syrians, so in the city of Rome, with expenses provided jointly, Christian schools might receive teachers of recognized learning, from which the soul might receive eternal salvation and the language of the faithful be adorned with chaste and most pure eloquence. But since, because of the wars then raging and the excessively turbulent struggles in the Italian kingdom, my desire could in no way be fulfilled—since peaceful undertakings find no place in troubled times—I have been compelled to this by divine charity, as is shown … .

How could that most pious son have raised the glory of the Bride of Christ, the Church, more exaltedly than by providing for the sacred education of young men, so that, adorned with the lights of every branch of learning, they might one day render the most useful service to their mother?

Although such a right and holy desire could not then be fulfilled because wars were raging everywhere, it could eventually be fulfilled in the monastery of Vivarium, where we shall see that sacred schools were opened by Cassiodorus the abbot.

§ XLIV. When Agapitus Went to Constantinople and How Cassiodorus Arranged for the Return of the Sacred Vessels. While Senator was laudably occupied with settling the affairs of the Empire and the Church, he devoted himself entirely to keeping war away from the borders of Theodahad’s kingdom. That unwarlike prince had long pleaded with the emperor for peace; but, observing that his efforts were fruitless, he induced Agapitus, the Supreme Pontiff, to travel to Constantinople and meet Justinian, so that the emperor might at least grant, through the prayers of Christ’s Vicar, what the king himself had been unable by any means to obtain.

Some writers believe that the pope departed at the very beginning of Theodahad’s reign. This is certainly false, since Cassiodorus’s letters and Procopius testify that the king had held several discussions with the emperor through ambassadors before Agapitus’s departure. Whatever the case, it is certain that Senator was administering the praetorian prefecture at that time. If he could not prevent Theodahad from deciding to send Agapitus to Constantinople, he certainly performed every duty of piety toward the most holy legate.

Compelled to obey the king’s will, Agapitus first attempted, before undertaking the journey, to obtain the money necessary for his embassy, but in vain, so completely exhausted was the treasury of the Roman Church. He therefore pledged the sacred vessels to the treasury. M. Cassiodorus, deeply moved by the stain of such disgrace inflicted upon the Church under the appearance of promoting its welfare, and stirred by religious zeal in virtue of his official authority, finally obtained from the king—otherwise exceedingly greedy for money—the return of the holy vessels deposited in the royal treasury, so that they might be restored to the church of Saint Peter.

He immediately wrote to Thomas and Peter, who were in charge of the royal funds, ordering them to return both the sacred vessels and the document of pledge (Var. XII.20):

> Therefore, having been warned by our command and made secure by the royal order, return without any delay the vessels of the saints, together with the document of pledge, to the representatives of Saint Peter the Apostle.

In this action he was considered worthy of far greater esteem because he wished the entire praise he had earned to be attributed to the king. For in the same letter he indicates that Theodahad had shown himself far more observant of Christian piety than Alaric: Alaric, although he had enriched himself by so great a devastation of the City, had refused to seize the vessels of the revered saints; Theodahad, by contrast, had religiously returned vessels that had seemingly become his own by right of pledge.

Cassiodorus brought forward this example of piety as especially worthy of remembrance. He was accustomed to transfer to the best uses the honor of his dignity and the favor he enjoyed in the highest degree with the ruler. Since he could not have employed the authority granted him by God’s favor more usefully or more gloriously for the increase of his own reputation than for the benefit of the Church, he nevertheless restrained himself with such moderation that he wished to be regarded not merely as the author of so great a good, but not even as a participant in it.

§ XLV. Cassiodorus’s Piety Toward Certain Nuns. He gave another demonstration of extraordinary piety by assisting certain nuns who had no means with which to pay their tax, because their fields had been damaged by the untimely flooding of overflowing waters.

The religious women appealed to Justinian, asking him to exercise his authority with Theodahad on their behalf. The emperor heard their prayers and sent a supplicatory letter to the king for this purpose. Moved by it, the king immediately wrote to Senator (X.26), instructing him, as part of his official duty, to examine the matter and, if the nuns were suffering any injustice, to release them entirely from the burden of the tax imposed upon them.

Such powerful incentives were scarcely necessary to incite Cassiodorus, renowned for his piety, to display his innate generosity toward consecrated virgins. The more deeply he revered their purpose of holiness, the more generous and beneficent he was toward them. Indeed, everyone will readily understand with what singular affection our prefect aided the nuns, provided that he remembers his paternal love in relieving the Romans, who were almost perishing from the scarcity of grain, and also knows with what concern he brought timely aid to the poverty of the Ligurians, Milanese, and Venetians oppressed by hunger, importing an abundant supply of grain.

§ XLVI. In What Year Famine Afflicted Liguria and the Neighboring Provinces. Authors are divided into various factions when they attempt to determine the precise time at which poverty afflicted the province of Aemilia. If we believe Baronius, it was in the same year—namely 534—that the Milanese suffered, while the Romans were being oppressed.

Some assign it to the year 537 and assert that Cassiodorus then wrote to Datius, bishop of Milan, for this reason alone. But, to state frankly what I think, I cannot agree with Baronius when he maintains that this famine occurred while Athalaric was ruling, since we see that it occurred under King Theodahad, while Cassiodorus was praetorian prefect.

Theodahad sent a letter to our Senator, already invested with this dignity, which appears as the twenty-seventh letter of Book X. In it he ordered grain to be transported from Ticinum and Dertona into Liguria, and from elsewhere into Venetia. In printed books the title prefixed to this letter reads “To Honorius, Prefect”; but from certain editions, in which the margin reads “To Senator, Praetorian Prefect,” it may be concluded that an error has entered the text.

The manuscripts I have seen clearly indicate the same mistake: they read “To Senator, Praetorian Prefect.” Moreover, Honorius was then prefect at Rome, as is clear from Letter 30 of Book X; responsibility for distant provinces such as Liguria was therefore not his.

Finally, in the same sense in which Theodahad wrote to Datius, bishop of Milan, or at least in accordance with Theodahad’s command as set out in the first part of the royal letter, Senator wrote that grain should be withdrawn from the storehouses of Ticinum and Dertona to relieve the Milanese in their poverty. He also provided for the Venetians, as the king had ordered, as may be read in Letters 26 and 27 of Book XII.

§ XLVII. How He Relieved the Provinces Suffering from Famine. But why should we linger any longer over identifying the time of the scarcity, when we must rather understand how earnestly the prefect labored to meet the calamity of those upon whom the hand of the chastising God weighed so heavily?

When he learned from Augustine how severely the Venetians were oppressed by hunger and want, he immediately wished provision to be made for them in such a way that they could suffer not even the slightest loss from the increasing scarcity of grain. He not only arranged for the greatest possible supply of grain to be furnished to them, but also ordered that all their taxes be remitted with the utmost generosity.

For, as he himself says (Var. XII.26), it seemed cruel to him to demand anything from those who were begging and then expect to receive what the province was known to need. He immediately adds this brilliant explanation of his humanity:

> From such people he demands only tears—the man who imposes what cannot be found.

The vigilant Senator knew that Datius burned with such ardent zeal of charity toward the sheep entrusted to him that no one could care for their interests with greater affection. He therefore wrote to him, asking him to distribute among the needy the grain collected from the cities of Ticinum and Dertona.

He began the letter with this splendid opening (XII.27):

> It is less useful to command a good deed unless we wish to accomplish it through most holy men.

Then, in the matter most relevant to our subject, he asks that nothing be done fraudulently:

> It seemed right to assist the needy, not the wealthy. Therefore we have arranged for two praetorian soldiers to be assigned to this task. Obeying the directions of Your Holiness, they shall do nothing on their own authority.

Finally, aware of the reverence with which bishops must be treated, he asks pardon for appearing to use the service of so great a man too freely:

> Therefore let Your Holiness not regard the duties of compassion as an insult, since everything is worthy of you wherever piety is found.

Nor was he content merely to have provided, with admirable vigilance, for so many provinces in distress. He sent an edict to the Ligurians (XII.28), whom a more severe famine was oppressing, and refreshed them with pleasant consolation by praising the piety of their ruler: he had compensated the poverty of his subjects with such abundant generosity that they seemed not to have experienced the hardships of scarcity.

He goes further in praising the king, whom he does not hesitate to compare with the patriarch Joseph. Indeed, he tries to show Theodahad as more humane than Joseph: Joseph had helped the Egyptians during a difficult period of want, but the king supplied an abundance of grain and added a remission of taxes.

> With respect to so great a father, let me say that it is far more excellent to sell grain while preserving freedom and to remit taxes out of indulgence.

He adds still greater praise by confidently asserting that Theodahad had given more to all his subjects than Joseph had given to his brothers:

> This man, Theodahad, has bestowed more generally upon those liable to taxes than that man, Joseph, appears to have given to his brothers alone.

Yet Senator modestly records that this indulgence had been granted by the ruler at his own request. I think this is why we read in Letter 28 of Book X that Theodahad granted Cassiodorus permission to regulate the price of goods with just moderation because of the high price of grain. He transformed this generosity of the ruler into an advantage for the common people, with such liberality that he remitted the taxes entirely, and with such humility that he took from himself the praise properly belonging to the deed and transferred it to another.

§ XLVIII. How He Provided Against Impending Scarcity. He not only drove scarcity away while it was present, but also anticipated its approach through shrewd foresight. For this reason, inferring that the fields would be barren in the future because of severe weather and difficult seasons, he wrote to Ambrose and ordered him to store in the granaries the abundant supply of grain gathered in the previous year, so that it might benefit the scarcity of the following year (XII.25):

> And therefore, let your prudence overcome future want with the old harvest, since the fruitful abundance of the past year was so great that what has been stored will suffice even for the coming months.

Anyone who reads this letter in full will not cease to marvel at Senator’s tireless concern for the peoples whom he embraced with the same affection with which a father embraces his children. He supplied food to the hungry and money to the needy. Thus, for the Ligurians, he ordered one hundred pounds of gold to be distributed (XI.15):

> In caring for the needs of devoted Liguria, our most glorious lords have, through that man and the other, in their customary piety, assigned one hundred pounds of gold. Let each person, in accordance with your judgment—for you know the circumstances thoroughly—rejoice in receiving as much of this gift as he is known to be burdened by necessity.

[Col. 0461C] XLIX. He Punished Those Who Plundered Church Property. We must acknowledge that Cassiodorus possessed truly paternal piety. The tenderness of his affection made him admirable, but his kindness was not corrupted by a culpable indulgence toward crimes. This is clearly proved by the law, or edict, promulgated against those who plundered Church property. In it he ordered that they be punished with greater severity, their fortunes assigned to the treasury, and they themselves stripped of every office.

He adds a memorable reason (XII.13), and one that testifies to his exceptional zeal in protecting the Church’s property:

> It surpasses every cruelty to wish to become rich from the poverty of a beggar.

He shows that the resources of the Church were not purchased with gold but, like a gift to a beggar, freely granted through the pious generosity of the faithful. Then he adds with great force:

> Whoever can assist people suffering such hunger, but does not feed them, destroys them.

§ L. What Dignities Cassiodorus Held under Vitiges, Who Succeeded Theodahad after His Murder. These works of Christian piety did not turn the compassionate man away from his duties, despite the injustice of the times and the deadly fury of the wars by which almost the whole of Italy was shaken. The exceedingly warlike Belisarius was pressing Theodahad fiercely, and the Goths, forming a conspiracy, removed him with an impious sword. They alleged his cowardice and weakness in repelling the strength of the enemy; in his place they installed Vitiges, who had been raised upon shields according to military custom, as may be gathered from Letter 31 of Book X of the *Variae*.

Vitiges the king honored Cassiodorus with the same distinctions that his predecessors had bestowed upon him. When he found him praetorian prefect, appointed by Theodahad in the year 537, he wished him not only to administer that dignity for the remainder of the year, but also to write letters through him to his subjects, announcing that he had been elected king with the support of the soldiers; to the emperor, requesting peace from him; to the bishops, commending himself to their prayers; and to several others concerning other matters.

In the year 538, Vitiges again placed M. Senator in the praetorian office, as Letters 16 and 22 of Book XII indicate; they are marked with the first indiction, corresponding to that year. Yet even then the king wished him to be free from the heavier cares of the quaestorship, as is indicated by the preface to the *Variae*, which he was writing at that time. There he speaks of the burden of the affairs pressing upon him:

> We add also that, being frequently burdened by the duties of the quaestorship, and so forth.

§ LI. How rightly he administered the praetorian prefecture under Vitigis

Before embracing the monastic way of life, he held the dignity of praetorian prefect for the last time, after being tested by almost immeasurable labors. For King Vitigis was pressing all Italy with the vast forces he was setting against the strength of Belisarius. Thus, besides the other burdens of his office, Senator had to take particular care that the soldiers inflicted no damage, that tribute was paid without undue hardship, that he could raise money to maintain so many troops without harassing the provinces, and finally that the laws—which ordinarily fall silent amid arms—were observed as circumstances and times permitted.

Overwhelmed by so many cares and weighed down by so great a burden of affairs, [Col. 0462B] some obscure and feeble spirit would surely have failed; but Cassiodorus, upright and prepared for great things, preserved amid so many difficult and troublesome responsibilities a firm and solid strength of mind. Indeed, in that final year during which he held the prefecture, this man distinguished for integrity seems to have scattered the purer rays of virtue in the manner of a brilliant star, whose radiance shines more splendidly the nearer it approaches sunset.

§ LII. He defended the Bruttii and Lucania from the harassment of the soldiers

Meanwhile the army of Vitigis was laying waste to the Bruttii and Lucania. When he heard this, the prefect’s extraordinary prudence immediately provided for them with such equity that neither the soldiers were left in want nor the inhabitants burdened: the former received the pay required for them, while part of the taxes was remitted to the latter.

“So that neither the proprietor may suffer losses nor the hard-pressed army endure want” (Book X, Letter 5).

Moreover, if the soldiers committed any offense, he ordered their officers to repair the damage and injury inflicted, and above all commanded them to be most scrupulous in observing military discipline (ibid.):

“Let them preserve discipline, from which the army is armed with greater strength.”

He also admonished the magistrates to restrain the citizens within the limits of their office and to keep the rustic and stubborn-minded from disturbance and sedition:

“So that, while the army of the Goths is waging war, the Roman people may remain at peace” (ibid.). [Col. 0462C]

§ LIII. How he provided for the tranquillity of the kingdom

Such was the bitter condition of the times that the Italians would easily have defected from the king to Belisarius, had the most watchful vigilance of M. Cassiodorus not foreseen what was coming and averted the rebellion of the peoples. Therefore, writing to the judges and magistrates, he says (ibid.):

“Restrain the intemperate movements of the landowners; let those whom no one drives headlong into uncertainties love quiet.”

And lest the plague of vice should spread with excessive license, “Let there be strength in the judges drawn from the laws,” he continues (ibid); “let the benches never cease thundering the laws against evil customs.” For this eminent man knew that a safe and tranquil peace is maintained when all are kept within their proper duties and the movements and attempts of the wicked are prevented. He therefore adds (ibid.):

“You will make everything peaceful if you suppress the leaders of crimes.”

And to inflame their spirits more ardently toward these duties, he adds that men of moderate ability may be able to sustain the administration of the provinces while peaceful times prevail; but amid the tumult of wars, that exceedingly demanding office could scarcely be borne except by men of uncommon ability and proven expertise.

Yet what he adds must certainly be remembered, as evidence of a virtue worthy of Cassiodorus: although he was otherwise a man of the highest dignity and authority, he did not wish his own people to be treated more gently than anyone else. For, he says (ibid.):

“My private concern slipped away from me once I began to consider the general safeguard. I wish well to my own people, but only in what can be common to all; for it is a great kind of injustice to wish for oneself a judge whom the community as a whole could not endure.”

§ LIV. How he wished the judges appointed under him to observe the laws of justice

It would take too long to pursue in greater detail Cassiodorus’ equity, which he required to be diligently practiced not only by the judges of the Bruttii and Lucania but also by all those whom he benefited by assigning them some office. Yet I considered it wrong to pass over what he wrote to one of his chancellors in these words (Book XII, Letter 1):

“Let your person be a refuge for the oppressed, a defense for the weak, a protection for one enclosed by some calamity. For you truly discharge the duties of our chancery if you break open the impious barriers of the injured.”

He then admonishes him (ibid.), more in the manner of an ecclesiastical preacher seeking to persuade than of a praetorian judge exercising authority, never to allow himself to be touched by the contagion of greed:

“Flee that queen of shameless vices, greed, to which all crimes serve with detestable devotion. Once it has entered a man’s breast, it admits in a body the treacherous cohorts as well. It cannot be endured once received, because it does not know how to be solitary. It has a most flattering procession; it takes up weapons from its talents, and through sweetness overcomes those whom it captures by bitter deception.”

With the same ardor of mind he always exhorted each administrator of justice to show such incorruptible fidelity in cultivating it that no one would disapprove of the magistrates whom Cassiodorus appointed to administer judgments. Thus Senator says to them (Book XII, Letter 6): [Col. 0463B]

“Return this favor to my judgment: since I have not burdened you with any personal recommendation, strive to ensure that my actions are praised in you.”

And in golden words he shows how much good they would bring both to themselves and to the commonwealth if, once all fear of injury had been removed and equity always preserved, they would serve the public interest:

“Serve the public welfare with steadfastness, since no private misfortunes will shake you” (ibid.).

He says that he repeated this exhortation frequently (Book XII, Letter 2), “because this is what we are required to say in our annual address, since there is no satiety in good things.”

§ LV. Cassiodorus’ moderation in collecting taxes and his generosity in rewarding his praetorian officials

I think the necessities of the times must be credited with the fact that he sometimes ordered the money owed to the treasury, and the money assessed for maintaining the royal armies, to be collected somewhat more rigorously by a fixed deadline. Yet he tempered his command with such kindness of spirit that he became more acceptable to the peoples and each person paid the tax imposed upon him more willingly.

On this matter Book XII, Letter 16 should be read, [Col. 0463C] where he clearly shows that necessity compelled him to demand the taxes again, but on the condition that the time for collection not be anticipated and that no one be forced to pay an unjust levy.

And how far he was from inflicting harm upon anyone is evident from the fact that he never failed eagerly to seize opportunities given him for aiding the provinces. The Bruttii are witnesses, and Lucania is a witness: he remitted half their assessment. The city of Rhegium is a witness, toward which we learn that this most generous man employed the same indulgence.

Indeed, the generosity of our prefect went so far that he even took pains to restore certain private estates and possessions afflicted by misfortune, entirely remitting the tax assessed upon them (Variarum, Book XII, Letter 7). And when he learned that the territory of Istria had produced a richer harvest than usual, we read that he sent money to its inhabitants so that they might gather the fruits more easily (Book XII, Letter 12).

What more? Anyone who examines Letters 36 and 37 of Book XI will readily perceive how ample were the rewards he bestowed upon his soldiers and upon other servants of the praetorian office. There he fixed no definite sum of money for the chief secretary; rather, he ordered him to receive as much payment as would allow him to enjoy the fruits of his just labors and his descendants to take from his example an instance of voluntary service, knowing that he had been well treated for his loyalty.

What else, indeed, would one expect from a most generous prefect, who seemed born solely to bestow benefits upon individuals with a liberal hand, who declared it most equitable that those who serve the public interest should receive the wages of their labor?

§ LVI. He grants freedom to those bound and confined in prison

It remained for the matter itself to prove how pious and kind he was. Some experienced this happily: they had been detained in prisons and chains, and, moved by a compassionate sense of pity, he ordered them to be released.

“The integrity of judges,” he said, “must indeed pursue the punishment of crimes at all times; but on the more solemn festivals it is fitting to be more inclined toward pardon than toward punishment, so that we may reach the Redeemer of all by the path of remission” (Book XI, Letter 40).

Then, in language adorned with such splendid and elaborate eloquence, he addresses indulgence itself by apostrophe that one is tempted to recount each of his words here. But lest we seem excessively long-winded to our readers, we shall quote several sentences from the longer course of his speech.

“Hail, indulgence,” he says (ibid.), “which releases even governors. Who does not need your gift, since to sin is common to all? By forgiving others, we spare ourselves.”

Then he addresses the guilty who have been released from their chains, urging them not to turn the benefit of life granted by the judge’s clemency into license for sinning, but rather to lay aside the ruined morals and perverse way of life that had delivered them to prison and death, and that would have caused them to pay the penalty due for their crimes had indulgence itself not intervened:

“You ought to hate what handed you over to death” (ibid.).

Afterward he concludes his speech with this saying: not only are the guilty bound by chains, but every human being suffers dangerous bonds [Col. 0464B] from which it is fitting that we be freed, so that, just as we are bound by nature, we may rejoice in the freedom of heavenly grace:

“Let the prison-bars release the guilty; let the bonds of wicked thought set us free” (ibid.).

§ LVII. He writes the books of the *Variarum*

Finally, we must especially consider that, although he was burdened with weightier cares and was granted not even the moments of the hours—for, as he himself says (in the first preface to the *Variarum*), “while one person increases his burden through the frequency of envious interruption, another chastises him with the weight of misery, and another surrounds him with the furious sedition of disputes; while even the nights themselves are encircled by inexplicable anxiety lest the cities lack provisions”—while, in a word, he was weighed down by the immense burden of the praetorian prefecture, his friends asked him to publish the various letters that he had written under the emperors or at the command of kings, through whose favor and beneficence he had been raised to the highest offices of the kingdom.

Cassiodorus could rightly have excused himself, without offending any of his friends, from those immense cares and from that heavy mass of affairs [Col. 0464C] with which he was then burdened. Nevertheless, out of his benevolence toward all, he published twelve books of letters, which he entitled *Variarum*, because of the varied subjects of affairs contained in them.

In the first five books he included letters and edicts that he wrote under Theodoric; in the eighth, ninth, and tenth, those that he wrote under Athalaric, Theodahad, and Vitigis; the sixth and seventh contain formulas of dignities that were in use under Gothic rule; and the eleventh and twelfth contain letters and decrees collected from those that he himself sent to various persons while presiding over the praetorian office.
