In collecting the letters he followed no order other than to place together those that he had written under each individual king. Similarly, he gathered into one collection those that he sent as praetorian prefect to different people, disregarding the time at which each had been written.

This is clear from the following example, which is sufficient to prove the point. Letter 20 of Book XII, addressed to Thomaces and Peter for the purpose of restoring the sacred vessels that Pope Agapetus had assigned to the treasury, is found placed before Letter 16 of the same Book XII, written under the first indiction—that is, in the year 538—although he wrote to Thomaces and Peter no later than the year 536. [Col. 0464D]

§ LVIII. He writes the book *On the Soul*

He had scarcely completed this collection of the *Variarum* when, at the repeated request of his friends, he wrote a book *On the Soul and Its Virtues*. In it, especially in the final chapter and in the conclusion of the book, he discloses such profound religious thoughts that one would say it had been composed by a man wholly devoted to the highest contemplation rather than by a praetorian prefect occupied by so many daily and nightly cares, so that he could not even have a moment free from public labor.

I know that in the final chapter of this book, and also in his *Commentary on the Psalms*, he holds that the souls of the just are not admitted into the bosom of blessed eternity, nor the wicked plunged into the abyss of eternal misery, before we receive the fruit of all our deeds through the examination of the final judgment. Yet no one is unaware what opinions the holy Fathers held on this matter, and these can easily clear Cassiodorus of blame.

§ LIX. How Cassiodorus’ piety shines forth at the end of the book *On the Soul*

Here I pause the reader and earnestly beg him to turn the final pages of this book with close attention, so that he may perceive the conspicuous marks of humility and of the other virtues displayed throughout, and observe how detached M. Cassiodorus was from earthly things, how free from vain desires, and how contemptuous of the false image of honors.

And indeed one will cease to wonder that this outstanding man, raised to the summit of dignities regarded as the highest of all, whose fortune had been so favorable that the mutability of circumstances and times had not touched it, and whom four kings had loved and honored—under whose reigns he had possessed authority so free and complete that he had acquired for himself an extraordinary reputation for glory and the most illustrious titles—one will not wonder, I say, [Col. 0465B] that, setting all these degrees of honor aside and despising riches, he withdrew from the court so that, within the enclosure of the cloister, he might confine himself through love of solitude and tranquillity, devoting himself to God alone and to the citizens of heaven.

§ LX. How and when he renounced the world

In the year 538 or 539, therefore, after laying down the dignity of the prefecture and bidding farewell to the world, Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus journeyed to the city of Scyllacium, longing for a quieter life. Near it he entered the monastery that he had built, as though it were an utterly secure harbor of salvation.

The Gothic people deeply mourned the loss of so great a man, and his departure created an ardent longing for him in the kingdom whose glory and ornament he had been. Not long after his departure came the ruin of the kingdom, already declining.

By contrast, the reception of this illustrious man brought a great increase of honor and splendor to the monastic profession. His life in the coenobitic institution was as conspicuous for monastic virtues as his life among the nobles had been glorious for the ornaments of integrity.

He had reached the age of sixty-nine or seventy when he withdrew into the monastery, possessing such vigor and strength of spirit that anyone would be unjust who said that he withdrew his head from the storms of the world and his shoulders from the burdens of government at the very time when, exhausted, he was no longer able to lend his country a helping hand. For, in the second part of this history, we shall demonstrate, with God’s help, how many labors and how severe hardships he endured with steadfast spirit in the monastic profession, where he prolonged his life to the age of ninety-three and beyond.

# PART TWO

[Col. 0465]

[Col. 0465B] § I. Cassiodorus’ condition when he renounced the world

Up to this point we have contemplated Magnus Cassiodorus shining in the courts of kings with the splendid ornaments both of piety and of dignities. I would not hesitate to call him an exemplary model of prudence and of the other virtues, so complete that even the wisest men could admire it more readily than imitate it. For he was not ashamed to join Christian humility to the splendors of purple in an unfamiliar partnership, nor did he obey the sacred oracles of the Gospel with less devotion than the laws of human justice.

Now it is a pleasure to behold him renouncing the honors of the world; exchanging the court for the monastery, the companionship of princes and the company of servants for the fellowship of monks; and trading riches for poverty in a most fortunate exchange.

§ II. The condition of the Gothic kingdom and of monasticism when Cassiodorus abandoned the former and embraced the latter

The empire of the Goths, which Cassiodorus had long supported by the protection of his virtues, was at last inclining with certainty toward ruin. Italy was already almost consumed by the fires of war, which the emperor Justinian and King Vitigis had kindled everywhere.

Meanwhile, the empire derived no small consolation amid its afflicted circumstances from the restoration of monastic discipline, which St. Benedict was striving to restore in the West to its former splendor and to secure with the strongest laws, since it had almost collapsed.

The foremost region of the world was being ravaged by the fury of war, and the fatal conflagration was enveloping its languishing peoples. Yet everyone confidently believed that the flames raging with impunity would soon be extinguished by the new legislator, Benedict, who, stationed upon the mountain like another Moses, stretched out suppliant hands toward heaven to obtain the richest abundance of grace.

Such was the calamity of the Italians that everywhere the clash of arms was heard, everywhere famine prevailed, everywhere death ruled. Yet around the heavenly initiate Benedict there was an earthly choir of angels—that is, a devout multitude of monks, instructed by the words and example of their most holy master. Their prayers, poured out continually before God, would undoubtedly obtain the most timely assistance for their unhappy homeland.

Since these things were so, one might reasonably affirm that Cassiodorus’ contempt and disgust for the world were stirred both by contemplation of the king succumbing to adverse circumstances and of the Gothic kingdom resounding everywhere with the tumult of so many wars, and by the fame of St. Benedict and his disciples, whose incredible triumphs all minds watched in amazement and whose praises all mouths proclaimed. [Col. 0466B]

§ III. The Centuriators’ opinion concerning the reason for Cassiodorus’ withdrawal is rejected

As for the claim that Cassiodorus, because of the unheard-of cruelty of the kings of Italy, who sacrificed the most innocent men to their own fury, seized the opportunity to hide in the cloister, and, as an eyewitness of the instability of fortune, lowered himself from that supreme height of dignity to the humility of the monastic condition so that he too might not become the sport of that most fickle mistress of human affairs—this is certainly an invented and reckless tale of the Centuriators.

When they perceived that the glorious act of this most noble man, an act deserving to be handed down to posterity, could not be passed over in silence, those envious men mentioned it so coldly that they said Senator—conspicuous for wealth, power, and, what is more important, virtues—had cast aside the highest offices and the greatest resources because he distrusted unjust fortune.

Nor is it surprising that those to whom the institution of the monastic life is distasteful should describe Cassiodorus’ worthy withdrawal with a fastidious circumlocution.

§ IV. Trithemius’ opinion concerning the reason for the same withdrawal is rejected

Trithemius likewise reports, in Book III, chapter 7, of *On the Illustrious Men of the Order of St. Benedict*, that Cassiodorus finally resolved to flee from the dangers of the court to the asylum of sacred religion, since Theodoric had inflicted death upon the illustrious Severinus Boethius.

But, in my opinion, no one will subscribe to the judgment of Trithemius, otherwise a most learned man and highly deserving of our order—especially since everyone knows that after the deaths of both Theodoric and Boethius, Cassiodorus was honored with many dignities by Athalaric, Theodahad, and Vitigis, and was weighed down by the burden of the kingdom’s greatest affairs.

§ V. The true reason for Cassiodorus’ withdrawal

Accordingly, it seems closer to the truth that so great a man despised wealth because it passes away, and dignities because they pass away, so that through religious humility he might devote himself to the supreme Governor of all things.

For the wisest of men knew that Christian servitude is far more excellent than any of the greatest empires. He gives, I think, a clear account of why he preferred it to all the dignities of the world, the riches of the world, and the pleasures of the flesh, when, at the end of his book *On the Soul*, the humble disciple addresses Christ, the humble Master, in these words:

“It is more useful to serve you than to seize the kingdoms of the world.”

§ VI. Cassiodorus withdrew not near Ravenna but near Scyllacium

But it is not sufficiently certain where he came ashore, as it were, in a safest harbor when he joyfully emerged from the stormy waves of the world. Some authors—Trithemius, Barrius, Rubeus, Ugellus, and Cuspinianus—maintain that he put on the monastic habit in a coenobium built near Ravenna. Others, whom we follow, judge more reasonably that Cassiodorus built the monastery in which he led his religious life in the region of the Bruttii, near Scyllacium, his native land.

Baronius supports this opinion with a twofold argument (under the year of Christ 562). The first is that Cassiodorus himself calls the Castellian coenobium, which can be inferred from two letters of St. Gregory the Great to have been situated near Scyllacium, his own monastery.

The second is that it is incredible that a man who had long been impatient of the noise of court and war, and who at last yearned with all his heart for the tranquil leisure of holy solitude, would have chosen a retreat near Ravenna, which had been shaken by the unaccustomed tumult of arms.

§ VII. The same is demonstrated more fully, and the identity of the river Pelena

Certainly Baronius did not know in which part of Italy Pelena rolled its waters. Yet our Senator asserts that its current was very near the Vivarian monastery, so that, when the river was judged necessary, it could easily be diverted by artificial means into the gardens ( *Divine Letters*, chapter 29).

An Italian writer who is soon to publish a sacred history of the Bruttii, as has been reported to us from Scyllacium—and who himself inspected these places—says that it is clearer than daylight that the river Pelena is the stream now called the river of Scyllacium, and that it gently irrigates with its flowing waters the land near the Vivarian monastery.

Thus it can be established by new and certain evidence that the coenobium to which Cassiodorus happily navigated from the swollen waves of the world was not far from Scyllacium, since he himself mentions that it was accessible by the waters of Pelena (*Divine Letters*, chapter 29). [Col. 0467C]

Add to this that the mountain commonly called Moscio and Castellesi—at whose foot he had excavated fishponds, and on whose summit Cassiodorus had assigned cells to monks wishing to pass from the coenobitic life to the eremitical life—descends with a gentle slope toward the city of Scyllacium.

And indeed, both ancient and modern geographers represent the territory of Ravenna as flat and everywhere marshy, without mountains enclosing it. Yet Senator asserts that Mount Moscio, or Castellesi, bordered, indeed was enclosed within, the boundaries of his monastery.

Finally, against Ugellus, Augustine of Florence, and certain others, the Italian author just mentioned proves that Cassiodorus, as a candidate for monastic discipline, never went to the Classian coenobium dedicated to St. Apollinaris, built three miles from Ravenna. For it is impossible that he should have entered monastic service in 538 or 539 in a monastery that was built only in 545, whose basilica was consecrated in 549, and in which monks are known to have been substituted for canons in 595. [Col. 0467D]

§ VIII. Why Cassiodorus is said to have flourished at Rome

As for the unraveling of the knots with which so many writers have entangled the histories, the kindly reader will excuse me if I have devoted some time and labor to disagreeing with them—or, shall I say, will fairly acknowledge that I have done him a great favor? For I have brought no little light to passages that are read in rather obscure verbal circumlocutions both in Paul the Deacon’s account of the deeds of the Lombards and in the Chronicle of the Abbot of Usperg under the year 527:

“Cassiodorus,” they say, “flourished at Rome in both secular and divine knowledge.”

I would not have you understand these words as though he had lived as a monk at Rome or founded a monastery there—for, as is clear from what has been said, he erected one near Scyllacium. Rather, I would judge that those most learned men meant to indicate either how much glory, not only at Rome but throughout all Italy, the contempt of wealth and withdrawal into solitude brought to this most devout and courageous deserter; or else they designated the period during which he shone with the highest honors, wrote elegant letters in the name of kings, and delivered speeches that bore witness to both sacred and secular eloquence. [Col. 0468A]

§ IX. Cassiodorus built a monastery on his native soil near Scyllacium

On his native soil near Scyllacium, therefore, M. Cassiodorus built a coenobium in the place where, when he had been placed in charge of the Lucanians and Bruttii, he had ordered fishponds to be excavated about a mile from the city, toward the Gulf of Scyllacium, at the foot of Mount Moscio (Book XII of the *Variarum*, Letter 15).

The Italian author cited above relates that the entire tract of land extending from the city to the sea was counted among Senator’s possessions. Moreover, there can still be seen there an estate formerly called Schilitano and now called Scallati, lying below the Vivarian monastery and situated within its territory. For the inhabitants were once obliged to pay an annual rent to the monks, as may be gathered from a letter of St. Gregory to John, bishop of Scyllacium, which is the thirty-third letter of Book VII of the *Registers*, under the first indiction. [Col. 0468B]

In the same place one sees a very beautiful villa called Castellesi, which Cassiodorus once possessed and which is now held by a citizen of Scyllacium, illustrious by nobility, descended from the ancient family of Geronda. That family recognizes as its founder Arnaldus Geronda the Norman, once especially dear to Count Roger.

§ X. The estates, revenues, and site of the monastery built by Cassiodorus

It is entirely probable that Cassiodorus endowed the Vivarian coenobium with this estate and with others that had come to him by hereditary right. I would confidently affirm that its annual revenues were abundant enough to correspond to its magnificent buildings, as Faber testifies.

Its site was especially agreeable, with the proximity of mountain and sea and the plain irrigated by the waters of Pelena. Cassiodorus himself described the character of the Vivarian soil in such a learned and careful style in chapter 29 of his book *On Divine Letters* that one can scarcely read what it is like without seeming to see it with one’s own eyes.

Therefore, lest I seem merely to repeat what has already been said, it will be enough here to recall from the immeasurable abundance of his praises those advantages of the fortunate place which he says were so great, and its fertility so abundant, that it could reasonably arouse the envy even of other, more perfect ascetics. For after describing the Vivarian lands, he addresses his monks as follows:

“Thus it comes about,” he says (*Divine Letters*, chapter 29), “that your monastery is sought by others rather than that you should desire foreign places.”

§ XI. Why Cassiodorus’ monastery was called Vivarian and Castellian

You may perhaps reasonably wonder whether the coenobium that Cassiodorus founded beneath the mountain and the cells that he built above it for hermits should be regarded as one monastery or two. For Senator himself seems to favor both opinions, at one time using these expressions: “the Vivarian monastery,” “your monastery,” “in the Vivarian monastery”; and at another using these: “the holy monasteries.”

Here we follow the abbot speaking of his own cloister.

That it was one monastery is first proved by its location within the same walls, by the communion in prayer between the coenobites and the anchorites, by the coenobites’ easy access to the mountain, and by the passage to the eremitical life.

That it was two is clearly demonstrated by their separation from one another in distance, food, conversation, and abbots.

Thus, if you take the word “monastery” in a narrower sense, you will distinguish the Vivarian establishments; if in a broader sense, you will combine them, as can be said in other cases of the Benedictine solitudes, and now of the Spanish solitudes of Montserrat and Camaldoli.

For this reason I think that in Cassiodorus’ time his monastery had a double name: the part called Vivarian belonged to the coenobites, while the part called Castellian belonged to the hermits.

§ XII. Who have inhabited the Vivarian monastery from its foundation to the present time

Nor, I think, will it be unwelcome to the curious reader to learn what we have recently received from the Italian author: namely, that Cassiodorus’ monastery was inhabited from its foundation, and for many years afterward, by Benedictines; that disciples of St. Basil succeeded them; and that these were eventually driven out either by the violence of wars, by the changing fortunes of the times, or by the fatal incursions of the Moors or Saracens throughout Calabria.

Nevertheless, that most ancient house still exists, bearing the illustrious title of St. Gregory Thaumaturgus and rich in sacred relics. Yet alas, it has experienced the wretched fate of human affairs, which are accustomed neither to preserve a stable and unhindered course for long nor always to shine with unfailing brilliance.

§ XIII. Whether Cassiodorus made his monastic profession in the monastery he built

That Cassiodorus was a monk in the monastery he had built has been accepted by the unanimous agreement of so many ancient and modern authors, not only Catholics but also heterodox writers—namely Cuspinianus and the Centuriators—that I cannot sufficiently wonder at certain critics of our own age who still wish to raise a dispute about the matter, especially since Senator himself frequently boasts in his works of the humble condition of a monk.

Thus he says in the preface to Psalm 130:

“Would that we were oxen, plowing the Lord’s field with regular furrows!”

And in the book *On Divine Letters* (chapter 23), speaking of Dionysius Exiguus, he says:

“He was accustomed to pray with us,” and so forth.

These passages show not only that Cassiodorus wore the monastic habit but also that he observed the prescribed laws of a regular institution. In the preface to his book *On Orthography*, he calls this discipline of right living the time of his conversion.

For this reason, in ancient manuscripts of the *Commentary on the Psalms*, he is called *Conversus*—“a convert”—and “Servant of God.”

§ XIV. Whether Cassiodorus embraced the Rule of St. Benedict

Until now the Benedictine family had counted among its members a man distinguished both for piety and for learning. Then Cardinal Baronius, otherwise a most judicious writer, dared—whether with sufficient deliberation I do not know—to deprive a mother who suspected nothing of her dearest son.

We examine in a brief dissertation whether that offspring should be restored to her; and, so that the sequence of the great man’s rightly performed deeds might not be interrupted, we have decided to append it to the end of this history.

§ XV. Cassiodorus most steadfast in regular observance

No one, I think, could demonstrate Cassiodorus’ holiness more easily than by first showing how firmly he adhered to the discipline of the Rule and how religiously he cultivated it.

The first step toward it is the pursuit of profound solitude. Senator cultivated this so carefully that, as soon as he withdrew from the crowds and the noise of courtiers into leisure, he lived completely removed from the company of mortals.

To achieve this more easily, when he was building the monastery he took special care that neither he nor his monks should have any need for intercourse or association with other people. Therefore he ordered gardens to be planted with every kind both of vegetable and of tree; fishponds to be dug that would never lack an abundance of fish; and mills to be built, as he testifies in chapter 29 of *On Divine Letters*:

“You have irrigated gardens and the nearby waters of the fish-filled river Pelena, which, diverted by artificial means, flows to you wherever it is judged necessary, sufficient both for your gardens and for your mills.”

Finally, with such shrewd foresight he enclosed within the monastery walls everything that the coenobitic life requires that nothing could thereafter be lacking for the monks’ comfortable habitation, nor was the slightest opportunity ever given to anyone to wander outside the Vivarian cloister.

§ XVI. Cassiodorus was abbot of the Vivarian monastery

We do not know with certainty who first presided as archimandrite over the Vivarian coenobium. We know only this: both from the preface to the book *On Orthography* and from the common agreement of nearly all writers, that Cassiodorus at some time held the office of abbot.

And indeed, who among the Vivarians could ever have been more worthy of such an honor? What virtue necessary to an abbot did not rule in Cassiodorus’ soul like a queen upon a throne?

Singular prudence shone forth in him: just as he had previously governed Italy, so afterward he governed the monastery. His longing for perfection was ardent; for he passed the whole span of his life in such a way that he became better and holier day by day, and by deed more than by speech he showed his disciples the way to self-restraint, humility, [Col. 0470A] and poverty.

He possessed courtesy in conversation and goodwill toward all; courage, by which he never permitted discipline to be relaxed; and, finally, all the virtues contended with one another in a kind of holy rivalry over which would first, and which most nobly, adorn the breast of Cassiodorus.

## § XVII. Cassiodorus’s utmost concern for the divine office

The abbot Cassiodorus’s concern, diligence, and assiduity regarding divine worship were extraordinary. Just as this most religious man rightly judged that nothing was nobler than the supreme Creator of all things, so nothing was dearer or more important to him than the work of God. He had established the same order and the same times for the divine office, both by day and by night, as St. Benedict had done in his Rule, as is understood from his words on Psalm 118, verse 164, “Seven times a day,” and so forth:

> “If we wish to understand it literally,” he says, “it signifies those seven occasions by which the devout piety of the monks consoles itself: namely, matins [that is, lauds], terce, sext, none, the lighting of the lamps [that is, vespers], and nocturns [that is, the night watches].”

That prime was customarily recited among them in choir he testifies in the preface to the Psalter:

> “The psalms themselves dedicate to us the first hour of the day.”

Finally, he designates compline in this way:

> “At nightfall they ensure that our mind is not darkened.”

This was the final hour of the day, which the eminent Cardinal Bona and many others whose authority he cites have noted was first instituted in the West by St. Benedict (*De Divinis Psalmis*, chap. 10).

It was no small achievement to arrange the canonical hours in so excellent an order; yet the monks still had to be stirred up to hasten to the oratory at the appointed times. Cassiodorus accomplished this admirably not only by words and example, but also by procuring both water clocks and sundials, so that the soldiers of Christ, warned by the surest signals to perform the divine work, might be summoned as though by the sounding of trumpets (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 30).

The monks’ supreme fervor corresponded to this vigilance of their abbot. You would have heard them, day and night, with equal exertion of mind and voice, singing a joyful paean to Christ the Victor. You would have seen them standing before the divine Majesty with a modesty that rivaled the reverence of angels:

> “In the silent night, the human voice bursts forth into music, and by words skillfully modulated causes it to return to Him from whom, for the salvation of the human race, the divine utterance came . . . Let there be one voice of those singing psalms, and with the angels of God, whom we cannot hear, let us mingle words of praise” (*Preface to the Psalter*).

## § XVIII. Cassiodorus’s and the Vivarians’ regular exercises

The distinguished abbot knew especially well that prayer drives out vices, searches out virtues, preserves stricter discipline, serves as the most fertile seedbed of pious thoughts, and acts as a bulwark against the assaults of raging demons. He therefore devoted himself to it with his Vivarians in such a spirit that no one could be excused from it by any consideration of domestic or public usefulness, nor by the necessity of pressing business.

Whatever free time remained after they had fulfilled the task of prayer and the divine office, they devoted entirely, without idleness, either to reading or to copying, after the manner of antiquarians, books of Holy Scripture or of the Fathers; the clocks allotting each exercise its proper periods. For this purpose, he testifies that they had also constructed their own water clocks and timepieces:

> “Nor have we allowed you to remain in any way unaware of the divisions of the hours, which are known to have been invented for the great benefit of the human race. Accordingly, I acknowledge that I have prepared for you one clock whose indication is given by the brightness of the sun; and another, a water clock, which continually indicates the quantity of the hours by day and night.”

## § XIX. The labors with which Cassiodorus exercised his monks

The most learned man believed that such power and importance lay in the sciences for preserving monasteries and enriching them with every good thing that he urged every one of his disciples toward the study of letters, setting before them the benefits ordinarily gained from it as though applying spurs.

If any happened to plead dullness of intellect, he reminded them that the fruits of the bitterest roots would be exceedingly sweet. What they considered harsh and unpleasant was, he said, so sweet and delightful that nothing sweeter or more pleasant could be desired, even in their most cherished wishes.

> “Then,” he said, “salutary perseverance will make learned men of those whom, at the first encounter, the profundity of reading terrified” (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 28).

Those whom nature had formed too dull ever to investigate matters that are mysteries to the unlearned and hold their minds in suspense, he at least took care to have the rudiments of letters traced out for their obtuse intellects, so that, supported by some modest degree of knowledge (*ibid.*), he might afterward order them to undertake rustic labor:

> “For he did not consider it alien to monks to cultivate gardens, work the fields, and rejoice in the abundance of fruit” (*ibid.*).

What cause impelled him to send idleness far away from the monks he himself reveals in this excellent saying:

> “Sin would certainly find no place if the restless mind of mortals had no idle time” (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 16).

And elsewhere:

> “Do not love idleness, which you know is hateful to the Lord” (*ibid.*, chap. 32).

## § XX. Cassiodorus teaches his monks philosophy and the liberal arts

What we have reviewed thus far is of such a kind that it could scarcely be expressed adequately in any mode of speech, not even in Ciceronian language. But what follows surpasses the capacity of the human mind so greatly that I can scarcely believe myself when I consider both Cassiodorus’s age and his rank.

Who could imagine an old man playing literary games with boy-monks? An abbot celebrated for so great a reputation undertaking to teach the liberal arts publicly? A man overwhelmed by many continual occupations bringing to light, in order to make the path to letters easier for his brothers, commentaries on Donatus and books on orthography, grammar, rhetoric, and dialectic, and taking Dionysius Exiguus as his associate in teaching the principles of philosophy?

These things would indeed seem incredible to us if we did not know how greatly this man, who had rendered such distinguished service to letters, wished the Muses always to reign in his monastery, and how much more highly this devoted promoter of monastic excellence always valued the progress of his disciples than his other affairs.

## § XXI. What Dionysius Exiguus, Cassiodorus’s associate, did in the Vivarian monastery

Since we have begun to mention Dionysius Exiguus, whom a bond of mutual affection had joined to the abbot and the monks of Vivarium, it will not be out of place to recall here with what light of virtue and learning he shone.

Because he was very well known to Cassiodorus, with whom he lived for many years in the closest friendship, we shall place before the reader’s eyes the true and almost breathing image of that most illustrious man who, by the splendor of his learning, wonderfully illuminated the Catholic Church, as it has been portrayed in the writings of our abbot.

Cassiodorus says:

> “In our times there was a monk named Dionysius, a Scythian by nationality, but entirely Roman in character, exceedingly learned in both languages, rendering in his actions the equity he had read in the Lord’s books. He had examined and understood the divine Scriptures with such great diligence that, whatever question he was asked, he had a suitable answer ready without any delay. He studied dialectic with me and, under the example of a glorious teacher, spent many years of his life, by the Lord’s favor, in this way . . .
>
> “In him great wisdom was joined with simplicity, learning with humility, and eloquence with restraint in speech; so that he never placed himself above even the lowest servants, although he was unquestionably worthy of conversing with kings . . .
>
> “When requested by Stephen, bishop of Salona, he composed from Greek exemplars ecclesiastical canons suited to his own character. Being plain and eloquent, he produced them with the great radiance of his eloquence; today the Roman Church embraces them in its most celebrated practice . . .
>
> “He also translated many other works from Greek into Latin which could contribute to the benefit of the Church . . .
>
> “He poured forth tears, moved by compunction, when he heard frivolous words of merriment . . .
>
> “But, to report the goodness of his mind without artificial praise, he was wholly Catholic and wholly steadfastly attached to the rules of the Fathers; and whatever readers might seek in various authors was known to shine in his learning . . .
>
> “But now, having abandoned the perversity of the world, and having been received, by the Lord’s favor, into the peace of the Church, he must be believed to have fellowship among the servants of God.”

He concludes this illustrious testimony about his friend with words full of modesty and humility:

> “I am ashamed to say of a companion what I cannot find in myself.”

## § XXII. Cassiodorus trains his monks in the study of Holy Scripture

But let us return, if you please, to Cassiodorus’s school, which, watered by the instructions of Cassiodorus and Dionysius as by the clearest waters of a double spring, flourished for the great benefit of the house of Castellum and of the whole world. I believe no one can doubt this.

Senator taught the Vivarians the liberal arts for no other reason than that, equipped by these exercises and, so to speak, raised by certain steps, they might finally reach the inner sanctuaries of sacred theology.

Nevertheless, he says:

> “Nor did the most holy Fathers decree that the study of secular letters should be rejected, since through it our understanding is instructed, and not to the least degree, for understanding the sacred Scriptures” (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 28).

Thus, just as eternal and heavenly things surpass what is transitory and earthly, he wished greater diligence to be devoted to the divine Scriptures than to lighter studies.

While still entangled in public affairs, he had once promised that he would open sacred schools, as we stated earlier in another part of this history. Now, in the monastery, he fulfilled the promise that he had been unable to fulfill at Rome, when wars were raging everywhere.

He therefore took particular care that the Vivarian ascetics should never appear to lack anything in this respect. He urged them, if only they would direct all their cares and studies toward knowledge of divine things, to dispel the darkness of ignorance; to implant virtue in the minds of posterity, since the road to its temple lies through the house of wisdom; and to instill in everyone a desire for the glory that flows from wisdom as from an abundant spring.

## § XXIII. Cassiodorus teaches his monks the method of undertaking the study of Holy Scripture

Cassiodorus was not unaware that whatever beginners did wrongly in the study of sacred letters was generally due to a disturbance of order: books that ought to have been read first were read later, and those that ought to have been read later were read first.

He therefore instructed his disciples to govern their desires wisely, learning in order what had to be read (*Preface to the Book on Divine Letters*). To ensure that they observed this method more faithfully, he published his book *On Divine Letters*.

> “I acknowledge,” he says, “that divine charity compelled me to prepare for you, in the role of a teacher, introductory books through which, as I believe, the sequence of the divine Scriptures and a concise knowledge of secular letters might, by the Lord’s gift, be disclosed.”

He adds that one must also ascend to Holy Scripture through the reliable expositions of the Fathers. Accordingly, he not only proposed that the books of divine authority—which he divided there into nine parts—be read, but also indicated which works of the holy teachers were suitable for explaining them.

And lest any stain of heretical contagion infect the purity of the faith, he identified the places where authors had deviated from the truth. Thus he turned them away from the reefs of Origen’s errors:

> “Accordingly, in the works of that same Origen, wherever I was able to find, in passing, passages contrary to the rules of the Fathers, I marked them with the rejection of useless things [Greek: **ἀχρήστων**, ‘of things useless’], so that the man whom such a mark shows must be avoided in depraved interpretations might not be able to deceive” (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 1).

For no other reason did he read with such diligence as he could muster the epistle to the Romans, which was then in everyone’s hands and was dividing Catholic teachers into opposing parties: because it was commonly believed to have been written by Pope Gelasius, he cleansed it of the impious opinions of Pelagian depravity.

## § XXIV. Cassiodorus establishes an excellent library

Our abbot provided, with truly incredible magnificence, the books he knew were needed for a clearer understanding of the Scriptures, as well as those he thought would assist in other kinds of study that were not unworthy of men devoted to contemplation. In procuring necessities he was piously generous; in purchasing superfluities he was piously frugal.

I do not think he ever displayed more clearly or convincingly his love for his disciples and for the Muses than when he enriched the library with a vast store of volumes brought not only from Italy but also from the most remote provinces, adorning it especially with sacred books, works of the holy Fathers, expositions by interpreters of Scripture, and treatises by writers on orthography, and giving it a marvelous beauty by the very order in which he assigned each author his proper place.

But, to pursue individually the care Senator devoted to acquiring books, when he first learned that explanations of the divine letters had been composed by the blessed Jerome, he immediately sent men to various regions of the earth to search for them diligently and bring them back quickly:

> “We have immediately sent them everywhere to be sought in different regions, trusting that, by divine mercy, we shall receive them” (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 8).

He also arranged for the commentaries on the Epistles of St. Paul by Peter, abbot of the province of Tripoli, to be brought from Africa to Italy:

> “By the support of divine grace, this is to be sent to you from the region of Africa among the other books” (*ibid.*).

When he learned that the interpreters who had diligently traveled through various regions had not come upon certain interpretations of Holy Scripture by the presbyter Bellator, he humbly requested that they be sent to him, so that he might remedy such a great scarcity. He likewise asked that the homilies of Origen on Ezra, translated into Latin, be transmitted to him.

He even prevailed upon a certain highly learned man, Epiphanius, who was also his close friend, to translate into Latin, both as a supplement to the library and for the use of the disciples, the work that St. Epiphanius had composed in Greek on the *Song of Songs*.

## § XXV. Cassiodorus’s depiction of the Tabernacle and Solomon’s Temple

I think the elegant image of Solomon’s Temple and Tabernacle should be counted among the most distinguished ornaments of Cassiodorus’s library. He had fitted it, as he himself says, into a large Latin pandect, carefully drawn with its proper lines.

That remarkable work had not yet perished in Bede’s time. Bede freely confesses that he had seen it and found it useful in his *Book II on the Tabernacle*, chap. 12, and in his books on Solomon’s Temple and Tabernacle. He evidently believed that nothing more perfect or more accurate could be devised than those figures.

> “Since we found these things distinguished in Cassiodorus’s painting,” he says, “we have thought it worthwhile to record them briefly. We believe that he learned them from the ancient Jews [perhaps: ‘we believe that he had learned them’], and that so learned a man would not have wished to set before readers as an example anything that he had not first recognized as true” (*Book on Solomon’s Temple*, chap. 16).

## § XXVI. Whether Cassiodorus had libraries at Rome and Ravenna

Just as Cassiodorus had cultivated the sciences not only in the leisure of Vivarium but also amid the noise of the court, so I have no doubt that he established a library both at Rome and at Ravenna while supporting the Gothic kingdom with its firmest defenses.

He himself mentions the Roman library in his treatise *On Music*:

> “In the library which we had at Rome,” and so forth.

I believe no one would likewise doubt the existence of the library at Ravenna, unless he wished rashly to assert that in that city—that is, in the very seat of the Gothic kings, from which Cassiodorus could scarcely be absent even for a single moment during the reigns of Theodoric, Athalaric, and their successors—this devoted fosterer and most zealous patron of the Muses neglected them for so long a period.

At last, after Senator left the court of Vitigis and had hidden himself within the cloister, he brought books untouched by the barbarians from Rome and Ravenna to enrich the Vivarian library.

For this reason he instructed the monks to bring to the monastery from Rome a certain book whose author was Albinus and whose title was *On Music*, if they found that it had not been carried off in the invasion of the pagans (*On Music*, at the end).

But let us pause here for a moment, if you please, and contemplate attentively the abbot’s exceptional diligence in supplying the monastery with the books it needed. What could the Vivarians have lacked? For, after the words just quoted, he adds that if the aforementioned book had perhaps not escaped hostile hands, they had the Latin work of Gaudentius Mutianus; if they read it with careful attention, he promises that the halls of this science—namely, music—would be opened to them (*ibid.*).

## § XXVII. Cassiodorus demonstrates to his monks how useful prayer is in the study of Holy Scripture

Who would not now consider the Vivarians exceedingly fortunate? They obeyed so holy an abbot, listened to so learned a teacher, and rejoiced that, because of the almost immeasurable abundance of books, access to every science, and especially to knowledge of divine things, lay open to them.

Who would not admit that Cassiodorus himself had rightly placed before his disciples the labors he had once undertaken in gathering books from every quarter, in these words?

> “Come now, dearest brothers, hasten to make progress in the Holy Scriptures, since you know that, for the abundance of your learning, I have gathered together for you such great and such excellent aids by the help of the Lord’s grace” (*Book on Divine Letters*, chap. 33).

It is astonishing how greatly these words must have inflamed the monks to pursue that teacher and queen of the disciplines, theology, and to penetrate the hidden meanings of the Scriptures.

Yet this most humble man believed that both he and his brothers would spend their oil and labor in vain unless, by the help of prayer, they obtained from God, the Lord of the sciences, what was too difficult and inaccessible to human powers.

Hence, at the very threshold of his book *On Divine Letters*, he exhorts them:

> “Let us pray that those things which are closed may be opened to us, and let us never withdraw from the study of reading.”

Elsewhere he asserts that perfect wisdom is obtained not so much by study as by good deeds and constant prayers, and that once obtained it is retained by them (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 28).

Since examples are usually more effective in encouraging people toward anything, he set before them David, who, although always intent upon meditation on the divine law, nevertheless continually struck heaven with these cries:

> “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments” (Psalm 118:73).

He said that a certain man whose weaker intellect had been closed had opened for himself an understanding of the most difficult scriptural text through very frequent prayer. He related that another man, ignorant even of the elements of the alphabet, had obtained through frequent prayer the ability to read the book given to him with the greatest ease.

Therefore, he said:

> “Let us pray that those things which are closed may be opened to us” (*Preface to the Book on Divine Letters*).

## § XXVIII. He teaches that understanding of Holy Scripture is acquired through labor as well as prayer

Cassiodorus nevertheless warned the monks who prostrated themselves before the divine presence that they should not pour out their prayers in such a way as to believe that their requests would be granted while they remained idle. Those who sought wisdom were to spare no labor.

Very few, he said, had been enriched with that most precious treasure—the hidden and inscrutable counsels of the divine mind—without labor and as though asleep. If they believed that they would receive so great a gift from heaven merely by folding their arms, they would pay the penalty of presumption and idleness rather than enjoy the rewards of empty and overbold prayers.

> “Read constantly, I beg you,” he says. “Return to the text diligently, for frequent and attentive meditation is the mother of understanding” (*Preface to the Book on Divine Letters*).

To impress this more deeply upon the minds of his disciples, he brings forward this excellent saying of St. Jerome:

> “Love the reading of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh” (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 32).

Finally, he impresses upon their ears that nothing whatever should be omitted in this work, so that nothing appears more important or dearer to him. Thus he addresses his monks once again:

> “Therefore, with all our strength, all our labor, and all our desires, let us seek to become worthy, by the Lord’s generosity, to attain so great and so remarkable a gift” (*Book on Divine Letters*, chap. 28).

## § XXIX. How far the Vivarians advanced under their teacher Cassiodorus in knowledge of Holy Scripture

Cassiodorus’s hope was not disappointed. At last he reaped what he had sown. He rejoiced to recognize that his monks had made such progress in the sciences that he could acknowledge them to be proficient in both divine and human letters. He said that he himself had begun the work merely with a light stroke of the brush, and asked them to complete it with a more practiced hand. His words testify no less to the humility of the teacher than to the learning of the disciples:

> “Therefore I beg you to complete in the name of Christ, with greater perfection, what we were able to explain only imperfectly by reading and even less by interpretation, you who have been nourished by abundant reading, both from the books we have left behind and from those you may fortunately discover” (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 15).

Nevertheless, fearing that such great understanding of divine things might perhaps inspire them with an overweening spirit, he teaches that what is hidden from the proud is revealed to little ones. Wisdom does not consist in letters alone; God grants perfect wisdom to each person as he wills (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 28).

## § XXX. How much Cassiodorus benefited the Vivarians and the whole Church

Thus did this abbot, distinguished above others in learning and holiness, cultivate the monks with equal devotion and knowledge. Thus the Vivarians responded by their own labor to the care of their abbot. Thus, with Cassiodorus as their encourager and instigator, they advanced so rapidly along the path of true glory toward which their nature already inclined them that everything in them conspired toward immortality of name and eternal happiness.

Nor is this surprising. For who could have applied stronger spurs to the Vivarians toward integrity of life and the finest arts than the man who frequently discoursed among them on the usefulness and glory that accompany understanding of the divine Scriptures?

> “For this is salutary, profitable, glorious, and everlasting for us: something that neither death, nor changeability, nor any forgetfulness can separate from us, but which will make us rejoice with the Lord in eternal exultation, with the sweetness of our native land” (*Book on Divine Letters*, chap. 28).

Who could have shone more brilliantly before his disciples than the man whose virtue, placed on a lofty height, itself sufficiently forced its way into everyone’s sight, and whose singular knowledge, not hidden under an envious bushel but displayed upon a lampstand, illuminated with its visible rays all who were then in the house of Castellum and throughout the universal Church?

God had kindled this most splendid sun so that, by its pure light, it might expose and consume with the most active fire both the monsters of vice springing up throughout the world and the heresies continually arising to the common ruin of all Christians, like so many heads of the Hydra.

## § XXXI. Cassiodorus orders some of his monks to occupy themselves with copying sacred books and assists them

But it is impossible to relate everything here. The labor of the antiquarians whom he ordered to occupy themselves with copying sacred books now summons us to him and no longer permits us to remain silent about his praises. Through their hands they were to preach to men, open tongues with their fingers, and fight against the devil’s snares with pen and ink.

Showing what fruit would result from this, he adds:

> “Their writings are to be spread throughout the whole world and read in the most holy places, with such immense benefit that, if they undertake their labor with an upright spirit, scarcely any reward could equal it. Nor will they be unable to receive a return for so many benefits, provided they are known to perform such things not from the ambition of desire but from upright devotion” (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 30).

To ensure that this kind of work might succeed as the antiquarians desired, he wished those who had cultivated their intellect especially well in divine and human letters to examine and correct the work of the copyists carefully, in case something defective had inadvertently slipped from them:

> “What is known to have been prepared for a simple and less learned congregation must be done by a few learned men” (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 15). “This kind of correction, as I believe, is exceedingly beautiful, and the task of highly learned men is glorious.”

He did not wish the expressions or Hebrew words of divine authority, when appropriate to things or persons and when the dignity and integrity of their own language had to be preserved, to be altered for the sake of greater clarity or any other reason:

> “For those things which are known to have been spoken under the inspiration of the Lord cannot be corrupted” (*ibid.*).

From this anyone can easily understand with what reverence and religious feeling Cassiodorus believed that the sacred pages should be handled. He demonstrates throughout the whole of chapter 15 of *On Divine Letters* that, so that they may shine with their own splendor, they ought not to be subjected to the mutilation of human preference.

To assist his disciples in their work, he wrote commentaries on Donatus the Grammarian and a book on Orthography. With their help the books would emerge so accurately corrected that they would be accompanied both by the applause of their contemporaries and, in future generations, by the joy of posterity, as well as by an enduring benefit to the Christian commonwealth.

## § XXXII. He orders others to devote themselves to copying the works of the Fathers

He also wished certain monks to devote themselves entirely to copying the works of the Fathers, and he indicated the path by which their work might soon reach a happy conclusion.

He ordered that the sermons and homilies of the saints be read with especially close attention, just as one reads treatises against heretics. If anything occurred in them that was suitable for clarifying obscure passages of Holy Scripture, he asked that they not hesitate to append it to the sacred volumes:

> “As we ourselves are known to have done in the Books of Kings.”

He then shows in magnificent words how fruitful and glorious their labor would be:

> “Consider, therefore, what kind of charge has been entrusted to you: the benefit of Christians, the treasure of the Church, the light of souls” (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 15).

For this reason he urges them to apply careful diligence to the task, so that no falsity may remain in the truth, no falsehood in purity, and no perversity in the integrity of the words.

## § XXXIII. Cassiodorus’s care in covering the manuscript books of Holy Scripture

One thing remained for the exceptionally vigilant foresight of our abbot: to ensure that the manuscript books would remain intact for as long as possible by having them bound and covered with the finest ornament he could provide.

> “We also added skilled artisans for covering the books, so that a beautiful exterior might clothe the beauty of the sacred letters” (*Book on Divine Letters*, chap. 30).

To share personally in this labor, he himself skillfully prepared designs for the bindings:

> “In a single book he had elegantly represented various kinds of workmanship, depicted in such a way that the diligent student could himself choose whichever form of binding he preferred.”

## § XXXIV. Cassiodorus constructs marvelous lamps

It would surely be almost a religious offense to remain silent here about those lamps, worthy not only of admiration but also of everlasting praise, which he fashioned with astonishing skill for the vigils of the brothers who worked far into the night:

> “We also prepared mechanical lamps for the night watches, keepers of their own illuminating flames, feeding their own fire, which, when human service ceased, preserved at length the abundant brilliance of the richest light; the thickness of the oil did not fail, although it was continually scorched by the burning flames” (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 30).

## § XXXV. Cassiodorus’s prudence in assigning tasks to each of his monks

It would be pointless to linger here over the contemplation of the prudence with which he governed the Vivarian monastery and arranged every matter suitably.

We can admire but cannot adequately express the tireless prudence of the wisest abbot, who assigned each person his task according to his industry and strength. No one was released into idleness; no one was worn out and overcome by labor; no one’s work failed to burn with zeal when he modeled himself on the abbot’s example; and no one who followed the abbot’s commands failed to complete his task quickly and successfully.

## § XXXVI. The fasts observed by Cassiodorus and the Vivarians

There is no doubt that very strict fasts flourished among the Vivarians, those most vigilant guardians of monastic discipline. It is certain that fasting held no lowly place in their Rule, as is clear from Cassiodorus himself, where he speaks of psalmody:

> “The psalms themselves, that is, loosen for us the fasts of none” (*Preface to the Commentary on the Psalms*).

In this passage he is speaking of the fasts that are called regular fasts. As for those prescribed by the Church on appointed days, the people of Castellum undertook them with religious devotion and, with holy scrupulousness, prolonged them until evening according to the ancient custom of Christians.

What need is there to demonstrate that they had adopted as a customary practice the perpetual abstinence from meat that was then familiar to all monks? Consult, if you please, the concluding pages of chapter 23 of *On Divine Letters*, where he discusses the cultivation of gardens and fields and instructs the monks to read the books of Aemilianus and Columella on raising doves and taming livestock—animals, Cassiodorus says, “which are prepared for the sick” (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 28). From this, I think, you will easily infer that the use of meat was entirely forbidden to the healthy and robust.

Moreover, someone might perhaps reasonably infer from the sentence that follows in the same place that they abstained from eating fish, or at least were not accustomed to eating such things very often. Senator says:

> “What is the point of feeding the weak with the offspring of doves, or nourishing them with fish?” (*ibid.*).

We leave this conjecture, however, to the judgment of the reader, so that we may turn our minds and our discourse to praising the care that the abbot used to devote to sick monks.

## § XXXVII. Cassiodorus’s devotion toward sick brothers

He wished a hospital to be maintained for these brothers (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 31), staffed by men who understood the medical art thoroughly and were moved by such charity toward the sick that no service of attention or devotion would be lacking to them.

He wanted these physicians to assist the sick in all their needs, so that by the monks’ remarkable diligence the illness itself might become not merely easy and tolerable, but also sweet and pleasant.

And so that every comfort for the sick might be supplied from his monastery and not from elsewhere, he determined that the brothers assigned to care for the sick should not merely prescribe medicines but also prepare them, and that they should learn the nature and properties of herbs.

Yet this most devout man, who habitually raised the minds of his disciples from earthly things to heavenly ones, forbade them to place their hope in herbs or their health in human remedies:

> “For although medicine is read to have been established by the Lord, it is nevertheless he himself who makes the healthy, he who grants life without end” (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 31).

For the refreshment of sick bodies he had also built baths, where the clear water of springs flowed agreeably, known to be most pleasant both for drinking and for bathing (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 29).

## § XXXVIII. Cassiodorus’s devotion toward guests and pilgrims

How he received guests and pilgrims with acts of devotion and humanity is shown by this one fact: he had ordered that they be welcomed before all others (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 31).

He had entrusted to those caring for sick brothers the care of guests as well (*ibid.*, chap. 32), so that if any of them happened to collapse from the hardships of travel or from some illness, they might immediately be restored by reliable remedies.

He repeatedly declared that, when such remedies were prepared for pilgrims, they became heavenly things, so that they might be offered with a more cheerful spirit (*ibid.*, chap. 28).

## § XXXIX. He orders his monks to devote themselves to contemplation and pious reading

Although the duties by which the Vivarians were occupied under their holy teacher were most sacred, he nevertheless exercised them in manual labor in such a way that, in order for them to advance ever further along the path of virtue, he also ordered them at fixed hours to devote themselves to sacred leisure: to pour out their hearts in prayer before the Lord, to open the secrets of their minds to God, who sees all things, and to handle frequently the pious books—especially the Rule, as well as the *Conferences* of Cassian and other volumes of that kind.

By these means they were to shape their conduct according to the norm of right reason, restrain their corrupt passions, and finally ascend more quickly to the highest summit of perfection.

> “Read attentively and listen willingly to the presbyter Cassian,” he says, “who wrote on the institution of faithful monks. He presents the harmful movements of the soul so suitably that he almost makes a person see his own excesses and compels him to avoid those which previously, through the confusion of darkness, he did not recognize” (*Lib. Divin. Litt.*, chap. 29).

And because this discerning man was not unaware of the errors into which Cassian had once fallen when dealing with free will, he seriously warned that Cassian—who had rightly been blamed by blessed Prosper—should be read with the safeguard of the Victoriana correction.

## § XL. Some Under Cassiodorus Passed from the Coenobitic Life to the Eremitic

Who would deny that the Castellenses possessed both a most flourishing solitude and an almost divine way of life? Does Cassiodorus not seem to have sketched their living customs in vivid colors when he pursued the praise of monasticism in these distinguished words (*Commentary on Psalm* 103:17)?

> Life in heaven upon earth, and the imitation of the faithful angels; to live spiritually in the flesh; [Col. 0478A] not to love the vices of the world; to despise the present life and continually seek the joys of future blessedness; finally, to become the temple of the One whose image the human condition has received.

Yet I suspect, not rashly, that many will be astonished that the Vivarienses shone with such purity of conduct and burned with such fervor of mind that not a few of them passed from the camp of coenobitic service to the solitary combat of the anchorites against spiritual wickedness, as veterans honorably discharged from service. Since Cassiodorus had foreseen their desires, he had ordered cells to be built on the summit of Mount Castellum for the retreat of hermits:

> “You have,” he says (*Book on Divine Letters*, chap. 29), “the pleasant seclusion of Mount Castellum, so that, with the Lord’s favor, you may happily live there as anchorites. Therefore it will be suitable for you, who are trained and already thoroughly tested, to choose that dwelling, if an ascent has first been prepared in your hearts.”

## § XLI. Which Books Cassiodorus the Monk Published

We have thus far considered what way of life Cassiodorus established for the coenobites—as founder of the monastery, as abbot, and as teacher. Now let us consider what he did from the beginning of his conversion as a private individual, and how successfully and diligently he devoted his mind to the study of sacred literature.

First, he undertook to illuminate the Psalter with a commentary. Next, he published books on Divine and Human Letters. Then he produced other works, which he enumerates in this order in the preface to his book *On Orthography*:

> After the commentaries on the Psalter, in which, with the Lord’s help, I first devoted the labor of study during the time of my conversion.
>
> 2. Next, after the *Institutions*, two books, as I believe, sufficiently completed on how divine and human readings ought to be understood, in which you will find more usefulness than ornament.
>
> 3. After the exposition of the Epistle written to the Romans, from which I removed the errors of the Pelagian heresy; and I admonished those who follow me to do the same in the remainder of the commentary.
>
> 4. After the book in which, with the Lord’s help, I collected Donatus’s works on grammar with their commentaries, the book *On Etymologies*, and another book by Sacerdos, *On Figures*, so that simple brothers, once instructed, might perceive similar statements without confusion wherever there was a likeness.
>
> 5. After this, the book of headings, collected from divine Scripture, which I wished to call the *Memorial*, so that those who dislike extended reading might run briefly through everything.
>
> 6. After the *Complexions* on the Epistles of the Apostles, the Acts of the Apostles, and the Apocalypse, which proceeded as exceedingly brief explanations.
>
> 7. With the Lord’s help, in the ninety-third year of my life I reached the work of examining matters for the devoted orthographers.

## § XLII. In What Order Cassiodorus Composed His Books

These words are indeed lucid and clear. Yet whether Cassiodorus followed the order just reviewed in publishing his works is open to doubt, if only because in his earlier books he mentions works that he says he wrote after a long interval of time.

Certainly, in the preface to his *Commentary on the Psalms*, he cites the book *On Divine Letters* in these words:

> “Many Fathers have spoken more broadly and at greater length about the forms of his eloquence; their names we have judged should be mentioned in the introductory books.”

He also mentions the book *On Geometry* in connection with that verse of Psalm 96: “His lightnings have shone forth”:

> “A fuller knowledge of these matters,” he says, “the diligent reader will find in the books on the discipline of geometry.”

And in fact, what he brings forward there from geometry is found in its entirety in the book he composed on that discipline, according to our edition, in which we restored, on the authority of the manuscripts, what was lacking in other copies.

Finally, in *On Divine Letters*, chapter 15, he gives the title of the book *On Orthography*:

> “I also gave this book, externally, the title *On Orthography*.”

And in chapter 30:

> “In the separate and completed book entitled *On Orthography*.”

These citations lead us to say that when Cassiodorus indicates the order in which he brought his works to light, he intended to refer to the time when he began to apply his hand to each of them—works that, beyond doubt, were not yet finished when he undertook others. Thus it may rightly be said that he began the *Commentaries on the Psalter* at the very beginning of his entrance into religion, [Col. 0479A] but completed them only in extreme old age.

From this arose the occasion for citing in them books that Senator published after a long intervening period. Or at least we must admit that he composed the preface—or rather the prolegomena—to the Psalter after completing the *Commentary*, and that in the meantime he wrote the book *On Divine Letters*, for there was nothing preventing him from praising it in that same preface.

As for the book *On Geometry*, we may perhaps reasonably assert that it had been completed when he interpreted Psalm 96. The same judgment should be made concerning the book *On Orthography*, which, as we have said, he mentioned in *Divine Letters*, chapters 15 and 30. Unless, perhaps, one prefers to suppose that when Cassiodorus reread his works, he inserted such references to later books into the earlier ones for the sake of assisting his readers’ memory. Our author himself seems to support this conjecture in those places where he speaks of his works.

## § XLIII. How Great Was the Labor of the Aged Cassiodorus in Explaining, Copying, and Purging the Books of Sacred Scripture of Errors?

Whatever the precise situation may have been, who could adequately describe Cassiodorus’s unremitting labor in explaining, copying, and purging the sacred Scriptures of errors? He himself admits that he devoted the greatest effort and labor to the Psalter, the Prophets, and the Epistles of the Apostles. If you ask why, he says:

> “They seemed to me to stir up a deeper abyss and to contain, as it were, the citadel of all divine Scripture and a glorious height.”

He discusses the brief explanations of the Acts of the Apostles and the Apocalypse that he published in the preface to the book *On Orthography*, just as he discusses the *Memorial of Sacred Scripture*, which, as I conjecture, was a concise compendium of Scripture, so that almost the whole of it might be placed before the eyes in a single glance.

He supplied new headings for the books of Chronicles, since the old ones had been lost:

> “Because I did not find the ancient headings,” he says in chapter 2 of *On Divine Letters*, “I therefore impressed new ones in the individual places, suitably, as I judge, in the likeness of those that preceded them.”

Neither the difficulty of the labor nor the chill of advanced age relaxed his ardent devotion to the sacred books, nor prevented him, in the final period of his life, from restoring the holy books to incorrupt integrity through comparison with older manuscripts, so that they might be preserved in the library.

Cassiodorus himself says (*Preface to the Book on Divine Letters*):

> “All these nine codices—for I had divided the sacred Bible into that many volumes—I went through with diligent reading, as an old man able to do so, by comparison with ancient manuscripts, while friends read them aloud before me.”

And lest anyone think that our abbot devoted only moderate effort to these night watches, let him hear what he adds in the same place—not arrogantly, but sincerely:

> “I confess, with the Lord’s help, that I labored greatly, so that I might neither fail through inadequately fashioned language nor mutilate the sacred books through rash presumption.”

## § XLIV. Cassiodorus Marked the Text of Sacred Scripture in the Books of the Holy Fathers with Marginal Red Ink

Yet amid such great labors and such great exertions, the unconquered spirit of the exhausted old man was nowhere broken. Again, for the benefit of his brothers, he displayed every care and diligence in searching out the works of the holy Fathers. In order to identify for his disciples the authorities of sacred Scripture cited in their various books, he marked each one with marginal red ink.

He himself testifies to this when he says (*Book on Divine Letters*, chap. 26):

> “As much as I was able to reread, whether as an old man or fatigued by a long journey, I inserted in certain codices of the Fathers these annotations marked in red ink—which are indexes of the codices—at each respective place, as I believe, suitably.”

How thoroughly Cassiodorus was versed in Scripture, and how worthy he is of immortal remembrance, may be proved by this one fact: at an age when the tenacity of failing memory begins to dissolve, he successfully assigned to their proper places all the passages of the sacred pages that occurred in the books of the Fathers, while they were read aloud to him by the monks.

I would indeed say that Cassiodorus meditated on the law of the Lord day and night. I would rightly call him an ark—not devoid of understanding, such as we know the ark of the Old Testament to have been, but living and possessed of the highest reason, embracing within the broad bosom of his memory not only the books of the ancient covenant but also those of the new.

## § XLV. How Greatly He Venerated the First Four General Councils

Cassiodorus knew well that the universal and holy councils had solidified the saving mysteries of our faith, and that in them the secret of true religion was recognized. Following the examples of the Fathers, he celebrated the reverence due to the first four councils with such praise that he judged it rightly comparable to holy authority (*Book on Divine Letters*, chap. 11).

He grieved that men impatient of quiet sometimes raised their heads from the darkness of hell, thinking it praiseworthy to hold opinions contrary to the ancients and to discover something new by which they might seem to perish. But he rejoiced that the aforementioned synods had provided such great lights for our faith that, if we are guarded by the Lord’s protection, we need not fall with blinded minds upon any rock of perversity.

Therefore, lest any opportunity for error be left to the monks, and so that the authority of the Fathers of Chalcedon might carry greater weight among them, he placed in the library the code of that synod, translated from Greek into Latin by Epiphanius: ἐγκύκλιον (*encyclical*), that is, the *Epistolary of the whole world*, or the letters of confirmation of the Council of Chalcedon.

If we believe Baronius (*Baronius, on the year 556*), by the Encyclical Code he understood that volume of letters composed, at the initiative of the emperor Leo, by very many bishops of his time in defense of the Council of Chalcedon.

## § XLVI. What He Thought about the Fifth Ecumenical Council

We have also thought it necessary not to omit what the annalist records concerning our abbot. He says that Cassiodorus, like the Western bishops and later Gregory the Great, remained entirely silent about the Fifth Ecumenical Synod.

For Baronius says (*ibid.*):

> “No one should be troubled if Cassiodorus, when listing the ecumenical synods, made no mention of the fifth, because that council dealt not with faith but with persons.”

Let learned men weigh how significant this argument is. I myself believe that something more certain can be extracted from Cassiodorus’s writings.

Our abbot teaches his disciples (*Book on Divine Letters*, chap. 1) that Origen had produced exceedingly eloquent homilies on the Octateuch; but he warns them to avoid Origen’s errors:

> “He whom the judgment of many Fathers identifies as a heretic … and whom, in the present time, the most blessed Pope Vigilius is again known to have condemned.”

Either that authority of the Fathers is identical with the anathema by which the Fifth Council struck Origen and his followers, or it is different.

If it is identical, Baronius has gratuitously invented Cassiodorus’s silence concerning the Fifth Council. If it is different, he could have argued more forcefully as follows: if Cassiodorus approved the Fifth Synod, he would have exhorted the monks to flee Origen not merely because of the opinion of certain Fathers, but especially because of the decrees of that ecumenical council. Since, as is supposed, he did not do so, we must admit that, like the Westerners, he neither accepted nor rejected the Fifth Synod, but passed over it in prudent silence.

Yet someone might perhaps rely on a conjecture that is not rash, and contend that by “the authority of many Fathers” Cassiodorus understood the Fifth Council, and that he deliberately used these words because the Westerners had not yet received that synod, although he knew that it had already been approved by Pope Vigilius.

But let us finally leave all these matters, whose judgment belongs to the critics. Certainly to be admired is Cassiodorus’s profound respect for the Roman See and the supreme pontiffs; his zeal, by which he wished above all to guard against those whom the provident Church had condemned; and his singular reverence—or rather, his imitation—for the judgments of the holy Fathers.

## § XLVII. Cassiodorus’s Assiduity in Reading through the Works of the Holy Fathers

I believe that those who read with greater care both the *Commentary on the Psalms* and the book *On Divine Letters*, and who consider with attentive minds and mature judgment how prudently he discerned when the opinions of others were to be embraced or avoided, will readily perceive how assiduous our abbot was in reading through the works of the holy Fathers.

From these purest fountains there flowed broad streams of that sound and orthodox doctrine by which Cassiodorus both more abundantly watered the thirsty fields of the Church and more successfully choked the insolent herds of heretics.

For this reason Bede the Venerable, moved neither by the disgraceful flattery of a lying intermediary nor by some blind Benedictine affection for his fellow, but by devotion to truth alone and justice, did not hesitate to place him among the sacred teachers (*Commentary on Ezra*, vol. IV, p. 379).

## § XLVIII. Cassiodorus’s Tripartite History and His Book on Orthography

The indefatigable archimandrite Cassiodorus collected in one work, as though in a continuous sequence of history divided into twelve books, the Greek histories of Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret, which his friend Epiphanius translated into Latin. He had already begun his *Commentary on all the Psalms*, but had not yet undertaken the book *On Divine Letters*. In that book, chapter 17, he says:

> “After the history of Eusebius among the Greeks, Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret wrote what follows. With God’s help, we had them translated by the most eloquent man Epiphanius in a single body of twelve books.”

Although he labored greatly over this work, even in arranging its parts in proper order, the reason why he omitted it from his list of the works he had written as a monk is not immediately apparent. I may perhaps reasonably attribute this to humility, which prevented him from counting among his own works a book that had chiefly been translated into the Latin language through the industry of another.

The nearer that great light of the Church approached its setting, the more splendidly did he scatter the rays of his virtues far and wide. Therefore, when some of his monks asked him to prescribe laws and precise rules of orthography, he was not ashamed—at the age of ninety-three—to set his hand to the work, offering an astonishing example both of humility and of charity.

## § XLIX. Cassiodorus Renounces the Abbatial Dignity, and What He Did Afterwards

The most holy man also demonstrated his humility, as I believe, through no lesser indications when, already worn down by advanced age, he entrusted his abbatial dignity to Chalcedonius and Geruntius. One of them governed the hermits who had withdrawn to Mount Castellum; the other governed the coenobites.

Relieved of pastoral care, the old man refreshed his mind more freely and sweetly through continual contemplation of heavenly things. Withdrawn and liberated from all earthly matters, he devoted himself entirely to divine and eternal concerns. Now mature for heaven, a veteran soldier of Christ, he tasted in advance the joys of future blessedness in the leisure of the most peaceful contemplation.

But before he hastened to his desired rewards, he finally displayed to his brothers the supreme signs of the charity that he had uniquely cultivated, foreseeing that he would shortly depart from those whom he therefore judged must be admonished with his final exhortations.

First, he addressed the abbots appointed in his place in a speech full of the tenderest love. He entreated them to pasture the sheep entrusted to them with such prudence and devotion that they might at last attain the rewards of eternal blessedness.

Let us receive these final words from his mouth (*Book on Divine Letters*, chap. 32):

> “But I beseech you, most holy men, the abbots Chalcedonius and Geruntius, to arrange everything in such a way that, with the Lord’s favor, you may lead the flock entrusted to you to the gifts of blessedness.”

Afterwards he asks that they receive the stranger above all, give alms, clothe the naked, and break bread for the hungry:

> “For he is truly to be called a consoler who consoles the afflicted.”

Then he warns them not to burden the monastery’s stewards with the weight of assigned payments, but to educate them in good morals. Let them be given a perfectly ordered way of life; let them frequently assemble at the holy monasteries, so that they may be ashamed to be called members of them and yet not be recognized by their formation.

Such was the zeal for charity in this religious man! Such concern for the salvation of others!

## § L. Cassiodorus’s Final Words to His Brothers

From Chalcedonius and Geruntius he turned his address to the brothers, exhorting them—with words capable of softening even iron breasts—to peace and concord, to meditation on Holy Scripture, and to observance of the Rule.

Finally, he asked them to repay him nothing in return for the benefits with which he had heaped them—when he had consecrated to them his possessions, estates, all his goods, his labors, and his entire self:

> “But for me,” he says (*Book on Divine Letters*, chap. 33), “deign only to beseech the Lord.”

And near the end of the book *On Orthography*:

> “Farewell, brothers, and deign to remember me in your prayers, so that, just as I wished you to be separated from the number of the ignorant, so may divine virtue not allow us to be joined in a punitive fellowship with the most wicked.”

## § LI. In the Year 562 Cassiodorus Published the Method of the Paschal Computation
