Some, including Baronius and Bucelinus, think that after completing the treatise *On Orthography*, Cassiodorus wrote another work useful for more easily indicating the indiction, epacts, and everything pertaining to the calculation of Easter.

It seems plausible to me that he published this work for the instruction of his monks for the year 562. The Paris and Geneva editions place this *Computation* among Cassiodorus’s works. Indeed, we do not see to whom else it could be attributed, since Dionysius Exiguus—who alone seemed to deserve the attribution—had died long before this year.

## § LII. In What Year of His Life and of Christ Cassiodorus Died

Cassiodorus made his final little work publicly available in the ninety-fourth or ninety-fifth year of his life. How many years he lived thereafter is not known.

We reported various opinions of various authors concerning his death in the first part, §§ 7 and 8. We do not repeat them here, to avoid tedium and excessive length. It will suffice to add several that we omitted there.

Baronius writes that he exchanged death for life at approximately his hundredth year (*On the Year of Christ 562*). Indeed, according to Bacon (*History of Life and Death*, p. 534), he did not end his life before his hundredth year.

Perhaps someone would not wrongly think that the most learned chancellor alluded to these words of Cassiodorus, speaking of himself at the conclusion of Psalm 100:

> “For it is shameful to say that, burdened with sins, I have advanced through the fertility of the hundredth number,” and so forth.

It is no clearer in what year of Christ Senator closed his final day. Augustine of Florence, Sixtus of Siena, Barrius—or Cardinal Sirletus—Trithemius, John Ferrerius, Gesnerus, Possevinus, Caferrius, Bucelinus, Stengelius, Angelus a Nuce, and many others think that he died in the year 575.

Baronius and certain others make no definite statement on the matter; they merely affirm that he was still alive in the year 562. We likewise do not believe that either the month or the year of his death can be determined.

## § LIII. Cassiodorus Rested in a Holy End

That Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator rested in a holy end, to speak in the words of Baronius, Ughelli, and Bucelinus, no one, I think, will deny. Even without our testimony, this is proclaimed by his love and veneration for the monastic life, for the Roman See, and for the universal Church—to whose benefit he always directed all his counsels and deeds as toward the most worthy goal of a Catholic man.

It is proclaimed by his singular reverence for the sacred books, as so many messengers of the holy Spirit. It is proclaimed by the sound faith that shines with perfect purity throughout all his works. It is proclaimed by the firmest hope: just as he always distrusted himself, so he always trusted in God. It is proclaimed by his most fervent charity toward God and neighbor.

Finally, it is proclaimed by his mercy toward the poor, his profound humility in word and writing, and those voluntary afflictions of the body in which he frequently asserted that the monks possessed their entire triumph (*Commentary on Psalm* 103:17).

Finally, if we believe Peter de Natalibus (*col.* 280, 1519 edition), “Buried, he lives in miracles.” But if anyone refuses to place faith in this writer, the life that Cassiodorus led on earth nevertheless gives us no slight grounds for believing that he lives among the blessed in heaven. Thus we may rightly acknowledge that Alcuin, when citing his authority (*Book V against Felix of Urgel*), gave him the title “Saint”; and that his name was rightly written long ago in Witford’s martyrology (Bollandus, [Col. 0484A] March 27), and later in the Benedictine menology (September 25).

# A Dissertation on the Monastic Life of Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus

No one ought certainly to dislike that genuine ardor of piety and that devout inclination implanted in the minds of monks toward their order, by which they vie with one another in advancing its usefulness and glory—provided that partisan zeal does not burn immoderately, ambition departs, greed is absent, and, above all, that supreme religious duty of writers is observed: that no cosmetic disguise be added to the truth.

Yet one may see many people so difficult and obstinate that they wish to concede nothing to authors who have given their names to some fellowship or religious order when those authors advance the interests of their own community, even though authority weighty in itself and reasoning balanced by its own force, brought forward in support of the case, counsels them otherwise.

The very name of the writer, or the title of the work, nauseates them; they are frightened by it as though it were an obstacle to truth.

Therefore, lest some person accuse me of being a Benedictine while dealing with a Benedictine controversy, I wish it to be understood that the purpose of this dissertation is not to add something new to my order, which is already rich and prosperous almost to the point of provoking envy and seeks nothing foreign or spurious, nothing taken by theft or granted on loan.

Conscience teaches that sacrifice must be made to truth, not to desire. Thus secure and free from suspicion of plagiarism, I propose this most noble thesis concerning the monastic affiliation of Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator: namely, whether he embraced the Benedictine Rule, which was flourishing at that time, or whether he followed some other institution—for example, that of Basil, Equitius, or another.

The constant assertion of the ancients was that he was a Benedictine. The first to disagree with the others was the most eminent Cardinal Baronius, followed perhaps by those who, dazzled by the brilliance of the purple, were less able to look upon the light of truth.

There is no doubt that the most learned champions on both sides believe that arguments can be marshaled in their favor. We shall first set forth our own arguments; then we shall hear Baronius. Wishing to be cautious no less toward sincerity than toward truth, as religious men ought to be, we shall not omit those considerations that may in some way appear to support his opinion.

Having weighed the arguments on both sides in this way and considered their force seriously, we have decided that nothing here should be definitively determined by us concerning so difficult a question. Let prudent and fair-minded men themselves judge whether Baronius can be abandoned without injury, and whether the Benedictine position can be defended without envy. Finally, let the learned reader adhere to whichever side of this celebrated problem he judges the better.

# FIRST ARGUMENT

For this argument, which first presents itself for resolving the dispute, to succeed according to our wishes, several points must first be set forth, from which, as they say, taken together, the reader may become persuaded of what we intend.

**First.** Everyone concedes—and even the heterodox do not deny it—that Cassiodorus, weary of the cares and dignities of the secular court, professed the monastic life and put on the cowl, as is shown from the cited passages in Part II, § 13 of his *Life*.

**Second.** This flight from the world and beginning of his monastic profession occurred in the year 538 or the following year, as we carefully noted in Part I, § 60 of the same *Life*.

**Third.** Cassiodorus lived until the year 575, according to the common chronology followed by Honorius of Autun, Augustine of Florence, and others whom the reader will find cited by us toward the end of the author’s life.

**Fourth.** It is no less certain that Blessed Benedict migrated to Cassinum in the year 529, established his residence on the summit of that mountain, and there, mature for heaven, died in the year 543, according to the more renowned chronological epoch.

**Fifth.** Such was the reputation for holiness of that most holy patriarch’s life, such the glory of his miracles, such the genius and character of his Rule, and finally such the discipline of regular observance among his disciples, that he made his name celebrated everywhere—not only throughout Italy, over all of which his fame spread abundantly, but also in Sicily, Gaul, Spain, and the other more distinguished regions of Europe, where, while he lived on earth, he showed himself wondrous or astonishing.

**Sixth.** While he was still alive, he had promulgated his Rule as legislator, and had entrusted it for observance to the Sicilians through Placidus and to the Gauls through Maurus, who had requested it.

**Seventh.** We must note that famous passage in the letter of the abbot of the monastery of Fundi to Simplicius of Cassinum (*Chronicle of Cassinum*, p. 355), who governed the monastery as the third abbot after Blessed Benedict and had been his disciple. From this all who devote themselves solely to truth conclude that around the year 560 the Rule of Saint Benedict was known not only throughout all the provinces of Italy but also commanded in each of their monasteries:

> “Hence it came about,” says the abbot of Fundi, “that all the monasteries of Campania, Valeria, Tuscany, Liguria, and the other provinces of Italy resolved to observe the certain and upright rule of life that your master, the most holy and God-beloved Benedict, established, so that, living according to it, they would presume to deviate neither to the right nor to the left.”

No one can justly call the authority of this letter into doubt. It was approved by the most learned Lucas Holstenius, prefect of the Vatican Library, after he had first examined and seriously discussed the most ancient parchments of the Cassinese Museum (*Chronicle of Cassinum*, p. 356), in which that venerable monument of antiquity is preserved. It is also commended and vigorously defended by Hugh Menardus, Haeftenus in his *Monastic Investigations*, Angelus a Nuce in his *Cassinese Monastery*, and certain others.

**Eighth.** It will also be useful to observe that, before this Benedictine Rule became publicly available, individual abbots had established particular laws for their monasteries according to their own wishes, as Cassian warns (*Institutions* 2.2):

> “We have seen almost as many types and rules in use as we have also seen monasteries and cells.”

The abbot of Fundi, cited above, agrees:

> “Experience has shown that the customs of many superiors have produced various forms of life in monasteries.”

As a kind of crowning addition, we append that the Vivarian coenobium was built by Cassiodorus near Scylacium in Calabria, in the kingdom of Naples, where D. Benedict had also founded his Cassinese monastery. The latter’s almost divine life was known to all Italians, and therefore could not have been unknown to our Senator, whether he was illustrious among the Goths or concealed among the Vivarienses.

From all these points, sincerely set forth in advance, and with the judgment of the abbot of Fundi standing firm, it is clear that Cassiodorus was thoroughly acquainted with Saint Benedict: he had heard of his most holy life and miracles, as well as the piety and holiness of his disciples. This is especially evident since he outlived the renowned legislator by more than thirty years.

He could not have been ignorant of the extent, fervor of mind, and efforts by which Benedict’s Rule, eagerly sought everywhere, had flown to other nations. Nor could it have failed to reach Senator’s hands after being accepted by so many monasteries; and he must have read it.

What other rule of life, then, would a genuinely good Christian man choose for himself and his monks—one who had hitherto been a novice in the cloister and was laying the first foundations of monastic perfection—if not the Benedictine Rule, which all Italy acknowledged to be superior and better than all others, and which all those most experienced in monastic discipline willingly embraced?

“While all the others were rushing toward the Rule of Saint Benedict,” asks his contemporary, the abbot of Fundi, “and while even the abbots themselves were entering anew, as it were, and being reborn in this new mother-city of the Church’s rule, would Cassiodorus alone have remained among the ruins of the ancient monasteries, raising for himself a new structure out of the broken and scattered walls of others? While all the others were abandoning their particular laws and embracing the Benedictine laws, would the wisest man have taken up a road abandoned by everyone else, or would the most modest man have prepared a new one for himself?”

I certainly would not doubt that, fired by the zeal of sincere piety, devoted above all to monastic perfection and especially dedicated to the advancement of his brothers, he proposed for himself and his coenobites that method and rule of progress which already prevailed over the others.

No one except someone plainly divining could assert that, while the particular laws of all the monasteries of Italy had been abolished in favor of the Benedictine Rule, the Vivarian house alone rejected it, though attached to no rule up to that time.

But let us press the matter more forcefully, if you please, and shed greater light on this argument.

For Cassiodorus, when he was about to profess the monastic life, it was necessary to choose both an abbot and monks under whom he might at least undertake his first training in the cloistered life. A man inexperienced in this discipline would not begin the study of humility and obedience by exercising authority as a teacher; a person not yet a novice would not act as superior, nor would someone who had not learned the first elements of the art shine before others by his instruction.

Nor would it have been consistent with the prudence of Senator or the customs of monks to establish a new congregation immediately out of secular people alone, without at least two or three experienced elders whose example and practice could instruct that newly formed community of Vivarienses.

Whom, then, would he summon as abbot, and what monks, unless Benedictines—immediately available, tested, and sought even from abroad in every direction?

Therefore, with due respect to Baronius, it stands that Cassiodorus, like the other founders of Italian monasteries, gave his name to Benedict; and that the Vivarian monks embraced no rule other than the Benedictine.

# ARGUMENT II

This argument is drawn from the practice of the same Benedictine Rule, or from the corresponding way of life familiar both to the Vivarienses and to Benedictine monks. From it one may clearly infer that they did not live under different laws.

To demonstrate this, the first point that presents itself is that in the first chapter of his Rule Saint Benedict approves only two kinds of monks—the coenobites and the anchorites. He establishes the former and recommends the latter to those who are trained and already veterans of accomplished service.

But Cassiodorus, diligently following the Master’s footsteps, set apart more secluded cells around Mount Castellum, which was enclosed by the monastery wall, so that those favored by God’s prompting and the abbot’s consent might, once well instructed, descend from the fraternal ranks into the solitary combat of the desert.

Having first set forth in chapters 29 and 32 of the book *Divine Letters* the matters that establish the strongest form of coenobitic life, he decrees the following for hermits:

> “You have the pleasant seclusion of Mount Castellum, where, with the Lord’s favor, you may happily live as anchorites, and so forth. Therefore it will be suitable for you, who are trained and already thoroughly tested, to choose that dwelling, if an ascent has first been prepared in your hearts.”

In sense and almost word for word, this is a Benedictine statement.

**2.** Regarding the hours of dinner and supper, the regular fasts, and the other stricter fasts imposed by the Church, Senator likewise agrees with our legislator, as is evident from a comparison of chapters 39 and 41 of the Rule of Saint Benedict with Cassiodorus’s preface to the Psalms, and with what we said in Part II, § 36 of his *Life*.

**3.** The care of the sick is alike in both, and their provisions for constructing baths for their benefit almost correspond word for word:

> “The use of baths,” says Benedict in chapter 36 of the Rule, “should be offered to the sick whenever it is beneficial.”

The other says in chapter 29 of the book *On Divine Letters*:

> “We have ordered baths suitably prepared for sick bodies to be built.”

Nor is the providence of either less in this respect; indeed, the same provision is found in chapter 36 of Saint Benedict’s Rule and chapter 21 of the cited book of Cassiodorus, namely, that the sick should not be neglected by the attendants.

**4.** The same cultivation of hospitality existed among them.

**5.** Cassiodorus had furnished a remarkable library so that the monks, in accordance with the command of D. Benedict, might receive each and every codex from the library (Rule of Saint Benedict, chap. 60; Cassiodorus, *Book on Divine Letters*, chaps. 28 and 32; Rule of Saint Benedict, chap. 48; Cassiodorus, *Book on Divine Letters*, chap. 8).

**6.** And, astonishingly, the son obeyed the father’s injunction concerning the lamp that was continually to burn so completely that he established the use of a perpetual lamp for the Vivarienses, as appears from chapter 30 of the book *Divine Letters* (Rule, chap. 22).

7. Nor did Baronius fail to mention, under the year 562, that Cassiodorus so carefully guarded against all association with the secular world that whatever might serve the needs of life and piety was contained within the monastery itself, and that, without compromising the discipline of silence or the leisure of contemplation, provision was made for all the brothers’ needs. This was set forth with exquisite wisdom in chapter 66 of the Benedictine Rule, which commands that the monastery be so constructed that everything necessary—that is, water, a mill, a garden, a bakery, and various crafts—may be carried on within the monastery, so that the monks have no need to wander outside, something wholly unfitting for their souls. Nor should it be passed over that Cassiodorus obeyed this command of the legislator with such religious care that, for the sake of the sick, he wished the books that discuss medicine, household management, and the care of feeding birds, especially pigeons—books useful only to the infirm—to be read by his own men.

But perhaps here you will object that most other monks lived under no other laws [Col. 0486C] than those just mentioned, and therefore that the argument drawn from the evidence cited does not establish that Cassiodorus was a Benedictine monk. We willingly grant that Cassiodorus observed certain of the aforesaid statutes that Saint Benedict shared with all monks. Yet we do not infer from this alone that he ought to be counted among the Benedictines. Rather, since we have shown that Senator obeyed both the common provisions and the particular ordinances of the holy legislator, we rightly conclude that he did not deviate even by a finger’s breadth from the entire Rule. Add that Cassiodorus ascribed to himself the practices we have called common in the same sense and almost the same words as Benedict, as will become still clearer from the following argument.

## ARGUMENT III

It is not only from what Cassiodorus did after becoming a monk that we may assert that he enrolled himself under Benedict, whether while Benedict was still alive or shortly after his death; what he wrote everywhere and repeatedly to the Vivarians in his works demonstrates this with certainty. For he appears to have composed, in scattered form, concise commentaries on the Benedictine Rule, in which, while leaving the legislator unnamed, he adopts his modes of expression. We shall offer a few examples from the many, enough to satisfy the reader without causing weariness.

First comes the arrangement of the office, or divine work, to be performed by day and by night. That Senator arranged it with exact conformity to the Benedictine system—or, more precisely, to sixteen complete chapters of the Rule—is proved by what he wrote in the preface to his Commentary on the Psalms and in other places, as we also showed in Part II, § 17, of his life.

2. The canonical hours are called “the divine work” by Benedict in chapter 43 of the Rule, and likewise by Cassiodorus in chapter 30 of the book *On Divine Letters*, and elsewhere.

3. In both authors, the part of the office that we call Matins is designated by the same term, “the nocturnal vigils” (Rule, chapter 43; Cassiodorus on Psalm 76). [Col. 0487A] And, so that access to them might be timely and easy, Cassiodorus ingeniously provided the ringing of clocks and the constant use of light: “These arrangements,” he says in chapter 30 of *On Divine Letters*, “were therefore made so that the soldiers of Christ, summoned by unmistakable signals, might be called to perform the divine work as though by the blare of trumpets.”

4. Scholars agree that no one in the West before Benedict’s time is remembered as mentioning Compline among the sequence of canonical hours, or as having prescribed its use and form for Western monks. The Roman Church itself owes its observance to that most holy Father, as Bellarmine, Francolinus, Hugh Menard, Cardinal Bona, and others cited by him properly write in chapter 10 of *On Divine Psalmody*. There can therefore be no doubt that Senator followed the Benedictine Rule when, in the prologue to his Commentary on the Psalms, in Psalm 118, and especially at the conclusion of Psalm 90, he ordered Compline to be sung at nightfall, after all the day’s activities.

5. There is a similar concern in both authors to prescribe manual labor for the monks [Col. 0487B], lest they grow sluggish through idleness, and a similar care in distributing tasks to each according to his strength. In nearly identical words, both strive to drive from the cloisters the idleness and sloth that are enemies of souls (Rule, chapter 48; Cassiodorus, *On Divine Letters*, chapter 30; Rule, chapter 48; Cassiodorus, *On Divine Letters*, chapter 32).

6. Both cultivated Cassian’s writings with equal reverence and placed them before their monks for reading. “Let all sit,” says Benedict in chapter 42 of the Rule, “and let one read the Conferences of the Fathers”—that is, those written by Cassian. “Read Cassian the presbyter diligently,” says Cassiodorus in chapter 29 of *On Divine Letters*, “and listen willingly.” Perhaps this means that, while the others sat, one person was to read Cassian’s Conferences aloud in their presence, as Benedict commands.

7. Cassiodorus commanded the Vivarians to exercise obedience above all other virtues. To make its observance more religious, he commended it to them in almost the very words with which Saint Benedict wished his disciples to be marked by it as by a kind of badge (Rule, chapter 5; Cassiodorus, *On Divine Letters*, chapter 32).

8. The Benedictine character of the Vivarian institution is no less persuasively indicated by the many distinctive expressions of Benedict that Cassiodorus carefully employed in writing to his own monks, so that he almost seems to have sworn allegiance to the Master’s very words. For example, in various places in *On Divine Letters* he calls his brothers “the soldiers of Christ,” in the familiar language of the Rule (Cassiodorus, *On Divine Letters*, chapter 30). Likewise: “And that ladder of Jacob,” and “But this is the step of humility” (Preface to Psalm 119), and so forth. Hence he speaks of that ladder of Jacob in part (Cassiodorus, *On Divine Letters*, chapter 32), and says: “Obeying salutary commands without any murmuring is the reward of a great recompense” (on Psalm 70, verse 15). Likewise: “Those things can be acquired at a lower price” (on Psalm 136, verse 11); and: “These thoughts, while they are still little, are struck against the rock” (Prologue to the Rule, chapters 7, 5, and 55). From these and other expressions encountered throughout his works, it is easy to infer that Cassiodorus could not have had the Rule of Benedict so readily at hand unless he had acquired it through use and long reading, which chapter 66 of the Rule commands should be repeated frequently in the congregation.

The same conclusion can be established, and not implausibly, from this statement of Senator, written to his own monks in chapter 32 of *On Divine Letters*: “Observe both the Rules of the Fathers and the commands of your own teacher.” By “the Rules of the Fathers,” quite a few men, and men of no little distinction, understand the Benedictine Rule. They judge that the holy legislator Benedict, out of modesty, suppressed his own name from his genuine offspring and designated it to posterity by the name of the Fathers, whose precepts he followed extensively. See Hugh Menard, *On the Origin of the Order of Saint Benedict*; Haeften, *Monastic Investigations*; and many others who hold this view, because, as Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, correctly notes in the preface to the *Concordia Regularum*, it is certain that blessed Benedict took his Rule from the rules of others.

And as is read in the *Life of Saint Martin of Vertou*: “They say that this Rule of Saint Benedict, established by the decrees of the earlier Fathers, was brought by him from the regions beyond the Alps.” It would be superfluous to assemble more evidence on this point; [Col. 0488A] for learned men cannot deny that this Rule was designated by that title even while the legislator himself was alive, and praised under it by contemporary authors. Gregory, the greatest of Benedict’s disciples, simply and absolutely calls it “the Rule of the Monks” in Book II of the *Dialogues*. It is cited in the same way in the most ancient charters, papal decrees, royal diplomas, and councils [Note: [Col. 0488D] In the *Chronicle of Saint Wandrille*. The Council of Rouen under Ansbert. Bede, in the *Life of Saint Wilfrid*. In Theodoric’s diploma in favor of the monastery of Saint Maur.], where “Law of the Monks,” “Holy Rule,” “Rule of the Fathers,” and “Norm of the Fathers” mean nothing other than the Rule of Benedict itself. Cassiodorus, observing that it had been composed from the better and more carefully selected sayings of the Fathers, appropriately called it, in the manner of others, the “Rules of the Fathers.”

But if some obstinately resist and prefer to claim that Senator’s words referred indiscriminately and generally to all the rules of the ancient Fathers, what pledge will they offer for their belief, so that anyone may safely think that this can be asserted without insulting so great a man? Cassiodorus’ prudence would certainly totter—indeed, would be entirely overwhelmed—under so great a mass of precepts if it were established that a man so eminent for discernment had bound so many unbearable burdens upon the shoulders of his monks: the rules of Antony, Pachomius, Macarius, Oresius, Basil, Cassian, and many others of that kind. It is indeed most useful to point these out to monks; it is harmful to compel them to follow them. The case is otherwise with the Rule that one has specifically professed, from whose commands the whole monk must necessarily depend.

But, to send our opponents’ replies packing and utterly demolish them, let us press one further point. By it anyone can easily believe, without scruple, that by “the Rules of the Fathers” Cassiodorus indicated no other book of rules than the Benedictine Rule. It is certain that the perfection of regular observance which he so often commended to his monks was the observance he wished to flourish in his monastery at Vivarium. A regular community must stand upon definite laws and definite practices, not upon vague, rash, or perfunctorily devised arrangements. But from Senator’s writings, instructions, and the matters we have reviewed above—and especially from the arrangement of Compline and of the entire divine office—it is clear that the practices of the monastery at Vivarium were none other than those prescribed by the Rule of Saint Benedict.

Cassiodorus therefore exhorts his monks to those observances of the Benedictine Rule that he had long before proposed to them—to that practice, I say, familiar to everyone and accepted throughout all Italy. He calls it the “Rules of the Fathers” because at that time it was not known by another name, and because he knew that the legislator had briefly reduced to his own Rule whatever lay scattered throughout the immense and varied collection of the ancient Fathers.

## ARGUMENT IV

This is established by the authority of writers who assert that Cassiodorus was a disciple of Saint Benedict and professed his Rule. Before bringing them forward, however, we should note—with no little astonishment—the profound silence among the ancients concerning a man so distinguished in the world and in the cloister by both his life and his writings. Later authors almost quarrel with Procopius, Jordanes of Ravenna, and even Isidore of Seville, who spoke either scarcely at all or far too sparingly about Cassiodorus and his manner of life, although they borrowed not a little from his works.

Yet there seems scarcely any ground for complaint if the subject is Cassiodorus’ Benedictine monasticism, which alone we are investigating. For there are not lacking witnesses who openly support our position, and we shall continue to cite a contemporary witness as long as the full and invincible authority of the abbot of Fondi, cited above, remains intact.

A second witness is Gabriel Vuarri, in Book III of *On the Situation and Antiquity of Calabria*, near the end:

“Yet if he was indeed the author,” says Paulus Aemilius Santorius in *The History of the Carbonian Monastery*, page 14, “although it was published under his name—for many, and perhaps not without good reason, attribute it to Cardinal Guglielmo Sirleto, a man distinguished by outstanding learning and by the polished discipline of his studies.” This author, whoever he may finally be, knew the antiquities and affairs of Calabria and Scylacium, where the monastery of Vivarium was situated, particularly well. He speaks of Senator as follows:

“Cassiodorus was easily the most learned man of his entire age in the secular disciplines; but, having despised the honors of the world and become a monk of Saint Benedict, he shone in knowledge of the divine Scriptures and also in holiness.”

The most learned Espencaeus says something similar in Book III of his *Digressions*, page 345, where he discusses chancelleries learnedly. Jerome Faber offers comparable testimony in Part I of his *History of the City of Ravenna*, page 1370. Among other things, he records that Cassiodorus, out of disdain for worldly glory, renounced the world and made greater progress in the school of Saint Benedict, after building the monastery at Vivarium at his own expense and enlarging it magnificently.

We read similar statements in Jerome Platus, Book II, chapter 32, *On the Good State of Religion*. In Sander’s *Belgian Manuscript Library*, a description of an ancient codex of Saint Amand in Flanders—which Sander himself had read, as he testifies—the title contains the following: “Of Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator, and later a Benedictine monk, the book *On the Soul*, and the first book only of his *Institution of Divine Letters*.”

The authors who should have led the procession will close it: those who expressly treat Benedictine matters and unanimously assert that our Senator must be assigned to their order, endeavoring to demonstrate this with many arguments. Thus Trithemius, Books II and III of *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*; Arnold Wion, Book V of *The Tree of Life*, chapter 5; Antonius Yepez, abbot of Valladolid, Volume I of his *Chronicle*; Stengelius; Bucelinus, in the *Menology* and in the *Benedictine Annals*; and others whom they cite.

But perhaps the authority of writers of our own order will seem suspect to Baronius and his adherents. On the contrary, since they are eyewitnesses and draw the truth from the fertile bosom of our libraries, greater faith ought to be given to them than to outsiders, to whom neither the archives of the Benedictine order nor its almost boundless collection of manuscripts were open. No one of sound mind would judge that such careful investigators of this matter, and such upright defenders of their opinion on the basis of arguments not to be despised, were carried away by a blind desire for the shadowy glory of their order.

What more is there to say? Among those who preceded Baronius, no one ever doubted Cassiodorus’ Benedictine profession. If some occasionally called him simply “a monk,” without qualification, as they say—such as Paul the Deacon, Honorius of Autun, Sigebert, Orderic Vitalis, Robert of Torigni, the abbot of Ursperg, Otto of Freising, Gesner, Sixtus of Siena, and very many others—they thereby indicated that he was a Benedictine under that name, either because in their age no monks other than disciples of Benedict proudly bore the designation, or because they did not mark with any other distinguishing character so many illustrious men whom no one in our order begrudges us.

In precisely the same sense, the title prefixed to older manuscript codices of Cassiodorus’ Commentary on the Psalms reads: “The Exposition of Cassiodorus, now, by the Lord’s grace, a Convert,” and so forth. For what else, I ask, does the word “convert” indicate except a monk who had professed the Benedictine Rule, already mature or advanced in age, and devoted to the duties of the choir? This is as opposed to the designation “nurtured,” applied to one not yet, or scarcely, pubescent, who put on Saint Benedict’s cowl through his parents’ vow rather than his own. This is clearly gathered from Gregory the Great, Book II of the *Dialogues*, chapters 17 and 18, and elsewhere; from Saint Lanfranc, *Decrees for the Order of Saint Benedict*, chapter 1, section 4; and especially from Saint Anselm, chapter 78 of *On Similitudes*, entitled “On the Dispute between Nurtured Monks and Converts.” Among all these authors, and many others, the same person is meant by “convert” as by “Benedictine monk.”

Let it therefore remain settled and entirely beyond doubt that Senator was always counted by his own sons among the members of the Benedictine order, until the most eminent Cardinal Baronius attempted, in our own age, to remove him from it. Let us now see by what right.

## BARONIUS’ ARGUMENT

Certain other objections against Cassiodorus’ Benedictine monasticism are considered.

[Col. 0490A]

It is certain from the foregoing evidence that Baronius did not remove Cassiodorus from the ranks of the Benedictines on the authority of any ancient writer. On what arguments, then, do you think that the most learned annalist contradicted so many authorities brought forward by us and so many reasons adduced? None, surely, except a single one—what they call a negative argument. We shall not merely diminish its force, if it has any; rather, for the sake of the most eminent cardinal, we shall enlarge it with stronger conjectures. And, so that nothing may be lacking to fairness, we shall not suppress points to which he perhaps did not attend and by which he might in some fashion have supported his opinion.

But first it is useful to hear him speaking in his own words. Thus he writes under the year 494:

“But why, following their own inclination, do they also count Cassiodorus as a monk under the rules of that same Saint Benedict, when, in treating of the monks whom he himself gathered together, in his *Commentary on Divine Readings*, chapters 29 and 32, he makes no mention at all—when he is dealing with that subject—either of Saint Benedict or of his rules, which certainly above all ought to have been placed before those monks’ eyes?”

This is the whole of Baronius’ argument, and no more, by which he attempts to show that Senator was wrongly assigned to the Benedictine community. “The abbot of Vivarium,” says the supreme historian of the Annals, “was silent about Benedict in those chapters 29 and 32, where no more appropriate opportunity could have been offered for praising him and citing his rules. He therefore could not have entered his order.”

Others will reply that he could have mentioned so great a Father and his Rule in other books, which are more certainly hidden from us or have perished. What then if we set against Baronius another cardinal, a man of no mediocre learning, likewise librarian of the Holy Roman Church—Guglielmo Sirleto, celebrated for his reputation for learning and for the testimony of authors of his own age—who counts Cassiodorus among the Benedictines in his *History of Calabria*?

But since a negative argument sometimes has force if it is weighed according to its proper grounds, let us grant Baronius’ reasoning every possible illumination and investigate what, after all, could have caused him to depart from the common path and from the consensus of others. “If Cassiodorus,” he says, “had vowed the Rule of Saint Benedict, he would undoubtedly have mentioned it in the chapters cited above, 29 and 32.”

This should readily be granted if no excuse for his silence were possible. But an excuse is available: when he wrote, the observance of that Rule was already entirely customary among the Vivarians; therefore Senator had no reason to exhort them to its practice, and believed that one thing alone remained for him to do—following the example of the holy patriarch and drawing resources from the reading of other Fathers: to urge his monks toward the summit of evangelical perfection.

There can certainly be no doubt that the Benedictine Rule was read most frequently, as it prescribes, in the monks’ daily assemblies; that it was worn smooth in everyone’s hands; and that, from the very beginnings of the order, it was learned by heart, as our most ancient parchments report. Who, then, I ask, after this, would have expected Cassiodorus [Col. 0490D] to invite, compel, or draw the monks to read that Rule? He was silent, I say, about Benedict, who was continually heard both privately and publicly in the monastery at Vivarium, and he indicated only the other teachers and Fathers of the cenobitic school, lest any help or support be lacking to those whose progress he watched over with unceasing diligence.

Indeed, Baronius’ argument seems no less inconvenient to himself and ought to be turned back against him, since he agrees that Senator was a monk and that the cenobites had subjected themselves to a definite rule before they all came together under the Benedictine Rule. For he argues as follows: “If Cassiodorus had been a monk of Saint Benedict, he would have mentioned him, or at least the Rule he promulgated—and indeed in those chapters 29 and 32. But he does not mention him; therefore,” and so forth.

We turn the argument back in this way: “If Cassiodorus had been a monk, he would in that passage have mentioned the rule to which he had committed himself and which the Vivarians followed. But he does not mention it. Therefore he was not a monk.” Yet Baronius himself writes that he professed monasticism. Therefore the negative argument is not entirely certain, and a fair-minded annalist should judge that it is endangered in both cases.

The most learned cardinal will not easily resolve this knot. For either he will answer that Cassiodorus had no concern or need to mention any rule in those chapters, in which case we agree; or he will say that he sufficiently indicated there which rule he himself followed. But if that were so, Baronius ought to have expressed clearly what the norm of the Vivarians was, and from its observance he ought to have established by a positive rather than a merely negative argument that the Benedictine Rule did not prevail as the common and customary—if one may so speak—canon of Cassiodorus’ monastery.

For his negative syllogism and dialectical quibble would have been no less playful than the following argument would be if someone wished to prove that Saint Bonaventure was not a Benedictine: “There is no mention of the Rule of Saint Benedict in his writings, although a convenient citation would have been possible. Therefore it is certain that he did not embrace it.” But he would have touched the matter with a sharp point [Col. 0491B] by stating this better proposition: “The Rule of Francis is different from the Rule of Benedict. Bonaventure observed the first; therefore he did not observe the second.”

Thus Baronius ought certainly to have indicated which rule Cassiodorus followed, if he was indeed certain that Cassiodorus discussed it in the chapters cited, 29 or 32. But he could not do so. Hence we return to the first part of the response already offered: nothing in that passage moved Senator to speak explicitly about the Rule of Saint Benedict. We shall demonstrate this once more in a few words.

Cassiodorus appears to have had one purpose throughout his entire book *On Divine Letters*: to instruct his cenobites in the study of sacred Scripture. For this reason he shows which books above all they should diligently read and learn. Then, around the middle of chapter 28, he prudently warns that, if anyone finds the study of sacred Scripture burdensome or altogether impassable, he should devote himself to cultivating gardens, planting trees, or raising fish—not to useless work, but to work that will benefit the brothers, guests, and the sick. These admonitions complete chapter 28.

Throughout chapter 29 he first discusses at length the resources of the monastery at Vivarium, carefully reviewing what he had contributed to the necessities and comforts of life. Then he urges his monks, having taken leave of all perishable and earthly things, to meditate seriously on heavenly matters. To pursue these with a more joyful spirit, he points to Cassian as a guide, whom Saint Benedict too had praised with equal commendation.

Third, following in the footsteps of that same legislator, though suppressing his name, he mentions the cells that he had ordered to be built for those who, after exhausting themselves in the labors of cenobitic life, desired the sacred leisure of the desert. But why did Cassiodorus need to commend the Rule of Saint Benedict in all these matters, especially to those monks whom—with Baronius’ permission—we at least assume here to have been Benedictines? The subject he was treating did not require it; nor did the fervor of the monks, for whom nothing was then more important than to cling strictly to the precepts of the Rule, desired by everyone’s wishes and celebrated on everyone’s lips.

Who would say that whenever a superior or abbot speaks to his monks about study, labor, or other regular exercises, he is compelled each time to recall to them the rule familiar to them and thoroughly known through use? Otherwise, would not so many most holy abbots, whose service in the order of Saint Benedict is certainly established, have to be excluded from the Benedictines because, in some exhortation to their own monks, they made no mention of Benedict or his Rule?

I readily admit that if a monastery of regular observance suffers any damage, no remedy is more immediate against impending or already raging evils than the recollection of the Rule itself, to whose words one has sworn by a public oath. But when matters are sound, and while the vigor of discipline remains unimpaired—as it did in the monastery of our Senator—repeated exhortation to observe the Rule at nearly every moment is superfluous, not to say burdensome.

Certainly, when Cassiodorus proposed other guides of monastic perfection to the Vivarians, who were already deeply devoted to the laws of their legislator, and drew out their teachings; when he unlocked the hidden fountains of divine wisdom both in sacred letters and in the orthodox Fathers; even though he was silent there about their rule, he rightly and deservedly believed that he had done more than enough for them and for his office.

Baronius’ objection to chapter 32 is still less fair. He does not show why Cassiodorus ought to have said more in that chapter than in the preceding chapter 29 about Saint Benedict and his institutions. What we said about his silence in chapter 29 would easily excuse his silence in the later chapter before everyone.

Nor would I immediately concede that Senator omitted the Rule of Saint Benedict there, since the conjecture already proposed is neither slight nor implausible: everyone may reasonably think that Cassiodorus alluded not obscurely to his teacher Benedict at the very beginning of that chapter, when he says, “Observe both the Rules of the Fathers and the commands of your own teacher.”

One should not listen to anyone who, serving grammar more than reason, insists that by the word “rules” not one rule but several are meant. For Baronius himself, when discussing the same Rule, repeatedly calls it by the plural word “rules.”

Finally, we add that the sole foundation of Baronius’ opinion completely overturns it. For the one thing he alone opposes to us—if it is true that Cassiodorus was silent about the Benedictine Rule in *On Divine Letters*—cries out that it was the rule of the monastery at Vivarium.

We demonstrate this by the following reasoning. Senator’s diligence in seeking out and procuring books from every direction is well known; through them, the celebrated library of Vivarium grew almost miraculously. It is no less evident how earnestly and in how many ways he labored to ensure that his monks lacked no human assistance by which they might cleave more sublimely to God through the constant reading of pious books.

Third, from the foregoing we take it as certain that the Rule of Saint Benedict, by its merit, reputation, and renown, was held in the highest esteem by Senator. How, then, could a man so deeply concerned for the salvation of his monks, while investigating other aids more extensively, pursuing them more eagerly, and purchasing them at greater expense, have neglected this one Rule—complete in every respect, approved by all, close at hand, and thoroughly known to him—which supplied the resources of piety and monastic perfection?

He was silent about it; let that be granted. But how loudly the walls of Vivarium resounded with it!

## SECOND OBJECTION

We submit this objection, and those that follow, proposed by a most learned man whom we honor for many reasons, for the sake of Cardinal Baronius, who perhaps did not notice them.

He objects that Cassiodorus was not a disciple of Saint Benedict but of Cassian, because he diligently commended Cassian’s writings to his Vivarian monks.

We reply:

1. This inference does not seem at all appropriate: “Senator approved Cassian’s writings and commended them to his monks; therefore, if Cassian published a rule, they embraced it.”

2. Someone could play the same enthymeme: “Cassiodorus likewise urges those same monks, with indefatigable labor, to devote themselves to reading the Fathers—for example, Jerome, Augustine, Basil, and the others—and he commanded them to read them through more than Cassian, saying: ‘Read, read diligently, read constantly.’ Therefore the Vivarian monks professed the rules of Saints Jerome, Basil, and the others by a solemn and special declaration of vows.”

3. Did not Saint Benedict establish an equal rule concerning reading Cassian privately and aloud, and at public communal assemblies? Who, nevertheless, would rightly say that the Benedictines lived under the rule of the *Collator*?

4. If Cassiodorus showed any particular diligence in praising Cassian, that is evidence of a mind thinking in harmony with the most wise legislator Benedict, who held Cassian in high esteem and devoted his monks to reading him. In chapter 42 of his Rule he commands: “Let all assemble together, and let one read the Conferences of the Fathers”; and in chapter 73: “Also the Conferences of the Fathers.” Our abbot follows him when he says in chapter 29 of *On Divine Letters*: “Read diligently Cassian the presbyter, who wrote on the instruction of faithful monks, and listen willingly.”

Finally, we reply that Senator’s purpose in that passage was not to propose Cassian’s writings as a particular rule of life, but to disclose certain errors in Cassian’s teaching to his disciples, lest the unwary be offended—especially in the matter of the aids of God and grace, in Conference 13, which Saint Prosper and others, following Augustine, the invincible defender of victorious grace, judged worthy of criticism.

Cassiodorus says as follows (*On Divine Letters*, chapter 29): “Read diligently Cassian, who wrote on the instruction of faithful monks, and listen willingly; yet he was rightly censured by blessed Prosper concerning free will. Therefore we warn you that you ought to read one who exceeds the bounds in such matters with caution,” and so forth.

Nor did he present himself as a critic only here. Whenever the opportunity arose, throughout his entire book *On Divine Letters* he took pains to point out the blemishes or dangers of other authors as well, with such diligence that this seems to have been, if not the sole purpose, at least the principal purpose of the book.

But what, I ask you, was unsound or less than orthodox in the Rule of Saint Benedict that required Senator’s scrutiny, so that it should have been cited as a defendant and brought before his tribunal? What could be found in a work so often approved by the Apostolic See, so highly praised by so many pontiffs, so many saints, and the universal Church, that Cassiodorus would brand it with the mark of censorial severity?

On the contrary, since that book contains nothing except what is praiseworthy, most holy, and divine, why should it be surprising that when Cassiodorus criticized Cassian, he remained silent about Saint Benedict?

Yet the most learned man presses the matter and yields nothing. He says: “How could Cassiodorus have been a Benedictine when he placed two abbots over his monastery, imitating the Africans who, as is read in the *Life of Fulgentius*, at one time subjected their monasteries to two abbots? Therefore, when Senator exhorts his monks to observe the Rules of the Fathers (*On Divine Letters*, chapter 32), he should be understood to be speaking not of the Rule of Benedict but of some mixed rule that he excerpted from the various rules of the legislators of the monastic order.”

We deny that two abbots presided over the Vivarian cloisters until the elder Cassiodorus appointed Chalcedonius and Geruntius as his successors. Nor do I see that what he did was alien to the Benedictine Rule. For Senator himself states more clearly and openly than anyone could bring into doubt that there were two monasteries among the Vivarians: one of cenobites and the other of anchorites.

First he describes the cloisters of the cenobites beneath Mount Castellium in chapter 29 of *On Divine Letters*: “For the place of the monastery at Vivarium invites you,” and so forth. Then he testifies that, if anyone should happen to feel a desire for the anchoritic life, he had assigned the pleasant recesses of Mount Castellium for such retreats.

Since these things were so, and since cenobites and anchorites differ considerably in their manner of life, the prudent man judged that their care should be entrusted not to one person but to two. This also contributes substantially to demonstrating Cassiodorus’ Benedictine monasticism, since, as we have already noted, the holy legislator speaks of that twofold type of monk in the very first chapter of his Rule. Nor was the arrangement formerly uncommon, or even now uncommon in some of our monasteries.

Hence you may infer that Cassiodorus did not follow the Africans, who were far removed from the Vivarian enclosure, but neighboring Europeans; and that he sought examples not from overseas but from the domestic Benedictines, who were already well known not only in Italy but also in other regions.

We learn this even from the very chapter 29 cited above. There, by presenting neighboring monks for imitation—no one would say that they were other than Benedictines—he so inflames his disciples with a desire for the eremitic life (*On Divine Letters*, chapter 29):

“For if, in the monastery at Vivarium, as it is worthy to believe, the custom of cenobitic communities should, with the support of divine grace, educate you suitably, and if it should happen that your weakened spirits desire something more sublime, you have the pleasant retreats of Mount Castellium, so that, like anchorites, you may, with the Lord’s assistance, happily be able to live there,” and so forth.

Moreover, Saint Benedict once placed twelve abbots over the twelve monasteries of Subiaco, although there was less distance between those monasteries than between Cassiodorus’ establishments. Three of them were situated on the summit of the same mountain and enjoyed the use of the same spring obtained through the prayers of the holy legislator, as well as the common use of other things.

Let the learned man therefore decide whether the Vivarian institution conflicts with our Rule—especially since, as I think, we have sufficiently shown that there is no reason to deny that by “the Rules of the Fathers” Cassiodorus wished to indicate the Rule of Saint Benedict.

“But perhaps,” you will say, “there was only one monastery in Senator’s time, since all its parts were enclosed by the same walls, and since he himself uses the word ‘monastery’ in his writings.”

Granted, let him use it. But does he not sometimes also use the plural, “monasteries”? Besides, who knows whether the same circuit of walls might not have enclosed several monasteries at Subiaco? Finally, if you take the word “monastery” broadly, there was one; if narrowly, we shall affirm and maintain that there were two at Castellium, and that nothing prevents a double Benedictine house, placed under two abbots, from having devoted itself entirely to the same Rule.

## THIRD OBJECTION

He objects again: By Cassiodorus’ command, the Vivarian monks devoted themselves to profane and humane letters, as is sufficiently clear from the book *On Divine Letters*. Yet we do not find this practice in the earliest beginnings of the Benedictine order. Therefore you must either admit that Cassiodorus transgressed the laws of his own Rule or concede that he was not a Benedictine.

But how will the most learned man prove that these studies did not flourish in the earliest age of the Benedictines, when he knows that the annals of that century have by no means come down to us intact?

Moreover, it must in no way be conceded that he who grew more than others within the order itself, and who notably matured in the use of the humane sciences, did not trace his beginnings back even to the order’s cradle. Indeed, who could believe that, when the noblest Roman youth flocked to St. Benedict as he was scarcely emerging from the hiding places of Subiaco, he intended so many adolescents and so many boys whom he subsequently took care to admit into his monasteries to remain in complete ignorance of polished literature? Unless, perhaps—and this is incredible—you were to say that the wisest legislator carefully instructed his monks to devote themselves wholly to the study of Sacred Scripture, prescribing both the hours themselves and the precise manner in which they were to apply themselves to sacred reading, while nevertheless barring them from access to the liberal arts by withdrawing them from the first rudiments of study.

I should certainly judge of St. Benedict—who was filled with the spirit of all the righteous—that he would have judged more wisely whoever said that the holy man established the following provisions concerning elementary learning, which our Cassiodorus records having been decreed by the ancient Fathers, when he says (*Book on Divine Letters*, chapter 28):

> The most holy Fathers—among whom he perhaps wished St. Benedict himself to be numbered—decreed that the study of secular literature should not be rejected, because through it our understanding is instructed in no small degree for the comprehension of the Sacred Scriptures.

We reply, thirdly, that when St. Benedict entrusted the boys’ education to the priors and deans, he wished them to place themselves under teachers who would initiate them not only into piety but also into the rudiments of the sciences. For, as Menardus testifies (*Concordance of the Rule*, chapter 75), Isidore of Seville, in his Rule—which, as the same author says in the preface to the *Concordance*, does not differ greatly from the Benedictine Rule—orders the holy man, wise and advanced in age, to instruct the little boys in literary studies.

“But,” you will object, “who in the first Benedictine community was equipped with so many of the exceptional gifts [probably *dotibus*] that Isidore requires?” At once that celebrated Gordianus presents himself, thoroughly learned in Greek literature. He wrote the life and acts of the martyrdom of St. Placidus as an eyewitness, with such elegance of language that even the emperor Justinian admired it—a fact which Baronius himself does not deny. His companion likewise was the monk Faustus, a disciple of St. Benedict from the seventh year of his life. He composed the life of St. Maurus in highly polished style, and the supreme pontiff Boniface IV strongly approved and praised it. From this, once again—and this bears more directly upon our subject—we must conclude that Faustus derived that remarkable learning from no other source than the abundant fountains of the monasteries, from which he had already tasted, as it were, with tender lips from early childhood.

We reply, fourthly, that some of these boys were enrolled by Blessed Benedict and by the first abbots of our order among the clergy, and were advanced to the exalted honors of the diaconate and priesthood. They therefore could not have lacked all that learning which such dignities rightly demand. Yet nowhere except in their own monasteries could they have been taught the first elements of that learning.

As a crowning addition to all these replies, let us, if you please, append the authority of Pope Boniface IV. For he asserts most aptly that whatever the most holy patriarch Benedict did not expressly prohibit, he permitted by his gracious silence. But if no law of St. Benedict establishes the study of literature, neither does any proscribe it; indeed, it seems not obscurely to accord with the decrees of the Benedictine Rule. Cassiodorus, therefore, not only did not depart from Benedictine statutes when he opened his schools at Vivarium, but I would confidently affirm that he conformed himself to their standard with still greater religious devotion.

## FOURTH OBJECTION

Finally, the objection is made that it is exceedingly likely that Cassiodorus lived under the same laws as Dionysius Exiguus, whom the objector supposes not to have followed the Benedictine Rule.

The answer would be easy, and perhaps not without proof, if one said that Dionysius’s monastic profession remains disputed—though writers of no mean reputation grant it to us. If that opinion stands, the objection collapses. Yet even if the opinion that associates the great Exiguus with the Benedictines did not prevail, the position that numbers the Senator among them would not therefore immediately perish; and the objection could be answered as follows.

1. Everyone agrees that Dionysius professed the monastic life somewhere other than Vivarium, and that he did not die there but at Rome; hence he was called a Roman abbot. But because the man enjoyed a most celebrated reputation for mastery of every branch of learning, the Senator, who was zealously concerned for his studies, wished him to come to him by right of hospitality and friendship, and for a time to preside over the school at Vivarium.

This is why he calls him his colleague and companion: he had admitted him as a partner in the chair of studies and in its responsibilities. “He reads dialectic with me,” he says (*Book on Divine Letters*, chapter 23); and shortly afterward: “I am ashamed to speak of my companion.”

Among monks, this alliance for the sake of learning was not unusual. Abbots either summoned more learned men to themselves or asked those who happened to arrive to remain for a while, so that the streams of their exceptional instruction and varied learning might flow more abundantly into the monasteries. If outstanding virtue was added to their learning, they were not merely received kindly; as St. Benedict advises in chapter 61 of the Rule, they were even invited to make the vows of stability.

Instructed by these counsels of the Benedictine Rule, the Senator summoned Dionysius to himself and arranged for him to be placed in charge of the brothers’ studies. But such an exchange of literary learning, the direction of a school, and what was virtually a foreign transmission of instruction by such newcomers and visiting teachers as Dionysius was among the people of Vivarium does not require the same profession of the Rule.

2. The reply may be made more plainly—assuming the disputed status of Dionysius Exiguus’s monastic profession—that he lived under laws different from those of the people of Vivarium, and that Cassiodorus, who elsewhere lavished abundant praise upon him, noted nothing in him that suggested the common life of his monastery, except the synaxes or assemblies for prayer, which he attended with greater devotion: “He was accustomed to pray with us,” he says (*Book on Divine Letters*, chapter 23).

Indeed, when the Senator describes Dionysius’s manner of life and character, he lists several things wholly at variance with the institution of the people of Vivarium. Thus he speaks of Dionysius:

> Extremely chaste, although he saw other men’s wives every day; he gladly attended banquets; he used little food, but nevertheless ate ordinary dishes; he did not disdain to take part in the company of secular people, and so forth.

How far both Cassiodorus and the people of Vivarium were removed from all these practices is made perfectly clear by his exhortations to his monks, and by what we have explained at greater length in Cassiodorus’s Life concerning their solitude and withdrawal, silence, and abstinences.

Here again the second objection discussed above collapses: it asserted that Cassiodorus either vowed or observed the institutions of Cassian. For if the same and equal pattern of regular observance applied to Exiguus and the Senator, then not only did both differ from the practices of the people of Vivarium—which scarcely anyone would admit concerning the latter—but neither agreed with Cassian. For nothing is more frequent in Cassian than the pursuit of stricter abstinence, the perpetual observance of silence, intimate withdrawal, very rare conversation with secular men, and none at all with women. How far this differed from Dionysius’s conduct while he presided over the school at Vivarium is even clearer from Cassiodorus’s preceding words.

Let no one count among the objections, or among those that might be raised, the opinion—or, rather, the dream—of a certain recent writer, who asserts in the *Augustinian Encomiast*, page 104, that Cassiodorus lived in concealment as a solitary among the Hermits of St. Augustine. “St. Aurelius,” he says, “or the great Aurelius Cassiodorus, Senator of the city of Rome,” and so forth.

He stumbles over almost every word of his own fable.

1. He supposes that the name “Senator” was an honorific title and a mark of one of Cassiodorus’s dignities, unaware that it was his proper name.

2. He says that Cassiodorus was admitted to the consular fasces in the year 510, although learned authorities establish from the consular lists themselves that his consulship occurred four years later.

3. He errs still more seriously when he makes Heliodorus the companion of Cassiodorus on his eastern journey and his colleague in the prefecture at Constantinople for eighteen years, although the Senator never held office at Constantinople.

4. He joins the Vivarium monastery to the walls of Ravenna, whereas geography places it in the Scylacian district of Calabria.

5. When he assigns Cassiodorus to his Hermits, he does not hesitate to cite Possevinus, Sixtus of Siena, and, astonishingly, Trithemius himself as witnesses, as though they had subscribed to his opinion—although the first two are completely silent about it, while the latter more than once expressly counts Cassiodorus among the Benedictines.

We have not thought that we were permitted, merely for the reader’s leisure, to pursue the errors of the many men who luxuriate abundantly in other people’s harvests—or, better, in imaginary spaces, as the saying goes.

## CONCLUSION

Having weighed the foregoing considerations and carefully examined them, and having diligently considered the arguments of Baronius and others, let the reader now be free to decide toward which side he himself inclines: the Benedictine side, or that of Caesar Baronius. Let him render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, to Benedict the things that are Benedict’s, and to God the things that are God’s.

Let him therefore reverently and submissively embrace the eminent purple of that most learned cardinal; let him acknowledge that the man is, by the judgment of all, worthy of the highest honors, and that for so many labors undertaken for the glory and benefit of the Church he ought to be crowned with the laurel of immortality.

Yet, on the other hand, in paying no lesser tribute of obedience to truth, let him consider whether Cassiodorus is justly denied his Benedictine origin. As we have seen, it is supported by the Senator’s life during the final years of Blessed Benedict and after his death, and by his monastic profession; by the renown of the Benedictine Rule itself and the universal rush to embrace it, of which Cassiodorus was not unaware; by the example of all the abbots and monasteries of Italy who professed it in Cassiodorus’s age; by the similarity between the manner of life at Vivarium and at Cassino; by the Senator’s familiarity with passages of the Rule of Benedict and by the scarcely dissimilar formulas of writing found in both; by the unanimous agreement of authors concerning Cassiodorus’s Benedictine profession down to the age of Baronius; and, finally, by the neither slight nor contemptible answer to the objections which we have honestly and faithfully reported.

## TESTIMONIES OF AUTHORS CONCERNING THE GREAT AURELIUS CASSIODORUS THE SENATOR

Saint Bede, commonly called the Venerable, *Book II on Ezra*, chapter 7:

> Cassiodorus, once a Senator and suddenly a teacher of the Church, carefully examined, in the excellent exposition of the Psalms which he produced, what Ambrose, Hilary, Augustine, Cyril, John, and the other brethren had said. He proved that he had undoubtedly been instructed by the elders of the Jews—that is, by those who confess and praise.

Paul the Deacon, *Book I of the History of the Lombards*, chapter 25:

> In the time of Justinian, Cassiodorus flourished near the city of Rome in both secular and divine learning. Among the other things which he wrote nobly, he especially unlocked with great power the hidden meanings of the Psalms. He was first consul, then Senator, and finally became a monk.

Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, *On the Diverse and Manifold Account of the Soul*, chapter 2:

> Cassiodorus, a man of exceptionally keen intellect and distinguished learning, shows in the book which he wrote on the Soul that in this matter, as in others, he follows the teachers of the holy Church.

He again cites several passages from Cassiodorus’s commentaries on the Psalms, chapters 25 and 33, concerning predestination.

Sigebert of Gembloux, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> Cassiodorus, consul and Senator, afterward a monk and abbot, composed treatises on the Psalms and divided the entire work into three parts, namely, into groups of fifty psalms. He wrote two books of the *Institutions*, explaining how divine and human readings ought to be understood; a book of *Etymologies*; and he compiled another book, *The Priest*, on figures of speech. He wrote a book of *Titles*, collected from Sacred Scripture, which he wished to be called the *Memorial*, so that those who dislike reading lengthy works might run through it briefly. He composed *Complexiones* on the Epistles of the Apostles, the Acts of the Apostles, and the Apocalypse; these are presented in the briefest explanation. He also arranged a catalogue of the Roman consuls. He condensed into one *Tripartite History* the three histories of Theodoret, Socrates, and Sozomen, translated from Greek into Latin by Epiphanius the Scholastic. Finally, in the ninety-third year of his life, at the request of his brothers, he wrote *On Orthography*, collecting its rules from twelve of the most renowned grammarians, as well as one book on the Soul.

Robert of Torigni, among the works of Guibert, page 718:

> I agree more with Cassiodorus the Senator and monk, a man learned in every field, who, considering the antiquity of his age—not to mention his manifold knowledge, since he was consul and apocrisarius of Theodoric, king of the Goths—must unquestionably be regarded as preceding Bede.

Honorius of Autun, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> Cassiodorus, one of the senators of Ravenna, prefect, philosopher by training, and monk by profession, magnificently expounded the Psalter and wrote many other works.

Helinand and Vincent of Beauvais, *Historical Mirror*, book XXI, cited and followed by St. Antoninus in the second part of his *History*, title 11, chapter 14:

> Cassiodorus first flourished as a Senator and afterward as a monk. He was chancellor of Theodoric, king of Italy, and on his behalf wrote many letters to various persons concerning court affairs. He also composed 150 treatises on the Psalms. He elegantly wrote a book on the Account of the Soul and a book on Orthography.

Jordanes, in his *Chronicle*:

> Cassiodorus was consul. Later, having been converted and made a monk, he built a monastery and shone brightly in secular and divine learning. He expounded the Psalms, wrote the books of the *Institutions* and the *Chronicle*, and arranged the *Tripartite History*.

Peter de Natalibus, page 280, 1519 edition:

> Cassiodorus the confessor, a monk from the senatorial order, once chancellor of Theodoric, king of Italy, an Apulian by birth, flourished in the time of Childebert, king of the Franks. Shining greatly in holiness of life and endowed with divine and human learning, he compiled several works of great usefulness to the Church of God. He wrote a book on the Trinity, one on the Soul, one on Friendship, and one on familiar letters; a book on Orthography; and 150 treatises on the Psalter, on the 150 Psalms. He also wrote the *Tripartite History* and paid the debt of humanity in the time of Justinian I. Buried, he lives on through miracles.

John Trithemius, *Book II on Illustrious Men of the Order of St. Benedict*, chapter 3:

> Cassiodorus, once chancellor of Theodoric, king of Italy, and afterward Senator of the city of Ravenna, a man most learned in secular writings and distinguished as a philosopher and rhetorician, heard of the fame and religious life of our holy Father. Inspired by divine love, he despised the world and became a monk in one of his monasteries. There, desiring to serve almighty God with all his heart, he devoted himself entirely to the study of Sacred Scripture. In this he advanced so greatly by writing that in his own time he scarcely had an equal in whom there was such abundant knowledge of both kinds of learning.

> This is proved by the many excellent little works which he wrote. Of these, for the present, I have found the following: an outstanding complete work on the Psalter in 150 treatises; one book on the Account of the Soul; our *Tripartite History* in twelve books; one book on the Song of Songs; three books on the Institution of Divine Readings; one book entitled the *Memorial of Divine Scriptures*; fourteen books of brief *Complexiones* on Paul’s Epistles; one book on the Acts of the Apostles; one book on the Apocalypse; one book containing a catalogue of the Roman consuls; works on Grammar, Dialectic, Rhetoric, Philosophy, Mathematics, Geometry, Astronomy, and Music; twenty-eight books of letters to various persons; one book of *Etymologies*; and one book on Tropes and Figures.

> He also published many other works which have not come to my knowledge. Several years after his conversion he was elected abbot and governed the monastery usefully for a long time. At the age of ninety-three, at the request of his brothers, he wrote a most elegant book on Orthography, collecting its rules from twelve of the most renowned grammarians. He flourished around the year of Our Lord 600. See more about him in the same author’s *Book I on Illustrious Men of the Order of St. Benedict*, chapter 6; *Book III*, chapter 7; and *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, page 241.

Those who have published catalogues of ecclesiastical writers, and nearly all librarians, follow Trithemius in almost the same words, including John Ferrerius, Gesner, Sixtus of Siena, Bellarmine, Possevinus, Philip Labbe, Vossius, and others.

From a letter of John Cochlaeus to the distinguished and God-worthy martyr Thomas More, dated the third day before the Ides of November, 1528:

> I found in the library of St. Stephen Cassiodorus’s *Chronicle*, a small book indeed, but distinguished by Roman nobility and deservedly desired by all learned men. This author gives the most certain testimony to his learning and piety in his commentaries on the Psalter; but anyone fortunate enough to possess his twelve books of letters will clearly recognize the integrity of his character, prudence, justice, and the full splendor of his dignities. This author shone among all ecclesiastical teachers through the honor of secular dignities, combined with the highest integrity, religion, and piety. Although his kings were Arians, he nevertheless defended the cause of the Catholic Church with the utmost fidelity throughout, as his various theological treatises prove, together with his own words written as prefect to Pope John II in Book XI, Letter 3.

> What is still more remarkable and more pious and religious is that, having finally abandoned the world with all the honors and dignities of the empire, he embraced the monastic life in such a way that he endowed the Vivarium monastery, situated not far from Ravenna, with very ample revenues, adorned it with various buildings, and furnished it with a very rich library. Anyone who reads his introductory books to the brothers of Vivarium will learn this more fully and admire it more worthily.

Gabriel Barrius, or rather the eminent Cardinal Sirletus, prefect of the Vatican Library, *On the Location and Antiquity of Calabria*, book III, near the end:

> In this city of Scylacium, or Sylacium, lived Cassiodorus, a man distinguished both by learning and holiness. He was easily the most learned man of his age in the secular disciplines; but, having despised the honors of the world and become a monk of St. Benedict, he shone in knowledge of Sacred Scripture and also in holiness. He wrote books of letters, and so forth. He flourished from the time of Justin to the end of the reign of Justin the Younger. He died at the age of ninety-six, in the year 575 after the birth of Christ. At Rome he held great and eminent honors and magistracies: he was Senator, quaestor, consul, master of the offices, head of the offices under the kings Theodoric and Athalaric, and prefect of all Italy.

The eminent Cardinal Baronius, under the year of Christ 562:

> The course of time now requires us to approach that most learned and equally holy man, the glory of the Roman nobility, long distinguished by countless prefectures, Aurelius Cassiodorus—not an idle man, although enjoying leisure, living in the monastery which he built. There, sitting as though in a harbor after the shipwrecks of the Gothic kings, whose realms he had administered through the praetorian prefecture, he devoted himself to God and to literature, and, until his death, continued to produce some offspring of his most fertile intellect. Thus, although exhausted by years, he passed his old age, fruitful in works. In this year he was writing a calculation of the paschal date, and so forth.

And below:

> Thus the man who had spent the vigor of his life usefully and honorably in the best administration of the kingdom, and who did not interrupt even for the least moment, in his decrepit old age, the labors he had turned toward divine things, finally rested in his monastery in a holy death. Two prefects and abbots, most holy men—Chalcedonius and Geruntius—were placed in charge of the monastery; one presided over the monks of Vivarium, the other over those of Castellum, who were joined there with the anchorites.

Gabriel Bucelinus, in his *Benedictine Menology*, under the seventh day before the Kalends of October:

> The great Aurelius Cassiodorus, born of a most noble family, excelled beyond belief and all praise in learning and in the skill of conducting affairs. First he was distinguished by the office of count of private affairs, then by that of the sacred largesses. He also held the prefectures of Sicily and of both the Bruttii and Lucania. Later he rose to the exalted dignity of the patriciate, served as palace quaestor, advanced to master of the offices, and soon gained the great honor of praetorian prefect; finally, the summit of the city’s dignities, the consulship, was granted to him.

> Yet he considered all this of little account, captivated by the glorious memory of our recently deceased and admirable patriarch and by the solid virtue and happiness of our people, confirmed by the most recent examples of his disciples, provided only that he might also attain that dignity. Accordingly, after founding at his own expense the monastery of Vivarium, or Castellum, and becoming more familiar with our monks whom he had summoned there, and after recognizing more deeply the lasting goods of religion, he soon grew weary of perishable things and, longing for eternal ones, put on the cowl himself, professed as a monk, and blossomed wondrously among the first and principal glories of the order, in the first flowering of its most holy institution.

> As great as was his majesty and glory in the world, so great was his humility of spirit in the monastery. Baronius calls him “most learned and equally holy,” and so forth.

He says more in the same place and in the first part of the *Benedictine Annals*, under the year of Christ 543, where he also cites Antonius de Yepez, Peter Opomerus, Possevinus, Charles Stengel, and others.

The eminent Cardinal Bona, in his book *On Divine Psalmody*, in the notice of authors and books:

> Cassiodorus the Senator, secretary of King Theodoric, afterward a monk, a serious and solidly learned man, whose sacred and profane studies are full of charm and grace.

Bollandus, in the *Acts of the Saints*, 17 March:

> Cassiodorus the Senator, greatly beloved by Theodoric and Athalaric, kings of the Ostrogoths in Italy, and renowned for his writings, held the consulship alone in the year 514 and was still living in 562, more than ninety years old, in his monastery near the city of Scylacium in Calabria, which he had built and enriched with a library filled with the best books.
