The first person found to have called him a saint and proposed him for veneration on this day with ecclesiastical worship was Witfordus in his *Martyrology*.

Alcuin, *Book V Against Felix of Urgell*; Aimoin, *On the Deeds of the Franks*, chapter 9; Jonas of Orléans, *Letters*, book I, *On the Worship of Images*; Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, book V, chapter 4; Orderic Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II; Augustine of Florence, *Camaldolese Chronicle*, book V, chapter 5; Espencaeus, *Digressions*, book III, page 345; Mauclerus, *On Ecclesiastical and Secular Monarchy*, part IV, book IX, chapters 2 and 3; Bacon, *History of Life and Death*, page 534; Ughelli, volume IX, folio 586; Rubeus, *History of Ravenna*, page 1370; and other historical writers on Italy and Ravenna have noteworthy accounts—though in fewer words—of both the holiness and the learning of the great Aurelius Cassiodorus.

## THE TWELVE BOOKS OF THE VARIOUS LETTERS OF M. AURELIUS CASSIODORUS (C)

## PREFACE

1. Since I had acquired the favor of eloquent men either through common tales or through gratuitous benefits—though by no genuine merits—they urged me to gather into one body the words which, often placed in positions of honor, I had poured forth to explain the nature of affairs. Thus posterity might recognize both the burdens of my labors, which I endured for the common good, and an action arising from sincere conscience, unpurchased [edition: *sincerae*; manuscript: *ineptam*].

[Note: He says *unbought* in the sense in which *bought-back praise* is used negatively below, Book V, Letter 40. See also “to fear a bought-back judgment,” Book VI, Formula 9.]

I said that their affection for me would instead prove harmful: what now seemed acceptable to me because of the requests of those who pleaded might later appear tasteless to readers. I added that they ought to remember the words of Flaccus [Note: Flaccus, that is, Quintus Horatius of Venusia, who says: “Once sent forth, the word flies irrevocably.” This is from the Rheims manuscript], who warns what danger a hasty utterance may incur.

You all see that everyone demands a speedy reply, and you believe that I am bringing forth words that cannot be repented. Expression is always uncultivated when it is not accompanied by carefully chosen meanings through delay, or when it is not explained by the exact properties of words. Speech has been given to us all in common; ornament alone distinguishes the learned from the unlearned.

The ninth year is granted to authors for writing, but I am allowed not even moments of an hour. As soon as I begin, threats arise amid shouting, and excessive haste is imposed, lest what has been begun be carried out more carefully. One man inflates our burden through the frequency of envious interruptions; another chastises us with the weight of our troubles; others surround us with the furious uprising of their demands [edition: *contentionum*]. Amid all this, why do you demand eloquence in dictation, when we can scarcely have an abundance of words?

An inexpressible concern also surrounds the nights themselves, lest provisions fail the cities, which, above all else, demand more for their bellies than for their ears. Hence we are compelled to travel in spirit through every province and to investigate everything that has been assigned to us, because it is not enough to order soldiers to perform their duties unless the judge’s continual attention appears to demand them.

Please do not love us harmfully. A request that contains more danger than honor must be avoided. But they wore me down by such arguments. Everyone knows that you are prefect of the praetorian seat, and that public duties always attend that dignity like attendants. From it military expenses are demanded; from it the peoples’ food supply is sought without regard to time; and upon it alone has the heavy burden of judgments also been placed. For this reason the laws seemed to impose an immense burden upon it, since, in honor’s name, they preferred almost everything to belong to it. What space could you steal from public labor, when whatever the common good requires flows together into a single breast?

We add also that, when you were heavily burdened by the duties of the quaestorship, frequent reflection deprived you of whatever leisure remained. And, as though you were sweating beneath moderate office, they seem to impose upon you matters concerning other dignities which their proper judges cannot manage.

Yet you do this by selling nothing. Following the example of your own father, you receive from those who hope for favors only labors; by providing freely for those who ask, you purchase everything under the service of self-restraint. They know that the glorious conversations of kings occupy you for the most part in the public interest, so that it is wearisome for idle people to await what they recognize you to be enduring through continual labor.

Still, this can contribute all the more to your praise if, amid so many and such great affairs, you have been able to produce things worth reading. Moreover, your labor can, without causing offense, instruct untrained men and men prepared for public affairs by a discerning eloquence; and those who live in tranquillity can more happily acquire the practical experience which you exercise while tossed amid the dangers of disputation.

Therefore, since you cannot conceal what your integrity requires you to acknowledge, if you allow such great benefits of kings to be forgotten, you have in vain preferred that they be granted through kindly haste. Do not call back into the darkness of silence those who, through your speech, deserved to receive illustrious dignities. You undertook to describe them with true praise and, in a manner, to paint them with historical coloring.

If you hand them down to posterity for celebration, you have, according to the custom of our ancestors, taken from the dead a fitting death. Moreover, you correct wicked morals with the authority of a ruler [manuscripts: *king*]; you break the audacity of the transgressor; you restore fear to the laws; and you still hesitate to publish what you prove capable of serving such great purposes?

You also conceal, so to speak, the mirror of your mind, in which every future age may behold you. It often happens that a dissimilar son is born [Note: See Sidonius Apollinaris, Book VII, Letter 18; St. Ambrose, Book I of *Duties*, chapter 18; and Cassiodorus below, Book V, Letter 22]; a speech unlike one’s character can scarcely be found. This, therefore, is a much more certain offspring of the will, for what is born from the secret heart is judged more truly to be the posterity of its author.

You have also frequently spoken in praise of queens and kings for the commendation of the whole community. You composed a history of the Goths in twelve books, selecting its prosperous achievements [Note: Jordanes also attests this in the preface to his *Chronicle*; Cassiodorus himself also does so below, Book XII, Letter 20]. Since you had success in those works, why do you hesitate to make them public, now that you are already known to have laid the foundations of your eloquence?

I have been overcome, I confess, to my embarrassment, and I could not resist persons so prudent [edition: *entreaties*], since I saw myself reproached out of affection. Now, readers, forgive me; and if there is any rash presumption, attribute it rather to those who persuaded me, because my judgments seem to agree with the person who decided to accuse me.

Therefore, whatever I was able to recover as dictated by me in various public acts during the dignities of the quaestorship, mastership, and prefecture, I arranged in twelve books, so that, although the reader’s attention might be stirred by the diversity of the cases, the mind might nevertheless be carried along more effectively as it moves toward the end.

But we did not allow others to undergo what we ourselves frequently experienced in the granting of honors: unpolished and hasty expressions demanded at a moment’s notice, so that they scarcely seem capable of being written down. I therefore included the formulas of all the dignities in Books VI and VII, both to provide for myself, though late, and to assist those who follow when time is short.

Thus, what I said concerning the past will apply suitably to the future [manuscripts: “And so I said of past matters, suitably and fittingly for future ones”], because I explained not persons but the offices themselves, which seemed suitable for explanation.

I prefixed to the books’ title, the index of the work, the herald of the cases, and the briefest expression of the entire discourse the name *VARIOUS*, because it was necessary for us to adopt not one style, since we had undertaken to address various persons.

One manner of speaking is required for those sated by extensive reading; another for those suspended in moderate enjoyment; another for those fasting from the taste of literature. Sometimes, therefore, it is a mark of expertise to avoid what pleases the learned.

Accordingly, the beautiful definition of the ancients is: “To speak suitably, so that you can persuade your hearers to accept the desires they have conceived.”

Nor did prudent antiquity define three styles of speaking without reason. The low style seems to creep along through ordinary expression itself. The middle style neither swells with grandeur nor grows thin through smallness; positioned between the two, enriched by its own grace, it remains within its proper bounds. The third style rises to the highest summit of discourse through refined meanings—that is, so that a variety of persons might receive a fitting eloquence and, although it flowed from one breast, might issue through different channels.

No one deserves the name of eloquent unless, girded with this triple power, he is prepared to act manfully as circumstances arise. To this is added the fact that we seem to speak now to kings, now to court officials, now to the humblest people. Some matters must be poured forth in haste, while others may be expressed only after reflection; and so it is rightly called *Various*, since it is composed with such diversity.

Would that, just as we are shown to have received these rules from the ancients, so they might display the merits of the discourse we have promised. Accordingly, we modestly promise the low style; we claim the middle style without shame; but we do not believe that we have touched the highest style, which, because of its nobility, has been placed on high [manuscripts: *in edictione*; others: *editione*].

Nevertheless, let unlawful presumptions be silent, since we are to be read. It is incongruous for us to thrust our own discussions about ourselves upon you, when we await your judgments instead.

## BOOK ONE

### LETTER ONE. TO THE EMPEROR ANASTASIUS

[Note: Baronius thinks that this letter was written in the year of Christ 493. Consult him, volume VI of the *Annals*, page 476 of the Antwerp edition. King Theodoric: He first called himself king, whereas Odoacer had earlier called himself Roman emperor, and before Odoacer there had been the Augustal. Sidonius Apollinaris elegantly describes the appearance and bearing of Theodoric, king of the Goths, in Book I, Letter 2. For how he invaded Italy, see Aimoin, *On the Deeds of the Franks*, Book I. Theodoric killed Odoacer when Albinus, *vir clarissimus*, was consul, in the year of Christ 493, the second year of Anastasius’s reign. This letter appears to have been written several years later. Guillelmus Fornerius.]

**THEODORIC, KING.** He asks for peace, which had been interrupted for definite reasons; praises the emperor; and sends ambassadors to him to settle the disputes and thereafter restore harmony to its own security.

It is fitting for us, most merciful Emperor, to seek peace, since we are known to have no grounds for anger—when the man who is found to be unprepared for what is just is already held liable by his character. For every kingdom ought to desire tranquility, in which both peoples prosper and the welfare of nations is preserved. For this is the noble mother of the liberal arts; this, multiplying the human race through renewed succession, extends resources and cultivates character. Anyone is recognized as ignorant of so many things who is perceived to have sought tranquility least of all.

And therefore, most pious of princes, it accords with your power and honor that we should seek your concord, by affection for which we continue to prosper. For you are the fairest adornment of all kingdoms, the saving protection of the entire world, which other rulers rightly welcome [others: “regard with admiration”], because they recognize that something unique resides in you [editions of Nivellus and Accursius: “as though”]. We especially recognize this, since by divine aid in your republic we have learned how we may rule the Romans with equal justice.

Our kingdom is an imitation of yours, a model of good purpose, an exemplar of unified rule; and to the degree that we follow you, we surpass other peoples. You frequently urge me to love the Senate, to embrace the laws of princes gladly, and to set in order all the members of Italy. How can you divide from august peace one whom you do not wish to differ from your customs?

There is also the revered affection for the Roman city, from which those who have joined themselves through the unity of the name cannot be separated. Therefore we have deemed it appropriate to send so-and-so and so-and-so [Note: Baronius thinks that these envoys were Faustus and Irenaeus. See volume VI of the *Annals*, under A.D. 493, p. 477] on an embassy to your most serene piety, so that the sincerity of peace—which is known to have been impaired by circumstances that arose—may, after the disputes have been wiped away, remain restored in its former firmness.

For we do not believe that you will tolerate the continuance of any discord between the two republics, which are shown to have always been one body under the ancient emperors. They ought not merely to be joined to one another in inactive affection; it is also fitting that they assist one another with reciprocal strength. Let there always be one will and one opinion concerning the Roman kingdom. Whatever we are able to do should be devoted to your praises.

Accordingly, while offering the honor of a respectful greeting, we earnestly beg you not to withhold from us the most glorious affection of your gentleness—an affection which I ought to have hoped for even if it had seemed impossible to grant it to others. We have entrusted the remaining matters to the bearers of this letter, to be conveyed orally to your piety, so that the letter itself might not become too long and we might not appear to have omitted anything concerning our interests.

## Letter II. To Theonius

[Note: Some read “Theodonius, a senator”; others, “Theodonius, Count of the Wardrobe”; others, “Theonius.”]

**Theodoric, King, to Theonius, a man of high rank.** He rebukes him for negligence concerning the purple garment, which he used to send to the royal court every year, and describes the origin and method of producing purple.

From the report of Count Stephen we have learned that the work on the sacred garment, which we wished to be completed with necessary haste, is being delayed by interrupted labor [manuscript of Remigius: “the upper parts”]. By withdrawing its customary course [edition: “use”], you are known to be imposing an utterly detestable delay.

For we believe that some neglect has occurred: either its milk-white threads, having been twice or three times saturated in a flesh-colored vessel [Juretus: perhaps “bronze-colored”], have taken on a less beautiful redness through their intoxication; or the wool has not absorbed the most precious quality of the venerated [manuscript of Audoinus: “adorned”] murex [Note: Here are described the imperial purple and the murex, together with their use. On this matter see Pliny, book IX, chapter 35; Virgil, book IV of the *Eclogues* and book IV of the *Aeneid*. Petrus Brosseus, jurist].

Therefore, if the investigator of the Hydruntine Sea had solemnly gathered the immersed [others: “inserted” or “thrust-in”] shellfish at the proper time, that Neptunian heap—the generator of ever-flowering purple [Note: “ever-flowering” is printed as a single word, as in Lucretius, book I, p. 52: “ever-flowering Homer”] and adornment of the throne—would, dissolved by an abundance of water, loosen the courtly rain in a flame-colored liquid.

The color, blooming with excessive charm; the red darkness; the bloodlike blackness distinguish the ruler and make the master conspicuous. It ensures for the human race that no one can mistake the appearance of the prince. It is remarkable that a substance prepared by death should, after so long a period, sweat out blood which ordinarily scarcely flows from living bodies wounded by injury.

For when the delights of the sea have been separated from vital strength for almost six months, they do not seem extremely offensive to acute noses—plainly so that the noble blood might not breathe anything dreadful. Once this substance has been dyed, it remains so and does not know how to be removed before the garment itself can be worn out.

If the quality of the shellfish is not changed, if that press has only one vintage, then clearly the fault will belong to the craftsman, from whom no abundance was withheld. But when the skilled director has dipped the silken, white hair into those ruddy fountains [Col. 0506B], he must possess the purest bodily chastity, because the secrets of such things are said to shun the unclean.

If all these conditions have been met, if the required solemnity appears to have been omitted nowhere, we are astonished that you gave no thought at all to your dangers, since negligence in such a garment constitutes a sacrilegious offense [others: “since the offense of sacrilege consists in negligent conduct”].

For what are all those craftsmen, all those troops of sailors, all those families of peasants doing? You too, carried along by your comitiva, issue so many commands and defend yourself with such presumption under this title that, although you are believed to be carrying out royal work, you appear in many respects to be commanding your own citizens.

Does your slackness, then, neglect the very thing that had raised you in the province and enabled you to come honorably into the prince’s presence? If concern for your resources has not yet deserted you, if regard for your own safety touches you, then, on the day when the bearer of this letter is approaching you, hasten to come with the *blatta* [Note: Achilles Statius mentions this in book II of *The Loves of Leucippe*; so do Cedrenus and Pollux in book I of the *Onomasticon*. The *blatta* is a light-shunning worm, because it cannot see daylight and therefore walks by night. It is named from its color; when caught, it stains the hand. Hence we also say *blatteus*, and a garment of this color is called a *blatta*. This note is taken from the manuscript of Rheims], which you have been accustomed to give to our chamber every year.

For now we are sending you not a prompter but an avenger, if you think that you may delay through any kind of deception.

Yet how easily, one reads, is such a great matter discovered! When a hungry dog, driven by greed, had crushed with its biting jaws the shellfish cast upon the Tyrian shore [Note: Tyre was once the most celebrated city of Phoenicia, one of the cities that formed Tripolis. Formerly an island, it was joined to the mainland by Alexander’s works. Pliny says: “Tyre, once an island separated from the deep sea by seven hundred paces, is now joined to the mainland by the works of Alexander, who was also attacking it. Formerly famous for its offspring, it produced the cities Leptis, Utica, and Carthage, that rival of the Roman Empire and covetous of the whole world; while Gades too was founded beyond the limits of the world. Now all its nobility consists in shellfish and purple.” This is what the author is indicating. Brosseus], those shellfish naturally released a bloodlike moisture and stained its mouth with a marvelous color.

And as is human custom, to turn sudden opportunities into arts, people reflecting on such examples made a noble adornment for princes out of a thing known to possess only modest substance [Note: On this matter see Arnobius, book II, p. 517, and Marius Victorinus, *On Genesis*, book II, p. 30].

Tyre of the East is Hydron of Italy [Note: Hydron is a city in Italy where shellfish are found, as they are at Tyre. This note is from the manuscript of St. Remigius. See Ammianus Marcellinus, book XIV, p. 24], certainly a courtly wardrobe—not preserving the ancient garment, but constantly sending a new one.

See therefore whether anyone will permit you to fail to fulfill what you know we so urgently demand.

## Letter III. To Cassiodorus, an Illustrious Man and Patrician

**Theodoric, King, to Cassiodorus, an illustrious man and patrician.** He extols him with the highest praises and confers upon him the dignity of the patriciate, after he had already been governor of Lucania and Bruttium and had held the praetorian prefecture.

Although he enjoys the honor proper to him—which is praiseworthy by nature—and although the fasces of an approved conscience are not lacking, since he carries dignities in his heart [Greek reading of Cujas: “bears”] (for all good things are joined to their rewards, and virtue separated from recompense cannot be believed), nevertheless the summit of our judgment is lofty. For the man whom we advance is considered distinguished and full of merits [manuscripts: “distinguished, full of merits”].

If the person whom a just man chooses is to be believed equitable; if the person whom a temperate man welcomes is endowed with self-control; then surely the one who has deserved to have as judge a man possessing every virtue can be capable of every merit.

For what greater thing can be sought [Note: Everyone desires praise, which is not blameworthy unless they place the end of right conduct in praise, as Ovid testifies in book I of *The Art of Love*, Juvenal in Satire 10, and Persius in Satire 1. Here the author indicates the distinction of being praised by a prince. Brosseus] than to have found testimonies of praise where gratitude cannot be suspected? The judgment of a ruler takes its measure solely from deeds, and the mind fortified by the authority of its lord does not stoop to flattery [editions of Nivellus and Gamonius: “of his domain”].

Let us certainly recall what you have impressed upon our senses, so that you may enjoy the fruit of your labor when you recognize that each of your qualities has sweetly remained fixed in our minds.

At the very devoted beginning of our rule, when the hearts of the provinces were wandering amid unsettled circumstances, and novelty itself did not allow a raw [Nivellus: “nameless”] master to be neglected, you diverted the minds of the Sicilians, who were suspicious, from headlong obstinacy. You removed guilt from them and deprived us of the necessity of vengeance. Sound persuasion accomplished what forceful severity might have corrected.

You won for the province the losses it had deserved not to know under devoted rule. There, while preserving civil rights under military discipline, you assessed public and private interests as an incorruptible judge. Neglecting your own wealth, and without envy of gain, you brought back riches of character; excluding either the hearing of complaints [edition of Accursius: “access”] or any opportunity for disparagement. From a place where the silence of patience is scarcely ever carried away, voices of those praising you served you.

For we know, as Cicero testifies in the *Brutus*, the nature of the Sicilians and how readily they turn to complaints, so that by their customary practice they can accuse judges even on the basis of suspicions.

But not content with this limit of praise, we gave you the conduct of Bruttium and Lucania, lest the fortune of your native soil remain unaware of the good that a foreign province had deserved.

You, however, by offering the accustomed devotion, bound us to yourself by a service through which we think you have repaid everything to us—indeed, by enlarging the debt from the point at which it might have been thought discharged [edition: “applying”].

Throughout everything you acted as a judge free from every error: neither depressing anyone through envy [Note: These are the duties of a true judge, for a judge is corrupted either by love, hatred, or money. Ovid offers a severe punishment of a corrupt judge in book I of the *Amores*. Brosseus], nor raising anyone through flattering favor.

Although this is difficult everywhere, it becomes glorious in one’s native land, where either family ties must provoke favor or long-standing disputes inflame hatred.

It therefore delights us to recall your conduct of the prefecture, the best-known [Nivellus: “newest”] good of all Italy, where, arranging everything through prudent order, you showed how light it is to pay taxes under the integrity of a judge. No one made a serious complaint about what he paid under equity, because whatever is exacted according to established order is not considered a loss.

Now enjoy your good fortune, and recover doubled the personal advantage which you had disregarded out of concern for the public. This is the glorious convenience of life: to have rulers as witnesses and citizens as praisers.

Moved, therefore, by so many extensive praises, we confer upon you the summit of the patriciate as a just recompense, so that what is a reward for others may be, for you, a repayment of merits.

Well done, great man, in your laudable prosperity: you have driven the mind of the ruler to this utterance, so that we confess that what we grant is rather the result of your good qualities. May these divine things be perpetual [edition: “accomplished under divine auspices”], so that, when we bestow these things as recompense, we may again be compelled by your merits to grant still greater things.

## Letter IV. To the Senate of the City of Rome

**Theodoric, King, to the Senate of the City of Rome.** He announces that he has raised Cassiodorus to the summit of the patriciate as a recompense for his merits, after he had administered the lesser offices with distinction. He praises Cassiodorus highly, as well as his father, grandfather, Heliodorus, and his entire family.

We wish, Conscript Fathers, that your crown might be depicted in the flower of various fasces. We wish that the genius of liberty might see the Senate as a pleasing assembly. For the gathering of such men is the dignity of rulers, and whatever is observed in you with festive rejoicing is truly added to our praises.

Yet we desire most eagerly that the lights of dignities adorn your body, since those who have grown through courtly authority fittingly restore increase to their homeland. Our attention searches out such men; we rejoice to find in them treasures of character, in which, as though in sculpted faces of honor, the mercy of our serenity is expressed.

For this reason we have given Cassiodorus, an illustrious and magnificent man, most renowned for exceptional distinction in public affairs, the seat of the patriciate as a recompense, so that the merits of a servant may be declared through the honor of a great name.

He was not advanced by fragile good fortune, flying to the summit of the fasces through the game of Fortune and sudden successions. Rather, as virtues customarily grow, he climbed to the height of renown by the steps of dignities.

For, as you know, the first entrance into public administration was founded upon the burden of the comitiva of the private estates. There he did not stumble through the weakness of apprenticeship, innocently erring through the fault of inexperience; rather, with the firm step of restraint established, he lived by an exemplary model.

Soon afterward, having received the honor of the sacred largesses, he grew as much in the praise of his conduct as he had advanced in dignity.

Why should we recount the discipline restored to the provinces, or the lessons of justice poured into every kind of person [others: “memorials of justice”]? He lived with such self-control that he both established equity by his admonitions and taught it by his example.

An innocent judge is an easy persuader of what is right; under his praiseworthy conduct, it is shameful not to possess respectable morals. Who would fear a crime when he sees its accomplice sitting in the lap of the judge? A man vainly assumes the appearance of feigned severity when, being greedy, he discourages the pursuit of money, or when, being unjust, he declares that the laws must be obeyed.

He has no place for the administration of justice whose authority is not supported by a free conscience [Juretus: “There is no spirit of strictness”], because offenses are feared only when they are believed to displease judges.

Thus, trained under the preceding king in the schools of administration, he came to our palace with well-earned praises. You remember, and the memory of recent events still assists you, with what moderation he sat in the dignity of the praetorian prefecture and, raised to the heights, looked down from there all the more upon the vices of those before his eyes [others: “of prosperous men”].

Unlike many who are raised up by Fortune’s favor, he did not exalt himself into the buskin of great power. Rather, moderating everything with equity, he did not make our favor toward him hateful.

He caused greater things to be wished for him by restraining great power within the bounds of modesty. This is the most welcome fruit of an approved conscience: although he could have attained the highest things, he was nevertheless judged by everyone to deserve still more.

He joined our advantages well with the joy of all: generous toward the treasury and gracious toward those who paid justly. Then the republic recognized in him, from that Romulean assembly, a man of innocence. Although he made himself glorious through self-restraint, he contributed something greater by leaving an example of good action to those who came after him.

For the person who appears capable of succeeding a praised man is ashamed to do wrong.

Thus, as you know, he was revered by soldiers, gentle toward provincials, eager to give, disdainful of receiving, a hater of crime, and a lover of equity. What was difficult for him to guard, when he had resolved to abstain from what belonged to others?

It is a sign of an unconquered spirit to cherish the advantage of reputation and instead hate the profits of litigation.

But those who did not know the very noble character of his father and grandfather may rightly marvel at these qualities in him. For the earlier Cassiodoruses are celebrated by fame.

Although this name appears to occur among others, it is nevertheless established as proper to his family. An ancient offspring, a praised lineage, they were distinguished among those who wore the toga and outstanding among brave men; they flourished both in bodily health and in stature.

His father, under the emperor Valentinian, honorably held the dignities of tribune and notary [Note: These two offices are often joined in imperial constitutions, as may be seen in book IV of the Code, *Concerning Advocates of Various Judges*; in book I of the Digest, *Concerning Mandates of the Emperor*; in the law *Neque*, book 61 of the Code, *Concerning Decurions*; and in book I of the Theodosian Code, *Concerning Those Who Receive Provisions*, cited by Sidonius Apollinaris in book V, letter 9. Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXVI, praises a certain Procopius who was tribune and notary. In a novel constitution of the emperor Valentinian concerning wills, Caesarius is named “a distinguished man, tribune and notary.” Brosseus].

That honor was then given to eminent men, since it is clear that such persons were chosen for the imperial secretariat in whom no fault of blame could be found.

But, as people of equal spirit customarily always choose one another [Grulard and Cujas: “love one another”], he was joined in great affection to the patrician Aetius for the advancement of the republic. The master of affairs [Note: Emperors are often honored by this title in the books of the ancients, as in Pliny’s letters, in book III of the Digest, *Concerning Things Deleted from Wills*. Sidonius, in his *Panegyric on Majorian*, writes:

> “My Gaul is still unknown to the masters of affairs.”

Sometimes “masters of affairs” is also used for princes. We likewise customarily call others besides emperors “masters,” as may be seen in Suetonius. Yet Suetonius, in his account of Augustus, says that Augustus especially detested the title “master” as a curse and insult, and afterward did not allow himself to be called master. Tiberius and Severus did the same. Hence Tertullian says: “I shall plainly call the emperor ‘master,’ but in the ordinary manner”; and elsewhere he argues that the word “master” is the title of supreme power. In civil law, the title “master” includes those who possess ownership, as in the law *Recte*, Digest, *Concerning the Meaning of Words*. Nevertheless, the word “master” properly applies only to slaves. I also find that in the age of Augustus and afterward children called their fathers masters, and flattering brothers called their brothers masters. They even addressed people they met as masters, as is clear in Seneca: “When a name does not come to mind, how do we greet those we meet? As masters.” Brosseus] followed him in every aspect of counsel because of his wisdom and his glorious services to the republic.

He was therefore sent on an embassy to Attila, powerful in arms, together with Carpilion, the son of the aforementioned man. Without fear he saw the power he had feared; trusting in truth [editions of Nivellus and Gamonius: “authority”], he looked down upon those terrifying and threatening faces. He did not hesitate to oppose the arguments of a man who, seized by some kind of madness, appeared to seek dominion over the world.

He found a proud king but left him pacified. He destroyed his slanderous claims with such truth that Attila would have wished to seek the favor of one with whom it was advantageous for him not to lack peace, despite that kingdom’s immense wealth.

His steadfastness raised up the side that was afraid; those who seemed to be armed with such ambassadors were not considered unwarlike. He brought back a peace that had been despaired of.

The success of his embassy may be understood from the fact that it was received with as much gratitude as it had been desired. Soon honored, he soon offered gifts of revenue as an equitable judge.

But he, richer in native moderation, accepted an unoccupied dignity and sought the most pleasant parts of Bruttium in place of a reward. The ruler could not deny the desired repose to one who had made him secure from a savage enemy; saddened, he released from his service one whom he knew had been necessary to him.

His grandfather Cassiodorus, illustriously adorned and surrounded by honor—which could not be denied to his family—freed Sicily and Bruttium from the incursions of the Vandals by the defense of arms, so that he deservedly held primacy in those provinces which he had defended from so savage and sudden an enemy.

The republic therefore owed his virtues the fact that Gaiseric did not invade those provinces so near to him—Gaiseric whom Rome later endured as a savage enemy.

These men also flourished in the eastern regions through the renown of their ancestors. For Heliodorus, who, in that republic and in our own time, admirably held the prefecture for twice nine years, was shown to be joined to their kinship.

A distinguished family in both worlds, fittingly suited to both Senates, shone with the purest brilliance, as though possessed of two eyes for two lights. How far can any nobility extend itself beyond this family, which deserved to be illustrious in both worlds?

He too lived in the province with the honor of a judge and the security of a private citizen. Superior to all of them in nobility, he attracted everyone’s minds to himself, so that those who could not be subjected by the right of liberty appeared instead to be gently bound by continual benefactions.

He even gloried in such abundance of his patrimony that, among his other goods, he surpassed princes in herds of horses and, by giving repeatedly, did not incur envy for his name [the word “name” is absent from the manuscript, and D. Juretus reads “of the man”].

That is why our candidate always arms the armies of the Goths; and, better because of the excellent practice he received from his parents, he preserves it through hereditary generosity.

Our dignity has passed through these matters in due order so that everyone may understand that those who choose to live by distinguished principles can also restore in our presence the praises of their parents.

And therefore, Conscript Fathers, since the honor of good men is advantageous to you, and your agreement accompanies our judgment, let his advancement be welcomed under a favorable auspice—he who has made the favor of everyone open to him.

For this is rather an exchange than a reward: those who have honored us through commendable action may rejoice in reciprocal favor.

## Letter V. To Florian, a Senator

**Theodoric, King, to Florien, a senator.** He orders that the decisions of Count Anna concerning the estate of Mazene be observed.

Completed lawsuits ought not to be dragged out indefinitely. For what peace will be granted to those who disagree if they do not even acquiesce in lawful judgments? There is one harbor prepared amid human storms; if people pass it by with heated resolve, they will always wander amid billowing quarrels.

And therefore, by this present decree we address your distinguished office, so that, if the matter is as it is suspected from the present circumstances [manuscript of Remigius and edition: “as it is requested”], and if the dispute concerning the estate of Mazene has been decided by lawful determinations in the judgment of Count Anna, with no appeal shown to have suspended it, the decrees may be observed.

For just as we do not wish to deny judgment to the oppressed, so we do not grant assent to unreasonable complaints. A person must be compelled to remain quiet when through his own fault he refuses to be peaceful.

Even a skilled physician frequently cures an unwilling patient, since in serious illnesses the proper will is absent and the patient instead desires what he senses may be burdensome according to the judgment of the physician of health.

## Letter VI. To Agapitus, Prefect of the City

[Note: The Audoinus manuscript reads “Agapitus, an illustrious man and bishop”; the Rheims manuscript, “Agapitus, a senator.” Grulard and Cujas read “Agapitus, an illustrious man, prefect of the city.”]

**Theodoric, King.** He writes that Rome should send its most skilled marble workers to Ravenna to complete the basilica of Hercules.

It befits a prince to care for what concerns the enlargement of the republic, and it is truly worthy of a king to adorn palaces with buildings. Let us not yield in ornament to the ancients, for we are not inferior to the blessings of the ages.

Therefore, having undertaken in the city of Ravenna the extensive work of the basilica of Hercules—a name to which antiquity fittingly attributed whatever it established in a court with admirable praise—we entrust the matter most diligently to your high office.

According to the brief appended below [Note: Below, book IV, letter 21: “Defined in the written briefs”; and book II, letter 39: “You will indicate, in written briefs, the money given to you.” Book II of the Theodosian Code, *Concerning Exemptions of Artisans*: “Artisans included in the attached brief.” Jerome, in his letter to Florentius, uses *brief* in precisely the same sense. *Briefs*: book XIII of the Theodosian Code, *Concerning Remission of Taxes*; the final book of the Code, *Concerning Fiscal Law*; Symmachus, book I, letter 34. Fornerius], send us from the City the most skilled marble workers, who may join together what has been finely divided and, by binding the pieces together with interlocking veins, may commendably imitate nature’s appearance [edition: “measure nature’s appearance”].

Let art produce what surpasses nature. Let the variegated veneers of marble be woven into the most pleasing variety of pictures. For whatever has been sought out for adornment is always held in value.

You will provide them with expenses and subsidies, so that none of our people may be burdened by an order which we intend for the benefit of all.

## Letter VII. To Felix, a Most Illustrious Man

[Edition and Grulard and Cujas: “Count.”]

**Theodoric, King, to Felix, a most distinguished man.** He orders him to restore the property of the ward Plutianus, which Felix had obtained from Neoterius, Plutianus’s brother, not so much by purchase as by theft, and rebukes him for failing to divide the inheritance equally among equals.

From the petition of Venantius, guardian of Plutianus, we have learned that you have engaged in conduct unworthy of you: you have afflicted with the loss of property one whom you ought to have helped at your own expense.

Your relationship by marriage ought to have been shown by the support you provided [manuscripts: “by support alone.”] What, then, does it seem like to do to those joined by blood what would be proved criminal in the case of strangers?

Therefore, by the present command we decree that whatever you know you obtained from Neoterius, who was wantonly prodigal, not so much by purchase as by theft, you must restore without delay for incorporation into the property of our soldier, lest you force us to avenge such conduct through the laws, when we now appear to have moderated everything through gentleness.

For we do not permit the ward to lose what we had bestowed upon his parents under our commendation. It is a grave matter for what was conferred by princely generosity to be taken away through false accusation.

As for the remainder, which you claim to have divided as your wife’s share, disregarding the path of justice—if it can indeed be called a division when it is clear that it was carried out under the will of one person—hasten to appear before our court, so that we may arrange among you whatever accords with justice.

For it is unjust that, from one estate, some to whom equal succession belongs should overflow with abundance while others groan under the hardships of poverty.

## Letter VIII. To Amabilis, the Executor

**Theodoric, King, to Amabilis, the executor.** He orders that the property of the ward Plutianus, wrongly sold by his brother Neoterius, be restored without delay to Venantius, Plutianus’s guardian. If the brother intervenes, he wants the case brought before his tribunal.

It is dear to our heart to protect everyone collectively, but especially those whom we know to have been unable to protect themselves. The balance of equity will thus be preserved if we offer assistance to the unequal and set our authority, on behalf of the little ones, against the insolent.

The weaker party seeks a prince, because those from whom public support withdraws fall into disrepute to our condemnation.

We have therefore learned from the tearful petition of Venantius, guardian of Plutianus, that his brother Neoterius, forgetful of brotherly affection, has torn apart the child’s property with the fury of an enemy.

This moved us because of the bitterness of the circumstances: we did not want our generosity, which we wish to stand as a title of piety, to appear to have been seized by unlawful presumptions.

And since there is no doubt that, in the recovery of a minor’s property, the losses caused by delay should be removed above all, therefore, fortified by our command, your devotion shall cause the requested property to be restored without delay to the aforesaid guardian, if there is nothing that can reasonably be brought against him by the person summoned.

Or, if the holder’s claim has anything to allege on his own behalf [Grulard and Cujas: “the claimant’s claim”], let him hasten to come to our court after a legal statement has been submitted, so that, once the allegations have been examined, we may judge according to our customary equity.

## Letter IX. To Eustorgius, a Venerable Man and Bishop of Milan

**Theodoric, King, to Eustorgius, a venerable man and bishop of Milan.** He says that he has restored the bishop of the city of Augusta to his former honor after the bishop was accused by clerics on false charges, and he sends those clerics to Eustorgius so that he may restrain them with the punishment they deserve.

The condition of subjects is secure where life is lived under the equity of rulers. Nor should one from whom unchangeable ordinances ought to be established be led astray by a doubtful rumor [manuscripts: “by reason according to custom”].

For we gather confidence in matters from reason, which is never hidden from those who seek it if it is pursued along its own traces.

And therefore, by the present document we declare what we trust will be most welcome to your blessedness: the bishop of the city of Augusta, accused by false charges of betraying his homeland, has been restored by us to his former honor and shall possess the entire right of the episcopate that he previously held.

For nothing may be rashly presumed in such an office. If a person is believed to have been guided by his purpose, even one who remains silent is excused from offenses.

Accordingly, manifest crimes in such cases scarcely find credence. Whatever is said out of envy is not considered truth.

We wish to strike his attackers with lawful punishment; but since they themselves also held the clerical office, we have sent everything to the judgment of your holiness for arrangement. It belongs to you to impose equity upon such conduct, since we know that you preserve ecclesiastical tradition.

## Letter X. To Boethius, an Illustrious Man and Patrician

**Theodoric, King, to Boethius, an illustrious man and patrician.** He writes that the household protectors of the cavalry and infantry, who keep continual watch over the royal court, have complained that they do not receive full-weight solidi from the treasurer of the prefects for their customary payments and that they suffer serious losses in the reckoning. He discusses arithmetic, the number ten, the solidus, the number six, the ounce, and the pound, and forbids any reduction of them whatsoever.

Although justice ought to be administered to all peoples, and truly deserves its name when it proceeds with equal moderation among the powerful and the humble, those who do not withdraw from service at the palace seek it with greater confidence. For something is freely granted by princely generosity to the idle; but custom is faithfully rendered as a kind of debt to one who serves obediently.

The *domestici patres* [D. Grul. and Cujacius: *protectores*] of cavalry and infantry, who seem to keep perpetual watch over our court—for this is usually done amid great hardships [Juretus: labors]—have jointly complained to us in a petition that, from the treasurer of the prefectures [Note: There were various treasuries, such as the theatrical treasury, mentioned by Julian in Novel 63; the quaestorian treasury; and the treasury of the praetorian prefect, in book 9 and the last book of the Theodosian Code, *On the Remission of Debts*, and in book 6 of the Code, *On the Collection of Taxes*. Hence the expression “treasurer of the prefectures.” There was also a pontifical treasurer, who once administered the treasury of the pontiffs; he is mentioned in an ancient monument: “Gaius Calpurnius, of senatorial rank, and Septimia Ammias his wife, purchased for themselves two memorials, and for Calpurnius Ammianus, Roman knight, their son, and for their freedmen, freedwomen, and descendants, a two-roofed treasury, with a shop and a little garden. If anyone should wish to sell this treasury, he shall then pay to the treasury of the pontiffs two [units].” There was also a wine treasury, as Symmachus attests in book 13 of his letters and in the Code, *On Receivers*. Hence a *treasurer* is a slave entrusted with the administration of the treasury in which the master’s money is stored—the same as a steward or dispenser. Scaevola, *On Testamentary Manumissions*: “Stichus, the treasurer, entered the names with his master’s approval.” Those who draw money from the house pay “from the treasury,” as distinct from payment made from the bankers’ table, according to book 1 of the Code, *On Things Recorded from Public Accounts*, book 4, *On the Regular Distributions*, and the last book, *On Receivers*. They call the treasury of the praetorian prefect a *trapeza*, that is, a table; and therefore Sidonius not improperly assigns to the treasurers the weights that are distributed together with measures to all the receivers, according to the final law of the Code, *On the Defenders of Cities*. BROSS.], they do not receive solidi of full weight as their customary emoluments [Col. 0514C], and that they suffer serious losses in the number.

Therefore let your prudence, trained by learned teachings, drive criminal fraud from the fellowship of truth, lest anyone find it desirable to subtract anything from that integrity. For this discipline, called arithmetic, rests upon the most certain reasoning amid the uncertainties of the world. We recognize it, equally with heavenly things, as manifest order, beautiful arrangement, simple knowledge, and immovable science: it contains the things above and safeguards those below. For what is there that does not have measure or exceed its weight? It embraces all things and regulates everything; and all things derive their beauty from this, that they are known to exist under its measure [editor: bushel].

It is pleasing to observe how the number ten, in the manner of heaven, both revolves within itself and is found never to fail. It grows by a new condition, returning into itself, the same calculation always being added to itself; so that, although ten does not seem to be exceeded, from small beginnings it prevails to embrace greater things. Repeated again and again by fingers bent and raised, it is always rendered extended; and the more the reckoning is brought back to its beginning, the more certainly it increases [manuscripts and editor: is rendered]. The sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the bright stars are enclosed within a countable quantity. Every creature is subject to number before its author; and whatever comes into existence cannot be removed from such a condition.

And since it delights us to speak with the learned about the more hidden matters of this discipline, it must be observed that, although coins themselves may seem worthless because of their very common use, the ancients nevertheless gathered them according to a reasoning of great significance. For they decreed that six thousand denarii should constitute one solidus, evidently so that the rounded form of radiant metal might appropriately enclose the age of the world [Note: Cassiodorus therefore thinks that the world will last six thousand years. Lactantius, book 7, *On the Divine Premises*, mocking the Chaldeans, says: “Let the philosophers who count the thousands of ages from the beginning of the world know that the sixth thousandth year has not yet been completed; when that number has been completed, the consummation must take place and the condition of human affairs be restored for the better.” The same author writes in the *Epitome of the Divine Institutes*: “Six thousand years have not yet been completed; when that number has been completed, then all evil will finally be removed, so that justice alone may reign.” This opinion of Rabbi Elijah appears in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter *Helek*, and in the book *Avodah Zarah*, in the chapter *Lifne Edhen*: “The world will exist for six thousand years and will then be destroyed. Two thousand are for desolation—that is, as the theologians prefer, two thousand before the Law; two thousand under the Law; and two thousand days of the Messiah.” Galatinus, book 4, chapter 20. Isidore, near the end of book 6 of the *Etymologies*, when discussing the division of times and the six ages of the world, concluded his discussion with these words: “The remaining time of the sixth age is known to God alone.” I gladly agree with him. FORNER.].

The ancients, learnedly, defined the number six as perfect [Note: Six is perfect because 1, 2, and 3 make 6. See Severinus Boethius, *Arithmetic*, and Jordanus on the power and sacred character of the number six. Macrobius, book 1 of the *Dream of Scipio*. Thus Julian extolled the number nine hundred with many praises in his letter to Serapion. Origen Adamantius, *Commentary on the Gospel of John*, tome 28: “Those who investigated the natures of numbers first defined six as perfect, since it consists of its own parts and a twofold composition: from one and two, which is three—the first number and the number into which doubling issued. I mean two; for two multiplied by three makes six itself.” FORNER.], and marked it with the name of the ounce, which is the first degree of measure. They calculated this twelve times, in likeness to the months, and gathered it into the fullness of the pound, corresponding to the circuit of the year.

O discoveries of the wise! O provisions of our ancestors! It is an exquisite arrangement, one that distinguishes what human use requires and figurally contains so many secrets of nature. It is rightly called a pound, since so many things have been weighed in its consideration.

To violate such secrets, and thus to wish to confuse things established with the utmost certainty—is this not a cruel and shameful tearing apart of truth itself? Let merchants conduct their business in merchandise; let things be bought broadly and sold more narrowly; let a reliable weight and measure be established for the peoples, because everything is thrown into confusion if integrity is mixed with fraud [Col. 0515C]. Certainly what is given to laborers must not be mutilated; but from one who is required to act faithfully, let reduced compensation be provided. Give a solidus, then take something from it if you can prevail; hand over a pound, then diminish it by something if you can. It is clear that all these matters have been provided for in the very names: either you give them complete, or you do not pay what they are called. You cannot, you absolutely cannot, give names signifying completeness and then produce criminal diminutions.

Therefore take care that the treasurer of the treasury retain his just customary practices [Note: Below, book 3, letter 23, and book 7, letter 2. Novel 43 belongs here; also the law of France promulgated by Charlemagne, book 3, title 12, *On Customs Duties*: “It is our pleasure that the ancient and just customs duties be exacted from merchants”; and book 4, title 24, *On Unjust Exactions and Customs Recently Instituted*, such as tribute; and title 52, *On Customs Duties and Cispadane Duties*: “Let them observe this: where there was an ancient custom, let the exactions be made; where new ones have been invented, let them be abolished.” This agrees with the single law, *On Crown Gold*, in book 10 of the Code. “Nothing” in the Theodosian Code, *On Extraordinary Exactions without Filth*. FORNER.], and that what we provide to those who deserve well may be received as an uncorrupted gift.

## LETTER XI. KING THEODORIC TO SERVATUS, DUKE OF RAETIA

He orders that the slaves taken from Maniarius by the soldiers called Breones be restored without any delay.

It is fitting that you display by your conduct the honor you bear in name, so that you do not permit any violence to be done throughout the province over which you preside, but compel everything to conform to justice, from which our rule flourishes. Therefore, moved by the petition of Maniarius [manuscripts: Moniarius], we address you by this present command: if you discover that the Breones have indeed taken his slaves without justification [Col. 0516B]—they are said to be accustomed to military duties and thus to oppress civil society while armed [Note: Restraint and strict discipline of conduct must be enforced in the army. For this reason there are three things without which an army has neither strength nor order: self-control, modesty, and abstinence. Self-control concerns food and sexual relations, from which weakness and softness arise; modesty concerns words, clothing, and actions; abstinence means not harassing provincials or seizing things indiscriminately. BROSS.]—and therefore disdain obedience to justice because they are always intent upon martial wars, since, somehow, for those who are constantly fighting it is difficult to preserve moderation of conduct, then, after removing every insolence that might be assumed under the pretext of courage, see that the requested property is restored without interruption. Otherwise, through the inconveniences of delay, they may appear to hate the victory of the petitioner.

## LETTER XII. KING THEODORIC TO EUGENITUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND MASTER OF OFFICES

After he has commendably administered the quaestorship, he confers upon him the dignity of master of offices and urges him to earn still greater distinctions.

[Col. 0516C]

The judgment of a king is the splendor of merit, because we know how to bestow these things only upon the deserving. And although, with God’s favor, everything we wish is subject to our power, we nevertheless measure our will by reason, so that we may be thought to have chosen what all can approve as worthy.

This is why, when you were commendably pursuing the studies of learned doctrine, we formerly chose you for the summit of the quaestorship, so that the dignity of literary office might become the reward of your honorable labor. For what is more splendid in the office of advocacy [Note: This is the duty of an advocate: according to the order of law, he pleads the case he has undertaken. But can his life, if it is disgraceful, harm the case he has undertaken? “The person of the advocate,” Augustine says, “can neither harm nor benefit the case.” For as the case is, so will the answer be. BROSS.], if it is performed purely, than to take a foreign matter upon oneself in order to relieve the labors of others? Trained in this field by the course of your achievements, you have reached the palm of our judgment.

Yet our kindness is not content with a single reward. It doubles your honor and arranges additions, and by its zeal renews gifts as though it owed everything it bestows. Therefore assume the insignia of the mastership, using all the privileges that your predecessors are known to have possessed. And so rejoice at having received such a judgment: in return for the honor of your labor, you have deserved to receive another honor.

What we thought of your former reward we declare by the increase of this second dignity. Fasces have been born from fasces, and, retaining their nature, arboreal offspring have sprouted again, decently pruned [Col. 0517B]. But let this reward not fill you with satiety, nor let the praise discovered by our judgment give your labors a holiday. Rather, let honesty become more desirable when it reaches its reward, and let it become more pleasing to have endured anxious labors when you understand that you have found their fruit.

Therefore return the honors you receive from documents through your merits. For you know well by what zeal one pleases us who comes from the innermost chambers of the council. You remember how often the innocent have been praised before us, and how often we have repaid good actions. We used to speak our judgments through your mouth; let examples such as these inspire you. Be a temple of innocence [Note: Thus he said in book 6, formula 3, that rightly exercising the praetorian prefecture is a kind of priesthood; and likewise in formula 19 of the same book. In a similar example, Ulpian, in book 1, *On Justice and Law*, calls jurists priests of justice; so does Symmachus in book 10, letter 54, and book 7, letter 58. JURETUS.], a sanctuary of self-restraint, an altar of justice. Let nothing profane enter judicial minds. Let service be rendered to a pious prince under something like a priesthood.

## LETTER XIII. KING THEODORIC TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

He announces that he has raised Eugenitus to the office of master of offices. Eugenitus is praised with the highest commendations because he competently exercised the quaestorship.

[Col. 0517C]

Conscript Fathers, dignity is a gift when it comes to one who is unknown; when it comes to one who has been tested, it is compensation for merits. The former is indebted to judgment; the latter is bound to favor. We raise some by esteem, others we advance by grace, and our humanity opens itself to every path of indulgence.

But consideration of your affection reminds us whenever one is brought into your assembly who is esteemed for glorious virtues. Whatever is the flower of the human race ought to have a place in the curia [Col. 0517D] [Note: Ennodius said this in his *Panegyric of Theodoric*: “You clothed the crown of the curia in countless flowers; no one whom a good conscience helped when he pleaded was touched by despair of honors.” Nazarius agrees: “You at last perceived, Rome, that you were the citadel of all peoples and queen of the lands, when from all the provinces you secured noble men as pledges for your curia, so that the dignity of the senate might be more illustrious not merely in name but in reality, since it consisted in the flower of the whole world.” I will not omit that Heliogabalus despised the senate so greatly that, according to Lampridius, he called senators “togate slaves.” BROSS.]. Just as it is the citadel and glory of cities, so it is the ornament of the other orders.

Therefore we have raised Eugenitus, an illustrious man shining with the reputation of learned doctrine, to the honor of the mastership, so that he might bear in title the dignity he possessed in merit. For who is unaware of all his dutiful labors, which he did not undertake from a base mind but preserved as an honor of advocacy? [Col. 0518A] We therefore gave a person equal to such honors, so that, each shining with the other’s distinction, they might adorn one another through their mutual fitness.

This is the man who formerly clung to our side as a truthful quaestor. No cloud of envy darkened him, nor did he seek, with the poison of malevolent zeal, arts of harming us through a tainted mind. In the sincere secrecy of his heart he obeyed our purity, and offered his innocence to the piety of our commands. For a deceitful mind does not follow the will of the one who commands, but rather unfolds its own [Col. 0518B] desires.

You have clear evidence of our judgment in this matter: after the summit of that office, he was to climb to another dignity. We did not allow him to remain idle whom his merits did not permit to be without office. He is to be judged by the customs of the serene sun: although he completes the day he has undertaken, he nevertheless illuminates another with the same grace of brightness.

Therefore, Conscript Fathers, let your favor receive this man, absolutely radiant with so many merits. You owe it to those who conduct themselves well that the agreement of your praise should accompany them. For if the running of horses is urged on by the cries of men and driven forward by resounding applause, so that mute animals seek speed, how much do we think human beings can be stimulated by this, when we find that they have been born uniquely desirous of praise?

## LETTER XIV. KING THEODORIC TO FAUSTUS, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He orders that the type of tax called the Tertiae, imposed upon the Cathalians, be paid every year.

[Col. 0518C]

We gladly give our assent in every way whenever the voice belongs to those making a just request [Note: Observe here that nothing should be refused to those who ask justly. Plautus says the same in the *Amphitryon*:

“I wish the just and easy thing asked of you to be granted.

For I have been appointed a just advocate by the just for a just cause.” BROSS.], because a benefit that suffers no loss through generosity ought not to be difficult. Therefore let your lofty magnificence cause the portion of the Tertiae that was being brought in by the Cathalians to be paid each year as part of the tributary sum, and let the petitioners not afterward suffer any inquiry concerning this matter.

For what difference does it make under what name the possessor pays, provided that he pays what is owed without diminution? Thus we remove from them the suspicious name of the Tertiae and, through our gentleness, eliminate the importunities of those who have a legitimate claim.

## LETTER XV. KING THEODORIC TO FESTUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND PATRICIAN

He entrusts him with protecting the house of the patrician Agnellus, who is departing for Africa.

[Col. 0519A]

It is pleasing to us whenever such an assessment of your greatness’s merits emerges that you are believed to be both the aid of the weak and the protection of the absent. For this reason you deserved to be first among the senators [manuscript: senate], so that, for the sake of justice, you might offer yourself to those who follow you.

Thus our good opinion of you grows through the example of glorious action. No departing person entrusts his own property unless he judges the recipient’s conscience to be good. Therefore by this present command we decree that the house of the patrician Agnellus, who is departing for Africa [Col. 0519B] and, seeking another’s kingdom, will serve our interests, be protected by your guardianship, without prejudice to the laws. Let it not suffer violent assaults because the owner’s defense has been withdrawn.

The resources of the absent are always exposed to injuries; and in a certain sense opportunity seems to draw people into wrongdoing when it cannot frighten the invading mind by the prospect of resistance. Therefore let your exalted position—which it is a pious desire to have nearby—raise up the humble, rescue those being oppressed, and, a rare quality in persons of power, advance all those among whom you are found to stand higher than everyone.

## LETTER XVI. KING THEODORIC TO JULIAN, COUNT OF THE PRIVATE ESTATE

He orders him to investigate the case of the contractors of grain from Apulia, who had complained that their grain had been burned through the thefts of enemies; and he orders that, if the facts are so, he deduct from the remainder of the first indiction after applying moderation.

[Col. 0519C]

We apply to our interests still more of what we grant through merciful humanity. The resources of a ruler become richer when he remits something; and he acquires noble treasures of reputation by neglecting the worthlessness of money. For this reason, reminded by the humanity of our customary practice, we extend help to the weary and a hand to those burdened, so that those who had fallen through the bitterness of fortune may rise through the remedy of our piety.

Some time ago the contractors of Apulia complained to us in a mournful petition that their grain had been burned through the thefts of enemies, asking that they not be compelled to make full payment, since the profits of their commerce had been diminished. We judge that this must be considered in accordance with our innate humanity, so that, since we cannot accuse them of negligence [Accursius: desires], we may instead consider their fortunes in need of relief.

We wish the established payments to be rendered from the source from which it is clear that the subjects have obtained their benefits. Therefore we order your Sublimity to investigate this case carefully, so that, insofar as it is established that they sold less, you may deduct that amount from the remainder of the first indiction after applying moderation. This must nevertheless be done in such a way that no fraud is inflicted upon our benefits, lest you become liable through negligence, since you have always pleased us by your watchful attention. For just as the losses of petitioners affect us [Col. 0520A], so their fruitful gains ought to benefit us.

## LETTER XVII. KING THEODORIC TO ALL GOTHS AND ROMANS RESIDING AT DERTONA

He orders them, while enjoying peace, to fortify the fortress situated near them and to build houses for themselves in it.

Moved by consideration of the public welfare—which has always willingly burdened us with its care—we order the fortress situated near you to be fortified [Note: It is clear from this passage that fortresses must be fortified in time of peace; for fortified camps, properly protected by ramparts and ditches, are necessary during long sieges, as is clear from Procopius, book 2, *On the Gothic War*. BROSS.]. The conduct of war is well arranged whenever it is considered in peacetime. A fortification becomes powerful if it has been strengthened by prolonged planning. Everything sudden is shown to be careless, and the construction of a site is badly considered when dangers are already feared.

Add that the mind itself cannot be inclined to boldness when it has been preoccupied by diverse cares. Our ancestors rightly called this an expedition, because a mind devoted to battle ought not to be occupied by other thoughts. Therefore the undertaking prescribed for the consideration of all must be embraced; it is not permissible to delay an order known especially to assist the devoted.

Accordingly, by this authority we decree that you eagerly build houses for yourselves in the aforesaid fortress, returning to our mind an equivalent service in kind, so that, just as we judge that what benefits you will also benefit us, so we may feel that you adorn our times with the most beautiful buildings.

Then it will happen that you will wish to gather fitting provisions for your households, and that your dwelling will not be unpleasant when its own construction can commend it to you. What, I ask, is it to live in one’s own homes [Col. 0520C] while the enemy is forced to endure the harshest quarters? Let him lie exposed to the rain; let roofs defend you. Let hunger consume him; let prepared abundance restore you. Thus, when you are most safely established, your enemy will suffer the fate of a destroyer before the outcome of battle.

It is clear that in a time of necessity the strongest man is proved to be the one who does not scatter himself among many tasks. For who would think that he had shown foresight if he began to work on buildings or store provisions only when he ought to be conducting war?

## LETTER XVIII. KING THEODORIC TO DOMITIAN AND UVILIA

He replies that estates occupied by usurpers must be restored unless a contract or a thirty-year prescription stands in the way; and that the slayer of a brother must be deported into exile.

[Col. 0520D]

You ought to cultivate and observe justice, since you have undertaken to speak equity to the peoples. When it is not permitted to transgress, how can one who is believed to keep others under the rule of equity transgress himself? Otherwise he becomes a bad example, having been chosen for an institution known to be praiseworthy [manuscript: suitable].

Therefore we have taken care to answer your inquiry, lest through doubt you should go astray—unless, which God forbid, you wish to overstep the mark. If a barbarian usurper has occupied a Roman estate without any *pyctacium* [reading uncertain] from a delegate [editor, Niv., and Gam.: petition]—from which, with God’s favor, we crossed the streams of the fountains when Italy first received our rule [Col. 0521A]—he must restore it to the former owner without delay.

But if he appears to have entered upon the property before the designated time, since a thirty-year prescription is proved to stand in the way, we order the petitioner’s claim to remain at rest. We do not wish to bring forward again those claims that we condemn as usurped in our own times, because no room for accusation remains when the obscurity of long time is passed over.

As for one who merely struck, and did not kill, his brother: although he is condemned by the common law of all, and although fratricide alone is a crime surpassing the whole tragedy of guilt, nevertheless our humanity, which seeks a place for mercy even among criminals, decrees by this authority [Col. 0521B] that such monsters be driven beyond the boundaries of the province [Note: Cicero, *In Verrem*: “The crime must be deported to the ends of the earth.” FORNER.]. Those who found the fellowship of their parents hateful [Note: The degrees of friendship. Cicero, *On Duties*, book 1. FORNER.] do not deserve the company of their fellow citizens, lest the pleasant brightness of a pure body be stained by cloudy spots.

## LETTER XIX. KING THEODORIC TO SATURNINUS AND VERBUSIUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MEN AND SENATORS

He orders them to compel anyone among the Goths who has refused to fulfill his obligation to the treasury to make restitution equitably.

We wish the treasury’s lawful advantage to be preserved, because our clemency appears content with its own resources. And just as we wish to burden no one, so we must not lose what is owed to us. We rightly avoid indigence, which encourages excess, since poverty in a ruler is a dangerous thing. Moderation is to be praised everywhere [Note: “Reason commands that nothing be excessive, but that all things be done with moderation.” Cicero, *On the Orator* and *On Old Age*, book 1 of *On Duties*; Columella, book 2. BROSS.] [Col. 0521C].

For why should culpable negligence drain what belongs to us, or shameful greed scrape away what belongs to others? Therefore by this present command we order you, after receiving the report of the curials of the city of Adriana, to constrain any Goth who refuses to make good the fisc to the equity of restitution. Let no poor person be compelled to pay from his own property what the well-to-do are clearly detaining without right.

The following rule must of course be observed: if anyone, through the fault of obstinacy, prefers to delay our commands, let him return with a fine what he ought to have offered even without compulsion, so that insolence, indecently raised by a stubborn spirit, may not be left unpunished for just generations.

## LETTER XX. KING THEODORIC TO ALBINUS AND ALBIENUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MEN AND PATRICIANS

He reminds them to assume the patronage of the Prasinus faction at the spectacles, and orders them to appoint, from Hellandius and Thodorus, whichever is judged more suitable for the public amusement, as the Prasinus pantomime, after removing the people’s confusion.

[Col. 0521D]

Although, amid the glorious concerns of the commonwealth and the salutary currents [editor: fruits] of royal anxieties, it may seem a small matter for a ruler to speak about spectacles [Col. 0522A], nevertheless, because of our love for the Roman commonwealth, we shall not be reluctant to admit these thoughts as well. Whatever we can provide from any source, we judge worthy of our attention, especially since the happiness of the times consists in the joy of the peoples.

That our labors are, with God’s favor, confirmed by success is shown by the fact that the community recognizes itself as enjoying leisure. Therefore, after the petition of the Prasinus faction had been presented, we learned—for this custom has been introduced, that the people may be called by their color—that turbulent riots are being incited by certain utterly wicked men, and that the cause of public joy has broken out into contests of fury. This cannot possess the quality of dignified rejoicing if it has not been granted the possession of common peace [manuscript Aud.: where].

It is therefore worthy of our clemency to inspect these matters also, so that moral integrity may shine everywhere. We are not considering empty popular words; we are excluding the seed of a destructive revolt. Accordingly, your illustrious greatness, admonished by this present command, should graciously assume the patronage of the Prasinus faction, which your father of glorious memory [editor: our] extended.

It must not be thought an injury to rule and govern the Roman people. For if the cause of all good things is weighed, those who deserved to receive the most glorious honors were chosen for their benefit. Therefore, after summoning the spectators, from Hellandius and Thodorus [editor: Theodorus], whichever is judged more suitable for the public amusement, appoint as the Prasinus pantomime, after removing the people’s confusion [Note: In these times the people in each city began to be divided into factions according to colors, namely the Venetians and the Prasini. Procopius says that certain people, taking their names from colors and dye-works, did not hesitate, for the sake of their factions, both to distribute money among spectators and to inflict terrible tortures upon bodies. He describes a revolt arising from this at Constantinople in book 1 of *The Persian War*. Justinian mentions it near the end of Novel 17 and orders the authors of the revolt who had fled to be sought out and brought back to the city for punishment. This formula is also mentioned below, in letter 33 of this book. FORNER.], so that we may appear to have bestowed upon the chosen man the expense we have incurred for the city’s spectacle [Col. 0522C].

Our ancestors called this branch of musical discipline “Mute,” namely, that which speaks with closed mouth through the hands and makes intelligible by certain gestures what could scarcely be recognized through a speaking tongue or the text of writing.

## LETTER XXI. KING THEODORIC TO MAXIMIANUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, AND ANDREAS, SENATOR

He decrees that they investigate whether the money assigned to the buildings of the City was entirely spent upon them without fraud.

We must be summoned by the citizens’ devoted zeal to increase the City, because no one can love what he understands the inhabitants not to love. Each person’s homeland is dearer to him when he seeks above all that it be safe, where he has dwelt from his very cradle [Col. 0522D].

Therefore let us be invited by equal wishes to make gifts, so that what we give freely we may bestow with doubled favor. For this reason, let it not be burdensome for anyone to render an account of the money assigned to Roman building works, since a pure conscience desires to be proved when it receives the fruit of its labor and recognizes that favorable reports about it have reached us.

Accordingly, by this present command we decree that you investigate the building works of the Roman city: whether the labor of the work corresponds to the expenses, or whether it is clear that money remains with anyone that has not been spent on the buildings; in that case he must return it for expenditure upon the assigned work. When these accounts have been clearly set out, send us a most faithful report, so that you may appear to answer our judgment, since you have been chosen to investigate the truth.

For we believe that no one wishes to defraud our generosity, when in such a matter we judge that he ought to spend even from his own resources.
