Birds themselves, wandering through the air, love their own nests; wild animals hurry to their thorny lairs; pleasure-loving fish, crossing the liquid fields, diligently search out their caverns; and every animal knows to take refuge where it desires to remain for the longest life [Col. 0523B]. What, then, should we say about Rome, which it is right that her own children should love even more?

## LETTER XXII. KING THEODORIC TO MARCELLUS, SENATOR AND ADVOCATE OF THE TREASURY

He appoints him advocate of the treasury after his service as a private advocate.

The praise of royal generosity is solid whenever grants accord with judgments; nor does it dare to attribute to chance what the examination of good arrangement has weighed. For where offices are fitted to merits, nothing is owed to uncertainty.

Your talent has indeed been praised in many ways, polished on the forum’s whetstone; you have nourished eloquence through the practice of cases; you have learned how sweet are the fruits produced by good faith, so that it wins over even the hearts of rulers. Our judgment, watchful for virtues, has observed these qualities in you.

By these testimonials you deserved to please us, so that you might be worthy of public cases, since until now you have conducted private ones with integrity. Therefore assume the responsibility of defending the affairs of our treasury, following the example of your predecessors in using the privileges of your office.

Proceed, then, governed by the middle path of justice, so that you neither burden the innocent with accusations nor relieve those who obstruct just petitions [Juretus: dishonor them]. We judge those to be true profits that we receive with integrity supporting us.

Let us therefore inquire not merely whether you prevail, but how you prevail. Aim at equity if you wish to please us; seek victories through law rather than through our power, since it is more praiseworthy for the treasury’s side to lose when justice is not present. If the master wins, there is the odium of oppression; equity, however, is believed to prevail if the petitioner happens to overcome.

We do not therefore plead cases at little risk, since our reputation prospers when an unjust advantage withdraws. Accordingly, the treasury’s case is sometimes made bad so that the prince may appear good. We lose with a greater profit than if an undeserved victory should support us.

## LETTER XXIII. KING THEODORIC TO CAELIANUS [Greek and Cujacius: FELICIANUS] AND AGAPITUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MEN AND PATRICIANS

These judges are chosen to settle the lawsuit of the patricians Festus and Symmachus against the patrician Paulinus.

[Col. 0524A]

It is fitting for the care of royal authority to preserve the harmony of the whole community, since it is counted to the ruler’s praise if peace is loved by everyone. For what could proclaim us better than a peaceful people, a harmonious senate, and the entire commonwealth clothed in the integrity of our conduct?

Therefore by this present command we decree that the distinguished men and patricians Festus and Symmachus bring before your court the claims they say they hold against the illustrious patrician Paulinus. After these have been received according to the requirements of the laws and, if the order of law permits, decided, let the patrician Paulinus in turn produce whatever complaint he claims to have against the distinguished men named above.

We do not wish the judgment on his side to be delayed either, since we desire everything between them to be settled and nothing left except what is owed to affection [Col. 0524B]. See, therefore, that you have been chosen as arbiters of so great a judgment; see that our expectation demands impartial justice. You will bring back the richest fruit of gratitude if the present dispute proves that those whom it judged worthy are not unequal to the task.

Special care must be taken concerning such men, since they can plainly provide examples to those beneath them. For anyone who neglects to conclude a lawsuit between the highest of equals undoubtedly permits others to imitate him.

## LETTER XXIV. KING THEODORIC TO ALL GOTHS

He states that he arranged for them, through his envoy Nandius, to be reminded to hasten to the Gallic expedition on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, sufficiently equipped with everything necessary, and that the elders should be examples to the young.

[Col. 0524C]

It is more necessary that contests be announced to the Goths than urged upon them, since for a warlike race it is a joy to prove itself. For one who desires the glory of valor does not shrink from toil. Therefore, with God’s help—God, by whose agency all things prosper—we have decided to send an army for the common good to Gaul, so that you may at the same time have an opportunity for advancement, and we may seem to have conferred what we have provided in accordance with your merits. For praiseworthy courage lies hidden in idleness; and while it has no opportunity to prove itself, the whole light of its merits remains concealed.

Accordingly, through our saio Nandio, we have arranged that you be admonished to set out for the expedition, in God’s name and according to your usual custom, adequately equipped with arms, horses, and every necessary provision, on the coming eighth day before the Kalends of July, and in every way, with God’s favor, proceed; so that you may show that the valor of your ancestors is present in you and successfully carry out our command.

Bring forth your young men for the discipline of Mars. Under your leadership, let them see what they may strive to report to posterity. For what is not learned in youth is unknown in mature age. Even hawks, whose food always comes from prey, drive their fledglings, stiff with inexperience, out of their nests, lest they grow accustomed to soft idleness; they beat their wings against those who linger and compel their tender chicks to fly, so that they may become such as maternal affection can confidently rely upon. You, however, whom both nature raises up and the love of reputation sharpens, strive to leave behind sons such as you are known to have had as fathers.

## EPISTLE XXV. TO SABINIANUS, A SENATOR. THEODORICUS, KING.

He orders the harbor of Lucina and the adjoining harbors to be repaired and more careful attention to be given to them in the future.

It is of no benefit to strengthen the beginnings of an undertaking if established presumption is able to destroy them. Those things are strong and lasting which prudence begins and care preserves. Therefore, greater [edition: “not lesser”] caution must be applied to preserving things than to discovering them: for praise is owed to the inventor for beginnings, but celebrated perfection is acquired through what has been preserved.

Some time ago, because of the walls of the city of Rome, toward which our tireless zeal will always devote its efforts, our order directed that the harbor of Lucina be repaired from assigned revenues, so that twenty-five thousand tiles might be supplied annually, likewise for the adjoining harbors, which formerly belonged to those places [manuscripts: “in antiquity”] and are now reported to have been seized through the usurpation of various persons. You shall therefore without delay restore everything to the prescribed contribution, since although our commands ought, out of respect for them, to be violated in no respect, we especially wish those things preserved which appear to adorn the face of the City.

Who could doubt that, through this provision, the marvels of buildings are being preserved and that vaulted chambers turned from suspended stone [manuscripts: “fashioned”] are being protected by a covering of tiles? Thus the ancient emperors ought rightly to owe us their praises, since by their buildings we have given long-lasting youth [Note: It is not unprecedented to attribute age to buildings. Mamertinus, in his *Panegyric on Julian*, said that the city walls, renewed by the emperor, had put on youth. In the same way we say that the ornaments and beauties of cities and marbles feel the old age of time, as may be seen in Book 16 of the Theodosian Code, *On Public Works*. Buildings also are said to be shaken by the old age of time in Book 15 of the same title. Ovid likewise says:

> “The neglected roofs grow gray with shameful squalor.”

Ennodius of Ticinum, in his letter to Boethius, writes: “His buildings grow old through neglect”; and elsewhere:

> “Under your guidance, the roofs renounce their former old age.”

So too the age of a document is mentioned in Book 1 of the Theodosian Code, *If a Certain Person Seeks Judgment*; and Gellius speaks of the age and end of a book, while Pliny, Book 23, chapter 1, speaks of age coming to wine. I also recall that the laws are assigned an age and are said by excellent authors to grow old, languish, die, and be killed. Constantine, in Book 23 of the Theodosian Code, *On Appeals*, orders the law that prohibited appeal from the judgment of the Urban Prefect to grow old. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book 16, speaking of sumptuary laws, says: “Sulla the dictator gradually restored them in their old age.” Claudian likewise says:

> “The laws resume their former  
> gray hair; the old ones are corrected,  
> and new ones are added.”

Aulus Gellius writes: “For he allowed those laws to die from such excessive punishment, decay, and old age.” In the same way Cicero said that the destruction of the laws, civil and domestic war, and the downfall of the whole City and empire were approaching. In the same sense, the age of wines, works, forests, and trees is read as referring to years and duration. Aggenus Urbicus transferred this usage to trees in his *Commentaries on Julius Frontinus*: “Another person, on the contrary, might similarly seek a comparison based almost entirely on similarity of cultivation—that is, whether the part of the forest destined for cutting is of the same age, and whether the age of the trees ordinarily left standing, which they call ‘left in advance,’ and the ages of the forests are equal; whether, in the case of vineyards, they are similar in comparison—whether the rows are equally distant, whether the arrangement is the same, and whether the kind of vines is similar.” Thus he. [BROSS.]]

so that they may shine again with their former freshness, which had already been darkened by the decay of old age.

## EPISTLE XXVI. TO FAUSTUS, PRAETORIAN PREFECT. THEODORICUS, KING.

He decrees that what he formerly granted to the Church of the Bishop of Versella shall remain valid forever, and that it shall not bear the extraordinary taxes paid since the time of Cassiodorus; nevertheless, he wishes the goods subsequently bestowed upon the Church to be subject to the burden of payment.

Among those to whom our repeated generosity is destined to provide other benefits, it is impious that confidence in an earlier benefaction should be diminished. But just as what we have once approved does not deserve to be rescinded forever, so those who have obtained our generosity through moderate petitions ought not, through excessive presumption, to overstep the limits of what we have granted.

Therefore, since we are reminded by the reverence due to religious devotion that what we formerly granted to the Church of the venerable Bishop of Versella should remain valid forever, we have now also thought it appropriate to admonish Your Illustrious Magnificence that the aforesaid Church shall not bear the burdens of the superimposed tax assessments [that is, extraordinary taxes] in the amount that was paid from the time of the illustrious man Cassiodorus, a patrician known to us for his pure faith and integrity.

But whatever property has been transferred by anyone to your Church from the time of the benefaction [manuscripts Greek and Cujacius: “profession”] shall acknowledge the common burden of payment together with all possessions [Greek and Cujacius: “possessors”], and shall be subject to the fiscal obligation of him whose rights of ownership it has obtained. Otherwise, the increases of those who prosper through loss to the treasury cannot be pleasing to us. Let the possessor’s saving consist in the reduction of his rent. Taxes belong to purple garments, not to cloaks. Gain accompanied by hatred is danger; how much better to manage everything moderately, so that no one may dare accuse it!

## EPISTLE XXVII. TO SPECIOSUS. THEODORICUS, KING.

He reports that the people of the Green faction, while coming to the court, suffered an ambush at the hands of the patrician Theodoricus and the consul Importunus, so that one man was killed; and he orders Speciosus to warn the aforesaid illustrious men to send properly authorized persons to the judgment of Coelianus and Agapitus, who are to settle the matter according to the laws. [Note: This letter was written in A.D. 509, for Importunus was consul in that year.]

[Col. 0526C]

If we regulate the customs of foreign peoples under the law; if whatever is joined to Italy obeys Roman law; how much more is it fitting that the very seat of civilization should show greater reverence for the laws, so that the favor of dignities may shine forth through the example of moderation? For where is a modest spirit to be sought if violence disgraces patricians?

The people of the Green faction have therefore represented to us in a petition that, while they were preparing to come to our court and requesting the customary remedies, they suffered savage ambushes from the patrician Theodoricus [manuscript of Remigius: Theodorus] and the illustrious consul Importunus, so that one of them is mourned as having been killed. This has moved us, if the matter is so, because of the atrocity of the deed: armed fury pursued an innocent populace, whom civic affection ought to have cherished.

But since the condition of the lower orders equally implores the ruler’s aid, we decree by the present command that the aforesaid illustrious men be admonished not to delay sending properly authorized persons, at your insistence, to the equal judgment of the illustrious Coelianus and Agapitus, so that, after the inquiry has been examined according to the laws, the matter may be ended by their sentence.

Yet, lest popular loquacity perhaps have offended the magnificent men, discretion must be exercised in judging this presumption. Whoever insolently inflicted an injury upon a most reverend senator passing by shall be held accountable, if he uttered evil wishes when he ought to have spoken well.

But who would demand serious manners at spectacles? Catos do not know how to assemble at the Circus. Whatever is said there to the rejoicing crowd is not considered an injury. The place itself defends the excess. If their garrulity is patiently tolerated, it is shown to adorn the rulers themselves.

Let those who are occupied with such enthusiasms certainly answer us whether they desire their opponents to be tranquil. Certainly they want them to be victorious when they rush into insults precisely when they are ashamed to have been disgracefully defeated. Why, then, do they wish to be angry at what they unquestionably acknowledge they wished for?

## EPISTLE XXVIII. TO ALL GOTHS AND ROMANS. THEODORICUS, KING.

By this letter he decrees that if anyone has stones of any kind lying in his fields that would be useful for walls, he should willingly devote them to the restoration of the cities.

[Col. 0527C]

The construction of a city is worthy of the care of a king, for the restoration of ancient cities is a glory of the times: in them the adornment of peace is acquired and the necessity of wars is forestalled. Therefore, by the present command, we decree as useful that if anyone has stones of any kind lying in his fields [manuscript of Audoin: *jacentibus* rather than *jacentia*], which would be useful for walls, he should willingly and without any delay make them available.

He will possess them more truly when he has devoted them to the benefit of his city. For what is more pleasing than to see public dignity grow where everyone’s advantage is contained in the common good? And although worthless things may be supplied, they will return to their owners with great benefit. For what is often given is received with greater usefulness. A person frequently embraces his own profits when he gives something necessarily in accordance with the circumstances of the time.

## EPISTLE XXIX. TO ALL THE LUCRISTANI ESTABLISHED ABOVE THE SONTIUS. THEODORICUS, KING.

He orders that the tracts of land which had formerly been permitted for the changing stations of the post-horses be recovered from the possessor and restored.

There is no doubt that the safeguarding of the public courier service belongs to the public good, since through it the swiftest execution is supplied for our arrangements. Therefore, as for a necessary undertaking, greater care must be applied so that those assigned to continuous journeys do not waste away in shameful emaciation; lest scant nourishment, overcome by toil, cause them to collapse, and the journey, which was clearly devised for speed, begin to become slow [Note: Many provisions on this subject are established in Book 8 of the Theodosian Code, title 5. FORN.].

Accordingly, your Devotion, admonished by the present command, shall restore the tracts of land which had formerly been permitted for their changes by the post-horses (see below, Book 5, Letter 5) [Note: “Changes” below, Book 4, Letter 47; they are commonly called *postas* [stations]. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book 21: “He departed early, carried by a change-station, and the swift course of the public route crossed the Julian Alps, etc.” FORNER.], after recovering them from the possessor; so that losses may not be imposed upon the former over a small tract [manuscript: *indicantur*, “are indicated,” for *inducantur*, “are imposed”], nor the recovered lands fail to suffice for the latter.

## EPISTLE XXX. TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME. THEODORICUS, KING.

He complains to them that armed servile fury attacked innocent people during the spectacles, and decrees that if the servant of any senator has taken part in the killing of a freeborn person, his master shall hand him over to be punished by the laws. If he delays presenting the accused to the judges, he shall know that he is to be fined ten pounds of gold.

[Col. 0528B]

Fathers Conscript, the complaints of the people have repeatedly struck our mind, which is heated by the concerns of the state and examines the counsels of diverse nations. Though arising from trivial causes, they have spewed forth serious excesses. The complaint is that, for the sake of the pleasure of the spectacles, they have reached the utmost limits of danger: after trampling upon the rule of law, armed servile fury pursued the innocent in desperation; and what our humanity provided for their enjoyment, punishable audacity converted into sorrow.

We restrain this through the customary foresight of our clemency, lest, by gradually allowing it, we should be compelled to avenge a graver offense. For it is characteristic of a benevolent ruler not so much to wish to punish crimes as to remove them: lest by punishing severely he be judged excessive, or by acting lightly be considered improvident.

Therefore, by the present decree, we sanction that if the servant of any senator should happen to have taken part in the killing of a freeborn person, his master shall hand him over to be prosecuted under the laws, so that, after the nature of the deed has been investigated, a sentence valid in law may be pronounced.

But if the master, in bad faith, delays presenting the accused of so great a crime to the courts, he shall know that he is to be struck with a loss of ten pounds of gold and exposed to the dangers of our displeasure [that is, indignation], which is far more serious.

But so that an equal balance might regulate the honor of all and the favor of civilized conduct [manuscripts and Accursius: *civitatis*, “of the city,” for *civilitatis*, “of civilized conduct”] might accord with restored morals, we have also sent our instructions to the people, which we gladly disclose to you, so that the torn harmony of the citizens may be repaired by the commands issued to both sides.

Accordingly, we remove no one from the enjoyment of the spectacles, but cut out the seeds of sedition by the roots. Let there therefore be a distinction between your splendor and mediocre manners: avoid such attendants as serve injuries, who strive to attribute to your honor what they themselves commit, and who, while wishing to assert their frivolities [manuscripts: “display them”], attempt to entangle your reverence.

You, whom gravity always befits, must not savagely pursue the empty words of the people. If something has perhaps been done that deserves punishment, let it be reported to the knowledge of the Urban Prefect, so that guilt may be restrained by the laws, not by presumptuous injury. For what difference is there between the offender and one who seeks to avenge himself through excess? Revenge upon a citizen that comes from the laws is not to be repented of; and he appears to have triumphed splendidly over the one who was struck when he is pronounced the victor by a judge.

Even among the adversaries themselves, as you know, their contests were not originally armed; rather, their fervent passion provoked one another with blows, and from this the contest received its name [Note: From *pugnus*, “fist,” of course. Gaius also writes that *pignus*, “pledge,” was derived from *pugnus*, because things given as pledges are taken by hand, Digest 50.16.238, *On the Meaning of Words*. A gift, or Greek *dōron*, is derived from *dōron*, that is, the palm, because offered gifts were taken by hand, as Vitruvius Pollio says in Book 2, chapter 3, and Pliny in Book 35, chapter 14. Paul may have alluded to this in Digest 39.6.35, *Senatus Consultum on Gifts in View of Death*. FORNER.]. Later Belus [Note: Cassiodorus attributes this to the father, while Isidore attributes it to the son, *Etymologies*, Book 18, chapter 1. Ninus, king of the Assyrians, was the first to introduce wars. Suidas: “*Arēs* properly means iron, but it also signifies war, since in war there is need not of speech but of action: ‘for in war there is need not of word but of deed.’ Homer likewise says: ‘For in the hands lies the end of war, but in counsel lie words.’ Eustathius, commenting on Homer’s *Iliad* 16, on the phrase ‘brazen Arēs’: ‘Arēs is iron.’ See Varro and Festus under the word *duellum*. FORNER.] first brought forth the iron sword, and from him it pleased people to call war by that name. A savage plan, a cruel defense, a bestial conflict. For even if it was granted to him first to defeat an unarmed man easily, nevertheless the fact must be charged as a crime because posterity could have perished through it.

Therefore, do not permit your servants to do to citizens what must still be condemned even in enemies.

## EPISTLE XXXI. TO THE ROMAN PEOPLE. THEODORICUS, KING.

He decrees that if anyone from the people has uttered savage insults against any senator, he shall know that he will be punished by the Urban Prefect according to the nature of the deed; and he orders the pantomimes to practice their arts in the places assigned to them.

The spectacles of pleasure ought, in our view, to be the people’s joy; and the excitement of anger ought not to arise from what was evidently invented for relaxation of the mind. For this reason we bear the burden of so much expense: so that your assembly may be adorned by peace, not filled with the noise of sedition.

Reject foreign manners; let the voice of the people be Roman, a voice whose being heard gives pleasure. Insults neither produce joy nor arise from gladness. This, certainly, was what you condemned in foreigners. Do not now acquire turbulent vices that you see others have discarded.

Therefore, by an edictal proclamation, we define (see the following book, Letters 24 and 25) that if an unjust voice presumes to utter savage insults against any senator, it shall know that it must be heard by the Urban Prefect under the laws, so that, after the deed has been examined according to its nature, it may receive the sentence promulgated by law.

But so that every seed of discord may be cut out completely, we order the pantomimes to practice their arts in the places assigned to them. The instruction given to the Urban Prefect will be able to inform you of this. Your only task is to carry out the city’s festivities with composed minds.

For there is nothing we wish you to preserve more diligently than the discipline of your ancestors [edition of Nivian: “men”], so that what you have always held as praiseworthy from ancient times may, under our rule, rather increase. For you customarily fill the very air with honey-sweet shouts [Note: The acclamation and applause were artistic performances, and the voices of the Roman citizens were composed and harmonized. Pliny calls this harmonized shouting “concord” in his *Panegyric*. The Roman people preserve their chosen prince, and with the same concord with which shortly before they celebrated another as handsome, they acclaim this one as strongest. BROSS.]; you produce voices sweeter than an organ; and thus, under a certain harmony of the lyre, the hollow theater resounds through you, so that anyone might believe them to be tones [understand: rather] than shouts.

Surely quarrels or inflamed contention are not fitting amid these things? Cast away your rages; rejoice, and exclude anger while celebrating. For in this way the spirits of others can be tempered when your expressions of favor are heard sweetly [edition of Niv.: “your supporters”].

## EPISTLE XXXII. TO AGAPITUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND URBAN PREFECT. THEODORICUS, KING.

[Note: Letter VI of this book was also addressed to him. Theodoric especially wished the Urban Prefect to restrain the disturbances customarily stirred up at the games; Letter XLIV of this book has the same object. FORNER.]

He informs him that he has written to the Senate and to the people, and orders that if anyone inflicts an injury upon a senator, that person shall immediately be punished with the severity of the laws; but if a senator has attacked a freeborn person with a criminal killing, he shall immediately suffer a fine. He further decrees that Helladius shall receive the same monthly allowance as the other pantomimes.

[Col. 0530B]

It is fitting that the prefect of the distinguished City should be its guardian of peace. For from whom should moderation more reasonably be expected than from the man to whom Rome could be entrusted? She is the mother of all dignities and rejoices to have men of virtue presiding over her.

Therefore, you must make your spirit equal to your honor, so that you may be thought to have found through your own merits what you obtained through our benefits. You ought to look around carefully lest any cause of sedition arise at the spectacles, because a peaceful people is your commendation. Let the custom of exchanging insults be moderate, so that neither honorable freedom may perish nor discipline be absent from conduct.

Accordingly, just as by our pronouncements we have instructed the most distinguished order and decreed that the people be admonished, so we also decree that Your Greatness observe this: if anyone inflicts an injury upon a senator, let loquacious recklessness immediately be punished with the severity of the laws.

But if a senator, forgetful of civilized conduct, causes any freeborn person to be attacked with a criminal killing, let him, as soon as the report has been transmitted, receive the blow of a fine from our perpetual authority.

Let everyone remember to divide the interests and factions of the spectacles in such a way that they remain harmonious in their fatherland. The contests of pleasure are not displayed to them so that hostile anger may grow from them.

But lest any furious contention arise again hereafter, let Helladius enter from the middle, to provide pleasure for the people, and let him receive the same monthly allowance as the other pantomimes of the factions [Nivian and Gamurrini, Greek and Cujacius: “the pantomime of the Greens”].

We also determine by the present command that, since repeated seditions among them are provoked by this matter, the admirers of Helladius, whom we have ordered to dance from the middle, shall have the freedom to watch him wherever they choose, without favoring either faction. But if their fickle inclination shifts in favor of one color, let the people pursue their enthusiasm in both the Circus and the theater for the faction they love; and let the person who presumes to do what is forbidden be judged to have sought discord himself.

## EPISTLE XXXIII. TO AGAPITUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND URBAN PREFECT. THEODORICUS, KING.

By the present ordinance he decrees that the pantomime selected by Albinus and Albienus shall receive the customary monthly allowance of the Green faction without reduction.

Our serenity’s judgment, once pronounced, does not know how to waver; nor does it change, through the intrusion of any circumstance, what it has established by prudent arrangement [others: *mutavit*, “changed,” for *mutare*, “to change”]. We remember that some time ago we gave orders to the patricians Albinus and Albienus to select a pantomime of the Green faction who would be more suitable for the spectacles. They disclosed to us in their report what had been done.

Therefore, by the present authority, we now decree that whoever is established as having been selected by the aforesaid magnificent men shall receive from you the customary monthly allowance of the Green faction without reduction, so that what our foresight established to remove confusion [manuscripts: “compulsion”] may not become a cause of sedition but of peace.

## EPISTLE XXXIV. TO FAUSTUS, PRAETORIAN PREFECT. THEODORICUS, KING.

He orders him to issue warnings at each maritime location that no one presume to load foreign ships with grain before the province has retained what it needs.

The abundance of grain ought first to benefit the province in which it is produced, since it is more just that the local fertility serve the inhabitants than that it be exhausted by the eager pursuit of foreign commerce. What remains ought to be supplied to foreign regions, and one should think of outsiders only after the calculation of local necessity has been satisfied.

Therefore, let Your Illustrious Magnificence ensure that warnings are issued at each place that appears to have responsibility for the shores: no one is to load foreign ships with grain for passage to foreign shores before public supplies have been able to reach the desired abundance.

## EPISTLE XXXV. TO FAUSTUS, PRAETORIAN PREFECT. THEODORICUS, KING.

He indicates that he is somewhat disturbed because the public grain, which customarily used to be transported by the chancellor from the Calabrian and Apulian shores during the summer, had still not been supplied even when autumn arrived; and he orders that this be corrected through the swiftest possible remedy.

[Col. 0531D]

Since the dryness of the present year, which is accustomed to rage locally at fixed seasons, has hardened the earth’s entrails with excessive heat and has produced not so much the abortive offspring of the crops as cast them forth in an imperfect abundance, what is ordinarily sought even in plenty must now be sought with greater diligence.

Therefore, we are greatly disturbed in every way that the public grain, which customarily used to be sent from the Calabrian and Apulian shores by your chancellor during the summer, has not arrived even by autumn. For the sun’s reflected course, moving through the southern constellations, alters the order of nature [edition: “altered by the order”] and revives turbulent storms through the mingling of the air; even the names of the months make this understood, since they received their names appropriately from the number of future rains [Note: September, as though “the seventh rain”; October and November likewise, following Varro, who approves of deriving the names of these months from the rains. FORN.].

What, then, is the reason for such delay, that swift ships have not yet been sent in such calm conditions, when the bright constellation of the stars that do not sink eagerly invites the sails to be spread and the reliability of the clear air cannot frighten the hopes of those who hasten?

Or perhaps, while the South Wind was blowing and the oars were assisting, the passages of the ships were held fast among the clear waves by the bite of the *echeneis* [Note: *Echeneis*, in Latin *remora*. From the Greek *para to echein tēn naun*, “because it holds the ship.” Pliny, Book 3, chapter 1; D. Gruter and Cujacius.]? Or perhaps shells of the Indian Sea, with a similar power, fixed the backs of the ships with their lips? Their motionless touch is said to hold back more than the agitated elements could drive forward [manuscripts and Accursius: “complete”].

The sluggish raft stands winged with swelling sails and does not have a course even when the wind smiles upon it; it is fixed without anchors and tied without ropes; and such tiny creatures resist more than all those aids to favorable progress can propel. Thus, although the wave beneath hurries the course onward, the ship is found standing fixed upon the sea’s surface; and in a marvelous way floating things are held motionless while the wave is swept along by countless movements.

But to mention another nature of fish: perhaps the sailors of the aforesaid ships became exceedingly sluggish through contact with the torpedo. By it the hands of those who touch it are so heavily numbed that, through the spear by which it has been wounded, it infects the hand of the person striking it, so that part of the living substance becomes rigidly numb and immobile, without any sensation. I believe that such things befell those who cannot move.

But for them the *echeneis* is obstructive commercial greed; the bite of the shells is insatiable avarice; the torpedo is fraudulent pretense. For they themselves deliberately create delays so that they may appear to have encountered adverse circumstances.

Let Your Greatness, to whom it especially belongs to consider such matters, have this corrected by the swiftest remedy, lest the shortage appear to have arisen not so much from the barrenness of the season as from negligence, its mother.

## EPISTLE XXXVI. TO THERIOLUS, A SENATOR. THEODORICUS, KING.

He orders him to assume Benedictus’s position in the city of Pedo and to surround Benedictus’s sons with civic protection.

The usefulness of good persons ought to be renewed through succession, lest some suspended undertaking suffer loss through a deficiency of those who serve it. Therefore, by our authority, we order you to assume the position formerly held by Benedictus in the city of Pedo, so that, providing for everything through vigilant administration, you may deserve an increase of our favor.

You ought to observe what reciprocity we strive to render to the living, since we cannot forget the loyalty of the dead. We are also reminded by our customary piety that, since the tested memory of those devoted to us does not fail, you should cause the sons of the aforementioned late Benedictus—who is known to have obeyed us with sincere devotion—to be surrounded with civic protection, so that, supported by the benefit of this present defense, they may rejoice that security has been bestowed upon them in return for their father’s services.

Let what could be provided through the devotion of one man therefore benefit his family: for it is fitting that we confer more than we appear to have received from those who serve us. This is not equality or justice; rather, our side weighs matters most justly when it is burdened by giving back more.

## EPISTLE XXXVII. TO CRISPIANUS. THEODORICUS, KING.

He recalls him from exile, if he truly killed a man caught in adultery, and orders that the money extorted from Crispianus’s surety, Agnellus, by the city vicar or his office be restored; he also grants Crispianus Candacis’s protection against every attack.

Although the first hearing of a homicide immediately detests the crime, and the eyes of judges recoil from a bloodstained hand, nevertheless, since the path toward mercy is always open to good minds, the matter must be weighed in light of justice: the injury inflicted upon each person must be distinguished from the wicked crime committed through a novel misfortune of fortune. The universal detestation will arise if the guilty man preserves himself as innocent.

For who would tolerate dragging before the laws a man who endeavored to violate the rights of marriage? It is implanted in wild beasts to defend their mating with their utmost struggle, since whatever is condemned by natural law is hostile to every living creature. We see bulls defend their females through the contest of their horns; rams rage to the point of death on behalf of their sheep; horses vindicate the females joined to them with blows and bites. Thus they devote their lives to their mates, though they are not moved by shame.

How, then, can a human being endure leaving adultery [Note: Compare this passage with the law *Marito*, Digest, *On the Julian Law on Adultery*. FORNER.] unavenged, when he is known to have neglected it to his eternal disgrace [editions of Nivian and Gamurrini: “committed it”]?

Therefore, if the truth of the petition submitted to us does not deceive you, and you washed away the stain of the marriage bed with the blood of an adulterer caught in the act, and if you are not advancing a case of modesty under the pretext of a bloodthirsty disposition, we order that you be removed from the exile that was imposed upon you. For to draw the sword on behalf of the love of chastity is not to trample upon the laws but to establish them.

Nevertheless, if a legitimate accuser appears, you must know that you will be heard concerning the nature of your deed, so that if you killed innocent men, the crime may be cut off by public rigor. If you separated adulterers who had entered into a wrongful embrace by killing them, let the act be judged rather vengeance than guilt.

But if anyone has caused you the losses of a false accusation, and if it is established, as you assert, that money was extorted from your surety Agnellus by the vicar or his office, let him, when summoned by our command [Accursius: “when convicted”], restore what was taken according to the laws. For we do not wish what our judgment appears to have set free to fall as prey to anyone.

Likewise, against the attacks of uncivil persons, we provide you with Candacis’s protection under equal defense, so that he may neither withdraw you from the laws nor again allow you to suffer on behalf of public rights.

## EPISTLE XXXVIII. TO COIO [others: Coino; others: Baio], A SENATOR. THEODORICUS, KING.

He orders him to restore as quickly as possible the property of his nephew Virilianus, which he had been detaining not with the intention of increasing it but even with the desire to diminish it.

It is not a benefit when something is provided to unwilling recipients; nor does anything appear useful to anyone when it is granted against his will. Therefore, Your Honor should know that we have been earnestly petitioned concerning your nephew Virilianus [edition: Hilarius], a young man, because you are detaining his father’s property not with the purpose of improving it but with the intention of making it worse.

Accordingly, whatever you recognize yourself to be retaining from the right of the aforesaid young man, restore without any delay, so that he may administer his parents’ property according to his own will. For a person who, having assumed the freedom of ownership, advances appears suitable to us.

Eagles nourish their bold young with carefully provided food until, gradually leaving behind their soft feathers, they grow wings in adulthood. Once their flight has become firm, they accustom their young talons to tender prey; they do not need to live by another’s labor when their own hunting can satisfy them.

Thus, it is disgraceful that our young men who have proved suitable for military service should be called weak when it comes to arranging their own lives, or be thought unable to manage their own household when they are believed capable of conducting wars. Among the Goths, valor creates legitimate age; and whoever is able to pierce an enemy must already be able to defend himself against every vice.

## EPISTLE XXXIX. TO FESTUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND PATRICIAN. THEODORICUS, KING.

He writes that Filagrius requested permission to return to his own household and that he sent his brother’s sons to Rome for the sake of their studies; and he orders Festus to establish them in the City in such a way that they may not leave it before he decrees otherwise by a second command.

[Col. 0534C]

Rational petitions of suppliants we willingly embrace, since even when not asked we ponder what is just. For what could be more worthy for us to turn over day and night in continual deliberation than that our commonwealth should be protected by equity, no less than by arms, inviolate? Accordingly, the distinguished Filagrius, residing in the city of Syracuse and long delayed by his attendance at our palace, petitioned that he be allowed to return to his own home; he had brought the sons of his brother to the Roman city for the sake of their studies. Your Illustrious Magnificence, retaining them in the aforesaid City in accordance with our command, shall establish them there; nor shall they be permitted to depart before we once again decree this by a second command.

[Col. 0534D] **Note:** [Col. 0533D] Book 11 below, letter 11: “by a repeated command,” which is more weighty. Justinian, Novel 17: “Nevertheless, you shall do nothing concerning him before, after informing us, you have received a second authorization from us concerning these matters.” And Novel 134: “So that a second command of ours concerning this matter may be issued.” For a repeated petition and grant concerning the same matter removes suspicion of concealment and error. The secondary command of the prior liberality and the repeated petition he calls “a second precept” in book 2, title 3, concerning incorporation. Code of Theodosius, book X, title 9. FORNER.

Thus both their intellectual advancement is promoted and consideration for our advantage is safeguarded. Let him not therefore think that something has been imposed upon him which ought to have been a matter of his own desire. Let no one find Rome unwelcome, since it cannot be called foreign.

[Col. 0534D] **Note:** Rome is defined as the common fatherland in Digest 50.1.33, *ad municip.*; and Digest 27.1.4, *de excusatione tutorum*. Hence Sidonius Apollinaris elegantly says that in that city of the whole world only barbarians and slaves travel as foreigners. Annaeus Seneca says: “Depart from this city, which may be called, as it were, the common fatherland; I have gone through all the cities: there is none in which you do not find a large part of the population foreign.” In Dio, Maecenas urges Caesar to grant Roman citizenship to all the allies, so that, made participants in it, they might become more loyal, and so that those living in Rome might regard it alone as truly a city, and their own fatherlands as fields and villages. Since Rome is therefore the common fatherland, it is not obscure why Ulpian writes in Digest 48.22.7, *de interdictione et relegatione*, that it had been established that one who had been forbidden his fatherland must also abstain from the City, which constitution was issued by Claudius, as Suetonius testifies in his Life of Claudius. Cicero, *Against Rullus*: “Rome, the common fatherland of us all.” Formerly, by the Julian law, Rome was the common fatherland of Romans and Italians; today it is the common fatherland of all who are subject to Roman rule. A person relegated cannot remain in Rome, because it is the fatherland of all, as Callistratus says in Digest 48.22, *The Relegated Person*, and Novel 78. See Cujas on Code 10.31.1, *de decurionibus*; Alciatus, book II, *Dispunctiones*, chapter 21; Brissonius, book III, *Selecta*, chapter 6; Decius on chapter *Meminimus*, no. 16, *Extra*, *de appellationibus*; Felinus on the final chapter, penultimate column, no. 26, *de foro competenti*; *Roman Singulars*, 146. Consult what I noted on letter 2 of book XI, below. BROSS.

It is the fertile mother of eloquence; it is the broadest temple of all the virtues: let what is renowned plainly be recognized. For the person to whom so great a dwelling is granted is not believed to be without distinction; and residence there may be beneficial, since at times it is advantageous to neglect one’s fatherland so that one may acquire wisdom. Had the Ithacan Ulysses not done this, he might perhaps have remained hidden in his own home [Ac., “labors”].

[Col. 0536C] **Note:** Thus Justus Lipsius reads, volume III, page 312, as does D. Juretus.

Homer’s noble poem especially established his wisdom on this account: that he traveled through many cities and peoples, since those are always considered wiser who are proved to have been educated through association with many people. For human nature, just as it is trained by hard labor, so through sluggish leisure it becomes foolish.

## LETTER XL. TO ASSUIN [ed. Accurs., ASSIO; D. Gr. and Cuj., ASSUM], ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND COUNT, KING THEODORIC

He orders him to provide the necessary arms for the soldiers of Salona before they set out for war.

[Col. 0535B]

Our arrangement must not be obstructed by delay, lest what has clearly been beneficially organized encounter an obstacle through the fault of tardiness. Therefore the arms must be distributed before necessity can demand them, so that when the occasion requires them they may be sufficiently prepared to obey orders. For the art of warfare, if it is not practiced beforehand, is not available when it becomes necessary.

Accordingly, Your Illustrious Sublimity shall provide the soldiers of Salona with the necessary arms, in accordance with our command, as soon as each of them is afforded the opportunity to equip himself; for an armed defender is the trustworthy safety of the commonwealth. Let the soldier learn during peace what he will be able to accomplish in war. Those who, after preliminary training, trust that they are fit for arms are the only ones who suddenly raise their spirits to battle. Calves eagerly engage in contests that will fill out their strength when mature; puppies play at early hunts. We begin to kindle fires with tender twigs; but if you apply logs to the first sparks, you extinguish the little flame that you are trying to foster. So, unless human minds have first been gently imbued, they cannot be found fit for the task toward which you are directing them. All beginnings are timid; and timidity is not removed except when unfamiliarity with necessary matters has been abolished.

## LETTER XLI. TO AGAPITUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND PREFECT OF THE CITY, KING THEODORIC

He orders him to enroll Faustus, the adult son of the illustrious Faustus, among those to be reported to the curia.

The exceptional care you show for your order makes us more cautious in issuing judgments; and the honor of the Senate compels us to examine more diligently whom we should admit to its venerable assembly. We wish it not merely to be increased in the number of citizens, but also adorned by the greatest brilliance of merit. Let another order perhaps admit men of mediocre quality; the Senate rejects those who have not been proven outstanding.

Accordingly, from where could we seek a colleague for nobility better than from the vein of nobles, one who promises by his character to shrink from baseness as much as he rejects it by his blood?

[Col. 0536C] **Note:** This expression is often found in authors. We read of “a vigorous fraternal vein” and “a vein fertile in good men.” Thus Macrobius calls it the vein of the Latin language; Cicero, the vein of the commonwealth; Spartianus, the vein of paternal discipline. Ennodius uses “the vein of languages.” Likewise, veins of water are mentioned by Sempronius in Digest 39.3.21, *de aqua et aquae pluviae arcendae*; Albericus de Rosate on Code 11.8, *forma*, § *salinae*; Coepola on Digest 50.16, *inter publica*, § *publica*, *de verborum significatione*; Paulus de Castro, consultation 5. The vein of a well is mentioned by Ulpian in Digest 39.2.24 § 12, *de damno infecto*. Veins of metals, quarries, and stones occur in Digest 7.9.13 § 5, *de usufructu*, and Code 11.6.3, *de metallariis*. Thus Bartolus speaks of a stony or iron vein in Digest 18.1, *venditor*, § *si constat*, *de communi praediorum*. Veins are also said of trees, as Pliny testifies, book XVI, chapter 38: “In the flesh of certain trees there are pulp and veins.” We also speak of veins of gold and silver, as is clear from Cicero, book II, *On the Nature of the Gods*: “We find the veins of bronze, silver, and gold buried deep.” BROSS.

Therefore Your Illustrious Magnificence shall decree that Faustus, the adult son of the illustrious Faustus, be granted what the ancient order has designated [others, “dictated”] concerning those to be reported to the curia. In issuing these instructions we diminish nothing of the sacred order’s customary authority of judgment, since it is a greater glory of rank to observe the decision of the leading men after a royal judgment. It is their adornment if we command what they themselves usually select, and if we earnestly request what is daily requested from them.

## LETTER XLII. TO ARTEMIDORUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND PREFECT OF THE CITY, KING THEODORIC

The prefecture of the City is conferred upon him, and he is adorned with the highest praises.

[Col. 0536C]

The rewarding of merits reveals the just rule of a sovereign, before whom the fact that someone has labored does not go unrewarded. For if we grant unexpected things, how can we deny what we owe? Every devotion places safely with us what it deserves; and he reaps a double fruit who recognizes that he has obeyed us in some matter.

Long ago you earned from us something more precious than rank, so that you might cling worthily to the royal side. Our affection allowed you to be delayed: with one who loved you, you obtained advancement only later, so that after the spirit of sacred friendship [that is, of the emperor] you might arrive at honors more richly adorned.

For everything through which humaneness seeks reputation was doubled in you: fatherland, lineage, and distinguished training. If any one of these completes nobility, collected together in you they will accomplish more, since you shine no less through the fortune of your native soil than you are adorned by the glory of your ancestry and virtue. Hence it is that now, in the third year of the twentieth indiction [that is, A.D. 510], we raise you to the summit of the urban prefecture.

[Col. 0537D] **Note:** See above, letter 32, and Digest 1.12.1, *de officio praefecti Urbi*. FORNER.

We grant you the fasces in that city where honors are perpetual.

[Col. 0537D] **Note:** Formerly only the magistrates of the Roman people, or those who held imperium in the provinces, used the fasces. Their use originated with Augustus, in whose honor the Senate decreed in the 735th year of the City that he should always possess consular authority and use twelve fasces. The emperors maintained this custom, though they did not add laurel to the fasces except in victory. Later, through flattery, it became customary for the fasces of all emperors always to be wreathed with laurel, and this became the principal distinction by which the emperor was marked off from the common people.

[Col. 0538D] The form of the fasces was as follows. After rods had been stripped from a birch tree, an axe was enclosed among them so that the iron blade projected at the top, while the rest was covered by the surrounding bundle. The ancestors devised this arrangement, as Plutarch testifies in the *Problems*, to show that the anger of magistrates in inflicting punishment ought not to be hasty: they possessed the fasces, but they were bound, and should not be loosened without just cause. Sometimes “fasces” denotes the magistrates themselves: Virgil, book II of the *Georgics*; Livy, book II; Pliny, book VII, chapter 30. BROSS.

We, who assess our offices with greater modesty, shall certainly acknowledge that you have deserved much from our judgment, so that you may preside over the assembly which you recognize to be revered by the human race.

[Col. 0537B] Is this merely to govern palaces and arrange private households? Honor is often acquired through recommendation; nor is undertaking the custody of a wine cellar the same as guarding precious diadems. What we believe to be more important we entrust for preservation to better men; and what we do not tolerate being exposed to loss we certainly entrust to more faithful minds. If Rome has an equal, consider that we have entrusted similar things to others as well; but if it is a unique good, we make you especially judge of the thing which we always desire to increase.

## LETTER XLIII. TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME, KING THEODORIC

He informs it that he has granted Artemidorus the fasces of the urban prefecture, praises him highly, and asks that the Senate confirm his choice by its votes.

[Col. 0537C]

You know, Conscript Fathers, that it is our delight [Niv., “bosom”; Acc., “joy”; Juret., “reward”] to confer the summits of rank; you know that it benefits you when we have been able to bestow the honor of the fasces. For whatever is undertaken by each individual is credited to the Senate, which deserves it. You recognize what we think of you, since to men tested by long labor we give this reward above all: that they may deserve to be participants in your body.

This is the man who, though he had left behind the sweetness of his native soil, preferred to cling to us. Although he was distinguished in his homeland, he nevertheless chose to submit to our fortune, surpassing the force of nature by the greatness of his loyalty. Under the emperor Zeno, who was not so much benevolent as related to him, he rejoiced. And what favor could he not obtain in that commonwealth from a parent who so readily favors strangers?

But excessive affection scorned all these things, so that we ourselves, for whom he is known to have done them, may rightly marvel that so many desirable things were despised for the sake of loyalty to one man. In addition to this exceptional fidelity, he added the comfort of his conversation, softening with the sweetness of his speech the harsh cares of the commonwealth which we sometimes undertake because of the necessity of emerging circumstances. Gentle in address, a faithful patron of suppliants, unable to accuse, but bold in commending.

He so distinguished himself by purity of spirit that, while he deserved courtly offices with us, he claimed for himself the most agreeable service through the organization of spectacles, so that under the appearance of free pleasure he seemed willing to serve freely [mss., “gladly”; some, “liberally”]. He abstained from burdens, but in no respect separated himself from us. Indeed, as a convivial companion, he adorned the royal table [ed., “loved it”]; there he strove to join himself to us, where it is certain that we can rejoice.

But what more need be said about his character, when for complete proof it is enough that he has continually deserved to possess our affection? There is no greater merit than to have found favor with rulers. For those who are entitled to seek the best among all men seem always to have chosen the deserving.

Therefore, weighing his labors with a reward, we have granted Artemidorus, an illustrious man, the fasces of the urban prefecture. To him, then, Conscript Fathers, who shines forth through so many and such great merits, show favor in your speech; show favor in your assemblies. It will also be praise for your benevolence if, by showing affection to the deserving, you encourage the rest by your example.

## LETTER XLIV. TO THE PEOPLE OF THE CITY OF ROME, KING THEODORIC

He informs them that he has given Artemidorus the fasces of the urban prefecture to govern, so that the innocent may have an utterly pure witness and the erring may encounter a supremely just avenger.

[Col. 0538C]

You can recognize from the very care we show you that we hold you in exceptional affection. For you we appear to be so concerned that we allow no admonition to be omitted. Caution reveals affection; and what we cherish more diligently we guard with greater favor.

Hence it is that we have given the fasces of the urban prefecture to the illustrious Artemidorus, long trained in our service, so that, since civic order is disturbed by the unlawful seditions of certain men, the innocent may have an utterly pure witness and the erring may encounter a supremely just avenger. Since we delight in the innocent, we have decided to make this known to everyone, so that no one may presume to transgress the customary bounds through an unexpected act of severity.

Therefore know that we have delegated such powers to the aforesaid man that, if anyone behaves uncivilly, he will immediately incur the severity of our command. And although the laws have given this power to the urban prefecture, we have nevertheless delegated it specifically, so that what a double authority has permitted may be carried out with greater confidence.

He will therefore dare, by our authority, to strike down seditious men and those who deviate from public discipline. Let the fervor of contentious spirits be quieted. Why are the blessings of peace which, with God’s favor, you have earned through our labor stained by unlawful seditions? Morals have never been endangered by greater harm than when Roman dignity is blamed. Let the honorable city therefore restore its moderation. It is shameful to have degenerated from one’s predecessors, especially at a time when you know that you have such a ruler, one who grants rewards to the well-deserving and vengeance to the troublesome.

## LETTER XLV. TO BOETHIUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND PATRICIAN, KING THEODORIC

He says that the king of the Burgundians has asked him to send water-clocks and a sundial to him, and he invites Boethius, who is thoroughly skilled in all the marvels of mathematics, to complete this work.

[Col. 0539B]

Requests made by neighboring kings in the spirit of presumption should not be scorned, since small things often have greater power to provide pleasure than great riches can obtain. Frequently, what arms cannot accomplish is supplied by entertainments of sweetness. Let it therefore be for the commonwealth, even when we seem to be playing. For we seek pleasures for this reason: that through them we may accomplish serious purposes.

The lord of the Burgundians therefore earnestly asked us to send him the clock regulated by water flowing through a calibrated device, and the one distinguished by the measured illumination of the immense sun, together with the masters of these things, so that, enjoying the pleasures he had obtained, he might regard as a marvel what is ordinary for us. For they rightly wish to observe what they marvel at in the reports of their envoys.

We have learned that you, nourished by vast learning, know this so well that, while the arts practiced by ordinary people are unknown to them, you have drunk at the very fountain of the disciplines. Thus, although far away, you entered the schools of Athens; thus you mingled the toga with the choirs of the cloak-wearers, so that you made the doctrines of the Greeks into Roman learning.

For in your translations Pythagoras the musician and Ptolemy the astronomer are read as Italians. Nicomachus the arithmetician and Euclid the geometer are heard by Ausonians. Plato the theologian and Aristotle the logician debate in the Quirinal tongue. You restored the mechanical Archimedes of Sicily to Latium [Note: He was a Syracusan, concerning whom see Cicero, book V of the *Tusculan Disputations*, and Vitruvius, book IX, chapter 3, *On Architecture*. Plutarch records his incredible and never-interrupted zeal in *Whether an Old Man Should Administer the Commonwealth*. FORNER. Juretus, instead of *Latialem*, thinks *Latiarem* should be read.]

And whatever disciplines or arts eloquent [ed., “fruitful”] Greece produced through individual men, Rome received through you as its single author, in its native language. You rendered those men illustrious with such brilliance of expression and conspicuous with such precision of language that they themselves might have preferred your work, had they learned both versions.

You entered the aforementioned art, born from the noble disciplines, through the fourfold gates of mathematics. You recognized it, seated in the inner sanctuaries of nature [Juretus, “penetrable places”], by the light of your heart, while the books of the authors invited you. Its purpose is to know difficult things through use and to display marvels. It endeavors to show what makes people astonished that it has happened; and, by changing the properties of nature in a marvelous way, it robs events of credibility while displaying a vision before the eyes.

It makes waters rise from below and fall headlong, makes fire run by weights, causes instruments to resound with unfamiliar voices, and fills pipes with foreign blasts so that they can sing by the art of music [ed., “joined”; mss., “diminished”]. Through it we see the defenses of cities already tottering suddenly rise with such firmness that the one found desperate in strength becomes superior through the aid of machines. Wet structures are dried in seawater; once hard, they are dissolved by ingenious arrangement.

Metals roar; in bronze the cranes of Diomedes trumpet; a bronze serpent hisses; artificial birds chirp [Note: Juretus thinks that instead of *fritiniunt* one should read *fringultiunt*, as in Apuleius, page 240: “Blackbirds chirp in the distant thickets.”]; and things that are not known to possess a voice of their own are proved to emit the sweetness of song [ed., “sweetness from bronze”].

We say little about an art to which it is permitted to imitate the heavens. It made a second sun move in Archimedes’ sphere; it constructed another circle of the zodiac by human ingenuity. It showed the moon, recoverable from its eclipse, through the illumination of art; and it rolled about with incomprehensible mobility a small machine pregnant with the world, a portable heaven, a compendium of things, a mirror of nature, fashioned in the likeness of the ether.

Thus the stars, whose course we know, do not appear to emerge to our deceived eyes. A certain passage among them stands still; and what you know by true reasoning to run swiftly, you do not observe moving. What could be more astonishing for a human being than even to do what it may be astonishing merely to have understood?

Therefore, since you are adorned by the knowledge of such things, which deserves to be proclaimed, dispatch the clocks to us at public expense, without loss to yourself. Let the first be one in which a pointer, the indicator of the day, customarily shows the hours by means of a small shadow. Thus an immovable and small ray accomplishes what the sun’s marvelous greatness travels through, and equals the sun’s flight even though it itself never moves. If the stars could feel envy of such things, they would perhaps deflect their course lest they be subjected to such mockery.

Where is that singular marvel of the hours coming from light, if a shadow also displays them? Where is the celebrated, unfailing dew, if metals, which are held in perpetual position, also perform this? O immeasurable power of art, which, while claiming to play, prevails over nature in publishing her secrets!

The second should be the one by which the hour is discerned apart from the sun’s rays, dividing the nights into portions.

[Col. 0540D] **Note:** Athenaeus wrote about the hydraulic clock.

Since it owes nothing to the stars, it converts the order of the heavens instead to the flow of waters. Through their movements it shows that the heavens revolve; and, conceived with bold presumption, art confers upon the elements what the condition of their origin denied them.

All the disciplines, and all the labor of the wise, seek to know the power of nature so that they may accomplish as much as possible. Mechanics alone seeks to imitate it through opposites and, if it is permitted to say so, in certain matters even strives to surpass it.

This is what mechanics is recognized to have done in making Daedalus fly.

[Col. 0541B] **Note:** A similar example occurs in Prosper, *On the Promises and Predictions of God*, part III, chapter 38; in Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 23; and in Laonicus, *On the Commonwealth of Muhammad*, book III, *On Turkish Affairs*. JUR.

This is what made the iron Cupid hang in the temple of Diana without any attachment. This is what today makes the mute sing, the senseless live, and immobile things move. The mechanic, if one may say so, is almost a companion of nature: he unlocks hidden things, transforms visible things, and plays with marvels, imitating so beautifully that what is undoubtedly constructed is judged to be reality.

Since we know that you have read these matters with exceptional diligence, you will hasten to send us the aforementioned clocks, so that you may make yourself known in that part of the world where you could not otherwise have arrived. Through you, let foreign peoples recognize that we possess nobles such as the authors whom they read. How often will they not believe what they have seen? How often will they think this truth a playful dream? And when they have recovered from their astonishment, they will not dare to call themselves our equals, since they know that wise men among us have conceived such things.

## LETTER XLVI. TO GUNDIBABUS [Note: Others, *Gundibaldus*; elsewhere, in Adon of Vienne. This Gundibaldus was defeated a few years later by Clovis, king of the Franks, according to Gregory of Tours, book II, chapter 32. Theodoric sends him two clocks, one representing the entire movement of the heavens, the other marking the hours.] KING OF THE BURGUNDIANS, KING THEODORIC

He sends him a sundial and a water-clock made by Boethius, together with those who constructed them.

Gifts that are proved to have been desired in every respect should be welcomed, since what can satisfy a desire is not contemptible. For through all costly things one aim alone is pursued: that the mind of the person desiring may be satisfied.

Accordingly, sending our customary greetings, we have entrusted the clocks, together with their constructors, to So-and-so and So-and-so, the bearers of this letter [their names are absent from the supplied text], as an agreeable gift for your presence [D. Juretus reads, “of your excellence”]: one in which human ingenuity appears to be gathered together, and which is known to traverse the spaces of the entire heaven; the other in which the sun’s course is known without the sun, and the intervals of the hours are marked by dripping water.

[Col. 0541C] **Note:** “Bearers” often signifies messengers by this name, also in book VIII, letter 8, and book X, letter 8. Before the use of paper, the words of letters were written on wooden tablets fashioned by cutting. Hence their bearers were called *tabellarii*, as Isidore says, book VI, chapter 8, *Etymologies*. Code of Theodosius 8.5.7, *Si certum petatur*, speaks of bearers and carriers of money and of a letter-carrier; likewise 8.5.23, *omnes*, and 8.5.31, *quoniam*. Code of Theodosius 8.4.1, *de appellationibus*. Otherwise *portitores* are toll collectors who occupied the harbor and questioned everyone in order to collect the toll. Nonius Marcellus; Donatus on Terence’s *Phormio*. FORNER.

Have in your own fatherland what you once saw in the Roman City. It is fitting that your favor should enjoy our goods, since you are also joined to us by kinship.

[Col. 0542C] **Note:** Gundibald had married a daughter of Theodoric. Gregory of Tours, book III, chapter 5. FORNER.

Let Burgundy under your rule learn to contemplate subtle things and praise the inventions of the ancients, through whom it lays aside its national disposition [Note: Clearly *per quos*—“through whom”—must be restored here, not *per vos*—“through you”—so that it refers to the preceding word *antiquorum*, “the ancients.” The other reading, *per vos*, seems to have arisen through the error of Pithaeus in his preface to Salvian’s books *On the Providence of God*, where he interprets the passage as referring to King Gundibald and understands the purpose of the nation as the treaty and alliance entered into with the Romans and the Gothic successors. JURET.], and, when it observes the wisdom of its king, rightly desires the achievements of the wise.

Let it distinguish the periods of the day by their activities and establish the moments of the hours with perfect precision. Life is conducted in confusion if such a distinction is not known according to truth. For it is the practice of beasts to sense the hours through the hunger of the belly and not to possess a fixed measure that has been allotted for human use.

[Col. 0542C] **Note:** Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIII, page 302.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0541]

## LETTER I. TO THE MOST PIOUS EMPEROR ANASTASIUS, KING THEODORIC

He announces that Felix the Gaul was created consul this year on account of his merits.

[Col. 0541D]

Solemn custom reminds us to give a name to the Fasti, the distinctive adornment of Rome and the earthly glory of the curia, so that through the numbering of years the favor of dignities may run its course and the memory of the ages may be consecrated by the gifts of rulers. Let the year take its auspices from a fortunate consul.

[Col. 0541D] **Note:** Formula 1, book VI: years were numbered by the consuls. “Let the year take its auspices from a fortunate consul.” It is clear from this passage that the consuls began and opened the year, as is evident from Code of Theodosius 8.11.1, *ne quid publicae laetitiae*, from Salvian, book VI, *On the Providence of God*, and many others. Thus “new year” was said of the first year of an emperor’s reign, as can be gathered from Seneca: “What happened in heaven on the third day before the Ides of October, when Asinius Marcellus and Acilius Aviola were consuls, in the new year, at the beginning of the happiest age, I wish to commit to memory.” “New year” is also that part of the year which produces new crops and new fruits. Tibullus:

> And whatever fruit the new year brings forth for me.

Thus Gellius appears to have called summer the “new year,” because summer brings new crops. It is also very often used for the beginning of the year, as in “new spring,” “new summer,” and “the beginning of summer.” Ovid:

> Tell me, why does the new year begin in the cold season?

BROSS.

And may the year dedicated by such a name enter as the gateway of the days, and may the fortune of its beginning favor the remainder. For what could be imagined more desirable for you than that Rome should gather her own children again to her breast and enroll a Gaul in the venerable assembly of her name?

[Col. 0543D] **Note:** D. Gronovius and Cujas think that the reading should be: “and enroll the Gallic Senate in the assembly of her venerable name.” Manuscripts: “and enroll the Gallic Senate in the venerable assembly of her name.”

[Col. 0543A]

Let the curia recognize the glory of transalpine blood, which has more than once clothed its crown with the flower of his nobility. Among the remaining fasces it knows how to draw consular men from that region, men whose honor is ancestral by the law of time, carried through a long line of descent and displayed on the trabea.

For who does not know that Felix possesses the character of the good, since at the first auspices he revealed his merit by appearing to hasten from here toward his fatherland of virtue? Prosperity followed a good judgment: his advancement grew along with freedom; nor did we allow him to remain without glory, since he deserved to reach the honor of the commonwealth.

He is plainly worthy of our generosity, since in the very flower of boyhood he restrained his slippery age with mature character; and, a rare good of self-control, deprived of his father, he became the son of gravity. He subdued desire, the enemy of wisdom; he despised the allurements of vices; he trampled upon the vanities of pride. Thus, having overcome his excesses, he seemed to have earned the consulship from his character before receiving it from us.

But we, who are won over by good training and attracted by integrity when we observe it, bestowed the curule fillets upon the candidate, so that through gifts we might call forth the aspirations to virtue; for zeal for a cause does not fail when it has a more generous reward.

[Col. 0543D] **Note:** A *fillet* is a band in the form of a diadem, from which ribbons hang on both sides. Some called the fillets of priests *filamenta*. Others write that fillets were white ribbons with which temples were adorned, and that it was customary for newly married women, before entering their husbands’ homes, to decorate the doorposts with fillets. Hence the term came to be applied to every dignity, since every dignity had its own insignia. There was also an imperial fillet, Code 1.40, final section. This is the diadem which Valerius calls “a cloth more noble than fortunate,” filled with many cares, anxieties, and miseries. There were also consular fillets and those of the praetorian prefect, Code 12.3.1 and Code 12.1.1 § 1. Likewise there were fillets of the master of offices, Code 12.7.2 at the end. There were also certain fillets or signs by which a free person was distinguished from a slave, Code 1.31, *jubemus*. Thus “fillets of honors” occurs in Code 7.51.1, *de temporum appellationibus*; “imperial fillets” in Code 7.37.1; and “fillets of higher administration” in Code 1.49.1. BROSS.

And therefore you, who can enjoy with undivided favor the benefits of both commonwealths, join your support and unite your judgment. He deserves to be chosen by the judgment of both who merits advancement to such great fasces.

## LETTER II. TO FELIX, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND ORDINARY CONSUL, KING THEODORIC

The dignity of the consulship is conferred upon him in the fourth indiction, and he is praised with many commendations.

[Col. 0544D] **Note:** [[Col. 0543C] This note appears at the foot of column 544, but the callout letter (d) has not been printed in the text.] The author speaks here of the distributions and expenses of the consuls for games and gifts. On this matter see Vopiscus in the *Life of Aurelian* and Dio, book LVIII, where he speaks of Valerius Asiaticus. BROSS.

[Col. 0543C]

We love to multiply our benefits, and a gift once conferred does not produce weariness; rather, those who have deserved to receive the beginnings of our favor prompt us to grant rewards frequently. For new men judgment is expended, but favor is shown to those who have once pleased us. For it is proper that a prince’s decisions should not remain fixed in one place, since earlier gifts are commended by later ones, and every unquestionable decision is strengthened by repetition.

Previously we bestowed upon you the rank of honors; now we grant you the summit of dignities, so that we may seem both to have conferred your earlier distinctions deservedly and to have maintained constancy in what follows through our benevolence. For we do not permit those who are celebrated for the brilliance of their lineage to remain without glory. Indeed, let the grace of honors run through parents, and under a good prince let everyone’s fortune advance. For who would despair of advancement where a gift is found in affection and a purpose to bestow it?

You maintain that you have approved the proofs of this clemency [mss.: “you hold that I have approved”], since, with only your native fortune left behind, you seemed to have returned to your ancient homeland by a kind of *postliminium*—a restoration to one’s former civic condition. Our affection received you, filled your hands with benefits, and made it a fulfilled wish that you had sought our rule. For it was fitting that one who seemed to have chosen better things should rise.

Fortune changes with rulers; and in the praise of the reigning sovereign, what the subject acquires prospers. But you showed yourself equal to this indulgence. Enriched with illustrious honor, you conducted yourself with such maturity that you allowed your years to lie lightly beneath a burden which the most vigorous force of nature had been unable to overcome in your first youth.

Enriched by your paternal estate—which always raises up new heirs—you preserved your wealth, although you had attained it without the exertions of labor. For what was found without difficulty is accustomed to slip away easily. You increased your patrimony through the persistent energy of your vitality [Grammarian and Cujas: “neighborliness”]. What clearer sign of good stewardship could be sought when the consulship itself bears witness? Amid such abundant resources you deserved to attain what is reached only with difficulty by those whose estates have been ruined.

Private frugality nourished public generosity.

[Note: Shortly afterward, by “outpouring” he names the consulships (*τὰς ὑπατείας*) and understands the consuls’ distributions; their gifts were issued to the people at their expense. See below, Book VI, Form 1, line 36. “Publicly,” *Digest* concerning conditions and demonstrations. This was later prohibited by the constitutions of Leo and Zeno and redirected toward the restoration of aqueducts: Code, Book XII, title “On Consuls,” laws 2, 3, and 4. The emperor Marcian likewise forbade consuls to scatter money: Novel 105, *On Consuls* (*περὶ ὑπάτων*). FORN.]

You surpassed the glory of your father through commendable stewardship, and what he was unable to assume, you accomplished from his resources. No one seeks lofty chariots without great confidence, since it is characteristic of a noble spirit to desire what is highest.

Self-confidence makes men daring, because nature does not allow one whom it drives forward to remain concealed. Through you the consulship has returned to a Transalpine family, and you have renewed the withered laurels with green growth. Behold the Sacred City made bright in answer to your wishes. Strive, therefore, toward the lofty footprints of praise, so that you may surpass in virtue your ancestors, whom you restore through honor.

Take up, therefore, in the fourth indiction [that is, in A.D. 511] the insignia of the consulship, and prove by your present generosity that you are worthy of the desires of so many. This is surely the place where outpouring deserves praise; and it is a kind of virtue not to love one’s own substance where as much reputation is gained as is taken away from one’s resources. See yourself flying above the shoulders and lips of everyone, and show yourself such that you may be judged worthy of your lineage, worthy of the City, worthy of our judgment, and worthy of the consular robes.

## EPISTLE III. KING THEODORIC TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME
