Felix Gallus, together with his father, is highly commended, and his promotion to the consulship is announced to the Senate.

Rejoice, Conscript Fathers, that the stipends of dignities have returned to you; rejoice that provinces long deprived of them are paying you consular men, and promise yourselves greater things from such an auspice. Beginnings usually foretell better things, when what begins from small origins raises itself in what follows to great heights of admiration.

A noble lineage lay prostrate beneath the Gallican interdict [Note: He seems to be referring to the time when Maximus seized tyrannical power in Gaul. JURET.], deprived of its honors and wandering as an exile in its own homeland. At last divine powers lifted up the oppressed, restored them to Rome with glory, and gathered the ancient laurels of their ancestors from the adorned forest of the Senate house. For who could deny a gift to a lineage whose possession you have, as it were, deposited in a citadel? Indeed, rumor has it that the consulship of the former Felix still lives: for good things know how to endure beyond a man, and what is gloriously performed is not confined by the passage of time.

Let us pass over his ancient ancestry, since you are sated with the abundance of former generations; his most noble father, the candidate’s, is still before everyone’s eyes. He shone so brightly in the Senate through the torches of his prudence that he was rightly considered distinguished among so many lights of dignity. Devoted to literary studies, he consecrated his entire life to the most learned disciplines. He did not, as they say, acquire eloquence merely with his first lips, but drank his fill from the whole Aonian spring. A vigorous disputant in books, an attractive declaimer in stories, a novel sower of words, he fully equaled the authors whom he had read repeatedly.

He also commended the excellence of his studies through distinguished acts of generosity, knowing that ignorance is more readily inflated by the breeze of pride when it is exposed to light gusts, because it is not held firm by the roots of virtue. He was a Cato of our own times, who by abstaining from vices shaped others through his example.

He also examined the causes of natural things with the greatest subtlety and fattened himself on the Attic honey of the Cecropian doctrine. It was wholly fitting knowledge in which a most honorable mind could rest—a mind that always embraces something beneficial, to which nothing unpleasant can happen because it commends to itself everything belonging to worldly affairs, and over which fickle Fortune alone has no power. It is enough for you to remember the rest about him, since, amid your occupations, there is no leisure to unfold the virtues of so great a man [mss. and editions of Nivardus and Gaimar: “when the father’s leisure does not permit it”].

Now turn your faces toward the candidate, so that you may recognize in him the imprint of his father’s praises, and so that he may be judged to have received from his father not merely the likeness of his body but also the signs of his virtue. For, as you know, he lived among you not with foreign customs but with Roman gravity. Joined to honors from his earliest beginnings, he always associated his boyhood, with emulative seriousness—which is the surest indication of probity—with the most glorious men, so that afterward, following examples of domestic virtue, he might adopt the judgment of public authority [ms. R and edition: “constancy”].

And although he pursued everyone’s favor with undiscriminating choice—a thing that can rarely be chosen in the case of great men—he so adorned himself with the affection of the patrician Paulinus that he thereby gave a remarkable sign of his conscience, since he seemed to hasten toward an eminent man. For desired friendship with superiors confers greater distinction than fellowship is able skillfully to impart through good morals, since through harmonious affection a person strives to make himself equal to the one whom he loves.

To him, therefore, Conscript Fathers, who shines through his ancestral goods together with his own merits, grant the radiance of your favor. One descended from a distinguished stock does not come ill-prepared for curial honors. Rome has often chosen the fasces from the Gallican walls [Note: An old manuscript reads “from the Gallican minds”; perhaps it should read “from the Gallican groves,” so that the expression is figurative, as at the beginning of this epistle, where he said “the forest of the Senate house.” JURET.], lest she either disregard outstanding men to her own disadvantage or leave approved virtue without honor.

Let the noble Senate house therefore be filled with provincial excellence, since it is its nature to regard whatever appears outstanding as its own. The year itself, the father of times, composes itself in fourfold variety; nor would it satisfy desire if it did not possess the grace of novelty. Favor, therefore, Conscript Fathers, your own advancement, which is also our judgment. For if the candidate is honored, what he deserves already benefits you.

## EPISTLE IV. KING THEODORIC TO ECDICIUS [editions of Nivardus and Gaimar: BENEDICTUS], AN HONORABLE MAN

He confers the titles of the *siliquaticum* or monopoly, formerly exercised by Antiochus, together with the assistance of the *saiones*.

We take pleasure in an invention of antiquity and willingly embrace adherence to established rules, because there is no room left for fraudulent encroachments whenever regulations reasonably established are observed. And therefore, having learned the substance of your petition, by the present authority we determine that whatever belonged by our command to Antiochus, who exercised the titles of the *siliquaticum* or monopoly, shall be transferred to you under the same terms, secured by the present authority against the attacks of all calumniators, with equity preserved.

You shall also have the assistance of the *saiones*, which our solemn authority has assigned to you for vindicating the aforesaid titles; yet with this proviso, that your protection must in no way be mixed with private business. For what we have granted as assistance must not be regarded as contrary to justice in any way; since another’s guilt reasonably concerns you if, while you seek to benefit someone through yourself, another person feels that he has been harmed by you.

## EPISTLE V. KING THEODORIC TO FAUSTUS, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He orders that the thirty soldiers stationed in the Augustan fortifications receive the same rations as those granted to the others.

[Col. 0546D]

Since our humanity seems to seek an opportunity for generosity and sometimes, out of love of clemency, grants its wishes even to persons of lesser necessity, how much more do we delight in spending for the benefit of the state, where whatever is given doubles the usefulness of the giver! Therefore, by the present authority we order Your Illustrious Magnificence to provide without hesitation to the sixty soldiers continually stationed in the Augustan fortifications [Note: “Sixty soldiers in the Augustan fortifications” should apparently be read “six thousand in the Augustan fortifications,” as in Code, Book I, title “On the Office of the Praetorian Prefect,” concerning fortifications and burgs, law 2, and Book I, title “On the Office of the Master of Offices,” law 4; and Book I, title “On the Office of Military Judges,” final law; and the heading of Epistle 19 of this Book II. In the Florentine *Digest*, however, *carcere clusus* should be read. See law 216, *On the Meaning of Words*, concerning the interpretation of Antoninus Augustus, Book I, chapter 8, *Emendations*. FORN.] the same rations decreed for the others, so that the usefulness of the state, which is aided by the advantages of these payments, may be completed with grateful approval.

For it is fitting to think of the soldier’s service, since he is known to labor in frontier places for the general peace and is shown to exclude the entry of foreign peoples, as if from a certain gate of the province. He will always be in battle array who strives to keep barbarians out, since fear alone restrains those whom a promise of faith does not hold back.

## EPISTLE VI [Note: Baronius thinks that this epistle was written in A.D. 515. See him for that year, volume VI, p. 655, Antwerp edition.] KING THEODORIC TO AGAPITUS, AN ILLUSTRIOUS PATRICIAN

A legate is chosen to be sent to the East.

The policy of our deliberation requires the service of prudent men, so that the public interest may be fulfilled through the ministry of the wise. And therefore, Your Illustrious Magnificence, with God’s help, should know that we have resolved to send an embassy to the East. Judging you suitable for it, we summon you by the present orders, so that honor may increase for you through our esteem and the desired result may be secured for our commands through you.

Although every embassy requires a wise man, since the welfare of the provinces and the condition of the entire kingdom are entrusted to him to be vindicated [edition of Accursius: “to be judged”] [Note: The words *judicare*, *indicare*, and *vindicare* are mutually exchanged. Seneca, *Controversies*, Book X, final controversy; Augustine, Letter 164. The exchange is also frequent in legal books: *Digest*, Book III, “Against Sylla”; Book XVIII, concerning delivery, section “Veterans”; Book XLIX, “On the Treasury”; the penultimate law, “On the Status of the Dead”; and the final law, *Digest*, “On Production”—the Florentine manuscript reads *vindicandos*, others *judicandos*, for “those who must be indicated as accomplices.” In the Theodosian Code, Book XI, title 39, law 12, it reads *indicare nititur*; read *vindicare*, for this is the sense of law 11, Code, title “On Claims to Inheritance.” FORNER.], it is now necessary to choose the most prudent man, one who can argue against the most subtle disputants and conduct himself in an assembly of learned men so that so many educated minds cannot overcome the cause he has undertaken. It is a great art to speak against those skilled in argument and to act before men who think they foresee everything. Rejoice, therefore, in so great a judgment, since you receive the gift of election before you could have demonstrated your own ability.

## EPISTLE VII. KING THEODORIC TO SUNA [edition: SURA], COUNT

He orders him to gather square blocks of marble, scattered and neglected everywhere, for the construction of the walls.

What can contribute to the beauty of the city ought not to lie unused, since it is not wisdom to despise something that can be useful. And therefore Your Illustrious Magnificence shall have square blocks of marble that lie scattered and neglected everywhere allocated to the construction of the walls by those to whom this task appears to have been assigned, so that the ancient structure may return to public beauty [Note: This concerns *Digest*, Book XLIII, concerning things imposed for a purpose; Book I, law 7, concerning the office of the Urban Prefect; Code, Book VIII, law 4, concerning public works; Code, Book VIII, laws 4 and 5, concerning private buildings; *Digest*, Book XLIII, section “If anyone to no one”; and the final law, “That nothing be done in a public place.” Pliny, Book X of the *Letters*, to Trajan, concerning a place for a bathhouse granted to the people of Prusa: “The city would now have gained a disfigurement through ruins, so that its ugliest appearance might be adorned.” See below, Book III, Epistle 29. FORNER.] and so that the stones lying after the ruins may adorn something.

Yet you must make it clear by demonstrable reasoning that the very materials have fallen from public places. For just as we do not wish the adornment of any city to be violated by anyone’s rash presumption, so we detest the infliction of harm under the pretext of private gain.

## EPISTLE VIII. KING THEODORIC TO SEVERUS, A VENERABLE BISHOP

One thousand five hundred solidi are sent through Montanarius for him to distribute to provincials who have suffered loss through the army.

[Col. 0548B]

Who is better chosen to uphold the rights of equity than one adorned with the priesthood, who, out of love of justice, knows how to judge without personal discrimination [Note: Without distinction of persons. This is called *προσωποληψία* by St. Paul in Romans II: the law is framed not for individuals but generally for all persons. *Digest*, Book I, laws 1 and 7, “On Justice”; Book I, law 8, “That…”; *Digest*, Book I, “On Laws.” Quintilian, *Declamation* 254. Philo, *On the World*: “For law is an evenly balanced god for us.” Leo likewise, at the beginning of Novel 21, concerning scales and the equality of laws, writes very elegantly. The emperor Comnenus appointed four men to preside over judgments, one of whom was a bishop, and exacted from them an oath that they would judge incorruptibly, without regard to persons—“to render judgments without partiality or bribery” (*ἀπροσωπολήπτως τε καὶ ἀδωροδοκήτως ποιεῖσθαι τὰς κρίσεις*). Nicephorus Gregoras, *Roman History*, Book IX. Philo Judaeus, *On the Judge*, gives the third instruction for a judge: “to examine matters before those being judged, and to try in every way to withdraw them from the appearance of the litigants, forcing himself into ignorance and forgetfulness of those whom he knew and remembered—relatives, friends, citizens, and again strangers, enemies, foreigners—so that neither goodwill nor hatred might overshadow knowledge of what is just”; that is, “to investigate matters before persons, and to try to remove them from the identity of the litigants; to come to forgetfulness of those whom he knows—relatives, friends, fellow citizens, and likewise strangers, enemies, foreigners—lest either goodwill or hatred rashly cause what is just and equitable to be offended.” FORNER.], and who, carefully considering everyone alike, leaves no room for envy?

Accordingly, recognizing an action suited to your merits, we inform Your Holiness that we have sent you, through Montanarius, one thousand five hundred solidi. You shall distribute them to the provincials whom you learn to have suffered loss this year as our army passed through, assigning each according to the assessment of his injury, so that no one whose own losses have afflicted him may be excluded from our generosity [Note: See Baronius, *Annals*, volume VI, under the year of Christ 509, chapter 22. JURET.]. For we do not wish to give indiscriminately what ought to be distributed according to a calculation, lest what we have clearly sent out of necessity to those afflicted be unnecessarily given to those unharmed.

## EPISTLE IX. KING THEODORIC TO FAUSTUS, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He decrees that the charioteer Sabinus receive a second solidus in addition to his monthly one, so that he will not be forced to beg.

[Col. 0548C]

Our humanity is known to incline to petitions, nor, out of a feeling of compassion, can it guard the boundaries of justice. For it is characteristic of a benevolent prince to cross the limits of equity for the sake of the benefit of clemency, since mercy alone is the virtue to which all the others honorably consent to yield [Note: See Seneca, *On Clemency*. FORNER.].

Previously, after assessing his merits, we had ordered one solidus to be given monthly to the charioteer Sabinus. Now, however, since Histrio [the manuscripts read *Ystrio*; Accursius, *Istorio*] has moved us by an honorable petition, asserting that one who serves the public joy ought not to be burdened by the most grievous poverty, by the present order we decree that the aforesaid driver of horses shall receive an additional solidus per month, which must be charged to the public accounts.

We rejoice whenever the pages of expenditure are burdened with such entries, since it is a great advantage to us whenever we distribute something to the poor in any form of life.

## EPISTLE X. KING THEODORIC TO SPECIOSUS, A DEVOTED *COMITIACUS*

The contract made by Agapita while she was separated from her husband is rescinded, and Theodoric orders that whatever property she had transferred into the possession of another be restored as quickly as possible.

[Col. 0549B]

It is a royal purpose to assist those oppressed by injustice, so that the punishment of wrongdoing may cause justice to be loved more. Nor can it be tolerated, consistently with the common life by which we live, that the reverend fellowship of the marriage bed should have public seducers [Note: Those who interfere in another’s marriage, even if they have not achieved the effect of their crime, are punished extraordinarily because of their intention toward pernicious lust. *Digest*, Book XLVII, title 11, law 1, “On Extraordinary Crimes”; Paul, Book V, title 4, sentence 12. FORN.] and that sacrament capable of propagating the human race [Note: St. Paul calls it a “mystery” in Ephesians V.] be profaned by criminal recklessness.

Moved, therefore, by the petition of Agapita, a distinguished woman—who asserts that everyone [Juret: perhaps “the wicked”] attempted to violate her privacy and even made proposals concerning the death of her husband, from whom they would more justly deserve to be destroyed—we decree by the present order that, from the time when, with her mind corrupted, she abandoned the marital union, every contract, which cannot remain valid because of the error of fickleness, having been annulled according to law, whatever is established to be possessed by those who wrongfully retain it shall be restored without any delay; lest criminals be able to claim the gains of their fraud as a mockery of justice. For it is exceedingly absurd that those whom punishment deserved to consume should also be able to claim profit for themselves.

## EPISTLE XI. KING THEODORIC TO PROVINUS, AN ILLUSTRIOUS PATRICIAN

He praises conjugal affection and orders Provinus to return to Basil, Agapita’s husband, the Areciretin house that had been transferred to him by Agapita without regard for legal procedure.

Among the burdens of the human race, conjugal affection has rightly claimed for itself a special care. Not undeservedly, since honor ought to belong to the source from which the renewal of posterity is obtained. Every crime pursues its authors alone [Note: Code, Book IX, law 22, “We decree,” concerning punishments; *Digest*, Book XLVIII, title 19, law 21, “A father’s crime,” concerning the same matter. Bion, in Plutarch, *On Delayed Punishment*, said that it was equally absurd to punish an innocent son for his father’s offense as to prescribe medicine for a son in good health because of his father’s illness. The crime of injured majesty is excepted: Code, Book IX, law 5, “Against the Julian Law on Majesty,” which I deny to have been abrogated, although Budaeus, Duarenus, and Balduinus think otherwise. In truth, the singular hatred of treason derogated from the common law stated in the general title on punishments, law 22, as is shown by the argument of that law and the whole of law 5, title “On Legal Rules.” FORN.]. The mother’s error passes to her children; and, through a new turn of misfortune, becomes their own disgrace though another’s crime.

For this reason divine and public laws alike command the bond of marriage to be guarded with such care that it is a great offense against conscience not to hold another’s affections in reverence. Basil, a distinguished man, informed us in a petition that certain persons had taken his wife Agapita from her own home through the vice of solicitation—for the female sex is open to the faults of instability. He confirmed this by submitting to us the petition of the aforesaid wife, adding that, when she had taken refuge within the precincts of the most holy church without her husband’s knowledge, she had transferred the Areciretin house to Your Magnificence without regard for legal procedure.

Now, recovering her senses, she laments the grievous stripping of herself that has been inflicted, condemning her own act: as if a poor woman should make a gift to a rich man, a wanton woman to a chaste man, and a foolish woman to a prudent man. Reject, therefore, the profits that do not seem to enhance an honorable person, since it is more fitting for you to acquire what can also increase your reputation. For this reason we had already issued orders, and now repeat them by a renewed command, that you return the aforesaid property without any hesitation.

The alienation of property requires a sound judgment [Note: That is, *προαίρεσις*—deliberate choice. It is as though he said: no one who is mistaken easily transfers or loses ownership of his property. *Digest*, Book XLI, law 35, “If an agent”; *Digest*, Book XXXI, law 18, “If I”; the penultimate law, *Digest*, title “On Law and Fact in Ignorance.” Error is opposed to judgment and consent: *Digest*, Book XLIII, law 15, “If through error,” concerning jurisdiction. FORNER.]. And clearly, in this matter, she is shown to have lost a firm judgment. For what could a respectable woman have done who abandoned her husband when no fault existed?

## EPISTLE XII. KING THEODORIC TO THE COUNT OF THE *SILIQUATARII*, ALSO IN CHARGE OF THE PORTS

He orders that salted pork not be sent to foreign provinces but be kept in Italy for domestic use.

[Col. 0550C]

If foreign trade serves our desires, if foreign loyalty is acquired by advancing gold, how much more ought Italy to abound in her own goods, when she is proved to suffer no losses in obeying! And therefore we absolutely order that no form of salted pork be sent abroad, but that, with the Divinity favorable, it be preserved for our own uses, lest something produced in our regions appear to be lacking through harmful negligence.

Take care, therefore, that no opportunity, however small, be offered for wrongdoing, knowing that the danger will be most serious if you strive even lightly to commit what has not been ordered. The sin lies in its quality, not its quantity; for injustice does not seek a measure. If imperial authority is despised in a small matter, it is violated in every respect [Note: Dignities are indivisible. Gloss on *Digest*, Book X, law 7, concerning the division of common property. Cornelius Tacitus, Book I, concerning Tiberius, in the Imperial Code. Section “Moreover,” concerning the prohibition of alienation of fiefs by Frederick; canon 7, “Among bees,” cause 7, question 1; canon “Of greater importance,” title “On Benefices.” Whoever touches one hair of a man seems to have injured the whole body of the man: *Digest*, Book XLVII, law 21, “Common,” concerning theft. FORNER.].

## EPISTLE XIII. KING THEODORIC TO FRUINARITH [edition: FRUINAIL], A *SAIO*

He orders him to summon Venantius in the name of Ulpianus, to whom a public debtor had bound himself by a surety for four hundred solidi.

[Col. 0551A]

We are moved by the zeal of compassion at the complaints of petitioners, but especially by those that concern the losses of innocent persons, so that those who gained no advantage in collecting what was owed may not suffer a serious loss in recovering it. It is clearly unbecoming to the justice of our age that one person’s contempt should burden another [Note: No innocent person ought to suffer from another’s hatred. Code, Book VI, law 33, “If anyone by his own will,” concerning undutiful wills; this has been incorporated by Boniface into the rules of law: canon “He ought not,” title “On the Rules of Law,” Book VI. FORN.], and that the innocent should bear guilt for another’s contempt.

Ulpianus, in a tearful petition, informed us that during his administration, at Venantius’s request, he had bound himself by a surety for four hundred solidi on behalf of a public debtor. Because that man, scorning to fulfill his pledge through the presumption of savage rustics, burdened the petitioner with the aforesaid sum of solidi, we decree that the aforementioned Venantius—whom the envy of many crimes repeatedly assails, though he is known only through persistent complaints—be summoned in the present matter, so that, once legally convicted, he may fulfill without any delay or evasive maneuver what he is alleged to have promised.

For boldness is always better restrained when pressed by the weight of the laws; and when fear is imposed on such men [Note: The same judgment is repeated by the authorities: *Digest*, Book XLVIII, law 16, “Whether a thing has been done”; Book XLVIII, law 28, “Capital offenses,” section “The notorious,” concerning punishments. Severity in avenging wrongdoing is often a good and prudent discipline for living properly. Sextus Caecilius apud Aulus Gellius, Book XX, chapter 1. FORN.], permission to sin is not granted.

## EPISTLE XIV. KING THEODORIC TO SYMMACHUS, A PATRICIAN

He sets out the crime of a certain Romulus, who was said to have laid violent hands upon his father Martinus; and he indicates that, if he is indeed guilty, punishing him is a form of compassion.

[Col. 0551C]

Who could accuse the remaining matters if the names of filial affection are proved cruel? A lesser offense is neglected when the great tragedy of a crime has thundered [variant: *tenuerit*, “has held”; Fornerius: *tenuerit*]; nor does anyone strive to avenge what is small if they see the greatest crimes escaping.

Reason itself reveals a savage enemy through his profession; in most cases you may find an associate who is angry. But humanity does not permit a disobedient son to evade punishment. Where is that force of nature which is appointed, through the embrace of union, for the continuation of descendants? The offspring of wild beasts follow their parents; shrubs do not differ from the ground from which they spring; the vine’s offspring serves its own origin—and does man differ from the beginning from which he was produced?

What shall we say of those benefits that can bind even an outsider? Children are nourished from infancy; labor is undertaken for them; wealth is acquired for them [Note: Simplicius, commenting in Epictetus on the origin, force, and effect of *patria potestas* as used among the Romans, expresses almost the same thought as Cassiodore here in these words: “The ancient laws of the Romans, looking to the superiority of nature and to the labors that parents undertake for their children, while also wishing to subject children in every way and trusting, I think, in the natural affection of parents, allowed parents, if they wished, to sell their children and even to kill them without punishment.” Quintilian, *Old Declamations*: “Certain animals,” and so forth, p. 218 and following. “By adoption of another…” “And afterward we choose your customs.” The Euripidean line from the *Erechtheus* is quoted by Stobaeus, chapter 74: “One ought to judge natural children superior to adopted ones; for it is necessary to regard those born as stronger than those selected.” FORN.].

And while each person believes that what he possesses is sufficient for him, when he is still being sought by his fathers, he sins for the sake of another generation. Alas! Shall we not deserve [edition: “shall we not mourn”] the affection of those for whom we do not refuse to undergo destruction [mss.: “departure”]? Even the sea, stirred by savage storms, does not shrink from a parent's concern, so as to acquire foreign merchandise to leave behind for its own offspring.

Birds themselves, whose life is always concerned with food, do not stain their nature with alien filth. The stork [Note: Aristotle, *Economics*: “the laws of storks” (*νόμοι πελαργικοί*); Quintilian, *Declamation* 387, and many others. FORN.], continual herald of the returning year, driving away the sadness of winter and introducing the joy of spring, offers a great example of filial affection.

When its parents’ feathers have loosened under the heat of old age and they are no longer able to seek food for themselves, the young birds warm their parents’ cold limbs with their own plumage, restore food to their exhausted bodies, and, until the aged wing has returned to its former strength, give back to the old through pious reciprocity what they received as young.

And therefore, not undeservedly, those who do not abandon the duties of filial affection are preserved for a long life. Partridges likewise have the habit of making good their lost eggs through the loss suffered by another mother, so that, by adopting another’s offspring [Note: Theophilus, concerning adoption; Cornelius Tacitus; Aulus Gellius, Book V, chapter 19; Timothy the bishop, Book II, *To the Catholic Church*. Many who have no children seek persons to whom they may assign the substance of their own property—that is, persons upon whom they may inscribe some shadowy name of kinship, whom imaginary parents make their children as if adopted, and who, through the treachery of dependents, take the place of those who do not exist. Code, Book VIII, the penultimate law, concerning adoption. FORN.], they may repair the disadvantages of their own bereavement.

But as soon as the young have begun to trust their ability to walk, they go out into the fields with their foster mother. When they have been summoned by their mother’s voice [Note: This is relevant to what Philastrius writes elegantly in the preface to his book *On Heresies*. JURET.], they seek the mother who is their true parent rather than the one by whom they were raised, even though they were nurtured by another through stolen offspring.

What, then, ought human beings to do, when they recognize that even birds possess this filial affection [Note: Cicero reasons in this way in the *Pro Roscio Amerino*, as does Lucian in an epigram: “He found nothing among human beings more grievous than a human being who falsely claims pure friendship. For we do not guard ourselves against him as an enemy, but, loving him as a friend, we are harmed more greatly by him.” FORN.]?

Therefore, have Romulus, who, polluted by the brutality of his deed, disgraces the Roman name, brought before your judgment. And if it is established that he laid hands upon his father Martinus, let him immediately experience the lawful vengeance. For this is why we chose your character: because you cannot spare the cruel, since it is a form of compassion to punish those who are taught to have entangled themselves in criminal acts against the order of nature.

## EPISTLE XV. KING THEODORIC TO VENANTIUS, AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

He confers upon him the *comitiva domesticorum vacans*, both because of the merits of his father, who is highly praised, and because of the literary studies to which Venantius himself had wholly devoted himself.

It is part of our foresight to consider future merits in tender youth and to judge the prospects of offspring from the virtues of their parents [Note: We are esteemed through the virtues of our parents. See above, Book II, Epistle 3, and Book III, Epistle 12. JURET.] 29, because those things are certain which draw their credibility from the beginning, when an origin does not know how to fail if it is accustomed to sprout from the root.

The life-giving vein of springs likewise flows in an unbroken course; and all flowing things possess this condition: that the taste granted to their source, unless perhaps corrupted by accidental causes, does not know how to be denied to the streams.

For this reason, having judged you by the merits of your magnificent father, we advance you through the honor of the *comitiva domesticorum vacans*, so that, being distinguished by your lineage, you may shine through your dignity. For who could fail to recognize in you, though still future, nevertheless certain prospects, when he recalls the dutiful labors of your glorious father? Fired by prudence, he was so attentive to sudden circumstances as though he had been trained by long experience.

He organized the prefecture—the most distinguished burden of all anxieties, whose successful completion alone would have been praiseworthy—together with the care of our army, so that neither administration was lacking to the provinces nor provident solicitude was withdrawn from the army. His tireless and ready prudence overcame everything; he brought barbarian customs to peace and ordered everything according to our wishes, satisfying those who received them in such a way that those who gave did not find grounds for complaint.

Yet, to let a little suffice concerning much, he proved so much about himself that his untested posterity was chosen. Amid these ornaments of lineage, however—which are the greatest indication of the most beautiful nobility—you do not lack the support of your own merits. For, diligently pursuing literary studies, which are worthy of the support of all honors, you add to the brilliance of your lineage the talent of a naturally eloquent mind.

Apply yourself, therefore, to such studies; love what you recognize as having been rewarded in yourself, so that you may direct our judgments along with your own advancement. For you demand from us only as much as you recognize yourself to be devoting to good actions.

## EPISTLE XVI. KING THEODORIC TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

The election of Venantius to the vacant *comitiva domesticorum* is announced to the Senate; his father, the patrician Liberius, is also highly praised.

[Col. 0553D]

Our policy is to confer a reward in accordance with upright purpose, and to kindle men of good character toward better standards through the fruits of generous expenditure. Examples of rewards nourish virtues, and no one fails to strive to rise to the highest standards of conduct when what is praised with conscience as witness is not left unrewarded.

For this reason we have advanced the illustrious Venantius, radiant with both his own and his father’s merits, to the dignity of the vacant countship of the household, so that the splendor implanted in his birth might be rendered more distinguished by the honors conferred. You remember, Conscript Fathers, that the patrician Liberius was praiseworthy even in our adversity. He obeyed Odoacer’s most upright commands in such a way that afterward he proved most worthy of our affection [ed., “election”], although he had seemed, as an enemy, to have done many things against us. For he did not migrate to us in the most contemptible condition of a deserter, nor did he feign hatred for his own lord in order to secure another’s affection. He awaited the divine judgments with integrity and did not allow himself to seek a king unless he had first lost his ruler.

Hence we were happy to give him a reward, because he faithfully assisted our enemy—an enemy who, with fortune favoring his opponent, became so acceptable to us as he could then be recognized as disloyal. Although his lord was already almost overthrown, Liberius was swayed by no terrors. He steadfastly endured the ruin of his prince, and even the novelty that had frightened the fierceness of the barbarian peoples could not disturb him. Prudently he followed the common fortunes, so that, while he firmly endured the divine judgments, he might find human favor more readily available to him.

We tested the man’s loyalty. He passed over sorrowfully to our laws, having turned his mind after being defeated, but without acting in such a way as to be defeated. As soon as we granted him the dignity of the praetorian prefecture, he administered the charge entrusted to him with such integrity that one might wonder how someone known to have been so ardently opposed could prove so simply devoted.

Thus, with tireless care, he appears to have secured public savings under the favor of the administration—a very difficult kind of virtue—by extending the census not through increasing it but through preserving it. While those resources that had customarily been squandered badly were gathered through good and diligent administration, we perceived that the assessments had increased, while you did not notice that additional taxes had been imposed. Both results were achieved with such admirable success that the treasury grew while private interests suffered no loss.

It pleases us to relate how, in the assignment of thirds [Juret., “of the baths”], he joined together both the estates and the dispositions of Goths and Romans. For [Note: It is well known that disputes arise among partners from common ownership, Digest 10.2.77, under “when a father,” section “the dearest”; Theophilus, section “certain matters.” Concerning actions: dividing judgments were therefore established so that common ownership, from which lawsuits ordinarily arise, might be removed: “For this purpose these courts are constituted, namely to put an end to common ownership and the contention arising from it.” Digest 10.2, final law; Code 3.38, “concerning the division of common property”; Book 84, under “moreover,” concerning the rule of law; Code 10.1.2, “when and to whom a fourth part is owed.” Aristotle, *Politics* II.3. Mamertinus, in the *Panegyric* that he delivered to Maximian, writes most elegantly; where, incidentally, for “straws of rivalry,” read “spurs.” Plutarch, on the family of the Tuberoes, in the Life of Marcellus. FORNER.] although people ordinarily clash with one another over neighborhood, the common ownership of these estates is known to have furnished the cause of their concord.

Thus it happened that, while the two peoples lived together in common, they came to agreement in a single purpose. Behold an unprecedented and wholly praiseworthy event: through the goodwill of the owners, a union was formed from the division of the turf; friendship among the peoples grew through shared losses; and a protector was acquired for one portion of the land, so that the security of the property might remain intact.

[Col. 0555A] One law and an even discipline embrace them. For it is necessary that a gracious affection grow among those who continually preserve the boundaries that have been established. The Roman state ought to credit the aforementioned Liberius with its tranquility, since he has instilled in such distinguished peoples the practices of charity.

Consider, Conscript Fathers, whether we ought to leave unrewarded this offspring whose originator we remember to have accomplished so many extraordinary things. May the powers above favor what has been arranged, so that, just as we invite virtues through benefits conferred, so we may approve consciences honored by the growth of their merits.

**30. LETTER XVII. TO THE HONORABLE POSSESSORS, DEFENDERS, AND CURIALES OF THE CITY OF TRIDENTUM, THEODORICUS THE KING.** He declares that he has exempted the presbyter Butilianus from payment of the fiscal assessment and forbids that what he remitted to him be exacted from others.

[Col. 0555B]

We do not wish our generosity to prove harmful to anyone, lest what is granted to one be applied to another’s loss. Therefore, by the present authority, know that, for the allotment which we have conferred by our generosity upon the presbyter Butilianus, he is to pay no fiscal assessment; rather, you are to understand that, in that payment, by however many solidi it amounts, you have been relieved of the assessments of the thirds. Nor do we wish anyone to impose what we have remitted to another through our clemency, lest—something impious even to say—the gift granted to a deserving man should prove a loss to the innocent.

**LETTER XVIII. TO GUDILA, BISHOP, THEODORICUS THE KING.** The case between the municipal citizens of Sarsena and the Church is referred to the bishop’s court. He wishes the bishop himself to settle it if equity lies with the people of Sarsena; but otherwise he orders that a properly instructed representative be sent to the prince’s court who may finally put an end to the opponents’ contentions. If the case should ultimately appear doubtful, he says that the bishop ought to ascertain justice before the controversy rather than depart defeated from the judgment.

[Col. 0555C]

The revered authority of the ancient laws dictates that no one born a curialis may in any way withdraw from the duties of his origin, nor may one who has been marked by such a fate of birth be drawn into another office of the state. If the laws forbade them even to advance to honors, how contrary it appears that a curialis should, after shamefully losing his freedom, serve the state and sink to the lowest condition, which antiquity called the lesser Senate (see below, Book VI, formula 3; Book IX, Letter 7).

Let your Reverence therefore know that the municipal citizens of Sarsena [Brisson., “Farcinates”] have claimed their fellow citizens, whom they say your Church wishes unreasonably to retain. Accordingly, let your Wisdom [ed., “Providence”], in accordance with its purpose of integrity, examine the truth and investigate the matters brought forward in complaint. If the petitioners’ claims rest upon truth [Note: If petitions are founded upon truth, let the lying petitioner go without what he has sought: Digest 4.6.3, “concerning restitution in full”; the penultimate law; the final law, Code 1.22, “if anything is done contrary to law or the public interest”; the final law, Code 1.23, “concerning various rescripts.” FORNER.], permit them to return to their own court in order to fulfill their duties.

But if you believe that your clergy has some reasonable support in these matters, send a properly instructed representative to our court by every means, one who ought to oppose the intentions [that is, the contentions] of the adversaries. If you doubt the nature of the case, it is consistent with priestly institutions that you yourself ascertain justice before the controversy rather than depart defeated from the judgment. One whom it is proper to find a lover of equity ought not publicly to be overcome.

**LETTER XIX [Note: A letter on the same subject is found in Sidonius Apollinaris, Book VIII, Letter 11, and in Pliny, Book III, Letter 14. They shed light upon one another. JUR.]. TO ALL GOTHS AND ROMANS, AND TO THOSE WHO ARE IN CHARGE OF PORTS OR FORTS [mss., “cloisters”], THEODORICUS THE KING.** He orders that the servants who murdered their master Stephanus and cast him out unburied be punished with the ultimate penalty.

[Col. 0556B]

We detest all crimes according to law, and a merciful hearing abhors everything unjust; but especially those crimes polluted by the shedding of human blood, which have stirred up our censure against them. For who could tolerate dangers existing within domestic protection, and the end of a cherished life discovered there, where the aid of defense ought to have arisen?

Therefore, by the present command, we order that, against the servants who murdered their master Stephanus in a punishable crime and also cast aside the reverence due to his unburied corpse [Note: Shall I further recall the ancient laws and examples concerning care for burial? It is enough to have indicated them even by a reference: title “concerning religious places and funeral expenses”; the penultimate law, “concerning conditions of appointment.” Lactantius VI.12. Agathias, *Gothic War* II, near the end. Valerius Maximus VI.3, “concerning severity.” Aelian, *Historical Miscellany* XII, concerning Alexander the Great; and below, Letter 22 of this book. FORNER.], you apply the strictness of the laws, so that those provoked by the worst examples may be restrained by punishments before their eyes.

Alas, compassion is found even among birds, while it is abandoned by the human condition. The vulture itself, whose life is another creature’s corpse, is not hostile to the body of such a great animal or to the smaller birds; rather, it strikes with its wings and tears with its beak the hawk that pursues the lives of feathered birds, and with all its weight strives to aid those in danger. Yet human beings cannot spare one whose kind they recognize themselves to be! The vulture does not wish to destroy what it could consume; the servants preferred to kill the man who, while alive, had habitually nourished them.

Let him therefore become food for the dutiful vulture who could cruelly desire the death of his shepherd. Let him who rendered his master unburied be received into such a tomb.

**LETTER XX. TO VUILIGIS [ed., “UNILIGIS”], SAIO, THEODORICUS THE KING.** He decrees that whatever ships he finds loaded with fiscal grain in the city of Ravenna be sent to Liguria, which was suffering from a shortage of crops and where the king then was.

[Col. 0556D–0557A]

It is fitting that all should willingly contribute what they see can benefit the public interest, since the limbs must feel what the body as a whole feels. Therefore, by the present decree, we order you to bring to us as many cargo vessels as you can find in the city of Ravenna, loaded with fiscal grain, so that, with the public food supply relieved by such provision, it may not have to endure the necessity of scarcity.

Let Ravenna restore to Liguria the abundance that it has been accustomed to receive from it. For the city that sustains our presence ought to find the assistance of many. Our court draws crowds of those who serve; and while people hasten to provide benefits, abundance is necessarily demanded for the peoples.

**LETTER XXI. TO JOHN, APPARITOR, THEODORICUS THE KING.** The king had granted the marshes of Speius and Domitius in the territory of Spoletium on the condition that, if the marshy waters were dried through their labor, the reclaimed fields would benefit them. But since the work begun had been rendered void through Domitius’ fault, he orders John to summon him, so that he may either complete the undertaking begun or yield his own share to Speius.

It is exceedingly serious that a diligent man be deprived of the fruit of his labor, and that one to whom a reward ought to be granted for assiduity should suffer an unjust loss—especially in a matter that concerns our generosity, where negligence ought to be allowed nothing, lest we appear to have decreed something less beneficial.

Some time ago our generosity granted to the distinguished men Speius and Domitius lands in the territory of Spoletium, uselessly occupied by muddy streams. There, an immense depth of water had swallowed up the fertility of the soil, which could have served no useful purpose. The land lay shipwrecked, confused by marshy torpor; battered by both kinds of loss, it had neither earned pure waters nor retained the dignity of solid earth.

We, whose concern it is to change everything for the better, granted it to the aforementioned men on this condition: if through their work or labor the foul marsh were dried, the liberated fields would benefit them. But, as the petition submitted by Speius’ agents [mss., “authors”] reports, through the fault of the distinguished Domitius, who, forgetful of the command, stubbornly spared expense, the labor of the workers was brought back to its beginning. The dried softness of the soil had already begun gradually to harden into the appearance of land, and the sun, unaccustomed to it, was warming the earth that had long been concealed by voracity.

We shall by no means tolerate that this be neglected, so that good beginnings may be destroyed by envious idleness. Therefore let your Devotion summon the aforementioned Domitius with measured enforcement, so that either he may diligently apply himself as the executor of the undertaking begun, or, if he considers this too costly for himself, yield his own portion to the petitioner. For if he himself cannot accomplish the work requested, he ought to allow his partner in the benefit to complete the glory of our age.

**LETTER XXII. TO FESTUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND PATRICIAN, THEODORICUS THE KING.** He orders that Festus command the sons of Ecdicius to return from the City to their father’s homeland for the purpose of burial.

It is equitable that royal piety assist those wounded by the blow of fate [Note: The discussions of the jurists concerning the burial of condemned persons’ corpses are relevant: Digest XLVIII, final title. Arrian, *Epictetus* I.9. On care for burial, see Letter 19 of this book. FORNER.], because those who have been pressed down by the adversities of their lot deserve more to be raised up.

Therefore, by the present authority, we declare to your Magnificence that you shall order the sons of Ecdicius, whom we had initially decreed should remain in the City, to return to their homeland with their father’s body—a return indeed desired, but made bitter by circumstance—lest, by denying their wishes, the wound of the afflicted be doubled [Note: Adversity must not be heaped upon those undergoing misfortune through a new grief. To the same effect: Digest 23.3.6, “concerning the law of dowry”; 1.14, “the Divine,” “concerning the office of the governor.” FORNER.]. And—something impious to say—lest we appear now to deny the wretched the dutiful tears with which we always wipe away the clouds of grief through our serenity.

For the weeping of one who is not permitted to attend the burial of bodies is insatiable, since he continually judges himself guilty if he does not render the final rites to the ashes. At what price did Priam redeem Hector for burial? He pleaded with the frenzied man, supplicated the armed warrior, and preferred to expose his own life rather than deny the corpse what was owed to it.

And since in such persons the duties of affection are mutual, it is unjust that a son should not freely render to his father what it cost the father great talents to accomplish.

**LETTER XXIII. TO AMPELIUS, DESPOTIUS, AND THEODULUS, SENATORS, THEODORICUS THE KING.** The king grants them pottery works and promises royal protection against wicked and deceitful men.

[Col. 0558C]

It is fitting to the discipline of our age that those who serve the public interest not be burdened with unnecessary obligations. Nor is it worthy that anyone’s envy should injure what has been ordered according to our customs. Therefore devote yourselves diligently to the pottery works granted to you by royal authority, and do not fear that you can be transferred to other assignments, from which we scarcely believe that the duties presently imposed can be discharged.

The wicked presumption of evil men against you will therefore cease, and our authority removes the effect of their obscure deceits. For hatred is useless against one whom the clemency of the prince has confronted.

**LETTER XXIV. TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME, THEODORICUS THE KING.** He says that he has learned from the reports of the provincial judges, sent to the praetorian prefect, that the time for the first tax assessment had elapsed in such a way that little or nothing appears to have been contributed by the senatorial houses, and that the poor, whom it would have been proper to assist, had consequently been oppressed. He therefore warns the Senate to arrange everything equitably, so that whatever each senatorial house declares may be paid through the appointed agents in the provinces in three installments.

It is clear that the Senate has provided the peoples with a rule of life. For whatever adorns the Roman name is understood to have been instituted by you. You were called Fathers at the outset so that, through you, the life of the sons might, as it were, be ordered. You decreed devotion for the provinces, laws for private persons, and taught subjects to obey willingly in every aspect of justice.

Therefore no sign of murmuring ought to emerge from the place from which an example of moderation could have shone forth [Greek and Cujas, “moderation”]. Our clemency, which is concerned to maintain measure in all things, has thought it necessary to bring this to your attention, lest excess be nourished by ignorance and error be allowed to persist perpetually under your awareness.

Accordingly, from the report of the provincial judges, sent to the magnificent praetorian prefect, we have learned that the time for the first transmission had expired in such a way that little or nothing appears to have been contributed by the senatorial houses. They allege that, because of this difficulty, the poor are being brought low, although they ought rather to have been raised up.

The result will be that, while the excessive demands of the collectors are despised by the powerful, they will rage against the poor, and the devoted man will pay what belongs to another instead of what belongs to himself. They add a much more bitter complaint: that each person, as he pleases, deigns to lodge some objection against those making demands.

All these losses, however, are said to be inflicted upon the curiales, so that those who had been restored through our provision for public purposes may be handed over to the injuries of the contumacious.

Therefore, Conscript Fathers, since you ought to share with us an equal zeal for the state, arrange matters equitably, so that whatever each senatorial house declares may be paid through the appointed agents in the provinces in three installments. Or, if you prefer what you used to seek in place of a benefit, fill the treasury of the vicariate seat in full, so that it may not be necessary for the curialis, through the repeated and ineffective labor of summonses, to suffer his own losses over your small assessments. Let the detestable result not occur that the devoted man, scarcely able to bear his own obligation, should be pressed down, weakened, by the burdens of others.

We cannot overlook this while preserving civil order: the oppressed must not be stripped of their possessions without the bitterness of war, and those who hasten to obey the state must not perish instead. Know also that we have brought this to the attention of all the provincials through an edictal proclamation, so that anyone who knows himself oppressed by the burden of another’s obligation may speak out freely in public. From us they will receive the fruit of justice, since we know how to give protection to the weary.

**LETTER XXV. OR, AN EDICT OF THEODORICUS THE KING.** The king complains that possessors, or curiales, have been oppressed because the leading men did not pay the sum assessed upon them; then, if anyone feels himself burdened for this reason, he orders that he bring his complaints to the king.

[Col. 0559D]

Although the voice of grief is plaintive, and diminished men do not restrain themselves, and an injured spirit feeds upon shouting, speech is nevertheless expressed more freely when our authority loosens it. For we detest the oppression of the wretched, and we are moved even by the sufferings of those who do not complain. What the silence of the sufferer conceals reaches us more swiftly.

And rightly so, since the injuries of all concern us, while we believe that whatever we experience through the losses of the humble is a loss to our clemency.

Recently, therefore, we learned from the report of the provincial judges that certain houses of the powerful were not fulfilling their obligations in due order. Hence, while the amount of the assessment is sought, the greater sum is exacted from the poor.

Then, through the arrogance of the contractors, the standard solidi—rather than being delivered in due order—were cast upon them under an unjust burden, and they did not solemnly contribute the entire siliqua that they had been accustomed to pay. Thus it happened that the curiales, whom we wish to have protected, compelled by the anxiety of the demands, suffered serious losses; and, if it is permissible to say so, they were pressed by the debts of others under savage collectors [ed. Niv. and Gen., “coercions”] and were even deprived through the loss of their own possessions.

To cut off this crime, we have also sent instructions to the most reverend Senate [Col. 0560B]. Now, through an edictal proclamation, we determine that any possessor or curialis who feels himself burdened by another’s fiscal obligation must hasten to come before the hearing of our Serenity. He shall know that we were wholly displeased by the earlier excesses when he sees beneficial measures taking their place.

The discretion of a just ruler has therefore been made evident to you, although it is always declared by many signs. Now either cover your patient suffering in silence or open a path for your voice under the protection of justice. The whole outcome of this counsel now rests with you, since it is yours to choose what you see will be beneficial for you.

**LETTER XXVI. TO FAUSTUS, PRAETORIAN PREFECT, THEODORICUS THE KING.** He forbids that the merchants of Apulia and Calabria be burdened in the future and imposes fines upon those who violate these commands of the prince. An edict concerning the goldsmiths follows.

[Col. 0560C]

We take no pleasure in unjust profits, nor do matters that abandon integrity for the sake of gain reach the disposition of our clemency. The state is always increased by the right of equity, and when moderation is cherished, beneficial results quickly follow.

Therefore, moved by the petition of the merchants of Apulia and Calabria, we have decided to instruct your Illustrious Magnificence that the grain purchased at public expense by the aforementioned merchants must not again be demanded from them in the quantity of solidi under the name *interpretium* [Note: This term also occurs in Cornelius Valens, *Concerning the Swineherds*, published by Pithaeus, p. 29. JUR.].

For if you do not require the commodity purchased at public expense, let the measure received by your office be faithfully disposed of [ed. Niv. and Gam., “moderation”]. The fiscal account will take the outcome into consideration, since it appears to have imposed unjustly what it rejects.

It is exceedingly unjust that the man who carried out another’s command should suffer a loss. We decree under the same condition concerning the sextarius, which the merchant of that province appears to contribute, so that no one may dare insolently to demand prices that have always been condemned.

To restrain excesses more forcefully, we impose a penalty of thirty pounds of gold upon the prefects of your seat if anyone attempts, with reckless audacity, to act against these salutary regulations. The office itself shall know that it is to be struck with a loss of ten pounds of gold if it presumes to carry out the prohibited commands.

In that matter too our clemency extends itself to the weary: if he pays the levy of this title to the siliquatarius, let the merchant also conduct the monopoly. But if the siliquatarius judges [ed., “indicates”] that this title should be abolished for merchants, let him demand no levy from them, because it is sufficiently absurd that one who receives no benefit from the activity should be afflicted with its losses.

Finally, let the ancient order be preserved among the goldsmiths, and let the obligation itself apply only to those whom the authority of antiquity wished to serve under this title. Therefore ensure in every way that our benefits toward merchants who are shown to be necessary to our titles are protected, lest a class of people who live by profits be brought to destruction by losses.

**LETTER XXVII. TO ALL JEWS RESIDING IN GENOA, THEODORICUS THE KING.** He permits them to repair their synagogue, but not to enlarge it, provided that the thirty-year limitation does not stand in the way.

[Col. 0561B]

Just as, when petitioned, we wish to grant a just consent, so we do not wish frauds to be committed against the laws through our benefits, especially in a matter in which we believe the reverence due to God is involved.

Therefore, so that the arrogant may not appear to insult, deprived of the grace of the Divinity, we decree by the present authority that you may place only a covering upon the ancient walls of your synagogue, granting your petitions permission only to the extent that the imperial constitutions have allowed. It is not lawful to add any ornament or to extend yourselves into enlarging the building.

Know that you cannot escape the severity of the ancient sanction if you do not abstain from unlawful acts. We grant permission to cover or form the walls themselves [ed., “repair them”] only if the thirty-year limitation cannot prejudice you.

Why do you desire what you ought to avoid? We grant permission, but we rightly disapprove the desire of those who err. [Note: The Christian religion cannot be imposed. Lactantius: Religion must be defended not by killing but by admonition; not by savagery but by patience; not by crime but by faith. The former belong to evil, the latter to good. For it is necessary that goodness, not evil, be involved in religion. If you wish to defend religion by blood, torture, or wrongdoing, it is no longer defended but polluted and violated. Nothing is as voluntary as religion; if the mind of the person making the sacrifice is opposed, religion has already been removed and is already nothing. The proper course, therefore, is to defend religion through patience or death; in this way faith is consecrated, pleasing to God himself, and adds authority to religion. Lactantius, *Institutes* V.20. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People* I.26. Gregory of Nyssa, chapter 31 of the *Catechetical Discourse*. Tertullian, *Apology* 23. Hilary, *To Constantius Augustus*. Ambrose, Letter 30 to Valentinian. And notably Constantine in the ancient Acts of Pope Sylvester I, in Baronius, volume III, under the year of Christ 324. JURET. Theodahad to the emperor Justinian, Book X, Letter 26: “Since the Divinity permits diverse religions to exist, we do not dare impose one. For we remember having read that sacrifice must be offered voluntarily to the Lord, not under the command of anyone who compels.” Tertullian, *To Scapula*, at the end: “It is not,” he says, “a matter of religion to compel religion; it must be embraced voluntarily, not by force.” Clement, at the beginning of Book X of the *Recognitions*, to James, the brother of the Lord. Saint Bernard, *On the Song of Songs*, Sermon 66: “Faith,” he says, “must be persuaded, not imposed.” FORNER. Moreover, prompted by the inscription of this rescript issued to the Jews of Genoa, I conjecture that it belongs to Book 8, “Concerning the Jews,” of the Theodosian Code. FORNER. And the final law, title “Concerning the Jews.” GRUL.] We cannot impose religion, because no one is compelled to believe against his will.

**LETTER XXVIII. TO STEPHANUS, SENATOR, COUNT OF THE FIRST ORDER, AND FORMER HEAD OF OUR OFFICE, THEODORICUS THE KING.** Stephanus is praised and granted the dignity of *spectabilis*, or count of the first order, together with certain distinguished privileges.

Compensation in the form of rewards must be granted for worthy labors, since a military career that passes without reward is considered reproached. The palm signifies to the peoples that the athlete is victorious. A civic crown bears witness to military toil. Even horses await their rewards, and so great is the force of justice that the price of labor is not delayed even for those who could not perceive that it had been denied.

If this is so, it is worthy to repay a man who is known to have pleased through honorable service. Through the slippery hazards of so many activities you maintained the steadfast mark of a proven military career. And what rarely occurs in a servant: the changing of judges never altered their affection toward you. No one among you was envious of another’s judgment, even when the arrangements of your predecessors were being opposed.

You deserved to please everyone because you always preserve what ought to be cherished: silence in confidential matters, effectiveness in action, and constant diligence in the labor of observation. And—an uncommon virtue of self-restraint, made rare by the frequent vices of men—although you offered services to many, you sold your assistance to no one.

You did not stain the name of the prince with any sordidness, preserving the dignity of the title through the exercise of virtue. Therefore, by the present authority, we confer upon you the honor of *spectabilis*, which ancient custom rightly assigned to one who has wiped away the sweat of military service, so that, with the watches of your labor finally concluded, you may now understand yourself secure through the reward of the countship of the first order [Note: See the final law, Code “Concerning the Jews.”].

And since the dignity of the prince does not assert favor when it stands bare, nor can something be called a benefit that is felt to have no practical value, we also grant you, with similar generosity, the privileges that the imperial constitutions ordained should be granted to your school’s former heads. You need fear nothing in these matters, even if they are perhaps being attempted through recent usurpation. Ancient authority has therefore justly protected you from every loss and sordid burden.

Although we now pay you what is worthy in the form of a present reward, we nevertheless promise the greatest hope for your future wishes. Since benefits are narrow if they promise nothing also for the future, the imperial Providence will be present, so that those whom we deem worthy of our favor may also be heaped with greater honor.

But because royal goodness ought not to be concealed, ensure that the favor obtained at present reaches the notice of the provincial judge, so that all may know your *spectabilitas* adorned by our testimony and so that, with your service to the military office considered discharged, appropriate respect may be preserved for you in keeping with the glory of our age.

**LETTER XXIX [Note: Baronius cites this letter in volume VI of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 504.]. TO ADILA, SENATOR AND COUNT, THEODORICUS THE KING.** He orders him to protect the estates and people of the Church of Milan situated in Sicily, but nevertheless wishes them to answer as soon as possible to public and private cases brought against them.

[Col. 0563A]

Although we do not wish anyone whom our clemency appears to protect to suffer any burden—for the glory of a ruler is the tranquil leisure of his subjects—we especially desire that Churches be kept free from every injury. When equitable treatment is provided for them, the mercy of the Divinity is gained.

Therefore, moved by the petition of the blessed Eustorgius, bishop of the holy Church of Milan, we admonish you by these present words to strive, while preserving civil order, to provide protection for the estates or people [ed. Niv. and Ga., “honors”] of that Church situated in Sicily. Do not allow them, contrary to right, to be oppressed by anyone of any nation, since, in view of the Divinity, they ought to be raised up.

Nevertheless, they must not delay answering the public and private cases reasonably brought against them. For just as we do not wish them to be overburdened by anyone, so we do not permit them to be found exempt from the path of justice.

**LETTER XXX. TO FAUSTUS, PRAETORIAN PREFECT, THEODORICUS THE KING.** One of the merchants of the Church of Milan, who was to be assigned to the service of the poor, is exempted from tax assessments; the same favor had previously been granted to the Church of Ravenna.

[Col. 0563C]

A personal exemption does not prejudice public law, since it is permissible for the prince to be beneficent, and royal generosity cannot be confined within the rules that have been established. Let anger be restrained by the gravest institutions; impatient ambition be curbed by law. Clemency has no law, nor should benevolence follow narrow limits when it deserves to be praised without end.

Therefore the defenders of the most holy Church of Milan desire that, for the expenses of the poor, which are poured out under the increase of profit, one of the merchants of their city be assigned to them. Acting in the capacity of a purchaser, he should fulfill what he undertakes while exempt from the burdens of commerce.

They remind us that we granted the same to the Church of Ravenna, moved by a reasonable argument. This example of piety they ask to have transferred to their own advantage as well.

Therefore your Illustrious and Exalted Magnificence, while preserving in other commercial matters the public benefit that is customarily contributed by the entire body, shall assign to them one person whom they appear to choose. Let him conduct commercial business in such a way that he pays nothing in the way of the *monopolium*, *siliquaticum*, or goldsmiths’ levy, nor suffer any burden from the permitted market activity.

Why should we delay approving what cannot cause us any loss?

**LETTER XXXI. TO THE DROMONARII, THEODORICUS THE KING.** He informs them that he has ordered the count of the sacred largesses that dromonarii be established at Hostilia, to whom he assigns fiscal money for making their customary journeys with the *veredarii* along the bed of the Po.

[Col. 0564A]

Those who have given their name to military service ought to labor for the public interest. For what should a man do if he fails in the service he professes, so that he finds neither private benefits nor gains the glory of energetic action?

Therefore our authority has ordered the count of the sacred largesses that you be established at Hostilia, so that, refreshed by fiscal generosity, you may make your customary journeys with the *veredarii* along the bed of the Po. In this way, with the labor divided, the public horses may be assisted, since your course is not worn down [Note: Juretus thinks this is what others call *evectio navalis*], being conveyed along liquid roads.

For you do not happen to limp under excessive labor when you travel by hand. Your vehicle does not feel the injury, nor does it suffer a defect, since it is carried forward instead by the flowing water.

**LETTER XXXII. TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME, THEODORICUS THE KING.** He decrees that two senators be sent to the marsh of Decennonium, which the patrician Decius had requested to have dried, and that they make the area of the marsh, marked out by fixed boundaries, the property of Decius himself.

[Col. 0564B]

Grateful to us, Conscript Fathers, is the devotion expended upon public interests, because, while we approve the citizens’ praiseworthy intentions, we find an opportunity for just benefits. For what is more senatorial than to devote one’s affection to public interests [Col. 0564C], so that one may benefit the fatherland to which one was born?

The magnificent and patrician Decius, therefore, bound by glorious love toward the commonwealth, voluntarily made a request of admirable ambition—one that could scarcely have been imposed even under the guidance of our paternal concern. He promised to swallow up the Decennonian Marsh, which devastates the neighboring region like an enemy, by opening the mouths of its trenches: that famous scourge of the age, which, through the long persistence of license, a marshy sea once possessed [ms. Rem. and ed. Ac., “settled upon”], pouring its waters over cultivated places as a flood hostile to them, and confusing the productivity of the land with a corresponding forest-like horror. Since it nourished nothing useful, the land, stripped of its fruits beneath the water, became subject to the marshes.

And so we marvel at a man of ancient confidence, that private hands have undertaken what public virtue long refused [Col. 0564D]. He has therefore promised, with praiseworthy determination, to undertake this bold labor, so that, when the destructive pool has perished, what had been lost might not thereafter perish. Hence he requests commands from our serenity concerning this matter, so that, with public authority, he may undertake an outstanding work that will benefit all travelers.

But we, Conscript Fathers, whose concern it is to assist a good desire by establishing appropriate support, assent by the present decree, so that you may send two men from your body to the very site of the Decennonian Marsh [Col. 0565A]. They shall determine, in their judgment, how much space the marshy flood has occupied through its stagnant incursions, and shall mark it out with fixed boundaries; so that, once he has completed the promised work, the land restored to its liberator may yield its benefits. Nor shall anyone presume to touch anything there that, although the invading waters had long occupied it, he was unable to reclaim.

## LETTER XXXIII. KING THEODORIC TO DECIUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND PATRICIAN

He grants Decius ownership of the Decennonian Marsh; then decrees that, if anyone chooses to undertake this labor jointly with him, that person shall receive, after the work has been assessed, an area of property proportionate to the share of the undertaking assumed.

It is consistent with justice that prosperity should follow a praiseworthy desire, and that what is undertaken with good will should also be fulfilled by royal ordinances [Col. 0565B]. Therefore, since you request justly desired things, by the present authority we grant that, once the ponds and marshes of Decennon have been dried, you may possess, without claim from the treasury, the fields restored to dry land; nor need you fear to cultivate the liberated land, which we release under the testimony of a general authorization.

For this reason we have also sent instructions to the most distinguished Senate, so that, once the space has now been defined, what has been reclaimed from foul pools may properly pass into your ownership. For it is equitable that each person should profit from his own labor [Note: An increase of patrimony is not sought without labor. Law *Si defunctus*, under the title *Arbitration*, *Quemadmodum et pecunia*; law *Quod si minor*, section Scaevola, Digest, *On Minors*; ecclesiastical benefices, chapter *Super*, *On Resignation*; increases of honour, law *Contra publicam*, Code, *On Military Matters*; stipends [are earned] by long sweat, final law, Code, *On All Deserted Lands*. Bross.], and that, just as he recognizes the disadvantages while spending, so he should obtain an increase when the work is completed.

We have also considered this, since we always watch over the interests of the commonwealth: if anyone chooses to undertake this labor in partnership with you, then, after the work has been assessed, he shall possess an area of property proportionate to the share he undertakes [Col. 0565C]. Thus you will not be crushed alone beneath immeasurable burdens, and the work undertaken with the assistance of a partnership [Note: Juretus reads “union.” That word is frequent in Cassiodorus, as in Book IV, Letters 33 and 36; Book V, Letter 3; and Book III, Letter 1. “Unite the sentences.”] will be carried out with greater courage.

In this way it will come about that the envy that is troublesome even to the greatest enterprises, and inimical to them, will be avoided. Therefore continue eagerly in your glorious undertaking [ed., “vigorously”], lest it be burdensome to your reputation that you have grown sluggish in the efforts you assumed. Look, indeed, upon the faces of all, and see that their eyes are turned toward you; consider that the judgments of our serenity await the completion of the work begun. Hasten with whatever courage you possess, so that you may be judged worthy to have emerged from so great an undertaking—one for which you are already praised with the admiration of all.

## LETTER XXXIV. KING THEODORIC TO ARTEMIDORUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

He decrees that the money assigned for the Roman public works, which was neither spent nor returned but withheld, be recovered and applied to the repair of the walls. He admits that those who concealed this money should indeed be punished, but mercifully pardons them.

[Col. 0565D]

We rejoice that our judgments have flourished in you; we are glad that you have proved yourself a worthy governor for the Roman citadels, since, with a noble spirit, you have not allowed a secret favorable to fraud to be concealed by friendship—lest either guilt make you accomplices or security encourage greater offenses [Col. 0566A].

Therefore, all the money that had been assigned to the Roman public works and that, as has now been established by the investigation of Your Magnificence [Note: The constitution of the emperor Zeno concerning this matter is set out in Book VII of the Code, under “The Accounting of Public Works.” Forner.], has been denied on oath [mss., “asserted on oath”; others, “repudiated”], since it was neither returned at the proper time nor shown to have been spent, must be recovered without any delay and, under your direction, applied once more to the Roman walls.

For it is wrong that things which Rome rightly laments as having been taken from her should pass into other uses. We ought therefore to punish with excessive severity those who concealed the assigned money, since in such a matter they defrauded our generosity. But mercy intervened—the mercy that is always joined to us—so that we might not punish heavily deeds that justice, aroused by them, urged us to punish [Col. 0566B]. Let it suffice for us that the greed of the person who wished to fulfill his desire has not been satisfied. No greater vengeance can arise than that the person who had judged himself to possess what he disgracefully suppressed should appear to lose it as though it were his own [ed., “had vindicated it”].

## LETTER XXXV. KING THEODORIC TO TANCILA, SENATOR

He urges him to search for a bronze statue stolen from the city of Como, promising one hundred gold pieces to whoever reveals the theft.

It is exceedingly bitter in our times that the works of the ancients should decline, when we daily desire to increase the adornment of cities. Therefore, by the present commands, we admonish you to search with every effort for the bronze statue from the city of Como whose disappearance has been reported [Col. 0566C]. We also promise one hundred gold pieces [Note: A reward is offered to the person who reports a theft, and this is also lawful. Digest 21.2.16, “They are accustomed,” concerning stipulations; Code 8.40.13, “If Balsatoram,” concerning sureties; Digest 12.5.4 and 12.5.5, concerning obligations on account of a shameful cause. That such a practice was customary at Athens is clear from the collections of Suidas, under Diagoras, Melus, and Ammonius, in the entry ἐπικηρύξαι, “to proclaim publicly” or “to offer a reward.” Forner.], if anyone should prefer to disclose this sacrilegious theft, so that the promise of our serenity may invite the fearful to hope for a confession, as the edicts sent to you also proclaim.

But when you have nevertheless promulgated these commands, if secrecy still conceals the crime, after the venerable day have the craftsmen of the region assembled. By threatening them, inquire from whom the deed was carried out. For the overthrow of the statue could not have been easy for people ignorant of such matters, unless the presumption of a skilled hand had attempted to move it from its place.

## 36. LETTER XXXVI, OR EDICT OF KING THEODORIC

The king promises one hundred gold pieces and pardon for the crime to anyone who voluntarily discloses the theft of the bronze statue. Then he threatens death to anyone who conceals the crime and is exposed by another person’s evidence.

[Col. 0566D]

Although a punishment relaxed so greatly for the betrayal of a crime ought to be sufficient, and although it is no small benefit to have escaped the terror of punishment, we nevertheless add a reward [Col. 0567A], as innocence is accustomed to receive—not because the offenses committed have pleased us, but because we delight in being generous when exacting vengeance.
