Therefore, let everyone know by the authority of this edict that he will earn one hundred gold pieces from our generosity if he reveals the person who carried off the statue from the city of Como; and let him know that he will receive pardon for his own deed, which is what the guilty person chiefly seeks. We give a golden reward for the recovery of bronze; we bestow metals more precious than that which we can recover, thereby redeeming through this liberality what is known to be forbidden from passing into use.

Who, then, would be condemned by such blindness of folly that he hesitated to come forward, when he finds both security and the reward of confession? But if anyone should perhaps think that the matter ought to be concealed, and our serenity should expose him through some evidence of the truth [Col. 0567B], let him know that he will be seized by the ultimate peril [Note: “Death,” which is defined as the ultimate punishment and final penalty: Code 9.47.12, final law, concerning punishments; Code 9.19.2, final law, concerning violation of tombs; Code 1.3.31, “All,” concerning bishops and clergy. “Ultimate punishment,” Suetonius, *Julius*; ἐσχάτη τιμωρία, “the final punishment,” in Harmenopulus and Novel 153. “The latest examples,” Tacitus, Books XII and XV. Forner.]. For it is unworthy that, after those who reject our pardon have been exposed, humanity should then come to their aid.

## LETTER XXXVII. KING THEODORIC TO FAUSTUS, PREFECT OF THE PRAETORIUM

The king grants the citizens of Spoleto an additional thousand beyond the customary amount for the maintenance of the baths.

The kindness of our reign ought to imitate its advancement, so that our humanity may relax its gifts to the same degree that the commonwealth has received increases. For we cannot otherwise preserve a praised moderation unless we must rouse our purpose to consider circumstances. Amid so many daily successes, with God’s favor, it would be a fault of stinginess to remain content with narrow generosity [Col. 0567C].

Therefore let Your Illustrious Magnificence know by the present authority that an additional thousand is to be assigned to the citizens of Spoleto for the maintenance of the baths, beyond the customary amount [Accursius, “for the third part”]. For we gladly wish to expend what we know contributes to the health of the citizens, since the joys celebrated by peoples are the praises of our age.

## LETTER XXXVIII. KING THEODORIC TO FAUSTUS, PREFECT OF THE PRAETORIUM

He prohibits the merchants of Sipontum, devastated by enemy plundering, from being harassed for two full years either over payment to the treasury or over the sums they had borrowed.

We desire our resources to be increased in the treasury of compassion, while we condemn profits acquired for us through the calamities of afflicted people. Our assessment is burdensome to our clemency when it is lamented, because whatever is paid amid grief is credited to the praise of the recipient [Col. 0567D].

The merchants of the city of Sipontum declare that they have been devastated by the plundering of the enemy. Since we regard relief for the needy as an increase of our own wealth, let Your Illustrious Magnificence ensure that those named above are not harassed by any collection during this full two-year period.

But since it is of no benefit to restore those who have fallen if another burden of payment is added [Col. 0568A], let Your Highness have those who are known to have lent money to the aforesaid merchants warned not to demand anything of the amount lent during these two years. Thus, under the respite mentioned above, they may recover the money they have given and the substance of the debtors may at least draw breath.

For what profit is it for a creditor to press his claim when he strives in vain to exact payment from those stripped bare? We provide better for them if, by forbearance, we enable them to meet their borrowed obligations.

## LETTER XXXIX. KING THEODORIC TO ALOISIUS, ARCHITECT

The king declares that he wishes the spring of Aponus, whose various properties he vividly describes, to be restored. To ensure that this succeeds, he orders the ancient solidity of the buildings there to be renewed and the palace, shaken by long age, to be repaired.

[Col. 0568B]

If we wish the miracles heard from the ancients to endure for the praise of our clemency—for the glory of a king increases when nothing declines under his rule—with what care ought that to be repaired which is also frequently presented to our own eyes?

It delights us to recall the power of health-giving Aponus, so that you may understand with what desire we wish to restore what cannot leave our memory. We saw a blue spring boiling in the shape of a cask, with hollow openings, and furnaces of steaming waters crowned by a smooth, encircling rim arranged with admirable natural design [ms. Aud., “with a tent-like rim”; eds. Niv. and Gam., “tent-like formation”]. Although, in the manner of hot water, they exhale misty vapors, they nevertheless reveal such pleasing clarity to human eyes [Col. 0568C] that anyone would desire to touch that charm, even while knowing that it burns.

With a completely open mouth [Note: The mouth of the spring. Below, in Book III, Letter 39, he calls it the “head of the spring”; likewise Ulpian, Digest 43.20.1, concerning daily and summer waters. Forner.], resembling a sphere, the backs of the waters swell above their boundaries. Hence the water flows down with such calm, and runs onward with such apparent stability, that you would not think it was increasing, except that you perceive something issuing from it with a hoarse murmur.

37 The waters come through icy channels, heated with such intensity that, after passing through winding spaces lengthened by art, they return with the greatest heat [ed., “return chiefly as heat”]. O ever-memorable skill of the craftsmen, who so tempered the fires of raging nature for the benefit of the human body that what at its source could have brought death, once most skillfully moderated, provided both delight and health!

It is pleasant to see the hidden process: waters exhaling fiery vapors, a warmth friendly to the waves, and heat coming through the course of a stream, from which it would ordinarily have been extinguished. The philosophers rightly say that the elements are bound together by mutual interweavings and joined by a wondrous alliance, although they are understood to fight one another through their contrasting qualities.

Behold: a watery substance is known to produce fiery vapors; then, when the water descends from the rocks to the beautiful buildings of the baths, it kindles the air with its own quality and becomes suitable for use when received in the bathing pools. From this comes not merely pleasurable delight but gentle medicine: treatment without torment, remedies without horror, health without punishment, baths assigned against various bodily pains [Note: Savaro, in his notes on Sidonius Apollinaris, Book V, Letter 3, restores *dolos*—“pains”—on the authority of ancient manuscripts and proves that the ancients spoke in this way. Juretus.].

For this reason antiquity named it Aponus in the Greek language, meaning beneficial [Note: If we love truth, no greater gift can be granted to a human being by God than sound bodily health; through it the condition of one’s character is to some degree regulated—Aelian, on Socrates. Hence *ἄπονος*, “free from labor,” is explained by Julius Pollux in the *Onomasticon* under *ἄνοσος καὶ ἀνόσητος*, “free from disease and not sick.” Cassiodorus therefore means that the spring Aponus is free from diseases, which is regarded as a supreme benefit and happiness. Forner.], so that the sick person might recognize the source of so great a remedy and have no doubt about a name of such significance.

Among the other blessings of the place, we have also learned that this is astonishing: the same nature of the waters appears suited to different functions. Immediately, when struck against the receiving rock, it exhales the sweating quality of the first chamber; then, descending into the ground after being softened and laying aside its threatening heat, it becomes mild through a pleasant tempering. Next, when carried into a neighboring chamber and allowed to cool somewhat, it grows warm much more gently. Finally, having abandoned even that warmth, it becomes cold in Nero’s pool to the same degree that it had previously been felt to boil.

Not without reason, sharing the name of its creator, it is a companion of the green color of gems; itself also transparent in the color of the glassy element, it sets certain trembling waves in motion while remaining still. But so that the bathing place itself might be made cleaner, by a remarkable discipline of restraint, if a woman descends into the water in which men are refreshed, the water is inflamed [Note: Hence Martial, Book VI: “The springs of Aponus are strange to girls,” according to D. Gruter and Cujacius.]. This is because another handsome provision has also been assigned to women, lest they think that the most fertile place of the burning waters lacked a source from which it might give abundantly, if both sexes shared a single benefit.

This perpetual flow of the waters provides evidence that, entering from within through hidden channels along the fiery veins of the earth, the irrigating purity of the baked spring bursts forth into the open air [Col. 0569C]. For if that fire had belonged to nature itself, it could not have been lost without the destruction of the substance [ed. Ac. and For., “admitted”]. But the tangible substance of water, just as it took on a foreign fire, so easily recovers its native cold.

That medicinal power also provides another kind of aid. Near the head of the spring, provident nature formed a channel for itself, a certain sparkling passage. Above it a seat has been constructed, perforated for human needs in the form of an apse; it receives the sick as the inner moisture flows down. When they have sat there, exhausted by excessive weakness, they are refreshed by the delight of the vapor; they restore their weary limbs and contract, by vital dryness, the fluids loosened by harmful infiltration [ed. Niv. and Gam., “relaxed”], so that, as if restored by some desirable food, they may immediately be found stronger.

Thus the medicinal substance derives from sulfur what makes it hot, and from salt what makes it dry. Not to hand such things down to posterity is to commit a grave fault over the course of a long life [Col. 0570A].

Therefore let the ancient solidity of the buildings there be renewed, so that, whether something must be repaired in the baths or in the underground passages, it may be rebuilt under your supervision. Let harmful shrubs also, growing inconveniently [Note: The roots of trees bring ruin upon buildings; below, Book VII, Formula 6; Code 3.41.1, concerning aqueducts; Code 8.1.1, concerning interdicts. Harmenopulus, Book II, title 4, “Concerning Plants”: “The planting of plants brings no ordinary harms upon houses, for plants put down roots,” etc. A passage similar and almost identical to this one. Forner.], be removed by pulling up the sod, lest certain root-hairs, gradually swelling, enter the vital parts of the structures and, like a viper, nourish offspring through a fertility hostile to itself, from which the framework might split and collapse.

Strengthen the palace as well, shaken by long age, through continual repair. Purify the space lying between the public building and the head of the fiery spring from its wild roughness. Let the beautiful face of the plain smile with flowering grass, which also rejoices in the fertility of the burning water; and, in a marvelous way, while producing barren salt nearby, let it nourish greenery as well [Col. 0570B].

But the land of Antenor is fertile not only in these benefits; it contains other things that will astonish you much more greatly. Those hearts of the mountains, so to speak, distinguish contentious matters in the manner of a record office. For if someone should presume, according to the customary practice, to strip stolen sheep of their natural wool, after repeatedly immersing the animal in the burning waters, he must boil it before he can succeed in cleaning it.

O tribunal truly worthy of reverence, since in these waters there is known to be not merely perception but also true judgment; and since what cannot be resolved by human dispute has been granted to the fairness of the springs. There silent nature speaks there while judging, and in a certain way pronounces a sentence that excludes the deceit of the denier.

But who would neglect to preserve such things, even though they become soiled through great accumulation? For it adorns the kingdom when it is uniquely renowned throughout the entire world. Therefore, if the money given to you will not suffice to complete the work undertaken, inform us by brief letters how much more you think must still be spent; for we do not regard it as burdensome to expend money in order to appear to preserve such great beauties of the countryside [ms. Rem., “the walls of the countryside”].

## 38. LETTER XL. KING THEODORIC TO BOETHIUS, PATRICIAN

He says that the king of the Franks has earnestly requested a lyre-player. He asks Boethius, an expert in music, to select one. He discusses at length the praise of music, the tones, modes, and related matters.

When the king of the Franks, attracted by the reputation of our banquet, had earnestly requested a lyre-player from us, we promised that the request could be fulfilled only through the proper means, because we knew that you were skilled in musical learning. It is appropriate for you to choose a learned man, since you have been able to attain a discipline established at a lofty level [Col. 0570D].

For what is superior to music, which embraces the structure of the heavens through resonant sweetness and, by the power of its nature, the harmony dispersed everywhere? Whatever exists within the conception of any modulation does not depart from the order of harmony. Through it we think suitably, speak beautifully, and move appropriately. Whenever it reaches our ears according to the law of its discipline, it commands song and changes the mind: an artisan of hearing and an elaborate delight.

When it proceeds from nature’s secret place, like a queen of the senses adorned with its figures, the remaining thoughts leap away, and it drives everything out so that it alone may delight when heard. It makes harmful sadness pleasant, diminishes swelling rages, renders bloody cruelty gentle, rouses sluggishness and drowsy languor [mss. Aud. and D., Gr. and Cuj., “sluggishness [and] drowsy humour”; ms. Rem., “flavours languor”], gives those awake the most healthful rest, recalls to honourable devotion the chastity corrupted by shameful love [ms. Aud., “buried”], cures the mind’s weariness, ever hostile to good thoughts, and turns destructive hatreds toward helpful grace. What is a blessed kind of healing, it expels the passions of the mind through the sweetest pleasures.

It gently caresses the incorporeal soul bodily, and by hearing alone leads it wherever it wishes. What it cannot hold by silent speech, it proclaims with its hands; it speaks without a mouth, and through the service of insensible senses it succeeds in exercising dominion over the senses.

All this is accomplished among human beings through five tones, each of which is called by the name of the province where it was found. Divine mercy distributed grace locally, making all its works greatly worthy of praise.

The Dorian tone is a giver of modesty and producer of chastity. The Phrygian arouses battles and inflames the desire for frenzy [Col. 0571C]. The Aeolian calms the storms of the mind and grants sleep to those already pacified. The Jastius sharpens understanding for the dull and generously produces a desire for heavenly goods in those weighed down by earthly desire. The Lydian, discovered against excessive cares and weariness of the soul, restores through relaxation and strengthens through delight.

By bending these things toward the dissolutions of a corruptible age, it made an honourable remedy into a shameful invention. This fivefold number consists of a threefold division. Every tone has a highest and a lowest note; these are said to relate to the middle. Since things that are referred to one another by alternating reciprocity cannot exist without one another, it was usefully discovered that artificial music—that is, music elaborated by the works of composers through different instruments—contains fifteen modes.

Human ingenuity, adding something greater to these matters, gathered through the most learned investigation a certain harmony belonging to the earth, called *diapason*, gathered, that is, from all the others, so that this wondrous union might contain the powers that the whole melody could possess.

Hence Orpheus effectively commanded mute animals and invited wandering herds away from neglected pastures to the feast of listening. While he sang, the Tritons loved dry land; Galatea played upon solid ground; the bears abandoned their beloved forests; the lions finally left their familiar thickets; beside their robber, the prey rejoiced. Contrary desires were gathered into a single assembly, and, while the lyre gave its pledge, all things believed what was contrary to their own nature.

Amphion of Dirce, too, is said to have built the Theban walls by singing to the strings [Col. 0572A], so that, when he lifted labor-weary men toward the pursuit of completion, the stones themselves were believed to have left the rocks and come to him.

The mighty tongue of Maro also celebrates Musaeus, both the son of Orpheus in art and the son of nature, saying that he was established in supreme blessedness among the dead, where he delighted happy souls through the strokes of his seven-stringed instrument across the Elysian fields. This signifies that the person to whom it has fallen to feast upon the sweetness of this discipline enjoys the highest reward.

All these things, however, appear to have been achieved through human effort by instrumental music. Natural rhythm is instead understood to have been assigned to the living voice. It preserves melody beautifully when it is silent at the proper time, speaks appropriately, and proceeds with a composed voice along the path of musical feet through accents [Col. 0572B].

A strong and sweet form of speech was also discovered to move the minds of orators, so that judges might become angry with criminals and pity those who err. Whatever eloquence can accomplish undoubtedly belongs to the glory of this discipline.

As Terence testifies, poets too were first assigned two principal meters: the Heroic and the Iambic—one to raise the spirit, the other to soothe it. From these, various forms were produced to delight the minds of listeners. Just as tones exist in instruments, so meters, pregnant with various emotions of the soul, have been produced in the human voice.

Antiquity reports that the Sirens sang wondrously [Note: Juretus thinks that *cariosa*, “worn” or “decayed,” or *cana*, “hoary,” should be read, as below in Book III, Letter 33, “hoary antiquity.”]. Although their song drew sailors away from the waves and the wind filled their sails, the sailors, sweetly deceived, chose to run upon the rocks rather than allow such sweetness to pass them by [Col. 0572C].

Only the Ithacan escaped them: he immediately blocked his sailors’ hearing against the beguiling sweetness. That most prudent man devised the most fortunate deafness and overcame by refusing to attend to what he could not overcome through understanding. He bound himself tightly with knots to the trunk of a tree, so that he might test the famous songs with unblocked ears and yet escape, bound, when the flood of the sweet-sounding voice carried danger with it.

But, so that we too may pass beyond such matters by the example of the wise Ithacan, let us speak of that Psalter which fell from heaven and which the man celebrated throughout the world composed and arranged for the salvation of the soul, so that through its hymns both the wounds of the mind might be healed and the singular grace of Divinity might be sought.

Behold what the age marvels at and believes: David’s lyre drove out the devil; sound commanded spirits; and, while the harp was playing, the king returned to freedom three times—the man whom an inward enemy had shamefully possessed. For although many instruments of this delight have been devised, nothing has been found more effective for moving the mind than the gentle resonance of the hollow lyre [Col. 0572D].

Hence, too, we think that a string was called a *chorda* because it can easily move the heart. In it so great a harmony of voices is gathered amid diversity that, when one neighboring string is struck, it makes another tremble spontaneously, although no one has touched it. So great is the force of harmony that it causes an insensible object to move of its own accord, because its companion is known to have been set in motion.

Hence different voices arise without a tongue; hence from varied sounds there is formed a certain most pleasing chorus: one high through excessive tension, another low through some relaxation, and a third in the middle, most gently tempered in its body [Col. 0573A]. Thus human beings cannot bring themselves to such unity as things lacking reason have attained through rational social harmony. For there, whatever sounds excellently, whatever with weight, whatever hoarsely, whatever with the greatest purity, and whatever with other differences, is gathered, as it were, into a single ornament.

Just as a diadem delights the eyes with the varied light of its gems, so the lyre delights the ear with the diversity of its sound. It is the speaking fabric of the Muses, the eloquent warp, the singing threads, in which the plectrum weaves what is pleasant to hear.

Mercury is said to have invented it in imitation of a many-colored tortoise shell. Astronomers, observing that it accomplished so many useful things, thought that it should be sought among the stars [Col. 0573B], arguing that there was a heavenly music because they were able to recognize the form of the lyre set among the constellations.

The harmony of heaven, however, cannot suitably be explained in human speech. Reason has given it only to the mind, while nature has not revealed it to the ears. They say that it must be believed so that heavenly blessedness may enjoy its delights—delights that neither fail at their limit nor wither through any interruption.

They report that the highest things dwell within the intellect itself, that heavenly beings enjoy those delights, and that beings adhering to such contemplations are continually held in blessed pleasures. They would have judged rightly if they had placed the cause of heavenly blessedness not in sounds but in the Creator: there, truly, joy exists without end, eternity remains forever without any weariness, and the mere vision of Divinity makes it impossible for anything to be more blessed [Col. 0573C].

This truly provides perpetuity; this accumulates joys. And just as no creature exists apart from it, so without it no creature can possess immutable happiness.

But since we have made a pleasurable digression—for it is always agreeable to converse about learning with experts—let your wisdom select at the present time the best lyre-player whom we said had been requested from us. You will accomplish something of Orpheus when, with sweet sound, you have subdued the savage hearts of the gentiles. And whatever thanks are given to us, an equal compensation from us will be returned to you, since you obey our command and bring about something that can bring you distinction.

## LETTER XLI. KING THEODORIC TO LUDUIN [Note: Luduin is so called below in Book III, Letter 4; he is also Clovis. See Baronius, *Annals*, vol. VI, under the year A.D. 499, chapter 27, p. 594. He thinks that this letter was written in the year cited above. Juretus. Luduin, that is, Clovis—because he was called Louis—says Hermannus Contractus in his *Chronicle*. He states that the victory over the Alamanni announced here occurred around A.D. 508, in the eighteenth year of the reign of Anastasius, with Felix and Secundinus as consuls [read: Venantius the Younger and Celer as consuls]. Forner.]

He congratulates Clovis on his victory over the Alamanni; then recommends clemency toward those who, terrified, were hiding within the boundaries of Italy; finally, he informs him that he has sent two envoys to Gaul with the requested lyre-player.

[Col. 0573D]

We indeed congratulate you on the glorious bond of your virtue [Note: Theodoric, in order to strengthen the power of his kingdom, had joined his sister in marriage to the king of the Franks. Matthew Palmerius. Forner.] because you have happily roused the Frankish people, long inactive, to new battles and have subjected the Alamannic peoples, brought low by stronger causes, with your victorious hand.

But since wrongdoing in the instigators of treachery always appears fit to be cut off—and since punishment for the culpable leaders ought to suffice as vengeance for all—moderate your anger against the exhausted remnants, because those whom you see to have fled for refuge to the protection of your kinsmen [Note: Theodoric had Clovis’s sister as his wife. Gregory of Tours. Forner.] deserve to escape by right of grace.

Be lenient toward those who, terrified, are hiding within our boundaries [mss., “foreigners”]. [Col. 0574B] It is a memorable triumph that the fiercest Alamannus has been so frightened as to be compelled to beg you for the gift of life. Let it be enough that he has fallen, together with the pride of his people; let it be enough that an innumerable nation has been subjected partly by the sword and partly to servitude.

For if you fight with the survivors, you will still not be believed to have overcome all of them. In such matters, accept the advice of one often tested by experience. Those wars have turned out favorably for me that were concluded with a moderate end. The person who knows how to moderate everything wins continually, since pleasing prosperity is more gracious to those who do not stiffen through excessive harshness.

Therefore, graciously yield to our disposition what kinship is accustomed, by common example, to remit to itself. Thus you will appear both to have satisfied my requests and not to be anxious about that side which you know belongs to us [Col. 0574C].

Accordingly, with the honor and affection he deserves, we have sent that man and that man, our envoys, to Your Excellence with our customary goodwill. Through them we hope to receive both news of your safety and the fulfillment of the request we have made. We have also entrusted to the bearers of these letters certain matters that have reached us for your benefit, to be conveyed to you orally, so that, having become more cautious, you may be able to complete the victory you desire with constancy.

Your safety is our glory, and we judge the kingdom of Italy to prosper as often as we learn good news concerning you. We have also sent the lyre-player, skilled in his art, whom you requested. By singing with a harmonious voice through mouth and hands [Note: Hence the expressions “most eloquent hands” and “talkative fingers.” Below, Book IV, final letter. Juretus.], may he delight the glory of your power. We believe that he will therefore be welcome, since you judged that he should be sent to you with such insistence.

# BOOK THREE

## 40. LETTER I [Note: Baronius assigns this letter and the three following ones to A.D. 507, volume VI of the *Annals*, p. 533, Antwerp edition.]

### KING THEODORIC TO ALARIC, KING OF THE VISIGOTHS

He warns him not to place confidence in the multitude of his ancestors or to declare war against the king of the Franks until he has sent envoys to him to settle the dispute that has arisen between them; for this reason he sends him envoys, who are also to meet Gundibad and the other kings.

[Col. 0575A]

Although the innumerable multitude of your ancestors may give confidence to your courage, and although you remember Attila the Mighty to have been brought low by the strength of the Visigoths, nevertheless, since the fierce hearts of peoples grow soft through long peace, beware of suddenly casting into danger men who plainly have had no military training for so long. Conflict is terrifying to men if it is not habitual; and unless confidence is acquired through practice, there is no assurance of suddenly engaging in combat.

Far be it that blind indignation should snatch anything from you. Prudent moderation is what preserves nations. Fury, however, generally rushes headlong in its urgency; and it is useful to take up arms only when justice cannot find a place with the adversary. Therefore wait until we can send our envoys to the king of the Franks, so that the judgments of friends may bring your dispute to an end. For between two men joined to us by kinship, we do not wish anything of such a kind to happen that one of them might perhaps be found the lesser.

You are not inflamed by the spilled blood of your ancestors; the occupied province does not yet grievously burn you; the dispute is still slight and concerns only words. You can settle it very easily if you do not irritate your spirits through arms. Let us oppose to him—even though he is our kinsman—exceptional peoples united with us by oath. Justice, which makes kings stronger, quickly turns the hearts of those who perceive such men armed against themselves.

And therefore, having first offered the honor of our greeting, we believe that we should send our envoys, So-and-so and So-and-so, to you. They will adequately make our instructions known to you and, with your consent, hasten to our brother Gundibad [Note: [Col. 0575D] The Visigoths, who then held Aquitaine. [Col. 0576D] Clovis and Alaric chose Theodoric as arbiter of the war; Alaric, unwilling to abide by his decision, was defeated by Clovis. Aimoin, Monk, Book I, chapter 20. FORNER.] and the other kings, so that you may not seem to be troubled by the intervention of those who wickedly rejoice in another’s conflict. For may the divine powers avert the possibility that such injustice should prevail over you. We judge your common misfortune to be our enemy. Indeed, the man who strives to oppose you will rightly have me as his adversary.

## LETTER II. TO GUNDIBAD, KING OF THE BURGUNDIANS. KING THEODORICUS.

He urges Gundibad, when envoys have been sent to him, to restore harmony between Alaric and Clovis.

[Col. 0575D] It is a grave evil when the wills of dear [others: concerned] royal persons are seen to be opposed to one another, and when one watches passively, by dissembling, to see whether something painful may emerge from the misfortune of one of them. It does not happen without our resentment if, while we remain passive, our kinsmen engage in battle and suffer ruin. Through me, you all possess pledges of great favor; no one is separated from the other. If you commit any offense against one another, you sin to my profound grief.

It is our task to restrain royal youths by reason placed before them, since those who, while desiring evil, cannot restrain the boldness of their will, truly perceive that we disapprove of such conduct in ourselves [others: in you]. Let the elders be respected, even though they burn with the vigor of flourishing age. Let them know that we are adversaries of their disagreements, and that we wish to pursue the course by which neither side may go beyond its proper bounds. For it is fitting that we speak harsh words, lest our kinsmen should have to reach the extreme.

And therefore we believe that So-and-so and So-and-so should be sent as envoys to your fraternity, so that, if it seems good to our son Alaric, we may send them to the king of the Franks together with the peoples allied with us; in order that the cause at issue between them may be reasonably cut short through the mediation of friends. For it is fitting that such great and powerful kings should not seek lamentable quarrels with one another, so that they may wound us also through their own misfortunes.

Therefore let your fraternity, joining your efforts with mine, strive to restore their harmony. No one can believe that they have come to these battles without our approval, unless it becomes entirely clear that, lest they come to conflict, these struggles are rather ours. We have also entrusted certain matters to be conveyed to you in the speech of the bearers of this letter, so that your prudence may arrange everything as it customarily does, with God’s help, and complete what it is accustomed to consider with the greatest diligence.

## LETTER III. TO THE KINGS OF THE HERULI, THE GUARNI, AND THE THURINGI. KING THEODORICUS.

He urges them to send envoys, together with their own and Gundibad’s, to Clovis, so that he may either restrain his expedition against the Visigoths and seek the laws of nations, or know that he will suffer attacks from all.

[Col. 0576C]

The agreement of all ought always to pursue pride, which is forever hateful to the Divinity. For whoever wishes to overthrow a renowned people through voluntary injustice is not intending to preserve justice toward the others. It is a most evil practice to despise truth. A man believes that everything yields to him if he happens to overcome an arrogant opponent in an abominable conflict.

Therefore you, whom the strength of conscience exalts and consideration of detestable presumption inflames, send your envoys, together with mine and those of our brother King Gundibad, to the king of the Franks, Luduin [edition: Ludovicum], so that he may either restrain himself from conflict with the Visigoths in view of the considered demands of equity and seek the laws of nations, or suffer the attack of all who judge that the arbitration of so many men must not be despised. What more does he seek when absolute justice is being offered to him?

I shall plainly say what I think: whoever wishes to act without law is preparing to shake the kingdoms of all. But it is better that a harmful undertaking be checked at the outset, so that what might have been an individual conflict may be brought to completion without the labor of all. Recall the goodwill of the elder Euric [edition: Henricus], how many gifts he always gave you, whenever he held back the impending wars of neighboring peoples from you. Return gratitude to his son, although you acknowledge that he has been appointed for your advantage. For if he should gain the upper hand over so great a kingdom, he will undoubtedly presume to attack you.

Therefore, after greeting your excellence in a letter, through our envoys, So-and-so and So-and-so, the bearers of this letter, we have entrusted certain matters to be said to you in person, so that you who follow what we have arranged may, with God’s help, be united in one agreement; and so that you may act externally to ensure that you are not able to fight within your own provinces.

## LETTER IV. TO LUDUIN, KING OF THE FRANKS. KING THEODORICUS.

He urges him not to prepare war against Alaric until their dispute has been settled through the mediation of friends; and threatens that he and his friends will take up arms against anyone who disregards this warning. For this reason he sends envoys to both sides.

[Col. 0577B]

The divine powers have wished the bonds of kinship between kings to become so firmly united that through their conciliatory spirit the desired peace of peoples may arise. For this is sacred, and must not be violated by any disturbance. For in whom can confidence be placed as hostages, if no trust is placed in their affections? The lords are joined by close relationship, so that divided nations may rejoice in a similar will, and, as though united through channels of concord, the wishes of peoples may be joined together.

Since this is so, we are astonished that your spirits have been so aroused by minor causes that you wish to undertake the harshest conflict with our son King Alaric, so that many who fear you may rejoice at your struggle. You are both kings of great nations; you are both flourishing in age. You do not lightly shake your kingdoms if, having given freedom to the parties, you engage in conflict. May your courage not become an unexpected disaster for your country, for it is a grave reproach to kings when the peoples suffer a serious ruin over trivial causes.

I shall say freely, I shall say affectionately, what I think: it is an impatient spirit to move immediately to arms at the first embassy. What is sought should be obtained from chosen judges appointed by your ancestors. For between such men, and those whom you wish to make mediators [manuscript R: to those], it is pleasing to grant this role.

What opinion could you yourselves form of us if you learned that we had abandoned your intentions? Far be that conflict in which one of you might be destroyed by being brought low. Cast aside the sword, you who wish to fight to my disgrace. By the right of a father, and as one who loves you, I threaten you. He shall have us and our friends as adversaries who—something we do not believe—judges such warnings unworthy of attention.

Therefore we have thought it most appropriate to send our envoys, So-and-so and So-and-so, to your excellence. Through them we have also sent our written message to your brother, our son, King Alaric, so that alien malice may in no way sow scandals between you; rather, remaining at peace, you should bring to a conciliatory conclusion, through the mediation of friends, whatever exists between you.

Through them we have also ordered certain matters to be said to you in person, so that the peoples who flourished in long peace under your ancestors should not be devastated by sudden upheaval. You ought to trust the man whom you recognize to be favorable to your interests, since one who wishes to cast another into precipitous disasters plainly does not advise him faithfully.

## LETTER V. TO IMPORTUNUS, AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, PATRICIAN. KING THEODORICUS.

He praises Importunus together with his father and uncle, and grants him the insignia of the patriciate in recognition of his outstanding merits.

[Col. 0578A]

If only nobility adorned you, or if you possessed distinction merely through the praise of your merits, we might perhaps weigh the honors to be conferred with a reasonable delay, lest great things become cheap when everything is poured out at once. But now, since all virtues accompany you in full array, and you do not lack anything that is praised in others, it is fitting for our justice that, since you have displayed abundant merits, the imperial munificence should fill you most generously.

For you do not follow here the order of advancement that is common to many: gradual promotion is considered a mark of ordinary virtue, when what is prepared with levity is recognized only after a tiresome delay. Your prosperity rises, as it were, by a leap, and only perfection is sought from you, since many virtues arise together with you.

The dignities of your family have been cultivated through a long age; they have established your household gods in your family’s most renowned dwelling. To pass over ancient ages, which appear to have produced an abundance of exceptional men, you shine conspicuous in the double splendor of your father and uncle. They provided not only an ornament to their family but also glory to the Senate itself. In the present age they were adorned with the customs of antiquity: endowed with goodness, glorious for steadfastness, inclined toward friendship, and difficult to provoke into hatred.

Thus, which is the greatest kind of good fortune, although they were acknowledged to possess great power, they escaped the envy of those who pursued them. Rather, the anxious prayers of the state depended upon them, and public affection for them grew beyond private affection. The Senate followed their judgment, and the crowd followed their purpose. It was necessary for Rome to desire what all seemed to wish; and, in a remarkable outcome of prosperity, the wavering will of the peoples maintained firm authority around them. We judge this, among all dignities, to be the chief gift.

For if the affection of a few is already rightly a glory, what praise can the affection of so great a state possess? Therefore, just as everything unloved seems obscure, so whatever is universally loved is splendid.

Adorned, then, by the praise of so many ancestors and conspicuous for such brilliance of character, receive, after the consular fasces have been completed, the insignia of the patriciate, the full gift of your dignities. Bind your mature hair with the white fillets of honor, since by the praise of your merits you have surpassed the prejudices of age.

For why should rewards come slowly to one for whom so many examples of his family spoke in support? In you, the glory of birth and the glory of life are both chosen; and although you draw much from your ancestors, you have deserved to please through your own qualities. From the very beginning of your life—a rare thing among crowds of flatterers—you have striven to show fidelity to noble virtues.

Therefore the firm trace of your training promises that, having attained glory in your earliest years, you will be increased in flourishing age by glorious honors. Finally, consider with how much exceptional praise your family has adorned you. It would be a kind of fault not to make you what is greatest. From your maturity, better things ought to come in abundance, since we have known you to have done praiseworthy things already in tender youth. For we trust that neither the training of your family nor our judgment concerning you can go astray.

## LETTER VI. TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME. KING THEODORICUS.

He extols the Roman Senate, just as he had extolled Importunus, whom he had raised to the dignity of the patriciate, and strongly commends him to the Senate.

[Col. 0579A]

It is indeed pleasing to us, Conscript Fathers, to advance new persons to the heights of honor. It delights us to insert men of foreign stock into the bosom of liberty, so that the Senate’s hall may put forth varied branches of virtue. Such a multitude adorns the assembly and gives the public face a joyful appearance through the presence of honored men.

But it pleases us much more whenever we restore to office those who are born from the very distinction of the curia, because our examination of you is not anxious while you transmit inherited goods and display merits together with their brightness. Birth itself is already a glory; praise is born together with nobility. For you, the beginning of dignity is the beginning of life. The Senate’s most exalted honor is born with you, though one reaches it only in mature years.

Although we judge all this truthfully of you all, so that favor may embrace the genius of the senatorial order, the blood of the Decii shines especially in the light of our serenity. It has shone with the brilliance of virtue through so many continuous years; and although glory is rare, it is not found to have varied in so long a lineage. Through its own ages, the noble stock produces foremost men. It does not know how to give birth to anything mediocre: as many approved men as born men, and—a difficult thing to achieve—a distinguished succession.

Behold, from one stock there grows a fourfold glory: the honor of citizens, the glory of the family, the increase of the Senate. Although they shine through a common share of merits, you will nevertheless find one whom you can praise for his own qualities.

Certainly look upon the young man who, through the grace of his appearance, pleases even more through the beauty of his mind. His face reflects the glory of his blood; the nature of his spirit is revealed through his countenance; and the serenity of his body wipes away even the clouds of his mind.

Yet the gifts of nature were adorned by the insignia of literature, so that, when the inner chambers of the mind had been polished by the whetstone of the liberal arts, he might shine more brightly [Note: Manuscript Aud.: “since he was eloquent in the great arts, he might please more in the innermost chambers of the mind.”].

In the books of the ancients he came to know the ancient Decii, a noble lineage living on through the benefit of glorious death. Most fortunate indeed is the labor of study to which it has fallen to learn the song of the ancients through one’s parents, and to educate a tender heart from the beginnings of ancestral praise.

It is pleasing to relate how, at that time, the gaze of the entire school was turned toward him as toward a great spectacle. When he listened to his father, the school immediately strained its attention, seeking the heir, so that what it had recognized the author saying it might approve through the son’s likeness. For just as an unworthy posterity denies the praises of an ancient family, so an excellent one confirms the distinguished words spoken of its fathers [others: gifts].

Everything that is read about them was believed, while the living stream of their virtues taught before their eyes the praises of the ancients, in the workshop of the lecture hall, where the flame of intellect glowed anew. He was formed by these examples, but was brought forth even more successfully by the commands of his household.

For, deprived of the support of a husband, his glorious mother undertook the burden of governing; and neither the extensive care of his patrimony nor the guardianship of so many sons could disturb her. She nourished them, increased their estates, and adorned them with good character; and as many young men as she produced for the family, so many consular men did she return to the curia.

Our mind, which searches out character, examined all this; it also investigates the goodness of domestic virtue, so that among private merits it ought to bestow public ornaments. Therefore, Conscript Fathers, we have granted the height of the patriciate to the illustrious and magnificent man Importunus, so that your assembly, just as it grows through the fortune of birth, may also be increased through the fasces.

Show favor to the son of such a father; unite your judgments. You possess the character that we approve. You certainly have something for which you may praise yourselves with ingenious commendation if, out of affection for your relations, you make the public judgment favorable; and what is given out of natural affection should be regarded as conferred by our commands.

## LETTER VII. TO JANUARIUS, A VENERABLE MAN, BISHOP OF SALONA. KING THEODORICUS.

He orders him to pay John the price of sixty amphorae of oil that he had received from him for supplying the lamps.

[Col. 0580B]

We indeed command everyone to cultivate and observe justice, but especially those who are raised by divine honors, so that they may become close to heavenly grace while they remain far from earthly greed.

John has therefore approached us with a mournful complaint, alleging that your holiness received from him sixty amphorae of oil for supplying the lamps, and that he now demands that their price be returned to him. It is a good request, provided that nothing contrary is mixed into it. For although justice ought everywhere to be preserved, it is especially necessary in those things that are offered to the divine sight, lest we suppose that God is unaware of their source if He accepts offerings obtained by fraud.

Therefore, if you recognize that the petitioner’s complaint is true, in consideration of the justice that you proclaim under holy law, see that what is justly owed is restored without delay, so that no one may groan that losses have been inflicted upon him by you, when you ought rather to provide assistance.

Therefore take care that, although you are not accustomed to go beyond the bounds in great matters, you may not appear—God forbid—to sin in a small one.

## LETTER VIII. TO VENANTIUS, A SENATOR, CORRECTOR OF LUCANIA AND BRUTTIUM. KING THEODORICUS.

He warns him to complete the appointed periods for the collection of the “twos and threes” assigned to him.

The principle of justice persuades us to demand from each person what is known to have been entrusted to him, and to pursue public funds diligently, lest neglect make the debtor’s burden heavier. For if leniency appears in warnings, contempt must necessarily involve everyone. In a certain sense cruelty arises from mercy if, by neglecting to warn someone, you later become compelled to exact payment from him.

It is useful, therefore, to give warning in advance, since this both removes the opportunity for offenses and leaves no place for unlawful conduct. Accordingly, from the report of the illustrious Count of the Sacred Largesses, we have learned that some time ago, according to ancient custom, the collection of the “twos and threes” [Note: For “twos and threes,” see below, Book VII, formula 20. FORNER.] was assigned to you.

We therefore admonish you by this present statement that, in accordance with the reliability of the accounts [or: the canonical record], you must complete the appointed periods, lest you be compelled to pay from your own resources whatever loss the public treasury may have suffered, since neither was the authority of so great an order respected nor the trust of your promise fulfilled.

## LETTER IX. TO THE OWNERS, DEFENDERS, AND CURIALS RESIDING AT AESTUNA. KING THEODORICUS.

He orders them to arrange for marble columns and unused stones lying about to be transported to the city of Ravenna.

It is indeed our intention to build new structures, but even more to preserve ancient ones, because we can acquire no less praise from things discovered than from things preserved. Therefore we wish to raise modern works without diminishing what came before. For whatever comes through another’s loss is not considered acceptable to our justice.

We have learned, therefore, that in your municipality columns and stones of antiquity, demolished by the hostility of age, are lying unused. Since it achieves nothing to preserve things lying dishonorably, they ought to rise again for renewed ornament before they reveal, through the memory of earlier ages, the pain of their ruin.

Accordingly, by this present authority we decree that, if the report of the informants is true and nothing there is considered suitable for public ornament at present, the aforementioned slabs [or: flat stones], or columns, are in every way to be handed over for transport to the city of Ravenna [editions Niv. and Gam.: collected]. Thus, when the collapsed structures have been restored, their obliterated appearance may once again be made beautiful by art; and what had been darkened by neglect may recover the quality of its ancient brilliance.

## LETTER X. TO FESTUS, AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, PATRICIAN. KING THEODORICUS.

He orders marble from the Pincian house to be transported to Ravenna by the *catabulenses*.

[Col. 0581C]

It is fitting for your prudence to obey the arrangements made for enlarging the royal buildings, since it is characteristic of a most noble citizen to consider the advancement of his country, especially when it is our concern to decree those measures which everyone is known to obey without personal loss.

Therefore, by this present admonition we inform your greatness that the marble known to have been removed from the Pincian house [editions Niv. and Gam.: Pincinian] is to be sent to the city of Ravenna under your direction by the *catabulenses* [Note: See the Theodosian Code, Book XIV, title 3; and below, Book IV, letter 47. Understand the term as derived from *catabulum*, which was a stable for animals serving the public interest, as indicated by a passage of an ancient author on the Roman pontiffs, in the life of Pope Marcellus, in Baronius’s notes on the Roman Martyrology, January 16. JURET.].

We have sent transportation immediately, lest either delay arise in our arrangements or the laborers suffer any losses.

## LETTER XI. TO ARGOLICUS, AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, PREFECT OF THE CITY. KING THEODORICUS.

The urban prefecture is conferred upon him, and excellent admonitions are offered for the worthy exercise of that dignity.

[Col. 0581D]

We desire that the whole day should pass filled with our benefits; we desire our gifts to shine everywhere, because what imperial munificence grants lives forever. For what is more royal than to make someone happy and to provide for him to such an extent that, raised up, he is amazed to have reached it?

Benefits are what exalt kingdoms; and the lord of liberty can continually increase if he strives to enlarge those subject to him. In accordance with this glorious purpose of our gentleness, and with the paternal affection by which we cherish you through the favor of all, in the fourth indiction [that is, in the year 511] we generously bestow upon you the insignia of the urban prefecture, so that a distinguished succession may rejoice in your paternal honors, and whatever deserved to reach our age may prosper under us.

Consider, therefore, how great it is that Rome, white-haired with age, could be entrusted to your beginnings; so that you may appear distinguished in the tribunal of judgment within that most exalted assembly where even to obtain membership is difficult.

Strive, then, to demand from your merits what you recognize that we have bestowed. Flee greed; pursue justice; cherish moderation; despise anger. What could be more pleasing than to have delivered a noble judgment amid that crowd of the great, where so many patrician hearts are summoned to favor, and where a good deed is celebrated by the mouths of the wise?

Virtue is never practiced with greater praise than when Rome is rightly governed. What wealth could you consider more suitable than to maintain the precious purity of your conscience before the eyes of the Senate, and to be captive to no vices before the very bosom of liberty?

We see with what glory the other offices are esteemed. The urban prefect is the dignity of dignities. That distinction cannot tolerate your committing what the noble crowd might fail to notice. Placed in the midst of all, you draw everyone’s gaze to yourself, and the reputation of the people proclaims the judgment of your entire life.

Your studies in literature make it believable to us that you will conceive these principles in your mind and explain them through evident actions, for in literature you learned everything that is fitting and formed your mind for a glorious life through the instruction of learned men.

Let learning, therefore, shun wrongdoing. It is a mark of an unteachable mind to be drawn into vices. A mind built up through books leaves no room for injuries; what is acquired in tender years is preserved in mature age.

Let the deeds of your elders encourage you along the path of right; let the authority of reading admonish you; and finally let the glorious choice of our judgment do so, so that you may receive greater things from us when you are known to have fulfilled what we have entrusted to you.

## LETTER XII. TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME. KING THEODORICUS.

He adorns Argolicus and his ancestors with many praises and expresses his approval of the Senate’s choice of him as urban prefect.

[Col. 0582D]

We love, Conscript Fathers, exceptional dignities arising from our benevolence. The ruler’s mind is the mother of public distinction; and whatever the sovereign’s judgment is, such is the appearance of liberty that it produces. For, if one may say so, it is easier for nature to err than for a prince to form a state unlike himself.

This is why we desire you to shine with perpetual honors, because whatever public opinion says about you is attributed to our instruction. Since you deserve everything exalted, it touches our reputation if anything should perhaps be lacking to you.

Therefore, under favorable auspices, we advance the illustrious Argolicus to the dignity of urban prefect, so that he may be increased by the fasces and you may by no means be deprived of the adornment of so great a judge.

For you know that exceptional men have often emerged from this family. Recall his grandfather, who was advanced and enriched by the honor of a perfected doctrine, whose blameless eloquence the courts admired. Although he abounded in eloquence, he deliberately cultivated the knowledge that a skilled speaker ought to be distinguished by purity [Note: “Eloquence is innocence.” Apuleius, *Apology* 1; and Book VIII, letter 12. JURET.].

Brought to the heights of honor by these merits, he protected the sacred treasuries with faithful custody, while also fulfilling through learning the dignity of the office of *magister* that he had undertaken [Note: “The dignity of the magistracies.” Concerning this, see below, Book X, letter 33. The *magister officiorum*, who was placed in charge of the praetorian soldiers; Zosimus, *History*; Cujacius on the last three books of the Code. FORN.]. He was praised in both respects, so that in each he was believed to be outstanding.

There is also his most noble father, who did not profane the insignia of the *comitiva privatarum* through any bitterness of calumny. Seeking the advantages of reputation, he neglected the increase of money; and—an uncommon example of virtue—he practiced self-restraint in an age when the crime of greed was not yet recognized.

For the purpose of the prince makes judges either neglectful or lovers of virtue. Having set forth so many proofs of his lineage [edition: promises], let us trust good things of a noble man, because a praiseworthy stock preserves its origin and faithfully transmits to its descendants what it has earned within itself through glorious inheritance.

Therefore, Conscript Fathers, show favor to the man consecrated by your dignities, so that you may arouse in those whom we summon by the example of our gifts a greater desire for virtue.

## LETTER XIII. TO SUNHIVADUS, A SENATOR. KING THEODORICUS.

He praises him and orders him to visit Samnium in order to settle disputes between Romans and Goths.

[Col. 0583C]

The long service of your labors and the many proofs of your tested fidelity provide us with this judgment: you who have governed your own passions should now be preferred over the character of others; and you should provide discipline to a province, since as a private man you loved self-restraint. For only one who has striven to conduct himself with dignity can govern others well.

Moved, therefore, by the supplication of the Samnites, we believe that relief can be brought to those in difficulty by this remedy, if we order your dignity to proceed to settle their disputes [others: to undertake their affairs]. Therefore strive now to answer so good a judgment with a praiseworthy performance, and make yourself fit for our commands, since until now you have pleased us by your own initiative.

Enter the province of Samnium. If a dispute exists between a Roman and a Goth, or if some matter has arisen between a Goth and Romans, you shall define it by consideration of the laws. We do not permit those whom we wish to protect with one will to live under indiscriminate justice. Therefore pronounce jointly what is in accord with justice, for one who considers pure equity knows no persons.

## LETTER XIV. TO AURIGENUS, A VENERABLE MAN, BISHOP. KING THEODORICUS.

He writes that Julianus has complained that his wife, or property, was taken away by the bishop’s subjects; and he orders that, if the matter is as alleged, the guilty party be punished at once.

[Col. 0584A]

Although we trust that all crimes displease your judgment, we especially expect you to detest [manuscript Aud.: to implore against] whatever attacks the marital affection of the marriage bed. For with what feelings can one receive from the continent what is condemned even by the detestation of laypeople?

Julianus has therefore complained to us in a tearful petition that his wife, or property, was seized by the unjust usurpation of your men. Therefore, if you recognize the petitioner’s claim to be true, and the person properly accused cannot clear himself, cut off the author of the deed without any delay.

For when evil persists, it increases; and accelerated correction is a good remedy for sin.

## LETTER XV. TO THEODAHAD [Note: He later obtained the Gothic kingdom; a letter of Theodoricus to him is preserved as letter 39 of the following book. FORN.], A SENATOR. KING THEODORICUS.

He commits to his judgment for examination a man who had avoided the judgment of Sona.

The injury is ours when justice is harmed, because we rightly take personally violations of the things we love. Therefore we do not permit that matter to remain unpunished which is known to have been undertaken in contempt of our command. For what presumption would not deserve punishment if it dared to despise the reverence owed to a sacred order?

Accordingly, we entrust to your examination the man whom we previously ordered to appear before the illustrious Sona, but who withdrew through long-established cunning [edition Ac.: discovered cunning]. Hear him, so that you may bring to an end the dispute that has been prolonged by punishable machination.

Therefore provide careful attention to the hearing, so that your reputation for justice may grow, since matters of doubtful dispute are entrusted to you as a remedy for those bringing suit.

## LETTER XVI. TO GEMELLUS, A SENATOR. KING THEODORICUS.

He is sent to Gaul to perform the office of the prefects’ vicar, and many useful admonitions are given to him.

A judgment is firm when it is supported by example, and no room for uncertainty remains where credible experience gives support. We have tested your effectiveness through various degrees of service; yet you have earned no lesser favor, having been equally approved in diverse actions.

For this reason, at the present time our authority sends you as vicar of the prefects to Gaul, which, with God’s help, has been subjected to us [edition: made subject; manuscript R: substituted] [Note: Theodoricus freed Gaul from Frankish oppression during the consulship of Venantius and Importunus, as our Cassiodorus himself records in the *Consular Fasti*. FORNER.], so that you may govern it.

Therefore consider what judgment we appear to hold of you when you are sent to correct those peoples whom we believe to have been specially acquired for us by our renown. Glory is dear to a prince; and one must necessarily be more concerned about those from whom one feels that an increase of triumphs has come.

Carry out our instructions, then, if you wish our judgment of you to advance. Do not love turbulence; avoid greed, so that the exhausted province may receive such a judge as it recognizes to have been sent by a Roman prince.

It desires outstanding men, constrained by its own disasters. Make it rejoice that it was conquered. Let it feel nothing like what it suffered when it sought Rome. Let all sadness arising from calamity depart. At last let its clouded face be brightened. Now it is fitting for it to rejoice, since it has attained its wishes.

## LETTER XVII. TO ALL THE PROVINCIALS OF GAUL. KING THEODORICUS.

He announces that he has sent Gemellus as vicar of the prefects to govern their province, and orders them to obey his commands.

[Col. 0585B]

It is fitting to obey the Roman custom, to which you have been restored after long ages; for a return is welcome where it is clear that your ancestors made progress. And therefore, recalled to your ancient freedom by God’s favor, clothe yourselves in toga-clad customs [that is, Roman customs] [Note: [Col. 0585D] Toga-clad customs are opposed to barbarian ones. The Roman toga is mentioned in book 32, but also in *Digest*, “On Fiscal Law,” title 2, even if the reading is accepted; Pliny, book IV of the *Letters*, “Have you heard?”; Cicero, *For Cornelius Balbus*. Foreigners, barbarians, and those against whom water and fire have been forbidden lack the use of the toga. Paul, book III, title 4. Macrobius notes that the Romans wore a belt, book VI, chapter 5 of the *Saturnalia*. Below, Cassiodorus likewise says in the formula for the urban prefect: “We have adorned you with the dress of toga-clad dignity, so that, clothed in Romulus’ garment, you ought to aspire to Roman laws.” FORNER.]; strip off barbarism; cast away cruelty of mind. For under the equity of our age [Note: [Col. 0585D] That it was customary for rulers to celebrate the character, happiness, customs, laws, and finally the praises of their own age is shown by the frequent mention of this in their constitutions. Above, book I, letter 6: “the blessedness of the age”; book II, letter 13: “the justice of our age”; Justinian: “The character of our age does not permit it,” final title, *On Covenants*. “Detractor of our age,” single title, *If Anyone Should Speak Ill of the Emperor*. In relation to this law, the Greek scholiast of the *Basilica*, book LX, gathers that one who condemns the emperor’s age appears to curse the emperor himself. I shall discuss this institution at some point in the *Selection*, whose publication I shall undertake shortly. FORNER.] it is not fitting for you to live by foreign customs.

Therefore, considering your needs with the gentleness innate in us—may this statement have a happy outcome—we have deemed it appropriate to send the distinguished man Gemellus, vicarius of the prefects, whose loyalty and industry we have found commendable, to put your province in order; trusting that he can do nothing wrong, since he understands that those who do wrong are gravely displeasing to us. Accordingly, obey his arrangements, issued on the basis of our commands, because we believe that he will decree what benefits you.

Gradually recover truthful [ed., legal] customs. Let no innovation that is honorable be burdensome. For what could be happier than for people to rely solely upon the laws and fear no other accidents? Public laws are the surest consolations of human life, aids to the weak, and restraints upon the powerful. Love that from which both security comes and conscience advances.

Heathenism indeed lives according to its own pleasure: there the person who can have whatever pleases him more readily meets his own death. Now, secure, display the wealth of your ancestors. Let goods hidden away through long neglect be brought into the light; for a person is noble in proportion as he shines both through honorable conduct and through conspicuous wealth.

For this reason we have sent you a vicarius of the prefectures, [Col. 0585D] so that, together with such dignity, we may appear to have appointed a civil governor. Enjoy what you used only to hear about. Understand that people are preferred not so much by bodily strength as by reason, and that those rightly increase in standing who can render justice to others.

## LETTER XVIII. TO GEMELLUS, A SENATORIAL MAN: KING THEODORIC

He orders that Magnus, who had returned from the enemy’s side to his native land, be restored without any delay to his property.

[Col. 0586A]

Property deserves to belong to those who appear to have chosen our clemency, so that we may demonstrate by their own advancement that we have judged them truly. And if it is fitting that such persons be provided for by public generosity, how much more is it right that they possess what is shown to be the common gift of justice?

Accordingly, the distinguished Magnus, having rejected association with the enemy and remembering where he was born, returned to the Roman empire; it is said that his absence caused his property to be lost. Therefore by this present command we decree that, whether in fields, urban or rural slaves, or anything else belonging to him that may in any way now be proved lost, he shall recover it without delay, retaining by our authority the full right of ownership that he possessed. Nor do we wish him to endure any legal dispute concerning things belonging to him by ancient possession, since it is also the purpose of our policy to grant new benefits.

## LETTER XIX, OR *COMMONITORIUM*. TO DANIEL: KING THEODORIC

This highly skilled marble-worker is granted authority to distribute marble sarcophagi in the city of Ravenna for the burial of the dead.

It is fitting that we provide for the rightful interests of those serving our palace, since public labor ought to be productive; and although services are rightly owed to us without payment, we should nevertheless encourage service through moderate profits.

Therefore, pleased by your skill in your craft, which you diligently practice in quarrying and decorating marble, we grant by this present authority that, under your reasonable administration, the sarcophagi distributed in the city of Ravenna for the burial of the dead may be allocated. Through their benefit, corpses are buried above ground, a considerable consolation to the bereaved, since souls alone depart from the intercourse of this world, while bodies do not abandon those dear ones who once survived them.

Thus, for some people, grief becomes a source of profit, and through the pitiable condition of their hopes the merchants’ gain from human death increases. Nevertheless, there must be no injustice in imposing a price on this occasion, lest we be forced, amid the harsh burdens of mourning, to lament the loss of the poor’s resources; and lest those constrained by impious devotion be driven either to destroy their patrimonies for the dead or, in grief, to cast their beloved bodies into the cheapest graves.

Let there be moderation in what the petitioners demand, since compassion itself makes a case for the purchasers [ed., moderation makes a case for those who deserve it]. For the person upon whom more appears to be imposed in fulfillment of a pious duty ought to be harmed less.

## LETTER XX. TO GRIMODA, SAJO, AND FERROCINCTUS, APPARITOR [Note: [Col. 0587D] Manuscript Aud., Tranvilae. Manuscripts R., Gruvialae; Cuj. and Forn., Trimulae.]: KING THEODORIC

He decrees that, if Faustus either burdened with titles or held by private usurpation anything that Castorius possessed, the usurper must immediately return the estate to Castorius, together with another of equal value, under the pressure of those officials.

[Col. 0587A]

Among the glorious concerns of the state that, with God’s help, we continually turn over in our thoughts, our heart is concerned with relieving the humble, so that we may raise an obstacle of our compassion against the power of the proud, and so that no act of audacity may prevail among us whose purpose is to trample upon the proud.

Moved, therefore, by the pitiable misfortune of Castorius, whom the deadly hostility of various persons has oppressed until now, we have found an occasion for salutary enactments, so that the aid of our compassion might prove stronger than the unjust cunning of wrongdoers.

Accordingly, by this present authority we decree that, if the magnificent prefect Faustus either burdened with titles anything that Castorius possessed or held it by private usurpation, the usurper must immediately return the estate to him, together with another of equal worth [Note: [Col. 0587D] No one is unaware that under civil law robbers are liable for three times the value. Against a usurper who invades another’s fields, an action for double value is available, according to Constantine’s constitution addressed to Bassus, which appears in Julius Frontinus, *On the Boundaries of Lands*, and in title 4, final law, *On Boundaries*. FORNER.], when you bring pressure to bear, so that we may provide a remedy of our compassion to one afflicted by cruel losses.

If, however, anyone is found implicated in this wrongdoing and unable to meet what has been ordered, bring him back to us bound in chains, so that the penalty may be exacted when the means available do not suffice for punishment. Let the impulse of an unjust mind now be quieted by such disgrace, lest he appear to have persecuted not so much Castorius as our own purpose.

But if thereafter that notorious agent should attempt to harm the often-mentioned Castorius on any pretext, let him immediately be struck with a fine of fifty pounds of gold. Let it be a greater torment for him to see unharmed the man whom he wished to see afflicted.

Here is an act that immediately restrains and corrects all powers: a prefect of the praetorium has not been permitted to rage in harming a humble man; and the power to harm the unfortunate is taken away from one whom we raise up. Let all understand how much we delight in justice, since we also wish to diminish the power of our judges, so that we may increase the benefits of a good conscience.

## LETTER XXI. TO FAUSTUS, AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN: KING THEODORIC

He grants him a four-month leave of absence from the city of Rome to withdraw to the province for his own benefit.

[Col. 0587D]

It is a custom of human life that things changed are enjoyed more [Ed. Ac. and old codex For., “understood”]; and although exceptional things may be kept in use, everything that satisfies eventually produces disgust.

Therefore, since you have continually remained within the sacred [that is, Roman] walls [Col. 0588A], you request that, for arranging your own affairs, leave of absence be granted to you—not because you are weary of so distinguished a residence, but because a return becomes sweeter when renewed.

Accordingly, our compassion grants your illustrious greatness four months’ leave to withdraw to the province, on condition that, when they have elapsed, you hasten back to your own household gods, so that Roman habitation—which we wish to fill with a numerous gathering—may not, through the withdrawal of its inhabitants, become less densely populated in that world-renowned city [Note: [Col. 0587D] Florus calls Rhodes “most renowned” in book II, chapter 7, as Pighius restored the reading from the *V.C.* in Valerius Maximus, book IV, chapter 8. Nevertheless, Doctor Juretus says that his interpretation ought to be rejected.].

We also judge this most suitable for you, since a Roman senator may elsewhere regret being detained. Where is that ancestral grace? Where can such beauty of walls be contemplated? It is a kind of sacrilege for one who can dwell in Rome, with his household established there, to make Rome absent from himself for too long.

## LETTER XXII. TO ARTEMIDORUS, AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN: KING THEODORIC

He summons him to court and to his company.

[Col. 0588B]

It is fitting for us to adorn our retinue with noble men, so that their desire may be fulfilled and our service be enhanced by the merits of individuals.

Therefore, by this official summons, we call your greatness to our presence, which we do not doubt is most welcome to you, so that you, who have spent many years with us, may be captivated by the sweetness of our presence. For the person who can at least see the ruler favorable hastens toward him. Anyone who is permitted to enjoy our conversation [Note: [Col. 0588D] King Theodoric considers conversation with the emperor a very great privilege, as well as being admitted to his table. On this matter see below, book VI, formula 9, and what we have touched upon in book III, chapter 13 of the *Selections*. FORNER.] believes that he has received divine gifts.

Therefore we do not delay the desire of one whose presence we wish to see. We believe that you will come rejoicing, and we eagerly await you.

## LETTER XXIII. TO COLOSSAEUS, AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND COUNT: KING THEODORIC

He entrusts him with the government of Sirmian Pannonia and instructs him with salutary admonitions for properly performing this office.

[Col. 0588C]

It is gratifying to entrust matters that must be organized to approved men, since the judgment of the chooser rejoices in such persons, and the interests committed to those approved are secure. For just as we desire to be those who [ms. Aud., “what”] please, so we take care that the person who has pleased us may shine.

Therefore, having begun under favorable auspices, proceed to Sirmian Pannonia [Note: [Col. 0588D] Sirmian Pannonia was once the seat of the Goths. Not a few constitutions of the emperors are preserved in the Code as having been issued at Sirmium, as their subscriptions indicate. FORNER.], once the seat of the Goths, girded with the dignity of an illustrious belt of office. Protect the province entrusted to you with arms and regulate it by law, so that the land which recognizes that it happily obeyed our ancestors may joyfully receive its ancient defenders.

You know by what sincerity of conduct you commend yourself to us. Your only way to please us is to imitate what we do. Favor equity [Note: [Col. 0588D] On Gothic justice, see Procopius, *On the Gothic War*. BROSS.]; defend innocence with courage, so that amid the perverse customs of nations [Col. 0589A] you may demonstrate the justice of the Goths [Note: [Col. 0589D] Yet Salvian calls the Gothic people faithless but chaste, book VII, *On Providence*: “among them there are no fornicators, no immoral persons, except Romans.” FORN.]. They have always stood at the center of praise because they both acquired the prudence of the Romans and possessed the courage of nations.

Remove customs that have grown abominably ingrained [others, “that have become unfamiliar”; others, “that have been introduced”] [Note: [Col. 0589D] “Customs ingrained,” below, book VII, formula 2, and above, book I, letter 10. By “custom” understand what is usually paid, namely a tax. Justinian calls them “customary imposts,” title 1, *Digest*, “On Duties and Honors”: τὰς ὠρισμένας συνηθείας, Novels 123 and 128. FORN.]. Let the matter be handled there by words rather than arms. Let it not be an insult to lose a case when a man who disowns another’s property [others, “properly, a repudiator of what belongs to another”] pays the penalty for theft, not with his life; lest a civil action carry off more than wars consume.

Let shields be raised against enemies, not against kinsmen. And lest poverty appear to drive anyone to death, incur for such persons an outlay that is plainly glorious. You will receive from us the richest fruit of gratitude if you can plant a civil policy there; and you will prove worthy of our true judgment if, as a judge, you undergo a loss so that a man otherwise destined to perish may gain life.

Therefore let our custom be implanted in savage minds until the brutal spirit grows accustomed to wishing to live.

## LETTER XXIV. TO ALL BARBARIANS AND ROMANS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT PANNONIA: KING THEODORIC

He orders them to obey Colossaeus and to abhor dueling, following the example of the Goths.

Our providence does not abandon its established purpose when, always attentive to those subject to us, it arranges what will benefit them, so that those who recognize that we have cared for them may be stirred to greater devotion [ms. Aud., “may be brought to the arrangement”].

This is why we have entrusted your government and defense to the illustrious Colossaeus, a man powerful in name and strength, so that one who has hitherto given many proofs of his own courage may rather increase in future deeds.

Therefore, demonstrate now, in his presence, your obedience [that is, compliance; Ed. Ac., “patience”] [Note: [Col. 0590D] “Obedience,” as below, book VII, formula 27; title 1, *Code*, “Those who act under their own jurisdiction.” “Obedience” is also used shortly afterward, as are “services,” in the same sense.
