Some read *parentiam*, title 1, where the common reading is *patientiam*; here, too, Jacobus Cujacius correctly restored the word, as he noted in book I, chapter 6 of the *Observations*. FORN.], which has often been approved, so that whatever he reasonably orders to be done for the benefit of our kingdom may be carried out with commendable devotion. For constancy proves loyalty, and the person who persists in continual service asserts the integrity of his own mind.

Furthermore, we believe that you must be admonished not to rage against one another but against the enemy. Let no trivial matter lead you into extreme dangers. Yield to justice, in which the world rejoices. Why do you resort to single combat when you have no venal judge? Lay down the sword when you have no enemy.

You raise your arm most wickedly against your kinsmen, for whom it is clear that one ought to die gloriously. What need has a man of a tongue if an armed hand conducts his case? Or how can peace be thought to exist if fighting takes place under the guise of civil conduct?

Certainly imitate our Goths, who know how to wage battles abroad and practice moderation at home. Thus we wish you to live, just as, by the Lord’s favor, you see our ancestors flourishing.

## LETTER XXV. TO SIMEON, AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND COUNT: KING THEODORIC

He entrusts him with the office of the *siliquaticum* throughout Dalmatia and orders him to investigate iron-bearing veins; he describes the uses of iron.

We love to place in public service persons conspicuous for the uprightness of their character, so that through the service of the faithful the increase of usefulness to us may grow.

Therefore, having learned your sincerity of mind through distinguished proofs [ms. A., “knowing the distinguished proofs of your sincere mind,” etc.], our administration entrusts to you throughout Dalmatia the office of the *siliquaticum*, which we had lawfully conferred under the guarantee of our lordship, for assessment in the first, second, or third indiction—that is, in A.D. 508, 509, or 510. If, while investigating, you discover any public loss bearing any trace of fraud, it must without doubt be brought into our treasury; for we seek not so much profits as we hasten to discover the character of our subjects.

Furthermore, we order you, by the path of truth, to investigate the iron-bearing veins of the aforesaid Dalmatia, where the softness of the earth produces the hardness of iron and it is refined by fire so that it is transformed into strength. From this, with God’s help, comes the defense of the fatherland; from this the usefulness of the fields is secured, and it is extended in manifold convenience for human uses. It commands even gold and compels the wealthy to serve the poor who are constantly armed.

It is therefore fitting to examine this resource with diligent investigation, through which profits are generated for us and destruction is prepared for our enemies. Be diligent, then, in the aforesaid examination [ms. A., “antefacta”] [Col. 0590C], and measured in public responsibilities, so that our reasonable gain may procure for you an increase in standing.

## LETTER XXVI. TO OSUN, AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND COUNT: KING THEODORIC

He orders him not to deny Simeon the assistance necessary for the tasks for which he was sent to Pannonia.

Although it is part of your prudence to give support to those assigned to public usefulness, our admonition adds further weight, so that the matter may be carried out more securely when our command is treated with reverence.

Accordingly, we have sent the most distinguished Simeon, whose loyalty and devotion have long been known and approved by us, to the province of Dalmatia by our arrangement, to administer the *siliquaticum* and also the ironworks. Do not deny him the assistance he requests [Col. 0590D], so that your greatness may become more commendable to us when it hastens to offer itself to public duties.

## LETTER XXVII. TO JOHN, A SENATORIAL MAN AND CONSULAR OF CAMPANIA: KING THEODORIC

He protects him, already battered by various persecutions, from the prefect of the praetorium, and also urges him to perform the office of the consulship with the utmost fidelity.

[Col. 0591A]

It is the purpose of royal compassion to remove the place of unjust hatred and to restrain the arrogance of armed power through reverence for commands. The offense of a superior is hostile to the humble, since it is converted into praise when vengeance is exacted from ordinary people.

Therefore, after being battered for a long time by varied persecution, you have not without good reason hastened to the remedies of our compassion, asserting that the most eminent prefecture was a source of terror to you, lest private hatreds be satisfied against you [ed., “be joined to you”] through public discipline.

But we, who wish offices granted to people to obey justice, not grief, surround you with our protection against unlawful presumption, so that, when the majesty of the king is brought to bear, the fury of heated minds may be shattered against its own rocks and arrogance may suffer punishment from itself while innocence is protected.

For a judge is called a judge only so long as he is thought just; the name that derives from equity cannot be retained through arrogance.

It remains for you now to fulfill the office of the consulship you have assumed and to devote yourself diligently and loyally to the public interests that your predecessors are known to have administered; and, in proportion as you are protected by us, hasten to obey modesty.

For if you rejoice that you know the prefects of the praetorium have been kept away from injuring you, while you are shown to be subject to them, what do you think you would suffer if you acted wrongly?

## LETTER XXVIII. TO CASSIODORUS, AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND PATRICIAN: KING THEODORIC

He summons him to his retinue, adorned with many praises.

[Col. 0591C]

The sight of those who have taken their place in our minds through glorious actions is always welcome to us, since those who have proved themselves devoted to virtue give us a perpetual pledge of their affection.

Therefore, by this present command, we summon your greatness—approved by us through glorious service—to our retinue, so that you may receive further adornment through royal service and may be exalted by appearing before us.

It is fitting that even you should be sought out, since you have caused our age to be exceptionally praised. You adorned the palaces through the integrity of your conscience; you gave the peoples profound peace. Hence you became known to all, because many do not know you placed in authority [Note: [Col. 0591D] Greek and Cujacius: “because the one who did not wish you placed in authority did not know you.”]; yet those brought before the tribunals saw in you a judge without any fear of harm.

You became more precious to everyone because you could not be bought by any reward [ed. Ac., “price”]. Who would not wish to see such a man, of whom it is clear that we have publicly expressed our gratitude? For although we have attempted to restrain another, we have also praised you, as the palace itself bears witness.

Advance your steps; hasten your arrival. It is fitting that one who knows he can be supported by the ruler should come eagerly.

## LETTER XXIX. TO ARGOLICUS, AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND PREFECT OF THE CITY: KING THEODORIC

He writes that he has granted the patrician Paulinus old warehouses, destroyed by age, so that he may rebuild them and convert them to his own uses.

Who does not know that it is advantageous for us to respond to a petitioner’s request, and that good rulers grow in what they can provide through benevolent generosity? Royal gifts are like seeds: scattered, they grow together into a crop; gathered into one place, they perish.

We therefore wish to distribute gifts among many, so that our benefits may sprout everywhere.

Accordingly, having received the petition of the illustrious and magnificent patrician Paulinus [reading uncertain: some have *actorum*, others *auctorum*, others *ac eorum*], concerning warehouses destroyed by the long passage of time, which are described in the document below and to which antiquity prefixed this and that designation, if they are now shown to be in no way necessary for public use and there is no collected property belonging to the treasury there, we grant them to the aforesaid man, with everything pertaining to them, in unrestricted generosity.

He may use the permission assumed for rebuilding and transmitting them to posterity and arrange them for the benefit of his own interests. For he confers a great gift upon the state who chooses to take up ruined structures for repair, especially in a city where everything deserves to shine when built, lest amid so many splendid walls the ruin of stones appear deformed [Note: [Col. 0591D] “Deformity” signifies the ruin of buildings and walls, as we showed below, book VII, formula 6, in the *Comitiva formarum*. Virgil, book XII of the *Aeneid*: “to kindle war,” “to deform the house,” that is, to overthrow it; title 23, *The Law Orders Guardians*, *Code*, “On the Administration of Guardianship,” orders a guardian to repair the building of his ward when it has been damaged. “Deformed ruins,” titles 4 and 5, *Code*, “On Private Buildings.” Lampridius says that Alexander Severus wished to restore the Theatre of Marcellus and gave money from tax revenues to many cities whose buildings had been disfigured by earthquakes, for the restoration of both private and public works; titles 4 and 16, “Whoever,” *Code*, “On Public Works.” Add what I noted below in the *Comitiva formarum*, book VII, formula 7. FORNER.].

In other cities, structures of lesser brilliance are tolerated [Col. 0592C]; in that city, however, we tolerate nothing even mediocre, since the whole world principally praises it.

## LETTER XXX. TO ARGOLICUS, AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND PREFECT OF THE CITY: KING THEODORIC

He orders him to assist John in repairing the Roman sewers.

The care of the Roman city is always watchful in our minds. For what more worthy matter should we undertake than to raise up its restoration [ms. Aud. and old manuscripts, Forn., “to choose”], since it is known to contain the ornament of our state?

Therefore let your illustrious sublimity know that we have sent the distinguished man John on account of the splendid sewers of the Roman city. They confer such astonishment upon those who see them that they can surpass the marvels of other cities.

There you may see rivers, as though enclosed within hollow mountains, flowing through enormous timbers [Note: [Col. 0592D] Doctor Juretus reads *ligna* in the *V.C.* Thus, in Symphosius’ riddle, chapter “In wood it travels through the middle,” which carried the timbers. Some read “through enormous signs” and others “through enormous timbers.” I suspect *stagna* should be read, on the authority of title 1, *On Navigation in Public Rivers*, and title 2, section “If Anyone Should [Interfere with] a Sewer,” section “Therefore,” *On Anything Done in a Public Place*; and Sallust, book IV of the histories, in Nonius: “The walls of the town were flooded when the sewers overflowed under the opposing tide of the sea.” Varro and Festus hold that *stagnum* is so called because water stands in it. But below, in the following book, letter 50, the phrase is “liquid streams flow.” FORNER. Manuscript Aud. and the edition read *signa*. Manuscript Rem. has *sagimina*, perhaps *signina*, as Doctor Cujacius noted. See book V, letter 38.], and you may see boats, constructed for the purpose, navigating through the rushing waters with no small anxiety, lest, when the torrent plunges downward, they suffer maritime shipwreck.

From this one may gather how great is the singular magnitude of Rome. What city would dare compete with your heights, when even your lowest parts cannot find a likeness?

Therefore we decree that you provide the aforesaid John with the assistance of your office, since we wish public persons to fulfill our arrangements, while removing private hands that plunge too boldly into unlawful acts.

## LETTER XXXI. TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME: KING THEODORIC

He writes that he has sent John to investigate those who had diverted the waterworks’ water for private use and also those who had removed bronze and lead from the decoration of the walls, and he urges the senators to assist him in these matters.

[Col. 0593B]

Although we desire to devote tireless care to our entire state and, with God’s favor, strive to restore everything to its former condition, the Roman city imposes upon us a more urgent concern, since whatever adornment is bestowed upon it is displayed for the common joy.

It has therefore come to our attention, through the report of many—which cannot conceal wrongdoing—that several detestable usurpers have undertaken actions prejudicial to the city of Rome, so that the city to which we most desire to devote our efforts may suffer unjust fraud.

Accordingly, we make our arrangements known to you, since we believe that nothing displeases you more than losses inflicted upon your city.

It is said, then, that for the sake of private advantage, the water of the waterworks [Note: [Col. 0593D] I emend to “the structure of the aqueduct,” on the basis of titles 1 and 6, “All,” *On Aqueducts*, *Code*, book XI; book VII, formula 6, in the formula for the *Comitiva formarum* of the City. *Formae* means a building or structure in title 27, “If Things Are Hanging,” section “If Anything [Pertains to a Sewer],” *Digest*, “On Usufruct”; Ulpian, in Harmenopulus, book II, title 1, discussing buildings constructed from another’s materials, calls them τὰ εἴδη, περὶ τῶν ἐξ ἀλλοτρίας ὕλης γινομένων εἴδων, “the forms of things made from another’s material.” FORN.]—which ought to be protected with the greatest care—has been diverted to operate water mills or irrigate gardens.

It is disgraceful and pitiable that this should occur in that city, although it would scarcely be tolerable even in the countryside. And because we cannot correct the nature of the offense beyond the limits of the law—for while wishing to benefit buildings, we must not destroy the heights of the law—if the owner of this most abominable act is protected by a thirty-year prescription [ed., “presumption”], let him sell his wrongdoing for an appropriate price, so that what inflicts injury upon public structures may no longer be presumed.

But if anything of this kind has been attempted through a recent presumption, let it be removed without hesitation. The general utility must take precedence over the wicked desire of one person, against which even in just cases it will rarely be possible to prevail.

We have also learned that slaves assigned by imperial provision to the service of the waterworks have passed into private ownership. Moreover, bronze—not a small quantity—and lead, which is extremely soft and very easy to steal, are reported to have been removed from the decoration of the walls, though their discoverers consecrated them to the ages. The Thessalian king Ionus discovered bronze, and Midas, ruler of Phrygia, discovered lead.

How pitiable it is that, from the materials by which others acquired a reputation for foresight, we should appear to have incurred a reputation for negligence. Temples and public places, too, which we granted to many petitioners for repair, are said instead to have been given over to destruction.

And since we take pleasure in correcting evil matters, lest silence appear to have granted permission, we have sent the distinguished John, selected by our justice, to investigate the matters mentioned above. When everything has been examined in due order, they will be made clear to us through the service of a report, so that, following the practice of our justice, we may determine what ought to be done in each matter and with the persons who presumed to commit them.

Now apply your efforts and provide assistance, so that you may be seen gladly to complete the investigation which you ought to have requested.

## LETTER XXXII. TO GEMELLUS, A SENATORIAL MAN: KING THEODORIC

He writes that he has remitted the taxes for the people of Arles who had favored the king’s side and, for that reason, had endured a siege and scarcity, for the fourth indiction.

It is clear to us that the services of the faithful do not perish, but receive repayment for what they have expended in sorrow through better fortune.

Therefore, for the people of Arles, who remained loyal to our side and endured the scarcity of a glorious siege [A.D. 511], our clemency remits the fiscal taxes for the fourth indiction, so that in the future they may return to their customary obligation. Thus we may appear to have repaid those who deserved well, and, when circumstances require it, their customary devotion may not be withheld from us.

Let those who preferred to hunger in hardship for our sake be filled in freedom. Let those who faithfully endured sorrow be joyful. It is not fitting for one who could scarcely escape the final catastrophe to be immediately concerned about taxes. We seek these from the peaceful, not from the besieged.

For what could you demand from the master of a field [Note: [Col. 0593D] Saint John Chrysostom attacks tax collectors made more greedy by the ruler’s demands, who exacted from farmers what not even the earth had produced; in comparison with the king and the monks, he calls them “common enemies of the region”: κοινοί τινες πολέμιοι τῆς χώρας, ἅπερ οὐκ ἐξήνεγκεν ἡ γῆ, ταῦτα τοὺς γεωργοὺς εἰσπραττόμενοι, “certain common enemies of the land, exacting from farmers what the earth had not produced.” Symmachus once donated 100,000 modii to the people of Puteoli, book I, letter 39. Julius Caesar, according to Suetonius, relieved tax-farmers seeking remission by one-third of the payment. Relevant here are title 25, “But You Will Add,” section “Force Majeure,” *Digest*, “On Letting and Hiring,” and below, book IV, letter 7, as well as what Bartolus discusses in this sense in title 11, “The Stone,” final section, *Digest*, “On Public Taxes and Confiscations.” FORNER.] whom you know not to have cultivated it?

They have already paid us a precious tax through their loyalty. It is unjust for us to exact worthless money from those who have offered glorious consciences.

## LETTER XXXIII. TO ARGOLICUS, AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND PREFECT OF THE CITY: KING THEODORIC

He orders that Armentarius and his son Superbus enjoy the same privileges as those being brought into the senate.

[Col. 0594D]

It is pleasing to us that our wishes concerning the advancement of the sacred order are succeeding. We rejoice that such men are emerging [Ac., “being chosen”] [Col. 0595A], men worthy to shine with senatorial light, so that praise may be accompanied by the grace of dignity.

For the senate is open to the disciplines of the ancients [ms. Aud., “is pleased by”]; nor can one be judged an outsider who is a student of the liberal arts.

Therefore let your illustrious magnificence arrange that, for the distinguished Armentarius and his son Superbus, there be provided what ancient tradition prescribes concerning those being brought into the senate [Note: [Col. 0595D] The old manuscript has “concerning the revered members of the senate.” Others prefer *referendarios*, “referendaries”; nevertheless *referendos* is also read below, book I, letter 41. Perhaps this is the Aeolic digamma, as in the Etruscan *Pandects*: *fi* for *vi* in *ventorum fi* for *ventorum vi*; *praefuerint* for *praebuerint*, title 9, “If Afterward,” *On the Risk and Sale of a Thing*; *advixa* for *affixa*, title 3, “On Exemptions and Excuses from Public Duties”; *provectae* for *profectae*, title 52, “Of Books,” section “If Anything, Therefore,” *On Legacies*; and the examples noted by Donatus on Terence’s *Andria*: *Dafus*, *cerfus*, *corfus* for *Davus*, *servus*, *corvus*. Quintilian, book I, chapter 13. Thus here *referendos* may have been written for *reverendos* in the same Aeolic manner. Let those who are more sharp-eyed in these minutiae and seek the praise of ingenious rules decide. FORN. Those being brought into the senate, or senate members, must not be confused with the court referendaries; the formulas for both are found below, book VI, formulas 16 and 17. JURET.].

For this Armentarius is commended to us both by the excellence of his parents and by his own intelligence, seeking through merit the dignity he hopes to obtain through petitions. For what could be more fitting than for a profession devoted to learning also to be clothed in senatorial honor?

Thus, among that crowd of learned men, he may dare to express a free opinion, not restrained by fear of incompetence, since the laws of eloquence encourage him to speak. The knowledge of letters is glorious, because its first benefit is to purify a person’s character, and its second is to supply grace of expression; thus, through both benefits, it wonderfully adorns both the silent and the eloquent.

Let them therefore be led into the inner chambers of freedom, praised for their own merit and adorned by our judgment. They will undoubtedly have a most welcome senate, since their art is to make the angry well-disposed, the suspicious pacified, the stern gentle, and the hostile favorable.

What, then, could he not impose upon the senators who has succeeded in bending the mind of a judge? [Note: [Col. 0596D] How great is the power of eloquence is testified by Virgil, book I of the *Aeneid*; Lucan, *To Piso*; Ovid, book XIII of the *Metamorphoses*; and Valerius Flaccus, book IV. BROSS.]

## LETTER XXXIV. TO THE PEOPLE OF MASSILIA: KING THEODORIC

He writes that he has sent Count Marabadus to protect them and orders them to obey him willingly.

[Col. 0595C] It is our policy to assign persons proven in courage and moderation to your administration and protection, so that the condition of the provincials may be relieved and the public interest strengthened under good governors. Accordingly, we have decided to send Count Marabad, whose equity we have found reliable, to the city of Massilia, so that, with God’s help, he may accomplish whatever pertains to your security or welfare; and, mindful of our favor, may take care to uphold justice: let him bring consolation to the humble, oppose the insolent with the severity of his authority, and, finally, suffer no one to be oppressed by unjust presumption; rather, let him compel everyone to what is just, by which our empire always flourishes. Therefore, obey the appointed man willingly in whatever he commands you for the public good, so that your loyalty—already demonstrated by earlier examples—may also be declared by subsequent [Col. 0595D] proofs; for obedience is more welcome when it is maintained through perpetual devotion. We, for our part, intend to repay in due course those whose services we cannot forget.

## LETTER XXXV. KING THEODORIC TO ROMULUS

He confirms whatever Liberius, by royal decree, had granted to him and his mother through a *pictatium*.

[Col. 0596A]

It is fitting that our generosity retain firm constancy, because a ruler’s resolve ought to remain unshaken, and what is known to have been confirmed by our command must not be overturned through the zeal of malicious persons. Therefore, by this present order we decree that whatever the patrician Liberius, acting under our arrangement, is established to have assigned to you and your mother by a *pictatium*—that is, by a tablet or written document—must remain in full force; and you need fear no unreasonable challenge from anyone, since you possess the security of our benefaction.

## LETTER XXXVI. KING THEODORIC TO ARIGERN, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND COUNT

He orders him to admonish Venantius to send a properly instructed representative to court, who will be able to answer before the judges appointed by the king concerning Firminus’s claims.

[Col. 0596B]

It is the purpose of our clemency not to deny a hearing to pitiable tears, especially since it is our custom to refer everything to the laws, so that the complainant may obtain a result and the defendant may not complain that he has suffered any prejudice. Accordingly, Firminus [edition: Firmius] says that he has a dispute with the magnificent patrician Venantius, and that Venantius has frequently disregarded his claims. And because power is always suspect in legal cases [Note: Cicero, at the beginning of the speech *For Publius Quinctius*. Juret.], since a person is believed to want whatever he is judged capable of doing, we order you, with due respect for the aforesaid man, to admonish him to promise that he will send a properly instructed [Col. 0596C] representative to our court under a lawful guarantee, who will be able to answer his claims before the judges delegated by our authority [manuscript Aud.: “by our admonition”; Ac.: “by the judgment of your authority”]. The plaintiff [others: author] will receive the penalty for his audacity if his claim against the magnificent man proves false.

## LETTER XXXVII. KING THEODORIC TO PETER, BISHOP

He orders him to restore the portion of property he was holding to Germanus, if Germanus is the legitimate son of Thomatis; but if he refuses, he wishes the case to be summoned before the court.

If it is appropriate for your Blessedness to intervene in the causes of others, so that through you the clamor of disputants may subside, how much more ought that which concerns you, as the parties responsible, to be referred to you? Therefore let your Holiness know that Germanus has approached us with a sorrowful petition. He asserts that he is the legitimate son of the late Thomatis, saying that a portion of his father’s property is being held by you, although it belongs to him by law. If this petition is supported by truth, and it proves that his father’s property belongs to him by right [others: “if you prove”], then, after justice has been considered, let what is owed be given to the petitioner, whom you admonish, without the loss occasioned by prolonged delay; for the nature of your cases ought to be settled by you as judges, since justice is more properly to be expected from you than imposed upon you. But if your judgment does not settle this case equitably, know that the petitioner’s complaint will be brought before our hearing. For you yourselves teach that the voices of the poor ought not to be neglected, since justice may accompany them.

## LETTER XXXVIII. KING THEODORIC TO VUANDIL

He orders him to ensure that Avenio suffers no violence from the army.

Although it is clearly the desire of our clemency that civil and moderate conduct prevail everywhere, we especially wish matters to be well managed in the Gallic regions, where recent devastation does not bring injury and where the very beginnings ought to establish the reputation of our name. For the protected security of subjects spreads the ruler’s reputation far and wide; and wherever an army is sent, it should be regarded as sent chiefly not to burden but to defend. Therefore, by this present authority, we delegate that you suffer no violence to be done at Avenio, where you reside [editions Niv. and Gam.: “which belongs to the king”]. Let our army live peaceably with the Romans; let the defense assigned to them benefit them; and do not allow our men to inflict anything upon those whom we are striving to free from hostile oppression.

## LETTER XXXIX. KING THEODORIC TO FELIX, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND CONSUL

He orders him to grant the charioteers of Milan what ancient custom had allowed.

[Col. 0597C]

Equity persuades us to preserve the ancient custom for those who provide public amusement, especially when it comes from a consul, whose policy is understood to be that he should be praised for generosity, lest his dignity appear to promise one thing while the senator wishes to accomplish another. Therefore, under the reputation of generosity, it is not fitting to be found miserly, since the obscurity of stinginess casts a shadow over the consul’s public reputation. Accordingly, let your Illustrious Magnificence know that the Milanese charioteers have approached us, saying that in your time they have been deprived of what ancient custom had granted them, although generosity displayed at the proper time has the force of law. [Col. 0597D] Therefore, if their assertions are not damaged by falsehood [manuscript Aud.: “are supported”], it is fitting that your Sublimity follow antiquity, which, by a kind of privilege of its own, demands as something owed what is granted. Nor is it permitted to deny what you recognize yourself to be granting in accordance with ancient custom.

## LETTER XL. KING THEODORIC TO ALL PROVINCIALS ESTABLISHED IN GAUL

After the provincials of Gaul had been devastated by the enemy, he takes account of their injury and remits their taxes, but on condition that they contribute something toward military expenses from whatever has remained untouched.

[Col. 0598A]

Although the multitude of our concerns occupied our mind and, with customary diligence, we considered the various regions of the kingdom, we nevertheless hastened to examine remedies for your welfare; for in our conscience it is a form of injury to delay what will be beneficial, and we cannot consider it pleasing when something agreeable has been suspended by unwelcome delay. For when treatment is postponed, disease is allowed to rage as it grows worse.

Since you have been devastated by enemy savagery, know that, in proportion to your injury, the tax obligation has been remitted for the fourth indiction—that is, in the year of Christ 511—for we do not rejoice in demanding what a sorrowful taxpayer is known to offer. Nevertheless, let military expenses be supported from those resources which are evidently untouched, because devotion ought not wholly to abandon those whom it recognizes as laboring on its behalf. A defender is ineffective when fasting, and courage supplies no boldness when strength has been deprived of bodily power.

## LETTER XLI. KING THEODORIC TO GEMELLUS, SENATOR

He decrees that grain for military expenses at the forts established above the Druentia be transported from the warehouses of Massilia at common expense.

Everything arranged by an equitable order becomes tolerable, because when a burden is divided through common participation, it is certain not to weigh heavily upon subjects. The final portion returns to each individual, while the total burden encompasses everyone.

The grain which, for military expenses, our foresight sent from Italy, so that the province would not be harmed by providing such supplies, is evidently to be transported from the warehouses of Massilia to the forts established above the Druentia. Therefore we order that the task of transporting the aforesaid grain be undertaken jointly, so that what appears to be assumed by the effort of all may be accomplished quickly.

## LETTER XLII. KING THEODORIC TO ALL PROVINCIALS ESTABLISHED IN GAUL

He announces that he has sent military supplies from Italy to the soldiers, so that Gaul would not be burdened excessively.

Subjects do not need to request remedies from a benevolent ruler [Note: Latinus Pacatus, in his *Life of Theodosius*, reports that the latter’s benefactions were so certain that they seemed already received when he promised them, because he did not weary people’s hopes [Col. 0598D] or employ an art of difficulty in granting gifts. Hence Arcadius and Honorius boast in book 2 of the *Theodosian Code*, *On the infirmity of those things which are under a tyrant*, where the emperor declares that he voluntarily offers benefits to those who do not expect them. Bross.], since humanity precedes supplication, and in a remarkable way requests come after gifts have been granted.

Recently, moved by justice, we had ordered that some portion of the province which had remained unharmed should provide sustenance for our Goths. But although it is always permissible to judge a ruler by his humanity—provided that what has been changed for the sake of a benefit is not considered a fault of inconsistency—and so that landowners would not be burdened by an excessive levy, we have sent military expenses from Italy, so that the army dispatched for your defense might be fed by our generosity and the province might feel only the assistance of so great a host. We have also sent the commanders and officers a sufficient quantity of money, so that the supplies which could not be transported might be purchased there without anyone’s loss; for we did not wish to impose upon our levy even those things which, as we believe, you were able to provide.

## LETTER XLIII. KING THEODORIC TO UNIGIS, SPATHARIUS

He orders that, when the army enters Gaul, slaves who have gone over to others be restored to their former masters.

We take pleasure that those whom we wish to defend by arms live according to Roman law; nor is our concern for moral matters less than it may be for wars. For what benefit is there in removing confused barbarians unless one lives according to the laws?

Therefore, when, with God’s favor, our army enters Gaul, if any slaves evading servitude [Col. 0599B] have gone over to others than those to whom they were understood to belong [edition Niv. and Gam.: “than those to whom they were legally owed”], we order that they be restored without any doubt to their former masters. For rights ought not to be thrown into confusion when justice governs; nor can the defender of freedom favor an abject servitude.

Other kings perhaps seek, in wars, the captives or plunder of conquered cities, or their destruction. Our purpose, with God’s help, is to conquer in such a way that subjects regret having acquired our dominion only so late.

[Note: Theodoric here orders runaway slaves to be restored to their former masters if they have gone to others to whom they did not belong. Moreover, the masters are granted the power to seek and reclaim runaway slaves in *Requirendi*, Code, *On Runaway Slaves*. The ancient writers testify to the great wickedness of slaves, for they regarded the character of slaves with suspicion and believed deceit to be innate in them. Hence Terence:

“Do not do what the common crowd of slaves usually does, deceiving me with tricks.”

In Salvian, *On the Government of God*, we read that vices are assigned to slaves and attributed to them, and that slavish dispositions, already bad in themselves, are made worse by the wickedness of their masters. Thus book 3 of the Code, *On Freedmen and Their Children*, speaks of “receiving the wickedness of a servile disposition.” Arnobius likewise speaks of “overshadowing the flame of wanton love with servile deceits.” Tacitus too says: “Our ancestors regarded the character of slaves with suspicion, even when they were born in the same fields or houses and received sufficient affection from their masters.” There is an old proverb, “We have as many enemies as slaves,” as found in Seneca. Bross.]

## LETTER XLIV. KING THEODORIC TO ALL LANDOWNERS OF ARELATE

He writes that he has sent them a fixed sum of money and provisions for the repair of the walls and ancient towers of Arelate.

Although it is our first duty to restore injured inhabitants and to display a sign of clemency especially toward human beings, our humanity joins both purposes together, so that we may assist the citizens by the remedy of generosity and hasten to restore the ancient walls to proper use. Thus the city’s fortune, which is raised up in its citizens, will also be displayed by the beauty of its buildings.

For the repair of the walls of Arelate and its ancient towers, we have therefore sent a fixed amount of money. We have also ordered provisions to be prepared that may relieve your expenses, so that they may be sent to you when the season of navigation is favorable [Note: Navigation is dangerous during winter; hence the seas are said to be closed. Vegetius, book 4, chapter 3; Code, book 6, *The City*, *On the Duties of Provincial Governors*. Cicero, book 2 of the letters to Quintus, letter 6: “I know that the sea was still closed, but they said that some people had nevertheless come to Ostia.” This passage also illuminates the example discussed by Scaevola in *Qui Romae*, section “Callimachus,” *On Verbal Obligations*. Forner.].

Now revive your spirits, and, encouraged by our promise [edition: “provision,”] maintain hope of future abundance; with divine favor, have confidence, for what is contained in our words is no less than what is contained in our storehouses.

## LETTER XLV. KING THEODORIC TO ARIGERN, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND COUNT

He entrusts to him the investigation of a dispute that arose concerning a certain house between the defenders of the Roman Church and the Jews.

It is consistent with our justice that we do not allow accusations to be brought against benefits that have been granted, and that whatever is concealed by perverse interpretation be brought to light once the cloud of falsehood has been driven away [Note: Valerius, book 3: “to obscure chastity with a cloud of disgrace.” Paulinus, letter to Severus: “to be surrounded by a cloud of earthly cares.” Virgil, book 10 of the *Aeneid*: “the cloud of war.” Paul Orosius: “the mists of war gathering into a great cloud of evils.” Bross.].

The defenders of the most holy Roman Church have therefore complained that Simplicius of blessed memory, now deceased, had solemnly purchased, through documents executed by the acolyte Eufrasius, a house situated in the most sacred City. They assert that the Roman Church possessed it in undisturbed right for many years and transferred it to other uses with secure title. Now, however, there exists a people hardened in Samaritan [manuscripts: “bitter”] superstition, who shamelessly falsely claim, through wicked efforts, that a synagogue had existed there, although the dwellings are shown to have been formed for human uses in a very different manner from the construction described.

Therefore, let your Magnificence investigate the case with careful examination, having demonstrated the justice of your conscience. If you discover that the matters brought forward in complaint are true, decide them after considering equity. For if calumnies must be removed from human affairs, how much more do we believe that what we judge to touch upon an insult to the Divinity must be corrected?

## LETTER XLVI. KING THEODORIC TO ADEODATUS

He changes the extremely harsh penalty to which he had been condemned by the governor of Lucania and Bruttium for the abduction of the grown girl Valeriana into six months’ exile, after which he is restored to his homeland and all his property. He then imposes a penalty of three pounds of gold on violators of such a decree and finally frees from all fear those who had participated in the offense in good faith.

The guilt of an offender is material for a ruler’s principal glory, because if occasions for fault did not arise, clemency would have no place. For what useful order could accomplish anything if moral integrity arranged everything? Arid dryness longs for the benefit of rain that makes the earth wet. Weak health needs the healing hands of physicians. Thus remedies are appropriately applied when one succumbs to weakness.

Accordingly, harsh circumstances must be met with moderation under the praise of justice, so that we neither allow vengeance to exceed the offenses nor permit guilt to mock the laws by remaining unpunished.

In your petition, therefore, you alleged that you, the distinguished Venantius, governor of Lucania and Bruttium [Juret.: that is, corrector], had been crushed by the bitterness of hatred, had long suffered confinement, and had been compelled to confess to the abduction of the grown girl Valeriana; so that it had been more welcome to seek the hope of a swift death than to endure cruel tortures. For amid the ultimate anguishes of one gasping for breath, the preference is to die rather than live, since the detestable experience of punishments drives out the desire for life’s sweetest salvation.

You also added something that justice could hardly tolerate: that when you repeatedly sought the advocacy of defenders, it had been withheld from you, although your adversaries, flourishing in ingenuity, could have bound even an innocent man in the snares of the law.

When this petition effectively entered the mind of our clemency and gradually inclined it toward the rights of mercy, a report sent by the governor of Bruttium intervened and suppressed your private allegation by the tragic force of its own account, denying that a petitioner who falsely pleaded against the public faith should be believed.

Therefore, by our gentleness we soften the severity of the penalty, decreeing that, from the day on which our decision is issued, you shall undergo six months of exile. After our decree, no one shall be permitted, under any interpretation, to charge you with the crime of infamy, since it is lawful for a ruler to wipe away the stains of a damaged reputation.

When this period has been completed and you have been restored to your homeland and all your property [others: “deprived of your homeland and all your property”], you shall have full right to everything you had at the beginning, because we judge that you should not groan under the brand of disgrace, since we wish you to be detained only in temporary exile.

We nevertheless threaten a penalty of three pounds of gold if anyone, whether by opposing or by interpreting otherwise, attempts to violate this present decree. But since we do not wish these provisions to extend to the innocent, lest ignorance appear to have benefited no one, by this present authority we free from fear those who, being unaware, are established to have participated in the same matter at any place or time. The person absent seems similar to one who has no guilty conscience.

## LETTER XLVII. KING THEODORIC TO FAUSTUS, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He writes that he has commuted the death penalty of his colleague’s killer Jovinus, who had taken refuge within the precincts of a church, to exile in the Vulcanian Islands, which he describes.

[Col. 0602A]

Mitigated severity falls within the sphere of clemency; and he punishes under a benefaction who, after considering the penalty with due moderation, has touched it lightly [editions Niv. and Gam.: “bestows it”].

Jovinus, a curial whom the corrector of Lucania and Bruttium reports to us as stained by the shedding of human blood [Note: Lactantius, book 1 and the *Epitome of the Divine Institutes*, Plato, book 9 *On Laws*, Philo, *On Special Laws*, and Porphyry, *On Abstinence from Living Things* (*περὶ τῆς ἀπὸ τῶν ἐμψύχων ἀποχῆς*). When the emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, along with the other defendants, pardoned crimes, they made an exception for the man who, seized by parricidal madness, stained his hand with his own blood, and for anyone stained by the killing of another human being. Code, book 9, *Paschalis*, title 38, *On Pardons*, book 9 of the Theodosian Code. Forner.], because, provoked by the passions of mutual contention, he carried a quarrel in words as far as the wicked death of his colleague, but, conscious of his deed, took refuge within the precincts of a church [Note: Theodosian Code, book 9, title 47, *On Those Who Flee to Churches*; Theodosian Code, book 1, title 12. Liutprand, book 1, chapter 9; book 3, chapters 4 and 6; the final title, *On the Immunity of Churches*. Sozomen, book 8, chapter 7. Socrates, book 13, chapter 5. Forner.], thinking that he could avoid the vengeance prescribed by the laws, we condemn to perpetual exile on the island of Vulcania [Note: The Vulcanian Islands are called the “Vulcanian cauldron” by St. Gregory, *Dialogues*, book 4, chapter 30. Juret.], so that we may appear both to have shown reverence toward the holy temple and not to allow a criminal wholly to escape vengeance, since he did not believe that an innocent person should be spared.

Let him therefore be deprived of his native hearth while destined to live amid destructive fire, where the bowels of the earth do not fail even though they are continually consumed throughout the ages. This earthly flame, which is nourished by the diminution of some body, if it does not consume, is extinguished. A mass of mountain burns continually amid the waves, undiminished; nor is it reduced, although it is understood to be capable of being dissolved, evidently because the inscrutable power of nature restores to the rocks as much growth as the devouring fire has taken from them. For how would the rocks remain intact if fire, continually joined to them, consumed them?

Divine power makes a perpetual wonder out of opposing things, openly restoring through hidden increases what has been consumed, so that it may endure through long ages. Although other mountains too boil with vaporous upheavals, none is regarded as comparable under the same name, because the one called by the name of Vulcan burns more violently.

Let the condemned criminal therefore be sent alive to the aforesaid place. Let him be deprived of the world in which we live, from which he drove another away by a cruel death, since the survivor receives what he inflicted through the event of death. Let him follow the example of the salamander, which often lives in fires. It is constricted by such natural cold that it is tempered amid burning flames. It is a subtle and small animal, akin to slippery worms, clothed in a yellow color. It grants life to the sun, which consumes all mortal things.

The preservers of ancient times [Juret.: perhaps “investigators” or “observers”] report that this island erupted some years ago, its fire bursting forth amid the terror of ruptured waves [Note: Juret: perhaps *imitus*, as Lipsius noted in Gellius, book 27, chapter 10, and Apuleius, p. 165. Thus Cassiodorus, letter 50, book 4, says that Mount Vesuvius “sends forth rivers of ash when it erupts.”], when Hannibal, at the court of Prusias, king of Bithynia, fought against poison within himself so that so great a commander would not fall into the mockery of the Romans. Still more remarkable was the fact that a mountain ignited by such a mass of flames was hidden beneath marine waves, while the fire there continued to live without interruption, although so great a flood appeared to overwhelm it.

## LETTER XLVIII. KING THEODORIC TO ALL GOTHS AND ROMANS RESIDING AROUND THE FORTRESS OF VERUCA

He writes that he has ordered Leodifridus, his *sajo*, to ensure that, under his direction, they build dwellings for themselves in the fortress of Veruca, which he describes.

The provident command of rulers ought to be a source of joy to everyone, when you see us offering what you ought to have sought. For what is more welcome than always to apply caution to human affairs, whether it is necessary or merely not burdensomely superfluous?

Therefore, by this present order, we have instructed our *sajo* Leodifridus that, through his diligence, you should build dwellings for yourselves in the fortress of Veruca, which received its appropriate name from its position. In the middle of the plains there is a rocky mound rising in a circular shape. Its steep sides, stripped of their forests, make the whole mountain resemble a single tower. Its base is narrower than its summit, and above it spreads out like the softest mushroom while remaining supported by its lower part. It is a rampart without battle and a secure refuge under siege: there the enemy dares nothing, nor does the one enclosed fear anything.

The Athesis, a river honored among rivers, flows past it with the purity of a lovely pool, providing both a means of defense and beauty. It is a fortress almost unique in the world, holding the gateways of the province, and is judged all the more outstanding because it stands exposed to savage peoples.

Who would not desire to inhabit this renowned stronghold and marvelous security, which even outsiders take pleasure in visiting? Although, with God’s help, we believe the province secure in our time, it is nevertheless prudent to guard against even those things that are not thought likely to arise.

Fortification must always be undertaken in peacetime [Note: “Let fortification be made in leisure.” Seneca, book 2, letter 18: “In security itself, let the mind prepare itself for difficult things and strengthen itself against the injuries of fortune amid its benefits. The soldier marches in the midst of peace without an enemy, digs a rampart, and grows weary through unnecessary labor, so that he may be able to suffice for what is necessary. If you do not want him to tremble in the crisis itself, exercise him beforehand.” Isocrates advises that voluntary labors be undertaken so that we may endure them more ardently. Forner.], because it is sought at the wrong time when it is judged necessary.

Dippers—water birds whose name derives from their behavior, fellow inhabitants of fish, and naturally foreseeing coming storms—seek dry ground and abandon ponds. Dolphins, fearing the waves of the sea, remain near shallow shores. Sea urchins, which are “fleshy honeycombs,” creatures of stony tenderness, and the saffron-colored delicacies of the rich sea, when they have recognized coming storms and wish to change their location—for they have no confidence in swimming because of the lightness of their bodies—embrace pebbles with which they can become equal in weight and, balanced by a kind of anchoring burden, seek rocks that they do not believe will be battered by the waves.

The birds themselves change their native places at winter’s arrival. Wild animals seek dens according to the season. Should human concern not provide what it may need to seek in adversity? There is nothing in the world from which human affairs are not shaken by change [edition Niv., Ga., Gr. and Cuj.: “by waves”; manuscript R.: “in the world one thing”]. This is why it is called foresight: so that future events may be considered.

## LETTER XLIX. KING THEODORIC TO THE HONORABLE LANDOWNERS, DEFENDERS, AND CURIALES OF THE CITY OF CATANIA

He permits them to use stones that have collapsed from the amphitheater through long neglect for the repair of the city walls.

[Col. 0604A]

Devotion that precedes a good command is desirable and welcome to us; and a request is rightly received with favor when it seeks what we are able to order. For a ruler’s happiness consists in those who serve him desiring what is expedient, since the burden of thought is removed from us when subjects arrange what will benefit themselves.

Therefore, having learned from the tenor of your petition what civic devotion you have undertaken in strengthening the walls, we decree that you have unrestricted permission in this matter. Fear nothing concerning it; rather, you should soon expect the rewards of our gratitude. For your fortification is likewise our strength, and whatever rescues you from uncertainty extends the reputation of our defense.

Accordingly, we grant you permission to use for public purposes only the stones which, as you report, have collapsed from the amphitheater through long neglect and now serve no public ornament except to display shameful ruins, so that what cannot be useful while lying there may rise into the face of the walls. Therefore confidently complete whatever prudence requires for defense and whatever adornment requires for beauty, knowing only this: what you do will be as pleasing to us as the gratitude of your city is thereby elevated.

## LETTER L. KING THEODORIC TO THE PROVINCIALS OF NORICUM

He decrees that the Alemannic oxen, exhausted by the length and hardships of the journey, be exchanged for Noric oxen.

[Col. 0604C]

An arrangement that benefits the giver and gladdens the recipient according to the needs of the moment ought to be received with gratitude. For who could regard something as a burden when the exchange produces an even greater advantage?

Therefore, by the present decree, we establish that you may exchange the oxen of the Alemanni, which appear more valuable because of their great size but have been weakened by the length of the journey, for animals smaller in limb but suitable for labor. Thus their departure will be assisted by healthier animals, while your fields will be furnished with larger cattle. The result is that they acquire animals strong in vigor, while you acquire animals remarkable in appearance; and, something that rarely happens, both parties appear to have received the desired advantages in a single transaction.

## LETTER LI. KING THEODORIC TO FAUSTUS, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He writes that the charioteer Thomatis, frequently victorious in the spectacles, to whom he had granted a just allowance of provisions, is to be supported by a monthly grant; he then speaks at length about the spectacles and the authority of the Augusti and the circus.

The rarer the steadfastness and honorable ambition among actors, the more precious it is when a commendable disposition is displayed in them. For it is dear to a person to discover something praiseworthy where he had not thought he would find anything. Some time ago our deliberation granted the charioteer Thomates, who had come from the regions of the East, a reasonable ration allowance, until we might test his skill and character. But since he is known to hold first place in this contest, and since, having abandoned his homeland, he has chosen to devote his will to fostering the seat of our empire, we have decided to support him with a monthly allowance, lest we continue to make uncertain one whom we know to have chosen Italy’s dominion. For he frequently flew victorious through the mouths of different peoples, carried more by favor than by chariots. He immediately won over a section of the crowd that had inclined toward him, and those whom he himself had made sorrowful, he labored once more to make joyful: at one moment surpassing the charioteers by his skill, at another exceeding them by the speed of his horses [Note: Charioteers, in order to make their horses faster, used magical arts, as may be gathered from Jerome, Hilary, Arnobius, Book I, and Book IX, chapter “On Sorcery.” JURET.].

The frequency of his victories caused him to be called a sorcerer [Note: Here this distinguished charioteer is praised because at one time he surpassed the charioteers by his skill and at another exceeded them by the speed of his horses. From this passage it should be noted that the speed of horses was extraordinarily popular at spectacles, so much so that Capitolinus relates that the emperor Verus made a golden statue of a winged horse of the Green faction; indeed, many of the charioteers hindered their opponents’ horses with demonic imprecations, so that they might more easily drive their own to the course. Arnobius speaks very aptly of the arts of magicians: “For who does not know that they break the affections of households, or unlock without keys what has been closed, or bind mouths in silence, or weaken, spur on, or slow horses in the racecourses?” Ammianus Marcellinus also writes that Apronianus, prefect of the City, condemned to capital punishment the charioteer Hilary, who had been convicted and confessed that, while his son was scarcely yet grown, he had handed him over to a sorcerer who taught the secrets of wicked arts forbidden by the laws, so that he might be assisted by occult means without anyone knowing. BROSS.]. Among such men, attaining crimes of this kind appears to be a great distinction. For it must be attributed to magical perversity whenever victory cannot be ascribed to the merits of the horses.

The spectacle drives out the gravest morals, invites the lightest quarrels, empties out decency, and is a well-watered fountain of disputes. Antiquity indeed held it sacred, but contentious posterity made it a mockery [some copies: slippery]. It is said that Oenomaus first introduced this custom at Elis, a city of Asia; later Romulus displayed it in a rustic fashion to Italy during the rape of the Sabines, before buildings had yet been founded. But Augustus, raising the work to the power of the lord of the world, extended into the valley of Murcia a structure wondrous even to the Romans, so that an immense mass, firmly enclosed by mountains, might contain the tokens of great affairs. They placed twelve gates, corresponding to the twelve signs. These are suddenly opened with equal alignment by ropes lowered from small pillars [Note: See Joseph Scaliger, *Readings on Ausonius*, chapter 14. JURET.], teaching that everything there was, as was thought, governed by a single design, where the image of a head is recognized as operating [Note: Lorippus, Book I *On the Praises of Justice*, p. 75; and Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XVIII, chapters “On the Colors of Horses,” “On the Desultores,” and “On the Obelisk.” See Suetonius, chapter 7, and Pliny, Book IX, letter 6. JURET.].

The colors are distributed in a fourfold division corresponding to the seasons: green is dedicated to the verdant spring, blue to the cloudy winter, rose-red to the fiery summer, and white to the frosty autumn, so that the complete year, passing as if through the twelve signs, might be represented. Thus it came about that the operations of nature were playfully imitated through the arranged imagery of the spectacles. The two-horse chariot was devised in imitation of the moon, and the four-horse chariot in imitation of the sun. The desultory horses, by which the attendants of the circus announce that the released competitors are about to come forth, imitate the heralding speeds of the morning star. Thus it happened that, while they thought they were honoring the stars, they profaned their religion by a playful imitation.

A white line [Note: Pliny, Book XXXV, chapter 17; and Seneca, Book XIX, letter 109. The author calls it a “white line” what Martial calls a “chalked cloth.” See Cedrenus in the *Compendium of History*: there the things the author says about the origin of the cloth are confirmed and illustrated. BROSS.] is extended not far from the gates toward both sides of the track, like a straight rule, so that as the four-horse chariots advanced, the contest might begin there; otherwise, if they always tried to dash past rapidly, they might seem to deprive the crowds of the pleasure of watching. The entire contest is completed in seven turns around the turning-posts [Note: See Suetonius, *Claudius*, chapter 21; and Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XVIII, chapter 30, and chapter 37, “On the Seven Courses.” JURET.], in imitation of the recurring week. The turning-posts themselves have three summits each, corresponding to the zodiacal decans, around which the swift chariots travel in the likeness of the sun’s chariot. The wheels mark the boundaries of East and West. The channel of glassy water gives the image of the sea; hence watery dolphins [Note: Alciatus, *Parerga*, Book V, chapter 27. JURET.] swim through the waters there. The elongated obelisks are also raised toward the height of heaven; but the higher one is dedicated to the sun and the lower to the moon. There the sacred signs of the ancients are indicated in Chaldaean characters, as though in letters.

The central barrier represents the fate of unhappy captives, where Roman commanders, walking above the backs of their enemies, enjoyed the rewards of their labors. The cloth [Note: The author calls the circus spectacle itself *mappa*, a word that is found in the Greek Novels. Suetonius mentions it in *Augustus*, chapter 45, where he speaks of chariot-driving, the Circus Maximus, racing horses, circus events, and the cloth that magistrates formerly dropped as a signal. Figuratively, the driving of horses in the circus was also called *mappa* by synecdoche, and this is understood not only in Justinian but also in Juvenal, *Satires* 12, when he says, “Meanwhile, the spectacles of the Megalesian cloth,” meaning the circus games, which were also called the Great Games and the Megalesian Games; and in Seneca, *On Anger*, Book III, chapter 30, where the cloth provokes bears and lions. BROSS. See the Novel “On Consuls.” GRUL. and CUJ.] which appears to give the signal for the circus races came into use in the following way. When Nero was prolonging his dinner and the crowd, eager for spectacles, was demanding speed as usual, he ordered the cloth with which he used to wipe his hands to be thrown out through the window, thereby giving freedom for the requested contest [some copies: for requesting; others: to the one requesting]. From this it developed that, when the cloth was displayed, it seemed to be a definite promise that circus games would follow [Note: Tertullian also relates this in *On the Spectacles*, in the chapter “On the Show.” So do Servius in his commentary on the *Aeneid* and Isidore, Book XVIII, chapters 24 and 41. JUR.].

The circus takes its name from *circuitus*, “circuit”; *circenses* is as though *circuenses*, because in the primitive antiquity, before spectacles had been brought into the adornment of structures, they were held in green places between swords and rivers [Note: The circus was a public place, “where especially,” as Herodian has it in Book II of his *History*, “the assembled multitude held an assembly,” where the people sat watching the games. Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book V: “And in the middle of the valley there was a circus of the theatre.” There were three circuses at Rome: the Circus Maximus between the Palatine and the Aventine; the Circus Flaminius, also called the Apollinarian; and Nero’s circus in the Vatican. BROSS.]. Nor is it without significance that the arrangement of this contest is completed by twenty-four releases [Note: *Missus*, *missus*: a race consisting of seven circuits, customarily completed by the charioteers in the circus game. Onuphrius Panvinius. The reading should be *missibus* rather than *missus*, according to V. C. [*variae codices?*]. Cassiodorus likewise has twenty-four in his *Chronicle* under Philip, during the consulship of Aemilianus and Aquilinus; so does Varro, *On Agriculture*, Book I, chapter 2. JUR.], so that the hours of day and night might be enclosed by that number. Nor should it be thought meaningless that the circuit around the turning-posts is represented by the raising of eggs: for the action itself, laden with many superstitions, professes through the example of the egg that it will produce something. Hence it is understood that flighty and highly inconstant morals arise from it, which they have adapted to the mothers of birds.

It would be lengthy to run through the other features of the Roman circus in speech, since everything appears to belong to particular explanations. We say only this: it is altogether astonishing that there, above all the other spectacles, the heat of people’s passions is swept away with unthinking intensity [Juret suggests *pravitate*, “depravity,” rather than *gravitate*, “gravity”] (see Cyprian, *On the Spectacles*). The Green faction passes, and part of the people mourns; the Blue faction takes the lead, and the greater crowd of the city is afflicted. Though they accomplish nothing, they hurl insults with fury; though they suffer nothing substantial, they are gravely wounded; and they descend into empty quarrels as though they were struggling over the fate of a homeland in danger. It is rightly believed to have been dedicated to abundant superstition, since it is so clearly cut off from honorable morals.

We support these things because of the necessity of the approaching crowds, whose desire is to gather for such events while they take pleasure in casting away serious thoughts. Reason captivates only a few, and a commendable purpose delights only the rare; the crowd is instead led toward that which is plainly devised for the relaxation of cares. For whatever it regards as pleasurable, it also judges applicable to the happiness of the times. Therefore let us grant expenses, though we should not always give them on the basis of judgment. It is sometimes useful to be foolish, so that we may contain the joys desired by the people.

### LETTER LII. KING THEODORIC TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS CONSULAR

He orders him to choose a land surveyor to settle the dispute that has arisen between Leontius and Paschasius over the boundaries of their cottages.

As we have learned from the excessively spiteful representation of the petitioners, a boundary dispute has arisen between the distinguished men Leontius and Paschasius, so that they believed the boundaries of their cottages were to be defended not by laws but by force. We are therefore surprised that they litigated with such passion over a matter that is evidently defined either by boundary-markers as witnesses, by mountain ridges, by riverbanks, by constructed arches, or by other clear signs. What would these men do if they possessed property in Egypt, where, when the flood of the Nile arrives, its vast torrent washes away the indications of boundaries and leaves the face of the land indistinguishable, since mud is known to cover everything? They ought not even then to have resorted to arms if an awakened dispute could not be settled to their satisfaction.

For this matter is recognized with such care through geometrical figures and the science of the *groma* [Note: Both editions and manuscripts read *grammaticam*, but this is an error; *gromaticam* must be read, for Hyginus once gave a book this title, as Volaterranus testifies, *Urban Commentaries*, Books XVI and XXX. It is a technical term of land surveyors. See Nonius Marcellus under *Grumus* and *Grumae*. JURET. Vossius also corrected this reading in *On Grammatical Art*, p. 3.], just as all speech is contained in letters. Geometry, indeed—as the human race is exceedingly acute and inquisitive—is remembered to have been first invented by the Chaldaeans. Gathering the principles of that discipline in general, they taught that it was applicable to astronomy, music, mechanics, architecture, medicine, the art of calculation, and whatever can be contained by general figures, so that none of these can attain the truest knowledge without it. Afterwards the Egyptians, burning with no less ardor of mind, transferred it, because of the annual increase of the Nile that they undergo in its wished-for inundation, to measuring land and recovering the shapes of boundaries, so that what seemed liable to contentious confusion might be distinguished by art.

Therefore let your Magnificence employ a most skilled land surveyor, who takes his name from his art, so that he may demonstrate by evident proofs everything already distinguished by manifest reasoning. For if that marvelous discipline achieved this, that it distinguished by certain reasoning fields without defined limits, how much more should this man demonstrate everything already proved to be bounded by its own limits? In the time of Augustus the Roman world was divided into estates and registered by census, so that no one might regard as uncertain the possession for which he had undertaken to pay a stated amount of tribute. The author Hyrummetricus reduced this to written doctrine, so that the student may learn by reading what he ought plainly to show with his eyes.

Let the skilled practitioners of this art see what public authority thinks of them. Those disciplines celebrated throughout the world do not possess this honor. You mention arithmetic: it is confined to lecture rooms. Geometry, when it disputes only about heavenly matters, is expounded only to students. Astronomy and music are learned for knowledge alone; but when a dispute over boundaries arises, it is entrusted to the land surveyor, so that the insolence of litigants may be cut short. Thus he is the judge of his art; his court is the deserted fields. You would think a man mad if you saw him walking along twisting paths. For he seeks out the evidence of facts among rough woods and thickets; he does not walk by common right. His textbook is his road; he shows what he says and proves what he has learned. By his footsteps he distinguishes the rights of disputants and, after the manner of a very great river [Note: Rivers too perform the office of assessors, in the opposite direction: Digest 41.1.30, *Ergo*, *Alluvion*. FORNER.], takes away tracts from some and grants fields to others. Therefore, supported by our authority, choose such a man that, after him, the parties may blush to litigate with shameless brow, so that the rights of possessors need not remain confused when they must cultivate their own property.

### LETTER LIII. KING THEODORIC TO APRONIANUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, COUNT OF THE PRIVATE ESTATE

He orders that, if he finds the water-finder who has come to Rome from Africa to be most skilled in this art, he should relieve his poverty with necessary rations and assign him a mechanic to assist him in his work.

From the report of your Magnificence we have learned that a water-finder [Note: Read *aquilegem*. For Seneca, *Natural Questions*, Book III, chapter 15, and Pliny, Book X, letter 38, call them *aquileges*. JUR.] has come to Rome from Africa, where the art itself has always been cultivated with great zeal because of the dryness of the country. He can provide running vein-water [Note: That is, water flowing from a perpetual vein. JUR. Others read *vernatiles*.] in dry places, so that by his service he may make habitable places parched by excessive barrenness. Know that this has pleased us, so that the craft set forth in the books of our ancestors may in our time receive approval.

By signs of green plants and the height of trees he suitably infers the neighborhood of waters. For in soils beneath which sweet moisture lies not far below, the luxuriance of certain shoots always flourishes: such as the water-reed, the slender cane, the vigorous bramble, the pliant willow [manuscripts Gr. and Cuj.: *laeta*, “lush”], the green poplar, and the remaining kinds of trees which nevertheless luxuriate beyond their natural condition in fortunate height. There are other signs of this art as well. When night comes, dry wool is laid upon ground already selected and left covered by an unbaked earthen pot; then, if the nearness of water favors it, it is found damp in the morning. When the sun has risen, the careful masters also inspect the places; wherever they see an exceptionally dense swarm of very tiny flies hovering above the ground, they gladly promise that what is sought will easily be found.

They add that a certain exceedingly thin vapor may be seen in the form of a column: by however great a height it has been extended upward, they know that waters lie concealed by so much depth below. Thus it is marvelous that by these and other signs a definite measure is predicted: at what depth the object sought will be revealed. They also predict the tastes of waters [Note: On the taste of water, Vitruvius, Book VIII, chapter 1; in that book, and in Seneca, *Natural Questions*, Book III, many matters concerning waters are discussed, which I now deliberately omit. FORNER.], so that neither harsh water need be sought by wasteful labor nor sweet and necessary water dishonorably despised. Among the Greeks one author and among the Latins Marcellus handed down this learning elegantly to their successors; they treated carefully not only of subterranean streams but also of the very outlets of springs.

For they say that waters which break forth toward the east and south are sweet and clear and, because of their lightness, found most healthful; whereas whatever flows toward the north and west is indeed proved very cold but troublesome because of its heavy thickness. Therefore, if your wisdom sees that the matters stated are confirmed for that man both by reading books and by practical experience, you shall relieve his travel and poverty by suitable rations assigned from public funds. You will receive the reward due to one to whom he has offered the gifts of his art. For although the Roman city abounds in flowing waters, rejoices in springs, and is exceedingly rich in the overflow of its conduits, many suburban places are nevertheless found that seem to require this skill. And one is rightly retained who is known to be necessary even in part.

Yet a mechanic must certainly be assigned to him, so that the former may raise the waters which the latter discovers and make them ascend by art when they cannot rise by nature. Let this man therefore also be counted among the masters of the other arts, lest anything desirable be thought to exist which the Roman city could not contain under our rule.

## BOOK FOUR

### LETTER I. KING THEODORIC TO HERMINAFRID [manuscripts: HERMAFRID], KING OF THE THURINGIANS

He gives him his niece in marriage, praising her, and announces that he has gladly received from him horses, whose beauty is described, as well as other gifts.

Wishing to join you to our family, with the favor of God we unite to you our niece, a dear pledge, so that you who descend from royal stock may now shine even more distantly through the splendor of imperial blood. We send you the adornment of a courtly household, an increase to your lineage, the comfort of faithful counsel, and the sweetest delight of marriage; she will both share your rule by right and shape your nation through better instruction. Fortunate Thuringia will possess one whom Italy nourished in letters, instructed in character [Note: A wife’s endowments are learning, character, beauty, lineage, and dignity; but the principal place is assigned to education. The ancients customarily educated girls: Livy, Book III, on Virginia; Pliny, Book I, letter 17; Athenaeus, Book XIII; Lucian, *On Those Who Associate for Hire*; Plutarch, *On the Education of Children*. In the time of the emperor Gallienus, girls and widows attended the school of the philosopher Plotinus for the sake of instruction; Julian, Book IV, *Where Pupils Are Educated*, and Gordian, Book XV, under “If the Father,” *On the Business Conducted by Another*. FORN.], and made distinguished not only by birth but also by feminine dignity, so that your homeland may shine no less through her character than through its triumphs.

Therefore, greeting you with fitting grace, we announce that, when your envoys arrived, we gladly accepted the appointed prices for an object indeed beyond price but received according to the custom of nations: horses adorned in silver-colored [Note: Just as the yellow color was dedicated to weddings, as the highly learned Turnebus proves from Catullus and Apuleius, *Adversaria*, Book XXVIII, chapter 2, so too was silver or white, as is clear from this passage: Apuleius, *The Golden Ass*, Book VII; Valerius Maximus, Book II, chapter 1; Plutarch, *Problems*. Hence white clothing was forbidden in mourning; Paul, Book I, *Sentences*, final title. “He who mourns,” he says, “must abstain from banquets, ornaments, and white clothing.” Aeschines, in his speech *Against Ctesiphon*, reproaches Demosthenes because three days after the death of his only daughter he sacrificed wearing a white garment (*λευκὴν ἐσθῆτα λαβών*—“having put on a white garment”). FORN.] color, such as was appropriate for wedding gifts. Their chests and legs are gracefully adorned with fleshy spheres; their ribs extend to a certain breadth; their bellies are drawn in by their shortness; their heads present the shape of a stag, imitating the speed whose likeness they appear to possess. These animals are gentle despite their excessive fatness, swift despite their great bulk, pleasant to look at, and more pleasing in use. They walk softly; they do not tire their riders with mad rushing. One rests upon them rather than labors, and, composed with delightful moderation, they know how to continue with constant agility.

Yet although you recognize this most noble herd, these well-mannered beasts, and the other exceptional gifts you sent, as defeated, everything is rightly surpassed by what adorns the dignity of royal power. We too have sent what the rank of a sovereign required; but we have paid nothing greater than joining you to the honor of so distinguished a woman. May divine blessings attend your marriage, so that, just as affection has joined us, so parental favor may bind our descendants.

### LETTER II. KING THEODORIC TO THE KING OF THE HERULIANS

He adopts him as a son through arms and gives him horses, swords, shields, and the other instruments of war.

It is widely proclaimed among nations that a son can be made through arms [Note: “Through arms” occurs below in Book VIII, letters 1 and 9. I would add no more here on this matter, except that I am hindered by the diligence of the most learned man, Pithoeus, that most acute investigator of antiquities, who discussed this rite in Book I of his *Adversaria*. In this way investiture was performed by the handing over of a staff and ring, chapter 4, *On the Granting of Benefices*. Among the Lombards, manumission was performed by means of an arrow, Paul the Deacon, Book I, *On the Deeds of the Lombards*. But perhaps these matters may be treated more fully elsewhere. FORN.], because no one deserves to be adopted unless he has earned recognition as the bravest. We are frequently deceived in offspring. But those whom judgment has produced cannot be cowardly. Such men possess favor not from nature but from their own merits alone, since they are bound by the tie of affection to those who are not their natural kin. There is such force in this act that they would rather die first than appear to allow anything harsh to be inflicted upon their fathers.

Therefore, according to the custom of nations and the condition of manhood, by this present gift we beget you as a son, so that you may be born through arms, since you are recognized as warlike. We indeed give you horses, swords, shields, and the other instruments of war; but we bestow upon you things stronger in every respect—our judgment. For you are believed to be supreme among the nations, having been approved by Theodoric’s judgment. Take, then, arms that will benefit both me and you. He asks devotion from you who intends rather to defend you; he tests your character and will have no need of obedience. One such as he adopts you, from whose people you would more properly be feared. The services of the Heruli to the Goths, with God’s help, are well known. We have given you arms; nations in former times have given pledges of valor.

Therefore, greeting you with fitting grace, we communicate the remainder through our envoys, this one and that one, in the language of our fathers. They will clearly explain our letter to you and add what must be said to confirm our favor.

### LETTER III. KING THEODORIC TO SENARIUS [Note: He soon says that Senarius often undertook the duties of difficult embassies and stood firm before kings. I therefore think he is the Senarius mentioned in an ancient poem or eulogy preserved in the *Ancient Epigrams*, Book III, p. 108. He also writes to him in Letter 7 of this book. JUR.], ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND COUNT

The dignity of the countship of the patrimony is conferred upon him, and he is praised most highly.

We believe that choosing persons suited to dignities contributes to the adornment of the palace, because the reputation of masters grows from the distinction of their servants. It is fitting for a ruler to advance such men that whenever he deigns to look upon one of his nobles, he may recognize that he has made sound judgments. The man who is given as an example for imitation ought to be distinguished in character. It is easy to choose anyone for oneself; but it is fitting that one chosen by many should live in such a way as to be seen by all.
