Accordingly, in the fourth indiction (A.D. 511), receive the dignity of the illustrious countship of our patrimony [Note: In that ancient eulogy of Senarius it is said: “For, a courtly count, he was illustrious for royal patrimonies.” JUR.], which royal authority has not undeservedly bestowed upon you. For a long time, having borrowed a double service from our arrangements, you were both a participant in counsel and completed what had been assigned through your commendable acceptance. You often undertook the duties of difficult embassies; you stood before kings as an advocate of no lesser worth, compelled to show our justice even to those who could scarcely understand reason through their harsh obstinacy. Royal authority inflamed by disputes did not frighten you. Rather, you subjected audacity to truth, and, obeying our commands, struck the barbarians in their own consciences.

Why should we recount your diligence, anxious through long night watches, and your blameless service of continuous labor? In the office of receiving petitions you used an eloquent talent; the listener himself, pleased by what he heard, favored you while you produced better arguments as soon as you began to recite them. Your delivery delighted our judgment, because you refreshed the spirit of those who dictated as much as the cares of those who thought could weary them. There was also another praiseworthy aspect of your life: you enclosed our secrets within the integrity of your character. You were privy to many things, yet, although you knew more, you were not lifted up. You pleased your colleagues by favor and your superiors by humility. Thus, from great diversity, a single spirit was formed in everyone on your behalf.

You will certainly reap the most welcome fruit of approved instruction, since your advancement has been able to make everyone joyful, so that all judge their own desires to have advanced in you. Preserve, then, this beloved and splendid steadfastness of the virtues; and, supported by the authority of our house, seek favor with as much greater diligence as you see that you have found a place suited to receiving benefits. Continue to extend your successes toward better things through good actions, knowing that our favor is always increased in the person who desires to be found worthy of the height he has attained [Note: Manuscripts read: “extending your successes toward better expressions, accepting our favor, desiring it in him,” and so forth.].

### LETTER IV. KING THEODORIC TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

He announces that he has raised the illustrious Senarius to the countship of the patrimony, and praises him in many ways.

It is indeed glorious for us, Conscript Fathers, to bestow honors everywhere; but it is more praiseworthy to grant worthy rewards to those who have deserved well. Whatever we grant to such men, we bestow rather for the common advantage. For advancement that steadfastly follows what is right benefits everyone; nor is any room left for injury when the rule of discipline reaches good men.

With this splendid aim, therefore, we have raised the illustrious Senarius to the dignity of the countship of the patrimony. He avoids the darkening of his spirit through venality; he does not rejoice in slander; nor, supported by the authority of the patrimony, does he make a profit for himself through our terror. Rather, he is able to uphold equal justice with the others, and from this he looks to pleasing us in the service he renders. The reliability of past times makes it possible to promise these things about his future. In the very flower of youth he entered our palaces already mature in merit; and, deceived by no error of novelty, turning toward the will of the ruler, he produced the effects of good commands—something that even robust ages find burdensome.

Now worthy of audiences, now most suited to receiving petitions, and frequently chosen for the honor of embassies, his manifold merit made his office uncertain among us. For he ought not to be called a man of one place whose accomplishments appear in many spheres. But humility commended these qualities still further [Ac. reads “utility”], a quality as bright as it is rare. For it is remarkable [Note: A very fine maxim. “It is remarkable to preserve modesty under the ruler’s affection”; that is, we would say, “It is difficult for those who have great influence with a ruler to conduct themselves with moderation and humility.” *Remarkable*, that is, “great,” as in the title *On Public Judgments*, “a remarkable punishment,” meaning an atrocious one. Servius Honoratus, on Virgil’s “And he himself composes remarkable songs,” and “Who is this remarkable man among our people?” Galen, in his commentary on Hippocrates, interprets *νεανικῶς* as *γενναίως*, *σφοδρῶς*, or *ἰσχυρῶς*, that is, “nobly,” “very greatly,” or “forcefully.” FORN.] to preserve modesty under the ruler’s affection, because joys always disturb the mind; even moderation is rarely imposed upon happy circumstances, whereas it more often intervenes in sorrowful ones.

Joy is a talkative thing [Note: Symmachus supports this judgment, Book I, letter 37. “For joy,” he says, “is a loquacious thing and displays itself, so much so that no precaution against it exists for a large part of humanity.” The following letter says the same [Note: This passage is not by Symmachus but by Nazarius in the *Panegyric*, as D. Juret says he observed in his note on Symmachus, Book I, letter 31.]. “In serene faces the signs of the mind are read. The greatness of overflowing joy cannot contain itself; disdaining the concealment of the breast, it projects so much brightness outward that it is understood to be not greater than it is genuine.” Apuleius, Book III of the *Florida*: “For now joy obstructs eloquence, thought is hindered by pleasure, and the mind, occupied by delight, prefers to enjoy its happiness for the present rather than proclaim it. What am I to do? I wish to appear grateful, but because of joy I do not yet have leisure to give thanks.” FORN. What is said here about joy being talkative agrees with what is read in Pacatus’s *Panegyric*: he says that joy and silence cannot coexist in the same person at the same time. Pliny likewise writes that joy possesses the power to compel. “Happiness without speech is incomplete; it is an image of grief to conceal what brings you joy, and it is a change into affliction not to have a voice in happiness.” We should not omit that Marcus Cato, in his speech on behalf of the Rhodians, asserts that prosperity thrusts us away from sound judgment and understanding through joy. Apuleius, *Florida*, Book III, says that joy obstructs eloquence and that thought is hindered by pleasure. These statements agree with the ancient proverb reported by D. Jerome: namely, that eloquence is not a sorrowful thing. BROSS.]; for the spirit cannot contain itself because of joy.

Yet amid these astonishing merits, his lineage also shines with a similar brilliance, so that one is uncertain in which respect he is richer, since he possesses both abundantly. Each quality separately has its own praise; joined together, they are a marvel. Therefore, Conscript Fathers, let hoary freedom rise to greet those entering in the flower of youth [Note: That is, the curia, or Senate. JUR.]. Nothing is taken away from your dignity when the novelty of those arriving is honorably welcomed. Public fathers [Note: That is, senators. JUR.], named from clemency, let a double consideration of kindness invite you: let the beginner deserve favor, and the advanced man goodwill.

### LETTER V. KING THEODORIC TO AMABILIS, DEVOTED MAN AND COUNT

He decrees that all shipmasters of Campania, Lucania, or Tuscany commit themselves to suitable guarantors in order to transport provisions to the Gallic provinces suffering from famine and distribute them at a price.

No one ought to receive our commands grudgingly, since they are known rather to advance the interests of the devoted. In the Gallic region, therefore, we have learned that provisions are scarce; to that region commerce hastens eagerly, so that purchased goods may be sold more extensively at a tighter price. Thus it happens both that the sellers are satisfied and that our provision assists those people.

Therefore let your Devotion know by this present authority that all shipmasters of Campania, Lucania, or Tuscany must commit themselves to suitable guarantors, so that they may set out for Gaul with provisions alone [or: with provisions to that extent]. They shall have permission to sell them as buyer and seller may agree. It is a great advantage to bargain with those in need [Note: Here the prices of goods vary: “Prices of goods,” Digest, title *On the Lex Falcidia*; “necessity is the mother of commercial transactions,” Digest, Book IV, title 4, *On Contracts of Sale*. FORN.], since hunger usually disregards everything [Note: In times of famine everything is sold more dearly; indeed, free persons are sold by their parents. Valentinian, Novel 11: “It is known that recently a most shameful famine raged throughout Italy, and that people were forced to sell children and parents in order to escape the danger of imminent death.” Paul, Book V, title 1, *Sentences*; Digest, Book XL, title 3, *On Parents Who Sell Their Children*. When Hannibal was besieging Cassitium, Strabo, Book V, testifies: *ὡς ὑπὸ λιμοῦ διακοσίων δραχμῶν πρατέντες μεδύμνου* [“as, owing to famine, [they were] sold for two hundred drachmas per medimnus”; the printed Greek is grammatically uncertain]. It is also reported by Pliny that during that siege a mouse sold for twenty coins.], so that it can drive away its own need [manuscripts: fulfill it]. For when a seller serves his own ambition, the person who sells at the buyer’s request seems almost to be making a gift. To go with merchandise to people already full is a contest; but the person who can carry provisions to the hungry sets the price according to his own judgment.

### LETTER VI. KING THEODORIC TO SYMMACHUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND PATRICIAN

He orders him to keep Valerian’s sons in Rome, where their father had brought them for the sake of study, and not to allow them to leave before he has decreed it.

We willingly welcome the reasonable petitions of suppliants, and even when not asked we think about what is just. For what is more worthy for us to turn over day and night in continual deliberation than this: that, just as arms protect our commonwealth, inviolable equity likewise should safeguard it?

Accordingly, the eminent Valerianus, residing in the city of Syracuse, petitioned to return to his ancestral home. He had brought his children to the Roman city for the sake of their studies. Your illustrious Magnificence, in accordance with our command, shall keep them in the aforesaid city and shall see that they remain there. They may not depart before our present rescript declares it permissible [manuscript Aud., “affection”]. Thus both advancement in their studies is acquired for them and reverence for our command is preserved. Let him not therefore think that something burdensome has been imposed upon him when it ought to have been welcomed as a favor.

Let Rome be unpleasant to no one, for it cannot be called foreign. She is the fertile mother of eloquence, the spacious temple of every virtue. Let it plainly be understood that what is cherished [edition, “celebrated”] is not believed to be without favor: one to whom so great a dwelling is granted.

[Note: [Col. 0615C] Justinian likewise, in the preface to the Institutes and in the single law, Code, “On Religion and Funeral Expenses.” Synesius, To Paeonius: “for the sake of the gift.” At Athens there was an Eleatic gymnasium, where they were trained with equal care and devotion in letters and arms, “a school in which they attended equally to discourse and weapons.” FORN.]

**62. LETTER VII. TO SENARIUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, COUNT OF PRIVATE AFFAIRS, KING THEODORIC.** He warns him that those who were carrying grain from Sicily to Gaul suffered a most grievous shipwreck, and therefore orders that the wheat which was lost be credited to them.

[Col. 0615C]

It is the purpose of our clemency to relieve the fortunes of those who have suffered misfortune without wrongdoing, because we cannot treat as an offense what is shown to have been imposed by an external force. For it is unjust that what is not governed by a person’s will should be charged to that person’s fault, or that a peril should be imputed to someone from which escape is rarely granted.

Accordingly, let Your Sublimity know that the carriers of grain who had been sent from Sicily to Gaul approached us with a tearful petition. After they had carried the cargo entrusted to them out into the open sea, they were overtaken by contrary winds. When the framework of the timbers began to give way, the force of the waves swallowed everything, and nothing remained for the wretched men from the overwhelming waters except their tears.

Therefore, instructed by this present authority, Your Illustrious Sublimity shall, without any delay, cause the measured quantity of wheat [*modiatio*] proved to have perished in this disaster to be credited to the aforesaid carriers.

[Note: [Col. 0615D] *Modiatio*: a modius, a measure. Epiphanius, “On Weights”; the final law, Code, “On Shipwreck”; Book XI, law 32, “When the shipmasters …”; “On Shipowners,” Book XIII of the Theodosian Code; law 16, “When grain is not …,” Code, “On Interest.” The calculation of the *modiatio* is set out in the aforementioned final law, where one may incidentally observe that the loss is called a “gap” in the sense in which Honorius and Theodosius speak of a gap in the treasury. Symmachus, Book I, Letter 19; Gellius, “a gap in reputation,” Book XI, chapter 3; Cicero, *Verrine Orations* 4. The Greek term μοδισμός means something quite different in Justinian’s maritime laws. FORN.

“Measured quantity of wheat.” This passage belongs to the law *On Shipwrecks*, 6, Code, “On Shipwreck.” That law provides that if, after the season suitable for sailing has passed, some public grain has been lost through a storm at sea by the shipowners’ fault, the risk shall fall proportionally upon the entire body of shipowners, not upon the treasury or the tax contributors. It must nevertheless be understood that what was lost in a shipwreck without fault on the shipowner’s part is to be borne by the treasury from the amount received, and does not fall upon the shipowner’s risk.

As for the word *modiatio*, it is found very frequently in the law, as in the aforementioned statute, in law 1 of the Code, “On the Annual Civil Tax,” and in many others. Some have incorrectly taken *modiatio* to mean the payment of grain, when it is rather a measure; others have likewise wrongly referred *modiatio* to a monetary valuation in the Rhodian law. BROSS.]

For it is a kind of cruelty to wish to rage beyond the shipwreck [Col. 0616B] and to compel those to bear losses whom the monstrous elements are shown to have forced into a life of poverty [manuscript, A., and editions of Niv. and Gam., “dangers”].

[Note: [Col. 0616C] A human legal principle. Ulpian’s statement seems similar: “If a blight has occurred and has destroyed the whole crop, the loss does not belong to the tenant, lest he be compelled, in addition to the loss of the seed, to pay the rent of the land.” For divine force—which they call θεοῦ βία, “the violence of God,” or, as it is called in Harmenopulus, θεομηνία, “a divine calamity”—ought not to be damaging to a tenant if the crops have been injured beyond what is tolerable. Law 11, *On Lease*, section “If force”; law 25, “If the rent,” Digest, “On Leasing and Conducting.”

The laws on shipwrecks likewise contain this provision: “Shipwrecks shall belong to the publicans,” law 1, Theodosian Code, “On Shipwreck,” Book XIII, title 8. That this is very ancient is clear from Hermogenianus and Fortunatianus, so that the treasury may not extract a sorrowful profit from the calamity of the unfortunate. In laws 1, 2, 5, and 11 of Justinian’s Code, “On Shipwreck,” a shipwrecked person receives a remedy through indulgence within the period of one year. The penultimate law adds that such cases are to be heard immediately, once the sail has been lowered. FORN.]

**LETTER VIII. TO THE HONORABLE LANDOWNERS AND CURIALES OF FORLI [edition, FOROJULII], KING THEODORIC.** He decrees that, after receiving payment, they are to transport beams from their country to Alsuanus without any delay.

What is decreed by our ordinance ought not to seem burdensome, for we know how to assess what you ought to fulfill. Indeed, you can reasonably be protected by us, since you have advanced without being burdened.

Therefore, by this present authority, we decree to your Devotion that, after receiving suitable payment, you shall transport beams from your lands to Alsuanus without any delay, so that our ordinance may achieve its effect and, having received your wages, you may not appear to suffer a loss.

**LETTER IX. TO OSUIN [edition, OSUNI], ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, COUNT, KING THEODORIC.** He orders that if anyone brings a lawsuit against Maurentius and Paula, who have been deprived of their father’s assistance, he is to send them to the royal court.

[Col. 0617A]

Choosing to come before us is a profession of innocence, for here there is no place for violence and the vices of avarice are not feared. Maurentius and Paula, deprived of their father’s protection, testify that they are exposed to the injuries of many; their youth appears exposed to misfortunes [Note: [Col. 0617C] The circumvention of young people was prohibited by the Laetorian law: Cicero, *On Duties* III and *On the Nature of the Gods*; Julius Capitolinus, in *The Philosopher Antoninus*; law 2, Theodosian Code, “On Gifts,” book [uncertain], title 12. Ambushes are laid for minors, law 1, “On Minors.” FORN.], since it can easily be snatched away even from unsupported young people.

They therefore deserve our protection, because the cunning of wicked men does not hold back from them. Accordingly, when Your Sublimity has recognized the tenor of this present command, let it know that the aforementioned adults are to be directed to our court if anyone of the litigants should prefer to bring a complaint against them [Col. 0617B]. There innocence can find refuge and accusers can find a strict application of the law.

**LETTER X. TO JOHN, SENATORIAL MAN, CONSULAR OF CAMPANIA, KING THEODORIC.** He decrees that he publish an edict against those who have voluntarily turned to the practice of seizure; and he orders that whoever perhaps invades another’s property for the purpose of taking a pledge, when he ought to have pursued a claim, shall lose his case by force of law. If anyone is unable to pay, he wishes him to be punished with blows.

It is disgraceful to grant private hatreds license among the public laws, and unconsidered passion must not be judged according to private whim. For it is exceedingly unjust that which pleases an angry person. Those who rage do not perceive what is just, because while they are stirred in spirit and rage for vengeance, they do not seek moderation in their actions.

This is why the sacred authority of the laws was discovered: so that nothing should be done by force [Note: [Col. 0617C] “Nothing by force”: χειρῶν νόμῳ, that is, “by violence.” Pomponius, law 2, “On the Origin of Law”: “All things shall be governed by the hand of the king.” Florentinus: “by the hand of kings.” Manuscript: “by the laws of hands.” Paulus: “against foreign persons, if they have done anything by force.” Those who understood this manner of expression less well have dared to substitute various readings for the complete reading of the Florentine Digest: sometimes *modo*, sometimes *manus*, sometimes *malum*. In Photius’s *Nomocanon*, title 9, chapter 7: “If a bishop who has an action against a fellow bishop, σύν-επίσκοπον, does not bring it but negotiates with him, χειρὶ πράξει, that is, ‘he shall act by hand and force.’ Henry Agyleus wrongly attempted to emend this to χειραπτήσει; the error is disproved by canon 121 of the Council of Carthage and Justinian’s Novel 1[.....]3. Every form of violence is hostile to the laws when, with the authority of the magistrate disregarded, private persons claim a right for themselves. The law “No one individually,” “On the Rules of Law,” calls this ἀναρχίαν δανειστῶν, “the anarchy of creditors.” Harmenopulus, *Epitome*, Book III, title 5, ἀνάρχως, “without authority”; Justinian, *Law Rustic*, title 1, law 6. FORN.], nothing by one’s own impulse.

For what difference will there be between the confusion of war and tranquil peace if disputes are settled by force [manuscript A., “if disputes are not settled by laws”]? Accordingly, from a report by the provincials of Campania and Samnium we have learned that certain people, disregarding the discipline of the times, have turned to the practice of seizure [Note: [Col. 0617D] Theodoric prohibits seizures of pledges, also called reprisals. Zeno likewise provides, in the single law, that no villager is to be held liable for the debts of fellow villagers; Justinian’s Code, Book XI, and Novels 52 and 134. He orders all violence to be absent from the commonwealth, so that one may seek a remedy not by force but by legal action. This accords with our law: laws “It stands” and “The final law,” “On Duress”; law 9, denying this, Code, “On Obligations and Actions.” FORN.] and, as though an edict had been issued, license for vice has increased among the populace [Col. 0618A]. They add things much more bitter still: that some are dragged into paying the debts of others, and that the sole reason appears acceptable if some connection with the debtor could be established in the city.

Oh, the unjust error of this persuasion [read: “invasion,” JURET.]. Causes are divided according to genuine relationships: a son is freed from his father’s obligations [Note: [Col. 0618D] Others read “attachments,” and so forth. Sextus Empiricus writes in Book I, chapter 14, at the end of the *Outlines of Pyrrhonism*, that among the Romans there was a law that one who renounced his father’s property did not pay his father’s debts. Among the Rhodians, however, he was compelled to discharge his father’s debt. Yet not every son is an heir, nor is he immediately unwillingly bound to the debt contracted by his father. If he renounced his father’s inheritance—as is permitted today—see the entire treatment “On the Law of Inheritance”; law 12, “When from the mother,” Code, “On Vindication of Property”; law 15, “Of Money”; law 24, “If to the father,” Code, “On Gifts”; canon “Not Every Son,” 32, question 2.

Therefore, when Pope Alexander writes without distinction that a son is bound to pay his father’s debts, chapter 1, “On Payment,” this must not be understood simply of a son, but, according to what most often occurs, of a son who has accepted only his father’s inheritance; compare laws 4, 5, and 6, “On Laws.” Ordinarily, he becomes the heir of his father, whose inheritance is assigned to the children by a certain tacit operation of nature. Law 11, “In the Father’s Own Heirs,” “On Children and Posthumous Heirs”; law 7, “When the Account,” Digest, “On the Property of the Condemned.” FORNER.]

A wife is not liable for her husband’s debts except through the bonds of succession; and audacity drags outsiders into payment, while the laws release those who are related. Perhaps our ignorance has until now allowed this to continue, but now what has come to our attention must receive a remedy from the laws.

Accordingly, after learning the tenor of the edictal proclamation, Your Eminence shall cause it to reach everyone’s notice: whoever perhaps invades property for the purpose of taking a pledge, when he ought to have pursued a claim, shall lose the protection of the law [Col. 0618B; manuscripts, “the voice of the law”]. No one may take a pledge on his own initiative unless the person is perhaps legally bound.

If anyone prefers to seize a pledge from one person on behalf of another—which is wicked even to say—he shall restore double to the person against whom he used force what he seized. For crimes are restrained more effectively by penalties, and only those who have suffered a loss of honor think about losses. But whoever is excused from this restitution by the disgraceful defense of poverty shall, according to the character of the offense committed, be punished by flogging. For we do not permit to go unpunished what we do not wish to be permitted.

**LETTER XI. TO SENARIUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, COUNT, KING THEODORIC.** He refers the case between the landowners of Volia and the curiales to him for careful examination and settlement.

[Col. 0618C]

There is certain hope of a remedy when the petitions of suppliants are entrusted to the judgment of a prudent man, so that through the benefit of an ordinance the uncertainty of confusion may be removed. Therefore, Your Greatness, under whose administration the province appears to lie, shall carefully examine the case between the landowners of Volia and the curiales, so that the complaint between them may be brought to rest and justice, made clear by you, may prevail.

For it is not fitting that after your hearing a matter should be prolonged which ought to have been heard by other judges before it reached you.

**LETTER XII. TO MARABADO, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, COUNT, AND TO GEMELLUS, SENATORIAL MAN, KING THEODORIC.** He entrusts them with the case between Archotamia and Aetheria, her daughter-in-law, to be heard according to the laws, so that, with the holy Gospels between them and three honorable jurists, they may deliver judgment according to the form of the ancient law.

[Col. 0619A]

It is our purpose that the provinces subject to us, with God’s help, should be ordered by laws just as we defend them by arms. For justice that is observed always increases rulers, and in proportion as life is conducted according to approved instruction, so much is added to the highest advancements.

Accordingly, Archotamia, an illustrious woman, lamenting bitterly, deplored the misfortune of her grandchild in the following complaint—since a grandmother’s care for her own is always more tender [Note: [Col. 0619C] Such is the force of natural affection, στοργὴ φυσική, toward children, that parents prefer their children to themselves and wish them to prosper; and love implanted in human beings by nature descends more than it ascends. Law 19, *Institutes*, Digest, “On Duress”; the penultimate law, section “Concerning One,” Digest, “On the Rites of Marriage.” This seems to be because nature, intent on preserving the propagation of offspring, devised a kind of immortality for the human race through the labor of raising children. Aristotle, in the *Economics*: “For in this alone the constitution of human beings, although mortal, attains through succession the condition of always existing, and all the prayers of parents are directed toward this.” Theophilus outlined the same thought under the title “On Natural Law”: “Nature, seeing each individual living creature consumed by death, contrived for them immortality through marriage, the procreation that follows from it, and the affection, upbringing, and succession relating to those who are born.” [Col. 0619D] Valerius Maximus, “On the Censor’s Mark”: “Nature writes for you the law of begetting just as of being born, and your parents, by raising you, have bound you—if there is any sense of shame—to the duty of nurturing grandchildren.” FORN.

Sidonius Apollinaris spoke similarly: “Roscia greets you—the shared concern which, in the most indulgent bosom of a grandmother and her friends (something rarely granted to other grandchildren), is raised both with discipline—which nevertheless does not weaken tender age, but rather forms the intellect.” And elsewhere: “After his wife’s death, he raises his only small daughter, left as the consolation of his celibacy, with the tenderness of a grandmother, a mother’s diligence, and a father’s kindness.” BROSS.]

—asserting that Aetheria, her daughter-in-law, had set aside her husband’s love and joined herself in a marital union to a certain Liberius; and that, wishing to appear more splendid in a new marriage, she had tried to destroy the resources of her former husband, alleging that she had been enriched by stripping her children, although those resources ought rather to have been gathered for them.

Therefore, since we are accustomed to refer the wishes of suppliants to the provisions of the imperial enactments, so that we neither reject the petition of the suppliants nor condemn the opposing party’s case with credulous ease, we entrust this case to Your Sublimity’s judgment for hearing according to the laws. With all incivility removed, and with the holy Gospels between the parties, together with three honorable men chosen by agreement of the parties who are able to possess knowledge of the laws, you shall pronounce whatever the form of the ancient law establishes between them [64], while taking into account the discipline of our own time.

[Col. 0619C] For it is not fitting that those who have deserved to come under our rule should do anything by force.

**LETTER XIII. TO SENARIUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, COUNT OF PRIVATE AFFAIRS, KING THEODORIC.** He informs him that he has decreed that provisions be supplied, according to ancient custom, to Colossaeus, who has been sent to Sirmium in Pannonia.

[Col. 0620A]

Those who labor ought not to be deprived of rewards, so that access to good hope may be opened and the complaint of those who toil may be closed by a just compensation. Therefore, know that our Providence, which surveys every part of the commonwealth under heavenly favor, has ordered that provisions be supplied according to ancient custom to the illustrious Colossaeus, who has been sent to Sirmium in Pannonia for his labors and merits. Thus, while what is necessary has been prepared for the aforesaid man, an end may be put to unjust presumptions.

For a hungry army cannot maintain discipline [Note: [Col. 0619D] This explains why so many provisions for military grain were established by our laws under a special legal arrangement; more elsewhere. FORN. Three things are necessary for conducting war: an apparatus of money, supplies, and arms. Grain is so necessary that anyone who does not prepare the necessary grain and provisions is defeated without the sword. In this respect we may blame present-day negligence, since near-starvation drives armed men to every form of despair. To speak with the emperor: a soldier who is clothed, armed, shod, fed, and possesses something in his belt is not afraid. BROSS.], while an armed man always presumes upon what is lacking. Let him have what he can buy [Note: [Col. 0620C] Polybius shows what the wretched military famine among the soldiers of Spendius meant; Porphyry, *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, Book II, discusses the same matter; and also what it meant among the Numantines, Valerius Maximus, Book VII, chapter 6. Livy, Book IV, and Ammianus Marcellinus discuss what it meant among the Romans; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III, chapter 4, Josephus, *Antiquities* IX, chapter 4, and the same author, *The Jewish War* VI, final chapter, and VII, chapter 6, discuss what it meant among the inhabitants of Jerusalem. See Book XII, Letter 5. FORN.], lest he be forced to think about what he might take.

Necessity does not love restraint [Note: [Col. 0620C] The authors show how great is the force and power of necessity. As Horace says:

> Necessity seizes all things  
> with equal law;  
> it casts lots among the distinguished and the lowly.  
> The urn moves every name that can be contained within it.

Moreover, the same author calls necessity the forerunner of Fortune, establishing Fortune’s rule and power, because whatever pleases necessity cannot be prevented by any force, however great. In an especially elegant fiction and conception he also assigns to necessity great structural nails, with which it fastens, strengthens, and holds everything in place. BROSS.], nor can many be commanded to preserve what very few are able to guard.

**LETTER XIV. TO GESILA, THE SAJO, KING THEODORIC.** He orders him to compel the Goths residing in both Tuscias to pay the taxes owed, and to punish the disobedient.

It is a grave kind of sin to burden one person with another’s debts, so that what can be demanded does not deserve to be heard. Let each person regard his own losses [Note: [Col. 0620D] In the name of tribute and tax, the estates themselves and their owners are sued, law 7, “The Emperors,” Digest, “On Publicans.” Demosthenes, *Against Timocrates*, says that taxes are owed not by bodies but by owners or estates: “that the estates, not the bodies, owe the contributions. For it is from these that we contribute.” Laws 1 and 3, Code, “If on Account of Public Payments,” and the title “Without Meaning,” or “If the Remaining Land Cannot Be Compelled.” Quintilian, *Declamation* 341, and Salvianus, Book V, *On Providence*, teach that the law concerning publicans and taxes was written not against persons but against property. FORN.], and let the person who is known to possess the benefit of the property pay the tax.

Therefore, by this present authority, we delegate to you the responsibility of ensuring that the Goths residing in Picenum or in both Tuscias are compelled, under your supervision, to pay their due assessments [Col. 0621A]. Excess must be checked at the very beginning, lest a shameful imitation, like a loathsome disease, gradually seize the rest.

If anyone, therefore, with a rustic spirit and a defiant posture, rejects our commands, you shall vindicate his huts for the rights of our treasury by affixing the appropriate notices, so that he who justly refused to pay a small amount may reasonably be seen to have lost something great.

For who ought to be more promptly devoted to the treasury than those who receive the benefits of a gift? When do they receive more from our humanity than is granted by right of military pay? For if the matter of our generosity is considered, we rather pay voluntary taxes, since we support the fortunes of everyone.

**LETTER XV. TO BENENATUS, SENATORIAL MAN, KING THEODORIC.** He orders him to select twenty-one sturdy *dromonarii* in place of those who have died and to test their strength.

[Col. 0621B]

From the report of the illustrious and magnificent Count of the Patrimony we have learned that twenty-one *dromonarii* [Note: [Col. 0621D] Justinian calls *dromones* swift ships, almost courier vessels, in law 4, Code, “On the Office of the Prefect of the Praetorium”; the Latins call them *celones* because of their speed, as Nonius testifies. “Appoint,” he says, “soldiers who can both protect the crossing itself and report to the illustrious commander everything that is being done in the regions of Spain or Gaul, whether by the Franks or others; and at that crossing have as many *dromones* as you provide equipped and arranged.” Isidore, *Etymologies* XIX. BROSS.

[Col. 0622D] *Dromones* were very swift ships with an unimpeded course, which he mentions below in Book V, Letters 16 and 17; elsewhere they are called courier vessels, as in Sidonius Apollinaris, Book I, Letter 4. From these, therefore, the *dromonarii* took their name: they were the oarsmen of the *dromones*. JUR.]

had been removed from the established number through the misfortune of death. Therefore, know that our Providence—whose proper task is to repair by deliberation what chance removes—has decreed that you hasten, without any hesitation, to select and approve replacement *dromonarii*, provided that they can be found suitable for this work.

The labor of oarsmen is arduous and requires men strong in mind and body, so that confidence of spirit may be able to confront the wave-tossed storms. For what is bolder than to enter in a small vessel that treacherous and vast sea, which only the presumption of despair causes one to struggle through?

Therefore, you ought to apply this precaution to our commands: do not complain about having gathered weak men, since you know that we sought the strongest [Imperial edition, “not the strongest”].

**LETTER XVI. TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME, KING THEODORIC.** He announces that he has entrusted the administration of the city of Rome to Count Arigernus, whom he praises for his distinguished deeds, and orders everyone to obey him.

For the sake of the public welfare, which our mind always regards, we formerly judged that it was necessary to send the illustrious Count Arigernus, almost one of your own citizens, to Gaul, so that by the maturity of his counsel the wavering hearts of the people might be strengthened. Wise rulers ought to treat anxious novelty prudently, so that, just as the order of life has been formed, loyal discipline may proceed.

When these matters had been arranged according to our wishes, he both restored the glory of civic life and, carefully displaying what he had learned among you, returned bearing the insignia of war. We have, as we think, restored him to your desired assembly, so that he who pleased you for so many years may now become even more pleasing, since the good qualities added to him commend him.

Therefore, let the Roman order restore itself to the discipline of the aforesaid man, so that what is commanded for the love of peace may be fulfilled with devoted minds; so that license may be removed from excesses and, above all, so that vengeance may find no place.

If any fault has arisen during his absence, correct it among yourselves with consideration for justice, as befits your nobility, which always takes pleasure in integrity. For know that we have expressly commanded that an error which has not been corrected by those responsible for it be cut away by the strictness of the laws.

Obey, therefore, Most Honored Fathers, a man already tested for many years, whose commendable actions must necessarily be followed; he has conducted himself until now to the praise of you all and, amid so great a multitude, has encountered no adverse judgment.

**LETTER XVII. TO IDA, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, DUKE, KING THEODORIC.** He orders him to arrange for the restoration of the possessions of the church of Narbonne, which have been occupied by certain usurpers.

[Col. 0622B]

We do not wish a matter settled by an ancient king—although it is clear that it was decreed reasonably—to waver in any uncertainty, for what is commended by an approved command ought to be firm. Why should we unsettle earlier decisions where there is nothing that we ought to correct?

Accordingly, by this present authority we order you to have the possessions of the church of Narbonne, which, according to the commands of Alaric of exalted memory, have been seized by any usurpers, restored in consideration of equity. We do not wish unlawful presumptions to continue at the Church’s expense, when it is fitting for our times to calm what has been thrown into confusion [manuscripts, “to oppose”].

Be entirely vigilant concerning such matters, so that you who are brave in war may also be made outstanding in civic life. With God’s help, you likewise strengthen your arms if you strive to preserve justice for the humble. For you cannot excuse yourself by saying that you were able to resist wicked men when everyone readily yields to you, knowing you as glorious in the contest of war.

Perhaps a coward can command nothing against the bold; no one exercises authority over presumptuous men more effectively than one whose own deeds commend him.

**LETTER XVIII. TO ANNAS, SENATORIAL MAN, COUNT, KING THEODORIC.** He decrees that he carefully investigate whether the presbyter Laurentius, after excavating the tombs of the dead, found treasures.

It is the custom of our clemency to entrust matters to men whose loyalty has been tested, so that when we appoint judges after mature consideration, no opportunity for wrongful fraud may be found [Col. 0622D].

Some time ago, indeed, a report from many people reached us that the presbyter Laurentius, after excavating the ashes, had searched among human corpses for accursed riches and had inflicted an outrage upon the dead, although he ought to preach peaceful conduct to the living.

He is said not to have held back his hands, dedicated to pious consecrations, from so cruel a contamination [Note: [Col. 0622D] The ancients testify that it was impious to exhume the bones of the buried: Horace, Ode 16 of the *Epodes*; Virgil, *Aeneid* IV. BROSS.]. He is reported to have sought gold with execrable desire, although he ought to have given his own substance to the needy, or what he had gathered equitably.

We therefore command you to investigate this matter carefully, so that, if you find that the statements correspond to the truth, you may confine the man’s ambition solely for this purpose: to prevent him from concealing gold which he was not permitted to find. For we believe that the crime which, out of priestly respect, we leave unpunished [Note: [Col. 0623D] Likewise in the laws of the Visigoths, Book IV, title 6: “We leave matters rather to be avenged by God than define them for cancellation by our own judgment.” JUR.] must be avenged with greater severity.

**66. LETTER XIX. TO GEMELLUS, SENATORIAL MAN, KING THEODORIC.** He writes that for the present he has remitted payment of the *siliquaticum* on grain, wine, and oil, so that he may provide abundance to the provinces.

It is fitting for imperial Providence to restore what is exhausted, so that the gentleness of its commands may mitigate the harshness of circumstances. For no hardship is felt if prosperity granted shows that what had been oppressed by adversity has been relieved.

Accordingly, we do not order the payment at the present time of the *siliquaticum*—which ancient prudence established for all goods sold in the marketplace—on grain, wine, and oil. This remission of payment may provide abundance to the provinces, and those wearied by the present decree’s benefit may gain some relief.

For who would not be encouraged to sell more generously when the customary expenses are removed? Let a ship entering our ports not fear them, so that they may be a secure refuge for sailors, provided they do not fall into the hands of collectors, whose exactions often afflict people more than shipwrecks usually strip them bare. This may perhaps be tolerated in a time of quiet; but now, while we desire to assist the provincials, let us meanwhile take care of the owners of the merchandise.

**LETTER XX. TO GEBERICH, SENATORIAL MAN, KING THEODORIC.** He decrees that one *iugum* (a unit of land) belonging to the church of Bishop Constantius, granted by the piety of earlier rulers and held by usurpers, be restored.

If we wish to find opportunities for benefits by which we may erect monuments to our clemency, how much more do we wish foreign benefits to be defended intact, since we desire to give our own freely—especially when there is also placed upon our conscience what is provided from the treasury under ancient solemnity?

Accordingly, from the petition of the venerable Bishop Constantius we have learned that one *iugum* (a unit of land) belonging to his holy church, granted by the benevolence of ancient rulers, is now being held through the violent usurpation of certain persons [Col. 0623D]. But since we wish no one to profit by his own frauds, especially when he is engaged in a detestable scheme at the expense of the poor [Col. 0624A], by this present authority we decree that what is shown to have been assigned in the past through the kindness of rulers be received by the aforesaid church without any diminution. The penalty against the usurper shall remain in force, since he is proved to have violated both the gifts of the ancient rulers and the church’s lawful revenues.

**LETTER XXI. TO GEMELLUS, SENATORIAL MAN, KING THEODORIC.** He admonishes him to be vigilant concerning the tasks assigned to him, since the needs of the time demand it.

Although we believe that you are applying yourself effectively to the tasks assigned to you and diligently avoiding whatever you have learned displeases us, nevertheless our admonition does not abandon its vigilance, so that you may be made more fully instructed after receiving what has been defined in the brief words written below.

Therefore, our ordinance ought to seem displeasing to no one, since the necessity of the times excuses the burdens of the command [Col. 0624B]. Be vigilant, then, concerning the tasks assigned to you, because although vigilance must always be applied, it is especially useful in a time of necessity.

You will therefore obey after this admonition, so that you may deal with the provincials in the way you perceive that we wish to provide for them. Thus, secure in our favor, you may obtain whatever, through vigilance, you have disdained to acquire by corrupt ambition.

**LETTER XXII. TO ARGOLICUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, PREFECT OF THE CITY, KING THEODORIC.** He states that he has learned from him that Basilius and Praetextatus were accused of magical arts, and decrees that, after taking five senators with him and also including Count Arigernus, he examine the case while observing the proper legal procedure, and, if they find them guilty, punish them with the severity of the laws.

[Col. 0624C]

It is an intolerable excess [Note: [Col. 0623D] This entire letter concerns the art of magic and declares that judges must be appointed against magicians, since, as he says, “it is not permissible to engage in magical arts in Christian times.” Since magicians among the Persians had chiefly been accustomed to devote themselves to the worship of the gods, their vanity later increased to such an extent that they claimed not only to predict the future by observing the stars, but also to know and be able to do everything through certain arts and spells. BROSS.] to seek an injury against the majesty on high and, forgetting piety, pursue the cruelties of error. For what hope of pardon did he have who despised the author worthy of reverence?

Let the already profane rite be removed from our midst; let the penal murmur fall silent [Note: [Col. 0623D] Justinian, Novel 115, uses γοητεία, that is, “magical whisperings,” according to the interpretation of Julianus; they are performed with summoned spirits, law 6, Code, “On Sorcery and Mathematics.” Aurelius Prudentius, Book I, *Against the Report of Symmachus*:

> For with a magical murmur to call forth delicate shapes,
And to know how to conjure sepulchral ashes. Cedrenus, in his account of the tricks of Apollonius of Tyana, p. 33, derives γοητείαν from lamentation at tombs, namely ἀπὸ τῶν γόων, καὶ θρήνων τῶν περὶ τοὺς ταφοὺς τοῖς τὸ τοιαῦτα ἐπιτηδεύουσι γινομένων, “from the wailings and lamentations made around tombs by those who practice such things,” below, Book IX, Letter 18. FORNER.] of souls. It is not permitted to engage in magical arts in Christian times (see Baronius, under the year of Christ 504).

From the report of Your Greatness, therefore, we have learned that Basilius and Praetextatus, already long polluted by the contagion of the sinister art, have been brought before your tribunal at the instigation of their accusers. Concerning this matter you assert that you await our judgment [Note: [Col. 0624D] *Spectare* for *exspectare*, “to await”; conversely, *exspectant* for *spectant*, Code 1.9.3, *On the Redemption of Actions*; Paul, *Sentences*, Book I, title 9; Book V, title 6. FORNER.], so that what the authority of our piety commands may be carried out with greater confidence. But we, who know that we must not depart from the laws and whose concern it is to maintain measured justice in all things, decree by the present authority that you, together with five senators [Note: [Col. 0624D] Here Theodoric orders Argolicus, Urban Prefect, to investigate the charge against Basilius and Praetextatus, accused of the sinister art, that is, magic, after summoning five senators. Valentinian and Valens likewise state in Code of Theodosius 9.16.10, *On Sorcerers*, that because members of the senatorial order were implicated in accusations of sorcery, such cases should be investigated by the urban prefect; if a question arose that the prefect could not conveniently decide, recourse was to be had to the prince, as is clear from that law. The final law of the Code of Theodosius, *On the Jurisdiction of All Judges*, expressly provides that the Urban Prefect cannot try a senator’s criminal case unless he admits to his council five senators, not chosen but selected by lot, lest persons selected by judgment should judge another concerning life and innocence; it adds that this had long since been established. [Col. 0626D] Indeed, Code of Theodosius, *On Accusations*, 13 shows that a criminal charge brought against a senator is also decided before the Urban Prefect by a five-man court, and forbids the use of approved judges voluntarily chosen, permitting only those selected by lot. BROSS.], that is, eminent and patrician men—Symmachus, Decius, Volusianus, and Coelianus, as well as the illustrious man Maximianus, examine this case with a lawful inquiry. And, with the whole legal procedure carefully observed, if the charge brought against them is proved, let them also be punished with the strictness of the laws themselves, so that those who are hidden and secret may by this kind of vengeance be deterred from such offenses—those whom uncertain knowledge cannot bring before the laws.

[Col. 0624D] We have also sent instructions to the illustrious man Count Arigernus, so that, once every forcible defense has been removed, if the accused conceal themselves, he may bring them before judgment; and, sitting with you in this case, may neither allow the innocent to be oppressed nor permit criminals to evade the laws.

[Note: “Impetitos,” that is, accused persons; for in the following letter he says “impeti accusatione,” “to be attacked by an accusation.” Also Book V, Letter 33; and Book XIV, *On Accusations*, Code of Theodosius. JUR.]

## LETTER XXIII

TO ARIGERNUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, COUNT, THEODORICUS THE KING.

He orders him to seek Basilius and Praetextatus, accused of magical art and escaped by flight, and to bring them, once found, before a five-man tribunal, where he is to arrange for the case to be examined and concluded.

[Col. 0625B]

Although the discipline of the Roman state entrusted to you ought in every respect to be maintained, you must nevertheless be especially diligent in those matters which you recognize as delegated to you by our authority, so that justice faithfully observed around you may increase your favor and you may gain the rewards of our judgment—you who have until now pleased us by your integrity. The Urban Prefect has therefore declared to us in his report that Basilius and Praetextatus, implicated in magical arts, are being prosecuted on the accusation of many persons, whom he reports to have escaped through the mental distraction of their guards.

We command you, wherever they are found, to bring them before the five-man tribunal which our authority has delegated for this present matter, and in which we order you to sit; so that, once every forcible defense has been removed, you may cause this case to be examined and concluded according to the laws. And if they are proved guilty of the crime of which they are accused, let them undergo the sentence established by the prescriptions of the law. But if their innocence is being assailed by detestable malice, do not allow them to be oppressed in any way, because in all cases, with divine consideration, we wish that to be done which increases the good opinion of our piety.

## LETTER XXIV

TO ELPIDIUS [OTHERS: HESPIDIUS], DEACON, THEODORICUS THE KING.

He grants permission to build in certain places of the city of Spoletium that have been ruined by age, provided that they are not devoted to public use.

Benefits bestowed upon those who deserve well turn to profit; and a gift yields even greater gain when worthy things are provided for the best men. Accordingly, from the tenor of your petition we have learned that certain places in the city of Spoletium, which long neglect had covered with the squalor of old age, require the splendor of restoration, so that to things disordered by antiquity the mature appearance of newness may be returned; and so that through your benefaction those structures may rise again which, bent down by age, had collapsed.

With regard to your merits and the service expended with long-standing devotion, we have gladly decided to grant this, so that both a just request may obtain its fulfillment and the city’s ornament may be increased by restoration. Therefore, by this present act of kindness, we grant authority to your petition, so that you may enjoy, with unrestricted generosity, the portico with its small square behind the Baths of Turasius, provided that it does not serve a public use.

[Note: The exception is nevertheless added: “provided that it does not serve a public use”; another is also added: “lest the structure built cause inconvenience to a neighbor.” Digest 39.2, *Ne quid in loco publico*. FORNER.]

For permissions to restore are accepted rather as rewards than granted as gifts. Supported, therefore, by this authority, take confidence to build in the places mentioned above; and henceforth fear no legal challenge, since both the advantage of the city protects you and the revered will of the prince supports you.

## LETTER XXV

TO ARGOLICUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, URBAN PREFECT, THEODORICUS THE KING.

He orders that Petrus, distinguished by birth and a candidate for senatorial rank, should obtain the fulfillment of his wish according to ancient custom.

It is evident that the man who desires to reach the heights of the sacred order presumes much of himself. Merits suggest the efforts of a worthy aspiration, and an honorable mind can be recognized in the character of its desire. For who ignorant of the athletic art would enter the stadium to wrestle? Or who would take part in a contest which consciousness of virtue does not recommend? In their very attempts, those things languish weakly which are not supported by the expectation of merits.

The profession of praise, therefore, is to have desired fellowship with the highest; and he gives a good judgment of himself who seeks the steps of lofty dignity. Our piety therefore gladly indulges these desires, and even raises languishing hopes, so that while advancement is sought, zeal for probity may be loved all the more.

Accordingly, let Your Illustrious Magnificence arrange that Petrus, conspicuous by the distinction of his parents and already a senator by his own gravity, be entered on the register of the sacred order according to ancient custom; so that the number of that great assembly may be increased and the candidate’s adornment may be enhanced by the sacred order.

## LETTER XXVI

TO ALL THOSE ESTABLISHED AT MASSILIA, THEODORICUS THE KING.

He confirms the immunity granted to their region by former princes, promises to free them from every burden, and remits the census of the present year.

We gladly preserve the ancient benefits bestowed upon you, while desiring to provide new ones for your advantage. Humanity does not know how to observe fixed limits, and it is fitting to charm people with new benefits restored after long periods. Accordingly, by this authority we grant you the immunity which your region is known to have obtained by imperial privilege; nor will we allow any new burden to be imposed upon you, since we wish you to be freed from every encumbrance.

Moreover, princely munificence remits to you the census of the present year, so that you may also receive what you did not happen to request.

[Note: Theodoric grants the people of Massilia exemption from the census. When the census began is not sufficiently clear. Some think it began under Julius Caesar, others under Augustus, and in my judgment the latter view is better, as Florus and Livy testify; Dio informs us that it occurred in the seventh consulship of Augustus. There were two forms of this census: for they appear to have assessed both persons and land, lakes, cattle, and other resources—persons, as may be seen in Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XVI; land, in the jurists, title *On Censuses*. BROSS.]

For this is perfect piety: before it is bent by petitions, it knows how to consider those who are weary.

## LETTER XXVII

TO TEZUTZAT, THE SAJO, THEODORICUS THE KING.

He entrusts him with the protection of Petrus, which he takes away from the sajo Amara because he had wished to kill Petrus; and he orders Amara to restore double whatever benefit he had received from Petrus, and to appear before the judgment of Count Duda to answer for the wound inflicted.

[Col. 0627B]

Every injury is indeed detestable, and whatever is committed against the laws is condemned by a just curse. But the extreme of all evils is shown when one suffers harm from the very source from which assistance was believed to come. Cruelty turned in the opposite direction magnifies the fault, and unexpected deception adds greater weight to guilt.

The illustrious man Petrus has therefore complained to us of an extraordinary misfortune: the protection of the sajo Amara, which we had granted him against violent men, had instead been directed against him, so that the obstruction of a post delayed for a while the sword-stroke driven into him. A hand was placed before the wound; and, lest it fall completely severed, the timbers of the doors, having been struck, held it up. When the force of the blow had weakened, the flashing edge of the sword grazed the outer parts of his body. [Variant: JUR. reads *laxato* (“relaxed”) for *lassato* (“weakened”).]

O detestable calamity! His own protection attacked the man, so that, once the benefit of assistance had been taken away, necessity increased because of the defense. Adding matters much more bitter than these, it was as though the injury had been assigned a price: his own crime was assessed by an outrageous exaction.

Therefore our anger rightly rises against those who have turned benevolent commands into savage acts of service. For what refuge will remain for petitioners if even our benefits inflict wounds? Accordingly, by this present order we decree that whatever the aforesaid Amara received from the causes of the aforementioned petitioner under the name of benefit, he, being constrained by you as an ungrateful assailant, shall be compelled to pay back to him double; for what is clearly extorted by wicked presumption deserves to be restored under penalty.

As for the wound which the reckless aggressor inflicted with a drawn sword, the aforesaid sajo, compelled by you, shall come before the judgment of Count Duda to be heard; so that, according to the wording of the edicts, he may without any delay make compensation for whatever wrongdoing is established.

[Note: *Tuitionem*—which our countrymen call *sauvegarde*, protection—is discussed also below, Book VII, Form 39. FORNER.]

You will provide protection to the petitioner against uncivil attacks by our order, while preserving civil order—not following the example of the accused, but in consideration of the honorable choice made.

## LETTER XXVIII

TO DUDA, SENATORIAL MAN, COUNT, THEODORICUS THE KING.

He appoints him judge of the case of the sajo Amara, who had wounded Petrus.

We approve the conscience of the man to whom we entrust judgments, because among others he is worthy to decide what should be followed who has seemed to impose upon himself the measure of lawful conduct. The illustrious man Petrus asserts that Amara, our sajo, who had been sent to protect him but, by an adverse turn of fate, acted against him, wounded him with a drawn sword and did as a defender what scarcely even an enemy could have dared.

We wish you to examine this matter by lawful deliberation and conclude it with a credible judgment, so that no one may dare attempt what he knows displeases us.

## LETTER XXIX

TO ARGOLICUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, URBAN PREFECT, THEODORICUS THE KING.

He reproves him because, led by his own advantage, he has not yet fulfilled the prince’s commands; and he decrees that he carry out the orders without delay.

If the authority of your office were considered, if concern for the dignity of the Roman [Note: Some read “reverence for the Roman curia.”] were present, you ought voluntarily to seek the very things for which you are being blamed. For what could you have considered more appropriate to the urban dignity than the increase of the Senate, when what the sacred order acquires advances the reputation of its head?

[Note: The dignity of the urban prefecture surpassed that of all urban magistrates. Code 1.28.3, *On the Office of the Urban Prefect*; Symmachus, Book I, Letter 22. Our Cassiodorus calls the urban governor “the dignity of honors” in the preceding Book, Letter 11; see also below, Book VI, Form 4. FORNER.]

But, as the petition sent by the most illustrious man Armentarius bears witness, you are perversely seeking advantages from delay through foul ambition, although it is clear that you ought to have desired its advancement. For what could be more incongruous than to suspend the wishes of petitioners after our commands had been expedited and, after the utterance of the sacred instruction, if it is permissible to say so, still to have suspended the judgment of the king?

But we, who are concerned not to desire vengeance immediately after a first fault, turn our commands instead toward admonition, lest our strictness be excessive when gentle patience has not preceded it. Therefore by this authority we decree that no cunning delay be introduced into our commands, because there is no place for pardon for one who transgresses after being admonished.

## LETTER XXX

TO ALBINUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, PATRICIAN, THEODORICUS THE KING.

He grants him permission concerning the curved portico, so that he may construct new buildings above it, provided that they do not harm public utility or public appearance.

[Col. 0629A]

It is fitting for everyone to consider the advancement of his fatherland, but especially for those whom the state has bound to itself by the highest honors, because the logic of affairs requires that the one who is seen to have undertaken greater things must owe more.

You have therefore testified in a petition that permission should be granted to place structures above the curved portico which stands beside the house called Palmata and suitably encloses the forum in the form of an open square, so that both the habitation of private houses may be extended and the appearance of newness may increase the old walls.

Thus what might have decayed through neglect appears to be sustained by the diligence of those who remain, because the collapse of buildings is easy when the guardianship of their inhabitants is withdrawn; and what human presence does not protect is quickly dissolved by the wasting of age.

[Note: Time devours everything, including buildings: Vitruvius, Book I, chapter 8; Pliny, Book 36, chapter 6; Digest 39.2.15, *Si quando*; Code 8.11.2, *On Public Works*; Digest 30.1.58, *Domus*, *On Legacies*. Paulinus, Tenth Birthday Poem of Felix. FORNER.]

Therefore we, who desire the City to be adorned by the splendor of rising buildings, grant the permission requested, provided that the proposed work neither harms public utility nor public appearance. Accordingly, rely securely upon what you have hoped for, so that you may appear a worthy inhabitant of Roman buildings and the completed work may praise its author. For nothing can better reveal both the intelligence of a prudent man and the effect of generosity.

## LETTER XXXI

TO AEMILIANUS, VENERABLE MAN, BISHOP, THEODORICUS THE KING.

He urges him to complete the aqueduct which he had undertaken, by the king’s authority, to repair.

What the intention of prudent men has appeared to undertake ought to be brought to completion, because just as completed works win praise, so those abandoned in the midst of their efforts generate blame. Failure in undertakings indicates either wavering judgment or a lack of strength.

Therefore, let Your Holiness, avoiding such criticism, quickly bring to completion the repair of the aqueduct which you undertook with commendable care by our authority. For what could be more fitting than that this most holy priest should provide water for a thirsty people, and that human foresight should satisfy those whom he ought also to have nourished by miracles?

You imitate the most ancient Moses, who, when the Israelite people had been dried out by prolonged aridity, drew abundant streams from the barrenness of a rock.

[Note: Psalm 113: “Who turns the rock into pools of water, and the cliff into springs of water.” FORNER.]

And, to fulfill the miracle, he made moist waters flow from the place where there had been dry hardness. But if you lead irrigating springs through the construction of stone channels, by this labor you provide the peoples with what he provided by miracles.

## LETTER XXXII

TO DUDA, THE SAJO, THEODORICUS THE KING.

He states that he has learned that the property of the proscribed Tupha was deposited with Johannes under the issuance of a written acknowledgment; and he orders him to summon the wife of Johannes and his son Januarius, and, unless they freely restore it, to have them come before the governor of Campania to be heard according to the laws.

[Col. 0630A]

Since we wish justice to be maintained in all cases—for the glory of a kingdom lies in its devotion to equity—we wish it especially in those cases brought in the name of our treasury, lest detestable slander afflict anyone with the ruler’s displeasure. We allow ourselves to be defeated by the laws while equity remains safe, so that we may always be victorious amid arms. For a subject who lawfully overcomes his ruler does not defeat him in battle.

From the report of Marinus we have learned that the property of Tupha was once deposited with Johannes under the issuance of a written acknowledgment. And since it is clear that whatever could have belonged to a proscribed person belongs to us,

[Note: The property of proscribed persons is assigned to the treasury. *Authentic Constitution, On the Property of the Condemned*. Code 9.49, *On the Property of the Proscribed*. BROSS.]

we therefore command by this authority that you summon the wife of the aforesaid Johannes and his son Januarius with measured enforcement. If they recognize that they are unjustly retaining the property (*intestata*; ed. *intentata*, “unclaimed”), let them restore it in consideration of equity; or, failing that, after first providing suitable security, let them come before the governor of Campania to be heard according to the laws, so that, with the parties present before you and under your supervision, judgment may be rendered according to the form contained in the imperial enactments.

Yet this must be done so that innocence is burdened by no prejudice, no injury, and no loss, lest you seem to make the malice of another’s accusation your own offense.

[Note: A judge is said to “make a lawsuit his own” by judging badly. Publilius Syrus: “If you tolerate the faults of friends, you make them your own.” FORNER.]

## LETTER XXXIII

TO ALL THE JEWS ESTABLISHED AT GENOA, THEODORICUS THE KING.

He confirms the privileges which the laws had granted them.

[Col. 0630C]

The observance of laws is an indication of civilization, and reverence for former princes also bears witness to the example of our devotion. For what is better than to wish a people to live under the command of justice, so that the assembly of many disciplined persons may be a union of wills?

[Note: Gellius, Book II, chapter 29: *adunare messem*, “to gather a harvest,” derived from Greek; in the same sense they use ἡνωμένον and συνήμενον, “united,” Digest 41.3.30, *Rerum*, *On Usucapion*: “united bodies”; Seneca, Book II, chapter 2, *Natural Questions*. FORNER.]

For this has gathered peoples from savage life into the order of human society. This principle has separated them from ferocity, lest those whom God wished to be governed by counsel wander according to chance impulse.

You have therefore presented a petition requesting that the privileges which prudent antiquity decreed should be preserved for you under Jewish institutions and laws be maintained. We gladly agree to this, since we desire the laws of former times to be preserved in reverence for us.

Accordingly, by this authority we decree that whatever the statutes of the laws have commanded shall remain inviolate among you, so that what is known to have been established for the use of civil society may be maintained with perpetual devotion.

## LETTER XXXIV

TO DUDA, THE SAJO, THEODORICUS THE KING.

He orders him to visit the places where treasures are hidden and, if they are found, to assign them to the public treasury.

It is the custom of prudence to recall to human use the talents hidden in the earth and not to call the commerce of the living the property of the dead, because such riches perish for us in a pit and, left to the dead, profit them in no respect. The abundance of metals is a source of human comfort.

For a vein of rich gold is like the rest of the earth if it lies unused; through use it increases in value, since what is enclosed in the hands of the grasping has been buried among the living. Therefore by a measured command we decree that you go, under public testimony, to the place where it is reported that many such things lie hidden; and if gold or silver, as is said, is discovered by your search, you shall faithfully claim it for the public treasury.

Yet you must keep your hands away from the ashes of the dead, because we do not wish profits to be sought that might be found through criminal acts connected with funerals. Let buildings cover the ashes, and columns or marble adorn the tombs; let not those who have abandoned the commerce of life retain talents. Gold is rightly removed from tombs where it has no owner; indeed, it is a kind of guilt to leave uselessly hidden among the dead what can sustain the life of the living.

For it is not greed to take away what no owner can lament having lost.

[Note: This is drawn from the law. A treasure, according to Paul, is an ancient deposit of money whose memory no longer exists, so that it has no owner; thus what belongs to no other becomes the property of the finder. Otherwise, if someone has buried something underground for profit, fear, or safekeeping, it is not a treasure, and its theft is still possible. Digest 41.1.31, *Nunquam*, *On the Acquisition of Ownership*. Scaevola, Book I of the *Responses*: A guardian bought a house for a ward and brought in a craftsman to repair it. The craftsman found money; the question was to whom it belonged. Scaevola replied: If it was not a treasure, but money accidentally lost or not removed through error by the person to whom it belonged, it nevertheless remained the property of its former owner. Digest 6.1.67, *A Tutore*, *On Vindication of Property*. FORNER.]

The first discoverers of gold are said to have been Aeacus and of silver Indus, king of Scythia, who handed them over to human use with the highest praise. We must not neglect this in the opposite direction, lest, just as hidden things are revealed with praise, things once found appear to be neglected with blame.

## LETTER XXXV

TO THE AGENTS OF ALBINUS, THEODORICUS THE KING.

He permits the property of Albinus to be restored to its former condition, if his age permits it and justice and the laws are preserved; he had suffered serious loss in it through wrongful contracts.

[Col. 0631C]

Antiquity, guided by deliberate prudence, wisely decreed that minors should not have full freedom to enter into contracts,

[Note: Dion Chrysostom, *On Distrust*: “The law does not allow the young, up to so many years of age, to enter into contracts, since they are untrustworthy.” FORNER. [Col. 0632D] Ulpian relates these matters in Book XI *On the Edict*, where he says that the judgment of persons of such ages is weak, exposed to many deceptions and greatly vulnerable to snares; therefore the praetor promised them assistance by edict and aid against deception. BROSS.]

so that the snares of those lying in wait might be frustrated and slippery youth might aid those who had fallen. Innocence would be overwhelmed if audacity were given free rein, and everyone would strive to deceive if fraud could obtain its secretly acquired profit.

You have therefore reported, in a petition submitted according to ancient custom, that your patron, while still under age, accumulated losses rather than resources, since inexperienced childhood undertook the opposite of what it thought would be beneficial; and that he is now at an age when we can assist those who have fallen through ignorance. You ask that what the laws have granted may also be bestowed by our beneficence.

Accordingly, if your petition does not depart from the truth, if he remains within the number of years for which the most sacred laws have provided this benefit, and if there is nothing that can lawfully be brought against him, our authority also permits your patron, after the case has been solemnly examined, to be restored to his former legal position.

This must nevertheless be carried out entirely according to justice and the laws, because we wish to assist petitioners without unjustly burdening their opponents.

## LETTER XXXVI

TO FAUSTUS, PRAETORIAN PREFECT, THEODORICUS THE KING.

He states that he has remitted the public tax for the third indiction to the provincials of the Cottian Alps, whose crops the passing army had devastated.

It is the part of a most provident ruler to remit the tax burden to those who have been gravely diminished, so that those exhausted by the bitterness of losses may be restored by renewed efforts to fulfill their customary obligations. For if the burden is not at all lightened for the weary, they are seen to lie prostrate from necessity. It is better to disregard present losses than, through a small gain, to lose lasting advantages.

Accordingly, let Your Illustrious Magnificence know that we have remitted to the provincials of the Cottian Alps the public tax for the third indiction—that is, the year of Christ 510—whose fields our army, passing like a river, overwhelmed even as it irrigated them. For although it burst forth in a roaring mass for the general security, in passing it nevertheless devastated their cultivated lands.

A river always erodes its own bed; and although, flowing out gently, it fertilizes the neighboring regions, it nevertheless leaves barren the place into which it has poured when gathered together. Therefore it was necessary to extend a saving hand to those cast down by civic devastation, lest they say that they alone had perished in defense of everyone. Rather, let them share in the joy, since they provided a route into Italy for its defenders.

Taxes ought not to be demanded sorrowfully from those through whom I have happily acquired taxpayers. Let our mind say on their behalf what a subject cannot charge against a king: at our own expense we purchased the prosperity of the Goths; we provided what was necessary so that the enemy might be defeated unharmed.

## LETTER XXXVII

TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS WOMAN THEODAGUNDA, THEODORICUS THE KING.

He informs her that Renatus has complained that, although he had won a judgment against Inquilina, his adversary has nevertheless not ceased her calumny; and he orders her to ensure that the matter, already concluded, remain firmly settled, provided that Inquilina has not appealed lawfully.

It is fitting for our prudence to apply careful protection to the affairs of subjects, because when we give orders, those things ought to be done which can demonstrate the royal presence. We believe this of you because, remembering your ancestry, you reject every fault and can love only those things which you know we also love. The examples of great-grandfathers may perhaps be forgotten if the achievements of a long line are remembered less; but sons quickly follow the praises of their fathers.

Renatus therefore complained to us in a tearful petition that, after we had delegated the matter to judges, he had obtained a judgment against a woman named Inquilina after a long lapse of time, and that, worn out by watchfulness and losses, he had at last looked to your justice. Yet the litigant’s wicked calumny had not ceased, since she pursued the poverty of the petitioner with renewed lawsuits, appearing to have sought not so much the desire to win

[Note: Papinian says: “The heir appears to deserve assistance when the litigant’s intention and desire to obtain the judgment admit this view.” Digest 35.2.11, *In ratione*, concerning the Lex Falcidia. FORNER.]

as the ruin of her adversary.

Therefore, if you know that the judgment was rendered at our command and it is not established that the adversary appealed lawfully, see to it that the matter, concluded according to law, remains in its own force, lest the long dispute of litigants increase their estates less than it overturns them; and lest what is done out of a desire for profit appear to become the cause of loss.

## LETTER XXXVIII

TO FAUSTUS, PRAETORIAN PREFECT, THEODORICUS THE KING.

He states that the Gravasiani and Pontonates have complained that they were burdened by unjust exactions imposed by Januarius and Probus; and he decrees that they pay nothing other than what they were accustomed to pay in the time of Odoacer.

Since we desire every part of our state to increase equally, the growth of fiscal taxes must nevertheless be weighed by the most equitable judgment, because the reduction of those who serve is an addition to this revenue; and by as much as one part advances, by so much does the other withdraw from stability.

But from us, who wish the advantage of the treasury to stand through enduring stability, every costly excess must always be excluded, lest the total, swollen by its increase, fail and begin to be more deficient because it has seemed to grow monstrously.

Accordingly, let Your Illustrious Greatness know that the Gravasiani and Pontonates have petitioned us, saying that they have been burdened by unjust exactions from Januarius and Probus, the assessors, although the barren sterility of their lands permits no increase to be made. When nature resists, every industry yields; nor does it profit to expend labor where the fertility of the place is not known to offer assistance. A tax can be increased where cultivation has advanced. Hence taxes vary, because the fertility of fields is not uniform.

Therefore we decree that their former custom be restored, so that just as they paid taxes in the time of Odoacer, so now also they may serve the public interest; and if anything more is proved to have been added, we remove it in consideration of their diminished resources. For we do not wish anything to be imposed that must necessarily be removed.

## LETTER XXXIX

TO THEODAHAD, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, THEODORICUS THE KING.

He writes that Domitianus has complained that his possessions were occupied with the greatest injustice; and he orders him, with the sajo Duda in attendance, to arrange for everything seized to be restored without any delay. If, however, he believes that anything favors the invaders, he orders a properly instructed representative to be sent to the court, so that, after both parties have been heard, a just judgment may be rendered.

[Col. 0634A]
