Among the various allurements by which the human race is troubled, the shameful coveting of another’s property must especially be avoided, because, once cast into the limitless, it is carried away unless pressed down by the weights of justice. Divine Scripture also testifies that avarice is the root of all evils,

[Note: It is called “the mother of all crimes”: Claudian, Book II *Against Rufinus*; Petronius Arbiter; Lucan, Books III and VII; Propertius 3.7.13; Tibullus 1.10; Martial, Book XII; Juvenal, Satire 14; Ovid, Book I *Fasti*; Horace, Book I *Satires*. BROSS.]

and it was punished in such a way that, although it seizes many things, it is always in want. Because of its kinship with our own nature, we do not wish it to grow together with your minds in such a way that we grant it even a beginning.

For what place have stains of the mind in the splendor of noble birth? You should rather choose what can adorn us. A man of Amalian blood should not have a common desire, since he sees that his lineage is clothed in purple.

Let us therefore correct you through the incentives of praise, in which we do not yet need to be strict. The illustrious man Domitius has complained in a petition presented to us that two possessions belonging to him—this one and that one—were invaded by your men in disregard of the laws, although they ought to have been received through civil process if they were lawfully claimed.

But because we cannot allow obscure accusations to be circulated against you any longer, you who shine with the distinction of your lineage, we decree by this authority that, with our sajo Duda in attendance, if the time of year permits it,

[Note: Annual legal actions are prohibited. Anianus, in title 6, Book V of Paul’s *Sentences*. FORNER.]

you shall arrange, without any delay, for the possessions recently occupied, together with everything seized, to be restored to the petitioner. And if you believe that anything may lawfully belong to your side, it is appropriate for you to send an instructed representative to our court, so that, after the claims of both parties have been examined with equity, the judgment dictated by the authority of law may be rendered.

For it is fitting that noble men conduct everything with moderated civility, because the resentment caused by injury grows in proportion to the power of those who inflict it, when the person proved to be inferior in fortune is believed capable of being oppressed.

## LETTER XL

TO THE AGENTS OF PROBINUS, THEODORICUS THE KING.

He reminds them that he ordered long ago that the Areciretine estate, which Probinus had bought from his wife Agapita, be returned to Basilius; now he orders that Basilius himself promptly answer the new claims of the purchasers.

[Col. 0634D] We are compelled, out of love for justice, to issue certain orders with greater strictness, although our policies are more merciful toward those of lesser fortune. For the one who could have been subjected draws us toward mercy; and this is the benefit of his modest station, that, while his evidence remains intact, he may meanwhile move us to compassion. For cruelty [ed. Niv. and Ac., credulity] relieves the humble and presses down the more powerful through envy.

Since, therefore, you have presented petitions alleging that Basil, a respectable man, had long ago deserved our order that the Areciretine estate—which your patron had formally purchased from his wife Agapita [Col. 0635A]—should, without delay and together with all its documents, be restored to the aforesaid wife, while he complained in a tearful action that his wife had been disturbed from her own household; and since you add that, in accordance with our customary justice, it was afterward ordered that, if your patrons presumed to rely on the merits of the case, they should promptly send a representative to our court, so that matters which could be resolved by reason might proceed as though from the fountains of justice:

Therefore, if the assertions have not been corrupted by any falsehood, we decree through the office of our seat that Basil be admonished: if there is nothing that he can raise on behalf of his own side to prevent his being summoned in this case, let him appear to answer your claims, whether he prefers to come to the court or to litigate in the competent forum. For we impose no necessity of distance upon anyone except those who recognize that it serves their own interests. Indeed, we offer our presence in place of a benefit; and therefore what deserves to be desired ought not to be imposed upon the unwilling.

## LETTER XLI. THEODORIC, KING, TO JOHN, CHIEF PHYSICIAN

He declares that he abolishes the judgment issued against him by the vicar of the city of Rome through Vivianus’s legal maneuvering, restores him to his country and all his property, and strengthens him for the future by the protection of the patrician Albinus.

It is a royal purpose to assist those oppressed by the stain of misfortune through the remedy of compassion, and to change bitter experiences of injustice into a better lot. In your petition, you complain that the respectable man Vivianus, elevated by his skill in the law, in which he is versed [Cor. and Gam., inflamed], pursued your person with accusations brought against you; and that matters proceeded so far that you were condemned, undefended and contrary to the order of law, by the judgment of the vicar of the city of Rome. But now, in the disposition of a pious mind, he has condemned worldly hatreds, and your danger has displeased its author.

And therefore, if the assertions are not weakened by any attacks, we do not allow an injury to cling to the unfortunate when it is clear that its contrivers themselves disapprove of it. Accordingly, by sending into abolition the judgment which the vicar of the city of Rome is known to have issued in this matter, our authority restores you to your country, your property, and everything else [Note: [Col. 0635D] Restoration of one who has suffered a judgment: in the preceding book, letter 46, there was an example of restoring a reputation. Antoninus: “I restore you completely to your province”; and he added: “But so that you may know what it means to restore someone completely, I restore you to your honors, your rank, and everything else,” Digest 1, Code, *On Those Who Have Suffered a Judgment and on Their Restoration*. The emperor Julian, recalling the physician Zenon, who was exiled for religious reasons, wrote in a rescript: “Return then honored, retaining your former rank.” Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIX: “But those who had been afflicted by exile and financial losses were recalled shortly afterward to the military service restored to them, with their dignities unimpaired and their splendor intact.” FORN.]; nor should you fear at any time that a charge will be brought against you on this account.

But lest the perhaps punishable rashness of anyone [Note: [Col. 0635D] Greek and Cuj., severity. Jur., perhaps savageness.] be able to renew an attack of audacity against you, the protection of the patrician Albinus, with the laws preserved, is assigned to guard you; for [Col. 0636A] we do not wish anything uncivil to be done, since his daily labor is to care for the general peace.

## LETTER XLII. THEODORIC, KING, TO ARGOLICUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

He orders that the circus tower and the site of the amphitheater be restored to Marcian and Maximus, the sons of Volusianus, who complained that these had been taken from them while they were occupied in mourning their father’s death.

Royal clemency rightly receives those whom paternal affection has abandoned, because under a public parent the loss of a father ought by no means to be felt [Note: [Col. 0635D] King Theodoric asserts that he is a public parent; and princes are several times said to have been born for the good of the commonwealth, while we read that an emperor was born for public welfare. For this reason Seneca calls princes and kings “guardians of the public order.” Ammianus Marcellinus writes that the condition of the world depends, as if by a thread, upon the safety of the prince, and that government is nothing other than care for another’s safety. Nor was it without reason that Christians prayed for magistrates and princes, even pagan ones, as Tertullian reports in the *Apology*, and Arnobius, since the safety of the prince is also the safety of private persons. See Seneca, book II of *On the Tranquility of Life*, chapter 6; Mamertinus, *Genethliacus*; Paul in Digest 1.3, *On the Office of the Prefect of the Night Watch*, who says that no one is better suited to protect the safety of the commonwealth, nor is anyone else sufficient for that task, than Caesar. BROSS.] For abandoned childhood has a rightful appeal to us, since the growth of all human beings is promoted through us.

The complaint of the illustrious youths Marcian and Maximus therefore moved us, when, during the Paschal days, they were wounded by the grief of their father’s death and, at the very season of joy, were forced alone to endure sadness. They had piously neglected their own interests, since even for a mature age it would seem madness to consider such matters amid tears. The pursuit of profit ceases when one is devoted to mourning; nor does the mind admit anything else when the quality of filial affection has filled it.

Taking advantage of this cruel fraud, they report that the tower of the circus and the site of the amphitheater, belonging to their father of illustrious memory, were sought from your offices through detestable ambition. No feeling of humanity recalled their plotter, nor did a similar misfortune terrify him. He burdened their childhood; and not to assist it is rightly judged a loss of honor.

But we, who observe the rules of the ancients and preserve the moments proper to compassion, decree by a salutary ordinance that, if their father, the once-patrician and magnificent Volusianus, possessed the aforementioned places by common right, they ought not to perish for his sons—especially since we desire to nourish the senatorial offspring [Note: [Col. 0636D] Senators, as heirs of paternal praises, were reckoned to possess a certain exceptional honor of nobility: Digest 50.2.6 and 7, *On Senators*; Digest 50.2.9, *Son*; Code 10.31.39, *On Decurions*; Digest 50.2. ult., *On Senators*. We have also made some observations on this, book I, chapter 12, *Selected Matters*. FORNER.] with new benefits, not to suppress, through some injury, the hope of their mature age at its very beginnings.

And therefore let your illustrious magnificence know that, if it remembers any such action having been committed, it must immediately be corrected, lest the venerable body of the senatorial order be violated by unjust presumption.

## LETTER XLIII. THEODORIC, KING, TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

He decrees that an inquiry be made into those who stirred up a riot and burned the synagogue of the Jews, and that punishment be inflicted upon the few perpetrators whom it may be possible to find.

The celebrated reputation of the city of Rome must nevertheless be preserved according to its own established character [Col. 0637A]; it does not admit foreign vices, since it has always boasted of the uprightness of its customs. For the frivolity of riots and the desire to set fire to one’s own city are not Roman behavior. Therefore the severity of the laws must be maintained against the perpetrators of the deed, lest the detestable spectacle of the fire seize the hearts of the populace for a criminal imitation.

We have learned from the report of the illustrious Count Arigern that we have been approached by a complaint from the Jews: that servile audacity had erupted into the murder of masters. When some of the offenders had been cut down in accordance with public severity, the people’s quarrel immediately flared up, and they rashly decided to burn the synagogue. They avenged the guilt of individuals by destroying buildings [Note: [Col. 0637D] The same principle was used by Honorius and Arcadius: “Just as we prohibit sacrifices in temples, so we wish the adornments of public buildings to be preserved. And lest those who attempt to destroy them flatter themselves with some authority,” and so forth. Code 1.11.3, *On Pagans, Sacrifices, and Temples*. Buildings are not to be punished as though guilty; rather, guilty citizens are to be punished. There survives a letter from Belisarius to Totila, asking him not to demolish the Roman walls; after reading it, the enemy immediately abandoned the destruction of the fortifications. Procopius, book III of *The Gothic War*. Sometimes, however, the houses of the guilty are razed to the ground or at least confiscated for the treasury—for example, those of traitors, tyrants, counterfeiters, and others whose guilt is more serious or whose obstinacy is punished by the destruction of their buildings as an example; or when public utility appears to demand it: Digest 48.19.24, *On Punishments*; Digest 10.2.20, *If the Person with Whom...*; Digest 43.8.2, section “If Anyone...”; Digest 43.8.3, *On Anything in a Public Place*; Digest 36.1.11, section “Whoever Unlawfully...,” *On Legacies* 3. FORN.], whereas, if any Jew were proved to have transgressed, he alone ought to have suffered the penalty for the wrong. It was not just, however, to rush together into the shameful business of riots or hasten to burn buildings.

But we, who, with God’s favor, take to heart the task of setting right what has been wrongly committed, so that everything may accord with settled conduct, decree by our present authority that you investigate the aforesaid matter through a lawful examination and, having exercised severity, cut down the few perpetrators whom you are able to discover as guilty of this fire. For we do not wish anything detestable to be done by which Roman dignity might be accused.

We likewise decree that, if anyone believes he has a reasonable claim against the Jews, he should come before your judgment to be heard, so that the one whom guilt has entangled may be condemned by the proper authority. For understand that we have been deeply displeased that the utterly empty claims of the populace have proceeded as far as the destruction of buildings, when we desire everything there to be beautifully ordered.

## 74. LETTER XLIV. THEODORIC, KING, TO ANTONIUS, A VENERABLE MAN AND BISHOP OF POLA

He writes that Stephanus complained that a house belonging to him had been occupied by subjects of the Church over which Antonius presided, and orders him to restore it to the petitioner. If anything supports the occupants’ case, he wishes a legally instructed representative to be sent to the court, where the matter is to be settled.

A complaint against one to whom the rights of reverence must be preserved is liable to provoke resentment, since something serious is believed to have been committed wherever silence is not maintained against such persons. Stephanus, in a sorrowful petition, complained that a house belonging to him, which he had possessed for a long time before your predecessor and his predecessor [Col. 0638A] [others, our predecessor], had, about nine months ago, been occupied by men of the Church over which you preside, with civil order disregarded.

If you recognize that this was indeed done [Note: [Col. 0638D] All restitutions in integrum were promised by the praetor after the case had been heard, so that he might examine their justice and determine whether they were genuine, and so forth. Digest 4.6.3, *On Restoration in Integrum*; above, letter 40 of this book. FORNER.], restore it promptly to the petitioner by a regard for justice [Note: [Col. 0638D] Above, letter 40 of this book. FORN.]. For it is fitting that you correct what ought not to have been committed by your associates.

Nevertheless, if you recognize that justice supports your side in the possessory action, whether the summary possessory action or the principal action [Note: [Col. 0638D] “Principal,” that is, concerning ownership, as it is called by Saint Gregory the Great, book VII, indiction 2, chapters 43, 44, 100, and 101; Symmachus says the same in book X, letter 41. See book X, *On Judgments*, Code. JUR.], first examine and investigate the matter carefully—for it is not fitting for a priest [Note: [Col. 0638D] It is unbecoming for priests to litigate improperly; indeed, they scarcely ought to litigate except through representatives, who are called *apocrisiarii*. Novel 123; nor should they stand surety or make claims on behalf of others, and so forth. Code 8.40.1, *On Sureties*; Apostolic Canon 20, “to give sureties” (ἐγγύας διδοῦναι); Synesius, letter 121; Optatus Afer, book I; Photius, *Nomocanon*, title 8, chapter 13. FORN.] to prolong an improper lawsuit—and send to our court a person instructed in the laws, where the nature of the case must be recognized and brought to an end.

Therefore let the mind of your holiness not be burdened, nor let it grieve at having been accused by deceitful words: [Col. 0638B] a reputation cleared is far greater than one that has not been attacked because the complaints have simply ceased.

## LETTER XLV. THEODORIC, KING, TO THE COUNTS, DEFENDERS, AND CURIAL OFFICIALS OF THE CITY OF TICINUM

He orders them to provide the Heruli with a ship as far as the city of Ravenna, together with grain provisions for five days.

By God’s authority we have ordered the Heruli, who are petitioners, to come to our court under our arrangements; they must be provided with transport by ship, lest they appear, while still in our country, to suffer the poverty of their own province. Therefore, warned by this order, provide them without any delay with the use of a ship as far as the city of Ravenna and with grain for five days, and ensure that they lack nothing necessary [Col. 0638C], so that they may recognize that, although they have left a hungry province, they have found an abundance greater than that of their homeland in a foreign land.

## LETTER XLVI. THEODORIC, KING, TO MARABADUS, AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

He states that Liberius reported that his wife had been placed at an unfair disadvantage in court. If this is so, he permits the case either to be examined by arbitrators chosen by the parties or for the parties to come to the court for judgment.

It is fitting that our compassion should arrange the petitions of suppliants through a salutary ordinance, since the spirits of subjects are relieved whenever the complaint of the grieving is settled. The respectable man Liberius therefore reported to us in a sorrowful petition that his wife had been placed at an unfair disadvantage in your court [Col. 0639A], contrary to the order of law.

If this is so, with prejudices removed, let the case be heard according to the laws before arbitrators chosen by the agreement of the parties, under your supervision. If the matter cannot be brought to an end there, we do not deny the parties permission to proceed to our court through legally instructed representatives, provided that the parties themselves do not choose to come; there, perhaps neither a bribe will be suspected nor a malicious [Niv. and Gam., envious] accusation be able to cause harm.

## LETTER XLVII. THEODORIC, KING, TO GUDISAL [ed. GODISCAL], A SAJO

He reports that he has learned from his envoys that the post-horses are being worn out by excessively frequent use and that those he had ordered to be preserved for public service are being taken for private use. He therefore decrees that he permit no Goth or Roman to leave Rome unless the prefect of the praetorium and the master of the offices have released him; that anyone who takes one horse against the will of those entrusted with this responsibility be compelled to pay one hundred solidi as a fine; and that no one place more than one hundred pounds of cargo upon a horse.

[Col. 0639B]

Things known to be subject to continual exertion must be restored through constant care. For how can the post-horses necessarily suffice for the labor imposed upon them if they are permitted to be overused [Note: [Col. 0639D] Greek and Cuj., “which are necessarily sufficient for the amount of transport of the post-horses ... to be overused.” See book V, letter 5.]? Neglect of supervision is an incentive to improper presumption. From the report of our envoys we have learned that the relay horses are being exhausted by frequent use, and that those which we wish to be preserved for public needs are being taken for private purposes.

Therefore we decree that, by arrangement of the prefect of the praetorium and the master of the offices, you remain in the city of Rome for as long as public utility requires [Col. 0639C], and that from now on you allow no Goth or Roman to depart unless those acting in the place of the aforesaid dignitaries have released him.

And concerning what is reported to have been frequently usurped: if anyone, regardless of his nation or rank, should presume to take a post-horse against the will of those entrusted with this responsibility, he must be compelled to pay one hundred solidi as a fine [Col. 0639D]. This is not because the injury to a single animal should be valued at so much, but because an excessive presumption must be restrained by a substantial penalty.

Moreover, do not allow any sajo to make repeated journeys; let him be permitted to approach or return from the assignment to which he has been sent by only one journey. Those whose prohibited repeated travel falls under the preceding fine are likewise included.

Nor may anyone exceed one hundred pounds in the loads of the pack-horses [Col. 0639D]. For we wish messengers to hasten unencumbered [Note: [Col. 0640D] That is, tax collectors or soldiers of the palace.], not to migrate. Anyone who carries many things with him reveals his own sluggishness; and one who prefers to conduct himself in a luxurious manner does not consider speed.

Finally, cranes about to cross the sea embrace small pebbles in their hooked feet, so that neither their lightness may be carried away by a powerful wind nor their natural speed be weighed down by unsuitable burdens. Those who know that they have been chosen for public necessities cannot imitate this.

Therefore whoever believes that a pack-horse should be loaded beyond one hundred pounds shall incur a fine of fifty solidi—not as a post-rider, but as a stable keeper [Note: [Col. 0640D] That is, a stable keeper. See book III, letter 10.].

We order you to observe those who preside in the City in place of the aforesaid dignitaries, so that any excess detected by them may be punished through your enforcement by the condemnation stated above. If any are struck by intemperate guilt, we wish the amount collected to be assigned through the acting officials to the managers [Note: [Col. 0640D] *Mancipes*; elsewhere, managers of the public post and managers of the wagon service: Code of Theodosius 8.5.15, 23, 26, 35, and 62, *On the Public Post*; Ammianus Marcellinus, book XX; and above, book I, letter 29.] of the changes of horses [Col. 0640B], so that the relay service may receive a remedy from the source from which it has hitherto suffered harm.

In worldly affairs, prosperity frequently arises from adversity; and people, when they wish to cause harm, often confer benefits. But you will carry out all these matters so effectively and carefully that, prompted by your good actions, we shall have to entrust greater responsibilities to your devotion.

## LETTER XLVIII. THEODORIC, KING, TO EUSEBIUS, AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

He permits him to withdraw to Lucania for eight months, after which he is to return to Rome.

After the tedious anxieties of the tumultuous City and the burdensome discomforts of official duties, your magnificence desires to be refreshed by the pleasantness of the province, asserting that the causes of your occupations have arisen in the present circumstances [Col. 0640C], in which, once they have been settled, you wish to enjoy rural pleasure.

And because that security is genuine which is granted by our commands, when the period of your occupation has been completed [Ac., emerged], we grant you, by our authority, a respite of eight months in the pleasant retreats of Lucania [Note: [Col. 0640D] Juret reads *secessus* (“retreats”), as he did in his commentary on Symmachus, book I, letter 29. “A respite for withdrawing,” above, book III, letter 21.]. Let the eight-month period be reckoned from the time when, by divine favor, you happen to leave the City.

When these months have passed, hasten to come to the Roman seat, desired by many, to be restored to the assembly of the nobles and to a way of life worthy of your character.

## LETTER XLIX. TO ALL THE PROVINCIALS AND THE CAPILLATI [Note: [Col. 0640D] The Capillati were said to be a certain people belonging to the Goths [Col. 0641D], and the name was a great and honorable one. Jordanes testifies to this in *Chronicle*, chapter 11. See Savaron on Sidonius Apollinaris, book I, letter 2. JUR.], THE DEFENDERS, AND THE CURIAL OFFICIALS RESIDING IN SUAVIA, THEODORIC, KING

He announces that he has appointed Fridibad as governor of their province.

[Col. 0640D]

Severity must never be withdrawn from a royal command [Col. 0641A], so that it may both restrain the bold through fear and revive the hope of the afflicted for the future. For a threatened punishment often accomplishes more than an imposed penalty can correct.

Therefore, with God as our guide, we have decreed that Fridibad preside over your regions, so that he may restrain cattle raiders with lawful severity [Ac., security], cut down murders, condemn thefts, and restore you to peace from the criminal assaults by which unjust presumption now tears you apart. Live in order; live instructed in good conduct. Let no nation [Ac., reason] [Note: [Col. 0641D] Fornerius wishes *ratio* (“reason”) to be read here on the authority of one manuscript, but not correctly. By the name “nation,” the author means those Goths who were called the Capillati by a special name, as in the heading of this letter. And, as I believe, they wanted to be permitted more than others, as below in book V, letter 39: “whatever people they may have been born from.” JUR.] excuse anyone, nor let any earned honor provide an exemption. Whoever complies with depraved conduct must necessarily submit to punishment.

## LETTER L. THEODORIC, KING, TO FAUSTUS, PREFECT OF THE PRAETORIUM

He orders him to send a man of proven loyalty to the territory of Nola or Naples, devastated by the fire of Mount Vesuvius, so that, after the fields there have been carefully inspected, the owner may be relieved of a tax burden proportionate to the damage he has suffered. The eruption of Mount Vesuvius is described remarkably.

The inhabitants of Campania, devastated by the hostility of Mount Vesuvius, poured forth supplicating tears to our clemency, asking that, stripped of the produce of their fields, they might be relieved of the burden of taxation [Note: [Col. 0641D] The remission of taxes and forgiveness of arrears on account of calamity is discussed in more than one place. [Col. 0642D] The signs preceding the mountain’s eruption should also be noted here; Pliny described some very similar ones in book VI, letters 16 and 20. FORN.]. Our compassion rightly agrees that this should be done.

But because the unexamined calamity of each individual is uncertain to us, we order your magnificence to send a man of proven loyalty to the territory of Nola or Naples [Col. 0641B], where necessity itself is spreading through a particular domestic injury, so that, after the fields there have been carefully inspected, the owner may be relieved in proportion to the extent to which his livelihood has suffered. Thus the amount of the benefit may correspond to what has been measured [Col. 0641C] [Gam., measured], while the full extent of the injury is ascertained.

This province suffers from one particular evil: its lands are stripped bare, and, lest it enjoy complete prosperity, it is repeatedly shaken by the bitterness of this fear. Yet that terrible event is not wholly without warning: it sends heavy signs in advance, so that the ensuing disasters may be endured more tolerably.

For, while nature struggles with such vast masses, the cleft of that mountain murmurs so loudly that some roused spirit seems to terrify the neighboring regions with a deep roar. The air of that place is darkened by a most dreadful exhalation, and almost all Italy recognizes when that anger is stirred.

Boiled ash flies across the great sea, and, when earthly clouds have been raised, it showers even the provinces across the sea with dusty drops. One can recognize what Campania may suffer when its misfortune is felt in another part of the world [Col. 0641D]. You may see there what seem to be dusty rivers flowing, and barren sand, driven by a boiling force, running down like liquid streams [Note: [Col. 0642D] Above, book III, letter 31: “running down like pools.” FORN.].

You would be astonished to see the backs of the fields suddenly swell as far as the treetops, and what had been painted with the happiest greenery suddenly laid waste by a mournful heat [Col. 0642A]. That perpetual furnace vomits reddish yet fertile sands. Although dried out by prolonged burning, they soon produce the seeds received into them in various crops, and with remarkable speed restore what they had shortly before destroyed.

What singular exception is this: that one mountain should roar in such a way as to terrify so many parts of the world through an alteration of the air [Note: [Col. 0642D] See Baronius, volume VI of the *Annals*, under the year A.D. 471, p. 297, where he criticizes Bodin for laughing at these matters. JURET.], and disperse its substance everywhere in such a way that it does not seem to suffer any loss [Note: [Col. 0642D] “To suffer loss,” that is, diminution. Paul, book 3, *On the Loss of Property*; Gellius, “the losses and increases of the moon,” meaning diminution and increase, book XX, chapter 7. FORN.]?

It sprinkles dust far and wide; toward the neighboring regions it belches out certain masses, and for so many centuries the mountain has been regarded as one that is expended through such great outpourings. Who would believe that such enormous clods, carried down onto the plains, had boiled up from such deep clefts and, blown out by some exhaling spirit from the mouth of the mountain, had been hurled forth like light straws [Col. 0642B]?

Elsewhere, great peaks of earth seem locally to burn; the fires of this mountain have been granted to almost the whole world to observe. How, then, should we not believe its inhabitants when what they attest can be recognized by the whole world?

Therefore, as stated, let your prudence choose a person who will both bring remedies to the injured and leave no room for fraudulent encroachment.

## LETTER LI. THEODORIC, KING, TO SYMMACHUS, THE PATRICIAN

He praises him for the many and splendid buildings which he had arranged to be constructed in the City and its suburbs, and asks him to strengthen and repair the ruined Theater of Pompey at the king’s expense. The theater and the events conducted in it are described.

[Col. 0642C]

Since you have devoted such attention to private buildings that you seem to have built a kind of fortification in your own homes, it is fitting that you should be known to have preserved Rome—which you have adorned through the beauty of its houses—in its own wonders: an outstanding founder of buildings and an exceptional embellisher of them, since both abilities arise from prudence: arranging things suitably and adorning what stands in an appropriate manner.

It is well known with what praise you have drawn Rome into its suburbs, so that whoever happens to enter those buildings does not feel that his view lies outside the City, except when he recognizes that he is also among the beauties of the fields. A most diligent imitator of the ancients and the noblest instructor of the moderns, your character is expressed by your buildings; for no one is recognized as diligent in them unless he is also found to be most refined in his own thoughts.

And therefore we believe that the structure of the theater, which is collapsing under its great mass, should be strengthened by your advice [Col. 0642D], so that what your predecessors are known to have granted for the adornment of the homeland may not appear diminished under better successors.

What will you not overcome, old age, which has shaken structures so strong? Mountains might more easily be thought to yield than that solidity to be battered [Col. 0643A], since the entire mass itself was made from rocks in such a way that, apart from the art added to it, it might also be believed to be natural.

We might perhaps have disregarded these things if it had not fallen to us to see such works: those apsidal tiers hanging from the rocks, joined by concealed connections into forms so beautiful that one would have thought them the chambers of a lofty mountain rather than something constructed.

The ancients made a place large enough for so many peoples, so that those who seemed to possess dominion over the world might have a singular spectacle. But since conversation with a learned man is pleasing to us, let us recall why antiquity is said, in its primitive state, to have founded these walls.

When farmers celebrated sacred rites to various divinities in groves and villages on festival days, the Athenians first gathered this rustic beginning into an urban spectacle. They called the theater by the Greek term for a viewing place, because a crowd standing at a distance could see everything without obstruction.

The front of the theater is called the stage, from the densest shade of a grove, where, at the beginning of spring, shepherds sang songs in various tones. There the musical performance and the sayings of the wisest age flourished. But little by little it happened that the most honorable disciplines, fleeing the company of the wicked, withdrew from there in modest contemplation.

Tragedy takes its name from the vastness of the voice. Strengthened by resonances in hollow spaces, it seems to produce such a sound that one scarcely believes it could come from a human being. It is raised on goatlike feet because, if anyone had pleased the shepherds with such a voice, he was given a goat as a gift.

Comedy is named from villages. For a *comus* is called a village where country people, in high spirits, mocked human actions in the happiest songs.

To these were added the highly expressive hands of the dancers [Note: [Col. 0643C] See the book *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 30, and Saint Cyprian, book *Against the Spectacles*: “A man broken in all his limbs, and a man more relaxed than feminine softness, whose art it is to make words clear with his hands.” And in the same work: “Breaking sounds at the proper point, he labors to speak with his fingers, ungrateful to the Craftsman who gave him a tongue.” See also above, book I, letter 20. JURET.], articulate fingers, clamorous silence, and silent exposition, which the Muse Polyhymnia is said to have discovered. It showed that human beings could express what they wished without the utterance of the mouth.

The Muses are called by the eastern term as though ὁμοῦσαι [Note: Some prefer to say that the Muses were named ἀπὸ τοῦ μασένειν, that is, “from seeking,” because through them, as the ancients wished, the power of poetry and musical modulation were sought [Col. 0643D]. Our Cassiodorus derives this from Clement of Alexandria in his work *On Music*. The author of the great *Etymologicum* says: “Some say that μοῦσα is μύουσα, for music differs in no respect from the mysteries; but according to others, it is μῶσα, for μῶ and μῶμαι mean ‘I seek,’” and so forth. See the entire passage. FORN.] because they seem to be mutually necessary to one another, like virtues.

The tips of light feathers are painted on their foreheads because [Col. 0644A] their intelligence, borne along by swift thought, looks upon the highest things.

As for the pantomime [Note: [Col. 0643D] Saint Augustine, book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 25, reports that, when a pantomime danced, it was customary for a herald to announce to the people what his movements were intended to signify. See Claudian, *Panegyric on Theodosius*, *On the Spectacles*: “Who by nod and hands [Col. 0644C] ... of tongues,” and so forth. An old and uncertain author, in an epigram on a pantomime:

> As many tongues as limbs, such wondrous art is in the man,
>
> Who makes his joints speak with a silent mouth.

JURET.], whose name comes from his manifold imitation, when he first enters the stage, invited by applause, choruses trained in various instruments stand beside him in harmony. Then that hand of the senses displays a melodious song to the eyes; through arranged signs, as though through certain letters, it instructs the gaze of the onlooker. In it the outlines of events may be read, and without writing it performs what writing has expressed.

The same body represents Hercules and Venus; it presents a woman and a man; it makes a king and a soldier; it renders an old man and a young man, so that you may believe there are many persons in one, distinguished by such varied imitation.

The mime, too, who is now regarded merely as an object of ridicule, was devised with such skill by Philistion that his performances were put into writing, so that he might temper with the happiest maxims the world, seething with devouring cares [Cuj. and Forn., restore].

What shall I say of the ringing of the small cymbals? What of the sweetest sounds, the melody produced by varied percussion? It is received with such an abundance of pleasurable grace that, among the remaining senses, people then judged that hearing had been granted to them for the highest purpose. But a later age, mixing in the slippery [Jur., playful] inventions of the ancients, drew them toward vices; and what had been discovered for the honorable purpose of delight drove minds rushing toward bodily pleasures.

The Romans, usefully adapting these practices, like their other cultural achievements, to their commonwealth, founded this building with lofty conception and astonishing magnificence. Hence it is not without reason believed that Pompey was called “the Great” from this place [Note: [Col. 0644C] Servius of P. Daniel, commenting on *Aeneid* I, “A name derived from great Iulus”: “Just as Alexander,” he says, “so Pompey.” For the Greeks call everything magnificent “great,” as in “Great Mother” and “great gods.” Lampridius, in *Alexander Severus*, writes that the name “Great” was taken by Alexander after his great achievements and by Pompey after his great triumphs, and that it was rejected by the emperor Alexander Severus when the Roman Senate offered it to him. Ovid writes elegantly of Pompey, book I:

> I call upon your name, Great One; your name is the measure of your deeds—
>
> But the man who conquered you was greater still in name.

Caligula deprived Gnaeus Pompey, of ancient lineage, of the name “Great,” Suetonius says. JURET.].

Therefore, whether it can be supported by massive piers or renewed through the zeal of repairing such a structure, we have arranged for expenses to be sent to you from our private treasury, so that both the reputation of so good a work may be acquired by you and antiquity may appear to have been restored more suitably in our time.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0643]

## 78. LETTER I. THEODORIC, KING, TO THE KING OF THE VANDALS

He writes that he most willingly received the weapons sent by him and, through his envoys, confers other gifts upon him in return.

[Col. 0644D]

With [uncertain: pitch-black objects], timber, and boys shining with a youthful [variant: pagan] brightness, and with swords that even cut through weapons, your Fraternity sent these gifts to us—richer in iron than in the price of gold. Their polished brilliance gleams so brightly that they faithfully restore the faces of those who gaze upon them; their edges descend to a sharp point with such evenness that they seem not to have been shaped by files but poured out in fiery furnaces. Their middles, hollowed out into beautiful channels, seem capable of being curled with little wormlike patterns. There so great a shadow of variety is enclosed [corrected reading: plays with variety] that you would rather believe the luminous metal to be woven with different colors.

Your whetstone carefully cleans this metal; your exceedingly bright dust so industriously polishes it that it makes the iron shine like a mirror for men. Nature, in her generosity, granted this dust to your homeland so that it might give us an exceptional impression of this craft. These are swords which one might think belonged to Vulcan, who is said to have refined works of the forge with such elegance that whatever was formed by his hands was believed to be not the work of mortals but divine.

Accordingly, through these and those envoys of ours, while conveying the affection of due greetings, we declare that we have gladly received your weapons, which have conveyed the purposes of good peace. In consideration of your expenses, we grant a reciprocal gift, so that what is returned to you may be as welcome as your gifts were pleasing to us. May the divine powers grant concord, so that by performing these agreeable acts toward one another with grateful minds, we may join the desires of our peoples and, mutually concerned for one another, bind ourselves through reciprocal benefits.

## Letter II. King Theodoric to the Haesti

He announces that he has gladly received the amber sent through their envoys, and describes its origin.

When these and those envoys of yours arrived, we learned that you had shown great eagerness to become known to us, so that, established on the shores of the Ocean, you might be joined with our mind. Your request was exceedingly sweet and welcome to us: you wished our fame to reach you, although we had been unable to send you any message. Love now the man whom you eagerly sought while he was still unknown. For to venture a road among so many peoples is not to have desired something easy.

Therefore, seeking you with affectionate greetings, we declare that we received with grateful mind the amber which you sent through the bearers of this letter. The wave of the Ocean, descending toward you, carries out this very light substance, as the report of your people also stated; but they said that you did not know from where it comes, although your homeland, before all others, offers it for your reception. According to the account of a certain Cornelius, it is read that amber flows from the sap of a tree on the inner islands of the Ocean, and hence it is called *succinum*; little by little it coalesces through the sun’s heat [Forn.: “rises toward the heavens”].

For it becomes a sweating metal of transparent softness, at one time reddening with a saffron color, at another growing rich with a flame-like brilliance. When it has fallen to the boundary of the sea, it is purified by alternating heat and is delivered exposed upon your shores. We judged that this should be explained lest you think that knowledge of what you believe you possess secretly has entirely escaped us.

Therefore seek us more often by the routes which your love has opened, since the acquired concord of wealthy kings is always beneficial: while they are appeased by a small gift, they always look forward to a greater recompense. We have also conveyed certain instructions to you verbally through your envoys, through whom we declare that we have sent what ought to be welcome.

## Letter III. King Theodoric to the Illustrious Honoratus, Quaestor

He confers upon him the office of quaestor, which his brother Decoratus held while he lived, and praises both brothers exceedingly.

It is customary for those who have deserved well to receive our gifts; but by the law of princely inheritance you have claimed the ruler’s benefits for yourself. You obtain your brother’s honor because you are also his equal in wisdom. We do not exclude from the same rewards one whom we have proved to be his equal. Let parents and children now go forth and, encouraged by likeness, compete in the pursuit of the liberal arts.

In you we have established a new law: that parents should succeed to their offices. This advancement is not removed but transferred, because although a substitute person has been appointed, the family does not lose what its most beloved brother acquired. Truly, both of you were chosen for your merits and honored under the auspices of your name! [Note: [Col. 0645] Forn.: “All were chosen by the deserts of nature. Parents foresee certain things when names are bestowed upon their offspring.”] Parents sometimes foresee things when names are bestowed upon their offspring; and since the course of future events proceeds from the high command of Divinity, the thought of one who foresees is instructed. One is enabled to speak what we do not know we have sensed; but after the event we remember what, in ignorance, we truthfully said.

Thus adorned by such an omen, he grew in strength—grew in strength, I say—and, praised by our judgment, entered the circle of palatine honors, assuming the dignity which we customarily bestow upon the prudent. In this he attained something above the rest: he was able to rise after the chosen.

Under the light of our genius he stood fearless yet reverent, appropriately silent and necessarily eloquent, an outstanding relief from our cares. Although he was enriched by the favor of our power, he was more satisfied with the praise of his character and preferred to make himself equal to men of moderate station. Among us the memory of good men lives, because human faithfulness does not know how to fail with death.

He concealed our secrets as though he had forgotten them; he retained our commands in order as though he were writing them down. He served without avarice and sought our favor with the greatest eagerness. We turn aside to praise one who deserved well, but by briefly recalling him we instruct you. He was certainly pleasing, since he does not cease to be so among us even after his death.

We seek in sorrow the man whose loss we mourn. Yet his bitter fate is softened by the fact that you succeed him through a corresponding excellence, because no one feels that he has lost what he recognizes that he has found again in another. Do not follow foreign examples, since such great praises are available to you within your own house. You are adorned through him; he is honored through you. Let merits unite when names have thus been joined.

We rightly expect better things from you, who follow him, because an imitator is always more diligent when he is permitted to choose the virtues of his predecessor and add new ones of his own. Therefore, from the third indiction, we raise you to the dignity of the quaestorship (A.D. 510 or 525), and by the brilliance of our counsel we cause Honoratus to live, so that you may now begin to be what you were previously called. Proceed now by clinging to justice, so that we who granted honor to one inexperienced may confer better honors upon you, who have been thoroughly proven.

## Letter IV. King Theodoric to the Senate of the City of Rome

He declares that he has chosen Honoratus, the brother of Decoratus, as quaestor. After speaking at length in praise of the quaestorship, he praises both brothers and asks that Honoratus be enrolled in their body.

It is certain, Conscript Fathers, that your council flourishes through prudent men; but it is also proved excellent that the dignity of letters is mingled among you. For all whom we raise to the summit of the quaestorship we consider highly learned [Note: [Col. 0647D] The office of quaestor is described here; see also the following book, formula 5; Book VIII, Letters 11 and 14. Fornaceus.]—such as it is fitting for interpreters of the laws and participants in our counsels to be.

This is a dignity found neither in wealth nor in birth alone; only learning joined with prudence can obtain it. For although we confer benefits in other offices, from this office we always receive them. It is indeed a fortunate portion of our cares: it enters the doorway of our thought, and recognizes the breast in which public concerns are revolved. Consider what ought to be judged of one who shares in so great a secret.

From him knowledge of the laws is sought; the prayers of petitioners converge upon him; and what is more precious than every treasure, the reputation of our civil administration is entrusted to him. Under a just quaestor the conscience of the innocent becomes secure, while only the hopes of the wicked are made anxious. When the hope of secretly plundering is taken from the wicked, attention is devoted to good morals.

He guards each person’s proper rights, restrained with money and generous in equity, ignorant of deceit and most ready to assist. He serves the ruler’s intelligence, which surpasses all things; he is compelled to speak with the voice of one for whom no equal can be found. Is this office, empty of vices and full of virtues, which he was able to discharge in our presence, not worthy of having him as your colleague?

You know from what distinguished stock he has advanced. You remember Decoratus laboring earnestly in advocacy [Note: “Advocacy” is discussed in *Digest* 9, concerning customs and penalties; and in *Digest* 1, at the end, concerning the office of the urban prefect. Pliny, *Letters* 1.21: advocacy, or *advocatia*, is a kind of right belonging either to an estate or to a benefit, which we commonly call a rent, in feudal usage, title “On maintaining peace”: “If anyone should hold his advocacy or any other benefit.” Theodore Balsamon establishes two kinds of advocates: one consisting of those who held a station in the forum and received grain-tickets from the emperor; the other of those who practiced it as a liberal profession and served in the office of advocacy. See title 8 of Photius’s *Nomocanon*, chapter 13.], by which he joined himself to every good man through integrity.

He attended your cases as a faithful advocate, assisting in necessary matters; he brought the spirit of a judge to the benches of those hearing cases. He deservedly received frequent applause, because he handled wisely what had to be argued. Those who correct themselves before becoming their own judges do not know how to suffer the loss of shame.

Though inferior in rank, he proved himself a patron to consular men; and although he was considered unequal to your honors, he was called a patrician and received with distinction in the most celebrated hearing [that is, as a client]. It is very rare, Conscript Fathers, to speak with substance and, when much must be said, not to utter words of hesitation. This was most certainly true of Decoratus, and you had proved it even before our judgments.

For who could have failed to recognize him in his day as a kind of helmsman of litigation, when he strove to pass through the reefs of lawsuits? The man who did not seek his assistance had less need of laws. We no longer complain of his premature death, for from his fruitful stock a brother has sprung. The man who had previously been sheltered in his brother’s shadow, once nature’s law removed that brother, spread the locks of his own fame into the open.

For he who was justly the early [Fornaceus and Cor.: “predecessor”] bearer of the family’s good qualities, being first in order of birth, grew in strength [Note: First-born children are held in greater honor and affection. Philo Judaeus, in his speech of Agrippa to Caius; Plutarch, *Life of the Ten Orators*. Hence Procopius, *Persian War* 1: the law called Cabades the elder by reason of age. The same author, *Vandalic War* 3: when the aged Gizeric was dying, he composed a testament directing the Vandals to transfer the succession of his kingdom to the nearest descendant of the male line, and among those descendants to the one who was older.].

The noble offspring preserved in the successor the fruit which it had lost in the predecessor. This agrees with that richly endowed branch which continually grows in Virgil’s verse:

> For when this one is torn away, another golden one does not fail,  
> and the branch grows green with metal of the same kind.

This man too cultivated eloquence through advocacy. Yielding to his brother the reputation of the city of Rome, he preferred to involve himself in the affairs of the people of Spoletium—a matter as difficult as it is understood to be removed from your prudence.

Among well-mannered people, to uphold what is just was very easy; among provincials, however, who conducted themselves with wandering freedom, it was exceedingly difficult. He seemed to have taught moderation in law, where even judges themselves are often carried away by wicked desire. And just as they seem to themselves to excel others in moderation, so they do not permit their own wishes to be opposed.

In such circumstances it is difficult to vindicate the laws, and great persuasive force is required to recall a judge’s venality to the purpose of right. Therefore, Conscript Fathers, gladly accept our judgment, and let your bosom gratefully receive Honoratus, raised to the summit of the quaestorship. He deserves to be loved by you, since he has proved worthy of such great honors.

## Letter V. King Theodoric to Mannila, the Sajo

He explains what he must and must not do in the office of *sajo*.

It is praiseworthy to double the guard in that sphere which is known to have been devised for the needs of the state. Through it, the usefulness of embassies and the speed of our commands are carried out. It also gives effect to the powers of the palace through various orders, and by frequent collections enriches our treasury, so that nearly everything conducted in the state is completed through its courier service.

What is proved suitable for public utility ought therefore always to be ready, lest what was devised for speed instead bring an unsuitable delay to those who are hastening. Therefore, when the prefects of the praetorium and the masters of offices have selected a place for public utility, we order you, stationed there by their command, to cut off the wicked presumption of those who exceed their authority with such severity that, whether Goth or Roman, anyone who presumes to use a post-horse without the authorization of our office or of those concerned must immediately be compelled by you to pay one hundred solidi for each horse.

With equal severity we impose this judgment upon those who presume to use courier horses beyond the number allowed by their travel authorizations. We also order that no more than one hundred pounds be loaded upon the pack-horses [see Book IV, Letter 47]. For it is exceedingly absurd that one from whom speed is demanded should be crushed by heavy weights. A bird itself grows sluggish when burdened with weight; ships whose hulls do not feel fatigue move more heavily when filled. What can a four-footed animal do when it collapses under excessive pressure?

If anyone is found to have more than the prescribed measure, let him be struck with a penalty of two ounces of gold. We decree that this sum, immediately exacted, should—as has already been established by earlier edicts—be advanced through the office of the master of the rank for the courier service. It is just that he be compelled to sell what he is known to have used to overload a public horse. Let the man who refused to be swift by choice be freed from his burdens.

Moreover, we admonish you not to presume upon the privileges of those placed over you, nor by any usurpation to debase [Note: Some read *deneges* (“deny”). The word *genius* and *geniatus* is frequent in Cassiodorus; hence I think *degeniare* means “to dishonor” or “diminish.” *Degeniatus* occurs below in Book XII, Letter 10.] whatever the revered antiquity has sanctioned them as possessing by authority [Greek and Cujacius and the edition: “deny”]. Through you we wish to double the guard, not to remove the safeguard of ancient custom.

## Letter VI. King Theodoric to the Stabularius of Comitiva

He orders him to apply all the property of Thomas, who owed twelve thousand solidi to the treasury for certain royal estates, to the fisc, to be returned to Thomas if he pays by the Kalends of September; otherwise it is to be handed over to John, who had promised to bring the aforesaid sum into the treasury.

A petition should be received when it does not conflict with public interests, and the desires of private persons should be embraced when they seek a remedy in such a way that they do not seem to cause us loss.

We have therefore learned from the complaint of the most illustrious John that Thomas received certain estates of our house—that is, this estate and that—and that he now remains a defaulter to our interests in the amount of ten thousand solidi, failing to discharge the debt through various deceptions. This also became fully clear to us through the representations of our nobles.

Therefore we believe that the matter should be secured by this remedy: you are to apply all the property of the aforesaid Thomas to public law under fixed inscriptions [Note: Just as at Athens marked estates were called pledged, while free estates were called *ἄστικτα* (“unmarked”), according to Harpocration under the word *ὅρος* and Pollux, *Onomasticon* 3, under *ἄστικτον χωρίον*, so inscriptions affixed to a private estate by the ruler—*panonceaux* in French—indicate that the property has been claimed for the treasury. See also the following letter and Book IX, Letter 18. For the interpretation of this passage, see my notes on Book IX, Letter 16; to these may be added Augustine’s words concerning those who affix the titles of powerful men to their own estates: “Lest some powerful person invade his house, he places there the titles of the powerful—lying titles. He himself wishes to be the possessor, and wishes the front of his house to be fortified by another’s title, so that when the title has been read, anyone terrified by the power of the name may refrain from invasion.”].

Thus, if Thomas has not paid by the day of the September Kalends the amount that has reasonably been laid out, the aforesaid property is to be handed over to the most illustrious John, who promised to discharge his debt into our treasury.

But if the aforesaid Thomas should perhaps be able to pay his obligation within the prescribed time, let everything taken from him be returned intact, so that neither our treasury seems to suffer loss nor we be thought to have denied our subjects the justice customary to us. We could indeed delay still further, if it were useful to endure the most negligent man, whom we have always found unprepared throughout so long a period.

## Letter VII. King Theodoric to John, Most Illustrious Man, Treasurer

He hands over Thomas’s property to him, provided that he pays ten thousand solidi into the treasury on Thomas’s behalf and Thomas himself does not satisfy the debt by the Kalends of September.

It is fitting to bring safely to fulfillment the wishes of those who prefer to preserve public interests; nor do we allow those who have made us secure against losses to be anxious about their own loss.

We have therefore learned from your representation that, during that indiction, we entrusted certain estates of our patrimony located in the province of Apulia—that is, this estate and that—to the honorable man Thomas under a *libellary* title [Note: The term *libellary* is discussed in Book I, title 5, “By what means a fief is lost under the name of a *libellus*,” and Book II, title 55, “On the prohibition of alienating a fief by Frederick.” Perhaps because the agreement was made by a brief *libellus* and written instrument as a perpetual arrangement: “when writing has intervened,” *Code* on emphyteutic law 1; Leo, *Novels* 13, “On perpetual emphyteuses”: “with the entire contribution evidently being entered in the documents of the grant.”], that is, by contract.

But through mismanagement of what he had received, he became a defaulter to the public accounts in the amount of ten thousand solidi from these and those collections. Although frequently admonished by our nobles, he negligently refused, with detestable cunning, to repay what he owed.

And lest some dispute arise for you in the future, you attest that you are willing to satisfy the amount owed to the public interests on this condition: that the estates of the aforesaid debtor be handed over to you in place of a pledge.

Therefore, by this present order we confirm your request, which was conceived according to justice. First, you are not to fear any public claim arising from this matter. Then, on this condition, we assign to you all the property of Thomas the debtor—both what he now possesses and what he possessed at the time when he first became liable to our accounts—which we previously caused to be claimed in our name by fixed inscriptions.

We relax this only out of consideration for humanity: he shall have time until the September Kalends to repay the amount due; or, if not, when you bring the money owed to the illustrious count of our patrimony on the aforesaid day, all his property, as we have said, shall be applied to your advantage. We do not think this will be a sad matter for the loser, since he does not seem to lose everything when he knows that you, his son-in-law [Cor. and Gam.: “kinsman”], are acquiring it. What you might have obtained by right of succession, you possess by the condition of a purchaser.

## Letter VIII. King Theodoric to Anastasius, the Consular

He decrees that he is to arrange for squared stones to be transported from the city of Faventia to Ravenna without anyone’s suffering loss.

It is fitting that your Sublimity should give steadfast obedience to our commands, so that what is arranged by a salutary order may be brought to completion. Prudence knows how to fulfill what is entrusted to it with moderation and to carry out delegated tasks with an effective plan, without the stain of ingratitude [Note: Elegant, although in some copies the word is written incorrectly, as Cicero used “the charge of ingratitude” in a letter to Atticus. Fornerius. Sidonius Apollinaris likewise speaks of “the stain of cruelty” and “the stain of suspicion,” and Honorius of “the stain of excuse” in *Code of Theodosius* 16, concerning agents in public affairs; Valentinian, *Novel* on thirty-year prescription; and Saint Ambrose, “the stain of error.”].

Therefore we order you to send a civil enforcement officer to the city of Faventia, so that, without anyone’s extortion or loss, squared stones [Note: He calls marble “squared,” as above in Book II, Letter 7, meaning stones. Hence *quadratores* (“squarers” or “stone-cutters”) are mentioned in Book II, “On exemptions for craftsmen,” *Code of Theodosius*, p. 418, and in Book I of the *Code of Justinian*, under the same title. In the ancient story of the Four Crowned Ones: “The stone-cutters began to cut the stone for the column’s polishing.”] may be transported to the city of Ravenna by our command, so that we may rejoice that our wish has been fulfilled and the opportunity for complainers to cry out may be removed.

## Letter IX. King Theodoric to the Possessors of Feltria

He orders them to assist in constructing the walls of a new city in the region of Tridentum.

Public necessity ought to be fulfilled through the devotion of many, because it is not fitting for a few to undertake what is known to benefit the majority. Otherwise royal commands grow lukewarm and slacken while a useful matter is entrusted to the weak.

Our authority has therefore ordered a city to be built in the Tridentine region. But because the smallness of the territory cannot support the magnitude of the work, our concern has provided that, after receiving appropriate wages, you all collectively undertake the measured extent of the walls [Note: Taken from civil law: neighbors and citizens contribute according to their means to the construction or restoration of public works. *Code* on public works 11, “All”; *Digest* “He who is from a village,” concerning municipalities and inhabitants. Indeed, this was expressly done even after ecclesiastical immunity had been removed: *Code* on public works, “To the harbors,” 6; *Code* on sacred churches, “For construction”; Novel 133.].

You who are joined by proximity are to do this, so that, with suitable assistance [Note: Above, Book III, Letter 26, meaning wages and salary; *Digest* “The seller,” final clause, concerning common estates; “From guardians,” final clause, concerning the administration of guardianship; *Code* on advocates of different courts 3 and 5; *Code of Theodosius* on the allowances granted to shipmasters 32. It is otherwise commonly understood as *παραμυθία* (“consolation” or “encouragement”), as in “women,” concerning adoption; *Digest* on the law of dowry 6; *Code of Theodosius* 2, “If a partner in a petition or an heir has died. Fornerius.”], what perhaps seems impossible to a few may be completed more securely.

This condition is expressly established: no one is to be excused from these burdens; consequently, not even the divine house is exempt [Note: *Code* on construction, “For instructions,” 7, concerning sacred churches; Harmenopulus 2.5. Here “the divine house” means the ruler’s house. See what Saint Juretus said to Symmachus, Book V, Letter 64.].

## Letter X. King Theodoric to Veranus, the Sajo

He orders him to ensure that the Gepids passing through, whom he was sending to guard Gaul, cause no damage to Venetia or Liguria, and therefore that all necessities be supplied to them.

Since, with God’s help, a most fortunate army is being led forth for the general defense, care must be taken lest they themselves be exhausted by unforeseen scarcity or—what must not be said—appear to suffer the devastation of our provinces. The first degree of prosperity is not to be harmful to one’s own people, so that we may not appear to have afflicted the fortunes of those for whose advantage we labor.

Therefore, by this present authority, we entrust to your devotion the task of making the multitude of Gepids whom we have ordered to hasten to Gaul for purposes of defense pass through Venetia and Liguria with every moderation. Lest any opportunity for excess be offered them, our generosity has sent them an allowance of three solidi each week, so that among our provincials they may have not the desire to plunder but the opportunity for commerce [Note: That is, for grain, according to Ulpian, the reciprocal right to buy and sell, *Fragments*, title 19. Theophilus, concerning useless stipulations, §1: “For *commercium* is the power to be able to sell or buy”; *Digest* on things pledged 1, § “that.” When Paulus speaks of acting for the sake of trade, *Digest* on contracts of purchase 12, “The senate,” Ulpian, treating the same matter, denotes it by the terms *commercium* and *promercium*, *Digest* on laws 1, 41, “The rest.” Marcianus and Alexander likewise use the verb “to trade” in the same sense, *Digest* on damages inflicted  ult.; *Code* on private buildings 2. The Greek interpreters explained the same expression as “for the sake of business” (*πραγματείας χάριν*), “through trade” (*δι’ ἐμπορίαν*), and “for the purpose of conducting business” (*ἐπὶ τῷ πραγματεύσασθαι*), Book XIX of the *Basilica*.].

For the peace of all, our indulgence also grants this: if either their wagons are damaged by the longer journey or their animals, worn out, grow weak, you, as guardian and mediator, are to arrange for them to be exchanged with the possessors without any oppression. Those who give animals in exchange, whether better in bodily condition or quality, are to be content with small but healthy animals, because the life of those exhausted by excessive fatigue is uncertain. Thus they will not lack the necessary transport, and no one will regard himself as injured by such an exchange.

## Letter XI. King Theodoric to the Gepids Sent to Gaul

He grants the Gepids departing for Gaul three solidi in gold per week.

It had indeed been our arrangement to order provisions to be expended for you as you traveled [Note: *Digest* on theft against sailors, innkeepers, and stable-keepers 1; *Code* on billeting and epidemics 5. In this passage, however, a learned man supplied the reading “traveling through.”], but lest the provisions themselves be spoiled or difficult to provide, we have chosen to send you three solidi in gold each week. Thus you may choose lodgings according to the abundance of pasture and buy whatever is most suitable for you.

This arrangement also helps the possessor, if he knows that you will purchase what you need. Move forward successfully; go with moderation. May your journey be such as befits those who labor for the safety of all.

## Letter XII. King Theodoric to Theodahad, the Illustrious Man

He orders the Palentian estate, seized from the heirs of Argolicus and Amandianus, to be restored; but if the invaders have any claim in their favor, he orders them to come to court to defend their right.

If we command everyone to cultivate and love justice, how much more must we command those who glory in our proximity—those who ought to conduct everything to their credit, so that they may display the splendor of royal kinship! This is true and unquestionable nobility, adorned by proven character, because it is a beautiful contribution to reputation to reject shameful profits of money.

The heirs of the illustrious Argolicus and the most distinguished Amandianus have therefore complained to us in a humble petition that the Palentian estate, which our generosity had transferred to them as compensation, so that they might console themselves for the loss of the Arbitanian estate by this advantage, was indecently seized by your men without any existing grounds. Thus the fault of culpable seizure grew from the place where an example of glorious moderation ought to have been given.

Accordingly, if their assertions are not invalidated by falsehood, let Your Greatness restore what was taken. And if you believe that anything may properly belong to you, send a person fully instructed in law to our court by every means, so that the civil dispute, established [Cor. and Gam.: “appeased”] according to law, may receive its conclusion.

For there everything done is attributed rather to your discredit, and you incur greater damage to your reputation while you do not strive to avoid such acts. Here, however, the cases contend according to their own rights, and anyone, however humble, is adjudged without derogation when he is overcome with justice as witness.

## Letter XIII. King Theodoric to Eutropius and Acretius

He admonishes them to provide the provisions established for the army, lest the provincials be exposed to its plundering.

You ought to devote your zeal to the state with a grateful mind, because you have recognized that we grant many things to those who have deserved well. For, out of regard for piety, we promise a reciprocal favor, although we order everything for your sake.

Therefore, by this present command, we believe that you must be admonished to provide the provisions established for the army, so that neither the army may be neglected contrary to our wish nor a ruinous act of plundering burden the provincials. An army is held more advantageously under the law of allotted expenses than if it is permitted to lay waste everything. Presumption does not know how to observe measure, and one cannot bring under control a person to whom license has seemed to be granted.

Accordingly, let the army receive its assigned food supply, lest any part of it be able to suffer the aforesaid violence [some copies: “annoyance”].

## Letter XIV. King Theodoric to Severianus, the Illustrious Man

He places him in charge of the taxes to be imposed upon each person according to the diversity of his possessions, and orders him to investigate whether the judges, because of their frequent journeys through the provinces, have inflicted unlawful expenses upon the inhabitants.

The logic of justice persuades us to restrain those who exceed their bounds, so that the sweetness of tranquility may reach everyone. For how can equality be maintained if the strength of ordinary people is not allowed to rise?

We have therefore learned, from the frequent complaints of our provincials, that the capable possessors of Suavia have not only left the tax obligation of their estates in a meager condition [for “rejected”; the Greek and Cujacius read “recoiled”], but have also, through criminal commerce, applied something of it here and there to their own profits, so that a public obligation becomes a private advantage.

We have long desired this to be corrected through many means; but until now it seems to have been delayed for your praise, so that confidence might be more readily placed in you when, after many negligences, you most effectively prove your diligence.

Therefore, with the prudence for which you are known, we order you to examine every possessor with considered justice and to regulate the equality of the tax on this basis: the public assessment is to be imposed according to the quality of the possessions and the persons, while whatever was done under other arrangements has been annulled by universal redemption. Thus justice is completed and the strength of our provincial subjects is restored.

Let the severity of the laws pursue those who are found to have imposed a census without our command and who, according to their own pleasure, have shifted the burdens of some onto others, so that they may repair every loss to those whom they improperly damaged.

We also order that an inquiry be made so that the account of collections may be examined among the defenders, curials, and possessors. Whatever, from the eighth indiction [that is, A.D. 515], the possessor proves to have recently paid beyond the taxable solidus, if it is not shown to have been paid into our treasury or to have been reasonably expended on necessary provincial expenses, must by every means be corrected as an unjust presumption.

Do not consider this part worthy of neglect either: if what the accountant of our chamber received is not reasonably shown to have been expended, it must be returned by the unjust holder. For what could be more absurd than that our generosity, which we wish to benefit everyone, should now be suppressed by the furtive profit of a few?

The provincial judges, curials, and defenders are also said to inflict unlawful expenses upon possessors, both through the courier service and in other matters. We decree that you investigate and correct this according to the laws.

Let the ancient barbarians who have chosen to be joined in marriage to Roman women, whatever title they used to acquire estates, be compelled to pay the fisc for the ground they possess and to comply with the additional imposed burdens.

The Roman judge, however, because of the expenses imposed upon provincials, which are reported to burden the poor, is to visit each municipality only once a year. He is to be provided with no more than three days’ provisions, as the safeguards of the laws have prescribed. For our ancestors wished the journeys of judges to be not a burden but an advantage to provincials.

The domestic officers of the Gothic count, and likewise the *vicedomini*, are said to have taken things from provincials through arranged [some copies: “continued”] threats. Once these matters have been brought by your justice [some copies: “by our urgency”] into examination, whatever you discover to have been done unjustly in this regard, you shall legally regulate without postponement.

After every such matter, and others relating to the public welfare or to the provincials, has been examined with complete care, we wish you in all respects to do what ought not to displease our gentleness.

Our foresight has also provided that, once everything has been discovered by you through careful and equitable inquiry, it be ordered to be entered in the *polyptychs* [Note: That is, in the registers of assessments and public accounts, according to Sirmondus. Below, in this same book, Letters 36 and 39; Andrea Alciatus, *Parerga* 2.26; Gregory, Book VII, Letter 40, and Book XII, Letter 30. Fornerius.]. Thus the proofs of your good faith may become clear, and no seeds of fraud that we wish to abolish may be repeated thereafter [Note: For this reason, tax tables were formerly engraved publicly. See century 6, chapters 34 and 40; century 1, chapter 72.].

## Letter XV. King Theodoric to All Possessors Established in Suavia

He writes that he has sent Severinus to them with edicts so that he may relieve those oppressed by the weight of taxation.

[Col. 0655B] Although our court, with God’s help, grants justice to all litigants, and although remedies for subjects flow from here to the remaining regions of the kingdom as though from a living spring, nevertheless, moved by frequent appeals, we have ingeniously discovered a way both to grant you equity and to abolish the fatigue of a long journey; for benefits obtained without any difficulty are sweeter.

Accordingly, we have sent the illustrious and magnificent Severinus, instructed in our commands, so that he may accomplish among you what he has always known to please us. For he has seen how highly we esteem the just [84] man, and how our clemency smiles upon good actions. He is exercising precisely what he rightly judges us to accept with gratitude; nor can rapacity please a temperate ruler by any compensation [Cuj., Gr. and For., reason].

Let the tumult of the injured therefore approach him confidently; let anyone oppressed by any injustice hope for relief. We remove from you the difficulty of lodging complaints, while crimes committed at their very beginnings are cut off. Let anyone burdened without cause by the weight of another’s tax cry out without fear, assured of receiving the remedy provided by the laws. For we trust that, through those whom our ordinances appoint, no harm will come to the innocent.

The decrees [Note: “Decrees”: Book I of the *Codex Theodosianus*, *De rei vindicatione*; law 2, *De episcopali audientia*; law 1, *Si per obreptionem*; law 5, *De haereticis*; law 18, *De medicis*, of the same title. The proud language of rulers concerning themselves: likewise the expression “at the prayer of our Eternity,” law 3 of the *Codex Theodosianus*, *De fabricis*; law 2 of the same title. Nor should such expressions be tolerated: “an offering was presented to our altars,” the final law, *De relationibus*, in the *Codex Theodosianus*. Novel constitutions of the *Codex Theodosianus*: *De mulieribus quae se servas esse profitentur*; Valentinian’s Novel I, *De testamentis*; Book VIII, *Quicumque*, *Codex Theodosianus*; “our divine power,” the sole law, *Codex Theodosianus*, *De imaginibus*—as though emperors were regarded not as subject to the mortal condition and law of human beings, but as possessing a unique and divine right. FORN. “Eternity,” “altars,” and “the divine power” of rulers were noted by D. Juret in his commentary on Symmachus, Book IV, Letter 54.] which we have issued concerning your tranquility and the equalization of taxes, and which we have delivered to the aforementioned illustrious Severinus, will make known what we have ordered, so that each person may clearly understand the matter concerning which he ought to petition.
