## LETTER XVI. KING THEODORIC TO ABUNDANTIUS, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He orders him throughout Italy to seek out and purchase timber for the construction of one thousand *dromones*, and to assemble a suitable number of sailors to serve the fleets.

[Col. 0656A]

Although, as is always our custom, we judge whatever benefits the commonwealth to be useful, and therefore whatever we command may be most welcome to all because it is known to benefit everyone, nevertheless we must take care that the ruler’s desire should become burdensome to no one. For if noble plans are not properly executed, they are unwelcome; and only that is called complete which is praised both in intention and in action.

Since frequent concern therefore troubled our mind with the thought that Italy possesses no ships, although it has such an abundance of timber that it sends sought-after supplies even to other [Col. 0656B] provinces, with God inspiring us we have decided for the present to undertake the construction of one thousand *dromones* [Note: *Dromones* are ships, as Ethicus Hister writes in Book V. Cassiodorus here mentions them as suitable for transporting grain; from them their sailors were called *dromonarii*. Procopius, Book III, *Gothic War*; Isidore, Book IX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1, calls *dromones* long ships. Since they are more suitable for flight and speed, they seem to have been named from δρόμος, “course” or “running,” as though they were swift vessels. Julius Pollux, *Onomasticon*, under the emperor Commodus, called them *holcades*; Fulgentius called a skiff a δρομάδην; and Moschopulus used θωὴ ναῦς, a term also familiar to the sailors living along our Loire, *Toue*, from παρὰ τὸ θεῖν, “from running.” FORN.], which can both transport public grain and, if necessary, confront hostile ships.

But we believe that the accomplishment of so great an undertaking must be secured through your Magnificence’s vigilance. Therefore send craftsmen throughout Italy to seek suitable timber for the work. If anywhere near the coast you find cypresses or pines, let the owners be consulted and paid an appropriate price. These alone are the trees that should be brought into the assessment. The rest, because of their low value, need not be appraised.

But lest our provision languish abandoned halfway through its execution, we now order you, with God’s help, to procure a suitable number of sailors under the following arrangement. If one whom we deem necessary is another person’s slave, either hire him to serve in the fleets or, if the owner himself prefers this, let him receive a reasonable price and cede to the public his rights of ownership over the man. If the person chosen enjoys freedom, he is to understand that he will receive five solidi as a gift and a suitable allowance of provisions.

Those who are stripped from their own masters are likewise to be treated in this way, since serving a ruler is itself a form of freedom. There are many who endure labor after harsh masters have pressed down their necks. Nevertheless, the aforesaid sailors should receive from our seat, by way of earnest money [ed., “expenses”], two or three solidi according to the standing of each man, so that whenever each is summoned he may be found ready.

We do not order fishermen to be included in this arrangement, because one is painfully deprived when a man possessed for the provision of delicacies is taken away, especially since another customary duty is to face raging winds and plow fish-rich waters.

## LETTER XVII. KING THEODORIC TO ABUNDANTIUS, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He praises him for the sudden construction of the ships and orders him to send them to Ravenna and arrange for others to be built. He also forbids fishermen from blocking the channels of the Mincius, Ollius, and other rivers with their fences against sailors.

We must apply ourselves energetically to undertakings once the nearness of completion has begun to smile upon them, since the hope of success removes weariness from labor, and it is a great source of encouragement to believe that what is desired is being brought to completion.

Some time ago, therefore, we ordered Your Magnificence to prepare sailors from the shores of Italy [Col. 0657B], so that the rowers’ hands would receive the *dromones* which industry had succeeded in constructing. But you, responding to our judgment and choice, have demonstrated how certain completion can be when what is sought is entrusted to men of the greatest effectiveness.

You report that what could scarcely have been believed to have been begun has already been completed [Note: This resembles what the Emperor Constantine says in Book VII, *De operibus publicis*, of the *Codex Theodosianus*: “The judges are to be admonished,” etc. JUR.], so that the construction of the ships has been completed almost as swiftly as ships themselves normally sail.

Nor have you merely related this in words: you have suddenly brought before our eyes a forest transformed into a fleet, dwellings upon the water, feet for an army, men who do not fail through labor but carry out their assigned tasks without wavering—a trireme revealing such a number of oars while carefully concealing the faces of the men. We read that the Argonauts first devised this arrangement.

It has proved suitable both for armed forces and for commerce, so that we, who once desired to behold foreign fleets, may now send both terror and splendor to other provinces [85]. You have adorned the commonwealth, restored through your undertaking. The Greek has nothing to reproach us for, nor may the African mock us. The envious see flourishing among us what they used to obtain only at great expense in order to fulfill their wishes.

Now provide the aforesaid equipment: above all, sails, which make the wings of ships; flying linen, as it were, a kind of spirit for speeding keels, heralds of cargoes, quiet aids to sailors. Through their assistance, men at leisure accomplish what even the swiftest birds scarcely manage to complete.

Isis is said to have first suspended this device when, with the daring devotion of a woman, she searched the seas for her son Apochran. Thus, while maternal love hastened to fulfill its desire, she seemed to reveal to the world something previously unknown.

Therefore, with divine assistance supporting us—the power of which is to fulfill the wishes of human beings—on the Ides of June, the entire assembly of ships is to gather at the city of [Col. 0658A] Ravenna, so that matters already rejoicing in their imminent completion may be brought to their fullest accomplishment.

But since, with God’s help, we desire the number of *dromones* to be increased, if any timber suitable for their construction can be found along either bank of the Po, we order that it be cut without obstruction. We wish what is enjoined for the present undertaking to be granted without prejudice to the owners. Let our Po send native ships out onto the sea, and let the fir tree, nourished and raised by the river’s waters, learn to surpass the piled-up waves of the sea.

We also consider it necessary to eliminate what we have learned was done at your suggestion: no one is to dare, in navigable rivers running through different territories—that is, in the Mincius, Ollius, Anser, Arno, and Tiber—to close the channels of the rivers [Col. 0658B] with disgraceful fences for the sake of fishing [Note: To obstruct the freedom of a river. Praetorian interdicts were issued on this matter to prevent navigation: “You shall do nothing in a public river or on its bank”; “You shall introduce nothing into a public river or onto its bank by which a station or passage for navigation may be made worse,” *Digest*, Book XLIII, *De fluminibus*, law 1. Likewise, that navigation on a public river should be permitted, *Pandects*, Book XLIII, titles 13 and 14. Aulus Gellius also reports and interprets the edicts of ancient praetors concerning the leasing of rivers for the removal of obstructions, Book XI, chapter 17. This corresponds to the established practice of clearing the bed of the Loire, which the inhabitants of Orléans call *balizer la Loire*. FORN.]; and whatever has been undertaken is to be removed immediately.

Let the river lie open for the passage of ships. Let it be enough to seek pleasures for human enjoyment by customary arts, and not to obstruct the freedom of a river by rustic contrivance [Ac., “fabrication”], lest—something shameful to say—private pleasure appear to have stood in the way of the public interest.

## LETTER XVIII. KING THEODORIC TO UVALIA, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND COUNT OF THE PATRIMONY

He writes that he has ordered sailors to be sought out and sent to Ravenna, and then commands that, if timber suitable for constructing *dromones* is found along the bank of the Po even on royal estates, it may be cut.

Just as the public interest concerns the preservation of all, so it must be advanced through the zeal and labor of everyone, because it is an opportunity for great praise if, in a common cause, something appears to have been accomplished by one person in particular [Col. 0658C]. For he creates a source of commendation for others who nevertheless recognize that he has benefited himself as well.

You will remember, therefore, that we previously ordered craftsmen skilled in navigation to be sought throughout our household. With God’s help, we now order that those who have been secured arrive without delay at the city of Ravenna on the Ides of June, so that their arrival may suitably assist the construction of the ships. Matters must not be divided in such a way that they seem to create delay for themselves; and it is of little use to complete one undertaking unless it happens that both can be managed.

If any timber suitable for constructing *dromones* can be found along the bank of the Po on royal estates, permission is to be granted to the craftsmen assigned to this work by the magnificent Abundantius, the praetorian prefect, to cut it [Col. 0658D]. For we wish to begin this example with our own estates [Note: “We wish to begin this example with our own estates,” so that no one may find burdensome an order that constrains even the ruler, *Codex*, Book IV, *De legibus*, law 4. A person who establishes a law ought to subject himself to the law. Seneca, on legislators, Letter 91. Ausonius, quoting Pittacus: “Obey the law, whoever you have sanctioned the law.” Although the ruler is released from the laws, *Digest*, “The Princeps,” *De legibus*. Dionysius, Book LIII: Λέλυνται δὲ τῶν νόμων, “They are released from the laws,” that is, “they are free from every compulsory observance and are bound by none of the written provisions.” Hence King Theodahad below, Book X, Letter 16: “Although we are able to do everything, we believe that only what deserves praise is permitted to us.” FORN.], so that no one may find burdensome an order that constrains even the ruler.

## LETTER XIX. KING THEODORIC TO GUDINAND, SAIO

He orders that the sailors who have been assembled be sent to Ravenna as quickly as possible.

[Col. 0659A]

Anyone who effectively carries out what has been entrusted to him causes greater things to be entrusted to him, because a task is undoubtedly committed to one who has been proved most capable. It is also an honorable support for a second judgment and evidence of the first [Note: Law “Not everyone,” section “by barbarians,” *Digest*, *De re militari*. FORNER.].

Therefore, by order of the magnificent Abundantius, praetorian prefect, and Uvalia, count of the patrimony, we order you to hasten to that province, so that, both from the royal household and from those living elsewhere, you may compel the sailors secured according to the earlier commands to hurry, with God’s help, to the city of Ravenna on the Ides of June. Thus no delay may be brought to commands of such distinction.

Take care, therefore, that venality does not stain you [Col. 0659B], nor disgraceful negligence envelop you; and do not allow yourself to be crushed by the weight of so great an undertaking falling upon you, should you prove unequal to matters of such magnitude and importance.

## LETTER XX. KING THEODORIC TO AVILFO, SAIO

He orders him to go to the bank of the Po with craftsmen to cut timber suitable for *dromones*, but without harming the possessors. He also orders the fences to be removed from the rivers Mincius, Ollius, Anser, Tiber, and Arno, so that the river channels may be open to the passage of ships.

[86] We have learned that timber suitable for constructing *dromones* is to be found along both banks of the Po. Therefore, by the present command, we assign you the task of going without delay, together with craftsmen, to the designated places [Col. 0659C], in accordance with the arrangements of the magnificent Abundantius, praetorian prefect, and Uvalia, count of the patrimony. Whether the timber is found on a royal estate or on private property, see that it is obtained without delay, for we believe that no one will find burdensome what, with God’s help, is being prepared for the common good.

Nevertheless, we wish you to carry out what has been entrusted to you in such a way that nothing appears to be deliberately sought in order to injure a possessor. Let only what is necessary for our advantage be taken. Do not demand anything from an owner which cannot afterward be said to have been received for public purposes. We order wild timber to be cut, not anything belonging to another’s property to be violently torn away. Such things benefit us as cannot burden our people. If the present necessity did not require them, the owner would consider himself not to possess them.

In the rivers Mincius, Ollius, Anser, Tiber, and Arno, we have learned that certain people have obstructed the course of the river, insofar as navigation is concerned, with fences [Col. 0659D]. We wish you, in accordance with the orders of the magnificent Abundantius, praetorian prefect, to remove this in every way. Nor are you to permit anyone to undertake anything of the kind again [Col. 0660A]. The unobstructed channels must be left open for the passage of ships [Note: Fishing is to be conducted with nets, not fences, and the rivers are to be cleared; this is likewise prescribed by the jurists, *Digest*, Book XLIII, title “That nothing be done in a public river”; the sole law of the *Codex*, Book X, title 29, *De Alexandrinis Primatibus*. This agrees with what Aulus Gellius interprets in the edicts of the ancient praetors concerning the public leasing of rivers for the removal of obstructions: they were to be cleared of nets—that is, trees projecting either from the banks of rivers or from their channels. They were called “nets,” as it were, because they impeded passing ships and seemed to entangle them. So he writes in Book XI, chapter 17, of the *Attic Nights*. FORN.].

For we know that fishing is to be conducted with nets, not fences. From this too the detestable greed of those people is revealed: they hasten to enclose for themselves as much as might have reached many.

## LETTER XXI. KING THEODORIC TO CAPUANUS, SENATOR

He praises him at length, appoints him rector of the decuries, and explains what this dignity entails.

If our judgments had chosen you as a novice, if you had come before the tribunal of examination unknown to us, we would think it necessary to advise you with what prudence and dignity you should conduct yourself. But everyone believes that you possess an understanding of every virtue, since you have deserved to be trained in the militia of letters.

You understand, therefore, with what modesty you ought to restrain yourself, since you appear to have fulfilled the wishes of another in his affairs. For if the suspicion of a harsh judge had touched you [Jur.: “awkward,” that is, “left-handed and perverse”], by praising justice you would correct his mind through a gentle yet penetrating remedy, obtaining through mild persuasion what you could not have imposed upon a superior.

Who, then, could doubt that you love those things which the public voice has shown you to have commended? Professed good qualities are not ambiguous; nor does anyone’s intelligence readily submit when what he himself, after earning distinction, could pursue is taught to him by others as though he were inexperienced.

You demanded that the authenticity of the document presented be established by lawful testimony, examining whether the record chests retained the truth uncorrupted. Judge, now display in yourself what you wished to obtain from others [Note: It should be noted that in the city of Rome there was a college of decurials who received, transcribed, and completed the acts and authorities of the Senate and kept the Senate’s record chests. They were men skilled in writing and speaking, and they were headed by a rector, whom the author calls a judge because he judged between the decurials and others. Thus the first law of the *Codex*, *De Decurialibus*, says that anyone wishing to bring an action against a decurial for removing a privilege or a right granted by ancient law must approach the judge of the decury. BROSS.].

Come now, lest your own speech be brought against you, for it is a burden of the gravest shame to be convicted by one’s own words. Therefore, with God as your author, assume the rectorship of the decuries, the truest witness of human actions, the security of property-holders, the most splendid temple of public trust. From this you will acquire as much praise as the number of persons whose interests are preserved there [Note: Others read “because their interests”; Cor. Gam., “as much as their interests.”].

May the wills of those who depart this life endure for you through all ages; may the judgments of parents pass to their descendants; may the peace of everyone be preserved in your record chests. Let others possess honors and terrifying fasces; to you the most welcome guardians of human life seem to serve. For there are acquittals of persons, bonds of cases, chains of lawsuits, and a prison for rage.

Of this the Mantuan poet would speak more truly:

> “The gates of War are closed;  
> impious Fury, shut within, roars with blood-stained mouth.”

Therefore choose the decurials after assessing their merits, for it is not fitting to summon what is worthless to serve so great a city [Col. 0660D]. When necessary, also make use of the judgment of the older men, having become senior to so many fathers and the voice of the Senate while so many remain silent.

Consider what dignity you have received [Col. 0661A]: among so many eloquent men you are to be foremost in speaking, men whom we too profess to revere. Take upon yourself, therefore, the authority to grant what we command and to provide what we entrust, so that you may open the doors of the curia to those whom our choice orders to enter the hall of liberty.

## LETTER XXII. KING THEODORIC TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

He announces that he has chosen Capuanus, distinguished by outstanding virtues, as rector of the decuries.

Although the man sent to you for approval must always be chosen with care—for he himself is entrusted to examination, and the judgment expressed concerning him is known to be weighed—we nevertheless wish those dignities to be joined to prudent men which, like noble gems, are affixed to the Roman citadels [Gr. and Cuj., “arts”] [Col. 0661B].

For where could an eloquent man advance more worthily than in the city of letters, so that he may display his merit where he nourished his talent? Every good thing is suited to its proper place; and all that is praiseworthy becomes shabby unless it possesses an appropriate seat.

A battle requires strong hands; a ship desires a courageous breast. So your record chests require a faithful purpose, and your curia an eloquent speaker. Accordingly, the man who is presented daily to your judgment must be weighed with much deliberation.

Our evaluation has therefore taken account of Capuanus, a noteworthy man, who could proclaim the judgment of your curia with the authority of an elder and preserve the Senate’s record chests with purity of conscience, so that he might make those acts, most renowned throughout the world, worthy of praise through his own integrity [87].

It is a great office, Conscript Fathers, to be chosen for integrity [Col. 0661C]; and the conscience to which the truth of the ages is entrusted is proved to be no ordinary one. If a witness who tells the truth in a present matter is praised, with what praise may he be judged who transmits certainty through all times?

Although in your alumnus you have all these things very well known, it is useful to repeat what everyone’s agreement can acknowledge. A certain chosen grace of speech is always present: it charms the ears, draws the mind, and employs the clarity of eloquence that ought to flow from a pure conscience. Speech is a kind of mirror of the character of the speaker; nor can there be a greater testimony to the mind than the observed quality of one’s words.

To describe his particular gift: in simple matters he suffers the restraints of the tongue; yet when he delivers a formal speech he is all the more impetuous [others: “more correct”]. Nature has bestowed this grace upon him, so that the man whom you have seen hesitating before the doors leaves you astonished by his eloquence in debate.

The memory which is rightly called the treasure of orators has settled in him with such firmness that you would think whatever he had once heard was stored with him in writing. It is a great gift not to know the failure of forgetfulness; and it resembles something truly heavenly always to possess as present what time has carried away.

We now declare these things so that you may understand that we regard the virtues of our subjects with approval, and that you may see that our judgment was conceived not through a casual wish but through deliberate choice.

Therefore, Conscript Fathers, we order that Capuanus, endowed with these good qualities, be rector of the decuries from the present indiction onward. We also raise him through the authority of seniority, so that he who has conducted himself with the gray maturity of character—which is the highest form of reverence—may rejoice in your order in the honor of age.

His eloquence will increase when enriched by a better office, since the man who dictates a judgment is much more eloquent than the man who petitions. Freedom nourishes speech, whereas fear frequently interrupts its abundance. His actual position will also be entirely different: he who once stood in attendance upon even modest and humble fortunes will now introduce consular men into your curia.

## LETTER XXIII. KING THEODORIC TO ABUNDANTIUS, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He orders him to provide provisions and ships for the archers sent to Count Julian.

[Col. 0662B]

We have judged that our *saio* Tatanes [Gr. and Cuj., Tanmem], together with the archers, should be sent to the illustrious Count Julian, so that the doubled army might gain greater strength. Let our young men display in war the virtue they learned in the training ground. Let the school of Mars send forth its companies, and let the man accustomed to train in leisure now fight in earnest.

Therefore we decree that Your Illustrious Magnificence provide them, according to custom, with provisions and ships, so that, with God’s help, they may reach the place to which they have been sent. We entrust the effectiveness of our commands to your vigilance, for whatever is begun under your arrangements with God’s help is believed in no way capable of being abandoned.

## LETTER XXIV. KING THEODORIC TO EPIPHANIUS, SENATOR AND CONSULAR OF THE PROVINCE OF DALMATIA

He advises him to attach Joanna’s property to the royal treasury, since she was said to have died intestate with no surviving relatives, provided that he discovers the matter to be as reported.

[Col. 0662C]

Joanna is said to have succeeded her former husband Andrea by operation of law; she is reported to have died intestate, with no close relatives surviving. Her property, it is alleged, is being possessed through voluntary usurpation by various persons supported by no legitimate right.

Since the laws, with due caution, have decreed that escheated property belongs to our treasury [Note: Under the law by which ἀδέσποτα καὶ ἀκληρονόμητα, “ownerless and without heirs,” pass to the ruler’s treasury—such things as treasures, vacant property that finds no heir, or property taken from those who are unworthy or incapable—see Ulpian, fragments, titles 17 and 18; the sole law of the *Codex*, *De caducis tollendis*; Pliny, *Panegyric to Trajan*, and Book VI, formula 3. FORN.], we therefore admonish you by the present decree that, after investigating the truth of the matter, if indeed, as has been reported to us, no heir existed for her either by testament or by right of kinship, you cause it to be added to the resources of our treasury.

For it is a profession of our innocence not to neglect legitimate gains, since calumny has never been able to find a place with us. In such cases it is proper that the ruler be asked, not defrauded, because it is a fault of negligence to leave unchecked usurpations which the laws command to be removed.

But if you discover anything to the contrary, you will allow the rightful possessors to remain undisturbed, since those patrimonies are more truly ours which are legitimately possessed by our subjects.

## LETTER XXV. KING THEODORIC TO BACAUDA, SUBLIME MAN

He grants him the administration of the tribunate of Milan in perpetuity.

[Col. 0663A]

Our generosity strengthens weary years, since it does not allow old age to feel the losses of poverty. The virtue of the young is animated by the prospect of labor; the only remedy available to the elderly is to find the tranquility of rest.

Moved therefore by your petition, we have decreed that the care of the designated tribunate [Note: D. Juret believes this should be understood as the tribunate of entertainments, mentioned below in Book VI, formula 19, and Book VII, formula 10.] is to be carried out most diligently by you in the city of Milan. Thus, in a new arrangement for service to the commonwealth, as long as you live no one’s punishable presumption shall ever appoint a successor to you.

Accordingly, through the favor of our clemency, you may continually enjoy the care of this office in providing entertainments, possessing in both respects what may console your age: the convenience of the place and the delight of its pleasures.

## LETTER XXVI. KING THEODORIC TO ALL GOTHS SETTLED THROUGH PICENUM AND SAMNIUM

He orders them to come to the palace on the eighth day before the Ides of June, without causing any harm to the provincials, to receive royal gifts.

[88] Although our generosity is everywhere most welcome to everyone, we believe that gifts conferred in our presence are much more acceptable, because peoples derive greater things from the sight of the ruler than they obtain from his generosity. For a person unknown to his ruler is almost like a dead man; and no one lives under any honor whom the recognition of his king does not protect.

Therefore, by the present command, we order you to come into our presence on the eighth day before the Ides of June, with God’s help, so that you may solemnly receive royal gifts [Note: See Liutprand, Book VI, chapter 5. These gifts were conferred on the Kalends of January. Nicephorus, Book X, chapter 23; Sozomen, Book V, chapter 17; Ambrose, Sermon 14. JURET.], if you hasten to come immediately.

We nevertheless necessarily admonish you that none of those who come may commit excess, nor may you ravage the crops or meadows of the possessors [Note: The passage of soldiers is to be harmless, and they must not damage crops. Thus some suspect that what Paulus wrote concerning the servitude of carrying a straight spear without damaging the crops, *Digest*, law 7, “Qui sella,” *De servitutibus rusticorum praediorum*, was derived from kings who permit a foreign army to pass through a region under their rule. Hence Lysander, commander of the Lacedaemonians, seeing that the Boeotians were of uncertain loyalty, asked, as he passed through their fields, whether he was to pass with upright or lowered spears. But I think the jurist was speaking of private law, not imperial authority: *Digest*, law 13; likewise the sections “army,” *Ex conducto*, law 15, under the words “an army passing through wantonly,” *Digest*, *Locati*. Justinian likewise established regulations concerning the passage of soldiers, Novel 130, περὶ παρόδου στρατιωτῶν, “concerning the passage of soldiers”; under these auspices and laws Belisarius governed the army. When some soldiers, roaming through the fields, touched the crops, he summoned them, marked them with disgrace, and addressed them as follows: “To use force and feed upon what belongs to another has always seemed shameful and disgraceful, because it is unjust in itself.” Authority: Procopius, Book IV, *Vandalic War*. See below, Book XII, Letter 5. FORNER.] but hasten with complete restraint, so that your arrival may be pleasing to us because of the discipline you have maintained [Col. 0664A]. For we willingly undertake military expenses so that civilized order may be preserved intact by armed men.

## LETTER XXVII. KING THEODORIC TO GUDUIM, SAIO

He orders him to admonish the *millenarii* of Picenum and Samnium to hurry to the palace, both to receive their gift and to render an account of what they have done in war.

The custom of royal liberality reminds us that we ought to bestow customary gifts upon our Goths [Note: Customary gifts and annual presents; below, Letter 42 of this Book V. FORNER.]. Therefore let Your Devotion, without any delay, admonish the *millenarii* of Picenum and Samnium to bring to the court, without delay, those who each year receive the rewards of our clemency, so that they may receive their gift. Thus those who have served us well may rejoice in greater generosity.

For the man who knows that he must present himself before rulers must necessarily live blamelessly. Praise accompanies the good, complaint the bad. On this occasion it is also fitting for us to investigate the deeds of individuals [Note: Lampridius attributes the same practice to Alexander, son of Mamaea. FORNER.], so that no deed performed in battle may be lost [Note: These royal gifts, in addition to the customary pay, went to soldiers as rewards for courage, and were not distributed randomly or indiscriminately to everyone without regard to fault. Under Justinian there was a quaestor of rewards, Agathias, Book III, *Gothic War*. “In the army,” he says, “he performed the office neither of commander nor of prefect, nor even of soldier. He was a quaestor and guardian of the royal funds, though not of those funds paid to soldiers as their stipend—for that responsibility was assigned to another—but of the funds sent from the emperor’s treasury to the army as rewards for those who had performed some distinguished deed in war. As a result he was not obscure but powerful, and indeed became one of those entrusted with secrets, so that the words of the rulers seemed to possess great firmness and reliability whenever they pleased him.” Cassiodorus seems likewise to hint at this when he says “the deeds of individuals,” as though there were in the camp some investigator of each soldier’s diligence and courage, whose report before the ruler could commend the active soldier. FORN.].

For if the army always expects only customary things, the neglected soldier cannot love valor. Let the timid man learn to come before the judge if he does not remember having done anything boldly, so that he may rise more violently against enemies after choosing to avoid the wounds of our accusation.

## LETTER XXVIII. KING THEODORIC TO CARINUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

He summons him to his court as an illustrious man necessary to him.

[Col. 0664C]

The merits of good men possess this glorious presumption: those who become known through honorable actions are not allowed to grow numb in idleness. Therefore, both to satisfy your desire and because we have judged you necessary, we summon you by the present commands, so that our service may be adorned by noble men and so that through you we may accomplish what we believe useful to us.

## LETTER XXIX. KING THEODORIC TO NEUDI, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

He orders that the blind Ocerus not be dragged into slavery if he is found to have proved himself freeborn.

[Col. 0665A]

The petition poured forth by Ocerus certainly moved us, but the man deprived of the adornment of his sight made his condition still more pitiable, since a calamity seen necessarily moves one more deeply than a calamity heard about. Surviving in perpetual night, he hastened to our remedies through the benefit of borrowed light, so that, though he could not see the person before him, he might at least feel the sweetness of clemency.

[89] He cries out that Gudila or Oppane is imposing upon him, unknown to his family, the condition of slavery, although previously he had followed our army as a free man. We were astonished that a man was being dragged into servitude who ought to have been expelled by his true master.

It is a new kind of extortion to seek out a man whom one can only dread and to call a slave someone whom, by divine consideration, one ought to serve. He adds that accusations of this kind had already been removed through the examination of Pythias, a count and a man of celebrated reputation.

Now, weighed down by the burden of his infirmity, he cannot vindicate himself with his own hand, although that hand is known to stand as a patron beside the strong. But we, whose proper task is to preserve equal justice among both equals and unequals, decree by the present command that, if he proved himself freeborn in the court of the aforesaid late Pythias, you are immediately to remove those who bring the accusation. They must not dare any longer to mock another’s necessities; once convicted, they ought to have condemned their own claims.

## LETTER XXX. KING THEODORIC TO GUDUI, SUBLIME MAN

He orders that servile burdens be removed from Costula and Daila, who enjoy the liberty of the Goths.

[Col. 0665C]

To those whom we choose as commanders we rightly entrust at the same time the weighty responsibilities of equity, because we desire to become distinguished not only through arms but also through judgments.

Since Costula and Daila, by God’s favor, rejoice in the liberty of our Goths, they complain that you are imposing upon them servile burdens which it would be unworthy for them to endure and which it is unreasonable for anyone to impose.

If you discover that this has been done, have it removed without delay, lest any further complaint be brought back to us and the accusation, returning against a commander, begin to weigh heavily upon our mind. A commander ought rather to perform such actions as we are pleased to hear about.

## LETTER XXXI. KING THEODORIC TO DECORATUS, DEVOTED MAN

He decrees that the presbyter Marcus, Andreas, and the others be compelled to pay money to the treasury if it is established that they are debtors.

[Col. 0665D]

Thomas, a most distinguished man, complains that, under the heading of *siliquaticum*, concerning the indictions of the eighth, ninth, eleventh, first, second, and fifteenth years, which he states belonged to his lease, certain persons are retaining [D. Grul. and Cuj.: “owing”; others: “returning”] a very large sum of money. [Col. 0666A] And since it is not fitting that the public interest be postponed through prolonged mockery, therefore, receiving this decree, your Devotion shall summon Marcus the presbyter, Andreas, Simeon, and the others whom the appended memorandum below names, preserving civility in every respect, so that, if it is established that they are truly—rather than calumniously—debtors to the treasury, they may pay, without any reduction, the sum that is reasonably demanded. For care must be taken lest the spirit of obstinate persons appear to inflict any loss upon the public accounts. Those, however, who realize that they have been subjected to less than was attempted shall, when you summon them, come before the competent tribunal, so that, after the allegations of both parties have been examined, what accords with equity may be carried out in accordance with the laws. [Col. 0666B]

## LETTER XXXII. KING THEODORIC TO BRANDILA

He admonishes him to correct Procula, his wife, who was said to have struck the wife of Patzenis most severely; but if Brandila believes that she has been falsely accused, he wishes him to come with his wife to the court to state the case.

The repeated complaint of Patzenis has reached us countless times. Although he was stationed on a most successful expedition, he asserted that his wife had been torn by a triple assault at the hands of Procula, your wife, so that she escaped only by the favor of despair, since she was believed not merely exhausted by blows but already dead. We cannot permit this audacity in a woman, if it is true, to pass unpunished, though we are greatly astonished by it. Therefore, by this present decree, we admonish you that, if you clearly acknowledge the deed, you should, with due regard for your honor, rebuke the complaint brought against her by the severity proper to a husband, [Col. 0666C] so that a just complaint arising from the same matter may not return to us; and you should know that what you ought to have corrected by domestic discipline can be cut off by the laws. But if, while accusing the petitioner of falsehood, you perhaps wish to plead the case, removing every obstacle of delay, come without hesitation to our court with the wife mentioned above, prepared either to receive punishment for an unjust presumption or victory over the woman’s wickedness.

[Note: [Col. 0665D] Tiberius was the first to authorize matrons of fallen chastity, when no public accuser was available, to be restrained by their relatives according to ancestral custom and by common judgment. Suetonius, *Life of Tiberius*, chapter 35. FORNER.]

[Note: [Col. 0666D] Fabius Quintilian says that women possess strength for crimes, *Declamations* 2. The final law of the Theodosian Code, *On the Cornelian Law concerning assassins*: “For the sentence ought to be milder toward those whom, because of the weakness of their sex, we trust will dare less.” FORNER.]

## LETTER XXXIII. KING THEODORIC TO WILITANCH, DUKE

He orders him to investigate the case of Brandila, who had taken Regina, the wife of Patzenis, in marriage while Patzenis was serving on the Gallic expedition; and, if he finds the accusation true, to punish the adulterers.

Patzenis’s grave complaint has been brought to the attention of our clemency. He testifies that, while he was stationed on the Gallic expedition, Brandila ventured upon such an outrage against him as to take his wife Regina and join her to himself in marriage; and that, to the injury of our times, adultery was committed under the pretended authority of marriage.

[Note: [Col. 0667C] I shall briefly demonstrate what the punishments for adultery once were. Under the law of Romulus, a matron guilty of that offense was handed over to her husband and relatives, who punished and fined her as they thought fit, even by death. For by that law itself, a woman married according to the sacred laws of Romulus was so under her husband’s authority that her children were under their father’s. Livy and Valerius say that, when women engaged in incest during the Bacchanalian rites, their relatives and husbands administered punishment within the home. See Valerius Maximus, book VI, chapter 3; Pliny, book XIV, chapter 13; Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 6. Moreover, adulteresses were expelled from the household and deprived of their dowry, as Plautus indicates in *Amphitryon*; see Valerius, book VIII, chapter 11. But if husbands and relatives concealed the matter—that is, to use Livy’s words, if no suitable private executor of punishment existed—the magistrates, and especially the aediles, not rarely pursued the crime by public judgment. Later came the Julian Law, enacted by Augustus, who punished adulterers by death or exile, so that the offense was capital, as is clear from Arnobius, book IV, and Salvian, book VI. Boniface, archbishop, attributes the same punishment for adultery to the ancient Saxons in his letter to Ethelbald, king of the English. “In ancient Saxony,” he says, “where there was no knowledge of Christ, if a maiden in her mother’s house, or a married woman under her husband, was found to have committed adultery, they strangled and burned her with their own hands; or chaste matrons, with her garments cut off as far as the belt, scourged her, and, as she was sent from village to village, new scourgers came to meet her and stabbed her with knives until they killed her.” BROSS.]

We cannot permit these things, if true, to pass unpunished. For when can anyone have secure affections, if he is subjected to crime precisely when he has fought for the safety of all? Look to the most chaste race of moaning turtledoves. If, through some intervening accident, one is separated from its mate, it binds itself by a perpetual law of abstinence. It does not seek again the favor of the union it has left; it preserves faith, while it knows nothing of the praise of chastity; and it is found to observe good morals, though it makes no display of a life of widowhood. Alas, women cannot restrain their desires, although reason persuades them to chastity, the penalty of the law imposes it, and the terror of a husband extorts it. Morals have surely perished if they cannot even be compared with creatures that are restrained without reason. Therefore let Your Sublimity cause the accused to appear for examination; and, after the truth of the matter has been investigated, let the adulterers be cut down, as our laws prescribe, with the favor of their husbands, since those who joined themselves by criminal presumption did not wish the defender of the state to return. Without doubt, those who attempted what is hostile to the laws desired everything to be thrown into confusion. But it is better that the purpose of wickedness be corrected by the loss of a few, because every marriage would remain uncertain, God forbid, if one could sin against such reverence without any fear.

[Note: [Col. 0668D] The ancients, according to Cicero in the *Pro Cluentio*, established that, if a military offense had been committed by many, punishment should be inflicted by lot upon some, so that fear might reach all while punishment reached only a few. From this arose the custom of decimation, which they called δεκατεύειν, “to take a tenth.” Livy, book II and book XXVIII; Polybius, book VI; Suetonius and Dio on Augustus; Xiphilinus on Galba; Capitolinus on Opilius Macrinus; Tertullian, *To Scapula*: “Carthage must be decimated.” It is therefore rightly said that, when the remaining citizens become wise through the punishment of a few, they are warned by the example of another’s evil; *Digest* 48.19.16, “or deeds”; Gellius, book XVI, chapter 14. FORNER.]

## LETTER XXXIV. KING THEODORIC TO ABUNDANTIUS, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He decrees that Frontosus be compelled without delay to pay the public money that he had squandered and had repeatedly promised to repay.

It has frequently been reported to us that Frontosus, a witness to his own name, had squandered no small amount of public money. We had him investigated by various judges according to due examination, lest, as often happens, it was not truth but envy that was defaming him [others: “weakening him”]. He confessed everything and declared that he could repay it if generous delays were granted him. When these had repeatedly elapsed, forgetful of his promise, he always appeared unprepared at the appointed times. He does not know how to flee, yet he is unaware of his own pledge: forgetful when left alone, trembling when held. He changes his words and alters his arrangements; not content with one form of statement, he is transformed into different shapes.

He is rightly compared with the chameleon, a beast resembling the form of small serpents, distinguished only by its golden head and by the remaining limbs being marked with a whitish-green color. Whenever it encounters human eyes, while the speed of flight is denied it, confused by excessive timidity it changes its colors in many different ways, so that it can now be found blue, now purple, now green, now deep blue. Hence it is remarkable to see so many different colors on a single surface. We may not unjustly say that it resembles a *Pandius* gem, in which a single radiance cannot remain fixed. It fluctuates before trembling eyes while the stone itself is held motionless. For what you see there now, you notice to be something else a moment later if you look at it more closely; thus you believe it changed, although you know that no one has removed it. [Col. 0668B]

When these transformations are considered, Frontosus’s mind is found to be most similar: it has no faith in its own word and contains as many varieties as it has uttered words. He must rightly be associated with the fables of Proteus, who, when suddenly seized, no longer possessed the form of his substance in any way. For in order to conceal the man, he either roared as a lion, hissed as a serpent, or dissolved into liquid waves.

And since he is known to be such, when he comes before your judgment, first act so that he does not make a promise; take care that he does not set a date. For it is the habit of a very flighty mind easily to promise what it has no intention of fulfilling. Whatever, after careful consideration of equity, he is able to pay, let him, once constrained, repay immediately and without any delay, since, after so many falsehoods, he may reckon among his clever tricks the fact that he knows he has repeatedly deceived himself.

[Note: [Col. 0668D] See Horace, book II, *Satire* 3. JURET.]

## LETTER XXXV. KING THEODORIC TO LUVIRIT, COUNT, AND AMPELIUS

He states that he ordered an ample supply of grain to be transported from Spain to relieve the scarcity of the Romans; nevertheless, the shipmasters carried it to Africa and sold it, and he therefore imposes upon them a fine of 1,038 solidi.

When, because of an uncertain turn of events, poverty was striking the Roman households with an emaciated face, and although rare, nevertheless appeared utterly disgraceful to so beautiful a city, [Col. 0669A] we judged it fair to provide it with the wheat supplies of Spain, so that fortunate Rome might recover its ancient revenue under our rule. The commendably worthy industry of the honorable Marcian served our orders. But what had clearly been most properly arranged was carried out with insufficient diligence. For those who had undertaken to transport the grain, unable to endure the tedium of delays, are said to have sold the grain destined for Rome in the regions of Africa for their own profit. Although this ought by no means to have passed unpunished—for love of private gain had suspended the hungry hopes of so many peoples—nevertheless, since it is implanted in us to remit faults that we can correct by prudent regulation, we have judged that the energetic men Catellus and Servandus should be sent. Since the shipmasters are said to have received 280 solidi for the wheat and 758 solidi in freight charges, if the truth of the deed becomes known to you, let the total be calculated and 1,038 solidi be exacted from them, so that, although we have remitted punishment, we may suffer no loss. In this matter Your Sublimity should apply itself diligently, so that it may appear to have satisfied both justice and the public interests.

[Note: [Col. 0669D] See Symmachus, book X, letter 50. JURET.]

## LETTER XXXVI. KING THEODORIC TO STARCEDIUS, A MOST DISTINGUISHED MAN

He exempts him from military service because of weakness in his limbs and permits him henceforth to lead a life of repose, though without the military donative.

You complain that your body, worn down by continuous labors, has brought weakness upon your limbs, so that although previously you were fit for military distinction, you are now scarcely found suitable even for a life of leisure. You ask not to be compelled to undertake the most successful campaigns, from which you are withdrawn not by choice but by necessity. Therefore, after your allegations had been investigated at length and brought to the truth of the matter, by this present order we grant you honorable leisure [Gr. and Cuj.: “not obscure”], since it is not the fault of idleness when pitiable misfortune provides the excuse.

But just as we grant you a life of repose, so by our present authority we deprive you of the donative, since it is not fair that, when you are known to be able to support yourself from your own resources, you should, while inactive, receive the reward of those who labor. Enjoy, therefore, a secure life, freed by our protection from the attacks of adversity. No one will charge you with the disgrace of desertion, since those whom illness causes to be withdrawn from military service ought rightly to be honored on account of their former deeds. For no one deserves rebuke who, by our judgment, merits acquittal.

[Note: [Col. 0669D] It is permissible to wipe away the shameful marks of a discredited ruler’s reputation. Thus, in *Code* 1.4, Tertullian says that stains are remitted by imperial favor; nevertheless, the ruler’s indulgence both liberates and marks those whom it frees. *Code* 1.2, *On the abolition of disgrace*; to this I add Suetonius, *Life of Claudius*, chapter 16. BROSS.]

## LETTER XXXVII. KING THEODORIC TO THE JEWS OF MILAN

He preserves the rights formerly granted to their synagogue, provided that they do not harm the rights of the Church.

We willingly grant what is requested without injury to the laws, especially since, for the preservation of civility, the benefits of justice ought not to be denied even to those who are still known to err in faith. Therefore let them learn the sweetest taste of good things, so that those who strive to seek human justice may begin more earnestly to consider divine judgments.

Since you frequently complain that you have been injured by the presumption of certain persons, and assert that the rights belonging to your synagogue are being rescinded, the protection of our gentleness will assist your petitions, so that no ecclesiastic may, by force, invade what legally belongs to your synagogue, nor intrude upon your affairs with unwelcome harshness. Rather, just as they are distinguished by the worship of religion, so also let them be distinguished in the conduct of their actions.

We grant the benefit of imperial assistance with this limitation, however: you must not yourselves attempt, in an uncivil manner, to touch what has been established by law to belong to the rights of the aforesaid Church or to other religious persons. The thirty-year prescription, the patroness of the human race, [Col. 0670B] shall be preserved for you by law in the same manner as for all others; nor do we order you irrationally to endure conventional [ed. Acc.: “commodated”] losses, so that, protected by this defense of our piety, your petition may rejoice to have been freed from unlawful disadvantages.

Indeed, in accordance with the custom of our clemency, we grant what you have requested. But why, Jew, do you ask while supplicating for temporal peace, if you cannot find eternal rest?

[Note: [Col. 0669D] In the laws of the Visigoths, book X, title 2, era 4, it is written that the thirty-year prescription became so firmly established in matters of legal actions that it now seems to have arisen not as a human institution but, as it were, from the very nature of things. A little later it adds: “Let no voice of any petitioner attempt to disturb this number, in which the truth of perfect maturity is completed.” See above, book III, letter 31, and book I, letter 18. JURET.]

## LETTER XXXVIII. KING THEODORIC TO ALL LANDOWNERS

He orders that the trees growing in the Signine channel be cut out by the roots.

The special care of the aqueducts admonishes us that whatever can grow harmfully must be cut away as quickly as possible, so that, with God’s help, the solidity of the water conduit may be preserved uncorrupted and the work required of you may remain light while the trees are young. For what are now shrubs will become, if neglected, full-grown timber. Things that can now be severed by an easy pulling will later scarcely yield even when struck by axes.

Therefore you must hasten together, so that by present diligence you may escape the hardships of future labor. This is civic [D. Grul. and Cuj.: “curial”; Juret.: perhaps “subtle”] destruction without assault, a quarrel without attack, an engine of war, so to speak, against the structures. Accordingly, we order every wood that rises in hostility to the walls to be cut out by the roots from the Ravenna aqueduct, so that the repaired construction of the Signine channel may bring us water of the purity with which it was able to receive it from its sources.

Then the bathing facilities will be splendid; then the pools will ripple with glass-clear springs; then there will be water that washes rather than pollutes, after which it will not be necessary to bathe repeatedly. It is also added that, if a pleasant stream flows in for drinking, everything is made acceptable to our nourishment, since no food becomes agreeable to human life when the clarity of sweet waters is lacking. [Col. 0671A] For if we desire to wash in the purest liquids, how much more eagerly do we hasten to be refreshed by such waters? If these future benefits are now taken into consideration, no one finds the labor burdensome when it is undertaken for the pleasure of all.

## LETTER XXXIX. KING THEODORIC TO AMPELIUS AND LIVERIA

He sends them to Spain to restrain, by the authority of the laws, both murderers and those exacting public money who were oppressing the estates of landowners through excessive weights, and finally all those engaged in evil and clandestine activities.

It is fitting that the provinces subject to our kingdom, with God’s help, should be ordered by laws and good morals, since that life is truly human which is contained within the order of law. For it is the way of beasts to live by accident: while they are driven by the impulse to seize, they succumb through unforeseen recklessness. Finally, the educated farmer clears his field of thorny thickets, since it is the glory of the cultivator if the rural soil is beautified by the sweetest fruits. In the same way, the most welcome peace of a people and the tranquil ordering of regions are proved to be the praise of rulers.

We have therefore learned from the complaints of many that in the province of Spain—which is the greatest crime among mortals—human lives are being destroyed by uncontrolled presumption, and that many are suffering death on the occasion of trivial causes. Thus, under a bad peace as though in a game, as many are falling as could scarcely have fallen under the necessity of wars.

Moreover, the provincials’ fortunes are said to be subjected not to the public registers, as is customary, but to the arbitrary will of those who compel them. This is plainly a form of plunder: each person must give according to the will of the man who hastens to exact more for his own advantage.

Desiring to remedy this matter by royal foresight, we have judged that Your Sublimity should be sent throughout Spain in the place of a commission, so that, under the novelty of your administration, the old custom may no longer be permitted anything. But, just as physicians apply accelerated remedies to more severe diseases, let the beginning of our treatment be made where the danger is known to be greatest.

We order the crime of homicide to be cut off by the authority of the laws. But the more severe the punishment, the more carefully the investigation of the matter must be conducted, lest, through love of vengeance, the innocent appear to be exposed to danger of their lives. Let only the guilty therefore perish for the correction of many, since it is also a form of mercy to restrain crime in its infancy lest it grow through increase. [Col. 0671D]

Those who exact the public penny are said to oppress the estates of landowners through excessive weights, so that the exaction appears to be not so much a levy as plunder. But, so that every opportunity for fraud may be removed, we order all public taxes to be brought to the standard of the weighing-house in our palace, which has now been given to you. For what is more wicked than for presumptuous persons to be allowed to cheat even in the very quality of the balance, so that what was assigned specifically to justice is discovered to have been corrupted by fraud?

After the truth has been fully investigated, we decree that the tenants of the royal household, whatever their nation of origin, pay only as much as our estates are established to pay. And, so that no one may find his labor unrewarded, we wish their wages to be fixed by your equity according to the nature of the property leased. For the fields should be called not ours but theirs if the amount of the rent is determined by the will of the tenant.

Therefore we order you carefully to investigate the schedule of overseas charges, where considerable fraud against the public interests is reported, and to determine the fixed amount according to the nature of the rights involved, since knowing what is to be paid is a useful remedy against fraud.

We have learned that the moneyers, who are clearly established specifically for public use, have passed into private profit. Once this presumption has been removed, let them be assigned to the public functions according to their abilities.

Moreover, do not allow the schedule of tolls to be confused by any usurpation. Set the most useful measure for the goods that ought to be supplied, and recall the license of commerce to an equitable standard, lest the ambitious enormity of the collectors extend into unrestrained excess.

The conduct of Laetus, whose integrity is strongly assailed by hostile suspicion, we likewise order to be investigated according to our customary equity, so that neither fraud may be concealed by cunning devices nor innocence be burdened by false accusations.

Those whom you find to have been involved in clandestine acts must, according to the value of the property suppressed, pay money as you determine. If it is established that these things were dispersed through others, those too shall be held liable who knowingly allowed themselves to be involved in such activity. For those who did not expose the deeds of the robber were accomplices in the crime.

The established allotment of provisions, which our humanity distributes in various ways, is reported to the provincials as an intolerable source of losses, since it is both exacted in kind and its price is demanded shamelessly. These are the proofs of detestable greed: to sell what is due to oneself and then immediately return to the insolence of exacting it.

This appears exceedingly wicked and absurd: that they should both disregard our regulations and seem to have injured the property of the taxpayers, whom they ought to support. Let them therefore be content with the amount fixed, whether they remain there or are nevertheless sent from here. Let them have the free choice of seeking only one of two things, provided that they do not burden the fortunes of others through doubled exaction.

The collectors’ license is also said to extort more from the provincials than is established to be brought into our treasury. After this has been carefully investigated, we decree that you restore the public taxes to the level at which they are known to have been imposed in the times of Alaric and Euric.

We have learned from the complaint of the provincials that those who have registered post-horses exact conveyances by means of them. You must permit no one at all to presume to do this, since through these most disgraceful profits both the landowner is worn down and the speed of travelers is impeded. [Col. 0673A]

We also wish the class of estate managers, which they complain was created for ruinous protection, to be entirely removed from both private and public property. For a defense imposed upon unwilling persons is not a defense; what unwilling people suffer is suspect. Indeed, this is truly a benefit if it is accepted without complaint.

Therefore we decree that the services needlessly rendered to Goths stationed in the city be removed. For it is not fitting to demand servitude from freeborn men whom we sent to fight for liberty.

[Note: [Col. 0671D] *Praebendarum*, elsewhere *praebendorum*. *Digest* 22.5.19, “Those unwilling,” concerning witnesses. Plautus, *The Persian*: “The aediles leased out provisions.” Aulus Gellius, book XV, chapter 4; Symmachus, book I, letter 19, says in the same form *tribuenda*, “to be distributed,” as provisions were distributed according to custom, book I, letters 6 and 28. FORN.]

[Note: [Col. 0672D] *Paraveredorum* is mentioned also below, book XI, letter 14, and *Code* 12.50.2 and 12.4.2, concerning the public postal service and the chief of the sacred bedchamber. FORN.]

## LETTER XL. KING THEODORIC TO CYPRIAN, COUNT OF THE SACRED LARGESSES

He confers upon him the office of Count of the Sacred Largesses and adorns him with many praises.

Although we are often glad to have granted benefits beyond the desires of petitioners and, what is most difficult, sometimes to have surpassed the wishes of human ambition, we embrace more willingly those things which we rightly boast of having done. For the man to whom official investigations are entrusted must be weighed for a long time, and one should be chosen by the prince who could be prescribed by the law itself.

Gem-rich veins are made precious by the brilliance of gold, and they acquire the glory of beauty because they are not sullied by any degenerate neighbor. In the same way, good merits joined to splendid dignities are strengthened by mutual praise [Ga.: “by the rewards of another”], and the appearance of one thing becomes more beautiful through added grace.

We have not believed any praise purchased for you or any loquacious fame, since you have often pleased us while we watched. You used to recount the confused complaints of petitioners in a most distinct and lucid report. Those who could not express their own grievances obtained what they sought when commended by your arguments; and, so that no excess of favor might be suspected, you made the desires of petitioners known in their very presence.

The desires of disputing parties met upon your lips; and, what is the most difficult kind of favor, you pleased both sides with impartial praise. This even places you above the advocates themselves. For while their task is to state the long-considered wishes of one side, you always had to explain a sudden case from both perspectives.

The very weight of the royal presence was added. Under it, you proved so readily effective that what they could scarcely obtain from judges through elaborate rhetorical figures, you were shown to obtain from the prince by straightforward arguments. [Col. 0673D] Our serene judgment was plainly prepared for the public good, since it tolerated no delay in investigating a case. As soon as the case had been narrated by you, it was understood; and why should the end of the matter be delayed when you concluded your presentation with lucid brevity?

You learned, as we believe, to judge by serving our judgments. Thus, what is the most effective kind of discipleship, you were instructed more by doing than by reading.

Educated in such disciplines, you undertook the office of ambassador to the East, sent to men of the highest expertise. Yet you were not confused by any hesitation among them, since nothing after us could be astonishing to you. Instructed in three languages, you found that Greece had nothing new to display; nor did even the subtlety in which it excels surpass you.

To all your merits was added faith, more precious than every praise—a quality loved by the divine and revered by mortals. For amid the world’s shifting storms, where could human frailty contain itself if weakness of mind were not absent from our actions [Niv.: “if firmness of mind were not present”]? Faith preserves friendship among companions; it serves masters with pure integrity; it offers reverence to supreme majesty through pious belief. And if you seek the benefit of so great a thing more broadly, everything that is lived well belongs to unchanging faith. [Col. 0674B]

Therefore, in the third indiction [A.D. 510 or 525], receive, with God’s favor, the dignity of Count of the Sacred Largesses.

[Note: [Col. 0673D] Claudian describes the office of the Count of the Sacred Largesses in the *Panegyric on Mallius*:

> “To him are entrusted the sacred riches and the tribute of the world,  
> Whatever gold is rolled forth by the rivers;  
> Whatever wealth, far from the light,  
> The skill of the pale Bessus mines from veins it has tracked.”

This office is frequently mentioned in the Theodosian and Justinian Codes. BROSS.]

Use the institutions appropriate to your birth. Thus far you have deserved that we should entrust you with the summit of honors; now act so that we may nevertheless confer upon you higher expressions of our gratitude.

## LETTER XLI. KING THEODORIC TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

He announces that he has raised Cyprian, distinguished by his own merits and the splendor of his birth, to the office of Count of the Sacred Largesses.

Although the imperial munificence has often produced candidates for you, and our fruitful indulgence is for you a second nature, [Col. 0674D] you now certainly have a man whom it was fitting for us to choose and appropriate for you to receive. Just as it was fortunate for him to be chosen by us, so it will be honorable for him to be joined to your assembly according to the law of honors.

This has come more auspiciously to the senate because, for us, an unpolished recruit is entering service, whereas it admits no one except one who can already be found worthy of honors. Your order is therefore rightly considered distinguished, since it is always assembled from the most approved men. Entrance there is not opened to the profane; those are permitted to approach who are also seen to depart from it as such.

Receive, therefore, as a colleague the man whom our palaces have tested by long examination. He served the royal utterances so fearlessly that he often carried out our orders while we watched and praised him. You certainly recognize what we are saying. For which of you was not assisted by Cyprian’s devotion? Whoever sought his aid soon received our benefits.

He often obtained through his reports what used to be done in the ancient consistories. Whenever we wished to lighten our mind, wearied by care for the state, we sought equestrian exercises, so that, through the very variety of activities, the firmness and vigor of the body might be restored. Then the delightful reporter brought many cases before us, and his presentation never became tedious even to a judge worn out by weariness.

Thus, while he skillfully introduced reasons for granting benefits, the mind, kindled by eagerness for benefactions, was refreshed. The candidate attached himself to such services and served our mind so well that no offense could weigh him down. We were often angered by disgraceful cases, yet the reporter’s tongue could not displease us. At times we condemned a matter whose advocate pleased us; and he frequently withstood the surge of our spirit, possessing the influence of favor.

He also boasts no ordinary distinction of birth. For his father, as you remember, was Opilio, a man chosen for palace guard duty despite the lowliness of the times. He could have risen much higher if faith had not lain beneath the most barren sterility of reward. For what could a poor donor contribute? Yet, although he did not enrich him, he made him known [Col. 0675B] [Note: [Col. 0675D] *Innotuit* is used actively for “made known,” as by Gregory the Great, book VII of the *Registrum*, indiction 2, chapters 113 and 114. Cassiodorus likewise says above *innotescenda*, “to be made known,” book I, letter 24. JURET.], since it is great praise, amid the poverty of the state, to have merited even moderate gifts.

He himself surpassed his ancestors through the good fortune of the age; and the fact that he advanced farther must be attributed to our times. For the measure of advancement among subjects is such as the difference between their masters has been.

Therefore, Conscript Fathers, we have raised the aforementioned Cyprian, distinguished by his own merits and the splendor of his birth, to the summit of the Sacred Largesses, so that both your number may be increased and the devotion of those who serve may be stimulated. Consider, most reverend Fathers, what opinion we hold of your order, since we praise at such length those whom we believe should be added to your ranks.

[Note: [Col. 0674D] For the sons of senators were born senators. *Code*, “If anyone [is of senatorial rank],” Theodosian Code, book VI, title 2. JURET.]

## LETTER XLII. KING THEODORIC TO MAXIMUS, AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND CONSUL

The ferocity of the spectacles, the amphitheater of Titus, and the games held there are described; and the consul is urged to distribute more generously the prizes for the combatants.

If those who wrestle with their bodies oiled and made flexible call forth consular munificence; if rewards are exchanged with those who sing to the accompaniment of an instrument; if a pleasing song receives its price, with what gift should the hunter be satisfied, when he labors through his own deaths to please the spectators?

He provides entertainment with his own blood.

[Note: [Col. 0675D] He calls the hunt and the spectacles in which men fought with beasts a cruel game and a bloody pleasure, just as theatrical performances, the presentation of spectacles, and other things of this kind are known to be called pleasures. Vopiscus confirms this in his *Life of Aurelian*: “On the following days pleasures were provided for the people—dramatic games, circus games, hunts, gladiators, and a sea battle.” Tertullian likewise says: “For all those profane pleasures of secular spectacles are composed of the things of God.” Lactantius, in condemning spectacles, repeatedly uses the word “pleasure.” Law 1, *Code*, *On Spectacles*; Law 1, *Code*, *On the Expenses of Games*. Trebellius Pollio, in the two books on Gallienus: “Lest the state, long devoted to theater and circus, should perish through the allurements of pleasures.” Salvian, *On the Government of God*, says that there is no crime or disgrace that is not present in spectacles, where men are torn apart for the pleasure of those looking on. Hence Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, when he urges Honorius to abolish the spectacles:

> “Do not permit the deaths of wretched men to be made an offering”

No one should fall in the world whose punishment is a pleasure. [BROSS.] And, bound by an unhappy fate, he hurries to please the people, who do not wish him to escape. Detestable performance, unhappy contest: to wish to contend with beasts whom he does not doubt to be stronger than himself. Presumption in deception is the only thing left; the sole consolation in the trickery. If he does not deserve to escape the beast, sometimes he will not even be able to find burial. While the man still survives, his body perishes; before it becomes a corpse, it is savagely devoured. Caught as bait, he becomes food for his enemy and (alas!) satisfies the one whom he longs to be able to destroy.

A spectacle magnificent only in its structures, but most dreadful in its action, was devised in honor of Scythian Diana, who rejoiced in the shedding of blood. O the miserable error of deception—to have desired to worship one who was appeased by the death of human beings! At first they fashioned her, known among rustic peoples through groves and forests and devoted to the chase [ed. Ac., “vows”], as a triple goddess through a false imagination, insisting that she herself was the Moon in heaven, Diana in the forests, and Proserpina in the underworld. But perhaps they did not unjustly consider her alone powerful in Erebus, since, deceived by such falsehood, they entered the deep darkness of the living with their errors.

This cruel game, this bloodthirsty pleasure, this impious religion, this human—as I might call it—savagery, the Athenians first introduced into the culture of their state, divine justice permitting it, so that it might arrive at the spectacle which the ambition of a false religion had discovered. The imperial power of Titus, pouring forth a lavish stream of wealth, conceived the construction of this building, by which the capital of cities might be able to be made.

Since a theater, which is a hemisphere, is called in Greek θέατρον, and an amphitheater is so called because two viewing spaces are joined into one, its name is correctly established: it enclosed the arena in the form of an egg [ed., “he who encloses its form with the arena”], so that a suitable space might be provided for those rushing together; and so that the spectators might see everything more easily, while an extensive circular shape gathered everything together.

People therefore go to such things as humanity ought to shun. The first, trusting in fragile wood, runs toward the mouths of the beasts, and seems with great force to pursue the very thing he wishes to escape. Predator and prey hurry against one another with equal speed; nor can he be safe in any other way unless he encounters the one whom he wishes to avoid.

Then, with his body raised into the air by a leap, his limbs thrown backward like the lightest garments, a bodily arch is poised above the beast; while it delays its departure, the beast’s speed passes away beneath it. Thus it happens that the one who is proved to be mocked may appear the gentler.

Another, arranging himself at the corners of the fourfold division of the world, relying on the turning facility of the device [Gr. and Cuj., “strengthened facility”], flees neither by going away nor by making himself more distant; he follows the pursuer, presenting his knees close to it, so as to avoid the mouths of the bears. That man, suspended by his belly from a slender rod [others, “by coming”], invites the deadly beast, and unless he has exposed himself to danger, gains nothing by which he can live.

Another, enclosed behind a movable wall of reeds against the fiercest animal, takes refuge after the manner of a hedgehog. Suddenly retreating upon its back, it gathers itself together and hides within itself; and, since it has gone nowhere, its little body is not seen. For just as the hedgehog, when its enemy approaches, rolls itself into a sphere and is protected by its natural spines, so this man, girded by a woven lattice, is made safer by the fragility of the reeds.

Others, with what I might call three arranged little gates [others, “little enemies”], presume to provoke the rage prepared against them. Hiding themselves behind latticed posts in an open area, they display now their faces, now their backs; so that it is astonishing that those whom you see darting about amid lions’ claws and teeth manage to escape.

One is offered to the beasts on a revolving wheel; another is raised by the same device in order to be removed from danger. Thus this machine, fashioned according to the treacherous character of the world, sustains some with hope and tortures others with fear; yet it smiles upon all in turn, so that it may deceive them.

It would be tedious to wander in words through all these episodes of danger. But it is appropriate to join to this what the Mantuan says of the underworld:

> Who could comprehend the shapes of crimes? Who could run through all the names of punishments?

But you, who are obliged to exhibit such things to the populace, pour out rewards with a generous hand, so that you may make these things objects of desire for the wretched. Otherwise it is violent coercion to withdraw customary gifts and command detestable deaths. Therefore, whatever has come down through long custom from ancient generosity, grant without any delay to the petitioner; for it is the guilt of homicide to be stingy toward those whom your exhibition has invited to death.

Alas, the world’s error, worthy of lamentation! If there were any regard for justice, as much wealth ought to be given for the lives of mortals as appears to be poured out for the deaths of human beings.

## LETTER XLIII. KING THEODORIC TO TRANSMUND, KING OF THE VANDALS

He praises his sister, whom Transmund had taken in marriage; and complains that Transmund himself had kindly received Gesalec, who had been expelled from the kingdom because of his treachery, and had sent him abroad with wealth.

[Col. 0677C]

Although, when various kings sought alliances for the strengthening of harmony, we have either given them our nieces or joined our daughters to them, with God inspiring us, we nevertheless judge that we have conferred nothing comparable to what we have done in making our own sister—the unique glory of the Amal line—your wife: a woman equal to your wisdom, who can be not merely worthy of reverence because of her royal rank, but remarkable for her judgment.

Yet I am astonished that you, bound to us by such benefits, received Gesalec—who, while he was being supported by us, joined himself to our enemies—in your defense [Col. 0677D] in such a way that he who had come to you stripped of strength and deprived of his possessions was, after being suddenly furnished with abundant money, sent on to foreign peoples. Although, with God’s help, he can do you no harm, he nevertheless revealed the disposition of your thoughts.

What should the rights of strangers expect if kinship is treated in this way? For if he was received into your kingdom out of compassion, he ought to have been retained; if he was driven from ours because of his offenses, he ought not to have been sent to foreign kingdoms with wealth [Col. 0678A]—wealth which, lest those kingdoms become hostile to you, made our conflicts wholly our own.

Where is that instruction in which you used to teach others about conduct, having been so richly nourished by reading? If you had wished to discuss this with our sister, it could certainly not have happened to you: for she would neither have permitted her brother to be harmed nor allowed her husband to be found involved in such matters.

And therefore, through our envoys So-and-so and So-and-so, who convey our greetings with fitting honor, we ask that your deliberation examine this injustice, lest the spirit of your parents, aroused by evident causes, should contemplate attempting something that might appear to break the peace. An injury that has occurred unexpectedly is indeed deeply painful; and even more so if treachery arises from the quarter from which assistance was expected.

We have also entrusted the bearers of this letter with certain matters to communicate to you orally, so that, having considered everything, your prudence may decide what ought to be done in so serious a case; for it is no light offense for prudent men to err in matters established for peace.

## LETTER XLIV. KING THEODORIC TO TRANSMUND, KING OF THE VANDALS
