He says that he has willingly accepted Transmund’s apology and exculpation regarding his reception of Gesalec, and returns the gifts that Transmund had offered him.

[Note: From Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book XVII, chapter 11. Transmund, a man of remarkable appearance and great spirit, sent an embassy to Theodoric, king of the Goths, asking to marry his sister Amalasuntha. He obtained her and in addition gave a thousand armed men and five thousand men to fill the ranks of his attendants. After Transmund’s death, Hilderic, the son of Honoric, who was descended from Gaiseric, reigned—a mild man and not, like Transmund here, an Arian and persecutor of Christian men. Athalaric writes below, in book IX, letter 1, to this Hilderic. FORN.]

Most prudent of kings, you have shown that, after an error has occurred, counsel can come to the aid of the wise; nor do you love the fault of obstinacy, which seems to belong to brutish men. You have bound my spirit to you by changing so swiftly for the better. For when a king gives satisfaction, he dissolves every hardship: humility is as glorious in princes as boastfulness can be hateful in ordinary men.

Recently we reproached you for the deceitful departure of Gesalec, once a king; but, mindful of your nobility and honor, you disclosed to us the true course of events. Thus it was not so blameworthy for a man [ed. Ac., “men”] to have given place to perverse suspicions as it is glorious that a ruler was able so quickly to clear himself.

For he who could least be compelled did not permit the secrets of his soul to be violated. Rendering, insofar as we can, a return for this praise, we have received his sincere exculpation with a pure mind; but we do not retain the gifts of gold that were sent, so that you yourselves may understand that the matter was moved by justice and that no bribery could bring it to an end.

Each of us has acted as befits a king. We have overcome tyrannical greed just as you, it is clear, have overcome error. Let the gifts return to your chamber, gifts whose offering alone appears to be most welcome. Let gold be disregarded where the reward of conscience has been chosen; let that which always commanded greedy kings suffer rejection.

Let this action now go through the nations: that a dear kinsman did not excuse guilt, and that wounded spirits rejected money. Thus what used to be sought through wars has been shown, through devotion to love, to be something that could be despised. Let your relatives understand that we were such men that they could not raise causes for themselves through devotion to avarice.

Affection has indeed conquered everything. The petition began to come to an end precisely when the one who had been confronted did not endure denying the charges brought against him. Receive, then, the gifts with your understanding, not with your hands. It was sweeter for us to return these things than to have received gifts of much greater size.

Now be cautious about similar matters and attentive to what is to come; for the mind is made wiser regarding the future when it is reminded by examples of the past. Therefore, as your envoys So-and-so and So-and-so return, we send back to you in full the affection of our greeting, wishing that the divine powers may grant you health, knowing that our minds are most firmly joined to yours.

# BOOK SIX

## I. FORMULA OF THE CONSULSHIP

[Col. 0679A]

How highly the consulship was regarded by the judgment of antiquity is made entirely clear by the fact that, among the eminent dignities of the world, it alone deserved to have robes marked with palms [Col. 0679B]—the robes bestowed by Fortune; the rewards of victors; the name of the years; the sole compensation to which everything was owed.

The state of the Roman commonwealth was protected by the right hand of a brave man; his counsels vindicated the fortunes and children of all; and for so many great debts this dignity alone was the repayment, discovered for the adornment of freedom and devised for universal joy.

Through it, unquestionably, the condition of the empire continually grew; through it fortunate Rome always received its leaders. It was rightly considered long ago [others, “indeed”] a kind of empire; rightly, he could exercise authority above all citizens who rescued his country from the enemy. Arranging public interests with equity, he administered justice even over life itself; yet the power of killing was safely entrusted to him who had been the author of safety.

This is why fasces and axes were ordered to be bound to so great an authority: so that, when they were released more slowly, they might provide time for deliberation if the consuls had resolved anything concerning the slaughter or death of a person. And since everything was entrusted to his judgment, so that he might not become insolent in spirit, the consul was named from *consulere*, “to deliberate” or “to take counsel.”

From this there flowed such generosity [Col. 0680A] that the hand which had shed the blood of enemies abundantly poured forth aid for the lives of citizens. Thus those whom it had made prosperous through wars it satisfied through devotion to generosity. As an increase [others, “proof”] also [Col. 0680B] of public glory, it released servants from the yoke of slavery [Col. 0680C], granting freedom to a state of such greatness.

[Note: *Digest*, sole law, “On the Office of the Consul”; laws 5 and 20, “If Requested,” “On Manumission by the *vindicta*.” Here Cassiodorus incidentally notes eight features of the consulship more carefully than anyone else has noted them: (1) giving one’s name to the official calendar; (2) possessing fasces and axes; (3) manumitting slaves; (4) the palm-marked robe; (5) the victory scepter; (6) gilded shoes; (7) the curule chair; (8) finally, the gifts thrown to the crowd, signified by this verse: “Come to these acts of generosity, you who recognize that you are equal to such expenses.” We discussed these above, book II, letter 2. The insignia of consular office and authority are described at the beginning of book VI of the *Theodosian Code*. FORN. Ammianus Marcellinus likewise says, in book XXII, that when Mamertinus, consul, gave games on the Kalends of January, slaves were brought in according to custom to be manumitted by the chief of the admissions office. Claudian, *Against Eutropius*, book I:

> And, about to give the freedom  
> Which he has not yet deserved, he climbs the lofty tribunal.

Likewise in book III of the *Theodosian Code*, concerning Heraclianus and the infirmity of those under a tyrant. JUR.]

[Note: Those who entered the consulship customarily expedited manumissions, laid the *vindicta* upon slaves, and brought them to freedom. This is why, I think, Ulpian, in book II *On the Office of the Consul*, treated of manumissions and said that the consul’s office was to provide counsel for those wishing to manumit. Ammianus recorded certain facts about the circus games and the manumissions which consuls expedited immediately upon entering office, in book XXII. Sidonius Apollinaris’s poem at the end of his panegyric to Anthemius, and Claudian’s poem on Honorius’s fourth consulship, bear on the same matter. BROSS.]

But now you receive these things more happily, since we have the labors of consuls and you the joys of dignities. Your palm-marked robes are proved to be our victories; and, through the outcome of the most prosperous condition [Col. 0679D], you grant freedom to servants in peace, while we provide security to the Romans through wars.

And therefore, by that indiction, we adorn you with the insignia of the consulship [Col. 0680C]. [Note: The insignia of a magistrate, παράσημα, are described by Justinian, *Novella* 24, concerning the praetor of Pisidia: “a silver curule chair, an axe, and rods,” and so forth. FORN.]

Clothe your broad shoulders in the palm-marked robe of varied colors; ennoble your strong hand with the victory scepter; go forth from your own home even in gilded shoes; climb the curule chair, striving upward through its many steps in proportion to its greatness. Thus, in the leisure of peace, as a subordinate, you may deserve what we, as rulers, assume through the greatest labors.

You carry out the affairs of victory, although you know nothing of war. We, with God’s help, govern; we deliberate; and your name designates the year. [Note: The Romans numbered the years by the names of the consuls; see below, book IX, letter 29. Justinian, *Novella* 105: “It will become the name of the year.” Seneca, *On Anger*, book III, chapter 31: “He gave twelve fasces, but did not make him ordinary consul; he wanted me to count the year by him, but I lack the priesthood.” The panegyrist Pacatus, addressing Theodosius the Elder: “Whoever is created consul is destined to possess the name of the year.” Apuleius, *Apology* 2, addressing the proconsul Claudius Maximus: “Let him recognize the signs that have been stamped, read the consuls, and count the years.” On an ancient stone:

> Three times the judge who unbound sacred disputes,  
> As consul, adorned the official calendars with an everlasting name.

Hence accounts were issued with the day and the consul, *Digest* 1 and 6, “If Anyone,” section “If the Beginning,” *On Issuing Documents*. The dates and consuls were written in the accusers’ petitions, *On Accusations*, law 3. Laws in the *Code* were promulgated without a date and consul. Thus I have no doubt that Lactantius, book VI, understands “consuls” in these words: “Those who devote their lives to holding magistracies, so that they may mark the official calendars and impose their name upon the years.” FORN.]

You have surpassed rulers in happiness, since you hold the highest honors without possessing the weariness of domination. Therefore raise the confidence of your mind: consuls ought to be magnanimous. Do not consider private wealth, since you have decided to obtain public favor by giving.

This is why we elevate other judges even when they do not ask, but promote consuls only when they hope for advancement: so that you alone may come to these acts of generosity, recognizing that you are equal to such expenses. Otherwise they would be burdens rather than honors if we imposed something beyond your strength against your will.

Enjoy, therefore, your wishes in fitting fashion. This is the ambition that receives approval. Be illustrious to the world, most prosperous for yourself, and a fortunate example for your descendants to imitate.

## II. FORMULA OF THE PATRICIATE

[Note: The patriciate, the highest honor, frees a man from paternal authority just as it frees him from the curia. See also the section “A Son under Paternal Authority,” title “In What Ways the Right of Paternal Authority Is Dissolved,” final law; *Code*, “On Decurions,” book X, final law; “On Consuls,” book XII, final law; below, book VIII, letter 21, and book X, letter 7. FORN. See Baronius, notes for 29 August, in the *Roman Martyrology*. JURET.]

If we investigate the order of antiquity in the origins of dignities, the family of the patricians [Gr. and Cuj., “Potitii”] is known to have been consecrated to Jupiter, so that the worship of the supreme god—as they thought—might possess the primary place.

But since it was fitting that you should possess something distinguished, and the name itself was closely joined to the fathers, after superstition was abandoned it migrated happily to your assembly, because the praise of priestly office could rightly belong to the conscience of the senate.

Thus we likewise read that kings were appointed from the augural family—not unjustly, since it was fitting that such a purpose should produce one who could administer public laws.

This is why the honor itself is girded even when it is inactive, possessing no jurisdiction, and does not lay aside the belt of the judge. In this arises perpetual happiness, since the ambition of a successor is not feared. For as soon as it has been bestowed, it becomes the man’s contemporary for the remainder of his life: an inseparable adornment, a faithful belt, which does not know how to leave him before men depart from the world.

I believe that the institution was formed in imitation of the pontificate from which it arose; priests do not lay aside their priesthood except when they relinquish the duties of life.

The laws also granted them such reverence that, when a man placed in sacred office had been girded with this honor, he was stripped of the bonds of paternal authority, unless the emperor expressly provided otherwise. This was evidently established for a credible reason: that one who had received the highest dignity of precious freedom should not share the lowest condition with his subjects.

He precedes prefects and men of the other dignities, yielding only to one splendor, which we too are sometimes known to assume. [Note: He means the consulship. See Symmachus, book IV, letter 8. JURET.]

Understand, therefore, that this dignity is necessarily to be praised, lest we appear to have given too little, or lest you treat it carelessly if you suppose that you have received something ordinary.

Accordingly, raised by our gift from that indiction, ascend the summit of the patriciate. Some jurists wished it to be called from the fathers [Note: Suidas: πατρίκιος, ὁ πατὴρ τοῦ κοινοῦ, “the father of the commonwealth.” Justinian, the cited section “A Son under Paternal Authority,” and the final law cited, *On Consuls*. FORN.], and perform everything that such reverence demands.

For although our clemency has conferred great things upon you, you still have something to expect if you strive to conduct yourself commendably.

## III. FORMULA OF THE PRAETORIAN PREFECTURE

If the origin of some honor is praiseworthy, and if a good beginning can provide a commendation for what follows, the praetorian prefecture boasts of such an originator: one who was most prudent in the world and especially acceptable to the Divinity.

For when Pharaoh, king of Egypt, was beset by unprecedented dreams concerning the danger of a future famine, and no human counsel could reveal such a vision, Joseph the blessed man was found—one who could both truthfully foretell the future and wisely assist a people in danger.

He first consecrated the insignia of this dignity [Col. 0682B]; he, revered, ascended the *carpentum* [Col. 0682C]. [Note: Praetorian prefects used the *carpentum* and could mount it, as could urban prefects. This custom had anciently been granted to sacred priests, as Suetonius makes clear in *Claudius*, chapter 11: he gave his mother a *carpentum* in which she might be carried around the Circus; and in *Caligula*, chapter 15: he instituted circus games and a *carpentum* for his mother, in which she might be borne in procession. Matrons too commonly used *carpenta* for sacred rites, as Ovid testifies in book I of the *Fasti*:

> For formerly Ausonian mothers rode in *carpenta*;
> I think these too were named after father Evander.

But later this custom fell into disuse. BROSS.] He was raised to this summit of glory so that through wisdom he might confer upon peoples what the power of a ruler had been unable to provide.

From that patriarch the prefect is even now called the father of the empire; the herald’s voice even today echoes him, instructing the judge not to allow himself to be unlike him. [Note: Below, book XI, letter 3, which was used in both public and private trials. *Digest*, “On the Right of Immunity,” law 2; penultimate law, “On Restoration in Full”; final law of the *Code*, “On Holidays.” Quintilian, book VI, chapter 4; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter 15. Agathias, describing the tribunal established by Justinian, says in book IV of the Gothic War: “Instructing the judge.” Donatus, commentary on Terence’s *Phormio*, act 1, scene 2; Demosthenes, *Against Ctesiphon*; Lucian, *The Double Accusation*. Perhaps we shall discuss this matter more fully elsewhere. FORN.]

It is deserved, therefore, that the one to whom such great power could be given should always seem to be subtly admonished.

Certain rights are shared by this dignity and by us. It produces distant persons without a plea of prescription; it fines offenders with great severity; it distributes the treasury according to its own judgment; it grants travel permits with similar authority; it proscribes ownerless property; it punishes the offenses of provincial judges; and it pronounces sentence by word. [Note: Among the rights and distinctive powers of the praetorian prefect is the privilege of not having to issue a sentence in writing, *Code*, “On Sentences Read from a Brief,” law 2. This was not permitted to other judges, who issued judgments to litigants from a written tablet. Symmachus, book I, letter 27; law 34; final law, *Code*, “On Rural Estates”; final law, *Code*, “On the Principal Agents in Affairs”; law “In Sacred Matters,” *Code*, “On the Chief of the Sacred Chancery,” book XII. We shall discuss this at a more appropriate place. FORNER.]

What is there that he is not entrusted with, when his very speech is judgment? He almost has the power to make laws, since his authority can conclude cases without appeal. Upon entering the Palace, he is frequently worshiped according to our custom; and this service seems to dissolve the custom by which he was able to accuse others.

No dignity, therefore, is equal to his in authority. He judges everywhere in the place of the emperor. No soldier prescribes to him concerning the authority of his court, except the officer of the master of the soldiers—perhaps so that antiquity might yield something even to those who appeared to conduct wars for the commonwealth.

He even scourges the curials, who are called by the laws the lesser senate. In his office he retains a singular right, and is known to command men of such rank and importance that even the judges of the provinces would not dare to despise them in any respect.

His office is plainly noble, effective, equipped, and powerful with the whole firmness of the spirit; its members carry out commands in such a way that they delay none of the orders given to them.

To those who have completed their military service he grants the honor of tribunes and notaries; and he makes his soldiers equal to those who, mingled among the leading men, obey our commands before our eyes [Gr. and Cuj., “commands”]. [Note: The jurist states, in *Digest*, “On the Office of the Praetorian Prefect,” law 1, that praetorian prefects were granted fuller license for the correction of public discipline. In the time of the emperor Constantius, all military and ordinary authorities always looked up to the praetorian prefects, according to the ancient custom of reverence, as the summit of all honors, as Ammianus Marcellinus records in book XXI. Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian define the merit of the prefecture as surpassing other dignities in *Code*, “On the Office of the Vicar,” law 1—and rightly so, for the praetorian prefecture was once a kind of principate of the empire, though without the purple. The distinction between the emperor and the prefect was established in the fact that the prefect did not wear the sacred purple or the imperial insignia. Moreover, supreme authority over affairs was entrusted to the praetorian prefects because of the dignity of their position, as the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius testify in *Code*, “Everyone,” law 40, “On Decurions,” book X. They are also called the fathers of the empire, as the author testifies. Anyone wishing to know more about the authority, office, and dignity of the praetorian prefect should consult Dion, book LII; Suetonius, *Galba*, chapter 14, and *Titus*, chapter 6. BROSS.]

We gladly fulfill what he has established; his authority binds us also in such a way that, without hesitation, we do what we know he has decreed.

This is not undeserved, since by his foresight he sustains the Palace, provides grain allowances for us who serve, extends acts of kindness even to the judges themselves, and satisfies the voracious envoys of nations through his arrangements. Although other dignities possess fixed titles, almost everything that is administered in our empire with balanced moderation is carried out through this one.

Accordingly, from that indiction we fittingly place upon your shoulders this most splendid burden of all responsibilities—which will be prosperous for us and useful to the commonwealth. Strive to bear it through the excellence of your intellect and to administer it with the highest fidelity.

The more this dignity is constrained by various anxieties, the more it triumphs in the highest praises. Therefore such a light of glory is added to your actions that it shines in our Palace and gleams in the distant provinces.

Let prudence be equal to your authority; let the fourfold virtue of conscience sit beside you. Know that your tribunal has been made so lofty for this reason: that, placed there, you should conceive nothing low or base.

Consider what you ought to say, since your words are received by such men. Let the public records contain things that no one will be ashamed to have read. A remarkable governor has no share in offenses, because unless he is continually doing something outstanding, he incurs blame even through idleness.

For if that holy and blessed originator mentioned above is recalled, to administer the dignity of the praetorian prefecture fittingly is a kind of priesthood.

## IV. FORMULA OF THE URBAN PREFECTURE

[Col. 0684A]

Since the praise of a judge is always assessed according to the dignity entrusted to him, and he ought to be considered superior to those over whom he is known to preside, no one seems to be raised higher than the one to whom Rome could be entrusted.

It is a great thing to be one of the leading men, but much greater to judge the leading men.

[Note: When Epictetus was asked by the emperor Hadrian what the senate was, he replied: “the ornament of the City, the splendor of its citizens.” Likewise, when Pyrrhus’s envoys were asked what they thought of the Romans, they replied that the City seemed to them a temple and the senate an assembly of kings. Some called it the teacher of right and good; others, the lights of the world. Probus, in Vopiscus, says that Roman senators are the rulers of the world, have always been such, and will be such hereafter. Petronius in the *Satyricon* calls the senate the teacher of right and good; Prudentius, in book I *Against Symmachus*, the lights of the world. Ammianus Marcellinus, describing Constantius approaching Rome, says that, contemplating with a serene countenance the offices of the senate and the venerable images of the stock of his native land, he judged not, like Cineas, Pyrrhus’s envoy, that a multitude of kings had been gathered into one place, but that the refuge of the whole world was at hand. Cicero calls the senate the chief of public safety and public counsel. See Majorian, *Novella* 3, “On the Rite of His Imperial Office”; Virgil, *Aeneid* VI; *Theodosian Code*, law 74, “On Decurions”; Quintilian, Declamation 329. BROSS.]

That senate, glorious in wondrous renown, is proved to have a governor whom the world receives as he establishes laws. Hence those who tremble to state their own cases before you exercise their full authority in the senate.

Yet this modesty too is known to deserve praise: that they should wish [ed., Niv. and Ga., “it was fitting”] to be bound by laws which they themselves know they can establish. In part, this matter is common to us; but we differ in this one respect: that we cannot be subject to another, since we have no judges.

Look upon so many learned men and consider what it means to address them, without fearing the embarrassment of error. You deliberate about men whom you recognize to be superior to yourself.

Therefore conduct yourself in your position so that everyone acknowledges you as the judge of an honored assembly. You sit above all the former consuls; you speak first; and you are viewed with reverence in that hall of freedom in which you are shown to have the leading men of the world entrusted to you.

Who could now think about some obscure fault [Gr. and Cuj. delete this word] when he recognizes that he is among so many lights of conduct? Do you wish not to incur hatred? Exclude from yourself the pursuit of personal gratification. You must possess public affection if you promise nothing in secret.

It will be a great and singular commendation if judges do not accept gifts where there are men eager to give much.

Not only Rome has been entrusted to your jurisdiction [D. Juret reads “dedication,” as in book XI, letter 7; Ac. reads “jurisdiction”]—although all things are contained within it—but ancient laws have also wished your authority to extend within one hundred miles, lest the walls of so great a city should enclose its judge, since Rome possessed everything.

You also hear appeals from the provinces designated by law. Learned advocates serve under you, since it is not difficult to fill the ranks of orators in that homeland where one continually has the opportunity to hear masters of eloquence.

You are carried in a *carpentum* through a noble populace; public prayers accompany you; most welcome acclamations proceed with you in harmonious voice. Act well, because when you come, the peoples are permitted to fall silent.

You have abundant means of winning the favor of so great a city, if diverse payments are not sold under any form of venality; if the profitable provision of the baths, once kindled, does not grow lukewarm amid the fires of robbery; if the spectacle provided for pleasure does not become a cause of litigation.

For anyone who avoids injustice in party contests pleasantly compels the people to be grateful. So great is the power of glorious truth that even in theatrical matters equity is desired.

Having therefore completed the order of admonitions, by that indiction we adorn you with the dress of the toga-bearing dignity, so that, clothed in Romulean attire, you may strive after Roman laws. [Note: He means the toga used by Roman citizens, *Code*, law 32, “But Even If Received,” “On Fiscal Rights,” to which he alluded in book III, letter 17: “Put on the customs of the toga-clad; strip off barbarism.” Dio, book L, notes Antony using ancestral dress: ἐσθῆτι ἐκ τῶν πατρίων ἔχρητο, “he used clothing from the ancestral customs.” Tertullian, *On the Pallium*; Salvianus, book IV, *On the Government of God*; Claudian, *Against Rufinus*:

> He brings back barbarism.

> Nor is he ashamed, while ruling Ausonian chariots and laws,  
> To assume the deformed customs and clothing of the Getae,  
> And to change the distinctive dress of Latium and the toga.

The toga of advocates is mentioned in *Code*, law 3, “On Advocates of Different Courts.”]

For if you prove equal to this dignity, there is nothing that you will not in due course obtain from us. You will be worthy of every such support if the senate praises your conduct. For the faith of a matter is complete when the highest men are proved to be unanimous witnesses.

## V. FORMULA OF THE QUAESTORSHIP

If dignities are as illustrious as they enjoy our words [Gr., Cuj., and Cor. N., “our presence”], if frequent presence reveals the affection of the ruler, no judge can be so glorious as the one who has been admitted to share our thoughts.

To some we entrust the administration of public money; to others we grant cases to hear; to others we delegate the rights of our patrimony [others, “marriage.”] But we receive the quaestorship with our whole heart, since we consider it to be the voice of our own tongue.

It is necessarily applied familiarly to our thoughts, so that it may properly say what it knows us to think. It lays aside its own will and receives our mind’s desire in such a way that what it says is thought to have proceeded from us rather than from it.

O how difficult it is for a subordinate to assume the words of the ruler, to be able to say what is believed to be ours, and, advanced into the public sphere, to make prosperity glorious!

Consider what weight and what distinction you possess together. [Note: It belongs to the quaestor’s office to make the emperors’ speeches and other matters known to the senate, as is clear from Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 65; *Nero*, chapter 15; and *Titus*, chapter 6; Aelius Spartianus, *Hadrian*, at the very beginning; Cornelius Tacitus, book XVI. Sidonius Apollinaris intended to designate this in his panegyric of Majorian:

> From whose mouth Caesar deigns  
> To speak throughout the world, although he has an eloquent quaestor too.]

May he flourish. [Col. 0686D] Ulpian likewise, in book 1 of *On the Office of the Quaestor*, reports that candidates devoted themselves solely to reading the books of the emperors in the senate. [BROSS.]

If we are uncertain about anything, we consult the quaestor, who is [Note: [Col. 0686D] The quaestor of the sacred palace subscribed petitions, or even issued replies; and, to summarize his entire office briefly at this point, he dictated laws and annotated petitions and replies, as is clear from the *Notitia of the Roman Empire*, Novels 53 and 114, and the final law of the *Code*, *On Various Rescripts*. Symmachus, writing to Ausonius: “You are quaestor, I remember; a participant in royal counsel, I know; arbiter of petitions, author of laws, I recognize.” Elsewhere: “The honor of the quaestorship and the practice of drafting enactments have exercised you more.” Procopius, book 1 of *The Persian War*: “For these reasons he is called the guardian of justice and laws, the treasury of public reputation, and the arsenal of laws,” as in the Novel of Valentinian, *On Accidental Homicide*. In short, he is plainly the quaestor whom in the court we call the chancellor. Memorials also belonged to the quaestor; that is, they received and completed laws and rescripts, meaning that they wrote them out or arranged for them to be written. BROSS.] the treasury of public reputation, the arsenal of laws, always ready for the unexpected; and, as Cicero, the master of eloquence, says, nothing seems more excellent than being able through speech to hold people’s minds, attract their wills, drive them wherever one wishes, and lead them away from whatever one wishes. For if it is the orator’s special quality to speak gravely and elegantly, so that he can move the minds of judges, how much more eloquent must he be who is known to admonish peoples with the emperor’s voice, so that they love what is right, despise what is wrong, praise the good without end, and denounce the worst with force? Thus, wherever the strength of eloquence prevails, the exercise of authority should almost be a holiday.

Let him be a most prudent imitator of the ancients; let him correct the conduct of others and preserve his own with proper integrity. In short, the quaestor ought to be such that he may fittingly bear the emperor’s image. For if it should happen, as usual, that we hear a case through official records, what authority will the tongue possess that can fulfill the royal majesty beneath our eyes? There must be knowledge of the law and caution in speech, [Col. 0686B] so that no one may reproach what it is established that the emperor judged. Moreover, firmness of spirit will be necessary, so that he may be removed from the path of justice by no gifts and no terrors. For we ourselves endure contradiction in order to preserve equity, and even the person who must be obeyed ought to accept it.

But see that you defer to learning only so far as to set forth everything after careful and credible investigation. Other dignities may seek the assistance of assessors, but your dignity supplies counsel to the emperor. And therefore, moved by the reputation of your prudence and eloquence, we grant you the quaestorship in that indiction—God permitting—as the glory of letters, the temple of civility, the mother of all dignities, the dwelling-place of self-restraint, and the seat of every virtue, so that you may act in such a way as to show yourself equal to the matters just mentioned.

For the provinces send their petitions to you; the senate seeks from you assistance in law; the learned are known to expect from you what they understand; and you must be sufficient for all those who happen to seek legal remedies from us. But when you have done all this, do not become elated by any arrogance, do not be consumed by envy, and do not rejoice in the misfortunes of others, because what is hateful to the emperor cannot befit a quaestor. Exercise the emperor’s authority as one subject to his condition.

Thus speak, glorified by truthful speech [others: “our speech”], yet believe that you will have to render an account to us as judges, when either the guilty person receives the requital of his conduct or the man praised wins the glory of a good purpose.

## VI. FORMULA OF THE DIGNITY OF THE MASTER OF OFFICES

[Col. 0687A]

Whoever receives the name of master assumes a venerable honor, because this title always arises from expertise, and from the name it is understood what must be judged concerning a man’s character. The discipline of the palace belongs especially to him; he successfully restrains the turbulent conduct of insolent schools within the bounds of his moderation. So many ranks are arranged without confusion, and he bears the burden of all, which the multitude has divided among them. Having discharged the gravity of his title, he adorns the authority of the emperor through his actions.

Through him the senator who comes is presented to our sight; he admonishes the fearful, composes the speaker, and habitually inserts words of his own, so that we may hear everything with decorum. His appearance is not unwelcome to the emperor; he is the herald of our conversation and the glorious giver of the court consistory, like a kind of morning star. For just as that star promises the coming day, so he grants to those who desire it the sight of the serenity of our countenance.

Moreover, we entrust the greatest burden of cases to the secure limits of his hearing [Ac.: “boldness”], so that, relieved by his faithful attentions, we may devote ourselves more vigorously to public affairs. [Note: [Col. 0687D] Travel permits are issued by the emperor, the praetorian prefect, or the master of offices; and if anything less than lawfully has been done in making use of the public transport system, the matter is referred to them. Law 3 of the *Code*, *On Public Transportation*, states that for this reason it is not surprising that they issue travel permits; governors, however, do not possess the power to issue them, according to the Novel of Majorian, *On Public Transportation*, except to those carrying out public functions. BROSS.]

He also preserves the timely speed of the *veredi*—whose condition is always one of travel—through the strictness of his diligence, so that by the benefit of speed he may expedite our concerns, which he assists by his counsel. Through him, kindness toward foreign peoples is arranged to the praise of our commonwealth; and those who did not wish to come return having been received with honor. Through him, moreover, the arrival of envoys, however hurried, is announced to us in advance; through him the conveyance of our name [Jur.: properly, “our divine power”] is dispatched; and to him above all is entrusted what is recognized as so necessary.

In view of these labors, antiquity also decreed the greatest authority to him, so that no judge throughout the provinces might assume the fasces unless he too had decreed that this should be done. It subjected the judgments of others to his discretion, so that what another appeared to have carried out would return to him. He does not, indeed, have the burdens of exacting money, but plainly enjoys the good of the power he has acquired [Grul. and Cuj.: “of the power preserved intact”]. I suppose this was done so that the dignity instituted for the emperor’s relief might be drawn out from various titles.

He also appoints, at his own discretion, the regulators of foodstuffs in the royal city and makes him judge of so necessary a matter. For he provides joy to the people; he provides adornment to our times when he places such men in charge of the public supplies that the complaining populace, once satisfied, does not know how to revolt.

His office is adorned with such a prerogative of rank that, having completed the duties of military service, he is honored with the name of imperial authority. In a remarkable manner, he seems to have found precedence among the praetorian cohorts and the soldiers of the urban prefecture, from whom humble service was rendered to you. Thus, in favor of a great honor, a certain injustice arises from the laws, when he who is declared to have served elsewhere is placed above the guards of others.

The assistant of the master is also presented to our sight, so that by a substitute distribution of favor we may choose the support of one who provides us with faithful assistance. Therefore, we entrust to you, for that indiction, this dignity, illustrious through so many titles and enriched by so many insignia, to be governed with fitting gravity, so that in everything you do you may appear to have acted as a master. For nothing is left over for character if—God forbid—one should fall into error after attaining such maturity.

## VII. FORMULA OF THE COMITIVA OF THE SACRED LARGESSES

It is altogether pleasing when titles immediately designate actions, because all ambiguity in hearing is removed when the matter being performed is contained in the title itself. The words testify that the comitiva of the sacred largesses presides over royal gifts. It was truly fitting, and in every respect carefully devised, to establish a dignity set apart in the distribution of royal gifts and to name another person’s honor, while it is established that we confer the gifts.

It is an innocent activity, an office of piety, always to provide what can increase the emperor’s reputation. It is a great happiness to serve royal gifts and to possess a dignity arising from public generosity. Other judges obey the remaining virtues of the ruler; this office alone serves only the moments of clemency. Nothing strict is carried out through it, and nothing severe is imposed; it obeys when petitions are offered on our behalf.

Through you we raise up the fortunes of petitioners, lavish gifts in abundance on the Kalends of January, and your service is public joy. But you adorn this generosity of ours with another service: you cause our likeness to be stamped on ordinary metal and make the coinage remind future ages of our times.

O great discoveries of the wise! O praiseworthy institutions of our ancestors! The image of the emperors seems to nourish their subjects through commerce, while the emperors’ counsels never cease to watch over the welfare of all. To this, so to speak, gift-bearing dignity we also add the office of chief secretary, the sign of our generosity and of public happiness, so that through you we may bestow honors, through the same person through whom we confer our financial largesses.

This is deserved, since both are provided through similar favor, and matters joined by equal praise ought to be administered by one judge. It is not enough that the judges of the provinces lie under your dignity: you also confirm the office of the leading men in matters of documents, since nothing is considered complete unless it has been formally completed by you.

It is also known that the sacred vestment was entrusted to you from ancient times, so that whatever pertains to the splendor of kings might obey your ordinances. You also undertake the administration of the shores with provision for incidental profit. Merchants, whom human life plainly requires, are subject to this authority. For whatever human ambition can possess as precious in clothing, bronze, silver, or gems obeys your arrangements, and those who have come from the farthest regions of the world flock to your judgment.

Antiquity also assigned to you the commerce in salt, between silk garments and the most precious pearl, not ineptly, so that it might plainly demonstrate your wisdom, to which such a commodity was entrusted to serve. Therefore, in that indiction, we confer upon you the dignities of the comitiva of the sacred largesses and of chief secretary, so that you may be adorned with many praises, being girded about with a multitude of honors.

Use your titles, therefore, with due ceremony; and if custom has taken anything from you by reason of your ancient privilege, it has certainly left much that you ought to claim, since the glorious but laborious care of two dignities brings you abundant fruit of honor if they are cultivated with upright character.

## VIII. FORMULA OF THE COMITIVA OF PRIVATE PROPERTY

The comitiva of private property, as the sound of its very name indicates, is said once to have governed the private substance of the emperors through the care of the financial officers [Cor. and Gam.: “through the care of the financial officer”]. And because it could not exercise the height of judicial authority among people reduced to the lowest conditions, it prudently undertook other titles as well, so that the Latial dignity might not seem to have dealings only with servants; instead, it occupied itself more successfully with urban affairs after it had fittingly abandoned the cases of rustics.

For what would those who had no legal standing first do among slaves under public law? [Note: [Col. 0689C] Slaves have no legal personhood and are therefore called ἀπρόσωποι, “without a person,” by Theophilus at the beginning of the title *On Stipulations of Slaves*. Concerning them, see Dio, *On Infidelity*, and the single law of the *Code*, *If by Force or in Another Manner*. Basil calls slavery ἀτιμία, “dishonor.” FORN.] No advocate was present there; the parties did not summon one another through a formal action. There was a secretariat confused by unpolished [Gr.: “undefiled”] disorder, and it was abusively called a court where the parties did not cite the statements of the wise.

Now the dignity deals with the cases of free persons, and is truly regarded as a legitimate magistrate when it is understood to be able to deliberate concerning the fortunes of freeborn people. First, a custodial duty has been decreed for you, as though for the public parent, against wicked lusts and the depraved desires of the human race, so that no one might pollute himself through shameful intercourse by failing to show reverence toward blood relations.

For public gravity, after due consideration, distinguished the sanctity of kinship and the grace of relationship, because nature’s proximity is owed something quite different from what we can permit to bodily license. Against such people you are chosen as the sole and self-controlled investigator, so that while pursuing such disgraces you may obtain the praises of chastity.

[Note: [Col. 0689C] See above, book 4, letter 18. Constantius, in laws 3 and 4, calls the houses and dwelling places of the dead “tombs,” title *On Violating Tombs*, Theodosian Code. This jurisdiction once belonged to the pontiffs, law 2, under the words “with the pontiffs,” in the same title; law 50, *Inheritance*, *Digest*, *On the Claiming of an Inheritance*; and the final law, *On the Dead*, here calls it “sacred repose.” See Suetonius, *Domitian*, chapter 17; Cicero, *On the Laws*, book 2, and letter 10. FORN.]

The equal laws have also entrusted the sacred repose of the dead to your conscience, so that no one might strip tombs clothed in marble, no one might presumptuously violate the beauty of columns through irreligious daring, and no one might expose foreign ashes, consumed either by the passage of time or by devouring flame, through criminal investigation, lest the body that had once escaped the troubles of the world should again suffer human ambushes.

For although corpses do not perceive theft, the person who is shown to have taken anything from the dead is recognized as alien to all piety. [Col. 0690B] See what has been entrusted to you: the chastity of the living and the security of the dead.

You also have throughout the provinces a considerable amount arising from the perpetual right of tribute. [Note: [Col. 0689D] See below, book 12, letter 13. These are the officials who exacted the public assessment. JUR.]

You direct the collectors of the public tax, admonish the possessors, and share no small legal rights with the other judges; you do not allow abandoned property to remain vacant. Thus, whatever usurpation could seize, you cause our treasury to obtain through lawful gains.

You legally place the nearest relatives of the dead before us, [Note: [Col. 0689D] In intestate successions the treasury occupies the final place and is postponed to agnates, cognates, colleagues, and fellow soldiers, title *On the Inheritance of Decurions*, Code. Hence Harmenopulus and the other interpreters of Greek law appropriately define vacant property as ἀδέσποτα καὶ ἀκληρονόμητα, “without a master and without an heir.” FORN.] because in this case the emperor’s person comes after everyone else. But for this reason we hope not to acquire it, provided that there are persons who ought to possess what has been left behind.

[Note: [Col. 0689D] *Depositivae*, according to the old reading; *repositivae*: both are correct, but the former is preferable, according to law 31, “Never,” *Digest*, *On the Acquisition of Ownership of Things*. There Paul defines a treasure as an ancient deposit of money whose memory no longer survives, so that it no longer has an owner, and grants it to the finder. Here, however, it is applied to the treasury, contrary to the legal discipline: section “Treasures,” *On the Division of Things*, Institutes, book 2; at the end of book 3 of the *Digest*, *On the Law of the Treasury*; and the single law of the *Code*, *On Treasures*. Plato, at the beginning of book 11 of *The Laws*, plainly denies that treasures should be removed.

Furthermore, for reasons of security, money was deposited in monuments and tombs, as is clear both from this and from the prologue to Terence’s *Eunuch*, though this practice was later forbidden. There is also a title in book 45 of the *Basilica*: “That it is not permitted to bury money with the dead,” οὐκ ἔξεστι συντάπτειν τεθνεῶσι χρήματα, “it is not permitted to bury money with the dead.”

What is read in the cited single law—movable goods or ornaments deposited by unknown owners in an earlier age—is likewise consistent with the description in this formula. Thus the Poet says:

“He opened up ancient aid from the earth for the journey,

treasures, an unknown weight of silver and gold.”

And the scholiast on Homer, *Iliad* 3, explained κειμήλια as ἀργὰ καὶ ἀπόθετα χρήματα, “idle and hidden wealth,” riches concealed and stored away. FORN. Here he is called the count of treasures, of the sacred largesses, and of the sacred remunerations or gifts, in law 2 of the *Code*, *On Travel Allowances*; the law “Palatines,” *On the Palatine Offices of the Sacred Largesses*; and law 41 of the Theodosian Code, *On Appeals*. He is also said to preside over imperial gifts; through him the fortunes of petitioners are raised up, and abundant largesses are made on the Kalends of January. The day of the largesses is noted in the law “Laudable,” *On Appeals from Divine Judges*, and by Nicephorus, book 10, chapter 23. BROSS.]

Money deposited long ago, whose rightful owners have been lost through the passage of time, is also assigned through your investigation to our treasuries, so that those who allow everyone to possess his own may willingly offer us what belongs to others. A person who finds without causing loss loses nothing, since he does not lose what is his own.

Therefore, under favorable auspices, we adorn you in that indiction with the honor of the comitiva of private property, which the laws have decreed equal even to the prefects. For it too is a courtly authority deserving of reverence in our palace by right; you will make it grow beyond its boundaries if you exercise the dignity you have undertaken with self-restraint.

## IX. FORMULA OF THE COMITIVA OF THE PATRIMONY

[Col. 0691A]

The reason of ancient custom persuades us to instruct through our documents those who, being far away, receive the dignities transmitted to them, so that those whom we could not instruct in person might be admonished by a credible reading. But you, whom the royal election has selected for the care of our patrimony [Gr., Cuj., and Forn.: “legal patrimony”], we instruct not so much through written commands as through the practice of our most serene conversation.

Our conversations will indeed be instruments of justice for you, once you have understood that what pleases us can also conform to divine commands. For we have entrusted our patrimony to you for the relief of private fortunes, not for their oppression. If you wish to consider the principle of our tranquility, you will see that you impose a kind of humiliating prejudice upon the servants of the royal house.

An evil master strives by every means to claim his own advantage; but the person known to pursue a good reputation is always more burdened by his own judgment. It is an insolent kind of freedom among rustics that they think everything is permitted to them merely because they are said to belong to our substance. Therefore, be moderate toward them while exercising your elevated authority. We grant the power together with its restraint.

Consider with what splendor the dignity you have undertaken ought to be handled, since through it you have earned the emperor’s familiarity above the other judges. For just as the rising sun reveals the colors of bodies after banishing the night, so the quality of your character will not remain hidden when you are constantly seen by the emperor.

Your mind will lie open to our eyes and ears. We recognize the character of servants in their face and voice. If a tranquil expression and a moderated voice make their suggestion, we believe the cases to be thoroughly sound. For whatever is said turbulently, we do not consider just.

Therefore, the ruler’s scrutiny will weigh your speech, since those who can express their words cannot conceal their desires. Words are the mirror of the human heart, since a person is believed to approve immediately in his character what he has shown himself to have chosen for action.

The proud person is also revealed by his crooked gait. [Note: [Col. 0691D] *Varicatis gressibus* means “with crooked steps,” that is, deceitfully; hence *praevaricatores*, law 212, “Prevaricators,” *On the Meaning of Words*, law 1, *On the senatorial decree Turpillianum*. Pliny, book 18, chapter 9: “The ploughman,” he says, “unless bent over, ploughs crookedly” (*praevaricatur*). From this the term was transferred to the forum; precaution must therefore be taken where it originated. Ulpian, however, following Labeo, in law 1, *On Prevaricators*, says that the name derives from a “varied contest”; this derivation could be defended, since wily deceivers are called *varii dolosi*, law 1, *Digest*, *On Fraud*, and the Greeks render this as ὁ ποικίλος κατηγορῶν, “the crafty accuser,” title 1, book 60 of the *Basilica*. FORN.] The angry person is declared by the heat of his eyes. The deceitful person always prefers a downward gaze. Inconstancy exposes the fickle through their eyes. The miser is made plain by his hooked fingernails.

And therefore, strive for the virtues appropriate to the rank to which you have been advanced, because no one can deceive the emperor, who is proven to investigate in you even the causes of natural traits with the greatest insight.

Therefore, in that indiction, with God’s help, we advance you to the comitiva of our patrimony, so that our palaces may attest that you are an incorruptible judge, whom we have judged worthy of advancement. What could you desire more than to know that the tongues of noblemen praise you?

Elsewhere, perhaps, unjust judges are feared; here, where immediate remedy is sought, a purchased judgment is not feared. Untangle the complaints of possessors without saleable delay [Gr. and Cuj.: “constrain”; Niv. and Ga.: “distinguish”]. Everything just becomes a benefit through the advantage of speed, and what is restored as a matter of duty is considered a gift because of such favor.

Let our possessions, whether because they are immovable or for another reason, not depart from their established boundaries, lest, through contrary conduct, what cannot be moved should nevertheless be extended through evil character. Also impart to your soldiers the chastity of spirit that you have chosen to pursue. How can the person under whom excess is not forbidden be called just?

Therefore, with God as your author, make fortunate use of the privilege of dignity granted to you. Let what you see most frequently incite you to desire good, because in what you do I shall be both judge and witness.

Even if you arrange banquets with careful organization, you must become renowned not only in our palace but also among foreign peoples. Envoys arriving from almost every part of the world, when they begin to share our banquets, marvel at the abundance they find, knowing that such things are exceedingly rare in their own country. They are also astonished that the abundance of a single table can satisfy such crowds of servants, so that they judge that what has been consumed grows again, from which so much is plainly seen to emerge.

They certainly have something to discuss in their own countries, when they eagerly tell their parents what they have seen. Thus the person who is found to be provident in our arrangements becomes celebrated throughout almost the whole world.

Add that your offices are the setting for the seasons of our joy, when our breast is made free from cares; and then you are granted an opportunity to make suggestions, when it is denied to everyone else. Deservedly, since you are the judge of so great an establishment and of its banquets, may your mind be indulged with delicate foods [Gr.: “most delicate”; Cor., Niv., and Ga.: “most delicate foods”].

[Note: [Col. 0692D] *Delinitus*, according to the old reading, “most delicate.” The custom should incidentally be noted by which envoys were admitted to royal banquets, something regarded as highly honorable. Ammianus Marcellinus, book 15: “Placed before others in the honor of the royal table.” Pacatus the panegyrist: “One was honored by conversation, another blessed by the table, another consecrated by a kiss.” Quintus Curtius, book 8: “The chief honor was considered to be that seated persons were permitted to dine with the king.” Valerius Maximus, book 5, chapter 1, speaking of Paulus: “Nor was he unworthy of the honor of the table.” FORNER.]

## X. FORMULA BY WHICH ABSENT NOBLES ARE MADE NOBLES THROUGH LETTERS PATENT

Good character would be gravely endangered if dignities were granted only to the wealthy or physically strong, since you will find many who avoid the palace watches but are able to shine more brightly through a praiseworthy way of life. For many lack sufficient means for triumph; many who pursue philosophy are deprived of bodily health; and it often happens that wise men lie unrewarded if people always reach honors through the courtly practice of attendance.

It is rare for many advantages to converge in one person, when the ruler’s clemency ought to assist everyone. What if a poor nobleman fears the expenses of the consulship? What if a man renowned for wisdom cannot bear the burdens of a prefecture? What if a man with an abundant tongue fears the weight of the quaestorship? What if others avoid the remaining fasces because they are weary of the burdens rather than because they lack merit?

If such offices are avoided by great men, do they not receive a kind of rejection through the shamelessness of our gentleness? How much more just is it for a good emperor to leave unrewarded nothing that nature makes praiseworthy? Wisdom is what deserves honors; everything else comes from outside. [103] Prudence alone is placed before all things when it is happily found in a person.

Let us have among us a consul unimpaired in fortune; let there be also chief men without prolonged labor; let exercises have their rewards. But let this honorable place also exist, which is attained solely through merit. For the most sacred laws did not judge absurdly when they decreed that those commended by the reputation of good opinion should be sought for such high offices through letters patent issued in their absence.

Even if means should abandon them in the display of so great an honor, conscious virtue would not conceal them. Those who seemed to despair of their own fortune are encouraged toward such offices. The strong man earns this through his labors; the physically weak earns it through his praises. For all are commended under different conditions whom the name of this honor embraces; and I do not know whether the person who is perceived to have earned while at leisure what laborers earned is thought to have extorted something more from merit [Gr., Cuj., Niv., and Ga.: “what”].

Therefore, by the present letters patent, from that indiction onward, with the Divinity favorable, defend this principle for yourself, so that, after considering the circumstances of the present time, you may enjoy the order of the honor you have attained. Yet in every respect let those be preferred who have appeared before us through the greatest labor. For one merit must yield to two merits that have overcome it [Ed., Ac., Niv., and Ga.: “must believe in one merit elevated by two”]. Otherwise everyone could hasten toward easy dignities if those who labor were not preferred to those at leisure.

Let those who can attain the former honors attain them, and let those whom we believe worthy not be absent from the latter. Thus, with both favors set in motion, they will be able to hasten to our palaces, and you will be accompanied by the joys of the honor you desired.

## XI. FORMULA OF A VACANT (HONORARY) ILLUSTRIOUS RANK

It is established that the commonwealth is happy when it shines, adorned with many citizens. For just as the heavens are made bright by the stars, so cities gleam with the light of dignities. This is not because a man becomes another person through honors, but because he becomes more modest, since a better order of conduct is expected from him.

Who would wish to handle his reputation disgracefully when he knows that it has been specially chosen for praise? Honors glorify the man whose life also commends him. For it is not permitted even to the emperor to live by a bad practice, since the people may secretly speak about him whose character no one has dared publicly to criticize.

Therefore, in return for your loyalty and labors, accept the vacant (honorary) illustrious rank of the comitiva of the household, so that you may appear adorned before your fellow citizens and, what is most delightful to good minds, may continually occupy yourself with your own interests.

For what is more fortunate than cultivating a field and shining in the city, where one’s own work delights its author and nothing is acquired through deception, while the granaries are filled by pleasant labor? Therefore, we have given you a delightful honor; join dignity to your conduct. For the two are connected to one another: one depends upon the other. Scattered seeds do not grow together unless the quality of the soil also does its work. You will have a rich harvest from our favor if we learn that you have managed our judgments with the greatest excellence.

## XII. FORMULA OF THE FIRST-ORDER COMITIVA

To many, and even in alternating circumstances, it seems a great thing to be born for the purpose of occupying oneself with public usefulness through upright actions. But how much happier it is to receive a splendid honor without having the burdens of thought!

Sometimes continual labors make dignities themselves unpleasant, since human weakness quickly tends to grow weary; and what one is believed previously to have sought ambitiously is later found to be something one wishes to avoid. But it is much more excellent to be present before royal eyes while absent from troubles; to possess the favor of one’s position while avoiding the insults of service.

It is pleasant to deserve something in such a way that no anxiety can disturb it, while prosperity becomes much more agreeable when one feels only its joys. Consider, therefore, this honor to have been granted to you as a reward in leisure. It is known to have been conferred by ancient provision upon men who had labored excessively, so that governors of provinces, praised after a year of service, could scarcely be raised to such a summit, although they acknowledged that they owed much to those who held it.

The counselors of prefects are also distinguished by the testimony of their conscience and preeminent in dictation. In the exercise of the most extensive prefecture they appear to exercise their eloquence in such a way that you might believe them to possess another quaestorship for dispatching public business. We therefore frequently take them on as judges, because we find them most learned.

Recognize, then, what is thought of such an honor: when accomplished men of prefectural rank, in return for so many praiseworthy institutions, receive rewards of this kind, and when an honor of such splendor is deservedly bestowed, one that is reckoned by the brilliance even of the senatorial order.

It is a distinguished rank, entirely worthy of our consistory, which enters among the illustrious and is summoned among the nobles; a dignity girded with the honor of a leisurely belt, which knows no offense and is known to burden no one, and above all does not know how to arouse envy against any good.

Therefore, moved by your character, we bestow upon you, from that indiction onward, with the favor of our majesty, the first-order comitiva, so that just as you enter our consistory in the toga [others: “when summoned”], you may adorn it by a character worthy of praise, since this honor stands near to that of the illustrious, while no intermediate rank is recognized.

Let it delight you to imitate those whom you approach in rank. You make the position broad and honorable if you conduct yourself with measured consideration. Let the fact certainly admonish you that the dignity you have undertaken is reckoned by the designation “first order,” since all those adorned with the honor of spectability follow you.

But see to it that no one surpasses you in reputation who follows you in dignity. Otherwise it is a grave burden of envy to shine with the brilliance of the belt while not shining with the lamp of character.

## XIII. FORMULA OF THE MASTER OF THE BUREAU AND THE FIRST-ORDER COMITIVA, TO BE GIVEN TO A *COMICIACUS* WHEN HE HAS COMPLETED HIS SERVICE

If honor is frequently bestowed upon men at leisure; if sometimes nobility is chosen, or merely personal favor supports someone in obtaining something, with what zeal must those be rewarded who have reached the prizes of their contest?

One must consider with what labor they have served, and then think about their reward. The measure of such matters comes from the opposite side: a gift ought to be given to the obedient such as could have been a danger to the unwilling.

Great are the burdens borne by those who keep watch; they compel the reluctant to obey; they track down those hiding in their bedrooms with prudent keenness; they impose the modesty of equality upon the proud. Thus what judges say briefly is completed by these men through effective service.

It is known what dangers they endure when they are sent to handle the cases of others. If he acts too slowly, the petitioner complains; if he acts strictly, the defendant cries out. Thus, between these two opposing sides, it is rare to find praise that deserves commendation.

Let us speak without offending the dignities: it is easier to find a praised judge than a soldier who completes an assigned task without causing offense. It is one thing merely to speak what is lawful; it is another to bring justice to its conclusion. A good act is indeed praiseworthily spoken of, but it is far more glorious when decrees are carried out.

Superiors direct only words, but soldiers are required to produce the result. After everything, they are exposed to danger if, once constrained, they make any plausible complaint. The very integrity of their conduct has often harmed others. For many whom they were compelled to distress in carrying out the judgment they afterward endured as hostile judges.

The ignorant frequently offend those to whom they must afterward submit; and while they preserve faith in the cases of others, they sometimes encounter dangers to their own safety. In the midst of all this, is it not rightly considered a miracle when a soldier escapes with praise?

Such merits, therefore, ought to receive their return, so that we may rouse those rendered sluggish by excessive labor through the compensations granted to them [Gr. and Cuj.: “allowed to them”]. Therefore, confidently use whatever generous laws have granted to veterans. You must not be subjected to any sordid burden, since you have conducted yourself with the purest character.

You will also claim, according to the imperial statutes, the first-order comitiva, which ancient times assigned to those who had completed such military service. You will indeed obtain this through the favor of the ancients, but you are surrounded by the perpetual protection of our name against uncivil attacks and contractual losses, so that the office which served our commands with special diligence may appear to have earned something more from us than other soldiers.

We also decree that anyone who believes our statutes may be violated on any pretext is to be struck with a fine of so many pounds of gold [that is, ten pounds, Gr. and Cuj.]. [Col. 0695D] Yet we do not permit anything attempted through deceitful plotting to have force against you.

## XIV. FORMULA CONCERNING THOSE TO BE REPORTED TO THE SENATE
We indeed wish the senate-house of the most distinguished Senate to be filled through natural fecundity [Col. 0696A], and its offspring to increase so greatly that it may appear to satisfy the wishes of its parents—which is the most difficult kind of appetite. Yet it is less loving not to seek further means by which it may increase so large a number. The diligent farmer, by anticipating, assists the heavenly rain; he waters the nurseries before they have earned the showers they desire. Moreover, striving to improve the offspring of trees, he establishes plantings of diverse stock, so that, through the multiplied sweetness of their fruits, he may impart the adornment of variety to his gardens.

Thus we desire to admit into the Senate a Greek endowed with the most delightful praises of virtue, so that foreign stock, bound by the embrace of favor, may grow accustomed to the customs of the Senate. Yet this cultivation is very different. For what is thought better is grafted onto trees; foreign shoots come to them so that they may become sweetened by the trees’ own [Col. 0696B] sweetness. To you, however, such things are offered so that what is rustic may advance. For although a fire shines at night, it is nevertheless obscure when brought before the sun. Hence nothing exceptional can be brought before that order except what is proved to be increased through it.

Therefore let the Senate receive one conspicuous for the brilliance of his birth and prudently kindled by the warmth of his intellect, as the Senate’s light. Until now he has been distinguished by his own merits; but now he will be made even more luminous by your brilliance. Open the Senate-house; receive the candidate. He has already been destined for the Senate, to whom we have conferred the dignity of the broad purple stripe. The fathers of the state must be benevolent, because this title owes its existence not so much to its own offspring as to general zeal and desire.

## XV. FORMULA OF THE VICAR OF THE CITY OF ROME

The custom of those who act in another’s place is to obey the will of judges in such a way that they possess no dignities of their own. They shine by borrowed light and rely upon another’s strength; in them there seems to be a kind of image of truth, since they do not possess the rights of their own radiance.

You, however, are called a vicar and do not relinquish your privileges, since the jurisdiction granted by the emperor is your own. For you share a certain portion with the prefects, and litigants bring their cases before you under praetorian advocacy. You pronounce judgment by sacred delegation, and—in what is the greatest sign of trust—human lives are entrusted to you in formal indictments, something that among mortals is acknowledged to be precious.

[Note: Above in this book, formula 6; *Sacra*, 1; *Si quis aliquid*, law 38, section 2, Digest, *On Punishments*. They judge by sacred delegation, formula 3, book VI. The praetorian prefect judged by sacred delegation, above, formula 3. Vicar of the City, formula 15. FORNER.]

[Note: “In formal indictments,” that is, in accusations, *Codex Theodosianus*, book IX, title 1, “On Accusations and Indictments.” No one is admitted to bring a charge unless he fulfills the formal requirements of an accusation and binds himself to the penalty that threatens accusers who make false charges: Digest 48.16.7, *On Calumny*; Digest 48.5.11 § “Some”; on the Julian Law on Adultery; Digest 48.2.3, *On Accusations*; Code 9.26.1, *Against Turpillianus*. On the bond of indictment, Code 9.2.11 and the final law, *No One*, “On Accusations”; the final law of the Theodosian Code, *On the Production or Transfer of Defendants*; the penultimate and final laws, *On Accusations*; the final Digest law, *On Private Delicts*. Example: Digest 48.2.3, *On Accusations*, and in Lucian; “the words spoken in court,” gloss of the Basilica, book LX, title 42. FORNER.]

The law has also decreed that you may not be greeted without your military cloak, so that, always seen beneath military dress, you might never be thought a private citizen. But we judge that all these things have been granted for the glory of the prefecture, so that one who is called the vicar of so great a seat might see nothing shadowy or insubstantial.

Consider what sort of things you must display, since you are carried along under such authority. One who is to be cleared of a charge should not be stripped [others: “should not appear stripped”] of innocent property. For what could he owe you if he attributed his escape to his least [Cor., Gam.: “merits”] services [Col. 0697A]?

You are carried in a chariot, in imitation of the highest officials.

[Note: He understands the fortieth milestone, or the fortieth mile. FORNER.]

Within forty miles you guard the laws of the most holy City. At Praeneste you hold games; appointed in place of a consul for the honor, you acquire a senator’s dignity, and those halls are opened to you which are recognized as having been bestowed upon the highest officials.

Hence, in the court of liberty, you occupy your ancestral place; and there you earn a seat where merely to have entered is itself a distinction. Even the senators themselves, who precede you in rank, seem to request certain necessary things from you. You have the power to assist those superior to you; and not without reason you are to be counted among the foremost, since you can either help or harm consular officials.

Raise your spirits beneath the guise of modesty. Every dignity is such as the will of those who administer it makes it. Nothing performed in the commonwealth is base unless it has been corrupted by bad character. For if the equality of humble private citizens is pleasing, how much more welcome is that equality preserved at the summit of power, which maintains a difficult measure while hastening to do its own will?

Accordingly, by the judgment of our serenity, we confer upon you the dignity of the vicariate, which you are to exercise at Rome in such a way as to make your conscience worthy of so great a city. You shall use all the privileges that your predecessors are known to have possessed, because just as we demand from you the institutions of the ancients, so we do not deny ancient rights to your dignity.

## XVI. FORMULA OF THE NOTARIES

There is no doubt that the emperor’s secretariat adorns those subject to it, since it is judged that nothing necessary can be entrusted to anyone except those who have been firmly established in great fidelity. Everything we do is public, indeed; but many matters ought not to be known beforehand until, with God’s help, they have been completed. The more eagerly they are desired to be known, the more they ought to be concealed.

It is fitting that only the most serious men should know the king’s counsels. They ought to imitate archives, which contain the records of documents and speak only when some instruction is sought from them; in everything else they should conceal their knowledge as though they knew nothing. For to inquisitors who are anxious, what is concealed is often betrayed even by the face.

Let innocence be present, for it commends everything, since royal words ought decently to be deposited in a tranquil mind. But since our concern, the huntress of good conduct, has observed you trained in approved character, from that indiction onward we decree that you are our notary, so that, after completing the ranks of service, you may happily reach the summit of the primiceriatus [Col. 0697D].

The honor that makes one a senator and opens the hall of the fathers is not undeserved; for he who serves our cares through constant nighttime labor seems rightly to enter the court of liberty. Another reward is also added to completed labor: if in any way he should deserve to attain an illustrious or vacant post, he must be preferred to all who are shown to be adorned with the rank of codicillary illustris.

Hence it is clearly established that the primiceriatus is granted according to merit, so that within one and the same title a dignity acquired equally might nevertheless be unequal in rank. You must therefore be encouraged toward labor when you see such a reward set before you as the highest offices rejoice to have found.

## XVII. [Note: Referendaries are those who report and explain the wishes of petitioners to the emperor and communicate the emperor’s commands to judges. Novels 10, 113, 124. Sometimes also, as Sigebert writes in his *Chronicle*, they confirm public documents with the king’s ring or seal. BROSS.] FORMULA OF THE REFERENDARIES

Although each dignity is as illustrious as the sight of our presence illuminates it—since the one who properly gains our conversations always receives honor—no one nevertheless deserves our words as much as the one who is recognized as a referendary.

Through him the sequence of legal cases is explained to us; through him we learn the wishes of those who appeal to us; and to them we return answers, so that we may release affairs that have been fettered [Cor., Gam.: “set in order”]. It is a great thing to serve prudence in this imperial contest and, when the need suddenly arises, to assert the troubles of others in such a way that one seems to satisfy the wishes of those who complain.

What is it to remain undisturbed amid our tumultuous processions, or not to be hindered at all by such great clamors? He must extract from the agitated crowd what he can communicate to us peaceably and report more distinctly than he could have heard it. It is difficult to compose the words of frightened people and to speak the truth: the petitioner does not fear the outcome of his case as much as this man bears the danger in reporting it.

If he says anything less than the truth, he is called an enemy; he is proclaimed to have been bribed. The master of the case can turn his own words under the protection of fear, but the reporter is not permitted to alter anything. Our decisions, moreover, must be held in the memory with such care that nothing appears either omitted or added.

You will often be about to repeat our words while we ourselves are listening; and, bound by a difficult condition, you are subject to our judgment while you strive to explain the cases of others. Therefore our choice has appointed you a referendary; but apply purity of conscience and truth of speech to our commands.

Our conversation grants you remarkable learning: while through you it organizes others, it adorns the quality of your mind. For under us it is not permitted to be unlearned, since we act in place of a whetstone and render brilliant minds bright, polishing them through the constant handling of cases.

Therefore report to all those matters that you ought or were able to receive as having been commanded by us. You approve what is ours if you report it justly. Love what glorifies us. Let your will be such as you see our purpose to be. Above all [Juret reads: “to the highest degree”], we want you to be such that through you we may even correct judges.

We require from you a particular tribute, so that, just as we mingle our words familiarly with you, our opinion may also deserve from you a special affection.

## XVIII. FORMULA OF THE PREFECT OF THE GRAIN SUPPLY

If dignities are to be assessed by this standard—that a man is regarded as honorable in proportion to the benefit he is known to have conferred upon citizens—then surely he must be glorious who is chosen to provide abundance for the Roman people.

[Note: He calls food and grain supplies “abundance,” as in Code of Theodosius 15.1.4, *On Public Works*; Digest 50.16.20, *On Compensation*; and Valerius Maximus, book V, chapter 1. Hence “to supply” (*copiare*) in the sense of providing a great convoy and enormous booty, in Aulus Gellius, book XXVII, chapter 2, and Nonius Marcellus. This is a military term and is not easily found elsewhere. BROSS.]

Your concern, indeed, is that grain should be prepared for the most sacred City [Col. 0699A], that an abundance of bread should overflow everywhere, and that so great a people should be satisfied as though at a single table. You move through the bakers’ workshops and among the food supplies; you demand the proper measure and cleanliness of the bread. You do not judge as insignificant the task through which Rome can praise you—rightly so, since the affection of that city is an exceptional glory.

And lest what you do be thought the lowest of duties, you mount the prefect of the City’s chariot amid a shared glorification. You are found closest to him at public spectacles, so that the people whom your industry feeds may recognize that you have been honored to their own reverence.

For if a complaint about bread, as usually happens, should be stirred up, you, the guarantor of abundance, dissolve civil disturbances through immediate satisfaction; and through you it is ensured that nothing excessive is done by complaining crowds.

Pompey is rightly said to have reached the summit of affairs after providing an abundance of supplies in sufficient quantity,

[Note: D. Juret thinks that *in honore* should be read as a single expression, “in honor,” as above, book III, letter 53, and below, book IX, letter 24. Also Mamertinus, *Panegyric* 198.]

because the people’s love is deservedly exceptional when they have been freed from scarcity. Hence he earned their gratitude and the applause of the people.
