Hence he was always uniquely loved, and in the favor of the citizens he surpassed the achievements of all his ancestors [Ac.: “evils”], so that, although he was never called “in honor,” he was addressed with the addition to his name “the Great.”

Let this example invite you to prosperity, since he is recognized as having occupied the place of your honor, whom fortunate Rome admired.

But lest anyone object that you command men of low status, the rights of the bakers have also been made subject to your dignity. Those rights extended through vast possessions in various parts of the world, lest what served Roman abundance through praiseworthy service become cheapened through scarcity. The pork merchants, too, established for the sake of Rome’s food supply, seem to have been assigned to your supervision.

Glory in the privileges you have acquired. Your tribunal is not among the least dignities, since you enjoy Roman favor and transmit commands to the provinces.

But if we examine fully the merits of this office itself, the praetorian prefecture manages the wheat supplies. Yet it is no lesser glory to administer them well than to gather the grain, since in any abundance complaint is not removed if no care is taken over the quality of the bread.

Thus Ceres is said to have discovered grain, while Pan is reported to have been the first to cook the grains after they had been kneaded; hence bread was also named after him. Both, therefore, were praised: she, because she discovered it, and he, because he suitably adapted it for human use.

And so, recognizing your industry, which is always a friend of wisdom, we confer upon you, by our choice, the prefecture of the grain supply for that indiction [Col. 0699D]. Consider now that it is not permitted to steal anything from the people. What is done to the detriment of the City is not concealed in silence. The plebs does not know how to remain silent, and sometimes even says that which no one has done.

Punish fraudsters; as a fair examiner, attend to the weights of the bread. Let that by which the Romans live—the bread—be weighed more carefully than gold, for the joy of the Roman people’s favor is more pleasing to us than an abundance of the most precious metal.

Pay attention, certainly, to what we say. What better thing can you desire than to seek the favor of that people, which we too are known to desire?

## XIX. FORMULA OF THE COUNT OF THE CHIEF PHYSICIANS

Among the most useful arts that the divine power has granted to sustain the needs of human frailty, none seems to offer anything comparable to what healing medicine can provide. It alone, with maternal kindness, always assists those endangered by illness. It alone fights against pain on behalf of our weakness and strives to raise us up where neither wealth nor dignity can offer help.

Experts in legal causes are considered outstanding when they have defended the great affairs of individuals. But how much more glorious it is to drive away what seemed to bring death and to restore health to one in danger, health from which he had been forced to despair!

It is an art that discovers more in a human being than he himself knows. It strengthens those in danger, reinforces what has been shaken, and, foreseeing what is to come, does not yield to illness when the sick person has been disturbed by present weakness. It understands more than it seems to; it trusts action [Ac.: “reading”] more than the eyes, so that to the ignorant what is gathered by reason may almost appear prophetic.

Is it not a proven forgetfulness of human affairs to lack a judge for this expertise? And when wanton pleasures receive a tribune, does this not deserve to have a chief?

Let them therefore have a governor to whom we entrust our safety. Let those who undertake the work of human health know that they must render an account to him. Let an art be called art not because of what it happens to do, but because of what it has learned; otherwise we are exposed to danger if we lie under the control of random impulses.

Therefore, if there is hesitation, let inquiry immediately be made [Ac.: “let the matter immediately be reported”]. Human health is exceedingly obscure, being a balance composed of contrary humors. Whenever one of these grows beyond measure, it immediately brings the body to illness. Hence, just as exhausted health is restored by suitable foods, so what is taken improperly becomes poison.

Let physicians therefore be held responsible for the safety of all. After their schooling, let them be free from their teachers and take delight in ancient books. No one reads more justly and continually than the one who has dealt with human health.

Put aside, practitioners of healing, the harmful quarrels of the sick,

[Note: See Sidonius Apollinaris, book II, letter 12. JUR.]

so that, when you refuse to yield to one another, you may not be seen to destroy your discoveries among yourselves. You have someone whom you can question without envy. Every wise person seeks counsel, since the more diligent man is recognized as the one who proves himself more cautious through frequent questioning.

Indeed, at the very beginnings of this art, a kind of priestly rite consecrates you through sacred vows.

[Note: He means the oath of Hippocrates, than which nothing is more sacred, chaste, or upright. FORN.—See Jerome, letter to Nepotianus, *On the Life of Clerics*, at the end. JURET.]

For you promise your teachers to hate wickedness and love purity. Thus it is not free for you deliberately to do wrong, since even before the moments of knowledge you are bound by the obligation laid upon your souls.

Therefore inquire with greater care into what cures the wounded and strengthens the weak. For I shall see whether any offense can be excused as a lapse. To sin against a person’s health is the crime of homicide.

But we believe that these things are already sufficient, since we are providing one who ought to admonish you. Therefore, from the present time,

[Note: Since there were several orders of chief physicians, in each order there were some who surpassed the others, and these were called counts of the chief physicians. Cassiodorus writes here about the manner of choosing them and their authority. There was not one count, but as many as there were orders of chief physicians. Cognat., *Observations*, book [and] chapter 15.]

we honor you with the countship of the chief physicians, so that among the teachers of health you alone may be regarded as outstanding and all may yield to your judgment—those who torment themselves through the ambition of mutual rivalry.

Be the arbiter of this excellent art, and settle [Juret thinks *discingue* should be read] their disputes, which the outcome alone used to judge [Niv. and Ga.: “which feeling alone used to judge”]. Care for the sick among them, if you wisely cut away harmful quarrels. It is a great responsibility to have wise subjects and to become honorable among those whom the others revere.

[Note: These men are called *περιοδευταί* (“traveling physicians”) by Modestinus, Digest 27.1.6, *On Excuses for Guardians*; and Luke calls them *περιερχομένους* (“going about”) in Acts 19. For physicians traveled around and walked through cities, as may be gathered from the law of Hippocrates: “going about the cities, they are to be regarded as physicians not only in word but also in deed.” So too philosophers strive to present themselves as frequent and useful to those engaged in the same branch of study, Digest 50.5.8, *On Exemptions from Public Duties*, *On Honors*. Suidas, under *δημοσιεύῳ*; the *Nomocanon*, title 1, chapter 34. FORN.]

Let your visitation be the health of the sick, the restoration of the weak, and the certain hope of the weary. Let the inexperienced ask those whom they visit—the sick—whether the pain has ceased and whether sleep has come. Let the sick person question you about his own illness and hear from you more accurately what he himself is suffering.

You, too, certainly have very truthful witnesses whom you can question. For to the skilled chief physician the pulse of the veins declares what the body’s nature is suffering within. Urine is also presented to the eyes, so that it would be easier to fail to notice the voice of one crying out than to fail to perceive signs of this kind.

You may also freely enter our palace; have confidence in entering a place that is usually purchased at great prices. Although others serve under the law of subjection, you are to show diligence to the Lord of all through your outstanding zeal.

It is lawful for you to weary us with fasts; it is lawful for you to oppose our desire and, in place of a favor, prescribe what may torture us for the sake of the joy of health. Finally, you recognize that we grant you such freedom as we are not proved to possess toward others.

## XX. FORMULA OF THE CONSULAR OFFICE

Although the testimony of the name itself seems to declare that your dignity descends from the consuls, such great insignia also surround you that no one can doubt that you shine with the radiance of that lamp.

The axes and fasces, which antiquity dedicated to their genius [Jur.: “to his genius”], seem assigned to your decorations, so that the jurisdiction granted to you, even when unspoken, may admonish the provinces. But what must you think of the fact that you are recognized as adorning the famous curule chairs?

Even the images of rulers are borne before you in the ceremonial pomp of attendance, so that you may be adorned not only with the reverence due to the highest judge but also with that due to sovereigns. O invention of great moderation! From the name of consul you are promised to be most merciful, and from the image of the emperors you are made an object of fear.

In some provinces you are still adorned with the *paenula*, and you are honored by conveyance in a chariot, so that by many indications it may be declared, through clearly expressed representations of these things, that you exercise the lofty duties of this dignity.

Consider that what you undertake is great, and do not corrupt it through any fall into crime. The authority of your name is praised because it confers many benefits. Act so that you are accused by no desires; and if you cannot give, at least hasten to show that you wish to exercise restraint.

For he is regarded as close to one who gives about whom it can be said, “He continually abstains from what belongs to others.” Certainly it is the vice of a most shameful contradiction to pursue thefts while bearing the title of generosity. Let what you are called arouse your spirit to praise. You certainly do not make yourself unequal to your merits if you trample underfoot the offenses of the most shameful ambition.

For to overcome harmful errors is to conquer stained vices, and this man truly is produced from the character of the consulship. The wisest of the ancients did not give such names to offices without purpose, when they sent a consul to the provinces as the governor of great self-restraint.

Triumph in public law; distribute justice; and imitate, to the best of your ability, the one whom you touch through the closeness of your name. A mediocre man may lack money [Ac.: “mediocre men”]; but one who is just cannot fail to possess the talents of character.

Do not fear the open-handed hands of consuls. Good poor men also have their riches. What is sought from you is what is born in the human breast, not what is contained in the bowels of the earth.

How much better to triumph from the treasury of the spirit, from which regret never arises! For you do not become poorer when you grant more; rather, you become as much richer as you recognize that you have scattered the goods of a good conscience [others: “of good conscience”].

Therefore, moved by the praise of your reputation, we order you, for that indiction, to exercise the consular dignity in that province, so that you may not welcome what the laws judge to be hostile. Love more those things that the laws of equity commend. Prove your name through your actions. Counsel the weary, and then you will truly be called consular.

But so that everything may be weighed with even moderation, make it your practice not to seek money, and you will recognize that abundant gifts come to you. For the divine powers have established this condition for human actions: the one who does not know how to desire shameful profits can grow rich more fully. Those who act well receive even without knowing it, because when the ambition of evils is despised for a little while, more is bestowed by a gift from above.

## XXI. FORMULA OF THE GOVERNOR OF A PROVINCE

Antiquity entirely and wisely decreed that judges should be sent to the provinces, so that mediocrity might not become burdensome by requiring people to come to us. For who would endure the boldness of robbers if they knew that discipline was far away? Violence could openly run rampant if the person who complained were believed to be heard only after delay.

But how much better it is to repress soft offenses while they are still in their cradle than to punish hardened crimes! We shorten the course of evils if we make judgments present. For who would dare to sin when he knows that punishment hangs above his neck?

Therefore our choice sends you as governor to that province for that indiction, so that you may truly strive to correct those whom you recognize as entrusted to you. Without doubt, place among the other features of your cloak the purple stripes, which you know were not placed there without purpose.

Thus it comes about that, when public officials see the purple,

[Note: Vulcatius Gallicanus, in *Avidius Cassius*: “so that you might recognize all the emperors dressed in purple.” Herodian, book I: “The royal purple received me emerging from the womb”; that is, “the imperial purple received me as I came from my mother’s womb.” The same author, book II, calls it “the royal purple” when he says that Niger was made emperor by the Syrian army and clothed in purple and the rest of the imperial apparatus. Lampridius, in *Alexander*, concerning Ulpian: “Whom he often defended from the anger of the soldiers by displaying the purple.” Trebellius Pollio called the emperors’ cloak the *peplum*, in *Saturninus*, chapter XXI, the tyrant. FORN.]

they may always be reminded of the emperor’s vigor.

[Col. 0703B] Clad in the *geniatus*, a pleasing garment—the garment that Venus is said to have woven for her son Priapus [Gr. and Cuj.: “Priam”]—you testify through the son’s exceptional beauty in a singular way to the adornment of his mother.

Consider how much the laws have granted, and extend yourself to the measure of your power. The collection of fiscal taxes has been entrusted to you.

[Note: It was the duty of judges or provincial governors to collect taxes. Code 10.19, *On the Collection of Taxes*, Novel 161. It is also the duty of the Catholic clergy, and, by the constitution of Augustus, has been so from the beginning of the proconsuls. Dio, book LIII. BROSS.]

It is established that you have been entrusted with the duty of reporting to the emperor whatever is proved to arise in the provinces. You are also ordered to hear the senator residing there, and to punish a soldier belonging to the prefect only with the prefect’s own knowledge. The laws have ordered your name to be placed before those of honored provincials in subscriptions.

It is granted to be observed what has been thought of you, since so many nobles appear to have been placed beneath you. It is added that you are called “brother” by the emperor,

[Note: The title “brother” was used as a term of friendship, Symmachus, book II, letters 21, 45, 67, and 71. “Friendship cannot be so fortunate that it imitates brotherhood,” Quintilian, *Declamations* 321. Hence, I think, Digest 28.5.58, *No One*, *On the Institution of Heirs*; Digest 17.2.63, *True*, where the partnership has in a certain way the rights of brotherhood. I have also observed that those who were in office were called “friends” by the emperors whom they served, and this remains customary: Code 4.38.1, *If a Slave Is Sold in Such a Way*; final Digest law, *On the Office of the Prefect of the Watch*; Code 5.4.11, *If During Life*; Digest 49.1.1, *On Appeals*; Digest 37.14.17, *Divi*, *On the Law of Patrons*. Thus Alexander called Ulpian his “friend,” not because of age, as the Glossator thinks, but because of esteem and dignity, Code 8.38.4, *On Contracting and Commutative Stipulations*. Julius Firmicus Maternus, book VIII, chapter 27 of the *Mathesis*: “They will be excellent advocates and friends of kings.” Here too “brother of the emperor” is used in this sense. For brotherhood is not contracted through letters, guarantees, or declarations, Code 4.20.13, *Not by Letters*, *On Proof*. To this should be referred Digest 28.5.58, final section, *On the Institution of Heirs*; Digest 17.2.63, final section, *True*, *On Partnership*. In no other sense, I think, did Theobald call Amalasuntha “sister,” nor did she call him “brother,” except that they were fellow rulers, below, book X, letters 1, 2, and 3. FORN.]

so that the nobility of this precious title may raise you above the baseness of crimes.

Consider that the fortunes of so many men have been entrusted to you. Your character will be the reputation of our age. Be restrained in your life [Gr. and Cuj.: “restrained in yourself”], so that you may be a judge of others.

The first form of equity is for governors to begin with themselves, so that criminals may fear one whom they cannot find to be like themselves. For the accused fears no faults in himself when he observes that the judge has them, since the one who acts badly considers that he displeases no one except those of good character.

No one condemns his own actions in another, because it is the nature of the human spirit to strive rather to avenge what it recognizes itself to have committed. O what a thing it is to sit freely upon tribunals and not be subject to one’s own defendant! Let him not begin to become more powerful because he has bought you. Let him fear the strict judge; let him fear the self-controlled judge; let him not hear a flattering one. Give him reason to fear a stern sentence.

Greedy judges do not know how greatly they offend; for when they sell the crimes of others, they make them their own sins. Therefore be attentive, so that we may hear rather the praises of your good actions. You confidently demand from us what you remit, because we think as much about your reward as we recognize that you have not sought money.

## XXII. FORMULA OF THE COUNTship OF SYRACUSE

It is characteristic of royal foresight to choose such persons as judges that those who happen to be staying in distant regions need not come to the imperial court to have their cases heard. For no legal matter could bear the expense of so long a Sicilian journey, when it would be more convenient to lose the case than to gain anything through such expenditures.

[Note: So that lawsuits might be settled in the province and it would not be necessary to approach the emperor’s court, Majorian uses almost the same words in his Novel *On Indulgences*, concerning the remaining matters: “Let no one who complains dare to come from the distant regions of the province to our court with great loss in expenses and costs. For the one who complains finds the plundering of a raging oppressor more tolerable beneath the hard groan of endurance than the result of obtaining vengeance, which must be endured amid the great inconvenience of vigilant attention.” Below, our Cassiodorus, book IX, letter 20; Justinian, Novel 17, *On the Emperor’s Mandates*, section “If It Is Your Concern”: “Especially so that they may define lawsuits with all possible speed.” Valentinian, Novel 4: “It is fitting to provide that poor provincials not be forced, through the lack of a defender, to come expensively to seek hearings.” Novel of Marcian 1 provides that no one is to be brought from a province to the imperial court except upon the report of the judge from whom the appeal was made: “It is clear,” he says, “that by the difficulty of a long interval and enormous expenses, people in need of lawful assistance can be freed. For you see crowds; you see endless throngs of those approaching, flowing not only from neighboring provinces but from the remotest boundary of the world and bringing complaints against their adversaries. This certainly would never have happened if integrity or strictness of judges had flourished in their own places.” FORN.]

For we do not want complaints from Sicily to come to us, but praises, since the action of a governor is burdensome to us if petitioners from so distant a place are able to accuse him. For a grievance is not believed to be false when the hardships of so great a journey are undertaken.

Therefore the matters in which envy is more greatly feared must be handled with greater care. Accordingly, for that indiction, with the favor of the divine power, we grant you the countship of the city of Syracuse, so that you may strive to conduct everything in the way in which you recognize that we have equipped you.

We endure the petitions of litigants who are near; from farther away we ourselves seek those whose arrival here we know to be difficult. You have what ought to adorn you, provided that you arrive there with a conscience cleansed of corruption.

A number of soldiers serves you at our expense. You are displayed among arms, clad in the *geniatus*; your procession is adorned for military array. You employ a peaceful army; you do not undergo the dangers of war, yet you are adorned by the pomp of arms.

Amid these things, however, consider civil discipline. Do not permit the soldiers to be insolent toward landowners. Let them receive their grain allowances with moderation; let them not become involved in foreign cases. Let the one who boasts of being armed recognize that he has been chosen for the security of all.

We neither wish the privileges of your dignity to be diminished nor command them to exceed their limits. Let it be sufficient for you to exercise only as much authority as your predecessors are established to have exercised reasonably.

## XXIII. FORMULA OF THE COUNTship OF NAPLES
Among the other achievements of antiquity, and the astonishing praises of ordered institutions, this deserves to be extolled with every commendation: that the distinguished appearances of different cities seem to be adorned by suitable administrations, so that both assemblies are brought together by the celebrated attendance of the nobility and the knots of legal cases are untied by judicial argument. Hence we too are recognized as possessing no lesser glory, since we renew the deeds of the ancients through annual ceremonies. For what would an invention have accomplished if it had not been continually preserved? Dignities go forth from us shining, [Col. 0705C] like rays from the sun [edition: “from the rays of the sun”], so that justice, preserved in our part of the world, may shine forth. For this reason we sow the benefits of so many advantages, so that we may gather the security of the provincials. Our harvest is the repose of all, which we cannot otherwise take into account than by ensuring that our subjects do not appear to have lost anything unreasonably. Therefore, during that indiction, we gladly appoint you to the comitiva of Naples, so that you may examine civil affairs as an impartial weigher and guard your reputation with as much maturity as you know that you can easily displease that people even by a slight fault.

It is a city adorned by a multitude of citizens and overflowing with delights of sea and land, so that you may judge that you have found the sweetest life there, provided that you do not mingle with any bitterness. Your praetorian offices fill the city, [Col. 0705D] and a crowd of soldiers guards you. You sit upon a jewel-encrusted tribunal [Niv. and Ga.: “a jeweled tribunal”]; but you endure as many witnesses as you recognize the ranks surrounding you to be. Moreover, by authorized command you guard the shores as far as the appointed place. Foreign commerce obeys your will. [Col. 0706A] You grant buyers an advantage in their purchases, and what the eager merchant acquires contributes to your favor.

Yet amid these splendid heights it is fitting to be an excellent judge, since one who is known to live among crowded peoples cannot conceal himself. Your action will become the city’s talk, while what has been done by the judge is carried through the mouths of the people. The multitude of men has its own revenge if I speak adversely [others: “if they speak”]; and what resounds with the support of many is believed to be judgment upon the judge. Conversely, what is better than to look upon that grateful people over whom you are known to preside? What is it like to enjoy the favor of many and to receive those voices which even merciful rulers delight to hear? We provide you with the means of advancement; it is your task to act so that your conduct may please the prince to increase his benefits. [Col. 0706B]

XXIV. FORMULA FOR THE HONORED LANDOWNERS AND CURIALS OF THE CITY OF NAPLES

You indeed pay us tribute with annual devotion; but in return we restore to you dignities adorned with greater reciprocity, so that those who obey our commands may defend you from the wickedness of aggressors. Your repose will be our joy; it will be a pleasant profit if you do not know hardship. Live with disciplined conduct, so that you may enjoy life under laws that are at rest. What need is there for anyone to do something by which he may incur punishment? Let the judge seek grounds for accusation against you and find none. Let reason regulate your movements, since you recognize yourselves to be rational. We appoint a judge for the wicked and a witness for those of good conduct, so that no one may feel himself compelled except the person whom the order of lawful conduct accuses. [Col. 0706C]

Therefore we declare that we have granted that man the comitiva of the city of Naples for that indiction, so that, commended by our governance, he may deserve another dignity through our judgment. It is fitting for you to obey him prudently, because both things are praiseworthy: that a good people make a judge benevolent, and that a gentle judge regulate a most grateful people with impartial reason.

XXV. FORMULA FOR THE SOLDIERS

All bodies of apparitors ought to have their own judges. For when a chief is taken away from someone, military service too is denied [Cor., Gam.: “apparitors. When a chief is taken away from someone, military service too is denied”]. But since we are concerned to keep all orders in their proper places, we declare that we have granted him, with God’s help, the comitiva of Naples, so that, as judges are renewed by annual succession, the solemnity of your activity may not perish. Therefore give the designated man appropriate obedience, so that, just as we do not allow you to lose the benefits of your emoluments, so you too must preserve the ancient rule of obedience.

LIBER SEVENTH

[Col. 0705]

110 I. [Note: In the *Notitia dignitatum* of the Roman Empire, the comes of Africa, Asia, Pontus, and Thrace are named; also the *comes rei militaris* for Egypt; the comes of Tingitana; the comes of the Saxon Shore; the comes of Isauria, and so forth. FORN.] FORMULA FOR THE COMITIVA OF A PROVINCE

Although the offices of all dignities are separated from armed authority [Col. 0706D] and those who are taught to exercise public discipline appear to be clothed in civilian garments, [Col. 0707A] nevertheless your dignity is adorned with terrors, since [Note: From this one may note the difference between a provincial governor and a comes: provincial governors were not military magistrates. FORN.] it is girded with a military sword even in peaceful circumstances. Observe by what judgment you have been elevated, when we see that others have been entrusted with the authority of the fasces, whereas it is established that iron itself has been extended to you by the laws.

[Note: The type of clothing was prescribed in Book IV, title 10, of the *Theodosian Code*, “Concerning the dress that ought to be worn within the City,” law 1: “None of the senators shall claim for himself military dress, but, laying aside the terror of the military cloak, let him put on the quiet garments of the colobium and paenula. When there is, however, an assembly, etc., we order him to attend in the toga.” This is evidently the civilian dress which it was established that magistrates should use within the City and outside the camp. It is mentioned in an ancient inscription of Trajan’s Forum: “The Senate decreed that a statue be erected in the Forum of the deified Trajan, in civilian dress and at public expense.” To this belongs Book 7, *Iisdem*, of the *Code*, “Concerning advocates of the divine courts.” FORN.]

They gave a bloody instrument to a peaceful mind, so that both the guilty might fear greatly and those who had been injured might rejoice in the vengeance they desired. [Col. 0707D] Otherwise the former rulers would be blamed if they had not moderated everything. But since you understand that you have been chosen for moderation, you should not readily desire a human being’s destruction. Let the person called defendant also be proved guilty. Know that the remedy of punishment has been given to you for the safety of many. These arms belong to law, not to rage.

This display of power was plainly established against wrongdoers, so that terror might correct more than punishment exhausts. For one who bends daring while it is still tender with words is not compelled to cut down with iron what is robust. [Col. 0707B] This fear is civil, not military; you will make it glorious if it is not proved to have exceeded its limits. You have iron as well, but it must likewise remain bloodless. Let those whom suspicion of minor crimes presses be confined in chains. Anyone who judges concerning a person’s safety must be slow to decide.

Another sentence can be corrected. [Note: A golden sentiment, worthy of Cassiodorus and treated by other authors. Juvenal, Satire 6:

“What crime did the slave deserve punishment for?  
What witness is there? Who brought the charge? Listen.”

No hesitation over a person’s death is ever too prolonged. [Col. 0708C] Digest 48.8.1; Code, *De poenis*, law 5; Cicero, *For Roscius of Ameria*; Aristotle, *Problems*: “Each of us would rather acquit the wrongdoer, on the ground that he is not doing wrong, than condemn the one who is not doing wrong, on the ground that he is doing wrong.” If one must err in either direction, it would be far more equitable to acquit the guilty than to condemn and destroy the innocent. The former is indeed a sin, but the latter is also impiety, as Stobaeus records from Antiphon, *Gnomologium*, chapter 44: “If one must err, to release unjustly is more pious than to destroy unjustly; the former is an error, but to kill unjustly is an act of impiety.” A notable example of this sentiment is found in Aelian, *Various History* 14, concerning Ptolemy and Berenice, and elsewhere. FORNER.]

The decision once made concerning a life does not allow itself to be altered. Let raiders fear your standards; let thieves dread them; let brigands shudder. Let innocence look upon you joyfully, believing that the assistance which the discipline of the laws has sent has arrived. Let no one bend your will through bribes. The sword is despised when gold is accepted [Niv., Gam.: “is concealed”]. You make yourself unarmed if you withdraw from manly courage through greed.

Accordingly, during that indiction we grant you the dignity of the comitiva in that province, so that you may carry out what pertains to your titles in a manner praiseworthy for its civility; and do not presume to do anything except what, as a private person, you could defend by the laws. For that is the proper administration which is defended even without power, so that a man is then proved to have been just when his enemy can bring against him whatever charge he prefers. [Col. 0708A]

Nor is your hope abandoned through any disdain. For if you preside well over the administrations of the provinces, the laws have rightly judged that you may hope for the highest honors. Hence what is known to have been voluntarily promised to you by so great an authority now appears almost a debt [Gr. and Cuj., Cor., Niv. and Gam.: “provided for”].

II. FORMULA FOR THE GOVERNORSHIP

Antiquity prudently and in every respect judged that provincial dignities should be renewed by annual succession, so that no one might become insolent through prolonged power and many might discover the joys of advancement. It is enough for each person to depart with praise, since, when a lengthy period of power is sought, the reproaches of faults are not avoided. [Col. 0708B] It is remarkable even to avoid them within a short period, since they often overtake those who depart from the fasces with haste. A whole year is sufficient both to display the good qualities of one’s conscience and to guard oneself more easily from error.

Let it be your intention to undertake the administration of one year; it is our task to extend the time of those who deserve it, since we do not readily wish to remove those whom we judge to be just. Therefore, invited by the character of your conduct, during that indiction we grant you the governorship of that province, with the favor of God, so that you ought to act in such a way that the landowner appears to repay us with thanks together with his taxes.

Follow the good examples of your predecessors; separate yourself from the imitation of the vicious. Let not every custom be considered acceptable. [Note: “Custom,” that is, a tax, *to telos* [τὸ τέλος], above, Book I, letter 10. Theodoricus, replying to Boethius: “Let the steward of the treasury hold just customs.” Again, Book III, letter 23: “Remove customs that have become abhorrent through long practice.” Julian, *Misopogon*: *eithismenōn eisphorōn pempton* [εἰθισμένων εἰσφορῶν πέμπτον], “a fifth of the customary taxes.” The same author, in his final letter: *eisoisetai kata to ethos* [εἰσοίσεται κατὰ τὸ ἔθος], “he will pay according to custom.” For custom is especially to be observed in exactions and taxes: Code of Theodosius 11.1.13, *De exactoribus*; Digest 50.16.23, *Aerariae*, concerning grain and taxes; Code of Theodosius 13.11, *Imperatores*, at the end; Digest 50.12, *De pollicitationibus* and concerning taxes; Digest 19.2.4 and 19.2.9, *Locatio*, section “Penalty.” FORNER.]

[Col. 0708C] An alien error ought to make a person cautious, not a follower. The man who follows one accused exposes the fault of his own folly. But the better course is chosen when the governor’s reputation is praised during his administration. Consider how full the province is of nobles. You have people who ought both to speak well of you and who may presume to disparage you, because no power exists that can remove the quality of its reputation from the mouths of men. Conversely, it is a benefit to pass through neighboring provinces with a reputation worthy of praise and to find the truest commendation where you do not rule by power.

Moreover, we do not leave unrewarded what we hear you have carried out commendably. Hate vice, and you will deserve the prince’s affection. You have the royal will in the laws: obey them, and you will be recognized as fulfilling our commands.

III. FORMULA FOR THE COMITIVA OF THE GOTHS THROUGH THE INDIVIDUAL PROVINCES

Since we know that Goths dwell mixed together with you, and lest, as commonly happens, some indiscipline should arise among partners, we considered it necessary to send to you as comes that eminent man, hitherto approved by us for his good character, who, according to our edicts, must cut short a dispute between two Goths. If some affair should perhaps arise between a Goth and a Roman, then, after associating with himself a prudent Roman, he will be able to resolve the conflict with balanced judgment. [Col. 0709B]

[Note: “After associating with himself a prudent Roman,” that is, a legal expert, who will not allow those whom he can settle through his jurisdiction to proceed to arms and quarrelling. Digest 7.9.13, “If someone,” passage “For it is necessary,” concerning usufruct. As the text continues: “In a case, let laws operate, not arms,” that is, force should not be used by litigants in debate. Among the Greeks this is called *ho cheirōn nomos* [ὁ χειρῶν νόμος], “the law of hands,” and among the Latins, *manus*. Pomponius: “Everything was governed by hand by kings,” Digest 1.2.2, concerning the origin of law. Paul, *Sentences* 5: “Those who violently wrest away a guard from a soldier escorting him are punished capitally.” FORN.]

Between two Romans, let Romans hear the cases—those whom we send throughout the provinces as judges—so that each person’s rights may be preserved and one justice may embrace everyone despite the diversity of judges. Thus, with God’s favor, may both nations enjoy gentle leisure in common peace.

Know, however, that we have one equal affection for all; but the man who loves the laws with moderate willingness will be able to commend himself more fully to our mind. We love nothing uncivil; we detest criminal arrogance together with its authors. Our piety curses the violent. In a case, let laws prevail, not arms. For why should those who are known to have present judges choose to seek violent remedies?

For this reason we give emoluments to judges; for this reason we maintain so many offices through varied grants: so that we may not allow anything capable of producing hatred to grow among you. Let one desire for the manner of life embrace you, since it is established that you possess one government. Let each people hear what we love. Romans, just as the Goths are your neighbors in property, so let them be joined to you in affection. And you, Romans, ought to love the Goths with great zeal, since in peace they make numerous peoples available to you and in war they defend the entire commonwealth.

Therefore it is fitting for you to obey the judge appointed by us, so that whatever he decides for the preservation of the laws, you may fulfill in every way, and thus appear to have satisfied both our authority [Col. 0709D] and your own welfare.

IV. FORMULA FOR THE DUKEDOM OF THE RHAETIAS

Although the honor of rank may appear to be one and nothing except length of service is usually preferred in such offices, nevertheless, when the quality of the circumstances is weighed, much seems to have been entrusted to those to whom peoples bordering the frontier are assigned. For it is not the same to administer justice in peaceful regions as to sit among suspect nations, where not only vices but wars are feared; nor does merely the herald’s voice resound, but the crash of trumpets frequently threatens.

For Rhaetia is the fortification of Italy and the province’s barrier. We rightly judge that it was so named, since it is positioned against savage and utterly wild peoples like an obstacle formed by nets. There the assault of the foreign nation is received, and the furious presumption is wounded by missiles sent across. Thus the foreign assault is your quarry, and you conduct as a game what you recognize yourselves to have continually and successfully carried out [Juret. reads “what we…”].

Therefore, hearing that you are strong in mind and bodily power, during that indiction we entrust to you the dukedom of the Rhaetias, [Col. 0710B] so that you may govern the soldiers in peace and with them traverse our borders with ceremonial vigor. For you recognize that no small matter has been entrusted to you, since the tranquility of our kingdom is believed to be guarded by your vigilance.

Yet let the soldiers entrusted to you live with the provincials according to civil law. Let the mind that knows itself to be armed not become insolent, because that shield of our army ought to provide peace to the Romans. They are known to have been stationed there so that within, life may be enjoyed in more secure freedom.

Therefore answer to our judgment, pleasing us by loyalty and diligence, so that you neither admit foreigners without investigation nor, through negligence, send our own people among foreigners [Gr., Cuj. and Forn.: “agents”]. The need for arms arises more rarely where it is believed that an intercepted intrusion can be guarded against. You will vindicate the privileges of your dignity through our commands.

V. [Note: Sidonius Apollinaris, chapter 23, page 348. See what Savaro says there. Pope Vigilius, in a letter preserved in volume IV of the Councils, page 164: “But also Justin, former consul, and *cura palatii*”; at this passage the editor noted that perhaps one should read “former consul and *ex curia palatii*.” But he is mistaken; I say that it should be restored as “former consul and *cura palatii*.” In the appendix to Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book XI, chapter 8: “He held the care of the palace.” JURET.] FORMULA FOR THE CARE OF THE PALACE

Just as our palace is known to have been established through skillful arrangements, so careful supervision by experts ought to exist in it. For that marvelous beauty is spoiled by creeping old age if it is not periodically restored. These are our delights, the splendid appearance of imperial power, the heralded testimony of kingdoms. They are shown to ambassadors with astonishment, and at first sight a lord is judged to be of the same character as his dwelling is proved to be.

Therefore it is a great pleasure [Gr. and Cuj.: “will”] for a most prudent mind to enjoy a beautiful residence continually and to refresh a spirit wearied by public cares with the sweetness of buildings. The Cyclopes are said first to have constructed such buildings in Sicily, immense and shaped like caves, after Polyphemus, in the caves of the mountains, had suffered from Ulysses the lamentable loss of his single eye. From there the skill of construction is said to have been transferred to Italy, so that what had been invented by such great and remarkable founders might be preserved for its own advantage by an emulative posterity.

For this reason we judge that, from that indiction, your Eminence [Juret. reads “your rank”] ought to undertake the care of our palace, so that you may preserve the ancient works in their original brilliance and produce new works with a similar antiquity. For just as it is fitting for a beautiful body to be clothed in one color, so the brilliance of a palace ought to extend uniformly through all its members. [Note: “Member of a building,” meaning part of a house: Digest 32.52.3, “Of books,” section “Fully,” concerning legacies; Pliny, Book II, letter 17; Apuleius, Book III, *The Ass*. Cicero, Book III, *To Quintus*, letter 1: “Nor could it have adjoining bedrooms and members of that sort.” It should not be concealed that the Greeks seem to have used *member* somewhat more narrowly to translate *koitōn* [κοιτών], “bedroom,” in the cited passage. FORN.]

You will be found capable of this if you frequently read the geometer Euclid; if you store his diagrams, drawn with marvelous variety, in the contemplation of your mind, so that when summoned at a moment’s notice an abundant knowledge may serve you. Let the most subtle investigator Archimedes, together with Metrobius, always assist you, so that you may be fully prepared for new projects.

For no minor responsibility is assigned to you when you are shown to fulfill, through the service of your art, our mind’s great desire for construction. For whenever we restore a city, wish to establish a new fortress, or are attracted by the appeal of constructing a praetorium, what we conceive is brought before our eyes under your direction. [Col. 0711B]

[Note: With you organizing and leading, according to your prescription; for the architect made and drew up the formulas, ideas, types, diagrams, and ground plans of the buildings that were to be constructed. FORN.]

It is a noble office, an altogether glorious undertaking, to send into such long ages something for which posterity ought to admire and praise you. For whatever the wall-builder, marble sculptor, bronze caster, vault-maker, plaster-worker, or mosaicist [Note: A mosaicist (*musivarius*) takes his name from mosaic work, which depicts forms and images of things with small cut pieces of varied colors. Aelius Spartianus, in *Pescennius*; Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVI, chapter 8. William Philander, on Vitruvius, Book VII, chapter 1, interprets *musivum* as what is now called mosaic; its craftsmen are here, and in Book X of the Code, title *De excusationibus artificum*, called *musivarii*. FORN.] does not know, he prudently asks you; and that great army of craftsmen turns to your judgment, so that nothing may remain confused.

See, therefore, how much the man must know who is able to instruct so many. Certainly you receive the richest fruit of your good administration when you are praised for their labor, if you show that their work has been carefully done. Therefore whatever pertains to you, we wish to have carried out with such elegance and strength that the only difference from the works of the ancients is the newness of the buildings.

But you make these things possible if you do not suppress our gifts through greed. For the craftsman is effectively commanded by the person who does not allow him to be defrauded of suitable compensation. A generous hand nourishes the talents of the arts, since the man who has no concern for his livelihood hastens to complete what has been ordered.

Consider also with what honor you are treated: adorned with a golden staff, [Col. 0712A] you appear to walk first before the royal feet amid numerous attendants. [Note: Cassiodorus records here that those who in the palaces of later Roman emperors held the honor and office of *cura palatii* walked adorned with a golden staff. Peter Fabricius, *Agon*, Book I; Gomes, Book I, chapter 3. JUR.] Or else, through the testimony of our proximity, we recognize that we have entrusted palaces to you.

VI. [Note: *Comitiva formarum Urbis*, that is, the comitiva of the city’s aqueducts. It is said of the person appointed as superintendent of buildings, from which come the disfigurement of buildings and ugly ruins. Suetonius, *Nero*: “Offended by the ugliness of the old buildings and by the narrowness and winding turns of the roads”; Code 8.10.22, “The law concerning tutors,” concerning the administration of guardianship; Digest 8.2.1, concerning beams built into another’s property; Digest 1.21.7, “The governor,” concerning the governor’s office. Cassiodorus, above, Book III, letter 29, at the end: “Lest amid so many distinguished walls the ugly ruin of stones appear.” And in Justinian’s pragmatic sanction, which is added to Julian’s old translation of the Novels: “For the repair of the aqueducts,” and so forth. Thus *eidos* [εἶδος] means “building” in Harmenopulus, Book II, *Epitome*. FORN.] FORMULA FOR THE COMITIVA OF THE CITY’S AQUEDUCTS

Although among the structures of Romulus it is scarcely possible to find any that can be compared with the outstanding ones—for everything seen there to have been founded is known to have been elaborated for admiration—we nevertheless judge that a distinction should be made between what utility makes pleasing and what recommends itself solely on account of beauty.

To see Trajan’s Forum even amid constant familiarity is a marvel. To climb the lofty Capitoline temples is to see human ingenuity surpassed. But do people live by those things, or is bodily health refreshed by any delight arising from them? [Note: “Aqueducts,” Book I, concerning aqueducts; Code 11.43.1, where Alciatus incorrectly understands *formae*: “For *formae* signify the construction and building of aqueducts.” Digest 7.1.27, “If things hanging,” section “If anything concerning sewers”; Digest 30.1.41, commonly 30.1.38, “When a slave,” section “The heir,” concerning legacies, for an aqueduct. FORN. — “In the aqueducts.” In imperial constitutions we read of *formae aquarum*, “aqueducts,” as in Code 8.11.1 and Novel 7, concerning imperial mandates. BROSS.]

But in the Roman aqueducts both features are pre-eminent: the construction is marvelous, and the healthfulness of the water extraordinary. When rivers are brought there, as though through constructed mountains, you might believe that solid masses of rock were natural channels, since the great force of the river has been able to withstand so many centuries securely.

Mountains hollowed out often collapse, and the channels of torrents are scattered; but that work of the ancients is not destroyed if it is preserved with the support of diligence. Let us consider how much ornament the abundance of water provides to the Roman walls. For what would the beauty of the baths be if they did not possess certain exceedingly sweet waters?

The Aqua Virgo flows in the purest delight. It is believed to have received this name because it is polluted by no filth. While other waters are disturbed by the excessive rains and mixture of earth, this one, flowing with perpetually clear water, seems to imitate the ever-serene sky.

Who could explain such things adequately in words? The Aqua Claudia has been brought across so great a height to the head of the Aventine that, when it falls there from above, it seems to irrigate that lofty summit as though it were a deep valley. The Egyptian Nile, rising at fixed seasons, surges turbulently across the level fields with a flood beneath a clear sky. But how much more beautiful that the Roman Claudia has sent the purest waters through so many dry mountain summits to baths and houses, pouring forth through abundant conduits, and flows so evenly that it can never withdraw itself from those who desire it!

For the Nile, when it recedes, is mud; when it arrives unexpectedly, it is a flood. Who, then, would not judge the famous Nile to have been surpassed by the rivers of our City, when it either terrifies its inhabitants by coming or abandons them by withdrawing?

We have recounted these things not as a superfluous reminiscence, so that you may understand what diligence is required of you, to whom such beauty has been entrusted. For this reason, during that indiction, after great deliberation we entrusted to you the comitiva of the aqueducts, so that you may strive with the utmost zeal to accomplish what appears appropriate to such great and remarkable works.

First, we decree that harmful trees, which cause the collapse of buildings while they become intolerable battering rams against the walls, be cut out by the roots. [Note: Trees that cause structural collapses. Wooden buildings are endangered by them: Code 8.5.1, concerning injunctions; Book II, letter 39. FORN.] No injury is removed whose origin is not taken away.

If anything has been demolished through the weakening effects of age, let it be repaired with vigilant speed [edition, Niv. and Ga.: “with vigilant clarity”], lest the defect increase and enlarge the cause of expense for us. The water channel is your fortune: you will remain secure if you strengthen it. You will advance in our regard to the extent that you prove yourself to have devoted yourself earnestly to it [Cor., Niv. and Ga.: “diligently”].

Let your skill and trustworthiness therefore act so that both the construction of the buildings remains unharmed and the distribution of the water does not withdraw through any venality among the custodians.

VII. FORMULA FOR THE PREFECT OF THE CITY WATCH OF ROME

[Note: Prefects of the watch ought not to determine capital cases by their own authority; should any such matter arise, they must refer it to the height of your authority, so that the said cases may be judged by a higher decision: law *Praefecti*, Code, *Concerning the Office of the Prefect of the Watch*. Hence he is called an obscure judge, a silent arbiter, and an investigator of incendiaries and thieves. The author elegantly says that he commits thefts against thieves while he outwits them by night. Harmenopulus, title *Concerning Dignities*, section 3, reports that the office of prefect of the watch was established to prevent fires and to investigate incendiaries, burglars, thieves, and receivers. BROSS.]

Although your name ought to rouse you to the watches of the City, so that you may fulfill what you are called to do, nevertheless the customary caution of our foresight does not desist until we also gently invite to obedience those whom we choose for action.

What could be more beautiful for you than to devote your service in that City, where such witnesses seem to stand beside your diligence? As soon as your vigilance has been applied, it runs through the mouths of patricians and consuls. You have scarcely managed to do something carefully, and you hear the leading men praising it with admiration.

You govern a moderate dignity, yet you move in the highest reputation. You are called the guardian of the Roman City when you defend it from an internal enemy.

Therefore be vigilant concerning thieves. Although the laws by no means command you to punish them by your own authority, they have nevertheless granted you permission to investigate them. I believe this was so that, although they were detestable robbers, because they were said to be Romans they might nevertheless be subjected to a higher dignity.

Accordingly, during that indiction make use of the dignity of the prefecture of the watch. The terror of punishments has been taken away from you, not the power; for the law, by commanding that the wicked be captured by whomever it wished, judged that person himself ought to be feared more.

You will be the security of those sleeping, the defense of houses, the protection of locks, an unseen investigator, a silent arbiter to whom it is lawful to deceive plotters and whose glory lies in outwitting them. Your activity is a nocturnal hunt which, if it is not seen in a marvelous way, is then feared [others: “is then held fast”].

You commit thefts against thieves, as it were, while you try to surround those whom you know can deceive everyone. What you do is a kind of conjuring, so that you can ensnare the stratagems of brigands. For we think it would have been easier to grasp the riddles of the Sphinx than to discover the fugitive presence of a robber.

He is watchful about everything, uncertain about what is to come, trembling at ambushes. How can he be captured who, like the wind, is not seen to be contained in any place? Keep watch tirelessly with the nocturnal birds. Let night open your eyes; and just as they find food in darkness, so may you find praise.

Now be vigilant concerning the duties assigned to you. Let venality not take away from you what diligence grants. Although these things appear to be carried out under deep darkness, no act can nevertheless be hidden.

You will also vindicate, by our authority, the privileges belonging to you and to the office assigned to you in a reasonable manner, since in so great a city it is necessary that matters be handled by various judges when one person cannot complete them.

114 VIII. FORMULA FOR THE PREFECT OF THE CITY WATCH OF RAVENNA

Although at first sight you are adorned with a dignity of great renown—for the supreme wisdom of the ancients could not designate both the highest and lowest offices by the same title, lest the brilliance it gave to the highest should be polluted by the baseness of another—one can nevertheless understand from this what the authority of our ancestors may have thought when they wished to call those “prefects of the watch” who run about for the general peace.

For the security of everyone’s fortunes, the ornament of the city, and the welfare of all have been entrusted to you: namely, so that you may wage a peaceful war against domestic aggressors if you perceive that any citizen is being harmed. Guard everyone’s fortunes. Secure sleep is enjoyed while you keep watch, and no disturbance is felt.

Placed in peace, you win victories over the nocturnal thief. In the morning the city rejoices in your laurels, defended; when it sees the captured men, it recognizes that it has been freed from a hidden enemy. You triumph every day if you keep good watch. And although the glory of military combat is rare, it continually serves you through the discovery of brigands.

O command assumed with such great affection for the citizens! You will undertake to seek out robbers whom their own master cannot find, and in two ways you will act as a benefactor: either you prevent future thefts or you bring those already committed to an end.

Is this not a kind of inexpressible grace of the city: to undertake within itself one task which it sees to be useful to all? The prudent antiquity rightly assigned you the glorious name of prefect, because no one could do this except one who loved his fellow citizens more than his own advantages.

Your office too is supported by no small grant, since even their jurisdiction in matters of small consequence has been enlarged—those who are known to serve as soldiers for the security of the citizens. [Note: Cujas explains this passage in his *Paratitla* to the Code, Book VIII, title 5.]

Since these things are so, we grant you the prefecture of the watch for that indiction, delighted by your reputation, so that you may carry out in every way both the care of this dignity and the privileges appropriate to you.

But although the general consensus pursues the most hateful name of thieves, nevertheless, since the shedding of human blood is involved, we command that nothing sudden or undeliberated be undertaken. Follow moderation, since you condemn audacity; cherish restraint, since you condemn thefts.

Let those brought to trial be heard if they have anything to say for their safety, since whatever is not examined is not considered justice. But once they have been convicted and have confessed, let the decrees be observed, since the man who follows the laws accomplishes nothing cruel.

IX. FORMULA FOR THE COMITIVA OF THE PORT OF THE CITY OF ROME
A more delightful than laborious military office is to hold the dignity of the comitiva at the Roman port. For there the plentiful arrival of ships is observed. There the sail-bearing sea conveys foreign peoples with the merchandise of various provinces, and amid so many spectacles of delightful goods your advantage is that those who arrive have escaped danger. At these mouths the pleasures of Rome are first felt, and upon the Tiberine waters, as through a channel, those goods proceed which ascend to the city’s commerce.

Well conceived is the dignity that appears to adorn the resources of Rome. For what can be conducted more elegantly than the means by which that people is shown to be nourished? O discovery of our ancestors! O refined wisdom of prudent men! Since Rome seemed to have been placed farther from the shore, they caused it to begin to exist there all the more fully where it possessed a seemly entrance for ships. For the two channels of the Tiber, like two lights, received highly ornamented cities [Note: [Col. 0715D] Namely, Portus and Ostia. JUR.], so that what supplied expenses to so great a city would not be without grace.

An exceptional responsibility is therefore entrusted to you, provided it is carried out with moderation. You create abundance when you treat those entering justly. A greedy hand closes the port; and when it draws in its fingers, it simultaneously shuts the sails of the ships. For all merchants rightly shun what they recognize to be costly to themselves. Therefore, an immoderate presumption is the contrary wind there. The man who heaps up the waves of greed condemns the calm sea.

Let each person, having been admonished according to the solemn custom, offer a voluntary gift. These are presents, not obligations. He who asks too much receives from few; and he who exercises moderation toward what is offered sends the gifts of life to himself [Gr. and Cuj., “he himself wishes to be sent”]. Let it therefore be your foremost concern not only to abstain yourself, but also to restrain the hands of those who presume; for it is no light offense to transgress amid that abundance which it is fitting that all should continually desire.

Accordingly, by that indiction we honor you with the office of the comitiva of the port, so that, just as the dignity administers delightful pleasures, you too may leave behind a commendable reputation for the honor [Col. 0715D].

## X. FORMULA OF THE TRIBUNATE OF PLEASURES

Although amusements [Note: [Col. 0715D] Thus the final book of the Theodosian Code calls the theatrical arts, in the title “On the Maiuma,” p. 469. The same error appears in Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XVIII, chapter 16, where, speaking of spectacles, he says: “These he also calls *lubrica*, because they are performed in games or on stages”; correct this to: “These he also calls *ludicra*.” Columella, in the preface to book I of *On Agriculture*, p. 4: “For without theatrical arts,” etc. So also Cornelius Tacitus, book XV of the *Annals*: “And he gave a circus performance.” Likewise Valerius Maximus, book II, chapter 4, *On Spectacles*, example 4; Ammianus Marcellinus, book XIV, pp. 19 and 21; Salvianus, *On the Government of God*. Below, in this formula 10, he calls it a “theatrical administration.” [Col. 0716D] JURET. Petrus Faber discusses this matter in *Agon*, book I, chapter 1.] [Others: *lubrica*, “slippery”] are removed from respectable conduct, and although the wandering life of actors may seem capable of being carried on through license [Col. 0716A], nevertheless prudent antiquity provided that these activities should not wholly disappear, since they too were subject to a judge. The presentation of pleasures must be administered under a certain discipline.

Let the stage performers be subject, if not to a real, at least to a shadowy, judicial order. Let these affairs also be regulated by the quality of the laws, as though propriety were commanding what is improper; and let those who do not know the path of upright conduct live by certain rules. They devote themselves not so much to their own pleasure as to the joy of others; and, by a perverse arrangement, when they surrender dominion over their bodies, they have rather compelled their souls to serve.

It was therefore fitting that they receive a moderator, since they do not know how to conduct themselves in a legally ordered manner [Gr., Cuj., Niv., Ga., “with moderation”]. Your office has been set over these groups of people as a kind of guardian [Col. 0716B]. For just as they protect tender ages with watchful care, so you must restrain ardent pleasures through assiduous maturity.

Carry out by good regulations what our ancestors are known to have devised with the greatest prudence. If modesty does not restrain a light desire, let pronounced strictness moderate it. Let spectacles be conducted in accordance with their customary rules, since they cannot win approval unless they imitate some form of discipline.

Accordingly, by that indiction our election appoints you as tribune of pleasures [Note: [Col. 0716D] From this it is clear that Rome had a tribune of pleasures, which I also find in the final law of the Theodosian Code, title “On Stage Performers,” where Diogenianus is called “tribune of pleasures.” I do not know whether what Suetonius writes in *The Life of Tiberius*, chapter 42, can properly be applied here: namely, that Tiberius established a new office “of pleasures,” placing the Roman knight Titus Caesonius Priscus over it. Book I of the Code, “On the Expenses of Games”; book V of the Theodosian Code, “On Stage Performers”; books 29 and 32 of the Theodosian Code, “On Praetors.” BROSS.], so that you may conduct everything in such a way that you win the city’s approval, lest what was evidently devised for joy appear, in your time, to have been turned toward wrongdoing.

Deal with those of impaired reputation while preserving your own good name. Cherish chastity, beneath which prostitutes are placed, so that it may be said with great praise: “He devoted himself to virtue who mingled with pleasures” [Col. 0716C]. For we desire that through a theatrical administration you may attain a serious dignity.

## XI. FORMULA FOR THE DEFENDER OF ANY CITY

If, for carrying out any business, a person is chosen who is praised for judgment and gravity, how much more distinguished must he be who takes up the affairs of a city? For if it is dangerous to deceive one person, what will happen if someone is found unequal to the judgment of so many? The well-conducted case of many ennobles a person, since he who is perceived to attend to the general desires is believed to conduct everything with good purpose.

Therefore, moved by the supplication of your fellow citizens, our authority grants you, by that indiction, the position of defender of that city, so that you may wish to do nothing venal or dishonorable, since you are called by such a name. Arrange commercial dealings for the citizens with even moderation, according to the character of the times. Preserve the limits you have ordered, for it is not difficult to sell while enclosing the sums; what is difficult is to guard the established prices with complete integrity.

You truly fulfill the office of a good defender if you allow neither your citizens to be oppressed by the laws nor to be consumed by high prices [Col. 0717A].

## XII. FORMULA OF THE CURATOR OF A CITY

Although a person is considered honorable in himself if he appears to devote even the slightest care to his own city, and although one who has professed to love his fellow citizens enjoys great reverence among them, nevertheless indisputable honor belongs to one conferred by our election, since a person to whom something is entrusted by the authority of the prince is believed to be endowed with good principles.

Therefore, from that indiction onward, we wish the care of that city to belong to you, so that you may govern the honorable orders of the curia wisely and cause moderate prices to be maintained by those whom the matter concerns. Let merchandise not rest solely in the power of the sellers; let equitable treatment be graciously preserved in everything.

The city’s prosperity—and hence the gratitude of its citizens—is gathered most abundantly [Col. 0717B] if prices are maintained within moderation, so that you may truly fulfill the office of curator when you have concern for the advantage of all. [Note: [Col. 0717D] *Consuetudines*: elsewhere, tolls and tributes; here, provisions. Moreover, in the formula for commending the princes to the count, both are joined together, “provisions and customs,” as written in the formula of this book 25, near the end. FORN.]

As for the customs dues, defend them by our authority, since it is established that your ancestors possessed them in that same place [Col. 0718D].

## XIII. FORMULA OF THE COMITIVA OF ROME

If the most wicked intention commonly lies in wait among closed and fortified houses, how much more does it appear to be enticed in the city of Rome, where someone finds in the streets a valuable object that can be carried away? For a very numerous population of statues and exceedingly abundant herds of horses must be guarded with the same care with which they appear to have been fixed in place. If there were any consideration for human affairs, Roman beauty would need to be guarded not by watchfulness but by reverence alone [Col. 0717C].

What shall we say of the marble, metal, and precious workmanship? If it were left free to seize them, how rare would be the hand capable of abstaining from such things? There are displayed there the works that general wealth and the labor of the world have been able to produce. Who would be permitted to be negligent amid these things? Who in such a matter would tolerate being venal, when the gravest damage could be inflicted upon singular beauty?

Therefore, by that indiction, we grant you the dignity of the comitiva of Rome, with its privileges and lawful advantages, so that with faithful zeal and great effort you may seek out criminal hands and bring before your judgment those who lie in wait either for private fortunes or for the city walls. After the truth of the matter has been examined, let them undergo the punishment appropriate to the laws.

For public indignation rightly pursues such men: they disfigure the beauty of antiquity by cutting off its limbs [Col. 0717D], and do to public monuments what they themselves ought to suffer. Compel your office and the customary soldiers to keep watch rather at night; during the day the city guards itself. Vigilance through devotion requires no external aid. Theft invites the attempt, but the presumptuous thief is easily caught when he least expects the guardian to appear.

The statues are not entirely mute: when struck by thieves, they seem to warn their guardians with their ringing. Accordingly, let us perceive your diligence through commendable devotion, so that to you, upon whom we now impose laborious fasces, we may later grant secure honors.

## XIV. FORMULA OF THE COMITIVA OF RAVENNA

[Col. 0718A]

If dignity is to be judged by labor, and if commendable attention to public affairs produces gratitude for one who serves generously, your position deserves the highest appreciation, since you are shown to remove delay from our orders by attending to your own responsibilities. Who does not know how abundantly you can procure ships with only a brief notice? It is scarcely recorded among the dignities of our palace in the transport documents, yet it is already completed by you with the greatest speed.

Amid the anxious haste of dispatches, scarcely another can attend to what you are able to fulfill with such vigor. Do not demand the customary services of merchants either excessively or with venality. Let there be a measure that cannot burden those who labor, so that, when you have handled troublesome matters without complaints, you may deserve greater favors from our judgment [Col. 0718B].

Accordingly, our serenity grants you the comitiva of Ravenna by that indiction, so that you may undertake and perform the privileges and labors of your dignity. Moderate your office with consideration for equity. For the person appointed to public actions always finds causes both to confer benefits and to inflict harm.

But since your administration is conducted among people of modest means, it must be weighed with equally measured fairness, because it is more important to maintain moderation when one is known to govern a diminished substance. Those who are well provided scarcely feel losses; the poor, however, are wounded by even a slight expense, since one who is known to possess little appears to lose everything through even a moderate injury.

## XV. FORMULA TO THE PREFECT OF THE CITY CONCERNING THE ARCHITECT OF PUBLIC WORKS

The splendor of Roman construction requires an expert guardian [Col. 0718C], so that, with diligence assisting it, that marvelous forest of walls may be preserved and the modern face of the work may be built according to skillful arrangements [Jur.: perhaps “of a skilled craftsman”].

For this purpose our generosity grants the appointment: that we may renew the works of the ancients after removing their defects, and clothe new works with the glory of antiquity. Therefore, let your illustrious greatness recognize that, from that indiction, he has been appointed architect of the Roman citadels.

And since it is clear that the arts must be nourished by lawful advantages, we wish everything that his predecessors are known reasonably to have obtained to belong to him. He will certainly see things better than he has read about and more beautiful than he could have imagined: those statues of their creators, still retaining the marks of their authors, so that, as long as the reputation of commendable persons survived, the image of the body might likewise preserve the likeness of living substance [Col. 0718D].

He will observe veins reproduced in bronze, certain muscles swelling with effort, and sinews stretched as though by movement; and he will see a human figure cast into various likenesses so that one would believe it rather to have been born than made. These statues are said to have first been discovered by the Etruscans in Italy; later generations embraced them and gave the City almost as large a population as nature itself had produced.

He will marvel that even statues of horses contain signs of ardor. With nostrils wrinkled, limbs rounded and tightly drawn, and ears drawn back, he may perhaps believe that they are eager for the race, even though he knows that metal cannot move.

What shall we say of the reedlike slenderness of the columns? [Col. 0719A] Of those loftiest masses of construction, as though held together by upright spears, excavated with hollow channels according to the nature of their substance, so that you might judge them to have been poured rather than built; of the waxlike appearance of what you see polished in the hardest metals; of the joints of the marble, which you might call generative veins? Here, while the eyes are deceived, praise is shown to have increased through marvels.

The narrators of the ancient age report that only seven wonders of construction were attributed to the earth [Note: [Col. 0719D] On the lamb of Olympian Jupiter and the temples, see Petrus Faber, *Agon*, book I. BROSS.]: the temple of Diana at Ephesus; the magnificent monument of King Mausolus, from whom mausoleums also received their name; the bronze statue of the sun at Rhodes, which is called the Colossus; the image of Olympian Jupiter, which Phidias, the first among artists, fashioned with supreme elegance in ivory and gold; the house of Cyrus, king of the Medes, which Memnon built with prodigal artistry, joining stones with gold; the walls of Babylon, which Queen Semiramis constructed of baked brick, sulfur, and iron; and the pyramids in Egypt, whose shadow, consuming itself in its proper position, is seen nowhere beyond the extent of their construction.

But who will henceforth consider those things preeminent, after seeing so many wonders in one City? They received honor because they came first in time, and in an unrefined age whatever new thing emerged was rightly proclaimed exceptional by human voices. Now, however, it may be truly said that all Rome is a wonder.

Therefore, it is fitting that a highly skilled man undertake such works, lest amid those exceedingly ingenious works of the ancients he himself appear to be merely metallic and fail to understand what the artistic antiquity of those men accomplished so that it might be perceived. Accordingly, let him apply himself to the books of the ancients and devote himself to their instructions, lest he know less from them than those in whose place he is known to have been appointed [Col. 0719C].

## XVI. FORMULA OF THE COMITIVA OF THE ISLANDS OF CURRITANA AND CELSINA

It is generally evident that matters can be managed well when a person to give warnings is not lacking. For everything is confused without a leader; and when each person thinks of living according to his own will, he is known to abandon the rule of discipline.

Therefore, following the custom of ancient practice, our authority grants you, by that indiction, jurisdiction as judge over the islands of Curritana and Celsina. For it is just that those who are separated from the society of other people should have someone go to their settlements who can organize them by a reasonable method, lest their remoteness and ignorance of common affairs become an occasion of injustice [Col. 0719D].

You therefore have, as has been said, someone among you who must both hear and settle the disputes that arise. And if anything has also been decreed by our benevolence, carry it out at the instruction of that same person; for opportunity for error is removed when it is made clear to you whom you must obey.

We believe that he will devote himself so to good actions that he may receive increases of our favor. For he must receive a reward from us if he arranges for you what will be beneficial.

## XVII. FORMULA CONCERNING THE SUPERVISOR OF LIME

It is a glorious task to serve the purpose by which the Roman city is shown to be adorned, since a person advances with us precisely to the extent that his own labor has proved useful to the City [Col. 0720A].

There is no doubt that fired lime, which is the color of snow and lighter than sponges, is a principal instrument of construction. To the extent that it is dissolved by the burning of fire, to that extent the strength of walls is reinforced by it thereafter: a dissoluble stone, a stony softness, a sandy rock, which is more fully kindled when it is drenched with abundant water. Without it, neither fixed stones nor the small particles of sand are solidified.

Therefore, the responsibility deserves to receive greater attention, since it is known to hold the first place in the walls of Rome. Accordingly, our authority appoints your industry, celebrated in the speech of many, over the firing and distribution of lime from that indiction onward, so that, abundantly supplied, it may suffice for both public and private buildings; and so that everyone’s enthusiasm for building may be aroused when they see that what is sought is ready [Col. 0720B].

You will vindicate the privileges of your position by our commands in a reasonable manner, so that you may deserve greater rewards if you complete well what has been entrusted to you.

## XVIII. FORMULA CONCERNING THE MAKERS OF WEAPONS

Consider what you are undertaking, and you will understand that you must give no place to wrongdoing. For to construct weapons well is to wish to preserve the safety of all: at first sight the enemy is terrified by them, and begins to yield in spirit if he recognizes that he does not possess similar weapons.

Accordingly, from that indiction onward, invited by the reputation of your character, we have placed you over the soldiers and the makers of weapons, so that you may demand from the craftsmen work of such a kind as you know can please us.

Let the security arising from our absence not lead you astray [Col. 0720C]. Whatever you do, we see: by the very practice of the most exact investigation we can immediately censure the craftsmen’s errors [Cor., Gam.: “detect”] and judge work that has been commendably performed. Therefore, consider with what diligence and zeal that work must be done which is known to come before our examination.

Act so that no venality and no fault may overwhelm you, since what is done wrongly in such a matter cannot be treated as venial, lest you be punished in the very area where you have committed the offense. This is work that generates death and safety, the destruction of wrongdoers and the protection of the good; it is always necessary assistance against the wicked.

Phoroneus is said to have offered this first to Juno, in order to consecrate his invention under the auspices of the deity, as he supposed. These things are necessary in war and honorable in peace. Finally, they make weak and fragile mortals stronger than all beasts [Col. 0720D].

## XIX. FORMULA TO THE PREFECT OF THE PRAETORIUM CONCERNING THE MAKERS OF WEAPONS

From the report of many we have learned that he, trained in upright conduct, can faithfully carry out what has been entrusted to him.
