Therefore, let your illustrious greatness recognize that we have chosen him so that he may both command the soldiers according to ancient custom and issue orders to the craftsmen of weapons, so that they may fulfill their customary duties with such care that no fault can be found in them.

Although wrongdoing causes harm everywhere, here it strikes with particular force [Col. 0721A] if he neglects the instruments of war. For it is like treason to withhold from an army what is known to arm it. Your foresight shall assign them their customary obligations, so that, once the provision-law has been removed from them [Cuj., Niv.: “once the total amount of provisions has been removed”], the necessities may be demanded with greater vigor.

## XX. FORMULA OF THE BINORI AND TERNORI, WHEN COLLECTED THROUGH A JUDGE

We believe it belongs to the spirit of your dignity if we appear to impose appropriate duties upon you, since a person is made more pleasing in proportion as he is shown to have undertaken more reasons for obedience.

Therefore, during that indiction, you shall hasten, through the management of your office, to transmit to the records office of the count of sacred largesses the titles of the *binori* and *ternori*, which ancient authority decreed should be exacted from the provincials [Note: [Col. 0721D] On the collection of the *binori* and *ternori*, see above, book III, letter 8, and below, in the two following formulas. FORN.]. Let the entire amount be solemnly completed by the Kalends of March, lest you be compelled to repay from your own resources what you neglected to procure.

It would have touched your own honor if another appeared to exact those titles which the most sacred laws ordered to belong to you [Col. 0721B].

## XXI. FORMULA OF THE BINORI AND TERNORI, WHEN COLLECTED THROUGH THE OFFICE

Although ancient custom ordered the collection of the *binori* and *ternori* to belong to you, nevertheless, lest multiple responsibilities weigh you down and doubled concern create obstacles for you, we have decided to send that man and that man, record-keepers of our office, so that they may assist you and your office.

Thus, with their help, the solemn amount may be conveyed by the Kalends of March to that illustrious man, the count of sacred largesses [Col. 0721C], lest you be made liable to public opinion if you should think that the sacred largesses could be delayed by any postponement. Do not therefore think that you are to be excused, since we have believed you should be assisted. For if anything is delivered in an amount less than required, know that it must be extracted from your own resources.

## XXII. FORMULA OF THE *COMMONITORIUM* FOR THAT RECORD-KEEPER AND THAT RECORD-KEEPER

[Note: [Col. 0721D] Vincent of Lérins, *Against Profane Innovations*: “For the sake of my forgetfulness, it will be enough that I have prepared a reminder for myself.” Augustine uses the same word in letters 129 and 158. Symmachus uses *monitorium* in the same sense. See the formula of book IV, title 4, law 1.]

We do not doubt that it is most welcome when someone is reminded to fulfill an office he has undertaken, since it is especially burdensome if a soldier lives in idleness, whose activity is his source of income and whose honor is his principal assignment. For a man left to ignoble torpor is regarded as resembling one without a belt [Col. 0721D].

Therefore, by that indiction, we order you to proceed to that province, so that, together with the judge or his office, you may send without delay to the records office of the count of sacred largesses, by the Kalends of March, the amount of the *binori* and *ternori* that is solemnly demanded.

This must be done in such a way that neither our treasury receives anything less than customary nor the landowner pays beyond the extent of his holding [Col. 0722A]. And do not doubt that you will incur the danger of our displeasure if we discover that anything has been done contrary to the ancient order.

## XXIII. FORMULA OF THE VICARIUS OF PORTUS

We specially grant the benefits of our favor to your merit if we approve that you are reasonably carrying out what has been entrusted to you. For you do not lie without reward if you receive foreign peoples wisely and regulate the commerce of our own people with measured equity.

Although prudence is necessary everywhere, it appears especially suitable in this activity, since quarrels continually arise between two peoples unless justice is preserved. Therefore, those whose character resembles the winds must be appeased by skill; unless their spirits are first tempered, they readily leap into the greatest contempt [Col. 0722B].

For this reason, moved by the reputation of your moderation, we decree that you shall have charge of that port by that indiction, so that you may conduct everything belonging to your title in such a way as to advance toward better things. For one learns in small matters whom greater responsibilities should be entrusted to.

## XXIV. FORMULA OF THE PRINCEPS OF DALMATIA

Whoever serves in the military under the title of *princeps* is adorned with great precedence among his colleagues. He is understood to occupy the first position, since in human affairs the greater part of titles asserts the excellence of dignities [Others: “of men”].

This is also demonstrated by the example of your office, without which neither access to the secretary’s office is granted nor the ceremonial business of petitions is conducted; and the whole authority of that tribunal is shown by the laws to have been entrusted to you in such a way that it cannot be complete without you.

Power has indeed been given to the count of the provinces, but the judge himself has been entrusted to you. You hold the vine-stick [Others: “life”] that threatens the wicked [Note: [Col. 0721D] Read “you hold the vine-stick.” This is the practice of military centurions. The vine-stick is read as an indication of authority, and they carried it; see D. in the title “On Military Matters”; Juvenal, satire 7; Pliny, book XIV, chapter 1. Spartianus, *Life of Hadrian*: “He gave the vine-stick to no one except a robust man of good reputation.” See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 14. JURET. See also Pithoeus, *Subseciva*, book I, chapter 15.]. You preserve discipline amid the laws; you have the right to strip away the insolence of an advocate, which the governor is not permitted to punish; moreover, the records of the entire proceeding are completed with your signature, and your consent is sought after the judge’s will has been expressed.

Act so that you may rightly be perceived to have fulfilled the duties of those over whom you are placed. Therefore, by that indiction, we order you to hasten to that province, so that, joined to the judge’s office, you may perform what is appropriate to your position; and so that, having departed from us as *princeps*, you may not be accused of any degradation [Col. 0722D]. For you make yourself most reverent in the eyes of all if what is believed about your title is also perceived in your conduct.

## XXV. FORMULA FOR COMMENDING PRINCES TO THE COUNT

A solemn custom invites us both to send you an ornament of office and to preserve the ancient ranks of the guards [Col. 0723A]. For our praise lies in the fact that Roman soldiers accompany you, since with such ministers you can carry out what appears to accord with ancient enactments.

Thus, with God’s help, we have brought forth our Goths in such a way that they are equipped with arms and ordered by equity. This is what the other peoples cannot possess; this is what makes you unique: that, accustomed to wars, you appear to live under the laws together with the Romans.

Therefore, we believe that this man and that man should be sent to you from our office, so that, according to ancient custom, those who obey your orders may govern them with due regard for antiquity. You shall grant him, by our command, your favor in preserving his provisions and customs dues. For he ought to be loved who has deserved to be appointed by us.

## XXVI. FORMULA OF THE COMITIVA OF VARIOUS CITIES

[Col. 0723B]

The honor of this age is an evident test of the human mind, because freedom of spirit always reveals its own will: a person who recognizes that others are subject to him does not seek to conceal himself. But the happy condition of the human mind is that which confines the exercise of its advancement within the limits of moderation and completes the brief course of dignity in such a way that it remains acceptable for all time.

Therefore, judges, sometimes descend to gentleness. It is indeed laborious, but not impossible, to persuade mortals to justice: the Divinity has granted it so deeply to the senses of all that even those who do not know the laws nevertheless recognize the reasoning of truth.

For what nature grants must necessarily be heard again, gently, when the same nature gives warning [Col. 0723C]. Therefore, do not labor to impose upon peoples what they are known to perceive by their own will. Those who believe they can be compelled by an admonisher easily follow the traces of another’s word.

Accordingly, by that indiction, with the Divinity favorable, we grant you the honor of the second rank of the comitiva in that city, so that you may govern the citizens entrusted to you with equity and consistently fulfill the commands of public ordinances. In this way we may grant you better things when we perceive from your present conduct that you have acted commendably.

## XXVII. FORMULA FOR HONORABLE LANDOWNERS AND CURIALS

It is useful always to choose one person whom the others must obey, because if the will of many is left to wander, confusion—the ally of wrongdoing—is generated.

Therefore, know that by that indiction we have granted the comitiva of your city to that man. Extend to him salutary obedience [Note: [Col. 0723D] Book I of the Code, “Those Who Act in Their Own Jurisdiction,” and above, book III, letter 14. FORN.], so that he may bring aid to your cases and procure the execution of public commands [Col. 0723D]. You should know that if anyone conducts himself with commendable devotion, he will not ask in vain for similar favors from our judgment.

## XXVIII. FORMULA OF THE PRINCEPS OF THE SOLDIERS OF THE COMITIVA

We are confident that it is welcome to you when we appoint judges of our military service, since you perform our orders whenever the presence of one who judges is not lacking [Col. 0724A].

These titles are relative to one another in meaning: if you remove the governor, you leave no soldier; for an attendant’s office is abolished whenever the person who could command is removed. Therefore, we believe it appropriate to send dignities to you, and we make you serve as soldiers only until we appoint judges. Do not consider this a slight benefit: while you know yourselves to be subordinate, the choice of those who will judge you comes before you.

Accordingly, by that indiction, know that we have appointed that count over your military service. We think that he will act in both public and private cases in such a way that the desired praise will accompany him. Granting him your most just devotion, obey solemnly whatever he commands you, because we believe our reverence to be honored if we perceive that our judges are well treated [Col. 0724B].

## XXIX. FORMULA CONCERNING THE GUARDING OF CITY GATES

There is no doubt about the faithfulness of one chosen to guard a city, since a person whose conscience has been tested must be believed when he serves the security of many.

Accordingly, by our authority we entrust you with the care of the gate of that city, so that it may not lie open to the arrivals of the wicked and may not delay the approach of the good. For if the gate is always barred, it is like a prison; if, on the other hand, it is continually open, it is useless for the walls to possess fortifications.

Let both conditions therefore be moderate, so that you may satisfy the night watches and not presume to close the gate inappropriately. You will indeed be the road of the citizens and the entrance for every kind of merchandise, while also being a friend to the abundance that you desire to enter [Col. 0724C].

Strive to invite those arriving with provisions. You have not been entrusted with something to be despised. You are placed over certain mouths of the city, and are shown to preside over the provisions entering it. You must complete this without complaint, so that in small matters we may recognize to whom we ought to entrust greater responsibilities.

## XXX. FORMULA OF THE TRIBUNATE OF THE PROVINCES

It is consistent with equity that each person should reach the fruit of military service after the passage of time and receive the reward of his labor in compensation for his merits.

Since the reasoning of ancient custom persuades us that the person who deserves to be tribune among you should be designated by us, we therefore decree by this authority that the man whom the position appears to demand shall preside over you in the aforesaid honor [Col. 0724D], so that when the appointed time arrives he may enjoy the desired dignity.

These are divine judgments, not human ones: when the heavenly power has chosen to bring someone to the proper time, he is rightly seen also to have received the rewards of his labor. Let him therefore obtain the appropriate privileges of his watches, since we do not wish anyone to be defrauded of his customary emolument whom we recognize to have reached primacy without fault.

Accordingly, obey in every way that man who makes arrangements for the public advantage, since those who hold precedence possess the judge’s authority [Cuj. Cor., Niv., and Gam.: “the judge’s skill”] whenever it is required of them to determine whether anything has been exceeded by you with excessive insolence.

## XXXI. FORMULA OF THE PRINCIPALITY OF THE CITY OF ROME

[Col. 0725A]

Since we judge that many things must be carried out in the city of Rome, and since it is necessary that the power of the count’s office be present there so that public advantages may be fulfilled, we have made provision according to our custom.

Because we do not permit the cardinal *princeps* to be absent from our services, you must solemnly occupy his place in the Roman city under the title of vicarius, so that he may enjoy the labors of his primacy and you may learn, in another’s honor, what you ought happily to display in your own.

If you should judge that any of the members of the count’s office ought to be sent to the court, then, in consideration of our service, the matter will be subject to your discretion. Those whom you judge should be retained shall enjoy the security granted to them. In this way, however, regulate everything in turn, so that continuous labor does not wear down those who keep watch, while the rust of idleness, which must be avoided, does not consume the inactive [Col. 0725B].

## XXXII. FORMULA BY WHICH THE MINT IS ENTRUSTED

Every public utility must indeed be completed through faithful action, since everything is conducted defectively where purity of conscience is absent. Nevertheless, the integrity of the mint must be sought above all, since our face is impressed upon it and the general advantage is found in it.

What will be safe if an offense is committed against our image? And how can a subject, who ought to venerate it in his heart, hasten to violate it with a sacrilegious hand?

Moreover, venality dissolves everything [Grul., Cuj., Niv., and Gam.: “everything is dissolved”] if the useful metals are adulterated, since what appears to be offered in commerce in a corrupt form must necessarily be rejected [Col. 0725C]. Who, then, would tolerate the criminal advantage of one person becoming the wicked loss of all, so that a detestable defect might reach a price?

Let what is brought to the likeness of our serenity be pure. Royal brilliance admits nothing contaminated. For if anyone’s face is painted in a true color, the sovereign favor is much more justly preserved through the purity of metals.

Let no wrongful admixture make the flame of gold pale; let the color of silver shine with the grace of its whiteness; let the redness of bronze remain in its natural quality. For if it is thought punishable under the laws to harm one person, what might the man deserve who has offended against so great a multitude of people?

We also command that the established weight of the denarii be preserved [120], which formerly were sold both by weight and by number. Hence antiquity, appropriately deriving the terms from their origin, beautifully called the difference between gain and loss *compendium* and *dispendium* [Col. 0725D]. Money, so called from the hide of cattle, was, according to Gallic authorities, transferred to metal before it yet bore any stamp. We do not permit it to be made contemptible by foul admixture, lest it be recognized as returning once more to its ancient baseness.

Therefore, because the integrity of your conduct has been praised by us, we command you to have charge of the mint from that indiction for a continuous five-year period. This is the mint that is said to have first been struck in bronze by King Servius. Do not doubt that any fraud discovered in it will be investigated at your own peril.

For just as you will undergo harsh consequences if you should perhaps commit an offense, so we will not leave you without reward if we perceive that you have acted without blame.

## XXXIII. FORMULA OF THE AMBASSADORS OF VARIOUS PEOPLES

[Col. 0726A]

Who could doubt that it is in the public interest that those to whom we are known to grant gifts should appear to suffer no inconvenience on their journey, since they cause you no loss through delays and themselves recognize that they have been well treated? Therefore you shall provide the envoys of that people without delay with the allowance specified below for their horses and persons, so that they may not reach their homes without compensation; for, when people are in haste, speed on the return journey is more welcome than any amount of gifts.

## XXXIV. FORMULA OF SUMMONS, WHICH THE PRINCE ADDRESSES.

We do not doubt that requests voluntarily offered are gratefully received when they are customarily presented in place of a gift; for remembrance of the lord always grants increase, and the judgments of a prince concerning favors cannot be empty. Therefore, by this present order, we summon you to our court, so that you may enjoy no ordinary pleasure. Accordingly, setting aside the delight of leisure, hasten to arrive at that city on that day, so that we may judge that our presence has been pleasing to you when we learn that you have hastened to us. For our palace desires the presence of good men, since, somehow, whatever is recognized as pleasing to royal wisdom is also approved by divine judgment: he who governs our hearts likewise grants us to understand what we ought to feel.

## XXXV. FORMULA OF SUMMONS GRANTED TO ONE WHO REQUESTS IT.

To have sought the presence of a just prince is an evident sign of a good conscience; only one who trusts in the great purity of his mind can desire it. Only bright eyes seek the sun’s gaze, since only those whose eyes are utterly pure can endure its radiant rays. So those who rely upon the sincerity of their hearts seek the prince’s presence.

Therefore, with a grateful mind, we generously grant you the confidence to come to our court, lest the honor of a summons—which was devised for our glory—be turned into an injury by being delayed in any way. Indeed, we welcome the wishes of those who come, since we grow greater when we attach noble men to our service.

## XXXVI. FORMULA OF LEAVE OF ABSENCE.

No one doubts that people are refreshed by variety, since continual sameness brings great weariness to the mind. The sweetness of honey becomes loathsome if taken constantly; even clear skies, however greatly desired, grow distasteful when enjoyed without interruption. This is not unreasonable, since human beings are changeable and desire to experience the qualities of their own nature.

Therefore, since you are eager to be refreshed by provincial pleasures, we grant you permission to remain for so many months in the aforesaid province—for a man seems almost confined when he is not free to change his place—provided that, after you have spent the leave granted you, with the Lord’s help, you hasten to return to the urban centers. For if it is wearisome to live continually amid the bustle of the city, how much more so to spend a long period in the countryside? We therefore gladly grant leave to depart, not so that Rome should be abandoned, but so that it may be more highly valued in your absence.

## XXXVII. FORMULA OF THE RANK OF SPECTABILIS.

[Col. 0727A]

With God’s help, we wish those subject to us to glory in the varied distinction of dignities. We desire to adorn a commendable class of men with the impressed grace of rank, so that each may live more worthily when he knows that he has received revered honors. For in this way one properly rises toward the pursuit of virtue, and the commonwealth is loved more greatly by good citizens.

Therefore we adorn you with the splendor of the rank of *spectabilis*, so that you may recognize that your judgment ought to be regarded in public assemblies, when you sit honorably among the nobles; and, if you conduct yourself in this praiseworthy manner, you may hereafter be increased by better rewards.

## XXXVIII. FORMULA OF THE RANK OF CLARISSIMUS.

[Col. 0727B]

It is evident that the taste of good things is pleasant, and that the pursuit of praise is useful when it is sought through the increase of virtue. We instill this zeal through provident generosity, so that the cultivation of character may increase while the desire for rewards grows.

The royal authority therefore bestows upon you the honor of *clarissimus*, an ornament of our judgment. It will provide testimony to a well-ordered life and promise an increase of future prosperity. Therefore, now that you shine with the dignity of *clarissimus*, do not permit yourself to undertake anything obscure. It is indeed a great testimony to one’s life to be called not merely “bright” but “most distinguished,” since almost everything excellent is believed to belong to the man who is called by the superlative name of such splendor.

### 121. XXXIX. FORMULA OF PROTECTION.

[Col. 0727C]

It may seem superfluous to ask a prince specifically for protection, since it is his purpose to defend everyone in common. But because the detestable rashness of certain violent men disturbs your security, we do not hesitate to be moved by the complaints of those who suffer and to be drawn toward this aspect of compassion, so that what we desire to provide for all we may confer especially upon one who begs for it.

Accordingly, since—as you complain—you have been wounded by the losses inflicted by various men, we mercifully receive you into the camp of our defense, so that you may be seen to contend with your adversaries not, as previously, in open battle, but under the protection of walls. Thus, pressed by savage forces, you will be made equal to them through royal assistance.

Therefore our authority grants you the protection of our name, like a very strong tower against uncivil attacks and contractual losses, provided that, strengthened by this assurance, you do not refuse to give a civil response, nor appear, in your insolence, to trample upon the public laws, when previously detestable audacity was oppressing you.

And since our command ought to have effective ministers, and it is not fitting for a prince to say what he cannot appear able to accomplish, by the order of this present benefit your confidence and diligence have easily protected you against the Goths in one matter and against the Romans in another. For no one takes trouble to defend a person unless he fears that person may be offended, when he fears that an eminent lord may prove ungrateful.

Enjoy our clemency, then; rejoice in the benefit you have received. For if anyone should thereafter attempt to treat you uncivilly, you will rather fulfill your wishes concerning your enemies.

> **Note:** This is the formula of protection—that is, of security, *ἀσφάλεια* (*asphaleia*)—discussed above, Book IV, Letter 27, at the end, and in Digest 1.6, *Illicitas*, § “Ne potentiores,” *On the Office of the Governor*; and Digest 1.12, § “Quies,” *On the Office of the Urban Prefect*. See an example in Livy, Book II, concerning Thrasybulus. —Forn.

## XL. FORMULA FOR CONFIRMING A MARRIAGE AND [Note: See Ambrose, Book I, *On Abraham*, chapter 3. Jur. —Thus this formula derogates from Codex 5.27.1, *On Natural Children*, which forbids this to be sought by imperial rescript. Forn.] LEGITIMATELY ESTABLISHING CHILDREN.

A benefit conferred for the sake of posterity is eternal; and nothing is more fitting for a king than to provide for human offspring. A person destined to come into the light does not deserve to encounter adverse circumstances, lest he suffer the burden of constraint before finding the joys of heavenly light.

You therefore state in the petition you have submitted that the woman to whom a pleasing [variant: gentle] embrace has bound you ought, through our favor, to be united to you in honorable marriage, so that children born from her may acquire the name of heirs. Since voluntary union joins all living creatures together, and what has been pleasing seems worthy of recognition, it is harsh that freedom should not have a free status from which free children are born.

Therefore, we decree that she, who is proved not to have been your equal in honor, as the law prescribes, shall become your legitimate wife; and we wish the sons born of that same wife—whether those already born or those yet to be born—to obtain the rights of heirs, so that you may love without any doubt those whom you know will plainly become your successors. Nature has given you sons, but we make them especially dear to you through this security.

## XLI. FORMULA OF A GRANT OF MAJORITY.

A petition that asks for a grant of majority is a glorious one, since its author confesses that he is acquiring the seriousness of character which he has not yet attained through the maturity of life. Younger by birth, you desire to be an elder in judgment. Thus, in a matter that is most daring among human affairs, you reject the benefit of years as an aid against error.

You therefore state in your submitted petition that, since your understanding is firmly prudent, your actions should not be left uncertain, lest a legal right be weakened by what cannot falter in practical usefulness. We, who take to heart the fulfillment of good desires, willingly accept this, since anyone who steadfastly seeks to possess unrestricted contracts professes that he does not wish to lay snares.

> **Note:** Above, Book IV, Letter 9. Here, as there, he calls deceit “a snare.” Codex 2.21, final law, *On Deceit*; Codex 4.58.8, *If by Consent*, *On Rescission of Sale*. Deceit must be demonstrated from the buyer’s craft and snares. It is appropriate that deceit be proved by manifest snares, Codex 2.21, final law, *On Deceit*. On this matter see also above, Book IV, Letter 35. —Forn.

Therefore, if the period has elapsed which the laws required to pass before this grant could be sought, we too do not deny permission to reasonable desires, so that in the proper court the venerable antiquity of the laws may solemnly prescribe what is to be done in such cases. The authority of the constitutions must be observed in alienating rural or urban estates, lest, while we wish to favor your reputation, we appear to harm the public interest.

Receive, then, through our favor, an age superior to your years; and demonstrate by your conduct what you request from the imperial authority. For a profession of premature maturity denies a place for legal action, since the authority that opposes its own promise is all the more seriously at fault.

> **Note:** That is, the twentieth year for males and the eighteenth for females, as defined by Constantine’s constitution, Codex 2.44.2, *On Those Who Obtain a Grant of Majority*. He elegantly calls this age “premature maturity,” as Ulpian does in Digest 4.4.2, under “Maturius,” and Digest 4.4.3, under “Quasi Ambitiosa,” *On Minors*. Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, Book I, likewise seems to indicate that adolescents were sometimes made independent earlier. Consequently, the alienation of estates was not permitted, nor even the mortgaging of immovables, Codex 2.44.3. Hence the customary Gallic clause, added in drafting such letters granting majority—commonly called *bail à gouvernement*: “on condition that the immovables not be alienated.” The force of this exception is likewise excluded by this formula, in the words “provided that in alienating …” At Athens, adolescents were entered and registered in the *Lexiarchic* register and thereby became independent, as Pollux writes; they then possessed the right to administer their patrimony. Suidas mentions this custom: “Those to whom it was permitted to manage their ancestral property” (*Οἷς ἐξῆν τὰ πατρῷα οἰκονομεῖν*). Aeschines also recalls it: “And he became master of the property” (*Καὶ κύριος ἐγένετο τῆς οὐσίας*). But concerning adolescents who obtained a grant of majority through the prince’s indulgence, it is certain that he discusses the matter more fully elsewhere. —Forn.

### 122. XLII. FORMULA OF AN EDICT TO THE QUAESTOR, THAT HE HIMSELF MUST GIVE SECURITY WHO SEEKS A *SAJON*.

[Col. 0729B]

We have frequently learned that the *sajones* whom we believed were granted by us out of pious good will have been burdened by the greatest complaints. Our benefit has been corrupted—alas!—and calamity has grown rather than healing, since, through the malignity of powerful men, they have been diverted to uses other than those to which our remedies transferred them.

It was therefore necessary for us to oppose pestilential demands with a salutary remedy, lest, while our zeal for compassion is drawn toward equal benefits, we suffer the most unjust frauds of surreptitious petition. Accordingly, by an edictal proclamation we decree that anyone who, because of unavoidable necessities, desires to obtain a strong *sajon* against violent snares must bind himself to our office by a punitive bond of security. Thus, if the *sajon* he obtains should exceed our commands through a punishable implementation of our order, he himself shall pay as a penalty so many pounds of gold and promise to compensate whatever losses, whether in property or in travel, his adversary may have suffered.

For when we wish to restrain uncivil dispositions, we must not oppress innocence. A *sajon*, however, who voluntarily exceeds the limits of the order shall know that he will be stripped of gifts and may incur the danger of losing our favor—which is more serious than every other loss. Nor may he thereafter be trusted if he becomes the violator of our command, whose executor he ought to have been.

## XLIII. FORMULA OF PROBATION FOR THE *CHARTARII*.

It is evident that military service is well performed when it is imposed upon men who have been approved, since a man can reflect upon what the judge was able to admonish him; especially when he is deemed worthy of approaching the patrimonies of such a divine household that he cannot be inflamed by detestable greed.

Moreover, since a most splendid office shines with a certain censorial gravity, and it is disgraceful for those who cannot be approved by worthy conduct to be mixed with its members, it seems fitting to seek men who ought to displease in no respect.

Accordingly, having learned of the recommendation of the tribunes of the *chartarii*, in whose hands the office possesses worthy dignity, we wish you from that day to acquire the name of *chartarius*, so that you, who promise to act well for us, may be approved by commendable documents. Avoid avarice; flee unjust profits as far as possible. Progress is much better made by serving good morals.

> **Note:** Cassiodorus mentions the *chartarii* in Book IX, Letter 3, and they are also mentioned in an ancient inscription at Nîmes. —Jur.

## XLIV. FORMULA CONCERNING COMPETITORS.

> **Note:** Codex 10.12.2, *On Claims to Property Taken Away*. —Forn.

One who desires to possess public places seems to promise something great of himself. This is fitting if [Note: The author means public works, or works pertaining to the commonwealth or to a city; see Codex, *If at Any Time*, *On Public Works*. —Bross.] a neglected thing is transformed into a better appearance and what previously seemed to lie uncultivated is restored to ornament.

Therefore, since you desire it, we grant you that place by right of ownership, except for bronze, lead, or marble, if any of these are discovered to lie hidden there. Act, then, so that what had lain neglected through carelessness and age may acquire beauty through you, so that you may deserve the praise of a good citizen if you adorn the appearance of your city, secure in the knowledge that you will transmit to posterity what has been fashioned by your own labor. For each person will possess something all the more firmly the more he proves that he has spent upon it, and that his predecessors spent upon it, in greater measure.

## XLV. FORMULA BY WHICH A TAX IS RELIEVED FOR ONE WHO POSSESSES A SINGLE OVERBURDENED HOUSE.

> **Note:** Today a petition for relief, transfer, conversion into money, and so forth, is forbidden; Codex, Book X, title 28, *On Assessments of Gifts or of Property Granted Relief*, etc. —Forn.

> **Note:** Digest 50.15.4, *On Censuses and Titles*, and Codex 10.15, *On Censors and Equalization*; Novella 163. Ulpian the Rhetorician, in his speech *On a Will Improperly Executed*, writes that exemption from public burdens was granted to the poor—called “men of moderate means” here—so that they might care for their household affairs. A constitution of Basil Porphyrogenitus is recorded by Cedrenus and in Book I of the *Eastern Law*, under which the tribute of the poor, who were less able to pay, was collected from the wealthy; this was called *allilengium*, about which more elsewhere. The entire subject of this letter accords with the discussion in Digest 50.15.4, *On Censuses*. —Forn.

Since life is sustained by the usefulness of the land, and everyone knows that a sure profit comes from it, you complain that the tax imposed upon the property established in that province is so burdensome that this vast lake of taxation has swallowed all your resources. What can be collected elsewhere only through great labor seems to be extracted through that property, whose assessment exceeds its usefulness, since more is returned to the collectors than is supplied by the diligent cultivator.

Therefore we believe that you can escape poverty if you lose ownership of this rural property [others: “urban property”], from which continual barrenness brings demands from the collectors, lest you serve, in a wretched condition, the necessity of which you deserved to be master.

But since the most sacred laws have decreed that this kind of benefit should be granted to persons of moderate means, so that one who is crushed by the excessive burden of a single plot and is not relieved by the advantage of another should be aided after due moderation, our greatness, which takes justice to heart, decrees by this present authority that, if the matter is as stated, you shall, after orders have been issued to those concerned, carefully erase so many solidi from the tax registers of the aforesaid property that no trace of this matter may thereafter be found in the public records, but that what has been settled in one common sum may endure without error through the ages.

> **Note:** The public *vasaria* here are the archives and tax registers, as in Codex Theodosianus 11.1.12, *Places*, *On Censors and Equalization*, in which the resources of individual citizens were recorded. Following Theophilus’s definition, they were “a tablet or sheet of paper on which the Romans recorded their own possessions, so that in time of war each might contribute in proportion to his own means” (*Σανὶς ἤτοι χάρτης, ἔνθα Ῥωμαῖοι ἀπεγράφοντο τὰς οἰκείας περιουσίας, ἐπὶ τὸ ἐν καιρῷ πολέμου κατὰ μέτρον τῆς ἰδίας ὑποστάσεως ἕκαστον εἰσφέρειν*). Otherwise, *vasarium* means money publicly given to magistrates traveling to the provinces, so that they might acquire horses, mules, vessels, furniture, and other things needed to equip a magistrate, purchased at public expense. Cicero mentions it in *Against Piso*: “One hundred and eighty thousand sesterces, which, under the name of *vasarium*, had been paid to you from the treasury at Rome for the sale of my person, you left behind as profit.” The same custom is mentioned by him in *Against Rullus*, Book II, and *Against Verres*, Book V; by Suetonius in *Augustus*; by Lampridius in *Alexander*; and by Budaeus, *On the As*, Book III. —Forn.

### 123. XLVI. FORMULA BY WHICH A COUSIN IS MADE A LEGITIMATE WIFE.

> **Note:** See Saint Augustine, *City of God*, Book IV, chapter 16; and Saint Ambrose, Book VIII, Letter 66. Jur. Today such a rescript is forbidden by our law, Codex 5.5.1, *If Marriage Is Sought by Rescript*. —Forn.

The institution of the divine laws provides the beginning for human law, since among those provisions inscribed on the two tablets there is found a command. For the holy Moses, formed by divine instruction, among other matters decreed for the people of Israel that they should abstain from intercourse with those of their own kin, lest by returning into such proximity they pollute themselves and fail to extend themselves prudently into an alien lineage.

Following this example, prudent men transmitted a more distant observance of chastity to posterity, reserving to the prince alone the benefit of joining cousins in marital union. They understood that what had been ordered by the prince would rarely be presumed unless it had been requested.

We admire this invention and praise, with astonishing deliberation, the measured arrangement of affairs by which this was left to the prince’s judgment: the ruler of peoples could himself loosen the restrained reins of desire in a measured way.

Therefore, moved by the substance of your petitions, if she is joined to you only by the closeness of cousin blood, and you are not proved to be closer to her in any other degree of relationship, we decree that she shall be joined to you in marriage. We order that no question shall thereafter be raised against you, since the laws consent to permit what our will permits, and your vows have been confirmed by the benefit of our present authority.

Thus, with God’s favor, your descendants will be your solemn heirs: a chaste marriage, a glorious union, since whatever is ordered by us to be done must necessarily be regarded not as a fault but as a matter for praise.

> **Note:** The reason for avoiding marriages between cousins or between first cousins is discussed by Saint Augustine, *City of God*, Book XV, chapter 16. Civil law once permitted marriages between cousins: Digest 23.2.23, *Uter*, at the end; the following law, *On the Conditions of Institutions*; Digest 23.2.66, *On the Rites of Marriage*; Codex 5.4.19, *On Marriages*, § “Of Two”; and the same title in the Institutes. Quintilian, in the preface to Book VI, *On the Death of His Son*, laments: “You, recently advanced to the consulship and destined by your praetor-uncle to be his son-in-law, you who had been brought near to your father’s hope of all honors?” Theodosius prohibited marriages between cousins in the cited chapter 16 of Codex Theodosianus 3.12, *On Incestuous Marriages*; see Ambrose, Letter 66; Book I of the Codex Theodosianus, *If Marriage Is Sought by Rescript*; Gaius, Institutes, Book I, title 4; and Harmenopulus, Book VI, title 4. Hence in Theophilus, under the cited § “Of Two,” some manuscripts read *οὐ δύνανται* (“they are not able”), although the negation is absent from the Latin archetype. —Forn.

## XLVII. FORMULA TO THE PREFECT, THAT HE MAY SELL ESTATES UNDER A CURIAL DECREE.

Human affairs, through their lack of foresight, often suffer this condition: what seems harmful may provide help, and what seems helpful may cause distress. But what is known to be beneficial must be preferred. For even poisons, if they are proved to heal, are acceptable. Conversely, the sweetness of honey must be rejected when it is known to cause injury. The wise man’s goal, therefore, is to love what is expedient; accordingly, the man who strives to provide benefit does not look merely to desire.

Antiquity prudently decreed that the estates of curials should not easily be sold, so that they might better suffice for public needs if they possessed more assistance from their resources. But it also provided in this matter that, if unavoidable necessity appeared among you, the sale of their property might provide relief. For what good does it do if someone seems financially capable but cannot be freed from the bonds of contracted obligations?

> **Note:** “Poisons” is a middle term; therefore, when someone says “poison,” he must add whether it is good or bad. Medicines too are poisons, since the term includes everything which, when applied, changes the nature of the thing to which it is applied. Digest 50.16.236, *He Who Gives Poison*. —Forn.

One who cannot repay what belongs to another resembles a needy man; nor can that be called his own which does not appear capable of freeing its owner from debt.

> **Note:** Everyone’s property is understood to mean what remains after the deduction of debts: Digest 50.16.11, *Subsignatum*, *On the Meaning of Words*; Digest 23.3.72, *Mulier*, *On Dowry Rights*; Digest 49.14.11, *Non Possunt*, *On Fiscal Rights*; Digest 35.2.69, *Usufruct*, *Against the Falcidian Law*; Quintilian, *Declamation* 233; and Harpocration, under the word *ἐνεπίσκημμα*. —Forn.

> **Note:** In an old manuscript the text reads “from the debt,” which I had myself emended before consulting the manuscript; whether the reading is more correct, others may judge. I was not altogether displeased by the conjecture, and I understood “free the owner who has been assigned” as referring to an opposite relation, since the debtor is bound to the creditor, *ὑπεύθυνος*, as Gordianus also says, almost like a client, Codex 8.41.3, *On Novation*. —Forn.

[Others: “added”; others: “assigned.”]

Although this was granted to your authority by the force of the laws, nevertheless, lest you suffer the unpopularity of an exceptionally rare act, moved by the petition of that municipal official, we too, by this present order addressed to Your Eminence, permit you—after the truth has been investigated—if the debt cannot otherwise be paid, to allow someone to sell the encumbered property he has chosen of his own will, so that he may repay the debt proved to have been contracted and not appear, infected by the vice of voracity, to have been permitted to consume his resources.

Let a credible cause for the losses be established before you, since we wish aid to be given to those proved to be constrained by harsh necessities. For either course can be blameworthy: loosening the reins for bad conduct or once again excluding just complaints.

Therefore antiquity wisely permitted you to decide in that matter for which it is useful to preserve the curia. For from whom could public burdens be sustained if the sinews of the cities were seen to be cut away indiscriminately?

> **Note:** Curials are the “sinews of the cities,” Book IX, Letter 2 below, and in a Novel of Majorian, where one should read “sinews,” not “slaves.” Novel 5. —Forn.

# BOOK EIGHT.

### 124. LETTER ONE. KING ATHALARIC TO THE EMPEROR JUSTINIAN.

He asks for his favor and friendship under the same conditions by which earlier emperors had entered into an alliance with Theodoric.

[Col. 0733B]

I could rightly be blamed, most merciful of princes, if I sought your peace half-heartedly, when it is known that my parents desired it with greater ardor; or I would be an unworthy heir if I were found unequal to my founders amid such glory.

It is not merely the purple-clad order of your ancestors that makes you illustrious; nor does the royal throne elevate you as much as your powerful favor, which ennobles you far and wide. We believe that everything in our kingdom is perfectly secure if we perceive that this favor is by no means lacking toward us.

It is also a proclamation of your piety to love those whose fathers you have had the fortune to love. No one is believed to have shown blameless purity toward the men of former times unless he is proved to have accepted their descendants. Let hatred be buried with the dead; let anger know how to perish with the insolent; favor ought not to die with those who were loved. Rather, the man who is found innocent in matters concerning the kingdom must be treated with greater affection.

Consider what the successor of good men deserves from you. You raised our grandfather to the highest curule offices in your city; you adorned my father in Italy with the glory of the palm-bearing robe. Through a desire for harmony, a son was also made by arms, although he seemed almost your contemporary. You will bestow this title more fittingly upon a young man, as you bestowed such titles upon our elders.

Our affection should now pass into the place of kinship; for, born from your son, he is not regarded as a stranger to you by the laws of nature. Therefore I ask for peace not as a distant relative but as a near one, because you granted me the favor of a grandson when you bestowed upon my father the joys of adoption.

Let us also be admitted into your mind, since we have obtained the royal inheritance. For me, it is above dominion itself to have so great and such a ruler favorable to me. May our beginnings therefore deserve the consolations of an aged prince; may our youth obtain the protection of your favor; and may we not be wholly abandoned by our parents when we are supported by such protection.

Let our kingdom be bound to you by the bonds of favor. You will reign more greatly in that sphere where you command everything through love.

Therefore we have judged that our envoys, this man and that man, should be sent to Your Serenity, so that you may grant us friendship under those pacts and conditions which your illustrious predecessors are known to have had with our grandfather, the lord of divine memory.

Perhaps I deserve something more on account of my sincerity, since neither my age appears suspect nor my lineage is now proved foreign. We have entrusted certain matters to be communicated verbally by the envoys mentioned above to your most serene mind. In accordance with your customary clemency, bring these matters to fulfillment.

### LETTER TWO. KING ATHALARIC TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME.

He informs the Senate that he has been made king by the unanimous consent of the Goths and Romans, and sends Count Sigismer with others to render oaths in his name.

[Col. 0734B]

It is surely the fullest joy, Conscript Fathers, to learn of the rise of a ruler, so that the man believed capable of protecting everyone may be heard to have reached the summit of kingship. The measure of joy arises from the greatness of the news, and the mind’s excitement is as great as its consideration of the event.

For if the anticipated advantages of companions raise prudent men, and announced safety relieves friends, with what jubilation should we receive the happy emergence of a ruler of all the lands—one whom no stirred-up revolt produced, whom no raging wars brought forth, and whose accession was not purchased through the losses of the commonwealth, but who was made in peace, as was fitting for the founder of civic order?

It is indeed a great kind of good fortune to obtain sovereignty without conflict and to make a young man ruler in a commonwealth where many are known to possess mature character. Counsel cannot be lacking at any age where so many public fathers are known to exist.

Our hope, therefore, has been preferred through the merits of all; and it was more certain that we should be trusted than that anything concerning others could be approved—not unjustly, since every other distinction of lineage yields to that of the Amal family. Just as one born from you is called of senatorial origin, so one who proceeds from this family is recognized as most worthy of kingship.

Our present act has proved what we say. When the sweetest memory of our grandfather, the lord, pressed upon us in his final moments in proportion to his benefits, he transferred the greatness of his rule to us with such speed that you might have thought not a kingdom but a garment had been changed.

So many nobles, glorious in hand and counsel, raised no murmur, as is customary; instead, they followed their prince’s judgments with such great joy that you would recognize the divine will rather than anything else flowing together there.

Therefore, with God’s favor, we considered it necessary to inform you of the rise of our kingdom, since the empire appears to have been extended rather than changed when it passes to descendants. In a certain sense, the man is thought to live himself whose offspring are known to rule over you.

These were your wishes; this was his unmistakable judgment: that he should leave as heir of his good works one who could increase his benefits among you. It was out of love for princes that the practice was devised of preserving the likeness of an image in bronze statues, so that a future generation might see the founder who had bound the commonwealth to himself through many benefits.

But how much truer is the man who lives in his descendants, through whom both bodily form is often restored and strength of spirit is extended? Therefore you must now show the fidelity of your nobility with greater zeal, so that both your former gifts may appear to have been bestowed according to merit, and we may confidently bestow future ones upon those whom we have not found forgetful of the past.

Know also that divine providence arranged that a general agreement of Goths and Romans should be extended to us, and that they should confirm by the solemnity of an oath the will which they offered with pure hearts.

We have no doubt that you will follow them in due time, though not from affection—for you might have begun what, overtaken by the passage of time, you now follow. It is evident that the most excellent Fathers can show all the greater love in proportion as they have appeared to receive greater honors from the other orders.

But so that you may recognize both our beginnings and our kindness toward you—for it is fitting that your curia should be entered through benefits—we have sent our illustrious Count Sigismer [others: Sigisin] to render an oath to you along with those who have been dispatched, since we desire to preserve inviolate what we promise by public authority.

If you believe that there is anything to be requested from us which may increase your security, ask without hesitation, having been encouraged to do so; indeed, we ourselves seem to urge you to pour out your prayers. This is a promise rather than an admonition: for he who commands the revered Senate to petition has thereby promised that it may obtain what it asks.

Now it is for you to hope for something capable of increasing the commonwealth.

> **Note:** The phrase is noteworthy because the word “more” is understood, as among the Greeks, *μᾶλλον* (“more”); see below, Book XI, Letter 8, and Book XII, Letter 25. Pindar, *Nemean Odes*: “We all sleep rather than believe” (*Ὑπνοῦμεν πάντες ἢ πιστεύομεν*). Tertullian, *Exhortation to Chastity*: “I think we are not permitted to kill one who is in the process of being born, whom we are not permitted to kill once born.” Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXXI: “He was terrified by the attack of the citizens, more rapid than deliberate.” In both passages, “more,” or some expression with comparative force, is understood; this seems to have the character of a Hellenism or Hebraism. Similar is the expression “They receive the office by payment rather than by appearance,” Digest 4.6.2, *If Someone Seeks a Certain Thing*; and “It was decided that children should be bound by merits rather than by agreements.” Paul, *Sentences*, Book IV, title 5: “Nothing is more pleasing to them than that liberty can be granted.” Digest 40.5.39, *On Trusts for Manumission*; Digest 5.2.2, at the end, *On Judgments*; Digest 16.3.7 § 1, *If a Slave*, *On Deposits*. Antoninus Augustinus, *Emendations*, Book IV, chapter 8, was the first of all to draw attention to this. —Forner.

### LETTER THREE. KING ATHALARIC TO THE ROMAN PEOPLE.

He extols King Theodoric with distinguished praises and announces to the Roman people that he has been raised to the throne by the common votes of Goths and Romans, promising through his envoys that he will preserve justice.

[Col. 0736A]

If an external heir had assumed the empire, you might perhaps have doubted whether, through envy, the successor would fail to love those whom his predecessor had loved—for somehow, when a successor strives to be praised more highly, the predecessor’s reputation is [textual variants: “gladdened” or “harmed”]. But now only the person has changed, not the favor shown you, since we believe that we deal rightly with you if we follow the venerable judgments of our grandfather. For it is in our interest that those whom he protected with the greatest kindness should also be nourished by us through steadfast ordinances and an abundance of benefits.

Those who succeed obscure rulers and men engaged in mediocre affairs think less deeply. Our predecessor was such a man that we must follow in the footsteps of his tested virtues. [Col. 0736B] Therefore, as may be said under God’s auspices, we announce to you that our glorious lord grandfather arranged the succession in such a way that the most harmonious consent of Goths and Romans alike should join our kingdom. And lest any suspicion remain because of adverse circumstances, they confirmed their wishes by the interposition of oaths: they swore that they were entering our rule with such joy as though our lord grandfather had not been removed from them by the decree of fate, so that they might prove themselves devoted not merely with their tongues but from the depths of their hearts.

If you, as we suppose, have willingly done likewise, we have caused the bearers of this letter to promise you under divine adjuration [Editors and Ac.: “display”; Forn.: “attestation”] that, with the Lord’s help, we shall preserve justice and equitable clemency, which nourish peoples, and that Goths and Romans shall have equal rights before us. Nothing is divided between you except that they undertake military labors for the common good, while your peaceful residence in the Roman city increases your numbers. Behold, by inclining our principate to the most merciful condition of an oath, we have raised it, so that the people whom our blessed founder nourished may have nothing doubtful or fearful. Behold, we restore to the ages the illustrious example of your Trajan.

[Note: For an understanding of this passage, see what we noted in the preceding letter. To that we may add Pliny’s words in the *Panegyricus* concerning the oath sworn to the emperor and by the emperor at the beginning of his consulship: “You approach the consul’s chair; you offer yourself to be compelled to words unknown to rulers except when they force others to swear.” A little later: “Moreover, while seated, he offered an oath to the standing man; and the latter swore. He expressed and explained the words by which the man would have pledged his own head and his household, had he knowingly deceived him.” From these passages it is clear that after the vows, magistrates, senators, and the people themselves customarily swore to the emperor. —Bross.]

He swears to you by him by whom you swear; nor can anyone be deceived by him whom, once invoked, it is not lawful to lie to with impunity. Now raise your spirits and, with God favorable, always hope for better things, so that, just as we began our royal power with affection, we may likewise pursue a tranquility pleasing to God in the times to come.

## LETTER IV. KING ATHALARIC TO ALL ROMANS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT ITALY AND DALMATIA

He writes that he has received the oaths of Goths and Romans as a safeguard for his acquired kingdom, and asks that they likewise swear the same oath.

[Col. 0737A]

We believe it honorable to report what you may have learned through the testimony of rumor. Anyone may rightly judge himself well regarded who is deemed worthy of royal address, since it is an honor for a subject to have merited an audience with his ruler—especially in a matter in which everyone’s hearts appear so anxious that, unless they know that events are prosperous, they always believe them adverse. For whoever hears that the government has changed fears a new regime nonetheless.

Indeed, I do not know what sad thought one is believed to harbor who delays making benevolent promises at the beginning. Therefore, cutting off every place for sinister thoughts, we do not permit you to believe anything about us other than what could have been judged concerning our parents. And so, as may be said under the favor of Divinity, while our glorious lord grandfather was happily arranging matters, we received the oaths of both the Goths and the Romans present as a safeguard for our acquired kingdom [Ms. A: “begun”]. We most willingly judge that you too will do the same, so that you who proved faithful to our parents may also obey us with similar devotion. For the heir is loved more sweetly by one who remembers the author of his benefits.

But so that the integrity of our goodwill may already be known to you, we have caused it to be promised to you under the religious sanction of an oath—a promise that may declare our purpose and strengthen the hope of all.

## LETTER V. KING ATHALARIC TO ALL GOTHS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT ITALY

He indicates that, while Theodoric was still alive, he received the oaths of everyone in the royal city, and urges them to follow that example. He also pledges his good faith to them through a count who has sworn an oath on their behalf.

[Col. 0737C]

We would indeed have wished to announce the joys of our lord grandfather’s long life. But since he was taken from those who loved him by a harsh decree, he appointed us heirs of his kingdom under God’s command, so that, through the succession of his blood, he might make perpetual the benefits he had conferred upon you, while we desire both to increase and to protect what we know to have been established by him.

While he was still alive and in the royal city, the wishes of all were joined to his arrangement by the interposition of an oath, so that you would have believed that one person was promising what the whole community appeared to desire. Following this example, carry out the same act with equal devotion, lest you appear to have done less than those present, who are believed capable of fulfilling everything in the same manner.

We have caused that count to promise you under oath that, just as you most devotedly reveal your disposition toward us, so you shall hear from our hearts what you desire. Receive, therefore, what is always a prosperous name for you: the royal lineage of the Amals, the purple-dyed scion, childhood clothed in purple, through which our parents, with God’s help, were fittingly raised and, throughout so long a succession of kings, continually received increase.

For we trust in the favorable Divinity who graciously helped our ancestors and who now also bestows the grace of his favor, so that, while we reign, you may bring forth the sweetest fruits of good things—you who flourished under our parents with an abundant reputation for virtue.

## LETTER VI. KING ATHALARIC TO LIBERIUS, PREFECT OF THE GAULS

He announces that Theodoric bestowed the kingdom upon him while still alive, and that Goths and Romans promised him their loyalty under the religious sanction of an oath. He then asks that those living in Gaul imitate them.

We know that your spirit is wearied by bitter grief at the death of our glorious-memory lord grandfather, while all good things that have been lost are mourned heavily. For one grieves more deeply when a beloved lord is taken away. It is fitting, however, to console a mind afflicted through devotion by a compensating remedy, since one whose successor is no stranger is scarcely felt to be lost.

Thus, under God’s command, he made provision while he was alive and provident even concerning what would follow his death, leaving peace to his realms so that no novelty might disturb their tranquility. He placed us as rulers in the seat of his kingdom, so that the glory of his lineage, which flourished in him, might immediately shine with equal light upon his successors.

The desires of Goths and Romans agreed with this arrangement, so that under the religious sanction of an oath they promised to preserve their loyalty to our kingdom with devoted hearts. We believe this should be brought to the attention of your illustrious magnificence, so that those in Gaul who are devoted to the kingdom of our piety may produce a similar example; and just as they do not wish our minds toward them to become less favorable, so they should be bound by a corresponding condition.

## LETTER VII. KING ATHALARIC TO ALL PROVINCIALS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT GAUL

He urges that Goths swear to Romans and Romans to Goths that they will render loyalty to the king.

[Col. 0738C]

Although the setting of our glorious-memory lord grandfather may seem sad to you because of his outstanding merits, nevertheless, since he fell under the human condition, he left us behind to continue the government which he had exercised uniquely, so that you would not feel the loss of a good ruler whose offspring is known to reign over you.

No one among us loses what obeyed him [others: “who obeyed him”]. Rather, with doubled generosity, we both repay what was owed to him and, through innate piety, lend benefits for future services. Therefore it is now fitting for you to display your former loyalty with greater devotion, since the one who serves the beginnings of rulers provides well for future affairs: one who is perceived to cherish the beginnings is believed to persevere thereafter as well.

We announce that, by divine favor, when we reached the summit of the kingdom, everything turned out for us so happily and peacefully that you would have believed one person was speaking what the whole community was proclaiming. It would not have been thought human that so many vows of mighty peoples should prove to have nothing contrary to them.

Therefore you too should imitate what has been stated, so that the Goths may swear to the Romans, and the Romans may confirm by oath that they are unanimously devoted to our kingdom. Thus your sincerity may become commendably known to us, and the concord promised by both sides may benefit your tranquility.

Let legally sanctioned peace pass among you; let the greater not be hostile to the lesser. Keep peaceful minds, since you have no external war. You can first please us by looking after yourselves in this way [Editors: “by benefiting yourselves”].

## LETTER VIII. KING ATHALARIC TO VICTORINUS, A VENERABLE MAN AND BISHOP

He announces that he succeeded Theodoric after his death. Commending himself to the bishop’s prayers, he asks him to exhort all the provincials to preserve their loyalty to the ruler.

Persons whose desires are shaken by differing fortunes ought to be admonished concerning faith and steadfastness. But since wisdom makes you firm and religious conviction strengthens you [Note: Aulus Gellius, Book II, ch. 29: “Let them come, lend mutual assistance, and gather this harvest for us.” Although “assist” is written in some books, it is wrongly read. —Forn.], it is more fitting that you be encouraged toward gatherings of the provincials, because one who deserves to be heard by many becomes rightly responsible for the judgment of others.

Therefore, greeting you with the reverence you deserve, we announce with the deepest grief the death of our glorious-memory lord grandfather, a report that may indeed bring you sorrow. Yet your sadness can be tempered by the fact that, with Divinity favorable, he placed us in the seat of his kingdom, so that he who has risen again for you in succession may not seem wholly torn away from your desire.

Now favor us with sacred prayers and willingly support our auspices, so that the heavenly King may confirm earthly kingdoms to us, crush foreign nations, forgive sins, and graciously strengthen and preserve what he in his glory deigned to grant our parents.

Therefore let your holiness admonish all the provincials that, maintaining concord among themselves, they should be wholly pure in their loyalty to our kingdom. For we desire to find in our subjects a faith which we may reward with abundant generosity.

## LETTER IX. KING ATHALARIC TO TULUM [OTHERS: THOLUIT], A PATRICIAN

The dignity of the patriciate is conferred upon him, and he is adorned with outstanding praise together with Gensemundus.

Although those whom Divinity has raised to the august summit thereby become fit to govern peoples—for age is no impediment where heavenly power pours itself forth—it nevertheless seemed appropriate, to relieve the cares of our flourishing youth, to employ you, a most prudent man, who is known to have adhered continually and commendably to the counsels of our lord grandfather.

If it was worthy of him to make such a man so great, how much more fitting is it for us to seek the support which, in the flower of youth, we may still properly need [Editors: “understand”]? Great, indeed, and limitless is wisdom; no one attains it so completely that he does not necessarily appear to seek it through others as well.

Old men themselves learn wisdom through counsel, and what is considered for the benefit of all is sought collectively from mature men. Mature kings frequently bring support to their cares; and they are judged better for not presuming to undertake everything alone.

Since long-lived rulers are assisted by the abilities of their subjects, we wisely relax the brief leisure of our age, so that, through its own growth, it may rise more prosperously, stronger for sustaining the burdens of empire.

Therefore, with divine favor, we raise you through the dignity of the present patriciate, so that a lofty seat may exalt you when you deliberate for our commonwealth, lest a salutary judgment, which ought humbly to be obeyed, appear to have come from an ordinary position.

This is an honor suited both to arms and to peace. Rich Greece, which owed so much to our most glorious lord grandfather, repaid it with gratitude: this Roman garment veiled his strong shoulders in a military cloak; this Roman shoe adorned his shins with silk, and he was deemed worthy to receive what he recognized that he was assuming through honor.

The eastern peoples’ desire to see our hero increased, while, I know not how, civil qualities were loved even more in one believed to be warlike. Content with this reward of honor, he labored tirelessly for foreign provinces and deigned to serve, together with his parents, a ruler who had been born from the stock of so many kings.

Thus the benefits of the great always exalt themselves, imposing the rights of reverence even upon those whom they cannot command. Everyone loves the author of his advancement, and those who are not held by benefits do not understand the laws of mortality [Greek and Cuj.: “A mindful person loves the author of his advancement. Those who are not held by benefits do not understand the laws of mortality”].

But it would take too long to speak adequately of the glory of one whom a fruitful age produced as a singular figure among nations. His labor trained you so that we might labor less. With him you discussed the certainties of peace and the uncertainties of war; and, what is a singular gift among wise kings, while he was anxious about everything, he safely opened to you the secrets of his heart.

Yet you never mocked anyone with ambiguous answers. You loved patience in listening and truth in counsel; often you corrected, out of zeal for what was right, matters that had falsely reached him.

[Note: Thus Saint Ambrose writes of Theodosius: “I loved a man who approved the one who reproved him more than the one who flattered him.” So also Ammianus Marcellinus, pp. 55, 259, and 341; Suetonius, *Life of Augustus*, ch. 56, and *Life of Tiberius*, ch. 31. Epiphanius in Ennodius: “Let no one fear to admonish the head of the Church if he finds him in error.” So below, Letter 13. See above, Book VI, Formula 5. —Juret.]

And, what is a rare form of confidence, you sometimes resisted the ruler’s wishes, yet in defense of the ruler’s judgment. That unconquered man in battle endured being overcome for the sake of his reputation, and rational opposition from an obedient counselor was sweet to a just ruler.

Now, in a higher position, love the justice which you loved while serving. Show yourself to be the disciple of one who never labored in vain. Joined to the Amal family, associate with yourself deeds of the highest nobility [others: “companionships”]. Royal affinity ought indeed to recommend every good thing.

You will act with your customary prudence, so that you may appear to have reached a lofty rank through the praise of your character. The Gothic nation possesses an example of this integrity: that Gensemundus, celebrated throughout the world, who had become a son through arms alone, joined himself to the Amals with such devotion that he displayed zealous service to their heirs, although he himself was being sought for the kingdom.

He bestowed his own merit upon others; and, most moderate of all men, he preferred to offer to the little ones what could have been conferred upon himself. Therefore our fame celebrates him together with them: he lives in reports forever because he despised what would one day perish. Thus, as long as the name of the Goths endures, his praise is recounted with universal testimony.

It is therefore right to expect better things from you, since it is known that you rejoice in affinity with our family.

## LETTER X. KING ATHALARIC TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

He displays Tulum’s outstanding achievements and writes that he has raised him to the summit of the patriciate.

[Col. 0741B]

You have, conscript fathers, reason to return thanks to a glorious ruler, since we have conferred the dignity of your order upon the eminent Tulum, who shines through our affinity. The genius of peace has been increased by the adornment of gleaming iron; the unbelted toga no longer lies idle, having now become a garment of military readiness.

Previously we bestowed honors upon you, but now we have raised the dignity itself. Splendor has plainly been poured over everything which a present patrician can possess, since the nature of the purest light is such that it shines also upon those nearby.

Although the candidate is well known to you, having adhered to our lord grandfather in such illustrious and enduring service, it is nevertheless worthwhile to repeat what evidently belongs to the glory of his instructor.

First, something exceptional among nations: he glories in the noblest stock of the Goths. As soon as he left childhood among his relatives, he immediately brought his inexperienced years into the secrecy of the sacred chamber, acting not as his age required but as his position demanded.

For although all service to kings must be performed with caution, there one acquires all the more fear the nearer one is held.

[Note: Complete silence must be observed in counsel when one wishes it to possess force or practical effect. When Alexander had read certain secret letters to Hephaestion, he brought a removed ring to his mouth; each man should understand that this was done for him, and at the same time he was admitted into the council, his mouth sealed and marked by the ruler. This was the custom of the Persians: no one was privy to counsels except silent and faithful nobles, as also among the Romans. Noteworthy is the case of King Eumenes, who, when he had come to Rome and accused King Perseus in the Senate, deliberated with the senators about the entire war. At the time, no one could know anything except that a king had been in the curia; only after the war had ended did everything said by the king and every answer given become known. Such was the remarkable and lasting fidelity of silence. —Bross.]

The master of self-control passed through these storms without offense: dear to the highest officials and always welcome to his colleagues. Even then it seemed a sign of great good fortune that he had earned everyone’s favor.

As his age began to mature and his tender years to harden into the vigorous courage of his people, he was sent on the Sirmian expedition.

[Note: Sirmium in Pannonia was once the seat of the Goths. See above, Book III, Letter 23. —Juret.]

There he was to display, in the freedom of the fields, what he had learned in words from that man of Mars. Among others, he celebrated a triumph over the Huns and, having begun his well-earned glory in his first encounters, put to death the Bulgars, terrifying throughout the world.

Such warriors are sent forth from our cradle; such hands are prepared when the spirit is trained. Raised in peaceful service, he conquered men accustomed to toil; and what he had not learned through exercise, his own valorous hand completed [Ms. A and Ac.: “his eager virtue”].

He returned suddenly to the ruler as a veteran, though he had departed as a youth, so that he might be believed to have devoted himself not to peaceful service but always to arms. The scrutinizer of deeds and bestower of honors, observing this, entrusted him with the vigor of the royal household, considering his virtue, so that one whom warfare had proved ingenious might be admitted to the counsels of the most valiant king: subtle in devising, strong in executing, and most cautious in concealing.

He deservedly occupied the place of keeper of the public secret. With him he arranged battles and equal matters of state; and he had joined himself so closely to the ruler’s thought that, once the circumstances were understood, he would carry out of his own accord what the ruler might have wished.

He assisted the defender of all peoples in his deliberations and, by supplying counsel, himself guided the guide. The Gallic expedition also bears witness to this, when, already placed among the commanders, he brought both his prudence to wars and his readiness to face danger.

[Note: Ausonius calls Arelate “the Rome of Gaul,” because it was both a very famous and a highly advantageous commercial center. Attracted by these advantages, the usurper Constantine—proclaimed emperor in Britain during the reign of the younger Honorius—established his imperial seat at Arelate and ordered that it be called Constantina. There remains a constitution of that same emperor concerning Arelate, noted by Joseph Scaliger, a man highly skilled in all antiquity, in his books of Ausonian readings. —Bross.]

Arelate is a city situated above the waters of the Rhône, which sends a level bridge toward the view of the East across the back of the river that bears its name. It was necessary both to seize this bridge from the enemy and to defend it for our people.

Therefore the Goths and Franks were stirred into the fiercest storm of battle. There the candidate’s courage was present amid doubtful circumstances. He fought with such a struggle against the enemy’s masses that he both drove his enemies away from their aims and received wounds as signs of his deeds: wounds, I say, an inseparable reputation, praise without an advocate, the proper language of valor.

[Note: The author calls bodily wounds “praise without an advocate,” just as we attribute a voice to letters alone and say that the stars cry out and birds speak destinies. To this may be added the elegant passage of Ammianus Marcellinus concerning the emperor Julian: “If the nocturnal lamps,” he says, “among which he studied by night, could have testified with any voice, they would certainly have shown how greatly he differed from certain rulers, whom they knew never to indulge in pleasures, not even to the extent required by nature.” —Bross.]

Although wounds bring immediate danger, they nevertheless adorn the remainder of life. An uninjured body needs witnesses to support its claims; it seeks others to publicize what they have seen. But there is no doubt about proven courage when it is confirmed by such testimony.

The clash of brave men drove back the weapons hurled by both sides; nor is the man who contends with a numerous enemy always safe. Perhaps a single blow can be skillfully avoided [Editors: “deflected”]; but the one who resisted many receives a wound from the direction he did not expect. These wounds are as glorious for him as the danger they then involved.

It is therefore pleasing to recount the peaceful example of this most courageous man’s good fortune, since a commander’s praise is not perfected by always asserting anxious labors. He was therefore sent again to protect Gaul while a Frank and a Burgundian were fighting, lest an enemy hand presume anything which our army had won through costly toil.

He acquired a province for the Roman commonwealth while others were contending, without any fatigue of his own; and our advantage became peaceful, since we incurred no danger through military conflict. Triumph without battle, a palm without labor, victory without slaughter.

We owe his glory as much as we have received utility from him. The arbiter of affairs judged that he should be honored with a grant of revenues, so that he might become lord of possessions where he had secured an increase for the public good.

The Aquileian storms are also rightly remembered among his successes, since dangers, when they end happily, leave behind the sweetest memory. As the foaming waves testified to the sea raging beneath violent winds, the long-tossed vessel was swallowed by swelling waves, leaving the brave man no support except the oars worked by his arms.

Then, while the sailors perished, he alone escaped with his cherished companion. There the love of the most devoted king and the merit of the endangered man were proved. When that ruler had scarcely reached the shore, he wished to enter the waves again so that he might rescue him from destruction.

Then he feared for the other’s dangers, though he himself did not know how to fear for his own safety. Do you not think, conscript fathers, that he was divinely rescued from harsh circumstances, for whom such an outcome had been prepared?

We have therefore raised this man, trained by wars, renowned for good fortune, and proved by prudence, to the summit of the present patriciate, as may be said under God’s auspices. Now favor the candidate’s auspices and open to our men the halls of liberty. It is fitting that the Romulean people should have men of Mars as colleagues.

## LETTER XI. TULUM, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND PATRICIAN, TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

He urges the senators to return thanks to the king because the king promoted him to the honor of the patriciate.

[Col. 0743D]
