I trust, conscript fathers, that the efforts of all of you should be stirred to give thanks to the best of kings, since you know that my advancement was devised for the benefit of all. Therefore what ought necessarily to have been hoped for should be received eagerly.

It is useful for everyone to follow the judgments of rulers; but the one who gratefully accepts another’s judgment makes it his own. You remember that I have always cherished the senate’s assembly, but especially now, when I appear to be entering your college.

The assumption of your order’s dignity has doubled our gratitude, since I feel myself among those by whom I trust I can be loved. There is also this most welcome pledge of your spirit: the genius of the patricians is evidently raised through me, since none of my countrymen believed that what is honored in me had been cast down in you [Ac.: “that the patrician class had been raised”].

In seeking honors from the ruler Theodoric of glorious memory, I often joined my wishes to yours, so that by a kind of foresight I may seem to have anticipated such things, destined to enter with glory among those with whom it was fitting for me to enter.

One seeks something more confidently when, after benefits have been conferred, one hastens toward it. I have often advanced consuls, patricians, and prefects after exercising intercession, striving to obtain for you what I could scarcely have dared to hope for myself.

Rejoice now, conscript fathers, in my auspices, as I have always favored your honors. Do you wish to know with what affection I embrace you? Inserted into the royal lineage, I wished to share a common name with you.

Live securely, with God favorable; and, what is the happiest kind of sweetness [Greek and Cuj.: “happiness”], rejoice with your children. Strive, as always, to be praised for Roman character, and seek the model of good deeds beneath profound tranquility.

It is part of our glory that, having increased your number, we should, with Divinity favorable, protect you.

## LETTER XII. KING ATHALARIC TO ARATOR [Ms. A: ORATOR], AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

He greatly praises him and his father for eloquence, and adorns him with the honor of the *comitiva domesticorum*.

We judge that the perfection of necessary matters is complete if, just as we have provided for the armed part of the commonwealth by choosing the magnificent man as patrician, so we also take care to associate with him a man highly skilled in letters.

It is fitting that the men entrusted with supreme power should have the most learned advisers, so that, with no deficiency obstructing their merits, the provision made for the commonwealth may be carried out.

Some honors are established by ordinary appointment. But for one concerned with the general security, a man had to be associated whose equal could not be found in his studies.

Nor are you recognized as less worthy because you came to honors in your first youth. The field of advocacy trained you; the summit of our judgment selected you. Although you possessed a broad profession in letters, your genius was so great within you that we could not allow it to grow old there.

You began as a soldier [Juret: “that is, an advocate”], although you could have fulfilled the role of an examiner [Juret: “that is, a judge”]. And although eloquence drew you toward speaking in defense, equity nevertheless urged you to set forth what ought to be judged.

It was proved how useful an eloquence armed with character can be. For just as it is harmful for the learned to give wicked advice, so it is a salutary service when eloquence does not know how to exceed the boundaries of truth.

But so that we may assert your merits through commendable examples rather than words alone, it is pleasing to recall the splendid embassy which you conducted not in ordinary language but in a torrent of eloquence.

Sent from the regions of Dalmatia to our lord grandfather, you argued the needs of the provincials and the public interests in such a way that, before that ruler—who was greatly and cautiously concerned—you were both abundant and free from tiresomeness.

Your words flowed in abundance with the sweetest charm; and when you finished, you were still sought to speak. By moving and delighting your audience, you fulfilled the effort of a true orator even after you had left behind the office of advocate.

You were also aided by your father’s eloquence and character. His speech could instruct you even if you had not spent time with the books of the ancients, for, as we know, he was exceptionally learned in letters.

And, to appear to say something carefully investigated, it is commonly reported that Mercury, inventor [Editors: “restorer”] of many arts, first collected the forms of letters through the flight of the Strymonian birds. Even today, when cranes join themselves into a formation, they trace the shapes of the alphabet, as nature instructs them.

By arranging them into an orderly system and suitably mixing vowels and consonants, he discovered a path for the senses by which the mind, seeking higher things, might swiftly reach the inner chambers of wisdom.

Hence Hellenus, the author among the Greeks, said many remarkable things, describing its virtue and composition in an extremely subtle account, so that from the very beginning the abundance of great letters might be recognized [Editors: “Hellenus said many remarkable things”].

But to return to our subject: you must be thought to have extended your genius by your father’s example, since you did not nourish your eloquence in the Roman Forum.

O blessed teacher and most fortunate student, who learned with affection what the terror of learned men had forced upon others! In the end, you did not discover Roman eloquence in its own regions; Tullian reading made you eloquent where the Gallic language once resounded.

[Note: Concerning the eloquence of the ancient Gauls, Juret stated that he had observed it in his note on Symmachus, Book IX, Letter 86.]

Where are those who claim that Latin letters must be learned at Rome and nowhere else? Caecilius would have escaped the burden of modesty had earlier ages produced this man. For that force of judgment has been released, and Liguria too sends forth its own Tullians.

Recognize what we have judged from your merits, since you see yourself joined to the counsel of the man who handles the secret affairs of our empire. For this reason we adorn you with the honor of the *comitiva domesticorum*, so that you should rightly hope for greater things from our judgments, since we still believe that better qualities may be found in you.

You see that a great responsibility has been entrusted to you: whatever you do is felt by the whole community. For one who can err in matters affecting everyone is very glorious if he knows how not to overstep.

## LETTER XIII. KING ATHALARIC TO AMBROSIUS, A QUAESTOR

He extols him with many praises because he wisely administered many dignities under Theodoric. He then confers the quaestorship upon him.

One who has proved himself in slightly lesser matters ascends securely to lofty positions; and one who gradually attains the desire granted to him proceeds with a firm step.

Everything sudden is thought to have been rewarded without merit; nor does what has arisen unexpectedly escape suspicion as something untested. In contrast, everything deliberate is strong [Ms. A: “What is untested is ... Everything deliberate is strong”]; and the one who is promoted after evidence of praised service is believed to have obtained everything through good actions.

Long ago, in the schools of letters, you were appointed by that examiner of merits who foretold even future things through his judgments. You presided over the offices of private largesses, undertaking the defense of merit, and increased the ruler’s favor so greatly that what did not yet possess the dignity was often entrusted to you.

If it is praiseworthy even to be equal to ordinary honors, how much more excellent is it to surpass courtly dignity through character? While you were carrying out these tasks, praised by so great a judge, you also found favor in another position.

You were approved for service in drafting documents, while another was expelled because of offenses; and your genius sustained your suspended honor in such a way that you did not allow the palace to lack a judge whose dignity, as we know, had for a time been taken away.

Our times are not inferior to those of the past. We have followers and rivals of the ancients. Behold, he returns once more to the quaestorship, endowed with immense genius [Greek and Cuj.: “he returns with immense genius”].

Restore Pliny now, and take up Trajan. You have great things to say if you too shine with a similar eloquence. The reputation of an age is generated by legitimate and eloquent command. For a fluent tongue heaps together every good thing; and what is commanded by us is adorned by the favor of the one who dictates it.

Be most ready to suggest good things to us, and steadfastly upright against the wickedness of those who presume evil. It will now speak to our ears what is entirely on our side.

That is a good ruler before whom it is permitted to speak for justice. Conversely, it is a mark of tyrannical ferocity to refuse to hear the established sanctions of the ancients.

We certainly renew that famous saying of Trajan: “Take—”

[Note: “*Dicationem*” should be read; this word occurs below, Book XI, Letters 7 and 9. From this comes the explanation of that passage in Sidonius Apollinaris, *Panegyric on Majorian*, near the end:

“With the Senate as witness …”]

Ulpius had also driven the drawn sword into himself [Col. 0746D]. See Nicephorus, Book III, chapter 23; Pliny, *Panegyric* 358. JURET.] *dicationem* [Others: *dictationem*, “dictation”], [Col. 0746C] “if I shall be good, for the republic and for myself; if bad, for the republic against myself.” But see what we ask of you, since we do not even permit ourselves to do anything unjust. Let our decrees, therefore, echo the enactments of the ancients, which find such sweetness in praise as they take on the savor of antiquity. We do not approve in others the precedents that we ourselves dread. We certainly bind you to the common good when we unreservedly command that the laws be observed. We say this now so that we may appear to have taken timely counsel for all through you. For it is fitting to give warning, lest we seem later to wish to correct you only after the dangers caused by others. Follow the examples of good men, and walk mindful of your nobility. Those return deservedly to the vices of their lineage who are born from a contemptible stock.

Having thus spoken these things for the public good, in the fifth indiction (A.D. 527), with God’s favor, we grant you the insignia of the quaestorship [131]: [Col. 0746D] the honor of prudent men, [Note: [Col. 0746D] These were the quaestor’s duties under the emperors: he composed laws and examined the truth of petitions, so that he might subscribe to them if they rested on sound justice, as may be seen in law 2 of the *Code*, “On petitions for property taken away”; and in the final law, *Code*, “On various rescripts”; and in the *Novels* of Valentinian, “On homicide committed accidentally or voluntarily.” BROSS.] the source of all dignities, since from it proceeds whatever has flowed from the generosity of our indulgence. Act so that, having been admitted to our council, you may be recognized as surpassing all in prudence and seriousness. For you see what is fitting for you. [Col. 0747A] [Note: [Col. 0747D] Sidonius Apollinaris, in the *Panegyric on Majorian*, near the end:

“From whose mouth Caesar is willing to speak throughout the world, although he also excels through an eloquent quaestor.”

And our Cassiodorus, Book VI, in the form for the quaestorship: “How much more eloquent ought he to be who is known to admonish peoples with the prince’s voice?” It is also known that emperors used the services of quaestors when they recited speeches or anything else in the senate, as is clear from Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 65; *Titus*, chapter 6; *Nero*, chapter 15. FORNER.] You are called the voice of the laws while we enact the laws (*nos iura*; Ed.: *nostra iura*). Apply yourself now to integrity or loyalty, so that, just as your first honor made you worthy of a second, so the second may make you worthy of a third dignity.

## LETTER XIV. KING ATHALARIC TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

He adorns Ambrosius with exceptional praise and announces that he has distinguished him with the dignity of the quaestorship.

Receive, enrolled fathers, the judgment that our judgments have rendered, since matters undertaken with caution are altogether more highly regarded; for what follows is believed to be such as its beginning is perceived to have been. No one expects a man to be diligent in the future whom, in the very newness of his reputation, he does not see to be watchful. If a provident cultivator strives to adorn his garden with fertile plants so that those tended with diligent labor may produce the desired fruits, how much more ought a kingdom to be arranged amid the pleasantness of peace at its beginning, lest it seem to bear the appearance of an uncultivated field? And so we thought that we should provide, as it were, a quaestor as a gateway through whom the summits of coming dignities might properly emerge.

You certainly know the candidate, as you also know the present matters of which we speak. When anxious hearts of our subjects were mourning the passing of our lord grandfather, of glorious memory—for a good that is lost is loved more when it is sought—through him the hopes both of our accession and of your security were opened to you. Understand by what fairness we bind ourselves regarding the future: we have made him the guardian of the laws who had become a promiser of the preservation of justice.

He was present at the royal commands [Ms. A.: “legal commands”] as their eloquent and graceful framer; moreover, his appearance was charming, and his speech rendered his hearers most pleased. Such ought courtly men to be, that they reveal the gifts of nature through the evidence of their countenance and can be recognized by their character when they are seen. A silent man is often contemptible if his tongue alone ennobles him; but a man whose spirit is tranquil always remains honored if an exceedingly serene appearance also commends him.

By this appointment, finally, we testify that we possess an abundance of prudent men, since such a man is chosen as can be praised from either side. Yet it would be foolish to praise the quaestor’s gifts of eloquence, since he has been admitted especially for this purpose: to commend the reputation of the age by the quality of his utterances. To some judges of the provinces is entrusted the collection of revenues; to others is delegated the custody of the private treasury. To him, however, are entrusted the distinctions of courtly reputation, so that through him a reputation celebrated throughout the world may be praised.

We have judged this so important, enrolled fathers, that you may believe we seek men such as it is expedient to find both for our praise and for your security. Learned men, recognize the good wish of your prince; you who are proved to possess knowledge of letters, put your confidence in his benefactions. It is the mark of the most sluggish to lie idle when he knows that he has invited the masters of affairs to advancement.

Therefore, enrolled fathers, let the favor of your kindness receive the illustrious Ambrosius, adorned with the summit of the quaestorship. There ought to be no doubt about a man whom your order already deserved to approve in his very first dignity.

## LETTER XV. KING ATHALARIC TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

He writes that it was most gratifying to him that they elected as bishop the man whom Theodoric had designated.

We profess that it is most gratifying to our mind that you followed the judgment of our lord grandfather, of glorious memory, in the election of a bishop. For it was proper to obey the decision of a good prince, who, after wise deliberation, although belonging to another religion, appeared to have chosen such a bishop as ought rightly to displease no one. Thus you may recognize that this was his particular wish: that religion might flourish through good priests in all the churches.

You have therefore received a man both commendably formed by divine grace and praised by royal examination. Let no one still be held by the former contention. The defeated man has no cause for shame when his wish happens to be surpassed by the prince. Indeed, he makes the choice his own who has loved the successful candidate in sincerity. For what cause for grief is there when he finds in this man also what he had desired another to possess?

These are civic contests [Ed.: *crinea*, “hair-like”]: a struggle without iron, a quarrel without hatred. The matter is conducted with shouting, not with pain. Even if one person has been removed, the faithful lose nothing when the desired priesthood is secured.

Therefore, as your legate, the illustrious Publianus, returns, we thought it reasonable to send greetings to your assembly. We enjoy great pleasure whenever we exchange words with our nobles. Nor do we doubt that this will also be most pleasing to you, if you recognize that what you did at his command is also agreeable to us.

## LETTER XVI. KING ATHALARIC TO OPILIO, COUNT OF THE SACRED LARGESSES

He extols him and his brother with the highest praise and grants him the office of count of the sacred largesses.

Men who approach courtly dignities are usually weighed through prolonged examination, lest the imperial judgment appear to approve anything doubtful, since it is the glory of a kingdom to discover exceptional judges. But your family’s most fortunate advancement is so constant, and its prudence has been displayed in so many persons, that even if someone were to choose you suddenly, he would appear to have done nothing uncertain.

A fortunate lineage preserves the likeness of its members, since a man is ashamed to do wrong when he cannot find similar examples in his own family. Hence it is more readily recognized that one has chosen a nobleman than that one has made a man fortunate: the former, once admonished, preserves himself through the deeds of his ancestors; the latter has no example except what he himself has done.

Therefore we confidently entrust to you what we rejoice has so often been entrusted to your family. Your father held these fasces, and your brother likewise shone with the same distinction. Dignity itself, as it were, established a household shrine in your home, and public honor became a domestic possession.

For you learned the order of military service under your brother’s praise. Joined to him by mutual affection, you fulfilled the role of a partner through your labors and of a brother through your participation in his counsels, judging that what your brother had received belonged rather to you. He leaned upon you as upon a staff, more fortunate because, relying on your resourcefulness, he neglected certain matters through confidence in you: through you he saw everything accomplished.

How sweet was the service of brothers, and how ancient the harmony of the present age! Judgment is rightly entrusted to such dispositions, when they are naturally recognized as preserving good character.

If pleasant retreats and provincial leisure had perhaps been your preference, crowds of litigants and the anxious prayers of the injured nevertheless ran to you. Among them you assumed the office of a good judge; and, under a kind of pressing foreknowledge of what was to come, you fulfilled through the assumption of honors what you could receive from us.

We also remember with what devotion you served us at the beginning of our reign, when the service of loyal men was especially necessary. After the passing [Juret.: that is, “death”] of our lord grandfather, of divine memory, when the anxious hopes of the peoples trembled and the hearts of our subjects were troubled by uncertainty about the heir to so great a kingdom, you brought the Ligurians the fortunate news of our accession. Strengthened by your wise address, they changed into rejoicing the grief that they had conceived at his death through the rise of our rule. The change of king passed without any disturbance, and your concern ensured that no one offended us.

And so, having been proved by such services, in the sixth indiction (A.D. 528), with the favor of God, we grant you the office of count of the sacred largesses. You shall enjoy all the privileges and emoluments known to have belonged to your predecessors. For those who stand firm through the strength of their conduct must not be shaken by any contrivance of accusation.

There was a time when even judges were harassed by informers. Lay aside fear now, since you have no fault. Enjoy the fruits of your dignities; for what longstanding custom under our lord grandfather, through our predecessors and ancestors, gave you, our indulgence also preserves.

We confer upon you the honor of your brother, but imitate his faithful service. If you follow him, you surpass many in praise: a man of the greatest authority and proven steadfastness [Ac.: “conscience”], who obeyed such a prince without fault and exercised justice to universal praise. It is easy to judge what he accomplished, since under an ungrateful successor the palace office could not remain silent about his praises. It is therefore not difficult to follow your brother in character, since those born from one seed often agree in the fruit of their way of life.

## LETTER XVII. KING ATHALARIC TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

He greatly praises Opilio, his father, and his brother, and asks them to favor his advancement to the office of count of the sacred largesses.

[Col. 0750A]

There is such an abundance of merits in the candidate, enrolled fathers, that we fear he may be thought to have been chosen too late rather than approved by judgment. When our grandfather, of divine memory, sought out the best men, more favorable fortune preserved him for us unrewarded. He obeyed him, served him with great devotion, and is known to have been left by the most generous master without any recompense of his benefactions. I believe the reward of his merit was postponed so that the occasion for granting it might become more fitting for us [Edd., Ac.: “more evident”].

For our piety ought to accord with the law of nature. It is fitting that the heir should discharge what is known to have been bestowed by the founder. Why should our munificence delay him, when the custom of his nobility urged him toward advancement?

His father was distinguished in military service and conspicuous for the highest nobility of character. Nor did raging wars reject him, though peaceful leisure praised him: strong in body, steadfast in friendship, he displayed the antiquity of former times, having cast aside the vices of the age [MS Aud.: *abjectis saeculis Odoacris*, “having cast aside Odoacer’s ages”], and was enriched by distinguished honors. In those times he was held to be exceptional, when the prince was not elevated.

But why should we retrace the ancient nobility of his parents, when the nearby light of his brother shines forth? It can be praised that he was connected not merely by kinship but even by friendship with this man. He so joined and bound himself to his brother’s virtues that it is uncertain which of the two is more praised through the other.

The brother excelled in keeping faith with friends; this man owes great steadfastness to his promises. The former was free from avarice, and the latter too is proved to be alien to greed. Hence they know how to keep faith with kings, because they do not know how to practice treachery even among their equals. Character is more easily tested where nature reveals itself under freedom. How, then, could they fail to serve their masters with purity, when they do not know how to deceive their colleagues?

Chosen for these praises by marriage, he is said to have been joined to Basiliana’s family—something that often happens when men of merit can be joined to noble families. If you wish, inspect also his private life, since such signs have often revealed industrious men to our ancestors. He arranged his private affairs with such moderation that he was neither mean through excessive thrift nor ruined through extravagant spending. He bound foreigners to himself through his hospitality and Romans through his judgments; and where ingratitude usually comes to dignities, he cultivated friendship for himself through adjudication.

See what noble nature can accomplish. Born from judges, he acted as an arbitrator; and this cannot occur in any way except through uprightness of character. The necessity of power can often compel obedience to office; only the integrity of judgments makes a man obey a private judge. Hence a voluntary judge seems to us to possess greater praise, since no one is chosen for a hearing unless he is judged just in character.

Therefore, enrolled fathers, favor your foster sons, and favor our judgments. For the second time there comes to your senate a man born from a senator and approved as honored by courtly dignities.

## LETTER XVIII. KING ATHALARIC TO FELIX, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND QUAESTOR

He celebrates him with the highest praises and grants him the quaestorship.

[Col. 0751A]

It is acknowledged to be the profession of justice to appoint judges skilled in the laws, since a man who knows equity can scarcely neglect it, and one whom learning has purified is not easily stained by the fault of error. The imperial eye formerly saw you laboring in forensic affairs; nor could it fail to observe with what fidelity you carried through the cases you had undertaken and with what clarity you argued them to conclusion.

Your eloquence and your conscience advanced together on an equal course. No client [Note: [Col. 0751] Understand “client” in the sense of one whose case has been undertaken. Juret. says that he observed this usage in his notes on Symmachus, Book V, letter 39.] whom you had undertaken had anything further to desire; no judge found anything in you that could be corrected. To this was added the charm of your face and the purity of your spirit. Your appearance alone showed you to be young, yet from your youthful mouth venerable words flowed. The bloom of age contended with the maturity of mind; but the latter prevailed, the quality that leads us to the heights of virtue and glory.

Therefore we adapt our gifts to your name and merits, so that you may receive the royal secrets in trust and, as an eloquent man, find a dignity grounded in learning. Now judge gloriously the cases that you used to argue laudably; let your own well-practiced learning sit beside you. The condition of affairs is now fortunate and secure, when the man gives judgment who cannot be ignorant of what he chooses.

It is not fitting for a judge to be the servant of another’s will, obeying another more than so many soldiers obey him. Even if such a thing might somehow be tolerated in others, it is exceedingly shameful in a quaestor, who is chosen for the prince’s council yet expects support from another.

And so, as God grants our auspices, in the sixth indiction (A.D. 528) we confer upon you the dignity of the quaestorship. But your honor is a reproach to the unskilled. For just as the conscience of one promoted by merit is joyful, so the man who recognizes himself unequal to the offices he has obtained lies under accusation.

You have ancient men whom it is fitting for you to imitate. Outstrip in renown those whom you follow in dignity. If private life exercised you in virtues, how much more clearly will advancement display them? You have taken your name from your merits; preserve it, so that you may always rejoice in the truth of your name. Since every name appears to have been imposed to declare realities, it is exceedingly absurd to bear another man’s name and to be called something that cannot be found in one’s character.

But let these words of a good conscience suffice, for a man who needs many admonitions is thought doubtful.

## LETTER XIX. KING ATHALARIC TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

He adorns Felix and his family with many praises and writes that he has chosen him as quaestor.

[Col. 0751D]

Although your assembly is always illuminated by its native [Ac. and Forn.: “double”] splendor, it becomes brighter whenever it is increased by the radiance of dignities. Even the sky shines more brilliantly with its abundant stars and presents to those who gaze upon it a wondrous beauty through its numerous splendor. For it is implanted in nature that an abundance of good things gives greater delight.

Meadows, finally, are painted with countless flowers, and the dense crop of a rich field is praised. Antiquity has made you be regarded as noble; we want the senate also to be praised for its numbers. Hence we wish to add to your ranks the man whom we have found preeminent everywhere. Although the senate is a nursery among you, nevertheless one who is attached to your assembly is also born from our indulgence. All courtly dignities produce foster sons for us; but the quaestorship is truly the mother of a senator, since it proceeds from prudence. For what is more worthy than that a man who has adhered to the prince’s council should become a member of the senate?

But since a general conclusion does not suffice for a prudent man, let us touch upon his particular and distinctive qualities. Know, enrolled fathers, that our quaestor first pleased through eloquence already practiced and then achieved such frequent victories in his advocacy [Ac., Niv.: “consistently”] [Col. 0752B] that the triumphant choice rightly selected him for itself, so that, inaugurated by fortunate palms, he might give you the omens of laurels.

Brought to the forensic school in his earliest youth, he always devoted himself to integrity of mind; and, most noble in modesty, he maintained bodily chastity through the greatest discipline. A fluent orator and most serious advocate, he supported the cases he undertook with his praises, since a case could not be thought unworthy when such a man appeared to stand beside it.

Would it not be a public loss to pass over this man? For what ought to be more welcome either to us or to you than that he should be joined to your side, since he deserved approval among the laws? He can love the laws through which he became distinguished by learning; for while each man seeks his own glory, the mind cannot forget from what side it was associated with us.

Perhaps you think, illustrious men, that a new and newly acquired prudence has appeared in this man. His origin claimed hereditary letters for itself: his father shone so brightly in the forum at Milan that he continued to spring forth with everlasting fruit from Cicero’s meadow. Therefore, although it is difficult even among ordinary men to be pleasing, he frequently deserved to find the praise of advocacy among the foremost men of eloquence.

He stood against the great Olybrius; he matched the abundance of the eloquent Eugenetis; and he proved equal to those whom Rome recognized as singular. For what is nobler than to have had so many leaders of letters as ancestors? If long-established wealth transmitted through a family makes men noble, much more distinguished is the man whose origin is found rich in the treasures of prudence.

Therefore, enrolled fathers, favor our judgment and the candidate on account of his merits; when you extend the hand of clemency to a colleague, you are lifting yourselves up instead.

## LETTER XX. KING ATHALARIC TO ALBIENUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He writes that he removed the praetorian prefect from office because of his misconduct and appointed Albienus in his place, praising him highly.

An assertion of merit is the fact that a man could be chosen after the accused judge’s misconduct: the excesses of predecessors are corrected only when an excellent successor is found. Medicine often follows contrary conditions. When vital heat has been applied, the deadly cold withdraws. The clouds themselves are cleared by the breath of the winds, and the north wind restores the calm face of the sky that the southern breeze had disturbed.

So we removed your predecessor out of concern for the common good, that you might arrive as a most salutary successor. Imitate what is contrary to his conduct, and you will accomplish what deserves praise. He was hateful through accusations; strive to be welcomed through justice. He was rapacious; be self-controlled. The brief definition of every good is to avoid what he did, since those things are truly beyond praise which he approved by his own judgment.

Consider, finally, the public hatred directed against him, and strive for the love of all. Let your character earn as much gratitude as his conduct has drawn accusations of harshness. Take courage from the disgrace of your predecessor, since after a man whose wickedness was openly declared, even abstaining from wrongdoing is praiseworthy.

For how fine it will be if you grant the provinces benefits that they have not previously possessed! An unfamiliar good is loved more, and preceding sadness adds sweetness to the joy that follows.

And therefore, in the sixth indiction (A.D. 528), with God’s help, we confer upon you the fasces of the prefecture. The more terrifying it has been through injury until now, the more it ought now to possess the benefits of gentleness, since those who have been wounded must be restored by your care. Let no one be burdened either by your hands or by those of others. For beyond every form of impiety is harming those who have been injured and whom one is believed to be healing [Gr. and Cuj.: *necare*, “killing”].

Let that prefecture of the praetorium, praised throughout the world, return to its ancient name. If we seek its origin, it began with Joseph, “from benefactions.” Not without reason is he praised by our laws as the father of the provinces and also the father of the empire, since they wished him to act so justly and prudently that they imposed upon him not the title of a harsh judge but the name of piety.

Through you, let our treasury grow by just and lawful economies. We reject profits that profane the safeguards of the laws; we want those revenues that the scale of justice supports. We do not permit wickedness to enter our halls, since we cannot admit privately (*privatim introducere*, MS and Gr.) what we condemn publicly.

Hear, judges, what we love; do not suspect anything else to the harm of the public. For whom do you think you will please through unjust appointments, when you know that we love only those things that can accord with the admonitions of justice? After this, if you offend, you sin against your own character.

Perhaps such things were done by those who attained dignities unknown to their parents. You, after your father’s praiseworthy prefecture, add something that may be praised as better; for the man who follows ought always to be more diligent, since we rightly wish both to imitate and to surpass the good qualities of our parents.

Your praises are also increased by the fact that you are proved to be imbued with the sayings of the wise. It is serious for a wise man to offend where he has found another has stumbled. Someone who did not know the laws might perhaps pass justice by; from you everything lawful is demanded, since your origin is not known to have been unlearned. The books of the ancients and the actions of your parents are your equals.

Make good your reputation; make good our judgment, so that you may not prove unequal to the merits whose dignities you have equaled through our benefactions.

## LETTER XXI. KING ATHALARIC TO CYPRIANUS, PATRICIAN

He praises him for outstanding deeds of military valor and for his well-trained sons, whom he has presented to the king. He then confers upon him the dignity of the patriciate.

Although you have often been praised through your own honors and through the dignity of your brother, nevertheless, since the nature of good men is not exhausted when it is recounted, we return, as it were, to a judgment about which many praises have already sounded.

Whatever ought to be judged concerning loyal and deserving men has been testified about you. Yet the man who has filled himself with upright conduct produces new praises whenever he wishes. Glory is like the perennial stream of a spring, a praiseworthy source [Note: [Col. 0753D] Basil, *On Almsgiving*: “As wells, the more often they are drawn from, have waters that flow more purely,” *ta phreata pollakis exantloumena, eurroōtera esti*—“wells, when repeatedly drawn from, flow more freely.” FORN.]: just as the spring is not exhausted by flowing, so glory is not dried up by celebrated speech. Even if past deeds are left unmentioned, you are proved to offer new material for praise, since you continually grow both in age and in merits. The course of years brings you an increase of praise. You grow old in body, but grow young in renown. It is deservedly wished that your life may be prolonged, since your fame is always found to grow stronger.

Under our lord grandfather, of divine memory, you always kept praiseworthy watch in both spheres. The still-pagan Danube saw you as a warrior; the Bulgarian host did not terrify you, although it was also preparing to resist our forces through the presumption of battle. It was distinctive of you both to attack barbarians who resisted and to pursue those who had been turned to flight in terror. Thus you aided the Goths’ victory not so much by numbers as by toil.

Afterward, in a service no less demanding than those battles themselves, you performed the office of referendary through laborious contests. Under that man, a man of every virtue, there were both military and peaceful services. For who would not wage war if he could provide him with an appropriate reply? He always demanded such firmness of spirit and such constancy of speech in asserting the truth that he rightly said he had conquered as an enemy the man who, in his presence, had been able to avoid error.

Hence prudent men rendered him their service, since caution always strengthens understanding; and when a man fears falling into fault, he strives to join himself to the wise.

He also conferred upon you the dignity of the sacred largesses—the most fitting [Ac.: “most obvious”] office for your labors—which you carried out with such pure and moderate judgment that you made yourself deserving of greater things, although you had accepted it as a great reward.

Through these duties your flowering youth was exercised, but our times preserved you in mature age. You possess great strength of counsel, yet you are not recognized as broken by age. [Note: [Col. 0753D] Jerome, *On Priests*, chapter following: “For it is not age in a man but virtue that must be considered.” Menander: “It is not white hair that makes one think wisely; rather, the character of some is old by nature” (*οὐχ αἱ τρίχες ποιοῦσιν αἱ λευκαὶ φρονεῖν, ἀλλ᾽ ὁ τρόπος ἐνίων ἐστὶ τῇ φύσει γέρων*). In the manner of this thought, Cicero, in *Cato the Elder*: “Neither white hair,” he says, “nor wrinkles suddenly confer authority; rather, a life rightly lived provides the final fruits of authority.” FORN.]

Thus you have acquired the good things of old age without undergoing its disadvantages. These are the qualities we judge ought to be increased [Ac.: “cultivated”] in you: just as you are endowed with a good conscience, so you may also be rendered venerable through honor.

The heavenly judgments of your life are also in harmony with our benefactions, since, having become the father of such sons, you appear to be a patrician by nature itself. It is not absurd to recount their flourishing virtues, since the more fortunate praise of those who raise children is to be praised for the integrity of their sons.

First—and this provides no small beginning of praise—their childhood is known to the palace. Thus your offspring, proving themselves in the manner of eagles, encountered royal eyes almost from their cradles. They also shine with the favor of their Gothic [or: “gentile”] heritage and do not cease to be trained in the strong disciplines of arms.

The boys of Roman stock speak our language, clearly indicating that they offer us future loyalty, since they already seem to have sought to adopt our speech. We have grounds for returning a reward to you, fortunate father, since you have offered us the hearts of your sons.

Therefore, since you have been approved through many labors and through great faith and steadfastness, with God’s favor we confer upon you the dignity of the patriciate: a lofty honor, certainly, but one proved equal to your merits. Enjoy your most highly approved institutions, so that, having doubled your own good qualities, you may meanwhile be increased by our benefactions.

## LETTER XXII. KING ATHALARIC TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

After enumerating the praises of Cyprianus and his sons, he writes that he has raised him to the honor of the patriciate and urges them to favor his election.

[Col. 0755C]

If a man is worthy of your favor who was able even once to obtain a royal judgment, what, enrolled fathers, will the illustrious Cyprianus deserve, who ought to become more welcome to you as often as he receives dignities from us?

Those who compete in the stadium are glorified by a more numerous crown; Olympic chariots (*currus*; Ac.: *cursus*, “races”) are ennobled by frequent palms. So even in lesser matters the man becomes more glorious to whom rewards are repeatedly returned.

There may be hesitation over a first advancement, since many deceive the prince’s mind and it is easy to mislead one whose constant wish has been to grant favors. But he displayed such steadfastness of mind and possessed such a purpose of goodness that he continually called forth the royal gift for himself.

This is certain glory, this is an indisputable judgment: that he has frequently been found worthy of the honor by which men are known to be adorned. It is fitting that such men should also enter our senate, men who do not exhaust their merit in their first honors but, after receiving great things, earn still greater ones.

Such men also adorn our judgments, since the man who is approved more than once is believed to have been chosen well in the first place. Good nature, joined to perseverance, is valued, since beginning good works is less praiseworthy than preserving one’s good purpose.

In former times, enrolled fathers, you had similar men in the Decii; antiquity likewise praises the Corvini as similar men. Nor has this man, of whom we are speaking, reconciled only our judgment to himself (*conciliavit*; Juret. V. C.: *reconciliavit*). To be advanced by one prince may perhaps seem a favor; but to have deserved advancement under another also proves that the judgment of both was unimpaired.

Everyone, therefore, follows the man who decides something according to truth. He deserved to be the author of his own advancement, so that he might most worthily find us the authors of his increase. The former laid the foundations of his goodness; we built the summit of his dignities.

And therefore, enrolled fathers, we have also added the office of the patriciate to the illustrious Cyprianus, distinguished by so many labors and praises, lest he should be greater in merits than in our honors. Now favor your colleague, whom you often honored as an outsider. He returns to you without anxiety, having already placed his honors in the hall of liberty.

He also possesses a reason to be more welcome to us, since he has produced for your senate such foster sons—sons who, although their father was eager for them, nevertheless surpassed his own hopes, not timid in childhood and not, as was permitted, ignorant of how to answer. They speak several languages excellently and mingle in fellowship with mature men. Thus, being known to us, they passed beyond adolescence at its very beginning.

May the divine majesty grant that, just as we have exalted through their father the name of munificence, so we may also increase in them the titles of our graciousness.

## LETTER XXIII. KING ATHALARIC TO BERGANTINUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND COUNT OF THE PATRIMONY

He orders him to hand over without delay to the agents of Theodahad certain estates that had come from the property of his mother, and praises Theodahad exceptionally.

[Col. 0756C]

Although it is fitting for a king’s munificence to shine daily like the sun and continually to do something through which the prince’s generosity may be made apparent, the debt owed by conscience is nevertheless discharged whenever it is shown equitably toward relatives. Princes profit from their gifts; and we truly place in our treasuries whatever we apply to the advantages of our reputation.

Let us not refuse our kinsman what we habitually preserve for our subjects, since one joined to us by blood deserves more; and a man who serves under a gracious judge cannot be defrauded of his own desire.

And therefore we order your illustrious greatness to restore to the illustrious and most distinguished Theodahad the estates listed below, amounting to so many solidi, from the patrimony formerly belonging to his magnificent mother, [Col. 0756D] so that they may be fully vindicated to his ownership; and in the portion we command, we grant him the entire right of succession.

We presume upon his faith and sincerity, so that at a later time he may deserve to receive the remaining matrimonial property [Others: “patrimonial property”] of the aforesaid woman, together with every amount added to it. [Note: [Col. 0755D] Fr. Conn(an)us, Book VIII, chapter 3, notes that this term sometimes signifies property that comes to children from their mother; others argue the same from Seneca, Valerius Maximus, and Suetonius. Plutarch, however, argues against this with no slight force in *Marriage Precepts* (*ἐν παραγγέλμασι γαμικοῖς*), where the reading “patrimony,” supported by the authority of two manuscript codices, favors the interpretation of this passage. FORN.] For what could we deny to such a man, who could obtain even better things through his services, even if he were not proved to be our kinsman?

Consider what such a man deserves from us: a man whom no elation over his nobility inflates, humble in modesty, always even in prudence. We count him toward our glory because we acknowledge him as our kinsman.

Therefore apply yourselves diligently [Juret.: “eagerly”] to this most equitable command, and through the beloved clerks of your office [Gr.: *directis*, “directed”] hand over without delay the designated estates to his representatives [Gr.: *actoribus*, “agents”], so that, joined to us by the greatest affection, he may be made still more welcome through the favor of the present gift.

## LETTER XXIV. KING ATHALARIC TO THE CLERGY OF THE ROMAN CHURCH

He refers those who have brought a suit against a Roman cleric to the pope’s judgment. He wishes anyone who has disregarded the authority of the holy see both to lose his case and to be punished by a fine of ten pounds of gold, to be distributed to the poor.

The greater the benefits we have received than other mortals, the more we owe to the Divinity. For what comparable return could one who possesses imperial power make to God? Yet although nothing adequate can be offered in compensation for so great a gift, gratitude is nevertheless rendered to Him when He is honored in those who serve Him.

And so, in a lamentable petition, you complain that this had long been established by custom: if anyone thought that a servant of the Most Holy Roman Church should be brought to court in some action, he would come before the bishop of the aforesaid city to state his case, so that your clergy, profaned by forensic disputes, might not be occupied with secular affairs instead. You further add that your deacon was compelled, to the disgrace of religion, with such harshness of enforcement that the saio [a royal official] considered him destined to be handed over to his own custody. You likewise assert that a presbyter of the Roman Church was criminally prosecuted for trivial causes.

We confess that this displeased us, out of the innate reverence that we owe to our Creator, since those who had formerly deserved to serve in sacred ministries were subjected irreverently to wicked injuries under color of legal summons. But the stealthy wrongdoing of others offered us an occasion for the fullest praise, since it provided an opportunity to do what might commend us to heavenly aid.

Therefore, considering the honor of the Apostolic See and consulting the wishes of those who petition, by the authority of this present decree we determine, in an orderly and moderate manner, that if anyone should think that a person belonging to the Roman clergy ought to be brought to court in any plausible case, he must first come to the judgment of the most blessed pope, where he is to be heard. The pope shall either himself examine the matter between the parties according to the custom of his holiness, or delegate the case to be concluded in the interest of equity. If—as it is impious to believe—the petitioner’s legitimate request should have been frustrated, then he may proceed to the secular courts, once he has proved that his petitions were despised by the bishop of the aforesaid see.

But if any litigant should prove so shameless, and should be condemned by everyone’s judgment as sacrilegious in mind, that he scorns to show reverence to so great a see and thinks that something may be gained from our pronouncements, then, before any summons has taken effect, he shall be struck with the loss of ten pounds of gold. This sum shall immediately be collected by the officers of the imperial treasury and distributed to the poor through the hands of the aforesaid bishop. Moreover, deprived of what he sought to obtain, he shall also be punished by the loss of his case. For he deserves to be struck by a double penalty who has violated both divine reverence and our commands.

Meanwhile, you, whom our judgments venerate, live according to ecclesiastical institutions. It is a great crime to commit an offense when your mode of life ought not even to be secular. Your profession is a heavenly life. Do not descend to the lowly desires and errors of mortals. Let worldly people be restrained by human law; obey sacred customs.

## EPISTLE XXV. ATHALARICUS, KING, TO JOHN, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND REFERENDARY

He confirms the generosity of Tulum, by which he had granted John a house situated in the Castrum Lucullanum.

It is very fitting to preserve the property of others for those to whom we ought to bestow gifts of our own. For how could you doubt that generosity, when you understand that you are receiving from us what you received from our predecessors? We therefore acknowledge that the gift belongs indeed to another, but that the decision is ours, and that the present ruler’s intention has anticipated that earlier and very swift liberality.

Accordingly, it is established that our grandfather, of divine memory, moved by your diligent services, wished to bestow the house situated in the Castrum Lucullanum. Following his arrangement, the patrician Tulum (see above, Epistles 9 and 10), after it had been granted to him by our generosity, transferred the aforesaid house by a lawful act into your ownership.

Therefore, by our present authority, we confirm both the desire of the intention already begun and the effect of Tulum’s fullest donation, so that the aforementioned house of the patrician Agnellus, remembered by our father [or: paternal] memory, situated in the Castrum Lucullanum, together with everything belonging to it, may remain in your possession and that of your heirs. Whatever you may thereafter wish to do with it, you shall have free authority to do. We remove any disturbance henceforth, whether under a private title or a public one; and if anything should perhaps be ambiguous through any circumstance or investigation, it is established that it has been rejected by the judgment of this authority of ours.

Enjoy, with God’s help, the property secured also by our authority. Others granted you lawful rights; we confer the peaceable possession and security firmly assured for all ages. But lest anyone should perhaps arise as an envious violator of our most excellent intention, we order that anyone who at any time attempts to raise any dispute concerning this matter, whether in the name of the treasury or of a private person, shall give you—or whoever you wish it to belong to—the house designated above, as a penalty, together with one hundred pounds of gold, and shall depart frustrated by his attempts and disgraced. Such is the fruit he deserves to find from his own will who appears to have sought anything contrary to our judgment.

## EPISTLE XXVI. ATHALARICUS, KING, TO ALL THE REATINI AND NURSINI

He appoints Quidilan over them and orders them to obey him.

Our glorious lord grandfather, learning of your wishes, was indeed preparing to make Quidilan, son of Sibia, your prior [governor] [Note: Cuspinianus, in *Austrian History*: “The first of the Roman Empire.” And Abdias of Babylon, Book I, on Zacchaeus. JUR.]. But because, when mortal fate intervened, he was unable to complete what he had planned, it is necessary for us to fulfill his wishes, lest so great a man should be judged to have thought well of something in vain.

Therefore, by this present authority we order that you are to have him happily as your prior, and that you are to obey in everything whatever he orders for the preservation of discipline, in which our greatest advantage is contained. For you have been trained in the customs of our lord grandfather in such a way that you willingly hear both laws and judges.

This is what accompanies our imperial power and magnifies our reputation among the nations: that you conduct yourselves in ways that are acceptable to us and most pleasing to the Divinity. Our enemies are defeated more effectively by good conduct, because those whom heaven protects cannot have happy adversaries. You fight effectively abroad while striving to foster justice in your own settlements. These two things are joined together in mutual embrace: whoever has honored equity will possess the fruit of victory.

For what necessity compels you to injustice, when both your own allotments support you and our gifts, with the Lord’s help, enrich you? And if anyone has something to seek, let him hope [JUR.: Supply “rather”] for it from the generosity of the ruler than from a presumption of valor. For it benefits you that the Romans are at peace: while they enrich our treasuries, they multiply your gifts.

## EPISTLE XXVII. ATHALARICUS, KING, TO DUMERIT, SAIO, AND FLORENTIANUS, DEVOTED COMES

He orders them to travel through the territory of Faventia and, if they find anyone who has harassed Gothic or Roman inhabitants, to impose both a fine and a penalty after assessing the damage.

Public severity, just as it refrains from the innocent, must necessarily apply the force of its strictness to criminals, because different merits of different persons do not always deserve the same judgment. Diseases themselves are healed by herbs with different juices: food restores health to some, iron to others, and the physician’s prescription deserves to vary according to the nature of the illness.

Therefore, let your devotion travel without delay through the territory of Faventia. If it finds any Goths or Romans involved in plundering landholders, let them be afflicted both with compensation for the damages and with penalties, according to the assessment of their deed. For those must be punished more severely who have believed that neither just admonitions nor the judgments of the ruler need be obeyed, since it is a greater ambition to desire to serve us as lords, so that, commended by good beginnings, they may enjoy the rest of their lives through the gift of security.

## EPISTLE XXVIII. ATHALARICUS, KING, TO CUNIGASTUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

He decrees that Tancan, who had taken from Constantius and Venerius a small estate called Fabricula and had reduced them to slavery, must appear before his judgment, so that he may receive a sentence consistent with the law.

The lamentable complaint of Constantius and Venerius moved our serenity. They complain that Tancan took from them their legally owned small estate, called Fabricula, together with its livestock and property. They add that, so that they might not press their claims for the recovery of their property, a condition of the most abject slavery was imposed upon them.

Therefore, let Your Greatness, obeying the present decrees, order the aforesaid man to appear before your judgment. When the entire truth between the parties has been examined, pronounce a sentence consistent with the law and consonant with your customs. For just as it is grievous for landholders to surrender their lawful property, so it is hostile to our age to press free necks beneath the yoke of slavery.

If they have a rightful claim, let what was seized first be restored [Note: This is a traditional legal maxim: one forcibly expelled from possession of his property, or despoiled, ought above all to be restored, *Codex* 8.4.1, *If by Force or Otherwise*; *Digest* 48.6.7, *If Anyone Against Himself*, under the Julian Law on Public Violence; chapter 7, *Conquerente*, on restoration of the despoiled. FORN.]. Nevertheless, let the lawful person not withdraw from the proceedings. Let violent presumption cease, so that the case may be examined at the judge’s discretion; and let him either retain the slaves proved against him, together with the property belonging to them, or release those proved free, unharmed and intact. For it is enough that we remit the penalty to the one who presumed to commit the injury.

## EPISTLE XXIX. ATHALARICUS, KING, TO THE HONORABLE LANDHOLDERS AND CURIALES OF THE CITY OF PARMA

He orders them to open the mouths of the city sewers and directs that Genesius press the work forward.

It is fitting that you undertake willingly what you know has been ordered for the benefit of your city. For what ought to have been undertaken at your own expense is now, as you see, being offered to you at little cost.

Your city has been suffering from prolonged dryness, but, with God’s help, our lord grandfather watered it with a most healthful stream. Now, through your diligence, let the mouths of the sewers be opened, lest the returning water, obstructed by the accumulation of filth, be driven against your buildings and be compelled to inflict upon you what it ought to have washed away.

Although civic love ought to urge you to this work, we order the distinguished man Genesius to supervise it, so that you may encourage us toward better things if you carry out what we have ordered with gratitude.

## EPISTLE XXX. ATHALARICUS, KING, TO GENESIUS, DISTINGUISHED MAN

He orders him to compel the citizens of Parma to cleanse the ancient channels so carefully that nothing obstructs the flowing water.

Out of love for your city, our lord grandfather constructed, with royal generosity, the structure of an ancient work [JUR.: Understand “aqueduct”]. But it is of no use to introduce abundant water into cities unless provision is now made for the proper arrangement of the sewers—just as the health of the human body is preserved when what someone takes in through the mouth is discharged through another part of the body.

Therefore, let Your Sublimity make the citizens of Parma apply themselves diligently to this work, so that they carefully cleanse the ancient channels, whether underground or joined to the edges of the streets [another reading: “repair them”]. Thus, when the desired liquid has solemnly flowed in to you, it will not be delayed by any obstruction of added manure [manuscript and some editions: “discarded matter”]. For water has no grace unless it continually flows in and is always seen to depart.

How beautiful is that water which, gracefully exercised in streams, laughs—and how deformed is it in stagnant pools! A marsh is neither pleasing to look upon nor useful to beasts of burden. Water is a most beautiful element, but only when it is preserved in its natural purity. Without it, fields grow barren and cities are exhausted by gasping thirst [Juret reads: “gasp”], so that ancient wisdom rightly punished by withholding water those whom it judged should be excluded from civic society [Note: Lucian, *Alexander*, or *The False Prophet*, on the oracles of the impostor: “No one any longer received such a man under a roof, nor did anyone share fire or water with him; rather, he had to be driven from land to land as an impious man and a denier of the gods.” That is: “No one received such a man under a roof, nor shared fire or water with him; instead, he had to be driven from one land to another, as an impious man and contemptuous of the gods.” [Col. 0762D] Victor of Utica, recounting the savage edicts against Christians in Book III of *The Vandal Persecution*, adds: “That no one should receive any of them as a guest or provide them with food.” FORN.].

Therefore, everyone ought to devote himself to so useful a matter, for he is not a true citizen whose heart is not held by the welfare of his city.

## EPISTLE XXXI. ATHALARICUS, KING, TO SEVERUS, DISTINGUISHED MAN

He describes the province of Bruttium and orders both provincials and curiales, after giving sureties and accepting a penalty, to promise that they will remain for the greater part of the year in whichever cities they prefer to inhabit.

[Col. 0761B] Since we believe that, by commendably adhering to the counsels of the prefects, you have learned everything relevant to arranging the condition of the state, you have especially learned, as an educated man, that the face of cities is beautiful when they are known to possess an assembly of peoples. In this way, the adornment of freedom shines in them, and the necessary effect of our arrangements is fulfilled.

Wild animals are permitted to seek fields and forests; human beings, however, ought to cherish their ancestral hearths above all things. Birds themselves fly in flocks and become tame through their harmless disposition. Melodious thrushes love the dense company of their own kind. Chattering starlings follow their companions in unceasing formations. Murmuring doves love their own cohorts; and everything belonging to simple life does not reject the grace of union.

By contrast, spirited hawks, hunting eagles, and birds that look more sharply than all others desire solitary flights, because predatory ambushes do not seek harmless gatherings. Those who do not wish to find prey with another seek to accomplish something alone.

Such is often the detestable will of mortals: it is shown to flee the sight of human beings, and nothing truthful can be believed about one whose life cannot find a witness.

Let the landholders and curiales of Bruttium return to their cities. Farmers are those who continually cultivate the fields. Let those who have been given honors and entrusted with public duties on the basis of a worthy evaluation allow themselves to be separated from rusticity, especially in a region where unworked delights [manuscript: “riches”] abound.

There Ceres luxuriates in great fertility; Pallas too rejoices in no small abundance [Juret.: Supply “of the olive tree”]. Level places laugh with fertile pastures, elevated ones with vineyards. The province abounds in herds of animals of many kinds, but it especially boasts of its horse herds—rightly so, since in the burning season the springtime character of its forests is such that animals are not wearied by the stings of flies and are filled with the abundance of ever-green grasses.

You may see the purest streams running over the mountain peaks; and, as though they flowed from an elevated source, they descend along the heights of the Alps. In addition, on either side it possesses abundant commerce through the frequent traffic of the sea, so that it overflows richly with its own produce and is filled with foreign provisions through the nearness of its shores [Note: Read Pliny, Book I, Letter 3, and Sidonius Apollinaris, Book VIII, Letter 8. JURET.].

There peasants live on the banquets of townsmen, and ordinary people abound in the plenty of the powerful, so that no one there is regarded as excluded from prosperity, however modest his fortune may be.

Do they therefore refuse to inhabit this province’s cities, although they admit that they love it entirely in their fields? What good is it for so many men, refined by learning, to remain hidden? Boys seek the company of liberal studies; and as soon as they become worthy of the forum, they immediately begin to be unknown through their rural dwelling. They advance in order to unlearn; they are educated in order to neglect; and when they love the fields, they do not know how to love themselves.

Let the educated man seek where he may become renowned; let the prudent person not reject the company of people, in which he knows that he can be praised. Otherwise, fame is taken away from virtues if their merits remain unknown among human beings.

For what sort of desire is it to abandon the company of citizens, when we see that birds too wish to mingle with human society? The nightingale confidently hangs its nests among mortal dwellings and fearlessly nourishes its young amid crowds of people living together.

It is therefore exceedingly disgraceful to raise the children of noblemen in desolate places, when birds can be seen to entrust their offspring to human society. Let the cities therefore return to their former dignity; let no one prefer the pleasantness of the countryside to the walls of the ancestors.

How can one take refuge in peace when war must be undertaken to preserve it from devastation? To whom would the meeting of noblemen seem less pleasing? To whom would it not be affectionate to mingle conversation with one’s equals, visit the forum, attend honorable arts, settle one’s own cases through the laws, occasionally occupy oneself with Palamedes’ counters, go to the baths with companions, and provide banquets through mutual arrangements? Surely he lacks all these things who wishes always to have his life among servants.

But lest a mind trained in the same habit slip back into it any further, let both landholders and curiales, after providing sureties according to their means and accepting a penalty, promise that they will remain for the greater part of the year in the cities they have chosen to inhabit. Let it be arranged that they lack neither the adornment of citizens nor the pleasure [Juret.: “the will”] of the fields.

## EPISTLE XXXII. ATHALARICUS, KING, TO SEVERUS, DISTINGUISHED MAN

He depicts the spring of Arethusa and orders him both to investigate and punish those who stole Nimfadius’s horses.

When the illustrious man Nimfadius was hurrying to the sacred court on his own business, exhausted by the length of the journey and wishing to restore his weary animals, he chose to make camp at the spring of Arethusa, situated in the territory of Scyllacium, because both the place itself and its pastures are fertile and it is made beautiful by an abundance of water.

For, as they say, beneath the foothills, above the sands of the sea, there is a fertile plain. From it a vast spring emerges, and the reeds surrounding it weave the edges of its banks into the shape of a crown. It is exceedingly pleasant because of the shade of the reeds and remarkable because of the power of the waters themselves.

When a quiet and deliberately silent man arrives there, he finds the waters of the flowing spring so still that, like a pond, they seem not so much to run as to stand. But whenever a resounding cough is uttered, or perhaps a louder word is spoken, the waters are immediately stirred by some unknown force and leap forth in that very place. You may see the mouth of the pool, gravely aroused, boiling up, so that you would think the rigid water had taken on the heat of a heated cauldron: silent for the silent man, but answering the speaker with noise and crashing; so that you marvel at how suddenly it has been disturbed, when no touch agitates it.

A new force, an unheard-of property: waters are moved by the human voice and, as though addressed, respond, so that, provoked by human speech, they seem somehow to murmur. You might believe that some animal lies there asleep, which, awakened by a great noise, answers you.

It is indeed recorded that certain springs gush forth with various wonders: some, when drunk, give animals a different color; another makes flocks white; some turn wood placed within them into stony hardness. But reason comprehends none of these causes, since what is applied only to natural things is recognized to lie beyond human understanding.

But to return quickly to the complaint of the petitioner: when the aforesaid Nimfadius had made his camp there, he asserts that his horses were driven away by the ambushes of peasants. It is not fitting that the discipline of our times should permit this, so that the delight of that place should be made horrifying by such damage.

We judge that Your Vigilance must examine the matter with careful inquiry. You appear to have gathered both authority from our palace and justice from the laws, so that, in the manner of that very spring, you may be seen to avenge the crime that has been committed.

Let the guilty be investigated in profound silence; let them remain quietly in their own homes, so that when the pursuer [JUR.: “executor”] soon rebukes them, their hearts may be disturbed, burst into cries, and thus be confounded by dreadful murmuring. In this way let them judge that the waters have given them an omen of their punishments.

Let there therefore be suitable vengeance among them, so that the places may remain passable. Let the discipline imposed invite travelers to use them, lest such a miracle, which is known always to delight those who seek it, be avoided because of the excesses of robbers.

## EPISTLE XXXIII. ATHALARICUS, KING, TO SEVERUS, DISTINGUISHED MAN

He decrees that, on the day before the feast of Saint Cyprian, Severus is to come, together with the landholders and tenants of various estates, to the Lucanian assembly at a place called Leucothea, in order to restrain the boldness of certain peasants who were stripping merchants of their goods. He then describes the place and the powers and wonders of the spring of Marcilianus.

Just as it is the mark of a prudent person to wish to know what is unknown, so it is madness to disregard what is known, especially when a harmful matter can be brought to the quickest correction.

For we have learned through frequent investigation that, at the Lucanian assembly which, because of an ancient superstition, received the name Leucothea, where there is water remarkably clear and bright, the resources of merchants are often torn apart by the hostile plundering of peasants acting unlawfully. Thus those who had come most devoutly to celebrate the feast of Saint Cyprian, and to adorn the face of the city with their merchandise, departed shamefully poor and empty-handed.

We believed that this could be corrected by a simple and easy remedy: at the appointed time, Your Distinction, together with the landholders and tenants of the various estates, must take anticipatory precautions for the peace of those assembling, so that you may find the perpetrators of the savage deed, whom punishment will consume.

If any peasant, or any man from any place, brings forward the grounds of a wicked dispute, let him be seized at the very outset and immediately subjected to the punishment of the cudgel; and, publicly paraded in disgrace [manuscript: “vows”], let him amend the hidden crime which he had previously been attempting to stir up.

For this assembly is both festive through its extraordinary celebrity and highly beneficial to the surrounding provinces. Whatever is especially notable or industrious Campania sends, whatever the wealthy Bruttians send, whatever the prosperous Calabrians send, whatever the capable Apulians send, or whatever the province itself can provide, is displayed for the adornment of that most beautiful marketplace, so that you may rightly judge such an enormous abundance to have been gathered from many regions.

There you may see broad fields gleaming with the most beautiful stalls and temporary houses suddenly woven from pleasant leafy branches, together with the movement of peoples singing and rejoicing [Note: Workshops and booths of the fair are meant. What else does Athalaric indicate by these words concerning merchandise and temporary houses, except booths? *Digest* 40.12.19, under *Heirs*, on judicial proceedings; *Digest* 43.8.5 at the end, on those who have been thrown down. FORN.].

Although you may not see there the work of city walls, you nevertheless see the adornment of a most celebrated city. Boys and girls are present, distinguished by different sexes and ages. It is not captivity that places them on sale, but freedom. Their parents rightly sell them [Note: *Codex* 4.43, on parents who sell their children. Jeremiah 5: “The people, oppressed by famine, burst out with these words: ‘Our sons and our daughters are very many; let us take grain as their price, and eat and live.’ Eusebius also testifies that this happened in the time of the emperor Maximinus. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VIII:

“And at last, with her fortune lowered into her very being,

A daughter remained, unworthy of such a parent;

This one too the impoverished man sells.”

FORNER.], since they profit from the servitude itself. For there is no doubt that slaves can be improved when they are transferred from agricultural labor to urban service.

Why should I mention garments distinguished by countless varieties? Why mention animals of different kinds, exceedingly fat from their sleekness [another reading: “shining”?]? Everything is offered there at such a valuation that even the most fastidious buyer may find what he wants. Thus no one returns dissatisfied from that commerce, if sound discipline arranges everything.

The place itself is spread out amid the pleasantness of fields, a kind of suburb of the most ancient city of Consilinum [JUR.: Perhaps “Consilini”], and it received the name Marcilianus from the founder of its holy springs. Here a clear and sweet abundance of waters bursts forth. A hollow, shaped like a natural cave and constructed in the form of an apse, pours out waters so transparent that you would think the lake empty, although you cannot doubt that it is completely full.

It is clear down to the bottom, so that you would judge that air rather than water appears to your eyes. The exceedingly fine water imitates a cloudless day, for whatever occurs below is displayed with unobstructed clarity [manuscript, Grul, and Cuj.: “to the eyes”].

There the most cheerful fish sport together in schools. They come fearlessly to the hands of those who ask for them [manuscript and Forn.: “feed them”], as though they knew that they were not to be caught; for whoever presumed to accomplish such a thing is soon known to have incurred the punishment of the Divinity.

It would take too long to describe all the memorable features of that spring. Let us come to its singular gift and sacred miracle. When, on the day of the sacred night, the priest begins to pour out the prayer of baptism [Note: Paschasius, bishop of Lilybaeum, tells similar stories of springs miraculously filled at Easter for those to be baptized, in his letter to Pope Leo I, which appears in volume II of the Councils among the letters of Leo. Add what Gregory of Tours reports concerning the springs of Spain. JURET.], and fountains of words begin to flow from his holy mouth, the water immediately leaps upward. It does not direct its waters through the usual channels but sends them upward into a mound and height.

The lifeless element rises of its own accord and, with a kind of solemn devotion, prepares itself for miracles, so that the sanctification of the Majesty may be displayed. For although the spring itself normally covers five steps and possesses only those in tranquil conditions, it is seen to rise by two additional steps, which it is never known to occupy except at that time.

It is a great and astonishing miracle that flowing streams should, at human words, either stand still or rise, so that you would believe they had not lacked the desire to listen.

Let this heavenly spring become venerable in everyone’s speech [JUR.: “memorable”]. Let Lucania too have its Jordan. The Jordan provided an example of baptism; this spring preserves the sacred ministry [JUR.: “mystery”] through annual devotion.

Therefore, both reverence for the place and the usefulness of the matter ought to grant the people a most holy peace, since by everyone’s judgment the person must be regarded as exceedingly wicked who attempts to violate the joys of such days.

Let what we have said be read aloud and proclaimed to the people, so that, when it is firmly believed that such offenses will not remain unpunished, no one may seek license to transgress.

# BOOK NINE

## EPISTLE I. ATHALARICUS, KING, TO HILDERIC, KING OF THE VANDALS

He complains of Amalafrida’s death, inflicted by Hilderic. He then sends envoys, before whom Hilderic is to explain the crime. If he refuses, Athalaric threatens him with war.

We are bound by an exceedingly harsh fate, so that those whom we formerly called dear parents we must now accuse of most bitter offenses—offenses that no one who is known to consider the memorials of filial piety can leave unmentioned.

For who does not know that Amalafrida, of divine memory, the outstanding glory of our family, met a violent end of life among you? You had formerly possessed her as your queen, yet you did not allow her to live even as a private woman [another reading: “now”].

If this relationship seemed burdensome to you contrary to the law of kinship, she ought to have been honorably sent back to us, since you had sought her with great supplications. It is a form of parricide that the royal marriage which made her your relative should have led you, through wicked actions, to participate in her death.

What such great evil did she deserve after being abandoned by her husband? If succession was owed to another, could a woman have been found in that contest? Indeed, she ought to have been regarded as a mother, since she transferred kingdoms to you. It would also have added to your nobility if, among the line of the Hasdiringi, you had retained the purple dignity of Amal blood.

Our Goths understand that this was attempted rather to their own disgrace. For whoever inflicted death upon a queen of another nation appears to have entirely despised the valor of her parents, since no one thinks that what he believes ought to be cut away [Greek and Cuj.: “avenged”; Forn.: “refused”] should be attempted.

Therefore, warned by moral reasoning, through these and those envoys of ours we first demand justice from you in words, awaiting what explanation can be offered for such events.
