For even if some matter had arisen concerning such a person, it ought to have been reported to us, so that she who had involved herself in the worst actions might perish by our judgment as well.

It remains for her death to be represented as natural. We do not allege impossibilities; we do not seek novelty. Hand over these men and those, through whom the matter may be brought to light. Let the complete proof of the whole case be established through them—without war, without slaughter—either making us peaceful or rendering you liable.

But if you believe this may be despised and do not prepare yourselves for reasonable answers, we are released from the terms of the peace that was made, since we are not bound by the bond of a treaty that has been violated.

Let the heavenly Majesty now avenge, by whatever means, the crime that has been committed, for it proclaims that the impious slaughter of a brother’s blood cries out to it.

## II. EDICT OF KING ATHALARICUS

He protects the curiales from every injury and threatens their harassers either with a fine of ten pounds of gold or with corporal punishment.

[Col. 0766D]

Anyone who wishes the condition of the commonwealth and the general eminence of the realm to endure must be attentive to everything, because there is no health in the body unless its members too are able to enjoy it. When one place suffers injustice, the whole structure is shaken; and so great is the force of solidarity that you would think one wound is received everywhere when that place begins to suffer. For the commonwealth is not the concern of one city, but the safeguarded custody of the entire kingdom. Therefore, if anything is diminished from it, losses are felt at the source. For whoever loses something must necessarily have less. And so our ever-watchful care for the various cities keeps us anxious, lest the evils permitted to continue too long should burden our palace.

[Col. 0767A] The tree that you see flowering, that you observe rejoicing in the highest verdure, is animated by the subterranean sap of fertility, returning to the surface what it contains in its root. The faces of human beings likewise are adorned with great cheerfulness if, with their inward parts healthy, they feel no burden from any injury. Thus a kingdom is rightly called wholly sound if it has nowhere been diminished. This can happen when unrestrained license is removed on every side and a malicious mind is not allowed, under an abhorrent freedom, to dare to sin.

The curiales, whose name derives from provident care, are said to be shaken by the gravest harassment, so that whatever is entrusted to them as an honor seems instead to have been turned into an injury. O monstrous crime, intolerable evil! When they ought to prosper by serving the commonwealth, they appear then to lose both their freedom and their possessions.

Therefore, by an edictal proclamation we determine that, if anyone has been involved in an injury or loss affecting a curialis, or has perhaps presumed to impose anything upon him—except what has been ordered by us or by the palace officials whose authority is concerned—he shall either be struck with a loss of ten pounds of gold, to the further benefit of the person who suffered such treatment, or, if the means for a monetary penalty are insufficient, he shall be torn apart by scourging and shall pay in penalties what he could not compensate with money. This is nevertheless subject to the condition that whatever has been entrusted for the public good shall be completed with freeborn diligence, since those whom we do not permit to endure the injustices of others thereby begin to owe more.

[Note: [Col. 0767D] The sale of curial estates is invalid unless it is made for a proved reason in the records of the governor, according to Book 2 of the Code, *On the Office of Him Who Holds the Office of Vicar or Other Judge*, or before the prefect of the praetorium, according to Majorian’s Novel on the curiales. Whoever buys a curial estate must restore the estate, together with its fruits, to the seller without a curial decree; nevertheless, he does not recover from him either the price or the improvements. It is therefore equitable that whoever entered into such a purchase should lose both the price and the expenses. — BROSS.]

[Note: [Col. 0768D] The same, in the last letter of Book VII. Justinian, Novel 101, forbids τὰς οὐσίας τῶν βουλευτῶν κατ` οὐδένα τρόπον ἀλλοτριοῦσθαι τῆς βουλῆς τῆς πόλεως ἧς εἰσι βουλευταί: “the property of councillors to be alienated in any manner from the council of the city of which they are councillors.” — FORN.]

No one is to seize the estates of curiales—through which snares are chiefly laid for men of modest means—by an illicit purchase, because a transaction cannot be called a contract unless it derives from the laws.

They are to be protected by the assistance of the judges from the harassment of *sajones* and soldiers. Our authority has even defended them from the very governors themselves; how much more severely must the person be punished if the one to whom assistance has been entrusted is proved to inflict harm?

Raise your necks, you who are bowed down; lift your spirits, you who are weighed down by burdens of misfortune; strive to recover what you know you have wickedly lost. To each citizen his own city is a commonwealth. Administer justice in the cities with a harmonious will. Let your orders live in equality. Do not oppress men of modest means, lest those of greater power be able, with good reason, to oppress you. The penalty of such sin is that each person may suffer in himself what he insolently inflicted upon another. Live justly; live temperately, because scarcely anyone dares to overstep against those in whom he cannot find faults.

Cranes know how to practice a moral harmony. Among them no one seeks primacy, because there is no striving for iniquity. They keep watch by turns and guard one another through common vigilance; even their feeding is alternated. Thus honor is taken from no one while everything is preserved in common. Their flight too is arranged in reciprocal equality: the last becomes first, and the one who held the first place does not refuse to become last. Thus, joined together in a kind of community, they obey one another without kings, submit without domination, and serve without terror. They are free because they serve voluntarily, and they are fortified by loving one another.

Observing their way of life, writers on natural things report that a kind of political order exists among them, since they have recognized that the birds live with civic affection. If you imitate them, you exclude from yourselves every accusation of wickedness. For you who receive the vows of upright men possess, by the laws, authority over your fellow citizens.

Antiquity did not grant you the curia for nothing, nor did it call you the lesser senate without reason; it also calls you the sinews and inmost parts of the cities.

[Note: [Col. 0768D] The curiales are the sinews of the cities, according to Majorian’s Novel on the curiales. — JURET.]

What do you not possess in this title, whether of power or of honor? For one who is compared with the senate is excluded from no distinction of eminence.

## EPISTLE III. ATHALARIC, KING, TO BERGANTINUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND COUNT OF THE PATRIMONY

He orders him to send a *chartarius* to the Rustician estate, in whose depths gold lies hidden, and to arrange for it to be dug out. He then describes the skill of the gold-workers.

If every persistent labor demands such diverse rewards that gold and silver are obtained through their customary exchange [Ac.: communion], why do we not diligently seek out the very things for which we seemed to require other things? Let Italy, rich in resources, bring us golden fruits. Every return is gained wherever the yellow metal is found. For why should the earth be exhausted by manifold fertility if greater prices themselves can be found within it?

Nature grants you grain in the customary manner, with industry assisting; wines pour forth everywhere; metal is produced rarely, so that it may be sought more eagerly. Therefore we order Your Greatness to send a *chartarius* to the Rustician estate belonging to our jurisdiction [Ac.: our rural estate], situated in the province of Bruttium. And if, as Theodore, an artisan skilled in these matters, says, the earth is fertile in the resources mentioned, let the inner parts of the mountains be searched after workshops have been solemnly [Greek and Cujacius: skillfully, in accordance with the duties] established. Let art enter, as a benefaction, into the earth’s innermost chamber, and let nature, rich as it is in its own treasures, be sought out.

For when the chambers have been opened through ingenious daring, the miners imitate the mole and dig passages that had previously been accessible to no one. Thus ambition leaves nothing hidden, nor does it know where it can sometimes endure an end. Men enter deep darkness, live without the upper world, and are exiled from the sun; and while they seek gains beneath the earth, they sometimes abandon the joys of the light. Their own route occasionally becomes their ruin, and those who made paths with laboring hands and feet cannot arrange their return.

But for those whose art is more cautious, life is more fortunate: they enter poor and emerge wealthy; without theft they seize riches, enjoy the desired treasures without envy, and alone among human beings seem to acquire valuable things without any bargaining. As soon as they have been restored to the light above, they separate from the mother earth each small particle from the heavier material by means of water; then, having enclosed it in earthen vessels, they cook it in a vast furnace until it is usefully melted into liquid. They also purify the streams that come from the fire with such intense heat until they reveal their beauty, which the earth’s depths had hidden lest it be desired.

Nature is conquered while industry improves it. It is more beautiful after it has burned and more valuable after it has been cooked, because it rises in price in proportion to the purity with which it has been cleansed. Its origin is indeed noble, but from the flame it receives the power of its color, so that you are more likely to believe it born from that whose likeness seems to adorn it. Yet while it gives gold a splendid redness, it confers upon silver the brightest whiteness, so that it is remarkable for one substance to convey what can be adapted to dissimilar things.

Accordingly, let your administration complete whatever you know belongs to the exercise of mastery in this art, so that the land of Bruttium too may discover within itself the tribute that it is able to provide, since it luxuriates in an abundance of fruits. For amid so many blessings it is fitting that those things which are considered pre-eminent should not be lacking. Why should something that can be an honorable gain lie unused [Ed., Niv., Ga., Greek and Cujacius: uncultivated]?

To seek gold through wars is a crime; through the seas, a danger; through falsehoods, a disgrace; but in its own natural place, it is justice. Those are honorable profits by which no one is harmed, and that is rightly acquired which has not yet been taken away from any owner.

Griffins, it is continually reported, dig up gold and rejoice at the sight of this metal. Since they have no striving for profit, they are not said to be inflamed by the crime of greed—plainly because every act depends upon the quality of its intention, and something is not blameworthy when no will has made it wanton. Let profits therefore continue through diligent work; let them fear no envy. What is called art is freed from crime.

## EPISTLE IV. ATHALARIC, KING, TO ABUNDANTIUS, PREFECT OF THE PRAETORIUM

He orders that Agenantia, the wife of Campanianus, and their children be removed from the register of the curiales and placed among the possessors.

A complaint is fortunate when the laws are surpassed by compassion; and the condition of subjects is blessed if they recognize that the one who has shown mercy to others also wishes to be gracious toward them. For the sacred laws bound the curiales for no other reason than that, when the sovereigns alone released them, they might discover the praises of indulgence—that is, when the lord, in a gracious contest, dissents from his own judgments. For it is itself a kind of justice that one who is called compassionate should not be held strictly to the limit of severity.

This too is a reasonable arrangement: finally to release from service those who are proved unequal to its labors. For a curialis who is not restrained by any bodily illness is assigned only to deceptions; and what good will it do for him to be present if he happens to be found lacking in strength? He is like an absent man, by whom the orders issued cannot be fulfilled.

Moreover, while the curia rejoices in its large numbers, it does not seem to be struck by the loss of a few from among the many. Therefore let Your Illustrious Magnificence carefully erase from the register of its curia Agenantia, the wife of the most eloquent Campanianus, established in the province of Lucania, and their sons, so that future generations may not know that what is forbidden to be brought forward once existed [Jur.: perhaps “objected”; Ms.: “to be imposed”], since a charge is not presumed where there is no proof.

Accordingly, let them instead be placed among the possessors,

[Note: [Col. 0769D] He says this because the curiales administered the taxes, and from them the system of distributions proceeded, as Juret says he noted in Symmachus, Book 9, Letter 10.]

while nevertheless suffering the burdens that they themselves used to inflict upon others. They will be disturbed by the customary taxes; they will dread the face of the collector—they had not known that orders had first come from the authorities—and, wearied by the ignorance they had once desired, they will begin to fear the assignments by which they had previously caused others to be afraid. They are also to be proved to have lived with scarcely any moral goodness in that respect, since they now endure living idly among those whose hatred they do not recognize themselves to have deserved. Otherwise [Niv. and Ga.: “some others”] they would not endure being under those whom they knew they had provoked to evil acts.

Let them therefore enjoy the benefit granted by the sovereign; let them live quietly in released peace, since they had been composed in the quality of their own actions.

## EPISTLE V. ATHALARIC, KING, TO THE BISHOPS AND HONORATI

He establishes that those who have hidden grain during a scarcity of provisions must sell it at a moderate price.

We have learned from the complaint of the possessors of your territory that they are enduring, beyond the necessity of the time, the execrable cruelty of certain fellow citizens. At the beginning of the crisis they bought up grain of the millet kind and converted it into their own property, watching the scarcity become burdensome to men of modest means, so that they might inflict detestable deprivation upon those who had stored away less, while people placed in danger of famine offer entreaties to those whom they know can strip them.

In the necessity of poverty, there is no dispute about price, when a person allows himself to be induced lest he be struck by any delay. Condemning these ambitions, we have sent the present bearers, so that, whether grain stores can be found in the public granary [Note: [Col. 0769D] *Panis gradilis*, bread customarily distributed to citizens from the steps without payment, as is shown by the individual laws in Title 17 of Book 14 of the Theodosian Code. See Prudentius, Book 1 *Against Symmachus*; Cujacius, on the title *On Grain Stored in the Public Granaries*, Book 10 of the Code. — FORN.] or in other places, each owner may retain for himself and his household as much as he knows he can consume. Let him sell the remainder to those in danger,

[Col. 0770D] in the presence, of course, of the bearers of this order, who are known to have been assigned to this task. The price, however, must be moderate, at the amount for which it is established that he purchased it from his provincials, so that the buyer is not burdened excessively and the seller is sustained by some profit.

Therefore fulfill what has been ordered with willing hearts, because in this matter you ought to consult one another, lest, while you seek excessive profit, you should instead—God forbid—wish something criminal upon yourselves. Let no one complain that a sale has been imposed upon him; let him know that freedom is not to be sought in a crime, but that it is rather the mark of a good disposition if he does not hasten to overstep.

Let the seller therefore sell according to a just measure. If he consents, he works for his own praise; if he resists, he makes our proclamation necessary. For the command is good when justice is imposed upon the unwilling.

## EPISTLE VI. ATHALARIC, KING, TO THE PRIMISCRINIUS

He permits him to go to the Baian baths for the sake of his health, while he is nevertheless to receive the emoluments of military service during that time.

Since you kept watch through prolonged labors, you assert that you have been so severely wounded by bodily weakness that you cannot even present yourself to receive the distinction of military service, toward which it is clear that you hastened with eager desire, fearing that in your absence the sweetest fruit for you might seem to be snatched away from the very jaws of opportunity. You also request that, constrained by the necessity of your chilled body, you may be loosened through the dryness [i.e. the dry heat] of the Baian bath.

This is plainly worthy of being granted among the highest rewards, so that, just as we offer hope to the defeated, we may likewise grant health to those who plead. Therefore we both release you from the obligation of the service allowance and relieve you through the gift of the bath mentioned above, so that, first refreshed by the joy of the mind, you may more easily recover the health of your limbs. For it is a natural form of care to give joy to the sick: make an invalid rejoice, and he is healed.

Go, then, to the pleasant retreats; go, so to speak, to a brighter sun, where, with the healthfulness of the air tempered, nature is more kindly toward the earth. There, while you ponder deeply upon the marvels, the human mind converses with the secrets of the world and does not cease to wonder at what it recognizes can be accomplished there.

First, the waters of Nereus are filled with marine delights; so many harbors have been opened by nature’s wisdom in earthly inlets; so many noble islands are enriched by the embrace of the sea. Then there is the sea, turned into a stagnant pool at Avernus, where the life of oysters is sheltered [Ms.: directed; Cujacius and Greek: generated] for human pleasure, and where mortal industry makes what is accidental elsewhere always appear abundant.

With what great masses have the boundaries of the sea been suitably invaded there! Over what distances has the earth been advanced into the depths of the waters! On the right and left, shoals of fish play. Elsewhere, let abundant delights be enclosed by industrious walls; let aquatic flocks be held captive. Here, everywhere, there are fishponds under freedom.

Add that fishing has been received in so pleasant a form that, before the sumptuous banquet, it feeds the eyes of those who watch. For it is a great joy to have captured what one desired; but in such matters the pleasure of the eyes is usually more gratifying than the usefulness of the catch.

But not to wander farther, the person to whom Baian leisure is granted is believed to dwell amid Neptune’s treasures. Thus, having been nourished by these delightful exercises, you will hasten to the most beautiful baths, which are both full of marvels and precious for the quality of their healthfulness. For although they are known to have been constructed through human care, they are certainly supplied by natural agencies.

There furnaces are not kindled by transported logs: when the flame is absent, perpetual heat performs the work. There smoky globes are unknown; the air is perfectly pure, supplying vapors and gently provoking warm, breathing perspiration. It is found to be so much healthier than ordinary baths as nature is higher than human industry.

There you may see waters perpetually steaming in swirling currents, which seem to fulfill the desires of bathers so completely that you would think they had been tempered by human skill. Let the ever-praised reputation of the Coral Sea give way; let the fame of the Indian Ocean, enriched by the whiteness of its pearls, rise up.

What have I to do with prices if the mind does not enjoy what it desires? Nothing can be superior to the shores of Baiae, where one has the opportunity both to feast upon the sweetest delights and to be filled with the priceless gift of health.

Enjoy, therefore, the good things you have so greatly desired. Through our benefactions you will attain your advantages. Through the remedies of Baiae, obtain the gift of health.

## EPISTLE VII. ATHALARIC, KING, TO REPARATUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

He extols his father and father-in-law with many praises. Then he grants him the urban prefecture.

[Col. 0772B]

After the distinguished administrations of parents, the most eminent dignities are rightly conferred upon their descendants, since no one’s character is content to lie within the estimation of his ancestors, when it is an honorable ambition to wish to surpass in praise those whom we follow in time. It is also added that those educated in the teachings of the ancients take pleasure in having their reputation increased. For the more each person recognizes that he has devoted himself to the better arts, the more boldly he presumes to aspire to greater things.

Some time ago, therefore, the Roman commonwealth experienced the diligence of your father, of illustrious memory. Presiding over the countship of the largesses and also serving in place of prefects, he exercised the praetorian dignity with complete integrity: restoring the curia and returning what had been taken from the poor. Although he had not been polished by liberal studies, he did not fail to please through his industry, because a good disposition can naturally commend itself by its own qualities even when it does not appear adorned by additional accomplishments.

But this is as much as concerns your literary knowledge. For learning distinguishes those whom it separates from the uneducated, and joins them in a friendly association with the wise. It is very easy for learning to adorn one who is noble,

[Note: [Col. 0771] See Tiraquellus, *On Nobility*, chapter 5, where he proves that learning makes people noble. — JUR.]

and it even makes a noble person out of one of obscure origin.

Your illustrious merits are also enhanced by the fact that, for the sake of affinity, a man chose you who has always been praised for the integrity of his judgment: ordinary in his conduct, unique in his conscience, and always making himself praiseworthy through his character, his dealings with friends, and his probity. What sort of person, then, must he be judged to have joined to his own blood, who never decided to add an immoral man to his community?

And therefore, although you come to honor at an early age, after the judgment of so great a man it would be foolish to say that you have not been tested and approved. For if we willingly lend a peaceful ear to those who advise us in matters concerning strangers, why should we not follow their judgments all the more in their own family, where even those who frequently go astray in other actions always carefully look to their own interests?

Therefore, as may happily be said, in that indiction we grant you the insignia of the urban dignity, so that, just as you are first in that order, you may also be regarded as pre-eminent in the praise of your merits. Almost the eyes of the world are fixed upon what is carried out in that city. What judge would now make himself acceptable to the senate of such benevolence if he offended it?

You recognize, in the assessment of that order itself, what maturity and prudence are, since its first shoots, as soon as they have grown, are called Fathers. Adolescence there begins with maturity of counsel. Young men deliberate with the modesty of old age [Others: old age itself], where the weight of character is permitted to flourish which elsewhere scarcely arises even in gray-haired age.

You will therefore conduct yourself with such moderation that, when you summon so many nobles to the curia, you will disclose before them a decision worthy of your will. For it is exceedingly difficult to say something among them that could fail to please such prudent men. Accordingly, a man who could receive a good judgment from that gathering of learned men should not be considered a man of only one dignity. For if it is pleasing to be praised even in rare instances, what joy must come to one whom the votes of so many nobles have praised?

Love justice; show gracious assistance to the oppressed; restore to your descendants the praises that you received from your ancestors [Jur. V. C.: better men].

## EPISTLE VIII. ATHALARIC, KING, TO OSUIN [Ed.: OSUM], ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND COUNT

He sends him again to govern the provinces of Dalmatia and Suavia.

It is our purpose to adorn honorable labors with the palm of reward, so that, by the reversal through which the promoted rejoice, the idle may be stung and may blame themselves for not deserving the rewards of our most merciful times.

Therefore, with God’s help, we have again decided to send Your Illustrious Greatness to the provinces of Dalmatia and Suavia, so that whatever you recognize to be useful to our interests you may arrange with balanced administration, and so that through your justice you may make the people devoted to us especially grateful to us. For an elected official is attached to the praises of his lords when he governs himself commendably.

Do not seek out the examples of others; remember what you have done, and you do not need to be admonished. For what reason should anyone doubt your conduct, when you recognize that your own good qualities still breathe their fragrance through those provinces? In a certain sense, it is already owed to that place that you should offer it your service, since you know that you were praiseworthy there.

For a disposition is rightly indulged in those who obey; and when we know people to remember benefits, we confidently show them favor again. Your age is advanced, but your conduct is also more mature. What could now steal upon you as a fault, when even your youth was not blameworthy?

But you did these things under the reign of our lord grandfather. Now display such qualities that you may seem to have reserved for our times whatever additional probity you possess.

## EPISTLE IX. ATHALARIC, KING, TO ALL GOTHS AND ROMANS

He announces that he has sent Count Osuin and Severinus to govern Dalmatia and orders the people to obey them.

Throughout the provinces granted to us by God’s favor, we wish to appoint men who are equipped with arms and illustrious for justice, so that you may be free both from fear of foreign peoples and from exposure to the snares of slanderers. For it is no less a good to have avoided the evil of war than to have escaped the cruelty of an inquiry.

True security is that which fears no impiety on the part of a judge. Therefore, under God’s auspices, we decree that the illustrious Count Osuin, distinguished at our palace and well known to the provinces through his long association with them, shall preside over Dalmatia. See to it that you obey him when he commands for our advantage, since you have so often experienced his justice that, remembering his earlier service, you ought to have obeyed him even without a royal order.

For the man who is just possesses a right of his own. Even if he is not raised up by the terror of supreme authority [Jur.: read “of the least authority”], he is always heard because equity persuades.

We have also decided to send to you the illustrious Severinus, so that, united in harmonious purpose, they may issue commands worthy of praise. For if unequal pipes can agree to produce a single melody [Ms., Greek, Cujacius, edition: “to proclaim”], it is much more fitting for very prudent men to recommend what is just with a concordant voice [Edition: “voice of the heart”].

But so that our beginnings might commence with benefits already granted, and so that you might perceive a most merciful lord at the very threshold of his reign, in the fourth indiction (the year of Christ 526) we have now ordered the illustrious Count of our Patrimony to remove what was being sought from you in the name of an augmentation.

We also grant you this additional concession: when, with God’s favor, we have brought the aforesaid man to our service, we shall send such persons as will enable us clearly to learn how the assessment of the census is to be imposed in the future. If we discover that you have been burdened, we shall relieve you, after equity has been considered, to whatever extent seems appropriate.

Thus you possess hope of a future benefit, you who have already obtained remedies in part. Therefore it is fitting that you serve our interests, since the royal munificence has voluntarily bestowed what you could more readily have hoped to obtain through prayers.

For we have learned this from the most merciful author who has granted us our rule: that we must not be idle in granting benefits to our subjects. The discipline of ruling, plainly, is to love what is useful to the many, because the commonwealth gains great solidity if the resources of the taxpayers remain unharmed.

## EPISTLE X. ATHALARIC, KING, TO ALL POSSESSORS AND DEFENDERS OF THE CITY OF SYRACUSE, AND TO ALL PROVINCIALS

He remits the taxes imposed upon them beyond custom and grants those harassed by the assessors the right to bring their complaints before the sovereign.

[Col. 0774D]

Some time ago we thought it right to announce to you the beginning of our rule. Now it is fitting that a benefit should follow, to increase the joy of all, so that those to whom our accession was most welcome may find the royal spirit generous toward them in some respect.

We desire everything to grow with us, with God’s help, because our true census is that which a joyful possessor pays. Accordingly, we subtract from the money that which adds to glory, and we strive, lavishly rather than greedily, to raise up the cultivators.

Previously, our lord grandfather, of divine memory, relying greatly upon his own benefits—since a long period of peace both provided agriculture with care and increased the population—established that a census should be demanded within the province of Sicily, under the customary moderation of his prudence, so that your devotion might grow as your resources expanded.

But his justice, worthy of praise, prepared a place for our clemency, so that what could rightly have been offered to him we might donate with a merciful spirit, as though it were an already rendered payment. By a certain foreknowledge of the divine mind, he also made pious what he was preparing for rule.

Therefore, in the fortunate fourth indiction (that is, in the year of Christ 526), whatever was either demanded from you or is known to have been exacted beyond the customary obligation in the name of an augmentation, our generosity grants to you. Although you could have paid it justly, we order you instead to offer the glory to our liberality.

But so that our clemency may extend more broadly, and so that you may experience a gracious lord through the benefits bestowed, whatever new assessment the collectors are proved to have imposed for the fifth indiction (the year of Christ 527), we have caused them to bring it to your attention. You are to bear what is judged reasonable with willing hearts, because observed justice harms no one.

But do not suppose that you can be burdened solely by the discretion of those appointed. If anyone thinks he has grounds for complaining about their conduct, let him hasten to the remedies of our compassion, so that we may correct those whom we judge, even though they were not asked, while we have graciously bestowed benefits.

Our lord grandfather, of glorious memory, had also been moved by their delay, for, as an investigator of profound wisdom, he judged that they were remaining in the province not without burdening us, although by repeated order he had already decreed that they return. But we, who ought to fulfill whatever he arranged with equity, are now, with God’s help, completing among you what he began.

Now return to our generosity a most prosperous pledge and faithful service. You have a sovereign whose accession has proved beneficial to you; and what is sweeter to subjects, his benevolence increases together with the growth of his age.

For this purpose we have decided to send our *sajo* Quidilan, through whom, with God’s gift, our most prosperous orders may be made known to you.

## EPISTLE XI. ATHALARIC, KING, TO GILDIAS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND COUNT OF THE CITY OF SYRACUSE

He forbids the possessors to be required to pay anything added by Victor and Witigisclus in the fourth indiction.

[Col. 0775D]

We have sent our instructions to the respectable men Victor and Witigisclus, assessors of the province of Sicily, ordering them not to demand from the possessors, in the fourth indiction, whatever they recently seem to have added to the tax obligation, because the imposition of a burden whose justice has not yet been established is severe.

We have also ordered their arrangements to be brought to us, so that, if whatever has been arranged in equality is judged proportionate to the resources, it may remain moderate. But if it is established that anyone has been burdened contrary to reason, let him be relieved by our decision.

This is nevertheless subject to the condition that, if anything is proved to have been imposed during the fourth indiction (the year of Christ 526), it must be returned to the possessors without any diminution, because a burden that is imposed and is known to have been borne for a long time ought to be accepted without complaint [Greek and Cujacius: “ought to be paid”].

What remains is that you should now admonish the provincials, so that we may experience in every respect the devotion of those to whom we have granted benefits, and so that what is owed to the sovereign may be seen to be paid with a grateful spirit.

## EPISTLE XII. ATHALARIC, KING, TO THE RESPECTABLE MEN VICTOR AND WITIGISCLUS

He orders that, if they have exacted anything from the provincials above the tax assessment during the fourth indiction, they return it without any diminution.

Your delay deservedly made you objects of suspicion to our lord grandfather, of glorious memory. He even considered it necessary to admonish you by subsequent orders [Edition: late orders], so that, finally abandoning the burden imposed upon the provincials, you should hasten to carry out his justice.

Now too your delay has greatly increased suspicion, since you were unwilling to attend to the beginnings of our reign—something that a clear conscience could have desired. Therefore, by the present authority, we decree that, if you exacted anything from the provincials above the tax assessment during the fourth indiction (the year of Christ 526), you must return it to them without any diminution, because we do not wish them to suffer any loss beyond the old census in the aforesaid indiction.

We have also thought it necessary to add this: through our love of clemency we do not wish to discover errors, lest we be forced instead to cut away what we cannot overlook without violating justice. If you have injured anyone through wrongful zeal, correct it by your own decision, because to correct one’s own offenses is equivalent to not committing them.

And lest you perhaps think that, because of the distance, what has been done can remain hidden, we have given the Sicilians confidence to pursue you. See now whether you can endure the complaining voices, which our authority itself has invited.

We have therefore admonished those whom it befits to be compassionate. He now appears to be accused by his own fault who was unwilling to be corrected of his own free will [Greek, Niv., Ga.: “He appears to be accused by his own fault who was unwilling to be corrected voluntarily”].

## EPISTLE XIII. ATHALARIC, KING, TO WILIA, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND COUNT OF THE PATRIMONY

He orders that the household troops who serve the provincial counts receive an additional annual payment of fifty solidi, beyond the two hundred solidi and ten rations they have received, to be charged to the accounts of the king.

[Col. 0776D]

We have learned from a report by Your Greatness that the provincials are being burdened by many losses through the excesses of the household troops who serve the counts assigned to them. We believe that this has been nourished by the smallness of their allowances, because a person who is not provided with what he needs is thought to be able to sin under a certain pretext.

Therefore, granting general relief through a special benefit, we order Your Greatness by the present authority to ensure that, beyond the two hundred solidi and ten rations that they have hitherto received, beginning with the fortunate fifth indiction you add to them without delay an annual fifty solidi,

[Col. 0777A] which are to be charged to our accounts. When the necessity that is the mother of crimes is removed, the desire to sin will be taken away.

But if anyone proves to be an insolent violator of our orders, so that in any circumstance he becomes involved in losses or prejudices affecting the provincials, let him be deprived of all allowances, because the one who is recognized to obey equity is worthy to receive rewards.

He receives from us for this reason: so that he may not seek from others. It is nobility for us to give. Royal gifts, however small, exalt their recipients, because the person raised up by a royal grant is also thought to have found the favor of merit.

## EPISTLE XIV. ATHALARIC, KING, TO GILDIAS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND COUNT OF THE CITY OF SYRACUSE

He decrees that whatever was extorted from the provincials for the repair of the walls must either be restored or spent on repairing the fortifications. He then rebukes him for claiming the property of the dead, without any judicial distinction, as forfeited to the treasury. He further says that the provincials complain that they have been burdened by every kind of summons and proceeding. Finally, he establishes that the edicts promulgated by Theoderic for regulating the conduct of the Sicilians must be observed in such a way that anyone who attempts to violate them in any respect is held guilty of sacrilege.

[Col. 0777B]

It has been reported to us, through the representations of the Sicilian provincials, that certain actions are being carried out by your authority whereby their fortunes appear to be afflicted. We have received this report leniently because they themselves did not wish past matters to be avenged. For it is clear that what an adversary concedes is doubtful; and one cannot lawfully be struck down when he prefers to forgive those who complain. But so that we may remove unjust suspicions in future cases, by the present command we decree that the following provisions must be continually observed, so that neither they may fear anything in the future nor you, through ignorance, incur the consequences of what is alleged.

At first sight, money is said to have been extorted from various provincials for the repair of the walls, although no promised construction has arisen from it. If this is established to have occurred, either walls shall be built from those funds for their protection, or each person shall recover what is proved to have been improperly taken from him. For it is exceedingly absurd to promise fortifications and give the citizens abominable devastation.

They also report that you claim, in the name of the fisc as ownerless property, the estates of certain deceased persons without any judicial discrimination, although you appear to have been entrusted with this only in the case of foreigners for whom no heir—whether testamentary or lawful—is found. For it is unlawful that what is ordered by us should be unlawfully claimed by you in our name.

Moreover, they lament that they are burdened in every way by summonses, so that, when brought to judgment, they appear to lose almost as much as the expenses they can scarcely be shown to have been condemned to bear. A judge’s summons ought to be the hope of justice, not a fine. For he himself is rightly regarded with suspicion before whose hearing burdens are felt. Therefore we decree that, if those summoned by your decrees are brought before you, the officer executing the summons shall receive no more compensation than our glorious lord and grandfather established, in a stated amount, that *sajones* should receive for the honors of persons. Compensation must be proportionate. If it exceeds the measure of equality, it will no longer possess the force of its name [*jur.*, *amoris*: “of law,” “of love”]. But if a summons is issued by your order, the officer shall receive only half the portion that he could have taken under royal commands, and only in those cases and with respect to those persons in which the edicts have wished you to intervene. For it cannot accord with justice that as much should be granted directly by you as is offered out of reverence for our command.

If anyone proves to be a violator of this most salutary enactment, we order that what was taken be restored fourfold, so that what is committed through the pleasure of greed may be punished through the severity of financial loss [Ms. and Ac.: “what is lost”].

As for the edicts of our glorious lord and grandfather, and all the commands that he sent to Sicily for the correction [Ed.: “movement”; Jur.: perhaps “ordering”] of the conduct of everyone, we wish them to be guarded with such obedience that anyone who, stirred by beastlike impulses [Ed.: “conduct”], attempts in any way to break through the protection of the commands shall be held guilty of sacrilege.

You are also said to summon to your judgment, even against their will, the affairs of two Romans. If you recognize that this has occurred, do not presume to do so again, lest, while improperly seeking jurisdiction, you appear instead to incur guilt. You must first remember the edict that you prefer to have established as a rule for yourself among others. Otherwise all authority to decide is removed from you if that rule is not observed by you.

The authority of the ordinary judges in their administrations shall remain unimpaired. Let a lawful body accompany their assessors. Do not be wounded by resentment of those observances. The glory of the Goths is preserved civility. All reputation flows toward you if a litigant observes that you are rarely approached. Defend rights by arms; allow the Romans to litigate in the peace of the laws.

You are reported to be taking possession of merchandise transported by ships and, through the pressure of detestable greed, defining only the ancient prices. This is not believed to be far removed from suspicion, even if it is not closely connected with an actual proceeding. Therefore, if you hasten to avoid such a rumor, let the city’s bishop and people stand as witnesses to your good faith. Let whatever must necessarily affect the fortunes of all be acceptable to all. Prices ought to be established by common deliberation, because there is no pleasure in commerce that is imposed upon unwilling parties.

Accordingly, we believe that your Sublimity should be admonished by the present commands, since we do not wish to exceed those whom we love; nor do we permit anything sinister to be said about those through whom we think the conduct of others ought to be corrected.

## LETTER XV. TO JOHN THE POPE

[Note: John II, the second of that name. His letter to the emperor Justinian, and Justinian’s letter to him, are found in the final law, *Inter claras*, in the Code, *On the Holy Trinity and the Catholic Faith*. He is mentioned below in this book, letter 17, and in Book XI, letter 2. He was the predecessor of Pope Boniface II. FORN.]

**ATHALARIC, KING.** He promulgates highly salutary decrees against simoniacs, in accordance with ancient senatorial decrees.

If ancient rulers took pains to seek out laws so that subject peoples might enjoy agreeable tranquility, it is far more excellent to enact provisions that can accord with the sacred rules. Let harmful profits be absent from our age [Note: Final law, *On Agreements*, above, Book I, letter 5; Book II, letter 13; Book VIII, letter 28. FORN.]. We can truly call only that a profit which it is certain that divine judgments do not punish.

Recently, the defender of the Roman Church came to us with a mournful allegation: when a bishop was being sought for the apostolic see, certain men, by a wicked scheme, had exploited the necessities of the time and so aggravated the resources of the poor through extorted promises that—even though it is an abomination to say so—the sacred vessels themselves appeared to have been exposed for public sale. As cruel as it was to commit this offense, so glorious is it to cut it away through the application of piety.

Therefore let your Holiness know that we have established by the present definition—and we wish this to apply also to all patriarchs and metropolitan churches—that, beginning in the time of the most holy Pope Boniface, when the senators, mindful of their own nobility, enacted senatorial decrees for prohibiting such payments [Note: See law 51, *Whomever*, Code, *On Bishops and Clerics*; the Novel *How a Bishop Ought to Be Elected*, chapter 9, in Platina; in the Canon, p. 88; and in Boniface, 3, p. 75. JURET.]:

Whoever is shown to have promised anything, either personally or through any other person, in order to obtain a bishopric, shall have the detestable contract annulled by every means.

If anyone is discovered to have been involved in this crime, we leave him no avenue of defense. Indeed, if he should believe either that what was given ought to be reclaimed or that what was received ought not to be returned, let him immediately be held guilty of sacrilege and be compelled by the competent judge to restore what he received.

For the most just laws, just as they open the way to good people, close it to evil conduct. Moreover, whatever was established in that senatorial decree, we command by every means to be observed against those who, in any manner, through any intermediaries whatsoever [Note: Fraud is often committed through their intervention. See law 18, *To Bring Forward*; law 45, *In Fraud*, § *The Lessee*; law 46, *It Is Conferred*, § *What Is Done by the Governor*, *On Fiscal Law*; the single law, *On Women Who Join Themselves to Their Own Slaves*; the single law, *On Contracts of Judgment*; law 9, *Although*, *On the Property of Wards*; Cicero, *In Defense of Cluentius*, concerning Avilius pretending to be Asinius: “He arranged for a false will to be sealed by substituting another person”; Novel 124, “Concerning Those Who Are Judged.” What most people fear to do themselves, they do not fear to accomplish through others—as in the case of Stolo, who, after proposing a law that no one should possess more than five hundred *jugera*, was found to possess a thousand by substituting the person of an emancipated son and was condemned under his own law. Varro, *On Agriculture*, Book I, chapter 2; Aulus Gellius, Book XXI, chapter 1; Pliny, Book XVIII, chapter 3. FORN.] have involved themselves in criminal contracts.

And because everything must be regulated with reason, and things that are excessive cannot be called just, if a dispute concerning the consecration of an apostolic pontiff should perhaps come before us [Jur.: “should arise”], and the quarrel of the people be brought to our palace, we decree that, with the collection of documents, we shall accept three thousand solidi. Nevertheless, we exclude from this amount all persons who are less suitable, after consideration of the matter itself, because the poor ought rather to be provided for from the resources of the Church.

As for the other patriarchs, when their ordination is discussed in our retinue, we order that two thousand solidi be expended under the conditions and for the persons mentioned above. In their own cities, moreover, let them understand that they are to distribute no more than five hundred solidi among the poorest people.

Those who receive more shall be constrained by the penalty both of the present edict and of the recently issued senatorial decree; and those who give shall likewise be pursued by the severity of the canons. But you, who preside in honor of the patriarchs over the remaining Churches, since our constitution has freed you from unlawful promises, must now, by imitating good examples, present pontiffs worthy of their majesty without any loss to the Churches.

For it is unjust that bribery should have a place among you when, through divine consideration, we have closed it to laymen. Therefore, if anyone believes that the bishop of the apostolic Church or a patriarchal bishop is to be promoted by the ambition of payment, whether personally or through parents or any servants whatsoever [Note: Justinian, when he prohibited magistracies from being conferred without payment—without “support,” that is, money and corruption—added with the utmost severity in Novel 8 that the sale of all magistracies is the source of every crime, the beginning and end of injustice: “to extract silver for offices is the prelude and culmination of every wickedness.” How much more necessary is it to avoid the ambition of gifts and the corruption involved in ecclesiastical offices when priestly dignities are conferred! The Council of Chalcedon: “If any bishop has performed an ordination for money and reduced the unbought grace to a sale,” and so forth. “Whoever has sold for a price the grace that cannot be sold,” and so forth. Code, *If Anyone Is a Bishop*, chapter *Of the Saints*, 1; chapter *From Many*, question 3. Anthemius also condemns this venality, law *If Anyone*, Code, *On Bishops and Clerics*. Constitutions of pontiffs against simony are also extant in Book V of the Decretals. The following letter of Athalaric to Salvantius, letter 16, likewise belongs here. FORN.], we decree that he himself must return what he received and suffer in every respect what the canons have established.

But if anyone who has given or promised anything fears to make it public while the recipient is still alive, let the Church whose support is found to have secured the bishop’s ordination reclaim it from his heirs or from those acting for his heirs; and let the surviving persons nevertheless be branded with the mark of infamy.

We likewise order that the remaining orders be regulated under the same strictness. But if, through the discovery of some deceitful scheme, a person has been bound by oaths imposed through intermediaries, so that, while preserving the condition of his soul, he can neither approve the iniquity entrusted to him nor dare to accuse it, we grant permission to any honest persons in each individual city to report this crime to the competent judges. Whatever may be recovered through such proof, so that we may encourage those who follow us in proving such matters, let the person who chooses to publicize the offense receive one-third of the adjudicated property [Ac.: “of that property”].

Let the remainder benefit the Churches themselves, since what appears to have been extorted will nevertheless be useful either for their buildings or for their sacred vessels. For it is fitting to convert to good uses what hostile wickedness sought to defraud.

Let the perverse greed of the malicious therefore cease. Where can those who have been shut out from the source proceed? Let the just condemnation of Simon be recalled and feared, for he believed that the Author of every gift could be purchased.

Pray for us, therefore, while observing our edicts, because you know that they accord with the divine mysteries. But so that the prince’s desire may more easily become known to everyone’s mind, we order this to be announced to the Senate and to the people through the Urban Prefect, so that the whole community may recognize that we pursue those who appear rather to oppose the divine majesty.

You too must announce this to all the bishops whom, by God’s favor, you govern. Let no one who was able to recognize the established provisions be free from guilt.

## LETTER XVI. TO SALVANTIUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, PREFECT OF THE CITY

**ATHALARIC, KING.** He orders that his edict and the senatorial decrees concerning the suppression of simony be engraved on marble tablets and placed before the atrium of the basilica of Saint Peter.

It is a welcome thing to make public everything that will benefit the community, so that what could have been merely a desired joy may become a general one. Otherwise, harm is understood to arise if benefits are concealed [Greek and Cujas: “is born”].

Recently, the most distinguished Senate, wishing to remove from its splendor the stain of the foulest suspicion, prudently resolved that, at the consecration of the most blessed pope, no one should pollute himself with abominable greed; a penalty was also established for anyone who should attempt such things. This was not unjust, since the merit of the chosen man is truly sought when money is not loved.

Approving and enlarging upon this discovery, we sent to the most blessed pope the provisions that had previously been issued and that shine with the same authority, so that profane ambition might be removed from the integrity of the holy Church.

[Note: Here I consider two matters worthy of incidental notice. Athalaric ordered that the senatorial decrees be engraved on marble tablets for lasting permanence, just as formerly they were engraved on bronze; see law 2, *On the Origin of Law*. Plato, in the *Minos*, relates that Talus, king of Crete, went around the villages each year carrying laws engraved on bronze tablets; hence he was called “Bronze,” “having the laws written on bronze tablets,” from which he was named “Bronze.” The second point is that they were to be placed in a prominent and conspicuous location—namely, the atrium of blessed Peter—so that they would be open to everyone and could be read from the ground. Thus Plato, in Book II of the *Laws*, orders that the laws concerning things for sale be affixed to a pillar in the middle of the marketplace, “the laws of the magistracy having been set up on a stele.” Demosthenes, *Third Philippic*: “Displaying the decrees of your ancestors, which they deposited after writing them on a bronze stele for the Acropolis.” FORNER.]

We wish you to bring this to the knowledge of the Senate and the Roman people without any delay, so that what we desire to be guarded through the zeal of all may be fixed in everyone’s heart.

But so that the principal benefit may remain attached both to the present age and to future ages, we order that our defined provisions and the senatorial decrees be suitably engraved on marble tablets and placed before the atrium of blessed Peter the apostle as a public testimony [Note: Laws were formerly placed in church atria; see Cujas, Book I of the *Feudal Law*, title 17; and Book III of Charlemagne’s *Capitularies*, title “How.” Thus the rector of the Church. See Justinian’s Novel S, at the end. JURET.].

For this is a worthy place to contain both the glorious reward of our work and the praiseworthy decrees of the most distinguished Senate. For this purpose we have sent the man whose return will inform us that what we ordered has been fulfilled. For he who gives an order appears to possess it uncertainly when he learns of the accomplishment of what he commanded only slowly.

## LETTER XVII. TO SALVANTIUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, PREFECT OF THE CITY

**ATHALARIC, KING.** He decrees that certain noble Romans, who were being held in prison merely on suspicion that a revolt had arisen, are to be released; and he permits them to seek redress under the just laws.

If ancient rulers sought the Roman walls for the exquisite joy of the peoples, so that citizens singularly deserving of them should not possess something in common with the rest, it is wrong, amid so many pleasant circumstances, for them to endure prolonged sadness. For the rejoicing of that city is a general wish; the rest must necessarily rejoice if it happens that the head of the world rejoices [Note: Theodoret, in his *Letter to the Romans*, says that public magistrates, “those who proclaim the favors,” tax collectors, and governors of provinces proceed from Rome, so that what happens at Rome must be known to everyone. Hence Justinian, in the preface prefixed to the *Digest*, says, concerning the composition of the Digest, that the custom of the city of Rome should be followed by all cities, because Rome is the head of the world, “the epitome of the inhabited world,” as Athenaeus writes: the world’s compendium and the common fatherland of all, law 33, *Rome*, Digest, *On Municipalities*. Nevertheless, the practice of the Roman city should be followed only when its example has not been corrupted. And, as Proculus elegantly says: “One must consider not so much what has been done at Rome as what ought to be done,” law 12, *But It Is Permitted*, Digest, *On the Duties of Governors*. FORN.]

From the report of the apostolic Pope John and our nobles we have learned that certain Romans have been worn down by the punishment of such prolonged imprisonment merely on suspicion of sedition, so that the entire city has contracted grief at their continual misfortune, and neither festival days nor any dignity of their own name—which is especially welcome among us [Ms.: “among you”]—has come to their aid.

This displeased us because of the harshness of what they had suffered, since they are not reported to have been convicted in judgment, yet they endured the punishments and tortures due to the wicked. Therefore we admonish your Greatness by the present commands not to delay releasing them wherever you may find them.

Even if it should become clear that they are involved in some offense, we decree that, through the intercessions mentioned above, they are now free from fear. But if they are confident that they endured tortures while innocent, we give their complaints a free voice, so that under the just laws they may seek redress for what they suffered through unjust acts. For we do not wish innocent people to be oppressed by judges when it is established that they have been raised up for the judges’ protection.

Let the Romans now be restored to their former joy. Let them not believe that anyone can please us unless he chooses to treat them with restrained equality. Let them understand that our parents undertook dangers through arduous efforts for their peace, while we act at great expense so that they may rejoice with outspoken exultation.

And if they have hitherto suffered anything unjustly or harshly, let them not believe that our gentleness will neglect it. We do not even allow ourselves leisure, so that they may enjoy secure peace and tranquil joy. Let them quickly perceive that we cannot love those whom they have abhorred for their offenses.

For whose favor can those obtain who have deserved to displease their own fellow citizens? And while they had time to gain public affection, they acted in such a way that they ought justly to be detested [Ms. A.: “cut down”]?

## XVIII. EDICT OF KING ATHALARIC

1. Against invaders of the property of others.  
2. Against those who affix titles in the public name.  
3. Against those who cunningly and perversely obtain decisions of the rulers.  
4. Against those who divide the marriages of others.  
5. Against adulterers.  
6. Against those who joined themselves to two wives.  
7. Against men and women who keep concubines.  
8. Against those who extort gifts through terror.  
9. Against sorcerers.  
10. Against murderers.  
11. Against those who appeal twice in the same case from ordinary judges.  
12. Against violators of the edicts both of Athalaric himself and of Theodoric.

Antiquity wisely decreed that the whole community should be admonished by general edicts, through which every offense may be corrected without burdening the offender with shame. Everyone thinks that an edict is addressed to him when no individual is identified; and a person becomes like an innocent man when he happens to be purged along with the community.

Thus our true piety is also preserved: fear arises while the sword remains sheathed, and correction is achieved without bloodshed. We are moved while remaining calm; we threaten while at rest; and we anger mercifully when we condemn only vices.

For a long time the complaints of various people have resounded in our ears through repeated whispers: certain persons, despising civilized conduct, aspire to live with beastlike savagery. Returning to a primitive, rustic condition, they regard human law as ferociously hateful to themselves.

We have now judged that such persons must suitably be restrained, so that we may pursue crimes hostile to good morals at the very time when, by divine power, we resist the enemies of the commonwealth. Both things are harmful, and both must be driven away; but vices rage all the more heavily when they are found within. One evil reclines upon another. The ranks of enemies fall more easily if we remove offenses from our own age.

### 1. Against Invaders of the Property of Others

First, we condemn with the severity of the laws and with our indignation the harmful practice of invasion, under which neither civilized conduct can be named nor possessed. We establish that the sanction of the divine Valentinian, long and wickedly neglected, shall be revived against those who, disregarding the order of law, presume personally or through their agents to enter violently, after expelling the possessor, upon urban or rural estates. We do not wish any part of that detestable strictness to be softened by moderation.

We further add that, if any freeborn person is not considered capable of satisfying the law defined above, he shall immediately be subjected to the punishment of deportation, because one who knew that he could not endure punishment elsewhere ought to have considered the public laws more carefully.

Therefore, if the competent judges to whom the committed offense may belong, although able to remove the invader, allow the usurpation to remain, they shall each be deprived of their office and made liable to our fisc for as much as the usurper could have been condemned to pay, while the established penalties remain in force against the actual authors of the crime.

But if anyone, driven to such madness and acting in a tyrannical spirit, neglects to obey the public law and, powerful in strength, despises the smallness of the office assigned to him [Ac.: “the perversity of the office assigned”], let him be brought by the judge’s report to our attention, so that, once the *sajones* have been authorized to execute the sentence, he may experience the vengeance of royal power because he refused to obey the judge.

### 2. Against Those Who Affix Titles in the Public Name

Since even the highest rulers must live under the common rule of law, if anyone, disregarding the legal procedure, presumes to affix titles in the public name [Note: It belongs solely to the fisc to place titles on the estates of others. A private person may not place either his own or public titles upon his own property, or upon the property of more powerful persons or of others; nor may he impress marks or hang royal curtains—or, as Ambrose says, royal draperies. Many passages concerning this matter are found in the Novels and the Code. The placing of titles upon churches was also prohibited by a synod held in the time of Gregory, during the reign of the Emperor Maurice. Titles are therefore lawfully imposed by the fisc alone—that is, with the fact attested, public persons present, and the solemn legal procedure observed. Gregory also complains in one letter about a certain chartularius named Stephen, because he invaded individuals’ properties in the name of the fisc and imposed titles without a case being heard. BROSS.], let him become liable to the possessor in the amount established by the sanction mentioned above.

Rightly, too, he is struck by the penalty for sacrilege who, by the weight of an unlawful invasion, has dared to burden the majesty of the royal name [Note: *To invade*: above, Book I, letter 15, and often elsewhere. *Action for invasion*: laws 5 and 6, Theodosian Code, *On Notification and the Publication of Rescripts*; Valentinian’s Novel 12, *On Episcopal Hearings*. We had long ago removed the same error from chapter 25 of Book V of Isidore’s *Etymologies*, but in the most recent edition we saw it repeated, with *persuasio* written for *pervasio*. What is more, the error occurs in other authors’ books as well. Vitruvius, Book IX, chapter 4, end: “Each month the sun, persuading the signs” [for *pervading* them], “increases and decreases the spaces of days and hours.” Salvian, Bishop of Marseilles, Book IV *On Providence*, where he censures the plundering of the rich: “through the persuasions of the powerful,” and so forth. In Book V he uses the same word twice correctly, *pervasoribus* and *pervasionibus*. Eusebius of Emesa likewise, Homily 11, *On Easter*: “He abandons the invader, remains deceived by the spoils, and is left bereft, the robber.” FORN.]

He shall also pay the expenses of the litigation when defeated in judgment. Such expenses are imposed because detestable quarrels are encouraged when wicked people are defeated without suffering harm; and calumniators do not grieve at the loss of their honor if they escape financial penalties.

### 3. Against Those Who Cunningly and Perversely Obtain Decisions of the Rulers

If anyone believes that something may be obtained from our archives, let him not conceal from his adversary, insofar as it concerns his case, anything in the complete sequence of the commands that have been issued [Ms. and Ac.: “the customary sequence”]. If he fails to do so, let him lose what he has obtained; or, if he attempts to act on any part of it, let it nevertheless be held invalid. For we wish only those to use our benefits whom we do not know to cultivate trickery.

### 4. Against Those Who Divide the Marriages of Others

Whoever attempts to divide another person’s marriage through blameworthy persuasion shall have his own marriage declared unlawful, so that he may feel that what he maliciously attempted to do to another has happened to himself.

But if, because of his interference with another’s union, he is deprived of conjugal affection, we legally deny him a future marriage, since he does not deserve to obtain the rewards of marital respect who has dared to attack the union of the marriage bed.

Yet, so that our vengeance may not leave some guilty persons untouched, those who have no hope of a present or future marriage, if they presume through deceitful scheming to interfere with another’s marriage, shall be deprived of half their property, to be immediately assigned to the rights of the fisc.

If, however, poverty prevents the penalty from being exacted from someone’s property, let them be punished by exile, so that—an abomination to say—they may not appear to escape the threat of public law merely because they are known to be subject to the lowest fortunes.

Thus our piety has decreed these provisions concerning those who solicit another’s affection.

### 5. Against Adulterers

As for adulterers, we wish everything to be observed with the utmost strictness that could be decreed by an imperial admonition.

### 6. Against Those Who Joined Themselves to Two Wives

No one may be joined to two wives at the same time, for he must know that he will be punished by the loss of his property. Either it is lust, and he is rightly prevented from enjoying it, or it is greed, and he is justly condemned to destitution.

### 7. Against Men and Women Who Keep Concubines

If anyone, through excessive and shameful desire, despising the honor of marriage, chooses to come into the embrace of a concubine, then, if she is freeborn, she shall be assigned in every respect, together with her children, to the yoke of slavery under the wife. Thus she shall perceive herself to be subjected by lawful judgment to the wife whom, through unlawful lust [Ac.: “promised lust”], she believed she could be placed above.

But if a slave woman has advanced to such an offense, then, apart from the penalty of blood, let her be subjected to a matron’s vengeance, so that she may suffer under the judgment of the woman whom she ought to have feared even in her absence.

### 8. Against Those Who Extort Gifts Through Terror

Let no one extort gifts through terror; let no one desire to acquire anything through fraud or detestable wantonness. For only honesty rightly gains profit from the laws.

In support of the most just generosity, we wish that the strictness be observed which antiquity, concerned for the truth, established by law. In this way, as antiquity itself testifies, no opportunity for fraud will remain open, and the authority of truth will grow stronger.

Otherwise we order that no one regard as valid what the person who created it made uncertain by failing to fulfill what the laws or rights prescribe.

### 9. Against Sorcerers

Let the severity of the laws also pursue sorcerers [Note: Constantine: “The others whom the common people call sorcerers because of the magnitude of their crimes,” law 5, Code, *On Sorcerers and Astrologers*. They are discussed in Book IV, letter 22. FORN.], and those who believe that something should be sought from their wicked arts. For it is impious for us to be lenient toward those whom heavenly piety does not permit to remain unpunished.

What greater folly is there than to abandon the Creator of life and follow instead the author of death? Let every shameful act be entirely alien to the judges. Let no one do what the laws condemn, because those who have involved themselves in forbidden excesses must be punished by the penalty decreed.

For what could they condemn in others if they themselves defile themselves through dishonorable contamination? Let a safe moderation also exist among the wealthy.

### 10. Against Murderers

Let the madness of killing be restrained. For the presumption of the hands is proven to be an act of war, especially in those whom the authority of our protection strengthens.

If anyone nevertheless attempts to act otherwise through wicked presumption, let him be held a violator of our command.

### 11. Against Repeated Appeals in One Case

We do not permit a subordinate to appeal a second time from the ordinary judges in a single case, lest what was devised as a remedy for the innocent appear in some way to be an asylum for criminals.

But if anyone attempts to repeat what has been forbidden, let him depart deprived of his case.

### 12. Against Violators of the Edicts of Athalaric and Theodoric

But lest, by touching upon only a few matters, we be thought unwilling to have the rest observed, we decree that all the edicts both of ourselves and of our lord and grandfather, which have been confirmed by venerable deliberation, as well as the customary public laws, be guarded with the full force of strictness. They protect themselves with such strong defenses that they are also surrounded by the intervention of our oath.

Why should we run through many matters? Let the customary rule of the laws and the integrity of our commands be observed everywhere [Note: See Theodosius’s Novel, title 44, *That They Should Not Be Led Away*, and Justinian’s *Institutes*, title *On the Penalty of Those Who Litigate Recklessly*. JURET.].

## LETTER XIX. TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

**ATHALARIC, KING.** He writes that he has issued an edict in twelve chapters and orders that it be read in the Senate and posted by the Urban Prefect for thirty days in the most prominent places.

The blameworthy excess of another usually provides the occasion for praiseworthy commands, and, in a remarkable way, the foundations of justice arise from an opportunity created by iniquity. Equity is silent if guilt is not loudly denounced; and the ruler’s mind rests inactive when it has not been provoked by some complaint.

Compelled by the voices of complainants and admonished by the appeals of frequent groups of people concerning certain matters, we have written, in the form of an edictal proclamation, twelve chapters necessary for Roman tranquility and to be preserved forever, just as civil law is understood to have been established. When observed, these provisions should not weaken the remaining law but rather strengthen it [Note: The reading of the preceding edict in the Senate follows Roman practice, by which the laws and constitutions of emperors were confirmed after being read in the Senate; see law 8, *Human*, Code, *On Laws and Senatusconsults*. We shall explain this custom more fully elsewhere. FORN.].

Let these provisions be read in the splendor of your assembly, and let the Urban Prefect, in the customary solemn manner, have them posted for thirty days [Note: Edicts, or the laws of rulers, remained posted for thirty days, as in the following letter. An example is found in Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book XIX, chapter 5. JUR.], in the most prominent places, so that, once our civil spirit has been recognized, hope may be removed from savage conduct.

For with what confidence would a headstrong man assume what he knows the ruler’s clemency has condemned? Let love of discipline return to everyone; through it, small things grow together and greater things are preserved.

For this reason, with God’s help, we admonish our armies through frequent expeditions, so that we may perceive the whole community living in accordance with the laws [Greek, Cujas, and Ga.: “we move”]. Let this exchange of rewards be returned to our mind: let the man whom you know to be occupied with the interests of the commonwealth be disturbed by the approach of complaints only very rarely [Ed.: “by the publication of complaints”].

Let the judges maintain their lawful strictness; let them reject the desire for the foulest venality [Note: We repeatedly read in Cassiodorus severe attacks on the monetary corruption of judges and magistrates in Philo the Jew, when he discusses the duty of a judge. FORN.]. Fear puts everything in order if the accused finds no crime in the judge.

## LETTER XX. TO ALL THE JUDGES OF THE PROVINCES

**ATHALARIC, KING.** He decrees that his edict be publicly posted for thirty days in accordance with the solemn custom.

Since, with God’s help, we appoint you to our provinces by annual renewal, and since courts are distributed throughout all the regions of Italy, we understand that an abundance of cases arises from a scarcity of justice.

For your negligence is shown to be at fault whenever people are compelled by us to seek the benefits of the laws [Note: Roman emperors were always particularly concerned that litigants should not be harassed by the expense and labor of pursuing their cases in distant courts. In this connection I may cite what Justinian writes in Novel 17, § “If It Is Your Concern,” and Novel 23, § “That Matter”; add Valentinian, Novel 10, title *On Confiscation*, and Marcian, Novel 1, *Let No One Be Produced*. BROSS.].

For who would choose to seek so far away what he saw had come to him in his own seat? But so that we might remove from you clever excuses and remove harsh necessities from the provincials [Note: It is also provided in formula 22 of Book VI and in Justinian’s Novel 17 that provincials should not be compelled to seek justice at the emperor’s court. FORN.], we have decreed, through the definition of an edictal proclamation, concerning certain cases hitherto neglected through the worst sluggishness, so that your confidence in judging rightly might increase and malicious audacity might gradually be diminished.

Have this proclamation posted for thirty days in public assemblies according to the solemn custom, so that anyone who presumes after these remedies to remain despairing may rightly be held condemned.

## LETTER XXI. TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

**ATHALARIC, KING.** He orders that teachers of grammar, eloquence, and law receive the emoluments established for them without any diminution.

We rightly recognize that the concerns of sons have been entrusted to their fathers, so that those whose interest it is that Roman studies flourish ought themselves to consider their advancement. For it cannot be believed that you can be less concerned with that from which both an ornament is added to your family and counsel is supplied to the community through constant reading.

Recently, since our concern for you is vigilant, we learned from the whispering of certain persons that the teachers of Roman eloquence were not receiving the established rewards for their labor, and that, through the bargaining of some, the sum assigned to the masters of the schools appeared to be diminished. Therefore, since it is evident that reward nourishes the arts, we judged it wrong that anything should be taken away from the teachers of youth, who ought rather to be urged toward glorious studies by increases in their benefits. [Col. 0787C]

For the school of the grammarians is the first and most beautiful foundation of letters, the glorious mother of eloquence, which teaches one to think for praise and to speak without fault. In the course of speech it recognizes an incongruous error just as good morals detest an external crime. For just as a musician produces the sweetest melody through harmonious choirs, so the grammarian knows how to chant a meter through accents appropriately arranged.

Grammar is the teacher of words and the adornment of the human race; through the practice of the most beautiful reading, it is known to assist us with the counsels of the ancients. Barbarians do not make use of this; among lawful rulers it is recognized as something unique. [Col. 0788A] Other nations possess arms, but eloquence alone is found to serve Roman rulers. From it the contest of orators sounds the trumpet-call of civil law; from it the most noble eloquence commends all the great men; and, to say nothing of the rest, our very speech comes from it.

For this reason, Conscript Fathers, with the Divinity favoring, we grant you this responsibility and authority [Note: [Col. 0787D] See Justinian’s Pragmatic Sanction after Julian’s novella above, chapter 22. GR. and CUJ.]: that the successor in the school of liberal letters—both the grammarian and the orator, as well as the interpreter of the law—may receive from those concerned, without any diminution, the benefits of his predecessor; and that, once confirmed by the authority of your first order and of the rest of the most illustrious Senate, he may suffer no wrongful challenge from anyone concerning the transfer or reduction of the allowances, so long as he is found fit for the work he has undertaken.
