[Col. 0788B] Rather, under your appointment and supervision, he shall enjoy the security of his emoluments, while the Prefect of the City likewise preserves what has been established.

And lest anything be left uncertain at the will of those who make the payments, as soon as six months have elapsed, let the aforesaid teachers receive half of the established sum. Let the remaining periods of the year be concluded with the due repayment of the allowances, so that they are not forced to depend upon the irritation of another, for whom it is a sacrilege to have been idle even for some part of an hour. For we wish what has been decreed to be guarded with the greatest firmness, so that if anyone whose concern it is should think this quasi-obligatory function ought to be delayed, he himself may suffer the losses customarily imposed by usury, because, through greed deserving punishment, he has withheld the just benefits from those who labor commendably [Mss., *commorantibus*, “those residing”]. [Col. 0788C]

For if we bestow our resources upon actors for the amusement of the people [Ed., *collectione*, “collection”] [Note: [Col. 0787D] This is an honorable collection, deriving its argument from pleasure toward the cultivation of morals; Demosthenes uses it in *Olynthiac* II, when he advises the Athenians that, setting aside the pleasure of spectacles, they should serve utility more, and that theatrical funds should be transferred to military uses: “He orders theatrical funds to become military funds” (*Θεωρικὰ χρήματα κελεύει γίνεσθαι τὰ στρατιωτικά*). Libanius. FORN.], and those who are not nearly so necessary obtain them with the greatest eagerness, how much more ought they to be provided without delay to those through whom both honorable morals arise and eloquent minds are nurtured for our palace!

We command this to be made known to your venerable assembly in the presence of the present teachers of letters, so that, just as they recognize that we are concerned for their benefits, they may likewise know that we are demanding from them, with greater insistence, the advancement of young men.

Let that saying now cease, which complaining teachers have appropriated from the satirists: that a talent ought not to be occupied with two concerns. [Note: [Col. 0787D] Quintilian, Book X, chapter 3: “For the mind cannot honestly apply itself to everything at once; and wherever it turns its gaze, it ceases to observe what had been its purpose.” For this reason the Emperor Justinian forbids anyone to enroll in several military services at once or to join one military belt to another, *Codex* XII.5, *Qui militare possint*. Justinian also enacted that no one should sit as assessor for two magistrates or undertake the care of both jurisdictions, *Codex*, final law, *De assessoribus*. Livy, Book IX on the Macedonian War, displays an ancient Roman law by which no one could hold two magistracies at the same time, especially curule magistracies, nor could he do so by hereditary right; nor is it fitting for several magistracies to be administered by one person, since one task is best completed by one person. “It is bad for the same person to rule several offices, for one task is best accomplished by one person” (*Φαῦλον εἶναι τὸ πλείους ἀρχὰς τὸν αὐτὸν ἄρχειν, ἓν γὰρ ὑφ’ ἑνὸς ἔργον ἄριστ’ ἀποτελεῖται*), Aristotle, *Politics* II.10. I judge this to be interpreted as follows: when the mind is drawn away into different occupations. Otherwise, nothing prevents a person from applying himself to several studies, provided that attention to one strengthens the way toward another—as the knowledge of civil law contributes substantially to the practice of advocacy and the administration of judgments; and conversely, we daily find that forensic practice contributes greatly to a true and genuine knowledge of the laws, so that we think each can scarcely preserve its proper bounds without the support of the other. FORN.]

Behold, they are now shown to possess a tolerable maintenance; therefore, with good reason, continually adhering to a single concern, let them devote the full vigor of their minds to the studies of the liberal arts. [Col. 0789A] [Note: [Col. 0789D] On this matter see law 1, *De variis et extraordinariis cognitionibus*; Seneca, Book XIII, Letter 89; Pliny, preface to Book XIV. FORN.]

## EPISTOLA XXII. TO PAULINUS, A MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND CONSUL, KING ATHALARIC

He adorns Paulinus and his family with splendid praises. Then he confers upon him the insignia of the consulship.

The conduct of human beings would wander indiscriminately and confusedly if either guilt had no fear or virtue no rewards. But since both are enclosed within their own limits and proper bounds, there must be no doubt concerning him who has deserved to be chosen by the judgment of the sovereign. For we decide nothing either from hatred or, seduced by some gratification, from favor. Our choice proceeds from merit, and a man is brought nearer to the royal spirit in proportion as he is joined to it by good pursuits.

Do not fear those who are absent, nor be anxious because the prince has not seen you. Perhaps the common sort of humanity can remain hidden; the offspring of the Senate cannot remain unknown. Those who are upheld by merit are well known, and whoever is praised with fame as witness is sufficiently recognized. Therefore, though situated at the greatest distance, the serene eye of our mind looked upon you and saw a merit that had not remained concealed.

Your purpose, widely celebrated, has been enlarged by public opinion, which testified to your lineage by the weight of your character, not by your age [Note: [Col. 0789D] The course of virtue is swifter than that of age, according to Marcus Tullius, *Philippic* V. “For neither gray hair nor wrinkles can suddenly confer authority; rather, an earlier life honorably lived offers the final fruits of authority,” as the same author says in *Cato the Elder*. Thus Jerome the presbyter says that the name “presbyter” is derived not from old age but from the gravity and maturity of character. FORN.]. Nor was it proper that our judgment should find anything in need of correction in one whom so great a family had produced.

You have restored the seed of your lineage through the fruits of your character. Long age has taken nothing away from you. Rome has recognized in you the ancient Decii—the Decii, I say, a lineage honored in former ages, the support of liberty, the glory of the Senate, and the singular proclamation of the Roman name. To one of them in particular it is attributed that, when the state was endangered, he emerged against the most savage enemy when the position of the republic was endangered; and among so great a multitude of brave men he alone was found to have loved his country more.

These examples continually kindle us by admonition, because the praise of parents is a great stimulus to modesty [Note: [Col. 0789D] “The praise of parents is a great stimulus to modesty,” a maxim resembling Virgil’s:

> “Both father Aeneas and uncle Hector stir him on.”

Here Athalaric means Theodoric, his ancestor. FORN.]; for we do not allow ourselves to be unequal to those whose authorship we rejoice to acknowledge.

Therefore, with God as our auspice, as has been said, in the twelfth indiction (A.D. 534), assume the insignia of the consulship—a lofty honor, but one native to your family. You complete the consular page; you are frequently named in the course of the years [Note: [Col. 0789D] Years were reckoned by the Roman consuls, and at Athens by the eponymous officials. Julius Pollux, Book VIII, *Onomasticon*: “This man is the eponym, and from him time is reckoned”; *Novella*: “Concerning the consuls”; and Novel 47, section 3, *Digest*, *De accusationibus*; see also above, Book VI, in the formula of the consulship: “The name of the years,” etc. FORN.]. And while abundance generally tends to produce weariness, your name, repeated again and again, is always made glorious.

Finally, Heaven has favored this lineage, granting the wishes of its fathers [Note: [Col. 0789D] The Voconian and Salic laws preferred males to females, as did Roman law, *Digest*, *De statu hominum*, law “In many matters.” Menander calls this the pillar of a family:

> “For sons, the males, are the pillar of a house.”

FORN.], in producing happy male offspring [Ed., *genera*, “kinds/offspring”]. Hence it is that, at that summit of affairs, you scarcely see an outsider as colleague: you have as judges those whom you have as parents.

O singular proclamation of the age! The Roman Senate is almost filled by your family. Truly, now one body must be spoken of, since it is clear that a fellowship of neighboring kin has been mingled together.

But do not let confidence in your family weaken your efforts, nor believe that it can suffice for you to rejoice in their renown. More is demanded of an heir to good things, since he is continually summoned onward by the virtues of his ancestors. Add distinguished praises to your elders; let the succeeding age follow with some memorable novelty. For if it is glorious for descendants to extend ancestral resources, how much more excellent is it to increase inherited virtues! [Col. 0790B]

We praised your domestic character in your private conduct; but now it is fitting for you to display something greater before the public, where neither tender age may flatter itself, nor fear claim anyone, nor a teacher take charge.

## EPISTOLA XXIII. TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME, KING ATHALARIC

He greatly exalts Venantius, Paulinus’s father, and Paulinus himself, whom he had created consul; and he asks that they favor his election.

Consider carefully, Conscript Fathers, what judgment we should form of you, when we choose for the highest summits of dignity men of your lineage whom we have never seen—not through the disdain of negligence, but through the honorable presumption of nature. Let matters thought uncertain come to examination. For who would think deliberation necessary where nothing is considered ambiguous?

Our kindness embraces everyone, but such men we proclaim with the testimony of truth. Favor precedes, but incorruptible judgment follows. For just as you are one body of the Senate, so you come together in one praiseworthy purpose. Therefore, to have loved you is itself a judgment, from which the increase of liberty and the ornament of our rule grow.

The causes of things are always in the seed; the fruit that is produced reveals its authors. Whatever we merit from the Divinity is gathered from fortunate offspring. Hence it is that we regard the patrician Venantius with admiration: he rejoices in fruitful offspring and is equal to so many consulships.

For he raised children whom no discrimination could distinguish in praise, equal in the weight of their moderation, alike in the liveliness of their intellect [Note: [Col. 0790D] The likeness of brothers or twins wins favor, *Digest*, laws 39 and 40, *De aedilicio edicto*; Pliny, Book VII, chapter 12, concerning Marcus Antonius the triumvir; Martial, Book IX:

> “What new Leda has borne you servants so alike?” etc.

See also law 22, *Proinde*, under the *Lex Aquilia*. FORN.], and truly brothers in their fellowship of character. Their infancy he nourished with good arts, and their youth he also trained in arms, forming their minds with letters and their limbs in the gymnasium; teaching them to show steadfastness to friends and loyalty to masters. Whatever divine favor granted that man, you may see transmitted to his descendants in complete perfection. [Col. 0791A]

Let others boast of being wealthy in possessions and regard riches alone as the highest good. In this household, however, inheritance is entered not only through patrimonies but also through virtues. This is what truly makes men rich, when no better profit can exist than to have succeeded to the praises of one’s ancestors.

It has also been proved in his case that good stewards lack nothing. Restraining what belongs to others, distributing his own with moderation, and admirable through an unusual excellence, he produced so many consuls without burdening anyone. Let him, hearing these things, receive the fruit of his good works; let him recognize that he has as herald the man whom he had as master, and that among so many lights of the nobility he has been praised in a singular manner.

For if receiving the palm once adorns men, what must we think of the man who deserves so many consulships in his sons? Therefore, Conscript Fathers, we clothe your ward Paulinus with the dignity of laurel [MS., *aurea*, “golden”], so that his youth, which shines with merits, may also gleam in the triumphal robe.

The family of the Decii does not marvel at this honor, since their halls are full of laureled fasces. To others this dignity comes rarely; in this succession of lineage it is almost born consular.

Favor, therefore, Conscript Fathers, our gifts and likewise your candidate. For although you are generally called fathers to all, to him you are also specifically parents. Your name, derived from the similarity of your care, confirms this by the most faithful naming of things [Ac., *applicatione*, “application”]—not through a commonplace and customary use of the word [Note: [Col. 0791D] He calls it a transferred, ordinary, customary, and almost neglected usage. Thus Pliny, Book VII, chapter 5: “In Egypt it is a transferred usage.” Book XXVII, chapter 2: “If a table is present, we see that nothing is placed upon it in the customary manner,” also because it is clear that many religious observances prevail. So too our jurists, *Digest*, law 55, *Si patroni*, *Ad senatusconsultum Trebellianum*. Nor should that transferred usage be omitted: law 1, *Digest*, *De iure patronatus*: “He should not carry out law 1 in a merely transferred manner”; law 1, *Digest*, *Ad senatusconsultum Turpillianum*: “He is a false accuser who performs the duty of accusing in a merely transferred manner,” that is, negligently, not truly, and without good faith fulfilling the role of accuser. BROSS.], but through the honorable lot of birth.

May the Divine Powers grant you this happiness perpetually, so that, although you extend favor to outsiders, you may rejoice more vigorously in your own offspring.

## EPISTOLA XXIV. TO THE SENATOR, PREFECT OF THE PRAETORIUM, KING ATHALARIC

He enumerates the dignities that Cassiodorus had held with the highest honor and integrity under Theodoric himself and under Athalaric. Then, after heaping extraordinary praises upon him, he confers the praetorian prefecture.

If our will had found you still concealed, or perhaps without honor, we would indeed rejoice at having discovered you; but we would rightly have doubts about your conduct, because in a new man there is more hope than fruit. But since you glory in the countless advancements and great judgment of our lord grandfather, it is inappropriate to submit to debate one whom we can scarcely proclaim without admiration. Such a judgment must not be examined but venerated, since there can be no doubt about his deeds when we are known to have been chosen by him himself. Always devoted to divine supplication, he earned by his merits the power to do what heavenly grace would preserve. [Col. 0792A]

What man did that ruler either appoint to command armies without receiving him back victorious, or gird as judge [Mss. Niv. and Gam., *ungens*, “anointing”; Jur.: perhaps *augens*, “exalting”] without proving him most just? You would think that he had treated of future affairs; for whatever his mind had conceived, the result always rendered back, and through an extraordinary devotion to wisdom he had no doubt about what he had truthfully foreseen would come to pass.

Finally, through you we can demonstrate the ruler’s excellent institution: when he took you, still young, into the office of quaestor, he soon found you endowed with conscience and mature in knowledge of the laws. You were truly the supreme glory of the age, making him, who was solicitous about everything, secure through your unoffending service, while you supported the immense burden of royal intellect by the powers of your eloquence. [Col. 0792B]

He had in you an agreeable stylist, a stern guardian of justice, and a man separated from avarice. You did not sell his benefits by any abominable assessment [Note: [Col. 0792D] *Novella* 8, and above, in this book, letters 15 and 16. FORN.], so that your honor might increase your wealth in reputation while being in no way subject to a price. Hence you appeared joined to the most equitable ruler by a glorious affection, because you were separated from vices by a praiseworthy withdrawal.

He burdened you, as the wisest judge, with the weight of those who appealed to you; and he presumed so much upon the deliberative judgment known to be in your mind that, in place of a favor, he offered your judgment without hesitation to those in distress.

How often did he set you against ancient nobles, when those whom such great length of years had equipped were not sufficient for your beginnings? Clearly there was something extraordinary to praise in you: a mind open to earning benefits and closed against the vices of greed. For, I know not how, a hand closed against greed and open to justice is rare among human beings. [Col. 0792C]

Let us come to the magisterial dignity, which you are known to have attained not through the dignity [The word *dignitate* appears corrupt; perhaps *indignitate*, “unworthiness.” Thus Seneca sometimes says that dignities are approached through unworthy means. JURET.] of money but through the support of character, and in which position you were always present for the quaestors. For when refined eloquence was needed, the case was immediately entrusted to your intelligence. The kindly prince demanded from you what he knew he had not entrusted to anyone else; and, by a certain preliminary favor, the labor of others was dispensed with [Mss. Gr. and Cuj., *labore*, “by labor”], so that he might crown you with the abundant praise of his judgment.

No dignity under your authority guarded its own proper limits, since it is clear that what many nobles would most sincerely have had to perform was entrusted to your conscience. No one knew how to mutter anything contrary about you, although you endured envy because of the prince’s favor. The integrity of your conduct overcame those wishing to disparage you; your adversaries often spoke what their minds did not hold, compelled to do so. For every form of malice fears to profess anything against manifest goodness, lest it be exposed to universal hatred. [Col. 0792D]

You acted as a familiar judge for the master of affairs and as an intimate nobleman. When he was free from public cares, he demanded from your discussions the judgments of the wise, so that he might equal the ancients through his own deeds. As a most searching investigator, he examined the courses of the stars, the curves of the sea, and the marvels of springs, so that, after more carefully investigating the natures of things, he might appear to be a philosopher clad in purple [Note: [Col. 0793] Below, in the following letter, “purple praises”; Book VIII, letter 5, “purple infancy.” FORNER.].

It would take too long to set everything forth. Let us rather turn to our benefits, so that what he was known to owe may rightly be felt by you to have been paid by the heir of the empire. Therefore, with God’s help, through whom all things prosper, from the twelfth indiction (A.D. 534) we place you in the seat and insignia of the praetorian prefecture, so that the provinces, which we have hitherto known to be wearied by the actions of bad men, may receive a proven judge without fear. [Col. 0793B]

Although you possess a paternal prefecture celebrated throughout the Italian world, we do not set before you the examples of others: you have fulfilled the old standards and the wishes of all through your character [Variant: *voto*, “wish”]. With God’s help, traverse the field of glory that we have always known you to desire.

For if this dignity also proves you to be self-controlled, as we believe, then you will have overcome the ambition of the age. You have been accustomed [MS., *sollicitus*, “solicitous”] not to sell justice, but now it is necessary to come more energetically to the aid of those injured by injustice. Let an incorruptible judgment watch against hands accustomed to wrongdoing; let fraudulent zeal be excluded everywhere, because it is worthy that this should proceed through a sincere judge.

By delaying for a long time, we wearied the wishes of everyone on your behalf, so that we might test the goodwill of the whole community toward you and make you arrive more desirable to all. Human nature has this characteristic: what is obtained quickly becomes tiresome, since everything precious grows cheap when offered; conversely, what is granted after some delay is received more sweetly.

But we are not content merely with the praise of your earlier years. Investigate everything belonging to the titles of the praetorian prefecture, which the greed of others appears to have defrauded. Let no one boast of his thefts or prejudicial acts. We have brought light to concealed matters through you, since no one will be able to deceive your prudence or tempt your loyalty by any offering.

Establish a rule for this dignity as well, you who in your former offices have offered admirable examples of self-restraint. Although you have held almost all the highest honors equally, you nevertheless have before you the good purposes of conscience, where no limit ought to exist. Here it is proper to have no boundary; here honorable ambition is approved, and even its excess is pleasing. For whatever is to be praised, the more abundantly it is sought, the more gloriously it is found.

## EPISTOLA XXV. TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME, KING ATHALARIC

He writes that he has granted the praetorian prefecture to Cassiodorus, whom he greatly commends.

We have indeed heaped our benefits upon a senator rich in virtues, wealthy in character, and filled with great honors, Conscript Fathers. If you consider his merits, we owe him everything we have bestowed. For by what recompense should he be commended, who so often filled the ears of rulers with brilliant praise?

He handled the dignities entrusted to him with extraordinary gravity, [Col. 0794A] and he strove to create periods that would rightly be praised in a ruler. Truth and the eloquence of his words drew on the ruler’s mind; he reported everything to him in such a way that the very man who had acted was astonished. He alone brought forward what would benefit everyone; and, while he struck his listener with purple praises, he made our rule pleasing to you.

He commends his people when, with a soothing speech, he charms the royal summit, since one such man is believed to have arisen from you, from whom similar things may be demanded. With what eloquence did he, devotedly and with the Senate’s own freedom, uphold the father of our clemency in that very Senate? You remember how, as our orator, he polished his deeds for us, making his virtues more marvelous than his honors.

What we say can be proved in the open. Consider, Conscript Fathers, with what favor you could have been regarded by him, from whose body he saw himself adorned. For praises are more pleasing to glorious rulers than tributes: a stipend is paid even to a tyrant, but praise is owed only to a good ruler.

What do you think, men of praise, was he content merely to strive to praise rulers while they survived, when perhaps the return of rewards is sought from them and the weariness of labor cannot be avoided? He also applied himself to our ancient lineage, learning through reading what scarcely the hoary memory of our ancestors retained.

He brought the kings of the Goths, hidden by long oblivion, out from the hiding-place of antiquity. He restored the Amals together with the splendor of their lineage, clearly showing that we possess a royal stock extending through seventeen generations. He made Gothic history Roman, gathering, as it were into a single crown, the flowering branch that had previously been scattered through the fields of books. [Col. 0794C]

Consider how much he loved you in praising us, since he taught that the nation of your ruler had been marvelous from antiquity, so that, just as you had always been judged noble by your ancestors, an ancient lineage might rule over you.

We believe, Conscript Fathers, that if we wished to continue recounting, the benefits already bestowed would be surpassed. With what labor did he devote himself to the beginnings of our rule, when the novelty of the kingdom demanded that many things be organized? He alone was sufficient for everything. Public dictation required him; our counsels required him; and through his labor it was accomplished that the empire did not have to labor.

We found him a master, but he fulfilled for us the office of quaestor; and, paying out revenues with the most righteous devotion, he willingly displayed to the interests of the heir the prudence he had learned from our predecessor. Yet adding something greater to these services, he aided the beginnings of our kingdom both with arms and with letters.

For while concern for the coasts pressed upon royal thoughts, he was suddenly drawn from the inner chambers of letters and, equal to his ancestors, fearlessly undertook a military command. Since he lacked an enemy, he triumphed through extraordinary character. He fed the Gothic troops assigned to him at his own expense, so that he would neither alarm the provincials nor burden our treasury with the weight of expenses. His arms inflicted no losses upon landowners. He was, in truth, the most faithful guardian of the provinces. For the man who protects without causing harm is properly called a defender.

But as soon as the season brought the passage of ships to a close [Col. 0795A] and the care of war was ended, he exercised his intelligence rather as a leader in the laws, healing without harm to the litigants [Niv. and Ga., *signans fine litigantium*, “recording an end to the litigants”; Ac., *sanans fine litigantium*, “healing with an end to the litigation”] what previously had clearly been torn apart for a price.

We read that the commands of Metellus in Asia and of Cato in Spain were of this kind; they were praised more for their discipline than for their arms. Not without reason: confronting an enemy always has a variable outcome, but preserving the measure of character brings unquestionable glory.

What then? Did he, presuming upon such conduct, boast of himself with any arrogance, since it is characteristic of human beings to exalt themselves when they know that they are esteemed favorably? Did he not conduct himself with such complete fellowship that he believed the prince’s favor toward him had been granted only for the sake of benefits? Benevolent to all, moderate in prosperity, and ignorant of anger unless seriously provoked [Col. 0795B], though stern in justice he does not remain harsh in granting remission of anger. He is an excellent distributor of his own possessions: while he does not know how to seek what belongs to others, he knows how to offer his own generously. [Col. 0796A]

Divine reading strengthened these qualities, since one always [Ed., *saepe*, “often”] acts well when heavenly fear is set against human impulses. From it comes the manifest knowledge of every virtue; from it wisdom is seasoned with the savor of truth. Thus the heavenly teaching makes him humble in all things.

To him, therefore, Conscript Fathers, with God as our auspice, from the twelfth indiction (A.D. 534) we entrust the dignity of governing the praetorian prefecture, so that, with God’s help, he may settle through his integrity all the complaints gathered by the trafficking of the faithless [Ac., *omnes inficiatione*, “all [the complaints] by denial”], and may make himself so greatly desired that he can be beneficial to everyone.

May Heaven attend what has been arranged, so that the man whom we have found prudent through long association may prove most prosperous for himself, most faithful to us, and useful to the republic; and may he leave to posterity a reputation through which he will make his family glorious for the ages. [Col. 0796B]

# BOOK TEN

## EPISTOLA I. TO THE EMPEROR JUSTINIAN, QUEEN AMALASUNTHA [MS., AMALASUNDA; OTHERS, AMALASUENTHA]

[Col. 0795C] The daughter of Theodoric and mother of Athalaric, whose virtues and greatness of spirit Procopius records in Book I of *The Gothic War* and Book I of *The Vandalic War*. From these works much may be gathered for understanding the following formulas, which I was unable to collect while hastily making these notes in my spare time. FORN. [Col. 0795D]

She writes that, after Athalaric’s death, she admitted Theodahad into partnership in the kingdom and sent ambassadors to request an extension of peace.

We have clung to you, most clement of rulers, with such affection that until now we delayed announcing the death of our son, glorious in memory [Note: [Col. 0795D] The mother is said to have devoted great care to raising this son; nevertheless, he was later corrupted by his peers. He died in A.D. 552 [read: 534], after reigning ten years [read: eight]. FORN.], lest, after the sad news, we wound the heart of one who loves us. But now, with God’s help—who is accustomed to change harsh circumstances into prosperity—we have chosen instead to convey to your knowledge those matters in which, sharing our position, you may rejoice with us in a common exultation. For it is pleasing to confess divine gifts to those who love them.

We have brought to the scepter a man joined to us by fraternal kinship [Note: [Col. 0795D] Theodahad, her cousin and partner in the kingdom. She rebuked him for many acts of plunder; but in the end, so that he alone might rule, he soon thrust her into prison, then ordered her killed, and held the kingdom for five years. Procopius, Book I of *The Gothic War*; Matthew Palmerius in his *Chronicles*; and Hermannus Contractus. FORN.], so that he might sustain royal dignity with us through the united strength of our counsel. Thus he might shine with the purple splendor of his ancestors [Note: [Col. 0795D] Born from kings. Aurelius Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, Book I, on the worship of Hadrian and his catamite:

> “Now him, in the purple bosom of the divine ruler, stripped of his manly lot…”

For Theodahad was born from royal stock, being the son of Theodoric’s sister Amalafreda, Procopius, Book I of *The Gothic War*, with the words “purple.” Parysatis, daughter of Cyrus and mother of Artaxerxes, ordered anyone who was going to address the king with greater freedom to use words more polished and weighty. Plutarch, *Apophthegmata*: “She ordered the man who was about to speak to the king with frankness to use fine-linen words.” He called his son “purple-clad” in the following book, Letter 1. This is a frequent and characteristic epithet of this author when it signifies something distinguished and royal, as in Ennodius’s panegyric addressed to King Theodoric: “Having used the purple-clad man as witness to the faith of your merits.” And near the end: “May the good fortune of the golden age enlarge from you a purple-clad king. May the heir of the kingdom play in your bosom,” etc.; see above, Book IX, letter 24, and Book X, letter 1. Procopius, near the end of Book II of *The Gothic War*: “He summoned Theudibald from Verona by the common consent of all the Goths, and when he came to him, immediately presented him with a purple garment and created him king amid the acclamation and applause of those standing by.” Pliny, Book XXII, writes that the cochineal dye was dedicated to imperial military cloaks; Plutarch, in *Crassus*, says that commanders of armies had earlier used this garment. FORNER.] and our spirits might be lifted by the consolation of a prudent man.

Join your happy prayers to ours, so that, just as we eagerly desire all things to prosper in the empire of your piety [Ac., *experimur*, “we experience”], we may likewise prove that your goodwill favors us. When the message has been completed—which, because of your innate clemency, we believe will be welcome to you—we add also the duty of a most agreeable embassy, asking that the peace which you always carry in your mind, and which you have also granted to me, may be prolonged by an addition of time. For although harmony between rulers is always becoming, yours nevertheless ennobles me absolutely, since the man who is joined to your glory by unanimity is thereby rendered still more exalted. [Col. 0796C]

But since the brevity of a letter cannot adequately set forth everything, we have entrusted our ambassadors with certain matters to convey to you orally, greeting you with suitable reverence. Receive these matters gladly, in accordance with your customary serenity, so that everyone may clearly recognize that we are justly confident in making our promises concerning your gentleness. For it is unquestionably fitting to presume this of you, since, in accordance with your wishes, we do for those whom you have commended such things as we know you hoped for. [Col. 0797A]

## EPISTOLA II. TO THE EMPEROR JUSTINIAN, KING THEODAHAD

He indicates that he has been taken by Amalasuntha as partner in the kingdom, and asks that the emperor favor him by his judgment.

It is customary for new kings [Note: [Col. 0797D] This custom is attested by the final law of the final title of Book XII of the Code; Philostratus, Book V of *The Life of Apollonius*, concerning Nero’s victory in singing, and the expression *εὐαγγέλια θύειν* (“to sacrifice thank-offerings”) in that sense; those who announce the thanks, *οἱ ἐπαγγέλλοντες τὰς χάριτας*, are so called by Theodoret in his commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans. FORN.] to announce throughout the various peoples the joys of their advancement, so that they may win the affection of a foreign prince through that very fellowship in kingship. When I did this, most pious Emperor, the Divine Powers granted me something far better: for I confidently seek your favor, which I know our most excellent lady and sister has pledged to you. It is certain that I shall in no way depart from her judgment; for she shines with so great a light of wisdom that she both orders her own realms with marvelous arrangement and guards the grace promised to all with steadfast strength. For this reason she made me a partner in her cares, so that I too might desire to honor those whom she herself has made peaceful toward her—judging according to her prudent custom, so as to choose the friendship of men who have no equal anywhere in the world. Nor is this affection new; for if you recall the deeds of our predecessors [Ms., “your predecessors”], you recognize that it is a kind of customary law that the Amals have always maintained friendship with that empire [Note: [Col. 0797D] The final letter of the preceding book; Book VIII, Letter 5, and the following letter. FORN.]. This friendship is all the more certain because it is more ancient, since what has been preserved through long centuries cannot easily be changed [Note: [Col. 0797D] Certainly it ought not to be changed: law 32, *On Matters Concerning Which*; the following law, *On Laws*. For in establishing new arrangements there must be evident utility before one departs from a law that has long appeared equitable: law 2, *On the Constitution of Princes*. Council of Nicaea, canon 6: “Let the ancient customs prevail.” The law of the places is sufficiently well known. FORN.].

Receive, therefore, with affectionate minds both my accession and that of our lady and sister, to whom you are singularly devoted; favor her judgment. For if you love me likewise, you in a certain sense make me king jointly with yourselves. But since our desire for novelty urges us to speak at greater length, while the brevity of a letter does not permit much to be recounted, after completing the honor of a greeting proportionate to such great merits, we have entrusted our envoys, the bearers of this letter, with certain matters to disclose to your Piety; for no one handles his wishes more effectively than one who has resolved to entrust them to your gentleness.

## LETTER III. QUEEN AMALASUNTHA TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

She announces that she has summoned Theodahad, adorned with many virtues and great wisdom, into partnership in the kingship, and asks them for this reason to give thanks to God.

After the lamentable death of our son, of blessed memory, [Col. 0797D] the affection of a devout mother prevailed over my spirit, [Col. 0798A] so that I might consider not the causes of my own grief but rather your advancement. We sought what consolation might support our royal cares. But that author of chastity and singular mercy, who was about to take our firstborn son from us, preserved for us the affection of a mature brother. With God’s blessing, we have chosen the most fortunate Theodahad as our partner in the kingship (See Baronius, volume VII of the *Annals*, p. 226), so that what until now I have borne alone through solitary deliberation concerning the burden of the state, we may now accomplish through united counsels for the benefit of all; so that in deliberations we may appear two, but in decisions one.

The stars themselves are governed by mutual assistance, and through shared labor they administer the world with their respective lights. To man also the Divine Powers have given two hands, paired ears, and twin eyes, so that the duty which was to be fulfilled through the partnership of two [Col. 0798B] might be carried out more robustly. Rejoice, senators, and commend our deed to the powers above. We desire to do nothing blameworthy, since with the counsel of another we have chosen to arrange everything. For the fellowship of kingship upholds good conduct, since he is rightly believed to be peaceable who is shown to have a partner in his power.

With God’s help, therefore, we have opened our palaces to a man conspicuous for the nobility of our race, descended from the stock of the Amals, and possessing royal dignity in his actions: patient in adversity, moderate in prosperity, and—what is the most difficult kind of mastery—long since master of himself. To these qualities was added a desirable training in letters, which renders an excellent nature especially adorned [Note: [Col. 0797D] Learned men should gladly be admitted to the council, but not those endowed with this single gift alone; for those who boast only of a bare knowledge of letters should be strongly rejected, and even the most learned are not always suited to public affairs. Other qualities of mind must also be present: they must be trustworthy, or upright in life; prudent in general and in particular; advanced in age; knowledgeable in both kinds of fortune; and, as Mithridates says of himself: “Fortune, after depriving me of many things, gave me the experience of giving good advice.” BROSS.].

There the prudent finds the means to become wiser; there the soldier discovers how to be strengthened in courage; from there the prince learns how to arrange peoples in equality; and there can be no fortune in the world that the glorious knowledge of letters does not increase. Receive what the common vows have deserved as something greater still. Your prince has also been educated in ecclesiastical letters [Note: [Col. 0798D] Procopius, Book I, writes that Theodatus, or Theodahad, was skilled in Latin literature and Platonic doctrines; he attributes to him no knowledge of theology, describes him as inexperienced in military discipline, and says that he was eager to collect money and accumulate possessions. FORN.]. From these we are always reminded of whatever pertains to humanity [Ed., honor]: to judge rightly, to have a good understanding, to venerate divine things, and to consider future judgments. For the one who believes that he will have to give an account of his own judgment must necessarily follow the track of justice.

I should like to see what reading sharpens the intellect; divine reading always strives to make it devout. Let us turn to that most liberal economy of his private household, which produced such abundance in gifts and such plenty at banquets that, when its ancient devotion is considered, nothing new seems to have been introduced into the kingdom. In hospitality [Col. 0798D] he was ready, in compassion most devout; and although he spent much, his resources increased through heavenly recompense. The whole community ought to have wished for a man such as we have proved ourselves to have chosen: one who, ordering his own affairs rationally, does not covet what belongs to others. The need for princes to exceed their bounds is removed whenever they have become accustomed to moderate what is their own. Truly praiseworthy [159] is the judgment that prescribes moderation in possessions, since even what is considered good is displeasing when excessive.

Rejoice now, senators, and offer prayers of thanksgiving to heavenly grace on our behalf, since I have appointed as my partner a prince who, by doing good through our equity, also displays the qualities of his own piety. For both the virtue of his ancestors admonishes him [Note: [Col. 0799D] They should be urged toward the moral excellences of domestic life by examples of ancestral praise. Law 1 of the Theodosian Code, *On the Correction of Relatives*. FORN.] and his uncle Theodoric effectively encourages him [Note: [Col. 0799D] Alludes to Virgil:

“And father Aeneas, and uncle Hector, stir him.” JURET.].

## LETTER IV. KING THEODAHAD TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

He writes that Amalasuntha, who is extolled with many praises, has advanced him to partnership in the imperial power.

[Col. 0799B]

We announce, senators, that the Divine Benefits have happily come to us: the mistress of the world, glorious throughout the earth, has made me her partner in kingship through her abundant piety, so that she would not lack faithful solace and our ancestral rule might fittingly be restored to us. Let what the whole community is known to have desired be received with the greatest gratitude [Ac., “adorned”]. Let the wishes of all now be disclosed without fear, so that from the source whence I suffered danger the whole community may recognize me as adorned.

You previously presumed to whisper, without my knowledge, what you could not openly undertake. From this it is clear how much I owe you: you hastened to make divinely come to pass for me what my spirit did not dare to seek. This is newer to us than it is unknown to you. Great gratitude, therefore, must be felt for the fulfillment of what appears to have been disclosed with such speed, when it ought to have been.

But if I have deserved anything from you, while nevertheless trusting that our glory has great influence among you, continually proclaim the glorious praises of our lady and sister, who wished the greatness of her empire to be strengthened by our participation, so that there might be one appearance in two lights, and no one might believe a harmonious understanding divided. For those whom grace joins and kinship reconciles are thus united. Those whose dispositions are unequal may perhaps consider this difficult. It is hard for those to live otherwise who can agree with one another through the likeness of good thoughts. The improvident refuses to change his counsel; but the wise man seeks wisdom in another, in whom there is greatness of knowledge.

[Col. 0799D] Among the various gifts that the Divine Powers have granted us together with royal majesty, this touches our spirit most deeply: that the most wise lady chose us after the great weighing of a serious inquiry. I therefore first endured her justice so that I might first attain the favor of her advancement. For, as you know, she made us plead our cases alongside private persons. O singular nobility of spirit! Behold an extraordinary equity, of which the world may speak. [Col. 0800A] She did not hesitate first to subject a kinsman to public law whom shortly afterward she wished to place even above the laws themselves. She examined the conscience of the man to whom she was about to entrust the governance of the kingdom, so that she might be recognized as mistress of all and might graciously lead me, once approved, to the kingship.

When shall we repay these gifts, when shall we discharge what we owe to such great grace—that she who ruled alone with her little son has now chosen to reign in partnership with me? In her lies the honor of all kingdoms; in her, the flower of the virtues of our origin. Whatever splendor we possess, we receive from her radiance, since she has conferred praise not only upon her parents but has also adorned the human race itself.

Who could adequately declare with what piety and with what weight of character she is adorned? Philosophers would surely learn new things if they were alive; [Col. 0800B] and they would admit that their books contain lesser things than those they would recognize as bestowed upon her. Sharp in deliberation, yet in speech supremely moderate and gravely restrained. This is unquestionably a royal virtue: to perceive what is necessary swiftly and to burst into words slowly. For the person who first submits what should be said to his own examination does not know how to say what he will later regret.

Hence her marvelous teaching is diffused with great abundance through many languages; her intellect is so ready for improvisation that it does not seem earthly. In the Books of Kings, the queen of the South is said to have come to learn Solomon’s wisdom; let princes here hear what they may recognize with amazement. Infinite meaning is enclosed in a few words, and with the greatest ease she composes what others now formulate only after long deliberation.

Blessed is the commonwealth that glories in the government of so great a lady. It was not enough for the community to serve under liberty; so much was added to her merits that even sovereign reverence was subjected to her. Through this obedience we rule most worthily. For when I obey such wisdom, I serve all virtues. Under such a guide we are not burdened by the weight of kingship, since whatever is unknown because of its novelty will become certain to us through her instruction.

For the public good, I am not ashamed to confess the truth. Recognize, princes and nobles, that whatever has been able to please us most is the possession of the wisest lady. We either understand matters better by questioning her or advance through imitating her. Live happily now; live, with God’s help, in harmony; and emulate the grace that you know sustains royal concord.

## LETTER V. KING THEODAHAD TO THEODOSIUS, HIS MAN [Note: [Col. 0800D] “His man,” that is, his household member and client: law 4 of the Code, *On Dignities*; the penultimate law of the Theodosian Code, *On Equalization and Inspection of Assessors*; law 1, *On Contractors and Members of the Household of the Augustan House*, Theodosian Code; law 5, *On Appeals for Reparation*, same Code. FORN.]

He forbids his household members to become arrogant in any way and orders them, through modesty and observance of the laws, to serve as examples to the rest.

[Col. 0800D]

We wish the moderation of our affairs to be the standard governing our power, so that, however many Divine Benefits [160] we have received, we may love equitable things all the more. Private interests are rightly excluded from our spirit, because, with God’s help, I have become the universal lord and guardian of all. And therefore by the present command we order that whoever is known to belong to our household and is shown to have been entrusted to your care must not grow insolent through any presumption; for only he should be called mine who can remain tranquil under the laws.

Increase our reputation through your patience. If anyone should perhaps have a dispute with another, descend to the common laws: let the courts protect you, not unjust presumption. We wish to begin discipline with our household, so that the rest may be ashamed to err when we are known not to grant our own people license to exceed the bounds.

We have changed our purpose along with our dignity; and if previously we defended what was just with severity, now we mitigate everything with clemency, because princes do not hold their household exempt from the law; rather, whatever we rule with divine assistance we openly confess to be properly ours. Be completely attentive, therefore, toward those who were formerly subject to our jurisdiction, and permit no one to transgress anything against the law. Let praise of you reach me before any complaint arises, because a good conscience truly rules when it hastens to provide for all alike.

## LETTER VI. KING THEODAHAD TO PATRICIUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND QUAESTOR

He praises him greatly and elevates him to the quaestorship.

It is evidently necessary for the commonwealth to choose persons suited to dignities, so that the man to whom justice is entrusted is not burdened by bad character. Otherwise it is ineffective to demand from a person what he is known not to possess; conversely, one confidently seeks what is perceived to be present.

And therefore it first pleased us to examine your character, without which any number of excellent qualities may be displeasing. Sincere kindness is the ornament of all virtues; it is not by itself, since it is recognized as generated from the virtues. Preserve the order of our judgment, so that, just as we sought this first, we may perceive that you guard justice above all else.

Our second concern was to investigate the streams of your eloquence. Although we value it exceptionally, we rightly place it second to character. In the former, life is recognized; here, only the tongue is praised. But in you the combination is especially fitting, because you are known to possess both. You shine equally through the merit of your conduct and the eloquence of your speech, so that it may rightly be understood that the prince’s will is carried out through you.

Among the other arts, we love oratory so much that we acknowledge it to be the ornament of all learning. Whatever is conceived in any discipline is presented by it with elegance. Let a philosopher discover something however great: what good will it do to perceive it if he cannot raise it up [Col. 0802A] [Ac., “cultivate it”] in a praiseworthy manner? Discovery is natural; but the eloquent man asserts it fittingly.

What could be more valuable than to speak to all who desire speech, and to express common matters in an address so eloquent that even the wise marvel at having heard them? In this art we have recognized you as exceptionally strong, so that you can persuade pleasantly and know how to mix nothing malicious into your recommendations.

And therefore [Note: [Col. 0801D] On the office and eloquence of the quaestor, see above, Book VI, Form 5; Book VIII, Letters 13 and 14. FORN.] we grant you, with the favor of the Divinity, the fasces of the quaestorship for the thirteenth indiction (A.D. 535), [Note: [Col. 0801D] From this it is clear what the functions of the quaestor were under the emperors: he drafted laws and scrutinized petitions, subscribing to them if they rested on just reasoning. This is evident from law 2, Code, *On Petitions for Confiscated Property*. See Symmachus, Book II, Letter 8; Book IV, Letter 50; Book V, Letter 52; and what we noted above concerning Form 5 of Book VI. BROSS.] so that you may satisfy the desire of the community by following the judgment of legal experts. Devote yourself wholly to the laws, wholly to the responses of the wise. You serve us best if you obey the enactments of the ancients [ed., “if you advise us”]. Consider that our principal praise is placed in your words. What you say is our reputation; what you feel, without doubt, is our conscience.

Understand how much is demanded of you, to whom our reputation is entrusted. It embraces our subjects and travels throughout foreign peoples; through it we are recognized where we are not seen. Our decrees convey speeches about us to cities and provinces. Those who obey even our commands can judge us. Therefore it is clear that what can pass judgment upon us must be guarded with the greatest diligence.

## LETTER VII. KING THEODAHAD TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

He announces that he has conferred the dignity of quaestor upon Patricius, distinguished by splendid virtues.

After the beginnings of our reign had been happily announced to you, [Col. 0802C] an appropriate subject for speech came before us, senators, so that you might recognize that we have chosen a judge whose tongue can adorn us. An eloquent quaestor is an ornament of the commonwealth, one who appears both to express our wishes most effectively and to guard the laws of the ancients with firm judgment.

This is Patricius, already honored by his very name. He enjoys perpetual praise because he bears honor in his name; his flowing eloquence was cultivated by Roman studies [Note: [Col. 0801D] Here he speaks of Roman eloquence; and indeed, when the dignity of the Latin language was already declining, those who knew Latin began to be held in esteem. It is established that from that time—certainly by the age of Justinian, when the language had contracted—documents written by notaries were composed in nearly the language now used by the common people of Italy. This is clear from a document in the royal library, by which Stephen, guardian of the orphan Gratian, reached an agreement with him. It was written at Ravenna in the thirty-eighth year of Justinian’s reign, in the twelfth indiction; I preserve a copy of it that I transcribed in my private archive. FORN.], rightly displaying a mastery proportionate to the distinction of the place.

For the man who could be formed there deserved to be praised everywhere. There the Latin language was purified; from there words radiant in their full brilliance are learned. Let other regions send wines, balsams, and fragrant incense: Rome gives eloquence, than which nothing has been heard more pleasing.

Thus educated in the liberal arts, he was soon fitted for the duties of the forum [Col. 0802D], so that he might display in corresponding declamation the orators whom he had absorbed through long study. It is also known with what moderation he contended with his colleagues. Modesty was always present in his contests. Carried away by the heat of speaking, he devoted himself to praiseworthy discoveries; [Col. 0803A] he did not, as most do, occupy himself with insults [Note: [Col. 0803D] The quaestor is praised here because, in conducting and pleading cases, he entirely abstained from insults; for the practice of reviling is most disgraceful, as the Emperor Valentinian attests in law *Quisquis*, Code, *On Pleading*. Moreover, speeches should not be filled with abuse. See Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXX. Advocates ought to restrain themselves from insults when pleading cases. See Book VI of the Code, *On Pleading*; and the notes on Symmachus, Book IX, Letter 28. BROSS.; JURET.]. He pleaded cases with such calmness that he always upheld his own character. He was found to have contended, not quarreled. For he made another’s case his own [161] glory. He was known to conquer in such a way that he was shown not to have injured the opposing spirit.

Such a man, therefore, ought no longer to have sought justice but to have taught it, since judicial virtue consists in abounding in the excellences of speech and guarding moderation of mind. Recognize, senators, what we wish to be done, since in the judges we first chose character, and did so in that dignity which is accustomed to proclaim the laws. In our times the quaestorship is not armed with royal power but is shown to be constituted by laws.

Our will is the will of the ancient princes, whom we desire to imitate to the extent that they followed justice. That is the reverence due to our predecessors which does not depart from the straight path. He has left posterity the necessity of following who has joined justice to his enactments.

And therefore, senators, in the thirteenth indiction (A.D. 535) we have conferred the dignity of quaestor upon the illustrious Patricius, so that he who is distinguished by name may also be magnificent in honor. Favor our judgment concerning him, so that what we have bestowed may likewise be felt to please you.

## LETTER VIII. QUEEN AMALASUNTHA TO JUSTINIAN AUGUSTUS

[Note: [Col. 0803D] Amalasuntha planned to travel from Italy all the way to Constantinople to the Emperor Justinian. Procopius, Book I, *On the Gothic War*. FORN.]

She asks him to order that the marble and other necessities that Calogenitus had procured be sent to the queen.

[Col. 0803C] Your Piety’s favor delights us so greatly that we willingly wish to request from your side whatever can contribute to our adornment, because the Divine Powers have granted you such things that you both abound richly in their gifts and grant what is necessary to those who hope for it with a kindly spirit.

And therefore, reverently offering your gentleness a greeting, I have sent the bearer of this letter to the benefits of Your Excellency, so that you may order the marble and other necessities that we once had Calogenitus procure to reach us through the present bearer [Ac., “pious bearer”], with the Lord’s favor. Thus we may know that we are truly loved by your Piety, since you cause our wishes to be fulfilled. For your glory is our adornment, when it is recognized that you have supplied what is applied to our praises.

[Col. 0803D] For it is fitting that this Roman world also [Note: [Col. 0804D] Law 17, *In the Roman World*, *On the Status of Persons*. Pliny, Book XVII, chapter 12; Book XXXIII, chapter 4. It was formerly read incorrectly as “in the Roman city” in the cited law 17, as the Florentine edition shows; Alciatus had already marked this in Book II, chapter 22 of the *Dispunctuationes*. This passage also supports him, as does law 1 of the Code, *On Eunuchs*. FORN.] should shine through your assistance, since the love of your serenity illuminates it.

## LETTER IX. KING THEODAHAD TO JUSTINIAN AUGUSTUS

He asks him to permit the things that Calogenitus purchased to be transported to Italy.

[Col. 0804A]

It is equitable, most wise Emperor, that you willingly cause those things to be expended for us which, if we were negligent, we ought rather to be urged by your clemency to undertake. For there is no doubt that whatever is accomplished through us for the adornment of Italy is pleasing to you, since it rightly advances your praises whenever what can contribute to the glory of our commonwealth appears to grow.

Therefore, offering your principate the most reverent affection of a greeting, we have sent the bearer of this letter to obtain those things for which Calogenitus had once been assigned, so that, although the person has been taken away from human affairs, your benefits may nevertheless reach us, with God’s help, lest the desire that reasonably rests secure in your anticipated favor be frustrated [ed., “followed”].

## LETTER X. QUEEN AMALASUNTHA TO THE AUGUSTA THEODORA

[Note: [Col. 0804D] To Theodora Augusta, wife of Justinian, whose courage of spirit Procopius records. Letters to the same woman appear below, Letters 20, 21, and 23 of this book. FORN.]

She asks her to inform her of her well-being through the envoys whom she had sent to Justinian.

Since it is our purpose to seek what is recognized as belonging to the glory of a pious prince, it is fitting to honor in speech those who are known always to be increased in every good thing. Concord is not limited to the present; rather, those who are joined by affection of spirit regard one another more deeply.

And therefore, returning the affection of a greeting to Your Augusta, I hope that, when our envoys return—those whom we sent to the most clement and glorious [Col. 0804C] prince—you will cause us to rejoice in your well-being. For your prosperity appears as welcome to us as our own, and it is necessary to receive with eager desire the well-being that we are known continually to wish for you.

## LETTER XI. KING THEODAHAD TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS MAXIMUS, A HOUSEHOLD OFFICIAL

He promotes Maximus, descended from the family of the Anicii, which is adorned with many encomia, and joined in marriage to a woman of royal descent, to the office of *primicerius*, or *domesticus*.

[Col. 0804D] [162] If it is the glory of good princes to make persons unknown to honors illustrious—since whatever is achieved by subjects is applied to the praise of rulers—how much more excellent it is for us to restore to a most noble family what we recognize it to have deserved even by the fortune of its birth! We follow justice in this way, if we do not deny the rewards of parents to worthy heirs. For those who have deserved to reach our times ought also to surpass their predecessors. [Col. 0805A]

The ancient age produced the Anicii, almost equal to princes; the dignity of whose name, conveyed to you through the source of your blood, has shone forth more brightly, restored with gathered strength. Who, then, would leave to posterity men of lesser honor [ed., “of honor”], when they are known to have been preeminent for so long? The ages would be accused [Note: [Col. 0805D] The discipline of the times and the happiness of the age are praised by princes: Book I, Letter 5; Book II, Letter 13; Book IV, Letter 10; this book, Letter 18; and very often elsewhere. FORN.—Pliny expressed something not very different in the *Panegyricus*, when speaking of the happiness of his own age: “Life is safe for all,” he says, “and the dignity of life; no longer is the thoughtful and wise man one who spends his life in darkness. Under the prince, the same rewards are given to virtues as under liberty; and there are not merely rewards for good deeds recognized by conscience, but also public honors.” BROSS.] if such a family could have remained hidden.

Would that a longer life had preserved for us Marius or Corvinus! The prince’s desire would scarcely have been satisfied if it had fallen to us to possess persons of such merit. How could we now neglect those whom we desire to have from the past? And therefore—may the announcement be auspicious—we confer upon you, beginning with the fourteenth indiction (A.D. 536), the dignity of the *primiceriatus*, also called the *domesticatus*. You are to use all the titles belonging to its functions.

Although this honor may appear inferior to such ancestry, it nevertheless seems more fortunate than all your offices, since during its tenure you deserved to receive as your wife a woman of royal descent—something you would not even have presumed to wish for in your curule offices [Gr. and Cuj., “in your consulship”]. Act now so that, just as it is wished for you, it may likewise prove acceptable to us. Consider what you have deserved, and conduct yourself as worthy of our kinship. For the man joined to the ruling family is placed in the bosom of praise.

Now let greater effort be devoted to gentleness; now let kind fellowship be offered to all, so that we may prove ourselves to have chosen one whom no prosperity can change. Act humbly in this matter of glory, since praise is derived from modesty and hatred is stirred by arrogance. Advancement is unquestionably close to envy; but envy is better conquered by endurance, whereas it is always increased by contention.

Above all other virtues, love patience as the friend of the wise. Raised up by us, you will be praised more for enduring than for taking revenge. Conquer anger, love kindness, beware lest your prosperity appear greater than your character. Rather, since you are joined to our family, prove yourself close to glorious deeds. Your parents have hitherto been praised, but they have not been honored by so great a connection. Your nobility has no further height to which it can grow. Whatever you do worthy of proclamation, you will be judged worthy of your own marriage [Note: [Col. 0805D] In the old and elegant manner of speaking, “one’s own wife.” Servius Honoratus, on that line of Virgil, Books I and IV of the *Aeneid*:

“I shall join her in a lasting marriage and make her my own.”

The prayer of Hersilia in Aulus Gellius, Book XIII, chapter 21: “May it be permitted to enjoy one’s own and prosperous marriage”; for a wife is not taken for a time, but into the companionship of perpetual life. Law 1, *On the Rites of Marriage*, section 1, *On the Institution of Paternal Power*, final chapter, *On Appended Conditions*. FORN. See Jerome, Book II *Against Jovinian*: “Among them no wife is one’s own,” etc.; and Altmus Avitus, Book II. JURET.].

## LETTER XII. KING THEODAHAD TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

He writes that he has granted Maximus, formerly consul, the dignity of *primiceriatus* or *domesticatus* and a wife of royal descent, and asks them to celebrate this marriage with abundant joy.

[Col. 0805D] Let no one, senators, think that we failed to consider the proper order in bestowing honors because, after the insignia of the consulship, we later confer what may seem lesser. Rather, the merits of the candidate advised us not to let a man already mature appear to undertake nothing, when he is known to have received distinguished honors in his youth.

It was the mark of a miserly prince to confine so great a span of life within a single honor, and therefore to grant nothing more because a man is first known to have deserved the highest things. On the contrary, let us grant everything indiscriminately. No dignity is lesser when it is well administered, since an office often seems to receive its prestige from the distinction of the person. These dignities are distinguished by rank only when they have been distributed among different people. For a consul always retains his own honor equally, whatever he may have done well.

Thus the names of lesser rivers are swallowed up by a greater stream; and although your Tiber receives very many tributaries, it nevertheless does not depart from its own name. And therefore—may the announcement be auspicious—we grant to the illustrious and magnificent patrician Maximus the dignity of *primiceriatus*, also called *domesticatus*, to be held from the fourteenth indiction (A.D. 536), so that the modesty of the office might increase through the merit of its holder.

For it is not right to call lowly what an Anicius holds: a family proclaimed throughout the world, truly called noble because the integrity of conduct does not depart from it. But to these advantages we add, senators, that the illustrious favor of your distinguished family may be joined to our kinship. Yet one man alone cannot claim this glory for himself, since we are shown to have conferred it upon the Roman name.

Return to my affection the fullest love. The subject is more to be loved by his lord when the lord has deigned to provide him with the name of a parent. But it is equitable, senators, that the man through whom such happy circumstances have come to you should be dear to you. [Col. 0806C] Rejoice together, and celebrate this marriage with overflowing joy. When the name of all is advanced, the wishes of all ought to be united. What prayers could have demanded from me what my spirit granted by spontaneous decision, namely, that we might truly call as parents men of your order who are to be joined to us through the glory of kinship?

## LETTER XIII. KING THEODAHAD TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

He reproaches the senators for failing, at the very beginning of his reign, to counter the fickleness of the populace and their groundless suspicions.

After we had dismissed the venerable bishops, having acknowledged their embassy, and although there were certain matters in your petitions deserving reproach, 163 our mind had not opposed them, some who came to us reported that the city of Rome [Col. 0806D] was still suffering from foolish agitation and was acting in such a way that, unless our clemency intervened, it would stir up against itself certain dangers from uncertain suspicions. Consider, then, to whom the empty fickleness of the people ought to be attributed, unless to your order, by which everything ought to have been settled [Col. 0807A]. For it was proper that, through your wisdom, all the provinces should have been admonished to undertake such measures as might seem to adorn the beginnings of a prince’s reign.

Yet what city would not become liable to reproach if Rome should do wrong? A lesser king follows the example of a greater, and rightly bears the odium of another’s deed when that deed sets an example for wrongdoing. But we give thanks to the Divinity, who has adorned His gifts rather through your outstanding merits. Behold, we forgive your faults before we perceive any acts of devotion. We owe nothing, yet we make payment; we show ourselves benefactors in advance, so that afterward we may be able to find you most grateful.

Although the gravity of our modesty is thereby asserted, we nevertheless do not wish ourselves to be praised so much that the kindness of Roman devotion cannot also be displayed. We are more nourished by your good reputation than if we were always praised for our own tranquility [Col. 0807B]. Remove from your order suspicions that have always been foreign to it. It is not fitting that the Senate should be corrected [Note: The senatorial order ought to be free from every fault. Law 74 of the Theodosian Code, *Concerning Decurions*: “Those who are burdened by the reproaches of their former life are judged unworthy of the most illustrious order,” [Col. 0808D] because “the gates of dignities are not open to infamous men.” See Cornelius Tacitus, Book XI of the *Annals*. BROSS.], when it ought to guide others by paternal exhortation. For from what source will their character derive its spirit, if they happen to find their public fathers inferior?

These things are sufficient for the noble; these things are sufficient for the modest, so that we may incite to the pursuit of perfect devotion those whom we have censured only slightly for their misguided suspicion. For when we sought your presence, we did not consider the injury of harassment, but, after deep reflection, the grounds of your advantage, so that you ought rather to have accomplished what we recognized to be expedient for you.

Certainly, it is a privilege to see a prince. We wish you to do this for the benefit of the commonwealth, which used to be sought through rewards. But lest the remedies themselves should seem harsh in any respect, whenever circumstances [Col. 0807C] require it, we order certain men to be summoned to us, so that Rome may not be stripped of her citizens and our counsels may be assisted by prudent men.

Return, therefore, to your former devotion, so that my concerns, which I bear for the whole community, may rather be aided by your judgment. For it has always been implanted in you to offer your rulers a pledge of purity—not to obey through the necessity of fear, but rather through love of the ruler. We have entrusted the remaining matters to be communicated verbally by the bearer of this letter, so that, once ambiguous thoughts have been removed, you may believe our admonitions.

## EPISTLE XIV. THEODAHAD, KING, TO THE ROMAN PEOPLE

He exhorts the people to preserve their loyalty to the king and to cast away empty suspicion.

[Col. 0807D]

Although it is implanted in you to love your rulers with a pure mind and to act through your obedience so that you may keep the reigning prince’s disposition favorable toward you, this was nevertheless always characteristic of your ancestors: just as limbs appear joined to the head, so they seemed joined to their own rulers. For what return should the one who is defended with the greatest labor, whose civic order is guarded day by day, make, except to love above all those through whom he is proved to possess everything [Ac., “immeasurable things”]?

Far be it from our times that we should find anything of this kind in you [Col. 0808A] that could suitably provoke our indignation. May your loyalty, which has hitherto upheld you, now display itself more clearly [Niv. and Ga., “be displayed”]. It is not fitting that the Roman people should be changeable [Ed., “empty”], deceitful, or filled with seditions. Evil conduct is shown to be hostile to your name.

But this too is remarkable: we are compelled to admonish your gravity, although it is known always to have been wise of its own accord. Let no foolish suspicion, no shadow of fear, deter you. You have a ruler who, out of devotion to piety, desires to find in you something to love. You should meet your enemies, not your defenders. You ought to have invited assistance, not excluded it.

But perhaps this opinion belongs to those who are judged less capable of understanding what could have been expedient for the whole community. Return rather to your own judgment. Did some new appearance of the race [Col. 0808B] frighten you? Why did you fear those whom you have hitherto called your fathers? Those who, leaving their families behind, hastened to come to you were concerned rather for your security. When, I ask, did such a return ever come from one to whom the rewards of safety were owed?

You ought to have known this concerning us: day and night, without ceasing, we desire that what is known to have been nurtured in the time of our parents may, under us, be increased rather through divine assistance. For where would the fame of a ruler be if we allowed you—God forbid—to be diminished? Do not entertain thoughts such as you see us least inclined to adopt.

Rather, if anyone has been weighed down by some injustice, let him not lose hope because of a good conscience, since we desire to raise up those whom we find striving toward honorable conduct. We have also entrusted certain matters to be communicated to you verbally by the bearer of this letter [Col. 0808C], so that, recognizing our disposition toward you to be favorable in every respect, you may remain devoted, as is proper, through constant obedience and sincere prayer.

## EPISTLE XV. THEODAHAD, KING, TO JUSTINIAN, EMPEROR

He commends to him a certain man sent to Constantinople concerning the affairs of the Church of Ravenna.

It is evident that the desire of our will is fulfilled whenever it happens that salutary letters are sent to Your Piety, because the one who speaks with you in a sincere spirit is always filled with joyful happiness. Therefore, saluting Your Clemency with fitting honor, I commend to you, with a petition most welcome to you, the bearer of this letter, who is coming concerning the affairs of the Church of Ravenna [Col. 0808D]. This is an occasion for conferring such a gift that a reward seems to be gained—something those who desire Your Serenity to flourish always long to do. For there is no doubt that those receive better things whom it happens to be their lot to grant what is just.

## EPISTLE XVI. THEODAHAD, KING, TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

He writes that he has sent certain men to administer the oath to the Senate.

164

It is a very commanding thing, Conscript Fathers, when our piety is overcome by our own will, although we are not bound by conditions imposed by others. For when, by God’s favor, we are able to do everything, we believe that only what is praiseworthy is permitted to us. You recognize, prudent men, the words that we speak; or recognize even now the clemency that you ought previously to have expected from us.

Behold, we do not even allow those to remain anxious whom we were thought to regard with hostility. This is how a grave suspicion should be overcome by a prince; this is how the one who did not wish to be harmful ought to have acted. Our authority has decreed that the requested oaths be administered to you by this man and that man. This is not difficult to persuade one who will rule well, because we have given you security in such a way that we seem to have added nothing to our purpose.

For we were going to do precisely what we promise, since we owe these things to God, not to man. For having passed through the ancient kingdoms in the sacred readings [Col. 0809B], what else can we desire except what we perceive to have pleased the Divinity in others? God Himself is the rewarder of all good things; for whatever act of piety we perform toward our subjects, we undoubtedly judge that He repays to us.

Therefore, show a faithful conscience after receiving security, because after such acts your affection is rather returned to our clemency than offered to it.

## EPISTLE XVII. THEODAHAD, KING, TO THE ROMAN PEOPLE

He writes that he has sent certain men to Rome to bind the king by oath.

Learn, Quirites, with what steadfastness your ruler has loved you, so that, when tested by difficult circumstances, he would not allow you to be anxious. Nor do we wish your hopes to be delayed any longer, since we always desire to see you rejoicing in the highest distinction of the commonwealth [Col. 0809C].

Your security is our adornment; and we truly receive this with gratitude when we perceive that you possess joy. Therefore, yielding to your petitions, we have judged that oaths should be administered to you by this man and that man, so that you may not remain ignorant of the disposition of your king. Nor should you wander into false suspicions when you plainly hold what you believe concerning your ruler.

Consider what kindness appears to be bestowed upon you when he swears who cannot be compelled. For we know that we have been given as a remedy for all; we do not disdain to heal our subjects. Therefore, although it might have seemed incongruous to our dignity, we gladly consented to do what we recognize the whole community desired.

Understand how much your ruler’s affection seems to impose upon you [Col. 0809D]: we are bound to you by faith, since even by a mere word we are admonished by the sacred readings to keep our promises. Now display your devotion; continually entreat the heavenly Majesty, so that the tranquil times which we desire you to possess may be granted by heavenly favor.

## EPISTLE XVIII. THEODAHAD, KING, TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

He writes that he has sent an army for the defense of the Romans and has placed Vaccenes, chief of the royal household, in command of it.

The remedy that we have considered [ed., “sent”] for you, Conscript Fathers, with pious [Col. 0810A] intent, we do not allow to be turned against you by harsh suspicion, because it is like an injury to counsel secretly and to display a different intention. Know, therefore, that our arms have been sent rather for your safety, so that, if anyone attempts to attack you, the hands of the Goths may, with divine assistance, confront them.

For if a vigorous shepherd excludes snares from his flock, and if a diligent master of a household cuts off an opportunity for deception from those who would mislead, with what vigilance ought we to defend Rome, which is known to have no equal in the world? Great things are not sent into danger, because the one who neglects to address adversity is proved to love less.

But lest the defense itself should prove burdensome to you in any respect, we have ordered that, under the command of that man, the grain allowances assigned to the army be calculated according to the market price of goods for sale [ed., [Col. 0810B] “procured”].
