Thus the soldiers would be deprived of the necessity of exceeding the proper amount, and you would be freed from the cause of expense.

We have also placed over them Vaccenes, chief of our household, who, by the quality of his virtues, would rightly be revered by warriors; by his example they would both avoid excesses and seek the means of courage. Nevertheless, we order them to remain in suitable locations, so that armed defense may be outside, while tranquil civic life remains within for you.

Understand what consoling ingenuity the ruler has devised for you: defense surrounds you, lest an enemy’s hand encircle you; and we have rescued from danger those whom we avenge through the blood of our own men. Far be it from our times [Note: The repeated insistence here sufficiently indicates how greatly rulers cared for the reputation of their age. Above, Epistle 11; in this book, Epistle 5; Book I, Epistle 13; Book VII and Book IV, Epistle 12. FORN.] that that City should seem protected by walls, which is known to have been a terror to nations even by reputation alone.

For we trust in divine assistance in such a way that she who has always been free [Col. 0810C] might not be disfigured by the disgrace of any confinement [F., “be disfigured”].

## EPISTLE XIX. THEODAHAD, KING, TO JUSTINIAN, EMPEROR

He praises the emperor, asks that peace be preserved, and sends Peter the ambassador back to Constantinople, adding his own ambassador to him.

We give thanks to the Divinity, to whom the tranquility of kings is always pleasing, because you have shown that our advancement is most welcome to Your Clemency. For it is evident that you can love one whom you rejoice to see elevated to the heights of kingship. It was fitting that the one who presumed to be raised through you should be received in this way.

Therefore, offer the world an example of your kindness, so that it may be understood how greatly the one who commends himself to you with pure affection is advanced. For you do not seek petty quarrels among kingdoms [165]; unjust contests, which are hostile to good morals, do not delight you [Col. 0810D], because it is evident that you desire nothing except what can adorn your reputation.

How will you be able to cast aside the peace for which you have been entreated, a peace that, through your innate piety, you have been accustomed to impose even upon wrathful nations? We do not conceal the blessings of your concord. Everything that has been joined to you by praiseworthy affection is believed to be excellent.

Yet something is also added to you, glorious princes, although you are absolutely admirable, when all kingdoms venerate you. It is common for everyone to be praised within his own dominions; but it is altogether exceptional to find one’s own praises among a foreign people [Col. 0811A], because judgments are true where no fear oppresses anyone.

You are indeed loved, most pious emperor, in your own kingdoms; but how much more splendidly are you loved in the regions of Italy, from which it is known that the Roman name has spread throughout the world! Our peace, therefore, ought to be preserved, since it has bestowed upon you the glorious beginnings of your title.

But so that we may seem to respond properly to your sacred utterances, after conveying our most reverent greeting, we inform you in our pious thoughts that the most blessed pope of the city of Rome and the most illustrious Senate were admonished by our command to receive, without any delay, an appropriate reply from Peter, the most eloquent ambassador of Your Serenity, supreme in learning and distinguished by the clarity of his conscience [Col. 0811B]. We did this so that he would not endure unsuitable delays against your will, since we desire to accomplish everything that could not displease your judgment, and since we know that Your Piety is likewise intent upon what we perceive to benefit us in every respect.

We have decided that this venerable man, our ambassador, should be joined to him, so that you may learn our wishes not through an opportunity arising from your embassy, but rather through our own deliberate appointment.

## EPISTLE XX. GUDELINA, QUEEN, TO THEODORA AUGUSTA

She gives thanks for the ambassador and her letters and writes that she has arranged for the pope and Senate to reply to her by letter. She then says that she has sent to her an ambassador endowed with many virtues and with learning.

I received the letters of Your Piety with the grace by which desired things are always received [Col. 0811C], and with most reverent congratulation I earned the privilege of conversations with your lips, surpassing all gifts, promising myself everything from so serene a spirit, since I received whatever I could wish for in such a gracious exchange.

For you urge us to place before your thoughts whatever we believe should be sought from the triumphant prince, our wedded lord. Who could now doubt that something will be brought to completion when such authority deigns to plead it? Previously, indeed, we trusted in the justice of our causes, but now we rejoice even more in your promise.

Our hopes cannot be delayed when the matter concerns things that deserve to be heard. Now fulfill your promises, so that you may bring to fulfillment the matter to which you have given the surest hope. My joy has also been increased by the fact that Your Serenity has sent such a man as both so great a glory ought to have sent and your service is worthy to retain [Col. 0811D].

For there is no doubt that she gives character to the one who is constantly attended to, while it is evident that a mind formed by good instructions is purified [ed., “retained”; Jur.: “Perhaps, ‘is presented’]. Therefore, having been admonished by your reverence, we decided to arrange that either the most blessed pope or the most illustrious Senate should reply without any delay to what you judged ought to be sought from them. Thus your glory would not be considered less deserving of reverence because the zeal for delay was set against it; rather, the grateful pleasure of accomplishment might be increased by its speed.

As for that person concerning whom something reached us by an insinuating remark, know that we have arranged what we believed suited your intentions. For our desire is such that, with your favor intervening, you may command no less in our kingdom than in your own [Col. 0812A].

We therefore inform you that we caused the aforesaid person to depart through the venerable pope before your ambassador, the bearer of this letter, could leave the city of Rome, lest anything occur that might oppose your intentions.

Therefore, greeting you with the reverence that ought to be shown to such merits, we have taken particular care to send to Your Clemency that venerable man, distinguished by character and learning and also worthy of reverence for the honor of his holiness, in the office of ambassador. For we believe that those persons are pleasing to you whom we judge acceptable to the divine ministries.

## EPISTLE XXI. GUDELINA, QUEEN, TO THEODORA AUGUSTA

She indicates that she and Theodahad earnestly seek her favor and asks that they be admitted into a share of her glory.

[Col. 0812B]

It is fitting for you, wisest of the Augustae, to estimate with what efforts I desire to seek Your Grace, and with what great zeal my wedded lord desires to obtain it. Although this is wholly dear to him, it is recognized to be especially important to me, since the love of so great a lady can raise me so high that I am known to find something greater than a kingdom.

For what could be more welcome than to seem joined to your glory through a share in your affection? Since you shine abundantly, may you willingly lend us something from your own splendor, since light suffers no loss when it bestows some of its brightness upon another. Foster our desires, which you recognize to be marked by exceptional sincerity.

May Your Grace commend us throughout all kingdoms [Col. 0812C]. You ought to make us illustrious, since we wish to shine through your light. Therefore, offering reverent greeting to Your Serenity, I commend myself with affectionate confidence to your hearts, hoping that your marvelous wisdom may arrange everything in such a way that the confidence given to us concerning your disposition may be increased more abundantly.

For although there ought to be no discord between Roman kingdoms, a circumstance has nevertheless arisen whose character ought to make us dearer to your fairness.

## EPISTLE XXII. THEODAHAD, KING, TO JUSTINIAN, EMPEROR

He asks him for peace through an ambassador distinguished by priestly rank and conspicuous for his reputation for learning.

You retain, wisest of princes, how eagerly we desire the harmony of Your August Serenity, both through our ambassadors [Col. 0812D] and through the most eloquent man Peter, whom Your Piety recently sent to us. Now once again, through that most holy man, we have believed that the same request should be repeated, so that you may judge to be genuine and affectionate what you know has often been sought.

We ask for peace with complete sincerity, since we have no cause for conflict. Let such a man therefore come to us, so ordered and so honorable, that we may rightly seem to have sought it with such great prayers. But far be it from us that what is entrusted to us should become burdensome. Deal rather on our behalf [Gr., Niv. and Ga., “on your behalf”] with what is fitting.

For the one whose cause is reasonably entrusted to him is drawn toward goodwill; nor can he put his own advantage first when it is more honorable for him to provide what will benefit the one who has trusted him [Col. 0813A].

Consider also, learned princes, and recall the historical memorials of your great-grandfathers, how much your predecessors strove to relinquish of their own right so that treaties with our ancestors might come to them. Consider with what gratitude those offerings ought to be received which they had been accustomed to request.

We do not speak arrogantly when we confess the truth. What we seek to demonstrate rather advances Your Glory, since now those who recognize themselves to be better than their ancestors voluntarily seek your favor. Let those whom you previously joined to yourselves through the generosity of your giving be associated with your hearts in a freely offered friendship, lest the good things of those times be thought to have been all that existed—things which you surpass both through abundant kindness and through lavish gifts.

Therefore, having first offered the honor of our greeting [Col. 0813B], we have sent that venerable man, distinguished by priestly rank and conspicuous for his reputation for learning, to carry the wishes of our embassy to Your Piety. For we trust in divine power that he will both please you abundantly through his own merits and obtain the desires of a proper petition. We hope that we may soon receive him back with the matter accomplished [ed., “with affection”].

But since the sequence of a letter could not contain everything, we entrusted certain matters to be conveyed verbally to your sacred thoughts, lest an extended reading of letters become tedious to you.

## EPISTLE XXIII. GUDELINA, QUEEN, TO THEODORA AUGUSTA

She writes that she received Peter, her ambassador, with a grateful spirit, and asks, through the man whom she sends to her, for the lasting establishment of peace between the two empires.

[Col. 0813C]

When we received your ambassador, the most eloquent Peter, and—something more honorable than the dignities themselves—one devoted to your service, the longed-for tokens of Your August Favor shone upon us [Note: “Tokens of favor,” perhaps “moments,” as below, Book XI, Epistle 23, where he says “moments of integrity”; and above, Book I, Epistles 4 and 19, “moments of justice”; and Book IV, Epistle 5, “moments of equity”; and Epistle 41, “moments of favor.” So in Symmachus, Book III, Epistle 4, *angusta momenta meriti*, “the narrow moments of merit,” for which Frobenius’s sole edition has *monumenta*, “tokens.” JUR.], so that through him we learned that you approved what is known to have occurred in this commonwealth.

You showed that you love whatever is recognized as belonging to justice, since, through divine providence, every suspicion having been removed, a desirable unanimity can remain. Now it is rather a fixed promise and a wished-for concord that unite kingdoms.

Therefore, we have decided to send to you that venerable man, truly worthy of your presence, as our special ambassador, so that, with your consent, the peace of our most serene wedded lord [Col. 0813D] may be made firm. Thus the whole community may clearly recognize that we have deservedly come to the sweetness of a treaty through such a bond of affection.

And because what has once been well begun ought not to be suspended by any contrary circumstance, if there is anything that ought not to be imposed upon us because of its difficulty, let it be softened by the moderation of your wisdom, so that we may increase through constant efforts the affection we have begun to hold toward your kingdom.

Therefore, display the steadfastness of your wisdom and specially claim for yourself this palm of concord. Just as the fame of the most merciful emperor is said to be renowned in battles, so may your reputation in the pursuit of peace be praised to the admiration of all [Col. 0814A].

Let the bearer of this letter, whom I have sent, see you familiarly and frequently, so that he may obtain a swift outcome, since he appears to have been sent in the expectation of your favor. For we hope for what is just, not burdensome, although nothing seems impossible when we know that such glory is pleading our cause.

## EPISTLE XXIV. GUDELINA, QUEEN, TO JUSTINIAN, EMPEROR

She indicates that she has written to him through Theodahad’s ambassador, so that, on his return, he may bring letters from the emperor bearing witness to the emperor’s safety and favor toward Gudelina herself and her husband.

When the most learned man Peter arrived, the love of Your Serenity filled us so completely that we thought we had seen the one whose conversation we had received with kindness. For who, having been received with such affability, would not return exceptional reverence to one to whom, even before the language of his condescension, the duty of commendation is rightly owed by all? [Col. 0814B]

Therefore, through that venerable man, the ambassador of our wedded lord, specially sent to you, we have taken care to dispatch salutary letters, so that the returning utterance of Your Serenity might both gladden us concerning your desired safety and make us rejoice in the exultation of your firmest favor.

Through such a shortening of affairs, the order of matters is well arranged, and the affection of our tranquility grows twofold. Let us therefore receive the good things of your heart, for this is truly a royal purpose: to live gloriously through the love of all.

We have entrusted certain matters to be suggested to you verbally by the bearer of this letter; receive them willingly, in keeping with your innate [Col. 0814C] gentleness, and, with God’s help, carry them into effect.

## EPISTLE XXV. THEODAHAD, KING, TO JUSTINIAN, EMPEROR

He states that he received the emperor’s letter from Heraclianus and immediately replies, announcing that he has written to the pope in accordance with the emperor’s wish.

Through the venerable man Heraclianus [Gr., Cuj. and For., “Eracemus”], the presbyter, the august page of Your Serenity shone upon us, graciously bestowing the favor of your speech and suitably conferring the gifts of your greeting. Truly, it is a great benefit to have deserved so pleasant a conversation with a prince.

We return a reply to him with all the affection of which we are capable, wishing that we may more often have the opportunity to hear of your safety and that the happiness of your kingdom may always increase [Col. 0814D]. For it is fitting that we should hold such a wish as can continually extend your glory and safety.

We also inform you that, in accordance with your wish, we have sent a letter to the pope of the city of Rome, so that he may reply without any delay to the bearer of this letter, and so that the one who deserved to be sent by you may obtain the favor of speed.

For it is our wish that circumstances arise in which we may obey your desires, since we effectively admonish ourselves to return your affection if we obey you in any respect.

## EPISTLE XXVI. THEODAHAD, KING, TO JUSTINIAN, EMPEROR

He says that he ordered Senator, the prefect of the praetorium, to go to the estate of certain nuns, so that, if a flood had inflicted any damage upon it, he might abolish the taxes. He then replies to what Justinian had written concerning Veranilda.

[Col. 0815A]

We understand that Your Serenity’s favor is richer than all gifts when you urge us to do things that can in every respect contribute to our reward. Such a wish is always characteristic of one who loves: that you want us to undertake works of mercy which can commend us to divine power.

Therefore, we inform Your Glory that the monastery of the servants of God which has been brought to your attention is suffering under the heavy burden of taxation because its field, drenched by an excessive flood [Col. 0815B], has contracted the defects of sterility from hostile moisture.

We have nevertheless given an order to the most eminent man Senator, prefect of the praetorium, that his prudent administration should send a careful inspector to the estate about which the complaint has been made, and that, after matters have been weighed through a moderate inquiry, whatever burden the property may bear should reasonably be abolished. This is to be done in such a way that a suitable and sufficient benefit may remain for the owners, since we truly judge it our most precious profit when we grant something at the request of Your Gentleness [ed., “our gentleness”].

As for the case of Veranilda, concerning which Your Serenity deigned to admonish me, although it occurred long ago under the rule of our parents, it was nevertheless necessary for us to settle the matter out of our own generosity, so that by such an action she would not regret her change of religion [Col. 0815C].

We do not presume to judge such matters when we do not have a specific mandate. [Note: [Col. 0815D] No one is to be compelled unwillingly to religion, which must be embraced voluntarily, not by force: above, Book II, Epistle 27. Theodoric to all Jews: “We cannot command religion,” he says, “because no one is compelled to believe against his will.” Athenagoras, in his *Embassy for the Christians* to the emperors Commodus and Antoninus, at the very beginning. [Col. 0816D] FORN.] For although the Divinity allows different religions to exist, we do not dare impose one religion. We remember reading that sacrifice should be offered to the Lord voluntarily, not at the command of anyone who compels it.

Whoever attempts to act otherwise has plainly opposed the commands of heaven. Your Piety therefore rightly invites us to do what the divine commandments enjoin upon us.

## EPISTLE XXVII. THEODAHAD, KING, TO SENATOR, PREFECT OF THE PRAETORIUM

He orders him to relieve the poverty of the Ligurians and Venetians.

Whoever hastens to assist taxpayers with some remedy seems not to give but to return expenses [Note: We have discussed the distinction between *dare*, “to give,” and *reddere*, “to return,” in Book III, Chapter 15 of the *Select Letters*. FORNER.]. For what is more just than to give to one who asks what he is understood to have worked for himself?

The idle may perhaps ask for mercy; but the cultivator of the land is abandoned to future hunger unless he is assisted when necessity requires it. Therefore, it is said that abundance has been taken away from the fields of industrious Liguria and devoted Venetia; but now let it be born in the granaries, since it is exceedingly impious for cultivators to hunger while the storehouses are completely full.

Accordingly, let Your Illustrious Greatness—whose office, as we read, was established for this purpose [Col. 0816A], so that you might feed the people from stored supplies—order that a third portion be distributed to the Ligurians, whom you nevertheless know to be in need, from the granaries at Ticinum and Dertona, at the rate of twenty-five modii per solidus [Cuj. and For., “fifteen”].

For the Venetians, likewise arrange for a third portion to be given from the granaries of Tarvisium and Tridentum, in the quantity specified above, so that the merciful Divinity may be able to bestow the abundance which He recognizes human beings to have exercised among themselves.

Therefore, appoint such men to these distributions that our indulgence may reach most fully those who have been least able to feed themselves by their own resources.

## EPISTLE XXVIII. THEODAHAD, KING, TO SENATOR, PREFECT OF THE PRAETORIUM

He confirms whatever Cassiodorus had established concerning the treasurers and distributors of grain, wine, and cheese; the meat sellers; and others in the cities of Rome, Ravenna, Ticinum, and Placentia. Then he forbids, under severe penalty, anyone to succeed them within five years. Finally, he orders that, because of the losses caused by sterility, the prices of goods be moderated.

[Col. 0816B]

168

It befits royal justice to preserve whatever has been arranged by judges who have acted well, especially when their conscience is so well known that they seem to have done nothing carelessly and nothing out of a desire for profit. Therefore, the treasurers and distributors of grain, wine, and cheese; the meat sellers, wine sellers, record-keepers of the granaries and taverns; the moneylenders and cellarers who belong either to the city of Rome or to the Ravenna station; and likewise those who are known to administer public offices along the banks of the Ticinum and at Placentia, or in any other places—these men, whom we have learned were appointed by you, whose judgments we embrace so willingly and desire to be preserved so firmly that they may be believed to have been made by us ourselves—we do not allow the malice of anyone to prevail against them, since they undertook public administrations by your judgment.

Therefore, let ambition, always hostile to justice, be quiet in the offices designated. Let us immediately remove the customary opportunity for envy against those who act well. Let no one be permitted to wish to succeed the aforesaid men within five years, provided that your inquiry finds them guilty of no fault.

Let those whom you have appointed, or have appointed previously, be fearless; let them provide themselves with what is necessary in security. Let no one fear being expelled within this five-year period if the integrity of his conduct has commended him.

Also, because of the sterility of the present time, arrange for the prices of individual commodities to be moderated according to what seems reasonably appropriate to Your Eminence [Col. 0816D], so that those entrusted with handling the several supplies do not complain of unjust burdens.

But since human ambition cannot be restrained except through fear of loss, anyone who, whether through influence or through the petitions of patrons, attempts to succeed any person whom we have appointed to these offices shall immediately be struck with a fine of thirty pounds of gold, which you are likewise to exact.

If he cannot be found capable of paying this loss [Col. 0817A], let him suffer corporal punishment, since he could not meet the penalty of the aforesaid blow [Note: Book 1, *Concerning Summons to Court*; above, Book IV, Epistle 10, at the end; and above, Book IX, Epistle 2: “If,” he says, “the means of exacting vengeance are insufficient, let him be torn apart by cudgel punishments.” Likewise, in the same Book IX, Epistle 18, in the edict of King Athalaric. FORN.]. Let the one who attempts to evade our prohibitions by any subterfuge be frustrated in his undertakings and branded also with the punishment of infamy.

For nothing can be found secure, nothing stable, if the wishes of the envious are always permitted to approach unlawful intrigues. Let Your Greatness make this known to everyone, so that no one may suppose that ignorance excuses him because he did not understand that the practice had been prohibited.

## EPISTLE XXIX. THEODAHAD, KING, TO VUINUSIADUS, COUNT

He grants him permission to seek the waters of Bormium for the treatment of gout, which is described graphically.

[Col. 0817B] Since the honorable nobility of your people and the proofs of your great loyalty had persuaded us to entrust to you in peacetime the governance of Ticinum, which you had defended through wars, you petitioned that, drenched by the sudden inundation of muddy gout, you wished instead to seek the waters of Bormiae, which are drying and especially beneficial for this ailment. We heal your desire by a remedial command, so that by the benefit of our order we may complete the recovery which we rightly seek for you.

For surely it would be intolerable that tyranny by so grievous a calamity should disarm a warlike man—a calamity which, in wondrous fashion, compels vigorous limbs to wither through the infusion of a painful humor, fills the mobile joints with swelling that grows like marble, and knows how to empty all the other joints. It seeks hollow depressions where, growing sluggish in a marshy station, it makes rocks out of liquid; [Col. 0817C] and what nature had relaxed for the beauty of movement, it constricts into the ugliest rigidity with a foreign solidity.

This disease is incurable, and health itself is liable to it; it binds what was loose, contracts the sinews, and causes bodies to shrink—bodies that have not been truncated by any mutilation. With the limbs remaining intact, the measure of one’s stature disappears, and a man is seen to be smaller although nothing seems to have been taken from him. The services of the limbs are withdrawn from the survivor: the body is alive but does not move; reduced to insensibility, it is now carried not by its own will but by another’s motion.

This living death is said to be worse than every other torture; and the man is thought better off who is not proved to have escaped the causes of so great a danger. The pain indeed leaves, but it leaves behind stronger remnants; and, in a new example of misery, the illness seems to depart while the sick man does not cease to be sick. [Col. 0817D] The appendages themselves are sometimes released from tortured debtors; but these are bonds which, once they have been able to bind their captive, do not know how to loosen him throughout his entire life.

In departing, it leaves unhappy signs, and, after the manner of barbarian peoples, violently defends the body’s occupied lodging by its marks, lest, once this savage power has begun to take possession, health—its enemy—should perhaps dare to enter there again. Although this may seem contrary to everyone, it is especially so to those who have flourished in the practice of arms, lest those exceptionally hard limbs should soften through the wasting process of illness; and lest those who could scarcely be overcome by an external enemy should instead be conquered by an inward adversary. [Col. 0818A]

Proceed, therefore, with God as your guide, on your own feet to the place mentioned above. Surely it would be intolerable for our warrior to walk on another’s feet. Let him be carried on a horse’s back, not by human transport; for it is burdensome for a brave man to live in such a way that he cannot even complete an inactive life [ed., “death”].

We have related these matters to you in an exaggerated account so that you may be seized by an exceedingly eager desire for health. Use those waters, therefore, first by drinking their soothing draughts, then by the drying applications of the baths, where that stubborn neck of the disease is rightly bent, when the inward parts are cleansed by abundant outpouring, the outward parts are freed by an attractive power, and the disease is overcome as though by two aids brought together and applied at the center. [Col. 0818B]

Let the gifts granted by heaven be loved there. Against that destroyer of the human race, the appropriate defenses of bathing have been provided; and what an unbroken ten years cannot subdue, what the entrance of a thousand potions cannot soften, is there driven away by delightful remedies. May the divine beneficence grant what is desired, so that by your recovery we may learn the truth of the place’s very celebrated reputation; for we desire to escape whatever deprives the body of health.

## LETTER XXX. KING THEODAHAD TO HONORIUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

He orders him to restore the tottering bronze elephants to their former condition and stability. He then gives a marvelous description of the elephants and their characteristics.

169. From the tenor of your report we have learned that, on the Sacred Way, which antiquity consecrated to many superstitions, bronze elephants are tottering on the verge of complete collapse; and those that are accustomed to live for more than a thousand years in bodily substance seem, in their bronze images, to be enduring an imminent downfall. Let your Providence restore to them their proper longevity by solidifying their gaping limbs with iron hooks, and also strengthen their lowered belly with a supporting wall, lest that marvelous mass collapse shamefully into ruin.

For collapse is also hostile to living elephants: when, through the ingenuity of men, they have entrusted their huge limbs to felled trees by the art of lying down, they cannot rise by their own strength once they have fallen, having been thrown onto their backs by their entire weight. This is because their feet bend at no joints [Note: [Col. 0818D] P. Gillius writes that this is false in his description of the elephant, appended to Aelian’s books on animals in the edition of Guillaume Rouillé, Lyon, 1565, p. 500. JURET.], but remain perpetually stiff and incapable of bending like columns. [Col. 0818D]

There they lie prostrate beneath such enormous bulk that you might then believe them more metallic than living, when you see them unable to move. Survivors lie there in the likeness of corpses: you would think them dead, although you cannot doubt that they are alive; and, like fallen structures, they do not know how voluntarily to leave the place which they have been able to occupy with their limbs.

That terrifying size is not even equal to the tiniest ants, since nature does not grant it the benefit which the lowest creatures appear to have deserved. They rise with human assistance, through whose skill [Col. 0819A] they had fallen. Yet once the beast has been restored to its own steps, it knows how to remember the favor: it accepts as its master the man whom it recognizes as having helped it; at his command it moves its feet, and at his will it takes food.

And—something that surpasses all the intelligence of four-footed animals—it does not hesitate at first sight to adore the one whom it understands to be ruler of all. If a tyrant appears to it, it remains bowed; nor can the beast be made to render to bad rulers what it knows it offers to good princes. It extends its trunk in place of a hand and gratefully accepts what will benefit its master, because it recognizes that it can live through his care.

For it is, so to speak, the beast’s nosed hand, through which it receives what is given and conveys it to its mouth to be swallowed. Although it is a tall animal, it is formed with a very short neck; thus, since it was not able to pick food up from the ground, it seemed capable of satisfying itself through this service. Always cautious, it proceeds by testing the ground, remembering that a fall had once proved harmful to it at the beginning of its capture.

When asked, it exhales its breath, which is said to cure human headaches. When it comes to water to drink, it pours out through the hollow of its trunk, like rain, a shower when requested; and thus it recognizes what it is suffering and willingly does what it is asked to do. By movements of its body it asks different persons for what it may offer its master, and it considers the provisions of its feeder to be its own food.

But if someone refuses to provide what it has requested, it is said to open the reservoir of its bladder and discharge such a great flood that a river seems to have entered that person’s household, taking revenge for the contempt through its stench. It also preserves an injury when wounded, and is said to repay it long afterward to the person whom it recognizes as having wronged it.

Its eyes are indeed small, but they move with solemn gravity. You might believe that its royal gaze was directed at something. It looks down scornfully on those who play the buffoon, but attends gratefully to anything honorable; and you perceive that it judges rightly when you discover that it dislikes frivolous things.

Its skin is furrowed by ulcerous valleys (from which the loathsome disease of travellers takes its name); it is hardened to such a degree that you might think it a skin of bone. No force passes through it, and no sharpness of iron penetrates it. For this reason the kings of Persia brought this beast into wars: it would yield to no blows and would terrify its opponents with its mass.

Therefore it is most pleasing to possess representations of them, so that those who have not seen the living creature may come to know the famous animal through such an image. And so do not allow them to perish, since it is worthy of Roman dignity to preserve in that city, through the skill of its craftsmen, what rich nature is known to have produced throughout the various parts of the world.

## LETTER XXXI. KING VITIGIS TO ALL THE GOTHS

He writes that he was created king by the army, according to ancestral custom.

Although every advancement must be referred to the gifts of Divinity, and nothing is established as good except what is recognized as bestowed by it, nevertheless the cause of royal dignity must above all be attributed to heavenly judgments, since He also ordained the one whom He knows his peoples must obey. Therefore, offering thanks to our Author Christ with the deepest humility, we declare that our Gothic ancestors, amid the drawn swords of the battle line, placed beneath a shield [Note: [Col. 0819D] Thus Ado of Vienne writes in his sixth age: “But, following the Franks, according to the custom of the people, he was placed upon a shield and established as king.” Likewise, Romans and barbarians lifted aloft the man whom they made emperor, as is clear from Jordanes, Chronicle, chapter 60, where I have noted other testimonies. That elevation was carried out with shields placed beneath him, as can be inferred from this passage. See Lorippus. JURET.], and by God’s favor conferred royal dignity upon us, so that arms might bestow the honor whose reputation the wars had produced.

You should know that I was chosen not in the narrow confines of a bedchamber but in wide-open fields; I was not sought amid the delicate conversations of flatterers but amid the blaring of trumpets, so that the Gothic people, stirred by such a roar and by a desire for innate valor, might find for themselves a warlike king.

For how long could brave men, raised amid raging wars, endure an untested leader, so that his reputation would be at risk, however confident he might be in his own valor? It is necessary that such an opinion of everyone should circulate as the people deserved to have of their ruler.

For, as you may have heard, summoned by the dangers facing my parents, I came to share the common fortune with all; but they would not permit me to be their leader, since they appeared to be seeking a tested king. Therefore, favor first the judgment of divine grace, and then that of the Goths, because you all make me king by joining your wishes with one accord.

Lay aside now your fear of losses; cast away your suspicions of expense; fear no hardship under our rule. We know how to love brave men, having often completed wars ourselves. Moreover, I stand as a witness to each of your virtues [ms., “to each of your men”]. [Col. 0820C] I do not need another person to recount your deeds to me, because I learned them all while sharing your labors.

The arms of the Goths must not be broken by any inconsistency in my promises [ed., “friends, etc., must not be broken”]. Everything we do will look to the advantage of the people; privately, we shall not love even ourselves. We promise to pursue whatever adorns the royal name.

Finally, we promise throughout our entire rule an empire such as the Goths ought to have after the illustrious Theodoric: a man singularly and nobly fitted to the cares of kingship, so that each of his successors may rightly be considered as distinguished as he is recognized to love his counsels. He should be regarded as his parent who is able to imitate his deeds. Therefore be concerned for the welfare of our kingdom, and, with God’s help, be secure regarding its internal conduct.

## LETTER XXXII. KING VITIGIS TO THE EMPEROR JUSTINIAN

[Note: [Col. 0820D] The subject of this letter arises from Justinian’s victory over the Goths, sufficiently attested by the histories; Vitigis therefore seeks peace from him through ambassadors. FORN.]

He sets forth the calamities which Italy was enduring because of the wars. He then asks the emperor for peace through ambassadors.

How great for us, most merciful emperor, is the welcome sweetness of your grace can be understood from this alone: after so many grievous injuries and so great a shedding of blood, we appear to seek your peace as though none of your people were thought to have injured us before. We have endured such things as might even offend those who inflicted them—persecution without guilt, hatred without fault, losses without debts.

And lest it could be neglected because of its smallness, the injury is proved to have been inflicted not only in the provinces but at the very head of the state. Consider what pains we cast aside so that we may find your justice. Such an event has occurred that Mundus may recount it [Note: [Col. 0821D] He was a commander of Justinian’s army, defeated the Dalmatians, and captured the city of Salona. Yet in that victory he himself was killed, together with his son Mauricius, struck down by a fleeing Goth. Procopius, Book I, On the Gothic War; Matthew Palmerius, Chronicle; Leonardo Aretino, On the Italian War against the Goths, Book I. FORN.]: it ought to be settled by you in such a way that the whole world must admire your equity.

For if vengeance against King Theodahad is being sought, I deserve to be loved; if the memory of the divine Queen Amalasuntha is held before your eyes, you ought to consider her daughter, whom it would have been fitting to bring to the throne through the efforts of all your people, so that all nations might recognize that you had repaid reciprocal favor to so great a pledge.

That fact ought to have moved you: by a marvelous dispensation, before the heights of kingship, Divinity caused us to know one another, so that it might give a cause for love to those to whom the grace of sight had been granted. With what reverence, then, could I have honored a prince whom I had revered while he was still subject to that fortune?

But even now you can restore everything that has been done, since it is not difficult to retain in affection one who is known eagerly to seek your favor. Therefore, greeting your Clemency with fitting honor, we inform you that we have sent our ambassadors, this man and that man, to the wisdom of your Serenity, so that you may consider everything in your customary manner, in order that, with concord restored, both commonwealths may endure; and that what was founded in the former times of the emperors with praiseworthy reputation may, under your rule, be increased still further by divine assistance.

We have entrusted the remaining matters to the aforesaid ambassadors to communicate verbally to your Serenity, so that the brevity of a letter might touch upon certain points while they, presenting our causes, might explain them more fully.

## LETTER XXXIII. KING VITIGIS TO THE MASTER OF OFFICES

He asks him to persuade the emperor to grant peace to Italy.

When sending our ambassadors, this man and that man, to the most serene prince, it was fitting that we should send through them salutary lines to Your Greatness, so that they might deserve your benefits in every respect, since they were carrying the affection of our conversation.

Therefore, offering you the grace of a letter in accordance with your merits, we hope that your prudence will support them in the heart of the most merciful emperor; for our requests are so just that they deserve the support of all wise men. What ought not to have been permitted can easily be corrected by you.

You can arrange everything graciously and peacefully, because favor is usually sweeter after bitterness has been cleansed away. An unknown man might have been able to flee you; but I, who have seen the adornment of your commonwealth and have come to know the hearts of so many noble leaders, do not wish to be separated from the favor of your most merciful prince, if he is willing to consider what is just toward me.

For if another deserved offense, I ought to be held most dear, since I succeeded an odious man together with his punishment. I followed your desires; rewards should have been returned to me, not injury. Therefore let favor not be denied to one against whom nothing at all can be charged; and let hatred be buried with the death of the offender.

Even if we perhaps deserve somewhat less from you, let Roman liberty be considered—the liberty that is shaken everywhere by the tumult of wars. Let these few words suffice for your wisdom, since in a lofty breast there extends that which is always enlarged by consideration.

## LETTER XXXIV. KING VITIGIS TO HIS BISHOPS

He asks them both to assist the ambassadors whom he has sent to the emperor and to pour out prayers to God on his behalf.

If we owe honor even to priests whom we do not know, how much more to those whom we have seen with affectionate reverence? We seek out a person we know in one way, and address an unknown person in another. The affection arising from what has been seen is always greater, since the person who is joined to us by constant and gracious speech is held most dearly.

Therefore, through the bearers of this letter, our ambassadors whom we have sent to the most serene prince, we present to Your Holiness the service of our due reverence, hoping that you will deign to pray for us and that, wherever necessity demands it, they may find your support; for it is necessary to wish well to those whom you recognize as joined to you by religion.

## LETTER XXXV. KING VITIGIS TO THE PREFECT [ed., “THE PATRICIAN, QUAESTOR”] OF THESSALONICA

He asks that the ambassadors sent to the emperor suffer no delay.

We have sent our ambassadors, this man and that man, to the most serene prince, with God’s favor. Through them it was necessary to return the affection of a greeting to Your Greatness, since your honor and wisdom deserve that we enjoy the pleasure of conversation with you.

We hope from Your Excellency that those whom you see us to have dispatched with all speed will not be made to suffer delay, so that we may attach them to your benefits if we learn that they have arrived without any tardiness.

# BOOK ELEVEN

[Col. 0821]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0821D]

The assistance of a preface generally arises from the contradiction of one’s activities, when what could have impeded the thinker proves helpful to the writer. Although this circumstance removes praise, when treated with kindness it grants pardon; for what everyone acknowledges that the idle owe, no one can demand from the occupied.

Therefore, if a most distinguished administrator is believed to have had leisure, it is a reproach; and even his privacy is said to be battered by tumultuous affairs. Yet a proof brought to completion will scarcely accomplish anything for us, since we are believed to have been occupied and are judged not at all to have been obliged to write badly. For it is much better to conceal faulty work in darkness than to publish what deserves blame through rash importunity.

An idle person, however, might object to me if I threw out a word with heedless haste, if I failed to adorn a thought taken from the middle with the beauty of language, or if I did not assign proper characteristics to the persons in accordance with the precepts of the ancients. But an occupied man, swept along by the diversity of affairs, continually obliged to give answers and dictate matters to be expedited for another, cannot condemn me when he recognizes that he himself has been endangered in such circumstances.

For one who is conscious of his own condition is easily acquitted regarding that of another; nor are we always capable of doing what we are sometimes judged capable of doing. A fertile intellect pours forth brilliant invention; an occupied mind conceives words that are lukewarm. Sometimes it is fitting that a sharp style should be consistently composed, since the art of speaking is recognized as lying within our power; but mental vitality belongs only to divine gifts.

What remains for our defense, then, is the unexpected brevity of the books—a matter no one can excuse at length except one who is believed likely to speak well. But lest anyone perhaps be offended that, established at the summit of the praetorian office, I have dictated so little while entirely occupied with affairs, let him understand that this was done at the initiative of the very prudent Felix, whose counsel I shared in every matter.

For he is a man first purified by the sincerity of his character, outstanding in knowledge of the law, distinguished by precision of language, an old man in youthful vigor, a gracious disputant, eloquent with measure. By elegantly fulfilling public needs, he brought himself, through his own labor, to favorable repute.

Otherwise, burdened by such enormous masses of affairs, I might either have proved unequal to them or perhaps been found arrogant. But it is better that, refreshed by his exertions, I attended to royal cares in such a way that I could not be judged deficient in difficult matters.

I have therefore appended two little books of my dictations concerning the work of the prefecture, so that I, who had spoken with the royal voice in ten books, might not be unknown in my own person; for it is exceedingly absurd for one who appeared to have spoken much on behalf of others to fall silent after attaining office.

But after I had brought my little work to its desired conclusion in twelve books, my friends compelled me to discuss the substance of the soul, or its virtues, so that, having said so much, I might appear to say something about the soul as well.

Now spare the eloquent and favor those who are beginning; for if I deserve nothing through the gift of eloquence, I should rather be considered for my most dutiful labor. Though occupied by such great necessities of the commonwealth, I was able to find leisure amid burning cares—if only I had been fortunate enough to boast of Tullian streams. For Cicero himself, that fountain of eloquence [Note: [Col. 0823D] Cicero freed a slave because he had announced that the assemblies had been postponed until the following day: so prepared and practiced did that great craftsman approach speaking. Plutarch. FORN.], is said, when asked to speak, to have excused himself on the grounds that he had not read the material the day before.

What, then, might happen to others, if so great a reputation for eloquence seemed to require the resources of its authors? The intellect surely grows feeble unless it is renewed by constant reading. Granaries are quickly exhausted if they are not supported by continual additions. How easily is the treasury itself emptied if it is not refilled with new money?

So the human understanding, when it is not filled with discoveries borrowed from others, can quickly be diminished in its own resources. If anything in us gives off a fragrance, it is the flower of study; yet this too becomes withered if it is plucked away from its mother, reading. For there it can be most flourishing, from which it is taught and born, since everything lives most fully at its origin before it is taken away from its natural wombs [ed., “boundaries”].

Accordingly, a large part of pardon lies in the fact that we write without leisure and are read without reading. But let us now withdraw from the plea of excuse, lest an overly contrived defense give greater offense.

## LETTER I. THE PREFECT OF THE PRAETORIUM, SENATOR, TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME

He praises Amalasuntha at length, as well as her parents and her son Athalaric. He then asks the senators to return thanks to the rulers for granting him the prefecture of the praetorium.

[Col. 0824B]

You have commended my advancement to me, Conscript Fathers, if I understand that it was welcome to you. For I believe that what so many fortunate men are known to have desired has turned out most auspiciously. Your desires are proved to be favorable omens of every good thing, since no one can be received with such favor unless Divinity has ordained that he be advanced.

Therefore borrow favor in order to demand service. It is the nature of things to love a colleague. Indeed, you exalt your own praises if you raise up the honor that has been bestowed upon a senator. Let the solicitude of the fathers drive me earnestly toward public usefulness, so that it may be attributed more to your commendation when I have deserved to please such patrons.

My second concern, after the rulers, is to commend myself to you, since we trust that you love what we also perceive the masters of affairs to command. First, let us consider useful whatever is honorable; let justice always accompany our actions like a handmaid; and let us not shamefully sell to anyone what we did not buy from a self-controlled ruler.

You have heard, distinguished men, what burdens I have taken up, having been praised for them. More is demanded than one’s strength can bear when a man who has entered the heights of dignity is praised. We do not dare call these judgments false, but we confess that they are greater than the truth. Such judgments did not find merits; they created them.

Nor do we boast on that account, since we understand that our lords wished to raise up the lowly, lest they appear to have bestowed such immense gifts upon the undeserving. The blessings of this age seize us as subjects of praise and, like people thirsting after a long drought, invite us to drink a sweetness most delightful.

O blessed fortune of the age! Under a prince at peace, a mother’s affection reigns; through it everything is conducted in such a way that we feel ourselves sheltered by a universal love. He renders glorious service to the woman whom all things obey, and, with marvelous harmony, before he could rule peoples he began already to rule himself by his character.

This is surely the most difficult kind of kingship: to exercise authority over a young man’s own faculties. It is an exceedingly rare good for a ruler to triumph over his character and to attain in the flower of youth what even gray-haired modesty is scarcely believed to reach.

Let us rejoice, Conscript Fathers, and offer thanks to the heavenly Majesty with humble devotion, since our prince will encounter no clemency difficult to approach in the course of time, having learned in his boyhood to serve piety.

But let us attribute this miracle to the character of both; for so great is the mother’s genius that even a foreign prince ought rightly to have served her. All kingdoms most worthily venerate her; to see her is an act of reverence, and to hear her speak is a marvel.

For in what language is she not proved to be most learned? She is eloquent in the brilliance of Attic expression, she shines with the splendor of Roman eloquence, and she takes pride in the abundance of her native speech. She surpasses everyone in their own languages while being equally marvelous in all.

For if knowing one’s native language well is a sign of prudence, what can be estimated concerning such wisdom, which preserves so many forms of eloquence through unimpeded practice? From this comes a necessary and great safeguard to different nations, because no one needs an interpreter in the presence of so wise a lady.

Neither does an ambassador suffer delay, nor does a petitioner suffer loss from the slowness of a mediator, since each is heard in his own words and answered in his native speech. To these qualities is joined, like an exceptional diadem, priceless knowledge of literature; through it, while the wisdom of the ancients is learned, royal dignity is continually increased.

But although she rejoices in such perfection of languages, in public action she is so silent that she might be thought idle. She resolves intricate disputes with a few words; she arranges raging wars beneath a calm exterior; the public good is conducted silently. You do not hear proclaimed what plainly appears to be undertaken, and with marvelous restraint she accomplishes by concealment what she recognizes must be hastened.

What similar achievement did antiquity honorably accomplish? We have learned that Placidia, celebrated in the opinion of the world and glorious through the lineage of some, devoted herself to her son in the purple. While she administered the empire with excessive mildness, it was known to have been diminished disgracefully. In the end she acquired a daughter-in-law for herself through the loss of Illyricum, and the union of the reigning house became a division to be mourned by the provinces. She also weakened the army through excessive repose. Protected by his mother, he endured what he scarcely could endure once abandoned.

Under this lady, however, who, with God’s help, has had as many kings as she has had parents, our army terrifies foreigners. Balanced by prudent arrangement, it is neither worn down by constant wars nor softened again by a long peace. At the very beginning, too, when novelty is always tested uncertainly, she made the Danube Roman against the wishes of the Eastern emperor.

It is known what the invaders endured; I judge that these things should be passed over lest the shared genius of the prince suffer the shame of a defeated man. For what he thought of your side [Ac., “of our fathers”] is clear from this: when injured, he granted peace which he had refused to grant to others even when entreated.

Furthermore, he adorned us by seeking us so rarely through such great embassies; and that singular power, in order to raise up Italian rulers, inclined the reverence of the Eastern throne. The Franks too, powerful through so many victories over barbarians, were thrown into turmoil by an expedition of such magnitude. Challenged, they feared to enter into battle with our men, who had always brought wars upon nations by rushing down precipitous passes.

Although that proud nation avoided the conflict, it could not avoid the death of its own king. For that Theodoric, long celebrated under a powerful name, died, overcome in the battle of illness rather than in triumph over our rulers: by divine ordinance, I believe, so that neither the wars of our neighbors might defile us nor an army rightfully brought forth lack some act of vengeance.

Hail, army of the Goths, made more joyful by every good fortune: you slay the enemy king and do not withhold from us the deeds of even a single least man.

The Burgundian, moreover, became devoted in order to recover what was his; he gave himself entirely once he had received something small. He chose, while intact, to obey rather than, diminished, to resist [Ac., “unprotected, to resist”]. He defended his kingdom more safely when he laid down his arms, for he recovered by petition what he had lost in battle.

Blessed are you, lady, with manifold praise, since by divine favor the necessity of every conflict is removed from you: you either conquer the enemies of the commonwealth by heavenly good fortune or join them to yourself by your commands and their voluntary generosity.

Exult together, Goths and Romans. It is a worthy marvel, one that all may proclaim. Behold, by God’s favor, the fortunate lady has fulfilled what is exceptional in both sexes: she has given us a glorious king and recovered a vast empire through strength of spirit.

These matters, insofar as they concern arms, have been reported in some fashion. But if we wish to enter the halls of her piety, scarcely could a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths suffice. Her justice and will are equal, but her kindness is greater than her power.

Let us therefore say little about great things, and a few words about many. You know how many benefits she has bestowed upon our order with heavenly kindness; there is no doubt of it, since the Senate is witness. She restored the afflicted to better circumstances, raised the unharmed to honors, and bestowed individual benefits upon those whom she guarded under universal protection.

The matters we assert have already grown. Consider, for example, the patrician Liberius, prefect also of the Gauls, a military man, most agreeable in fellowship, renowned for his merits, conspicuous in appearance but more beautiful through his wounds, who received the rewards of his labors. He neither lost the prefecture which he had administered well, nor did the doubled honor fail to adorn this outstanding man. His merit was acknowledged, yet his single honor was insufficient as a reward. [Col. 0826D]

For he also received an immediate dignity, lest, having deserved well of the commonwealth, he should be thought ungrateful because of his long absence. O admirable benevolence of our lords! It raised the aforesaid man so high that, after granting him the insignia of office, it judged that his patrimony also ought to be increased. This was received gratefully by everyone, so that all considered themselves enriched by his gift, since whatever is entrusted to a worthy man is unquestionably felt to have been bestowed upon many.

What, then, shall I say of the firmness of spirit that overcame even philosophers celebrated with great praise? A beneficent word proceeds from the lady’s mouth, and a promise remains secure. These are not matters of which we, Conscript Fathers, have less experience; the true witness is the man who praises what he has tested.

You know what opposing hopes fought against me: neither gold nor great prayers prevailed. Everything was attempted so that the glorious constancy of the wisest lady might be proved. The order of my discourse demands that I compare the splendor of the august women of old with modern examples. But how could those female examples suffice for one to whom the praise of men altogether yields?

If that royal company of ancestors could behold her, it would immediately see its own praises reflected as in the purest mirror. Amalus shone in good fortune, Ostrogotha in endurance, Athala in gentleness, Munitarius in equity, Unimundus in beauty, Thorismuth in chastity, Unalamer in faith, Theudimer in piety, and her illustrious father in endurance, as you have already seen.

All of them would certainly recognize here their own qualities individually, but would happily confess that they had been surpassed, since the praise of one person cannot rightly be equaled by a multitude of virtues. Consider what joy they would have felt in such an heir, who was able to surpass the merits of them all.

Perhaps you may ask separately about the prince’s virtues: the offspring is abundantly praised by the man who praises her author. You also retain the excellent saying of the most eloquent Symmachus: “I happily behold the growth of his virtue, while I postpone praising its beginnings.” [Note: [Col. 0827D] These words do not occur in the editions of Quintus Symmachus currently published. JUR.]

Come to my aid, Conscript Fathers, and, by acting on my behalf, return thanks to our common lords and discharge my debt through your acknowledgment. For just as one person cannot satisfy the wishes of everyone, so many people can fulfill the intentions of one.

## LETTER II. THE PREFECT OF THE PRAETORIUM, SENATOR, TO JOHN THE POPE

He asks that he be assisted by John’s prayers, admonitions, and even corrections.

[Col. 0827C]

It must be requested of you, most blessed father, that we may feel the joy which, through you and by God’s gift, we have received preserved for us by your prayers. For who could doubt that our prosperity should be attributed to your merits, when we attain an honor which we do not deserve by being loved by the Lord, and receive good things by an effective exchange, while we do not perform deeds of such a kind? Indeed, through ecclesiastical fasts popular hunger has been driven away; through tears of fitting dignity, shameful sorrow has departed; and through holy men it has been hastened that what weighed upon us should not be prolonged further.

And therefore, greeting you with the dutiful respect that is proper, I beg you to pray more earnestly for the welfare of the rulers, so that the heavenly Prince may make their life long, diminish the enemies of the Roman commonwealth, and grant peaceful times. Then, as that which adorns peace, may he bestow upon us the necessary supply from the storehouses of his abundance. May he also open to me, your son, the understanding of intelligence, so that I may follow what is truly useful and avoid what ought to be shunned. May that rational vigor of the soul provide us with counsel; may the face of truth grow bright, lest bodily darkness cloud our mind; may we follow what is within, lest we be outside ourselves. May it instruct what has a taste for true wisdom and illuminate what shines with heavenly radiance.

Finally, may public office receive such a judge as the Catholic Church sends forth as a son [Greek and Cuj.: “nurtures”]. May holy virtue also preserve us in its own gifts, because we undergo the heavier ambushes of the ancient adversary precisely when we receive his gifts.

Do not cast upon me alone the care of that city, which is made secure rather by your praise. For you preside as guardians over the Christian people; in the name of a father you love all things. The security of the populace therefore pertains to your reputation, to which its guardianship has been divinely entrusted.

Accordingly, it is fitting that we guard certain things, but that you guard everything. You feed the flock entrusted to you spiritually; nevertheless, you cannot neglect those matters which seem to contain the substance of the body. For just as a human being consists of a duality, so it is the duty of a good father to foster both.

First, remove by holy prayers the scarcity of the present time, which sins have deserved. If something should nevertheless happen—which God forbid—necessity is then well excluded when it is dealt with amid abundance [Greek and Cor.: “truth”; Jur. thinks “freedom” should be read]. Carefully advise me concerning what must be done. I desire to act well even when corrected, because the sheep that longs to hear the shepherd’s voice is less likely to go astray; nor does one easily become vicious when a constant admonisher attends him.

I am indeed a palatine judge, but I shall not cease to be your disciple. For we conduct these matters correctly only if we depart in no way from your rules. But since I desire from you both admonition through counsel and assistance through prayers, it is now for you to answer if anything in me should be found otherwise than was hoped.

May that seat, wondrous throughout the whole world [Note: “He means Rome, which Sidonius calls the dwelling-place of the laws, the school of letters, the senate-house of dignities, the summit of the world, and the homeland of freedom. Jerome too, in a certain letter, wonders that a certain inhabitant of Gades was moved more by the mere name and fame of Titus Livy than by the splendor of the city of Rome when he was traveling toward Rome. But now Rome, the squanderer of her own name, lies as nothing other than the foul corpse of her former beauty.” BROSS.], shelter its own devoted adherents with affection. Although it has been granted to the world in general, it is also known to have been assigned to you locally. We possess something belonging particularly to the holy apostles, provided that it is not made alien to us by sins that divide us, since Rome has been deemed worthy to hold within her bosom those shrines of confession [Note: “Those confessors—Peter and Paul. By the name ‘confession’ they meant the part of a church where the bodily relics of the saints were buried beneath the altar, not the whole church itself, as Baronius notes in his commentary on the Roman Martyrology under 6 July. Aimoinus likewise uses ‘the keys of the confession of Saint Peter’ in *History of the Franks*, book IV, chapter 84. Add the passage of Ennodius cited by Baronius, volume VI, page 601.” JURET.], whom the whole world longs to see.

We therefore fear nothing with such patrons, provided that the bishop’s prayer does not cease. It is certainly difficult to satisfy the desires of many, but Divinity knows how to provide great things. May it itself blunt the envious; may it itself make us, through heavenly aspiration, exceedingly pleasing to our fellow citizens; and through your supplications may it grant us times in which heavenly grace may be proclaimed as bestowed.

## EPISTLE III. TO THE VARIOUS [edition: “ALL”] BISHOPS, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He commends himself to their prayers and asks them to proclaim a fast for the welfare of the rulers and for the attainment of peace. Then he urges them to drive every vice far from the people.

[Col. 0829A]

It is the natural custom of bodily fathers to rejoice in the advancement of their sons, since whatever praise is granted to illustrious offspring is applied to their upbringing. But you are spiritual parents, who behold the Creator of all things with enlightened minds. Earnestly supplicate the holy Trinity for me, so that it may cause the lampstand placed in the midst to shine far and wide, so that neither inward sight may be lacking to me nor the outward gaze upon me be concealed from others.

What benefit would it be for a judge to be clear-sighted to others, if he were rather made obscure to himself? May he who has deigned to confer tribunals grant dignity of conscience. May he make the judge blameless, lest he condemn one who is in error. May he be most favorably present to us, so that harmful vices may be made absent. May he grant his love, so that in pity he may exclude the opportunity for sinning.

Therefore, true parents of the soul, I beseech you with affectionate and commendable petition to supplicate the Lord with a proclaimed fast, that he may extend the life of our rulers through a flourishing reign, that the defender may diminish the enemies of the commonwealth, grant quiet times and abundant times for the praise of his name, establish tranquility in all things, and deign to make me pleasing to you.

But so that your prayer also may be heard more easily, be astonished [Ac.: attentive] concerning those whom we appoint. What we do not know ought not to be attributed to us. Let your testimony follow their actions, so that one who is praised may find favor with you, while one who is accused may find offense before you. For they will not be able to blame you if they commit offenses, when they are not ordered to give evil things, so as to be compelled to receive them wrongly.

Provide orphans and widows with comforts pleasing to God against savage attacks, but do so in such a way that—what happens through excessive compassion [Note: “Through excessive compassion. In this sense an old and uncertain author writes in *Homily 14 on Matthew*, chapter VI (wrongly attributed commonly to Saint Chrysostom): ‘Mercy is truly mercy if it is done in such a way that justice is not despised through it; but if mercy is practiced with justice despised, that mercy is not mercy but foolishness.’” JURET.]—while you seek to help the wretched, you do not remove the place of the laws. For if something should perhaps offend strict authority, give everyone such admonitions that you may be able to render the laws inactive for a time.

Holy men, drive away among the unclean spirits the implacable furies of vice; restrain violence, expel greed, remove theft, and separate from your people the luxury that lays waste the human race. You defeat the author of iniquity effectively if you remove his persuasions from human hearts. Let the bishop teach, so that the judge may find nothing to punish. The administration of innocence has been given to you. For if your preaching does not cease, it is necessary that punitive action come to rest.

And therefore I commend my dignity to you in every respect, so that our actions may be assisted by the prayers of holy men, since we place less confidence in human power. Advise me also familiarly concerning what is just. I am not a cunning repudiator [edition: “pleader”; manuscript: “arbiter”]; I pay without compulsion what I owe generally. I also return to your holiness the duty of an honorable greeting and conclude the text of the letter with an affectionate ending, so that sweeter things may remain in your mind, since the mind properly commends what comes afterward to itself.

## EPISTLE IV. TO AMBROSIUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, ACTING AS DEPUTY, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He admonishes him to carry out faithfully the office entrusted to him.

We confidently entrust our reputation to you with God’s help, since over a long period we have tested your integrity through the varied practices of legal cases. For if you shone with the clarity of justice in the practice of advocacy [Note: “When advocates’ proceedings come to an end, dignities then begin,” says Sidonius Apollinaris, book I, letter 11. JURET.], what will you now do, having been advanced to our councils? Merit grows in the one to whom a greater office is given, when one who has deserved to sit among the powers of the court must now be counted among the judges.

Let the benches therefore be adorned by him whose voice once made the courts resound. While absent, cleave to our side, destined to gain fuller praise from this, because whatever you arrange well by yourself will be reckoned wholly to your credit. When you were present, you shared this care and glory with me; now, however, we are compelled to owe you alone whatever praise we may receive from it, with God’s favor.

Therefore we judge that you should observe the office which obeys our commands. We also order obedience to your instructions, duly designated for the public advantage, so that you may have confidence to send orders for the public benefit and no one may take the audacity to despise you. If you should think it necessary to commit some persons to sureties, take them on confidently, because it can relieve our mind all the more if we learn that something has been accomplished through you. Before, you would have offered us only words in person; now, however, actions are owed to us in your absence.

The counsel of so great a seat is undoubtedly the great reputation of its merits. But consider what is demanded of one upon whom such a name is imposed. Let your labor procure quiet for me in all things. You know what disgrace neglect has brought about. One must avoid the rock where another has stumbled. Yet my concern prompts me to admonish you more than distrust of you does. For we believe that you will do all those things which, with God’s help, we judge useful to our reputation and to the commonwealth.

## EPISTLE V. TO AMBROSIUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, ACTING AS DEPUTY, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He urges him to come to the aid as soon as possible of the Roman people suffering from scarcity.

[Col. 0830D]

I believe that you rejoice in those things which I judge your affection to have desired; for in a way the matter of the one whose wishes are fulfilled in another is being carried out. But from this I understand that the fruit of our ancient friendship, made happier by its charm, has flowed forth into sweetness of the most pleasant flavor: if, before anything else, through those concerned you offer to our household the abundance of the Roman state as an exceptional gift.

For this reason we entered upon the hardships of travel, for this reason so many anxious reflections, so that that people, accustomed to ancient pleasures, might enjoy the most blessed times of the rulers, with their necessities driven away. Far be it from us to be satisfied while any inhabitant of that city is hungry. Their need—which God forbid—is our scarcity. What more is there to say? We cannot be happy unless we hear that they too are rejoicing with us.

Therefore let grain of unimpaired quality be gathered with such vigor that the bread baked from it may seem offered not as an object of disgust but as a delicacy. Let just measurement be maintained. Let supplies surpass the desires of minds. What is sought is not thought to abound. Flee criminal profits; avoid wicked gains. Whatever is wrongly presumed there strikes at my own mind. Let no one think it pardonable to presume upon anything in this matter.

We more readily consent to being exceeded in our own affairs than to allow the interests of the Romans to be diminished—not in order to obtain popular favor and applause, but so that, with the Lord’s help, I may fulfill my judgment of affection toward them. All citizens must indeed be cherished, but the Romans deserve something more. A city adorned with so many outstanding senators and blessed with peoples so noble ought to resound with praise of our rulers—praise which a man of foreign nation might marvel to hear.

For popular joy rightly exalts itself there, since it is known to have victorious rulers. Therefore everything that fidelity and great caution can provide must be expended, because that is truly our advantage which secures their affection for me. Let those who were anxiously suspended over our action rejoice in present joys; their desires and their vows have helped me. It also benefited me before the lords of all things that their wishes were universally heard.

Now act so that this love may endure, with the Lord’s help, because I believe that in the future they will do more of what they happily feel they have begun in me. Let us now seek abundance with common prayers; let us humbly entreat heavenly mercy, so that divine clemency may first grant us the safety of our rulers. As for the yield which it provides, let neither negligence diminish it nor any venality withdraw it. I pledge my good faith, but together with them I uphold the gifts of Divinity; I offer vigilance and exclude the shameful practices of the most fraudulent market-dealing. Let them themselves glory in the abundance deserved from the Lord.

## EPISTLE VI. TO JOHN, THE CHANCELLOR, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

John is appointed chancellor by Cassiodorus, and he is admonished concerning what must be done in this dignity.

Although every service is performed through established grades, and those who obey the commands of judges observe their proper periods, your honor is known not to be held by the customary order, since it has deserved to be placed before its own superiors. Those whom you are known to precede render you their services; and, by a reversal of the order of rank, you are regarded with reverence by those whom you are shown to be able to follow.

You carry out this unequal equality, this special decree, this singular favor, under the gaze of the judge; nor can it reasonably be blamed that something seems to be assumed in opposition to the established order. No one prescribes to you concerning the quality of time. Your action is a transgression of the register, and alone you confidently neglect what you insist that others observe [manuscript: “despise”]. But such things are granted to you because of your outstanding merits, since you are believed to surpass everyone in diligence and fidelity—one whom we plainly chose.

For no one approves a successor unless commendable virtue associates him with himself, since it is blameworthy to raise an inferior unless he appears to surpass others in merits. This therefore commendable precedence, this gracious decision, this household service, assigns to you from the twelfth indiction (A.D. 534) the distinction of the chancellorship, so that you may guard the secrets of our consistory with faithful integrity.

Let the petitioner approach through you for presentation; through you let the desire of the suppliant become known to our ears; expedite our commands without the zeal of venality; and conduct everything in such a way that you may commend our justice. For your actions are the judge’s reputation. And just as the inner chamber of a house can appropriately be understood from its doors [Note: “Book I, chapter 2, of Nazarius’ panegyric, page 206. Saint Ambrose, *On Virgins*, book II: ‘A good house ought to be recognized in its very vestibule.’ So too Apuleius and Jerome, in the letter to Marcellinus and Anapsychus: ‘When you have read them and seen the vestibules, it will be easy to conjecture what the house itself will be.’” JURET.], so the mind of the governor is rightly recognized from you, not without reason, because each person seems to choose for his responses such a man as he has resolved to consider himself [Greek, Niv., and Ga.: “a guardian … to be judged”].

Are not the very garments applied to our bodies able to disfigure us if they become dirty through some stain? How much grace, however, they seem to lend us when they shine with commendable purity! So the soldier who has approached the judge’s secrets either adorns or stains the reputation [manuscript and Ac.: “appearance”] of his governor. Those who stain others sin against us; and while the property of the petitioner [edition: “the one who watches”] is pursued, the reputation of the presiding official is stripped away.

Consider whether we ought to neglect anything by which we may be known to deserve blame. He is excessively merciful [Note: “The old reading is ‘beyond the insane.’ The error was easy because of the similarity of *cl* and *d*, just as Gellius, book V, chapter 14, suffers from the same kind of mistake in the name of the servant recognized by a lion, who is truly *Androclus* in Aelian. Nemesianus likewise has ‘the gods lying gently on the slopes’ for ‘on the hills.’ He is describing the ascent of the Capitoline, where slopes certainly existed, as is also clear from Alfenus, book 52, ‘On the slope,’ under the Aquilian law. A similar error among the Greeks occurs in *χαλήβια* for *χαδήσια*, and *χαλήσια* for *χαδήσια*, as Hartung discovered.” FORN.] who does not wish to avenge one whom he has found assailing him in his own disgrace [Greek, Cuj., and Forn.: “beyond the insane”]. Consider by what name you have been called. What you have done among the grilles [Note: “In the ancient glosses, *caula* means an enclosure; the grilles before the judge are outside the enclosure, facing the courts.” JURET.] cannot remain hidden.
