You hold bright doors, open barriers, and latticed entrances. Although you close them carefully, it is necessary that you open yourself to everyone. If you stand outside, you are corrected by my gaze; if you enter inside, you cannot avoid the sight of those who watch. See where antiquity wished you to be placed: you are observed from every side because you move in that brightness.

Therefore turn your ears and mind toward our admonitions; fix in your memory everything that we command. Do not let our words pass through you like an empty pipe [Note: “A similar saying by the comic poet:

> I am full of cracks; I leak through here and there.

FORN.], which is seen to be full only so long as it is known that waters can flow into it. Be rather a receptacle that guards what it has heard and does not pour out what it has received. For it will do no good if things passing through your ears please you, while nothing fixes itself in the recesses of your heart.

## EPISTLE VII. TO ALL THE JUDGES OF THE PROVINCES, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He orders that the taxpayers be admonished to pay the customary taxes in three installments and at the appointed times.

What is provided through annual devotion is rightly sought, when it is clear that what is paid according to natural law is brought forward with a certain joy. For it is a stipend that makes the subject be called generous; and the giver receives the name of one who recognizes that he owes what is paid. How splendid it is to stand fearlessly in the court, not to fear the public authority, and to be placed among the devoted as one worthy of praise, when one is not forced in a way that leaves no room for modesty!

Everything compelled is dishonorable [edition: “everything done is dishonorable”]; and one who is driven to pay taxes by his own losses does not possess the grace of a giver. Conversely, what could be more worthy of a free man than to owe nothing to those who compel? That field alone is pleasing to its master in which the tax collector is not feared when he arrives.

Therefore the security of payment is rightly called a testimony [Note: “A receipt is called security. Petronius, in the *Satyricon*: ‘Give me the final receipt,’ that is, release from old age. Sidonius speaks of security against taxes, and so forth.” BROSS.], by which not only the mind but also the property is fortified.

And therefore, in the twelfth indiction (A.D. 534), with the customary administration maintained throughout the diocese of your jurisdiction, we order you and your office to admonish the possessors that, devotedly paying in three installments at the appointed times [Note: “All installments were paid into the treasury in three payments, namely every fourth month. *Code*, ‘On Receipts,’ book X, title 22.” FORNER.], they complete their obligation. In this way let that venal delay cease [Note: “Venal delays: below, book VIII, letter 35; and book XXII, ‘If properly,’ under *On Interest*.” FORN.], which is known to have been devised not for the advantage of taxpayers but through the ambition of fraud.

For those who claim that they are relieving people of such burdens impose another, greater burden of detestable bargaining. Far be detestable and avoidable cunning from our times. Let the possessor pay nothing except what is owed to the public; for those who attempt to defraud anyone under our authority are rather bringing loss upon themselves.

Therefore, just as we do not wish fiscal burdens to be increased by any pretext, so we order that the prescribed installments be completed at the appointed times, with God’s help, so that both the devotion of the possessors may be known to the rulers as most pleasing and the confusion wrapped up in delay may be removed from our accounts [edition: “prayers”].

Accordingly, send to our archives at each appointed time the lists duly prepared according to custom, just as both the ancient authority of the laws and the present authority of our command seem to admonish you, lest, if you should judge any of these matters negligible, you absolutely make the danger your own.

Nevertheless, so that more diligent zeal for the most just commands may be secured, have this man and that man—proved by their earlier merits—attend upon you and your office, so that negligence may be unable to cause harm where doubled diligence is applied.

Therefore act continuously if you desire to extend your advancement further. Let impious profits be entirely alien to you. You make the possessor devoted if he is not burdened by fraudulent disadvantages. Progress comes through equity rather than rapacity. Unjust presumption always fears. For what is thought to be gained where a good conscience is lost? Or in what respect can a person advance if he is proved to have lost his innocence?

Do not believe that those things which seem to pertain to a good conscience will be without reward. Those who act well will have us as hearers in whatever way we can assist. For I promise to be a rewarder of the man whom I discover to have conducted himself with some degree of honesty.

Act, then, so that praise of you rather than complaints reaches me. Seek no greater advantage than that of selling nothing. Those profits alone should be pursued which the possessor can offer joyfully and the soldier receive with solemn security. I desire to be your praiser, not your censor.

Take care, therefore, that the man who wishes to be beneficial to you is not made hostile. For the one who is stirred contrary to his intention is always more severely angered.

## VIII. EDICT THROUGHOUT THE PROVINCES, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He offers many excellent admonitions and promises that he will be a judge of complete integrity.

[Col. 0834C]

It was the custom of the ancients to decree new laws [Note: “Thus Ulpian says that a proconsul ought to send an edict containing some commendation of himself, and so forth, *Digest*, book I, ‘On the Office of the Proconsul.’” FORN.] so that they might add to the succeeding people something that seemed to have been omitted. Now, however, it is sufficient praise of conscience to preserve the decrees of earlier times.

Under this novelty there had previously been a class of people anxious, since they understood the rule of their life to depend upon another’s will. Now, however, each person knows what is fixed, since he does not doubt that it was fully established by the ancients. The laws are sufficient for you, provided that exceptional willingness is not lacking.

Why do you endure the voices of heralds and the dangerous judgments of governors with ears raised [Note: “Above, book VI, form 3, final section; *Code*, ‘On Holidays.’” FORNER.]? He imposes a limit upon his own life who understands that he has been appointed judge of himself. All of you should devote yourselves to good actions and know nothing of what must be feared. Do not burn with desire for illicit presumptions; love to live in tranquility; always conduct yourselves harmlessly.

Why do you confuse honorable matters with lawsuits? Why do you do things that you may soon fear? If you seek profits, avoid rather damaging litigation. If some civil dispute should nevertheless arise, be content with the laws of your fathers. Let no one rise to sedition; let no one resort to violence. It is a kind of madness to pursue a turbulent purpose in a peaceful world.

But since a reasonable fear of judges arises among you, even if it is not well founded—since inexperienced power tends rather to produce fear—as far as my purpose is concerned, with God’s help and while the lords of all things reign, I promise you that everything will be just and everything moderate.

First, the thing that most disgraces a judge—venality—will not be found foully practiced by me. For my words are not sold, like garments hung out for sale [Note: “The emperor Constantine: ‘Let the judge’s word not be for sale; let there be no purchased entrance; let there be no secretariat made infamous by bids,’ *Theodosian Code*, book I, ‘On the Office of Provincial Governors.’ Some read *verbum*—‘word’—as *velum*—‘curtain’; I change nothing rashly. Compare *Code*, book V, ‘On Shipwreck’; book VI of the *Theodosian Code*, same title. See below, book XI, letter 32: ‘the harmless hands of the office,’ Greek *τῶν ταξεωτῶν χεῖρες καθαραί*—‘the pure hands of the officials.’ Seneca, book VII of the *Controversiae*, novelty 8: *καθαραὶ χεῖρες*—‘pure hands.’” FORN.].

Need alone the scarcity of certain goods make you expect something from me, not malicious venality, provided that there is a moderate command which softens the passage of time. We do not impose something to be purchased, nor do we drag into assessment things that are not considered necessary.

Be concerned only about what is customary and secure concerning novelty, because we have judged that the sole advantage for us is to preserve you unharmed, with the Lord’s help. No soldier will shake you down according to his own will; no tax collector will burden you with additional disadvantages. We have guarded not only our own hands but also those of our office from wrongdoing.

Otherwise, it is a useless good not to receive a judge while giving many permission to receive one. For our officials do not depart from us in such a way that they may rightly appear to have done to others what they themselves have suffered. The recommendations that had previously grown through everyone’s loss have been diminished out of love for you.

With God’s help, we have displayed restraint in ourselves, so that we may command it of the soldiers without shame. Speech cannot possess authority if it is not supported by example, since it is unjust to command good things and not to have done them. Our administration, therefore, will look only to the public advantage, not to private theft.

We know what prayers you have poured out for us and with what anxiety you have been suspended. It is disgraceful for us to do things that would prevent you from rejoicing fully in your own exultation. By God’s favor, our ears will be open to receive the desires of suppliants. The author of the case will see us with his own eyes in freedom; he will speak with his own tongue, not with one that has been purchased.

For neither servitude will command you, nor will venerable nobility be wearied by us. Finally, no shameful action has entered our praetorium; no one has returned from us poorer than when he came. The inner chamber of the household has not learned to differ from the judicial benches. Whoever observes me will find me a judge.

Mindful of modesty, with God’s help, we wish to act in the manner in which we received the commands of the lords of all things. Be devoted to all just things, so that you may make me a father of the provinces rather than merely a judge [Note: “*Quam*, without a comparative particle, requires something such as ‘more’ or a similar word to be supplied. See above, book VIII, letter 2, and book IX, letter 25.” FORN.]. For he who has least expectation of upright conduct becomes angry more severely when he is disappointed.

For if you have rendered obedience to injuries, what ought you to offer to the man whom you recognize as striving earnestly on your behalf? Let the customary allowances [Note: “Customary allowances, that is, salaries; *Code*, ‘Allowances,’ under ‘On Judicial Matters’; Vitruvius, preface to book I; and below, book VIII, letter 33.” FORN.] of your seat not be denied to the soldiers who labor, because the one who does not permit what is just to be paid provides the means for excess.

Also render obedience to our commands with even moderation. Your own reason reasonably urges you not to let armed terror compel you. He excites hatred against himself who resists just commands. I shall not love the man whom I have already compelled. For we wish everything that must be done to be carried out in such a way that we diminish you with no coercive agent.

We want the benefits formerly granted by the lords to be preserved for you, not alienated by any detestable presumption. We wish you to feel our honor only through gratitude, and to ask good things of the rulers, who, you recognize, have granted your desires [edition: “unless”]. Live now rejoicing in the security you have obtained.

One whom it was not right to compel, you were able to bind by voluntary promises. For the person who hesitates to promise what is just under God’s protection wishes to retain the freedom to alter what he has not promised. Hold, therefore, in my free will a reliable guarantor, a mirror of the heart, an image of the will, so that those who do not know me by face may recognize me by the quality of my character.

Look upon me rather in that aspect through which absent persons are revealed. My absence is not a loss to you; it is more useful to know a judge by his mind than by his body.

## EPISTLE IX. TO THE JUDGES OF THE PROVINCES, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He urges them to love justice and to ensure that it is observed by their subjects.

Knowing that those who had been diminished by earlier evils might believe the contrary—for the human mind easily suspects in anyone what it has suffered—we promised the purpose of our policy in the form of an edict, so that, with God’s help, we might not burden by the very anxiety even those whom we desire to be secure.

For it is no small torment to fear that something adverse is going to happen, since what is feared is always judged more serious when it emerges. Far be even the slightest belief in injury from our times. One who is thought to be wicked is already near being a criminal, because something is persuaded upon the mind when a suitable suspicion enters the heart [edition: “an enacted suspicion”].

Therefore let your jurisdiction cause what has been sent to be posted in the most frequented places. It is fitting that those whom we have decided to admonish should learn our commands. Let the love of all now be aroused around the fortunate rulers, so that, just as we did not wish to keep anyone suspended through contrary thoughts, so they too may show themselves devoted to the pious rulers.

You make our promises true [edition: “your promises”] if you preside over the provincials with equal treatment. Love justice, which will make you both beloved and grant you a glorious advantage through your participation in it. Know that offices stand before you like witnesses of your actions. How great, then, is it to do, in the sight of so many, what everyone’s lips can proclaim?

Recognize that a judicial office is called, as it were, a ‘declaration of law’ (*jurisdictio*). It is not fitting for a governor to do what another accuses. What should a criminal fear when he sees the crime established in the insignia of office? For the wicked, the only tortures are those that arise when they perceive public wishes to be contrary to their own conduct. It cannot be called discipline when discipline itself must be corrected.

Therefore strive with us to give good morals to the provincials, but to remove destitution. Deal rather with remedies than with injury. It is a grave evil for anything to be done in order to bestow the benefits of the law and for it to be found mixed with injuries. Act so that, when tested justice is sought, your year may seem short [Note: “See Apuleius, book II of the *Florida*, where, addressing the proconsul of Africa, he writes among other things: ‘Would that it were permitted to enjoy you forever! What have we to do with these changes of proconsuls? What have we to do with short years and months that hasten away? O swift days of human beings! O rapidly approaching dangers of the best governors!’” JURET.].

Let honors rather be offered to you. For you lose the necessity of canvassing if you join to yourselves the wishes of the provincials. We appoint no overseers of your actions, nor do we bend the judge’s character under private control; but conduct everything in such a way that what we now believe to be most disgraceful does not become necessary.

You are acting in keeping with our dignity if you conduct yourselves with purity of conscience. Oppose evils; nonetheless cherish the innocent. If there is someone who rises through reckless daring against your insignia and you are unable to exercise what is just, either send the petitioner immediately with your report, or, if he is abandoned by his resources [edition and Ac.: “by his legal rights”], make the matter known through a prepared report, since you have also received public conveyances and it pleases us to hear about such matters.

And therefore every pretext for excuse has been removed from you, since either through your dignity you can conduct what is right, or at least report to us what is necessary.

## EPISTLE X. TO BEATUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, CHANCELLOR, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He announces that the king has granted Davus permission to seek Mount Lactarius in order to recover his health, and orders him to supply him with whatever is necessary.

[Col. 0837C]

When the clemency of the Lord of all was considering the health of his servant Davus [others: David] (whose wish is to rejoice in everyone’s well-being), it ordered him to seek the remedies of Mount Lactarius, so that the benefit of that celebrated place might help one for whom human medicine had achieved nothing. His body had been weakened by a frequent cough that resounded through his panting chest, while the powers of nature, weakened by excessive disturbance, were unable to exercise their strength for his recovery. For when the foods supplied to support the human body are not properly processed, they are rendered useless. For such people it makes no difference whether they take food or endure fasting. Day by day their living substance diminishes; and, like a cracked vessel, gradually draining away until it is emptied, it is consumed. To this most violent affliction the Divine powers granted the benefit of that mountain. There, the healthfulness of the air, harmonizing with the fertility of rich soil, produces herbs seasoned with the sweetest quality. Herds of cows, fattened on their pasture, make milk of such healthfulness that for those whom so many medical prescriptions cannot help, that drink alone seems capable of providing relief, restoring to its former order the natural strength dissolved by disease. It fills emptied limbs, renews exhausted strength, and assists the sick with a kind of restorative fomentation, just as sleep assists those wearied by labor.

To see these herds exhausted despite such abundant fodder is a marvel: the milk’s fluidity does not surpass its source, although it is proved to restore damaged human bodies; and, in a wondrous manner, animals do not thrive on the herbs from which human limbs grow plump. They range thinly through the mountain thickets, appear lean, and, like the one whom they heal, endure the disease. Yet their milk is so rich that, when expressed into vessels, it clings to the fingers.

Therefore provide the arriving man with the allotted provisions and necessary assistance, so that, healthfully nourished in the aforementioned place, his youth may be restored by the same food by which his infancy was nourished. Take heart, you who suffer from such an illness. You will no longer recoil from a most sweet life because of bitter medicine. Drink with pleasure what you find most healthful. It is a kind of happiness to be cured by that which a sick person can gladly consume to satiety.

## XI. EDICT ON THE PRICES TO BE MAINTAINED AT RAVENNA

He declares that he has fixed prices for commodities and that violators of the edict’s regulations shall incur a monetary and corporal penalty.

### 180. Sale prices [Note: [Col. 0837D] This was treated above in the formula for the defender and curator of the commonwealth, book VI, formula 18, and book VII, formulas 11 and 12. Fair prices should be established for goods offered for sale: Novel 122, edict 6, of Justinian; above, book IX, letter 5, chapter 1, outside the law on buying and selling; Cedrenus, under the emperor Theophilus; Athenaeus, book VI of the *Deipnosophists*, chapter 2, on fish sellers; Moschopulus and Suidas, under [Col. 0838D] Σιτοφύλακες (*grain keepers*). FORNER.]

The sale of seasonal provisions [Niv. [Col. 0838C] and Ga.: of the buyer] ought to be subject to regulation, so that neither dearness be sought amid cheapness nor cheapness amid dearness; rather, with equality carefully weighed, both complaints from purchasers and burdens upon querulous merchants may be removed. Therefore, after everything has been weighed and the calculation brought to a precise account, we have affixed below the prices of the various commodities, so that, with every ambiguity removed, the required supervision of the specified goods may remain in force.

But if any seller fails to observe what the wording of this present edict declares, let him know that for each offense a fine of six solidi will be exacted from him and that he may be subjected to flogging [Note: [Col. 0838D] This is frequently mentioned in the law: book 7, *Saccularius*, at the end, concerning extraordinary crimes, Novel of Majorian; Papinian, *Responsa*, titles 14 and 21; book 5 of the Theodosian Code, concerning bishops and clergy; Paulus, book V of the *Sentences*, titles 4 and 21; and above, book IX, letter 2; book IV, letter 10; book VIII, final letter; book 2, final title, of the Code, concerning those who flee for refuge to a church. Pope Adrian, in Gratian: “Whoever publicly fabricates a written document or insulting words against another’s reputation shall be flogged,” canon 1, 5.1. He renews the law of the Twelve Tables, which ordered the author of defamatory pamphlets to be punished by flogging. Cornutus, on Persius, satire 1. FORNER.], so that both fear of loss may frighten him and the aforementioned punishment may severely afflict him.

## XII. EDICT OF PRICES THROUGH FLAMINIA

He orders that guests be charged only the prices established by his soldier, the citizens, and the local bishop. Whoever acts otherwise shall incur a fine of six solidi and the punishment of flogging.

[Col. 0839A]

If the idle populations of individual cities are restrained by the justice of fixed prices, how much more ought assistance to be given to those who labor, lest the usefulness of travelers be injured by accidental danger! Therefore the reception of travelers ought to be a relief from cares, lest what was clearly devised for alleviation instead impose a detestable burden. Let a guest be received at the established prices; let the person invited to receive favor not suffer greedy injustice, since it is a shameful practice [Ac.: occupation; Niv. and Ga.: bird-catching] to terrify someone with the enormity of a price while flattering him with hospitality.

He resembles a predatory robber who wishes, with unjust intent, to sell at an unfair price. For both are plainly intent on plundering what belongs to others and have no regard for justice. Do you not know how much you can acquire by moderation? Those who know that you can act temperately come voluntarily to your advantage. Therefore let no one suppose that he can protect himself through forgetfulness of distance—a practice always familiar to those who are absent—when people who suffer from your commerce come to us every day. Rather, beware of harming the many while pursuing greed for profit.

Let him know that he must bear a loss of six solidi and be punished by bodily laceration if anyone thinks that goods should be sold otherwise than the soldier whom we have sent for this purpose, after deliberation with the citizens and bishops of the places, has determined. Honest profits from citizens ought to suffice for everyone, lest the roads appear to have been occupied by robbers.

## LETTER XIII. THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME TO THE EMPEROR JUSTINIAN

It asks him to grant peace to the king. To obtain this more easily, it adds to its own prayers those of Rome and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0839C]

It seems an exceedingly honorable and necessary undertaking to supplicate a devout ruler for the security of the Roman commonwealth, since it is fitting to ask from you what can advance our liberty. For among the other blessings that the Divine power has singularly granted you, nothing is shown to be more glorious than that you understand yourselves to be capable of providing everywhere.

Therefore we ask, most merciful emperor—and from the lap of the senate we extend our hands in supplication—that you grant your firmest peace to our king. Do not allow us to become hateful, since we always seemed to be esteemed because of your concord. [Col. 0839D] You commend the Roman name if you grant kindness to our lords. Your favor raises and protects us; and we recognize that we deserve what is perceived to proceed from your mind.

Let your treaties, therefore, establish peace for Italy, since we can then be loved if, through you, a desired affection is joined to us. If our prayers still do not seem sufficient for this matter, imagine our fatherland breaking forth in these words of supplication:

“If I was ever pleasing to you, most merciful of princes, love my defenders. Let those who rule me be in concord with you, lest they begin to do things against me that they know differ from your wishes. Do not be the cause of my cruel destruction, you who have always granted me the joys of life. Behold, under your peace I have doubled my offspring; behold, adorned with citizens, I have shone forth in splendor. If you permit me to be harmed, where do you now display the name of your mercy? For what more will you strive to do for me, whose religion—which is yours—is known to flourish in this way?

“My senate grows in honors and is continually increased in resources. Do not dissipate through discord what you ought to defend through wars. I have had many kings, but none so learned [ed.: of letters]; I have had prudent men, but none so powerful in learning and piety. I love Amal, nourished at my abundant breast, a brave man formed by my association, dear to the Romans for his prudence and revered by the nations for his virtue.

“Join your wishes to mine; share in my counsels, so that it may contribute to your glory if some prosperity comes to me. Do not seek me in such a way that you cannot find me. [Col. 0840B] I am yours nonetheless through your affection, if you do not cause anyone to tear my limbs apart. For if Libya deserved to receive liberty through you, it is cruel for me to lose what I have always seemed to possess.

“Command the movements of anger, excellent triumphant ruler. More is accomplished by what is asked in a general voice than if your spirit were overcome by the offense of any ingratitude. Rome speaks these words while it supplicates you through its senators.

“And if this is still too little, let the most holy petition of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul be considered. Since they are proved often to have defended Roman security from enemies, what will your imperial power fail to grant through their merits? But, so that everything may seem to accord with your reverence, we believe that our prayers should be presented to your clemency through that venerable man, the ambassador of our most devout king sent to you, so that so many may accomplish what even individuals might obtain from devout minds.”

## LETTER XIV. TO GAUDIOSUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, CHANCELLOR OF THE PROVINCE OF LIGURIA, FROM THE SENATOR, PREFECT OF THE PRAETORIUM

He describes the city of Como and indicates that its king has granted its inhabitants a permanent benefaction.

Since the city of Como is sought through many journeys, the owners of the relay horses report that they are so exhausted by constant service that they themselves are worn down by the horses’ excessive running. By royal indulgence, we order that the benefit granted to them be continually preserved, lest that city—pleasantly habitable because of its situation—become sparse in inhabitants because of the damage inflicted upon them.

It lies beyond the mountain passes and the vastness of the purest lake, like a kind of wall of level Liguria. Although it is recognized as a fortified barrier of the province, it is brought to such beauty that it seems to have been established solely for pleasures. Behind it stretch cultivated plains, suitable for pleasant travel and generously supplied with provisions. In front, for sixty thousand [paces], it enjoys the charm of the sweetest waters, so that the spirit may be filled with refreshing delight and the abundance of fish may not be withdrawn by any storm.

Como therefore rightly received its name, since it rejoices in being adorned with such gifts. Here indeed is a lake received within the depth of a very broad valley. Gracefully imitating the shapes of shells, it is painted with the whiteness of a foaming shore. Around it, the most beautiful summits of lofty mountains meet in the form of a crown. Its shore, attractively adorned with the lights of praetorian residences, is surrounded as if by a belt of Palladian forest, with perpetual greenery.

Leafy vineyards climb the side of the mountain above it. The very summit, curled as though with hair by the density of chestnut trees, is depicted by nature’s adornment. From there, streams gleaming with snowy whiteness descend into the lake’s basin, plunging down from the height.

The river Addua, coming from the south, is received into its bays with open mouths [Note: [Col. 0841D] It is a river in Insubria that flows through the middle of Lake Larius, so that its waters do not mingle. Hence Claudian:

“Where the Addua drives its divided waters, more foamy.”

It nourishes good fish, especially tench. See Pliny, book II, chapter 103. BROSS.].

It received this name because, formed from two springs, it flows down as if into its own sea. It strikes the waves of the enormous body of water with such force that, retaining its name and color, it is produced toward the north through the lake’s deeper-bellied channel. You might think that a darker line had been drawn in the whitened waters. In a wondrous way the contrasting nature of the inflowing river is visible, although it is understood that waters of similar substance ought to be able to mix.

This also occurs, indeed, in the waves of the sea through the inundation of rivers; but the explanation is commonly apparent: torrents rushing down, corrupted by muddy sediment, are of a different color from glasslike water. Here, however, it will rightly be considered astonishing that water of such similar qualities can be seen moving with great speed through a sluggish lake, so that you might think a river was running across solid fields, while you do not see it able to mingle its color with the foreign waters.

For this reason the inhabitants are rightly spared these burdens, since all pleasant things are delicate in relation to labor, and those accustomed to enjoy agreeable pleasures easily feel the weight of affliction. Let them therefore enjoy the royal benefaction perpetually, so that, just as they rejoice in their native banquets, the imperial generosity may cause them likewise to exult.

## LETTER XV. TO THE LIGURIANS, FROM THE SENATOR, PREFECT OF THE PRAETORIUM

He makes known that the king has granted one hundred pounds of gold to relieve their needs and exhorts them to give thanks to the king.

A royal gift obtained ought to be the joy of all, so that you may be encouraged to better things when you recognize that what has been granted through us is most welcome. For if it is always characteristic of one who loves to assist, what sort of people do you understand yourselves to have been judged, when you feel that you have been relieved?

But lest we delay your joy with lengthy prefaces—for recognition of good things is always desired as quickly as possible—most illustrious lords, while providing for the needs of devoted Liguria, have, in their accustomed mercy, sent one hundred pounds of gold through this and that man from their chamber [Col. 0841D]. Thus, in your judgment, to whom the matter is thoroughly known, let each person rejoice in a share of this gift proportionate to the need under which he is known to labor. Let what was given to the afflicted not be appropriated by the unharmed; rather, let those whose strength has been restored rise again who had fallen beneath the burden of their losses.

The city of Asta, which is reported to have been burdened above the others, should especially be relieved by the justice of your arrangement, so that it may enjoy the benefit in proportion to the amount of its loss. Receive, taxpayers, the stipend of mercy, and esteem the clemency of your lords, since, with your condition changed, you see yourselves receiving from the treasury what you had been accustomed to pay into it.

But so that your lords’ benefits may be increased by the removal of the inconveniences of taxation, let your report promptly inform us what you judge should be remitted to each person from this sum, so that we may suspend from the initial levy as much as the information conveyed to us reports. Therefore render to your most devout lords the salutary vows that you owe, so that your account may accomplish through supplication what the whole community recognizes itself to have received from this very source.

## LETTER XVI. TO THE LIGURIANS, FROM THE SENATOR, PREFECT OF THE PRAETORIUM

He promises to weigh the complaints brought concerning the pound and measures and, if he discovers anyone engaged in fraud, to compel him to repair the injury inflicted. He then asks them promptly and willingly to procure whatever is necessary for the army’s equipment.

[Col. 0842B]

We ought diligently to raise up those whom royal mercy has decided to support. For those toward whom the clemency of their lords has chosen to incline ought also to demonstrate their own dignity toward those subject to them. Recently you gave me thanks because I had brought you both hope of good things and some actual benefit. You invited me to grant benefits because you received promises with great gratitude. We have fulfilled the vow of a bound judge. What was promised is now proved to have been accomplished.

Let us therefore begin with the pound, because where conscience may rightly be directed, there the judge’s speech ought to begin. This is why you report that you have been burdened in weights and measures. Our care will therefore provide that injustice may no longer trouble you in this respect, since we judge it a serious crime either for measures to exceed their proper standard or for the pound not to possess the justice of an exact weight.

We have summoned by our commands the soldiers of our office, as well as the collectors and receivers, from whom you have complained that serious losses were inflicted upon you, so that, once the accounts have been brought to a precise reckoning, they may pay without any delay whatever fraud is found to have occurred. For we confess that nothing is more hostile to our times than one person rejoicing in another’s misfortune.

Now turn your wishes toward the equipment of the most flourishing army, procuring everything without complaint or any delay. You bind me effectively to every kindness if you gratefully complete what has been ordered. Let him whom the cause of the common good summons obey gladly. Only those losses ought to cause grief that appear to have been imposed through deliberate greed. For what is ordered out of necessity for the commonwealth does not burden the mind of the prudent.

## XVII. PROMOTIONS IN THE PRAETORIAN OFFICE, MADE ON THE LORD’S BIRTHDAY

If on this day of redemption we have found a life-giving remedy, if the hope of salvation is opened through heavenly favor, it is also fitting for us to bring the medicine of joy to those wearied by long labor, so that the heavenly blessings bestowed upon a world in danger may be generally felt.

Otherwise it is a kind of sacrilege to wish to rejoice among the sorrowful, and he avoids the impulse of humanity who does not follow another’s grief. On the contrary, how much better does one rouse oneself through shared joy! What an incentive to great eagerness it is to see many people rejoicing! Hence the wise have testified that the mortal race is one human being, since they wished all people to be inseparable from one another in all their circumstances.

Therefore let each person be announced according to the sequence of the register and by your designation, so that the order of the place may receive the advancement of rank that it requires. Let one man step forth to take precedence over all. He draws the entire sequence of those who follow toward advancement, once the man before him has completed his military service and departed.

## XVIII. CONCERNING THE CORNICULARIUS WHO DEPARTS

The welcome solemnity of promotions should be embraced, for it releases the watches of those who have served well, while hope of labor is granted to recruits once the veterans have received their due in turn. Therefore let Antianus, who is reported to have served the praetorian offices blamelessly, hasten among the tribunes and notaries to adore the imperial presence, so that, presented according to custom, he may be adorned with the insignia of a *spectabilis*.

## XIX. CONCERNING THE CORNICULARIUS WHO ENTERS

May the man who reaches what he desired obtain the fulfillment appropriate to his name. Therefore we decree that the aforementioned man, approved by continual labors, assume the office of *cornicularius*, so that he may rightly stand among the foremost who blamelessly performed the watches of a recruit.

## XX. CONCERNING THE PRIMISCRINIUS WHO DEPARTS

In former times you effectively carried out the commands and earned the good judgments of many; but now you are also raised up, commended by divine favor, when you are shown to have completed the labors of military service. Therefore, supported by the honor of *spectabilitas*, come among the tribunes and notaries to adore the venerable purple [Note: [Col. 0843] For an understanding of this passage, see what I noted on letter 31 below, in this same book. BROSS.], so that your firmness of rank may endure through the sacred presence of the emperor.

## XXI. CONCERNING THE PRIMISCRINIUS WHO ENTERS

We do not permit the merits of faithful men to be deferred, so that we may encourage the wishes of all toward good actions. Let us therefore give what is just to labors, so that by advancing those who came before we may invite the hearts of those who follow.

Therefore let Andreas, who is known to have served the praetorian insignia blamelessly, happily ascend the rank of *primiscrinius*, so that he may rejoice to have found through upright conduct the position that cunning did not know how to seek.

## XXII. CONCERNING THE SCRINIARIUS OF THE ACTS

He rightly attains higher office who is praised for completing the business entrusted to him. Therefore our authority has also ordered Catellus, whom the sequence of the register caused to advance, to assume responsibility as *scriniarius* of the acts.

## XXIII. CONCERNING THE CARE OF LETTERS

Although many affirm the merits of Constantinianus, our own testimony also commends him. For such is the sincerity of his mind that, with the judge as witness, he deserves to be praised. Therefore let him receive advancement to the care of the canonical letters, so that he may display even more fully the qualities of his integrity when he sees that the public trust has been entrusted to him.

## XXIV. CONCERNING THE SCRINIARIUS OF MILITARY ADMINISTRATION

The uprightness of one’s actions appropriately brings an increase of honor; nor is it fitting that a man be delayed whom it has frequently happened to prove effective [ed.: decently]. Hence we order Lucillus to be *scriniarius* of military administration, so that he may offer service to the office to which he does not doubt that he has been deservedly assigned.

## XXV. CONCERNING THE PRIMICERIUS OF THE EXCEPTORES

It is fitting for us without delay to grant advancement to those whom continual military labor deserves. For just as it is fair to deny the rewards of labor to the idle, so it is fitting to grant the desired remuneration to those who keep watch. Therefore let Patricius know that we have appointed him *primicerius* of the *exceptores*, so that, brought to such an office, he may rejoice that the merits of his actions have pleased us.

## XXVI. CONCERNING THE SIXTH SCHOLARIS

He is worthy, in our judgment, of promotion who has deserved the approval of many superiors. To have pleased one person is sometimes merely favor; to have pleased many is judgment. Therefore let Justus know that he has obtained the position of sixth *scholaris*, destined to find the reward of military service when he strives to join himself to faithful actions.

## XXVII. CONCERNING THE PRAEROGATIVARIUS

Who would not judge John worthy of promotion, since once he assumed the office of the chancery by our judgment, and even then earned the prerogative of his integrity when he received the responsibility of judicial secrecy? Let him therefore enjoy the joy both of rank and of honor, since he is known to have pleased us through praised conduct. Our decision therefore confirms him as *praerogativarius*, so that the rank of one who has earned it may more readily and publicly obey the command with devoted spirit.

## XXVIII. CONCERNING THE COMMENTARIENSIS

It is pleasing to respond with corresponding benefits to the wishes of those who have served well, so that one who has deserved precedence may be able to serve with more devoted mind. Therefore let Cheliodorus enjoy the office of *commentariensis*. We rightly entrust to his integrity what we judge must be guarded.

## XXIX. CONCERNING THE REGENDARIUS

It seems suited to equity that those praised for effective action should receive a worthy return corresponding to their conduct. He possesses his own glory who is known, after carefully measured watches, to advance his military fortune. Hence we decree that Cartherius happily obtain the place of *regendarius*, so that, encouraged by the hope of future advancement, he may cling more eagerly to the labors of the praetorian office.

## XXX. CONCERNING THE PRIMICERIUS OF THE DEPUTATI AND THE PRIMICERIUS OF THE AUGUSTALES

It is worthy that the fruit of labors should follow the wishes of the faithful and that a higher rank should receive those whom the integrity of their achievements commends. Hence we decree Ursus to be *primicerius* of the *deputati* and Beatus to be *primicerius* of the *Augustales*, so that those who are being advanced toward greater offices may follow examples of conscience worthy of praise.

## XXXI. CONCERNING THE PRIMICERIUS OF THE SINGULARES WHO DEPARTS

It is fitting that the rewards of victory be obtained by those who appear to have completed their military oaths, since prolonged labor claims for itself what inexperienced nobility can scarcely find. Therefore, since Urbicus is known to have completed the period of his *primiceriatus*, let him come among the *domestici* and *protectores* to adore the sacred purple [Note: [Col. 0845D] It is clear that there is a distinction between *domestici* and *protectores*. For the latter, undertaking armed military service, endure the responsibility not only of defending their own bodies but also of protecting our side; hence they received the name *protectores*, and they are in the battle line. Others, as the meaning of the name indicates, serve more familiarly and are *domestici protectores*. Of these, some were infantrymen and others cavalrymen, so that some were counts of the household cavalry and others counts of the household infantry: illustrious men who governed the *domestici*, when it was permitted them to approach and adore the emperor’s purple. Book 2 of the Code, concerning the *fabricenses*; book 1 of the Code, concerning the *domestici*. They were also admitted to greet and kiss the vicars of the prefect of the praetorium, and still more the governors; all these privileges were granted as marks of the highest honor. Thus in book 109 of the Theodosian Code, concerning the *decurions*, the privilege of kissing provincial judges and of sitting with them was granted. BROSS.], so that, made illustrious by the venerable presence, he may rejoice that he has been released from military watches.

## XXXII. CONCERNING THE PRIMICERIUS OF THE SINGULARES WHO ENTERS

The integrity of the judge is present in military service, since he willingly fulfills what he recognizes to be justly owed. Therefore let Pierius know that by our authority he has been made *primicerius* of the *singulares*. If there are any matters of this kind, let them be confidently reported, since there is no fear of hesitation where the judge’s hearing is not for sale [Note: [Col. 0845D] One might reasonably wonder whether *aditus* (“access”) should be read somewhat more correctly. Compare book 1 of the Theodosian Code, concerning the office of the provincial governor: “Let neither the judge’s curtain be for sale, nor access be redeemed.” Cicero, *Against Verres*: “To approach him, you will pay this much.” Salvian of Marseille, book III, *On Providence*: “Within the doors not only of illustrious men, but also of governors and superiors, not everyone dares to enter indiscriminately, except those whom either the judge has summoned, or business has brought in, or the very dignity of their office has allowed to enter; so that if anyone has entered insolently, he is either beaten, driven away, or punished by some disgrace and stain upon his reputation.” The emperors Valentinian and Valens: “With the doors opened, call everyone inside,” and so forth. Book 2 of the Theodosian Code, concerning the office of the provincial governor; book 9, “Whoever,” of the Theodosian Code, concerning heretics: “Let him open the court,” and so forth. Nevertheless, I would not readily depart from the ancient and published reading, *auditus* (“hearing”). For the judge is said to provide ears. Marcian, Novel 1, book III: “He should provide full ears to those approaching from the provinces.” On the contrary, “ears closed,” Valerius Maximus, book VII, chapter 3. FORNER.].

## XXXIII. CONCERNING DELEGATORY PAYMENTS TO BE GRANTED

The man whom the custom of granting benefits constrains cuts through delays [manuscript: hours], since the person moved by innate benevolence is more strongly compelled to confer benefits. Nor is it fitting that we should be unlike our own actions, while the number of remedies ought to increase for one whose periods of administration appear to be lengthening. Therefore our generosity now grants you your delegatory payments, so that you may then possess the advantages of the reward when you have also reached the end of your labor. We do not suspend you through anxious delay or weary you with torturous postponement. Let there be one end to anxiety and labor. For who would think that something should be delayed if he does not hesitate to sell his own benefits?

## XXXIV. THE FOLLOWING WAS SAID AT ANTIANUS’S REQUEST

Your petition will be retained by the office until, when opportunity permits, we inquire into the consent of those who follow, since it is unsafe to trust one person with what must be affirmed by many. [Col. 0846B] Go forth, all who have been advanced. Be happily approved, all of you. You endured no uncertainty while every judgment was held to be uncertain. Only the letter alpha embraces us, where that letter is not feared. Thus each person made use of his own wish, as though he had not depended upon another’s judgment.

## XXXV. DELEGATORY PAYMENT

If the driver of the Olympic chariot snatches the prizes after his labors, if the dishonorable contest with wild beasts ordinarily crowns its victors swiftly, what speed of remuneration will he deserve by whom the military oath is laudably fulfilled? Why should a soldier of the office of *agentes in rebus* suffer any uncertainty after so many labors, when by keeping watch through repeated actions he has deserved to bear the emperor’s name precisely because he surpasses the others in military service?

For he will continually observe imperial commands, and, to exalt the reverence owed to the praetorian seat, he came into its service when he began to bear a distinguished title. Therefore it is sacrilege to delay such men, since no one is postponed after victory. What a sorrowful man receives cannot be called a gift of his wishes. Let those who have been released fear no burdens, lest the harbor inflict upon free men what the storm could do to those battered by it.

Therefore let your administration pay without any delay, from that province, out of the third levy, the solidi of fiscal taxes that provident antiquity assigned to the *princeps* of the Augusti [that is, of the *agentes in rebus*]. You should know that they are to be charged to the accounts of the thirteenth indiction (A.D. 535). But beware of delays for sale [Note: [Col. 0847] “Delay for sale” above, in this book, letter 7. “The saleability of diligence,” Novel 7 of Majorian, concerning ownerless property. FORNER.]; avoid ruinous annoyances, so that, while you desire to obtain similar benefits, you may not seem to have imposed an example of loss upon yourself.

Therefore do not dismiss one who petitions with reason [Gronovius: lest], if you bind yourself by the quality of your action [Ac.: if he binds himself]. Veterans must indeed be honored by all, but especially by those who are occupied with military labor. Thus you benefit yourself when you spare another, since the preservation of the one who came before becomes rather the profit of the one who follows.

## LETTER XXXVI. TO ANATHOLIUS [ed.: ANATOLICUS], ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, CHANCELLOR OF THE PROVINCE OF SAMNIUM, FROM THE SENATOR, PREFECT OF THE PRAETORIUM

He decrees that seven hundred solidi be given to one who has honorably completed the office of *cornicularius*, and he commends his own integrity.

[Col. 0847B]

He who discovered laborious watches and duties requiring great diligence reasonably also established fixed limits of time, so that what had been placed within the term of life would not have an uncertain reward. Otherwise, who could always be sufficient and keep watch, when daylight itself was withdrawing from mortals? Therefore, amid uncertain life, military service has a fixed term. He has nothing to fear who has deserved to reach the appointed time without offense.

Even the stars themselves, as astronomers hold, although they revolve through constant repetition, preserve the fixed limits of their courses. What is enclosed within its own terminus cannot be uncertain. Saturn traverses the spaces of heaven assigned to it in thirty years. The star of Jupiter illuminates the region allotted to it in twelve years. The star of Mars, carried along with fiery speed, travels through its assigned course in eighteen months. The sun passes through the signs of the zodiacal circle in the space of a year. The star of Venus surpasses the spaces granted to it in fifteen months. Mercury, girded with speed, passes through the intervals appointed to it in thirteen months. The moon, nearer to us through its special proximity, completes in thirty days what the golden sun, revolving over the span of a year, accomplishes.

Mortals therefore rightly find an end to their labor, since, as the philosophers say, even those things that cannot fail except with the world have received the termini of their courses according to a rational order—though with this difference: they complete their work in order to return to their beginning, whereas the human race serves in order to rest when its labors have been completed.

Therefore, to the man who has blamelessly completed the office of *cornicularius*, hand over seven hundred solidi, which longstanding custom has also assigned, from the third levy of the province of Samnium during that indiction, without ambiguity. For the man whose true commendation by the emperor supports him cannot doubt his reward.

He presided over the horns [or: insignia] of the praetorian secretary, from which his name is derived, and was approved by praised actions. While he served, we wrote down the reckoning [Gronovius; Cuj., Niv., and Ga.: calculation] for what was desired to be fulfilled at great expense, without purchase; we granted favor to the one whom the laws supported; we denied it to the one to whom justice made no promise. No one was saddened by his victory, because he obtained it with his resources intact, since he did not purchase advancement. You know everything that we say; for our secretarial affairs were not conducted in our chambers. The cohorts know what we did.

We were private persons in the capacity to harm, judges in the capacity to grant. Our strictness was displayed in words, and our kindness was perceived in deeds. We were angry while reconciled, we threatened while harmless; and, so that we might not be able to injure, we appeared to inspire terror. You have, as you were accustomed to say, a most chaste judge; I shall leave you as wholly upright witnesses.

## LETTER XXXVII. TO LUCINUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, CHANCELLOR OF CAMPANIA, FROM THE SENATOR, PREFECT OF THE PRAETORIUM

He orders that a customary payment of solidi from the register of the province of Campania be granted to a *primiscrinius* who has already completed his office.

[Col. 0848B] It was wisely provided by ancient moderation that those who serve the public interests should receive the rewards of their labor, so that no one who had deserved praise for a commendable action might be passed over. For to whom would remuneration be paid for service, if rewards were delayed for praetorian labors? Almost everything, indeed, that is done in the commonwealth is accomplished through their energy; and—since this is the most difficult kind of service, being compelled to fulfill everything without being permitted to exceed its bounds—it obeys the armies and submits to the armed forces, yet receives gratitude precisely where it may encounter another’s offense.

Why should we recount that the public accounts [Mss. and Ac.: actions] are assembled through exceedingly difficult details, composed with great exactness, and demanded from those whom they do not presume to offend? To their exertions also must be assigned the provisions which, although gathered from places far away, are collected without complaint from the provincials as though they had been produced in the royal city: for when something suitable is sought at its proper time, it is not regarded as an expense by the giver.

[Col. 0848C] Their actions are our glory, the reputation of the age, the virtue by which commands are carried out; and whatever gratification we receive for holding everything together, we justly apply to their prudent arrangements. Their labors, which keep men constantly prepared, shine through use itself: labors, I say, that are harsh teachers and vigilant tutors, through which a person becomes more cautious because he fears encountering dangers. Let one man be trained in forensic letters, another taught by whatever discipline; nevertheless, the better instructed is the one educated by the practice of continual devotion.

And therefore what they deserve must be paid to such men with honor, [Col. 0848D] so that the man who was always acquiring benefits for the public interests may at last receive something for himself. Accordingly, we decree that you solemnly give Primiscrinius, now discharged from military service, so many solidi from the assessment of the province of Campania, from the third levy, so that he may enjoy the rewards of just labors and his descendants may receive an example of free service, when they learn that he was well regarded for his loyalty.

### LETTER XXXVIII. TO JOHN, CANONICARIUS OF TUSCIA, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He describes the manner of making paper, as well as its usefulness. Then he orders that a prescribed sum of money, transported from the province of Tuscia, be distributed to a certain man.

[Col. 0849A]

Antiquity, which governs all things, carefully considered that, since many matters had to be dealt with through our archives, an adequate supply of prepared paper should not be lacking [Note: [Col. 0849D] See Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book VI, chapter 10; Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book [VI], where he speaks of Daphne; Saint Jerome, *To Niceas*; Alcimus Avitus, p. 31; and Cassiodorus, in the preface to *On the Arts*, p. 558. JURET.], so that when judges issued decisions beneficial to many, pleasing benefits would not carry the burden of hateful delays. This gift was granted to petitioners, lest those for whom it was known to have been received from public generosity should be stingily constrained in their access to it. The most shameless opportunity for exactions was removed: it specifically protected from losses those on whose behalf the emperor’s humanity had given it.

Memphis’s ingenious workmanship plainly conceived a beautiful product, to clothe all the archives with what the labor of a single place had elegantly woven. The Nilotic [Col. 0849B] forest rises without branches, a grove without foliage, a harvest of waters, a beautiful shearing of marshes, softer than shrubs, harder than grasses, full through some inexplicable emptiness and empty through its fullness, a sponge-like wood with thirsty tenderness. In it, as in a fruit, strength lies in the rind, softness in the pith; its height is slight, yet it contains itself. It is the most beautiful fruit of a foul inundation.

For what comparable thing grows in any cultivated land to that material in which the thoughts of the wise are preserved? Before this, the sayings of the sages and the reflections of our ancestors were exposed to danger. For how could what resisted the hardness of bark and could scarcely be prepared have been written swiftly? The heat of the mind endured those pointless delays; and when words were postponed, intellects were forced to grow cold.

Hence antiquity also called the works of the ancients “books.” Even today [Col. 0849C] we call the husks of green wood a *book*. It was unbecoming, I admit, to entrust learned discourses to unpolished tablets and to impress upon withered branches what the elegance of the intellect could discover. With hands weighed down, it recalled only a little to memory; nor was someone encouraged to say more when such a page seemed to offer itself.

But this was appropriate to the beginnings, since an uncultivated beginning [Note: [Col. 0850D] That the beginnings of all things are uncultivated is shown by Seneca, *Letters* 96; Aelian, *Various History*, Book X, concerning painting; Apuleius, Book I of the *Florida*; and the *Panegyric to Maximinus*, p. 270. JURET.] ought to have such an invention, one that would stimulate the ingenuity of those who followed.

The inviting beauty of paper is said to abound wherever there is no fear that the material for writing will run short. For on its snowy surface it opens a field for eloquence, always stands ready in abundance, and, so that it may be manageable, is gathered by being rolled upon itself while great treatises are unfolded. Its joining is without cracks, its continuity made from minute fibers, its interior snowy, its surface suitable for writing and receptive of blackness for ornament. There, with raised letters, a most fertile crop of words is planted [Grul., Cuj., Niv. and Ga.: “planting”]; it yields fruit most pleasing to minds whenever it finds a reader’s desire. It preserves a faithful testimony of human actions, speaks of things past, and is the enemy of forgetfulness.

For although our memory retains the matters themselves, it changes the words; on paper, however, what will always be heard in the same form is safely stored. Therefore we decree that you provide to him the assigned sum of so many solidi from the province of Tuscia [Col. 0850A] 186, from the third levy [Gr. and Cuj.: to be charged to the thirteenth levy], to be calculated from the accounts of the tenth indiction; so that the public archive may preserve the integrity of its trust through praiseworthy permanence. Knowing nothing of decay among mortal things, it continually grows through annual accumulation, constantly receiving new materials and preserving the old.

### LETTER XXXIX. TO VITALIAN, A MAN OF ILLUSTRIOUS RANK, CHANCELLOR OF LUCANIA AND BRUTTII, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He orders him to ensure payment of the public assessment which the Lucanians and Bruttians used to pay to the City each year in place of their own and their oxen. Then he recounts the benefits with which he had enriched his homeland.

[Col. 0850B]

It is clear how great the population of the Roman state must have been, since supplies provided even from distant regions were needed to satisfy it, so that the surrounding provinces could suffice for the sustenance of foreigners, while the abundance brought to them was preserved. For how small could the population have been that possessed the dominion of the world?

The immense expanses of the walls, the extended circumference of the theaters, the astonishing size of the baths, and that whole collection of mills—which is known to have been specially contributed for food—bear witness to the crowds of citizens. For this instrument, unless it were in ordinary use, would not be considered necessary, since it could contribute neither to ornament nor to any other purpose. In short, these things are like costly clothing for bodies and therefore are signs of cities, since no one is willing to produce superfluities when he knows that they can be displayed at great expense.

Hence it came about that mountainous Lucania paid its swine, and that the Bruttians supplied a herd of oxen through the abundance native to their land. Both arrangements were truly remarkable: provinces could supply so great a city, and so extensive a city, through their benefits in provisions, did not suffer a shortage of food.

It was indeed glorious for them to feed Rome; but at what expense did it seem possible to provide what had to be brought over so many routes, delivered by weight, when no one could charge against them whatever was plainly diminished in transit! The obligation has been converted into a payment, where it could suffer no loss: it is neither reduced by journeys nor damaged by labor.

Let the provinces understand their own benefits. For if their ancestors were devoted to incurring expense, why should their descendants not be generous in making payments that bring advantage? And [Col. 0850D] therefore your diligence has now arranged both titles, converted into a public assessment, through the prescribed levies, so that in my time those who obeyed other dignitaries with praiseworthy integrity may not appear negligent.

Although I have also sought to restore other provinces, nothing was done in the others [Ac. and Cor., Ga.: in those] that I would wish to claim for myself. They experienced me as their judge; and those whom, as a private citizen, I had benefited through my ancestors and great-grandfathers, I strove more vigorously to assist through my official power, so that they might recognize that I retained affection for my homeland—those whom I saw rejoicing with eager delight in my advancement.

Let them therefore obey, not because of any compulsion, but out of love, since I have also reduced this sum for them, which used to be offered. For when they were paying twelve hundred solidi in annual contributions, I brought them back to one thousand through royal generosity, so that they might rejoice in the increase of their happiness through the reduction of their burdens.

### XL. CLEMENCY

[Note: [Col. 0851D] The *Theodosian Code*, Book IX, title 39, concerning acts of clemency, is extant. Here the reference is to the joy of the holy Easter day; and in Books III, IV, and VI of the *Theodosian Code*, the religious observance of an annual supplication is mentioned, in Book VII as well. There is also clemency on account of the commonwealth’s liberation from tyranny, in the final book. Constantine likewise granted clemency on account of the birth of Crispus and Helena, Book I of the same title. FORN.]

The Senator, moved by compassion, frees many detained in prison.

Although the very name of judge appears to be dedicated to justice, and we are ordered to walk throughout the whole year in the footsteps of equity, on these days we turn by right toward the dwelling of compassion, so that we may reach the Redeemer [Col. 0851B] of all by the road of remission. For from this virtue we read of the sweetest fruits, and by forgiving others we spare ourselves. Since we are dangerously just, we always forgive under the protection of security [Note: [Col. 0851D] Plutarch says that justice ought to be a pure, incorrupt, modest—or bashful—temperate, and useful virgin. Juvenal, *Satire* II, moreover assigns modesty as the companion of justice. This means reverence, as though a ruler who is just and civil should fear—not receiving, but inflicting—some evil, harm, or injury upon his subjects. Modesty is therefore called the companion of justice, as though the ruler ought to respect and fear inflicting rashly, on a false pretext and contrary to law, a penalty on any of his subjects—especially since forgiveness is also granted under the protection of security, and no one can be just except with danger. BROSS.].

Therefore we renounce punishments, condemn torture, and then are truly judges. Hail, Clemency, who releases and presides! You are the patroness of the human race, the singular physician of afflicted circumstances. Who does not need your gift, when wrongdoing is common? You are necessarily sought by all, since under you the hope of life is taken up, which is not available under justice.

For although you enjoy, by heavenly grace, the company of three other sisters and are joined to them in loving embrace, all of them—although they too are virtues—yield honorably to you, when they recognize that you bring salvation to the human race.

[Col. 0851C] But why should we speak so much about earthly life? It is compassion that governs even the heavens. O, if only it were permitted to dwell with you for long ages! All guilt would be excluded, and, by sparing, it would come about that the Fates would be abolished [others: “that the Fates would be spared.”]

But such a great gift has most providently been granted only for sacred seasons, so that the world might receive more gratefully what it rejoices in because of its unusualness. Therefore, lictor, refrain from the harmful axe, with which you are permitted to do with impunity what you are known to punish in others; for a little while love the bright iron, not the bloodstained. May happier rust receive your chains, wet with tears; put away instead the instrument that used to enclose them. Let the hearing chambers of deadly cries grow silent under better fortune. Thus you truly preserve your title as guardian, without the deaths of others.

[Col. 0852A] Why do you always toil among the dead? At times serve among the living as well. A merciful act commands you to rest. Whoever keeps watch over unyielding justice must necessarily be loosened by kindly compassion.

And therefore let the cell of groans [Note: [Col. 0852D] The prison was first built in the middle of the city, overlooking the Forum, as Livy testifies. In it was a pit into which condemned criminals were thrust for ultimate punishment; it was called the Tullianum. On this matter see Dionysius, Book XLVI. Sallust says: “There is a place in the prison called the Tullianum; when one has climbed up a little, it is about twelve feet below the ground on the left. Walls enclose it on every side, and above it a chamber joined with stone vaults; neglected, dark, foul with odor, and terrifying is its appearance.” BROSS.], the house of sorrow, Pluto’s lodging among the gods above, a place blinded by perpetual night, at last grow white with an infusion of light. In it the accused endures not one torment alone, for the man tortured by the prison’s squalor is killed by manifold death before he encounters the end of execution, having already been cut off from the upper world.

First, that filth, the companion of chains, torments him with loathsome misery; the hearing is disturbed by the sound of another’s groans and lamentations; long fasts weaken the taste; burdens pressing down weary the sense of touch [Note: [Col. 0852D] Concerning these matters, see Book III of the *Theodosian Code*, “On Exactors”; and Aulus Gellius, Book XX, chapter 1. There were also stone weights by which martyrs were burdened, as Baron says under 16 September in the *Roman Martyrology*. JURET.]; the eyes, dulled by prolonged darkness, grow numb.

For those shut in, death is not one thing only; the man tormented by the prison’s filth is destroyed by many forms of death. Now therefore send forth from your own Avernus [Col. 0852B] 187 the accused who are to live; let those return to the upper world who have endured, in large part, the condition of the underworld; let your halls be filled with emptiness. Let that place of everlasting tears lose its once-sorrowful inhabitants. There are no happy people there; it will surely have received gratitude when it appears deserted.

Come out, prisoners, always pale with the nearness of death; return to the light, you whom darkening shadows possessed, destined to suffer nothing more through the death you longed for, except that you could still be killed. But you who ought no longer to be deceived by any ambition, leave your crimes behind with your chains, released by the benefits of these days.

Live honorably now, you who learned, while survivors, how to die. Learn how beneficial good conduct is: the former brought about the most dreadful prison; this one knows how to grant splendid freedom. The latter will make you wish to live; the former made you choose to die.

If the laws bind you, no one will imprison you again. Fear secret places; come to the Forum without trembling. Shun those things rightly through which you suffered sorrow. Let those who saw you accused marvel at you set free. You ought to hate what delivered you to death.

Even animals know how to avoid what they recognize as having harmed them; they do not retrace the paths where they fell into a pit. A captured bird avoids tenacious snares and, wary of sticky birdlime clinging to its wings, does not perch upon it.

The fish called the wolf buries itself in soft sands to escape the traps of weighted nets. When the nets drawn over it have torn its back in vain, it leaps lively into the waves and, freed from danger, recognizes the joys of having escaped it.

The scarus, enticed by bait, when it has begun to enter a reed enclosure, as soon as it realizes that its destruction has been invited inside, slips backward onto its tail, gradually withdrawing itself from the narrow passage. If another of the same species sees it caught in the net, it pulls its extremity firmly with its teeth, so that the one unable to help itself after being caught may prove able to escape through the aid of another.

So too the sauri, a clever species of fish named from their speed, when they have thrust themselves into knotted snares and are bound together as though by certain ropes, pull backward with all their strength and try to free their captive companions. There are many further examples, if such matters are investigated. For everything that can have an opposite disposition would be swept away by an easy accident if it did not take care for its own safety.

Let us turn our words back to you, master of the prison cells. [Col. 0854A] Allow your penal chamber to remain harmlessly shut. You are tormented because no one is being afflicted; you are received sadly from the common joys, since the general pardon alone does not spare you, and you are comparable to livid envy. Bear the loss of everyone’s security, since you once had joy in the affliction of many.

But, to console your own groans as well, exact punishment from only those whom the law of compassionate clemency does not release, lest, by sparing the savage, you make the most atrocious crimes seem lighter.

Let us therefore release all those entangled in worldly actions. Every person endures dangerous bonds from which he hastens to escape. Let the prison cells release the accused; let us be freed from the chains of wicked thought.

## BOOK TWELVE

[Col. 0853]

### 188 LETTER I. TO THE VARIOUS CHANCELLORS OF THE INDIVIDUAL PROVINCES, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

Salutary admonitions are given to the chancelleries chosen by the praetorian prefect and sent to the various provinces, instructing them how to perform their office well and especially how to avoid avarice.

[Col. 0853B]

A man is thought distinguished when he is sent from the judge’s inner chambers, since he is esteemed all the more to love justice the more frequently he is known to have heard it from that judge. A judge is understood through his soldiers; and just as disciples reveal their teacher’s knowledge [Note: [Col. 0853] On this matter Salvian writes well, *On the Government of God*, p. 97; Ennodius, p. 327. JURET.], so the conduct of those who obey us reveals us.

A rash man is not thought to have observed moderation; an avaricious man is not considered to have obeyed restraint; a fool is not believed to have served the wise. I admit that we are endangered by your actions [Col. 0853C] if you conduct yourselves with evil intent; and, although none of you experiences it, another’s vice is celebrated as our disgrace. We endure circumstances of the kind that we cannot judge in others, and the law enjoyed by all cannot be maintained in us.

But on the other hand we have this consolation: your good qualities are believed to be our instructions, and while we are at leisure, whatever glory is achieved through your labors accrues to us. For if someone sees you acting wisely, he immediately exalts the reputation of your instructor, since it is believed that such an education produced actions of this kind.

The common judgment of the people is that judges are such as those whom we have happened to approve. Therefore great care must be taken lest the man whose opinion you have previously torn apart should begin to judge you. He avenges through punishments [Col. 0853D] what you spread in stories, and through your torments compensates for what the wounded people exaggerate [Ac.: “so that he may restrain through our torments”].

How dangerous it is to suffer a judge reasonably angered, and to have him decide concerning your fortunes whom you are known to have seriously provoked! Therefore strive rather to be praised by our voice, since just as the judge’s speech can bring you down, so a most favorable judgment can raise you up.

Proceed, then, during that indiction, with God’s help, to that province, adorned with the pomp of the chancellery and girded with glorious dignity. Though absent, consider the sense of shame proper to one who is present. For what base thing ought you to attempt [Cor., Ga.: “what do you see as base”], when you serve under honor?

The judges’ fasces obey you; and while you are believed to carry the orders of the praetorian seat, you reverently assume, in a certain sense, the power itself. Observe our edicts first [ed.: “especially”]; show those under your authority the good path. For whose duty is it to guard the judge’s commands if our soldiers appear to neglect what has been established?

Flee that queen of brazen vices, avarice, to which all crimes serve with detestable devotion. Once it has entered a man’s breast, it admits whole troops of bad faith. It cannot be tolerated once received, because it does not know how to be solitary. It has a most alluring retinue, takes up arms from its talents, and by sweetness overcomes those whom it captures through bitter deception.

Therefore be solicitous for the public interests; administer what has been entrusted to you with moral compulsion. The one who inculcates reason accomplishes more than one who can exercise terror. Let your person be a refuge for the oppressed, a defense for the weak, and a protection for one enclosed by some calamity. For you truly conduct our chancellery if you release the impious enclosures of the injured.

### 189 LETTER II. TO ALL THE JUDGES OF THE PROVINCES, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He invites the judges to imitate him. Then he orders them to admonish landholders that the taxes of the thirteenth indiction be paid with devoted intent and at the appointed times, and to send a faithful account of expenses to the praetorian archives.

I give thanks to the Divinity, because the provincials have done what I advised and I have fulfilled everything I promised. [Col. 0854D] For no one has perceived me polluted by any venality, nor have I encountered taxpayers who were disloyal. Each of us has something that we ought to love in the other: they have found judges affectionate toward them, and we have acquired completely upright heralds.

Let us therefore accomplish, with God’s assistance, what we have begun. Let the landholder willingly bring public money to me; I shall pay him the taxes at the assemblies of justice. It is appropriately repeated to you that what has been done faithfully inspires great hope for the future from past events.

For you have proved that we compelled no one to give what he ought not to have offered. [Col. 0855A] No one was afflicted by public or private losses at my hands. We caused the terrors of investigations to be forgotten. Nor did we seek extraordinary payments, since we wished everything to be conducted according to the laws.

But you too must not be unlike us in this respect. The laws have willed that governors be imitators of our dignity, granting them through the provinces almost the same jurisdiction as ours. Justice rejects no one who follows it; it ennobles all whom it elevates by sharing in itself. Only the man who departs from justice makes himself lesser.

Why should we pursue the acceptance of gifts? No glory belongs to the man called rich; by contrast, the man declared just is adorned with every praise. Let us desire instead what makes us more valuable than the wealthy. We receive the fasces so that we may be weighty. We ascend the tribunals so that we may be raised through the steps of good character.

[Col. 0855B] Nothing base, nothing greedy, becomes judges. For they make their own stains conspicuous if those to whom many look become sullied by any reproach. Otherwise it is better not to appear than to be marked by the ridicule of everyone.

Therefore let all of us who seek the heights of offices [ed.: rewards] abandon the low places of vices. Let our brow be open, so that we may correct the sins of others. Every crime makes equal those whom it stains; therefore the person who judges must differ from the accused.

This is fitting for us to say in our annual address, because there is no satiety in good things. I confess the eagerness of my desire: I want to be praised together with you [Note: [Col. 0855D] See Pliny, *Panegyric*, p. 357: “Vows which always …” JUR.].

Let us now come to customary matters, which ought to be received gratefully because they are known to be traditional.
