Therefore, as has fortunately been said, we order you and your office, with God’s help, to admonish the landholder [Col. 0855C] that they pay the taxes of the thirteenth indiction (in the year of Christ 535) with devoted intent, so that, while the regulation of the three levies is preserved, they may bring the due contribution to the commonwealth.

The appointed times of collection must be observed, but in such a way that no one complains of being exacted from under the injury of premature compulsion, nor is the damaging generosity of extensions again offered under shameful venality. Delay in paying taxes becomes a greater cause of expense when what cannot be avoided by any postponement is uselessly suspended.

You shall also hasten to send to our archives a faithful account of expenses, organized according to the established practice in four-month periods [Note: [Col. 0855D] Hence the four-month statements, which are prepared by the record-keepers for each installment and sent to the palace office or to the praetorian prefect. It is established that the taxes of each year’s indiction are paid in three installments, *Codex*, final book, “On Grain Supply and Taxes”; *Theodosian Code*, Books XV and XVI, same title. Thus the statements for the individual installments are four-monthly, as may be seen here. Accursius used the author’s words in Book I of the *Code*, “On Public Receipts”; and Majorianus, in the novella *On the Indiction*. BROSS.], so that, once every obscurity of error has been wiped away, the clarity of the public accounts may appear.

For if you act otherwise, the losses that are imposed upon the public interests through your neglect will concern you. And so that, with God’s help, you may more easily accomplish what has been established, we order that this man and that man, soldiers of our seat, customarily attend upon you and your office, so that our arrangement may achieve its effect without blame.

Take care, therefore, not to show yourself unequal to our admonitions, since it is exceedingly shameful for us to approve as needing removal what we ask you to make worthy of praise.

### LETTER III. TO ALL THE SAJONES WHO HAVE BEEN ASSIGNED TO THE CHANCELLERIES, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He admonishes how the *sajones* assigned to the chancelleries ought to perform their office.

[Col. 0856A]

Everything ought indeed to be carried out peacefully, in a manner compatible with good morals. But such is the diversity of the commonwealth arising from the variety of human character that no one can defend the laws unless terror appears to exercise some restraint.

The sick do not all have the same path to health: one is restored by food, another is weakened through the benefits of abstinence; one seeks gentle baths, another iron for his wounds. Different conditions of illness demand different remedies. So the man known to preside over peoples is not found equipped with only one policy.

The fierce must be pressed by strictness, [Col. 0856B] the gentle admonished civilly; the deceitful treated cautiously, the simple with mildness. Prudence is therefore everywhere proved necessary, since it appears suitable for application to all circumstances.

Accordingly, we assign your devotion, in the customary manner, to the assistance of our most illustrious chancellor, so that you may rise against no one except him who has disdained to obey the laws. Drag to the Forum the man who refuses to accept what is just; be angry under restraint, impose discipline with maturity.

We want you to be feared more than approved, since your vigor will be credited with the greatest achievement if no one sins through presumption. Let the faithful collection of public money be considered above all else. Let your advantage be another’s contempt. Let the man who neglected to fulfill what was just voluntarily do it under compulsion.

Devote yourself only to the cases assigned to you. If you follow orders, you do not seek forbidden paths. The man who fulfills what was commanded is free from blame. In an executor, the worst fault is to leave discretion to the judge. Do not boast that no one can oppose you; do not wish to assume arrogance because the humility of many fears you.

Brave men are always modest in peace, and those who have often engaged in battles love justice exceedingly. How pleasing it is if, returning among your relatives, you bring back no reproach from complaints, but they recognize that you acted as devoted people are known to wish!

We too gladly receive with praise the man who returns, and we do not allow him to remain idle when we judge that he has acted commendably. The lord of all things also entrusts greater responsibilities to those whom a good conscience has shown to have handled his interests well. How much can wise men acquire! No one gains more than the man who has conducted himself through good behavior.

### LETTER IV. TO THE CANONICARIUS OF VENETIA, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He orders that choice fish and *acinaticum* wine, praised by many, be provided for the king’s table.

The very rich preparation of the royal table is proved to be no small ornament of the commonwealth, because the ruler is believed to possess as many novelties as he enjoys at table. It is a private person’s prerogative to have what the place contains; at a royal banquet, what is seen ought to be sought out so that it may inspire admiration.

Let the Danube send carp; let the *anchorago* come from the Rhine; let the Sicilian *exormiston* be supplied regardless of the labor required; let the sea of the Bruttians send sweet *acerniae*; let fish pleasing to the palate be brought from diverse regions. It is fitting to feed a king in such a way that ambassadors of foreign peoples believe him to possess almost everything.

Therefore wines must be procured which fertile Italy uniquely produces, lest, while we desire foreign things, we appear not to have sought our own. A report from the count of the patrimony has declared that *acinaticum*, whose name derives from *acinus*, “grape,” had been made scarce in the palace cellars.

Since all dignities ought to provide one another with necessities that are shown to belong to the lords of the world, we order you to go to the Veronese possessors, where special care for this product is taken, so that, once a suitable price has been received, no one delays selling what ought to be offered to royal favor.

It is plainly a product worthy of Italy’s boast. For although ingenious Greece commends herself through the varied subtlety of her care and either seasons her wines with fragrances [Note: [Col. 0857D] It should be noted here that the ancients frequently used wine seasoned with fragrances, as Athenaeus testifies, Book II, chapter 1; Aelian, Book XII of the *History*; Eunapius of Sardis, in his account of Iamblichus; and Arnobius, Book V. BROSS.] or flavors them with marine mixtures, nevertheless, after such elaborate refinement, nothing similar is found.

This wine is pure, royal in color, and outstanding in flavor, so that one might think that the purple dye itself had been steeped in its springs, or that its liquids had been pressed from purple. There an ineffable sweetness is perceived; it is strengthened by some firmness of texture; its touch grows rich through density, so that you might say it is either a fleshy liquid or an edible drink.

It is worth reporting how singular its collection appears to be. In autumn, grapes picked from the vines are hung upside down in household arbors; they are preserved in their own vessels and kept in natural cases. They stiffen rather than dissolve with age; then, exuding their foolish fluids, they become sweet with great pleasantness.

They are kept until December, until the season of winter opens their flow; and in a marvelous way the wine begins to be new precisely when it is found aged in every cellar. Winter must, the cold blood of grapes, the vintage in rigidity, a bloody liquid, drinkable purple, violet nectar: it first cools in its origin; and when it has been able to mature, it begins to possess perpetual newness.

It is not beaten injuriously by feet, nor darkened by any admixture of filth; rather, as is fitting, such nobility is elicited. It flows while water hardens; it is fertile when every fruit of the fields has departed. It distills a liquid comparable to gems, shedding something delightfully tear-like; and besides the pleasure of its sweetness, its appearance possesses a singular beauty.

Seek this out as quickly as possible, gather it at suitable prices, and deliver it to the record-keepers who have been sent for this purpose. Do not think that the other product should be neglected, the one that gleams in a milky cup, since it is more marvelous when what you have been able to find is more difficult to obtain.

Its whiteness is beautiful and its purity serene, so that the former may be believed to have been born from roses, the latter from lilies. In color they are different, but in flavor alike; their appearance differs, yet the sweetness of each is similar. For what tastes sharply and what quickly refreshes are understood to be common to both, but the difference visible between them is great.

You behold this one joyful in redness; you see the other festive in whiteness. Therefore their procurement must be exceedingly swift, since both are known to contain equally what is sought.

### LETTER V. TO VALERIAN [ms. A: VALERIUS], A MAN OF SUBLIME RANK, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He announces that the king has reduced the prices of goods in the fields of Lucania and the Bruttii because of the injury inflicted by the army. Then he orders that the people be kept to their duty by the judges and the soldiers by the commanders. Finally, he forbids any household—not even his own or the royal household—from being exempted from feeding the troops.

[Col. 0858B]

Generally, it is fitting that a most distinguished administrator should extend benefits, since one who is known to preside over all is considered obliged to bestow what will profit everyone. Yet, since nature favors them, we owe more to those who are joined to us by some degree of proximity, although it may seem a kind of right purpose to depart from equality. We show modesty to colleagues, offer reverence to fathers, owe fellow citizens a common goodwill, but a special affection to sons; and so great is the force of family ties that no one should judge himself despised if he recognizes that another’s pledges have been preferred to his own. Therefore it is not unjust to be more solicitous for one’s homeland, especially at a time when we seem to be coming to its aid in its dangers. For we are believed to love more those whom we hasten to rescue.

Accordingly, a numerous army, known to have been assigned for the defense of the republic, is said to have devastated the cultivated lands of Lucania and Bruttium and, through its zeal for plunder, to have reduced the abundance of the regions. But since, according to the circumstances of the time, it is necessary both to give to some and to take from others, learn that the prices established by ancient custom have been moderated by order of the lord of affairs, so that what is supplied should be charged to the public treasury at a much lower rate than that at which you used to sell it, so that neither the landowner may have to bear losses nor the struggling army suffer want.

Do not, therefore, be anxious. You have escaped the hands of the collectors; the present military apparatus removes the taxes from you. But so that your understanding might more easily be informed, we have thought it appropriate to set out below, in brief statements, the sums to be charged, so that no one may sell you as a favor what you know has been bestowed through public generosity.

Therefore restrain the landowners’ intemperate agitation. Let those love peace whom no one drives toward uncertainties. While the army of the Goths is waging war, let the Roman population remain at peace. What is commanded is a fortunate wish. Let not the peasants, that rustic class of men, while fleeing the burdens of labor, become inflamed by unlawful ventures and begin to rise against you—men whom you could scarcely restrain in peacetime.

Therefore, by royal command, admonish each lessee of estates and substantial landowner not to contract any barbarity in the struggle, lest they hasten to be useful in war no more than they are destructive in peace. Let them take up iron, but iron with which to cultivate the fields; let them take pointed implements, goads for oxen, not for rage. The greatest praise belongs to defenders if, while those others appear to be protecting the aforesaid regions, these men do not cease cultivating their ancestral possessions.

Let there be vigor in the judges, proceeding from the laws; let the benches never cease to thunder out the law against evil conduct. Let the thief fear the judgment which he has always dreaded. Let the adulterer tremble before the judge’s bosom [Note: [Col. 0859D] Juret thinks that *genium* should be read instead of *gremium*, as in Book I, Letter 4, although he used *gremium curiae* in Book XI, Letter 13. By this formula a tax is remitted on account of the passage of soldiers, which is established to be innocent, *Novell.* 130; for the same reason, assessments are legally remitted to private contractors, *Digest*, Book XIX, Title 2, *Locati et conducti*, above, Book V, Letter 26. FORN.]. Let the forger dread the herald’s voice. Let the thief not smile at the courts, because liberty rejoices when such things do not flourish.

For you will perceive that the war is being conducted most successfully if you share a common resolve for civic order. Let no one oppress the needy: attack the violators, pursue the persecutors. You have a fitting civic battle. You will restore everything to peace if you suppress the leaders of crimes.

In reckoning the grain allowances, be vigilant, lest anyone’s craft defraud another. As for the army’s commanders, learn that they have been delegated by the lords of affairs in my presence, so that, whenever they have necessarily been admonished by you, they may be aided when burdened by injustice. Nevertheless, let them maintain discipline, from which the army is always armed with greater strength.

A further kind of benefit has also been added: by the present decree of the king, not even the divine household is to be considered exempt; rather, everything assessed for the general levy is to be borne communally. Now, therefore, rise diligently with all your brothers and take every necessary precaution, so that it may truly profit the noblest homeland to have placed such responsibilities before you.

To govern peaceful affairs and administer provinces according to established practice is within the ability even of men of ordinary intelligence. But this is the task, this is the labor: to govern that which cannot contain itself when abandoned. For the skill of sailors ceases in calm weather, nor does a craftsman’s name bring distinction unless the force of danger has been great. You therefore have an opportunity in which you may acquire the reputation of wise men and, with the Lord’s help, preserve yourselves honorably in every respect.

As for my own people, I do not commend them above the others in any special way, because we desire that the same thing happen to everyone which we wish to happen to our own household [ed., *labors*]. My personal concern has fallen away since I began to consider the guardianship of all. I wish well to my own, but only in a way that can be shared by everyone, because it is a great form of injustice to want for oneself a judge different from the one that the community as a whole can endure.

## EPISTOLA VI. TO ALL WHO ADMINISTER THE OFFICES OF THE PREFECTURE, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He threatens unjust judges with punishments and urges the good to attend tirelessly to the public welfare.

Although the commands issued by the lords of affairs in their innate piety are fully sufficient, we nevertheless double the threats against the importunate and foolish by applying strictness, so that those who cannot feel shame may at least restrain themselves through fear. For who would rejoice in his own presumption when he is going to lose his reputation if he attempts what has been forbidden?

Let the blind ambition of those who desire things be blunted [Ac., “Let it be concealed”]; let insolent boldness be curbed; let the man who seeks profit from wrongdoing be terrified by the penalty set before him; let the man who desires honor through abominable acts be disturbed instead by the loss of his reputation. It is also added that in our times criminal money will have no power; nor can one redeem his guilt when he knows himself to be guilty. No opportunity will lie open for unjust frauds: we pursue those who transgress; we do not sell them off.

When both the lords of affairs and your own judges threaten you, where will you now have hope of taking things by wrongful means? [Col. 0860B] But you whom our election has enabled to reach public administrations, trust in the honesty of your conduct, since no venality excludes you if integrity has governed your actions. Serve the public welfare steadfastly, since no private losses will shake you. Repay this favor to my judgment, so that you who were not burdened by any personal support of mine may strive to have my actions praised in yourselves.

Know, therefore, that the period fixed by the lords of affairs must be observed, but in such a way that you must provide for and discharge whatever has been decreed for the public welfare.

## EPISTOLA VII. TO THE CANONICARIUS OF VENETIA, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He indicates that the king has remitted the fifteenth-indiction tax to certain persons whose property was devastated by an incursion of the Suebi.

[Col. 0860C]

Under the clemency of a good ruler, nothing is considered subject to chance, since they correct adverse circumstances who are accustomed to provide for prosperity with the greatest success [Ms. and Ac., “who have judged”]. For how can a naked man endure savage barbarism and a strict ruler, when, having been stripped, he refuses by right what he had learned to impose when prosperous?

Therefore, to those whose lands had been devastated by an incursion of the Suebi, royal serenity has remitted the treasury payment of the fifteenth indiction (in the year of Christ 537), as the decree read again will be able to inform you. Accordingly, while commending your obedience, do not exact from the aforesaid landowners, for those estates which you ascertain to have been devastated, the taxes of the present indiction. For the remainder, however, see to it by the customary compulsion that you supply the remaining amount to our treasurer at the appointed times.

Take care, therefore, lest you become more burdensome to enemies if you still wish to strip those who have already been stripped. Let those who feared arms not fear cloaks; let those who have suffered plunder not suffer it after the plunderers. They have found strong receipts against you; their calamity has given them inviolable securities; the violent man has taken away what you were seeking. One who appears to have been left with nothing is plainly freed from taxes.

## EPISTOLA VIII. TO THE CONSULAR OF THE PROVINCE OF LIGURIA, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He exempts certain estates from paying their public taxes to the collectors, provided that the owners themselves carry the payment to the royal treasury in their own hands at the prescribed time.

[Col. 0861A]

It seems to be a new kind of saving for petitioners to acquire something while those who provide it suffer no loss. For something is received from one person in such a way that it cannot perish for another: it is given without loss; it is transferred without diminution; and it bears the name of generosity, while never departing from the ruler’s rights.

Therefore, the owner of the estates situated in that province, which the brief statement written below reports to be harassed by the excessive zeal of collectors, desires to pay to our treasurers the due obligation without any diminution of the public interest. We, who are known to pursue no one’s losses, willingly assent, provided that what is owed to the treasury is paid by reasonable satisfaction. For it is as bad to thwart good desires as to commit unlawful acts.

Accordingly, after admonishing the curials and the compulsors, as well as those whose interest you recognize, your Eminence shall arrange for the collection from the aforesaid estates to be suspended from that indiction onward under this condition: if the amount owed has not been paid to the treasurer within the stated deadlines, customary collection shall be carried out throughout the province.

If, by the treasurers’ receipts, he proves that the assurance of his promise has been fully met [the reading *minusve* is uncertain], the designated estates shall be freed from all harassment by the compulsors, because those offerings ought rather to be chosen which are proved to be made willingly and without suspicion of loss. For collection without the pressure of a compulsor is pleasing to us; and it is a devoted act to do voluntarily what one could scarcely have fulfilled under compulsion.

Would that a willing landowner might both remove from us the necessity of delays and abolish for himself the losses arising from the required payments! For he makes what is necessary imminent who delays providing the customary payments.

## EPISTOLA IX. TO PASCHASIUS, PREFECT OF THE GRAIN SUPPLY, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He indicates that an African has claimed the property left by a certain man who died without surviving children or heirs, and orders that the African be formally introduced into possession according to custom.

It is full of piety to bind a foreign people to public benefits, and not merely to permit blood relatives to gain the profits of an inheritance, but also to invite newcomers themselves. An inheritance without near relations is succession without kinship; [Col. 0861D] the sole proof of lineage is to speak ancestral speech.

For this African seeks the benefit in such a way as to show that it was once granted to him: a gift bestowed without the recipient’s name, apart from the person, because it was first conferred upon the nation, so that afterward the designation of individual petitioners could be attached to it. Hence they claim foreign inheritances by a certain right, and they alone seem to possess what a Roman cannot obtain in comparable cases.

They did not have such a benefit in their homeland, but here all are relatives under this condition: the entire nation is one family insofar as the benefit of succession is concerned. Therefore let your Experience examine his petitions through careful inquiry; and if the man whom he alleges to have departed from this life truly left no children, and the property is not reasonably established to be possessed by someone else, let your office carry out the formal introduction into possession of the aforesaid property according to custom, so that the ancient piety of the rulers may restore the benefits of the present lords, and he may be able to pray for those under whom he understands himself to have deserved votive favor.

Let him recover the property which he had sighed to have lost. He can no longer call himself a foreigner, since he acquires the desired lands [Ac., “rights”]. Let him possess the same dignity as the landowners, and, restored to the position of a taxpayer, let him now make the payments that he sought from alien hands. Let him rejoice that he has been brought to the point of giving what clearly cannot arise except for one who possesses it; in this one respect he is less fortunate than the other lords, because he cannot alienate what he has managed to possess.

We also believe this to have been discovered through great equity: that the man who succeeds in place of a pledge may preserve his property for strangers with the affection [Grul., Cuj., Niv. and Ga., “with the effect”] due to a father. Nourished by compassion, let him now nourish others as well. A fortunate and celebrated captivity has fallen to him: to enjoy Roman citizenship and to have been able to share in the privileges of the Africans.

## EPISTOLA X. TO THE VARIOUS CHANCELLORS OF THE PROVINCES, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He orders them to exact without any delay the amount of the coming indiction. If they do otherwise, he threatens to treat them more severely.

The remnants of public accounts are to be compared to an unhappy illness, which burdens and weakens unless it departs swiftly. To be under a debt is a kind of guilt, and one cannot truly be called free who is proved to be liable.

A prudent man compels himself; the less cautious man is driven by another. For what has the collection undertaken throughout the whole year accomplished? Let the amount and quantity of the coming indiction be exacted. By sparing, you do not spare; by relieving, you increase the burden. While you seek delays for sale, you double the burden of the tax.

Abandon at last this cruel mercy, these benefits made bitter by utter detestation. The man who proceeds violently under the appearance of flattery strikes more severely; and the man who delays collecting taxes at the customary times injures under the guise of indulgence.

Therefore cease at some point to trade in the landowners’ losses, because through the hardships you impose you return in full what you have taken away through unjust delays. After this, do not expect to be warned again by words, but compelled by unremitting collection.

Accordingly, if by that day you have neither brought nor sent to our treasurer the amount customarily demanded from the provinces, with the accounts properly itemized, you will swiftly pay back in the province, after being degraded, what you acknowledge that you have wrongly delayed. For it is exceedingly unjust that public money should lie idle through your negligence, while the treasury continually spends borrowed money on public purposes.

## EPISTOLA XI. TO PETER, A MAN OF CLARISSIMUS RANK, DISTRIBUTOR OF THE FOOD ALLOWANCES, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He orders him to distribute without fraud the food allowances granted by the king to the Roman people.

He who is appointed to distribute princely benefits ought to possess a proven conscience, lest any portion of what flows from such great generosity be dried up by greed. The hands of those who seize things alter every kind of generosity. Just as the purity of a spring is corrupted by mud, so the abundance of a good king is altered by avaricious distributions.

Gold itself, when dissolved into liquid, is contaminated unless it is received in the purest vessel, since only those things preserve their purity which are darkened by no admixture of filth. How pleasing it is to see streams running through snow-white vessels, and, as it were, nature’s own unbounded purity smiling, when it is disfigured by no stain or injury!

So the gifts of the lord of affairs must not be darkened by any pollution. Just as they issue abundantly from him, so they must reach the Romans in complete purity. For although every fraud seems serious, that fraud is intolerable which operates among the Roman people: a crowd that lives peacefully; a people unknown except when joyful; a cry without sedition; a tumult ignorant of rage; people whose only struggle is to flee poverty and not to love riches.

They do not know how to pursue profit, nor do they torment themselves through any crafty practice of refusal. They live by the fortune of the middling and the conscience of the rich. Is it not sacrilege to rob such people, who do not know how to defraud others?

Therefore, beginning with that indiction, we grant the food allowances to be distributed to the Roman people, with the Divinity favorable to you, so that they may receive without any diminution what they have earned through royal generosity. Take care that what they have earned is not received by another, and that you are made a stranger to our favor if you depart from civic affection.

Let no one be made Latin by purchase who does not possess the rights of that citizenship by birth. What gave its name to nations must always be honored, since it becomes superior among human affairs when something is bestowed from its glory. These are gifts of the Quirites. Let servile fortune not usurp the place of the free.

He sins against the majesty of the Roman people who stains the purity of that blood by associating it with slaves [Note: [Col. 0863D] See what Dionysius writes concerning the gifts of the emperor Tiberius, Book LVII, p. 787. JURET.].

## EPISTOLA XII. TO ANASTASIUS, CHANCELLOR OF LUCANIA AND BRUTTIUM, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He praises above all the Palmatian wine and the Silanian cheese, and orders him to search for both with particular care so that they may be sent to the royal court.

When we were dining according to customary practice with the lord of affairs, and the delicacies of various provinces were being praised, conversation, as usual, reached the wines of Bruttium and the sweetness of Silanian cheese. Through the benefit of the grasses, it is made there with such natural delight that you would not think the taste of honey lacking, although you see no honey mixed into it.

There, when gently provoked, milk flows lightly from full, tubular udders and, as though gathered by nature’s abundance into other bellies, does not fall in drops but flows in sudden streams. A sweet and varied fragrance of herbs exhales; the pasture of the flocks is recognized by the nostrils, and, burning with diverse strength, is perceived to breathe forth something resembling incense.

Such richness accompanies it that you might think the Palladian liquid were flowing along with it, except that it is distinguished from that green color by snowy whiteness. Then, when that remarkable abundance has been received with great delight by the joyful shepherd in broad, open vats, and, mixed with rennet, has begun to harden into a tender, compact mass, it is brought into the form of a beautiful circle. Gathered for a time in underground storehouses, it gives the cheese lasting substance.

You shall send this by ship as quickly as possible, so that we may seem to have satisfied the royal desires with a small gift. As for the wine which antiquity, wishing to praise it, called Palmatian [Forn. and Cor., Ga., “Palmatine,” or “Palmary”] [Note: [Col. 0863D] See Baronius on this passage, vol. VIII, for the year of Christ 591, p. 21. JURET.], search for it carefully: it is not harshly astringent, but pleasing in sweetness.

For although it seems the least among the wines of Bruttium, it has nevertheless become almost universally regarded as pre-eminent. There is also a wine equal to Gazetan [Note: [Col. 0863D] Gazetan wine is mentioned by Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapters 5 and 6, and by Sidonius Apollinaris in Poem [Col. 0864D] 17, to Omatius:

> My wines are not Gazetan, Chian, or Falernian.

This expression comes from the region of Gaza, that is, Palestine, as Isidore writes, *Etymologies*, Book XX, chapter 3. JURET.] [Cuj., “Gazean”], similar to Sabine wine, and remarkable for its powerful fragrances.

But since that wine has claimed for itself the most distinguished reputation, this one too should be sought as exceptionally elegant in its own kind, lest the wisdom of our ancestors seem to have given it an improper name. It is thick with a pleasantly sweet richness [Gr., Cuj., Niv. and Ga., “well planted”], exceedingly firm in its vigor, powerful in aroma, and also clear in its whiteness. It smells so strongly when belched from the mouth that the name seems rightly to have been given to it from the palm.

It constricts weakened bowels, dries moist wounds, restores a weary chest, and what a prepared medicinal drink scarcely manages to accomplish, this wine naturally provides without artificial treatment.

But take care that you send the aforesaid varieties exactly as required, because we cannot be deceived, having retained this knowledge through ancestral tradition [ms., “variety”]. For the present, we have supplied from our cellars what was requested. You, however, act at your own risk if you make substitutions, since you know that their judgments can already be held against you.

## XIII. EDICT. Against Those Who Stole the Gifts Granted by the King to the Churches

The generosity bestowed by the rulers ought to be maintained in practice, since what they have been proved to have done at the prompting of the Divinity must benefit the whole community. For the piety of rulers protects the entire empire, and when a fitting return is made to them, the members of the republic are preserved unharmed.

Some time ago, imperial enactments assisted the holy Churches throughout Bruttium and Lucania with a certain devotion of gifts. But, as is customary with sacrilegious minds—to sin even in the very sphere of divine reverence—certain *numerarii* among the *canonicarii* were withholding part of these gifts under the name of accounting charges, turning the property of clerics into a lay profit.

Our own *numerarii*, rejecting this with detestable execration, report that they never received for themselves what impious hands defrauded them of through such a crime. What will you not attempt next, human audacity, if you extend theft even where you know that you cannot remain hidden? To deceive mortal eyes, an act of presumption may perhaps appear in some sense plausible, though unjust. How, then, is the man condemned for such blindness who thinks he can perpetrate what the Divinity cannot perceive?

But lest similar presumption continue to rage or frequent excess provoke divine patience, we decree by edict that whoever is thereafter involved in this fraud shall both lose his office and forfeit the profit of his own property. For he must be punished with a heavier penalty who has extended his audacity even to the point of injuring the Divine.

Let the poor have the gifts of the rulers; let those who possess no means possess something. Why is another’s property, placed in the generosity of the king, invaded? Its possession is a gift of the ruler. How should a subject presume to touch what the humility of the ruler considers proper to offer to God?

It is also added that not to give such people what is due is to take it away—and rightly so, since one who can aid the hungry destroys them if he does not feed them. Let them be ashamed to take from those whom we are commanded to support. It exceeds every cruelty to wish to become rich through the poverty of a beggar.

Let honest profits be loved; let harmful gains be abhorred. Let no one dare to take away what he could distribute once it has been collected. By adding to his wealth he destroys it, if he has accumulated it by withholding; and he draws poverty toward himself if he does not reject the money of those who exact it.

## EPISTOLA XIV. TO ANASTASIUS, CHANCELLOR OF LUCANIA AND BRUTTIUM, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He describes the region of Rhegium and prohibits the continued requisition of lard and wheat from it in the name of compulsory purchase.

[Col. 0865C]

The citizens of Rhegium, the furthest people of Bruttium, whom the violent force of the sea once separated from the body of Sicily, from which their city received its name—for division is called *ῥήγιον* (*rhēgion*, “division”) in Greek—report that they are being unjustly harassed by the presumption of collectors. They implore remedies known not merely to our ears but to our eyes, since we can see that their territory does not possess what is being demanded.

The land there is exceedingly poor in mountain stones, dry in its pastures but watered in its vineyards; hostile to grain crops but suited to olives. Therefore all its cultivation depends on the hoe, because its dry surface cannot nourish what grows above it. There the naked field is clothed more by human effort than by nature. For it is covered with the greenery of Palladian forests, although the soil itself is found to be extremely arid.

In such places, those plants thrive whose tall roots descend into the depths of the earth. Grain crops are irrigated in order to live; and, with the condition reversed, what is supplied to vegetables is lavished upon the ears of grain. How large a harvest is there that is gathered by hand [Ac., “cultivated”]? Rarely does the farmer come from the threshing floor burdened on his shoulders, so that the harvest may be stored in granaries; rather, he can scarcely fill a few baskets from the summit of abundance.

In the gardens of the peasants there is a laborious multitude, because every vegetable there is sprinkled with the flavor of the sea by marine irrigation. What human industry is accustomed to produce, the land received while it was being nourished. Contrary to Maro’s judgment, the fibers of chicory there are exceedingly sweet; enclosed by twisted leaves, they gather into a tough yet tender mass. Hence, like natron [Ac., “glass”], something cut away is broken off when it is separated from the fertile turf.

If you wish to know, that region is fertile in these foodstuffs. It also enjoys the delightful abundance of marine produce, because there the upper and lower seas, joined where their fronts meet, bring the delicacies of both seas into a single gathering through the revolving motion of their gulf. Fish must necessarily hurry there, where it is clear that the water too can flow away.

The exormiston [Note: [Col. 0865D] A kind of fish so called by the Greeks who inhabited the farthest coast of Greece in Italy, because it is accustomed to leave the bottom of the sea and swim to the surface. The term is properly used of a ship when its anchors have been raised; conversely, when it is anchored, it is said to have been *ὁρμισθῆναι* (“to be moored”). BROSS.] is also a royal kind among fish. It resembles the moray in body but differs in color; it has bristling nostrils, the delicate tenderness of a soft oyster, a fatty and sweet liquid congealed within it, and a pleasing, appetizing richness.

When it begins to swim amid the foaming waves at the boundary between water and air, it does not know how to return to the resting places it has left. I believe this is either because it has forgotten the way back or because, softened by its extreme tenderness, it cannot struggle against the rising waves and sink beneath them. It is carried along like a lifeless body, avoiding danger with no effort and by no art. Thus, deprived of strength, it is not believed capable of returning, since it is not perceived to be able to flee.

This fish is plainly recognized as possessing such sweetness that none of the fish can be compared with it. These are the things we have described on the shore of Rhegium, which we know not from another’s report but retain through visual observation.

Therefore we decree that no variety of lard or wheat is to be demanded from there at any time in the name of compulsory purchase, since what the nature of the place does not possess is demanded with excessive injustice. Moreover, the defense of truth and the testimony of the judge ought to suffice, because it is an exceedingly detestable evil if the conscience knows one thing while the tongue decrees another.

It is also added that the region is wearied by the arrivals of so many travelers and worn down by the tearing away of so many departing parties, so that it ought reasonably to have been granted remission of what is established either to be capable of growing there [Grul., Cuj., Niv., Ga., “incapable of growing there”].

## EPISTOLA XV. TO MAXIMUS, A MAN OF CLARISSIMUS RANK, CHANCELLOR OF LUCANIA AND BRUTTIUM, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He describes the city of Scyllacium, his homeland, and the fishponds he had excavated at the foot of Mount Moscius. He then issues certain regulations concerning relay horses, grain allowances, and the judges’ *pulveraticum*.

[Col. 0866D]

Scyllacium, the first of the cities of Bruttium, which Ulysses, the destroyer of Troy, is believed to have founded, is said to be irrationally harassed by the excess of presumptuous men—something that ought not to have been undertaken while we preside, since we are compelled to grieve all the more over its injuries because they touch us through ancestral affection.

The city, situated above the Adriatic gulf, hangs like a cluster of grapes upon the hills—not because it swells through a difficult ascent, but so that it may pleasantly look out upon the green fields and the blue back of the sea.

It observes the rising sun from its very cradle, where the coming day does not send the dawn ahead of it. Rather, as soon as the sun begins to rise, the brightness, shaking its lamp, displays it. It looks upon Phoebus in joy; there it shines with the splendor of its own light, so that it might be thought more truly the homeland of the sun itself, surpassing Rhodes in reputation.

It enjoys a clear light and is also endowed with a temperate climate: it experiences sunny winters and cooled summers, and life passes without sorrow where hostile seasons are not feared. Hence human beings too are freer in their understanding, because moderation governs everything.

A hot homeland makes people light and sharp; a cold one makes them slow and crafty. Only a temperate homeland shapes human character according to its own quality. Hence the ancients said that Athens was the seat of the wise: an atmosphere purified and polished it, preparing the clearest minds by a fortunate generosity for contemplation.

For is it the same for the body to drink muddy water as to draw in the clarity of the sweetest spring? So the vigor of the soul is burdened [Note: [Col. 0867] “The situation of places shapes the minds of men,” says Curtius Rufus, Book VII and Book VIII. See Stobaeus, Sermon 99, p. 327; Cicero, Book II, *On the Nature of the Gods*. JURET.], when it is compressed by a heavier air. We necessarily lie under the influence of such things: we become sad under cloudy skies and naturally rejoice again under clear ones, because the heavenly substance of the soul delights in all that is untainted and pure.

It also enjoys abundant marine delicacies, since it possesses nearby the enclosures of Neptune which we have made. For at the foot of Mount Moscius we properly introduced the waters of Nereus’ whirlpool into excavated hollows in the rock. There a multitude of fish, playing in free captivity, both refreshes the spirit with delight and charms the eyes with wonder.

They eagerly run toward human hands; and before they become food, they seek food. A man feeds his delicacies, and while he has at his disposal what he might capture, it frequently happens that, once filled, he leaves everything behind.

Nor is the spectacle of those laboring beautifully denied to the city’s inhabitants. Abundant vineyards are seen; the rich threshing of the threshing floors is observed; the faces of flourishing olive trees are also revealed. No one needs the beauty of fields who has been granted the ability to see everything from the city.

Because it now has no walls, you might believe it a rural city; you might judge it an urban villa. Placed between the two, it is known to be enriched with abundant praise. As travelers frequently desire to visit it, and wish to escape the burdens of labor, the citizens are wearied at their own expense by the city’s beauty through the provision of relay horses and grain allowances.

Therefore, lest its beauty injure the city or its reputation become the cause of expense, we decree that the provision of relay horses and grain allowances, according to the authorized conveyances, be charged to the public treasury. We also abolish the judges’ *pulveraticum* entirely and decree that grain allowances be provided to governors for only three days, according to ancient regulations, with the delay in transport borne at their own expense.

For those who administer the laws wished them to be a remedy, not a burden. Accordingly, in view of equity, it is the duty of judicial office to relieve your city; what we set before you is not a remission. Live, with God’s help, by the justice of the age and with the singular joy of security. Let others speak of islands; I would rather call your dwellings fortunate.

## EPISTOLA XVI. TO THE CANONICARIUS [ms. Aud., “CANONICARIA”]

He orders him to admonish his subordinates to pay the customary taxes willingly; no one is to exceed the established weights; he himself is to send a reliable account of expenses to the praetorian archives every fourth month.

The season, ever suited to human affairs—since a continually cherished expectation reconciles even harsh circumstances to us—admonishes us to renew our care for fiscal payments through an annual observance, since the order of the republic is seen to stand upon such an institution. And rightly that is seen to be a votive offering which is performed for the benefit of all.

These things must be cherished, through which the republic is seen to be most firmly established. While it is renewed by the returning census, it is held together by the firmest strength of its condition. Therefore devotion displayed at any time is great; but it becomes more welcome when it is recognized as more necessary.

Let the landowners provide the stipends that will benefit their own good standing. A debt that cannot be avoided ought always to be offered with a willing mind, so that what is clearly paid without compulsion may become a benefit.

Therefore, in the first indiction [in the year of Christ 338], as has happily been said, we order you to admonish the landowners in your diocese, with the threefold payment preserved, to pay the total tax devotedly, so that no one may lament that it has been exacted from him prematurely, nor may anyone say that he has been passed over through a delayed remission.

Let no one exceed the amount of the proper weighing, and let the pound be exactly correct. There will be no limit to robbery if it is permitted to exceed the weights. You shall also regularly send a reliable account of expenses to our archives every four months, so that, once the darkness of every error has been removed, the truth may shine forth in the public accounts.

But so that, with God’s help, he may more easily complete what has been established, we order that this and that soldier of our office remain close to you and your office, mindful of their own dangers, so that what you recognize as commanded may obtain its effect without blame.

Take care, therefore, lest the guilt of improper redemption or sluggish negligence affect you, and lest what you neglect to expedite bring losses upon your own fortunes.

## EPISTOLA XVII. TO JOHN, THE RAVENNATE *SILIQUATARIUS*, THE SENATOR, PRAETORIAN PREFECT [ms. “KING ATHALARIC”]

He orders him to admonish the landowners to open great mouths of ditches beside Mount Caprarius and in the places lying around the walls.

Fortification of cities is the sure hope of all, since in peacetime one learns from foreign peoples what must truly be feared in battle. For the inhabited quarters of individual cities are filled with people of diverse kinds. Who knows with what people he may have to contend? Therefore all must recognize what it would not please future enemies to hear. Accordingly, by our command you shall warn the possessors that beside Mount Caprarius and in the places surrounding the walls, enormous mouths of ditches are to be opened [Ac., constructed]; and such a gap must be made there that no entrance is left.

Why, wicked men, do you investigate illicit approaches by which entry through the gates is freely permitted? I do not know what you seem to be concealing, since you do not wish to enter openly. A righteous conscience keeps to public roads and rejoices in the conversation of those it meets; and when it cheerfully inquires after different people, it is not burdened by the weariness of the undertaking. It is characteristic of guilt, however, to wish not to be known; and whoever hides his roads betrays his conscience.

Therefore let the ancient routes be restored to general use, lest, while they seek to shorten their labor, they suffer the loss of their lives. For he must rightly be regarded as an enemy who strives to violate the defenses of a city.

## LETTER XVIII. TO CONSTANTINIANUS, A MOST EXPERIENCED MAN, SENATOR, THE PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He orders him to repair the Flaminian Way; to provide the prescribed number of post-horses; to collect provisions without loss to the possessors; and diligently to seek out the foods prepared for the royal tables.

Royal service brings danger to the negligent, but honor to those who labor energetically, because it is the reward of life to serve, under the eyes of the lord, one from whom neither fault can be concealed nor good action hidden. How pleasing it is to travel the appointed route without any offense, to see judgments guided by diligence, to pass uncertainties without fear, to climb mountainous places with an easy step, not to tremble at the bridge’s [*contrabium*] crossing, and to complete the journey in such a way that everything is judged to have accorded with the intention!

You rise above your military service if you are able to please the lord of all things. For the one whom we strive to obey: it is a great advancement if you prove worthy to come into his peaceful presence. Therefore join together the banks of the Flaminian Way, cut through as they are by streams, with very broad bridges; strip the crushed margins of the highways of their most rugged forests; let the prescribed number of post-horses be provided, with an excellent selection of animals; and let the assigned quantity of provisions be collected without any loss to the possessors. You make everything pleasing in this way, if you commit no offense in any respect. One thing withheld disfigures everything; and everything is believed lacking wherever even the slightest harshness of complaint is aroused.

Moreover, seek out with complete diligence the products prepared for the royal tables. For what will it profit you to satisfy the army if you should happen to fail in the very feeding of the lords [ms. and Ac., “suffering”]? Let the provincials obey when warned; let each city supply what has been declared in the brief written orders. For whenever one approaches a joyful prince, benefits are effectively requested.

Consider also that I am judging your present actions, either joyfully returning the lords’ thanks to you or, in anger, assigning you the prince’s reprimand. Act, therefore, so that your excess may not be charged to me, since I satisfy everyone concerning you by saying that I have been offended by your faults. Let the whole army rather render me thanks. Great will be your glory if you make me secure and merit the good judgment of so many.

## LETTER XIX. TO MAXIMUS, VICAR OF THE CITY OF ROME, SENATOR, THE PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He warns him to prepare everything necessary for solemnly receiving the king.

You can recognize the king’s arrival from the very multitude of those traveling to and fro, because it is necessary that a great event always send appropriate signs ahead of it. The rising Morning Star reveals the coming day; a favorable wind shows that clear weather will follow; by a certain foreknowledge of the mind we discern impending blessings; and it is difficult for a great event to take place without being announced in advance by signs.

Nevertheless, we necessarily warn you also to dress the Tiberian waters solemnly by joining the bridge, so that it may provide an unshaken passage, with the vessel fixed by its chains, and, from its fixed position, provide us a swift passage. Let it not be moved by sluggish ropes, as it used to be; let so great a mass not grow numb under the hands of those pulling it. Rather, let it provide through its fixed position the speed that previously it could not provide while moving. Let the crowds of travelers pass; surely the divided water should not carry us in boats. The lord must be received in such a way that he may have cause to rejoice at some novelty.

The strongly fastened joining of the planks must provide the necessary solidity, so that by its likeness to solid land it may remove the fear of those who distrust the waves. Indeed, once it has been crossed safely, one should wish it had been longer. Let the protection of railings be suitably fitted on the right and left. The passage is made prosperous when a harsh accident has been excluded.

See how you should prepare the rest of what concerns you, since you know that you will be among those who come to meet him. For how great a thing it is, amid so great a multitude, not to have been found blameworthy! Whoever withholds anything necessary from the king afflicts everyone, because although all rejoice in his being desired, they are all saddened if he is shown to have been offended.

Add that it is especially illustrious to be praised amid such a gathering of senators: to receive the prince in such a way that everyone understands that nothing is lacking, and even that the lord himself comes cheerful rather than confused by any apprehension. It is an unexpected blessing if the person to whom the danger of deception belongs secures an increase of favor for himself.

For this purpose, know that we have sent a soldier of our office, who must keep watch over you and your office, so that he may report to us that everything is prepared, since what is known to have been assigned to our danger cannot be entrusted to chance.

## LETTER XX. TO THOMAS AND PETER, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MEN, TREASURERS, SENATOR, THE PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He orders them to return to the agents of Saint Peter, under a written bond, the sacred vessels that Pope Agapitus, sent as envoy to the East, had pawned to the royal treasurers for money received.

You remember with me, most faithful men, that when the holy Agapitus, pope of the city of Rome, was being sent to the ruler of the East on an embassy, he formally received from you so many pounds of gold, by way of a payment made for the pledges given at the royal command, so that the provident ruler might provide even for the sudden urgency of his need. He first acted kindly by lending money in a time of need; but how much more gloriously he acted by also granting what could have been offered with thanksgiving! Necessity was overcome without loss: the pope’s hands gave what his substance did not possess; and the journey was rendered free of liability because it was completed through gifts.

What, I ask, could seem more fitting than for a bishop to give to those petitioning the Church, while the Church suffered no detriment? He was rather a distributor than a donor, since the expenditure necessarily had to be charged to the one from whose resources it appeared to have been made. What would such an embassy not accomplish with a devout prince, when it is known to have been appointed as a singular example?

Therefore, warned by our command and made secure by the royal order, return the sacred vessels, under a written bond, to the agents of the holy apostle Peter without any delay, so that, returned at a profit, the desired objects may seem to have been obtained quickly [ms., “may seem to obtain the desired objects”]. Let the sacred ministrations be restored to the hands of the Levites, to be proclaimed throughout the whole world. Let what was his own be restored, since by a just act of generosity he receives back what the priest had legally pledged.

The example that we recounted at length in our history has been surpassed. For when King Alaric, satiated with the plundering of the city of Rome, had received the vessels of the apostle Peter as they were being carried by his men, as soon as he learned the circumstances of the matter after an inquiry, he ordered them to be carried back to the sacred thresholds by the hands of those who had seized them, so that the greed which, in the course of the plunder, had committed the crime might erase its excess through the most devoted generosity.

But what wonder if he refused to plunder the venerable things of the saints [Note: “In a similar expression he said, *the reverence of the sacred command*, Book III, Letter 15; and *the astounding character of merits*, Book IV, Letter 4. JUR.], when he enriched himself through such a devastation of the City? Our king, however, in accordance with his religious purpose, returned the vessels that had appeared to have become his own by right of pledge. And therefore let prayer frequently be offered for such deeds, since we believe that joyful things can be granted when we ask for repayment through good actions.

## LETTER XXI. TO DEUSDEDIT, SCRIBE AT RAVENNA, SENATOR, THE PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He describes the duty and usefulness of scribes.

The office of scribes is customarily the security of all, since the rights of everyone are guarded by their vigilance. Fires ravage some; furtive theft strips others; through negligence, what a diligent owner acquired perishes for some; but whatever private persons lose [ms., “admit”] is restored most firmly by public trust.

Care concerning another’s property is more diligent than care can be concerning one’s own: without being warned, it does what one would scarcely fulfill when asked; and when required, it cannot deny what the person concerned admits he has lost [ms., “admitted”]. His archive is the fortune of everyone; and it is rightly called the refuge of all, where the security of all is found.

He takes on the duties of a father if truth is guarded incorruptibly. For just as a diligent parent preserves what an idle successor will find, so the arbiter of the arts allows no one to be defrauded of his own advantage. And therefore we continually command you to be guardian of so great a matter, so that you who have pleased us until now by your integrity may not be darkened by any change.

Consider what ancient trust is committed to you, and how by daily diligence you settle the quarrel of those who dispute. Your care is contested before all magistrates; and you rather act as judge, since you dissolve the bonds of cases. When this honorable distinction, this indisputable testimony, this ancient voice of documents, has proceeded incorruptibly from your inner chambers, the examiners receive it with reverence; and the litigants, however wicked, nevertheless obey under compulsion [perhaps “heed”]. Even though it is permitted for a promulgated judgment to be suspended, it is not permitted to oppose you.

Therefore let your purpose not be for sale. A malignant offering from one who buys it is the moth of documents, while they seek to destroy what they know they have obstructed. Let the honorable publication [Gr. [Col. 0872B] and Cuj., “edict”] of truth nourish you; let integrity be considered your resource. Give petitioners what was formerly done. Be a transcriber, not an author, of ancient records. Impress the copy upon wax like a ring, so that, just as an engraved likeness cannot escape its marks, your hand may not differ from the authentic text.

But if someone maligns you by a fraudulent surreptitious act, how can he in another case consent to be believed on your authority, when he knows that you could be corrupted? He attacks you by his own fraud and easily convicts the one whom he deceived in one respect. Love justice, of which no one complains, so that even an angry person may be able to give you wholesome testimony—one who wished to make you deviate in vain. Everything you do is public, since whether praised you can find favor, or accused you can encounter offense.

## LETTER XXII. TO THE PROVINCIALS OF ISTRIA, SENATOR, THE PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He orders them to pay the tax in wine, oil, and wheat, with which the province abounded this year; and he sends Laurentius with money to purchase a larger quantity of such goods and transport it to Ravenna. He then portrays that province in detail.

Public expenses, wavering through the various changes of time, can be kept steady by this arrangement, if the soundness of commands follows the produce of the regions. Administration is easy where the harvest has been more abundant. For if what barren sterility has refused is demanded [Juret. reads “is imposed”], then the province is harmed and the desired result is not achieved.

Therefore, from the testimony of travelers, we have learned that the province of Istria, renowned with praise for three excellent products and made fruitful by divine generosity, is rejoicing this present year in the fertility of wine, oil, and wheat. And therefore give the aforesaid products in so many solidi as your tax payment, to be credited to you from this first indiction (A.D. 538); but we leave the remainder, for the customary expenses, to the devoted province.

Since, however, we must seek the goods mentioned in a larger quantity, we have also sent so many solidi from our treasury, so that the necessary products may be gathered in abundance without loss to you. For frequently, when you are compelled to sell to outsiders, you suffer losses—especially at a time when your foreign buyer has been taken away from you; and it is rare to receive gold when you know that merchants are not present.

How much better it is to obey your lords than to supply distant buyers, and to pay what is owed with produce than to endure the disdain of purchasers! In the name of justice, we also reveal what you might have suggested to us, since we ought not to injure you in the price, from which we are not burdened by the provision of transport charges.

For a region lies close to you, situated above the Gulf of the Ionian Sea, filled with olives, adorned with grain fields, and rich in vines. There, as if from three abundant breasts, every product has flowed forth in splendid fertility and desirable fruitfulness. It is not improperly called the Campania of Ravenna, the granary of the royal city, an exceedingly pleasant and delightful retreat; extending toward the north, it enjoys an admirable tempering of the climate.

It also has, if I may say so without absurdity, certain bays of its own, where the billowing sea, entering earthly hollows, settles into a beautiful appearance through the level surface of a lagoon. These places nourish many delicacies and boast an abundance of fish. There is not just one Avernus. Numerous pools of Neptune are visible, in which, even when human industry ceases, oysters arise everywhere without being ordered.

Thus neither effort in cultivating delicacies nor uncertainty in capturing them appears to exist. You might think the brightly shining praetorian residences had been arranged like pearls, so that from this it becomes clear what the judgments of the province’s ancestors must have been, since it is known to have been adorned with such great buildings.

A most beautiful chain of islands is also added to that shore. Arranged with pleasing usefulness, it both protects ships from dangers and enriches cultivators with great abundance. It plainly sustains the guards of the imperial court, adorns the dominion of Italy, supplies the leading men with delicacies, and feeds the people of moderate means at the cost of provisions; and nearly everything produced there is possessed in the royal city [Ac., “principal city”].

Let the devoted province now willingly offer its resources and obey more fully while it is being asked, since it used to act most agreeably when it was scarcely asked at all. But lest any uncertainty arise concerning our commands, we have sent Laurentius, a most experienced man, proven to us through great labors for the republic, with the present authority, so that according to the written orders appended below he may promptly carry out what he knows has been assigned to him for the public expenses.

Now procure what has been ordered. You make the soldier devoted when you willingly accept the command. We shall declare the prices to be moderated for you in the following order, when the bearer of this message has informed us in a report of the quantity of the produce. For nothing can justly be assessed unless the abundance of the commodity has first been clearly investigated. The arbiter who sends a judgment into uncertainty [ms., “in vain”] is unequal; and the person who intends to make an undeliberated statement proves himself conscious of wrongdoing.

## LETTER XXIII. TO LAURENTIUS, A MOST EXPERIENCED MAN, SENATOR, THE PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He orders him to visit the province of Istria to purchase wine, oil, and wheat.

The judge’s deliberation ought to employ proven men in public actions, so that what appears to be sought amid a time of scarcity may easily be accomplished. In an abundance of goods, any person can manage; chosen soldiers are needed when the pressure of necessity has arisen.

And therefore we order your experience, which has been frequently pleasing to us by such devotion, to hasten to the province of Istria, so that you may procure so many solidi’ worth of wine, oil, or wheat from the taxable solidus. With the other so many solidi that you received from our treasurer, you shall hasten to purchase from both merchants and possessors, as the written report delivered to you by the moneyers has instructed.

Therefore now raise your spirits for obedience, you who have pleased us by an undivided record through such great watches. Let the example of your former conduct admonish you, since it is exceedingly serious for a veteran to commit an offense when it is entirely established that, as a recruit, he never erred.

But report to us truthfully, as we believe you will, how abundantly the aforesaid products have unfolded into the desired supply, so that, having determined the quantity, we may establish what will neither injure the provincials nor burden the public expenses.

## LETTER XXIV. TO THE TRIBUNES OF THE MARITIME DISTRICTS, SENATOR, THE PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He orders them to prepare ships to transport wine and oil from the province of Istria to Ravenna. He then discusses navigation and the labor of sailors, especially in working the salt pans.

In a command issued some time ago, we decreed that Istria should successfully send to the Ravenna station the wine and oil whose abundance it has been granted to enjoy in the present year. But you, who possess numerous ships in its vicinity, provide for this with equal devotion, so that what it is ready to hand over you may strive to transport swiftly. The grace of completion will be similar for both parties, since the result cannot be fulfilled if one of them is separated from the other.

Therefore be most prompt in going to nearby places, you who often traverse boundless distances. You travel, in a manner of speaking, through your own lodgings when you sail through your homeland. It also contributes to your advantage that another route is opened to you, tranquil in perpetual security. For when the sea has been closed by raging winds, a path is opened to you through the most delightful rivers.

Your keels do not fear harsh blasts; they touch land with the greatest good fortune; and they do not know how to perish, since they frequently run aground. From a distance they are thought to be carried across meadows whenever their channel happens not to be visible. Drawn by ropes, they walk, although they are accustomed to stand by their cables; and, with their condition changed, people aid their ships with their feet. They pull the carriers without labor and, in place of the favor of sails, use the sailors’ more fortunate footsteps.

It is pleasant to recount how we saw your dwellings situated. The once-renowned Venetiae, full of noble inhabitants, touch Ravenna and the Po on the south, while on the east they enjoy the delight of the Ionian shore, where the alternating tide, flowing out, now closes and now opens the face of the fields through its reciprocal flooding.

Here your home is, as it were, in the manner of aquatic birds. For what is now seen as mainland is presently seen as an island, so that you might think you were looking at the Cyclades, where suddenly you behold the appearance of the places transformed. Indeed, by their likeness, dwellings appear scattered across far-extending waters—places not produced by nature but established by human care.

For there, by binding together flexible reeds, the gathered solidity of the earth is made into a mass; and this fragile fortification is not hesitantly opposed to the sea’s waves, especially since the shallow shore does not allow the mass of the waters to cast it out, and what is carried without force is not aided by the support of depth.

The inhabitants therefore have one common resource: they are filled solely by fish. Poverty lives there on equal terms with the rich. One food restores everyone; one similar dwelling encloses all; they do not know how to envy one another’s households, and living under this measure they escape the vice to which the world is known to be subject.

In working the salt pans, however, all the struggle is concentrated. In place of plows and sickles, you roll cylinders; from these all your produce arises, since in them you possess even what you do not produce. There, in a manner of speaking, edible money is struck. Every wave is devoted to your craft [ms., “every product”]. Someone may seek gold less eagerly, but no one fails to desire finding salt—rightly so, since every food owes its pleasantness to it.

Therefore carefully repair the ships that you have tied to your walls like animals, so that when the most experienced man Laurentius, who has been sent to procure the products, attempts to warn you, you may hasten to set out. Thus you will not delay the necessary expenses by any difficulty, since, according to the state of the weather, you can choose the shorter route for yourselves.

## LETTER XXV. TO AMBROSIUS, AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, ACTING AS DEPUTY, SENATOR, THE PRAETORIAN PREFECT

From certain signs he infers a future scarcity; to avert it, he orders a great quantity of old grain to be collected.

People generally become anxious when they observe changes in the established order of things, because such changes often portend events judged contrary to custom. Nothing happens without a cause, nor is the world entangled in chance events; rather, whatever we see approaching its conclusion is known to be part of the divine plan.

People are disturbed when kings change their established practices and appear in different dress from that to which their usage has accustomed them. Who would not be greatly troubled by such things if, in a reversal of customary patterns, something obscure seemed to be coming from the stars? For just as it is a sure security to mark the seasons as they run their appointed courses, so we are filled with great curiosity when we sense such things being changed.

What is it, I ask, to behold the chief of the stars and not see his customary lights; to look upon the moon, the glory of night, full in its sphere, yet deprived of its natural brightness? We all still see what is like a blue-green sun; we marvel that at midday shadows have no bodies, and that the strength of that most powerful heat has reached the uttermost weakness of the season. This was not the momentary failing of an eclipse, but something that nevertheless continued through nearly the whole course of the year.

What fear, therefore, is there in enduring for so long what usually terrifies peoples even with the greatest speed? We have thus had winter without storms, spring without mildness, and summer without heat. From where can temperate weather now be expected, when the months that could have ripened the crops were intensely chilled by northern blasts? For what can produce fertility if the earth does not grow warm during the summer months? What can open the bud if it does not receive the nourishing rain as its mother?

We recognize two things as contrary to all the elements: perpetual cold and opposing dryness. The seasons have changed by failing to change [Niv. and Ga., “by being about to change”]; and what used to be produced by rains mixed with sunshine cannot be obtained from dryness alone.

Therefore let your prudence overcome the future scarcity through old grain, since the fortunate abundance of the preceding year was so great that supplies stored for the coming months will suffice. Let everything required for nourishment be stored away. A private person easily finds what is necessary when the public provision has been replenished.

But lest the present matter torment you with great hesitation, return to consideration of natural things, and make certain by reason what seems ambiguous to the astonished crowd. For it is established that this has been arranged by divine ordering: the stars in their present dwellings have come together in mutual administration in such a way that winter has become drier and colder than usual.

Hence the air, thickened by snow with excessive cold, was not rendered thin by the heat of the sun. Rather, remaining in the density it had assumed, it both resisted the sun’s heat and eluded human sight. For the intermediaries that exist between us and the stars dominate our vision, and through them we can see only as much as the thinness of their substance allows us.

That great emptiness which, like an element, extends between heaven and earth truly opens the way for your sight when it is clear and sprinkled with the brightness of the sun. But if it has been gathered together through some admixture, then, stretched out as though it were a kind of hide, it prevents the stars’ proper colors and heat from reaching us. This is also frequently produced for a time in other ages by a clouded atmosphere.

Hence the rays of the stars have for so long been darkened by an unusual color; hence the reaper was terrified by the new cold; hence, as time advanced, the fruits hardened; hence the ripeness of the grapes is bitter. But if this is entrusted to divine providence, we ought not to be anxious, since by its command we are forbidden to seek prodigies.

Nevertheless, we know without doubt that it is hostile to earthly fruits whenever we do not see the customary nourishment being cultivated according to its proper law. Therefore let your concern act so that we do not appear to be disturbed by the barrenness of a single year, since that first administrator of our dignity has provided in such a way that the preceding abundance might have been able to mitigate the following scarcity.

## LETTER XXVI. TO PAULUS, A VIGOROUS MAN, SENATOR, THE PRAETORIAN PREFECT

He willingly and freely comes to the aid of the Venetians suffering from scarcity because of the year’s barrenness, remitting taxes and granting provisions.

Public welfare is often preserved by economical compassion, when it gains more by remitting something through the intercession of good men. The venerable man Augustine, illustrious in life and name, came and reported to us the needs of the Venetians in a sorrowful petition: no wine, no wheat, and no millet had been produced among them. He asserted that the fortunes of the provincials had reached such extreme scarcity that they could survive the dangers to their lives only if royal compassion, in its customary humanity, came to their aid.

It seemed cruel to us to demand anything from those who were petitioning, or to expect that in which the province was known to be deficient. For from such people the one who imposes what cannot be found exacts only tears.

And therefore, moved by the petition of so great a man, we remit by the present authority the wine and wheat that we had ordered to be collected for the army’s provisions from the cities of Concordia, Aquileia, and Forum Julii. We provide only meat from those places, as the brief delivered to you contains. From this source, whenever necessary, we shall send a sufficient supply of wheat.

And since we have discovered that wine has grown abundantly in Istria, request from there as much as had been expected from the aforesaid cities, at the price found in the market for goods offered for sale, so that they too may not be harmed when fair prices are preserved for them.

Therefore do not suppose that any monetary charge is to be imposed for this present indulgence, so that, while it is a free remedy, it may nevertheless prove glorious. For you should know that you can be subjected to severe punishment if anything forbidden to be given should appear to have been accepted by you.

## LETTER XXVII. TO DATIUS, BISHOP OF MILAN, SENATOR, THE PRAETORIAN PREFECT

[Note: [Col. 0877D] This document was written after the consulship of Belisarius, at which time Belisarius was resisting Witigis, king of the Goths (some of whose rescripts appear above, in Book X), while holding Rome by force. For in that year there was such great famine throughout the whole region that Datius, bishop of Milan, clearly took care in his report to state that certain women in the parts of Liguria, from the household of his Church, had eaten their own children because of excessive hunger. This is found in the *Liber Pontificalis*, in the Life of Pope Silverius, which appears in Volume II of the Councils, and likewise in Paul the Deacon, Book XVII. FORNER.]

He sends a great quantity of millet to be distributed among the people suffering from scarcity.

It is of little benefit to command what is good unless we wish to accomplish it through the most holy men. For the upright will of the just increases the benefit, and whatever is done without fraud is truly attributed to the merits of the giver. It is fitting that priestly purity should carry out princely generosity. For one whose concern is to do good from his own resources can laudably fulfill the wishes of another.

And therefore we ask your holiness—whose purpose it is to serve divine commands—to arrange, under our direction, that from the granaries at Ticinum and Dertona, as the prince has ordered, one-third of the millet be sold to the hungry people at the rate of twenty-five modii for one solidus, so that, through no one's mercenary dealing, it may reach those who appear able to manage from their own resources.

Let the one who has less receive the prince’s indulgence. The command was judged to assist the needy, not the rich [Niv. and Ga., “it was judged”]. The one who sends into a full vessel pours out rather than stores away; for what is gathered into empty vessels is more truly stored.

Therefore let your holiness not regard the duties of compassion as an injury, since everything is worthy of you wherever piety is found. For faithfully carrying out the desires of another is to perfect one’s own good deeds.

For this purpose, with God’s help, we have arranged to send this man and that man, who, obeying the orders of your holiness, are to do nothing on their own but strive only to obey you. Report to us how many solidi can be gathered from the aforesaid quantity of millet, so that, stored with the treasurer [Ac., “in the secret place”], it may be reserved for restoring the aforementioned supply in times to come, with God’s help—like a renewed garment whose joined structure is unraveled through its threads, so that it may instead be woven into a new form with splendid beauty.

## XXVIII. EDICT
