It announces to the people of Liguria the victory won over the Burgundians and the flight of the Alemanni. It then says that, because of their scarcity, the king remitted half of their tax and opened his granaries to relieve them.

[Col. 0878B] Who does not know that divine providence wishes to withdraw certain things from our ordinary use, in order to test the human spirit? For if it happened that no one were in need at all, generosity would consequently have no place. Scarcity has been given to the provinces for the praise of our king; the fields have become barren, so that the lord’s abundance may be recognized. A gift would be less welcome if hardship had not preceded it. Rejoice, provinces, and rather give thanks for your misfortunes, since they prove such a disposition in your prince that he yields to no adversity. Behold the wondrous piety that everywhere withstands our troubles.

For when the savagery of former times had stirred itself up, and your Aemilia and Liguria—as you must remember—were being shaken by the incursion of the Burgundians and were waging a furtive war because of their proximity, suddenly the fame of the present government shone forth [Col. 0878C] like the rising sun. The enemy groaned that he had been conquered by his own presumption when he learned that the ruler of the named people was the very man whom he had recognized, under the name of a soldier, as pre-eminent. How often did the Burgundian wish not to leave his own borders, lest he fight against our prince? Though he escaped his presence and was thereby relieved, he nevertheless encountered his fortune in his own downfall.

For as soon as the Goths devoted themselves to the conduct of war with a twofold strength, the force of the rebels was cut down in so favorable an engagement that it seemed as though the armed had been made to stand on one side and the naked on the other: an equitable judgment of God, so that the plunderer should fall on the very fields he had presumed to ravage. Exult, province adorned with the corpses of your adversaries; laugh at the heap of funerals which is plainly known to have been produced by the enemy’s wrongdoing. Now Liguria is better cultivated: although the fruit of the grain harvest was denied you, an enemy harvest has sprung up. For even if your tribute could be collected only in diminished measure, you have happily offered triumphs born within you.

To this is added the recent incursion of the Alemanni, routed at the outset. It was so thoroughly crushed in its first attempts that its arrival and departure were joined together, as though it had been cleansed by the salutary cut of a sword: both so that the excess of those who had presumed wickedly might be punished and so that the destruction of the subjected people might not [Col. 0879A] spread without limit. I could indeed enumerate for you how great a multitude of enemies has fallen in other places; but, following the custom of the human mind, since we hasten toward your successes, you wish us to say only what you recognize as pertaining especially to you.

Let us therefore return to the pleasing beginning, since he who defended you from the disaster of war does not allow you to suffer the dangers of want. For he who struck down the enemy of the province also ordered famine to depart. O contest worthy of proclamation throughout the whole world! Against cruel need, the humanity of the glorious prince wages war. His true camps are storehouses filled with grain; if he had wished to close them, then an unbearable enemy would have entered. But because he opened them still further, he immediately drove away the raging adversary.

I do not know which wars of our prince the world should admire more; nevertheless, I shall say what I think. It is customary for brave men to have fought battles successfully, but it is plainly a virtue beyond human capacity to have conquered scarcity. Yet although the prayers of suppliants could never have been sufficient for such great and such remarkable benefits, he has also endured the remission of half the fiscal levy, lest he make sad in any respect those to whom he had granted so many blessings.

We read that Joseph, in opposition to the deadly famine, gave the joy of purchasing grain; but he set such a price that the man eager for his own relief sold himself in order to buy food. What, I ask, was life like then for those wretched people, to whom harsh relief seemed to deprive them of their freedom? There the freedman groaned no less than the captive could weep. I believe that the holy man was constrained by this necessity so that he might both satisfy a greedy prince and aid a people in danger.

With the peace of so great a father, let me say how much better it is to sell grain while preserving freedom, and to relax tribute on account of want. This sale is free of charge, since both what you were buying has been remitted and he has imposed a price that delights you. Thus public generosity sells twenty-five modii, whereas the landowner cannot find [a buyer] at ten; [Col. 0880A] humanity has changed the order of worldly affairs. We are ordered to sell cheaply, while the hungry person is ready to buy more dearly.

O novel outcome worthy of proclamation! A transaction has arisen from the desire to suffer loss; the seller’s wish is to lose more, so that the one seeking profit may be able to find it. Such commerce surely becomes a king; such a market is fitting for piety to conduct: he is then least willing to receive when the buyer is driven to offer the most.

It is pleasant to report what affection the ruler has shown toward you, since at first he yielded as much as he thought sufficient, and now he has doubled the requests once more. It was embarrassing for you to hope for anything after the gifts, although the prince’s humanity still had benefits in reserve. He did not reject requests not yet heard, when he himself bore witness to what had been seen. Happy the calamity that first found a merciful witness, so that it would not have to face a strict judge afterward.

Rejoice, therefore, Ligurian, now accustomed to good fortune: a second [manuscript and Ac., “ages”] age has come into your experience. With great prosperity you have overcome the Egyptians bestowed upon you; you escape the times of necessity and do not lose the rewards of freedom. Rather, you were restored secure from the enemy at the very time when you were also recognized as freed from the danger of famine.

The example mentioned above still adorns you; there is still a respect in which you surpass it. For we read that Joseph secretly returned the money to his brothers only in their sacks. Is it surprising that, compelled by nature, he appeared more humane toward his kinsmen? But this man sold abundantly to everyone and remitted the levy owed; and in general he gave more to those subject to tribute than Joseph appears to have given to his brothers alone. Let what was poured out be stated briefly: from this let the whole world learn its own blessings, [Col. 0880C] since our age is compared not with kings but with prophets.

But so that we do not detain those eager for royal benefits any longer, know that our orders have reached those concerned, so that the princely munificence may come to you according to the tenor of the command.

[Col. 0879]

# M. AURELIUS CASSIODORUS’S ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY, CALLED THE TRIPARTITE HISTORY, EXCERPTED FROM THREE GREEK AUTHORS—SOZOMEN, SOCRATES, AND THEODORET—TRANSLATED BY EPIPHANIUS SCHOLASTICUS AND REDUCED BY CASSIODORUS HIMSELF TO A COMPENDIUM (C, S)

## PREFACE

[Col. 0879D] 203 A preface is placed most usefully at the beginning of a book, where the character of the work to come is indicated. For what is more advantageous than first to learn something through it, lest an unexpected discourse cause confusion? This Ecclesiastical History, which is shown to be exceedingly necessary for all Christians, was admirably composed by three Greek authors: namely, Theodoret, a venerable bishop, and two most eloquent men, Sozomen and Socrates. Since we are rendering them into Latin speech through Epiphanius Scholasticus, we judged it necessary, with the Lord’s help, to bring their selected statements into the course of a single style and to make one discourse from three authors.

It must be clearly understood that the writers mentioned above arranged the events from the time of the emperor Constantine, of blessed memory, up to Theodosius the Younger, of august remembrance. But when we had reread their works and carefully considered each one, we recognized that they had not all explained every matter equally clearly and precisely; rather, sometimes one, sometimes another had treated a different part better. Therefore we decided to gather selected material from each teacher [manuscripts Lyr. and Santheod., “writers”; edition, “dictators”] and arrange it in order under the name of its author. Let whoever, by the Lord’s gift, reaches these little works read without fear; he will gain much usefulness and knowledge if he carefully stores in his memory what has been set forth throughout these twelve books.

Moreover, lest an undifferentiated subject trouble anyone, let the reader observe that titles have been placed throughout the entire text of this work, so that at the appropriate places he may seek what he recognizes as having been stated under the corresponding number.

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0881]

### CHAPTER ONE. Sozomen’s Address to the Emperor Theodosius (p. 393)

[Col. 0881B]

They say that among ancient rulers it was the care and concern of their admirers to prepare ornaments, purple robes, crowns, and things of that kind for them; while those devoted to books, occupied with various stories, composed writings that would soothe the hearts of their hearers. Those who pursued warfare, moreover, sought to direct an arrow at the proper moment, fell a beast, cast a spear well, or mount a horse gracefully. Each person presented to the kings gifts corresponding to the things most pleasing to the ruler. One therefore offered precious stones that were difficult to find; another, purple dye; many, distinguished poems or various writings; another, fine belts or an excellent display [edition, “proclamation”] of the use of weapons. The greatest and most imperial part of this popular virtue was thought to be that toward which the admirer’s attention at the time inclined.

But concerning piety, which is the true ornament of empire, no one seems to have spoken with comparable diligence. But you, most powerful Theodosius—to state the matter comprehensively—have, with God’s help, surpassed every virtue. For the purple and crown with which you appear to be surrounded for the sake of those who look upon you, since they are signs of majesty, constantly nourish piety and clemency within you. Hence writers, prefects, and the rest of your subjects devote themselves to your actions and those of your household.

But when appointed judge and arbiter of books, you are not captivated by ornate speech, nor do you permit truth to be stolen by any figure of speech; [Col. 0881D] rather, you measure both perfectly, adapting the proper expression to the subject. You examine deeply the figure of the discourse, its parts, order, appropriateness, diction, composition, collections, meaning, and history. You reward those who recite both according to your judgment and with timely favors, as well as with golden portraits, the placing of statues, gifts, and every kind of honor.

Such, indeed, as you show yourself toward those who recite, were the judges of old [edition Niv., “the Cretan judges”] toward sweet-speaking Homer; the Alevadae [others, “Alevas”] toward Simonides; Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, toward Plato, the disciple of Socrates; Philip of Macedon toward the historian Theopompus; and Caesar Severus toward Oppian, who described in verse the kinds and natures of fish and the methods of catching them.

[Col. 0882A] The Cretans, rewarding Homer’s poem with a thousand coins and boasting as though of the greatest generosity, inscribed their gifts on a public statue. The Alevadae, Dionysius, and Philip were in no way more sparing in spirit than the Cretans, who boasted of their proud commonwealth and philosophy; they could quickly have imitated the statue of those men, had they not been inferior in the work of giving. Severus, however, by giving Oppian a gold coin for each verse of his metrical poem, displayed such a marvel of generosity that Oppian’s golden verses are still so called by many.

Such were the gifts once made by lovers of letters and learning. But you, most powerful of princes, are found inferior to none of your predecessors in the generosity you have shown toward writings. Yet I think that you do such things quite appropriately. For since you have surpassed everyone in virtues, you diligently elevate what is yours toward ever greater increase, because you have learned with complete integrity the truth of the deeds once performed among Romans and Greeks.

They say that during the day you exercise yourself in arms and in bodily activity, conduct the affairs of your subjects, judge and administer at once, and consider what must be done, sometimes privately and sometimes in common; but at night you devote yourself to the divine books. It is reported that a lampstand made by mechanical art supplies you for the pursuit of their knowledge and pours oil of its own accord into the lamp, so that no one stationed near the imperial quarters is forced to suffer through your labors, while you do violence to nature by resisting sleep.

Thus you are gentle and mild toward those near you, and especially toward all people, imitating your heavenly King and patron, to whom it is pleasing to rain upon the just [Col. 0882D] and unjust and to make the sun rise (Matt. 5:45), and to bestow other gifts as well when envy has departed. Through extensive learning, I also hear that you know the natures and powers of stones, the effects of roots, and the results of remedies no less than Solomon, the son of David; indeed, you are superior to him in virtues. For he, having become a slave to lust, did not preserve piety to the end, although it had been the cause of his blessings and wisdom. But you, most powerful prince, by applying reason to negligence, appear to rule not only human beings justly but also the passions of body and soul.

If this too ought to be said, I hear that you overcome even every desire for food or drink. You do not crave sweet fruits or anything else attractive, except insofar as it is suitable to the touch and agrees with the taste—and even then only after first blessing the Creator of all things. Accustomed to enduring thirst, heat, and cold, you seem through daily exercises already to possess the very nature of self-restraint.

Some time ago, while hastening to see in Pontus the city of Heraclea, named after Hercules, and to relieve it after its long distress, you traveled through Bithynia in the heat of summer. When the sun was burning fiercely around midday, one of the travelers, seeing you covered at once with much sweat and dust, approached as though he were about to render service. He offered you a very clear cup, gleaming as if with rays, and poured into it a particularly pleasant drink, diluting it with cold water.

But you, most powerful prince, took it, praised the man for his generosity, and shortly afterward increased his reward with princely largesse. Yet when all the soldiers were gazing too eagerly at the brightness of that cup and calling blessed the man who would drink from it, you returned the cup to him, ordering him to use it as he wished.

In this respect, therefore, you seem rightly to have surpassed even Alexander, of whom those who admire his deeds relate that, while he was hastening with the Macedonians through waterless regions, a devoted soldier found some water, drew it, and offered it to him. He did not drink it, but poured it out.

To put the matter plainly, we ought to call you, according to Homer, the foremost of all the former princes—if it is permissible to say so. For we find that some former kings possessed nothing worthy of mention, while others adorned the empire with one or two qualities. But you, most serene prince, embracing all virtues at once, are recognized to have surpassed everyone in piety, clemency, courage, [Col. 0883C] chastity, justice, generosity, and magnanimity suited to imperial dignity.

Everyone boasts that your empire is without bloodshed and free from slaughter, surpassing that of all the ancients. You order your subjects to be instructed with delight in scholarly pursuits, and you direct everyone to show favor and reverence toward love for you and toward the common good.

Therefore, since I am composing an Ecclesiastical History, it seems necessary to me to address you first on account of all these things. To whom would I more appropriately dedicate this work, when I am about to relate the virtues of many venerable men and the events that occurred around the catholic Church, including the storms through which she passed before reaching the harbors of you and your parents?

Come now, you who know all things and possess every virtue, especially piety, which the divine word teaches to be the chief of wisdom. Receive this writing from me and examine it willingly; applying additions and omissions according to your integrity, cleanse it through your own labors. Whatever pleases you will assuredly appear useful and clear to readers, and no one will criticize what you have approved.

My composition proceeds from the third consulship of the Caesars Crispus and Constantine to your seventeenth [Note: That is, from the year of Christ 323 to 439]; and it seemed good to me to divide the whole work into nine books. The first and second volumes will contain what happened to the Church under the emperor Constantine. The third and fourth will contain what occurred under his sons. The fifth and sixth will recount what is known to have taken place under Julian, the cousin of the sons of the great Constantine, and under Jovian, as well as Valentinian and Valens. The seventh and eighth volumes will disclose what happened under the brothers Gratian and Valentinian up to the time of the empire of your most blessed grandfather Theodosius: namely, when your most merciful father, the most sacred Arcadius, succeeding to his paternal empire, received the task of governing the Roman world together with your most pious uncle Honorius. I have dedicated the ninth book to your Christian and venerable majesty. May the eternal God preserve you, prevailing over your enemies with unconquerable magnanimity, holding all beneath your feet, and directing your pious empire to your sons’ sons, with Christ’s assent—Christ with whom, together with God the Father and the Holy [Col. 0884B] Spirit, there is one glory forever and ever. Amen.

### CHAPTER II. Why the Gentiles Accepted the Faith of Christ More Readily than the Hebrews

A thought has sometimes occurred to me: why, do you suppose, was faith in the word of the Lord quicker among some other peoples, while it was incredible to the Hebrews, although from the beginning they received the divine commandments concerning the presence of Christ and learned through the prophets how these things would be before they came to pass?

Abraham, the founder of their race and of circumcision, was deemed worthy to behold and entertain the Son of God (Gen. 18). Isaac, his son, was honored through the imitation of a sacrifice, bound by his father and offered upon the altar as a type of the cross (Gen. 22), just as, they say, happened in Christ’s passion, according to those who have collected the sacred Scriptures with complete accuracy.

Jacob, moreover, foretold the expectation of the nations, which now exists in him, as well as the time when he would come (Gen. 49:10), when he said that at that time the rulers of the Hebrews would cease from the tribe of Judah, the ruling tribe. He was indicating the rule of Herod, who, although of Idumean ancestry on his father’s side and Arab on his mother’s, received the Jewish people from the Roman senate and Caesar Augustus.

Some other prophets, too, clearly prophesied Christ’s birth, that sacred and ineffable conception, the mother remaining a virgin after giving birth, his lineage and homeland. Others foretold his passion, resurrection from the dead, ascension into heaven, and the outcome of each individual event. Anyone devoted to the sacred writings can know that the Hebrews did not fail to understand these matters.

Josephus, son of Mattathias and a priest, a man most noble among the Jews and also highly esteemed among the Romans, will be a witness to the truth concerning Christ (Josephus, *Antiquities*, book 18, chapter 6). He does not dare to call him a man, as one who performed remarkable deeds and taught truthful sayings. He openly calls him Christ, says that he was condemned to the punishment of the cross and appeared alive on the third day, and does not fail to recognize that countless other miracles concerning him had been foretold by the holy prophets. He also testifies that at that time there were many whom he chose, both Greeks and Jews, who continued in his love, and that the people named after him did not cease to exist.

It seems to me that, in reporting these things, Josephus appears almost to proclaim that Christ is God through his deeds, standing amazed at the miracles of the events. Yet after saying this, he himself passes by in the middle of the account, without contradicting those who believed in him, and rather agreeing with them.

As I reflected on these matters, it seemed rightly astonishing to me that the Hebrews had not been able to convert to Christianity before other peoples. For although the Sibyl and other oracles among the Gentiles foretold what was to come in Christ, not all Greeks should therefore be blamed for unbelief. Only a few, who appeared more learned, especially understood such prophecies, which were often metrical and expressed to the people in more eloquent language.

It was therefore, as it seems to me, part of heavenly providence that, for the harmony of future events, what was to come should be entrusted not only to its own prophets but also in part to the Gentiles—just as a composer of melodies, for the usefulness of a foreign sound, might run over other strings with the plectrum or add others above those already present.

The Hebrews, although they possessed more numerous and clearer prophecies, were found inferior to the Greeks in the presence of Christ. Nor will it seem contrary to reason that the Church believed so greatly from the other nations. First, because it is pleasing to God that changes in divine and most important matters should arise from miracles; and second, because the religion is shown from the beginning not to have been rendered hopeless by the chance virtues of its leaders [reading uncertain]. For although they did not possess a tongue eloquent in expression or beauty of speech, nor employ philosophical arguments or demonstrations, they were nevertheless no less zealous in persuading. They were stripped of their possessions, despised and abandoned their property, and, as though in other bodies, endured many of the worst tortures. They submitted neither to the populace of cities, nor were enticed by the flatteries of judges, nor, perhaps, deterred by threats. Thus they made clear to all that they endured such contests for the sake of the greatest rewards.

Therefore there was no need for verbal persuasion, since the very events themselves compelled belief throughout houses and cities—events that at first had not seemed to have been heard.

*SOZOMEN, book I, chapter 1, p. 398.*

### CHAPTER III. What Sozomen’s Purpose Was in Writing His History, and From What Sources He Collected the Deeds of Earlier Times

[Col. 0885D]

After such a great and wondrous change had taken place throughout the world, so that both the former religion and the laws of the ancestors were despised, it was exceedingly cruel that the Calydonian boar, the Marathonian bull, and other things of this kind occurring or reported in stories throughout the provinces and cities should be celebrated with such enthusiasm that many of the Greeks and most distinguished writers, possessing a talent for composition, had devoted themselves to such matters—while I should fail to employ the power of my own nature to narrate the deeds of Ecclesiastical History.

For I think that, since the subject of this work was not devised by human beings, its author too will unexpectedly appear not to be without God’s aid. At first, indeed, I attempted to carry this work from the origin of the world [edition, “arrange”]. But when I considered that others had treated such matters up to their own time—namely, the very learned Clement and Hegesippus, following the succession of the apostles, and the writer Africanus, and Eusebius, surnamed Pamphilus, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and in the poets and orators of the Greeks—I then gathered into two books whatever had happened in the Churches after Christ’s ascension into heaven up to the overthrow of Licinius. Now, with God’s favor, I shall attempt to disclose what happened afterward.

Accordingly, I shall recall the events in which I took part and those which I heard from people who knew or witnessed them, both events that occurred in my own generation and those before it. I shall explain the knowledge of the remaining matters from laws issued for the sake of religion, from councils convened over time, from innovations that occurred, and from imperial and priestly letters. Some of these are preserved to this day in palaces and churches, while others are found scattered among diligent investigators.

For some of these matters I judged it better to embrace the account rather than the whole text in this work, because of the length of the reading, so that their meaning might be indicated briefly—unless perhaps certain matters could be called into doubt, concerning which many people hold differing opinions. Then, if I am able to find any document in support of the truth, I do not omit to include it.

But lest anyone accuse the composition of falsehood through ignorance of the facts, on reading perhaps contradictory letters, [Col. 0886C] it must be understood that, on the occasion of the Arian doctrine and of those who arose afterward, the bishops of the Churches, being at odds with one another, wrote individually to their own followers about the causes they were pursuing. When gathered in councils, they decreed what they wished; and, holding contrary opinions, they often condemned one another in their absence. Over time, their rulers and leading men bent them by whatever power they could, and made them agree with one another, so that by their consent they might be thought to cultivate what was right.

Some favoring one side and others another compiled collections of letters sent in support of their own heresy, and left them contradictory to one another. It was extremely difficult for us to discover everything that arose concerning such matters. But since the chief concern must be truth, I considered it necessary, for the purity of the history, to examine such letters also insofar as possible.

Therefore, if I explain the ecclesiastical uprisings that took place among them concerning episcopal office or the honor of primacy, as well as their particular heresy, this should not seem burdensome or ill-willed. First, as has been said, a writer ought to subordinate everything to truth; second, he ought to declare the doctrine of the catholic Church with complete accuracy. This doctrine is often found attacked by the plots of its adversaries, yet, as though strengthened by God, it has remained in its own power and drawn all Churches and peoples to its truth.

Although I wished, if it were permitted [edition, “fitting”], to write only what appeared to have come to my knowledge concerning the Church established in the Roman Empire, nevertheless I decided, insofar as I could, to record also what had happened concerning religion among the Persians and the barbarians.

Nor will it be absurd for an Ecclesiastical History, in this work as well, to include those who were once fathers and teachers of monks, or those who afterward, through succession, were seen to be useful, as we have heard and verified. We shall not appear ungrateful by consigning their virtue to silence; nor will those who left behind such examples of philosophy be excluded from this history, since their successors, making use of them, will attain a most blessed and happy end.

But as the discourse proceeds, it will observe these matters as it is able. I shall now turn to the narration of events, invoking God as my helper. From this point the present writing will take its beginning.

*SOZOMEN, book I, chapter 1, p. 400.*

### CHAPTER IV. From What Time He Began the History, How the Sign of the Cross Was Shown to Constantine, and Which Emperors and Caesars Existed at That Time

When Crispus and Constantine were Caesars and consuls (A.D. 322), Sylvester was presiding over the Roman Church. Alexander presided over the Alexandrian Church, and Macarius over Jerusalem. At Antioch on the Orontes, however, no one had yet been ordained after Romanus, because the persecutions prevented it. Not long afterward, those who had gathered at Nicaea, admiring Eustathius for his wisdom and eloquence, judged him worthy to preside over the apostolic see. Although he was bishop of neighboring Beroea, they transferred him to Antioch.

At that time, therefore, the Eastern Christians living around Libya as far as the borders of Egypt did not dare to assemble openly in churches, since Licinius had changed the favor he had once shown them. Nor, throughout the West, did the Greeks, Macedonians, or Illyrians continue freely in their religion because of Constantine, who was the Roman ruler in those regions (A.D. 315).

We have learned that many other things subsequently happened to this man, through which he was moved to venerate Christian doctrine; but above all this occurred because of the sign divinely shown to him.

*SOZOMEN, book I, chapter 2, p. 403.*

Since we have reached this point, let us report something at greater length. When Diocletian and Maximian Herculius had chosen a private life, and Maximinus Galerius, who had ruled with them, held Italy and had appointed two Caesars—Maximinus in the East and Severus in Italy (A.D. 306)—Constantine was proclaimed emperor in Britain after his father’s death, in the first year of the 271st Olympiad, on the twenty-seventh day of July.

At Rome, Maxentius, son of Maximian Herculius, was made emperor by the praetorian soldiers. Hence his father, desiring to rule, wished to deprive his son of the kingdom, but could not do so. After this he died at Tarsus in Cilicia. Severus, coming from Rome against Maxentius, was killed through the treachery of the soldiers. Maximinus Galerius, after appointing Licinius Augustus, died.

Maxentius was consequently regarded at Rome as a tyrant, shamelessly practicing adultery and killing the husbands of the women involved. Wishing to crush him and free the Romans from their disasters, Constantine considered which god he should have as his helper in war. He knew that the gods worshiped by Diocletian were of no benefit, and that his own father, having rejected the religion of the pagans, had lived successfully.

*SOCRATES, book I, chapter 2, p. 5.*

While he was occupied with these anxieties, he saw in sleep the sign of the cross splendidly placed in the sky. As he marveled at the vision (A.D. 315), angels stood beside him and said: “O Constantine, conquer by this.” It is also reported that Christ himself appeared to him, showed him the sign of the cross, and ordered him to make a similar figure and to have this as his aid in battles, by which he might win the rights of victory.

Eusebius Pamphilus reports that he heard the emperor himself affirm under oath that, around midday, when the sun was already declining, he had seen a sign of the cross made from light, with an inscription joined to it saying, “BY THIS CONQUER”—and that the soldiers who were then with him had seen it as well. As he was traveling with his army along some road, he said, this miracle was shown to him. While he was considering what it might mean, night came on, and Christ appeared to him in sleep with the sign he had seen in the sky. He ordered him to make an image of that sign, which would be a source of aid in the encounters of battle.

*SOZOMEN, book I, chapter 3, p. 403.*

### CHAPTER V. How Constantine Came to Know Christian Doctrine, and Concerning the Miracles of the Cross and the Death of Maxentius

Since an interpreter was no longer needed, but it had been openly shown to the emperor what he ought to believe concerning God, as soon as day came he summoned the priests of Christ and consulted them about the doctrine. They, presenting the sacred books, spoke about Christ and supported their statements from the prophets.

They said that the sign which had appeared to him was the trophy of victory over hell—a victory Christ achieved when he ascended into heaven after being crucified and dying and rising on the third day. They said that this was to be expected because, after the end of this life, at the conclusion of the present age, all human beings would rise again and become immortal: some to the rewards of the deeds by which they had lived well, others to punishment because they had done evil.

They taught, however, that even in the sins committed here there is an opportunity for salvation and purification from sin: for the uninitiated, the reception of baptism according to ecclesiastical law; [Col. 0888D] for the initiated, observance so that they may not sin. But since only a few holy men are wholly capable of this, they also taught a second purification established through repentance. For God is merciful and grants forgiveness to sinners if, by repenting, they strive to strengthen their repentance through their deeds.

As the priests explained these things, the emperor, amazed at the prophecies concerning Christ that had been made in this manner, ordered skilled men to transform the sign into a standard of the cross made of gold and precious stones. This standard was called the Labarum. Among other military standards it was more precious because it was customary for it to precede the emperor and to be worshiped by the soldiers.

Therefore, I think that Constantine changed the most illustrious glory of the Roman Empire into the sign of the cross so that his subjects, through frequent sight of it and care for it, might grow unaccustomed to their former practice and might consider as God alone the one whom the emperor worshiped or under whose leadership and with whose aid he acted against his enemies.

This sign was always displayed before all the ranks, and he ordered it especially to be present for the hard-pressed battle lines during combat. He therefore appointed certain standard-bearers to attend to it. Their duty was to carry it on their shoulders in shifts and to pass through all the battle lines with it.

It is reported that once a certain man, while carrying this sign, was suddenly frightened when the enemy attacked and gave it to another to carry. When he withdrew from the battle and avoided the javelins, he was suddenly struck and died. The man who had received the sacred trophy, however, remained unharmed despite the many javelins cast at him.

For, through the wondrous direction of divine power, the enemy’s arrows stuck in the sign, while they immediately flew away from the standard-bearer amid the dangers. It is also said that no other attendant of this sign ever died in war from a wound, as usually happens, or suffered the disaster of captivity.

*SOZOMEN, book I, chapter 3, p. 404.*

Accordingly, he engaged Maxentius near the Milvian Bridge and conquered him, Maxentius being drowned in the river. For it was the seventh year of Constantine’s reign. During this period Diocletian died at Salona (A.D. 315).

*SOCRATES, book I, chapter 2, p. 7.*

### CHAPTER VI. On the Abolition of Pagan Practices
I am not unaware that the Greeks report that Constantine, because he had killed certain close relatives by blood [Col. 0889C] (A.D. 316), and had taken part in the murder of his son Crispus, was moved to repentance and consulted the philosopher Sopatrus about purification. At that time Sopatrus presided over the school of Plotinus. He is said to have replied that there was no purification for such crimes. Constantine, however, disturbed by this prohibition, found bishops who promised that through repentance or baptism he could be cleansed from every offense. He then rejoiced in those who had said what he wanted, admired their doctrine, became a Christian, and brought his subjects over to his own likeness.

It seems to me, however, that these stories were fabricated by those who seek to disparage the Christian religion. For Crispus—the reason they say Constantine needed purification—died in the twentieth year of his father’s reign (A.D. 329). While he was still alive, he enacted many laws with his father on behalf of the Christians; for he was honored in the second rank of the empire and was Caesar, as even the names and dates of the rulers appended to the laws now testify. Nor is it credible that Sopatrus could have come to a conversation with Constantine, who ruled only in the part of the world around the Ocean and the Rhine, while he was living in Italy because of the campaign planned against Maxentius. At that time the Roman state was in turmoil, and it was not easy for Britons and Gauls to meet with those among whom Constantine is known to have shared the Christian religion, except when he was encamped against Maxentius and proceeded to Rome.

The dates of these events, as well as the laws that he enacted in favor of the religion, are again witnesses. But even if we grant that the emperor could easily have spoken with Sopatrus, or consulted him by letter about whatever he wished, it is nevertheless not plausible that the philosopher was unaware that Hercules, after the murder of his son, was purified at Athens in the rites of Ceres, and that after the killing of Iphitus he unjustly slew a stranger and friend. Since, therefore, the Greeks announce purification for such crimes, what has been said is sufficient, and they should accuse of falsehood those who invented the claim that Sopatrus gave Constantine the opposite answer. For I do not believe that the most distinguished Greek of that time in literary learning was ignorant of these matters. SOZOMEN, Book I, chapter 5, p. 406.

## CHAPTER VII. On Constantius, Constantine’s father

Thus, under Constantine’s rule, the churches conducted themselves cheerfully [Col. 0890B] and increased from day to day, while the favorable and harmonious ruler raised them up with many benefactions [ed., “raised them up with his many benefactions”]. Previously also, the Lord had preserved them unharmed from dangers and disturbances. For while the churches in other parts of the world were suffering various persecutions, Constantius alone, Constantine’s father, freely permitted Christians in his territory to remain in their religion.

Finally, I have learned that he performed a certain memorable miracle of this kind. Wishing to test whether some Christians in his palace were good and steadfast men, he summoned them all and ordered them, saying that if they came to sacrifice and worship his gods, they should remain around him and retain their position in his retinue; but if they refused, they should leave the palace, giving thanks that they were not punished.

When both groups had revealed themselves—some as deserters from their religion, others as preferring the divine things to those present—he decided to use as friends and advisers those who had steadfastly remained faithful in better things. The others he rejected as effeminate and expelled from his presence, believing that those who had been so ready to betray their God would never be devoted to the emperor.

Therefore, while Constantius was still alive, it did not seem unlawful for anyone to be a Christian among those who lived beyond Italy, Gaul, and Britain, and among those who inhabited the region around the Pyrenees as far as the Western Ocean. When Constantine succeeded to his empire, however, the affairs of the churches flourished still more.

After Maxentius, the son of Herculius, had been killed, and his territory had fallen to Constantine, those who lived around the river Tiber and the Eridanus—which the provincials call the Po—and those who lived around the Aquila, were now at liberty to flourish in their religion. Tradition says that the Argo was brought by ship to this place and carried to the Tyrrhenian Sea. For the Argonauts, avoiding a powerful wind, did not use the same ship on their return; instead, [p. 209] crossing the sea above Scythia, they came by these rivers to the borders of Italy. There they spent the winter and founded the city called Aemonia.

When summer came, with the help of the inhabitants, they dragged the Argo by mechanical means for nearly four hundred stades overland to the river Aquila, which mingles with the Eridanus. The Eridanus has its mouths in the Italian Sea. After the battle, the Cibalaeans, Dardanians, Macedonians, those who then lived around the Ister, as well as the Greeks and the entire Illyrian people, were brought under Constantine. SOZOMEN, Book I, chapter 6, p. 407.

## CHAPTER VIII. How Licinius was driven away, persecuted the Christians, and was finally defeated

Licinius, driven away from this region, had previously been a follower of Christian doctrine. But after changing his mind, he afflicted many priests within the authority of his own faction, and many others as well, especially those belonging to the military class. He was exceedingly hostile to the Christians because of Constantine’s war, thinking that Constantine could be distressed by the misfortune of his religion. At the same time, he believed that the Christians were praying and striving to bring the whole empire under Constantine’s sole rule.

Moreover, when he was preparing to fight Constantine again, he placed his hope of victory in divinations and sacrifices. Misled by certain people who promised that he would defeat Constantine in war, he turned to paganism (A.D. 325). The Greeks even say that he then consulted the divination of the Milesian and Didymaean Apollo; when he asked the god about the war, the demon replied with these verses of Homer:

> Old man, the young warriors watch you closely,  
> and your life is released; cruel old age will overtake you.

From many circumstances, therefore, it seemed to me that the Christian doctrine had been established by divine providence and had advanced to such great growth, especially through the future persecution by the pagans. For while Licinius was persecuting the churches established in his empire, a war took place in Bithynia, where he and Constantine finally fought against one another.

Constantine was assisted by such great divine favor that he defeated his enemies on land and sea. After Licinius had lost both his land and naval forces, he withdrew to Nicomedia, and, reduced to private status, remained for some time at Thessalonica, where he was killed (A.D. 329). Thus this man, who at the beginning of his reign had advanced greatly through wars and other achievements and had been honored by marriage to Constantine’s sister, met such an end. SOZOMEN, Book I, chapter 7, p. 408.

## CHAPTER IX. On the laws Constantine enacted for the Christians; on the alteration of pagan rites; on the advancement of the Christians; on his victories; and on his veneration for religion

[Col. 0891D]

When, therefore, the entire Roman Empire had come under Constantine alone, he issued public edicts so that his Eastern subjects might fearlessly worship the religion of Christ and diligently serve the Divinity. They were to believe that this was the only Divinity who truly existed and who possessed sufficient power at all times. Those who devoted themselves to such things, he said, would receive every good in abundance, and whatever they regarded as adverse would be accompanied by better hope; but those who offended against God would find everything difficult, both individually and collectively, in war and in peace.

Giving thanks and not claiming the credit for himself, he added to this law, saying that God had deemed him a suitable minister of his own purpose and had brought him from the British Sea to the regions of the East, so that the Christian religion might be increased; and that those who had steadfastly endured in confessing the faith and martyrdom should appear more illustrious through his honors.

After delivering this speech and saying many other things by which he believed he could lead his subjects to the worship of religion, he decreed that the measures conceived or carried out against religion under the persecutors of the churches were invalid. He ordered that all those who, because of their confession of Christ, had been compelled against their will to move to islands or elsewhere, to suffer in the mines, to perform public works, to serve women or wool-workers, or to be assigned to municipal councils when they had not previously been municipal officials, should receive remission.

Those whom the persecutors had branded with infamy he released from that infamy. Those deprived of military service he left free to choose whether to remain in the rank in which they had served or instead to enjoy an honorable retirement. Having restored everyone to his former liberty and customary honors, he also restored their property.

If any who had been condemned to death had also been stripped of their property, he ordered that their relatives by blood should receive the inheritance. If no such relatives existed, each provincial church was to assume the right of inheritance. Whether anything from such property had been taken by a private person or by the public authorities, it was to be restored. For those who had purchased anything from the public treasury or received gifts, he promised to make provision in a possible and proper manner.

These measures, as has been said, pleased the emperor, were confirmed by law, and were brought to completion with an excellent result. At that time Christians administered all the offices of the Roman state. Henceforth everyone was forbidden to sacrifice, and there was no place for offerings or divinations; nor was it any longer permitted to dedicate idols or celebrate pagan festivals.

Many practices in the cities of the pagans were also altered from their ancient custom. From that time, among the Egyptians, a cubit was no longer offered in the pagan temples according to the former ceremonies, but rather in the churches, signifying the rise of the waters of the Nile. Among the Romans, the spectacles of gladiatorial combat were then first abolished. Among the Phoenicians who lived in Lebanon or Heliopolis, it was no longer lawful for virgins to practice fornication before being joined to legitimate husbands—namely, after undergoing the disgraceful experience of the first unlawful union.

The holy buildings that appeared to have sufficient size were repaired. Others were enlarged in height and breadth. Elsewhere, where there had been no such buildings, they were built from their foundations and shone forth. The emperor [p. 210] spent money from the royal treasuries with great liberality, writing to the bishops and civic governors in each city that the bishops should give whatever orders they wished, and that the governors should obey their commands, so that the work might be completed quickly.

Under his joyful rule, religion also flourished greatly. Even after the war against Licinius, he was so successful in the wars prepared against foreign peoples [Col. 0893A] that he defeated the Sarmatians, and the people called Goths finally entered into treaties with him as a gesture of goodwill. At that time this people lived beyond the river Ister. Inclined to war, and always trained in arms because of the number and great size of their bodies, they prevailed over the other barbarians; only the Romans stood against them.

It is said that this battle also demonstrated to Constantine through signs and dreams how greatly he was governed by God’s providence. After he had overcome all the wars waged under him (A.D. 333), as though repaying Christ, he burned ever more ardently with zeal for his religion. He ordered his subjects to acknowledge this religion alone as true and saving.

From the land subject to him, taking a fixed public tax from each city, he distributed it to the provincial churches and clergy, and decreed that the donation should remain valid forever. Accustoming his soldiers to worship God as he did, he marked their weapons with the sign of the cross.

In the imperial residence he built a chapel, and he also carried about a tent fashioned in the likeness of a church while he was encamped against his enemies, so that neither he himself while on campaign nor the army would be deprived of the sacred light in which it was fitting to praise God and offer prayers [Mss., “so that he might deem it fitting to praise … to offer”]. Priests and deacons serving the tent accompanied it as well, fulfilling the sacred orders according to ecclesiastical law.

From that time, the Roman cohorts, which are now called *numeri*, each made its own tent and had priests and deacons assigned to it. On the day called the Lord’s Day, which the Hebrews call the first day and the Greeks the day of the sun, and on the day before the seventh [that is, Friday], he decreed that everyone should have freedom from lawsuits and other affairs and be occupied only with prayers.

He honored Sunday because on that day Christ rose from the dead, and another day because on it he had been crucified. He held the most exalted veneration for the most holy cross, both because of the successes granted him through its aid in the wars undertaken against his adversaries and because of the sign that seemed to have been divinely shown to him concerning it.

Finally, he prohibited by law the punishment of crucifixion, which had formerly been customary among the Romans. He ordered this sign always to be inscribed and represented on the designs of solidi and on images, as his portraits decorated with this form still testify.

In all things, but especially in legislation, he labored to appease the Divinity. It appears that the shameful and extremely foolish unions that had not been prohibited before his time were then corrected, as can be learned from the laws he himself enacted.

But it is now necessary to set forth what he decreed for the honor and standing of the religion, since these matters seem to belong to ecclesiastical history. SOZOMEN, Book I, chapter 8, p. 409.

Among the Romans there had long been a law that excluded from the privileges of married persons those over twenty-five who had no wives. It also imposed many other requirements, ordering that such people should gain nothing from a will, even if they were related by blood [Col. 0894A]. Those who had no children lost half of what had been left to them.

The ancients established these laws because they wanted Rome to be populous and the whole earth to be subject to it, and because shortly before those laws had been enacted they had lost many people in civil wars. The emperor therefore saw that those who, for God’s sake, devoted themselves to virginity and childlessness were being treated unjustly. He judged it foolish to imagine that the human race was increased by human diligence and effort, since nature always undergoes diminution and increase through heavenly distribution.

He proposed a law to the entire people so that those without spouses and children might enjoy equal privileges with those who rejoiced in possessing them. He also decreed that those who lived in virginal continence should have greater privileges, granting men and women—even if under age—the right to make wills contrary to the common law.

For he judged that all those think rightly whose concern was always to please God and devote themselves to true philosophy. For this reason, even the ancient Romans permitted the Vestal Virgins to make wills, and decreed this during the sixth period of their lives.

The pious emperor’s greatest judgment concerning reverence for religion was this: he wished the decisions of all civil administrators to be regarded as incomplete everywhere, and decreed that anyone wishing to reject a civil judge should appeal to the bishops. He regarded the bishops’ judgment as firmer than that of other judges and, as though issued by the emperor, ordered it to be observed by all; synodal decrees were to be unalterable boundaries.

Nor should we pass over the provision enacted for the benefit of those who are emancipated in the churches. Since, because of the subtlety of the laws, even unwilling owners experienced difficulty in granting the better form of freedom that they call Roman citizenship, he enacted three laws. He decreed that all who were emancipated in churches under the testimony of priests should, through this pious innovation, enjoy Roman citizenship. The evidence of this practice is preserved even in the present day.

For it had been customary for written laws concerning freedom to be placed before the acts of emancipation. Constantine, therefore, earnestly honoring this religion in all things, held it in high regard; it was already glorious in itself because of the virtue of the many who at that time excelled in it. SOZOMEN, Book I, chapter 9, p. 413.

## CHAPTER X. On various confessors and their manner of life

[Col. 0894D]

When the persecutions had ceased, many confessors who were still alive continued to adorn the churches. Among them were Hosius, bishop of Córdoba; Amphion of Epiphania in Cilicia; Maximus, who held the episcopate of Jerusalem after Macarius; and Paphnutius the Egyptian. Through him, they say, God performed many miracles, subjected demons, and granted him the power to bestow healings for various diseases.

They report that Paphnutius and Maximus were among those confessors whom the emperor Maximinus condemned to labor in the mines, after tearing out their right eyes and cutting their left calves. SOZOMEN, Book I, chapter 10, p. 414.

[Col. 0895A] 211

We have learned that Spiridion, bishop of Trimithus in Cyprus, was also among them. To demonstrate his virtue, I think the opinion about him that has survived to the present is sufficient. The provincials know many of the deeds accomplished through him by divine assistance; I will not remain silent about those that have reached us.

He was a farmer who had a wife and children, but that did not make him lesser in divine matters. They say that one night wicked men came to his sheepfolds and, when they tried to steal, the thieves were suddenly bound without anyone tying them. At daybreak he came and found them bound. He released them from their invisible bonds, but blamed them and said:

“Why, brothers, when you were permitted to take what you desired, did you choose instead to steal it and pass the night continually in misery?”

Then, taking pity on them, or rather teaching them better things, he said:

“Go from here, taking a ram with you. You have labored through the night watches, and it is fitting that you depart from my sheep without complaint.”

Anyone may rightly admire this deed. Yet the following is no less remarkable.

A certain acquaintance had deposited some property with his daughter, a virgin named Irene. She took the deposit and hid it underground, believing that it would be safely guarded there. Meanwhile the girl died without telling her father anything. The man came to reclaim his deposit, while Spiridion did not know what he was talking about. After searching the entire house without finding it, the depositor wept, tore his hair, and seemed close to death.

When Spiridion saw this happening, he hurried to the tomb and called the girl by name. When she answered, he asked her about the deposit. After learning the facts from her, he returned and, finding the place she had indicated, gave the man what he was seeking.

Since I have come to speak of this man, it is not inappropriate to add the following. Spiridion had the custom of distributing some of the produce that grew for him to the poor and lending some of it freely to those who wished to borrow. He neither gave nor received anything personally, but merely showed them a storeroom, inviting those who requested something to take as much as they needed and to return again whatever they knew they had taken.

A certain man, after receiving a loan, returned some time later to repay what he had taken. Spiridion, following his custom, ordered him to put it back in the storeroom from which he had borrowed it. But the man turned to injustice and, believing that Spiridion was unaware, did not return what he owed. Taking the debt away, he departed as though he had repaid it.

This, however, could not remain unknown for long. After some time he came again and asked Spiridion for a loan. Spiridion sent him to the storeroom, giving him permission to measure out for himself as much as he needed. Finding the same place empty and recognizing this by his own observation, the man reported it to Spiridion.

Spiridion answered him:

“It is strange, man, what you are saying. How has it appeared to you alone that the storeroom has become deficient in necessities? Consider rather within yourself whether, when you borrowed on the previous occasion what you owed, you failed to repay it at the outset. If this is not so, you will certainly not be deprived of what you need; return again and you will find it.”

Thus the man was caught and confessed what he had done wrong.

It is therefore worthy of admiration that this most sacred man was so pure and so careful in the ecclesiastical order. It is said that at a certain time the bishops of Cyprus assembled for some useful purpose, and that Spiridion was among them, together with Triphyllius, bishop of Ledra, a man endowed with eloquence and wisdom and educated in the law [ed., “educated in the laws of Berytus, etc.”].

When the gathering was being held, Triphyllius was instructed to address the people. When he came to the passage, “Take up your bed and walk” (Matthew 9:6), he used the word *couch* instead of *bed*, changing the term. Spiridion became indignant with him and leapt from his episcopal chair:

“Are you better,” he said, “than the one who said ‘bed,’ since you are ashamed to use his words?”

He did this before the people, teaching moderation to a man who was puffed up with the pride of eloquence. He was able to inspire shame because he was venerable, renowned for his deeds, and at once advanced in age and dignity of priestly office.

His conduct toward the reception of strangers is shown by the following incident. Lent was already approaching. A traveler came to him during the days when Spiridion customarily continued his fast with his household and ate on a fixed day, passing the intervening days without food. Seeing that the traveler was very weak, he said to his daughter:

“Go, wash the traveler’s feet and set food before him.”

When the girl replied that there was neither bread nor ἄλφιτα [that is, flour]—for during the fast they were accustomed to keep none of these things stored—Spiridion first prayed and asked forgiveness, then ordered his daughter to cook the salted pork that they had in the house.

When it had been cooked, he sat down with the traveler, placed the meat before them, and asked him to eat with him. When the traveler refused and professed himself a Christian, Spiridion said:

“For that very reason you ought not to refuse. For ‘all things are clean to the clean’ (Titus 1:15), as the divine word teaches.”

This is sufficient concerning Spiridion. SOZOMEN, Book I, chapter 11, p. 415.

## CHAPTER XI. On various monks and their discipline

Above all, those who at that time practiced the monastic way of life displayed the Church in its greatest distinction and spread the doctrine through the virtues of their life. This philosophy, a most beneficial gift from God to humanity, despises the study of many disciplines and of dialectical technique as something petty that obstructs the time required for better work and offers nothing for right living.

This philosophy, expressed in an admirable manner of life, teaches through natural and simple prudence whatever destroys wickedness and produces what is useful. It does not merely proclaim virtue but rather practices it, setting no value on human glory and manfully resisting the passions of the soul. It neither submits to the necessities of nature nor yields to bodily weakness.

Possessing the virtue of the divine mind, it continually contemplates the Creator of all things. Worshiping him night and day, it unquestionably appeases him with prayers and litanies. By purity of soul and a life of good deeds, preparing itself for divine service, it disregards purifications and sprinklings, considering only sins to be defilements. It overcomes external accidents that rush upon it and absolutely masters all such things.

It is not altered by any inclination through the stability and necessity of life; it does not avenge itself when it suffers harm; it is not oppressed or embittered by illness or lack of necessities, but rather glories in such circumstances. 212

It meditates on patience, gentleness, and moderation throughout life. As far as human nature permits, it seeks to be near to God, using present things as though passing through them. It is not constricted by being occupied with the possession of things, nor perhaps compelled to make provision for the present beyond what is necessary.

Always praising the simplicity and discipline of this instruction, it contemplates eternal blessedness and hastens with all its vitality toward a happy end. Sighing without interruption with the fear of God, it rejects obscene speech and does not even allow the utterance of words whose actions it is known to expiate by its own deeds.

Grasping the necessities of nature in brief and compelling the body to need only modest things, it subjects luxury to chastity, punishes injustice with justice, and falsehood with truth. Discipline shares in the proper measure of all things. It lives with its neighbors in harmony and communion; it is provident toward friends and strangers; it makes what is its own common property for the needy and protects what is useful to each person. It is not intrusive toward those who rejoice but brings the afflicted the remedy of consolation.

Always extending its diligence toward the true good, it teaches and cares for its hearers with chaste words and wise counsels, setting aside ornate and vain eloquence, as though with medicines. It conducts its arrangements with honor and reverence, free from contention, rivalry, and anger. For since it is rational, it flees every irrational impulse and generally conquers the passions of both body and soul.

The founders of this most elegant philosophy were, as some say, the prophet Elijah and John the Baptist. Philo the Pythagorean reports in his own time (Philo the Jew, *On the Contemplative Life*) that distinguished Hebrews from every region practiced philosophy on a certain estate near Lake Mareotis, situated on a hill. He describes their dwelling, food, and manner of life as resembling what we now observe among the monks of Egypt.

For he writes that when they began their philosophy, they relinquished all the things belonging to them and renounced every form of intercourse, dwelling outside the walls in solitary fields and gardens. Their houses, he says, were sanctuaries, which among us are now called monasteries. In them they celebrated honorable mysteries in solitary living, diligently appeasing the Divinity with psalms and hymns, and tasting no food before sunset.

Some even went three days or more without food, and on certain days had the floor as their bed. They always abstained from wine and from anything containing blood. Their food was bread, salt, and hyssop, and their drink was water. Women lived with them, older virgins voluntarily abstaining from marriage because of their love of philosophy.

In reporting this, Philo seems to reveal that those who, in his view, had become Christians from among the Hebrews were still living in a Jewish manner and observing their established practices. For this manner of life is not found among others. Hence I infer that among the Egyptians this philosophy had its beginnings. SOZOMEN, Book I, chapter 12, p. 417.

Others, however, say that the cause of this way of life was the persecutions that arose over time on account of religion. Since they fled and lived in mountains, valleys, and deserts, they became accustomed to this manner of life. But whether Egyptians or certain others presided over this philosophy from the beginning, everyone agrees on this: that Antony, the greatest of the monks, brought it to the highest reverence and perfection through fitting morals and disciplines [Col. 0898B]. At that time he was living in the deserts of Egypt (A.D. 334). Because of the glory of his virtue, the emperor Constantine had made him his friend, honored him in letters, and sought his written replies on whatever matters he wished.

This man was Egyptian by birth, born in a notable village situated in the district of Heraclea among the Egyptians. When he was left an orphan as a boy, he gave his paternal fields to his fellow villagers; and, disposing of his other property, he distributed its value to the poor. He considered true philosophers to be those who not only stripped themselves of money but also distributed it profitably. Joining himself to men who were devoted to philosophy like himself, he zealously pursued the virtues of all. He found that a good life becomes pleasant through habit itself, although at first it had been difficult.

He devised increasingly rigorous forms of abstinence and grew daily through discipline. As though always beginning anew, he continually introduced some fresh practice: punishing lust through bodily afflictions, and resisting the soul’s passions through the will directed toward sacred wisdom. His food was only bread and salt, his drink water, and his time for eating sunset. Frequently he remained without food for two days or more. He kept vigil, so to speak, throughout the unbroken night, and by his prayers he reached into the day; if sleep overcame him, he slept standing for a little while, usually lying on the pavement and having only the bare earth as his bed of rest [ms., “for rests”]. He avoided in every way the anointing with oil, bathing, and similar practices, lest his body, through its moisture, be changed into softness. They say that he was never seen naked [Col. 0898D].

He neither knew letters nor admired them [ms. Lyr., “pondered them”], but regarded a good mind as superior to letters, although he rightly praised their inventor. He was especially gentle, chaste, courageous, and agreeable to those who spoke with him, without any gloom. Even when those disputing with him introduced contentious questions, he would often calm the growing quarrel in his customary wise and disciplined manner, immediately bringing it back to its proper measure; he moderated the clamor of those speaking with him and, as though by a rule, ordered their behavior.

[Col. 0899A]

Thus, although divine providence abounded in such virtues, he did not consider it a virtue to know the future in advance; for this reason he advised that one should not labor uselessly over such matters. He declared that neither the person ignorant of the future necessarily falls under punishment, nor is the person who knows it thereby holy. He said that true blessedness consists in the worship of God and the observance of his laws. If anyone was concerned with such matters, he taught that the person should cleanse the soul so that it might be capable of seeing and possessing knowledge of future things, with God’s foreknowledge making them clear.

He did not permit himself to be idle, and he always commanded those who wished to live well to work, examine themselves, and reckon with themselves concerning what they had done by day and by night. If anyone did something improper, he was to write it down, so that thereafter he might refrain from the offense—being ashamed of himself if he discovered many offenses of his own, and at the same time fearing that the written record might make him known to others. He was industrious, especially in providing relief for the oppressed [Col. 0899B].

Who else was so fervently devoted to those for whose sake he often came to the cities? Many, compelled by force, made [p. 213] him act as their envoy before judges and magistrates. Each of them considered it exceedingly distinguished to see him, glorious to hear him speak, and honorable to obey his commands. Yet, though he was such a man, he sought to remain unknown and hidden in the wilderness. If necessity brought him into a city, once he had settled the business for which he had come, he immediately returned to the desert.

He used to say that fish are nourished by a moist substance, whereas monks are adorned [ed. V., “are destined”] by the solitary life. And just as fish waste away when they touch the earth, so the glory of monks is stained by approaching cities. Yet he showed himself obedient and agreeable to those who saw him. [Col. 0899C] He took pains neither to have an inflated and proud nature nor to be thought to have one.

I have been compelled to mention these few things about Antony’s virtues so that through these examples we may consider the philosophy of so great a man. He had many highly distinguished hearers. Some of them became renowned in Egypt and Libya, others in Palestine, Syria, and Arabia. Each exercised himself no less than the teacher with whom he had lived; they taught many and led them to a similar virtue and philosophy. Thus some people made it their task to travel through cities and provinces, or through the countryside, carefully seeking out Antony’s disciples and their successors.

[Col. 0899D]

But how could they easily be found, when they took the greatest care to conceal their way of life and did not, as many people now do, puff themselves up with glory, parade themselves, and make themselves known to everyone? Among the most distinguished disciples of Antony whom we have come to know were many others, and also one called Paul the Simple.

They say that, while he was a farmer and had a wife of attractive appearance, he caught her in the very act of adultery, smiled quietly, and swore that he would never again have intercourse with her. Then he said to the adulterer, “Take her,” and immediately departed for the desert to Antony. They say that he was exceedingly gentle and patient. Finally, when he was already an old man and unaccustomed to perseverance in the monastic life [ed., “to monastic perseverance”], Antony tested him with every kind of trial and found him inferior in nothing. He testified that Paul possessed perfect philosophy and commanded him to live separately, as one who had no need of a teacher [Col. 0900A]. God confirmed Antony’s testimony and showed by his deeds that Paul was a glorious man, superior even to his teacher, and prepared to afflict and drive out demons.

**SOZOMEN, Book I, chapter 13, p. 420.**

Around this same time Ammonius the Egyptian was practicing philosophy. Concerning him it is reported that, compelled by his parents, he took a wife, but never had intercourse with her. At the beginning of the marriage, receiving his bride as a bridegroom in the bridal chamber and remaining alone with her, he said: “Woman, our marriage has been celebrated only up to this point.” From the sacred Scriptures he then taught her what a great good it is to remain a virgin, and he attempted to live alone and apart.

But although the woman, being a virgin, had praised his discourse on virginity, she considered separation from him difficult. Therefore she slept in another room and remained with him for eighteen years, without meanwhile abandoning monastic abstinence. In the meantime, jealous of her husband’s virtue, the woman judged that it was not right for so great a man to remain hidden at home because of her, but that each of them ought rather to practice philosophy separately. For this reason she entreated her husband.

He gave thanks to God for this thought of the woman and said: “You keep this house; I shall build another for myself.” He then went to the southern part of the desert of Lake Maria, near the place of Scetis, to the mountain called Nitria, and practiced philosophy there for twenty-two years, visiting the woman every second year [Col. 0900C].

Many worthy disciples came from this most sacred founder of these monasteries, as their succession demonstrates; and through him many excellent and venerable practices arose, which are especially and perfectly preserved among the Egyptian monks. For they take the greatest care, through the succession of mutual tradition, to hand down to memory the virtues of the ancient monks. I, however, must mention those who have come down to our own time.

It happened that this man and his disciple Theodore were traveling and had to cross a river called the Lycus. So that they might not see each other naked, Ammonius [elsewhere Amos] ordered Theodore to withdraw from the water. Since he was himself ashamed to look upon his own nakedness, he was suddenly transported by divine power to the farther bank.

Theodore crossed the water and, seeing that neither Ammonius’ clothing nor his feet had become wet [Col. 0900D], begged the old man to explain the event to him. When Ammonius refused to speak, Theodore declared that he would not continue on his way unless he learned what had happened. Theodore promised that, while Ammonius lived, he would tell no one, and so Ammonius confessed what had occurred.

A miracle close to this one also took place, which I shall now relate. Unjust parents brought to him a son who had been bitten by a rabid dog and was almost dead, and they begged him amid lamentations to heal him. He said to them: “He does not need my healing. But if you wish to return to its owners the ox you stole, the sick boy will immediately recover.” And so it happened. As soon as the ox had been restored, the boy’s illness departed.

When this Ammonius was dying, Antony is said to have seen [Col. 0901A] his soul being carried up into heaven, with divine powers preceding it with psalmody. When those around him asked about the cause of this miracle, he did not conceal it. They knew that Antony, gazing intently into the air, had been looking with astonishment upon a miraculous vision. Later, when some people arrived from Scetis and reported the hour of Antony’s vision, and it agreed with the time of that man’s death, they blessed both men: the one because he had passed over to manifest blessings, the other because he had been worthy to behold such a vision from so great a distance. The places where the two men lived were separated by a journey of many days.

This, then, is how the story has been reported. During this episcopate I heard that Eutychianus, who lived in Bithynia near Olympus, practiced philosophy with the highest distinction [Col. 0901B]. He was filled with divine grace for the healing of illnesses and for miracles of things and deeds, so that Constantine himself became his friend because of the virtue of his life.

At that time a certain sword-bearer, who had come under suspicion as though he had attempted to seize power, fled; after being sought, he was captured near Olympus. His relatives begged Eutychianus to act as his envoy before the emperor. He replied: “First, we must see to it that this man is freed from his chains, lest he die from cruel restraint.” He is then said to have sent word to the keepers of the chains, asking them to release the man from such distress. When they refused to do so, the closed doors opened of their own accord, and the prisoner’s chains suddenly broke.

Afterward Eutychianus went [p. 214] to the emperor, who was then residing in Byzantium, and very readily obtained the favor he had requested [Col. 0901C]. Constantine could not refuse his petitions, since he showed him the highest honor.

These brief remarks by us concerning the monks who at that time practiced philosophy with distinction should suffice. Whoever has a more detailed interest in these matters will find, by searching, that the lives of many others have not been written here.

**SOZOMEN, Book I, chapter 14, p. 423.**

[Col. 0901D]

# CHAPTER XII. How Arius arose against the Church

Although the Church was flourishing in every respect, the enemy could not endure it. He saw it at once exalted and greatly radiant, and began to devise malicious plans, striving to submerge the Church governed by the Lord and Creator of all things. He saw that pagan error had been stripped bare, that the various devices of demons had been overthrown, and that the creature was no longer worshiped by many, but hymns were fittingly offered to the Creator.

For this reason he no longer openly raised war against our Lord and Savior. Instead, he found men who professed themselves Christians in name but, drawn back into servitude by their love of honor and empty glory, and he made them instruments of his scheme. Through them he led many back to their former error—not by commanding that the creature again be worshiped, but by asserting that the Creator himself, the Maker of the world, was equal to the creature.

Where this began, and how the enemy sowed this tares, I shall now relate. Alexandria is a very large city, rich in a multitude of inhabitants, and holds primacy not only over the Egyptians but also over the Thebans and the Libyans around Egypt [Col. 0902A].

After that celebrated defender Peter, who under the impious tyrants Diocletian and Maximian received the crown of martyrdom when they finally and voluntarily laid down the imperial power (A.D. 310), Achillas succeeded to the episcopate of this city. Under that distinguished Peter, Arius had been ordained a deacon; after being caught up in the innovations of Meletius and expelled from the Church, he was received again at the request of the faithful, and Achillas ordered him to minister.

After Achillas, Alexander, a most courageous preacher of evangelical doctrine, was ordained bishop. At this time (A.D. 322), Arius was among the presbyters and appeared to have been entrusted with the exposition of the divine Scriptures [Col. 0902B]. When he saw Alexander assume the reins of the episcopate, he could not endure the passage of time. Driven on by bitterness, he sought the beginning of a dispute.

He saw, indeed, that the man’s way of life was praiseworthy and could not construct accusations against him. Nevertheless, envy prevented him from remaining quiet. The enemy therefore found in him an opponent of the truth and attempted through him to stir up a storm against the Church.

Arius openly persisted in resisting Alexander’s apostolic teachings. Alexander, following the divine utterances, proclaimed that the Son possessed equal honor with the Father and the same substance as God the Begetter.
