Arius, on the other hand, resisting the truth, said that the Son was a creature and something made, adding: “There was when he was not,” along with other insane statements recorded in his writings.

[Col. 0902C]

He continued teaching these things not only in the Church but also in private gatherings and assemblies; going from house to house, he persuaded everyone he could.

**THEODORET, Book I, chapter 2, p. 6.**

Someone, however, censuring such men, also blamed Alexander, as though he had not wisely remained silent while innovations were being made against the doctrine. Alexander judged it better that the disputed matter should be presented from both sides, so that the contest would appear to have been removed [ed. Frob. and Niv., “introduced”] not by compulsion but rather through satisfaction. He therefore sat in judgment with the clergy and brought both parties into debate.

As usually happens in verbal contests, each side strove to prevail. Arius, however, was entirely unwilling to yield, because he would not admit that the Son is consubstantial and coeternal with the Father [Col. 0902D].

**SOZOMEN, Book I, chapter 15, p. 426.**

Alexander, the preacher of apostolic doctrines, first tried to recall him through admonitions and counsels. But when he saw him growing proud and openly proclaiming deeds of impiety, he removed him from the priestly order. For he had heard the divine law cry out: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you” (Matt. 5:29).

At this time Sylvester governed the Roman Church, succeeding Melchiades, who had assumed the rights of the episcopate after Marcellinus had been glorified in the persecution of the pagans. At Antioch, when peace was beginning in the Church after the tyrant, Vitalis was bishop (A.D. 314). He also rebuilt the ancient church [Col. 0903A] that had been destroyed by tyrants after many years. After him Philogonius assumed the episcopate, added the remaining parts of the building, and displayed zeal for piety during the reign of Licinius (A.D. 316).

In Jerusalem, after Hermon, Macarius was ordained, a man worthy of his name and adorned with every virtue. At the same time Alexander held the episcopate of the sacred ministry in Constantinople, highly distinguished for his apostolic gifts.

At that time Alexander of Alexandria, seeing Arius driven on by the goad of a contentious love of judgment, deceiving and arousing many toward blasphemies, and holding assemblies of his own, informed the bishops of the Churches of his blasphemy by letter.

**THEODORET, Book I, chapter 2, p. 7.**

# CHAPTER XIII. Letter of Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, to all the Churches against Arius

[Col. 0903B]

To the beloved and dearest fellow ministers everywhere in the Catholic Church, Alexander sends greetings in the Lord.

Since the Catholic Church is one body, and since the sacred Scriptures command that the bond of unanimity and peace be preserved (1 Cor. 12:26), it follows that we ought to write and make known to one another what is happening among each of us, so that whether one member suffers or rejoices, we may suffer or rejoice with one another.

In our diocese, therefore, impious men and rebels against Christ have now arisen. They teach an apostasy that anyone might rightly suspect to be a forerunner of Antichrist. I wished to consign this matter to silence, if somehow the evil might be confined among the apostates alone and not, by penetrating other places, pollute the ears of the simple [Col. 0903C].

But since Eusebius, now at Nicomedia, thinks that the affairs of the Church depend upon him—because, after leaving the city of the Berytians and desiring the Church of Nicomedia, no punishment followed him—he also supports these apostates and has attempted to write everywhere in their favor, commending them, in the hope that he may draw some ignorant people into this most evil heresy and rebellion against Christ.

Therefore I judged it necessary, knowing what is written in the law, no longer to remain silent but to make this known to all of you, so that you too may recognize the apostates and beware of the exceedingly wicked words of their heresy. If Eusebius writes to you, do not receive him, nor accept his writings. Wishing to renew through these men an ancient cunning that had been suppressed for a time, he pretends to write on their behalf; but his actions show that he is hastening [Col. 0903D] to pursue such interests for himself.

These apostates are Arius and Achillas. The following also apostatized with them: Aithales, Carponius, another Arius, Sarmatius, Euzoius, Lucius, Julius, Menas, and Helladius, as well as Gaius, Secundus, and Theonas, who at some time were called bishops.

Their opinions and statements are as follows: “God the Father did not always exist, nor did the Word of God always exist; rather, there was a time when God the Father did not exist. The Word of God was made from things that did not exist. For since God existed, he made what did not exist from what did not exist. Therefore there was a time when he did not exist.

“The Son is a creature and something made. [Col. 0904A] He is not like the Father according to substance; he is not true, nor is he the Father’s true Wisdom, nor is he naturally the Father’s true Word. He is one of the creatures and things made. He is called Word and Wisdom improperly; he too was made and exists in God’s own Word and Wisdom, in which God made all things, including him.

“Therefore he is subject to conversion and change by nature, like all rational beings. The Word is foreign, alien, and remote from the Father’s substance, and the Father is invisible to the Son. The Son does not know the Father perfectly and completely, nor can he see him perfectly. Indeed, the Son does not know even his own substance as it is.

“He was made for our sake, so that God might create us through him as through an instrument; and he would not have continued to exist at all [Col. 0904B] if God had not wished to make us.”

Someone then asked them whether the Word of God could be converted, just as the devil had been converted. They were not afraid to say that he certainly could, since he existed by nature as subject to conversion: “He was made,” they say, “and is subject to conversion.”

These are the statements of Arius and those who are with him. They persist shamelessly in these assertions, as do their followers. We met with the bishops of Egypt and Libya, nearly one hundred in number, and anathematized them.

But those around Eusebius have welcomed them, striving to mix falsehood with truth and join impiety to piety. They will not prevail. Truth will conquer, for light has no communion with darkness, nor does Christ have concord with Belial (2 Cor. 6:14).

Who has ever heard such things? Or who, hearing these words now, will not be afraid [Col. 0904C] or immediately stop his ears, lest his hearing be polluted by the filth of such words? Who, hearing John say, “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1), would not condemn those who say, “There was a time when he was not”? Or who, hearing in the Gospel, “the only-begotten Son” and “all things were made through him” (John 1:18, 3), would not hate those who say that the Son is one of the creatures? How, then, can he be one of those things known to have been made through him? Or how can he be the Only-begotten if, according to them, he is counted among all the others?

How also can he be from things that did not exist, when the Father says, “My heart has uttered a good Word” (Ps. 44:2), and again, “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3)? Or how can his substance be unlike the Father’s, when he is the perfect image and radiance of the Father, who says, “Whoever sees me sees the Father [Col. 0904D] also” (John 14:9)?

If the Son is the Word and Wisdom of God, how was there a time when he did not exist? It is as though they were saying that God once existed without Word and without Wisdom. Or how is he subject to conversion and change when he says of himself, “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 14:10), and again, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30)? Through the prophet he says: “See me; see that I am, and I will not change” (Mal. 3:6).

Although that apostolic statement says that he became human, he was not changed; rather, as the Apostle said, “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Heb. 13:8).

What cause, do you suppose, persuaded them to say that he was made for our sake, when Paul writes, “from whom are all things and [Col. 0905A] through whom are all things” (Rom. 11:36)? It is not surprising that they blaspheme by saying that the Son does not know the Father perfectly. Once they had resolved to rebel against Christ, they also resisted his saying: “As the Father knows me, so I know the Father” (John 10:15).

If the Father knows the Son only in part, it is clear that the Son also does not know the Father perfectly. But if it is impious to say this—for the Father does know the Son perfectly—it is clear that, just as the Father knows his own Word, so the Word knows his own Father. There is no other possibility.

By saying these things and examining the holy Scriptures, we frequently convicted them. Then again, like chameleons, they changed themselves, striving to apply to themselves what is written: “When the wicked comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3).

[Col. 0905B]

There have been many heresies before them. Presuming more than was proper, they fell into their own folly. These men, however, seeking in all their words to rise up against the destruction of the divinity of the Word, tried rather through these arguments to strengthen those earlier heresies, becoming more closely allied with Antichrist. Therefore they were rejected and anathematized by the Church.

We grieve over their destruction, especially because they too once heard the things belonging to the Church and now utterly depart from it. Yet we are not surprised. The same thing happened to Hymenaeus and Philetus, and before them to Judas, who followed the Savior but afterward became a traitor and apostate.

We are not ignorant concerning such men. The Lord foretold this, saying: “See that no one deceives you. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he,’ and [Col. 0905C] ‘The time is near,’ and they will lead many astray. Do not go after them” (Luke 21:8).

Paul learned this from our Savior and said: “In the last times some will apostatize from the sound faith, attending to spirits of error and teachings of demons, which reject the truth” (1 Tim. 4:1).

Since our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ himself foretold such men, and the Apostle also identified them, we, having heard their impiety for ourselves, consequently anathematized them, as we have said, showing that they are strangers to the faith and to the Catholic Church.

We have made these things known to you, beloved and dearest fellow ministers, so that if any of them should attempt to come to you, you may not receive them, nor obey Eusebius or anyone else [p. 216] who writes on their behalf [Col. 0905D]. For as Christians we ought with all our strength to reject everyone who speaks and thinks against Christ, as rebels against God and corrupters of souls. We should not even say “greeting” to such men, lest we appear to share in their sins, as the blessed John says (2 John 11).

Greet the brothers who are with you. Those who are with us greet you.

**SOCRATES, Book I, chapter 3; edition of Christopherson and Valesius, chapter 6, p. 10.**

I shall not omit inserting into this work not only this letter but also the one he sent to Alexander, bishop of Constantinople, which clearly sets forth all his positions, so that no one may suspect that I have composed these things fictitiously. After it I shall include Arius’s own letter and the other letters as well, since the historical narrative requires them, so that they may testify to the truth of the writing [Col. 0906A] and clearly teach what took place. The Alexandrian wrote the following to Alexander of Constantinople.

**THEODORET, Book I, chapter 3, p. 8.**

# CHAPTER XIV. The same man’s letter to Alexander, bishop of Constantinople

To Alexander, my dearest brother and of one mind with me, Alexander sends greetings in the Lord.

The desire for power of the worst men, and their determination to pursue greed, habitually lie in wait for the truth, which is held to be of the highest importance, through various pretexts that resist ecclesiastical devotion. Driven on by malice, with the devil working in them toward the lust they have set before themselves, and recoiling from all reverence, they trample underfoot the fear of God’s judgment. Concerning these matters it was necessary for me to inform your patience and reverence [ed., “patient reverence”], so that you may beware of such people, lest anyone presume to enter your parishes, either personally or through others.

For magicians are skilled at using fabrications to deceive, or letters composed with falsehood, which can cast a spell over those who look upon them with simple and pure faith. Arius and Achillas, therefore, having recently formed a conspiracy, followed the arrogance of Colluthus, and something far worse than his. For while Colluthus blamed these very men, he found an opportunity for his own evil will. But they, looking upon [ms. Lyr., “rejecting”] his activity as worthy, could by no means endure subjection to the law of the Church. Instead, building dens of robbers for themselves, they hold unceasing assemblies in them, acting against Christ and against us by night and by day, and practicing depraved lusts.

They accuse all pious and apostolic glory, and, rebelling against Christ in a Jewish manner, have established a workshop for themselves. They deny the divinity and equality with the Father of our Savior Jesus Christ, and, tearing away all the sayings concerning his saving dispensation and the humility he assumed for our sake, they strive by uttering these words to carry on the proclamation of their impiety. For, wholly avoiding any account of his divinity and of the ineffable glory that he possessed with the Father from the beginning, they confirm the impious opinion of pagans and Jews concerning Christ. Seeking, as is their custom, their own praise, they traffic in every kind of mockery that they can bring against us; and every day they create seditions and persecutions against us, proposing quarrels through the interventions of shameless women whom they seduce, while also undermining the whole Christian community, as their young women go about all the streets. Moreover, they now presume to tear apart Christ’s seamless tunic, which the soldiers refused to divide (John XIX, 2).

As for us, because their life and their ungodly schemes had been concealed, we recognized them only slowly; but now, by a general decree, we have expelled them from the Church that worships Christ’s divinity. Yet they have tried to make use of wanderings and to plot against us, pretending among our like-minded fellow ministers to practice the dignity of peace and unity. But what is true is that they hurry to snatch some people into their own plague by means of fabricated pleasant words, and demand from them open and unambiguous letters, so that, when they reread these to persons whom they have deceived, they may cause them to remain in their sins without repentance, as though they had bishops of like mind with themselves who had reached the same decisions.

For they do not confess the things they taught and did wickedly among us, on account of which they were also expelled. Rather, they either consign these matters to silence or conceal them beneath fabricated arguments and certain disguises. Covering their corrupt doctrine with plausible and grandiloquent speeches, they draw every unwary person into their deception, and do not even refrain from slandering our piety before everyone.

Hence it has happened that some who subscribed to their letters have been received into the Church, with, as I believe, the greatest danger impending, when fellow ministers presume to do such things, since neither does apostolic rule tolerate this, and they pour over these people a diabolical influence against Christ.

Therefore, dearest ones, I have roused myself, without any sluggishness, to make their faithlessness known to you. For they say that there was once a time when the Son of God did not exist, and that afterward he was made, although previously he had not been made such; for at some time he too was made, as it happens that every human being is made. They say that God made everything from things that did not exist, wishing to include the Son of God among all rational and irrational creatures.

Consequently, in these words they say that he is of a mutable nature, capable of virtue and wickedness, since he is said to exist from things that did not exist. For they destroy the divine Scriptures by which it is shown that he always exists, and by which the unchangeableness of the Word, the Wisdom, and the Divinity—which are Christ—is openly designated.

“We too,” say these polluted men, “can become sons of God, just as he did.” For it is written: “I begot sons and exalted them” (Isaiah I, 2). When what follows is brought before them—“But they themselves rejected me”—which is not natural to the Savior, since he is immutable by nature, they strip themselves of all reverence and say: “He has no special relation to God. Rather, since he is mutable by nature, God knew beforehand and foresaw concerning him that he would not reject him; therefore he was chosen from among all the others. For by nature,” they say, “he possesses nothing exceptional among the other sons. He is neither naturally the Son of God nor does he possess any special relation to God. Since he himself is mutable by nature, God chose him on account of his moderation, diligence, and virtue, because he did not change for the worse. And if Paul or Peter had attained this, Jesus would have differed in nothing from their sonship.”

To refute this mad teaching, therefore, and after examining the divine writings, we set forth what is said of Christ in the Psalms: “You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm XLIV, 8).

Since the Son of God was neither made from things that did not exist nor was there ever a time when he did not exist, the evangelist John is sufficient to instruct us when he writes concerning him: “The Only-Begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father” (John I, 18). For God, intending to show that these are undivided realities, named the Father and the Son who exists in the Father’s bosom.

But since the Word of God is in no way numbered among the things made from things that did not exist, he says: “All things were made through him” (John I, 3). He indicated his own substance when he said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made” (ibid., 1–2).

For if all things were made through him, how could he who granted creatures existence himself once not have existed? There is no reason why the maker should be of the same nature as the things that are made. If he was in the beginning, while all things were made through him, then he made them from things that did not exist; and what exists is contrary to and wholly distinct from those things that were made from things that did not exist.

Between the Father and the Son no interval can be shown to exist, nor can the imagination of the soul perceive such an interval even in thought. The world, however, created from things that did not exist, has a new and recent birth of substance from the Father through the Son, a substantiality of the kind received by all things.

The most blessed John, contemplating still more deeply the divinity of the Word, which transcends the whole understanding of created things, did not wish to call his generation a making, nor by the elements of syllables to call him the ungenerated Maker. For there is one ungenerated being: the Father. But because the ineffable substance of the Only-Begotten Son surpasses, I think, the perception not only of the evangelists but also of the angels, and transcends all things, I do not think that those who consider matters piously presume to inquire into it, on account of what has been said: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not examine what is beyond your powers” (Ecclesiasticus III, 22).

For, as with many other things, knowledge of this too has been hidden from human perception, as in Paul: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (II Corinthians II, 9). God also said to Abraham: “You cannot count the stars, nor the sand of the sea”; and who can count the drops of rain (Genesis XV, 5; and Ecclesiasticus I, 2)?

Who, then, unless he is insane, would dare to investigate inwardly [ed., “outwardly”] the subsistence of the Word of God? Concerning it the prophetic Spirit says: “Who will recount his generation?” (Isaiah LIII, 8). Our Savior himself, wishing to benefit all the pillars of this world in this matter, hastened to relieve them of knowledge of it, indicating that this understanding is beyond the nature of all things and that the mystery of this knowledge belongs only to the Father: “No one,” he says, “knows who the Son is except the Father, and no one knows who the Father is except the Son” (Matthew XI, 27).

I do not think, therefore, that wise people are unaware that it is madness to say that the Son was made from things that did not exist, since he plainly has no temporal beginning, as something made from things that did not exist is shown to have. For if what they say—“There was when he was not”—had to exist within time, or within any interval of the age; and if it is true that all things were made through him, then it is clear that every age, time, interval, and “once,” among which they place the statement “there was when he was not,” were made through him.

How, then, is it not incredible to say that he who made times and moments, among which is that “there was when he was not,” once did not exist? For it is foolish and full of every sin to say that the one who is the cause of something came into being later than the thing of which he is the cause.

According to them, therefore, the Wisdom of God, which created all things, precedes the interval in which they say that the Son had not yet been made by the Father—while Scripture lies, according to them, when it says that he is “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians I, 15). The eloquent Paul also cries out in agreement with them when he says of him: “Whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages” (Hebrews I, 2).

Moreover, “in him all things were created, those in heaven and those on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things” (Colossians I, 16–17).

Since, then, the argument by which they say that the Son was made from things that did not exist is shown to be impious, the Father must always be Father. The Father is always Father with the Son present, on account of whom he is called Father. With the Son always present to him, the Father is always perfect and remains without diminution, not generating the Only-Begotten Son temporally, through an interval, or from things that did not exist.

What could be more wicked than to say that the Wisdom of God did not once exist, although it says: “I was beside him, dwelling with him” [ed., Niv. and Frob., “fitting myself to him”], “I was the one in whom he rejoiced” (Proverbs VIII, 30)? Or to say that the Power of God once did not exist, or that his Word received a beginning, or to say anything else by which the Son is recognized and the Father represented?

For whoever does not say that he is “the radiance of glory” (Hebrews I, 3) destroys at once the primordial light, whose radiance he is. And if the image of God did not always exist, it is clear that the one of whom he is the image did not exist either. If he is not the figure of God’s subsistence, then the one who is represented by him in all things is also destroyed at once.

From this the sonship of our Savior becomes evident: it has no admixture with the sonship of the others. Just as his ineffable subsistence is proved to transcend, with incomparable excellence, all things to which he himself granted existence, so also his sonship, which exists naturally in the Father’s divinity, differs with ineffable sublimity from those who through him have been adopted as sons.

For he, being unchangeable, is perfect by nature and lacking in nothing; but they, in both respects, are subject to mutability and need his help. In what could the Wisdom of God progress, or in what could its truth increase? Or how could God the Word be improved, since he is life and true light?

If this is so, how much more witless is it to say that the Wisdom or Power of God was once capable of weakness, or that the Word was capable of irrationality and thereby reason was darkened, or that darkness was mixed with the true light, when the Apostle says: “What fellowship has light with darkness? Or what agreement has Christ with Belial?” (II Corinthians VI, 15).

Moreover, since Solomon cries out (Proverbs XXX, 19), it is impossible even in imagination to discover the ways of the serpent upon the rock, which according to Paul is Christ.

But human beings and angels, his creatures, received his blessing, striving to advance in virtues and lawful commandments, so that they would not sin. Our Lord, however, being naturally the Son of the Father, is worshiped by all.

They, laying aside the spirit of slavery, receive the spirit of sonship from good works and progress; aided by the natural Son, they too become sons by adoption. Paul also made this Son’s own, natural, and preeminent sonship manifest concerning God, saying: “He who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us”—that is, for us who are not sons by nature—“gave him up” (Romans VIII, 32). To distinguish him from those who are not his own, he called him his own Son.

In the Gospel he says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew III, 17). In the Psalms the Savior says: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son” (Psalm II, 7). Declaring the kinship of nature, he signifies that no other sons besides this one are his natural sons.

And what of the statement: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Psalm CIX, 3)? Does it not clearly demonstrate the sonship of natural generation from the Father—a sonship he received not through diligence in conduct or progress by exercise, but through the propriety of nature? Hence the Only-Begotten has an untransgressible sonship from the Father.

Reason knows that the sonship of rational beings is not natural to them, but is also mutable, arising from the suitability of their conduct and from God’s gift. For we read: “The sons of God saw the daughters of men, and they took wives for themselves from among them” (Genesis VI, 2). Again, we have learned through Isaiah that God said: “I begot sons and exalted them; but they themselves rejected me” (Isaiah I, 2).

I pass over many things that I could say, dearest ones, because I think it burdensome to admonish like-minded teachers with more words. You yourselves have been divinely instructed and do not fail to know that the doctrine that has recently arisen against ecclesiastical piety is that of Ebion and Artemas, and the zeal of Paul of Samosata of Antioch, who were expelled from the Church by a synodal gathering of all the bishops. Lucian, succeeding him, remained outside the churches for a very long time under three bishops.

Having swallowed the dregs of their impiety, these men—Arius and Achillas, and the council of the wicked with them—have now caused those hidden plantings to sprout among us from things that did not exist. And somehow in Syria three bishops have been ordained because they agreed with them and have been inflamed toward worse things.

Let the judgment concerning them rest upon your discernment, since you retain in memory the saving humility of the Passion, the self-emptying, the voluntary poverty, and the sayings that the Savior assumed for our sake.

Therefore, to display his heavenly and ancient divinity, these things are fitting; and in significant expressions his natural glory, authority, and dwelling with the Father are explained more clearly. Consider the saying: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30). He does not call himself the Father, nor does he declare two substantial natures to be one; rather, because the Son possesses the Father’s fullness of saving power in a perfect nature, bearing the Father’s likeness in all things, existing as his unchangeable image, and being the expressed representation of the primary cause, he speaks in this way.

Accordingly, when Philip desired to see the Father, the Lord showed himself without jealousy. For when Philip said, “Show us the Father,” he replied: “Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John XIV, 8–9), as though he were contemplating the Father through a spotless and living mirror, through the divine image in Christ. The holy men likewise sing of him in the Psalms, saying: “In your light we shall see light” (Psalm XXXV, 10).

Therefore whoever honors the Father honors the Son also; and whoever honors the Son honors the Father also—and rightly so. Every impious word that anyone presumes to speak against the Son is referred also to the Father.

It is not surprising, dearest ones, that I should report the false accusations brought against me and against our most pious people. Those who set up a camp against the divinity of the Son of God do not fear to level ungrateful slanders against us. They do not deem any of the ancients worthy of comparison with themselves, nor do they permit themselves to be equated with the teachers by whom we were instructed from childhood. They do not count any fellow minister anywhere as their equal in wisdom, as though they alone were wise, possessing nothing in common with others, inventors of new doctrines, and the only people to whom realities unknown to anyone else under the sun have been revealed.

O wicked pride, immeasurable madness, frenzy of empty glory, and wisdom of Satan, violently rushing into their most evil souls! The exposition of the ancient Scriptures beloved of God did not deter them; nor did the shared reverence of their fellow ministers tame their savagery toward Christ. Even demons cannot endure their wicked deeds, since they do not presume to utter a blasphemous voice against the Son of God.

Let these darts, therefore, be directed according to the present power against those who are sharpened for battle against Christ by an [ed., “unlearned”] learned argument and strive to bring accusations against his piety.

For they say that, while opposing the fables from which it has been invented that he is said to be “from things that do not exist,” we preach an impious and unwritten blasphemy against Christ—namely, two ungenerated beings. Rather, they themselves, being unlearned, say that one of two alternatives must necessarily be true: either the Son must be understood as being from things that do not exist, or one must unambiguously say that there are two ungenerated beings.

These ignorant men do not know that there is a great difference between the ungenerated Father and the rational and irrational things created by him from things that did not exist. Between them stands the nature of the Only-Begotten, through whom the Father, God of the Word, made all things from things that did not exist; yet the Son has his birth from the Father himself, as the Lord himself testified somewhere, saying: “Whoever loves the Father loves the Son who was born from him” (I John V, 1).

Concerning these matters we believe as the apostolic Church approves: in one ungenerated Father, who had no cause for his existence, unchangeable and immutable, always the same and consistently so, receiving neither increase nor diminution, giver of the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospels, Lord of the patriarchs and apostles and of all the saints;

and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Only-Begotten Son of God, born not from one who did not exist but from the existing Father—not according to the likenesses of bodies, through divisions or outflows of substances, as Sabellius and Valentinus hold, but ineffably and indescribably, according to the one who said, as we quoted above: “Who will recount his generation?” (Isaiah LIII, 8).

His subsistence [ms. Theod., “substance”] is inscrutable to every created nature, just as the Father himself is inscrutable, since the nature of rational beings cannot comprehend the knowledge by which the Father begot the Son.

It is not fitting for a man filled with the spirit of truth to say this on his own; for Christ’s voice instructs us when it says: “No one knows who the Father is except the Son, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father” (Matthew XI, 27). It also declares him unchangeable and immutable like the Father, lacking nothing, perfect, and equal to the Father, who alone is ungenerated.

For he is the Father’s most complete and immutable image. An image must be wholly complete, so that nothing is lacking from its equality with the one whose image it is, as the Lord himself taught when he said: “My Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28), in accordance with the belief that the Son has always existed from the Father.

“For he is the radiance of glory and the figure of the Father’s substance” [ed. V., “subsistence”] (Hebrews I, 3).

But let no one take the word “always” as suggesting that the Son is ungenerated, as those whose minds are blinded suppose. For “was,” “always,” and “before the ages” are not the same as “ungenerated.” Nor can any human understanding, by whatever names human beings have assigned, indicate what we call “ungenerated.” I believe that you too understand this, and I am confident in the purpose of all of you: under no circumstances can the ungenerated be expressed by any names [ed., Niv. and Frob., “those declaring it”].

These names appear to be productive of temporal extension; nevertheless, they cannot adequately signify the divinity of the Only-Begotten or, so to speak, his antiquity. The holy men, each according to his own virtue, have tried to disclose this mystery, asking pardon from their hearers through reasonable explanations and saying of themselves: “We have brought forth what we were able to reach.”

But if any people expect something beyond the human level, and strive toward more exalted speech, having already supposed that the statement “We know in part” (I Corinthians XIII, 9) has been abolished, it is clear that they fall far short of their hope.

Therefore, whatever “was,” “always,” and “before the ages” may be, it is nevertheless not the same as “ungenerated.” The proper dignity of the ungenerated Father must therefore be preserved [ms. Lyr., “conferred”], and no cause for his existence asserted. But an honor suitable to the Son must be assigned.

Let us know that his birth from the Father is without beginning, and, as we said earlier, piously attribute worship to him, proclaiming in a sound understanding concerning him that he “was,” “always was,” and existed “before the ages.” We investigate his divinity, while devoting to the image and investigation of the Father perfect equality in all things.

We say that the Father’s sole distinctive property is that he is ungenerated, since the Savior himself said: “My Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28).

In this pious judgment concerning the Father and the Son, as the divine Scriptures teach us, we confess one Holy Spirit, who filled both the holy men of the Old Testament and the most sacred teachers of the New Testament.

We confess one and only catholic and apostolic Church, which has always been invincible, even if the whole world fights against it, and which is victorious over all opposing impiety. The head of its household makes us secure when he cries: “Have confidence: I have overcome the world” (John XVI, 33).

We know that this was accomplished after the resurrection from the dead, of which our Lord Jesus Christ became the firstfruits. He was clothed in true flesh and was not merely apparent flesh from Mary, the Mother of God. In the last times he came to the human race for the condemnation of sin, and was crucified and died; but for that reason he was not diminished in his divinity. For he rose from the dead, was taken up into heaven, and sits at the right hand of Majesty.

I have outlined these matters in part in this letter, considering it burdensome to write out each point with painstaking precision, since I know that your holy zeal is not ignorant of such things. These are what we teach; these are also what we preach; these are the dogmas of the apostolic Church. For them we also die, and we do not fear in the least those who wish to destroy them. Even if they extort these things from us by blows, we nevertheless do not abandon our hope.

Their opponents, therefore—Arius and Achillas, and the enemies of the truth who are with them—have been expelled far from the Church and made strangers to our pious doctrine, in accordance with the blessed Paul, who says: “Whoever announces to you anything beyond what you received, let him be anathema, even if he pretends to be an angel from heaven” (Galatians I, 8). He also speaks of anyone who is puffed up by other words of our Lord Jesus Christ and by the doctrine that accords with piety, knowing nothing, and so forth.

Therefore let none of you receive these men, who have been anathematized by the brotherhood, or allow yourselves to have anything that they say or write.

For, like magicians, they lie about everything, since they cannot speak the truth. Finally, they go about the cities doing nothing except, under the appearance and name of friendship and peace, giving and receiving letters through fabrications and flatteries, so that by these means they may lead astray the little women whom they have deceived.

Therefore turn away from these men, dearest ones, who presume so greatly against Christ, who have so openly undermined Christianity, who do not cease, as far as lies in them, to stir up persecutions against us amid judicial proceedings, and who strive to weaken the ineffable mystery of Christ’s birth [ed. V., “Christianity”]. Stand united with us and contend against their insane presumption, after the example of our fellow ministers, who were indignant and wrote to me against them, and who subscribed the letter that I also sent to you through my son the archdeacon [otherwise, “Architus the deacon”—uncertain], namely the priests of all Egypt and the Thebaid, as well as of Libya and Pentapolis, Syria, Pamphylia, Asia, Cappadocia, and other provinces. I am confident that you too will receive it after their example.

Since I have many remedies against those who cause harm, this useful medicine has also been discovered: the peoples deceived by them are turning back, now obeying our priests and hastening through them to repentance.

Greet the brotherhood that is among you mutually. I wish you health in the Lord, dearest ones.

Those who have been anathematized are these: among the presbyters, Arius; among the deacons, Achillas, Euzoius, Aithalis, Lucius, Sarmatius, Julius, Menas, another Arius, and Helladius.

He also sent a letter agreeing with these matters to Philogonius, bishop of the city of Antioch, and to Eustathius, who at that time governed the Church of Beroea, and to other defenders of the apostolic doctrines.

But Arius too did not remain quiet. For he himself wrote to those of like mind with him. Since the most sacred Alexander had written nothing false against him, Arius himself protested in a letter written to Eusebius of Nicomedia. I shall not omit inserting that letter, so that I may make those who shared in his impiety manifest to those who are ignorant of it.

THEODORET, Book I, chapter 4, p. 8.

## CHAPTER XV. Arius’s Letter to Eusebius

[Col. 0914B]

To my most desirable lord, the man of God, faithful and orthodox Eusebius: Arius, who unjustly suffers persecution from Alexander the pope on account of the truth that conquers all things—which you too defend—sends greetings in the Lord.

When my father Ammonius was coming to Nicomedia, I thought it reasonable to greet you through him, knowing both the love and the affection that you are recognized as having toward the brethren for God’s sake.

Bishop Alexander is violently laying waste to and persecuting us, and is stirring every kindly disposition against us, so much so that he would even have expelled us from the city as godless men, because we do not agree with him when he publicly says:

“Always God, always Son; Father together, Son together; the Son coexists with the ungenerated God; he has always been begotten; he was begotten from the ungenerated; God the Father does not precede him even in thought or by a single instant; the Son is always from God himself.”

And because your brother Eusebius of Caesarea, together with Theodotus, Paulinus, Athanasius, Gregory, Aetius, and all those throughout the East, say that God existed before the Son without beginning, they have been anathematized, except for Philogonius, Hellanicus, and Macarius—heretical and unlearned men. Some of these say that the Son is an effusion, others a proposition, and others co-generated.

We cannot even listen to such impieties, although the heretics threaten us with countless deaths.

But because we say, think, have taught, and teach that the Son is not ungenerated, nor in any way a part of the ungenerated, nor from anything underlying; rather, that by will and counsel he subsisted before times and before the ages as complete God, Only-Begotten, and mutable; and that before he was begotten, created, predestined, or established, he did not exist—for he was not ungenerated—we suffer persecution because we have said: “The Son has a beginning, but God is without beginning,” and because we have said: “He is from things that do not exist.”

We said this in the sense that he is neither a part of God nor from anything underlying; for this reason we suffer persecution.

For the rest, you know. I wish you health in the Lord, remembering our tribulations, truly Eusebius, fellow Lucianist—that is, piously.

Eusebius, then, was bishop of Caesarea; Theodotus of Laodicea; Paulinus of Tyre; Athanasius of Anazarbus; Gregory of Berytus; and Aetius of Lydda. Lydda is the city now called Diospolis.

Arius boasted that these men were of like mind with him. He called Philogonius, bishop of Antioch; Hellanicus of Tripolis; and Macarius of Jerusalem his enemies, and heaped accusations against them, because they proclaimed the Son eternal and existing before the ages, equal in honor with the Father and of the same substance.

When Eusebius had received this letter, he too vomited forth the poison of his impiety, writing as follows to Paulinus, bishop of Tyre.

THEODORET, Book I, chapter 5, p. 20.

## CHAPTER XVI. Eusebius’s Letter to Paulinus, Bishop of Tyre

[Col. 0915B]

To my lord Paulinus: Eusebius sends greetings in the Lord.

Nor has my lord Eusebius’s zeal for the truth of the Word remained hidden; it has reached us, and neither has your silence, my lord, concerning this matter remained hidden. As was fitting, therefore, we rejoiced in my lord Eusebius, but we grieve over you, believing that the silence of so great a man is our defeat [mss. and ed. V., “devotion”].

I therefore ask you, knowing that it is unbecoming for a wise man to hold other opinions and remain silent about the truth, to begin, moved by spiritual reasoning, to write about such matters, since this will be useful both to you and to those who hear you—especially if you wish to write everything according to the sequence of Scripture, the traces of his words, and his will [mss., “pleasure”].

For we have never heard of two ungenerated beings, nor of one divided into two. Nor have we learned or believed, my lord, that anything corporeal suffered; rather, that there is one ungenerated being and another truly from him, but not made from his substance—and, to speak generally, that the latter in no way participates in the ungenerated nature or exists from his substance, but was perfectly made, different in nature and power, insofar as concerns the complete likeness, disposition, and authority of the maker, made in an ineffable manner.

We judge and believe this to be incomprehensible not only to human thought but also to thought that is beyond all human beings.

We say these things not because we are bound by our own arguments, but because we learn them from Holy Scripture. Scripture teaches us that he was created, established, and begotten in substance, and that in nature, which is unchangeable and ineffable, he was made in the likeness of his maker, as the Lord himself says:

“The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways, for his works; before the ages he established me; before all the hills he begot me” (Proverbs VIII, 22).

If he were from him—that is, from the Father—as a part of him or from an outflow of his substance, he would certainly not be said to have been created or established. Nor are you unaware, my true lord, that to say that what exists from the ungenerated was already created by another, or by him, or established from the beginning, provides a kind of demonstration, as though he had been born from the Father’s substance and possessed equality of nature from him.

For we know that Scripture speaks of being begotten not only concerning one who is like him but also concerning those who are entirely unlike him in nature. For it says of human beings: “I begot sons and exalted them, but they themselves rejected me” (Isaiah I, 2); and again: “You abandoned the God who begot you” (Deuteronomy XXXII, 18). Another says: “Who begot the drops of dew?” (Job XXXVIII, 28). He is not describing nature from nature, but the birth of each creature from God’s will.

For they are not from his substance; rather, all things were made by his will, just as they were made. He is God; these things, made according to his likeness by the Word, came into being through spontaneous movement. And although all things were made by God through him, nevertheless all things are from God.

Understanding and explaining these matters according to the grace divinely given to you, hasten to write to my lord Alexander. For I am confident that if you write to him, he will be converted.

Greet all who are in the Lord. May the grace of God preserve you in health and prayer for us, my lord.

THEODORET, Book I, chapter 6.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the Power of Eusebius of Nicomedia

[Col. 0916B]

Such things they also wrote to one another, arming themselves for battle against the truth. The evil grew worse, fueling the fire of contention among those who received these writings. Accordingly, those who agreed with Alexander also subscribed to his letter, while others acted in the opposite manner. Above all, however, Eusebius of Nicomedia was stirred to opposition, because Alexander had spoken of him severely in his letter [Col. 0916C].

At that time Eusebius wielded considerable power, because the emperor was then residing at Nicomedia. For shortly before this, Diocletian and those around him had established the imperial court there. Consequently, many of the bishops obeyed Eusebius. He frequently wrote to Alexander, urging him to abandon the question that was causing the tumult and to receive Arius and his followers; and he wrote to the various bishops throughout the cities, urging them not to agree with Alexander’s writings. Thus everything was greatly disturbed. For it seemed that not only were the leaders of the Churches contending with one another in argument, but the people also were divided. Some sided with these men, others with those. The matter became so inflamed that Christianity was disparaged in public, even in the theatres themselves.

The men situated in Alexandria, as though they had already become victors over the earlier persecutions, were more vigorously armed and sent embassies to the provincial bishops; while those who had separated into the opposing party shared in their similar sedition.

SOCRATES, book I, chapter 3; editions of Christopherson and Valesius, chapter 6, [Col. 0916D] p. 13.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Meletians, how they were separated from the Church, and how, when Alexander refused to receive Arius, the Arians held councils in various places

The Meletians therefore joined the Arians (A.D. 315), although they had long before been separated from the Church. Who these men were must now be explained.

Under Peter, bishop of the city of Alexandria, who suffered martyrdom during the reign of Diocletian, a certain Meletius, bishop of one of the cities of Egypt, was deposed both for many other reasons and especially because, during the persecution, he had denied the faith and sacrificed. Accordingly, after he had been condemned, he acquired many followers and became the founder of the heresy of those who to this day are called Meletians in Egypt—having no just justification for remaining separated from the Church [Col. 0917A].

He claimed that he had suffered injustice, repeatedly spoke against Peter, and disparaged him. But Peter, having received the crown of martyrdom during the persecution, died. Meletius then directed his attacks against Achillas, who succeeded Peter in the episcopate, and again against Alexander, who is known to have been ordained after Achillas.

Meanwhile the Arian controversy arose, and Meletius, together with his followers, defended Arius, having entered into a conspiracy with him against the bishop. For all those to whom the sect of Arius seemed wicked always accepted Alexander’s judgment [ed., *super Ario*, “concerning Arius”], as though his decree against Arius’s adherents appeared to be just.

Those who were around Eusebius [Col. 0917B] of Nicomedia also wrote, as did others who approved Arius’s opinion, asking that the condemnation pronounced earlier be revoked and that the condemned men be restored to the Church, as though they professed nothing evil.

Thus, by sending various letters to the bishop of Alexandria, they made collections of these letters: Arius collected those that favored his cause, while Alexander collected those directed against Arius. From this arose the occasion for the contentions of the heresies that now fly about everywhere—namely, those of the Arians, the Eunomians, and all who bear the name of Macedonius. Each of these groups used the letters themselves as witnesses in defense of its heresy.

SOCRATES, book I, chapter 3; editions of Christopherson and Valesius, chapter 6, p. 14.

When those who were around Eusebius [Col. 0917C] repeatedly approached Alexander with petitions, yet failed to move him, they became malicious as though they had suffered an injury, and grew more zealous in strengthening Arius’s doctrine. They assembled a council in Bithynia and wrote to all the bishops, urging them to communicate with the Arians as though they were orthodox and to act so that Alexander too might communicate with them.

When their efforts failed because Alexander would not agree, Arius was sent as an embassy to Paulinus, bishop of Tyre; to Eusebius Pamphilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine; and to Patrophilus of Scythopolis. Together with his followers, he asked that they be ordered to celebrate the Church’s solemn sacraments with the people who were with him, since he had previously held the office of presbyter. He claimed that it was the custom in Alexandria—as it remains even now—that, although one bishop presided over all, the presbyters held separate churches and the people solemnly celebrated their assemblies in them [Col. 0917D].

At that time those bishops, gathered with other bishops in Palestine, issued the following decree concerning Arius’s petition: they ordered them to conduct their assemblies as before, but required them to remain subject to Alexander the bishop and always to entreat that they might enjoy his peace and communion.

When the heresy also spread throughout Egypt after many councils had been held, so that it reached even the imperial court, the emperor Constantine was greatly distressed. The religion had only recently begun to grow, yet the disagreement over doctrine was drawing many people away from Christianity [ms. Lyr., “he saw many disagreeing with the doctrine of Christianity”].

Therefore he blamed Arius and Alexander, and, writing to them, reproached them because, although this question could have remained hidden, they had brought it into the open and had stirred up with intense zeal a dispute that ought neither to have been sought nor contemplated from the beginning—or, rather, once contemplated, ought rightly to have been entrusted to silence—since they could not in any case have been separated [Col. 0918A] from one another, even if they disagreed in some part of their doctrine.

Thus he wrote to Alexander and Arius, sometimes blaming them and sometimes offering advice. It is not inappropriate to set down here part of his letter. The entire letter is included in the books of Eusebius, in the *Life of Constantine*.

SOZOMEN, book I, chapter 14; editions of Christopherson and Valesius, chapter 15, p. 427.

## 222 CHAPTER XIX. The letter of the emperor Constantine to Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, and to Arius, in which he urged them to return to peace

Victor Constantine Maximus, Pius, to Alexander and Arius.

[Col. 0918B]

I learned when the origin of the present controversy arose: when you, Alexander, were asking the presbyters what each of them thought about a certain passage written in the Law [ms. Lyr., “word”], or rather, which side of a certain vain question each preferred.

And you, Arius, rashly brought forward at once what ought not to have been contemplated in the first place and what, once contemplated, ought rather to have been committed to silence. From this, when disagreement arose between you, the mysteries are despised. The holy people, divided between the two sides, are separated from the harmony of the common body.

Therefore, let each of you equally offer your will in obedience to what your fellow servant rightly urges you to obey. It is neither worthy to ask such questions nor to answer those who inquire about them. Questions of this kind, which are not proposed by the necessity of any law, demand time that would otherwise be spent in useless leisure [Col. 0918C].

Even when they arise from someone’s natural intellectual exercise, we ought nevertheless to confine them within our own understanding, rather than readily carry them into public gatherings or carelessly commit them to everyone’s ears. For what human being is so great that he can either fully perceive or adequately interpret the power of matters so great and difficult? Or, if someone could do this—though with difficulty—to what portion of the people could he persuade them? Or who could sustain the subtleties of such questions without endangering himself through error?

Accordingly, in such matters we must avoid excessive speech, lest, while the weakness of our nature is unable adequately to explain what is proposed, and while the minds of those learning cannot attain a perfect understanding of the question because of their slower comprehension, the people be led into the necessity of blasphemy or schism [Col. 0918D].

Therefore, let both the careless questions and the imprudent answers receive equal pardon from each of you. The occasion of this quarrel was not inflamed among you by the supreme command of the Law, nor has some new heresy been introduced on behalf of the worship of God. You hold one and the same doctrine, just as you share one sign of communion.

Since, then, you are contending with one another over childish and very minor matters, it is neither fitting nor at all credible that you should cause so great a people of God—whom it is your duty to govern through your prayers and prudence—to disagree [Col. 0919A].

To remind your wisdom by a small example, you know that even the philosophers all agree in one doctrine. When they disagree in some part of an opinion, although they are distinguished by the excellence of their discipline, they nevertheless remain united with one another in bodily fellowship.

Since this is so, how much more just is it that you, ministers of the great God, should be united with one another in the purpose of religion? Let us therefore consider the matter with greater reason and think with a more expansive understanding: is it right that, because of small and empty verbal disputes, brothers should clash with brothers and that you should tear apart the honor of the council through impious contention, while you quarrel with one another over matters so small and entirely unnecessary?

These are commonplaces, more suited to the foolishness of children than consonant with the understanding of holy and prudent men [Col. 0919B].

Let us therefore willingly withdraw from diabolical temptations. Our great God, the Savior of all, has shone forth as the common light of everyone. By his providence, permit this effort of mine, ministers of God, to reach its fulfillment, so that through my address, service, and earnest admonition I may restore his people to synodal communion. For, as I have said, you possess one faith, one understanding of heresy according to your own account, and the commandment of the Law tends in its several parts toward the purpose of one will.

The matter that has stirred up contention among you does not concern the whole force of the Law and therefore ought not to produce separation and sedition between you. I say this not as though I were compelling you in every respect to agree with this entirely excellent question, whatever its character may be. For you can preserve the honor of the council intact and maintain one and the same communion among all, even if some particular dispute arises among you over a minor matter, since we do not all desire the same thing in every respect, nor is one nature present in us all, nor is one will recognized in us [Col. 0919C].

With respect to the divine providence, let there be among you one faith, one understanding, and one consent in God. As for the matters argued between you concerning these frivolous questions, even if they are not brought together into one opinion, they must nevertheless remain within your understanding, while the ineffability of the mind is preserved.

But the chief sacrament of common charity, the faith of the truth, and honor toward God and the religion of the Law must remain among you without disturbance.

Return, therefore, to friendship and favor toward one another; restore your embraces to the whole people; and, cleansing yourselves as though you were your own souls [ms. Lyr., “and cleansing yourselves before your friends”], recognize one another again. Friendships restored to harmony after causes of hostility are often sweeter [Col. 0919D].

Restore to me, then, tranquil days and secure nights, so that the joy of a certain delight in pure light and peaceful life may be preserved for me. Otherwise I shall be compelled to groan, to be weighed down continually by tears, and to endure unwillingly the wickedness of this age.

It is now time for the people of God—that is, my fellow servants—who have been so unjustly and harmfully divided by your contention, to be gathered together [Col. 0920A].

To make you understand the magnitude of my sorrow, listen. Not long ago, when I came to the city of the Nicomedians, I was suddenly hastening to proceed toward the East. As I was making my way toward you and was already, for the most part, with you, I was detained by the news of this affair, lest I should be forced to see with my own eyes what I had judged impossible for the ears even to hear.

Therefore, open to me now, through your concord, the roads of the East that you have closed against one another through contention [Col. 0920B]. Quickly grant me the opportunity to see you and all the other peoples rejoicing, and to offer to God, through favorable words, the thanksgiving owed for the common concord and freedom of all.

SOCRATES, book I, chapter 4; edition of Christopherson and Valesius, chapter 7, p. 15.

## 223 CHAPTER XX. How Constantine caused a council to be held at Nicaea both concerning the Arian controversy and concerning the determination of the feast of Easter

It is known that Constantine wrote these things to Alexander and Arius, sometimes blaming them and sometimes admonishing them. He was also deeply troubled when he heard that certain people were celebrating the feast of Easter contrary to the ordinance of all.

At that time, in certain cities of the East [Col. 0920C], some people were divided from one another on this matter, although they were not separated from one another in fellowship; nevertheless, they celebrated the Lord’s feast according to Jewish custom and, as usually happens, marred the splendor of the assembly by such a distinction.

The emperor therefore hastened to restore peace to the Church on both matters. Thinking that he could prevent the evil before it reached many people, he sent a man distinguished among those around him alike in faith and life, and approved by the doctrine of the confessions of earlier times, to address the Egyptians, who were in turmoil over doctrine, and the Easterners, who were divided over Easter.

This man was Hosius, bishop of the city of Corduba. But when the affair proceeded contrary to expectation, and the heresy proved stronger than the hoped-for peace, the man who had been sent for the peace of the Churches returned without accomplishing anything [Col. 0920D].

Then the emperor’s zeal stirred up that most famous council at Nicaea. He ordered the bishops and those accompanying them to come to the synod in public wagons, mules, and swift horses.

SOZOMEN, book I, chapter 15; edition of Christopherson and Valesius, chapter 16, p. 429.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0919]

## 224 CHAPTER I. On the leaders of the Churches who attended the Council of Nicaea

The following took part in the Council of Nicaea (A.D. 527): from the apostolic sees, Macarius of Jerusalem; [Col. 0920D] Eustathius, already presiding over the Church of Antioch on the Orontes; and Alexander of Alexandria, which is situated by Lake Mareotis.

Julius, bishop of Rome, was absent because of his old age; in his place there were present Vitus and Vincentius, presbyters of the same [Col. 0921A] Church.

Besides these, many other good and excellent men from various peoples gathered together. Some were exceptionally capable of understanding and speaking, trained in knowledge of the sacred books and in other learning, and distinguished by the virtue of their lives. Others were men highly approved in both respects. I consider it useful to mention even their names.

SOZOMEN, book I, chapter 16, edition of Christopherson.

They were, in the words of the holy Apostle, like those who bore the marks of the Lord Jesus in their bodies.

There was James at Antioch of Mygdonia, which the Syrians and Assyrians call Nisibis. He raised the dead, healed the living, and is proved to have performed countless other miracles. But I consider it superfluous to insert again into this work matters that I have narrated more fully in my history beloved of God [Col. 0921B].

Paul was from Neocaesarea, a fortress situated beside the banks of the Euphrates. Licinius’s fury had destroyed him. Both his hands had been bound and burned with heated iron, by which the nerves of his joints had been dried up and deprived of their movement.

Others had had their right eyes gouged out; others had had their right shins cut off. One of these was Paphnutius the Egyptian. In short, the people there appeared to be a company of Christ’s athletes and martyrs gathered together in one place.

Concerning these men Eusebius Pamphilus also speaks in this manner in the third book of the *Life of Constantine*.

THEODORET, book I, chapter 7, p. 24.

The foremost ministers of all the Churches that filled Europe, Libya, and Asia were gathered together [Col. 0921C]. Like a house of prayer enlarged inwardly by God, it contained all of them together in unity: Syrians, Cilicians, Phoenicians, Arabs, and Palestinians, among them Egyptians, Thebans, and Libyans, as well as those who came from Mesopotamia. Even a Persian bishop came to the council.

Nor was a Scythian absent from their company. Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, and Pamphylia supplied exceptionally distinguished men. Thracians, Macedonians, Achaeans, and Epirotes were present, as were those living farther inland among these peoples.

The famous Hosius of Spain was also there, sitting among the many. Alexander, the bishop of the imperial city, was absent because of his old age; the presbyters who were present filled his place.

Thus the one emperor, Constantine, adorning Christ’s crown with the bond of peace, dedicated to his Savior, God, a lesson in victory over enemies and foes; according to our understanding, he established an image of thanksgiving with apostolic acclamation [ed. and ms. Santheod., “a declaration”] [Col. 0921D].

Then that saying was fulfilled: “Men devoted to religion were gathered from all the nations under heaven, among them Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and those who inhabit Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the regions of 225 Libya near Cyrene, and visitors from Rome, Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs” (Acts 2:5, 9–11).

Yet one thing was lacking in those earlier people: unlike those gathered here, they did not all consist of ministers of God.

In the present assembly there was a multitude of bishops, exceeding three hundred in number, followed by presbyters, deacons, and acolytes, whose number could not be reckoned. Some of God’s ministers shone with the word of wisdom; others glittered through self-restraint and endurance of life; still others were adorned in moderate measure with these virtues [Col. 0922A].

Among them were men honored by the length of their service, and others distinguished by youth and strength of spirit, who had recently entered upon the course of this ministry. For all of them the emperor had generously ordered provisions to be supplied at public expense each day.

These matters concerning those who had gathered there were recounted by Eusebius Pamphilus. When the emperor had celebrated the festival of victory over Licinius, he himself also came to Nicaea.

Among the bishops, Paphnutius from Upper Thebaid and Spyridion of Cyprus were especially notable. I shall explain later why I have mentioned these men [Col. 0922B].

SOCRATES, book I, chapter 5; edition of Christopherson and Valesius, chapter 8, p. 19.

## CHAPTER II. On the petitions presented to the emperor and ordered by him to be burned, and on the discussion of Arius’s doctrine

There were present with the bishops men experienced in disputation and eloquent in speech, eager to benefit the council.

As usually happens, many priests had gathered as though to contend for their own causes and thought they had found an opportunity to correct what distressed them. Each man, perhaps blaming another for some offense, presented a petition to the emperor and described in it the matters that had been committed by the other.

Since this happened easily every day, the emperor ordered that on a fixed day each person should make public the charges [Col. 0922C] by which he blamed another.

When the appointed day arrived, he received the petitions that had been presented and said:

“These accusations will have their proper time—that is, the day of the great judgment—and their Judge will be the one who will then judge all things. But I, a human being, am not permitted to hold a hearing concerning such matters, with priests serving at once as accusers and accused, when they ought by no means to be shown as men who must be judged by others.

“Come, then: imitating divine clemency, let us pardon one another and abolish the accusations against one another. Let us devote ourselves to matters pertaining to the faith, for the sake of which we have gathered here.”

After saying this, the emperor declared that each written accusation was void and ordered the petitions to be burned. He also fixed a day on which it would be appropriate to resolve the matters that were uncertain [Col. 0922D].

Before that appointed day, however, the bishops gathered among themselves and summoned Arius. They discussed together the opinions he had put forward and subjected them to careful examination.

As usually happens, when the matter was drawn into various questions, some argued that nothing should be changed concerning the ancient tradition of the faith, especially when the simplicity of conduct had been handed down without investigation to those approaching the mystery of the faith.

Others replied that the opinions of the ancients ought not to be followed without examination.

Many of the bishops who had then assembled, and of the clergy who followed them, were skilled in disputation and distinguished for their training in such rhetorical forms. They became known to the emperor and to those around him.

Among them was Athanasius, then still a deacon and serving with Bishop Alexander [Col. 0923A]. He appeared to be one of the principal participants in this activity. Some Greek philosophers also took part at suitable points in these discussions: some seeking to understand what kind of doctrine this was; others, hostile to the Christians because the religion of the Greeks was newly beginning to decline, dragging the mysteries of Christian doctrine into verbal quarrels, so that they stirred up disputes against one another, engaged in contests among themselves, and repeatedly argued in opposition.

SOZOMEN, book I, chapter 16; edition of Christopherson and Valesius, chapter 17, p. 430.

## CHAPTER III. How a simple lay confessor overcame a dialectician, and how a simple old man expounded Christian doctrine to a philosopher

[Col. 0923B]

When many were being drawn along by the pleasure of disputation, one of the lay confessors, possessing a simple understanding, confronted the dialecticians and said:

“Listen, then. Christ and the apostles did not hand down to us the art of dialectic and the empty deceit of words, but pure knowledge [ms. Lyr., “conscience”], to be observed through faith and good works.”

When the young man, old in spirit, had said this, those present were astonished and approved his statement. The dialecticians, having received the answer, ceased, for they had heard a simple account of the truth [Col. 0923B].

SOCRATES, book I, chapter 5; edition of Christopherson and Valesius, chapter 8, p. 20.

Another incident is also reported. When one of the philosophers was exalting himself through the magnificence of his speech and mocking the priests, a certain simple, innocent, and exceptionally worthy old confessor could not tolerate his arrogance [ms. Lyr., “deed”]. He came forward to speak against him [Col. 0923C].

This action caused laughter among the insolent and among those who knew the simple confessor, but it inspired fear in the more mature, who foresaw that the man might be led into ridicule by one skilled in words. Nevertheless, they yielded and allowed him to say what he wished; for, since he was such a man, they were exceedingly reluctant to oppose him.

“In the name of Jesus Christ, O philosopher,” he said, “hear the doctrines of the truth. There is one God, Creator of heaven and earth and of all things visible and invisible. By the power of his Word he made all these things and established them by the holiness of his Spirit.

“This Word, whom we call the Son of God, having taken pity on human beings, freed them from error and savage religion. He suffered to be born from a woman, lived among human beings, and died for them; and he will come again to judge the life of each person.

“We believe that these things are so without investigation. Do not therefore labor in vain, seeking to destroy what we have received by faith. Do not investigate the manner in which these things could or could not have happened. If you believe me, who offer you this counsel, answer these matters.”

The philosopher, astonished, replied: “I believe.”

Then, giving thanks for his defeat, he embraced the same position as the old man [ms. Lyr., “testified the same as the old man”] and persuaded his former companions to be of one mind with one another. He swore that he had not changed his position rashly, but had immediately been invited to Christianity by some ineffable power. 226

SOZOMEN, book I, chapter 17; edition of Christopherson and Valesius, chapter 18, p. 431.

## CHAPTER IV. How Alexander, bishop of Constantinople, silenced a pagan philosopher in debate

[Col. 0924A]

It is said that something resembling this miracle occurred through Alexander, bishop of the city of Constantinople [Col. 0924A].

When the emperor Constantine came to Byzantium, certain philosophers approached him and complained that he did not worship God as he ought and was introducing innovations into sacred matters by bringing a new religious practice into the state, contrary to what his ancestors and the rulers of the Greeks and Romans in past ages had considered and approved.

They wished to dispute with Bishop Alexander concerning doctrine. He, however, was inexperienced in this kind of verbal exercise and relied upon the quality of his life [Col. 0924B]. For he was a great man, admirable in his conduct.

When, at the emperor’s command, he accepted the challenge, and the philosophers had assembled, all of them wishing to speak, our father Alexander of holy memory asked them to choose from among themselves whichever one they wished. He ordered all the rest, whoever they might be, to keep silent and to attend only to what was said by each side.

When one of them undertook the business of the entire dispute, Saint Alexander said to the philosopher:

“In the name of Jesus Christ, I command you first of all not to speak.”

With these words the deed was accomplished. As soon as that man heard the command, his mouth was bound and he became silent.

Which would be more fitting to consider as the greater miracle: that a human being, and a philosopher at that, should so easily lose the faculty of speech, or that a stone should be split by the force of a word, which some say Julian the Chaldean accomplished [Col. 0924C]?

These events took place as they are reported.

SOZOMEN, book I, chapter 17; edition of Christopherson and Valesius, chapter 18, p. 432.

## CHAPTER V. On the first session of the bishops in the palace at Nicaea, and on the deposition of Arius

Meanwhile the priests frequently assembled and brought Arius forward for examination, conducting a careful investigation of his propositions. They were afraid to express an opinion rashly in either direction [Col. 0924D].

This sacred and venerable company did not appear free from the mixture of adversaries. Among them were certain men—few indeed, but cunning—who concealed their cleverness while imitating brevity, and who did not openly defend Arius’s blasphemy.

When everyone had assembled, the emperor prepared a great hall in the imperial residence and ordered seats and benches to be placed in it sufficient for the rank of the priests. Thus he prepared for them an honor appropriate to their dignity, invited them to enter, and asked them to deliberate about the matters before them [editions of Niv. and Frob., “to hold a council”].

The emperor himself entered last with a few attendants. His greatness was worthy of praise, his appearance remarkable, and his dignity even more remarkable, with a noble modesty displayed upon his face.

A seat smaller than those of the others was placed for him, and he sat in their midst, first asking that this be granted him by the command of the bishops. Then that most holy assembly sat down with him [Col. 0925A].

First came the great Eustathius, who had received the episcopate of the Church of Antioch. Philogonius, whom we mentioned earlier, had already passed to the better life, and the bishops, priests, and the entire Christian people had compelled this remarkable man, even against his will, to assume the governance of that Church by common decision.

Eustathius therefore adorned the emperor’s head with flowers of praise and offered him blessings for his zeal concerning sacred matters.

After him came Eusebius, surnamed Pamphilus.

When these men had taken their seats, the famous emperor delivered a speech on unanimity and concord, reminding them of the cruelty of the tyrants and of the honorable peace that had been divinely bestowed under his rule. He also pointed out how wicked and exceedingly cruel it would seem if, after the enemies had been destroyed and no one dared to resist, priests should hurl accusations at one another and confuse one another, providing amusement and laughter for impious and godless people.

This was especially so since they were treating of divine matters and had the teaching of the Holy Spirit in written form. “For,” he said, “there are the books of the Gospel and of the apostles, and the ordinances of the ancient prophets, which teach us what we ought to think concerning the sacred Law.

“Let us therefore drive hostile contention from the words inspired by God and receive in our minds the resolution of these questions [Col. 0925B].”

The emperor offered these and similar words to the priests as a son who loves his father offers them to fathers, striving to destroy the discord among the apostolic doctrines [editions of Niv. and Frob., “to reconcile concord”].

Most of the council obeyed what was said and willingly embraced unanimity among themselves and the soundness of doctrine.

A few men, whom we have already mentioned, and in addition Minophantus of Ephesus, Patrophilus of Scythopolis, Theognius, bishop of Nicaea, Narcissus of Neronias—which is in Cilicia Secunda and is now called Irenopolis—and, with them, Theonas of Marmarica and Secundus of Ptolemais in Egypt, resisted the apostolic doctrines and defended Arius [Col. 0925C].

They drafted a statement of faith and handed it to the assembled company. When it had been read by everyone, it was suddenly torn apart and declared adulterated and fraudulent.

When the whole crowd raised a tumult against them and everyone accused them of betraying piety, they rose in fear and were the first to depose Arius, with the exception of Secundus and Theonas.

When that impious man had been overthrown, all the others unanimously drafted the faith and confession of glory that has remained in the Churches to this day, strengthened it with their subscriptions, and dissolved the council.

Nevertheless, the men mentioned above assented to the conclusion of the faith deceitfully and in an unsound manner [Col. 0925D], as is shown both by the schemes they later devised against the defenders of piety and by what they are known to have written themselves.

THEODORET, book I, chapter 7, p. 24.

## CHAPTER VI. The account of Eustathius, bishop of Antioch, concerning the Council of Nicaea
