Eustathius, bishop of Antioch, whom I mentioned at the beginning, reported the following concerning them, explaining what had happened and refuting their blasphemies. 227 In this account he also interprets the proverbial saying: “The Lord created me at the beginning [ed., ‘as the beginning’] of his ways, for his works” (Proverbs 8:22).

I shall now proceed from this point to the events that took place.

When, because of these matters, the great synod had come to the city of Nicaea [Col. 0926A] and the standard of the faith was being sought, Eusebius, with open shamelessness, produced a blasphemous document. When it was read aloud before everyone, it suddenly inflicted an unbearable disaster of division upon those who heard it, while providing its author with an incurable disgrace.

When the workshop had been captured, Eusebius’s document of iniquity was unmistakably torn apart in the presence of all. Certain men, explaining the name of peace from the treatise, restrained the others, although everyone was making a just complaint.

The Arians, fearing that they would be expelled by the great council gathered there, leapt up and anathematized the condemned doctrine of Arius. They subscribed unanimously to the document, assented with their own hands, and professed that they thought alike with the entire synod.

When they had prevailed over the bishops, so to speak, by the evil art of cunning, although they ought rather to have done penance, they began at first secretly and later openly to invoke opinions that had been condemned. They repeatedly laid traps for those by whom they seemed to have been convicted and wished to establish the shoots of tares.

At that time, fearing and avoiding the investigators of so great a council, they later attempted secretly to attack the preachers of piety. But we do not believe that godless men can prevail against the sacred, venerable, and evangelical teaching.

For even if they are strengthened greatly, they are again overcome with strength and magnificence, according to the prophetic voice of the glorious Isaiah [Col. 0926C].

Thus far the great Eustathius.

THEODORET, book I, chapter 8; edition of Christopherson and Valesius, chapter 7, p. 26.

## CHAPTER VII. Athanasius’s account to the Africans
Athanasius, champion of this cause and tower of the bulwark of truth, successor of the renowned bishop Alexander, when he wrote to the Africans, added the following as well:

“For the bishops, when they met, endeavored to destroy the words of impiety invented by the Arians—namely, ‘from things that do not exist’; and what they said, that the Son was a creature and a work; and ‘there was once when he was not’; and that he is of a mutable nature. But they set forth the clear expressions of the Scriptures: that the Son is naturally the only-begotten from God, the Word, Power, and Wisdom of the Father alone, true God, as John says; and, as Paul wrote, ‘the radiance of glory and the exact representation of substance’ (Hebr. I, 13), teaching that he is the Son of the Father.

“But those who were around Eusebius, driven by their own madness, spoke among themselves and said: ‘Let us agree, for we too are from God. There is one God, from whom are all things; and, “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new from God” (II Cor. V, 17).’ They also considered what is written in the Shepherd: ‘First of all, believe that there is one God, who created and completed all things, and established them from what did not exist, so that they might exist.’

“But the other bishops, seeing their wickedness and the worst artifice of their impiety, said more openly and, so to speak, more explicitly—or rather, they wrote—that the Son is ‘from God,’ that is, from the substance of the Father. Thus creatures, because they do not possess existence from themselves but have a beginning of existence, are said to be from God; whereas the Son alone is believed to be properly from the substance of the Father. For this is proper to the Only-Begotten and to the true Word of the Father. This, then, was the reason why he was said to be from the substance of the Father.

“Again, when the bishops asked a few of those who were thought to be Arians whether they said that the Son was not a creature but the Father’s sole Power and Wisdom, his eternal Image, in every respect not dissimilar to the Father, and true God, those who were around Eusebius were caught as they indicated to one another that these things also applied to us: ‘For we too,’ they said, ‘are called the image and glory of God. For it is said and has been said concerning us: “Always we who live,” and, “There are many powers”; and, “Every power of God went out from the land of Egypt”; and the locust too is called “a great power”; and again, “The Lord of powers is with us” (Ps. XLV, 8). But we too are properly God’s. We possess this not simply, since he also called us brothers. If they call the Son true God as well, this does not trouble us. For he became true.’

“This is the corrupt mind of the Arians. But the bishops themselves, seeing their deceit, gathered from the Scriptures that ‘radiance,’ ‘source,’ ‘river,’ and ‘image’ pertain to substance; and also, ‘In your light we shall see light’ (Ps. XXXV, 10); and, ‘I and the Father are one’ (John X, 30). And now, more clearly and briefly, they wrote that the Son is consubstantial with the Father. For all the expressions mentioned above have this meaning.

“Their murmuring—as though these words had not been taken from the authority of the Scriptures—is thereby also shown to be empty. For they themselves impiously put forward expressions not found in writing, since they are nowhere at all discovered: ‘from things that do not exist,’ and ‘there was once when he was not’; yet they blame others. Therefore they were condemned on account of unwritten expressions, though understood in a pious sense. They themselves, as though finding these things in dung [ed., Niv. and Frob.: ‘crawling’], spoke words that truly came from the earth.

“But the bishops did not invent the words for themselves; they had them from the Fathers and wrote down the testimonies. For nearly one hundred and thirty ancient priests before them, of the great city of Rome and of our own city, condemned all who said that the Son was a work or creature and not consubstantial with the Father.

“Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, also knew this. At first he defended the Arian sect, but at the end subscribed to the Council of Nicaea. He also wrote to his fellow citizens, affirming that he had recognized certain learned and distinguished ancient bishops and writers who had used the name ‘consubstantial’ in speaking of the divinity of the Father and the Son.

“Thus, fearing the council, these men agreed to the faith that had been set forth, in accordance with the prophet’s rebuke, who says: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me’ (Isa. XXIX, 13). Theonas and Secundus, however, refused to comply and were condemned. Afterwards, when they came to the council, they wrote twenty regulations concerning ecclesiastical conduct.”

THEODORETUS, book I, chapter 8, p. 27.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Sabinus, bishop of the Macedonians.

Let us not believe Sabinus, who called them ignorant and inexperienced. For Sabinus, bishop of the Macedonians at Heraclea in Thrace, having assembled a collection of what had been produced in writing by 228 priests in various councils, disparaged those who had gathered at Nicaea as ignorant and simple-minded. He did not perceive that he was also thereby disparaging Eusebius himself, who confessed the faith with much proof, as an ignoramus. He passed over some matters because he wished to do so, and softened others; nevertheless, he took everything according to his own intention.

He praises Eusebius Pamphili as a witness worthy of faith, and at the same time praises the emperor as one who laid down the doctrines of the Christians. But he censures the faith set forth at Nicaea as having been handed down by ignorant people who knew nothing; and the very man whom he was accustomed to call wise and a witness without deceit, he voluntarily despises.

For Eusebius says: “Of the men of God who gathered at Nicaea, some shone with the discourse of wisdom, while others were praised for the restraint of their life; and, since the emperor was present, he showed them all to be harmonious and followers of his unity.””

Thus the contradictory statements of Sabinus, and likewise of Eusebius and their associates, are recognized as contradicting one another. If the need arises anywhere, we shall speak further about Sabinus.

The harmony of faith brought forth by the great council at Nicaea and praised by Eusebius in a clear voice is as follows.

SOCRATES, book I, chapter 5. Edition of Christophorus Valesius, chapter 8, p. 22.

## CHAPTER IX. On the faith of the Council of Nicaea.

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father, only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth.

Who for us human beings and for our salvation came down, and was incarnate and became human; he suffered, rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was when he was not,” or, “He was not before he was made,” or, “He was made from things that did not exist,” or who say that he is from another substance or essence, or call the Son of God created or mutable—such persons the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes.

This venerable faith three hundred and eighteen men both acknowledged and embraced; and, as Eusebius says, they explained it in writing, harmonious and unanimous. Only five did not accept it, criticizing the word “consubstantial”: Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia; Theogonius of Nicaea; Mares of Chalcedon; Theonas of Marmarica; and Secundus of Ptolemais. They said that “consubstantial” meant what comes from something either by division, by flowing forth, or by planting: by planting, as a shoot comes from a root; by flowing forth, as sons come from a father; and by division, as two or three rings come from a mass of gold. “The Son of God,” they said, “is none of these.”

Therefore they said that agreement should not be given to the faith. For, strongly disparaging the word “consubstantial,” the men mentioned above refused to subscribe to the deposition of Arius. Accordingly, the synod anathematized Arius and all his adherents, adding that he should not even enter Alexandria. And, by the emperor’s command, Arius himself, those around Eusebius and Theogonius, and those who were with them were suddenly sent into exile.

SOCRATES, book I, chapter 5. Edition of Christophorus Valesius, chapter 8, p. 22.

## CHAPTER X. How Eusebius and Theogonius were received after submitting a written plea of repentance.

After a short period of exile, Eusebius and Theogonius presented a written plea of repentance and agreed with the faith of consubstantiality, as we shall explain in what follows. At that time, however, in the synod, Eusebius, surnamed Pamphili, who had obtained the episcopate of Caesarea in Palestine, paused briefly to consider whether the definition of faith ought to be accepted. Together with all the others—that is, with the entire assembly—he agreed and subscribed. He also wrote to the people placed under his diocese concerning the definition of faith and sent the document everywhere, carefully interpreting the name “consubstantial,” so that no one could have any suspicion against it.

The words written by Eusebius himself were as follows.

SOCRATES, book I, chapter 5. Edition of Christophorus Valesius, chapter 8, p. 23.

## CHAPTER XI. Letter of Eusebius Pamphili concerning the faith of the Council of Nicaea, addressed to the Palestinians.

We suppose, beloved, that you too have learned from other sources that the customary report has already gone ahead of the full account of what has taken place. But, so that the truth may not be reported to you otherwise on the basis of such hearsay, we have necessarily sent you first the written statement of the faith proposed by us. For when our Lord also sent his disciples to preach, he said: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19).

Concerning these matters we affirm that they stand thus and are thus understood; indeed, that they have long stood thus and been so understood, and that we shall persist in this faith until death, anathematizing every godless heresy. We testify truthfully before almighty God and our Lord Jesus Christ that we have understood and held all these things in our heart and soul from the time when we came to know ourselves, and that we now understand and profess them. We shall demonstrate this by proofs and satisfy you that in former times also we believed and preached in this way.

Once this faith had been set forth by us, no room for resistance remained. But our first, God-beloved emperor himself also testified that it was entirely correct, and professed that he understood it in this way. He ordered everyone to agree, subscribe, and be united in these doctrines, with only one word written and inserted: “consubstantial.”

He himself also interpreted it, saying that “consubstantial” is not spoken according to bodily passions, nor according to division, nor according to some separation by which the Son would subsist from the Father. For it is impossible to understand an incorporeal nature without matter as subsisting through some bodily passion. Rather, the term must be understood according to certain sacred and ineffable principles. Thus the very wise and pious emperor reasoned.

After the explanation of the faith had been dictated, the expressions “from the substance of the Father” and “consubstantial with the Father” were not left without examination. For consultations and answers followed, and the mind investigated the meaning of the words.

They therefore agreed that what they were saying concerning “substance” signified indeed that the Son was from the Father, but not that he was a part of the Father. Consequently, it also seemed right to us to agree in mind with the pious teaching that the Son is from the Father, but is not a part of his substance.

Therefore we too agreed in mind, neither rejecting the word “consubstantial” nor losing sight of the intention of peace that had been set before our eyes and of the most correct understanding. In the same way we accepted the expressions “begotten” and “not made.” For they said that “made” was a term common to the work of the other creatures made through the Son, and we confess and preach that the Son has nothing similar to them. Therefore we do not say that he is a work, in the manner of those things known to have been made through him, but that he is superior in substance to the whole creation, whom the divine utterances appear to teach was begotten from the Father, the mode of generation for the maker of all nature being inexpressible and inconceivable [ed., Niv. and Frob.: “for created nature”].

Thus a reasoned examination also recognizes that the Son is consubstantial with the Father, not according to the manner of bodies nor as resembling mortal living beings. For this is not through division of substance, nor through diminution [ed., “perfection”] or change of the Father’s substance or power. The unbegotten nature of the Father is foreign to all these things.

Rather, one must preach that the Son is consubstantial with the Father because the Son of God has no equality with created things, but is in every respect like the Father who begot him; and because he is not from any other substance or essence, but from the Father’s.

This interpretation also seemed rightly suited to agreement, because we recognized that certain ancient bishops and eloquent and distinguished writers had used the name “consubstantial” in the theology of the Father and the Son—that is, in their divine reasoning.

Let this suffice concerning the faith that was set forth, in which we all agreed—not without examination, but in accordance with the meanings explained before the God-beloved emperor himself, who examined them, and in harmony with the arguments stated above. After the faith, we believed that the anathema pronounced against them was not distressing, because it prohibited the use of words not found in Scripture. For this reason almost complete confusion and disorder arose in all the churches. Since no divinely inspired Scripture says “from things that do not exist,” or “there was once when he was not,” or the other expressions they produced, it seemed irrational to us to say or teach such things, since we had never previously been accustomed to use such language.

We have necessarily written all this to you, beloved, making known to you the judgment of our examination and our agreement. For, although at that time certain written statements offended us in other ways, later we accepted without distress what was in them beyond doubt. Therefore, after magnanimously examining the meaning of the words, we resolved to agree with what had been confessed by us in the exposition of the faith.

Thus Eusebius Pamphili explained these matters in a letter to Caesarea in Palestine. To the Church of Alexandria, to Egypt, Libya, Pentapolis, and the neighboring regions, the council wrote the following by common decree.

SOCRATES, book I, chapter 5. Edition of Christophorus Valesius, chapter 8, p. 23.

## CHAPTER XII. Letter of the Council of Nicaea sent to Alexandria and Egypt.

To the holy and great Church of Alexandria, established by the grace of God, and to the beloved brothers throughout Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis: the bishops gathered at Nicaea and celebrating the great and holy synod send greetings in the Lord.

Since, by the grace of God and of our most God-loving prince Constantine, who gathered us in the city mentioned above from various provinces and cities, a great and holy synod has been celebrated, it seemed altogether necessary that this holy and sacred council should also send a letter to you, so that you may know what matters were raised and examined, and what matters were approved and confirmed.

First of all, the impious, unjust, and godless doctrines of Arius and those who agreed with him were investigated in the presence of our most God-loving emperor Constantine. By the decision of all, it pleased the council to anathematize his impious, unjust, and godless sect, together with the words and names that he used in blaspheming the Son of God and saying that he was “from things that do not exist,” and again, “There was once when he was not.” For how was he, or how again was he not? And, saying that the Son of God was capable, by free choice, of wickedness and virtue, they called him a creature and a work.

The holy and universal council therefore anathematized all these foolish, childish, and blasphemous notions, and did not lend an ear or give its understanding even to the impious sect and this madness or to the meaning of its unjust expressions. What happened to them and what end their affairs had, you have either already heard or will hear; lest we seem to speak against a man who bears punishments deserving of his crime.

His impiety had such force that even Theonas of Marmarica and Secundus of Ptolemais adopted it. They too were condemned.

But since the ineffable grace of God, destroying by the admonition mentioned above those evil sects, blasphemies, discord, audacity of persons, and division, has freed Egypt from them, there remain the things done through the insolence of Meletius and those ordained by him. We therefore make known to you, beloved brothers, what the synod has also decided concerning this matter.

It pleased the merciful council that Meletius, although by strict and true judgment he deserved no pardon, should remain in his own city but should possess no authority whatsoever—neither to elect nor to ordain—and should not be seen in the province or in any city, possessing only the bare name.

Those whom he ordained, however, are to retain the honor and ministry confirmed by their mystical ordination, but in every respect are to remain subordinate to all those ordained in the individual parishes and churches by our most beloved fellow minister Alexander. They are to have no authority to elect persons of their choice, to put their names forward, or to do anything at all apart from the will of Alexander, bishop of the catholic Church.

For those who, by the grace of God and your prayers, have been found in no schism but remain without blemish in the catholic and apostolic Church ought to have authority to elect anyone and to present the names of those worthy of the clergy, and freely to do everything according to the law and regulations of the Church.

If someone should happen to rest in the Church, then those who have recently been admitted may be advanced to the honor of the deceased, provided that they appear worthy and the people elect them, with the bishop of the great city of Alexandria simultaneously deciding and confirming the matter.

This has been granted to all the others. In the case of Meletius, however, the same arrangement was by no means approved, because of his former disorder, his insolence, and his willful arrogance, so that no authority or power might be granted to a man capable of again organizing the same disorders.

These are the principal matters relevant to Egypt and to the most holy Church of the Alexandrians. If anything else has been arranged or decreed, our lord, most beloved fellow minister and brother Alexander, who was present and participated in the proceedings, will be able to explain it to you more precisely, since he was an author of the acts and a participant in them.

We also announce to you the agreement concerning the most holy Pascha: through your prayers this matter too has been settled, so that all the Eastern brothers who formerly celebrated it with the Jews must from this time celebrate it in agreement with the Romans, with you, and with all who have observed Pascha from the beginning.

Therefore, rejoicing in what has been accomplished, in common peace and concord, and in the fact that every heresy has been torn out by the roots, receive with greater honor and fuller affection our fellow minister, your bishop Alexander, who gladdened us by his presence and endured so great a labor for your peace even in his advanced age.

Pray together for us all, that what has been rightly approved may remain firm through our Lord Jesus Christ, having been accomplished according to the good will of God the Father in the Holy Spirit, to whom be glory for ever. Amen.

THE ETERNAL CONSUBSTANTIAL TRINITY IS GOD.

THEODORETUS, book I, chapter 9. Edition of Christophorus Valesius, chapter 6, p. 30.—SOCRATES, book I, chapter 6. Edition of Christophorus Valesius, chapter 9, p. 27.

## CHAPTER XIII. That Constantine summoned Acesius, bishop of the Novatians, to the council.

From this letter of the synod it is clear that they anathematized not only Arius and his associates but also the words of his sect, and that, while agreeing concerning Pascha, they received the arch-heretic Meletius.

The emperor’s zeal moves me to preserve the memory of his intention in another matter as well, and to show how he thought about concord. In his concern for the peace of the churches, he summoned to the synod Acesius, bishop of the religious body of the Novatians.

After the definition of the faith had been written and subscribed by the council, the emperor asked Acesius whether he too agreed with the faith and with the definition of the feast of Pascha.

He replied: “The synod, O emperor, has defined nothing new. For long ago, and from the time of the apostles, I myself received both this definition of the faith and the appointed time of the Paschal feast.”

When the emperor asked him again, “Why, then, do you separate yourself from communion?” Acesius recounted what had happened during the persecution under Decius and brought forward the strictness of his very severe rule: those who sin after baptism with the sin that divine Scripture declares to be unto death ought not to be made worthy of communion in the sacraments. They should indeed be invited to repentance, but they should look for hope of forgiveness not from priests but from God alone, who has the power to forgive sins.

When Acesius had said this, the emperor replied: “O Acesius, set up a ladder, and, if you can, climb into heaven by yourself.”

Neither Eusebius Pamphili nor the others said these things. I heard them from a man who was by no means a liar, who was very old and who reported them as one who had seen what had taken place at the council.

SOCRATES, book I, chapter 6. Edition of Christophorus Valesius, chapter 9, p. 29.

## CHAPTER XIV. That ecclesiastical canons were written at Nicaea, and concerning Constantine’s twentieth anniversary.

The synod, wishing to correct the conduct of people and of those dwelling in the churches, established laws that we call canons. In the discussion of these, some proposed introducing a law that bishops, presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons should not sleep with the wives whom they had married before their ordination.

But Paphnutius the Confessor rose in the midst of them and objected. He declared marriage honorable and said that intercourse with one’s own wife is chastity. He urged the council not to establish such a law, asserting that it would be a grave matter if the law became an occasion of fornication either for the men themselves or for their wives.

Paphnutius explained these matters, although he himself had no experience of marriage. The synod praised his judgment and enacted nothing on this point, but left it to each person’s will rather than imposing it as a necessity.

SOZOMEN, book I, chapter 22. Edition of Christophorus Valesius, chapter 23, p. 437.

When the council had arranged these matters in this way, Constantine’s twentieth anniversary came around. It is the custom of the Romans to celebrate each decade of the emperors’ reigns with a public festival.

Constantine therefore judged the occasion suitable and invited the synod to a banquet, honoring it with appropriate gifts. After exhorting them concerning harmony of faith and mutual peace, and asking for their prayers, he bade farewell to everyone at Nicaea. He wrote to those who had been absent about what had been accomplished at the council, inviting them to withdraw from every disagreement and to agree in the faith set forth by the council. This faith seemed to be nothing other than the judgment of God, established by the Holy Spirit through the agreement of so many and such distinguished priests, and confirmed after the most careful inquiry and examination of every doubt.

SOZOMEN, book I, chapter 23. Edition of Christophorus Valesius, chapter 25, p. 438.

## CHAPTER XV. Constantine’s letter concerning Arius and his writings.

Victor Constantine the Great, Augustus, to the bishops and people.

Arius imitated wicked and impious men, and it is fitting that he should also receive their punishment. Thus Porphyry, the enemy of divine piety, who produced wicked books against religion, deservedly met with a fitting reward, one that would make him a disgrace for the future and fill him with the greatest infamy.

Now, therefore, it has pleased us that Arius and his adherents should be called Porphyrians, so that they may enjoy the name of those whose conduct they have imitated.

Moreover, if any writing composed by Arius is found, let it be committed to the fire, so that not only may his wicked teaching perish, but none of his writings may remain. I also command that, if anyone is discovered to have concealed any of Arius’s writings and does not immediately produce them and burn them, he shall be subject to the penalty of death. As soon as he is caught in this matter, he shall suffer capital punishment.

May God preserve you. Amen.

SOCRATES, book I, chapter 6. Edition of Christophorus Valesius, chapter 15, p. 32.

## CHAPTER XVI. The same emperor’s letter to Eusebius of Palestine concerning the production of sacred books and the cleansing of the Lord’s tomb.

Victor Constantine the Great, Pius, to Eusebius.

Since, by the provident assistance of our God and Savior, we have learned that a very great multitude of people in the city bearing our name has devoted itself to the most holy Church, and since this growth is advancing so greatly that it seems fitting that more churches should also be built there, it is appropriate that we make our will known to your wisdom.

Therefore see to it that fifty well-prepared and serviceable parchment codices be written by skilled antiquarian craftsmen who thoroughly understand their art—namely, copies of the divine Scriptures, whose production and use you know to be especially necessary for the churches.

Letters have been sent from our tranquillity to the governor of the province, so that he may ensure that everything necessary for their production is supplied. Your diligence will be required so that the codices may be completed and prepared more quickly. You should also receive, by the authority of our rescript, two public vehicles for transporting them.

In this way, the well-written codices will be brought to our presence, with one deacon of your Church carrying out this task. When he comes to us, he will experience the generosity of our piety.

May God preserve you, dearest brother.

These matters are sufficient to suggest, and indeed to show more clearly, how the renowned emperor established his devotion concerning sacred things. Nevertheless, I shall add what he also did concerning the saving tomb.

For he recognized that the arrogant pagans, drunken with the worship of idols, had covered the Lord’s tomb with filth, striving to consign its saving memory to oblivion. Above it they had built a temple of the most wanton demon, Venus, so that there they might mock it with the songs of virgins. He ordered the most criminal temple to be destroyed, the soil polluted by its abominable sacrifices to be cast out, and it to be scattered far from the city.

Then he ordered a shrine to be built for God, the greatest and most beautiful, as is shown by his letter sent to Macarius, bishop of that city.

THEODORETUS, book I, chapter 16, p. 45.

## CHAPTER XVII. The written plea of repentance submitted by Eusebius and Theogonius.

Eusebius and Theogonius, therefore, sent a written plea of repentance to the chief bishops. By imperial command they were recalled from exile and received back their churches, expelling those who had been ordained in their places: Eusebius expelled Amphion, and Theogonius expelled Chrestus.

The text of the plea is as follows:

Although we were condemned some time ago before your reverence, we ought patiently to have endured what was decreed by your holy council. But since it is exceedingly absurd to provide our accusers with proof against us through our silence, we therefore state that we ran together in the one faith, and that, after examining the meaning of the word “consubstantial,” we were all reconciled. We did not follow heresy, but recalled to mind, as a safeguard for the churches, the considerations that occurred to our understanding [ms. Lyr.: “dwelling”].

And, satisfying those whom we ought to have persuaded through ourselves, we subscribed to the faith. But we did not subscribe to the anathema—not as accusing the faith, but because we did not believe that the man who had been accused was of such a character, being certain from the letters he had sent to us and from the discussions held among us.

If, then, our holy council has been satisfied, we too, not resisting but agreeing with your decrees, satisfy you by this written statement. We do not take exile heavily, but reject the suspicion of heresy. For if you now deem us worthy to be received into your presence, you will find us agreeing in all things and likewise following the decisions you have established, since your reverence also judged it fitting that the man accused in these matters should obtain your mercy and be recalled.

For it is absurd that, if the man who is thought guilty is recalled to satisfy those matters in which he was disparaged, we should, by our silence, furnish a judgment of reproach against ourselves.

Therefore deign, as befits your reverence, both to remind the God-beloved emperor and to consider our petitions, and quickly to deliberate [ms. Lyr., “discuss”] concerning us what is fitting for you.

This is the written statement of the return of Eusebius and Theogonius. From its words I infer that they subscribed to the faith that had been dictated but were unwilling to agree to the condemnation of Arius. From this it is also understood that Arius was recalled before them.

But although this appears to have been the case, he was nevertheless forbidden to enter Alexandria. This is demonstrated by the schemes he is later found to have undertaken, through the fabrication of his repentance, as will suitably be made clear.

SOCRATES, book I, chapter 10. Edition of Christophorus Valesius, chapter 14, p. 43.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the dedication and adornments of the city, the embellishment of Jerusalem, the wood of the cross, and the nails with which the Lord was pierced.

Meanwhile, after the council, the emperor lived joyfully. After celebrating the public festival of his twentieth anniversary, he immediately hastened to erect churches. He did this in the individual cities and in the city that bore his name.

SOCRATES, book I, chapter 12. Edition of Christophorus Valesius.

Since everything was prospering for him, he wished to inhabit a city of his own. Coming to the plain situated before Ilium near the Hellespont, above the mound of Ajax, where the Achaeans had their camp while fighting against Troy, he marked out a city and built gates that are still visible to sailors.

While he was engaged in these works, God appeared to him during the night and warned him to seek another place. He directed him to Byzantium in Thrace and ordered him to dwell there.

SOZOMEN, book II, chapter 2. Edition of Christophorus Valesius, chapter 3, p. 444.

Although it had originally been called Byzantium, he enlarged it, surrounded it with a very great wall, and, adorning it with various buildings, made it equal to imperial Rome (A.D. 333). He renamed it Constantinople and established by law that it should be called the Second Rome. The law itself is known to have been written on a marble tablet and set up in the Strategium beside his equestrian statue.

In this city he also built two churches, one of which he named Irene and the other the Church of the Apostles. But Constantine, as I have said, not only enlarged the doctrines of the Christians; he also destroyed the temples of the pagans. He publicly displayed adorned images in the city of Constantinople and placed the Delphic tripods in the circus as a spectacle. They are reported to be displayed there together with the statue of Constantine himself.

SOCRATES, book I, chapter 12. Edition of Christophorus Valesius, chapter 16, p. 45.

Meanwhile the emperor’s mother Helena—after the emperor had made the village of Drepanum into a city and named it Helenopolis after her—was warned in a dream and hurried to Jerusalem. Finding Jerusalem, once deserted, like a garden for keeping fruit, she sought Christ’s tomb. Although with the greatest difficulty, she found it (A.D. 325).

She immediately ordered that that most criminal temple be demolished. When the Lord’s monument had been exposed, three crosses were found buried around it, together with nails and a title written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters:

“JESUS THE NAZARENE, KING OF THE JEWS.”

SOCRATES, book I, chapter 13. Edition of Christophorus Valesius, chapter 17, p. 64.

It is said that even a dead person rose when touched by the cross. Concerning this wood, the Sibyl said among the pagans:

“O thrice-blessed wood upon which God was stretched!”

Then they began to doubt which cross belonged to the Lord and which to the thieves. Accordingly, Macarius, the bishop of the city, resolved the doubt by the following test.

Bringing one of those crosses with earnest prayer to a woman distinguished by noble birth and worn down by a long illness, he recognized the power of the Savior. As soon as the cross touched the woman, it drove away the cruel disease and restored the woman to health.

SOZOMEN, book II, chapter 1. Edition of Christophorus Valesius.

Thus the emperor’s mother, recognizing what she desired, had some of the nails with which Christ’s hands had been pierced inserted into the emperor’s helmet, taking care for the protection of her son’s head so that he might avert warlike weapons. She mixed others with a horse’s bridle, both taking precautions for the emperor and fulfilling an ancient prophecy.

For long ago the prophet Zechariah had cried out, saying (chapter XIV, 20): “And that which is on the bridle shall be holy to the Lord Almighty.”

Of the saving cross, however, she distributed one portion among the royal household.

THEODORETUS, book I, chapter 18, p. 48.

Constantine, receiving it and believing that the city in which this fragment was preserved would be saved, devoutly enclosed it in his statue, which, as is said, was placed in the Forum of Constantine atop a porphyry column. SOCRATES, Book I, chapter 13; edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 17, p. 47.

He entrusted the remaining part, enclosed in a silver chest, to the city’s priest. Gathering craftsmen from every quarter, he built there [Col. 0937C] the largest and most splendidly adorned churches. When these things had been accomplished, after a banquet had been provided for the sacred virgins—and while she herself performed the duties of a servant—she, now more than eighty years old and doing similar things, returned to her son. She passed from this life with joy, entrusting many instructions in piety to her son and bestowing her final blessings upon him. THEODORET, Book I, chapter 18, p. 48.

After this, therefore, the emperor, taking the greatest care of the Christians, detested pagan superstitions. He abolished gladiatorial combats and ordered that his images be placed in the temples; and he decreed that the cubit by which the Nile is measured should no longer be carried every year into the temple of Serapis, but into a church. SOCRATES, Book I, chapter 14; edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 18, p. 48.

Since he wished Constantinople to be shown equal to Rome [Col. 0937D] in every respect, he was not disappointed. For it became greater both in population and in wealth. I believe this happened because of the city’s love for God and the assistance its inhabitants provide to the needy. Faith grew so greatly there that many of the Jewish citizens—and nearly all the pagans—were converted to the Christian faith. As time passed, religion there is known to have expanded; no altars, pagan temples, or sacrifices were found there except for a short time under Julian, and this was soon extinguished. Constantine therefore dedicated this city, newly founded as it was, to Christ under his own name, adorning it with many large churches. The Divinity aided the emperor’s wishes, and by many apparitions it was made known that the churches being built [Col. 0938A] there were holy and beneficial. SOZOMEN, Book II, chapter 2; edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 3, p. 445.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the place where Vesta was once worshiped and where the basilica of the archangel now stands, and on the miracles performed there in Christ’s name

From that time onward, therefore, a notable place became renowned among visitors and city-dwellers alike: Vesta had once been worshiped there, but afterward a church was built. The place is now called the Michaelium. It lies on the right-hand side of those sailing from the Pontus to Constantinople, about thirty-five stades from the city by sea; by land, for those traveling around the entire gulf, the distance extends to seventy stades and more. The place received and still retains its name because [Col. 0938B] the divine archangel Michael is clearly seen to appear there. I too, having been exceptionally [helped—*jutus* in the text], affirm that this is truly so, 233. Divine power has shown this to be the case to many others as well through their own experience of these events.

Some, falling into cruel or unavoidable dangers, and others into illnesses or obscure afflictions, prayed to God here and obtained deliverance. But it would take too long to recount what miracles occurred for each person and in what manner. What happened to Aquilinus, our acquaintance and associate in legal matters, I must disclose, partly from hearing it from him and partly from my own knowledge.

When an extremely violent fever, brought on by red bile [manuscripts: “marked by red colors”], seized him, the physicians gave him a drink while he was burning with fever; he vomited it up, and immediately the bile discharged with the vomit [Col. 0938C] stained the surface of his face with a color like its own. Consequently, whatever he ate or drank, he vomited. When he had suffered this for a long time and food did nothing to nourish him, the physicians’ art was at a loss. As he was near death, he ordered his servants to take him to this place, believing that either he would die there or be freed from his illness.

While he lay there through the night, divine power appeared to him and commanded him to dip whatever he ate into a potion made from pepper, wine, and honey. When he had done this, he was freed from his illness, even though, according to medical reasoning, it appears contrary to medicine to administer hot drinks to those suffering from an excess of bile.

I also heard that Probianus, a man serving in the palace and holding a military medical post, was afflicted with a cruel attack of gout but was freed from his pains there, and that a holy vision miraculously appeared to him (A.D. 339). Although [Col. 0938D] he had long been a pagan and afterward became a Christian, he followed the doctrine only to some extent. He was unwilling to worship the most sacred cross, the source of complete salvation. Divine power appeared to him while he held this opinion and showed him the sign of the cross that had been placed on the altar of that church. It plainly revealed that, since Christ was crucified, everything done for the benefit of the human race had been accomplished in some manner through the power of the cross that must be worshiped—neither by holy angels nor by pious human beings had anything been done apart from it. SOZOMEN, Book I, chapter 2; edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 3, p. 445.

## CHAPTER XX. On the destruction of the temples

When the peoples and cities were therefore turning to the worship of Christianity [Col. 0939A], and the others, fearing for their sons and wives lest they suffer some harm if they resisted, remained quiet, the worshipers and priests of the temples, stripped of the support of the multitude, handed over the most precious images kept among them, as well as those objects called Jupiter’s thunderbolts. They themselves brought these out from the inner sanctuaries and hidden places of the temples. Things that had previously been invisible among them and known only to the priests became utterly despised by everyone.

Other images and statues made from the most precious materials were burned in the fire and their monetary value added to the public funds [F. reads: *pubicae*]. Those that appeared to have been wonderfully made of bronze were brought to Constantinople for purposes of adornment (A.D. 335) and have remained set up in public places: in the streets, in the circus, and in the imperial residences—that is, the Pythian oracle of the divining [Col. 0939B] Apollo, the Muses of Helicon, and the Delphic tripods.

The temples were stripped of their doors; some were deprived of their ceilings; others, neglected, were brought to filth and finally to ruin. At that time, therefore, the following were destroyed and utterly overthrown: the temple of Asclepius at Aegeae in Cilicia, and the house of Venus at Aphaca, near Mount Lebanon and the river Adonis—both of them famous among those peoples. The people of Aegeae boasted that the sick in body were healed there, when a demon appeared by night and effected the cure. At Aphaca, they said that on a certain day, through some invocation, a shining fire like a star descended swiftly from the summit of Mount Lebanon into the nearby river; they called it Venus. SOZOMEN, Book II, chapter 4; edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 5, p. 449.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the conversion of the barbarians

[Col. 0939C]

Meanwhile, when a very large multitude of peoples had crossed from Thrace into Asia, and other barbarians from elsewhere had made war against the Romans, many priests of Christ were held captive with them. When these priests healed the sick and drove out demons, naming Christ alone and invoking the Son of God, and when, by their blameless way of life, they displayed philosophical wisdom and overcame every stain through their virtues, the barbarians admired both the men’s life and their remarkable deeds. They concluded that they would think rightly and have God favorable to them if they imitated better men and appeased God as those men did. They appointed some of them as guides in good conduct, received instruction, and were baptized; afterward [Col. 0939D] they hastened to the churches. SOZOMEN, Book II, chapter 5; edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 6, p. 451.

## CHAPTER XXII. How Eusebius of Nicomedia seized the episcopate of Constantinople, and concerning Constantine’s letters against him

The supporters of Arius did not abandon their wicked schemes. For even in the confession of faith they had agreed with their hands, although afterward they imitated the deeds of wolves. When the most holy Alexander—who had struck at Arius with his prayers, that is, the bishop of Byzantium, for that was what Constantinople was then called—had been transferred to a better life, Eusebius, the defender of impiety, disregarding the rules that he himself had written [Col. 0940A] shortly before with the other bishops, suddenly abandoned Nicomedia and seized the see of Constantinople, although the rules loudly declared that bishops and priests were not permitted to transfer from one city to another.

But it is not surprising that those who rage in this way against the divinity of the Only-Begotten should also freely transgress other laws. For this was not the only time he had committed such an offense; he had perpetrated a similar one earlier. While he was bishop at Berytus, he leapt over to Nicomedia, and from there he was expelled again after the council, when his manifest madness and impiety became clear, together with Theognius of Nicaea. The emperor Constantine made this known in a letter. I have decided to insert the letter into this work as its conclusion. He wrote the following to the Nicomedians:

“Who is this man who has taught an innocent [Col. 0940B] people in such a way? Eusebius, of course, the cultivator of tyrannical cruelty. That he is everywhere known as a tyrant’s client is clear from many things. The deaths of truthful bishops bear witness to this; the most savage persecution of Christians also cries it out openly. I say nothing now about the wrongs inflicted upon me, through which, when the plots of the opposing faction were at their height, he too kept his eyes fixed upon me. The only thing lacking was that he should also have openly offered an armed force to the tyrant.

“Let no one suppose that I am insufficiently prepared to prove these matters. The judgment is manifest, since it is plainly established that I caught the priests and deacons who followed Eusebius. But I pass over these matters, which are now known to have been brought forward by me [Col. 0940C] not out of indignation but for their confusion. This alone I fear and consider: I see that you are being summoned to share in the crime. Through Eusebius’s seduction and subversion, you have received a conscience separated from the truth.

“Yet this matter will soon have a salutary outcome if, now choosing a faithful and upright bishop, you turn your eyes toward God. This should certainly be your concern at present, and it ought to have been your concern; it would long ago have depended upon your judgment, had the aforementioned Eusebius not come here with the worst protection of his accomplices [manuscripts and edition V: ‘here’] and most shamelessly confused the order of rectitude.

“But since it is fitting that we speak briefly to your charity about the aforesaid Eusebius, listen. Your patience remembers the council held in the city of Nicaea. I myself properly paid the tribute of [Col. 0940D] my conscience to it, desiring nothing else than to establish concord for everyone, and above all to condemn and remove this cause, which began through the pride of Arius of Alexandria but was strengthened by the wicked and pestilential vote of Eusebius.

“But Eusebius himself, O beloved and dearest men, with what sort of examination do you think he lived—overcome, of course, by his own conscience—and with what confusion, when his lie had been exposed? He sent various people to me to plead on his behalf, asking me for some consolation so that, although convicted of so great an evil, he might not be deprived of his honor. God is my witness in this matter, the God who dwells in kindly love both in me and in you. For he even misled me and seized me indecorously, as you also know. Then [Col. 0941A] everything was done as he desired, because he was concealing every evil in his conscience.

“But, leaving aside his other perverse actions, listen, I ask, to what he did above all with Theognius, his partner in wickedness. I had ordered certain Alexandrians who were departing from our faith to be sent here [manuscripts and edition V: ‘here’], because through their ministry he was inflaming men’s minds. But these exceedingly kind and excellent bishops, whom the truth of the council had reserved for repentance, not only received them and kept them among themselves, but also resolved to share in their evil desires. Therefore I decided to deal with these ungrateful men by having them seized and transported far away into exile.

“Now it is your responsibility to turn toward God with that faith which you have always been obliged to possess, which it is fitting for you to possess, and by which you ought to act. We rejoice that we have purified, orthodox, and merciful bishops. [Col. 0941B] But if anyone should perhaps presume to rise up in memory or praise of those pestilential men, he will suddenly be crushed in his presumption by the minister of God—that is, by my action. May the Lord protect you, dearest brothers.” THEODORET, Book I, chapters 18 and 19, p. 49.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How Eusebius again obtained pardon from Constantine and acted on behalf of the Arians

At that time these men were condemned and expelled from their cities. Amphion [edition: Appion] was appointed bishop at Nicomedia, and Chrestus at Nicaea. But again they practiced their customary schemes, and, finding the emperor’s clemency accessible to their deceptions [Col. 0941C], they were restored and recovered their former power.

For Eusebius, as I have already said, also held the episcopate of Constantinople tyrannically and acquired still greater presumptuous power. He frequently came to the emperor and, by gaining his confidence through repeated conversation, initiated fierce conflicts against the defenders of the truth. At first he declared that he desired to see the places of Jerusalem, and he cleverly enticed the emperor by presenting himself as though he wished to see the famous building project. He was therefore dismissed with great honor, the emperor providing him with vehicles and other assistance. Theognis of Nicaea, a participant in his evil counsels, set out with him, as we have already said. THEODORET, Book I, chapters 20 and 21; edition of Christoph Valesius.

## CHAPTER XXIV. By what fraud Eustathius of Antioch was deposed from the episcopate and transported into exile, and who were ordained after him

[Col. 0941D]

When they came to Antioch, they put on the appearance of friendship and received the greatest hospitality [edition of Valesius and editions Niv. and Frob.: “ministration”]. For Eustathius, the great defender of the truth, offered them generous fraternal hospitality. When they had reached the most sacred places and had seen that the following men were united—Eusebius of Caesarea, Patrophilus of Scythopolis, Aetius of Lydda, Theodotus of Laodicea, and others who had accepted Arius’s leprosy—they announced to them what they had planned [Col. 0942A], and came with them to Antioch.

Their arrival was presented outwardly under the guise of honor; what they were preparing, however, was war against piety. They hired a prostitute for money [edition of Valesius, Niv. and Frob.: “engaging” her] and persuaded her to lend them her tongue, then came to the council (A.D. 331). Ordering everyone else to go outside, they brought in the thrice-wretched woman. Pointing to an infant at her breast, she said that she had conceived and borne him from intercourse with Eustathius, repeatedly calling him a shameless man.

But Eustathius, who knew that her accusation was so clearly false, ordered that, if anyone knew the facts, they should bring them forward. When she said that she had no witness to her accusation, the most just [Col. 0942B] judges administered an oath to her, since the law openly declares (Deut. 19:15) that what is said must be held true on the testimony of two or three witnesses; and the Apostle also commands (1 Tim. 5:19) that no accusation against a presbyter be received without two or three witnesses.

But these men, despising the sacred laws, accepted an accusation against such a man without testimony. When the woman had sworn the oath, she added, affirming that the infant had been born from intercourse with Eustathius. Then these lovers of truth issued a decree as though against an adulterer, while other bishops—many of whom were present, opposed the apostolic doctrines, and knew nothing at all of what had been contrived—openly protested, praised the great Eustathius [Col. 0942C], and prevented their unjust decree from being accepted.

After this had been done, the fabricators of this charge quickly went to the emperor and persuaded him that the accusation was true and that Eustathius’s deposition was a just sentence. They had him expelled as an adulterer and a tyrant, although he was an outstanding practitioner of both piety and chastity. He was led through Thrace to a city of Illyricum.

At first these men appointed Eulalius in his place. When Eulalius had lived only a short time, they wished Eusebius of Palestine to transfer there. When he fled from the change, and the emperor at the same time forbade it, they appointed Euphronius. When he too died in the episcopate [Col. 0942D] after a year and a few months, they entrusted the episcopate of that church to Placitus.

[Note: [Col. 0941] One of the Greek manuscripts had Πλακεντίῳ (*Plakentio*); another had Φλακείτῳ (*Phlakeito*).]

All these men concealed Arius’s plague. For this reason many of those living piously—both priests and others—left the ecclesiastical communities and gathered privately among themselves. Everyone called them Eustathians, because after his departure they assembled separately.

But that thrice-wretched woman, having fallen into a cruel illness, exposed the plot and at the same time stripped bare the whole tragic fabrication. She revealed to not merely two or three but very many priests what had been contrived. She said that she had dared to make the accusation for money. Yet the oath had not been [Col. 0943A] entirely false, because the infant about whom she had sworn was the son of a certain Eustathius, a blacksmith. THEODORET, Book I, chapter 21, p. 52.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the division of the people of Antioch on account of Eustathius

At that time a serious uprising arose in Antioch over Eustathius’s deposition, and afterward such a fire was kindled over the election of a bishop that almost the entire city was destroyed, as the people split into two factions. Some insisted that Eusebius of Palestine should be transferred to Antioch, while others worked for Eustathius’s return.

Both factions included the city’s populace and military forces, and everyone was stirred up as [Col. 0944A] though against enemies, so that they almost came to blows with swords, had not God and fear of the emperor restrained them. The emperor suppressed the uprising by his letters. Eusebius of Palestine rejected the proposal [Theodoret manuscript: “returned”]. The emperor, admiring this, wrote to him, praising his resolve, calling him blessed, and declaring that he deserved to be appointed bishop not of one city but rather of the whole world.

Afterward, it is said, the see of the Church of Antioch remained vacant for eight years. At last, through the efforts of the enemies of the Nicene faith, Euphronius was ordained. Since these matters have now been properly woven together in this volume, it is time to arrange the beginning of the following book [edition: “let us begin”]. SOCRATES, Book I, chapter 18; edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 24, p. 59.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0943]

236 ## CHAPTER ONE. On the conversion of the Indian and Persian peoples

[Col. 0943B]

In the time of the religious emperor Constantine, both the peoples of India and the Iberians received the beginnings of Christian doctrine. I also heard that the Armenians at that time first became Christians. For they say that Tiridates, king of that people, was then made a Christian through a certain marvelous sign of God that occurred near his house, and by a single command ordered all subject to his rule likewise to submit their necks to God. From there Christian doctrine also passed among the neighboring peoples and spread widely.

Among the Persians, I believe the beginning of Christianity was celebrated when some of them, coming on account of trade to the Osroënians and Armenians, as is customary, conversed with those holy men and experienced their virtues. SOZOMEN, Book II, chapter 7; edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 8, p. 454.

## CHAPTER TWO. How the Jews accused the Christians before the Persians, and who suffered among the Persians, how many they were, and in what ways
As they increased with the passage of time, they began to have churches, priests, and likewise other ministers. This greatly grieved the magi, who are known to possess the religion of the Persians, as a kind of priestly tribe, entrusted to them from the beginning through hereditary succession. It also affected the Jews, who were, in a way, naturally hostile to Christian doctrine. Therefore they accused Symeon before Sapor, then king, the archbishop of Seleucia and Ctesiphon, the royal cities in Persia, alleging that he was a friend of the Roman Caesar and disclosed Persian affairs to him.

Believing these accusations, Sapor first burdened the Christians with immense taxes, since he recognized that many of them preferred poverty; and he imposed such exactions upon cruel men, so that, oppressed by want of money and the excessive demands of the collectors, they might disregard the laws of their own religion. After this he put to death with threatening swords the priests and ministers of God, overthrew the churches, and confiscated all their vessels.

He ordered Symeon to be brought before him as a traitor to the Persian kingdom and religion. The magi, assisted by the Jews, hastened to destroy the holy churches. Symeon was seized, bound in irons, and led before the king. He proved to be a great man, distinguished by every kind of courage. When Sapor ordered him to be brought in for torture, he neither feared nor prostrated himself. The king, becoming still more enraged at this, asked why he had not prostrated himself, since he had previously been accustomed to do so.

Symeon replied: “Before, I was not brought in chains in order to deny the worship of the true God; and, having no hesitation about this, I fulfilled the king’s customary rites. But now it is not lawful for me to do this. For I have come to contend on behalf of our doctrine and piety.”

As he was saying this, the king ordered him to worship the sun and promised that, if he did so, he would give him many gifts with the highest honors. But if he resisted, he threatened that both he and the entire Christian people would die. When he could move Symeon neither by threats nor soften him with promises, but Symeon remained steadfast and refused ever to worship the sun, lest he become a betrayer of his religion, Sapor ordered him to be kept in chains, believing that he could bend him over time.

As Symeon was being led to prison, a certain elderly eunuch named Ustazades [aliter: Ustazanes, and Ustazares], Sapor’s tutor and a senior member of the royal household, saw him. He rose and prostrated himself before him. He had been sitting before the king’s doors. Symeon rebuked him harshly, cried out angrily, turned away, and looked upon him with contempt. For although he was a Christian, not long before he had been compelled to worship the sun.

At this, the eunuch suddenly began to weep. With a groan he removed the bright garment he was wearing, took a mourning cloak, and sat before the royal palace, weeping and lamenting:

“Alas!” he said. “What sort of God can I believe is concerned with me, when I denied him, since my former dearest friend Symeon, on account of this matter, did not even return a word to me, but turned away in anger and passed by?”

When Sapor heard this, he summoned him and asked the reason for his mourning, or whether some misfortune had befallen him in the royal household.

Ustazades answered: “O king, I have suffered no misfortune in this house of the world. Would that, in exchange for what has now happened to me, I had fallen into every other calamity! For I mourn because I am alive, though I ought to have died long ago. I see the sun, which, wishing to obey you, I worshiped against the desire of my own will. Therefore it is most just that I die for both reasons: I am a betrayer of Christ, and I have also deceived you.”

After saying this, he swore by the Creator of heaven and earth that he would never again change his resolve. Sapor, astonished at the eunuch’s steadfastness, raged still more fiercely against the Christians, as though they were able to do this by magical arts. Sparing the old man, he tried by turns through gentleness and threats, with every means, to overthrow his resolve.

When he accomplished nothing, and Ustazades declared that he would never be so foolish as to worship, in place of the God who created all things, those things which had been created by God, the king, moved to anger, ordered that his head be cut off with a sword.

As he was being led to execution, Ustazades asked the executioner to wait a little, as though he wished to send a message to the king. Calling one of the faithful eunuchs, he ordered him to say this to Sapor:

“For the favor which I have enjoyed until now, from my youth, in your household, serving your father and you with appropriate devotion, I need no witnesses; you know it well. Therefore, in return for everything I once did for you, grant me this compensation: let no one who is ignorant suppose that I am suffering punishment as an unfaithful servant of the kingdom or as a man of some evil disposition. Rather, let it be made clear what is happening. Let the herald proclaim to everyone that Ustazades is being beheaded—not as an enemy of the king, but because he has professed himself a Christian and refused to deny his own God before the king.”

The eunuch reported this to the king. Sapor then had the herald proclaim it according to Ustazades’ request. For he believed that other Christians might be turned away from Christianity if they understood that he spared no Christian, since he had killed his old tutor and a devoted member of his household. Ustazades, however, wanted the reason for his death to be proclaimed, believing that, when he had worshiped the sun through fear, he had led many Christians into fear; but that now, when they learned that he had died for his religion, he would make many imitators of his courage.

In this way, therefore, Ustazades was taken to glory by a most glorious death.

SOZOMEN, Book II, chapter 8. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 9, p. 455.

Symeon, learning of this in prison, offered God hymns of thanksgiving for him. On the following day, which was the sixth day of the week of Holy Week, on which the annual memorial of the saving Passion is celebrated before the feast of the Resurrection, the king also decided to put Symeon to death by the sword.

Brought again from prison to the royal palace, he spoke to Sapor with the utmost fearlessness about the doctrine; and he would not worship either him or the sun. On that same day, a hundred others who were being held in prison were likewise ordered to be put to death. Finally, Symeon was ordered to be killed, so that he might witness the death of them all. Among them were some bishops, some presbyters, and others clerics of various ranks.

As they were all being led to death, the chief of the magi arrived and asked them whether they wished to live, practice the king’s religion, and worship the sun as well. Since none chose that life, the executioners set about the death of the martyrs.

Symeon, standing beside them, encouraged them all. He spoke of the resurrection and of piety, and, drawing confidence from the Holy Scriptures, said:

“True life consists in dying in this way; manifest death consists in denying God. Moreover, after a little while death comes of its own accord, without anyone inflicting it. For this is the unavoidable end of all who are born. After this, however, eternity does not come to all in the same way; rather, as though from some reckoning, people will render an account of this life and will receive the reward of the things they have done well, as well as, without doubt, the punishments of their evil deeds. Nothing is greater or more blessed among all good things than to choose to die for God.”

As Symeon said these things, teaching them as though they were his children, each, trained in the sacred contests in the manner appropriate to him, eagerly ran toward death. When the executioner had passed through all one hundred, he came last to Symeon, Abedecallam, and Ananias. The latter two were elderly, white-haired men serving under Symeon’s Church; they had been seized together with him and were in chains.

SOZOMEN, Book II, chapter 9. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 10, p. 458.

At that point Pusicius, who was in charge of all the king’s craftsmen and was standing there, saw Ananias trembling as he was being prepared for death. He said: “For a little while, old man, close your eyes and be confident; soon you will see the face of Christ.”

As soon as he had said this, he was suddenly seized, led before the king, and exposed as a Christian, because he had spoken freely on behalf of the martyrs in defense of the doctrine. The king then ordered him to die in a strange and cruel manner: his neck was pierced, and his tongue was pulled out through the opening.

After this had been done, some also accused his daughter. The sacred virgin was then seized and put to death.

In the following year, on the day when the Passion of Christ was commemorated and the feast of the Resurrection awaited, Sapor’s most savage order spread throughout the entire land of Persia: those who professed themselves Christians were condemned to death. At that time, it is said, an innumerable multitude of Christians fell by the sword. The magi carefully searched for others through the cities and villages and found them in hiding; still others offered themselves voluntarily, without anyone instructing them, lest they appear to deny Christ by their silence.

Thus, while all Christians were being killed without mercy [ed., “and no one was spared”], many were also killed within the royal household, among them the eunuch Azanes, who was especially dear to the king. When Sapor heard this, he became sorrowful, revoked the general slaughter, and ordered only the teachers of the religion to be killed.

At that time the queen fell ill (SOZOMEN, Book II, chapter 10. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 11, p. 459). Tharbua, the sister of Bishop Symeon, was seized together with her servant, who shared her way of life. They happened to be detained through the plot of Jews who accused them of having worked magic against the queen on account of Symeon’s death. The queen—for the sick are accustomed to lend their ears to such matters [ed., Niv. and Frob.: “to such hopes”]—suspected that the accusation was true, especially since it had been made by Jews; she herself held similar views and considered them truthful and favorable to her.

The magi took Tharbua and the others and struck them with the punishment of a cruel death. They bound them to stakes, split them through the middle with a saw, and mangled them in a cruel death; then, as though purifying the queen, they made them pass between the stakes.

They say that Tharbua was exceedingly beautiful and was loved by certain magi. They secretly sought her for intercourse, promising that she and the others would be spared if she consented to the vice. She could not even endure hearing such a lustful proposal; after returning insults for the shameful request, she went eagerly to her death, lest she surrender her holy virginity.

As the magi and their leaders traveled throughout the entire province according to Sapor’s order, to seize the priests and teachers of the Christian doctrine, they punished bishops and presbyters, especially in the region of Adiabene. This is a Persian region with a very large number of Christians.

SOZOMEN, Book II, chapter 11. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 12, p. 460.

At this time they also seized Bishop Acepsimas and many of his clergy. Holding the bishop, they considered that sufficient for their purposes, while releasing the others after stripping them of their possessions. A certain presbyter, James, followed Acepsimas of his own accord [printed: Ponti; ms.: sponte], and, by repeatedly pleading with the magi, eventually succeeded in being ensnared. For he served the old man eagerly and somewhat lightened his suffering, never ceasing to care for his wounds as far as he could.

After a short time the magi tortured him with cruel punishments, forcing him to worship the sun. When he refused, they sent him back into chains. They also held many other presbyters and deacons in prison after flogging them.

After a little time had passed, the chief of the magi consulted the king about them. Having received authority to do whatever he wished if they would not worship the sun, he communicated the king’s will to them in prison. When they openly replied that they would never become betrayers of Christ and would not worship the sun, he tore them apart with blows, without the slightest mercy. Among them Acepsimas also died courageously for his confession of the doctrine.

Some Armenians, who were hostages among the Persians, secretly carried away his body and committed it to the burial owed to him. Others, although flogged no less severely, survived beyond hope; since they did not change their resolve, they were led back into chains. Among them was Aithalas. When he was beaten while stretched out extremely tightly, his shoulders were dislocated, so that afterward he appeared to carry dead hands, while others brought food to his mouth.

Under this reign, presbyters, deacons, monks, sacred virgins, and others holding ecclesiastical offices, as well as innumerable multitudes laboring for the doctrine, were taken away with the testimony of a good life. At the same time Bishop Bichor suffered together with Marea and about two hundred and fifty clerics who had been captured with him and seized by the Persians.

At that time a man named Milesius was also crowned with martyrdom. He had first served as a soldier among the Persians; afterward he abandoned military service and devoted himself to an apostolic way of life.

SOZOMEN, Book II, chapter 12. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 13, p. 461.

For it is said that, when he had been ordained bishop in a Persian city, he often suffered greatly, being beaten and dragged about, yet endured it with a manly spirit. When he could persuade no one there to become a Christian, he took this deeply to heart, cursed the city, and departed.

After a short time, when the leading men of that place had sinned against the king, an army arrived with three hundred elephants, overthrew the city, and plowed and sowed it as though it were a desolate field.

Bishop Milesius, carrying only a bag containing the sacred book of the Gospels, went to Jerusalem to pray, and from there to Egypt, in order to see the monks living there. The Syrians, who wrote an account of his deeds and life, bear witness to what sort of holy man he was and how he worked miracles.

It is therefore reported that, among those crowned with martyrdom under the reign of Sapor, the number of men and women was approximately sixteen thousand.

SOZOMEN, Book II, chapter 13. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 14, p. 462.

## CHAPTER III. The Letter of Constantine to the King of the Persians on Behalf of the Christians

In Persia, Constantine Augustus voluntarily took thought for the supporters of piety. Recognizing that they were being severely afflicted by impious men, and that their king, serving error [ed., “raging”], was inflicting various dangers upon them, he sent him, through the envoys who were then present, admonitions concerning piety, asking that the worshipers of God be treated with the honor due to them. But the zeal of the pious ruler can better be recognized from his letter itself.

### LETTER OF THE EMPEROR CONSTANTINE

### To Sapor, King of the Persians: On God’s Providence toward Human Beings

Guarding the most sacred faith, I have shared in the light of truth; governed by the truth of the light, I recognize the sacred faith. Finally, through these things, as the facts themselves confirm, I perceive that this is a venerable religion, offering to all the teaching of the knowledge of the most holy God, and I profess that I practice such worship.

Because I have the power of this God as my help, beginning from the ends of the Ocean, I have secured the whole world with the firmest hope of salvation, so that all those who had been subjected to daily disasters by so many tyrants and brought even into darkness might, recovering the vengeance owed to the common order of things, rise again through a kind of renewed healing.

I worship this God, whose sign my army, dedicated to God, carries upon its shoulders; and when something is requested from him in righteous speech, it is obtained. From the very insignia of the trophy I suddenly receive benefits. I therefore profess that I honor this God with immortal remembrance, and I believe that he is supreme over all, with the purest mind.

I shall invoke him with bent knees, fleeing all abominable blood, horrible and detestable odors, and every earthly fire, which I avoid above all. Through all these things, that wicked and unspeakable error has cast down many peoples and entire nations and handed them over to hell.

For the things which the God of all, in his providence and clemency, brought forth into the world for the sake and benefit of human beings, he does not permit to be dragged toward the desire of each individual. Rather, he requires only a pure mind and an unstained soul from all [ed., “from human beings”]; he demands deeds of virtue and piety; he delights in works of gentleness and mercy; he loves the mild and hates the turbulent; he loves faith and punishes faithlessness; he despises every power accompanied by arrogance; he punishes the harshness of the proud; he destroys those lifted up by vanity; but to the humble and patient he grants fitting rewards.

Thus, highly valuing a just kingdom, he extends it through the aid of his power, and guards royal wisdom with the tranquility of peace. Therefore, my brother, I do not think that I am mistaken in confessing that this is the God, ruler and father of all, whom many rulers among us, seduced by mad errors, have attempted to deny.

A destructive end overtook all of them, so that the entire human race arising after them seems to set their disasters before itself as an example of a curse. I consider Valerian to have been one of these: like a rod of divine wrath, he was driven out of our lands and handed over to your regions for punishment. He is known to have displayed among us a trophy most notorious for his shame [ed., Niv. and Frob.: “a most noble trophy”].

This, however, was turned to good account, so that such punishment became manifest in our age. I too saw the end of those who recently disturbed the people devoted to God with their wicked commands. Therefore I return many thanks to God, because, through his undiminished providence, the whole human race, honoring the divine law, rejoices appropriately in the peace restored to it.

Hence I also believe that everything proceeds excellently and securely for us, since through their pure and commendable religion and divine concord he deigns to raise all things to himself.

How willingly, then, do you think I hear of such a fellowship of human beings—that is, of Christians, for whom this entire discourse is intended—when even the distinguished regions of Persia are adorned by them more than I desire? You will therefore govern excellently if you become like them and share what they possess. In this way you will have the Lord of all as gentle, peaceful, and gracious.

Since you are so great and so distinguished, I commend these people to you, for you are also proven outstanding in piety. Love them suitably, and make them participants in your clemency, thereby providing both yourself and us with an immense right to gratitude through faith.

Thus did that excellent emperor, adorned with piety, act, caring not only for his subjects but also for those who were governed under foreign rulers. Therefore he too obtained divine protection, and, holding all Europe and Libya, as well as the greater part of Asia, he had devoted subjects everywhere.

Some of the barbarians also served him voluntarily, while others had been conquered. Everywhere triumphs were seen, and the emperor was recognized as victor in all things.

THEODORET, Book I, chapter 24, p. 56.

## CHAPTER IV. The End of Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, and the Beginning of the Episcopate of Athanasius

Meanwhile, after Alexander, that remarkable old man who had overthrown the blasphemies of Arius, died, Athanasius assumed the episcopate of the Alexandrian Church five months after the Council of Nicaea. I have postponed recounting his persecutions, flights, insults, and frequent dangers; Rufinus has ennobled them with his eloquence.
