THEODORET, Book I, chapter 26, p. 59. Year of the Lord 328; Baronius, 326.

## CHAPTER V. What Was Done against Athanasius, and How He Fled to the Emperor

After many deliberations had been filled with disturbances and seditions, and after the cries of accusers demanding that Athanasius be condemned as a violent magician unworthy of the priesthood, men sent by the emperor, fearing that they might kill him through some attack, secretly removed him from the council.

But he knew that it was unsafe for him to proceed against so many accusers, especially since the judges were also his enemies. Leaving the synod, he hastened to come to the emperor.

SOZOMEN, Book II, chapter 24. Edition of Christoph Valesius.

Thus Athanasius came to the emperor and informed him of the entire charge brought against him by the bishops. But those men, assembling at Mareotis, sent to the emperor certain priests who agreed among themselves—namely, Theognius of Nicaea, Theodorus of Perinthus, Maris of Chalcedon, Narcissus the Cilician, and others like them—fabricating lies, inventing certain fictions, and composing utterly bare slanders as though they were genuine accusations.

After this they came to the city of Aelia. For the emperor had ordered the entire council to come from Tyre to Aelia. He had also ordered others to be gathered from every direction, so that the newly built temples might be dedicated.

Accordingly, he sent devoted men of outstanding piety and faith, ordering that expenses be provided most generously, not only for the bishops and priests but also for all the needy who were flocking together from every direction. The sacred altar had also been adorned with royal hangings and vessels decorated with gold and precious stones.

THEODORET, Book I, chapter 30, p. 64.

## CHAPTER VI. How Arius Was Recalled from Exile, What Sort of Statement He Gave to Constantine, and the Frauds of the Arians

Meanwhile the emperor recalled Arius from exile and ordered him to set forth in writing what he believed concerning God. Arius then avoided the novelty of the terms he had previously devised, composed another explanation, confirmed it with simple words and divine reading, and also gave an oath that he believed in this way, held these views in his mind, and understood nothing otherwise. The text of his statement is as follows.

### To Our Most Pious and God-Loving Lord, the Emperor Constantine

### From Arius and the Presbyter Euzoius

As your God-loving piety, lord emperor, has commanded, we set forth our faith and profess in writing before God that we believe in this way, both we and all who are with us, as follows:

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, and in the Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, who was born from him before all the ages: God the Word, through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth; who came, assumed flesh, suffered, rose again, ascended into heaven, and will come again to judge the living and the dead; and in the Holy Spirit; and in the resurrection of the flesh; and in the life of the age to come; and in the kingdom of heaven; and in the one holy catholic Church of God, which extends from end to end.

We have received this faith from the holy Gospels, where the Lord says to his disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

But if we do not believe and receive these things in this way, truly acknowledging the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as the whole catholic Church does, and as the holy Scriptures teach—which we follow in all things—God will be our judge, both now and on the future day.

Therefore we ask your piety, God-loving emperor, that, since we are members of the Church and possess the faith and understanding of the Church and of the holy Scriptures, you order that we be united, through your peaceful and God-worshiping piety, to our mother the Church, with questions and superfluous investigations removed; so that we and the holy Church, reconciled with one another, may all together celebrate solemn prayers for the peaceful and pious empire and for your entire family.

Some said that this exposition of faith had been skillfully composed, so that the emperor might appear to be appeased by its language while Arius’s doctrines were nevertheless insinuated into it; thus the exposition would give him confidence and possess a double meaning.

The emperor, however, believing that Arius and Euzoius held the same beliefs as those who had assembled at Nicaea, was greatly pleased. Nevertheless, he did not persuade himself to receive them into communion with the Church before a judgment and examination by suitable persons according to the law of the Church. Instead, he sent them to the bishops then assembled at Jerusalem, writing that they should examine the statement of their faith and pronounce a merciful judgment concerning them—whether they had been unjustly persecuted out of envy despite believing correctly, or whether, since they had no grounds on which to accuse their judges, they should be recalled through repentance.

The supporters of Arius, however, taking advantage of the opportunity, received them into communion on the authority of the emperor’s letters. After doing this, they wrote back to the emperor and to the bishops and clergy of the Alexandrian Church, Egypt, the Thebaid, and Libya, ordering them all to receive Arius and Euzoius eagerly, since the emperor testified that their faith was correct; they appended this statement of faith to their own letters.

These events are known to have taken place at Jerusalem.

SOZOMEN, Book II, chapter 26. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 27, p. 484.

Athanasius, fleeing from Tyre, came to Constantinople and recounted to the emperor what he had suffered, asking that the proceedings at Tyre be examined in the emperor’s presence as well. The emperor Constantine, judging his request reasonable, wrote the following to the bishops who had assembled at Tyre.

SOZOMEN, Book II, chapter 27. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 28, p. 486.

## CHAPTER VII. The Letter of Constantine Summoning the Bishops so That He Himself Might Examine Athanasius’s Case

The emperor therefore summoned the council by a sacred letter, so that Athanasius’s case might be examined in his presence. Its words are these:

### Victor Constantine, the Pious, to the Bishops Gathered in the City of Tyre

I do not know what has been turbulently and stormily decreed by your council. For it is apparent that truth has been suppressed by a kind of tumultuous disorder, since you have failed to consider what pleases God and, because of the quarrels you have with your neighbors, insist that your purposes are unconquerable.

But it will be the work of divine Providence that this dispute may be openly exposed and brought to nothing, and that it may become clear to us whether, when you assembled there, you acted out of some favor or because of enmities.

Therefore I want all of you to hasten with every speed to my presence, so that through your own testimony you may demonstrate the integrity of what was done. You will learn from what follows for what reason I have written this to you and summoned you to me by letter.

As I was already proceeding toward the most fortunate city that bears our name, and was about to mount my horse, the bishop Athanasius suddenly approached us in the middle of the street with certain priests who were around him. He came upon us so unexpectedly that he immediately gave us cause for a certain alarm.

God, who sees all things, is my witness that at first I was unable even to recognize who he was, until one of our men explained who he was and what injustice he had suffered. At that time I neither conversed with him nor held any discussion with him. When he asked to be heard, while I rejected him and had almost ordered him to be driven away, he asked nothing else of us with greater insistence than that you should come, so that in your presence he might necessarily explain through his lamentations what he had suffered.

Since this seems to me reasonable and suitable to the present circumstances, I have gladly ordered this letter to be written to you, so that all of you who celebrated the council at Tyre may hasten without delay to the presence of our gentleness. There you will demonstrate by your actions the purity and uprightness of your judgment before me, whom you yourselves do not deny to be God’s own minister; for I too am God’s minister as emperor.

Thus the name of God is everywhere made peaceful and fully blessed through my worship of God, even among those barbarians who until now were ignorant of the truth. For it is certain that whoever is ignorant of the truth cannot know God.

Nevertheless, as has been said, the barbarians too have recognized him through me, his faithful minister, and have learned to fear the Lord, whom their actions have shown everywhere to be my protector and provider. Hence they especially know God.

They indeed revere God because of their fear of us. But you, who ought to proclaim the holy mysteries of his clemency—not to mention guarding them—do nothing except what is known to belong to contention and hatred, and, to speak plainly, what appears to aim at the destruction of the human race.

But hasten, as I have said, to come to us immediately, knowing that I shall strive with every power to ensure that the things contained in the law of God are observed above all, without any hesitation. No reproach or evil superstition can be attached to these things once the enemies of the most sacred law have been scattered, openly crushed, and utterly destroyed—those who, under the appearance of the holy name, introduce various and differing blasphemies.

SOCRATES, Book I, chapter 22. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 34.

## CHAPTER VIII. How the Bishops Who Favored Arius, When They Came, Slandered Athanasius, So That He Was Sent into Exile

This letter threw the men who had assembled in the synod into agitation, since many of them had already returned to their own cities. Those who were associated with Eusebius, Theognius, Maris, Patrophilus, Ursacius, and Valens came to Constantinople. They did not permit an inquiry into the broken chalice, the overturned altar, or the alleged killing of Arsenius, which they had contrived in the synod. Instead, they discovered another slander, suggesting to the emperor that Athanasius had threatened not to send grain from Alexandria regularly to Constantinople.

[Note: Through the generosity of the elder Constantine, approximately eighty thousand modii of grain were sent from Alexandria to Constantinople for the poor. The matter appears to have been entrusted to the bishop.]

They also claimed to have heard this from Athanasius, who had allegedly said it to the bishops Amantius, Anubion, Arbathion, and Peter.

Slander is very powerful when the slanderer is believed to be worthy of confidence. Deceived by this trick and driven to anger, the emperor sent Athanasius into exile and ordered him to live in Gaul. Some say that the emperor did this in order to unite the Churches, since Athanasius avoided communion with the Arians.

Athanasius lived at Trier in Gaul.

SOCRATES, Book I, chapter 23. Edition of Christoph Valesius.

No one should therefore be surprised that so great a man was deceived and went astray when priests were speaking falsely, since even the divine prophet David was deceived—not by a high priest, but by the servant Ziba, who spoke lies against Mephibosheth.

THEODORET, Book I, chapter 33, p. 66.

## CHAPTER IX. How Marcellus of Ancyra Was Deposed, and Concerning Asterius the Sophist

The bishops who had assembled in Constantinople deposed Marcellus of Ancyra in Galatia for the following reason.

A certain Asterius, practicing the art of sophistry in Cappadocia, abandoned it and professed that he was embracing Christianity. He attempted to write books that are still extant and through which Arius’s doctrine was strengthened. For he said that Christ was the Power of God in the same way as it is said in Moses: “The locust and the grasshopper are the power of God,” and many similar things.

Asterius frequently associated with bishops who did not especially avoid the Arian sect. He also attended councils, seeking the episcopate in some city. But he was frustrated in obtaining the priesthood because he was proved to have sacrificed during the time of persecution.

As he traveled through the cities of Syria, he displayed the books he had composed. When Marcellus learned of this and wished to write against him, he exceeded the proper measure of opposition. For he rashly ventured to say that the Lord Christ was a mere human being, like Paul of Samosata.

When the bishops who had then assembled at Jerusalem learned of this, they said nothing about Asterius, since he was not among the order of priests. But, requiring Marcellus, who held the priesthood, to give an account of his book, and discovering that he was stained with the doctrine of Samosata, they ordered him to withdraw from that sect.

When reproved, he promised that he would burn the book. When this effort had been undertaken [ed., Niv. and Frob.: “had subsided”], the college of bishops, summoned by the emperor, came to the imperial city. With Eusebius and the bishops who were with him present, the case against Marcellus was again pursued in Constantinople.

When Marcellus refused to burn the unlawful composition, as he had promised, they deposed him from the episcopate. In his place they sent Basil to Ancyra. Eusebius later refuted this composition in three books, strongly censuring its superstition.

Afterward, at the Council of Sardica, Marcellus recovered the episcopate, saying that his book had not been understood and that he had therefore been deposed as though he were a follower of Paul.

SOCRATES, Book I, chapter 24. Edition of Christoph Valesius.

## CHAPTER X. How Arius, While Seeking to Be Received into Communion by Alexander of Constantinople, Died

[Col. 0954C]

Therefore, when Arius had come to Egypt after the Council of Jerusalem, and the Alexandrian Church was avoiding communion with him, he came again to Constantinople, where his followers gathered, under the leadership of Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, and wishing to hold a council. Alexander, then bishop of Constantinople, learning of their endeavor, tried to dissolve it. Since he was unable to accomplish this, he openly opposed Arius’s efforts, declaring that Arius could not be regarded as a member of the Church, nor could the judgment of nearly the whole world’s bishops, who had assembled with him in the city of Nicaea, be weakened.

But when Eusebius and those around him were initially unable to bend Alexander by argument, they later threatened him with intimidation: unless he received Arius, Alexander himself would certainly be sent into exile on a fixed day, while Arius would be received into the communion of all. After this, the two sides withdrew from one another. The former awaited the appointed day in order to carry out their threats; Alexander, however, prayed that Eusebius’s words might not reach their fulfillment.²⁴² He was especially terrified because they had almost persuaded the emperor to do what they wanted. But before the appointed day arrived, he prostrated himself beneath the altar and lay there face downward all night, asking God to thwart the deadline set by his enemies.

SOZOMEN, book II, chapter 28. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 29, p. 488.

Alexander was praying in this posture. The emperor, wishing to test Arius, summoned him to the palace and asked whether he upheld the decrees of the Council of Nicaea. Arius, without hesitation, immediately subscribed to the decrees of the faith, cleverly evading them by means of a cunning subscription. The emperor, amazed, then imposed an oath upon him. Arius also dealt fraudulently with this, in a certain sense mocking the oath by trickery.

I record what I have heard about this deception. For it is said that Arius wrote down his sect’s teaching on a sheet of paper which he carried beneath his armpit; thus he truly thought that he was swearing when he said that he believed what he had written. Hearing that this had happened, I wrote it down; but I learned from the emperor’s letters that he also gave an oath. The emperor therefore believed him and ordered him to be received into communion by Alexander, bishop of Constantinople. It was then Saturday. He expected them to communicate with one another on the following day; but the presumptuous schemes of Arius were overtaken by the judgments of God.

For when Arius had gone out from the imperial palace, he was being honored by the attendants of Eusebius and appeared conspicuously in the middle of the city. When he came near the place called Constantine’s Forum, where a porphyry column had been set up, a sudden terror seized him, arising from some hidden secret of conscience, and a violent discharge from his bowels followed with fear. He asked whether there was a privy nearby, and, learning that one lay beyond Constantine’s Forum, he went there. Once inside, he was seized by a kind of collapse accompanied by an evacuation, and his rectum prolapsed together with the feces. He then fell down, and a great quantity of blood flowed out afterward, together with his small intestines; his internal organs, including his spleen and liver, flowed out at the same time. Thus death followed suddenly.

The privy where these things occurred was pointed out in Constantinople, as I have said, beyond Constantine’s Forum and the market, in a portico. All who passed by marked the place with their finger, remembering with detestation the death of Arius.

SOCRATES, book I, chapter 25. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 38, p. 73.

After some time, one of the wealthy and influential supporters of the Arian madness made an effort to purchase that same place from the public. He demolished what had originally stood there and built a house on the site, so that the event might be forgotten and its memory gradually disappear. Nevertheless, the story spread throughout the entire city and proclaimed Arius’s death to the whole world.

SOZOMEN, book II, chapter 28. Edition of Christ.

## CHAPTER XI. That at first the Arians agreed and communicated with the orthodox, and concerning Constantine’s law by which he ordered the meetinghouses of heretics to be assigned to the churches

Although Arius’s teaching was exalted in disputations among many people, it had not yet been distinguished as belonging to a separate people, nor was it established under its author’s name. Rather, all met together and communicated in the church, except the Novatians, those called Phrygians, the Valentinians, the Marcionists, the Paulianists, and those who practiced other heresies. Against all of these the emperor enacted a law, decreeing that their meetinghouses should be taken away and assigned to the churches. He did not permit them to hold gatherings in private houses or to celebrate publicly. For he judged it better that people should communicate in the catholic Church, and he urged everyone to assemble in it.

I think that the memory of the heresy was destroyed because of this law. In the time of the earlier emperors, although those who worshiped Christ differed in the diversity of their sects, among the pagans Christians were nevertheless regarded as one group, and they were subjected in the same way to sufferings. Because of the persecutions they shared, they could not examine one another, and therefore they easily came together and celebrated their services with one another. Although they were few, they did not appear to be divided.

After this law, however, they could meet neither publicly in the churches nor secretly, since the bishops and clergy of the cities observed such matters and prohibited them. Consequently, many, out of fear, withdrew to the catholic Church. Others remained in their own belief, but left no successors to the heresy.

SOZOMEN, book II, chapter 30. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 32, p. 492.

## CHAPTER XII. How and where the emperor Constantine left three sons as emperors, and died after receiving baptism

Since the most religious emperor rejoiced in Christianity and recognized that the faith of Nicaea was being strengthened by the testimony of the true God, he was pleased with what had been done concerning Arius. Having three sons, he called them Caesars and established each of them as ruler for ten years of his reign.

That is, he arranged that his first son, Constantine, who bore his own name, should hold the principate over the western regions during his tenth anniversary; he appointed the second, Constantius, named after his grandfather, Caesar in the East at the twentieth anniversary of his reign; and he appointed the younger Constans at the thirtieth anniversary of his reign.

After another year had passed, when he was entering his sixty-fifth year of life and had been seized by illness, he left Constantinople, as though going to warm baths.

SOCRATES, book I, chapter 25. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 38, p. 74.

While he was staying at Nicomedia, weighed down by illness and not unaware of the uncertainty of this life, he obtained the grace of holy baptism. He had delayed this until that time (A.D. 339), desiring to receive it in the river Jordan. Moreover, he left his three sons as heirs of the empire and ordered the great Athanasius to return to Alexandria, although Eusebius was present and tried to persuade him to do otherwise.

THEODORET, book I, chapter 23, p. 65.

At Nicomedia, in a suburb, he was initiated into the gifts of holy baptism.

SOZOMEN, book II, chapter 32 [repeated as “chapter chapter 32” in the source]. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 34, p. 945.

After making his will and appointing his three sons as heirs, he died. The emperor’s body was placed in a golden coffin, transported to Constantinople, and deposited in an elevated place in the palace. It was honored and revered in many ways as though he were still alive, until one of his sons might be present.

Afterward, when Constantius came from the East, his funeral was conducted with imperial rites, and he was buried in the Church of the Apostles. Constantine had built that church so that emperors and priests might not be deprived of the apostles’ relics.

The emperor Constantine lived sixty-five years and reigned thirty-one. He died during the consulship of Felicianus and Tatianus (that is, A.D. 336; Cassiodorus’s Chronicle gives 338), on the twenty-second day of May, in the second year of the 208th Olympiad.

SOCRATES, book I, chapter 26. Edition of Christophorus.

# BOOK FOUR

## ²⁴⁴ CHAPTER I. How the teaching of Arius began to flourish through a certain presbyter

Under Constantine’s rule, such events occurred throughout the churches. When he died, the teaching of the Council of Nicaea again became a subject of complaint. Although, while Constantine lived, not everyone accepted it, they did not dare openly to reject it. After his death, many unquestionably withdrew from that council.

These were the men who had earlier appeared suspect—especially Arius’s followers, Eusebius and Theogonius. They believed that they could strengthen their teaching if they prevented Athanasius from returning and handed the rights of the Egyptian diocese over to their partisan. They carried out these actions with the assistance of the presbyter through whom Arius had been recalled from exile during Constantine’s reign.

This presbyter was also dear to Constantius, because he had preserved his father’s will for him, and thus had access to the emperor and to the powerful men of the palace. Eusebius, moreover, appeared so prominent at the royal court that he made his followers Augusti and high officials.

For this reason, disputes concerning the teaching were once again frequently brought forward, both privately and publicly, along with insults, hostilities, and the many events that usually arise from such circumstances.

SOZOMEN, book III, chapter 1, p. 497.

## CHAPTER II. How Athanasius returned to Alexandria through the favor of the younger Constantine, and Constantine’s letter

Meanwhile Athanasius returned to Alexandria from the West; Constantine, while still alive, had also preferred that he return. It is said that Constantine even wished to record this in his will. But since he died before doing so, his elder son Constantine, ruler of the western regions, carried it out and sent the following letter to the Alexandrian people.

### Constantine Caesar to the people of the Catholic Church established at Alexandria

I do not think that your most sacred mind is unaware that Athanasius, preacher of the revered law, was sent for a time to Gaul because the ferocity of his cruel enemies threatened the safety of his sacred person, lest through the cunning of the wicked he should suffer some unsuitable harm. To prevent this, he was removed from the dangers threatening him. At my command he was ordered to live in such a way that, in the city where he was staying, he would not lack the necessities of life.

Such is his venerable virtue, supported by divine aid, that he even despises the troubles of harsher fortune. Therefore, although our lord Constantine, of blessed memory, the pious emperor and my father, had proposed restoring this same bishop to his own place among you, because he was overtaken by human fate and found rest before he could fulfill this desire, I considered it fitting to carry out the will of the emperor of divine memory.

When he returns to you, you will recognize what honor he has received from me. It is not surprising if we have done something in him that deserves praise. For the image of your desire and the form of so great a man moved and invited my soul to this action. May divine providence guard you, dearly beloved brothers.

SOZOMEN, book III, chapter 2, p. 498.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the plots of the Arians against Athanasius

Relying on this letter, Athanasius came to Alexandria, and the Alexandrian people gladly received him. The Arians, however, having formed a conspiracy against him, repeatedly stirred up serious disturbances. These gave Eusebius an opportunity to disparage him before the emperor, claiming that Athanasius had seized the Church on his own authority, without a common council of the bishops having decreed it.

Their disparagement achieved so much that, when the emperor became angry, Athanasius was expelled from the city of Alexandria. At the same time, when Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, surnamed Pamphilus, died, his disciple Agapius received the episcopate. Agapius also produced many other books and wrote much about the life of his teacher.

SOZOMEN, book IV, chapter 2, p. 499.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the death of the younger Constantine

Not long afterward, the emperor Constantine, the son of Constantine the Great, was killed near Aquileia in a battle while attempting to invade the territory of his younger brother Constans, during the consulship of Acindynus and Proclus (A.D. 339). Consequently, the rule of the Roman Empire in the western regions passed to Constans, while the eastern regions passed to Constantius.

SOCRATES, book II, chapter 3; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 5, p. 83.

## CHAPTER V. How Athanasius withdrew to Italy when the Arians again stirred up war against him

When Constantine passed to the eternal empire, distributing the temporal kingdom among his sons by his will—for none of them was present—he entrusted his will to a presbyter whom his own sister had commended to him. He ordered that it be given to Constantius, who appeared to be the nearest of the others and was thought likely to arrive first.

Thus this man became known to Constantius and, after delivering the will, gained confidence to approach him. Seeing that Constantius’s disposition was easily swayed, as a reed is shaken by approaching winds, he presumed to undertake war against the evangelical teachings and to raise a most violent storm against the churches.

He said that those who had placed in the doctrine of the faith the word “consubstantial,” which was not found in Scripture, were culpable, because it created discord between the priests. Thus, accusing Athanasius and his followers, he prepared plots against him.

His collaborators were Eusebius and Theogonius, and Theodorus of Perinthus, who appeared more eloquent and wrote explanations of the Gospels. Many call him Heracleotes (A.D. 341).

These men, repeatedly seeing the emperor, asserted that Athanasius’s return was the cause of many evils. They said that not only Egypt but also Palestine, Phoenicia, and the neighboring peoples had been disturbed because of him. Accordingly, by such words they besieged the emperor’s extremely unstable resolve and persuaded him to expel Athanasius from the Church again.

Recognizing their advice, Athanasius went to the western regions.

THEODORET, book II, chapter 3, p. 70.

## CHAPTER VI. What Julius, the bishop, decreed concerning Athanasius

Eusebius and his associates sent to Julius, the Roman pontiff, the accusations they had made against Athanasius. Following ecclesiastical law, Julius ordered them also to come to Rome and regularly summoned the venerable Athanasius to judgment.

Athanasius immediately came upon receiving the summons. The bearers of the accusations, however, did not travel to Rome, knowing that their lie could easily be exposed. But when they saw the sheep abandoned by their shepherd, they set a wolf over them as shepherd—that is, Gregory. After treating the flock more cruelly than savage beasts for six years, he paid the penalty for his wickedness, being torn apart most bitterly by everyone.

THEODORET, book II, chapter 4, p. 71.

## CHAPTER VII. That the emperor Constans supported Athanasius’s cause

When Athanasius came to Constans, after the younger Constantine had died in war, he described with groans the plots of the Arian faction and the war waged against the apostolic faith. He recalled his father’s name and the great council held by him, and stated that the synod appeared to have been strengthened by a common law.

By presenting these matters with tears, he stirred the emperor to filial zeal. As soon as he heard them, Constans sent instructions to his brother, advising him to preserve inviolate the inheritance of their father’s piety—since their father, by governing his kingdom with piety, had defeated the Roman tyrants and subdued the peoples situated around him.

THEODORET, book II, chapter 5; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 4, p. 72.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the death of Alexander, bishop of Constantinople, and the ordination of Paul among the orthodox and Macedonius among the Arians

At that time another and greater disturbance arose in Constantinople from this cause. Alexander, bishop of the Church of Constantinople, departed this life after the struggle with Arius had ended, in the thirty-third year of his episcopate and the ninety-eighth year of his life (A.D. 326). He appointed no one in his own place, but instructed them to choose one of two men whom he himself would name.

If they wished to choose someone at once teachable and adorned by the testimony of an excellent life, they were to make Paul, whom he had ordained a presbyter, their bishop—a man young in age but old in wisdom. But if they wished to choose someone merely on the basis of external dignity, they were to choose Macedonius, who was then a deacon and appeared older in age.

For this reason a greater dispute arose over the ordination of the bishop and disturbed the Church, since the people were divided into two parties: some defended the Arian teaching, while others defended the decrees of the Council of Nicaea.

Therefore, while Alexander lived, the Homoousians were stronger than the Arians, because the Arians were daily convicted and diminished. When Alexander died, however, conflict was again stirred up on both sides. Accordingly, the Homoousians ordained Paul as bishop, while the Arians ordained Macedonius.

Paul was ordained in the church called Irene, which is nearby, beside the Basilica of Sophia; in this, Alexander’s judgment appeared to have prevailed.

SOCRATES, book II, chapter 4; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 6, p. 83.

## CHAPTER IX. That after Paul was removed, Eusebius of Nicomedia seized the bishopric of Constantinople; concerning the council at Antioch, the appointment of Eusebius to Alexandria, and Gregory after him; and concerning the alteration of the Council of Nicaea

After a short time, the emperor came to Constantinople and became angry over the ordination carried out by the Arian bishops. He therefore had Paul removed and decreed that Eusebius, transferring from Nicomedia to Constantinople, should be bishop.

After this, the emperor went to Antioch. Eusebius, however, would not cease by any means but stirred everything up until he brought his plan to completion. He therefore arranged for a synod to be held at Antioch in Syria, ostensibly for the dedication of the church that the father of the Augusti had begun to build [Lyr. manuscript: “had built”], and which Constantius, after his death, completed in the tenth year from the time its foundations had been laid; but in reality, for the overthrow and destruction of the Council of Nicaea.

Ninety bishops from various cities assembled at this synod. Maximus of Jerusalem, the successor of Macarius, was not present, thinking that he might be deceived into subscribing to Athanasius’s condemnation. Nor did Julius, bishop of great Rome, attend, nor did he send anyone in his place, although ecclesiastical rule plainly commands that councils should not be held without the judgment of the Roman pontiff.

Thus a synod was held at Antioch in the presence of the emperor Constantius, during the consulship of Marcellinus and Probinus—that is, A.D. 340 according to Cassiodorus, or 341 according to Baronius. It was the fifth year after the death of Constantine, the father of the Augusti. Placitus, the successor of Euphronius, was then presiding over the Church of Antioch.

The supporters of Eusebius, therefore, considering it worthwhile to disparage Athanasius, first accused him of having acted outside the rule that they themselves had then established: he had not received the episcopate according to the judgment of the common council of the bishops but had entered the Church by arrogating it to himself. They then alleged that, when he arrived, the population had been disturbed and many had died in the uprising, and that certain people whom Athanasius had beaten were said to have been handed over to the judges.

SOCRATES, book II, chapter 5; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapters 7 and 8, p. 84.

After this disparagement had been presented, they appointed as bishop of Alexandria, first, Eusebius, surnamed Emisenus.

SOCRATES, book II, chapter 6; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 9, p. 85.

When Eusebius had been ordained but feared going to Alexandria, they made Gregory bishop. After these actions, they altered the faith—not indeed condemning anything in the Council of Nicaea, but providing a beginning whereby, through frequent councils that repeatedly changed and recited other formulations, the boundary of the faith might gradually return to the Arian madness.

SOCRATES, book II, chapter 7; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 9, p. 86.

## CHAPTER X. The letter of the Council of Antioch concerning the faith, the Frankish war, and the earthquake at Antioch

“We were not followers of Arius—for how could we bishops follow a presbyter? Nor did we accept any other faith apart from the one expounded from ancient times. Rather, we too became examiners and judges of that faith, and we judged it instead of following it.

“For from the beginning we learned to believe in one God, the creator and providential ruler of all things intelligible and sensible; and in one only-begotten Son, existing before all ages and remaining with his Father, through whom all things visible and invisible were made. In the last times, through the good will of the Father, he descended, took flesh from the holy Virgin, and fulfilled all the will of his Father. He suffered, rose again, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. He will come to judge the living and the dead, and he remains forever both king and God.

“We also believe in the Holy Spirit. If anything further must be added, we believe also in the resurrection of the flesh and everlasting life.”

Writing these things in their first letter, they sent it to the cities. Shortly afterward, however, they dictated another letter at Antioch.

At the same time, the state also happened to be greatly disturbed. The people of the Franks, established around Gaul, were hostile to the Romans. At that time a very great earthquake also occurred in the East, especially at Antioch, which was shaken continually for a year.

SOCRATES, book II, chapter 7; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 10, p. 86.

## CHAPTER XI. How Gregory came to Alexandria, Athanasius fled, and what evils were perpetrated by Gregory

Meanwhile Syrianus, the military commander, escorted Gregory to Alexandria, accompanied by five thousand armed soldiers. Arius’s followers who lived there were also with them.

How Athanasius, driven from the church, escaped capture ought, I think, to be related. It was evening, and the people were keeping vigil; an assembly was expected. During this time the military commander arrived and stationed his soldiers in cohorts around the church.

When Athanasius saw what was happening, he considered how to prevent any harm from coming to the people on his account. He ordered the deacon to complete the prayer and again caused a psalm to be begun. While the psalmody was being sung in unison, everyone went out through one door of the church.

Once this had been done, the soldiers stood without disturbance. Athanasius departed unharmed through the midst of those singing. Fleeing in this way, he went to Rome.

Gregory then presided over the Church of Alexandria. The Alexandrian people, unable to endure what had happened, burned the church called that of Dionysius.

SOCRATES, book II, chapter 8; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 11, p. 88.

## CHAPTER XII. That after Eusebius’s death Paul was again brought into the church, while Macedonius was appointed by the Arians

Eusebius sent an embassy to Julius, bishop of the city of Rome, asking him to act as judge against Athanasius. But Eusebius did not live long enough to learn what Julius had decreed concerning Athanasius; for, after surviving only a short time following the council, he died.

Consequently, the people of Constantinople again brought Paul into the church. The Arians likewise appointed Macedonius in the church now called Paul’s. These actions were carried out by the supporters of Eusebius and the successors of his presumption: namely, Theogonius of Nicaea, Maris of Chalcedon, Theodorus of Heraclea, and the others.

Ursacius and Valens, however, later presented a petition of repentance to Bishop Julius, and, consenting to the word “consubstantial,” deserved to be admitted to communion.

SOCRATES, book II, chapter 9; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapters 11 and 12, p. 89.

## CHAPTER XIII. How Hermogenes, the military commander, was killed by the people when he wished to expel Paul from the church, and what vengeance followed

Meanwhile, because of Macedonius, a huge blaze of conflict arose, and civil war among the Christians began in the city with the shedding of much blood.

When the emperor Constantius, who was staying at Antioch, heard of this, he ordered Hermogenes, military commander of Thrace, to expel Paul from the church. Hermogenes came to Constantinople and caused the greatest disturbances [edition: “stirred up”], compelling the bishop to be expelled.

When the revolt began, the people were prepared for revenge. Hermogenes persisted in expelling Paul by military force, but the enraged people, as commonly happens in such circumstances, resisted him irrationally. They burned his house, dragged him away, and killed him.

These events occurred during the consulship of Constantius for the third time and Constans for the second time—that is, A.D. 341. At that time Constans subjected the Franks to the Roman Empire.

Constantius, dealing with Hermogenes’s death, came from Antioch to Constantinople by relay horses. He expelled Paul from the city [edition: “punished the city with a fine”], while imposing a penalty on the city by taking away more than forty thousand modii of grain that had been supplied by his father and distributed daily. For nearly eighty thousand modii were supplied each day, sent from the city of Alexandria.

After this, he postponed appointing Macedonius bishop of the city. He was angry with Macedonius as well—not only because he had been ordained against Constantius’s will, but because many had died in the disturbances that had arisen between him and Paul, and the military commander had also been killed.

Constantius therefore allowed Macedonius to celebrate services only in the church in which he had been ordained, and then departed again for Antioch.

SOCRATES, book II, chapter 10; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapters 12 and 13, p. 90.

## CHAPTER XIV. How Gregory was removed from Alexandria and the Arian George was summoned there

Moreover, the Arians removed Gregory from Alexandria as hateful, both because the fire had occurred on his account and because he gave insufficient support to their error. They summoned George of Cappadocia, a supporter of the Arian madness.

SOCRATES, book II, chapter 10; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 14, p. 91.

## CHAPTER XV. When Athanasius, Paul, and other orthodox bishops were established at Rome, what Julius the Roman bishop wrote to the Easterners

Athanasius, therefore, left Alexandria and went to Rome. At the same time Paul, the bishop of Constantinople, also happened to arrive there, as did Marcellus of Ancyra and Asclepas of Gaza.

Because Asclepas opposed the Arians, they brought an accusation against him, alleging that he had overturned an altar, and he was condemned. For this reason the Church of Gaza was entrusted to Quintianus.

Lucianus, bishop of Hadrianopolis, had been deprived of his church on another accusation and was living in Rome. The Roman bishop, therefore, learning the charges against each of them and discovering that they all agreed with the Council of Nicaea, received them into communion, as one who cared for everyone on account of the dignity of his own see.

He restored their churches to each of them and wrote to the Eastern bishops, censuring them for having dealt unjustly with blameless men by expelling them from their churches and for failing to preserve the decrees of the Council of Nicaea.

He ordered a few of them to appear before him on a fixed day, so that he might show them that he had issued a just judgment concerning them. He also threatened that, in the future, he would tolerate none of this unless they ceased from such disturbances and innovations.

This is what Julius wrote. Athanasius and Paul, for their part, sent Julius’s letters to the Eastern bishops, and each of them recovered his own see.

SOZOMEN, book III, chapter 7; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 8, p. 507.

## ²⁴⁸ CHAPTER XVI. What the Easterners wrote in reply to Julius

The Eastern bishops, however, taking this very badly, assembled at Antioch (A.D. 346) and sent Julius a reply. It was composed in an elaborate style, but was filled especially with irony and was not without the character of a threat.

They acknowledged that, in all matters, the Roman Church was generous [Santheod. manuscript: “unique”], as one that possessed apostolic care and had existed from ancient times as the mother of piety, although preachers of the teaching had come to it from the East.

They did not, however, think that they should for that reason be regarded as second, since they did not fall short in the quality of their lives merely because they lacked the size or number of churches. They charged Julius with having appeared to communicate with Athanasius’s followers, as though he had inflicted insults upon them and destroyed their judgment; and they accused him of an unjust action discordant with ecclesiastical regulations.

After writing these things, they added that, if Julius accepted the condemnation they had pronounced and confirmed the bishops ordained in place of those they had condemned, they would maintain peace and communion with him. But if he resisted their decisions, they would hold contrary assemblies—especially since the Eastern bishops had not resisted when Novatus was expelled from the Roman Church.

Concerning what they had done regarding the Council of Nicaea apart from the common judgment, however, they preferred to write him nothing.

SOZOMEN, book III, chapter 6; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 8, p. 507.

## CHAPTER XVII. What happened when Athanasius returned to Alexandria

This, then, is what the Eastern bishops wrote in reply to Julius, the Roman pontiff. When Athanasius entered Alexandria, the oppression of the people by the faction of George, who had been ordained bishop there, became severe.

They said that disturbances and deaths had resulted from this, and they attributed such crimes to Athanasius as though he were the author of the wrongdoing, although such things frequently occur in conflicts.

For this reason Sabinus, bishop of the Macedonian heresy, repeatedly accused Athanasius. If he had considered how many evils the Arians had perpetrated against Athanasius and the Homoousians, how many councils had been held because of him, or how many evils Macedonius, the arch-heretic, had perpetrated against all the churches, he might perhaps have been ashamed and remained silent.

SOCRATES, book II, chapter 11; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 15, p. 91.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How Paul was again expelled from Constantinople, and what deaths occurred when Macedonius was brought into the church

The emperor Constantius was staying at Antioch when he heard that Paul had again recovered the see of Constantinople. In anger, he sent his imperial orders to Philippus, who then possessed the greatest authority among the judges and was regarded as second after the emperor, ordering him to expel Paul from the church and introduce Macedonius.

The prefect Philippus, fearing a popular uprising, employed a stratagem against Paul and concealed the emperor’s command. Pretending that he was going to hold a public hearing, he proceeded to the baths called the Zeuxippus Baths and summoned Paul there with honor, as though his presence were necessary.

When Paul arrived, the prefect suddenly displayed the emperor’s orders. The bishop patiently endured the unjust sentence there. The prefect, however, fearing an attack by the multitude that had assembled, ordered one of the baths’ windows to be opened because of the danger posed by the crowd. Through it Paul was led to the palace, placed on a ship prepared for such purposes, and quickly carried into exile.

The prefect ordered that Paul be kept at Thessalonica, from which he had originated, so that he might live there freely and in the other cities of Illyricum, but not approach the eastern regions. In this way Paul was unexpectedly expelled from the Church.

Philippus then hurried from the baths to the church, accompanied by Macedonius, who sat in a carriage with the prefect, as well as by soldiers dressed in armor. When this happened, terror seized the people, and all the Homoousians and Arians rushed together to the church.

When the prefect and Macedonius reached the church, irrational fear seized both the people and the soldiers. Since the crowd was enormous and the prefect could not enter, the soldiers began violently pushing the people. Because the people could not retreat in the confined space, the soldiers thought that they wished to resist them, drew their swords, and began slaughtering them.

Then, as the story goes, about 3,150 people were killed. Some were killed by the soldiers; others died from the crush.

After these events, Macedonius, as though he had done nothing evil and as though he were pure and innocent, received the episcopate entrusted to him by the prefect rather than by ecclesiastical rules. By means of such slaughter, he and the Arians held the rights of the Church.

At this time the emperor was building the larger church now called Sophia. It was joined to the church called Irene, which the emperor’s father, when it had previously been small, had developed into a structure of beauty and grandeur. These two churches are now known to be contained, as it were, within a single circuit.

SOCRATES, book II, chapter 12; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 16, p. 92.

## CHAPTER XIX. Again concerning the accusations against Athanasius
Meanwhile another plot was contrived against Athanasius. The father of the Augusti had given the Church of the Alexandrians grain to distribute to the poor; they said that Athanasius was selling it and appropriating it for his own purposes. Believing this, the emperor ordered him to be killed. When Athanasius learned of this, he secretly escaped.

At that time Julius, bishop of the city of Rome, recognizing the plots that the Arians had devised against Athanasius, [Col. 0966A] summoned Athanasius after receiving Eusebius’s letter and learning where he was concealed. Meanwhile he also received letters from the Egyptian bishops, asserting that the accusations made against Athanasius were false. Julius therefore wrote back to those who had assembled at Antioch, first blaming them for the insults contained in their letter, then asking why they had not summoned Athanasius to their synod, since the canons required that nothing be decided outside Rome without the Roman pontiff; moreover, he accused them of secretly corrupting the faith, of having produced the proceedings at Tyre by stealth and artifice, and of having unlawfully drawn up records against him from one side only [ms. Santheod.: “contrary to the law”]. He also reported the falsehood fabricated concerning Arsenius. I have omitted reproducing the letters themselves because of the tedium of a long reading. [Col. 0966B]

After a short time, Paul, pretending that he was traveling to Corinth, came to Italy and, together with Athanasius, reported his proceedings to the emperor Constans. SOCRATES, book II, edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 17, p. 94.

## CHAPTER XX. On the envoys sent by the Eastern bishops to Constans concerning what had been done

The emperor wrote to his brother Constantius, asking him to send some Eastern bishops who could give an account of the condemnation of certain men. Accordingly, three were chosen: Narcissus of Irenopolis [ms. and ed. V.: “of Hermipolis”], a Cilician bishop; Theodore of Heraclea in Thrace; and Mark of Arethusa in Syria. When they came [Col. 0966C] to Italy, they defended their own actions, striving to persuade the emperor that the judgment of the Eastern council was just. When they were required to give a confession of their faith, they concealed the creed published at Antioch. Instead, composing another confession, they presented it, although it differed greatly from the Council of Nicaea.

But when Constans saw that men had been unjustly oppressed, and that the charges for which they were said to have been suspended from communion were not true, but that the proceedings had arisen from disagreement over the faith, and when they were unable to give the satisfaction for which they had come, he sent them back to their own country.

After three years, the Eastern bishops again sent another letter to the Westerners. They called it a “long-form composition,” because it appeared to have been written with more extended language than the earlier one. In it they made no mention of the substance of God. They repudiated those who said that the Son of God was from things that did not exist, or from another essence rather than from God, and those who said that there had once been a time or age when he did not exist.

Moreover, the Western priests refused to receive Eudoxius, bishop of Germanicia, and Martyrius and Macedonius, the bearers of the letter, saying that the Nicene doctrines were sufficient and that nothing further ought to be discussed. When Constans, asking his brother to restore Athanasius to his see, was unable to obtain anything because the heretics resisted, Athanasius and Paul then approached him and requested that a synod be held, since they had been expelled for defending orthodox doctrines. SOZOMEN, book III, chapter 9; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 10, p. 510.

## CHAPTER XXI. How Constans was moved on behalf of the faith, and how Constantius ordered the Council of Sardica to be convened

[Col. 0967A]

When Constans heard this, he wrote to his brother, warning him to preserve inviolate the inheritance of their father’s piety, since he had both governed the empire, defeated the tyrants of the Romans, and subdued the barbarian peoples round about.

Moved by this letter, Constantius ordered both the Eastern and Western bishops to assemble at Sardica, a city of Illyricum. For many other afflictions likewise required the medicine of a synod. The Arians had driven Paul, bishop of the city of Constantinople, almost to the point of death because of his orthodox doctrines, treating him as the author of sedition and adding certain other charges dear to slanderers. Yet at that time the people of Sardica did not allow him to be taken away because of the plots of his enemies.

Shortly afterward Constans died. The Arians, taking advantage of the emperor’s exceedingly weak disposition and expelling Paul from the royal city, transferred him to the small town of Cucusus, which at that time belonged to Cappadocia but now belongs to the Second Armenia [ed.: “sent him away”]. But the wondrous life of Paul, although he was living in solitude, did not suffice to satisfy those who were disturbing everything. For they sent agents of murder and delivered him to a most violent death. Blessed Athanasius reports this in his defense of his own flight, saying as follows. THEODORET, book II, chapter 5; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 4, p. 72.

## CHAPTER XXII. Athanasius’s account of the death of Paul, bishop of Constantinople

[Col. 0967C]

While persecuting Paul, bishop of Constantinople, and discovering him, they decided that he should be openly strangled at Cucusus in Cappadocia, having the prefect Philip as their accomplice. He was then the patron of their heresy and the agent of their wicked plans. Such cruelties were produced by the blasphemy of Arius. His ministers of presumption rage against the Only-Begotten.

Thus, after Paul had died—or rather had been led to the heavenly kingdoms—they installed Macedonius as bishop, as one who shared their pursuits, since he blasphemed especially against the Holy Spirit [ms. Lyr.: “most of all”]. But shortly afterward they expelled him as well, because he did not confess as a creature the one whom the Scriptures call the Son. Therefore, in answering them [ed.: “having been condemned by them”], he appeared as the author of his own heresy: he said that the Son was not consubstantial with the Father, yet taught that he was like the Begetter in all things, and openly called the Spirit created.

These things, as we have said, happened not long afterward. THEODORET, book II, chapter 5, p. 73.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the assembly of the bishops at the Council of Sardica

It was therefore the eleventh year after the death of the father of the two Augusti. The consuls at that time were Rufinus and Eusebius, when the Council of Sardica was celebrated [Col. 0968A] (A.D. 347).

From the Western regions, therefore, about three hundred bishops assembled, as Athanasius says. From the East there were only seventy-six, as Sabinus says. Among them was counted Ischyras, as though he were bishop of Mareotis, whom the condemnors of Athanasius had put forward as bishop of that province [ed.: “into the episcopate”].

Some excused themselves on account of bodily illness; others complained of the shortness of the notice and for that reason blamed Julius, the Roman bishop, although the synod had been announced a year and six months earlier and Athanasius was staying at Rome, awaiting the synodal judgment.

When the Easterners had assembled at Sardica, they refused to come into the presence of the Westerners, saying that they would not come to terms unless the Athanasians and Paulinians were expelled from their company. But when Protogenes, bishop of Sardica, and Hosius of Cordova in Spain would not allow the defenders of Paul and Athanasius to be removed from the council, the Easterners suddenly withdrew.

They went to Philippopolis in Thrace, held a council separately, and openly anathematized consubstantiality. Composing letters that defended the doctrine of unequal substance, they sent them everywhere.

Those who had assembled at Sardica first condemned the Easterners’ madness; then they deprived the accusers of Athanasius of their rank. Confirming the definition of the Nicene faith and rejecting the doctrine of inequality in the divine substance, they proclaimed consubstantiality more explicitly and likewise sent their own writings everywhere.

Each side therefore thought that it was acting correctly: the Easterners because the Westerners had received those whom they had condemned; the Westerners because the condemnors had fled before the case was heard, and because the Westerners preserved the Nicene faith whereas the others had dared to corrupt it.

They therefore restored Paul and Athanasius, as well as Marcellus of Ancyra in Galatia, who, as has already been said, had previously been condemned. SOCRATES, book II, chapter 16; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 20, p. 101.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The letter of the Council of Sardica to all the bishops

What was done at Sardica (A.D. 350) will be made clearer by the letter of the council, which I have not omitted to insert into this work because of the manner in which it explains the matter.

[Col. 0968D]

The holy synod assembled at Sardica by the grace of God, from the city of Rome, Spain, Gaul, Italy, Campania, Calabria, Africa, Sardinia, Pannonia, Mysia, Dacia, Dardania, the other Dacia, Macedonia, Thessaly, Achaia, Epirus, Thrace, Rhodope, Asia, Caria, Bithynia, the Hellespont, Phrygia, Pisidia, Cappadocia, Pontus, Cilicia, the other Phrygia, Pamphylia, Lydia, the Cycladic islands, Egypt, the Thebaid, Libya, Galatia, Palestine, and Arabia, to all the bishops and fellow ministers of the holy and apostolic Church, our most beloved brothers in the Lord: greeting.

The ministers of Arian madness have often and in many ways presumed against the servants of God and those who guard the true faith. For, proposing adulterated doctrine, they attempted [Col. 0969A] to expel the orthodox. They rose up against the faith to such an extent that even the things they did did not remain hidden from the emperors beloved of God.

Therefore, with the grace of God cooperating, the most devout princes themselves gathered us from different provinces and cities and ordered this holy council to be celebrated in the city of Sardica, so that, every disagreement being removed and all perfidy driven far away, the piety of Christ alone might be preserved inviolate among all.

The Eastern bishops came, invited by the most devout emperors, especially because of the report that had been spread concerning our beloved brothers and fellow ministers: Athanasius of Alexandria, Marcellus of Ancyra in Galatia, and Asclepas of Gaza. Perhaps accusations of this kind have also reached you, since they even attempted to spread them to our ears, so that what they reported against innocent men might be believed true and the wicked opinion of this heresy concealed.

But they were not permitted to do this any longer. For the Lord is the overseer of the Churches, and he endured death for them and for all, and on their account granted us all his ascent into heaven.

Some time ago Eusebius, Maris, Theodore, Theognius, Ursacius, Valens, Minophantus, and Stephen wrote to our fellow minister Julius, pontiff of the Roman Church, against the aforementioned fellow priests: Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria; Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra in Galatia; and Asclepas of Gaza.

Bishops from other regions also wrote, bearing witness to the purity of our fellow priest Athanasius and affirming that the things done by Eusebius and [Col. 0969C] his followers were nothing but full of lies and slanders. Since they had been summoned by our beloved fellow priest Julius but did not appear, as is demonstrated by the writings of that same bishop Julius, they plainly appear to be slanderers.

For if they had confidence in the proceedings held against these men, they would not have delayed appearing. Yet their plot is also clearly evident from what they did in this holy and great council. They came to the city of Sardica and, seeing our brothers Athanasius, Marcellus, Asclepas, and the others, were afraid to appear for judgment. Though summoned once, twice, and repeatedly, they refused to obey the summons, while Hosius of advanced age—who, because of his age, his confession, and his great labor, appeared worthy of every honor—and the others assembled in council waited for them and invited them to enter into judgment, so that they might demonstrate in person whatever they had spread abroad and written against their absent fellow priests.

But, as we have said, they did not come when summoned, thereby also displaying their own slander and, as it were, by rejecting just judgment, proclaiming their plots and schemes. For those who trust in their own statements do not avoid proving them even face to face.

Since they did not appear, we are confident that none of you is unaware of this concerning them. And if perhaps they should again attempt to contrive something there, let everyone know that, having nothing with which they can accuse our fellow priests, they slander the absent and flee from those present. [Col. 0970A]

For they fled, beloved brothers, not only because of the slander prepared against these men, but also because they saw their own accusers appear with charges of various crimes. Shackles and chains were brought forward. Men came from exile, together with fellow priests, and likewise their relatives and friends, who were known to have died because of these men.

And what is astonishing, bishops were present, one of whom carried the chains and fetters with which he had been bound because of them. Others testified that death had been inflicted upon them by their plots, since these men had been led to such arrogance that they even attempted to kill a bishop who would have died had flight not saved him.

Our fellow priest, the blessed Theodulus, also came, fleeing the schemes by which they had ordered him to be killed. Others displayed wounds from swords; others lamented that they had suffered hunger at their hands. These things were testified not by random individuals, but by whole Churches. Those who appeared and those who acted as envoys reported the plagues of violence, armed soldiers, crowds with clubs, the terrors of judges, and the production of false letters.

The letter of Theognius against our fellow priests Athanasius, Marcellus, and Asclepas was read, so that it appeared that even the emperors had been stirred up. The deacons of Theognius had circulated this letter. In addition, there were reports of virgins being stripped naked, churches being burned, and prisons being used against our priests. All these acts are known to have been committed for no other reason than the detestable heresy of the Arians [ed.: “not for any other struggle, but only for”]. Whoever rejected their ordination and communion was necessarily subjected to these outrages.

Seeing, therefore, the straits caused by their crimes, they withdrew in confusion. Unable any longer to conceal these things, they came to the city of Sardica, so that by their arrival they might make it appear that they had never perpetrated such acts.

But when they saw those against whom they had brought slanders, and the accusers whom they themselves had oppressed, and had the denunciations before their eyes, they could not enter when summoned to judgment. Our fellow priests Athanasius, Marcellus, and Asclepas acted with confidence, lamented deeply, confronted and challenged them, and promised not only to expose their slanders openly but also to reveal what they had done wrong in their Churches.

Those men, however, were so bound by the terror of conscience [Col. 0970D] that they fled. By fleeing, they exposed their slanders and confessed their crimes by avoiding judgment. Although their malice and slanders are evident not only from earlier events but also from these, we nevertheless took care to investigate their schemes truthfully, so that they might not use their flight as an opportunity for some further injustice.

After examining what had been done, we found them to be slanderers and found that they had contrived nothing except plots against our fellow priests. Arsenius, whom they said had been killed by Athanasius, is alive and is known to dwell among the living; from this it is also proved that other matters were fabricated.

Because they had also spread the report that a chalice had been broken by Macarius, Athanasius’s presbyter, those who had come from Alexandria and Mareotis testified that nothing of the kind had happened. The bishops of Egypt likewise wrote to our fellow priest Julius, firmly asserting that there had not even been any suspicion of such an event.

Accordingly, they said that records had been prepared against these men, although it was proved that the proceedings had been conducted by one side only. In those proceedings pagans and catechumens were examined. One catechumen, when questioned, said that he had been inside when Macarius came to that place. Another, when interrogated, said that the notorious Ischyras was then ill and lying in his cell. From this it is clear that none of all the alleged sacramental acts had occurred, since catechumens had been inside and Ischyras [ms. Santheod. and ed. V.: “Squiras”] had not been present but was lying sick.

That extremely wicked man Ischyras lied by claiming that Athanasius had burned certain sacred books; yet he was shown to have been ill at the time when Macarius was there. Thus he too appeared as a slanderer.

Finally, as a reward for this kind of slander, they gave Ischyras the name of bishop, although he had never even been a presbyter. For two presbyters who had once lived with Meletius and who afterward were received by the blessed Alexander, bishop of the city of Alexandria, and assigned to Athanasius, testified that he had never been a presbyter of Meletius, that Meletius had neither a church nor a minister in Mareotis, and that this man, who had never been a presbyter at all, had now been put forward as a bishop, so that by that title they might seem to intimidate their hearers in their slanders.

The letter of our fellow priest Marcellus was also read, [Col. 0971C] and the wickedness of Eusebius and those like him was exposed. For what Marcellus had said as though making a complaint, they accused him of saying as though he himself were confirming it.

These matters, together with the rest and the earlier inquiries, were read, and this man’s faith was found to be correct. He had not, as they asserted, given the Word of God a beginning from holy Mary, nor had he said that his dominion would have an end; rather, he had written that his kingdom was without beginning and without end.

Asclepas, our fellow minister, presented the records drawn up at Antioch in the presence of the accusers and showed himself innocent by the judgment of the bishops who had rendered the decision.

They were right, therefore, beloved brothers, to refuse obedience when repeatedly summoned, and they were right to flee. Terrified by their own conscience, they revealed their slanders by their flight and confirmed what the accusers present had said against them.

Moreover, they not only received those who had previously been accused and expelled because of the Arian heresy; they also placed them in higher orders, promoting deacons to the presbyterate and presbyters to the episcopate, for no other reason than that they might sow and spread impiety and corrupt the piety of the faith.

Their leaders are Eusebius; Theodore of Heraclea; Narcissus of Neronias in Cilicia; Stephen of Antioch; George of Laodicea; Acacius of Caesarea in Palestine; Minophantus of Ephesus; Ursacius of Singidunum [ed. Frob.: “Mygdoni”] in Moesia; and Valens of Mursa in Pannonia.

When these men assembled with the Easterners, they would not allow them even to enter the holy council [Col. 0972A] or to approach the Church of God at all. When they came to Sardica, they held private gatherings among themselves in various places and fabricated certain proceedings with threats, so that nothing whatever might reach judgment and we might be unable to celebrate a holy council.

We were able to learn all this from our fellow priests Macarius of Palestine and Asterius of Arabia, who had come with them but had withdrawn from their perfidy. Coming to the holy council, these men related the violence they had suffered. They said that nothing right was being done among the others; they added that, although they held the orthodox faith, they had been prevented from coming to these places, and that because of their threats they had only with difficulty been able to withdraw from them [ed. Niv. and Frob.: “depart”].

For this reason, when they came to Sardica, they all stayed in one house and did not allow themselves to separate from one another even for a short time.

Since it was not right for us to remain silent or to leave unpunished their slanders, chains, murders, wounds, fabrications of false letters, beatings, the stripping of virgins, exiles, destruction of churches, burnings, transfers from smaller cities to larger Churches, and above all the Arian madness now cruelly rising through them against the orthodox faith [Col. 0972B], we therefore determined that our beloved brothers and fellow ministers—Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria; Marcellus of Ancyra in Galatia; and Asclepas, ministering to Christ at Gaza—were innocent and pure.

We wrote to the parish of each one, so that the peoples of the individual Churches, recognizing the purity of their own bishop, might know that they both have and hope to have him as bishop.

But those who entered their Churches like wolves—namely, Gregory in Alexandria, Basil in Ancyra, and Quintianus at Gaza—are not to be called bishops or Christians. No communion whatsoever is to be maintained with them; their letters are not to be accepted, and no letters are to be written to them.

As for Theodore of Heraclea in Europe; Narcissus of Neronias in Cilicia; Acacius of Caesarea in Palestine; Stephen of Antioch; Ursacius of Singidunum in Moesia; Valens of Mursa in Pannonia; Menophantus of Ephesus; and George of Laodicea: although they did not come from the East because they were afraid, nevertheless, because they had been condemned by the bishop Alexander of Alexandria, of blessed memory, because they had Arians with them, and because of the crimes charged against them, the holy council by general decree deposed them from the episcopate.

We decreed not only that they were not bishops, but also that they did not deserve communion with the faithful. For it is fitting that those who divide the Son from the substance and divinity of the Father and alienate the Word from the Father should be divided from the Catholic Church and be strangers to the Christian name.

Let them therefore be anathema from us and from all, since they appear to have trafficked in the word of truth. For the apostolic command is: “If anyone announces to you anything besides what you received, let him be anathema” (Galatians 1:9).

Announce, therefore, that no one is to communicate with these men; for there is no communion between light and darkness (2 Corinthians 6:14). Drive them far from everyone [ms. Lyr.: “from men”]; for there is no harmony between Christ and Belial.

Guard yourselves, beloved brothers, so that you neither write to them nor receive their writings. Strive together, beloved brothers and fellow ministers, as though present in spirit at our council, to consent to it and by your subscription to decree that the same agreement be preserved everywhere by all our fellow ministers.

We repudiate and cast far outside the boundaries of the Catholic Church those who do not affirm [Note: [Col. 0973D] Editions Frob. and Niv. read: “who affirm: that Christ is God, but is not true God; that he is the Son, but is not the true Son; that he is begotten and at the same time unbegotten.”], that Christ is God, but say that he is not true God because he is the Son; and that he is not the true Son, lest he be both begotten and unbegotten.

For they claim to understand his birth in this way, because they said: “What is born has been made.” And since Christ exists before the ages, they gave him a beginning and an end—although he has this not in time but before the ages.

Accordingly, two vipers have proceeded from the Arian asp: Valens and Ursacius. They boast and do not hesitate to call themselves Christians, professing that the Word and the Spirit were wounded, killed, died, and rose again. The whole company of heretics declares that the substances of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are different and divided.

But we have received and been instructed in this tradition, and we hold this Catholic and apostolic faith and confession: we name one substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0974D] “As it seems to me, either *esse* or *nominantes* is redundant. EDIT.].

And if they ask what the substance of the Son is, we profess that it is the same as the Father’s. We firmly believe that the Father never existed without the Son, nor could it have been otherwise with the Word and the Spirit.

For it is absurd to say that at some time the Father did not exist as Father. The Father could neither be named nor exist without the Son. For the Son himself testifies: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:11); and, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

None of us denies that he was born; but born before what? [Note: [Col. 0974D] Editions Frob. and Niv. read: “But begotten before all things, both invisible …”] Before all things called invisible and visible.

He is the maker of archangels, angels, the world, and the human race, since Scripture says: “Wisdom, the craftsman of all things, taught me” (Wisdom 7:21). And, “All things were made through him” (John 1:3).

For he could not always have existed if he had received a beginning; since the Word, which always exists, has no beginning. God, however, never has an end.

We do not say that the Father is the Son, nor again that the Son is the Father; the Father is Father, and the Son is the Son of the Father.

We confess that the Son is the power of the Father. We confess that he is the Word of God the Father, besides whom there is no other; and we hand down that the Word is true God, Wisdom, Power, and the true Son.

We do not call him Son in the same way as other sons are called sons. For they become gods either by the grace of regeneration or because they are deemed worthy and are called sons—not because of the one substance which belongs to the Father and the Son.

We likewise confess both the Only-Begotten and the Firstborn. We call the Word the Only-Begotten, who always was and is in the Father; but Firstborn with respect to humanity. Yet he differs from ordinary creation, since he is also the firstborn from the dead.

We confess that there is one God. We confess one divinity of the Father and the Son. No one denies that at some time the Father was greater than the Son—not because of another essence or a difference, but because the very name “Father” is greater than “son.”

But this is their blasphemy and corrupt interpretation. For this reason they insist that he said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), referring to agreement and unanimity.

But all we Catholics have rejected their foolish and base understanding, like that of mortal men. Since such men began to be corrupted, they are known to quarrel and to rise toward changes, saying that distance and disagreement could exist between God the almighty Father and the Son. It is absurd to understand or even to suppose this.

But we believe, affirm, and understand as the holy Scripture has spoken: “I and the Father are one,” because of the unity of essence, which is one and the same in the Father and the Son. We believe that he reigns forever with the Father, without beginning and without end, and that his dominion has neither time nor failure, because he always exists. He never began to exist and therefore cannot cease to exist.

We also believe and receive the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, whom the Lord himself promised and sent to us, and we believe that he was sent. But he did not suffer; rather, the man whom he had put on, whom he had assumed from the Virgin Mary, suffered, since he could suffer as a mortal. God, however, is immortal.

We believe that he rose on the third day—not God in man, but man in God rose—and that he offered the man to his Father as a gift, the one whom he had delivered.

We believe that at the appropriate and appointed time he himself will judge all people and all things.

Their foolishness is so great and their minds are so blinded by the density of darkness that they cannot see the light of truth or understand why it was said: “So that they too may be one in us” (John 17:21).

It is clear why he said “one”: the apostles received the Holy Spirit of God, but they were not themselves the Spirit, nor was any one of them the Word, Wisdom, Power, or Only-Begotten.

“As I and you,” he says, “are one, so may these also be one in us” (ibid.). Therefore divine Scripture most certainly made the distinction: “in us,” it says, “may they be one.” It did not say, “as we, I and the Father, are one”; rather, the disciples, joined and united among themselves, may be one, and through the confession of faith, in the grace and piety of God the Father and through the gift and love of our Lord and Savior, they may be one.

From this letter the slander of the accusers, the injustice of the earlier judges, and the true saving soundness of the doctrines are recognized. For the blessed Fathers not only taught us about the divine nature but also explained the instruction contained in the divine dispensation. THEODORET, book II, chapter 8, edition of Christ.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the envoys of the Sardican council sent to Constantius, and on the wicked plot contrived against them by Stephen, bishop of Antioch

[Col. 0975A]

When Constans learned these things, he was distressed as he observed his brother’s fickleness, and he raged against the instigators of evil who were deceiving the emperor’s gullibility in this way.
