He chose two bishops from the Council of Sardica and sent them to his brother with letters, together with the military commander Salianus, a man distinguished by piety and justice. The letters contained not only admonition and advice but also a threat appropriate to a devout ruler.

First, he informed his brother that he should grant the bishops a hearing, recognize the injustices committed by Stephen and the others, and restore Athanasius to his own flock, since the slander and the injustice and cruelty of the former judges had been exposed. He added that, unless Constantius wished to do what was just, he himself would go to Alexandria, restore Athanasius to the sheep who desired him, and drive the bands of his enemies far away.

Constantius received this letter at Antioch and promised to do what the circumstances of the time permitted. But the enemies of truth, terrified by these developments, contrived a most wicked crime.

The priests sent by the council had settled in a more remote place. The military commander, however, had taken another lodging.

At that time Stephen, bishop of Antioch, together with other accomplices in tyranny, was preparing a shipwreck, by which he sought to engulf the defenders of orthodox doctrines in various slanders. Their leader was a certain young man named Onager, who came with a harsh manner [ed.: “living licentiously”] and delighted in wicked conduct. He not only subjected various people in the streets to tortures and tore them with clubs, but also shamelessly invaded houses and dragged away highly respectable men and women.

Not to extend the account of his cunning further, I shall relate the crime he contrived against excellent men.

Onager went to a prostitute and said that some strangers had recently arrived and needed a prostitute for the night. Then he took fifteen undisciplined men, hid them nearby in the lodging of the bishops, and went with the prostitute to the door where the men were resting.

Finding the door open, he persuaded one of the servants, after giving him money, to bring the woman inside the doorway he pointed out. There, he said, both priests appeared to be sleeping, and he ordered the woman to go farther inside. He himself went out, saying that he was going to call his companions.

It happened that one elderly bishop named Euphratas was sleeping in an outer room. Vincentius—for that was the other man’s name—was resting in an inner chamber.

When the girl had entered through the doorway, Euphratas recognized the sound of footsteps. Since it was dark, he asked who was walking. When she spoke, Euphratas was terrified and, thinking that a demon had imitated a woman’s voice, suddenly called upon the Savior Christ for help.

Onager, the leader of this iniquity, then entered with his companions, shouting that the men were wicked and that judges had been appointed to deal with their wickedness. After much shouting, the servants also rushed in. Vincentius rose, and, closing the doors of the house, they managed to seize seven of the slanderers. Onager, however, fled with the rest. The woman was also detained with them.

At dawn they woke the military commander who had come with them and proceeded to the palace. Proclaiming Stephen’s crimes, they said that there was no longer any need for a trial or for beatings to expose his wickedness.

But the military commander repeatedly cried out, asking that the emperor order the wicked crime to be investigated not synodically but judicially. He promised first to hand over the bishops’ clergy and said that Stephen’s ministers too ought to be subjected to the same treatment.

When Stephen shamelessly insisted that the clergy should not be subjected to beatings, both the emperor and the judges agreed that the examination of the case should take place inside the palace.

First they questioned the woman: who had brought her to the bishops’ lodging? She said that a certain young man had come to her, told her that strangers had arrived and what they needed, and that in the evening he had led her to a certain dwelling. He had ordered her to enter through the door of the house and into the portico.

She added that the bishop had questioned her, that terror had followed, that he had prayed, and that the attackers had suddenly burst in.

These judges, recognizing this, brought forward into the midst the young man who had been seized among the others. Without waiting to be subjected to torture, he disclosed the contrived plot and confessed that Onager had perpetrated all these things. When Onager was brought forward, he said that Stephen had ordered all this. Thus, recognizing Stephen’s iniquity, they permitted the bishops who were then present to condemn him, and he was expelled far from the Church. Yet the Church was not freed from the Arian plague. For Leontius was ordained after him, a Phrygian by birth and utterly wicked in intention. But Constantius, learning by experience what had been contrived against the bishops, wrote to Athanasius the Great once, twice, and three times, inviting him to return from the western regions, as the letters themselves indicate. THEODORET, Book II, chapters 8, 9, and 10, pp. 83–84.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Constantius’s Letter to Athanasius, Inviting Him to Come to Him

**Constantius, Victor Augustus, to Athanasius the bishop.**

Our clemency did not permit you to be carried about and tossed upon the savage waves of the sea. Although you had been stripped of your native land, deprived of your possessions, and were wandering through places impassable for beasts, our unfailing devotion did not disregard you. Therefore I delayed for a long time to write to you concerning my intention and wish, hoping that you might perhaps come to us of your own accord and seek from us recompense for your labors.

Nevertheless, since fear may perhaps have hindered the purpose of your will, we have sent letters full of generosity to your blessedness [Ms. Lyr., “kindness”], so that without fear you may hasten to present yourself swiftly before us. Thus, having obtained what you desire, you may experience our clemency, restored to your own possessions. For this reason I also asked my lord and brother, Constans, Victor Augustus, on your behalf to grant you permission to come to us, so that, with the consent of us both, once restored to your native land, you might possess the greatest pledge of our favor. SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 18. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 23, p. 107.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Another Letter of the Same Emperor Concerning the Same Matter

**Constantius, Victor Augustus, to Athanasius the bishop.**

Although in our previous letters we informed you that you ought to come to our court without anxiety, since we especially desire to restore you to your own possessions, nevertheless we have now sent this letter also to your holiness. By it we invite you, without any disbelief or fear, to mount the public vehicles and hasten to come to us, so that you may obtain what you desire. SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 18. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 23, p. 108.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Constantius’s Third Letter Concerning the Same Matter

**Constantius, Victor Augustus, to Athanasius the bishop.**

While we were staying at Edessa, in the presence of your presbyters it was agreed that, after presbyters had been sent to you, you ought to hasten to our court, so that, seeing us in person, you might immediately hurry to Alexandria. But since a considerable time has passed since you received letters from us without coming, we have therefore hastened to admonish you even now, so that you may at least now strive to present yourself swiftly before us and thus be restored to your native land and safely enjoy your own prayer. For full information we have sent the deacon Achitus, from whom you may learn both the intention of our mind and that you will be able to obtain what you desire.

Receiving these letters at Aquileia—for he had remained there after leaving Sardica—Athanasius immediately returned to Rome. He showed the letters to Bishop Julius and caused the Roman Church to be in the greatest joy. For it was thought that even the emperor of the East had agreed with their faith, since he confidently summoned Athanasius to himself. Julius then sent to the clergy and people in Alexandria what had been written concerning Athanasius. SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 18. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 23, p. 108.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Julius’s Letter to the Alexandrians on Behalf of Athanasius

**Julius, archbishop, sends greetings in the Lord to the presbyters, deacons, and people dwelling in Alexandria, his most beloved brothers.**

I too rejoice with you, dearest brothers, because you already see before your eyes the fruit of your faith. Anyone can truly recognize this in our brother and fellow bishop Athanasius, whom God has restored to you because of the purity of his life and your prayers. From this it is believed that your pure and charity-filled prayers have always ascended to God.

For you remember the heavenly promises and the love which you learned from the teaching of my aforementioned brother Athanasius, and you recognized its integrity according to the faith implanted in you and received by you: that he could not be taken away from you to the end, whose prayers you always held as present in your most holy souls. Therefore I have no need to write many words to you. Whatever could be said to you by me, your faith has already anticipated, and divine grace has fulfilled the desires of our common prayer.

I rejoice with you; indeed, I say it again, I rejoice, because you have preserved souls unconquered in the faith. But I rejoice no less with my brother Athanasius, because although he suffered much sorrow, he did not forget your longing and love for even a single hour. Although he was separated from you in body for a time, nevertheless he seemed always to dwell with you in spirit.

And I, dearest brothers, judge that no glory was absent from the trial that arose against him. For both your faith and his have become known and have been approved by all. If such great and extraordinary events had not occurred, who would have believed either that you would have shown such judgment and such love toward such a bishop, or that he could have been surrounded by such virtues, through which he was not deprived of heavenly hope?

Therefore, in every way, he has now and will also in the future deserve the glorious martyrdom of confession. Frequently tossed about upon land and sea, he trampled upon all the wickedness of the Arian heresy; and often driven by envy almost to danger, he despised death, fortified by almighty God and the Lord Jesus Christ, our Savior. He hoped both to escape his enemies and to be restored for your consolation, bringing you greater trophies from his most courageous conscience, on account of which he appeared glorious even to the ends of the whole earth.

Thus, possessing confidence in his purpose and in heavenly teaching, he has been glorified by immortal judgment and is returning to you. He is therefore now more illustrious and worthy of love among you than when he departed from you. For if fire tests precious materials—that is, gold and silver—for purification, what worthy thing can be said about such a great man, who, after overcoming so many tribulations and dangers, is now returned to you undefiled—not only approved by us, but confirmed by the entire council?

Receive now, dearest brothers, with all divine grace, your pastor and bishop, truly as Athanasius, together with those who have become participants in his great labors; and rejoice, enjoying the prayers of him for whom you hunger and thirst as your pastor, even as you yourselves nourished and gave drink to your holiness with salutary writings. For while he lived among strangers, you were his consolation, and amid persecution and dangers you strengthened him through your most faithful souls and minds.

I already rejoice, considering and foreseeing by reason, at his return the joy of each one of you, the people’s joyful welcomes, and the glorious festival of those gathering together; and I foresee what a great and remarkable day that will be for you when my brother returns and the old evils, repaired by the plotting of certain persons, come to rest, while his precious and long-desired return joins everyone together in a certain fullness of joy.

The greatness of this joy reaches even to us, to whom it is also granted by God that we should rise up in praise of so great a man. But it is better that we close the letter with a prayer. May almighty God, and his only-begotten Son, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, grant you this joy forever, assigning a worthy reward to your admirable faith, which you demonstrate toward your bishop by glorious testimony, so that both you and those who are with you may possess better things here and in the future: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9).

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory belongs to almighty God for ever and ever. Amen. I wish you health, dearest brothers. SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 18. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 23, p. 109.

## CHAPTER XXX. What Constantius Asked of Athanasius and What Athanasius Asked of Constantius, and How, When the Orthodox Bishops Received Their Churches, the Heretics Were Expelled

Trusting in these letters, Athanasius came to the East. The emperor Constantius did not receive him harshly at that time; but, prompted by the machinations of the Arians, he attempted to ensnare him and said to him:

“You have indeed recovered your see by the decree of the council and with our consent. But since there are some people in Alexandria who reject your communion, permit them to have one church in the city.”

Athanasius immediately answered this proposal and said:

“O emperor, you have the power both to command and to carry out whatever you wish. But I too ask a favor from you, which I beg you to grant.”

When the emperor immediately declared that he would grant it, Athanasius suddenly added that he asked to be granted the same favor that the emperor was asking him to accept. For he too requested that one church be given in each city to those who rejected communion with the Arians.

The Arians, recognizing that Athanasius’s demand was useless to them, said that this should indeed be postponed and that whatever pleased the emperor should be done, since the emperor had restored their own sees to Paul, Athanasius, Marcellus, Asclepas of Gaza, and Lucius of Adrianople, according to what had been decided at the Council of Sardica. Therefore imperial decrees [that is, the emperor’s official letters] were sent to their churches in each city, ordering them to receive these men immediately.

Thus, at Ancyra, after Basil had been expelled and Marcellus introduced in his place, a disturbance not due to chance arose, bringing reproach upon those who held contrary opinions. Asclepas, however, was immediately received by the people of Gaza. In Constantinople, Macedonius succeeded Paul for a short time and held gatherings privately in a church apart.

For Athanasius alone, however, the emperor wrote to the bishops, clergy, and people, ordering them to receive him willingly. In addition, he ordered by other letters that the proceedings conducted against him in the courts be annulled. What was written concerning both matters is known to have been as follows. SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 18. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 23, p. 111. (A.D. 350.)

## CHAPTER XXXI. Constantius’s Letter by Which Everything Done Against Athanasius Was Annulled

**Victor Constantius Maximus, pious, sends greetings to the bishops and presbyters of the Catholic Church.**

The most reverend Bishop Athanasius has not been abandoned by the grace of God. Although for a short time he was subjected to human testing, nevertheless he is known to have received the decree owed to the providence that sees all things: by God’s will and by our judgment, he has recovered his native land and likewise the Church of which, by divine ordinance, he was bishop.

It was therefore fitting that our gentleness should be directed toward him, so that everything defined against him and against those in communion with him, and every suspicion and deception contrived against him, should henceforth be empty and void; and so that the relief previously granted to his clergy should remain suitably firm.

We have also judged that this should be added to his favor: all those of the sacred order should know that permission has been granted to all who are joined to him to be without fear, whether they are bishops or clergy. For unity of right intention toward him is sufficient for each person. Therefore, all who, having adopted the better judgment and side, choose his communion, we order, in accordance with the preceding providence, to receive even now, by God’s will, the generosity of our favor. SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 18. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 23, p. 112. (A.D. 350.)

## CHAPTER XXXII. Constantius’s Letter to the Alexandrians, Ordering Them to Receive Athanasius

**Victor Constantius Maximus, Pius, sends greetings to the Alexandrian people of the Catholic Church.**

In all things we demonstrate the intention of our equity, and we know that for a long time you have been separated from the one who watches over you—that is, from the bishop Athanasius—who, because of the rectitude implanted in him and the uprightness of his conduct, has become known to all. We have therefore decided to send him back to you.

Receive him accordingly in the customary and appropriate manner, and, having the merciful God as the helper of your prayers, hasten sufficiently to preserve everywhere the concord and peace fitting for you and pleasing to us, according to the ordinance of the Church, which has been approved [Ms. Lyr., “proclaimed”] everywhere.

For it is not reasonable that any discord should be stirred up among you, or any disturbance contrary to the discipline of our times; and we emphatically desire this to be absent from you. We solemnly admonish you to persevere sufficiently in prayers, with that bishop as your intercessor and helper before God, so that, when such a purpose reaches the desires of all, even the gentiles who until now have served the error of idols may hasten eagerly to the knowledge of the sacred religion.

O Alexandrians, most dear to us, we therefore admonish you again to persist in the matters that have been stated, and to receive willingly and piously the bishop sent by heavenly decree and by our judgment, and to regard him as one whom you ought to embrace with your whole mind and will. For this is fitting for you and is known to accord with our gentleness.

But so that every opportunity for the sedition of the crowd may be destroyed, we order by our letters that the judges stationed among you subject to lawful punishment all whom they recognize as seditious. Therefore, considering both matters—the judgment we share with God, and the reasonableness of your confession, as well as the punishment decreed against the seditious—preserve suitably and appropriately the laws of the sacred religion.

Honor the aforementioned man, beloved of God, with every reverence and honor; and together with him joyfully offer prayers to God, the Savior of all, for yourselves and for the prosperity of our life [Ms. Theod., “the supporter”]. SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 18. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 23, p. 113.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Constantius’s Letter on Behalf of Athanasius, Ordering the Annulment of Everything Done Against Him

**Victor Constantius Augustus sends greetings to Nestorius.**

The same form was written to the provincial governors of Augustamnica, the Thebaid, and Libya. Whatever is found to have been done previously to the injury and wrong of those in communion with Bishop Athanasius, we now order to be annulled. For we also wish the ministry from which his clergy had been deprived to be restored to them.

We therefore judge that this order of ours must be observed, so that, once Athanasius has been restored to his Church, those in communion with him may have the ministry they have always possessed, which the other clergy are also known to possess, so that they too may share in the joy. SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 18. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 23, p. 114.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How Athanasius Returned to Alexandria

Strengthened by such great and numerous letters, the most holy Athanasius traveled through Syria and came into Palestine. Making his way to Jerusalem, he informed Bishop Maximus of the proceedings of the Council of Sardica and of the fact that the emperor Constantius had agreed with its decree and judgment. He therefore arranged for a synod of the bishops residing there to be held.

Maximus, who was in no way sluggish, summoned all the bishops from Syria and Palestine. After the council had been held, he too restored communion and dignity to the blessed Athanasius. The synod also wrote to the Alexandrians, to everyone in Egypt, and to the bishops, clergy, and people in Libya concerning what had been done and decreed regarding Athanasius.

For this reason the bishops who disparaged Athanasius strongly reproached Maximus: because, having first deposed Athanasius, he had again, as though nothing had happened, out of repentance issued a judgment on behalf of Athanasius that restored communion and dignity to him.

When Ursacius and Valens, who had earlier been ardently devoted to the Arian doctrine, learned this, they abandoned their former intention and went to Rome. They offered a written confession of repentance to Bishop Julius, agreed in their statement with the doctrine of consubstantiality, and sent letters to Athanasius, professing that henceforth they would be in communion with him.

Thus Ursacius and Valens, overcome at that time by the proceedings concerning Athanasius, were converted [Ms. Lyr., “returned”]. Athanasius therefore traveled through Pelusium toward Alexandria. As he passed through the cities, he instructed everyone to reject the Arians and embrace the doctrine of consubstantiality. In certain churches he also performed ordinations. This became the beginning of another complaint against him, because he had presumed to ordain in the churches of others. Such were the events concerning Athanasius. SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 19. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 24, p. 114.

## CHAPTER XXXV. The Circumstances by Which the Commonwealth Was Then Disturbed, and the Division of the Antiochene People on Account of the Faith

Meanwhile the commonwealth was being afflicted by unexpected events; hence it is not inappropriate briefly to explain the principal matters. It has already been narrated that, when the founder of Constantinople died, his three sons assumed the empire.

It should also be known that their cousin, named Dalmatius, who bore the name of his father, ruled together with them. After ruling for a short time, he was killed by the soldiers—not because Constantius had ordered that he be killed, but because he had not prevented it.

When Constantine the Younger invaded his brother’s territories, he too was killed by the soldiers after an engagement. This has already often been mentioned. After the death of Constantine the Younger, war arose between the Persians and the Romans. Constantius was unable to prevail in it; for when a battle had been fought at night near the borders of the Romans and Persians, the Persians were found for a short time to be the stronger.

At that time Christians were not living in peace either, but through Athanasius there was a struggle among the Churches concerning the expression “consubstantial.” SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 20. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 25, p. 115.

Finally, at Antioch, clergy and people did not agree in their confession. Rather, in the choral singing customary at the end of the psalms, they displayed their respective opinions in the hymns sung to God. Some said “glory to the Father **and** to the Son,” indicating equal honor; others said “glory to the Father **in** the Son,” showing, through the insertion of the preposition, that the Son was second to the Father.

When these things had occurred, Leontius, who at that time governed the see of Antioch while belonging to the opposing heresy, was at a loss what to do. He did not dare forbid those who sang to God according to the tradition of the Council of Nicaea, because he feared that sedition would arise among the people. He is said to have touched his already gray head and said:

“When this snow melts, an enormous quantity of mud will be heaped up.”

By this he indicated that, after his death, the disagreement expressed in the hymns would generate sedition among the people, since his successors would not tolerate agreeing with the diversity of the people.

When Athanasius therefore came to Egypt, he made known the synodal letters of Julius, the Roman pontiff, and also the synodal letter of Maximus of Jerusalem, which are recognized to contain the following. SOZOMEN, Book III, chapter 19. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 20, p. 533.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The Letter of the Council of Jerusalem to the Egyptian Bishops

**The holy synod assembled at Jerusalem sends greetings in the Lord to the presbyters, deacons, and people established throughout Egypt, Libya, and Alexandria, its most longed-for brothers.**

We are unable, dearest brothers, to give God worthy thanks for all things. For in the places where he has always performed miracles, he has now also acted with your Church: in his goodness restoring to you your pastor, lord, and fellow priest Athanasius.

For who ever hoped to behold with bodily eyes the one whom both we and you now behold, looking upon the man whom you desired to see? But truly your prayers have been heard by the God of all, who cares for his Church and has always looked upon your tears and groans; therefore he has heard your petitions. You were like rejected and wearied sheep, without a shepherd. For this reason the true Shepherd visited you from heaven and, caring for his own sheep, restored to you the one whom you are known to have desired.

Behold, we too, doing everything for ecclesiastical peace and joining ourselves to your love, have gone before you into his embrace; and by communicating with him, through him we address you and send this present letter. Therefore, in accordance with your grateful prayers, know that we too are bound with him by the bond of love.

You ought therefore to pray without ceasing for our pious and God-beloved emperors, since they too, recognizing your longing, resolved to restore him to you. Receive him, then, with every honor and with hands outstretched, and offer grateful prayers to God, who has granted you such blessings. Hasten always to rejoice in God and glorify the Lord, through whom and with whom glory belongs to the Father for ever and ever. Amen.

When Athanasius came into Egypt, he deposed those whom he recognized as followers of Arius. After deposing them, he ordered their Churches to hold the faith of the Council of Nicaea and to preserve it with the greatest zeal. SOZOMEN, Book III, chapter 21. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 22, p. 535.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. The Tyrant Magnentius, and Britannion and Nepotian

While matters stood thus, the tyrant Magnentius arose in the western regions (A.D. 352). By treachery he killed Constans, emperor of the western regions, in Gaul. After this, civil war broke out. For the tyrant Magnentius held all Italy, Africa, Libya, and Gaul. In Illyricum and Sirmium, another war likewise arose among the soldiers, under a tyrant named Britannion.

Nor was Rome free from a considerable disturbance. For Constantine’s cousin, named Nepotianus, had assumed the empire, supported by the strength of gladiators. The soldiers of Magnentius deposed Nepotianus, while Magnentius advanced and ravaged all the western regions.

Thus an immense convergence of all these evils arose in a short time. These events are recorded as having occurred in the fourth year after the Council of Sardica, during the consulship of Sergius and Nigrianus (that is, in A.D. 350). From these reports it became clear that the authority of the empire had come into the hands of Constantius alone. Accordingly, he prepared himself as best he could against the tyrants. SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 20. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 25, p. 116.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Plots Laid Against Athanasius and the Inconstancy of Constantius

The opponents of Athanasius, judging that they had found an opportune moment, again plotted against him. They then suggested to the emperor Constantius that he had overturned all Egypt and Libya. They especially increased the resentment against him because he had performed ordinations in parishes belonging to others.

Meanwhile Athanasius, having come to Alexandria, assembled a synod of the Egyptian bishops. They issued decisions agreeing with those of the Council of Sardica and of the council held at Jerusalem.

The emperor Constantius, who had himself long been preoccupied by the Arian sect, therefore changed into the opposite all that had pleased him shortly before. First, he ordered Paul, the bishop of the Church of Constantinople, to be carried away into exile. Those who led him away strangled him at Cucusus in Armenia. When Marcellus was again expelled, Basil once more seized the Church of Ancyra. Lucius of Adrianople, bound in chains, died in prison.

So powerful were the accusations made against Athanasius that the emperor, falling into immense fury, ordered him to be killed wherever he might be found, together with Theodulus and Olympius, bishops of the Churches of Thrace. Athanasius was therefore not unaware of the emperor’s intention; foreseeing it, he escaped by flight and evaded the ruler’s threats.

The Arians publicized his flight, especially Narcissus, bishop of Neronias; George of Laodicea; and Leontius, then bishop of the Church of Antioch. When Leontius was a presbyter, he had been deprived of his dignity because, while living with a woman named Eustolia and wishing to conceal a shameful suspicion, he is known to have castrated himself. Thereafter, however, he lived openly with the woman. Later, through the efforts of the emperor Constantius, he was ordained bishop of the Church of Antioch after Stephen, who had first succeeded Placitus. Let this suffice concerning these matters. SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 21. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 26, p. 116.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Macedonius and His Cruelty

At that time Macedonius held the churches in Constantinople, after Paul had been removed in the manner described above. Presuming upon the emperor, he stirred up war against Christians, no less than what the tyrants of that time were doing. For by persuading the emperor to support him as he devastated the churches, he brought it about that whatever he attempted to do most wickedly was confirmed by law.

Fortifying himself with many monasteries, which he established in the city of Constantinople by his own will, and with the agreements of the bishops situated around it, he is frequently said to have afflicted those who followed Paul’s doctrine. First he expelled them from the churches; then he compelled them to communicate with him, so that many perished from the severity of the blows, others were deprived of their property, others of their civic status, and marks were placed on the foreheads of still others, so that they would be identified by such a sign.

They did these things throughout all the cities of the East, but especially at Constantinople. The persecution, which Macedonius the bishop had initially delayed, he intensified. The cities of Illyricum in Hellas, as well as the western regions, remained unmoved. SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 22. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 27, p. 117.

# BOOK FIVE

## CHAPTER I. How, After the Death of Constans, the Arians Again Stirred Constantius Against Athanasius

After a short time had passed, when Constans, the emperor of the West, had died, the supporters of Arius compelled Constantius to recall Athanasius to mind, as though Athanasius himself had made Constans hostile to him, so that they almost descended to war after the bonds of nature had been torn apart.

Incited by these men, Constantius ordered that the most holy Athanasius be not only expelled but also killed. Sending a certain Sebastianus, a commander, with a very large military force, he ordered him to be killed as though he were a criminal. But how Sebastianus came with his army and how Athanasius escaped, the man who suffered these things and was wonderfully delivered will tell more accurately himself; for in his defense of his flight he says the following. THEODORET, Book II, chapter 13, p. 87.

## CHAPTER II. What Athanasius Reported in Defense of His Flight

Nevertheless, let them inquire into the manner of my departure and learn it from their own people. For the Arians were advancing with the soldiers in order to incite them and expose us to those who were unaware; and although they are without compassion, let them at least, when they hear this, withdraw in confusion.

It was already night, and some of the people had come for the vigils; the assembly for the following day was being awaited. Suddenly the commander appeared with more than five thousand armed soldiers, with drawn swords, bows, arrows, and clubs. He himself surrounded the church, stationing soldiers close together so that none of those leaving the church could escape their hands.

I judged it unreasonable to abandon the people amid such confusion and not rather to endure the dangers before them. Therefore, sitting in my seat, I ordered the deacon to read a psalm, while the people responded: “For his mercy endures forever” (Psalm 117:1). Thus they all went to their homes [ed., “were going”].

But afterward, when the commander entered and the soldiers surrounded the sanctuary so that they might capture us, the clergy who were found there and the people alike cried out, asking that we too depart together with the people. I, however, said the opposite: that we would not leave until everyone had first gone out individually.

Then, rising after prayer, I ordered everyone to depart, saying that it was better for me to be exposed to danger than for any one of them to suffer harm. When many had gone out and the rest were following, certain monks who had been there with us, together with some of the clergy, came up and pulled us away. Thus the truth itself bears witness.

While some soldiers surrounded the sanctuary and others ran throughout the church, we passed through their midst, the Lord opening and guarding our way, and escaped every danger, glorifying God magnificently. For we had neither handed the people over to slaughter nor failed to act for their preservation, and we prevailed in escaping the hands of those who sought us. THEODORET, Book II, chapter 13, p. 87.

## CHAPTER III. What Athanasius Again Reported in His Book *On His Flight* Concerning the Deeds of George

Let us also recount in the voice of Athanasius himself what George did in Alexandria at that same time, since Athanasius himself suffered these things. For in the book which he wrote concerning his flight, he says:

“Then in Alexandria they again rose up seeking to kill us. ‘And the last things became worse than the first’ (Matthew 12:45). Suddenly the soldiers surrounded the church and conducted battles instead of prayers.

“When Lent began, George, who had been sent by them from Cappadocia, increased the evils which he had learned through their cunning. After Easter week, virgins were sent to prison; bishops were led away in chains by soldiers; the houses of orphans and widows were seized; invasions were carried out in homes; Christians were seized at night; houses were sealed; and the brothers of the clergy endured dangers in place of their brothers.

“These things were indeed exceedingly evil, but worse things were afterward attempted. In the week after holy Pentecost, the fasting people went out to the cemetery for the sake of prayer, since they all rejected communion with George. But that most wicked man, learning of this, himself stirred up Sebastianus, a Manichaean commander, who, with a multitude of armed soldiers carrying drawn swords, bows, and arrows, made an assault on the people on the very Sunday. Finding a few people praying, since most had already departed, he did such things as were fitting for them to carry out.

“After lighting a fire, he placed virgins beside it and compelled them to profess themselves Arians. When he saw that they were victorious and in no way concerned about the fire, he tore their faces so savagely that afterward they could scarcely be recognized. He also seized forty men [Ms. Lyr., ‘four hundred’] and tore them apart with a new kind of torture.

“For after cutting branches from palm trees, still bearing their thorns, he lacerated their backs with blows so severely that some of them had to be cut open repeatedly by physicians because of the thorns embedded in their backs; others, unable to endure the torture, died. Those who were able to survive, and one virgin, he deported into exile in the Great Oasis [ed., ‘Stasis’].

“At first he did not allow the bodies of the dead to be returned, but concealed them, leaving them unburied, as though he wished such cruelty to remain hidden. But this is what those who are deranged by error do. For when the parents of the dead rejoiced, indeed, on account of their confession, but wept because of the bodies of the deceased, the judgments of their impiety resounded all the more loudly.

“After this they deported into exile from Egypt and Libya the bishops Ammonius, Muius, Gaius, Philo, Hermen, Plenius, Psenosiris, Nilamon, Agathon, Anagamphus, Ammonius, Mark, Dracontius, Adelphius, and Athenodorus, and the presbyters Hierax and Dioscorus. They drove them with such severity along the roads that some of them died on the journeys themselves, while others died in exile.

“They drove away more than thirty bishops, displaying a zeal like that of Ahab, so that, if they could, they might utterly cut off the truth.” SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 23. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 28, p. 118.

In addition to these things, Athanasius also wrote books of consolation to those virgins who had endured the most cruel sufferings, saying among other things:

“Therefore let none of you be sad, even if the impious deny you burial and prevent you from being carried out. For the wickedness of the Arians has advanced even to this point: they closed the gates and sat around the places of burial like demons, so that none of the faithful beloved [Ms. Lyr., ‘elect’] might be buried.”

George was doing these and similar things in Alexandria. But Saint Athanasius considered no place secure enough for his protection, since the emperor had ordered that he either be brought in alive or beheaded in death, with his head brought to the emperor. For this reason he also promised a very great reward to anyone who reported anything of this kind. THEODORET, Book II, chapter 14, p. 90.

## CHAPTER IV. How Britannio Was Deprived of the Empire

[Col. 0987C]

Meanwhile the emperor had pitched camp in Illyricum, compelled by public necessity and especially by the situation of Britannio, who had been proclaimed Augustus by the soldiers. When he came to Sirmium, he met Britannio after mutual agreements had been made. It was arranged that the soldiers who had appointed him should transfer their allegiance to Constantius. Having done this, they proclaimed only Constantius emperor Augustus with a public acclamation (A.D. 354). When no further mention was made of Britannio, he suddenly realized that he had been betrayed and prostrated himself at the emperor’s feet. Constantius, taking away both his crown and his purple, spoke to him mercifully, advising [Col. 0987D] him to rest in the condition of a private citizen, which was certainly more suitable to his age than to bear a title burdened with anxieties; and he ordered that very generous expenses be supplied to him from the public revenues. While Britannio was residing at Prusa in Bithynia, Constantius wrote to him, saying that he had been the cause of many benefits to him, since he had freed him from so many concerns and evils that would otherwise have come upon him; yet he had not acted well, because what he ought to have provided for himself he had instead expended on Britannio. SOCRATES, book II, chapter 23. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 28, p. 120.

## CHAPTER V. On Gallus Caesar, and on the Sign of the Cross That Then Appeared in the Sky

At that time, therefore, the emperor made his cousin Gallus Caesar. Giving him his own name, he sent him to Antioch in Syria, so that through him the eastern regions might be guarded. When he came to Antioch, a sign of the Savior appeared in the East. For a column in the form of a cross was seen in the sky, to the great astonishment of those who beheld it. He sent other commanders of his with a large army against Magnentius. He himself remained at Sirmium and awaited the outcome of events. At that time Photinus, bishop of the Church, was also openly expounding the doctrine that he himself had discovered. SOCRATES, book II, chapter 24. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 28, p. 120.

He said:

“Indeed, there is one almighty God, who created all things in his own Word. But he avoided speaking of the Son’s birth and existence before the ages, [Col. 0988B] and taught that Christ was born from Mary” (A.D. 355). SOZOMEN, book IV, chapter 5. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 6, p. 542.

## 261 CHAPTER VI. On Photinus the Heresiarch and His Condemnation

For this reason, when an uproar arose, the emperor ordered a council to be assembled at Sirmium. From the Easterners there came Marcus of Arethusa and George of Alexandria, whom the Arians had appointed after removing Gregory. Basil also came, after Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra, had been expelled; Pancratius of Pelusium; and Hippacianus of Heraclea. From the Westerners came Valens of Mursa and the then most famous of men, Hosius, bishop of Corduba, likewise unwillingly. These men assembled at Sirmium after the consulship of Sergius and Nigrianus—that is, A.D. 351—the year in which, because of the turmoil of the wars, no consul had been formally appointed; and they suddenly condemned Photinus, repeatedly recognizing [in him] the doctrine of Sabellius the Libyan and Paul of Samosata. SOCRATES, book II, chapter 24. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 29, p. 121.

## CHAPTER VII. The Faith Set Forth at Sirmium, with the Following Chapters

After this they issued statements concerning the faith, one in Greek and another in Latin, very much in agreement with one another both in wording and in meaning. SOZOMEN, book IV, chapter 5. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 6, p. 542.

At that time, as though criticizing the ancient doctrines of the faith, they enacted other statements concerning the faith. Marcus of Arethusa issued one in the Attic language, but it had no agreement with the Roman language either in expression or in composition, nor was it even consistent with Greek usage itself. We shall therefore append here one composed by Marcus in Latin; the second, which they later reread at Ariminum, we shall place in its proper location when we have related what happened there. Both, however, have been translated into Greek. Marcus therefore dictated the exposition of the faith in the following manner:

“We believe in one God, the Father almighty, creator and maker of all things, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named; and in his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who was born from the Father before all ages: God from God, light from light, through whom all things were made in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible; [Col. 0989A] existing as the Word, and Wisdom, and true Light, and Life; who in these last days was made human for us from the holy Virgin, and was crucified, died, and was buried, and rose from the dead on the third day, and ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come at the consummation of the age to judge the living and the dead, and to repay each according to his works. His dominion, existing without end, remains forever throughout the endless ages. For he will sit at the Father’s right hand not only in this age but also in the age to come. And in the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete—that is, the Comforter—whom, promising that he would be sent to the apostles after his ascension into heaven, he sent in order to teach them and remind them of all things. Through him also the souls of those who truly believe in him are sanctified.

“The holy Catholic Church recognizes as alien those who say that the Son is from things that did not exist, or from another substance, and not from God; and those who say that there was a time or an age when he did not exist. Therefore we say again:

“1. If anyone says that the Father and the Son are two gods, let him be anathema.

“2. If anyone does not confess that God the Son, before the ages, ministered to the Father in the creation of all things, let him be anathema.

“3. If anyone presumes to say that he is unbegotten, or that his Father was born from Mary, let him be anathema.

“4. If anyone says that, according to foreknowledge, the Son existed before Mary, but does not say that he was born from the Father before the ages and existed with God, and that all things were made through him (John 1:3), let him be anathema.

[Col. 0989C] “5. If anyone says that the substance of God is extended or contracted, let him be anathema.

“6. If anyone says that the Son makes the substance of God extended, or calls the Son the extension of his substance, let him be anathema.

“7. If anyone calls the Son of God an affective or prolate Word, let him be anathema.

“8. If anyone says that the Son who is from Mary is merely a man, let him be anathema.

“9. If anyone, while speaking of God and man from Mary, understands him to be the unbegotten God himself, let him be anathema.

“10. If anyone, hearing what is written, ‘I am God first, and I am afterward, and besides me there is no God’ (Isaiah 44:6)—which was spoken for the destruction of idols and nonexistent gods—understands it in a Judaizing manner, rather for the destruction of the only-begotten God who existed before the ages, [Col. 0989D] let him be anathema.

“11. If anyone, hearing ‘the Word became flesh,’ thinks that the Word was changed into flesh, or that he took flesh by a conversion having occurred, let him be anathema.

“12. If anyone, hearing that the only-begotten Son of God was crucified, says that he underwent corruption, suffering, conversion, change, or destruction, let him be anathema.

“13. If anyone asserts that what is written, ‘Let us make man’ (Genesis 1:26), was not spoken by the Father to the Son, but that God spoke it to himself, let him be anathema.

“14. If anyone says that, in wrestling with Jacob, it was not the Son as man [Col. 0990A] who wrestled (Genesis 32:24), but the unbegotten God or his Father, let him be anathema.

“15. If anyone does not understand what is written, ‘The Lord rained from the Lord’ (Genesis 19:22), as referring to the Father and the Son, but says that he rained from himself, let him be anathema. For the Lord the Son rained from the Lord the Father.

“16. If anyone, hearing ‘the Lord the Father,’ or ‘the Son the Lord,’ and ‘the Lord the Father and the Son,’ and ‘Lord from Lord,’ asserts that there are two gods, let him be anathema. For we do not make the Son equal to the Father, but recognize him as subject. For he did not descend into the body without the Father’s will, nor did he rain from himself, but from the Lord, namely, with the Father granting authority. Nor did he sit at the right hand from himself, but he hears the Father saying, ‘Sit at my right hand’ [Col. 0990B] (Psalm 109:1).

“17. If anyone says that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one person, let him be anathema.

“18. If anyone, while calling the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, asserts that he is the unbegotten God, let him be anathema.

“19. If anyone does not say, as he taught us, that the Paraclete is another apart from the Son—for he says, ‘And the Father will send you another Paraclete, whom I shall ask’ (John 14:16)—let him be anathema.

“20. If anyone says that the Spirit is a part of the Father or of the Son, let him be anathema.

“21. If anyone says that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three gods, let him be anathema.

“22. If anyone asserts that the Son of God was made by God’s deliberation like one of the creatures, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0990C] “23. If anyone says that the Son was born against the Father’s will, let him be anathema. For the Father did not beget the Son unwillingly, under compulsion and constrained by natural necessity, as though unwilling; rather, as soon as he willed, even without time and without suffering, he begot him from himself.

“24. If anyone calls the Son unbegotten and without beginning, as though there were two without beginning, and by saying that there are two unbegotten beings makes two gods, let him be anathema. For the Son is the head and beginning of all things, but God is the head of Christ. Thus all things are piously referred through the Son to the one beginning of all things, which is without beginning. Again, examining Christian meaning with precision, we say:

“25. If anyone does not say that Christ, God the Son of God, existed before the ages and ministered to the Father in all creation, but says that, from the time he was born from Mary, from that moment he was called Son and Christ and received a beginning in order to be God, let him be anathema, like Paul of Samosata.” SOCRATES, book II, chapter 25. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 30, p. 121.

## CHAPTER VIII. Another Faith Set Forth at Sirmium in Latin, Which We Have Translated from the Greek; and on Photinus’s Debate

Since it was decided that a certain discussion concerning the faith should be held, everything was carefully investigated and set forth at Sirmium in the presence of Valens, Ursacius, Germanus, and the others. It is established that there is one God, the almighty Father, as is also proclaimed throughout the whole world. And there is one only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ, our Lord and God and Savior, begotten from him before the ages. Two gods, however, ought not to be spoken of, since the Lord himself says: “I am going to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20:17). Therefore he is also the God of all, as the Apostle likewise taught: “Is he the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Greeks and of the Gentiles?” Certainly. “Since circumcision is from faith, and uncircumcision through faith” (Romans 3:29–30); and everything else agrees, and no disagreement seems to remain.

But because many are troubled by the Latin word *substantia*, which in Greek is called οὐσία (*ousia*, “substance”), so that it may be understood with the greatest precision whether ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*, “of the same substance”) or ὁμοιούσιον (*homoiousion*, “of similar substance”) is intended, these expressions ought not to be mentioned at all, nor should anything be expounded about them in the Church. [Col. 0991B] The reason for this is that nothing of this kind is written in the holy Scriptures; that such matters exceed human knowledge and understanding; and that no one can narrate the generation of the Son, as it is written: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8). For this must be understood: the Father alone knows how he begot the Son, and, again, the Son knows how he himself was begotten from the Father.

No one doubts that the Father is greater in honor, dignity, and divinity, and is superior even in the name “Father,” as the Son himself testifies: “The Father who sent me,” he says, “is greater than I” (John 14:28). No one is unaware that this is catholic teaching: that the Father and the Son are two persons; that the Father is greater, while the Son is subject, together with all that the Father subjected to him; and that the Father has no beginning, is invisible, immortal, and impassible. [Col. 0991C] The Son, however, was born from the Father, God from God, light from light; and no one knows his birth, as was said above, except the Father alone.

The Son himself, our Lord and God, assumed flesh or a body—that is, a human being—as the angel announced and all the Scriptures teach, especially the Apostle himself, the teacher of the Gentiles: Christ assumed a human being from the Virgin Mary, through whom he suffered.

The summit and foundation of the whole faith is that the Trinity should always be preserved, as we read in the Gospel: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). The number of the Trinity is complete and perfect. The Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, sent through the Son, came according to the promise in order to sanctify the apostles and all believers.

With these explanations, they also urged Photinus, even after his condemnation, to agree and subscribe, promising to restore his bishopric if, through repentance, he anathematized the doctrine he himself had discovered and agreed with their judgment. He, however, did not accept their proposal but challenged them to a debate. Therefore, when a day had been fixed by the emperor’s will, the bishops who were present assembled, together with many senators whom the ruler had ordered to attend the debate. Among them Photinus was opposed by Sabinus, then bishop of Ancyra, while scribes recorded their statements. Great verbal contests between the two parties are reported to have taken place, and Photinus, defeated, was condemned. [Col. 0992A] Remaining in flight, he thereafter composed books in both languages, since he did not appear ignorant of Latin either. He also wrote against all the heresies, striving to establish his own doctrine.

Let this suffice concerning Photinus. It must nevertheless be known that the bishops who assembled at Sirmium were led by repentance concerning the exposition of the faith that had been issued in the Latin language. For after its publication they judged it contrary to themselves. They tried to have it returned by the bishops who had already subscribed it, since it was being concealed [ms. Santheod.: *celebrabatur*, “was being celebrated”] by many. The emperor, however, ordered by edicts that the document itself be sought out, threatening punishment if anyone were found to have concealed it. Yet terror could not destroy what had once been established, since it was held by many. Let this suffice concerning these matters. SOCRATES, book II, chapter 25, edition of Christ.

## CHAPTER IX. On Hosius the Spaniard

Since we have also mentioned Hosius the Spaniard, who came there unwillingly, something must briefly be said about him as well. A short time earlier this man had been sent into exile through the machinations of the Arians. At that time, at the urging of those who had assembled at Sirmium, the emperor summoned him, wishing him either through persuasion or through compulsion to agree with those present. For this was considered the strongest testimony to their faith. Therefore, as I said, he came under compulsion. When he refused to agree with them, he endured prolonged tortures and beatings; hence, under extreme necessity, he agreed with and subscribed the expositions then issued. This, then, was the conclusion of what is known to have taken place at Sirmium. The emperor Constantius remained at Sirmium and awaited the outcome of the war being waged against Magnentius. SOCRATES, book II, chapter 26. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 31, p. 126.

## CHAPTER X. On the Tyrant Magnentius and the Tyranny of Silvanus

Meanwhile Magnentius, reaching elder Rome, killed many senators and members of the people. When he realized that the soldiers of Constantius were near him, he withdrew to Gaul, in the western region. While they repeatedly waged war against one another there, now one side and now the other seemed victorious. Finally, Magnentius was defeated [Col. 0992D] and fled to Mursa, a fortress of Gaul. Seeing his soldiers grieving as though over destruction, he stood in a higher place and tried to encourage them in his customary manner of address. Then, prepared to show Magnentius their customary support, but unwilling to do so in the opposite direction, they all shouted: “Constantius Augustus, may you conquer!” Magnentius interpreted this omen as applying to himself, as though imperial power had not been granted to him by divine will. Therefore, abandoning the fortress, he proceeded farther.

When Constantius’s soldiers pursued him, an engagement took place near Mount Seleucus. Fleeing alone, he came to the city of Lyons. When he learned that his mother and the brother whom he had appointed Caesar had been killed, he finally killed himself as well, during the sixth consulship of Constantius and the second of Constans Gallus—that is, A.D. 353—on the fifteenth day of August. Not long afterward Decentius, his other brother, also strangled himself. Yet even then no peace came to the state. For shortly afterward a certain tyrant named Silvanus arose in western Gaul, whom Constantius’s commanders quickly killed. SOCRATES, book II, chapter 27. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 32, p. 127.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Revolt of the Jews, and on the Tyranny and Death of Gallus Caesar

The Jews, resisting at Diocaesarea in Palestine, were disturbing the neighboring regions; taking up arms, they attempted to revolt against the Romans. After this, while Gallus Caesar was residing at Antioch, he sent an army against them, captured them, and devastated the city. When he seemed to have conducted matters successfully, unable to bear his good fortune, he proceeded to tyranny. Without revealing his intention to the emperor, he killed the quaestor named Magnus and Domitianus, prefect of the East. Constantius, angered by this, summoned him. Since Gallus could not refuse to obey, he proceeded to the emperor. When he had come near the island of Flacona, Constantius ordered him to be killed there. SOCRATES, book II, chapter 27. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 33, p. 128.

## CHAPTER XII. On Julian Caesar, and That Liberius Succeeded Julius

Shortly afterward Constantius appointed Julian, the brother of Gallus, Caesar and sent him against the barbarians in Gaul. Gallus, who was killed in the seventh consulship of Constantius and his own third—that is, A.D. 354—was put to death in this manner. In the following consulship of Arbition and Julian [read, from Cassiodorus’s *Chronicle*, “Lollianus”], Julian was appointed Caesar on the seventh day of the month of November. SOCRATES, book II, chapter 27. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 34, p. 128.

With the tyrants removed, Constantius seemed to have obtained relief from his troubles. Leaving Sirmium, he went to elder Rome, wishing there to celebrate a triumph with the spoils of the tyrants. Believing that on this occasion he might bring the bishops of both parties into agreement concerning doctrine, he again decided that a synod should be held in Italy. Meanwhile Pope Julius, after having governed the Roman Church for fifteen years, died. Liberius succeeded him. [Col. 0993D] SOZOMEN, book IV, chapter 7. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 8, p. 545.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Aetius the Heretic

Then another heresiarch, Aetius, emerged in Syrian Antioch, surnamed “Godless” (*Sine Deo*) (A.D. 356). He held the same opinions as Arius but separated himself from the Arians because they had admitted Arius into their communion. As was stated above, Arius had one intention in his mind but confessed another in words: he had accepted and subscribed the decree of the Council of Nicaea, wishing at that time to deceive the ruler. For this reason Aetius avoided the Arians.

Aetius had previously been a heretic and seemed to defend the doctrine of Arius with the utmost fervor. Having acquired some education, he returned to Alexandria. Coming to Syrian Antioch, from which he originated, he was ordained deacon by Leontius, then bishop of the city of Antioch. People would come to him, and he would deceive them through sophistical arguments. He did this by following Aristotle’s *Categories*, arguing and fabricating certain theories that he himself did not hold; nor had he recognized the purpose of Aristotle from the learned. Aristotle had written that work for the instruction of young men because sophists at that time were ridiculing philosophy, and he opposed dialectic to the sophists through such disputes. Contemplative philosophers, however, in explaining the books of Plato and Plotinus, refute those matters that Aristotle composed artificially.

Aetius, lacking a contemplative teacher, therefore persisted in sophistical commentaries. For this reason he could not understand how generation can be without beginning, or how that which is born can be coeternal with the one who generates it. Aetius was therefore only lightly instructed and ignorant of the divine writings, prepared solely for disputes—a thing that any rustic can do. Although he had not read the ancient writers who had interpreted the Christian writings, he claimed to take great pleasure in the books of Clement and Africanus, as well as those of Origen, even though those men had been instructed in every virtue of wisdom.

This man therefore wrote letters to the emperor Constantius [264] and to certain others, entangling them in disputes and composing various theories. For this reason he was also called “Godless.” Although he maintained the same positions as Arius, he was thought a heretic by his own associates, who were unable to understand the intricacies of his syllogisms, because he held the same opinions as Arius. Consequently, he was believed to have been expelled from their Church, although he himself had rather refused to communicate with them. From these people came those who were then called Aetians and are now called Eunomians. For at a later time Eunomius, his secretary, instructed by him, published his heretical exposition. We shall explain Eunomius in the appropriate places. SOCRATES, book II, chapter 28. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 35, p. 129.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Enemies of Athanasius

The enemies of the faith, thinking that they had found an opportunity against its defenders, worked very hard with the ruler [Col. 0994D] to expel from the Churches all those whom they regarded as having been deposed by their opponents, as adherents of another faith; or because, while Constans was alive, they had resisted the emperor Constantius, so that matters had nearly come to war.

They accused Athanasius above all, because, through excessive envy, they did not desist from harassing him, neither while Constans was alive nor while Constantius professed to love him. Assembling at Antioch, Narcissus the Cilician, Theodore of Thrace, Theogonius of Nicaea, Patrophilus of Scythopolis, Minophantus of Ephesus, and about thirty others wrote to all the bishops: Athanasius had returned to Alexandria contrary to ecclesiastical decrees and had been found not free from blame at the council; therefore they ordered that no one should communicate with him or send him letters, but should communicate with George, who had been ordained by them. But Athanasius made no response to this. [Col. 0995A] SOZOMEN, book IV, chapter 7. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 8, p. 546.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Synod Held at Milan

After Magnentius had been defeated and Constantius alone held the empire of the Romans, he worked with every effort to induce the Western bishops to agree with those who denied that the Son was consubstantial with the Father. He did this because he did not wish from the beginning to employ force openly, but craftily to persuade them to agree with the decree made by the Eastern bishops against Athanasius. For he hoped that, if Athanasius were condemned by a common decree, he could more easily accomplish his own will in religious matters [editions Valesius and Frobenius: “in the region”].

SOZOMEN, book IV, chapter 7. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 8, p. 546.

[Col. 0995B]

At that time not many Eastern bishops assembled in Italy, since old age or the length of the journey prevented most of them from coming. More than three hundred Western bishops, however, assembled so that, at the emperor’s command, a council might be held at Milan. When the Easterners arrived, they demanded above all that a common decree be made against Athanasius, so that, once this had been done, access to Alexandria might be completely closed to him.

When Paulinus of the Gallic city of Trier, Dionysius of Alba, the metropolitan see of the Italians, and Eusebius, bishop of Vercellae, realized that the Easterners were attempting to act against Athanasius for the destruction of the faith, they rose up and loudly cried out that deceit and circumvention were being inflicted upon Christian doctrines through what was being done. For they said that the charges against Athanasius were not genuine, since such measures were evidently being devised for the revocation of the faith. While they were proclaiming these things, the council of the bishops was dissolved. SOCRATES, book II, chapter 29. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 36, p. 130.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Exile of the Orthodox Bishops, Which Athanasius Recorded in His Defense of His Flight

After Athanasius had been deposed, the heretics tried to set forth another exposition of the faith, or rather a doctrine. But neither of these things could be brought to completion, since, in the presence of the ruler, people cried out that the proceedings were unjust and impious. After this, those men themselves were expelled from their Churches and ordered to live at the furthest ends of the earth.

The remarkable Athanasius records this again in the following manner in that defense:

“Who will be able to recall how much they did? [Col. 0995D] For when the Churches were enjoying peace (A.D. 360), and the peoples were praying in their assemblies, Liberius, bishop of the city of Rome; Paulinus, metropolitan bishop of Gaul; Dionysius, an Italian; Lucifer, metropolitan bishop of the islands of Sardinia; and Eusebius from Italy—all good bishops and preachers of the truth—were seized and sent into exile, having no guilt except that they did not wish to agree with the madness of the Arians, nor did they subscribe to the accusations brought against us.

“Concerning the great and excellent old man, and true confessor, Hosius, I believe it unnecessary even to speak. For it is known to everyone that they also caused him to be carried into exile. He is known not to have been obscure but exceedingly famous among all. Over what council, after all, did he not preside, or whom did he not satisfy by speaking rightly? [Col. 0996A] What Church does not preserve the memory of his protection? Who ever came to him in sorrow and did not return healed? Who, in need, ever asked him for something and did not obtain what he requested? Yet they dared to act in this way even against him, because, recognizing their impious schemes, he refused to confirm them by his own subscription.” THEODORET, book II, chapter 15, p. 90.

The emperor therefore sent those men into exile. He was planning, however, to hold a general council, so that, if possible, he could make all the Eastern bishops who came to the West agree with one another. Since this seemed difficult because of the distances involved in travel, he arranged for two synods to be held: the Italians who were then present were to assemble at Ariminum, while the Easterners were to assemble at the city of Nicomedia in Bithynia.

While the emperor was arranging this, the outcome did not occur as he wished. Neither council agreed with itself, but each was divided. For the bishops who assembled at Ariminum could not agree among themselves, and the Easterners, gathered at Seleucia in Isauria, suffered another schism. This will be related in its proper place. SOCRATES, book II, chapter 29. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 37, p. 131.

## 265 CHAPTER XVII. The Dialogue Held Between Liberius and Constantius, and How Liberius Was Sent into Exile
I indeed wish to recount Liberius’s most celebrated dialogue, conducted wholly for truth against Constantius, since it was written down by faithful men of that time. For after Julius, the successor of Sylvester, he governed the Roman Church.

[Col. 0996C]

The Emperor Constantius said: “Because you are a Christian and the bishop of our city, we have judged it fitting to summon you and warn you not to delay renouncing communion with the utterly wicked Athanasius, who is held fast by unspeakable pride. For the whole world has approved this as rightly done and, by synodal judgment, has declared him alien from ecclesiastical communion.”

Bishop Liberius said: “O Emperor, ecclesiastical judgments ought to be pronounced with the greatest justice. Therefore, if it pleases Your Piety, order an inquiry to be instituted; and if Athanasius appears worthy of condemnation, then let a sentence worthy of him be pronounced according to the form of ecclesiastical procedure. For it is impossible to condemn a man whose case has not been examined.”

The Emperor Constantius said: “The whole world has judged his crimes; but he, as from the beginning, mocks the passage of time.”

[Col. 0996D]

Bishop Liberius said: “Those who signed did not themselves see what was done; but because of honor, fear, and lest they suffer insults from you, they gave their assent.”

The Emperor said: “What do you mean by honor, fear, and insults?”

Liberius said: “Those who do not love the glory of God prefer your gifts. Thus, without seeing the man and without examining the case, they judged him in a manner alien to Christianity.”

The Emperor said: “He was certainly condemned in his presence at the Council of Tyre, and all the bishops of the entire world likewise decreed against him in council.”

Liberius said: “That man was never judged in his own presence. For those who then assembled and condemned him pronounced sentence after Athanasius had withdrawn from the proceedings.”

[Col. 0997A]

The eunuch Eusebius said: “He was proved alien to the Catholic faith at the Council of Nicaea.”

Liberius said: “Only five of those who sailed with him to Mareotis judged him—men whom they sent to accuse him and prepare a record against him. Of those who were sent, two are dead, Theognis and Theodorus; the remaining three are alive, namely Maris, Valens, and Ursacius. Because of these men who had been sent from Sardica, a synod was held: at that synod they presented written petitions, asking pardon, because at Mareotis they had fabricated the proceedings against Athanasius on one side through calumny. We now have their petitions before us. Whom is it proper for us, Emperor, to believe and join in communion with: those who first condemned him and later asked pardon, or those who still strive to bring these accusations?”

[Col. 0997B]

Bishop Epictetus said: “O Emperor, he is not speaking today on behalf of the faith or of ecclesiastical judgments, but so that he may boast before the senators established in the city of Rome, as though he had overcome the Emperor.”

The Emperor said to Liberius: “What portion of the whole world are you, since you alone defend that most wicked man, so as to dissolve the peace of the world and of the Church?”

Liberius said: “The faith is not diminished because I alone stand for it. In ancient times, too, only three men were found resisting the king’s command.”

The eunuch Eusebius said: “Are you making our Emperor into Nebuchadnezzar?”

Liberius said: “No. But is a man who has not been examined to be judged so irrationally?” [Niv. and Froben editions: “judged” (*adjudicatus*) rather than “to be judged” (*adjudicandus*).]

[Col. 0997C]

“Therefore, I ask first that a general subscription be produced, confirming the faith proclaimed at Nicaea; then, when our brothers have been recalled from exile and restored to their own places, if those who are causing disturbances in the Churches are seen to agree with the apostolic faith, let us all assemble at Alexandria, where both their accusers and their defender are present, so that, after the case has been examined, we may pronounce sentence.”

[Col. 0997D]

Bishop Epictetus said: “But the *cursus publicus* is not sufficient for transporting the bishops.”

[Note: *Cursus publicus.* Hence *curiosus*, the *cursus publicus praesentalis* and *curiosi* throughout all the provinces, who were under the authority of the illustrious master of offices. See the book *On the Images of Roman Magistrates*.]

Liberius said: “Ecclesiastical cases do not require the public transport system. For the Churches are able to escort their bishops as far as the sea.”

The Emperor said: “What has already been given legal form cannot be dissolved; the judgment of the greater number of bishops ought to prevail. You alone are defending friendship with that criminal.”

[Col. 0998A]

Liberius said: “Emperor, we have never heard of a judge pronouncing a man’s crimes when the accused is absent, unless these proceedings seem to arise from personal hatred.”

The Emperor said: “He has harmed everyone through communion, yet no one as he has harmed me. Since the death of my elder brother was not enough for him, nor did he cease repeatedly to incite the blessed Constans against me in his hostility, unless we, restrained by greater gentleness, had moderated the force of his incitement. Therefore I have no victory—not even over Magnentius or Silvanus—unless I expel that criminal from ecclesiastical affairs.”

Liberius said: “Do not use the bishops to avenge your hostilities; the hands of ecclesiastical men ought to remain free for sanctification. Therefore, if it pleases you, order the priests to be summoned to their own places; and if they appear to agree with the man whom we are now defending according to the orthodox faith established at the Synod of Nicaea, then, assembling together, they will make provision for the peace of the world, so that a man who has not sinned may not be unjustly rejected.”

[Col. 0998B]

The Emperor said: “There is one matter at issue: I want you, embracing ecclesiastical communion, to be sent back again to Rome. Therefore agree to peace, sign, and return to Rome.”

Liberius said: “I have already said farewell to the brothers at Rome; for ecclesiastical ordinances are greater than residence in the city of Rome.”

The Emperor said: “Then you have three days in which to deliberate. If you wish to sign, return to Rome; otherwise, consider to what place you wish to be deported.”

Liberius said: “A period of three days cannot in any way change my resolve. Therefore, send me wherever you wish.”

After two days, the Emperor examined Liberius, but could not turn him from his purpose, and ordered him to be deported into exile at Beroea in Thrace.

[Col. 0998C]

As Liberius was leaving, the Emperor assigned five hundred solidi for his expenses. Then Liberius said to the man carrying the money: “Go, give it back to the Emperor; he needs to distribute it to his soldiers.”

Likewise, 266 solidi, and the Empress sent him an equal amount. Liberius said: “Return this to the Emperor; he needs it for the expenses of his soldiers. But if the Emperor has no need of it, let him give it to Auxentius and Epictetus; they need it.”

When he had accepted nothing from them, the eunuch Eusebius offered him other solidi. Liberius said to him: “You have desolated the Churches of the whole world, and you bring this to me as though I had been condemned? Go first and learn to be a Christian.”

[Col. 0998D]

After these events, he was sent into exile three days later, having accepted nothing.

THEODORET, Book II, chapters 15 and 16, p. 92.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How Liberius was brought back from exile through the intervention of the Roman matrons

Thus the champion and victor of truth reached Thrace, as he had been ordered. After two years had passed, Constantius came to Rome. [Niv. and Froben editions: “to Rome” (*Romam*).]

The wives of the nobles and senators urged their husbands to entreat Constantius to restore the shepherd to his flocks. For they said that, unless their husbands softened the Emperor’s disposition, they themselves would leave them and hasten to that greatest shepherd.

[Col. 0999A]

But the men replied: “We fear the Emperor’s fury, and perhaps we shall not obtain any pardon.”

“Yet,” they said, “if you ask more insistently, perhaps he will spare you; one or the other will happen: either he will accept your requests, or, if he cannot be moved, he will dismiss you without doing you any harm.”

When those women—worthy to be praised with the highest commendation—understood this advice, they approached the Emperor in their customary finery, so that, judging them distinguished and noble by their splendid dress, he might show them respect and spare them.

As they approached the Emperor, they cried out in these words: “Have mercy on so great a city, which has no shepherd’s care and lies exposed to the snares of wolves.”

He replied: “The city does not lack another shepherd; for there is a bishop who cares for it.”

[Col. 0999B]

For after the great Liberius, one of his deacons, named Felix, had been ordained. He steadfastly preserved the faith set forth at Nicaea, but communicated indiscriminately with those who corrupted it. Nevertheless, none of the inhabitants of Rome entered the basilica while he was inside.

The matrons also said this to the Emperor. Moved by their appeal, he ordered that this man, outstanding among all others, be recalled and that the two govern the Church jointly.

When these letters were reread at the circus spectacle, the people shouted that the Emperor’s sentence was just: just as the spectators were divided into two groups by their colors, so one man ought to preside over one group and the other over the other.

[Col. 0999C]

Although at first they had thus applauded the Emperor’s letters, later, moved by a change of heart, they cried out with one voice: “One God, one Christ, one bishop.”

I have judged it right to record those very words. After these pious words, adorned with justice, of the people beloved by Christ, the most holy Liberius returned. Felix, however, withdrew and lived in another city.

THEODORET, Book II, chapter 17, Christ. Edition.

## CHAPTER XIX. How Eudoxius usurped the episcopate of Antioch

At that time, when Leontius was dying—the man who had ordained the heretic Aetius as a deacon—Eudoxius, bishop of Germanicia, a city of Syria, was then present at Rome. He pretended that a pressing necessity required him to return and spoke craftily to the Emperor, claiming that the city of the Germanicians needed his oversight and protection. He therefore asked permission to return to his own country.

[Col. 0999D]

The Emperor, failing to see through him, let him depart. But Eudoxius, having the chamberlains as his collaborators, abandoned his own city and usurped the episcopate of Antioch. For he was eager to support Aetius.
