For this reason he attempted to convene a council of priests and restore Aetius to the diaconate. This was not done, because hatred of Aetius proved stronger than Eudoxius’s desire.

It is sufficient for us to know this much about the matter.

SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 29; Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 37, p. 132.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Council of Ariminum and the controversies conducted there

[Col. 1000A]

The Easterners who had assembled at Ariminum, consigning to silence the proceedings concerning Athanasius, said that they had come together for the council. Ursacius and Valens supported their efforts. At first they had held the Arian doctrine; later they had agreed with the Homoousians, having given a written petition to the Roman bishop, as has already been stated. These men always inclined toward the side of those who held power at the time.

Their assistants were Germinius, Auxentius, Demophilus, and Gaius. While those present at the council were each trying to put forward a different proposal, Ursacius and Valens said that everything that had been said about the faith ought to be suspended and that a new exposition should be accepted, which those who had recently assembled at Sirmium had issued.

As they said this, they had a document in their hands and caused it to be read according to the exposition of the faith produced at Sirmium. As I have said, they had concealed it there, but at Ariminum it was displayed. Its text is as follows:

### THE FAITH SET FORTH AT SIRMIUM

In the presence of our lord Constantine Augustus, in the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June [22 May], in the year of our Lord 559.

[Col. 1000B]

We believe in one true God, the almighty Father, creator and maker of all things.

And in one only-begotten Son of God, begotten before all ages, before every beginning, before every time that can be conceived, and before every conceivable notion, begotten impassibly from God, through whom the ages were perfected and all things were made.

The Only-Begotten alone was begotten from the Father alone, God from God, like the Father who begot him according to the Scriptures. No one knows his generation except the one who begot him, the Father.

We know that this only-begotten Son of his, Jesus Christ, came from heaven at the Father’s will for the destruction of sin; that he was born of the Virgin Mary; that he lived with the disciples; and that he fulfilled the whole dispensation according to the Father’s will; that he was crucified and died, descended to the underworld, and administered what was there. The gatekeepers of the underworld saw him and were terrified. He rose again on the third day and lived with the disciples; after completing forty days, he ascended into heaven and sat at the right hand of the Father; and he will come on the last day in the glory of the Father to render to each according to his works.

[Col. 1000C]

And in the Holy Spirit, whom the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, promised to send to the human race as Comforter, according to what is written: “I go to my Father, and I will ask my Father, and he will send you another Comforter, the Spirit of truth; he will receive from me and will teach you and remind you of everything” (John 14:16).

But because the term “substance,” having been introduced by the Fathers in a simple manner, is unknown to the peoples and causes scandal, and because the Scriptures do not contain it, it has seemed good that it be abolished and that henceforth absolutely no mention of “substance” be made in relation to God, since the divine Scriptures nowhere speak of the substance of the Father and the Son.

We say that the Son is like the Father in all things, as the holy Scriptures say and teach.

[Col. 1000D]

When these words had been read, those who were displeased with them rose and said: “We have not come here because we lack the faith—for we preserve intact the faith that we received from the beginning—but rather so that, if there is any novelty concerning these matters, we may prohibit it altogether.

“If, then, what has been read introduces no novelty, openly anathematize the Arian heresy, just as the rule of the Church has rejected the other heresies as blasphemous. For it is very well known throughout the whole world that Arius’s blasphemous doctrine stirred up the disturbances that still afflict the Churches, as well as seditions.”

When Ursacius, Valens, and the others did not fully accept this proposal, it divided the Church. Some agreed with what had been read at Ariminum, while others again strengthened the faith of Nicaea. They mocked the written form of that reading, especially Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, in a letter that he sent to his friends. Whoever reads it will find how forceful its language is.

[Col. 1001A]

SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 29; Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 37, p. 132.

For the Arians who had assembled at Ariminum said, wishing to persuade the simple-minded Westerners, that the body of the Church ought not to be divided over two words that were not found written anywhere; rather, they should profess that the Son was like the Father in all things and remain silent about the term “substance.”

But the Homoousian bishops, recognizing their deception, rejected them. They themselves informed the Emperor by letter of their own resolve, saying that they were sons and likewise heirs of the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea.

THEODORET, Book II, chapter 18, p. 97.

[Col. 1001B]

It must nevertheless be known that the synod condemned Ursacius and Valens, Auxentius and Germinius, Gaius and Demophilus, and their associates, because they avoided anathematizing the Arian doctrine. Angered by this condemnation, they quickly went to the Emperor, carrying the faith that had been read at the council.

SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 29; Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 38, p. 136.

Their letter to Constantius will show more clearly the complete rule of their faith. Its words are as follows.

THEODORET, Book II, chapters 18 and 19, p. 97.

## CHAPTER XXI. Letter of the orthodox bishops of the Council of Ariminum to the Emperor Constantius

[Col. 1001C]

By divine command and by the injunction of Your Piety, we trust in what was established long ago. For we have all assembled together at Ariminum from all the cities of the West, so that the faith of the Catholic Church might be recognized and those who hold contrary opinions might be exposed.

After much discussion, we found it best that the faith established in ancient times should remain—the faith that the prophets, evangelists, and apostles are known to have proclaimed through Jesus Christ our Lord, who is also the protector of your kingdom and the helper of your salvation—so that, holding it, we may guard it, and guarding it, preserve it to the end.

For it seems improper and impious to alter anything from what has been rightly and justly defined: namely, what was jointly deliberated and fixed at Nicaea with your most glorious father, the Emperor Constantine. Their teaching and understanding have spread abroad and have been proclaimed to the hearing and minds of all human beings.

[Col. 1001D]

This faith alone attacked and destroyed the Arian heresy; through it not only that heresy but also the remaining heresies were condemned. It is truly rash to add anything to it and dangerous to take anything away. If either of these things is done, our enemies will have the opportunity to act as they wish.

Therefore Ursacius and Valens, because they were participants in and agreed with the Arian doctrine, were separated from our communion. In order to be received back, they acknowledged the offenses they had committed and asked to obtain repentance and pardon; their written statements testify that this was so, and through them they obtained forgiveness for their crimes.

[Col. 1002A]

There was a time when these events are known to have occurred, when the synod was held at Milan in the presence of priests of the Roman Church. We also know that, after the death of the most worthy of memory, Constantine, he had set forth the faith in a document with complete integrity and examination. Since he departed this life after receiving baptism and went to the rewards of the peace he had deserved, we judge it improper to admit any novelty after him or to despise so many holy confessors and martyrs, the authors and originators of this doctrine, who are known to have thought in all things according to the ancient ordinance of the Church.

God transmitted their faith into the period of your reign, through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom such power was granted to you that you might also possess the boundaries of our world.

[Col. 1002B]

Again, then, these wretched and most worthless men in wisdom, preachers of impious thought, have announced themselves with wicked presumption and are attempting to alter the limit of truth. While, according to your command, the rights of the council were being conducted, they disclosed the plan of their deception.

For by a certain cunning and sedition they were striving to introduce some novelty. We found that a certain Germanus, Auxentius, and Gaius had been caught in this kind of wickedness, creating heresy and contention. Although their teaching was one, it is shown to surpass the entire mass of blasphemies.

When they saw that we were neither of their mind nor in agreement with what appeared to be their erroneous opinions, they withdrew from our council, so that they might seem to write something different. The brief time that followed also revealed their intentions.

[Col. 1002C]

But lest ecclesiastical affairs should continually fall into the same disturbances—for repeated disorder and sedition throw everything into confusion—it seemed firm to us that what had been decreed earlier should be preserved legally and immutably.

We separated the men mentioned above from our communion. For this reason we sent envoys to Your Mildness, who would announce the council’s judgment through our letter.

Above all, we instructed the envoys to affirm the truth by explaining the ancient and just reasons, and also to instruct Your Piety: for, contrary to what Ursacius and Valens say, there will be no peace if any just ordinances are altered. For how can peace be expected among those who overturn the laws of peace? Through this, contention and sedition will arise rather among the other cities and the Roman Church.

[Col. 1002D]

Therefore we beseech Your Mildness to receive our envoys with calm ears and look upon them with a tranquil eye; do not permit anything new to be changed to the injury of the dead, but allow us to remain in what was defined and sanctioned by our forefathers, whom we trust to have celebrated everything with deliberation, wisdom, and the Holy Spirit.

For what they are now introducing as novelty brings unbelief to those who believe, but belief to those who do not believe.

We therefore beseech you to order those who are being detained in various places, whom both the burden of age and the hardship of poverty afflict, to return to their own homes, lest the Churches appear to remain desolate after their bishops have been taken away.

[Col. 1003A]

In addition, we ask this: that nothing be added to or taken away from what has already been settled, but that everything remain inviolate which was preserved both by the piety of your father and in your own time.

Do not permit us henceforth to be wearied or to be separated from our own parishes, so that the bishops may pray in peace and devote themselves to divine worship together with their own people, beseeching God for the peace of your empire and likewise for your salvation, which may the Divinity grant you forever.

Our envoys carry the subscriptions and names of the bishops; through the reading of divine Scripture they will also be able to instruct Your Piety.

THEODORET, Book II, chapters 18 and 19, p. 97.

The synod therefore wrote this letter and sent it through the bishops. But Ursacius and Valens, anticipating their arrival, disparaged the council and showed the Emperor the exposition of the faith that they were carrying.

[Col. 1003B]

The Emperor, favoring the Arian doctrine, became angry against the synod and honored Ursacius and Valens instead. For this reason those who had been sent by the council were delayed, unable to obtain a response.

At last Constantius sent the following letter to the synod through the bishops who were present.

SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 29; Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 37, p. 139.

## CHAPTER XXII. Letter of Constantius to the Council of Ariminum

Constantius, victorious and triumphant Augustus, sends greetings to all the bishops assembled at Ariminum.

[Col. 1003C]

Your Benevolence is not unaware that I have always thought, above all else, about the sacred and worshipful law. At present, however, I have been unable to see the twenty bishops whom your wisdom sent on their embassy, since necessity requires us to travel among the barbarians, and, as you know, the divine law ought to be examined with a pure mind, free from every other thought.

We have therefore ordered the bishops to await our return at Adrianople, so that, once the whole state has been properly organized, we may hear what they have done.

Let it not seem burdensome to Your Holiness to await their return, so that, when they come back and report our answer to you, you may bring to completion what is known to be useful to the Catholic Church.

When the bishops received this letter, they replied as follows.

SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 29; Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 37, p. 139.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Letter of the Council of Ariminum sent to the Emperor Constantius

[Col. 1003D]

We have received the letter of Your Clemency, lord Emperor beloved of God. It states that, because of public necessity, you were temporarily unable to see our envoys, and orders us to await their arrival until Your Piety may learn from them what we have decreed and what is known to agree with our forefathers.

Therefore, through this letter, we now declare and affirm that we will in no way depart from our purpose. We have also imposed this upon our envoys.

We beseech you, then, to order that even this letter of our insignificance be reread with a tranquil mind and to receive willingly what we have conveyed through our envoys.

[Col. 1004A]

Your Mildness ought to consider with us how great the sadness and grief now are: that, in the most blessed times of your reign, Churches so great should appear to be deprived of their bishops.

Therefore once again we implore Your Clemency, lord Emperor beloved of God, to order us to return to our Churches before the harshness of winter—if indeed this pleases Your Piety—so that even now we may celebrate solemn prayers with the people to almighty God and to our Lord and Savior Christ, his only-begotten Son, for your empire.

SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 29; Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 37, p. 139.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How Constantius became angry when the bishops departed

After writing this, and waiting for a short time without receiving any answer from the Emperor, they withdrew to their own cities.

[Col. 1004B]

The Emperor, who had already been striving to sow the Arian sect throughout the Churches, seized upon their departure as a pretext for his own outrage, saying that he had been despised because the council appeared to have been dissolved contrary to his command.

Therefore he gave Ursacius and those around him permission to act against the Churches with confidence, whatever they wished.

He ordered the exposition of the faith read at Ariminum to be sent throughout the Italian Churches, commanding that those unwilling to subscribe to it be expelled from their Churches and that other bishops be substituted in their places.

SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 29; Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 37, p. 140.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the synod held at Nicaea in Thrace

[Col. 1004C]

Ursacius and those who agreed with him, departing from Italy, came to a city of Thrace named Nicaea. After staying there for a short time, they held another council.

They translated into Greek the exposition of the faith read at Ariminum, published it, and confirmed it. Afterwards they spread the claim that it was the faith dictated and issued by the universal council at Nicaea, so that, through the similarity of the name Nicaea, they might deceive the simpler-minded by this trick. For they thought that the faith dictated at Nicaea in Bithynia was meant.

But this contrivance did them no good. Shortly afterward they were exposed and mocked.

SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 29; Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 37, p. 141.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How Athanasius again avoided the fury of Constantius

[Col. 1004D]

Meanwhile, Athanasius perceived that plots were being prepared against him. He did not dare to come to the Emperor and did not judge it useful to do so. Instead, he sent five bishops chosen from Egypt, among them Serapion of Thmuis, a man especially holy in his life and very eloquent in speech, to the Emperor, who was then residing in the West.

He also sent with them three priests, through whom he might appease the Emperor, make satisfaction for the disparagements uttered by his enemies, and do whatever else might be useful to himself or to the Churches.

While they were sailing, letters from the Emperor arrived shortly afterward summoning Athanasius. For this reason both Athanasius and the people were disturbed: it was not safe to obey a heretical Emperor, yet it was dangerous to resist him.

[Col. 1005A]

Nevertheless, Athanasius delayed going, and the bearer of the letters returned without accomplishing anything.

When summer arrived, another man sent by the Emperor came with the provincial judges and pressed him; he was also exceedingly hostile to the clergy. But when he saw that the people were prepared for war, he too returned.

Not long afterward, troops from Egypt and Libya assembled. When it was reported that Athanasius was hiding in the church called Theonas’s, their commander took soldiers and Hilary, who had again been sent by the Emperor, and unexpectedly broke down the doors and entered the church. Searching everywhere for Athanasius, he did not find him.

It is said that Athanasius often escaped many dangers through a divine message, and that, by God’s providence, he likewise escaped this peril.

SOZOMEN, Book IV, chapter 8; Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 9, p. 547.

[Col. 1005B]

## CHAPTER XXVII. How he foretold future sorrow when pagans mocked him

Because of these and similar events, which God had foretold to him, he was called a magician by pagans and heretics.

For a story is told that once, as he was passing through the city, a little crow happened to fly away, crying out. When this occurred, a crowd of pagans stood nearby and, mocking him as a magician, asked him to explain what that little crow signified.

He is said to have replied silently with a smile: “Tomorrow,” which in the Latin language signifies the coming day. “By crying out in this way, it signifies for you a sorrowful day tomorrow, by order of the Roman Emperor.”

And so it happened that Athanasius’s words, although they had been mocked, came to pass.

[Col. 1005C]

For on the following day letters from the Emperor arrived for the judges, ordering that the pagans no longer be permitted to enter their temples or celebrate their solemn superstitious rites and festivals.

Thus their venerable and universal festival was destroyed.

SOZOMEN, Book IV, chapter 9; Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 10, p. 549.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. What evils were carried out by Georgius in Alexandria

Although Athanasius, as has been said, had frequently escaped danger, the clergy and people, favoring him, held the Churches until the prefect of Egypt and the military commander expelled them, took possession of the Churches, and handed them over to Georgius.

[Col. 1005D]

Georgius came shortly afterward and took possession of the Churches by his own authority. Since he was violent beyond the conduct and customs of the priesthood, especially toward the supporters of Athanasius, whom, like a tyrant, he subjected to chains and beatings—men and women alike—the people, inflamed with anger, almost killed him, unless he had barely been rescued and fled to the Emperor. [Lyranus manuscript: *vi* (“by force”) for *vix* (“barely”).]

After this, the followers of Athanasius again held the Churches for a long time. When the commander of Egypt came again, he is said to have handed them over to Georgius’s supporters.

After this, when an imperial secretary arrived, many Alexandrians were handed over to punishment. After him Georgius himself arrived, even more terrifying and more hated than before, as though he had moved the Emperor to put many to death.

[Col. 1006A]

The Egyptian monks certainly denounced him; the entire multitude followed their reputation and judged their testimony true, because they lived in the virtue of the highest philosophy.

SOZOMEN, Book IV, chapter 9; Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 10, p. 550.

Since all the soldiers of truth, and especially those living in the West, condemn the faith set forth at Nicaea in Thrace, letters sent by them to Illyricum bear witness to this.

The author of this letter was Damasus, bishop of the Roman Church at that time, who had assumed the rights of the pontificate after Liberius and was adorned with many notable virtues.

In this letter he had ninety associates who had assembled in the city of Rome from Italy and Gaul. Because of their number, I have postponed giving their names. The text of the letter is as follows.

270

## CHAPTER XXIX. Letter of Damasus and the others to Illyricum against the council held at Nicaea in Thrace

[Col. 1006B]

Damasus, Valerianus, and the other bishops send greetings in the Lord to their most beloved brothers, the bishops established in Illyricum.

We believe that you hold fast to our holy faith, founded on the teaching of the apostles, and that you expound this faith to all peoples—a faith which in no respect departs from the decrees established by the Fathers, through whom it is right that the others should be instructed. Yet, from the report of our Gallican and Venetian brothers, we have learned that certain men favor heresies. This evil must not merely be avoided by bishops; they must also resist those things which have been done through the ignorance [Col. 1006C] or simplicity of certain men deceived by wicked interpretations.

Therefore the judgment of our Fathers ought not to be weakened by various doctrines, but rather strengthened. It has accordingly been prescribed that Auxentius of Milan has been condemned especially in this matter. Hence it is right that all teachers of the law throughout the Roman world should hold the things of the law, and not stain the faith with varying doctrines.

Thus, when the wickedness of the heretics first began to sprout—as even now the blasphemy of the impious Arians is evident—our Fathers, three hundred and eighteen in number, chosen and assembled in the city of Nicaea, established this strongest wall against the weapons of the devil. By this remedy the deadly poisons were driven away, so that the Father and the Son should be believed to possess one divinity, one power, and one greatness, and likewise one essence or substance, together with the Holy Spirit. They judged, however, that those who thought otherwise were strangers to our communion.

Certain men wished to corrupt and violate this salutary boundary and this venerable decision by other ideas. But from the very beginning the matter was corrected by those same men who were being compelled at Ariminum to renew and reconsider it, to the point that they confessed either that it had been secretly taken from them through some other deception, or at least that, because they had not understood the judgment established by the Fathers at Nicaea, it was contrary to it.

Nor could any prejudice have been created by the number assembled at Ariminum, since it is clear that neither the Roman bishop—whose decree above all they ought to have awaited—nor Vincentius, who had guarded the episcopate inviolate for so many years, nor others had given their consent to such things. This was especially so because, as we have already said, those very men who seemed to have strayed through the assembly later, having adopted better counsel, declared that these things displeased them.

Your sound judgment therefore perceives that this one faith, founded at Nicaea upon the authority of the apostles, must be preserved with perpetual firmness; and that the Easterners who recognize themselves as Catholics do this together with us, while the Westerners also glory in it. We believe, moreover, that those who languish in this undertaking should soon be separated from our communion, and that the name of bishop should be taken away from them, so that their peoples, freed from error, may recover their breath. For those held in the snare of deception can in no way correct the people whom they deceive.

[Col. 1007B] Let your judgment, therefore, agree with all the priests of God; and we judge that you remain steadfast and firm in it. Thus we too ought rightly to believe together with you. Gladden us with letters in return from your charity. Farewell, dearest brothers.

THEODORETUS, Book II, chapter 22, p. 102.

But the great Athanasius also discussed the council of Ariminum in the following manner in the letter that he wrote to the Africans.

## CHAPTER XXX. From a Letter of Athanasius Concerning the Council of Ariminum

After these things have been brought forward, who would receive those who dare to name Ariminum—or any council other than Nicaea? Or who would not regard as hateful those who reject the decrees of the Fathers, yet set above them the things recently composed contentiously and violently at Ariminum? Who would agree with such men, who do not even accept what is their own?

For, when at their ten and more councils, as I said earlier, they wrote one thing at one time and another at another, they have shown themselves plainly, since they are known to accuse each of their own statements. And they suffer what the traitorous Jews then suffered. For just as those men, abandoning the sole Fountain of living water, dug cisterns for themselves that cannot hold water (Jer. 2:13), as is written by the prophet Jeremiah, so these men, resisting the universal council, dug many councils for themselves, which are plainly empty among them and possess no power.

Let us not, therefore, tolerate those who, besides Nicaea, presume to name Ariminum or any other council; especially since even those who accept Ariminum are known not to have understood what was done there—for they could have remained silent. For you know, dearest brothers, and have learned from your own people who were present at Ariminum at that time, that Ursacius and Valens, Eudoxius and Auxentius, together with Demophilus, were condemned because they wished to write something other than what had been established at Nicaea. When they were compelled to anathematize the Arian heresy, they rejected it, although they had tried rather to defend it.

But the bishops who were truly upright servants of the Lord and who believed correctly—nearly two hundred of them—declared in writing that the Nicene faith alone was sufficient, and that they wished neither to seek nor to hold anything more or anything less than it. They also made this known to Constantius, who had ordered the council to be celebrated.

THEODORETUS, Book II, chapter 23, p. 104.

## CHAPTER XXXI. What Evils Macedonius Committed in Constantinople, and How He Subsequently Offended the Emperor

[Col. 1008A]

Meanwhile Macedonius was disturbing the provinces and cities neighboring Constantinople, stirring up the ministers of his own sickness against the Churches. At Cyzicus he made Eleusius bishop, and at Nicomedia Marathonius, who had formerly been a deacon and was zealous for establishing monasteries of men and women.

After Macedonius had obtained the episcopate, he afflicted those who fled from agreeing with him—not only the orthodox, but also the Novatians, knowing that they too accepted the term “consubstantial.” Their bishop Agelius fled because of the persecution. Many distinguished men, however, were detained and punished because they refused to communicate with him. After being tortured, they were compelled by force to receive and retain communion in their mouths. For, opening people’s mouths with a piece of wood, they placed the sacrament in them.

Moreover, seizing women and children, they forced them to communicate. If anyone resisted, blows, chains, and tortures immediately followed. They even cut off the breasts of women who refused to communicate, pressing them in a chest; in the case of others they burned the same members either with iron or with heated eggs. I heard this from the old man Auxonius, who suffered these same punishments.

SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 30; edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 38, p. 141.

[Col. 1008C] Such, then, were the actions, killings, struggles, enticements, and civil wars that arose from Macedonius under the pretext of Christianity. This produced intense hatred not only among those who were injured, but also among his own associates.

He also offended the emperor himself, both for this reason and for another matter of the same kind. The house in which there was a chest containing the body of the emperor Constantine threatened to collapse, and therefore its guards and those who entered to pray were placed in fear. Macedonius accordingly considered transferring the emperor’s bones, lest the collapse of the building crush the chest.

When the people learned of this, they prevented it, saying that the emperor’s bones ought not to be moved, lest they appear to have been exhumed [quasi exorbiri; ed. Frob. and Niv.: exsopiri]—that is, dug out of the tomb. For this reason the people were divided into two parties: some saying that moving a dead man caused no injury, while others maintained that it was impious. The defenders of the consubstantial faith were also among the latter.

Macedonius, however, disregarding the words of those who opposed him, transferred the emperor’s body to the church where the body of the martyr Acacius lay. When this had been done, opposing crowds gathered at that church, and the conflict reached the point of hand-to-hand violence, so that many people died and the vestibule of the church and the neighboring portico were filled with blood.

When the emperor learned of this, he became angry with Macedonius, both because of those who had died and because Macedonius had dared to move his father’s body without his advice. He therefore left Julian Caesar as governor of the Western regions and proceeded himself to the East.

SOCRATES, in the same place; and SOZOMEN, chapter 20, edition of Christoph Valesius.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning Leontius, Bishop of Antioch, and Aetius, Who Was the Teacher of Eunomius

[Col. 1009A]

Leontius, bishop of Antioch, although he was an Arian, tried to conceal his sickness. Seeing the priests and people divided, with some saying, “Glory to the Father and to the Son,” and others, “Glory to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit,” he himself recited the prayer in silence. Those standing nearby heard nothing from him except when he said, “for ages of ages.”

If he had done this without malice, it might have been said that he did it for the sake of the people’s unity. But because he was also sharpening his opposition against the soldiers of truth and promoted no one except heretics, he was shown to be concealing the disease—at one time under fear of the people, at another oppressed by dread of the emperor, who had forbidden the Son to be called unlike [the Father].

At that time Aetius, the teacher of Eunomius, who had increased Arius’s blasphemy by his own opinions, was serving in the order of deacons. Flavianus and Diodorus, however, while embracing the monastic life and laboring openly on behalf of the apostolic doctrines, rebuked Leontius, the bishop of Antioch, for the plots he was contriving against piety. They said that he had chosen a man imbued with wicked studies, who had attained the height of power for the sake of impiety and possessed the title of deacon for the ruin of the Church.

They also threatened to suspend him from apostolic communion and, when they came to the West, to expose what was being craftily done. Fearing this, Leontius suspended Aetius from office, although he continued to support him in other matters.

That remarkable partnership—namely, Flavianus and Diodorus—had not yet attained sacerdotal office, but pleased the people greatly and armed everyone, night and day, with zeal for piety. They were the first to divide the choirs of singers into two groups and to teach them to sing David’s melody antiphonally. This first began to be done at Antioch and spread as far as the boundaries of the entire world.

They summoned lovers of divine things to the tombs of the martyrs and celebrated vigils, praising God with them. When Leontius observed this, he judged that forbidding it would be imprudent, since he saw that a very large crowd was devoted to those excellent men. But, using gentle words, he asked them to celebrate these festivals in the churches instead.

Recognizing his cunning perfectly, they did what he commanded and gathered their followers in the churches, so that they might praise God joyfully with one harmonious voice. But Leontius was not moved to restrain his wickedness. Wearing an appearance of gentleness, he concealed the iniquity of Stephanus and Placitus [manuscript and editions V.: Flacitae].

For he received adversaries of the true doctrine, although they led disgraceful lives, and raised them to the orders of presbyter and deacon. Those who were adorned with every virtue and defended the apostolic doctrines he abandoned without honor. Through this favor the clergy contained many heretics, while the people fought especially for the correctness of the doctrines, so that even their teachers did not dare to reveal their blasphemy.

What Placitus [manuscript and edition V.: Flacitus], Stephanus, and Leontius did at Antioch in impiety and injustice requires a separate account. Let us now proceed to the remaining matters.

THEODORETUS, Book II, chapter 24, p. 106.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning Eudoxius, Who Seized the Bishopric of Antioch, and the Earthquake That Occurred at Nicaea in Bithynia

Germanicia is a city situated at the meeting point of Cilicia, Syria, and Cappadocia. Eudoxius presided over the Church of this city. When Leontius died, he seized the see of Antioch and began, in his ferocity, to ravage the Lord’s vineyard.

He no longer concealed his wickedness as Leontius had done, but openly resisted the apostolic doctrines and afflicted the orthodox with many calamities. At that time Basil presided over the Church of Ancyra after Marcellus, while Eustathius presided over Sebastia in Armenia. When they learned of Eudoxius’s injustice and rage, they informed Constantius by letter while he was in the West.

They were known to the emperor and enjoyed his favor because of the excellence of their lives. When Constantius learned this, he wrote to the Antiochenes that he himself had not granted Eudoxius the episcopate of the Church, as Eudoxius claimed. He ordered Eudoxius to be expelled and to pay the penalty for his deeds at Nicaea in Bithynia, commanding that a council be held there.

Eudoxius himself had arranged with influential men of the palace that the synod should be held at Nicaea. But God, who knows all things beforehand and knew the future as though it had already happened, prevented the council from being celebrated by a terrible earthquake (A.D. 364). For that earthquake destroyed a very large part of the city and killed many of its inhabitants.

When those who had assembled learned this, they returned to their own Churches. I believe that this was done by God’s wisdom. For it was in that city that the holy Fathers had brought forth the teaching of the apostolic faith against Arius. Perhaps a second gathering there might there have held [ed. Niv., Frob.: sanctioned] contrary views, giving the Arians an opportunity [ed.: an accusation] under that name by which they could more easily capture the simple-minded, as though they were bringing forward that earlier synod. But the guardian of the Churches quickly dissolved such a council.

THEODORETUS, Book II, chapters 25 and 26, pp. 108–109.

In a moment, when the city was shaken, they were unable to flee and were killed at the first experience of danger. It is said that before this disaster occurred, a certain soldier named Ursacius [others: Arsacius], a Persian by birth [ed., Frob.: former soldier], had foreseen it. Under Licinius he had become a confessor; then, abandoning military service, he practiced divine philosophy in a tower of the city.

A heavenly visitation openly commanded him to leave the city, which was soon to suffer the things that afterward became manifest. Having done so, he ran quickly to the church and informed the clergy that they should beseech the Lord to free them from the impending danger. When they thought this ridiculous, he returned to the tower and began to shed tears, lying prostrate.

Meanwhile, when the earthquake came, many perished, while the survivors were scattered across the fields [Latin: per agnos; the context may reflect an OCR error for *per agros*, “across the fields”] and mountains. Ursacius, however, was found dead in that tower, lying prostrate, just as he used to pray.

There is nevertheless a report that, before he died, he asked God to end his life before he could behold the destruction of the city in which he had first come to know Christ and seemed to have shared in ecclesiastical philosophy. For by a way of life worthy of him he also drove away demons.

On one occasion, when someone was being tormented by a demon, Ursacius drew his sword and began to run through the entire city. While everyone else fled, he alone ran toward the man, invoked Christ, cleansed him by his word, and made the man’s madness cease.

Among his various adornments of virtue, this too ought to be remembered. There was a dragon before Nicomedia that killed passers-by with its breath, and it had a lair near a certain valley. Ursacius came there and prayed. Then the serpent came out of its own accord, and, when Ursacius struck it on the head a second time, it was killed. Those who saw Ursacius himself reported this to me.

SOZOMEN, Book IV, chapter 15; edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 16, p. 559.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Concerning the Council Celebrated at Seleucia

I shall now relate briefly the proceedings of another synod, which the emperor Constantius had ordered to be held in the East, as though in imitation of the council of Ariminum. At first he had arranged for the bishops to assemble at Nicaea in Bithynia. Their gathering was prevented by a great earthquake.

This occurred during the consulship of Tatianus and Cerealis (A.D. 358), on the eighth day of the month of August. They therefore considered transferring the synod to a city near Nicaea. When this proposal was rejected, they again wished to assemble at Tarsus in Cilicia. Finally, it was decided to celebrate the council at Seleucia in Isauria, which is called “the Rugged.” This took place during the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius (A.D. 359).

Those who assembled numbered one hundred and sixty. With them was a distinguished palace official named Leonas. In his presence the emperor’s command ordered that the question of faith be proposed. It had also been ordered that Lauricius, a soldier and governor of Isauria, should be present, so that he might assist the bishops wherever necessary.

They assembled on the twenty-seventh day of September and debated while the official record was being prepared. Notaries were also present, recording the words of both parties; these records are preserved in one collection under Sabinus. We, however, set out these matters point by point.

On the first day Leonas ordered each man to propose whatever seemed appropriate to him. Those present, however, did not initially say that any question should be raised unless the others were present. The absent bishops were Macedonius of Constantinople, Basil of Ancyra, and certain others who feared accusation.

Macedonius pretended to be ill, Patrophilus claimed to suffer from an eye ailment, and others invented similar excuses for their absence. When Leonas said that the question should nevertheless be proposed even in their absence, the bishops again replied that nothing should be done until the lives of those being accused had been examined.

For Cyril of Jerusalem, Eustathius of Sebastia in Armenia, and certain others had already been accused. As a result, a dispute arose among those present. Some said that the lives of the accused should be investigated; others maintained that nothing should be sought before the question of faith.

The emperor’s differing opinion also raised the issue. In his letters it was stated at one time that the question of faith should be addressed first, and at another that the conduct of the accused should be examined. This matter led those present into schism, and the mass of the synod was divided into two parties.

Acacius of Caesarea in Palestine was the leader of one party, together with George of Alexandria, Ursacius of Tyre, and Eudoxius of Antioch; thirty-two others followed them. The other party included George of Laodicea in Syria, Sophronius of Pompeiiopolis in Paphlagonia, and Eleusius of Cyzicus, whom very many followed.

When it was decided that the question of faith should be raised first, those of Acacius’s party openly denied the Nicene faith and attempted to dictate another faith. The other party, greater in number, accepted everything in the council of Nicaea [Col. 1012B], except that they objected to the term “consubstantial.”

After many disputes between the two sides had continued until evening, Sylvanus, bishop of Tarsus, finally cried out in a loud voice that a new faith ought not to be dictated, but that the faith previously set forth at Antioch at the time of the dedication should be preserved. After saying this, his followers withdrew.

The other party brought forward the faith recited at Antioch. After reading it again, they dissolved the council for that day. On the following day they assembled in the oratory at Seleucia, closed the doors, and subscribed the faith that had been reread.

Present readers and deacons also subscribed on behalf of the absent, through whom the absent declared that they regarded this definition as valid.

SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 31; edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 39, p. 146.

Acacius and the others of his party complained that the subscription was being made in a closed church, saying: “Things done secretly are full of suspicion of wrongdoing.” They acted in this way because they wanted to present another explanation of the faith. He himself also read the statement he had prepared, in the presence of the judges Lauricius and Leonas, striving to give it authority.

These things were done on the second day. On the third day Leonas hurried to assemble the bishops’ parties again. On that day neither Macedonius of Constantinople nor Basil of Ancyra was absent. When both had assembled with one party, those around Acacius again refused to attend, saying that those who had formerly been condemned, as well as those currently accused, ought first to be expelled from the council.

As the dispute increased, those who appeared to be under accusation withdrew, and those around Acacius entered. Leonas then said that a document had been given to him by those with Acacius, concealing the fact that it contained a statement of doctrine. When the bishops present remained silent, judging that the document contained something other than an exposition of the faith, Acacius’s written faith, together with its preface, was immediately reread in the following form:

“We who assembled at Seleucia in Isauria, in accordance with the emperor’s will, yesterday, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October (A.D. 359), made every effort to preserve ecclesiastical peace with discipline and to consider the faith steadfastly, as our God-loving emperor Constantius commanded, in accordance with the prophetic and evangelical utterances, introducing nothing beyond the Scriptures into the ecclesiastical faith.

“Because certain men in the council have insulted some of us, forbidden others to speak, confined others against their will, brought condemned men with them from various provinces, and introduced with them those who were ordained contrary to the canons, so that the synod was filled with tumult on every side, as the illustrious Count Leonas and the illustrious governor of the province, Lauricius, also observed, for this reason we make the following declaration.

“We do not depart from the faith authoritatively set forth at the dedication in Antioch, but bring it forward, although at that time our Fathers had gathered to address the question under consideration, because the term ‘consubstantial’ disturbed many people in the past and continues to do so to the present.

“Now, however, because certain men are said to have introduced the doctrine that the Son is unlike the Father, for this reason we reject the terms ὁμοουσίου and ὁμοιουσίου—that is, ‘of the same substance’ and ‘of similar substance’—as foreign to the Scriptures. We anathematize the word ἀνομίου, that is, ‘of dissimilarity,’ and we regard all who hold such views as alien to the Church.

“We openly confess that the Son is similar to the Father, according to the Apostle, who says of the Son: ‘He is the image of the invisible God’ (Col. 1:15).

“We confess and believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, and of all things visible and invisible.

“We also believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, begotten from him without suffering before all ages, true God [ed., Niv. and Frob.: the Word] from God, the only-begotten, light, life, truth, wisdom, and will, through whom all things were made in heaven and on earth, whether visible or invisible.

“We believe that, at the consummation of the ages, for the destruction of sin, he took flesh from the holy Virgin Mary, became man, suffered for our sins, rose again, and was taken up into heaven. He sits at the right hand of the Father and will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead.

“We also believe in the Holy Spirit, whom our Lord and Savior called the Paraclete—that is, the Comforter (John 15:26)—promising that after he departed he would send him to the disciples. He also sent him, and through him he sanctifies believers in the Church and those baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

“We decree that those who preach anything other than this faith are alien to the Catholic Church.”

This was the statement of Acacius concerning his faith. He himself subscribed to it, as did those who agreed with him, in the number mentioned shortly before.

After this faith had been read, Sophronius of Pompeiiopolis in Paphlagonia cried out these words: “If each person is permitted to produce his own faith every day, the integrity of the truth will not remain.”

These were Sophronius’s words. I, however, say that if those who came before and after these men had spoken these words about the Nicene faith from the beginning, every dispute could have ceased.

Then, after they had spoken and listened to many words among themselves on this matter and concerning those who had been accused, they departed.

On the fourth day they all assembled and again raised contentious arguments. Among them Acacius expressed his opinion in these words: “If the Nicene faith has once been changed, nothing prevents us from dictating another faith now as well.”

Eleusius of Cyzicus replied to this in the following words: “The present council has been convened not to learn an anathema or to receive an exposition of the faith as though it did not possess one, but, possessing the faith of the Fathers, it will preserve it until life and death.”

By these words Eleusius opposed Acacius’s opinion, calling the faith declared at Antioch the faith of the Fathers. Anyone could rightly answer him: “How do you call these men Fathers, Eleusius, when you do not accept their Fathers? Those who assembled at Nicaea, agreeing in the term ‘consubstantial’ established for the faith, are properly called Fathers, both because they preceded the others in time and because those who later assembled at Antioch received from them the rights of the priesthood.

“But if those who assembled at Antioch denied their own Fathers, then their successors consequently followed the destroyers of the Fathers. How, then, and whose faith did those men reject as wicked, while these men accepted it as sound?

“Moreover, if those men did not possess the Holy Spirit—which is received through the ministry of the laying on of hands—then these men did not receive the priesthood either. For how could they have received from men who did not possess it what was given?

“Anyone, therefore, could bring these replies against Eleusius.”

While these matters were being discussed, they came to another question. Since Acacius had said in the faith that was read that the Son was similar to the Father, they asked one another in what respect the Son was similar to the Father.

Those around Acacius said that the Son was similar to the Father only according to will, not according to substance. All the others, however, declared that he was also similar according to substance. They remained in this dispute for the entire day.

They accused Acacius because, in the writings he had composed, he had said that the Son was similar to the Father in all things, whereas now he denied that he was similar according to substance. When they had argued at length without reaching any agreement, Leonas rose and dissolved the council.

This was the end of the synod assembled at Seleucia. On the following day Leonas was asked to attend, but he refused, saying: “I was sent to bring the council to agreement; while you remain divided, I cannot be present.”

After this, those around Acacius also refused to attend the synod. The other party came to the church and summoned Acacius and those with him so that an examination might be held concerning Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem.

It must be understood that Cyril had long before been accused and condemned. For, having frequently been summoned to judgment, he avoided it continually for two years, fearing his accusers. After being condemned, he sent his condemners a petition of appeal, appealing to a higher judgment. The emperor Constantius also agreed to this appeal.

Cyril, therefore, alone and first among bishops, did this contrary to ecclesiastical custom and rule: he used a written appeal, as in civil courts. He was then present at Seleucia to be judged.

For this reason the bishops summoned Acacius and those who agreed with him, so that, after investigating the accusations, they might issue a common decree. They also summoned certain others who had been accused and had attached themselves to Acacius.

When these men refused to appear after repeated summonses, they condemned them. They also condemned Acacius, George of Alexandria, Uranius of Tyre, Theodulus of Charea, Penum of Phrygia, Theodosius of Philadelphia in Lydia, Evagrius of the island of Mytilene, Leontius of Tripolis in Lydia, and Eudoxius, who had first been bishop of Germanicia and afterward seized the episcopate of Antioch in Syria.

They likewise condemned Patrophilus, because he too, having been accused by the presbyter Dorotheus, refused to obey when summoned. These men, then, they condemned.

They excommunicated Asterius, Eusebius, Abgarus, Basil, Phoebus, Fidelis, Eutychius, Magnus, and Eustathius, decreeing that they should remain in this condition until, after making satisfaction, they cleared themselves of the accusations.

After these proceedings, they made the condemnation known to their parishes. In Eudoxius’s place they appointed Anianus as bishop. Those around Acacius seized him and handed him over to Leonas and Lauricius, by whom he was sent into exile.

After this, the bishops who had ordained Anianus presented a formal protest to Leonas and Lauricius against Acacius and those who agreed with him, saying that the judgment of the synod had been violated. When they accomplished nothing, they went to Constantinople so that the emperor might be informed of what had taken place.

SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 32; edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 40, p. 148.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Concerning the Delegates of the Council of Seleucia, the Examination of Aetius, and the Proceedings at Ariminum

This was the conclusion of the synod established at Seleucia. Whoever wishes to know all the details precisely must reread the records of the notaries.

Afterward the following events took place. Those who agreed with Acacius reached the emperor as quickly as possible. The bishops of the other party each returned to his own place. Only ten of them were sent by common decree. When they came to the emperor, they found ten delegates sent from the council of Ariminum.

The followers of Acacius had already arranged for influential palace officials to protect their party, and through them the emperor’s favor smiled upon them. They said that some of the others agreed with them, while others had been corrupted by ecclesiastical money and still others deceived by unsuitable seductions [ed. V.: seditions].

Acacius was naturally cunning and prepared both to understand and to speak. He also possessed a distinguished church, namely that of Eusebius Pamphilus, whose episcopate he held after him, and he boasted that Eusebius had been his teacher. Being such a man, he easily persuaded others of whatever he wished.

When there were twenty bishops from both councils at Constantinople, together with others who happened to be present, Honoratus was first ordered to judge the case of Aetius in the presence of the leading officials. The emperor, on returning from Rome not long before, had appointed him the first prefect of Constantinople.

Afterward, when Constantius himself was listening together with the judges, Aetius was found to be sick in the matter of the faith, so much so that even the emperor and the others were stirred against what appeared to be his blasphemous words.

It is said that Acacius and those who agreed with him initially pretended to be ignorant of this heresy and acted under a certain pretext with the emperor, so that he himself might judge the matter with his leading officials. They believed that Aetius could not be defeated by argument, but that they could more readily win over the judge’s hearing by necessity, and that the undertaking of the heresy would prevail without opposition.

When this could not be accomplished, they demanded that the document issued at Ariminum be brought forward and that those sent by the synod of Seleucia accept it. When the question concerned the term “substance,” they affirmed under oath that they in no way confessed the Son to be unlike the Father according to substance, and declared themselves ready to renounce this heresy.

And because the Westerners had unexpectedly abandoned the term “substance” at Ariminum, they acknowledged that such a document was necessary. They said that if the term “substance” were left unmentioned, then together with the term “substance” the decree concerning consubstantiality would undoubtedly also be left unmentioned—a decree that many Western priests embraced most earnestly out of reverence for the council of Nicaea.

The emperor too was persuaded to praise this document, considering the multitude assembled at Ariminum and believing that one who called the Son similar to the Father did not sin. He believed that the confession of “consubstantial” and that of “similar in substance” were the same in power and differed in meaning only through words unknown to divine Scripture.

Holding this opinion, he ordered the bishops to agree in the faith of the council of Ariminum. When he was preparing for the consulship—which is celebrated according to Roman custom on the first day of January—he spent the entire day and most of the night engaged in conflict among the bishops, until the bishops who had come from Seleucia subscribed to the document brought from Ariminum.

SOZOMEN, Book IV, chapters 21 and 22; edition of Christoph Valesius, chapters 32 and 33, p. 577.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. How They Affirmed the Faith of the Council of Ariminum and Deposed Aetius Together with Others
Acacius, however, and those who were with him, after staying for some time in Constantinople, summoned bishops from Bithynia. Among them were Macarius of Macedonia [read: Mares of Chalcedon] and Ulfilas, bishop of the Goths. All fifty of them assembled and confirmed the document read at Ariminum, adding that henceforth neither “substance” nor “essence” should ever be named in reference to God, and that, apart from this document, all other statements—whether already made or still to be made—should be completely repudiated.

Having done this, [Col. 1016D] they deposed Aetius from the order of the diaconate, as one who held heretical opinions, who composed certain writings of human wisdom contrary to ecclesiastical custom, who dictated dialogues full of blasphemy, and who proved to be the author of ecclesiastical disturbances and sedition. Some say, however, that they did not depose him with a sincere heart, but wished to commend themselves to the emperor because they were said to hold similar opinions.

When they saw the emperor’s indignation against Macedonius at that time, they deposed him as well, together with Eleusius of Cyzicus, Basil of Ancyra, Ortasius of Sardica, and Dracontius of Pergamum. Although they appeared to disagree with them in doctrine, at the time of their deposition they paid no regard to their faith; instead, they brought separate charges against all of them, [Col. 1017A] by which they claimed that the men had transgressed the ecclesiastical canons.

SOZOMEN, Book IV, chapter 23. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 24, p. 579.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. For what reason Cyril of Jerusalem was deposed

Among these they also deposed Cyril of Jerusalem, on the grounds that he was in communion with Eustathius and Elpidius. These men had held opinions contrary to those who had assembled at Mitylene. Cyril himself had also attended that gathering and, as though after the deposition carried out in Palestine, had shared communion with Basil and George, bishops of the city of Laodicea.

When Cyril of Jerusalem had assumed the episcopate, he disputed with Acacius [Col. 1017B] of Caesarea in Palestine concerning the rights of the metropolitan, as though he were the bishop of an apostolic see. Therefore, when they were established at Antioch, they disparaged one another, as though neither held correct opinions about God. Indeed, each had previously appeared suspect to the other. Acacius praised the doctrine of Arius, whereas Cyril followed those who proclaimed the Son consubstantial with the Father.

Acacius therefore, finding an opportunity together with the bishops who agreed with him, deposed Cyril on this account. When famine had seized the province of Jerusalem, the crowd of needy people looked to him as their bishop for food. Since he had no money with which to relieve [editions of Niv. and Frob.: “to attend to”] their poverty, he sold sacred vessels and hangings and came to the aid of the people’s necessity.

SOZOMEN, Book IV, chapter 24. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 25, p. 583.

[Col. 1017C] This moved the emperor’s mind, especially because Acacius was known to have plotted against Cyril. They say that Cyril had sold the sacred vestment which the most famous emperor Constantine had given to Macarius, bishop of that city, for the honor of the Church of Jerusalem, so that, clothed in it, he might perform the ministry of holy baptism. The vestment was woven with gold and silk. A certain dancer named Thymelicus bought it; and when he had put it on, he fell during the very dance, was crushed, and was handed over to death.

THEODORET, Book II, chapter 27, p. 110.

With this charge in hand, Acacius deposed Cyril from the episcopate. The followers [Col. 1017D] of Acacius then drove the condemned bishops out of the city of Constantinople. But the bishops who agreed with them, while unwilling to subscribe to those depositions, were ten in number; they ordered them meanwhile to live apart, neither to perform their ministry nor to govern churches, until they subscribed. If within six months they did not repent and give written assent to all the decisions and actions of that council, they too would be deposed.

After this, the bishops who agreed with them appointed others throughout the individual provinces. Having conceived such plans, they wrote to all the bishops and clergy, instructing them to observe and carry them out.

Not long afterward, therefore, Eudoxius succeeded Macedonius; Athanasius succeeded Basil; and Eunomius succeeded Eleusius—he who later became the leader of the Eunomian heresy. In place of Eustathius, Meletius assumed the episcopate of the Church [Col. 1018A] of Sebaste. of the Church of Sebaste.

SOZOMEN, Book IV, chapter 24. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 41, p. 583.

An exposition of the faith, with an addition, was also read in the city of Constantinople. But since we scarcely ever find our way through the labyrinth of expositions, we shall also arrange their number.

SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 32. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 41, p. 154.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Enumeration of the various heretical expositions after the explanation of the faith of the Council of Nicaea

After the Council of Nicaea, at the dedication at Antioch, they composed a twofold exposition. The third is the one known to have been presented to the emperor Constantius by Narcissus in Gaul. The fourth was that of Eudoxius, which was sent to Italy. At Sirmium three were composed [Col. 1018B], one of which was reread at Ariminum during the consulship [edition: “was left behind”]. The eighth was issued at Seleucia by the associates of Acacius; the last was recited at Constantinople with an addition. For it had been added that neither “substance” nor “subsistence” should be spoken of in reference to God.

At that time Ulfilas, bishop of the Goths, first gave his assent [manuscript of Lyr.: “first wrote it down”]. Previously he had embraced the faith of Nicaea, following Theophilus, bishop of the Goths, who had been present at the Council of Nicaea and had subscribed to it.

Acacius and Eudoxius, therefore, together with their associates, were engaged at Constantinople in a dispute concerning the condemnation of certain bishops of the opposing party [A.D. 363]. Seeing that the emperor was angry with Macedonius, they first condemned him as the author of many deaths and because he had received into communion a deacon who had been caught in fornication.

SOCRATES, in the same place.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. How Eudoxius the Arian, after Antioch, seized the episcopate of Constantinople, and concerning Aetius’s wicked doctrine

After Macedonius had been expelled, Eudoxius, rejecting the see of Antioch, seized the Church of Constantinople with the support of Acacius. These men, forgetting their own actions, enacted decisions contrary to their previous judgments. For although they had earlier deposed Dracontius because he had passed from Galatia to Pergamum, without considering what had been done, they themselves transferred Eudoxius to another see.

After this, they sent everywhere the faith read at Ariminum, together with the addition they themselves had made in the city of Constantinople, ordering that those who did not subscribe should be sent [Col. 1018D] into exile by imperial command. They also made their actions known to the other Eastern bishops who agreed with them and to Patrophilus, bishop of Scythopolis, who had promptly returned from Seleucia to his own city.

After Eudoxius had been installed at Constantinople, the greater church called Sophia was also dedicated, in the tenth consulship of Constantius and the third of Julian Caesar (A.D. 360), on the fifteenth day of February.

When Eudoxius had taken his seat in that church, he was the first to utter the saying that became famous everywhere: “The Father is ἀσεβής, the Son εὐσεβής.” These two Greek words have different meanings among the Greeks. ἀσεβής means both “impious” and “without worship”; εὐσεβής means “pious” and “worshiping rightly.”

When he had spoken these words, a disturbance arose among the people, as though he had called the Father impious and the Son pious. [Col. 1019A] Then he said, “Do not be disturbed by what I have said: the Father is ἀσεβής because he worships no one, whereas the Son is εὐσεβής because he worships the Father.”

When Eudoxius had said this, the disturbance among the people was indeed calmed, but great laughter filled the church. The saying continued thereafter as an object of ridicule. By such seductions and speeches the heresiarchs busied themselves while tearing the Church apart.

With such an outcome, therefore, the synod at Constantinople also came to an end.

SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 33. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 43, p. 156.

Acacius and his associates did not cease, however. They assembled at Antioch and destroyed what they had previously approved. From the document that had been read at Ariminum and Constantinople, they tried to remove the term “similarity,” introducing the claim that the Son was unlike the Father in every respect, both in substance and in will [Col. 1019B], and that he had been made from things that did not exist, as Arius had first taught. The Aetians also agreed with them. For after Arius, Aetius was the first to dare to use these terms openly.

For this reason he was called “Godless”; and his followers were consequently called “Unlike” and “Non-existential” by those who at Antioch agreed with the consubstantial doctrine.

When the adherents of the Council of Nicaea asked them why, in their exposition of the faith, they dared to call the Son, while saying that he was God from God, unlike the Father, and to name him as being from things that did not exist, they replied in these words:

“It is said that the Son is God from God in the same way as it is written in the Apostle: ‘All things are from God’ (Romans 11:36). Therefore the Son of God also is one of all things; and for this reason the phrase ‘according to the Scriptures’ was placed in the expositions.”

SOZOMEN, Book IV, chapter 28. Edition of [Col. 1019C] Christoph Valesius, chapter 29, p. 588.

The leader of this doctrine was Gregory, bishop of Laodicea. While teaching such things, he did not know how extensively Origen, at an earlier time, had examined and interpreted the Apostle’s distinctive usages.

SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 35. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 45, p. 157.

## CHAPTER XL. Concerning the cruelty of George at Alexandria, and those who held the episcopate after Cyril of Jerusalem

Meanwhile, while Athanasius was still in hiding, George cruelly afflicted the pagans at Alexandria as well as the Christians who opposed him. He compelled both groups to adopt his own opinion and punished those who refused. Among educated people he was hateful, as though he despised [Col. 1019D] them and issued commands to the judges; among the populace he was regarded as a tyrant and as exalted above the powerful.

Above all, however, he oppressed the pagans, whom he forbade to sacrifice and to observe the festivals of their fathers. At that time he brought soldiers and the prefect of Egypt into the city under arms and removed the images and ornaments from the temples. This afterward became the cause of his death.

After Cyril had been deposed, as was stated above, Herennus took possession of the Church of Jerusalem; after him came Heraclius, and after Heraclius, Hilary. We understand that these men governed that Church until the reign of the emperor Theodosius, when Cyril returned once more to his own episcopate.

SOZOMEN, Book IV, chapter 29. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 30, p. 589.

## CHAPTER XLI. Concerning Macedonius and the Macedonians

[Col. 1020A]

Macedonius, therefore, having been driven from the Church of Constantinople and unable to endure his condemnation, refused to remain quiet. He went over to the party that had deposed Acacius and his associates at Seleucia. He sent an embassy to Sophronius and Eleusius, urging them to defend the faith previously set forth at Antioch and afterward confirmed at Seleucia, and reminding them that the faith of “similar substance” ought to be proclaimed.

Many of his associates gathered around him, and they are now called Macedonians after him. Those who had rejected Acacius at the Council of Seleucia openly established the term “similar substance,” although previously they had not declared this with such manifest evidence.

Many hold the opinion [Col. 1020B] that this teaching was not discovered by Macedonius but rather by Maratonius, bishop of Nicomedia; hence they are also called Maratonians. Eustathius, expelled from Sebaste, took refuge with them.

When Macedonius avoided including the Holy Spirit in his treatment of the divine Trinity, Eustathius likewise said: “I neither allow the Holy Spirit to be called God, nor do I presume to call him a creature.”

For this reason those who agree in the exposition of consubstantiality call such persons “opponents of the Spirit.”

SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 35. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 45, p. 158.

When Macedonius had been expelled from the Church of Constantinople, he did not hold the opinions of Acacius and Eudoxius. Rather, he taught that the Son, God, was in every respect and according to substance similar to the Father. But he said that the Holy Spirit did not participate in those things [Col. 1020C], but was a minister and performed a service, as may be said of the holy angels.

SOZOMEN, Book IV, chapter 26. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 27, p. 585.

## CHAPTER XLII. Concerning what the Arians again did against the Arians themselves; how Eustathius exposed the wickedness of Eudoxius; and the letter of the Council of Constantinople to George of Alexandria condemning Aetius and his writings

The followers of Acacius therefore assembled at Antioch with great enthusiasm, driven by repentance because they had called the Son similar to the Father. In the following consulship, that of Taurus and Florentius (A.D. 361), while Euzoius was governing that Church and the emperor was stationed [Col. 1020D] there, a few again revived the views that had previously pleased them. They said that the phrase “similar substance” ought to be removed from the exposition of the faith delivered both at Ariminum and at Constantinople. They did not conceal the matter but said openly that the Son was unlike the Father in every respect, not only according to substance but also according to will, and that he was from things that did not exist, just as Arius had taught. The followers of Aetius were with them.

SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 35. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 45, p. 159.

At that time, while Eudoxius’s perfidy was being denounced, Eustathius, among others, said:

“Since, O emperor, you wish an examination to be made concerning the faith, consider Eudoxius’s blasphemies.”

He produced Eudoxius’s exposition, which contained, among other things, the following:

[Col. 1021A]

> What is expressed as unlike is unlike according to substance.
>
> There is one God the Father, from whom are all things; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.
>
> But “from whom” and “through whom” are unlike. Therefore the Son is unlike God the Father.

Moved by this reading, the emperor asked Eudoxius whether he acknowledged it as his own. Eudoxius denied this, saying that it belonged to Aetius. When the emperor ordered Aetius to be brought in, Aetius, on being questioned, professed that the writing was his, although it had not been his originally; and for this reason he was sent into exile.

Eustathius nevertheless continued to proclaim that Eudoxius held the same opinion, demanding that he anathematize Aetius’s writing. Although he did so only reluctantly, he eventually complied and condemned what he had previously and subsequently preached.

Then Eudoxius also demanded that Eustathius anathematize the term ὁμοούσιον [Col. 1021B], “consubstantial,” since it was not found in Scripture. At this point Sylvanus said: “The phrases ‘from things that do not exist,’ ‘creature,’ and ‘of another substance’ are nowhere written. It is therefore right that these should be rejected.”

The emperor also decreed that this should be done, and, although with difficulty, they complied. After this, they demanded that they themselves should also reject ὁμοούσιον. Then Sylvanus said, disputing both dialectically and truthfully:

“If he is not from things that do not exist, and is neither a creature nor God the Word from another substance, then he is consubstantial with the Father who begot him, just as God is from God and light from light, and he has the same nature as the one who begot him.”

The emperor then became angry and threatened them with exile. But they said: “You have the power to punish; nevertheless, we are not destroying the decrees of the Fathers.”

The emperor then ordered them to be expelled from the [Col. 1021C] churches and others to be appointed in their place.

At that time Eudoxius, while tyrannically holding the Church of Constantinople, expelled Eleusius of Cyzicus and appointed Eunomius as bishop. They also repudiated Aetius in writing, although they appeared to be his associates, and wrote to George about what had taken place.

THEODORET, Book II, chapter 27, p. 111.

### Copy of the Letter of the Entire Council to George against Aetius, on Account of His Wicked Blasphemy

The holy synod assembled at Constantinople sends greetings to the honorable George, bishop of the city of Alexandria.

When the synod reproved Aetius on account of his wicked [Col. 1021D] writings, full of scandals, action was taken against him by the bishops in accordance with the sequence of ecclesiastical ordinances. He was deposed from the diaconate and made a stranger to the Church.

These warnings also proceeded from us: his wicked letters were not to be brought forward for anyone’s reading, but were to be rejected because they were exceedingly harmful. We add that he is also to be anathematized if he persists in that purpose together with his followers.

It was fitting that all the bishops assembled in the synod should depose the author of scandals and schisms created among the Churches throughout the whole world and should agree on the sentence justly pronounced against him. But, contrary to our votes and hope, Serras, Stephen, Heliodorus, and Theophilus refused to agree with our judgment or to subscribe to his deposition.

Serras in particular also accused Aetius of another insane arrogance of his. For he said that Aetius presumed to claim—and had said—that the things God had hitherto concealed from the apostles had been revealed [Col. 1022A] to him.

After Serras had protested against Aetius’s insane and arrogant statements, those men could not be moved by prayers to agree with our decision. Nevertheless, restrained by patience, we tolerated them for a long time: now expressing indignation, now making requests, now issuing threats, and again making entreaties that they should agree with us and issue a decision consonant with the entire council.

We continued to tolerate them in the hope that perhaps they would listen, perhaps understand, perhaps see the situation clearly. When, [Col. 1022B] after we had persevered for a long time, they were not moved to follow the sentence pronounced concerning the aforesaid man, we judged the honor of the Church more important than the friendship of these men.

We therefore concluded the period of their excommunication, granting them six months for repentance, so that, if within that time they should turn back and agree with the decisions of their brethren, they might be received into the Church and recover their former confidence and charity.

If, however, they persisted without repentance and placed human friendships above the rules of the Church and our concord, then we judged them to be strangers to the dignity of the episcopate. Once they had been deposed, it would be necessary for other bishops to be appointed in their places, so that the lawful Church, receiving an appropriate order, might be in harmony with itself. [Col. 1022C]

All the bishops were to preserve the bond of charity and to say the same things with perfection, in one understanding and one essence.

So that you may know what pleased the council, we have sent these writings to your reverence, praying that, while preserving these things by the grace of Christ, you may govern peacefully and lawfully the churches placed under your care.

THEODORET, Book I, chapter 28, p. 114.

## CHAPTER XLIII. Concerning Eunomius, how he was ordained at Cyzicus and again expelled, and how he became the author of a heresy

Aetius is exalted by Eunomius in his books, where he calls him a man of God and honors him with many expressions of praise. At that time Eunomius was also present when Aetius was repudiated and himself received episcopal ordination from those men.

Eudoxius and Acacius, together with their associates, gave their assent to what had been done [Col. 1022D] at Nicaea in Thrace and appointed other bishops in place of Basil and Eleusius. I consider it unnecessary to speak of these men now; I shall narrate only what concerns Eunomius.

When Eunomius had obtained the Church of Cyzicus while Eleusius was still alive, Eudoxius saw the people’s well-being and observed that the emperor was raging against those who professed the only-begotten Son of God to be created. He compelled Eunomius to conceal this opinion and not reveal it to those who were investigating and accusing him. He said to Eunomius as well:

“In due time we shall preach what we now conceal. We shall teach those who are ignorant, and those who oppose us we shall either bend, compel, or punish.”

Persuaded by these promises, Eunomius presented his impiety under a veil. But those who had been trained in divine [Col. 1023A] teachings saw the cunning of his words and were distressed; they judged that to contradict him openly would be an act of presumption rather than wisdom.

They therefore assumed the appearance of heretical wickedness, pretending that they shared it, and approached his house. They asked him to explain the truth of the doctrine openly and not allow them to be carried here and there by different teachings.

Eunomius then, taking courage, revealed the opinion he had been concealing. When they said that it was exceedingly wicked for not everyone subject to him to enjoy the truth, he was deceived by these and similar words and revealed his blasphemy in the assembly of the church.
