But they, inflaming their souls with zeal, went to Constantinople. First they lodged a written accusation against Eunomius before Eudoxius. [Col. 1023B] When he did not receive them, they approached the emperor and disclosed with groans the plague of Eunomius. They said that Eunomius’s statements were more impious than those of Arius.

The emperor, angered on their account, ordered Eudoxius to bring Eunomius before him and, once convicted, to strip him of the priesthood. Eudoxius repeatedly endured the importunity of the accusers and tried to avoid the matter. They therefore approached the emperor again, groaning that Eudoxius had done nothing of what he had commanded and was despising so great a city, which was being polluted by Eunomius’s blasphemies.

Constantius then threatened to expel Eudoxius unless he brought Eunomius to judgment and punished him once he had been convicted by the accusation.

Fearing this, Eudoxius wrote to Eunomius that he should flee from Cyzicus and blame himself, since he had in no way obeyed Eudoxius’s warning. Eunomius, however, frightened, did indeed depart [Col. 1023C], but, unable to endure the insult, accused Eudoxius of betrayal and asserted that both he and Aetius had been wronged. He then formed a faction of his own.

All who followed his doctrine in agreement with him withdrew from Eudoxius, accusing him of betrayal and joining themselves to Eunomius. They are known to have derived their name from him to this day.

Eunomius thus became a heresiarch and increased the blasphemies of Arius by adding to their mass of impiety. That he served the passion of arrogance and proved to have established a separate college is proclaimed by the events themselves.

For when Aetius had been repudiated and expelled, Eunomius did not go out with him, although he called him his teacher and a man of God; instead, he remained attached to Eudoxius. But when the punishment for impiety was demanded, he did not accept the council’s decree; rather, though deprived of episcopal dignity, he ordained bishops and presbyters. [Col. 1023D]

THEODORET, Book II, chapter 26, p. 115.

## CHAPTER XLIV. Concerning Apollinaris the father and Apollinaris the son, and their heresy

At that same time there were in Laodicea of Syria two men bearing the same name, father and son, both called Apollinaris. The father held the rank of presbyter, while the son served as a lector. Both were teachers of Greek eloquence. The father was a grammarian; the son was a rhetorician.

The father was Alexandrian by birth. After first teaching at Berytus, he later came to Laodicea, married, and had a son named Apollinaris.

At that time both studied [Col. 1024A] under the sophist Epiphanius and, since they were his friends, strongly supported him. Theodotus, bishop of Laodicea, feared that through frequent conversation with the sophist they might turn toward paganism and forbade them to attend his classes. They disregarded the bishop and embraced Epiphanius’s friendship all the more.

Later George, Theodotus’s successor, was unable to prevent them from doing so and deprived them both of communion.

Apollinaris the son then considered this an injustice and, relying on the inflated power of sophistic eloquence, himself introduced the novelty of a heresy that now bears the name of its inventor.

Some say that they were provoked against George not only for the reason stated above, but also because they saw him putting forward varying doctrines: at one time professing that the Son was similar to the Father, as had been established at Seleucia, and at another turning toward the Arian [Col. 1024B] position.

Therefore, taking this as a convenient opportunity, they withdrew. Since no one paid attention to them, they introduced the plague of heresy under the guise of religion.

At first they said that the soul had not been assumed by God the Word in the dispensation of the incarnation. Then, as though led to repentance, they corrected themselves by adding: “The soul was indeed assumed, but it did not possess a mind; rather, God the Word was assumed in a human being in place of the mind.”

They are said to have fallen into error concerning this single point, and those who now bear their name are called after them; for they profess that the Trinity is consubstantial.

SOCRATES, Book II, chapter 36. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 46, p. 160.

## CHAPTER XLV. How the king of the Persians was unable to prevail against the Romans because of the prayers of Bishop James

[Col. 1024C]

While these events were taking place, King Sapor was encamping against the Romans. Constantius came to Antioch with a great army and drove away the enemy (A.D. 357). This was accomplished not by Roman military power but by God, whom the Romans worship.

I shall now undertake to recount the trophy of that victory. Nisibis—which some call Antioch of Mygdonia—lies on the boundary between Persian and Roman territory. Its bishop, ruler, and leader was James, illumined by the rays of apostolic grace. I judged it unnecessary in this history either to write out or enumerate all his worthy and praiseworthy miracles. For the sake of the narrative, however, I shall describe one of his deeds.

The Persian army besieged this city, which was subject to the Romans. [Col. 1024D] Although it kept watch over it continuously for seventy days, captured many cities, made numerous preparations and earthworks around it, and constructed embankments and ditches for taking the city, it could not capture it.

Later the Persians held back from a distance the force of the river Mygdonius, which rushed through the middle of the city, and raised both its banks, so that the water collected within them might build up and then burst forth with greater force.

When they saw that the raised banks they had constructed were now filled, they suddenly removed the dams they had made and released the force of the river against the wall. The wall, unable to withstand the weight of the violent water, tilted and fell.

After this, the water entered with great force and also brought down another section of the wall, [Col. 1025A] through which the river ordinarily flowed out, with a great collapse.

When Sapor saw this, he believed that he could capture the city without a battle. He rested that day so that the riverbed might be cleared and it might be possible to walk through the river.

On the following day, believing that he could enter the city with his entire army through the places where the walls had collapsed, he saw a wall constructed on both sides.

That most holy man had armed the soldiers and other inhabitants of the city with his prayers. In this way he restored the wall and built fortifications with which to repel those who approached. He accomplished this not by coming to the wall but by completing it within the holy temple while supplicating the Lord.

Sapor was terrified not only by the construction of the wall but also by another vision. He saw someone standing above the wall, clothed in imperial attire and shining with both purple and a diadem.

Believing that he was the Roman emperor, he threatened with death those who had told him that the emperor was not present there. When they affirmed that they had spoken the truth and that Constantius was staying at Antioch, Sapor recognized from the face [Col. 1025B] he saw that their words were true, and he said that God was fighting on behalf of the Romans.

Deeply distressed by this, the unhappy man shot an arrow into the air. When he saw that he could not strike the man in the body, he nevertheless did not withdraw from the assault of his madness.

Then Ephrem, a remarkable man and an excellent writer among the Syrians, pleaded with the most holy James to come to the wall and, seeing the barbarians, send arrows of cursing against them.

The venerable man was persuaded and climbed a certain [Col. 1025C] tower. When he saw armies numbering thousands upon thousands, he asked no other curse against them except gnats and mosquitoes, so that through these small creatures they might recognize the power from above.

Clouds of gnats and mosquitoes followed his prayer. They filled the trunks of the elephants—for those trunks are hollow—and likewise the ears and nostrils of the horses and other beasts of burden.

Unable to endure the force of the small creatures, the animals threw their riders and commanders from their backs, broke up the battle lines, and threw them into confusion; the riders abandoned the army and fled with the greatest speed.

In this way the most wretched emperor, recognizing that a small and merciful correction had been inflicted upon him by God, who watches over the souls of those who devoutly worship him, led his army away from the siege. From it he gained confusion, not victory.

THEODORET, [Col. 1025D] Book II, chapter 30, p. 117.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Concerning the council again assembled at Antioch

At this time Constantius was staying at Antioch. While the war against the Parthians was at rest, he again gathered the bishops, compelling everyone to reject the terms “of one substance” and “of another substance.”

But after Eudoxius had seized the see of Antioch following Leontius and, after many councils, had been expelled and had unjustly held the episcopate of Constantinople, the Church of Antioch appeared to be deprived of a shepherd.

The bishops therefore assembled. Since they were numerous and had gathered from every direction, they told the emperor that a shepherd ought [Col. 1026A] first to be appointed and that only then should questions of doctrine be considered with him.

THEODORET, Book II, chapter 31, p. 119.

## CHAPTER XLVII. Concerning the translation of Saint Meletius to the episcopate of Antioch and his exposition concerning the unity of the Trinity

At that time the most holy Meletius, governing a certain city of Armenia and teaching the barbarians, appeared to be living in tranquility. The Arians, supposing him to agree with them, asked Constantius that he be appointed head of the Church of Antioch.

The orthodox also joined them in subscribing to the decree because of the excellence of his life and the soundness of his doctrines. Both parties entrusted the decree itself to Eusebius, bishop of Samosata.

When the great [Col. 1026B] Meletius arrived, the people of both parties went out to meet him. Jews and pagans likewise wished to see that famous man, Meletius.

The emperor then ordered him and the others who were able to explain it to expound to the people the passage: “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways, for his works” (Proverbs 8:22). He instructed shorthand writers to record their words.

George of Laodicea was the first to spew forth the stench of heretical corruption. After him came Acacius of Caesarea, who tried to put forward a kind of middle doctrine and withdrew far from their blasphemy, although he did not preserve the supreme doctrine of apostolic integrity.

Third, the great Meletius arose and displayed the correctness of the rule in sacred discussion. Using the truth as a kind of balance, he avoided both what was excessive and [Col. 1026C] what was deficient.

When the entire crowd applauded and asked him to give them a brief outline of the doctrine, he held up three fingers, then joined two together and extended one, and uttered this admirable statement:

“There are three things understood, but we speak as though concerning one.”

THEODORET, in the same place.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. How, after Meletius had been expelled, Euzoius the Arian was ordained bishop of Antioch

At that time it is said that, while he was still speaking, the archdeacon [Col. 1026D] of his Church extended his hand and closed Meletius’s mouth. But Meletius indicated his opinion more clearly with his hand than with his voice.

For he opened three fingers, then closed them again, and once more extended only one finger. By the figure of the thumb he proclaimed that the three are one.

Then, while the archdeacon held his hand and allowed his mouth to be released, he cried out in a free voice that the Council of Nicaea ought to be preserved.

SOZOMEN, Book IV, chapter 27. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 28, p. 587.

Against this doctrine the Arians sharpened the tongues of their slanders, asserting that Saint Meletius was a Sabellian. For this reason they persuaded the emperor to send him into exile in his own province.

The aforesaid Euzoius openly praised the Arian doctrine; for the great Alexander had deprived him of the diaconate together with Arius.

After this had been done, the Christian people, divided from the heretics, assembled in the apostolic church located in the place called the Old Church. For thirty years after the great Eustathius had been expelled, the orthodox endured the burdens [Col. 1027A] imposed by the Arians, awaiting a useful change in circumstances.

THEODORET, Book II, chapter 31, p. 120.

Those who had preserved the Nicene doctrine from the beginning refused to communicate with the followers of Meletius. They said that Meletius had been ordained by an Arian decree and that his followers had been baptized by him. For this reason the Church of Antioch was divided into another party.

SOZOMEN, Book IV, chapter 27. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 28, p. 588.

When the orthodox saw that the impiety of the heretics was increasing and that the defenders of the apostolic doctrine were being openly crushed, while holy Meletius had been expelled and the heretic Euzoius ordained, they remembered the words spoken to Lot:

“Save,” he said, “save your life” (Genesis 19:17).

They also recalled the evangelical [Col. 1027B] saying:

“If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you” (Matthew 5:29).

The Lord established the same concerning the hand and foot, adding:

“For it is better for you that one of your members should perish than that your whole body should be thrown into Gehenna” (Matthew 5:30).

THEODORET, Book II, chapter 31. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 32, p. 121.

## CHAPTER XLIX. Concerning the steadfastness of Eusebius on behalf of Meletius
Furthermore, the remarkable Eusebius, whom I mentioned earlier as having been entrusted with the decree, seeing the treachery being contemplated concerning the agreements made about Meletius, returned to his own city. The Arians, however, fearing the written testimony, persuaded Constantius to send [Col. 1027C] someone to recover from Eusebius the decree that had been issued concerning Meletius. Then a courier was sent to carry this out swiftly. When he arrived and announced the emperor’s words, the admirable Eusebius said: “I shall not return the common deposit unless all who entrusted it say so.” When the man who had been sent reported this, the emperor, angered, sent again, ordering him to return what he had received; he added in writing that, if Eusebius refused to return it, his right hand should be cut off, while verbally ordering the man he sent not to do what was written in the letter. When Eusebius had read the letter and found the punishment decreed by the emperor, he offered his left hand as well as his right, asking that both be cut off. “I shall not surrender the decree,” he said, “for it is a clear indication of the Arian plague.” Seeing this steadfastness of his, [Col. 1027D] Constantius praised him highly. For even the impious admire those who resist them when they are overcome by the greatness of their deeds. THEODORETUS, book II, chapter 32, p. 121.

## CHAPTER L. How Julian, having rejected the Christian religion, prepared war against Constantius, and concerning the death of Constantius

[Col. 1028A]

Such, then, were the events taking place among the Eastern churches. Meanwhile Julian Caesar, having defeated the barbarians dwelling near the river Rhine (A.D. 361), killed some and captured others. Crowned with a famous victory, and pleasing to the soldiers because of his moderate way of life and gentleness, he was proclaimed Augustus by them. After this, thinking nothing of Constantius, he courted with honors the judges appointed by him; and, to arouse hatred against him, he produced letters in which he showed that Constantius, because of the war waged against Magnentius, had brought barbarians into Italy.

But suddenly, changing his religion, although he had previously been thought to be a Christian, he called himself chief priest; and, coming to the temples of the pagans, he sacrificed and urged his subjects to worship such things.

[Col. 1028B]

While Constantius was staying at Antioch because of the Persian war, Julian, hoping that he could retain Illyricum without a war, was making his way toward them. He said that he wished to make amends to Constantius, as though he had received the imperial insignia not of his own will but at the will of the soldiers.

It is said that, when he had approached those regions, although the grape harvest had already been gathered, grapes were brought forth again around the setting of the Pleiades. Moreover, rain descending from the sky formed individual drops in the shape of crosses on his garment and likewise on the garments of the others. When this occurred, both he and the others thought that the grapes appearing out of season disclosed a favorable indication of the event, while the rain falling upon the garment strengthened the sign upon which it fell. 281 Others, however, said that the sign of the grapes appearing out of season signified the destruction of the emperor, after the manner of such clusters, and that his reign would be short.

[Col. 1028C]

Concerning the cross, they said that the sign foretold this because it was the heavenly doctrine of the Christians and everyone ought to be marked with the sign of the cross. Thus it is evident that, although they interpreted the matter differently from what the emperor had said, they were not deceived by the truth: the time that followed showed that both interpretations had been appropriately stated.

When Constantius heard that Julian was coming against him, he abandoned the preparations for the Parthian war and went to Constantinople. SOZOMEN, book V, chapter 1, p. 394.

At Mopsucrenae, between Cilicia and Cappadocia, he died of an apoplectic seizure brought on by excessive brooding, in the consulship of Taurus and Florentius, on the third day of November, in the forty-fifth year of his life (A.D. 361). Of these years, he reigned thirteen with his father and [Col. 1028D] twenty-five after him. SOCRATES, book II, chapter 37. Edited by Christoph Valesius, chapter 47, p. 161.

After his death, Julian already held Thrace. Not long afterward, when he came to Constantinople, he was proclaimed emperor. SOZOMEN, book V, chapter 1, p. 591.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 1027]

## 282 CHAPTER I. Concerning Julian’s lineage and education, and how he attained the imperial power

[Col. 1027D]

Now, therefore, a few things must be said about Julian, his lineage and education, [Col. 1028D] and how he came to the imperial power [ms. Lyr., “the principate”].

Constantine, who called Byzantium Constantinople after his own name, had two brothers by the same father but not by the same [Col. 1029A] mother. One was called Dalmatius and the other Constantius. Dalmatius had a son bearing his own name; Constantius had two sons, Gallus and Julian.

After the death of Constantine, the founder of the city of Constantinople, when the soldiers had killed the younger Dalmatius, these two also, their father already dead, nearly suffered death together with Dalmatius, had not an illness, thought to be incurable, rescued Gallus, and Julian’s age—he was eight years old—saved him.

When the emperor’s anger toward them had subsided, Gallus was staying near Ephesus with teachers; he also possessed estates there inherited from his ancestors. Julian, meanwhile, as he grew, was trained in the lecture halls of the city of Constantinople, in the basilica where the teachers were, appearing in private clothing. [Col. 1029B] He had as tutor an eunuch named Mardonius, and Nicocles of Lacedaemon as grammarian. He studied rhetoric under the sophist Euboulus [ms. Frob. and Niv., “Ecebolus”], who at that time was a Christian. This was done through the foresight of Constantius, so that, by studying under a pagan sophist, Julian would not turn toward the doctrines of that superstition. For Julian was a Christian from the beginning.

As he advanced in his studies, a rumor spread among the people that he might even govern the Roman commonwealth. When this became more widely known, it aroused anxiety in the emperor Constantius. Therefore he removed him from the royal city and sent him to Nicomedia, ordering that he not meet with the sophist Libanius of Syria. At that time Libanius, expelled by the tutors of Constantinople, was residing at Nicomedia.

Julian was therefore forbidden to study under Libanius [Col. 1029C] because he was a pagan; nevertheless, Julian made use of his books by reading them. As he progressed in rhetoric, the philosopher Maximus came to Nicomedia—not that Byzantine Maximus who was the father of Euclid, but the Ephesian—whom the emperor Valentinian later ordered to be killed as one practicing magical arts.

Maximus had come to Nicomedia for no other reason than that he had been drawn by Julian’s reputation. After Julian had tasted the philosopher’s teachings under him, he also began to imitate his religion. For Maximus had also implanted in his mind a desire for the imperial power.

When these things did not escape the emperor’s ears, Julian, caught between hope and fear and wishing to conceal the suspicion—for one who had formerly been an upright Christian had afterward become a traitor [Col. 1029D]—had his hair cut and pretended to lead a monastic life. In secret he devoted himself to philosophy; publicly he read the sacred books of the Christians.

Finally, he was appointed reader in the church of Nicomedia; and under this guise he avoided the emperor’s anger. He did all this out of fear, without in any way abandoning the hope he had conceived in his mind. He also said to many of his friends that the times would be more favorable when he himself possessed the imperial power.

283 While these things were thus being done against him, his brother Gallus, appointed Caesar, came to Nicomedia to visit him as he was proceeding to the East. Not long afterward, when Gallus had been killed, Julian too suddenly became suspect to the emperor, who ordered him to be kept under guard. When he had escaped, he saved himself by traveling through various places. [Col. 1030A] At last the emperor’s wife, Eusebia, discovered where he was hiding and begged the emperor that he suffer no harm, but rather be sent to Athens to study philosophy. SOCRATES, book III, chapter 1, p. 164.

Julian therefore began to desire the imperial scepter. For this reason, traveling throughout Hellas, he sought prophets who would give responses, asking whether he would attain his own empire. He found a man who claimed that he could tell him the answer he desired. This man led him to a certain place of idols and admitted him into the sanctuary; then he summoned deceptive demons.

When they appeared in solemn fashion, Julian was compelled by fear to form the sign of the cross upon his forehead. Then the demons, seeing the figure of the Lord’s trophy and remembering their own defeat, suddenly disappeared.

Recognizing this, the magician began to rebuke Julian. But Julian both explained his fear and said that he had been astonished at the power of the cross, since the demons had vanished when they saw that sign. The magician, however, said: “Do not suppose this, good man, that they were afraid, as you say; rather, they withdrew because they abhorred this sign.” Thus, by deceiving the wretched Julian, he filled him with hatred of the Christian sign. THEODORETUS, book III, chapter 3, p. 126.

After this the emperor summoned Julian and appointed him Caesar (A.D. 360). Giving him his sister Constantia as wife, he sent him against the barbarians in Gaul. These barbarians, from whom the emperor Constantius had sought assistance against Magnentius, had been of no help against the usurper and were ravaging the cities of the Romans.

[Col. 1030C] Since Julian was still a young man, Constantius ordered him to attempt nothing without the advice of the generals. But when the generals, having received authority, neglected it, and the barbarians consequently gained the advantage, Julian allowed the generals to devote themselves to their pleasures. Taking the soldiers and promising them the spoils of the enemies they killed, he began to defeat the barbarians and secured the soldiers’ affection.

It is said that, when he entered a certain city, a laurel crown of the kind with which cities are customarily adorned, hanging between the columns, fell upon his head when its cord broke and crowned him most fittingly. After this, everyone shouted that it was a sign of imperial power. Some say that Constantius sent him against the barbarians for this very reason, so that he might perish there.

[Col. 1030D]

But I do not know whether this suspicion is true. For the man who gave him his own sister as wife would, if he had entertained such a plan, have stirred up plots against himself instead.

When Julian therefore complained to the emperor about the generals’ negligence, another commander was sent, suited to Julian’s vigor. With his assistance Julian confidently engaged the barbarians. When they showed the emperor’s letters to their envoys, inviting them to the provinces, Julian sent those envoys in chains. He then fought and conquered them, even sending their captured king to Constantius.

Raised up by this success, he was proclaimed Augustus by the soldiers. Since there was no imperial crown, one of the standard-bearers took the torque he wore around his neck and placed it around Julian’s head. In this way Julian became emperor.

[Col. 1031A] Let those who hear judge what that philosopher did afterward. At the very beginning, without sending an embassy to Constantius or attempting to appease the mind of his benefactor, he did whatever seemed good to him: at one time changing the provincial judges, at another disparaging Constantius, and throughout the individual cities publicly having read the letters issued concerning the barbarians.

For this reason many followed him, abandoning Constantius. At that point he also cast off the pretense of Christianity that he had maintained. As he traveled through various cities, he opened the temples, offered sacrifices to idols, and called himself chief priest of the pagans.

While doing these things, he prepared an internal war against Constantius, seeking an opportunity and advancing it as far as he could. For his philosophical ambition could not be fulfilled without much bloodshed, unless God, the judge of plans, had brought one of them to an end without the other’s [Col. 1031B] contest.

When Julian had come to Thrace, he was informed that Constantius had died. In this way the Roman empire was freed from civil war.

When Julian came to Constantinople, he began to consider how he might win the people’s favor and acquire their support in a fitting manner. He accomplished this by the following strategy.

He knew well that Constantius was hated by all the peoples who embraced the doctrine of consubstantiality; for this reason they had been excluded from the churches, and the bishops had been deprived of their property and sent into exile. He also knew that the pagans had been grieved by the prohibition of sacrifices and desired the time when their temples would be opened and they would have permission to sacrifice to idols.

Thus, recognizing that both peoples had been wounded by grief, and that everyone alike [Col. 1031C] groaned under the violence of the eunuchs and especially under the plundering of Eusebius, he commended himself to everyone under an artfully constructed appearance. To some he made false promises; to others he was generous out of vainglory. To all alike, however, he displayed what his religion was.

First, disparaging Constantius’ cruelty toward his subjects and publicly reproving him before the entire people, he ordered that the bishops who had been transported into exile be recalled and that their confiscated property be restored. He also quickly ordered the pagan temples to be opened to their custodians.

He decreed that those who had been oppressed by the eunuchs should recover what had been wrongly taken from them. He condemned Eusebius, who presided over the imperial household, to death—not only because he had oppressed many, but because he had heard that his accusation had led to the killing of Gallus, his own brother.

[Col. 1031D] He buried the body of Constantius with royal honors. He expelled the eunuchs, barbers, and cooks from the palace: the eunuchs because his wife had died and he had not taken another wife after her; the cooks because he used simple foods; and the barbers because, as he said, “one is enough for many.”

He restored many of the writers to their former fortunes and ordered that the others be paid the compensation due for their writing. He also cut back the public transport service involving mules and horses, ordering them to be assigned to public uses.

A few praise these actions of his, but many condemn them, because, once the splendor of the palace had been removed, the imperial office seemed contemptible. [Col. 1032A] He stayed awake at night writing books and, descending into the senate, read them publicly. He was the only emperor after Julius Caesar to recite speeches in the senate-house.

He also honored cultivators of the disciplines, especially those devoted to philosophy. For this reason his reputation drew such men from every direction, and they crowded around the palace. Wrapped in cloaks, they displayed themselves more by their dress than by their teaching. They were burdensome to all Christians, seductive men who always favored the emperor’s religion.

Julian, therefore, possessing a great defect of vainglory, attacked all the emperors who preceded him in the speech he wrote about the Caesars. Moved by this arrogance, he also wrote books against the Christians.

[Col. 1032B] In expelling cooks and barbers, he acted as a philosopher, though not as an emperor; but in slandering and attacking others, he acted neither as a philosopher nor as a ruler. SOCRATES, book III, chapter 1, p. 166.

## CHAPTER II. How Julian came to the pagan rite, and concerning the sacrifices to idols

It is reported that, right at the beginning, Julian openly and shamelessly denied the Christian faith, so that by certain sacrifices and invocations—which the pagans call expiations [ed., “expeditions”]—and by the offering of blood, he sought to wash away our baptism and renounce the confession of the Church.

From that time onward, both secretly and publicly, the pagans freely celebrated sacrifices in the temples. It is also reported that, while he was once sacrificing, a sign of a cross [Col. 1032C] surrounded by a crown appeared to him in the entrails of the slaughtered animal.

At this sight the other ministers of the sacrifice were terrified, judging that such a display revealed the power of this religion and the eternity of Christian doctrine: the crown surrounding the cross was an indication of victory, and the circle’s circumference, having no end at its starting point, returned again into itself.

While the others marveled, the chief authority in this knowledge encouraged them, saying that favorable and useful signs had been shown to him, and that the sign of Christian doctrine was being restrained, since it could not expand as far as it wished, being enclosed within the boundary of the circle. SOZOMEN, book V, chapter 2, p. 599.

## CHAPTER III. How he had secretly been a pagan even before becoming emperor

[Col. 1032D]

For Julian, fearing Constantius, who killed his relatives because he feared tyranny, joined the company of the readers and read the divine books in the church while the people listened. He also built the Basilica of the Martyrs, which divine providence did not accept. THEODORETUS, book III, chapter 2, p. 125.

While Gallus and Julian were still boys and living in Cappadocia, they are said to have undertaken to build a very large basilica for the burial of the martyr Mamma [ed., “Mamae”]. They divided the work between them.

While both were competing in the construction, each trying to surpass the other, a certain miracle is said to have occurred; and unless those who claim to have heard this from eyewitnesses were still alive to recount it, it might perhaps seem unbelievable.

[Col. 1033A]

Gallus’s portion increased and grew continually; but Julian’s labors were, in some places, dug up [ms. Lyr., “defiled”], while in others the earth itself, spewing them out, filled them with rubble. Several times the foundations that had been laid could not be joined to the earth, as though some violent power from below had struck them back and driven them away. The cause appeared to everyone to be miraculous.

From that time they judged that this man was not sound in the Christian religion. SOZOMEN, book V, chapter 2, p. 594.

## CHAPTER IV. How hostile Julian was toward the Christians

When he alone had secured the empire, reopened the temples, and restored others, he lavished every form of devotion upon the temple officials. [Col. 1033B] He often sent public letters to the citizens urging them to embrace pagan rites and enjoy his generosity, openly identifying himself as an enemy of the Christians, so that he did not even wish them to come to him or receive their embassies.

Finally, when the Persians had begun a war, the people of Nisibis sent an embassy as Christians generally did, since they neither opened the temples nor wished to attend pagan rites. Julian threatened them that he would provide no assistance, receive no embassy from a polluted city, and not come to them first unless he learned that they had converted to paganism.

He also sent a complaint about the people of Constantia in Palestine. This place, since it was the port of Gaza and was called Maiuma, and since it was full of Christians, had received the dignity of a city from Constantine and had been named Constantia after his son.

[Col. 1033C] Constantine had judged it unjust that it should appear subject to the pagan Gazans. Thus, when Julian was reigning, the Gazans brought a lawsuit against the people of Constantia. When he sat as judge, he again subjected Constantia to them, although it was about twenty stadia distant. From that time, after its former name had been removed, it was called Maritime Gaza.

The two places had common judges and governors, but the rights of the Church appear to show that they were two cities: each has its own bishop and clergy. The vigils of the martyrs and the assemblies are held separately among them, and the boundaries of each episcopate and church remain distinct.

[Col. 1033D] At one time, after the bishop of Maiuma had died, one of the bishops of the Church of Gaza sought to subject both clergy to his authority, saying that it was not lawful for two bishops to preside over one city. When the people of Maiuma resisted, the provincial synod decided that a bishop of their own should be appointed for them. It judged that those who, under Constantine, had deserved to possess the privileges of a city because of their pious religion, but had lost them through the judgment of a pagan ruler, should not in their priesthoods and ecclesiastical order be deprived of the honor granted to them in ancient times. SOZOMEN, book V, chapter 3, p. 596.

At that time he also forbade Caesarea of Cappadocia, a very great and flourishing city, to be called by that name, and removed the ancient designation of Caesarea, which it had received from Claudius Caesar; previously it had been called Mazaca.

[Col. 1034A] He had long hated it because all its people were Christians and had destroyed the temple of Jupiter and that of their ancestral Apollo. When, during his reign, the Christians also destroyed the shrine of Fortune, which alone had remained, he became violently hostile to the city. He severely blamed the pagan population living there because they had not avenged themselves and had endured anything whatsoever for Fortune.

By beatings he extorted all the possessions and money of the Caesarean churches and ordered them to be brought before him. He immediately deposited three hundred pounds of gold from them in the public treasury.

[Col. 1034B] He ordered all the clergy to be gathered among the soldiers and made subject to the service of the provincial governor, which was extremely harsh and highly insulting. He commanded that the Christian people, together with their wives and children, be registered and pay taxes like village-dwellers. He swore with threats that, unless they promptly rebuilt the temple, he would afflict the city severely and would not permit the Galileans to retain even their heads. This was his customary name for Christians.

This might indeed have happened, had he not soon met his end. SOZOMEN, book V, chapter 4, p. 598.

## CHAPTER V. That at the beginning of his reign he spared the Christians more

At the beginning, sparing the Christians, he appeared more merciful, knowing that the earlier persecutors [Col. 1034C] had accomplished nothing toward increasing paganism by punishing however many Christians they had punished; rather, the Christians had increased because of this and had become glorious by dying for the true doctrine.

Therefore, envying their glory, he abstained from tortures. He judged that it was necessary instead to persuade the people, by speech and admonition, to worship paganism, believing that by doing this he would also demonstrate his clemency. SOZOMEN, book V, chapter 4, p. 599.

## CHAPTER VI. How Bishop Mares of Chalcedon rebuked Julian to his face

It is said that, while Julian was sacrificing at Constantinople before Fortune, Mares, bishop of Chalcedon, approached him and publicly called him impious, ἄθεον—that is, “without God”—and an apostate. Julian, in turn, reproached him only for his blindness. For Mares was an old man and, because of the weakness of his eyes, was led by the hand of another.

Moreover, wishing to insult God as well, Julian customarily said: “Nor can your God, the Galilean, cure you.”

[Col. 1034D] Mares replied: “I give thanks to my God for my blindness, because this has happened so that I might not see you stripped of piety.”

The emperor made no reply and went away. He thought that paganism would be strengthened if he showed himself patient and gentle toward the Christian people. SOZOMEN, book V, chapter 4, p. 599.

## CHAPTER VII. That he recalled those whom Constantius had deported, and concerning the harassment of the clergy and the Christian people

Having done these things, he recalled those who had been driven into exile by Constantius for their religion and restored their confiscated estates. He ordered the people not to harm any [Col. 1035A] Christian or compel anyone unwilling to sacrifice. Those who voluntarily approached the altars, however, he prepared first to be purified before the demons and cleansed by their customary sacrifices.

He removed from the clergy all privileges, honors, and customary rights, repealed the laws established on their behalf, and handed them over to the municipal courts. He also ordered that the things which virgins and widows, maintained among the clergy because of poverty, had formerly appeared to receive from the public treasury be exacted from them.

For the emperor Constantine, arranging the affairs of the churches, had provided for each city so that the clergy would receive sufficient revenues, and had confirmed this by law. This law has remained in force to the present, after Julian’s death.

They say that this exaction was exceedingly cruel. He repeatedly seized money and sacred ornaments; [Col. 1035B] temples founded under Constantine and Constantius were destroyed; and the money given for their construction was demanded back. On this pretext the priests, clergy, and Christian people were cruelly harassed. SOZOMEN, book V, chapter 5, p. 600.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the uprising that arose against the pagans at Alexandria

At the same time an uprising occurred in the great city of Alexandria for the following reason.

There was a certain place in the city that had long been deserted and neglected and was filled with much filth. In ancient times the pagans had sacrificed human beings there to the goddess Mithras. Constantius had granted this place, as though it were vacant, to the Church of Alexandria.

When George wished to build a chapel there, he was clearing it. During this work, a sanctuary was discovered, constructed at considerable depth, [Col. 1035C] in which the pagan mysteries were celebrated [ms. Theod., “concealed”].

There were many human skulls there, belonging both to adults and to children, who were said to have been killed there so that magical arts might be practiced from their entrails.

When the Christians discovered these things in the sanctuary of Mithras, they sought to expose all these crimes publicly, to the ridicule of the pagans, and they spread abroad the human heads they had found.

When the pagans of Alexandria saw this and could not endure the disgrace, they were inflamed with anger. Everything they found at hand they regarded as a weapon. Attacking the Christians, they killed many: some with swords, others with clubs or stones; they strangled some with ropes and crucified others, in insult to the holy cross; and they afflicted very many with various [Col. 1035D] wounds.

The violence was such that they spared not even their relatives. A philosopher struck a philosopher, a brother struck a brother, a father his children and parents, and they raged against one another in mutual slaughter.

For this reason the Christians were unable to cleanse the same place. SOCRATES, book III, chapter 2, p. 170.

## 286 CHAPTER IX. How George of Alexandria was killed

Meanwhile, when the judges had announced that Constantius was dead and Julian was reigning, the pagan people of Alexandria began a revolt. Attacking George, they bound him in chains.

Shortly afterward they came to the prison and killed him. Placing his corpse on a camel, they carried it through the entire city from morning [Col. 1036A] until evening and toward evening burned it. [ms. Santheod., “paraded it.”]

Many Arians report that this was done by supporters of Athanasius. But I am firmly convinced that the pagans did it, since they certainly had grievances against him because of the idols and the injuries done to the temples, and because of the prohibition of their festivals.

Julian himself confirms this in a letter sent to the Alexandrians, in which he blames them and remits the penalty, as though out of reverence for Serapis, whom he calls the protector of the city, and for its founder Alexander, as well as for his own uncle Julian, devoted to paganism and a great hater of Christians. SOZOMEN, book V, chapter 7, p. 603.

## CHAPTER X. How Julian, the uncle of Julian the Apostate, closed the churches and plundered their ornaments

[Col. 1036B]

It is said that he was intent on storing many precious vessels of the Church of Antioch in the imperial treasuries, and that he closed the churches, drove out all the clergy, and left only the presbyter Theodoretus standing there.

When he had seized Theodoretus as guardian of the vessels and cruelly wounded him, he finally ordered him to be killed with the sword. Through all his tortures he answered courageously and prevailed by his confession [ms. Lyr., “defense”] of the doctrine.

After collecting all the vessels and garments dedicated to God, Julian threw them on the ground, treating Christ with insults and outrages as he wished; he even sat upon them, increasing the accumulation of injuries.

Soon afterward, it is said, his private parts and the areas around his thighs were struck, and he progressed to such a degree of putrefaction that worms formed, while the physicians labored without being able to overcome the disease.

All kinds of expensive medicines were prepared from fat birds, so that, because of their thickness, they might be spread over his corrupted and putrid limbs. By this treatment the worms were drawn to the surface; boiling up from the depths, they tore apart the living flesh. Until he died, he was never free from this affliction.

It therefore became clear that this had occurred through divine indignation, since the guardians of the imperial treasuries and many others who rose up against the churches also died unexpected and pitiable deaths, as though condemned by heavenly anger. SOZOMEN, book V, chapter 7. Edited by Christoph Valesius, chapter 8, p. 604.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the martyrs Eusebius, Nectarius, and Zeno

[Col. 1036D]

Having said this, it is time to recall Eusebius, Nectarius, and Zeno, Christian brothers. The people of Gaza, exercising their hatred against them, found them hidden in a house, seized them, bound and scourged them, and afterward assembled in the theater, where they began to shout against them as though they had destroyed their temples and previously committed many acts of insult against the pagans.

As they incited one another, as is customary among the mob, they rushed to the prison, brought the brothers out, and cruelly killed them. Sometimes they dragged them face down, sometimes on their backs, beating and wounding them with pieces of wood, stones, and clubs.

I have heard [Col. 1037A] that women also came out and wounded their bodies with the beams of looms; that public cooks—some pouring water over them, others boiling pots—pierced their limbs with spits.

After tearing them apart and smashing their heads so that their brains lay on the ground, they carried them outside the city, where dead animals were customarily thrown. There they burned their bodies and mixed the bones that remained among the corpses of camels and asses, so that they could not easily be found. This did not remain hidden for long.

For a certain Christian woman, though not from Gaza, gathered the bones by night in accordance with a divine command, placed them in an urn, and entrusted them for safekeeping to Zeno, their cousin.

God had [Col. 1037B] revealed this man to the woman in a vision. He was unknown to her and was hiding because the persecution had recently taken place. In this way, therefore, he received their relics through the woman and kept them at home for the time being.

When, under the reign of Theodosius, he assumed the episcopate of that same church, he built a basilica before the city, established an altar, and placed the bones of the martyrs beside those of the confessor Nestor.

During his lifetime Nestor had lived with these relatives. He was arrested by the people together with the martyrs and shared their chains and scourging. As he was being dragged along, he had a very handsome body and moved the persecutors to pity. They threw him down alive but near death before the gates.

Some people picked him up and brought him to Zeno. While he was being cared for there, he died. SOZOMEN, book V, chapter 8. Edited by Christoph Valesius, chapter 9, p. 605.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning Hilarion the monk, the cruelty of the people of Heliopolis and Arethusa toward the Christians, and Bishop Mark and his martyrdom

[Col. 1037C]

Meanwhile, when the Gazans were searching for the monk Hilarion, he fled to Sicily. There he made his daily living by gathering wood from the mountains, selling it in the city, and carrying it on his own shoulders. When his power had become known there through the demons, he came to Dalmatia; there, by divine power, he performed many miracles, so that by his prayer he even drove back the sea, which had occupied certain places. But he departed from there again, because he avoided living wherever he was praised. He made it his practice to change locations and remain uncertain to everyone, so that by frequent migration he might destroy his reputation. Finally, while sailing to Cyprus, he came to Paphos. Invited by the bishop of Paphos, he came to love the place and lived as a philosopher near an estate called Charybdis. Flight prevented him from becoming a martyr there. For he fled because the divine command is not to await persecutors; those who are arrested during persecution, however, are commanded to endure bravely.

The Gazans and Alexandrians, indeed, are known to have committed such acts against Christians. But the inhabitants of Heliopolis and of Arethusa in Syria reached such cruelty—as people of those times have described it—that they forced consecrated virgins, whom the people had never before seen in such a condition, to stand publicly naked in the theater. At first they mocked them; afterward they sheared them; finally, after cutting them in two, they urged pigs to eat them.

[Col. 1038A] In my judgment, the Heliopolitans were driven to this cruelty against the consecrated virgins because their ancestral custom—by which their virgins engaged in fornication before marrying—seemed to have been prohibited. For Constantine, after destroying the temple of Venus in that city, was the first among them to build a church and forbade their customary fornications by law.

The Arethusians, however, put to a marvelous death Mark, the bishop of their city, an old man worthy of reverence for his life and conduct. They had already hated him because, during the reign of Constantius, he had destroyed their exceedingly ornate and most costly temple in order to bring the pagans back to Christianity. When Julian became emperor, he was moved against him and ordered him either to repay the assessed value of the temple or to rebuild it. Since both alternatives were impossible for the Christians and the priest, Mark first fled in accordance with the evangelical law. But afterward, when many people were being subjected to dangers and hardships on his account, he returned from flight and voluntarily handed himself over to the people, allowing them to do whatever they wished to him.

Although they ought to have praised the philosopher, they instead regarded him as a contemptible man. They fell upon him and dragged him through the individual streets, while men and women alike tore his hair and limbs apart, even cutting off his ears with thin cords. Schoolchildren placed under teachers mocked him, striking him with slaps and pricking him without the slightest restraint with their styluses. They also lowered him into foul sewers. While he was still breathing, they smeared him with honey and fish sauce, put him into a basket, and hung him in the air.

[Col. 1038C] It is said that, when wasps and bees then touched him and fed on his flesh, he said to the Arethusians that he himself was exalted, whereas he saw them placed in a lowly position; but afterward they too would suffer this fate. SOZOMEN, book V, chapter 9. Christian Valesius’s edition, chapter 10, p. 607.

While carrying out these acts, they compelled him to rebuild the temple or provide the funds. When he refused, thinking him poor, they first demanded half the money; finally, they demanded at least some small amount. He said to them: “I will not give a single obol for all of it.” Thus defeated, they ceased inflicting their tortures on him. THEODORET, book III, chapter 6. Christian Valesius’s edition, chapter 7, p. 131.

[Col. 1038D] The story is told that at that time the prefect, who was especially a pagan, admired Mark’s steadfastness and went to the emperor to complain. He said that it was shameful for so many tortures to be inflicted on one old man, and that while Christians became glorious by suffering such things, he himself was increasingly brought into disgrace. Mark, therefore, was crowned with such an end. SOZOMEN, book V, chapter 9. Christian Valesius’s edition, chapter 10, p. 609.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the martyrs Macedonius, Theodulus, and Tatian

At the same time Macedonius, Theodulus, and Tatian, Phrygians, also obtained the pledge of martyrdom. When the provincial judge had opened a temple in the city of Meroe in Phrygia and had spent a long time clearing it of rubble, these men entered during the night and smashed the idols. When many people were arrested on this account and led to punishment, they identified themselves. Although the judge, as though satisfied with the punishment of the offense, did not wish to kill them, he chastised them with various kinds of torture at the insistence of the crowds. Finally, he ordered them to be placed on a grate and burned.

As they were being burned, they said: “If you take pleasure in roasted flesh, O Amatus”—for that was the judge’s name—“turn our other sides toward the fire, lest, when you begin to eat, you find the flesh half-raw.” Thus they too overcame their adversary in a most courageous contest.

They say that Busyris in Ancyra of Galatia gave a most celebrated and courageous confession, although he belonged to the heresy called that of the Encratites, that is, the Abstainers. When the judge had arrested him as one who had attacked the pagans, he wished to torture him publicly and ordered him to be hung on a piece of wood. Then Busyris quickly stretched out his hands above his head and bared his sides, saying that there was no need for the attendants who hung him and took him down to labor, since he himself was ready for whatever punishment they wished to inflict and was preparing his sides for the executioners.

The judge, astonished at his offer, was even more amazed when the event was put to the test. While iron claws were tearing his sides with increasing force, he kept his hands stretched out until the judge was satisfied, and received the wounds cheerfully. After this he was taken back to prison and rested there. Soon afterward, when Julian’s death was announced, he lived until the reign of Theodosius; after doing penance for his former heresy, he lived within the Catholic Church. SOZOMEN, book V, chapter 10. Christian Valesius’s edition, chapter 11, p. 610.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the martyr Basil and Eupsychius

At that time, they say, Basil, a presbyter of the Church of Ancyra, and Eupsychius of Caesarea in Cappadocia, who had recently married and still appeared to be like a bridegroom, ended their lives by martyrdom. Eupsychius was killed because of the temple of Fortune, which, as we have already said, had been demolished. The people of Caesarea generally experienced the emperor’s anger, and some were punished with death, others with exile.

Basil, however, was a zealous man, approved in matters of doctrine. While Constantius lived, he resisted the Arians. For this reason, by decree of Eudoxius, he was removed from the ecclesiastical order. [Col. 1039D] When Julian held the imperial power, Basil publicly admonished Christians to preserve their own doctrine and not defile themselves with pagan superstition, and to regard as worthless the honors bestowed by the emperor—temporal honors and indeed causes of everlasting condemnation.

For this reason he fell under the suspicion and hatred of the pagans. He would stand watching them sacrifice publicly, groaning, praying, and crying out that no Christian should become subject to such an error. He was arrested and handed over to the provincial judge. After bravely enduring many tortures, he was crowned with martyrdom. I have gathered these accounts together, although the years and days of their martyrdom appear to have been different. SOZOMEN, book V, chapter 10. Christian Valesius’s edition, chapter 11, p. 611.

## CHAPTER XV. On the cruel acts committed against Christians in Gaza, Sebastia, and Phoenicia

Many were the acts committed at that time by those subjected to the seductions of idols, and they would require books of their own; but from the many I shall recount a few. In Ascalon and Gaza, they cut open the bellies of men worthy of the priesthood and of women distinguished by a life of virginity, filled them with barley, and exposed them to be eaten by pigs.

In Sebastia, a city of the same province, they opened the tomb of John the Baptist, consigned it to the fire, and scattered the bones and ashes.

But who could either describe or hear without tears the crime they committed in Phoenicia? In Heliopolis, which lies near Lebanon, there was a deacon named Cyrillus. During the reign of Constantius, inflamed with divine zeal, he had smashed and burned many idols that were worshiped there. Remembering this deed, certain men whose names ought not to be mentioned not only killed him but also cut open his belly and ate his liver.

Yet they could not escape God, who observes everything; rather, they paid penalties worthy of their presumption. All who took part in that crime lost their teeth and all became tongueless, for their very tongues likewise fell away, consumed by decay. They also lost their sight and, through their sufferings, proclaimed to everyone the power of piety. THEODORET, book III, chapter 6. Christian Valesius’s edition, chapter 7, p. 129.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the androgynous image set up by the pagans in a church

[Col. 1040C]

In Emesa, which lies on the border of that city, they dedicated to Dionysus *gynidi*—that is, to Bacchus in feminine form—a church that had recently been built for God. As an object of ridicule, they set up there an image that was androgynous, that is, one that displayed both a man and a woman.

In Dorostolus, a distinguished city of Thrace, the invincible champion Aemilianus was handed over to the fire by Capitolinus, judge of all Thrace.

As for the deeds or martyrdom of Mark, bishop of Arethusa, they are known to require the public eloquence of Aeschylus and Sophocles [edited text: “competition”], so that the tragedy of his acts might be recounted in fitting order. THEODORET, book III, chapter 6. Christian Valesius’s edition, chapter 7, p. 130.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the laws Julian established against Christians

[Col. 1040D]

Countless other things were also committed at that time throughout land and sea by the impious against the devout. Then the emperor, openly hateful to God, established laws against piety. First, he forbade the sons of the Galileans—for this is what he called the worshipers of our Savior—from studying the disciplines of poets, rhetoricians, and philosophers.

“We are wounded,” he said, “by our own feathers, according to the proverb. Armed with our writings, they wage war against us.”

After this he established another law, ordering the Galileans to be expelled from military service. THEODORET, book III, chapter 7. Christian Valesius’s edition, chapter 8, p. 131.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Athanasius’s return to Alexandria

[Col. 1041A]

Accordingly, when Athanasius returned from exile, the people of Alexandria welcomed him gladly. They expelled the Arians from the churches and handed the venerable enclosures over to Athanasius. The Arians, however, gathering in obscure houses, accepted Lucius in the place of George. SOCRATES, book III, chapter 4, p. 173.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Lucifer and Eusebius

At that time the bishops Lucifer of Cagliari and Eusebius of Vercelli were recalled from exile by order of the emperor. Both returned from exile beyond the boundaries of the Thebaid and considered how they might restore the Church’s corrupted rule. It was therefore decided that Lucifer should go to Antioch in Syria and Eusebius to Alexandria, so that, after taking counsel with Athanasius, they might restore the doctrines of the Church.

Lucifer, however, sent a deacon in his place, through whom he declared that he would regard as binding whatever the council established. When he himself came to Antioch, he found the Church in turmoil. The people were divided among themselves. Not only did the Arian heresy, which was under Euzoius, divide the Church, but the followers of Meletius, devoted to their own bishop, had also withdrawn from their associates.

Lucifer therefore ordained Paulinus as bishop for them and departed again. Eusebius, coming to Alexandria, held a council with Athanasius. SOCRATES, book III, chapters 4 and 5. Christian Valesius’s edition, chapters 5 and 6, p. 173.

## CHAPTER XX. On the council held at Alexandria with Athanasius

[Col. 1041C]

Bishops gathered from various cities and discussed matters of the greatest importance and necessity. While discussing the divinity of the Holy Spirit, they included him in the consubstantial Trinity. They also declared that the Word made human was endowed not only with flesh but also with a soul, as had long pleased ecclesiastical writers.

They did not introduce a new religion into the Church, but the one that ecclesiastical tradition had taught Christians from the beginning. For all the ancients, after discussing this matter, left us writings of the highest authority. Irenaeus, Clement, Apollinarius of Hierapolis, and Serapion, bishop of the Church of Antioch, declared in their writings that the one who was made human was ensouled.

Likewise, when a synod had been held concerning Beryllus, bishop of Philadelphia in Arabia, it wrote to that same Beryllus in opposition to him on these very points. Origen too, throughout his books, called the one who was made human “ensouled.” His ninth tome on Genesis, in particular, fittingly explains this mystery: there he expounded Adam as Christ and Eve as the Church at greater length.

Saint Pamphilus and Eusebius, who derived his surname from him, are worthy witnesses to these statements. Both, while jointly commending Origen’s life, resisting his adversaries, and composing notable books in his defense, say that Origen was not the first to introduce this discussion but had interpreted the Church’s mystical tradition.

Those who gathered at Alexandria, however, did not leave the question of substance and subsistence without careful investigation. Hosius, bishop of Corduba in Spain, whom we have already mentioned, had been sent by the emperor Constantine to extinguish the flame then kindled by Arius. He also destroyed the doctrine of Sabellius of Libya and raised the question concerning substance and subsistence. SOCRATES, book III, chapter 5. Christian Valesius’s edition, chapter 17, p. 174.

Meanwhile, many bishops gathered at Alexandria with Athanasius and confirmed the decisions of the Council of Nicaea. They confessed the Spirit to be consubstantial with the Father and the Son and named the Trinity. Since the question of substance and subsistence was disturbing the Churches, it was wisely decreed that these terms should be used only against the Sabellians, lest, through a lack of terms, subsistence be thought to be the same as substance. SOZOMEN, book V, chapter 11. Christian Valesius’s edition, chapter 12, p. 612.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the difference between substance and subsistence

Such, then, was the synod at that time. It is not inappropriate for us briefly to indicate what we know concerning substance and subsistence. Those who explained Hellenic philosophy defined οὐσία (*ousia*), “substance,” in one way, but made no mention at all of ὑπόστασις (*hypostasis*), that is, “subsistence.”

The grammarian Irenaeus, in a book in which he collects words letter by letter, even calls this term barbarous. He says that it was not used by any of the ancients, and that, even if it is found somewhere, it does not signify what is now understood by it. In Sophocles’ *Phoenician Women*, he recalls, “subsistence” signifies a place of ambush. In Menander, he says, it designates something like the sediment that collects from wine in a jar.

It should nevertheless be understood that, although the ancient philosophers left this term aside, later philosophers used the term “subsistence” in place of “substance.” They explained the definition of substance in different ways. If, then, substance is circumscribed by a definition, how can we properly use this term of God, who cannot be comprehended?

Evagrius, however, in his *Monastic Book*, prohibited speaking about God in a presumptuous and careless manner. He entirely forbade defining the Divinity. For he says that definitions belong to composite things. Thus he writes:

“Every proposition,” he says, “either has a genus that is predicated, or a species, or a difference, or a property, or an accident, or an expression composed from these. But none of the things just mentioned can be comprehended within the Holy Trinity. Therefore let what is ineffable be worshiped in the silence of reason.”

Such is Evagrius. Although we may seem to have said these things by digression, we do not regret having included them as a matter useful to the history. SOCRATES, book III, chapter 5. Christian Valesius’s edition, chapter 7, p. 176.

## CHAPTER XXII. Part of Athanasius’s book *On the Defense of His Flight*

[Col. 1043A]

Athanasius then read before those present a book on the defense of his flight, which he had formerly composed. Here, inserting the useful portions that may be of benefit, I urge the diligent to seek out and read the entire book, which contains many verses. He says:

“Behold the kind of presumption shown by the impious when they do these things without blushing. First, after contriving evil against us, they accuse us to this day because we were able to avoid their hands prepared for murder. Rather, they groan bitterly because they could not cut us off completely. They reproach us for fear, unaware that, while muttering this, they turn the blame more against themselves.

“For if it is evil to flee, it is far worse to pursue. One man hides so that he may not die; another pursues in order to kill. Scripture says that one should flee; but he who seeks to kill transgresses the law and himself provides the greater occasion for flight. If persecutors reproach those who flee, let them instead blush at themselves. Let them cease laying ambushes, and those who flee will immediately cease fleeing.

“But they do not cease their cunning; with every effort they hasten to capture us, knowing that the flight of those enduring persecution is the greatest judgment against their persecutors [manuscript: ‘indication’]. No one ever flees a gentle and merciful man, but rather one who is both savage and cunning. Everyone who groaned and was harassed by Saul fled and came to David (1 Sam. 22:2).

“But these men therefore seek to kill those who hide themselves, lest they seem to be reproving their wickedness. In this too they are blinded. For the more evident the flight is, the more plainly their ambushes, murders, and exiles are exposed to everyone. Whether they kill, death continually cries out against them; or whether they threaten exile, they are known everywhere to be creating a memorial of evil against themselves.

“If they possessed a sound mind, they would see that they are trapped by these things and injuring themselves by their own counsels. But because they have lost their understanding, they are deceived by persecution; seeking to kill, they do not behold their own impiety.

“If they reproach those who flee while seeking to kill, what will they do when they see Jacob fleeing from his brother Esau (Gen. 27:44), and Moses going down to Midian because he feared Pharaoh (Exod. 2:15)? How will they answer concerning David fleeing from Saul, who sent into the house to kill him while he was hidden in a cave (1 Sam. 19:11; 24:4), and who changed his appearance until he withdrew from Abimelech, thereby escaping the ambushes of his enemies (ibid. 21:13)?

“What will these men, who speak so presumptuously about everything, say when they see that the great Elijah raised a dead man by prayer, yet hid himself because of Ahab and fled because of Jezebel’s ambushes? At that time the sons of the prophets who were sought were also concealed, hiding in caves with Obadiah (1 Kings 17:22; 19:3).

“But if they have not read these things because they are ancient, let them at least remember the Gospels. The disciples too withdrew because of fear of the Jews, hiding themselves (Acts 8:1). Paul, sought by the ruler of Damascus, was lowered from the wall in a basket and escaped the hands of his pursuer (2 Cor. 11:33).

“Since Scripture speaks thus about holy men, what excuse do you think they can find for their presumption? Whether, then, they reproach fear, they speak like madmen against themselves; or whether they say that this is done against the will of God, they appear completely ignorant of the divine Scriptures.

“For in the Law it was commanded that cities of refuge also be designated for flight (Num. 35:9), so that those sought for death might somehow be freed. At the final age of the world, the Father’s Word himself, who spoke to Moses, came and gave this command again, saying: ‘When they persecute you in this city, flee into another’ (Matt. 10:23).

“And shortly afterward he says: ‘When you see the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel standing in the holy place—let the reader understand—then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains; let the one who is on the roof not come down to take anything from his house; and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak’ (ibid. 24:15–18).

“Knowing these things, the saints adopted this manner of conduct. What the Lord now commands, he also spoke to the saints before his presence in the flesh. This is the goal of human beings, leading to perfection: that they do what God commands.

“For this reason the Word himself, made human for us, when he was being sought, deigned to hide himself just as we do (John 8:59); and again, when he was suffering persecution, he fled and withdrew from the ambushes (John 11:54). It was fitting for him to endure this as he endured hunger and thirst, and in this way to show himself made human.

“From the beginning, as soon as he became human, while he was still a child he commanded Joseph through an angel: ‘Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt. For Herod is about to seek the child’s life’ (Matt. 2:13). After Herod’s death, he appears to have fled to Nazareth because of Archelaus, his son.

“And when he was already making God known in himself and had restored the withered hand to health, the Pharisees went out and took counsel against him in order to kill him; but Jesus, knowing this, withdrew from there (Matt. 12:14–15).

“When he raised Lazarus from the dead, it is said: ‘From that day they planned to kill him.’ Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews but departed from there to a region near the desert (John 11:53–54).

“Then, when the Savior said, ‘Before Abraham was, I am,’ the Jews took up stones to throw at him. But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple. Passing through their midst, he departed (John 8:58–59; Luke 4:30), and thus withdrew.

“When they see—or rather hear—these things, how can they fail to understand that, according to what is written, they ought to be burned by fire because they think and speak in opposition to what the Lord does and teaches?

“When John had suffered martyrdom and his disciples had buried his body, Jesus, upon hearing it, departed from there by boat to a deserted place apart (Matt. 14:13). Thus, by doing these things, the Lord was also teaching.

“Would that these men were ashamed even of this and made their presumption known only among human beings, rather than appearing increasingly insane by attacking the Savior himself and directing blasphemies against him [edited text: ‘meditating blasphemies’]. Yet no sane person could endure them, since they are exposed as not even knowing the Gospels themselves.

“There is a reasonable and true cause for our withdrawal and flight, which the evangelists recorded in the case of the Savior. We too ought to think of such things in the case of the saints. For what has been written about the Savior in human terms is also attributed generally to the human race. He took up what belongs to us and displayed the sufferings of our weakness.

“John wrote this: ‘They sought to seize him, and no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come’ (John 7:30). Before these things occurred, he himself had said to his mother: ‘My hour has not yet come’ (John 2:4). And to those who were called his brothers he said: ‘My time has not yet come’ (John 7:6).

“Again, at the time of his passion, he said to the disciples: ‘Sleep now and rest. Behold, the hour has drawn near, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinners’ (Matt. 26:45).

“Before the time came, he did not allow himself to be seized; when the time came, he did not hide himself but even handed himself over to his adversaries. In the same way, the blessed martyrs guarded themselves during temporal persecutions and fled through hiding places when they were sought; but when they were found, they submitted themselves to martyrdom.”

This is sufficient to have reported concerning Athanasius. SOCRATES, book III, chapter 6. Christian Valesius’s edition, chapter 8, p. 176.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How Eusebius, coming to Antioch because of Paulinus and seeing the people divided, became indignant

[Col. 1045C]

Meanwhile Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, came suddenly afterward from Alexandria to Antioch. Finding Paulinus consecrated by Lucifer and the people divided, with the followers of Meletius holding their assemblies separately, he was deeply disturbed because not everyone had consented to the ordination. He reproved in his own mind what had been done, but out of reverence for Lucifer departed in silence, promising at a gathering of bishops that what had been done would be corrected. Although he took the greatest care, he was unable to unite them.

Meanwhile Meletius also returned from exile. Finding his associates celebrating their assemblies separately, he presided over them. The churches, however, were held by Euzoius, the bishop of the Arian doctrine. Paulinus retained only one small church within the city, from which Euzoius did not expel him out of respect for him. Meletius celebrated the solemn rites outside the city gates.

Thus Eusebius departed from Antioch. Lucifer, however, realizing that Eusebius did not accept his ordination, considered this insulting, became intensely angry, and avoided communion with Eusebius. He also attempted, through contention, to reject the decisions approved by the synod.

While these things were taking place during a period of distress between them, they removed many people from the Church, and another heresy of the Luciferians arose. But Lucifer could not bring his anger to fulfillment, for he was bound by his own declarations: through his deacon he had promised to regard as binding whatever the council had determined. Therefore he himself, preserving the faith of the Church, returned to Sardinia and his own see.

Those who had earlier been grieved with him, however, remained thereafter separated from the Church. Eusebius, meanwhile, traveling through the East like an excellent physician, restored the sick in faith, instructing and teaching everyone through ecclesiastical preaching. From there he crossed into Illyricum, and afterward traveled through Italy, proclaiming these same things. SOCRATES, book III, chapter 7. Christian Valesius’s edition, chapter 9, p. 180.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Hilary of Poitiers

[Col. 1046B]

Hilary, bishop of the second Aquitania, had long sown the doctrines of the true faith among the Italian and Gallic bishops, since he was the first to return from exile (A.D. 364). Thus both men labored bravely in the faith. But Hilary, as an eloquent man, composed in his books a defense of the consubstantiality of the Trinity. In them he explained this sufficiently and vigorously destroyed the Arian doctrine.

These events, therefore, are known to have taken place after the brief period of their exile. SOCRATES, book III, chapter 8; Christian Valesius’s edition, chapter 10, p. 181.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Macedonians

At that time the followers of Macedonius, Eleusius, Eustathius, and Sophronius were all called Macedonians after one Macedonius, and they frequently held councils. They summoned those who had followed them at Seleucia and anathematized the bishops of the opposing party, that is, those who agreed with Acacius. Rejecting the faith of the Council of Ariminum, they instead confirmed the statements that had been recited at Seleucia and set forth at Antioch.

When some asked them: “You who are now called Macedonians, if you believe something different from the followers of Acacius, why have you until now shared communion with them, as though you believed the same things?” they gave this poisonous answer through Sophronius, bishop of Pompeiópolis in Paphlagonia:

“The Westerners,” he said, “were diseased in their doctrine of consubstantiality. Aetius, throughout the East, preached dissimilarity according to substance. Both positions were wrong: the Westerners improperly joined the divided substances of the Father and the Son under the name of consubstantiality, while Aetius openly separated the nature of the Son from the Father’s nature, believing that he was piously proclaiming the Son to be dissimilar to the Father in substance.

“Since these men held such opinions, we were pleased to possess the truth of piety by a middle course.”

In this way they tried to satisfy those who questioned them. SOCRATES, book III, chapter 8. Christian Valesius’s edition, chapter 10, p. 182.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How Julian also persecuted Athanasius

Accordingly, when the emperor heard that Athanasius, established in the Church of Alexandria, was lawfully preaching to the people and that many pagans had been converted to Christianity, he ordered him to leave the city (A.D. 365). If he remained, he commanded that he suffer the greatest penalties, finding an occasion for accusation against him because, although he had been condemned to exile during the reign of the previous emperor, he had not received the episcopal see by Julian’s order.

Therefore he prepared to flee in accordance with the emperor’s command. Seeing the Christian people around him weeping, he said: “Have confidence, little children; it is a cloud, and it will quickly pass.” With these words he took his leave, entrusted the Church to his devoted friends, and departed from Alexandria. SOZOMEN, book V, chapter 14. Christian Valesius’s edition, chapter 15, p. 615.

## CHAPTER XXVII. How Julian favored Cyzicus because of its pagan worship

Meanwhile, when the people of Cyzicus were serving as an embassy before the emperor concerning their own affairs and the restoration of the pagan temples, he praised them for their concern for the sacred rites and granted everything they had requested.

He removed Eleusius, the bishop of that city, as though he were a destroyer of temples, because he had established provisions for widows and monasteries for consecrated virgins, and had persuaded the pagans to abandon their ancestral religion and turn to Christian doctrines.

He also forbade Christian foreigners to come to Cyzicus, believing that they would stir up disturbances on religious grounds and that the other Christians of the city would support them.

The public workers and craftsmen of the mint [Note: [Col. 1047] From this it is evident what sort of moneyers they were, those mentioned in the *Pandects*], who had been divided into two groups by the command of earlier emperors, were ordered to live at Cyzicus with their wives and children. Every year they contributed a fixed offering to the public treasury: some supplied soldiers’ cloaks, while others supplied new money.
