Since Julian was determined by every means to establish the pagan rite, he judged it foolish to use force and torture against people unwilling to sacrifice. He therefore ordered only that their number be recorded in each city; yet he did not forbid them to pray in any way. For he knew that no compulsion could restrain what spontaneous willingness had suggested.

Moreover, he hastened to remove clerics and the leaders of the Churches from the cities, seeking gradually to dissolve the Church through their absence, so that there would be neither ministers of the sacred rites nor people to teach or participate in the mysteries, and so that over a long period they would suffer the loss of memory of their own religion. SOZOMEN, book V, chapter 14. [Col. 1047D] Christian Valesius’s edition, chapter 15, p. 615.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Titus, bishop of Bostra
So he publicly ordered the people of Bostra to drive out Titus, then bishop of their city. When he had issued this order and threatened the clergy, as though they themselves were causing disturbances among the people, Titus sent a petition to the emperor, warning and saying that the pagan and Christian crowds were hostile to one another, and that, at his urging, the Christians were more inclined to refrain from sedition. After this, the emperor tried, on the basis of these words, to stir up the hostility of the people against Titus. He wrote to the people of Bostra that Titus had been their accuser, saying that the people had ceased from sedition at his admonitions, not of their own accord; and he urged them to drive him out as an enemy of the people. For he did not order what was just or lawful to be done; rather, out of hatred for religion, he sought to condemn it in words while accomplishing evil in deeds. Therefore the Christians scattered throughout the cities and provinces.

Many of my ancestors shared in this persecution. My grandfather also did so. He was born of a pagan father, but he himself, together with his entire household and those who belonged to the family of Alaphion, first became Christians at Bethelea, a very populous village in the region of Gaza. It had ancient temples and very beautiful buildings, especially the Pantheon, situated in the citadel of the city and towering over the entire village. I believe that this place was named from the Syrian and Greek expression meaning “dwelling place of the gods.” It is said that the monk Hilarion was the author of the conversion of all these people to Christianity.

When Alaphion was being tormented by a demon, the pagans and Jews had long employed incantations and purifications on his behalf, but none of this benefited him. Hilarion, however, invoking only the name of Christ, drove out the demon and suddenly brought him over to the Christian religion. My grandfather therefore flourished in the exposition and interpretation of our Scriptures, for he was gifted and supported by learning. He was even skilled in the mathematical art, and for this reason was greatly valued by the people of Ascalon and Gaza and by the Christians throughout the surrounding region, as one necessary to religion and useful for resolving difficulties in divine Scripture.

These men were the first in that place to build churches and monasteries and to adorn them equally with decency and hospitality toward travelers and the needy. From this family down to our own time there have been excellent men, whom, when I was a young man, I myself saw in their old age.

SOZOMEN, Book V, chapter 14. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 15, p. 616.

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### How Julian ordered the pagans also to offer prayers and alms according to the Christian custom, to present tithes to the temples, and to perform the other practices customary among Christians

The emperor had long been striving to spread paganism throughout all his dominions, and he was deeply distressed to see that the Christians were gaining greater approval. The temples were indeed open, and pagan sacrifices were being carried out throughout the cities according to his will. But he was tormented by the fear that the abundance of Christians would render his zeal fruitless. He was especially troubled because he heard that many of his priests had Christian wives, children, and slaves.

Believing that the condition of Christianity rested upon a good life and proper conduct, he endeavored everywhere to adorn the pagan temples with the construction and order of the Christian religion—with seats, processions, pagan doctrines, and admonitions. He appointed readers for his superstition after the model of the clergy, so that they might solemnly observe fixed hours, days, and prayers. He likewise ordered them to have [perhaps delete this word] care for men and women skilled in philosophy, to provide lodging for travelers and the poor, and to exercise other forms of concern for the needy, thereby organizing the pagan religion and giving it the name of piety. If anyone sinned voluntarily or unwillingly, he established, according to Christian tradition, that after penance the person should undergo moderate correction.

He is also said especially to have envied the letters of the bishops, by which those writing to one another customarily commended travelers, indicating in every way where they were going and from whom they had come, and obtaining assistance as though they were known and friends by virtue of the testimony of the dispatched letter. Considering these things, he hastened to accustom the pagans to the practices of the Christians.

But since many find it incredible that he wished to imitate the Christians, this must be demonstrated from the emperor’s own words. He sent the following letter to Arsacius, the high priest of Galatia:

“The rite of the pagans has not yet been conducted according to our intention, because its worshipers have been negligent. For the splendor, greatness, and sublimity of the gods surpass every reason and every hope. But may the gods be gracious to our minds because of the negligence we have shown, since through their providence so much has been accomplished in a short time—so much that no one had previously dared even to pray for.

“Why, then, do we believe that this can be sufficient, and why do we not consider how the care of the Christians for travelers has increased their superstition, together with their many services concerning graves and the dead and their devotion to honorable conduct—not genuine, but fabricated? I believe that such practices ought to be carried out among us in truth.

“It is therefore not enough for you alone to be such a man. You must either entreat all the priests throughout Galatia, bend them by reason, or certainly remove them quickly from the priestly ministry unless they bow their necks to the gods together with their wives, children, and slaves. They must no longer tolerate their slaves or children despising this practice, nor Galileans impiously acting against the gods and preferring impiety to piety.

“Then instruct everyone that a priest must neither attend spectacles nor drink in taverns, nor preside over any disgraceful or shameless trade or occupation. Honor those who obey; expel the disobedient.

“Establish hostels in every city, so that travelers may enjoy our benevolence—not only our own people, but also strangers in need of money. And so that you may have the means to do this, for the present I have decreed that thirty thousand measures of grain be distributed each year throughout all Galatia, together with sixty thousand sextarii of wine. One fifth of this must be spent on the poor who attend the temples, and the remainder distributed among needy travelers.

“For it is disgraceful that the impious Galileans should not only refuse to reject the Jews but rather nourish both their own people and ours, while our people are deprived of the assistance of their own. Therefore teach the pagans also to make contributions for such services, and instruct the pagan villages to offer the first fruits of their crops to the gods. Teach them to practice such beneficence, explaining that this work was formerly customary among our people. Homer proves this, for he introduces Eumaeus doing such things.

“Thus we do not imitate even the good practices of our own people; instead, through negligence and without shame, we allow others to practice them, or rather we reject reverence for the gods. If I learn that you are doing these things, I shall be filled with joy.

“Receive the governors of the provinces at home less frequently; send them letters often. When they enter a city, let no priest go out to meet them. When they come to the temples of the gods, let no soldier or official attendant precede them through the doors; whoever wishes may follow. When he reaches the very threshold of the temple, let him be a private citizen. For you, as you know, are judge within. This too seems to be required by the sacred ordinance.

“Those who obey are therefore pious in truth; those who resist are shown to be lovers of empty glory. For what should the person suffer, or what aid does the person deserve, who has refused to have the mother of the gods propitious? Those who neglect her will not merely be without complaint; they will also endure the assault of our indignation. For it is not right to spare one who has made the gods his enemies. Persuade them, then, that if they wish to enjoy my protection, they should all strive to offer worship to the mother of the gods.”

SOZOMEN, Book V, chapter 16. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 15, p. 619.

## CHAPTER XXX  
### By what means he attempted to exalt paganism and incline the soldiers toward the worship of idols

By these measures the emperor sought the destruction of the Christians. Yet he could neither persuade his subjects to accept this nor openly commit violence without shame. Meanwhile, in order to accustom the soldiers to paganism, he tried to restore to its ancient form the higher standard of the Romans, which Constantine, as stated above, had changed into the shape of a cross.

In public images he depicted Jupiter as though bringing him a crown and purple robe from heaven, while Mercury and Mars looked toward him, as though testifying to his wisdom and courage. He did this with the images so that, under the pretext of imperial authority, the gods might secretly be worshiped, and the subjects might in this way be deceived without realizing it. He believed that, if he imposed this upon them voluntarily, he could afterward accomplish whatever he wished. If he discovered that they refused, he would remove their pardon and torture them, as though they were resisting Roman ceremonies and committing an offense against the state and the empire itself.

A few, even when subjected to punishment, recognized the deception because they refused to worship as was customary. The crowd, however, as usually happens, worshiped the images simply through ignorance. This nevertheless benefited the emperor nothing.

When he devised many measures by which to exalt pagan rites, he found a means that bestowed upon many Christian soldiers the glorious crown of martyrdom. When the time came at which soldiers customarily received imperial gifts—for this was usually done on the Kalends of January, on the birthdays of emperors, and on the anniversaries of royal cities—he sought a way to deceive them simply and in accordance with ancient custom. He ordered that each person approaching the emperor’s hand, after being instructed by the officials, should first offer incense. Frankincense and an altar had been placed before him according to the ancient Roman ceremony.

Some then freely displayed their courage and would neither offer incense nor accept the gift from the emperor. Others, because of the occasion, the law, and the antiquity of the custom, did not even realize in their minds what sin they had committed. Others, however, overcome by gain, shaken by fear, or trapped by the sudden command, were unable to avoid paganism, even though they understood what was happening.

Many, deceived through ignorance, were invoking Christ among themselves over food and drink, as was customary, when one of them replied: “Why do you suffer while invoking Christ, whom you denied a short while ago, when, as you received the gift from the emperor, you threw incense into the fire?”

When the soldiers heard this and recognized what they had done, they immediately leapt up and ran publicly, crying out to their God. They declared before everyone that they were Christians, that they would remain in that name, and that they had acted through ignorance—or, if it could be said so, that only their hands had been pagan, while their consciences had taken no part in the deed.

When they came before the emperor, they threw down the gold they had received and loudly demanded that he take back what he had given and kill them. They confessed that they were doing penance because their right hands had sinned thoughtlessly, and that, for Christ’s sake, they were eager to surrender their entire bodies to punishment.

SOZOMEN, Book V, chapter 16. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapters 17, pp. 620–621.

These events aroused the emperor’s fury. At first he ordered their heads to be cut off. As they were being led to execution, with the people following and admiring the courage they had shown for piety, they came to the place where criminals were customarily punished. Then the eldest of them asked the executioner to cut off first the head of a certain Roman, still a young man, so that he would not lose courage while looking upon the others.

When the young man had fixed his knees upon the ground and the executioner had drawn his sword, a messenger suddenly arrived, forbidding the killing with a shout. The young man, thus deprived of death, said: “Roman was not found worthy to be called a martyr of Christ.”

Although the malicious emperor, led by envy, had forbidden their blood to be shed, he nevertheless did not permit them to live in the cities, but sent them into exile in the remotest regions of the Roman world.

THEODORET, Book III, chapter 16. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 17, p. 140.

Afterward he ordered that those who refused to sacrifice should not enter the palace. He also ordered that they should share neither in the council nor the forum, neither in judicial authority nor in any dignity or administration.

SOZOMEN, Book V, chapter 17. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 18, p. 623.

## CHAPTER XXXI  
### Concerning the body of the martyr Babylas and the image of Apollo consumed by lightning

When Julian was going to the Pythian oracle at Daphne to seek an answer concerning victory in the Parthian war, and the oracle accused the proximity of the body of the martyr Babylas, he ordered the body to be removed. For this reason, while the Christians were celebrating a festival and singing psalms as the body was carried away, and while a certain young man named Theodore had endured many tortures because of the emperor’s anger, the deceitful demon thereby increased the martyr’s glory but exposed its own falsehood more clearly.

For lightning sent down from heaven set the entire temple ablaze and reduced the image of the Pythian Apollo itself to ashes. It was made of wood and gilded on the outside. The prefect of the East at that time, Julian, the uncle of the emperor Julian, learned of this during the night and hurried to Daphne, wishing to offer assistance to his god. When he saw the image reduced to ashes, he afflicted the νεωκόροι—that is, the temple attendants—with beatings, believing that some Christian had committed the deed.

Although they were tortured, they refused to lie, crying out that the fire had begun not below but above. At this, peasants from the neighboring places also came and said that they had seen the lightning brought down from heaven.

THEODORET, Book III, chapters 9 and 10. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapters 10 and 11, pp. 132 and 134.

## CHAPTER XXXII  
### Concerning the confiscation of the church vessels and how the aforementioned Julian and Felix, after destroying the church, were divinely punished

In the meantime orders were given that the sacred vessels of the churches be assigned to the treasury of the fisc. After the doors of the greater church had been removed, the sanctuary became accessible to everyone.

When Julian, the prefect of the East, entered the church, Felix, prefect of the imperial treasuries, entered with him, as did Elpidius, count of the private estates. It is said that both Felix and Elpidius had originally been Christians but had then departed from piety, wishing to obey the impious emperor.

Julian the prefect shamelessly urinated against the sacred altar. When Euzoius tried to stop him, Julian struck him on the head. He is said to have declared that the Christian religion had been laid waste by divine providence.

When Felix saw the ornamented vessels that Constantine and Constantius had frequently offered, he said: “Look at the vessels in which service is rendered to the son of Mary!”

Not long afterward, however, they suffered punishment for these impious and mad presumptions. Julian was suddenly seized by a terrible illness and died with his entrails rotting. He did not discharge the feces through the digestive passages; rather, the criminal mouth that had served his blasphemies became the instrument of this excretion.

It is said that his wife was outstanding in faith, and that she said to him: “It is fitting for you, husband, to praise Christ the Savior, because through this correction he has shown you the greatness of his own power. You did not know against whom you wished to fight, unless, in his customary patience, he had brought these scourges upon you from heaven.”

Recognizing through these words and the sufferings that threatened him the cause of his illness, he begged the emperor to restore the church from which it had been taken. But this did not move him, and Julian himself reached the end of his life.

Felix also suddenly received a scourge by divine power. Blood poured from his mouth all day and night, the veins throughout his body were emptied, and all his strength was spent. He too was quickly extinguished and delivered over to eternal death.

THEODORET, Book III, chapters 11 and 12. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 12, p. 134.

## CHAPTER XXXIII  
### How the son of a priest was converted at Antioch

After these events, a certain young man, the son of a priest and raised in paganism, was transferred to the company of Christians. At that time there was a woman of distinguished reverence who held the rank of deaconess. She had been a friend of the young man’s mother. Whenever his mother came to her, she would embrace the child and invite him to the worship of the Christian name.

After his mother died, the young man would come to her and receive his customary instruction. When he had firmly accepted her counsel, he asked his teacher by what means he could escape both his father’s superstition and attain the proclamation of the truth.

She told him to flee from his father and follow instead his own Creator and his father’s Creator, and to go to another city, where he could secretly escape the hands of the impious emperor. She promised that she herself would care for him.

The young man replied: “I shall return later and entrust my soul to you.”

After a few days had passed, Julian came to Daphne to celebrate the public sacrifices. The young man’s father came with him, for he was a priest and accustomed to follow the emperor. The boy and his brother were also with him, serving in the capacity of attendants who placed food before the emperor.

The festivals at Daphne customarily lasted seven days. On the first day, while the young man was standing before the emperor’s couch and had solemnly sprinkled the food, he was filled with horror. He hurried to the city of Antioch and came to the remarkable woman.

When he arrived, he said: “I have come, and I have not deceived you concerning my promise. You, however, concerned for the salvation of us both, must fulfill what you promised.”

She immediately arose and led the young man to the holy man Meletius. He ordered him meanwhile to live in an upper room.

In the meantime the father searched for his son. He went throughout all Daphne, and when he came to the city he walked through all the streets and alleys, his eyes searching everywhere and longing to find him. When he reached the place where the holy Meletius had his dwelling, he looked up and saw the boy looking out of the window.

He ran up, dragged him down, and took him home. First he struck him with many lashes; then he heated coins and placed them upon the boy’s hands, feet, and back. After this he bound him, shut him in a room with the doors closed, and went back to Daphne.

I heard this from the man himself when he was already old and was telling the story. He added that, filled with the divine Spirit and grace, the boy crushed all his father’s idols and began to heap blasphemies upon their weakness.

When he realized what he had done, he feared his father’s presence and begged the Lord Christ to help him, break his bonds, and open the doors: “For you, Lord, I have endured such things, and I was not afraid to do this.”

When he had said this, the bolts suddenly fell and the doors were opened. He returned to his instructress, who immediately dressed him in a woman’s clothing and settled him on the roof. Shortly afterward she presented him again to the holy Meletius.

Meletius entrusted him to Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, and they traveled by night to Palestine. After Julian’s death, the young man also brought his father to the Christian truth. He related this to us among other matters.

THEODORET, Book III, chapter 13. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 14, p. 135.

## CHAPTER XXXIV  
### How Julian polluted everything with sacrificial water and how Juventius and Maximinus resisted him

Meanwhile Julian was arming himself more shamelessly against the piety of the faith. In appearance he pretended to be gentle, but he prepared snares by which to deceive the innocent.

First, he polluted the city fountains with water used in the sacrifices at Daphne, so that everyone who drank the water might partake of its horror. When he had also infected the foods sold in public with that crime—for bread, meat, fruit, vegetables, and everything eaten were sprinkled with it—those who had received the saving name groaned and lamented when they saw such a great abomination.

Nevertheless, they ate, obeying the Apostle’s rule: “Eat everything sold in the market, making no distinction for the sake of conscience” (1 Corinthians 10:27).

There were, however, two men distinguished in military service—for they were the emperor’s shield-bearers—who, at a certain banquet, were inflamed by this horror with even greater fervor. They used the words of the noble youths who had shone in Babylon, saying: “For you have delivered us to an unjust king who has departed from you beyond all the nations that are upon the earth.”

One of the banqueters reported this to the emperor. He immediately summoned the two brave men before him and asked what they had said. Taking the emperor’s question as an opportunity for confidence and confirming the praiseworthy zeal they possessed, they replied in the manner of men raised in piety:

“O prince, until now we have faithfully obeyed the laudable laws established by Constantine and his sons. Now we groan as we see everything filled with abomination and food and drink polluted by wicked sacrifices. We have lamented this at home, and in your presence we likewise cry out. This is what displeases us in your rule.”

When the man called gentle and philosophical by his associates heard this, he displayed the appearance of mildness but immediately revealed the face of impiety, ordering them to be beaten with the most bitter blows. He also deprived them of daylight—or rather, to speak more truly, he freed them from the unhappiness of that time and arranged for victorious crowns to be offered to them.

He pretended that he was defending in them the cause of an insult to imperial authority, and he ordered this to be publicized, begrudging the champions of truth the title of martyrdom and honor alike. Their names were Juventius and Maximinus. The city of Antioch revered them as defenders of piety, placed them in a precious monument, and honors them to this day in its annual festivals. Many other distinguished men, too, who possessed rank and dignity, gained equal crowns by displaying such courage.

THEODORET, Book III, chapter 14. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 15, p. 137.

## CHAPTER XXXV  
### How Valentinian, who ruled after him, struck the temple attendant because of the sprinkling of sacrificial water

Valentinian, who shortly afterward assumed the empire, was at that time a commander of the lancers stationed around the palace, with the rank of commander of a thousand. He did not conceal the zeal that he possessed for piety.

At that time, when that man marked for lightning was entering the temple of Fortuna in procession, temple attendants stood on both sides of the doors. They sprinkled those entering, claiming that they thereby purified them. Valentinian, walking before the emperor, saw a drop of the sprinkling on his cloak. Indignant, he struck the temple attendant with his fist, saying that he had been polluted rather than purified.

When the emperor saw this, he ordered Valentinian to be placed in custody and sent into the wilderness. But after a year and a few months had passed, Valentinian received the empire as the reward of his confession.

For God honors not only those who love him in the life to come; sometimes even in the present he grants rewards for good works and confirms what is hoped for there by rewards received here.

THEODORET, Book III, chapter 15. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 16, p. 138.

## CHAPTER XXXVI  
### Concerning the martyr Artemius and the abbess Publia

As for Artemius, who had been commander of Egypt in the time of Constantius, because he had destroyed many of the idols of that period, Julian not only stripped him of his property but also punished him by beheading. Such were the deeds of that gentle man, removed from anger, as the impious called him.

I shall add to these matters also the miracle involving a woman who, through divine zeal, despised his impiety. There was at that time a woman named Publia, highly renowned and adorned with precious virtues. Although she had briefly undertaken the marriage yoke, she bore to the Creator a most worthy fruit.

John, who long served as presbyter at Antioch and often fled decrees appointing him to apostolic presidency, sprang from the soil of that remarkable woman. She kept with her a company worthy of their manner of life—women who preserved their virginity—and with them she always praised God, their Maker and Savior.

When the emperor passed by, they sang psalms together more loudly, judging the deceived man contemptible and laughable. They especially repeated those songs that seemed to expose the weakness of idols and to ridicule them. With David they said: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands.” And again: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Psalm 113:4, 8).

When Julian heard this and became violently enraged, he ordered them to be silent as he passed by. They disregarded his law and formed their chorus in greater numbers. Again, as he passed, they sang: “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered” (Psalm 67:1).

Then, raging, he ordered the leader of the chorus to be brought before him. When he saw that she was worn down by old age, he neither pitied the whiteness of her body nor took care to honor the virtue of her spirit. Instead, he ordered certain sword-bearers to strike her on the face.

She received those insults as though they were the highest honor, returned home, and denounced him in her customary spiritual melodies, just as the composer of that song had driven the evil spirit away from Saul. For Julian, the deceived man, drawing demons to himself, was raging against the gift of piety.

THEODORET, Book III, chapter 17. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 18, p. 140.

## CHAPTER XXXVII  
### Concerning Basil and Gregory

Apollinaris the Syrian, a man exceedingly well instructed in every branch of knowledge, caused him no small distress, as did Basil and Gregory of Cappadocia, Christian rhetoricians of that period, together with many other eloquent men. Some of these were zealous for true glory; others were afflicted by the madness of the Arian heresy.

Believing that the Christians were being armed from this quarter, Julian prohibited them from being instructed in the doctrines of the Greeks and from being educated through their literature.

At that time Apollinaris, being both learned and gifted, composed a Hebrew history in heroic verse in place of Homer’s poetry, carrying it down to the reign of Saul. He divided the entire work into twenty-four books, giving each book the name of a letter according to the Homeric arrangement.

He also produced another work modeled on the plays of Menander and comparable in form to comedy; he likewise imitated the tragedies of Euripides and the lyric poetry of Pindar. In short, taking his subjects from the divine Scriptures, he composed in a short time works corresponding to all the branches of Greek learning—in number, excellence, moral character, composition, style, and arrangement. If people had not honored antiquity and considered what was customary agreeable, I believe that they would have judged the little works of Apollinaris equal to those of the ancients.

He also composed a by no means insignificant book addressed to the emperor himself—or against the pagan philosophers—which he entitled *For the Truth*. In it, while remaining silent about the sacred testimonies, he proved that the pagans had indeed been deceived, whereas he himself possessed true knowledge of God.

Considering these things, the emperor wrote to the bishops who were then distinguished: “I have read it, and I have criticized it.”

They replied: “Although you have read it, you have not understood it. For if you had understood it, you would never have criticized it.”

Some say that this letter came from Basil, the bishop of the Church of Cappadocia; this is not incredible. Whether it was his or another’s, it is right to praise the teaching of virtue.

SOZOMEN, Book V, chapter 17. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 18, p. 623.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII  
### Concerning those who departed from the faith through love of money

Many did not possess the Christian name with a sound mind. They preferred money and present honor to the happiness of true faith and descended into the crimes of sacrifice.

One of these was Eubulus, a Constantinopolitan sophist. Following the conduct of the emperors, he had pretended under Constantius to be an exceedingly fervent Christian, but under Julian he quickly became a pagan. After Julian, he again wished to be a Christian.

Throwing himself face down before the doors of the church, he cried out in a loud voice: “Trample me, senseless salt.”

SOCRATES, Book III, chapter 11. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 13, p. 184.

## CHAPTER XXXIX  
### How Julian took money from the Christians

When Julian was going to the Persians, wishing to avenge upon them the fact that under Constantius they had invaded the Roman frontier, and knowing that reverses frequently occur in battles and that he needed large sums of money, he devised a way to take the Christians’ money.

Accordingly, he imposed a heavy monetary payment on those who refused to sacrifice, and it was exacted from genuine Christians. Each of them contributed according to his means, and the emperor was unjustly made capable by an unjust collection. Where the tax did not exist, he introduced the law; where it existed, he made use of it.

At that time the pagans severely oppressed the Christians and sometimes afflicted them with bodily tortures. When the emperor heard of this—and the Christians came to him—he refused to defend them, saying: “It is your duty to endure your sufferings patiently, for this is the command of your God.”

SOCRATES, Book III, chapter 11. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapters 13 and 14, p. 185.

## CHAPTER XL  
### How he was mocked by the people of Antioch

The emperor came to Antioch in order to fight against the Persians. When the people complained that goods were abundant but were being sold at high prices, he wished to display the greatness of his generosity and set prices in the marketplace lower than they ought to have been.

When the shopkeepers and various merchants withdrew, necessary goods became scarce. The people of Antioch, bearing this very heavily, hurled insults at the emperor.

SOZOMEN, Book V, chapter 18. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 19, p. 624.

They complained against him, making jokes about his beard, which was exceedingly long. They therefore said: “Let it be cut, so that his beard may be useful for ropes.”

Because he frequently sacrificed a bull to idols for the sake of his superstition, he ordered an altar or a bull to be fashioned in his solidus. For this reason they tore into him, saying: “This bull will overturn the world.”

Provoked to anger by these insults, he threatened to inflict punishment upon the city of Antioch. Therefore, wishing to return to Tarsus in Cilicia, he ordered the necessary preparations to be made.

The sophist Libanius recalled him from this intention by writing one book of intercession on behalf of the Antiochenes and another to the Antiochenes concerning the emperor’s anger; he did not publish either book. The emperor, however, rejecting the idea of taking revenge by deeds, dispelled the anger of his indignation by returning the insults.

He composed a witty and sufficiently urbane book against the Antiochenes, which he called *The Antiochene*. Nevertheless, he also committed many evils against the Christians in that city.

SOCRATES, Book III, chapter 15. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 17, p. 190.

## CHAPTER XLI  
### Concerning the image of Christ that Julian removed

I shall not refrain from relating also what occurred under Julian. It was a sign of Christ’s power and an indication of God’s anger against the emperor.

When Julian learned that in Caesarea Philippi, a city of Phoenicia called Paneas, there was a notable image of Christ, which the woman who had been freed from an issue of blood had erected, he removed it and placed his own statue there.

A violent fire falling from heaven split Julian’s statue around the chest. Its head and neck, together with one part, were thrown down and fixed in the earth; the remaining part has survived to this day and preserves the mark of the lightning.

At that time the pagans dragged away and broke the statue of Christ. Later the Christians gathered it up and placed it in a church, where it is preserved to this day. According to Eusebius, this image is known to be a remedy for every kind of suffering and illness. Near it a certain herb sprang up, whose appearance no physician of our land, however experienced, was able to recognize.

SOZOMEN, Book V, chapter 20. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 21, p. 629.

## CHAPTER XLII  
### Concerning the benefit of the herb that grew beside the image of Christ and the miracles that occurred in various places through the name of Christ
It seems to me, then, that when God is involved, no miracle and no benefit ought to be considered incredible. For many other miracles, too, have long been handed down in cities and villages among numerous provincials, and they possess the character of truth; I shall now demonstrate this immediately.

There is, then, a city of Palestine called Nicopolis. While it was still a village, the sacred book of the Gospels calls it Emmaus. After the devastation of Jerusalem and the victory over Judaea, the Romans called it Nicopolis, evidently from the outcome of the victory. Before this city, at the crossroads where Christ is known to have walked with Cleopas after the resurrection, intending to go to another village, there is a healing spring in which human ailments are washed away, and other animals likewise are cleansed of various illnesses.

It is reported that this comes about because, on a certain journey, Christ appeared at the spring with his disciples and washed his feet there; from this the water became medicinal for various illnesses. It is also said that in Hermopolis of the Thebaid, a tree called the Perseid overcame the illnesses of many people if its fruit, leaf, or a piece of its bark was tied around the necks of the sick.

They tell of this tree that, when Joseph had fled from Herod into Egypt with Christ and the holy Virgin Mary and had come to the city of Hermopolis, as soon as he entered the city, the tree—unable to endure the arrival of the great Savior Christ—bent down to the ground and reverently worshiped him. I have related what I heard from many people about this tree.

I think, however, that this sign was performed for the citizens as an indication of the divine presence; or certainly, because this tree was worshiped according to pagan custom on account of its size and beauty, it was moved because it could not endure Christ’s divinity. For the demons trembled when they saw the destroyer of such things, and, in accordance with the prophecy of Isaiah, all the idols of the Egyptians likewise fled; once the demon had been driven away, the tree remained empty as a testimony to Christ. Thus, among the Egyptians and Palestinians, testimonies to these events are preserved.

SOZOMEN, Book V, chapter 20. Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 22, p. 629.

## CHAPTER XLIII. How Julian armed the Jews against the Christians, and concerning the Temple of Jerusalem

Julian, then, also armed the Jews against the Christians. First he summoned them and asked why, although the Law commanded them to sacrifice, they did not make offerings at all. When they replied that they had been permitted to offer sacrifice in only one place, the god-hated man suddenly ordered the destroyed temple to be rebuilt, believing in his folly that he could destroy the Lord’s word—whose truth he thereby demonstrated all the more clearly.

The Jews gladly received these words and sent instructions to Jews throughout the world. They came running from every direction and eagerly contributed money for the construction; the emperor also supplied a great deal, not out of generosity but in opposition to the truth. He likewise sent a governor, most worthy to execute the commands of the impious.

For they say that, in clearing the site, they used silver mattocks, baskets, and carrying-trays. When they had begun to dig, a very large crowd was carrying out this work on the appointed day. At night, however, earth spontaneously rose from the valley. After even the remains of the former foundation had been removed, they prepared everything anew.

When they had prepared many thousands of measures of gypsum and lime, a great force of winds suddenly arose; storms and violent squalls immediately followed and scattered everything that had been collected. Yet while they continued their madness and were not corrected by divine patience, a great earthquake first occurred. Whoever had not been instructed in the divine mysteries was violently shaken.

When they were not frightened even by this sign, fire came forth from the foundations they were excavating; it burned many of the diggers and tore apart the limbs of others. At night, when many were sleeping in the nearby portico, the portico itself suddenly collapsed with its roof and crushed those who were sleeping.

On the following day, a shining sign of the saving cross appeared in the sky. The garments of the Jews, too, were filled with the sign of the cross—not marked in a shining color, however, but in black. When these rebels against God saw this and trembled at the divine scourges, they returned to their own homes, confessing that there is a God who is shown to have been hung upon wood by their ancestors.

When Julian heard this, although it was being proclaimed by everyone, he did not fear, like Pharaoh with his hardened heart.

THEODORETUS, Book III, chapter 17. Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 20, p. 142.

## 298 CHAPTER XLIV. Concerning the Persian war, and how Julian proceeded there

When the Persians learned that Constantius was dead, they took courage and came to the borders of the Romans, announcing war. For this reason Julian, after gathering an army, sent to Delphi, Delos, and Dodona to receive responses as to whether it was advisable for him to undertake the war.

Then all the seers both gave confidence for battle and promised victory. I shall not hesitate to insert one response as an example of their falsehood and deception. It was as follows:

> Now all the gods advance, bearing the trophies of victory beside the river Thiren. I, Mars the warrior, shall be their leader.

It is fitting that those who call the rational lord and prince of the Muses the Pythian should publicize the absurdity of these verses. But when I discover the falsehood of his deception, I groan. For by the river Thiren he intended to name the Tigris, since “Thiris” resembles its name. That river, flowing down from the mountains of Armenia and running through the fields of Assyria, descends into the Persian Gulf.

Deceived, then, by these responses, the wretched man both dreamed of victory in his mind and prepared to wage war against the Galileans after the Persian [another reading: Parthian] battle—for that is what he called the Christians. He thought he was insulting them by this name, although he ought rather to have considered their virtue.

For Socrates, although he was called Critias, and Pythagoras, although he was called Phalaris, did not thereby share in any plague through a change of name; nor did Nereus, when called Thersites, lose the natural beauty he possessed. Understanding none of this, Julian thought that by this designation he was inflicting some monstrous insult upon us.

Trusting the deceptive response, he threatened that he would set up idols of demons in the churches.

THEODORETUS, Book III, chapter 18. Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 21, p. 143.

After these threats, he was defeated by one man in Beroea. This man was noble and presided over the council of that city; the zeal of Christ made him even more renowned. Seeing that his son had been plunged into the impiety then prevailing, he expelled him from his house and disowned him publicly.

The son, having encountered the emperor on the road to a neighboring city, informed him of his own wishes and of his father’s disavowal. The emperor ordered the young man to be quiet and promised that he would reconcile him with his father.

When he arrived in Beroea, he summoned the nobles and distinguished men to a banquet. Among them was the young man’s father, whom he ordered to recline and dine at table with his son. Then, in the middle of the meal, he said to the father:

> It does not seem right to me to do violence to someone’s will by forcing him to turn toward something else and change his mind toward things he does not want. Do not, therefore, use violence against your son, who refuses to follow your doctrines. For I do not force you to follow mine, although I could compel you very easily.

Understanding that the matter concerned divine religion, the father replied:

> You are speaking, O emperor, about a misguided man, hated by God, who places falsehood before the truth.

Then the emperor again assumed an expression of gentleness and said:

> Stop insulting him.

Turning his face away from the father, he said to the young man:

> I shall take care of you, since I cannot persuade your father to do this.

I have not related these events without purpose, but in order to show not only the courage of that remarkable man, but also that Julian’s power was despised by very many.

THEODORETUS, Book III, chapter 18. Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 22, p. 144.

In Antioch there lived a certain excellent man who was a teacher of young men. The famous sophist Libanius was also there, an impious man who awaited Julian’s victory and kept his threats before his eyes.

So he asked the teacher, apparently mocking our religion:

> What do you suppose the carpenter’s son is doing now?

But the teacher, filled with divine grace, foretold what happened shortly afterward. He replied:

> O sophist, the Creator of all things, whom you have called the carpenter’s son, is preparing a burial coffin for Julian.

A few days later, the death of the misguided man was announced. He was placed in a coffin and brought back, emptied of the arrogance of his threats.

THEODORETUS, Book III, chapter 18. Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 23, p. 145.

## CHAPTER XLV. How Julian the monk foretold the death of that Julian [that is, the impious Julian] before he heard of it

At that time the most religious Julian, surnamed Saba, who seemed to imitate the life of the bodiless angels through his bodily way of life, and whose life we have also written, was offering longer prayers to God after hearing the threats of that impious man.

At the hour when Julian was struck, this holy man learned of his death while praying, although more than twenty stages seemed to lie between that place and the emperor’s army. For they say that, while he was continually groaning and entreating the merciful Lord, suddenly the stream of his tears stopped, he was filled with joy, and his face became cheerful.

When his attendants saw this change of spirit, they asked him to reveal the reason for his sudden joy. Then he said:

> The savage devastator of the sacred vineyard has paid the penalty for his devastation. He lies dead, deprived of the power of his terrors and threats.

When they learned this, they all rejoiced and offered hymns of thanksgiving to God. Later, messengers confirmed that the day and hour of Julian’s death had been exactly the same as those which that most holy elder had perceived and foretold.

THEODORETUS, Book III, chapter 19. Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 24, p. 145.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Concerning Julian’s ill-considered command

The outcome of his death demonstrated that he had always conducted himself without sound judgment. For when he had crossed the river dividing the realms of the Persians and Romans with his army, he suddenly burned the ships, not persuading the soldiers by argument or exhortation but compelling them to fight.

The commanders, however, filled with enthusiasm, encouraged the soldiers and comforted them with various hopes—hopes which the emperor had cut off when, by burning the ships, he denied them any possibility of return.

Moreover, although he ought to have gathered provisions for the soldiers, he neither ordered food to be brought from his own territories nor commanded that anything be taken from the abundance of the enemy. Abandoning the inhabited route, he proceeded through deserted regions. There, deprived of food and drink and without guides for the journey, but wandering through a desolate province, the soldiers recognized the plans of their most sagacious prince.

THEODORETUS, Book III, chapter 20. Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 25, p. 146.

[Col. 1061D] 299

After taking many villages and military camps, he was already capturing cities as well. When he came to the city of Ctesiphon, he besieged the king so severely that the king repeatedly sent embassies, offering to surrender part of his homeland if Julian would withdraw from the war.

Julian refused. He neither showed mercy to the supplicants nor understood that although victory is a good thing, complete triumph is excessively liable to provoke envy. He trusted especially in the magical arts that the philosopher Maximus displayed to him, and he imagined that he would attain the glory of Alexander of Macedon—or even surpass it.

For, according to the teaching of Pythagoras and Plato, he thought that he possessed Alexander’s soul through the transmigration of bodies, or rather that another Alexander existed in another body. For this reason he refused to hear the prayers of the Persian king.

SOCRATES, Book III, chapter 18; Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 21, p. 194.

When he had at first used captives as guides into the desert regions, an old man later promised to show him a shortcut, under the guise of a traitor. After they had walked for three days and reached an even greater wilderness, they killed the old man with clubs. He confessed that he had done this for the freedom of his country and that he was willing to endure every torture.

Meanwhile, the Persian army, angry with the Roman army exhausted by the journey, encountered it and prepared for battle.

SOZOMEN, Book VI, chapter 1, p. 635.

The Romans complained about their emperor, asking why he had refused to end the war when a profitable settlement had been offered. Nevertheless, when the Persians pressed them, they resisted, so that they frequently put the enemy to flight.

Julian was present on horseback and encouraged the army. He was unarmed, relying confidently upon the expectation of his own good fortune.

SOCRATES, Book III, chapter 18; Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 21, p. 194.

## CHAPTER XLVII. Concerning Julian’s death

A javelin suddenly came against him, passed through his arm, and lodged in his side. From this wound he received the end of his life. Who inflicted this most just wound remains unknown to this day.

Some say that one of the invisible beings inflicted it; others, that it was one of the shepherds of the Ishmaelites; others, that it was a soldier exhausted by hunger and the journey. But whether it was a human being or an angel, it is clear that he served the divine commands.

For they say that, when he had been wounded, he immediately filled his hand with his own blood and threw it into the air, saying:

> Galilean, you have conquered.

And by this very act he confessed, though blasphemously, the victory.

THEODORETUS, Book III, chapter 20; Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 25, p. 146.

Callistus, who was then serving among the emperor’s companions and wrote his history in heroic verse, says that Julian was wounded by a demon and died.

Julian, therefore, during his fourth consulship, which he held with Sallustius (A.D. 363), died in the Persian region on the sixth day of the month of June, in the third year of his reign and the seventh year from the time when he had been appointed Caesar by Constantius, at the age of thirty-one.

SOCRATES, Book III, chapter 18; Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 21, p. 195.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. What magical practices were discovered after his death

[Col. 1062D]

After his death, his magical practices were discovered. The city of Carrhae still preserves remains of his impiety. Passing through this city, he had refused to travel by way of Edessa because of its observance of the true religion, and had entered a temple worshiped by pagans.

There, after celebrating certain sacrilegious rites with his companions, he arranged the doors and bolts and ordered some soldiers to keep watch there, so that no one might enter until he returned. When he had died and a pious government had succeeded his impious one, those who entered the temple found astonishing images of the emperor, revealing his wisdom and famous piety.

They saw a woman hanging by her hair, with her hands outstretched and her abdomen opened, so that he might inspect the Persian victory in her liver. This crime, then, was discovered at Carrhae.

At Antioch, however, they say that many chests were found in the palace filled with human heads, and innumerable bodies of the dead had been submerged in wells. When his death was announced in that city, everyone held a public festival. They rejoiced not only in the churches and at the tombs of the martyrs, but also proclaimed the victory of the cross in the theaters, rejoicing with the priests [editions of Niv. and Frob.: mocking his magical practices].

I have judged it necessary to set down here even their cry of rejoicing, so that this memory may be preserved for posterity. For everyone shouted together:

> O utterly foolish Maximus, where are your prophecies? God and his Christ have conquered!

This, then, is to be regarded as the end of the book, lest the power of impiety be joined to a pious government.

THEODORETUS, Books III, chapters 21 and 22; Christ. Valesius edition, chapters 26 and 27, p. 147.

# BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 1063]

## 300 CHAPTER I. Concerning the accession of the emperor Jovian, and how he departed from the territory of Persia

[Col. 1063B]

The soldiers, therefore, arriving in the greatest distress, without allowing any delay, placed the imperial diadem upon Jovian the following day. He was a brave and noble man, and at that time was a commander of a thousand, when Julian proposed to the soldiers, under a legal order, that they either sacrifice or leave the army.

Jovian chose to lose his military belt rather than obey the emperor’s impious commands. Julian therefore kept him among the military men at that time because of the necessities of the war.

When the soldiers forcibly dragged him toward the imperial office, he cried out that he did not wish to rule pagan men, since he himself was a Christian. When the unanimous voice of all proclaimed that they too were Christians, he accepted the empire.

SOCRATES, Book III, chapter 19. Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 22, p. 195.

[Col. 1063C]

Jovian was concerned for the common safety and with how he might free the army unharmed from the midst of the enemy. He did not require any elaborate plan, but reaped the most useful fruit from the seeds of piety.

For God suddenly displayed his providence and brought his troubled situation into the harbor of peace. When the king of the Persians learned of his distress, he sent an embassy seeking peace. He then sent provisions to the soldiers and ordered a market for the sale of goods to be prepared for them in the desert. After the treaties had been concluded, Jovian led the army back unharmed.

THEODORETUS, Book IV, chapter 2, p. 152.

These terms were disgraceful as far as Roman glory was concerned, but they suited the circumstances. He departed after Syria had been lost and Nisibis, a city of Mesopotamia, had been handed over to the Persians.

When this was announced, it comforted the Christians and brought grief to the pagans. The soldiers, moreover, strongly blamed Julian’s reckless fervor and attributed to him rather than to anyone else the loss of Roman territory, since, deceived by a Persian as though by a traitor, he had burned the ships that were to transport grain along the river and had brought famine upon the soldiers.

SOCRATES, Book III, chapter 19. Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 22, p. 196.

## CHAPTER II. What the sophist Libanius wrote against the Christians, and how the historian Socrates refuted his statements

The sophist Libanius then composed a book of lamentation about Julian, which he entitled *Julian*, being utterly captivated by praise of him. In it he also mentions the books that Julian had published against the Christians.

If the sophist had merely praised the emperor, I would have remained silent, following the path of history. But since, like a clever rhetorician, he seems through his recollection of Julian’s books to attack the Christian religion, a few things must therefore be said against him, after first setting out his own words.

> Extending the nights of winter by devoting himself [manuscript: by composing] to books concerning the Palestinian man who is God and the Son of God, the emperor fought with great vigor and prevailed in refuting them, so as to expose the absurdity and a certain emptiness of what such people worship. In these labors he was found wiser than the old Tyrian.

May that Tyrian be gracious and receive my words calmly: he has been defeated by a son.

These are the words of the sophist Libanius. I know that he was an excellent sophist; yet if he had not belonged to the religion of which the emperor was a member, he too would at that time have said everything that Christians say about Julian, and perhaps, as a rhetorician, would have exaggerated it.

For while Constantius was alive he poured out praises, but after Constantius’s death he poured forth insults filled with accusations against him. And if the old Porphyry had been emperor, he would have preferred Julian’s books to Porphyry’s works. Julian too, if he had been a sophist, might perhaps have called him evil, just as he did Eubulus.

Since, then, Libanius spoke as one of the emperor’s sect, as a sophist and his friend, saying what seemed right to him, let us oppose him as best we can.

First, he said that Julian devoted himself to his books, extending the nights of winter. “To devote oneself” signifies that he applied his attention to composing a denunciation, as is the custom of sophists. For he had known these books long before; but at that time he was devoting himself to them and striving in a great battle.

It is therefore clear that Julian did not prevail by refuting, as Libanius thinks, but was inflamed by the weakness of his own case and labored, like a detractor, to tear apart what had been set down there well and carefully.

For everyone who resists someone, now twisting the truth and now concealing it, lies against the person with whom he is arguing. And one who is hostile to someone strives not only to act but also to speak about everything as an enemy would.

Since Julian and Porphyry, whom he calls the old Tyrian, were both detractors, they are exposed by their own words. Porphyry tore apart the life of the great philosopher Socrates in the history of philosophy that he himself composed, and reported such things about him as are usually employed in disparagement.

This was Socrates, who among the Greeks was regarded as remarkable for chastity, justice, and other virtues; whom Plato, that remarkable philosopher among them, and Xenophon, and the other philosophical company—that is, chorus—not only honor as beloved by God but also declare to have been wiser than a human being.

Julian, however, out of zeal for a faction, exposed his own passion in the *Caesars*, criticizing the lives of all who had reigned before him and sparing not even the philosopher Marcus.

Thus both were detractors. I have no need to use many words. I inferred their character from the words of both and have said this.

But let us hear what Gregory of Nazianzus reported about Julian. In the second book *Against the Pagans*, after other remarks, he says:

> “These things concerning Julian were handed down to others by experience itself and by the power he assumed; but I had long since learned his character, when I came to know the man more clearly at Athens. He had come there when his brother seemed to be an enemy of the emperor. His arrival had a twofold purpose: one, apparently more respectable, for he said that he had come to see Hellas and to be educated; the other more secret and unknown to most people, to seek out demon-worshiping sacrificers and deceitful men, since he did not yet possess the license for his impiety.
>
> “At that time, then, I did not observe the man without reason. I did not see these things by chance; rather, the instability of his character and its excessive deviation made me cautious. For the one who observes well is indeed an excellent prophet.
>
> “No favorable sign appeared to me in him. His neck was inflexible, his shoulders restless, his eyes darting about, directed here and there and looking furiously; his feet impatient, his nostrils breathing insult and contempt; his gestures ridiculous, and always displaying the same thing; his laughter uncontrolled and seemingly bubbling up; agreement and denial at once; reasoning that held together by no reason; questioning disorderly; and answers that did not correspond to one another.
>
> “But why should I run through everything? I saw him before his deeds and recognized him by the deeds themselves. And if those who were present then were here, they would testify that, when I saw these things, I suddenly said: ‘What an evil the Roman state is nurturing!’
>
> “After I had foretold these things, I wished that I might be proved a liar. For that would have been better than for the earth to be filled with such crimes.
>
> “I do not think that such prodigies ever existed, even when many floods, many fires, many pestilences, and chasms in the earth occurred, although men are reported to have been inhuman and savage and composed of dissimilar natures. For this reason he was brought to an end worthy of his arrogance.”

These are Gregory’s words concerning Julian.

Since those who speak many words against the Christians strive to do violence to the truth, perverting certain passages from the sacred writings and altering others, while nevertheless taking everything according to their own purpose, many people opposed them and clearly demonstrated the falsity of their empty sophisms, destroying and refuting them. Before all the others was Origen, although he lived many years before Julian.

When certain passages seemed to trouble readers of the most sacred writings, Origen set them before himself and interpreted them, thereby eliminating the sophistical inventions of detractors. If Julian and Porphyry had read these writings more often, they might have accepted them willingly, changed their words in another direction, and not turned them toward sophisms of blasphemy.

That the emperor endeavored to attack the Scriptures by addressing ignorant and simple people rather than those who possessed the truth of the divine Scriptures is clear from the following. He gathered passages that had been expressed in more human terms for the sake of the divine dispensation, and after collecting many examples of this kind he finally says:

> “Each of these statements, if it does not contain some ineffable contemplation, is filled with the greatest blasphemy against God.”

Julian said this in the third book *Against the Christians*.

In his book composed on Cynicism, while teaching how sacred myths ought to be fashioned, he says that their truth should be concealed. Thus he speaks:

> “Nature loves to be hidden, and the substance of the gods, concealed from view, does not endure to enter polluted ears in bare words.”

From this it is evident that the emperor suspected the divine Scriptures because they contained mystical words possessing a certain ineffable mode of contemplation. But he was indignant that everyone did not hold the same opinion, and he attacked those among the Christians who seemed to accept the divine utterances simply.

He ought not, therefore, to have risen up against simple people, nor on their account to have swollen with rage against the sacred writings, nor to have hated and rejected what others had understood more correctly, simply because not everyone then thought as he wished.

He thus became like Porphyry. Porphyry, having been beaten by certain Christians at Caesarea in Palestine, could not endure his anger and, in his fury, abandoned Christianity. By writing blasphemies out of hatred for his enemies, he deprived himself of Christianity, as Eusebius Pamphilus demonstrated in refuting him and destroying his arguments.

The emperor, however, became proud among the ignorant Christians and, through the same passion, turned toward the blasphemies of Porphyry. Both sinned willingly, and by sinning knowingly were punished with the most deserved penalty.

When the sophist Libanius, seemingly in mockery, said that Christians make a man from Palestine into God and the Son of God, he appears to have forgotten his own words. At the end of his book, he deified Julian, saying among other things:

> “For they had nearly killed the first messenger of his death, because he was thought to have lied about a god.”

A little later he says:

> “O fosterling of demons, disciple of demons, and observer of demons.”

Although he understood this differently, he nevertheless said of Julian the very things that Christians assert in reproaching him. If, then, he intended to praise Julian, he ought to have avoided this name and not indicated that Julian was devoted to demons, just as he avoided another expression and removed it from his books when he was criticized.

How Christ, who was a human being, is deified; how he was openly human but invisibly God; and how both are true—the sacred reasoning of the Christians knows. Pagans, however, cannot understand this before they believe. For the divine word says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7:9).

They are therefore not ashamed to deify many human beings—and would that they were men trained in good morals, or just, or chaste, rather than lewd, wicked, and drunken men, namely Hercules, Dionysus, and Asclepius, just as Julian frequently is not ashamed to swear by them in his books.

If I wished to enumerate their male and female Cupids, a lengthy digression would result. But it is enough for those who wish to know these things to consider Aristotle’s *Pallium*, Dionysus’s *Crown*, and the book of Eginius, together with the multitude of poets who, writing about such matters, truly expose the absurdity and emptiness of pagan theology.

Since it is characteristic of pagans to deify human beings with the greatest ease, let us demonstrate this. When the Rhodians were afflicted by a certain calamity, an oracle was given that they should appease the Phrygian Attis, priest of the madness of the Phrygians, with their public celebrations.

The oracle was as follows:

> Appease Attis, the great and pure god Adonis, giver of a good life and riches, and the long-haired Dionysus.

By this oracle, Attis, who killed himself in mad love, called the same person Adonis and Dionysus.

When Alexander, king of the Macedonians, crossed into Asia, the Amphictyons, favoring Alexander, composed these verses:

> Consult Zeus, king of the gods, and honor thrice-born Athena; you who conceal in mortal form the heavenly king, whom Zeus sowed among the generations of heroes as an ally. Let good laws of joy establish Alexander as king.

The demon uttered this at the Pythian [edition: Parthian] oracle. While flattering the powerful, it deified them.

What shall we say when they even deified the athlete Cleomedes [manuscript of Lyr.: Diomedes], saying:

> The last of the heroes, Cleomedes, athlete of the city: honor him with sacrifices, because he is no longer mortal.

For this reason Diogenes the Cynic and the philosopher Oenomaus rebuked Apollo, the Pythian.

The people of Cyzicus called Hadrian the thirteenth god. Hadrian himself also deified his beloved Antinous.

And does Libanius not call these things absurd and empty? Let these remarks, therefore, which we have made in digression because of his disparagement, suffice for us.

SOCRATES, Book III, chapter 19. Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 22, p. 196.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the uprightness of Jovian’s faith, and what Athanasius of Alexandria wrote

Jovian [editions of Valesius and Frob.: Jovinianus], then, as soon as he entered the territories of his empire, first wrote that the bishops should return from exile and that the churches should be restored to those who had inviolably preserved the faith set forth at Nicaea.

He also wrote to Athanasius, who was the chief defender of these doctrines, asking him to write back to him concerning the complete discipline of the divine doctrines. Athanasius gathered the more eloquent bishops and replied, asking him to preserve the faith set forth at Nicaea as agreeing with the apostolic doctrines.

The words of his letter are as follows.

THEODORETUS, Book IV, chapter 2, p. 152.

To the most pious and merciful, victorious Augustus Jovian: Athanasius and the other bishops, appearing on behalf of all the bishops of Egypt, the Thebaid, and Libya.

It is fitting that a ruler beloved by God should possess the will and desire to learn heavenly things. For then, truly having your heart in God’s hand, you will govern the empire in peace through many years.

Since you wished to learn from us the faith of the Catholic Church according to your piety, we gave thanks to the Lord for this and took care to present to your piety the faith proclaimed by all the Fathers at Nicaea.

Certain people who rejected it frequently plotted against us because we did not agree with the madness of Arius. They became the authors of heresy and schisms throughout the universal Church.

The true and pious faith in our Lord Jesus Christ is therefore manifest to everyone and is known and read from the divine writings. In this faith the holy martyrs were also brought to completion, and now, resting in the Lord, they stand firm.

That faith would have remained unharmed had not the cunning of certain heretics dared to violate it. For a certain Arius and his followers attempted to break out and introduce impiety against it, saying that the Son of God was from things that did not exist, a creature, a product, and changeable. Through such teachings they led very many astray, so that even those who seemed to possess some standing were drawn into this kind of blasphemy.

But our holy Fathers, assembling long ago, as we said, in the Council of Nicaea, anathematized the Arian sect and, with the testimony of Scripture, professed the faith of the Catholic Church. By that proclamation the heresy that appeared to have been kindled everywhere was extinguished.

This faith was therefore read and preached throughout all the churches. But because certain people, wishing to renew the Arian heresy, dared to anathematize the very faith set forth by the Fathers at Nicaea, while others pretend to profess it but are known to deny the truth itself by interpreting “consubstantial” differently and blaspheming against the Holy Spirit when they say that he is a creature and a product brought into being through the Son, we have necessarily considered the harm produced among the people by this matter and have taken care to offer your piety the confession of the Council of Nicaea.

Thus your pious religion may learn with how much precision it was written and how greatly those who wish to teach anything outside it are in error.

Know, beloved emperor, that this faith has been proclaimed from ancient times and that the Fathers who assembled at Nicaea professed it. In this faith all the churches established in Spain and Britain agree, as do those in Gaul, Italy, and Dalmatia, in Mysia and Macedonia, and throughout Hellas as a whole; likewise those throughout Africa, Sardinia, Cyprus, Crete, Pamphylia, Lycia, Isauria, all Egypt and Libya, Pontus and Cappadocia and the neighboring regions, and the churches of the East, apart from a few followers of Arius.

For we have learned the opinion of all those mentioned above through experience, and we possess their letters; and we know them, beloved emperor. Since only a few contradict this faith, they cannot prejudice it throughout the whole world. For, having long been driven away from the Arian heresy, they now oppose piety with the greatest contentiousness.

So that your piety may know this—even though you already know it—we have taken care to append the faith professed at the Council of Nicaea by the three hundred and eighteen bishops. It is as follows:

This is the faith of the Council of Nicaea:

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord, our Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father as the only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things were made, both in heaven and on earth. He, for us human beings and for our salvation, descended from heaven [the editions omit “from heaven”], was incarnate, became human, suffered, and on the third day rose again. He ascended into heaven and will come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” and “Before he was born he did not exist”; and that he was made from things that did not exist, or is from another substance or subsistence; and who assert that the Son of God is created, changeable, or mutable—the holy catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes them.

It is necessary, God-beloved Emperor, for us to stand in this faith as in a sacred and apostolic faith, and not to unsettle it through any verbal deception or contentious argument—as the Arians did from the beginning, saying that the Son was from things that did not exist, and that there was a time when he did not exist, and that he was created, made, and changeable.

Therefore, as we have already said, the Council of Nicaea also anathematized such heresy, but professed the faith of truth [Lyr. manuscript: “of the Trinity”]. For they did not simply call the Son “like” the Father, lest he be thought merely to be a god like God, rather than true God [Col. 1069C]; they also wrote that he is consubstantial, which is proper to a genuine [edition: begotten] and true son, born from a true and natural father.

Nor did they separate the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son; rather, they glorified him with the Father and the Son in the one faith of the Holy Trinity, since the Godhead in the Holy Trinity is one.

THEODORETUS, Book IV, chapter 3, edition of Christ. Valesius.

When the Emperor read this letter, he confirmed the knowledge and devotion toward sacred matters that he had possessed. He also composed another law, so that the customary grain allowance would be restored to the churches—the allowance that the great Constantine had established and Julian had prohibited from being distributed. Since the famine arising from Julian’s impiety did not permit the whole amount established by Constantine to be distributed at that time, Jovian promised that, for the present, one-third would be expended, so that, when the famine had ceased, the grain would be supplied in full.

THEODORETUS, Book IV, chapter 4, p. 155.

## CHAPTER IV. How the orthodox flourished in the time of Jovian and the heretics were suppressed

The Emperor therefore recalled from exile the bishops whom Constantius had sent away and who had not returned during Julian’s reign. At that time all the temples of the pagans were also being closed, and the priests themselves were fleeing everywhere. They put on their cloaks, then laid the cloaks aside, and returned to ordinary dress. The pollution of blood also ceased—the pollution that they had publicly and insatiably practiced under Julian [Col. 1070A].

The Christians, however, did not remain quiet. The leaders of the religious factions frequently approached the Emperor, believing that they could secure his will against their own opponents. First the Macedonians presented the Emperor with a petition, asking that those who preached that the Son was unlike the Father be expelled from the churches and that they themselves be admitted to them.

Those who presented the petition were Basil of Ancyra, Silvanus of Tarsus, Sophronius of Pompeiopolis, Pasinicus of Zela, Leontius of Comana, Callicrates of Claudiopolis, and Theophilus of Castabala. The Emperor received their petition and dismissed them without an answer, saying only:

“I hate quarrels, but I love and honor equally those who hasten toward concord.”

When those who were preparing for contention heard this, they became quiet [Col. 1070B].

This, therefore, was done according to the Emperor’s wish. For at that time the intention of the followers of Acacius was revealed; and, as they were accustomed to do, they adapted themselves to the Emperor’s wishes. Meeting at Antioch in Syria, they held discussions with Meletius, who shortly before had separated from them and now seemed to defend the doctrine of consubstantiality. They acted in this way because they saw that he was honored while the Emperor was residing there.

Accordingly, after composing a petition by common agreement, they professed consubstantiality, confirmed the Nicene faith, and presented it to the Emperor. The words of the petition are these:

“To our most devout and God-beloved lord Jovian, victorious, Augustus: the synod of the bishops presently assembled in the city of Antioch from various provinces.

“Since your piety first endeavored to celebrate ecclesiastical peace and concord, we too know this well, God-beloved Emperor. And since you have rightly embraced the summit of such true unity and orthodox faith, we are not unaware of this either.

“But lest we be reckoned among those who adulterate the doctrine of truth, we submit to your piety that we both accept and hold the faith of the holy council formerly celebrated at Nicaea and established from the beginning.

“We also say that the word ‘consubstantial’—which appears to some to have another meaning—received a careful interpretation from the Fathers, since they signified that the Son was born from the substance of the Father and that, in substance, he is like the Father. 304

“For it is not believed to involve any kind of suffering in the ineffable birth. Nor did the Fathers understand the term ‘substance’ according to any pagan usage; rather, they used it to destroy the Arians, who had presumptuously dared to preach something impious about Christ, namely, that he was from things that did not exist.

“Those who now assert inequality have likewise, with even greater harshness and audacity, unwisely dared to do this, to the destruction of the Church’s concord. For this reason we have appended to our present statement a copy of the faith of the Council of Nicaea, which we also rightly embrace. It is as follows:

“‘We believe in one God, the Father almighty,’ and the rest.

“And the subscription:

“‘I, Meletius, bishop of Antioch, have presented this, consenting to the foregoing: Eusebius of Samosata, Evagrius of Sicily, Uranius of Apamea, Zoilus of Larissa, Acacius of Caesarea, Antipater of Rhosus, Abraham of Urima, Aristonicus of Seleucobelos, [Col. 1071A] Barlabentus of Pergamum, Uranius of Melitene, Magnus of Chalcis, Eutychius of Eleutheropolis, Josacius of Greater Armenia, Titus of Bostra, Pelagius of Laodicea, Arabianus of Adada, Piso of Adada through the presbyter Lamyrion, Sabinianus of Zeugma, Athanasius of Ancyra through the presbyters Orphitus and Aetius, Irenaeus of Gaza, Piso of Augusta, Patricius of Palti through the presbyter Lamyrion, Anatolius of Beroea, Theotimus of Aramenus, Lucianus of Arca.’”

We found this petition written in Sabinus’s collection of synodal documents. The Emperor’s purpose, however, was to cut off the disputes of the dissenting parties through conciliatory language and persuasion. He said that he would trouble none of those who believed in any manner whatsoever, but that he loved and highly honored those who offered a beginning to ecclesiastical unity.

That he acted in this way is also stated by the philosopher Themistius in the praise he delivered during the Emperor’s consulship. There he marvels that the Emperor permitted each person to worship as he wished; and, mocking the customs of flatterers, he says that they were revealed by the purple [Note: Editions V and Froben read “to reveal the purple.” The Niv. edition adds, “that they worship not God but the purple more.”].

SOCRATES, Book III, chapters 20 and 21; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapters 24 and 25, p. 202.
