At that time the Emperor also gave Secundus, who was governing the prefecture, a praetorian law providing that anyone who dared to violate a sacred virgin in the marriage bed, or even look upon her with an immodest gaze—not to mention attempting to abduct her—would be punished by capital sentence. He enacted this law because, during Julian’s reign, certain men had dared to take such virgins as wives.

SOZOMEN, Book VI, chapter 3, p. 640.

## CHAPTER V. That Athanasius came to Jovian and was suitably honored by him

[Col. 1071C]

Meanwhile Athanasius, bishop of the Alexandrian see, after consulting with a few of his associates, judged it necessary to visit the Christian Emperor. Coming to Antioch, he instructed the Emperor about matters that required attention. Some say that the Emperor himself had summoned him, so that he might explain what appeared necessary for religion and the right faith; and, having arranged ecclesiastical affairs as was fitting, he was considering his return.

Euzoius, however, the bishop of Antioch belonging to the Arian faction, was trying to have a certain eunuch named Probatian ordained bishop in the city of Alexandria. While this was being done, Lucius of Alexandria, ordained by the presbyter George, approached the Emperor. He slandered Athanasius, alleging that Athanasius had been formally indicted during his episcopate [Niv. and Froben editions: “had been accused”], had endured many exiles under earlier emperors, and had caused discord concerning sacred matters. He further begged that another bishop be ordained in the city of Alexandria.

But the Emperor, knowing how great were the plots laid by Athanasius’s enemies, paid no attention to such disparagement. He ordered Lucius to be silent, with severe threats, and commanded that Probatianus and his eunuch followers [Col. 1072A], the authors of such crimes and disturbances, be punished.

He sent Athanasius, now made his very dear friend, to Egypt, so that he might arrange the affairs of the churches and the people as he thought best. It is reported that he praised him for the exceptional virtue of his conduct and wisdom.

Some say that, before the Arians held the churches under the Emperor Constantius, the monk Antony saw a dream in which asses had overturned the sacred altar with their kicks. When he awoke, he said that the Church would be trampled by adulterers and mongrel people. Later events showed that this was not false.

SOZOMEN, Book VI, chapter 5, p. 642.

## CHAPTER VI. On Jovian’s consulship and death

[Col. 1072B]

The Emperor, then, restraining the attack of the heretics, departed from Antioch and came to Tarsus in Cilicia, where he buried Julian’s body. After performing all the customary rites for his funeral, he was designated consul (A.D. 364).

As he hastened toward Constantinople, he came to an estate called Dadastana, between Galatia and Bithynia. There the philosopher Themistius, meeting him with other senators, delivered a consular address.

The affairs of the Roman state, as well as ecclesiastical matters, could then have been prosperously arranged under a kindly ruler, had sudden death not taken such a man from the human race. At the aforesaid estate, during winter, seized by an illness of the phraxis, he died during his own consulship and that of his son Varronianus [Col. 1072C], on the seventeenth day of February. He had reigned seven months and lived thirty-three years.

SOCRATES, Book III, chapter 22; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 26, p. 205.

## CHAPTER VII. On the rise of the Emperor Valentinian and how he himself made his brother Valens Emperor

When the army had come to Nicaea in Bithynia, he appointed Valentinian Emperor, an excellent man and one most worthy of imperial rank.

SOZOMEN, Book VI, chapter 6, p. 644.

Valentinian was therefore appointed on the twenty-fifth day of the same month of February. He was a Pannonian by birth, from the city of Cibala, and had at that time been entrusted with the command of the soldiers [Col. 1072D], because he knew military discipline with outstanding skill. He was also a great-hearted man and always appeared better than his present circumstances.

SOCRATES, Book IV, chapter 1, p. 210.

He excelled not only in courage but also in prudence, temperance, justice, and bodily stature. He was at once regal 305 and civilized, so that when the army attempted to associate another partner with him, he replied with what is repeated by all:

“‘It was your task, soldiers, when there was no emperor, to give me the government of the empire. But once I had undertaken it, it is now my task, not yours, to consider the common affairs.’”

The soldiers admired his words and followed his will. But he called his brother from Paeonia [Santheod. manuscript: Pannonia] and, contrary to what he ought to have done, made him his partner in the empire.

THEODORETUS, Book IV, chapter 5; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 6, p. 156.

Thirty days after his accession.

Handing over to him the scepters of Asia and likewise of Egypt, he assigned Europe to himself. Coming to the West, he immediately instructed everyone there in equity, beginning with exhortations to piety.

SOCRATES, Book IV, chapter 1, p. 210. THEODORETUS, Book IV, chapter 5; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 6, p. 156.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the episcopate of Ambrose of Milan and his confidence in speaking

[Col. 1073B]

After Auxentius had died—he had held the episcopate of Milan and had been deposed by many councils—the Emperor summoned the bishops and addressed them as follows:

“You know clearly, since you are learned in the divine words, what a bishop ought to be and that it is not fitting for him to govern his subjects by word alone, but also by his conduct; he must show himself an imitator of virtue in every respect and possess good conduct as a witness to his teaching.

“Therefore establish in the episcopal see a man to whom we too, who govern the empire, may sincerely bow our heads, and whose admonitions, whenever we necessarily sin as human beings, we may receive as medicines from a physician.”

THEODORETUS, Book IV, chapter 5 [Col. 1073C]; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 6, p. 156.

When the Emperor had said this, the synod asked that he himself make the decision, since he was wise and devout. But he replied:

“Such an election belongs to you. For you, having received divine grace and shining with that splendor, will be better able to choose.”

The priests then went out and discussed the episcopal see. Meanwhile the inhabitants of the city, as usually happens, created an uproar, some asking that one man and others another be ordained. Those belonging to the sect of the Arian Auxentius were striving to have someone like themselves appointed, while the orthodox were trying to have a bishop of their own doctrine.

Ambrose, who at that time had been entrusted with the civil administration, learned of this disturbance and feared that some disorder might arise. He therefore hurried to the church. But when the disturbance had ceased, the people gave a unanimous response [Col. 1073D], asking that Ambrose be ordained shepherd of the flock, although he had not yet been baptized.

When the Emperor learned this, he immediately ordered him to be baptized and ordained bishop as a worthy man. For he knew that his will was more certain than any weight of argument and that he understood the decrees of the entire rule with greater precision. He also judged that a divine decision was at work in him, since even the opposing party agreed in his election.

Thus, after receiving the gift of holy baptism, Ambrose also received at the same time the grace of the episcopate. It is said that, once this had been done, the excellent Emperor offered the following hymn to the Savior and Lord—for he had been present at the events:

“‘I give you thanks, almighty Lord and our Savior, because I entrusted bodies to this man, while you entrusted souls; and you have shown that my choice accords with your justice.’”

A few days later, when Saint Ambrose complained to the Emperor with great confidence that the judges were acting unjustly, the Emperor said:

“‘I recognized this confidence of yours long ago. And, clearly approving it, I not only did not resist but was also a partner in your election and ordination. Therefore hasten to heal, as the divine law commands, the offenses of our souls.’”

Thus the Emperor both said and did these things at Milan.

When he learned that certain people in Asia and Phrygia were doubting the divine doctrines, he ordered a synod to be held in Illyricum and sent to those who were doubting the decrees that had been made and confirmed concerning them. Those who assembled there decreed that the faith set forth in the city of Nicaea should be preserved.

He also wrote himself, associating his brother with him in the letter, so that they might persevere in the decisions that had pleased them. It is therefore now necessary to set forth the law itself, which openly proclaims his piety and unquestionably demonstrates the sincerity of Valens at that time.

THEODORETUS, Book IV, chapter 6; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 7, p. 157.

## CHAPTER IX. The edict of Valentinian and Valens concerning the consubstantial Trinity

“The most exalted, devout, victorious Emperors, Augusti, Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian, to the bishops of the dioceses of Asia, Phrygia, Carophrygia, and Pacatiana, greetings in the Lord.

“Since a great council has been held in Illyricum and the question concerning the saving Word has been examined with precision, the thrice-blessed bishops have shown that the Trinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is consubstantial. Without deviating from it, they exercise the ministries of religion under the great King.

“Our power has therefore also decreed that this faith be preached, but in such a way that no one says: ‘We follow the religion of the Emperor who governs this country,’ rather than obeying him who gave us the commandments of salvation. For the Gospel of our Christ says: ‘Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s’ (Matthew 22:21).

“What, then, do you say, bishops and leaders of the saving Word? If your profession is such, cease abusing imperial dignity while loving one another, and do not persecute those who serve God perfectly. By their prayers earthly wars are calmed, the assaults of angels who have departed from God are driven away, and all demons, corrupters of prayers, are confounded by the constancy of their petitions. They do not refuse to pay taxes according to the laws, nor do they resist royal authority; rather, with sincere devotion they observe the commandments of the heavenly God and submit to our laws.

“You, however, are shown to be disobedient. We submit to him who is first and last, whereas you claim authority for yourselves. We therefore desire to keep ourselves pure from you.

“And just as Pilate, when examining our Christ and unwilling to kill him, turned toward the East, asked for water, and washed his hands, saying, ‘I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man’ (Matthew 27:24), so our Majesty has always ordered that there be no persecution, no disturbance, and no envy toward those laboring in the Lord’s field; nor are the stewards of the great King to be expelled.

“Otherwise you may appear to prosper for the present under our rule, but afterward you will subject the Lord’s testament to suffering, as in the blood of Zechariah. But after the coming of the heavenly King, our Lord Jesus Christ, those men were destroyed and handed over to death together with their helper, the corrupting demon.

“We gave this order to Megetius, Ciceronius, Damas, and Lampo, and to Brintisius, who were hearers. We have also sent you the official records themselves, so that you may know what was celebrated in the eminent council.

“To this letter he also appended the decrees of the council, which in summary contain the following:

“‘We profess, following the great and orthodox council, that the Son is consubstantial with the Father. We do not understand “consubstantial” in the way that certain persons formerly explained it, without truly subscribing to it; nor in the way that others now call those men “Fathers” while rejecting the force of the term and following those who wrote that consubstantiality signifies likeness, on the ground that the Son is like none of the other creatures made through him, but only the Father.

“‘Those who explain matters in this way impiously teach that the Son is God’s chief creature. We, therefore, hold—as did the councils recently held at Rome and in Gaul—that the substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one and the same in three persons, that is, in three perfect subsistences.

“‘In accordance with the Nicene exposition, we confess also that the incarnate Son of God is consubstantial, from the holy Virgin Mary; that he dwelt among human beings; and that he completed the entire dispensation for us in his birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven. He will come again to restore to us the divine likeness, being God who became flesh and human being who bears God.

“‘We therefore anathematize those who hold views contrary to what has been stated, as well as those who do not truly anathematize the one who said, “Before he was born, the Son did not exist,” but wrote that, before he was born in actuality, he existed in the Father’s power.

“‘This is true also of all creatures, which do not always exist as God does. The Son, however, is always with the Father, begotten by an eternal generation.’”

The Emperor therefore indicated these matters in summary. I, however, think that the actual letters of the council should also be set forth.

THEODORETUS, Book IV, chapter 7; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 8, p. 158.

## CHAPTER X. Letter of the Illyrian bishops to the Eastern bishops, professing the consubstantial Trinity

“The bishops of Illyricum to the bishops of the churches of God in the dioceses of Asia, Phrygia, Carophrygia, and Pacatiana, greetings in the Lord.

“When we assembled together and held a very serious inquiry concerning the saving Word, we proved that the Trinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is consubstantial [Col. 1076A]. It was therefore right to send you a letter—not setting forth the faith of the Trinity through arguments, but asking in humility.

“We have sent this letter through our most beloved brother and fellow priest, the presbyter Elpidius. In this present letter, it is as though the following words were being recalled, words written in the books of our Savior Jesus Christ: ‘I belong to Paul,’ ‘I to Apollos,’ and ‘I to Cephas.’ ‘Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul?’ (1 Corinthians 1:12–13).

“These words would have been sufficient for our humility, even if we had not sent you a universal letter, because of the great fear with which you proclaim throughout all your provinces that the Holy Spirit is separate from the Father and the Son.

“For this reason we considered it necessary to send to you our lord and fellow minister, the presbyter Elpidius, bearing this letter from the imperial government of the Romans, so that, if this is indeed your preaching, you may know that those who do not preach the consubstantial Trinity are anathema. And if anyone is found not sharing this confession, let him be anathema.

“But for those who preach the consubstantial Trinity, the kingdoms of heaven have been prepared. We therefore ask you, brothers, not to teach one thing and introduce another, but, always and everywhere preaching the consubstantial Trinity, you will possess the kingdom of God.

“For this reason we write and remind you, sending this letter.

“Concerning bishops to be appointed and fellow ministers already appointed: if they remain sound to the end, well; otherwise let them be removed from the presbyterate [Col. 1076C]. Likewise, we have determined concerning presbyters and deacons in the priestly order that they must be blameless in every respect and free from both the municipal council and military service.

“For this reason we did not wish to write at greater length, since we have sent to you from among us our lord and fellow minister Elpidius, who will carefully learn your preaching, whether it is as we heard from our lord and fellow priest Eustathius.

“Moreover, even if you have at some time been in error, put off the old person and put on the new (Colossians 3:9–10). For our brother and fellow minister Elpidius himself will teach you to preach the true faith: that the Holy Trinity, consubstantial with God the Father, and the Son together with the Holy Spirit, sanctified, glorified, and manifested itself; the Father in the Son, the Son in the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, forever.

“When this has been declared, we shall be able openly to confess that the Holy Trinity is consubstantial, according to the faith formerly set forth at Nicaea and confirmed by the Fathers. When this faith has been preached, we shall be able to avoid the erring demon. Once he has been destroyed, we shall greet one another in peace, living peacefully by our letters.

“We have therefore written to you so that you may know that the Arians have been condemned because they are unwilling to confess the Son from the Father’s substance, and the Holy Spirit. Their names are appended: Polychronius, Telemachus, Faustus, Asclepiades, Amantius, and Cleopater.

“These things therefore stand as stated, to the glory of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

“We wish you health in the Father and Son, Christ the Savior, together with the Holy Spirit, for many years.”

THEODORETUS, Book IV, chapter 8; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 9, p. 160.

## CHAPTER XI. On the heresy of the Audaeans

The most famous Emperor therefore showed concern for the apostolic doctrines. Meanwhile a certain Syrian, Syrian both by origin and by language, named Audaeus, was at that time reviving new doctrines. He had long been beginning to entertain evil notions, but then became openly manifest.

At first, foolishly understanding what is written, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26), he thought that the Godhead possessed human form and was divided according to bodily members. He paid no attention to the meaning of divine Scripture, which often applies the names of human limbs to divine operations, because through such expressions those who cannot easily understand more subtle matters recognize God’s providence more readily [Col. 1077B].

He added other doctrines akin to this impiety. Tainted by the madness of Manes, he asserted that God was the creator neither of fire nor of darkness. These teachings, and whatever resembles them, are concealed by the participants in Manes’s madness, as he preached, who were separated from the Church. Some of them declare marriage accursed; others, living with women outside the law [V edition: “not far from the law”], live contrary to the law. For this reason they say that one must live at a greater distance, while concealing the blasphemy of their doctrines.

Nevertheless, their dwelling is full of arrogance, and they are an offspring of Pharisaic teaching. Those men accused the physician of souls and bodies in the temple, saying to the apostles, “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” (Luke 5:30). And through the prophet God says of such people:

“Those who say, ‘I am clean; do not touch me,’ these will be smoke in my wrath, a fire burning all day” (Isaiah 65:5).

But it is not now the time to refute their foolishness; therefore let us proceed with the rest of the narrative.

THEODORETUS, Book IV, chapter 6; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 10, p. 162.

At that time the heresy of the Messalians arose. They are called Εὐχῆται, that is, “those who pray,” and by another name Ἐνθουσιασαί, that is, “sacrificers.” For there they await the operation of a certain demon and suppose it to be the presence of the Holy Spirit.

Those who participate fully in this disease reject the work of their hands as though it were evil, abandon themselves to sleep, and call the fantasies of their sins prophecies. The leaders of this heresy were Dadosius, Sebas, Adelphius, Hermas, Symeones, and others. They did not withdraw from ecclesiastical communion at all, saying that the divine food neither benefits nor harms anyone, although Christ the Lord said:

“Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood will live forever” (John 6:55).

When they wish to conceal this disease, even when convicted they shamelessly deny it, and they utterly reject others who hold the very views that they themselves retain in their minds.

Litoius, therefore, bishop of the Church of Melitene, suitably adorned with divine zeal, saw that this disease was invading many monasteries—or rather, as I should say, dens of thieves. He burned them and separated the wolves from the sheep.

Likewise Amphilochius, that most famous bishop of Lycaonia, when this plague was growing there, suppressed it vigorously and rescued the sheep that were afflicted by such contagion.

Flavian, the universally praised bishop of Antioch, hearing that these people were living at Edessa and spreading their own poison through the neighboring cities, sent a crowd of monks and brought them to Antioch. He refuted them in the following way:

“Accusers,” he said, “are slanderers and witnesses are liars.”

Then, calling the very old Adelphius gently and ordering him to sit beside him, he said:

“We, elder, who have already passed through a large part of life and have learned human nature very well, have recognized the contrivances of hostile demons and, through experience itself, have been taught the ministries of grace. These men, however, since they are young and have no better understanding of such matters, were unable to hear spiritual words.

“Tell me, therefore, how do you believe that the opposing spirit departs and the grace of the Holy Spirit arrives?”

Melted by these words, the old man vomited out all the poison he had concealed and said:

“Baptism brings no benefit at all to those who are baptized; only earnest prayer drives out the indwelling demon.”

He further maintained that every person at birth draws from his parent, along with his nature, service to demons. Once these demons have been expelled through earnest prayer, the Holy Spirit arrives and marks his presence sensibly and visibly [Col. 1078C]. It rescues the body from the passions of every impulse and completely frees the soul from evil will, so that thereafter the person has no need either of fasting, which afflicts the body, or of teaching, which restrains it, or of discipline, which willingly instructs one to advance.

Moreover, he said that the person who obtained this was not only freed from the exultations of the body but also clearly foresaw the future and saw the Holy Trinity with his eyes.

Flavian, therefore, having dug up this most foul spring and brought out its cups for all to examine, said to the wretched old man:

“Most ancient of evil days, your mouth has rebuked you, and not I; for your lips testify against you.”

When this disease had become known to everyone, they were expelled from Syria and advanced to Pamphylia, filling it with this plague [Col. 1078D].

THEODORETUS, Book IV, chapter 10; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 11, p. 163.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Council of Lampsacus

Valentinian, then, held the same doctrine as the Fathers of Nicaea and benefited those who professed similar views; toward those who held different opinions, however, he was not oppressive.

At the beginning of his reign, as he was traveling from Constantinople through Thrace toward Rome, the bishops of the Hellespont and Bithynia, and all who preached that the Father and the Son were consubstantial, sent Hypatianus, bishop of Heraclea Perinthus, as an envoy, so that he might deign to take part in correcting the doctrine.

When he approached the Emperor and explained the bishops’ embassy, Valentinian replied:

“Since I am merely one of the people, it is not lawful for me to investigate such matters. Let the priests, whose responsibility this is, assemble among themselves wherever they wish.”

After the Emperor had given this answer, the bishops assembled at Lampsacus. After deliberating for two months, they finally decreed that the proceedings conducted at Constantinople through the efforts of Eudoxius and Acacius should be annulled.

They likewise decreed that the exposition of the faith should be annulled—the exposition which they had presented as that of the Western bishops and under which they had induced certain people to subscribe, promising that they would utterly reject the doctrine concerning the term “unlike in substance,” though they had lied about this.

They asserted that the Son was like the Father in substance, saying that the addition of “like” was necessary because of the distinction between substances [manuscripts: “subsistences”]. They held that the faith promulgated at Seleucia and set forth at the dedication of the church at Antioch should be prescribed throughout all the churches.

They also decreed that those who had been deposed by people asserting that the Son was unlike the Father should recover their own sees. If anyone wished to accuse them, they sanctioned that he should do so at equal risk, appointing as judges bishops who held the correct doctrine and who would assemble from neighboring provinces into the church, where they would be witnesses concerning each person said to have been oppressed.

Having made these decrees, they summoned Eudoxius and those who had been with him and granted them a place for repentance. When they refused to obey, they announced to all the churches what had been decided.

Since they believed that Eudoxius was striving to make the entire royal power favor his party and would certainly disparage the others, they thought it necessary to forestall him and report what had been done at Lampsacus.

Accordingly, they approached the Emperor Valens as he was returning from Thrace at Heraclea. He had separated from his brother and gone as far as a certain place. At that time Eudoxius already held the highest position with the Emperor and the leading men.

When the envoys sent from Lampsacus approached, the Emperor ordered them not to separate themselves from Eudoxius. When they resisted and complained about the proceedings held against Eudoxius at the council of Seleucia, the Emperor was provoked to anger. He sent them into exile and ordered that the churches be handed over to Eudoxius.

SOZOMEN, Book VI, chapter 7, p. 646.

## CHAPTER XIII. How Valens became an Arian
At the time when Valens assumed the empire, he was adorned with apostolic doctrines. But when the Goths had crossed the Danube and were traversing Thrace, he gathered an army and was considering fighting against them. It seemed good to him not to engage in battle unarmed with respect to sacred grace, but fortified with the arms of holy baptism; and this was indeed good and very wise. What he did afterward, however, signifies great weakness of spirit and treachery toward the truth. For he suffered the same misfortune as his ancestor Adam. He was seduced by his wife’s address and ensnared by feminine words. For she, having first been entangled in the snares of the Arian deception, persuaded him also to fall with her [Col. 1080A] into the pit of blasphemy; Eudoxius was the author of this seduction. He still held the reins of the Constantinopolitan Church—not governing it, but rather sinking his own ship. At that time, therefore, during the very administration of baptism, he bound the wretched man by an oath to remain in the impiety of the doctrine and to expel everywhere those who held contrary opinions. Thus, abandoning apostolic teaching, he took the opposing side, and shortly afterward fulfilled what he had sworn.

THEODORET, book IV, chapter 11. Christ. Valesius’s edition, chapter 12, p. 165.

## CHAPTER XIV. With what cruelty Valens acted against the orthodox

Meanwhile he came to Euroea; for he feared that the Persians might perhaps break the treaty concluded under Jovian for thirty years. Since they made no movement, he remained in Antioch. At that time he sent Bishop Meletius into exile, but, out of respect for Paulinus, spared his life. Those who refused communion with Eudoxius he expelled from the churches, condemned to fines, and afflicted with blows and other punishments.

For it is said that he even drowned many in the river Orontes.

SOZOMEN, book VI, chapter 7, p. 647.

From Samosata he expelled the holy Eusebius, and deprived Pelagius, the remarkable shepherd of the Laodiceans, of his city. Although Pelagius had married in his youth, on the very first day of his marriage, in the bridal chamber, he persuaded his bride to prefer purity to shared pleasure and, so that she might attain fraternal charity, instructed her in place of marital intercourse.

SOCRATES, book IV, chapter 2, [Col. 1080C] p. 212.—THEODORET, book IV, chapter 12. Christ. Valesius’s edition, chapter 13, p. 165.

## CHAPTER XV. The tyranny and downfall of Procopius

While these things were happening in Syria, a tyrant named Procopius arose in Constantinople. Gathering a considerable army for himself within a short time, he hastened against the emperor. When this was reported, Valens was disturbed and delayed his advance for a little while. While the outcome of the war was meanwhile being brought forth, an earthquake destroyed many cities. The sea also altered its proper boundaries, and in some places it advanced so far that it flooded areas where people had previously been able to walk; in other places it withdrew so far [Col. 1080D] that dry land appeared. This occurred during the first consulship of the two rulers (A.D. 365).

SOCRATES, book IV, chapter 3, p. 212.

In the following year, during the consulship of Gratian and Dagalaiphus (A.D. 365), wars were being prepared. When the tyrant Procopius had departed from Constantinople and was moving his camp against the emperor, Valens heard of it, came from Antioch, and engaged him near the Phrygian city of Nacolia. At the first battle he was defeated. Shortly afterward, however, he captured Procopius, who was handed over by the soldiers Agelo and Gomarius; these men he later ordered to be executed by unexpected punishments. Disregarding the oath he had given them, he cruelly killed them by cutting them apart with saws. [Col. 1081A] As for the tyrant, he bent two nearby trees toward one another and had each of his feet tied to one of them. When the trees were released and sprang back into the air, they tore Procopius apart. In this way the tyrant perished.

SOCRATES, book IV, chapter 5, p. 213.

309

## CHAPTER XVI. The exile of the holy bishop Eusebius of Samosata, and how his citizens, out of love for the faith, refused to submit to another bishop

Meanwhile Eusebius, bishop of Samosata, having been deported into exile in Thrace, was laboring zealously in apostolic works. Seeing many churches deprived of pastors, he assumed military clothing, covered his head with a cap, and traveled through Syria and Phoenicia, [Col. 1081B] as well as Palestine, ordaining presbyters and deacons and filling the other offices of the Church. Whenever he found bishops who agreed with him, he appointed them as leaders over churches that lacked pastors.

I consider it necessary that those who do not know it should recognize the courage and wisdom he displayed when he received the imperial command ordering him to live in Thrace. The bearer of this order had arrived toward evening. Eusebius ordered him to remain silent and to conceal his arrival, saying:

“If this crowd learns of it, inflamed by sacred zeal, it will kill you; and I shall be compelled before God to pay the penalty for your death.”

After saying this, he celebrated the customary evening service. At the beginning of the night, revealing the secret to one of his servants, the old man went out alone. The servant followed, carrying only a small mattress and a book. When he came to the bank of the Euphrates, laid out beside the very walls of the city, he boarded a ship to sail to Zeugma; and he ordered the sailors to row. At daybreak he reached the region of Zeugma.

But Samosata was filled with groans and lamentation. When that servant had disclosed to his close associates what had been ordered, and who had departed with him, and which books he had carried, everyone lamented, deprived as they were of their shepherd. The river was filled with those sailing after him and pursuing him. When they arrived and saw their longed-for shepherd, they wailed even more. Sighing and pouring forth fountains of tears, they tried to retain him, lest his sheep should fall among wolves. When they could not move him, they heard him reading the apostolic law (Titus 1:1), which openly commands us to be subject to rulers and authorities.

After this, some offered him gold, others silver, others clothing, and others servants, as though he were departing for a foreign and distant land. He accepted only a few things from people well known to him, armed everyone with his teachings and prayers, instructed them to fight for the apostolic doctrines, and departed for the Danube.

They returned to their own city, exhorting one another, and wisely watched for the ambushes of the wolves.

The ardor and purity of these people’s faith must now also be related. I believe I would be at fault if, through this account, I did not ensure that they were always remembered. When, therefore, the Arians had stripped the flock of its excellent shepherd and appointed another in his place, a man named Eunomius, [Col. 1082A] making him bishop, none of the inhabitants—not poor or rich, servant or craftsman, farmer or gardener, man or woman, young or old—went to the customary ecclesiastical assembly. The bishop lived alone, with no one seeing or addressing him at all, although it is said that he lived with considerable gentleness.

The following event confirms this. When he wished to bathe, and his servants had closed the doors of the bathhouse and prevented those who wished to enter, he himself saw the people before the doors and ordered them opened, gladly inviting everyone to share the bath with him. He did the same in the bathing pool. For when he saw certain people standing near him while he bathed, he ordered those who were standing silently to enjoy the warm water together with him.

But the bishop, thinking that this was being done out of honor, quickly climbed out and departed. The people, however, judging even the water to be polluted by the filth of that most wicked heresy, immediately consigned it to the drainage channels and had another pool prepared. When he learned this, he left the city, considering it disgraceful to live in a city hostile to him and sharing a common horror of him.

After he had departed from Samosata, they openly appointed Lucius in his place, a wolf and enemy of the sheep. But the sheep, although deprived of their shepherd, nevertheless did what belonged to the shepherd. For they remained steadfast in preserving apostolic teaching inviolate.

How all of them also came to hate Lucius, I shall explain in another account. Young men were amusing themselves in the street, passing a ball to one another. As Lucius passed by, the ball happened to fall and roll beneath the feet of his donkey. The boys then wailed loudly, thinking that the ball had been filled with pollution. When Lucius understood this, he ordered one of his attendants to wait and observe what was happening. The boys kindled a fire and threw the ball through the middle of the flames, believing that in this way they had purified it.

I know that this is a youthful act and a remnant of ancient custom. Nevertheless, it provides evidence of the hatred that the entire city harbored toward the Arian madness.

Lucius did not imitate Eunomius in gentleness. Instead, through the judges, he had many priests deported into exile, especially those who fought courageously for the sacred doctrines, [Col. 1082D] even to the remotest boundaries of the Roman empire. Evolcius, who had served in the diaconate, he caused to be sent into the desert of Oasis. Antiochus, distinguished by the lineage of the great Eusebius—for he was his cousin—and shining with many virtues and resplendent in the dignity of the priesthood, he persuaded the authorities to send to the boundaries of Armenia. Who could adequately explain the deeds he performed for the divine doctrines?

When the holy man Eusebius, after many struggles and many virtues and countless victories, had also received the crown of martyrdom, a provincial synod assembled in the customary manner, together with Jovian, then bishop of the city of Pergena [ms. Perrena], who had been stained for a short time by communion with the Arians. When everyone had chosen Antiochus, his own uncle’s successor, and had brought him to the sacred altar and compelled him to bend his knees for ordination, Antiochus turned and, seeing Jovian placing his right hand upon his head, pushed his hand away, saying that a right hand which had once received sacraments celebrated with blasphemies was not to be endured.

But these events occurred somewhat later. At that time, as I have said, he had been led into Inner Armenia. During that period the holy man Eusebius was staying near the Danube, while the Celts were devastating Thrace and besieging its cities, as his writings record.

THEODORET, book IV, chapters 12, 13, and 14. Christ. Valesius’s edition, chapters 13 and 14, p. 166.

310

## CHAPTER XVII. The exile of Bishop Barses

Valens also ordered Barses to live first on the island of Aradus. Barses is still held in the greatest glory, not only in Edessa, which he governed, and the neighboring provinces, but also in Phoenicia, Egypt, and the Thebaid, lands through which he had passed with the greatest splendor of his virtue. When Valens learned that countless crowds were flocking to him—for, since he was full of grace, he healed illnesses by his word—he sent him into exile at Oxyrhynchus, an Egyptian city. When even there his fame inflamed everyone, the old man, worthy of the heavenly city, was taken to a remote fortress near the barbarians, called Pheno.

Some say that his bed is still preserved at Aradus, worthy of exceptional veneration; for many sick people, when placed upon it, [Col. 1083C] receive health through faith.

THEODORET, book IV, chapter 15, p. 167.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Again, the cruelty that Valens exercised against the orthodox after the death of Procopius

After Procopius had been killed, the emperor, advanced in prosperity, once more stirred up battles against the Christians, desiring to bring every form of religion into agreement with Arian doctrine. The synod held at Lampsacus especially provoked him to fury—not only because it had renounced the Arian bishops, but because it had anathematized the promulgation of the faith of Rimini.

Coming, therefore, to Nicomedia in Bithynia, he summoned Eleusius of Cyzicus, for, as I have already said, Eleusius followed the sect of Macedonius. Having convened a council of Arian bishops, Valens compelled Eleusius to agree with their doctrine. At first Eleusius refused; later, when the emperor threatened him with exile, he was frightened into consenting to the Arian doctrine.

After this had been done, he was immediately struck by repentance. He came to Cyzicus and complained publicly before the entire people about the coercion, saying that his consent had been obtained by force, not by his will. He urged them to seek another bishop for themselves, since he had denied his own doctrine under compulsion.

The people of Cyzicus, however, out of affection for him, refused to submit to another bishop and remained under him, although they did not change their own heresy. When the bishop of Constantinople heard this, he ordained Eunomius bishop of Cyzicus, as one who might be able, by the craft of his words, to win the people over to his agreement.

When Eunomius arrived, Eleusius was ordered by sacred commands—that is, by imperial letters—to be expelled and Eunomius to be installed in his see. After this had been done, the partisans of Eleusius built a place of prayer outside the city and held their assemblies there.

Let this suffice concerning Eleusius. We must now report concerning Eunomius.

SOZOMEN, book VI, chapter 8, p. 648.

## CHAPTER XIX. Eunomius the heresiarch

Eunomius was the secretary of Aetius, who was called “Godless,” whose memory we have mentioned. While he was with Aetius, he imitated his sophistical method. Occupying himself with certain arguments and constructing sophisms for himself, he did not understand that, through these things, he was being puffed up and falling into blasphemies. For he zealously defended the doctrine of Arius and opposed the doctrines of the truth in many ways.

He had learned little from the sacred writings and was unable to understand them. He was frequently occupied with words, constantly twisting them, and could not fulfill the purpose of his own intention, as his seven books demonstrate. He composed these books on the Apostle’s Epistle to the Romans, but although he poured forth many words there, he could not discover the meaning of the epistle. There are also other books similar to these; whoever wishes to read them will recognize their worthlessness by experience.

Eudoxius therefore made this Eunomius bishop of Cyzicus, attempting to expel Eleusius. When Eunomius arrived there, using dialectic in his customary manner, he introduced something strange to his listeners. Consequently, a disturbance arose at Cyzicus, and they drove him from the city, unable to tolerate the arrogance of his words.

Coming to Constantinople, he remained with Eudoxius, without a bishopric. But lest we seem to slander him, listen to Eunomius’s own voice, with which he presumes to speak sophistically against God. For he says:

“God knows nothing more of his own substance than we do, nor is it known to him more fully and to us less; but whatever we know concerning it, he also knows in every respect. And whatever he, in turn, knows, you will find unalterably in us.”

Eunomius did not realize that these and similar sophisms—that is, deceptions—were leading to his ruin. How he was separated from the Arians shortly afterward, we shall relate in its proper place.

SOCRATES, book IV, chapter 7, p. 215.

## CHAPTER XX. Valens’s savagery against the orthodox of Constantinople

The inhabitants of Constantinople who professed the Nicene doctrine were also being harassed. The emperor ordered all of them to be expelled from the city, and the churches of the Novatians likewise to be closed. He found none of the churches of the other heretics to close, since they had already been confiscated under the emperor Constantius [ms. Lyr., Constantine].

He also condemned Agelius, the bishop of the Novatian church established at Constantinople, to deportation into exile. For he was said to conduct himself admirably according to ecclesiastical rules. His life was philosophical and detached from the possession of money; the character of his way of life also showed this. He wore only one tunic and always walked barefoot.

Not long afterward he was recalled and recovered the churches. The author of this restoration was a certain Martianus, remarkable in life and learning. Formerly he had served in the imperial court; at that time, as a Novatian presbyter, he taught grammar to the emperor’s daughters Anastasia and Carosa. The public baths at Constantinople are still called Anastasiana and Carosiana after their names.

SOZOMEN, book VI, chapter 9, p. 649.

## CHAPTER XXI. The destruction of the walls of Chalcedon

The emperor Valens ordered the walls of the city of Chalcedon, situated opposite Byzantium, to be destroyed. For he had sworn that he would do this once the tyrant had been defeated, because the Chalcedonians, out of favor toward the tyrant, had inflicted shameful insults upon him and had closed the city gates.

The wall was therefore being demolished at the emperor’s command, and the stones were being carried to Constantinople for the construction of the baths called Constantianae. Among these stones one was found bearing an inscription containing a prophecy—formerly hidden, but then revealed. It signified that when an abundance of water came to the city, the wall would serve the bath; but countless barbarian nations, ranging throughout the Roman territories and committing many atrocities, would finally perish themselves.

After some time, it happened that Valens built an aqueduct and supplied Constantinople with an abundance of water. At that time the barbarian nations also rose in motion. Yet the prophecy was fulfilled in another way as well. After the aqueduct had been brought into the city, Clearchus, then prefect of the city, built a very large fountain in the street now called the Street of Theodosius, where the abundance of water was released. The city held a great festival there.

But this prophecy was fulfilled shortly afterward. While the wall was being dismantled, the Constantinopolitans asked the emperor to desist from destroying it. The landowners of Bithynia, together with the people of Nicomedia and Nicaea, also made this request. The emperor, however, full of fury, barely received the petitions of those who pleaded with him.

Nevertheless, wishing to fulfill his oath, he demolished the wall and then rebuilt it with smaller stones. This can still be seen in certain parts of the wall, where inferior construction has been placed above the largest and most remarkable stones.

SOCRATES, book IV, chapter 8, p. 216.

## CHAPTER XXII. The birth of the younger Valentinian, the immense hailstorm, and the elevation of the emperor Gratian

At this time these things were taking place. It must nevertheless be understood that the war against the tyrant Procopius occurred during the consulship of Gratian and Dagalaiphus, around the end of May (A.D. 366). Shortly afterward, in the same consulship, a son was born to the emperor Valentinian, who was established in the western regions. He bore his father’s name. Gratian, however, had been born before his father’s accession to the empire.

In the following consulship, that of Lupicinus and Jovian (A.D. 367), a great quantity of hail was violently poured down upon the city of Constantinople on the second day of June, resembling stones. Many said that this happened because of the emperor’s actions, since he had deported many priests into exile for fleeing communion with Eudoxius.

Shortly afterward, in the same consulship, the emperor Valentinian appointed his son Gratian emperor, on the twenty-fourth day of August. In the following consulship, that of the second Valentinian and the second Valens (A.D. 368), a very great earthquake around Bithynia overturned the city of Nicaea on the eleventh day of October. It was the twelfth year after the fall of Nicomedia.

A short time later, another earthquake destroyed many parts of the city of Germa, situated in the Hellespont. When these things had occurred, neither Eudoxius, the Arian bishop, nor the emperor Valens was moved by any reverence or fear. For they did not cease their persecution.

The earthquakes appeared to signify the disturbances of the churches. When many priests were being carried into exile, only Basil and Gregory, through divine providence and because of the eminence of the reverence owed to them, did not suffer exile. One of them, Basil, was bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia; Gregory was bishop of the exceedingly insignificant city of Nazianzus, which lies near Caesarea. We shall speak of Basil and Gregory in the following account.

SOCRATES, book IV, chapters 9 and 10. Christ. Valesius’s edition, chapters 9, 10, and 11, p. 218.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How the Arians persecuted the Macedonians, and how the latter withdrew to Liberius

At that time, while those who professed the doctrine of consubstantiality were being severely afflicted, the persecutors again rose against the Macedonians (A.D. 367). Bound by fear and violence, the Macedonians sent embassies from city to city to one another, deciding that under compulsion they ought to flee to the emperor’s brother and to Liberius, bishop of the city of Rome. They embraced Liberius’s faith rather than Eudoxius’s communion.

They therefore sent Eustathius of Sebaste, who had often been deposed, Silvanus of Tarsus in Cilicia, and Theophilus. They instructed them not to avoid Liberius for the sake of the faith, but to enter into communion with the Roman Church and to strengthen the faith concerning consubstantiality.

With letters drawn up at Seleucia, these men reached Italy. They could not see the emperor, for he was occupied in Gaul and was fighting against the Sarmatians. They presented their letters to Liberius, but he absolutely refused to receive them, saying that they were Arians and that the Church could not receive those who did not accept the Nicene faith.

They replied that through repentance they had come to know the truth, that they had long since rejected the faith of dissimilarity, and that they professed the Son to be in every respect like the Father, and that “like in every respect” differs in nothing from “consubstantial.”

When they said this, Liberius demanded that they provide a written profession of their position. They presented a document in which they also set forth the words of the faith of the Council of Nicaea. I have not written here, because of the length, the letters composed at Smyrna in Asia, Pisidia, Isauria, Pamphylia, and Lycia. [312] The words of the document given to Liberius by Eustathius and the others are known to be as follows.

SOCRATES, book IV, chapter 11. Christ. Valesius’s edition, chapter 12, p. 219.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The document given by the Macedonians to Liberius, bishop of Rome

To the lord brother and fellow priest Liberius:

Eustathius, Theophilus, and Silvanus send greetings in the Lord.

Because of the insane suspicions of the heretics, who do not cease creating scandals for the catholic churches, we remove every opportunity for their attacks by professing the synod held at Lampsacus and those of the orthodox bishops held at Smyrna and in various other places.

As envoys of this synod to your fatherhood, and to all the bishops of Italy and all the bishops of the West, we carry letters affirming that we hold the catholic faith and preserve what was confirmed at the holy Council of Nicaea under Constantine of blessed memory by three hundred and eighteen bishops. This faith has remained until now, and shall remain forever, in a perfect and immovable condition. In it consubstantiality was defined in a holy and devout manner against the wickedness of Arius.

We likewise profess with our own hands that we, together with those mentioned above, have held and do hold the same faith and shall preserve it to the end. We condemn Arius and his impious teaching, together with his disciples and those who hold opinions like his, as well as every heresy: the Sabellians, Patripassians, Marcionites, Photinians, Marcellians, and also the followers of Paul of Samosata and their teaching, all who hold opinions similar to theirs, and every heresy contrary to the sacred faith stated above, which was expounded piously and catholicly at Nicaea by the holy Fathers.

We especially anathematize the exposition read at the Council of Rimini, as contrary to the aforesaid faith of the holy council held in the city of Nicaea. When this exposition was approved at Nicaea, a city of Thrace, they were captured by deceit and perjury and subscribed to it at Constantinople.

Our faith, and that of those for whom we serve as envoys, is this:

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one only-begotten God, the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father, that is, from the substance of the Father; God from God, light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made; consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things were made, those in heaven and those on earth.

For us human beings and for our salvation he descended, was incarnate, and became human; he suffered and rose again on the third day; he ascended into heaven and shall come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was when he was not,” and “Before he was begotten he was not,” and that he was made from things that did not exist, or who say that he is from another essence or substance, or who say that the Son of God is convertible or mutable, the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes.

I, Eustathius, bishop of the city of Sebaste, and Theophilus and Silvanus, envoys of the councils of Lampsacus, Smyrna, and the others, have subscribed this profession with our own hands and of our own will.

If anyone should wish to bring any charge against us or against those by whom we were sent, apart from the faith set forth by us, send your holiness’s letters concerning us to whichever orthodox bishops you approve, and let them plead the case with us before those bishops. If any charge is proved, let punishment without doubt fall upon the one responsible.

Having bound the envoys by this document, Liberius received them into communion. Giving them letters of this kind, he ordered them to depart.

SOCRATES, book IV, chapter 11. Christ. Valesius’s edition, chapter 12, p. 220.

## CHAPTER XXV. The letter of Liberius, bishop of the city of Rome, and of the Sicilian council to the Macedonian bishops after their repentance

To our most beloved brothers and fellow priests Eustathius, Cyril, Hypericius, Heron, Elpidius, Maximus, Eusebius, Eucarpius, Ortasius, Neon, Eumathius, Faustinus, Proclus, Passinicus, Arsenius, Severus, Didymion, Britanius, Callicrates, Damabius, Edessius, Eustochius, Ambrosius, Gelonius, Pardalius, Macedonius, Paulus, Marcellus, Heraclius, Alexander, Adolius, Martianus, Sthenelus, John, Macer, Charisius, Silvanus, Photinus, Antonius, Authus, Celsus, Euphranor, Milesius, Patricius, Severianus, Eusebius, Eumolpius, Athanasius, Diophantus, Minodorus, Diocles, Chrysampelus, Eugenius, Eustathius, Callicrates, Arsenius, Eugenius, Martyrius, Hieratius, Leontius, Philagrius, Lucius, and all the orthodox of the East:

Liberius, bishop, and the bishops of the West send greetings in the Lord.

Your letter, radiant with the light of faith, has brought us the desired joy of peace and concord, dearest brothers. It was delivered to us by our most beloved brothers and fellow bishops Eustathius, Silvanus, and Theophilus. We rejoice especially because they have affirmed and demonstrated that your judgment and your thoughts agree and harmonize with my humility and with all the Italians and the Westerners.

We recognize that this is the catholic and apostolic faith which was preserved whole and immovable down to the Council of Nicaea. They themselves have professed that they retain it, and, filled with joy and casting away every trace and cloud of foolish suspicion, they have professed it not only in speech but also in a written document.

We have judged it necessary to append a copy of that document to this letter, lest we once again leave the heretics any opportunity to lay snares. By rekindling the flames of their own wickedness, they customarily revive the fires of discord.

Our beloved brothers Eustathius, Silvanus, and Theophilus further professed that your charity has always held this faith and will preserve it to the end: the faith approved in the city of Nicaea by three hundred and eighteen orthodox bishops, which contains perfect truth and closes and dissolves the mouth of the entire heretical multitude [Ms. Lyr., wickedness].

For the number of so many bishops was not assembled by spontaneous human impulse but by divine command against the madness of Arius, just as blessed Abraham destroyed so many thousands by faith. This faith, since it is contained in the substance and name of consubstantiality, like a very strongly fortified and impregnable camp, fittingly avoids all the darts and schemes of Arian unbelief.

When all the Western bishops had assembled at Rimini, at the time when the madness of the Arians gathered them, they tried, through a certain persuasion—or, to speak more truly, through worldly power—to remove or secretly deny what had been more securely established in the faith. Yet their cunning accomplished nothing. For nearly all those who had assembled at Rimini, then moved by fear and deceived, are now recovering their senses and anathematizing those who assembled there, or subscribing to the catholic faith decreed in the city of Nicaea and entering into communion with us. They are now inflamed more fervently against the doctrine of Arius and his disciples.

Your own city’s envoys, recognizing evidence of this, joined you to themselves in their subscription, anathematizing Arius and the acts carried out at Rimini by his followers against the faith decreed at Nicaea. In these matters you too, having been deceived, subscribed under perjury.

Therefore it seemed appropriate to us to write to your charity and to assist you in your just requests, especially because through the profession of your envoys we have learned that the repentant Easterners agree with the orthodox Westerners [ms. Santheod., “coming together”]. We inform you so that you may know that the blasphemers of Rimini, who then appeared to have been polluted through deception, have now been anathematized, and that everyone has returned to the faith of Nicaea.

You must make this known to all, so that those who have been injured by force may at last pass from the darkness of heretics into the divine light of catholic freedom. After this synod, if they refuse to reject the poison of faithlessness, to cast away all the blasphemies of Arius, and to anathematize them, let them know that they are companions of Arius and his disciples and of the other serpents, whether Sabellians, Patripassians, or members of any other heresy, and that they have been deprived of communion by the ecclesiastical synod, which does not admit adulterous children among its own.

May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brothers.

After receiving this letter, Eustathius and the others again came to Sicily. There they held a synod of the Sicilian bishops and, in their presence, professed the faith of consubstantiality. Having strengthened the Nicene faith and received from them letters in agreement, they returned to those by whom they had been sent.

Those men, accepting Liberius’s instructions, sent embassies throughout the cities to the bishops and preached the consubstantiality of the faith. They invited them to assemble together at Tarsus in Cilicia, so that, by strengthening the Nicene faith, they might thereafter put an end to every dispute.

This could have taken place, had not Eudoxius, the bishop of the Arian religion, then highly influential with the emperor, prevented it. Angered still more by the journey that had been announced to Tarsus, he inflicted worse injuries upon them.

Because the Macedonians, through the envoys they had sent, entered into communion with Liberius and confirmed the Nicene faith, Sabinus himself professed this in his collection of synodal acts.

SOCRATES, book IV, chapter 11. Christ. Valesius’s edition, chapter 12, p. 222.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Why Eunomius separated from Eudoxius

Around this time Eunomius separated from Eudoxius and held services on his own, because, although he had repeatedly asked Eudoxius to receive his teacher Aetius, Eudoxius did not listen to him. He did not reject this request because he avoided Aetius’s sect—for he himself was preaching it—but because all unanimously acknowledged Aetius as belonging to another sect.

This, therefore, was the reason Eunomius separated from Eudoxius.

These things were taking place in Constantinople.

SOCRATES, book IV, chapter 12. Christ. Valesius’s edition, chapter 13, p. 225.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Athanasius’s hiding place

Then an order from the prefects, sent to Alexandria through Eudoxius’s efforts, disturbed the Church. Athanasius, however, fearing the irrational fury of the people and afraid that he himself might appear to be the cause of the evils being committed, hid himself for four months in his father’s tomb.

When, because of his absence, the people stirred up a riot out of longing for him, the emperor, recognizing that Alexandria had been disturbed on this account, indicated by letter that Athanasius might freely retain the churches.

This was the reason that the Alexandrian Church was not disturbed until Athanasius’s death. Since after his death the Arians again invaded those churches, I shall relate this after a short interval.

SOCRATES, book IV, chapter 12. Christ. Valesius’s edition, chapter 13, p. 225.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The Council of Tyana, where the letters of Liberius and of the Westerners were received
At that time a council was being held at Tyana by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia; Athanasius of Ancyra; Pelagius of Laodicea; Zeno of Tarsus; Paul of Emesa; Otreius of Melitene; Gregory of Nazianzus; and many others who, during the reign of Jovian, had decreed at Antioch that the term “consubstantial” should be retained. There the letters of Liberius and of the Western clergy were read aloud. Therefore, filled with joy, they wrote to all the churches that they should read the decrees of the bishops held in Asia, together with the letters of Liberius and of the Italians, Africans, Gauls, and Sicilians. For envoys sent from Lampsacus had brought the letters of these men, so that they might ascertain the number of all who agreed with one another. Their multitude greatly exceeded that of the Council of Ariminum. They likewise wrote that they should assemble on a fixed day at Tarsus in Cilicia; and in this way they invited one another.

While the synod was being prepared at Tarsus, the Asian bishops—thirty-four in number—assembled at Antioch in Caria. They indeed praised the zeal for ecclesiastical concord, but rejected the name “consubstantial,” and endeavored to strengthen the creed issued at Antioch and Seleucia, claiming that it was the creed of the martyr Lucian and had been approved by the labors of many of their forefathers. But the emperor, acting at Eudoxius’s instigation, prohibited the synod from being held in Cilicia.

SOZOMEN, book VI, chapter 12, p. 652.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Eudoxius, the Arian bishop, and Valens’s persecution on account of Evagrius, the orthodox bishop

Accordingly, the emperor Valens, hastening to Antioch after departing from Constantinople, came to Nicomedia and remained there for the following reason. Eudoxius, who belonged to the Arian religion, died soon after the emperor’s departure, in the third consulship of Valentinian and Valens (A.D. 370), having held the see of the Church of Constantinople for eleven years. Therefore the Arians appointed Demophilus in his place.

But the preachers of consubstantiality, judging that they had found an opportune moment, appointed a certain Evagrius, who shared their faith, as bishop. He was ordained by Eustathius, formerly bishop of Antioch, who had previously been recalled from exile by Jovian. At that time he was secretly residing in Constantinople, in order by his presence to strengthen the preachers of consubstantiality.

SOCRATES, book IV, chapter 13. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 14, p. 225.

After this had been done, the Arians began another persecution from a new starting point. When these events had reached the emperor, he feared that the city might be disturbed by an uprising and sent a military force from Nicomedia to Constantinople, ordering that both the ordainer and the ordained should be arrested and that one should be sent into exile elsewhere. Eustathius was therefore sent to Besa, a city of Thrace, while Evagrius was dispatched to another place.

After these events, the Arians, becoming still more enraged, violently harassed the orthodox: beating them, assaulting them with insults, locking them in prisons, frequently inflicting financial losses upon them, and doing everything against them in an intolerable manner. Since they could not endure these things, they came to plead with the emperor, hoping somehow to deserve escape from the violence. But in thinking this, they were thoroughly deceived, believing that they could obtain justice from an unjust man.

SOCRATES, book IV, chapter 13. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 15, p. 226.

When eighty chosen men from the ecclesiastical college had arrived at Nicomedia—Urbasus, Theodorus, and Menedemus being their leaders—they presented petitions to the emperor, protesting against the violence and reporting what they appeared to have suffered.

SOCRATES, book IV, chapter 13. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 16, p. 227.

## CHAPTER XXX. How eighty orthodox men were burned by Valens in a ship

The emperor, therefore, was indignant. For the moment he concealed his anger, but secretly instructed the prefect Modestus to have them arrested and killed. The manner of their death was in some way unusual, and for that reason was handed down to memory.

For the prefect feared that a popular uprising would arise if he openly put them to death. He therefore pretended that he was sending these men into exile. When they had innocently accepted this, the prefect ordered them to be placed on a ship, as though they were to be transported into exile. He instructed the sailors that, when they reached the middle of the sea, they should drown them, so that they would die in this manner.

After they had been taken into the middle of the gulf called Astacenus, what the prefect and the emperor had ordered was carried out. The sailors then transferred themselves to another boat that was following and set the ship on fire. A wind from the southeast happened to blow with great force, and thus the ship was quickly consumed. Its remains reached the place now called Acidiza, where they were completely destroyed along with the religious men.

They say, however, that this did not pass without punishment. For famine suddenly followed among the peoples of Phrygia, so that the inhabitants were compelled to leave their homeland and hasten to Constantinople and to various provinces.

SOCRATES, book IV, chapter 13. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 16, p. 227.

## CHAPTER XXXI. What Valens did in Antioch and Cappadocia

Valens, therefore, leaving Nicomedia, proceeded to Antioch. Meanwhile, when he had come to Cappadocia, he was disturbing the churches of that region in the usual manner [the Lyr manuscript reads *sollicite*, “zealously”], wishing to hand them over to the Arians.

He believed that he could accomplish this quickly because Basil seemed to be estranged from Eusebius, who at that time governed the Church of Caesarea, on account of certain hostilities. Basil had withdrawn into Pontus and lived there with monks devoted to philosophical pursuits.

The people, especially the noble and learned, suspected Eusebius, as though he himself had been responsible for the flight of the man whose life and teaching were perfected by philosophy. They wished to abandon him and celebrate the solemn rites of the Mass among themselves.

Basil, however, so that no disturbance might arise among the people through the seditions of heretics, remained silent in Pontus with his bishops, who had always adhered to him. It also happened that hatred of Eusebius arose among the people.

When Basil was informed that Valens was coming into Cappadocia, he left Pontus and came to Caesarea. After making an agreement with Eusebius, he strengthened the Church for the time being by his exhortations. But when Valens was unable to accomplish his intention, he departed with the bishops who were accompanying him.

SOZOMEN, book VI, chapter 15, p. 656.

Accordingly, the emperor Valens, disregarding [the Valesian edition reads “observing”] the advance of famine, came to Antioch in Syria. While he remained there, he laid waste to those who refused to agree with the Arians and violently persecuted the preachers of consubstantiality. After he had expelled them from nearly all the churches of the cities of the East, this was still not enough for him: he also subjected them to various punishments and killed many who had been condemned to different forms of death, while he drowned very many in the river.

SOCRATES, book IV, chapter 14. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 17, p. 228.

## CHAPTER XXXII. How, in Edessa, a woman hastening with her son to martyrdom caused the prefect and the emperor, astonished, to withdraw from their cruelty

It should also be related what is known to have happened in Edessa of Mesopotamia. In this city there is a basilica of the apostle Thomas, exceedingly famous and splendidly adorned. Because of the reverence due to the place, assemblies were frequently held there.

When the emperor wished to inspect it and learned that all those whom he hated had gathered there, he is said to have struck the prefect with his hand, asking why he had not expelled all the orthodox from that place. Although the prefect had suffered this insult, he tried unwillingly to carry out the emperor’s anger—for he did not wish to inflict slaughter upon so many people—and secretly ordered that no one should remain in that basilica.

But no one heeded either his advice or his threats. For on the following day they all flocked together to the place of prayer.

When the prefect was hastening to the basilica with a large force of soldiers in order to carry out the emperor’s command, a certain poor woman, dragging her son by the hand and hurrying toward the basilica, interrupted the prefect’s mission.

The prefect, indignant, ordered the woman to be brought before him and said to her:

“Unhappy woman, where are you running so indecently?”

She replied, “To the place where the others are hastening.”

Then he said, “Have you not heard that the prefect will kill everyone whom he finds there?”

“I have heard,” the woman replied, “and that is why I am hurrying, so that I may be found there among them.”

“And where are you dragging this little child?”

The woman answered, “So that he too may deserve to receive martyrdom.”

When the man heard this, he considered the determination of those who were gathering. He immediately returned to the emperor and reported that they were all prepared to accept death for their faith, saying that it was unreasonable to kill so many people in such a short time. By saying this, he recalled the emperor from his anger.

In this way, therefore, the people of Edessa escaped the emperor’s fury.

SOCRATES, book IV, chapter 14. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 18, p. 228.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the examination and exile of very many orthodox Christians

When the prefect had reported these things to the emperor, the emperor did not endure putting the people themselves to the test. Instead, the prefect was ordered to question their leaders—that is, the presbyters and deacons—so that they might choose one of two alternatives: either communicate with the wolf or be driven from the city and sent to certain remote regions.

After he had gathered them all together, he used gentle words, trying to persuade them to follow the emperor’s laws. He said that it was a sign of madness for a few men to resist so great an emperor.

When everyone remained silent, the prefect said to their leader Eulogius, a man greatly worthy of praise:

“Why do you not answer what we are saying?”

He replied, “One ought not to answer a question that has not been asked.”

Then the prefect said, “I have spoken many words, advising you about what is sufficiently advantageous.”

Eulogius replied that these words had been addressed to everyone, and that it would be improper for him alone to answer while disregarding the others. “But if you question me alone,” he said, “I shall declare my opinion.”

The prefect said, “Communicate with the one who possesses the kingdom.”

He replied peacefully and with great composure, “I too have a share in the kingdom and in the priesthood.”

Then the prefect, perceiving the mockery, became furious and insulted the old man. He added:

“That is not what I said, thunderbolt; I advised you to communicate with those with whom the emperor communicates.”

When the old man said that he had a shepherd and obeyed his commands, the prefect sent eighty men who had been arrested at the same time into Thrace. As they were being led away, they were treated with great honor along the route. Cities and villages came out to meet them, honoring them as victorious athletes.

But envy armed their enemies, so that they might tell the emperor that the great honor shown to these men was regarded as an insult to him. When the emperor learned this, he ordered that they be separated into pairs and sent some into Thrace, others into the remotest parts of Arabia, and still others into the cities of the Thebaid. For they say that the most savage man separated even brothers whom nature had joined, dividing them bodily.

He sent Eulogius, their bishop, and Protogenes, who succeeded him, as far as Antinoopolis. I cannot allow their virtue to be handed over to oblivion.

When they saw that the city’s bishop was orthodox and shared communion with the ecclesiastical college, they observed that few people were attending the churches. After investigating the matter, they discovered that the inhabitants of the city were pagans. Grieving over their unbelief, they lamented it; yet they did not think that they should mourn for long, but considered with every effort how to provide a remedy.

THEODORET, book IV, chapter 16. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapters 17 and 18, p. 170.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the miracles of the confessors

The most holy Eulogius, therefore, confined to his dwelling, prayed to God all day and all night for everyone.

Protogenes, a man of exceptional worth, educated in the writings of Eunomius and well prepared for writing swiftly, found a suitable place and set it apart for himself in order to teach. He became the teacher of the young men, whom he instructed both to write quickly and in the divine utterances.

He dictated to them the melodies of David and instructed them to meditate on readings corresponding to apostolic teaching.

When one of the young men fell ill, Protogenes came to his house. Taking the sick man’s right hand, he drove away the illness through his prayers. When the parents of the other children learned of this, they led him to their homes and begged him to help the sick.

He said that he would not first ask God to drive away their illnesses unless the sick first received the gift of holy baptism. They gladly complied, for the desire for salvation compelled them, and they enjoyed the health of soul and body together.

Whenever he persuaded someone to receive the sacred grace, he led him to Eulogius. Knocking on the door, he asked him to open it and impose the Lord’s sign upon the person who had been reborn. When Eulogius opened only with difficulty, so as not to interrupt his prayer, Protogenes would say that the salvation of the erring was more necessary.

Everyone therefore marveled when they saw Protogenes doing such things. Although he bestowed upon them so great a light of divine knowledge, he nevertheless reserved primacy in everything for Eulogius, offering to him especially those whom he had won. From this they inferred that Eulogius’s virtue was still greater.

When the turmoil had ceased and tranquility had been restored, all those who had been ordered to return were led away amid groaning and tears, especially the bishop of the Church, who was deprived of their affection.

When they had returned to their own places, the holy Eulogius assumed the governance of the Church after the great Barse had departed for the most blessed life. The remarkable Protogenes, meanwhile, was ordered to cultivate the deserted city of the Carrhaeans, filled everywhere with the thorns of the pagans—a place that certainly required very great labors.

THEODORET, book IV, chapter 16. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 18, p. 171.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the demon’s response concerning who would rule after Valens, and how Valens consequently killed many people

At the same time, a certain erring demon, taking advantage of Valens’s cruelty, persuaded him to investigate who would assume the empire after him. For this reason he practiced necromancy.

When these arts had been completed, he killed very many people, since the demon, as usual, gave responses not openly but obliquely. When he was consulted about the empire, he displayed four letters—θ, ε, ο, δ—and said that a person whose name began with this sequence would receive the height of imperial power after Valens.

When this reached the emperor’s ears, he was driven by jealousy and killed many whom he judged likely to seize the tyranny.

Thus Theodoretuses, Theodors, Theodotus, Theodosiuses, Theoduluses, and everyone who had these letters at the beginning of his name were killed. Among them a certain Theodosiolus was also killed, a brave man descended from the province of Spain.

Because of this fear, many people changed their names. They denied under oath the names they had previously borne, so that they might avoid danger.

SOCRATES, book IV, chapter 15. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 19, p. 229.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On Basil, bishop of Cappadocia, and how he escaped the threats of exile

When the emperor Valens had stripped, so to speak, all the churches of their shepherds, he came to Caesarea of Cappadocia, whose bishop at that time was Basil, the light of the whole world.

He sent the prefect ahead, ordering him either to bend Basil so that he would join in the doctrine of Eudoxius or, if unwilling to do this, to expel him.

Having heard of the glory of so great a man, Valens did not wish to enter into conflict with him immediately, lest Basil, by bravely avoiding his attacks, become for the others an even clearer image of virtue.

The prefect’s schemes were like webs made by spiders. The ancient stories of the Fathers had been sufficient for the other priests’ benefit and, like certain towers, had preserved the wall of faith unshaken.

The prefect, therefore, coming to Caesarea and summoning the great Basil, honored him and addressed him in gentle language. He advised him to yield to the times and not allow so many churches to be troubled over a minor subtlety of doctrine.

He also promised the emperor’s friendship and offered many benefits that would follow from it.

But that most holy man said that such words were suited to young men:

“They and those like them,” he said, “look to promises of this kind. But those who are nourished by divine utterances do not tolerate the corruption of even a single syllable of the divine doctrines. For their sake, if necessary, they embrace every kind of death.

“As for the emperor’s friendship, I judge it great when joined with piety; without piety, however, I call it ruin rather than friendship.”

When the prefect raged against him and repeatedly called him foolish, Saint Basil said:

“I continually pray that I may always possess this foolishness.”

When the prefect then ordered him to leave so that he could consider what he ought to do and give his decision the following day, that famous man is said to have replied:
