“I myself shall return tomorrow also, provided that you do not change your decision; but make use of your threats.”

After these words, the prefect went to the emperor and reported what had been said, as well as the man’s virtue, courage of soul, and confidence. The emperor then entered in silence.

After this it happened that Valens perceived that divinely inflicted blows had come upon him. For his son, being ill, was in danger at the very gates of death. His wife, too, was afflicted by various illnesses.

Recognizing the cause of his sorrow, Valens asked the most holy man, whom he had threatened to punish, to come to the palace. The officers carried out the imperial commands.

The great Basil then came to the palace. Seeing the emperor’s son near death, he promised that the child would return to life if he received holy baptism through pious men. Having said this, he departed.

But Valens, mindful of the oath he had made at the time of the baptism, ordered the child to be baptized according to the foolish error by the Arians who were present. When this had been done, the infant immediately reached the end of his life.

Valens, however, moved to repentance and judging the truth of his oath to be harmful, entered the sacred temple, joined himself to the teaching of the great Basil, and offered the customary gifts at the altar.

He ordered Basil to come within the curtains where he himself was seated and spoke many words with him about the divine doctrines, listening willingly as Basil taught.

A certain man named Demosthenes was present there, in charge of the imperial kitchens. When he attempted to criticize the teacher of the world, he committed a barbarism.

Saint Basil then smiled and said:

“We have seen an illiterate Demosthenes.”

When the man instead began to threaten him, Saint Basil said:

“Your task is to think about the dishes, not to prepare divine doctrines.”

After this, the emperor loved the man so greatly that he even offered to the poor under Basil’s care the excellent estates that he possessed there. From these, provisions were supplied especially to lepers.

In this way the great Basil avoided Valens’s first attack.

When Valens later returned there, however, he had forgotten what had happened earlier, because his will was besieged by deceivers. He again tried to move Basil to adopt the heretical position.

When he could not persuade him, he ordered a decree of exile to be written against him. Wishing to confirm it with his own signature, he was unable to complete a single letter, for the pen was broken.

When a second and a third pen suffered the same fate, and he still attempted to ratify the impious decree, his right hand was shaken and suddenly seized by trembling. Then, his mind filled with fear, he tore the document with both hands.

The God who provides for all thus showed that he had permitted others to suffer while rescuing this man from the plots against him. Through what happened in this case, he displayed a sign of his own power, and through other events proclaimed the strength of the best men by his providential ordering.

THEODORET, book IV, chapter 17. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 19, p. 173.

It should be known, moreover, that while Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, was alive, divine providence delayed disturbing Alexandria or Egypt. The emperor knew that Athanasius was loved by the entire populace and feared that, if a revolt arose, the state might be troubled.

Athanasius, however, died in the second consulship of Gratian and that of Probus (A.D. 371), after frequent struggles on behalf of the Church. He had governed the episcopal see for forty-six years amid many dangers.

SOCRATES, book IV, chapter 16. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 20, p. 230.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the death of Athanasius of Alexandria, the succession of Peter, the revolt made against him, and his journey to Rome

When Athanasius, victorious in Alexandria after many struggles and countless crowns, had reached the end of his life and departed to the rewards of his labors, Peter, an excellent man, assumed the episcopate. Blessed Athanasius had chosen him long before, and everyone agreed: the priests, the nobles, and the entire populace, all displaying their will through their favor toward him.

Peter had shared in Athanasius’s labors both while he was in the city and while he passed through various hiding places, enduring many dangers with him. Therefore all the priests gathered together and proclaimed Peter the worthy heir of Athanasius.

THEODORET, book IV, chapter 18. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 20, p. 175.

After they had installed him in the episcopal see, the provincial judge suddenly gathered a pagan crowd together with the Jews and surrounded the church precincts. He ordered Peter to come out and threatened to drag him out if he refused.

He did this because he wished to please the emperor by subjecting those who thought differently from him to misfortune. But, as is true, the fury of impiety had taken possession of him: he was trying rather to please the idols and regarded the storm against the Church as a splendid festival.

Peter, a remarkable man, seeing an unexpected attack, secretly went out, boarded a ship, and departed for Rome.

THEODORET, book IV, chapter 19. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 21, p. 176.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. With what cruelty Lucius was brought into Alexandria

After a few days had passed, Euzoius came from Antioch with Lucius and handed the churches over to him. The people of Samosata are also known to have experienced his impiety.

The populace, first satisfied with the teachings of Athanasius and then disgusted that food contrary to what they desired was being offered to them, withdrew from the ecclesiastical assemblies.

Lucius, using idol-worshiping soldiers, beat some, hanged others, compelled others to flee, and devastated the homes of still others like a barbarian.

But the remarkable Peter will relate these things more fully in his own letter. I shall nevertheless report one of Lucius’s crimes and insert Peter’s letter.

Certain men in Egypt, imitating the life of angels and avoiding the crowds of the cities, chose to live in the desert. They made sandy and barren ground fruitful, producing for God an exceedingly sweet fruit—the excellent fruit of their virtue.

Many appear to have been victorious inhabitants of that desert. But from childhood the most famous Antony grew up there, showing the monks the virtue of spiritual combat.

THEODORET, book IV, chapter 19. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 21, p. 176.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. What miracles the hermits performed when Lucius sent them into exile

Lucius, that wretched man, expelled the inhabitants of this place, the followers of Antony. Driving from their caves their most holy bishops—Macarius the venerable, another Macarius, Isidore, and the others—he sent them to a certain island inhabited by impious men, an island that had never received a teacher of piety.

When the ship reached the island’s shore, the demon who was worshiped by those people abandoned the idol in which he had formerly been accustomed to dwell. He entered the daughter of his priest and, making her rave like a bacchant, led her as far as the place where the monks’ ship had arrived.

Then, using the girl’s tongue, the demon cried out, just as it had done at Philippi through the Pythoness. All the men and women heard the demon proclaim:

“O your power, O ministers of Christ! Everywhere we are driven away by you—from cities and villages, from mountains and hills, from the desert, which is shown to be deprived of human beings.

“We had hoped that, by dwelling on this island, we would be freed from your darts; but we are known to have been disappointed in that hope. Your persecutors sent you here, not to trouble you, but so that through you they might drive us out even more completely.

“Behold, we are departing from this island, for we are struck by the rays of your virtue.”

After saying these and similar things, they threw the girl to the ground and then themselves disappeared completely.

The most holy company then raised the girl through prayer and restored her healthy and sound to her father.

Those who had witnessed the miracle, however, fell at the feet of the saints and begged to receive the provisions of salvation. They destroyed the temple of the demons, and, illuminated by the rays of their teaching, received the grace of holy baptism.

When these things were reported in the city, all the people gathered and denounced Lucius, saying that divine wrath threatened him unless the company of saints returned.

Thus, fearing the city’s tumult, Lucius ordered the most holy men to return to their caves.

These events are worthy to reveal the abomination of his impiety.

THEODORET, book IV, chapter 19. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 21, p. 176.

## CHAPTER XL. The letters of Peter, bishop of Alexandria, in which Lucius’s crimes are reported

The letters of the remarkable Peter will in fact teach us the injustices of his presumption. Avoiding their length, I shall not omit setting down what is placed in the middle.

THEODORET, book IV, chapter 19. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 21, p. 177.

The provincial judge Palladius, he says, being a pagan in religion and always worshiping idols, repeatedly attempted to wage war against Christ. Gathering the aforementioned people, he launched an assault against the church, as though he were trying to subdue barbarians. At that time many cruel deeds were committed. Merely wishing to dictate them, I was moved by the memory of the event to the deepest grief [Col. 1099A], and I poured forth a stream of tears; indeed, I could scarcely have endured it for long had I not relieved my spirit by reflecting upon divine providence.

When the crowd entered the church called Theona, instead of words of honor they shouted acclamations in praise of the idol. In place of the sacred reading of Scripture, shameful clapping of hands was performed. And, with disgraceful cries, they uttered insults against Christ’s virgins—insults that the human tongue cannot bear to repeat. Any wise person who heard such things closed his ears and would rather have been deaf, lest he be compelled to hear words of that kind.

Would that they had ceased after sinning merely in words and had not surpassed the shamefulness of their words by their deeds. Such slander is easy for those in whom the wisdom of Christ and devotion to his teaching have taken up residence. These men, vessels of wrath [Col. 1099B], made for destruction, mocked, emitting a horrible sound from their nostrils and—so to speak—pouring forth a stench as though from some sewer. They tore the garments of Christ’s holy virgins, whose continence imitated the form of the holy angels. Then, as human nature dictates, they led them naked throughout the entire city and, in whatever manner they pleased, abused them with obscenity. If anyone attempted to restrain them out of compassion, he was driven away after being mangled with wounds.

Woe to those calamities! Many endured the violent violation of their bodies; very many virgins, struck on the head with bars, remained speechless. Even their bodies were forbidden the rites of solemn burial. Finally, many corpses, sought to this day by grieving parents, cannot be found.

But why do I speak of small matters amid great ones? Why linger over these things rather than return to what is now necessary? In these matters I know well that everyone will marvel with us, standing aghast at the Lord’s patience, because he did not bring everything to an immediate end. Things that had never been done, nor heard of in the days of our fathers through the Scriptures, these impious men committed upon the very altar.

For, standing as though upon a shameful stage, they made a certain boy—denying his male nature and wearing a woman’s garment, with his eyes painted, his face colored with a silken dye, and dressed in an actor’s costume—imitate an idol “of feminine form” (as it is written in the prophet). They had him circle back and forth upon the very altar where we invoke the coming of the Holy Spirit, and perform a gesture with his hands [Ed. V.: “abomination”; Ed. Niv. and Frob.: “dance”], while they laughed and uttered abominable cries [Col. 1099D].

Then, judging this a small matter and considering what had happened before more ornamental than shameful, they placed one of their own men, notorious for his depravity, naked in both clothing and genitals, upon the church’s seat, and shamelessly elevated him as a foul preacher against Christ. In place of sacred words he uttered crimes; instead of praising what was honorable, he praised luxury; and instead of piety, impiety; instead of continence, fornication and adultery; intercourse between males; theft; food and drink; and whatever is useful for this life.

When these things had occurred, and I had withdrawn from the church—for I could not remain there, where there were invasions by soldiers, where the populace, redeemed [mss.: retained] for the sake of sedition by the generosity of money, and a multitude of pagans summoned by great promises [Col. 1100A] were present—a certain Lucius was sent as our supposed successor, or, as though purchasing a worldly dignity in place of the episcopate. He hastened to possess the wickedness and actions of a wolf. He was not elected by a council of orthodox bishops, nor by the decree of truthful clergy, nor by the petition of the people, as the ecclesiastical ordinances proclaim. No bishop, presbyter, or deacon preceded him; nor did a multitude of people, nor monks singing hymns from Scripture.

Euzoius was with him, formerly condemned with Arius in the holy and great Council of Nicaea. Now Magnus, through the patronage [ms. Lyr.: “parish”] of the Antiochenes, was a devastator of the Church, count of the largesses, and a military commander notorious for every kind of impiety. In the time of Julian he set fire to the church of the Berytians, and in the time of the blessed emperor Jovian he was compelled to repair it from his own resources; he would then scarcely have escaped losing his head had he not, through the efforts of many, obtained the emperor’s clemency [Col. 1100B].

I beg you to consider these matters with your zeal and to be roused to vengeance: how great and how terrible are the crimes committed against the Church of God, when such a tyrant has been stirred up against us. That Lucius, who, through your religious authority and that of all the orthodox bishops, has frequently been rejected for reasonable causes, now took his stand before the city. Not only, like a blasphemer and fool, does he say in the psalms, “Christ is not the true God”; he has also been corrupted in times of opportunity and has corrupted others, rejoicing in blasphemies against those who are known to worship the Savior [Col. 1100C].

Since he is close in mind to the pagans, this misguided man presumes to worship a new God. For some shouted such praises before him: “You have come well, bishop, who do not defend the Son.” Others said: “Serapis loves you and has brought you here,” naming the idol of the pagans.

At that very moment [ms. Lyr. and Ed. V.: “at the prompting”], the aforementioned Magnus, his inseparable companion in impiety, his most bitter arms-bearer and minister of cruelty, having gathered a crowd of people, seized nineteen presbyters and deacons, some of whom were more than eighty years old, and treated them under the laws as though they had been captured in some crime and were enemies of the Romans. He did not know the power of the Christian law or the faith of the apostles handed down to us through the Fathers [Col. 1100D]. He even declared that these actions were pleasing to the most merciful emperor Valens.

“Yield,” he said, “wretched men, and agree with the doctrines of the Arians. Yield, for the Divinity will forgive you. Even if you show devotion to the true religion, you do so not willingly but under compulsion. Necessity lacks satisfaction; but a voluntary will is followed by a deserved accusation. Therefore, keeping such considerations before your eyes, follow promptly and subscribe to the Arian doctrine now preached by Lucius. Know well that if you obey, you will receive money, profits, and honors from the emperor; but if you resist, you will endure prisons, punishments, tortures, scourging, and chains. Deprived of your money and possessions, and afterward expelled, you will be condemned to inhabit cruel places [Col. 1101A].”

Thus this most powerful seducer, mixing threats with his seduction, invited and compelled them all to depart from the pious confession. But they considered nothing more bitter than betraying piety and answered him with words that overcame his seduction and threats through courage and firmness of mind:

“Be silent—be silent now! Stop frightening us with these speeches; cease uttering vain [ms. Lyr.: mad] words. We worship neither a new nor a recent God. Even though you rage in vain and shake yourself like a violent wind, we shall remain steadfast unto death in the doctrines of piety. We do not confess God to be powerless, foolish, or at any time without truth; nor do we say that he once existed, as Arius’s impiety teaches when it declares the Son to be temporal.

“For if, according to his madness, the Son is a creature and did not exist with the Father, then the Father also once did not exist, since, according to them, the Son did not yet exist. But if the Father is eternal, since the true Son exists from him—and not according to an outflow of generation, for God is impassible—how is he not foolish and mad who professes this concerning the Son, saying: ‘There was when he was not,’ through whom all things were established by grace so that they might exist?

“Our Fathers—those from whom these men have fallen and, rightly, have been made fatherless—came to Nicaea and anathematized the sect of Arius, whose patron this young man now is. They did not say that the Son, of another substance—which you now compel us to confess—was outside the Father, but that he was from the Father’s essence. Understanding this well and with a pious mind, they professed, after collecting many sacred testimonies, that he is consubstantial.”

Saying such things and many others like them, he harassed them for many days, thinking that he could turn them from their pious confession. But they became stronger, like men strengthened in the arena; trampling down fear, arming themselves with the arguments of the Fathers, and judging their dangers an exercise of virtue, they possessed an even firmer understanding of piety [Col. 1101C].

While they thus contended and became a spectacle, as the blessed Apostle writes, “to angels and to men” (1 Cor. 4:9), the whole city gathered to behold Christ’s athletes. By their steadfastness they overcame the judge’s blows and scourging, and through endurance they obtained a pious triumph over the Arians—those whom he believed he could conquer and hand over to their impiety.

When he grew weary of afflicting them with tortures, while everyone wept and mourned, he again gathered an irrational multitude and had them brought to judgment—or rather, to prejudgment—near the harbor [Col. 1101D]. While pagans and Jews customarily shouted against them there, and they refused to consent to the impieties of the Arians, he pronounced sentence. With everyone groaning before his tribunal, he ordered that they be taken from Alexandria and brought to Heliopolis in Phoenicia, whose inhabitants could not endure even to hear the name of Christ, for they were pagans.

After ordering them to board a ship, he himself stood in the harbor brandishing a naked sword, thinking in this way to frighten those who had often wounded hostile demons with the two-edged sword. Thus he sent them away without provisions and without any consolation, ordering them to sail upon a foaming sea that, so to speak, was unwilling to receive men compelled by an unjust command to comply with it [Col. 1102A].

The whole city groaned and continues to mourn to this day. Some struck their breasts with their own hands; others stretched out their hands and eyes toward heaven, protesting the violence and saying, as it were: “Hear, O heaven, and listen with your ears, O earth, for the things being done are unjust.” Everything was filled with groaning together; it was as though a mournful song ran through the city, and a river of tears flowed.

When that judge ordered the ship’s sails to be raised, then a great groan from everyone—virgins and women, old men and young—mingled with tears. As they sailed toward Heliopolis, where diabolical superstition was celebrated, everyone throughout the city, both collectively and individually, was driven to groan [Col. 1102B] and mourn. Yet, by order of the city prefect Palladius, they were not even permitted to weep openly; for he too was a pagan.

Finally, many of those who wept were seized and led to prison; then they were punished, mangled, scourged, and finally handed over to the mines: men of the Church, fighting with great zeal for the divine cause. Very many of them were monks, inhabitants of the desert, twenty-three in number. Shortly afterward, a deacon sent by our beloved brother Damasus, bishop of the Roman city, carrying letters of consolation and fellowship for us, was led publicly by the very executioners with his hands bound behind his back, as though he were some notorious criminal, fit to be compared with murderers. His neck was battered with stones and lead, and he was led to the sea; then, like the others, he was transported into exile in the mines without provisions and without any consolation [Col. 1102C].

When that judge had also tortured many infants, some of them died without receiving the solemn funeral rites of their parents or brothers. O immense [ms. Lyr.: drunken] inhumanity of the judge—or rather, the prejudging judge! Those who fought for piety could not even be compared with murderers, and their bodies were left unburied. Having labored piously, they were thrown out as food for beasts and birds. Those who, by natural human feeling, wished to sympathize with the fathers of the slain were, as though they were criminals, beheaded.

What Roman law, what barbarian judgment, punishes those who feel compassion for fathers? When did any of the ancients commit such an impiety? Pharaoh indeed ordered the male children of the Hebrews to be killed [Col. 1102D], but envy and fear produced that command. Yet how much more humane were those deeds in comparison with what has happened now; how much more desirable when set beside the injustice of this time!

Although wickedness is in no way separated from wickedness, the things reported here are nevertheless unbelievable: inhuman, cruel, savage, barbarous, bitter, and without mercy. The Arians exulted in them, forming choruses while the whole city groaned. “There was no house in which there was not someone dead,” as it is written in Exodus (Exod. 12:30).

And when these things had been done—for the authors of the injustice did not stop, but proceeded to worse deeds—they spread their own poisons even among the bishops of the provinces, having as the companion of their iniquity the associate of bribe-giving whom we mentioned, Magnus [Col. 1103A]. They handed some bishops over to the magistrates and subjected others to various devices, wishing to bind everyone to impiety and, in imitation of their father the devil, seeking whom they might devour in their fury.

Moreover, they sent eleven Egyptian bishops into exile in a city of the Jews called Diocaesarea. These men had inhabited the desert almost from childhood to old age; by word and deed they had overcome lust; they proclaimed the pious faith without shame; they taught the doctrine of piety; performed many victories over demons; and exposed the Arian sect with the wisest reasoning. Like a most savage hell, never satisfied with the death of their brothers, the Arians wished to leave behind a memorial of their cruelty.

Recently, they also prepared to send the clergy of the Catholic Church living in Antioch, together with faithful monks, to Neocaesarea in Pontus, wishing to expose their crimes and inflaming the imperial ears [Col. 1104A]. I think that, because of the harshness of the place, they were even deprived of life.

Such tragedies did that period enact—tragedies worthy of silence and oblivion, yet worthy of being recorded in writing as a rebuke to those who sharpened their tongues against the Only-Begotten. Armed with the fury of blasphemy, these men strive not only to hurl weapons against the Lord of all, but have also undertaken an unrelenting war against his servants.

THEODORET, Book IV, chapter 20; edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 22, p. 178.

# BOOK EIGHT

321. **CHAPTER ONE. On the conduct, miracles, and answers or writings of various monks, as well as of bishops**

[Col. 1103B]

At that time Arsenius was superior of a monastery. He did not excommunicate delinquent young men, but rather those advanced in age. For he said: “An excommunicated young man despises it, but an older man is quickly corrected by the pain of excommunication.”

Another man, named Pior, ate while walking. When asked why he ate in that manner, he replied: “I do not wish to use food as though it were necessary, but to treat it as something foreign.” When another person therefore questioned him about the matter, he said: “So that, while I am eating, my soul may not experience bodily pleasure.”

Isidore used to say that he had completed forty years since he had begun to perceive sin mentally, yet had consented neither to desire [Col. 1103C] nor to anger.

Pambo, although unlearned, went to someone to be taught a psalm. When the teacher recited the first verse of Psalm 38, “I said, I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue,” he did not allow him to hear the second verse, saying: “If I can fulfill this in practice, this one verse will be enough for me.” When the teacher who had given him the verse reproached him for not coming to him for six months, he replied: “Because I have not yet fulfilled that verse in practice.”

Later, after he had lived many more years, a certain acquaintance asked him whether he had learned the verse. He replied: “For forty-nine years I scarcely managed to fulfill it.”

When someone gave this man gold for the nourishment of the poor and said, “Count it,” he replied: “What you have given does not need counting, but an attitude conducive to salvation” [Col. 1103D].

That same Pambo, at the request of Bishop Athanasius, came down from the desert to Alexandria. When he saw a theatrical woman there, he wept. Those present asked him why he was crying, and he replied: “Two things moved me: one was her ruin; the other, that I do not strive as earnestly to please God as she does to please depraved human beings.”

Another man said: “Unless a monk works, he is judged equal to one who uses violence.”

Piterius used to provide many natural explanations and frequently explain one matter or another when others asked about them. Yet he prayed through each explanation.

At that time there were among the monks two men beloved by God, both named Macarius: one from Upper Egypt, the other an Alexandrian. Both were distinguished in many ways—by abstinence, conduct, character, and the miracles performed through their hands.

Macarius the Egyptian performed so many cures and expelled so many demons that a separate book is filled with his deeds. He was reverent and strict toward those who made inquiries [Ed.: “those who offended”].

Macarius the Alexandrian, although in every respect like the Egyptian, differed in this: he appeared more cheerful toward those who consulted him, and with a joyful expression led young men toward conversion [mss. Frob. and Niv.: “induced them”].

Their disciple Evagrius possessed philosophy in practice. Previously he had philosophized only in speech; then, in the city of Constantinople, he was ordained deacon by Gregory of Nazianzus. Afterward he went down with him into Egypt, observed the men mentioned above, and zealously imitated their conduct. As many miracles were performed through his hands [Col. 1104C] as through the hands of his teachers.

He composed books of great usefulness. One is entitled *The Monk* and concerns practical matters. Another is *The Gnostic*, according to the state by which someone becomes worthy of knowledge; it contains fifty chapters. Another is *The Antirrhetic*, collected from the divine Scriptures against tempting demons; it is divided into eight parts, corresponding to the eight thoughts. He also composed six hundred propositions concerned with contemplation, which he called *γνωστικὰ προβλήματα*, that is, “gnostic propositions.”

In addition, he composed two works in verse: one for monks living in coenobitic communities or traveling, and one for virgins. Readers understand how extraordinary and necessary these works are.

It is appropriate, I think, to report a few of his sayings about monks and Scripture. He says:

“It is necessary to seek out the paths rightly followed by earlier monks and to train ourselves according to them. For many things were found among them that were well said and at the same time well done” [Col. 1105A].

Among them, one man also said: “A dry and even diet, joined with love, quickly leads a monk to the haven of dispassion.”

When he saw one of the brothers troubled at night by fantasies, he cured him in this way: he ordered him to fast and serve food to those who were ill. When asked about this, he replied: “Nothing extinguishes passions of this kind as mercy does.”

A certain philosopher came to the righteous Antony and said: “How do you manage, Father, deprived of the consolation of books?” Antony answered him: “O philosopher, my book is the nature of created things. It is present whenever I wish, and it rereads God’s words to me.”

Macarius, the Egyptian elder, the chosen vessel, asked me: “Why, while retaining a memory of evil against human beings, do we dissipate the soul’s memorable virtue? But when we retain a memory of evil against demons, do we remain innocent?”

When I was perplexed by the question contained in this inquiry, I asked him to explain his statement. He replied: “The first passion is anger contrary to nature; the second [that is, the following one] is according to nature.”

At the very hour of blazing midday I reached the holy Father Macarius. Burning intensely with thirst, I asked for water to drink. He said: “Let the shade be sufficient for you. For many who are now traveling or sailing are deprived even of this refreshment.”

Afterward, when I was discussing abstinence with him, he said: “Take courage, son. For twenty years I was satisfied neither with bread, nor with water, nor with sleep. I ate my bread by weight and drank water by measure; leaning against the walls, I snatched a little sleep” [Col. 1105C].

A monk was informed that his father had died. To the messenger he said: “Go away, and do not blaspheme; for my father is immortal.”

One of the brothers possessed only the Gospel, which he sold and distributed to the poor. He offered a worthy and memorable saying: “I sold the very word that always says to me, ‘Sell all that you have and give to the poor’” (Matt. 19:21).

There is an island near Alexandria, beyond the Mareotis marsh, in which lived a monk most distinguished in contemplation [mss.: “most contemplative and approved.”] He said: “Everything done by monks is done for five reasons: for God, for nature, for custom, for necessity, or for the work of their hands” [Col. 1105D].

The same man also said that virtue is one according to nature, but that it assumes different forms through the qualities of the soul. “For,” he said, “although the light of the sun is without form, it seems to create a varied pattern in the windows through which it enters.”

Another monk said: “For this reason I cut off lusts, so that I may remove the occasions of anger. For I know that anger always contends on behalf of lusts, troubling my mind as it pursues knowledge.”

One of the elders said: “Love does not know how to store up a reserve of food or money.”

The same man also said: “I do not know of having been deceived by demons in the same matter.”

Thus Evagrius recorded these sayings in his book *The Practical*.

In *The Contemplative* he says:

“We learned from Gregory the righteous about four virtues and their contemplations: prudence, courage, temperance, and justice” [Col. 1106A].

He said that the work of prudence is to contemplate the intellectual and holy powers without words, since wisdom has declared that they are signified by such powers. The work of courage is to remain steadfast in the truth, even if someone is overthrown, and not to approach things that are nothing. He answered that the characteristic of temperance is to receive the seeds of the first farmer and plant them appropriately. The work of justice is that each person be given words according to his merit: some things are spoken obscurely, others indicated through riddles, and certain matters openly arranged for the benefit of the simple.

Basil the Cappadocian, the pillar of truth, says: “Frequent meditation and exercise make human knowledge better; but justice, patience, and mercy make that knowledge better which is granted by the grace of God” [Col. 1106B]. Those who are still subject to passions can receive human knowledge, but only the dispassionate are capable of divine knowledge. At the time of prayer they also shine with the proper light of the mind and behold themselves.

Athanasius, the most sacred light of the Egyptians, says: “Moses commanded the table to be placed toward the northern side. Therefore, let contemplatives recognize who it is that blows against them, let them endure every temptation with a courageous mind, and let them nourish with eagerness those who approach them.”

Serapion, the angel of the Church of Thmuis, said: “The mind, once possessed of spiritual understanding, is perfectly purified. Love heals the members swollen with anger; continence restrains unlawful desires and their inflowing impulses” [ms. Theod.: “iniquities flowing from desires”] [Col. 1106C].

Didymus, the great teacher of contemplation, says: “Always practice within yourself discourses concerning providence and judgment, and retain in memory the material for study. For almost all of us sin in these matters. You will find the account of judgment in the differences among bodies, in which the world itself also consists; and the account of providence in the ways by which a person is raised from wickedness or ignorance to the heights of virtue and knowledge.”

We have reported these things from the sayings of Evagrius.

There was also another remarkable man among the monks named Ammonius. He was so free from curiosity that, when he came to Rome with Athanasius, he inspected none of the city’s works except the basilicas of Peter and Paul.

When Ammonius was being urged toward the episcopate and was fleeing from it, he cut off his right ear so that, being mutilated in half his body, he might escape the work of ordination [Col. 1106D]. Later, when Evagrius too was being pressed toward the episcopate by Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, he fled without cutting off any part of his body. When he came to Ammonius [ms. Lyr.: “and conversed with him”], he jokingly said, as though Ammonius had done wrong, that he had cut off his ear and thereby incurred guilt for it [ms. Theod.: “God”].

Ammonius answered him: “You do not know, Evagrius, that you ought to be punished because you cut out your tongue. And lest you seem to claim credit for yourself, you do not make use of the grace of God.”

There were very many worthy men at that time. If anyone wishes to learn their sayings and miracles, and how even beasts were subjected to them, let him read the book of the monk Palladius, who was Evagrius’s disciple. He explained everything about these men with precision [Col. 1107A], and in it he also recorded the conduct and imitation of women.

Evagrius and Palladius therefore flourished shortly after Valens had died.

SOCRATES, Book IV, chapter 18. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 23, p. 233.

This period also provides as many examples as I can recall of those among the Christians who practiced philosophy at that time. One of them was John in Egypt, to whom God revealed things future and otherwise uncertain no less than to the prophets of old, and granted the gift of healing incurable diseases. From his youth he praised God, living in solitude, eating herbs and roots, and drinking water whenever he found it. When he reached old age, he migrated by divine command to the Thebaid and became the superior of many monasteries. By prayer alone he drove away sicknesses and demons; and although he had never learned letters, he did not need books in order to remember anything, because whatever he once grasped in his mind he retained with complete accuracy.

In that region Ammon, superior of the Tabennesiots, practiced philosophy, having about three thousand disciples. Theonas too was superior of many monks. Both were workers of astonishing deeds, filled with divine providence and prophecy. Theonas is said to have been learned in Egyptian, Greek, and Latin literature, and to have maintained silence for thirty years. Moreover, no one ever saw him angry, swearing, lying, or uttering anything frivolous, harsh, or discouraging.

At that time there were also Copres, Hellin, and Elias. Copres, they say, possessed the divine gift of bringing about the healing of illnesses and driving out demons. Hellin, brought up from childhood in a monastery, performed many astonishing miracles, even carrying fire in his bosom without his clothing ever burning. Elias, however, was then living in the desert not far from the city of Antinoe, at about one hundred and ten years of age. Before that, he had lived alone in the wilderness for nearly seventy years, and he reached this age by fasting and conducting himself manfully.

There was also Apelles in Egypt, formerly a blacksmith. One night, while practicing his trade, a demonic shadow in the form of a beautiful woman tempted him concerning chastity. He drew from the furnace the iron he was working and struck her in the face. Then, shrieking and groaning, she fled far away.

Among these there was also Isidore, who fortified his monastery on every side and took care that no one should leave it, while ensuring that everyone had all necessities within. Serapion likewise had about ten thousand monks under him, all of whom he trained to obtain necessities through their own labor and to serve them to others in need.

Dioscorus was superior to no more than one hundred monks. As a presbyter, when celebrating the sacred offerings, he applied the utmost perfection in examining and carefully judging those who approached the holy mysteries, so that they might cleanse their minds and have no guilty conscience. Eulogius the presbyter is said to have possessed foreknowledge of the thoughts of all who came to him. He openly reproved their offenses and disclosed whatever they had secretly thought, since it had been revealed to him. Those who had done something evil or entertained a wicked intention he suspended from the altar, making known to them the sin they had committed; after they had been cleansed through careful penitence, he received them again.

Apollo in the Thebaid was like these men. He had lived for forty years in the inner desert, possessing a small cave on a nearby mountain; but, having become famous in a short time because of the multitude of his miracles, he became superior to many monks.

At that time many excellent men practiced philosophy diligently in Alexandria—about two thousand. Some lived in solitude, while others dwelt around Mareotis. Among them Dorotheus, a Theban by birth, stood out exceptionally. His way of life was this: every day he gathered stones from the sea and each year built a lodging-house, giving it to those unable to construct one for themselves. At night he made baskets in order to sell them and provide their food.

His food was six ounces of bread, one small bundle of greens, and water to drink. He had lived in this manner from youth and did not weaken in old age. He was never seen asleep in a bed, stretching out his feet for rest, or sleeping at will, except insofar as his eyes might close naturally when weariness overcame him through working or eating. Indeed, often, while eating, he fell asleep and the food slipped from his mouth.

Once, overcome by very heavy sleep, he fell into a dung heap and fell asleep there. When he awoke and was distressed, he said quietly: “If you persuade angels to sleep, you will persuade me also hereafter.” Perhaps he was speaking to sleep, or to the demon who was trying to hinder him from good works.

When he was laboring, someone asked him: “Why are you destroying your body in this way?” He replied: “Because it has destroyed me.”

The presbyter Piamon is said, while celebrating the sacred offering, to have seen a holy angel standing near the sacred altar, recording the monks who were present in a book and erasing those who were absent.

God is also known to have granted John such power against diseases and infirmities that he healed many sufferers from gout and those whose joints had become dislocated.

Among these men the elder Benjamin was held in very high esteem. He possessed the gift of God by which, without medicine, the touch of his hands, or oil, after prayer, he healed the sick. It is said that he himself fell into dropsy, and that his body became so swollen that he could not be carried out through the doors of his cell, where he lived, unless the doors, together with the boards set before them, were removed.

During his illness, for nearly eight months before his death, he sat in an extremely broad chair and solemnly treated the sick. He did not take it badly that this brought no benefit to his own illness; rather, when they saw him, he consoled them and begged them to pray to God for his soul and not to be concerned about his body. “For even when it was healthy,” he said, “it did nothing for me.”

Mark, who lived in Scetis, is said to have been very gentle and wise even in his youth, and to have possessed an excellent memory of the divine Scriptures. He was so beloved by God that, whenever he approached the Lord’s body, an angel gave him the sacraments. He said that he saw only the angel’s hand as far as the joint of the arm.

Macarius was granted power to surpass demons. The occasion of his conversion was a murder he had committed. While still a boy and tending sheep around the marsh of Mareotis, he killed a companion of his own age in play and, fearing the consequences, fled into the desert. After living under the open sky for three years, he built a small lodging for himself and lived there for twenty-five years. Many said that they had heard him give thanks for that calamity and call that involuntary murder salutary, since through it the means of blessedness had come to him.

Apollonius, although throughout his life he had learned nothing of the monastic way of life, realized that because of his age he could neither write nor practice his former trade. He therefore purchased, at his own expense, all medicines and suitable foods for the sick. From early morning until the ninth hour he went around the doors of the monasteries, visiting the sick and supplying whatever they needed. When he was about to die, he handed over what he possessed to another [Ed. Niv. and Frob.: to someone else], ordering him to preserve such vows.

Moses, however, had been a slave and was expelled from his master’s house because of his offenses. He devoted himself to robbery and committed many murders. Later, after his conversion, he was suddenly filled with the power of this philosophy. Since the fantasies of his former lust still stirred him with the natural force of life, he subdued his body through great abstinence, eating only bread and performing much labor.

For six years he prayed standing throughout the entire night, neither bending his knees nor closing his eyes in sleep. In addition, he went around the monks’ cells at night and filled each man’s water jars, even when water was flowing ten, twenty, or thirty stadia away. Although he so disciplined his body, he did not lose his former physical strength. For it is said that when four robbers attacked his lodging, he seized and bound them all, carried them on his shoulders to the church, and left it to the monks to decide what should be done with them.

Thus he attained the highest philosophy, was terrifying to demons, and was appointed presbyter in Scetis. He lived for nearly seventy-five years.

Under this emperor Paul of Libya was in Scetis, with no fewer than five hundred monks under him. He neither worked nor received anything except what he ate. He prayed alone; and as though he had been assigned a tribute, he rendered three hundred prayers to God each day. To avoid making a mistake in the number, he placed three hundred stones before him and cast one into his bosom for each prayer. When the stones had been used up, he knew that the prayers were complete.

At that time Abbot Pachomius was flourishing in Scetis, having conducted himself excellently from youth to old age. A demon had never deceived him, either concerning bodily health or concerning the soul’s affliction.

Stephen lived around Mareotis, conducting himself perfectly and with complete self-control. For about sixty years he was a tried and approved monk and was well known to Antony the Great. He was gentle and wise, sweet and useful in speech. He consoled the hearts of the sorrowful and restored them to cheerfulness, even when necessary tribulation occurred.

He was the same in his own misfortunes. When he contracted an incurable illness and physicians cut away his rotting limbs, he nevertheless worked with his hands, plaiting palm leaves and persuading those present not to grieve over such matters or think of anything except a good end. “Everything God has made,” he said, “is useful. I know that such sufferings occur because of sins. It is better to pay the penalty here than to endure everlasting punishments after death.”

When Pior left his father’s house to turn to the philosophical life, he promised that he would never again see any of his relatives. After fifty years, however, his sister, having learned that he was alive and living in the desert, did not cease until she saw him. When the local bishop saw that, on account of this, the woman—already advanced in age—was being afflicted, he wrote to the superiors of the desert that they should send Pior.

Since it is wrong to resist [ms. Lyr.: despise], Pior obeyed the commands of the elders. Taking someone with him, he went to his native land. When he approached the doors of his house and announced his arrival, his sister came. With his eyes closed, he said: “Here I am, Pior. Satisfy yourself with looking at me as much as you wish.”

She then gave thanks and praised God. After praying, he returned to the desert, where he dug for water, found it bitter, and used it until the last day of his life. After his death, no one was able to live there. I believe that through prayer he made it sweet for his own use, just as by prayer he had merited that water should flow where it had not existed elsewhere.

For once, when Moses and his monks were digging a well and found no vein of water, while the depth no longer permitted them to dig farther, Pior arrived at midday. After praying, he descended into the pit; when he struck the earth for the third time, water immediately flowed out. When he was leaving after praying, they asked him at least to taste the water. He replied: “I was sent here for this purpose, and what I came for has been accomplished.”

Ammon is said to have been extremely learned, a disciple of Origen and Didymus, and from youth until the last day of his life to have eaten nothing except bread and salt. When certain people tried to drag him into the episcopate and he could not avoid them by argument, he cut off his own ear, saying: “Now surely no one will tolerate ordaining me against my will, since ecclesiastical discipline seeks men perfect in body.”

When they had left and returned again, saying that the Church sought perfection of character rather than of body, he even swore that he would cut out his tongue if they tried to force him. On hearing this, those who had come desisted [Ed.: withdrew].

At that time Evagrius was a man of very eloquent and gentle character, properly educated by Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus, whose archdeacon he also was. He is said to have been extremely handsome in appearance and elegant in the arrangement of his clothing.

When a jealous senator realized that Evagrius was very well known to his wife, he prepared an ambush to kill him. It would have succeeded had not a terrifying yet salutary vision foretold the danger to him. In a dream he saw that he had been arrested as though for a crime, bound hand and foot in chains, and led away to punishment.

As this was taking place, someone brought out a Gospel and promised that he would be released from his bonds if he departed from the city of Constantinople; he compelled Evagrius to promise this by oath. Touching the Gospels, Evagrius promised that he would fulfill it. When his bonds were removed, he awoke; trusting the sacred vision, he escaped the danger. He then went from Constantinople to Jerusalem.

There were also in Rhinocorura men who were not foreigners but natives, flourishing in philosophy. Among them Bishop Melas is said to have possessed such kindness.

When men had been sent to deport resisting bishops into exile and came to his church, they found him preparing the church’s candles like the lowest servant. They asked where the bishop was. He replied: “I will announce you to the bishop.”

He led them, weary from their journey, into the bishop’s residence and, having set a table before them, fed them as well as he could. After the meal had been served, he said that he was the bishop. Astonished at the man, they disclosed the reason for their visit. Having shown him due respect, they departed.

Then he said: “I will not evade what men like me have gladly accepted; willingly, therefore, I accept the order of exile.”

His brother Solomon, converted from a life of commerce, rose to the highest summit of philosophy.

At this time Epiphanius, who later became bishop of Cyprus, was held in the highest esteem among the hermits.

There was also Protogenes, bishop in Carrhae after Vitus. He is said to have professed that, on the Lord’s Epiphany, it had been revealed to him that he saw the emperor Constantine, and that God showed him future events and commanded him to obey whatever Constantine said.

Among these men such abstinence prevailed that, because of his many fasts, Protogenes’ teeth boiled with worms [ms. Lyr.: fell out and were torn away]. Others are said not to have tasted bread at all for as many as eighty years. Heliodorus passed many nights without sleep and continued fasting for seven days at a time.

There were also many monks in Palestine, Syria, and among the Persians. If anyone wished to write down even their names, they would fill many books.

SOZOMEN, Book VI, chapter 28, p. 677.

## CHAPTER II  
### How the Arians in Constantinople seized orthodox Christians and burned many of them in a ship

At that time, in the city of Constantinople, the Arians seized certain presbyters of the true religion, put them into an unarmed ship, and towed them out to sea, while others followed in another ship. They set the ship on fire and burned them. After this had been done, the holy men struggled against both fire and sea; finally they were swallowed up and crowned with the triumph of martyrdom.

THEODORET, Book IV, chapter 22. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 24, p. 187.

## CHAPTER III  
### How Valens granted pagans, Jews, and heretics permission to celebrate their festivals, while prohibiting the orthodox everywhere; and concerning the virtues of Flavian and Diodorus

Valens remained for a long time in Antioch and granted everyone—pagans, Jews, and heretics alike—permission to celebrate their festivals. The pagans celebrated their festivals, serving demons; and after Jovian had extinguished the vanities of idolatry, this emperor allowed them to flourish again. The worship of Jupiter and Dionysus, and the rites of Ceres, which under a devout emperor would have been celebrated only in secret, were now performed openly; the revelers ran everywhere through the middle of the streets.

At that time the ruler was hostile only to those who appeared to preach apostolic doctrine. First he had them expelled from the sacred basilicas, to which the renowned emperor Jovian had given a new church. When they celebrated sacred rites on the mountain, praising God with hymns and delighting there in the divine utterances—although they often endured the harshness of the weather, sometimes being tormented by rain, sometimes snow, sometimes frost, and frequently by the heat of fire—he did not allow them to enjoy divine praise even in such places, but sent soldiers to drive them away.

Then Flavian and Diodorus, like defensive ramparts, resisted the missiles directed against them. When Meletius, their shepherd, was compelled to live apart [ms. Lyr.: attempted to live apart], they took care of the flocks, opposing their own courage to the wolves and continually offering the sheep appropriate care.

Thus expelled from the mountainous places, they pastured the sheep beside the banks of the neighboring river. For they did not allow themselves, like the Israelites in captivity at Babylon, to hang up their instruments; rather, they praised God the Creator and Giver in every place of his dominion.

But the enemy of Christ’s servants did not allow the assembly of the devout to remain undisturbed even there. Nevertheless, their remarkable harmony—as disciples of the great Shepherd, nourishing the holy sheep through training—provided spiritual pastures.

Diodorus, supremely wise and courageous, like a clear river and a rushing stream, watered his own sheep while completely washing away the blasphemies of the wolves. Disregarding the nobility of his family, he willingly endured every calamity for the faith.

Flavian, an excellent man and himself of the noblest birth, judged that only uprightness was piety. Like a trained boy, he urged the great Diodorus, as though he were an athlete of innumerable contests, to exert himself.

At that time Flavian did not preach among the ecclesiastical assemblies; instead, while others performed that task, he supplied abundant assistance through counsel, the Scriptures, and explanations [ms. Lyr.: through explanations of the Scriptures]. The teachers drew their bows against the Arian blasphemies, while he, as though drawing arrows from quivers, offered the fitting arrows of his mind. Resisting the heretics not only at home but also in public, he more easily tore through their nets and exposed their labors as the work of spiders.

THEODORET, Book IV, chapter 22 [printed: chapter chapter 22]. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 24, p. 187.

## CHAPTER IV  
### Concerning the praises of the monk Aphraates and the confidence with which he answered Valens

Aphraates labored with these men; we have recorded his way of life elsewhere. Preferring the salvation of the sheep to his own quiet, he left his cave and undertook pastoral labors. It would now be superfluous to recount how great a wealth of virtue he accumulated. Only one thing should be mentioned about him, since it is highly relevant to this history.

On the north side a river called the Orontes flows near the palace; to the south there is a very large portico with tall towers on every side. Between the palace and the river lies a street that leads those leaving the city toward the suburban fields. As Aphraates was passing along this street, hurrying toward hostile battles so that he might provide the sacred sheep with the care they needed, the emperor looked down from the palace and saw him dressed in a very shabby cloak and hurrying along despite his advanced old age.

When someone said that this was Aphraates, upon whom the whole city depended, the emperor said to him: “Tell me, where are you going?”

He wisely and appropriately replied: “To pray for your reign.”

The emperor then said: “You ought to pray at home, according to the monastic custom.”

The most holy man replied: “You speak very well—if you also allowed me to do so, I ought to act in that way. I have done this until now, while the sheep of Christ enjoyed their former peace. But since they are being thrown into the greatest turmoil and the burden of danger presses upon them lest they be held captive, it is necessary to run everywhere and rescue them from their distress.

“But tell me, most tranquil emperor: if I were a girl sitting in a bedroom and occupied with wool, and I saw my father’s house burning with fire, what would be appropriate for me to do? To sit inside and disregard the burning house? Or rather to run about everywhere, carrying water and extinguishing the flames? I believe that you would say the latter ought to be done; for that is the task of a wise girl. This is what is happening now, emperor. Since you are sending flames against our ancestral house, we are running about to extinguish them quickly.”

When he had said this, the emperor threatened him but remained silent. One of the emperor’s chamberlains, however, responded harshly to the holy man and is known to have suffered the following calamity.

He was in charge of the bathhouse. After these words, he went down to prepare the emperor’s entrance; but, his mind shaken, he descended into boiling water and died there. The emperor sat waiting to bathe when the man returned. When he delayed, he sent other men to ask why he was taking so long. They entered and found him dead and dismembered in the boiling bath [ms. Santheod.: vat].

When this was reported to the emperor, they recognized the power of Aphraates’ prayer. Nevertheless, they did not withdraw from their impious doctrines [ms. Lyr.: did not cease], but, like Pharaoh, their hearts were hardened.

THEODORET, Book IV, chapters 23 and 24. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapters 25 and 26, p. 188.

## CHAPTER V  
### Concerning the monk Julian

At this time that famous Julian, leaving his solitude, came to Antioch. Since the heretics, accustomed to patching their lies with ease, claimed that this man belonged to their error, Flavian, Diodorus, and Aphraates sent to him Acacius, a man distinguished for his virtue who later became bishop of Beroea. They asked him to aid many thousands of people, refute the deceit of the adversaries, and confirm the doctrines of truth.

We have related in the history composed by us, beloved of God [variant: in the Philothean history], how many miracles that most holy man performed when coming, returning, and remaining in the great city itself. Since the entire population of the city came together in our assemblies, I am confident that no age will doubt this. Extraordinary events prove themselves capable of attracting everyone.

But because that man performed the greatest miracles, even the enemies of the truth cannot deny them. The great Antony did the same in Alexandria during the time of Constantius. Leaving the desert, he went around all the cities, assuring everyone that Athanasius was a preacher of apostolic doctrine and that the enemies of the truth were Arius’s adherents.

Thus those most holy men knew what was appropriate to each time: when it was necessary to enjoy quiet and when it was necessary to prefer cities to solitude.

THEODORET, Book IV, chapter 25. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 27, p. 190.

## CHAPTER VI  
### Concerning Acepsemas and others

At that time the celebrated Acepsemas was shut up in a cell in the wilderness of the Cyrestenians, and for sixty years was neither seen nor heard speaking.

There was also the remarkable Zeugmatius. Although deprived of his sight, he went everywhere, strengthening the sheep and resisting the wolves. For this reason they burned down his monastic cell; but Trajan, a most faithful military commander, built another for him and supported him with abundant assistance.

At this time Ephraem was in Edessa, and Didymus in Alexandria. Ephraem, using the Syrian language, emitted rays of spiritual grace. Although he did not know Greek doctrine, he refuted many learned Greeks and exposed the weakness of every heretical error.

At that time Harmonius the Bardesanite composed certain songs, mixing impiety with the sweetness of melody. By this means he enticed his listeners and captured them in the plague of error. Ephraem therefore took those melodies and mingled piety with the songs, offering his listeners an exceedingly sweet and useful medicine. These songs continue to make the festivals of the triumphant martyrs more glorious.

THEODORET, Book IV, chapter 26. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 28, p. 191.

## CHAPTER VII  
### Concerning the evils perpetrated under Valens in Alexandria and throughout Egypt

When the emperor Valens had ordered by law that all the orthodox in Alexandria and Egypt should be persecuted, everything was laid waste. Some were dragged before tribunals, others were sent into chains, and others were driven on by beatings. Very many punishments were inflicted upon lovers of quiet.

While these things were being done in Alexandria according to the will of Lucius, and Euzoius had returned to Antioch, the military commander with a multitude of armed men, together with Lucius the Arian, immediately proceeded against the monasteries established throughout Egypt.

Although they inflicted many evils upon the holy men and could not overcome them in any way, at Lucius’s persuasion the fathers of the monks were sent into exile. Among them were Macarius the Egyptian and another Macarius of Alexandria.

When they came to a certain island, they found the daughter of a priest seized by a demon and crying out to those men: “Why have you come here as well, to drive us out?” Through their prayers they freed her and restored her to her father. At the same time they brought the priest and the other inhabitants of the island to Christianity. They immediately cast down the images and transformed the temple into a church. They were baptized and were most gladly taught the practices of Christianity.

Thus, because of their faith in consubstantiality, those admirable men became even more credible. By healing others, they demonstrated through their works that their faith was stronger.

SOCRATES, Book IV, chapter 19. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 24, p. 238.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### Concerning Didymus and his writings; and Gregory of Pontus and his miracles

At that time God brought forth another faithful man, Didymus, an extraordinary man who then flourished in every branch of learning, so that through him he might bear witness to the faith.

While he was still a child and being taught the first elements of letters, he lost his sight through an eye disease. In place of visible eyes, God granted him intellectual ones. For what he could not learn through his eyes, he came to know through attentive hearing. Since he had been gifted from childhood, he surpassed even those who saw clearly.

He easily learned the rules of grammar and rhetoric. When he turned to philosophy, he learned and stored in his mind, with remarkable ability, dialectic, arithmetic, music, and the other philosophical disciplines, so that he quickly matched those who had learned such things with the aid of their eyes.

He also knew the Old and New Testaments so perfectly that he produced many books. He composed three books on the Trinity and interpreted Origen’s work *On First Principles*—that is, *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*Peri Archōn*, “On First Principles”)—leaving in it outstanding explanations.

It is said that when Antony came to Alexandria during the time of Valens because of the Arians, he saw Didymus and said to him:

“Do not be troubled, Didymus, by the loss of your bodily eyes. For you lack only such eyes as can recognize flies and fleas. Rather, rejoice, because you possess eyes with which even angels look, through which God is seen and his light is contemplated.”

SOCRATES, Book IV, chapter 20. Edition of Christ. Valesius [printed: Vates], chapter 25, p. 240.

Didymus, deprived of his eyes from infancy, learned through hearing grammar, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, Aristotle’s syllogisms, and Plato’s eloquence—not as though these disciplines taught the truth, but as though they were weapons of truth against falsehood.

THEODORET, Book IV, chapter 27. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 29, p. 192.

Since some people are known to err because of the similarity of names, it is necessary to show that Gregory of Pontus was a different person: he came from Caesarea of Pontus, was very ancient, and was a disciple of Origen.

There is much discussion of this Gregory in Athens, Berytus, and Pontus, and, so to speak, throughout the entire world. After leaving Athens, he came to Berytus, where he studied law. When he learned that Origen was expounding the sacred books at Caesarea, he went there to hear the explanations of that eloquent man.

Having been instructed by him in true philosophy, he returned to his homeland when his parents summoned him. There, while still a layman, he performed many signs: healing diseases, driving out demons through letters, and subjugating pagans to himself through words and deeds.

The martyr Pamphilus also mentions him, as does Eusebius in the books he composed about Origen. This Gregory, therefore, was the ancient Gregory, Origen’s disciple, distinct from Gregory of Nazianzus, the brother of Basil. There was also another Gregory of Alexandria, an Arian.

SOCRATES, Book IV, chapter 22. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 27, p. 244.

## CHAPTER IX  
### How the Novatians changed the festival of Easter; and concerning the schism between Cornelius, bishop of Rome, and Novatus over the reception of those who had gone astray

At that time the Novatians living in Phrygia changed the festival of Easter. I shall explain how this happened, first recounting why ecclesiastical discipline is maintained more strictly among the peoples of Phrygia and Paphlagonia.

The presbyter Novatus separated himself from communion with the Roman Church because Cornelius, the bishop, had received into communion the faithful who had sacrificed during the persecution carried out under Decius.

For this reason Novatus separated himself and, summoned to the episcopate by his fellow bishops, wrote to the churches that those who had sacrificed to demons should not be received into the sacraments, but should indeed be invited to repentance; remission, however, should be left to the power of God, whose alone it is to forgive sins.

When the churches in each province received such letters, they gave responses according to their own judgments. When Novatus therefore commanded that those who had sinned after baptism with a sin leading to death ought not to participate in the sacred mysteries, this rule seemed exceedingly bitter and harsh to some, while others accepted it as just and right.

While this question was being debated, letters arrived from Cornelius, the Roman prelate, promising forgiveness to sinners even after baptism. Thus, since both men wrote different things and supported their opinions from the divine utterances, the provincials followed differing judgments.

For those who supposed that the promised remission would be granted continued to sin thereafter. Hence it appears that the peoples of Phrygia are known to be more morally pure than others.

Although Novatus separated himself because of his exceptionally strict way of life, he did not change the festival of Easter. According to the Western fathers, he too celebrated it. Among them Easter has long been observed after the equinox, from the time they first became Christians.

Novatus himself later ended his life in martyrdom during the persecution under the emperor Valerian. Those who took their name from him and shared his views, however, held a council of a few bishops in the village of Pazenum, where the springs of the river Sagarius are located. They established a rule that they should observe the Jews when they made unleavened bread and celebrate Easter with them.

Later, because of that council, the Church of the Novatians also became divided.

SOCRATES, Book IV, chapter 23. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 28, p. 245.

## CHAPTER X  
### Concerning Damasus and Ursinus, who were ordained bishops of Rome at the same time

At that time, while the emperor Valentinian disturbed no heresy, Damasus was ordained bishop of Rome after Liberius; at the same time Ursinus, a deacon of that church, was secretly ordained in the Basilica of Siricius.

For this reason, after many had been punished by sedition or by the intervention of the prefect Maximinus, Ursinus was removed and Damasus remained bishop.

SOCRATES, Book IV, chapter 24. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 29, p. 247.

At that time in the West, Damasus of Rome and Ambrose of Milan struck the enemies with spiritual weapons. Those who had been sent into long exiles also encouraged their own people by letters and destroyed the adversaries. Divine providence prepared them as governors amid the storm and as supremely wise commanders of soldiers in battle.

THEODORET, Book IV, chapter 28. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 31, p. 193.

## CHAPTER XI  
### Concerning the death of Valentinian the Elder, the omens concerning Valentinian the Younger, and how Valentinian took another wife while his first wife was still alive

[Col. 1117C]

Meanwhile, the emperor Valentinian of the West, violently enraged against the envoys of the Sarmatians, died from a hemorrhage caused by the rupture of his veins, after the third consulship of Gratian and the consulship of Equitius [A.D. 375], on the seventeenth day of November, in the fifty-fourth year of his life and the eleventh of his reign. When he died, the soldiers of Italy, on the sixth day after his death, elevated his young son Valentinian to the summit of imperial power. His brother Gratian and his uncle Valens, although reluctantly [Col. 1117D] (since it had been done without their knowledge), nevertheless later accepted his rule. Thus the younger Valentinian succeeded to his father’s empire. He had been born to Justina, whom Valentinian is shown to have married while his former wife Severa was still alive, in the following manner.

Justus, Justina’s father, when he was governor of Picenum in the time of Constantius, saw in a dream that he had given birth to imperial purple from his right thigh. When the vision was being recounted by many people, it eventually reached the ears of Constantius. But he, interpreting the dream as meaning that an emperor would be born from Justus, sent men to kill him. His daughter Justina, left fatherless, remained a virgin.

Later, she came to the attention of Severa, to whose house she frequently went, and she became beloved by her, so much so that she even bathed with her. When Severa had gazed for a long time at Justina bathing beside her, she became captivated by the virgin’s beauty and told the emperor that the virgin Justina was so beautiful that even she, although a woman, had been overcome by love for her. The emperor, having taken her words to heart, considered marrying Justina, but did not wish to cast aside Severa, by whom Gratian had been born and whom he had shortly before confirmed as emperor.

He therefore publicly promulgated a law, posted throughout the cities, decreeing that those who wished might have two wives. Once the law had been enacted, he joined himself to Justina. By her were born the younger Valentinian and three daughters, Justa, Grata, and Galla. Two of these remained virgins, but the elder emperor Theodosius later married Galla; by her he is known to have had Placidia as a daughter [Col. 1118B]. For it is known that he had Arcadius and Honorius by his former wife Flacilla.

SOCRATES, Book IV, chapter 26. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 31, p. 248.

## CHAPTER XII. How the philosopher Themistius diverted Valens from killing the orthodox

Meanwhile, while Valens was residing in Antioch of Syria, he was violently persecuting the worshipers of consubstantiality, had not the book of the philosopher Themistius recalled him from this course. In it Themistius argued that he ought not to be hostile on account of disagreements over ecclesiastical doctrines, since even among the pagans there appeared to be a difference of more than three hundred sects, and each person maintained a different opinion in accordance with his own doctrine.

And perhaps this was more pleasing to God, since he is not easily known and is glorified in different ways; for each person fears him more greatly when he is more ignorant of the fullness of his knowledge, or of how, what sort, and how great he is. Through these arguments of Themistius the emperor became somewhat more lenient.

SOCRATES, Book VI, chapter 36, p. 695.

## CHAPTER XIII. How the Goths came to Valens, and how the Arian plague reached the Goths

Yet he did not entirely suspend his anger, but decreed exile instead of the death penalty for the most sacred men, until a public emergency of the following kind turned aside his attack.

The barbarians established beyond the Hister, who are called Goths, stirred up a civil war among themselves in two [Col. 1118D] factions. Fridigern commanded one, and Athalaric the other. When Athalaric had prevailed, Fridigern fled to the Romans and requested their aid. When Valens learned this, he ordered the soldiers of Thrace to provide assistance to the barbarians. With this support Athalaric was defeated and also put to flight.

For this reason Fridigern, wishing to repay Valens with some favor, embraced, together with all his people, the doctrines of Valens’s religion. Hence the Goths are still known to be Arians. At that time Vulfilas, bishop of the Goths, also devised Gothic letters and translated the divine Scriptures into that language.

When Vulfilas was instructing not only Fridigern’s Goths but also Athalaric’s, Athalaric, seeing the ancestral religion violated, delivered many [Col. 1119A] Arians to punishment; the Arians now call them martyrs.

After a short time the barbarians again made peace among themselves, but they were plundered by the neighboring people, the Huns. Driven from their own lands, they fled to Roman territory, preferring to serve the emperor. When Valens learned this, without foreseeing what would happen, he granted them lands in Thrace, thinking that he had thereby prepared assistance for himself against all the barbarians. Consequently, he neglected the soldiers thereafter and despised those who had previously labored against the enemy. He even demanded from the provincial tax collectors, throughout villages and cities, eighty solidi for each soldier, although previously he had relieved them of their taxes.

This, then, was the beginning of the subjection of the Roman state to calamities. For when the barbarians had occupied [Col. 1119B] Thrace [p. 329], they ravaged the Roman province freely. When Valens heard this, although he did not cease the exiles of the orthodox, he nevertheless restrained himself from that course because of this necessity. Troubled, he came from Antioch to Constantinople; consequently, the persecution of the Christians also ceased for a time.

SOCRATES, Book IV, chapters 27 and 28. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapters 32 and 33, p. 250.

Meanwhile, when the emperor Valens had stirred up the Gothic people for battle near the Bosporus, then, at last recognizing the weakness of his own strength, he sent to his brother asking for assistance. But his brother replied that it was not religiously right to aid such a man, who was rebelling against God; rather, it was just that his pride should be humbled.

When that most wretched man recognized this, although constrained by an even greater necessity, he nevertheless did not desist from his excesses but remained rebellious against God and the truth.

At this time Terentius returned victorious from Armenia, an excellent man, suitably adorned with piety. Valens ordered him to ask for whatever gifts he wished. He replied with what a pious man ought to have considered: he asked for neither gold, nor silver, nor an estate, nor a belt, nor a gift [ms. Theod., a house], but that a single church be provided for those who had endured dangers on behalf of apostolic doctrine.

But when Valens recognized the written petition and tore up what had been written there, he ordered him to request something else. The other, however, gathering together the words of his prayer, said: “Receive it, emperor, and count it as a gift; I ask for nothing else. The Judge of all is the judge of my intention.”

[Col. 1119D] When Valens, having crossed the Bosporus, came into Thrace, he first remained at Constantinople, preparing for war. Then he sent Trajan with a mobile force against the barbarians. When Trajan returned defeated, Valens reproached him for weakness and attributed the outcome to cowardice. But Trajan, with the confidence appropriate to a very brave man, said:

“Emperor, it is not I who have been defeated; rather, you have lost the victory by resisting God and making his assistance more useful to the barbarians. For while he is being attacked by you, he fights on their behalf; and it is necessary to follow God’s victory. Do you not know whom you have expelled from the churches, or to whom you have handed them over?”

Arantheus and Victor, the masters of the soldiers, made this same declaration and warned the emperor not to become angry at that time.

They say also that the monk Isaac, who had a cell there, saw Valens entering the battle and cried out:

“Where are you going, emperor, you who are fighting against God, whom you do not have as your helper? For he himself has stirred up the barbarians against you, since you have raised many blasphemous tongues against him and expelled from the sacred houses those who sing psalms to him. Stop rebelling, and he will make the wars cease. Restore excellent shepherds to the flocks, and you will receive victory without battle. But if, doing none of these things, you persist in fighting, you will learn by experience how hard it is to kick against the goad (Acts 9:5). For you will neither return, nor will you fail to lose a great part of your army.”

Betranion, renowned for every virtue and bishop of all Scythia, having a heart inflamed with zeal for the faith, often rebuked Valens for the corruption of doctrine and the injustices [Col. 1120B] that he committed against the saints, crying out with the most holy David: “I spoke of your testimonies in the presence of kings, and I was not ashamed” (Psalm 118:46).

How, however, the barbarians were infected with the Arian disease, I shall now relate. At the time when they crossed the Hister and made peace with Valens, Eudoxius, the bishop then present [ms. Lyr., the bishop], suggested to the emperor that the Goths should enter into communion with him. “For,” he said, “having long been imbued with the rays of divine knowledge, they were nourished on apostolic doctrines.
