Communion in one doctrine will make the peace more secure.”

Valens approved this and demanded from the Gothic leaders that they also maintain agreement in doctrine. They replied that they could not change the teaching of their fathers. At that time Vulfilas was their bishop, whom they followed closely and whose words they regarded as immutable laws.

Eudoxius, bending him by words and money, induced him to make the barbarians embrace communion with the emperor, thus deceiving them by saying that the dispute concerned words, not a difference of doctrines. Consequently, the Goths to this day say that the Father is greater than the Son; but they do not at all tolerate anyone’s saying that the Son is a creature, although they appear to communicate with those who assert this.

THEODORET, Book IV, chapter 29 and following. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 31 and following, p. 693.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the return of Bishop Peter to Alexandria, his death, and the succession of Timothy

At this time, therefore, when the emperor departed from Antioch, those who were suffering persecution from him were encouraged [Col. 1120D], especially the Alexandrians. Peter had returned from Rome with letters from Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, confirming the faith of consubstantiality and strengthening Peter’s episcopal ordination.

After this, the people, taking courage, expelled Lucius and restored Peter. Lucius, however, sailed to Constantinople. Peter lived only a short time and left his brother Timothy as his successor.

SOCRATES, Book IV, chapter 30. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 37, p. 254.

## CHAPTER XV. How Valens was defeated and killed while fighting against the Goths

Now when the emperor Valens came to Constantinople on the thirtieth day of May, in his sixth consulship and the second of the younger Valentinian (A.D. 378), [Col. 1121A] he found the people in mourning. For the barbarians, roaming throughout Thrace, were even devastating the suburbs of Constantinople, and there was no one capable of resisting them effectively.

When they had come as far as the city walls, the afflicted city murmured, as though the emperor had summoned them there, since he neither resisted them nor brought the wars to an end. The circus games were therefore being held, and there they shouted to the emperor: “Give us weapons, and we shall fight.”

Inflamed by this, the emperor went out on the eleventh day of June, threatening that when he returned he would exact punishments from the citizens of Constantinople for their insults, since they appeared previously to have given support to Procopius; he even threatened to turn the city over with a plow.

He therefore led the citizens as far as Adrianople, which lies on the border of Macedonia.

[Col. 1121B] SOCRATES, Book IV, chapter 31. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 38, p. 254.

After sending the army ahead, he himself awaited victory in a certain village. But the soldiers, unable to withstand the attack of the barbarians, fled in some cases and were killed in others [p. 330]. [Col. 1122A] The barbarians then came to the village where Valens, having recognized the betrayal, was attempting to lie hidden and conceal himself. They set fire to it and burned down both the village and that enemy of piety.

THEODORET, Book IV, chapter 31. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 36, p. 195.

He met the end of his life on the ninth day of August, in the same consulship, that is, in the fourth year of the 289th Olympiad (A.D. 378). Some say that he was consumed by fire after fleeing into the village that the barbarians burned. Others report that, after changing his imperial clothing, he went to the infantry; when the cavalry had surrendered and refused to fight, the entire infantry was suddenly stabbed in the engagement. They say that Valens himself was also struck down by an unknown wound.

[Col. 1122B] He died in the fiftieth year of his life. He had reigned with his brother for thirteen years and, after his brother’s death, for three years. Such was the manner of his death.

SOCRATES, Book IV, chapter 31. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 38, p. 255.

# BOOK NINE

[Col. 1121]

331 ## CHAPTER I. How, after the death of Valens, the barbarians devastated Constantinople

[Col. 1121B]

After Valens had died, the barbarians once again came as far as the walls of Constantinople and devastated its suburbs. Therefore, the citizens carried whatever weapons they found and resisted the enemy as best they could.

For Dominica, the wife of the emperor Valens, according to military custom, distributed rewards from the public treasury to those who fought well. The Saracens also provided assistance; their queen, named Mavia, who was allied with the Romans [Mss. and ed. V., allied with the Romans’ people], had sent them.

SOCRATES, Book V, chapter 1, p. 259.

## CHAPTER II. On the kindness of Gratian and the correctness of his faith

Gratian, the son of Valentinian, had long held the scepter of Europe after his father’s death. When Valens died without offspring, he also assumed the kingdoms of Asia and Libya. Soon he demonstrated by his actions the piety he had received in his heart and dedicated the beginnings of his reign to the Lord of all things.

He therefore issued a law [Col. 1121D] ordering that the expelled shepherds return to their own sheepfolds and that the sacred basilicas be restored to those who followed the communion of Damasus. For Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, a man worthy of praise and remarkable in every respect, was always distinguished, hastening to say and do everything on behalf of apostolic doctrines; after Liberius, he assumed the governance of the Church.

The emperor therefore sent with this law a certain Sapor, then a highly distinguished military commander, and ordered that the preachers of Arian blasphemy be expelled from the divine enclosures like wild beasts, while everything was restored to the best shepherds and the sacred sheepfolds.

He decreed that this be observed throughout all the provinces.

THEODORET, Book V, chapters 1 and 2, p. 199.

[Col. 1122B] Thus Gratian, having obtained the empire together with the younger Valentinian, recalled everyone from exile and enacted a law that each religion might freely celebrate its sacred rites. He prohibited only the Eunomians, Photinians, and Manichaeans from the churches.

SOCRATES, Book V, chapter 2, p. 260.

## CHAPTER III. On the dispute that arose at Antioch between Paulinus and Meletius, and on Apollinaris of Laodicea and his sect

[Col. 1122C]

At that time a dispute of the following kind arose in Antioch, which presides over the East. Those laboring on behalf of the apostolic doctrines, as has already been said, were divided. Some, after the accusations brought against Eustathius and abhorring the Arian madness, celebrated the sacred rites among themselves and had Paulinus as their bishop. Others, after the ordination of Euzoius, assembled with Meletius and enjoyed his teaching.

In addition, Apollinaris of Laodicea assumed the episcopate of the other party for himself. While he put on the appearance of piety and pretended to preserve the apostolic doctrines, after a short time he appeared openly as an enemy.

For concerning the divine nature he employed adulterated arguments, generating certain degrees [p. 332] [Col. 1122D] of dignity and presuming to explain the mystery of the dispensation as incomplete; he also maintained that the rational soul, which governs the body, had been deprived of salvation. For if God the Word did not assume a soul according to the soul’s own rational nature, he neither provided it with a remedy nor bestowed honor upon it. Rather, the earthly body is adored by invisible powers, while the soul, made according to the divine image, remained in the lower realm, clothed in the insults of sin.

That madman asserted many other things in addition. At one time he too confessed that flesh had been assumed from the holy Virgin; at another, that it had descended from heaven together with God the Word; at another, that the Word himself had become flesh and had taken nothing from us. He joined many other empty and nonsensical tales to the sacred promises, which I have judged it superfluous to recount here.

By saying such things he not only filled his own followers with the plague, but also caused certain members of our community to share in this leprosy. After a short time, when they saw their own disgrace and the splendor of the Church, almost all returned and were deemed worthy to receive ecclesiastical communion. They did not, however, lay aside their former disease; rather, they secretly wounded many of the steadfast.

From this root there sprouted in the churches the doctrine of one nature of flesh and deity, as well as the doctrine that suffering is joined to the divinity of the Only-Begotten, along with whatever other disputes arose among peoples and priests. But these things happened later.

When Sapor, the master of the soldiers, arrived and displayed the emperor’s law, Paulinus admitted that he shared Damasus’s communion. Apollinaris also made the same promise, concealing his disease. The most sacred Meletius, living quietly, avoided their disputes.

Flavianus, then established in the rank of the presbyterate and exceedingly wise, first spoke to Paulinus when the master of the soldiers arrived:

“If you follow the communion of Damasus, friend, show us openly your agreement in doctrine. For while he confesses one substance of the Trinity, he openly proclaims three subsistences; yet, in the opposite direction, you destroy the subsistences of the Trinity. Show us, therefore, your agreement in doctrine, and receive the churches according to the laws [Ms. Lyr., according to the ecclesiastical laws].”

[Col. 1123C] After rebuking him with these words, he turned to Apollinaris and said:

“I am astonished, friend, that you resist the truth so shamelessly, when you plainly know that the praiseworthy Damasus says that our nature was completely assumed by God the Word, whereas you confess the contrary. You deprive our mind of salvation. But if we are speaking falsely in accusing you, deny now the novelty that has arisen from you; embrace the teaching of Damasus and accept the venerable sect [Mss., the venerable enclosures] of truth.”

With these arguments the exceedingly wise Flavianus refuted their presumption.

Meletius, however, the gentlest, most peaceful, and most modest of all, said to Paulinus:

“Since the Lord has entrusted me with the care of these sheep, and likewise entrusted you with the care of others, accept this responsibility and communicate with one another under the doctrine of piety. Let us join the flocks as friends and end the dispute over the episcopate. Let us feed the sheep together and jointly offer our care for them.

“But if the dispute concerns the seat, I too shall try to remove this contention. Let the holy Gospel be placed on the seat, and let us sit on either side of it. If I reach the end of life first, you alone shall be bishop; but if this happens to you first, I shall again care for the flock.”

When Meletius had spoken these words with complete gentleness, Paulinus did not agree to comply. Then the master of the soldiers, acting as judge between their words, handed the churches over to Meletius. Paulinus, however, remained bishop of the other sheep.

Apollinaris, deprived of the episcopate of the Church, openly and shamelessly proclaimed the novelty of his doctrine [Col. 1124A], displaying himself as the leader of the heresy. He himself frequently stayed in Laodicea. In Antioch, however, he had previously ordained Vitalis, a man adorned with an excellent way of life and nourished on apostolic doctrines [Ms. Lyr., instructed in them], but later corrupted and putrefied by this disease.

The most sacred Meletius appointed as shepherd of Tarsus that Diodorus whom we have already mentioned, who during that exceedingly fierce storm had preserved the ship of the Church from sinking, and entrusted him with the care of the people of Cilicia.

In Apamea he gave the episcopal charge to John. Although John shone by birth and nobility, he adorned his ancestors by his own virtues. Both his speech and his life, therefore, gave him distinction.

During the time of the storm he governed the number of his fellow believers, [Col. 1124B] having as a coworker the praiseworthy Stephen, whom the most sacred Meletius sent to other struggles. For when he learned that Germanicia had been corrupted by the disease of Eudoxius, he sent Stephen there as a most wise physician. He was full of every kind of Greek learning and stuffed with divine doctrines [Ms. Lyr., saturated with them]. Thus his hope was not disappointed: by using the gift of spiritual teaching, he changed wolves into sheep.

The great Eusebius, returning from exile, ordained Acacius, a man of the highest distinction, bishop in Beroea; Theodotus in Hierapolis, whose admirable way of life is still celebrated; Eusebius in Chalcis; and Isidore in our Cyrrhus.

For they say that he also ordained Eulogius bishop of Edessa. Eulogius had fought on behalf of the apostolic doctrines and had been sent into exile at Antinoe with Protogenes [Col. 1124C]. The most sacred Barses had already departed from this present light.

Finally, the holy Eusebius made Marinus bishop in the city of Doliche. At that time this small city possessed Arian madness. When Eusebius came there to install Marinus, a man adorned with many virtues, in the episcopal seat, a woman filled with the Arian plague threw a roof tile down upon him and severely crushed his head. Shortly afterward he departed this life for a better one.

As he was dying, he bound those present by oath not to exact punishment from the woman who had done this, imitating his Lord, who said concerning those crucifying him: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34), and also his fellow servant Stephen, who, after many stones had been thrown, cried out: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:59).

In this way the great Eusebius died. He who had escaped the barbarians of Thrace could not avoid the hands of impious heretics, but through their ferocity received the crown of martyrdom.

These events took place after the return of the bishops.

THEODORET, Book V, chapter 3. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapters 2 and 3, p. 200.

333 ## CHAPTER IV. On the command of Theodosius; how he was appointed by the emperor Gratian, sent to the Eastern Empire, benefited the orthodox, and confined the heretics

[Col. 1125A]

When Gratian learned that the barbarians were devastating Thrace, he left Italy and came to Phoenice [Ed. Frob. and Niv., Paeconia or Pannonia].

At that time Theodosius was highly renowned both because of the nobility of his parents and because of his own courage. For this reason, worn down by the envy of fellow governors, he was residing in Spain, where he had been born and raised.

When the emperor was uncertain what to do—for the barbarians, elevated by victory, appeared invincible—he believed that the war could be brought to an end under the command of Theodosius. He therefore suddenly summoned him from Spain, declared him master of the soldiers, and sent him with a mobile force against the barbarians.

Strengthened by faith, Theodosius set out confidently for Thrace. When he arrived and saw the barbarians, he arranged his army for battle. When the engagement took place, the barbarians, unable to withstand the attack, abandoned their battle lines. They fled, while the Romans followed them bravely. A vast slaughter of the barbarians then took place.

After many had been killed and a few had secretly crossed the Hister, the excellent commander, having dispersed the army through the neighboring cities, quickly returned to the emperor, so that he himself became the messenger of his own triumphs.

Yet, while the emperor marveled at what had happened, it did not seem credible even to him. For the envious were saying that Theodosius had also fled and had lost his army. He therefore asked that men be sent who could see the multitude of slain enemies.

Moved by these words, the emperor sent men to inspect what had happened and report back to him.

Meanwhile the excellent commander saw a divine vision, plainly shown to him by God himself. In a dream he saw that the holy Meletius, bishop of the city of Antioch, was clothing him in an imperial cloak [Col. 1125C] and placing a crown upon his head.

When he had seen this during the night, he reported it in the morning to one of his friends [Ed., clerics]. The man said that the dream was clear and contained nothing enigmatic or uncertain.

Only a few days later, those who had been sent to investigate the victory returned and reported that many thousands of the enemy had been killed. Therefore the emperor, rejoicing, made Theodosius emperor.

THEODORET, Books IV, V, and VI, p. 203.

In the consulship of Ausonius and Olibrius (A.D. 379), on the sixteenth day of January.

SOCRATES, Book V, chapter 2, p. 260.

Having entrusted to Theodosius part of Valens’s scepters, Gratian himself returned to Italy and sent Theodosius to the kingdoms assigned to him [Col. 1125D].

As soon as he assumed the empire, Theodosius thought above all about the concord of the Church and ordered the bishops of every episcopal see to assemble at Constantinople. The East alone was full of the Arian contagion; the West had remained free from this disease.

For Constantine the Elder, the son of Constantine the Great, and Constans the Younger had preserved their father’s faith intact. Again, the emperor Valentinian of the West had guarded the piety of the faith inviolate. The regions of the East, however, had been filled in many ways with this corruption.

For Arius, a presbyter of the city of Alexandria, had generated this blasphemy there. After him, Eusebius, Patrophilus, and Aetius, from Palestine; Paulinus and Gregory, from Phoenicia; Theodotus of Laodicea [Ms. Santheod., Theodolus]; and with them George; after these, Athanasius and Narcissus, from Cilicia; and many others nurtured the seeds that had been badly sown.

Constantius and Valens cooperated with these most wicked devotees. Therefore, for this sole reason, Theodosius ordered the bishops subject to his empire to assemble at Constantinople.

THEODORET, Book V, chapter 6, p. 205.

## CHAPTER V. How the Macedonians were again divided from the orthodox

Meanwhile, after the embassy sent to Liberius, the Macedonians for some time communicated without distinction with those who from the beginning had accepted the definition of the Nicene faith.

When the law of the emperor Gratian had granted religions permission to communicate as they wished, they were again divided. Having assembled at Antioch, they decided that the word “consubstantial” should be removed and that communion should not be maintained with those who venerated the Nicene faith.

Many, however, seeing their inconsistency, withdrew from them and joined the followers of consubstantiality.

SOCRATES, Book V, chapter 4, p. 261.

## CHAPTER VI. How the emperor Theodosius was baptized at Thessalonica

After Theodosius had defeated the barbarians in war, and they begged to be permitted to have the Romans as friends, he came to Thessalonica after accepting hostages as the basis of a treaty. There, when he fell ill, he was baptized by Acholius, bishop of that city, although from his forebears he followed Christian doctrine and the faith of the Council of Nicaea.

SOZOMEN, Book VII, chapter 4, p. 707.

At that time, wishing to be baptized because of his illness, he asked the bishop of Thessalonica what faith he held. The bishop replied that the Arian plague had not been able to enter Illyricum, but that they had preserved inviolate the faith of the Council of Nicaea from the beginning. Gladly accepting his words, Theodosius was baptized and freed from his illness.

SOCRATES, Book V, chapter 6, p. 262.

## CHAPTER VII. Theodosius’s profession of faith

The emperor considered that it would be better to declare to his subjects what faith he held, so that he would not appear to use force by suddenly compelling anyone unwilling to practice a religion. He therefore published a law at Thessalonica and posted it for the people of Constantinople.

This seemed appropriate, so that the written declaration, as if from a certain citadel of the city, might make his position manifest to all his subjects and to the other cities. The words of the law are as follows.

334 The Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius Augusti, to the people of the city of Constantinople.

“We desire all the peoples ruled by the governance of our Clemency to live in the religion that the divine Apostle Peter is declared to have handed down to the Romans, and that the religion transmitted from him to the present day makes known; and which the pontiff Damasus and Peter, bishop of Alexandria, a man of apostolic holiness, clearly follow. That is, in accordance with apostolic discipline and evangelical [Col. 1127A] teaching, we are to believe in one Godhead of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, under equal majesty and within the pious Trinity.

“Following this law, we order that they embrace the name of catholic Christians. As for the others, whom we judge demented and insane, we decree that they bear the disgrace of heretical doctrine [ed. V., madness], to be punished first by divine vengeance and afterward by the penalty of our judgment, which we shall assume by heavenly decree.”

Given on the third day before the Kalends of March at Thessalonica, in the fifth consulship of Gratian and the consulship of Theodosius Augusti (A.D. 380).

After enacting this, he shortly afterward traveled to Constantinople.

SOZOMEN, Book VII, chapter 4, p. 708.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the transfer of Gregory of Nazianzus to Constantinople

At that time Gregory of Nazianzus was transferred to Constantinople by common decree [Col. 1127B] of many bishops, and within the city he celebrated the sacred rites in a small oratory. Later, when the emperors joined a great basilica to that place, they called it Anastasia.

SOZOMEN, Book VII, chapter 5, p. 708.

## CHAPTER IX. On the basilica of Saint Anastasia

It is known to have been illumined not only by beauty and size, but also by the most evident manifestation of God. For divine power is recognized as having come to the aid of many there, both in dreams and openly, frequently assisting many who were sick and those who were meanwhile placed in perilous circumstances.

Some therefore believed that this was the holy Mary, Virgin and Mother of Christ, since she appeared to many in such clothing. They call the basilica Anastasia because, as I think, the doctrine of the Council of Nicaea, almost dead in Constantinople, rose again in that place through Gregory’s teaching.

I have nevertheless heard some truthful men report that, while the people were assembled there for the services, a pregnant woman fell from the upper portico and died. After a common prayer had been offered over her, she came back to life and was saved together with her child.

For this reason it received the highly remarkable name Anastasia, that is, “resurrection.”

SOZOMEN, Book VII, chapter 5, p. 708.

## CHAPTER X. How Theodosius expelled the Arians from the Church of Constantinople

Gregory, a most eloquent and venerable man, [Col. 1127D] recognizing that some were murmuring because he came from another city, avoided living in Constantinople when the emperor arrived.

The emperor, however, finding the churches in such a condition, considered how he might reconcile everyone and enlarge all the churches. He therefore suddenly sent a message to Demophilus, who at that time presided over the Arian religion:

“If you wish,” he said, “to believe according to the doctrine of the Council of Nicaea, let the people be united and receive peace.”

When Demophilus rejected this proposal, the emperor said:

“If you decline peace and concord, I also order you to flee from the sacred basilicas.”

When Demophilus heard this, and considered that it would be difficult to resist those in authority, he summoned the people into the church. Rising in the midst of them all, he addressed his subjects in these words:

“Brothers, it is written in the Gospel: ‘If they persecute you, flee from this city to another’ (Matthew 10:27). Since, therefore, the emperor needs the churches, know that tomorrow we shall celebrate our assembly outside the city.”

Having said this, he went out, though he did not understand the Gospel’s words in the way they were intended. For the command there is that, fleeing worldly habitation, people should seek the Jerusalem above.

Having gone out of the city, therefore, he held meetings before the gates. Lucius, who had been expelled from Alexandria and was then living in Constantinople, went out with him.

Thus, unable to endure the concord of Theodosius, after forty years they abandoned the churches that they had held by force. They left the city in the fifth consulship of Gratian and the first of Theodosius (A.D. 380), in the month of November. After this had been done, the followers of the Nicene faith recovered the churches.

SOCRATES, Book V, chapter 7, p. 263.

## CHAPTER XI. On the cunning of Eunomius

When Eunomius had withdrawn from his own clergy during the time of Valens, he lived by himself in Bithynia. He was a cunning man, skilled in speaking, and many people flocked to him: some wishing to test him, others wishing to hear what he would say.

His fame reached the emperor, with whom Eunomius himself also wished to converse; but the Augusta Flacilla detained him by her prayers. For she was exceedingly faithful and preserved the rights of the Nicene doctrine in their integrity. She feared that the emperor, as often happens, might be captivated by the eloquence of a cunning man and easily fall into his sect.

SOZOMEN, Book VII, chapter 6, p. 710.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Council of Constantinople against the Macedonians
Meanwhile, when one hundred and fifty bishops had assembled at Constantinople, the emperor ordered that no one should reveal who that great Meletius was. For he wished, in accordance with the memory of his dream, that the man should be identified to him. Accordingly, when that entire multitude of bishops had entered the imperial palace, leaving everyone else behind he ran to the great Meletius and, like a son who loves his father and, after a long time, has obtained the sight of his father, embraced him and kissed his eyes, lips, breast, and head. He also clasped the right hand with which Meletius had crowned him in his dream, and explained to him the vision he had seen. After he had appropriately greeted the others as well, he asked them, as Fathers, to deliberate about present affairs (THEODORETUS, Book V, chapter 7, p. 206), and to ordain a bishop for the city of Constantinople.

Hoping that the Macedonians might be united, he also summoned their bishops. Accordingly, the following assembled concerning the faith of consubstantiality: Timothy of Alexandria; Cyril of Jerusalem, who after his repentance had assented to the doctrine of consubstantiality; Meletius of Antioch; and Acholius of Thessalonica, together with many others, so that the number of one hundred and fifty was completed. Elusius of Cyzicus presided over the Macedonians, and Marcianus over Lampsacus; there were thirty-six of them altogether, most of whom appeared to come from the cities of the Hellespont. They assembled, therefore, in the consulship of Eucharius and Evagrius (A.D. 381), in the month of May.

The emperor and the bishops of his party then labored to unite Elusius and his followers to the Church. They reminded them of the embassy which they had sent to Liberius, then bishop of the city of Rome, through Eustathius, and of the fact that they had formerly communicated with him of their own accord; it would not be honorable suddenly to exchange what had previously been approved. But they disregarded his admonitions and open reproaches, and chose to follow the Arian plague rather than call the Trinity consubstantial. Having confessed these things, they departed from Constantinople and wrote to one another that none of them should assent to the doctrine of the Council of Nicaea. SOCRATES, Book V, chapter 8, p. 264.

## CHAPTER XIII. The ordination of Maximus the Cynic and his deposition; the proper ordination of Nectarius; and the canons established at that synod

[Col. 1129B]

Gregory, who at that time governed the Church of Constantinople, was intending to return to Nazianzus. Since the episcopal see of the Church of Constantinople was therefore vacant, Timothy of Alexandria, the successor of Peter, ordained a certain Maximus the Cynic as bishop, although he had only recently tonsured him. For he was also stuffed with the madness of Apollinaris. But the most holy men assembled at Constantinople did not tolerate this evil. While the Egyptians had chiefly separated themselves on account of his ordination, they were celebrating the sacred offices with Gregory.

Grieving deeply that the division had been renewed, Gregory begged them all to seek a man worthy of praise whom they could ordain as bishop. They then accepted his words and appointed Nectarius, distinguished by the nobility of his birth, as bishop of the city of Constantinople. But Maximus, afflicted by the contagion of Apollinaris, they stripped of his episcopal dignity and cast out. THEODORETUS, Book V, chapter 8, p. 206.

At that time they also issued the rule that the bishop of Constantinople should possess the privileges of honor after the bishop of Rome, because it is New Rome. They again confirmed the Nicene faith and established patriarchs, assigning provinces so that the bishops of each diocese would not go to churches belonging to others. During the time of persecution this had originally been done indiscriminately.

They therefore assigned the greatest city and Thrace to Nectarius; the Pontic diocese to Helladius, who succeeded Basil; Caesarea of Cappadocia to Gregory of Nyssa, Basil’s brother; they also granted Troilus of Melitene in Armenia the rights of a patriarch; Amphilochius received the Asian diocese of Iconium; Optimum received Antioch of Pisidia; and they assigned Egypt to Timothy of Alexandria. They entrusted the governance of the Eastern Churches to their bishops, Pelagius of Laodicea and Diodore of Tarsus, while reserving the privileges of the Church of Antioch, which they then granted to the present Meletius.

They likewise determined that if anything arose in any province, it should be settled by the council of that province. In all these matters the emperor also gave his assent. SOCRATES, Book V, chapter 8, p. 265.

[Col. 1130A] After a short time had passed, the holy Meletius died and was buried by all the wise with the greatest praises. THEODORETUS, Book V, chapter 8, p. 206.

In the following summer, several bishops again returned to Constantinople on ecclesiastical business. There they received a synodical letter from the Western bishops inviting them to Rome, so that a great council might be celebrated there. They, however, avoided the journey, as though it would yield no benefit, but sent a letter to Damasus and the other bishops, which I have judged necessary to append below for the sake of clearer information. THEODORETUS, Book V, chapter 8, p. 207.

## CHAPTER XIV. Letter of the Council of Constantinople to Pope Damasus and the Western bishops

[Col. 1130B]

To our honorable and venerable lords, brothers and fellow ministers, Damasus, Ambrose, Brittonius, Valerianus, Acholius, Basil, and the other holy bishops gathered in great Rome: the holy synod of orthodox bishops assembled in the great city of Constantinople sends greetings in the Lord.

It is perhaps unnecessary to inform and recount to your Reverence, as though you were unaware, the multitude of sufferings repeatedly inflicted upon us by Arian power. For we do not believe that your holiness has been so negligent that you still need to learn about those whom we know you grieve with. Nor did such storms constrain us that they could have remained hidden because of their smallness. The time of persecution is not new; it still preserves the memory of the past, not only in those who suffered but also in those who share the lot of those whose own sufferings they reveal.

Only yesterday, so to speak—or today—those released from the bonds of exile have returned to their own churches after countless tribulations. The bodies of others who died in exile have been brought back. Some, returning from exile but detained by the burning fury of the heretics, endured in their own country things more bitter than those they had suffered in exile; they were buried beneath stones by them, like blessed Stephen. Others, tortured by various punishments, are still known to bear the marks of Christ and wounds upon their bodies.

Who could count individually the financial losses, the deprivation of honors, the confiscations and machinations against individuals, the injuries and imprisonments? All our tribulations have truly been multiplied beyond number. This is just, because we have sinned greatly. Or rather, the merciful Lord wished to train us through the multitude of our sufferings.

For these things, therefore, we give thanks to God: because through such great tribulations he chastises his servants, and according to the multitude of his mercies he has led us back again to refreshment. We therefore needed time and very great labor, so that the correction of the churches might come about; so that, as with a long illness, care applied gradually might restore their former health of piety. In this way we shall be thought to have been freed from the fiercest persecutions and to have restored anew the churches that had long been held by heretics.

Nevertheless, wolves are still a grave danger to us. After they have been driven from the folds, they snatch sheep from the very pastures, striving to hold assemblies, stirring up the peoples, and showing no lack of zeal in harming the Church. As we have said, time was therefore necessary for this work.

Since, however, out of fraternal charity toward us you have, by God’s will, held a synod in the city of Rome and summoned us there as your own members by letters from the emperor beloved of God—so that, whereas we had previously been devoted only to tribulations, under the pious concord of the emperors you might not reign without us, but that we too might reign with you, according to the apostolic saying (I Cor. 4:8)—our wish was that, if possible, we might all leave our churches together and join you in a useful desire.

For who will give us wings like those of a dove, so that we may fly and rest with you (Ps. 54:7)? But since this would have left the churches entirely without protection, when their rest had only recently begun, and since the matter was impossible for very many—for we had gathered in the city of Constantinople because of the letter sent to us the previous year by your charity after the Council of Aquileia, addressed to the emperor beloved of God, Theodosius, and had hurried to Constantinople for this sole purpose, carrying with us only the agreement of the bishops who had remained in the provinces—we neither expected nor had heard beforehand that a longer journey would be required before we came to Constantinople.

Moreover, since the brief period of the truce made it impossible for us either to prepare for a long journey or to notify all our communicants residing in the provinces and obtain their agreement, it appeared that these and many other considerations prevented the arrival of a great number. Accordingly, in proportion to the actual circumstances [ed., “according to the effect,” instead of “in proportion to the circumstances”], and as a demonstration of your charity toward us, we have done the following: we have eagerly begged our most venerable and beloved brothers and fellow ministers, the bishops Cyriacus, Eusebius, and Priscianus, to undertake the journey to you. Through them we display our peaceful will and intention of unity, and we make known our zeal for the most salutary faith.

For we have willingly endured persecutions, tribulations, imperial threats, the cruelties of judges, and every other temptation of the heretics for the sake of the evangelical faith, which is known to have been confirmed at Nicaea in Bithynia by the three hundred and eighteen Fathers. We trust that this faith is pleasing both to you and to us and to all who do not overturn the word of the true faith. We know it to be most ancient, following baptism, and teaching us to believe in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

For we believe in one divinity, power, and substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; equal honor and dignity; and coeternal dominion in three most perfect subsistences, or three perfect persons. Thus there is no place for the weakness of the Sabellians through confusion of the subsistences or destruction of their properties; nor may the blasphemy of the Eunomians, Arians, and Pneumatomachi—that is, those who resist the Spirit—prevail, by which the substance, nature, or divinity is divided, and some final element, either created or of another substance, is assigned to the uncreated, consubstantial, and coeternal Trinity.

As for the doctrine of Christ’s incarnation, we preserve it without any violation. We do not accept an incarnation without a soul, without a mind, or an incomplete dispensation of the flesh; rather, we know that the Word of God existed perfect before the ages, and that in the last days he became a perfect human being for our salvation.

Thus, the matters of faith which we openly proclaim may be summarized as follows. You will be able to learn more about them if you deign to read both the tome composed at Antioch by the synod established there and what is known to have been issued the preceding year at Constantinople by the universal synod. In these documents we professed the faith at greater length and issued written anathemas against the recent innovations of heresies.

As for the particular administration of the churches, as you know, ancient law has prevailed, as has the decision of the holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea, according to each province: if the bishops wish it, they may celebrate ordinations with neighboring bishops for the sake of usefulness. You should understand that the other churches among us have consequently been built according to these principles, and that the priests of the distinguished churches have approved them.

As for the new Church of the city of Constantinople, so to speak, we have dragged it from the jaws of the lion, pierced through by the blasphemies of the heretics. Through the mercies of God, we ordained the most venerable and God-beloved bishop Nectarius before the universal council, with common agreement, in the presence also of the emperor Theodosius, beloved of God, and with the whole clergy and the entire city jointly deciding the matter.

In the ancient and truly apostolic Church of Antioch in Syria, where the venerable name of Christian was first used, the most venerable and God-beloved bishop Flavianus was canonically ordained by those who had gathered from the entire province and Eastern diocese, with the whole Church deciding together and honoring this man as though with one voice. The common council received this ordination as lawful.

In the mother of all the churches, established at Jerusalem, we declare that the most venerable and God-beloved Cyril is bishop. He had formerly been canonically ordained by the provincial bishops and had suffered many struggles at various times because of the Arians.

Since these things have been carried out among us so lawfully and canonically, we ask that your Reverence rejoice with us, with spiritual love intervening, together with fear of the Lord. Through these, human offense is removed and the building up of the churches is placed above all else. Thus, when we are united in the word of faith and Christian charity is strengthened among us, we have ceased to say what the Apostle condemned: “I am of Paul,” “I am of Apollos,” and “I am of Cephas” (II Cor. 1:12), while all of us clearly appear [ms. Lyr., “seem”] to belong to Christ, who is not divided among us. If, with God’s help, we preserve the body of the Church without schism, we shall stand with confidence before the tribunal of the Lord.

These men wrote against the madness of Arius, Aetius, and Eunomius, and also against Sabellius, Photinus, Marcellus, Paul of Samosata, and Macedonius. They likewise openly rejected the innovation of Apollinaris, saying: “We preserve the incarnations of the Lord without violation; we do not accept an incarnation without a soul, without a mind, or an incomplete dispensation of the flesh.”

Moreover, Damasus, most worthy of all praise, recognizing that this heresy had arisen, rejected not only Apollinaris but also his disciple Timothy. He reported this in his own letter to the bishops governing the East, which I have taken care to append below. THEODORETUS, Book V, p. 208.

## CHAPTER XV. Letter of Damasus concerning the condemnation of Apollinaris, addressed to Timothy

Because your charity has shown due reverence to the apostolic see, you have rendered us, most beloved sons, a very great service. For although we hold, in some manner, the helm of the Church in which the holy Apostle sat and taught, and which we have received, we nevertheless confess that we are inferior in honor. Therefore we hasten in every way to attain the glory of his blessedness.

Know, then, that some time ago we condemned the profane and unlearned Timothy, disciple of the heretic Apollinaris, together with his impious doctrine, and that henceforth we do not permit his remnants to prevail in any manner. But if that ancient serpent, struck once and a second time, revives for its own punishment, and, although expelled from the Church, does not cease to test some of the faithful with its deadly poisons, avoid this corruption as something pestilential. Thus, mindful of the apostolic faith, which was set forth especially in writing by the Fathers at Nicaea, may you remain steadfast and unchanging in the faith, and may you not allow your clergy or people to hear from him empty words and destructive questions.

We have already once established the rule [Ed. V., “we have learned”] that anyone who recognizes himself as a Christian must preserve what is known to have been handed down by the Apostles, as the holy Paul says: “If anyone announces to you anything beyond what you received, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1:9).

For Christ, the Son of God, our Lord, bestowed complete salvation upon the human race through his own passion, so that he might free the whole human being, subject to sins, from all sins. If anyone says that he possessed anything less either in divinity or in humanity, he has shown himself, filled with the spirit of the devil, to be a son of Gehenna.

Why, then, do you ask me again for Timothy’s condemnation? He was condemned here, by the judgment of the apostolic see, in the presence also of Peter, bishop of the city of Alexandria, together with his teacher Apollinaris; and on the day of judgment he will endure the torments and deserved punishments. If he persuades some people with lesser concessions, as though he had some kind of hope, he who altered the true hope in the confession of Christ, let them know that they too will perish with him, when the ecclesiastical regulations resound against him.

May God keep you safe, most beloved sons. THEODORETUS, Book V, chapter 10, p. 212.

## CHAPTER XVI. Decrees of the apostolic see against various heresies

Or, according to the manuscript of Saint-Théodard: The Catholic confession of faith which Pope Damasus sent to Bishop Paulinus in Macedonia, who was in Thessalonica.

But they also collected certain other materials in eminent Rome and wrote against various heresies, which I have judged necessary to append to this work.

1. Since after the Council of Nicaea an error arose such that some dared with profane lips to say that the Holy Spirit was made through the Son, we anathematize those who do not proclaim with complete freedom that the Holy Spirit exists with the Father and the Son, of one and the same substance and power.

2. Likewise, we anathematize those who followed the error of Sabellius, saying that the Father is the same as the Son.

3. We anathematize Arius and Eunomius, who, although they differ in words, nevertheless with similar impiety affirm that the Son and the Holy Spirit are creatures.

4. We anathematize the Macedonians, who, deriving from an Arian root, changed not their impiety but their terminology.

5. We anathematize Photinus, who, renewing the heresy of the Ebionites, confesses that our Lord Jesus Christ is from Mary alone.

6. We also anathematize those who profess that there are two sons: one before the ages, and another after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin.

7. We anathematize those who affirm, in place of a rational soul, that the Word of God was changed into human flesh. For the Son himself, the Word of God, was not made in his body in place of a rational and intellectual soul; rather, he assumed and saved our soul—that is, a rational and intellectual soul—without sin.

[Col. 1134D] 8. We also anathematize those who say that the Word of God was separated from the Father by generation and corruption and without subsistence [Ed. Niv., “substance”], and who blasphemously assert that he must be terminated [or: circumscribed].

[Note: At this point the manuscript of Saint-Théodard inserts the number nine and alters the subsequent numbers.]

We regard those who have migrated from one church to another as excluded from our communion until they return to the cities in which they were originally ordained.

9. If someone, having migrated from another place, was ordained to the post of a living man, he who abandoned his own city shall remain without the dignity of the priesthood until his successor rests in the Lord.

10. If anyone does not say that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit always exist, let him be accursed.

[Col. 1135A] 11. If anyone does not say that the Son was born from the Father—that is, from his divine substance—let him be accursed.

12. If anyone does not say that the Son of God is true God, as his Father is true God, and that he is almighty, all-knowing, and equal to the Father, let him be accursed.

13. If anyone says that, while dwelling in the flesh, the Son of God, when he was on earth, was not in heaven and with the Father, let him be accursed.

14. If anyone says that in the passion of the cross the Son of God, who is God, suffered pain, and not the flesh with the soul with which the form of a servant was clothed and which he assumed for himself, as the holy Scripture says, let him be accursed.

15. If anyone does not say that, in the flesh which he assumed, he sits at the right hand of the Father and in that same flesh will come to judge the living and the dead, let him be accursed.

[Col. 1135B] 16. If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit is truly and properly from the Father, just as the Son, the Word of God, is from the divine substance and is God, let him be accursed.

17. If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit is almighty, all-knowing, and present everywhere, just as the Son and the Father are, let him be accursed.

18. If anyone says that the Holy Spirit is a creature or was made through the Son, let him be accursed.

19. If anyone does not say that the Father made all things through the Son and through the Holy Spirit—that is, visible and invisible things—let him be accursed.

20. If anyone does not say that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one deity, power, divinity, might, glory, dominion, sovereignty, will, and truth, let him be accursed.

[Col. 1135C] 21. If anyone does not say that the three persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are true, equal, ever-living, encompassing all things, almighty, judging all things, giving life to all things, creating all things, and saving all things, let him be accursed.

22. If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit is to be adored by every creature, just as the Son and the Father are, let him be accursed.

23. If anyone has a right understanding of the Father and the Son but does not believe rightly concerning the Holy Spirit, he is a heretic. For all heretics who think wrongly about the Son of God and the Holy Spirit are proved to remain in the unbelief of the Jews and Gentiles.

24. If anyone divides God the Father, saying that there is also God the Son and God the Holy Spirit, affirming that they are called gods and not one God because of the one deity and power which we believe and know to belong to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—one God—while removing the Son and the Holy Spirit and supposing that only the Father is God, let him be accursed.

For the name “gods” has been given and assigned by God to angels and to all the saints. But concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because of their one and equal divinity, it is handed down [ms. Lyr., “is believed”] and signified not as the name of gods but as the name of our God. Thus we believe that we are baptized in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit alone, and not in the names of archangels and angels, as the heretics, Jews, and Gentiles foolishly claim.

This, therefore, is the salvation of Christians: that, believing in the Trinity—that is, in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—and being baptized in it, we believe that in it there is one deity, power, divinity, and substance.

These things were done while Gratian was still alive. THEODORETUS, Book V, chapters 10 and 11, p. 213.

## CHAPTER XVII. How Theodosius had the body of Paul, bishop of Constantinople, brought back from Ancyra

Meanwhile the emperor Theodosius had the body of Paul, bishop of Constantinople, brought back from Ancyra. The prefect Philip, on account of Macedonius, had sent Paul into exile and had caused him to be strangled at Cucusus in Armenia. Receiving the body with the greatest honor and reverence, Theodosius buried it in the church that is now known by his name, which the Macedonians had then occupied after being separated from the Arians. They were expelled by the emperor because they refused to follow his faith. SOCRATES, Book V, chapter 9, p. 266.

In that basilica many people, unaware of the truth, believe that the Apostle Paul lies there, especially women and the common people. At this time the relics of Meletius were also brought back to Antioch and are known to have been buried beside the tomb of the martyr Babylas. It is said that, by order of the emperor and with all the cities providing assistance, his body was brought back along the entire route to Antioch with psalmody and due honor. SOZOMEN, Book VII, chapter 10, p. 716.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The inauguration of the emperor Arcadius

[Col. 1136C] Meanwhile the emperor Theodosius designated his son Arcadius as Augustus, in the consulship of Merobaudes for the second time and Saturninus (A.D. 383), on the sixteenth day of January. Not long afterward, in the same consulship, in the month of June [ms. Lyr., “July,”] bishops of every religious party were present from every direction. SOCRATES, Book V, chapter 10, p. 267.

## CHAPTER XIX. How, after examining the heretics, Theodosius expelled them all and supported only the orthodox

Meanwhile the emperor summoned Nectarius and discussed with him what should be done so that Christianity would not be divided but the whole Church would be united. He said:

“The question separating the churches must be examined. When disagreement withdraws, concord will gather the churches together.”

When Nectarius heard this, he reflected on it. He summoned Agelius, then bishop of the Novatians, as a partner in the faith, and told him of the emperor’s desire. Although Agelius was venerable in other matters, he was unable to give an account of the doctrine. He therefore appointed his lector, named Sisinnius, to present the argument in his place—a man eloquent and experienced in practical matters, and thoroughly knowledgeable not only in the deepest points of sacred literature but also in philosophical doctrines.

Sisinnius said that disputation would not merely fail to unite the schisms; it would also bring the heresies into sharper contention. He therefore gave Nectarius the following advice. He knew well that the ancient Fathers had avoided assigning the beginning of subsistence to the Son of God, because they had perceived him to be coeternal with the Father.

He therefore advised him to avoid argumentative controversies, to bring forward testimony from ancient tradition, and to ask the leaders of the heresies whether they wished to speak about the ancient teachers of the Church who had flourished before the division, or whether they would reject them as strangers to Christianity. If they denied them, they should be challenged: “Then dare to anathematize them.” If they dared to do this, they would be expelled by the people. This would make the victory of truth manifest.

But if they were not offended by the earliest teachers, Sisinnius said: “It will be our task to provide the books of the ancients, by which our doctrine may be strengthened through their testimony.”

When Nectarius had willingly listened to Sisinnius speaking, he hurried to the palace and told the emperor the advice he had received. After considering the proposal, the emperor wisely arranged the matter. He then summoned the leaders of the heresies and asked whether they accepted as teachers of the Church those who had existed before the time of the division.

Since they did not deny them but honored them as teachers, the emperor asked them again whether the testimony of these men concerning Christian doctrine pleased them. When the leaders of the heresies and their disputants heard this—for many of them were prepared for contests of argument—they were greatly perplexed in their response.

A great disagreement broke out among them: some said that the emperor’s proposal was good; others, thinking more carefully, saw that it did not serve their purpose, since the others appeared to hold differing views about the books of the ancients. They could not agree among themselves. They were divided not only against other heresies but also among themselves, although they had previously appeared to belong to one heresy.

Thus their shared wickedness was divided like the tongues of the ancient giants, and their tower was utterly overthrown. The emperor, recognizing their confusion and seeing that they trusted only in disputation and not in the ancient interpretations, proceeded by another route. He ordered them to set forth in writing the boundary of the faith of each religion.

The clever men of each heresy then carefully shaping their words wrote down their own doctrine. A day was appointed on which the bishops would assemble at the palace. Nectarius and Agelius were present as leaders of the consubstantial faith; Demophilus represented the Arians; Eunomius himself represented the Eunomians; and Elusius of Cyzicus represented the Macedonians.

The emperor received those who had assembled and the writings of each doctrine, then withdrew and prayed earnestly that God would assist him in choosing the truth. After reading through the writing of each doctrine, he condemned all the others as introducing division into the Trinity. He suddenly tore them apart and accepted only the doctrine of consubstantiality with praise.

This occasioned the Novatians, who were acting rightly, once again to have churches within the city. The emperor, admiring their agreement concerning the faith, ordered by law that they should retain their own houses of prayer and possess the privileges of their Church and faith.

The leaders of the other religions, however, because of their disagreement, came under the reproach of their own people. They departed in anguish and confusion, comforting one another by letter so that they would not be distressed because many were leaving them and approaching the faith of consubstantiality. They said: “Many are called, but few are chosen.” Yet they certainly did not say this when by their power they were gathering a great multitude to themselves. SOCRATES, Book V, chapter 10, p. 267.

Meanwhile the emperor enacted by law that the heretics should possess neither churches nor the right to teach about the faith, nor should they ordain bishops or others. He ordered some to be expelled from the cities, while permitting others to remain without honor and without enjoying the common civic privileges. In addition, he wrote severe punishments against them into the law, although he did not carry them out. He was concerned that through this they should become united, rather than be subjected to punishment. SOZOMEN, Book VII, chapter 12, p. 719.

## CHAPTER XX. The schism between the Easterners and the Egyptians on account of Flavianus of Antioch

But even those who defended the faith of the Council of Nicaea were not entirely free from sorrow. The Antiochenes avoided those who had been present at the council. The Egyptians, Arabs, and Cypriots said that Flavianus should be expelled from Antioch. The Palestinians, Phoenicians, and Syrians, however, labored on Flavianus’s behalf. We shall relate the outcome of these matters in its proper place.

At the time when the synods were being discussed at Constantinople [Col. 1138C] [ms. Lyr. and ed. V., “this synod”], the following events occurred in the West. Maximus rose from the regions of Britain against the Roman empire and brought war upon Gratian, who was engaged in fighting the Alamanni. In Italy, while Valentinian was still a very young boy, Probus, a former consul and prefect, managed affairs.

Justina, the mother of Valentinian, was an Arian. While her husband was alive, she had not been able to harm the orthodox; but after his death, when her son was still very young, she came to Milan and became hostile to Ambrose the bishop, to such a degree that she ordered him to be sent into exile. SOCRATES, Book V, chapters 10 and 11, p. 269.

When Ambrose was ordered to leave the Church, he said: “I do not do this willingly, lest I seem to hand the sheepfolds over to wolves or to those who blaspheme God. If this pleases you, kill me here; in this place I willingly receive death.” THEODORETUS, Book V, chapter 13, p. 217.

When the people, who loved Ambrose with exceptional devotion, protested and strongly resisted those who were dragging him into exile, Justina, becoming even more indignant, summoned Benivolus, then quaestor, and ordered him to publish quickly the law that confirmed the faith issued at Rimini. Since he refused to do this—for he was orthodox—she invited him with higher belts of office. Benivolus, however, unfastened his belt and threw it at the feet of the Augusta, saying that he wanted neither that honor nor any greater one as the reward for impiety. When he completely refused to do this, others were found who would serve wicked commands. SOZOMEN, Book VII, chapter 13, p. 720.

340 ## CHAPTER XXI. How Justina persecuted Ambrose, and concerning the death of Gratian and the invasion of Maximus

[Col. 1139A]

Meanwhile word was brought that Gratian had been killed by the treachery of the tyrant Maximus. Andragathius, the general of Maximus, was carried in a litter in order to kill Gratian. He spread the following report among the people: that Gratian’s wife was hurrying to meet her husband at the city of Lyon in Gaul, as he crossed the river.

Gratian, believing that his wife was truly coming—the woman whom he had recently married—did not guard against the plot. Like a blind man falling into a pit, he fell into the hands of the enemy. When Gratian arrived, supposedly to meet his wife’s carriage, Andragathius suddenly leapt out and treacherously killed him.

He died in the consulship of Merobaudes and Saturninus (A.D. 383), in the fifteenth year of his reign and the twenty-fourth year of his life. After this had happened, Justina’s anger against Ambrose temporarily subsided. Valentinian, although unwilling, yielded to the empire of Maximus, compelled by the circumstances of necessity.

Probus, fearing the power of Maximus, then left Italy for Illyricum and stayed at Thessalonica in Macedonia. SOCRATES, Book V, chapter 11, p. 270.

When Maximus heard what was again being done against Ambrose, the eloquent preacher of truth, he wrote to Valentinian that the war being waged against the churches should cease. He urged him not to abandon his father’s piety, and he added threats of war, saying that if Valentinian did not desist, he would fulfill his words by deeds.

Accordingly, he took an army and came to Milan, where Valentinian was then staying. Recognizing his invasion, Valentinian fled to Illyricum, learning by experience what evils he was suffering because of his mother’s counsel. THEODORETUS, Book V, chapter 14, p. 217.

Theodosius, having heard what Justina had done and what had been written by the tyrant, replied in writing to Valentinian, who was fleeing, that it was no wonder that terror was increasing for the emperor but power for the tyrant, since the emperor had rebelled against piety while the tyrant was lending assistance to piety. Therefore, the former was fleeing unarmed, while the latter was arming himself against an unarmed man. THEODORETUS, book V, chapter 15, p. 217.

Then the emperor Theodosius, placed in the greatest anxiety, prepared an army against the tyrant, fearing lest the tyrannical conspiracy should also prevail against the younger Valentinian. At that time an embassy from the Persians was also present, seeking peace. During this period a son, Honorius, was born to him by his wife Placilla, in the consulship of Richomer and Clearchus (A.D. 384), on the ninth day of September; in that consulship Agelius, bishop of the Novatians, also died. SOCRATES, book V, chapter 12, p. 271.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the death of Timothy of Alexandria and the ordination of Theophilus

In the following consulship, that of Arcadius Augustus for the first time and of Bauto (A.D. 385), when Timothy, bishop of the city of Alexandria, had died, Theophilus assumed the episcopate. [Col. 1140A] After a year, when Demophilus, the Arian bishop, had died, the Arians ordained for themselves a certain Marinus as bishop. He did not, however, live long; under him the Arian religion was divided. After his death, they brought Dorotheus from Antioch in Syria and had him as their pontiff. SOCRATES, book V, chapter 12, p. 271.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Theodosius’s battle against Maximus and his victory

Thus, hastening against Maximus, the emperor left his son Arcadius as emperor at Constantinople. When he had come to Thessalonica, he found Valentinian’s judges in the deepest sorrow, because they had accepted the tyrant as emperor under the pressure of necessity. Theodosius, however, neither openly rejected nor accepted Maximus’s embassy; nevertheless, he could not tolerate the Roman empire’s being placed under a tyrant. Taking his entire army, he proceeded toward Milan, where Maximus also was.

Meanwhile, the Arians established at Constantinople, sowing various opinions among the people, said both that the emperor had lost his army and that he himself had been subjected to the tyrant’s commanders, along with many other claims that enemies commonly blurt out in accordance with the desire of their wickedness. Thus, because they repeatedly heard these things, the people came to believe them already not as opinions but as facts. Inflamed by these Arian speeches, the people burst into a kind of irrational boldness and burned down the house of the bishop Nectarius, in the second consulship of Theodosius and of Cynegius (A.D. 388).

But when the emperor Theodosius attacked the tyrant, Maximus’s soldiers recognized the presence of the imperial army and the arrival of his standards. They were unable to withstand even the force of his reputation; instead, they seized the tyrant and immediately brought him to Theodosius in chains. He was put to death in that same consulship, on the twenty-seventh day of August. Andragathius, who had killed Gratian, threw himself into a neighboring river and died.

Then the emperors Valentinian and Theodosius, having accomplished their victory, came to Rome. Honorius was also with them, still a very young boy. After the victory over Maximus, Theodosius had summoned him from the city of Constantinople.

While they were staying in Rome and celebrating festivals in honor of the victory, the emperor Theodosius displayed his goodness toward Symmachus, the former consul. Symmachus was regarded as one of the foremost among the senators and was remarkable for his mastery of Roman eloquence; many of his books are also extant. He had written a panegyric of Maximus and recited it, and for this he later seemed liable to a charge of treason. Fearing death, he took refuge in a church.

The emperor, however, being of the most perfect Christian character, honored not only the priests of his own faith but also the Novatians, who adhered very closely to the decrees of his faith. Therefore, when Leontius, then the Roman bishop of the Novatian Church, requested this favor, he released Symmachus from the charge. When Symmachus had obtained pardon, he composed an apologetic—that is, a book of satisfaction—during the reign of the emperor Theodosius. SOCRATES, book V, chapters 12, 13, and 14, p. 271.

## 341. CHAPTER XXIV. How the emperor Theodosius removed the robberies carried out in Rome through the bakeries, and concerning the law enacted against adulterous women

[Col. 1141A]

Thus the emperor Theodosius, while residing in Rome, greatly benefited the city, providing some things and usefully removing others. He prohibited two practices, however, that were especially disgraceful.

From the beginning, there had been in the city of Rome houses built on a vast scale in which bread was made for the supply of the entire city. In time, the managers of these establishments turned the public bakeries into places of robbery. Since mills had been established in underground locations, they set up shops along each side of them and made prostitutes stand there, so that through them they might deceive very many people—some who came for bread, and others who hurried there to indulge in the disgrace of lust. By a mechanical device, people fell from the shop into the mill. This happened especially to foreigners. In this way, many who had labored up to old age were not permitted to leave, their relatives believing that they had died.

A soldier of the emperor Theodosius fell into such a snare. When he had been shut up in the mill and was not allowed to leave, he drew his sword and killed those who were preventing him. Terrified, they then let the soldier go. When the emperor learned of this, he put the managers to death with punishments and also ordered the bakeries themselves to be completely destroyed.

He abolished another practice of this kind. If a woman had been caught in adultery, she was not corrected; rather, she was handed over to increase the sin. They shut her in a narrow brothel and admitted men to fornicate with her. At the hour when she was being joined to them in disgrace, bells were struck, so that by that sound her dishonor might be made known.

When the emperor heard of this, he would not permit it to continue. He ordered the brothels themselves to be destroyed and decreed that the adulteress be punished by other penalties. After these things, leaving Valentinian at Rome, he himself returned with Honorius to Constantinople, in the consulship of Dacianus and Symmachus (A.D. 391), on the tenth day of November. SOCRATES, book V, chapter 18, p. 277.

## CHAPTER XXV. How Amphilochius persuaded Theodosius to prohibit the Arians’ assemblies

When Theodosius was returning from the western regions, Amphilochius came to him—a remarkable man, whom we have often mentioned—and begged him to prohibit the Arians’ councils in each of the cities. The emperor, however, judging the request cruel, rejected him.

The very wise Amphilochius remained silent at that time, but prepared a memorable remedy for the matter. A few days later, entering the palace and seeing his son Arcadius, already emperor, standing beside his father, he solemnly greeted Theodosius. He passed by the son without offering him a greeting. The emperor, believing that Amphilochius had forgotten him, invited him to kiss Arcadius. But he replied: “His own honor is sufficient for him.”

The emperor then became distressed and judged that an insult had been inflicted upon his son. [Col. 1142A] The very wise Amphilochius disclosed the intention of his counsel and exclaimed: “Do you see, emperor, how you cannot endure an insult being inflicted upon your son? Believe, then, that the God of all likewise abhors those who strive to blaspheme his only-begotten Son, and that he always holds them in hatred as ungrateful toward the Savior and benefactor.”

When the emperor understood this and marveled at both the deed and the words, he immediately issued a law prohibiting the councils of heretics. THEODORETUS, book V, chapter 16, p. 218.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the death of Paulinus, bishop of Antioch, the ordination of Evagrius, and how Flavian was reconciled to Damasus

About this time, when Paulinus, bishop of Antioch in Syria, was dying, his congregation avoided Flavian in every way. For this reason they ordained Evagrius as bishop of their party. When he died shortly afterward, no one else was appointed in his place, since Flavian resisted.

Those who avoided Flavian because of his violation of an oath celebrated the solemn rites separately. Flavian, however, made every effort to bring them over to himself. It is understood that this happened shortly afterward in the following manner.

When Damasus, the Roman pontiff, and Theophilus of Alexandria were indignant against Flavian—not only because of his perjury [ms. Lyr., “quarrel”], but also because he himself had caused the faithful people to fall into discord—Theophilus later, at Flavian’s request, sent the presbyter Isidore to appease Damasus, who was displeased with Flavian as bishop. He said that harmony among the people would be beneficial if the fault already committed by Flavian were forgiven.

In this way, communion having been restored to Flavian, the people of Antioch gradually recovered their unity. The Arians, however, expelled from the churches, held their assemblies in the suburbs of Antioch. Meanwhile, when Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, had died, John succeeded him in his see. SOCRATES, book V, chapter 15, p. 273.

## CHAPTER XXVII. How the temples of the pagans were destroyed at Alexandria

At that time a similar disturbance also arose in Alexandria. The emperor had ordered that the temples of the pagans be destroyed in Alexandria at the initiative of Theophilus. Having received this authority, Theophilus undertook to destroy the pagan mysteries. He cleansed the temple of Mithras and overthrew that of Serapis.

He publicly exposed the rites of Mithras, where murders had been committed. He showed that the rites of Serapis and the other temples were full of ridicule, ordering that through the middle of the street the private parts be carried which the pagans had worshiped with the greatest honor.

When the pagans saw this, especially the philosophers, they could not endure the insult. In a single assault against the Christians [342; ms. Santheod., “approaching”], they committed countless murders. When the Christians resisted, the disaster progressed into immense conflicts. In that clash, few pagans and many Christians were killed, while innumerable persons on both sides were wounded.

After the pagans had been sated with slaughter, they hid themselves in various places out of fear of the emperor; many also fled the city. Among them were the grammarians Helladius and Ammonius, under whom I myself studied at Constantinople when I was still very young. Helladius was said to be a priest of Jupiter, and Ammonius of the Ape.

After these events, the prefect of Alexandria and the commander of the military forces provided Theophilus with assistance in the destruction of the temples. The idols of the gods were melted down to make cooking pots and for various needs of the Alexandrian Church, since the emperor had donated the gods to it for the expenses of the poor.

When Theophilus had shattered all the gods, he left only one image of an ape, ordering it to be publicly displayed and preserved, lest in later times the pagans deny that they had worshiped such gods.

I know this because the grammarian Ammonius took the matter very badly. He said that the pagans had suffered nothing so grievous except that the image itself had not been melted down, but that this one idol had been preserved for mockery. Helladius, for his part, boasted that during the clash he himself had killed nine Christians. SOCRATES, book V, chapter 16, p. 274.

When the emperor heard what had been perpetrated at Alexandria, he indeed pronounced the Christians blessed, attributing to them the palms of martyrs because they had endured such dangers for their doctrine; but he granted pardon to the pagans, so that he might more easily persuade them to become Christians. He ordered that the temples which had been the cause of the slaughter be utterly destroyed.

When his letter had been read publicly and the Christians attacked the pagans, the guardians of Serapis, overcome by fear, fled; and from that time it is known that the Christians occupied those places.

The philosopher Olympius, as I heard not long ago, on the daybreak of the day on which this occurred, heard someone singing “Alleluia” in the temple of Serapis. Since the doors were closed and, at that quiet hour, he saw no one there but only heard the voice of the singer, he recognized by the sign what was going to happen. He secretly departed, found a ship, and sailed away. SOZOMEN, book VII, chapter 15, p. 724.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the deceptions that the pagans practiced in their temples

Theophilus therefore cleansed the city of Alexandria of the error of idols. He not only overthrew the temples from their foundations but also exposed the deception of the priests to those who were being led astray.

There were bronze and wooden images that were hollow inside and had their backs joined to the walls. They left certain openings there; then, ascending through the inner sanctuaries [ed. V, “hidden places”] and entering the images, they spoke through their mouths whatever they wished. In this way, those who continually heard them were deceived.

When Theophilus went up into the temple of Serapis, he saw an image whose size terrified those who looked at it. A deceptive story was also circulated: if anyone approached it, the earth would immediately be shaken and pestilence would invade everyone.

Confident that these words were full of old women’s tales, he disregarded its size as though it were lifeless and ordered someone who had an axe to smash Serapis with a powerful blow. When it fell, everyone cried out, fearing those old wives’ tales.

Serapis, however, neither suffered pain—for he was wooden—nor uttered a voice, since he was lifeless. When they had removed his head, swarms of mice ran out from within. For the god of the Egyptians was a dwelling place for mice. They then cut him into pieces and burned him in the fire, while they dragged his head through the whole city. THEODORETUS, book V, chapter 22, p. 228.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the characters made in the form of a cross that were found in the temple of Serapis

When the temple of Serapis was stripped bare, letters carved in the stones were found. These letters are called sacred among the Egyptians, and their characters had the form of a cross. When the Christians and pagans saw this, each group assigned the sign to its own religion.

The Christians said that it was the sign of Christ’s life-giving passion; the pagans, however, asserted through this sign that there was some association between Christ and Serapis. The interpreters said that the sign of the cross indicated the life that was to come.

For this reason the Christians were raised to the highest esteem. Since other letters, which among them are called sacred, also indicated that the temple of Serapis would have an end when the character of the cross appeared—a character that unquestionably declared the life to come—very many hastened to Christianity, confessed their sins, and were baptized.

I do not, however, believe that the priests of the Egyptians had foreseen the coming of Christ and had indicated the sign of the cross. For if the mystery of the Lord’s coming was hidden from the ages and generations, as the Apostle says (Ephesians 3:9), and remained unknown to the prince of wickedness, the devil, how much more was it unknown to his servants, the Egyptian priests?

But divine providence prepared this beforehand, so that what was also demonstrated in the Apostle Paul might come about in a matter concerning the interpretation of letters. For he too, enriched by the Holy Spirit, led many Athenians to faith when he explained, according to the meaning of his own discourse, what had been written on the altar.

Unless perhaps someone should say that God also worked among the Egyptian priests as he did through Balaam and Caiaphas; they too are said to have prophesied. SOCRATES, book V, chapter 17, p. 276.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the massacre that took place at Thessalonica under Theodosius, and on the repentance of Theodosius and the steadfastness of Ambrose

[Col. 1144D]

It is not easy for human beings to avoid all the snares of the enemy. For when someone has escaped the passion of lust, he falls into greed. When that has been avoided, a pit of envy is prepared. If he has crossed beyond this, he falls into the vice of rage. The enemy sets many other snares by which he may capture the unwary.

He has bodily passions readily serving him, so that he may kill the soul. But a mind watchful through divine consolation destroys the arguments of his schemes.

The emperor Theodosius, participating in human nature, also shared in its passions. Mingling immense cruelty with a justifiable anger, he committed an unjust act of passion. It is necessary to recount this, both for the benefit of readers and for the memorable reputation of virtue.

Thessalonica is a large and populous city. When a disturbance had arisen there, certain judges were stoned and butchered. Theodosius became angry at this and did not restrain the weakness of his wrath; instead, he ordered unjust swords to be drawn against everyone and the innocent to be killed together with the guilty.

For, as is reported, seven thousand people were killed without any prior trial. Like a harvest, they were all cut down together.

When Ambrose heard of this disaster, filled with groans, and the emperor had come to Milan and wished to enter the holy church solemnly, Ambrose met him outside at the doors [Col. 1145B] and prevented him from entering the sacred threshold with these words:
