“Do you not know, emperor, how great is the magnitude of the slaughter you have perpetrated? Even after such an outburst of fury, your mind does not recognize the weight of its presumption. Perhaps the power of the empire prevents you from recognizing your sin. Yet reason ought to overcome power.

“You must know your nature, its mortality and dissolution, and the dust of your forefathers from which we were made and to which we shall be reduced. You must not, trusting in the flower of purple, remain ignorant of the frailties of the body which it covers.

“You are ruler of human beings equal to yourself, O emperor, and of fellow servants. For there is one Lord of all, the king and creator of all. With what eyes, then, will you look upon the temple of our common Lord? With what feet will you touch his holy pavement? How will you extend hands from which unjust blood still drips? How will you receive the holy body of the Lord with such hands? With what presumption will you take the cup of precious blood with your mouth, when through the fury of your words so much blood has been unjustly shed?

“Withdraw, then; withdraw, lest you seek to increase your former wickedness by a second sin. Accept the bond with which the Lord of all has now bound you, for it is the greatest medicine of health.”

The emperor obeyed these words—for he had been nourished by divine instruction and clearly knew what belonged to priests and what belonged to kings—and, groaning and weeping, returned to the imperial palace.

Eight months passed continuously, and the festival of the Nativity of our Savior drew near. The emperor, sitting in the palace amid constant lamentation, poured forth continual tears without ceasing.

Rufinus, then master of the offices, entered. He possessed exceptional confidence with the emperor and, seeing him prostrate in lamentation, approached to inquire the cause of his tears.

The emperor, groaning most bitterly and shedding tears even more abundantly, said: “You are playing, Rufinus, and do not feel my misfortunes. I lament and mourn my calamity, because the temples of God are open to servants and beggars, and they may enter freely and pray to their own Lord, but I have no entrance to him. Moreover, heaven itself is closed to me.”

As he said this, he interrupted each sentence with sobs.

Then Rufinus said: “If it pleases you, I will go and persuade the bishop by my prayers that the bond with which he has bound you should be released.”

The emperor replied: “You will not persuade Ambrose. I know that his decree is just, and he will not fear imperial power so as to violate the divine law.”

When Rufinus continued at length and promised that Ambrose could be moved, the emperor ordered him to go quickly. After a short while, he himself followed, trusting Rufinus’s promises.

But the remarkable Ambrose, as soon as he saw Rufinus, said: “You have imitated the shamelessness of dogs, Rufinus. Though you were the author of such a great slaughter, you wipe shame from your forehead and are neither embarrassed nor afraid to bark against the divine image.”

When Rufinus pleaded and said that the emperor was coming, Ambrose, inflamed by heavenly zeal, said: “I declare, Rufinus, that I will prevent him from entering the sacred threshold. If he changes his imperial authority into tyranny, I too will gladly accept death.”

Rufinus heard these and many other words and reported the bishop’s resolve to the emperor, warning him not to leave the palace. When the emperor learned this while already in the middle of the street, he said: “I will go and receive the just reproaches upon my face.”

When he reached the sacred threshold, he did not presume to enter the holy basilica. Instead, he came to the bishop and found him sitting in the place of welcome. He begged him to release his bonds.

Ambrose declared that his presence was tyrannical and that Theodosius was raging against God and trampling upon his laws.

The emperor replied: “I am not rising against ecclesiastical decrees, nor am I unjustly trying to enter the sacred threshold. I ask you to release my bonds and to implore for me the mercy of our common Lord, so that the door may not be closed to me which our Lord has opened to all who repent.”

Then the bishop said: “What repentance have you shown after such great iniquities? By what medicines have you healed incurable wounds and injuries?”

The emperor replied: “It is your task to teach and to prepare the medicines; mine is to receive what is offered.”

Then Saint Ambrose said: “Because you entrusted your judgment to fury, and your sentence was issued not by reason but rather by anger, write a law that annuls the decrees of fury. Let a sentence of death and proscription remain in writing for thirty days only and await the judgment of reason. When those days have passed, with anger now having subsided, let reason judge the case and determine according to truth what it has discovered.

“During those days it will be recognized whether the sentence you have pronounced is just or unjust. If reason proves that what has been issued is unjust, it will annul it; if just, it will confirm it. The number of days will be sufficient for examining these matters.”

The emperor willingly accepted this admonition and confessed that it was excellent. He immediately ordered the law to be written and confirmed it in his own hand. After this had been done, Ambrose released his bond. This law is observed to the present day. It is as follows:

**The Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius Augusti to Flavian, praetorian prefect of Illyricum.**

“If we should order that certain persons be punished more severely than is customary with us, in view of the circumstances of the case, we do not wish them immediately either to undergo punishment or to receive sentence. Instead, for thirty days their fate and fortune shall remain suspended regarding their condition. Let custody receive and bind the accused and watch over them vigilantly with attentive guards.”

Thus the most sacred emperor, presuming to enter the threshold, did not stand and beseech the Lord, nor did he bend his knees; rather, he lay prostrate on the pavement and proclaimed David’s words: “My soul clings to the pavement; give me life according to your word” (Psalm 118:25).

Tearing his hair with his hands, striking his forehead, and sprinkling the pavement with drops of tears, he begged to obtain pardon. When the time approached at which he was accustomed to offer a gift at the altar, he rose and entered with tears.

After he had made his offering, as was customary, he stood inside the chancel. Ambrose, however, did not remain silent but instructed him concerning the distinction between places. First he asked what he was waiting for. When the emperor said that he was waiting to receive the sacred mysteries, Ambrose sent word through the archdeacon:

“Emperor, the inner places have been assigned only to priests; the others are not permitted either to enter or to touch them. Go out, then, and share this waiting with the others. Purple makes emperors, not priests.”

The most faithful emperor willingly accepted this tradition as well and sent back the reply:

“I did not remain inside the chancel out of boldness. I learned that this was the custom in the city of Constantinople. Therefore I give thanks for this medicine” [ed. V, “discipline”].

Thus both the bishop and the emperor shone with such great virtue. I admire the deed of each: the confidence of the one and the obedience of the other; the fervor of the one’s zeal and the purity of the other’s faith.

After he returned to Constantinople, he also observed the rules of piety that he had received from the great priest. When he had gone to the church during a festival, he placed his gifts upon the altar and immediately departed.

When Nectarius, then bishop of the Church, sent to ask why he had not wished to remain inside, the emperor replied: “I could scarcely learn what distinction there is between an emperor and a priest; scarcely have I found a teacher of truth. I know only Ambrose to deserve the name of pontiff.”

So great was the benefit produced by the rebuke delivered by a man flourishing in virtues. THEODORETUS, book V, chapters 16 and 17; edition of Christ. Vales., chapters 16, 17, and 19, p. 218.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the virtues of Theodosius’s wife

[Col. 1147D]

The emperor therefore had another occasion for benefit, through which he might triumph in good works. His wife frequently admonished him concerning the divine laws, while first instructing herself perfectly. She was not exalted by the heights of royalty; rather, she was inflamed by divine love.

The greatness of the benefit bestowed upon her increased her desire for the benefactor. As soon as she had suddenly come to the purple, she showed the greatest concern for the lame and the weak. She did not use servants or other attendants, but acted personally: she went to their dwellings and provided each person with whatever he needed.

She also went through the xenodochia of the churches and ministered to the sick with her own hands. She cleaned their pots, tasted their broth, offered spoons, broke bread, served food, rinsed cups, and did everything else that servants and attendants customarily perform in an orderly manner.

To those who tried to prevent her from doing such things, she would say: “To distribute gold is the work of imperial power; but I offer this service on behalf of the empire itself, which has bestowed all good things upon me.”

She often said to her husband: “You ought always, my husband, to consider what you were formerly and what you are now. If you always consider this, you will not be ungrateful to your benefactor. Rather, you will govern the empire you have received lawfully and will appease the author of these things.”

With these words she offered her husband a most excellent benefit and an abundance of virtue. THEODORETUS, book V, chapter 18; edition of Christ. Vales., chapter 19, p. 223.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Theodosius’s anger and reconciliation on account of the Antiochenes, who removed his wife’s statue

She died before her husband. Some time afterward, an event occurred through which the emperor displayed the great love he had borne toward her.

Theodosius, compelled by the continuation of many wars, imposed a new levy upon the cities. The city of Antioch could not bear the new tax. When the people saw various persons being hanged, they did what the populace commonly does when it finds an opportunity for sedition: they took down the image of the most highly honored Placilla—for this was the name by which she had been called as Augusta—and dragged it throughout the city.

When the emperor heard this, he became angry, removed the city’s privileges, and transferred the primacy to the neighboring city, Laodicea, believing that this would afflict the Antiochenes most severely. Afterward he threatened to burn Antioch, destroy it, and reduce it to the condition of villages.

The local administrators, having seized certain people, killed them before the emperor learned of this presumption. The emperor indeed ordered all these things, but they were not carried out, because of the law that Ambrose had caused to be issued.

When the men who carried the emperor’s threats arrived—Hellebichus, master of the soldiers, and Caesarius, master of the offices—everyone was overcome with fear. Many men living in the desert, defenders of virtue, men of great excellence at that time, offered them abundant admonitions and prayers, for they had been sent by the emperor.

Macedonius, however, a holy man who knew nothing of this life and was entirely inexperienced in the divine books, lived in the heights of the mountains and offered pure prayers to the Savior of all day and night. He was not moved by the emperor’s anger or by the judges sent by him. In the middle of the city, he seized the cloak of each of the two men and ordered them to descend from their horses.

At first they were indignant when they saw a little old man dressed in the most wretched rags. But when some of those who had served the man disclosed his virtue, they suddenly leapt from their horses, grasped his knees, and humbly begged pardon.

Filled with divine wisdom, he addressed them as follows:

“O friends, say to the emperor: [345] ‘You are not merely an emperor, but also a human being. Do not look only to your imperial authority; consider nature as well. For since you are human, you are recognized as ruling human beings of the same nature, and human nature was created according to the image and likeness of God.

“‘Do not therefore subject the image of God to slaughter with cruelty and extreme savagery. You provoke the Creator when you punish his image.

“‘Consider also that you yourself are so distressed on account of a bronze image. How much the inanimate differs from the animate, the living and rational, is clear to all who possess understanding.

“‘Consider further that it is easy for us to replace one image with many bronze images; but for him it is utterly difficult to restore even one hair of those who have been killed.’”

When they heard these words and conveyed them to the emperor, they completely extinguished the flame of his anger. He sent back a reply of satisfaction in place of his threats and made known the cause of his indignation:

“It was not right that, although I had sinned, a woman deserving every honor should endure such an insult after death. Those who were angry and indignant against me ought to have armed themselves against me.”

He added that he was troubled and grieving because he had heard that some had been killed by the judges. THEODORETUS, book V, chapter 19; edition of Christ. Vales., chapters 19 and 20, p. 244.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How Theodosius became hostile toward the pagans

The most faithful emperor therefore then directed his efforts against the error of the pagans and composed laws ordering the temples of the idols to be overthrown.

Constantine the Great, who deserves every praise and who first adorned the empire with piety, prohibited all sacrifice to demons; yet he did not destroy their temples but ordered them to be inaccessible. His sons followed in their father’s footsteps.

Julian, however, renewed impiety and rekindled the flame of the ancient deception. Jovian, after assuming the empire, again prohibited the sacrifices of idols.

The elder Valentinian governed Europe by means of laws of this kind. Valens permitted everyone else to practice their religions as they wished, attacking only those who fought for the apostolic doctrines. Throughout his reign, fire was kindled upon the altars, libations and sacrifices were offered to idols, public festivals were held through the streets, and the Orgia of Dionysus were celebrated. They ran with shields [ms. Santheod. and ed. V., “sacred objects”], disemboweled dogs, raged and reveled, and performed all the acts that reveal the wickedness of their own teacher.

When the most faithful emperor Theodosius found all these practices, he tore them up by the roots and consigned them to oblivion. THEODORETUS, book V, chapter 20; edition of Christ. Vales., chapter 21, p. 226.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How Marcellus, bishop of Apamea, destroyed the temples
The first among the others, therefore, was Marcellus, bishop, who used the emperor’s law in place of weapons and destroyed the temples of his own city [Col. 1150A], trusting in God rather than presuming on human strength. I shall not fail to recount an event worthy of remembrance.

After John, bishop of the city of Apamea, had died, Marcellus, a most holy man, was ordained in his place, fervent in spirit according to the Apostle. Meanwhile the prefect of the East came to Apamea, accompanied by two commanders of a thousand and their subordinates. As a result, the people were terrified by fear of the soldiers. At that time there was a particularly important temple of Jupiter, adorned and embellished in many ways, and the prefect attempted to destroy it. But when he saw that the building was exceedingly large and strong, he judged it impossible for human beings to break apart the joints and connections of the stones. For the stones were enormous, fastened to one another, and moreover joined with iron and lead.

Marcellus, seeing the prefect’s faintheartedness, sent him to other cities [Col. 1150B], while he himself prayed to God to provide an opportunity for destroying the temple. Meanwhile a certain man came of his own accord at dawn. He was not a builder, nor a stonecutter, nor skilled in any other craft, but accustomed to carrying stones and wood upon his shoulders. Approaching, he promised that the temple could easily be dismantled; he asked only to receive the wages of craftsmen. When the holy bishop had promised him this, the man set about his undertaking.

A portico, built at the established height, was attached to the temple on all four sides. It had enormous columns, equal in height to the temple. The circumference of each column was sixteen cubits. The nature of the stone was exceedingly hard and could not easily be broken by tools of any kind. He therefore dug around three of them [Col. 1150C], placed strong pieces of wood beneath their bases, and set them on fire.

When this was done, the fire could not naturally ignite the wood. For a certain exceedingly foul demon appeared and prevented the flame from exercising its power. When they had attempted this frequently and could not complete their undertaking, they reported the matter at noon to the bishop, who was asleep. But he immediately ran to the church, ordered water to be brought in a vessel, and placed the water beneath the altar. Then, with his forehead on the pavement, he prayed to the merciful Lord that He would no longer permit the demon to possess any confidence in its tyranny, but would expose its weakness and display a sign of His own power, lest this become an occasion for the unbelievers to exult [ms. Lyr., “for insult”].

After saying this, he made the sign of the cross over the water. He ordered one of his deacons, Equitius, armed with faith and zeal, to take the water, run quickly, sprinkle the wood in faith, and set fire to it. When this had been done, the demon fled, unable to endure the power of the water. The fire, however, treated that water as though it were oil: the wood caught fire and was suddenly consumed.

The columns, stripped of the support that had propped them up, also fell and brought down twelve others with them. Then the side that had been attached to the temple was brought down by the violence of the collapse. The sound shook the entire city and caused everyone to hurry there. When the enemies of the demon clearly recognized that it had fled, they gave free expression to their mouths in divine praises.

In this way that most holy bishop also destroyed the other temples. He wrote to the victorious martyrs, received their replies, and finally was himself crowned with martyrdom. THEODORETUS, book V, chapter 21, p. 226.

346  
## CHAPTER XXXV. For what reason the presbyters appointed over penitents were removed

At that time, therefore, it was decided that the presbyters who had been appointed over penitents should be removed, for the following reason. After the Novatians had separated from the Church because they refused to communicate with those who had sinned during the persecutions under the emperor Decius, from that time the bishops, in accordance with ecclesiastical regulation, appointed a presbyter over the penitents. SOCRATES, book V, chapter 19, p. 278.

[Col. 1151B] Since it is recognized that not to sin at all is divine and beyond human nature, while God commanded that forgiveness be granted to those who sin and repent, those who refuse to confess acquire [ms. Lyr., “assume”] a greater burden of sins. For this reason the ancient bishops decided that sins should be disclosed, as though in a theater, in the presence of the ecclesiastical people.

For this purpose they appointed a presbyter of good conduct, one who kept secrets, and a wise man. Those who sinned would approach him and confess their own offenses. He then imposed penance [ed., “punishment”] according to each person’s fault.

This practice is still carefully observed in the Western Churches, especially at Rome, where there is also a designated place for penitents. The guilty stand there, as though placed in mourning. When the sacred celebration has been completed, they do not receive communion, but with groaning and lamentation they prostrate themselves on the ground. The bishop runs to them and likewise prostrates himself with tears and spiritual groaning, while the whole congregation of the Church is flooded with weeping.

After this, the bishop rises first and raises those lying on the ground. Then, after offering an appropriate prayer for the penitents, he dismisses everyone. They, meanwhile, voluntarily devote themselves to afflictions—fasts, abstaining from bathing, suspension of food, or other practices that are commanded—and await the appointed common time established by the bishop.

When the appointed time arrives, having paid what was in a certain sense a debt and been cured through the afflictions of sin [mss. and ed. V., “sin”], they participate in communion [Col. 1151C] with the people.

The Roman bishops preserved this practice from ancient times down to our own day. At Constantinople, however, there was a presbyter over the penitents until the time when a certain noblewoman, after confessing her sins and receiving from the presbyter the command to fast and to entreat God through good works, repeatedly observed this practice in the church and confessed that she had slept with a deacon.

When the people learned of this, they raged against the priests, as though the injury to the Church had been caused by them. Then Bishop Nectarius removed the wicked deacon. When certain people advised him to leave each person to the judgment of his own conscience regarding admission to communion, he also ordered that there should no longer be a presbyter over the penitents.

From that time the ancient custom was abolished, lest, as I think, lesser sins should be committed because of the shame of confession and the minute scrutiny of the examiners. SOZOMEN, book VII, chapter 16, p. 726.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the division of the heretics among themselves

I consider it worthwhile not to remain silent about what happened among the others, namely, among the Arians, Novatians, Macedonians, and Eunomians. The Church was divided, and each group gathered separately among its own members. As the account proceeds, we shall explain how and for what reasons they were divided.

This, however, must be understood: the emperor Theodosius persecuted none of them except Eunomius, who held gatherings in a house at Constantinople and read books that he himself had written, so that many were corrupted by his teaching. For this reason the emperor punished him with exile, but he troubled no one else and compelled no one to communicate with him. Rather, he permitted each group to hold its gatherings in its own places and to maintain Christian worship as it was able.

He allowed some of them to build oratories outside the city; but to the Novatians, who were united in their faith, he granted permission to have churches within the city. A few things must be said about them.

Agelius was their bishop for forty years, from the time of Constantine until the sixth year of Theodosius. When he approached death, he ordained the presbyter Sisinnius as bishop, a man of exceptionally eloquent speech who had been educated in literature by the philosopher Maximus together with the emperor Julian.

When the Novatian people criticized the ordination, asking why he had not ordained Marcian instead, through whom the Novatians had remained free from persecution under Valens, Agelius, wishing to calm the people’s grief, also ordained Marcian as bishop.

When he had recovered somewhat, he went into the church and delivered a sermon, saying: “You have Marcian after me, and after Marcian, Sisinnius.” A few days later he died.

During Marcian’s episcopate, their Church was also divided for the following reason. SOCRATES, book V, chapter 20, p. 279.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On Sabbatius, the heresiarch

A certain Sabbatius, a Jew who had become a Christian and had been promoted by Marcian to the dignity of the presbyterate, nevertheless continued to serve the Jewish sect. Together with this crime, he was also striving for the episcopate.

Taking with him two presbyters who shared his desire, Theoctistus and Macarius, he attempted to defend the new observance of the Paschal festival that had been established under the emperor Valens in the Phrygian village of Pazo. At first, as though he were safeguarding the integrity of the Church, he said that certain people were unworthy to participate in the sacraments. As time went on, however, he was exposed when he began holding gatherings of his own.

Meanwhile Marcian recognized his error and the fault of his own ordination, because he had ordained presbyters who were men of empty glory. With a groan he would say: “It would have been better to place my hands upon thorns than to ordain Sabbatius presbyter.”

Accordingly, he held a synod of Novatian bishops at Sangarus in Bithynia. When they had assembled, they summoned Sabbatius and his associates [Col. 1153A] to present before the synod the reasons for their separation [ed., “dissension”].

Sabbatius said that the disagreement over the date of Easter was his grief, and insisted that it ought to be celebrated according to the Jewish observance, as had been established at Pazo. The bishops judged that Sabbatius was doing these things out of ambition and imposed an oath upon him that he would never desire the episcopate.

After he had sworn, they issued a rule concerning the Paschal festival, allowing each person to celebrate Easter whenever he wished, so that the Church would not be divided because of disagreement over the festival. In ancient times, although churches close to one another disagreed about such a festival, they nevertheless communicated with one another. The Novatians established in the imperial city of Rome had never followed the Jews, but had always celebrated Easter after the equinox [Col. 1153B].

When this rule had then been established by them, Sabbatius, bound by his oaths, whenever the Paschal festival fell on a different date, would fast privately beforehand and celebrate the solemn day of Easter during the night on Saturday. Then he would again assemble with everyone in the church and partake of the mysteries.

By doing this for many years, he could not remain concealed. Therefore certain simple people, especially Phrygians and Galatians who believed that they were justified by this practice, became zealous for him and celebrated Easter with him.

Later Sabbatius began also holding separate gatherings, and, disregarding his oath, he was ordained bishop by the choice of his followers. SOCRATES, book V, chapter 20. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 21, p. 281.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On Easter, or the diversity of institutions and observances celebrated in the various Churches

[Col. 1153C]

It does not seem to me that such men argued rationally about the festival of Easter, nor do those who now follow the Jews do so. They did not understand that, once Judaism had been changed into Christianity, the subtle and figurative elements of the Mosaic law had come to rest. This is evident from the following.

No Christian nation has commanded the practice of Judaizing. On the contrary, the Apostle also opposed it, not only forbidding circumcision but also warning that disputes about festivals should be rejected. For, writing to the Galatians, he says: “Tell me, you who wish to be under the law, have you not heard the law?” (Galatians 4:21).

Speaking briefly thereafter, he shows that the Jewish people were a slave population, while those who come to Christ have been called into freedom. He also warns that days, months, and years are in no way to be observed.

Writing to the Colossians, he cried out in a loud voice that the ancient observances had been shadows. “Therefore,” he says, “let no one judge you concerning food or drink, or with regard to a festival, or the beginning of a month, or a sabbath, which are a shadow of things to come” (Colossians 2:16).

The same Apostle says to the Hebrews: “For when the priesthood is changed, there is necessarily a change of the law” (Hebrews 7:12).

Thus neither the Apostle nor the Gospels imposed upon those who came to the preaching the yoke of slavery. They did, however, say that the festival of Easter and other celebrations ought to be honored.

Since people love such celebrations because they rest from their labors during them, the inhabitants of the various provinces, according to their own preferences, traditionally celebrated the remembrance of the saving Passion from a certain established custom [Col. 1154A]. The Savior and our Apostles did not proclaim this by law, nor did the Gospels or the Apostles threaten us with punishment, penalty, or a curse as the Mosaic law did the Jews.

It is recorded in the Gospels only as a reproach to the Jews that they committed murder during their festivals, and that the Savior suffered at the time of Unleavened Bread. The Apostles’ intention was not to legislate a festival according to particular days, but to proclaim upright conduct and the worship of God.

It therefore seems to me that, just as many other practices came to be customary in the provinces, so also the festival of Easter was handed down, since none of the Apostles had legislated anything about it.

For many in the region of Asia Minor observed the fourteenth day, without regard to the day of the sabbath [Col. 1154B]. Yet in doing this they did not separate themselves from those who celebrated differently, until Victor, bishop of the Roman Church, sent an excommunication against the Quartodecimans in Asia.

When this happened, Irenaeus of Lyons, a Gallic bishop, rebuked Victor in a letter, saying that the ancient people had also celebrated in this way, and that Polycarp, bishop of the city of Smyrna—who was later crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Gordian—had communicated with Anicetus, bishop of Rome, without making any distinction concerning the Paschal festival, although he himself was a Quartodeciman, as Eusebius teaches in the fifth book of his Ecclesiastical History.

Thus, as I have said, some in Asia Minor observed the fourteenth day. Others in the eastern regions also observed the sabbath [Col. 1154C], but they disagreed about the month.

Some said that the Jews should be followed in the sacred festival, although they did not preserve the observance in its entirety. Others celebrated after the equinox, avoiding the Jews and saying that Easter ought to be celebrated when the sun was in Aries.

According to the Antiochene practice, it was celebrated in the month Xanthicus; according to the Roman practice, in April. This was not to be done by following the Jews of the present day, who are known to be in error in every respect, but rather the ancient Jews and Josephus. For Josephus wrote this in the third book of his Antiquities.

We therefore find that all the Westerners as far as the Ocean celebrated Easter after the equinox according to ancient tradition, and that they never had any disagreement. The council celebrated under Constantine did not, as some say, change the festival of Easter.

For Constantine himself, writing to those who disagreed, urged the minority to imitate the majority. I have not omitted to include part of his letter. After other remarks, he said:

“There is indeed an orderly arrangement that all the Churches throughout the world situated in the West, the South, and the North are known to preserve, as well as certain churches in the East. Therefore, at the present time, everyone has judged the matter to be in a good state, and I myself have promised that it would also please your wisdom that what is willingly observed in one agreement in the city of Rome, Italy, Africa, all Egypt, Spain, Gaul, Britain, Libya, all Greece, the diocese of Asia, Pontus, and Cilicia, should also be accepted by your wisdom.

“Consider not only the multitude of the places mentioned and the number of their Churches, [Col. 1155A] but also that you ought all to celebrate together above all that which careful reasoning appears to demand: that we have no communion with the perjury of the Jews.”

Such were the words of Constantine.

Some, however, say that the Apostle John handed down this observance to the Quartodecimans. Others say that the Apostles Peter and Paul handed down the solemnity of Easter to the Romans and Westerners. But no one is known to possess written proof of these claims.

Since Easter is celebrated throughout the provinces according to a certain custom, I therefore think that no religious sect appears to observe the same solemnities. For although many share one faith, they nevertheless disagree concerning the proper observances of Easter. A few things must therefore be said.

Even in the matter of fasting we find different practices among different peoples [Col. 1155B]. The Romans fast continuously for six weeks before Easter, except on Saturday and Sunday [ed. Niv. and Frob., “three weeks”].

The Illyrians, all Greece, and Alexandria also fast for six weeks before Easter, and they call these fasts Lent. Others are known to begin their fasts seven weeks before Easter, but fast for only three weeks—namely, for five days at a time, with intervals during the other two weeks—and nevertheless call this period Lent. I therefore wonder how they call it Lent when they do not possess the number forty.

They also do not have a uniform abstinence from foods. Some abstain entirely from animals; others eat only fish among animals; some eat fish and birds, saying that according to Moses these have their substance from water. Others are also known to abstain from vegetables and eggs. Some eat only dry bread; others do not even eat that. Others fast until the ninth hour and then take nourishment without distinguishing among foods. Innumerable customs are found among different peoples.

Since no ancient reading is found on this subject, I think that the Apostles left this to the judgment of each person, so that everyone might do what is good, not from fear or necessity.

There is also some diversity concerning the celebration of gatherings. Although sacrifices are celebrated throughout the Churches established across the whole world on every Sabbath, week by week, this is not done at Alexandria and Rome according to a certain ancient tradition.

The Egyptians living near Alexandria and the inhabitants of the Thebaid hold gatherings on the Sabbath, but on Sunday, as is customary, they receive the sacraments. After they have feasted and been filled with all foods, they make an offering toward evening and then communicate.

At Alexandria, on the other hand, Scripture is read on the fourth and sixth days of the week, and the teachers interpret it. Everything is done except the customary solemn offering. Origen appears to have expounded [ed., “instructed”] a great deal on these days.

For, being a wise teacher and considering that the impossibility of observing the Mosaic law literally was weak, he elevated the meaning of Easter to the level of contemplation. He said that only one true Easter had taken place: the one celebrated by the Savior when He accepted the cross and used this trophy against the opposing powers, that is, against the devil [Col. 1156A].

In Alexandria, readers and reciters of psalms are appointed without distinction, whether they are catechumens or already Christians, since all the Churches appear to regard the faithful as eligible for these offices.

I also learned of another custom in Thessaly. When a certain cleric had lawfully taken a wife before entering the clergy, he was deposed because he had had intercourse with her, whereas in the East everyone—even bishops—abstains from intercourse of his own free will and not from any compulsion. Many of them had children by a lawful wife even while they were bishops.

I also learned that this practice is observed in Thessaly because among them baptism is administered only during the days of Easter. Consequently, many die without baptism.

At Antioch in Syria they have the altar not toward the east of the church [Col. 1156B], but rather toward the west.

In Greece, Jerusalem, and Thessaly, they hold prayers at the evening hour similar to those of the Novatians living in Constantinople.

In Caesarea of Cappadocia and in Cyprus, on the Sabbath and on Sunday toward evening, the bishops and presbyters interpret the Scriptures by lamplight.

At Alexandria the presbyter does not deliver a sermon. This practice began from the time when Arius disturbed the Church.

At Rome they fast on every Sabbath.

In Caesarea of Cappadocia, those who sin after baptism are suspended from communion, as the Novatians and Macedonians do in the Hellespont, and the Quartodecimans in Asia.

The Novatians around Phrygia do not admit those who have married twice. At Constantinople they neither openly admit them nor are they known publicly to exclude them. In the Western regions, however, they openly admit them. SOCRATES, book V, chapter 21; edition of Christ. Valesius, chapter 22, p. 282.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the Easter of the Montanists

The Montanists, whom they call Phrygians, introduced a certain foreign innovation and celebrate Easter according to it. They blame those who follow the course of the moon and say that only the solar cycles should be followed.

They define each month as consisting of thirty days and say that the first month begins with the spring equinox, which according to the Romans is the eighth day before the Kalends of April. “At that time,” they say, “the two great lights were made, by which the seasons and the years are revealed.”

They say that this is indicated by the fact that over eight years the moon runs in harmony with the sun, and that both have the same new month. Because the eight-year cycle of the moon is completed and this day is, as it were, the beginning of the first month, they reckon the aforementioned day as the fourteenth day in Scripture. They say that this is the eighth day before the Ides of April, and according to it they always celebrate Easter—provided that the day of the Resurrection also happens to fall on Sunday; otherwise, when Sunday arrives, they celebrate it. For, they say, it is written that the festival is to be celebrated from the fourteenth through the twenty-first day. SOZOMEN, book VII, chapter 18, p. 733.

Among the Romans, Alleluia is sung only once each year, on the first day of Easter, so that the Romans seem almost to regard it as an oath that they may be worthy to hear this hymn [Col. 1157A]. In that Church neither the bishop nor anyone else teaches before the people [ms. Santheod., “speaks”].

Among the Alexandrians, it is considered remarkable that, while the Gospels are being read, the bishop does not stand. I know of no other place where this happens. There, the archdeacon alone reads this lesson; in other places, deacons do so; in many churches, only priests. At Constantinople, on the first day of the Lord’s Resurrection, the bishop does so. SOZOMEN, book VII, chapter 19, p. 734.

349  
## CHAPTER XL. On the division of the Arians

Divisions also arose among the Arians for the following reason. Their separate disputes led them into foolish arguments.

Since it was believed in their Church that God the Father was the Father of the Son, the Word [Col. 1157B], a question arose among them: could God the Father have been called Father even before the Son existed? For they believed that the Word of God had been brought into being not naturally from the Father but from things that did not exist.

Thus, while they were going astray over the first point, they properly rushed from a matter of mere terminology into an unlawful controversy.

Dorotheus, whom they had summoned from Antioch, said that the Father could neither be nor be called Father if the Son did not subsist.

Marinus, whom they had summoned from Thrace before Dorotheus, found a suitable opportunity—he was opposed to Dorotheus—and gave the contrary answer concerning this question. For this reason divisions arose among them.

Divided over this statement, they celebrated their solemnities separately. Some followed Dorotheus; others followed Marinus, saying that the Father had always been Father, even when the Son did not exist.

These people were called Psathyrians, because a certain Theoctistus, a Syrian by birth and a seller of pastries—*Psatyropola*, that is, “one who sells double [or paired] goods”—strongly defended this proposition.

Selenas, bishop of the Goths, also followed them. But these people too were soon separated, when Marinus disagreed with Agapius, whom he himself had made bishop at Ephesus.

Yet they waged their quarrels and conflicts not on account of religion but on account of the episcopate. The Goths supported Agapius. For this reason many of their clergy, fleeing empty glory, profitably joined the faith of consubstantiality.

The Arians remained divided from one another for thirty-five years. Later, under the rule of Theodosius the Younger, during the consulship of Plinta (A.D. 419), they withdrew from the heresy of the Psathyrians and were reunited, as though establishing by law that they would never mention the issue over which they had been divided.

This occurred at Constantinople. In the other cities, however, they remained divided.

So much for the Arians. The Eunomians also did not remain free from division. Eunomius himself had earlier been separated from Eudoxius, who had ordained him bishop of Cyzicus, on the occasion that he had refused to receive Aetius, his teacher, after Aetius had been expelled.

The others were divided from him through various schisms. First, a certain Theophronius, a Cappadocian who had been taught by Eunomius to engage in disputes and who understood something of Aristotle’s *Categories* and *Περὶ ἑρμηνείας* (“On Interpretation”), wrote books [Col. 1158A] which he entitled *On the Exercise of the Mind*.

When he offended his followers, he was expelled as though he were withdrawing from them. He then gathered people separately and left behind a heresy named after himself.

At Constantinople, a certain Eutychius separated from the Eunomians over a very minor dispute. To this day he holds gatherings separately. Some of these people are called Eunomian-Theophronians, while others are called Eunomian-Eutychians.

Nevertheless, these people corrupted baptism. They baptize not into the Trinity, but into the death of Christ. SOCRATES, book V, chapters 22 and 23. Edition of Christ. Valesius, chapters 23 and 24, p. 291.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the division of the Macedonians

At a certain time a division also arose among the Macedonians, when the presbyter Eutropius held gatherings separately and Carterius by no means agreed with him.

There may have been other divisions among the heresies, but, as a Constantinopolitan and one raised here, I have taken care to recount those that seemed clearer to me. SOCRATES, book V, chapter 23, p. 293.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the recession and subsequent rise of the river Nile

At that time, they say, the Egyptian river withdrew backward around the first rising of the waters. As a result, the Egyptians raged because they were not permitted to perform their customary sacrifices to the river.

When the judge perceived that a rebellion was being stirred up, he reported the matter to the emperor. The emperor, however, judged it better to serve the divine faith than the cups of the Nile and to prefer piety to sacrilege.

“Let that river never flow,” he said, “if by magical arts and the flow of blood the waters of the sacred Paradise are to be polluted” [Col. 1158C].

After this had been done, the Nile shortly afterward poured forth so abundantly that its flood spread even higher than usual. When it had filled its customary measures and continued to rise toward the summit, the Egyptians were reduced to extreme terror, fearing that it might perhaps destroy Alexandria and the regions of Libya as well.

At that time the pagan Alexandrians are said to have shouted in the theater that the Nile had vanished like an old and senile man.

For this reason many Egyptians, abandoning their ancestral religion, turned to the laws of Christianity. SOZOMEN, book VII, chapter 20, p. 736.

## CHAPTER XLIII. How the head of John the Baptist was carried to Constantinople

[Col. 1158D] At the same time, they say, the head of John the Baptist was brought to Constantinople—the head that Herodias requested from Herod the Tetrarch.

The head is said to have been discovered by Macedonian monks who at first lived in Jerusalem and later migrated to Cilicia. Before this reign, Mardonius, the chief officer of the imperial household, had reported this to the emperor. Valens ordered the sacred head to be carried to Constantinople.

Those sent for this purpose placed it on a vehicle and carried it away. When they had come to a place called Pantichium, which is near Chalcedon, the vehicle could not be moved at all, although the pack animals were beaten with many blows.

When this seemed inexplicable to everyone, including the emperor himself, they stored the sacred head [Col. 1159A] in a village called Cosilai. The place itself was an estate belonging to Mardonius. At that time, whether by God’s direction or at the prompting of the prophet himself, it had been brought as far as this place.

Later, when the emperor Theodosius wished to remove these relics of the Baptist, they report that only one woman remained: a sacred virgin who guarded the head.

The emperor repeatedly entreated her—not violently, but with tears—to allow him to fulfill his desire. She thought that, just as in the time of Valens, the Baptist would not permit himself to be carried farther, and she yielded.

The emperor then wrapped in his purple the chest in which the Baptist’s head lay, carried it away, and deposited it at the seventh milestone outside Constantinople. There he built a large and very beautiful church to God [Col. 1159B].

He repeatedly pleaded with the woman and promised her very generous gifts if she were willing to be reconciled. She did not yield, however, for she had been corrupted by the Macedonian heresy, although her presbyter Vincentius, one of her followers who likewise guarded the prophet’s tomb, had been converted and had entered into communion with the Catholic Church.

For they say that the Macedonians have a conspiracy never to depart from their sect. But this presbyter, when the matter of transferring the sacred head was being discussed, decided in his heart that if the Baptist followed the emperor, he too would communicate with the emperor. Having done this, he was converted. SOZOMEN, book VII, chapter 21, p. 737.

## CHAPTER XLIV. How Flavian alone obtained the Antiochene episcopate

[Col. 1159C]

At Antioch, therefore, Flavian succeeded the great Meletius. Together with Diodorus, he had endured many struggles on behalf of the sheep.

Paulinus had wished to assume the leadership of the Church, but the chorus of bishops resisted him, saying that the man who had not accepted Meletius’s policy ought not, after Meletius’s death, to occupy his seat. Instead, the position should go to the man who had shone forth through the greatest labors and had endured dangers for the care of the sheep.

This action made the Romans and Egyptians hostile to the Easterners. Nor were the hostilities destroyed by Paulinus’s death. After him, when Evagrius had obtained his seat, they remained vehemently hostile to Flavian, although Evagrius had been ordained contrary to ecclesiastical regulation.

Paulinus alone had appointed him, violating many ecclesiastical rules. For the rules do not prescribe that anyone may ordain a successor for himself, but that all the priests of the province must be summoned; they absolutely forbid an ordination from taking place without three bishops.

Nevertheless, disregarding all this, they embraced communion with Evagrius and incited the emperor against Flavian. The emperor, frequently urged on, brought Flavian to Constantinople and ordered him to proceed to Rome [mss. and ed. V., “at Rome”].

Flavian, however, using the excuse of winter and promising that he would go to Rome at a suitable time, then returned to his own region.

When the Roman bishops—not only the remarkable Damasus, but also Siricius and Anastasius after him—pressed the emperor vehemently, saying that although he defeated his own tyrants, he allowed those who resisted the laws of Christ to go unpunished, the emperor summoned Flavian again and compelled him to proceed to Rome [mss. and ed. V., “at Rome”].

Then the exceedingly wise Flavian, displaying worthy confidence, said:

“If certain people accuse my faith, O emperor, as though it were unsound, or say that my life is unworthy of the priesthood, I do not refuse to have those very accusers as judges, and I gladly accept their judgment. But if they are disputing about the see and the episcopate, I neither quarrel nor resist those who wish to possess these things. I withdraw and suspend myself from the episcopate. Give the see of Antioch, therefore, O emperor, to whomever you wish.”

The ruler admired his courage and wisdom and ordered him to return to his homeland and govern the Church entrusted to him [Col. 1160B].

After some time the emperor came again to Rome and was subjected to the same complaints by the bishops, as though he had been unwilling to suppress Flavian’s tyranny. But the emperor ordered them to describe the supposed tyranny which they said was Flavian's.

When they said that they could not contend with the emperor, he urged them thereafter to preserve peace in the Church, to abandon their dispute, and to extinguish their foolish controversies.

“Paulinus,” he said, “died long ago. Evagrius was ordained contrary to the rules. The Eastern Churches, however, have granted the episcopate to Flavian, and Asia, Pontus, and Thrace are joined in communion with him. All Illyricum knows that he presides over the bishops throughout the East.”

Moved by these admonitions, the priests of the West promised that they would end their hostilities and said that they would receive envoys sent by him.

When the most holy Flavian learned this, he sent to Rome [mss. and ed. V., “at Rome”] certain bishops worthy of praise, together with Antiochene presbyters and deacons. They were led by Acacius of Beroea, celebrated throughout the whole land and sea.

Coming to Rome [mss. and ed. V., “at Rome”] with the others and healing the long-standing disease of hatred, he restored peace to the Churches after seventeen years.

When the Egyptians learned this, they extinguished their hostilities and embraced concord.

At that time Innocentius, the successor of Anastasius, presided over the Roman Church, a man suitably adorned with prudence and understanding; Theophilus presided over the Alexandrian Church. THEODORETUS, book V, chapter 23, p. 229.

## CHAPTER XLV. On the tyrant Eugenius, and how he was defeated

[Col. 1160D]

At that time the state was being thrown into confusion in the western regions for the following reason. A certain grammarian named Eugenius, a teacher of Latin letters, abandoned his schools and served in the palace. He was the emperor’s secretary and, because of his eloquence, was honored by many. Then, as is reported, after considerable deliberation he took as his associate Arbogastes, born among the lesser Gauls, a commander of the military order, a savage man prepared for slaughter. Having done this, he turned toward tyranny. Thus the two of them plotted the murder of the emperor Valentinian, corrupting his chamberlains and eunuchs. But those men [Col. 1161A] strangled the sleeping prince. When Eugenius suddenly learned of this, he seized power in the West and acted as was fitting for a tyrant.

Hearing this, the emperor Theodosius, once again burdened with anxieties, prepared a second campaign, after the one against Maximus. Gathering his military forces and designating his son Honorius as emperor during his own consulship and that of Habundantius (A.D. 393), on the tenth day of January, in the 351st month [sic], he hastened anew with great zeal toward the western regions. SOCRATES, Book V, chapter 24; Christ. Valesius’s edition, chapter 25, p. 293.

Meanwhile, considering the outcome of the war, he sent to the Thebaid for the monk John, then famous for his foreknowledge. He sent to him the eunuch Eutropius, his most faithful servant, so that he might either bring John back, if he wished to come, [Col. 1161B] or ask him, if unwilling, about the outcome of the war. But he was unable to bring John back; instead, he reported his reply: that Theodosius would win the war and destroy the tyrant, and that after the victory he would die in Italy. SOZOMEN, Book VII, chapter 22, p. 740.

Accordingly, Theodosius left both his sons in the city of Constantinople and set out to fight against Eugenius. Very many barbarians from beyond the Danube followed him, intending to fight against the tyrant; and after a short time he arrived in Gaul with a very large force. There he was preparing for battle, since he already had many thousands of soldiers. SOCRATES, Book V, chapter 24; Christ. Valesius’s edition, chapter 25, p. 294.

When he found an oratory on a certain mountain, he prayed there to the Lord during the night. Around cockcrow, overcome by sleep, he dreamed that he was lying in a field and that two men stood beside him, wearing white garments and seated upon exceedingly white horses. They commanded him to have confidence and, at daybreak, to arm his soldiers for victory; they said that they had been sent for his consolation. One of them said that he was John the Evangelist, and the other that he was the apostle Philip. After learning of this vision, he did not cease from prayer but shed even more abundant tears. This vision was also revealed to a certain soldier, and through various people it reached the emperor. But he said: “That man did not see this on my account; rather, it was shown to him so that no one might believe that I had invented what I myself saw. Therefore it was also shown to him; for the common Lord first revealed this to me.” THEODORET, Book V, chapter 24, p. 232.

Battle was therefore joined near a river called the Frigidus. [Col. 1161D] In the sector where Romans were fighting Romans, the battles were evenly matched. But because of the barbarian auxiliaries of the emperor, the side of Eugenius appeared to be stronger. When the emperor saw the barbarians being destroyed, he was overcome by the greatest distress, threw himself upon the ground, and called upon God for help; nor was his petition frustrated. For a certain Bacurius, his master of the soldiers, was suddenly so encouraged that he charged with the foremost commanders into the sector where the barbarians were being pressed. By this action he broke the battle line and immediately put the enemy to flight.

At that same hour another miracle occurred. A very powerful wind blew and turned back the arrows shot from Eugenius’s side against them, while carrying those from the emperor’s side toward the enemy with great force. [Col. 1162A] Such was the power of the emperor’s prayer. When the combat had thus ended, the tyrant ran to the emperor’s feet and begged to be granted safety. While he was at the emperor’s feet, soldiers cut off his head. These events took place on the seventeenth day of September, in the third consulship of Arcadius and the second of Honorius (A.D. 394). Arbogastes, however, the cause of so many evils, fled two days after the battle. When he realized that he could not remain alive, he killed himself with his own sword. SOCRATES, Book V, chapter 24; Christ. Valesius’s edition, chapter 25, p. 294.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On the miracles of Bishop Donatus at Beroea

At that time many bishops shone brightly, among them Donatus of Euroea in Epirus. Although the provincials testify to many miracles performed by him, the greatest was what he did concerning a dragon. Lying near a bridge on the public road, it seized and devoured sheep, goats, horses, and human beings for food. Donatus came to the beast without a sword or any weapon. When it lifted its head as though about to devour the man, he traced the sign of the cross in the air before its face with his finger and spat into its mouth. The beast immediately received the spittle in its mouth and died. As I have heard, eight pairs of oxen dragged it to a nearby field, where it was burned with fire so that it would not pollute the air with its stench.

The burial place of this Donatus is renowned. An oratory there is called by his name, and it has a spring of water which, it is said, he discovered by his prayers. For when the place was without water and he had once arrived there while traveling, they say that, after those who were with him had grown weary, he prayed, and immediately a flood of water burst forth and has continued there from that time until now. SOZOMEN, Book VII, chapter 25; Christ. Valesius’s edition, chapter 26, p. 747.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On Bishop Theotimus of Tomis

At that time Theotimus governed the Church of Tomis and Scythia. He was a man trained in philosophy, and the barbarians living beyond the Danube, admiring his virtue, declared that he was the god of the Romans. For they had repeatedly experienced in him manifestations of divine things.

Once, while he was traveling, the barbarians of that region encountered him. While those who were with him were disturbed by fear, as though they were about to die immediately, he dismounted from his horse and prayed. The barbarians then passed by without seeing either him, his followers, or the horses from which they had dismounted.

As he repeatedly crossed among the naturally savage Scythians and softened them by feasts and gifts, one barbarian, supposing him to be wealthy, began to plot how he might seize, bind, and drag him away. Having prepared this plan and holding out his right hand in order to throw a noose over him, the hand was immediately bound in the air, and the barbarian was fettered by invisible bonds. Then, when others pleaded on his behalf, Theotimus prayed to God that the barbarian might be released. SOZOMEN, Book VII, chapter 25; Christ. Valesius’s edition, chapter 26, p. 748.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On Epiphanius of Cyprus

[Col. 1163A]

At that time there was also Epiphanius, bishop of the Cypriots, at whose tomb demons are expelled even to the present day. He had distributed his own property to those suffering want and, when many people also offered him money, dispensed it with a most generous hand. It happened that, when the money ran out, the steward of the Church began to complain.

Then someone who was present in the house where the steward was staying gave him a bag containing a large amount of money and disappeared so completely that it was impossible to determine either who had given it or who had sent it. Everyone judged that this had been done by divine providence.

It is also worth reporting another miracle of his. Certain poor men wished to deceive Epiphanius by trickery in order to obtain something from him. While he was traveling, one of them stretched himself out on the ground on his back, while another stood grieving over him as though he were dead and had no means by which he could bury him. When Epiphanius arrived, he prayed that the man might sleep peacefully, provided what was necessary for burial, and consoled the one who was weeping, saying: “Cease your tears, my son; he cannot be brought back to life by weeping. What has happened is inevitable.”

When Epiphanius had departed, the man began to strike his companion so that he would rise. After doing this once and again, he said: “Get up; today let us feast from your earnings.” But when the other did not sense anything at all, he realized that he was truly dead. He ran back to Epiphanius, weeping and asking him to restore his companion to life. Epiphanius consoled him so that he would not take what had happened too hard, but he did not raise the dead man again. For I believe that this was providentially done [Col. 1163C] so that the ministers of God would not easily be deceived.

At that time Aeas [Valesius: Ajax] and Zeno were pursuing philosophy in Gaza, Palestine. Aeas is said, after marrying a very beautiful wife, to have had intercourse with her only three times and to have fathered three sons; afterward he devoted himself earnestly to the monastic life. Zeno, however, was bishop until he reached the age of one hundred years and was never absent from the customary services or rested from his duties. SOZOMEN, Book VII, chapters 26 and 27; Christ. Valesius’s edition, chapters 27 and 28, p. 749.

## CHAPTER XLIX. How the bodies of the prophets Habakkuk and Micah were discovered

At that time it was not only religion that was ennobled; the bodies of the prophets Habakkuk and Micah also, as I have heard, were revealed by divine revelation. Zebennus then governed the Church of Eleutheropolis, in a village formerly called Ceila, on the estate of Berethasia, about ten stadia from the city. Near this place was the burial site of Micah. Since the provincials did not know what to call it, they called it “the memorial of the faithful” [edition: “of the faithful”]. SOZOMEN, [Col. 1164B] Book VII, chapter 28; Christ. Valesius’s edition, chapter 29, p. 752.

## CHAPTER L. On the end of the emperor Theodosius

The emperor Theodosius, exhausted in body after his public labors and expecting to die from that illness, was thinking chiefly about the state, considering what usually happens to human affairs when an emperor dies. He therefore summoned his son Honorius quickly from Constantinople, intending to organize the western regions.

When his son had arrived at Milan, Theodosius recovered somewhat from his illness and celebrated his victory in the circus. Before lunch he presented himself at the spectacle as though he were well. After lunch he suddenly became more seriously ill and could not come to the spectacle; nevertheless, he ordered his son to attend the games. During the following night he died, in the consulship of Olybrius and Probinus (A.D. 395), on the seventeenth day of January, in the first year of the 294th Olympiad. The emperor Theodosius lived sixty years, of which he reigned sixteen. SOCRATES, Book V, chapter 25; Christ. Valesius’s edition, chapter 26, p. 295.

# BOOK TEN

[Col. 1163]

353

## CHAPTER I. On the succession of Arcadius and Honorius

[Col. 1163C]

After Theodosius’s death, his sons succeeded to his empire: Arcadius in the East and Honorius in the West. At that time Damasus presided over the Roman Church, Theophilus over Alexandria, John over Jerusalem, Flavian held the see of Antioch, and Nectarius that of Constantinople.

Around the eighth day of November, in the same consulship (A.D. 395), the body of Theodosius was brought with solemn honor and handed over for burial to his son Arcadius. A few days later, namely on the twenty-seventh of the same month, the army that had been with the emperor Theodosius against the tyrant also returned. When the emperor Arcadius, according to custom, had gone out to meet the returning army at the gates, the soldiers killed the emperor’s prefect Rufinus. [Col. 1164C] He was suspected of being capable of seizing the tyranny. It was also said that he himself had summoned the Huns into the Roman provinces; they were then devastating Armenia and [Col. 1164D] the eastern regions very severely. SOCRATES, Book VI, chapter 1, p. 299.

## CHAPTER II. How Honorius abolished the gladiatorial games

When Honorius assumed the empire of the West, he abolished the gladiatorial games, which had long been celebrated at Rome, for the following reason. A certain Telemachus, living the monastic life, came to Rome from the East for this purpose. While that abominable spectacle was taking place, he himself entered the arena, descended into it, and tried to separate the gladiators who were fighting one another with swords.

When the spectators became enraged against him and continued their bloodshed, they killed the advocate of peace with stones. When the remarkable emperor learned of this, he counted him among the victorious martyrs and completely abolished the abominable spectacle. THEODORET, Book V, chapter 26, p. 234.

## CHAPTER III. On the death of Nectarius, bishop of Constantinople, and the ordination, deeds, and character of John

After a short time Nectarius, bishop of Constantinople, also died, in the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus (A.D. 397), on the twenty-seventh day of September. Immediately, therefore, factions arose over the episcopate, with different people wishing to ordain different candidates. Finally, it was decided that John, a presbyter of the Church, should be summoned from Antioch. The reputation of his teaching was extraordinary.

Within a short time, therefore, by the common decree of all the clergy and laity, the emperor Arcadius summoned him. Since many bishops were present by imperial command for the dignity of the occasion, Theophilus of Alexandria also came. He was indeed eager to disparage John and to ordain his own presbyter Isidore. He loved Isidore because the latter had once endured such danger on his behalf.

When the emperor Theodosius was fighting against the tyrant Maximus, Theophilus sent gifts to the emperor through Isidore and sent two letters, instructing him to give one set of letters to the man who did not win and to present both the gifts and the other letters to the victor. When Isidore had carried these things and arrived at Rome, he waited for the outcome of the victory; but the matter did not remain hidden for long. A certain lector seized the letters and showed them to the emperor. For this reason Isidore, seized by fear, fled to Alexandria, wishing to conceal what he had been ordered to do. For this reason Theophilus loved Isidore.

But the judges of the palace appointed John. When many people accused Theophilus, they presented written accusations against him before the bishops concerning various matters. Then the head of the palace, named Eutropius, took the written accusations and showed them to Theophilus, saying: “Either ordain John, or let the accusations come to trial.” Terrified by this, Theophilus ordained John bishop. John assumed the episcopate on the sixteenth day of February, in the consulship of the emperor Honorius and the prefect Eutychianus (A.D. 398).

Since John was an altogether distinguished man, this can be recognized from the books he left behind. I shall set forth his life, lineage, manner of life, the way in which he was deposed, and how he was honored more greatly after his death [edition Valesius: “later honored in death”]. SOCRATES, Book VI, chapter 2, p. 300.

John was an Antiochene, the son of Secundus and Anthusa, noble persons; he was a pupil of the sophist Libanius and a student of the philosopher Andragathius. When he was preparing for advocacy, he considered the troubles of litigants and the unjust aim of life, and chose a quiet life instead. He did this in imitation of Evagrius, who, although he too had pursued the same studies, had chosen a quiet life.

Soon afterward, changing both his appearance and his manner of walking, he devoted himself to sacred readings and went more frequently to the holy church. By doing this he persuaded Theodorus [Col. 1166A] and Maximus, who had been his fellow students under the sophist Libanius, to abandon their ostentatious life and pursue a simple one. Theodorus was later ordained bishop of the Church of Mopsuestia, while Maximus became bishop of Seleucia in Isauria.

At that time these men became pupils in sacred reading under Diodore and Carterius, who then presided over holy monasteries. Diodore was later ordained bishop of Tarsus and wrote many books, examining the sacred Scriptures literally.

While John was living with Basil, who had then been made deacon by Meletius and was later appointed bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, the bishop Zeno, returning from Jerusalem, appointed him lector in the church of Antioch. While he still held this office, he published a book against the Jews. After a short time he also received the diaconate from Meletius, wrote another book, On the Priesthood, and explained many other works.

Later, when Meletius died in the city of Constantinople, John withdrew from the Meletians and did not communicate with Paulinus; he lived quietly for three continuous years. Then, after Paulinus died, he was ordained presbyter by Evagrius, Paulinus’s successor.

Before becoming a bishop, therefore, he lived in this manner. He was, as they say, a man made more severe by his zeal for chastity; from his youth he gave himself more to anger than to respect, and, because of the rectitude of his life, was careless about looking ahead to the future. Because of his simplicity, he was lavish in freedom of speech and used it without moderation with those with whom he conversed. He was outstanding in teaching and effective in correcting the conduct of his hearers; but in conversation the uninformed considered him arrogant.

When he had such a character, after receiving the episcopate he conducted himself with greater arrogance than he should have, wishing to correct the life of his clergy. Thus, from the very beginning, when he appeared harsh to the clergy of the Church, he became hateful to many, and everyone avoided him as though he were mad. His deacon Serapio compelled him to offend everyone; on one occasion, in the presence of the clergy, Serapio loudly addressed him as follows: “You will never be able to correct these men, O bishop, unless you strike them all with a single staff.” This remark provoked still greater hatred against him.

Before long he removed many of the clergy for various reasons. But they conspired against him and also used disparaging reports among the people. They gave the greatest credibility to these accusations because he would not allow anyone to eat with him, nor would he himself go when invited by another. Some say that he refused to eat with anyone because he ate disgracefully and took food in an unbecoming manner; others declared that he did this because of his extraordinary restraint in food. SOCRATES, Book VI, chapter 3, p. 301.

Nevertheless, I heard from a truthful man who reported it that, because of his abstinence, he often suffered pain in his head and stomach, and for that reason avoided the banquets at midday. SOZOMEN, Book VII, chapter 9, p. 769.

The people, however, loved him because of the sermons he delivered in the church and paid little attention to the accusations of his enemies. What his books are like need not now be stated, since they can reveal this to their readers. Because he was hostile only toward the clergy, plots against him did not entirely succeed. But when he also began to rebuke many of the nobles, greater envy was kindled against him. Many things were said, and many things were also done that gave credibility to the accusations. SOCRATES, Book VI, chapter 4, p. 304.

## CHAPTER IV. How Eutropius, the emperor’s chamberlain, was killed

A homily delivered against Eutropius at that time added weight to these disparagements. Eutropius, the eunuch who was the emperor’s chamberlain and held the dignity of consul, wished to punish certain people who had taken refuge in churches. He therefore sought to have the emperors enact a law [Col. 1167B] ordering that no one should flee to churches and that those who had previously taken refuge there should be dragged out.

But divine judgment suddenly followed. The law had been published. A few days later, when Eutropius himself had offended the emperor, he was among those who had taken refuge at the church. While Eutropius lay beneath the altar, struck by extreme fear, the bishop sat upon the ambo where he customarily delivered sermons and preached a homily of rebuke against him.

For this reason he offended many people even more, since he not only failed to pity a man placed in misfortune but also did not cease rebuking him. Therefore the emperor ordered the head of Eutropius, who then held the dignity of consul, to be cut off for certain faults, and his name was completely removed from the list of consuls (A.D. 399). For this reason [Col. 1167C] only the name of Theodorus, who had been consul with him, was entered. He repeatedly rebuked many people boldly for various reasons and was hateful to many.

Accordingly, Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, immediately after John’s ordination investigated the grounds for his deposition and secretly spoke against him in the presence of certain people; he also wrote to many who were far away. He was distressed not only by John’s boldness but also because he had been unable to ordain his own presbyter Isidore bishop of Constantinople. SOCRATES, Book VI, chapter 5, p. 304.

Bishop John urged the priests to live according to the ecclesiastical ordinances. Whoever presumed to violate them, he prohibited from approaching the temple. For he said that those who disdained to imitate the life of the priesthood ought not to enjoy the honor of the priesthood.

He was responsible not only for the administration of the city of Constantinople but also for the whole of Thrace, which is divided into six provinces and administered through eleven jurisdictions. By these ordinances he also regulated the Pontic region, which is known to be governed by the same number of judges.

When he learned that sacrifices were still being offered to demons in Phoenicia, he sent chosen monks, armed with imperial decrees, against the worshipers of idols. He gave money to be distributed to the destroyers of the temples, not from the public treasury but from funds that he voluntarily received from faithful women who offered them. THEODORET, Book V, chapter 28, p. 235.

## CHAPTER V. On the conversion of the Celts through John

[Col. 1168A]

Seeing that the people of the Celts were also ensnared in the nets of the Arians, and considering how their salvation might be captured, he devised the following strategy for this hunt. He appointed presbyters, deacons, and lectors who spoke the same language and gave them one church. By this means he captured many of them, since he himself frequently went there and explained the sacred readings through a Celtic interpreter.

By doing this repeatedly within the city, he recalled many Arians of that people to the apostolic doctrines. Among the Scythians, however, there were certain people who desired salvation but could not attain it. When John learned of this, he sought out men burning with apostolic zeal, sent them there, and supplied the grace of salvation to those who desired it.

I also read a letter of his to Leontius, bishop of Ancyra, in which he reported that the Scythians had been converted in our province. When he learned that the disease of Marcion had grown in certain villages, he wrote to the pastors of that place to drive them out. In addition, he asked that an imperial decree be issued for this purpose. [These words are absent from the manuscript codices and from edition Valesius.] That he had the care of the churches in his heart, in accordance with the divine Apostle, is sufficiently demonstrated by these things. [These words are absent from Valesius’s edition.] It is also possible to understand his boldness from another source. THEODORET, Book V, chapter 30, p. 236.

## CHAPTER VI. On Gainas, master of the soldiers, and his rebellion

[Col. 1168C]

A certain Gainas, Celtic by birth, barbarian in judgment, and greatly elated by tyrannical ambition, was at that time master of the soldiers. He had many men of his own race and many Romans under his command, and by his contemplation of tyranny he inspired terror in very many people, even in the emperor himself. He was also an Arian.

He therefore asked the emperor to give him one church within the city. The emperor promised that he would appease him. Then, summoning John and telling him of Gainas’s power and his contemplated tyranny, he asked him to restrain Gainas’s purpose by giving him a church.

But John, most courageous in virtue, said: “Do not make such promises, O emperor, nor give what is holy to dogs. I cannot drive out those who bless God and unjustly surrender a holy temple to blasphemers. Nor should you fear this barbarian, O emperor. [Col. 1168D] Instead, order both of us to be summoned, and secretly listen to what is said between us. I shall restrain his tongue so completely that he will not dare to ask for what ought not to be given.”

Hearing this, the emperor rejoiced and summoned both men on the following day. Gainas then pressed his request, while John opposed him, saying: “It is not lawful for an emperor who guards piety to presume to do anything contrary to the divine commandments.”

When Gainas replied that he too ought to have an oratory, John said: “The divine house is open to you everywhere, and no one prevents you from praying.”

But Gainas said: “I belong to another sect, and I request that I and my people have one temple. I have undertaken many labors for the Roman state, and I ought not to be disregarded in my request.”

John replied: “You have received very many rewards, rewards surpassing your struggles, having become master of the soldiers and having moreover been adorned with the consular robe. It is appropriate for you to consider who you once were and how you are now seen, what your former poverty was and what your present possessions are; what clothing you wore before you crossed the Danube and what you wear now. Consider, therefore, that a few labors have brought you the greatest rewards, and do not be ungrateful toward the one who honors you.”

By these words that great teacher closed Gainas’s mouth and compelled him to remain silent. THEODORET, Book V, chapter 32, p. 237.

Gainas desired to obtain the empire. Although he had earlier promised the emperor Arcadius, before the blessed martyr Euphemia at Chalcedon, that he would remain faithful, he was considering various plans and persisted in his purpose.

Since he had been unable to accomplish anything in the city of Constantinople during the day, he devised a plan to send barbarians by night to burn the palace. Then it was openly demonstrated how God protects the city. When the barbarians he had sent for arson and plunder appeared, a host of angels appeared, forming a vast body of armed men. Thinking that they were soldiers, the barbarians withdrew.

When this was reported to Gainas, it seemed unbelievable to him. He knew that the entire army had been stationed throughout the cities. Therefore, on the following night, he sent others. When the same report was made to him—for the angels again displayed the same vision to the barbarians—finally he himself went out with a multitude and experienced the miracle, believing that an army truly lay concealed during the day and was stationed at night to guard the city.

Thus, since he could accomplish nothing within the city, he withdrew into Thrace and openly revealed his hostile intention. SOCRATES, Book VI, chapter 6, p. 307.
