After some time had passed, Gainas revealed the tyranny he had long been contemplating. Having gathered an army, he ravaged all of Thrace. When the judges and the people learned of this, they were terrified; no one dared to resist him or undertake an embassy to him, because they feared his barbarian harshness.

Then the emperor, leaving all the others aside as though they were afraid, imposed the burden of the embassy upon John, a most holy man. John, remembering neither Gainas’s resistance nor the enmities that seemed to have arisen from it, eagerly set out for Thrace.

When Gainas learned that the envoy was approaching and that John had assumed such boldness on behalf of piety, he went out to meet him far along the road and placed John’s right hand around his own eyes. He also ordered his sons to kiss John’s sacred knees. Such was John’s virtue that he compelled even men who were exceedingly terrifying to humble themselves and feel fear. THEODORET, Book V, chapters 32 and 33, p. 238.

## CHAPTER VII. On the dispute that arose among the Egyptian monks: whether God is corporeal or incorporeal

At that time a dispute had arisen over whether God was corporeal and possessed the form of a human being, or whether he was incorporeal and altogether alien to human form. From this dispute many quarrels and struggles arose, with some affirming one position and others another. Most of the simpler monks, however, judged that God was corporeal and of human form. Many others, rejecting them, said that God was incorporeal and separate from bodily form.

The bishop Theophilus of Alexandria agreed with the latter, so that in the church, before the people, he argued against those who asserted that God was of human form and defined God in accordance with his doctrine as incorporeal. When the Egyptian monks learned of this, they came to Alexandria and raised a revolt against Theophilus as though he were impious, even attempting to kill him.

When he realized this, he considered how he might avoid death. Receiving them with flattery, he said to them: “I see you as the face of God.” With these words he turned the monks away from their attack.

But they said: “If you truly say that the face of God is like ours, anathematize the books of Origen. For some of their teachings oppose our opinion. If you do not do this, you will certainly suffer from us what belongs to the impious and rebellious against God.”

Theophilus replied: “I shall do what pleases you; do not rage against me. I too am an enemy of Origen’s books and condemn those who accept them.” Thus he turned the monks aside, and perhaps for this reason the dispute was suppressed for a time.

After this, the following event occurred. Four venerable brothers, Dioscorus, Ammonius, Eusebius, and Euthymius, presided over monasteries in Egypt. Because of their bodily stature they were called the “Tall Ones.” They shone in speech and life and were therefore distinguished among the Alexandrians. The bishop Theophilus also honored them.

For this reason he forcibly brought Dioscorus and made him bishop of Hermopolis. He asked two of the others to live with him and obtained their consent only with difficulty. He made them clergy and appointed them stewards of the church.

When they were distressed that they were accomplishing less of the purpose of their way of life and, as time passed, saw that their souls were being harmed—since the bishop lived for money and was eager to amass much gold [editions Nivardus and Froben: “since he had much money and was eager…”]—they refused to remain with him and preferred to live in a deserted dwelling.

Since he did not know their wishes, he asked that they remain with him. Later, when he saw that they themselves rather disliked him, he became angry and threatened them. But they paid no attention and departed.

Theophilus, however, being inflamed in spirit, attempted by whatever means he could to harass those men. Meanwhile he hated their brother Dioscorus. He was distressed because the crowd of monks loved and revered them, and he knew that he could harm them in no other way than by attacking the monks.

He had also discovered that, in frequent conversations with them, they confessed that God was incorporeal and not of human form, lest human passion also follow from the necessity of a human form. Although Theophilus himself held this view, he changed what he had formerly taught well in order to avenge himself.

Sending into the desert, he hunted down many simple monks who lacked spiritual training, saying that they ought not to follow Dioscorus or his brothers, who said that God was incorporeal. For, according to divine Scripture, God has eyes, ears, hands, and feet, just as human beings do. Dioscorus and his followers, following Origen, introduce a blasphemous doctrine, as though God had neither eyes nor ears nor hands nor feet.

Many monks were deceived by this seduction, and a most violent revolt was stirred up. The trained men were not deceived, but the simple monks, suddenly inflamed with zeal for the faith, rose against their brothers. A division arose, and they attacked one another.

The followers of Theophilus called their brothers Origenists and impious; the others called the followers of Theophilus “Human-formists.” Because of this a monstrous revolt arose, and Theophilus came to Nitria with an armed multitude against Dioscorus and his brothers. They were scarcely able to escape the dangers by flight. SOCRATES, [Col. 1171B] Book VI, chapter 7, p. 309.

## CHAPTER VIII. How John began the nocturnal hymns

While these things were happening in Egypt, John of Constantinople flourished in teaching and was regarded favorably by everyone. He was the first to increase prayers during the nocturnal hymns, for the following reason.

The Arians, as has been said, held their gatherings outside the city. On Saturdays and Sundays, however, they assembled within the gates and under the porticoes, singing hymns and antiphons composed according to Arian doctrine. They did this for most of the night, and at daybreak, singing the same antiphons, they passed through the middle of the city and hurried to their church.

Since they repeatedly continued doing this almost as an insult to the orthodox—for they frequently also sang: “Where are those who say that the one has a threefold power?”—John, fearing that simple people might be drawn away by such songs, instructed his own people to occupy themselves likewise with nocturnal hymns, so that the work of the Arians might be obscured and the profession of the faithful strengthened.

John’s very useful undertaking ended amid crowds and dangers. For when the hymns of the Homoousians appeared more splendid at night—for he had also made silver crosses, which were carried with candles, and the Augusta Eudoxia supplied the expenses for this—then the Arians, driven by zeal, rose even to murder.

One night, when a clash took place, Brison, the Augusta’s eunuch, who had been appointed to organize the hymns, was struck in the forehead with a stone. Some people of both parties were also killed. Because of these disturbances, the emperor prohibited the Arians from singing hymns publicly. SOCRATES, Book VI, chapter 8. Christ. Valesius’s edition, chapters 7 and 8, p. 312.

## CHAPTER IX. That a vision of angels praising God was shown to Bishop Ignatius
It must nevertheless be explained from where the practice of singing antiphons in the church took its beginning. Ignatius, the third bishop of Antioch in Syria after the apostle Peter, who had also lived with the apostles themselves, saw a vision of angels and how, through antiphonal chants, they sang hymns to the Holy Trinity. He is accordingly thought to have handed on the manner of this vision to the Church of Antioch, and from there it passed to all the Churches. SOCRATES, book VI, chapter 8, p. 313.

## CHAPTER X. On the Enemies of John

[Col. 1172A]

It is reported that, among other causes, John had also incurred the empress’s hatred on account of Severian, bishop of Gabala. Severian and Antiochus of Ptolemais were both exceptionally eloquent and prepared to teach before the church. Antiochus came first to Constantinople; advanced by his eloquence and enriched with money, he returned to his own city.

Because of his zeal for Antiochus, Severian later came as well. He saw that John frequently appeared remarkable when preaching in church and was honored by many nobles, by the emperor himself, and likewise by the empress. When John departed for Asia, he entrusted the church to Severian. He believed that Severian’s flattering behavior [Col. 1172B] showed that he truly loved him. But Severian was more concerned to commend himself to his hearers. When John learned of this through Serapion, he became jealous. When John returned from Asia, it happened that, as Severian was passing by, Serapion deliberately did not rise for him. Enraged, Severian shouted: “If the cleric Serapion has died, Christ has not become human.” For this he was accused by Serapion of insult and blasphemy against God, and John expelled him from the city.

When the empress learned of this through Severian’s associates, she immediately had him recalled from Chalcedon. John, however, refused to see him despite the entreaties of many, until, in the Church of the Apostles, the empress placed her son Theodosius at John’s knees, begging and repeatedly adjuring him to restore Severian to his favor. SOZOMEN, book VIII, chapter 10, [Col. 1172C] p. 770.

Meanwhile, monks came from the desert to Constantinople with Dioscorus and his brothers; among them was Isidore, who had formerly been Theophilus’s closest friend but later became his enemy for the following reason.

There was a certain Peter, archpresbyter of the Church of Alexandria. Theophilus expelled him from the Church, accusing him of having admitted into sacred communion a certain Manichaean woman who had not first renounced heresy. When Peter said that he had admitted her at Theophilus’s command, and Theophilus denied this, Peter appealed to Isidore’s testimony, since the bishop was not unaware that the act had taken place.

At that time Isidore was living in Rome, having been sent by Theophilus to Damasus in order to reconcile Flavian, bishop of Antioch, with him. When Isidore returned, he confirmed that Peter’s reply was true, saying that the Manichaean woman had been admitted at the bishop’s command. Enraged by this, Theophilus expelled both men from the Church.

For this reason Isidore came to Constantinople with Dioscorus and the others, in order to report their treatment to the emperor and to John. When John learned of these events, he at first honored the men and enjoyed their prayers; but he did not wish to participate with them in sacred communion before the case had been examined.

After these events, a false report reached Theophilus that John had communicated with them and was offering them assistance. He prepared not only to avenge himself on Dioscorus and Isidore, but also to depose John from the episcopate.

He therefore sent letters to the bishops of the individual cities, [Col. 1173A] concealing his intention but accusing the books of Origen. Then he made Epiphanius of Cyprus his friend, although previously he had been his enemy, as though Epiphanius had insufficiently correct views about God and believed that God possessed human form. Thus, as if out of repentance, Theophilus professed that he followed Epiphanius’s sect [ms. Lyr., statements], and arranged for a synod of the bishops of Cyprus to be held, so that Origen’s books might be condemned.

Epiphanius, however, misled through excessive self-regard and simplicity, convened the synod, prohibited the reading of Origen’s books, and sent a letter to John, warning him to abstain from reading Origen and, once the synod had assembled, to confirm himself whatever had been approved.

Thus Theophilus, having deceived the highly renowned Epiphanius and recognizing that his wishes were succeeding, himself too, [Col. 1173B] after assembling the bishops, condemned Origen’s books, although Origen had died nearly two hundred years earlier—not because Theophilus had any such intention in itself, but because he was striving to injure Dioscorus and his followers [mss., to deceive Dioscorus and his followers].

John, however, paid little attention to what had been announced by Epiphanius and Theophilus. He was occupied with ecclesiastical teaching and flourished in it; he repeatedly gave no thought to what was being plotted against him.

When Theophilus now appeared openly intent on deposing John from the episcopate, John’s enemies also followed Theophilus. Many clerics and many palace nobles, finding the opportunity favorable, sought to have a synod held at Constantinople against John. They conveyed this both to one another by letters and by word of mouth.

The case of Severian and Antiochus, the bishops mentioned above, therefore increased the hostility against John. SOCRATES, book VI, chapters 9 and 10, p. 314.

## CHAPTER XI. How Epiphanius of Cyprus Became an Enemy of John

After a short time, Bishop Epiphanius came to Constantinople, bringing the condemnation of 358 books of Origen. They had not decreed Origen himself excommunicated, but had merely censured his books.

He went out to the basilica of Saint John, situated seven miles from the city; after holding an assembly there and ordaining a deacon, he returned to the city. He declined John’s invitation because of Theophilus and preferred to live in his own lodgings. He then summoned the bishops who were present and read to them the condemnation of Origen’s books. Some, out of reverence for Epiphanius, subscribed to it; most refused to do so.

Among the latter was Theotimus, bishop of Scythia, who replied as follows: “I, Epiphanius, neither insult him who long ago entered blessed rest, nor dare to attempt anything impious by condemning what our predecessors did not reject. Therefore I do not perceive any evil teaching in Origen’s books.”

Then, producing Origen’s books [ms. Santheod., his books], he read from them and displayed their ecclesiastical interpretations. Afterwards he continued: “Those who insult these things do not understand themselves.” Thus, it is reported, Theotimus, renowned above all for the uprightness of his life, replied to Epiphanius. [Col. 1174A]

Since many detractors, however, insidiously reject Origen as a blasphemer, it does not seem unreasonable to say a few words about them. Worthless men, who cannot make themselves distinguished by their own qualities, try by disparaging better men to show that they themselves possess some merit.

This happened first to Methodius, bishop of Olympus, a city of Lycia; then to Eustathius, who was a bishop for only a short time; after him to Apollinaris; and finally to Theophilus. These men disparaged Origen, while others approached his accusation for a different reason [ms. Santheod., and otherwise].

After Methodius had initially disparaged Origen at length, he later, as though in repentance and admiration of the man, said in the dialogue that he entitled *Xenon*:

“But why should I say anything further about the complaints made against Origen? While they blame him for what they think are grounds for blame, and find nothing in him as one who holds evil beliefs about the Holy Trinity, they are shown instead to bear witness in him to greater piety and uprightness.”

Athanasius, the defender of the Council of Nicaea, clearly calls this man a witness to his faith in his own books against the Arians, joining Origen’s books to his own and saying:

“Origen, remarkable and most industrious, bearing this testimony to us concerning the Son of God, says that he is co-eternal with the Father.”

Thus Origen’s detractors do not understand themselves: in blaspheming his praiser Athanasius, they also blaspheme Origen. Let this suffice concerning Origen. Now let us follow the history. SOCRATES, book VI, chapters 11 and 12. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapters 12 and 13, p. 318.

## CHAPTER XII. How John Received Epiphanius

[Col. 1174C]

John of Constantinople was not indignant that Epiphanius had performed an ordination in his church without observing the regulations; nevertheless, he asked him to remain with him among the bishops. Epiphanius replied that he would neither remain with him nor pray unless John expelled Dioscorus and those who were with him from the city and personally subscribed to the condemnation of Origen’s books.

While John delayed doing these things and said that nothing should be done rashly before a Catholic examination, Epiphanius was driven to this course by John’s enemies. When an assembly was to be held in the Church of the Apostles, they induced Epiphanius to come forward before the entire people, condemn Origen’s books, declare Dioscorus and his followers condemned, and at the same time disparage John as their defender.

This was reported to John. The next day, when Epiphanius had already come to the church, John sent him the following words through Serapion:

“You have done many things contrary to the regulations, Epiphanius! First, because you performed an ordination in a church subject to my jurisdiction; next, because, without my command, you celebrated sacred rites there on your own authority; again, because, although invited, you excused yourself; and now once more you presume upon yourself. Therefore take care lest an uproar arise among the people and you yourself bear the danger of this matter.”

When Epiphanius heard this, he withdrew from the church in fear. As he was about to return to Cyprus, some report that he sent John this message: “I hope you will not die a bishop.” John replied: “I hope you will not return to your homeland.” I do not know whether these words were truly spoken; [Col. 1175A] both men, however, met the following fate. Epiphanius did not reach Cyprus alive but died on the ship, and shortly afterwards John was deposed from the episcopate. SOCRATES, book VI, chapter 13. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 14, p. 320.

## CHAPTER XIII. Why the Empress Became More Hostile, Through Whom John Became Her Enemy, and How He Was Carried into Exile

After Epiphanius had departed, word reached John that the empress Eudoxia had armed Epiphanius against him. Enraged by this, he delivered a speech to the people, with the fullness of his eloquence, filled with criticism of all women.

The entire people seized upon this speech as though it had been delivered against the empress, and it reached the emperor’s ears. When the empress learned of it, she described it to the emperor as an insult against herself, saying that the insult directed against the emperor’s wife was principally an insult against him. Consequently, arrangements were made for Theophilus to convene a synod against John as quickly as possible. Severian was acting in the same cause, for he was still John’s enemy.

Meanwhile Theophilus arrived, stirring up many bishops [ed. V., admonishing many bishops]. Many of John’s enemies therefore flocked together. Those whom John had removed from the episcopate were also present. They all assembled in agreement at Chalcedon, where Cyrinus was then bishop; Cyrinus said many things against John, calling him impious and arrogant. The bishops took pleasure in such accusations.

Maruthas, bishop of Mesopotamia, unwillingly stepped on Cyrinus’s foot. Cyrinus, overcome by the pain, could not cross to Constantinople with the bishops; the others, however, crossed. SOCRATES, book VI, chapter 14. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 15, p. 321.

Afterwards, when his leg frequently suffered pain, it was amputated, because putrefaction had invaded almost his entire body and had already begun to spread into the other foot. Not long afterward he died. SOZOMEN, book VIII, chapter 16, p. 779.

When Theophilus came from Alexandria, no one went out to meet him, nor was he received with customary honor, since he was an open enemy. Alexandrian sailors, however, who had then arrived with grain, came out to meet him and received him favorably.

When he reached Constantinople, he refused to enter the church and instead lived in a house of the empresses called the Placidiana. [Col. 1175D] From this point they began to bring charges against John. The matter was no longer presented as concerning Origen’s books; rather, they stirred up these unlawful accusations.

When these preparations had been made, the bishops assembled in the Chalcedonian suburb called Rufinianum, where a basilica dedicated in honor of the apostles Peter and Paul had been established. They summoned John to give satisfaction for the charges brought against him, and ordered Serapion, Tigrius the eunuch presbyter, and Paul the lector to come with him, since they too were being accused.

John rejected those who summoned him as enemies and called for a universal synod. They nevertheless summoned him four times without delay. When he refused to come and continued to call for a synod, they condemned him, [Col. 1176A] finding no fault in him except that, when summoned, he had refused to obey.

When this was announced toward evening, the people were stirred to the greatest revolt. They rushed together during the night and would not permit him to be dragged from the church, but shouted that his case should be examined before a larger council.

The emperor’s order, however, was imminent: he was to be expelled quickly and carried into exile. When John learned of this, on the third day after his condemnation, around midday, he surrendered himself without the people’s knowledge. He was thinking that no uprising should arise because of him.

He was led away into exile. Among the people, however, an intolerable revolt broke out, so that even many of his enemies were moved to pity, saying that a man who had shortly before been desired as deposed had suffered calumny.

Therefore everyone shouted against the emperor and the council of priests, [Col. 1176B] and especially against Theophilus. His plot could no longer remain hidden, for it was apparent from many indications, especially because immediately after John’s deposition he had communicated with Dioscorus and his brothers.

At that time, while Severian was also teaching in the church, he disparaged John, saying: “Even if John is to be blamed for nothing else, his arrogance is nevertheless a crime sufficient for condemnation. For all sins are forgiven to human beings, but God resists the arrogant” (James 4:6), as the Holy Scriptures teach. SOCRATES, book VI, chapter 14. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapters 15 and 16, p. 322.

## CHAPTER XIV. How John Returned and Was Again Attacked by His Calumniators

[Col. 1176C]

When an immense revolt had arisen, with the people running about and shouting even at the imperial palace, the empress, moved by the situation, asked the emperor to order John’s return. The eunuch Breson was then sent, and John, although unwilling to enter the city, was compelled by necessity to do so.

When he returned, the people came to meet him at the church with great honor. As soon as John entered, they asked him to sit on the episcopal throne and offer the people the prayer of peace. He refused, saying that this ought to be done by a synodal judgment and that those who had condemned him should withdraw their sentence.

Everyone was nevertheless eager to see him seated in his proper place and to hear the words of the teacher. Although he delayed for a long time, the people prevailed, [Col. 1176D] compelled him to sit on the episcopal throne, and required him to offer the customary prayer of peace. Compelled as well, he delivered a speech to the people.

This gave his enemies another opportunity. At first, Theophilus was said to have raised a charge against him concerning the ordination of Heraclides [ms. Theod., the appointment], in order to depose John on this pretext. Heraclides was not present, however; he was judged as though present, on the accusation that he had unjustly blinded certain people and sent them bound in chains in a procession through the middle of Ephesus.

When John’s party said that a proper hearing ought to be established, the Alexandrians insisted that Heraclides’ accusers should be admitted. A violent riot and slaughter consequently arose between the Constantinopolitan and Alexandrian peoples. [Col. 1177A] Many were wounded, and a few were killed.

When Theophilus saw this, he suddenly fled to Alexandria. The other bishops did the same, except for a few who supported John. After these events Theophilus was found blameworthy. His unpopularity was increased by the fact that he again occupied himself with Origen’s books.

When someone asked him how he could again embrace what he had previously rejected, he replied: “Origen’s books are like a meadow full of every kind of flower. Whatever good I find in them, I pluck; but if I encounter anything thorny, I leave it aside, as though it might prick me.”

Theophilus said this without considering the words of the wisest Solomon, who says that “the words of the wise are like goads and nails” (Ecclesiastes 12:11). [Col. 1177B] For this reason Theophilus appeared blameworthy to everyone.

After Theophilus’s flight, Dioscorus, bishop of Hermopolis, died a short time later. He was buried with honor in the basilica established at Illicum, where the synod had been held on John’s account. SOCRATES, book VI, chapters 14 and 15. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 16, p. 324.

John was then sent into exile and lived at the mouth of the Pontus, a place called Hieron. When an earthquake invaded the imperial city during the night, envoys were sent to him in the morning, asking him to return quickly to the city and remove the dangers by his prayers. Others were sent after them, and then still others, so that the Bosphorus was filled with envoys.

When the most faithful people learned of this, [Col. 1177C] the ships of the Propontis were covered with waves of people. Everyone went out to meet him, lighting candles and lamps for the return of their shepherd. THEODORET, book V, chapter 34, p. 239.

Meanwhile, when Theophilus arrived by ship at Hierapolis, the citizens chose the monk Nilamnion after the bishop of that city had died. Nilamnion repeatedly refused, but Theophilus urged him not to reject the priesthood. Then he promised, saying: “Tomorrow what pleases the Lord will be accomplished” [ms. Lyr., replied].

The next day, the people came to his cell and compelled him. Then Nilamnion said: “First, let us pray.” When Theophilus approved this, they prayed together. During that prayer Nilamnion suddenly reached the end of his life. SOZOMEN, book VIII, chapter 19, p. 784.

## CHAPTER XV. How John Treated the Empress

[Col. 1177D]

John was occupied with teaching and appointed Serapion bishop of Heraclea in Thrace. As a result, even greater hatred was stirred against him.

Not long afterward the following events are said to have occurred. A silver statue of the empress Eudoxia was erected on a porphyry column, wrapped in a cloak. It stood neither near nor far from the Church of Hagia Sophia, from which it was separated only by the course of a street. Public games were customarily held there.

John considered this an insult to the Church and once again armed his tongue with his customary boldness. When it would have been necessary to turn the rulers away from such a spectacle by a word of supplication, he did not do so; instead, relying on the force of his eloquence, he attacked those who ordered such things to be done.

The empress again interpreted this as an insult directed against herself and prepared once more for a synod of bishops to be held against him. When John learned of this, he delivered in the church that famous homily whose opening is:

“Again Herodias rages; again she is troubled. Again she dances; again she desires to receive John’s head on a platter.”

This action inflamed the empress to still greater anger. SOCRATES, book VI, chapter 16. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapters 17 and 18, p. 326.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Plots Laid Against John

Meanwhile a certain man was arrested who wanted to kill John. He was handed over to the prefect for punishment, but John rescued him so that he would not be executed.

Later, the servant of the presbyter Elpidius also approached the bishop at a run and attempted to kill him. When someone seized him, he suddenly struck that man, as well as another bystander and a third. When an outcry arose and many people gathered, he killed several before finally being captured and handed over.

From that time the people guarded John by night and by day, sitting around his house. SOZOMEN, book VIII, chapter 21, p. 787.

## CHAPTER XVII. On John’s Second Deposition and the Schism Made on His Account

After a short time the bishops Leontius of Ancyra in Galatia, Ammonius of Laodicea, Breson of Philippi in Thrace, Acacius of Beroea in Syria, and several others were present. In their presence the former accusers were again stirred up.

John therefore trusted in such circumstances and asked that the accusation be brought forward properly. When the festival of the Savior’s birth arrived, the emperor did not come solemnly to the church; instead, he sent John word that he would not communicate with him unless John was first cleared of the charges.

Although John’s accusers were greatly frightened for his safety, the bishops who were present demanded nothing else except that, after his deposition, he had sat on the episcopal throne without observing the council’s decree.

When John replied that sixty-five bishops who communicated with him had decreed this, Leontius and the others protested: “But very many bishops had deposed you, John.”

John again maintained that this regulation belonged not to the orthodox Church but to the Arians. For when they had assembled at Antioch to condemn the faith proclaimed concerning consubstantiality, they had introduced this regulation out of hatred for Athanasius. The others then condemned him without a proper examination, failing to understand that, when they used this regulation, they had also deposed Athanasius.

These events took place around the festival of Easter. The emperor sent word to John that he could not come to the church because two councils had condemned him. John therefore remained inactive and did not go down to the church.

Immediately, all those who supported him withdrew from the church and celebrated Easter in the baths called Constantianae. Many bishops, presbyters, [Col. 1179A] and clerics of the sacred order were moved to join them, celebrating assemblies separately in various places. For this reason they were also called Johannites.

John did not appear anywhere for two months, until the emperor ordered that he be taken into exile. He was dragged from the church and led away. On that day some of the Johannites set the church on fire. As it burned, the wind also carried the flames to the basilica of the senate, which was likewise consumed.

This happened on the twentieth day of January, during the sixth consulship of Honorius and the consulship of Aristenes (A.D. 404). For this reason the city prefect Optatus, although a pagan, tore many Johannites apart with various kinds of torture out of hatred for Christians. SOCRATES, book VI, chapter 16. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 18, p. 326.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On John’s Exile and Death

[Col. 1179B]

John was not only expelled from the city but also sent to a certain small and deserted city of Armenia, Cucusus. From there he was sent again to Pityus, at the boundaries of the Pontus and the Roman Empire, places near savage barbarians. But the merciful Lord did not permit the victorious athlete to remain long in such regions. THEODORET, book V, chapter 34, p. 240.

Meanwhile Innocent, the Roman bishop, hearing about John, being distressed, and wishing a general council to be held, wrote to John and to the clergy of Constantinople that John ought not to be given a successor and that his clergy should not obey another bishop. I have not translated these letters because of their length.

They say that, while John was being led into exile, he learned through a vision the day on which he would die; the day was shown to him by Basiliscus the martyr at Comana. Exhausted by the journey and unable to endure the headache and the heat of the sun, he ended his life through illness. SOZOMEN, book VIII, chapters 26 and 28, pp. 793 and 798.

On the fourteenth day of September, during the seventh consulship of Honorius and the second of Theodosius (A.D. 407). SOCRATES, book VI, chapter 19. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 21, p. 329.

## CHAPTER XIX. How Illyricum and the West Withdrew from Communion with the Eastern Bishops on John’s Account

[Col. 1179D]

The bishops of Europe especially abhorred the causes of this injustice and withdrew themselves from communion with the eastern bishops. All the Illyrians of that region likewise took their side.

Many of the eastern bishops avoided the injustice, but did not wish to divide the body of the Church. After that teacher of all the lands had died, however, the Western bishops did not embrace communion with the Egyptians, the Easterners, the Bosphorans, and the Thracians until the name of that most holy man had been placed among the bishops who had preceded them.

They did not consider Acacius, who was ordained after John, worthy of any mention. Later they accepted Atticus, the successor of Arsatius, who repeatedly sent embassies and sought pledges of peace, once John’s name had been entered in writing in the diptychs. THEODORET, book V, chapter 34, p. 240.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Ordination of Arsatius of Constantinople and the Hatred Directed Against Him on John’s Account

After a few days had passed, Arsatius was ordained bishop of Constantinople. He was Nectarius’s brother, very long-lived and more than eighty years old, and he governed the episcopate with exceptional gentleness. SOCRATES, book VI, chapter 17. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 19, p. 328.

His reputation was later damaged by what was done against John’s supporters [ms. and ed. V., his reputation]. Since they refused to communicate with Arsatius or to join with him in prayer, but, as has been said, celebrated sacred rites separately in various hidden places at the edge of the city, Arsatius reported this to the emperor.

When the emperor ordered that they be dispersed by military force, the soldiers drove the people into flight with stones and clubs. They imprisoned the nobler people and those more ardent in their love for John.

The soldiers, taking the opportunity—as is customary—plundered women’s ornaments: gold belts, bracelets, necklaces, wash-vessels [mss. Lyr. and ed. V., libation vessels], rings, diadems, and earrings, tearing them away together with the women’s ears. As a result, immense public mourning and lamentation arose in the city.

Even so, the people did not abandon their devotion to John. Many did not dare to gather publicly, either in the square or in the bath. For some, even remaining at home was dangerous, and they avoided the city. Indeed, many men and many women of noble birth, distinguished for virginity and virtuous living, fled. SOZOMEN, book VIII, chapter 23, p. 789.

At that time a violent hailstorm also descended upon Constantinople and its surrounding suburbs. This occurred in the same consulship of Honorius and Aristenes, the sixth (A.D. 404), on the thirtieth day of September. They said that it happened because of God’s anger, since John had been condemned without a judgment.

The death of the empress, which followed immediately, gave force to these words. She died on the fourth day after the hailstorm. SOCRATES, book VI, chapter 17. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 19, p. 328.

At that time Cyrinus, bishop of Chalcedon, who had frequently attacked John, also died after his foot had been amputated. SOZOMEN, book VIII, chapter 16, p. 780.

Others, however, said that John had justly suffered these things because he had removed many churches belonging to the Novatians, Quartodecimans, and other heretics [ed. V., had taken away]. SOCRATES, book VI, chapter 17. Edition of Christoph Valesius, chapter 19, p. 328.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Eutropius the Lector, Who Was Cast into Prison on John’s Account

At that time the lector Eutropius was detained, as though he too had set fire to the church. After suffering many tortures, he was confined in prison and died a short time later.

What happened to him, however, should, I think, be recorded. Someone saw in a dream a man standing beside an altar, distinguished by beauty and stature, as though he were stationed in honor of the martyr Stephen and pondering the fact that good men could nowhere be found. He seemed to search throughout the entire city and to have found absolutely no one except Eutropius.

When the person who had seen this awoke, he reported the dream to faithful men. He then searched for those who had been arrested by the prefect and tormented with beatings. Finding Eutropius, he reported the vision to him.

Weeping, Eutropius begged the man who had seen it to give him his prayers. When the prefect was afflicting various people and could not identify the perpetrators of the fire, he also seized certain women and urged them to accept communion with Bishop Arsatius. Many avoided this; but Olympias, believing it unjust to yield to wickedness, said:

“Add accusers against me and impose even greater violence. But it is not lawful for me to communicate or to do what pious people are not permitted to do.”

Since the prefect could not induce her to communicate with Arsatius, he released her, then arrested her again a short time later and stripped her of much gold, believing that by this means he could break her steadfastness.

At that time the presbyter Tigrius was stripped of his clothing and beaten on the back. He was stretched so violently that the joints of his feet and hands were dislocated. SOZOMEN, book VIII, chapter 24, p. 791.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Death of Arsatius and the Ordination of Bishop Atticus

Arsatius lived only a short time and died in the following consulship, the second of Stilicho and of Anthemius [A.D. 405], on the eleventh day of November.

After his death, a major dispute began over the episcopate of Constantinople. Since it remained vacant for four months, Atticus was ordained bishop in the following consulship, the sixth of Arcadius and of Probus [A.D. 406]. He was Armenian by descent, a monk by habit, and from his youth endowed with natural wisdom. SOCRATES, book VI, chapter 18, p. 244.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Succession of Various Patriarchs

Meanwhile, after Siricius had governed the Roman episcopate for five years, Anastasius succeeded him. After him Innocent assumed the rights of the pontificate.

Flavian also died, refusing to consent to John’s condemnation. After Flavian’s death, Porphyry assumed the episcopate of Antioch.

Since many had consented against John, great division consequently arose in the city of Constantinople, so that many celebrated services among themselves and scandals arose. For the sake of Arsatius and Porphyry, and also of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, a law had previously been enacted at the urging of the nobles, ordering everyone to assemble in the church and those who did not communicate to be expelled far away. SOZOMEN, book VIII, chapter 24, p. 792.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Ravages Inflicted upon the State by the Barbarians

At that time, while discord among the priests was also disturbing the state with great upheavals, the Huns crossed the Danube and devastated Thrace.

The brigands of Isauria likewise assembled in enormous numbers, came as far as Carenae and Phoenicia, and plundered the cities and villages lying between them.

At the same time Stilicho was master of the army under Honorius, endowed with great power, and had many Romans and barbarians under his command. Having incurred hostility with the commanders of Arcadius, he was considering engaging them in battle.

He therefore acted with Honorius and had Alaric, king of the Goths, appointed master of the soldiers. Alaric advanced against Illyricum, and Stilicho appointed Jovius prefect [ms. Lyr., Jovianus], so that he would raise arms against the Romans and subject the provinces of Honorius to his authority.

When Alaric had gathered the barbarians placed under his command and living throughout Dalmatia, he came to Epirus. After remaining there for a long time, he returned to Italy, because when he wanted to depart he was detained by a letter from Honorius, as he himself acknowledged. SOZOMEN, book VIII, chapter 25, p. 793.

## CHAPTER XXV. How Alexander, Bishop of Antioch, Recalled a Divided People to the Unity of the Church

At that time Cyril, Theophilus’s cousin, assumed the episcopate of Alexandria. John, a remarkable man and Cyril’s successor, presided over the Church of Jerusalem. Alexander was bishop of Antioch, a man learned in speech and demonstrating virtue through great works.

He succeeded Porphyry, who had been ordained after Flavian, and left many memorials of his clemency. Flavian indeed flourished in subtle wisdom. The most holy Alexander, however, abounded in exemplary conduct, the highest eloquence in philosophy, and very many acts of goodness.

By his prayers he also joined to the rest of the body the party of Eustathius, which Paulinus had formerly been unable to bend, nor Evagrius after him. He then held a festival such as no one had ever been able to see before.

Having gathered all the faithful priests and peoples, he came to the place where the Eustathians assembled. Taking with him singers who proclaimed a single hymn in fitting harmony, he filled the entire street with people from the city’s farthest gate to the larger church, and displayed a rational stream flowing along like a river.

When the Jews, the Arians, and the small remnant of pagans saw this, they groaned, observing other streams rushing into the sea of the Church.

This bishop was therefore the first to insert the name of the great John into the ecclesiastical diptychs. THEODORET, book V, chapter 35, p. 241.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How John’s Body Was Brought Back to Constantinople
The relics of this teacher were later conveyed to the imperial city. Once again the most faithful people, crossing the sea as though over land, covered the waves of the Bosphorus with lamps and candles. The emperor deposited this treasure in that city. He had inherited both his grandfather’s name and his piety, which he preserved inviolate. Fixing his eyes and forehead upon the saint’s shrine, he prayed for his parents Arcadius and Eudoxia, asking that he might pardon those who had sinned in ignorance. For his parents had died some time before, leaving him an orphan. But the God of fathers and ancestors did not allow him to experience the trials of an orphan. Rather, he caused him to be piously brought up, guarded his empire without fear of upheaval, and restrained the designs of tyrants. THEODORETUS, Book V, chapter 26, p. 242.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the praises of Theodosius the Younger

For he, always mindful of benefits, honored the giver of the benefit. His sisters, who preserved their virginity in their way of life, shared in his hymns, considering sacred meditation upon the divine utterances their greatest delights [Ed. Niv. and Frob., “luxuries”], and regarding the hands of the needy as an inexhaustible treasure [Ed. Niv. and Frob., “an unremovable treasure”]. The ruler himself, however, is adorned with many other praises, especially clemency, gentleness, and tranquility of spirit, never admitting the storm of anger, possessing a true and approved faith. We ought to present a clear proof of this.

A certain man, monastic in his way of life but harsher in judgment, approached the emperor to ask for a particular favor. When he had done this repeatedly and had not obtained what he requested, he excluded the emperor from ecclesiastical communion, imposed the bond of excommunication upon him, and departed. But the most faithful emperor, having returned to the palace, said to those serving the meal at lunchtime that he would not take food unless the man’s bond were first loosed. For this reason he sent to the bishop of the city, asking him to order the one who had imposed the bond to release him from it. When the bishop said that no one ought to accept an excommunication from an ordinary person, and sent word that the emperor was absolved, he nevertheless did not accept the absolution until the one who had imposed it had been sought out with much effort and restored to him the communion from which he had excluded him.

He therefore ordered that the abandoned temples of idols be torn up from their foundations, so that later generations might find no trace of their former error. He had written this same principle into his own law. When, therefore, Roilas, duke of Scythia, crossed the Ister and ravaged Thrace with an innumerable army, threatening to besiege and overthrow the imperial city itself, divine majesty struck him with darts and thunderbolts from above and burned up both him and his entire army at once. THEODORETUS, Book V, chapter 36. Christ. Valesius edition, chapters 36 and 37, p. 242.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the miracles performed against the Persians

The Lord, his comforter, also accomplished something of this kind during the Parthian war. When the Persians learned that the Romans were unoccupied elsewhere, they attacked the cities situated on the frontier and violated the terms of peace. Their territories having been devastated, scarcely anyone brought them aid. For the emperor, relying upon the peace, had sent his commanders and soldiers to other wars. Then God, sending down extremely heavy rain and hail, did not permit them to advance farther, and bound the movement of their horses, so that in twenty days they were unable to travel even as many stadia.

But when our commanders came, gathered the army, and besieged the city named after the emperor, as in the earlier war, they were found to be wicked. For while King Gororanus besieged the aforesaid city on every side for more than thirty days, built many engines of war, and raised lofty towers against the city walls, Eunomius alone, the city’s most holy bishop, resisted and destroyed their attack and their engines. Although our commanders had been defeated in battle by the enemy and the besieged citizens did not dare to resist, he alone, fighting, preserved the city without devastation.

Now one of the enemy party, while habitually blaspheming, uttering the words of Rabshakeh and Sennacherib, and madly threatening to burn the holy temple, was not endured by that most holy man. He ordered a ballista [ed. V., “a bow-ballista”] to be placed beside the fortification that bore the name of the Apostle Thomas. Having fitted a very large stone into it, he said: “In the name of the one who has been blasphemed, release the stone from the drawn bow.”

The stone, once released, came as far as the face of the abominable blasphemer, grievously disfigured his countenance, crushed his head, and scattered his brain upon the ground. When the commander of the army, who had threatened that he would capture the city, learned of this, he fell silent, acknowledged by the facts themselves that he had been defeated, and, fearing, sought peace. Thus the King of all preserved this most faithful ruler, since he professes himself a servant and offers the Lord an appropriate ministry. THEODORETUS, Book V, chapter 36. Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 37, p. 243.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the succession of bishops

[Col. 1184C]

In the meantime, Boniface succeeded Innocent, the remarkable bishop of the city of Rome; Zosimus succeeded Boniface; and Celestine succeeded Zosimus. At Jerusalem, Praylius succeeded John and assumed the episcopate of the Church. At Antioch, however, after the holy Alexander, Theodotus was ordained bishop of the Church, a mirror of chastity, adorned with gentleness and purity of life. He joined the Apollinarians to the sacred sheep, asking them to be united with the flocks. At that time Isdigerdes, king of the Persians, stirred up wars against the Churches for this reason. THEODORETUS, Book V, chapter 37. Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 38, p. 244.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the virtues of Abdas, bishop among the Persians

[Col. 1184D]

There was a certain bishop named Abdas, adorned with very many virtues. Exercising no ordinary zeal for God, he destroyed a *pyreion*—that is, their fire or Vesta. For pagans call *pyrea* temples in which they keep fire; they believe that fire is God.

When the king learned of this from the magi, he summoned Abdas. At first he gently reproved the deed and ordered him to rebuild the *pyreion*. When Abdas resisted and firmly declared that he would never do so, the king threatened to destroy all the churches. The threat was followed by its fulfillment. For he first ordered that the man be killed and then commanded that the churches also be destroyed.

I do not think that the destruction of Vesta was undertaken at an opportune moment. For when the holy Apostle came to Athens and saw the city filled with idols, he did not destroy the altars honored by them; rather, he refuted their ignorance by reason and demonstrated the claims of truth. But because Abdas refused to rebuild the destroyed temple and chose death instead, I greatly admire him and consider him worthy to be honored with many crowns. For worshiping fire is the same as building a temple for it.

From this point the storm began, swelling most savagely and fiercely against the followers of piety, and a dreadful persecution, driven as if by certain storms from the magi, continued for thirty uninterrupted years. The Persians call those who deify the elements “magi.” We have exposed their fables in another work, in which we offered answers appropriate to their questions.

Gororanus, the son of Isdigerdes, therefore obtained the empire after his father’s death and also undertook wars against Christian piety. It is not easy now to recount the kinds of torture and inventions of punishment that he inflicted upon the godly. They flayed the hands of some, the backs of others, and the heads of others, beginning at the forehead and leaving the skin bare as far as the neck. They covered others, naked, with reeds split lengthwise, fitted the cut reeds to their flesh, and bound them from head to foot with cords; afterward they violently pulled the reeds from their bodies, so that, as the sharp sections of the reeds were dragged away, they cut their flesh and inflicted the bitterest pains of torture.

Then, digging pits and closing them in on every side, they put flocks of large mice into them and gave them the athletes of piety as food. They bound their hands and feet so that they could not drive the beasts away from themselves. They also inflicted many other, still more savage tortures, having as their teacher an enemy of the truth.

Yet they could not overcome the steadfastness of the athletes. They ran willingly, so that through the opportunity of this death they might receive the gifts of incorruptible life. I shall mention two or three of them, so that through these the courage of the others may be displayed. THEODORETUS, Book V, chapter 38. Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 39, p. 245.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On Hormisdas, a most noble confessor among the Persians

There was a certain very noble Persian named Hormisdas, whose father had been a prefect. When the king learned that Hormisdas was a Christian, he had him brought in and ordered him to deny the God who saves. But Hormisdas said:

“You command what is neither just nor useful, emperor. For whoever is taught easily to despise and deny the God of all will also very easily despise the emperor, since the emperor too shares mortal nature. And if one who has despised your scepters is worthy of the greatest punishment, emperor, then one who has denied the Creator of all ought to be subjected to manifold tortures.”

But although the emperor ought to have admired his prudence, he stripped the most courageous athlete of his wealth and rank and ordered him, naked, to drag the army’s camels. When many days had passed, the emperor looked down from above and saw that eminent man inflamed by the rays of the sun and covered with the squalor of dust. Remembering his noble birth, he ordered him to be brought to him and clothed in linen garments.

Then, thinking that he would be softened both by his previous affliction and by the emperor’s compassion, he said: “Now at least, deprived of that obstinacy, deny the son of the carpenter.”

But Hormisdas, filled with zeal for God, tore off the garment and threw it down, saying: “If you think that because of this I shall depart from piety, keep your gift together with the impiety that you possess.”

Having witnessed his courage, the emperor cast him naked out of his dominion. THEODORETUS, Book V, chapter 38. Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 39, p. 246.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Sanne, a confessor among the Persians

Sanne [ms. Santheod., Samin], who was lord of a thousand servants, resisted him and could not bear to deny the Creator of all. The king inquired which of his servants was the most savage and handed Sanne over to that servant’s authority; he also ordered Sanne’s wife to serve him. By this means he thought that he could bend the defender of the truth.

But he was deceived in his hope. For Sanne had a house built upon a rock. THEODORETUS, Book V, chapter 38. Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 39, p. 247.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Benjamin, the Persian deacon, and his martyrdom

The king also seized the deacon Benjamin and shut him in prison. When two years had passed, a Roman envoy arrived to conduct other business. When he learned of this, he asked the king that the deacon be released. The king ordered Benjamin to promise that he would not dare preach Christian doctrine to any of the magi, and that then he might go free.

The envoy promised that he would see to it that Benjamin observed what the king had commanded. But when Benjamin heard the envoy’s admonition, he said:

“It is impossible for me not to share with others the light that I myself have received. For the sacred history of the Gospels testifies how great a punishment is deserved by the one who hides his talent.”

At that time the king understood none of this and ordered him to be released from his bonds. But Benjamin did not cease preaching at all. He continually seized those held in the darkness of ignorance and offered them to the intelligible light.

When a year had passed, his deeds were reported to the king. He had Benjamin brought before him and ordered him to deny the true God whom he worshiped. Benjamin asked the king:

“What honor is deserved by one who, abandoning his own kingdom, tries to invade another’s?”

When the king answered, “Death and the final punishment,” that most wise man replied:

“What punishment, then, should a person justly suffer who abandons the Maker and Creator of the world, its Nourisher and Savior, and wishes to deify one of his fellow servants, offering him the worship owed to God?”

Enraged by these words, the king ordered twenty reeds to be sharpened and as many to be inserted beneath the fingernails of his fingers and toes. When he saw that Benjamin mocked this punishment, he ordered another sharp reed to be inserted into his thigh, from which human generation proceeds. Since it was repeatedly expelled and inserted again, it caused him unspeakable pain.

After this punishment, the impious and savage man ordered a thick staff covered on every side with thorns to be thrust through his passage, so that in this manner the most courageous combatant might give up his spirit. Many other things were also attempted by those impious men.

Yet it is not astonishing that God, who is Lord of all, patiently endures their savagery and impiety, since before the reign of the great Constantine all the Roman emperors were violently enraged against the ministers of the truth [ms. Lyr., “preachers”]. For on the day of the saving Passion, Diocletian destroyed the churches throughout the entire Roman Empire. But after nine years had passed, the churches flourished again and acquired great size and beauty; whereas Diocletian, after the frenzy of his impiety, was extinguished.

The Lord also foretold that wars of this kind would come and proclaimed the victory of the Church. Yet the events themselves teach us that wars are more useful to us than peace: peace makes us delicate, lax, and timid, whereas war sharpens the mind and persuades us to despise present things as transitory. We have recounted these matters more frequently in another work. THEODORETUS, Book V, chapter 38. Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 39, p. 247.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On Theodorus, bishop of Antioch, and Theodorus, bishop of Mopsuestia

At the time when the most holy Theodotus governed the Church of Antioch, Theodorus, bishop of Mopsuestia but teacher of the entire Church, after fighting valiantly against the whole host of heretics, reached the end of his life. He had received the teaching of the great Diodorus. He was also the companion and fellow worker of the most holy John. Together they had received the spiritual cups of Diodorus. Diodorus remained in the episcopate for thirty-six years, fought most courageously against the forces of Arius and Eunomius, extinguished the ambushes of the brigand Apollinaris, and prepared excellent pastures for the divine sheep.

His brother Polychronius governed the Church of Apamea and was adorned with eloquence of speech and the splendor of his conduct. THEODORETUS, Book V, chapter 39. Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 40, p. 248.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the death of the emperor Arcadius

Not long after John died, the emperor Arcadius also died. He was a gentle and quiet man and, because of what occurred near the end of his life, is considered worthy of reverence.

In the city of Constantinople there is a very large house called Caria, that is, “of the walnut.” In the vestibule of this house there is a walnut tree, about which the story is told that the martyr Acacius was hanged and died. For this reason an oratory was also built there.

Wishing to see this place, Arcadius came to pray and, having completed his vow, was returning. Accordingly, all who lived around the oratory ran to see the emperor. Some went ahead outside the house, so that they might have a better view of the ruler and the order of his retinue; others followed.

When everyone—women and children, as well as slaves—had gone out of the house together, suddenly the enormous house adjoining the oratory collapsed completely. A cry of astonishment followed, because the emperor’s prayer had freed so many people from the danger of the impending collapse.

Arcadius therefore died, leaving his eight-year-old son Theodosius, about whom much has already been related, during the consulship of Bassus and Philippus (A.D. 408), on the first day of May, in the second year of the 297th Olympiad. He had reigned thirteen years with his father Theodosius and fourteen years after his father’s death. He lived thirty-one years. SOCRATES, Book VI, chapter 21. Christ. Valesius edition, chapter 23, p. 332.

# BOOK ELEVEN

## CHAPTER I. That the empire of Theodosius the Younger was governed by the prefect Anthemius

[Col. 1187C]

When the emperor Arcadius had died, his brother Honorius governed the western regions, while the eastern provinces remained under the authority of Theodosius the Younger, who was eight years old, with the prefect Anthemius arranging everything.

Anthemius was the nephew of Philippus, who under Constantius had expelled Bishop Paul from the Church and introduced Macedonius. He surrounded the city of Constantinople with a very large wall. He was considered, and indeed was, the wisest man among those of his time. He did nothing rashly but deliberated, with the advice of many people, about what needed to be done; above all, he relied upon the sophist Troilus. SOCRATES, Book VII, chapter 1, p. 338.

## CHAPTER II. On Bishop Atticus and his character

While the emperor was entering his eighth year, Atticus was in the third year of his episcopate [ms. Lyr., “in the pontificate”]. He was a distinguished and learned man, venerable and prudent. Accordingly, it happened that the churches received great increase under him.

He was not generous only toward those belonging to his own faith; he also displayed the wonder of his wisdom to heretics, whom he did not wish to weary. When he had attempted to frighten them, he again displayed gentleness; and amid all this he did not neglect eloquence. He devoted himself to reading the ancient authors, applying himself to them at night. Therefore philosophical or sophistic writings did not disturb him. He was agreeable in conversation, sorrowful with the sorrowful, and, simply put, according to the Apostle, he became all things to all people (1 Cor. 9:22).

At first, when he was a presbyter, he both wrote books and recited before the Church what he had prepared. Later, having also acquired confidence through labor, he brought forth praiseworthy [mss., “remarkable”] teaching before the eyes of all. Yet his sermons were not such that they were also transmitted in writing by his hearers. I shall recount what memorable events occurred in his time. SOCRATES, Book VII, chapter 2, p. 339.

## CHAPTER III. On Theodosius, bishop of Synnada, and how the Macedonians were converted there

In Synnada, a city of Phrygia Pacatiana, there was a certain bishop named Theodosius. Since there were many Macedonians there, he persecuted them and, with excessive cruelty, expelled them not only from the city but also from the countryside, although the Church of the orthodox does not usually inflict persecutions. He did this not out of zeal for the true faith but for love of money.

He armed all the clergy and the provincial judges against them and especially harassed Agapitus, their bishop. When he did not think that the provincial judges were sufficient to inflict tortures upon them, he went to Constantinople to obtain the assistance of the prefects.

While Theodosius was there for this reason, Agapitus, bishop of the Macedonians, turned to the better side. After consulting with all the clergy and summoning the entire people subject to him, he persuaded them to accept the faith of consubstantiality. Having done this, he came suddenly with a very large crowd—indeed, so to speak, with the whole city—to the church of the orthodox. After prayer had been offered, he took the seat in which Theodosius had been accustomed to preside.

Then, uniting the peoples and thereafter teaching the faith of consubstantiality, he took possession of the Church of Synnada. When these things had occurred, not long afterward Theodosius came with the assistance of the prefects, knowing nothing of what had happened, and hurried to the church. Expelled from it by everyone, he returned again to Constantinople and laid before Bishop Atticus what had been done against him, alleging that he had been irrationally expelled from the episcopate.

Atticus, recognizing that a useful outcome for the Church had occurred, consoled Theodosius in words and urged him to bear it patiently. Preferring the general good to personal considerations, he wrote to Agapitus that he should retain the episcopate and should think nothing of Theodosius’s hostility. SOCRATES, Book VII, chapter 3, p. 339.

## CHAPTER IV. How a Jewish paralytic was healed through baptism

This is one of the useful events that occurred in the Church during the time of Atticus. Nor were miracles and healings absent from those times.

A certain Jew, being paralyzed, had lain in bed for many years. After every medical treatment had been administered to him, and the prayers of all the Jews had proved ineffective, he finally fled to the grace of Christian baptism, entrusting himself to this medicine of truth alone.

This was quickly reported to Bishop Atticus. He ordered that the man, having become a catechumen and professing hope in Christ, be carried to baptism with his bed [ms. Lyr., “that he be carried in his bed”]. The Jewish paralytic received baptism with true faith, and when he had been lifted from the font, he was suddenly freed from his illness and remained healthy thereafter.

Thus the power of Christ also demonstrated this healing in our own times. For this reason many pagans believed and were baptized. The Jews, however, although they sought signs, were not moved to faith by these events. When these things had occurred among the Christians, many people, treating them with contempt, remained in their wickedness [ms. Lyr., “malice”]. And not only did the Jews resist such great wonders; their followers also proved to have held similar opinions. SOCRATES, Book VII, chapter 4, p. 341.

## CHAPTER V. On Sabbatius the heresiarch and his followers

Sabbatius, whom we mentioned earlier, did not wish to remain in his rank as presbyter but desired the episcopate. At the same time he withdrew from the Church of the Novatians, using as his pretext something resembling an observance of the Jewish Passover.

He held assemblies against his bishop Sisinnius in a place of the city called Xerolophus—that is, “the dry hill”—in the Forum of Arcadius. There he committed a very dangerous offense. On the day of the festival, during the Gospel reading where it is written, “For it was the Passover of the Jews” (Mark 14:1), he presumptuously added words that are nowhere written or heard: “Cursed is the one who celebrates the Passover apart from unleavened bread.”

When this was heard, it spread among the people, and the simple-minded, deceived Novatian laypeople gathered to him. Yet this evil did not remain unpunished; in the end his wicked falsehood was overturned.

Shortly afterward, when many people had gathered for a certain festival to celebrate the customary vigils, sudden demonic terror fell upon them, as though their bishop Sisinnius were coming with a very large crowd. A tumult arose; and, finding themselves in a confined place at night, they crushed one another, so that more than seventy people died.

This event kept many people from the sect of the Sabbatians, though some remained in his rustic folly. SOCRATES, Book VII, chapter 5, p. 341.

## CHAPTER VI. On the death of Dorotheus, the Arian bishop, the ordination of Barbas, and what occurred under him

At that time Dorotheus, the Arian bishop whom they had transferred from Antioch to Constantinople, died at the age of one hundred and nineteen, during the seventh consulship of Honorius and the second of Theodosius [A.D. 407], on the sixth day of November.

After him Barbas was ordained bishop of the Arian superstition. Under Barbas, therefore, the Arian religion flourished through two highly eloquent presbyters, one called Timothy and the other George. George had been educated in Hellenic learning, while Timothy devoted himself to the sacred writings. George always had Aristotle and Plato in his hands; Timothy had Origen, so that he even spoke the Hebrew language.

Timothy had formerly belonged to the heresy of the Psathyrians. Barbas ordained George as a presbyter. I myself saw Timothy and learned how ready he was to answer those who questioned him, resolving the most obscure questions found in the divine utterances and calling the most truthful Origen as his witness.

Yet it seems remarkable to me how such men remained within the Arian religion: one of them always had Plato in his hands, while the other continually looked to Origen. Nowhere does Plato assert that the second or third cause, as he himself customarily calls it, received the beginning of subsistence; and Origen everywhere confesses the Son to be coeternal with the Father.

Although these men remained in their own position, they nevertheless secretly led the Arian religion toward better things. For through their own teachings they expelled many of Arius’s blasphemies. SOCRATES, Book VII, chapter 6, p. 342.

## CHAPTER VII. On the ordination of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria

In the meantime, Theophilus died of a lethargic illness during the ninth consulship of Honorius and the fifth of Theodosius (A.D. 412). A dispute arose over the episcopate between Timothy and Cyril, and on the third day after Theophilus’s death Cyril was ordained bishop. He held the episcopate with greater pomp than Theophilus had.

At the beginning of his episcopate he immediately closed the churches of the Novatians, seized all their sacred vessels, and stripped their bishop Theopompus of all the property he possessed. SOCRATES, Book VII, chapter 7, p. 343.

## CHAPTER VIII. How Christianity was expanded among the Persians through Bishop Maruthas

At the same time Christianity was expanded among the Persians. Embassies were always sent between the Romans and the Persians for various reasons. It happened then that Maruthas, bishop of Mesopotamia, whom we mentioned earlier, was sent by the Roman emperor to the king of the Persians.

Finding great reverence in Maruthas, the king honored him suitably and regarded him as a divine man. This angered the magi, who feared that Maruthas would persuade the king to become a Christian. For the king had long been tormented by a headache. When the magi were unable to cure him, Maruthas restored him to health through his prayers.

For this reason the magi devised a certain deception. Since the Persians worship fire, and the king customarily adored a perpetually burning fire with humble devotion in a certain house, the magi hid a man underground. At the time when the king customarily worshiped, they made the man shout such words as these:

“Send the king out! For he has acted impiously, judging that the priest of the Christians ought to be venerated.”

When Isdigerdes, king of the Persians, heard this, although he held Maruthas in reverence, he nevertheless considered casting him out. But Maruthas, a man truly venerable to God, devoted himself to prayer, through which he discovered the deception fabricated by magical arts.

Coming to the king, he said: “Do not be deceived, king. Enter, and when you hear the voice, order the place to be dug up; you will discover the cause of the deception. For it is not fire that speaks; rather, it is clear that human schemes of this kind are at work.”

At these words the Persian king was persuaded. He entered again where the inextinguishable fire was kept, and, when he heard the voice, ordered the place to be dug up. The man who had been sending forth what seemed to be a divine voice was found and exposed.

The king, enraged, ordered the class of the magi to be reduced to a tenth of its former number. After this had been done, he told Maruthas to build whatever temples he wished. From this point Christianity began to increase among the Persians.

Maruthas then returned from Persia to Constantinople. Not long afterward he was sent there again. Once more the magi plotted to prevent the king from receiving him. They created a certain foul odor in a place through which the king customarily passed and alleged that Christians had done it.

Since the king already suspected the magi, he investigated the matter carefully and again discovered that the odor had been contrived by them. For this reason he handed many of them over to punishment. He honored Maruthas with still greater distinction, greatly loved the Romans, and embraced their peace.

He nearly became a Christian when another miracle occurred through Maruthas and Ablates, bishop of Persia. The two of them, devoting themselves to prayer and fasting, drove an oppressive demon from the king’s son.

After these events, Isdigerdes died before becoming a Christian, and the empire passed to his son. During the latter’s reign, the treaties between the Persians and the Romans were broken. SOCRATES, Book VII, chapter 8, p. 344.

## CHAPTER IX. How Alaric ravaged Italy

At the same time Innocent I began to persecute the Novatians at Rome and took away many of their churches [mss. and ed. V., “seized”]. At that time Rome was plundered by the barbarians.

A certain barbarian named Alaric, subject to Roman authority and to the emperor Theodosius, had provided assistance against the tyrant Eugenius and had therefore been honored with Roman dignities. Unable to endure his good fortune, he did not choose to rule; instead, he departed from the city of Constantinople and came to the western regions.

When he reached Illyricum, he overturned everything. Crossing Thessaly, he engaged in battle near the river Peneus at Nicopolis in Epirus, and the Thessalians killed nearly three thousand of his men.

Afterward, destroying whatever they encountered, they finally came to Rome [mss. and ed. V., “at Rome”]. As they ravaged it, they burned many of its marvels with fire, carried off its money, and subjected many members of the senatorial order to various punishments.

Mocking the Roman Empire, they made a certain man named Attalus emperor. On one day they made him proceed as an emperor, but on the next they made him serve in the guise of a slave.

After Alaric had done these things, he suddenly turned to flight, when word spread that the emperor Theodosius had sent an army against him. The report was not false; an army was truly coming.

It is said that, as Alaric was marching against Rome, a venerable man of monastic way of life warned him not to dare to commit such evils or to rejoice in slaughter and bloodshed. Alaric replied: “I am not going to Rome of my own will. Someone troubles me every day, tormenting me and saying: ‘Go and destroy the city of Rome.’”

Let this suffice concerning these matters. SOCRATES, Book VII, chapters 9 and 10, p. 346.

## CHAPTER X. On Celestine, bishop of Rome, how he persecuted the Novatians, and on Sabbatius

[Col. 1193A]

In the meantime Celestine was ordained bishop at Rome. He also took away the churches of the Novatians and compelled their bishop, named Rusticulus, to hold assemblies secretly.

For until that time the Novatians possessed very many churches. The Constantinopolitans, however, did not tolerate such actions; because they loved the Novatians, they even allowed them to hold assemblies within the city.

When Sisinnius, bishop of the Novatians, died, Chrysanthus was being drawn toward the episcopate. He was a man honored with many Roman dignities. When he fled, Sabbatius, believing that he had found an opportune time for the episcopate, had certain low-born men lay hands upon him, disregarding the oath he had given.

When the people recoiled from his character, they searched everywhere for Chrysanthus. Finding him in Bithynia, they compelled him, against his will, to accept the priesthood. He received nothing from the Church except two loaves on the Lord’s Day. SOCRATES, Book VII, chapters 11 and 12, p. 347.

## CHAPTER XI. On the sedition and killings of Christians caused by the Jews at Alexandria
## CHAPTER XI. On the Riot and Killings of Christians That Occurred at Alexandria at the Hands of the Jews

[Col. 1193C]

At that time, then, the Jewish people was expelled from Alexandria for the following reason. The people of Alexandria is more devoted to riots than other peoples; if it obtains an opportunity, it commits intolerable evils. For it does not cease from quarrelling except through bloodshed.

It happened, therefore, that at that time they were engaged in disputes with one another—not on account of any necessary cause, but because of their enthusiasm for the pantomimes. Since the performer who danced on the Sabbaths had a very large Jewish following, and they were occupied in leisure not with hearing the Law but with the theaters, that day became contentious between the parties.

Although this had been corrected to some extent by the prefect of Alexandria, the Jews nevertheless remained hostile to the opposing party. Since they were always hostile to the Christians, they fought even more vigorously against the Christians’ pantomimes.

At that time, therefore, Horestes, the prefect of Alexandria, was celebrating a certain festival in the theater which they call the *Politia*. Some admirers of Cyril were also present there, wishing to learn the prefect’s arrangements [Col. 1193D]. Among them was a certain Gerax, a teacher of children’s letters and a most fervent listener to Cyril, accustomed to stir up applause during his explanations.

When the Jewish crowd saw this Gerax in the theater, they shouted against him, saying that he had come for no other reason than to provoke riots among the peoples in the theater. But Horestes, who had long borne hatred toward Cyril’s arrogance, seized Gerax and publicly had him dragged about and beaten in the theater.

When Cyril learned of this, he summoned the leading men of the Jews and, as was proper, warned them not to provoke further riots against the Christians. But the Jewish crowd disregarded this and devised greater plots against the Christians.

They therefore gave one another a sign, so that all of them would wear a ring made from palm on their finger, and in this way they attacked the Christians. They sent some of their own people through all the districts of the city during one night, shouting that the Alexandrian church was burning. For this reason the Christians rushed from every direction, as though to extinguish the flames of the church.

The Jews, however, killed them without being recognized, identifying one another by the sign of the ring and sparing one another. But when day came, they could no longer remain concealed.

Moved by this, Cyril came with a very large crowd to the synagogues of the Jews. He removed the synagogues, expelled the Jews from the city, and ordered the people to plunder their property. Thus the Jews, who had inhabited that city since the time of Alexander of Macedon, were then expelled completely naked and scattered through the various regions [Col. 1194B].

Adamantius, however, a sophist of medicine, came to Constantinople and professed himself a Christian, but afterward returned to Alexandria. The prefect of Alexandria, Horestes, was therefore deeply grieved when he suddenly saw the populous city so devastated. He consequently reported what had happened to the emperor.

Cyril also did not conceal the Jews’ offenses from the emperor, and, compelled by the people, he sought a reconciliation with Horestes. When the prefect rejected the proposal of reconciliation, Cyril offered him the Gospels. But when even this did not subdue his heart, the following events occurred.

Some monks living on Mount Nitria, supporters of Theophilus from the time when he had been unjustly arrayed against Dioscorus, willingly undertook battles also on Cyril’s behalf. Nearly five hundred men left their monasteries [Col. 1194C] and came to the city, where they shouted that the prefect, proceeding in his carriage, was a pagan idol-worshiper and sacrificer.

Thinking that this had been done at Cyril’s instigation, the prefect began to cry out: “I am a Christian, and I was baptized by Atticus at Constantinople.” Since they despised these words, one of them, a certain Ammonius, struck the prefect on the head with a stone. He was immediately covered in blood, and when his officials withdrew and avoided the assault of the stones, he remained with only a few men.

Meanwhile the people ran together to avenge the prefect’s injury. They seized Ammonius and punished him with blows until they delivered him to death.
