Before long, these events were reported to the emperor. Cyril took Ammonius’s body and buried it in a certain church, giving him another name, so that he would be believed to have died not for his own crime but for Christ. He offered him praises as though he were a martyr.

But those who truly knew that Ammonius had received punishments deserving of his crime severely blamed Cyril. Nor did the hostility between Cyril and Horestes cease with this alone, for afterward another event arose.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapters 13 and 14, p. 349.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Philosopher Hypatia and How She Was Killed at Alexandria

There was at Alexandria a certain woman named Hypatia, daughter of the philosopher Theon. She was so learned that she surpassed the philosophers of her time. She herself inherited the succession of the Platonic school descending from Plotinus and expounded all philosophical teachings [Col. 1195A].

Therefore everyone hastened to her because of the honorable confidence inspired by her learning [Lyr manuscript: “having confidence in her teaching”]. She even went to the judges and, mingling modestly with men, had no shame, since all revered her for her chastity.

At that time, therefore, envy was aroused against this woman. Since she frequently went to Horestes, the ecclesiastical people were stirred up against her, as though she herself were preventing him from maintaining friendship with the bishop.

Accordingly, men conspiring together and driven by the fiercest zeal—led by a certain Peter, a reader—watched for the woman as she was returning home. They pulled her from her carriage and dragged her to the church called Caesareum. There they stripped her and killed her with stones. Afterwards, tearing her limbs apart, they burned her in the place called Cinarus [Col. 1195B].

This deed caused no small scandal to Cyril and to the Church of Alexandria. For killings and battles are foreign to Christians.

These events took place in the fourth year of Cyril’s episcopate, in the consulship of Honorius for the tenth time and Theodosius for the sixth time (A.D. 415), in the month of March, during the fasts.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 15, p. 332.

## CHAPTER XIII. How the Jews Paid the Penalty for Their Presumption

After a short time, therefore, the Jews were punished there for acting unlawfully against the Christians, in a place called Mestar, situated between Chalcis and Antioch of Syria.

There the Jews were celebrating certain customary ridiculous festivities [Col. 1195C]. Inflamed by drunkenness, they began, among other things, to insult the Christians and Christ himself, mocking the cross and those who placed their hope in the one who had been crucified.

They seized a Christian child, bound him to a cross, and hung him there. At first they mocked and derided him; afterward, seized by madness, they killed the child with blows.

For this reason a dreadful conflict arose between them and the Christians. When the emperor learned of it, the judges of the provinces were instructed to seek out and punish the perpetrators of such deeds. In this way they received a deserved vengeance for their wickedness.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 16, p. 353.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Jew Who, Though Frequently Baptized, Caused the Water of the Font to Disappear

[Col. 1195D]

At that time, a certain Jewish deceiver repeatedly received baptism while falsely professing Christianity, and by this device accumulated money. After deceiving the Arians and Macedonians through many heresies, he finally came to the orthodox Church.

When a period of fasting had been imposed upon him and he was still occupied for many days, he began to hurry, as though, in his fervent eagerness for baptism, he wished to receive its gifts.

The baptism was prepared, together with the appropriate baptismal garment [Santheod manuscript: “for the baptized”]. When the font had been filled, the Jew was led to be baptized. Then a certain invisible power of God commanded the water to disappear.

Since those present, not considering God’s power, suspected that the water had flowed away through its own channel [Col. 1196A], they carefully sealed it everywhere and filled the font again. When the Jew was brought forward a second time, the water disappeared.

Then the priest said: “What evil have you done, man? Or perhaps, without knowing it, you have already received baptism?”

For this reason, when various people gathered, someone recognized the Jew—the very man whom he himself had received after he had been baptized by Bishop Atticus—and in this way his fraud became evident to everyone.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 17, p. 354.

## CHAPTER XV. How Barabanes, King of the Persians, Persecuted the Christians and Was Defeated by the Romans

Meanwhile, after Isdegerd, king of the Persians, had died, his son Barabanes succeeded him. Instigated by the Magi, he tortured Christians with cruel punishments.

When the Christians were oppressed among the Persians, they fled to the Romans and sought their aid. Bishop Atticus gladly received them and supported them as far as possible, reporting to the emperor Theodosius what had taken place.

At that same time another matter had also arisen that made the Romans hostile to the Persians: the Persians refused to return the gold miners whom they had received from the Romans for payment, and they had violently seized the burdens of Roman merchants.

To this ingratitude was added the flight of the Christians to the Romans. The king of the Persians soon sent envoys demanding the fugitives. The Romans, however, were by no means willing to return those who had fled to them, wishing not only to liberate suppliants but also willingly to endure everything for the sake of Christianity [Col. 1196C].

For this reason they chose to fight rather than hand over the Christians to destruction. The treaties were therefore dissolved on this account, and a cruel war began.

It is not inappropriate to recount a few details of it. The Roman emperor sent an army commanded by the master of the soldiery, Ardaburus. Entering Persian territory through the borders of Armenia, he laid waste a province of it called Azazena. Narseus, commander of the Parthian king, met him there with a very large army, but after an engagement was defeated.

After this, Narseus planned to invade the Roman province, which was situated in Mesopotamia without a guard, and in this way take revenge on the Romans. But the Roman commander could not remain unaware of Narseus’s plan. After swiftly ravaging the region of Azazena, he too came into Mesopotamia [Col. 1196D].

Although he had a very large army, he could not enter Roman territory. Instead, he came to Nisibis, a Persian city situated on the frontier, and sent word to Ardaburus that he should designate the day and place of battle.

When his messengers arrived, Ardaburus replied: “Tell Narseus that Roman commanders will not fight whenever you wish.”

The emperor, however, placing his hope for the war in God alone, dispatched his army. That he suddenly obtained help because he faithfully entreated God may be recognized from the following event.

While great anxiety concerning the outcome of the wars was arising at Constantinople, angels of God appeared to travelers passing through Bithynia toward the city of Constantinople. They commanded them to be confident, pray, and believe in God, because victory would follow the Romans; they said that they had been sent by God as mediators of the war.

When this was heard, it strengthened not only the city but also the soldiers. When the war had been transferred from the Armenian region to Mesopotamia, the Romans bravely besieged the Persians shut up in Nisibis. They constructed wooden towers against them and placed them against the walls, killing many of those who fought against them from the walls.

When Barabanes, king of the Persians, heard that the Romans had devastated the region of Azazena and were besieging those who appeared to be shut up in Nisibis, he prepared to meet them with a large army [Col. 1197A].

Amazed at the Romans’ power, he requested the aid of the Saracens. Their king at that time was Alamundarus, a strong man and a warrior. Since he had many thousands of Saracens, he promised the Persian king victory and said that he would hand over Antioch of Syria to him.

But what he expected did not occur. For God secretly cast an irrational fear upon all the Saracens, so that they thought the Romans were attacking them. Confused and having nowhere to flee, they threw themselves fully armed into the Euphrates River. There more than one hundred thousand men were killed and swept away.

When these events had occurred, those besieging Nisibis heard that the Persian king was bringing many elephants. Terrified, they burned all the apparatus of the siege and returned to their own places.

The engagements that took place afterward, and how Areobindas, another Roman master of the soldiery, killed the strongest Persian champion in single combat; or how Ardaburius captured and killed seven very brave Persian commanders by an ambush; or how Byatianus, another Roman commander, destroyed the remaining Saracens, must be passed over, lest I seem to have departed too far from the proposed account.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 18, p. 355.

What was then taking place was quickly reported to the emperor Theodosius. It is not burdensome to explain how he learned of these events so quickly.

He found a certain man named Palladius, very strong in disposition and bodily constitution, who traveled by post-horses with such speed that he reached the boundaries of the Romans and Persians in three days and returned to the city of Constantinople in the same number of days. He also rapidly traversed the other boundaries of the Roman Empire.

Concerning him, a certain most eloquent man said: “Although the Roman state is broad, this man makes it appear small through his speed.” The king of the Persians also frequently marveled at him.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 19, p. 357.

Although the Roman emperor plainly saw that the victory granted to him by God had been achieved, he nevertheless did not conceal his desire for peace. He sent Helio, a prudent and honored man, to discuss peace with the Persians.

When Helio reached Mesopotamia, where the Roman trenches were located, he sent a certain Maximus to seek peace. Maximus was a most eloquent man and counselor to Ardaburus, the master of the soldiery.

When he came to the Persian king to seek peace, he asserted that he had been sent not by the emperor but by the commanders, saying that this war had not reached the emperor because of his contempt [Col. 1198A].

The Persian was prepared to receive the envoy’s words, since his army was suffering from hunger. But Numerus, who among them is called the Immortals—for it consists of ten thousand very brave men—arrived and declared that peace should not be made with the Romans until they themselves attacked the Romans, who were stationed without a guard.

The king was persuaded by these words to suspend negotiations for peace. He ordered the envoy to be held in confinement and sent the Immortals to fight against the Romans.

When they arrived, divided into two battle lines, they placed the Romans between them. The Romans saw one of the Persian lines and prepared to attack it; they did not see the other, which gradually approached the battle.

When the engagement was almost underway, by God’s providence another Roman army appeared from a certain hill, with the commander Procopius. When he saw his allies in danger, he pressed upon the Persians from the rear.

Those who had first surrounded the Romans were thus enclosed in the middle and were immediately destroyed by them. After this, the Romans rushed against the others who had been placed in reserve and struck them down vigorously with their missiles.

Thus those who were called the Immortals appeared altogether mortal, as Christ exacted punishment from the Persian people because they had killed many of his servants.

The king of the Persians, recognizing the cause of his misfortune, pretended not to know what had happened. He accepted the embassy, saying to the Roman envoy: “I do not embrace peace because I yield to war; rather, I wish to grant this favor to you, since I recognize you as the wisest of all the Romans.”

In this way the war that had arisen against the Christians ceased in the region of the Parthians. This occurred in the consulship of Honorius for the thirteenth time and Theodosius for the tenth time (A.D. 422).

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 20, p. 358.

## CHAPTER XVI. How Acacius, Bishop of Amida, Redeemed Persian Captives from the Roman Soldiers by Selling the Church’s Vessels and Sent Them Fed and Supplied Back to Their Own Country

At that time, therefore, Acacius, bishop of the city of Amida, was made more illustrious by an excellent deed.

When the Roman soldiers were unwilling in any way to return to the king of the Parthians the Persian captives taken from the devastated region of Azazena, the captives were being consumed by hunger. They numbered about seven thousand, which greatly distressed the king of the Persians [Col. 1198D].

Acacius then summoned the clergy subject to him and said: “Men and brothers, our God has no need of dishes or cups, for he neither eats nor drinks. Since our church possesses many golden and silver vessels from the offerings of Christians, it is fitting that these be used to free the army of captives and provide food for the needy.”

After saying these and similar words, he melted down the vessels and gave their value to the soldiers as the price of the captives. When he had restored the captives with food, he sent them back to their own king, supplying them with provisions for the journey.

The king of the Persians was even more astonished at this remarkable deed of Acacius, since the Romans had conquered both by war and by benefactions. They say that the Persian king even wished to see Acacius, but that the emperor Theodosius prevented this.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 21, p. 359.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Eudoxia, the Wife of Theodosius, and on the Praises of Theodosius Himself

[Col. 1199A]

After the victory had been granted through God’s help, many Romans skilled in eloquence composed praises of the emperor. His wife composed many poems in heroic meter.

She was eloquent, the daughter of the Athenian sophist Leontius, and had been educated by her father in every branch of learning. When the emperor was about to marry her, Bishop Atticus made her a Christian and, at her baptism, changed her name from Athenais to Eudocia.

Many people, therefore, as I said, wishing to make themselves known, or to display their eloquence, composed imperial panegyrics. I, however, desiring neither to make myself known nor to display the eloquence of my speech, strive to recall the emperor’s good qualities truthfully, since it is harmful if they are passed over in silence [Col. 1199B].

First, he was born and raised in a royal manner and possessed nothing lukewarm. He was so wise that among those conversing with him he was believed to have knowledge of every matter.

He endured cold and likewise heat. He frequently fasted, especially on Wednesday and Friday, out of Christian devotion. In other respects, the palace seemed no different from a monastery. For in the morning he went to his sisters and recited the divine praises.

Therefore he could recite the sacred Scriptures without a book. When bishops were speaking, he responded from the divine reading as though he had long ago become a priest. He gathered sacred books and studied whatever interpreters or commentators of them anyone seemed to have written, more diligently than Ptolemy Philadelphus had studied [Col. 1199C].

He surpassed all people in patience and clemency. Although the emperor Julian was called a philosopher, he did not endure the injury done by the Antiochenes; rather, in his anger, he imposed the greatest tortures upon Theodore.

Theodosius, however, greatly delighting in the syllogisms of Aristotle, practiced philosophy through his deeds, conquering anger, grief, and lust, and desiring to take revenge on no one.

When one of his attendants asked why he did not subject any of those who injured him to death, he replied: “Would that it were possible for me even to restore the dead to life.”

When another questioned him about this, he said: “It is neither great nor difficult for a man to die, since it belongs to God alone [perhaps: ‘it is fitting for God alone,’ etc.] to raise a dead man to life once he has died, through repentance.”

He was so merciful [Col. 1199D] that whenever someone committed an offense deserving death, the person did not reach even the gates of the city before he was to die; rather, through the emperor’s clemency, a reprieve immediately followed.

Once, while he was waiting in the amphitheater at Constantinople, the people began to shout: “Let the maker of parables [or: the craftsman of the cruel beast] fight!”

But he said: “Do you not know that we are accustomed to await things mercifully?”

He excelled in such great piety that he honored all who were consecrated to God, but especially those whom he heard to be distinguished by venerable conduct [Lyr manuscript: “honorable conduct”].

It is said that when the bishop of Cherson had died at Constantinople, the emperor sought his extremely filthy cloak and wrapped himself in it, believing that he might obtain some benefit from the dead man’s holiness.

On one occasion, when there was a storm, he was waiting in the circus for the sake of the people. A violent storm arose throughout the entire circus, pouring down a great quantity of rain.

When this was happening, the emperor revealed his will and had the herald proclaim: “It would be better to disregard the spectacle and ask God that we be preserved unharmed from the threatening storm.”

When this had been said, everyone prayed to God with great joy and offered hymns together, and the entire city sang as though it were one church.

The emperor, however, was in their midst and proceeded in private attire. Nor was his hope disappointed. For suddenly, through divine clemency, the weather was restored to calm and provided an extraordinarily fruitful year for all crops.

Whenever wars arose, he took refuge in God, following David. Knowing that God is the author of battles, he overcame his enemies through prayers.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapters 21 and 22, p. 360.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How the Tyrant John Was Overcome in the West

A short time after the Persian war, when the emperor Honorius had died in the consulship of Asclepiodotus and Mariniani (A.D. 423), in the month of August, I shall relate how Theodosius, committing himself to God, overcame John.

Just as at that time it happened to the Hebrews under Moses that they crossed the Red Sea, so similar things occurred to Theodosius’s commanders when he sent them against the tyrant.

After the emperor Honorius had died, as we have said, Theodosius learned of the event but concealed it, and by saying various other things forestalled the suspicions of different people [Col. 1200C].

Meanwhile he sent the master of the soldiery to the city of Salona in Dalmatia, so that, if any disturbance of war arose in the western regions, he might be a nearby source of aid. After doing this, he disclosed his uncle’s death.

Meanwhile John, the first among the imperial officials, unable to endure that his good fortune should pass him by, attempted to seize the empire. He sent envoys to the emperor Theodosius, asking him to accept his rule.

The emperor imprisoned the envoys and sent the master of the soldiery, Ardaburus, who had labored greatly among the Persians. Ardaburus came to Salona and from there sailed to Aquileia. It happened that an adverse wind blew, so that he fell into the hands of the tyrant.

After Ardaburus had been captured, John hoped to bring Theodosius to a point of necessity, so that by this means he might proclaim him emperor if Theodosius wished to free the master of the soldiery.

When the emperor heard what had happened, he was deeply agitated, fearing that Ardaburus might suffer harm. Aspar, the son of Ardaburus, learned that his father was being held by the tyrant and that many thousands of barbarians were serving as the tyrant’s auxiliaries. He did not know what to do.

But at that moment he prevailed through the emperor’s prayer. For an angel of God, in the guise of a shepherd, led Aspar and all who were with him through the marsh beside Ravenna, and they reached the places they had hoped to reach.

In that city the tyrant was residing with his army. It was said that no one had ever crossed through that place. Then God made impassable land passable.

They crossed through the marsh over dry water and, finding the city gates open, also seized the tyrant [Col. 1201A].

Then the most pious emperor demonstrated the reverence he held toward the Divinity. While he was looking around, he was informed that the tyrant had been killed.

For this reason he addressed the people, saying: “Come, if it pleases you, abandoning this intention and proceeding to the church, let us offer hymns of thanksgiving to God, whose hand has opposed the tyrant’s presumptions.”

When he had said this, the spectacle ceased. Everyone came with him through the middle of the circus to the church, giving thanks together, so that the entire city appeared to be one church.

When they reached the place of prayer, they gave thanks to the Lord throughout the whole day.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapters 22 and 23, p. 362.

# BOOK TWELVE

[Col. 1201]

## CHAPTER I. On the Birth of the Emperor Valentinian, Son of Placidia

[Col. 1201A]

After the tyrant had been killed, the emperor Theodosius considered to whom he ought to entrust the kingdoms of the West. Valentinian was then a very young boy, born of his mother Placidia—Theodosius’s own paternal aunt, daughter of the elder Theodosius and sister of Arcadius and Honorius—and of his father Constantius, who had received the rights of empire from Honorius and had reigned with him for a short time [Col. 1201B].

Theodosius therefore made this Valentinian, his cousin, Caesar and sent him to Italy, entrusting his mother Placidia and the entire administration of the empire to him with her. He himself also wished to go to Italy, in order to raise his cousin to the height of imperial power and, by his strength, remove the audacity of the tyrants. But when he had come as far as Thessalonica, he was prevented by illness.

Accordingly, he afterward sent the imperial crown to his cousin through the patrician Stilicho and returned to Constantinople. Let this account of these matters suffice.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 24, p. 364.

## CHAPTER II. On the Good Deeds of Atticus, Bishop of Constantinople

[Col. 1201C]

Bishop Atticus administered the affairs of the Church wonderfully by his wisdom and encouraged the people by his teachings toward the pursuit of virtue. Seeing the Church divided, while the Johannites separately celebrated the sacred rites among themselves, he ordered that John be commemorated in the prayers, as was customary for the other departed bishops. By this means he hoped to bring many back to the Church.

He was so generous that he sent large sums of money for the relief of the needy not only to the poor of his own parishes but also to neighboring cities [edition: “in neighboring cities”]. Thus, when sending three hundred gold coins to Calliopius [Theod. manuscript: Caelpius], presbyter of the Church of Nicaea [Col. 1201D], he wrote as follows.

> Atticus to Calliopius, greeting in the Lord.
>
> I have learned that ten thousand persons in the city are hungry and need mercy to be shown by the pious. When I say ten thousand, I mean a multitude, not an exact number. Therefore, since I have received a prescribed sum from him whose hand is generous and who fittingly supplies those who distribute it, and since some have come to be in need—[the text is corrupt]—most dear head, spend these three hundred solidi as you wish, especially upon those who are ashamed to ask, and not upon those who make a trade of such matters chiefly for the belly’s sake. Therefore do not consider religious affiliation in this matter; observe only this one thing: feed those in need, and do not consider whether they seem not to share our beliefs.

Thus Atticus cared even for the needy at a distance [Col. 1202B]. But he also endeavored to cut off the superstition of some people. Having heard that the Novatians, following the Jewish Passover, had been divided because of Sabbatius, and that his body had been brought from the island of Rhodes, where he had died, and that many prayed at his tomb, he secretly sent men by night and ordered Sabbatius’s body to be hidden in another grave. When they came as usual and found the tomb dug up, they thereafter ceased to venerate that place.

He was also attentive to the names of places. For when a certain harbor situated at the mouth of the Black Sea had from ancient times been called Pharmacus, that is, “poisonous,” he changed its name and called the place Sanatorium, lest, when assemblies were preached there, the place itself should be designated by a blasphemous name. For a similar reason he also named another place Argyropolis [Col. 1202C]. Chrysopolis is situated at the head of the Bosporus, and many ancient writers mention it. Xenophon says of this city in the first book of the *Hellenica* that Alcibiades altered it and established there that those sailing from the Pontus should pay tithes there.

Seeing, therefore, on the opposite shore from Chrysopolis a pleasant and beautiful place, Atticus said: “Let it be called Argyropolis”; and the place immediately acquired that name.

When some people said to him that the Novatians ought not to celebrate Masses within the city, he replied: “Do you not know how much they suffered with us in the persecution of Constantius and Valens, and that they are also witnesses to our faith? For when the Church was formerly divided, they introduced no innovation concerning the faith.”

Once, when he came to Nicaea for the ordination of a bishop, he saw Asclepiades, bishop of the Novatians, a very old man, and asked how many years he had held the episcopate. When he answered, “Fifty,” Atticus said: “You are a happy man, having had charge of a good work for so long a time.”

He also said: “I praise Novatus, but I do not approve of the Novatians.” Then Asclepiades said: “How can you say this, bishop?” But Atticus replied: “I praise him because he refused to communicate with those who had sacrificed; I myself would have done the same. But I do not praise the Novatians because they exclude laypeople from the grace of communion for trivial faults.”

Asclepiades said: “Apart from the sin of sacrificing, there are also many other offenses which, according to the Scriptures, lead to death; because of these, you forbid clerics, but we even laypeople, to communicate, committing the judgment of their forgiveness to God alone” [Col. 1203A].

Atticus also foretold his own death. For when he was leaving Nicaea, he said to the presbyter Calliopius: “Hasten to come to Constantinople before autumn, if you wish to see me alive again. If you delay, you will not see me.” What he said was not false. For in the twenty-first year of his episcopate, on the tenth day of October, he died, in the consulship of Theodosius for the eleventh time and of Valentinian Caesar for the first time (A.D. 425).

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 25, p. 365.

## CHAPTER III. On the Ordination and Character of Sisinnius; and on Proclus, Ordained for Cyzicus but Not Received

[Col. 1203B]

When the emperor Theodosius returned from Thessalonica, he did not find Atticus’s funeral. For Atticus had been buried one day before Theodosius entered the city. A few days later, that is, on the twenty-third day of October, it was announced that Valentinian had received the insignia of empire.

After Atticus’s death a great dispute arose about the ordination of a bishop, different parties demanding different men. Some sought Philip the presbyter; others likewise Proclus the presbyter. But all the people together desired Sisinnius to be ordained. He too was a presbyter, though he had not been ordained in any city, but ministered in a suburban place of Constantinople called Olive. This suburban place lies opposite the city, where the day of the Savior’s Ascension is solemnly celebrated.

All the laity loved this man because of his dignity, and especially because he supported the poor beyond his means [Col. 1203C]. Thus the wish of the laity prevailed, and Sisinnius was ordained on the twenty-eighth day of February, in the following consulship of Theodosius for the twelfth time and of the younger Valentinian for the second time (A.D. 426).

Philip the presbyter, over whom Sisinnius had been placed, severely attacked Sisinnius’s ordination in his *Christian History*, which he himself wrote in thirty-six books, disparaging both the man ordained and those who ordained him, and especially the laity. This Philip had been ordained deacon by Bishop John and also wrote much against the emperor Julian. Yet his history seems to me to contain much confusion and to be of insufficient benefit to its readers.

After Sisinnius had been ordained, it happened that the bishop of Cyzicus died [Col. 1203D]. Sisinnius then consecrated Proclus at Cyzicus. Before Proclus departed for Cyzicus, however, the citizens had forestalled him by ordaining for themselves as bishop the monk Dalmatius, disregarding the rule which commanded that no ordination should be performed there apart from the bishop of Constantinople. The Cyzicenes neglected this because that law seemed to have been granted personally to Atticus alone.

Proclus therefore remained without a church of his own, though he flourished greatly in teaching in the churches of Constantinople. Sisinnius, having completed two years in the episcopate, died in the consulship of Hierius and Ardabius (A.D. 427), on the twenty-fourth day of December. He was a man most renowned for chastity and uprightness of life, gentle in character, without any pretence, and removed from lawsuits [Col. 1204A]. For this reason he seemed melancholy and ineffective to inquisitive men.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapters 25 and 26, p. 367.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Ordination of Nestorius, and the Evils That Befell the Churches under Him.

After Sisinnius’s death, the emperors decided to appoint no pontiff from the Constantinopolitan Church, because its members were vain-glorious and presumptuous, although many desired Philip and very many Proclus. Meanwhile, it was decided at Antioch that an outsider bishop ought to be summoned. For there was a certain man there named Nestorius, by nationality a Germanician, of good voice and eloquence. Therefore they summoned him as a man seemingly suitable for teaching. When three months had passed, Nestorius came from Antioch; he was regarded as outstanding among many for chastity. But what sort of character he had been trained in did not escape the notice of sensible people from his first sermon. For, having been ordained on the tenth day of April, during the consulship of Felix and Taurus 375 (A.D. 426), he immediately uttered publicly before the whole people the following speech, addressing the emperor:

“Give me,” he said, “O emperor, a land cleansed of heretics, and I will give you heaven. Fight down the heretics with me, and I will fight down the Persians with you.”

Although some hated the heretics, his frivolity of judgment, the beginning of his indignation, and the swelling of his vainglory nevertheless displeased him greatly. For he had not even endured a short time before descending to such words and, as the proverb says, so to speak, before he had yet tasted the city’s water, he appeared as a most fervent persecutor.

On the fifth day after his ordination, wishing to take away the Arians’ oratory, where they used to meet secretly, he drove them to such fury that they burned the same oratory. This act also consumed the neighboring houses, and a violent disturbance arose in the city. The Arians, however, were preparing to defend themselves; but God the Lord, guardian of the city, thwarted their plan.

After this, not only the heretics but also those who agreed with his faith called Nestorius himself “the incendiary” [Valesius, “fire-raiser”]. For he could not keep silent; always plotting against heresies, he overturned the city utterly, so far as lay within him. He also attempted to ravage the Novatians, because their bishop Paul was said to possess reverence [Col. 1204D]; but the leading men restrained his attack.

How many evils he committed against the Quartodecimans throughout Asia, Lydia, and Caria, and how many died because of him when sedition broke out around Miletus and Sardis, I now pass over. What vengeance he received on account of these things and his unbridled tongue, I shall relate shortly. For now, a memorable event must be indicated.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapters 29, p. 370.

A certain people beyond the river Rhine are the Burgundians. They lead a quiet life, and nearly all of them are woodworkers; from this craft they earn their livelihood [editorial reading: “wage”]. The Huns were devastating their territory through frequent invasions and killing very many of them. Although constrained by anxiety [manuscript of Lyons: “trusting in him”], they nevertheless had recourse to no human beings, but were considering committing themselves to some god.

Then, hearing that the God of the Romans strongly helps those who fear him, they all, by common agreement, fled for refuge to belief in Christ. Coming to a certain city of Gaul, they asked to receive Christian baptism from the bishop. He made them fast for seven days and instructed them in the faith; then, on the eighth day, he ordered the baptized men to depart.

Taking courage, they hastened cheerfully against the tyrants, and were not deprived of their hope. For when the king of the Huns, named Suptarus [manuscript of Theodore, Sumptarus], had been overcome during the night by excessive indulgence in food, the Burgundians found the hostile people without a leader. Though few, they resisted the many, and after an engagement [Col. 1205B] they won. Although they numbered three thousand, they killed about ten thousand. From that time the whole people remained most fervently Christian.

At that time Barbas, the Arian bishop, died, during the thirteenth consulship of Theodosius and the third of Valentinian (A.D. 430), on the twenty-fourth day of June; Sabbatius was ordained in his place.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 30, p. 371.

Nestorius, therefore, acting contrary to the custom of the Church, stirred up very many against himself, as his actions show. In Germense, a city of the Hellespont, there was a bishop named Antonius who, recognizing Nestorius’s zeal against the heretics, hastened to persecute the Macedonians as well, as though imitating the patriarch’s example.

The Macedonians endured this for a while. But when Antonius pressed them violently and they could no longer bear the harassment, they resorted to a most grievous crime. They sent certain men who, putting what is right in second place, killed him.

This deed of the Macedonians gave Nestorius an opportunity for a greater persecution. For he persuaded the emperors that their churches should be taken away. Consequently, in Constantinople their church, situated before the city’s old wall, was taken from them, as were the church at Cyzicus and many others that they possessed in the Hellespont. Some of them took refuge in the Church, agreeing in the faith of consubstantiality.

But, as Scripture says, “Wine is never lacking for drunkards, nor quarrels for contentious people.” So it happened also to Nestorius, who loved persecutions: he continually persecuted the Church of God.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 31, p. 372.

Anastasius, a presbyter from Antioch, had also been sent with him. Nestorius honored him excessively and kept him as an adviser in affairs. Once, therefore, Anastasius was teaching before the church and said:

“Let no one call Mary the Mother of God. Mary was a human being, and it is utterly impossible for God to be born from a human being.”

When this was heard, it disturbed very many clergy and laypeople alike. For they had long since learned to confess Christ as both God and man, and in no way to separate him from divinity through the dispensation as though he were merely human, believing the apostolic statement:

“And even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him thus” (2 Corinthians 5:16).

Therefore, leaving aside the discussion of Christ, let us proceed to its completion.

When, as I have said, a tumult had arisen in the church, Nestorius wished to confirm Anastasius’s sermon rather than rebuke him as a blasphemer, since Anastasius appeared to be honored by him. He therefore frequently taught this publicly in the church. As he pursued the question with increasing contention, he rejected the expression “Mother of God.” Hence division arose in the Church; and, divided as though in a nocturnal quarrel, people sided now with one group and now with another, disowning their own words.

Among many, Nestorius was thought to say that Christ was only a human being and to be introducing into the Churches the doctrine of Paul of Samosata and Photinus. But [Col. 1206B] a very great controversy and tumult arose over these matters, so that a universal synod was held.

As for me, having read Nestorius’s books and understood what I found him to mean, and having observed it in accordance with the truth, I shall explain it neither because of hostility toward him nor out of favor toward another. It does not seem to me that Nestorius followed Paul of Samosata or Photinus, or said that Christ was altogether merely human. Rather, he was simply terrified of the expression, as though it were something to be feared. This happened because he had not been properly educated.

Although he was naturally eloquent, he considered himself learned and disdained to apply himself to the books of the ancient interpreters, thinking himself superior to them all. He did not know that in the Catholic Epistle of John, in ancient copies, the following is found:

“Every spirit that separates Jesus from God is not from God” (1 John 4:3).

Those who wish to separate divinity from the human dispensation removed this meaning from the ancient copies. Therefore the ancient interpreters were unwilling to accept this very reading [manuscript of Theodore: “designated it”], because some had corrupted the Epistle, wishing to separate the human being from God.

Humanity is joined to divinity; they are no longer two, but one. Trusting in this reasoning, the ancients were not afraid to call Mary the Mother of God.

For Eusebius Pamphili, in the third book of his *Life of Constantine*, said:

“For our sake, the God who is with us also wished to undergo birth; and the place of his incarnate birth is called Bethlehem among the Hebrews. Therefore Helena Augusta, beloved of God, adorned with wondrous memorials the spacious place where the Mother of God gave birth, fittingly illuminating this most sacred cave.”

But Origen, in the first volume of his commentary on the Apostle Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, says:

“Consider more fully how she may be called the Mother of God.”

It is therefore evident that Nestorius was ignorant of the readings of the ancients.

[Therefore, as I said, he dwelt only on the expression, and not only uttered that expression sincerely, but also altogether denied that the one who was born was God. We confess that the one born of the holy Virgin, who was crucified, is the Lord of glory, as the Apostle said: “For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). Nestorius, however, says: “Do not boast, Jew; you did not crucify God”—as though the Lord of glory himself were not also God.] [Note: These words are absent from Christopher and Valesius.]

That he did not say that Christ was merely human, as Photinus or Paul of Samosata did, is also shown by the homilies he delivered. For nowhere does he abolish the subsistence of the Word of God; rather, everywhere he confesses that it subsists and possesses substance, unlike Photinus and the followers of Samosata, who abolish its existence. The Manichaeans also presume to teach this doctrine from Montanus.

This, then, is what I find Nestorius to have understood from his books. His lukewarm reasoning nevertheless stirred up no slight upheaval throughout the world.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 32, p. 373.

Meanwhile, a certain crime occurred in the Church. Some slaves of barbarian origin belonging to powerful men, having experienced a cruel master, fled for refuge to the Church and entered the altar area carrying swords. When they were asked to leave, they refused in every way. For many days they prevented the solemn services from being celebrated, holding their swords drawn and ready to avenge themselves, and they attacked everyone who approached them.

At last they killed one cleric and wounded another, and then killed themselves as well. After this had happened, one of the passersby predicted that the crime signified nothing good for the Church; nor was he deprived of the truth. For it signified the division of the people and the downfall of the one who had been the cause of the division.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 33, p. 375.

## CHAPTER V. The Council of Ephesus against Nestorius

Not long afterward, an imperial command ordered bishops from everywhere to assemble at Ephesus. Soon after the Paschal festival, Nestorius came to Ephesus with a very large crowd and found that many bishops had already gathered there. Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, arrived somewhat late, around Pentecost. On the fifth day after Pentecost, Juvenal of Jerusalem also arrived.

Since John of Antioch was delayed, the bishops who were present raised the question. Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, was making certain extracts from Nestorius’s books, wishing to trouble him, for he was his enemy.

Although many confess Jesus to be God, Nestorius said: “I do not confess a two-month-old or three-month-old child [variant: ‘a twofold and threefold child’] to be God. For this reason I am innocent of your blood [Col. 1207D], and from now on I shall not come to you.”

After saying this, he joined the other bishops who followed his opinion. Thus those present were divided into two groups.

Cyril and his supporters then held a council and summoned Nestorius. But he did not obey, postponing his appearance until John of Antioch arrived. Those around Cyril, repeatedly rereading the homilies that Nestorius had delivered on this question and judging him from them, condemned him as one who blasphemed the Son of God.

After this, those around Nestorius held another council among themselves and condemned Cyril, together with Memnon, bishop of the city of Ephesus.

Not long afterward John, bishop of Antioch, also arrived. When he learned what had happened, he was angry with Cyril, regarding him as the author of the sedition because he had condemned Nestorius with such fervor. Cyril, wishing to avenge himself with Juvenal against John, condemned John as well.

When matters had become confused through this mixture of actions, Nestorius recognized that the dispute had reached a certain ruin and called Mary the Mother of God, saying:

“Let Mary also be called the Mother of God, and let the things that bring grief cease.”

But no one accepted him when he said such things in repentance. Accordingly, he remained condemned and was sent into exile; he is known to have lived in the Oasis.

Such was the outcome the synod then had. These events occurred during the consulship of Bassus and Antiochus (A.D. 431), on the eighteenth day of June.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 33; edition of Christopher Valesius, chapter 34, p. 376.

## CHAPTER VI. How John of Antioch condemned Cyril

[Col. 1208B]

John then came to Antioch and gathered many of the bishops. He condemned Cyril, who was already in Alexandria. After a short time, however, they set aside their hostility, returned to friendship, and restored each other’s sees.

After Nestorius’s condemnation, a harsh disturbance arose at Constantinople against the Church. The people had been divided because of his lukewarm treatment, as I have said. Nevertheless, all the clergy anathematized him by common decree.

For this is how we Christians customarily call a decree issued against blasphemers: when we display it openly to everyone, as though it had been written on marble.

SOCRATES, [Col. 1208C] book VII, chapter 33; edition of Christopher Valesius, chapter 34, p. 377.

## CHAPTER VII. The ordination of Maximian at Constantinople

When these events had occurred, the question of electing a bishop arose again. Many were choosing Philip, whom I have already mentioned, and very many Proclus. Proclus could have held the pontificate if certain leading men had not prevented it, saying that ecclesiastical regulation did not permit one who had been appointed bishop of another city to migrate to another city. This statement recalled the people.

When four months had passed after Nestorius’s condemnation, Maximian was ordained bishop. He had lived a monastic life but had been enrolled in the college of presbyters. He had long enjoyed the reputation of a venerable man because he built tombs at his own expense, so that the bodies of religious people might be buried in them. He was uneducated in speech and preferred to live in quiet.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 34; edition of Christopher Valesius, chapter 35, p. 377.

## CHAPTER VIII. That bishops have been transferred from one Church to another

Since some people said that ecclesiastical regulation prohibited Proclus from holding the Church of Constantinople because he had been ordained at Cyzicus (Cyzici; manuscripts and Valesius’s edition, Cizico), I wish to say a few things about this matter.

They do not seem to me to have spoken truthfully, but either envy or ignorance of ecclesiastical ordinance caused them to prohibit what is frequently known to have been done beneficially in the Churches. Eusebius Pamphili, in the sixth book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, reports that Alexander, bishop of a city in Cappadocia, came to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer, was detained by its citizens, and was appointed in the place of the bishop Narcissus. Thereafter he presided over that Church for the rest of his life.

Thus among the ancients a bishop migrated from one city to another without any distinction whenever usefulness summoned him. The regulation itself must also be joined to this discussion, so that it may be shown that those who prevented Proclus from being enthroned were lying.

**Rule XVIII.** If a bishop ordained for the parish to which he was ordained does not go there, not through his own fault, but either because the people reject him or for any other reason not arising from necessity, he is to share only in the honor and ministry, and is not to be involved in the affairs of the Church in which the Church celebrates its assemblies; rather, he is to await whatever the synod of the province determines by its judgment.

This, then, is the rule. Since many bishops have migrated from one city to another because of the circumstances of the times, we have added the names of those who were transferred.

Perigenes was ordained bishop at Petrae. Since the citizens refused to receive him, the bishop of the Roman city ordered him to be enthroned in Corinth, the metropolis, after its bishop had died; and he presided over that Church for as long as he lived.

Gregory of Nazianzus was first bishop of one of the cities of Cappadocia [Col. 1209C] and was afterward appointed at Nazianzus.

Meletius first presided over the Church at Sebaste and afterward was appointed bishop of Antioch.

Alexander, bishop of Antioch, caused Dositheus, bishop of Seleucia, to migrate to Tarsus in Cilicia.

Reverentius migrated from Arca in Phoenicia to Tyre [manuscript of Lyons: “migrated”].

John was transferred from Gordo in Lydia to Proconnesus, and presides over the Church there.

Palladius was transferred from Helenopolis to Aspona.

Alexander migrated from Helenopolis to Adrianople.

Theosebius was transferred from Apamia in Asia to Eudoxiopolis, formerly called Salmbria.

Polycarp was transferred from the city of Antapristus in Mysia to Nicopolis in Thrace.

Hierophilus migrated from Trapezopolis in Phrygia to Plutinopolis in Thrace.

Optimus was transferred from Argadamia in Phrygia [Col. 1209D] to Antioch in Pisidia.

Silvanus was transferred from Philippopolis in Thrace to Troas.

It is enough for us to have mentioned as many as we have presently found to have migrated from their own cities to others. Concerning Silvanus, however, who was transferred from Philippopolis in Thrace to Troas, I judge it useful to relate a few things.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 35; edition of Christopher Valesius, chapter 36, p. 378.

Silvanus had previously been a rhetorician under the sophist Troilus. Having become a complete Christian, he devoted himself to the monastic life. He disdained to wear the teacher’s cloak. Later, Bishop Atticus seized him and ordained him bishop of Philippopolis.

After living in Thrace for three years, and being unable to endure the cold because his body was very weak and delicate, he asked Atticus to appoint him elsewhere, saying that he wished to move from that region for no other reason than the cold. When another man had been ordained in his place, Silvanus remained at Constantinople, observing the monastic life perfectly.

He was so entirely free from arrogance that he often went out amid the great crowds of the city wearing sandals made of rushes.

After some time had passed, the bishop of Troas died, and the Trojans came asking for a bishop. While Atticus was considering whom he ought to ordain, it happened that Silvanus suddenly came to pay him a visit.

When Atticus saw him, he immediately stopped thinking. Then he said to Silvanus:

“You no longer have an excuse by which you can avoid ecclesiastical duties. Troas has no cold; and behold, God has prepared a place suitable for your body. Prepare yourself, therefore, and depart at once for Troas.”

Thus Silvanus was transferred.

I shall relate the miracle that occurred through his hands. A very large ship, which had recently transported huge columns, was being built on the shore of Troas. When they wished to drag it down to the sea with many ropes and with the people pulling, it would not move at all.

When this had continued for many days, they suspected that the ship was being held back by a demon. Then they came to Silvanus the bishop and asked him to offer a prayer at the place, believing that in this way the ship would be moved.

In humble language he said that he was a sinner, asserting that this work belonged to some righteous man, not to him. When they pressed him, he came to the shore. After praying, he touched one rope and ordered them [Col. 1210C] to persist in the work with effort.

Then, when they pushed briefly, the ship swiftly moved into the sea. This miracle caused all the provincials to hold that man in reverence.

Since he was also outstanding in other matters, and saw that clerics were conducting cases arising from disputes among litigants, he ordered that no cleric should ever judge. He himself received the petitions of those making requests and asked one of the faithful laymen, a lover of justice, to be present among the litigants and determine the limit of justice.

For this reason he acquired the greatest renown among everyone.

When Maximian had been ordained bishop in the city of Constantinople during the consulship of Bassus and Antiochus (A.D. 431), on the twenty-fifth day of October, ecclesiastical affairs came to rest.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 36; edition of Christopher Valesius, chapter 37, p. 381.

378

## CHAPTER IX. How, in Crete, many Jews died through the deception of a certain Jew who claimed to be Moses, while the rest became Christians

Around this time many Jews in Crete became Christians because of the following calamity.

A certain Jewish deceiver pretended to be Moses and to have been sent from heaven to lead the Jews who inhabited that island across the sea. He claimed to be the one who had once saved the children of Israel through the Red Sea.

For an entire year he went around each city of the island and urged the Jews to believe. He advised them to leave behind all their money and possessions, since, after being led across the dry sea, they would reach the joys of the Promised Land.

Captured by this hope, they neglected all their own work, even despising their possessions and handing them over to whatever persons they could find.

When the day appointed by that deceiver arrived, everyone followed him with their wives and children [manuscript of Lyons: “sons”]. He led them to a certain cliff sloping sharply downward and ordered them to unroll themselves in the manner of rolls. The ones in front did this. As they came to the cliffs, they suddenly died, being torn apart by the sharp rocks or drowned in the water.

More would have died if, by God’s providence, certain Christian fishermen [Col. 1211B] and merchants had not arrived. They rescued and revived some while they were dying. Then, realizing the evil caused by their folly, they restrained others so that they would not kill themselves by leaping, announcing the deaths of those who had previously been thrown down.

When they recognized the deception, they blamed themselves for having believed so easily. They wished to kill the deceiver, but could not capture him. He suddenly disappeared, giving rise to the suspicion that he had been a wandering demon clothed in human form.

Because of this calamity, many of the Jewish Cretans were then converted to the Christian faith.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 37; edition of Christopher Valesius, chapter 38, p. 383.

## CHAPTER X. The great fire at Constantinople, the death of Maximian, and the appointment of Proclus

[Col. 1211C]

Meanwhile, a fire broke out in the city of Constantinople. It gradually reached the baths called the Achilleae and then the place called Pelargus, so that it encompassed the church of the Novatians.

It is said that Paul, their bishop, stood amid the flames of the church, supplicating God that the church should not burn as well. That place was saved, and to this day the Novatians celebrate an assembly there on the seventeenth day of August. From that time not only Christians but also pagans have venerated the place.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 38; edition of Christopher Valesius, chapter 39, p. 384.

After governing the Church for two years and six months [Col. 1211D], Maximian died during the consulship of Ariobindus and Aspar (A.D. 434), on the twelfth day of April, in the major week of the fasts, on Thursday.

The emperor Theodosius then wisely took care that the question of a disturbance or tumult in the Church should not arise again concerning the episcopate. While Maximian’s body still lay there, he ordered Proclus to be enthroned in the presence of the bishops.

This was also confirmed by a letter from the Roman bishop Celestine, which he sent to Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, to John of Antioch, and to Rufus of Thessalonica, saying that nothing prevented a bishop from one city from migrating to another.

After being enthroned, Proclus celebrated the funeral rites for Maximian’s body. It is now time to say a few things about him.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 39; edition of Christopher Valesius, chapter 40, p. 385.

## CHAPTER XI. The conduct and character of Proclus

From his earliest age Proclus was a lector, and among his teachers he was also an eager student of rhetoric. When he reached full maturity, he was often with Bishop Atticus as the recorder of his speeches. As he advanced, Atticus ordained him deacon and afterward presbyter. Sisinnius then consecrated him bishop of Cyzicus.

These things happened to him at first; afterward he obtained the throne of the Church of Constantinople. He was a man of excellent character and, having been beneficially instructed by Atticus, imitated everything in him. But in Proclus patience appeared more prominent.

Atticus showed himself suitably terrible to heretics; Proclus, however, was gentle toward everyone and tried to bend them by this means rather than by violence. He did not wish to harass any heresy, imitating the emperor Theodosius in this respect. The latter judged that imperial power should not be used against the guilty. Proclus, for his part, did not take it badly if someone did not think about God as he himself did.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 40; edition of Christopher Valesius, chapter 41, p. 386.

In these matters the emperor also praised him, since he himself imitated true priests and did not admit those who wished to persecute. I nevertheless say boldly that Proclus surpassed all true priests in gentleness.

For this reason he subdued his enemies without the contests of war, as is shown in the case of John the tyrant and in the subsequent destruction of the barbarians.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 41; edition of Christopher Valesius, chapter 42, p. 386.

## CHAPTER XII. The victory over the barbarians

After the tyrant’s death, the barbarians whom he had summoned to his aid against the Romans were prepared to invade Roman territory.

When the emperor heard this, he customarily entrusted the concern to God and, occupied with prayers, quickly obtained what he sought. What happened to the barbarians must be related.

Their leader, named Rugas, was struck by lightning and died. Then a plague followed and killed the greater part of those people. Nor was this alone sufficient: fire descended from heaven and consumed very many of those who seemed to have survived [Col. 1212D].

This event placed the barbarians in great fear, not only because they had dared to raise arms against the very powerful Roman people, but because they saw that the Romans were being helped in this way by a powerful God.

At that time Bishop Proclus delivered a sermon before the Church on the prophecy of Ezekiel concerning the salvation that had been granted, and was praised by everyone. The words of the prophecy are these:

“And you, son of man, prophesy against Gog, ruler of Meshech and Tubal. I will judge him with death and bloodshed, and I shall rain down upon him and all who are with him a flood of rain, hailstones, fire, and sulfur” (Ezekiel 38:1).

And shortly afterward:

“And they shall know that I am the Lord.”

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 42; edition of Christopher Valesius, chapter 43, p. 387.

## CHAPTER XIII. How Theodosius’s daughter was joined in marriage to Valentinian

[Col. 1213A]

Therefore God granted the emperor, on account of his gentleness and many other virtues, numerous benefits, one of which was the following.

He had a daughter by Eudoxia, named Eudoxia. Valentinian, his cousin, whom he had made emperor of the western regions, asked for her in marriage.

When Theodosius agreed, he considered celebrating the wedding at some place midway along the journey. It had been arranged that both men would come to Thessalonica. Meanwhile Valentinian sent word that Theodosius should not tire himself, for he himself promised to come to Constantinople.

After securing the western regions, he came to Constantinople for the wedding. When the ceremony had been celebrated during the consulship of Isidore and Senator (A.D. 436), he returned with his wife [Col. 1213B].

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 43; edition of Christopher Valesius, chapters 43 and 44, p. 388.

## CHAPTER XIV. How the body of Bishop John was brought back to Constantinople

Not long afterward, Bishop Proclus restored to the Church those who had separated themselves because of John’s deposition. By his wisdom he alleviated their grief in the following way.

He had John’s body, which had been buried at Comana, brought back to Constantinople by imperial order in the thirty-fifth year after his deposition. After it had been publicly displayed, he reburied it with great honor in the Church of the Apostles.

This occurred in the sixteenth consulship of Theodosius (A.D. 438), on the seventeenth day of January.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 44; edition of Christopher Valesius, [Col. 1213C] chapter 45, p. 388.

Paul, the bishop of the Novatians, also died during that consulship, on the twentieth day of July. When he fell ill, he neither exceeded his customary diet nor omitted his usual prayers.

When he was near death, he summoned all his clergy and said:

“Consider choosing a bishop while I am alive, so that afterward they may not have to endure disturbances in our Church.”

When they instead offered him the election, Paul said:

“Then give me a written declaration of this kind, stating that you will choose the one whom I shall appoint.”

When they had done this and subscribed it, he wrote the name of the presbyter Marcian on the document and signed it. He likewise had the presbyters who were present sign it, and deposited the document with Marcus, bishop of the Novatian Church of the Scythians [Col. 1214A], saying:

“If I live, return it to me; if I die, here you will find whom ought to be ordained.”

After his death, on the third day they opened the document and found Marcian’s name. Praising his election, they immediately sent for him at Tiberias in Phrygia, where he was then living. They seized him, brought him back on the twenty-first day of the same month, and ordained him bishop.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 45; edition of Christopher Valesius, chapter 46, p. 389.

## CHAPTER XV. How Eudoxia, the emperor’s wife, traveled to Jerusalem

The emperor Theodosius therefore returned thanks for the benefits God had bestowed on him, repaying his vows to Christ with many honors. He sent his wife Eudoxia [Col. 1214B] to Jerusalem.

She too had made this vow if she should see her daughter married. She honored both the churches established at Jerusalem and those situated in each of the cities, both as she traveled there and as she returned.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 46; edition of Christopher Valesius, chapter 47, p. 390.

## CHAPTER XVI. How Proclus, by his authority, made the senator Thalassius bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia

At the same time, in the seventeenth consulship of the emperor Theodosius (A.D. 439), Bishop Proclus performed a remarkable act, such as none of the earlier bishops had done.

When Firmus, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, had died, the Caesareans were present asking for a bishop. While Proclus was considering whom he ought to ordain for them, it happened that all the senators came to greet him on Saturday.

Among them was Thalassius, who had administered the office of prefect of Illyricum. Since, as rumor had it, he was about to govern the Eastern prefecture, Proclus laid a bishopric upon him by extending his hand, in place of the prefecture’s dignity, and assigned him to the city of Caesarea.

These things were being done in the Church at that time. Let us now bring our history to an end, praying that all the Churches may be governed in peace.

Therefore, O most holy man of God Theodore, we have fulfilled your command, bringing the history to an end in the second year of the 305th Olympiad, during the seventeenth consulship of the emperor Theodosius.

SOCRATES, book VII, chapter 47; edition of Christopher Valesius, chapter 48, p. 391.

[Col. 1213]

# THE CHRONICLE OF M. AURELIUS CASSIODORUS, TO KING THEODORE (C)*

## PREFACE

[Col. 1213D] 380 In accordance with your princely wisdom, by which you always ponder great matters, you have judged that I should arrange the consuls in order, so that you who had adorned the year with a glorious name might restore to the official records their former truth [Col. 1214D].

I willingly obeyed your commands. After removing the variations of the copyists, I impressed upon the work the authority of historical reliability, so that your spirit, delighted by illustrious events [Col. 1215A], might traverse the very long age of the world through an agreeable abridgment.

From Adam, the first man, to the Flood, which took place under Noah, 2,242 years are reckoned.

The Flood occurred because of the excessive savagery of the giants [Col. 1216A], who, prevailing in bodily size and equal ferocity of spirit, had utterly confounded every right belonging to humanity.

From the Flood to Ninus, who was the first of all to reign among the Assyrians, there are 899 years.

## CHRONICLE

[Col. 1215]

## ASSYRIAN KINGS

[Col. 1215A]

Ninus therefore reigned among the Assyrians for 52 years. In the 43rd year of his reign Abraham was born. He also founded Nineveh. Semiramis, the wife of Ninus, reigned for 42 years. She is remembered as having restored the walls of Babylon, not as having founded them. [Col. 1215B]

Ninias, son of Ninus and Semiramis, reigned for 38 years. Arius reigned for 30 years. Arelius reigned for 40 years. Xerxes, also called Baleus [ed. Niv. and Orry., Balaneus], reigned for 30 years. Armametres reigned for 38 years. Bolechus [Cusp., Belochus] reigned for 35 years. Baleus reigned for 52 years. Altadas reigned for 32 years. In his time Prometheus was a wise man. Mamithus reigned for 30 years. Manchaleus [Cusp., Magelaus] reigned for 30 years. In his time Atlas, the brother of Prometheus, was regarded as a foremost astrologer. [Col. 1215C]

Spherus [ed. Niv. and Onuph., Iphereus] reigned for 20 years. Mamylus reigned for 30 years. Sparetus reigned for 40 years. In his time Athens was founded by King Cecrops. Ascades [Cusp., Astacades] reigned for 40 years. In his time Moses received the divine law on Mount Sinai. Amynthes reigned for 45 years. In his time Jesus, the successor of Moses, distributed the land of the Palestinians to the Jewish people. Belochus reigned for 25 years. Bellepares [Cusp., Belopares] reigned for 30 years. Lamprides reigned for 32 years. [Col. 1215D]

Sosares reigned for 20 years. In his time the swiftest horse, Pegasus, was discovered. Lampares reigned for 30 years. Panias reigned for 45 years. Sosarmus reigned for 19 years. In his time the voyage of the Argonauts took place, and Orpheus, the Thracian musician, was regarded as famous. 381 Mithreus reigned for 27 years. In his time Hercules practiced athletics, and Priam reigned at Ilium. Through these Assyrian kings, therefore, 852 years are reckoned.

## LATIN KINGS

Latinus reigned for 32 years. From him the Latins received their name. [Col. 1216A] In the 25th year of his reign Troy was captured; the exiled Aeneas came to him and, having become his son-in-law, succeeded him in the kingdom. Eight years after the capture of Troy, Aeneas reigned in Italy for 3 years. His son Ascanius reigned for 38 years; he founded Alba [Cusp., Alba Longa]. [Col. 1216B]

Silvius, the son of Aeneas by Lavinia, reigned for 29 years. In his time the poet Homer is said to have lived. Aeneas Silvius reigned for 31 years. In his time David, king of the Hebrews, reigned at Jerusalem. Latinus Silvius reigned for 50 years. In his time the Amazons ravaged Asia. Carthage was founded by Carchedon the Tyrian, as some say. Solomon also, the son of David, reigning at Jerusalem, founded the celebrated Temple.

Alba Silvius reigned for 39 years. Aegyptius Silvius reigned for 24 years. Capys Silvius reigned for 28 years. Capetus [Cusp., Calpetus] Silvius reigned for 13 years. [Col. 1216C] Tiberinus Silvius reigned for 8 years. Agrippa Silvius reigned for 40 years. Aremulus Silvius reigned for 19 years. In his time Lycurgus established laws among the Lacedaemonians. Aventinus Silvius reigned for 37 years. From him the Roman mountain received its name, because he was buried there. Procas Silvius reigned for 23 years. Amulius Silvius reigned for 44 years. He expelled his brother Numitor from the kingdom; Numitor’s period has been joined to his.

## ROMAN KINGS

Romulus reigned for 38 years. From him Rome was founded, and the Romans were named [Al. ed., founded] from the Latins. [Col. 1216D] He first appointed one hundred senators. In his time Syracuse and Catina were founded in Sicily.

Numa Pompilius reigned for 41 years. He added two months to the year, January and February, since before his time the Romans had only ten months. He also built the Capitol from its foundations. In his time, too, the Sibyl on Samos was held in high renown.

Tullus Hostilius reigned for 32 years. He was the first among the Romans to use purple. In his time Chalcedon and Byzantium, now called Constantinople, were founded.

Ancus Martius reigned for 23 years. In the sixteenth mile from the city of Rome he founded Ostia. [Col. 1217A]

Tarquinius Priscus reigned for 37 years. In his time Massilia was founded in Gaul. Servius Tullius reigned for 34 years. He was the first to establish a census of Roman citizens. In his time Cyrus first began to reign among the Persians.

Tarquinius Superbus reigned for 35 years. In his time Pythagoras, the distinguished natural philosopher, was held in renown. After Tarquinius had been expelled, two consuls at a time began to administer the state annually in place of one king.

## FROM THIS POINT, THE CONSULS

L. Junius Brutus and L. Tarquinius Collatinus. They did not hold office for a full year; others were substituted to complete the term, namely P. Valerius, Sp. [Col. 1217B] Lucretius, and Horatius Pulvillus.

In their consulship, after the capture of the City, the Roman commander Camillus destroyed the Gauls as they were returning; celebrating a triumph over them in the City, he deserved to be called Romulus, as though he too were the founder of his country.

Then the offices were changed. In place of the consuls, military tribunes served for 17 years. After these were removed because of their arrogance, consular and tribunician authority ceased for 4 years. Then the state was again administered for three years by military tribunes; after the twenty-fourth year, consular authority returned.

In their consulship destructive disagreements concerning Pompey [Col. 1226A] and Caesar were fomented in the senate-house. But C. Julius Caesar, coming from Gaul, drove Pompey from Italy; at Rome he removed the gold and silver from the treasury, and was the first Roman to obtain sole rule. From him Roman emperors were called Caesars. He ruled for four years and six months. The following consuls served under him.

## ROMAN EMPERORS

### C. JULIUS CAESAR I

C. Julius Caesar II and P. Servilius.

Q. Fusius and P. Vatinius.

C. Julius Caesar V and M. Antonius.

In their consulship, during the Lupercalia, M. Antonius placed a diadem on Caesar, who was seated on a golden chair and refused it; and on the Ides of March Caesar was killed in Pompey’s senate-house. Octavian Caesar succeeded him and ruled for fifty-six years and six months. During that period the following consuls served.

### OCTAVIAN AUGUSTUS II

Our lords Eutharic Cillica and Justin Augustus, consuls. In that year Rome witnessed many spectacles at each successive celebration; and even Symmachus, the ambassador of the East, was astonished. He bestowed wealth and honors upon Goths and Romans alike. In the Senate-house, he displayed wild beasts of various kinds in the amphitheatrical entertainments—animals at which the present age would marvel because of their novelty. Africa, in its devotion, also sent across the sea the rare delights of this spectacle. When everything had been completed with extraordinary praise, he had so won the love of the Roman citizens that, while they still longed for his presence, he returned to Ravenna to behold his glorious father [Cusp., “to hear his address”], where, by repeated celebrations, he lavished such gifts upon Goths and Romans that he alone was able to surpass the consulship he had celebrated at Rome.

## EPILOGUE

Therefore, to compress into a brief summary the extended succession of years arranged according to the testimony of authors:

From Adam to the Flood, as we gather from the Chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome, there are 2,242 years. From the Flood to Ninus, king of the Assyrians, there are 899 years. From Ninus to King Latinus there are 852 years. From King Latinus to Romulus there are 457 years. From Romulus to Brutus and Tarquinius, the first consuls, there are 240 years [Cusp., 242]. From Brutus and Tarquinius to your consulship, as we have gathered from Titus Livy, Aufidius Bassus, and Paschalis [Bucherius thinks that *Victorii canone* should be supplied], confirmed by the authority of distinguished men, there are 1,031 years [Cusp., 1,270].

And if the entire sequence of ages up to your consulship is added together, there are 5,721 years [Cusp., 5,741; but this is a numerical error].

[Col. 1249]

## PASCHAL COMPUTATION (C, G)

[Col. 1249A] If you wish to know what year it is from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, multiply thirty-six by fifteen: the result is 540. Always add twelve to this: the result is 552. Add also the indictions of whatever year you wish—for example, the twenty-first after the consulship of Basiliscus junior: the result is 562. These are the years from Christ’s incarnation. Remember this point with particular care: whenever you have completed the fifteenth indiction, so that the calculation may remain exact, do not take fifteen; instead, add one to the first total—that is, to thirty-six—so that, for example, after the fifteenth indiction has ended, which you add in the preceding calculation, you will calculate thirty-seven by fifteen instead of thirty-six, and you will be able to find the years of the Lord without any error. [Col. 1249B]

If you wish to know which indiction it is—for example, the twenty-first after the consulship of Basiliscus junior—take the years from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, namely 562; always add three to them: the result is 565. Divide this by fifteen; ten remain. The tenth is the indiction. If nothing remains, it is the fifteenth indiction.

If you wish to know how many epacts there are—that is, lunar additions—take however many years there have been from the Lord’s incarnation, for example 562; divide these by nineteen: eleven remain. Multiply these by eleven: the result is 121. Divide this again by thirty: one remains. One is the lunar addition.

[Col. 1249C] If you wish to know the solar additions—that is, the concurrent days of the week—take however many years there have been from the Lord’s incarnation, for example 562; for the tenth indiction, always add a quarter of the years that have elapsed, that is, now 140, making a total of 702; add four to this and divide by seven: six remain. Six are the solar epacts, that is, the concurrent days of the week for the above-mentioned twenty-first indiction after the consulship of Basiliscus junior.

If you wish to know which year of the nineteen-year cycle it is, take the years of the Lord, for example 562, and always add one: the result is 563. Divide this by nineteen; twelve remain. The twelfth year is [Col. 1250A] the year of the nineteen-year cycle. If nothing remains, it is the nineteenth year.

If you wish to know which lunar cycle it is—the cycle contained within the nineteen-year cycle—take the years of the Lord, for example 562, and always subtract two: the result is 560. Divide this by nineteen; nine remain. The ninth is the lunar cycle of the nineteen-year cycle; whenever nothing remains, it is the nineteenth year.

If you wish to know when a leap year occurs, take the years of the Lord, for example 562, and divide them by four: if nothing remains, it is a leap year. If one, two, or three remain, it is not a leap year. And so that perhaps no obscurity of error may arise for you, throughout every calculation that you perform, if nothing remains, recognize that the calculation is the number by which you divided: for example, if, when dividing by nineteen, nothing remains, know that it is the nineteenth; if by fifteen, the fifteenth; if by seven, the seventh. [Col. 1250B]

If you wish to know on what day of the moon the Paschal feast occurs: if Easter is celebrated in March, count from September through February: the result is six. Always add two: the result is eight; and add the epacts, that is, the lunar additions of whatever year you wish—for example, one for the tenth indiction: the result is nine. Add the day of the month on which Easter is celebrated, that is, the thirtieth of March: the total is forty. Subtract thirty; ten remain. The moon is on the day indicated above.

If, however, we celebrate Easter in April, count the months from September through March: the result is seven; [Col. 1250C] always add two: the result is nine; add also the epacts, that is, the lunar additions of whatever year you wish—for example, one for the tenth indiction, making ten; and add the ninth day of the month in which we celebrate Easter, that is, April ninth: the total is nineteen. But if the total exceeds thirty, always subtract thirty; then it will be the nineteenth day of the moon.

If you wish to know which day of the week it is, take the days from January through whatever month you wish—for example, through April 9: the result is ninety-nine days. Always add one: the result is one hundred. Also always add the solar epact of whatever year you wish—for example, the sixth of the tenth indiction: the total is 106. Divide this by seven; one remains. That is the Sunday of Easter.

# APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF CASSIODORUS

[Col. 1251]

## JORNANDES, OR JORDAN, BISHOP OF RAVENNA, ON THE ORIGIN AND DEEDS OF THE GETAE OR GOTHS, TO CASTALIUS (C)

## PREFACE

[Col. 1251A] 397. As I wished to reach the shore of a calm coast in a small vessel and, as someone says, gather tiny fish from the pools of the ancients, you compel me, brother Castalius, to spread my sails into the deep. You urge me, setting aside the little work I have in hand—namely, *On the Abridgment of the Chronicles*—to compress into this one small book, in my own words, the twelve volumes of Senator [that is, Cassiodorus], *On the Origin and Deeds of the Getae*, descending from ancient times to the present through generations and kings.

These are sufficiently harsh commands, imposed as though by one who does not know the weight of this work. Nor do you consider that my spirit is too feeble to fill so magnificent a trumpet of eloquence. This burden is greater than we can bear, [Col. 1252A] since we are not given access to the books themselves, so that we may serve their meaning. Yet, not to lie, through the kindness of its custodian I previously reread those books during a three-day reading. Although I do not remember their precise words, I believe that I retain their meaning and the events described in full. To these I have added certain relevant materials from Greek and Latin histories, mingling my own composition into the beginning and end, and in many places in the middle.

Therefore accept willingly what you have requested, and read it most willingly; and if anything has been said too briefly, add to it yourself—as one who is close to this people and recalls the matter. Pray for me, dearest brother.

## CHAPTER ONE. On the Division of the Whole World

[Col. 1251A]

Our ancestors, as Orosius reports, represented the circumference of the whole earth, enclosed by the rim of the Ocean, as triangular; and they called its three parts Asia, Europe, and Africa.
