[Col. 1251B] Concerning this threefold extent of the world, there are almost innumerable writers who explain not only the positions of cities and places but also—and this is clearer—the measurement of miles and stadia. They also determine the islands mingled among the sea’s waves, both larger and smaller, which they call the Cyclades or Sporades, situated in the immeasurable expanse of the great sea.

No one has undertaken to describe the farther boundaries of the unnavigable Ocean; indeed, no one has been permitted to cross them, because they are thought to be impassable owing to the obstructing seaweed and the stillness of the winds, and known to no one except him who established them. But the nearer shore of that sea, which we mentioned, encircling the whole circuit of the world like a crown, has become very well known to curious people and to those who wished to write about it, because the circuit of the earth is possessed by its inhabitants.

Some islands in that same sea are habitable, such as, in the eastern region and the Indian Ocean, the Hippodes and Jamnesia, scorched by the sun; although uninhabitable, they are nevertheless very extensive in length and breadth. Taprobane also contains, apart from its towns and estates, as they say, strongly fortified cities: beautiful Sedalia, highly agreeable Silestantina [variant: Silephantina], and also Etheron [variant: Theron]. Although they are not made clear by any author, they are nevertheless abundantly populated by their inhabitants.

In its western part the same Ocean contains several islands, almost all known because of the frequency of those who travel to and fro. Near the Strait of Gades are two islands, one called Beata and the other Fortunata. Some, however, place in the islands of the Ocean those twin promontories of Galicia and Lusitania. On one of them the temple of Hercules can still be seen, and on the other the monument of Scipio. Yet because they form the extremity of the mainland of Galicia, they belong rather to the great land of Europe than to the islands of the Ocean.

It also contains other islands farther within its waters, called the Balearic Islands, and another called Mevania; also the Orcades, thirty-four in number, although not all of them are cultivated. At the extreme western region it has another island called Thyle, concerning which the Mantuan poet says:

> May the farthest Thyle serve you.

398. This same immeasurable sea also has, in its northern—that is, Arctic—part, a large island named Scanzia [Note: [Col. 1251C] Pliny likewise calls it this. Jacobus Ziegler says that it was called Scondania, while the name Scondia remained because it signifies pleasantness and beauty [Col. 1252C], since it yields to no blessed region. B. Vulcanius.] [variant: Scandia], from which, if the Lord helps, our account must begin; for the people whose origin you request burst forth from the bosom of this island like a swarm of bees and came into the land of Europe. How and in what manner, if the Lord grants it, we shall explain in what follows.

## CHAPTER TWO. On the Island of Britain

[Col. 1252C] Now, however, I shall briefly treat, as best I can, of the island of Britain, which lies in a bay of the Ocean between Spain, Gaul, and Germany. Although, as Livy reports, no one in former times sailed around its whole extent, many various opinions about it have nevertheless been expressed. For so long as it was inaccessible to Roman arms, Julius Caesar made it passable by battles undertaken solely for glory; thereafter, when it had been opened to many mortals for trade and other reasons, the age which followed made its situation known more accurately and carefully than we set it forth from what we have received from Greek and Latin authors.

Many have called it triangular, like a cone, projecting between the north and west: with one great angle facing the mouths of the Rhine, then narrowed in an oblique width and drawn back so as to end in two other angles; and with its two longer sides extending toward Gaul and Germany. Its breadth, where it is wider, is said to be 2,310 stades; its length to extend no more than 7,132 stades. At one point it lies in a bushy, at another in a wooded plain, and rises also in certain hills; it is surrounded by a sluggish sea, which yields neither readily to oarsmen nor swells with the blasts of winds, because lands lying farther away prevent the causes of its movement, since there the expanse of water spreads more widely than anywhere else.

Strabo, the distinguished Greek writer, reports that, when its soil is moistened by the Ocean’s frequent incursions, it exhales such great mists that throughout almost the whole day the sun’s obscured face is denied to view, even though it is clear; and the night is brighter. At its extremity is Memma [variant: Miniamque], which Cornelius, likewise a writer of annals, says is rich in many metals, abundant in herbs, and more productive than all these because it feeds cattle rather than human beings. Through it flow and return many very great rivers, rolling gems and pearls. The Silures are born with dark complexions, mostly with twisted black hair. The inhabitants of Caledonia, however, have red hair and large but loose bodies; they are judged to resemble Gauls or Spaniards, from whomsoever they are observed. Hence some have conjectured that it received settlers continually summoned from these peoples. Dio, the most celebrated writer of annals, states that all the uncultivated peoples and their kings nevertheless yielded to the Caledonians in the naming of their metal [Note: [Col. 1253D] Variant: “yielded in the names of the Caledonians and the Maeatae,” etc. Perhaps read *Memmatanum*.].

They dwell in huts of reeds, sharing roofs with cattle, and forests are often their homes. For adornment, or for some other reason I do not know, they mark their bodies with iron [Note: [Col. 1253D] Perhaps read *pungunt*, “prick.” Thus Ammianus Marcellinus, p. 432. Jur.]. They frequently wage war among themselves, either from desire of dominion or to enlarge what they possess, not only with cavalry or infantry but also with two-horse chariots and scythed cars, which in the common speech they call *essedae*. Let these few remarks on the form of the island of Britain suffice.

## CHAPTER THREE. On the Location and Peoples of the Island of Scanzia

Let us return to the location of the island of Scanzia, which we left above. In the second book of his work Claudius Ptolemy, the outstanding describer of the world, mentions it, saying: “There is situated in the Arctic waters of the Ocean a large island named Scanzia, in the shape of a cedar [variant: citron] leaf, closing in upon itself after a long course with spreading sides; the Ocean flows around its shores. It lies opposite the Vistula River, which rises in the Sarmatian Mountains and, in sight of Scanzia, flows with three mouths into the northern Ocean, separating Germany from Scythia.”

This island has to the east an enormous lake, situated within the bosom of the world; from it the Vagus River, generated as though from a womb, rolls in waves into the Ocean. To the west it is surrounded by an immense sea; to the north it is enclosed by the same vast, unnavigable Ocean. From this Ocean, as though from an arm extending outward in a broad inlet, the German Sea is formed.

Here are peoples who live only on meat; there, too, they say, are arranged small but numerous islands. If wolves cross to them over the frozen sea because of the extreme cold, they are said to lose their sight. Thus the land is inhospitable not only to human beings but also cruel to beasts.

In the island of Scanzia, which is the subject of our account, although many diverse nations dwell there, Ptolemy records the names of seven. Because of the extreme cold, a swarm of honey-making bees is never found there. In its northern part lives the people called the Adogit, who are said, in midsummer, to have continuous daylight for forty days and nights; likewise, in winter, for the same number of days and nights, they are said not to know clear daylight.

Thus, alternating sorrow with joy, they are unlike others in benefit and loss. And why is this? Because during the longer days they see the sun returning toward the east along the edge of the axis; during the shorter days it is not seen there in the same way, but differently, because it travels through the southern signs, and the sun which appears to us to rise from below is said by them to circle along the edge of the earth.

Three other peoples live there, the Crefennae [Note: [Col. 1254D] B. Rhenanus, in his *Castigations on Tacitus*, p. 174, writes *Scritofennae*]. They do not seek nourishment from grain but live on the flesh of wild animals and birds; the breeding in their marshes is so abundant that it supplies both growth to the species and food and plenty to the people.

Another people lives there, the Suethans, who, like the Thuringians, use excellent horses. They are also the people who, through commercial exchange, send Saphirian skins to the Romans through countless other nations, famous for the beautiful blackness of their pelts. Although they live in poverty, they dress most richly.

Next follows a crowd of diverse nations: the Theusthes, Vagoth, Bergio, Hallin, and Liothida. All of them dwell in level, fertile country and are therefore harassed by the incursions of other peoples. 399 After them come the Athelnil, Finnaithae, Fervir, and Gautigoth, a fierce race of men and extremely ready for war. Next are the mixed Evagerae and Othingis. All these inhabit excavated rocks as though they were fortresses, in bestial fashion.

Among these, in the outer regions, are the Ostrogoths, Raumarici, Raugnaricii, and the very gentle Finns, milder than all the inhabitants of Scandia. There are also their equals, the Vinoviloth and Suetidi; the Cogeni are physically taller than the rest of this people. The Dani too, having sprung from their stock, expelled the Heruli from their own territories. Among all the nations of Scanzia, the Heruli claim a distinctive reputation for their extraordinary height.

There are also, in their arrangement, the Grannii, Augandzi [printed: Aganziae], Unixae, Ethelrugi, and Arochiranni. Not before all, but many years ago, their king was Rodulf, who despised his own kingdom, hastened to the protection of Theoderic, king of the Goths, and found there what he desired.

These peoples, greater than the Romans in body and spirit, were hostile in the savage violence of battle [variant: “they fought with bestial savagery”].

## CHAPTER FOUR. From Where the Goths First Departed and How They Gradually Advanced Their Settlements into Scythia near the Pontic Sea

From this island of Scanzia, then, as from a workshop of peoples—or certainly as from a sheath of nations—the Goths are once said to have departed with their king, named Berig. As soon as they came out of their ships and touched land, they immediately gave the place a name. To this day, it is said, that place is called Gothiscanzia.

From there they soon advanced to the settlements of the Ulmerugi, who at that time occupied the shores of the Ocean, and established a camp. After engaging them in battle, they drove them from their own settlements; and, already subjugating their neighbors the Vandals, they added them to their victories.

When the population there had greatly increased, under nearly the fifth king after Berig, Filimer, by the counsel of Filogud and Arigis, it was decided that an army of Goths with their families should advance from there. While it was seeking suitable settlements and appropriate places, it reached the lands of Scythia, which in their language were called Ovim [variant: Oium].

There, as the army delighted in the great fertility of the region and half of it had crossed over, the bridge by which it had crossed the river is said to have collapsed disastrously, and from then on no one was permitted either to go or to return. For that place, as is said, is enclosed by a surrounding chasm amid trembling marshes; nature has made it impassable through this double confusion.

Nevertheless, even today, from the testimony of travelers, one may believe that the sounds of cattle are heard there and traces of human beings detected, although they are heard from afar.

That part of the Goths which, under Filimer, crossed the river into the lands of Ovim [variant: Oium] is therefore said to have reached the desired soil. Without delay, they came upon the people of the Spali and, engaging them in battle, gained victory. From there, already like conquerors, they hastened toward the farthest part of Scythia, which lies near the Pontic Sea.

This is also recalled collectively in their ancient songs, almost in the manner of history; and Ablabius, an outstanding historian of the Gothic people, confirms it with a most reliable account. Some of our elders also agreed with this view.

Josephus too, a most truthful narrator of histories, while everywhere laying down the rule of truth and tracing the origins of causes back to the beginning, omitted for some reason the beginnings of the Gothic people that we have described. Nevertheless, when he recalls their stock from this point, he asserts that they were called Scythians both by nation and by name. Before we proceed to anything else, it is necessary to state the boundaries of that land as they lie.

## CHAPTER FIVE. The Location and Description of Scythia, and the Goths’ Various Settlements There

[Col. 1255B]

Scythia, then, borders the land of Germany as far as the point where the river Ister rises, or where the Mysian lake spreads out; it extends to the rivers Tyras, Danastrus, and Vagosola, and to that great Danube and Mount Taurus—not the Taurus of Asia, but its own, that is, the Scythian Taurus—around the whole circuit of Maeotis. Beyond Maeotis, through the straits of the Bosporus, it reaches Mount Caucasus and the river Araxes; then, turning back toward the left beyond the Caspian Sea, it rises at the farthest limits of Asia from the Ocean called Euroboreus, at first narrow like a mushroom and afterward in a broad, rounded form, and stretches as far as the Huns, Albans, and Seres.

This country, I say, namely Scythia, extending far and opening out widely, has the Seres in the east, at its very beginning, dwelling on the shore of the Caspian Sea; in the west, the Germans and the river Vistula; on the north, that is, toward the region of the pole, it is enclosed by the Ocean; on the south, by Persia, Albania, Iberia, Pontus, and the final channel of the Ister, which is called the Danube, from its mouth all the way to its source. [Col. 1255C]

On that side where it touches the Pontic shore, it is surrounded by no obscure cities: Borysthenis, Olbia, Callipode, Cherson, Theodosia, Pareon, Myrmecion, and Trapezuntum. The untamed nations of the Scythians permitted the Greeks to found these cities so that they might provide trade for themselves.

In the middle of this Scythia lies the region that divides Asia and Europe from one another, namely the Rhiphaean Mountains, which pour forth the enormous Tanais as it enters Maeotis. The circumference of this marsh is 144,000 paces, and nowhere does it sink more than eight cubits in depth.

In this Scythia the first people settled from the west were the Gepids, who are enclosed by great and remarkable rivers. For the Tisianus runs along their northern side and around them. On the southwest is the great Danube itself; from the east the river Tausis cuts across them, rushing swiftly and whirlpooling as it rolls furiously into the waters of the Ister. Within their territory lies Dacia, fortified in the form of a crown by lofty Alps.

Along the left side of these mountains, which faces north and extends from the source of the river Vistula across immense distances, the populous nation of the Uvinidi settled. [Col. 1255D] Although their names now vary among different families and places, they are principally called Sclavini and Antes.

The Sclavini dwell from the New City, the Sclavino Rumunnense, and the lake called Musianus, as far as the Danastrus, and northward to the Viscla. They have marshes and forests in place of cities.

The Antes, however, who are the strongest of them and bend toward the Pontic Sea, extend from the Danastrus to the Danube—two rivers separated from one another by many days’ journeys.

On the shore of the Ocean, where the waters of the river Vistula are swallowed through three mouths, the Vidioarii dwell, gathered together from different peoples. Beyond them the coast of the Ocean called Itemestis is occupied by a thoroughly peaceful race.

To their south settled the very powerful nation of the Agazziri, ignorant of agriculture and living by livestock and hunting.

Beyond them, above the Pontic Sea, extend the settlements of the Bulgars, whom the evils of our sins have made notorious. [Col. 1256A]

From this stock the Huns, like a most fertile patch of the strongest peoples, sprang forth into a twofold fury of populations. Some are called Aulziagri, others Aviri, although they occupy different settlements.

The Aulziagri live near Cherson, to which the greedy merchant imports the goods of Asia. In summer they roam across the open plains, establishing their settlements wherever the pasture of their herds invites them; in winter they withdraw again above the Pontic Sea.

The Hunagari are known for this reason: from them comes the trade in mouse pelts. The courage of such mighty men was feared.

We read that their first dwelling was on Scythian soil beside the Maeotian marsh; their second, in Moesia, Thrace, and Dacia; their third, above the Pontic Sea; and again they lived in Scythia. Nowhere do we find written the tales of those who say that they were reduced to slavery in Britain or in one of the islands and once redeemed for the price of a single horse.

Or, if anyone should say that they arose in our world otherwise than as we have stated, he contradicts us. [Col. 1256B] We prefer to trust what we have read rather than agree with old women’s tales.

To return, then, to our subject: those whom we mentioned as dwelling in the first part of Scythia near Maeotis, the region about which we are speaking, are known to have had Filimer as their king.

In the second region, namely the land of Dacia, Thrace, and Moesia, they had Zamolxis, whom most writers of annals attest to have possessed extraordinary philosophical learning. Before him they had the learned Zeutas, and afterward Diceneus, and thirdly Zamolxis, of whom we have spoken above.

Nor were there lacking men who instructed them in wisdom. Consequently, the Goths have always been wiser than almost all barbarians and nearly comparable to the Greeks, as Dio relates, who composed their histories and annals in the Greek style.

He says that they were first called Zarabos Tereos, and afterward Pileati—those who stood out among them by noble birth. From these men their kings and priests were appointed.

So highly, then, were the Getae praised that they are said to have maintained that Mars, whom the poets’ falsehood proclaims the god of war, arose among them long ago. Hence Virgil says:

> “And Father Gradivus, who presides over the Getic fields.”

The Goths always appeased this Mars with the most savage rites. The deaths of captives served as his victims, since they believed that the commander of wars should more suitably be appeased by the shedding of human blood.

The first spoils of war were vowed to him; his trophies were hung upon tree trunks. Among them there was a religious devotion to him surpassing all others, since they seemed to offer devotion to their ancestral deity by name.

Their third settlement was above the Pontic Sea. By then they had become more civilized and, as we said above, more prudent, and the peoples were divided among families. The Vesegoths served the family of the Balti; the Ostrogoths served the illustrious Amali. [Col. 1256C]

Their first concern among the neighboring peoples was to bend bows with sinews, as Lucan, more historian than poet, testifies:

> “And to bend Armenian bows with Getic sinews.”

Before them, too, the deeds of their ancestors were sung in song and accompanied by the lyre: those of Ethespamara, Hanala [perhaps Amala], Fridigerna, Uvidicula, and others, whose reputation is great among this people, men whom venerable antiquity astonishingly boasts to have scarcely been heroes. [Col. 1256D]

Then, as the story goes, Vesosis brought upon the Scythians a war more grievous to himself—namely, against those whom ancient tradition says were the husbands of the Amazons. Orosius also openly bears witness to these warrior women in the first book of his work.

Thus we clearly prove that he fought against the Goths, since we know that he fought outright against the husbands of the Amazons. At that time they lived from the river Borysthenes—which the inhabitants call the Danube [or Danabrus]—as far as the river Tanais, around the inlet of the Maeotian marsh.

By Tanais I mean the river that falls from the Rhiphaean Mountains and rushes downward with such precipitous force that, while the neighboring rivers, Maeotis, and the Bosporus are hardened by frost, it alone, warmed by the rugged mountains, never freezes under the cold of Scythia.

This is regarded as the famous boundary between Asia and Europe. There is another river, however, which rises in the mountains of the Chrinni and flows down into the Caspian Sea. [Col. 1257A]

The Danube, for its part, rises from a great marsh and pours forth as though from the sea. As far as its middle course it is fresh and drinkable, and it produces fish of extraordinary flavor, lacking bones and possessing only cartilage to hold the body together.

But when it becomes nearer to Pontus, it receives a small spring called Ampheus. This spring is so bitter that, although the river is navigable for a journey of forty days, its scanty waters alter it; polluted and unlike itself, it flows into the sea between the Greek cities of Callipidas and Hypanis.

At its mouth there is an island lying directly before it, called by the name of Achilles. Between these places lies an enormous land, planted with forests and made uncertain by marshes.

## CHAPTER VI. The Goths rout Vesosis, king of the Egyptians, and on their return subjugate Asia. Also, concerning the origin of the Parthians.

While the Goths were dwelling there, Vesosis, king of the Egyptians, invaded them in war. At that time their king was Taunasis. [Col. 1257B]

In the battle at the river Phasis—from which the birds called pheasants originated and which abound throughout the world in the feasts of the powerful—Taunasis, king of the Goths, confronted Vesosis of Egypt. He defeated him severely and pursued him as far as Egypt. Had the impassable waters of the Nile not blocked his way, or the fortifications that Vesosis had previously ordered to be built for himself against the incursions of the Ethiopians, Taunasis would have destroyed him there in his own country.

But because he was unable to harm him while he remained there, Taunasis returned and subjugated almost all Asia. He made it tributary to himself, including the Medes, who were then ruled by his dear friend King Sornus [or Sormi].

Some of the victorious men from his army, seeing the subject provinces and their abundant fertility, voluntarily settled in the regions of Asia, abandoning the main body of their own people. Pompey Trogus says that the lineage of the Parthians arose from their name or stock.

For this reason, even today they are called in the Scythian language *Fugaces*, that is, “Fugitives” (*Parthi*). True to their origin, they alone among almost all the nations of Asia are archers and extremely fierce warriors. [Col. 1257C]

As for the name by which we have said they are called Parthians, that is, “Fugitives,” some have derived the etymology in this way: they were called Parthians because they fled from their own parents.

The Goths then worshiped this king Taunasis, after his death, among the divine beings of their people.

## CHAPTER VII. The Amazons, while their husbands are absent at war, resist various attacks by their enemies and overcome diverse peoples of Asia in battle.

After his death, while his army and his successor were conducting an expedition in other regions, the women of the Goths were attacked by a neighboring people and led away as plunder by the men [or: trained for plunder]. They resisted bravely and drove back the enemies who came against them, to the great disgrace of the attackers.

After achieving this victory and gaining greater courage, they encouraged one another, seized weapons, and chose two of the boldest women, Lampeto and Marpesia, to assume the leadership. [Col. 1257D]

While they took care to defend their own possessions and ravage those of others, Lampeto remained behind by lot to protect the ancestral territories. Marpesia, however, taking an army of women, led this new kind of force into Asia. She overcame various peoples in war, reconciled others through peace, and reached the Caucasus.

There she remained for a fixed period and gave the place the name Marpesian Rock. Hence Virgil says:

> “As though it were hard flint or the Marpesian crag standing firm.”

It was in this place that Alexander the Great later established gates and called them the Caspian Gates. The people of the Lazes now guard them as a Roman fortress.

The Amazons therefore dwelt there for a certain period and grew stronger. From there they went out, crossed the river Alym, which flows past the city of Garganum [or Gorgarum], and subdued Armenia, Syria, Cilicia, Galatia, Pisidia, and all the cities of Asia with equal success. [Col. 1258A]

Turning toward Ionia and Aeolia, they made those provinces subject to themselves. After ruling there for a long time, they also dedicated cities and military camps to their own name.

At Ephesus, because of their devotion to archery and hunting—arts to which they had devoted themselves—they built, at enormous expense, the temple of Diana, a work of marvelous beauty.

Thus, by this turn of fortune, the women born from the Scythian people gained possession of the kingdom of Asia and held it for nearly one hundred years. At last they returned to their own companions at the Marpesian crags, which we mentioned above, namely, to Mount Caucasus.

Since this mountain has now been mentioned again, I think it appropriate to describe its extent and position, for it is known to encircle a very large part of the world in one continuous range. [Col. 1258B]

Caucasus rises from the Indian Sea. On the side facing south, heated by the sun, it burns; on the side open to the north, it is exposed to freezing winds and frost.

Then, bending at an angle toward Syria, it turns back. Although it sends forth many rivers, it pours the Euphrates and the Tigris, navigable rivers, into the region of Asia with the abundant richness of mighty perennial springs.

These rivers embrace the lands of the Assyrians and cause Mesopotamia both to be called and to appear as such, depositing their waters into the gulf of the Red Sea.

Then turning northward, the aforesaid range traverses the lands of Scythia in great curves. There, pouring into the Caspian Sea rivers of the greatest renown—Araxes, Cyssus, and Cambyses—it extends in an unbroken ridge as far as the Rhiphaean Mountains.

From there, providing a boundary for the Scythian peoples with its back, it descends as far as Pontus. Joining hill to hill, it also reaches the waters of the Ister; when that river splits and opens out, it too is called Taurus in Scythia.

Such and so great a mountain range, almost the greatest of all mountains, raising its lofty summits, naturally provides the peoples with impregnable defenses. [Col. 1258C]

For where it is cut back and, after the ridge has been broken, a valley opens in a gap, it forms, according to the locality, now the Caspian Gates, now the Armenian Gates, now the Cilician Gates, or others corresponding to the region. It is scarcely passable even by a wagon, with its sides rising vertically to great heights on either hand.

It is called by different names according to the variety of peoples. The Indian calls it Jamnium [perhaps Imaus], then Propanismus; the Parthian calls it “the first camp beyond Niphaces.” The Syrian and Armenian call it Taurus; the Scythians call it Caucasus and Rhiphaeus, and again, at its end, Taurus. Many other peoples have also given this ridge numerous names.

Since we have briefly touched upon its continuity, let us return to the Amazons, from whom we digressed.

## CHAPTER VIII. Of the intercourse of the Amazons with neighboring peoples and of their offspring.

Fearing that their offspring might become too few, they sought intercourse with neighboring peoples. Once a year they held a kind of market, arranging that, when the men returned at the appointed time, whatever male offspring had been born should be given back to its father, while whatever was born female should be trained by the mother in the arts of war. [Col. 1258D]

Or, as some prefer to believe, after male children had been born, they broke the pitiable lives of the infants with stepmotherly hatred. Thus childbirth was hateful among them, although everywhere it is agreed to be a source of joy.

This cruelty, according to the widespread report, added greatly to the terror inspired by them. For what hope, I ask, could there be for a captive when it was considered unlawful even to spare one’s own son?

Against them, as the story goes, Hercules fought, and Melanes subdued them almost more by cunning than by force. Theseus carried Hippolyta away as booty, and by her he fathered Hippolytus.

Afterward these Amazons also had a queen named Penthesilea, whose deeds in the Trojan War are recorded in the clearest testimony. These women are said to have retained their kingdom down to the time of Alexander the Great.

## CHAPTER IX. Of the men of the Amazons and their king Telephus, and of his birth and deeds.

But lest you say, “Since the discussion has turned to the men of the Goths, why does it remain so long among women?” listen also to the distinguished and praiseworthy courage of the men. [Col. 1259A]

The historian Dio, a most diligent investigator of antiquities, who gave his work the title *Getica*—and whom we have already proved above to mean the Goths when he speaks of the Getae—says, according to Orosius Paulus:

> “This Dio, after a long interval of time, mentions that they had a king named Telephus.”

And lest anyone say that this name is wholly foreign to the Gothic language, no one is unaware that peoples commonly adopt many names through usage: the Romans adopt names from the Macedonians, the Greeks from the Romans, the Sarmatians from the Germans, and the Goths frequently borrow from the Huns. [Col. 1259B]

This Telephus, then, son of Hercules, born of Auge, the sister of Priam, and joined in marriage, was tall in body but still more formidable in strength. Equaling his father’s courage by his own virtues, he also bore, in the nature [or genius] of Hercules, a likeness to him in appearance.

Our ancestors therefore called his kingdom Moesia. This province has the mouths of the Danube on the east, Macedonia on the south, Istria on the west, and the Danube on the north.

The aforementioned king waged war against the Danaans. In that battle he killed Thessander, the commander of Greece. While he attacked Ajax with hostility and pursued Ulysses, his horse fell and he himself was thrown down; wounded in the thigh by Achilles’ spear, he could not be cured for a long time.

Although wounded, he nevertheless drove the Greeks from his territory.

After Telephus died, his son Eurypylus succeeded him in the kingdom. He was born of a sister of Priam, king of the Phrygians. Desiring to take part in the Trojan War out of love for Cassandra and to bring aid to his parents and father-in-law, he was killed as soon as he arrived.

## CHAPTER X. Of the various wars and victories of the Goths against the kings of Persia and Macedonia.

After a long interval, Cyrus, king of the Persians—nearly six hundred and thirty years later, as Pompey Trogus testifies—brought upon himself a fatal war against Thamiris, queen of the Getae. [Col. 1259C]

Elated by his victory in Asia, he attempted to subjugate the Getae, among whom, as we have said, Thamiris [or Thomiris] had ruled.

Although she could have prevented Cyrus from approaching by blocking his passage at the river Araxes, she nevertheless allowed him to cross, choosing to defeat him by arms rather than drive him away through the advantage of the terrain.

This is what happened. When Cyrus advanced, fortune at first favored the Parthians so greatly that they killed both Thamiris’ son and a very large part of her army.

But in a second battle the Getae, together with their queen, defeated and crushed the conquered Parthians, and carried away rich booty from them. It was then that the Gothic people first saw silk tents.

Queen Thamiris, having achieved victory and obtained such great booty from her enemies, crossed into the part of Moesia that, borrowing its name from Greater Scythia, is now called Lesser Scythia. There she is honored at the Moesian bridge, and she built a city named Thamiris after herself.

Afterward Darius, king of the Persians and son of Hystaspes, sought the daughter of Antriregirus, king of the Goths, in marriage, making requests while also issuing threats if they did not do his will. [Col. 1259D]

The Goths rejected his proposed alliance and frustrated his embassy. Rebuffed, he was inflamed with fury and led an army of eighty thousand armed men against them, seeking to avenge his humiliation through a public disaster.

He constructed ships, almost from Chalcedon to Byzantium, joined together with planks in the manner of bridges, and marched against Thrace and Moesia. Then, having built a bridge over the Danube in the same fashion, he was worn down for two months by repeated *intaphis* [a corrupt word whose meaning is unknown; B. Vulcanius conjectures a connection with Italian *intopo*, “an encounter,” and further suggests that Italian and Spanish *topar* may have been borrowed from Gothic; alternatively, *in scaphis*, “in skiffs”]. He lost eight thousand armed men.

Fearing that the bridge over the Danube might be seized by his opponents, he fled swiftly back into Thrace and did not consider even Moesia safe enough for him to remain there for any length of time. [Col. 1260A]

After his death, his son Xerxes again considered himself bound to avenge his father’s injuries. He set out to war against the Goths with two hundred thousand of his own men [or seven hundred thousand], three hundred thousand auxiliaries, one thousand seven hundred beaked warships, and three thousand cargo ships.

But without even testing the matter in battle, he failed to prevail, overcome by the steadfastness of their courage. He withdrew with shame exactly as he had come, without any engagement.

Philip, the father of Alexander the Great, also entered into friendship with the Goths and took Medopa, daughter of the Gothic king Gudila [or of the king of the Medes, Gudila], as his wife, so that, strengthened by such an alliance, he might secure the kingdom of the Macedonians.

At that time, according to the historian Dio, Philip suffered from a lack of money and resolved to ravage the Moesian city of Udisitana with a well-equipped force. Because of its proximity to Thamiris [or Tomheae], it was then subject to the Goths.

Some Gothic priests, called Pii, suddenly opened the gates and came out to meet him with lyres and white garments, singing in supplication to their ancestral gods that, being favorable to them, they might repel the Macedonians. [Col. 1260B]

The Macedonians, seeing them approach so confidently, were astonished; and, if it may be said, the armed men were held fast [or tormented] by the unarmed.

Without delay they broke up the battle line they had formed for war. They not only withdrew from the destruction of the city but also returned those whom they had captured outside the city by the right of war. After making a treaty, they returned to their own land.

After a long time, the distinguished Gothic commander Sitalcus remembered this stratagem and, having gathered 150,000 men, waged war against Perdiccas, king of Macedonia, upon the Athenians. After Alexander had met death by drinking poison near Babylon through the treachery of his attendants, Perdiccas had been left as his successor to the leadership of the Athenians by hereditary right.

After a great battle with Perdiccas, the Goths were found to be victorious. Thus, in retaliation for the injury that the Athenians had previously inflicted upon them in Moesia, the Goths marched through Greece and ravaged all Macedonia.

## CHAPTER XI. Of Diceneus’ arrival among the Goths under Boroista, by whom he taught them all philosophy, and of his supreme authority among the Goths. Also, of Comosicus, Diceneus’ successor.

[Col. 1260C]

Afterward, while Sitalces was reigning among the Goths, Diceneus came to Gothia under Boroista. This occurred at the time when Sulla gained control of the Roman state. Boroista, receiving Diceneus, granted him almost royal power. On his advice the Goths ravaged the lands of the Germans that the Franks now possess.

Caesar, who was the first of all the Romans to claim imperial power for himself, who subjected almost the whole world to his authority and conquered every kingdom, even occupying islands placed beyond our world in the basin of the Ocean, and making tributary to the Romans peoples who had never even heard the name of the Romans—Caesar, I say, nevertheless tried repeatedly and could not subjugate the Goths.

Gaius Tiberius was already reigning as the third emperor of Rome, but the Goths remained unharmed in their own kingdom. [Col. 1260D] It was beneficial, advantageous, and desirable for them that whatever Diceneus, their counsellor, commanded, they should carry out in every way, judging it wholly worth seeking and useful. [403]

When he saw that their minds obeyed him in everything and that they possessed natural intelligence, he instructed them in almost the whole of philosophy, for he was a skilled teacher of this discipline.

He taught them ethics, restraining their barbarous customs. By handing down physics, he made them live according to the laws proper to nature—laws that they still call *Bellagines* in writing.

**Note:** I do not believe anyone will persuade me that *Bellagines* is a Gothic word; rather, it is corrupted from Gothic. I believe it was originally *Wel-hagen*, contracted for brevity from *Wel-behagem*, meaning “well-pleasing,” so that *bellagines*, in my opinion, are nothing other than the decrees of princes. —B. Vulcanius. [Col. 1259D; Col. 1260D]

By instructing them in logic, he made them more skilled in reasoning than the other nations. By showing them practical philosophy, he persuaded them to conduct themselves in good actions. By demonstrating theoretical philosophy, he taught them to contemplate the twelve signs of the zodiac, the courses of the planets through them, and the whole of astronomy. [Col. 1261A]

He explained how the lunar sphere undergoes increase or suffers decrease, and showed how much the fiery globe of the sun exceeds the earthly sphere in size. He also explained by what names or signs 344 stars, inclining or returning in the pole of heaven, rush headlong from east to west.

What, I ask, must their willingness have been, since men of the greatest courage, whenever they had been free from arms for as many as four days, were immersed in philosophical instruction?

You might see one of them investigating the structure of the heavens, another examining the natures of herbs and crops; one observing the advantages and disadvantages of the moon, another the labor of the sun; and one learning through reason how the sun, carried along by the rotation of the heavens, is drawn back toward the western region although it hastens toward the eastern quarter.

As Diceneus taught these and many other things to the Goths through his own expertise, he became remarkable among them [or: shone forth], so that he commanded not only ordinary men, but even kings. [Col. 1261B]

He chose from among them the most noble and prudent men. Instructing them in theology, he persuaded them to venerate certain divine beings and shrines, and made them priests. He gave them the name *Pileati*, as I suppose because, with their heads covered by tiaras—which we call caps by another name—they performed sacrificial rites.

He ordered the rest of the people to be called *capillati*, “long-haired.” The Goths accepted this name as a great honor and still recall it in their songs today.

When Diceneus died, they honored Comosicus with almost equal veneration, because he was not inferior in skill. Indeed, because of his expertise he was regarded both as their king and as their priest, and in his supreme [perhaps: “greatest”] justice he judged the peoples.

## CHAPTER XII. Of Corillus, king of the Goths. Also, a description of ancient Dacia. Also, a description of the Danube.

After Comosicus had passed beyond human affairs, Corillus, king of the Goths, ascended the throne and ruled his people in Dacia for forty years. [Col. 1261C]

I mean ancient Dacia, which the peoples of the Gepids are now known to possess. This country, lying opposite Moesia beyond the Danube, is encircled by a crown of mountains and has only two approaches, one through the Bontas and the other through the Tabas.

This Gothic land, which our ancestors called Dacia and which is now, as we have said, called Gepidia, was bounded on the east by the Roxolani, on the west by the Tamazites, on the north by the Sarmatians and Bastarnae, and on the south by the waters of the Danube.

The Tamazites [A.: Taziges] are separated from the Roxolani only by the channel of a river.

Since the Danube has been mentioned, I think it appropriate to indicate a few notable facts about such a river. Rising in the Alemannian plains, it receives sixty rivers from its source to its mouths as it turns toward Pontus, taking in tributaries from either side over 1,200,000 paces, like a spine whose ribs are woven together into a lattice.

It is altogether enormous. In the language of the Bessi it is called the Ister. Its channel is only two hundred feet deep.

This river, enormous among the other rivers, surpasses all except the Nile. Enough has been said about the Danube. Let us return, with the Lord’s help, to the subject from which we digressed.

## CHAPTER XIII. Of Dorpaneus, king of the Goths, and of their various battles and victories against the Romans under the emperor Domitian.

After a long interval, while Domitian was reigning as emperor, the Goths, fearing his greed, broke the treaty that they had earlier made with other rulers. They ravaged the bank of the Danube, which had long been held by the Roman Empire, after overthrowing [or selecting] the soldiers and their commanders. [Col. 1262A]

At that time Poppaeus Sabinus [editorial reading: Pompeius] governed that province after Agrippa.

Dorpaneus was leading the Goths. When battle was joined, the Goths defeated the Romans, cut off the head of Poppaeus [or Oppius] Sabinus, and, invading many forts and cities, openly plundered the emperor’s territory.

Because of this emergency among his people, Domitian hastened into Illyricum with all his forces. Under the command of Fuscus, he compelled soldiers from almost the whole Roman state, together with the most select men, to cross the Danube in assembled ships arranged like a bridge, against the army of Dorpaneus.

The Goths were then found to be no less ready. They took up arms and, in the first armed clash, soon defeated the Romans. After killing their commander Fuscus, they stripped the soldiers’ camp of its wealth.

Having achieved a great victory across the region, they began to call their nobles—men who seemed to conquer through fortune—not ordinary men but demigods, that is, *anses*. [Col. 1262B]

**Note:** I interpret *semideos* as “heroes,” whom Hesiod also calls ἡμιθέους, or “demigods.” But the heroes of whom the present passage speaks we do not place in the middle region of the air, as Hesiod does, “clothed in air,” as he says; nor do we make them, as Apuleius does in his *On the God of Socrates*, messengers and interpreters of the gods. Rather, they are men of the highest nobility and dignity among the Gothic people. In much the same way the Gauls call them *les pairs de France*, “the peers of France”; the Spaniards, *los grandes del reyno*, “the grandees of the kingdom.” Consider also whether the Teutonic word *Ansa*, and the federated Hanseatic cities, derive their name from this term, although I am not unaware that others offer different interpretations or etymologies of the word. —B. Vulcanius. [Col. 1261D; Col. 1262D]

## 404. CHAPTER XIV. The genealogy of the Gothic nobles, whom they called *anses*, that is, demigods, and concerning their origin and end.

According to their own tales, the first of these heroes was Gapt, who begot Halmal. Halmal begot Augis; Augis begot the man called Amala, from whom the lineage of the Amali descends.

Amala begot Isarna; Isarna begot Ostrogotha; Ostrogotha begot Unilt; Unilt begot Athal; Athal begot Achiulf.

Achiulf begot Ansila, Ediulf, Widulf, and Hermerich. Widulf begot Valeravans; Valeravans begot Winitharius; and Winitharius begot Theodemir, Walamir, and Widemir. [Col. 1262C]

Theodemir begot Theoderic; Theoderic begot Amalasuentha. Amalasuentha, by her husband Eutharic [or Utheric], begot Athalaric and Mathasuentha. Through this husband she was connected with the lineage in the following way.

The aforementioned Hermerich, son of Achiulf, begot Hunnimund; Hunnimund begot Thorismund; Thorismund begot Berimund; Berimund begot Wideric; and Wideric begot Eutharic.

Eutharic, joined in marriage to Amalasuentha, begot Athalaric and Mathasuentha.

When Athalaric died in his childhood, Mathasuentha was married to Witichis [or Vitigis]. She had no child by him. They were brought together by Belisarius to Constantinople, and when Witichis had passed beyond human affairs, Germanus, a patrician and cousin of the emperor Justinian, took her in marriage and made her an ordinary patrician. By her he fathered a son, also named Germanus.

After Germanus died, she resolved to remain a widow.

How and in what manner the kingdom of the Amali was destroyed, we shall explain in its proper place, if the Lord wills. For now, let us return to the subject from which we digressed and explain when the order of the people about whom we are speaking completed the course of its history.

For the historian Ablavius reports that there, on the shore of Pontus where we said they dwelt in Scythia, the part of them that occupied the eastern region and was ruled by Ostrogotha were called Ostrogoths—although it is uncertain whether they received this name from Ostrogotha himself or from the eastern region. The remainder, in the western part, were the Vesegoths. [Col. 1262D]

We have already said that, after crossing the Danube, they lived for some time in Moesia and Thrace.

## CHAPTER XV. Of Maximinus, emperor, born from the Gothic people, his remarkable courage, and how he attained the imperial power.

[Col. 1263A]

Among their descendants was the emperor Maximinus, after Alexander, son of Mammaea [editorial reading: Mammeam], as Symmachus says in the fifth book of his history.

He says (Niv. ed.: “Maximinus,” he says, “Caesar having died, Alexander,” etc.): “After Alexander Caesar died, Maximinus was made emperor by the army. He was born in Thrace of the humblest parents: his father was a Goth named Mecca, and his mother was an Alani woman called Ababa.”

After reigning for three years, he took up arms against the Christians and lost both the empire and his life.

While the emperor Severus was reigning and celebrating the birthday of his son, Maximinus, after an early life spent in rustic circumstances, came from the pastures into military service. The emperor Severus had provided military games.

When Maximinus saw this—although he was a half-barbarian young man—and the prizes had been set out, he asked the emperor in the barbarian language to grant him permission to wrestle with experienced soldiers. [Col. 1263B]

Severus was greatly astonished by his physical size—for, as the story goes, he was more than eight feet tall—and ordered him to wrestle with the camp servants in bodily contests, so that no injury might come to the military men from an untrained man.

Then Maximinus, with such success, threw down sixteen camp servants that, by defeating them one by one, he allowed himself no rest between the contests.

After receiving the prizes, he was ordered to be enrolled in the army, and his first pay was that of a cavalryman.

Three days later, when the emperor had gone out [Niv. ed.: “went out”] into the field, he saw Maximinus leaping about in barbarian fashion and ordered a tribune to restrain him and train him in Roman discipline.

When Maximinus understood that the emperor was speaking about him, he approached him and began to run on foot ahead of him while he rode.

Then the emperor drove his horse [Niv. ed.: “added his horse”] into a gallop with the spurs and made many circuits [Juretus: *intripedavit*], here and there, through various turns, until he himself was exhausted. He then said to him:

> “Thracian, do you wish to wrestle after the ride?” [Col. 1263C]

He replied: “As much as you wish, emperor.”

Severus therefore leapt down from his horse and ordered the freshest soldiers to compete with him.

Maximinus threw seven of the strongest soldiers [or young men] to the ground, without taking any time to breathe, just as before.

He alone was rewarded by Caesar with silver prizes and a golden torque, and was afterward ordered to serve among the emperor’s bodyguard.

Later, under Antoninus Caracalla, he advanced through the ranks and, repeatedly increasing his reputation by his deeds, passed through many military grades and received the reward of his courage in the centurionate.

When Macrinus afterward entered upon the imperial power, Maximinus refused military service for nearly three years. Although he held the honor of tribune, he never appeared before Macrinus, considering his rule unworthy because it had been sought through the crime committed by Heliogabalus.

Afterward, as though returning to the son of Antoninus, he took up his tribunate again. Later, under Alexander, son of Mammaea, he fought brilliantly against the Parthians.

When Alexander was killed at Mainz amid a military revolt, Maximinus himself was made emperor by the choice of the army, without a decree of the senate. [Col. 1263D]

He stained all his good qualities with an evil purpose through the persecution of the Christians. He was killed at Aquileia by Pupio and left the empire to Philip.

We have borrowed this account from Symmachus’ history, Book V, for this reason: to show that the people about whom we are speaking reached even the summit of the Roman Empire.

For the rest, the subject requires us to return to the point from which we digressed.

## CHAPTER XVI. The Goths, formerly federates of the Romans, become enemies because their pay was withheld, and devastate Moesia and Thrace under the leadership of King Ostrogotha.

For this people became known in a remarkable manner in the region where it dwelt—that is, on the shore of Pontus, in the Scythian land—undoubtedly possessing such vast stretches of territory, so many inlets of the sea, and so many river courses that often a Vandal lay beneath its right hand, a Marcomannian stood at its price, and the [Col. 1264A] princes of the Quadi were reduced to slavery.

For when the aforementioned Philip was reigning over the Romans—the only Christian before Constantine, together with Philip, that is, his son—and in the second year of his reign Rome completed its thousandth year, the Goths, as usually happens, bearing their withheld pay with resentment, became enemies instead of friends. For although they lived under their own kings at a distance, they were federates of the Roman state and received annual gifts.

What more need be said? At that time Ostrogotha crossed the Danube with his people and devastated Moesia and Thrace. Decius the senator was sent by Philip to repel him. When he arrived and was unable to prevail against the people, he removed his own soldiers from military service and made them live as private citizens, as though the Goths had crossed the Danube through their negligence; and, having supposedly taken vengeance upon his own men, he returned to Philip.

But when the soldiers saw that after all their labors they had been expelled from military service, they became indignant and fled for assistance to Ostrogotha, king of the Goths. He received them, and, inflamed by their account, immediately led thirty thousand [Col. 1264B] armed men into battle, together with a number of Taiphali and Astringi [variant: Thaifali and Astingi]. He also brought three thousand Carpi [variant: three hundred thousand], a people exceedingly swift in warfare, who had often been hostile to the Romans. Later, under the emperor Diocletian, Caesar Galerius Maximian [edition: and Maximian] subjected them to the Roman state.

Thus, possessing Goths and Peuceni—so called from the island of Peuce, which lies beside the mouth of the Danube where it empties into Pontus—he appointed Argaitus and Gunthericus, the most distinguished men of his people, as commanders. They soon crossed the Danube, ravaged Moesia a second time, and attacked Marcianopolis, the famous metropolis of that region. After besieging it for a long time, they withdrew after receiving money from those who were inside.

Since we have mentioned Marcianopolis, it is pleasing briefly to explain something about its situation. The emperor Trajan is said to have built this city for the following reason. While Marcia, his sister’s daughter [variant: Marcia, his sister], was bathing in the river called Potamus, which rises in the middle of the city with extraordinary clarity [Col. 1264C] and flavor, she wished to draw water from it. By chance, the golden vessel she was carrying fell into the depths, weighed down by the metal, and resurfaced only much later. This was certainly not something usual: either for an empty vessel to be swallowed, or for one once swallowed to be cast back up by the returning waters. When Trajan learned of these marvels and believed that the spring contained something divine, he named the city he founded after his sister: Marcianopolis.

## CHAPTER XVII. Fastida, king of the Gepids, makes war upon Ostrogotha, king of the Goths; the Goths emerge victorious. Also concerning the kinship between the Goths and Gepids.

After this, as we said, the Goth, enriched by the reward received after the long siege, withdrew to his homeland. When the nation of the Gepids saw him suddenly [Col. 1264D] victorious everywhere and enriched with spoils, it was moved by envy and took up arms against its kinsmen.

If you ask how the Getae and Gepids are related, I shall explain briefly. You should remember that at the beginning I said that the Goths had departed from the bosom of the island of Scanzia with their king Berich, carried in only three ships to the shore of the nearer Ocean. One of these three ships, as usually happens, was carried more slowly and is said to have given its name to the people; for in their language “slow” is called *gepanta*. From this it happened that, gradually and through corruption, their name arose as an insult.

The Gepids undoubtedly derive their origin from the stock of the Goths. But because, as I said, *gepanta* signifies something slow or sluggish, the name Gepids arose as a gratuitous insult [variant: as a serious insult]. Nor do I believe that the name itself is entirely false. For they are slow in understanding and heavier in bodily speed.

These Gepids, therefore, touched by envy and having long despised the province, lived together on an island surrounded by the shallows of the river Vistula, which in their native language they called Gepidos. Now, it is said, the [Col. 1265A] nation of the Vividarii inhabits that island [uncertain reading: “island”], while the Gepids themselves have moved toward better lands. The Vividarii were gathered from various nations as though into a single refuge and are known to have formed one people.

Thus, as we said, Fastida, king of the Gepids, who also roused his peaceful people and enlarged its ancestral boundaries by force of arms, destroyed the Burgundians [variant: Burgozones] almost to extermination and subdued several other peoples. He also wickedly provoked the Goths and first violated the bond of kinship through an unwarranted quarrel. Inflated by exceedingly proud arrogance, while he began adding lands to his growing people, he made the native inhabitants fewer.

He therefore sent ambassadors to Ostrogotha, under whose rule both the Ostrogoths and the Visigoths—that is, both peoples of the same nation—were still subject. Fastida complained that he was confined by the ruggedness of the mountains and hemmed in by the density of the forests. He demanded one of two things: either that Ostrogotha prepare war for him, or that he provide him with room for his territories.

Then Ostrogotha, king of the Goths, being a man of steadfast courage, replied to the ambassadors that he indeed dreaded such a war, that it would be harsh [Col. 1265B], and that it was altogether wicked to fight with relatives; but he would not surrender his lands.

What more need be said? The Gepids rushed into battle. Ostrogotha also mobilized his forces against them, lest he be thought too weak [variant: lest he be thought inferior]. They met near the town of Galtis, beside which the river Aucha flows [variant: Houna], and there the two sides fought with great vigor, since the similarity of their weapons and warfare stirred them against one another.

But the Goths were aided by the better cause and their lively spirit [variant: by the vigor of their intelligence]. Finally, when the Gepid line began to give way, night [edition: soon] ended the battle. Then Fastida, king of the Gepids, abandoning the slaughter of his people, hurried back to his homeland, humbled by shameful disgrace as greatly as he had been lifted up by arrogance.

The victorious Goths returned, satisfied with the Gepids’ departure, and our people lived peacefully in their homeland until Ostrogotha became their leader.

## CHAPTER XVIII. After the death of Ostrogotha, Cniva, king of the Goths, leads an army into Moesia and harasses the Romans in various battles, in which Decius is slain.

After Ostrogotha’s death, Cniva divided his army into two parts and sent some of it to ravage Moesia, knowing that it had been left without defenders because its rulers were negligent. He himself, with seventy thousand men [variant: eighty thousand], climbed toward Eustesium—that is, Novae. From there, having been driven away by the commander Gallus, he approached Nicopolis, a very famous city situated beside the river Iatrus, which Trajan built after defeating the Sarmatians and called the City of Victory.

When the emperor Decius arrived there, Cniva at last withdrew toward the regions of Haemonia, which were not far away. From there, after arranging his preparations, he hastened to Philippopolis. When the emperor Decius learned of his withdrawal and desired to bring assistance to the city itself, he crossed the mountain ridge [variant: Haemus] and came to Berroea.

While he was resting his horses and his exhausted army there, Cniva [Col. 1265D] suddenly fell upon him with the Goths like a thunderbolt. After devastating the Roman army, he drove the emperor, with the few who had been able to flee, back across the Alps into Moesia, toward Thuscia, where Gallus, commander of the frontier, was stationed with a very large force of fighting men. Gallus gathered an army both from that region and from the enemy and restored his battle line for the war to come.

Cniva then attacked Philippopolis, which had long been under siege. After obtaining the spoils, he won over the commander Priscus, who was inside the city, to his side, as though Priscus intended to fight against Decius. When they came to battle, they immediately struck Decius’s son with an arrow, inflicting a cruel wound.

When his father perceived this, although he is said to have declared, to encourage the courage of the soldiers, “Let no one grieve; the loss of one soldier is not the diminution of the state,” he could not bear his paternal grief. He attacked the enemy, demanding either death or vengeance for his son.

When he came to Abruptum, a city of Moesia [variant: “to Abitrum”], he too was surrounded and killed by the Goths, thus bringing his imperial rule and his life [Col. 1266A] to an end. That place is still called Decius’s Altar, because before the battle he had there pitiably sacrificed to idols.

## CHAPTER XIX. How Gallus and Volusianus made a treaty with the Goths, and Aemylianus harassed Moesia.

After Decius’s death, Gallus and Volusianus gained rule over the Romans. At that time a pestilential disease [variant: a pestilential year of diseases], almost like the calamity we experienced nine years ago, disfigured the face of the whole world. It devastated Alexandria and the regions of all Egypt beyond measure. The historian Dionysius lamented this disaster in writing, as did our own venerable martyr of Christ, the bishop Cyprian, in the book entitled *On Mortality*.

At that time a certain Aemylianus, observing that the Goths were often devastating Moesia because of the negligence of the emperors, and seeing that this was permitted and that they could not be removed by anyone without [Col. 1266B] great damage to the state, likewise judged that the same might happen to his own fortune. He seized the tyranny in Moesia and, having gathered an entire military force, began to devastate cities and peoples.

Against him, within a few months, the growing mass of preparations produced no small disaster for the state. Yet he was killed almost at the very beginning of his wicked attempt and lost both the life and the rule he had seized [variant: desired].

The emperors Gallus and Volusianus mentioned above, although they departed this life after remaining in power scarcely two years, nevertheless during those two years ruled everywhere peacefully and enjoyed favor everywhere. The sole misfortune attributed to their fortune was the general disease [Niv.: “the things because of which”]. This judgment, however, came from the ignorant and the slanderers who habitually tear the lives of others apart with a malicious tooth.

As soon as these men obtained the empire, they made a treaty with the Gothic people. Soon afterward both kings died, and Gallienus seized the leadership.

## CHAPTER XX. During the reign of Gallienus, the Goths invade Asia, burn the temple of Diana at Ephesus, destroy Chalcedon, ravage Troy, and harass Thrace.

[Col. 1266C]

While Gallienus was entirely given over to dissipation, the Gothic commanders Respa, Veduco, Thuro, and Varo [variant: Tharvaro] took ships and crossed into Asia, conveyed across the Hellespont. After plundering many cities of that province, they set fire to the celebrated temple of Diana at Ephesus, which, as we said earlier, was founded by the Amazons.

Carried into the region of Bithynia, they destroyed Chalcedon, which Cornelius Avitus later restored in part. Although today it rejoices in the status or proximity [variant: vicinity] of a royal city, it still preserves some signs of its ruins as indications for posterity [variant: of its former power].

After this success, by which the Goths had entered the regions of Asia and gained booty and spoils, they crossed the Hellespont again. [Col. 1266D] Along their route they ravaged Troy and Ilium, which had scarcely begun to recover [variant: to restore themselves] from the war of Agamemnon before they were again destroyed by the hostile sword.

After such a catastrophe in Asia, Thrace experienced their savagery. There, at the foot of Mount Haemus and near the sea, they immediately attacked the city of Anchialus. This was the city which, long ago, King Sardanapalus of the Parthians had placed between the coast of the sea and the roots of Haemus.

They are said to have remained there for many days, delighting in baths of hot water. These springs lie fifteen miles from Anchialus [variant: twelve miles from Anchialus], bubbling up from the fire [variant: fiery depths] at the bottom of their source. Among all the countless thermal springs in the world, they are especially effective for the health of the sick.

From there they returned to their own settlements.

## CHAPTER XXI. The emperor Maximian won great victories over the Parthians and Persians with the aid of the Goths. Constantine likewise accomplished many notable things with their assistance.

[Col. 1267A]

After this, the emperor Maximian summoned them to serve as auxiliaries of the Romans against the Parthians. Once their auxiliary troops had been supplied, they fought faithfully.

But after Caesar Maximian had almost defeated, with their assistance, Narseus, king of the Persians and grandson of the great Shapur, and had plundered all his wealth, together with his wives and children; after he had defeated Achilles at Alexandria together with Diocletian; and after Maximian Herculius had crushed the Quinquegentians in Africa [Niv.: Quinquangentians; variant: Quinquagintani], the Romans, having obtained peace for the state, began to neglect the Goths.

For previously the Roman army had fought with difficulty against any peoples without them. It is often evident how frequently they were invited to assist, as they were also summoned under Constantine in 407, and took up arms against his relative Licinius. After defeating Licinius and shutting him up in Thessalonica, they killed him, deprived of imperial power, by the sword of the victorious Constantine.

When Constantine was founding a city in his own name, exceedingly famous and a rival [Col. 1267B] of Rome, the Goths also took part in the work. Having made a treaty with the emperor, they supplied him with forty thousand of their men as assistance against various peoples. Their number and their thousands are still designated in the state by the name “Federates.”

At that time they flourished under the rule of their kings Araric and Aoric [variants: Arian and Atric]. After their deaths, Geberich succeeded to the kingship, a man of exceptional courage and nobility.

## CHAPTER XXII. Geberich, king of the Goths, makes war upon Visumar, king of the Vandals, and defeats him. The few Vandals who survive the disaster seek and obtain Pannonia from Constantine as a place to inhabit.

For Geberich, born of his father Helderich, his grandfather Ovida, and his great-grandfather Chivida, equaled the glory of his lineage through illustrious deeds. Wishing immediately to extend the beginnings of his reign among the Vandal people, he marched against their king Visumar, [Col. 1267C] who came from the stock of the Hasdingi, a lineage outstanding among them and indicative of a most warlike race.

As the historian Dexippus reports, the Hasdingi scarcely reached our frontier from the Ocean within a year, because of the immense breadth of the lands. At that time they were living in the place where the Gepids now dwell, beside the rivers Marisia, Miliare, and Gilfil, and the Grissia, which exceeds the aforesaid rivers.

At that time the Goths were to their east, the Marcomanni to their west, the Hermunduri to their north, and the Ister, also called the Danube, to their south.

While the Vandals were dwelling there, King Geberich of the Goths declared war against them on the bank of the aforementioned river Marisia. A long and evenly matched battle was fought there. But soon Wisumar, king of the Vandals, was struck down with a large part of his people.

The outstanding Gothic commander Geberich, having defeated and plundered the Vandals, returned to the places from which he had come.

Then the very few Vandals who had escaped gathered together a force of their unwarlike countrymen and, abandoning their unfortunate homeland, [Col. 1267D] requested Pannonia from the emperor Constantine. Having settled there for approximately forty years [Niv.: sixty years], they served as inhabitants by imperial decree.

Much later they were invited by Stilicho, master of the soldiers, former consul, and patrician, and occupied Gaul. There, while plundering the neighboring peoples, they did not establish very permanent settlements.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning Ermanaric, king of the Goths, who was compared with Alexander the Great because of the many peoples he conquered, and concerning his campaigns and victories against the Heruli, the Veneti, and the Aesti.

After Geberich, king of the Goths, had departed from human affairs, Ermanaric, the most distinguished of the Amali, succeeded him in the kingdom after some time. He subdued many northern and exceedingly warlike [Col. 1268A] peoples [variant: eleven northern peoples] and compelled them to obey his laws.

For this reason some rightly compared him with Alexander the Great. Among those whom he conquered were the Goths, Scythians, Thuidi in Aunxis, Vasinabroncae, Merens, Mordensimni, Caris, Rocas, Tadzans, Athual, Navego, Bubegentae, and Coldas.

Although he was esteemed because of the service of so many peoples, he did not rest until he had slaughtered a large part of the nation of the Heruli, ruled by Alaric, and subjected the remainder to his authority.

According to the historian Ablavius, the Heruli lived beside the Maeotian marshes, in stagnant regions which the Greeks call *helē* (“marshes”). They were called Heruli, a people as swift as it was exceedingly proud. At that time there was no people that did not choose from among them men of light armor for its battle line.

Although their speed was often not overcome by other combatants, it nevertheless yielded to the steadfastness and slowness of the Goths. Fortune brought it about that they too served Ermanaric, king of the Getae, among the other nations.

After the slaughter of the Heruli, Ermanaric [Col. 1268B] likewise took up arms against the Veneti. Although inferior in arms, they relied upon their numbers and at first attempted to resist. But numbers are of no value in war [variant: the multitude of unwarlike men], especially when an armed multitude arrives.

As we began to say at the beginning of our account or catalogue of this people, they arose from one stock and now bear three names: Veneti, Antes, and Sclavi. Although today, through the fault of our sins, they rage everywhere, at that time they all served under the commands of Ermanaric.

He likewise subdued the nation of the Aesti, who occupy the longest shore of the Germanic Ocean. Through his wisdom [variant: wisdom and courage] and strength, he ruled all the nations of Scythia and Germania as though by his own labors.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the accursed origin of the Huns, namely the intercourse of sorceresses with unclean spirits; and concerning the Huns’ campaign against the Scythian Ostrogoths, including the savage and terrifying appearance of the Huns.

[Col. 1268C]

After a short interval of time, as Orosius reports, the nation of the Huns, more savage than every form of ferocity, burst upon the Goths.

We have learned from ancient tradition that they arose in the following manner. Filimer, king of the Goths and son of Gandaric the Great, who held the leadership of the Getae in the fifth place after the departure from the island of Scanzia and had entered the Scythian lands with his people, discovered among his subjects certain magical women whom he himself called *Aliorumnae* in the language of his people [Note: [Col. 1267D] Otherwise *Aliorunas*, who are also now called *Alrunae*, Spanish *bruxas*—witches. B. VULC.].

Suspecting them, he drove them from his midst and, having expelled them far from his army, forced them into the solitude of the land [variant: forced them to wander in the wilderness]. When unclean spirits saw them wandering through the desert and mingled with them in sexual intercourse, they produced this exceedingly savage race.

At first it was small, foul, and meager among the marshes, almost a human race, and known by no speech except one that gave the appearance of human language. Thus created from this stock, the Huns came into the territories of the Goths.

Their [Col. 1268D] savage nation, as the historian Priscus reports, occupied the farther bank of the Maeotian marsh. It knew no occupation except hunting, until, after it had grown into a people, it disturbed the neighboring nations by fraud and plunder.

While the hunters of this people, as is their custom, were searching for game on the farther bank of Maeotis, they noticed a hind suddenly appear before them. Entering the marsh, now advancing and now stopping, it offered itself as a guide to the way.

Following it, the hunters crossed the Maeotian marsh on foot, although they had considered it as impassable as the sea. As soon as the Scythian land appeared to them, unknown as it was, the hind disappeared.

I believe that the spirits from whom they derive their origin brought this about out of hatred for the Scythians. The Huns, who had known absolutely nothing of any other world beyond the Maeotian marsh, were filled with wonder at the land of Scythia. Being astute, they judged that the route [Col. 1269A], previously known to no one of that age, had been divinely shown to them. They returned to their own people, reported what had happened, and praised Scythia.

After persuading their people, they hastened to Scythia by the route they had learned from the hind, their guide. They sacrificed to Victory all those whom they encountered at the entrance to the Scythian lands and subdued the rest under their rule.

For as soon as they had crossed that vast marsh, they immediately swept away, like a whirlwind of nations, the Alipzuros, Alcidzuros, Itamaros, Tuncassos, and Boiscos [Note: [Col. 1269D] Variants: Alpidzyros, Aiobridzuros, Itimaros, Tuncarcer, and Bairchos], who occupied the bank of that part of Scythia.

They also subdued the Alans, who were their equals in battle but differed from them in food, civilization, and appearance, wearing them down through frequent combat. Those whom they perhaps could not overcome in war, they drove to flight by inflicting extreme terror through the horror of their appearance.

Their aspect was terrifying in its blackness, like a shapeless lump, if one may call it that, rather than a face, with more points than eyes. Their fierce gaze revealed the confidence of their spirits. They even attacked their own children on the first day of their birth.

For male infants [Col. 1269B] they cut their cheeks with iron, so that before they could receive the nourishment of milk they would be forced to endure wounds. Thus they grow old without beards and are unbeautiful youths, because the face furrowed by iron removes the proper beauty of hair through its scars.

They are small in stature, but shrewd, quick in movement, and exceedingly ready for riding; broad-shouldered and prepared for bows and arrows; firm-necked and always proudly upright.

They live under human form with the savagery of beasts.

When the Getae saw this exceedingly swift people, the ravager of many nations, they were terrified and deliberated with their king how they might withdraw from such an enemy.

For Ermanaric, king of the Goths, although, as we have related above, he had triumphed over many peoples, was deceived on the occasion of the Huns’ arrival by the faithless nation of the Roxolani, who at that time rendered him service among the other peoples.

When the king, enraged over a woman named Sanielh from that nation because of her husband’s treacherous [Col. 1269C] departure, ordered her to be tied to wild horses and torn apart by their racing in different directions, her brothers Sarus and Ammius, seeking to avenge the death of their sister, attacked Ermanaric’s side with a sword. Wounded by this blow, he endured a sickly life in bodily weakness.

Taking advantage of his impaired condition, Balamir, king of the Huns, set his forces in motion against the Ostrogoths. The Visigoths had already withdrawn from their association, which they had formerly maintained united among themselves.

Meanwhile, Ermanaric, unable to endure either the pain of his wound or the incursions of the Huns, died, an old man full of days, in the one hundred and tenth year of his life.

His death gave the Huns the opportunity to prevail over those Goths whom we said lived in the eastern region and were called Ostrogoths.

## CHAPTER XXV. After the Ostrogoths had been defeated by the Vandals, the Visigoths seek and obtain Moesia as a place to inhabit from the emperor Valens. Wishing to become Christians, they receive Arian preachers from Valens, who infect them with the poison of his perfidy.

[Col. 1290D]

The Visigoths—that is, the other allies of the Goths and inhabitants of the western land—were terrified by fear of their kinsmen and were uncertain what decision to make concerning themselves because of the nation of the Huns.

After long deliberation, they finally agreed and sent ambassadors to Romania, to the emperor Valens, brother of the elder emperor Valentinian. They asked him to grant them a part of Thrace or Moesia for cultivation, promising that they would live under his laws and submit to his commands.

To make their pledge more credible, they promised that, if he provided teachers in their own language, they would become Christians.

When Valens learned this, he immediately agreed with joy to what they had willingly requested. He received the Getae into the regions of Moesia and established them as a kind of wall of his kingdom against the other peoples.

Since the emperor Valens was then wounded by the [Col. 1270A] perfidy of the Arians and had closed all the churches of our confession, he sent preachers who supported his own party. When these arrived among the ignorant and inexperienced people, they immediately poured out upon them the poison of their perfidy.

Thus the Visigoths were made Arians rather than Christians by the emperor Valens. Thereafter they evangelized both the Ostrogoths and the Gepids, their kinsmen, through the grace of affection, teaching them the observance of this perfidy and inviting every people of their language everywhere to the worship of this sect.

They too, as has been said, crossed the Danube and, with the emperor’s permission, settled in Dacia Ripensis, Moesia, and Thrace.

## CHAPTER XXVI. The Visigoths, subjects of the Romans, oppressed by severe famine and treated most harshly by the Roman commanders, assert their freedom and occupy Thrace and Dacia Ripensis. The emperor Valens, who had arranged for them to be infected with Arian perfidy, is burned by them as divine vengeance.

As usually happens to peoples not yet firmly established in a place [Col. 1270B], famine befell these nations. Their leading men and commanders, who ruled them in place of kings—Fridigern, Alatheus, and Safrach—began to grieve over the army’s scarcity and sought supplies through trade from Lupicinus and Maximus, the Roman commanders.

But what does the accursed hunger for gold not compel people to accept?
