Driven by greed, the commanders began to sell them not only the flesh of sheep and oxen, but also the carcasses of dogs and unclean animals, and to give them anything at all at a great price. They bartered a single slave for one loaf of bread or ten pounds of meat.

When slaves and household goods were already exhausted, the avaricious merchant demanded their children under the necessity of sustenance [variant: the necessity of famine]. Their parents indeed did no differently: seeking to preserve the lives of their children, they judged it better for freedom to perish than for life to perish, and that a person should be sold so that he might be mercifully fed rather than preserved only to die.

At that sorrowful time it happened that Lupicinus, the Roman commander, invited Fridigern, the Gothic [Col. 1270C] prince, to a banquet and, as the outcome later showed, plotted deception against him.

Fridigern, unaware of the plot, came to the banquet with a small retinue. While dining inside the headquarters, he heard the cries of the miserable men who were dying. Meanwhile, in another part, his companions had been shut up while the commander’s soldiers attempted to slaughter them on his orders. The harshly uttered voices of the dying were already resounding in suspicious ears.

Fridigern immediately recognized the treachery. Drawing his sword at the banquet, he escaped with great daring and speed, rescued his companions from the impending death, and incited them to kill the Romans.

Seizing this welcome opportunity, these bravest men chose to perish in battle rather than in famine, and immediately armed themselves for the slaughter of the commanders Lupicinus and Maximus.

That day deprived the Goths of famine and the Romans of security. The Goths began, not as newcomers and strangers but as citizens and masters, to give orders to the possessors and to hold all the northern regions as their own right as far as the [Col. 1270D] Danube.

When the emperor Valens learned this at Antioch, he immediately set out with an armed army toward the regions of Thrace. There a lamentable battle was fought, and the Goths were victorious.

The emperor himself, wounded, fled to a farmhouse near Hadrianopolis. The Goths did not know that the emperor was hiding in such a wretched hut. When the fire, as often happens, was raging because an enemy had set it beneath the building, he was burned with all the splendor of royalty—plainly as though by the judgment of God.

For he was burned by those whom he himself had turned away from the true faith into perfidy when they sought faith from him, and he had twisted the fire of charity into the fire of Gehenna.

At that time the Visigoths, after the glory of so great a victory, began to inhabit Thrace and Dacia Ripensis as though they had gained possession of their native soil.

## CHAPTER XXVII. While the emperor Theodosius was plotting the destruction of the Visigoths, they withdraw, during his illness, to plunder Thessaly, Epirus, Achaia, and Pannonia. The emperor Gratian makes a treaty with them, which Theodosius also confirms.

[Col. 1271A]

The emperor Gratian appointed Theodosius, chosen from Spain, to the eastern imperial office in place of his uncle Valens. As military discipline was soon restored to a better condition and the cowardice and negligence of the former rulers were removed, the Goths became afraid when they perceived this.

For the emperor was altogether distinguished in intellect, courage, and judgment. Through the severity of his commands, together with his generosity and graciousness, he encouraged the weakened army to brave deeds.

When the soldiers gained confidence after the change to a better emperor, they attempted to attack the Goths and drove them from the borders of Thrace. But because the emperor Theodosius was then almost reduced to despair by severe illness, the Goths were again given courage.

After dividing his army, Fridigern withdrew to plunder Thessaly, Epirus, and Achaia, while Alatheus and Safrach with the remaining forces proceeded toward Pannonia.

When the emperor Gratian, who had withdrawn from Rome into Gaul because of the invasion of the [Col. 1271B] Vandals, learned this, and saw that the Goths were becoming more savage as Theodosius succumbed to a fatal illness, he immediately gathered an army and came against them.

Yet he did not rely upon arms. He intended to conquer them through favor and gifts, granting them peace and provisions, and he made a treaty with them [variant: he made treaties with them].

When the emperor Theodosius recovered afterward and learned that Gratian had made a treaty with the Goths and Romans—the very treaty he himself had desired—he received the news with the greatest gratitude and likewise maintained this peace.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Atanaric, king of the Visigoths and successor of Fridigern, is summoned to Constantinople by the emperor Theodosius and treated with great honor; he dies there. Also concerning the Federates and the victory won with Visigothic assistance by Theodosius against the usurper Eugenius, who had occupied Gaul.

Theodosius also won over King Atanaric, who had succeeded Fridigern [Col. 1271C], by giving him gifts and treating him with his characteristic kindness. He invited him to come to him at Constantinople.

Atanaric readily agreed, entered the royal city, and marveled. “Behold,” he said, “I see what I often heard about without believing: the fame of so great a city.” Turning his eyes here and there, he admired now the situation of the city and the movement of its ships, now its splendid walls, and its peoples of different nations, as though water were springing from different quarters from one fountain.

Then, observing the soldiers drawn up in order, he said: “Without doubt, the emperor is a god upon earth, and whoever moves his hand against him becomes guilty of his own blood.”

Thus, sustained by such admiration and by even greater honor from the emperor, he departed this life a few months later. The emperor, honoring him through affection almost more in death than in life, committed him to a fitting burial and himself went before his bier in the funeral procession [Note: [Col. 1271D] From this infer the ancient custom. Formerly the crowd and procession went before the funeral, as is clear from Ammianus Marcellinus, p. 440. JURET.].

After Atanaric’s death, the entire army remained in the service of the emperor Theodosius and, submitting itself to Roman rule, formed one body with the Roman army. Those thousands of Federates formerly established under the emperor Constantine were renewed, and these men too were called Federates.

From among them the emperor led more than twenty thousand armed men, faithful and friendly to him, against the usurper Eugenius, who had occupied Gaul after killing Gratian. He gained victory over that usurper and exacted vengeance.

## CHAPTER XXIX. After the customary gifts were withheld from the Visigoths by the sons of Theodosius, they grow weary of inactivity, choose Alaric as their king, and invade Italy.

After Theodosius, a lover of peace and of the Gothic people, had departed from human affairs, [Col. 1272A] his sons began to destroy both empires through luxurious living and to withhold the customary gifts from their auxiliaries, that is, the Goths.

Soon the Goths became disgusted with them. Fearing that their strength might be weakened by prolonged peace, they appointed Alaric as king over themselves. After the Amali, he possessed the second-highest nobility, and his remarkable origin was from the family of the Balthi. Because of his courage, he had long before received among his people the name *Baltha*, that is, “the bold.”

As soon as the aforementioned Alaric had been made king, he deliberated with his people and persuaded them that it was better to seek kingdoms through their own labor than to remain subject to others through idleness.

Taking an army, he entered Italy through Pannonia, during the consulships of Stilicho and Aurelianus, and through Firmium [perhaps Sirmium], on the right side, as though it were empty of men.

With no one at all resisting him, he reached the bridge of Condinianus, which was three miles from the royal city of Ravenna.

This city lies among marshes and the sea, and among the waters of the Po. It has only one point of access. Long ago, as our ancestors relate, its inhabitants were called Eneti, that is, “praiseworthy.”

It is situated in the bosom of the Roman kingdom upon [Col. 1272B] the Ionian Sea and is enclosed, like an island [perhaps “the island should be added”], by the overflow of the surrounding waters.

To the east it has the sea. Anyone who sails there in a straight course from Corcyra and the regions of Hellas has on his right first Epirus, then Dalmatia, Liburnia, and Istria, and thus passes by Venice with a small vessel.

To the west it has marshes, through which a single extremely narrow entrance remains open like a gate. On the northern side it has an arm of the Po called the Fossa Asconis.

To the south is the Po itself, which they call the king of rivers, with the name Eridanus. The emperor Augustus led it through a very deep channel. One-seventh of its riverbed flows through the middle of the city, and at its mouths it provides a most pleasant harbor.

According to Dio, it was once believed capable of receiving a fleet of 240 ships in a very safe anchorage. Now, as Fabius says, what was once a harbor displays very spacious gardens full of trees—not trees from which sails hang, but trees bearing fruit.

The city itself [Col. 1272C] boasts three names and rejoices in a triple arrangement: first Ravenna, last Classis, and in the middle Caesarea [variant: Cessuria], between the city and the sea, full of softness, fortified with sand, and suitable for transport.

## CHAPTER XXX

Alaric defeats Stilicho, who had unexpectedly attacked the Goths in war; he devastates Italy and plunders Rome. Then, while planning to cross into Africa, he dies with his spoils. The Visigoths bury Alaric in the bed of the river Busentinus by a remarkable stratagem.

But when the army of the Visigoths had arrived at that city and had sent an embassy to the emperor Honorius, who was inside it, proposing that, if he allowed the Goths to settle peacefully in Italy, they should live with the Roman people so that both might be regarded as one nation—and, if not, that in war either side should drive out the other as far as it was able, with the victor then safely exercising rule—Emperor Honorius, fearing both proposals, took counsel with his senate [Col. 1272D] and deliberated how he might expel them beyond the Italian frontiers.

At last the following opinion prevailed: Alaric, with his people, should claim as their own homes the distant provinces—that is, Gaul and Spain—which Honorius had already almost lost and which the invasion of Gizeric, king of the Vandals, was ravaging, if he could do so; and this grant was to be confirmed by a sacred decree. The Goths agreed to this arrangement and set out for the homeland assigned to them.

After their departure, when no further harm had been inflicted in Italy, Stilicho, patrician and father-in-law of the emperor Honorius—for he had married both of his daughters, Mary and Hermant(h)ia [al. Thermantia], whom the emperor had joined to him one after the other, and whom God commanded to depart this life both virgins and untouched—this Stilicho, then, deceitfully approached the city of Pollentia, situated in the Cottian Alps [Col. 1273A]. The Goths suspected no evil, but he rushed into battle, bringing ruin upon all Italy and disgrace upon himself.

When the Goths suddenly saw him, they were initially terrified; but soon recovering their courage and rousing one another with exhortations, as was their custom, they routed almost Stilicho’s entire army and cut it down almost to annihilation. Then, abandoning the route which they had undertaken in their furious spirit, they turned back into Liguria, through which they had already passed. Having taken possession of his plunder and spoils, they devastated Emilia in like manner; and running along the Flaminian road between Picenum and Tuscia as far as the city of Rome, they seized as plunder whatever lay between the two regions.

At last, after entering Rome, they plundered it only at Alaric’s command; they did not, however, as other peoples are accustomed to do, set it on fire, nor did they allow any injury whatsoever to be inflicted upon holy places. From there they departed and, after inflicting similar devastation through Campania and Lucania, reached Bruttium. Remaining there for a long time, they planned to cross to Sicily and from there to Africa.

The region of Bruttium lies in the extreme southern part of Italy. One corner of it forms the beginning of the Apennine mountain, and, extending like a tongue, separates the Adriatic Sea from the Tyrrhenian waters; it once took its name from the queen Bruttia [Col. 1273B].

There, then, Alaric, king of the Visigoths, arrived with the wealth of all Italy that he had seized as plunder. As has been said, he intended from there to cross through Sicily into Africa, a peaceful homeland. But since whatever a human being plans cannot be accomplished freely without God’s will, that terrifying strait submerged several ships and threw many more into confusion [411]. Repelled by this disaster, while Alaric was deliberating with himself what he should do, he was suddenly overtaken by an untimely death and departed from human affairs.

Mourning him with extraordinary devotion, they diverted the river Barentinus [al. Busentinus] from its channel near the city of Consentia. This river, flowing down from the foot of the mountain beside the city, runs with health-giving water. In the middle of its channel, therefore, after gathering a crowd of captives, they dug a place for the burial. In the hollow of the excavation they buried Alaric with many riches [Col. 1273C]; then, restoring the waters to their channel so that no one might ever recognize the place, they killed all the diggers.

## CHAPTER XXXI

Athaulf, Alaric’s successor, plunders Italy. He marries Placidia, the sister of Emperor Honorius. From Italy he crosses into Gaul to expel the Vandals and Alans from there. From there he goes into Spain, where he is killed. Regeric, the third king of the Visigoths, is likewise killed.

When Alaric the Visigoth had died, they entrusted the kingdom to his kinsman Athaulf, distinguished in appearance and mind. Although he was not particularly tall in stature, he was well formed and handsome in body and face.

Having assumed the kingdom, he returned once more toward Rome and, like a swarm of locusts, stripped away whatever had initially remained. He deprived Italy not only of private wealth but also of public property, since the emperor Honorius was unable to resist him. He also carried away from the city as a captive Placidia, the emperor Theodosius’ daughter by another wife [Col. 1273D].

Yet, considering her noble birth, her beauty, and the integrity of her chastity, he lawfully joined her to himself in marriage at the city of Forum Livii [al. Forum Cornelii] in Emilia. He did this so that, when the peoples learned of the alliance, they might be more effectively terrified, as though the Roman state had been united with the Goths. He then left Augustus Honorius, although exhausted of resources, as a kinsman toward whom he nevertheless showed gratitude, and proceeded toward Gaul.

When he arrived there, the neighboring peoples, terrified, began to remain within their own boundaries—those who had previously harassed Gaul cruelly, both the Franks and the Burgundians. The Vandals and Alans, whom we mentioned above, had settled in both Pannonias with permission from the Roman authorities. Since they did not think it safe to remain there or to return, out of fear of the Goths, they crossed into Gaul.

But soon, fleeing from Gaul, which they had occupied not long before, they shut themselves up in Spain. They still remembered, from the reports of their ancestors, what harm Geberic, king of the Goths, had once inflicted upon their people [Col. 1274A] and how by his valor he had driven them from their ancestral soil.

Thus, by this turn of events, Gaul lay open to the advancing Athaulf. After securing the Gothic kingdom in Gaul, he began to grieve over the plight of the Spaniards and, intending to rescue them from the attacks of the Vandals, entered inner Spain through Barcelona with a select group of loyal men and an unwarlike populace. There he often fought the Vandals; in the third year after he had subdued Gaul and Spain, he died, pierced by the sword of Vernulf, whose stature he had been accustomed to mock.

After his death Regeric was established as king; but he too was killed through the treachery of his own people and quickly surrendered life together with the kingdom.

## CHAPTER XXXII

Valia, the fourth king of the Visigoths, makes peace with Emperor Honorius and restores Placidia to the Romans. Also concerning Constantine, Constans, Jovinus, and Sebastian, the invaders of Gaul.

[Col. 1274B]

Next Valia was established as the fourth king after Alaric, a man exceedingly severe and prudent. Against him the emperor Honorius sent Constantine [al. Constantius], a man distinguished by military ability and celebrated in many battles, with an army. He feared that Constantine might disrupt the treaty previously made with Athaulf and again contrive some threat against the state, after neighboring peoples had been repulsed. At the same time, he desired to free his sister Placidia from the disgrace of subjection.

He therefore made an agreement with Constantine that, whether by war or peace, or by whatever means he could, Constantine should recall her to his kingdom and join her to himself in marriage. With this agreement Constantine, exultant and accompanied by a large armed force, and almost equipped with royal splendor, set out for Spain.

King Valia of the Goths met him at the Pyrenean passes with no less preparation. There, after both sides had sent embassies, they reached the following agreement: Valia would return Placidia, the emperor’s sister, and would not refuse his support to the Roman state whenever necessity required it.

At that time a certain Constantine had invaded the imperial power in Gaul [Col. 1274C] and had made his son Constans, formerly a monk, Caesar. But he did not hold the usurped kingdom long: soon, after the Goths and Romans had joined forces, he himself was killed at Arles, while his son was killed at Vienne.

After them Jovinus and Sebastian, likewise supposing that they could seize the state with equal rashness, perished by an equal fate.

In the twelfth year of Valia’s reign, when, after Pannonia had been invaded almost fifty years earlier, the Huns were expelled from it by the Romans and Goths, Valia saw the Vandals in his own territories—that is, on Spanish soil—having boldly emerged from the interior regions of Gaul [al. Galicia], where Athaulf had once driven them. He saw them laying everything waste in plunder at the time when Hierius and Ardaburius were consuls. Without delay he moved his army against them.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

The succession of the Vandal kings in Africa for nearly one hundred years, and how Belisarius triumphed after bringing Gelimer to Constantinople, and Africa was again added to the Roman Empire. Also concerning the death of Valia.

[Col. 1274D]

But Gizeric, king of the Vandals, was already being invited to Africa by Boniface, who, having fallen into disfavor with the emperor Valentinian, could avenge himself in no other way than by harming the state.

Thus, at his own request, he invited them and transported them across the narrow passage called the Strait of Gibraltar, which separates Africa from Spain by scarcely seven miles, and through whose mouth the waters of the Tyrrhenian Sea drive the ocean tide.

Gizeric was already well known in the city for the disaster he had inflicted upon the Romans. He was of moderate stature, lame from a fall from a horse, deep in character, sparing in speech [al. shrewd], contemptuous of luxury, turbulent in anger, greedy for possessions, exceedingly skilled in stirring up peoples, and ready to sow the seeds of conflict and mingle hatreds.

Such was the man who, invited by Boniface’s appeals, as we have said, entered the African state. There, after reigning for a long time, as is said, by authority received from the Divinity [Col. 1275A], he summoned an assembly of his sons before his death and arranged that there should be no dissension among them over the pursuit of the kingdom. Instead, each in his own order and rank, whichever survived the others would become the next successor to his elder brother, and then the brother younger than he would succeed him.

Observing this arrangement over many years, they possessed the kingdom successfully. They were not, as commonly happens among other peoples, disfigured by civil war; each one in turn assumed the kingdom and ruled the peoples in peace.

Their order and succession was as follows: first Gizeric, the father and master; next Huneric; third Gundamund; fourth Transamund; fifth Hilderic. Gelimer, to the ruin of his people, expelled and killed Hilderic, forgetting the commands of his ancestor, and usurped the tyranny. But what he had done did not go unpunished.

For the vengeance of the emperor Justinian appeared against him. Brought to Constantinople with his entire family and with the wealth upon which he had preyed like a brigand, by the most illustrious Belisarius, master of the soldiers in the East, ordinary consul, and patrician, he became a great spectacle for the people in the circus. When he saw himself cast down from royal eminence and reduced to the private life to which he had refused to submit, he died in belated regret for himself [Col. 1275B].

Thus Africa, which in the division of the earth is described as the third part of the world, was rescued after almost a hundred years from the Vandal yoke and restored to the freedom of Roman rule. The hand of a foreign people had once torn it away from the body of the Roman state under incompetent masters and faithless commanders; now, restored by a diligent master and faithful leader, it rejoices together with us even today.

Although after this it lamented having been somewhat weakened by civil war and the treachery of the Moors, nevertheless the triumph granted to it by God through the emperor Justinian carried what it had begun through to completion.

But why should we speak of matters that the subject does not require? Let us return to our purpose.

King Valia of the Goths was so fierce, with his own forces, against the Vandals that he would even have pursued them into Africa, had not the disaster that had once befallen Alaric as he was heading toward Africa [Col. 1275C] recalled him.

Having become renowned in Spain and achieved a bloodless victory, he returned to Toulouse. After the enemies had been expelled, he left several provinces to the Roman Empire, as he had promised. Then, when an adverse illness came upon him after a long period, he departed from human affairs.

This occurred at the time when Berimund [al. Beremuth], son of Torismund—whom we mentioned above in the catalogue of the Amal family—migrated with his son Witiric from the Ostrogoths, who were still subject to the oppression of the Huns in the land of Scythia, to the kingdom of the Visigoths.

He was conscious of his valor and noble birth, believing that leadership would more readily be transferred to him by his relatives, since it was clear that he was the heir of many kings. For who would doubt an Amal, if the opportunity for choosing arose?

Yet he himself did not wish to reveal too openly who he was. After Valia’s death, they appointed Theoderic as Valia’s successor. Berimund came to him and, possessing great strength of character, discreetly concealed the exceptional greatness of his lineage [Col. 1275D], knowing that those born from royal stock are always objects of suspicion to reigning monarchs.

He therefore allowed himself to remain unknown, lest he cause the arrangements that had to be made to become confused. King Theoderic received him and his son with the greatest honor, so that he excluded him neither from his counsel nor from his table—not so much because of the nobility of his birth, which he did not know, as because of his courage and the strength of his people, which he could not conceal.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

Theoderic, the fifth king of the Visigoths. The Romans, with Hunnic auxiliaries, lead an army against him after breaking the peace. Treaties are strengthened. Attila is pacified. Also concerning Attila’s court.

After Valia’s death, to repeat what we said above, Theoderic succeeded to the kingdom. Valia had brought little good fortune to Gaul, but Theoderic was most prosperous and fortunate: a man of the greatest moderation, abundant in manly strength of mind and body [Col. 1276A; al. usefulness].

When Theodosius and Festus were consuls, the Romans, having broken the peace and joined Hunnic auxiliaries to themselves, took up arms against the Goths in Gaul. The hand of the federated Goths had disturbed them, for it had entered into a treaty with the count Caina at Constantinople [al. had advanced].

The patrician Aetius was then in command of the soldiers. He was descended from the stock of the bravest Moesians, born in the city of Dorostena to his father Gaudentius. He endured military labors and was uniquely born for the Roman state; by immense slaughter he had compelled the pride of the Suebi and the barbarism of the Franks to serve the Roman Empire.

With the Hunnic auxiliaries also led by Litorius, the Roman army advanced in battle order against the Goths. For a long time both sides drew up their lines; since both were brave and neither was stronger, they exchanged right hands and returned to their former harmony. After the treaty had been confirmed and each side had secured a faithful peace, both withdrew.

By this agreement Attila, lord of all the Huns and almost the sole ruler in the world of nearly all the peoples of Scythia, was pacified. He was renowned among all peoples with a fame remarkable for its brilliance [Col. 1276B]. Priscus, sent to him as an ambassador by the younger Theodosius, reports the following among other things.

After crossing great rivers—the Tysia, the Tibisia, and the Dricca—we came to the place where, long ago, Vidicula [al. Vidogoia], the bravest of the Goths, fell through the treachery of the Sarmatians. From there we approached not far away a village in which King Attila was staying—a village, I say, of immense size, resembling a great city. There we found wooden walls constructed of polished planks, whose joints imitated such solidity that it was scarcely possible for an attentive observer to detect the joining of the boards.

One might see dining halls extending in a broad circuit and porticoes arranged with every kind of splendor. The courtyard, moreover, was enclosed by a vast perimeter, so that its very size displayed a royal palace. These were the residences of King Attila, who held the whole barbarian world; he preferred these dwellings to captured cities.

## CHAPTER XXXV

Concerning Attila, king of the Huns: his father and brothers, his stature, appearance, and character. Also concerning the sword of Mars, which he appropriated. An important passage from the historian Priscus.

[Col. 1276C]

Attila was born from his father Mundzuccus. His brothers were Octar and Roas, who are said to have held the kingdom of the Huns before Attila, although not over all of them.

After their deaths, Attila succeeded to the kingdom of the Huns together with his brother Bleda [al. Buda; Prosper: Budam]. To make himself equal to the expedition he was preparing, he sought an increase of strength through fratricide, extending his designs to the destruction of all his relatives.

But, though he grew by this detestable remedy, justice weighing the matter against him, he found a hideous end for his cruelty. After his brother Bleda [al. Buda], who had ruled a large part of the Huns, had been killed by treachery, Attila subjected the entire people to himself. Gathering also the multitude of other nations that he then held under his authority, he greatly desired to subjugate the foremost peoples of the world, the Romans [Col. 1276D] and the Visigoths.

His army was said to number nearly five hundred thousand men. He was born into the world to shake the nations, the terror of all lands; by some fortune or other he frightened everyone, for a terrifying opinion of him had spread everywhere.

He was proud in his gait, turning his eyes this way and that, so that even in the movement of his body the power of his arrogance was apparent. He loved wars, although he himself exercised restraint in combat; he was exceedingly strong in counsel, lenient toward those who pleaded with him, and gracious toward those once admitted to his allegiance.

He was short in stature, broad-chested, large-headed, small-eyed, scantily bearded and sprinkled with gray, flat-nosed, and ugly in complexion, displaying the marks of his origin.

Although he was by nature such a man that he always placed great confidence in himself, the discovery of the sword of Mars nevertheless added to his confidence. This sword had always been regarded as sacred among the kings of the Scythians.

The historian Priscus relates that it was discovered on the following occasion:

“A certain shepherd,” he says, “noticed that one heifer of the herd was limping, but could find no cause for so great a wound. Anxiously following the traces of blood, he eventually came upon a sword [Col. 1277A] which the heifer, carelessly grazing the grass, had stepped upon. He immediately dug it up and carried it to Attila.

“Attila rejoiced at the gift. Being magnanimous, he judged that he had been appointed ruler of the whole world and that, through the sword of Mars, power over wars had been granted to him.”

## CHAPTER XXXVI

Attila, by his own nature prepared to devastate the world, is urged to do so by Gizeric, king of the Vandals, through many gifts. He attempts by every means to sow discord between the Romans and Goths, but in vain. The letter of Emperor Valentinian to the Visigoths and their reply.

Learning that Attila’s mind was prepared for the devastation of the world, Gizeric, king of the Vandals, whom we mentioned shortly before, drove him through many gifts into war against the Visigoths. He feared that Theoderic, king of the Visigoths, would avenge the injury done to his daughter.

She had been married to Huneric, Gizeric’s son, and at first had rejoiced in so great a marriage [Col. 1277B]. But afterward, since Huneric was savage even toward his own children, merely suspecting that she had prepared poison for him, he mutilated her by cutting off her nose and ears, stripped her of her natural beauty, and sent her back to her father in Gaul. Thus he intended her always to present the shameful spectacle of a pitiable funeral and, by a cruelty that would move even outsiders, to obtain her father’s vengeance more effectively.

Attila, therefore, bringing forth the wars he had long conceived through Gizeric’s bribery, sent ambassadors to the emperor Valentinian in Italy, sowing discord between the Goths and Romans. Those whom he could not shake by battle, he sought to destroy through internal hatred.

He asserted that he was in no way violating his friendship with the Roman state, but that his conflict was with Theoderic, king of the Visigoths, and that he would gladly wish him to be received. He filled the rest of the letter with the customary flattering greetings of letters, striving to give credibility to his falsehood.

In the same manner he sent a written message to Theoderic, king of the Visigoths, urging him to withdraw from the alliance with the Romans and to recall the battles that had recently been stirred up against him with excessive ferocity [Col. 1277C].

Before he waged war, this subtle man fought by cunning. Then Emperor Valentinian sent an embassy to the Visigoths and their king Theoderic in the following words:

> “It is the mark of your prudence, bravest of peoples, to conspire against the tyrant of the City [al. the world], who desires to impose universal servitude, who does not seek causes for war but considers whatever he has done legitimate. He measures his ambition by his arm; through arrogance he satisfies his license. Disregarding right and justice, he shows himself the enemy of all nature. Indeed, he deserves hatred who proves himself the common enemy of all.
>
> “Recall, I beg you, what certainly cannot be forgotten. The calamity wrought by the Huns has been spread abroad; but what he seriously pursues, he pursues by ambush. Therefore, leaving ourselves aside, can you endure this arrogance without avenging it? You who are powerful in arms, favor your own grievances and join your common hands. Help the state, of which you are a member. Ask the enemy’s plans how greatly our alliance should be desired [Col. 1277D] and embraced.”

Through these and similar words, Valentinian’s ambassadors moved King Theoderic. He replied:

> “You have what you desire, Romans: you have made Attila our enemy as well. We shall follow him wherever he summons us. Although he swells with pride over victories against various arrogant peoples, the Goths nevertheless know how to fight the arrogant. I would call no war difficult except one whose cause is weak; for nothing grievous terrifies the man whom majesty favors.”

The duke’s companions applauded this reply, and the joyful populace followed it. Everyone desired the battle; the Huns were already eagerly awaited as enemies.

King Theoderic of the Visigoths therefore led out an innumerable multitude [Col. 1278A]. He left four sons at home—Frideric, Turic, Rotemer, and Himmerit—and took with him only Thorismund and Theoderic, his elder sons, as companions in the struggle. Fortunate is the campaign that has the pleasant fellowship of auxiliaries and the support of those who are glad to undergo the dangers themselves together.

On the Roman side, the foresight of the patrician Aetius, upon whom the state of the Western region then depended, was equally great. He gathered warriors from every direction and met the fierce and endless multitude with a force that was not inferior [414].

His auxiliaries included Franks, Sarmatians, Armoricians, Litians, Burgundians, Saxons, Riparians, and Ibriones—formerly Roman soldiers, but by then enrolled among the auxiliaries—as well as several other Celtic or Germanic nations.

The two sides therefore met on the Catalaunian Plains, also called the Maurician Plains, extending for 100 leagues [Note: [Col. 1277D] “Leuga” is a word of the Gauls and purely Frankish, as is clear from St. Jerome on Joel, Paul the Deacon, book XV; Ammianus Marcellinus, book XV, p. 68, and book XVI, p. 91; from the laws of the Bavarians; and from Rutello, book II of the Itinerary. For just as the Romans used miles, so the Gauls were accustomed to measure by leagues. Juret.], as the Gauls call them, in length and 70 in breadth. A Gallic league is measured as 1,500 paces.

Thus that region became the field of an innumerable multitude of peoples [Col. 1278B]. Both armies of the greatest strength drew up their lines. Nothing was done by stealth; they fought in open battle.

What worthy cause could be found for the movements of so many peoples? What hatred had animated all of them against one another and armed them? It was proved that the human race lives under kings, since the mad impulse of one man’s mind brought about the slaughter of peoples, and by the will of an arrogant king what nature had produced over so many ages was cast down in a moment.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

Concerning the events that occurred amid the movements of the armies themselves before the battle was joined between the Romans and Huns.

Before we recount the order of the battle itself, it seems necessary to state what occurred during the movements of the armies, since the battle was as complicated and perplexing as it was famous.

Sangiban, king of the Alans, terrified by fear of what was to come, promised to surrender himself to Attila [Col. 1278C] and to transfer the Gallic city of Aureliana, where he was then stationed, under Attila’s authority.

When Theoderic and Aetius learned this, they fortified the same city with great ramparts before Attila’s arrival. They kept Sangiban under suspicion and placed him, together with his own people, in the midst of their auxiliaries.

King Attila of the Huns, therefore, struck by this event, lost confidence in his forces and feared to enter the conflict. Turning over flight within himself—more grievous than death itself—he decided to inquire into the future through haruspices.

As usual, they examined now the entrails of animals, now certain veins in scraped bones, and announced ill omens to the Huns. Yet they predicted this small consolation: that the supreme leader of the enemy would die, and that, although victory would remain behind, he would stain his triumph by his own death.

Since Attila considered Aetius, who opposed his designs, deserving of death even at the cost of his own destruction, he was troubled by such omens. Being, as he was, an expert in military counsels, he began the battle hesitantly at about the ninth hour of the day, so that, if matters did not go well, the approaching night [Col. 1278D] might come to his aid.

The two sides met, as we have said, on the Catalaunian Plains.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

The position of the place where the battle between the Romans and Huns was fought on the Catalaunian Plains, and a description of both armies.

The site rose in a sloping swelling, growing upward in the form of a hill. Since both armies desired to gain it, because the advantage of the location would confer no small benefit, the Huns with their forces occupied the right side, while the Romans and Visigoths with their auxiliaries occupied the left.

After abandoning the contest for the crest of its summit, Theoderic held the right wing with the Visigoths; Aetius held the left with the Romans [Col. 1279A]. They placed in the center Sangiban, whom we mentioned above as commanding the Alans, taking the military precaution of enclosing him with a crowd of loyal men, since they had less confidence in his intentions. The necessity of fighting is readily accepted by the man for whom the possibility of flight has been made difficult.

The Hunnic line, by contrast, was arranged so that Attila and his bravest men were placed in the center. By this arrangement the king was looking after himself, so that, positioned among the strength of his own nation, he might be protected from the imminent danger.

Various peoples and different nations whom he had subjected to his authority surrounded his wings. Among them the army of the Ostrogoths stood out, led by the brothers Walamir, Theodemir, and Widimir—men more noble even than the king whom they then served, because the power of the Amal lineage ennobled them.

There was also, with an innumerable host of Gepids, that most brave and famous king Ardaric, who, because of his excessive loyalty toward Attila, took part in his counsels. Attila, recognizing his intelligence [Col. 1279B], loved him and Walamir, king of the Ostrogoths, above the other petty kings.

Walamir was secretive, gracious in speech, and ignorant of deceit. Ardaric, as we have said, was renowned for loyalty and counsel. Against their Visigothic kinsmen, Attila could reasonably trust such men as fighters [Niv. “about to fight”].

As for the remaining multitude—if it is permissible to say so—of kings and leaders of various nations, they attended Attila’s nod like attendants. Wherever he signaled with his eyes, each one stood by without a murmur, in fear and trembling, or carried out whatever had been ordered.

But Attila alone, king of all the kings, was concerned for everyone and above everyone else.

The struggle therefore began over the advantage of the location just mentioned. Attila sent his men to seize the summit of the hill, but Thorismund and Aetius forestalled him. They struggled up the heights of the hill and gained the upper position; coming down upon the Huns, they easily threw them into confusion through the advantage of the ground.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

Attila’s speech to the Huns, exhorting them to undertake battle against the Romans.

[Col. 1279C]

When Attila saw that his army had been thrown into confusion by the preceding event, he judged that it had to be strengthened by an address delivered on the spot:

> “After victories over so many nations, after the world has been subdued, if you were to stand still, I would consider it foolish to sharpen you with words as though you were ignorant of war [415]. Let a new commander or an inexperienced army seek such treatment. It is not right for me to say anything commonplace, nor is it fitting for you to hear it.
>
> “What else are you accustomed to do but fight? What is sweeter to the brave than to seek vengeance by hand? Nature has granted a great gift: the ability to satisfy the spirit with revenge.
>
> “Let us therefore attack the enemy eagerly; those who bring on war are always the bolder. Despise the discordant nations joined together. It is a sign of fear to be defended by an alliance.
>
> “Look: even before the attack they are already being driven by terror. They seek high ground, seize mounds, and, in late regret, demand fortifications in the open fields.
>
> “We know how light the Roman weapons are. At first they are weighed down not by a wound, I say, but by the dust itself. While they gather disorderly and join their lines and their shield-wall, clash with them in your accustomed superior courage. Despising their battle lines, attack the Alans and press upon the Visigoths.
>
> “From that point we must seek a swift victory, since the war depends upon it. When the sinews are cut [perhaps: ‘with the sinews cut’], the limbs soon collapse; nor can a body stand when you have removed its bones.
>
> “Let courage rise; let your accustomed fury swell. Now, Huns, bring forth your counsels, now your weapons. Let the wounded demand the death of his opponent, or let the uninjured satisfy himself with the slaughter of the enemy.
>
> “No weapon can reach those destined to win; those destined to die are hurried toward their fate even in leisure.
>
> “Finally, why would fortune declare the Huns victorious over so many peoples unless she had prepared them for the joys of this battle? Who else would have opened to our ancestors the route through Maeotis, closed and hidden for so many ages [Col. 1280A]? Who made the armed yield to the unarmed?
>
> “The united multitude will not be able to endure the face of the Huns. I am not deceived about the outcome: this is the field that so many successes have promised us.
>
> “I shall be the first to hurl weapons at the enemy. If anyone can remain at rest while Attila fights, he is already buried.”

Inflamed by these words, everyone rushed into battle.

## CHAPTER XL

The outcome of the battle fought between the Romans and Visigoths against the Huns. The death of King Theoderic. Attila surrounds himself with wagons.

Although the circumstances themselves were frightening, the presence of the king removed hesitation from those who were wavering. Hand to hand [perhaps read: “hands to hands”] they came together: a savage, complex, monstrous, and stubborn battle, such as no antiquity has ever recorded as its equal.

Events of such a kind are reported that an eminent man who was deprived of the sight of this marvel would have had nothing in his lifetime that he could have witnessed comparable to it.

For, if it is permissible to believe the elders, the stream of the field just mentioned, flowing down along a low bank [Col. 1280B], was carried onward by the abundant blood from the wounds of the slain—not increased by rains, as usual, but transformed into a torrent by an extraordinary liquid, augmented with gore.

Those whom the wound inflicted there drove to a parched thirst were carried along by waters mingled with slaughter. Bound by this pitiable fate, they were stained as they drank the blood they themselves had shed when wounded.

Here King Theoderic, while moving through the army and encouraging it, was thrown from his horse and trampled under the feet of his own men; thus he ended his life in ripe old age.

Others say that he was killed by the weapon of Andag of the Ostrogothic side, who at that time followed Attila’s command. This was what the haruspices had previously predicted to Attila, although he had suspected Aetius.

Then the Visigoths, separating themselves from the Alans, attacked the Hunnic companies and would almost have killed Attila, had he not prudently fled beforehand and immediately shut himself and his men inside the enclosure of the camp, which he had surrounded with wagons.

Although the fortification was fragile, those who shortly before could not be resisted by any rampart sought in it a refuge for their lives [Col. 1280C].

Thorismund, the son of King Theoderic, who had seized the hill with Aetius and driven the enemy from the higher ground, believing that he was making his way to his own ranks, unknowingly ran into the enemy wagons in the blind darkness of night.

While he was fighting bravely, someone wounded him in the head and threw him from his horse. Saved by the vigilance of his men, he abandoned his intention to continue fighting.

Aetius, likewise separated by the confusion of the night, wandered among the enemy. Anxious lest some misfortune had befallen the Goths, he searched for them and eventually reached the allied camp, where he spent the remainder of the night under the protection of the shields.

At dawn the following day, when they saw the fields filled with corpses and observed that the Huns did not dare to break out, they considered the victory theirs. They knew that Attila had fled from the battle only after being overwhelmed by a great slaughter.

Yet he did nothing cowardly or abject even when defeated. Clashing his weapons, he sounded his trumpets and threatened an attack. Like a lion pressed by hunting spears, pacing around the entrance of its cave, neither daring to rise up nor ceasing to terrify the neighborhood with its roars, so the most warlike king, shut in, disturbed his victorious enemies [Col. 1280D].

The Goths and Romans therefore came together and deliberated what they should do about Attila, who had been overcome. They decided to exhaust him by siege, since he had no supply of provisions, while access was prevented by the repeated shots of his own archers stationed inside the camp’s enclosure.

It is also reported that, in desperate circumstances, the aforementioned king—still magnanimous even at the point of death—built a pyre from horse saddles and intended to throw himself into the flames if his adversaries broke in, so that no one might rejoice over his wound and the lord of so many nations might not fall into the power of so many enemies [Note: [Col. 1279] Perhaps read: “or, as lord of so many nations, fall into the power of the enemy,” etc.].

## CHAPTER XLI

Thorismund prepares the funeral rites for his father, King Theoderic; and, on the advice of the patrician Aetius, who feared the Goths after the Huns had been utterly destroyed, returns to the Roman Empire and succeeds his father. The Franks and Gepids wear one another down in mutual slaughter. The number of those killed in the battle between the Romans and Attila.

[Col. 1281A]

In the meantime, during these delays in the siege, the Vesegoths seek their king, the father of his sons, wondering at his absence, since victory had followed. After searching for a long time—as is customary among brave men—they found him amid the thickest corpses, honored with songs, and carried him away while the enemies watched. You might have seen the Gothic companies, with discordant cries and still raging amid the battles, paying funeral honors to the dead. Tears were shed, but the kind ordinarily offered to brave men; it was a death of our own, yet glorious in the presence of the Hun, since the enemy’s pride was thought to have been humbled when they saw them carry forth the body of so great a king with his insignia.

But the Goths, still rendering the due honors to Theoderic, bore forth the majesty of the king amid the clashing of arms. [Col. 1281B] 416. Thorismund, most valiant and highly renowned, accompanied the funeral rites of his beloved father, as befitted a son, to the realm of the dead. When this had been completed, moved by the grief of bereavement and by the force of the courage with which he was endowed, while he sought to avenge his father’s death among the remains of the Huns, he consulted the patrician Aetius—as though an elder and mature in wisdom—about what ought then to be done.

Aetius, however, fearing that, once the Huns had been utterly destroyed, the Roman Empire might be oppressed by the Goths, offered this advice: Thorismund should return to his own territories and seize the kingdom his father had left him, lest his brothers, having taken possession of their father’s wealth, invade the kingdom of the Vesegoths, and he should thereafter fight against them and his own people—what would be worse, pitiably. Thorismund accepted this reply without hesitation, not as it had been given but rather for his own advantage; leaving the Huns, he returned to Gaul. Thus human frailty, while attempting to forestall suspicions, is cut off from a great opportunity for action.

In this most famous war, fought by the bravest nations, 162,000 are reported to have been killed on both sides, excluding the 90,000 Gepids and Franks who, encountering one another by night before the public battle, fell by mutual wounds: the Franks fighting on the Roman side, and the Gepids on the side of the Huns.

When Attila learned of the departure of the Goths, and—judging, as is usually inferred from disordered circumstances [variant: unexpected circumstances]—thinking rather that it was a trick of the enemy, he remained inside his camp for a long time. But when the enemy’s absence was followed by prolonged silence, his mind was raised toward victory, his joy anticipated it, and the spirit of the powerful king returned to its former destiny.

After the death of his father, Thorismund, immediately invested with royal dignity on the Catalaunian Plains where he had fought, entered Toulouse. Although he rejoiced in the company of his brothers and warriors, he moderated the beginnings of his rule in such a way that he found no one disputing the succession to the kingdom.

## CHAPTER XLII

Attila, informed by the Romans of the withdrawal of the Vesegoths, turns all his forces toward the oppression of the Romans. He devastates Aquileia, Milan, and Ticinum. Pope Leo approaches him and obtains peace for Italy under definite conditions. Attila returns to his own territories beyond the Danube.

[Col. 1281D]

Attila, seizing the opportunity created by the withdrawal of the Vesegoths and seeing the dispersal of the enemy in separate parts—something he had often desired—soon, now secure, set out in battle order to oppress the Romans. At his first assault he besieged the city of Aquileia, the metropolis of Venetia, situated at the point or tongue of the Adriatic gulf.

The river Natissa, flowing from the east, washes its walls from Mount Picis. When Attila had besieged the city for a long time and achieved absolutely nothing, because the bravest Roman soldiers within resisted him, his army began to murmur and desired to withdraw. Attila, walking around the walls while deliberating whether to break up his camp or remain longer, noticed white birds—storks—which nest on the roofs of houses, carrying their young out of the city and, contrary to their custom, transporting them into the fields outside.

When, as a remarkably perceptive observer, he recognized what this meant [Niv.: anticipated it], he said to his men:

“Observe the birds, foreseeing future events: they are abandoning the city destined to perish and, as danger approaches, deserting the towers that are about to fall. Let this not be considered meaningless or uncertain; fear of what is to come makes them change their custom.”

What more is needed? The spirit of his men was again inflamed to attack Aquileia. They constructed siege engines and employed every kind of artillery; without delay they invaded the city, plundered, divided, and savagely devastated it, leaving scarcely any trace by which it might be recognized.

From there, now bolder and still unsated with Roman blood, the Huns raged through the remaining cities of Venetia. They likewise devastated Milan, the metropolis of Liguria and once a royal city; nor did they spare Ticinum, which they overthrew in the same manner. They ravaged and demolished the neighboring places and nearly destroyed all Italy.

When Attila was intent on approaching Rome, his own men, as the historian Priscus relates, dissuaded him—not out of concern for the City, which they hated, but by setting before him the example of Alaric, formerly king of the Vesegoths. They feared for the fortune of their own king, because Alaric had not lived long after breaking Rome but soon departed from human affairs.

Thus, while his mind wavered over the uncertain question of whether to go or not to go, and while deliberation caused him to delay, an embassy pleasing to him arrived from Rome. Pope Leo himself approached him at Acroventus Mamboleius [variant: in the field of the Venetians at Ambuleium], where the river Mincius is crossed by frequent travelers.

Attila immediately laid aside the fury of his army and, returning by the way he had come—that is, beyond the Danube—departed after promising peace. Above all else, however, he declared and emphasized with threats that he would inflict still greater devastation upon Italy unless Honoria, the sister of the emperor Valentinian and daughter of Augusta Placidia, were sent to him together with the portion of the royal wealth due to her.

For it was reported that Honoria, being confined at her brother’s command in the interests of courtly dignity and chastity, had secretly sent a eunuch to invite Attila to use his protection against her brother’s power—an utterly disgraceful act, as though she sought to purchase license for lust at the price of public disaster.

## CHAPTER XLIII

Attila advances against the Alans settled beyond the Loire. Defeated in battle by Thorismund, king of the Vesegoths, he is forced to flee to his own territories. The killing of Thorismund.

Attila had returned to his own territories, but, as though regretting leisure and taking it hard that he had ceased from warfare, he sent envoys to Marcian, emperor of the East, threatening devastation of the provinces because Marcian was by no means paying him what the former emperor Theodosius had promised, and presenting himself as more inhuman than usual toward his enemies.

While doing this, however, as he was crafty and cunning, he threatened in one place, moved his weapons in another, and turned the face of his indignation toward the Vesegoths. But he did not achieve against them the outcome he had achieved against the Romans. Returning by routes unlike those he had previously used, he determined to bring under his power part of the Alans settled beyond the river Loire, so that, by changing through them the appearance of the war, 417. he might emerge more terrifying.

Accordingly, Attila left the provinces of Dacia and Pannonia, where the Huns then dwelt together with various subject nations, and set out against the Alans. But Thorismund, king of the Vesegoths, detecting Attila’s trick with no less subtlety, arrived first among the Alans with every subtle device [Niv.: with all speed]. There he was prepared for the movements of Attila, who was already approaching, and met him. Having joined battle, he deprived him of hope of victory in almost the same manner as before, on the Catalaunian Plains; he drove him from his own country without triumph and compelled him to flee to his native territories.

Thus the famous Attila, master of many victories, while seeking to cast off the reputation of a loser and erase what he had previously suffered at the hands of the Vesegoths, endured a second defeat and withdrew without glory.

Thorismund, having driven back the Hunnic bands from the Alans, migrated to Toulouse without any injury to his own men. After establishing peaceful order among his people, in the third year of his reign he fell ill and, while having blood removed from a vein, was killed by Ascalernus [variant: Ascahhamus], a dependent who had informed his enemies and caused his weapons to be taken away. Yet with the one hand that remained free, he held a footstool and became the avenger of his own blood, killing several of those who had plotted against him.

## CHAPTER XLIV

Theoderic, brother of Thorismund, king of the Vesegoths, defeats Riciarius, king of the Sueves, who had invaded Spain. He places the dependent Achiulf over the Sueves. Achiulf, aspiring to tyranny, is executed. With Theoderic’s permission, the Sueves choose Remismund as their king. The death of King Theoderic.

[Col. 1283B]

After Thorismund’s death, his brother Theoderic succeeded him as king of the Vesegoths. He soon found his kinsman Riciarius, king of the Sueves, hostile to him. Riciarius, relying on his relationship with Theoderic, believed that nearly all Spain ought to be occupied by him, judging the time favorable for attempting the disorderly beginnings of a seizure against the reigning king.

The Sueves had formerly held Gallicia and Lusitania, which extend along the ocean on the right side of Spain. To the east they had Austrogonia; to the west, on a promontory, the sacred monument of Scipio, the Roman commander; to the north, the Ocean; and to the south, Lusitania and the river Tagus, which, mixing gold-bearing ores with its sands, carries riches together with the lowly sediment.

Riciarius, king of the Sueves, therefore set out and attempted to occupy all Spain. His kinsman Theoderic, being a restrained man, sent envoys to him and peacefully told him not only to withdraw from another’s borders but also not to presume to make such an attempt, lest by such ambition he acquire hatred for himself.

But Riciarius, in his arrogance, replied: “If you grumble here and blame me for coming, I will come to Toulouse, where you reside; there, if you are able, resist me.”

When Theoderic heard this, he took it badly. Having entered into alliance with the other nations, he moved against the Sueves, with the Burgundian kings Gaudiacus and Hilperic as auxiliaries devoted to him.

The battle took place near the river Urbicus, which flows between Asturica and Iberia. When battle had been joined, Theoderic, fighting with the Vesegoths on the rightful side, won a victory and overthrew nearly all the Suevic nation to the point of annihilation.

Their king Riciarius, abandoning his unfinished victory and fleeing from the enemy, boarded a ship. Driven back by a contrary storm at the mouth of the Tyrrhenian Sea, he was delivered into the hands of the Vesegoths, and did not delay a pitiable death, although he had changed the elements.

Theoderic, however, having achieved victory, spared the conquered and did not permit further fighting to rage. He placed over the Sueves whom he had subdued his dependent Achiulf. Within a short time Achiulf, persuaded by the Sueves, changed his mind toward treachery. He neglected to fulfill the commands imposed upon him, instead growing proud in tyrannical arrogance and believing that he possessed the province by the same virtue with which he had once subdued it together with his master.

He was born of the stock of the Varni, far removed from the nobility of Gothic blood; therefore he neither pursued liberty nor kept faith with his patron. When Theoderic learned of this, he immediately sent men against him, intending to overthrow him from the kingdom he had seized. They came without delay, defeated him in the first engagement, and exacted from him a fitting punishment for his deeds.

Captured and deprived of the support of his own people, he was executed. At last he felt the anger of the master whom he had believed could be despised when favorable.

Then, seeing the death of their ruler, the Sueves sent the priests of their regions as suppliants to Theoderic. He received them with episcopal reverence and not only granted immunity to the Sueves but, moved by compassion, allowed them to appoint a ruler from their own people. This was done, and the Sueves appointed Remismund as their prince.

When these matters had been completed and peace had been secured for all, Theoderic died in the thirteenth year of his reign.

## CHAPTER XLV

Euric succeeds Theoderic as king of the Vesegoths, while Roman emperors are killed one after another. Gizeric, king of the Vandals, invades Italy and devastates Rome. Euric invades Gaul, defeats the Britons serving as Roman auxiliaries, and occupies Arverna, a city of Gaul.

Euric, his brother, succeeded Theoderic with excessive eagerness, driven by cruel suspicion. While these events and various others were taking place among the Vesegoths, the emperor Valentinian was killed by the treachery of Maximus, and Maximus himself seized the kingdom in tyrannical fashion.

When Gizeric, king of the Vandals, heard this, he came from Africa to Italy with an armed fleet, entered Rome, and devastated everything. Maximus, fleeing, was killed by a certain Ursus, a Roman soldier.

After him, by order of Marcian, the eastern emperor, Majorian assumed the government of the Western Empire. But he too did not reign long. While he was marching against the Alans who were troubling Gaul, he was killed at Dertona near the river called the Ira.

Severus seized his position and died at Rome in the third year of his reign. Seeing this, the emperor Leo, who had succeeded Marcian in the eastern kingdom, appointed his own patrician Anthemius and made him emperor at Rome.

Anthemius immediately sent his son-in-law Ricimer against the Alans—a distinguished man who at that time was almost unrivaled in Italy as a military commander. Ricimer defeated the great multitude of the Alans and their king Beurgus in the very first engagement and put them to death.

Euric, king of the Vesegoths, observing the frequent changes of Roman rulers, attempted to occupy Gaul as his rightful possession. When the emperor Anthemius learned this, he immediately requested the assistance of the Britons.

Their king Riothimus arrived with twelve thousand men and, disembarking from ships at the city of Bituriga [variant: Veturiga], was received there. Euric, king of the Vesegoths, came against them with an innumerable army. After a long struggle, he defeated Riothimus, king of the Britons, before the Romans could join his side.

Riothimus, having lost a large part of his army, fled with those whom he could gather and reached the neighboring Burgundian nation, which at that time was allied with the Romans.

Euric, king of the Vesegoths, occupied the Gallic city of Arverna after the death of the emperor Anthemius. Anthemius, raging in civil war against his son-in-law Ricimer, had worn down the Roman state; Ricimer himself killed him and left the kingdom to Olybrius.

At that time, in Constantinople, Aspar, the foremost of the patricians and illustrious by Gothic descent, was killed in the palace by the swords of the eunuchs together with his sons Ardabur and Patriciolus—the former formerly a patrician, the latter a Caesar and called the son-in-law of the emperor Leo.

418. Olybrius died before he had entered upon eight months in the kingdom. Glycerius was then made Caesar at Ravenna more by presumption than by election. After barely one year had passed, Nepos, the son of the sister of the former patrician Marcellinus, removed him from the kingdom and ordained him bishop at the Roman harbor.

Observing these great changes and variations, Euric, as we said above, occupied the city of Arverna. At that time the most noble senator Decius, formerly the son of the emperor Avitus—who had seized the kingdom for only a few days—was in command there.

Avitus had held the empire for only a few days before Olybrius, then voluntarily withdrew to Piacenza, and there was ordained bishop. His son Decius fought for a long time against the Vesegoths but, unable to withstand them, abandoned his homeland and especially the city of Arverna to the enemy and withdrew to safer places.

When the emperor Nepos heard this, he ordered Decius to leave Gaul and come to him, appointing Orestes, master of the soldiers, in his place. Orestes took command of the army and, setting out against the enemy, traveled from Rome to Ravenna. He remained there and made his son Augustulus emperor.

When Nepos learned this, he fled to Dalmatia, where he died as a private citizen, deprived of the kingdom. Glycerius, formerly emperor, was already holding the bishopric of Salona, while Augustulus had been appointed emperor at Ravenna by his father Orestes.

## CHAPTER XLVI

Odovacer, king of the Turcilingi, invades and subjugates Italy.

Not long afterward, Odovacer, king of the Turcilingi, accompanied by the Sciri, Heruli, and auxiliaries from various nations, occupied Italy. After killing Orestes and expelling his son Augustulus from the kingdom, he condemned him to exile in the fortress of Lucullanum in Campania.

Thus the Western Empire of the Roman people, which Octavian Augustus, the first of the emperors, began to hold in the 709th year after the founding of the City, perished with this Augustulus in the 522nd year of the reigns of his predecessors and successors. Thereafter the kings of the Goths held Rome and Italy.

Meanwhile, after Odovacer had subjugated all Italy, he immediately killed the count Brachila at Ravenna, thereby displaying his terror to the Romans. Once his kingdom had been strengthened, he held it for nearly fourteen years, until the arrival of Theoderic, about whom we shall speak later.

For the moment, however, let us return to the order from which we digressed.

## CHAPTER XLVII

Euric, king of the Vesegoths, subjugates Arles, Marseille, and the Burgundians. He dies. Alaric, the son of Euric, becomes the ninth king of the Vesegoths.

Euric, king of the Vesegoths, observing the instability of the Roman kingdom, brought Arles and Marseille under his own rule. Gezeric, king of the Vandals, had enticed him to undertake these actions with gifts, so that Gezeric himself might guard against the plots that Leo or Zeno had directed against him.

He arranged matters so that the Eastern Empire would be ravaged by the Ostrogoths and the Western Empire by the Vesegoths, enabling him to reign peacefully in Africa while enemies fought one another in both states.

Euric accepted this with gratitude. By his own right he now held all Spain and Gaul, and he also subdued the Burgundians. Residing at Arles, he died in the nineteenth year of his reign.

His own son Alaric succeeded him. He was the ninth in succession from that great Alaric to obtain the kingdom of the Vesegoths. For, just as we stated above concerning Augustulus, the same pattern is seen among the Alarics: kingdoms often fail among those whose names provide their beginnings.

For the moment we pass over this matter. As we promised, let us weave together the whole origin of the Goths. Since both nations—the Ostrogoths as well as the Vesegoths—had once been united, I have, as far as I was able, reviewed the statements of our ancestors and followed the Vesegoths separately from the Ostrogoths in full detail. It is therefore necessary for us to return again to their ancient Scythian territories and to set forth the genealogy and deeds of the Ostrogoths in the same manner.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

The genealogy of the kings of the Ostrogoths, from the death of King Ermanaric to Walamir, son of Thorismund, and the death of Attila.

After the death of their king Ermanaric, the Ostrogoths were separated from the Vesegoths. Subject to the power of the Huns, they remained in the same homeland, although Winitharius, an Amal, retained the insignia of his own principate.

Imitating the courage of his grandfather Ataulf, though inferior to Ermanaric in good fortune, he nevertheless resented being subject to the rule of the Huns. He withdrew somewhat from them and, while striving to display his own courage, marched in battle order against the territories of the Antes.

When he attacked them, he was defeated in the first engagement. Thereafter he fought bravely and crucified their king, named Boz, together with his sons and seventy leading men, as an example of terror, so that the corpses hanging there might double the fear of those who had been subjected.

But after he had ruled with such liberty for scarcely a year, Balamber [above: Balamir], king of the Huns, would not tolerate it. He summoned to himself Sigismund [variant: Gesismund], son of the great Hunimund, who, mindful of his oath and loyalty, was subject to the rule of the Huns together with a large part of the Goths. Renewing his alliance with him, Balamber led an army against Winitharius.

After a long struggle, Winitharius won the first and second engagements. No one can adequately recount the slaughter Winitharius inflicted upon the Hunnic army. In the third battle, with the help of a surprise attack, when both sides had come together at a river named Erac, Balamber shot an arrow that wounded Winitharius in the head and killed him.

Balamber took his niece Waladamarca [variant: Vallamarica] in marriage and then possessed the entire Gothic people, now subdued in peace. Yet the Gothic nation always had its own ruler, although he governed with the counsel of the Huns.

Immediately after Winitharius’s death, Hunimund, formerly the son of the most powerful king Ermanaric, ruled the Goths. He was fierce in war and excelled in the beauty of his whole body. Afterward he fought successfully against the Suevic nation.

When Hunimund died, his son Thorismund succeeded him. Adorned with the flower of youth, in the second year of his rule he led an army against the Gepids and gained a great victory over them. He is said to have been killed by an accident involving his horse.

After his death the Ostrogoths mourned him so deeply that no other king succeeded him in his place for forty years [Niv.: sixty], so that they might always keep his memory on their lips and so that time might come for Walamir to restore his manly vigor.

Walamir was born of Wandalarius, Thorismund’s cousin. For, as we said above, 419. Wandalarius’s son Berismund had already abandoned the Ostrogothic nation because of the domination of the Huns and followed the nation of the Vesegoths into the western regions. From him Vedericus was born.

Vedericus in turn had a son named Eutharicus. Eutharicus married Amalasuenta, the daughter of Theoderic, and thereby reunited the Amal line, which had already been divided. He fathered Athalaricus and Mathesuenta.

Since Athalaricus died in childhood, Mathesuenta was taken to Constantinople. By her second husband, Germanus, the nephew of the emperor Justinian, she bore a posthumous son, whom she named Germanus.

But for the order we desire to follow, we must return to the offspring of Wandalarius, whose line flourished in three branches. Wandalarius, the cousin of Ermanaric and of the Thorismund mentioned above, took pride in the Amal nation after producing three sons: Walamir, Theodemir, and Widemir.

Of these, Walamir succeeded to the kingdom by hereditary succession, while the Huns still generally held them subject among the other nations. At that time these three brothers presented a pleasing spectacle, when the remarkable Theodemir fought for the rule of his brother Walamir. Walamir, for the honor of the other, issued commands; Widemir considered it his duty to serve his brothers.

Because they protected one another with mutual affection, none of them lacked a kingdom, which both held in peace. Yet, as has often been said, they ruled in such a way that they themselves served under the authority of Attila, king of the Huns.

They could not refuse battle against their kinsmen, the Vesegoths. But the command of a master must be fulfilled, even if it orders parricide. Nor could any Scythian nation break away from Hunnic domination until the death of Attila came—a death desired by all nations alike, and by the Romans as well. It was so beneficial [perhaps: destructive] that his life had been extraordinary.

## CHAPTER XLIX

The death of Attila, king of the Huns, from excessive drunkenness, and the magnificent funeral rites performed for him.

As the historian Priscus relates, at the time of his death Attila took a very beautiful girl named Ildico in marriage, after innumerable wives, as was customary among that people. At the wedding he gave himself over to great merriment, then lay on his back, weighed down by wine and sleep.

The blood that habitually flowed from his nostrils, when prevented from following its usual channels, descended through a fatal passage into his throat and killed him. Thus drunkenness gave a shameful end to a king made glorious by wars.

On the following day, when a large part of the day had passed, the royal servants, suspecting something grievous, broke down the doors after loud shouting. They found Attila dead without a wound, his death having been caused by the flow of blood, and the girl beneath a veil, weeping with downcast face.

Then, according to the custom of that people, they cut off part of their hair and disfigured their ugly faces with deep wounds, so that the exceptional warrior might be mourned not with feminine lamentations and tears but with manly blood.

A remarkable event was added to this. While the emperor Marcian of the East was anxious about such a savage enemy, the Divinity appeared to him in a dream and showed him that Attila’s bow had been broken that same night, as though to indicate that the nation itself placed great confidence in that weapon.

The historian Priscus says that he confirms this by truthful testimony. Attila was held so terrifying by the great empires that the powers above revealed his death to their rulers as a gift.

Let us not omit to say a few things, out of many, about the ways in which his people honored his spirit. His body was placed in the midst of the open fields and beneath silk tents, and a remarkable spectacle was solemnly displayed.

The most select horsemen from the entire Hunnic nation rode around the place where he lay in circus-like courses and recited his deeds in a funeral song, in the following manner:

“Attila, the foremost king of the Huns, born of Mundzuccus, lord of the bravest nations, who alone possessed the Scythian and Germanic kingdoms with power unheard of before him, terrified both empires of the Roman world by capturing their cities, and, appeased by prayers so that he might not subject the remainder to plunder [read: *praedae reliqua subderet*], accepted an annual tribute.

“After accomplishing all this through the prosperity of fortune, he fell—not by an enemy’s wound, not through the treachery of his own people, but unharmed among his nation, joyful amid rejoicing and without any awareness of pain. Who, then, would call this an end that anyone could regard as requiring vengeance?”

After he had been mourned with such lamentations, they celebrated a *strava*, as they themselves call it, over his tomb with an immense feast. Joining opposites together, they expressed funeral grief mixed with joy. At night, secretly, they buried the body in the earth.

They fortified the bier [variant: coverings] first with gold, second with silver, and third with the hardness of iron, signifying by this device that everything was appropriate to the most powerful king: iron, because he subdued nations; gold and silver, because he received the adornment of both states.

They added weapons acquired by the slaughter of enemies, precious horse trappings gleaming with various gems, and insignia of different kinds by which courtly splendor is honored. So that human curiosity might be kept away from such vast riches, they slaughtered those assigned to the work with an accursed reward. Thus sudden death overtook both the burial workers and the one who was buried.

[Note: [Col. 1287D] The meaning of the Gothic word *strava* is not unreasonably doubtful. The commentator on Statius, concerning the passage in *Thebaid* 2, “Hostiles super ipse it,” says that this should be read in that form, not as “victor acervos”: “He goes over the heaps,” he says, “the masses of spoils.” For the spoils of enemies were heaped up for the burial of dead kings. Barbarians are said still to preserve this burial rite, which they call *straba* in their own language. I would rather argue that the word *strava* is a genuinely Gothic term, pronounced by them *straffa* [Col. 1288D], meaning punishment and penalty, as it does even today among the Germans and Belgians, from the verb *straffen*, which means “to punish” or “to exact a penalty from someone.” It is therefore plausible that the Huns honored Attila not only by heaping up heaps of enemy spoils over his tomb but also by slaughtering captives. Let the learned judge whether my conjecture is *εὔστοχος*—well aimed. B. VULCAN.]

## CHAPTER L

[Col. 1287D]

After Attila’s death, a dispute over the succession arises among his innumerable sons. Ardaric, king of the Gepids, kills Ellac, Attila’s son, in battle and drives the remaining sons as far as the Pontic Sea. The emperor Marcian grants various Goths and Gepids different settlements.

When these matters had been completed, a dispute over the kingdom arose among Attila’s successors, as the minds of young men are accustomed to being stirred by ambition for power. Since all foolishly desired to rule, they all 420. lost the empire together. Thus kingdoms are often burdened more by an abundance than by a scarcity of successors.

Attila’s sons, whose indulgence in lust had made them almost a people in themselves, demanded that the nations be divided among them by equal allotment, so that, like the household of a warlike king, they might be assigned peoples as their shares.

When Ardaric, king of the Gepids, learned this, he was indignant that so many nations were being treated as though they were the condition of the basest slaves. He was the first to rise against Attila’s sons and, through the success that followed, wiped away the shame of servitude that had been imposed. By his departure he freed not only his own nation but also the others that were being oppressed in the same way, since everyone readily embraces undertakings attempted for the common good.

They therefore armed themselves for mutual destruction, and war was joined in Pannonia near the river called the Netad [variant: Neda]. There the various nations whom Attila had held under his rule came together. Kingdoms were divided together with their peoples, and diverse limbs were made from a single body—not limbs that would sympathize with the suffering of one part, but limbs that, once the head had been severed, would rage against one another. Nations that had never found equals to oppose them tore themselves apart only by wounding one another with mutual blows.
