I think there must have been a remarkable spectacle there, where everyone could see [variant: every spear could see] a Goth fighting furiously with his sword; a Gepid breaking all the weapons in the wounds of his own people [variant: breaking the weapons of his own king]; a Sueve daring with his foot; a Hun with his arrow; an Alan forming the line in heavy armor; and a Herul in light armor.

After many severe conflicts, unexpected victory favored the Gepids. Ardaric’s sword and those of his conspirators killed nearly thirty thousand, both Huns and members of other nations who had brought assistance to the Huns.

In that battle Ellac, Attila’s eldest son, was killed. His father is said to have loved him so greatly above the others that he preferred him in the kingdom to all his various sons. But fortune did not agree with the father’s wish. After the slaughter of many enemies, Ellac was killed so bravely that his surviving father would have desired such a glorious death.

After his death, his remaining brothers were driven toward the shore of the Pontic Sea, where we previously described the Goths as having settled.

Thus the Huns yielded, although it had been thought that the whole world would yield to them. So destructive is division that those who had terrified others when united in strength fell when divided.

This success of Ardaric, king of the Gepids, benefited the various nations that had unwillingly languished under Hunnic rule. It raised their long-mournful spirits toward the joy of desired freedom. Many came through envoys to the Roman soil and, being most graciously received by the ruler Marcian, received assigned settlements in which to live.

The Gepids, claiming by force the territories of the Huns, took possession of the whole region of Dacia as victors. From the Roman Empire they asked for nothing except peace and the customary annual gifts, as brave men, under a friendly agreement. The emperor at that time gladly consented, and this customary gift continues to the present day, since the nation receives it from the Roman ruler.

The Goths, seeing the Gepids defending the Hunnic territories for themselves and the Hunnic people occupying their ancient lands, preferred to request territories from the Roman kingdom rather than invade those of others at their own peril. They received Pannonia, an extensive plain bounded on the east by Upper Moesia, on the south by Dalmatia, on the west by Noricum, and on the north by the Danube.

This homeland was adorned with many cities, the first being Sirmium and the last Vindomina.

The Sauromatae, whom we have called Sarmatians, the Cemandri, and some of the Huns occupied the settlements assigned to them in part of Illyricum, near the fortress of Martena.

Blivilas, commander of the Pentapolis, belonged to this people, as did his brother Froilas and Bessa, the patrician of our own time.

The Sciri, Satagarii, and the remaining Alans, together with their leader named Candax, received Scythia Minor and Lower Moesia.

Peria, the father of my father, that is, my grandfather, was notary to Candax for as long as Candax himself lived. The son of Candax’s sister was Gunthigis, also called Baza, master of the soldiers; he was the son of Andagis, son of Andala, descended from the line of the Amals.

I too, Jornandes, although uneducated, was a notary before my conversion.

The Rugii and several other nations requested settlements in Biozimetas and Scandiopolis [variant: Brisium and Arcadiopolis] in which to dwell.

Hernac, Attila’s younger son, also established settlements with his people at the far end of Scythia Minor.

His kinsmen Emnedzar and Uzindur [variants: Emedzar, Eumezur, and Ulzindur] settled in Riparian Dacia.

Uto and Iscalmus [variant: Histo and Alivus], who gained possession of those regions, and many Huns who poured out in various directions then gave themselves over to Romania. From these people the Sacromontisi and Fosatisi are still named.

## CHAPTER LI

The settlements of the Goths called the Minor Goths, and of Vulfila, their bishop, who instructed them in letters.

There were also other Goths, called the Minor Goths, an immense people with their own bishop and leader, Vulfila, who is said to have instructed them in letters. Even today they dwell in the region of Moesia, at Encopolis [variant: Necopolis].

At the foot of a mountain [variant: Haemus] there settled a numerous people, poor and unwarlike, possessing little except herds of various kinds of livestock, pastureland, and woodland for timber. They have little wheat, but the land is fertile in other kinds of produce.

As for vineyards, even if there are any elsewhere, they have no certain knowledge of them; they obtain wine for trade from neighboring regions, for they are nourished by milk.

## CHAPTER LII

The various settlements of the Ostrogoths in Pannonia after the death of Attila; how they repelled Attila’s sons when they attacked and drove them into Scythia; and the friendship of the Ostrogoths with the Romans, with Theoderic, son of Theodemir, sent to Constantinople as a hostage of peace.

[Col. 1289C]

Most of them, then—to return to the people under discussion, namely the Ostrogoths, who were dwelling in Pannonia under King Walamir and his brothers Theodemir and Widemir—although they occupied separate districts, nevertheless held their plans in common. Walamir lived between the rivers Scarniunga and Aqua Nigra; Theodemir beside Lake Pelso; and Widemir between the two. It happened, then, that Attila’s sons came against the Goths, seeking them as though they were deserters from their rule, like runaway slaves; and, while the other brothers were unaware, they attacked Walamir alone. Yet he, although accompanied by only a few, confronted them and, after wearing them down for a long time, so crushed them that scarcely any portion of the enemy remained. Those who survived turned to flight in 421 and made for those parts of Scythia through which the waters of the Danube [variant: Danabri] flow, which in their own language they call Hunnivar [Note: [Col. 1289D] Hunnivar, that is, “the Crossing-place of the Huns.” B. Vulcan.].

At that time, when he had sent news of the victory to his brother Theodemir, a messenger arriving on that very day found an even happier joy in Theodemir’s house. For on that same day Theoderic, his son—though born from the concubine Erelieva, yet a boy of good promise—had been born.

Not long afterward, King Walamir and his brothers Theodemir and Widemir, while they were receiving the customary gifts from the emperor Marcian, which they received in the manner of a *strena* (a customary ceremonial gift), in order to preserve the treaties of peace, sent an embassy to the emperor. There they saw Theoderic, son of Triarius [variant: Trianus], flourishing in every respect with his people and joined in friendship with the Romans, receiving the annual ceremonial payments, while they themselves were treated with contempt. Immediately, stirred by anger, they took up arms and, ranging through nearly the whole of Illyricum [Col. 1290A], devastated it for plunder. But the emperor at once, changing his mind, returned to his former friendship. Through an embassy he granted both the past gifts and the present ones, and promised without any dispute to provide them in the future as well; and from them he received as a hostage for the peace the infant Theoderic of Theodemir, whom we mentioned above. He was already advancing through his seventh year and had entered his eighth. When his father hesitated to give him, his uncle Walamir became an intercessor, asking only that peace between Romans and Goths might remain firm.

Thus Theoderic was given by the Goths as a hostage and brought to the city of Constantinople to the emperor Leo. Since he was an attractive child, he deserved to enjoy imperial favor.

## CHAPTER LIII. The Ostrogoths move against the Satagans after Attila’s death. They resist the Huns, led by Dinzio, Attila’s son, and drive them back. Various battles of the Ostrogoths with the Suevi and Sciri. The death of Walamir. The Sciri destroyed to the last.

[Col. 1290B]

After firm peace had therefore been established between the Goths and Romans, the Goths saw that the assistance they received from the emperor was not sufficient for them; and, wishing at the same time to display their valor, they began to plunder the neighboring peoples all around them. First they took up arms against the Satagans, who possessed inner Pannonia.

When Dinzio [variant: Dinclzic], king of the Huns and son of Attila, learned this, he gathered with him those who still seemed to have remained under his command, although they were few: the Ulzingures, Angiscires, Bittugores, and Bardores. He came to the Pannonian city of Bassiana, surrounded it with siegeworks, and began to ravage its territory.

When the Goths learned of this, they abandoned the expedition they had assembled against the Satagans and, wherever they were, turned against the Huns. They drove them ingloriously from their borders, so that from that time onward the Huns who survived—and their descendants to this day—have feared Gothic arms.

[Col. 1290C]

When the Hunnic people had at last been quieted by the Goths, Hunimund, leader of the Suevi, while passing through Dalmatia to plunder it, carried off the herds of the Goths that were wandering in the fields. Dalmatia was near Suevia and not far from Pannonia, especially from the place where the Goths then lived.

What more need be said? When Hunimund returned to his own country with the Suevi after devastating Dalmatia, Theodemir, Walamir’s brother and king of the Goths, grieved not so much over the loss of the herds as he feared that, if the Suevi gained this profit with impunity, they might advance to still greater license. He therefore watched their passage so carefully that, in the dead of night, he attacked them while they were sleeping beside Lake Pelso. Joining battle unexpectedly, he overwhelmed them so completely that, after King Hunimund himself had been captured, he subjected to Gothic servitude the whole of his army that had escaped the sword.

But since he was greatly devoted to mercy, after exacting vengeance he granted pardon. Reconciled with the Suevi, he adopted as his own son the man whom he had captured and sent him back with his people to Suevia.

Yet Hunimund, forgetful of this paternal kindness, after some time brought forth the treachery he had conceived. He incited the people of the Sciri, who then lived above the Danube [Col. 1290D] and dwelt peacefully with the Goths, so that, breaking away from their alliance with them and joining Hunimund, they might take up arms and attack the Gothic people.

Then, while the Goths expected no evil—especially because they trusted in both peoples as friendly neighbors—war suddenly arose. Compelled by necessity, they resorted to arms; and, entering upon their customary struggle, they avenged themselves and their wrong.

In that battle their king Walamir, while riding before the line on horseback to encourage his men, had his horse thrown into confusion and brought down, casting its rider to the ground. He was immediately pierced by the spears of the enemy and killed.

The Goths, seeking vengeance both for the death of their king and for their own injury inflicted by the rebels, fought so fiercely that they extinguished virtually the whole Scirian people, leaving scarcely any except those who bore the name alone and had no distinction remaining.

## CHAPTER LIV. The Suevian kings Hunimund and Alaric, advancing against the Ostrogoths with the Sarmatians, Sciri, Gepids, and Rugians, suffer a great disaster.

[Col. 1291A]

Fearing the destruction of the Sciri, the Suevian kings Hunimund and Alaric took up arms against the Goths. They relied on the aid of the Sarmatians, who had come to support them with their kings Beuga and Babai. They also summoned the remnants of the Sciri, who were eager to fight more fiercely for their own vengeance, together with their leaders Edica and Vulfo [variant: Hunulfo]. Along with them they had both Gepids and considerable support from the people of the Rugians. Gathering others from every direction and assembling a vast multitude, they encamped beside the river Bollia in Pannonia.

The Goths, Walamir having died, took refuge with his brother Theodemir. Although he had long been ruling jointly with his brothers, Theodemir assumed the insignia of greater authority. He summoned his younger brother Widemir, shared the burdens of war with him, and, compelled to arms, sprang into action.

[Col. 1291B]

When battle was joined, the Goths were found to have the upper hand, so much so that the field was drenched with the blood of the fallen enemy and appeared like the Red Sea. Weapons and corpses were heaped up like hills, and the field was overwhelmed by more than ten thousand [422; the wording is corrupt or incomplete in the source]. Seeing this, the Goths rejoiced with indescribable exultation, since they had avenged the blood of their king Walamir and their own wrong with the greatest slaughter of their enemies.

Of the innumerable and varied multitude of the enemy, those who were able to escape were scattered and, scarcely reaching their own country, arrived there without honor.

## CHAPTER LV. King Theodemir advances against the Suevi, devastates them, and nearly subdues them. Theoderic, son of Theodemir, while still almost a boy and without his father’s knowledge, attacks and kills Babai, king of the Sarmatians. He captures the city of Singidunum.

After a certain time, when the severe cold of winter was pressing on and the Danube had frozen as it usually does—for this river becomes so rigid that it carries an infantry army [Col. 1291C] like stone, as well as wagons and sledges, or whatever sort of vehicle there may be, without the need of a boat or skiff—King Theodemir of the Goths saw it frozen and led an army on foot across it. Having crossed the Danube, he appeared unexpectedly behind the Suevi.

That region of the Suevi has the Baiobarians to the east, the Franks to the west, the Burgundians to the south, and the Thuringians to the north. At that time the Alemanni were also joined to the Suevi. They completely controlled the elevated Alps [perhaps the Brecian Alps], from which several streams flow into the Danube, descending with a tremendous roar.

Thus, with the place fortified in this way, King Theodemir led the Gothic army during winter. He defeated, devastated, and nearly subdued both the Suevian people and the Alemanni, who were allied with one another.

From there, returning victorious to his own settlements—that is, to Pannonia—he gladly welcomed his son Theoderic, whom he had given as a hostage to Constantinople and whom the emperor Leo had sent back with great gifts.

Theoderic had by then reached the years of adolescence [Col. 1291D], completed childhood, and was in his eighteenth year. He gathered his father’s retainers and associated with himself men from the people as lovers and clients, nearly six thousand in number. Without his father’s knowledge, he crossed the Danube with them and attacked Babai, king of the Sarmatians. Babai had then gained a victory over Camundus, a Roman commander, and was ruling in the swelling pride of arrogance. Theoderic fell upon and killed him, plundered his household and wealth, and returned victorious to his father.

Afterward he attacked the city of Singidunum, which the Sarmatians themselves had occupied. He did not restore it to the Romans but subjected it to his own authority.

## CHAPTER LVI. The Ostrogoths, weary of peace, harass Italy, Gaul, and Illyricum. Theodemir makes a treaty with the Romans and dies.

As the plunder of the neighboring peoples [Col. 1292A] diminished on every side, food and clothing also began to be lacking for the Goths; and for the men whom war had long provided with sustenance, peace began to be burdensome. All the Goths therefore, approaching King Theodemir with a great outcry, begged him to lead the army wherever he wished.

He summoned his brother and, casting lots, urged him to go to that part of Italy where Glycerius was then ruling as emperor, while he himself, as the stronger [variant: more vigorously], would advance toward the stronger kingdom, namely the eastern one. And this was done.

Widemir soon entered the lands of Italy, but, paying the final debt of fate, departed from human affairs and left his son Widemir as successor to the kingdom.

The emperor Glycerius, after giving him gifts, transferred him from Italy to Gaul, which was being hard-pressed on every side by various peoples. He explained that their kinsmen, the Visigoths, who were neighbors to him, were ruling there.

What more need be said? Widemir, having received gifts and instructions from the emperor Glycerius, set out for Gaul. Joining himself to his kinsmen, the Visigoths, he became one body with them, as they had formerly been; and, holding Gaul and Spain [Col. 1292B] by their own right, they defended them so effectively that no other power could prevail against them.

Meanwhile Theodemir, the elder brother, crossed the river Saus [variant: Spadus], threatening war against the Sarmatians and soldiers if anyone opposed him. Fearing this, they remained quiet; indeed, they were not strong enough to withstand so great a multitude.

Seeing prosperity come to him from every direction, Theodemir attacked Naissus, the first city of Illyricum. Joined by his son Theoderic, he stood ready and sent his companions through the fortress of Hercules to the village of Ulpiana. When they arrived, they soon received both the town and its wealth into surrender. They also made certain inaccessible places of Illyricum passable for themselves for the first time. For they gained possession by right of war of the cities of Heraclea and Larissa in Thessaly, after first taking them as plunder.

King Theodemir, observing both his own success and that of his son, was not satisfied even with this. Leaving the city of Naissus with a few men behind to guard it, he himself proceeded toward Thessalonica, where Clarianus [variant: Hillarianus], a Patrician sent by the emperor, was stationed with an army.

When Clarianus saw Thessalonica [Col. 1292C] being fortified with a rampart and realized that he could not resist their efforts, he sent an embassy to King Theodemir. By offering gifts, he turned him back from the siege of the city.

A treaty was concluded, and the Roman commander voluntarily handed over to the Goths places for them to inhabit: Ceropella, Europa, Mediana, Petina, Bereum, and others called Sium [variant: Phium]. There the Goths, laying down their arms with their king and establishing peace, remained at rest.

Not long afterward, King Theodemir was seized by a fatal illness in the city of Cerras. He summoned the Goths, designated his son Theoderic as heir to his kingdom, and soon afterward departed from human affairs.

## CHAPTER LVII. Theoderic, king of the Ostrogoths, is summoned to Rome by the emperor Zeno, adopted by him, and presented with the consulship and an equestrian statue. He inflicts a great defeat on Odoacer in the West and assumes the insignia of the Roman kings.

[Col. 1292D]

When the emperor Zeno heard that Theoderic had been appointed king of his people, he received the news favorably. He sent him a summons and ordered him to come to him in the city. Welcoming him with fitting honor, he placed him among the nobles of his palace.

After some time, to increase his honor in arms, he adopted him as his son and granted him a triumph [423] in the city from his own resources. He was made ordinary consul, which is declared to be the highest and foremost distinction in the world [the text has *docus*, perhaps *decus*, “honor”]. Nor was this all: he also placed an equestrian statue before the palace entrance, to commemorate so great a man.

Meanwhile Theoderic, joined by treaty to the rule of Zeno, was himself enjoying every good thing in the city. Yet he heard that his own people, who—as we have said—were settled in Illyricum, were neither fully equipped nor abundantly supplied. He therefore preferred, according to the customary way of his people, to seek a livelihood through his own labor rather than enjoy in idleness the wealth of the Roman kingdom while his people lived in moderate circumstances.

After deliberating with himself, he said to the emperor:

“Although [Col. 1293A] nothing is lacking to us who serve your empire, still, if your piety considers it worthy, may it willingly hear the desire of my heart.”

When he was granted permission to speak familiarly with him, as was customary, he said:

“The region of the West, which was formerly governed by the rule of your predecessors and forebears, and that City which is the head and mistress of the world—why does it now fluctuate under the tyranny of the king of the Turcilingi and Rugians? Send me with my people, if you command it, so that here you may be free from the burden of expense; and if, aided by the Lord, I am victorious there, the fame of your piety may shine forth.

“For it is fitting that I, who am your servant and son, should, if victorious, possess that kingdom as your gift; and that he whom you do not know should not oppress your senate and a part of the commonwealth under the yoke of a tyrant and the service of captivity.

“If I am victorious, I shall possess it by your gift and your generosity; if I am defeated, your piety loses nothing. Rather, as we have said, it gains the expense.”

When the emperor heard this, although he was distressed by Theoderic’s departure, he nevertheless did not wish to sadden him and agreed to what he requested [Col. 1293B]. He dismissed him enriched with great gifts and entrusted to him the Roman senate and people.

Theoderic therefore left the imperial city and returned to his own people. Taking with him the whole Gothic nation—so far as it had given him its consent—he proceeded toward the West. He followed a straight route through Sirmium and ascended toward the neighboring parts of Pannonia.

From there he entered the territory of Venetia and encamped at the bridge called the Sontius. After remaining there for some time to restore the strength of his men and animals, Odoacer sent an armed army against him.

Theoderic met it in the Veronese fields and destroyed it in a great slaughter. Breaking camp, he entered the territory of Italy with greater confidence. After crossing the river Po, he established his camp near the royal city of Ravenna, about three miles from the city, at a place called Pineta.

When Odoacer saw this, he fortified himself inside the city. From there he frequently went out secretly at night with his men and harassed the Gothic army—not once or twice, but repeatedly [Col. 1293C], and he continued this effort for almost three years.

But he labored in vain, because all Italy already called Theoderic its lord, and the commonwealth obeyed his will. Odoacer alone, with a few retainers and the Romans who were present, suffered daily within Ravenna from both famine and war.

When he accomplished nothing, he sent an embassy and begged for pardon. Theoderic first granted it to him, but afterward deprived him of this life.

In the third year after his entry into Italy, as we have said, Theoderic—following a private consultation with the emperor Zeno [variant: “having privately consulted”]—laid aside the clothing of his own people and assumed the insignia of royal dress, as though he were now ruler of both Goths and Romans.

## CHAPTER LVIII. Concerning King Theoderic’s wife Audefleda and his concubine, his sons and daughters, and their marriages and other alliances with various kings. Also concerning the brigand Mundo and the victory won over the Franks.

Theoderic sent an embassy to Lodoin, king of the Franks, and asked for his daughter [Col. 1293D] Audefleda [variant: Oldebfleda] in marriage. Lodoin granted her gladly and willingly, believing that through this alliance his sons Ildebert, Cheldepert, and Thuidepert would be joined by treaty to the Gothic people.

Yet this union did not contribute so greatly to peace and concord that they did not often fight bitterly with one another over the lands of Gaul. Nor did the Goth ever yield to the Franks while Theoderic lived.

Before he had offspring by Audefleda, Theoderic had daughters born from a concubine while he was still in Moesia: one named Theudicoda [variant: Thiudigota] and another Ostrogotho. As soon as he came to Italy, he joined them in marriage to neighboring kings: one to Alaric of the Visigoths and the other to Sigismund of the Burgundians.

From Alaric was born Amalaric. While his grandfather Theoderic [Col. 1294A] was nourishing and protecting him after he had been deprived of both parents in childhood, he learned that Eutharic, son of Witeric and grandson of Beremund and Thoresmund, descended from the stock of the Amals, was living in Spain. Eutharic was in the vigor of youth and distinguished by prudence, courage, and bodily integrity.

Theoderic had him come to himself and joined his daughter Amalasuntha to him in marriage.

To extend his lineage fully, he sent his sister Amalafreda—mother of Theodatus [variants: Theodahatus; and so forth], who later became king—to Trasemund, king of Africa and of the Vandals, as his wife. He also married her daughter, his niece Amalaberga, to Hermenfred, king of the Thuringians.

He sent his own count Petza, chosen among the foremost men, to take possession of the city of Sirmium. Petza expelled its king, Transaric, son of Trafstila, and took possession of the city while retaining Transaric’s mother.

From there, against Sabinian, the Illyrian master of the soldiers, who at that time had prepared a conflict with Mundo, Petza came to Mundo’s aid with two thousand infantry and five hundred cavalry at the city called Margoplanum, which lay between the rivers Danube and Martian [variant: Margus] [Col. 1294B], and destroyed the Illyrian army.

For this Mundo, once descended by origin from Attila [perhaps “from the Attilans”], had fled from the people of the Gepids and, beyond the Danube in uncultivated places without any tillers of the soil, had run wild. Gathering from everywhere many cattle-raiders, *scamarae*, and robbers [Note: [Col. 1293D] Perhaps “assassins,” unless the same term has both meanings among the Goths], he seized a tower called Herta, situated above the bank of the Danube. There, plundering the neighbors in barbarian fashion, he called himself king over his brigands.

When Petza came to the aid of this man, who was almost desperate and even considering betraying his own cause, he rescued him from Sabinian’s hands and, with thanks, made him subject to his own king, Theoderic.

Theoderic also gained no lesser a trophy over the Franks through his count Hibba in Gaul, where more than 30,000 Franks were killed in battle.

He also appointed Thiodem, his arms-bearer, after the death of Alaric his son-in-law, as guardian in the kingdom of Spain [424] of Amalaric, his grandson. Amalaric, however, already [Col. 1294C] in adolescence, became entangled in the treacheries of the Franks and lost both his kingdom and his life.

After him, Thiodis, his guardian, seized that kingdom and drove the Franks’ deceitful calumny from Spain. He kept the Visigoths under his control for as long as he lived.

After him, Thiodigis Glossa [variant: Thodigis of Toulouse] obtained the kingdom but did not reign to completion; he was killed by his own men.

Hactenusagil succeeded him and continued the kingdom. Against him Athanagild rose up and summoned the forces of the Roman kingdom. Liberius the Patrician was also sent there with an army.

There was no people in the western region that, while Theoderic lived, did not serve him either through friendship or through submission.

## CHAPTER LIX. The aged King Theoderic proclaims Athalaric, son of his daughter Amalasuntha and fatherless, king. When Athalaric is taken by premature death, his mother appoints her cousin Theodatus king, and he confines her to an island, where she is strangled.

[Col. 1294D]

When Theoderic had reached old age and knew that he would soon depart from this life, he summoned the Gothic counts and the leading men of his people. He appointed Athalaric, the still scarcely ten-year-old son of his daughter Amalasuntha, who had been deprived of his father Eutharic, as king.

He gave them instructions, declaring them almost as if in a testamentary speech: they were to honor the king, love the senate and Roman people, and always keep the eastern emperor appeased and favorable.

They observed this command in every respect for as long as Athalaric and his mother lived, and they ruled in peace for almost eight years. Although the Franks, despairing of the boy’s kingdom—or rather holding it in contempt—were preparing and attempting to make war because his father and grandfather had occupied Gaul, Theoderic allowed them that territory. Everything else was possessed in the tranquility of peace.

When Athalaric was advancing toward the hope of youth, he commended both his own adolescence and his mother’s [Col. 1295A] widowhood to the emperor of the East. But soon, most unhappily overtaken by premature death, he departed from human affairs.

Then his mother, deliberating with herself lest the Goths despise her because of the weakness of her sex, summoned her cousin Theodatus from Tuscany under the pretext of kinship. He was living a private life there, occupied with his own troubles [perhaps “in his own home,” as in Book I, Letter 3]. She placed him on the throne.

He, forgetful of their blood relationship, after some time dragged her from the palace at Ravenna and confined her in exile on an island in Lake Bolsena. After living there in sorrow for a very few days [variant: “There Amalasuntha lived for several days, etc.”], she was strangled in a bath by his retainers.

## CHAPTER LX. The emperor Justinian sends Belisarius with an army against the Goths. He occupies Sicily. The Goths choose Witigis as their king and kill Theodatus. Witigis gives Ravenna, together with Mathasuentha and the royal treasures, to the Romans.

[Col. 1295B]

When the eastern emperor Justinian heard this, as though the death of those entrusted to him had rebounded as an injury to himself, he was deeply moved. At that very time he was returning in triumph from Africa over the Vandals through his most faithful Patrician Belisarius [variant: Betramus]. Without delay, while the weapons were still wet with Vandal blood, he sent an expedition against the Goths under the same commander.

That most prudent commander judged that he could subdue the people of the Goths if he first occupied Sicily, their nurse; and this was done. When he entered Trinacria, the Goths who were holding the stronghold of Syracuse saw that they could accomplish nothing. With their leader Sinderich, they voluntarily surrendered to Belisarius.

When the Roman commander had overrun Sicily, Theodatus, learning this, dispatched his son-in-law Evermor [variant: Evermundus] with an army to guard the strait lying between Campania and Sicily, from which the vast Adriatic surge flows out of the basin of the Tyrrhenian Sea.

When Evermor arrived there, he established his camp near the town of Rhegium. No sooner had he seen that his cause was deteriorating than he went over to the side of the victor with a few trusted servants who shared his secrets. Throwing himself at the feet of Belisarius, he desired to serve the rulers of the Roman kingdom.

When the Gothic army learned this, it loudly declared that the suspect Theodatus should be expelled from the kingship and that their commander Witigis, who had been his arms-bearer, should be raised to the throne. This was done.

Witigis was immediately raised to the kingship in the barbarian fields and entered Rome. He sent trustworthy men of his own to Ravenna and ordered the death of Theodatus.

Those who came carried out the orders given to them. They reported to Witigis that Theodatus [Col. 1296A] had been killed, while the king whom Witigis had sent was arriving; Theodatus was still in the barbarian fields [the syntax is uncertain].

Meanwhile the Roman army crossed the strait, approached Campania, overturned Naples, and entered Rome. A few days earlier King Witigis had left Rome and departed for Ravenna. He had taken Mathasuentha, daughter of Amalasuntha and granddaughter of the former king Theoderic, as his wife.

While he delighted in this new marriage and maintained the royal court at Ravenna, the imperial army, having left Rome, attacked the fortified places of both Tuscanies.

When Witigis learned this through messengers, he sent the Gothic commander Cumunila to Perugia with a force fully armed. While they were attempting, through a long siege, to dislodge a great count who was stationed there with a small army, the Roman army arrived. The Goths themselves were dislodged and completely destroyed.

When Witigis heard this, like a raging lion he gathered the entire Gothic army. Leaving Ravenna, he exhausted the Roman strongholds with a long siege.

But his boldness was frustrated. After fourteen months he fled from the siege of the Roman city [Col. 1296B] and prepared to attack Ariminum. There, frustrated and driven off in the same manner, he withdrew to Ravenna. Once besieged, he soon voluntarily surrendered to the victorious side, together with Mathasuentha, his wife, and the royal treasures.

Thus Justinian, emperor and conqueror of nations, finally defeated through his most faithful consul Belisarius that famous kingdom and that most powerful people, which had ruled for a long time, in the thirteen-hundredth year [the chronological statement is as printed]. He brought Witigis to Constantinople and honored him with the rank of Patrician.

Witigis remained there for more than two years, lived in the emperor’s favor, and then departed from human affairs.

As for Mathasuentha, the emperor joined her in marriage to his brother, the Patrician Germanus. A posthumous son of Germanus, the father, was born to them [425], also named Germanus. In him the people of the Anicii, joined with the stock of the Amals, promise—by the Lord’s favor—a future hope for both lineages.

Up to this point the origin of the Goths, the nobility of the Amals, the deeds of brave men, and the praiseworthy succession have yielded to a more praiseworthy ruler and given their hands to a stronger commander [Col. 1296C], whose fame no age and no generation will silence.

Thus the victorious and triumphant emperor Justinian and the consul Belisarius are called Vandalic, African, and Gothic.

You who read this should know that I have followed the writings of the ancients and gathered a few flowers from their spacious meadows, so that, according to the capacity of my talent, I might weave a crown for the inquirer. Let no one believe that, in favor of the people mentioned above, as though I derived my origin from them, I have added anything except what I read or learned.

Nor have I embraced everything that is written or reported about them; and I have set these matters forth not so much for their praise as for the praise of him who conquered.

**Wealth.** Small things often have greater power to provide what great riches cannot obtain, 21.

Learning makes a noble person out of one who was obscure, 144.

Learning makes the person it imbues humble in all things, 156.

The moth of documents is the wicked offering of one who ransoms them, 197.

A deceitful mind does not follow the command of the one giving orders, 10.

*Dolos* for *dolores*, 37.

**Lord.** Fortune changes along with its masters, 24. The reputation of masters increases through the distinction of those who serve them, 60.

Domnica, wife of the emperor Valens, 331.

Dominical. See *Day*.

Domitian orders himself to be called a god, 387.

[Col. 1309] Princes profit from their own gifts, 135.

Royal gifts, although small, exalt their recipients, and why, 147.

Royal gifts to soldiers, 88.

When the donatives of princes were customarily given, 293.

A donative, 84, 88.

The benefits of a donative, 64.

The burial of Bishop Donatus at Beroea is distinguished, together with his miracles, 351.

Donatus the grammarian is regarded as distinguished, 392.

The labors and astonishing vigils of Dorotheus, 333.

The death of Dorotheus, bishop of the Arians, 367.

Dromons—that is, ships—are built in Italy, 84 and following.

A duel is discouraged, 48.

He who cannot return what belongs to another is like a needy man, 123. Hegesippus, most wise, wrote a history, 266.

Hatred is aroused by arrogance, 162. Electus. He is commended by the praises of his lords when the elected man conducts himself commendably, 145. On the elements: what the philosophers think, 37. Where the power of eloquence prevails, enforcement is almost on holiday, 99.

What a bishop ought to be, 305. What is required for the episcopal office, 318. What the integrity of bishops ought to be, 26. Administration of innocence is entrusted to bishops, 175. The election of bishops, 230. Bishops transferred from one church to another, 377. Bishops determine the prices of goods, 180. The king sends fifteen hundred solidi to a bishop for distribution among the provincials, 26. It is fitting that a bishop correct what ought not to have been admitted by his associates, 74. Theodoric orders the bishop of Aurigenum to punish a subject who had stolen Julian’s property and wife, 45. A case between the municipal inhabitants of Sarsena and the Church is referred to the bishop’s court, and how, 30. Constantine permitted appeals to bishops, 210. Theodoric summons the case of the bishop of Pola, 74. See Athanasius, Clerics, Priests.

Bishops who had been deposed and subjected to injury go to Rome, 247. Condemned bishops, 274. Various punishments of bishops, 275. Deposed bishops, 275. Excommunicated bishops, 274. Eleven Egyptian bishops relegated to Diocaesarea, [Col. 1310] 319. Orthodox bishops driven into exile, 311. Exiled bishops are restored, and pagan temples are opened, 283. Episcopal letters for pilgrims, 292. The designation “bishops.” See Chrysostom, Cyril of Jerusalem.

A canonical epistle, 182. Description of excellent horses, 59. Public horses of the couriers, 34. Relay horses, 56. Judgments are shared with knights and senators, 384. What miracles occurred among the hermits sent into exile by Lucius, 317. See Monks.

To overcome harmful errors is to overcome blemished vices, 107. An alien error ought to make one cautious, not a follower, 111. The hungry. Whoever can help the hungry, if he does not feed them, destroys them, 194. It is exceedingly impious that, when storehouses are full, the cultivators should hunger in emptiness, 167.

What books Evagrius published, 321. What Evagrius wrote in his book on monks, 322. Certain distinguished testimonies of the Fathers from Evagrius’s book *On Contemplation*, 322. The Eucharist was formerly given to the laity in their hands, 343. The Euchite error concerning the Eucharist, 307. See Macedonius. Eudoxia, wife of the emperor Arcadius, dies, 361. The education of Eudoxia, wife of Theodosius, 371. How she went to Jerusalem, 379. Eudoxia, daughter of Theodosius, married to Valentinian, 379.

Eudoxius, Martyrius, and Macedonius, envoys of the Eastern bishops, 249. Eudoxius usurps the bishopric of Antioch, 266. He strives to restore Aetius, ibid. Eugenius the grammarian seizes the empire, 350. He is killed, 351. The conversation of Eulogius with the prefect Modestus, 315. Eulogius and Protogenes labor for the conversion of the pagans, 315. They return from exile, 315. See Protogenes. Eulogius knew the thoughts of others, 323.

Eunomius the bishop freed his city from the Persian siege, 363. Eunomius, Aetius’s secretary, 264. He increases Arius’s blasphemies, 278. He is accused before the emperor, 278. He flees, ibid. On his craft and knowledge, 334. He is sent into exile, 346. See Eudoxius. The schisms of the Eunomians, 349. See Aetians.

Euphronius becomes bishop at Antioch, 235. Why Eupsychius suffered martyrdom, 287. Euric invades Gaul, 417. He routs the Britons, ibid. He subdues them, 418. He occupies the Gallic city of Arverna, 417. He subdues Arles and Marseilles, 418. He dies, ibid.

Eusebia, wife of Constantius, pleads for the emperor Julian, 283. Eusebius of Gaza is crowned with martyrdom, 286. The steadfastness of Eusebius of Samosata on behalf of Meletius, 279, 280. His greatness of spirit in undergoing exile, 309. In other provinces he initiates many into the sacred orders, ibid. After returning from exile he appoints several bishops, 332. He is killed by a tile thrown by an Arian woman, 332. He was crowned with martyrdom, 309.

Eusebius of Vercelli is sent into exile, 264. He is recalled from exile, 288. He holds a council at Alexandria with Athanasius, ibid. What he did at Antioch, 290. Eusebius. See Basil, Marcellus.

Eusebius Pamphili delivers an address to the emperor Constantine at the Council of Nicaea, 226. He subtly interprets the term *ὁμοούσιον* (*homoousion*, “consubstantial”), 228. He refuses the bishopric of Antioch, 235. Eusebius Pamphili is praised by the emperor, 235. He wrote the *Life of Constantine*, 221. He dies, and Agapius succeeds him, 245. The letter of Eusebius of Nicomedia to Paulinus, bishop of Tyre, 220. His power with the emperor, 221. At the Council of Nicaea he proposed a written statement full of blasphemies, 227. After presenting a written confession of repentance, he agrees with the faith of consubstantiality, 228, 231. He seizes the bishopric of Constantinople, 233, 234, 216. He acts before Constantine on behalf of the Arians, 234. What he did so that Arius might be received into communion with the Church, 241. His power at the court of Constantius, where he tried to establish the Arian doctrine, 244. He writes to Julius, the Roman pontiff, making accusations against Athanasius, [Col. 1311] 245. Eusebius of Emesa is appointed bishop of Alexandria, 246. Eusebius the eunuch, chamberlain, replies to Liberius, the supreme pontiff, 265. He is condemned to death, 283. Alexander of Antioch unites the Eustathians with the orthodox, 362.

Eustathius, bishop of Beroea, is ordained bishop of Antioch by the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea, 207. He delivers an address to Constantine at the Council of Nicaea, 226. Eutharic marries Amalasuntha, 395, 423. What happened during his consulship, 395. Eutropius, the emperor’s chamberlain, is killed, 354. Eutropius. See Chrysostom. Eutropius the lector is thrown into prison because of John Chrysostom, 361. Eutychianus the monk, distinguished for miracles, 113. The heresy of Eutyches, 349. Euzoius the Arian is ordained bishop at Antioch after Meletius has been expelled, 280. When Meletius returns, he presides over the Arian churches, 290.

*Evectus* and *evectiones*, 80, 97. A formula of summons, 120. Evolcius is sent into exile, 309.

Examination. He to whom examinations are entrusted must be weighed for a long time, 93. Matters considered uncertain come to examination, 153. Exception. A personal exception does not prejudice public right, 34. Excesses are feared when they are believed to displease judges, 5. In the authors of treachery, excess always seems subject to excision, 39. Excess must be restrained at the very beginning, 64. Whoever can sin against the whole community is excessively glorious if he does not know how to go too far, 130.

Examples. The mind is made ready for the future when it is reminded by examples of the past, 95. Speech cannot possess authority when it is not supported by example, 178. Exercises. What is subject to continual exercises must be refreshed by constant care, 74. Expenses for exercises, 53. Army. A fasting army cannot preserve discipline, 64. An army is more conveniently maintained under a law of expenses, 83. It is like treason to withhold from an army what is known to arm it, 117. An army is always more strongly armed by discipline, 191. See Military service.

Existentials. See Aetians. Existence. “From things that do not exist,” or “there was once when he was not”: these are expressions not found in the divine Scriptures, 229. See Arians.

### F

The seven wonders of construction, 116. No one is recognized as diligent in construction unless he is also found highly cultivated in his own faculties, 76. Every crime pursues its authors alone, 27.

Fame. Whoever strives for a good reputation is always more burdened by his own judgment, 102. No power can remove the quality of reputation from the mouths of men, 111. A longer life is desired in which reputation is always found stronger, 134. Famine in retaliation for the killing of the orthodox, 314. During famine children are sold, 409. During famine grain is ordered to be sold at a moderate price, 143. Famine commonly despises everything in order to satisfy its need, 61. Fasces born from fasces, 9.

Felix. It is better recognized that one has chosen a noble man than made a fortunate one, and why, 132. Felix is ordained supreme pontiff in place of Liberius, 266. Felix is divinely punished, 296. The praise of Felix, 23. Commendation of Felix, 172. The female sex is open to the vices of changeability, 27. The uses of iron, 48. Iron itself commands gold and compels the wealthy to serve the poor who are constantly armed, ibid. Iron mines in Dalmatia, 48.

The feast days of Christians, and what Socrates thought about them, 347. Hymns at the feasts of the martyrs, 326. The annual feast day of Saints Juventius and Maximinus, 295. See Christ.

Nine expositions of the faith, 275. Some fell away from the faith through love of money, 296. See Heresy. Praise of faith, 93. Faith produces fruits so sweet that it even wins the hearts of rulers, 12. Constancy proves faith, 48. No one is compelled to believe unwillingly, 33. Faith is inferred from things by reason, 7. A man’s faith does not know how to fail with death, 79. Those are good and certain things that transmit the faith from the beginning, [Col. 1312] 29. One must not believe a petitioner who deceitfully pleads against the public faith, 54.

Confidence. Confidence in themselves makes men bold, 24. Tileworks are granted by the king, 31. How the Son of God is consubstantial with the Father, 306. Whence he is, 149. How he is both Only-Begotten and First-Born, 252. Why the Father is sometimes said to be greater than the Son, ibid. A son is released from his father’s obligations if he is not the heir, 63. Like sons quickly follow their fathers’ praises, 71. He does not seem entirely rescued who rises restored in succession, 127. It is a more fortunate praise for parents to be praised for the integrity of their sons, 135. Humanity does not permit a disobedient son to avoid punishment, 28. See Adoption.

The fisc must always exclude costly excess, and why, 71. It is more praiseworthy for the fisc to suffer loss when justice is not maintained, 13. Barbarians are ordered to pay the fisc for occupied turf, 83. Lapsed goods belong to the king’s fisc, 87. The property of proscribed persons is assigned to the fisc, 69.

Flacillus of Antioch, successor of Euphronius, 246. When the Circus Flaminius and the Via Flaminia were built, 383. The virtues of Flavian, 325. He rebukes Adelphius, 307. A schism arises between the Easterners and the Egyptians because of Flavian, 339. He is reconciled with Damasus, 341. Flavian’s outstanding speech to Theodosius, 350. Flavian alone receives the bishopric of Antioch, 350. He vigorously rebukes Leontius, 271. See Porphyrius.

The channels of rivers ought to be free, 85. The Claudia spring is compared with the Nile, 113. The virtues and miracles of the Marcilian spring, 140. A spring near Nicopolis that drives away diseases, 297. Formulas of dignities among the Goths, 96 and following. Brave men are always modest in peace, 190. The hand of the brave is a patron, 89. Praiseworthy courage lies hidden beneath leisure; while it has no opportunity to prove itself, the whole light of its merits remains concealed, 13.

The Franks, headlong in their assaults, have always brought battles upon nations, 173. The Frankish nation, established around Gaul, hostile to the Romans, 426. Constans subjected them to Roman rule, 247. See Gauls. The sweet concord of brothers, 132. The killer of his brother is relegated into exile, and why, 11. Every fraud is serious, 193. Everything is thrown into confusion if integrity is mixed with frauds, 8. Fridigern ruled part of the Goths, 228. Fronto, a distinguished orator, 388.

The abundance of grain ought first to benefit the province in which it grows, and why, 17. Grain must not be exported until the need of the region has been satisfied, 17. The enraged do not perceive what is just, and why, 63. Anger generally rushes headlong through insistence, 40. The punishment of fustuarium, 63, 142, 180. Fustuarian vengeance, 139.

Gainas attempts to set fire to the palace of Constantinople, 355. The rebellion of Gainas, 355. See Chrysostom. Gallus becomes Caesar, 260. His rebellion and death, 263. Gallus, grandson of Constantine the Great, 282. He applies himself to studies at Ephesus, and under which teacher, ibid. An omen when Julian and Gallus erect a temple of Memma, 284.

Gizeric, king of the Visigoths, invades Italy and devastates Rome, 417. The games of gladiators. See Honorius. Sword. See Belus.

Glory. Whoever desires the glory of virtue does not shun labor, 13. What is done gloriously is not held by the end of time, 24. Everyone seeks his own glory, 133. This is certain glory: to have frequently been able to earn what plainly adorns men, 135.

King Cororanes of Persia is divinely driven back in battle, 363. Where the Goths first came out from, 399. How they moved their settlements into Scythia, 399. They enter Gaul, ibid. They return Placidia to Constantius, ibid. They defeat Vesosis, king of the Egyptians, 400. They subjugate Asia, ibid. Their wars and victories against the kings of Persia and Macedonia, 402, 403. They devastate Moesia and Thrace, 405. Under Ostrogotha they defeat the Gepids, 405. Under King Cniva they harass the Romans, 406. Under Gallienus they harass Asia, Chalcedon, Troy, and Thrace, 406. The lesser Goths inhabit Moesia, 420. How the Goths approached Valens, 328. They enter into a treaty with Gallus and Volusianus, 406. Their kinship with the Gepids, 405. Their justice, 47. Their privileges, 89. They received annual gifts from the Romans, 405. They are wiser than the barbarians, 400. Their custom in choosing kings, 169. The king of the Goths received the oaths of the Romans, 126, 127. How the Arian plague reached the Goths, 328. Virtue makes the Goths legally mature, 18.

The praises of grammar, 152. A hailstorm resembling stones falls at Constantinople, 311. A violent hailstorm falls there again, 361. Grace. Grace is usually sweeter after bitterness has been expiated, 169. Grace ought not to perish with the beloved, 124.

Gratian becomes emperor, 311. His kindness and correctness of faith, 331. He recalls the orthodox bishops from exile, 331. See Andragathius. The fame and miracles of Gregory of Pontus, 327. Gregory the Cappadocian, an eloquent man, 296. Gregory of Nazianzus depicts Julian, 301. He is transferred to Constantinople, 334. He leaves Constantinople, 335.

Gregory is intruded as bishop of Alexandria, 245, 246. Syrianus brings him to Alexandria with a military escort, 246. The skill of cranes when they cross the sea, 75. The concord of cranes, 142. Griffins are said to dig up gold continually, 143.

The bodies of the prophets Habakkuk and Micah are found, 352. Dwelling-place. At first sight, the Lord is believed to be such as his dwelling-place proves him to be, 112. The emperor Hadrian ceases the persecution of Christians, 388. He constructs a library of marvelous workmanship, ibid. He deifies his beloved Amasius, 302. See Alexandria, Laws, Aelia.

Heretics change like chameleons, 215. Constantine’s law ordering the meeting-houses of heretics to be assigned to the churches, 242. Jovian drives them back, 303. Alaric. See Goths. Hamilcar, Hannibal’s father, is killed, 383. Hannibal prepares for war, 383. He perishes by poison, 384. What Helena discovers near the Lord’s monument, 232. The city of Helenopolis is dedicated in her name, ibid. She encloses the nails in the helmet and bridle of her son, 232. She dies, ibid. The solitude of Elijah, 323. The vigils and fasts of Heliodorus, 325. Heliodorus, from the family of Cassiodorus, 6. Heliopolis in Phoenicia, 319. Helladius the grammarian, teacher of Socrates, 342. Hellin performs miracles, 323. Heraclea, a city of Pontus, 205. Heraclides. See Chrysostom.

Basilica of Hercules constructed by Theodoric, 6. Heir. An heir who remembers the author of his benefits loves his benefactor more sweetly, 126. It is fitting that an heir should pay what is known to have been bestowed by the benefactor, 132. An heir is continually compelled by the virtues of his ancestors, 153.

Hermanaric, king of the Goths, is compared with Alexander the Great, 407. He defeats the Heruli, Veneti, and Ostrogoths, ibid. Theodoric gives his niece in marriage to Herminafrid, king of the Thuringians, 59. Hermogenes, master of the soldiers, is killed by the people when he wishes to drive Paul from the Church, 247. Herod the Idumaean, 206. The king of the Heruli is adopted as a son by Theodoric through arms, 59.

Jerome the presbyter, established at Bethlehem, is considered remarkable throughout the world, 393. The Church of Jerusalem, mother of all churches, 336. Those who held the bishopric of Jerusalem after Cyril, 276. The letter of the council of Jerusalem to the Egyptian bishops, 257. See Arius. The restoration of the Jerusalem temple is divinely prevented, 297.

The miracles of Hilarion, 286. Hilarion the monk, apostle of the Easterners, 292. Hilary, returning from exile, wrote books on the Trinity, 291. Hilderic. See Amalafrida. The tax of Spain, 90. The province of Istria described, 198. The rare steadfastness and honorable vow of actors, 56.

The hearing is the first to detest the crime of murder, 18. It is murder to sin against a person’s salvation, 106. He avoids the feeling of humanity who does not follow another’s grief, 182. Humanity does not know how to preserve boundaries, 68. Every person suffers dangerous entanglements, 188. Homoousians. See Arians.

Honesty alone rightly derives profit from the laws, 150. Honor. He continually enjoys praise who has honor in his name, 160. Honor of the second order, 118. Honoratus, prefect of the city of Constantinople, judge in the case of Aetius, 274.

Honorius, son of Theodosius, is born, 340. He is designated emperor, 350. He succeeds Theodosius, 353. He abolishes the gladiatorial games, 353. He marries two sisters unlawfully, with an unhappy outcome, 410. He dies, 372. The extremely talkative hands of the Horcistae, 76. Orestes. See Cyril. Hormisdas, a most distinguished confessor among the Persians, 364.

A water clock, 21. A sundial, ibid. Water and solar clocks made by Boethius, 22. Granaries. Granaries are quickly exhausted if they are not strengthened by continual additions, 172. Humility is as glorious as it is rare, 60. Humility in rulers is glorious, 95. Hunimund and Alaric, kings of the Suebi, suffer the greatest disaster, 421. The accursed origin of the Huns, 407. Their terrifying faces, 408. They overcome the Scythian Ostrogoths, ibid. They march against the Goths, 328. They devastate Thrace, 362. They are driven from Italy, 393. ### I

The conversion of the Iberians to Christ, 236. Which emperors prohibited or permitted the worship of idols, 345. How the voices of idols were produced, 342. On a hermaphroditic image set up by pagans in a church, 288. See Alexandria.

To forgive. We who are perilously just always forgive in security, 186. Formula for a vacant office of illustris rank, 103. The letter of the Illyrician bishops to the Eastern bishops, 306. Images. See Christ.

When one yields to weakness, appropriate remedies are assigned, 54. To imitate. The imitator of an earlier person is always more diligent, 79. Whoever is given as an example to imitate ought to be conspicuous in character, 60. Who among the Persians were called immortals, 371. See Romans.

The emperor had bodyguards, 404. The imperial decennials, 230. See Constantine the Great. The empire that passes to descendants has been extended rather than changed, 125. See Altar. The discipline of ruling is to love what benefits many, 145. Weakness in a ruler is a pernicious thing, 11. Piety is the true adornment of empire, 204. What very few cannot guard cannot be commanded of many, 64. No one commands more boldly than the man whose own deeds commend him, 65. Whoever resists just commands arouses hatred against himself, 178. If imperial authority is despised in a small matter, it is violated in every part, 27.

Ignorance is further inflated by the wind of pride, 24. Prices of a priceless thing, 59. The imprudent refuses to change his plan, 159. The continence of turtledoves is proposed to immodest women, 90. Unpunished. It is impious for us to be lenient toward those whom heavenly piety does not permit to remain unpunished, 150. Let us neither allow vengeance to surpass sins nor permit guilt to insult the laws by remaining unpunished, 54. We do not leave unpunished what we do not wish to be permitted, 63.

Figures and prophecies of the Incarnation, 205. Incentive. It is a great kind of encouragement to believe that desired things can be accomplished, 84. How the indiction may be recognized, 396. Need encourages excesses, 11. It is a great advantage to make terms with the needy, and why, 61. He who imposes what cannot be found demands only tears from the needy, 200. The conversion of the Indians, 236.

Indulgence. It is unworthy that humanity should subsequently plead for those who reject indulgence when they are exposed, 36. Industry is always a friend of wisdom, 106. Nature is conquered when industry improves it, 143. See Labor. Failure to assist infancy is considered a loss of modesty, 73.

Inferior. It is blameworthy to elevate an inferior unless he appears to surpass others in merits, 176. Unbelievers. For the preservation of civic order, the benefits of justice must not be denied to those who are still known to err in faith, 91. The intellect ought not to be occupied by two concerns, 152.

Beginning. A good beginning can provide praise for what follows, 97. Once begun well, things ought not to be suspended for any contrary reason, 166. Beginnings commonly promise better things when they start from small matters that later raise themselves to greatness with remarkable splendor, 24.

Injury. An unexpected injury causes severe grief, 95. Injury does not seek measure, 27. Every injury is detestable, 68. Innocence commends everything, 105. Hardly anyone dares to go too far against those in whom he cannot find faults, 142. Innocent, Roman pontiff, a man suitably adorned with prudence and understanding, 350. He persecutes the Novatians, 368. An inscription predicting the future is found on a stone, 311.

Integrity. It is a great gift to be chosen for integrity; the conscience entrusted with the truth of the ages is tested no lightly, 87. *Interpretium* [uncertain term], 32.

Envy. Whatever is said out of envy is not considered truth, 7. Envy does not seek measure, 27. Envy oppresses those who are superior, 72. Royal splendor admits nothing unfinished, 119. Whatever is known to be pleasing to royal wisdom and approved by divine judgment, 120.

It is fitting for a king to give greater things than he seems to have received from those who serve him, 17. The increases of royal glory occur when nothing diminishes under the king, 36. # ORDER OF THE MATTERS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME

## POPE VIGILIUS

Notice from the Pontifical Book. 9

### LETTERS AND DECREES

15. **LETTER OF VIGILIUS, STILL A PSEUDOPOPE, TO EUTHERIUS.**—He replies to Eutherius’s consultations. *Ibid.*

**LETTER TO PROFUTURUS.** 19. Testimonies of the ancient canons in favour of triple immersion. 20.

**LETTER OF VIGILIUS, STILL A PSEUDOPOPE, TO CAESARIUS OF ARLES.**—He replies to Sylverius, who consults him concerning the penance to be imposed on King Theudebert for his incestuous marriage. 21.

**LETTER TO JUSTINIAN.**—When the emperor Justinian had professed the faith before Vigilius, legitimately elected, the latter, changed from an enemy into a defender, from a persecutor into a preacher, from a blasphemer into a confessor, pronounced a sentence of anathema against Anthimus and his heretical associates. *Ibid.*

**LETTER TO MENNAS.**—He congratulates him, now that the heretics have been condemned, on embracing the four holy universal synods; those returning from heresy ought to be received. 25.

**LETTER TO AUXANIUS OF ARLES.**—He postpones the use of the pallium which Auxanius requested, until he informs the emperor more certainly. 26.

**LETTER TO THE SAME.**—He delegates his authority to him in Gaul and grants him the use of the pallium, admonishing him to pray to God for the emperor and to strive to preserve peace between him and King Childebert. 27.

**LETTER TO THE SAME.**—Concerning the examination of the case of Bishop Praetextatus. 29.

**LETTER TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL.**—He announces that Auxanius has been appointed vicar of the Apostolic See, explains the duties of that office, and orders all to obey him. *Ibid.* Decree of the emperor Justinian. 30.

**LETTER TO AURELIAN OF ARLES.**—After Auxanius’s death, he delegates his authority in Gaul to Bishop Aurelian. 37.

[Col. 1334] **LETTER TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL.**—He announces that he has delegated his authority to Aurelian in Gaul and orders them to obey him. 39.

**LETTER TO AURELIAN OF ARLES.**—That nothing contrary to the general councils and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs has been admitted by him. He urges him to suggest to King Childebert that he write to the king of the Goths, lest he allow anything in the Roman Church to be disturbed. 41.

**LETTER TO RUSTICUS AND SEBASTIAN.**—He excommunicates them. 43.

**LETTER TO VALENTINIAN.**—What was done at Constantinople concerning the Three Chapters. 51.

**LETTER TO THE WHOLE CHURCH.**—He sets forth the reasons for his withdrawal to St. Euphemia, and what he did there with Justinian’s envoys; at the same time he inserts a confession of his faith. 53.

**Fragment of the condemnation of Theodore.**—Theodore the bishop is deprived of priesthood and communion. The bishop of Constantinople and the other bishops aware of his crime are excommunicated. 59.

**Letter of Eutychius to Vigilius.**—He professes the Catholic faith and asks that the question of the Three Chapters be decided in a council. 64.

**LETTER TO EUTYCHIUS.**—He commends his faith and agrees that the Three Chapters be discussed in a council. 66.

**VIGILIUS’S CONSTITUTUM CONCERNING THE THREE CHAPTERS.** 67.

**Letter sent by the clerics of Italy to the envoys of the Franks.**—They urge them to endeavour to give comfort and assistance to Pope Vigilius and Datius, bishop of Milan, who were harassed in that city by the emperor Justinian because of the controversy over the Three Chapters. 113.

**Copy of the sacred letter of Justinian to John, metropolitan.** 119.

**Another letter of Justinian to Cosmas, bishop of Mopsuestia.** *Ibid.*

[Col. 1335] **Petition of the Second Ecumenical Synod of Constantinople to Vigilius.** 120.
