## POPE PELAGIUS I

Notice from the Pontifical Book. 391.

### LETTERS OF PELAGIUS

393. **LETTER TO NARSES.**—He urges him to give assistance to the envoys in correcting bishops who disturb the Church. *Ibid.*

**LETTER TO THE SAME.**—He admonishes him to restrain the schismatics. 394.

**LETTER TO THE SAME.**—That he should restrain the schismatics by whom he had unjustly been excluded from communion. 396.

**Critical observation on the two preceding letters.** 397.

**LETTER TO THE SAME.**—He admonishes him to send the bishops of Aquileia and Milan to the prince under guard. 397.

**LETTER TO THE BISHOPS OF TUSCIA.**—He rebukes them for schism. *Ibid.*

**LETTER TO THE WHOLE PEOPLE OF GOD.**—On the Catholic faith. 399.

**Admonition of Jacques Sirmond on the following letters.** *Ibid.*

**LETTER TO SAPAUDUS OF ARLES.**—A letter of greeting before he had received a letter from Sapaudus. 401.

**LETTER TO THE SAME.**—He modestly rejects the praises with which Sapaudus had adorned him in his letter. *Ibid.*

**LETTER TO KING CHILDEBERT.**—He pronounces anathema upon those who think otherwise concerning the faith than is contained in the letters of Leo and in the Council of Chalcedon. He sends relics of the saints through the subdeacon Hominembonus. 402.

**LETTER TO SAPAUDUS.**—He commends to him the return of the subdeacon Hominisbonus, and asks that he suggest to his father Placidus the purchase and dispatch to Rome of garments to be distributed among the poor. 404.

**LETTER TO THE SAME.**—He delegates his authority to him in Gaul and grants him the use of the pallium. 405.

**LETTER TO KING CHILDEBERT.**—He states that he has granted his authority and the use of the pallium to Sapaudus, whom he commends to the king. 406.

**LETTER TO KING CHILDEBERT.**—Concerning Sapaudus of Arles, who had been ordered, contrary to the privilege of his see, to submit to the judgment of another bishop. *Ibid.*

**LETTER TO SAPAUDUS.**—Concerning his letter which he previously wrote to the king on the Catholic faith. He commends the Romans who had fled there through fear of the enemy, and again discusses garments to be sent to the city. 407.

**LETTER TO CHILDEBERT.**—He sends his confession of faith and admonishes him to take care not to allow dissensions to be stirred up in Gaul by heretics. 408.

**FRAGMENTS** of letters rescued from obscurity by Lucas Holstenius. 411.

**Other fragments from the collection of Deusdedit.** 417.

**APPENDIX** to the letters of Pope Pelagius I. 419.

**LETTER OF PELAGIUS TO BISHOP VIGILIUS.**—He proves that the Father and the Son are one God. *Ibid.*

## CASSIODORUS

*[The supplied source ends here, with this heading and no following contents.]*
Epistle of Dedication. 421  
Preface to a new edition of Cassiodorus’s works. 425  
Life of Cassiodorus. 437  
Treatise on Cassiodorus’s monastic life. 483  
Testimonies concerning Cassiodorus. 497  
THE TWELVE BOOKS OF THE VARIOUS LETTERS. 501  
Preface. Ibid.

BOOK ONE. 503

LETTER ONE (King Theodoric to the Emperor Anastasius). — He requests the restoration of peace, interrupted for definite reasons; praises the emperor and sends envoys to him to settle the disputes and thereafter restore concord to the stability of his rule. 503

LETTER II (Theodoric to Theonius). — He rebukes him for negligence concerning the purple, which he used to send to the royal court each year, and describes the origin and method of preparing purple.

LETTER III (Theodoric to Cassiodorus). — He extols him with the highest praises [Col. 1336] and bestows upon him the summit of the patriciate, after he had already been governor of Lucania and Bruttium and had held the praetorian prefecture.

507 LETTER IV (Theodoric to the Senate). — He announces that he has raised Cassiodorus to the summit of the patriciate as a reward for his merits, after he had administered the lower offices with distinction. He praises Cassiodorus, his father, his grandfather, Heliodorus, and his entire family to the highest degree.

508 LETTER V (Theodoric to Florianus). — He orders that the provisions established by Count Anna concerning the estate of Mazene be observed.

511 LETTER VI (Theodoric to Agapitus). — He writes that Rome should send the most skilled marble-workers to Ravenna to complete the basilica of Hercules.

512 LETTER VII (Theodoric to Felix). — He orders him to restore the property of the ward Plutianus, which his brother Neoterius had not so much acquired as stolen, and rebukes him for not having divided the inheritance equally among equals. Ibid.

LETTER VIII (Theodoric to Amabilis). — He orders him to ensure that the property of the ward Plutianus, improperly sold by his brother Neoterius, be restored without delay to Venantius, Plutianus’s guardian. If his brother intervenes, he wishes the case brought before his tribunal.

513 LETTER IX (Theodoric to Eustorgius, bishop of Milan). — He says that he has restored the bishop of the city of Augusta, accused by the clergy on false charges, to his former honor, and sends those clerics to Eustorgius so that he may restrain them with the punishment they deserve. Ibid.

LETTER X (Theodoric to Boethius). — He writes that the household protectors, cavalrymen and infantrymen who continually keep watch at the royal court, have complained that the prefects’ treasurer does not pay them solidi of full weight as their customary emoluments, and that they suffer serious losses in the reckoning. Here he treats of arithmetic, the number ten, the solidus, the number six, the ounce, and the pound, and forbids any reduction whatever in these measures.

514 LETTER XI (Theodoric to Servatus). — He orders him to have the slaves taken away by the soldiers of the Breones restored to Maniarius.

516 LETTER XII (Theodoric to Eugenites). — After his praiseworthy administration of the quaestorship, he confers upon him the dignity of master and urges him to earn still greater distinction.

516 LETTER XIII (Theodoric to the Senate). — He announces that he has raised Eugenites to the office of master; Eugenites is adorned with the highest praises because he administered the quaestor’s office well.

517 LETTER XIV (Theodoric to Faustus, praetorian prefect). — He orders that the class of *tertiarii* imposed upon the Cathalians be paid each year.

518 LETTER XV (Theodoric to Festus). — He entrusts to him the protection of the house of the patrician Agnellus, who is departing for Africa.

519 LETTER XVI (Theodoric to Count Julian). — He orders him to investigate the case of the grain contractors Apodorus, who had complained that their grain had been burned through the thefts of their enemies; and he commands that, if the matter is as alleged, he deduct from the remainder of the first indiction after allowing for a reasonable adjustment. Ibid.

LETTER XVII (Theodoric to the Goths and Romans residing at Dertona). — He orders them, while enjoying peace, to fortify the fortress situated near them and to build houses for themselves within it.

520 LETTER XVIII (Theodoric to Domitianus and Uvilla). — He replies that estates occupied by usurpers must be restored, unless either a contract or a thirty-year prescription stands in the way; and that the slayer of a brother must be deported into exile. Ibid.

LETTER XIX (Theodoric to Saturninus and Verbusianus). — He prescribes that whoever among the Goths has refused to fulfill his fiscal obligation be compelled to make restitution equitably.

521 LETTER XX (Theodoric to Albinus and Albienus). — He warns them to support the Prasinian faction at the spectacles, and orders them, after popular disorder has been removed, to appoint from among the Prasini pantomimes Helladius and Theodoron, whichever of them is judged more suited to public entertainment. Ibid.

LETTER XXI (Theodoric to Maximianus and Andreas the senator). — He decrees that they investigate whether the money assigned for the city’s buildings was all spent on them without fraud.

522 LETTER XXII (Theodoric to Marcellus the senator). — He appoints him, from being a private advocate, advocate of the fisc.

523 LETTER XXIII (Theodoric to Caelianus and Agapitus). — These men are chosen as judges to settle the lawsuit of the patricians Festus and Symmachus against the patrician Paulinus. Ibid.

LETTER XXIV (Theodoric to all the Goths). — He states that through the saio Nandius he had them warned to hasten to the Gallic expedition on 8 Kalends of July [June 24], adequately supplied with everything necessary, and that the elders should set an example for the younger men.

524 [Col. 1337] LETTER XXV (Theodoric to the senator Sabinianus). — He orders the harbor of Lucina and the adjoining harbors to be repaired and more careful attention to be given to them in the future.

525 LETTER XXVI (Theodoric to Faustus, praetorian prefect). — He decrees that what the bishop of the Church of Vercellae formerly obtained shall remain valid forever, and that he shall not feel the extraordinary taxes paid since the time of Cassiodorus; yet he wishes the property later granted to the Church to remain subject to the burden of payment. Ibid.

LETTER XXVII (Theodoric to Speciosus). — He reports that the people of the Prasinian faction, while coming to the court, suffered an ambush at the hands of the patrician Theodoricus and the consul Importunus, so that one man was killed; and he orders that Speciosus warn the aforesaid illustrious men to send properly authorized representatives to the judgment of Caelianus and Agapitus, who are to settle the case according to law.

526 LETTER XXVIII (Theodoric to all Goths and Romans). — By this letter he decrees that, if anyone possesses stones of any kind lying on his fields that would be useful for walls, he should willingly devote them to the restoration of the cities.

527 LETTER XXIX (Theodoric to all the Lucristani). — He orders that the tracts of land formerly permitted to the *veredi* for their relays, once claimed by the possessor, be restored. Ibid.

LETTER XXX (Theodoric to the Roman Senate). — He complains to them that armed servile fury persecuted innocent people during the spectacles, and decrees that, if a senator’s servant has taken part in the killing of a free man, his master must hand him over to be punished according to law. If he delays producing the accused before the judges, he is to know that he will be fined ten pounds of gold.

528 LETTER XXXI (Theodoric to the Roman people). — He proclaims that, if anyone from the populace has inflicted atrocious injuries upon any senator, he must know that the prefect of the City will punish him according to the nature of the offense; and he orders the pantomimes to practice their arts in the places assigned to them.

529 LETTER XXXII (Theodoric to Agapitus, prefect of the City). — He reminds him that he has written to the Senate and the people, and orders that, if anyone has inflicted an injury upon a senator, he be immediately punished with the severity of the laws; but if a senator has subjected any free man to an unlawful killing, he must immediately undergo the penalty. He further decrees that Helladius shall receive the same monthly allowance as the other pantomimes.

530 LETTER XXXIII (Theodoric to the same). — By the present ordinance he decrees that the pantomime chosen by Albinus and Albienus receive the customary monthly allowance of the Prasinian faction without diminution.

531 LETTER XXXIV (Theodoric to Faustus, praetorian prefect). — He orders him to give notice at every maritime place that no one should dare load foreign ships with grain before the province has retained whatever is necessary for itself. Ibid.

LETTER XXXV (Theodoric to the same). — He states that he is somewhat disturbed because the public grain customarily transported by the chancellor from the Calabrian and Apulian coasts during the summer had not yet been brought in by autumn, and orders that this be corrected with the utmost speed.

Ibid. LETTER XXXVI (Theodoric to Theriolus the senator). — He orders him to assume the post at Pedona formerly held by Benedictus and to surround Benedictus’s sons with civil protection.

532 LETTER XXXVII (Theodoric to Crispianus). — He recalls him from exile, if he truly killed a man caught in adultery, and orders that the money extorted from Agnellus, Crispianus’s surety, by the urban vicar or his staff be restored; he also grants Crispianus the protection of Candacis against every attack.

533 LETTER XXXVIII (Theodoric to Coio the senator). — He orders him to restore as quickly as possible the property of his nephew Virilianus, which he had retained not merely with a view to increasing it but even with a view to reducing it.

534 LETTER XXXIX (Theodoric to Festus). — He writes that Filagrius had asked to return to his ancestral home and had sent his brother’s sons to Rome for study; he orders Festus to establish them in the City in such a way that they may not leave before he gives a second order. Ibid.

LETTER XL (Theodoric to Count Assius). — He orders him to provide the necessary weapons for the soldiers of Salona before they depart for war.

535 LETTER XLI (Theodoric to Agapitus). — He orders him to enroll the adult Faustus, son of the illustrious Faustus, among those to be reported to the curia.

536 LETTER XLII (Theodoric to Artemidorus). — The prefecture of the City is conferred upon him, and he is adorned with the highest praises. Ibid.

LETTER XLIII (Theodoric to the Senate). — He announces that he has bestowed upon Artemidorus the fasces of the urban prefecture.

537 LETTER XLIV (Theodoric to the Roman people). — He informs them that he has bestowed the urban prefecture upon Artemidorus.

538 LETTER XLV (Theodoric to Boethius). — Having been asked by the king of the Burgundians to send him a water-clock and a sundial, he invites Boethius to undertake and complete this work.

539 LETTER XLVI (Theodoric to Gundibadus). — He sends the clocks made by Boethius [Col. 1338].

541 BOOK TWO. Ibid.

LETTER ONE (Theodoric to the Emperor Anastasius). — He announces that Felix the Gaul has been made consul. Ibid.

LETTER II (Theodoric to Felix). — The consulship is conferred upon him.

543 LETTER III (Theodoric to the Senate). — The promotion of Felix the Gaul to the consulship is announced.

545 LETTER IV (Theodoric to Ecdicius). — He confers the titles connected with the *siliquaticum* or monopoly.

546 LETTER V (Theodoric to Faustus, prefect). — He orders him to provide the thirty soldiers stationed at the Augustan frontier posts with the same grain allowances as are given to the others. Ibid.

LETTER VI (Theodoric to Agapitus). — He is chosen as an envoy to be sent to the East.

547 LETTER VII (Theodoric to Suna). — He orders him to collect for the construction of the walls the squared marble blocks scattered about, ruined, and neglected. Ibid.

LETTER VIII (Theodoric to Severus, bishop). — Fifteen hundred solidi are sent through Montanarius so that he may distribute them among provincials who have suffered losses through the army.

548 LETTER IX (Theodoric to Faustus, prefect). — He decrees that Sabinus the charioteer receive, in addition to his monthly solidus, another one, so that he may not be forced to beg. Ibid.

LETTER X (Theodoric to Speciosus). — The contract made by Agapita while she was separated from her husband is rescinded.

549 LETTER XI (Theodoric to Provinus). — He orders him to restore to Agapita’s husband the house at Arecira that Agapita had conferred upon him. Ibid.

LETTER XII (Theodoric to the count of the *siliquatarii*). — He orders him not to allow salted pork to be sent to foreign provinces.

550 LETTER XIII (Theodoric to Fruinarith). — He orders him to summon Venantius to appear on behalf of Ulpianus.

551 LETTER XIV (Theodoric to Symmachus). — He sets out the crime of a certain Romulus, who was said to have laid violent hands upon his own father, and requests that punishment be inflicted upon him. Ibid.

LETTER XV (Theodoric to Venantius). — He confers upon him the office of count of the household troops.

553 LETTER XVI (Theodoric to the Senate). — The appointment of Venantius as count of the household troops is announced. Ibid.

LETTER XVII (Theodoric to the honored possessors, defenders, and curials residing in the city of Tridentum). — He declares that he has exempted the presbyter Butilianus from payment of the fiscal assessment and forbids anyone else to exact what he has remitted to him.

555 LETTER XVIII (Theodoric to Gudila, bishop). — He decrees how the lawsuit between the municipal citizens of Sarcina and the Church is to be settled. Ibid.

LETTER XIX (Theodoric to all Goths and Romans and to those in charge of harbors and frontier posts). — He orders that the servants who slaughtered their master Stephanus be punished with the ultimate penalty.

556 LETTER XX (Theodoric to Uniligus). — He decrees that whatever ships he finds in the city loaded with fiscal grain be sent to Liguria, which is suffering from a shortage of crops. Ibid.

LETTER XXI (Theodoric to John the apparitor). — The king had granted the marshes in the territory of Spoleto to Speius and Domitius on the condition that, if the waste water were drained through their labor, the reclaimed fields would benefit them. But since, through Domitius’s fault, the work begun had come to nothing, he orders John to summon him either to complete the undertaking or to yield Speius his own share.

557 LETTER XXII (Theodoric to Festus). — He orders him to require the sons of Ecdicius to return from the City to their father’s homeland for burial.

558 LETTER XXIII (Theodoric to Ampelius, Despotius, and Theodulus). — Potteries are granted to them by the king, and royal protection against dishonest and deceitful persons is promised. Ibid.

LETTER XXIV (Theodoric to the Senate). — He says that, from the reports of provincial judges sent to the praetorian prefect, he has learned that the time for the first collection of taxes had passed in such a way that little or nothing had apparently been paid by the senatorial houses; consequently the poor, whom it would have been proper to relieve, had been oppressed. He therefore warns the Senate to arrange everything equitably, so that whatever each senatorial house declares may be paid through the appointed agents in the provinces in three installments. Ibid.

LETTER XXV (or, Theodoric’s edict). — The king complains that possessors or curials have been oppressed because the leading men had not paid the sum assessed upon them; and he orders that, if anyone feels himself burdened for this reason, he bring his complaints before the king.

559 LETTER XXVI (Theodoric to Faustus). — He forbids the merchants of Apulia and Calabria to be burdened in the future and imposes fines upon those who violate these commands of the ruler. Then follows an edict concerning goldsmiths.

560 [Col. 1339] LETTER XXVII (Theodoric to all the Jews of Genoa). — He permits them to repair their synagogue, but not to enlarge it, provided that the thirty-year prescription does not stand in the way.

561 LETTER XXVIII (Theodoric to Stephanus the senator). — Stephanus is praised, and the dignity of *spectabilis*, or a first-order comitiva, is conferred upon him, together with certain distinguished privileges. Ibid.

LETTER XXIX (Theodoric to Adila the senator). — He orders him to protect the estates and people of the Church of Milan located in Sicily; yet he wishes them to answer as soon as possible the public and private lawsuits brought against them.

563 LETTER XXX (Theodoric to Faustus). — One of the merchants of the Church of Milan, who was to be assigned to the service of the poor, is exempted from the payment of taxes, a privilege previously granted to the Church of Ravenna. Ibid.

LETTER XXXI (Theodoric to the *dromonarii*). — He informs them that he has ordered the count of the sacred largesses to station *dromonarii* at Hostilia and has assigned them public money for their customary expeditions with the *veredarii* along the channel of the Po.

564 LETTER XXXII (Theodoric to the Senate). — He decrees that two senators be sent to the marsh of Decennonium, which the patrician Decius had requested to have drained, and that they make the area marked out by fixed boundaries the property of Decius. Ibid.

LETTER XXXIII (Theodoric to the patrician Decius). — He grants Decius ownership of the marsh of Decennonium; then he decrees that, if anyone chooses to undertake this labor together with him, that person shall, after the work has been assessed, possess as his own the area corresponding to the portion of the work he has undertaken.

565 LETTER XXXIV (Theodoric to Artemidorus, prefect of the City). — He decrees that the money assigned to the Roman buildings, not spent but embezzled, be recovered and applied to the repair of the walls. He admits that those who concealed this money ought to be punished, but mercifully pardons them. Ibid.

LETTER XXXV (Theodoric to the senator Tancila). — He warns him to search for a bronze statue stolen from the city of Como, promising one hundred gold pieces to anyone who reveals the theft.

566 LETTER XXXVI (Theodoric’s edict). — The king promises one hundred gold pieces and pardon for the crime to anyone who voluntarily discloses the theft of the bronze statue. He then threatens death to anyone who conceals the offense and is discovered through another person’s testimony. Ibid.

LETTER XXXVII (Theodoric to Faustus, praetorian prefect). — The king grants the citizens of Spoleto, for the maintenance of the baths, an additional thousand beyond the customary amount.

567 LETTER XXXVIII (Theodoric to the same). — He forbids the merchants of Sipontum, devastated by enemy depredation, to be harassed for two full years on account of fiscal payments and the sums they had borrowed. Ibid.

LETTER XXXIX (Theodoric to Aloisius the architect). — The king states that he wishes the spring of Aponus, whose various powers he vividly describes, to be restored. To ensure the success of this undertaking, he orders the ancient solidity of the buildings there to be renewed and the palace, shaken by long age, to be repaired.

568 LETTER XL (Theodoric to Boethius). — He says that the king of the Franks had earnestly requested a harpist. He asks Boethius, an expert in music, to select one. He discusses at length the praise of music, tones, modes, and related matters.

570 LETTER XLI (Theodoric to Clovis). — He congratulates Clovis on his victory over the Alamanni; then advises clemency toward those who, driven from the borders of Italy, were hiding; finally, he informs him that he has sent two envoys to Gaul with the requested harpist.

573 BOOK THREE.

575 LETTER ONE (Theodoric to Alaric). — He warns him not to trust in the multitude of his kinsmen and not to declare war against the king of the Franks until he sends envoys to him to settle the dispute that has arisen between them; for this reason he sends him envoys who are also to approach Gundibadus and the other kings. Ibid.

LETTER II (Theodoric to Gundibadus). — Through the envoys sent to him, he urges Gundibadus to restore concord between Alaric and Clovis. Ibid.

LETTER III (to the kings of the Heruli, Warni, and Thuringi). — He urges them to send envoys, together with their own and Gundibadus’s, to Clovis, so that either he may restrain his expedition against the Visigoths and seek the law of nations, or may know that he will suffer attacks from all of them.

576 LETTER IV (Theodoric to Clovis). — He urges him not to prepare war against Alaric until their dispute is settled through friendly mediation; and he threatens that he and his allies will take up arms against anyone who disregards these warnings. For this reason he sends envoys to both parties.

577 LETTER V (Theodoric to Importunus). — Importunus is praised together with his father and uncle, and, on account of his distinguished merits, the insignia of the patriciate are conferred upon him.

578 [Col. 1340] LETTER VI (Theodoric to the Senate). — He extols the Roman Senate, as well as Importunus, with many praises; he had raised Importunus to the dignity of patrician, and commends him highly to the Senate.

579 LETTER VII (Theodoric to Januarius). — He orders him to pay John the price of sixty *orcae* of oil, which he had received from him for supplying the lamps.

580 LETTER VIII (Theodoric to Venantius the senator). — He warns him to complete the appointed periods for the collection of the twofold and threefold assessment entrusted to him. Ibid.

LETTER IX (Theodoric to the possessors, defenders, and curials residing at Aestunum). — He orders them to arrange for marble columns and unused stones lying about to be transported to the city of Ravenna.

581 LETTER X (Theodoric to Festus). — He orders the marbles from the Pincian house to be carried by the *catabulenses* to the city of Ravenna. Ibid.

LETTER XI (Theodoric to Argolicus, prefect of the City). — The urban prefecture is conferred upon him, and distinguished advice is given to him for carrying out that dignity honorably.

LETTER XII (Theodoric to the Roman Senate). — He adorns Argolicus and his relatives with many praises and expresses his wish that the Senate’s approved choice of him as prefect of the City be confirmed.

582 LETTER XIII (Theodoric to Sunhivadus the senator). — He praises him and orders him to proceed to Samnium to settle disputes between Romans and Goths.

583 LETTER XIV (Theodoric to Aurigenus the bishop). — He writes that Julian has complained that his wife, or his property, had been taken away by the bishop’s subjects; and he orders that, if the matter is indeed so, the guilty party be punished as soon as possible.

584 LETTER XV (Theodoric to Theodahadus the senator). — A person who had evaded the judgment of Sona is entrusted to his judgment for examination. Ibid.

LETTER XVI (Theodoric to Gemellus the senator). — He is sent to Gaul to discharge the office of deputy to the prefects, and is given many useful instructions.

LETTER XVII (Theodoric to the provincials of Gaul). — He announces that he has sent Gemellus as deputy to the prefects to govern their province and orders them to obey his commands.

585 LETTER XVIII (Theodoric to Gemellus the senator). — He orders that the property of Magnus, who had returned from the enemy’s side to his native land, be restored without any delay.

586 LETTER XIX (Theodoric to Daniel). — This highly skilled marble-worker is granted permission to distribute marble coffins in the city of Ravenna for burying the dead. Ibid.

LETTER XX (Theodoric to Grimoda the saio and Ferrocinctus the apparitor). — He decrees that, if Faustus has either burdened with charges what Castorius possessed or retained it through private usurpation, the estate, together with another of equal value, be immediately restored to him by the usurper under their compulsion.

587 LETTER XXI (Theodoric to Faustus). — He grants him a four-month respite to withdraw from the city of Rome into the province for his own advantage. Ibid.

LETTER XXII (Theodoric to Artemidorus). — He summons him to court and to his companionship.

588 LETTER XXIII (Theodoric to Colossaeus). — He entrusts him with the administration of Sirmian Pannonia and furnishes him with salutary instructions for performing this office well. Ibid.

LETTER XXIV (Theodoric to all the barbarians and Romans residing in Pannonia). — He orders them to obey Colossaeus and to abhor single combat, following the example of the Goths.

589 LETTER XXV (Theodoric to Count Simeon). — He entrusts him with the title of *siliquaticum* throughout Dalmatia and orders him to search for iron deposits; he describes the uses and benefits of iron.

590 LETTER XXVI (Theodoric to Count Osunus). — He orders him not to deny Simeon the assistance necessary for the tasks for which he was sent to Pannonia. Ibid.

LETTER XXVII (Theodoric to John the senator). — He protects him, already shaken by various persecutions, from the praetorian prefect, and also urges him to perform the office of consulship with the greatest fidelity. Ibid.

LETTER XXVIII (Theodoric to Cassiodorus). — He summons him, adorned with many praises, to his court.

591 LETTER XXIX (Theodoric to Argolicus). — He writes that he has granted the patrician Paulinus warehouses ruined by age so that he might rebuild them and convert them to his own uses.

592 LETTER XXX (to the same). — He orders him to assist Joanna in repairing the Roman sewers. Ibid.

LETTER XXXI (Theodoric to the Senate). — He writes that he has sent John to investigate those who had diverted the water of the aqueducts for their private use, as well as those who had removed bronze and lead from the adornment of the walls, and he warns the Senate to assist him in these matters.

593 LETTER XXXII (Theodoric to Gemellus the senator). — He writes that he has remitted, for the fourth indiction, the taxes of the people of Arles who had supported the king’s side and for that reason had endured siege and scarcity.

594 LETTER XXXIII (Theodoric to Argolicus). — He orders that Armentarius and his son Superbus enjoy the same privileges as those who are to be reported to the curia. Ibid.

LETTER XXXIV (Theodoric to the people of Massilia). — He writes that he has sent Count Marabadus to protect them and orders them to obey him willingly.

595 LETTER XXXV (Theodoric to Romulus). — He confirms whatever Liberius had granted to him and his mother by royal edict through a *pictatium*.

596 LETTER XXXVI (Theodoric to Arigernus). — He orders him to warn Venantius to send an authorized representative to court who can answer before the judges appointed by the king concerning Firminus’s accounts. Ibid.

LETTER XXXVII (Theodoric to Peter the bishop). — He orders him to restore to Germanus the share of property he was retaining, if Germanus is Thomatis’s legitimate son; if he refuses, he wishes the case brought before the court.

Ibid. LETTER XXXVIII (Theodoric to Vuandil). — He orders him not to allow any violence by the army to be committed at Avignon.

597 LETTER XXXIX (Theodoric to Felix the consul). — He orders him to grant the charioteers of Milan what ancient custom had allowed them. Ibid.

LETTER XL (Theodoric to all the provincials residing in Gaul). — Since the provincials of Gaul had been devastated by the enemy, he remits their taxes in proportion to the damage suffered, but on the condition that they contribute something toward military expenses from whatever has remained untouched. Ibid.

LETTER XLI (Theodoric to Gemellus the senator). — He decrees that grain for military expenses be transported at common cost from the warehouses of Massilia to the forts situated beyond the Durance.

598 LETTER XLII (Theodoric to all the provincials residing in Gaul). — He announces that he has sent military supplies from Italy to the soldiers so that Gaul would not be excessively burdened. Ibid.

LETTER XLIII (Theodoric to Uniges). — He orders that, when the army has entered Gaul, slaves who have gone over to other masters be restored to their former owners.

599 LETTER XLIV (Theodoric to all the possessors of Arles). — He writes that he has sent them a fixed sum of money and provisions for repairing the old walls and towers of Arles. Ibid.

LETTER XLV (Theodoric to Count Arigernus). — He entrusts to him for investigation a dispute that had arisen concerning a certain house between the defenders of the Roman Church and the Jews.

600 LETTER XLVI (Theodoric to Adeodatus). — He changes the most severe punishment to which he had been condemned by the corrector of Lucania and Bruttium for the abduction of the adult girl Valeriana, commuting it to six months’ exile, after which he is restored to his homeland and all his property. He then imposes a penalty of three pounds of gold upon violators of such a statute; finally, he frees from all fear those who had taken part in the crime in good faith. Ibid.

LETTER XLVII (Theodoric to Faustus, praetorian prefect). — He writes that he has commuted the capital punishment of Jovinus, the slayer of his colleague, to exile on the Aeolian Islands because he had taken refuge within the precincts of a church; the islands are described.

601 LETTER XLVIII (Theodoric to all Goths and Romans residing around the fortress of Veruca). — He writes that he has ordered the saio Leodifridus that, at his instigation, they build dwellings for themselves in the fortress of Veruca, which is described.

603 LETTER XLIX (Theodoric to the honored possessors, defenders, and curials of the city of Catana). — He permits them to use stones from the amphitheater, which had collapsed through long age, to repair the city walls.

604 LETTER L (Theodoric to the provincials of Noricum). — He decrees that the oxen of the Alemanni, exhausted by the length and hardship of the journey, be exchanged for oxen of the Noricans. Ibid.

LETTER LI (Theodoric to Faustus). — He writes that Thomates, a charioteer frequently victorious in the spectacles, to whom he had granted proper grain allowances, is to be supported by a monthly grant; then he speaks at length about the spectacles and the circus of the Emperor Augustus. Ibid.

LETTER LII (Theodoric to the Consular). — He orders him to choose a surveyor to settle the dispute that had arisen between Leontius and Paschasius concerning the boundaries of houses.

607 LETTER LIII (Theodoric to Apronianus). — He orders that, if he finds the water-engineer who had come to Rome from Africa to be highly skilled in this art, he relieve his poverty with the necessary grain allowances and assign him a mechanic to assist him through his work.

609 BOOK FOUR. Ibid.

LETTER ONE (Theodoric to the king of the Thuringi). — He gives him his niece in marriage, and she is praised; he announces that he had gladly received from the betrothed woman horses, whose beauty is described, as well as other gifts. Ibid.

LETTER II (Theodoric to the king of the Heruli). — He adopts him as a son through arms and gives him horses, swords, shields, and the other instruments of war [Col. 1342].

611 LETTER III (Theodoric to Count Senarius). — The dignity of count of the patrimony is conferred upon him, and he is praised to the highest degree.

612 LETTER IV (Theodoric to the Roman Senate). — He announces that he has raised the illustrious Senarius to the office of count of the patrimony; he is extolled with many praises.

613 LETTER V (Theodoric to Count Amabilis). — He decrees that all the shipowners of Campania, Lucania, or Tuscany entrust themselves to suitable guarantors to transport provisions to Gaul, which is suffering from famine, and distribute them for payment.

614 LETTER VI (Theodoric to Symmachus). — He orders him to keep in Rome the sons of Valerianus, whom their father had brought there for study; they are not to be permitted to leave before he gives the order.

615 LETTER VII (Theodoric to Count Senarius). — He informs him that those who were transporting grain from Sicily to Gaul suffered the most grievous shipwreck; therefore he orders that the wheat lost be credited to them. Ibid.

LETTER VIII (Theodoric to the possessors and curials of Fréjus). — He decrees that, once the price has been received, they transport beams from their homeland to Alsuanus without any delay.

616 LETTER IX (Theodoric to Count Osuinus). — He orders that, if anyone brings a lawsuit against Maurentius and Paula, deprived of their father’s assistance, he send the parties to the royal court.

617 LETTER X (Theodoric to John the senator). — He decrees that an edict be promulgated against those who voluntarily devote themselves to the practice of taking pledges; and he orders that anyone who may have seized something, for the sake of taking a pledge, that he ought to have reclaimed, lose it by force of law. If anyone is unable to pay, he wishes him punished with clubs. Ibid.

LETTER XI (Theodoric to Count Senarius). — He sends back to him for careful examination and settlement the case between the possessors of Volia and the curials.

618 LETTER XII (Theodoric to Count Marabadus and Gemellus the senator). — He entrusts to them the case between Archotamia and Aetheria, her daughter-in-law, to be heard according to the laws, so that, with the sacred Gospels present and with three distinguished legal experts, they may deliver a judgment in accordance with the form of the ancient law.

619 LETTER XIII (Theodoric to Count Senarius). — He informs him that he has decreed that grain allowances be provided according to ancient custom to Colossaeus, who had been sent to Sirmian Pannonia.

620 LETTER XIV (Theodoric to Gesila the saio). — He orders him to compel the Goths residing in both Tuscanies to pay their due taxes and to punish the recalcitrant. Ibid.

LETTER XV (Theodoric to the senator Benenatus). — He orders him to select twenty-one sturdy *dromonarii* in place of the deceased and test their strength.

621 LETTER XVI (Theodoric to the Senate). — He announces that he has entrusted Arigernus, the count whom he praises for his distinguished achievements, with the administration of the Roman city, and orders everyone to obey him. Ibid.

LETTER XVII (Theodoric to Ida the duke). — He orders him to ensure that the possessions of the Church of Narbonne, occupied by certain usurpers, be restored.

622 LETTER XVIII (Theodoric to Anna the senator). — He decrees that she investigate carefully whether the presbyter Laurentius, after excavating the graves of the dead, found treasures. Ibid.

LETTER XIX (Theodoric to Gemellus the senator). — He writes that, for the present, he has remitted payment of the *siliquaticum* on grain, wine, and oil, so that he may be able to supply abundance to the provinces.

623 LETTER XX (Theodoric to Geberich the senator). — He decrees that one *jugerum* belonging to the Church of Bishop Constantius, granted through the piety of the rulers and held by usurpers, be restored. Ibid.

LETTER XXI (Theodoric to Gemellus the senator). — He warns him to be diligent in the tasks assigned to him, since the urgency of the times requires it.

624 LETTER XXII (Theodoric to Argolicus, prefect of the City). — He reports that he has learned from him that Basilius and Praetextatus were accused of magical practices, and decrees that, taking five senators with him and also calling upon Count Arigernus, he examine the case while observing the proper legal procedure; if they find them guilty, they are to be punished with the rigor of the laws. Ibid.

LETTER XXIII (Theodoric to Count Arigernus). — He orders him to search for Basilius and Praetextatus, accused of magic and escaped by flight, and, when found, bring them before the five-man tribunal, where he is to ensure that the case is investigated and concluded.

625 LETTER XXIV (Theodoric to Elpidius the deacon). — He grants permission to build in certain places of the city of Spoleto that have been worn out by age, provided that they do not serve a public use. Ibid.

[Col. 1343] LETTER XXV (Theodoric to Argolicus, prefect of the City). — He decrees that Peter, distinguished by birth and a candidate for senatorial rank, obtain the fulfillment of his desire according to ancient custom.

626 LETTER XXVI (Theodoric to the people of Massilia). — He confirms the immunity granted to their region by the rulers and promises that he will free them from every burden; he also remits their assessment for the present year. Ibid.

LETTER XXVII (Theodoric to Tezutzat the saio). — He entrusts to him the protection of Peter, which he takes away from the saio Amara because Amara had wished to kill Peter; and he orders Amara to restore twofold whatever advantage he had received from Peter and to appear before the judgment of Count Duda to answer for the wound he inflicted.

627 LETTER XXVIII (Theodoric to Duda the senator). — He appoints him judge of the case of the saio...

Amarae, who had wounded Peter. 628

**LETTER XXIX (Theodoric to Argolicus, Urban Prefect).**—He reproaches him because, led by his own advantage, he has not yet fulfilled the prince’s commands; and he decrees that he carry out the orders without delay. Ibid.

**LETTER XXX (Theodoric to Albinus).**—Permission is granted him to use the curved portico, so that he may construct new buildings upon it, provided that they do not prejudice public utility or beauty. 629

**LETTER XXXI (Theodoric to Aemilianus, bishop).**—He urges him to complete the aqueduct which, by royal authority, he had undertaken to repair. Ibid.

**LETTER XXXII (Theodoric to Duda, saio).**—He states that he has learned that the property of the outlaw Tupha had been deposited with John under the security of a written bond; and he orders him to summon John’s wife and his son Januarius, and, unless they freely return it, to have them come before the governor of Campania to be heard according to the laws. Ibid.

**LETTER XXXIII (Theodoric to the Jews established at Genoa).**—He confirms the privileges which the laws had granted them. 630

**LETTER XXXIV (Theodoric to Duda, saio).**—He decrees that he visit the places where treasures lie hidden and, if they are found, assign them to the public treasury. Ibid.

**LETTER XXXV (Theodoric to Albinus’s agents).**—He permits Albinus’s property to be restored in full, if his age permits and justice and the laws are preserved—property in which he had suffered serious loss through fraudulent contracts. 631

**LETTER XXXVI (Theodoric to Faustus).**—He announces that he has remitted the public tax for the provincials of the Cottian Alps for the third indiction, whose fields the passing army had devastated. 632

**LETTER XXXVII (Theodoric to Theodagunda).**—He makes known that Renatus has complained that, although he had obtained a judgment against Inquilina, his adversary nevertheless did not cease from calumny; and he orders that the matter, already concluded, be maintained in its own validity, provided that Inquilina has not appealed lawfully. Ibid.

**LETTER XXXVIII (Theodoric to Faustus).**—He states that the Gravasiani and Pontonates have complained that Januarius and Probus had burdened them with unjust exactions; and he decrees that they pay nothing other than what they had been accustomed to pay in the time of Odoacer. 633

**LETTER XXXIX (Theodoric to Theodahad).**—He writes that Domitianus had complained that his possessions had been seized with the greatest injustice; and he orders him, with the saio Duda attending, to arrange without any delay that everything taken away be restored. If, however, he should believe that anything favors the invaders, he orders a properly instructed person to be sent to the court, so that, after both parties have been heard, a just sentence may be issued. Ibid.

**LETTER XL (Theodoric to Probinus’s agents).**—He reminds them that he had long ago ordered that the Areciretine estate, which Probinus had bought from his wife Agapita, be restored to Basil; now he orders that Basil himself promptly answer the new purchasers’ claims. 634

**LETTER XLI (Theodoric to John, chief physician).**—He declares that he annuls the sentence promulgated against him by the deputy of the city of Rome through Vivianus’s contrivance, restores him to his homeland and all his possessions, and henceforth places him under the protection of the patrician Albinus. 635

**LETTER XLII (Theodoric to Argolicus).**—He orders that the tower of the Circus and the site of the amphitheater be restored to Marcianus and Maximus, the sons of Volusianus, who complained that they had been taken from them while they were occupied in mourning their father’s death. 636

**LETTER XLIII (Theodoric to the Roman Senate).**—He decrees that an inquiry be made into those who had stirred up a riot and burned the synagogue of the Jews, and that punishment be inflicted upon the few perpetrators whom he is able to discover. Ibid.

**LETTER XLIV (Theodoric to Antonius, bishop).**—He writes that Stephanus had complained that a house belonging to him had been occupied by subjects of the Church over which Antonius presided; he orders him to restore it to the petitioner. If anything should support the occupants, he wishes a properly instructed person to be sent to the court, where the matter is to be brought to an end. 637

**LETTER XLV (Theodoric to the counts, defenders, and curiales of the city of Ticinum).**—He orders them to provide the Heruli with a ship as far as the city of Ravenna, and grain rations for five days. 638

**LETTER XLVI (Theodoric to Marabadus).**—He reports that Liberius had suggested that his wife had been placed at a disadvantage in court. If this is so, he permits the case either to be examined by arbitrators chosen by the parties or for the parties to come to the court for judgment. Ibid.

**LETTER XLVII (Theodoric to Gudisal, saio).**—He states that he has learned from his envoys that the post-horses are being exhausted by more frequent travel, and that those which he had ordered to be kept for public use are being appropriated for private use. Therefore he decrees that no Goth or Roman be allowed to leave Rome unless the prefect of the praetorium and the master of offices have released him; that whoever takes even one horse against the will of those entrusted with this responsibility be compelled to pay one hundred solidi as a fine; and that no one place more than one hundred pounds of weight upon a horse. 639

**LETTER XLVIII (Theodoric to Eusebius).**—He permits him to withdraw to Lucania for eight months, after which he is to return to Rome. 640

**LETTER XLIX (Theodoric to the provincials, capillati, defenders, and curiales residing in Suavia).**—He informs them that he has appointed Fridibad as governor of their province. Ibid.

**LETTER L (Theodoric to Faustus).**—He orders him to send a trustworthy man to the Nolan or Neapolitan territory devastated by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius, so that, after the fields there have been carefully inspected, the possessor may be relieved of a burden of taxation proportionate to the amount of damage suffered. The eruption of Mount Vesuvius is described at length. 641

**LETTER LI (Theodoric to Symmachus).**—He praises him for the many splendid buildings which he had arranged to be constructed in the City and its suburbs, and asks him to strengthen and repair the ruined Theater of Pompey at the king’s expense. The theater and the events taking place in it are described. 642

**BOOK FIVE.** 643

**LETTER I (Theodoric to the king of the Vandals).**—He writes that he most willingly received the weapons sent by him and, through his envoys, presents him with other gifts in return. Ibid.

**LETTER II (Theodoric to the Haesti).**—He makes known that he gladly received amber through their envoys; he describes where it originates. 645

**LETTER III (Theodoric to Honoratus, quaestor).**—He confers upon him the office of quaestor, which his brother Decoratus had held while alive; both brothers are praised exceedingly. 646

**LETTER IV (Theodoric to the Roman Senate).**—He declares that he has chosen Honoratus, the brother of Decoratus, as quaestor. After he has spoken splendidly of the quaestorship, both brothers are praised, and he asks that Honoratus be enrolled in their company. 647

**LETTER V (Theodoric to Mannila, saio).**—He teaches what he is and is not to do in the office of saio. 648

**LETTER VI (Theodoric to the comitiacum Stabularius).**—He orders him to attach to the treasury all the property of Thomatis, who owed twelve thousand solidi on account of certain estates belonging to the royal house, but to return it to him if he pays by the Kalends of September; otherwise it is to be handed over to John, who had promised that he would pay the aforesaid sum into the treasury. 649

**LETTER VII (Theodoric to John).**—He hands over Thomatis’s property to him, provided that he pays ten thousand solidi into the treasury on Thomatis’s behalf and that Thomas himself does not satisfy the debt by the Kalends of September. 650

**LETTER VIII (Theodoric to Anastasius, consular governor).**—He decrees that he arrange for squared stones to be transported from the city of Faventia to Ravenna without anyone’s loss. 651

**LETTER IX (Theodoric to the possessors of Feltria).**—He orders them to devote themselves to building the walls of a new city in the region of Tridentum. Ibid.

**LETTER X (Theodoric to Veranus, saio).**—He orders him to ensure that the passing Gepids, whom he was sending to guard Gaul, cause no damage to Venetia or Liguria; for this reason, all necessities are to be supplied to them. 652

**LETTER XI (Theodoric to the Gepids).**—To the Gepids departing for Gaul he grants three gold solidi per week. Ibid.

**LETTER XII (Theodoric to Theodahad).**—He orders that the estate of Palentiana, seized from the heirs of Argolicus and Amandianus, be restored; if, however, anything should support the invaders, he orders them to come before the court to defend their right. 653

**LETTER XIII (Theodoric to Eutropius and Acretius).**—He warns them to provide the army with the stipulated grain rations, lest the provincials be exposed to its plundering. Ibid.

**LETTER XIV (Theodoric to Severianus).**—He places him in charge of the taxes to be imposed on each person according to the variety of his possessions, and orders him to investigate whether the judges, because of their more frequent traveling through the provinces, have inflicted unlawful losses upon the inhabitants. 653

**LETTER XV (Theodoric to all possessors established in Suavia).**—He writes that he has sent Severinus to them with edicts, so that he may relieve those oppressed by the burden of taxation. 655

**LETTER XVI (Theodoric to Abundantius, prefect of the praetorium).**—He orders him to search throughout Italy and purchase timber for building one thousand dromons, and to gather a suitable number of sailors to serve the fleets. 656

**LETTER XVII (Theodoric to the same).**—He praises him for the sudden construction of the ships and orders him to send them to Ravenna and arrange for others to be built. He then forbids fishermen to block the channels of the Mincius, Ollius, and the other rivers with their fences. 657

**LETTER XVIII (Theodoric to Uvilius, count of the patrimony).**—He writes that he had ordered sailors to be sought and sent to Ravenna; then he orders that, if any timber suitable for building dromons is found along the bank of the Po, even on royal estates, it may be cut down. 658

**LETTER XIX (Theodoric to Gudinandus, saio).**—He orders that the sailors who have been gathered be sent to Ravenna more quickly. 659

**LETTER XX (Theodoric to Avilfus, saio).**—He decrees that he go to the bank of the Po with craftsmen to cut timber suitable for dromons, but without harming the possessors. He also orders that the fences be removed from the rivers Mincius, Ollius, Anser, Tiber, and Arno, so that the river channels may be open to the passage of ships. Ibid.

**LETTER XXI (Theodoric to Capuanus, senator).**—He raises him up with many praises and confers upon him the administration of the decuries; he explains what this dignity is. 660

**LETTER XXII (Theodoric to the Roman Senate).**—He announces that he has chosen Capuanus, adorned with outstanding virtues, as administrator of the decuries. 661

**LETTER XXIII (Theodoric to Abundantius).**—He orders him to provide grain rations and transport vessels for the archers assigned to Count Julianus. 662

**LETTER XXIV (Theodoric to Epiphanius, senator).**—He warns him to attach to the royal treasury the property of Joanna, who was said to have died intestate and without surviving relatives, provided that he discovers the matter to be so. Ibid.

**LETTER XXV (Theodoric to Bacauda).**—He grants him permanently the administration of the tribunate of Milan. 663

**LETTER XXVI (Theodoric to all Goths).**—He orders them to come to the court on the eighth day before the Ides of June, without any damage to the provincials, to receive royal gifts. Ibid.

**LETTER XXVII (Theodoric to Guduim, saio).**—He orders him to notify the millenarii of the provinces of Picenum and Samnium that they must hasten to the court, both to receive a donative and to give an account of their deeds in war. 664

**LETTER XXVIII (Theodoric to Carinus).**—He summons him to his court as an illustrious man indispensable to him. Ibid.

**LETTER XXIX (Theodoric to Neudes).**—He orders that the blind Ocerus not be dragged into slavery if he is found to have proved himself freeborn. 665

**LETTER XXX (Theodoric to Guduim).**—He orders that servile burdens be removed from Costula and Daila, who enjoy the freedom of the Goths. Ibid.

**LETTER XXXI (Theodoric to Decoratus).**—He decrees that Marcus the presbyter, Andreas, and the others be compelled to pay money to the treasury if it is established that they are debtors. Ibid.

**LETTER XXXII (Theodoric to Brandila).**—He warns him to correct his wife Procula, who was said to have struck Patzenis’s wife most severely. If Brandila believes, however, that she has been falsely accused, he wishes him to come to the court with his wife to plead the case. 666

**LETTER XXXIII (Theodoric to Wilitanchus).**—He orders him to examine the case of Brandila, who had married Regina, the wife of Patzenis, while he was away on the Gallic expedition; and, if he finds the accusation true, to punish the adulterers. Ibid.

**LETTER XXXIV (Theodoric to Abundantius).**—He decrees that he compel Frontosus without delay to pay the public money which he had squandered and which he had repeatedly promised to repay. 667

**LETTER XXXV (Theodoric to Luvirit and Ampelius).**—He warns them that he had ordered a supply of grain to be transported from Spain to relieve the Romans’ scarcity; the shipmasters, however, had carried it to Africa and sold it. He therefore imposes upon them a fine of one thousand and thirty-eight solidi. 668

**LETTER XXXVI (Theodoric to Starcedius).**—Because of the weakness of his limbs, he exempts him from military service and permits him thereafter to lead a life of leisure, though deprived of the donative. 669

**LETTER XXXVII (Theodoric to the Jews of Milan).**—He preserves the rights formerly granted to their synagogue, provided that they do not harm the rights of the Church. Ibid.

**LETTER XXXVIII (Theodoric to all possessors).**—He orders that the trees growing in the bed of the river Signinus be cut out by the roots. 670

**LETTER XXXIX (Theodoric to Ampelius and Liveria).**—He sends them to Spain to suppress, by the authority of the laws, both murderers and those exacting the public tax who, through burdensome weights and measures, were oppressing the estates of the possessors; and, finally, all those engaged in evil and thieving acts. 671

**LETTER XL (Theodoric to Cyprianus, count of the sacred largesses).**—He confers upon him the office of count of the sacred largesses and adorns him with many praises. 673

**LETTER XLI (Theodoric to the Roman Senate).**—He announces that he has raised Cyprianus, radiant with his own merits and the splendor of his birth, to the office of count of the sacred largesses. 674

**LETTER XLII (Theodoric to Maximus, consul).**—The savagery of the spectacles, the amphitheater of Titus, and the games held there are described; he urges the consul to distribute rewards more generously to the combatants. 675

**LETTER XLIII (Theodoric to Transmundus, king of the Vandals).**—He praises his sister, whom he had given in marriage to Transmundus, and complains that Transmundus had kindly received Gesalecus, expelled from the kingdom for treachery, and sent him abroad with riches. 677

**LETTER XLIV (Theodoric to the same).**—He writes that he willingly accepted his apology and defense concerning the reception of Gesalecus, and returns the gifts he had offered him. 678

**BOOK SIX.** 679

Formula of the consulship. Ibid.

Formula of the patriciate. 681

Formula of the prefect of the praetorium. 682

Formula of the urban prefecture. 684

Formula for the master of the registry and for the office of first-order count, to be given to the comitiacus when he enters military service. Ibid.

Formula concerning matters to be referred in the Senate. 695

Formula of the deputy of the city of Rome. 696

Formula of the notaries. 697

Formula of the referendaries. 698
