Formula of the governor of a province. 702

Formula of the Syracusan countship. 704

Formula of the Neapolitan countship. 705

Formula for the honored possessors and curiales of the city of Naples. 706

Formula for soldiers. Ibid.

**BOOK SEVEN.** 705

Formula of the provincial countship. Ibid.

Formula of the governorship. 708

Formula of the Gothic countship in the individual provinces. 709

Formula of the command of Raetia. Ibid.

Formula of the administration of the palace. 710

Formula of the countship of the aqueducts of the City. 712

Formula of the prefect of the city watch of Rome. 713

Formula of the prefect of the city watch of Ravenna. 714

Formula of the countship of the port of Rome. 715

Formula of the tribune of entertainments. Ibid.

Formula of the defender of any city. 716

Formula of the city curator. 717

Formula of the Roman countship. Ibid.

Formula of the Ravennate countship. 718

Formula addressed to the Urban Prefect concerning the architect of public works. Ibid.

Formula of the countship of the islands of Curritana and Celsina. 719

Formula concerning the superintendent of Calcis. Ibid.

Formula concerning weapons manufacturers. 720

Formula addressed to the prefect of the praetorium concerning weapons manufacturers. Ibid.

Formula for pairs and groups of three when brought before a judge. 721

Formula for pairs and groups of three when brought through the official staff. Ibid.

Formula of a warning addressed to such-and-such registrars. Ibid.

Formula of the deputy of the port. 722

Formula of the governor of Dalmatia. Ibid.

Formula for commending governors to a count. Ibid.

Formula of the countship of various cities. 723

Formula for honored possessors and curiales. Ibid.

Formula of the commander of the soldiers’ countship. Ibid.

Formula concerning the guarding of the city gates. 724 [Col. 1347]

Formula of the provincial tribunate. 724

Formula of the principate of the city of Rome. 725

Formula by which the mint is entrusted. Ibid.

Formula of envoys to various peoples. 726

Formula of a summons issued by the prince. Ibid.

Formula of a summons granted to a petitioner. Ibid.

Formula of a travel permit. Ibid.

Formula of the rank of spectabilis. 727

Formula of the rank of clarissimus. Ibid.

Formula of protection. Ibid.

Formula concerning the confirmation of marriage and the establishment of children as legitimate. 728

Formula of a concession of age. Ibid.

Formula of an edict to the quaestor, requiring the person who deserves a saio to provide security. 729

Formula of a certificate for registrars. Ibid.

Formula concerning competitors. 730

Formula by which a census assessment is relieved for one who possesses a burdened house. Ibid.

Formula by which a female cousin is made a lawful wife. 731

Formula addressed to a prefect, authorizing him to sell estates by curial decree. 732

**BOOK EIGHT.** 733

**LETTER I (Athalaric to the emperor Justinian).**—He seeks his favor and friendship under the same conditions by which the earlier emperors had entered into an alliance with Theodoric. Ibid.

**LETTER II (Athalaric to the Roman Senate).**—He informs it that he has been created king by the unanimous consent of Goths and Romans, and sends Count Sigismer with others to administer oaths in his name. 734

**LETTER III (Athalaric to the Roman people).**—He exalts King Theodoric with splendid praises and announces to the Roman people that he has been raised to the throne by the common votes of Goths and Romans; through his envoys he promises to preserve justice. 736

**LETTER IV (Athalaric to all Romans established throughout Italy and Dalmatia).**—He writes that he has received the oaths of Goths and Romans as the protection of the kingdom he has acquired, and asks them to take the same oath. 737

**LETTER V (Athalaric to all Goths established throughout Italy).**—He states that, while Theodoric was still alive, he received the oath of all in the royal city, and urges them to follow their example. Through a count he also pledges them his faith under oath. Ibid.

**LETTER VI (Athalaric to Liberius, prefect of Gaul).**—He announces that Theodoric, while still alive, bestowed the kingdom upon him, and that Goths and Romans promised him loyalty under the sanctity of an oath. He then asks that those living in Gaul imitate them. 738

**LETTER VII (Athalaric to all provincials established throughout Gaul).**—He urges the Goths to swear to the Romans, and the Romans to the Goths in turn, that they will render loyalty to the king. Ibid.

**LETTER VIII (Athalaric to Victorinus, bishop).**—He announces that he succeeded after Theodoric’s death. Then, commending himself to Victorinus’s prayers, he asks him to exhort all the provincials to preserve loyalty to the prince. 739

**LETTER IX (Athalaric to Tholuit).**—The dignity of the patriciate is conferred upon him, and he is praised splendidly together with Gensemundus. Ibid.

**LETTER X (Athalaric to the Roman Senate).**—He sets forth Tulus’s outstanding deeds and writes that he has raised him to the summit of the patriciate. 741

**LETTER XI (Tholuit to the Senate).**—He urges the senators to give thanks to the king because the king has promoted him to the honor of the patriciate. 743

**LETTER XII (Athalaric to Arator).**—He praises him and his father greatly for their eloquence, and adorns him with the honor of the countship of the household troops. 744

**LETTER XIII (Athalaric to Ambrosius, quaestor).**—He extols him with many praises because he had wisely administered many offices under Theodoric. He then confers the quaestorship upon him. 745

**LETTER XIV (Athalaric to the Roman Senate).**—He adorns Ambrosius with exceptional praise and announces that he has marked him with the dignity of quaestor. 747

**LETTER XV (Athalaric to the Senate).**—He writes that it was most pleasing to him that they had chosen as pontiff the man whom Theodoric had designated. 748

**LETTER XVI (Athalaric to Opilio, count).**—He extols him and his brother with the highest praises and grants him the office of count of the sacred largesses. Ibid.

**LETTER XVII (Athalaric to the Roman Senate).**—He greatly praises Opilio, his father, and his brother, and asks that they support his promotion to the office of count of the sacred largesses. 749

**LETTER XVIII (Athalaric to Felix, quaestor).**—He celebrates him with the most ample praises and grants him the quaestorship. 751

**LETTER XIX (Athalaric to the Roman Senate).**—He adorns Felix and his family with numerous praises and writes that he has chosen him as quaestor. Ibid.

**LETTER XX (Athalaric to Albienus, prefect of the praetorium).**—He writes that he removed the prefect from office because of his wickedness and appointed Albienus in his place; Albienus is praised exceedingly. 752

**LETTER XXI (Athalaric to Cyprianus, patrician).**—He praises him for outstanding deeds of military valor and for his well-raised sons, whom he has presented to the king. He then confers upon him the dignity of the patriciate. 754

**LETTER XXII (Athalaric to the Roman Senate).**—After enumerating the praises of Cyprianus and his sons, he writes that he has raised him to the honor of the patriciate and urges them to support his election. 755

**LETTER XXIII (Athalaric to Bergantinus, count of the patrimony).**—He orders him to hand over without delay to Theodahad’s agents certain estates which had fallen to Theodahad from his mother’s property; Theodahad is praised extraordinarily. 756

**LETTER XXIV (Athalaric to the clergy of the Roman Church).**—He refers to the pope’s judgment those who have brought a suit against a Roman cleric. Whoever has despised the authority of the Holy See is to be held to have lost the case and punished with a fine of ten pounds of gold, to be distributed to the poor. 757

**LETTER XXV (Athalaric to John, illustrious man).**—He confirms Tulus’s generosity by which he had granted John a house situated in the Lucullan fortress. 758

**LETTER XXVI (Athalaric to all Reatini and Nursini).**—He places Quidilanus over them and orders them to obey him. Ibid.

**LETTER XXVII (Athalaric to Dumerit, saio, and Florentianus, comitiacus).**—He orders them to travel throughout the territory of Faventia, and, if they find anyone who has harassed Gothic or Roman inhabitants, to inflict both a fine and a penalty upon him after taking the amount of the damage into account. 759

**LETTER XXVIII (Athalaric to Cunigastus).**—He decrees that he order Tancanus, who had taken the small estate of Constantius and Venerius under the name of Fabricula and had reduced them to slavery, to appear before his tribunal, so that he may undergo a sentence consistent with the law. Ibid.

**LETTER XXIX (Athalaric to the honored possessors and curiales of the city of Parma).**—He orders them to open the mouths of the city sewers and that Genesius press this work forward. 760

**LETTER XXX (Athalaric to Genesius).**—He orders him to compel the ancient municipal inhabitants of Parma to clean the old channels so thoroughly that nothing impede the inflowing water. Ibid.

**LETTER XXXI (Athalaric to Severus).**—He describes the province of the Bruttii and orders both the provincials and the curiales, after providing guarantors and stipulating a penalty, to promise that they will remain for most of the year in whichever cities they prefer to inhabit. 761

**LETTER XXXII (Athalaric to the same).**—He depicts the spring of Arethusa and orders him both to seek out and punish those who had stolen Nimphadius’s horses. 762

**LETTER XXXIII (Athalaric to the same).**—He decrees that, on the day before the feast of Saint Cyprian, he meet with the possessors and tenants of various estates at the Lucanian assembly, called Leucothea, to repress the audacity of certain peasants who were stripping merchants of their goods. He then describes the place and the powers and marvels of the spring of Marcilianus. 763

**BOOK NINE.** 765

**LETTER I (Athalaric to Hilderic, king).**—He complains of Amalafrida’s death, inflicted by Hilderic. Then he sends envoys, through whom he asks him to excuse the crime. If he refuses, he threatens him with war. Ibid.

**LETTER II (Edict of Athalaric).**—He protects the curiales from every injury, imposing upon their harassers either a fine of ten pounds of gold or corporal punishment. 766

**LETTER III (Athalaric to Bergantinus, count of the patrimony).**—He orders him to send a registrar to the Rustician estate, within whose depths gold lies hidden, and to arrange for it to be dug out. He then describes the skill of goldsmiths. 768

**LETTER IV (Athalaric to Abundantius, prefect of the praetorium).**—He decrees that Agenantia, the wife of Campanianus, and her children be struck from the roll of the curiales and placed among the possessors. 769

**LETTER V (Athalaric to the bishops and honored men).**—He establishes that those who have hidden grain during a grain shortage sell it at a moderate price. 770

**LETTER VI (Athalaric to the first registrar).**—He permits him to go to the Baian bath for the sake of his health, while continuing during that time to receive the emoluments of military service. 771

**LETTER VII (Athalaric to Reparatus, Urban Prefect).**—He extols his father and father-in-law with many praises. Then he confers the urban prefecture upon him. 772 [Col. 1349]

**LETTER VIII (Athalaric to Osuin).**—He sends him again to govern the provinces of Dalmatia and Suavia. 773

**LETTER IX (Athalaric to all Goths and Romans).**—He announces that he has sent Count Osum to govern Dalmatia, together with Severinus, and orders them to obey them. Ibid.

**LETTER X (Athalaric to all possessors and defenders of the city of Syracuse, or to all provincials).**—He remits the taxes imposed upon them beyond custom, granting those harassed by the tax assessors permission to complain before the prince. 774

**LETTER XI (Athalaric to Gildias, count of the city of Syracuse).**—He forbids them to exact from the possessors anything added by Victor and Witigisclus to the taxes of the fourth indiction. 775

**LETTER XII (Athalaric to Victor and Witigisclus).**—He orders that, if they have exacted anything from the provincials beyond the taxable solidus during the fourth indiction, they return it without any reduction. 776

**LETTER XIII (Athalaric to Wilius, count of the patrimony).**—He orders him to arrange that fifty solidi be added annually, chargeable to the king’s accounts, to the domestic troops who serve the provincial counts, beyond the two hundred solidi and ten grain rations. Ibid.

**LETTER XIV (Athalaric to Gildias, count).**—He decrees that whatever has been extorted from the provincials for the repair of the walls either be restored or be spent on repairing the fortifications. He then reproaches him for claiming, in the name of the treasury’s right of escheat, the property of the dead without any distinction required by justice. Moreover, he says that the provincials complain that they have been burdened by every kind of summons. Finally, he establishes that the edicts promulgated by Theodoric for regulating the customs of the Sicilians be observed so strictly that anyone who attempts in any way to violate them is to be held guilty of sacrilege. 777

**LETTER XV (Athalaric to Pope John).**—He promulgates highly salutary decrees against simoniacs, in accordance with ancient senatorial resolutions. 778

**LETTER XVI (Athalaric to Salvantius, Urban Prefect).**—He orders that his edict and the senatorial resolutions concerning the abolition of simony be engraved on marble tablets and placed before the atrium of the Basilica of Saint Peter. 781

**LETTER XVII (Athalaric to Salvantius, Urban Prefect).**—He decrees that certain noble Romans be released, men who were being held in prison on the mere suspicion that a revolt had arisen; and he permits them to defend themselves according to the just laws. Ibid.

**LETTER XVIII (Edict of Athalaric).**

1. Against invaders of another’s property.
2. Against those who affix titles in the name of the public authority.
3. Against those who cunningly and perversely obtain a judgment from the princes.
4. Against those who separate other people’s marriages.
5. Against adulterers.
6. Against those who joined themselves to two wives.
7. Against men and women living in concubinage.
8. Against those who extorted gifts by intimidation.
9. Against sorcerers.
10. Against murderers.
11. Against those who appealed a second time in the same case from the ordinary judges.
12. Against violators of both his own edicts and Theodoric’s. 782

**LETTER XIX (Athalaric to the Roman Senate).**—He writes that he has issued an edict in twelve chapters, and orders that it be read in the Senate and displayed by the Urban Prefect for thirty days in the most frequented places. 786

**LETTER XX (Athalaric to all provincial judges).**—He establishes that his edict be read publicly for thirty days in the assemblies according to the customary ceremony. Ibid.

**LETTER XXI (Athalaric to the Roman Senate).**—He orders that professors of grammar, eloquence, and law receive their stipulated emoluments without any reduction. 787

**LETTER XXII (Athalaric to Paulinus, consul).**—He adorns Paulinus and his family with splendid praises. Then he confers upon him the insignia of the consulship. 789

**LETTER XXIII (Athalaric to the Roman Senate).**—He greatly extols Venantius, Paulinus’s father, and Paulinus himself, whom he had created consul, and asks them to support his election. 790

**LETTER XXIV (Athalaric to Senator, prefect of the praetorium).**—He enumerates the offices which Cassiodorus had held with the greatest honor and integrity under Theodoric and under Athalaric himself. Then, after heaping exceptional praises upon him, he confers the praetorian prefecture upon him. 791

**LETTER XXV (Athalaric to the Roman Senate).**—He writes that he has granted the praetorian prefecture to Cassiodorus, whom he greatly commends. 793

**BOOK TEN.** 795

**LETTER I (Amalasuntha to the emperor Justinian).**—She writes that after Athalaric’s death she admitted Theodahad into partnership in the kingdom and sent envoys to request an extension of the peace. Ibid.

**LETTER II (King Theodahad to Justinian).**—He states that Amalasuntha has taken him as her partner in the kingdom and asks him to favor his cause. 797 [Col. 1350]

**LETTER III (Amalasuntha to the Roman Senate).**—She announces that she has called Theodahad, adorned with many virtues and great wisdom, into partnership in the kingdom, and asks them on this account to give thanks to God. 798

**LETTER IV (Theodahad to the Roman Senate).**—He writes that Amalasuntha, who is exalted with many praises, has raised him to partnership in the rule. 799

**LETTER V (Theodahad to Theodosius).**—He forbids his household officers to grow arrogant in any way and orders them to serve as examples to the rest through modesty and observance of the laws. 800

**LETTER VI (Theodahad to Patricius, quaestor).**—He praises him greatly and raises him to the quaestorship. 801

**LETTER VII (Theodahad to the Roman Senate).**—He announces that he has conferred the dignity of quaestor upon Patricius, who shines with outstanding virtues. 802

**LETTER VIII (Amalasuntha to Justinian).**—She asks him to order that the marble and other necessities which Calogenitus had purchased be sent to the queen. 803

**LETTER IX (Theodahad to Justinian).**—He asks him to allow the things Calogenitus had bought to be transferred to Italy. 804

**LETTER X (Amalasuntha to the Augusta Theodora).**—She asks her to send, through the envoys whom she had sent to Justinian, a message concerning her well-being. Ibid.

**LETTER XI (Theodahad to Maximus).**—He promotes Maximus, descended from the family of the Anicii, which is adorned with many encomia, and joined in marriage to a woman of royal lineage, to the office of first secretary, or domesticus. Ibid.

**LETTER XII (Theodahad to the Roman Senate).**—He writes that he had formerly granted Maximus, once consul, the dignity of first secretary or domesticus and a wife of royal lineage, and asks them to celebrate this marriage with overflowing joy. 805

**LETTER XIII (Theodahad to the Roman Senate).**—He reproaches the senators because, at the very beginning of his reign, they had not checked the fickleness of the populace and its empty suspicions. 806

**LETTER XIV (Theodahad to the Roman people).**—He urges the people to preserve loyalty to the king and cast off empty suspicion. 807

**LETTER XV (Theodahad to Justinian).**—He commends to him a certain man sent to Constantinople on an affair of the Church of Ravenna. 808

**LETTER XVI (Theodahad to the Roman Senate).**—He writes that he has sent certain men to administer oaths to the Senate. Ibid.

**LETTER XVII (Theodahad to the Roman people).**—He writes that he has sent certain men to Rome to bind the king’s loyalty by oath. 809

**LETTER XVIII (Theodahad to the Roman Senate).**—He writes that he has sent an army for the defense of the Romans and placed Vaccenes, master of the royal household, over it. Ibid.

**LETTER XIX (Theodahad to Justinian).**—He praises the emperor, asks for the preservation of peace, and sends Peter the envoy back to Constantinople, assigning his own envoy to accompany him. 810

**LETTER XX (Gudelina to the Augusta Theodora).**—She gives thanks for her envoy and letters and writes that she has arranged for the pope and the Senate to reply to her by letter. Then she says that she has sent to her an envoy endowed with many virtues and learning. 811

**LETTER XXI (Gudelina to the same).**—She states that she and Theodahad earnestly seek her favor and asks that they be admitted into participation in her glory. 812

**LETTER XXII (Theodahad to Justinian).**—He asks him for peace through an envoy distinguished by priestly office and conspicuous for the praise of his learning. Ibid.

**LETTER XXIII (Gudelina to Theodora).**—She writes that she received Peter, her envoy, with a grateful heart, and through the man whom she is sending to him asks for firm peace between the two realms. 813

**LETTER XXIV (Gudelina to Justinian).**—She states that she had written to him through Theodahad’s envoy, asking that, on his return, he bring letters from the emperor attesting his safety and goodwill toward Gudelina herself and her husband. 814

**LETTER XXV (Theodahad to Justinian).**—He states that he received from Heraclianus the emperor’s letters, to which he immediately replies, announcing that he
on his behalf, had written to the pope. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XXVI (Theodahad to Justinian).**—He says that he ordered the praetorian prefect to proceed to the estate of certain nuns, so that, if an inundation of waters had inflicted any injury upon the estate, he might remit its taxes. Then he replies to what Justinian had written concerning Veranilda. 815

**EPISTLE XXVII (Theodahad to Senator, praetorian prefect).**—He orders him to relieve the poverty of the Ligurians and Venetians. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XXVIII (Theodahad to the same).**—He confirms everything that Cassiodorus had established concerning the treasurers, purveyors of grain, wine, and cheese, butchers, and so forth, in the cities of Rome, Ravenna, Ticinum, and Placentia. Then he forbids, under severe penalty, that anyone should succeed them within five years. Finally, he orders him to adjust the prices of goods because of the losses caused by the sterility of the land. 816

[Col. 1351]

**EPISTLE XXIX (Theodahad to Count Vuinusiadus).**—He grants him permission to seek the waters of Bormiae for the treatment of gout, which is described graphically. 817

**EPISTLE XXX (Theodahad to Honorius, prefect of the City).**—He orders him to restore the tottering bronze elephants to their former condition and stability. Then he wonderfully depicts the elephants and their properties. 818

**EPISTLE XXXI (King Vitigis to all the Goths).**—He writes that he was created king by the army, according to the custom of his ancestors. 819

**EPISTLE XXXII (Vitigis to Justinian).**—He sets forth the calamities that Italy was enduring because of the wars. Then, through ambassadors, he asks the emperor for peace. 820

**EPISTLE XXXIII (Vitigis to the master of offices).**—He asks him to persuade the emperor to grant peace to Italy. 821

**EPISTLE XXXIV (Vitigis to his bishops).**—He asks them both to assist the ambassadors whom he has sent to the emperor and to pour forth prayers to God on his behalf. 822

**EPISTLE XXXV (Vitigis to the prefect of Thessalonica).**—He asks that the ambassadors sent to the emperor suffer no delay. Ibid.

## BOOK ELEVEN

821

**Preface.** Ibid.

**EPISTLE I (Senator to the Roman Senate).**—He praises Amalasuntha, her parents, and her son Athalaric at length. Then he asks the senators to return thanks to the rulers for the praetorian prefecture conferred upon him. 824

**EPISTLE II (Senator to Pope John).**—He asks that he be assisted by his prayers, admonitions, and even corrections. 827

**EPISTLE III (Senator to various bishops).**—He commends himself to their prayers and asks them to proclaim a fast for the welfare of the rulers and for the attainment of peace. Then he exhorts them to drive all vices far from the people. 829

**EPISTLE IV (Senator to Ambrose).**—He admonishes him to discharge faithfully the office entrusted to him. 830

**EPISTLE V (The same to the same).**—He urges him to come to the aid as quickly as possible of the Roman people suffering from scarcity. Ibid.

**EPISTLE VI (Senator to John the chancellor).**—John is created chancellor by Cassiodorus, and he is instructed concerning what must be done in this dignity. 831

**EPISTLE VII (Senator to all provincial judges).**—He orders them to admonish the taxpayers to pay their customary taxes in three installments and at the appointed times. 833

**EPISTLE VIII (Senator’s edict).**—He offers many excellent admonitions and promises that he will be an utterly incorruptible judge. 834

**EPISTLE IX (Senator to the provincial judges).**—He urges them to love justice and to ensure that it is observed by their subjects. 836

**EPISTLE X (Senator to Beatus the chancellor).**—He announces that the king has granted Davus permission to seek Mount Lactarius in order to recover his health, and he orders him to supply him with everything necessary. 837

**EPISTLE XI (Edict concerning the maintenance of prices at Ravenna).**—He declares that he has fixed prices for the various commodities, prescribing a financial or bodily penalty for violators of the edict. 838

**EPISTLE XII (Edict of prices along the Via Flaminia).**—He establishes that guests are to be charged only the prices fixed by his soldier, the citizens, and the local bishop. Whoever acts otherwise is condemned to a fine of six solidi and punishment by the cudgel. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XIII (The Roman Senate to Justinian).**—It asks him to grant peace to the king. To obtain this more readily, it adds to its own prayers those of Rome and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. 839

**EPISTLE XIV (Senator to Gaudiosus, chancellor of Liguria).**—He describes the city of Como and states that its king had endowed its inhabitants with a perpetual benefaction. 840

**EPISTLE XV (Senator to the Ligurians).**—He makes known that the king has granted one hundred pounds of gold to relieve their needs, and he urges them to return thanks to the king. 841

**EPISTLE XVI (Senator to the Ligurians).**—He promises to weigh the complaints brought concerning the pound and the measures, and, if he discovers anyone engaged in fraud, to compel him to repair the injury inflicted. Then he asks them promptly and willingly to procure everything necessary for the army’s preparations. 842

**XVII.**—Promotions in the praetorian office. Ibid.

**XVIII.**—Concerning the cornicularius who is leaving office. 843

**XIX.**—Concerning the cornicularius who is entering office. Ibid.

**XX.**—Concerning the primiscrinius who is leaving office. Ibid.

**XXI.**—Concerning the primiscrinius who is entering office. Ibid.

**XXII.**—Concerning the records clerk. Ibid.

**XXIII.**—Concerning the management of correspondence. 844

**XXIV.**—Concerning the records clerk of the military administration. Ibid.

[Col. 1352]

**XXV.**—Concerning the chief of the exceptores. 844

**XXVI.**—Concerning Sextus the scholarius. Ibid.

**XXVII.**—Concerning the prerogativarius. Ibid.

**XXVIII.**—Concerning the commentariensis. Ibid.

**XXIX.**—Concerning the regendarius. 845

**XXX.**—Concerning the chief of the deputati and the chief of the Augustales. Ibid.

**XXXI.**—Concerning the chief of the singulares who is leaving office. Ibid.

**XXXII.**—Concerning the chief of the singulares who is entering office. Ibid.

**XXXIII.**—Concerning grants of delegatoria. Ibid.

**XXXIV.**—A decree proposed by Antianus. 846

**XXXV.**—Delegatoria. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XXXVI (Senator to Anatolius).**—He decrees that seven hundred solidi be given to the man who has commendably completed the office of cornicularius, and he himself commends his integrity. 847

**EPISTLE XXXVII (Senator to Lucinus, chancellor of Campania).**—He establishes that the primiscrinius, having completed his office, shall be solemnly paid solidi from the assessment of the province of Campania. 848

**EPISTLE XXXVIII (Senator to John the canonicarius).**—He describes the method of preparing paper, as well as its usefulness. Then he orders him to give a certain person the prescribed sum of money brought from the province of Tuscia. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XXXIX (To Vitalianus, chancellor of Lucania).**—He orders him to arrange for payment of the public as, which the Lucanians and Bruttians annually paid to the City in place of their own and their oxen’s [assessment]. Then he lists the benefits with which he had enriched his native land. 850

**EPISTLE XL.**—A pardon. 851

## BOOK TWELVE

853

**EPISTLE I (Senator to various chancellors).**—To chancellors chosen by the praetorian prefect and sent to various provinces, salutary instructions for the proper administration of their office, and especially for avoiding avarice, are delivered. Ibid.

**EPISTLE II (Senator to all provincial judges).**—He invites the judges to imitate him. Then he orders them to admonish the landowners to pay the tax of the thirteenth indiction with dutiful obedience and at the appointed times, and to send a faithful account of expenditures to the praetorian records offices. 854

**EPISTLE III (Senator to all *saiones* assigned to the chancellors).**—He instructs the *saiones* assigned to the chancellors concerning how they ought to perform their office. 856

**EPISTLE IV (Senator to the canonicarius of Venetia).**—He orders him to provide the king’s table with choice fish and acinatic wine, which is praised by many. Ibid.

**EPISTLE V (Senator to Valerian).**—He announces that the king has reduced the prices of goods in Lucania and the lands of the Bruttians because of the injury inflicted by the army. Then he orders that the people be kept in order by the judges and the soldiers by the commanders. Finally, he forbids any household—even his own or the royal household—from being exempted from supplying provisions for the troops. 858

**EPISTLE VI (Senator to all administrators of the prefecture’s offices).**—He threatens unjust judges with penalties and urges the good ones, without growing weary, to attend to the public interests. 859

**EPISTLE VII (Senator to the canonicarius of Venetia).**—He reports that the king has remitted the tax of the fifteenth indiction for certain people whose lands had been ravaged by an incursion of the Suevi. 860

**EPISTLE VIII (Senator to the consular governor of the province of Liguria).**—He exempts the houses of certain persons from paying public taxes to the tax collectors, provided that they themselves deliver those taxes into the royal treasuries with their own hands at the prescribed time. Ibid.

**EPISTLE IX (Senator to Paschasius, prefect of the grain supply).**—He reports that an African has sought the property left by a certain man who died without surviving children or heirs, and orders that he be formally installed in possession of it. 861

**EPISTLE X (Senator to various provincial chancellors).**—He orders them to collect without any delay the amount of the coming indiction. If they act otherwise, he threatens to deal with them more severely. 862

**EPISTLE XI (Senator to Peter, distributor of provisions).**—He orders him to distribute without fraud the provisions granted by the king to the Roman people. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XII (Senator to Anastasius, chancellor of Lucania).**—He especially praises Palmatian wine and Silanian cheese, and orders him to seek out both with particular diligence for shipment to the royal court. 863

**EPISTLE XIII (Edict).**—Against those who had stolen gifts bestowed by the king upon the churches. 864

**EPISTLE XIV (Senator to Anastasius, chancellor of Lucania).**—He describes the region of Rhegium and forbids henceforth that bacon and wheat be demanded from it under the pretext of compulsory purchase. 865

**EPISTLE XV (Senator to Maximus, chancellor of Lucania).**—He describes the city of Scyllacium, his native city, and the fishponds that he had excavated at the foot of Mount Moscius. Then he issues certain regulations concerning the riding horses, grain allowances, and dust-money of the judges. 866

**EPISTLE XVI (To the canonicarius).**—He orders him to admonish his subjects to pay their customary taxes willingly; no one is to exceed the established weights; and he himself is to send a faithful account of expenditures to the praetorian records offices every fourth month. 868

**EPISTLE XVII (Senator to John the siliquatarius).**—He orders him to warn the landowners to open enormous mouths of pits beside Mount Caprarius and in the places lying around the walls. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XVIII (Senator to Constantinianus).**—He orders him to repair the Flaminian road; to provide the prescribed number of riding horses; to gather grain allowances without expense to the landowners; and diligently to seek out the foods prepared for the royal tables. 869

**EPISTLE XIX (Senator to Maximus, vicar of the City).**—He reminds him to prepare everything necessary for the solemn reception of the king. 870

**EPISTLE XX (Senator to Thomas and Peter, treasurers).**—He orders them to return to the agents of Saint Peter, against a written bond, the sacred vessels that Pope Agapitus, when sent as ambassador to the East, had pawned to the royal treasurers in exchange for money. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XXI (Senator to Deusdedit, Ravenna secretary).**—He describes the office of secretaries and its usefulness. 871

**EPISTLE XXII (Senator to the provincials of Istria).**—He orders them to pay the tax in wine, oil, and wheat, with which the province was plentifully supplied that year; and he sends Laurentius with money to purchase a larger quantity of such goods and transport them to Ravenna. Then he carefully depicts that province. 872

**EPISTLE XXIII (Senator to Laurentius).**—He orders him to go to the province of Istria to buy wine, oil, and wheat. 873

**EPISTLE XXIV (Senator to the maritime tribunes).**—He orders them to prepare ships to transport wine and oil from the province of Istria to Ravenna. Then he discusses navigation and the labor of sailors, especially their work in operating the saltworks. 874

**EPISTLE XXV (Senator to Ambrose).**—From certain signs he infers a future scarcity; to meet it, he orders a vast quantity of old grain to be gathered. 875

**EPISTLE XXVI (Senator to Paul).**—He willingly and freely comes to the aid of the Venetians, who are suffering from scarcity because of the year’s crop failure, by remitting their taxes and granting them grain allowances. 876

**EPISTLE XXVII (Senator to Datius, bishop).**—He sends a vast quantity of millet to be distributed to the people suffering from want. 877

**EPISTLE XXVIII (Edict).**—He announces to the Ligurians the victory won over the Burgundians and the flight of the Alemanni. Then he says that, because of their scarcity, the king has remitted half of their tax and opened his own granaries to relieve them. 878

## ON THE ORIGIN AND DEEDS OF THE GOTHS, BY THE AUTHOR JORDANES

1251 **Preface.** Ibid. **CHAPTER I.—**The division of the whole world. Ibid. **CHAPTER II.—**The island of Britain. 1252 **CHAPTER III.—**The situation of the island of Scandza and its peoples. 1253 **CHAPTER IV.—**Where the Goths first came from, and how they gradually advanced their settlements into Scythia near the Pontic Sea. 1254 **CHAPTER V.—**The situation and description of Scythia, and the various settlements of the Goths there. 1255 **CHAPTER VI.—**The Goths defeat Vesosis, king of the Egyptians, and on their return from Egypt subjugate Asia. Also, concerning the origin of the Parthians. 1257 **CHAPTER VII.—**With their husbands absent in battle, the Amazons resist various attacks by their enemies and overcome different peoples of Asia in war. Ibid. **CHAPTER VIII.—**The intercourse of the Amazons with neighboring peoples and their offspring. 1258 **CHAPTER IX.—**The husbands of the Amazons and their king Telephus, together with his birth and deeds. Ibid. **CHAPTER X.—**The various wars and victories of the Goths against the kings of Persia and Macedonia. 1259 **CHAPTER XI.—**The arrival among the Goths of Diceneus of Boroista, who taught them every branch of philosophy; and his great authority among the Goths. Also, Comosicus, Diceneus’s successor. 1260 **CHAPTER XII.—**Corillus, king of the Goths. Also, a description of ancient Dacia. Also, a description of the Danube. 1261 **CHAPTER XIII.—**Dorpaneus, king of the Goths, and their various battles and victories against the Romans under the emperor Domitian. Ibid. **CHAPTER XIV.—**The genealogy of the Gothic nobles, whom they called *anses*, that is, demigods, and concerning their origin and end. 1262 **CHAPTER XV.—**The remarkable courage of the emperor Maximinus, who was of Gothic descent, and how he attained the imperial power. 1263 **CHAPTER XVI.—**The Goths, formerly federates of the Romans, become enemies because their pay was withheld; under the leadership of King Ostrogotha they devastate Moesia and Thrace. Ibid. **CHAPTER XVII.—**Fastida, king of the Gepids, makes war upon Ostrogotha, king of the Goths; the Goths emerge victorious. Also, concerning the kinship between the Goths and the Gepids. 1264 **CHAPTER XVIII.—**After the death of Ostrogotha, Cniva, king of the Goths, leads an army into Moesia and harasses the Romans in various battles, in one of which Decius is killed. 1265 **CHAPTER XIX.—**How Gallus and Volusianus made a treaty with the Goths, and how Aemilianus ravaged Moesia. 1266 **CHAPTER XX.—**While Gallienus was emperor, the Goths invade Asia, burn the temple of Diana at Ephesus, overthrow Chalcedon, devastate Troy, and harass Thrace. Ibid. **CHAPTER XXI.—**The emperor Maximianus, with the aid of the Goths, won great victories over the Parthians and Persians. Constantine likewise accomplished many notable deeds with their assistance. Ibid. [Col. 1363] **CHAPTER XXII.—**Geberich, king of the Goths, makes war upon Visumar, king of the Vandals, and defeats him. A few Vandals who survived the disaster ask Constantine for Pannonia as a place to inhabit and obtain it. 1267 **CHAPTER XXIII.—**The expeditions and victories of Ermanaric, king of the Goths—who was compared with Alexander the Great because of the many peoples he subdued—against the Heruli, Veneti, and Ostrogoths. Ibid. **CHAPTER XXIV.—**The accursed origin of the Huns, namely, the intercourse of witches with unclean spirits. Also, the expedition of the Huns against the Scythian Ostrogoths, including a description of the Huns’ monstrous and terrifying appearance. 1268 **CHAPTER XXV.—**After the Ostrogoths had been defeated by the Vandals, the Visigoths seek and obtain Moesia from the emperor Valens as a place to inhabit; and, since they desired to become Christians, Valens, being an Arian, sends Arian preachers to them and infects them with the poison of his treachery. 1269 **CHAPTER XXVI.—**The Visigoths, subject to the Romans, oppressed by great famine and treated most harshly by the Roman commanders, assert their freedom and occupy Thrace and Riparian Dacia. The emperor Valens, who had arranged for them to be infected with Arian treachery, is burned by them as divine vengeance. 1270 **CHAPTER XXVII.—**While the emperor Theodosius was preparing their destruction and was ill, the Visigoths disperse to Thessaly, Epirus, Achaea, and Pannonia to plunder them. The emperor Gratian makes a treaty with them, which Theodosius also confirms. Ibid. **CHAPTER XXVIII.—**Atanaric, king of the Visigoths and successor of Fridigern, is summoned to Constantinople by the emperor Theodosius, receives great honors from him, and dies there. Also, concerning the Federates, and the victory won with the aid of the Visigoths by Theodosius against the tyrant Eugenius, who had occupied Gaul. 1271 **CHAPTER XXIX.—**After Theodosius’s sons withheld their customary gifts, the Visigoths, weary of peace and idleness, choose Alaric as their king and invade Italy. Ibid. **CHAPTER XXX.—**Alaric defeats Stilicho, who had unexpectedly attacked the Goths in war; he devastates Italy and plunders Rome. Then, while contemplating Africa, he dies with his spoils. The Visigoths bury Alaric in the bed of the river Busentinus by a remarkable method. 1272 **CHAPTER XXXI.—**Athaulf, Alaric’s successor, plunders Italy. He marries Placidia, the sister of the emperor Honorius. From Italy he crosses into Gaul to drive out the Vandals and Alans from there. From there he goes into Spain, where he is killed. Also, Regeric, the third king of the Visigoths, is killed. 1273 **CHAPTER XXXII.—**Vallia, the fourth king of the Visigoths, after making peace with the emperor Honorius, returns Placidia to the Romans. Also, concerning Constantine, Constans, Jovinus, and Sebastianus, the invaders of Gaul. 1274 **CHAPTER XXXIII.—**The succession of the Vandal kings in Africa for nearly a hundred years, and how Belisarius celebrated a triumph after bringing Gelimer to Constantinople, and Africa was again added to the Roman Empire. Also, concerning the death of Vallia. Ibid. **CHAPTER XXXIV.—**Theoderic, the fifth king of the Visigoths. The Romans, with Hun auxiliaries, lead an army against him after breaking the peace. Treaties are renewed. Attila is appeased. Also, concerning Attila’s court. 1275 **CHAPTER XXXV.—**Attila’s father and brothers, and the stature, appearance, and character of Attila, king of the Huns. Also, concerning the sword of Mars, which he claimed for himself. A notable passage from the historian Priscus. 1276 **CHAPTER XXXVI.—**Attila, naturally prepared to ravage the world, is incited to do so by Gizeric, king of the Vandals, through many gifts. Gizeric tries by every means to sow discord between the Romans and the Goths, but in vain. The letter of the emperor Valentinian to the Visigoths and their reply. 1277 **CHAPTER XXXVII.—**The events that occurred amid the movements of those wars, before the battle between the Romans and the Huns was joined. 1278 **CHAPTER XXXVIII.—**The location where the battle between the Romans and the Huns was fought on the Catalaunian Plains, and a description of both armies. Ibid. **CHAPTER XXXIX.—**Attila’s speech to the Huns, in which he urges them to undertake battle against the Romans. 1279 **CHAPTER XL.—**The outcome of the battle fought between the Romans and Visigoths against the Huns. The death of King Theoderic. Attila fortifies himself with wagons. 1280 **CHAPTER XLI.—**Thorismund prepares the funeral rites for his father, King Theoderic, and, on the advice of the patrician Aetius—who, after the Huns had been utterly destroyed, feared the Goths—returns to the Roman Empire and succeeds his father. The Franks and Gepids wear each other down in mutual slaughter. The number killed in the battle between the Romans and Attila. 1281 **CHAPTER XLII.—**When Attila learned of the Visigoths’ withdrawal from the Romans, he turned all his strength toward crushing the Romans. He devastates Aquileia, Milan, and Ticinum. Pope Leo approaches him and obtains peace for Italy on specified conditions. Attila returns to his own settlements beyond the Danube. Ibid. **CHAPTER XLIII.—**Attila marches against the Alans settled beyond the Loire. After a battle was joined by Thorismund, king of the Visigoths, he is forced to flee to his own settlements. The killing of Thorismund. 1282 **CHAPTER XLIV.—**Theoderic, brother of Thorismund and king of the Visigoths, defeats Ricarius, king of the Suebi, who had invaded Spain. He places Achiulf, a client, over the Suebi. When Achiulf aspired to tyranny, he was executed. With Theoderic’s permission, the Suebi choose Remismund as their king. The death of King Theoderic. 1283 **CHAPTER XLV.—**Euric succeeds Theoderic as king of the Visigoths, while Roman emperors are killed one after another. Gizeric, king of the Vandals, invades Italy and devastates Rome. Euric invades Gaul, defeats the Britons, auxiliaries of the Romans, and occupies the Gallic city of Arverna. 1284 **CHAPTER XLVI.—**Odoacer, king of the Turcilingi, invades and subjugates Italy. 1285 **CHAPTER XLVII.—**Euric, king of the Visigoths, subdues Arles, Marseille, and the Burgundians. He dies. Alaric, son of Euric, the ninth king of the Visigoths. Ibid. **CHAPTER XLVIII.—**The genealogy of the kings of the Ostrogoths, from the death of King Ermanaric up to Walamir, son of Thorismund, and the death of Attila. Ibid. **CHAPTER XLIX.—**The death of Attila, king of the Huns, from excessive drunkenness, and the magnificent funeral rites performed for him. 1286 **CHAPTER L.—**After Attila’s death, a dispute arose among his countless sons concerning the succession. Ardaric, king of the Gepids, kills Ellac, Attila’s son, in battle and drives the remaining sons as far as the Pontic Sea. The emperor Marcian grants various settlements to different Goths and Gepids. 1287 **CHAPTER LI.—**The settlements of the Goths called the “Lesser Goths,” and their bishop Wulfila, who instructed them through writing. 1289 **CHAPTER LII.—**The various settlements of the Ostrogoths in Pannonia after Attila’s death, and how they repelled Attila’s invading sons into Scythia; also, the friendship of the Ostrogoths with the Romans, on account of the hostage Theoderic, son of Theodemir, who was sent to Constantinople as a pledge of peace. Ibid. **CHAPTER LIII.—**After Attila’s death, the Ostrogoths move into Satagi. They repel the Huns who resist them under Dinzio, son of Attila. Various battles between the Ostrogoths and the Suebi and Sciri. The death of Walamir. The Sciri are destroyed to the last man. 1290 **CHAPTER LIV.—**The Suebi kings Hunimund and Alaric, advancing against the Ostrogoths with the Sarmatians, Sciri, Gepids, and Rugians, suffer a crushing defeat. 1291 **CHAPTER LV.—**King Theodemir marches against the Suebi, devastates them, and almost subdues them. Theoderic, son of Theodemir, scarcely yet a boy, attacks Babai, king of the Sarmatians, without his father’s knowledge and kills him. He captures the city of Singidunum. Ibid. **CHAPTER LVI.—**The Ostrogoths, weary of peace, harass Italy, Gaul, and Illyricum. Theodemir dies after making a treaty with the Romans. Ibid. **CHAPTER LVII.—**Theoderic, king of the Ostrogoths, is summoned to Rome by the emperor Zeno, adopted by him, and presented with the consulship and an equestrian statue. He inflicts a great defeat upon Odoacer in Hesperia. He assumes the insignia of the Roman kings. 1292 **CHAPTER LVIII.—**The wife of King Theoderic, Audofleda, and his concubine, together with his sons and daughters, their marriages with various kings, and other family alliances. Also, concerning Mundo the raider, and the trophy won from the Franks. 1293 **CHAPTER LIX.—**When King Theoderic was old, he proclaimed Athalaric, the fatherless son of his daughter Amalasuntha, king. After Athalaric was carried off by an untimely death, his mother made her cousin Theodahad king; he banished her to an island, where she was strangled. 1294 **CHAPTER LX.—**The emperor Justinian sends Belisarius with an army against the Goths. He occupies Sicily. The Goths choose Witigis as their king and kill Theodahad. Witigis surrenders Ravenna, together with Mathasuenta and the royal treasures, to the Romans. 1295
**END OF THE SIXTY-NINTH VOLUME.**
